en: 1. Prakaraṇa: Detachment, First Chapter.
The All-pervading Lord is within me, as well as outside me—in heaven, on earth, and in the sky.
Salutation to that Self of the universe who shines as the essence of light.

He who possesses the firm conviction, "I am bound; may I be liberated,"—neither one who knows that [reality] to the absolute extent nor one who does not know it at all—is qualified for this scripture.
Vālmīki:
Having first reflected upon the means to the stories, one who is wise then reflects upon these means to liberation is not born again.
O crusher of enemies, having previously composed these means of narration in the work named *Rāmāyaṇa*, which yield great fruit,
I [taught them] first to this disciplined and wise disciple, Bharadvāja.
With one-pointed mind, he bestowed these beautiful jewels upon the seeker, just as the ocean does;
thereafter, these means of instruction were proclaimed by the wise Bharadvāja in the presence of Brahmā in a certain thicket on Mount Meru.
Then the blessed Lord Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, being pleased with him, spoke thus:
"O son, choose a boon," said that noble-minded one.
Bharadvāja:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, this boon is pleasing to me today:
please proclaim that by which these people may be liberated from suffering.
Brahmā said:
Quickly and with great effort, seek out the teacher Vālmīki here;
for by him this irreproachable Rāmāyaṇa was begun. When that is known, a person will cross over all delusion entirely.
"Like one with boundless virtues crossing to the far shore of the ocean by means of a raft," having said this to Bharadvāja, the Supreme Lord,
the Creator of Beings, came to my hermitage together with that Bharadvāja.
Having been quickly honored by me with water for the hands, feet, and other offerings, that god,
the Great Being who delights in the welfare of all creatures,
said to me: "O supreme sage, because of this narration of Rāma's true nature by you..."
One must not abandon one's effort until the blameless completion [of this work].
By knowing this, this world will quickly cross over the peril of saṃsāra, as if by a boat from the ocean.
"I have come here specifically to tell you this very matter:
for the sake of the welfare of the world, compose a scripture," so said the Unborn One (Aja). Having spoken thus, he vanished from that holy hermitage of mine in an instant.
In a moment, he rose up loftily like a wave of water.
When that Blessed One had departed, I was filled with wonder;
once again, with a clear mind, I questioned Bharadvāja on that matter.
"What was this that was spoken by Brahmā? O Bharadvāja, tell me quickly!
When he had been addressed thus, Bharadvāja spoke again to me, O sinless one:
Bharadvāja said:
This was said by the Blessed One: "Compose the Rāmāyaṇa quickly for the welfare of all the world, as a boat for the ocean of saṃsāra.
And tell me, O Blessed One, how [one may cross] the peril of saṃsāra. (MU 1.1.19)
Rāma, though engaged in worldly affairs here, as well as the high-minded Bharata,
Śatrughna, Lakṣmaṇa, and the illustrious Sītā—
these were his followers, as were the sons of the ministers, who were possessed of great intelligence.

"O King of Kings, when I was addressed with reverence by Bharadvāja, saying, 'Tell me clearly how you have attained freedom from suffering; in that same way, I shall cross over [the ocean of existence] along with the people,'" MU 1.1.22.
Then, in order to carry out the command of the Lord, I began to speak:
"Listen, dear Bharadvāja; I shall tell you according to what was asked, by hearing which you will be able to cast far away your delusion."
O wise one, conduct yourself in such a way that you may live happily,
like the lotus-eyed Rāma,
Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and the high-minded Śatrughna, who all acted with an intellect free from all attachments.
Kausalyā, Sumitrā, Sītā, and Daśaratha;
Kṛtāstha, Avirodha, and Vasiṣṭha, who had reached the further shore of awakening; Vāmadeva and the other eight ministers.
Ghṛṣṭi, Vikuṇṭha, Bhāma, Satyavardhana,
Vibhīṣaṇa, Suṣeṇa, Hanumān, and Indrajit—
these twenty-eight are said to be those whose minds are free from passion.

The great-souled ones who are liberated while living follow whatever comes to them. My son, if you conduct yourself in the same way as these men— with respect to what was taken, given, received, dwelt upon, or remembered— then you are indeed liberated from all distress.

Having attained supreme yoga, the noble being who has fallen into the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra experiences neither sorrow nor dejection; free from fever, he remains eternally satisfied. This concludes the chapter named "The Mere Sūtra."
The second canto:
Bharadvāja said:
"O Brahmin, having first described the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukta) regarding Rāghava..."
"Tell me in due order how I may become eternally happy.
Vālmīki replied:
"This worldly delusion, once born, is like the color of the sky."
"O virtuous one, I consider non-remembrance to be better than remembrance;
for that [non-remembrance] cannot be experienced without the realization of the absolute non-existence of the object of perception.
Therefore, let that realization be sought by someone at some time."
And that [reality] is indeed possible here; for that purpose, this scripture has been composed. If you listen to it, you will attain the truth, and not otherwise.
This delusion of the world, though visible, is experienced as being non-existent at all.
O sinless one, through this inquiry, as with the color of the sky, there is no weariness; when,
by the realization that "the visible does not exist," the cleansing of the visible from the mind is accomplished,
then the supreme bliss of Nirvana has arisen.

Otherwise, for you who wallow in the pits of the scriptures, there will be no peace even after many eons, for your knowledge here remains unauthentic. The renunciation of latent tendencies (vāsanā) is said to be the supreme liberation.
O Brahmin, this very one is the stainless path that illuminates knowledge.
When latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have perished, the mind dissolves quickly,
O Brahmin, like a speck of frost when the continuity of cold has ceased.

This body, a cage of elements, is sustained by latent impressions (vāsanā), just as a multitude of pearls is strung together by a fine thread inserted within. Latent impressions are said to be of two kinds: pure and likewise impure.

The impure [vāsanā] is the cause of birth; the pure destroys birth. The wise declare that impure latent impression (vāsanā) is characterized by dense ignorance, possesses thick egoism, and brings about rebirth. (MU 1.2.11–12)
Having abandoned the sprout of rebirth, she remains like a parched seed; known through what is to be known, she persists until the end of the body and is called "the Pure.
She effects the state of no further birth among embodied beings who are liberated while living.
Pure latent impression exists within the body like the whirling of a wheel.
Those whose impressions are pure do not again become vessels for the miseries of birth;
having known that which is to be known, they are called the high-minded ones liberated while living.

I shall fully explain to you, O highly intelligent Bharadvāja, this auspicious method of Rāma, by which the great-minded Rāma attained the state of liberation while living, for the sake of pacifying old age and death.
Listen, I shall speak; by that you will understand everything in every respect.
Having departed from the house of learning, the lotus-eyed Rāma spent his days at home in playful diversions, free from all fear.
Then, as time passed while that king was protecting the earth,
and while his subjects remained free from sorrow and devoid of distress,
his mind became eager to behold the series of hermitages of the sages at the sacred fords.
Once, while the virtuous Rāma was there, he became deeply distressed.
Having reflected thus, the descendant of Raghu approached his father’s feet and grasped them—
those with their nails as their bristling filaments— as a swan might grasp two fresh lotuses.
Rāma said:
"O father, my mind is indeed very eager to see sacred fords, temples of the gods, forests, and shrines."
"Therefore, you ought to fulfill this former request;
for there is no petitioner in the world, O dear one, who has ever been disregarded by you.
Thus entreated by Vasiṣṭha, the king then [acted] together with him.
Having deliberated, he released Rāma first, as the petitioner.

On an auspicious lunar day and under a favorable constellation, the descendant of Raghu, his body adorned with auspicious ornaments and having had benedictions pronounced by the twice-born, set out together with his two brothers.
Accompanied by a few affectionate and excellent princes, as well as by Brahmins sent by Vasiṣṭha who were learned in the scriptures,
he was adorned after being embraced again and again by his mothers who had pronounced their blessings upon him.
He departed from that house, intent upon a pilgrimage to sacred fords. Having left his own city, he was cheered by the citizens with the sound of musical instruments,
while the women of the city gazed at him with eyes curved like swarms of bees.
He was strewn with showers of parched grain offered from the lotus-like hands of the village women,
like the Himalaya mountain covered by snow;
he gratified the assemblies of Brahmins and listened to the blessings of the people.

Gazing toward the horizons, he wandered through the forest. Then, starting from his own territory of Kosala, he proceeded in due order and beheld [the lands], preceded by ritual bathing, charity, austerity, and meditation.
Rivers, sacred fords, holy forests, and sanctuaries;
jungles at the edges of the woods, and the shores of oceans and mountains;
the Mandākinī, which resembles the moon, and the Kālindī, pure as a blue lotus.
The Sarasvatī, the Śatadru, the Candrabhāgā, and the Irāvatī;
the Veṇā and the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, as well as the Nirvindhyā and the Sarayū; the Carmaṇvatī, the Vitastā, the Vipāśā, and also the Bāhudā.
Prayāga, Naimiṣa, Dharmāraṇya, and likewise Gayā;
Vārāṇasī, Śrīgiri, Kedāra, and likewise Puṣkara;
Mānasa, Kramasaras, and likewise Uttaramānasa.
Vaḍavā and Maḍavā, along with the multitude of holy fords (tīrthas) and their siblings; Agnitīrtha, the great holy ford, as well as Indradyumna-saras;
the lakes and ponds, and likewise the series of oblong ponds and wells.
He likewise beheld his master Kārttikeya, Sāligrāma Hari,
and the sixty-four sacred sites of Hara, the lord of Girijā,
as well as the shores of the four oceans, variegated with many wonders.
He saw the caves and groves of the Vindhya mountains, the plateaus of the principal mountain ranges,
as well as the auspicious and purifying hermitages of great royal sages, Brahman-sages, gods, and Brahmins.
Again and again that bestower of honor wandered with his two brothers to all the horizons of the four quarters and across every part of the earth’s surface;
having surveyed this entire world, he was honored by gods, kinnaras, and humans.
The joy of the Raghus returned to his own home, having traversed the quarters like the Lord [Śiva] after visiting the realm of Śiva.
This is the third canto, titled "The Undertaking of the Pilgrimage."
Vālmīki:
Strewn with handfuls of parched grain and flowers by the city-dwellers,
the illustrious Jayanta entered his home like [Indra] entering heaven.
Then Rāghava, having arrived first, bowed down to his father Vasiṣṭha, his maternal relatives, the Brahmins, and the elders and teachers,
together with his friends, mothers, father, and the assembly of twice-born ones.
Then Rāghava could not contain himself amidst those repeated acts of embracing;
in that son of Daśaratha, as they conversed privately with firm and sweet words of affection,
the quarters of the sky seemed to tremble like the soft sounds of bamboo flutes.
Many days passed there, filled with the festival of Rāma’s arrival—
a celebration tumultuous with playful clamor, releasing the people into great joy.
From that time forward, the descendant of Raghu lived happily in his home.
Describing the various customs and the local practices of this and that region,
Rāma rose in the morning and, having performed his twilight devotions according to the rules,
then beheld his father seated in the assembly hall, equal to Indra.
Having spent a quarter of the day with Vasiṣṭha and the others, engaged in most diverse conversations that were filled with wisdom and attended with respect,
he departed, permitted by his father and surrounded by a great army.
[He went] to a forest filled with boars and buffaloes, desiring to hunt.
Then, having returned to his residence and performed his bath and other rites in due order,
he ate together with his friends and kinsmen and passed the night with his companions.
Rāghava, whose daily conduct was of this nature, returned with his two brothers from his pilgrimage and dwelt in his father’s house;
he was like moonlight to the hearts of the virtuous, delightful through his royal deportment.
The sinless one passed the days with actions made delicate by the nectar-like essence of sacred learning.
The Fourth Canto, titled "The Description of the Daily Routine."
Vālmīki: Now, while the sixteenth year was current for the scion of Raghu,
Rāma, as well as for Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa, who were following him— MU_1,4.1
While Bharata remained constantly in his maternal grandfather’s house in happiness,
the queen protected this entire earth according to dharma;
and for the sake of her sons' marriage, she deliberated daily with her ministers.
While King Daśaratha— the possessor of great wisdom, skilled in counsel, and knowledgeable in those matters—
was engaged in his pilgrimage to sacred fords, Rāma, remaining in his own home,
grew thinner day by day like a stainless lake in autumn.
Gradually his large-eyed face took on a pallor,
like a white lotus with petals blossoming from ripeness, surrounded by rows of rice stalks. With his hands resting upon the surface of his cheeks, he remained seated in the lotus posture.
Overcome by anxiety, he became silent and inactive. With his limbs emaciated, possessed by worry, exhausted, and deeply dejected, he said nothing to anyone, appearing as if fixed in a painting.
Though entreated again and again by his attendants out of weariness,
he performed his daily ritual with his lotus-like face withered.
Thus [he attended upon] that Rāma, who was distinguished as a sage and a mine of multitudes of virtues.
Seeing his two brothers in that very same state, they too fell into that condition. While those sons were thus distressed and emaciated,
the protector of the earth, together with his wife, succumbed to the helplessness of anxiety.
"Son, what is this heavy anxiety of yours? Thus he asked Rāma again and again with affectionate words, but Rāma did not tell him anything.
Sitting on his father’s lap, he said, "Father, I have no sorrow at all."
Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals, remained silent.
Then King Daśaratha asked Vasiṣṭha, the best of speakers and knower of all affairs, "Is Rāma distressed? (MU 1.4.12–13).
"There is a reason for this, O illustrious one; let there be no sorrow for you, O King.
Thus addressed by the sage Vasiṣṭha, the king was filled with anxiety. For the virtuous do not harbor anger, dejection, or widespread joy except under the influence of a significant cause.
O King, without the momentum of creation— that force of conjunction— beings in this world do not undergo transformation.
The fifth chapter, titled "Lamentation over Emaciation," is concluded.
Vālmīki:
When the lord of sages had spoken thus, the king remained filled with doubt,
overcome by distress, observing silence for some time while awaiting [the sage’s response].
While all the queens in the royal palaces were exhausted and remained on guard,
keeping watch everywhere for every movement of Rāma,
at that very time, the one known as Viśvāmitra arrived.

The great seer came to Ayodhyā to see that lord of men. At that time, the sacrifice of that wise one, who desired righteousness, was reportedly destroyed by Rākṣasas intoxicated by their power of illusion, heroism, and strength.
For the sake of protecting that sacrifice, he desired to see the king;
for that sage was not able to attain that ritual without obstacles.
Then, the treasury of asceticism prepared himself for their destruction.
The immensely radiant Viśvāmitra arrived at the city of Ayodhyā. Desiring an audience with the king, he spoke to the gatekeepers:
"Quickly announce that I, Kauśika, the son of Gādhi, have arrived."
Having heard those words of his, all the gatekeepers went to Rājagṛha,
their minds agitated, impelled by that speech. Having gone to the royal palace, they [sought] the seer Viśvāmitra.

Then they announced his arrival to the lord of the chamberlains. Thereupon, that staff-bearer, approaching with haste the king who was seated in the assembly hall and surrounded by a circle of royal attendants, addressed him.
"O King, at the gate stands a glorious man of great splendor, radiant like the rising sun, with a mass of matted hair as red as flames.
He is accompanied by chowries and banners, and possesses horses, elephants, men, and weapons."
He made that region appear as if strewn with gold by his splendors. The staff-bearer said to us quickly in a humble voice, "Report to the King that the sage Viśvāmitra has arrived."
Having heard these words of Yashṭika, that best of kings,
together with his ministers and his feudatories, rose from his golden seat;
though protected by a great multitude of kings, he departed on foot alone.
Accompanied by Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva, and praised by the surrounding assembly,
he went to the place where the great sage Viśvāmitra was;
there he beheld that tiger among sages stationed at the gateway.
For some reason, he had come to the surface of the earth like the sun,
pervading it with Brahmanic splendor and the great majesty of the Kṣatriya;
yet he was constantly worn down by old age, which was parched by the expansion of his asceticism.
His shoulders were covered with matted locks, like a mountain shrouded by evening clouds;
he bore a radiant body that was both tranquil and lovely, yet blazing, unimpeded, serene, and possessed of a majestic form.
With a splendor that was both charming and most formidable, serene yet agitated, profound and overflowing, he delighted the people;
she alone was blameless, a companion to the state of infinite life.
Holding a smooth lute in his hand, his mind was unfading;
because his heart was overcome with compassion, he seemed to drench these creatures with nectar through his clear and sweet glances.
Having beheld from afar the sage— whose outer corners of the eyes were white and black, whose brows were white and arched,
and who bestowed both joy and fear upon the beholder within—
the king assumed a bowed posture.
He bowed down so that the ground was adorned by the garlands of jewels from his falling crown.
The sage also greeted the Lord of the Earth with sweet and noble speech, just as the radiant sun greets Indra.
Then all the twice-born ones, headed by Vasiṣṭha,
respectfully honored him according to the sequence beginning with a welcome.
Daśaratha said:
O holy one, we have been graced by your radiant vision, which has appeared unexpectedly, just as beds of lotuses are graced by the sun.
That which is beginningless, undisturbed, and free from decay— [by that you have favored us].
O Sage, by beholding you today, we have attained that blissful happiness;
indeed, by virtue of your arrival, we have truly come to stand at the forefront of those who practice righteousness. (MU 1.5.28–29)
Thus conversing there, the kings and the great seers took their seats in the assembly hall and sat down.
Seeing that seer approaching, blazing with splendor, he was struck with fear.
With a joyful countenance, the king himself offered the guest-offering (arghya).
Having accepted the king’s arghya according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures,
he honored the king as he performed a circumambulation.
Honored by the king, he then, with a joyful countenance,
inquired after the welfare and well-being of that lord of men.
Having met with Vasiṣṭha, that bull among sages smiled.
Having honored him as was fitting, he then inquired after his health.
Having met and honored one another as was appropriate for a moment,
they all, with joyful minds, entered the residence of the great king.
Seated upon their respective appropriate seats, their splendors mutually enhanced,
they all respectfully inquired after one another’s well-being.
To that wise Viśvāmitra who had thus taken his seat, [he spoke].
He repeatedly offered water for the feet, the guest-offering (arghya), and cows;
and having honored Viśvāmitra according to the prescribed rites,
the king, with palms joined in reverence and a joyful mind, spoke these words.

Just as the attainment of nectar, just as rain in a time of drought, just as the recovery of sight for one who is blind— such is your arrival. It is like the acquisition of desired wealth, or the birth of a son to one who is childless.
The attainment of an object seen in a dream, so too is your arrival;
union with one's desire, the arrival of what is wished for,
and the recovery of what was lost— your arrival is just like that.
Just as there is joy for one who has died because of returning through travel in the sky, so too, O Brahmin, is there joy from your arrival; welcome to you, O great sage!
For whom indeed would dwelling in the world of Brahmā not bring delight?
O Sage, your scripture is likewise; I tell you this as the truth itself.
What is your supreme desire? And what may I do for you?
You have come to me as a worthy recipient, O Brahmin, having attained the highest righteousness.
Worthy of being addressed by the title of "royal sage" (rājarṣi), with your subjects illuminated by your ascetic power,
and having subsequently attained the status of a "brahmin sage" (brahmarṣi), you are worthy of my worship, O Blessed One.
May the joy that arises in me from the sprinkling of the waters of the Gaṅgā [be equal to the joy I feel at seeing you].
Thus, from the sight of you, a joy cools me as it were within.
O Brahmin, that you have come to me— free from desire, fear, and anger, devoid of passion, and free from affliction— is a most wonderful thing.
O best among those who know what is to be known, I perceive myself as having entered a pure field, free from stain, like the orb of the moon emerged [from the clouds].
I consider your arrival before me to be like the direct presence of Brahman itself.
"I am purified, O Sage; I am graced by your arrival.
O Holy One, because my heart has been delighted by the merit of your coming, today my birth has become fruitful and my life well-lived."

Having seen you arrived here, having honored and bowed to you, I bow within my very self, like the ocean that bows when it beholds the moon. O bull among sages, for whatever purpose and for whatever task you have come, [please speak].
"Know that it is already done; for you are indeed highly honored by me.
O Kauśika, you ought to deliberate upon your own task. Blessed One, there is truly nothing that should not be given to you, whatever may be requested. (MU 1.5.52–53)
"And you ought to deliberate upon the matter according to dharma;
I shall be your agent for it all, while you are the supreme deity.
Having heard these exceedingly sweet words, spoken with humility by one who knows the truth and pleasing to the ear, [the king was moved].
On account of his renowned virtues, the bull among sages experienced supreme joy at being distinguished by those qualities.
The sixth canto, titled "The Arrival of Viśvāmitra."
Vālmīki:
Having heard those words of the lion among kings, which were so wonderful in their detail,
the highly effulgent Viśvāmitra, his hair standing on end with joy, spoke.
"O tiger among kings, this is indeed worthy of you alone upon this earth—
you who are born of a great lineage and follow the tradition of Vasiṣṭha.
As for the matter that is in my heart, regarding the decision on what must be done,"
"O tiger among kings, you must act; uphold the Dharma! O bull among men, I am observing a vow for the sake of spiritual perfection, and terrible Rākṣasas stand as obstacles to it."
"Whenever I performed a sacrifice for the assembly of gods,
at that very time the night-stalkers would destroy that sacrifice of mine. Even though it was performed many times, those leaders of the Rākṣasas [continued to do so]."
They covered the earth at that sacrifice with flesh and blood.
When that assembly of sacrifices had thus been cast down, I,
having exerted myself in vain, lost my enthusiasm and departed from that place.
"O King, my mind does not incline toward releasing anger;
for such was that deed, and no curse can take effect upon it.
And such, O King, is my forbearance toward him in that great sacrifice."
"By your grace, may I attain the great fruit without obstacle.
You ought to protect me, who am afflicted and have come seeking refuge;
for the hopelessness of those who seek is indeed a defeat for the virtuous."
"You have a glorious son, Rāma, who possesses the prowess of a proud tiger,
a hero equal to Mahendra, the destroyer of demons. O tiger among kings, [entrust] that son Rāma, whose valor is truth, [to him]."
"You ought to give me your eldest son, the hero who wears the side-locks of youth;
for he, protected by me with my own divine splendor,
is capable of crushing the heads of those Rākṣasas who do you harm."
"I shall bring him manifold and infinite welfare,
by which he will become worthy of worship even by the three worlds;
and having encountered him, the night-stalkers will not be able to stand before him."
Seeing him enraged in battle, they were like deer in a forest seeing a lion;
no man other than a descendant of Kakutstha dared to fight them,
just as no one dares to face angry lions except for rutting elephants.
For those wicked ones, O tiger among kings, will not withstand Rāma’s arrows in battle; they are arrogant with valor, like the Kālakūṭa poison,
the servants of Khara and Dūṣaṇa,
resembling enraged Yamas.
Like the incessant streams from a cloud or the rising dust, [all things come and go].
O King, you ought not to harbor affection for your son;
there is nothing in this world that must not be surrendered by one of great soul.
"Ah, now I truly understand; know that those Rākṣasas have been slain.
For wise people like us do not engage in action when there is doubt.
I know the high-souled Rāma, whose eyes are like lotuses."
Vasiṣṭha of great splendor and those others who are far-sighted—
if righteousness, greatness, and fame are established in your mind,
then you ought to give me your own desired son.
And my sacrifice shall last for ten nights, at which the Rākṣasas— the enemies who act as obstacles to my sacrifice— must be slain by Rāma.
O descendant of Kakutstha, let your ministers grant their permission for this.

"O knower of time, let all these men, headed by Vasiṣṭha, dismiss Rāma before the appointed time passes for me, O descendant of Raghu. Act accordingly; may prosperity be yours, and do not set your mind on grief."
"Even a minute task, when performed at the proper time, becomes a source of benefit;
but even a great one, through being done out of season, becomes empty of benefit.
Having spoken these words, which were consistent with righteousness and purpose, that righteous-souled one—
The great ascetic Viśvāmitra, lord of sages and possessed of immense splendor, ceased speaking.

Having heard the words of that best of sages, he of great power remained silent, for this was the appropriate thing for him to say; yet the wise man finds no satisfaction in a discourse lacking logical consistency, nor does the world find contentment when its heart’s desire remains unfulfilled.
The seventh canto, titled "The Speech of Viśvāmitra," by Vālmīki.
Having heard those words spoken by Viśvāmitra, that tiger among kings remained motionless for a moment and, with a sense of dejection, spoke as follows:
"This lotus-eyed Rāma is less than sixteen years of age."
"I do not see his fitness for battle against the Rākṣasas.
O Lord, I am the master of this full Akṣauhiṇī army;
surrounded by it, I shall give battle to the flesh-eaters."

"For these servants are brave, valiant, and skilled in weapons; and I, bow in hand, shall be their protector at the head of the battle. Together with them, [I can withstand] even the enemies of yours who are as great as Mahendra."
I shall give him battle, as a lion does against rutting elephants.
But Rāma is but a boy; he knows nothing of strength and weakness in armies, for other than the inner apartments, no battlefield has ever been seen by him.
He was neither equipped with supreme weapons nor skilled in warfare;
nor was he an expert in the frowns of soldiers at the forefront of battle.
He spent his time only among groves of flowers and in the city parks.
Always accustomed to the groves and forest thickets of the gardens,
he knows how to enjoy himself with the princes in his own courtyards, which are strewn with flowers.

But today, O Brahmin, due to a reversal of my fortune, he has become exceedingly pale and emaciated, like a green lotus struck by frost. He is unable to eat food or even to move about in the courtyard of his home.
With his soul overwhelmed by inner anguish, he remains merely silent.
O leader of sages, for his sake, I, along with my wife and servants,
have surely reached a state of helplessness, like a cloud in autumn.
"Such is this young son of mine, rendered helpless by mental anguish;
how can I give him to you to fight with the night-stalkers?
O virtuous one, even more than the company of a young woman, and even more than the essence of nectar—"

O Great-minded One, this affection for a son brings greater happiness even than sovereignty. Even the virtuous do not resort to those things which, though undertaken with great effort, have miserable ends and bring weariness throughout the three worlds, because of their love for a son.

"O tiger among sages, men easily renounce their pleasures—sensual desires, wealth, and even wives—but not their sons; for such is the nature of living beings. Yet there were Rākṣasas of cruel deeds, experts in treacherous warfare."
The mere statement, "Let Rāma fight them," is utterly unbearable. Separated from Rāma, I do not have the strength to live for even a moment, though I desire life; you ought not to take Rāma away.
"O Kauśika, nine thousand years have passed for me;
these four sons were produced by me with great hardship.
Among them, the lotus-eyed Rāma is the most preeminent."
Without him, even those other three do not maintain their lives.
That very Rāma is being led by you toward the Rākṣasas;
if he is gone, know me to be as good as dead this very moment, bereft of my son.
Indeed, my affection for my four sons is supreme;
therefore, you ought not to take away Rāma, the eldest, who is the very embodiment of dharma, O Sage,
if it is your desire to destroy the army of the night-stalkers.
"Lead an army endowed with the four divisions along with me.
Tell me clearly: what is the prowess of those Rākṣasas, whose sons are they, how are they, what is their size, and who are they?"

O Brahmin, tell me everything: how should Rāma strike those Rākṣasas who fight with deceit—with my forces or with me himself—in battle? O Blessed One, explain this to me as it concerns them and me in combat.
One must remain [vigilant] regarding wicked beings, for the *rākṣasas* are indeed arrogant in their prowess.
For it is heard that there is a great hero among the *rākṣasas* named Rāvaṇa,
the actual brother of Vaiśravaṇa and the son of the sage Viśravas.
"If that evil-minded one indeed creates an obstacle to your sacrifice,
then we shall not be able to withstand that wicked-souled one in battle,
O Brahmin, for at various times our great power and majesty manifest differently."
Beings attain prosperity and dissolve away through the power of time.
Today, at this time, we are not capable of standing before our enemies, Rāvaṇa and the others; such is the certainty of destiny.
Therefore, O knower of dharma, show favor toward my little son;
for you are indeed the incomparable deity even to me, who am of such meager fortune.
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, monkeys, and serpents—
They are not even able to fight Rāvaṇa, much less other men in battle.
He robs the great heroic power of those who consume nectar;
therefore, we are not capable of fighting him, nor can we withstand his boons in combat.
This was one such time when the virtuous were rendered weak;
even Rāghava, worn out by old age, fell into a state of wretchedness.
Or rather, O Brahmin, that son of Madhu, the salt-sprinkler who destroyed the sacrifice—
"Tell me, O you who resemble a god, where indeed shall I release my little son?
If you do not wish it, O Brahmin, then I am surely subject to your will;
otherwise, I see no eternal victory for myself."
Having spoken these gentle words, he was overwhelmed by fear and submerged in the turbulent uncertainty regarding the sage’s doctrine;
like one being swept away in an ocean with rising waves, that great-souled man could not discern even a single drop of certainty.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Words of Daśaratha."
The Eighth Sarga. Vālmīki:
Having heard those words of his, whose syllables were choked with affection, [he spoke].
The wrathful Kauśika replied to the lord of the earth:
"Viśvāmitra said:
'Having promised, "I shall do it," do you now wish to abandon your vow?'"
Having become a powerful lion, you desire the state of a deer!
O descendant of Raghu, this reversal of fortune is unworthy of this lineage;
rays of darkness never arise from the cool-rayed moon.
"If you are not able [to grant my request], O King, I shall depart as I came; having failed in my vow, O descendant of Kakutstha, may you remain happy along with your kinsmen. Vālmīki:
Then, when that great-souled Viśvāmitra was overcome with anger,
the entire earth trembled and the gods were seized by fear;
for they perceived that the great sage, a friend of the world, was overwhelmed by wrath.
The steadfast, virtuous, and wise Vasiṣṭha spoke these words:
"Born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, you are like another Dharma incarnate."

You, the illustrious Daśaratha, are adorned with virtues throughout the three worlds; having become one who is ethical and firm in his vows, you ought not to abandon dharma. You ought to carry out the word of the Sage, the Lord of the Three Worlds.
Renowned throughout the three worlds and endowed with righteousness and glory, practice your own duty; you ought not to abandon dharma.
O King, having promised "I shall do it," you have failed to perform that for me.
"The merit of sacrifices and charitable works would perish; therefore, O Rāma, let him go.
Protected by that lion among men, he will be like nectar guarded by fire;
whether he has mastered the divine weapons or not, the Rākṣasas shall not behold him."
"Even though you are born of the Ikṣvāku lineage and are yourself Daśaratha,
if you do not uphold the word [of the sages], who else will uphold it?
By means of the conventional practice established by you and others, living beings [proceed]."
They do not abandon their boundary; you ought not to forsake it here.
He is dharma incarnate, he is the best among the valiant, he is preeminent in wisdom in this world, and he is the ultimate refuge of asceticism.
He knows every kind of weapon in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile;
no other man knows these, nor will anyone ever know them. Neither any of the celestial seers, nor the immortals, nor the rākṣasas [know them].
"O King, neither nāgas, yakṣas, nor gandharvas are equal to him.
This weapon, which is exceedingly difficult for enemies to conquer, was given long ago by Bhṛśāśva to Kauśika when he ruled the kingdom. (MU 1.8.16–17)
For those heroic sons of Bhṛśāśva, resembling the sons of Prajāpati,
radiant and of great prowess, followed him. Jayā and Suprabhā, both slender-waisted daughters of Dakṣa, likewise followed.

As for their offspring, which were a hundred and exceedingly invincible— Jayā, having previously obtained a boon, gave birth to fifty sons for the destruction of the asura armies; they were indestructible and able to assume any form at will.
Suprabhā gave birth to fifty other sons named Saṅgharṣas, who were invincible, difficult to assail, irreproachable, and exceedingly powerful.
Such was the prowess and great splendor of the great sage Viśvāmitra.
"You ought not to harbor a despondent thought regarding Rāma’s departure.
While this Lord of Sages, who is composed of great being, stands nearby, even a man facing death attains immortality; do not fall into dejection like one who is utterly deluded."
The Ninth Sarga, titled "Vasiṣṭha’s Speech," by Vālmīki.
While Vasiṣṭha was speaking thus, King Daśaratha, intending to dispatch his son Rāma, summoned him along with Lakṣmaṇa.
Daśaratha said:
"O doorkeeper, bring quickly and without hindrance the mighty-armed Rāma, whose valor is truth, along with Lakṣmaṇa, for the sake of the sage.
Having been thus dispatched by the king, he went to the inner apartments.
Having arrived in a mere moment, he spoke to the lord of the earth:
"O King, you whose arms have crushed all enemies, Rāma remains in his own palace dejected at night, like a bee within a lotus."
"I shall come in a moment," he says, yet he meditates all alone;
with a weary mind, he does not wish to remain in the presence of anyone.
When this was said by him, the king [addressed] that attendant of Rāma.

He comforted them all and questioned them in due order. When asked by the king, "O Rāma, how is he? In what state is he? the distressed attendants of Rāma spoke these words to the lord of the earth: "O King, we have searched for him everywhere—on the mountains, in the forests, in the cities, and in the villages. We have searched along the rivers, in the oceans, and in the caves; yet we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. He is not in Ayodhyā, nor in the city of Mithilā, nor in the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, nor in the abode of Agastya. We have searched through the lands of the Kurus, the Pāñcālas, the Matsyas, and the Śālvas; we have searched through the regions of the Kosalas, the Videhas, and the Magadhas. We have searched through the lands of the Kaliṅgas, the Āndhras, the Draviḍas, and the Keralas; we have searched through the lands of the Kāśmīras, the Saurāṣṭras, and the Sindhus. We have searched through the lands of the Kāmbojas, the Yavanas, the Kirātas, and the Daradas; we have searched through the lands of the Cīnas, the Tukhāras, and the Barbaras. But we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Guptas, the Mlecchas, and the Pulindas; we have searched through the lands of the Śakas, the Pahlavas, and the Hūṇas. Yet we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Mālavas, the Śibis, the Niṣādhas, and the Madras; we have searched through the lands of the Aṅgas, the Vaṅgas, and the Kaliṅgas. But we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Pārasīkas, the Tāmilas, and the Kāñcīs; we have searched through the lands of the Cola, the Kerala, and the Pāṇḍya. Yet we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Khasas, the Daradas, and the Pārvatīyas; we have searched through the lands of the Bhūtas, the Yakṣas, and the Rākṣasas. But we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Siddhas, the Cāraṇas, and the Gandharvas; we have searched through the lands of the Nāgas, the Piśācas, and the Guhyakas. Yet we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Vidyādharas, the Kinnaras, and the Kiṃpuruṣas; we have searched through the lands of the Apsarases, the Sādhyas, and the Viśvedevas. But we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Maruts, the Rudras, and the Vasus; we have searched through the lands of the Ādityas, the Pitṛs, and the Ṛṣis. Yet we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Brahmakāyikas, the Mahārājikas, and the Trāyastriṃśas; we have searched through the lands of the Yāmas, the Tuṣitas, and the Nirmāṇaratis. But we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Paranirmitavaśavartins, the Akaniṣṭhas, and the Bhavāgras; we have searched through the lands of the Anabhrakas, the Puṇyaprasavas, and the Bṛhatphalas. Yet we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Ābhāsvaras, the Śubhakṛtsnas, and the Apramāṇaśubhas; we have searched through the lands of the Parīttaśubhas, the Anabhrakas, and the Puṇyaprasavas. But we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Brahmapurohitas, the Mahābrahmans, and the Parīttābhas; we have searched through the lands of the Apramāṇābhas, the Ābhāsvaras, and the Śubhakṛtsnas. Yet we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Parīttaśubhas, the Apramāṇaśubhas, and the Śubhakṛtsnas; we have searched through the lands of the Anabhrakas, the Puṇyaprasavas, and the Bṛhatphalas. But we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Avṛhas, the Atapas, and the Sudṛśas; we have searched through the lands of the Sudarśanas, the Akaniṣṭhas, and the Bhavāgras. Yet we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Kṛtsnāyatanas, the Vijñānānantyāyatanas, and the Ākiṃcanyāyatanas; we have searched through the lands of the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanas and the Saṃjñāvedayitanirodhas. But we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Cāturmahārājikas, the Trāyastriṃśas, and the Yāmas; we have searched through the lands of the Tuṣitas, the Nirmāṇaratis, and the Paranirmitavaśavartins. Yet we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Bhūtas, the Pretas, and the Piśācas; we have searched through the lands of the Asuras, the Nāgas, and the Rākṣasas. But we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Siddhas, the Cāraṇas, and the Gandharvas; we have searched through the lands of the Kinnaras, the Kiṃpuruṣas, and the Mahoragas. Yet we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Vidyādharas, the Yakṣas, and the Guhyakas; we have searched through the lands of the Piśācas, the Bhūtas, and the Pretas. But we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Mlecchas, the Barbaras, and the Pulindas; we have searched through the lands of the Śakas, the Yavanas, and the Kambojas. Yet we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Khasas, the Daradas, and the Pārvatīyas; we have searched through the lands of the Bhūtas, the Yakṣas, and the Rākṣasas. But we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Siddhas, the Cāraṇas, and the Gandharvas; we have searched through the lands of the Nāgas, the Piśācas, and the Guhyakas. Yet we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Vidyādharas, the Kinnaras, and the Kiṃpuruṣas; we have searched through the lands of the Apsarases, the Sādhyas, and the Viśvedevas. But we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Maruts, the Rudras, and the Vasus; we have searched through the lands of the Ādityas, the Pitṛs, and the Ṛṣis. Yet we have not found the son of Daśaratha anywhere. We have searched through the lands of the Brahmakāyikas, the Mahārājikas, and the Trāyastriṃśas; we have searched through the lands of
"O Lord, we who support this slender body of ours are exhausted,
O All-pervading One, now that your son Rāma has withered away from grief.
Since the lotus-eyed Rāma first arrived," [so they said].
From that time forth, Savitṛ became dejected regarding his pilgrimage;
though we entreated him with great effort, he would perform his daily duties—
whether he did them or not— with a face that remained unfaded at evening.
Even when entreated, the Lord, weary from his bath, worship of the gods, and customary rites,
does not eat his food to satiety;
for in the courtyard, the women of his restless harem have set up swings.
And he does not sport with pleasures, like a *cātaka* bird with drops of rainwater;
nor do armlets, bracelets, and rows of necklaces set with rubies and pearls delight him,
O King, as the heavens fail to gladden one who is helpless under a falling rain.
In these bower-houses of creeping vines, where playful young women wander and where the breezes carry the scent of flowers, he becomes filled with extreme despondency—
regarding whatever is beautiful, appropriate, sweet, delicate, or heart-stealing. *Mūla-kārikā 1.9.14*
As if his eyes were filled with a flood of tears, he is distressed by that very [sight];
"Why do these sorrow-bringing women appear before me?"—thus he censures the amorous gestures in the dance. (MU 1.9.15–16)
Food, sleep, bathing, pleasure, drink, and sitting—he does not welcome these when they are censured, as if they were the behavior of a madman.
What is the use of prosperity? What is the use of adversity? What is the use of home? What is the use of worldly pursuits?
Having declared that "everything is indeed non-existent," he remains alone in silence.
He does not respond in jests, nor does he sink into enjoyments;
he does not remain occupied with worldly affairs, but maintains only silence.
Women with creeper-like, tossing tresses and eyes that roll with playful charm do not bring him joy, just as does deer do not delight a forest tree;
[he seeks them] in solitary places, at the ends of the quarters, on riverbanks, and in the depths of the woods.

He finds delight in the forests as if among beings who have been sold; O King, by that very aversion to the taking of clothing, drink, and food, he follows the path of the ascetics who possess the dharma of the wandering mendicants.
Dwelling alone in a region devoid of people, O Lord of Men,
he neither laughs with a singular intellect, nor sings, nor weeps;
seated in the *padmāsana* posture with his mind vacant, he rests his left hand upon his lap.
Taking hold of the surface of the cheek, it remains alone;
it assumes no pride, nor does it desire sovereignty;
it neither rises nor sets amidst the fluctuations of pleasure and pain.
We do not know what he has become, what he does, what he strives for, what he meditates upon, from where he comes, or how and why he pursues this [world].
Day by day he grows emaciated; day by day he becomes pale.
Day by day he moves toward dispassion, like a tree at the end of autumn.
O King, Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa followed him;
they were exactly like him, as if they had arisen as his very reflections.
Although questioned again and again by his servants, kings, and mothers,
he said nothing at all and remained silent and motionless.
"Do not set your mind upon enjoyments that are pleasing only at first sight."
Thus he instructs his worthy friends who stand by his side.

Regarding women, delightful with their various splendors, and regarding social gatherings and conversations, he, being devoid of attachment, perceives them as nothing but destruction, as if they were standing right before him.
He repeatedly sings with a falsetto voice (*kākalyā*), employing gestures that are devoid of rhythmic flow, sweetness, effort, and proper placement of words;
even when a courtier standing nearby says to him, "Be an emperor! (MU 1.9.32).
The sage laughs at one who talks like a madman, his mind turned elsewhere;
he does not listen to what is said, nor does he look at what stands before him;
he shows contempt everywhere, even toward matters of great importance.
Even regarding a lotus in the sky or a great forest in the sky,
no wonder arises in him as to how this could be so;
even when he is in the midst of beloved women, his mind is not pierced by the arrows of Love.
They cannot break that which is difficult to break, just as streams cannot split a great rock.
"Why do you desire wealth, the sole dwelling place of calamities?"—
having thus instructed him, he bestows his entire possession upon the seeker.
"This is calamity, this is prosperity"—this delusion, consisting of conceptual construction, has arisen in the mind; thus, out of grief, he cries out:
"Alas, I am ruined! I am helpless! even while being intent on lamentation. (MU 1.9.38)

People do not attain dispassion; they simply say, "It is wonderful. Because Rāma, the slayer of enemies, remains thus intensely fixed within the forest-thicket of the Raghus, we have come to great distress.
"O mighty-armed one, we do not know what we should do for such a person as he, O lotus-petal-eyed one; for you alone are our refuge in this matter.
[Should it be] a king, or a brahmin, or a teacher who stands at the forefront?"
O Lord, he disregards this expansion known as the world that has arisen here, just as one who is unperturbed disregards a beast;
having reached the firm conclusion, "This is not a real entity, nor am I it," he remains established [in that state]. (MU 1.9.42–43)
Neither in woman, nor in himself, nor in a friend, nor in his kingdom, nor in his mother;
neither in prosperity nor in adversity—there is no place for that All-pervading One within or without.
Free from attachment, free from hope, free from effort, and without a support.
"He has been liberated from delusion; because of that, we are tormented.
What is the use of wealth? What is the use of mothers? What is the use of a kingdom? What is the use of worldly striving?"—thus resolved within himself, he remained intent on giving up his life.
He experienced supreme agitation regarding enjoyments, life, sovereignty, friends, father, and mother,
like a cātaka bird during a drought.
For him, whose nature was such, [there arose] that which was endowed with complete prosperity...
O Lord, the expansive web of saṃsāra acts as a counter-poison [to liberation].
Who on this earth could be such a great being (mahāsattva)—one capable of establishing [the world] within the ordinary course of worldly affairs? (MU 1.9.48–49)
Thus, may he who is devoted to compassion arise sufficiently to rescue this calamity that has come upon us, spreading like the extension of branches;
for the high-minded one, having cast away delusion from his mind, indeed possesses the goodness to alleviate all the suffering of those in distress.
Just as the sun dispelling darkness brings about its own fruitfulness by attaining the state of the "light-maker" (bhāskara) upon the earth, so does he bring success here.
The tenth canto, named "The Despair of Rāghava."
Viśvāmitra:
If this is so, then let your honors quickly bring that highly wise delight of the Raghus here, as lions bring a deer.
This delusion of the Lord of the Raghus arose neither from calamities nor from passion;
this awakening, born of discernment and dispassion, is of great consequence.
Let Rāma come here in an instant; we shall remain right here for an instant.
"O Maruts, we shall dispel his delusion, just as a cloud [dispels] mist from a mountain.
O descendant of Raghu, when this delusion has been cleared away by means of reasoning,
he will find rest in that supreme state, just as we have."
Having attained truth, joy, wisdom, and rest,
he will attain fullness and a most excellent complexion, as if having drunk nectar;
and he will [resume] his own natural, ongoing succession of worldly activities.

With a fulfilled mind, he will honor his teacher and practice the path without flaw. This Great Being will come to know the high and low of the world; indifferent to the states of pleasure and pain, he will regard a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal.
When the Lord of Sages had spoken thus, the king, his heart fulfilled,
dispatched a succession of messengers once more to bring Rāma back.
And in that much time, Rāma [rose] from his own seat at home.
Rising like the sun from a mountain to come into his father’s presence,
he arrived accompanied by a few servants and his two brothers at that holy assembly hall of his father,
which was like the heaven of the Lord of the Gods.
Then, from afar, Rāma beheld Daśaratha surrounded by a multitude of kings like Vāsava by the hosts of gods,
attended on both sides by Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra.
It was protected by a circle of ministers who were experts in the meaning of all the scriptures;
it was attended by beautiful women with lovely chowries in their hands,
standing as was appropriate like the quarters of the sky personified.
Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and others, as well as Daśaratha and his kin,
beheld from afar Rāghava approaching like Guha,
with a pride born of his steadfastness of character, like the Himālaya with its coolness.
He was attended by one worthy of all service, and possessed a deep voice;
he was gentle, with an even and auspicious appearance, noble in his modesty, and majestic;
his body was both beautiful and serene, and he was a vessel for the highest goal.
His youth had fully commenced, yet he was graced by both exertion and tranquility;
he was free from agitation and effortless, his desires being almost entirely fulfilled.
Having investigated the course of the world, his sphere of experience was characterized by pure virtues.
Out of singular longing for the Great Being, as if taking refuge in his virtues,
[I beheld] that hollow of the inner heart, filled with noble essence,
displaying the unsurpassed state through its undisturbed activity.
Thus, the scion of Raghu’s line, adorned with a multitude of virtues, bowed from afar—
his garment-like shoots being his white,
pure, and translucent turban— as he did so, the rays of his shimmering crest-jewel flickered.
With his head possessing the beauty of mountains swaying from the trembling of the earth,
he first bowed to his father, then to the sages with singular reverence;
thereafter to the Brahmins, then to his kinsmen, and finally to his teachers of superior virtue.
Having seen them, he accepted with his own voice the salutations offered by the circle of kings in a slightly sweet tone;
and Rāma, whose mind was tranquil, received the blessings bestowed by the two sages.
The godlike youth approached his father’s holy presence.
Then the lord of the earth, intent on receiving the prostration of his feet,
quickly embraced him upon the head and kissed him again and again.

Then that slayer of enemy heroes embraced Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa with deep affection, just as a royal swan embraces a lotus. Then, as the lord of the earth said, "O child, stay on my lap," [the two brothers sat there].
Then Daśaratha sat down upon a garment spread on the ground by his attendants.
Daśaratha said:
"My son, you have attained discernment and are a vessel for all that is auspicious."
One should not subject oneself to weariness with an intellect that has grown old like the common folk;
rather, by one such as you who practices what is taught by aged brahmins and gurus,
the meritorious state is attained, not by one who pursues delusion.
"O son, calamities remain far away and utterly fragile for as long as no opening is given to the spread of delusion. Vasiṣṭha said:

O mighty-armed prince, you are a hero; by you these enemies that are the sense-objects—so difficult to sever and so difficult to confront—have been conquered. Why do you act like one ignorant in this ocean of delusion, which is the proper domain of the unwise?
You are sinking into the dense mass of waves characterized by dullness.
Viśvāmitra:
O you whose eyes are like a cluster of swaying blue lotuses, [why this] fickleness?
Speak, O mind: having abandoned what you have created, for what reason do you become deluded?
Upon what are they based, how many are they, by what means, and for what cause do these anxieties plunder the mind, just as rats ravage a house?
I consider you the foremost among those who have not become the abode of mental agonies;
for that steadfast man who remains composed in calamities has conquered his anxieties. Speak quickly what you desire, and you shall attain it without fault.
"Furthermore, by this [knowledge], all your mental afflictions shall be shattered.

Having heard these words of the supreme sage, which were filled with the graceful beauty of appropriate meaning, the banner of Raghu’s lineage abandoned his sorrow— just as a peacock does when the rain-cloud roars and it has inferred the attainment of its desired goal.
The eleventh canto, titled "The Consolation of Rāghava," by Vālmīki.
Thus questioned by the Lord of Sages and comforted, Rāghava spoke these words, which were beautiful, steady, full of meaning, and measured. Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, since you have now asked me as is fitting, I shall speak, though I am ignorant; for who can transgress the words of the virtuous?
First, I was born here in this, my own father’s house."
Having gradually attained maturity and acquired knowledge, I remained there;
then, O leader of sages, becoming devoted to virtuous conduct,
I wandered over the earth girdled by the oceans for the purpose of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.

After this much time, my own discernment (*svaviveka*) removed from within me this attachment to *saṃsāra*, just as a rushing current sweeps away a creeper growing on a riverbank. With my self encompassed by that discernment, I thereafter [proceeded] of my own accord.
With an intellect indifferent toward enjoyments, he reflected upon this:
"What indeed is this so-called happiness that is this wandering through saṃsāra, where the world is born for death and dies for birth? (MU 1.11.6–7)
All these beings, including those that move and those that are stationary, remain established in their own states;
yet they are the masters of calamities, sinful, and the very grounds of worldly existence— like iron rods, they are entirely unattached to one another.
Entities merely cling together through their own mental construction.
This expansive world is seen as dependent upon the mind;
yet the mind itself appears as non-existent here—by what have we been utterly deluded?
Alas, we of deluded intellect have been sold for nothing,
like bewildered deer in the forest lured by the water of a mirage from afar.
We have not been sold by anyone, yet we remain as if we were sold.

"Alas, we are all deluded, even though we know Śambara! What indeed are these enjoyments within these manifold worlds, so utterly wretched? For in vain have we remained, bound by our conceptions through ignorance."
Unaware for a long time, we have fallen in vain into this dense delusion, like bewildered deer into a pit—fools indeed!
What use have I for kingship, what use for enjoyments; who am I, and what is this that has come upon me?
"Let that which is false remain false; for whom indeed has anything come to pass?
O Brahmin, as I reflected thus, a distaste for all existing things arose within me, like that of a traveler in the deserts.
Therefore, O Blessed One, tell us this: what is it that perishes? What is it that is born again? What is it that increases?
Aging, death, misfortune, birth, and likewise prosperity—[what is it that undergoes these?]

Through repeated manifestations and disappearances, we are indeed led to decay by those very same trivial states of being, just as mountain trees are brought to ruin by the winds. Observe this! (MU 1.11.18–19)

Like insentient beings, people stand making sounds through the winds called "vital breaths," just like hollow bamboo flutes; I am tormented by the thought, "How can this suffering be stilled?"* MU_1,11.20 *The commentary notes that the winds (prāṇa) here refer to the vital breaths. The term kīcaka-veṇu refers to a hollow bamboo that whistles when struck by the wind. The verse likens living beings to these whistling bamboos, driven by the winds of life. I am distressed by the anxiety of how this misery might come to an end.
Like an old tree with a fierce fire dwelling within its hollow,
though my heart is packed solid with the stones of the sorrows of saṃsāra,
I do not weep with falling tears merely out of fear for my own world.
But my mental states are empty, parched by dry weeping and devoid of flavor;
only discernment, dwelling within my heart, beholds me in solitude.
I am utterly bewildered as I recollect this condition composed of both existence and non-existence.
Like one who is fortunate [in the world] despite poverty, he remains far removed from the anxieties of saṃsāra.
Prosperities, which are intent on deception, utterly delude the activity of the mind, thoroughly shatter the virtues, and bestow a web of suffering. (MU 1.11.24–25)
Wealth, which turns toward a mass of anxieties, does not lead to my joy;
nor do houses filled with wives, like those of men beset by calamities.
This is due to constant reflections on states of manifold defects, fashioned from causes that are perpetually fragile.
O Sage, my mind finds no peace, like that of a wild elephant bound in chains.

At every turn, throughout the night, when the world is shrouded by the thick mist of sharp delusion, the clever thieves of the senses—those who seize objects by force—have set out in every direction, intent on plundering the very faculty of discernment. Tell me, O wise ones, who is capable in battle against them?
"Today, O brave warriors!
Thus ends the twelfth canto, titled "The First Lamentation. Canto Twelve.
Rāma:
O Sage, this Śrī was fashioned for diversion in this saṃsāra; yet even she surely brings about delusion and bestows misfortune.
Like a river in the rainy season, she pours forth vast, dull, and surging waves within her that are agitated and out of order;
many daughters of anxiety issue from her, driven by excessive restlessness.
Fickle states arise in her like the waves of a river. For this unfortunate one does not fix her footing in any single place; like a bewildered girl, she runs hither and thither with no fixed conduct.
Producing intense burning when touched,
she brings about her own destruction within herself, like a streak of lamp-soot,
even without the deliberation of merits and defects by one standing at her side.
Like the nature of a king, this deluded [intellect] clings to what is difficult to ascend;
by various actions it undergoes expansion,
such that the force of the venomous serpent of its defects spreads out like a flow of milk.
People are cold and gentle in their touch toward both strangers and their own kin only so long as they have not been made harsh by prosperity, like snow driven by a whirlwind.
Those who are wise, brave, grateful, refined, and mild— [are rare].
By your splendor, jewels have been rendered as dull as mere handfuls of dust.
O Blessed One, prosperity does not lead to happiness; indeed, it conduces only to suffering.
Like a poisonous creeper, it conceals its own destruction until it brings about death.
The illustrious man, the one beyond reproach, and the hero who does not boast—
these three types of men are difficult to find, for they possess equal vision and mastery.
Indeed, this cave of those who experience suffering is treacherous and deep.
It is a great forest on Mount Vindhya for the lordly elephants of dense delusion;

it is a moonlight night for the lotuses of the theory of pre-existent effects (*satkārya*), a moonlight for the night-lilies of suffering; it is a whirlwind for the lamps of right vision, and a river surging with a flood of waves.
It is the path to the mountain of the clouds of agitation, the nourisher of the poison of despondency;
it is a small field for conceptual constructions, a pit for the serpents of evil enjoyments,
frost for the creepers of dispassion, and the night of the owl of mental transformation.
Discrimination is the fang of Rāhu to the moon of goodness;
it is as enchanting as Indra’s bow with its various flickering colors,
and like a shimmering flash of lightning, it arises and perishes while resting upon the dull-witted.
Fickle and devoid of delight, she is a female mongoose born of a mongoose;
she is a mirage, the cause of intense delusion and pursuit. Like a wave, she remains uniform in nature, never establishing a steady footing for even a moment.
Like the flickering flame of a lamp, its course and sphere of activity are exceedingly difficult to discern;
like a lioness, it strikes down the pride of the elephant-herd of conceptual constructs;
like the edge of a sword, it is cool yet sharp, resting upon a sharp intention.
"Behold, this unfortunate Fortune— afflicted by this [misery], overwhelmed by grievous suffering, and incapable of anything else— sees no happiness at all except for sorrow.
Driven out through the gateway, Fortune returns once more with the enemy of darkness."
Alas! Prosperity, though dwelling in the heart, is shameless and the abode of the wicked;
it captivates the mind's movement yet is difficult for the miserly to achieve and momentarily fragile.
Like a flowering creeper that has emerged from a pit but whose body is enveloped within a swarm of serpents, such is the nature of fortune.
The thirteenth canto, titled "The Banishment of Lakṣmī," Canto 13:
Rāma.
The body departs unexpectedly, like one who has gone mad, abandoning life which is as fragile as a drop of water hanging from the tip of a sprout's edge;
for those whose minds are worn out by attachment to the poison of sensory objects, [the world] is like a forest fire.
For those whose self-discrimination is immature, life is a cause of exhaustion;
but for those who have known what is to be known, who have found rest in the expansive state,
and who are composed in the equilibrium of existence and non-existence— for them, life becomes a source of happiness.
O Sage, we have reached a certainty established through limited forms; yet, amidst this mass of lightning in the clouds of saṃsāra, we find no peace in our lifespan.
It might be possible to wrap the wind or to break open the sky.
The binding together of waves and reliance upon life are not fitting.
Like an autumn cloud, like a lamp without oil,
and like a wave that is restless, it is perceived only as having already passed away.
I do not fix my resolve upon grasping the moon reflected in a wave, a mass of lightning in a cloud, or the sky within a rain-cloud;
yet, with an unquiet mind, I strive for this empty, protracted life whose duration has already passed.

Like a female mule conceiving in her womb, the deluded person suffers only for his own misery. O King, in this ocean of creation, the water of worldly existence is but foam; life is like sap to the creeper of the body—it does not please me.
That by which the goal to be attained is reached, by which one no longer grieves, and which is the abode of supreme bliss—that is called true life.
For even trees live, and deer and birds live; yet their life is not like that.
He truly lives whose life does not depend on the activity of the mind;
those alone are born in this world as beings with a noble life who are not born here again. Know, O asses, that all others are merely born.
The scriptures are a burden to the undiscerning; knowledge is a burden to the passionate;
an unpeaceful mind is a burden; and the body is a burden to one who does not know the Self. Form, lifespan, mind, intellect, ego, and likewise effort—[these belong to the non-Self].
Like a burden for one who carries it, everything leads to suffering for the person of dull intellect. Life is a state of constant mental unrest, the supreme abode of calamities,
a nest for the birds of disease, and a firm source of exhaustion.
Daily casting off weariness, one should strive steadily and without ceasing;
for in time, the pit of birth is quickly buried.
[This is done] by those who have rested within the cavity of the body, yet who bring about the burning of poison.
It is consumed by fierce diseases, like the forest breeze by predatory beasts;
it is dragged away by cruel sufferings that arise within and cut it down, like an old tree by woodworms.
Surely death watches incessantly for the sake of swiftly swallowing away dense pride,
just as a cat watches a mouse;
[for one] who is filled with qualities such as pride, yet is empty and subject to incapacity.
Food is digested by old age just as it is by a voracious eater;
after only a few days, having recognized its nature,
one is cast off by youth with indifference, just as a good person is abandoned by a wicked man.

Form is constantly coveted by Death— the eternal friend of destruction and kinsman of old age and death— just as a supreme libertine covets [a woman]. It is perpetually abandoned by stability and the capacity for happiness, and is both excellent in appearance yet utterly fragile.
In this world, there is nothing so devoid of merit as this life acquired through death.
The fourteenth canto, titled "Censure of Life."
Rāma:
It is in vain that I have risen up out of delusion; it is in vain that [this state] continues to grow.
I am terrified by this enemy of false ego, which consists of nothing but illusion.
It is solely through the power of egoism that this world, with its manifold forms, inflicts the torment of a treasury of defects upon those who are most wretched;
through the power of egoism comes calamity, and from egoism come troubled anxieties.
"Even this striving arises from the power of egoism; egoism is a great illusion.
Relying upon that egoism, my supreme and long-standing enemy, I neither eat nor drink water—how much less, O Sage, could I indulge in worldly enjoyments?"
The long rope of saṃsāra, which deludes my mind,
has been stretched out by the fault of egoism, like a snare set by a hunter.
Whatever sorrows there are— long, harsh, and great— [they are all produced by it].
They have issued forth from egoism like *khadira* trees from the earth.
I abandon this egoism, which is the great thunderbolt for the lotus of the qualities, the mouth of Rāhu to the moon of tranquility, and the autumnal cloud for the rain of knowledge.
I am not Rāma, nor do I have desire for worldly objects, nor does my mind dwell upon them;
I wish to remain tranquil within my own self alone, like a Jina.
Whatever I have enjoyed, done, or taken under the influence of egoism—
All that is indeed non-substantial; the substance is the emptiness of egoism.
O Brahmin, if there is an "I," then I am pained in adversity and happy in prosperity;
therefore, the wealth is the state of being without egoism.
"O sage, having abandoned the ego, with a peaceful mind and free from agitation,
I remain established in the flood of enjoyments as one whose abode is indestructible. O Brahmin, as long as the cloud of egoism continues to expand,"

The cluster of *kuṭaja* blossoms that is craving continues to bloom only so long as the dense cloud of egoism remains. Once that cloud has subsided, the fresh lightning-streak of craving will quickly vanish somewhere, like the flickering of a lamp’s flame when it has been extinguished.
In the great Vindhya mountain of egoism, the intoxicated elephant of the mind roars with the crashing of clouds, like a rain-cloud with its thunderous peals.
Here, within the vast cave of the body, the lion of dense egoism [roars].
By that which expands and shines forth, this entire world is pervaded.
The succession of many births, strung upon the threads of craving,
has been fashioned by the fierce hunter of egoism into a necklace around his neck.
Wife, children, and family— this entire web, devoid of mantra,
has been spread out here by this enemy of false ego; yet,
when the state of "I" was wiped away, he himself remained untroubled.

All anxieties indeed become completely wiped away. When the "I"-notion has been stilled, gradually becoming characterized by perfect tranquility, the mist of the mind’s conceptualization and delusion vanishes somewhere beyond reach.
"O Brahmin, since my mental state is free from egoism yet I am sinking in grief due to my own folly,
you ought to tell me whatever is appropriate here.
I do not take refuge in this unstable body, which is the abode of all calamities, situated within, and abandoned by the Supreme Being."
O Great-Souled One, with all effort, instruct me further regarding the state of egoism, which is surrounded by extreme suffering.
Thus ends the fifteenth canto, titled "The Loathing of Egoism."
Rāma:
The fickle mind, having reached a state of decay through its faults, wavers from the noble deeds practiced by the virtuous, like a fragment of a *tapiñcha* feather blown by the wind.
It runs aimlessly and distractedly here and there,
like a miserable village dog that wanders further and further away;
it attains nothing at all anywhere, even though great wealth has been acquired.
The mind never attains fullness, like a basket with water; it is eternally empty, yet entangled in the snare of desires,
and finds not even the slightest peace, like a deer strayed from its herd.
Bearing a state as flickering as a wave and falling into a condition of being cut and shattered,
the mind does not attain peace even for a moment.
Agitated by its own thinking, the mind runs through the ten directions.
Like the water of the milk-ocean churned by the strike of Mount Mandara,
I am unable to stem this great ocean of mental delusion, which possesses whirlpools formed by surging waves and is garlanded with the crocodiles of *māyā*.

O Brahmin, like a deer captivated by the desire for the sprouts of *dūrvā* grass while disregarding the fall into a pit, my mind runs far astray; never indeed has it reached that state of being neither torn nor shattered.
With its agitated state of being, it abandons stability, just as the ocean loses its steadiness through turbulence.
With its flickering activity, the mind— restless with a multitude of anxieties—
does not fix its resolve upon any one thing, like a lion in a cage.
The mind, mounted upon the chariot of delusion, seizes the bliss of tranquility from the body—
having exerted its effort— as a swan draws milk from water.
The fluctuations of the mind lie nestled upon the broad bed of conceptual construction.
O Lord of Sages, they do not awaken; therefore I am tormented and distressed. O Brahmin, with my mind bound by the threads of craving in firm knots, I am caught like a bird in a net.

O Sage, I am consumed by my mind as dry grass is by fire— fire whose smoke is constant resentment and which is thick with the flames of anxiety. I have become cruel and dull-witted, following after my wife, Craving.
"O Brahmin, I have been devoured by the mind as a corpse is by a jackal;
O Brahmin, I have been carried away by the mind, which is inert in nature and characterized by a fluctuating motion like that of waves, just as a tree on a riverbank is swept away by a torrent."
Driven far away by my mind— as a blade of grass is tossed by a fierce wind— I am cast toward intermediate falls and assailed by emptiness.
Though I am constantly intent on crossing over this ocean of saṃsāra, [I am swept away].

I have been dammed by my evil mind, just as a flood of water is held back by a dike; I am indeed encircled by my mind, which goes from the surface to the underworld and from the underworld back to the surface, like a well-wood driven by a wicked rope.
I have been seized by my own mind, which is falsely expansive in form yet fragile under investigation, just as a child is seized by a Vetāla;
it is hotter than fire and more difficult to traverse than a mountain.

O Brahmin, the mind is harder than even a diamond; this fierce grasper of the mind is difficult to restrain. It falls upon sense-objects like a bird upon pieces of meat, yet in an instant it turns away from them like a child from a toy.
O dear one, this ocean of the mind— insentient by nature, restless, possessing the movement of vast whirlpools, and filled with serpents in the form of desires— drives me far away.
Even more than drinking the great ocean or leaping over Mount Sumeru, [it carries me off].
Moreover, O virtuous one, the restraint of the mind is more difficult than even the avoidance of food.
The mind is the cause of all objects; when it exists, the three worlds exist, and when it is extinguished, the world is extinguished. Therefore, that mind must be treated with diligent effort.

Surely these hundreds of joys and sorrows have come from the mind, just as forests emerge from the best of mountains; I believe they skillfully dissolve away, O Sage, when that mind has been thinned through the power of solitude.
Against that enemy—the mind—upon which the great ones have fixed their hope for victory over all virtues, I have now risen to conquer it.
Because I have become free from passion within, I do not delight in worldly splendor— which is dull, impure, and vast— any more than the moon delights in a mass of clouds.
The sixteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Wickedness of the Mind."
Rāma:
By means of this endless thirst, which is a night of internal darkness,
rows of owls that are the defects roam here in the sky of consciousness.
My essence and softness have been utterly consumed by this anxiety, which brings internal burning; I am being dried up by it, just as mud is dried by the radiance of the sun.
In the great forest of my mind, which is crowded with the darkness of delusion—
In this void, the demoness of hope dances wildly and is utterly intoxicated;
with the mist of passion woven about her and radiant with a mass of gold,
the cluster of my sorrowful thoughts surely puts forth its blossoms.
Enough with this craving that devours the inner disposition;
it leads to a turbulent agitation like a wave in the ocean.
It seems to flow down my mountain-like body with the roar of unrestrained billows.
With its form made even more wavy by surging waves of craving,
this mind-cataka bird has been led away somewhere by a turbid intellect, like an old blade of grass driven by a whirlwind that has arisen to check its momentum.
Whatever excellence of virtue I have studied and whatever refuge I take,
craving cuts it away for me, just as a field mouse gnaws at a string.
Like an old leaf in water, or like withered grass in the wind, [so does craving destroy my gains].
Like an autumn cloud in the sky, I wander within the wheel of anxiety.
We, whose intellects are powerless to reach our own true abode,
are utterly bewildered by the snare of thought, like birds caught in a net.
"O Father, I am thus scorched by the flame called craving that I do not hope for the cessation of this burning even through ambrosias.
Having gone far, far from here, and having met again and again,"
The mare of craving, intoxicated by thirst, gallops swiftly to the ends of the quarters. Clinging to the dull-witted, this craving performs its upward and downward movements;
agitated and full of knots, it is like the harsh rope of a water-wheel.
Like a powerful ox driven by a rope knotted within its body that is being pulled with frantic haste, a person is swiftly led away by thirst for children,
wives, and possessions— a thirst that is perpetually dark.

Just as Kirātī spreads her net among birds, so is this [thirst] woven here among the worlds. Like the night of Kṛṣṇa, this thirst terrifies even the wise, blinds even the eye of insight, and exhausts even the joyful.
Crooked, with a soft touch, proclaiming the imbalance of poison,
