craving burns like a black female serpent even when only slightly touched;
it pierces the hearts of men, creating a web of illusion.
Bestowing misfortune, wretched craving is like a black ogress; O Brahmin, a lute worn out by craving does not shine in joy, even while it holds its bundle of strings coiled within its case.
The creeper of the abyss of craving is eternally and exceedingly filthy, characterized by bitter madness; it is long, slender, and thick with attachment,
yet it brings no joy, is empty, utterly fruitless, and excessively lofty.
Craving is inauspicious and cruel, like a withered cluster of blossoms;
though its heart is never won over, it pursues everything,
yet it obtains no fruit at all, like an aged woman full of desire.
In the great dance of saṃsāra, crowded with various sentiments,
upon the stages of the vast expanse of the worlds, craving is the aged dancer;
she has mounted the blossoms of old age and bears a succession of fruits that are falls and rises.
In the long jungle of saṃsāra, the poisonous creeper of craving spreads; even there, it adopts a dancing gait that it cannot otherwise manage. Devoid of true joy, craving dances like an aged dancer.
When the mist flickers intensely, light subsides upon its arrival;
the peahen of craving, restless with thirst, sets foot amidst the floods of suffering—
she who is thick with dull waves and for a long time has an utterly empty interior.
The river of craving momentarily surges with joy;
having abandoned one who has perished, it moves from one person to another like a restless bird flying from tree to tree. (MU 1.16.27–28)
Even upon that which cannot be transgressed, she sets her foot; though satisfied, she still seeks further fruit;
she does not remain long in one place—such is the restless female monkey of craving.
Having done this, she proceeds to that; everything is utterly inconsistent.
And she strives incessantly, like a divine impulse of craving:
for a moment she descends to the underworld, for a moment she ascends to the vault of heaven;
for a moment the bee of craving wanders through the bowers of the quarters—the lotus-heart of craving.
Craving alone is the giver of long-lasting suffering among all the defects of saṃsāra;
it casts even one dwelling in the inner apartments into extreme distress.
Obstructing the supreme light, it bestows the highest dullness.
The dense cloud-banks of craving, with their deceptive illusions,
are the garlands woven from the minds of all the hosts of living beings engaged in the affairs of saṃsāra; craving is the binding rope.
Thirst has variegated colors, is devoid of virtues, long-lasting, and its very nature is impurity;
it is empty, the abode of emptiness, possesses the character of Indra’s bow (the rainbow),
is like a thunderbolt to the crops of virtue, and bears fruit only in times of calamity.
She is the frost to the lotus-pond of worldly prosperity, the long night of darkness,
the actress on the stage of saṃsāra, the bird dwelling in the cage of the body,
the doe in the forest of the mind, and the lute for the song of passion.
It is a wave in the ocean of worldly affairs, a chain for the elephant of delusion,
as beautiful as a banyan tree at the crossroads, and moonlight for the night-lotus of suffering.
It is the singular casket of jewels containing the miseries of old age and death.
The goddess of desire is eternally intoxicated by the play of mental and physical afflictions;
for a moment she is pure with light, and for a moment she is a fragment of dense darkness;
at times she is like the path of the sky, and at times she is thick with mist.
Let craving go to its pacification for the sake of calming the exertion of activity,
just as the thick, black darkness of night ceases for the sake of warding off demons.
For so long this world remains deluded, mute, and with its inner disposition agitated.

To whatever extent one continues to pursue [objects], one suffers from the cholera of the poison of craving. This entire world abandons all suffering when it is free from anxiety; indeed, the abandonment of anxiety is said to be the mantra for the cholera of anxiety.
Grasping at everything— grass, stones, wood, and so forth— with the suspicion that it is a source of enjoyment,
craving throbs within like a female fish in a pond.
Craving, which dwells within the limbs as disease and pain, [overcomes] even a man who is profound.

It quickly brings one to a state of openness, like the rays of the sun to a lotus. Desire is like a bamboo vine: empty within, knotted, and possessing long shoots as its thorns; yet it constantly possesses the luster of a pearl gem.
Oh, how truly wonderful! Even those of great intelligence cut through craving—which is so difficult to sever—with the stainless sword of discernment.
Neither the edge of a sword, nor the fire of a thunderbolt, nor the glowing sparks of heated iron [are as formidable as this].
O Brahmin, this craving that resides in the heart is as sharp as that [flame];
like the wicks of a lamp, it has a black soot-like point, is long with its oil, and, though luminous, is painful to touch when burned. (MU 1.16.48–49)
Even the wise man who is like Mount Meru, even the brave, even the steadfast—
even the best of men— thirst alone makes as light as a blade of grass in the blink of an eye.
Vast, dense, terrifying, and filled with a web of clouds and dust, [it is thus].
Craving is a great Vindhya forest, thick with blinding darkness and heavy mist;
it is one alone, having found its mark within the interior of all worlds, appearing as if it has become difficult to perceive even while standing right before us.
Craving abides in the world like the power of sweetness in the mass of waters of the milk-ocean, amidst its rows of restless waves.
The seventeenth canto, titled "The Censure of Thirst," ends here. Rāma:

The body, dense with the strings of moist intestines, subject to transformation, and possessed of feverish heat, throbs within saṃsāra; even that [body] leads only to suffering. Though ignorant, it appears like one who knows, its self-delight being merely a turning [of the mind].

Though capable by reason, he is yet incapable for me; he is neither inert nor conscious. Suspended between the views of the inert and the non-inert, his evil intent wavers; he is neither a man of discernment nor a fool, but yields only to delusion.
With a slight [cause] it attains joy; with a slight [cause] it falls into distress.
There is no object of grief equal to the body, which is base and devoid of virtue, though it is always adorned with teeth like filaments and is subject to constant coming and going.
Adorned at every moment by the blossoming flower of his smile,
with the multitude of his branch-like arms as its supporting pillars,
well-established upon the trunk of his teeth, with the bees of his eyes hovering about it, and bearing the great fruit of his head upon its pedestal; (he was like a tree).

This tree of the body has flowing streams of blood and fluids, beautiful sprouts in the form of hands and feet, possesses ankles, and serves as a resting place for the birds that are the collection of bodily functions; it has true shade and is the dwelling place for the multitude of travelers that are living beings.

Whose is "one's own" and whose is "another"? For what purpose, indeed, are there here [the notions of] reliance and non-reliance? When the boat of the body-plant has been repeatedly taken up for the sake of crossing over the burden, for whom could there be the conceit of "self"?
In this empty forest called the body, crowded with many pits and filled with countless trees that are hairs—
who can find confidence therein?
This firm drum of the body is bound together with skin, sinews, and bones.
Like a cat, I do not remain still amidst the incessant noise;
the monkey of my flickering mind has grown wild in the forest of saṃsāra, appearing like a cluster of wish-fulfilling flowers yet riddled with the woodworms of long-standing suffering.
This glorious tree has craving for its female serpent-dwelling, anger for its crow-nest, smiles for its flowers, and the great fruits of good and evil;
it has well-formed trunks, a network of vine-like arms, and is beautiful with clusters of hands for its blossoms.
With the sprouts of all his limbs and members trembling in the wind,
he was a support for the birds of all the senses; with well-formed knees, excellent skin, and a lofty stature,
he was endowed with a lustrous grace and frequented by the travelers of desire.
Upon its head is grown a long line of hair like blades of grass;
its hollow interior is a nest for the vultures of egoism;
and because its root—the web of latent impressions—is torn asunder, it has become frail in form.
This tree of the body, which ceases its exertion, brings me no pleasure.
O Sage, this physical frame is the great house for the householder that is the ego; whether it rolls about or attains stability, what does it matter to me?

This house of the body is not desired by me: it has the sense-faculties as its tethered cattle bound in rows, the courtyard of its inner rooms is the leaping thirst, and all its limbs are stained with dust;
its hollow interior is a cramped space where logs of bones clash together.
Bound by strings of entrails, this house of my body is not desired;
with its spreading sinews for cords and the blood for its mire,
white with the *makkola* fruit of old age, this house of my body is not desired.

This house of the body is not desired by me; its structure is occupied by endless activities performed like painted figures, and it has false delusion as its great pillar. It is filled with the wailing of the infant of suffering, yet it is charming with the bed of pleasure.
This house of my body— supported by pillars whose tops are the knees, resting on the threshold of the ankles, and made very firm by the timber of long arms— is not desired by me;
it has the windows of its open eyes and the courtyard where the wisdom-dweller plays within.

O Brahmin, this body-house of mine, which has anxiety as its daughter, is not desired by me. This body-house of mine— with the beauty of the ears covered by the thatch of hair, and with the long fingers as its protruding windows— is not desired by me.
This house of the body is not desired by me, for it has sprouts of thick hair growing on all its walls, its seats and vessels are utterly empty,
and its interior is filled with the rustling sound of nails, hair, and the navel.
This body-house of mine,

with its winds making whistling sounds, is not desired by me; this body-house of mine, with its constant force of wind agitated by the incessant entry and exit [of breath], and with its wide windows of the sense-organs, is not desired by me.
This house of the body is not desired by me; its gateway to the mouth is terrifying, overrun by the monkey of the tongue, and fragments of teeth and bone are visible within.
It is smoothed by the plaster of your skin, yet it is as fickle as the movement of a mechanical engine.

This house of my body, dug up by the rat of the restless mind, is not desired by me. This house of my body, which shines for a moment with the light of the lamp of a smile, beautiful with bliss, yet for a moment pervaded by floods of pain— this is not desired by me.
This body of mine is not desired by me; it is the abode of all diseases, a city of wrinkles and grey hair, a forest of the deer of all mental afflictions,
as unstable as the tossing of stars and constellations, empty, and hollow within.
This forest of the body, with its thicket of the heart shrouded in darkness, is not desired by me,
O lords of sages; I am unable to maintain this abode of the body,
just as one of little strength cannot rescue an elephant sunk in the mud.
Of what use is prosperity, and of what use is the body, of what use is desire, and of what use is worldly effort?
In just a few days, Time cuts away everything.
O Sage, this [body] consists of blood and flesh, both internally and externally.
Tell me, what beauty can there be in this body,
which is subject to destruction? O dear one, what reliance can a wise man place upon these ungrateful bodies that do not follow the soul at the time of death?
As long as this body— trembling like the tip of an elephant’s ear in rut, fragile as a dangling drop of water—
does not abandon me, so long shall I abandon it.
This sprout of a body is delicate and flickering with the movement of the wind.
Worn out, thin, and shriveled, this body— bitter and sapless— is not desired;
having eaten and drunk for a long time, as fragile as a young sprout,
it reaches a state of emaciation and pursues its own destruction without effort.
Indeed, this ordinary body feels no shame while repeatedly experiencing those very same pleasures and pains, consisting of both existence and non-existence;
for even after exercising sovereignty for a very long time and enjoying the glory of great wealth, it remains the same.
The body attains neither height nor stability; why, then, is it preserved?
At the time of old age it undergoes decay, and likewise at the time of death it meets its end;
for one who lacks discernment, the body is exactly the same whether it belongs to a wealthy man or a pauper.
Within the belly of the ocean of saṃsāra, in the midst of the hollows of craving,
this mute tortoise of a body remains asleep, though it is destined for liberation.
Abundant logs of bodies are fit only to serve as fuel for the fire.
In this ocean of saṃsāra, people are carried away; among them, the wise know only a rare few.
For one who possesses discernment, there is no purpose whatsoever in this physical body, which is unstable due to long-standing wickedness and whose fruit is only downfall.
Having suddenly reached old age within the mire-filled pits of the bathhouse,
it is not known where or how this frog-like body will soon depart;
all its undertakings are devoid of essence, for bodies are as fleeting as the wind.

"Moving along the path of the dust, they are not seen here by anyone. O Blessed One, the movement of the wind, of a lamp, and of the mind going away is known, but not that of our body-arrow as it comes back."
Fie, fie again and again upon those who have fixed their hopes on bodies and those who have fixed their hopes on the maintenance of the world—they who are intoxicated by the wine of delusion!
I am not the body, nor is the body mine; likewise, this [body] is not I.

Thus, O Sage, those whose minds are at rest are the supreme among men. But those who perceive faults, who are full of honor and dishonor, and who find delight in abundant gain, destroy a man whose attachment is bound solely to the body.
We have been deceived by the trickery of the wondrous ego, which dwells in attachment to the body like a female demon with graceful limbs;
for all poor wisdom has been bound to this body by its persistent clinging.
Alas, she has been deceived by the villain of false knowledge while left all alone!
By that ruined soul, for whom nothing at all is true, the people are being deluded by his wondrous, burnt body. (MU 1.17.56–57)
In just a few days, this withered sprout of a body falls away without effort, like a drop from a mountain stream;
this body is soon to perish, like a bubble upon the ocean.

O twice-born one, when this body— a city born of the delusion of dreams— is subject to the fluctuations of futile actions and is clearly destined for destruction, no attachment remains in me for even a moment toward this transformation of false knowledge, which is utterly fruitless. (MU 1.17.59–60)
He who has determined stability in lightning, in autumnal clouds, and in cities of the Gandharvas— he places his trust in physical conflict,
which triumphs over a succession of ever-perishing effects and achieves victory through deceitful means.
Having cast off this wretched body, which is full of every defect, like a blade of grass, I remain in happiness.
The eighteenth canto, titled "Loathing the Body."
Rāma:
O you whose form is as flickering as a wave, even having obtained birth in this ocean of worldly existence that surges with the burden of duties, childhood leads only to suffering.
Incapacity, calamities, craving, muteness, dullness of intellect,
greed, fickleness, and wretchedness— all these prevail in childhood. Amidst fits of rage and weeping, amidst fierce and wretched states, and amidst those shattered by misery—
In all stages of life, there is bondage and childhood, like the tethering of female elephants;
those anxieties which tear at the heart during childhood do not cease in death, nor in old age and disease, nor in adversity, nor even in youth.
The undertaking of animal births is utterly despised by all;
the fickle conduct of the ignorant brings suffering even beyond death.
It is a mere reflection of dense ignorance, as fragile as various mental constructs.

To whom would childhood bring happiness, when the mind is torn asunder and shattered? What calamity could there be in youth that would produce such fear as that which arises at every step through an intellect darkened by dullness? (MU 1.18.6–7)
In playful diversions, in wicked amusements, in evil pursuits, and in base intentions,
the fool incurs supreme delusion and powerful calamity; for such play is turbid with conceptual constructions, full of wickedness, and a miserable refuge.
Childhood exists for the sake of instruction alone, not for peace. Whatever faults, whatever misconducts, whatever evil ways, and whatever wicked anxieties there may be—
all these reside in childhood like owls in a ruined dwelling.
"Childhood is delightful"—those of vain intellect who speak thus, O Brahmin, are fools; fie upon those men of ruined consciousness!
For therein the mind, restless in form, flickers among its mental fluctuations.
How, indeed, could even sovereignty over the three worlds bring satisfaction? For the minds of all beings, O Sage, become ten times more restless in childhood than in any other state.
The mind is restless by its very nature, and youth is the height of restlessness;
O dear one, when these two are joined together, who can bring an end to such wicked fickleness?
It is like the eyes of women, which are like masses of lightning, garlands of flames, and shifting waves.
"O Brahmin, this fickleness was learned either from childhood or from the mind itself.
For both childhood and the mind, in all their activities,
are observed to be like two brothers whose state is constantly shifting."
All wicked spirits, all faults,
and all evil intentions subsist upon childhood alone, just as men depend upon one who possesses wealth.
If a child does not experience something new and delightful every single day, [he does not grow].
He attains that state and undergoes the stupor of the poison's onset. With the slightest [provocation] he comes under control, and with the slightest [cause] he falls into a state of agitation;
like a young dog, the fool delights only in impurity.
With a face constantly streaming with tears, his mind sluggish within the mire,
the infant resembles a patch of ground scorched by the sun and then drenched by rain;
he is wretched, intent on fear and food, and desires whatever he perceives.
A child of fickle intellect assumes a body that leads only to suffering.
Failing to obtain the things desired by his own imagination, the weak-minded child, his intellect tormented, falls into misery as if his very heart were being cut away. (MU 1.18.21–22)
O Sage, those sufferings of a child— which have their aims frustrated by wicked efforts and are intensified by many adversaries— do not belong to anyone else.
A child is indeed like one who is powerless against a powerful man sporting with his desires.
He is constantly tormented in his mind, like a forest glade by the summer heat. Having entered the house of learning, the youth undergoes supreme suffering,
as terrifying as the agitation of poison, like a lordly elephant confined to its tethering post.
Consisting of various desires, this false imagination born of ignorance— a fragile disposition— is for the sake of extreme and long-lasting suffering.
[It is like] wishing to eat frost that has been scorched, or attempting to seize the moon from the sky.

How can that which is desired by such ignorance lead to happiness? O one of great intelligence, what difference is there between an insentient tree and a child, both of whom are incapable of warding off cold and heat?
Driven by hunger, they desire to fly up with their two wings;
children, possessing the nature of birds, are constantly intent on fear and food.
In childhood, there is fear of the teacher, as well as of the mother and the father.
Childhood, for both the wise and the foolish, is a temple of fear;
its disposition is struck down by the state of all defects, and it is a refuge even for those who revel in a lack of discernment.
O great sage, in this world, childhood never brings sufficient satisfaction to anyone.
The nineteenth canto, titled "Disgust with Childhood," ends here. Rāma: [to be continued].

Then, having abandoned the miseries of childhood, a man whose mind is struck down mounts the dizzying precipice of youth for his own downfall. Therein lies his own fickle mind, full of endless diversions.

Following after the fluctuations of the mind, the dull-witted man goes from sorrow to even greater sorrow. Helpless, he is overcome by the demon of desire dwelling within the cave of his own mind, which forcibly creates manifold agitations.

Just as one who is powerless hands over his own son to the flames, so do those various evils arising from wicked undertakings forcibly direct the mind toward such a disposition on all sides, like women of fickle conduct.

O Sage, those who are not destroyed by youth— which plunders the young and is the seed of great hells that grants continuous delusion— are indeed not seen at all. Those people who have not perished through youth have not perished through anything else.
He who has crossed the terrifying realm of youth— which consists of manifold flavors, is variegated, filled with a multitude of events, and is full of restlessness— is called wise. Youth,
which possesses a form flashing with the movement of the eyes and the rolling thunder of dense clouds, [is thus overcome].
Youth, which shines like lightning yet is never constant, does not please me. Abounding with various whirlpools, mired in mud, possessing a dull depth,
fragile as breaking waves, and terrifying— youth does not please me.
Youth, which precedes all men, charming for but a moment, resembling a city of the Gandharvas— this does not please me;
for it lasts but the flight of an arrow, providing pleasure while flashing with suffering.
"Youth, which constantly brings about the affliction of burning passion, does not please me.
Sweet, pungent, and bitter, it is a corruption disguised as an ornament; youth, which resembles the surging waves of wine, does not please me."
Unreal yet appearing as real, soon bringing about deception,
and like union with a woman in a dream— such youth does not please me;
it is flickering like a momentary flash of light, a wheel falsely constructed.
Youth, which resembles a whirling firebrand, does not please me. Youth,
which is soft yet expansive and vast, yet hollow within and perishing in an instant,
resembling an autumn cloud, does not please me.

"Youth, which is delightful only at its onset but devoid of true essence within— resembling union with a courtesan— is not pleasing to me. Whatever wicked undertakings there may be, they all bring about every kind of suffering."

In youth, calamities draw near like great portents at the end of an eon. Even the Blessed One fears the night of ignorance that is youth, which creates darkness in the heart and possesses a terrifying form.
This delusion of youth causes extreme confusion, which utterly forgets virtuous conduct and brings about a failure of the intellect;
it burns with an irresistible fire born of separation from one's beloved within the heart.
In youth, a living being is consumed like a tree by a forest fire.
For even though it may be expansive, clear, and purifying, the intellect in youth becomes turbid, like a river in the rainy season.
A river, terrifying with its thick, surging waves, can be dammed;
but not so the longing that flickers with youth and agitates the inner heart.
That beloved, those two full breasts, those graceful charms, and that face—
Through anxieties regarding youth, a person reaches a state of decay.
Here in this world, the virtuous honor a young man who is afflicted by ever-rising and flickering thirst,
but they do not honor one whose desire is trivial, like a withered blade of grass.

Indeed, youth is the eternal tethering post for the great elephant of self-conceit— that which is blinded by intoxication and wears the pearls of its own faults— for the very purpose of its destruction.
[It is the tether] for those whose roots are vast as the mind and who harbor the venomous serpents of the defilements.

Know that youth is a new forest for the trees of anger and weeping; it is a lotus for the bees of evil thoughts—a lotus thick with the filaments of passion and crowded with the petals of false conceptualizations. MU 1.19.26–27.
Fresh youth is the abode of the birds of mental and physical afflictions, which frequent the shores of the lake of the heart and possess both formed and unformed wings;
it is the playground for the playful, insensate waves that have passed beyond all counting.
The ocean, disregarding all bounds, has reached full youth;
therefore, the fierce wind of youth stands ready, skillful in stripping away the dust from all the leaves of virtue.
The fierce dust-storms of youth turn the face pale and cause the hands to tremble;
these harsh particles of youth ascend to the highest peak and awaken the multitude of faults while cutting down the garland of virtues.
The exuberance of youth in men is the playfulness of the fortune of evil deeds.
This moon of youth, having bound the flickering bee of the mind to the pollen of the body-lotus, deludes man.
The lovely creeper of youth, sprouting from the thicket of the body,
intoxicates the bee of the mind as soon as it has attached itself and reached its full growth.
[This] is like the mirage of youth arising from the heat of the body's breath.
The deer of the mind, as they run wild, fall into treacherous pits.
The moonlight of the night of the body is but the mane of the lion of the mind;
the wave of the ocean of life—youth—does not please me.
This autumn of youth has borne fruit in the wilderness of the body for only a few days; indeed, you ought not to place your trust in it.
For this bird of youth departs from the body in an instant.
In an instant, it is like the *cintāmaṇi* slipping from the hand of one with little fortune. Whenever youth ascends to its highest peak, passionate desires leap up, leading only to destruction.
Right then do the demons of passion and hatred prowl about;
they do not set until the night of youth has entirely passed away— this wretched [life],
filled with manifold duties and perishing in an instant.
Exercise compassion toward youth, as if toward a son who is dying.
That man who, out of delusion, feels joy because of youth— which is subject to momentary destruction— is indeed called a "human deer," utterly bewildered.
That fool who desires youth, which is intoxicated by pride, delusion, and passion,
will before long be joined with remorse.
They alone are righteous, they alone are great-souled, and they alone are true men on this earth.
O virtuous one, those who have easily crossed over the peril of youth—
indeed, the ocean, that abode of formidable sea-monsters, can be crossed with ease; but youth, when it has passed, is fraught with faults and does not possess the splendor of surging waves.

Adorned with discipline, the abode of noble beings, radiant with compassion, and encircled by virtues— indeed, O dear one, such a youth is rare in this world, like a forest situated in the sky. The chapter titled "The Censure of Youth."
The twentieth canto: Of Rāma;
and [of the flesh-puppet] within the cage of limbs agitated by machinery.
What indeed is beautiful about a woman who is adorned with sinews, bones, and joints?
Having separated the skin, flesh, blood, tears, and watery moisture from the eye, look closely; if it is still charming, why do you delude yourself in vain?
"Here are the hairs, here is the blood"—this is the body of a woman.
What can a person of vast intention do with this censured thing?
Those [limbs] which were repeatedly cherished with garments and ointments...
Flesh-eaters tear away those very limbs of all embodied beings;
yet it was upon her breast that pearls were seen, radiant with the splendor of a necklace and resembling the forceful current of the Gaṅgā gushing from the slopes of Mount Meru’s peaks.
In cremation grounds at the ends of the quarters, that very same breast of a woman is licked by dogs in time, like a small lump of food.

In the same way, what attachment can there be even for the limbs of a beloved woman? O Sage, I consider that even the quality of being momentarily delightful, which is attributed solely to a woman, does not exist here, as it has delusion as its sole cause.
O Sage, what distinction is there here between intoxicating liquor, which bestows vast exhilaration by first agitating one's passion, and a woman, who is a source of transformation? O Sage,
the elephants of men are bound to the hitching post of women.
They do not attain awakening even by means of the long hooks of tranquility.
Bearing hair like collyrium, sharp by their very nature,
and possessing the flames of the fire of evil deeds, women burn a man like straw.
They are to be revered, they are great-souled ones, and they alone are true men on this earth,
who have happily crossed over the perilous strait of youth, O virtuous one. Even that which is flaming, even if it is far away, and even if it is full of flavor, becomes sapless [for them].
For women are both the wood that feeds and the fire of the hells, beautiful yet terrible.
With tresses like scattered darkness, eyes like shimmering stars,
a face like the orb of the full moon, she smiles like a cluster of white water-lilies.
Fickle in her playful charms yet harsh, she brings about the destruction of one's undertakings;
she is a woman who utterly deludes the intellect, a long night for the seeker.
She is as delightful as a flower and as sweet as honey, her hand-like sprouts ever graceful.
Rich in the playful grace of bee-like eyebrows, bearing clusters of blossoms for breasts,
her body fair as the filaments of flowers, and intent on slaying men,
this lovely and most dangerous *hālā* creeper bestows supreme subjugation.
By the mere sound of "sīt" and a sigh,

a lover eager to crush his serpent-like rival draws out the man from his heart, just as a female elephant drags a snake from its hole; thus, by the hunter named Desire, it is bestowed upon those of simple minds.

Women are the snares that bind the limbs of men, who are like birds. O Brahmin, the intoxicated elephant of the mind, tied to the vast tethering post of a woman by the chain of passion, remains as if mute.
For men who are like fish in the pond of birth, moving within the hollow of their karma,
a woman is the baited hook on a line made of the cords of evil tendencies;
she is like a stable for horses or a tethering post for elephants.
To men who are attached to them like bees to a lotus, beautiful-eyed women are a bond.
O Sage, this variegated field of enjoyment, consisting of manifold pleasures,
attains its supreme stability here by depending upon women.
"Enough for me of this woman, who is a casket for all the jewels of faults and a constant chain of suffering!
What is the use of her breasts, what of her eyes, what of her hips, and what of her brows?"
"With this unsubstantial thing, whose sole essence is mere flesh,
I [act]. "O Brahmin, in just a few days, a woman goes to ruin— from here the flesh, from there the blood, and from here the bones."
O Sage, those women who were cherished by their husbands with soft cotton-like caresses now sleep upon the ground of their fathers, their limbs separated from one another. Upon that [ground],
where there is thick, fresh moisture, the beauty of leaf-sprouts appears on their faces.
O Brahmin, that which is fashioned by a beloved perishes in the wilderness;
the hair becomes like the bristles of a *cāmara* on the trees of the cremation ground,
and the bones shine like stars upon the circle of the earth within a few days.
"Dust drinks the blood, and many carnivorous creatures devour it;
the flames of fire consume the skin, and the vital breaths depart into the sky.
Thus, this is what will soon happen to the limbs of women.
I have explained the nature of your stability; why do you pursue delusion?

How could one endowed with intelligence fail to understand that this thing called the "lalanā," which is the structural arrangement of the conjunction of the five elements, carries [the vital essence] through its own inherent nature?
Thick with the spreading canopy of its branches and bearing bitter and sour fruits,
the anxiety that pursues one's beloved reaches a towering height;
at times, the mind— blinded by greed for wealth— is agitated by the reality of what has occurred.
He incurs supreme delusion, like a deer strayed from its herd;
he reaches a state of extreme pitiability,
like a young elephant who, out of longing for a female, is bound in a pit in the Vindhya mountains.
He who has a wife has a desire for enjoyment; for one without a wife, there is no ground for enjoyment. By abandoning a woman, the world is abandoned; by abandoning the world, one becomes happy.
I have no interest in enjoyments that are pleasant only at first sight, full of hidden dangers, and as fragile as the wings of a bee.
O Brahmin, out of fear of death, disease, old age, and the like, I take delight [in renunciation]; I find peace and, with great effort, I go to the supreme forest.
The twenty-first canto, titled "Loathing of Women."
Rāma:
Indeed, childhood is insufficient, for childhood drinks up youth;
and later, old age consumes youth—behold their mutual harshness.
Just as a thunderbolt destroys a lotus, as a whirlwind disperses an autumn cloud,
and as a river erodes a tree on its bank, so does old age wither the body;
it makes every limb slack and long, a frame decayed by aging.
Lustful women look upon a man and a camel as the same.
When people are seized by old age, which torments them with labored breathing and exhaustion,
wisdom flees away like a wife who has fled from a rival woman.
Servants, sons, wives, kinsmen, and friends likewise laugh at a man trembling with old age, as if he were a madman—
him who is of poor intellect, decrepit, wretched, and destitute of both virtue and prowess.
For greed, like a vulture toward a tree, approaches old age without delay.
In old age, the longing for things grows—a long-lasting companion to all calamities, consisting of the fault of wretchedness, and causing burning pain within the heart. (MU 1.21.6–7)
"What painful and most terrible deed must I perform for the sake of the next world? Indeed, in old age, this fear increases—a fear that is incurable.
Who am I, a wretch; what indeed can I do, or how?"

"I shall remain in silence alone"—such dejection arises in old age. Greed arises with delight for the sake of enjoyment, yet it cannot be fulfilled; indeed, the heart is scorched by the frailty of one's powers in old age.
As long as this female crane, worn out by old age, perched upon the top of the tree of the body, cries out while afflicted by disease and emitting the harsh sounds of coughing,
so long will someone suddenly appear from somewhere and be seen approaching.
O Sage, the owl of death, longing for the thick darkness of night,
pursues the twilight as soon as it has arisen;
likewise, old age, as soon as it is seen upon the body, pursues death.

O Brahmin, as soon as she sees from afar the tree of the body in full bloom with old age, the female bee of death approaches the man with great eagerness. A city appears empty, and a tree shines with its branches severed.

A region suffering from drought is conspicuous, but a body worn out by old age is not. Like a vulture seizing its prey, old age swiftly devours a man, producing the wheezing cough of death in an instant.
Upon seeing it, as if eager, old age instantly seizes the body and shatters it in a moment, just as a young maiden plucks a white water-lily;
it makes one gasp with distress, becoming harsh with dust and utterly decayed.
This [old age] withers the body, just as a whirlwind withers the sprout of a tree.
Stricken by old age, the body, having reached a state of decay,
bears the beauty of a withered lotus strewn over with a mass of frost.
Like the rising moonlight of old age upon the mountain-peak of his head,
this [old age] causes the lily-cluster of coughing to blossom, stirred by the violent wind. Having observed it fully ripened, grey with the ash of the caustic of decay—
Time, it is said, is the Lord who devours the head of man like a pumpkin gourd.
Old age, exerting herself like the daughter of Jahnu (the Ganges), swiftly cuts away the roots of this unstable tree of the body, which is its very life-span.
Old age is like a female cat; nourished by the mice of youth that it has devoured, it reaches its highest delight, greedy for the flesh of the body.
Is there anything else in this world so inauspicious?
Just as a female jackal born in the forest of the body causes decay and shrieks,

so too does this flame of old age blaze forth— filled with the smoke and darkness of suffering, accompanied by coughing, labored breathing, and whistling sounds— by which that person is indeed utterly consumed.

O dear one, through old age the slender body of men— whose sprouts are its white limbs— becomes crooked, like a flowering creeper bent down by its blossoms. Old age makes the camphor-tree of the body white with the camphor of its own decay.
O Sage, the elephant of death surely uproots one in an instant.
O Sage, as King Death approaches, old age— with its white fly-whisks— goes out before him, followed by his army of mental anguish and disease.
Those who were not conquered by enemies in battle— those who crushed the peaks of mountains—
behold them quickly conquered, O Sage, by an old ogress worn out by age.
Within the interior of the body-palace, white as the frost of old age...
The young dice are unable to move even slightly.
Upon this head of the sandalwood chamber of the wandering through saṃsāra,
the beauty of the yak-tail whisk named "old age" shines upon the staff of the body.
O Sage, while the city of the body remains white with the moonrise of old age, the night-lily of death suddenly comes into bloom within the inner apartments of the body,
which have been whitened by the plaster of the nectar of aging.
"Incapacity, affliction, and calamity remain while women live in comfort;
where old age, preceded by their absence, triumphs over living beings—what consolation is there for me, of dull intellect, in this world, O Sage? (MU 1.21.33–34)
What is the use of that miserable life and wretched grasp, for even one who has reached old age continues to live?
Yet, O dear one, old age—which is unconquered by men in this world—overcomes all their desires.
This is the chapter titled "Loathing Old Age."
The Twenty-second Sarga:
Rāma:
By those of small intellect, who imagine through the manifold fabrications of conceptual construction;
The delusive wandering of saṃsāra has been brought to a state of height by its various divisions. How could those who are wise have any reliance here upon this cage of a net?
Only children desire to grasp the fruit reflected in a mirror.
Even here, there exists this fragile cultivation of happiness;
yet Time cuts it away entirely, just as a rat gnaws through a thread.
There is nothing here that this all-devouring Time does not consume.
He devours the world-born, as the submarine fire [Vāḍava] devours the great ocean;
the formidable Time, the Great Lord, being all-pervasive in its universality,
is intent upon swallowing this entire existence of the visible.
Even for the great, O Lord, Time— having become the soul of the universe and having swallowed the infinite world— awaits not even a moment;
it becomes slightly manifest through what are called ages, years, and kalpas.

With a form that cannot be perceived through forms, he stands pervading everything. Those things which are delightful, those which are auspicious undertakings, and even those as massive as Mount Sumeru—
all have been swallowed up by Time, like serpents by a young camel.
Merciless, hard, cruel, harsh, wretched, and base—
there is nothing that even now this Time does not swallow up.
Time, whose mind is solely intent on devouring, devours even the mountains.
Even with infinite floods of enjoyments, this great consumer is never satiated.
Like an actor in the various roles of the dance of saṃsāra, Time takes away, destroys, creates, devours, and slays. (MU 1.22.10–11)

Established in its state of differentiation, it incessantly shatters the seeds of the elements within the world with its beak of non-existence, just as a parrot pecks at pomegranate seeds; it shears away the sprouts of living beings with the tips of its horns of good and evil.
The elephant that sustains the rows of living beings among the swelling multitudes thunders;
encompassing the vast Brahma-forest, which is like a great bilva tree containing the cosmic egg as its core,
it stands pervading the expansive realm of Brahmā.
Creating clusters of days filled with nights like female bees,
and blossoms of years like creepers of kalpas, he is never weary;
though pierced, he is not broken, and though burnt, he is not consumed.

O Sage, though he is not easily seen, this crest-jewel of rogues is nevertheless perceived. In a single moment, he is capable of raising up something and utterly destroying something else, spreading out like a vast kingdom of the mind.
With his conduct, which was like that of a wanton woman of depraved dalliance and nurtured by hardship,
he remained turning the people around like a cook stirring a soup with a ladle;
[he treated] a blade of grass, a particle of dust, Mahendra, Mount Sumeru, a leaf, and the ocean as one.
Striving to assimilate everything to itself through the expansion of its own self, cruelty is fully contained right here; greed is established right here;
all misfortune is right here, and all fickleness is right here.
Playfully impelling the sun and moon, he sports here in the vault of the sky like a child with two balls placed in his hands;
his form is encircled from head to foot by garlands of the bones of all living beings.
This Time, which fashions its own imaginings, sports at the end of the aeon;
at the end of the aeon, Mount Meru trembles in the sky like a birch-bark leaf tossed by the winds that have issued from the limbs of this wild dance.
Becoming Rudra, he becomes Mahendra, then the Grandfather (Brahmā), Śukra, and Vaiśravaṇa; yet again, he becomes nothing at all.
He assumes infinitely radiant creations that arise incessantly and pass away.
Like the ocean [casting off] various waves within itself— neither different nor non-different—
he stands casting down from the trees called "great aeons" the ripened clusters of fruits that are the hosts of gods and asuras.
He has attained the state of a vast tree for the multitudes of *uḍumbara* worlds that fall away, humming with the swarms of moths that are restless beings;
he is the moonlight of consciousness that causes the lily of pure existence to blossom.
One [the yogin] delights his body while accompanied by action as his beloved;
another remains established, leaning upon his own body which is like a massive mountain— tall, firmly rooted, and reaching to the end of infinite calamities.
In some places meditating on his own nature as dark as the deepest shadow, in other places as pervasive and endowed with splendor,
and in others as empty of both, he remained thus;
with his own essential being, which had absorbed the essence of countless transmigrations.
As if burdened by a heavy load, he becomes one whose steps are bound;
yet he neither suffers nor dies, he neither comes nor goes,
he neither sets nor rises, even in hundreds of great aeons.
Merely through the effortless play of initiating the world, with profound ease, he passes his time by means of the self for the sake of the self, having attained a state free from egoism—
like a row of day-lotuses amidst the thick mud of the night.
Remaining with the delusion of activity superimposed upon the lake of his own self,
the Terrifying One takes up the dark night as a worn-out broom and sweeps the golden dust of light all around the earth.
Moving the sun-lamp with his finger around the corners of the house of the world,
he gazes out of compassion to see what exists and where;
having fully observed the days that have ripened, he does so in the blink of an eye with the sun as his eye.
This [Time] eats the fruits that are the world-protectors from the withered forest of the universe;
it deposits the jewels of the world, which are the qualities of the three strands, one by one into the casket of Death within the fierce hollow of the decayed hut of the cosmos.
Having taken upon his body that very series of world-jewels which is so abundantly filled with virtues,
as if for the sake of ornament, he repeatedly cuts it away—
like a night-blooming lotus garland followed by the swan of day.
The restless one incessantly whirls about the pollen of the stars;
he is a butcher of the world’s wool, [shearing] the mountains, the spider-silk of the sky, and the peaks of the earth.
Day after day, having sprinkled them, he drinks even the red drops of the stars.
He is the moon for the lotus of youth and the lion for the elephant of life;
there is nothing, whether trivial or significant, that he does not plunder.
By his playful sport at the end of the eon, he has ground all living beings into dust.
Through the joy of the emergence of [the world] from its state of subordination, he delights in himself by means of his own self.
(MU 1.22.43) He is the agent, the enjoyer, the destroyer, and the rememberer; having attained the state of all, he performs all this, yet he does nothing at all. (MU 1.22.44)
Revealing and suddenly concealing the entire body— which, though devoid of internal parts, assumes both beautiful and ugly forms— the power of Time indeed sports among men here.
This is the chapter titled "The Refutation of Time."
The Twenty-third Sarga:
Rāma—
of him whose play was so formidable, and from whom all calamities were cast far away.
In this saṃsāra, which is like a forest thicket worn out by the hunt of King Time— whose power is immeasurable— he pursues his chase with wretched and deluded herds of living beings as his prey.
The great ocean at the end of the eon (*kalpa*) is a delightful pleasure-pool, wherein the beautiful submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*) shines as a lotus in one part;
it is filled with oceans of curd, milk, and salt water, enriched by pungent, bitter, and sour elements.
By means of those very worlds that have become stale, the turning of time occurs.
Caṇḍī, whose movement is fourfold and who is accompanied by the entire host of Mothers,
is a she-wolf that drags away the human deer placed within the forest of saṃsāra.
The earth is in the palm of his hand, the earth is his wine-cup filled with nectar,
garlanded with swaying clusters of lotuses, water-lilies, and white lilies;
the roaring Nṛsiṃha, with his formidable outstretched arms, is the cage.
With shoulders broad, formidable, and muscular, he is a lovely play-bird;
sweet-toned like a gourd-lute, with a complexion as pure as the autumnal sky,
the Lord Mahākāla is indeed a playful young cuckoo.
With a form of incessant throbbing, having vomited forth the thunderbolts of suffering,
and possessing a bow named Non-Contemplation (*abhāvanā*), it flashes forth everywhere—
increased by the play of supreme throbbing, wandering, seizing, shimmering, and tearing asunder.
Here, Time, whose body quivers like an old, decrepit, and restless monkey, exerts himself.
The twenty-fourth chapter, named "The Play of Time."
Rāma:
It is here alone that another, like a crest-jewel of all misfortunes,
is called by the world "Fate" and "Time," as if it truly exists.
Apart from mere activity, no other form of action is perceived for that which consists of its own internal vibration, nor is any intended result [perceived]. Therefore,
this entire succession of beings is eternally fragile.
Like a garland of snow brought to a state of extreme distress by heat,
so too is this entire expansive sphere of the world;
it is his theater for dancing, and here he performs his dance.
And thirdly, bearing the most terrible name Kṛtānta,
Fate dances in this world in the intoxicated form of a Kāpālika. Indeed,
as Kṛtānta dances, he never ceases for a moment.
O Sage, for you who are eternally and supremely enamored of Niyati (Fate),

Śeṣa— white as a digit of the moon— and the current of the Gaṅgā serve as your two sacred threads (*upavīta*), which possess the luster of the *avīta* sacrifice; these two rest upon the chest of *saṃsāra*.
The two golden bracelets upon his wrists are the orbs of the moon and the sun;
in his hand is the playful lotus whose pericarp is the cosmic egg,
studded with stars as its seeds and possessing the flickering Puṣkarāvarta clouds as its petals.
The single sky, washed by the waters of the universal ocean, is the sole covering. Before Him of such a form, Necessity (niyati), eternally longing,
dances with her efforts, her fervor never ceasing.
In the hollow of the pavilion of the world, that woman who delights in dancing— her movement unimpeded and her coming and going ever-flitting—
possesses a series of celestial realms as beautiful ornaments upon her limbs.
Her massive circle of braided hair hangs down to the depths of the underworld;
and her anklet-garland, filled with a tinkling clamor, is strung upon the thread of evil deeds and moves about her feet that roam the nether regions.
In that very night, Citragupta painted upon the tablet of her face a musk tilaka prepared by his friend Kriyā;
meanwhile, at the end of the kalpas, she assumed the form of Kālī, surrounded by the host of Kriyā.
This goddess dances again, making the solid mountains resound;
behind her, the peacocks on the chariot of Kumāra flutter with their tails trailing low,
terrifying with the loud, deep humming from the great cavities of their three eyes.
With the hair on Śiva’s head bestowed by the long, dangling autumn moon;
with the whisks of Gaurī’s beautiful, rising, and pale tresses of mandāra flowers;
and with the bellies of Bhairava, who resembles a mountain in his wild dance, resembling gourd-vessels.
With begging-bowls in the form of Indra’s bodies, possessing thousands of ringing apertures,
and filling the sky with the broken fragments of the skeletal staffs of dried-up corpses,
she strikes terror even into herself, though she is as dark as a black cloud.

She shines amidst the great cosmic cycles (*mahākalpa*), dancing with the beautiful lotus-garland that is the wheel of Viśvarūpa’s head, as she moves restlessly during her *tāṇḍava* dances; she resounds with the terrifying cries of the intoxicated Puṣkarāvarta clouds and the *ḍamaru* drum.
It is said that at the end of the world, Tumburu and the other celestial musicians flee from her—
the dancing Goddess of Death who laughs with the orb of the moon,
and whose peacock-feather crown is the sky, beautiful with the moonlight of the stars.
In one ear there is the long Himalaya as a ring;
in the other, the great Mount Meru is a lovely golden earring.
Right here, the swaying earrings are the moon and sun, and the circular cheeks are the two discs.
The range of the Lokāloka mountains forms a girdle around her waist on all sides;
and the lightning-bands, moving here and there like streaks of color,
shine like silken scarves of clouds tossed by the wind.
With maces, spears, spikes, lances, barbed missiles, and clubs—
sharpened and gathered like the Destroyer himself who has exhausted the multitude of living beings—
he stood within the long noose of worldly bondage cast forth by the hand of Time.
His garland shines, strung upon the great thread of his remaining enjoyments;
blazing with the brilliance of jewels in the form of playful sea-monsters representing living beings,
the row of bracelets formed by the seven oceans is the ornament of his two arms.
The great whirlpool of worldly affairs, a succession of pleasure and pain, filled with passion and dark with ignorance— this row of hair upon him shines forth.
At the end of such an eon, Death, fierce in his wild dance, [seizes] her.

Having withdrawn his dance together with the creation, Maheśvara again extends this playful dance consisting of laughter, which embodies all forms and is adorned with the dramatic gestures of old age, suffering, and grief.

Again he creates worlds, forest interiors, and other realms, as well as the arrangement of the web of living beings and the beautiful performance of conduct, both stable and unstable— just as a child tirelessly constructs a structure out of mud.
This is the chapter titled "The Play of Fate."
The Twenty-fifth Chapter.
Rāma said:
"O great sage, when this [creation] of Kāla and the others has occurred..."
What reliance can there be here for those like me upon this thing called *saṃsāra*?
We stand as if sold by these cheats— fate and the rest—
who are clever in their deceptions, like innocent forest deer.
This ignoble conduct is Time itself, intent upon devouring;
it incessantly casts the world into an ocean of calamity.
At the end, Fate, through its cruel workings, consumes [beings] with its evil desires.
Just as a fire consumes the world with its flame-like clusters of blossoms,
so too does a single beloved woman, though beautiful in form, disturb one's steadfastness;
for by her very nature as a woman, she is fickle, while destiny is inclined toward restraint.
Like a serpent seizing the air, the cruelly acting Kṛtānta (the Ender) incessantly devours the multitude of living beings; having brought the world-body to old age,
that merciless king of Yama does not show compassion even for one who is suffering.

A person whose conduct is characterized by compassion for all beings has become rare. O Sage, all classes of living beings possess but meager resources; they are fields of greed that lead only to suffering and to endless, terrible consequences.
Life is exceedingly fickle, yet death alone is cruel;
youth is extremely unstable, while childhood is stolen away by dullness.
The world is stained by its own artifice, and kinsmen are but the shackles of existence.
Worldly enjoyments are the great diseases of existence, and craving is but a mirage.
The senses themselves have become enemies; truth has turned into untruth. The mind itself, as the enemy of the mind, strikes down the self by means of the self.
Egoism leads only to blemish; intellects have become feeble;
actions yield only bitter fruits; and pastimes have come to depend entirely upon women. Desires, though possessing their objects, have been rendered devoid of wonder.
Women are banners of faults; the aesthetic flavors have become tasteless.
Reality has been grasped as unreality, and the mind is surrendered to the ego.
Entities are obstructed by non-existence, and the end of existence is not attained.
O virtuous one, the mind, its interior agitated, suffers in vain;
the serpent of passion plays about and does not approach dispassion.
The vision struck by the quality of *rajas* increases further through *tamas*.
And no being is apprehended, for reality is exceedingly remote.
Stability has become instability; death is on the verge of arrival;
fortitude falls into despondency; and delight finds its constant object in that which is unreal.
The intellect is clouded by dullness, the body is intent solely on falling [to the ground],
old age seems to blaze within the frame, and evil deeds crackle forth.
Youth departs with effort, while association with the virtuous remains far away.
No course whatsoever exists, and nowhere does reality arise.
The mind seems utterly bewildered within; joy has gone far away.
Radiance does not dawn, and compassion does not arise; from afar, baseness approaches.
A person, intent on rising and falling, moves between states of fortitude and lack of fortitude;

association with the wicked is easily found, but union with the virtuous is difficult to attain. Phenomenal entities arise and pass away, and their mental cultivation is the bond of worldly existence.
The eternal succession of beings is merely led away somewhere;
for even the directions are not seen, nor is there any place that remains unnameable.
Even mountains crumble away—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
Even the oceans overflow and even the stars shatter;
even the perfected ones fail to achieve perfection—what hope, then, for a person such as I? Even the sky is devoured by non-existence, and the world itself is destroyed.
Even the earth falls into distress; what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
(MU 1.25.25) Even the Dānavas are shattered; even Dhruva’s life is transient; even the immortals are slain; what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I? (MU 1.25.26)
Even Śakra is assailed by other Śakras, and even Yama is brought under control;
even Vāyu possesses a state of non-wind—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
Even Soma reaches the state of the sky, and even Mārtaṇḍa suffers fragmentation.
Even fire falls into a state of sickness; what reliance can there be on a person such as I?

Even the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) is subject to non-attainment of his goals, even the Unborn (Aja) seizes Hari, and even Bhava goes to a state of non-existence; what reliance can there be on a person such as I?
Time reaches a state of fragmentation, destiny is also led away, and even space dissolves into the infinite; what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
By one whose form is unknown through a system that is difficult to hear, difficult to speak, and difficult to perceive—
The worlds are imitated by a certain deluder who dwells within everything,
having assumed a portion of egoism; there is no one in the three worlds who is not afflicted by him here.
Upon the ridges of rocky mountains, the sun, together with its horses and charioteer,
is constantly whirled about helplessly like a forest stone;
it is a sphere of earth containing within it the abodes of hosts of gods and asuras.
It is encircled by the wheel of the hearths, like a ripe walnut by its husk.
In heaven the gods, on earth men, and in the underworld the asuras and serpents—
all fashioned merely by a moment of thought— are led to a state of decay.

And Kāma, whose prowess was won through battle with the Lord of the World, having displayed his valor in a most disorderly manner, leaps about after having assailed the world. Spring is like an intoxicated elephant, with its rutting ichor consisting of showers of flowers.
Fragrance that perfumes the entire circle of the quarters leads the mind to crookedness.
Even great discernment is unable to clarify the mind when its form has been gazed upon by the eyes of an impassioned woman.
I consider only the Buddha truly happy, for his mind is cooled by its own self-interest, whereas others are tormented by a feverish concern for the welfare of others.
All conditioned things arise and perish, falling into the submarine fire of time.
By whom can the waves of the ocean of life be numbered?
All men, through delusion, fall into the snares of wicked desires;
they are like deer caught in thickets of vice, swallowed up in the wilderness of birth.
By those evil deeds here in this world, the lifespan of people throughout the succession of births is exhausted;
for we do not know the fruit of those acts, which is like a noose made from the creepers of trees in the sky, even though we are wise in reflection.
"Today there is a festival, this is the season, likewise there is a procession here, these are your kinsmen, this is happiness, and that is special enjoyment."
Thus, with a mind as fickle and fragile as a trembling leaf, the world here perishes while vainly weaving the web of its own conceptual constructions.
The twenty-sixth canto, titled "The Description of Wicked Amusements."
Rāma:
Furthermore, dear father, in this nature of the world— whether exceedingly desolate or delightful—
there is not even the slightest collection of objects by which the mind attains supreme rest.
When childhood has passed and the deer of youth— restless with imagined play— is scattered among the caves of old age,
and when the little body has reached a state of decay, the world suffers only in its utter desolation.
Having abandoned from afar the lotus-pond of the body, which has been struck by the frost of old age, [the world withers].
In an instant, when the bee of life has departed, the lake of worldly existence for humanity is utterly dried up.
Whenever it surely reaches its full maturity,
this creeper of the human body then bows down, shattered by the weight of old age as if by the fire that withers fresh blossoms.

In this world, the river of craving flows on, its exceedingly powerful current sweeping away the entire multitude of infinite objects; it is skilled at rubbing away the roots of the sturdy tree of contentment that stands upon its banks.
The boat of the body, its mooring tied with skin, tossed about and wandering in the ocean of existence—*Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* 1.26.5.

Flowing downward, it is driven by the five so-called senses, which act like sea-monsters. These deer of the mind, wandering through the forest of the creeper of thirst upon the trees of desire, exhaust themselves roaming among the hundreds of branches; they do not attain the fruit of their longing.

In times of hardship, those who have cast far away despair and delusion; in times of sovereignty, those whose minds are not arrogant but remain pleasingly composed—such great men, whose inner hearts are unassailable by beautiful women, are now very difficult to find.
Those who cross the ocean of battle, which has the masses of elephants for its waves, are not heroes in my eyes.
Only those are heroes here who cross this ocean of the senses, which is like a wave upon the mind;
for no one’s action is seen to be delightful with an untroubled ultimate fruit— no action performed by one whose mental state is struck down by evil desires, reaching which the world finds its rest.
Those who fill the world with their fame, the hollows of the quarters with their majesty, their homes with their splendor, and prosperity with the strength of their virtue—
those men, whose bond to Dharma remains unbroken, are not easily found in this world.
Even if [an enemy] were situated within the interior of a mountain crag, or stationed inside a fortress of diamond;
All prosperities and all calamities come together with full force;
O dear one, sons, wives, and wealth are mentally constructed like an elixir,
yet in the end they do not provide any benefit, being as utterly delightful as the intoxication of poison.
Overwhelmed by despair and having reached a precarious state at the end of his physical life and youth, the person,
remembering his own past states which were empty of the Abhidharma, burns within when overcome by old age.
Having spent the days at first with activities that were internally emaciated by their pursuit of sensual pleasures, wealth, and dharma;
By what means can the mind of a man—fickle like the trembling plumage of a peacock—attain rest?

For, by the power of fate, men are mocked by the fruits of their actions, which, though appearing before them, do not yield their true form; they are like the lofty waves of a river, for people have diverse tastes.
These and those tasks, analyzed as being endlessly delightful,
wear out the minds of people through the pursuit of pleasing one's wife until the end of old age,
just as the withered leaves of trees, having come together at birth, quickly go to their destruction.
In the very same way, people devoid of their own discernment come together from somewhere and depart with the days.

Having wandered further and further away from here and there, they enter their homes at the close of day; when the day has passed—devoid of the virtuous deeds of those who rely on the world of the discerning—who can truly find sleep? (MU 1.26.18–19)

When the entire host of enemies has been put to flight and prosperity has arrived from all sides, one enjoys these pleasures— yet at that very moment, death arrives from somewhere unknown. From somewhere, through these transient things whose forms have grown so trivial, which are seen for a moment and then vanish, [death comes].
Bewildered by the world, people on this earth do not perceive what has come nor what has gone—alas!
Those who, desiring to depart, prepare for the mouth of Death with their human-sheep flocks, are bound by their own wretched karma;
for they have indeed attained corpulence through force within the confinement of the body. (MU 1.26.21–22)
This restless multitude on earth comes incessantly with haste and likewise goes away without ceasing with haste; from wherever it arises, it is like a garland of waves, momentary in its destruction.
Intent solely on seizing the life-breath of men, they captivate the mind by means of their charm.
Women are like poisonous trees with red blossoms and eyes as flickering as bees;
they are like restless creepers that have approached from here and there in vain, bound by a common agreement.
Like a gathering at a festival, the deceptive practice of men regarding wives and friends is merely a transient association.
Just as in the lights of lamps whose many wicks have been consumed and which are bound by excessive oil,
the true nature is not known within these illusory transmigrations, which are flickering and devoid of reality.
This wheel of the breast of worldly activity, though as fragile as a bubble in the rain-clouds of the monsoon, [continues its course].
It produces a long-lasting conviction in the mind of a person who is inattentive.

(MU 1.26.27) Splendor once radiant, now ruined by wretchedness; virtues that remain now in a state of decay; consolation has departed far away—just as the winter has left the lotus plants. (MU 1.26.28)
When a tree, having repeatedly approached by the power of fate and caused harm with the weight of its own body,
is cut down with axes— what occasion indeed is there for consolation in that?
Even for something as charming as the mind, when it has arisen within to cause destruction through its excessive and faulty activity...
From association with people who are like poisonous trees, one now encounters only a state of fainting.
What eyes are there in which no defects exist? What directions are there in which there is no burning pain of suffering?
What beings are there in which there is no fragility? What actions are there in which illusion does not indeed reside?
Even the Viriñcas, who live for a single moment within a named kalpa, are themselves counted by the number of kalpas in the flood of time;
therefore, in the web of Time which possesses all its parts (kalās), even the notions of shortness and length are unreal.
Everywhere, mountains are made of stone, the earth is made of clay, and trees are indeed made of wood.
People whose minds are bound to the state of manhood do not perceive here anything unprecedented or free from modification;
rather, what is perceived by consciousness as interwoven with thought is a collection of atoms situated in space, bound together like milk.
This world exists through the distinct differentiation of the characteristics of objects, and nothing else whatsoever exists.

In this world of the wise, a marvel that causes wonder in the hearts of men— though it be of variegated form— is never, even in a dream, within the reach of anyone, O virtuous one. Yet now, even when the greatness of conceptualization has passed away like the fruit of a creeper in the sky, [the state remains].
For those who have not been struck by even a trace of greed, there arises no discourse whatsoever concerning such noble deeds.
Desiring to attain the state of the supreme ones, the world today is ruined by its own mind;
it leaps recklessly from the mountain peak like a beast, out of a longing for the leaves of a dark blue creeper.
With their branches of foliage, flowers, and fruits merely the shadows of shoulders placed across them,
the trees in ravines— deprived of their wealth of fruit— and the men of today are exactly alike.
In one place people wander through regions beautiful with softness, and in another, through places that are terrifying.
Like black antelopes in the dense thickets at the edge of a forest, [they move] through the ten intermediate spaces without interval.

Whose minds are not amazed by the Creator’s new deeds performed day after day—deeds that are both terrifying and beautiful, in which all men are thrown into turmoil, and where the onset of fortune is destroyed by the ripening of bitter fruits? (MU 1.26.39–40)
People are attached to desires and intent on practicing various base arts; even in a dream, a virtuous person like me is not easily found in this world today.
All activities, due to their connection with suffering, are surely distressed and more than distressed; I truly do not know how this state of life must be conducted.
The twenty-seventh canto, titled "The Exposition of Impermanence," [from] Rāma:
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving,
all that is unstable, O Brahmin, resembling a union in a dream.
That which is seen today as a dug-out pit resembling a dried-up ocean—
O Sage, that mountain which is enveloped by clouds in the morning becomes a forest;
that immovable mountain, vast with its array of woods and licking the sky,
in just a few days reaches the level of the earth or turns into a well.

That very limb which today is clothed in silk garments, garlands, and ointments, shall tomorrow be naked and cast far away into a pit. That city which today is seen, vibrant with its diverse activities, [shall likewise vanish].
In that very place, within days, there arises the state of a desolate forest and desert.
O King, that man who today stands as a radiant sovereign over the realms will, in just a few days, become a heap of ashes.

The great and terrifying forest, which resembled the vault of the sky and whose canopy of banners covered the atmosphere— that very same thing has now become a city. That formidable row of woods, entwined with creepers, shines today as a city.
O Sage, in mere days that place becomes a desert land;
water turns into dry ground, and dry ground becomes a watery place. Indeed, the entire world—including its wood, water, and grass—is utterly overturned.
Youth, childhood, the body, and accumulations of wealth are impermanent;
like waves, they pass incessantly from one state to another. In this world, life is as flickering as the flame of a lamp in the wind.
The splendor of objects in the three worlds is like the flickering of lightning;
this succession of many beings undergoes transformation,
constantly sprouting again and again like a heap of seeds.
With the thick cloth of the elements' dust tossed about by the wind of the mind,
adorned with the graceful gestures of falling,
rising, and revolving, this worldly state is perceived as a mere illusion.
Like an actress on the stage of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) revealed through the possession of dance,
she produces the illusion of a city of Gandharvas; she is enchanting with her noble conduct, which is as fleeting as a sidelong glance.
O Brahmin, repeatedly casting forth a light as flickering as lightning, the passion for worldly existence shines like a woman intoxicated by dancing.
Great are those days, great are those riches, and great are those actions.
Everything has become a mere object of memory; we too shall depart in an instant.
Day by day it decays, and day by day it is born again;
even today there is no end to this burnt-out cycle of worldly existence.
Men fall into the state of animals, and animals even attain the state of men; gods likewise become non-gods. O Lord, what indeed is stable here?
Weaving day and night again and again with its web of rays, [the sun moves on].
Having passed through the time, the Sun beholds the limit of destruction.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and all classes of beings alike rush toward their own destruction, just as bodies of water rush toward the submarine fire.
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the quarters—
this entire world is the fuel that will be consumed by the submarine fire of destruction.
Wealth, kinsmen, servants, friends, and all possessions— these too shall perish.

For one terrified by the fear of destruction, everything has become devoid of flavor. These objects in the world remain pleasant to the wise man only so long as the wicked demon of destruction does not enter the path of his memory.
In one moment sovereignty arrives, and in a moment poverty comes;
in one moment freedom from disease, and in a moment the onset of illness. By this great force that brings about reversal at every moment—
Who indeed, even among the wise, has not been deluded by the world’s illusion? For a moment the circle of the sky is smeared with the mire of darkness;
for a moment it is beautiful with a soft radiance like a flowing stream of gold.
At one moment its hollows were encircled by garlands of dark-blue lotuses like clouds;
at another moment it resounded with a tumultuous roar, and at another it remained silent.
At one moment it was radiant with stars, and at another it was adorned by the sun.
At one moment bringing delight like the moon, at another moment cast out from everything;
by this state characterized by coming and going, and by its instability and destruction—
who here in this saṃsāra would not be afraid, even if he were wise?
Calamities arrive for a moment, and prosperity arrives for a moment;
birth and then death come for a moment—O Sage, what indeed is not momentary?
Previously one was born here as someone else, and in days he becomes yet another.
"O Blessed One, is there even a single thing that exists in a fixed state?
For the nature of a jar has been seen as a cloth, and the state of a cloth as a jar.
There is nothing that, once perceived, does not undergo reversal; such is the nature of cyclic existence."
A hero slain by one who is not a hero—even a single man has slain a hundred;
commoners have attained lordship, and the entire world revolves.
This generation constantly follows such a reversal.
Just as a series of waves arises from the perception of the movement of inert matter,
so too does childhood today, then the beauty of youth, and thereafter old age appear within the body; if even the body lacks a single fixed form, what stability can there be in external objects?
In one moment the mind attains joy, in another moment it reaches despondency;
in a moment it becomes gentle—like an actor, the mind acts in every way. By this means and by that, and by this other means as well, such is the nature of this mental process.
Creating the world, he does not experience weariness, like a child at play;
the Creator gathers this born universe here, intoxicates it, devours it, slays it, strikes it down, and makes it his own through hundreds of calamities and upheavals.
In one moment one thing, on another day another, and in the morning yet another— arranging things thus here and there, the Creator, though skilled in deception, is not seen by anyone.
That which exists today does not exist tomorrow morning, and that which exists tomorrow morning did not exist today.
But that which was otherwise at another time does not recur at all today. Here, sufferings are continuous while pleasures are rare; they revolve incessantly for every person, like nights and days.
For people subject to worldly existence, who are partakers of appearance and disappearance,
neither calamities nor prosperities attain stability.
This sinner, causing everyone to fall from one misfortune to another, [is himself cast down].
The entire world is tossed about in sport by the wicked fragment of Time as it stands;
the floods of fruits consisting of the successions of beings in the three worlds, divided by the ripening of their favorable and unfavorable conditions,
fall day after day from the vast trees of saṃsāra, cast down by the wind of destiny.
The twenty-eighth canto, titled "The Demonstration of the Reversal of Delusion," [spoken by] Rāma.
Thus, when the great mind has been consumed by the forest fire of wisdom,
desires for enjoyments do not flicker forth, like mirages in lakes.
And day by day, the wandering through the cycle of existence becomes exceedingly bitter.
Just as the neem vine, its fibers swelling under the influence of the ripening of time, so too,
O King, does wickedness increase and goodness diminish day by day within the hearts of people, which have become as hard as the *karañja* thorn.
The boundaries on earth are instantly shattered in every direction with a sharp,
harsh *ṭāṅkāra* sound, like parched bean stalks snapping.
Anxious for their kingdoms and heaps of enjoyments, the lords of the earth—
Better is the practice of solitude, with all thorns of anxious thought cast away. (MU 1.28.5) Neither my garden brings me joy, nor my riches bring me happiness;
neither does the hope for wealth bring me delight; I am at peace along with my mind. (MU 1.28.6)
The world is impermanent and unhappy, and craving, my dear, is difficult to bear;
my mind is struck by restlessness—how shall I attain peace?
I do not rejoice in death, nor do I rejoice in life.
Just as I remain, so I remain free from the fever [of passion].
What use have I for kingship, what use for enjoyments, what use for wealth, or what use for my endeavors?
By the power of egoism, all that has dissolved away from me.
On the rope of the succession of births, the knots of the senses are firm;
those who strive for their release from that which has ensnared them are the best.
The hearts of proud women have been crushed by the god whose banner is the sea-monster.
Just as a lotus is crushed by the gentle trampling of an elephant's hooves,
O Lord of Sages, if today you do not treat me with a healthy mind,
then what occasion indeed remains for further treatment of the mind, and from where could it come?
Poison is the inequality of sense objects; poison is not called [mere] poison.
Sense objects destroy future lives, whereas [ordinary] poison destroys only a single body.
There are neither pleasures nor pains, neither friends nor kinsmen.

For the mind of the knower, there is neither life nor death that leads to bondage. O Brahmin, best among those who know the past and the future, instruct me quickly so that I may become such a knower, free from sorrow, fear, and exertion.

O Sage, I am able to endure the harsh gnawing of the saw in this forest of ignorance, which is entangled in a web of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), crowded with the thorns of suffering, thick with falls and upheavals, and terrifying in form.
This [knowledge] destroys the calamity of the poison of destruction arising from the worldly conventions of saṃsāra—
the delusion of common folk that "this exists" or "this does not exist"—
just as the wind shakes away a mass of dust from a flickering mind.
