The pearl-string of the multitude of living beings, strung upon the threads of craving,
with the mind as its ever-evident leader due to its nature as a part of pure consciousness—
this necklace of saṃsāra is loathed by the dispassionate, yet it serves as an ornament for the serpent of Time.
I shall tear asunder this cruel snare, like a lion [tearing] a trap;
O best among those who know reality, quickly shatter the mist of mental darkness within the forest of my heart with some lamp of knowledge.

O Great-souled One, those afflictions do not exist here for you, nor do they reach destruction, just as the sharp blades of the mṛṇāla plant are [dissolved] by the moon through its contact with the minds of the most excellent beings. Life is as fragile as water hanging from a cluster of lotus petals tossed by the wind; enjoyments are as flickering as lightning flashing amidst a canopy of clouds.
Considering that the torrent of the waters of youthful indulgence is likewise fickle, I have indeed swiftly placed a seal as firm as a mountain upon my mind for the sake of long-lasting peace.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Demonstration of Non-Attachment Toward All Objects."
The twenty-ninth canto:
Rāma:
Thus, [the world] has become a hollow pit of peril, filled with a multitude of rising calamities.
Beholding the world submerged in the mire of mental construction,
my mind seems to wander and agitation arises within me;
my limbs tremble like the leaves of an aged tree.
The mind, its lap agitated by conduct that lacks supreme contentment,
fears here as it has found no abode in the Void, like a child whose protector is weak;
and these fluctuations of the internal organ wallow amidst conceptual constructions.
Like female deer lured into pits by a deceptive and hollow object,

those wretched ones— the eye and the other senses— have fallen from the ground of discernment; having strayed into a miserable state, they have not established themselves in the true path, like those who have stumbled into a blind well.

Thought does not remain stable, nor does it proceed according to its desire; dependent on the Lord of Life, it is like a mistress in an unpleasant household. Wearing things down and then casting them away, it likewise continues to sustain them.
Like a creeper at the end of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, her fortitude has become frail.
Having cast aside all objects of purpose, instability has taken hold;
having grasped and then abandoned the self, non-abiding has become established.
My mind is mocked by an internal support that is both moving and unmoving,
like the root of a tree that has been cut down by a poor man;
and my consciousness is flickering, expansive, and wandering through the interior of the worlds.
He does not abandon this agitation, like an immortal [gods] in his own celestial chariot.
Therefore, what is that excellent state of stability— free from emptiness, free from effort, free from limiting conditions, and free from delusion— in which no doubt exists?
All undertakings and enterprises, as well as good people such as Janaka and others, were solely devoted to worldly activity; how then did they attain the state of supreme excellence?
O bestower of great honor, even though [the body] was indeed attached to many parts of the limbs...
How is it that a person here is not smeared by the mire of saṃsāra? Relying upon what view do you great ones, free from stain, wander here as high-minded ones liberated while living?
Objects of sense, which are like serpents of enjoyment, incite desire only for the sake of fear;
how can they, whose power is of a fragile nature, ever lead to well-being? Crushed by the elephant of delusion and stained within by blemish—
How does the lake of one's intellect attain supreme clarity?
How is it that a person, though dwelling within saṃsāra and even engaging in worldly affairs,
incurs no bondage, just as water on a lotus leaf?
How can one who creates this entire world— treating it as himself or as a blade of grass—
attain supremacy without touching the mind’s passion?
Who is that Great Being who has reached the further shore of the ocean of existence?
Following established conduct, this person proceeds and does not commit an evil deed.
What is that which is appropriate and beneficial? What would be that appropriate fruit?
And how indeed should one conduct oneself in this discordant cycle of existence?
Therefore, O Lord of this world, tell me something by which I may understand the beginningless and endless, unstable course of the Creator’s activity,
and the cleansing of the impurity of the mind, which is like the moon in the sky of the heart.
"O Brahmin, act so that it may be accomplished for me without obstacle.
What here is to be accepted, what is to be rejected, or what is otherwise?
How may the flickering mind find rest, like a mountain? (MU 1.29.22–23)
By what purifying mantra is this cholera of miserable transmigratory existence—
causing hundreds of labors— pacified without effort?
How does it attain internal coolness, becoming a cluster of blossoms on the tree of bliss?
Like the full moon, I attain the unimpaired Rākā;
having reached internal fullness within, I no longer grieve as before.
May you virtuous ones, knowers of reality, instruct me in that very same way.

O Great-souled One, the mind— which finds its supreme rest in the state of unsurpassed bliss— is utterly wasted here by conceptual constructions, just as the body of a small creature in the forest is devoured by dogs. This creation, indeed, has no purpose.
The thirtieth canto:
Rāma [traversed] the place where water droplets were as transient as those hanging from the trembling leaves of lofty trees.
In this body, as tender as the digits of the moon, lord of life;
fragile as the throat-skin of a frog croaking in a field;
and like a snare for a creature, is the gathering of friends and kinsmen.
When the cloud of the mist of delusion flashes intensely with the lightning of base desires, stirred by the wind of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it thunders and roars;
and when the fierce and fickle peacock of greed dances its frantic dance, [the world trembles].

In the tree of the useless *kuṭaja*—which is in full bloom, bursting open, cruel, like a cat of Death (*kṛtānta*), and a stealer of the mice that are all living beings; which lacks the movement of sound or vibration, yet falls from somewhere above—[how can there be safety]? 1.30.4–5.
What is the means? What is the way? What is the reflection? What is the refuge? By what means might this forest of life, which yields such inauspicious results, not exist?
There is nothing on earth, nor in heaven among the gods, anywhere at all— ... [by which one could escape]. (MU 1.30.6)
Even this [world], though trivial, does not fail to become delightful to the wise.
For how could this burnt-up cycle of existence— crowded with incessant mental constructions and devoid of essence— attain sweetness without the state of folly?
By what bathing in milk can the poison of hope be made delightful?
It becomes so through the white blossoms of [wisdom], just as a beautiful creeper is by honey.
When its impurities are wiped away by this cleansing, it rises with the luster of nectar.
By what means can the mind— which is stained by desire— be purified from the moon?
By one who has seen the course of saṃsāra and who has destroyed both the seen and the unseen,
by whom should one navigate through the pathways of the forest of saṃsāra?
How is it that the great diseases of passion and hatred, preceded by the pursuit of enjoyments and extreme impurities,
do not afflict a living being wandering in the forest of saṃsāra?
And how is it that one is not consumed even when falling into the fire of heroic aversion?
Just as by means of water one quenches fire, so too [is this done] by means of a flavorful essence;
for indeed, in this world, no stability is possible without the performance of worldly activity, just as there is no water for one who has fallen into the ocean.
Free from passion and hatred, devoid of pleasure and pain,
like a flame of fire that lacks heat, there is no virtuous action here for one who is proud of the mental reflections of the mind, which cause torment throughout the three worlds.
"O most excellent ones, tell me that reasoning by which there is no destruction without logic;
tell me that supreme path by which suffering does not come to me through worldly activity,
or else, tell me the highest state for one who is beyond worldly activity."

Therefore, O Blessed One, tell me how, by whom, and what was done by one of supreme mind in the past, by which the mind attains this most holy rest? Tell it to me as you know it, for the cessation of delusion.
"Tell me, O virtuous ones, by what means you have attained freedom from suffering.
Or else, O Brahmin, if such a method does not exist,
or if someone knows it clearly but does not tell me."
Yet I myself do not attain that unsurpassed rest;
therefore, having abandoned all worldly effort and attained a state free from egoism,
I shall neither eat, nor drink water, nor shall I put on a garment.
I perform no activity such as bathing, giving gifts, or eating;
nor do I dwell upon worldly affairs in times of prosperity or in states of adversity.
O Sage, I desire nothing at all except for the casting off of this body.
Free from doubt, devoid of the sense of "mine," and without envy,
I remain here in silence alone, as if fixed in a painted image;
then, gradually abandoning even the consciousness of inhalation and exhalation.
"I abandon this arrangement called the body, which is a source of misfortune.
I am not it, nor does it belong to me; I become extinguished like a lamp without oil.
Having renounced everything, I cast off this physical frame."
Having spoken thus, Rāma— delightful as the stainless, cool-rayed moon, his mind blossoming with the most profound discernment—
became silent before the great ones, like a peacock ceasing its cry out of exhaustion from the sound of thunderclouds.
This is the canto named "The Question of the Descendant of Raghu."
The Thirty-first Sarga.
Vālmīki spoke these words, which bring about the cessation of the delusion of the mind:
While that prince Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals,
was there, everyone present became wide-eyed with wonder,
as if their hairs stood on end to hear his words.

Those words of that noble Rāma, in which all worldly tendencies were cast off by the latent impression of cessation, for a moment seemed as if they were painted upon a canvas, like waves tossed upon the ocean of nectar.
It was heard by the sages such as Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra, who were seated in the assembly with their hearts overflowing with joy;
and by the ministers headed by Jayanta and Ghṛṣṭi, all of whom were experts in counsel.
By kings such as Daśaratha, by the citizens including the Pāraśavas and others, by vassal lords and princes, by Brāhmaṇas who discourse on Brahman,
as well as by servants, ministers, and even by birds kept in cages.
With pet deer motionless and horses ceasing their chewing,
and with groups of women standing at their own windows led by Kausalyā, their ornaments silenced and their bodies still; MU_1,31.7–8.
With birds dwelling in garden creepers and even in the eaves of houses,
their flocks undisturbed and their cries silenced;
and with Siddhas moving through the sky, as well as Gandharvas and Kinnaras.

Those words of Rāma, rich in diverse meanings and most noble, were heard by the preeminent sages headed by Nārada, Vyāsa, and Pulaha, as well as by others— the lords of the gods, the Vidyādharas, and the great serpents.
Then, while the lotus-eyed Rāma—
so beautiful like the moon in the sky of the Raghu dynasty— remained silent, a cry of "Well done! was uttered by the assembly of Siddhas.
A rain of flowers fell from the sky like a canopy,
resounding with pairs of bees resting within the buds of *mandāraka* flowers,
and gladdening the intoxicated people who were delighted by its beauty and the fragrance of wine.
Like a succession of stars scattered by the wind in the sky,
like the flash of a celestial woman’s laughter fallen to the surface of the earth,
it was like a row of fragments from a single-autumn cloud fallen amidst the rains.
It was like a continuous succession of balls of fresh butter,
like a noble shower from the Himalayas, comparable to a string of pearls,
like a garland of moonbeams, or a series of waves of milk.
Enveloped by the fragrance of filaments, with swarms of bees hovering about,
sweetened by the scent of the wind singing with whistling sounds, it was shaken by the breeze;
it possessed clusters of wandering *ketaka* flowers and spreading throngs of night-lilies.
With its circles of *kunda* flowers falling away, its home for the *kuvalaya* lilies curling,
its courtyards filling the roofs of the women’s gardens and houses,
it was gazed upon by the excellent city-dwelling women who stood with upturned necks.
A rain from the cloudless sky, resembling blue lotuses, fell without agitation;
it was never seen before by any person and inspired wonder.
Stirred up by the hands of the multitude of perfected beings (*siddha*), it had never been witnessed previously.

In the fourth part of a muhūrta, a rain of flowers fell; when the assembly hall was filled and the shower of blossoms had subsided, those members of the assembly heard these words from the hosts of Siddhas: "In the fourth part of a muhūrta, a rain of flowers fell; when the assembly hall was filled and the shower of blossoms had subsided, those members of the assembly heard these words from the hosts of Siddhas."
Wandering all around the heavens until the end of the aeon among the hosts of perfected beings (siddhas),
we have today heard for the first time this nectar for the ears,
which has indeed been spoken so nobly by this moon of the Raghu dynasty.
For, due to its freedom from passion, that state is indeed beyond the reach even of the Lord of Speech.
Oh, what great merit has been gained by us today,
having heard these words issuing from the mouth of Rāma, which bring the refreshment of nectar to the intellect!

Because this descendant of Raghu has spoken what is fitting— attaining with diligence the state of supreme excellence, beautiful with the nectar of tranquility— we have been instantly awakened by him. The chapter named "The Praise of the Sky-Travelers."
The thirty-second canto is completed: of these purifying words spoken by the banner of the Raghus.
"It is fitting to hear the decision that shall be spoken by the great seers.
O foremost of sages, headed by Nārada, Vyāsa, and Pulaha,
let all you great seers come here quickly and without hindrance."
"Let us wander all around this holy assembly hall of Daśaratha,
like bees about a lotus pond filled with dense golden lotuses.
Vālmīki said:
Having spoken thus,

that entire divine succession of sages, dwelling in their celestial abodes in the sky, descended into that assembly; led by the lord of sages, they played vīṇās upon the surface of the wind moving before them.
Its interior was made variegated by the dark clouds of the Milky Way;
it was adorned by the leaders of sages such as Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Pulastya,
and protected by Cyavana, Uddālaka, Uśīra, Śaraloman, and others.
Through their mutual observation, she appeared with her deer-skin garment poorly arranged;
holding a rosary, bracelets, and a beautiful water-pot,
she enhanced each other's beauty like a row of stars.
It was like a rain of flowers, like a second solar orb; Vyāsa shone there like a cloud amidst a cluster of stars. Nārada shone there like the cool-rayed moon amidst a multitude of stars.

There Pulastya shone like the lord of the gods among the deities, and Aṅgiras shone like the sun among the gods. Then, as that army of Siddhas descended from the sky to the earth, it appeared like the sun among the gods and Aṅgiras among the deities. MU_1,32.10.
Now, as this army of Siddhas was falling from the heavens to the surface of the earth...
Then the assembly hall of the son of Daśaratha, filled with sages, rose up.
Those sky-dwellers and earth-dwellers, mingled together, shone forth;
their bodies and radiance intermingling with one another, they illuminated the ten directions.
Holding flutes and bells in their hands, they carry play-lotuses;
their hair-tips are entwined with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, and their locks of hair are adorned with crest-jewels.
Their matted locks are tawny like a forest thicket, and their heads are crowned with garlands.
With bracelets of beads upon their forearms and adorned with rings of rubies,
they were clothed in rags and bark garments yet veiled in garlands and silk;
they had dangling girdles and moving clusters of pearls.
In an instant, Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra honored those great hosts of sky-dwellers with offerings of water for the hands and feet, as well as with words;
the king likewise honored the multitude of Siddhas with every form of respectful conduct.
The multitude of Siddhas greeted the king with inquiries concerning his welfare;
having received mutual honors through various expressions of affectionate zeal,
the sky-dwellers and the earth-dwellers sat down upon their seats.
With words, a rain of flowers, and shouts of "Well done!",
they honored Rāma from all sides as he stood bowed before them.
And there, resplendent with royal fortune, he took his seat.
Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, and Vāmadeva were his ministers;
as were Nārada, the son of a god, Vyāsa, the preeminent among sages,
Marīci, Durvāsas, and the sage Āṅgirasa.
Kratu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Śaraloman, the lord of sages, Vātsyāyana, Bharadvāja, Vālmīki— the preeminent among sages—
Uddālaka, Ṛcīka, Śaryāti, and likewise Cyavana.
Ūṣmapa, Ghṛtārcis, Śāluḍi, and Vāluḍi—
these and many others who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, great-souled leaders who knew all that is to be known, were present there.
Together with Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra, those masters of sacred lore, Nārada and the others, spoke these words to Rāma, whose face was bowed in humility:
"Oh, how wonderful! By this prince, who is endowed with auspicious virtues..."
Speech was uttered, pregnant with the essence of most noble dispassion;
its meaning was perfectly established, easy to understand, appropriate, clear, sublime,
worthy of being practiced as a pleasing act, undisturbed, and unerring.
Whom does this speech uttered by Rāghava— not only clear in its manifest words, but desired, nourishing, and pleasing— not fill with wonder?
It is as if it were the voice of a single person from among a hundred, yet possessing every noble and marvelous quality.
Speech becomes uniquely capable of bestowing the desired object;
O Prince, in whom else but you does this fresh vine of wisdom, bearing the fruit of discernment, thus attain its full bloom?
That man is considered truly wise in whom the flame of the lamp of wisdom dwells within the heart, blazing brightly like that of Rāma and providing illumination.
[He perceives] many machines of blood, flesh, and bone, stretched out in great extension.
They drag down all objects; there is no consciousness in them.
Again and again they undergo the suffering of birth, death, and old age;
like cattle, utterly deluded, they do not reflect upon saṃsāra.
Somewhere and somehow, a single person of pure intention is seen who is worthy of being examined from beginning to end, such as this slayer of enemies;
for those of auspicious form yield the fruit of unsurpassed wonder.
For those capable [of liberation] are rare in the world, like mango trees.
Within this noble mind, this right vision— which possesses the wonder of its own discernment regarding the birth of the world— is seen as if it were something else entirely.
Worlds that are easy to attain and auspicious, abounding in fruits and sprouts, grow as trees in every land; yet sandalwood trees do not.
Truly, there are trees in every forest with fine fruits and foliage.
But a novel wonder, O Lavaṅga, is never easily found.
A marvel seen in a beautiful woman is like moonlight from the cool-rayed moon, like a cluster of blossoms from a fine tree, or like a trail of fragrance from a flower.
O best of the twice-born, from this burnt-out cycle of existence fashioned by the workings of fate and unrestrained wickedness, the essence is indeed extremely difficult to attain;
yet those who are treasuries of glory strive with their intellect for the attainment of that essence.
Blessed are they, counted as leaders among the virtuous; they alone are the best of men.
It is our conviction that there is no one in these three worlds equal to Rāma—none who possesses such discernment, such a noble soul, and such a great spirit.

Even though it causes wonder to the entire world, if that which is desired by the heart of Rāghava does not bear fruit, then we ourselves are clearly sages of ruined intellect. Thus ends the canto titled "The Arrival of Siddhas, Munis, and Lords of Sages."
The chapter on Detachment, titled the Second Sarga, is completed. Chapter One: The Conduct of the Seeker of Liberation.
Vālmīki:
When these great words had been spoken by Nārada, Viśvāmitra, who was present in the assembly, also spoke with affection to Rāma, who stood before him.
Viśvāmitra:
O Rāghava, best among the wise, there remains nothing further for you to know;
by your own subtle intellect, you have understood everything.
In you, whose intellect is like a mirror naturally pure and eternally bright, mere wiping away is required only to a slight degree;
your mind is like that of Śuka, the son of the blessed Vyāsa.
"Even one who has known the object of knowledge requires only internal rest.
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, how was it for Śuka, the son of the venerable Vyāsa?"
"At first it did not rest even with the intellect, and then it rested once more with the intellect.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O Rāma, this account of my own life, as it is being described by me, is equal to your own."
Listen to the news concerning the son of Vyāsa, which is the cause for the end of [his] births:
this venerable Vyāsa, who has the luster of the sun and the hue of collyrium, is seated upon a golden throne at the side of your father.
To him was born a son named Śuka, moon-faced, skilled in statesmanship,
and possessed of great wisdom, who stood like the sacrifice (Yajña) incarnate. As he reflected deeply upon this worldly course within his heart, it was sufficient [to dispel his delusion].
Indeed, it is said that a profound sense of discernment arose in him as well, just as it did in you.
O high-minded one, by means of his own discernment,
he himself reflected for a very long time and attained that which is beautiful and true.
Because his mind did not find rest even when the supreme reality was spontaneously attained,
he could not gain the conviction within himself that "this is the reality"; rather,
his mind simply ceased its restless wandering.
Like a *cātaka* bird from rain-clouds on earth that are subject to many breakages, [he turned away] from enjoyments.
Once, that one of pure wisdom, with devotion, questioned his father, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, who was staying in solitude on Mount Meru.
"O Sage, how has this grand display of saṃsāra arisen?
How does it come to rest? To what extent, by whom, and when?"—when thus questioned, the sage Vyāsa explained everything to his son.
"What has been declared as stainless must be spoken exactly as it is by one who knows the Self.
Then Śuka, with his pure intellect, did not think much of his father’s words, [thinking], "I already knew this before. 2.1.15–16.
The venerable Vyāsa, having understood his son's intention to be such, replied again to his son: "I do not know [him] in truth;
there exists on the surface of the earth a king named Janaka."

"He knows the knowable exactly as it is; therefore, you shall obtain everything. Having been addressed thus by his father, Śuka departed from Sumeru for the surface of the earth and reached the city of Videha, which was protected by Janaka.
O King, that high-souled Janaka was informed by the staff-bearers at the gate: "The son of Vyāsa, Śuka, is standing here.
Out of disdain, he said, "Let him remain right there for the sake of his inquiry."
Having spoken thus, Janaka remained silent for seven days.
Then Janaka ushered Śuka into the inner apartments;
there he stayed for those same seven days, remaining with his mind fixed on the Supreme.
Then Janaka had Śuka enter the inner apartments for seven days, thinking, "The king is not to be seen for that long. There,
he was entertained by intoxicated, lovely women with food and an abundance of enjoyments.
Janaka cherished Śuka, whose face was like the moon.
Those enjoyments and those sorrows did not disturb the mind of Vyāsa’s son,
just as a gentle breeze cannot move a mountain that has its foundation firmly fixed.
There Śuka remained, solitary, tranquil, pure, silent, and joyful in mind, like the full moon;
King Janaka recognized that Śuka had realized his true nature.

Having brought him near, he looked upon him with a joyful soul and bowed down. Then, having offered a welcome, he quickly said to him: "O you who have completed all duties for the world and attained every heart's desire, what is it that you wish for?"
Śuka said:
O Guru, how has this grand display of saṃsāra arisen?
How does it come to rest? Tell me this properly and quickly.
Viśvāmitra: When questioned thus by Janaka, Śuka related exactly what had been told to him previously by his high-souled father.
Śuka said:
"I myself had previously understood this through discernment;
this is all that was stated by my father when he was questioned."
O best among those skilled in speech, you too have stated this very same point; and this indeed is the meaning of the sentence as it is observed in the scriptures:
that this [world], which arises from one's own conceptual construction, [ceases] through the complete exhaustion of one's own conceptual construction.
"The cycle of existence, being devoid of essence, is consumed and destroyed; this is the certainty.
"O mighty-armed one, tell me this truly and purely: how may my mind find rest in you, so that the world no longer wanders in delusion?"
Janaka said: O Sage, there is no other certainty beyond this;
you have known this yourself and have heard it again from a teacher. (MU 2.1.35)
The one conscious Self alone exists here as the person, uninterrupted; there is nothing else.
Bound by the power of volition, he is liberated when free from volition.
But for that great-souled one by whom this is clearly known, there is nothing further to be known.

"O Great Hero, your mind has reached a state of renunciation; it has become sufficient for you to turn away from enjoyments here, whether they be all those visible objects or even from the entire world of appearance.
Since you have turned away from enjoyments that are like chronic diseases, what else do you wish to ask?"
The fullness of the great treasure-house of omniscience did not arise for your father while he remained in extensive asceticism in such a manner as it has for you;
therefore, though I am the son of Vyāsa’s disciple, I am indeed superior to Vyāsa himself.
"By the attenuation of your desire for enjoyments, you have become even greater than I.
Everything that was to be attained has been attained by you, whose mind is now full.
O Brahmin, you do not fall back into the realm of the visible; you are liberated—cast off this delusion! (MU 2.1.40–41)
Having been thus instructed by the high-souled Janaka,
Śuka became silent and rested in the pure, supreme reality— free from sorrow,
fear, and exertion, devoid of worldly effort, and with all doubts severed.

He went to the faultless peak of Meru for the sake of meditative absorption. Having remained there for ten thousand years in unwavering samādhi, he was extinguished within himself like a lamp whose oil has been consumed.

Then, in that pure and sanctifying state which is naturally stainless and free from the stain of temporal succession, that Great-Souled One attained oneness, with all distinctions dissolved, like a drop of water in the ocean. The Chapter Named "The Nirvāṇa of Śuka."
The Second Chapter: Viśvāmitra;
the removal of the slight measure of pride from that son of Vyāsa.

O Rāma, lord of the earth, as much as has been employed by you is precisely what is required; by this, the knowable has been understood in its entirety. To him, worldly enjoyments no longer taste sweet, appearing instead like diseases to one of sound intellect.
This is indeed the characteristic of a mind that has known what is to be known:
that all varieties of enjoyments no longer taste sweet.
Through the mental cultivation of enjoyment, bondage—which is devoid of substantial reality—attains firmness.
By that very tranquility, bondage in the world goes to attenuation.
O Rāma, the attenuation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is called liberation by the wise;
the firmness of the latent impressions regarding the objects of experience is designated as bondage.
For most men, there occurs an approach to the reality of the Self;
thereafter, a distaste for sense objects arises from [the realization of] their worthlessness.
That wise man who knows the truth sees correctly, having known that which is to be known.
Sensual enjoyments do not please that great-souled one by force alone;
moreover, he for whom worldly enjoyments no longer have any appeal on earth, being devoid of motives such as fame and the like— he is called liberated while living.
O dear one, as long as that which is to be known has not been realized,
a person’s lack of attachment toward sense objects does not arise, just like a creeper in a desert land.
Therefore, O scion of Raghu, know that this occurs only when that which is to be known has been realized.
Since these delightful lands of enjoyment do not truly delight him,
Rāma hears from the presence of the True One that "that which he knows is the Reality," and thus a rest for his mind arises within the descendant of Raghu.
The intellect of Rāma requires only rest in the state of absolute oneness (*kevalībhāva*), just as the beauty of autumn requires the stillness of the waters. Here,
for the sake of the rest of the mind of the great-souled descendant of Raghu—
"Let the illustrious and venerable Vasiṣṭha speak the reasoning;
he is the lord and eternal family preceptor of all the Raghus,
omniscient, all-seeing, and possessed of stainless vision regarding the three periods of time."
"O venerable Vasiṣṭha, do you perhaps remember what happened previously,
when for the sake of pacifying our enmity and for the welfare of great-souled beings,
[you led us] to the peak of Mount Niṣadha, which is thick with *sarala* trees and frequented by sages?"
O Brahmin, much knowledge has been taught by the Blessed One, the Lotus-born,
by which rational knowledge this worldly tendency (*vāsanā*) of the transmigrating soul surely comes to rest, just as darkness [is dispelled] by the sun.
O Brahmin, you should quickly teach that very same reasoned knowledge to Rāma, who dwells at the end of the path, by which he will attain rest;
for this is no harassment, as Rāma is indeed free from all taint.
Just as a face reflects effortlessly in a spotless mirror,
so too is that knowledge, that meaning of the scripture, and that unimpaired proficiency which is taught by a virtuous teacher to a dispassionate and worthy disciple. (MU 2.2.19–20)
Whatever is taught to one who is not a disciple and who lacks dispassion becomes impure, like cow’s milk in a dog’s skin.
Those who are free from passion, fear, and anger, who are devoid of the sense of "mine," and whose sins have dissolved— [to them alone is this teaching intended].
"But that which those like you say, upon this the intellect here comes to rest.
When the son of Gādhi had spoken thus, those sages, headed by Vyāsa and Nārada, honored him for that very meaning, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Then the illustrious sage Vasiṣṭha, of great splendor, standing by the side of the king like Brahmā’s son Brahmā himself, spoke: Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Sage, I shall perform without obstacle whatever you command me.
For who, even if capable, is able to transgress the word of the virtuous?
Indeed, I shall dispel the darkness of mind from the princes, such as Rāma and others."
Today, by means of knowledge, I dispel [ignorance] as a lamp dispels the darkness of night;
I remember it all without interruption for the sake of pacifying the delusion of saṃsāra—
that knowledge which was formerly proclaimed on Mount Niṣadha by the Lotus-born One.
Vālmīki:
Having spoken thus, that great-souled one, his splendor as a venerable teacher enhanced by his formal attire,
Vasiṣṭha explained this for the sake of pacifying ignorance— the sole awakening to the supreme state.
The third canto, titled "The Words of Viśvāmitra," [spoken by] Vasiṣṭha:

"What knowledge was previously spoken by the Blessed One, who was born from the lotus, for the sake of the peace of the world at the beginning of creation— that very thing I shall now relate. Rāma said:
“O Blessed One, you shall speak at length on that which is connected with liberation;
first, however, dispel this doubt that has arisen in me for this moment.
Vyāsa, the great sage and omniscient teacher, was the father of Śuka.
"How is he liberated as one whose body has vanished (videhamukta), and how is that son of his liberated?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"The motes of dust in the three worlds end within the light of the supreme sun."
Those who have arisen again and again and then dissolved cannot be numbered.
And as for those millions of hosts of beings existing in the three worlds at present,
they likewise cannot be counted by anyone.
In the supreme ocean, there will arise waves that are the creations of the world;
there is not even a mention of anyone who could count them.
Rāma said:
"It is appropriate to investigate those successions of world-creations that have been and those that will be; what need is there to speak of those occurring in the present?
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, whatever being— whether animal, human, god, or other— perishes,
in that very place and at that very moment,
he perceives this triple world within his own heart by means of what is called the *ātivāhika* (the subtle body).
In the sky, with a body of consciousness, the unborn one experiences the nature of space.
Thus, millions of beings have died, are dying, and will die;
for these worlds of living beings have arisen individually and separately.
Like a whirlwind or an earthquake; like a child terrified by a *piśāca*;
like a string of pearls in the stainless sky; like a tree or a vehicle that does not move;
like a city perceived in a dream; or like trees in the sky born of memory.
Having died within itself, one experiences the wandering of the world by oneself.
There, through extreme transformation, that very [space] attains density;
thus, "this world" unfolds within the space of the living soul (jīvākāśa).

Furthermore, in that very place, one who experiences birth, death, and so forth imagines a world beyond; having died there, he likewise [imagines] it again. Within that interval are other persons, and within them, others still.
These so-called "saṃsāras" appear like the surface of a plantain leaf;
there exist neither the collection of great elements such as earth and the rest, nor the sequences of worlds,
even for those who have died— nevertheless, they still experience the delusions of the world.
Thus, this ignorance is infinite and characterized by manifold productions;
it is a long river for the dull-witted, a stream of waves that is the creation of the world.
O Rāma, within the vast ocean of ultimate reality, these waves of creation [arise].
Again and again, they and others in great numbers undergo rebirth;
some are similar in every respect through their lineage, conduct, mind, and qualities,
some are similar by half, and some are utterly different.
There, I remember this sage Vyāsa as the thirty-second,
through the vision of knowledge that arises according to its possibility and is like a mirror; there,
the twelve other mental faculties are equal to him in their forms and dispositions.
The remaining ten possess all common characteristics and are distinguished by their lineage.
Even now, others will arise— such as Vyāsa and Vālmīki—
as well as Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, and yet others besides them.
The hosts of various asuras, ṛṣis, and gods arise in great numbers together, and at times they dissolve again, each separately.
There have been, are, and will be seventy-two Tretā ages of Brahmā.
"I know that he is indeed another, as well as the world, you, and I. Thus, in due order, this tenth incarnation of the far-sighted sage Vyāsa, whose deeds are marvelous, is clearly perceived.
We have been joined with Vyāsa and Vālmīki many times;
we ourselves have appeared in these various forms while possessing the same underlying intention.
Indeed, he must yet appear here once more for eight more ages.
Furthermore, he will compose the *Bhārata*, his own history (*itihāsa*).
Having divided the Vedas and brought his lineage to preeminence through this work, he will then attain the state of Brahman; thus shall it be for the liberator of Videha.
Free from sorrow and fear, peaceful, liberated, with all conceptualization gone—
this Vyāsa is described as one who is liberated while living, having conquered his mind through [the transcendence of] wealth,
kin, age, ritual action, learning, specialized knowledge, and worldly activity.
In every creation, beings exist again and again as equals;
at times, through hundreds of creations, they come into being or cease to be. Yet this illusion is sometimes devoid of such ends.
This vast succession of beings proceeds toward perversion,
like a heap of seeds being sown incessantly again and again,
in that very same configuration and yet in another, over and over.
Forms of creation proceed like waves from the ocean of time.
With his inner organ at rest, his conceptual constructions exhausted, consisting of the essence of his own true nature,
and satisfied by the nectar of supreme peace, the wise man remains unobscured.
The Fourth Chapter, titled "The Repeated Experience of Creation," by Vasiṣṭha.
Just as the state of being water remains the same in the ocean whether it is in the form of gentle waves or in its nature as water,
so too is the state of liberation identical whether one is embodied or disembodied.
[Rāma:]
Whether with body or without body, your liberation is independent of objects;
for how can there be experiences of food for one who has not tasted it?
O best of sages, the one liberated while living is indeed like an insentient object.
"We see him before us, yet we do not know his inner disposition.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"What difference can there be between those who are liberated while in the body and those who are liberated beyond the body, when they both possess the nature of non-duality?"
Just as that very same water remains the same whether it is in the state of a wave or in its calmness,
there is not even the slightest difference between the embodied and the disembodied liberation.
Whether it is with movement or without movement, it is indeed air that is called the wind.
Whether with body or without body, liberation is not an object of valid cognition for us;
for when its own oneness exists as undivided, [it is self-evident].
Therefore, listen to this very subject at hand, which is an ornament to hearing.
O descendant of Raghu, you must always understand that this knowledge being taught by me destroys the blindness of ignorance; for in this world of saṃsāra,
everything is always obtained through every properly applied human effort.
For here, as in the case of the moon, a cooling refreshment arises in the heart;
[it is known that] the attainment of the fruit of activity comes from human effort alone and from nothing else.
That which is not seen through direct perception to be like the fruit of human exertion—
Nothing such as "destiny" (daiva) exists, which is merely imagined by the dull-witted who are deluded.

That which is performed by the mind and the limbs through the instruction of the scriptures of the virtuous is human effort (pauruṣa); that alone is fruitful, while anything else is the behavior of a madman.
Whoever desires a particular object and strives for that object in due order will certainly attain it, provided he does not turn back halfway;
through human effort, even the beautiful lady who rules over the three worlds [is won].

For a certain particular living being attains the state of Śakra through human effort; indeed, a certain flash of consciousness alone attains the state of Brahmā by suddenly reaching the abode of the lotus.
By his own essential human effort alone, this certain man has attained the state of Puruṣottama, the one whose banner bears Garuḍa;
through human exertion alone, he has assumed the form of the Goddess who bends the world.
A certain embodied being here has indeed attained the state of having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
Know that human effort is of two kinds: that belonging to the past and that belonging to the present. The former is quickly overcome by present human exertion.
By those who are diligent, firm in their practice, and endowed with wisdom and energy, even Merus are swallowed; what need is there to mention former human efforts?
That which is the supreme humanity of a person consists in human effort governed by the scriptures.
For that [practice] leads to the accomplishment of the desired fruit, whereas the other indeed leads to misfortune.
In a certain state of a person who, due to his own internal instability, gradually [drinks] many drops of water for rinsing from a single cup squeezed by the tip of a finger.

In some [other world], the earth— adorned with masses of water, mountains, cities, and islands— would not be "earth" at all, were it not for the distribution of its portions according to what is appropriate for action.
This is the chapter titled "The Commencement of Human Endeavor."
The Fifth Canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"In this manner, for those who sport according to the scriptures, such is the initial engagement."
Like light for the various colors, she is the accomplisher of all actions.
Whatever is desired by the mind according to the scriptures is accomplished not by action;
she is the playful intoxication that deludes, not a means for achieving worldly goals.
Just as it is intended by one, so is it experienced by that same person;
let it be one's own karma alone, for there is no other separate thing called "fate.
Human effort is traditionally held to be of two kinds: that which is contrary to the scriptures and that which is in accordance with the scriptures.
In this regard, that which is contrary to the scriptures leads to misfortune, while that which is in accordance with the scriptures leads to the supreme goal.
Two human aims, equal and unequal, fight like two rams;
of these two, one's own [aim] and another's, the more powerful one prevails.
When misfortune is encountered even through effort prescribed by the scriptures,
one should recognize that one's own personal exertion is more powerful than the agent of that misfortune.
Relying on supreme human effort, one should crush the teeth against the teeth.
One who is intent on the auspicious shall conquer past inauspicious human effort (pauruṣa). The thought, "This past human effort is impelling me," must be forcibly cast down;
for that [past effort] is not superior to what is directly perceived.
To that same extent, one should strive with effort according to one's own human capacity,
until past karma naturally subsides.
Past defects undoubtedly subside through present virtues.
The illustration here is the destruction of yesterday’s defects by today’s virtues.
Having cast aside what is merely illusory, one should strive with a mind constantly applied to the goal to cross over saṃsāra and establish prosperity within oneself.
One must not associate with those who lack diligence, for they are like human donkeys; rather, one should exert effort according to the scriptures for the sake of accomplishing both worlds.
One must emerge from this cavern of saṃsāra by one's own strength.
Relying on human effort, as [one would escape] from the cage of enemies like Hari,
a man should examine his own conduct every day;
he should abandon that which is equal to the behavior of beasts and take refuge in that which is appropriate for virtuous men.
Having tasted something pleasant, such as delicious food and drink, within the home—
tender like an insect in a wound— one should not let one's life be reduced to ashes;
for by auspicious human effort, an auspicious fruit is swiftly attained.
"From the impure, the impure always arises; there is no such thing as fate.

He who rejects what is directly perceived and relies instead on inference would flee in terror upon seeing these two snakes with his own eyes, thinking, "These are snakes!"—even though they are merely his own arms. (MU 2.5.16–17)
Seeing the faces of those of deluded intellect who say, "Fate impels me," and whose vision regards the unseen as supreme, Prosperity turns away.
Therefore, one should resort to full discernment through human effort.

One should investigate those scriptures whose purpose consists of the knowledge of the Self. Fie upon the wicked desires of those fools who, though contemplating the goal in their minds according to the scriptures through their own efforts, do not actually accomplish it.

Human effort is not infinite; that which is not destined to be obtained cannot be attained even with great exertion, just as oil is not extracted from a stone. As a jar is limited, so too is a cloth limited.
In the same way, for you, the goal of human life is fixed and established within its own measure.
And it is the very nature of that [goal] to yield its own fruit through the study of scripture, the company of the virtuous, and right conduct; otherwise, it leads to misfortune.

This is the true nature of manhood: a person who conducts himself in this way never finds his efforts to be fruitless. Even others who are afflicted by wretchedness, poverty, and suffering have become supreme among men.
By human effort alone, they have attained equality with the Lord of the Gods.

For by means of those qualities— such as the study of scriptures and association with the virtuous— which have been practiced thus from childhood, one's own goal is indeed attained through human exertion.
Those of perverted intellect who think that what is seen directly, experienced, heard, or performed was brought about by fate are destroyed.
If laziness did not exist in this world, who would not be wealthy or highly learned?
Out of laziness, this earth, bounded by the oceans, is filled with human-beasts who are destitute.

(MU 2.5.28) When childhood has passed—restless with incessant play—a man should, from the age of adolescence and its adornments onward, diligently apply himself through the company of the virtuous to awaken his intellect to the meaning of words and their referents, and perform investigations into his own virtues and faults. (MU 2.5.29)
Vālmīki:

When the sage had spoken thus, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
The sixth canto, titled "The Establishment of Manhood," by Vasiṣṭha.
Therefore, having cast far away that which is other than human effort and destiny,
one should forcibly rescue the living soul by means of the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures.
To the extent that there is exertion, so shall the fruit quickly come to be.
Thus, human effort alone exists; let that very thing be your "destiny.
Just as at a time of suffering one cries out, "Alas, what misery! when expressing pain, so too the phrase "Alas, destiny! is merely a synonym for the word "misery."
There exists no such thing as "fate" (daiva) other than one's own prior karma;
it can be conquered here by a fool through effort, just as a powerful man overcomes another.
Even a wicked conduct of yesterday can be overcome by virtuous conduct today.
Just as one’s former misdeeds quickly attain purity,
so too do those who strive for that victory— not being greedy for even a fraction of gain—
become fools, commoners, and wretched ones, remaining dependent on fate.
When an action performed through human effort is destroyed by fate,
it should be understood that in such a case, human effort is the more powerful force.
Even among two fruits on the same stalk, one may be hollow within while the other is sound.
In that state, effort manifests, as does the consciousness of its aesthetic flavor (rasa).
Even those things that have attained perfection go to destruction when they become worldly states;
one should recognize therein the great power of the effort that causes destruction.
Whatever a mendicant king seizes by force from a state elephant is the great fruit of the diligent efforts of the ministers, the elephants, and the citizens;
just as food is seized through human effort and crushed between the teeth.
Having overcome their meager human effort, they are likewise crushed by the hero.
For the insignificance of even great beings who exert themselves is experienced;
they are employed at will in tasks by him like clods of earth.
Whatever human effort of a capable person may be visible or even invisible,
that is perceived as "fate" by one who is incapable and lacks wisdom within himself.
It is established that for living beings, fate is the exertion of a powerful being.
Even for those who remain stationary, this mutual nature of the ruler, the ministers, the elephant, and the citizens is clearly evident; it is that very nature which, beyond all doubt,
acts as the sustainer and maintainer of the kingdom of the mendicant and the stability of the subjects.
The present [action] overcomes the past, and the past [action] overcomes the present by force;
in this regard, that person who is always free from agitation regarding human activity is the victor.
Between these two, the present alone possesses strength because it is directly perceived.
Therefore, destiny can be overcome through efforts, just as a child can be surpassed by a youth. Or, when a harvest acquired over a year is carried away by a cloud,
it is the human effort of that cloud— possessing superior exertion— that triumphs.
Even when wealth acquired through gradual effort is lost, one should not feel distressed;
for where my strength was powerless, what cause is there for lamentation? If I were to suffer grief over that which I am unable to prevent, [it would be futile].
Therefore, for me, who have not honored Death, this daily weeping is appropriate.
All these states of the world, though they flash forth by the power of place, time, action, and substance, are conquered by one who exerts superior effort.
Therefore, relying on human effort, and having brought your wisdom to purity through true scriptures and the company of the virtuous, cross over the ocean of saṃsāra.
Both past and present human efforts are like fruit-bearing trees.
And between those two, the human goal pertaining to this life prevails as the superior one.
That ignorant creature who does not destroy his insignificant past karma through auspicious efforts is powerless over the pleasure and pain of speech and mind. (MU 2.6.23–24)
But he who possesses noble wonder and dwells in virtuous conduct emerges from the delusion of the world, like a lion from its cage.
"Someone is impelling me thus"— such a vain and harmful imagination [is abandoned].

He who stands having abandoned what is seen [by the senses] should be shunned from afar as the lowest of men. One should conduct oneself according to the scriptures amidst the thousands of worldly transactions that come and go, having renounced both pleasure and pain.
For one who does not abandon their own established boundaries as prescribed by the scriptures,
all treasures come to them, just like those from the ocean;
this singular dedication to the effort of accomplishing one's own purpose is what is praised by the wise.

That [power], which is expressed by the word "pauruṣa" (human effort), when constrained by the scriptures, leads to success. The capacity of action— which is characterized by vibration— to accomplish its own purpose is inferred by an intellect sharpened by the company of the virtuous and the study of authentic scriptures.
The wise know the infinite bliss of equanimity to be the ultimate truth;
those from whom this is obtained forever are the virtuous ones who should be served as masters of the scriptures.
If that which was previously called human effort is here designated by the term "destiny," [then it is the same].
Therefore, this is appropriate; we do not find fault with this name.
Those fools who have imagined a separate destiny (daiva) are those who have gone to ruin;
[one's] welfare in both worlds should always arise from human effort alone.
Just as yesterday’s misdeed attains beauty through a virtuous deed today, so too does today’s [misdeed] through that of the past; therefore, strive with effort to accomplish what is good.
For that fruit which is seen to arise from human exertion alone is like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one’s hand.
The deluded man, casting aside direct perception, sinks into the delusion of fate.

O noble-minded one, disregarding that fate— which is devoid of all causes and effects, imagined merely through the power of one's own conceptual constructions, and composed of unreality— take refuge in your own human effort.

When that fruit which has been conceived by the scriptures and the long-established local customs of virtuous conduct—having become deeply rooted—flashes within the heart, the mind does not turn toward anything else; they call this sequence of bodily movements "human effort" (*pauruṣa*). Having understood that human nature is indeed the fruit of such effort, one must always remain intent upon personal exertion.
Then, by serving true scriptures, virtuous people, and the learned, that [effort] shall attain supreme fruitfulness.

With minds made beautiful by the discernment of fate and human effort, and constantly contemplating that "human exertion alone triumphs," one should make an effort to serve noble persons. (MU 2.6.38–39)
Having understood that this disease consisting of the continuous chain of births is cured only by innate human effort in this world,
may this living being lead to peace through the unfailing supreme medicine of serving the most excellent sages with contentment.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Refutation of Fate."
The Seventh Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
Having obtained a body free from disease and afflicted by only slight suffering, [he remained there].
One should thus compose oneself so that one is not born again. He who wishes to overcome destiny through human effort shall conquer his every desire, both in this world and in the next.
Those who, having abandoned exertion, remain dependent on destiny, destroy virtue, wealth, and pleasure; they are enemies of themselves.
Consciousness-vibration, mind-vibration, and indeed sense-organ-vibration—these are the three.
These are the forms of the human goal; from these arises the emergence of results.
As the mind experiences [an object], it undergoes an internal vibration;
in that very way the body moves, and in that very way there is the state of being an enjoyer of the result.
This has been established from childhood: that wherever and however it may be, fate is never seen to prevail; therefore, human effort triumphs.
By means of human exertion, even this preceptor Bṛhaspati became the lord of the gods.
Śukra attained the status of preceptor to the lord of the Daityas through human effort alone.
O virtuous one, even the best of men, though afflicted by wretchedness, poverty, and suffering,
have reached equality with the lord of the gods through human exertion alone.
Those who were great and rich in power, the abodes of various wonders,
have become guests of hell through the very fault of their own human exertion,
amidst thousands of existences and non-existences and in various conditions.
The various classes of beings have evolved solely through the power of their own human effort.
Success in every human goal arises from three sources— the scriptures, the teacher, and oneself— never from fate alone.

One should diligently draw the mind away from unwholesome states and establish it in wholesome ones alone; this is the swift summary of the meaning of all the scriptures. That which is supreme, that which is not trivial, and that which is free from misfortune—[this is the goal].
"O son, perform that [action] with effort"—thus stand the teachers.
"In whatever measure my effort is applied, in that same measure shall the fruit come quickly";
thus, by human exertion alone am I the enjoyer of the fruit, and not through destiny.
Success is seen to arise from human effort; the method of the wise is based on human exertion.
Destiny is merely a consolation for those of feeble intellect when faced with suffering.
The method of human effort is always grounded in the means of valid cognition, foremost among which is direct perception.
Consequently, it is observed in the world that [the soul] undergoes such things as traveling to another country:
the enjoyer experiences satisfaction, not the non-enjoyer; the goer goes, not the non-goer;
the speaker speaks, not the non-speaker; and human effort bears fruit for men.
Those of sound intellect cross over insurmountable difficulties through human effort without exertion, but not by this state of muteness.
Whosoever exerts himself in whatever manner, he alone reaps the corresponding fruit.
But no fruit is obtained here by anyone who remains merely silent.
A favorable fruit is attained through a favorable human effort; an unfavorable one through an unfavorable effort, O Rāma. Do as you wish.
The attainment of the fruits of human effort here, occurring according to place and time—
whether it be reached after a long duration or quickly— is what is traditionally known as destiny (*daiva*).
Destiny is not perceived by the physical eye, nor does it exist in another world.
It has been said that what is called "fate" (daiva) in the world is actually the fruit of one's own past actions.
A person is born in the world, grows, and then decays again;
yet fate is not seen therein, for [the body] possesses childhood, youth, and old age.
The movement from one place to another, the holding of objects in the hand,
and likewise the activity of the limbs, are due to human effort and not through fate.
The wise maintain that the sole focus of exertion is on the action that brings about the desired goal.

That which is designated by the term "human effort" (pauruṣa) achieves everything through it. But that which consists solely in the exertion of effort toward an end that results in the attainment of what is harmful is called a "madman's act"; nothing at all is achieved by it.

The capacity of action, which is characterized by vibration, to accomplish its own purpose is itself raised up by an intellect sharpened by the company of the virtuous and the study of true scriptures. Those who know the infinite bliss of equanimity recognize it as their own ultimate reality.
Therefore, those scriptures and virtuous persons from whom [this knowledge] is obtained with effort should be served.

Through the intellect, the qualities of good scriptures and the like increase; through the intellect, the qualities of good scriptures and the like increase; these two grow mutually through practice, like a lake and the ocean over time.

Through human effort, one's own beneficial goal is attained by means of qualities such as the study of scriptures and association with the virtuous, which have been thoroughly practiced since childhood.
By human exertion, the Daityas were conquered and the activities of the world were established.
The worlds here have been fashioned by Viṣṇu, and not by fate.
O Lord of the Raghus, exert yourself long in this world where human effort is the cause,
so that you, O fortunate one, may never fearfully fall into the state known as that of trees or reptiles.
The eighth canto, titled "The Demonstration of Manly Effort," by Vasiṣṭha.
It has no form, nor actions, nor a locus, nor prowess;
what is this so-called "fate" that is spoken of as something as potent as false knowledge?
Those [notions] which, regarding the attainment of the fruits of one's own actions, think "this is thus," [are merely delusions].

These words have attained renown under the name of "destiny" (daiva). Likewise, the conviction held by those of deluded intellect that "destiny exists" is grasped through a lack of understanding, like a snake imagined upon a rope.

Just as yesterday’s misconduct attains beauty through good conduct today, so too does today’s [conduct] depend on what was done previously; therefore, strive with effort to be one who performs virtuous deeds.
For that person of evil mind for whom destiny is established by the fallacious reasoning of fools—
"Whether there be burning by fate or not—it must be said thus regarding the fire.
(MU 2.8.5) "If indeed fate alone is the agent here, what is the use of human exertion?
Fate itself will perform the acts of bathing, giving, eating, and conduct. (MU 2.8.6)
Or what is the use of instruction from the scriptures? This person is supposedly mute;
he is merely moved by destiny—what can be taught here to whom?
Furthermore, no lack of movement is observed in this world except in the case of a corpse.
There is vibration and the attainment of results; therefore, destiny is purposeless.
Nor can there be joint agency between the formless destiny and that which has form;
for the hands and other limbs exerting themselves, nothing is ever accomplished by destiny.
Even as in the case of the mind and cognition, this destiny is not experienced here [in the world];
indeed, down to the cowherds, it is held by the wise that destiny is always non-existent.
If there were an object distinct from cognition, then what would be the difference between the two? If they are one and the same, how can there be any distinction between them?

If conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) were a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), why is it not postulated as being human? Since that which is formless has no contact with that which possesses form— just as the sky [has no contact] with a corporeal body—
and since a corporeal object is seen to be joined [to another], therefore fate (*daiva*) does not exist.
Furthermore, there exists another director of all beings within these three worlds;
let the multitudes of beings lie down, for destiny will accomplish everything.
"I am thus directed by destiny; what can I do, given that things stand as they are?"
This speech regarding destiny is merely for consolation; in the ultimate sense, destiny does not exist.
Those who are deluded imagine destiny to be real and have gone to their destruction by being devoted to it;
the wise, however, have attained the highest state through human effort.
Tell me, by whom among those who are brave, those who are valiant, those who are wise, and those who are learned— by whom in this world is destiny proclaimed?
For it has been determined by those who know time that for some there is long life.
If he survives even with his head severed, that is the supreme destiny;
O Rāghava, if one who knows the time [of death] has determined it, and he remains untaught yet knows that [destiny], that is the supreme destiny. (MU 2.8.17–18)
"O Rāma, by the sage Viśvāmitra, having cast fate far aside,
brahminhood was attained through human effort alone and not otherwise.
O Rāma, by these other men as well, who have attained the state of sages— "

By human effort alone they attained the power of traveling through the sky for a long time; by human effort alone did the lords of the Dānavas, having destroyed the hosts of gods, establish their empire within the three worlds.
By their prowess alone, the lords of the gods forcibly seized from the Dānavas this expansive world, which had been torn asunder and shattered;
O Rāma, it is by the application of human effort alone that water is sustained [in its place].
A basket remains closed for a long time through skillful means; fate is not the cause therein.
O Rāma, in matters of seizing, giving, exertion, agitation, and delusion, it is seen that power resides in the agent, not in fate, just as it does in medicine.

O you of noble intent, disregarding fate— which is devoid of all causes and effects, merely imagined through the power of one's own conceptual constructions, and composed of unreality— take refuge in supreme human exertion.
This is the chapter titled "The Refutation of Fate."
The Ninth Sarga:
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, [this matter] has reached its full conclusion."
"O Brahmin, tell me what is called 'fate' in this world; how is it defined?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O Rāghava, human effort alone is the agent of all actions, and nothing else."

And everywhere the enjoyer of the fruit is [the self]; destiny (*daiva*) is not the cause therein. Destiny does nothing, nor does it enjoy; it does not exist, it is not perceived, and it is not respected—it is merely such a conceptual construction.

For those who possess the fruits of human effort, the attainment of what is auspicious or inauspicious once that effort has been accomplished in this world is designated by the term "destiny" (daiva).
[Yet] the constant arrival of desirable or undesirable things brought about by human effort—

Whether desired or undesired, attainment is designated by the word *daiva*. That future object which is necessarily to be accomplished solely through human effort is what is designated by the word *daiva* in this collection of worlds.
But for no one in the world, O Raghava, does destiny— which is like the sky— ever actually do anything at all,
whether it brings about the arising of good or evil fruits from human effort already accomplished, or fails to do so.

Whatever statement is made that "the state of affairs is thus," that is called destiny (*daiva*). "Such was my thought, and such indeed was my conviction"— whatever statement is made regarding the attainment of the fruits of action, that is called destiny (*daiva*).
"Regarding the attainment of desired or undesired results, that which expresses 'it is so'— the mere words of consolation— are called destiny (daiva). Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, Knower of All Dharmas, that which was previously accumulated as karma is called 'fate' (daiva); how has this been refuted by you? Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Excellent, O Rāghava! You understand; listen, for I shall tell you everything by which your intellect will become firm in the conviction that there is no destiny (*daiva*).
That latent impression (*vāsanā*) which formerly existed in abundance and was submerged..."
This very [consciousness] undergoes transformation into the state of karma for human beings. Whatever latent impression (*vāsanā*) a living being possesses, that becomes their karma in an instant;
it is simply not tenable that one could have a different karma or a different state of being.
One who goes to a village reaches a village, and one who seeks a city reaches a city;
whatever one's latent impression (*vāsanā*) may be, so does that person strive.
Whatever action was performed here in the past with intense momentum, [that alone bears fruit].
That very thing is indeed expressed by the synonymous term *daiva* (fate).
Thus, *daiva* is one's own actions; action is one's own latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
latent impression is nothing other than the mind; for the mind is traditionally known as the person (*puruṣa*).
That which is called destiny (*daiva*) consists of those very actions; for action, O virtuous one, is indeed the mind.
The mind is indeed the person (*puruṣa*); therefore, it is certain that there is no such thing as destiny.
For whatever way the single mind of a living being exerts itself, [that is what results].
Surely one attains that very thing through one's own self, not through destiny.
O Rāma, mind, consciousness, latent impression, action, destiny, and self-determination— these are the names for the determination of the person as proclaimed by the wise.
"O Rāma, just as a man of such-and-such a name attains a result in full measure by constantly striving with firm resolve,
so too, O scion of Raghu, everything is achieved through human effort."
It is attained here by no other means; therefore, may it grant you auspiciousness.
Rāma said: "Just as the web of past latent impressions (vāsanā) impels me,"
"O Sage, I remain exactly as I am; what can I, a wretched man, do?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"For this very reason, O Rāma, you shall attain eternal welfare."

It is achieved only by human effort brought about by one's own exertion, and not otherwise. O Rāma, your two-fold accumulation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—both auspicious and inauspicious—exists from the past; or perhaps only one of the two remains.
If you are led there today by a pure flood of latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
then through that very auspicious process you shall attain the eternal state.
But if an inauspicious disposition joins you to a crisis, [the opposite occurs].
Therefore, that former [self] must be conquered by you through effort and force.
O wise one, you are pure consciousness alone; you are not the body, which is insentient by nature.
If that very [consciousness] is perceived by another within the mind, then where indeed could you be found?
But if another causes you to perceive, then since you do not exist, who else could there be? And whom would that other cause to perceive? Therefore, an infinite regress is not real.
The river of latent impressions flows along two paths, the auspicious and the inauspicious.

One should be joined to the auspicious path by means of human effort. O best among the strong, one should cause one's own mind— which has entered into inauspicious things— to descend into only auspicious things through the power of human exertion.
The mind of a living being, like a beast, wavers from the unwholesome toward the wholesome, and from that again toward the other; therefore,
one should always guard it with the soothing balm of equanimity— swiftly at first, and then gradually, not all at once.

One should protect the child of the mind through human effort. O Rāma, the flood of latent impressions (vāsanā) that you previously made dense through practice— whether auspicious or inauspicious— you must now make the auspicious one dense.
O crusher of enemies, know that when your latent impressions (vāsanā) arise by the force of prior practice, then you should recognize the success of that practice;
O sinless one, even now your latent impressions are reaching density.
Therefore, by the power of practice, apply yourself to the cultivation of the auspicious.
If your latent impression (*vāsanā*) has not previously reached density through practice, it will certainly increase now; therefore, my dear, be happy.
Even when there is doubt, gather only what is intensely auspicious;
for in this increase of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), no fault whatsoever arises from the auspicious.
Whatever is practiced in the world, one becomes permeated by that very thing.
Thus has this been observed among the wise, free from doubt, even down to children.
Therefore, endowed with auspicious latent impressions (*vāsanā*), apply yourself here to your own welfare by relying on supreme human effort and conquering the five senses.
"As long as your mind is unrefined and you have not yet realized that supreme state, practice that which has been determined by the authority of the Guru and the scriptures. Then,
through the ripening of your spiritual impurities, you will surely come to know the reality."
Even this auspicious flood of meditative cultivation must be abandoned by you, O one free from desire.

Having pursued that which is most beautiful and practiced by the noble ones—the auspicious—through the perception of it as a desirable state, attain the state forever free from sorrow; and having subsequently relinquished even that, remain perfectly established.
The tenth chapter, titled "An Inquiry into Karma," by Vasiṣṭha.
Therefore, relying on human effort which is a constant companion to the highest good,
make your mind one-pointed for the sake of spiritual welfare, and listen to these words of mine: [Do not let them] fall midway, having mounted upon the chariot of your desire.
Quickly restraining the senses through human effort, bring them to a state of equanimity.

For the sake of accomplishment both in this world and the next, I shall proclaim the Saṃhitā, which is equal to the essence [of all teachings], bestows the fruit of the goals of human life, and consists of the means to liberation.
Having abandoned the latent impressions of saṃsāra so as never to grasp them again,
and having taken up tranquility and contentment with a noble intellect,
he [attains] that which is honored by the investigation into the meaning of the preceding and succeeding statements.

Having made the mind equanimous and continuous within the Self, O Rāma, listen to this means to liberation that will be described hereafter; it brings about the destruction of pleasure and pain and is the sole means for attaining great bliss. MU_2,10.6
Having heard this discourse on liberation together with all those who possess discernment,
you shall attain the state free from suffering, where no destruction exists.
This was spoken in a former age by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
"It brings about the destruction of all suffering and is the supreme consolation for the intellect.
Rāma said: "O Brahmin, by whom was this spoken previously, and for what reason, by the Self-existent One?"
"And how was this attained by you? Tell me, O Lord.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"There exists the Self of infinite manifestations, all-pervading and the refuge of all."
The sky of consciousness, whose nature is indestructible, is like a lamp within all things.
From it, Viṣṇu was born through the common form of both vibration and non-vibration,
like a wave from the ocean filled with the essence of vibration.
From the heart-lotus of that [Supreme Being], which has Mount Sumeru as its pericarp, the quarters of space as its petals,
and the stars as its filaments, the Parameṣṭhin was born;
he who is garlanded by the Vedas, the meanings of the Vedas, the lords of the gods, and the circles of sages.
He created the entire creation as a flood of mental constructs, just like the mind itself.
In this corner of Jambūdvīpa, in the region named Bhārata,
he produced beings overwhelmed by mental anguish and physical disease through his sons.

Seeing the suffering of those beings in this creation— who were despondent over existence and non-existence, intent on calamity and destruction, and [yet] the source of supreme nourishment for the various classes of living beings— the Creator of all the worlds, having perceived that, [acted].

The Lord felt compassion just as a father would from the suffering of his son. "What end might there be for the sorrow of these wretched ones, whose lives are spent? the Lord of Beings reflected with one-pointed concentration for a moment.

Having reflected thus, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, created once again austerity, righteousness, charity, truth, and the sacred fords. Having created these, the divine Creator of beings reflected further.
"By this alone, for men, there is no end to all suffering. [He said:
"That which is called Nirvāṇa is the supreme bliss, by means of which a person is neither born nor dies; that is obtained through knowledge alone. (MU 2.10.19–20)
For the crossing over of saṃsāra, knowledge alone is indeed the means for a living being;
austerity, charity, and likewise pilgrimage are proclaimed to be inferior means.
Therefore, for the sake of this high-souled person’s liberation from suffering, [knowledge is required].
"I shall quickly reveal a fresh means for crossing over.
Having thus reflected, the Lord Brahmā, seated upon the lotus,
formed this mental resolve and brought me into existence.
O sinless one, having arisen from somewhere, I quickly appeared before that father of mine as swiftly as one wave rises from another;
I was there, O Lord, bearing a water-pot, accompanied by my own water-pot.
Adorned with a rosary, he bowed down and was greeted by him.
Having said to me, "Come, my son," he placed his hand upon the white northern petal of his own lotus,
like the cool-rayed moon upon a white cloud.
Clad in a deer skin, with a deer skin as his own garment,
my father Brahmā spoke to me like a swan to a crane:
"O son, for even a moment your mind has been as fickle as a monkey."
"May ignorance enter you, just as the hare-marked moon enters the hare!
Having been cursed by him thus, immediately upon reflection,
I, the twice-born, forgot my entire stainless true nature.
Then, having fallen into a state of dejection, though I remained with a mind awakened by perfect enlightenment, I became like a base person, tormented by suffering and grief:
"Alas! How has this fault called 'saṃsāra' come to be?"
Having thought thus within himself, he remained silent.
Then my father said to me: "Son, why are you so sorrowful?
Ask me about the destruction of suffering, and you shall be eternally happy."
Then, seated upon the petal of a golden lotus, I asked that Blessed One, the creator of all worlds, about the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra:
"How indeed has this great suffering of saṃsāra come to be?"
When he was asked by me, "And how does the suffering of a living being perish?",
he spoke at great length about that supreme purifying knowledge, knowing which I have come to stand, as it were, even above my father.
Then the Creator of the world, the speaker and the cause of all things, spoke to me, who had realized what was to be known and was established in my own true nature:
"Having reduced you to a state of ignorance by means of a curse, I have made you my questioner."
These sons of Jñānasāra [were born] for the accomplishment of all people.
Now, with the curse pacified, you have attained supreme awakening;
you stand as one with the Self, like gold [separated] from gold.

"Now, O virtuous one, go for the sake of favoring the worlds to Bhāratavarṣa, situated within Jambudvīpa upon the surface of the earth. There, my son, you shall find those of great intelligence who are devoted to the ritualistic section [of the Veda]."
Those who follow the sequence of ritual action (kriyākāṇḍa) and proceed step by step should be instructed;
likewise, those whose minds are detached, who possess great wisdom, and who are free from passion—
O virtuous one, they should be instructed by you with knowledge that bestows bliss.
"Thus commissioned by my father, the lotus-born Brahmā, I remain here, O Rāghava, as long as the succession of beings endures.
Indeed, there is nothing at all left for me to do here; with this resolve, I am established upon the earth."
With a mental state that is utterly tranquil, as if my intellect were perpetually asleep, I perform my duties, yet I do nothing at all.
The eleventh canto, titled "The Descent of Knowledge."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus I have related to you everything concerning the descent of knowledge upon earth,
as well as my own endeavors and what was ordained by the Lotus-born One.
"O sinless one, because of the ripening of my great merit, my heart is today intensely yearning to hear this supreme knowledge from you.
Rāma said:
