"O Brahmin, how did the intellect of the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, proceed after the creation, in order to bring about the descent of knowledge into the world? Vasiṣṭha replied:

In the supreme Brahman, Brahmā himself was born by the power of his own nature, eternally consisting of vibration like a wave in the ocean. Having thus created this extended creation and all the destinies of that creation, he... [continued].

The Supreme Lord beheld those situated in the past, the present, and the future. When the time for the sequence of ritual acts, beginning with the Kṛta age, had come to an end, the Lord, perceiving the delusion of the worlds, was moved by compassion.
Then the Lord, having created me and repeatedly endowed me with knowledge,
dispatched me to the surface of the earth for the sake of pacifying the ignorance of the world.
Just as I was sent by him, so too were other great seers.
Led by Sanatkumāra and including Nārada and others in great numbers,
they were sent forth by means of the sequence of meritorious action as well as the sequence of knowledge,
in order to uplift the world that is afflicted by the great disease of the mind.

Then, in the past, when the Kṛta Yuga had waned and the pure sequence of ritual action had gradually diminished upon the earth, those great seers [acted] for the purpose of establishing the system of ritual action and for the sake of defining the boundaries of conduct.
The protectors of the earth were assigned according to the division of separate regions.
Furthermore, many treatises on traditional law (*smṛti*) and treatises on sacrifice (*yajña*) were composed and proclaimed upon this earth for the sake of accomplishing virtue, pleasure, and wealth.
While this Kālacakra was flowing, and that sequence had subsequently dissolved,
people were daily intent on eating and devoted to the acquisition of rice; thus,
the dualities of kings arose for the sake of sense objects.
Numerous beings on earth fell into a state where they were subject to punishment.
Consequently, the kings gradually became incapable of protecting the earth without war; thus, together with their subjects, they fell into a state of wretchedness.
In order to dispel their dejection and for the sake of the proper process of creation,
great visions of knowledge were then proclaimed by us and others;
therefore, this science of the self (adhyātmavidyā) was first described to kings.

Thereafter, it spread throughout the world and is proclaimed as the "Royal Science" (rājavidyā). Having understood this Royal Science, this Royal Secret, the supreme treatise on the inner self (adhyātma), O Rāghava, kings have attained the state beyond all suffering.
Now, after many kings of stainless fame have passed away,
you, O Rāma, have been born today here on this earth from this Daśaratha.
And in your mind, which is exceedingly serene, there has arisen that which purifies.

This beautiful dispassion, O crusher of enemies, is signless (nirnimitta). For indeed, O Rāma, in every fortunate and discerning virtuous person, dispassion preceded by a specific cause arises as that which is characterized by passion (rājasa).

But this unprecedented state that has arisen in you, which causes wonder among the wise— this dispassion of yours, which is without external cause, characterized by goodness, and born from your own discernment— is truly remarkable.
For who indeed would not become detached upon seeing the loathsome and the foul?

But for the virtuous, supreme detachment arises from discernment alone. Indeed, those great ones of great wisdom, in whom detachment arises without any external cause, they alone possess stainless minds.
Indeed, by means of an intellect dispassionate through the contemplation of the wonder of its own discernment, a living being shines like a youth with a forest garland; for,
having contemplated this structure of saṃsāra through discernment, [he becomes liberated].

Only those who attain dispassion are the supreme among men. By the power of one's own discernment, having investigated this again and again, one must forcibly abandon this magical illusion, both external and internal.
Who would not become dispassionate upon seeing a cemetery, calamity, and wretchedness?
That dispassion which arises spontaneously is the supreme good. You have attained greatness through this unartificial dispassion.
You are worthy of the essence of knowledge, like soft soil for a seed.
By the grace of the Supreme Lord, the Protector, the Supreme Self,
the auspicious intellect of one such as you pursues discernment.
When evil karma has been exhausted through a great sequence of ritual actions, austerity, observance, charity, pilgrimages, and long-term discernment,
one becomes fit for the investigation of the supreme reality.
The intellect of a living being functions through a chance occurrence, like the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow.
People here continue to wander, devoted to ritual actions and intent on the revolutions of the wheel, as long as they do not behold the supreme state.
Having seen this saṃsāra as it truly is, and having abandoned the mind absorbed in it, they go to the supreme state like elephants freed from their tethering posts.
O Rāma, this progression through saṃsāra is a treacherous path of endless striving.

The great thread that has escaped from the body is not destroyed without knowledge. O descendant of Raghu, those of great intelligence have crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to cross, by means of the boat of the application of knowledge alone, and not by any other means.
Listen with an attentive intellect to this method of knowledge which carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra, for by means of this constant attentiveness, you shall [be liberated];
since the ways of suffering in the world involve endless turmoil.
O blameless Rāghava, these pairs of opposites— cold, wind, heat, and so forth— which burn within for a long time,
how could they be endured by the virtuous without the application of knowledge? (MU 2.11.38–39)
Afflictions fall upon a foolish man at every step and at their appointed time, and they consume him just as a flame of fire burns straw;
yet these mental agonies do not affect the wise man who has realized true knowledge and possesses right vision.

Like crests of fire, they do not burn the forest that has been rained upon. Even when the desert wind of saṃsāra— revolving with mental agonies and physical diseases— is stirred up, the knower of reality is not shattered, like the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
Therefore, in order to know reality, only a wise person should, with effort and full of devotion, question a wise person who is authoritative and awakened in soul;
for when an authoritative speaker is questioned by one of the highest mind, [the truth is revealed].
One should grasp speech with effort, just as one takes saffron from a cloth;
O best among those skilled in speech, there is no one more foolish than that man who questions one whose words are not to be accepted because he does not know the truth.
There is no person more base than one who, having been diligently questioned by an authoritative speaker who knows that [truth], does not carry out his word.
One should first determine whether the speaker knows that [truth] or not by means of his prior actions.
The man who poses a question is a wise inquirer; however,
the fool who asks a question without first determining the nature of the speaker is a base inquirer and not a fit vessel for the great meaning.

When a question is asked by a wise person, it should be answered by one whose blameless intellect is capable of reconciling what precedes and what follows; it should not be told to a base person who follows the nature of a beast,
nor without first considering whether the questioner possesses the fitness for the authoritative subject matter.

The wise in this world call that man the most foolish who speaks [without being asked]. O descendant of Raghu, you are an exceedingly great repository of virtues as an inquirer, and I am capable of speaking; thus, this is a fitting union between us.

O you who are skilled in the meaning of words, whatever I say should be carefully determined by you as being the actual fact, and held in your heart without wavering. You are great, you are dispassionate, and you are a knower of the true state of worldly existence.
Just as saffron water sinks deep into a garment, so does your intellect—
intent on attending to what has been said and discerning the ultimate truth— penetrate your inner reality like sunlight entering the midst of water.
Whatever I say to you should be taken to heart and applied with effort;
otherwise, I should not be questioned by you here in vain.
For the mind, O Rāma, is fickle—a monkey in the forest of saṃsāra.

Restraining [the mind] with effort within the heart, one should listen to the wisdom of the ultimate truth. Having kept for a long time at a very great distance the person who lacks discernment, is ignorant, and delights in the company of the wicked, one should indeed honor the virtuous.
Through constant association with the virtuous, discernment arises;
enjoyment and liberation are said to be the two fruits of this tree of discernment.
Four gatekeepers are proclaimed to stand at the gateway to liberation.
Tranquility, discernment, contentment, and fourthly, association with the virtuous—
these four should be cultivated with effort, or perhaps three or even two;
these forcibly open the door to the royal palace of liberation.
Or rather, one should resort to even a single [virtue] by every possible effort, even at the cost of sacrificing one's life;
for when this one is brought under control, all four likewise come under control.
Indeed, it is through discernment that mastery over the scripture, knowledge, austerity, and splendor is attained.
The vessel takes on the form of its ornament, just as the sun [is the source] of all splendors. Indeed, for those devoid of consciousness, the dullness of their intellect reaches a state of density;
through this rigidity, it becomes like a stone, just as water turns to stone from coldness.
But you, O Rāghava, with your heart blossomed by kindness, virtue, and insight into the meaning of the scriptures, stand like a lotus at sunrise; O noble-minded one,
you are fit to hear and understand this vision of knowledge.
But a person whose ears have been extracted, O worthy one, is like [one hearing] the sound of a lute.
Through the yoga of the practice of dispassion and through the perfection of equanimity and nobility,
that state is attained, O Rāma, wherein no destruction exists.
Through the scriptures, preceded by association with virtuous people, and through excellent austerity and self-restraint,
one should first increase wisdom alone for the sake of liberation from saṃsāra;
[for saṃsāra is] the fierce watering of the poisonous tree of worldly existence and the abode of calamities.
One should diligently destroy the collyrium of ignorance, which is delusion, by means of folly; know that this very thing is the supreme destroyer of folly:
namely, this scripture which is being examined with a somewhat refined intellect.
When the serpent-hole of false hope leaps within the heart through folly,
the mind undergoes contraction, like a piece of leather placed in fire.
In a wise person, however, this vision of reality becomes clarified as it accords with the true nature of things.

Like the vision of the moon when its entire orb is stainless and free from clouds—[so too is he] whose mind is expansive and endowed with the beautiful skill of investigating what precedes and follows; such a person is called a "man. (MU 2.11.71–72)

With your blossoming, white, mind-stealing heart— cool-rayed through its excellent discernment and endowed with virtue— you shine like the stainless moon in the sky. The chapter entitled "The Characteristics of the Speaker and the Questioner."
Canto Twelve. Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāghava, you are one whose mind is perfected and who is worthy of honor; you know how to ask questions."
"You know what was said by him, and so I have proceeded to speak out of respect.
Having established your mind— free from passion and ignorance and following pure goodness— within yourself, remain steady to hear this knowledge."
Within you exists the entire array of qualities of an inquirer,
and within me the series of qualities of a speaker, just as the glory of jewels resides in the ocean.
O Sage, you have acquired detachment born from the association with discernment.
Like a moonstone that becomes moist when struck by the rays of the moon,
your long-standing practice with pure and noble qualities has been continuous from childhood, like the ever-expanding fibers of a lotus.
Therefore, listen; I shall tell you a story, for you alone are its worthy recipient.
Indeed, without the moon, the white water-lily does not bloom in its pure splendor.
Whatever undertakings there may be, and whatever philosophical views there may be—
When that state is perceived, both those [defilements] and these [mental fluctuations] indeed go to complete rest.
If the mind of a fortunate person were not to find repose in pure consciousness,
who in this cycle of existence could endure such constant anxiety?
Through the attainment of the Supreme, all mental fluctuations dissolve,
like the rocks of the great mountain ranges through contact with the multitude of suns at the end of an eon.
O Rāma, the cholera-like affliction of the onset of the poison of saṃsāra is difficult to endure.
It is pacified by the purifying *yogagāruḍa* mantra.

And that yoga, consisting of the knowledge of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-jñāna*), is indeed obtained through the investigation of the meaning of the scriptures with a virtuous person. (MU 2.12.11)
Indeed, it must be understood that when inquiry is conducted here, the total destruction of all suffering necessarily occurs;
therefore, those who possess the vision of inquiry should not be viewed with contempt.
By the power of inquiry, a person casts off this entire cage of worldly existence, just as a snake sheds its fully ripened skin.
One who possesses right vision (*samyagdarśana*), being free from the fever of passion and possessing a tranquil inner heart, beholds the entire world as if it were a mere diversion.
For one who lacks right vision, this [world] is indeed supreme suffering;
for this disease of *saṃsāra* is exceedingly treacherous, biting like a serpent.
It cuts like a sword;
it pierces like an arrow;
it entangles like a rope.
It burns like fire;
it blinds like the night;
and it renders one helpless like a harsh stone unexpectedly dropped from above.
It carries away wisdom,
destroys stability,
and casts one into the blind well of delusion.
Craving wears one down;
there is no suffering in cyclic existence that a transmigrating being does not encounter.
This craving is indeed a chronic cholera-like affliction caused by the poison of the objects of the senses.
If it is not treated, then it produces various effects that result in a succession of experiences like those found in a multitude of hell-cities:
where the falling of hundreds of cold swords feels like being struck by blue lotuses, and where the burning of fire feels like a drenching with snow.
The laceration of limbs is the application of sandalwood paste;
the crushing within a whirling wind is the massaging of the body;
the incessant falling of a shower of yak-tail fans and iron arrows flickering in the flames of a fire is the sprinkling of spray from a cooling fountain-house to dispel the summer heat.
The severing of the head is a peaceful sleep;
being rendered mute is the seal of proficiency—a great accumulation.
Therefore, O Rāghava, one must not treat with indifference this wheel of saṃsāra, which is so volatile and filled with thousands of such agonizing exertions.
This must certainly be investigated;
and it should be understood in this way: that indeed, through investigation, the attainment of the highest good occurs.
Furthermore, O moon of Raghu’s lineage:
If these great sages, great seers, brahmins, and kings— whose bodies are enveloped in the armor of knowledge—

are unable to endure suffering, how is it that they remain constantly joyful in mind while experiencing the afflictions of saṃsāra, which consist of suffering and are preceded by the activity of darkness?
For here, just as Hari, Hara, Padmaja, and the others remain free from curiosity and devoid of the disturbances of conceptual construction,
so too do those supreme among men— whose intellects are awakened and who have attained the lamp of the Self— remain in this world.
And thus:
when delusion is utterly exhausted, when the dense cloud of ignorance has dissolved, when reality is fully known, and when the beloved Self is attained;
when, having deliberated with the Noble Ones, the two—existence and non-existence—have had their forms dissolved by the intellect and reality is seen, there is delight in wandering.
This world belongs to the Supreme;
and furthermore, O Rāghava,

when the essence of consciousness (cittattva) is serene within the heart, the Supreme Being dances in its full majesty, while all perceptions of mental constructs have become completely absorbed into it.

When the activities of the internal organ have subsided before him, and when the reality has been perceived by the intellect with its essence firmly established, this wandering through the world becomes a delight.
And furthermore:
The chariot is the expansive body, the arrangement of horses is the movement of the senses, and the motion is from the wind; I am the ungraspable, infinite, and peerless one.
Whether as another or as this self, I, the embodied soul, wander through the world—when the reality is thus seen with a stainless intellect, wandering through the world becomes a source of delight.
This is the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Greatness of Reality."
Vasiṣṭha:
Holding fast to this view, those of noble soul and keen intellect move about without arrogance, like great beings who have attained their goal. MU 2.13.1
They do not grieve, they do not beg, and they do not desire good or evil;
they perform everything, yet they perform nothing at all.
They remain established in their own natural state, they act with composure, and they move about with composure.
Free from the dualities of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, they abide in their own self;
they come and yet do not come, they go to the forest and yet do not go;
they do not act and yet they act, and they do not speak and yet they speak.

Whatever undertakings there may be, whatever views there may be, and whatever perceptions of what is to be rejected or accepted— these all perish once the state [of the Self] has been realized. The mind, having abandoned all egoism, possesses a sweet disposition.
From every side, happiness approaches him as he stands like the orb of the moon;
even when free from the effort of mental construction and with all curiosity extinguished,
it does not find room within himself, just as an elixir does not fit within the moon.
He performs no magical illusions (*indrajāla*) and does not pursue latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
having cast off the fickleness of a child, he shines forth as truly full.
For such states of being are obtained through the vision of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*).
Not from anything else.
Therefore, the Self must be sought through inquiry; it must be meditated upon and known by a person throughout his life, and nothing else.
(MU 2.13.9) There is perfect harmony between one's own experience, the excellent scripture, and the teacher.
Wherein the self is beheld through that continuous practice;
one who has disregarded the meaning of the scriptures, who has been despised by great men,
and who has fallen even into a painful calamity, should not fall into equality with the foolish.

Neither disease, nor poison, nor calamity exists upon the earth that causes such distress to men as the folly residing within their own bodies. Just as this treatise is to be heard by those whose intellects are somewhat refined, [so too is it for others].
There is no other scripture whatsoever that so effectively removes ignorance.
This work is worthy of being heard, it brings happiness, and is beautiful with its narratives and illustrations;
it is entirely consistent with the meaning and spirit of all scriptural teachings.
Those calamities which are difficult to overcome, and those empty, wretched births—
all these are produced from folly, just as thorns grow from the *khadira* tree.
Better it is for one to wander with a bowl in hand through the streets of outcaste dwellings;
Wandering for alms, O Rāma, is not a life ruined by folly.
Having attained this light consisting of the means to liberation,
no person ever again falls into blindness, even within the darkness of delusion.
The night-blooming lotus of humanity is shriveled by the darkness of craving only so long as the stainless radiance of the sun of discernment has not arisen.
For the sake of liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra, [one should strive] together with kinsmen such as myself.
Having known the true nature of the self through the authority of the Guru and the scriptures,
those liberated while living move about here in this world, just as Hari, Hara, and others do,
and as other Brahman-sages do; so too, O Rāghava, do you conduct yourself.
In this world, sufferings are endless while happiness is like a mere moment;
therefore, one should not fixate one's vision upon pleasures that are followed by suffering.
That state which is infinite and effortless is for the sake of attaining the essential goal.
This must be accomplished with effort by a man who possesses discernment.
They alone are the supreme men, the vessels for the goal of human existence,
whose minds— free from all feverish distress— rest upon the unsurpassed state.
Know those of wicked mind who are satisfied with mere enjoyments, such as sovereignty and other pleasures, to be like blind *duṇḍubha* snakes;
they who [rely] on the deceitful, the miserable, and those characterized by the undertaking of evil deeds.
Those who place their devotion in enemies disguised as friends, or in those who enjoy worldly pleasures,
go from the difficult to the more difficult, from sorrow to sorrow, and from fear to fear— from one hell to another— those fools whose intellects are dulled by delusion.

O Rāma, the two states of pleasure and pain— which are ever eager to destroy one another, which are never conducive to the highest good, and which are as fragile as a flash of lightning— are never truly beneficial. Those great-souled ones who are detached, such as yourself, remain perfectly discerning amidst them.
Know those men to be venerable who partake solely in enjoyment and liberation;
having resorted to supreme discernment through the yoga of the practice of dispassion,
one shall cross over this terrible river of worldly existence and its calamities.
A discerning person who understands this world should not sleep amidst the illusions of saṃsāra, for they bestow the stupor and delusion of a toxic faint.
Having encountered this saṃsāra, he who remains indifferent to it—
He lies within a house made of straw that is burning fiercely.
That state which, once attained, one does not return from, and reaching which one no longer grieves—that state is indeed obtainable through wisdom; of this there is no doubt.
If that [self] does not exist, what fault would there be for you in this investigation?
If it does exist, then you will have crossed over the ocean of existence. Thus, a person’s engagement here is in the investigation of the means to liberation.
When that occurs swiftly, then one is said to be a partaker of liberation.
An undecaying, fearless state of well-being, free from delusion,
does not exist within the three worlds without the state of absolute oneness (kevalībhāva).
In attaining that, in attaining the supreme, neither affliction is of use,
nor do friends provide assistance, nor wealth, nor kinsmen;
there is no movement of hands and feet, nor travel to another land.
Or rather, that state is not to be accomplished through the excellence of [external] afflictions nor by resorting to the abodes of heretics;
it is attained solely through the conquest of the mind alone, by means of an action whose purpose is the single goal of the person and whose function is the unification of latent impressions.
That state, which is to be accomplished through solitude alone and is certain to be reached through exclusive inquiry,
is attained by a man who abandons the snares of suffering while seated upon a comfortable seat and reflecting for himself.

Having attained that state, one does not grieve, nor is one born again. The virtuous know that to be the ultimate limit of the essence of all happiness; they call that supreme elixir the unsurpassed outflow [of bliss].
Because all states of existence in both heaven and the human realm are subject to decay,
there is no happiness in these two at all, just as there is no water in mirages.
Therefore, one should contemplate the conquest of the mind, which has tranquility and contentment as its means.
From that, infinite bliss is attained, which is the enjoyment of ultimate peace.
Whether living, moving, wandering, or falling;
whether a *rakṣasa*, a *dānava*, a god, or a human being.

Having attained that supreme bliss born from the pacification of the mind, which is the fruit of the lofty tree of discernment whose blossoms are expanding tranquility— one who, though engaged in worldly affairs, does not accumulate a multitude of duties; ||| MU_2,13.45 ||| [remains] even while intent upon conventional activity, without gathering a mass of tasks.
Like the sun situated in the sky, it neither abandons nor desires anything.
When the mind is perfectly tranquil, utterly pure, rested, and free from delusion;
when it is effortless and devoid of longing for desired objects, it neither yearns nor rejects.
Listen now to these gatekeepers at the door of liberation in their proper order;
by devotion to even one of them, one enters the door of liberation.
The long cycle of saṃsāra is a desert expanse characterized by the states of suffering and defects.

A living being attains coolness through the cooling water of tranquility. Through tranquility, the highest good is attained, for tranquility is the supreme state. Tranquility is auspiciousness; tranquility is peace; tranquility is the warding off of delusion.
For a man who is satisfied by tranquility, whose self is cool and clear,
and whose mind is contented through peace, even an enemy becomes a friend.
Those whose inner disposition is adorned by the moon of tranquility—

The supreme purity of those [virtuous ones] arises like that of the oceans of milk. In the hearts of those virtuous ones, the lotus of tranquility has blossomed within the sheath of the heart-lotuses; for they are like Hari, possessing two lotus-hearts.
Those whose stainless moon-like faces shine with the glory of tranquility—
these lords of their clans, who have surpassed the moon in beauty, are worthy of homage.
The glories existing within the belly of the three worlds do not bring such joy as that [found in them].
Just as the manifestations of tranquility are like the wealth of universal sovereignty,
whatever sufferings, cravings, and unbearable anxieties there may be— all that perishes in those whose minds are peaceful, just as darkness vanishes before the suns.

For the mind of all beings follows after serenity; it does not do so toward the moon as it does toward a person who is tranquil, full of curiosity, and possessed of friendliness toward all creatures. (MU 2.13.57)
In a virtuous person, the supreme reality becomes manifest by itself. Just as with a mother, all beings— whether harsh or gentle— attain a state of trust toward one who is endowed with tranquility.
A person does not attain such happiness through the drinking of elixirs nor by the embrace of Fortune as they do through inner tranquility—
[happiness] which is otherwise enveloped by all manner of mental and physical afflictions and assailed by the triple bond of craving.
O Rāghava, comfort the mind with the sprinkling of the nectar of tranquility.

Whatever you do and whatever you eat, when performed with an intellect cooled by tranquility, that will taste exceedingly sweet and delicious to you, O dear one; nothing else can be so in the mind. (MU 2.13.61–62)
O Rāghava, I believe that even severed limbs grow back again for one whose mind has attained such bliss as comes from bathing in the nectar-essence of tranquility.
Neither Piśācas, nor Rākṣasas, nor Daityas, nor enemies can harm him.
Tigers, serpents, and other such creatures do not hate one who is endowed with tranquility;
nor do sufferings pierce one whose every limb is well-armored by the nectar-like mail of peace, just as arrows cannot penetrate a diamond stone.

A king, even when surrounded by his ministers and the women of his inner apartments, does not shine as much as he does when adorned with tranquility through a balanced and healthy mode of conduct. Furthermore, people do not experience such satisfaction upon seeing something dearer than their own life.
He who conducts himself well with a conduct that is impartial and tranquil, which brings peace to people upon seeing it and inspires confidence—
only he lives here in this world, and no other.
When one who is undisturbed in mind and tranquil performs a virtuous deed,
all these beings born of reality rejoice in it entirely—
whether they have heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled what is auspicious or inauspicious.
He who neither rejoices nor desponds is said to be at peace.
He who is equal toward all states of being, neither longing for nor rejecting them,
having conquered his senses through effort— he is said to be at peace.
He whose mind is as clear as the orb of the moon and remains undisturbed even in death, festivals, or battles—he is called "peaceful.
Even when standing, he is as if not standing; he neither rejoices nor is he provoked to anger.

He whose mind is as if in deep sleep and who remains established in his own nature is called "peaceful. He whose joyful gaze extends toward all people, blessed with the flow of the nectar of immortality, is called "peaceful."

He whose actions are seen with a clear and pure intellect, such that they are the same within as they are without, is called "peaceful. Even amidst calamities of endless duration, even when the eons are burning at their end.
He whose mind is not attached to trivial things is said to be peaceful.
He who has attained inner coolness and does not sink into worldly objects,
who engages in daily affairs without being deluded— he is said to be peaceful.
He whose mind, though constantly engaged in its own activities, remains ever like space and incurs no stain— that one is called "peaceful.
Among ascetics, the learned, officiating priests, and kings—
Among those who are powerful and rich in virtues, it is the one possessed of tranquility alone who shines.
For the great ones, whose minds are devoted to tranquility and who abound in virtues,
bliss arises from the heart like moonlight from the cold-rayed moon.
Peace, the glorious one, shines forth as the boundary of all multitudes of virtues, the exclusive ornament of manliness, and the place of fearlessness in times of distress.
Having taken recourse to peace— the immortal, unshakable, supreme state cherished by the noble ones— they have gone to the highest goal.
O son of Raghu, like those of great majesty, follow that very same sequence for the sake of success.
The fourteenth canto, titled "The Description of Tranquility."
Vasiṣṭha said:
One who knows the cause should, with a mind purified by the stainless understanding of the scriptures and with a self-restrained soul, engage in inquiry.
Having attained sharpness through reflection, the intellect perceives the supreme state;
for reflection is indeed the great medicine for the disease of long-lasting saṃsāra. Saṃsāra is a forest of calamities, its form overspread with the blossoming of endless desires.
That which has been cut by the saw of discernment never grows again.
O one of great wisdom, in delusions, the loss of kinsmen, calamities, and errors— in all such circumstances, discernment is indeed the refuge of the virtuous.
Without discernment, there is no means for the pacification of suffering;
through discernment, the intellect of the wise abandons the unwholesome and attains the wholesome.
Strength, intelligence, vigor, resolve, and the fruit of action—these all depend upon it.
All these bear fruit for the wise man through discernment alone.
Relying upon extensive discernment— the great lamp that distinguishes the appropriate from the inappropriate and the means of accomplishing one's desires— one may cross the ocean of saṃsāra.
The noble lion of inquiry, being a pure self, tears asunder the great elephant of delusion which has lacerated the lotus of the heart.
Fools, by the power of time, have here reached the supreme state.
That is the unsurpassed manifestation of the lamp of inquiry.
Sovereign kingdoms, abundant wealth, expansive enjoyment, and eternal liberation—
these, O Rāghava, are the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree of inquiry.
Those thoughts of the great here that delight in solitude do not sink in adversity, like gourds in water.
Those who conduct their affairs with an intellect that captivates through the arising of inquiry—
For they become the vessels for exceedingly noble fruits.

But the flower-clusters of those who dwell in the forest of the fool’s heart— those who obstruct the expansion of hope and are like *karañja* trees that yield no reflection— are the ways of suffering.
O Rāghava, may that sleep— stained by the soot of delusion, possessing the fragrance of wine, and consisting of a lack of discernment— come to an end for you.
Even in great calamities or long durations, a man who is devoted to right discernment [remains steadfast].
He does not sink into delusions, like a mass of light in the midst of darkness.
He in whose clear lake of the mind the multitude of lotuses of inquiry has surely blossomed shines like the Himavat mountain.
For one whose intellect is devoid of discernment and has fallen into dullness,
suffering arises like a thunderbolt from the moon, or like a phantom from a child.
It is a termite mound for the thicket of sorrows, a honey-spring for the withered creepers of misfortune.
O Rāma, that lowest of men who lacks discrimination must be abandoned from afar.
Whatever undertakings are wicked, whatever conduct is evil, and whatever anxieties are base—
these appear through lack of inquiry like ghosts in the darkness.
O scion of the Raghus, keep far from me one who lacks discernment, who resembles a solitary, withered tree, and who is incapable of performing virtuous deeds;
for when a person’s mind is secluded and freed from the helplessness of desire, it becomes tranquil.
One attains supreme bliss within oneself, like the full moon;
the discernment that has arisen thoroughly cools the entire body and adorns it exceedingly,
like a fresh moonlight adorning the world.
The investigation into the intellect, which is the white fly-whisk for the banner of ultimate reality,
shines for a living being like the moon in the night;
the states of being, made beautiful by investigation, illuminate the ten directions.

Those whose fear and disease of rebirth have been shattered shine like the sun. The life-robbing vampire imagined by the child’s own deluded mind dissolves through inquiry, just as it does in the darkness of night.

All worldly phenomena are charming only so long as they are not investigated; their true existence is non-existent, for they disintegrate upon analysis. This world, imagined by the delusion of a person’s own mind, bestows no small amount of suffering.
The long-standing vampire of saṃsāra dissolves through inquiry.
Know this state of absolute liberation (*kevalībhāva*)— equanimous, pure, unobstructed, infinite,
and independent— to be the fruit of the fierce tree of inquiry.
By him, through his steady composure and the vast, manifest splendor of his majesty,
a state of desirelessness arises like the coolness produced by the risen moon;
he is seated within the virtuous mind, which serves as a great medicine for the fever of anxiety.
Because it bestows the state of supremacy, one neither desires it nor abandons it.
That mind, having attained a vast manifestation with that as its constant support,
neither sets nor rises, like the sky which is an exceedingly expansive interior.
It neither abandons nor takes up; it neither suffers nor attains peace.
Merely observing like a witness, it remains within itself as the world.
It does not attain peace, nor does it abide within, nor does it abide without.
He does not cling to inaction, nor does he sink into action;
he remains indifferent toward what has passed and follows what has arrived.
Neither agitated nor excessively unagitated, he shines like the full ocean.
With such a mind, the great-souled ones of noble intent—
those yogins liberated while living— indeed wander about in this world;
having dwelt for a very long time, those steadfast ones remain for as long as they desire.
Having cast off the body at the end, they attain the pervasive state of absolute oneness.
Even in times of calamity, a wise person should strive with effort and by means of remedies to reflect: "Who am I? And whose is this cycle of existence? (MU 2.14.36–37)
O Raghava, a king understands the doubt regarding the difficulty of a task—
whether it will be fruitless or fruitful— only through deliberation and not otherwise.
The established doctrines of the Vedas and Vedanta are the cause of stability.
They are determined through investigation, just as the features of the earth are discerned at night by means of a lamp.
Even that which is obscured, the eye of investigation— beautiful and unclouded— beholds it clearly, even amidst thick darkness, provided it is not blinded by excessive light.
For the one who is blind to discernment is like one born blind; such a person of evil intellect is pitiable to all.
But he whose soul is discernment and who possesses the divine eye triumphs over all things.
That which consists of the Supreme Self must be protected, for it is the sole means to supreme bliss.
The wondrous power of discernment must not be abandoned for even a single moment.
A person who is beautiful through discernment is pleasing even to the great, just as a fully ripened mango fruit is delightful.
Men whose minds delight in reflection and who have known the upward path do not fall again and again into the many pits of suffering;
neither does the sick man nor one shattered by hundreds of misfortunes lament in such a manner.
One whose self is destroyed by a lack of inquiry laments like an ignorant man. Better is the state of a worm in the mud, better is being a thorn in a pit,
better is dwelling in a blind cave, than the lack of inquiry for a human being.
One should abandon that which is the abode of all misfortune, despised by all the virtuous, the ultimate limit of all instability, and devoid of discernment; rather,
the great-souled one should always be engaged in inquiry.
For those falling into the dark well of worldly existence, discernment is indeed the support.
By supporting oneself with one's own self through discernment,
one may cause the deer of one's own mind to cross over the ocean of delusion that is saṃsāra.
"Who am I? How has this fault called saṃsāra come upon me?"—this investigation according to reason is what is called *vicāra*.
[Otherwise,] it is merely for the sake of long-lasting suffering, like the talk of one blind with delusion leading another blind man.
A heart of stone has been made of the wicked-minded and thoughtless man.
For here, O Raghava, among those who perceive through the grasping and abandoning of existence and non-existence,
no reality whatsoever is properly known except through inquiry.
Through inquiry, reality is known; from reality comes rest in the Self.
Then, when the mind is stilled, all suffering is utterly destroyed. Indeed, the fruitfulness of actions on this earth becomes manifest through the highest [inquiry].
May this very vision of clear discernment, when examined, shine forth even for you who are established in tranquility.
The fifteenth canto, titled "The Description of Discernment."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Contentment is indeed the highest good; contentment is called happiness.
O destroyer of enemies, one who is contented attains supreme rest.

For the virtuous who are happy in the sovereignty of contentment and whose minds have long found rest, even a universal empire is like a blade of withered straw. O Rāma, the intellect possessed of contentment [finds no pleasure] in the activities of worldly existence.

Undisturbed even by adversities, they are never pained. For those who have attained supreme satisfaction by drinking the nectar of contentment, even incomparable worldly prosperity acts as a poison toward them.
These waves of nectar-like flavor do not satisfy one as much as contentment,
which possesses a sweet taste and destroys all defects. Having abandoned the longing for what has not been attained, one who has reached equanimity toward what has been obtained—
One who is free from weariness regarding the unseen is called "content" within this world.
As long as the mind does not attain contentment within itself by means of the Self,
calamities continue to arise like creepers from a forest of the mind.
The mind, cooled by contentment and possessing the vision of pure gnosis,
attains full blossoming like a lotus under the rays of the sun. But when the mind is overwhelmed by the helplessness of desire and devoid of contentment, it withers away.
Knowledge does not reflect [in one] like a face in a withered mirror.
The lotus of man does not undergo contraction through the night of dense ignorance for him in whom the sun of contentment has eternally risen.
Even though he possesses nothing, that person enjoys the happiness of sovereignty,
for his mind is contented and liberated from mental and physical afflictions;
he does not long for what has not been attained, and he enjoys what has been obtained in due order.
O gentle one, he who possesses good conduct is called "contented.
In the mouth of that great person, whose mind is full and who is completely satisfied by contentment,
splendor shines forth like that of the pure Ocean of Milk.
Relying fully upon perfection within one's very own self by means of the self itself,
one should abandon craving everywhere through human effort;
for one who is filled with the nectar of contentment, there is naturally a coolness within the heart.
Stability comes permanently to one who is not empty [of contentment], just as it does to the moon;
to him whose mind is nourished by contentment, great riches approach like servants,
having entered into a state of servitude, as they do unto a king.
When the person remains established in the self by means of the self alone— pure and contented—
all mental afflictions are pacified instantly, like dust in the rainy season.
[This occurs] through that which is eternally cool and free from blemish.

Through pure conduct, a person shines with fullness like the moon. Just as people find satisfaction by beholding a face beautiful in its equanimity, they do not find such satisfaction through the acquisition of wealth.

O descendant of Raghu, even the great sages who roam the heavens bow down to that stainless king of men, who is adorned here by his equanimity, his wisdom, and his possession of virtues. This concludes the canto titled "The Description of Contentment."
The Sixteenth Chapter.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O one of great intelligence, [this is] especially for men in crossing over the cycle of existence.

In every way, association with the virtuous benefits one here in this world; it is truly a meeting with the good. Those great-souled ones who protect the auspicious flower of discernment born from the tree of association with the virtuous are the vessels for the glory of its fruit.
The empty becomes crowded; even death turns into a festival;
misfortune appears like prosperity in the assembly of learned men.
Frost is to the lotus-pond of adversity, and delusion is the wind that brings a veil of mist.
Victorious in this world is the one thing: the company of the virtuous.
Know that the company of the virtuous is the supreme nourishment of the intellect, the felling of the tree of ignorance, and the complete departure from mental anxieties.
From association with the virtuous, the supreme lamp of discernment arises—
truly as enchanting and radiant as a cluster of blossoms from an *aśoka* tree.
It leads to a bliss that is free from danger, free from affliction, and eternally abundant.
The riches of association with the virtuous bestow the unsurpassed [state].
Even by men who have fallen into most miserable conditions and reached a state of helplessness, association with the virtuous must not be abandoned even slightly. (MU 2.16.7–8)
In this world, association with the virtuous is a bright lamp for the auspicious path of the righteous;
it dispels the darkness within the heart and is the radiance of the sun of knowledge.
He who has bathed in the Ganges of association with the virtuous—cool and pure—[is truly purified].

What is the use of gifts for him, what use are sacred fords, what use are austerities, or what use are sacrifices? O sinless one, if there exist virtuous men who are free from passion, whose doubts are severed, and whose knots are untied, what is the need for the accumulation of austerities and pilgrimages?
Those whose minds are at rest are indeed worthy of worship with the utmost effort;
for the virtuous are to be gazed upon by the wise just as jewels are sought by a poor man. The intellect of the wise is graced by the beauty of association with the good.
She always shines like a lotus amidst a host of celestial nymphs; by that fortunate one, whose pure grace is thus manifest, the pinnacle of that state has been reached,
since he has never abandoned the company of the virtuous.

Those who have severed the knots, who know that reality, who are virtuous, and who are honored by all— these should be served by every means, for they are the very means for crossing the ocean of existence.
Indeed, these [saints] have turned the fires of hell into dry fuel that has been completely consumed.
By those who have seen with ease that the virtuous are like water for the fire of hell,
the treacherous delusion— that poverty, death, and suffering are real—
is completely extinguished by the medicine of association with the holy.
Contentment, association with the virtuous, inquiry, and likewise tranquility—these alone are the means for men to cross the ocean of worldly existence.
Contentment is the supreme gain; association with the good is the supreme goal.
Discernment is supreme knowledge, and tranquility is indeed supreme happiness.
These four pure means exist for the shattering of worldly existence;
those by whom they have been practiced have crossed over the ocean of existence, which has delusion as its waters.
O best among the wise, when even one of these has been cultivated and its stainless emergence attained, all four are indeed considered cultivated;
for each one is like the source of birth for all the others.
Therefore, for the sake of complete success, one should diligently rely upon a single [practice].
Association with the virtuous, contentment, and discernment proceed without effort toward pure tranquility, like currents in the ocean.
In a person who possesses association with the virtuous, discernment, contentment, and tranquility proceed just as fortunes do for one who has taken refuge under a wish-fulfilling tree.
Discernment, tranquility, and association with the virtuous [abide] in a human being endowed with contentment.
Just as beauty and other virtues manifest in the full moon,
contentment, tranquility, and discernment flourish in one who possesses right understanding and reflection,
like the glories of victory in an excellent minister.
Therefore, O descendant of Raghu, having conquered one of these [faculties]— the mind— which is eternal through human effort, one should diligently cultivate virtue.
Relying on supreme human exertion and having subdued the elephant that is the mind, one should strive for excellence.

As long as not even a single virtue has been attained, there is no supreme state. O Rāma, with manly effort, grinding tooth against tooth, exert yourself until your mind is fully intent upon the acquisition of virtue.
Whether you are a god, a yakṣa, a man, or even a tree,
O mighty-armed one, as long as this single fruit has not ripened and attained its full power, there is no remedy whatsoever for you here.
All defects of one whose mind is free from poison perish quickly.
When a quality increases, qualities that bring about the destruction of defects increase;
when a defect increases, defects that destroy qualities increase.

For in this great forest of the mind, the swift river of latent impressions (vāsanā), with its vast banks of the auspicious and inauspicious, flows constantly among living beings. Indeed, by one's own effort, wherever that river is cast down, [there it remains].
It flows toward the shore by that very [means]; do as you wish.

O noble-minded one, by the speed of human effort, gradually lead the great river of your own nature—which has reached the auspicious bank—to the forest of the mind; for by that means, you will not be carried away even slightly in this world.
The seventeenth canto, titled "The Description of Right Conduct," by Vasiṣṭha.
Thus, O Rāghava, you who possess such self-seclusion are worthy of hearing the words of knowledge, just as a king is worthy of hearing the discourse on statesmanship; for you are pure, noble-minded,
and a vessel for pure wisdom.
Free from attachment to the insentient and worthy like the sky for the autumnal moon,
you are graced by this unbroken splendor of virtues;
listen now to these words about to be spoken, which remove the delusion of the mind.
This effort to hear [this teaching] belongs to that person for whom the wish-fulfilling tree of merit stands bowed under the weight of its fruit, which brings about the liberation of living beings;
it is for those who are purifying, noble, and who bestow the singular realization of the supreme awakening.
One who is worthy becomes a vessel for words for the sake of prosperity, not one who is base.
This compendium, which sets forth the means to liberation, is equal in essence to the *Sāra*;
consisting of thirty-two thousand [verses], it bestows nirvāṇa upon those who know it.
Just as light proceeds from a lamp that has been lit while one is awake—
even against one's will— so too shall nirvāṇa arise through this [practice].
Whether known by oneself or heard from another, it bestows happiness simply by the cessation of delusion.
The word of the authoritative teacher, when described, is immediately like a river of nectar.
Just as the delusion of a snake in a rope perishes through inspection,
so too does the suffering of saṃsāra come to rest through this contemplation.
In this work, there are six chapters composed of logically consistent statements of meaning, each formulated individually, and containing the essence of illustrative examples and well-spoken verses.
The first chapter is proclaimed as that named "Detachment" (Vairāgya).
By means of which dispassion increases, like a tree in a desert through irrigation;
when that text of one thousand verses is reflected upon within the heart, a pure radiance arises, as if from a polished gem. (MU 2.17.11–12)
Thereafter, a chapter titled "The Conduct of Those Seeking Liberation" was composed;
it consists of about a thousand verses and is beautiful with its string of well-spoken words.
For it describes the true nature of those men who seek liberation.

Thus it is understood that one who possesses such a nature is fit for liberation. Now follows the section on origination, consisting of illustrative narratives and containing five thousand verses, which sets forth the doctrine of consciousness (vijñāna).
The *jāgatī* is the splendor of the seer and the seen, consisting of the forms of "I," "you," and so forth;
it is described as being neither arisen nor as if arisen, wherein this entire world is understood within the hearing upon that [Reality] being heard. MU 2.17.16.
That [world], along with ourselves and you, in its full extent, including the space of the world and its mountains—
devoid of any grasping at material form, without a foundation, and without mountains,
free from the elements such as earth— is like a city existing only as a mental construction.
It is like an entity perceived in a dream, as expansive as a kingdom of the mind,
resembling a city of the Gandharvas— an apprehension devoid of objective reality;
it appears like the illusion of two moons and is spread out like the water of a mirage.
Resembling a mountain shimmering on the ocean, yet devoid of the attainment of truth;
appearing like a demon of mental delusion, yet seedless and radiant;
resembling the flash of meaning in a story, and like a string of pearls in the sky.
Just as the state of being a bracelet [arises] in gold, just as the state of being a wave [arises] in water,
and just as blueness arises in the sky— though it is non-existent— in the same way,
that which is without a wall and devoid of color is perceived as captivating to the mind.
Whether in a dream or in the sky, a painting is a non-action yet shines for a long time.
Just as a non-fire assumes the state of fire in the case of a painted fire,
so too does [the intellect] assume the unreal nature of the world in the form of words and their meanings.
It rose up like a stone leaf adorned with a garland of wave-lotuses,
appearing like a heap of filth produced from the grinding of the *cakras* and *śūtkāras*.
It was like a sapless forest in summer, its leaves withered and fallen away.
It resembles a frantic dance at the time of death, yet it brings forth the laughter of a stone woman;
it is like a solitary dance within a house of darkness, a madman’s gesture.
It is the autumnal sky of pure consciousness, from which the mist of ignorance has been stilled.
It is as if carved upon a pillar, or depicted on a painted wall;
it is fashioned from clay, yet it possesses consciousness or lacks it.
Thus, the fourth section, "The Nature of Stability" (sthitiprakaraṇa), is fully established.
Three thousand verses consisting of well-spoken narratives—
thus has the world, whose nature is the sense of "I," reached its state of existence,
fully developed through the sequence of seer and seen; so it has been described here.
"This delusion of the world, radiant throughout the expanse of the ten directions,
has thus come to increase"— this is what is said there for a long time.
Then follows the *Upaśāntiprakaraṇa* consisting of five thousand [verses].
The fifth purifying [chapter] is proclaimed, beautiful through the lineage of sages.
"This world, I, and you—this delusion has arisen;
thus it is pacified"—this is what is told in this compendium of verses.
When the section on tranquility is heard, the cycle of existence subsides;
though perception remains somewhat clear due to delusion,
it becomes reduced to a hundredth part, its form being that of stilled error.
Residing in a mind occupied by another's volition, it is unreal like the splendor of a city [in the sky];
it is unobtainable, like the cries of a battle in a dream occurring beside one;
and it is like the terrifying sound of a thunderbolt from a cloud whose fury has subsided.
She is like a city created by the imagination of a forgotten dream;
she is like the dark-bodied maiden of a future city’s garden festival;
she is like the experience of the meaning of a fierce tale being told by a tongue that is about to perish.
It was like a wall covered by a painting whose colors had not yet been applied;
it resembled a city of imagination that is being forgotten;
it possessed the indistinct form of a supreme, unarisen dance occurring in all seasons.
Coloring with the essence of spring through the form of future excellent flowers,
it is like a river of calm water whose surging waves are hidden within;
therefore, the sixth chapter, called "Nirvāṇa," has been proclaimed.
The remaining portion of the text should be known as its extent, which bestows great meaning.
When that [text] is understood, the listener becomes one who has attained nirvāṇa, with all conceptual constructions stilled;
he is the self whose nature is the light of consciousness beyond the object of thought, the self of pure awareness, free from all affliction.
Transparent as the sheath of the supreme ether, with all wandering through existence stilled;
having brought the journey of the world to its conclusion, he remains well-established, having accomplished what was to be done;
like a diamond pillar amidst all extensive undertakings, he is like the sky itself.
Fully satiated by having swallowed the entire web of the world exactly as it exists,
with all perceptions of form, mental constructs, and the elements of space completely vanished;
he is liberated from the states of cause and effect, agent, rejection, and acceptance.
Possessing a body yet bodiless, involved in saṃsāra yet free from transmigration, consisting of consciousness alone, he is like the interior of a solid stone;
though the sun of consciousness shines in the world, it is as if within the depths of darkness.
Though his nature is that of supreme illumination, he has, as it were, entered into a state of ultimate blindness;
his wicked play of worldly existence is checked, the poison of his desires is destroyed,
the vampire of egoism is lost, and though possessing a body, he is bodiless.
On the tip of some single hair-pore,
this splendor of the world remains for him, like a bee on a flower somewhere upon Mount Mahāmeru;
within every single atom, in the hollow of the space of consciousness.
Having created them, he sustains and beholds thousands of world-glories.

O Great-minded One, even by hundreds of thousands of Lakṣmīs belonging to Hari, Hara, and Brahmā, the expansion of the heart of one who possesses liberation cannot be equaled; alas, there is surely no such expansion for that which is insubstantial.
The eighteenth canto, titled "Description of the Occasion," by Vasiṣṭha.
Within this very measure of consciousness, the supreme awakening arises,
just as a certain and excellent fruit inevitably follows from a sown seed. Even human effort is to be accepted if the scripture provides the awakening through reasoning.
One who adheres solely to logic must abandon even the words of a seer (*ārṣa*) if they are otherwise; one should accept that which is joined with reason even from a child,
while rejecting anything else like a blade of grass— even if it was spoken by the Lotus-born One (*padmajanman*).
Who would instruct that passionate man who, thinking "this is my father's well," drinks the bitter water of a pit while abandoning the Ganges water standing right before him?
Just as when the dawn has broken, light will surely follow.
Or rather, within this very measure of consciousness, one's own discernment will likewise arise—
either from hearing it from the mouth of a wise man, or by having understood it oneself,
or through gradual inquiry once an impression has been formed in the intellect.
First, there arises within him a highly refined command of speech,
pure and lofty like a garland of pearls, which serves as the ornament for the assembly hall;
thereafter, there arises a supreme dispassion, endowed with the quality of greatness.
By that [wisdom], even kings and pythons become affectionate;
a man who knows what precedes and follows becomes wise in all matters,
just as one with good eyesight holding a lamp in the night [discerns] objects.
Defects such as greed, delusion, and the like gradually diminish sufficiently,
just as the mists of autumn near its end fade from the quarters of the sky;
the intellects require nothing more than the practice of discernment.
No action bears any fruit without diligent practice. The mind attains clarity like a great lake in autumn;
it achieves supreme equanimity like the ocean when the Mandara mountain has ceased its churning.
Free from internal darkness, like a vajra-flash that has cast away the veil of gloom,
wisdom— which discerns the true nature of things— blazes forth intensely.
Wretchedness, poverty, suffering, and the like are seen as having their inner essence revealed.
The arrows do not cut his vital points, as if he were clad in armor;
the terrifying fears of cyclic existence do not tear at his heart, for even when standing before him, they cannot affect the wise man, just as rats cannot affect a great boulder.
"How could there be a beginning for birth and action, whether they belong to fate or to human effort?"—
such a multitude of doubts is pacified, just as darkness is dispelled by the day;
for in every way, attachment to all things comes to rest.
When the night has passed as it were and the light of wisdom has arrived, there arises in the one who investigates:
a depth like that of the ocean, a stability as firm as Mount Meru,
and an inner coolness like that of the moon.
That state of liberation while living gradually reaches its full fruition for that yogi who has stilled all mental constructs, entering him as a pure,
supremely illuminating, and wise clarity that remains cool toward all objects.
It attains supreme illumination, like the full lunar light.
When the sun of discernment rises in the stainless sky of the heart, shining with the light of tranquility,
the deceptive banners of strife that create a multitude of misfortunes no longer arise.

The cravings subside, attain purity, and remain gentle and well-restrained; they become motionless and inert, like a mass of clouds in autumn. Cruel vulgarism, which performs all manner of base acts, turns away.
Like the wretched countenances of *piśācas* at the break of day,
mental afflictions (*ādhayaḥ*) do not ravish the intellect that is firmly fixed upon the wall of Dharma and has mounted the yoke of fortitude, just as winds cannot uproot a painted creeper.
A living being does not fall into the pit whose nature is attachment to sense objects; for who indeed, once they have known the path, would run headlong into a chasm?
This applies when one's action is not in conflict with the true scriptures and the conduct of the virtuous.
The intellect rejoices in whatever it has attained, like a virtuous woman in the courtyard of the inner apartments.
With an intellect free from the notion of creation, it perceives within each and every one of the atoms found throughout millions of worlds the creations situated therein.
For a person whose inner organ is purified by the realization of the means to liberation,
the flood of enjoyments neither causes distress nor brings joy at any time.
Within every single atom, multitudes of creations arise without restraint.
He beholds those who fall and spring up like waves upon the water;
he neither hates actions that have begun nor longs for those that have ceased. Though awakened, he is like an unawakened tree regarding his duties.
He appears like an ordinary person, conforming to whatever circumstances he encounters;
yet, in the attainment of desired or undesired results, his heart remains unconquered.
Having understood this entire scripture, whether by reciting it or by discerning its meaning, [one attains this state].
This is indeed experienced, and not merely stated like a boon or a curse.
This scripture is easy to understand, adorned with various ornaments;
it is a beautiful poem, dense with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and instructive through its illustrative examples.
One who knows even a little of the words and their meanings understands this by himself;
however, he who does not know this by himself must hear it from a learned teacher.
When this has been heard, reflected upon, and realized, [the fruit of] austerity, meditation, recitation, and so forth [is attained].
But for the attainment of liberation here, nothing else is required;
for this [attainment] comes from the repeated and intense study of this scripture,
preceded by wisdom and the purification of the mind.
The arrogant demon of the seer and the seen, manifesting as "I" and "the world," subsides of its own accord and without obstacle, just as a ghost vanishes at the rising of the sun.
The delusion consisting of "the world" and "I," though seemingly established, subsides [upon realization].

The delusion of a dream, once fully understood, no longer delights us at all. Just as joy and sorrow caused by an imaginary city do not afflict a person, so too the internal error of the world does not trouble one who has fully realized its nature.
Just as a painted snake, once fully understood, does not cause fear of a snake,
so too a visible snake, once fully understood, does not bestow pleasure or pain.
Through thorough understanding, the "snakeness" of the painted snake perishes.
In that very same way, saṃsāra remains as it is and yet becomes tranquil.
O you who are impatient with the sprouts of the mind’s flowers, there might be some disturbance;
but upon attaining the state of ultimate reality, there is no disturbance for us.
The movement of limbs occurs when crushing the petals of a flower;
however, in this state, there is only the awareness of pure consciousness, not the awareness of the parts of the body.
This happens for one seated in a comfortable posture, eating as is appropriate.
One should not remain among those whose conduct is contrary to righteous practice; rather,
one should dwell in happiness by reflecting upon this scripture— or others— as well, according to the opportunity, according to the place, and through association with the virtuous as it may occur.
Great awakening to knowledge, which brings peace to saṃsāra, is attained by him through which he no longer undergoes the crushing of the machine of rebirth.
Those beings who, having obtained enjoyments, remain fixed in the flavor of them only to this extent—
Those lowest of beings, the worms in the excrement of their own mothers, are not even worth mentioning.
Now, O Rāghava, listen as I describe this expansion of knowledge, which is the most essential core of the intellect.
Listen now in detail to that by which this scripture is heard,
and by which definition its true meaning is investigated;
[it is] that by which, in this world, there is an understanding of an unperceived object through the perception of another object.
The wise know that to be an illustration which yields the fruit of assisting awakening.
Without an illustration, O Rāma, a novel matter is not understood,
just as in the night one cannot perceive the vessels and furnishings in a house without a lamp.

O descendant of Kakutstha, whatever analogies I have used here to awaken your understanding, all of them possess causes; for that which is to be attained is indeed without cause. The relationship of cause and effect has been described through the comparison of the illustrative examples and the subjects illustrated.
Except for the Supreme Brahman, this [nature] exists in all things indeed.
For when an illustration for the instruction on Brahman is stated here, it is accepted as having a commonality with only one part of that [Brahman]. (MU 2.18.53–54)
Whatever illustration is given here for the realization of the reality of Brahman,
each of them should be understood as pertaining to a world seen in a dream.
This being so, how can that which possesses form exist within the formless Brahman?
Regarding the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the fallacious arguments of the ignorant do not arise;
nor does any other [fallacy], such as the unestablished (*asiddha*) or the contradictory (*viruddha*), emerge when the example is scrutinized, because the world is like a dream. (MU 2.18.56–57)

The unreal is that which does not exist in the past or the future; the present is analyzed as being like the waking state, while the dream state is established as undisturbed by everyone, even down to children.
[This is known] through dreams, volitions, meditations, boons, curses, medicinal herbs, and so forth.
Those things which are the subject matters here serve as examples, because the state of the world is of that very nature.
As for the other treatises composed by the author as means to liberation,
this single system alone is the one established therein for the awakening of what is to be known.
And that the world has the nature of a dream will be understood from the sacred scriptures;
it cannot be stated quickly, for speech indeed proceeds sequentially.
The world is comparable to a dream, a mental construction, a city of the gods, or a vision in meditation.
Since only those [examples] are seen here, and not others, they appear as such;
for when a non-cause is used as an illustration to bring about the understanding of a cause,
it is impossible for there to be complete similarity in all respects due to the delusions of comparison.
The wise person, free from dispute, must accept that the object of comparison shares a single quality with the standard of comparison in order to achieve understanding; for indeed,
in the perception of an object, it is said to be like a lamp that provides nothing more than a mere illumination.

Not even a small amount of anything—such as a vessel, oil, or wick—is employed [in this case]. Rather, my dear, the means of comparison (*upamāna*) brings about the cognition of the object of comparison (*upameya*) because it shares the same properties in one respect, just as a lamp illuminates an object by means of its radiance. (MU 2.18.65–66)
When the awakening of understanding arises through even a mere portion of an illustration,

the determination of the meaning of the Great Sentence (mahāvākya) should be grasped as something to be adopted. One must not, having fallen into the state of a sophist, destroy that awakened consciousness.
Because they involve the denial of direct experience and consist of impure conceptualizations,
[these views] have become mere verbal proliferation among people like us, even though they are prompted by inquiry into experience.
Furthermore, even if another statement were uttered by a woman or were Vedic in origin, it would still be merely the prattling of words and not authoritative scripture (āgama).

Our conviction is indeed this: since the unification of all scriptures into a single voice has borne fruit, for us there exists no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) other than that consciousness which is nourished by its own limbs consisting of the scriptures whose content is merely phenomenal. This concludes the chapter titled "The Determination of Means of Valid Cognition and Examples."
The nineteenth canto: Vasiṣṭha says:
In similes, a state of shared characteristics with the most distinguished part is apprehended.
If there were total similarity between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison, what distinction would remain?
Through the knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures on the realization of the single Self— derived from the Buddha as an exemplar—
and through the direct realization of the meaning of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya), peace is called Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, enough with these outbursts of conceptualizing the illustrative example and the thing illustrated;
by whatever reasoning one may, one should quickly take recourse in the meaning of the Great Saying.
Know that peace is the supreme good; one should be diligent in attaining it.

"Rice to be eaten has been obtained; what is the use of conceptualizations regarding its perfection? By those who seek to understand the cause, that which is not the cause is compared for the sake of awakening, using analogies that resemble the object of comparison only in certain respects."
One whose soul is devoid of discernment should not remain here amidst enjoyments,
like a blind frog grown fat within the belly of a stone.
Through examples and reasonings, one should strive to abandon all that is contrary [to liberation] and desire the other.
One should be possessed of discernment and be endowed with the meaning of the treatises on peace; through the scriptures,
tranquility, gentleness, wisdom, and association with those who know them,
one should from time to time perform the practice of acquiring wealth in accordance with the Dharma.
The wise person should investigate until he attains within himself that rest known as the fourth state (turya)— the peace from which there is no further destruction.
For one who is endowed with rest in the fourth state and has crossed over the ocean of existence, [there is liberation].
Whether living or dead, whether a householder or an ascetic,
he has no concern with what is done or left undone, nor with the fluctuations of the Vedas and Smṛtis;
like the ocean without Mount Mandara, he remains as he is.

The similarity of the objects of comparison with the objects of comparison must be understood through a single aspect for the sake of awakening to what is to be known; one should not remain fickle in raising objections. By whatever means possible, you should quickly understand that which is indeed to be understood.
Therefore, those who are agitated and eager to raise objections do not perceive that which leads to liberation.
When the reality— which is the very nature of experience— rests within the heart as the space of consciousness,
he who asks about what is not a true concern is called one who is "eager to raise objections."
The ignorant one, conceptualizing cognition through portions of his own conceit,
defiles his internal awakening just as a snake defiles its own pure mouth;
he is the locus of all existing means of valid knowledge, like the ocean is for waters.
"O Rāma, listen: in this world, perception alone is the single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The wise know that direct awareness, which is the essence of all objects, is supreme.
That which is established in relation to that [awareness] is indeed declared to be perception."
That which consists of experience, feeling,
and cognition as they truly exist is here given the name "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), and that very thing is the living soul (*jīva*).
That itself is consciousness (*saṃvit*), and it further consists of the nature of the notion of "I-ness" (*ahantā*).
That consciousness by which it arises is known as "the object" (padārtha).
Through delusions such as conceptualization and discursive thought,
it manifests as the world with its various successions, just as water appears as waves and the like.
Previously, at the beginning of creation, having first manifested as a causeless state through the play of creation,
it itself became the manifest cause within its own self; thus,
although the causality of this individual soul (jīva) was non-existent, it came to exist through investigation.

As if it were real, the perfection of the world’s form has attained manifestation within this [intellect]. But inquiry itself, having destroyed its own nature— which is the meaning of the negative particle *san*— quickly brings about the supreme state as a direct perception.
When even the act of discernment, upon being scrutinized, no longer perceives a self,
then that which is beyond description remains as the supreme reality.
When the mind is free from striving and stilled, along with those functions of the intellect and the senses, [the supreme remains].

There is no purpose here for those things performed by anyone, nor for those not performed, because of the absence of mental cultivation. When the mind is desireless and tranquil, the organs of action do not engage in action and the like at all, like a machine that is not set in motion.
They know that sensation is the cause for the movement of the mental mechanism,
just as a rope is contained within the wooden frame of a ram.
The world is agitated by forms, light, mental attention, objects, and so forth.
Just as there is a vibration within the wind,
so too does the pure perception of the Self of all exist; arising as that very essence,
it shines forth, manifesting forms both internal and external, transcending space and time.
The Seer alone remains, maintaining his own nature while appearing as the manifestation of the visible;
just as his own form shines forth therein, so indeed is it. Just as everything there has, as it were, attained the state of being a mental construction, so too is the Self.
It remains there quickly and shines as if it were that very form.
Because the Seer is the self of all, it is appropriate for the object of sight to appear as if it were the Seer;
but while the state of being a Seer exists when the Seer is present, it does not exist for that which is non-existent.
Therefore, this world remains as the Brahma-cosmos, existing without any other cause;
it is directly perceived as the creator itself, while its constituent parts are free from limiting adjuncts (*anupādhi*).
That which consists of nothing other than its own effort—having cast far away the meaning of the word "destiny" (*daiva*)—[is the true agent].
O virtuous one, that supreme state is indeed attained within by the hero through his own manly effort alone.
First, investigate according to the true and pure teachings of the lineage of teachers,
until you yourself reach that ultimate reality which is pure, awakened, and infinite in form.
The twentieth canto, titled "The Definition of the Means of Valid Cognition," by Vasiṣṭha.
Through association with the noble, through reasoning, and so forth, one should forcibly increase one's wisdom;
from that comes the state of a Great Person by means of the marks of a Great Person.
Whatever person shines here by whatever quality, [that quality he shall attain].
Therefore, for the sake of increasing one's intelligence, one should quickly train in each and every one of those [virtues].
O Rāma, this state of being a Great Person (mahāpuruṣatā), which is characterized by qualities such as tranquility (śama) and the rest,
does not attain perfection for anyone without right knowledge (samyagjñāna).
Through knowledge, the qualities such as tranquility increase by following the path of the virtuous;
they are praiseworthy within, like fresh sprouts from rain.
And through the qualities such as tranquility, supreme knowledge increases.
Just as excellent rain from the clouds brings forth rice, so too do the qualities such as tranquility arise from sacrifices that are essentially material;
and from those qualities like tranquility, knowledge arises.
Thus, knowledge and these qualities mutually increase one another, just as a cloud and a lake augment each other.
Knowledge arises from the conduct of the virtuous, and from knowledge comes the practice of the virtuous;
thus, knowledge and the practice of the virtuous increase through their mutual interaction.
Yet, even one of these two cannot be accomplished by a person in this world.
Just as the joy of singing is accomplished by the female guardian of the *kalama* reeds through her wide-reaching, high-pitched song accompanied by the driving away of birds,
so too [is liberation accomplished] by means of knowledge and the effort of the true person, who, though non-doing, appears as a doer.
In the same way, a man free from desire attains the supreme state.
O descendant of Raghu, this sequence of right conduct has been declared by me;
