now, this sequence of knowledge shall be correctly explained.
This [teaching] brings fame and long life, and bestows the fruits of the goals of human existence;
it should indeed be heard by a wise person from a reliable teacher who has mastered the meaning of the scriptures.
Having heard it, through the clarity of your intellect, you will surely attain the state of the virtuous by its power.
Just as water inevitably becomes clear through contact with the *kataka* nut,
O Sage, so too this mind, having known that which is to be known, goes helplessly to the supreme state;
for that which has been realized as the indivisible, supreme reality never again abandons the state of that realization.
The chapter titled "The Succession of the True Man of Knowledge" is concluded. Section 3: The Chapter on the Conduct of One Seeking Liberation.
Section 4: Origination.
Vasiṣṭha:
Through the radiance of speech, the knower of Brahman perceives Brahman within himself as if in a dream;
let him who knows this very thing by means of its own words and meanings understand it for himself.
By this reasoning, when the entire creation exists within the ether of Brahman, one who is eager to raise objections—asking "What is this? or "To whom does it belong?"—is refuted.
As for me, I shall speak according to my knowledge, according to the reality of things, and in due order.
I shall speak this according to its true nature; let all of it be heard, O wise ones.
One perceives the world as the sky of consciousness, consisting of the body and the mind, like a dream.
The analogies for the dream and the cycle of existence are fully applicable right here within this very context.
Following this treatise consisting of the discourse on the conduct of one seeking liberation, I shall now fully describe this "Treatise on Origination":
This bondage is the existence of the visible; in the absence of the visible, there is no bondage.
But listen now in due order to how this visible world does not truly come into being:
"Whatever is born in the world, that indeed grows; that very same thing attains liberation, or heaven, or even hell. (MU 3.1.6–7)

Therefore, for the sake of your own understanding, I shall first relate that very account of how one enters into the cycle of existence (saṃsṛti) and how it originally arose. O Rāghava, listen briefly to this subject matter of the present treatise.
Thereafter, I shall explain to you in detail whatever you desire.
All this world that is seen, both the stationary and the moving,
perishes at the end of the aeon like a dream in deep sleep.
Then there remains something that is neither light nor pervasive darkness, motionless and profound, ineffable and unmanifest— whatever it may be.
It is called *ṛta*, the Self, the Supreme Brahman, and Truth by the wise.

The name of that Great Self is merely imagined for the sake of conventional usage. Being exactly as he is, that Self shines forth as if it were something else; he enters, as it were, into the state of being a living soul, undergoing the indignities of future names.
Then, having fallen into the agitation of conceptualizing the meaning of the word "jīva," it becomes the mind (manas), which is by nature silent but becomes sluggish through the act of thinking;
through that, it becomes the intellect (manas) [in relation] to the Great Supreme Self.
Like a wave of the ocean, it takes a transient form from that which is stable;
it itself constantly and spontaneously conceives [these forms] at its own will, and by that means,
this splendor of a magical illusion is spread out as if extended.
Just as the referent of the word "bracelet" exists separately within gold,
yet that [separateness] does not exist in the bracelet itself; so too, the referent of the word "world" does not exist in the Supreme,
but this world exists as nothing other than Brahman itself, just as it is.

The world has no reality apart from the word "world," just as bracelets and such have no reality apart from gold. The world-appearance, which is as unreal as a wave upon a heated river, is spread out by the mind alone like the splendor of a magician’s illusion.
Ignorance, transmigratory existence, bondage, illusion, delusion, and the great darkness—
these are the names given to it by those who know all things.
Now, listen to this description of the nature of bondage as it is being told.
Then you shall know the true nature of liberation, O moon-faced one.
My dear, the state of the seer being subject to the seen is called bondage;
the seer is bound by virtue of the seen and is liberated through the absence of the seen.
The world, "you," "I," and so forth—the nature of creation—is called the visible (dṛśya). As long as this exists, liberation is not found.
It is not pacified by useless prattle such as "this is not it" or "that is not it."

On the contrary, the disease of the visible world increases through those things that give rise to conceptual construction (saṅkalpa). Neither by the grinding of the weight of logic nor by pilgrimages, observances, and the like,
can the real visible world be overcome, because these [means] are merely investigators of it.
If the world of appearances exists, it can never be stilled;
for there is no coming into being of what is non-existent, nor the cessation of what is existent.
Wherever this Self, whose nature is consciousness yet is beyond the objects of cognition, abides—
In each and every place, the splendor of the visible world arises for him, even within the interior of an atom.
Therefore, the visible world exists; yet I have wiped it away and abandoned it through austerity, meditation, and recitation, like one who is satisfied with a mere drop of sour gruel.
If indeed this visible world exists,
it is reflected without doubt in this mirror of consciousness, even within the interior of a single atom;
O Rāma, wherever it may be situated, it is reflected therein just as in a mirror.
For in that mirror of consciousness (cid-ādarśa), mountains, the earth, rivers, and the quarters appear exactly as they are.
Thence, within it, there again arise suffering, old age, death, and birth;
existence and non-existence, grasping and relinquishing, the gross and the subtle, the moving and the unmoving.
This visible world has been wiped away by me; I no longer abide within it.
This very [realization] is the inexhaustible seed for the recollection of saṃsāra during meditative absorption (samādhi).
However, while this visible world still exists, through non-conceptual absorption—
Neither inexhaustible deep sleep nor the fourth state (turya) is possible [for one who has not realized this].
For upon emerging from meditative absorptions, all this suffering of the world appears exactly as it is, unbroken, just like at the end of deep sleep. (MU 3.1.33–34)
O Rāma, what indeed is gained by meditative absorptions (*samādhi*)? For even if there is a momentary equanimity, what happiness is there when one is again struck down by misfortune?
Or even if one should attain a state free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) within meditative composure, [what is the use]?
I consider that stainless state to be like an imperishable deep sleep;
it is not attained by anyone as long as this visible world exists,
for the delusion of the world arises wherever the error of the mind goes.
If, moreover, the observer remains by force contemplating the state of being like a stone,
even at the end of that, the state of being an object of perception arises for him once again.
Furthermore, non-conceptual meditative absorptions (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) are not equivalent to the state of being a stone.
It is experienced by all that for some these attainments reach a state of stability;
yet these meditative absorptions (samādhis) do not become like a stone-like rigidity,
nor do they reach the supreme, peaceful state which is the unborn and imperishable nature of consciousness.
Therefore, if this visible world were real, it could never cease;
the notion that it might cease through asceticism, recitation, and meditation is a firm delusion of the ignorant.
It is like the form of a clinging creeper within the hollow of a lotus seed.
Just as the seed of a lotus remains [within it], so does the perception of the visible reside in the seer.
Just as sap is in substances, as oil is in sesame seeds and the like,
and as fragrance is in flowers, so does the perception of the visible reside in the seer.

Just as the fragrance of camphor and other substances arises wherever they are situated, so too does the world arise within the belly of the element of consciousness (ciddhātu). And just as here, in your own mind, there is the perception of dreams, volitions, and the kingdom of thought; [so is this world].
Therefore, by one's own direct experience alone, the realm of the visible exists within the heart as a metaphor. Thus, just as a demon residing in a child's imagination destroys the child,
so too does this world of the visible, existing within the observer, destroy him.

Just as a sprout situated within a seed manifests a radiant body according to place and time, so indeed does the perception of the visible expand. Just as a wonder resides within a substance, ever-arisen in its interior and free from rising or setting; so it is with the inner self.
In this same way, the existence of the world resides within the belly of the Substance whose body is pure consciousness; it is its very nature.
The Second Chapter, titled "Description of the Cause of Bondage."
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, listen to this narrative called "The Birth from Space," an ornament for the ears, which is the section concerning origination by means of which you shall attain understanding.

There was here a twice-born man named Ākāśaja, supremely righteous, constantly devoted solely to meditation and intent on the welfare of all creatures. When he lived for a long time, Death reflected: "MU_3,2.2 When he lives so long, Death thought:"
"I indeed devour all beings in due order, for I am imperishable.
Why then, O Brahmin, do I not devour you, who are born from space?
My power is blunted here, like the edge of a sword upon a stone."
Having reflected thus, he then went to that city to kill him;
for no one who has exerted effort ever abandons their undertaking.
Then, as Death himself entered that dwelling,
For that long, the fire, resembling the conflagration at the end of an aeon, burned him.
Even though he had entered within a great mass of blazing flames,
upon seeing the twice-born man, he strove with effort to seize him with his hand.

And although he was powerful, he was unable to seize the Brahmin, even though he had seen him before and was within a hundred cubits' reach, just as one cannot grasp a person created by mere thought (*saṅkalpapuruṣa*).
Then Death, having approached Yama, who cuts through all doubts, questioned him.
"Why is it, O Lord, that I am unable to eat that which is born of space?
Yama said:
"O Mṛtyu, you alone are not capable of killing anything by force."
The actions that lead to death are those which bring about that result here, and no others.
Therefore, diligently seek out the deeds of this Brahmin who is to be killed; with their assistance, you shall devour him.
Then Death wandered about, intent on searching for that deed,
through circles, the ends of the quarters, lakes, rivers, and directions;
through forests, thickets, and networks of woods, as well as the slopes of mountains and oceans.
Other islands, forests, cities,
and towns; villages, entire kingdoms, and the deep recesses of distant regions—
having thus wandered over the circle of the earth, he found nothing whatsoever anywhere.
Having obtained those actions born of space, Death, though striving,
was like a wise man facing the son of a barren woman or another person facing a mountain of mere imagination;
then, having approached, he questioned Yama, who is skilled in all matters.
"For you are indeed the refuge and the source for your dependents in times of doubt.
Death said:
"O Lord, tell me, where do the actions of one born of space reside?"
Then Dharmarāja, having reflected for a very long time, spoke this:
Dharmarāja said,
"O Mṛtyu, there are no actions whatsoever belonging to one who is born from space."
For this Brahmin was born from space, produced from space alone;
he who is born from space itself becomes as pure as the sky.
There are no auxiliary causes whatsoever for him.
There is not even the slightest connection between this [being] and prior karma,
just as there is none for the son of a barren woman or for one who has never been born. Therefore, this self-existent one is indeed unborn and eternal.
For him there is no prior karma, like a great tree in the sky.
This mind of his is not subject to necessity because of the absence of prior karma;
indeed, nothing else has been accumulated by him as karma up until today.

This Self, whose nature is the sheath of space, is eternally established in a meditative absorption that has the form of the clear sky; for it, there are no actions whatsoever. Its prior actions do not exist, nor does it perform any actions today.
In this regard, this [self] is likewise nothing but consciousness and space;
the movement of its vital breath is perceived as its activity by people such as us.
This is seen by us alone, yet it possesses no cognition of action here.
His body is seen by us, yet he does not perceive it as distinct from the supreme state,
just as one might not see a carved statue on a pillar of consciousness as separate from the pillar itself.
Just as a statue remains uncarved while situated upon a pillar, so too is this body.
In the same way, O twice-born one, this Supreme Self remains established within as one's own self;
just as liquidity exists in water, emptiness in space,
and motion in the wind, so does this [Self] exist in the Supreme State.
Indeed, he possesses neither present-day accumulated actions nor past ones; therefore, he has not fallen under the power of saṃsāra here. He who is born in the absence of auxiliary causes—
It is experienced that this [Self] does not become distinct from its own cause;
O twice-born one, this self-existent one has the nature of the stainless ether.
He was not a creator in the past, nor is he one today—tell me, how can he be overcome?
When he performs with his intellect that mental construction called death,
at that very moment he will die by himself, divested of that intellect.
He who possesses the firm conviction, "I am this one consisting of earth and the other elements," [is bound].
That which is earthen can be grasped quickly, and it is indeed possible to grasp it;
but this, which has no earthen form and consists of the nature of pure consciousness,
cannot at all be grasped, just as the sky cannot be bound by a strong rope.
Mṛtyu said: "O Blessed One, tell me how it is that one is born empty;
tell me also how earth and the other elements exist, or how they do not exist."
Yama said:
"This twice-born one was never born, nor is he ever non-existent;
he is solely the light of pure consciousness, and thus he remains."
Upon the occurrence of the great dissolution, nothing whatsoever remains;
only Brahman exists—peaceful, undecaying, the infinite Self, and absolute.
Know that to be the pure consciousness (cinmātra) freed from all objects of thought, subtler than the subtlest atom.
Thus, that [self] is subtle, because of which the sky near it appears like a mountain.

Since its true nature is pure consciousness, it perceives through that [subtle self] the form appearing in the mind as "I am the body," which has arisen by mere chance, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit.
This very Brahman, at the beginning of that creation within the belly of the ether,
self-luminous and having attained the state of the Self-born, shines forth, ageless and immortal.
He has no body, no actions, no agency, and no latent impressions.
This is the pure space of consciousness, an expansive mass of pure awareness.
No prior web of latent impressions exists within it,
for it is of the nature of the void alone, like a light of the nature of radiance.
In this way, he is perceived solely through the mere experience of sensation;
yet when that mere sensation is completely stilled, even such a perception is no longer seen.
Therefore, just as the space of consciousness is, so too are the means of its realization.
"From what indeed could the earth and other elements possibly arise here, and in what manner?
Therefore, O Death, do not strive so hard to seize me;
it is never possible for anyone to grasp the sky."
Rāma said:
"O Brahman, you have described to me my great-grandfather as being none other than Brahmā himself;
it is my conviction that he was the self-existent, unborn, singular Self, whose nature is pure consciousness."
Vasiṣṭha said: "It is even so, O Rāma; this Brahman has been described by me to you.
On account of this, Death formerly engaged in a dispute with Yama."
In that Manvantara, when Death, devouring all beings as he carried away the creatures,
attained power, he himself made an effort to overcome the one born from the lotus.
Thus was he swiftly subdued by Yama, the King of Dharma.
Whatever is performed constantly, therein alone does delight arise.
How indeed can Brahmā, whose body is the supreme ether, be ascended?
He is mind-only, free from conceptualization, and devoid of forms such as earth and the other elements.
That which is indeed the wonder of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), possessing the experience of space, is consciousness-space itself; it possesses neither causality nor the state of being an effect.
It is like a person of volition whose form flashes forth as space.
Devoid of earth and the other elements, the Self-existent (Svayambhū) shines; likewise, he manifests.
In the absolute Supreme Self, there is neither the visible object nor the seer;
nevertheless, because of its own consciousness, it shines as the Self-existent.
This mind, which is mere volition, is called Brahman;
it is the person of the ether of volition, and for it, earth and the other elements do not exist.
Just as a bodiless figure appears within a painting created by an artist, so does this [Brahman] appear.
In that very same way, Brahmā shines forth as a being born from the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
The self-existent one (svayambhū) appears as Brahmā—pure, infinite, and without beginning or middle within the sky of consciousness—by virtue of his own mind;
yet, though appearing here as if possessing form due to his creative power, in reality he has no body, just like the son of a barren woman.
The Third Sarga, titled "The Description of the Original Creation," [spoken by] Rāma:
Thus it is: this pure mind, devoid of earth and the other elements, is like the sky;
O Sage, it is called Brahman—the truth that is free from earth and the rest.
Why, then, is the prior memory not the cause here?
"Tell me: as it is for me, so is it for others and for all living beings?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"He for whom there exists a prior body today, accompanied by his past karma—"
Memory arises as the cause for the persistence of his transmigratory existence.
When no prior karma of Brahmā exists,
from where and how could his recollection of the past arise?
Therefore, it appears either without a cause, or its sole cause is its own consciousness;
being non-different from its own cause, the Self-born is himself possessed of his own self.
This very body of that Self-born one is indeed the *ātivāhika* (subtle) body.
"But, O Rāma, a material body is not possible for the Unborn.
Rāma said:
"There is one subtle body (ātivāhika), but there is another, the material body (ādhibhautika)."
"Is there for all classes of beings only one Brahmā?
Vasiṣṭha replied: "For all beings whose nature is causal, there are indeed two bodies."
Because the Unborn has no cause, it alone is the *ativāhika* (the conductor).
Of all classes of beings, the one Unborn is the supreme cause;
since there is no cause for the Unborn, it possesses only a single body.
The body of the first Prajāpati is not at all composed of the elements;
possessing a subtle, transportable body (ātivāhika-deha), he appears as having the nature of space.
His body consists of mind alone; it is not made of earth and the other [gross] elements.
The primordial Lord of Creatures, whose body is the void, extends forth all creatures;
and they are of the nature of liberation, even without other external causes.
That whatever arises from whatever source is of that very same nature is experienced by everyone.
First there is mere nirvāṇa, and that very thing is supreme awakening;
it is merely mind, and it remains as such, not becoming the earth and other elements.
[This is so] for all beings and minds engaged in the worldly cycle of existence.

This first [emanation] is the *praticchanda*, the body of consciousness, arising from itself. From that preceding *praticchanda*, this creation has issued forth as non-different from its own nature, like the perception of movement from the wind.
Because this creation possesses the form of mere creative intuition (*pratibhā*) derived from that which has the nature of creative intuition,
it shines forth in this way, existing like a real experience.
In this regard, the examples are a city in a dream and likewise sexual union with a woman in a dream.
Though non-existent, it shines forth through the perfection of its purpose, radiant with the experience of reality.
Though not composed of earth and the other elements, bodiless and having the form of space,
the Lord of Beings, who is his own self, appears in human form as if possessing a body.
Because it consists of the nature of mental volition, that [universe] arises and then subsides;
but because its own nature is self-dependent, it neither arises nor subsides.
Brahmā is devoid of volition, and his form is devoid of earth and the other elements.
The mind alone, consisting of pure consciousness, is the cause of the existence of the three worlds.
Just as this volition shines forth according to its own arising,
so too does it appear as the nature of space, like a mountain born of your own imagination.
Due to the firm-rooted and total forgetfulness of its purely subtle nature,
it appears in vain like a ghost through the perception of the material body.
This occurs for one whose great consciousness has been awakened by the initial effort [of inquiry].
Because of the purity of his consciousness, the forgetfulness of the subtle body (ātivāhika) does not arise;
therefore, the demoness of materiality (ādhibhautikatā) does not arise for him—
she who is unreal like a mirage, falsely bestowing the delusion of dullness.

When Brahmā consists of mind alone and is not composed of earth and the other elements, therefore the universe is mind alone; for whatever is from what [source], that is indeed that very thing. Since there are no auxiliary causes for the Unborn, [he is independent].

Even for that which arises from them, those [causes] do not truly exist; therefore, there is no diversity of effects whatsoever arising from a cause. Whatever kind of pure cause exists here, an effect of that same nature is established.
But here, the relationship of cause and effect is not at all tenable;
for exactly as is the Supreme Brahman, so too is the triple world.
The world is stretched out by Brahman, as if it had attained the state of the mind.
Like liquidity is not different from water, all this that is spread out by the mind is merely the unreal, extended from the pure Self;
it is like a city of imagination, like a city of the Gandharvas.
There is no materiality there, just as there is no serpent in a rope;
how then could Brahmā and the other gods remain there once they have awakened?
Indeed, for one whose mind is awakened, only the subtle body (ātivāhika) exists.
Why and how could there even be a discussion here regarding a physical body?
For the world is the kingdom of the mind— belonging to the human being called "mind"— which assumes various forms and stands as if it were real.
Know that the mind alone is Viriñca, whose nature consists of volition;
having brought its own form to expansion, this [universe] is stretched out by the mind.
Viriñca is the form of the mind; the mind is the body of Viriñca.
Earth and the other elements do not exist here; therefore, earth and the rest are merely imagined.
Just as a lotus plant exists within a lotus seed, the state of being visible exists within the heart-pleasing mind.
The mind and the object of vision are never, in any way, distinct from one another.

And so, in this matter, your own dream and mental construction—the intellect that rules the mind—are themselves the examples seen through direct experience; therefore, the ground of the visible exists within the heart. Thus, like a demon residing in a child's mental projection, [it appears].
In this way, appearing in the form of the visible, it destroys the internal seer.
Just as a sprout situated within a seed manifests its radiant body according to place and time, so indeed does the cognition of the visible expand itself.
If the suffering of the visible world does not ever subside while the visible world persists, then there is no isolation (kaivalya) for the knower.
However, when the visible world is impossible, the state of being a knower subsides even while the knower remains; indeed, they call that his liberation.
The Fourth Sarga, titled "The Cause of Bondage," by Vālmīki.

While the leader of sages was thus speaking these unrestrained words, the assembly remained silent, intent on listening with single-minded devotion; and while the tinkling of the network of small bells had subsided, there was no further movement.
Even the hārīta birds and parrots within their cages had ceased their play;
even the women remained with their amorous dalliances utterly forgotten;
and the entire royal palace stood as if fixed upon a painted wall.
When only a single *muhūrta* remained of the day, its heat became mild;
worldly activity waned along with the rays of the sun.
Winds blew, rich with the intoxication from clusters of blossoming lotuses.
The winds arrived with a sweet vibration, as if for the purpose of hearing [his words].
Having heard them, the sun, like one weary from the movement of day and night,
abandoned his solitary course and went to the peak of the western mountain, the void.

In the forest lands, the darkness produced by the onset of mist arose like the inner coolness of tranquility resulting from hearing the teaching on consciousness. People became scarce in their movements even throughout the ten directions.
As if to listen with full attention, they ceased all movement;
their shadows grew long as if to hear the sequence of descriptions concerning Vasiṣṭha, while all the creatures stretched out their necks.
The doorkeeper, bowing before him, said to the lord of the earth:
"O King, the time for bathing and the worship of the twice-born has indeed passed by far.
Then the venerable Vasiṣṭha, having withdrawn his sweet speech, [fell silent].
"O Great King, let this much suffice for you to hear today; tomorrow morning we shall speak of another matter. Having said this, he became silent.
Upon hearing this, the king said, "So be it," for the sake of increasing his prosperity.
With flowers, water for honor, water for the feet, respectful salutations, the giving of sacrificial fees, and worship,
he reverently honored the gods, celestial rishis, forest hermits, and brahmins. Then the entire assembly, including the circle of kings and sages, rose up.
Their faces were encircled by a halo from the mass of rays radiating from their earrings;
their armlets and bracelets jingled as they brushed against one another's shoulders;
and the golden fillets upon their broad chests were struck by the weight of their necklaces.
With the sounds of awakened bees resting upon the laps of their crests,
the upper parts of their heads seemed filled with a humming sound as if their hair were falling away;
the quarters of the sky were turned golden by the radiance of their golden ornaments.
With the functions of their senses completely stilled by the meaning of the words of the Buddhist Sage,
the sky-dwellers went to the heavens and the earth-dwellers to the circle of the earth;
everyone performed their own daily activities in their respective homes.
In the meantime, the dark night appeared like a young woman in a house empty of crowds of people;
the leader of the day departed to illuminate another region.
To illuminate everything everywhere is the true vow of a noble man.
The twilight arose on all sides, bearing a multitude of stars,
like the splendor of spring appearing with forests of blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees.
At that time, the birds settled within the mango, *nīpa*, and *kadamba* trees, at the tops of village shrines, and inside temple-houses, just as those mental states settle within the mind;
they were adorned by fragments of clouds tinted by the sun’s rays, as if by a slight glow of saffron.
The western mountain, clad in yellow garments, joined by the sky adorned with the beauty of its necklace of stars, emerged from the ocean of darkness.
When the twilight worship was concluded and she had departed as she had come,
the darknesses rose up like a circle of *vetāla* spirits.
A cool breeze blew, soft and whispering of the night-lotus, its spray dripping with dew-drops and its tender shoots shaken by its playful motion.
Even the quarters of the sky, though their stars were clearly visible, fell into a profound darkness.
With their very long, hanging hair, they were like widowed women;
then the moon-milk ocean, whose form consisted of elixir, arrived filling the sky and the world with a flood of radiant milk.
Masses of darkness fled and vanished somewhere beyond sight,
like the ignorance of kings from their minds when the voice of scriptural knowledge is heard;
likewise, the seers, the protectors of the earth, the sages, and the brahmins [departed].
Like various objects in the mind, they found rest in their own abodes.
A thick darkness, dark as a mass of *yamaka* flowers, departed;
there, the dawn slowly approached them, taking the form of a mist.
The bright stars in the sky became invisible,
like showers of saffron powder swept away by the morning breeze; then the night,
its eyes opened by the light of the sun, came into view.
The conduct of the great ones, characterized by discernment, arose like a fresh dawn within their minds.
Then the sky-dwellers and earth-dwellers returned to the assembly hall,
having performed their morning rites in the same sequence as the previous day.
She entered the vast assembly hall with her former composure;
she became motionless in appearance, like a lotus pond released from the wind.
Then, finding the opportunity, Rāma spoke with a sweet voice.
Rāma said to Vasiṣṭha, the tiger among sages and the best of speakers:
"O Blessed One, tell me clearly: what is the nature of the mind?"
For it is by this that this entire cluster of defects is spread out.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, not even the slightest form of this mind is perceived.
Apart from its mere name, like the sky which is empty and inert by nature,
the mind exists neither externally nor within the heart;
know, O Rāma, that it is situated everywhere, just like space.
This unreal form that has arisen for him is like the water of a mirage;
now hear in brief about form, which is comparable to the delusion of a second moon.
O virtuous one, this manifestation of an object that has reached the state of appearing—
Know that the mind is either existent or non-existent, and nothing other than that;
whatever appears as an object is designated as "mind," for there is never anything else whatsoever called "mind."

Know that the mind is volition; it is not distinct from volition. Just as water [is inseparable] from fluidity, and just as movement [is inseparable] from the wind, so too, my dear, where there is volition, there the mind is situated.
Volition and mind are never distinct from one another for anyone. Whether it be true or false, know that the mind is merely that which appears as an object; that is Brahman, the Grandfather.
The self consisting of the subtle body (ātivāhikadeha) is designated as the mind (manas);
the intellect pertaining to the material realm (ādhibhautikabuddhi), however, is the constant ideation that persists for a long time.
Ignorance, transmigratory existence, consciousness, mind, bondage, impurity, and darkness [are all one].
Thus the supreme ones know these to be the synonymous names for the visible world.
For there is no form of the mind whatsoever apart from the visible world;
and yet, I shall explain again that this visible world has never actually arisen.
Just as the lotus bud exists within the seed of the lotus,
so the visible world exists within the atom of the Great Consciousness;
just as there is light for illumination and movement for the wind.
Just as liquidity belongs to water, so does visibility belong to the seer;
as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold, as water exists in a mirage,
and as a wall exists in a dream-city, so does the perception of the visible exist in the seer.
Thus, I quickly wipe away from the mirror of your mind that impurity which exists as if non-different from the seer, yet is the state of being an object of sight;
for in the absence of an object of sight, this [seer] would necessarily become a non-seer.
Know that from this very state of the non-existent becoming existent arises the state of absolute oneness (kevalībhāva).
When the objective world has attained its true nature, the latent impressions of passion, aversion,
and the like subside, just as the agitation caused by movement ceases when the wind is stilled.
When everything consisting of the directions, the earth, and space has ceased to exist as an object of illumination,
the form of the light itself becomes stainless;
likewise, when the visible world— including the three worlds, you, and me— has attained non-existence, [the pure consciousness remains].

For such a pure-souled seer, there would be the state of absolute isolation (*kevalībhāva*). For just as the nature of a mirror remains as the mirror itself when it contains the reflections of all infinite mountains and other objects, so too is the nature of the absolute Self.

"When the delusion of the visible world has been stilled in such states as 'I', 'you', and 'the universe', there arises that same state of absolute isolation while the Seer remains established, yet non-observing. Rāma said:
"If this does not subside, or if there is no such thing as non-existence for that which exists,
and we perceive no absence within this visible world which bestows defects—
then, O Brahman, how can this cholera of the visible be pacified?"
"It causes confusion through the appearance of various things and bestows a continuous stream of suffering.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Hear this mantra for the pacification of this demon of the visible world."
"O Rāma, because of this, he will reach death and perish utterly.
O Rāghava, that which exists can never be destroyed;
therefore, even though it has perished outwardly, it remains as a seed within the heart."
The perception of the visible world, arising again from the seed of memory within the space of consciousness,
spreads a vast defect in the form of the worlds, mountains, and sky;
thus there would be the defect of non-liberation, yet no part of that [defect] can possibly exist.
Because gods, sages, and seers are seen to be recipients of liberation;
for if this world were real from the very beginning, there would be no liberation for anyone.
Whether the visible world resides outside or within the heart, it exists solely for the sake of destruction.
Therefore, O Rāma, listen to this most terrifying proposition,
which you will surely understand through the subsequent text:
"This [universe], consisting of space, the elements, and so forth, is characterized as being 'I'."
Indeed, there is no referent for the word "world" at all.
Whatever web of visible objects is seen here before one,
all that is but the one Brahman— undecaying, immortal, and immutable.
In the full, the full expands; in the tranquil, the supreme tranquil abides.
Space has arisen within space itself; Brahman stands within Brahman.
There is neither the visible nor the sight, neither the seer nor the act of seeing.
"It is neither empty, nor inert, nor consciousness; it is simply this all-pervading peace.
Rāma said:
"The mountain is ground by the son of a barren woman, and the horn of a hare is being sharpened!"
"Stretching out its mass of arms, the rock performs the *tāṇḍava* dance;
the sands drip oil, and the stone figurines recite; the painted clouds thunder"—such, O Lord, was this speech. (MU 3.4.70–71)
The world consists of the sky-like expanse of the suffering of old age, death,
and so forth; why do you say even to me that "this does not exist," as if this entire universe were neither established, nor arisen, nor found?
"Tell me that, O Brahmin, so that this may become certain.
Vasiṣṭha replied: "I am not one whose speech is inconsistent; listen, O Rāghava, it shall be told."
Just as this non-existent appears like the son of a barren woman or a mirage;
so too, this world was unproduced at the beginning, and therefore it does not truly exist.
For this appears through the mind, just like a city in a dream or the like.
And the mind alone, at the beginning of creation, was unarisen and of non-existent form;
listen now as I shall explain how this is experienced:
the mind, consisting of the visible world, extends this defect which is of the nature of decay.
Just as one dream follows another, that which is non-existent indeed appears in a non-existent form;
it spontaneously and effortlessly conceives a body for itself,
and by means of that extended [conception], this splendor of a magical illusion is spread out.
It throbs, it moves, it leaps, it begs, it exists, it sinks, and it withdraws by itself;
it even attains immortality and yet merely flickers due to the nature of its flickering power—the mind.
(Chapter titled "Description of the Section," Verse 79)
Fifth canto.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, tiger among sages, what indeed is this delusion of the mind here?
How does the mind, which is illusory in nature, exist? From where has it arisen?
O Lord, tell me briefly about its origin at the outset;
thereafter, O best of speakers, you shall explain the remainder that remains to be said.
Vasiṣṭha said: When the great dissolution has occurred and the entirety of the visible world has reached non-existence at the beginning of creation, only the tranquil remains.
The unborn, undecaying, radiant Lord, free from all ailment—
the Supreme Self, the Great Ruler, who is everything, the creator of all at all times—
abides; he from whom words turn back, and who is realized by the liberated.
And for whom notions such as "self" and so forth are merely imagined and not born of intrinsic nature;
who [is the self] for the followers of Sāṅkhya views, for the Vedāntins who speak of Brahman,
and for the knowers of consciousness, who is pure consciousness alone and absolutely stainless.
He who is the illuminator of the void for the proponents of emptiness, he who is the splendor of the suns;
he who is the speaker, the rememberer, the knower of truth, the enjoyer, the seer, and the eternal doer;
he who, though existing, is non-existent in the world, and who, though situated within the body, is far away.
For this manifestation of consciousness is like the light of the sun;
from it the gods, Viṣṇu and the others, emerge like rays from the sun;
and from it the infinite worlds arise like bubbles from the ocean.
That into which all visible multitudes dissolve like waters into the great ocean;
that which illuminates both itself and objects like a lamp;
which exists in space, in the body, in stones, in water, and in creepers.
Established in the dust, in the mountains, in the winds, and in the netherworlds,
he is that which violently floods the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka) here and there;
by him the dull-witted are rendered mute, remaining as if fixed in meditation like stones.
By whom the sky was made empty, by whom the mountains were made solid,
by whom the waters were made fluid, and by whose power the sun blazes;
from whom the diverse, unsubstantial visions of saṃsāra emanate.
From which, like rains from an ocean filled with imperishable nectar,
the waves of the three worlds— consisting of manifestation and disappearance—
vibrate incessantly, like rays of light from the sun.
That which is of the nature of non-destruction, whose essence is indestructible, which dwells within all things,
which is hidden though distinct, and which is established in all existents;
it is the creeper of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) grown in the void, bearing the great fruit of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
That wind by which the mind-rooted petals dance; that jewel of consciousness which shines within the casket of every body,
in which moon these rays of the world-web quiver.
In that dense mass of tranquil consciousness, which rains down nectar,
all beings flash like streams of water and clear visions like lightning;
by the light of that [consciousness], objects manifest their wondrous nature to one another.
That by which the non-existent becomes born, and by which the existent attains its state of being;
in whose presence this inert body moves even though it has no desire,
while that supreme jewel remains peaceful within itself.
Destiny, place, and time, as well as movement, vibration, and actions— by him, who pervades all beings, these have attained existence; for he,
being composed of pure consciousness, becomes the void through the awareness of space.
The state of being the knower of categories remains unestablished as an object; [the Self] persists as that which is not fixed.
Even while appearing to perform the infinite vibration of the great worlds, He never does anything at all;
established solely in His own self, which is changeless consciousness without setting, He remains as the One alone, having abandoned the notions of arising and abiding.
The Sixth Chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of the Deity who is the Root Cause," by Vasiṣṭha.
For this supreme Self, the God beyond gods, the highest perfection comes from knowledge alone, and not from the exhaustion of ritual performance.
In this matter, knowledge is the practice; nothing else is of use.
That which consists of the perception of the cessation of the delusion of water in a mirage is its true form.
It is neither far away, nor in the sky, nor unattainable, nor difficult;
having the nature of the radiance of one's own bliss, it is attained from one's very own body.
In this regard, asceticism, charity, vows, and the like do not provide any assistance;
there is no means of accomplishment here other than resting solely in one's own true nature.
In this matter, there is only dependence upon the scriptures, the company of the virtuous, and the great yogis.

The means for awakening is that which is the unartificial unraveling of the web of delusion. Merely by the thorough recognition that "this is that God," suffering no longer arises for a person, and they attain the state of liberation while living.
Rāma:
Merely by means of this self thoroughly knowing itself within itself,
faults such as death and the like shall never again cause affliction.
"From what distance can this great God of gods be reached,
and by what intense austerity or how much hardship?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
O Rāma, that Lord is known through one's own effort and exertion, and through blossoming discernment; He is not known by means of asceticism, ritual bathing, or formal rites.
[He is known] through the abandonment of passion, hatred, delusion, anger, intoxication, and envy.
O Rāma, without the gift of austerity, even suffering is not real.
When the mind is afflicted by passion and the like, one acquires wealth by deceiving others;
of that wealth, the fruit belongs to him who gives it away.
Whatever vow or other practice is performed when the mind is afflicted by passion and the like is called hypocrisy; its fruit is either negligible or non-existent.
Therefore, by human effort, one should obtain the primary medicine.
Association with true scriptures and virtuous people is the destroyer of the disease of worldly existence.
In this regard, apart from one human effort,
no other means is found to lead to the attainment of the destruction of all suffering.
Listen to what kind of human effort is required for the attainment of self-knowledge,
by which the cholera-like fevers of passion and hatred are entirely pacified.
This should be done through such means as may be possible, provided they are not in conflict with worldly custom or sacred scripture.
With a mind contented by satisfaction, abandoning greed for enjoyments,
one should first resort to devotion to the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures, through one's own effort as far as possible and with a state free from agitation.
He who is content with whatever is obtained, who disregards what is censurable,
and who delights in the company of the virtuous and the study of true scriptures, is swiftly liberated.
For the one of great intelligence whose own nature has been fully understood through investigation— *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 3.2.18.
These—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śaṅkara—are worthy of compassion.
He whom people, for the most part consisting of good men, declare to be virtuous is distinguished; he would be a true saint. One should take refuge in him with diligent effort.

Among all branches of knowledge, the science of the inner self (adhyātmavidyā) is preeminent; they call that treatise which rests upon its discourse a "true scripture" (sacchāstra), and one who investigates it is liberated.
Through the discernment born of true scriptures and the company of the virtuous, impurities are thus forcibly destroyed.
Just as by contact with the *kataka* nut the impurities of water are removed, and just as by the application of the *abhaya* plant the dullness [of the mind] is cleared away—
this concludes the seventh chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Effort of Those Seeking Liberation."
Rāma:
"O Lord, tell me where this deity resides of whom you have spoken— the knowledge of whom brings liberation— and how I may obtain him."
Vasiṣṭha:
This deity who has been described does not stand at a distance;
it is eternally established within the body, renowned as pure consciousness alone (cinmātra).
This [Self] is this entire universe, yet this all-pervading one is not the universe;
for he alone exists as the one, and there is no perception of a world-appearance apart from him.
This moon-bearer is pure consciousness alone, and the one whose banner is Garuḍa is pure consciousness alone.
The sun is indeed pure consciousness alone; the lotus-born Brahmā is pure consciousness alone.
Rāma said: "Even children say this, if it is merely consciousness."
"What kind of instruction could there possibly be here regarding that which is called 'the world'?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"That you have realized is that the entire universe is pure consciousness and the conscious principle."

This which delivers one from existence has not been understood at all by you. That which is called consciousness is transmigratory existence; this is known as the individual soul (*jīva*), a bound beast (*paśu*).
From this very source emerge the waves of old age and death.

For the individual soul (*paśu*), though insentient and formless, is indeed a vessel for suffering alone; yet because it possesses consciousness, it perceives this [world], and thus, remaining in its own state, it becomes the very essence of misfortune. Whether it be the state of being free from objects of thought (*cetya*) or the state of being oriented toward that which is not an object of thought, [it remains bound].
That is its state of fullness; having known that, one does not grieve.
When He—the one who is both the transcendent and the immanent—is seen, the knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are severed, and one's karmas are exhausted. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9–10)
Moreover, its tendency toward being oriented toward an object of thought cannot be obstructed without the non-existence of that object;
for how indeed can the visible world, which is the object of thought, be stilled?
Rāma said:

"O Brahmin, tell me: what is that Supreme Self like, which is seen through the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures as the one who carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra? Vasiṣṭha replied:

Those who desire this conscious individual soul (*jīva*), which is shattered in the jungle of birth, are ignorant even though they are considered wise. For it is the *jīva* itself that constitutes transmigratory existence here, due to its consciousness and its continuous stream of suffering.
When this is known, nothing remains unknown anywhere.
O Rāma, if the Supreme Self is known, the succession of sufferings comes to an end,
just as cholera ceases when the influence of poison has subsided.
Rāma said:
O Brahman, describe to me accurately the form of the Supreme Self,
by seeing which a person shall cross over all delusion in its entirety.

Vasiṣṭha said: That form which exists in the interval between consciousness that has traveled a great distance from one place to another, occurring in the mere twinkling of an eye— that is the nature of the Supreme Self.
The absolute non-existence of the cycle of existence and the world's condition exists within that great ocean of consciousness which is the nature of the Supreme Self; therein,
the sequence of seer and seen, though present, has utterly set.

That which is non-space is space; that is the form of the Supreme Self. That which is empty as if not empty, wherein the world remains empty—though the flood of creation exists—that which is empty is the form of the Supreme Self.

That which is composed of pure consciousness, though vast like a great stone, is insentient on the outside yet sentient within; that is the form of the Supreme Self. Having attained union with that by which everything—both external and internal—is pervaded, [one realizes the truth].
It attains the existence of its own nature, which is the form of the Supreme Self.
Just as light is to illumination and emptiness is to the sky,
so is this established wherein that form of the Supreme Self resides.
Rāma:
How indeed can this Supreme Self be understood as being everywhere? Whence is the non-existence of this visible world called "the universe"?
Vasiṣṭha said: If there were sufficient firm conviction in the absolute non-existence of this worldly delusion, which has arisen like the color of the sky, [then one would be liberated].
That form of Brahman is known through this [means] and not by any other action;
for there is no other auspicious path than the absolute non-existence of the visible world.
When the absolute non-existence of this visible world is accomplished according to its true state, [that is the goal].
That which remains is the ultimate reality (paramārtha); it is therefore awakened to and known.
There is no consciousness anywhere that is not a reflection, apart from the absence of the visible object;
for where indeed does a mirror exist without a reflection?
Without the possibility of the existence of this visible world named "the universe," the supreme reality can never be understood by anyone at any time.
Rāma said:
O Sage, how can there be non-existence for this vast web of the visible—the cosmic egg and the stability of the world? Where is Mount Meru within the interior of a mustard seed?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
O Rāma, if you remain for a few days with an undaunted mind,
intent upon the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures, then in an instant I shall wipe away the world of appearances from your vision, just as a mirage vanishes in one's awakening.
When the object of sight is absent, the state of being a seer is stilled, and pure consciousness remains.
The state of being a seer exists only when this object of sight exists; the state of being an object of sight exists only when there is a beholder.
Indeed, unity exists only when duality exists, and duality exists only upon the perception of unity.
Indeed, in the absence of one, the establishment of both does not occur here;
when duality, unity, the seer, and the seen have ceased, the Real alone remains.
I shall wipe away for you all this world of perception, including the sense of "I" and so forth.
The impurity of the mind arises from the perception of that which is absolutely non-existent.
There is no existence for the non-existent, nor is there non-existence for the existent;
since that which does not exist by way of its own nature has no reality, what effort can there be in cleansing it?
This world, which was unproduced in the beginning and is seen spread out here,
is indeed Brahman itself, expanded within its own pure self by virtue of its consciousness.
That which is called "the world" has never been produced, it does not exist, and it is not perceived.
Just as the state of being a bracelet or other ornaments [is not real] in gold, why this effort to polish it?
We shall explain this here at length with many arguments,
so that it may indeed be experienced by oneself as something uncontradicted.
For how can there be existence here for that which has never arisen from the very beginning?
How could there be a river of water in a desert, or a planet in the second moon? Just as the son of a barren woman does not exist, so water does not exist in a desert.
Just as there is no tree in the sky, so too there is no delusion of a world.
O Rāma, that which is seen here is nothing but Brahman, free from all affliction;
we shall explain this to you later through reasoning, and not merely by words.
O noble-minded one, it is improper for one of exalted intellect to show contempt for that which those who know the truth proclaim here through reasonings;
for they know him to be truly ignorant who, out of a deluded mind, disregards what is consistent with reason, thereby bringing about his own suffering.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Proposition Concerning the Non-existence of the World and Other Perceptible Objects."
The Eighth Chapter.
Rāma said: "By what reasoning is this known, and how can it be established?"
"When this has been realized through right reasoning, nothing remains to be known.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"This cholera of false knowledge has been deeply rooted for a long time."
That which is called the world does not subside through mantras except by means of inquiry.
O Rāma, I shall relate these narratives for the sake of attaining awakening;
if you listen to them, O virtuous one, you will indeed be liberated and wise.

If, out of a habit of agitation, you rise from the midst of it and depart, then nothing at all will be accomplished for you today, for you are behaving like an animal. He who desires an object and likewise strives for that purpose—
He will certainly attain that, provided he does not turn back out of weariness. O Rāma, if you are devoted to the company of the virtuous and to the true scriptures,
then in days, and certainly not in months, you shall attain the supreme state.
Rāma said:
O best among those who know the scriptures, what is the name of that preeminent scripture for the awakening of self-knowledge, by knowing which one no longer grieves?
Vasiṣṭha:
O Great-minded One, for those for whom self-knowledge is paramount,
this very work titled the Mahārāmāyaṇa is the supreme scripture among all scriptures.
From this supreme history, a higher understanding proceeds;
this is declared to be the essence of all histories.
Since, upon hearing this body of sacred word, the state of liberation while living remains unimpaired.

From this very [realization], this world arises by itself; it is indeed most purifying. Through inquiry, the visible world, though already existing, comes to its setting, just as when a dream is fully recognized, the mental impression of the dream-objects vanishes.
"What exists here exists elsewhere; what does not exist here exists nowhere else.
The wise know this to be the treasury of all the sciences of consciousness.
For one who hears this constantly, there arises a noble sense of wonder."
Even for a child, the intellect attains supreme awakening; of this there is no doubt.
But for that unfortunate person to whom this does not appeal due to the ripening of past evil deeds, let him investigate whatever scripture consists of mere intellectual talk.
But when this [scripture] is heard, the state of liberation while living (jīvanmuktatva) is experienced by oneself,
just as freedom from disease is realized when an excellent medicine has been drunk.
For when this scripture is being heard, the listener understands this through his own self.
We have not stated this as we ought to have, like a boon or a curse. This suffering of saṃsāra is stilled for you by the great discourse on the investigation of one's own self alone;
it is not stilled by wealth, gifts, austerity, sacred learning, or the Vedas, nor by hundreds of efforts devoid of that discourse.
The ninth canto, titled "The Determination of the True Scripture," by Vasiṣṭha.
With their minds fixed on That and their lives dedicated to That, awakening one another and constantly speaking of That, those who find contentment and delight [in it]—
for them, whose sole steadfastness is in knowledge, through the investigation of self-knowledge— [there arises the realization].
That state which is liberation while living arises as that very liberation after death.
Rāma said: "O Brahmin, what are the characteristics of one liberated after death and one liberated while living?"
"Tell me, so that I may likewise strive with an intellect guided by the vision of the scriptures.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"He for whom this world remains exactly as it is, even while engaged in worldly affairs,"

When the sky [of the mind] has set and remains [in its true state], he is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). Having attained exclusive steadfastness in pure awareness, he who remains as if in deep sleep even while awake,
and who conducts himself in the world of affairs, is called one liberated while living.
He whose facial radiance neither rises nor sets in pleasure or pain,
remaining as it is naturally obtained— he is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
He who is awake while abiding in deep sleep, for whom no waking state exists— [he is liberated].
He whose awakening is free from latent impressions is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Even while acting in accordance with passion, hatred, fear, and the like,
he who is internally as utterly pure as the sky is called liberated while living.
He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not stained—
whether he is acting or not acting— he is called liberated while living.
And he for whom the creation and dissolution of the world occur through the opening and closing of his eyes...
He who perceives the three worlds as equal to space is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
He who is both the enjoyer and yet not the enjoyer, having attained oneness with pure consciousness,
remains inwardly like one awakened from sleep— he is called liberated while living.

He who is always both the seer and the non-seer, who, though living, is like one dead, and who, though engaged in worldly activity, is as immovable as a mountain— he is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta). He from whom the world does not tremble, and who does not tremble before the world;

One who is liberated from joy, impatience, and fear is called "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta). One whose mental constructions regarding worldly existence have ceased, who, though possessing parts, is partless, and who,
though possessing a mind, is mindless— he is called "liberated while living."
He who remains cool even while engaged in all kinds of worldly affairs,
his self being as full as it is in matters concerning others— he is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Having abandoned the state of being liberated while living, when the body is destroyed by the power of time, [he becomes liberated in death].

Consciousness attains the state of disembodied liberation (videhamukti), just as the wind reaches a state of motionlessness. The one liberated while in the body (videhamukta) neither rises nor sets, nor does it cease;
it is neither existent nor non-existent, neither far away, nor "I," nor anything else.
Becoming the sun, Viṣṇu blazes;
as Rudra, he destroys all; and as the lotus-born Brahmā, he creates all.
Having become the ether, he supports the masses of winds along with the stars, gods, and demons.
Becoming the range of the principal mountain ranges, it becomes the abode of the cities of the world-protectors;
becoming the earth, it sustains this unbroken stability of the worlds;
and becoming grass, shrubs, and creepers, it yields a continuous succession of fruits.
Bearing the forms of both water and fire, it blazes and, when liquefied, flows;
as the moon it produces nectar, yet as the *hālāhala* poison it brings death;
appearing as light, it reveals the quarters, yet becoming darkness, it spreads blindness.
Being empty, it attains the state of space; being a mountain, it completely obstructs.
Being consciousness, it creates the moving and the stationary;
having the form of the stationary, it becomes the ocean and encircles the earth-woman like a bracelet.
Having become the body of the supreme sun, spreading its light within,
it remains perfectly tranquil, [like] the mass of motes in the three worlds.
Whatever appears here, has appeared, or will come to appear— [all this is that].
"Or rather, he is everything—the visible world existing throughout the three periods of time.
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, how can you speak thus? For my mind is indeed troubled."
"But this vision is difficult to attain and difficult to ascend; such is the certainty.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāma, this is called liberation; this is declared to be Brahman."
This is what has been called Nirvāṇa; hear now how it is attained.
This visible world that is perceived, which is joined with the sense of "I" and so forth—by realizing through the intellect that even though this exists, it is unproduced, it is attained.
Rāma said:
"O best among those who know what is to be known, when those liberated while in the body attain the three worlds, I consider that they have merely reached the state of being created."
Vasiṣṭha said:
If the three worlds exist, let them attain that state where not even the slightest meaning of the word "the three worlds" can possibly occur.
In that regard, how could there be an understanding of the meaning of the statement "Brahman has become the three worlds"?
Therefore, no other conceptualization of the referent of the word "world" is possible for us;
it is non-different [from Brahman], peaceful, a mere appearance, and as stainless as space.

For those who have realized the truth, the truth is simply that the world is Brahman alone. Just as, when one examines a golden bracelet, the state of being a bracelet is not seen anywhere at all apart from the pure gold itself.
Apart from water, I do not perceive anything at all in the waves of the ocean;
for that which is perceived as "waviness" by those like you does not exist there at all. Likewise, the state of vibration is never, anywhere, other than the wind.
The wind is always merely vibration; therefore, the world does not exist.
Just as emptiness is the sky, and water is but a mirage in the desert, just as light is but fire, so the three worlds are but Brahman.
Rāma:
O Sage, teach me that supreme method by which liberation from the world of the visible arises through the attainment of its absolute non-existence. *Muktikopaniṣad* 3.9.37.
[Vasiṣṭha: When the seer and the seen, having come together, undergo the dissolution of one,
and both cease to exist, reaching a state of non-duality, only nirvāṇa remains.
[Rāma:
Tell me how Brahman, which is thus established in its own nature, is understood in such a way that there is the absolute non-arising of this visible world.
"How is this known through reasoning, and how is it established? But once this is proven, O Sage, nothing remains to be accomplished.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
This cholera of false knowledge has been rooted deep for a long time;
it will surely be eradicated by the mantra of inquiry.
It cannot be destroyed all at once in a single instant.
For on a mountain of even effort, the ascending and descending are equal.
Therefore, listen as this is explained so that the delusion of the world may be stilled through the yoga of practice, by means of reasoning, and through logical justifications. MU 3.9.43–42.
O Rāma, I shall relate this narrative for the sake of attaining awakening;
if you listen to it, O virtuous one, you will indeed be liberated and wise.
Now, this chapter on origination is being told by me to you.
"O Rāma, that which indeed arises becomes liberated by that very arising.
Thus, this delusion of the world, though unborn and of the nature of space, appears in this manner;
this is now being explained by me in this chapter on origination.
Whatever is seen here in this world, both stationary and moving— everything rich in all its various forms, including gods, asuras, and kinnaras— all that,
when the great dissolution has arrived, undergoes transformation within Rudra and the others.
It becomes non-existent and invisible, it goes somewhere, or it perishes.
Then, there remains something that is existent—tranquil and profound, neither light nor pervasive darkness, indefinable and unmanifest. (MU 3.9.48–49)
It is neither empty nor space, neither the visible nor the act of seeing;
it is not the flood of real entities, for it abides in infinity.
It is an indescribable essence, a form more full than the full, arising from the Full.
It is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent; it is neither a non-entity nor a becoming.
It is pure consciousness, devoid of any object of thought, infinite, undecaying, and auspicious;
it is without beginning, middle, or end, free from mental affliction, and beyond all disease.
In whom the world vibrates like a pearl, a swan, or a vision;
who is both this and not this—the God whose nature is both being and non-being;
who is without ears, tongue, nose, skin, or eyes, yet is everywhere and at all times.
He who hears, tastes, smells, touches, and sees—
he alone is that by whose light the nature of existence and non-existence is perceived,
as well as the beginningless and endless variegated creation and his own form, which is free from attachment.
He who perceives the world as his own nature— a constant manifestation consisting of the void itself, with the pupils of the eyes situated between the eyebrows like half-closed lids—
and for whom there is no other cause for that all-pervading Lord, just as there is none for a hare's horn; // MU 3.9.56 //
He for whom this world is an effect, like a mass of waves from water;
he who, blazing incessantly on all sides, abides within the vessels of the mind;
by the light of that lamp of pure consciousness alone, the three worlds shine.
Without which even these luminaries such as the sun are like darkness;
when it exists, the three worlds proceed like a mirage. When it is active, it seems to arise; when it is motionless, it seems to have entered within.
In him this fortune of the world revolves like a circle of fire;
he is the pervasive Great One, whose nature is the play of the creation and dissolution of the universe,
consisting of both motion and stillness, pure and imperishable.
The existence of that [Self], which consists of both movement and stillness like the wind and is omnipresent,
appears as if divided by name alone for the sake of conventional usage, but not in reality.
He who is always awakened and he who is always asleep— [these two are one].
He who is neither asleep nor awake, who is always and everywhere [the same];
he whose non-vibration is auspicious peace, and whose vibration is the existence of the three worlds;
he who is the single one, whose nature is the play of both vibration and non-vibration, and whose form is all-pervading.
Like fragrance in flowers that perish, it does not vanish even when they are destroyed;
though present before the eyes, it is ungraspable, like the whiteness in white cloths.
He who speaks is like one mute, and he who thinks is like a stone.
He who is the enjoyer, though eternally satisfied; he who is the agent, yet possesses nothing;
he who is limbless, yet possesses all limbs, with a thousand hands and eyes;
and by whom this entire world is pervaded, even though he remains as nothing at all.
He whose sensory functions are entirely devoid of the power of the senses,
and whose mental constructs proceed even though he is without a mind; from the non-perception of whom the fears of the serpent of saṃsāra vanish.
Upon seeing whom all calamities flee in every way and at all times;
in whom, the witness, the pervasive manifestation, and the eternal— like actions in a lamp—
various activities proceed, preceded by movement.
Because hundreds of rows of objects in the form of jars, cloths, and so forth arise from that very [consciousness] as its transformations—
just as waves, droplets, surges, and billows arise from the ocean—
he alone arises through the delusions of hundreds of objects.
Just as gold [is not distinct] from bracelets, armlets, earrings, and anklets; so you,
who are the self-luminous essence, and I, and these people here, and that which is not you—
O one whose nature is unawakened— that is neither I, nor these people here.
In that [Reality] wherein the world of appearances flashes forth like a series of waves upon the water— appearing as both distinct and non-distinct, as existent and non-existent, and as transient—
from which arises the reckoning of time and from which comes the visibility of the visible; MU_3.9.74.
By whatever mental construction there is the manifestation of speech;
by which you perceive action, form, taste, smell, touch, sound, and consciousness—
that is the God, and that by which you perceive is also He.
O virtuous one, through focused attention, you shall realize your own Self— that which exists as the act of seeing among the seer,
the seeing, and the seen; the unborn, undecaying, non-inert, eternal, constant Brahman, auspicious, stainless, beginningless, and beyond reproach by those whose objects of knowledge are barren.
Devoid of all parts and divisions, the cause of causes; experience itself, unknowable as an object, yet the very essence of consciousness within.
The Tenth Chapter, titled "The Description of the Supreme Cause."
Rāma:
That which remains when the great dissolution has occurred—let this be called "formless"; there is no doubt about this.
How could it not be empty? How could it not be luminosity?
Or how could it not be of the nature of darkness? Or how could it not be of the nature of space?
Or how could it not be of the nature of consciousness? Or how could it not be the living soul (jīva)?
"How could it not be the principle of consciousness (*buddhitattva*), or how could it not be the mind (*manas*)?
Or how could it not be 'nothingness,' or even 'everything'?
By this turn of phrase, a kind of delusion has arisen within me. (MU 3.10.3–4)
Vasiṣṭha said:
This question posed by you is exceedingly difficult;
yet I shall resolve it without effort, just as the sun dispels the darkness of night.
Listen as this is explained: that which remains as the existent at the end of the great aeon (mahākalpa) is not non-empty; it is said to be "this.
Just as a carved figure (sālabhañjikā) exists within a pillar even before it is carved out, so too does that [reality] exist.
Likewise, the universe is situated therein; therefore, that state is not empty.
This world, known as the "universe," appears in this manner with its great enjoyments—whether it be real or unreal, where in that [state] could there be emptiness?

Just as a pillar that has not been carved with a female figure is not empty of that figure, so too, my dear, the world is Brahman; therefore, that state is not empty of it. Just as a wave in gentle water neither exists nor does not exist, [so is the world in Brahman].

In this same way, this world has entered into Brahman, which is the state of both the empty and the non-empty. Since space, time, and so forth are stilled within it, why is one not deluded internally regarding the unborn essence, just as the carving of a doll occurs within a tree?
That [comparison] regarding pillars, statues, and so forth, is similar only in one respect to the ultimate state of the world, and not in every way.
This [world] never arises from another, nor does it ever cease.
Thus, the absolute Brahman, whose nature is such, abides within its own self.
The conceptualization of the meaning of the word "empty" depends upon the non-empty;
since non-emptiness is impossible [in the absolute], how can there be emptiness or non-emptiness?
Indeed, this luminosity arising from the elements is not possible in Brahman;
for how could the sun, fire, moon, stars, and so forth exist there in that imperishable state?
The absence of the luminosity of the great elements is called darkness.
But because it is not born from the great elements (*mahābhūta*), there is no darkness whatsoever here.
For this [Self], which has the nature of space, its illumination is solely through self-experience (*svānubhūti*);
that which exists within is experienced by that very [self-experience] and not by anything else.
That which is liberated from both darkness and light— know this undecaying state to be the very sheath of space, the sheath within which the world exists.
Just as there is no difference whatsoever between a wood-apple and that which is called a wood-apple, so too is there no difference here.
Likewise, in this case, there is not even the slightest difference between Brahman and the world.
Just as a wave exists within water, or a jar within clay, so too,
since the existence of the world is [identical] to that [Brahman], how could it be of the nature of emptiness?
The beauty of analogies such as water and clay does not equal that of the Formless here;
for Brahman is as pure as space, and that which resides within it is likewise so. Therefore, the space of consciousness is such that it is even purer than physical space.
That which exists within it is exactly like that, even in its aspect as the referent of the word "world.
Just as pungency within a peppercorn is not perceived without a taster,
so too pure consciousness within the supreme ether is not perceived without the element of the object of thought.
Therefore, even consciousness, being of a non-material nature, exists within itself as something distinct from the object of cognition;
this world-existence is likewise exactly such, by virtue of its essence consisting solely of that [consciousness].
Form, light, and mental attention are composed of that very [consciousness] and nothing else.
Therefore, the universe as it truly exists is either deep sleep or indeed the fourth state (turya).
By that [realization], the yogi—though engaged in worldly activity—is one whose self is in deep sleep and whose intellect is tranquil;
he abides in Brahman, which is beyond all appearances and is the source-container of all appearances.
Just as the process of fluidity exists within calm water that possesses form,
so too does the universe exist within the Supreme, which is formless and yet resembles it;
from the Full, the Full flows forth, from the formless, the formless.
The universe has appeared from Brahman, yet it is devoid of any objective reality.
From the Full, the Full proceeds; that which is established remains the Full alone.
Therefore, the universe is unproduced; and whatever is produced, that is indeed That itself.
Since there can be no object of cognition (*cetīya*) in that state, how could there be any objective referent?
Just as there is no pungency in black pepper when there is no one to taste it, so too this consciousness (*cit*),
though appearing as the mind (*citta*) within the Supreme, is truly unreal.
Since the reflection does not exist, how can there be the capacity for reflection?
That which is even subtler than the subtle atom,
purer, more refined, and more tranquil than even the interior of space— [that is the Self].
Because its nature is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, it is exceedingly vast;
it is without beginning or end, a manifestation devoid of anything to be manifested. Where this very form of consciousness is not found, there life is not obtained.
How could there be the nature of consciousness, which has the form of the wind of latent impressions?
Precisely because the nature of consciousness does not arise, there is no state of being a living soul (jīvatā) therein;
there is no intellectuality, no mentation, no sensory organ-ness, and no latent impressions.
Thus established, this undecaying state is full even while dissolution begins;
from our perspective, it remains peaceful, empty, and more vast than space. Rāma said:
"What is the nature of the ultimate reality (paramārtha), which has the form of infinite consciousness?
Explain this again with precision for the increase of my awakening.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
Listen as this Supreme Brahman is described— that which remains at the occurrence of the great dissolution, the cause of all causes—
when one has dissolved one's own self through the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. MU 3.10.38.
That form which is inexpressible is the true form of that reality.
There is no visible world, nor a seer; due to the absence of the visible, it is as if dissolved.
That which is the manifestation of "it shines" is the true form of that reality.
If that which is the nature of the living self (*jīva*), when directed toward an object of cognition, is its body;

yet that which is pure consciousness, stainless and peaceful, is the cause of all causes. (MU 3.10.41) Furthermore, when there is no contact with wind or other sensations by means of the thumb or a finger, [the self is perceived].
That form of the mind which exists while one is alive is the supreme form of the Self.
O sinless one, that form which remains after long contemplation— of that state which is dreamless, infinite, non-inert, and firmly established— is what is left.

That which is the heart of space, or of stone, or of the wind— that is the form of the Supreme Self, the sky of consciousness, which is beyond the reach of thought. It belongs to that which is beyond thought, devoid of mind, yet living and active.
That stability is the supreme, peaceful existence of that primordial reality.
That which is the center of the light of consciousness, or of dense light,
and that which is the center of vision— that is the form of the Supreme Self.
The experience of sensation, light, the visible, and likewise darkness—
that which is without beginning or end is the form of the Supreme Self,
from which the world seems to arise, even though its nature is eternally unarisen.
That form of the supreme Self is as if divided, though it is undivided;
that form of the supreme Self is like the state of being space for that which is not space, even while remaining as motionless as a stone for one intent on worldly activity.
Furthermore, that wherein these three forms— the object of knowledge, the act of knowing,
and the knower— arise and set, is the supreme and most excellent reality.
