Wherein this triad of the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, and the knower is reflected, [that is the supreme].
In the great mirror of the absence of intellect and so forth, that form is remembered as supreme.
That form of the Great Consciousness which is free from the six senses including the mind remains at the end of creation, whether in the moving or the stationary.
If the form of immobile beings were to consist of consciousness,
being free from mind, intellect, and the rest, it would be equal to the Supreme.
When Brahmā, Arka, Viṣṇu, Hara, Śakra, Sadāśiva, and the others have attained peace, this one supreme Śiva alone remains here.
The remaining, the ordained, the undestroyed, the effortless, the desired, the mixed, the unmixed, the subtle, and that which is not dependent upon the dependent.
This is the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Ultimate Reality Remaining at the End of the Great Kalpa."
Rāma:
O Brahmin, where does this radiant world, known as the visible universe of such a nature, go when the great dissolution occurs?
Vasiṣṭha said:
From where does the son of a barren woman come, or what is he like, and where does he go?
Tell me, where does the forest of the sky go, and from where does it come?
Rāma:
The son of a barren woman and the forest of the sky neither exist nor will they ever exist.
What kind of visibility could there be for him, and what kind of non-existence?
Vasiṣṭha:
Just as the son of a barren woman and the forest in the sky never exist at any time,
so too the entire visible world, beginning with the universe, never exists at any time.
That which did not exist at the beginning is neither arisen nor destroyed.
What kind of arising could there be for it? What talk can there be of the word "destruction"?
Rāma said:
For the conceptualization of the son of a barren woman or a tree in the sky certainly exists;
just as that [conceptualization] is subject to destruction, birth, and so forth, why should this [world] not be the same?
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Phulla, properly perform the decoration of your incomparable face with your curls;
for just as speech is devoid of external sequence, so indeed is the existence of the world.
Just as in a golden bracelet, even though it is clearly visible...
But the state of being a bracelet does not exist at all; likewise, the state of being the world does not exist in the Supreme.
Just as emptiness does not exist in space as something distinct from it, so too the state of being the world does not exist in Brahman, even though it is perceived.
Just as blackness is not separate from collyrium, nor coldness from snow,
so the world is perceived as distinct [from it], yet it does not exist in the supreme state;
and just as the coolness of the moon is not different from the moon itself.
The creation of Brahman does not exist as something distinct [from it].
Just as there is no water in a mirage-river, and just as there is no moonhood in a second moon, so too this world does not exist at all; though seen, it does not exist within the pure Self.
This light of the eye of consciousness shines in the sky of consciousness,
like a string of pearls in the stainless firmament called the world.
In the space of consciousness, that which is the space of consciousness shines by itself through its own nature as consciousness.
That very thing perceives itself as the world in that form.
For that which does not exist from the very beginning due to the impossibility of a cause cannot exist even in the present; what kind of destruction could there be of that?

How could insentience, which is impossible in that which has arisen from the elements, be capable of being the cause of an insentient object such as earth and so forth? Just as sunlight cannot be the cause of shade, this effect has not arisen from any such cause; therefore, it is nothing at all.
That which exists as the very cause is itself situated in this manner:
that which appears, though unborn, is the manifestation of consciousness itself;
the world that is seen in a dream is nothing but the shining forth of consciousness.
Just as the delusion of a dream-world is merely the internal manifestation of consciousness,
so too, at the beginning of creation, the manifestation of the world is extended within Brahman.
Whatever is seen here exists as the Real alone, abiding within the Self.
Nothing in the world ever sets nor does it ever rise.
Just as liquidity is water and mobility is wind,
and just as light is its own manifestation, so too the three worlds are Brahman alone.
Just as the knower of the inner self dwells within as if it were a city during the perception of a dream,
so too does one's own self alone appear as the world within the Supreme Self.
Rāma said:
"If that is so, O Brahmin, tell me how this poison of the visible world has arisen with such firm conviction, like the experience of an unreal dream. [Vasiṣṭha:]
When there is an object of sight, there is indeed a seer; when there is a seer, there is the state of being an object of sight.
When both exist within a single being, there is bondage; when one is destroyed, both are liberated.
As long as the destruction of the object of sight has not been realized by the Buddha, its absolute non-existence cannot occur.
As long as the visible object exists at first and subsequently undergoes destruction, the seer’s state of non-seeing— which bestows liberation—
is not possible; thus, bondage, consisting of the recollection of that visible object, does not cease.
Wherever it may be situated, this world— consisting of the memory of creation— indeed adheres to the movement of consciousness, just as a reflection adheres to its own mirror;
for if the visible world had never arisen from the very beginning, it would not exist by itself.
Because of the absence of the delusion of the seer and the seen, that liberation is possible.
[Rāma:
Therefore, having dispelled my doubt regarding the impossibility of liberation through reasoning—
"O best among the knowers of the Self, tell me how that which is absolutely impossible in the realm of the visible can appear," [asked the King].
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Just as that which is non-existent appears as the creation of the world, so it is."

Listen, O Rāma; I shall tell you through a long narrative. As long as that [account] has not been fully described by means of words in this discourse on resolve, it will not find rest in your heart, just as dust does not settle in a lake.

Having realized the absolute non-existence of this delusion of world-creation, you, with your self established in one-pointed meditation, will carry out your worldly activities. [You will see that] existence and non-existence, grasping and abandoning, the gross and the subtle, the moving and the unmoving— [are all unreal].
"Views will pierce you, but not like arrows piercing a great mountain.
This very Self exists as one alone; there is no second conceptualization.
O Rāghava, I shall explain to you how the world has arisen within this."
Therefore, all these manifestations have unfolded; for he who is the Great Soul, O dear one, is the entirety within the entirety.
He himself arises and dissolves as the locus of the treasury that illuminates the observation of forms and the mental reflection upon them.
This is the chapter titled "The Description of Ultimate Reality."
The Twelfth Chapter:
Vasiṣṭha said:
From this supreme, tranquil, and most purifying state...
Listen with the highest intelligence to how this universe has arisen:
deep sleep appears like a dream, and Brahman alone appears as the creation;
all is one and that is peaceful—now hear the sequence therein. MU 3.12.1–2.
The incessant manifestation, by its very nature, which consists of mere existence, belonging to that gem of consciousness whose form is infinite light—
that [manifestation] itself appears within the Self as if it were something to be perceived.
Not grasping an external object, it indicates consciousness, effort, and reflective awareness;
its form is slightly inferred through the mental constructions of future objects.
Subtler than space and pure, it is the awakening to all things yet to be.
Then that supreme reality, being oriented toward consciousness from the state of pure existence (*satī*),
becomes fit for the name "consciousness" (*cit*) by virtue of being slightly attainable;
subsequently, through dense self-awareness, it comes to be designated as the "living soul" (*jīva*) and so forth.
When that mental construction of a self, moving away from the supreme state,
becomes oriented toward the cycle of transmigration— having as its sole essence the mere contemplation of oneness with itself—
then these subtle bodies remain within it by virtue of their own inherent nature.
Immediately following this, emptiness arises as the *khasattā*;
it is the seed of the qualities such as sound, and it bestows the future meaning of designations.
Thereafter, the sense of "I" (*ahantā*) arises together with the existence of time (*kālasattā*).
That seed is the primary cause for the existence of the world, according to your doctrine concerning the meaning of "that which is to be.
Yet, this net— which is of an unreal nature— arises throbbing as if it were real, consisting merely of the self-awareness of that supreme power.
Such is that consciousness (*cit*), the seed of the tree of volition (*saṅkalpa*).
Therein, the hand of egoity (*ahaṅkāra*) is its wind, by virtue of being its vibration.
Consciousness, possessing the nature of "I-ness," through the contemplation of the subtle element of sound within space, [becomes the organ of hearing].
Having gradually become condensed from itself, it becomes the subtle element of space (*khatanmātra*).

That is the seed of the tree of the flood of words, containing the forms of future objects; it is that which undergoes transformation into the multitude of Vedas enriched by words, sentences, and means of valid cognition.
Therefore, the entire glory of the world will arise from that which has the nature of sound;
spreading through the transformation of the multitude of objects produced by the flood of sounds,
consciousness itself, possessing such an entourage, is designated by the term "jīva."
The seed of the tree of the multitude of beings, through the web of future words and meanings,
will then cause the fourteenfold collection of beings— the entire mass of the world-machine— to expand, enveloping the sky.
That very consciousness, whose essence has not yet attained the state of being named and which throbs with a body due to its vitality,
becomes in an instant through contemplation the subtle element of touch (*sparśatanmātra*).
It is the seed of the tree that has touch as its sole branch, expanding into a mass of wind.
From that, the vibration of the activity of all beings will spread forth.
Therein, whatever light arises from experience through the play of consciousness (*cidvilāsa*),
that will become the subtle element of fire (*tejomātra*), which bestows its respective designations and objects.
That seed of the tree of light, through the blossoming of the sun and other luminaries,
will from that cause the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) to spread forth by way of the differentiation of forms;
and thus, for you who have descended into the four states of being, it proceeds as if from the existent, yet from the non-existent.
The tasting of that assembly is called the subtle element of taste (rasatanmātra). That seed of the tree of taste consists of the future play of flavors;
from this mutual tasting, saṃsāra will expand forth.
This [element], consisting of mental construction and named after its future fragrance,
being of the nature of ideation, bestows the state of the subtle element of fragrance upon the ideation itself.
It is like the seed of a tree, which, by virtue of becoming the future terrestrial globe, possesses the form of that tree.
From that Self which is the support of all, the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) shall expand forth.
The subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi), being conceptualized by consciousness, transform themselves within one another without interval,
like waters within water.
In this way, whether these [elements] are mixed or separated again,
they are not found in their pure state; for indeed, until the end of all destruction,
they remain within the belly of space as forms consisting of mere consciousness.
Just as networks of banyan trees exist within the interior of a tiny seed,
they are seen to produce fruit with hundreds of branches and they expand;
within a single atom, they fit, and in an instant, they become vast aeons.
They run toward mere illusory manifestations, yet they remain free from such manifestations;
for all that is known by consciousness indeed condenses in an instant.
That group of subtle elements (tanmātra) is composed of Consciousness's own volition.
At the occasion of sensation, she perceives the flood of atoms as being indeed formless.
Is it not the case that the seed within the worlds consists of merely the five [elements]? Its seed is the supreme, primordial power of consciousness, which is concealed.
That which is born from it is always experienced as being that very same thing; therefore, the glory of the world is but the one, unborn, and primordial pure consciousness.
The thirteenth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Seed of Saṃsāra," by Vasiṣṭha.
In the supreme Brahman— vast, equal, abiding in absolute evenness,
whose nature consists of the non-arisen, space, light, darkness, existence, and so forth—
there was previously the conceptualization of being an object of cognition, arising from the consciousness of its own objective aspect.

From the consciousness of the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) arises the notion of being the mind (*citta*); from that, the notion of being the individual soul (*jīva*) arises through the consciousness of the nourishment of objects of thought; and from that, the notion of "I-ness" (*ahambhāva*) arises by virtue of exclusive devotion to the object of thought.
Then, from the transformation of egoity (ahaṃtā), there arises the measurement of intellect (buddhi) and skin;
this very [state] possesses the nature of the mind (manas), the word-tanmātras, and so forth.
From the swelling [of the tanmātras] through the contemplation of other tanmātras, it takes on the form of the gross elements.
Thus this great thicket, the beginning of the world, is perceived—
either instantaneously or gradually— like a city constructed in a dream,
arising again and again only to perish within the vast forest of the Great Space.
This seed, born from which the groves of the *karañja* trees of the world arise,
does not require anything at all— such as earth, water, air, and so forth.
This very consciousness-nature will subsequently, it is said, produce the earth and the other elements.
Like a city in a dream, that [world] consists of pure consciousness alone;

though it exists here and there as the first sprout of the universe, it is cast off [as unreal]. Consciousness is the imperishable seed of the fivefold world, and the fivefold world is the seed of that [consciousness].

Know that whatever is the seed, that is the fruit; therefore, the world consists of Brahman. Thus, at the beginning of creation, this group of five elements exists within the great space as the self-nature of the ether-like power of consciousness; it is conceptualized, not real.
Even that which, having attained swelling through this [process], is further expanded,
is not composed of reality because its nature is a mere mental construction (*kalana*) based on the form of space.
Indeed, nothing whatsoever is ever established that is proven by means of what is itself unestablished.
How could that which is of the nature of conceptual construction (vikalpa) attain the status of reality?
If, on the other hand, the pentad [of elements] is Brahman by virtue of its being identical with Brahman,
then the delusion of the three worlds is nothing but Brahman itself, matured through the manifestation of that pentad.
Just as this [universe], born of the pentad [of elements], vibrates at the beginning of creation,
so too here in the present it itself becomes the cause of the state of the elements.
Thus, nothing whatsoever is born, yet the world is perceived as having been born.
"Like a city of dreams or a city of mental construction, the unreal is experienced as real;
the space of Brahman, the supreme space, exists within the self as the space of the individual soul (jīvākāśa).
Thus does the one of purified self know this, because of the non-existence of earth and the other elements.
Thus has this living being been described as the self of space, just as it arises in the void. Now hear how the living being, as space, enters this body:
that living being as space is indeed the ether itself within that supreme sky.
In this regard, one perceives by thought, "I am a spark of light," and then,
as if that very [spark] were swelling, one contemplates it within oneself in the space of the mind;
just as the moon of conceptualization [perceives] the hare-mark, though it is non-existent, as having the form of a rabbit.
Meditating upon that very [Self], abiding in the form of both the seer and the seen,
it becomes two though being one alone, like one who perceives his own death in a dream.
Then, as if assuming a slight degree of grossness, it attains the state of the "star" (the individual soul).
In this context, the state of being "as-it-is" (yathābhāvitva) arises from the cultivation of the object and from the nature of consciousness itself.

Just as a traveler perceives "you" as "I" within a dream due to his state of mind, so too does this [Self], though eternally of the nature of space and identical with space, assume the notion of "I" by virtue of its consciousness.
Then, meditating upon the form of the star, which is designated as the future body,
the mind attains that state, just as it [attains] the nature of the object of thought.
Having abandoned that external [perception], [it remains] thereafter within the hollow of the star.
Just as a mountain, though situated outside, appears within a mirror;

or just as one perceives a body located in a well or contained within a casket, so too does consciousness perceive the individual soul (*jīva*) within the subtle body (*aṇuka*). Just as in dreams and mental constructs, consciousness itself knows [the soul].

Whatever the living soul (*jīva*), situated within the star-like point (*tāraka*) which is its own true nature, perceives by itself— that is this very thing consisting of intellect (*buddhi*), mind (*citta*), and so forth, taking the form of a continuum of cognition (*jñāna-santāna*).
Therefore, the space of the living soul (*jīvākāśa*) exists there, contained within the treasury of the space of the star-like point.
With the thought "I shall see," it seems to expand into the sky in order to look;
then, as if through two apertures, that by which it sees again what is called the external world shall be known by the name of the pair of eyes.
That by which it touches is its skin; that by which it hears is its sense of hearing.
That by which it smells is its nose; it perceives its own self within itself. Subsequently, that same faculty will manifest as the tongue, known by the name of tasting.
That which vibrates is the activity of the wind and the collection of the organs of action;
contemplating the entire aggregate born of form, light, and mental attention,
he whose self is the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) remains in the sky within the sky.
Thus, while contemplating such swelling within that spark of fire—
unreal yet appearing as real— the Brahman remains bearing the designation "living being" (jīva).
In this way, he has fallen into the confusion of conceptualizing the meaning of the term "living being."
The self whose nature is the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), having the form of the sky that is the body of consciousness,
perceives through its own imagination a form situated within the cosmic egg; some perceive it as being within the waters, while others perceive it as having the nature of a sovereign emperor.
He perceives and even experiences the formation of future universes from his own mind,
as if they were composed of his own volitions within the inner chamber of his self;
he is that which experiences the perception of space, time, action, and substance.
Fashioning words, the creator binds [beings] with imagined sounds.
This is the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) within the unreal delusion of the world;
it appears as something unreal, just like flying in dreams.
Thus, this very one— the self-arisen,

primordial Lord and Progenitor, whose nature is the *ātivāhika* body— has arisen by himself, even though he is fundamentally unmanifest. Even when this delusion, which takes the form of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), has come into being...
Nothing at all has been accomplished, nor has anything been born, nor is anything seen.
That Brahman is the sky, remaining as the very sky, free from doubt;
it has the form of a city of one’s own imagination, and though it exists, it is not real at all.
This painting has arisen in the sky, uncreated and bodiless;
it is both unmade and yet experienced, not real, yet standing as if it were real.
This is undoubtedly because Brahmā and the other gods are liberated throughout the great aeon (mahākalpa).
No prior memory whatsoever can be the cause of that which is self-existent (*svayambhu*).
Therefore, this world is considered to be born from that which is self-existent in whatever manner that self-existent being is.
Thus, the beginningless experience is exactly as it is through the earth and the other elements.
Just as the earth and other elements experienced in a dream appear upon waking,
so too this entire world is always remembered as being of the nature of mere space.
Wherever fluidity exists in water, it is found in that very place and in that manner.
In each and every place, there is no other creation within the Supreme Self.
Thus this mature creation exists, and thus this world-egg appears; it is indeed the very nature of space, devoid of any constructed form.
Thus, this visible world is peaceful, of the nature of space, without foundation, and free from delusion;
it is without support, without anything to be supported upon, non-dual, and devoid of unity.
Even when the consciousness of the world has arisen, nothing at all has been born.
The supreme space remains as utterly empty and transparent as it was during the dissolution of all things;
therein there is neither the contained nor the container, neither the visible nor the state of being a seer.
There is no cosmic egg, no Brahmā, and nowhere any belonging to the cosmic egg;
there is no world, nor is there a world-creature; everything exists as nothing but peace. Only Brahman, pure and transparent, thus shines by itself within itself through itself.
Due to its nature as consciousness and its fluidity, it revolves within itself like water in a whirlpool.
This which is non-existent appears here as if it were existent;
it is experienced as real, yet at the end it perishes as something non-existent, just like one's own death in a dream.
Alternatively, because its nature is pure consciousness (*vāja*), this very Reality is indeed free from affliction,
undivided, without beginning or end, and has the interior of the sky of pure knowledge as its belly.
In the supreme space itself, the first Lord of Creatures shines eternally by himself, identical with emptiness.
For he possesses a subtle, transportive body (*ātivāhika-vapuḥ*) and not a form composed of the elements such as earth; therefore, that which has not been born does not exist.
The fourteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Self-Existent One's Origin."
Vasiṣṭha:
Thus, this entire visible world consisting of "I," "you," and so forth, is nothing at all;
because it is unproduced, it does not exist, and that which does exist is only the Supreme.
This very supreme space itself perceives among living beings,
like water within the womb of the motionless ocean comes to possess movement;
without ever abandoning its nature as space, it seems to perceive— that which is to be seen.
Just as in dreams, mental constructs, or mountains [seen in visions], the internal activity of consciousness [is the cause];
that great body of the Virāj-self, which is devoid of earth and other elements,
is purely *ātivāhika* (subtle), consisting of the void of pure consciousness alone.
It resembles an inexhaustible dream-mountain, like a city seen in a stable dream;
it has the appearance of an army depicted in a painting situated within the mind of a painter;
it is comparable to a multitude of dolls on great pillars that have not been carved out.
In the ether of Brahman, he whose self is not fixed is like a statue upon its own pillar.
The first Lord of Creatures, formerly renowned as the Self-Existent (Svayambhū),
was without a cause because of the absence of his own prior effects.
At the conclusion of the great dissolution, it is said that even the primordial Grandfathers are liberated; therefore, what prior karma could there be for them?
The self of the wall must indeed be liberated, whether it exists as visible or invisible.

There is neither the visible nor the seer, nor indeed is there a creator; this alone is the reflection of all objects. From it arises the series of living beings, like a row of lamps from a single lamp.

"By mere volition alone, indeed, he goes from one volition to another, devoid of earth and the other elements, yet appearing as if possessing them, like one moving from one dream to another without leaving his bedchamber. From this very reflection, these individual souls (jīvas) emanate. (MU 3.1.11)
And because of the absence of auxiliary causes, that very [consciousness] is for you the cause of the effect.
In the absence of auxiliary causes, this cause and effect are one;
therefore, there is no other delusion of creation apart from that.
Brahman alone is the primordial Virāṭ Self; the state of emanation is the Virāṭ Self itself.
That very one exists thus as the space of the individual soul (jīvākāśa), since the earth and other elements are unreal.
Rāma said:
Is the mass of living beings limited, or is it infinite?
Or rather, is there an infinite aggregate of souls, as immovable as a mountain?
Like streams from a rain-cloud, or like spray from the ocean.
"Why do individual souls emerge like sparks from heated iron?
O Blessed One, tell me this definitive resolution regarding the web of living beings.
This has been mostly understood by me; please clarify that very point."
Vasiṣṭha:
There is not even a single living soul; how then can there be the arising of aggregates?
Your words are like saying that the horn of a hare has flown up into the sky.
There is no individual soul (*jīva*), nor are there multitudes of souls, O Rāghava;
nor does there exist any single mass of soul resembling a mountain.
All conceptualizations associated with the meaning of the word "soul" are themselves accompanied by every form of conceptualization.
Let your firm conviction be that "nothing whatsoever exists.
For here, indeed, there is everywhere only the pure, stainless Brahman, which is mere consciousness;
and because it possesses all powers, it assumes whatever form it wills for itself.

Indeed, by means of the very sequence of pure consciousness alone, one quickly perceives that [consciousness] itself— whether embodied or unembodied— as if it were a fully blossomed creeper. Furthermore, [the notions of] the individual soul (jīva), intellect (buddhi), the vibration of activity (kriyāspanda), the mind (manas), duality, and unity [are all that same consciousness].
It directs that [intellect], which shines forth as its own existence, toward cognition.
Thus, it becomes truly awakened; through awakening, it becomes Brahman itself.
Non-awakening perishes upon investigation, yet that [non-awakening] is not itself cognized.
Just as darkness perishes when illuminated by a lamp,
yet its true nature is not known [by the lamp itself], so it is indeed with the unawakened.
In this way, Brahman alone is the individual soul (jīvātman), undivided and continuous.
Possessing all powers, without beginning or end, it assumes the form of the essence of the Great Consciousness.
Because of its universal infinity, no conceptualization of difference exists within it; for whatever conceptualization there may be, that is itself [the reality] through direct experience.
Rāma:

This is so. But how, O Brahmin, is it possible that all the living beings of the world do not act according to the will of a single living being, under the influence of their identity with the Great Soul?
Vasiṣṭha said: That Brahman, which is the Great Living Self (mahājīvātman) and consists of all powers,
remains here exactly as it desires— undivided and without interval.
Whatever that Great-Souled One desires comes to him immediately;
yet if his desire first perishes, then duality arises from that.
Subsequently, for those powers divided by duality, [the world] is fashioned according to their own capacities.

For by this [power], it comes to be thus; such is the sequence of action established by that divine power. Without that restriction which has been fashioned by her, the other powers do not arise; rather, the will of the Pradhāna alone brings them forth.
That desire of the power called *jīva* which bears fruit does not do so without the performance of the regulation of the primary power (*pradhāna-śakti*).
If the regulation of the primary power were not well-established, [the desire would not bear fruit].
Therefore, due to the presence or absence of capacity, that fruit does not arise anywhere for those who have not exerted effort.
Thus, the Great Soul, Brahman, exists devoid of end or beginning;
through the living soul, it becomes many millions and billions of souls, and yet it remains nothing at all.
Through the perception of the object of thought, the individual soul comes into being and enters the cycle of transmigration;
through the non-perception of that [object], form attains peace from transmigration.
Thus, by means of the sequence of activities of the elder souls, [the state of] the younger souls [is reached].
The state of being a living soul first arises, just as the state of gold arises from copper.
Here, in this infinite supreme space, even though this entire multitude is non-existent,
it arises as if existent— being nothing other than the void itself— consisting of the wondrous manifestation of consciousness.
That which is experienced by consciousness as a self-manifesting wonder—
the future body, name, and so forth— is known as the contemplation of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāvanā).
That which is the light of consciousness within consciousness is infinite because it consists of that [consciousness] alone.
This very expanse of the worlds is reflected within her.
By means of such terms as "transformation" (pariṇāma) and "modification" (vikāra), that very same immutable Consciousness,
though indivisible due to its uniform nature, becomes aware through its own power alone.
That which is the self-sustained relishing of consciousness, whose nature is uninterrupted play, is this very world— the manifestation of that light which is beyond being an object of thought.
This pervasive power of consciousness is subtler even than space.

By her very nature, she perceives this non-duality (ahantā). Whatever within herself flashes forth by itself like water, reaching to the end of the world as a minute atom of non-duality— that very thing she beholds.
That consciousness which, being beautiful and wondrous, performs a marvel within itself—that very thing has spread out what is called the "world.
O Rāghava, the state of being consciousness is the ego; it is that very same [consciousness] which is the mental construction.
Therefore, since the subtle elements and so forth are indeed consciousness alone, where can duality and unity reside?
As long as you do not abandon the cause of the individual soul—the notions "you" and "I"—abandon them!
Remain in the remainder that lies between existence and non-existence, and become one whose nature is the ultimate goal.
Just as that consciousness was first conceived as its own existence, so it has arisen;
it is seen as non-different from space, for I know both existence and non-existence.
Consciousness is space, space is the world and its activities, and space is the oceans, gods, and mountains.
Indeed, because it consists of the wonder of the consciousness that takes on various forms, there is nothing else whatsoever.
Whatever is a manifestation of something, that can never be separate from it;
this is true even for a reality with parts—what need is there to mention that which is partless?
One should always cite that there is no consciousness for that which is beyond the reach of thought, nor for that whose form is unmanifested;
whatever is the form of the world, that is the form of its own radiance.
Mind, intellect, ego, the elements, the mountains, and the directions—[all these are but its manifestation].

Thus, through this arrangement of synonyms, [it is shown that] the world exists from the reality of consciousness (*cit*). Know that the world is the consciousness-nature of consciousness; for there is no consciousness-nature that is not the world.
Since it is non-worldly, consciousness would be non-consciousness; because there is no difference between being and non-being, how could there be a world?
To cite the innate wonder at the end of the seed-syllable *marīca*:
it is this very [wonder] that exists as the world, consisting of nothing more than the subtle element of life (*jīvatanmātra*).
Because of its consciousness, the manifestation of its own power is the consciousness’s sense of "I-ness" (*ahambhāvana*).
For this living being (jīva) is essentially of the nature of vibration and action, and it is indeed designated by its future name.

That which is the mental construction (kalana) through consciousness regarding objects and directions to be accomplished by itself is differentiated by limitations and modifications; therefore, [in its true nature], it does not exist [as such].
There is no difference between the agent and the action, for both consist of the vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*).

Action is merely vibration, and that very [vibration] is known as the person (*puruṣa*). The individual soul (*jīva*) is the movement within consciousness; for men, consciousness is that very [movement].
But the mind, though having the form of a sense organ, moves indeed in manifold ways. For the world is a flash of the light of consciousness in which all particularities are stilled;
therefore, nothing other than that exists, such as the relationship of cause and effect.
"I am indestructible, I am unburnable, I am indeed neither moistened nor dried up;
I am eternal, all-pervading, stable, and immovable"—this is my established nature.
Let them dispute as they wish regarding this matter with their delusions.
We, however, are not wandering; we have been born free from delusion.

While in the case of a visible, embodied form established in the ignorance of the unwise, modifications and the like may appear as distinct; but this is not so in the case of the formless, which is the consciousness of the knower of that [Reality], the sky of consciousness whose nature is both being and non-being.
The mind, which is the essence of the object of thought, expands its powers called Time and the rest—
powers that are as clear as space— as its own blossoms, beautiful with the honey of consciousness.
The unstruck bow of consciousness itself flashes forth in manifold variety.
The jewel of consciousness shines forth by itself in manifold ways, without any external cause.
The wind of consciousness, whose nature is non-inert, vibrates by itself in diverse manners; the water of consciousness, which does not remain stagnant, turns by itself in various directions.
The lofty peak of consciousness, fashioned from various elements, is itself manifested;
the moonlight of consciousness, which is the constant radiance of the joy of manifold flavors, is itself ever-arisen.
The light of consciousness, whose nature is stainless, is itself eternally manifest.
In the ignorant, consciousness has set of its own accord; in the wise, it has arisen through knowledge. In the insentient, it has reached the state of deep sleep through its own inertia;
yet, by virtue of its nature as consciousness, the great sky of consciousness is both vibrating and non-vibrating.
For the world exists and does not exist as the radiance of the light of consciousness;
the world exists and does not exist as the singular voidness of the space of consciousness.
The world exists and does not exist as the great form of the light of consciousness.
The world exists and yet does not exist as the dense vibration of the wind of consciousness.
The world exists and yet does not exist as the blackness of the darkness of the mass of consciousness.
The world exists and yet does not exist as the day of the light of the sun of consciousness.
The delusion of the world is a single atom of the mountain of consciousness’s collyrium;
the streak of the world is the heat of the fire of consciousness; the whiteness of the world is the whiteness of the conch of consciousness;
the world is the interior of the mountain of consciousness; and the world is the liquidity of the water of consciousness.
The world is the sweetness of the sugarcane of consciousness; the world is the oily richness of the milk of consciousness.
The world is the coolness of the snow of consciousness; the world is the blazing of the flame of consciousness.
The world is the viscosity of the ghee of consciousness; the world is the wave of the river of consciousness.
The world is the sweetness of the honey of consciousness; the world is the golden armlet of consciousness;

the world is the fragrance of the flower of consciousness; the world is the fruit at the tip of the creeper of consciousness. The existence of consciousness alone is the existence of the world, and the existence of the world alone is the very body of consciousness.
In this regard, differentiation, transformation, and so forth do not exist [in Him], like impurity in the sky.
Thus, because of its nature as Pure Being (sanmaya), this triple world—whether existent or non-existent—is that very Being itself;
for, due to its being the undifferentiated Self, existence and non-existence are one with it.
Fie upon those who, in order to deny direct experience, imagine that the meanings of the words "part" and "whole" are like a hare's horn!
There exists no world therein— not even the mountains, the heavens, the earth, the rivers, or their lord.
Since consciousness is one, how could there be any contingency regarding the delusion of "the other" therein?
Though as solid as the heart of a stone, consciousness is as clear as its own space;
it holds within itself the entire tranquil arrangement, just as a stone [holds its internal structure].
In the space of the multitude of objects, you are like a mere fragment of space;
for you, there are no delineations of "you-ness," "I-ness," "self-ness," "that-ness," or "existence.
Like the pervasive arrangement of a mass of lines within the interior of a leaf, [all things are spread out].
This consciousness, by its very nature, internally maintains a character that is both different and non-different from all things.
Know that the state of consciousness— which is, by its own nature, devoid of causality— is the primordial grandfather of the entire multitude of causes, as established through direct experience.
Nor can the non-existence of the inconceivable consciousness be established even by words;
for it is observed that whatever exists arises, like a sprout from a seed.
O dear one, within this Great Consciousness there exists the three worlds, which, though distinct, are as utterly empty as the sky.
"Through the experience of your being, you have reached the certainty that this entire visible world consists of the supreme state.
Having spoken thus, the sage, the day departed, and the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites.
Having offered her salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, she returned along with the rays of the sun.
This is the fifteenth canto, titled "The Establishment of the Office of Brahman."
Vasiṣṭha said: This world is indeed just like space; for just as a pearl shines in the pure sky, so the world, which is of the nature of space, shines in the sky of consciousness.
The statue of the three worlds appears as if carved,
yet it is not carved upon the pillar of consciousness, nor is there any carver here.
Like the stillness of water within the ocean, though they do not deviate from their own nature, [they remain unmoved].
Likewise, those who know the visible world perceive the objects of knowledge as if they were external;
even the lattice-like arrangements that are reflections of the sun within water appear gross to the world-perception, yet they are as immovable as atoms.

The appearance of the world has no appearance of its own because it is non-different from Brahman; however, the mass of rays from the sun reflected in water gives rise to the experience of difference. Even these things experienced in the world are of the nature of space.

The earth and other elements do not exist at all, just as in dreams and mental constructions (saṅkalpa). Within this grasp of a solid mass, which is in reality of the nature of the space of consciousness, they are not possible anywhere, like water in a mirage.
In this world, which lacks any substantial core and is like a city of Gandharvas in the desert,
that which appears as a visible object is merely an illusion, like a river seen in a mirage.
There is no comparison whatsoever between this world and a mountain in a dream.
Fulfilled and free from mental construction, the splendor of the visible world is nothing but the void.

(MU 3.15.9) Excluding the conceptualization of the meaning of the words "world" and "Brahman" as known by the ignorant, there is indeed no difference between the referents of the words "world," "Brahman," and "void. (MU 3.15.10)
But this manifestation of the sun of pure consciousness, which is devoid of objects of thought, is as subtle toward the sky as a cloud formed by mere volition is toward a cloud;
it is as transparent as a city in a dream is toward a magnificent city in the waking state.
In the same way, this world is transparent toward the imagined world. Therefore, the world, whose nature is consciousness beyond the object of thought, is nothing but the void.
Know that the words "void" and "world" are synonyms, both being composed of consciousness and empty of objective reality.
Therefore, nothing whatsoever has arisen here in this world that is visible;
it remains as it is, unnameable and unmanifested.
The world itself is the great space, the space of consciousness, without walls.
It does not fill even an atom of space or the capacity of a scale;
it is purely of the nature of space, transparent, devoid of any solid form,
consisting of space within space, variegated, and existing like a city of one's imagination.
In this regard, hear this narrative of the pavilion, which is an ornament for the ears, so that this matter may find rest in your mind without doubt. Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, for the sake of increasing true awakening, tell me briefly and quickly the entire narrative called 'The Pavilion' (Maṇḍapa), by which awakening may increase.
Vasiṣṭha said:
On this earth there once appeared a blooming lotus of a lineage,
a glorious king named Padma, who had many sons and vast treasuries;
he was an ocean in the maintenance of moral boundaries and a sun to the darkness of his enemies.
He is the moon to the night-lotus of beloved women, and the fire that consumes the grass of their faults;
he is Mount Meru for the hosts of gods, and the ocean from which the moon of his fame arises;
he is the lake for the swans of virtuous qualities, and the sun for the lotuses of his artistic skills.
A wind to the ocean of enemies, a lion to the elephants of pride,
beloved of all branches of knowledge, a mine of all marvelous virtues;
he was a Mount Mandara shining as he churned the ocean of the enemy Śūra.
He is the honey from the multitude of flowers that are his playful charms; he is the flower-armed god of love who is the very fortune of the world.
He is the wind that causes the play-palm trees to dance; he is the Keśava who is the festival of daring deeds.
He is the moon for the night-lotuses of goodness; he is the fire for the creepers of wicked conduct.
He had a fortunate wife named Līlā,
a playful woman endowed with every grace, like a lotus risen upon the earth;
she was charming with all prosperity and spoke with sweet, playful words.
Gently turning with joy, her smile like the rising of a second moon;
her lotus-face captivating with its mass of curls; her limbs cool and her complexion as fair as a *karṇikāra* flower; she was like a moving lotus-pond.
Laughing like a mass of *kunda* flowers with the grace of creepers, full of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*),
with hands of coral and rich in blossoms, she was like the embodied splendor of spring;
pure-bodied and holy, she bestowed joy upon the people.
Like the celestial river Gaṅgā, sporting with swans, having descended to earth,
she appeared like another Rati arisen to perform for a long time the service of that Puṣpaka, who bestowed delight upon all.
When [the world] was anxious, she was deeply agitated; when it was joyful, she was delighted; when it was utterly distraught, she was overwhelmed with confusion.
Like a reflection, the beloved was merely terrified when it was enraged.
This is the chapter titled "The Description of the King" within the Narrative of the Pavilion, concerning the manifestation of the world as like space.
The sixteenth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
He, whose wife was none other than the Apsaras Bhūtalā, [remained] a husband to no other woman.
He took delight with that beloved wife in the unfeigned essence of love within the garden groves, in the thickets of *tamāla* trees,
upon couches made of flower-canopies, and in the dwellings formed by the circles of creepers.
Upon flower-laden palace beds, in pathways strewn with heaps of blossoms,
on swings in the spring gardens, and in pleasure ponds;
amidst groves of sandalwood trees and beneath the shade of *santānaka* trees.
In houses made of *kadamba* and *nimba*, and within those of *pāribhadra*;
in mountain caves and marshy banks, and in cities with many windows; on the shores of rivers and in huts, and in dwellings atop elephants.
In summer, they dwell in houses of snow, in vine-arbors,
beneath trees that are golden palaces, and in walls of pearls and rubies,
all fragrant with the nectar of blossoming *kunda* and *mandāra* flowers.
In the forest groves of spring, where rows of cuckoos warble,
upon grounds of various jeweled grasses with soft luster,
and at waterfalls raining down showers of shimmering spray; MU_3,16.8–MU_3,16.8.
Upon the golden and ruby stone-slabs of the mountains,
in the dwellings of divine sages and seers, in remote and meritorious hermitages,
and amidst blooming water-lilies and smiling lotus-pools.
In forest glades where trees were in bloom and lotus ponds were in full flower,
they entertained themselves with riddles, narratives, and word-games; likewise with *aṣṭāpada* puzzles, brilliant displays of wit, and verses with hidden fourth lines.
Through dramas and narratives, through verses and the confusion of *bindumatī* meters,
through regional dialects and the activities of cities and villages,
and through arrangements of garlands, wreaths, and various ornaments;
With playful, restless movements that were vessels for various aesthetic sentiments;
with the chewing of betel leaves mixed with moist areca nuts and camphor;
with the play of applying unguents and the graceful sport of swinging on a cradle.
In their homes, they engaged in the rhythmic swinging of flower-cradles back and forth,
and took delight in hiding within the bodies of flowering creeper-thickets;
they traveled by boat, carriage, elephant, horse, camel, and other mounts.

Through the playful sport of water, by splashing one another, through dancing, singing, and the arts of *lāsya* and *tāṇḍava*, with musical performances, conversations, and the playing of the *vīṇā* and *mṛdaṅga* drums; MU_3,16.16–17.
In gardens, on trees by the banks of rivers, in forest paths,
in inner apartments, in palaces— in such various places as these— she,
that young woman raised in luxury, was his devoted and beloved wife.
Once, she whose thoughts were pure reflected:
"This lord of the world, my husband, is dearer to me than even my own life;
endowed with the splendor of youthful exuberance, how might he become free from old age and death?"
"How might I, with my high breasts, sport for a long time at will for hundreds of years with this husband in flower-pavilions?
I shall strive accordingly through the successive practices of austerity, recitation, and self-restraint."
"May I be a king as radiant as the moon at night, free from old age and death.
For now, I shall ask those twice-born ones who are advanced in knowledge, advanced in austerity, and advanced in learning: 'How might death not exist for men?'"
Then, having quickly honored the invited brahmins with humility, she asked them again and again, "O brahmins, how might immortality be attained? The brahmins replied:
"O Goddess, all the perfections and the powers of perfection are attained through austerity, recitation, and self-restraint;
however, immortality is never obtained. Having heard this from the mouth of the twice-born, she reflected once more.
"Terrified by the thought of separation from my beloved, I shall quickly [resolve this] by my own wisdom alone:
'If, by fate, death should come before my husband,
then, liberated from all suffering, I shall abide happily in the Self.'"
Then, even if my husband should die first after a thousand years,
I shall act in such a way that his life-force will not depart from this house;
while his life-force remains wandering here in my own inner palace pavilion.

split asunder in her heart like a parched bean pod.
Having become a corpse along with her husband and casting off her body far away,
she approached her husband by means of a subtle, transportable body (*ātivāhika-deha*).
Like a river following its course, she followed after her husband who was buried there.
He attained freedom from sorrow, like a flower-cluster in springtime.
There, this Brahmin possessed abundant houses, lands, immovable property, and so forth;
yet today, on the eighth day since his death, his soul remains in a temple in the village of Giri.
The twentieth canto, titled "The Death of the Brahmin," from the Līlopākhyāna; the goddesses said:
That husband of yours has now been accomplished as a twice-born man who has attained the status of a king;
and she who was the Brahmin woman named Arundhatī, you are she, O lady.
Here, you two, as a noble couple, shall rule this kingdom.
Like two young ruddy geese born upon the earth, or like Śiva and his consort.
Thus has been described to you in its entirety that former delusion of transmigratory existence;
it is mere illusion, nothing more than space itself assuming the form of the individual soul.
This delusion has been reflected in the mirror of consciousness from that [prior] delusion;
though it is entirely unreal, arising from the unreal, it brings about the destruction of worldly existence for you both.
Therefore, who could be composed of delusion, or who could be free from delusion?
"Creation manifests from unimpeded and vast consciousness; nothing else expands.
Having heard this, Vasiṣṭha’s eyes remained wide open for a long time with beautiful wonder.
Having become [visible], Līlā spoke these words, her syllables slow with playful grace:
"O Goddess, how has your word come to be so false?
Where is the life-force of the Brahmin in his own home, and where are we standing here?"
How can such another world, that earth, those mountains, and those ten directions fit within the interior of my house where my husband resides?
Even Airāvaṇa was bound by me within the belly of a mustard seed.
A battle was fought by a mosquito against a pride of lions within the hollow of an atom;
Mount Meru was placed upon a lotus-stalk and swallowed by a honey-drinker;
having heard the thundering of dream-clouds, peacocks dance in a painting.
"Just as this is inconsistent, O Sovereign of all sovereigns,
so too is it inconsistent that the earth and the mountains are within the house;
O Mistress of the Gods, explain this correctly with your stainless intellect."
For those of great majesty do not tremble when [a request] is well-received with favor.
The Goddess said:
"I do not speak this falsely; listen to it exactly as it is, O beautiful one."

For the breaking of established laws is not something performed by those such as myself. Whatever boundary I have established, even while being challenged by another, who else will maintain that very boundary once it has been broken by me?
The soul of the twice-born, while in that very same house,
perceives this earthly kingdom as being in the sky itself, for it is of the nature of space;
that former memory of yours has been lost, and another has arisen.
Just as the memory of waking occurs in a dream, O lady, so is this death.
As the three worlds appear in a dream through mental construction, as the triple universe exists [in thought],
as the battle for the sake of a story, and as water in a desert land.
This earth, together with its mountains, forests, and cities, exists within that brahmin’s house like a mental construction or a reflection;
though it appears as if real, this dense manifestation is entirely unreal.
Within the hollow of the sheath of that sky of consciousness (cidvyoman), which is an appearance of unreality,
that which is called "memory" arises from the unreal; it too is unreal,
for even a wave in the river of a mirage is not real.
Know this abode of yours to be contained within the space-receptacle of that house; know me, yourself, and everything else to be nothing but the void alone.
These successions of experiences—dreams, unions, volitions, and self-perceptions—are likewise so.
In this regard, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are primary for the sake of awakening, like a lamp.
Established within the house of a Brahmin, the life-force of the twice-born dwells therein;
within it, the earth with its oceans and forests is situated, like a bee upon a lotus.
Within a certain single, delicate hollow of that [tree],
this city appears like a mass of hair in the sky.
O slender lady, in this very city stands this residence of yours.

Therefore, how could it be that within even a minute atom there exists a multitude of elephants? My child, who indeed could possibly count the worlds that exist within, one after another, inside every single atom which is of the nature of consciousness?
Līlā said: "O Supreme Goddess, that Brahmin died on the eighth day;
many years have passed for us since then, so how can this be?"
The Goddess said:
"Just as there is no length of space, so too there is no length of time. Listen as I explain, according to the proper method, how this is indeed not the case."
Just as this manifestation of the creation of the world is mere appearance,
so too is this manifestation of moments and aeons mere appearance.
[This applies] to the states of being, existence, and birth of moments, aeons, the creation of the world, and living beings.
O child, listen to this sequence of how appearances manifest as they truly are:
having experienced for a moment the swoon of false death, the living being,
though consisting of space itself, [arises] in space itself by means of a mere opening of the eyes.
"I am that which is to be supported here in this support," so it perceives;
"this body, possessing hands, feet, and so forth, is mine," thus it views it. At the very moment it perceives the body, at that same moment it perceives this [world].
"I am the son of this father; these years are mine.
These are my delightful kinsmen; this is my lovely dwelling.
I was born, I became a child, and I have grown to be such as I am now."
And all those relatives of his likewise continue to live in that same way;
yet, because of their essential unity with the single mass of the space of consciousness, they exist even within his own self.
Thus, although this grove of saṃsāra has arisen within this consciousness, it is [nothing but] consciousness itself.
Nothing at all has arisen; it is like the stainless sky, remaining as it is.
Just as consciousness exists in the dreamer, so too is that same consciousness in the object seen;
because it is always one and the same, the seer and the seeing in a dream are but consciousness.
Just as consciousness arises in a dream, so does it arise through the perception of the next world;
and just as it arises in the next world, so too does it arise here in this world.
Thus, for both the unreal and the real, there is no difference between the states of dreaming, the next world, and this world.
There is not even the slightest difference [between them], like waves in water.
Therefore, this entire universe is unborn; because it is unborn, it is indestructible.
And because its nature is that of the Knower (kha), it does not exist at all; that which appears is only consciousness (cit).
Just as this [consciousness] is of the nature of the supreme ether even when devoid of an object of thought,
so too it remains of the nature of the supreme ether even when accompanied by an object of thought.
Therefore, the object of thought is not other than this [consciousness], just as a wave is not other than water.
And yet, the state of being a wave does not exist at all, for it is just like the horn of a hare.
That very [consciousness], though never falling from its own nature, appears as if it has become the object of cognition;
therefore, the visible object does not exist at all—how, then, can there be the notion of a seer and a seen?
In the very moment immediately following the delusion of death for the living being,
the splendor of the visible creation of the three worlds enters into manifestation—
according to its location, according to its time, according to its inception, and according to its sequence.
According to their birth, according to their mother, according to their father, and according to their lineage;
according to age, according to agreement, according to station, and according to their endeavors;
according to kinship, according to servants, and according to the rising and setting of their worldly activities.
The one whose form is consciousness perceives that he was born even before being born,
as well as space, time, action, substance, mind, intellect, and the sense organs;
and instantly, at the end of death, he perceives his body in its youth.
"This is my mother, this is my father, and I was once a child"—
whether such a sequence consisting of memory has been experienced or not,
it arises later like the emergence of fruit from a flower.
It is experienced that everything passes in the mere blink of an eye;
yet for Hariścandra, a single night became like twelve years.
For those separated from their beloveds, even a single day stretches out like a year.

In the realm of dreams, one thinks, "I am dead," or "I am born," or "This is another, my father. (MU 3.20.51) The notion that an object yet to be experienced has already been experienced arises for one who has not actually experienced it; conversely, the notion that something has been experienced arises even when it was not experienced—this is clearly seen among gamblers and the like. (MU 3.20.52)
In the consciousness of intoxication, sleep, and so forth, emptiness turns into crowding, misfortune becomes equal to festivals, and even separation is perceived as gain.

Just as pungency resides within the tiny seed-particle of a black pepper, or as a mass of carved figures exists within a pillar; ||| MU_3,20.53 ||| just as it resides within its own self, or like a network of crafted statues inside [the wood].
Thus, this visible world exists as non-different from the Unborn and is quiescent; for whom, then, could there be the perception of bondage or liberation, and from what, or by what means?
The twenty-first canto, titled "The Demonstration of the Ultimate Reality of the World," within the narrative of Maṇḍapa, also known as the narrative of Līlā.
The Goddess said:
Immediately after the delusion of death, all worlds appear clearly to the living being,
just as all forms appear fully to one whose eyes have opened.
And those things composed of the divisions of space and time, of ether, of phenomena, and of karma— vast, infinite, and enduring until the end of the aeon—
even that which has not been experienced and not seen, [the thought] "this was done by me," [arises].
In that very instant, it becomes an object of memory, just as one’s own death is experienced in a dream.
Thus, this infinite delusion shines within the void of the sky of consciousness—
an imaginary city called "the world" that is devoid of walls.
"I am this world"— thus the memory of creation expands, producing a singular confusion through the reversal of distance and the eon into a single moment. Consciousness,
being both experienced and unexperienced, is thus twofold in form.
Previously, as if empty of causes, it proceeds as the very form of consciousness alone.
Even when there is no actual experience, the state of having been experienced arises within consciousness,
just as the memory of a father arises toward one who is not actually a father due to a dream-delusion.
Sometimes, having abandoned the state of memory,
that which exists as mere intuition shines forth in the form of the Lord of the first creation;
subsequently, this visible world, beginning with the three worlds, remains established within the memory of what has been experienced.
O slender one, for some it remains as a memory of what was experienced,
while for others this appears as mere manifestation without any recollection;
for the lordship over subjects belongs to certain atoms of consciousness (cidaṇu) by mere chance, like the "crow and the palm fruit" coincidence.
The visible world, when completely forgotten, is designated as liberation;
therein, neither the desired nor the undesired exists for anyone at all.
Without the attainment of absolute non-existence, the state of "I" and the world persists.

Liberation, consisting of non-arising, does not arise at all. Just as the delusion of a snake in a rope does not cease without the cessation of the referent of the word "snake," so too liberation, though eternally peaceful and consisting of non-arising, does not become quiescent [without the cessation of its conceptual object]. MU 3.21.12–13.

Being only half-pacified, he is not truly pacified; for by meeting with another state again, even after one demon has been destroyed, another demon arises for the wise man. And this expansive cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is indeed the Supreme itself—this is the certainty.
Whatever appears here due to the absence of a cause, that becomes non-existent. Līlā said: In the creation consisting of the forms of the Brahmin and the Brahmin woman, memory is the cause.
"How could that [vision] have arisen without this being remembered?
The Goddess replied:
"The recollection of the Grandfather (Brahmā) is the cause there, and his recollection [is the cause of mine]."
It is simply not possible for there to be a prior state, because of the liberation from previous birth.
Consciousness itself cannot be remembered as something prior;
it assumes the state of being born from a lotus and so forth, according to the nature of the sentient being.
Another person is born with the consciousness "I existed," while someone else arises by chance, as if by the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow, consisting merely of a flash of intuition.
Thus, when the world has arisen in this manner, there is nothing that does not exist at any time.
In some places, that which is called "risen" exists solely as the sky of consciousness.
The supreme state is the cause of this twofold memory;
this relationship of cause and effect is the single sky of consciousness alone.
The existence of cause and effect [is established] by means of auxiliary causes;
the identity of cause and effect does not cease due to their absence.
Know this very world to be the form of the Great Consciousness (mahācidrūpa) through recollection.
In this regard, the relationship of cause and effect exists; therefore, sound is not ultimately real.
Thus, nothing whatsoever has arisen, including the visible world of the three realms and so forth;
it is only the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) abiding solely within itself, in the space of consciousness.
Līlā said:
"O Goddess, what a supreme vision has been shown to me by you!
The beauty of the world’s forms is like the splendor of the morning light to the radiance of the eyes."
"Now, O Queen, while my vision has reached this state of maturity, pierce this mystery through practice alone— this mystery wherein that Brahmin dwelt in his house together with his Brahmin wife."

"Lead me to that creation, to that mountain village, so that I may behold it. The Goddess replied: "Behold this supreme, purifying vision, which consists of the nature of consciousness yet is beyond the reach of thought."
Having adopted this form and cast off the impurities of existence,
you will then undoubtedly attain the self that is like space, abiding in the sky—
just as one who is on the ground may conceive of a city within the expanse of the heavens.
We two behold him thus situated, together with the creation immediately following;
for in this way, through the gateway of that vision, the body is indeed the supreme bolt.
Līlā:
"O Goddess, by means of this very body another world is attained, or perhaps not; why is this so? Please explain the reasoning here out of your grace.
The Goddess said:

These worlds, which are formless, have been perceived by you as possessing form through a vain grasping, just as gold is perceived as a ring when one thinks it to be so. Even though the nature of a ring exists within the gold, the state of being a ring does not actually exist in the gold itself.
In whatever way the world appears, the state of being a "world" does not exist within the state of consciousness.
This world is indeed just space; it is Brahman alone, and not a visible object.
Not even a speck of dust can be seen here, like [a grain] in the ocean.
Brahman alone perceives Brahman; that which is not Brahman does not perceive Brahman.
Its very nature is such that it is designated by names such as "creation" and so forth. There exists no relationship of cause and effect between Brahman and the world.
Due to the absence of all auxiliary causes,
as long as your perception of duality has not been stilled through the practice of yoga,
you certainly do not perceive Brahman, which is not of that [dualistic] nature.
In this regard, those such as ourselves have attained proficiency;
for through the practice of the realization of Brahman, we indeed perceive that state.
My body, composed of space, is like a city of one's own mental construction.
"I behold this very wind as Brahman itself, that state [attained] by means of this body;
I am one whose body is pure knowledge, just like these [beings] born from the lotus and others.
O lady, this world, beginning with Brahmā and the self, is but a limb of ours."

Without practice, a fool does not attain the state of Brahman despite his form; remaining as one whose nature is the self of mental construction (*kalanā*), he therefore does not perceive that [Brahman]. Wherein the city of one's own volitions is not perceived within one's own body.
In that regard, the city of another's mental construction is not perceived within one's own body.
Therefore, having abandoned this body, you who are of the nature of the space of consciousness, behold that very [reality] immediately; do so, O best among those who know what must be done.
Just as a city of one's imagination is real for the one who imagines it—
whether with a body or without a body, but nothing at all for anyone else—
so too has this delusion of the world come to endure since the beginning of creation.
In that way, from that very moment, destiny attained its full maturity.
Līlā said:
"O Goddess, you said, 'Let us go to the house of the Brahmin and his wife.'"
"I say this: 'How, O Mother, am I to go? [He replied:
'Having cast off this body here, with a mind following pure being (*śuddhasattva*), I shall go to that supreme world; you may speak thus.'"
The Goddess said:

Just as the tree of your mental construction, though it exists, is of the nature of space—neither having the nature of a wall nor being obstructed by a wall, nor destroying a wall—so too is this [world]. *Muktikopaniṣad* 3.21.48.
That [body], it is said, consists of the form of a mind manifested solely for the sake of pure beings;
therefore, its manifestation differs only slightly from that supreme [mind].
Such as this is this body; I shall not depart, having abandoned it.
By this very means, I reach that place, just as the wind reaches a fragrance.
Just as water mingles with waters, fire with fire, and air with air,
so too does the mental body mingle with other bodies composed of mind.

For consciousness that is not of the nature of earth does not attain oneness with that which is of the nature of earth; where is there a collision between a mountain of imagination and an actual rock? This mental body of yours is indeed merely *ātivāhika*.
But when it is grasped through the notion of materiality due to long-standing mental habituation—
just as in a dream, just as in meditation over a long period, just as through delusions,
just as in the imagination of one addicted to vice, and just as in the city of the Gandharvas.
Līlā said: "When the attenuation of your latent impressions (vāsanā) has indeed reached its stable state,
then this body shall never again return to the condition of being composed of material elements."

When the conviction that the body is merely a subtle, transportable vehicle (ātivāhika-deha) becomes firm, this [gross] body attains that state; it perishes when delusion regarding its condition ceases.
Thus spoke the Goddess.
The process of destruction and non-destruction could only occur there if something actually existed;
but if it does not exist in reality, what kind of destruction could there be?
Just as when the delusion of a snake in a rope has ceased through the power of true knowledge, O son.
"What is the point of such talk as 'the snake is lost' or 'it is not lost'?
Just as the physical body is no longer seen through the thorough knowledge of reality,
so too the physical body is no longer seen through the knowledge of the subtle body (*ativāhika*)."
If that which is imagined were imagined by someone, then conceptual construction would cease;
but that [imagined object] has never existed here at all, being like a mere stone cast away.
This body and so forth exist as mutually filled with the other.
"Thus, O blessed lady, we see the truth; you do not see it.
When, at the beginning of creation, consciousness becomes conditioned by conceptual construction, then from that time forward, the single self is perceived as if it were an object."
Līlā:
Since the supreme reality alone exists— tranquil, undivided by space, time, and so forth—
whence could there be occasion for conceptual construction?
The Goddess said:

Just as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold, just as the state of being a wave exists in water, and just as reality exists in dreams, mental constructs, cities [of the gandharvas], and the like; MU 3.21.64.

Just as there is no dust in the sky, so too there is no conceptualization of a separate self within the experience of reality or in the state of consciousness, because its own nature is free from affliction. MU 3.21.65. Just as there is no dust in the sky, so there is no such part (kalā) in the Supreme.
Therefore, this one unborn reality is peaceful, devoid of both parts and their perception.
Whatever appears here is merely its own stainless manifestation,
like the radiance of a beautiful, supreme jewel known as gold.
Līlā said:
O Goddess, tell us this: for how long a time have we been thus deluded by these conceptual constructions of duality and non-duality?
The Goddess said:
"O fickle one, you have long been deluded and distressed by non-investigation.
Non-investigation arises from one's own nature; it perishes through investigation."
Non-investigation perishes through investigation in a mere moment;
thus, since this non-existence exists within, this ignorance does not truly exist.
Therefore, there is no such thing as non-investigation, nor is there ignorance, nor indeed any bondage.
There is no liberation free from affliction; rather, this world is pure consciousness.
Since you did not reflect upon this for so long, you were not fully awakened, but were merely wandering, agitated, in the ocean of delusion.
From this day forward, you are awakened; you are liberated and discerning.
The seed has fallen from your mind as the latent impressions have been attenuated.
For from the very beginning, the drama of saṃsāra—the world of the visible—has never arisen.
When [that state occurs], how, by what, or even what kind of latent impression (*vāsanā*) could it be perfumed?

Therefore, when the absolute non-existence of the seer, the seen, and the seeing has been attained, and supreme non-conceptual absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) is firmly established in single-minded meditation; 3.21.74–75.
When this seed for the exhaustion of latent impressions has sprouted even slightly within the heart,
the perceptions of passion, hatred, and so forth will gradually cease to arise;
and this very origin of saṃsāra will reach a state of rootlessness.

You shall attain a firm foundation in non-conceptual meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi). Free from the stain of the darkness of mental constructions, as pure as the expanse of the sky, you shall— by your own power— become the end of all the functions and causes of the senses, yet remain active through the necessity of a few specific tasks.
The twenty-second canto, titled "The Instruction on Rest," from the Narrative of Līlā.
The Goddess said:
Just as the dream-body is not real upon the full recognition of it as a dream,
so too this waking body, though experienced, is not real.
Just as the dream-body subsides through the recognition of it as a dream, [so does the waking body].
In the same way, through the thinning of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the waking body also subsides.
Just as this body is perceived at the end of a dream-constructed body,
so too does the subtle body (*ativāhika*) arise within the waking state of contemplation.

Just as the state of deep sleep arises in a dream when the seeds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are absent, so too does liberation arise in the waking state when the seeds of latent impressions are absent. That which is called "latent impression" for those who are liberated while living is not, in fact, a latent impression.
That which is designated as pure being (*śuddhasattva*) is called the generality of existence (*sattāsāmānya*).
That sleep in which latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are dormant is known as deep sleep (*suṣupta*);
that waking state in which latent impressions are dormant is called dense delusion (*ghano moha*).
Sleep in which all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been exhausted is designated by the term "the Fourth" (*turya*);
this state occurs even while one is awake when the supreme state has been realized.
For those who have exhausted their latent impressions here, this is the very nature of their existence as living beings.
When these are not yet released and not fully understood, that state is called liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
The mind, having fallen into a state of pure sattva and having its latent impressions (vāsanā) shattered,
attains the state of the subtle body (ātivāhika), just as snow melts when immersed in heat.

The mind, having attained the state of a subtle body (*ātivāhika*), meets with other Buddhas and with perfected beings (*siddhas*) who have passed through various births and creations, but not with anything else.
When this sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*) of yours reaches peace through its own practice...
Then, at the end of your vision, expansive awareness will manifest of its own accord.
Once the state of being *ativāhika* is known, your existence attains eternal stability;
then, through the light of other-worldly resolve, you become naturally pure.
Therefore, O blameless one, exert yourself toward the attenuation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
when that [attenuation] reaches full maturity, you will become liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
As long as this stainless moon of awakening has not been fully filled, [you must strive].
Therefore, having left the body here, let the other world be observed.
A body of flesh enters into union only with another body of flesh,
and not with a mental body in worldly activities and actions.
This has been stated exactly as it exists, according to experience;
it is established even among children, being perfectly proven, and is not like a boon or a curse.
Through the intense practice of awakening, this very body comes to be transformed.

The attenuation of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of saṃsāra is indeed the state of having a mental body (*cittaśarīratā*). While this [mental body] is about to arise here, it is not perceived by anyone;
rather, people merely observe the physical body as it dies.
But this body neither dies nor does anything whatsoever live;
for who indeed [is there] in the delusion of dreams and mental constructs regarding death and life?
Just as this life and death exist in a person created by imagination, so too are they in the world.
"O daughter, this very body appears as though it were real, yet it is truly unreal.
Līlā said:
"O Goddess, this pure knowledge has been taught to me by you."
When this [reality] is heard, all maladies go to peace.
For what benefit does it provide here, or what is its practice like?
How does it come to growth, and what would happen when it is fully nourished?
The Goddess said: Whatever is done by whomever, whenever, and in whatever manner,
that never attains perfection here in this world without practice.
The wise know that the practice of Brahman consists of reflecting upon That, speaking of That, mutually awakening one another to That, and directing one's vital breath and thoughts toward That.
For those people of meritorious deeds whose evil has come to an end, [this practice is fully realized].
Those who are liberated from the delusion of dualities should be known as servants of Brahman.
Those whose nights pass in reflections upon the scriptures of the supreme self,
intent on the thinning of latent impressions, are established as practitioners of Brahman.

Those noble souls who, being detached, cultivate within themselves the attenuation of the tendency toward enjoyment for the sake of non-becoming— they, being worthy of liberation, are victorious on this earth.
Adorned with the beauty of exalted generosity and colored by the essence of dispassion, they shine forth.
