Those whose intellects overflow with bliss are the supreme practitioners. Those who strive through reasoning and scripture to understand the absolute non-existence of any object of knowledge are established as practitioners of Brahman.
The wise know that from the very beginning of creation, the visible world has never arisen; it does not exist at all, neither this universe nor "I. This is what they call the practice of awakening.
Through the realization of the non-existence of the visible, passion, hatred, and the like are thinned away.

That delight which arises from strength is declared to be the practice of Brahman. Through the realization of the non-existence of the visible world, the attenuation of passion, hatred, and the like is called "austerity" (tapas) in this world; for the defect of the visible world is the cause of suffering.
For when the impossibility of the object of perception is realized, that is said to be the knowledge of the knowable;
through the practice of that [knowledge], there is Nirvāṇa—thus, practice is of great consequence.
The long-lasting sleep of the night of worldly existence is ended by the constant sprinkling of the water of discernment.
"In autumn, it overflows in the mind like a great frost, as if with intensely cold snow"—thus spoke Vālmīki.
When the sage had spoken these words, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites.
Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of night, it returned together with the rays of the sun.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, this is the twenty-third canto, titled "The Description of the Practice of Knowledge."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus conversed, O beautiful lady, while that night was falling and the attendants were asleep in the pavilion of the inner apartments, he surely [proceeded].

In that chamber whose doors and windows were secured with all the bolts firmly fastened, where the air was heavy with the abundant and thick fragrance of flowers filling the space, and which stood beside a corpse adorned with unfading garlands and garments; in that place where the mind was focused with skillful intent.
In that place illuminated by the face of the entire, stainless full moon,
they went to the site of their meditative absorption and stood with motionless limbs,
as if carved from jeweled pillars or set into a painted wall.
They both abandoned all their anxieties as contraction set in,
like two lotus plants at the end of the day when their streaks of fragrance have spread;
they became intensely tranquil, pure, and devoid of movement.
Like two rows of clouds on a windless mountain in autumn during the rains,
they abandoned their consciousness in the sky through unwavering meditative absorption,
just as two lovely wish-fulfilling creepers abandon their full essence at the end of the season.

When, through these two [means of knowledge], one realizes that the error "I" and "the world"— the very object of perception— has from the outset never arisen, and that its nature is absolute non-existence,
then this demon of the visible world completely vanishes for those two.
And because it is non-existent, O sinless one, the world is like the horn of a hare for us;
for that which does not exist at the very beginning likewise does not exist in the present. Therefore, though it appears, the world is as if unmanifest, like the water of a mirage.
The two women became that very nature, which is exclusively peaceful,
like the sky utterly free from the multitude of objects such as the moon and the sun;
by means of that very body of knowledge, the goddess of cognition crossed over.
But the human woman, by means of the other [power], quickly— conforming to her knowledge or lack thereof—
ascended from within the house itself to a height of a span toward heaven;
they both became of the nature of the space of consciousness, having the form of birds in the sky.
Then those two playful women, with their graceful eyes,
having by their very nature moved far away from the consciousness of objects as if into the sky,
remained there and floated across the expanse of the heavens through the activity of their single-minded awareness.
Though their bodies were composed of space and separated by an interval extending for millions of yojanas,
they became two companions devoted to affection, gazing at each other’s forms here through the very nature of their own continuous perception of the visible.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the twenty-fourth canto, titled "The Travel of Līlā and Prajñapti through the Body of Consciousness to the Sky," Vasiṣṭha says:
Having leaped from afar to even further, they slowly ascended to a high station;
placing hand in hand, as they proceeded, they beheld the sky—
vast like a single swelling ocean, deep, and pure within.
It bestows the blissful enjoyment of contact with the exceedingly gentle breeze;
it is intensely refreshing and serene due to its immersion in the waters of emptiness (śūnyatā),
and it is utterly pure and profound, like a gracious noble person.
They rested upon the pure, moon-like belly of the mountain-peak, which was like a dwelling of nectar, as stainless as the water of a cloud, and as beautiful as the interior of the full moon;
it was enchanting with the fragrance of the mandāra garlands of the *siddhas* and *gandharvas*.
As the moon’s orb emerged and a sweet breeze blew, they sported together;

at the end of the summer heat, they bathed in a mass of clouds that was thick with water and resembled a lake filled with water, agitated by its own flow, and strewn with red lotuses like flashes of lightning.
Like two female bees wandering extensively among the lotus-stalk sprouts rising from the great mountains upon the earth in every direction, they wandered through the lakes;
and with the thought that it was a fountain-house, they stayed by the mountain cascade of the Ganges, which possessed a steady flow.
They wandered within a pavilion formed by circles of clouds agitated by the wind;
then, resting according to their strength, those two sweet and amorous women beheld the empty sky, sluggish with great turbulence.
Never before seen, one after another, with various narrow hollows,
being filled and yet emptied even by hundreds of millions of worlds;
situated one above the other, high upon high, each surrounded separately by others.

The sky was completely filled on all sides by the primary mountains, Meru and the rest, which were covered with various forms of veils— living beings, clouds, rays of light, and celestial palaces— and which,
with the radiance of their ruby slopes, resembled the interior of the flames at the end of an aeon.
Beautiful with the peaks of the Himavat filled with floods of pearl-like radiance, it was radiant with golden plateaus shimmering like the light of a mountain of gold;
the dark green of its grassy meadows was intensified by the luster of great emeralds.
For the observer, it was a darkness arising from the blackness of ignorance born of the non-truth of the destruction of vision;
yet it was like a floor of lapis lazuli, its form blossoming with the clusters of awakening, and bearing the banners of hosts of celestial palaces swaying like *pārijāta* creepers.

It was filled with the sounds of the songs and instrumental music of celestial women in their palatial mansions, where the movement of the wind was conquered by the great siddhas who travel with the speed of thought;
its intervals were thinned by the shifting movements of the multitudes of beings wandering through the three worlds.
It was crowded with hosts of gods and asuras moving about, each gazing upon the other;
it contained circles of Kumbhāṇḍas, Rākṣasas, and Guhyakas stationed at its borders;
and it held multitudes of celestial chariots being carried along by the great force of the wind-spirits.
It resounded with the clatter of moving celestial chariots and possessed the dense roar of thunderclouds graspable by the fist;
its wind-machines were set in motion by the movement of the hosts of planets and constellations,
while the dwellings of those perfected ones who had achieved only minor siddhis were scorched by the nearby heat.
The winds from the mouths of the sun’s horses had scorched that charming celestial chariot,
which was restless with the movement of throngs of world-protectors and *apsarases*,
and enveloped by clouds of incense smoke burned by the women of the gods’ inner apartments.
It was strewn with ornaments fallen from the limbs of celestial women carried off by birds;
it possessed a mass of unbearable, fierce radiance common to the perfected ones (siddhas), yet it had the power of darkness;
and it was agitated by the coming and going of powerful hosts of siddhas as they collided with one another.
It was dense with Himavat, Meru, and Mandara mountains standing at its sides like silken garments;
it was filled with swarms of crows, owls, and vultures gathered together and moving about;
and it was crowded with dancing *ḍākinīs* on their mounts, like waves upon the ocean.
It was filled with throngs of dancing yoginīs who had faces like dogs, crows, camels,
and donkeys, coming and going for no purpose across a hundred yojanas;
its mansions were shrouded in clouds of incense smoke billowing from the cities of the world-protectors.
Where pairs of Siddhas and Gandharvas had begun the festival of love;

where the path was traversed by Khadira trees intoxicated by hearing the songs of heaven; and where hundreds of thousands of birds were distinguished by their constant flight toward the celestial mansions.
The waters of the triple-pathed river (Ganges) flowed within the hollows dug out by the mass of winds;
young gods wandered about, preoccupied with gazing at the wonders;
and there were those carrying thunderbolts, discuses, tridents, swords, and spears, moving amidst the masses of doubt.
In some places, it contained Tumburu and Nārada dwelling in abodes that were not built upon walls; in other places, it was agitated by the great onset of massive clouds in the path of the sky;
and in others, it resembled clouds at the end of an aeon, rendered silent as if depicted in a painting.
In some places, it possessed clouds as beautiful as great mountains of rising wings smeared with collyrium;
in other places, it had water-bearing clouds lovely with streams of molten gold;
and in yet other places, it was clothed in garments of silent clouds rained upon by the splendor of moon-like heat.
In some places, it was the water of emptiness, tranquil like an ocean devoid of wind; in some places, it was the grass and sprouts of celestial palaces tossed by the fierce rivers of wind;
and in some places, it was as pure as the brilliance of the skin on the backs of swarms of moving bees.
In some places it was grey with the dust stirred up by winds in the caves of Mount Meru;
in other places its courtyards were variegated by the splendors of celestial chariots and gods;
in some places it was garlanded by circles of naked, frantic mothers.
In some places, there were hosts of masters of yoga whose constant speech was agitated; in others, circles of sages rested in peaceful meditative absorption,
their agitation long since cast away, delighting the minds of the virtuous.
In some places there were circles of singing kinnaras, gandharvas, and celestial women;
in some places it was filled with motionless cities; in some places it carried away the best of the gods; in some places it blocked the flow of cities, and in some places it besieged great cities.
In some places it was a city created by illusion, and in others a future city;
in some places a lake with a revolving moon, and in others a lake of still water;
in some places a multitude of Siddhas moving through the air, and in others the rising of the moon.
In some places it consists of the rising sun; in some places it is filled with the darkness of night;
in some places it is tawny with the garments of twilight; in some places it is grey with mist;
in some places it is white with celestial chariots; and in some places it is like a rain-cloud.
In some places the sky was like dry land, where the guardians of the world had come to rest;
in some places it was crowded with hosts of gods and asuras busily moving upward and downward;
and in some places it was agitated by the movement of beings traveling toward the east, west, north, and south.
In some places it extends for hundreds of thousands of yojanas, with incense difficult to reach;
in other places it is like the sky, filled with indestructible darkness as seen by the eye;
and in some places it is an indestructible, vast radiance, comparable to the sun or fire.
In some places, it was as cold as the interior of a great mass of snow; in others, it was the abode of the moon and other celestial bodies.
In some places, there were forests of *kalpa* trees and creepers where great cities danced;
in others, there were lofty cities of the gods falling down, having been struck by the Daityas.
In some places it was marked by streaks of fire from the falling of celestial chariots;
in some places it was struck by the mutual clashing of hundreds of rising comets;
and in some places, even auspicious beginnings were seized upon by hosts of malevolent planets.

In some places it was pervaded by the darkness of night, and in others it was radiant with day; in some places there were clouds thundering in the fastnesses, and in others the clouds were motionless and silent;
in some places there was a mass of white cloud-fragments scattered by the wind like a heap of flowers.
In one place it was utterly empty, pure, and boundless;
like the heart of a wise man, it was spread out, blissful, soft, peaceful, and clear.
In another place, it resounded with the croaking of swarms of frogs riding upon parrots.
The realm of those who dwell in the sky was overspread by emptiness;
in some places it was covered by birds such as the peacock with its golden crest,
which had made their abodes upon the mounts of the Vidyadhara goddesses.
In some places, there were circles of peacocks belonging to Guha dancing amidst the clouds;
in other places, the ground appeared dark with fire-parrots as if it were a patch of green grass;
and in some places, there was a cloud serving as a vehicle for the majesty of the buffalo of the Lord of the Dead.
In some places, horses seized by the suspicion that dark clouds were mouthfuls of grass;

in some places pervaded by the cities of the gods, and in others accompanied by the cities of the Daityas; with cities so vast they could not reach one another, yet terrifying with the gaps between them.
In some places it was radiant with Bhairava dancing in the form of the Kulācala mountains;
in other places it bound hosts of celestial women in Gandharva cities;
and in some places it covered the ocean with hundreds of thousands of trees destroyed by trembling mountains.
In some places it was as cool as the water of a lotus-pond in the sky created by illusion;
in some places, elephant-headed deities (Vināyakas) were dancing upon great winged mountain-kings;
and in some places, mountains were being launched into the air by wings fanned by a gurgling wind.
In some places there was a wind, cooled and refreshing by showers of moonbeams;
in others, trees, mountains, and clouds were scorched by the heat of blazing fires.
In some places, there was absolute silence due to the complete stilling of the winds and other elements.
In some places, it had the rising of flames resembling mountains;
in some places, it was filled with the gurgling roar of clouds intoxicated by the weight of the rainy season;
and in some places, it was impassable due to battles waged by hosts of gods and asuras.
In some places, he was summoned by the sound of the swans of the celestial lotus-lake;
in others, by the breeze plundering the lotuses on the banks of the Mandākinī—
due to the proximity of embodied rivers such as the Gaṅgā.
With hollows between leaping fish, crocodiles, and crabs;
with a belly as dark as the shadow of the earth cast by the sun when it has entered the netherworld (pātāla);
and in various regions, with the orbs of the moon and sun swallowed within its circles.
In some places, there were forests of illusory flowers shaken by the breezes of heaven,
where the women of the celestial chariots were terrified by the falling showers of blossoms;
in others, there were masses of living beings contained within the three worlds, whirling like gnats inside the hollows of udumbara fruits.
Having leaped over that [space], O beautiful woman, she prepared to release the sky and return once more to the surface of the earth.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Sky," in the *Līlopākhyāna*.
Vasiṣṭha said:
As the two women were traveling from the sky toward a mountain village, their minds remained fixed on the thought [of the earth], and they beheld the surface of the ground.
The heart-lotus of the man within the cosmic egg is vast, with the eight directions as its petals;
it is densely packed with the filaments of the mountains, beautiful with the abundance of its own fragrance,
has the rivers as its stalks, and bears dewdrops as its water droplets.
It was swarming with the confusion of night-bees, agitated by the mosquitoes of the multitudes of living beings;
it was filled with swarms of internal woodworms and covered with hollows like fine holes;
it was being carried away by floods of water, possessing the splendor of the light of day.

Sometimes it was like a lotus stalk: moist with nectar, with a swan wandering in the sky, serving as a vessel for the contraction of the night, and having the lord of serpents submerged in the mud of the underworld;
at other times, its petals were the quarters of the horizon, trembling from the shaking of the ocean that serves as its base.
Below, it has the nagas, the infinite daityas,

and the dānavas as its thorns; its heart is the great seed of the mountains, pervaded by the creeper of the wounds of the asuras, which is both delicate in enjoyment and yet the very essence of the seed.
There, one should visualize a vast pericarp known as Jambudvīpa,
with rivers as its filaments, cities and villages as its pistils,
and made beautiful by the seven great mountain ranges as its lofty, protruding seeds.
The surface of the sky was overspread by the seeds of Mount Mahāmeru, the lofty center;
it contained lakes, dewdrops, forests, and groves of jasmine;
and within the circle of its own lines, it contained the swirling circles of the multitude of people situated therein.
It was pervaded by oceans that served as bees, extending for hundreds of yojanas in every direction and awakening at every new moon;
these bees rested upon the eight petals of the quarters, humming amidst the lotuses.
Divided into nine parts by the nine brothers who were kings,
it was a hundred thousand *yojanas* in extent, filled with particles of dust,
and thick with the spray of hoarfrost from the dense clusters of various inhabited lands.
Twice the size of the continent, it is encircled on the outside by the belt of the salt ocean, which, like a conch shell, appears as if it were a wrist-ornament;
beyond that, it possesses a body twice its size, shaped like a bracelet.
It was encircled by the strip of land known as Śāka-dvīpa, which, like a vine,
enveloped the world; and beyond that, it was surrounded by a band of ocean filled with fresh milk, cool and sweet, possessing twice the extent of the former.
Beyond that, it was encircled by the coastal strip of the continent named Kuśa, which is twice its size and adorned with various peoples.
Beyond that, it was enveloped by [the ocean] possessing a form twice as large.
It was constantly gratifying the hosts of gods with the ocean of curd,
and it was encircled by the island-streak named Krauñca, which was of the same dimensions and surrounded by a moat as deep as the sky, like a new royal city.
Beyond that, there is a strip of the ocean of ghee of such a measure;
beyond that, a strip of Śālmalidvīpa filled with gods;
and beyond that, a strip of the great ocean of wine, white as flowers.
The remainder, by its bodily form, appeared as if it had taken refuge in the body of Hari;
then, by the coastal strip of Gomedaka Island of such a measure,
and likewise by the strip of sugarcane fields as pure as the slopes of the Himalayas.
Beyond that, situated at double the distance, is the line of Puṣkaradvīpa;
at its edge is the line of the Sweet-water Ocean (Svādūdakāmbhodhi) of equal measure. Thus, among the seven lines of oceans in the southwestern direction, [the lands are arranged].
Then, for ten million leagues, it was marked by sparks from the submarine fire blazing with water as its fuel; beyond that, it was encircled by the earth, which possesses the luster of molten gold,
is radiant with beauty, and is the domain of the gods.
Then, by way of measurement, [the earth] consists of seven oceans and continents; ten times that size below is the foundation of the netherworld (pātāla),
which takes the form of a vast accumulation of chasms and is like a deeply sunk circular moat.
Winding through the path leading to the netherworld with a terrifying nature,
[the river] is indeed ten times more extensive than all this;
reaching up to the sky in the four directions, it is fearsome with its mass of chasms.

On one side, she was adorned with a garland of blue lotuses clinging to her form, which was like a fading darkness; on the other, she possessed a residence of vast, lofty watchtowers as high as the Lokāloka mountain, featuring various peaks of rubies and white, pink, and red lotuses.
It was like the gathered tresses of the hair-knot of the Fortune of the Three Worlds;
and beyond all this, it was protected by a forest ten times its size, known as A-jñāta-bhūta-sañcāra (where the movement of beings is unknown).
Then, from all this [world], by means of that which is ten times its magnitude,
it was pervaded in the four directions like the sky with pure water.
Then, from all this, by means of that which is ten times its magnitude...
Adorned with a mass of flames eager to melt Mount Meru and the other mountains,
[the yogin] then, by means of that power increased tenfold over all this,
leads even the immovable Meru and the rest like blades of grass or particles of dust.

It was surrounded on all sides by a wind that carried the fire from the wood of the Kārī tree— [the fire] which causes the bursting of the great lords of mountains— and which, due to its emptiness, was devoid of sound;
then, beyond all this, [there was a layer] ten times its magnitude.
It was surrounded on all sides by the sky, which is of a single uniform nature yet devoid of emptiness;
and it was pervaded by a solid golden shell of the cosmic egg, a hundred thousand leagues thick and radiant as the sun.

Thus, having surveyed the interior of the world— comprising the oceans, great mountains, world-protectors, the city of the gods, the heavens, and the earth— the daughter of Manu first beheld her own dwelling within a hollow on the ground. This concludes the chapter titled "Description of the World of Mortals" in the Narrative of Līlā.
The twenty-sixth canto:
Then the two perfected women beheld their own abode,
a pavilion that was the dwelling place of Brahman, invisible to the world.
With handmaidens overwhelmed by anxiety, the faces of the women drenched in tears,
its usual arrangement mostly ruined and resembling a lotus with withered petals;
it was like a city where all festivities have vanished, or like the ocean reaching as far as Agastya’s hermitage.
Like a garden scorched by summer heat, like a tree consumed by lightning,
like a cloud torn apart by the wind, or like a lotus withered by frost;
it is like a lamp whose oil is nearly spent, providing light only at the cost of exhaustion.

That house, struck by the separation from its master, became like a forest of withered, decaying tree leaves whose luster has been destroyed by the beauty of the mouths of youths on the verge of death; it became parched and grey, like a region desiccated by the cessation of rain.
Endowed with the power of true resolve and possessing true desires like a goddess,
she thought: "Let these kinsmen behold me and this queen as bearing the common form of a woman."
Then his household members saw there two women,
who illuminated the palace like a pair of Lakṣmī and Gaurī;
they were beautiful with various unfading garlands draped down to their feet.
Like a pair of springtimes that have caused the forests to blossom,
it filled the entire collection of medicinal herbs and groves with elixirs; like two risen moons, it bestowed coolness, refreshment, and happiness.
Scattering heaps of *mālatī* flowers mixed with blue water-lilies, with glances from eyes that trembled like long, creeper-like tresses;
captivating with a flow as charming as a river filled with the essence of molten gold.
By the power of the radiance of his body, he turned the forest into gold;
through the natural beauty of his form, which sported upon the playful swing of grace,
he seemed to cross the ocean of his own loveliness, so rich with waves.
With her pair of trembling vine-like arms and her reddish hands,
she seemed to scatter a fresh forest of golden *kalpavṛkṣa* creepers;
with her feet, tender as flowers and sprouts that never fade even when trodden upon, she moved.
Furthermore, with the beauty of garlands of full-blown lotus petals that did not touch the ground,
it produced young sprouts for the clusters of dried *tālī* and *tamāla* trees through the nectar-sprinkling of the moonbeams.
Having said, "Homage be to the two forest goddesses," Jyeṣṭhaśarman then cast a handful of flowers along with his household;
that handful of flowers fell at the feet of those two goddesses.
Like a shower of frost-drops upon the two lotuses of a lotus-pond;
Jyeṣṭhaśarman and the others said: "Victory to you, O forest goddesses, who have come for the sake of destroying our suffering!"
"For the virtuous, the protection of others is generally their own inherent duty.
Thus [thinking], the two deities became here a Brahmin couple, affectionate toward one another,
hospitable to all guests, the founders of a lineage, and the very pillars of the twice-born's standing.
Today, having abandoned their home along with their children, cattle, and kinsmen, our parents have gone to heaven; because of that, the three worlds are empty.
Like birds perched upon a tree, they are scattering [their branches] at every moment.
In the empty house, the kinsmen, longing for the deceased, lament with sweet voices;
the mountain, its cave filled with the confused sounds of moaning and wailing,
weeps aloud with thick streams of tears like rivers.
The quarters of the sky were ravaged by the cries of mountain torrents, stripped of their garments of clouds, shattered by the heat of sighs, and reduced to extreme emaciation;
every limb was mangled and wounded, and the air was harsh with piteous lamentation.
The village is intent on fasting, wretched, and stands ready for death. Day after day, from the bud-eyes of the clusters of trees, teardrops of dew fall downward, heated by the sun's glare.
The streets, where the movement of people has ceased, are grey with dust;
the widows, their joy departed, have reached a state of empty hearts.
The creepers, once made to warble by cuckoos and bees, are now struck down by the tears of rain.
With their hands of tender shoots, they strike their bodies with intensely hot breaths;
these waterfalls fall from the surface of a great chasm onto the rocky ground, their own forms scorched by the heat, as if to shatter themselves into a hundred pieces.
Devoid of conversation, their splendor departed, mute and with agitated hearts, the houses— filled with blinding darkness— have fallen into a state of desolation;
from the flower-beds of the gardens, they seem to weep with the humming of bees.
A foul odor emanates, known by the other name of "sweet fragrance. Day after day, the playful mango trees become tasteless;
the creepers wither away, their bud-eyes closing.
Agitated and intent on casting their bodies into the ocean, they began to move;

the small streams, restless with a tumultuous clamor, tossed their forms upon the ground with an extreme restlessness that made even the slightest quiver from the landing of a mosquito seem like a matter of grave concern.
The ponds stand as if measuring out within themselves a bliss unmoving;
surely today the sky has become adorned by our fathers with singing *kiṃnaras*, *gandharvas*, *vidyādharas*, and celestial nymphs.
"Therefore, O two Goddesses, let the destruction of our grief be accomplished for now;
for the sight of the great is never without fruit.
Having spoken thus, she touched her son on the head with her hand.
Bowing low with her sprout-like hand like a lotus plant bending over its root-knot,
she— by that touch of his— cast off her distress, misfortune, and hardship, just as a mountain sheds the heat of summer through contact with the clouds of the rainy season.
Then, upon seeing those two goddesses, all the members of the household became endowed with prosperity and liberated from suffering, like drinkers of nectar. Rāma said:
"By her, through such playfulness, why was the sight of her son Jyeṣṭhaśarman not granted to me, or why was he not even mentioned? Vasiṣṭha said:
The Buddha, through the awakening to earth and the other elements, is one whose assembly consists of earth and the rest;
he alone maintains the nature of a unified whole, while for others there is only the void.
Indeed, my dear, that which is non-existent appears as if existent due to the perception of earth and the other elements.
Just as a ghost does not appear to a child because he does not perceive it,
so too the appearance of earth and other elements would cease to be earth and so forth in an instant;
this is clearly the case both in a dream through the recognition of the dream, and likewise in the waking state.
Earth and the other elements are perceived as empty space; indeed, they are experienced simply as "space.

For instance, even in the case of those whose elements are agitated, their exertion toward a wall is as if directed toward empty space. Likewise, in a dream, one perceives a city or the earth as being empty and excavated like space.
And a woman in a dream, though empty, performs causal functions for men.
Space is perceived as earth and so forth, and earth and so forth arise in an instant;
even the next world is directly experienced through fainting.
The ignorant man perceives a ghost in the sky, one who is dying sees the forest as the sky, another sees a mass of hair in the void, and yet another perceives a pearl in the sky;
likewise, those who are terrified, intoxicated, half-asleep, or traveling by boat always perceive [objects] in the sky.

And like a vetāla, they see and even experience trees and other such things. This form of these objects, which has been cultivated through mental projection, is produced by habitual practice; in ultimate reality, not a single one of them exists.
But that earth and so forth, which are perceived as objects through mere play, do not exist;
for they are declared to be nothing other than space, because they are manifested through consciousness.
For the sage who possesses the realization that the Self is Brahman, the mere expanse of pure consciousness, [the world] is thus described.
How, what, when, and from where do sons, friends, and wives come to be?

That the hand was placed playfully upon the head of Jyeṣṭhaśarman is the fruit of consciousness, for the purpose of awakening the intellect to the activity inherent in the flow [of worldly existence].
For consciousness perceives exactly as it shines forth; though subtle, it is far more pure than space.
O Rāghava, that very consciousness alone is the entire web of objects everywhere, just as what is experienced in dreams within imagined cities.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Explanation of the Cause for the Siddhas' Vision" in the Līlopākhyāna.
The twenty-seventh canto: Vasiṣṭha said:
On that mountain slope, in that village, within the interior of that pavilion—

Those two women vanished instantly while remaining right there. Then, with their household members' suffering pacified and standing ready for the completion of their merit, [the king thought]: "A favor has been bestowed upon us by the forest goddesses."
Sarasvatī, who is of the nature of space, spoke playfully to her— who was likewise of the nature of space and remained silent out of a smile— while she was dissolved in the space of the pavilion;
it was a mutual recounting of the futility of actions in the realms of imagination and dreams.
Just as those two [dream and imagination] produce purposeful action here, so too is their discourse;
even without earth, channels, vital breaths, and the like,
that consciousness of discourse arises for them, just as in dreams and mental constructions.
Sarasvatī said:
"The knowable has been known in its entirety; the perceptions of all that is to be seen have been witnessed.
Such is this reality of Brahman; tell me, what else do you ask?"
Līlā said:
"If this soul of my deceased husband rules a kingdom there, why was I not seen by them? Why was I seen here by my son?"
Sarasvatī said:
"O child, without practice, that certainty regarding duality of yours has surely not set,
just as one season does not end during the transition between seasons."
How can one who has not attained non-duality be joined with the practices of non-duality?
For one established in asceticism, how could there be an experience of the limbs of a shadow?
Without practice, the thought "I am Līlā" did not cease to exist therein.
When you were a living being, you did not possess the power of true resolve;
even today, my resolves are based on experience, yet they have reached me because of you. O beautiful one, your desire, "May he see me," has borne fruit.
"If you now go into the presence of that husband of yours, then your dealings with him will proceed just as before. Līlā said:
Right here in the space of this temple, a Brahmin became my husband;
right here he died and was reborn as a lord of the earth.
Right here, within that very cycle of existence, in that same region of the world.
In that royal capital city, I was established as a matron. Right here in that inner apartment, my lord of the earth died;
right here in the space of that very inner apartment, he became king once again.
Accomplished on the surface of the earth as the lord of various lands,
this entire state of flux remains right here;
within this very space of the house, all the manifestations of the cosmic egg reside.
They stand like heaps of mustard seeds within an opened casket.
I consider that circle of my lord to be not far away;
act in such a way that I may see it somewhere situated nearby here.
Śrīdevī said:
"O daughter of Arundhatī on earth,
you now have three husbands by name, or perhaps there were many, numbering in the hundreds."
"O twice-born one, among those three who were closest, he was reduced to ashes;
the king, clothed in garlands and garments, lies as a corpse within the inner apartments.
Even in this pavilion of worldly existence, there is a third lord of the earth."
Fallen into the great ocean of saṃsāra, he has come to wander;
his consciousness is agitated and distracted by the surging waves of enjoyments,
and with his mental states shattered by dullness, he is like a tortoise in the sea of worldly existence.
Even while performing diverse and highly tumultuous royal duties, he remains asleep due to his abiding in splendor and does not wake to the delusion of worldly existence; [he thinks]:
"I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am perfected, I am powerful, and I am happy."
"Thus, bound by the endless great rope and brought under control—
tell me, O woman of excellent complexion, to which master shall I lead you from this forest,
like a streak of fragrance carried by the wind to another wood?"
This cycle of worldly existence, this pavilion of the cosmic egg, is indeed something else;
and those successions of worldly transactions, O child, are likewise something else.
Even though those spheres of worldly existence stand right here by one's side, they remain distinct.
Surely the distance between them here is tens of millions of millions of *yojanas*;
behold, their bodies before you are nothing but empty space.
Within them, tens of millions of peaks of Mount Meru and Mandara are situated here.
In every single atom, multitudes of creations flash forth without restraint from the Great Consciousness, like motes of dust in a sunbeam.
And even the cosmic eggs, though heavy with their vast undertakings, [arise in this same manner].
In the balance, they do not exist even as much as a grain of rice.
Just as a forest shines in the sky with the brilliance of mountains of various jewels,
so does consciousness shine like the world, devoid of the elements such as earth and the rest.
This very consciousness shines forth under such names as "the world" and so on;
however, at the beginning of creation, there was not the slightest thing consisting of earth and other elements.
Just as a wave in a river, having arisen again and again, may come into being once more.
Thus, O Mother of the World, this world has become for you a mere play, fashioned with its various forms and arrangements. Now, by me, it has been brought here to its end.
"This birth of mine is rajasic and tamasic, not sattvic.
"But for me, who have descended from Brahman, eight hundred births in various wombs have passed; I see them now as if before my eyes."

O Goddess, in a certain part of the circle of saṃsāra in the past, I was a Vidyādhara woman, a bee among the lotuses of other worlds. Then, defiled by evil latent impressions (*durvāsanā*), I came to exist as a human being.
In another circle of saṃsāra, in that same region, I was a Śabara woman, the beloved of the lord of that tribe; dwelling in groves of *karañja*, *kuñja*, *jambīra*, and *kadamba* trees,
dark-complexioned and clad in garments of leaves, I then became a Śabarī.
Deluded by my dwelling in the forest, I have now become a creeper;
with clusters for eyes and leaves for hands, I am a forest-dweller. Sanctified by association with sages, I am that very sacred creeper of the hermitage.
"O great sage, having been consumed by a forest fire, I became the daughter of that very same great sage.
Due to the ripening of those karmas which yield the fruit of non-femaleness,
I became a glorious king in Surāṣṭra for a hundred years."
Due to the fault of the king's evil deeds,
I became a female mongoose with limbs destroyed by leprosy for nine years in the marshy thickets of the palm groves.
For eight years, O Goddess, I was made a cow by me in the lands of Surāṣṭra.
Just as a bird in the forest glades easily endures the snares set by its enemies through the playful movements of wicked, ignorant cowherd boys,
so too have these mental impressions (vāsanās) been severed today with great effort.
He rested with the bee upon beds within the heart of the lotus filaments,
having enjoyed the pollen in secret within the buds of the lotuses;
he wandered with the fawn-eyed doe over mountain peaks of lofty summits.
In beautiful forest regions where the vital organs of Kirātas were struck down,
she was seen in the eight directions being carried away by the waves of the ocean, amidst the leaping,
roaring, and striking of fish, horses, and turtles.
On the banks of the Carmaṇvatī, he was completely and spontaneously delighted by her singing with a sweet voice during passionate lovemaking;
she, whose face and eyes were tremulous, [dwelt] amidst groves of *tālī* and *tamāla* trees.
She intoxicated the bees of the gods with her glances, which were agitated by passion, as she cast her looks upon her beloved;
and with her lap-lotuses, beautiful with the flow of molten gold,
she quickly gratified those bees who were like the lotus-thickets of the celestial nymphs.
On the ground strewn with heaps of jewels, gold, rubies, and pearls,
he took pleasure with his youth in the groves of wish-fulfilling trees on Mount Meru;
and along the shores agitated by billows, where the gulugulu sounds resounded.

For a long time he remained in the form of a tortoise within the caves of the coastal forests of the ocean; and in the form of a royal swan, he performed the sport of swinging upon the lotus-stalk swings amidst the breezes from the lakes and among the clusters of trembling leaves.
Having observed the state of sleep induced by the swaying of the blades of grass on the meadow, I saw the wretched male mosquito standing with his female companion;
they were kissing the tips of the dancing waves as they moved upon the rising, high ripples.

Formerly, afflicted by love, a young Vidyādhara fell at her feet in the palace of the Mandāra trees on Mount Gandhamādana, while she wandered among the mountain streams like a young female water-creeper.

Afflicted by calamity, I have long wallowed upon beds purified with scattered camphor, like the luster of the moon upon the orb of the moon itself. With my limbs agitated by rising and falling, I have wandered through wombs fraught with hundreds of manifold sufferings.
By means of the shifting wave of the long river of saṃsāra, following the course of a doe pursued by an irresistible wind—
this concludes the twenty-eighth canto, titled "The Description of Previous Births," within the narrative of Līlā.
Rāma: How did both of you emerge from the wall of the cosmic egg, which is as solid as the core of a diamond, densely compacted, and extends for millions of yojanas?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Where is the cosmic egg, where its wall, and where in this context is that adamantine hardness,
when the two goddesses must necessarily remain within the supreme space of the inner apartments?
In that very mountain village, in that very space of his dwelling,
that brahmin named Vasiṣṭha enjoys sovereignty;
he [perceives] that very corner of the pavilion’s sky as mere emptiness.
He experienced the surface of the earth bounded by the four oceans.
Upon that royal city, which was a terrestrial plane within the self of space,
he experienced the royal palace, as did she, Arundhatī.
She became known as Līlā, and by her Jñapti was honored.
Together with Jñapti, having leaped up into the sky which was wondrous and delightful,
she remained right there within the interior of the house in a space the size of a span.
Having reached another world-egg and the mountain that is Indra’s abode,
he emerged from that world-egg and came to rest in his own home,
just as a man lying on a bed moves from one dream to another.
All this is merely a flash of creative intuition, consisting of nothing but empty space;
there is no cosmic egg, no cycle of existence, no walls and such, and no distance.
It is one's own mind alone that shines forth as those two [the sun and moon], appearing so enchanting.
Where is the cosmic egg, which is merely a manifestation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and where is worldly existence?
This infinite space of consciousness is indeed without obstruction;
it is slightly raised up by one's own mind, just as the wind is set in motion by the principle of vibration.
The sky of consciousness is unborn and tranquil, indeed everywhere and at all times;
yet, because it is consciousness, it appears by itself as the world within itself, through itself.
But for one by whom this is realized, it is more empty even than space.
Because he does not perceive a Buddha, this [body] of his is like a mountain of adamantine essence.
Just as a brilliant city appears within a dream even while one is at home,
so too does this unreal thing appear brilliantly within the interior of the element of consciousness.
"Just as the state of being water appears in a mirage and the state of being a bracelet appears in gold—
though unreal, appearing as if real— so too does this state of being an object of perception appear within the Self.
Reflecting thus, those two women, possessing the forms of beautiful women, [continued their discourse].
They departed from their home to the outside with graceful strides;
while the villagers looked on, they beheld the mountain before them,
which kissed the hollows of the sky and touched the solar orb.
A carpet of diverse forests, all in full bloom and of many colors;
with forest birds warbling as they are stirred by various waterfalls;
and a circle of clouds tawny with clusters of variegated flower-stalks.
The sound of birds resting on the tips of the branches of *abhraka* trees resounded there;
the entire riverbank was concealed by the spreading thickets of *sāra* and *vañjula* trees;
and the wind caused the vines hanging from unfinished stone cavities to dance.
The sky was like a casket covered by clouds of flowers, while the water-bearing clouds were like a jeweled floor; the falling streams of long rivers appeared like strings of white pearls,
and the winds from the shifting groves of trees brushed against the horizons.
Then those two women themselves beheld there that mountain village, which was perpetually cooled by the shade from its borders crowded with various groves,
as if it were a fragment of heaven fallen from the sky.
The surface of its flowing channels was filled with the water of full lotus-pools;
its hollows and marshy banks resounded with the warbling of *kurukuca* birds;
and every thicket within it was made formidable by the lowing of herds of bellowing cattle.
Abounding with thickets and groves of *guñjā* shrubs, it possessed cool and dense breezes;
its sunbeams were difficult to penetrate, and it was grey with scattered mist,
while the interior of its pathways was tangled with clusters of rising flower-stalks.
With its vast white waterfalls gushing forth from stone slabs,
it recalled the splendor of the milk-ocean churned by the mountains;
with its courtyard trees radiant with the heavy burden of garlands of fruit.
It was crowded with those who stood as if bringing forth a multitude of flowers;
it was like a great rain of scattered blossoms from trees agitated by winds that produced the sound of *jhāṅkāra* as they trembled, as if filled with sap.
With the *jhāṅ* sounds of water droplets trickling from unsuspected masses of rock,
the birds— hidden, unafraid yet suspicious— uttered slight cries;
they were agitated by tasting the spray at the edges of the leaping waves.
The river was filled with birds wheeling in soaring circles, while young children—
frightened by the sight of crows perched on the tall palm trees—
concealed lumps of sugarcane that had been left behind by their own parents.
[He saw] a village boy wearing a garland of flowers, carrying a load, and dressed in garments,
who was cooled by the dense thickets of *kadamba*, *nimba*, and *jambīra* trees at the edge [of the forest];
[she approached him] with haste, her ears filled with flower clusters and wearing linen garments.
With hunger endured while wandering through the streets of villages and hamlets,
he remained in a state of solitary seclusion, desired because of his dense fear of the deafness of his ears to the clamor arising from the collision of river waves.
The courtyard was crowded with naked children whose faces, hands, and feet were smeared with curd, who wore garlands of flowers as lower garments, and who were marked with streaks of cow-dung;
it was made charming by swings suspended from the creepers growing on the grassy banks.
Its sandy banks were marked by streaks of water being carried along by the waves;
there, flies moved slowly, intoxicated by the thick fragrance of curd and milk;
and young boys, their garments frayed by tears shed while begging for their morning meal, wandered about.
People were laughing at women who, enraged by the water-sprinkling in the courtyards smeared with cow dung, were busily twisting their braided hair; meanwhile,
crows were swooping down to peck at the humps of oxen covered by the flicking of their tails.
The courtyards and doorways of the houses were strewn with baskets of *kunda* flowers;
every morning, the courtyards were covered knee-deep in blossoms fallen from flowering trees growing in the hollows situated at the sides of the dwellings.
With its forest thickets swaying like autumnal fly-whisks, where fawns slept upon the young grass grown in the *guñjā* groves;
where the throbbing of a single ear of a calf at the edge of the pasture signaled the absence of flies; and where there was no dust.
The flies were motionless from contact with the curd left over by the cowherds;
in all the houses, the bees had perished, driven away by the honey;
and the dwellings were made crimson by the glow of the blossoming *aśoka* trees.
With trees perpetually moistened and blossoming by the wind carrying showers of spray,
with heaps of *saptacchada* leaves pierced by *kadamba* buds,
and garlanded by clusters of creepers and blooming *ketaka* flowers;
It resounded with the loud "ruṭ-ruṭ" cries of flocks of birds from the broad water-channels; clouds rested within the palaces as if in mountain caves emerging from the windows;
and the interior of its royal roads was purified by rows of full lotus ponds.
With cool and pure grassy meadows shaded by dense foliage,
where the stars were reflected in droplets falling from every flower,
and whose dwellings were white with a constant snowfall of falling blossoms; MU 3.28.48.
It possessed ponds and trees with various clusters of blossoms and leaves; within its inner courtyards, young women were sheltered by clouds resting against the houses,
while the lightning from clouds hovering over the mansions rendered the lamps unnecessary.
The pavilion was filled with the deep, humming resonance of the wind whistling through the mountain caves;
the temple was enchanting with wandering *cakora* birds, *hārīta* birds, and does;
and it was made languid by the thick fragrance exhaled by blossoming *kandala* plants.
The trees, with their trembling shoots, began to be gently shaken by the Maruts;
the place was filled with throngs of women engaged in the playful chatter of quails,
and it was made tumultuous by the clamor of ruddy geese, cuckoos, and crows.
It was adorned with *sāla*, *tālī*, and *tamāla* trees, and garlanded by dark ponds;
its brow was surely curved with the playful arrangement of folds and circles.
It was filled with dwellings entwined by swaying creepers and shoots, and made fragrant by blossoming *kandala* and *silindhra* flowers.
[He saw] herds of cows agitated by the splashing of the water's current, beautified by dark-blue young grass and flowering meadows;
[he saw] the courses of rivers hidden by rows of trees on their banks, with dense canopies formed by flowering creepers;
[he saw] places fragrant with the nectar of garden jasmine, where clouds were obscured by swarms of bees blinded by the scent.
Of those whose mansions surpassed the abode of Indra in beauty; whose skies were reddened by the pollen from rows of lotuses;
whose waters resounded with the gurgling of mountain rivers borne by the current; which shone with the brilliance of clouds as white as jasmine;
where flower-creeper bowers flourished upon the grounds of the palaces; and where sweet-voiced birds flitted about playfully.

It was filled with young men reclining on carpets of blooming flower petals, and with playful women whose garlands trailed down to their feet; it was a place where the forest paths were crowded with wild creepers swaying in the breeze, bristling with all manner of beautiful new sprouts,
thick with tender leafy shoots, and where dwellings were veiled by the canopies of rain-bearing clouds.
Of the expansive green meadows, enchanting like frost; of the women in their palaces agitated by clouds and lightning;
of those beautiful with the fragrance rising from blooming blue lotuses; of the herds of cows looking upward toward the green pastures, captivated by lowing sounds;
of the dwellings of charming fawns scattered about; and of the cascades of spray from the peacocks in their frenzy.

Where the winds, intoxicated by fragrance, carry away the scents; where the lamps are forgotten due to the blazing of medicinal herbs on the mountain ridges; where the dwellings of birds are agitated by a tumultuous clamor; where the banks of the streams are filled with the sweet warbling of flocks of birds; and where all the trees, creepers, grasses, and sprouts are cooled by the falling of drops as beautiful as clusters of pearls.
Who is able to measure the splendor of the mountain-dwellings, which possess flowers blooming that never set?
The description of the Mountain Village, titled the Chapter on the Narrative of Līlā.
The twenty-ninth canto: Vasiṣṭha said:
There, those two goddesses fell into the village that was inwardly cool in its nature.
In that peaceful one who had realized the Self, the two splendors of worldly enjoyment and liberation were present like [two qualities] in a man.
Through that practice over such a long period of time, she became a playful manifestation;
because her sole body was pure knowledge, she possessed stainless vision of the three times.
Then Līlā spontaneously recalled, by her own natural inclination, all those former states of her transmigratory existence, including her previous births, deaths, and so forth.
"O Goddess, having seen this place, through your grace I remember all that former conduct of mine here, including its inner details.
Here I was, aged, with limbs covered in veins, emaciated and dark."
The Brahmin woman, whose palms were rough from handling the tips of dry *darbha* grass,
was a wife who brought prosperity to her husband’s lineage, gracing the milking and churning of the ritual offerings;
she was a mother to all her sons and a bringer of joy to her guests.
Devoted to the gods, the twice-born, and the virtuous, her limbs were moistened with clarified butter and cow’s milk;
she was the cleanser of vessels and utensils such as jars, sacrificial pots, and water-pots,
and her single bracelet of glass and shell was constantly smeared with fragments of food.
Constantly honoring her son-in-law, daughter, brother, father, and mother,
she spent her days and nights solely in the service of the household;
distressed, she incessantly uttered the words "for a long time, for a long time" until her life was exhausted.
"What am I? What is this cycle of existence?"— such talk is not even found in the dreams of a foolish,
ignorant Vedic scholar who is so dull-witted that his sole devotion is to the collection of fuel made of cow dung.
Clad in a withered woolen blanket, her body covered in prominent veins,
she was intent on extracting worms from the ears of a young calf;
she was busily engaged in household chores, hastening to water the garden of domestic vegetables.
Her calves were nourished by grass moistened by the waves of the blue riverbank;
every moment she applied sandalwood paste to the doors of her house;
for the sake of policy, she maintained the authority of the household servants and the cavalry.
Like the shore of the ocean, she never deviates from her established bounds;
she is marked by a single ear-ornament resembling a withered leaf,
as if bearing the insignia of a servant to the living who fears the agony of old age.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, she herself showed [the place] to Sarasvatī as she was wandering within a hollow of the Śikharin mountain village.
This is my flower garden, adorned with groves of *pāṭala* trees;
this is my walled enclosure containing pavilions within a blossoming park. This is my lotus pond, its banks lined with trees and thickets of young grass.
This is that very calf named Karṇikā, who used to eat leaves;
this is that poor girl who carried water, now wasted away by fatness.
Today, for the eighth day, she weeps with eyes filled with tears.
"O Goddess, here I have spoken; here I have dwelt; here I have stayed;
here I have slept; here I have passed away; here this was given; here this was brought.
This son of mine, named Jyeṣṭhaśarman, weeps in the house."
This milch-cow of mine wanders in the forest upon the lush grass; behold this body of mine here, known as the five elements— a withered, parched, and ash-grey thing that perishes in the house.
This kitchen area, entwined by fierce gourd-vines like cravings,
is like another body of mine;
these kinsmen with eyes copper-red from weeping are but a bondage upon the earth.
Wearing rudrākṣa beads as armlets, they gather fuel for the fire; meanwhile,
the waves— incessantly snapping at the clusters of moss on the rocks— touch the leaves of the creepers on the shore with their towering forms.
With the edges of the grassy meadows sprinkled by spray from the tossing of water,
with droplets of foam leaping up as they strike the surfaces of stone slabs,
and with the clusters of rays of the midday sun turned into frost;
With its banks of trees eager to bestow a downpour of masses of full-blown flowers,
it was covered by heaps of blossoms that caused great splendor, appearing like corals through the reflected beauty of the blooming *kiṃśuka* flowers.
It was encircled by a village stream whose waters were turbid with a flood of fruit being carried along by the very busy village children, and which was caught in the whirlpools of a great clamor;
its surface appeared as if washed by the water lashed by the tossing waves.
Constantly cooled by the shade of a canopy formed by dense-leaved trees,
this palace pavilion is visible, beautiful with its winding flowering creepers; its windows are covered by dangling clusters of blossoms.
"Here resides my husband, who has the form of a mere fragment of the space of life,
the lord of the earth girdled by the four oceans.
It was previously remembered that this very person had once harbored such a desire."

"May I quickly become like the king," [he thought] with a nature of intense spiritual urgency. O Supreme Goddess, in just eight days he obtained a prosperous kingdom that provides security for a long time.
"O King, that husband of mine, my lord, remains here in the house within the ether,
invisible like the wind in the sky or like fragrance in the breeze.
Even here, at the tip of my thumb, his station is established as if in the ether."
"My husband's kingdom has become for me as if it were ten million yojanas away.
O Sovereign Lady, both we and that sky are indeed the sky;
my husband's kingdom is full of thousands of mountains—oh, how vast is this illusion!"
"Therefore, O Queen, it is my desire to go once more to my husband's side.
So come, let us go there; for how far can distance be for those who are resolute?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess bowed to the Goddess, and quickly entering the pavilion,
she flew with her into the sword-like sky,
which resembled a mass of crushed collyrium and was as beautiful as a single, serene ocean.
Resembling the body of Nārāyaṇa, with a complexion as pure as the back of a bumblebee,
he transcends the path of the clouds and likewise the region of the winds; then,
having ascended the solar path, he passes beyond the lunar path.
Having traveled beyond the path of the fixed stars (dhruvamārga) and the path of those who are being perfected (sādhya),
and having completely passed over the earth and transcended the sphere of heaven (svargamaṇḍala),
he went into the interior of the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka) and the sphere of the Tuṣita gods.
Having transcended Goloka, Śivaloka, and Pitṛloka,
and having crossed far beyond even the bodiless gods (videha-devas),
she traveled further and further until, having gone to a place exceedingly remote, she was somewhat obstructed.
Afterwards, he looked back toward the sky that had passed away,
until not even a trace of the moon, sun, stars, or anything else was perceived below;
it was a darkness, motionless and profound, filling the hollows of the quarters.
It stands like the interior of the single universal ocean, as solid as a mountain of rock.
Līlā said:
"Then, O Goddess, tell me, where has the light of the sun and other luminaries gone beneath it?"
How can there be darkness that is motionless like the interior of a stone and graspable by the fist?
The Goddess said:
O sir, you have come this far along the path of the sky!
For even luminous bodies such as the sun are not seen [from below];
just as a firefly at the bottom of a great dark well is not perceived,
so too here the sun is not seen from below by one who is behind it.
Līlā said:
"Oh, how far we have come along this path!
Even the sun is not perceived in the slightest, appearing like a tiny speck of dust below."
“Beyond this, what other path might there be, and of what nature? How is it to be traversed, O Goddess? Tell me this.
Sarasvatī said:
Beyond this, ahead of you, is the shell of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*),
from which even diamonds and other such things have arisen as mere specks of dust.
Vasiṣṭha said:
As they were thus conversing, they reached the shell of the cosmic egg;
like two bees reaching the dense surface of a mountain crag,
they emerged from it without any difficulty, as if from the sky.
For that which is the object of certainty is the vajra-nature and nothing else.
Then, with unobstructed consciousness, she beheld here and there,
beyond the veil of water and other elements, the exceedingly radiant [realms] within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
The water-element is established as ten times the size of the Brahma-egg;
it stands enveloping that [egg], like the skin covering the surface of a walnut. Fire is ten times greater than that, and wind is ten times greater than fire.
Beyond that, space is tenfold; beyond that, the supreme ether.
In that supreme ether, no conceptualizations of middle, beginning, or end arise at all, like the talk of the son of a barren woman.
That which is absolute, stainless, peaceful, beginningless, free from delusion, and devoid of beginning, middle, and end, abides within the Great Self.

If the Lord of Śivā, by his supreme power, were to remain there until the end of the kalpa, or if the one whose banner is Garuḍa were to rise up there by force; [the world would still not perceive it].
For by that meditation, even the wind, moving with a single impulse, reaches the end of the stainless sky for the duration of a kalpa.
The thirtieth canto, titled "Description of the Supreme Space," from the *Līlopākhyāna*.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Here, having in an instant transcended the veils of earth, water, fire, air, and ether, each ten times greater than the preceding; MU 3.30.1.
She beheld that supreme space, devoid of all dimensions;
this entire world was spread out therein such that it appeared there no larger than a mere atom.
Within the cosmic eggs, she saw such creations as those, veiled by similar obscurations.
They flash forth by the millions in the sky like motes of dust in a sunbeam;
in the great ocean of the vast ether, within the waters of great emptiness,
they arise as bubbles and multitudes of blisters born from the state of the fluidity of Great Consciousness.
Some were falling downward, some were moving upward,
others were going crosswise, and still others remained motionless through their own self-awareness;
wherever consciousness arose for whomever, and in whatever manner.
In each respective place, their form arises in that particular way;
yet there is no name for it there, neither above nor below, nor any coming and going.
For that state is something entirely other than our bodily existence.
There, consciousness arises by itself from its own nature again and again;
it comes to rest through one's own volitions, like the web of volitions born of a child.
Rāma said:
"What would be below, what would be above, and what would be across in that radiant [state]?
Tell me this, O Brahmin, if there is no stability even here.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
Within this great, infinite, and boundless [reality], all the eggs of Brahmā, along with all their veils, appear like a hair-net in the sky;
for all entities whatsoever run about, lacking independence.
The cosmic egg is a portion of the earth; below that is space, otherwise it would be different.
For ants moving upon a round clod of earth in the sky, the ten directions are such that their feet are downward and their backs are said to be upward.
To some, the surface of the earth appeared as a web of trees and anthills;
the pure sky was surrounded by the moon, the sun, gods, and demons;
and the desert land was seen to have arisen together with villages, cities, and mountains.
This kalpa is like a ripe walnut still encased in its skin.
Just as female elephants roam within the vast expanse of the Vindhya forest,
so too do the atoms of the cosmic egg exist within that supreme expanse.
In that [reality], everything is contained; from it, everything arises; it is everything and exists everywhere.
It is eternally composed of all things, and likewise, it resides within every single atom.
In that ocean of supreme light, which consists of pure awakening, [all this is established].
The waves known as world-eggs (brahmāṇḍa) come and go incessantly;
some remain empty within, lasting for nights that end with the dissolution of the kalpa,
being carried away like waves in the ocean of water upon the ocean of emptiness.
For some, the gurgling roar of the end of the eon has already begun within;
it is neither heard nor known by others who are distracted by the flavors of their own inherent natures.
For others, at the very first beginnings, the desire to emerge expands.
Just as sprouts and creepers emerge from the seed-vessel when it is moistened by the rain of creation; so too,
upon the occurrence of the great dissolution, some whose supports have been melted by the rays of the sun proceed to fall away, like drops of frost under the heat.
Some indeed fall [into hell] for an entire kalpa without attaining the spiritual stages (*bhūmi*);
it is said that they remain there until, having been shattered, they are born again as beings composed of consciousness (*saṃvinmaya*).
Others remain completely paralyzed, like a hair-tuft in the sky.

Those whose prosperity has arisen in such a manner appear like the vibrations of the wind. Due to the conduct prescribed by the Vedic scriptures, the undertaking of others is entirely different and proclaimed otherwise; it is extensive and its established sequence is not like this.
Some are beings such as Brahmā and others; some are creators and protectors of the world such as Viṣṇu and others;
some are other lords of creatures; and some are beings without a protector.
Some are lords of diverse creations; and some are those whose nature consists of animals.
Some are filled with a single ocean, devoid of anything other than water;
some are masses of solid rock, while others are the internal paths of worms.
Some consist entirely of gods, and others consist entirely of men.
Some are filled with eternal darkness, inhabited by creatures accustomed to such conditions;
some are teeming with gnats, possessing the appearance of the fruit of the *uḍumbara* tree;
some are eternally hollow within, their inhabitants being creatures whose very nature is the vibration of emptiness.
Other creations of that same kind, which do not even enter the range of imagination here in our minds— being like the sky, the mute, or mountains— fill those [other worlds].
Between these [worlds], the great space remains situated in such a manner.
That which is not bestowed even by Viṣṇu and the other gods who grant life itself— that earthly portion,
situated within each cosmic egg like a magnet,
possesses by its very nature the power to attract the elements.
Since the nature of creation is beyond the scope of our intellects,
I lack the power, O Great-minded One, to describe that world.
Like those intoxicated by liquor dancing in a vast forest thick with terrifying darkness, unable even to see one another, [we wander in ignorance].

Just as many Yakṣas appear within the vast expanse of the supreme sky, so do very many great worlds flash forth. This concludes the thirty-first canto, titled "The Description of the Cosmic Egg," within the Narrative of Līlā.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Reflecting thus, the two of them emerged from their own world and suddenly beheld their inner apartments as if they were fast asleep.

It was filled with the great corpses of great kings, their bodies heavy with the weight of blooming flowers; within it, the playful forms of women sat by the sides of the corpses. It was crowded with people in deep sleep, as if it were a dense, dark night.
Perfumed by the fragrance of incense, sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, Līlā,
beholding that [world] again, became intent on returning to her husband’s cycle of existence;
she fell right there from that sky with her body of mental resolve.
Having pierced through the shell of the cosmic egg and repeatedly breaking through the veil of worldly existence, he entered a certain vast cycle of rebirth governed by his master’s will;
together with that goddess, he reached once more a realm possessed of further veils.
Having thus entered that vast pavilion of the universe with such speed,
that female swan beheld the world-born from her husband’s volition as a muddy pool, with mountains for its lotuses and the clouds of darkness for its silt.
Those two goddesses entered that sky within the world-egg, which is itself of the nature of space,
just as an anthill made of baked clay enters a small bilva fruit;
there, they passed beyond the intermediate worlds, the mountains, and the atmosphere.
They reached the surface of the earth, crowded with mountain ranges and oceans;
Jambudvīpa, adorned by Meru like the pericarp of a nine-petaled lotus.
Then, within that land of Bhārata, they arrived at the domain of Līlānātha.
In the meantime, in that circle upon the adorned earth,
a certain neighboring king launched an assault;
he was joined by those who had arrived for the sake of witnessing the fury of the battle.
The sky became utterly congested with the beings of the three worlds.
Then those two goddesses, arriving unexpectedly,
beheld the firmament crowded by hosts of sky-dwellers, as if garlanded with clouds.
It was accompanied by hosts of Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and Vidyādharas; it was surrounded by Apsarases from the heavenly world who were eager to seize the heroes;
and it was filled with Bhūtas, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas dancing with mouths full of blood and flesh.

It was filled with Vidyādhara women whose hands were laden with flowers rained down from the sky, and it was surrounded by Vetālas, Yakṣas, and Kumbhāṇḍas who, out of eager curiosity to witness the duels,
held mountain slopes as shields to protect themselves from the falling of weapons.
The circle of spirits fled from the expanse of the sky along the path of the missiles;
it was radiant with the soldiers of Indra, busy bringing forth heroes worthy of heaven;
and its lofty elephants, the foremost among the world-protectors, were adorned for the sake of those heroes.
The assembly of brave warriors arrived, with gandharvas and cāraṇas looking up expectantly;
the noble soldiers were gazed upon by the side-long glances of celestial women eager for battle,
while the spectators were formidable in their agitation and shouting as they cheered one another on.
[He saw] a city where rumors of an imminent and terrifying battle were circulating from one to another,

where beautiful women, eager for playful laughter and amorous gestures, waved their fly-whisks, and where the foremost sages offered hymns of benediction (*svastyayana*) employed for the sake of righteousness.
It was filled with the constant intimacy of the wives of many perfected world-protectors; it was a source of throngs of women eager for the embrace of the circle of heroes' arms;
and by the white fame of its warriors, it turned the sun into the moon.
Rāma:
Venerable sir, what kind of warrior is designated by the word "hero"?
Who would be the ornament of heaven, and who would be one struck down like a mere child?
Vasiṣṭha said: He who, for the sake of his lord who is endowed with conduct prescribed by the scriptures, dies or becomes victorious in battle, is a hero and partakes of the world of heroes.
But otherwise, the man who meets death in battle with his limbs severed,
having been struck down in a chaotic melee while fighting for wealth through conduct that deviates from the scriptures, is said to be destined for hell.
For that man who dies in battle, there is the inexhaustible hell.
He who fights while following the meaning of the scriptures as they apply and conforming to worldly conduct— only such a person is called a hero by virtue of his devotion.

For the sake of a cow, for the sake of a Brahmin, and for the sake of a friend, one who possesses right-mindedness dies through his effort to protect those who have sought refuge; such a person is an ornament in heaven. Always protecting his own country, he maintains the state that must be protected alone.

The king who dies for that cause is a hero who attains the world of heroes. But those who die in battle for the sake of a king or a lord who is intent on oppressing his subjects, they indeed go to hell.
If there were a righteous war conducted in such a manner,
they would utterly destroy this established order— being intoxicated and devoid of fear for the world—
by means of those base sayings which declare that "wherever a hero is slain, he goes to heaven."
"A warrior who fights righteously is a hero"—such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.
Those who endure the edge of a sword for the sake of those who follow virtuous conduct are called heroes; all others are merely slain in the fray of children's play.
For their sake, celestial women stand in the sky of battle with longing hearts, eager for the embrace of those great beings who have become gods;
they are filled with the sweet, languid songs of the Vidyādharīs and are agitated by the jealous anger of their wives as they clutch at Mandāra garlands.
With the rows of celestial chariots of the gods and Siddhas resting [there], it shone as if its beauty had been fashioned for a festival in the sky.
Thus ends the thirty-second canto, titled "The Description of the Sky Filled with Spectators of the Battle of the Sky-Travelers," within the narrative of Līlā.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then Līlā, standing amidst the Apsarases who were dancing out of longing for Vīravara, beheld the earth endowed with the sciences in the sky.
In a certain vast forest within the realm of Surāṣṭra, protected by its lord and garlanded with groves,
which was as terrifying as a second sky,
two armies remained undisturbed, resembling two tranquil oceans.
It was like a great, intoxicated, and steady cloud at the onset of a storm, accompanied by two kings; it was fully armed and prepared for battle, like a consecrated sacrificial fire,
its eyes agitated as it awaited the impact of the first strike.
It was a place where people were being submerged by the torrential downpour from the edges of uplifted, stainless swords;
it was crowded with the splendor of glittering battle-axes, spears, and slings;
and it trembled at the falling of forests agitated by the flapping of Garuḍa’s wings.
Their golden armor gleamed with the light of rising sunbeams;
their weapons were brandished in anger as they glared at one another's faces,
appearing as if fixed upon a painted wall because of their mutual, fixed gazes.
Its stability was established by long-established boundaries of writing;
its clamor was an unavoidable, great, and irresistible roar, yet its discourse was not heard; the drums had long since been silenced out of pride at having struck the first blow.
The army was sluggish, its ranks rendered motionless by the positions of the stationed warriors;
it was divided by a single bridge in the middle, which was empty for the space of two bows,
like a single ocean agitated by the wind at the end of an eon.
Its lord was overcome by the anxiety of the agitation caused by the crisis of his duties;
its inner chambers were filled with hearts distressed and broken by the croaking of frogs;
and it possessed countless soldiers ready to sacrifice their very lives for the sake of vital breath.

The bow-bearers had their bows raised, ready to release a flood of arrows held at their ears; countless soldiers stood motionless, watching for the fall of the blows; and the field was crowded with warriors whose brows were knit in fierce mutual defiance.
The armor produced a harsh *kaṭuṭāṅkāra* sound as it struck against one another's shoulders;
the hollows [of the chariots] were abandoned by cowards who could not withstand the heroic warriors; and life was held in doubt for a mere moment by the mutual positioning of the combatants.
With its human inhabitants appearing aged by the dust clinging to all their limbs,
and with the sound of its waves stilled as if sealed in sleep because the life-breath of its people was distracted by watching the previous blow; (3.32.15–16)
The clamor of the conchs, the multitude of musical instruments, and the kettledrums had subsided;
all the clouds of dust on the surface of the earth had settled,
and those intent on flight had abandoned [the road] step by step.
It shone like an ocean filled with fish in the form of spreading arrays of *makara* monsters;
its principal trees were fanned by clusters of flower-stalks serving as banners,
and the expanse of the sky was turned into a forest by the trunks of elephants raised aloft like pillars.
With all his weapons appearing as if winged by the flood of his shimmering, trembling radiance,
and filling the intermediate space of the sky with the sounds "dham-dham" arising from his breath,
he— having crushed the wicked Asura warriors within the circular military array (cakravyūha)— [advanced].
The mass of serpents was agitated by the fury of the *garuḍa* formation;
the fierce array of the *śyena* (hawk) formation rose up with a thundering sound;
and throngs of heroes fell as they struck and crushed one another.
It was arranged with various diverse displays, terrifying with internal roars,
and resembled a temple of intoxicated mallets raised aloft by hands;
it darkened the sun with the web of rays from the weapons of Kṛṣṇa.
The sound of the arrows was like the whistling of *śalmali* trees shaken by the wind;
it stood as if possessing the same nature as many kalpas and the end of kalpas,
like a single ocean arisen, agitated by the winds of universal dissolution.
Like darkness rising unagitated from the caverns of the netherworld,
like the Lokāloka mountain with its slopes shimmering and swaying in the wild dance of the intoxicated,
it appeared as if the earth had risen up after piercing through the mass of the great hells.

With the rays of their swaying spears, maces, swords, and axes, it seemed as if they were turning the entire vessel of the world into a single ocean with masses of rainwater; it was like preparing to make the abyss an immeasurable expanse in an instant with its endless floods.
The *Līlopākhyāna*, the chapter titled "Description of the Manifestations at the Commencement of Battle."
The Thirty-third Chapter.
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, tell me briefly and in brief about this battle."
Vasiṣṭha said: "Then those two goddesses remained there in the sky to witness that battle, by which the hearing of the listener is gladdened through these utterances."
In that lovely, fashioned celestial chariot, which was now obstructed, the two remained firm and ascended. In the meantime, there, on account of his opposition to the Lord of Līlā,
he grew weary, unable to endure the onset of suffering in battle.
