Like a towering wave in the ocean of dissolution, the fierce warrior leaped up and hurled a mallet at the chest of the other warrior, as if striking a rock upon a mountain peak. Then he began to attack with violence, possessing the momentum of the ocean at the time of universal destruction.
In the two armies, there was a clash of weapons, scattering sparks like fire and lightning;
the surface of the sky was marked by lines of rising, trembling droplets,
while amidst the clanging *jhaṇajhaṇa* sounds, the whizzing *jhāṅkṛti* of arrows was clearly perceived.
Devouring with the gurgling roar of his bowstring mingled with heroic *huṃ* cries,
he was like a canopy of solar rays amidst the clouds of flowing showers of arrows;
the fire of his *kaṇapa* missiles flew up at the clanging sound of his ringing armor.
The sky became a forest where the trees were the arms of heroes, shaken by their movement; the fragments of weapons severed by mutual blows were its scattered leaves;
and the courtesans of the celestial chariots fled in terror at the twanging of bows and the whirling of discuses.
The deep roar of the clouds was turned into the great tumultuous din of bees;
by virtue of its singular density, it was as if the army were established in a state of non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*).
The heads of heroes were severed into fragments by the torrential showers of iron arrows.
It was crowded with armor clashing and rattling against one another on their shoulders;
it resounded with the harsh *ṭāṅ* sounds from the impact of weapon-tips struck down by the *huṃ* cries;
and its entire horizon was jagged and fierce with the surging waves of flowing torrents.
With the clashing and agitation of weapons, a rattling sound grasped by the fist;
with the bursting of exploding shells and the crackling *caṭacaṭa* roar;
with the ringing of brandished swords and the crackling sound of flaming hemp and *śaṇa* grass.
The air resounded with the soft, gasping breaths of autumnal deer;
blood gushed from wounds arising from severed throats with the sound "dhag-dhag-dhag";
and the sky was filled without any gaps by fragments of severed arms, heads, and swords.
His hair was scorched by the flickering flashes of fire arising from his armor;
he produced a thick *jhaṇajjhaṇa* sound from the multitude of clashing swords falling against him;
and blood welled up from the waves of elephants blunted by his spears.
Rough with the *kreṅkāra* sounds produced by the crushing of tusks against tusks,
it resounded with the loud cries of throngs ground to powder by the impact of great pestles;
the sky was covered by a profusion of lotus-like heads of *taraccha* beasts.
A cloud of dust was formed by the lordly serpents with their arms tossed about in the sky;

it brought about the counter-action of hair-to-hair combat between Keśin and the one who had severed his head; and it caused great terror as eyes, hands, noses, and ears were torn out by nails against those who possessed no nails.
The earth trembled under the falling elephants in rut, and chariots rolled about;
the battlefield was draped with the blood from wounds inflicted by the fury of the conflict,
while weapons gleamed as they flashed through the mist created by rising dust.
Proud of his ocean-like army, which was a single mass of dense agitation,
he was devoured by Death with the playful laughter of a madman;
his thundering roar was dwarfed by the bellowing of the great lordly elephants and the mountains of his pride.
With wheels, spears, swords, and mallets resting against the slopes at the sides of the trees;
with trees so densely packed by the warriors that even the threads of woolen yarn could not pass between them;
and with its banners, cloths, and chowries scattered by the tossing of the clouds.
The sky-dwellers were swiftly scattered by the flood of mechanical stones and wheels;
it was exceedingly gurgling with the wailing of warriors whose limbs were hacked while they were preoccupied with death;
and it was scarred by wounds upon heads split open by the impact of blows from sharp-edged axes.
The sky was starred with fragments of swords flashing as they soared far aloft; the earth was covered by a mass of spears hurled from pikes that remained stuck there;
and mallets were cast down by the leaping of Vetālas agitated within the army.
The lofty archway of his heroic lances was raised high toward the sky;
the rows of sword-blades shattered by his *bhuśuṇḍī* mallets formed earrings for the firmament;
and the forest of his spears, scattered like a grove of reeds, acted as the flickering crest-fire upon the hair of the parched heavens.
His soldiers were honored by kings who were satisfied by showers of sword-blades and spears;
he endeavored to capture true heroes by intimidating them with his own prowess, causing celestial nymphs to be seized;
and as his mace moved along its path, it caused his shimmering armlets to fall, casting light toward the quarters of the sky.
The fierce warriors, whose miserable efforts were crushed by force with spears,
were rendered helpless as their four tusks were severed by the movement of the discus’s rim;
the rutting elephants fell down, struck by the falling mass of axes.
The warriors leaped up, brandishing clubs and roaring fiercely as they struck;
the standards, chariots, and trees were crushed by the falling stones from the siege-engines;
and the white lotuses of the royal umbrellas were severed by sharp swords.
It was characterized by the earth strewn with soldiers destroyed by the agitation of being hurled [into the fray];
its flanks were crushed by the falling of headless trunks and intoxicated elephants;
and its elephants were held back by heroes stationed on conch shells who were wary of the [enemy] spikes.
He laments the heroes who know the specific ways of entering the noose;
he is one whose belly is pierced by a razor-edged dagger and from whom the lotus-like entrails fall out;
he performs a dance for Śiva with a trident held high like a face.
It resounded with the cacophony of whistling quivers filled by rushing archers;
it was a theater for the frantic dancing of soldiers brandishing slings,
and it was a perilous place where brave warriors were crushed by diamond-hard fists.
Like a hawk, he soared into the path of the sky with his spear and sword;
his banner bore the great elephant and horse of Lord Śiva, which were subdued by his hook;
and the mountain of the host of gods, agitated by the effortless destruction of Hālāhala poison, was struck down.
The surface of the earth was marked by pits dug by sharp-pointed spades that had been pulled up from beneath;
the rows of stones in the world were severed by missiles discharged with double the force of a bow; and the rutting elephants were cut down on both flanks by saws.
The battle was a cloud where the mortars were filled with the world’s rice-grains;

its birds were the soldiers bound by chains as vast as masses of clouds; it was a hero-surge like a choice rain-cloud raining down iron arrows, where the dancing headless trunks were peacocks bewildered by the intoxicated clouds.
The tumult of battle was like the upheaval at the end of an eon, as it was surrounded by mountain-like elephants reeling with speed.
This concludes the thirty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of the First Clash of the Two Armies," within the *Līlopākhyāna*.
Vasiṣṭha:

Then, among the kings eager for battle, the warriors, the ministers, and the impetuous spectators, these words arose there: MU_3,34.1: "Then, among the kings eager for battle, the warriors, the ministers, and the impetuous spectators, these words arose there."

The sky, strewn with the heads of heroes, shines like a lake with swaying lotuses or like one filled with migrating birds, its appearance marked by the stars. Behold it, reddened by the winds carrying floods of blood-drops and vermilion.
At midday, these clouds and sunbeams shine like the twilight.
"Sister, why does this sky stand here filled with straw?
"This is not straw; for heroes, these are clouds laden with showers of arrows."
For as many subtle particles of dust as are settled upon the earth by their blood, for that many thousands of years shall these warriors have their abode in heaven.
Do not fear; these are not swords possessing the luster of blue lotus petals.
These are the playful glances of the goddess Lakṣmī as she surveys these heroes; meanwhile,
the flower-weaponed god has begun to loosen the girdles on the hips of the celestial nymphs who long for the embrace of a hero.
With hands like trembling red shoots upon their swaying creeper-like arms,
with eyes intoxicated by flower-clusters and fragrant with the scent of honey,
the deities of the Nandana grove entreated her with sweet words.
Suspecting your arrival, they have begun to dance;
this army strikes at its own enemy within with harsh axes, like a village woman with her wicked behavior striking her lover.

"Alas! My father’s head, adorned with flaming earrings, has been carried by my broad-headed arrow to the vicinity of the sun, like the eighth planet [Rāhu] drawn near the sun by Time. His two massive feet, bound by chains and spinning, resemble two large stones."
Whirling with speed the wheel called Citradaṇḍa with his arms raised high,
the warrior approaches from the southern quarter like Yama himself;
withdrawing the army from all sides, he says, "Come, let us go back the way we came."
Behold the headless trunks (kabandhas) dancing on the battlefield, as tall as palm trees, crowded with flocks of herons swooping down into the cavities of their recently severed necks.
A conversation has begun among the assemblies of the hosts of gods.
"Speak, O heroes! How will they go to the other world, who are they, and from where?
These armies that have arrived swallow [everything] like oceans swallowing rivers;
alas, how formidable are these warriors, with their battle arrays of fish and crocodiles!"
Upon the hides of elephants were strewn heaps of sharp-edged iron arrows, like full-fledged showers of rain fallen upon the clusters of mountain peaks.
"Alas! My head has been carried away by a spear"—thus did he wish to say.
"His head has been brought here!"—thus was it cried out like the shriek of a bird in the sky.

"Let a net of chains be forcibly cast upon this army by which he drenches us with a rain of stones from his machines!"* MU 3.34.18–19 *(Note: The term *yantrapāṣāṇavarṣeṇa* refers to a shower of stones discharged by mechanical contrivances.)*
"O lowest of men, lead all these fools together—who are already half-dead—away by striking them with your own feet; do not kill them yourselves!
While the throngs of celestial nymphs, filled with intense longing, are busy arranging their braided hair..."
"Behold the soldier who has arrived at my side with a divine body!
Look upon him who has come from afar upon the banks of the celestial river, where golden lotuses are in bloom and where the shade, cool waters, and breezes [provide relief]."
With the sharp peaks of mountains shattered by the clashing of various weapons,
they moved through the sky like stars falling in death amidst the *jhaṇat* sounds;
in the void, a river of emptiness flowed with arrows for its waters.
Even mountains become like mere dust as they travel upon the revolving wheel;
for the heads of the heroic mountain-kings, whirling in the paths of the planets,
have their sword-blade thorns caught upon the stalk-like creepers of the light-rays from their weapons.
With the banners as its lotus stalks and the fallen arrows as its petals,
the sky was turned into a lotus pond by the swaying lotuses of the wind-blown flags. Like ants upon a mountain covered with a multitude of dead elephants, [the soldiers lay there].
The timid ones hide away, like women [hiding] from the chest of a man.
Winds blow, ruffling the tresses of the Vidyādhara women, heralding their union with beloveds of unprecedented and supreme beauty.

When the umbrellas had flown up and vanished, having been severed, the moon descended upon the sky’s moonlight and, in the form of his own glory, became a white parasol for him. Then the warrior, at the end of his swoon from death, in a mere moment attained a divine body.
It was like reaching a city in a dream, fashioned by the artisan of one's own imagination.
Showers of spears, javelins, double-edged swords, and discuses were released with open fists;
they stood like heroes in the ocean of the sky as schools of fish, crocodiles, and crabs.
The sky shines as if covered by hundreds of thousands of full moon discs gathered together, like swans falling from their umbrellas severed by arrows; and it is filled with beautiful,
low-sounding chowries flying upward into the heavens.
The splendor of the multitude of waves shaken by the wind is seen;
those parasols, fly-whisks, and banners appear like grains of rice of fame sown in the field of the sky, utterly shattered.
Behold the shower of spears being brought to destruction by countless arrows flying through the sky,
like the beauty of a grain crop destroyed by locusts.
This [shower] is accompanied by the clashing of swords from warriors with outstretched, staff-like arms.
Born from the harsh armor of Death himself, they were like his fierce roar;
shattered by the wind of the logic of causes, they were like mountains whose elephants have been destroyed, with their cascades of teeth now silenced at this time of the destruction of mankind.

"Alas, alas! Woe! The city of chariots has been submerged, fallen, and destroyed in the great lake of blood from the battle array—the horses, chariots, and masters of the wheels!"—amidst the clanging sounds produced by the striking together of sharp armor and swords.
As Kālarātri dances in battle, she is played upon like a lute;

behold how the quarters of the sky are reddened by the wind sprinkled with droplets from the streams of blood falling from the corpses of men, elephants, and horses, which serve as her mountain-sounding-boards.
In the sky, the mass of her hair, dark as Kālī’s locks, appeared like a flash of lightning amidst the ocean of the rays of weapons,
adorned with a garland of the weight of arrow-buds;
it was surrounded by weapons whose blades were as red as the earth drenched in blood from the army.
The world shone with excessive radiance, as turbulent as the realm of Agni;
showers of *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons, spears, tridents, swords, clubs,
and javelins reached the state of scattered fragments through their mutual cutting and piercing.
Because of the singular, unshakeable strike, the combatants— whose wisdom sought out one another’s fury— stood as if asleep, their mutual movements unobserved by others,
amidst the incessant *jhaṇajhaṇa* clashing of weapons that produced no other sound.

The terrible roar of battle, exulting in the agitation of destruction, seemed to sing; the ocean of war, filled with the dust from the tips of weapons struck against one another, became as if composed entirely of sand, with severed umbrellas for its waves.

This mountain of battle, skilled in fierce wings and filling the world of the world-protectors with the echoes of drums split by the force of extreme impetuosity, seems to perform a widespread dance in the sky like that at the end of an eon.
Alas, alas! Fie upon these blazing flashes of manifest lightning, leaping up as they strike against the vast iron armor!
Resounding with the twang of their vibrating strings, these iron arrows, splitting mountain rocks as they whiz by, carry us away.
Before these shafts, blazing like a raging fire, sever our desires and shatter our limbs with a sharp *chham* sound, come quickly, friend, let us go; this fourth watch of the day is now passing away.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the thirty-fifth canto, titled "Description of the Words Spoken by the Spectators of the Battle," Vasiṣṭha said:
Then that ocean of battle became like one intoxicated in a wild dance, with its waves of horses intent on leaping upward;
it was filled with shoals of fish that were white arrows resting upon the foam of parasols and staffs.
Its hollows were agitated by the surging waves of cavalry and elephant forces;
it possessed the swirling eddies of armies carried along by the rivers of various weapons;
and it was filled with the shifting mountain ranges that were the massive bodies of rutting elephants.
With his head whirling as it spun through the hundred revolutions of the sword-wheel, he was like a blade of grass;
the water-like luster of his brandishing sword was swallowed by the clouds of dust.
His fierce ship of warriors—neither broken nor surrendered—was shattered by the vast array of crocodiles.
Its deep caverns resounded with the thick echoes of great gurgling whirlpools;
its mustard-seeds were the swarms of fish emerging from their beds of reeds; and the circles of its waves were formed by banners torn away by the clashing of weapons upon the ripples.
With earrings like whirlpools in the ocean wounded by weapons and water,
with the dense movement of fury as its crocodiles and timingilas,
and terrifying with the waters of the moving army clad in black iron armor; MU_3,35.7.
Terrifying with mountains that were the armies gathered within the lines of whirlpools formed by headless trunks;
with the quarters of the sky shrouded in the darkness of the mist-like spray of arrows;
and possessing a single, dense roar of *ghuṅghuma* that left no other sound behind.
It was filled with the spray from fragments of heads tossed up and down;
within its circular whirlpools, soldiers spun like pieces of wood;
it was formidable with the waves of bow-strings twanging in painful *ṭāṅkāra* sounds, resembling the crashing of jars.
Without hesitation, like a rising ocean of soldiers from the underworld (pātāla),
it was foamy with the banners and parasols of endless troops engaged in coming and going; it bore away the trees that were the chariots, swept along by the force of the flowing rivers of blood.
With great bubbles of blood produced by elephants resembling [massive] clouds,
and with horses and elephants as aquatic creatures tossing about in the flowing current of the army—
that battle was as wondrous to men as a celestial village in the sky.
It was as restless as mountains shaken by the earthquake at the time of universal dissolution; with leaping horses for its birds and falling masses of elephants for its banks;
with herds of timid deer wandering about and resounding with a loud, rattling roar.
With its army as fragile as a śarabha struck by a flight of autumn arrows,
with its swift horses like śarabhas, and its earth bearing the weight of the śarabhas;
with the trumpeting of elephants circling as its roar and the mountain caves serving as its sounding halls for the musical instruments.
A cloud of the retreating army, with the leaping warriors as its lions;
a cloud of spreading dust, with the retreating troops as its mountain peaks;
rich with the falling limbs of excellent chariots, and with circles of falling swords.
Rich with fluttering silk flowers, bearing banners and parasols like clouds,
with surging rivers of blood flowing through it, and with great elephants falling within it—
that battle became like the end of an aeon, agitated by the devouring of the world.
With its chariots and infantry, along with its banners, umbrellas, and flags overturned; radiant like the intense light of many suns from the mass of falling, stainless weapons;
it scorched all human beings with the heat of its harsh life-force.
The sky was filled without interval by the continuous showers of arrows from the *puṣkarāvarta* clouds of his bow;
the firmament was encircled by flashes of lightning in the form of the streaks of sword-blades flashing forth;
and the mountain ranges were the multitudes of elephants fallen from the swelling red ocean of blood.
The stars were the masses of stones from the mechanical engines scattered and falling through the sky;
the clouds of arrows filled the expanse of the heavens like the whirlpools of clouds at the end of an aeon;
and the intermediate spaces between the worlds were the intervals between the armies consumed by the fires of the divine weapons.
The earth and its mountains were shattered by the thunderbolt-like rain of arrows;
the multitudes of people were crushed by the falling mass of elephant-kings like mountain ranges;
and the earth and sky were covered by clouds in the form of a host of arrow-bearing showers.
It resounded with a harsh noise from the clashing and agitation of a great ocean of armies;
it was pervaded by water-monsters, fires, and mountains tossed up by fierce winds,
all intent on crushing one another and arisen as portents of weapons.
Piercing one another and resounding with the clash of pikes, swords, discuses, arrows, spears, maces, *bhuśuṇḍīs*, and darts,
hundreds of blazing weapons whirled about, assuming the appearance of objects tossed by the winds at the end of an aeon;
thus ends the chapter titled "The Description of Battle" within the "Līlopākhyāna."
The thirty-sixth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, while the Śabaras and others stood there with their horns held high like banners;
While rivers of flowing blood, equal to the Gaṅgā, were being produced;
while headless trunks with flailing arms danced together with their companions;
and while men, elephants, horses, and chariots sank into the waters of blood.
When all the armies had departed and become scattered,
when all the cowards were broken and fled in the ten directions,
and when the rows of clouds rested upon the mountain-like corpses of elephants;
While the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas were sporting in the ocean of blood,
there arose [the sound] of great heroes— those devoted to dharma, endowed with virtue, vigor, and courage, pure lotuses of noble lineage, and never-retreating warriors.
Duels broke out like the roaring of clouds,
eager to swallow one another like the meeting of the surging tides of the ocean.
A mass of elephants with their riders engaged in combat with a multitude of elephants equipped with armor.
The pressing-stone met with the pressing-stone by force, as stone meets stone;
the flood of horses met with the multitude of horses, roaring with great speed,
like a terrible surge of waves meeting a surge of waves in the ocean.
The army of men fought the army of men with equal weapons,
like a stream of bamboos driven by the wind clashing against a stream of bamboos tossed by the wind;
and the mass of chariots crushed the entire body [of the enemy] with the mass of chariots.
As if the city itself had been carried into the sky by fate,
the army of archers, with its banners obscuring the heavens, fought against the autumnal downpour of arrows that formed an unprecedented cloud.
When warriors of feeble resolve flee by some stratagem during battles with uneven weapons amidst the fire of the world-ending kalpa,
then those who wield discs join with discs and archers with archers.
Swordsmen fought with swordsmen, those with *bhuśuṇḍī* clubs with those with *bhuśuṇḍīs*, mace-wielders with mace-wielders, spear-bearers with spear-bearers,
those armed with *ṛṣṭi*s with those bearing *ṛṣṭi*s, and those with darts in hand with those holding darts.

Those with mallets fought with mallet-wielders; those with gleaming clubs fought with those armed with clubs; those skilled in the use of spears fought with spears; those who hurled axes fought with battle-axes;
those with masses of cudgels fought with cudgel-bearers; and those whose weapons were stones fought with those armed with stones.
With nooses they were supreme in binding; with spikes they bore spikes;
with daggers they carried daggers; and with slings they held those weapons. They wielded diamond-hard maces, and with hooks they were raised up by their hooks.
Those skilled in striking with clubs fought with clubs, and those bearing tridents with tridents;
those equipped with chains fought with nets, using those nets that were as soft as bees;
those armed with spears fought with spears, and those expert in pikes fought with pikes.
They were agitated like masses of waves in an ocean tossed by the dissolution of an eon;
the single ocean of the sky appeared with its churning whirlpools of wheels, winds of arrow-spray, and the makaras of whirling weapons.
With the surging waves of leaping weapons and the aquatic creatures of the army hosts,
that ocean of the earth’s hollows became impassable for the gods;
it was as if the armies of the people of the eight directions had become its two wings.
Thus it remained, divided half and half by the two kings.
Behold these provinces situated in the eastern direction according to their number;
hear now of the districts belonging to the side of Padma, the lord of Līlā.
In the east are Kāśī, Magadha, Kosala, Mithilā, Utkalā, Mekalā, Kavaṭa, Puṇḍra, Auṇḍra, and all the Gauḍakas;
as well as Drimaya, Madra, Suhma, and likewise Tāmralipta.
The Prāgjyotiṣas, the horse-faced ones, the Ambaṣṭhas, and the cannibals;
those with ears for eyes, those without ears, and likewise those who eat raw fish;
the tiger-faced ones, the Kirātas, the Śavaras, and the one-footed ones.
There is the mountain named Mālyavat, as well as Śibi, Vāñ, and Jñāna;
likewise the mountains Vṛṣabhadhvaja, Padma, and others, along with Udayakara.
Now, to the southeast, these are the inhabitants of the Vindhya mountains.
The Cedis, Vatsas, Dāśārṇas, Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, and Upavaṅgas; likewise the Kaliṅgas, Puṇḍras, Jaṭharas, Vidarbhas,
Mekhalas, Śabaras, Nagnaparṇas, Kaṇṭhas, Tripuras, and Pūrakas.
The Kaṇṭakasthalas, the Pṛthudvīpakas, the Komalas, the Kaṇṭhadrās, the Śoṇikas, as well as the Carmaṇvatās;
the Kokakas, the Hemakuḍyas, and likewise the Śmaśrudharas.
Baligrīva, Mahāgrīva, Kiṣkindhā, and Nārikelina;
then, to the south of this Lord of Līlā, are these mountains:
Vindhya, Kusumāpīḍa, Mahendra, and Dundura.
Malaya, Sūryavān, the Gaṇarājya and Nṛrājya peoples, those known as Avanti, and likewise the Sāmbavatīs;
Daśapura, Ekakaccha, the Ṛṣikas, Turuṣkas, and Śakas.
Vanavāsa, Upagiri, and Bhadragiri;
Nāgara, Daṇḍaka, Gaṇarājya, and Nṛrājyaka; Sahāra, Ṛṣyamūka, Kārkoṭa, and Vanatimbiḷa.
The Padmanivāsins, the Caurakas, the Karkavīrakas,
the Vairikas, the Pāśikas, the Dharmapattanas, and the Pāṃsikās; the Śākikas, the Kṛṣṇacelūras, the Nārmadas, and the Tāmraparṇakas.
The Gonandas, the Kanakas, those named after the city of Cīna,
the Tālīkaṭas, the Saritkīrṇas, the Rahakas, the Veṇnakārhaṇas,
the Vaivuṇḍakas, the Tumbavanas, the Lājinadvīpas, and the Karṇakas.
The Karṇikāras, Śivayas, Kuṅkuṇas, Citrakūṭakas, Karṇāṭas, Mañcakaṭakas, Mahākaṭavikas,
as well as the Āndhras, Kollaśinas, and Śivātakacavairikas.
The Baladevas, Pattanakas, Krauñcas, and likewise the Ṭīvas;
the Śilākṣas, Radatas, Nandanas, and those called Nandanandanas;
they [dwell] on the peaks of Citrakūṭa, which are the abodes of the hosts of Rākṣasas who protect Laṅkā.
Then, in the south-eastern direction, there are the Mahārāṣṭras and Surāṣṭrakas;
those known as Sindhus, Sauvīras, and Śūdras; likewise the Ābhīras and Dramiḍas; the Koṭakas, those called Ṣaṇḍasindhvas, and also the Kaliruhās.
Herein lies the Hemagiri mountain, as well as the Raivataka mountain;
there is the Mayavana forest called Nabhuka, where the Yavanas dwell as its inhabitants,
along with the Pahlavas, Mārgaṇāvartas, and those known as Dhūmras and Ambaṣṭhakas.
Likewise, there are the Lājakaṇas and those who dwell on Mount Āmraka;
then there are the people of Līlāpati, together with the ocean and the submarine fire (aurvāgni).
Now, hear of these regions situated as adversaries to that [kingdom].
In the western direction, these great mountains stand firm:
the king of mountains named Matimān, as well as Kṣurārpaṇa-giri,
Vanaukahā, Meghavān, Cakravān, and the Asta mountain.
The people known as the Pañcanadas, the Kāśas, the Brahmāvasātakas, as well as the Tārakṣatayas, the Pāravas, and the Śāntikas; likewise,
those on the slopes of the Vatakapokrāṇas and the Girivānavamas.
Those lowest tribes of Mlecchas have abandoned the boundaries of dharma.
Beyond that lies the land of Janapada, two hundred yojanas in extent;
beyond that is the peak of Mount Mahendra, a ground composed of pearls and jewels.
Then there is the mountain named Āsta, surrounded by hundreds of peaks;
beyond that lies the great ocean, and on the shore of the formidable Pāriyātra mountain,
in the northwestern quarter, stands the region of Girimati.
Likewise Veṇumat and Turamati, and then the earth [was ruled by them];
as well as the Phalgunakas, the Māṇḍavyas, and the Ekanetrakas;
the Purukundas, the Tukhāras, and the Tālamallalahāvahas.
The people will be bowing, yet not bowing; their hair, limbs, and arms will be long;
they will be colorful, sky-faced, trembling, slayers of their teachers, and laughing beautifully.
Then there will be an incomparable kingdom of women, where the bull is the vessel for offspring.
Then, in the north, there are Himavat, Kāñja, and the Madhumat mountain;
Kailāsa, Vasumān, and Meru—these are the people along those paths:
the Madras, Pauravas, Yaudheyas, Mālavas, and Śūrasenas.
Likewise, the Rājanyas, the Aśvinīs, the descendants of Arjuna, the Trigartas, the Kekayas, the Kṣudrakas, the Mācellas,
those dwelling in Cūta, the Ambalas, the Prasthalas, the Śākas, and the Kṣemadhūrtis.
Then there are Antaradvīpa, Gāndhāra, Vandivaṭa, and Tava; then the place named Takṣaśilā, followed by Lavaṇāvatī,
the region of Puṣkalāvatī, and then the earth of Yaśovatī.
Then there were the Maṇimantīs, the Śyāmākās, and the Khacarās;
likewise the Dāśadānas, the Gavyasanas, and the Daṇḍahavyasanās;
the Dānadās, the Śūrakas, and the Vāṭādhāras as well.
Kohaka and Nagara, as well as Surabhūtipura;
then indeed Taṭakādarśa and Danturādarśa;
and thereafter those named Piṇḍala, Mālavya, Yāyana, and Īya.
Mālahālā, Hūnahematālāśva, Svamukha, Himavat, Vasumān, Kauñja, Kailāsa, and likewise Agra;
from there the country is a land of eight thousand yojanas.
Now, listen to these countries situated in the north-east:
the Kaulūtas, the Brahmaputras, the Kuvindas, the Dinādanās, the Maḍavas, those whose kingdoms have perished, and likewise the Vanarāṣṭras.
The Kaiḍabhallas, Siṃhapuras, and likewise the Cāmavaṭaṅgas;
the Sārpātakas, Pārvatakas, Kaśmīras, and Daradas; the Abhisārajas, Dārvākās, Pallolas, Urukaciras, and Oḍunas.
Then there were the Kirātas and the Paśupālas, and the land of Cīna and the Golden Land; after that, the ground of the divine groves; then the glorious abode of Viśvāvasu;
then the mountain Kailāsa with its supreme prosperity; and then Mount Muñjavat, the playground for the Vidyādharas and gods and the site of their celestial chariots.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the thirty-seventh canto, titled "Description of the Country," Vasiṣṭha said:
In that battle, fierce with men and elephants violently torn apart,
where crowds of warriors rushed forward crying "I first! I first!",
these and many others there were reduced to ashes.
Entering with great effort like moths into a fire—
here, other people from the Middle Country have not been mentioned by me;
listen as I shall describe these partisan followers of King Līlā.
The Uddehikas, Śūrasenas, Guḍas, Aśvatthas, Nīpakas,
Uttamajyotikas, Drāṇis, Padamadhyamikas, and so forth; the Sālvakas, Ketakas, Matsyas, Dauleyakas, and Kapiṣṭalas.
Māṇḍavya, Pāṇḍunagara, Sauragrīva, and Gurugraha; the Pāriyātras, Kuraḍhya, and also Yāmuna and Uḍumbara; Gajāhvā, Ujjihāna, Kālakoṭika, and Mathurā.
And likewise the people of Kapāla, Dharmāraṇya, Uttara, and Dakṣiṇa;
the Pāñcālas, the Kurukṣetras, and the Sārasvata folk; and those of Avanti, Syandanaśreṇī, and Kunti, driven by the arrows of Pañcanada.
Flowing and fleeing, she fell upon a great mountain precipice.
The *kāśa* reeds and the *brahmāvasāta* grasses, severed by the people of Sāmbavatī,
fell to the ground, crushed by rutting elephants.
The heroes of Daśapura, their noble necks severed by weapons,
were attacked by Tārakṣati and cast into the Yojana lake;
likewise Ṛṣya, Kāruru, and Kakṣa, marked by hundreds of Śaivya’s arrows.
The earth became mired in mud by the trampling of the army;
seeking shelter in their forest dwellings,
the mountain-dwellers ran about on all sides and fell into the pool of the Yamunā.
Bound by the strings of their own entrails emerging from their torn bellies,
the *rātrikas* ceased their wandering at night,
having been devoured by *piśācas* on the path of battle with the fierce Udra Bhadragiris who were consecrated for war.
Cast into the pits of the earth like lotuses deprived of their sap;
fleeing with their blood flowing, the great chariot-warriors of the Haihayas were scattered like deer driven by the wind through the Daṇḍaka forest.
Shattered by the tusks of elephants and crushed by the teeth of warriors,
the enemies were carried away by the great river of blood like the sprouts of trees;
the Chinese, chewed by iron arrows, had their lives worn away and shattered.
They cast their bodies, which had become a burden, into the ocean; with the mountain caves carved by the spears hurled by the brave warriors of Karṇāṭa,
the heroic Ābhīras crossed over like clusters of stars in the sky.
Struck by the force of the array of elephants and sea-monsters, their weapons shattered,
and engaged in hand-to-hand combat, the Daśakas and Śakas were routed.
From Daśārṇa came those who feared nets, like thunderbolts released from their chains.
They lay hidden in the blood-mud like small fish in a shallow puddle.
By the destruction of the Gūrjara army, the plucking out of the hair of the Gūrjara women was accomplished by the sharp,
lofty spears of the Tāṅgaṇas.
They drenched [the enemies] with a rush of weapons, like flashes of lightning flashing from the sky,
as if from a cloud that bestows fish-like weapons;
while those who were terrified by the portentous appearance of the sun turned dark by the glare of the circle of *bhuśuṇḍī* spears.
The enemies fell upon the Ābhīras like herds of cattle upon green pastures.
The naked army of the Taṅgaṇas, their limbs as beautiful as refined gold,
was ravished by the Gauḍa warriors with the pulling of their fingernails and hair.
By the slicing of the wheels of the chariots stationed in the roaring sky,
the Taṅgaṇas were scattered in pieces among the herons and vultures by the Rudrakas; while the Gauḍas, tossed about by the stirring of clubs, rose up with a gurgling roar.
Hearing [the sound] from the fierce Gandhāra region, they fled like those whose strength was exhausted.
Resembling the ocean of the sky and carrying a multitude of weapons,
it caused the Pārasīkas to experience the delusion of thick nocturnal darkness.
In that place, beautiful as the Milky Ocean rising from the Mandara mountain,
the rows of forest trees served as weapons upon the snowy peaks of parasols;
for the sky was filled with masses of weapons that seemed like clouds rising up.
That forest of the sky was seen as if flooded by the waves of the ocean, shimmering with ripples;
it appeared filled with hundreds of moons in the form of white parasols, dense with locust-like arrows,
and packed as thickly with spears as a crow-filled thicket.
The peacocks, who had been making long-drawn cries while huddled together, were rendered silent by the herons,
whose heads rose up into the sky as they crowded together in flocks;
thus, at will, the clamor of the daughters of the Himavat mountains was silenced.
Having rendered their limbs bodiless, they roared like Bhairavas;
then, as if by invisible birds out of compassion, they were overtaken by withered *uddehakas*— like dust stirred up by agitated winds whose wings have been shaken off.
Shaken by the weapons of the mad [demons] and having abandoned their missiles on the battlefield,
they— those who create joy in the Nandana grove— danced, laughed,
and sang as the shower of spears arrived with its network of tinkling bells.
Stirred up by the wind of the Sālva’s arrows, it took on the appearance of a shower of raindrops.
The Kauntas, shattered by Śaivya’s weapons and struck down by his whirling spears, became like corpses;
they were seen being led to heaven as if they were Vidyādharas.
The cities of Pāṇḍu were shaken by the steady Vīrasenā, who possesses the nature of supporting the earth, through the mere thrill of her movement;
the Uddehakas were crushed by the Pañcanadas, the intoxicated Kāśis.
Like lotus-pools by wild elephants with tusks scarred by wounds from spears,
the hosts of Brahma and Vasanta were cut down by discuses and fell to the earth like flowering trees hewn by saws.
The Bhokkāṇa forest was mown down by axes driven from bellies;
as it fell, Bhadreśa, standing at its side, consumed it with the fire of his arrows.
Withered elephants, clinging to the saliva of their drivers, were [consumed].
They entered into dissolution, like fuel in a kindled fire, as long as they were conscious.
Having wandered through the whirlpools and pits of Trigarta, the Auṇḍras, who were like blades of grass,
fled with their heads shattered and entered the depths of Pātāla.
In the Māgadha army, which was as radiant as the ocean stirred by a gentle breeze,
the dull-witted Vandilas were submerged like old elephants in the mud. Then Jahnu restored consciousness to the Taṅgaṇas on the field of battle.
Like the heat [fading] from the fragility of flowers withered on the road,
the Kosalas, unable to endure the roar of the Pauravas, crossed over [the battle] like children,
having cast aside their showers of maces, spears, arrows, pikes, and double-edged swords.
With their limbs mangled by broad-headed arrows, they shone like coral trees made of stone upon a mountain, their forms drenched in streams of blood and thick with entrails as they fled;
while floods of iron shafts, their forms driven by winds of great weapons, [fell upon them].
Resplendent like swarms of bees, they whirled about as if in the ocean. The clouds, which were like rain-bearing monsoon clouds, dark as if filled with the fibers of reeds,
and the trees covered with arrow-leaves, roared and drifted swiftly along.

The forest kingdoms were worn away by speed; the creatures dwelling on the ground of the camps snapped asunder when violently dragged along, like fragile threads. On the chariots with wheels turned upward, their heads were buried and then raised up again.

Multitudes of people fell like clouds upon forested mountains. Having reached that dense forest of *sāla* and *tāla* trees, which was a thick thicket of human beings, there occurred the severing of arms, while the groves were filled with upright trunks [or: standing men].
The beauties of the Nandana grove, intoxicated by their youth,
rejoiced in the regions of the forests and gardens of Mount Meru, frequented by the most excellent heroes.
Meanwhile, that lofty forest-army shone forth with a tumultuous roar.
As long as they were not overcome by the opposing side with the power of the fire at the end of an aeon,
the Daśārṇas— whose weapons had been snatched away by the Hūṇas and who were joined by Piśācas—
fell upon Karṇa like young calves.
Their voices broken, they lost their luster through the power of the Tājikas and the Āji-janās, like lotuses in the Kāśī region withered by the force of a dried-up stream.
The ground was strewn with arrows, spears, double-edged swords, and mallets, as well as with girdles and armlets.
Fled and cast into the hell named Kārkoṭasthala,
the inhabitants of Kurukṣetra were surrounded by ascetics who fought with deceit;
like virtues overcome by the wicked, they clearly fell into a state of powerlessness.
The Drimi warriors, seizing the heads of the Vaṭadhānas in an instant with their crescent-headed arrows (*bhallas*),
quickly fled away like lotus plants whose stalks have been severed.
Thus did the Sārasvatas and Ādityas mutually achieve victory from beginning to end.

Like wise men in debate, they were neither agitated nor defeated. Like doors closed by those dwelling in low and mean dwellings, they attained supreme splendor, like fires extinguished by the lack of fuel.
How much of this can be described, even with a multitude of tongues, for it is a chaotic mass of blood?
Even Vāsuki is not capable of fully describing that excellent battle named Raṇavara.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Description of the Battle between the Two Nations" within the *Līlopākhyāna*.
The thirty-eighth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, while the battle was exceedingly tumultuous and crowded with warriors clapping their arms,
From beginning to end, amidst the unobstructed clamor of hard armor clashing,
as showers of stones were being carried along, flying up, and falling,
and as rivers rose from the tossing of weapons and rows of lotuses formed by fluttering banners; (3,38.1–2)
In the sky, as the rivers of arrows arrived and fell from afar— spraying the fire arising from the tips of their mutually clashing heads—
and as they surged with waves formed by the whirling circles of severed heads like lotuses, drifting along;
The ocean was filled with masses of weapons like the streams of the Mandākinī; the gates resounded with the wind, thick with clouds of pulverized armaments,
while the perfected ones (siddhas) had their limbs constantly burning, as if afflicted by the pain of *kapikacchu* bristles.

With his splendor and sweet form diminished by the loss of eight parts of his lifespan, he became emaciated like a hero who has lost his vigor from the wounds of weapons; his brilliance, once like a mass of blazing weapons, was now faded as his horses grew weary and his foremost troops were broken.
Along with Dineśa, the armies lost their former prowess.
Then, after the two commanders-in-chief had deliberated together with their ministers,
they dispatched messengers to one another saying, "Let the battle be withdrawn."
Then, due to exhaustion, all of them agreed upon the cessation of battle at that time, as their arrows, weapons, and prowess had become sluggish.
Thereupon, [the enemy] took up a position on the tip of the lofty banner of a great chariot-warrior.
One warrior mounted onto the two horses like Dhruva;
he brandished his silken garment, visible throughout the circle of all directions,
like a long ray of the moon in the sky, crying out, "Let the battle be concluded!"
Then the kettledrums resounded, their echoes filling the quarters of the sky,
like the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds at the subsiding of the great dissolution,
amidst the vast expanse of the firmament where the rivers of arrows and other weapons flowed.
The armies began to wither away like rivers in the autumn;
the movement of the trees that were the warriors' arms gradually became thin,
like the trembling of a forest at the end of an earthquake, or like the ocean when the wind has ceased.
The two armies proceeded to emerge from the forest of battle,
like a flood of water flowing in four directions from the single ocean at the time of universal dissolution,
agitated by the churning of Mount Mandara in the milk-ocean.

The army, with its whirlpools of tranquility, gradually attained a state of equanimity. In the course of a moment, the battlefield became as terrifying as the belly of Vikaṭodara, and like the ocean swallowed by Agastya, it was utterly empty.
It was filled with a continuous succession of corpses and a great lake of flowing blood;
it resembled a forest of *khillī* trees filled with the sounds of moaning and gurgling,
and it resounded with the roar of waves from the currents of a vast river of blood.
It was filled with men agitated by their own cries, lamentations, and calls for protection;
it was like a mountain torrent with streams of blood flowing from heaps of bodies, some dead and others half-dead;
and it struck terror with the throbbing of corpses still mounted on the backs of living men.
With fragments of clouds resting upon the peaks of the heaps of slain lordly elephants,
it possessed great forests formed by the clusters of shattered chariots;
with the force of flowing rivers of blood, it carried away chariots and elephants.
It was crowded with arrows, spears, double-edged swords, maces, clubs, and darts;
its ground was covered by saddles, saddle-cloths, armor, and mail,
while the bodies of infants were hidden beneath a multitude of banners, chowries, and silk streamers.
The wind whistled through the groves of quivers with their wide-open fastenings;
the Lord of the Dead lay asleep upon a bed of heaps of arrows like a thicket of palāśa leaves;
and the area was covered by the forest of his discus and bow, radiant with the light of his crown, necklaces, and armlets.
It was a place where long ropes of thick entrails were pulled by dogs, jackals, and birds;
it was jagged with the few remaining living beings shrieking in the field of blood;
and it was filled with the groaning of living men submerged in the mire of gore.
It possessed hundreds of rivers of terrible red blood flowing from the multitude of wooden beams that were its arms, while its hundreds of protruding eyes appeared like heaps of cowrie shells;
it was filled with half-dead men surrounded by their wailing kinsmen.
The space between them was filled with all manner of weapons, chariots, horses, and elephants, along with their saddles;

the sky was turned into a forest by the multitude of staff-like arms of dancing headless trunks, and the cavities of the nostrils were smeared with masses of the stench of rutting ichor, fat, and marrow.
Leaping horses and elephants were being struck down, their lives ebbing away; the drums were shattered by the blows of waves in the flowing rivers of blood.
Dead horses and elephants were carried along like sea-monsters in the surging streams of gore.
The wind was thick with blood spat out by the hosts of dying men;
its sound was marked by the gasping of those whose lives were nearly spent as they filled their mouths with arrows;
and it was reddened by the pressure of the wind carrying the stench of fat from the funeral pyres.
With headless trunks (kabandhas) trampled by the trunks of lordly elephants that were half-buried in the nostrils [of others],
and with headless trunks leaping up as elephants and horses fell down without riders;
with the sound of blood being stirred up from corpses abandoned by weeping kinsmen and friends.
There was a noble woman who had given up her life by thrusting a weapon into the throat of her deceased husband;
there, kinsmen stood with necks upturned, examining the bodies in the place where the corpses lay;
and it was crowded with men mingled together, being dragged along by the asses that carried the dead.
[He saw] a great river flowing with blood, rich with high surging waves, where the hair was the *śevala* weed, the lotus-faces were the whirlpools, and the dancing was the churning;
[he saw] his beloved sons, mother, deities, and wealth, remembered at the moment of death, as its name.
There was the cry of "Hā! Hā! Hī! Hī! uttered amidst the agony of having one's vital organs torn asunder;
half-dead men were frantic to pull away weapons stuck in their limbs;
and there were Hūnas, Taṅgas, and Tājikas crying out for those who had died in a foreign land.
A battle of chariots has begun between those who hate one another and are now dying;
they are unable to fight with their tusks, having forgotten the beloved deities of their homes. On the path of death, there is shameless flight resorted to by even the brave.
The ground was eager for movement, carried away by whirlpools of unexpected blood;
there was the sound of "huṃ" uttered from the pain of volleys of arrows piercing the vital organs,
and the sequence of Vetālas beginning their gyrations upon the heaps of headless trunks.
With its rows of beautiful lotuses consisting of fluttering banners, parasols, and chowries,
it scattered a crimson glow from the twilight toward the quarters of the sky like radiant red lotuses;
possessing whirlpools like the wheels of chariots, it was like an eighth ocean of blood.
Rich with masses of foam in the form of banners and possessing beautiful bubbles in the form of yak-tail whisks, the city—
with its chariots overturned— resembled a town destroyed by an earthquake,
like a vast forest strewn with trees uprooted by a cataclysmic wind.
It resembled the world scorched by the fire at the end of an eon, like the ocean drunk up by a sage;
it was like a region devastated by excessive rain, with its human inhabitants utterly exterminated;
it was filled with iron spears like black iron spikes and crowded with circles of *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles.
It had the appearance of the carcasses of intoxicated elephants, with its curved spears and mallets;
it was spread out like a grove of palm trees growing on a mountain peak,
and the lances rising like tall trees stood upon the banks of the flowing rivers of blood.
The sky was filled with trees of weapons entwined by serpents and covered in the flowers of arrows;
its atmosphere was webbed with clusters of entrails for girdles dragged out by herons;
and its lotus-pools were the lakes of blood where fallen banners served as its lotuses.
It was a place where friends were summoned by men submerged in blood-red mud;
it was gazed upon by terrified people emerging from the dwellings of the corpses of lordly elephants;
and its fierce headless trunks (kabandhas) were suspected to be trees whose creepers had been severed by weapons.
A river of blood flowing, with a multitude of boats in the form of elephant trunks and skull-bowls;
with masses of foam in the form of white garments shimmering in the currents of gore;
where men were swiftly cut down by death as they wandered about and fell.
Headless trunks fell here and there like headless demons;
the masses of visible wheels standing upright cut through the fleeing soldiers;
and there was the sound of the gurgling flow of blood mixed with the gasping of those half-dead.
The silver-winged birds were washed by streams of blood gushing from the openings of the veins;
it was perilous with the frantic *tāla* dances of *vetālas* rendered more violent by the *tāla* beat.
Fallen chariot timbers obstructed the path, while brave warriors remained hidden within the forest-like interior of the wreckage.
It struck terror into the chariots of the soldiers stationed within;
its mouth was filled with blood-mud, and it bore the groaning corpses of those barely alive;
dogs and crows were seen there, their necks craned in agony as they watched those who were half-alive.
It was agitated by the clamor of battle among fierce carnivores vying for a single piece of meat;
it was crowded with immortal-like warriors and flesh-eating beasts contending in the struggle for that same morsel.
Rivers of blood surged forth, flowing from the severed necks of countless horses, elephants, men, lords, and chariots that had been overturned.
That battlefield became a garden of Death, with its unwithered creepers of weapons; like the entire world overturned at the end of an aeon, it stood together with its mountains.
The Chapter on the Description of the Battle, titled "The Narrative of Līlā."
The twenty-ninth canto:
Vasiṣṭha said—
Then, like a hero flushed with blood, the sun set by the power of time.

His majesty, whose splendor had long been fading, was cast into the ocean. At that moment, as the sun’s head was severed from the day, the streak of twilight— reflected in the mirror of the sky, which possessed the crimson glow of blood from the battle— suddenly arose.

From the earth, the netherworld, the sky, and all directions, masses of darkness arrived like the surging waters of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution, resembling circles of *vetālas*. It was seen that the head of the great serpent-king of the day had been severed by the sword of gloom.
The sky was strewn with the pearls of clusters of stars, reddened by the glow of twilight.
In lakes devoid of life and blinded by darkness, and lacking their usual flavor,
the lotuses closed up like the hearts of the dead.
In an instant, the birds fell asleep with their wings closed and their necks tucked into their armpits within their nests,
like arrows lodged in every limb; meanwhile,
the rows of night-lotuses were graced by the approaching light of the moon.
Her heart became radiant, like the goddesses of fortune among the ranks of heroes;
that lotus-pond, consisting of blood-water and protected by arrows as its concealed bees,
became like the battlefield, with her lotus-face now shrunken.
Above was the lake of the sky, adorned with the lilies of the stars;
below was the water of the firmament, shimmering with lilies that were the stars.
Even the darknesses, whose effects had not yet been absorbed, and all living beings were fully present.
Like various kinds of flesh spread out in every direction,
the battlefield became crowded with throngs of singing *vetāla* spirits,
where *kaṅka* and *kākolaka* crows sported upon the throats of rattling skeletons.
Resplendent with the stars of the flames from the funeral pyres of chariot wood,

it was a fire consisting of fat and flesh, crackling with the sounds of "paca-paca-paca," where the logs of corpses were clearly bursting apart and the torches rolled about upon the heaps of the pyre.
It was obscured by water-sports commenced by female Vetālas;
it was intense with the clamor of dogs, crows, Yakṣas, and Vetālas;
and through the gathering of spirits, it resembled a forest where birds are taking flight.
The *ḍākinīs* were preoccupied with extracting blood, flesh, fat, and marrow;
the *piśācas* had their lips dripping with chewed blood, fat, and flesh;
and in the midst of the assembly, a multitude of blood-stained corpses was laid bare by the light of the funeral pyres.
It was filled with great corpses being carried away by jackals,
its interior made terrifying by circles of fierce Kumbhāṇḍas engaged in wild dancing;
it ended with the "chamacchami" sound of lamentation, and possessed clouds of fat, blood, and tears.
It was filled with the forms of land-dwelling beings carried along by the swift currents of flowing rivers of blood;
it was crowded with *vetālas* and filled with crows agitated by the dragging of skeletons;
and within it were young *vetālas* sleeping in the chests formed by the bellies of dead elephants.
He saw a rākṣasa stationed at a secluded spot beneath a solitary tree, engaged in drinking games;
there was a tumultuous quarrel among intoxicated vetālas, blazing with funeral pyres and firebrands,
and a wind fragrant with the scent of flowing blood and fat.
In the jeweled caskets, there was the tumultuous clamor of the *vegaraṇa* and *duṭaruṭa* birds;
it was filled with the joyful yakṣas who were greedy for the taste of half-cooked corpses;
and there flew birds perched upon the limbs of beautiful women from Tuṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, and Aṅga.
It bore the appearance of flames facing outward like the falling of stars;
it was beautiful with blood amidst the exultant spirits of falling *vetālas*,
while the throngs of *yoginīs* sang nearby as they were overheard by the *piśācas*.
The playing of musical instruments was mostly provided by great lutes with entrails stretched out for strings;
men who had become female *piśācīs* after their *piśāca*-nature had been displaced by latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
and brave warriors who were half-dead from the unprecedented terror caused by the sight of the *rūpikās*.
In some places, it was like a battlefield where days were being raised up by vetālas and rākṣasas;
in others, night-stalkers were terrified by the hides falling from the shoulders of those wearing donkey-skins,
while the sky was crowded with throngs of previously unseen hordes of bhūtas.
It was a heap of corpses scattered by the glances of hungry yakṣas who were watching for their prey, while kings were being forcibly carried off as they died;
it was further marked by the severed fragments of those moving about at night, mangled by the flames from the fire in Śivā’s mouth.
It was as if a cluster of *aśoka* flowers had blossomed all around;
young *vetālas* were clinging restlessly to the necks of headless trunks (*kabandhas*),
while *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, *piśācas*, and *ajikas* hurled firebrands into the sky.
The sky was filled with a mass of darkness resembling a mountain thicket or a cave, like a vast expanse of water;
it was as if the world were a door-panel being shaken by the apocalyptic winds agitated by the violent onset of elemental beings.
This concludes the chapter titled "Description of the Battlefield at Night, Turbulent with Night-Rangers," from the *Līlopākhyāna*.
The fortieth canto:
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, on the battlefield that had become long-terrible through the conduct of the night-stalkers,
While the Vetālas were uttering their terrifying shrieks with loud clamor,
the armies in the sky, acting as spectators, departed as they had come; and the kings, along with their chariots and other vehicles, rested as it were in their own abodes.
On the battlefield, where people appeared like the waters of a great lake,

while the conduct of men remained as fixed as the day and the movements of women were as dark as night; in the house at night, where the walls were clearly visible through the mass of darkness that could be grasped by the hand— *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* 3.40.3.
While the host of spirits danced with hearts leaping in the celebration of their gain,
and while the multitude of directions lay sealed in sleep, moving in silent stillness,
the noble-souled lord of Līlā appeared as if somewhat dejected in mind.
Having quickly deliberated upon the morning duties with his ministers, who were experts in counsel,
he [lay] upon a bed as cool as snow, shaped like a long crescent moon,
in a bedchamber resembling the rising of the moon, within a cool inner chamber.
For a moment he fell asleep, his lotus-eyes closed;
then those two women, leaving that sky, entered that house through its openings like a gust of wind entering a lotus bud.
Rāma said:
O best among those who know speech, O Lord, how does this gross body, which is merely this much in size, enter through an opening as thin as a thread?
Vasiṣṭha:
O sinless one, he whose deluded mind perceives this body as merely material cannot pass through the subtle aperture.

It is experienced that the cognition "I am obstructed by this" or "I do not sink here" is one that experiences what has already been experienced. He by whom the first half [of the experience] was previously experienced, thinking "I am going," is the agent of that action.
How does one become conscious of being intent on departing for the other world?
Water does not rise upward, nor does fire go downward;
in whatever manner consciousness has set forth, it remains exactly so.
For one seated in the shade, how could there be experiences of heat?
An object perceived by one consciousness is not experienced by another.
In whatever manner consciousness has arisen, it remains established in that very same way.
By supreme effort, one is led again to another state:
the cognition of a snake regarding a rope is forcibly turned back by the cognition of its unreality;
otherwise, however, this [cognition] remains exactly as it was.
As is consciousness, so is the mind; as is the mind, so is one's striving.
This is well-established even for a child; who does not experience it?
Furthermore, that which has the form of a person in a dream or a mental construction—
Having the form of mere space, how and by what could it be obstructed?
For the body of everything indeed consists of mind alone;
yet, because of its nature as experience, it seems to go somewhere from within the heart.
For him, the setting and rising occur exactly as desired;
at the initial creation, they arise from inherent nature, while subsequently there is the contemplation of duality and unity.
The space of the mind, the space of consciousness, and the third, the [outer] space—these three are one.
Know that these three are indeed one, by virtue of their inseparable nature.
Know this to be the mind-body (*citta-śarīra*), which arises as all-pervading,
just as it arises according to the nature of its perception and according to the arising of its perception.
It dwells within a mote of dust, it is led into the belly of the sky;
it dissolves within the sheaths of sprouts and turns into sap in the leaf.
It surges as a wave upon the water and dances within the heart of a stone.
Becoming a cloud, he rains; becoming solid stone, he remains stationary.
He travels at will through the sky and even into the bellies of mountains.
Having the body of infinite space, he then assumes the state of a subtle atom.

He becomes the support for the best of mountains, with his seat firmly fixed at the summit of the sky; he possesses excellent body-hair both within and without his body. He becomes space itself and assumes millions of lotus-seated abodes.
Non-different from its own self, like the formation of whirlpools in the ocean,
that [Self], at the beginning of creation, possesses a body of consciousness;
having become the Great One whose nature is space, it perceives itself as having attained the state of primordial matter (prakṛti).
Having realized that non-existence itself is the state of being obstructed, it arises as if it were real,
just as a man in a dream-delusion thinks, "I am the son of a barren woman.
Rāma said:
"What is this mind? Or what does it not become?
How is it that from such a form it does not become something else, or even from a moment?
Vasiṣṭha replied:

Each individual mind possesses such power; thus, the delusions of the world arise separately for each momentary state of consciousness. Through their association with the world—whether for a moment or an eon—they emerge and dissolve.

For some it occurs in the blink of an eye, for others after a kalpa; hear that sequence. Immediately after death and the great delusion, this state arises—either in an instant or after a long time; hear now this sequence regarding that.

The fainting that consists of death and so forth is experienced by each individual; know this, O wise one, to be the very night of the great dissolution. At its end, everyone brings forth a creation individually.
Just as the mountain-like fluctuations of innate dreams and mental constructs [arise],
so too at the end of the night of the great dissolution, the Virāj-self, whose body is mind,
expands this universe; in the same way, each individual does so immediately after death.
Rāma:
Just as the creation after death is experienced through memory, so does the Virāj experience it; therefore, the universe is not without a cause.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, during the great dissolution, all beings, including Hari, Hara, and the others, attain the state of disembodied liberation; what possibility, then, is there for memory?
One whose self is awakened like ours is indeed necessarily liberated;
how then could Brahmā and others be unliberated and bodiless?
For those living beings who exist at present, in their deaths and births...

In this world, memory becomes the cause [of rebirth] due to the absence of liberation. For that which, at the end of death and fainting, appears as if awakening within the individual soul (jīva), yet remains unawakened— that is designated as Pradhāna.
That space is said to be *prakṛti*, and that is the unmanifest (*avyakta*), both insentient and sentient.
This is the sequence for the arising of existence, due to both worldly involvement and the lack of recollection [of the Self].
For when it becomes oriented toward awakening, that which is great (*mahat*) becomes fully awakened.
Then, from the void (ākāśa), the subtle elements, space, time, action, the primary elements, and so forth arise.
That very [void], when swollen and awakened, becomes the fivefold sense-faculties.
That same [void] perceives the body; this is the *ātivāhika* (subtle) body.
Through the cognition of long duration, this very [mind] of yours, thickened by conceptualization,
brings about the perception of materiality;
thereafter, the divisions of space and time remain as its substratum.
Like the act of vibration in the wind even before it has arisen,
this delusion of the world has thus come to increase in vain;
though experienced by oneself, it is composed of unreality, like union with a woman in a dream.
At the very moment a living being dies, he immediately perceives there itself this entire expanse of the world situated in such a manner.

Like space itself, the living being (*jīva*), whose nature is space, experiences the delusion "I am the world," appearing as if it has become a self-possessing entity; though it is of the nature of space, it perceives the world as variegated with cities, towns, mountains, suns, and clusters of stars. *Maitrāyaṇīya Upaniṣad* 3.40.48.
It is a hollow place of distress caused by old age, death, and disease;
it is characterized by the agitation of existence and non-existence, and is both gross and subtle, moving and unmoving;
it includes the mountains, heavens, earth, rivers, the directions, days, nights, kalpas, and their destructions and arisings.
"I was born here by this father"—thus one forms a firm conviction;
"this is my mother, this is my wealth"—thus latent impressions arise;
and "this is my merit and this my demerit"—thus conceptual constructions are made.
"I was a child, but today I am young"— thus rejoicing in his heart,
the forest grove of saṃsāra appeared to each person as if blossoming with stars and possessing leaves as flickering as dark clouds.

Within the seed of the lotus of the mind, the sprout of experience lies hidden.
Wherever this living soul dies, there it instantly perceives [the world] in this manner,
as each vast multitude of worlds arises in abundance.
Tens of millions of visions of Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, the Maruts, Viṣṇu,
and Vivasvat have reached the sight of Meru, the oceans, the circles, the islands, and other worlds;
these visions have passed, will pass, and are passing away within that which is of imperishable form.
Who is capable of counting those [qualities] in the Brahman, which is richly augmented?
Thus, the universe consisting of walls does not exist at all apart from mental construction; and since mental construction is itself like space, reflect upon that now.
That which is the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) is remembered as the supreme;
the act of thinking is the space of consciousness, and that alone is the supreme state.
Just as a whirlpool is merely water and no separate entity called a "whirlpool" exists as a reality, so it is with this.
Having seen it, one remains as if seeing the visible; yet that visible object does not exist as a real entity.
That which is the manifestation of the space of consciousness within the elemental ether—like the light of a gem—is this world, appearing as a jewel of manifold forms, like a hollow in the sky.
The word "world" exists as the object of my intellect as the supreme state;
however, the object of your intellect does not exist at all, nor do the words "you" and "I.
Therefore, Līlā and Sarasvatī remain with bodies of ether.
O all-pervading one, supremely pure, omnipresent, unobstructed, and sinless!
Wherever you may be in that space, just as the sky extends according to desire,
by that [power] you two have brought about your rising and have taken up residence in that house.
The sky of consciousness exists everywhere; within it, its perception, conceptualization, and expansive reflection occur.
They say that this body here is merely *ativāhika* (transmigratory), being indeed wall-less. Tell me, how, like what, and what could possibly obstruct it?
This concludes the chapter titled "The Experience of Transmigration Immediately Following Death" from the *Līlopākhyāna*.
The forty-first canto:
When those two goddesses had entered, that lotus-palace became beautiful,
its interior radiant and white with the light of the rising of two moons.
By its power, the battlefield— where the king was asleep and others were overcome by slumber— became a garden of fortune and delight, with gentle breezes from the soft and stainless *mandāra* trees,
and with the pain of wounds driven away.
Like a forest in full bloom during spring, or like a lotus at dawn;
refreshed by the floods of light from their bodies, which were as cool as the flow of moonlight,
he woke up as if sprinkled with nectar by the king.
He beheld two celestial nymphs resting upon two seats,
appearing like two risen moons nestled upon the two peaks of Mount Meru.
Reflecting for a moment as if in a trance, the king’s mind was filled with wonder.
He rose from his bed like the wielder of the discus and mace rising from the serpent Śeṣa; with his hanging garlands, necklaces, and excellent garments firmly adjusted,
he took up a handful of flowers like a cluster of blossoms upon a full-blown tree.
Emerging from within the fold of his own garment at the place where it was draped,
he sat upon the ground in the bound lotus posture and, bowing low, spoke these words:
"Victory to you, O moonlight for the burning affliction of the world's existential instability!"
"O two Goddesses, possessing the radiance of the sun that dispels both external and internal darkness!
Having spoken thus to them, he offered a handful of flowers at their feet,
just as a tree on a riverbank casts its blossoms upon the lotuses of a pair of female elephants.
Then, in order to explain Līlā’s birth as a king, the Sovereign Goddess Sarasvatī awakened the minister standing at her side through her resolve.
Having woken up and seen the two apsarases, he bowed and offered a handful of flowers.
Having abandoned them at their feet, he entered before them, bowing low.

The queen said, "O King, who are you? Whose son are you? When were you born here? Having heard these words, the minister spoke this speech: MU_3,41.12–13: "Having abandoned them at their feet, he entered before them, bowing low. The queen said, 'O King, who are you? Whose son are you? When were you born here? Having heard this, the minister spoke these words."
O Goddesses, by your grace, I am now able to speak even before you;
therefore, hear this account of the birth of my lord.
There was once a lotus-eyed king born of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
The illustrious one named Kuṇḍaratha covered the earth with the shadow of his arms.
He had a son named Bhadraratha, whose face was like the moon;
his son was Viśvaratha, and his son was Bṛhadratha.
His son was Sindhuratha; his son was Śailaratha;
his son was Kāmaratha; his son was Mahāratha;
his son was Viṣṇuratha; and his son was Kalāratha.
His son was Sūryaratha, and his son was Nabhoratha. This is our lord; he is the son of Pūrṇāmaladyuti, whose chariot is filled with nectar, like the moon from the Ocean of Milk.
Through great accumulations of merit, he was born to his mother Sumitrā as one renowned by the name Vidūratha, like a second Guha born of Gaurī;
when he was ten years old, his father gave him the kingdom and departed for the forest.
From that time forth, he has protected the surface of the earth according to righteousness.
Today, when the tree of our good deeds has borne fruit, we two goddesses— whose sight was difficult to obtain even through hundreds of hardships of long penance— have come together.
"Thus this lord of the earth, known as Vidūratha,
has today attained supreme purification through your grace.
When the minister had spoken thus and remained silent, the king likewise [fell silent].
While he stood on the ground with palms joined, face bowed, and seated in the lotus posture,
O King, Sarasvatī touched him on the head with her hand as she spoke: "Remember this former birth of your own through discernment."
Then the darkness of illusion within the heart came to an end;
and through the touch of pure cognition, the heart became expanded.
He remembered his former history as if it were still shimmering within him.
Having understood that his sovereignty over another body was merely the unfolding of playful sport,
and having realized that the entire course of his perceptions was the manifestation of a divine play,
he became like one being carried away upon the ocean, lost to himself.

He said to himself: "Alas! This pervasive illusion in the cycle of existence has now been fully understood by me here through the grace of the two Goddesses. O Goddesses, what indeed is this—that for me, though dead, a single day has passed?"
Seventy years of life have passed away here today.
I remember my many past deeds; I remember my great-grandfather;
I remember childhood, youth, and the circle of friends and kinsmen.
The formal announcement:
O King, immediately after the fainting caused by the great delusion of death, once that interval between worlds had passed, at that very moment— MU_3,41.32.
Now, in this very house, you will not recognize it; therefore, I shall tell you:
this royal pavilion is indeed situated within the void inside that house of the Brahmin from the mountain village.
Within that [ether], this world-house appears individually;
indeed, by my grace, your life-spirit (jīva) resides within the house of a Brahmin.
Right there is his earthly surface, and within that, his own pavilion.
And within that very house is this circle of saṃsāra;
right there, your own house stands, slow in its construction.
And right there, within your mind—which is as pure as the clear sky—[it exists].
"This pervasive delusion of worldly convention has come to appear as such.
Vidūratha said:
"Just as this birth is mine, so too is the Ikṣvāku lineage mine."
"These were my grandfathers, bearing these very names, who existed before me. Having been born as a child, when I was ten years old,
my father became a wandering mendicant and departed for the forest after consecrating me here in this kingdom."
Then, having accomplished the conquest of the quarters and having made my kingdom free from thorns,
I shall protect the earth with these ministers and citizens,
performing the sequence of sacrificial rites and protecting my subjects in accordance with dharma.
Seventy years of my life have passed away. This enemy force has arrived for a fierce conflict; having fought this battle, I have come home as I am now situated.
"These two goddesses have arrived at my home;
I shall worship them both, for when deities are worshipped, they grant one's own desired object. Of these two, this one [here] bestows knowledge and the recollection of past lives."
Here, the Goddess has bestowed [upon me] what is like the blossoming of a lotus.
Now I have accomplished my purpose; I am born, freed from doubt.
I am stilled, I am fully extinguished, and I abide in absolute bliss.
Sarasvatī said:
Thus, this delusion of yours has expanded with great agitation,
abounding in various foods and pastimes, and wandering through other worlds.
At the very moment when you previously met with death,
this very intuition arose spontaneously within your heart;
just as one abandons a single whirlpool and takes up another.
Just as the swift current of a river flows in various streams, so too does yours; just as one whirlpool, merging with another, continues to revolve,
so too does the splendor of creation sometimes increase, both mixed and unmixed.
At that moment of death, this insight occurred to you:
"This net, though unreal in nature, appears as if real within the sphere of consciousness;
just as within a moment of dream, there occurs the succession of a hundred years."
Just as death occurs again after life within a creation of one's own imagination;
just as walls, pavilions, and enclosures appear in a city of the Gandharvas;
and just as trees and mountains seem to move during the turbulence of a ship's voyage.
Just as cities and mountains dance during the agitation of one's own elements,
and just as the cutting off of one's own head appears in a dream,
so too is this mature delusion here entirely false, though it manifests in an expansive form.
In reality, however, you have never been born, nor have you ever died;
you are of the nature of pure consciousness and abide peacefully within the Self.
You perceive all this as if seeing it, yet you do not perceive anything at all.
By virtue of being the self of all, you shine eternally within yourself by means of yourself—
noble like a great jewel and radiant like light.
In reality, however, this is not the surface of the earth, nor are you this [person].
These mountains are not villages, nor am I here, nor indeed are we; yet,
within the small pavilion of the Brahmin of this mountain village,
that entire world— rich with the kingdom of King Līlāpati— shines forth in its splendor.
Within that, the pavilion of the capital city of Līlā, adorned in form,
shines in the midst of the sky; within its belly is this vast universe of yours,
in which world we stand here inside a house.
Thus, for those pavilions, the sky is nothing but pure space.
Within those pavilion-regions, there is no earth and no city;
nor are there forests, nor mountain ranges, nor clouds, rivers, or oceans.
Only people dwell there in that utterly empty house;
they see neither the world, nor kings, nor even mountains.
Vidūratha:
"If this is so, O Goddess, how is it that these followers of mine here exist as complete beings by their own nature? Are they not themselves possessed of a self?
The world appears like the objects of a dream; therein, in that dream, there are new mountains."
"Tell me, how could they exist when the self exists, or how could they not exist?
The Goddess replied:
"O King, among those who have known what is to be known and whose sole nature is pure awakening,"
This world, within those whose nature is the sky of consciousness, possesses no real form whatsoever.
How indeed could the delusion of a world appear to one whose self is pure awakening?
Once the delusion of a snake in a rope has ceased, how could the delusion of a snake arise again?
When non-existence is fully understood, how can there be existence in the delusion of the world?
Once the water of a mirage is recognized [as such], how can there again be the notion of water?
When one's own death in a dream is recognized during the time of dreaming, how can there be [fear]?
In one's own dream, the fear of death within a dream arises as if it were [the fear of] immortality itself.
For the awakened one— who is pure, whose splendor is like the autumnal sky, who is clear and bright, and whose disposition is profound—
the notions of "I" and "the world," which are devoid of the meaning of false words, are merely what is expressed by the speech of a young woman.
Vālmīki:
When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites;
the assembly, having offered salutations, departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
The forty-second canto, titled "An Examination of Delusion," from the *Līlopākhyāna*:
He who is dull-witted and foolish, and has not established himself in the expansive state—
This world belongs to him who possesses the essence of the diamond; though non-existent, it appears as existent.
Just as a ghost causes suffering to a child until his death, so does this world appear in the form of reality to the deluded mind, though it is utterly non-existent.
Just as a mirage of water causes delusion for deer,
so too does this world appear real to those of deluded intellect, though it is utterly unreal.
Just as the death of a creature in a dream appears real despite being unreal, so is this world.
Thus this world appears to those of poor discernment as incapable of performing purposeful action; just as for one who is untrained, there is only the cognition of a bracelet in gold or base metal,
and not even the slightest thought of it being gold.
Just as for an ignorant person there is the conceptualization of houses, mountains, and lordly elephants,
