so too this perception of the visible exists, but it is not the vision of ultimate reality.
Just as in the sky there appear rows of pearls, peacock feathers, hair-tufts, and floating hairs, [so does this world appear].

Just as that which is unreal attains the state of reality, so too does this world appear to those of false vision. Know this entire universe to be a long dream, joined with the sense of "I" and so forth;
hear now how others here are real, just like the people in a dream.

There exists the all-pervading, tranquil, solid ultimate reality, pure, whose body is pure consciousness beyond thought— an expansive supreme space. It is all-encompassing, omnipotent, everything itself, and the self of all.
In whatever place and in whatever manner it arises, it indeed remains exactly so in that very place. Therefore, those inhabitants of the city whom the observer perceives in the dream-city—
those men truly become men for him in an instant.
That which is the seer’s nature of consciousness (citsvarūpa) resides within the space of the dream; for it is conceived as "I am a man by means of this consciousness of the dream-space.
By virtue of its identity with the side of consciousness, it is perceived as being merely a man.
Therefore, by means of these two perspectives, the reality of both is established.
Rāma said: "O Sage, when those dream-men in your dream are not real, [how can they be otherwise]?"
Tell me, what fault could there be in that which has as its very body mere illusion?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
In a dream, those residing in another city are in fact real in nature.
In this matter, hear from me the authority: it is perception alone, and nothing else.
At the beginning of creation, the Self-born shines forth as one whose nature is experience, appearing like a dream;
the world is merely a portion of his volition, and thus it is indeed like a dream.
In this way, this entire universe is a dream; therein, you are real to me.
Just as you are, so are others; likewise, for men, a dream is a dream within a dream.
If these inhabitants of the city in the dream were not real, [then how could they appear so?]
Therefore, in this case as well, even you, sir, are not real to me in that form [of the dream], just as I am not real to you;
yet, just as I am the real self for you, so too are you the real self for me.
Such a mutual establishment occurs in the perception of dreams and in the cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
"Just as I am real to you within this vast dream of saṃsāra, so too are you real to me in all dreams; such is the sequence. Rāma said:

"O Blessed One, it is my view that just as that dream-city remains exactly as it was seen by the dreamer while he is awake— because it possesses the nature of reality— it is so with this world. Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus it is exactly so; because of its reality, it remains just as it is, like a city in a dream.
Even for one who has awakened from sleep, it appears with the clear form of space to the dreamer.
Let this matter rest for now—this which you consider to be "waking."
Know that this is merely a dream within, filling out space, time, and so forth.
Thus all this appears; it is not real, yet it stands as if real.
Though it is utterly false, it delights the mind, like union with a woman in a dream.
Everything exists everywhere, both inside and outside the body;
whatever consciousness perceives in a certain way, it sees exactly in that way.
Just as when one sees the wealth contained within a treasury, it is thereby obtained.
"Likewise, everything that is perceived exists within the sky of consciousness.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Immediately thereafter, the goddess Jñapti spoke these words to Vidūratha:
Having made it beautiful with the sprouts of discernment through the sprinkling of the nectar of awakening—
Sarasvatī said:
"Therefore, O King, you have been described in this manner for the sake of the narrative."
"May it be well with you; we shall depart, having seen the views illustrated by these examples.
Thus was it spoken by Sarasvatī in a voice of sweet syllables. Vasiṣṭha said: [Thus].
The wise King Vidūratha spoke these words:
"O Goddess, even my sight of you would not be in vain when I am a petitioner;
how much more so will it be for you, who bestows such great fruit?"
"O Goddess, having cast off this body from here, I shall go henceforth to another world, as one goes from one dream to another;
O Mother, quickly give instructions to me, who have approached you for refuge."
Disdain toward a devotee does not become those who grant boons.
"Let this minister and this maiden come to the very place where I go; have mercy on me, for she is but a child. (MU 3.42.32–33)
Sarasvatī said:
"Come, rule the kingdom, which is as beautiful as the graceful movements of its limbs; enjoy it without hesitation in this excellent realm of your previous birth.
Know this: we have never at any time seen the rejection of a supplicant's desire."
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the forty-third canto, titled "The Determination of the Reality of the Dream-Man," Sarasvatī said:
"O King, you must now die in this excellent battle;
that former kingdom of yours is to be regained, and this is evident even to me. [It shall be restored] by the princess, by the minister, and by you to the former city."
One must return when it has become a corpse; that body must be reached.
We two shall go as we came, and you too in the form of the wind.
That place must be visited by the maiden and by the minister as well.
The gait of a horse is one thing, the gait of a donkey or a camel another,
and the gait of an elephant with temples moistened by rut is yet another.
While this conversation was thus proceeding between the two who spoke so sweetly to one another—
Then, having entered in great agitation, a man stood above and said: "O Lord,
a great enemy force has arrived, raining down arrows, discuses, swords, maces, and clubs, like a surging, single vast ocean."
Resembling a boulder from the Kulācala mountains tossed by the winds at the end of an aeon,
he released showers of maces, spears, and *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons like rain.
A fire, having caught hold of the city which resembled a mountain, pervaded the horizons.
With crackling and crashing sounds, he causes the highest cities to fall;
great mountains of smoke, resembling jars of clouds at the end of an eon,
begin to rise forcefully into the sky like Garuḍas.
Vasiṣṭha:
While the man was speaking thus with harsh cries in agitation,
a great clamor arose outside, filling all the quarters of space.
Of bows whose ends were drawn back with force and which rained down arrows;
of great, swift, and utterly intoxicated elephants;
and of blazing fires crackling with loud pops as they leaped about within the city.
With the great tumultuous cries of the city folk whose wives had been consumed by fire,
with the harsh "ṣvak-kāra" sounds of fragments of fire leaping across,
and with the "dhvaga-dhvagi" roar of the blazing flames as they flickered and quivered.
Then, from the window, the two queens, the minister,
and King Vidūratha beheld at the dead of night that great city with its towers raised high,
resembling the force of a single full ocean agitated by the winds of universal dissolution.
It was filled by the force of the enemy, like a surging mass of clouds;
it was being consumed by great networks of flames that filled the sky, shining like mountains whose bodies were melting in the fire at the end of an eon.
With the fierce, tumultuous clamor of the thundering and terrifying roar of great clouds graspable by the fist, and with the powerful mutterings of the mantra-reciters,
the sky was shrouded by smoke-clouds resembling the Puṣkarāvarta storm.
The sky was rendered continuous by masses of flames resembling soaring golden clouds; it was made shimmering by the stars that were fragments of glowing embers drifting through it,
and it was agitated by the masses of flames blazing from the multitude of bodies dwelling within one another.
The hollows of the clouds were filled with embers shaken from the falling cities whose armies had been destroyed;
the fierce roar [of the battle] scorched the multitude of people with its harsh cries;
and the sky was rendered without interval by sparks of fire like iron arrows.
It was a place where heaps of burnt cities were being tossed about by a vast mass of blazing fire-tongues; where fierce, noble warriors were crushed by the clashing of trumpeting herds of elephants;
and where great wealth was strewn along the paths as fleeing thieves were cut down.
Men and women wail piteously as they fall upon heaps of glowing coals;
burning wood rolls about with a crackling *caṭacaṭā* sound;
and the sky is filled with hundreds of suns in the form of vast, whirling circles of firebrands.
The entire surface of the earth was strewn with heaps of glowing coals;
it resounded with the crackling of burning firewood and the whistling of blazing flames,
while all the buffaloes wept and wailed as they cried out in distress at the perishing creatures.
The fire’s great crest was active in its endeavor to swallow everything, having snatched away the food from the mouths of the king’s women and elders who were resting upon the floor-cloths;
the house resounded with the crackling of the fire as it consumed the hard fuel of ladles, spoons, and other utensils.

Then King Vidūratha heard there the cries of the warriors as they were being consumed by fire— cries that expressed a longing for fuel released from the fire of food that is the sustenance of infinite beings, even as they watched and rushed forward.
Alas! The intoxicated wind stands blowing down the trees that were like houses of glowing coals, where birds were chirping and fire was hidden;
alas! The edge of the sword, as cold as frost, [cuts] into the bodies of the elephants.
The wise words of insight cling to the minds of the great, just as [flames] cling to the grass of a young woman’s braid.
Alas, father! The arrows, like heaps of dry leaves fanned by the fire of heroes, blaze forth as they strike the grass of a young woman’s tresses.
This long, wavy river of smoke, turning in eddies and flowing upward,
appears to me as it rushes toward the celestial Gaṅgā;
this river of smoke moves upward, carrying embers and wood.
It blinds the inhabitants of the celestial palaces; behold, it is like a mass of fire-sparks and bubbles.
His mother, father, brother, son-in-law, grandson, and daughter have been consumed by fire in this house; now, having burnt them, it seeks its end.
"Alas, alas! Go quickly, O man, from this house of burning coals, which has begun to fall like the peak of Mount Sumeru!
Oh, the arrows, stones, spears, lances, darts, swords, and other weapons!"
Like moths entering a mass of twilight clouds, streams of weapons enter the fire; oh, they all enter it from the sky like floods of water from the ocean entering the blazing submarine fire.
The great clouds smoke amidst millions of crests of flames;
even the lush [forests] wither like the hearts of the passionate.
These rows of trees are being treated by the elephants as if they were angry hitching-posts.
With loud *kaṭakaṭa* cracking sounds and accompanied by shrieks of distress,
the house-trees— whose beauty of flowers, fruits, branches, and fragrance has been scorched— are cast down;
having lost all their possessions to the flames, they have fallen into a state of wretchedness like householders whose entire wealth has been consumed.
Children, deprived of their parents, blinded by rows of darkness,
are struck down and killed on the streets by the falling of walls as they scramble over their limbs; alas,
like elephants routed at the front of a battle by one whose sight has been destroyed!
The bitter cries of those carrying loads of burning coals:
"Alas, what misery! A stone from a machine has fallen upon a man like a thunderbolt, while his shoulder is pierced by a sword and his firm torch is extinguished."
"Alas! A terrible battle has begun here, obstructing the path, waged by agitated cows, horses, buffaloes, goats, camels, donkeys, jackals, and wolves;
with the flapping sounds of cloths and the wind fanning the rows of blazing flames."
The wailing women go forth like ponds filled with land-lotuses;
behold, the flickering flames lick the creepers of their tresses, making them resemble female serpents with the luster of *aśoka* flowers, while the flames act like young elephants.

Alas, alas! Upon the lashes of the fawn-eyed woman’s thickly-eyelashed eyes, the flame of the fire rests as if upon the tips of blades of *kuśa* grass. Even while being consumed by fire, a man does not depart without his wife.
Alas! How difficult it is for living beings to sever the snares of affection!
Like an elephant, with blazing charcoal trees violently torn apart by its fury, the beast, in its rage, churns up a lake whose lotuses have been scorched, tossing the flowers about.
Having reached the region of the clouds, which is filled with flickering streaks of firebrands and lightning,
the smoke pours down a shower of blazing embers and clusters of iron arrows.
Here, the smoke, accompanied by sparkling sparks of fire, moves in the form of whirlpools.
Stationed in the sky, wearing a floral crest (*āpīḍa*), he appeared like a flood of jewels in the atmosphere.
The white garment shone with the brilliance of the tips of his flaming crests,
like a distressing mark of saffron applied for the festival of Death.
"Alas! How terrible is this enmity that has arisen, devoid of all moral conduct!
Even the noble wives of kings are being carried off by excellent heroes with uplifted weapons—women who used to scatter garlands of trembling flowers along the royal path."
With their braided hair half-burnt and the garments on their chests scattered;
with the regions of their hips and loins barely visible through their fluttering clothes;
with their ruby bracelets falling off as they rolled across the circle of the earth.
Pure pearls were scattered from the lattices of broken necklaces;
the golden luster rising from their breasts, hips, and sides was seen and unseen;
and the roar of battle was dulled by the harsh wailing of female ospreys.
Their consciousness was shattered by showers of falling tears like volleys of iron arrows;
their garments were soaked and clung to them by the mud of blood and the water of their tears,
as they were being led away by force by men who had placed their arms around their shoulders.
With their eyes fixed upon the calamity, crying out, "Who indeed might be our protector?",
they made the soldiers weep as if with falling blue lotuses;
[the soldiers] whose thighs were like clusters of lotus stalks, tender and exceedingly pure.
Visible against the surface of the clear sky like lotuses in the celestial waters,
with their garlands, garments, ornaments, and unguents swaying, and with the creepers of their eyebrows moving over faces agitated by jealousy,
they appeared like royal fortunes emerged from the ocean of desire, which was being stirred without restraint by the beauty of bliss.
The forty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of the Burning by Fire" in the Narrative of Līlā; Vasiṣṭha said:
In the meantime, the queen, intoxicated by her youth,
entered that house like Lakṣmī entering the hollow of a lotus;
her garlands and garments were swaying, and she was disarrayed with broken strings of pearls.
Followed by her companions and servant girls, she was overwhelmed with fear;
with a moon-like face and fair limbs, her breasts trembling from her sighs,
and her teeth like stars, she stood there like the sky incarnate.
Then one of her companions addressed the king, as an apsaras might address the lord of the gods when he is enraged for the battle with Vṛtra: "O King,
the queen has fled from the inner apartments along with us."
The king’s wives, seized by powerful thieves with raised weapons, sought refuge with the god like a wind-tossed creeper seeking a tree;
they were like trees and creepers on the shore of great oceans, overwhelmed by masses of waves.
All the masters of the inner apartments have been crushed by the arrogant enemies who have attacked unexpectedly,
like forest trees by winds that have suddenly arisen.
Our city has been seized by the enemy forces that have arrived unexpectedly like a flood.
At night, as if during the rainy season,
our city was pervaded by fires with smoky trails and loud roars, licking the sky with their cresting flames like water-borne surges, and by the numerous enemy warriors.
"The queens, who were the delights of their retinues, having been seized by their hair and forcibly led away while crying out like female ospreys by fishermen—
this very branch of ours has arrived, spreading forth with its tendrils."
"Only the Lord has the power to lift up this calamity.
Having heard this and looked [upon them], he said: "I am going for battle;
may this wife of mine, who is a bee at the lotus-feet of you two goddesses, be forgiven."
Having spoken thus, the king, his mind agitated by anger,
went forth like a lion from a mountain cave that has been breached by a rutting elephant.
Then Līlā beheld Līlā, whose form was identical to her own appearance.
"Like a reflection appearing in a mirror, O lady of beautiful appearance—Prabuddhalīlā said:
'What is this, O Goddess? Tell me; why am I standing here?'"
"How is it that she who was my own being in the past is situated here now?
These ministers and others, the citizens, and the warriors with their armies and vehicles—
all these are exactly the same ones who were stationed there in that very way."
Even there, O Queen, [he asked]: "How is it that all these are situated here, both outside and inside, like reflections in a mirror? Are they conscious?
The Queen replied:
Just as a cognition arises within, so does consciousness experience it in an instant;
consciousness takes on the nature of the object of thought, just as the mind takes on the nature of its own objects.
Whatever kind of mental cultivation the conscious being extends within, that very thing it projects as memory.
In that very moment, the world appears there with such a form of objects;
there is no distance of space or time, nor is there any variety born of external things.
There is nothing external; it shines as internal—of this, the objects of a dream are the illustration.
That which is the manifestation of consciousness within, like a dream or a city of creative imagination—
that very thing stands here, clearly manifest under the name of "external," due to one's own habitual practice.
Such was the state of your husband when he died in that city at that time.
A being of such a nature encounters that very same object in that very place.
For these servants are indeed different from those [previously encountered], even though they are similar to them;
yet for him, they are of the same essential nature, like an army in a dream or a mental construction.
Tell me, how or in what way could there be unreality for that which is experienced as non-contradictory and possessing the form of all objects? Or else,
it may be that at a later time it is not substantially real because of its perishability.
Thus, all this is exactly like that; what room is there for atheism?
In the waking state, the dream is unreal; in the dream, the waking state is unreal.
Death is unreal in relation to birth, and birth is likewise composed of unreality in relation to death.

O beautiful one, because of the fragility of discursive thought and because of experience, this world is neither existent nor non-existent; it appears as mere delusion. Whether at the arrival of the end of a great aeon, or today, or in another age, [it remains thus].
That which never perishes is indeed Brahman; that is this world. In its midst, these delusions called "creations" shine forth like clusters of hair in the sky, yet they do not exist in reality.
Just as waves arise in the ocean, so do these creations in the Supreme;
rising again and again, they dissolve like dust motes in a great wind.
Therefore, falsity resides in the appearance consisting of delusion, which is of the nature of the "I."
What reliance can there be on the flow of water in a mirage, or on the ashes of creation?
There are no other delusions therein; those very [delusions] are the supreme state.
In dense darkness, the appearance of a yakṣa is merely darkness itself, not the yakṣas.
Therefore, birth, death, and delusion, as well as the sky, the "I," you, and this all-pervading "that"—
all of this remains at the end of the great aeon (*mahākalpa*) when it has subsided. Hence,
this is seen to be neither real nor ever unreal.
This is indeed a duality, or rather, Brahman alone arises therein.
Whether within the space of an atom, or even within a subtle particle (*aṇuka*) among substances and so forth,
wherever the atomic soul (*jīvāṇu*) is, there it perceives this world as its own body.
Just as fire perceives its own heat arising from its inherent nature,
so too does the Self perceive this world as its own being, through its pure consciousness.
Just as motes of dust whirl about in a house illuminated by the sun’s rays, so does the mind wander within the body.
Likewise, these atoms of the cosmic egg exist in the supreme space;
just as vibration resides in the wind, fragrance in the air, and coolness in the sky,
so does the universe abide in the Supreme, free from any material aggregation.
Now you must understand that for the sake of realizing Brahman— which is devoid of parts such as existence and non-existence, grasping and abandoning, gross and subtle, moving and stationary—
these very qualities are to be known as its forms.
They would be non-different from their own self, like the limbs of a tree.
This universe, as it exists, arising through the sequence of its own inherent nature,
is empty of the referents of the word "universe" and remains non-different from Brahman.
That is neither real nor unreal, like the delusion of a snake in a rope;
it is real due to false experience, but unreal upon investigation.
Having understood the supreme cause, one fully realizes it as being like the state of the individual soul (*jīvatva*).

Therefore, experiencing that very [state], it clearly attains the condition of being a living soul (*jīvatva*). Whether real or unreal, this world appearing even in the sky truly delights the atomic soul (*jīvāṇu*) with its own arising experiences.
Some of these experiences arise from previous experiences, while others are entirely new; they are both similar and dissimilar.
At some place and at some time, those very same experiences may occur again, even when they are similar.
Unreal experiences, appearing as real, shine forth within the space of the living soul (jīvākāśa).
Those very people of that lineage, those with that same conduct, born of that [same source], and performing those same actions—
those alone shall become your ministers and citizens within your visionary manifestation.
And those very [perceptions] are truly sufficient within the Self, equal in all respects regarding place, time, and benefit;
such is the established state of the intuition (*pratibhā*) whose nature is that of the universal Self.
Just as a perception consisting of reality arises within the King’s own self, which is like the sky.
Likewise, as it arises in succession, it shines forth as truth itself:
"Possessing your character, possessing your conduct, belonging to your lineage,
and embodying your form"— thus does this play appear, a manifestation born from reflection.
In the all-pervading mirror of consciousness, a manifestation reflects;
whatever [manifestation] is where [it is], it arises there without interruption. That manifestation which resides within the space of the individual soul shines forth by itself.
This [universe] exists externally as a reflection in the mirror of consciousness within the void.
This sky, this "I," the world, the earth and so forth, and the king—all this is indeed unborn, a mere manifestation.
Know, my dear, that the space of consciousness is like the interior of a wood-apple fruit; understand this, and remain at peace, exactly as you are here.
In the narrative of Līlā, the forty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Burning by Fire, the Night Battle, and the World as Brahman," Sarasvatī said:
"Vidūratha is your husband; having cast off his body on the field of battle, he will reach that very inner apartment and become such a self once more. Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard these words of the queen, that Līlā, whose home was in that city,
stood again with bowed head and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words. Second Līlā:
"O Goddess, the divine Jñapti has been constantly worshipped by me;
O Goddess, she grants me a vision during the nights in my dreams.
O Mistress of the Gods, O Mother, you are exactly as she is."
"O fair-faced one, out of compassion for my wretched state, grant me a boon.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed thus, Jñapti then recalled that feeling of devotion.
The Goddess Prasannā spoke thus to Līlā, who was dwelling there:
"With undivided devotion that remains undiminished throughout your life..."
"I am well-pleased with you, my child; accept the boon you desire.
Taddēśalīlā said:
"In that place where my husband lies, having cast off his body in battle,"
"With this very body, may I become that woman there. The Goddess said:
"So be it; I have been worshipped by you for a long time, O daughter, and you shall be free from obstacles."
"O Queen, through worship with flowers and incense performed with undivided devotion.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Then, when the festival of that region had blossomed due to the rise of that bridegroom..."
Pūrvalīlā, her mind agitated by doubt, spoke to the Goddess:
Pūrvalīlā said:
"Those whose desires are true, whose resolutions are solely true, and who are of the nature of Brahman—"
"For those like you, everything they desire is swiftly accomplished.
Therefore, O Sovereign, for what reason was I not led by you with this very body to another world, or to that mountain village?"
The Goddess said:
"O woman of excellent complexion, I do nothing for anyone;
it is the individual soul (jīva) itself that swiftly accomplishes all its own desires."
For I am the straightforward consciousness, the presiding deity of pure awareness;
I am the individual power of consciousness, manifesting in the form of the individual soul (jīva). In whatever manner the power of "I" arises for whichever individual soul, [so it appears].

It shines forth eternally, bestowing its fruit upon each [practitioner] in whatever manner is appropriate. When one propitiates me quickly, the power of life (jīvaśakti) arises in such a way that, while still in the body, one thinks for a long time: "I am liberated in her."
In various ways, you have been fully awakened by me;
through that reasoning, O fair-complexioned one, you have been led to a stainless state of being.
When I had thus been awakened for a long time by this very cultivation of thought,
Attaining that very same object at that time through the power of its own consciousness,
it bestows upon each person, in accordance with their long-standing mental effort, a corresponding fruit in due course.
Whether becoming austerity or even a deity, that very same immutable consciousness bestows the fruit at will, like the falling of fruit from the sky;
for there is never anything other than the illumination of one's own self-awareness.
The fruit follows swiftly; therefore, act as you desire.
Indeed, the inner self, which is the very nature of consciousness, is all-pervading; whatever it perceives and strives for, that it attains, and that is its glory.
Therefore, having deliberated whether something is pleasant or unpleasant, and having understood that which is purifying, abide within that.
In the Līlopākhyāna, the forty-sixth canto, titled "The Abiding in Truthful Desire and Truthful Resolve," Rāma said:
While they were thus conversing within that house,
what did Vidūratha do after departing from the home in anger?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Vidūratha, having emerged from his own palace,
was surrounded by a vast retinue like the moon by a multitude of bears;
with all his limbs armored and adorned with clinging necklaces and ornaments.
Amidst great shouts of victory and triumph, like the Lord of the Gods, the king departed;
commanding his host of warriors, listening to the arrangement of the battle circles,
and surveying the heroic combatants, he ascended his chariot.
Resembling a celestial mansion, adorned with pearls and rubies,
and pervaded by clusters of banners, it was like a heavenly chariot descended from the sky;
with golden sprouts falling from the streams flowing down its moon-like walls.
With beautiful masts of coral that produced a pleasant jingling sound like pearls, [the chariot] was drawn by excellent,
white, and lean horses endowed with auspicious marks;
they seemed to be shedding their hooves due to the speed that increased their momentum.
With their natural gaits, they seemed to outstrip even the winds;
with their hindquarters leaping upward, they seemed to drink in the sky,
as if filled with moons formed by the brilliance of their chowries.
It was yoked to eight horses whose neighing fulfilled all desires; then there arose the sound of kettledrums, filling the air like the roar of wild elephants or clouds,
harsh with echoes from mountain walls.
It was filled with the clamor of shouting soldiers,
the tinkling of networks of small bells,
the clanging sounds produced by the collision of weapons, the crackling of bows, and the whistling songs of arrows.
With the clanging sounds of masses of armor being crushed against one another’s shoulders,
with the crackling of blazing fires, with the cries of those suffering in pain, with the mutual challenges of warriors, and with the agitated wailing of captive bards; MU_3,46.12–13.
A roar arose that filled the hollows of the entire universe with solid stone;
it was tangible to the touch, terrifying to you, and filled the groves of the ten directions.
Then there rose up [a cloud] thickly obstructing the path of the sun.
With the surface of the earth obscured by dust as if about to fly up into the sky,
that great city became like one that had entered the womb;
darkness reached its full density, as if through the folly of youth.
The multitudes of lamps departed somewhere like stars with the day;
the restless successions of nocturnal spirits arrived with their forces. Those two girls and Kumārikā beheld that great battle as if it were a play.
Then, with their hearts throbbing as they were beheld by the great gaze bestowed by the Goddess,
those fires in the houses subsided amidst the rising crackling sounds,
like submarine fires quenched by the surging waters of the single universal ocean.
Drawing his army along with his arrows, the king entered the midst of the enemy forces like Mount Meru, soaring on its wings into a single ocean.
Then there arose the clear, crackling sound of the bowstring: *caṭaccaṭat*.
The successions of arrows, having become oceans of their own essence, surged forth;
taking to the sky, various weapons became like birds,
and the flashes of the weapons spread abroad through the quarters like mists.
Blazing with the clashing of weapons like the fire of a brand,
those heroic clouds rumbled as they rained down torrents of arrow-showers. Cruel weapons, like herons, pierced the limbs of the warriors.
Crushed by weapons in the sky, they shrieked with a *paṭapaṭa* sound;
the darkness was quickly pacified by the lamps of blazing weapons,
and all the armies became bristling with new iron arrows like hair.
Rows of headless trunks (*kabandha*) rose up like dancers in the procession of the battle;
the female *piśāca* demons, acting as war-maidens, loudly sang the treasonous cries of combat; and from the force of the elephants, there arose the trumpeting sounds of their intoxicated collisions.
The rivers of blood, intoxicated by the stones hurled from catapults, surged across the expanse of the sky; and masses of chariots fell like parched forest leaves,
while rivers of blood flowed forth from the mountain of battle, raining down death.
The dust was stilled by blood, the darkness by the fires of weapons,
the sounds by the singular focus on battle, and the fears by the certainty of death;
only the battle remained, tumultuous, incomparable, and full of noise.
With the gurgling sound of sword-blades moving like unimpeded clouds,
with the clatter of showers of arrows flying swiftly, with the *kaṭakaṭa* sound of falling *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons,
and with the clanging noise of great missiles colliding, that army lay as if asleep at night beneath its new cover.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the forty-seventh canto, titled "The Departure of Vidūratha," Vasiṣṭha says:
While this terrible tumult of battle was occurring,
the two Līlās spoke thus to the Blessed Jñapti who stood before them.
The two Līlās said:
"O Goddess, why does our lord suddenly conquer us in battle?
Tell us, for even though you are pleased, he has put this elephant to flight.
Sarasvatī said:
I have been long propitiated by this enemy of King Vidūratha for the sake of his victory, whereas I have not been so by King Vidūratha;
therefore, he alone is victorious, and Vidūratha is defeated.
This consciousness, which is internal cognition, impels whatever [object] in whatever manner and at whatever time;
at that very moment, I accomplish that for him.
In whatever way anyone impels me, I abide as the fruit thereof for him.
"This [victory] does not arise from my own inherent nature, just as heat belongs to fire;
rather, I have been honored by him with the thought, 'May victory be mine in battle.
Thus, taking the form of an image, he obtains such a fruit."
"By Vidūratha I was awakened to this matter, having reflected upon it;
and I was resolved that by him alone I might be liberated. Therefore, Vidūratha, having attained that body together with his wife—"
"In time, O child, he shall be released by you and her;
for this enemy of his, the lord of the earth named Sindhu,
having been slain upon the surface of the world, he shall rule the kingdom as a victor."
Vasiṣṭha said:
While the queen was speaking thus and the two armies were engaged in battle,
the sun, as if to witness the marvel, ascended the mountain of sunrise.
At twilight, the stars in the sky were like corpses; they appeared as if they had been cast out by the masses of darkness, which took on the form of armies.
Gradually, the mountainous terrains of the battlefield assumed a formidable appearance;
the world shone as if it had been cast up from the ocean of soot.
The rays of the sun fell, beautiful like streams of molten gold.
Among those excellent heroes who were like mountains, there appeared a spray of blood as if from a battle;
then the sky and the field of battle were seen alike,
with arms whirling like serpents and strewn with splendors like scattered gold.

With heads strewn with earrings like a mass of scattered jewels, it was filled with aged lotuses; dense with swords like its blades and brimming with *śarabha* deer due to its arrows; rich with a twilight of blood-red luster and unsteady light, it was filled with corpses as if with perfected beings (*siddha-puruṣa*).
With necklaces it was like the sloughed skin of a serpent; with garments it was crowded with rays of light. With its thighs, which were like shimmering creeper-banners, it formed an archway;
with its hands and feet it was made to sprout like shoots, and with its arrows it resembled a forest of reeds.
Dark as a meadow of young grass from the luster of weapons, with sands strewn with blades of sword-grass and covered with garlands of arms, it was as terrifying as a place possessed by madness;
it had the appearance of a grove of blossoming *aśoka* trees due to the fires produced by the clashing of weapons.
With loud shouts of "udghuṅghuma," the leaders of the Siddhas were put to flight;
its form was fashioned of gold, with weapons as radiant as the rising sun, and the space between its ranks resounded with spears, swords, discs, javelins, double-edged blades, mallets, and arrows.
In the meantime, all the armies met their destruction;
the battlefield became as if empty, with only a few soldiers from both sides remaining.
Men were cut down, shattered, slain, destroyed, or had fled in flight.
It was a place where great heaps of falling corpses formed a mire and streams of blood flowed; it was filled with the force of rushing rivers of gore that swept away multitudes of corpses,
and it was crowded with *bhuśuṇḍī* slings, spears, lances, swords, and large stones.
In the empty battlefield, accompanied by the falling of headless trunks severed by the blows of heroes' weapons,
and filled with the tumultuous clamor raised by a host of Vetālas performing a frantic palm-clapping dance,
the two radiant chariots— the Lotus and the Elephant— moved about.
They appeared like the sun and moon, the two signs of the sky, in the heavens;
they were surrounded by thousands upon thousands of heroes, and were crowded with discuses, spears, *bhuśuṇḍi* missiles, javelins, and lances as their weapons.
Wandering at will upon the ground spread out within the mandala, they—
some crushed by the great wheel that emits a whirring sound, others rendered immortal—
crossed the rivers of blood with the grace of elephants in rut.
Their wheels were covered with hair like moss, and their blood-stained waters were drenched;
elephants, thrown down in agitation by the shock of being struck by the revolving wheels, lay scattered about;
and the hollows of their poles resounded with the tinkling of jewels and pearls.
The fluttering cloth at the tips of their banners made a rustling sound as they were pursued by numerous great heroes and terrified soldiers,
who bore the weight of spears, arrows, and bows.
Amidst the flashing luster of spears, spikes, and whirling discs,
the two of them, having moved for a moment in circles and vast mandalas,
both became like clouds of weapons facing one another.
As those two lions among men struck each other with showers of iron arrows that were as thick as a mass of hailstones, they roared at one another like two intoxicated oceanic clouds.
As those two lions among men struck each other with their arrows, the earth—
They took the form of stones and maces, extending across the sky;
some had the blades of swords, others had faces like mallets,
some had sharp wheels for mouths, and others had axes for faces.
Some arrows had heads shaped like spears, some even like razors;
some had heads like spikes, iron blades, or crescent moons;
some had heads like lion-stones, and some had heads like the points of tridents.
Some, with faces like tridents, were as massive as great boulders;
then the feathered arrows moved about like masses of rock cast down by the winds of universal dissolution.
At that moment, the encounter between the two became like the tumultuous agitation of the oceans unleashed at the time of the world's end.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the forty-eighth canto, titled "The Meeting of Vidūratha and Sindhu," Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reached the city, the king beheld Sindhudvīpa standing before him with his neck held high;
with a wrath as radiant as the midday sun,
he became enraged and drew his bow, making it resound through all the quarters of the sky.
Like the slope of the mountain of the immortals struck by the winds at the end of an aeon,
the powerful king released at dawn a succession of arrows that had been bound to his quiver during the night, just as the sun emits its rays.
A single great arrow of his, released from its string, would fly forth;
while traveling through the sky, it would fall by the thousands, and as it went, it would descend by the hundreds of thousands.
The ocean likewise possessed such power and such swiftness of hand.
Indeed, there was a resemblance between the sun and Viṣṇu’s face, and between those two, their skill as archers.
Those arrows named *musula*, shaped like *musula* clubs,
covered the sky with loud roars like the mountains at the end of an eon.
Those rows of golden shafts shone in his sky like stars falling, distressed by the winds of the cosmic dissolution, as they became his targets.
From Vidūratha, a continuous shower of arrows issued forth.
Like masses of water from the ocean, like rays from the sun,
like flowers shaken from a great tree by a fierce wind,
or like rows of sparks struck from a heated iron ball.
Like torrents from a rain-cloud, like spray from a waterfall,
or like brilliant sparks from the great conflagration of that city’s fire;
hearing the crackling and snapping sound of those two bows— *caṭacaṭāsphoṭam*— he [listened].
The two armies became as silent as the ocean at rest, their gaze fixed and motionless. Floods of arrows flowed through the sky like the current of the Gaṅgā,
rushing toward the ocean with the gurgling roar of yakṣas.
From the cloud that was his bow, there issued forth incessant showers of whetted iron arrows,
accompanied by the "śava-śava" sound of falling corpses;
it was like the flood of the Mandākinī river of arrows flowing toward the filling of the ocean.
Seeing him from the window, Līlā, a resident of that city,
suspecting victory for her husband by means of that multitude of arrows,
spoke these words, her lotus-like face blossoming with joy.
"Victory, O Goddess! Victory! Behold this our Lord;
indeed, by this flood of arrows, even Mount Meru would be reduced to powder.
While she was speaking thus, [the air] became filled with the sounds of intense affection.
While the two goddesses, intent on gazing at him, laughed in their hearts at the mortal,
the submarine fire of the ocean drank that surging sea of arrows,
just as Jahnu drank the Mandākinī with its unapproachable heat.
Having pierced that entire mass of arrows with a shower of his own shafts,
and having brought even that down, he cast them into the ocean of the sky;
just as the movement of an extinguished lamp is no longer perceived.
The course of that multitude of arrows was not perceived in such a way.
Having cut through that downpour of shafts, he spread forth his own dense cloud of arrows in the sky, accompanied by the whistling sound of autumnal winds.
Vidūratha also swiftly shattered him with his finest arrows,
just as the wind at the end of an aeon scatters an ordinary cloud;
thus did the two lords of the earth engage with showers of arrows, each countering the other's deeds.
Rendered useless, they ceased their incessant striking.
Then Sindhu took up the *mohana* (stupefying) weapon, having obtained it through his friendship with a Gandharva; by its power, all beings fled except for Vidūratha, who remained unmoved.
With their weapons and garments cast aside, mute, and with dejected faces and eyes,
the warriors became like the dead, or as if they were figures depicted in a painting,
while Vidūratha’s chariot was reduced to sluggishness by his delusion.
Then King Vidūratha took up the weapon of awakening;
thereupon the subjects regained consciousness like a lotus-pond at dawn,
while Vidūratha became like the ocean surging in rage against a Rākṣasa.
He discharged the terrible Nāga-missile, which causes distress through the binding of nooses;
by it, the sky became pervaded with serpents resembling mountains,
and the earth was entwined with snakes like a lake with lotus stalks.
All the mountains were completely covered with blankets of black serpents;
all these objects, including the expanse of mountains and forests, were shrouded by the bodies of snakes, and the earth fell into a state of helplessness.
Scattered with sparks from the *dhūta* rite, signaling the onset of poison,
winds carrying dust and fire blew with intensely hot frost.
Then Vidūratha, skilled in great weapons, discharged the *sauparṇa* weapon.
The Garuḍas rose up like mountains of gold;
they made all the quarters golden, fulfilling every desire,
and their violent flapping of wings generated winds like those at the time of universal dissolution.
With circles of hissing serpents drawn in by the movement of his nostrils,
filling the masses of clouds with a roar like that of a great thundercloud,
that cloud-like Suparṇa drank up the flood of snakes that covered the earth.
Like Agastya [drinking] the ocean, he drained the earth which was being torn asunder with a *śala-śala* sound;
the circle of the earth shone, freed from its serpent-bedding,
like a vast, dense, waterless heap.
Then that host of Garuḍas vanished somewhere from sight,
like a mass of lamps by the wind or a circle of clouds in autumn;
it was like a range of winged mountains fleeing again out of fear of the thunderbolt.
Like a world seen in a dream, or like a city created by mere imagination;
then Sindhu released the weapon of darkness, which produces blinding gloom,
and by it the darkness increased, resembling the interior of a black cloud.
Spreading through the cavity of the earth, it became like a single vast ocean;
the mountains became like fish, and the stars became like jewels.
Darkness prevailed, resembling an ocean of ink and mud.
The mass of collyrium-mountains was shaken even by many kalpas;
all subjects were as if fallen into a blind well,
and worldly affairs toward every direction were as if dissolved at the end of an aeon.
Then Vidūratha, the best among those skilled in weapons, having performed the ritual procedures with potent mantras, bestowed the Mārtāṇḍa weapon within the pavilion of the universe.
Thereupon, like Agastya with his rays, the Sun rose from the ocean of darkness.

He drank in Kṛṣṇa like the stainless autumn season drinks up the dark cloud. Freed from the garment of darkness, the pure quarters of the sky shone forth before the lord of the earth like beautiful women with lovely breasts.
All the forest ranges within became visible,
like the intellects of the virtuous when they are freed from the soot-like net of greed. Then, agitated by anger, the ocean unleashed the most terrifying *rākṣasa* weapon.
In an instant, he discharged that which consisted of arrows produced by mantras.
From all directions, the forest-rākṣasas rose up in fury like great oceans agitated by the *hūṃ*-cries of the subterranean elephants.
The fires, with their smoke-colored, upward-pointing tawny matted locks and emitting crackling *caṭa-caṭa* sounds,
were like those with fierce, licking tongues and half-consumed fuel;
they moved in whirlpools in the sky, making terrifying *ḍakkā-raṭa* cries.
They were like great fires with massive smoke and flaming brands;
their lotus-like faces and bodies were overrun by fang-like poison-sprouts,
and they appeared as if their matted locks were the fierce flames emerging from their pores.
Swallowing [their foes], charging forward, and roaring with threatening intent,
they were like water-laden clouds with masses of lightning flashing from their matted locks.
In that interval, Vidūratha, the lord of Līlā, [arrived].
He bestowed the Nārāyaṇa weapon, which wards off wicked beings. As soon as this king of weapons was invoked, the hosts of Rākṣasas were extinguished, like darkness at the rising of the sun.
The three worlds were cleared of the Rākṣasa host;
like the sky in autumn when the clouds have departed, it shone forth stainless. Then Sindhu released the fiery weapon (*āgneya-astra*), which set the heavens ablaze.
By that [fire], the quarters blazed as if enveloped by the fire of cosmic dissolution;
all directions became shrouded by clouds of smoke,
as if agitated by the darkness rising from the netherworld and piercing through the sky.
The mountains appeared like mountains of gold with their forms ablaze,
as if they were forests of dense, blossoming *caṃpaka* groves.
The sky, the mountains, and the mountain-caves took on the tangled appearance of masses of flames.
As if anointed with the blood of Death during a festival of saffron,
the people blazed like oceans encircled by the coils of the thousand-formed serpent, as he touched the nearby sky while inspiring singular dread in the multitude.
Having conquered his enemy,
Vidūratha, honoring him, discharged the Vāruṇa weapon just as he had struck back;
floods of water came surging from all sides like masses of darkness.
From below, above, and from all directions, they were like mountains in liquid form;
like portions of the autumnal sky, like clouds with swift flight,
like great oceans standing upright, and like the rocks of the principal mountain ranges.
Like masses of *tāla* trees flying up, like nights gathered together,
like heaps of collyrium tossed upward, like the Lokāloka mountain reaching its summit,
and like the vast expanses of the subterranean caves desiring to see the sky; [so did they appear].
With their forms augmented by the force of a great, deep-thundering roar,
that mass of water swallowed the spreading line of flames from the fire of heat—
just as the night, pervading the world, quickly swallows the twilight.

Having drunk that continuous stream of fire, the beauty of the waters completely filled the surface of the earth, her body having attained a state of manifest fluidity. Such delusions caused by weapons are indeed contradictory; they are not otherwise.
At first, they saw and experienced one another as being composed of illusion; then,
like those carrying heavy loads of weapons who are swept away by the waters of the ocean,
they were carried off like blades of grass, and his chariot was carried along as well.
In the meantime, Sindhu remembered the weapon Śoṣaṇa;
and the god, who provides protection in times of distress, gave it to him in the form of an arrow. By that radiant [weapon], the illusion consisting of water was extinguished.
Those who had died remained dead, and the earth was parched.
Then, like a fool enraged by asceticism, he tormented the subjects;
he yawned with a harshness like the vast expanse of a withered and decayed forest.
With the complexion of his limbs made beautiful by the luster of refined gold, he clung to the major and minor limbs of the women of the quarters, as if he were the best of kings;
because of him, those who were his adversaries fell into a feverish swoon.
Like tender sprouts scorched by a summer forest fire, [the enemy's forces were withered].
Then Vidūratha, having bent his bow so that its long,
tinkling string produced a whirring sound, took up the Parjanya weapon.
Rows of clouds rose up like accumulated nights,
sluggish with the frantic onset of rising from the tamāla groves;
they moved with a wild roar upon a flood of water consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

The winds blew, scattering sprays of mist like noble necklaces of pearls; they shattered the mass of clouds and served as earrings for the entire circle of the quarters, which were made sluggish by the frost. (MU 3.48.77–78)
The lightnings in the sky flickered like the retreating of terrified golden serpents, or like the darting side-glances of the Daitya women; the mountain caves,
thick with echoes swollen by thundering roars, resounded.
The quarters of the sky resounded with the deep growls of elephants, lions,
and bears; torrential rains fell with the force of great mallets,
harsh with the sound of *kaṣṭa-ṭāṅkāra*, like the glares of Death himself.
First, there arose from the earth a very hot vapor, mountain-like,
resembling masses of clouds rising from the netherworld as if for battle;
then, in the mere twinkling of an eye, those mirages subsided.
Just as the latent impressions of worldly existence [are washed away] by the floods of the essence of supreme awakening,
so the entire circle of the earth was once marked with mud and impassable;
yet it was filled by full streams, just as a river is filled with water from another river.

He discharged the Vāyavya weapon, which made the hollows of the sky whirl and was as terrifying as the roaring of Bhairava engaged in the dance at the end of an eon. Thunderbolts fell, their masses like solid lumps, and fragments of shattered rock scattered across the quarters of the sky.
The winds, signaling the time of dissolution and terrifying the soldiers with their harsh, artificial *ṭāṅkṛta* sounds;
thus ends the forty-ninth canto, titled "The Description of the Battle of Weapons," within the narrative of Līlā.
Vasiṣṭha said: Winds blew, swirling with frost and scattering thick foliage; they shook the multitude of trees, fierce in their power to uproot and cast them down.
Then, by that exceedingly terrifying wind, which tore apart the thickets of the forest and split the walls of the chasms, even Vidūratha’s chariot was carried away like a withered leaf in a river.
Then Vidūratha, a master of great weapons, discharged the mountain-weapon (*parvatāstra*),
by which the wind ceased its blowing as if the sky itself were striving to assume density through that impact of the mountain-weapon.
And by that peaceful wind he proceeded toward where the rows of trees situated in the sky fell to the earth;
they were like millions of crows upon a vast array of food for various people.
The sounds of "śemuḥ," "śītkāra," "ḍakkāra," "bhākkāra," and "ukkāra" issued from the quarters of the sky,
like the incoherent chatter of creepers in a gale whose grandeur was destroyed;
they saw mountains falling from the heavens like scattered leaves.
Like the Sindhunada [river] encountering the Maināka and other mountains scattered here and there,
he discharged the blazing vajra-weapon; then the clouds of thunderbolts surged forth,
swallowing the mountains like fires consuming counter-mountains through the heat of their flames.
With the crushing blows of their beak-tips against mountains and cities,
they shattered the heads [of the enemies] like fierce winds felling fruits.
Then Vidūratha discharged the Brahmā weapon to neutralize the Vajra weapon.
Then, when the Brahmāstra and Vajrāstra had been simultaneously pacified,
the king then unleashed the Piśāca weapon, which was darkly black.
By that [weapon], rows of Piśācas arose, inspiring infinite terror.
As if out of fear of the twilight, the day turned to darkness;
the *piśācas*, resembling pillars of ash and sporting with the swaying of palm trees, seized the world like masses of gloom.
Some appeared with massive forms, yet were as nothing more than what could be grasped in a fist;
some had hair standing erect, others were emaciated, and some even had beards.
These sky-dwellers were lean-limbed and soiled in body, appearing like common villagers.
In the assembly, they are of deluded vision, doing whatever comes to hand, and wicked;
they are wretched, gluttonous, and cruel, like base villagers.
They are fickle, dwelling in empty houses situated at the foot of trees, in mud, or along the edges of roads.
Licking their lips, appearing like hungry ghosts, with blackened limbs like outcaste dog-cookers,
those intoxicated men then seized the remnants of the enemy's army that had survived the slaughter. There, the soldiers who were nearby became terrified and their minds grew agitated.
Having cast aside their weapons and armor, their lives trembling and their steps faltering,
they caused alarm with the distortions of their eyes, limbs, faces, and feet;
stripped of their loincloths and utterly naked, they were overcome with loud laughter.
While discharging excrement and urine, yet remaining firmly engaged in his dance,
the king of the Piśācas then began to overwhelm King Vidūratha; at that moment, the wise monarch recognized that it was an illusion.
That lord of the earth knew the illusion that creates battles with *piśācas*.
With that, he deployed that army of *piśācas* against the enemy's army;
consequently, his own soldiers remained healthy, while the enemy warriors became possessed by *piśācas*.
Then, out of anger, he gave her that Rūpikā weapon and another;
from the earth and from the sky there emerged Rūpikās with stiff hair,
naked, with hideous eyes, and with pendulous hips and breasts.

They were women of advanced age whose youth had already blossomed, with stout limbs yet now decayed; their hips possessed both beauty and formlessness, and their vulvas bloomed like ill-performed dances; they held human heads by the hair in their hands, their bodies crimson with blood.
With their cheeks wet from the flowing blood and half-chewed flesh,
they twist and turn their various limbs, raising and lowering their faces;
their veins, arms, mouths, thighs, breasts, flanks, hands, and bodies are all visible.
With ropes of entrails dragged from the corpses of infants they had beaten,
their mouths, jaws, and bellies sunken, and their faces like those of dogs, crows, and owls,
they seized those Piśācas as if they were weak children.
Then that army of female piśācas became a single mass;
they were naked, dancing with their faces, limbs, and eyes turned upward,
trampling one another and terrifying each other.
With great tongues protruding and displaying various contortions of the face,
they were laden with the weight of corpses, dragging one another's severed limbs;
their shimmering bodies sank and rose again in a sea of blood.
With protruding belly, protruding arms, and protruding ears, lips, and nose,
they were wallowing together in the mud of blood, flesh, and fat;
it was as tumultuous as the resonant clamor arising from the Milk Ocean when churned by Mount Mandara.
Just as he had previously performed the movement of illusions,
so too did he quickly perform it in return, having recognized the other's swiftness;
then the Vetāla weapon was bestowed by him, and from that, throngs of corpses rose up.
Headless trunks with heads reattached, leaping with the possession of *vetālas*,
and then, like a flood of *piśācas*, *vetālas*, and headless torsos,
a terrifying army capable of swallowing the earth arose.
Then the other king also, having employed another illusion,
quickly discharged the Rākṣasa weapon, intent on the conquest of the three worlds;
from all sides there arose massive Rākṣasas, shaped like mountains.
Having emerged from their bodies like hells emerging from the netherworld (pātāla),
that army then became terrifying, striking fear even into the gods and asuras;
it was filled with roaring rākṣasas like a vast ocean and with dancing headless trunks (kabandhas) amidst the sounding of musical instruments.
The form of the maiden Rūpikā was firmly established in the abode of a Piśāca; it was enriched by the sound of whistling flutes, its head crowded with heaps of lotuses,
encircled by a dangling garland of intestines, and sprinkled with the water of blood.
It was radiant with the splendor of dancing *vetāla*s, a shimmering abode of *piśāca*s,
rich with fat, flesh, and marrow, and beautiful with the wine of blood;
it was crowded with the frantic dances of intoxicated *vetāla*s, *kumbhāṇḍa*s, and *yakṣa*s.

The bridge was established over the stream of blood by the *bhūtas*, who were beautiful with the tips of their masses of hair like streaks of twilight clouds, and who were sprinkled by waves tossed up by the blood agitated by their feet, which acted as staffs for the frantic dance (*kuttāṇḍava*) of the *kumbhāṇḍas*.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, this is the chapter titled "The Second Battle of Weapons."
Fifty-fifth canto. Vasiṣṭha:
While that terrible confusion of agitation was then occurring,
For the sake of destroying the entire army of his enemies and for the pacification of his own forces,
the mindful one, who possessed infinite and noble fortitude, inwardly recollected the glorious Vaiṣṇava weapon— the lord of weapons— which was like Śaṅkara himself.
Then, from the tip of that arrow which had been consecrated with the Vaiṣṇava weapon when it was released, there emerged rows of blazing discs like firebrands,
filling the horizons as if with hundreds of suns.
The skies were turned into a hundred reeds by the approaching maces;
the skies were turned into autumnal antelopes by the broad-edged thunderbolts;
and the skies were turned into trees on a riverbank by the sharp-edged spears and barbed missiles.
Then the second king, for the sake of neutralizing the Vaiṣṇava weapon,
discharged the very Vaiṣṇava weapon that vomits forth missiles. Thereupon, rivers of weapons issued forth from it, destroying the opposing weapons.
A battle took place in the sky between those rivers of weapons and missiles— arrows, spears, clubs, darts,
and axes— which caused the destruction of the space between heaven and earth and shattered the great lords of the principal mountain ranges.
Where spears were felled by arrows, axes shattered by swords, and clubs struck down by well-aimed darts;
where pikes were cut away by lances,
and the Mandara mountain of the mallets was intoxicated by churning the ocean of arrows.
It resembled an irresistible mountain thunderbolt intent on shattering maces;
it possessed a lunar orb of whirling spears that quelled the rain of double-edged swords;
and it brought about the end of all things with upraised spikes, eager to devour darts.

The mountain peaks were shattered by half-moons and high mountains were rendered feverless by thunderbolts; the surfaces of the rocks were pierced by spears hissing with the sound of "shut-kāra" as they struck like spikes;
and the circle of trees was devastated by fierce *bhiṇḍipāla* missiles struck by *bhusuṇḍī* slings.
It was crowded with many who bore axes and spears in their hands, and it was struck by axes and spears; it carried whisks that were sharp and severed by the friction of wheels and blades;
and it shattered the river of the three paths (the Gaṅgā) with the bursting, crackling, and snapping sounds of explosions.
A vast canopy of great clouds formed by the mass of weapon-dust,
with lightning flashing from the whirling collisions of weapons striking one another;
the cosmic egg of Brahmā vibrating with sound, and the principal mountain ranges shattered by the blows.
As the two warriors fought with a torrent of weapons severed by their own blades,
time passed for the powerful-souled one solely through his skill in warding off missiles;
he stood effortlessly upon the ocean to see how much strength he himself possessed.
Vidūratha discharged the fiery weapon (*āgneya-astra*), which resounded like a thunderbolt;
it set Sindhu’s chariot ablaze, as if burning dry grass in a forest thicket.
In that interval, within the sky whose interior was cleared of all obstacles by the weapon—
Like two armored warriors, or like two masses of monsoon clouds,
having made the king of weapons their eyes, they engaged in a most terrible battle;
then, like two valiant soldiers, those two powerful ones reached a state of mutual peace.
In the meantime, the fire-weapon (Agni-astra), having quickly reduced the chariot to ashes and consumed the forest,
reached the Sindhu like a lion from its mountain cave.
The Sindhu king, from close range, neutralized the fire-weapon with the Varuna-weapon (Varuna-astra).
Abandoning his chariot and reaching the ground, he took up sword and shield.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, with his sword he swiftly severed the hooves of the enemy's chariot horses as if they were lotus stalks.
Vidūratha, too, became deprived of his chariot and took up shield and sword;
armed and equally spirited, they moved in circular maneuvers.
As the two struck one another, their swords became like saws.
"This is his very row of teeth as he devours the subjects," [thought Vidūratha].
Abandoning his sword, Vidūratha took up a spear and hurled it into the ocean with a gurgling roar, like a thunderbolt portending a great calamity.
Arriving without interruption, she fell upon his chest like an unwilling mistress upon her unpleasant husband. By that blow from the spear, he did not meet his death.
The serpent shed its stream of blood like water;
seeing him broken like darkness by the moon, Līlā of that region,
blooming with intense joy, spoke to Pūrvā-līlā.
"O Goddess, behold! This husband of ours, the Daitya with his towering neck, has been slain by Nṛsiṃha with the tips of his millions of nail-claws,
like water driven away by the *hūṃ*-roar of a lordly elephant standing at the edge of a lake."
"Alas! From this one and that one, blood flows out with cries of 'shul-shul.
Oh, what a tragedy! The chariot has been brought; Sindhu is preparing to mount it, like Puṣkarāvartaka ascending the golden peak of Mount Meru."
"Behold, O Queen, this chariot of mine has been crushed by the mallet,
like a golden city by the fall of a revolving mountain.
My husband is now intent on mounting the chariot that has been brought."
"Alas! Like a thunderbolt hurled by Indra, this mace has been cast by the Lord of the Sindhus.
Having evaded it with grace and swiftly mounting his chariot, behold—this husband of mine shines resplendently on the battlefield!"
"Alas! What a tragedy! This elephant has forcibly mounted the chariot of my noble lord, just as a monkey climbs a tree from a boat or a dog climbs into a pit.
Look! As he mounts it, his master’s shoulder has been severed by his sword."
The mountain of rubies seems to shed its luster as blood.
Alas, alas! Woe is me! By this ocean-like blade, my husband has been severed from his thighs, like a tree cut by a saw.
"Alas, alas! I am ruined, I am consumed, I am dead, and I am utterly destroyed;
both knees of my husband have been severed like lotus stalks.
Having spoken thus and beholding him, she was then overcome with fear for her husband's fate.
Like a creeper severed by an axe, she fell to the ground in a swoon.
Vidūratha too, his knees shattered as he was still striking the enemy,
quickly fell from his chariot like a tree whose roots have been cut.
As he was falling, being carried away by his charioteer in the very chariot,
at that moment the surging ocean struck him on the neck;
then, with his throat half-severed, he was pursued by the sea.
He entered the palace by carriage, just as Lakṣmī enters a lotus; yet,
due to the power of Sarasvatī, he was unable to enter that house,
just as a drunken gnat cannot enter the midst of a great flame.
With his garments and armor splattered by the spray of blood mixed with wind flowing from the wound in his throat, which had been severed by a sword,
the charioteer entered the interior of the house and left him— the enemy who had passed away— upon the bed on the floor.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Death of Vidūratha" in the *Līlopākhyāna*.
The fifty-first canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"The king has been slain, the king has been slain by a rival king in battle!"
When these words were uttered, the kingdom became overwhelmed with fear;
its entire population fled, laden with burdens of goods and utensils,
while the city was impassable as the citizens ran away with their wives crying out in distress.
With crowds of women being seized on the roads by those fleeing and crying out,
with a great battle joined by people busy plundering one another,
and with the clamor of the exultant dancing of the enemy kingdom’s host of women; MU 3.51.3.
There were no elephants, horses, footmen, or people left standing;
it resounded with the *gharghara* roar of treasure-chests flying open as their lids were shattered;
and it was filled with fierce enemy warriors clad in countless plundered silken garments.
The courtyard of Rājagṛha was filled with the raw entrails torn out by knives;
it was crowded with Cāṇḍālas and Śvapacas resting in the king’s inner apartments;
and the common folk were intent on eating the food and provisions plundered from the houses.

The young trees were shaken by the feet of the throngs of thieves carrying loads of gold; the women of the inner apartments had their hair disheveled by unprecedented youths; and the paths and directions were bristling with priceless jewels fallen from the hands of the robbers.
The circle of vassal kings was occupied with the crowding of horses, elephants, and chariots;
the chief ministers were intent on the instructions for the preparations of the consecration;
and the master architect stood upon the ridge where the royal capital was being constructed.
[He saw] the royal favorites falling into wells, windows, and pits;
[a place] filled with the roar of hundreds of shouts of victory from the lords of the Sindhu region;
and one where stability was maintained by the ocean-like multitude of his own countless kings.
The beloveds of kings fled as they were overtaken by the advance of other villages; plundering of cities and villages broke out within the various districts;
and the coming and going of travelers was blocked by endless theft and clamor.
It was like a day of sunlight obscured by the mist of the absence of those of great majesty;
it possessed a dense resonance, formed by the wailing of deceased kinsmen, the sounds of trumpets heard from afar,
and the noises of horses, elephants, and chariots.

"Sindhudeva is victorious, the sovereign of the earth under a single umbrella!"— immediately after this, kettledrums were sounded in every city at that time. Then Sindhur entered the capital with his neck held high in pride.
Like another Manu at the end of an eon, he set out to create progeny;
then, from the ten directions, men began to enter the city of Sindhura,
like oceans filled with jewels entering the sea, bringing with them houses for men, elephants, and horses.
The ministers quickly established markers, signs, and instructions for every direction around the mandala;
in no time at all, they appeared in every region and every city.
Just as there is a fixed rule for life, death, and honor according to one's self-restraint (yama),
so too did the calamities and disturbances of the land cease in an instant, like the subsiding of portents and the stilling of winds that cause the upheaval of objects.
The entire region, extending through the ten directions, quickly attained a state of serenity,
like the Ocean of Milk when its churning whirlpools have subsided after Mount Mandara has been withdrawn.
Winds blew, tossing the masses of hair and the bee-like faces of the women of Sindh, whose lotus-faces were agitated.
In an instant, the winds, agitated by the swirling spray of water, became as if possessed of inauspicious qualities on all sides.
This concludes the fifty-second canto, named "The Kingdom of Sindhu," within the narrative of Līlā.
Vasiṣṭha said: In the meantime, seeing her husband lying ahead of her with only his breath remaining, Līlā spoke to Sarasvatī.
"O Mother, this husband of mine has set out here to cast off his body,
and Līlā stands here like one dead, her limbs motionless. This wife of a hero must depart with this very body."
"O Mother, how are we two to go to that place?
Jñapti replied:
"In such a great undertaking, in battle, and in the turmoil of the kingdom..."
Even when it has come into being, even when it remains, and even when it is high and slow with various undertakings—
nothing at all has truly come into being, nor does the kingdom exist, nor the surface of the earth;
for this world is nowhere established as such, since it is of the nature of a dream.
O sinless one, within that pavilion of yours, in the space near the corpse,
the kingdom of your husband’s life-force appears in this manner;
this very inner apartment of yours has the entire realm contained within its belly.
The world stands within the house of the deceased, even within the home of the Brahmin Vasiṣṭha.
Thus, this great undertaking— the delusion consisting of the three worlds—
is joined by you, me, and her, along with the earth and its oceans.
Within the house of the village on the mountain, inside the hollow of the sky,
the ether-self shines forth clearly, or perhaps it does not shine at all anywhere.
In this same way, even between those two pavilions, though they are dense with their respective beginnings.
In the belly there is only empty space; there is no delusion of a world.
For in the absence of a deluded observer, what kind of delusion could there be in the act of wandering?
There is no existence of delusion at all; that which exists is the unborn state.
In delusion, that which is seen is unreal; for the seer, how could there be a state of seeing?
Since the sequence of seer and seen is absent here, that which is indeed innate—know that to be the supreme state, devoid of destruction and arising.
One’s own [nature] shines forth as luminous, peaceful, primordial, and free from affliction. Indeed,
within the interior of the pavilion-house, people dwell according to their own established conventions, abiding in the Self that has arisen from its own essential nature.
Neither the world nor any creation whatsoever is experienced by them;
therefore, I tell you that the world is space and unborn.
All is the cognition of the void-natured self, like the network of mountains beginning with Meru.
This is not anything made of walls, like a great city in a dream;
even in a space the size of a span, there arise within every single atom voids consisting of networks of mountains that have the hardness of a diamond.
By means of the arrangement of the clusters of plantain leaves,
the three worlds exist extensively within the atom of consciousness, like a city in a dream;
and within that [city] as well, the world exists one by one in succession through further division.
O auspicious one, among those [worlds], in that very world where King Padma resides,
your co-wife Līlā reached him even earlier; this is Līlā who has now fainted right before you.
At that very moment, Līlā stood near the corpse of her husband Padma. She asked: "O Goddess, how did she come here? How did she become embodied there?"
How, or in what manner, did she come to attain the state of being his wife?
Tell me, what form do those women dwelling in that excellent house perceive when they see her, or what do they say? Tell me this in brief.
The Goddess said:
Listen; I shall tell you everything in brief exactly as it was seen—O Līlā, the account of my own play, which brings an end to the miseries of all that is visible.
"This husband of mine is indeed Padma himself"—thus does he perceive this vast delusion, consisting of the entire world, within his own very abode.
This battle is a battle of delusion; these people are people born of delusion.
Death exists here only through delusion, and this world itself is of the nature of delusion.
By this very sequence of delusion, his beloved Līlā stands before him;
both you and she, O fair-limbed lady, are merely a dream.
Just as this husband of yours is such, so too am I myself;

you are seen here as the very splendor of the world within saṃsāra, and thus it is said. When this very [truth] is fully understood, one abandons the referential meaning of the word "the visible" (*dṛśya*).
Thus you are so constituted, and that king is so;
and I, having attained the reality of the Self through the all-pervasiveness of the Self,
am here with these others, mutually integrated like words uttered by oneself.
Thus, because she abides as a mass of great consciousness through her nature as the self of all,
this Queen remains in such a state, radiant with a captivating smile;
her eyes are playful and rolling, and she is graced with fresh youth.
Sweet with her graceful conduct, speaking with sweet and noble words,
her voice resembling that of the cuckoo, languid with passion and desire,
her eyes like the petals of a blue lotus, and her breasts full and rounded.
With limbs as fair as lovely gold and lips like the ripe bimba fruit,
she is a digit of the mind of her husband, who is composed of your own volition;
thus, at that time, she remained within the wonder of consciousness, possessing a form identical to yours.
Indeed, immediately upon the death of your husband,
this very husband of yours was seen before you by the subtle atom whose nature is your own volition;
for the mind itself experiences its own objective state.
Therefore, one knows that the conception of the subtle body (*ātivāhika*) consists of unreality;
for when one perceives this material state (*ādhibhautika*), it is not known to consist of reality.
At that time, that conception of a subtle body arises for another [person].
Therefore, within the delusion consisting of rebirth following the perception of death,
he perceived you by means of this [consciousness],
and you perceived him; thus he saw you, and you were seen by him.
You are established within the self because the conscious self is all-pervading;
for since Brahman is all-pervading, whatever arises in whatever place and in whatever manner,
it immediately becomes so there, and one perceives it by its own power alone.
Because it possesses all powers everywhere, wherever it raises whichever power,
it remains there and shines forth in that manner due to the cause of intense momentum.
By the very moment of death and delusion, these two, husband and wife, remained thus.
At that very moment, this was realized by the two of them in their hearts through the power of mental appearance:
"These two are our fathers, and these others are our mothers;
this is our body, this is our wealth, and such was our former karma."
In this very way, we two have been married and have thus attained oneness;
and the people of those two [cities] have likewise attained reality right there.
In the same manner, there is a perceptible illustration for this case: the experience of a dream.
"O Līlā, by meditating thus, I was then worshipped by you with play;
'May I not become a widow'—this boon was granted by me as well. Thus, this young girl here has indeed died previously, as if she were a petitioner.
"I am the one whose nature is consciousness, belonging to you who are portions of consciousness;
therefore, as the family deity (kuladevī) who is always to be honored, I perform this.
Then Jīvaka, assuming the form of the vital breath (prāṇa-māruta), departed from her body."
Having been drawn by the mind, he reached the tip of the mouth and abandoned his body;
then, at the end of the fainting spell of death, while in this very house,
the awakened one was perceived by her through the conscious self as a manifested form.
This doe-eyed woman, possessing the splendor of a full moon face, exalted in pride and embraced by her lover, desires to enjoy her beloved;

with her face turned forward in haste due to the memory of the past, yet restrained within by her own nature, she is like a lotus-pond at dawn, appearing as if in a dream, manifesting her natural majesty.
*The Līlopākhyāna, the chapter titled "The Manifestation of the Body Immediately Following Death," Canto 52.49.*
The fifty-third canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, having obtained the boon, [she] addressed the lord of the earth with this very body.
"I shall go through the path of the sky to the celestial realm to reach my husband"—
having thus reflected with joy, she whose love-god was unrestrained,
possessing a graceful form, leaped into the expanse of the sky like a bird.
There, the maiden perceived that beneficial [vision] sent by Jñapti alone,
as if it had emerged from before her from the great mirror of her own volition.
The maiden said:
Līlā: "I am your daughter, my friend Jñapti; welcome to you, O beautiful one!
I have been standing here on this path through the sky, waiting for you alone."
"O Goddess with water-lily eyes, lead me to my husband's presence;
for the sight of the great is never in vain.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Come, let us go right there," said that young woman;
standing before her in the sky, she was intent on showing the way.
Then, following after her, she reached a hollow in the heavens.
Like a line of auspicious marks upon the stainless blade of a sword,
she then soared above the path of the clouds, rose into the midst of the mass of winds,
passed beyond the path of the sun, and reached the realm of the stars.
Having leaped over the worlds of Vāyu, Indra, the Suras, and the Siddhas with such lightness,
he reached the shell of the cosmic egg belonging to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa;
