just as the coldness of snow situated inside a jar would manifest outside its walls.

Thus, having achieved her resolve, she emerged outside the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). Possessing a body consisting solely of her own mind, she indeed experiences within herself such a delusion born from the power of her own volition.
Then, having leaped over the nine coverings beginning with water that stand beyond the shell of the universe,
he reached the vast expanse of the sky of great consciousness ahead,
its farthest limits unseen, as he rushed forward with extreme speed.
Even for Garuḍa, it is inaccessible from all sides even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Therein exist countless and abundant hundreds of thousands of Brahmā-eggs;
they are not seen by one another, like fruits in a vast forest.
There, having pierced through a single city situated in the midst [of others], which was provided with extensive enclosures,
he entered within like a worm into a mouth; then,
having leaped over the radiant worlds of Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and the rest.
She descended from the path of the stars onto the glorious surface of the earth.
Having reached that region there, she entered the city and that pavilion,
and stood near the corpse hidden by flowers.
In the meantime, that beautiful-faced woman did not see the maiden there; she had vanished somewhere like an illusion once recognized,
as she gazed upon the face of her husband in his form as a Śava.
"This is the truth, O Buddhavatī; it appears to me of its own accord: this is that husband of mine, slain in battle by the Sindhu;
having reached these worlds of heroes, he lies for a moment as he pleases."
"By the grace of the Goddess, I, blessed, have reached him here in such a state with his very body; there is no one else like me. Having reflected thus, she took a beautiful fly-whisk in her hand.
And the sky fanned that orb of the earth with the moon;
Līlā said:
"Those were his servants, or those were his maidservants, and he was the awakened king."
"O Goddess, what will those who speak say, with what comparison, and with what wisdom?
The Goddess replied:
'That king and all those servants of yours shall [speak] to one another.'"
Through our power and by virtue of the union with the oneness of the space of consciousness,
and due to the certainty of the great cosmic order (*niyati*),
the manifestations of the Great Consciousness will thus recognize one another as mutually reflected within each other.
"This is my co-born wife; this is my co-born friend;
this is my co-born queen; this is my co-born servant.
Only you, I, and she [know] exactly what occurred, without interruption.
"We shall witness a great marvel, yet no one else at all.
Līlā said:
"Why did she not come to her husband with this very body?"
Even when such a boon was obtained, the goddess Līlā, speaking with charming words, said:
"Those of unawakened intellect [desire] the worlds of the Siddhas that arise through the power of merit."

They are unable to reach it with their own bodies, just as shadows cannot reach the sunlight. Indeed, at the beginning of creation, Niyati was established by the enlightened ones such that truth never mingles with falsehood in any way whatsoever.
As long as a child possesses the conceptualization of a *vetāla*, how and when can there be the arising of that [realization] for one whose mind is free from the *vetāla*?
As long as the feverish heat born of non-discrimination exists within the self, [how can there be liberation]?
How then can the coolness of the moon of discernment arise sufficiently?
One who internally possesses the conviction, "I am a body composed of earth and other elements; I have no supreme movement through the sky," how could he ever possess the conviction of the opposite?
Therefore, by means of the discernment of knowledge, or by merit, or even by some excellence,
those with meritorious bodies do not go to the next world by this [path].
Just as a dry leaf is surely consumed instantly upon falling into glowing embers, so too are they consumed.
This very body, composed of the divine, perishes as soon as it is attained;
this is all that occurs through the expansion of the attainment of boons.
Just as consciousness is, so am I—that is the established state of "I remember."

How can that cognition of a snake regarding a rope perform the function of a snake? For how can there be causal efficacy for that which does not exist even in its own nature? As for this experience of "it is dead," which is perceived as false—
This is merely the manifestation of previously cultivated habituation.
When the web of the world is easily understood through one's own experience, there is no delusion regarding cyclic existence;
indeed, such a practice of creation and so forth does not exist in that which is not imagined by another.
The transmigrations experienced within [the self] are as far removed from those who perceive the external web of elements as the lunar orb is from men who do not know what is to be known.
This concludes the chapter titled "Instruction on the Investigation of Transmigration" within the *Līlopākhyāna*.
Fifty-fourth canto.
The Goddess said:
Therefore, those who are knowers of what is to be known, or those who have taken refuge in the supreme Dharma—
They indeed attain the state of a subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*), and not others;
for the state of a material body (*ādhibhautika-deha*) is false and consists of delusion.
How could others remain [in that state], and how could shadows exist in the sunlight?
Līlā, who knows all that is to be known and has taken recourse to the supreme Dharma,
went solely because she was sent by her husband to the city.
Līlā said:
"Behold my husband, O Mother, as he thus departs;
he has set out to relinquish his life-breaths. What should be done here now?
How has the necessity regarding the existence and non-existence of all things come to pass?"
How is it that there is again no fixed rule regarding death, birth, and so forth?
How is the establishment of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) [accounted for], and how does existence reside in entities?
How is there heat in fire and the like, and how is there stability in earth and the like?

How is there coldness in snow and the like? What is existence in space, time, and so forth? How do the perception and rejection of existence and non-existence occur for those with gross and subtle vision?
And how is it that grass, shrubs, sprouts, and the like attain such extreme height?
Even when the cause of its own height remains undestroyed, the object does not come into being.
The Goddess said:
"When the great dissolution has occurred and the state of creation has come to an end,"
The infinite space, which has reached its ultimate end, remains as the eternal Brahman alone.
Through its nature as consciousness, it perceives itself as "I am a spark of light," just as in a dream your consciousness experiences such things as traveling through the sky.
A spark of light attains a state of grossness within itself by itself;
this very [spark], though unreal, appears as real and is known as this cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Within that, one knows that Brahman, thinking, "I am this Brahman."
He creates this world as his own mental kingdom; it is his very self.
Whatever cognitions were described in that first creation—how, where, and in what manner—they remain there even today, fixed and unchanging.
In whatever manner the nature of consciousness manifests, in that very same way it becomes something else;
since it is itself unrestricted, there would be nothing here at all.
Yet, for that which has consciousness as its essential nature, it is not possible that it should be a mere nothingness.
Having abandoned all structural forms, how indeed can it remain?
Just as at the beginning of creation consciousness itself shines forth within itself,
so even now it remains by its own existence in the form of snow, fire, and so forth.
Therefore, it is not logical for that which exists to abandon its own being;
since consciousness and the rest [of phenomena] are thus, this necessity does not perish.
Whatever is manifested in whatever manner, even that which is of the nature of space appears as if it were material.
From the beginning of creation until this very day, it is not possible for that [consciousness] to move.
Whatever consciousness has manifested in a certain way, in the absence of one who perceives its opposite,
it does not deviate from that state by itself through the force of habitual perception.
That which is experienced here, though unproduced at the beginning of the world,
is the manifestation of the sky of consciousness, like the sexual union with a woman in a dream;
it is established that this appearance is indeed unreal, though appearing as real.

Thus is the self-awareness of one's own nature; such are the experiences of beings. At the beginning of creation, whatever continuous stream of consciousness arose in its particular form, that remains even today, established by another as destiny, though it appears to be moved.
The consciousness of space having been grasped, the sky of consciousness has attained the state of space;

the consciousness of time having been grasped, the ether of consciousness has attained the state of time. The consciousness of water having been grasped, the sky of consciousness is established as water.
For in a dream, a person likewise perceives within himself things that are obstructed;
through the consciousness of his own vital breaths, it shines forth and becomes established just as it is.
This collection of unreal things is gathered together by the skillful wonder of consciousness.
Just as consciousness itself knows within itself, as in dreams, volitions, and meditations, so too it may become a bedstead, the wind, the earth, water, or even fire.
[This describes] the sequence of experiencing the fruits of karma immediately after death.
Listen to that which brings welfare and is conducive to the pacification of all karmic afflictions here.

Regarding the established creation, destiny (*niyati*) is measured by one, two, three, or four [units] for men in terms of their lifespan during periods such as nourishment; now listen to that destiny.
The purity or impurity of place, time, action, and substance regarding one's own deeds,
as well as their deficiency or excess, are the causes of human lifespan.
When the dharma of one's own actions diminishes, the lifespan of humans here on earth diminishes accordingly.
In the case of an increase, it attains increase; in the case of equality, it becomes equal.

Through actions that bring death to a child, a child meets death; through those that bring death to a youth, a youth meets death; through those that bring death to an old man, an old man meets death. (MU 3.54.30–31)
He who performs his own duty as it has been undertaken according to the scriptures becomes a fortunate vessel for a lifespan in accordance with the scriptures. Thus,
by following his karma, a living being departs from this world at the final stage.
Līlā said:
O moon-faced one, tell me briefly of my death, which brings the cessation of speech and the agony of the piercing of the vital organs of the eyes.
"What is happiness at death, or what is suffering? And what becomes of one after dying?
The Goddess replied:
"There are three kinds of persons who, at the end of the body, are about to die."

Now, there is the fool, the one who practices concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and likewise the man possessed of skillful means (*yukti*). Having practiced concentrations and performed their exercises, the practitioner of concentration and the one endowed with skillful means alike depart from the body at will and proceed [to their respective goals]. (MU 3.54.35–36)
He who has not attained the practice of *dhāraṇā* does not partake in liberation;
at the time of his own death, this fool, with his mind rendered helpless, encounters suffering.
Contemplating the helplessness brought about by the onset of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he remains fixed in the objects of the senses.

He falls into the deepest despondency, like a lotus that has been torn asunder. One whose mind is not refined by the scriptures and who is devoted to the company of the wicked experiences an internal burning at the time of death, like one who has fallen into fire.
When this entity, whose nature is destruction, undergoes a hoarseness of voice and deformity of appearance and complexion, it then becomes dejected in mind; its vision becomes utterly dark,
and day becomes like night.
The expanse of the quarters whirled about, and the sky became as dark as thick clouds;
the circle of trees was tossed about, distressed by the agony of its vital parts;
the earth became like the sky, and the interior of the sky became like the earth.
With the circle of the quarters revolving as if upon an ocean,
his mind was about to awaken from its deep sleep, as if being carried away into the sky;
he felt as though he had fallen into a blind well or been cast within a solid rock.
His tongue becoming numb of its own accord, as if his heart were being cut away,
he felt as if falling from the path of the sky like a woodworm trapped in a whorl;
he was like one mounted on a swift chariot, on the verge of plunging over the Himalayas.
As if illuminating the cycle of existence, as if touching the midst of fire,
as if whirled around by a sling, or standing like a wind-machine;
or as if whirled like a spinning top, or dragged along by a rope.
Like one whirling in a whirlpool of water, like one placed upon a mechanical weapon,
like straw being carried away by the great wind of the ocean,
like one swept far away by a flood of water, or like one falling into the submarine fire; MU_3,54.47–48.
As if falling into the infinite sky, into a chasm, or into a whirlpool; as if experiencing a state where mountains, heavens, and earth are overturned;
he remains as if constantly falling or as if leaping up on all sides.
Agitated by hearing the sound of the *ghūtkāra*, with the entire collection of his sense-faculties overwhelmed,
all his perceptions of objects gradually turn dark,
just as the quarters of the sky fade away when the sun sets due to the dimness of light.
He no longer knows what is before or behind him, as his memory has reached a state of attenuation;
just as at the end of the western twilight, vision is lost in the eight directions,
so too does he, utterly deluded, lose the mind’s capacity for conceptualization.
Through that lack of discernment, he sinks into great delusion.
When he takes on such delusion, the vital air (pavana) no longer sustains him;
it does not take up his life-breaths as before, and thus he falls completely into delusion.

Through the delusions of perception that have reached a state of mutual reinforcement due to ignorance, a living being attains the state of a stone; this has been established since the beginning of creation. Thus [ends] the *Līlā*.
"Why does this body come to pain, delusion, fainting, dizziness, disease, and unconsciousness, even though its limbs are intact?"—
thus [asked] the Goddess.
Thus, this perceived activity— the vibration of consciousness at the beginning of creation—
is such that if suffering were to exist at this time due to such a duration of time,
it would simply manifest by its own nature, like a cluster of blossoms on a branch.
One perceives [this] as arising from the expansion of consciousness; there is no other cause here.
When, due to the force of distress, the channels abandon their contraction and expansion, the vital breaths depart from the body and return to their own state.

When the winds enter but do not exit, or exit but do not enter, due to their being confined within the channels (vināḍī), then death occurs because of their lack of movement. Or, when the vital air neither enters nor exits at all, [death follows].
When the channels of the body are impaired, one is said to be dead at that time; then,
the consciousness that was previously known as "I must return after such a period of time" departs,
impelled by that very [consciousness].
The consciousness born at the beginning of creation, which thinks, "I must become such a thing in this way," never undergoes the destruction of its seed-potency. Indeed,
the very nature of consciousness is the act of perceiving, which is inseparable from it.
Therefore, birth and death are nothing other than the consciousness of one's own nature (svabhāva).
Just as there is turbulence like a whirlpool in some places and calm water in others within a river,
so too this sentient being possesses the qualities of a living entity— sometimes gentle and sometimes turbulent.
Just as the nodes of a long creeper appear at intervals along its length,
so do births and deaths occur within the existence of consciousness.
The conscious person is never born, nor does it ever die.
One perceives this world as nothing but an error, like a dream or a delusion.
When and how could that person, who is pure consciousness, ever perish?
And tell me, what else could a person be apart from consciousness?
"Tell me, until today, who has ever died? Of whom, what, and how?
Millions of bodies perish, yet consciousness remains inexhaustible.
For if you were the mind, then when that one [body] dies, you alone would have died."
If all were indeed dead at the death of one,
then the very variety that a living being experiences for itself would be nothing but mental impressions (*vāsanā*);
it is only to this [stream of impressions] that the names "birth" and "death" are conceptually attributed.
Thus, nothing whatsoever dies, nor is anything born;
the living soul merely wallows in the pits of the whirlpools of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
And that [perceived world] is itself a latent impression, because the visible object is absolutely non-existent.

Through the inquiry "it does not exist at all," firm knowledge perishes. Having correctly perceived the continuity of the world—both the unarisen and the arisen—as a calamity arising from the fear of existence, the living being whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have ceased is truly liberated; let this be the truth here.
The fifty-fifth canto, titled "Reflections on Death," from the *Līlopākhyāna*. Līlā:
O Goddess of the gods, tell me how this living being dies and how it is born again, for the further increase of my understanding. The Goddess said:
When the flow of the channels is disturbed and a person falls into a state of deranged wind,
his consciousness indeed seems to subside;
for pure consciousness, being eternal, neither arises nor subsides.

It abides in the stationary, the moving, in space, in the mountain, in fire, and in the wind. When, due to the cessation of the vital breath, its vibration subsides, that body is called "dead" and is designated as inert.
When that body has become a corpse and the vital air has returned to the state of the wind in space,
the consciousness— endowed with latent impressions (vāsanā) and having space as its essence— remains right there.
That [consciousness], though atomic, is called by the name "jīva" because it possesses latent impressions.

He remains right there in that charnel house, as well as in the sky; therefore, he is called by those engaged in worldly affairs by the term "preta. He is conscious, mixed with latent impressions (vāsanā), and exists like a fragrant breeze.
When one remains within another philosophical system (darśanāntara), having renounced all this,
then that [system] appears in various forms like a dream or a mental construction (saṅkalpa).
Within that very same location, there would be a portion of memory as before.
At that very moment, at the end of the swoon of death, he perceives another body within himself— one nourished by a jar of bones— while there is only the empty space of another,
together with the earth as its support, the sun, and the latent impressions of the people of the sky.
Listen now to this classification of those who become such pretas:
there are those of ordinary sin, those of middling sin, and those of gross sin;
likewise, those possessing ordinary qualities, those possessing middling qualities, and those possessing superior qualities.
Among these, there may be a distinction for some, or perhaps two or even all three for another.
One who has committed a great sin (mahāpātaka) experiences death and fainting for years,
remaining internally stupefied like a heart of stone.

Then, in the course of time, the Fully Awakened One experienced for a long duration the unimpaired suffering born of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) arising from the womb; having endured hundreds of births,
he passed from one great misery to another.
Sometimes this delusion of the dream of saṃsāra comes upon them;
or else, at the end of the stupor of death, they experience for a moment that which resides in their hearts as something insentient, agitated by hundreds of sufferings, and even as trees and such.
Furthermore, having experienced sufferings in hell that correspond to their own latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
they are then born after a long time on earth in various wombs.
Now, as for one who is of middling evil, immediately after the delusion of death—
For some time he beholds a state of dullness, like a stone within a belly; then,
after awakening in some way or another,
having experienced the sequence of births as animals and so forth, he shall enter the cycle of transmigratory existence.
A certain person who has committed an ordinary sin experiences, even while dead,
a body that is fully formed and unimpaired, according to his own latent impressions;
he perceives it as such, just like a mental resolve.
At that very moment, a memory arises in him as follows:
"Those who, immediately after death, through the delusion of their own great merit, experience heaven or the city of the Vidyādharas by means of memory... (MU 3.55.21–22).
Then, having experienced elsewhere the fruit of their own karma that resembles other actions,
those who possess middling qualities are born in the world of humans, which is glorious and the abode of the virtuous, immediately after the delusion of death.
Those who perform the rite of extraction here behold the body remaining;
then those whose qualities are common, immediately after the delusion of death,
enveloped by space and wind, proceed to the sprouts of medicinal herbs.
Having become a beautiful fruit there and having entered the hearts of men,
they then preside over that womb according to the sequence of births arising from their own latent impressions (*vāsanā*); thus do these *preta*s establish this state.
At the end of their fainting spell, they experience within themselves [the world] both sequentially and non-sequentially.
At first, they perceive, "We have died," and subsequently,
through the offering of funeral cakes and other rites by their kinsmen, they become aware that they have been reborn.
Then [he thinks]: "These are the servants of Yama, equipped with the nooses of Time;
being led away by them, I shall go in an instant to the city of Yama.
Again and again, he beholds gardens and beautiful celestial palaces.
One is called "meritorious" simply because one has acquired merits through one's own actions; likewise,
one is called "sinful" because one has encountered these thorns, pits, and forests of sword-leaves, which have arisen from one's own evil deeds.

"This earth before me is pleasant to tread upon, with its cool grassy meadows, its glossy shadows, and its ponds; it lies ahead"—this is the intermediate [thought]. "This one has reached the city of Yama; this is that Lord of Beings."
"I have performed this investigation of karma"— possessing such an experience,
the vast thicket of saṃsāra approaches him individually,
radiant with the conduct of all things exactly as they exist without exception.
In the utterly void space, the one who possesses such expansive awareness is himself of the nature of emptiness;
though radiant with the vastness of space, time, and action, he is nothing at all.
From this [state], I am directed here to experience the fruit of my own karma.
I shall go quickly to auspicious heaven or indeed to hell from here.
This heaven has been experienced by me, or this hell has been experienced;
these wombs have been abandoned, yet I am born again in the cycle of transmigration.
"This rice plant has been born from me; gradually, the fruit stands here"—awakened by such a realization of the future, he will come to understand this.
Thus, with his latent tendencies (vāsanā) dormant, he attains the state of a seed within that man.
That seed, fallen from the womb, becomes an embryo within the mother.
That embryo is born in the world according to its prior karma;
it may be fortunate or unfortunate, a child of graceful form.
Then, indeed, one experiences this youth that is inclined toward passion;
then, O lotus-faced one, one encounters old age, like a thunderbolt fallen from the sky.
After that, there is disease and death, and again the fainting away of death.
Again, like a dream, it assumes a bodily form through the *piṇḍas*;
it goes again to the world of Yama, and again undergoes this cycle of wandering,
repeatedly experiencing it while possessing a space-like form within space itself.
Līlā said:
O Goddess, just as delusion alone proceeds at the time of the initial creation,
tell me that again out of your grace, for the increase of my understanding.
The Goddess:
The mountains are the solid mass of ultimate reality; the trees are the solid mass of ultimate reality;
the earth is the solid mass of ultimate reality; the sky is the solid mass of ultimate reality.
Since that Lord of Consciousness, whose self is everything, arises in whatever manner,
He becomes fully established therein as the pure Self of the supreme ether. At the beginning of creation, by the analogy of a person in a dream, He becomes the First Progenitor.
Just as it was manifesting and shining forth, so does its state remain even today.
This first reflection is indeed the prototype of all objects;
that which is reflected from it remains established even now.

The wind situated within those hollow places of the bodies causes the movement of the limbs; therefore, one is said to "live. This very principle of sustenance has been established by me in mobile beings since the beginning of creation.
Volition, too, is motionless; therefore, those are called "trees" (pādapa).
This very space of consciousness (cidākāśa) produces a portion manifested as volition;
that itself becomes consciousness (saṃvit), while the remainder is not even that.
If a person perceives the tip of a hoof but not the eye-lid,
then for him there is no life in the eye, nor is there non-life at all in every respect.
Likewise, space is perceived as space, earth as earth, and water as water.
"In whatever way it wills by its own freedom, it knows itself as having that very form.
Thus, the Self of all remains pervading everything— moving things with their moving nature through all moving bodies,
and stationary things with their stationary nature through all stationary bodies.
Therefore, that which is called "mobile" possesses the nature of both existence and non-existence;
because it was awakened by Him, it remains exactly as such even today.
Furthermore, that which is designated as "insentient" and "immobile" was indeed awakened by Him.
Know that even today the insentient consists of stones, trees, grass, and so forth;
yet there is no such thing as "insentience" existing separately, nor is there "sentience.
There is no distinction here at the beginning of creation other than through the universal property of existence (*sattāsāmānyaka*).
Those internal self-cognitions of trees, stones,
and so forth, which are directed toward the intellect and other faculties— those alone constitute their existence here.
For those [cognitions] of the knower residing within stationary beings and the like are indeed their intellect and other faculties.
However, other things which have different names and different meanings are established through other conventions.
For worms, insects, and moths, whose internal cognitions exist within themselves,
those very same [faculties] such as the intellect and so forth serve as their objects, even though they bear other designations.
Just as the people of the northern ocean know nothing at all of the condition of those born in the southern ocean except through their own individual perception,
so too do all things, both stationary and moving, remain dissolved within the experience of their own consciousness.
All are mutually inert and devoted solely to their own conventions;
just as there is no perception of those situated inside a stone by those situated outside,
so too is the non-existent and inert state of frogs dwelling together within one another.

Therein, that which is perceived by the sky of consciousness (cidvyoman) due to its omnipresence and sentience is the wind; it was the impeller at the beginning of creation, and it remains established here even today.
That which is known as the lightness within the head is the ether (nabhas), and therein resides the wind.
"Having the nature of vibration," and so forth, and "that Great One [resides] within all objects"—this is the introductory statement.
But consciousness (*cittva*), in the ultimate sense, resides in both the stationary and the moving;
it is by means of the winds alone that these introductory functions arise and cease.
Thus, this entire universe consisting of delusion— these objects of experience, which are fragments of consciousness—
exist even today exactly as they were during the beginning of creation and other such periods.
Just as the manifestation of the intrinsic nature of all these worldly objects [occurred then], so it continues now.
This which has been told to you is indeed unreal, though it appears to be real.
Behold, King Vidūratha, who is now almost departed,
enters the secret chamber of your heart, which is like a garland of lotuses for its lord.
Līlā said:
"O Queen of the Gods, by what path do they go to the pavilion of the corpse?
O most excellent one, let us both go quickly so that we may see him."
The Goddess said:
"Abiding within the latent impressions of humanity, she proceeds by resorting to the path;
she is composed of consciousness, thinking, 'I am going to another world far away.'"
That which is practiced by one who has no fixed abode on the path alone is approved by that very path;
for mutual desire and mere social intercourse do not truly bind one in friendship.
Vasiṣṭha said:

Thus, when the sun of awakening had risen and the sequence of the discourse on tranquility had been established within the noble mind of the king’s daughter, the aged Vidūratha became one whose ignorance had dissolved. In the *Līlopākhyāna*, this is the chapter titled "The Movement of Saṃsāra and Death."
The fifty-sixth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
In the meantime, the king’s eyes rolled back in their sockets.
Immediately his single body became lifeless, his dry lips turned white,
his complexion took on the hue of withered leaves, the luster of his pale face faded,
and he was convulsed by a mass of sighs whose resonance resembled the humming of bees.
With his mind fallen into the dark well of the great swoon of death,
with the functions of all his senses such as the eyes completely withdrawn within,
he is insentient, visible only as a mere form like a figure in a painting.
With all his limbs motionless, as if carved out of stone—
what need is there for much speaking here? With his palate, he abandoned that life-breath which was about to fly away, like a well-winged bird from a tree in the sky.
Those two children, possessing divine vision, saw him situated in the sky—
the living soul composed of vital breath, like a trace of fragrance from consciousness carried by the wind.
That consciousness of life, being enveloped by the wind of the atmosphere, remained there.
The consciousness of the living being began to travel far through the sky, following its latent impressions; then the two women followed that very consciousness,
like a pair of female bees following a trace of fragrance caught by the wind.
Then, in just a moment, when the fainting from death had subsided,
his consciousness awakened in the sky like a scent-trail carried by the wind.
He saw the messengers of Yama and his own body being led away by them.
Through the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) by his kinsmen, his own body—
though situated on the distant path shimmering with the fruits of karma—
proceeds unimpeded toward the city of Vaivasvata.
He reached the city of Vaivasvata, and was then instructed there:
"There are never any unwholesome deeds whatsoever belonging to him;
he is eternally the performer of pure and auspicious actions."
"By the grace of the Blessed Sarasvatī, this youth has been restored;
his former body, now like a corpse, remains here with its flowery garments.
Let him go and enter that [body]; let him be abandoned [here]," he said, observing thus.
Then, abandoned by him, it leaped into the path of the sky like a stone hurled from a machine.
Thereupon, the triad consisting of Jīvakalā, Līlā, and Jñapti flew through the sky;
however, the formless Jīvalekhā did not see them.
Following him alone, they leaped across the vault of the sky;
having passed through other worlds and emerged from the house of the universe,
they reached a second world and arrived at the terrestrial sphere.
Having reached Padmarājapura and the pavilion of Līlā’s inner apartments, those two beloved ones, who were embodiments of resolve, united with the thread of life and entered at will in an instant,
like two streaks of wind entering a cloud.
"Just as sunlight [awakens] the lotus, and as the breeze [awakens] the fragrance.
Rāma said: "O Brahmin, how did he reach that house near the corpse?"
"How was the path realized by him whose body was dead?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O Rāghava, that which resides within his own latent impressions (*vāsanā*) must necessarily [be realized]."
Since all that is contained within the heart, how could he not attain it?
Who indeed does not see that the immeasurable world exists within the interior of a minute living being,
like a banyan tree within a seed?

Just as a person standing in one place constantly perceives with their mind a treasure situated in a far-off land, so too does the atom of consciousness, which is the very nature of reality, perceive the entire collection of the three worlds.
Just as one whose body is alive perceives the living sprout within the heart,
so too does one perceive their desired object situated within their own latent impressions (vāsanā),
even if that living being is burdened by hundreds of births or enveloped in delusion.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, what kind of body does one become who is devoid of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and the like—
a body for whom no funeral cake is offered?
Vasiṣṭha:

If the thought "Let a rice-ball be given to my mother" or "The rice-ball has been given to me" is firmly rooted as a latent impression (vāsanā) in the heart, then that person partakes in the fruit of that rice-ball offering.
That a living being becomes identical with whatever its mind is directed toward is a matter of experience;
this occurs among those with bodies as well as those without bodies, and never otherwise.
For even one who is bodiless becomes possessed of a body through the cognition, "I am one with the physical aggregate."
"Through the realization 'I am formless,' even one who possesses a body is no longer possessed of a body.
For the reality of these objects corresponds to their mode of contemplation,
and that contemplation indeed arises from the objects themselves as its causes."

Just as poison becomes nectar for a living being through habitual conditioning (*vāsanā*), so too does an unreal object attain the status of reality through intense mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Nothing ever arises for anyone without a cause.
O friend,
be certain that there is no effect whatsoever without a cause, until the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).
Nothing has ever been seen or heard of anywhere as being produced by itself, in its own singularity, apart from [the ultimate reality].
Indeed, it is latent impression (*vāsanā*) alone that assumes the status of an object, as in a dream;
it enters into the relationship of cause and effect, yet it remains as something other [than the object].
Rāma said:
If a deceased person who is possessed by latent impressions thinks, "The Dharma does not belong to me," and a friend, having performed extensive Dharma, offers it to him—
would that Dharma be lost in this world or the next, or would it rather become a mental cultivation for him?
"Is meditation more powerful than that which has a true object or even one that lacks a true object?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Meditation [is strengthened] by the excellence of place, time, action, and substance."
Wherever that [consciousness] arises through equanimity, it is the superior victor over the two.
If the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the giver of merit has increased, then by that [impression], the mind of the deceased is instantly filled;
if not, it is quickly filled by the thought of the deceased.
Thus, in this struggle for mutual victory, the one of superior vigor triumphs;
therefore, with auspicious effort, one should cultivate the practice of the virtuous.
Rāma said:
O Brahmin, if it is argued that latent impressions (*vāsanā*) arise as superior to space and time,
then at the beginning of creation in a great aeon (*mahākalpa*), from where would the emergence of space and time come?
By what auxiliary causes (*sahakārī-kāraṇa*) would this [world] then arise?
"In the absence of auxiliary causes, how could there be latent impressions?
Vasiṣṭha replied: "It is so, O illustrious one; for when the Self is real, [this is never the case]."
At the beginning of creation following the great dissolution, in the absence of any auxiliary causes such as space and time,
this perceptual cognition does not exist,
has not arisen, and nothing whatsoever manifests.
Because of the impossibility of the visible object, whatever is seen here is in fact Brahman alone, existing in this way as a luminous form and free from all affliction;
we shall indeed explain this to you further with hundreds of arguments.
For this purpose, here is an effort; listen to the present narrative.
When they reached the palace, they beheld its beautiful interior, strewn with offerings of flowers and as cool as springtime.
In that capital city, which was the very essence of the commencement of the morning rites,
lay a corpse whose garments fluttered like clusters of garlands made of *mandāra* and *kunda* flowers;
at the head of the bier stood auspicious objects such as a preeminent full water-jar.
The house had its doors, windows, and bolts firmly secured;
the walls were spotless and darkened by the fading light of the lamps;
and from one part of the dwelling came the sound of snoring and hissing breath as someone slept.
With a beauty as lovely as the interior of a full moon’s crescent, she surpassed the splendor of Indra’s palace;
with a charming radiance like that within a lotus bud of Brahmā, she was silent and stainless like a moonstone.
The chapter titled "Description of the State of the Dead Immediately Following Death" in the *Līlopākhyāna*.
The fifty-seventh canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then they both saw her there, lying on one side upon a bed of corpses.
Before Vidūratha, she appeared as one who had died and returned;
she possessed her former dress, her former conduct, her former body, and her former latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
and she was beautiful in every form and limb, resembling her previous appearance.
There she remained alone, her former movements of limbs now stilled by memory, her former face turned away, and her former burden of ornaments cast off;
yet she was beautiful, holding a fly-whisk and fanning the lord of the earth.
She stood in silence, her face like a moon resting in her left hand,
appearing like a blossoming woodland thicket with the flower-like rays of light from her ornaments;
with her glances, she seemed to rain down *mālatī* jasmine and blue lotuses in every direction.
She was emitting from her own beauty drops like rising moons,
appearing like the goddess Lakṣmī come forth from Viṣṇu, the soul of the lord of men;
she was like the splendor of the springtime emerging from its abundance of flowers.
She appeared as if her gaze were fixed upon the face of her husband through her very gestures;
with her face somewhat faded like a night when the moon has lost its luster,
that woman was seen by them, yet she was not noticed by those two.
Because her resolve was true, she did not manifest in that manner until then.
Rāma said: "In that region, having established her body for that former pastime,"
It has been described that she departed through meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) accompanied by the formal declaration (*jñapti*).
Now, O Lord, tell me: why was her play (*līlā*) not described there? What did she become, and where did she go? Tell me this.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Where is that body of play? For how could it possess reality?
That was indeed merely an illusion, like the perception of water in a desert.

Just as this playfulness gradually underwent transformation within Awakening, so too did its form dissolve away like snow upon the Supreme. Through time, an illusion arose regarding the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*).

"I am the physical body" is like [the perception of] a snake in a rope. Whatever is conceived as the visible world—earth and so forth—is merely a designation made for that very subtle body (ātivāhika-deha); it is what is called the "physical" (ādhibhautika).
In its actual form, however, the physical world consisting of earth and so forth does not exist as either sound or object; both sound and object are like the horn of a hare.
For one whose thought arises in a dream, "I am a deer," [the deer is likewise unreal].
When his own state of being a deer has perished, what deer would he seek?
Thus, the unreal arises quickly and likewise the unreal dissolves;
for it is like the grasping of a snake in a rope by one who is deluded.
This very perception has attained a false ascension through the delusion of some unawakened being born of the mind;
everyone remains experiencing their own perception of creation, known as a dream.
"For a long time, his body and self have been withdrawn, like the vibration of the earth's wheel.
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, as a yogin moves through the worlds situated before him, his own..."
"What kind of body is this that is seen as being of a transportive nature (ātivāhika)?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"The attainment of another body from the current body brings about the destruction of the previous body."
For in the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), [the yogi's power] blossoms as if in dreams;
just as a drop of frost or a white cloud in the autumn sky, though visible, becomes invisible when exposed to heat, so too does the body of the yogi.
Or else, suddenly, the body of a certain yogi is no longer perceived by other practitioners of yoga,
like a bird that has flown swiftly into the sky before their eyes;
in some cases, some [bodies] disappear at some time or other solely through the sequence of their own latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Those walking ahead see a certain yogin and think, "He is dead. But that notion of theirs—that the body is the self—is merely an illusion; it subsides through the realization of truth, just as the perception of a snake in a rope ceases when the rope is known for what it is.
What is the body? Whose is its existence? Whose is its destruction? How and from where does it come? That which has thus arisen is indeed stable; only ignorance has departed. Rāma said:
Does the purely material body itself attain the state of being a vehicle for transport, or is it something else? Tell me this, O Lord, so that I may be carried across as if by a vehicle.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
Although I have said this many times, why do you not grasp the answer?
There exists only the *ātivāhika* (the subtle, transmigrating body); here, the *ādhibhautika* (the material body) does not exist at all.
Through the repeated practice of that [subtle body] alone, the notion of the *ādhibhautika* arises.
When that [mind] subsides, then its former [nature] proceeds.
At that time, heaviness, hardness, the state of having walls, and the stubborn grasping would subside—
just as for a man in a dream, through the healthy awakening of the knower.
From that, the meditative attainment of lightness (laghutūla-samāpatti) arises;
just as the body becomes light in a dream through the recognition of the dream,
so too, through awakening, this body becomes capable of leaping like something gross.
For those whose selves have been transformed through the mental constructs of many days,
once this corpse-like body has been burned, they attain a state of existence right there; indeed,
the experience of a subtle body is then necessarily inevitable.
Due to the excellence of awakening, even for yogins while they are still living,
when memory has arisen there, the notion "I am the self consisting of volition" ceases entirely;
whatever kind of body that [previous] one was, such is this body of the awakened one.
Thus this delusion appears, like the form of a snake in a rope.
When it has perished, what is lost? When it has arisen, what is produced?
Rāma:
"Immediately thereafter, if those inhabitants see Līlā, they perceive her through the power of their own true resolve; what of it, O Lord?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
Thus they will think: "This queen is staying here in distress;
this must be some other female companion who has come to her from somewhere.
What doubt could there be for them? For they are like animals, lacking discrimination.
They act according to what they have seen; how could there be any deliberation for them?
Just as a clod of earth, rolling away, quickly bypasses a tree, so too the ignorant masses proceed without even knowing the mountains, fire, the gods, and so forth.
"Just as I know that the body of a dream goes nowhere upon waking,
because it is unreal, so too is this physical body here.
Rāma said:
“O Blessed One, where does the peak of a dream go upon awakening?
Cut through this doubt of mine, as the wind disperses an autumn cloud.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
In dreams, in delusions, and in mental constructions, objects such as mountains and the like merge within consciousness, just as vibrations enter the wind.
Or rather, just as the internal vibration of the motionless wind enters [itself] fully.
But when not flickering, it attains oneness with that very [object], becoming identical with its nature.
No duality is ever found between consciousness and the object of a dream,
just as there is none between liquidity and water, or between motion and the wind.
But that which here is the non-awakening to duality is supreme ignorance;
this is said to be transmigratory existence (saṃsṛti), arisen as the nature of false knowledge.
Indeed, in the absence of auxiliary causes, what kind [of state] could there be?
The duality of the objects of consciousness in a dream is meaningless within that dream.
As is the dream, so is this waking state; there is no doubt about this.
Just as an unreal city appears in a dream, so does the unreal world appear at the beginning of creation.
An object presented in a dream is not capable of existing as real;
for consciousness is eternally true, while dream-objects are unreal.
Just as a mountain in a dream instantly becomes like space, [so too do all objects vanish].
Or, through such gradual awakening, the physical body becomes like space;
those standing nearby wonder, "Has he flown away, or is he dead?
because his own nature has been destroyed by the transformation into the *ativāhika* body of knowledge.
These creations are indeed false views, views born of delusion;
they appear as mere illusions, empty like the experiences of a dream.
These experiences of a dream—these appearances of a manifest creation—are the perceptions of delusion that flash forth within the consciousness at the moment of death.
All these things, arising from false imagination, shine forth within the subtle transportive body (*ātivāhika-śarīra*) in the manner of the death of a mirage.
Fifty-eighth Sarga. Vasiṣṭha said:
In the meantime, Jñapti quickly obstructed the life-force (jīva) of Vaidūratha before her with a mere thought, just as one restrains the movement of the mind.
Līlā said:
"Tell me, O Goddess, how much time has passed here in this palace while I was absorbed in samādhi and the corpse of the king remained?
Thus spoke Jñapti.
"A month has passed here, and these two maidservants remained standing by you while you slept in the bedchamber for the sake of protection.
Listen, O woman of excellent complexion, what has happened to your body here."
Indeed, within a fortnight, the body reaches a state where its sinews are moistened with decay;
lifeless and fallen upon the ground, it is like a withered leaf—
a corpse as cold as frost, resembling a piece of wood or a wall.
Then the ministers arrived and, having personally determined from the appearance of decay that she was indeed dead, they cast her out of the house in fear.
What need is there for much speaking here? Having taken her away, they burned her with sandalwood logs.

Having been cast upon the funeral pyre, it was suddenly reduced to ashes along with the clarified butter. Then, after the queen had died, your entire retinue, overcome with grief, raised a loud wail and performed the funeral rites.
"Now, seeing you here in this world, having arrived with your very body,
it will be a great marvel that you have come from the other world.
But you, O daughter, by virtue of your power of true resolve, shall [return] with that very same body."

You appear with that same pure radiance, and because of it, your mind is directed toward him. Whatever latent impression (*vāsanā*) you possessed regarding the body, that very form has arisen within you; therefore, O child, you resemble your former self.
Indeed, everyone perceives everything according to their own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
In this regard, the example of children seeing a ghost (*vetāla*) is non-contradictory.
You have become a beautiful perfected one (*siddha*), endowed with a transportive body (*ātivāhika-deha*).

That former body of yours has been forgotten; as you lead it yourself, it subsides for one who possesses a firm vision of the subtle body (ativāhika). Even while being perceived, the physical body (ādhibhautika) vanishes like an autumnal cloud in the sky for the enlightened one.
Once the state of being the subtle body (ātivāhika) has taken root,
the corpse becomes like a cloud without water, resembling a flower devoid of fragrance.
From this day forward, when the consciousness of the subtle body has fully developed...
In my youth, my body has become as if forgotten, like one dwelling within a womb.
Today is the thirty-first day since we arrived here in the sky;
at dawn, these two maidservants were stupefied by me with sleep.

Therefore come, O Līlā; by means of our creative will (*saṅkalpa*), let us both reveal ourselves to Līlā so that her worldly activity may proceed. As soon as we thought, "Let Līlā see us two," [it was done].
Then, by the power of that command, the two goddesses became visible there in all their splendor.
Then Vidūratha’s wife, Līlā, her eyes agitated with emotion,
beheld that house, radiant with a mass of light.
Having beheld before her a house that seemed as if carved from the orb of the moon, or washed with liquid gold,
or like a cool flame, or possessing walls of exquisite proportions,
she observed the playful commands [of her attendants].
Rising up in agitation, she fell at their feet:
"O goddesses who have come for my immersion, may you both be victorious, O givers of life! I arrived here first, to clear the path for you both."
When she had spoken thus, those proud women, intoxicated by their youth,
sat down upon the seats like creepers upon the peaks of Mount Meru.
Jñapti said:
"Tell me, daughter, how did you come to this place from the beginning?
What has happened to you? What have you seen on the road, and where?
Vidūrathalīlā replied:
O Goddess, in that place she then fell into a swoon;
I was like the crescent of the second lunar day enveloped by the flames at the end of an aeon.
I perceived nothing at all—neither what was even nor what was uneven.
Then, having closed my eyes whose lashes were trembling,
O Supreme Goddess, I beheld at the end of the swoon of death that as soon as I had risen,
I was swiftly leaping into the belly of the sky.
Likewise, having mounted a chariot of wind in the elemental ether,
I was brought by him to this abode like a streak of fragrance;
here I see the residence adorned by its lord.

While this Vidūratha lies here— his limbs concealed by flowers like the springtime honey-bee in a flower-grove— I shall behold my husband, who is like a brightly lit lamp, secluded and provided with a costly bed.
Then, thinking, "This man is exhausted by the toil of the fury of battle, so let him sleep," O Queen of the Gods, I did not prevent his sleep.
Immediately thereafter, [I saw] that these two goddesses had arrived at this place.
"O you who bestow grace upon me, it has been told exactly as it was experienced.
[The Goddess] replied: "O Līlā and Lalitalocanā, you who move with the gait of swans!"
"Let us raise this king from the surface of his bier," she said,
and as she spoke, she released the life-force like a lotus releasing its fragrance;
taking the form of a gust of wind, it went near his nostrils.
It quickly entered his nostril as the wind enters the hollow of a bamboo flute;
containing within it hundreds of its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), like the ocean holds jewels.
His face, with the living soul dwelling within it, attained that same splendor.
As if a lotus had entered into water when the lotus-pond was covered,
all his limbs gradually shone with vitality,
like clusters of creepers in a king during the flowering season.
Then he shone like the lord of stars on a full-moon night,
his face illumining the palace profusely with the rays of its moon;
he expanded his limbs, which were both tender and full of aesthetic flavor.
Like the month of Mādhava causing the blossoming of sprouts radiant with the luster of gold,
he opened his two eyes— the cause of pure light—
which were as captivating and full of auspicious splendor as the moon and sun illuminate the world.
He rose up with his body radiant, like the Vindhya mountain increasing in height, and said:
"Who is this standing here, whose abode is reddened by the light [of the sun]?
Then Līlādvaya spoke before him: "Let it be commanded."
He saw before him Līlā and Advaya standing bowed,
identical in their support, identical in appearance, identical in form,
and identical in posture; identical in speech, identical in effort, identical in joy, and identical in origin.
Looking about, he asked, "Who are you? Who is she? And from where has she come?
To him Līlā said: "O Lord, listen to what I say.
I am your wife Līlā, who grew up together with you in a former life."
"Speech is as closely attached to its meaning, remaining in a state of intimate union;
this is your second *līlā*, a woman acquired by me with ease for your sake—I shall speak of such a one. (MU 3.58.46–47)
Seated here upon this great golden throne at the head of the assembly is the goddess Sarasvatī, the auspicious mother of the three worlds;
she has appeared here in person through the accumulation of our merits.
"By her, the lord of the earth was brought here from the other world.
Having heard this, the lotus-eyed king rose up,
wearing hanging garlands and garments, and fell at the feet of Jñapti.
"O Sarasvatī, salutations to you, the bestower of welfare upon all the worlds;
O granter of boons, bestow upon me wisdom, long life, and riches.
To him who had spoken thus, the goddess Jñapti touched him with her hand.
Accompanied by the words, "May you become rich in sons and desired objects," Sarasvatī said:
"May all calamities and the visions of all evil deeds go to their destruction for you, and may infinite happinesses arise perfectly."
May the people always be joyful, may they remain steadfast in the kingdom, and may fortunes ever flourish there.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, this is the chapter titled "The Life of Padma," the fifty-ninth chapter.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Sarasvatī, having spoken thus, vanished right there;
at dawn, all the people awoke together with the lotuses."
Līlā embraced her lover Ghanavāhana in turn,
and he, the king, experienced great bliss as if dead and revived again and again.
At that time, the royal palace became languid with intoxication and passion.
The populace was intoxicated with joy, filled with the clamor of instrumental music and song;
it resounded with the deep, humming roar of cries of "Victory!", "Auspiciousness!", and "A Holy Day!";
and its courtyards were crowded with throngs of royal attendants and people who were both delighted and well-fed.
It was accompanied by the hissing sounds of showers of flowers released by accomplished *vidyādharas*,
and by the resonant beating of mṛdaṅgas, murajas, kāhalās, conchs, and dundubhi drums;
it was made intense by the thundering of herds of elephants with their great trunks raised aloft.
It was filled with the resonant sounds of women performing wild, exuberant dances;
it was bristling with various presents falling from their mutual collisions,
and it was beautiful with garlands and wreaths consisting of heaps of flower-crests.
The sky was filled with land-lotuses consisting of the scattered and torn silken garments of ministers, vassals, and citizens, who were dancing wildly with their hands stained red; meanwhile,
the earrings of intoxicated women swayed gracefully as they turned their necks.
The courtyard of the palace was filled with mud from the flowers tossed up by the stamping of dancing feet;
it was overspread by a canopy of autumn clouds made of fine powders,
and the faces of beautiful women dancing there served as the moonlight for the house.
"The king has brought back his own self and his husband from the other world"—
thus did the people in that foreign land sing in verses of such occurrence.
King Padma, having heard this account of events, was somewhat moved.
He performed his ablutions with waters brought from the four oceans.
Then the brahmins, ministers, and a hundred kings consecrated him,
who had attained his rise and possessed infinite energy, just as the immortals consecrated the Lord of the Immortals.
Then Līlā, Līlā, and the king— those great-minded ones liberated while living—
delighted in recounting their former adventures as if they were acts of sexual union,
through the grace of Sarasvatī brought about by their own human effort.
The king Padma attained the excellence of both worlds;
awakened through the knowledge of conventional designations and endowed with the two-fold play,
he ruled an irreproachable kingdom there for eighty thousand years.
Liberated while living, having conquered the mind and the delusion of the five senses,
with an unattached heart, silent, and following whatever comes to him—
of that ocean of grace, he is like a drop of water drawn forth as the moon.

Like a spark arising from the fire of his majesty, which was like the fire of universal destruction, Bhanu emerged. Having ruled the kingdom for eighty thousand years, those who were liberated while living and possessed perfected consciousness attained liberation beyond the body (videhamukti).
That which arose—clear, wise, charming, beneficial to the self, and elegant—bestowed satisfaction upon all people; having long protected that sovereign kingdom, the noble couple attained liberation.
Thus ends the chapter titled "Nirvāṇa" in the *Līlopākhyāna*.
The Sixtieth Sarga. Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāma, this has been told to you for the sake of removing the defects of the visible world."
O sinless one, abandon the density of the world through the narrative of Līlā.
The existence of this visible world is already quiescent; its further pacification is not required.
For the cleansing away of what exists is a hardship, but never so for that which does not exist.
Having perceived that the object of knowledge, which has the nature of solidity, is unified with knowledge in the form of space, the knower remains like the sky;
this world is devoid of earth and other elements, being only the self-manifesting radiance of consciousness.
That which is established by one who is unestablished is neither dual-natured nor truly established.
Just as consciousness exerts itself in whatever manner, so it appears as an external trace; it spreads within the river of creative thought until it is awakened through effort.
This world is understood to be merely the manifestation of the space of consciousness;
within the pure self of the sky of consciousness, even down to the smallest atom.
Thus, what reality can there be for this vain delusion, or what kind of latent impression (vāsanā) could possibly exist?
Tell me, what is *kāsthā*, what is *niyati*, what is *īhā*, and what is called *avaśyambhāvin*?
All this exists exactly as it is perceived, established in this way without fragmentation;
it is simply this infinite *māyā*, yet there is no such thing as *māyā* at all.
Rāma:
Oh, how supreme a vision has been shown by you, O Blessed One!
It is like the lunar light for the quenching of the burning of those whose very stages of existence are visible as forest fires.
"Aha! After so long, this imperishable object of knowledge has been realized by me—just as it is, what it is, of what nature it is, from whence it comes, and when it arises.
O best of the twice-born, I feel as if I am becoming tranquil, as if I have attained nirvāṇa, free from all conceptual construction."
This is a marvelous narrative and an exposition according to the perspectives of the scriptures.
O Lord, knower of all things, tell me this to dispel my doubt;
I am not yet satiated by drinking the nectar of your words with the vessels of my ears.
Indeed, for the Lord who acts out of divine play, that time which constitutes the three creations is, through his yoga,
sometimes a single day and night,
sometimes merely a month, sometimes many years, and for some it is exceedingly subtle.
"For some, is it very long; for others, does it last but a moment?
O Blessed One, please tell me this correctly out of your grace, for what I have heard but once does not settle within me, like water on a clod of earth."

Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one, by whatever means, at whatever time, whatever thing, and in whatever manner it is perceived, by that very means, at that very time, that very thing is experienced in that very manner.
Poison always becomes nectar through the perception of it as nectar;
an enemy becomes a friend through the perception of him as a friend. Such is the inherent nature of these objects, according to how they are cultivated in the mind.
For that very consciousness, through long practice, comes under the sway of necessity;
whatever it manifests as, consisting of a single form of appearance,
it immediately becomes that way therein, because its sole cause is its own inherent nature.
If one perceives a multitude of kalpas within a single moment, then that very moment becomes a kalpa;
of this there is no doubt.
And if one perceives a single moment within a kalpa, then even that kalpa [becomes a moment].
For consciousness, being of such a nature, quickly becomes like that [object];
indeed, for one who suffers, a night is a kalpa, and for one who is happy, that same night is a mere moment.
In a dream, a moment may become a kalpa, and a kalpa may become a moment.
And likewise, one experiences: "Having died, I was born; I am a youth standing here;
I have traveled a hundred yojanas"—as in a dream.
Hariścandra experienced a night as lasting twelve years.
Lavaṇa enjoyed a lifespan of one hundred years within a single night;
that which is a blink of an eye for the Lord of Creatures (Brahmā) is the life of the sage Manu,
and that which is the life of Viriñca is indeed a single day for the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu).
For the yogin whose mind has been dissolved in meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), there are no days and no nights;
there are no objects, nor is the world real, nor even the self.
That which is sweet becomes bitter when contemplated with a sense of bitterness.

Even that which is bitter attains sweetness when it is perceived as sweet. O mighty-armed one, an enemy becomes a friend through the perception of friendship, and a friend becomes an enemy through the perception of enmity; thus the world exists according to one's own cognition.
Those categories of reality, such as the recitation and chanting of scriptures, which have not been previously practiced—

through the repeated cultivation of awareness of these, they certainly attain the state of being one's own nature. However, for those traveling by boat who are afflicted by delusion, [this awareness] turns away from them due to their perception.
Even for those afflicted by delusion, this [nature of reality] does not change due to their lack of perception;
through perception, the empty appears as crowded, just as in dreams.
Through perception, even what is not blue is experienced as blue, or white as yellow.
To the utterly deluded, even a festival causes distress like a calamity;
the conduct of one whose elements are disordered is seen to be like empty space even within a wall.
An unreal yakṣa even snatches away the lives of those who are bewildered.
From sensation, the woman of a dream bestows pleasure just as if she were awake.
Whatever comes about through repeated practice attains stability in that very way;
even that which is non-existent [appears] in the sky, and in the sky itself, within the self of consciousness.
Know that the world is like a dance performed by the shadows of a hundred elephants' hooves spread across the sky; it is a movement of the mind, not a real substance.
It is the formless manifestation of the demon of false knowledge.
This [world] consists merely of the body; it is without obstruction and without foundation.
The wise know this luminous appearance, which is like a vision in a dream, as something entirely unprecedented that has arisen for the Consciousness while it is asleep, just as it does for a man.
Just as a pillar carved in relief perceives the figures of women,
so does the Great Pillar of ultimate reality perceive the created worlds.
Just as a man beside his bed perceives himself agitated by great warriors in a dream, [so does the Great Pillar perceive the world].
Such is the creation of Brahman, which is indeed like the state of deep sleep;
just as the sap at the end of winter exists within the earth, joined with grass, shrubs, and creepers,
so does creation abide in the supreme state.
Just as liquidity resides within gold without manifesting externally, so does creation reside within the Supreme; it is the self of space, leaping from atom to atom.
Just as the arrangement of the limbs is not other than the body itself, [so is the world not other than Brahman].
Thus, this world belongs to the bodiless one, whose nature is space, who is the Brahman whose nature is space.
Just as a dream-war of one man against another man is of such a nature—
neither real nor unreal— so too is this world, which moves in the void, of the nature of space.

At the beginning of creation at the end of a great aeon, this body, whose nature is consciousness, perceives itself as a cause for one another; subsequently, it perceives that which is unreal as real.
If, once this Brahman is liberated, there should arise another Brahman born of memory, [it would likewise perceive the unreal as real].
The memory of that [creation] remains as if established within the creation born of cognition, by virtue of being mere cognition.
Rāma said:
"Tell me the lineage of Vidūratha and his chief ministers."
"How is it that [the world] appears there simultaneously to everyone?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"All cognitions conform to the primary consciousness."
Just as from a vast whirlwind there arise common streaks of wind, so too,
O Protector of the People, by mutual influence do those perceptions arise among the inhabitants and ministers of the realm.
"In the city of Vaidūrathe, those who know the inhabitants say, 'This king of ours was born from such a lineage; he is indeed Kacita.
Yet, for that which is of the nature of consciousness (cit-svabhāva), there is no search for a cause."

It is as appropriate for a great gem to possess its own distinct radiance by its very nature. Even the thought, "I alone am the royal lineage and the king of this earth," was the splendor of intuition arising from the jewel of Vidūratha’s knowledge.
However many beings there may be in whatever creation at whatever time, they all,
due to the omnipresence of the element of consciousness (*cid-dhātu*), have come to perceive one another.
Therein, that consciousness which is free from conceptual construction (*akalpita*) and possesses intense momentum [becomes manifest].
That very [consciousness] attains supreme stability, having the singular form of liberation itself.
Through the mutual persistence of the playful manifestations of powerful forces,
their inherent natures reflect one another due to the nature of the mirror of consciousness.
There, that consciousness, through great effort, conquers those other perceptions and assimilates them to itself,
just as a river flowing toward the ocean absorbs the smaller streams along its way. Those who are established here in equanimity strive by the very nature of their consciousness.
While one might prevail there, the second sinks away;
even as things are being born, perishing, and existing in great numbers,
so it is throughout thousands of creations, down to every single atom.
Nothing is pervaded by anything, nor does anything abide anywhere;
this entire world is the unborn, peaceful sky of consciousness, devoid of any foundation.
This dream appears here, yet it is without sleep and devoid of a dreamer.
And that awareness of what is necessarily so, though experienced, is composed of unreality;
just as a single tree situated in itself consists of the essence of flowers, leaves, and fruits,
so too the all-pervading Lord is one alone, consisting of infinite and all powers.
The unborn state, which consists of the knower, the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and so forth,
is never forgotten by anyone at any time.
Though it appears as the rising and setting of emptiness, as darkness and light, and as space, time, and form, it is the one Reality, beginningless and pure.
Devoid of beginning, end, and middle, it remains as a single, pure entity, like the surface of water rich with the rippling of waves;
it shines as the very nature of the world—“I,” “you,” and so forth—as the sole manifestation of pure consciousness.
Within the expanse of space, there is only its own emptiness; where, then, are the conceptual constructions of duality and unity?
The sixty-first canto, titled "Description of the Purpose" in the Līlopākhyāna. Rāma:
"O Brahman, please explain to me thoroughly once more how this delusion that 'I am the world' arises from something other than its own cause. Vasiṣṭha replied:
Since one perceives all things together within consciousness simultaneously, therefore the unborn, single Self of all is everything, in every way and at all times.
These minute portions of the meanings of all words, beginning with "all," are Brahman alone; they are not separate from it.
In these [powers], there exists no form of primordial matter (māyā) consisting of all objects, words, and so forth.
Just as the state of being a bracelet cannot exist separately from gold, nor can the state of being a wave exist separately from water,
even so the world does not exist separately from the Lord.
The Lord alone is the form of the world, but the form of the world is not the Lord;
just as gold alone is the nature of bracelets and the like, while the nature of the bracelet is not the gold.
Just as the form of a whole consists of many parts, [so too does the Lord consist of the manifold world].
Likewise, for those who are partless, the consciousness of the intellect is of the nature of all things.
That which is the simultaneous perception of the entire totality within the Supreme is this world that shines forth as "I" and also as "this."
Just as the arrangement of lines of writing exists within a stone,
so too do the world and "I" exist densely within the mass of consciousness as non-different from it;
just as waves exist within water that is internally surging with waves.
Likewise, the higher creations are devoid of the meaning of the word "creation.
The supreme [reality] does not abide as a creation, nor does the lower [reality] abide as a creation;
for these two possess an existence that is partless, like a whole and its parts.

Through the consciousness-nature and the self-awareness of the void, the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*) is manifested as its own very form or as the heart, just as vibration is manifested by the wind. At that moment, this atom of sound assumes the nature of the wonder of consciousness.
Just as a thought is perceived within the mind by the tranquilized mind itself,
so too does the wind then perceive its own nature as air, consisting of its innate existence and the essence of internal vibration, just as it perceives its own state of blowing.
At that very moment, it itself attains a manifestation consisting of its own existence,
like light within a sheath attaining the state of manifest radiance;
at that very moment, the Unborn perceives that which has attained the nature of its own existence.
Just as water perceives its own liquidity as being essentially the subtle element of taste residing within the heart,
so too does the Unborn perceive the earth as being essentially his own mind,
with the subtle element of smell situated within it, like the quality of stability.
Cognitions are a hundred-thousandth part of a moment’s duration;
that constant manifestation of consciousness is the succession of the floods of creation.
Thus, within its own nature, it is eternally free from affliction, even while appearing as the midst of the visible world.

Brahman, free from rising and setting, remains unestablished; it is both conscious and associated with manifestation, yet it is equal [to that which is not]. Unconscious, its nature is the form of manifestation, and it is always characterized by emission.
In whatever way and by whatever means the Consciousness-Brahman attains its own nature within itself, it experiences all that accordingly; for it possesses all powers.
That is the Truth, because it is the play of consciousness and because its form is eternal experience.
That is unreal because it has transcended all designations, with the mind as the sixth [sense].
Just as that movement exists in the wind, so does creation exist in the Supreme;
though it is like an unreal construction, it is an unreal construction within the Real, appearing as if unreal even in the Real.
Just as light and heat within fire appear as if different yet are not other than it,
so too the splendor of the universe exists within Brahman— the Self whose nature is both real and unreal.
Or, just as a figurine might be uncarved in clay or wood, [so is the world within the Supreme].
Just as colors exist within a mass of soot, so do the creations abide in the Supreme.
The reality of Brahman alone shines forth in the desert of the ultimate truth;
this triple world is a mirage, consisting of unreal and impermanent existence.
By means of the Brahman consisting of consciousness, the Self alone is manifested as the source of creation;
yet, due to its non-duality, it is not manifested [as something separate], just as a tree is not perceived apart from the seed within it.
Just as sweetness belongs to milk and pungency to black pepper, so too does the nature of the Self abide within itself.
Fluidity belongs to water, and motion to the internal wind;
though established as non-different from the Self, it appears as if different and yet is not so established within the Self.
Thus, creation—which is the unimpeded form of consciousness—assumes the nature of the Self while being the Supreme Self itself.
That which exists as the world is indeed the golden jewel of Brahman;
therefore, being without cause, it is not distinct from Him.
The perception of latent impressions, mind, the individual soul, and so forth, arises from that very perception.
It does not arise merely from the absence of sensation, for that which is not the Self is simply the human ego.
Nothing whatsoever ever sets nor does it rise anywhere at any time;
everything is the peaceful, unborn Brahman, a mass of consciousness as solid as a stone.
Toward every atom, thousands of floods of emanations appear by virtue of its consciousness;
within each and every one of those atoms, there are others—what counting could there be here, and how?
Just as waves and other powers exist both hidden and manifest within water.

The states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth, are likewise situated within the individual soul (jīva). If even a slight distaste for enjoyments arises, then by that alone he has attained the highest state; such is the Vedic revelation.
From whatever one is separated, from that one is liberated;

therefore, who would go toward the consciousness of birth from the absence of the consciousness "I am"? [One realizes] the Consciousness, which is both supreme and non-supreme, unborn, formless, and nameless.
Those who know her, who consists of the moving and the unmoving and the earth itself, are victorious.
(MU 3.61.36) In the supreme consciousness there exists the unmanifest and non-dual [reality], like a whirlpool within a mass of water;
alas, it is by that [consciousness] that the three worlds are sustained—worlds which, though belonging to the Supreme Self, neither exist nor do not exist. (MU 3.61.37)
The mind, consisting of the "I" and the meditation on the lotus-born [Brahmā], expands the universe through the diversity of its volitions;
within itself, it experiences the infinite as if it were the end of an eon in the mere fraction of a ten-millionth part of a moment—though all this is in vain.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Description of the Appearance of the World."
The sixty-second canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Even in the calculation of a hundred-thousandth part of the smallest atoms and the blink of an eye, [the world appears as such].
Thousands of world-ages appear as if they were truly real;
yet within them, and likewise within each individual atom,
this very same infinite delusion appears, manifesting in such a manner.
These successions of creations, being essentially unreal, flow away like the currents of water within a lake— tranquil, yet possessing indistinctly turning whirlpools—
even as they carry along this splendor of creation in the great desert of this world.
Like a river shedding flowers from the trees and creepers on its banks,

the ground of the experience of creation appears as utterly unreal as a dream, a magical illusion, a city [in the sky], or a mountain appearing in a conversation; it is like a mere mental construction.
Rāma:

O best among those possessed of perfect knowledge, when, through right inquiry, there arises such a state of oneness with the single Self within the non-conceptualizing consciousness— *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.6* (as cited in the source)
