"For what reason do the bodies of even those who know the principles remain here, as if overcome by destiny? And what indeed is this 'destiny' in this case?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
Here exists the Brahma-necessity (*niyati*), whose nature consists in the touch of the power of consciousness;
its sole reality is that which must necessarily come to pass, and it persists throughout all kalpas. Indeed, at the initial creation, necessity [establishes] the inexhaustible variety of beings.
"By this, one should always meditate in this manner"—thus it is accomplished as the Supreme.
She is called the Great Being (*mahāsattā*), known as the Great Consciousness (*mahāciti*);
she is renowned as the Great Power (*mahāśakti*) and established as the Great Vision (*mahādṛṣṭi*).
She is called the Great Action (Mahākriyā), she is heard of as the Great Source (Mahodbhavā),

she is the Mature One known as the Great Pulsation (Mahāspandā), and she is proclaimed as the Oneness of the Great Self (Mahātmaikatā). She is the grasses, she is the worlds, she is the Daityas, and she is the gods.
"Thus the serpents, thus the mountains—such is the state until the end of the aeon.
(MU 3.62.12) Sometimes a deviation from the existence of Brahman is inferred, like a painting in the expanse of space; otherwise, there would be no stability for the cosmic order. (MU 3.62.13)

Because she causes the expansion of those whose self is unknown for the sake of awakening, by means of the Buddhas beginning with Viriñca, she alone is called "Necessity" (niyati); this is what is termed "this creation. The unmoving Brahman, established in the noble ones, is seen as if it were moving.

The Teacher, who is without beginning, middle, or end, stands within the Self like a tree in the sky; by means of Brahmā— who, like a series of inscriptions on the interior of a stone, abides within the Self— he perceives the creation as if awakening the void through the principle of cosmic necessity (*niyati*).
Just as in the body the limbs and so forth are touched by the embodied one due to the nature of consciousness,
so too is the body composed of parts such as necessity (niyati) [touched] by Brahman through its state as the Lotus-born.
This is declared to be "fate" (daiva), which is everything existing throughout all time.
Having thoroughly transcended the objective entity, pure consciousness remains as it is.
There must be movement by the object, or there must be the state of being an enjoyer;
"by this it must be thus, by that it must be thus"—this is the notion of destiny.
This very [consciousness] is the entire world, including the movement of the person, the grass, the shrubs, and so forth;
this very [consciousness] is all beings, as well as the world, time, and their functions.
Through this, the existence of the person is established, and through the person, the existence of this [world] is established.
For when both have entered the body, they are perceived as having a single nature;
indeed, both effects consist of existence through human effort alone.
Such is destiny, and such is the union of destiny and human effort.
"O Rāma, you must ask me for the determination of fate and human effort;
it is the fixed law that you must maintain the human effort I have described.
One who is devoted to fate thinks, 'Fate will feed me.'"
That he remains silent and inactive is the certainty of destiny;
and that a man, having acquired enjoyments through human effort, experiences them—
ranging from sovereignty up to liberation— is the certainty of destiny.

Liberation from saṃsāra does not occur even through multitudes of kalpas for those wandering with throngs of bodies; this is the certainty of destiny (niyati). It has no intellect, no actions, no transformations and the like, and no form.
However, it is established that [the world] must remain in this state until the end of the kalpa.
For such is the fixed order: "This must necessarily come to be in this way," which cannot be transgressed even by the intellects of Rudra and others.
A wise person should not abandon human effort,
for it is by relying on this very human effort that destiny (niyati) acts as the regulator;
indeed, destiny is non-human, yet it is that same destiny which, when directed toward creation, takes the form of human effort.
Fruitless and devoid of human agency, yet fruitful and consisting of human effort;
where does that movement of the vital breath go when it remains inactive due to the muteness of destiny and the absence of human action?
Now, if one remains even after having brought about the cessation of the activity of the vital breaths and granted rest to them, then that virtuous person is indeed liberated; what more need be said?
The supreme good is the state of being solely the Self through human effort; liberation is the absolute absence of action.
But this variegated position leads only to suffering for the great-souled ones.
If destiny— which is the non-manifestation of the reality of Brahman— is transformed within that [reality],
which is indeed supremely pure, then surely the supreme goal is attained.
Through these great diversions of necessity and the like, Brahman alone, the universal self, vibrates forth;
it is like the existence of water residing within the earth, manifesting as grass, creepers, trees, shrubs, and thickets.
This concludes the chapter titled "An Inquiry into the Meaning of the Word *Daiva*."
The sixty-third canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
This is the reality of Brahman—always, in every way, from every side, possessing all powers, having all forms, and being the Lord of all.

"All-pervading, indeed all"—this Self, because it possesses all powers and infinite powers, manifests the power of consciousness (cicchakti) in some places, the power of insentience (jaḍaśakti) in others; it manifests radiance (ullāsa) in some places, quiescence (śānti) in others; it manifests something in some places, and nothing at all in others.
Whatever, wherever, whenever, and in whatever manner he contemplates, that very thing he perceives in that same way, at that time, and in that place.
For whatever arises from the All-Powerful One does so in that very manner;
thus, by its own nature, it is its own power, manifesting in various forms.

This web of conceptual constructs—such as "these are the powers" and "this is the self"—has been imagined by the wise for the sake of worldly convention; however, no such differentiation exists within the Self.
Just as there is a conceptual cognition of waves and ripples in water, or of bracelets, armlets, and necklaces in gold, so too is the cognition of parts and the whole merely imaginary.
It is not real in either of these two ways.
For in whatever manner something is perceived, it does not arise as consciousness from either the external or the internal;
rather, because it is the self of all, Brahman—which consists of all forms—perceives its own manifestation here or there as this or that. It is Brahman alone that exists therein.

Those possessed of false knowledge imagine power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) in the form of parts and the whole; these are not ultimately real, whether they be existent or non-existent.
Whatever the mind, being deeply attached, conceives, it perceives all that, and it appears as if it were a truly existent thing.
The sixty-fourth canto, titled "The Entry into the Mind," by Vasiṣṭha.
This God who is omnipresent, the Supreme Self, Maheśvara, is transparent,
whose nature is the bliss of self-experience, and is devoid of end, beginning, and so forth.
From this supreme bliss, which consists of pure consciousness alone...
The living being is born first, and from that mind, the world arises.
Rāma said:
"O Brahman, in this case where the expanded Brahman is the means of valid cognition through one's own direct experience..."
"How does Jīvaka attain existence in that which is devoid of duality?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"The internal Brahman, though appearing as non-existent, exists here in its full expansion."
The body of Bhairava is the expanding consciousness, the imperishable one named Bliss.
That which is its equal, full, pure, and unmarked essence—
undefinable even for those who know it— that is the peaceful, supreme state.
The very rising of that great peace—which is the reality whose essence is consciousness—is a vibration arising from its own nature; that is what is designated by the term "jīva.
In that regard, these [perceptions], which consist of experience, exist within the supreme mirror of the space of consciousness.
The unreal successions of the web of the world are reflected [therein].
Know, O Rāghava, that whatever slight vibration of Brahman there is— like that of a windless ocean or a windless lamp— that is the *jīva*.

O dear one, when its state of tranquility has departed, that natural vibration of the space of consciousness (cidvyoman), which consists of a subtle self-awareness, is the individual soul (jīvaka). Just as movement belongs to the wind and heat to fire, so it is with this.

Just as coolness belongs to frost, so too does the state of being a living soul belong to the Self. That initial, slight self-awareness which arises spontaneously by virtue of the inherent nature of the reality of the Self, whose form is consciousness, is traditionally known as the "living soul" (jīva).
That very dense consciousness gradually attains the state of "I-ness," just as a spark of fire, due to an abundance of its own fuel, attains its own power of illumination.
Just as the blueness of the sky manifests during the creation of stars, so does it manifest within this [consciousness].
Even for this soul (*jīva*), which is empty, there arises such a cultivation of the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*).
The soul assumes the ego-function (*ahaṅkṛti*) through the fuel of volitional constructions (*saṅkalpa-kalpanā*),
or by its own density, just as the sky [assumes] the quality of blackness.
For the state of "I-ness" (ahambhāva) has a form marked by the delimitations of space and time;
residing in the void, it vibrates through the power of volition like the movement of the wind. Having turned toward volition, it remains designated as the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).

It is known by the names *citta*, *jīva*, *manas*, *māyā*, and *prakṛti*. When that mind, consisting of volition (*saṅkalpa*), forms the conception of the subtle elements (*bhūtamātra*), it truly attains the state of those elements; through volition, it undergoes the process of dissolution into the five elements (*pañcatā*).
The mind, taking on the form of the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), becomes a spark of fire,
like a delicate star in the sky where the world has not yet been born.
By the conceptualization of the subtle elements, the mind assumes the state of a spark of fire.
Slowly, like a seed reaching the state of a sprout from its own internal vibration,
that spark of light— due to the conceptualization called "the egg"— attains the state of an egg, with Brahma manifesting within it, just as water attains the state of being squeezed into a mass.

Someone, through the sudden conceptualization of a body and so forth, assumes the state of a body— arising from delusion and consisting of both that and its opposite— just as the desire of a Gandharva manifests as the splendor of a city.
One attains the state of an immobile being, while another attains even the state of a mobile being.
Someone goes forth from his own kind by means of volition (*saṅkalpa*) in the form of ether, water, and so on.
At the beginning of creation, the first-born body arises from the volition of the living being;
having gradually attained the station of Brahmā (*vairiñca*), it brings about the world.
Whatever the self-born one, whose nature is conceptualization, conceives in an instant,
that very thing he perceives as already born, solely by the power of its own inherent nature.
Having attained from the nature of consciousness the state of Brahman, which is the cause of all, [he perceives it thus].
In the cycle of existence, action subsequently stands having fashioned its cause;
the nature of consciousness flashes forth from the essence of the Intellect like foam from water,
and it is subsequently bound by actions like curdled milk by ropes.

Volition is the seed of action; for that very self is indeed the living soul. Having first embraced the sprout, it holds the state of being its own seed, and subsequently, having arisen, it expands the sequence of action beyond mere inaction. MU 3.64.27. The seed, having first taken hold of the sprout, maintains its own nature as a seed.
Thereafter, they come to possess diversity through the delusions of leaves, sprouts, and fruits.
Other living beings who exist in the void itself have likewise assumed such forms;
once the world has first arisen, they take up their station supported by the elements.
Then, through their own actions which have become the cause of birth and death, beings go upwards or downwards; action is said to be the vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*).
That vibration of consciousness is action, that itself is destiny (*daiva*), that itself is the mind (*citta*), and that itself is the auspicious, the inauspicious, and so forth.
Therefore, from this [source], the worlds and living beings arise quickly, just as flowers first emerge from a tree;
thus ends the sixty-fifth canto, titled "The Determination of the Seed and the Sprout."
Vasiṣṭha: For this very reason, the mind first arose in this way;
consisting of thought and expansive in nature, it attained its state while remaining established in that [Brahman] alone.

Because of the oscillation of the power of existence and non-existence, this creation is perceived as having the appearance of both being and non-being, just as a city appears through the will of a *gandharva*.
There exists no distinction whatsoever consisting of the conceptualization of duality or unity.

Through the surging waves of consciousness— without limit or expansion— this very Self, a single ocean of consciousness, manifests itself as the appearances of Brahman, the individual soul, the mind, māyā, the agent, the action, and the world.
Unreal due to its lack of stability, yet real from the perspective of its own appearance;
just as a dream, so too the world, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, resides within the mind.
This delusion of the waking mind is neither existent nor non-existent.
Like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*) arisen from the combination of medicinal herbs,
this long dream called *saṃsāra* has come to abide by the power of the mind;
due to incorrect vision, it is like the vain notion of a person in a wooden post.
Because it perceives what is not-self as self, the mind grieves for itself as a mind,
like a fool who fears a phantom conjured up by his own imagination.
[This occurs] regarding the ineffable essential nature, which transcends all constituent parts.
Through its orientation toward objects, consciousness becomes "mind" (citta); from being mind, the conception of "livingness" (jīvatva) arises.
From livingness comes the sense of "I-ness" (ahambhāva), and from I-ness comes the state of being mind.
From the state of being mind comes the state of the senses and so forth, and from that, the delusion of the body and other such things.

Due to delusion regarding the body and so forth, heaven and hell, liberation and bondage, arise like the seed and the sprout; thus the undertaking of the body and karma becomes firmly rooted. Just as there is no duality between consciousness and the reality of the Self, likewise there is no difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the mind (citta).
Just as there is no difference between the living being and the mind, so too there is no difference between the body and action.

Indeed, action is the body, and the body is the mind; that very thing is the "I," which is the living being (*jīva*). That living being is the consciousness of the Lord (*īśvara-cit*), and that is the Self (*ātman*). All this arises from the single state of Śiva.
The sixty-sixth chapter, titled "An Inquiry into the Living Being," by Vasiṣṭha.
In this way,
even the manifoldness of various women is sufficient to become like a multiplicity, just as a hundred lamps arise from a single lamp.
If one perceives the self as it truly is— in its unreal form— then [it is seen as such].
Having reflected with a mind free from the sense of "I," one does not grieve. When that which is merely mind is stilled, this world is stilled;
for to one whose feet are encased in shoes, the earth is indeed as if covered by leather.
Just as nothing exists for the plantain tree other than its mere leaves,
so too nothing exists for the worlds other than mere delusion.
It is born, it reaches childhood, youth, and likewise old age.
For the mind dances through delusion, [experiencing] death, heaven, and hell;
just as there is the power of alcohol to produce various rising bubbles that are not distinct from the liquor itself, so too is the power of the mind in the cycle of existence (*saṃsṛti*).
Just as one with eyes clouded by impurity perceives duality in the moon and such, so too does the consciousness (citi), when overcome by a fraction of sentience, perceive it within the Supreme Self.
Just as a drunkard, deluded by intoxication, sees trees as reeling.
In this way, consciousness perceives the various parts of saṃsāra as agitated by volition;

just as a child, due to the delusion of a toy, sees the world as the spinning wheel of a potter, so too, because of its nature as consciousness, consciousness indeed perceives the visible world as such.
When consciousness perceives duality, then there is the delusion of duality and unity;
when it does not perceive duality, then there is the cessation of both duality and unity.
That which is perceived as an object does not exist as something separate from consciousness.
Through the cessation of the thought "nothing exists," the consciousness of the mind is stilled.
When you remain motionless, having attained oneness with the mass of consciousness, then—
whether you are at peace or engaged in worldly activity— you are said to be perfectly tranquil.
The subtle [consciousness] perceives the object of perception, whereas the dense [consciousness], alas, does not perceive at all.
One who is slightly intoxicated becomes agitated, while one who is deeply intoxicated becomes tranquil.
This is the state of one who has attained oneness with the mass of consciousness and is firmly established in the supreme station.
The teaching occurs through such synonyms as "selflessness" (nairātmya) and "emptiness" (śūnya).

One perceives this delusion thus: that consciousness (cic), by means of its conscious nature (cetana), is the state of being an object of cognition (cetyatva); [and one perceives] the unreal [notion]: "I am born, I live, I perish, I transmigrate. (MU 3.66.14–15)
But apart from its own nature, there is no consciousness belonging to consciousness;
just as there is no movement in the wind without motion, therefore, what could be perceived by what?
Indeed, nothing at all that is perceived by consciousness can possibly exist as an object of perception.

The wise know that appearance of the delusion of a snake in a rope to be the delusion of ignorance. O sinless one, why do you exert yourself in this disease called saṃsāra, which consists merely of the vibration of the mind and is curable by pure consciousness alone?

If you remain having renounced everything and transcended all latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then in this very moment you are liberated; of this there is no doubt. Just as the fear of a snake in a rope vanishes in an instant without the movement of a limb.
For in this way, transmigratory existence perishes through the manifestation of pure consciousness alone.
My dear, if one remains having utterly renounced that which is the object of desire, liberation is already attained; what is difficult in this?
In this world, high-minded men renounce even their lives as if they were a blade of grass;
how then could there be any meanness in relinquishing only that which one desires?
Having abandoned with an unrestrained mind whatever objects one desires, [one attains liberation].
O friend, remain as one who perceives through the organs of action what is obtained, and who accepts or rejects what is desired.
Just as a bilva fruit or a mountain might appear directly before the palm of one's hand,
so too is the birthlessness of the Supreme Self directly evident to him.
The Self alone shines as the world, like the immeasurable ocean appearing as waves at the end of an aeon;
for when known, that very Self grants the perfection of liberation, yet when unknown, it leads to long-term bondage through the mind.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Yoga of the Cessation of Transmigration."
The sixty-seventh canto.
Rāma said: "What could this individual soul (jīva) possibly be that is unfit for the mind, as compared to the Supreme Self?"
"How has he arisen in this [body], or who indeed is he? Tell me again.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Brahman, the Lord of All, is eternally composed of all powers."
By that very power through which it vibrates, it perceives that [power] once it has been attained.
That consciousness, whose nature is sentience, which the Self knows for itself as the soul of all—
that is designated by the word "jīva," and it is that same [consciousness] which performs volition.
Having first conceived of itself as consciousness (cit) in its own nature as the cause of duality,
it subsequently assumes the state of various causes during birth, death, and maintenance.
Rāma said:
This being so, O best of sages, what is meant by "destiny" (daiva)? What is meant by "action" (karma), and what is said to be the cause? Vasiṣṭha replied:
For here, there exists only pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), whose very nature consists of both vibration and non-vibration;
through its vibration, it is full of joy like the wind in the sky, otherwise it is quiescent.
The wise declare that the "consciousness-ness" of consciousness, when cultivated, is called "vibration."
This state of being free from the objectivity of the visible is known as "the motionless" (aspandana).
Consciousness (cit), throbbing through vibration (spanda), is the creation; when devoid of vibration, it is the eternal Brahman.
The individual soul (jīva), the cause, karma, and so forth, are known as designations for the vibration of consciousness.

This very vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*), which is of the nature of experience, is indeed what is called the "living being," the "cause," and "karma"; for this is the seed of transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*).
When the body has appeared through the power of the manifestation of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*)—which has been made twofold—[this seed persists].

Having experienced for a long time the various objects of volition, the vibration of consciousness (citspanda) attains a state of manifold causality; after a long time, this vibration of consciousness is liberated—
some after a thousand births, some after a single birth.
Due to its own inherent nature as a cause, consciousness, having come together as a duality,
gradually becomes the cause for bondage in heaven, liberation, or hell—
just as gold takes the form of bracelets and the like, or as wood and clods of earth remain in their common state.

While residing in the body, the mind perceives multiplicity born of the modifications of states within the insentient matter; though unborn and non-existent in nature, it views this delusion, thinking,
"I am born," "I am standing," or "I am dead"— just like falling into the midst of a further delusion.
The mind perceives only that which is unreal in the form of "I" and "mine"; because it has not seen the ultimate truth, it remains subservient to its desires,
just like the agitation of a king, the lord of Mathurā, over a low-caste outcaste.
For it was thus that this existence of the world flashes forth from the mind;
everything is indeed the unfolding manifestation of the delusion of the mind alone.
This which is called "living being" vibrates like a ripple upon water.
Prior to Śiva, the causal ground, consciousness arises, oriented toward the apprehension of objects of thought,
like a slight movement of water from a tranquil ocean.
Through its vibration, having attained the state of the wheel of living beings, it reaches the condition of a wave of the mind.

In the ocean of Brahman, consciousness creates the bubble of creation; that slight manifestation of consciousness within Brahman— which is as clear, gentle, and equanimous as the yawning of a lion— is itself, as it were, the object of cognition.

When consciousness (cit) is called "the object of consciousness" (ceti), it becomes the individual soul (jīva); through volition (saṅkalpa), it becomes the mind (manas); and as the intellect (buddhi), the object of consciousness, and the ego (ahaṅkāra), it subsequently receives such designations as "illusion" (māyā) and so forth.
First, the mind, through the conceptualization of the subtle elements (tanmātra), expands this world.
Unreality appears like reality, just like a city of the Gandharvas;
just as one who perceives emptiness sees a garland of stars and such,
and just as there is delusion in a dream, so too is the cycle of existence for the mind.

The pure self, as if eternally satisfied, peaceful, and established in equanimity, does not see, yet as if seeing, this delusion called the mind, which is like a dream. It is said that transmigratory existence is the waking state; they know the ego-sense to be the dream.
The mind in the state of deep sleep is called *cinmātra* (pure consciousness), which is said to be the fourth (*turya*).
That transformation which occurs for a long time within the absolutely pure *cinmātra* is the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*); one who stands firm in that does not grieve again.
In that [Self], all this arises; in that very [Self] it is dissolved;
and in that very [Self] it expands, like a string of pearls seen in the eye.
Because it offers no obstruction, space is the cause for the upward growth of trees.
Although it is not an agent, consciousness is likewise an agent, because the world exists as conscious;
just as a mirror, through its mere presence, becomes the cause of a reflection,
so too does this [Self] consisting of consciousness [become the cause] in the cognition of objects.

Just as a seed becomes a fruit through the process of sprouts, leaves, and so forth, so too does pure consciousness (cinmātra) become the mind through the process of objects of thought, the individual soul (jīva), and so on.
Just as a seed, naturally casting off its fruit and other parts, becomes a seed once again; [so it is with the mind].
Likewise, having abandoned consciousness, the object of consciousness, the mind, and so forth, one remains in a state of natural composure.

Even though there is a difference between the states of non-awakening and awakening— just as there is a difference between a seed and a tree within the seed— there is no such difference between the world and Brahman, nor between these two states of consciousness.
Nevertheless, when awakening occurs, the indivisible nature of the Self is manifested,
because it attains the light of pure consciousness, just as the beauty of form is revealed by a lamp.
Whatever is dug out from the earth becomes, in that very act, the sky itself.

Whatever ignorance is investigated, in that very way it becomes the Supreme. Just as the arrangement of atoms within a crystal appears diverse even though it is pure because of its perception, so too does the world appear within the belly of Brahman.
"Brahman is the entire substance of the world, a single undivided mass,
existing like a seed within its fruit, leaves, creepers, shrubs, and roots.
Rāma said:
Oh, how wondrous is this world! Though unreal, it appears as if real;
oh, how vast! Oh, how pure! Oh, how manifest! Oh, how subtle!
It is the very nature of manifestation within Brahman, a sphere consisting of the mere collection of those elements.
I have heard how this one, who feeds on particles of dew,
quivers; tell me, O Lord, how he turns away from it, how he becomes the self-born, or how he attains his own essential nature.
Vasiṣṭha:
That which is absolutely impossible in form, non-different from its own nature,
and never before experienced, appears as if it were being experienced right before one’s eyes.
Just as the words "hulla," "sabullo," and "ghullāṅgha" clearly arise in the heart of a child,
so too does the state of being a living soul (jīvatā) arise within the Supreme Brahman.
That which consists of the means and objects of knowledge is impure and unreal, yet it stands as if it were real.

And though appearing divided, she is not different from this Brahman, whose nature is expansion (bṛṃhaṇa). Just as the individual soul (jīva), which lives by means of mental construction (kalana), quickly becomes Brahman,
so too the soul quickly becomes the mind (manas), characterized by the perception of thought.
The mind, perceiving itself as mere ideation, quickly beholds its own nature;
this assembly, resembling a fragment of wind, vibrates within the void.
It experiences a state of emptiness, comparable to a drop of frost.
Perceiving within himself that which consists of pure sensation, which is exclusively determined by time—

the awareness of the meaning of the word "I" as "what am I?"— the individual soul (jīva), experiencing the consciousness of his own limbs, perceives the object of the word "thing" as possessing its true significance.

Then, through such a consciousness, that living being experiences the meaning of the word "taste" (rasa) in a moment, by means of a portion of the name of the object for the tongue that is yet to come. From such a consciousness, the individual soul becomes oriented toward the meaning of words.
The manifestation occurs within a portion of that which will later be called the "eye.
That is a corresponding perception; then, because of the perception of its function, it is the "nose.
As long as one remains in that state, the stability of the future sight and other senses persists therein.
In this manner, that individual soul, by chance and gradually,

perceives within itself the state of being a specific configuration, even though it was previously unmanifested. It [perceives] that configuration, whether it be non-existent or existent, as if it were real.
Through the sense of hearing, it perceives its status as a portion of the nature of sound;
through the sense of touch, it perceives its status as a portion of the nature of touch;
and through the form of the tongue, it beholds its status as a portion of the nature of taste.
One perceives the form-aspect as a portion of the eye and as the shape of the object; one perceives the odor-aspect as a portion of the nose.
Thus, this [consciousness] is capable of manifesting its nature as consisting of these very states.

"It perceives that opening in the body which will later be called the sense-faculties. In this way, for the soul— whether belonging to Rāghava or to someone else today— the subtle body (*ativāhika-deha*), which consists of appearances, arises within the very physical body.
The supreme reality is indeed ineffable;
through the cultivation of its nature as such power, it moves as if toward a subtle body while remaining unmoving.
When the knower, the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and so forth, are realized as Brahman alone through direct experience, [then all duality ceases].
"In that case, what relevance do the statements regarding the *ātivāhika* have? That very thing is it.
Rāma said:
"The *ātivāhika* is distinct from the Supreme Self because of the perception of its otherness."
Brahman is known through the realization of its nature as Brahman; for otherwise, it would not be consciousness.
Or rather, since non-consciousness is impossible due to its being identical with the Self that is Brahman, what would liberation be, and what would inquiry be?—thus said Vasiṣṭha.
Enough with these conceptualizations of duality.
O Rāma, this question of yours is fitting only at the time of the final conclusion;
for even a garland of out-of-season flowers does not shine, however beautiful it may be.

Just as a garland of flowers that is out of season, though beautiful, becomes useless when untimely, so too is the speech of a living being; for everything is truly splendid when done at the proper time.
It is observed that Time is the giver of both prohibitions and permissions.
"Is it not true that all things attain their fruit through time?
In this same way, this living self, having entered the state of sleep,
perceives within itself through time the swelling forth of its grandfatherhood."
He who first perceives the Vedas through the consciousness of their utterance and creates a kingdom of the mind quickly becomes one whose intellect is fixed upon that [reality].
Perceiving this very [universe] as non-existent yet appearing as existent, like a son in the sky within his own self, he attains such a state.
The world, appearing like a mass of mountains, expands within the void of space.
Nothing whatsoever is born here, and nothing whatsoever perishes here;
the world, expanded by Brahman, has the form of a city of Gandharvas.
Just as the existence of living beings such as Brahmā and others consists of both being and non-being,
so too is it for all beings down to the crawling insects and the demons;
this entire manifestation has arisen as a mere delusion of consciousness, though it is unreal.
From the consciousness of a Brahmā down to that of a worm, there is the cessation of perfect cognition.
Just as a Brahmā attains his state, so too does a worm;
for the worm, due to the surging of the mass of elements that have taken root, acts with trivial karma.
Whatever life one lives directed toward the source of consciousness and free from the sense of "I," that alone is human effort; in that [life], that alone is the essence, and that alone is action.
Whether it be the creative impulse of Brahmā or the base emergence of even a worm, [it is the same].
When error, which consists of nothing but mind, has perished through the arising of mere discernment, and when the objects of the knower,
the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge are nothing other than pure consciousness,
then the meaning of doctrines concerning duality or unity is like a lotus growing from the horn of a hare.

The false cosmic egg of Brahmā, consisting of the firmness of phenomenal existence, is imagined just as the self itself is [imagined] by a silkworm to consist of the nature of its own saliva. Whatever appears through the existence of Brahmā shines forth exactly as it is perceived.

That is seen as such by those who know it; this is the certainty regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Just as whatever entity has arisen cannot exist without that [nature], whether for a moment or for an eon—this is the certainty regarding intrinsic nature.
This has arisen as false, and it grows as false;
it tastes as false, and likewise it dissolves as false.
Pure, all-pervading, infinite, and non-dual Brahman appears as if impure, as if non-existent, and as if manifold due to the power of difficult-to-comprehend ignorance.
One perceives it as if it were not all-pervading;
through the conceptualization of the ignorant, a distinction is indeed imagined such that "the water is one thing and the wave another," yet this is not real.
Therefore, this appearance of difference is merely imagined by those who do not know reality, like the notion of a snake in a rope.
Thus, because the powers of difference and non-difference exist within Brahman itself as non-distinct from it, duality— as it were— is brought about by that very nature which is non-dual,
just as waves are imagined in water or a bracelet is imagined in gold.
Thus, for this reason, it perceives itself as if it were something other than itself by means of its own self; from this, the act of conceptualization (*kalana*) arises.
That very [act], having attained expansion, becomes the mind (*manas*).
Therefore, the state of "I-ness" (ahambhāva) is imagined. That which is first of the nature of non-conceptual perception is the mind (manas).
Through the cultivation of the meaning of the word "I," that [mind] quickly becomes the "I.
Subsequently, memory is connected by both the mind and the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).
By means of those three, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) experienced therein are conceptualized.

When the subtle elements exist, a structural arrangement possessing hands, feet, and so forth is seen to be conceptualized by the living being (*jīva*)—whose nature is mind—spontaneously, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit;
for whatever the mind conceptualizes, that very thing it perceives, whether it be real or unreal.
The mind, when conceptualizing and becoming attached, perceives each of those things as if they were real, appearing as manifestations just as in a dream.
Within pure consciousness alone is creation; within all things, there is only pure consciousness.
In reality, all existences are either pure consciousness alone, or everything is indeed pure consciousness.
Pure consciousness alone—whether external, internal, above, or below—assumes the state of the knower (*mātṛ*), as well as the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
Because it is eternally quiescent, all existence is eternally established as one, perfectly equal, and devoid of a fourth.
The sixty-eighth canto, titled "The Instruction on Truth," by Vasiṣṭha:
In this very context, they cite this ancient history:
the entire web of great questions spoken by the Rākṣasī, which encompasses everything.
There exists a fierce statue, like a pillar carved from a mountain of collyrium paste.
On the northern side of the Himālaya mountain dwells a Rākṣasī named Karkaṭī; she is the maiden called Viṣūcikā, who subverts all logic, and who has,
by a clever stratagem, attained emaciation through her body as if she were the Vindhya forest itself.
With eyes like a fire of great power, she filled the cavity between heaven and earth;
clad in blue garments, she was black as the night embodied,
veiled in a garment of mist with thick clouds for her head-cloth.
Her breasts are like the form of long, hanging clouds; she is eternally above the darkness, risen high. Her eyes are steady streaks of lightning, her pupils are like *tāla* trees.
The tips of her nails are like *vaiḍūrya* winnowing baskets, and she smiles with the frost of ashes.
Adorned with garlands of flowers formed from the fleshless bodies of men,
she shone with a necklace of corpses strung together with the entrails of her entire limbs;
her earrings were black skeletons twitching as they were possessed by *vetālas*.
With a circle of arms fierce and terrifying like clouds blazing with the rising sun,
her digestive fire remained unsatiated due to the vastness of her body and the scarcity of her own food, like the submarine fire at the edge of the ocean.
That large-bellied woman never attained satiety;
like the tongue of the submarine fire, she once thought to herself:
"If I were to swallow all the people residing in Jambudvīpa..."
Like the ocean [absorbing] masses of water incessantly and without ceasing,
my hunger is quenched by that cloud-like [food], just as a mirage is [quenched] by a cloud;
for that method alone is consistent by which one lives in times of distress.
Who can oppress all people equally when they are protected by mantras, medicines, austerity, charity, worship of the gods, and so forth, and are free from harm?
With an unwearied mind, I shall perform supreme austerity.
"By means of most fierce austerity alone, even that which is difficult to attain is obtained.
Having reflected thus, she, with a desire to devour the entire multitude of living beings,
then remembered a place inaccessible to other creatures for the sake of performing penance.
And she, whose eyes were steady lightning-flashes and whose body possessed hands, feet, and other limbs, ascended that peak like a dark cloud-mass;
there, wearing only the sky as her garment, she took up residence to perform austerities and bathe.
She stood on one foot, her eyes motionless as the moon and sun;
days, fortnights, months,
and seasons passed for her in succession as she remained unshaken by cold and heat, like a rock hewn from a mountain.
She became like a mass of clouds, her form rendered motionless;
with her black hair standing erect, she seemed to raise her arms to seize the sky.
Seeing her, her skin and limbs shattered by the wind, rendered powerless, and shaken by the whistling wind that rattled through the branches—
Wearing a mass of hair standing on end like a veil of darkness, she bore a multitude of stars like pearls; thus Aja approached her.
This is the sixty-ninth canto, named "The Description of the Rākṣasī."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, after a thousand years, the Grandfather (Brahmā) approached him;
for even the fire of excrement, when engaged in fierce austerity for the sake of perfection, dispels the cold.
Having mentally bowed to him, the virtuous woman remained there saying, "So be it," and became filled with the thought: "What boon would be sufficient to destroy my hunger?
May I become both non-metallic and metallic, a needle for the living."
By means of this speech, having become a two-fold needle and becoming imperceptible,
I enter the hearts of all along with their vital breath (*prāṇa*), like a fragrant scent;
through this, I may devour every person according to my desire.
To her, who was reflecting, "The gradual destruction of hunger is the supreme happiness," the Lotus-born One said:
"She saw something never seen before, resembling the sun amidst clouds of nectar."
Brahmā said:
"Daughter Karkaṭikā, you who wear a garland of clouds upon the mountain-like race of Rākṣasas!
Arise; I am pleased with you, so accept a boon as you desire."
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, may I become a needle for living beings—both one made of non-iron and one made of iron; please grant me this boon. Vasiṣṭha said:
Having said "So be it" to her, the Grandfather spoke again to Sūcī: "In the creation, you shall become Viṣūcikā;
through subtle illusion, you shall bring about the destruction of all the worlds."
"You shall indeed inflict violence upon those who eat poorly, those who undertake evil deeds, the foolish, those of wicked conduct, those dwelling in improper places,
and the audacious; having entered their hearts, you shall pierce their vital organs, such as the lotus and the spleen, with your life-breaths."

"You shall become the disease known as *viṣūcikā*, consisting of a streak of wind. You will encounter people who are either virtuous or devoid of virtue; however, for the sake of treating you when you have encountered a virtuous person, this mantra is being spoken by me."
Brahmā said:
On the northern side of the Himālaya mountains, there is a rākṣasī named Karkaṭī;
she is the maiden called Viṣūcikā, who is a subverter of justice.
Her mantra is:
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ rām / Namaḥ to Viṣṇu’s Śakti.
O Blessed One, Viṣṇu-śakti, burn her, burn her! Cook her, cook her! Grind her, grind her! Slay her, slay her! Destroy her, destroy her! Drive her far away! Svāhā!
O Viṣūcikā, *rkhaḥ* *rkhaḥ* *rkhaḥ*! Go to the Himavat, go to the Himavat; live!
*Saḥ saḥ saḥ*; you have gone to the orb of the moon.
*Svāhā!*
Having thus placed this mantra, the great mantra, within the hollow of the left hand,
one should, with self-restraint, wipe away the form of the afflicted person with that hand;
one should then visualize her as having fled toward the Himalayan mountain.
One should visualize the patient as a female crab, emitting harsh cries, crushed by the mallet of the mantra;
[then] one should contemplate him situated in a lake of elixir within the moon,
free from old age and death, and liberated from all mental anxieties, diseases, and delusions.
"For the practitioner, having become pure, having sipped water for ritual purification, and being well-composed,
cuts through all forms of cholera by means of this sequence.
Thus spoke the Lord of the Three Worlds, who dwells in the sky and whose perfected mantra has been grasped by the sky-faring Siddhas.
Being praised by Śakra upon his arrival, he returned to his own imperishable and foremost city of radiant splendor.
This is the seventieth canto, titled "The Narration of the Sūcī Story and the Recitation of the Viṣūcikā Mantra."
Vasiṣṭha: Then that great black Rākṣasī, with horns shining like lapis lazuli,
was like a streak of collyrium upon a cloud, as she prepared to depart.
It became like the form of a cloud when abandoning its tree-like appearance;
it was then the size of a man, then it became the size of a cubit,
then it appeared the size of a span, and finally it took the form of a finger.
Then she became equal in size to a black gram seed, and from that she became a needle.
Then she attained the state of a silken needle, beautiful with lotus filaments;
it was shaped like a peak, as vast as a mountain of one's own volition.
The black needle, smooth and composed entirely of iron,
shone as it moved through the sky, enveloped by the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) and driven by the wind.
This needle was indeed visible, yet no such thing as iron existed there.
This is merely a flicker of delusion within consciousness, appearing like a needle in a dream;
smooth as a needle set in jewels, joined with the mind’s own reflection,
it is beautiful as a continuous line of luster from a streak of lapis lazuli.
Like a filament-stalk of collyrium-lotus carried by the wind,
the pupil of the eye— clear as the sky seen through a minute aperture—
is [perceived] by means of the subtle thread of its own face, with its fine tail-tip.
For the sake of the peace of the vastness of the visible, she has attained the supreme vow of silence.
Like a lamp seen from afar, that which was perceived has come to a state of extreme subtlety;
even from a distance, she seems to be emitting the sky through her lovely mouth.
With her long eyes visible as they were slightly contracted, she was as delicate as a fine silk garment;
she was a playful girl with a forehead swollen from a recent bath,
appearing like a fiber of lotus stalk that had flown away out of curiosity for outward wandering.
Like the channel of Brahmā, she is exerted outwardly, beautiful as a portion of the moon;
her own power of the senses being restrained, she is cast out by the *jīva* as it were,
remaining unperceived like the stream of consciousness (*vijñāna-santāna*) of the Buddhist outsiders.
Like the needle-like rays of a dying lamp, or like the tip of a hair, she is unperceivable due to her fear of the slightest breath from the openings of the doctrine of emptiness;
though she has been indicated as an object for consumption, that [consumption] is of no use to her.
"She reflected, 'This is not so; alas, it is the manifestation of folly! She considered that the needle did not possess the nature of a minute object;
seeing only the activity of the mind, she remained as she pleased."
Without even investigating, that person of deluded intellect requested the state of being a teacher;
for one whose mind is occupied with various objects, reflection upon what precedes and follows does not manifest.
That which is purposeful and possesses supreme capacity undergoes transformation through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

The object [of her desire] was rich with the intended meaning, like a mirror [reflecting] through a sigh. Even for this Rākṣasī, who had assumed the state of a needle and was casting off her bulky body, the great death remained exceedingly pleasant.
Alas, how treacherous is the course of those who are attached to a single object!
Even her own body was cast away like a blade of grass by the Rākṣasī according to her own will.
Indeed, through excessive pride in one thing, other perceptions are utterly destroyed.
Out of pride in her meal, the rākṣasī did not even consider the destruction of her own body.
Even though her body was destroyed, it brought pleasure to the ignorant one who is excessively attached to a single object;
for the rākṣasī was quite content even when she had become as thin as a needle.
Another [power] arose, clinging to that [Self], which is the indicator of life;
it is of the nature of space, formless, having the functions of space as its body,
appearing like a stream of threads of light, and consisting of the threads of the vital breaths.
Having the form of the sensation of a piercing pain, yet beautiful as the rays of the sun through its openings;
it stands as if separate like the edge of a sword, and like a series of atoms,
or like a streak of fragrance from a flower, it consists of the subtle divisions of time.
For that evil mental disposition of hers remained fixed in such a way,
being solely intent on the ultimate reality of piercing the vital breaths of others.
Thus her body became composed of two needles.
Thin as the awn of wild rice and as delicate as a thread of cotton,
she entered the hearts of men through those two slender forms;
then, piercing them, that cruel woman roamed through the ten directions.
By the power of one's own volition, everything becomes light or heavy;
having cast off its fierce body, the karkaṭī fruit assumed the state of a needle.
Even a trivial object becomes highly desirable for those of little strength of character.
The state of being a Piśācī with the body of a needle was acquired by the Rākṣasī through her ascetic penance.
Even for those with meritorious bodies, the bond of birth does not cease;
thus, the state of being a Piśācī with a needle-like form was fully earned by the Rākṣasī.
While she was thus engaged in wandering to the ends of the quarters along with the winds,
her body, having become thick there, dissolved away like an autumn cloud—
either upon some helpless-limbed man, or a drunken one, or a large one.
Having entered within, it becomes a needle of wind, causing intense piercing pain.
Even for someone with a subtle body, who is pure and wise,
once the "life-needle" has entered, there arises an internal piercing pain.
Thus, in some places that evil-minded one dwelling in his heart finds satisfaction,
while in others she is cut away by merits and by the application of mantras and medicinal herbs.
For many years she remained solely intent on wandering.
Moving through both the sky and upon the surface of the earth with her two bodies,
she is concealed by dust on the ground; she is concealed by the fingers in the hand,
concealed by light in the sky, and concealed by thread in the garment.
Situated within the river of sinews, it is ill-fated and pale with dust;
it is a dry channel carved by the rivers of lines, where the fine lines are like withered grass;
it is devoid of purpose, shorn of luster, empty, and yet it causes one to breathe.

In that place, which repels the wind of flies and is devoid of sacred fig trees (śrīvṛkṣa), which is entwined with thick bones and joints, where the surface is in constant tremor and throbbing, and where the delusion of pure white silk is created by the mist of one's own breath; Upon the scars and the tips of stumps rest flies, sparrows, and crows;
on the rough, wind-blown sap that has risen, there are fingers like trembling branches.
In this world, which is like a streak of impure clouds, there are the hollows of wounds upon one's own fingers.

In places defiled by sweat, dew, and spittle; on hills of anthills and mountain ridges; where there was the shimmering illusion of dust and water; where the ground was as rough as the scales of a *ajagara* snake;
and here and there, paths for travelers who were terrified of the lice that had fled from the rivers.
In a place where there are scattered, withered, visible pustules like putrid pools,
amidst a flood of paths marked by middle-lines, within the reach of cold winds,
and where the mouths, nails, and faces of swarms of men are filled with the blood of swallowed lice;
When the yakṣa Dadhatāṅguṣṭha, who can leap everywhere,
had traversed it, the horse— exhausted by its coming and going— remained there for a very long time, like a variegated painting on a cloth or a city of diverse designs.
Carrying her bundle of thread and tools from city to city,
she arrived at the Karatala forest; there,
while resting briefly in a secluded spot, she let it slip from her hand as she turned to look at her oxen.
Worn out by pulling at the face fixed upon the thread, she eventually falls apart somewhere;
though hard, she does not pierce when pressed against the ear.
For even if sharp, one who possesses a base nature does not abandon that baseness in outward action.
Whirled by the needle of the mind, that iron needle wandered about;
though its limbs were not actually whirled, it moved like a stone-heavy boat upon the waters.
It spread out to the ends of the quarters along with the existence of the internal organ.
Like a blade of grass by the power of the wind, she is carried along by the form of worldly existence;
with her mouth, she casts off the end of a fine thread while supporting her beautiful head,
as if suddenly filled with a heart through the effort of filling herself with the Supreme.
As if with the essence of a fulling-liquid, the heart is thoroughly expanded by the needle;
like the fine thread being wound during weaving, it is incessantly vomited forth.
Even when worn away over a long time by sharp [tools], it is filled again without hesitation.
The illustration here is a tattered cloth filled with a needle in a single moment.
The heart has been made fit by the needle through the threads of the fibers;
and its brilliance is instantly ignited like the light of the sun for the very purpose of filling the other.
Suddenly, by that [needle] which had entered and whose nature was to diminish and fill,
she felt as if her heart were being tormented by the activity of a female demon; moved slightly, it seemed to pierce with the very sound of its point.
Worldly activity, even when performed with one's own natural disposition, leads only to exhaustion.
Like a four-eyed needle threading a long strand of thread through garments,
the thread of latent impressions (vāsanā) weaves itself through bodies like the sensation of pain.
Moving with speed as if running when the eyes are cast about,
wicked people who pierce the vital spots remain unseen by their faces; yet,
when threaded upon the needle of the shoulder-cloth, they are seen easily by the eye of the piercer.
"How shall I break him?"—this is the desire of the sharp-witted.
For who, indeed, even if dull-witted, would remain indifferent to the presence or absence of a quality, whether it be in silk or in linen cloth? (MU 3.70.60–61)
Holding a blazing thread pressed between her thumb and fingers,
she gazes as if vomiting forth an endless intestinal cord;
due to the sharpness of her face and heart, she finds no pleasure whatsoever in any sensual objects.
Even when the subject matter has been set forth in the sūtras, understanding enters only slowly;
even if it is very sharp, the intellect is not fixed upon the face of a donkey.
Even if she is pierced, a princess who lacks a heart is nonetheless unfortunate.
Without having harmed anyone else, it seeks refuge in a sharp object;
pierced and obstructed, the needle hangs from the ear-ornament.
Furthermore, like a lovely act of friendliness, it lies fallen upon the chaff, discarded by the hand.

To whom indeed would a friend who resembles one's own nature not be pleasing? (MU 3.70.66) When mingled with the dispositions of the ignorant among worldly people, who would wish to abandon an association that is equal to oneself? (MU 3.70.67)
It becomes like a forge fashioned by a blacksmith, abandoned [by the body] and moving inward;
stirred by the blasts from the bellows, it is intent on soaring into the sky. Abiding within the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, it moves into the interior of the heart-lotus.
The power of suffering is most terrible, rising up like the power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti).
By its similarity and its opposite, it moves together with the breath of equality (samāna); by its opposition to the upward-moving breath (udāna), it moves together with the upward-moving breath.
Established in the *vyāna* [vital energy], it generates disease; it circulates through the essence of all the limbs and causes pain in the heart and throat, swelling, discoloration, and madness.
It generally resides in the hand of a tailor or within the hollow of a sleeping woolen blanket.
Sporting with the palm of a child’s hand as her sole pleasure,
entering the feet and spreading across the courtyard where blood is drunk, she is exceedingly satisfied by meager food— she who is nourished by meager food.
She lies for a long time with her face turned downward, situated within a sheath of mud;
for who would abandon a dwelling once they have found it to their heart's content?
By means of piercing probes, she reveals her own self as one whose soul has been stolen away by cruelty.
For even from a festival, strife brings pleasure to the base.
A single cowrie shell makes the inner self of those in Valabhī feel very important;
indeed, the wondrous display of egoism in living beings is difficult to eradicate.

By means of obtaining a pair of white garments and by taking [them] with oneself, one brings about the death of men through a wondrous act; for delusion does not arise regarding one's own purpose. Through the separation of the threads of my garment, may there be a swift and supreme destruction.
When this is accomplished, she becomes utterly stainless.
Just as a needle, when set aside without being sharpened, takes on rust,
so too does disease arise for her due to the absence of piercing by another.
Subtle, piercing, and causing forgetfulness in an instant,
she is sharp, divisive, and cruel like a divine needle;
she is satisfied merely by piercing the thread, thinking, "Another has been struck."
By that very means by which he was destroyed, the wicked man recognizes his own evil nature.

He sinks in mud, he travels through the sky, he sports with the winds of the atmosphere, he lies on the edges of the quarters, in dust, on the ground, on the road, in a house, in a marketplace, in a forest, or in the inner apartments.
In the hand, in the soft lotus-ear, in the soft cheek, in the cavity, in the heart of wood and clay, and in the hollow of a tube—
that very same reality of the substance exists there.
Vālmīki:

When the sage had spoken thus, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun. The Chapter on the Needle, titled "Description of the Needle’s Conduct."
The seventy-first canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, after a long time, that Rākṣasī named Karkaṭī—
She surely attained satisfaction from all the human flesh;
yet it is said that she was already satiated by a single drop of blood on the previous day.
For what can fit inside a needle? But the needle of craving is difficult to fill.
He thought: "Alas, what misery! Why has this happened?
I have become subtle and my power is destroyed; even a morsel does not fit within me.
Where have those broad limbs of mine gone, O evil-minded one?"

Like the play of dark clouds in the forest, they have withered away like fallen leaves; yet within me, this unfortunate woman, not even a slight taste of savory meat broth or liquor scented with fat finds any room.
I am sinking deep within the mud; I fall upon the surface of the earth.
I am struck down by the floods of people and crushed by bandits.
Alas! I am destroyed, I am without a protector, without comfort, and without refuge.
I sink from sorrow into sorrow, and from calamity into further calamity.
I have no friend, no servant, no mother, and no father;
I have no kinsman, no dependent, no brother, and no son.
I have no body, no place, and no one to rely upon;
finding no comfort in staying in one spot, I wander like a leaf in the forest.
I stand at the forefront of calamities and am settled in a most dreadful state.
I long for non-existence, yet even that does not come to pass for me. My own body was abandoned by me with a deluded mind,
like a fool who, with the notion that it is mere glass, lets the wish-fulfilling gem fall from his hand.
Striking down the delusion of the mind, it first delivers a blow; afterwards, it expands in the form of a vast proliferation of misfortunes.
I have fallen asleep among the chaff and have been tossed about upon the paths.
Sent into wounds within, alas, what a succession of my miseries!
Constantly performing the service of others, always wandering on the errands of others, I have fallen into extreme wretchedness; I have become subject to the will of others.
I perform this service as one who is utterly insignificant, yet even that takes the form of piercing pain!
Alas, for me of such meager fortune, even misfortune is difficult to obtain;
for while I am performing my peace-offering, a massive vetāla has arisen.
"The total destruction [of my merit] has arisen for me because I engaged in taking wealth.
"Why did I, blinded by passion, abandon that great body? Or rather, an inauspicious thought arises in such a way that it must inevitably lead to destruction."
Who indeed will rescue me, who am half-burnt, diminished even below a tiny insect,
and lost amidst heaps of dust?
Where can those of ruined hopes appear in the intellect of those whose minds are solitary?
Like grass along a village path for those dwelling upon a mountain,
how could there be any prosperity for the awakening of the ignorant?
Even the slightest radiance does not arise for one who follows after fireflies.
Therefore, I do not know for how long I shall have to wallow in the pits of the abyss of misfortune, my hopes destroyed. When shall I become like the daughter of the great mountain Añjana?
She assumes the form of beryl pillars for heaven and earth;
her arms are like rows of clouds, her eyes are flashes of steady lightning,
her garment is a veil of mist, and her hair is high-tufted and dark as the sky.
With her peacock-feathered crest dancing at the sight of the cloud-like belly of Lambodara,
she had pendulous, swaying breasts; wine flowed from her dark body,
and the mass of ashes from her laughter covered and obscured the orb of the sun.
Assuming a singular form intent upon the act of devouring the Destroyer at the end of time,
she carries a pestle, a mortar, a grass mat, a winnowing basket, and garlands of flowers;
she sports from mountain to mountain, placing her foot upon each peak.
When shall that great belly of mine become radiant with its wide caverns?
When shall my row of claws become thick like clouds of refuge? When shall my smile bring about the flight of the great rākṣasas?
When, intoxicated, shall I dance in the great forest with my own buttocks and other limbs?
When, with great jars of fat and liquor, and heaps of dead flesh and bones,
shall I bring an end to the filling of my sweet belly?
When, having drunk the blood of the great world,
shall I become intoxicated and dance with rising joy, only then to be sealed by sleep? Having myself burned that radiant body in the fire of austerity, [I shall attain that state].
The state of being reduced to ashes has been accepted by gold, just as the state of being a mere needle has been accepted [by iron].
Where, indeed, is that body which resembles a mountain of collyrium and fills the horizons?
And where is this state of being a needle, as fragile as grass and like the hoofprint of a mouse?
The ignorant man quickly casts away the earth even after obtaining a golden bracelet;
thus, out of greed, I have cast away my radiant body which I had revealed.
Alas, Mahodara! [My body] was like a cave of mist upon the Vindhya mountains.
Today you do not bring an end to the lions, deer, and elephants— how is this?
Alas, O arms, with your tips bent by the weight of the *bhara* bow and possessing nails like the moon,
why do you not today rush toward the moon with the thought that it is a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)?
Alas, O chest, as beautiful as the slopes of the great mountains of crystal and lapis lazuli!
Today, that abode of lions and other beasts has been replaced by you with a forest of hair.
Alas, O eyes, radiant like a dry forest ablaze under the black night!
"Why do you not adorn the quarters with the garland of flames from your eyes? Alas, O friend of my shoulder, you are lost; you have fallen upon the surface of the earth!
You have been overtaken by Time; you have been crushed within the belly of a rock."

Alas, O moon of a face! Why do you not today [shine] with the rays of your teeth, you who are as captivating as the lunar orb when it has been extinguished by the fire at the end of an aeon? Alas, alas! Where have those two great hands of mine gone today?
"Am I now truly accomplished? Am I like a needle, a fly, or a hoof-print?
Alas! O Bhagīrathī, rich with fierce *karañja* trees, beautiful with pleasant horse-tracks;
O Vindhya mountain, with vast forest slopes and pure orb-like forms!

Where is this form that fills the sky, and where is this new body as empty as a needle? Where is the cavity of its mouth, equal to the space between heaven and earth, and where is this needle-pointed opening?
Where is the mouthful thick with a great mass of flesh, and where is the blocking by a single drop of water? Oh, how this subtle face has been fashioned by me alone!
The Drama of the Destruction of One’s Own Self.
The seventy-second canto, titled "The Lamentation of Viṣūcikā."
Vasiṣṭha, having reflected upon those words that had been uttered, conceived this plan:
"I shall quickly become an ascetic woman once again in order to regain that body."
Having reflected thus, she withdrew that murderous intent fixed upon living beings and went to that very peak of the Himalayas to practice steady austerity. There,
she perceived within her own mind that state of being a needle.
Consisting of the vital breaths and having entered by means of those very breaths, she killed the man;
then, appearing as a needle within his own self,
she whose body was composed of vital breath and wind went to the peak of the Himalayas.
There, in that place where a fierce forest fire raged, devoid of all living beings,
parched by the agitation of great boulders and grey with dust,
she stood alone upon a vast, grassless expanse.
Suddenly, like a dry tuft of grass in a desert, she withered away;
having resorted to only one subtle quarter along with its half,
she began to perform the penance of her own self-awareness, which consists of that single-quartered self.
With the soles of her feet, she has barely prevented this earth from being covered with dust;
holding her steps back with effort, she stands with her face turned upward. Her blackness, ferocity, heat, and sharpness are like those of serpents that feed on wind.
Striving with effort to place her foot amidst the gravel, dust,
and pebbles, she imitated a female serpent agitated in the forest, who has risen to see from afar and is swaying her tail as she stands upon its tip.
The ray of the sun, emerging from the aperture of her mouth,
became her companion— shining like a needle— and remained as her sole protector at her back.
Even toward one who has become a lowly kinsman, people extend affection.
Even by Dīdhitī, her conduct as a friend was indicated by the needle she had pointed out;
for that second ascetic woman who had been so pure became like a stained needle, rendered impure by her afterwards.
Her eyes, which had been narrowed with a smile at the sight of the sunbeams emerging from the needle's eye,
were later seen by her to have been directed toward nothing but the dust there;
even that dust which she beheld was itself seen by the trees, creepers, and other things.
Who would not long to see Sūcī, the great ascetic?
As she stood there with her feet firmly planted and her disposition as noble as a flower,
the winds agitated her with whistling sounds issuing from their mouths.
"Having been swallowed by her, we shall soon be born as the flower-dust within her"— thinking thus, they filled her mouth with pollen. The dust,
driven by the wind sent by Indra to carry away her ascetic merit, was like sacrificial meat.
But because of her lack of greed, she did not swallow them even though they were in her mouth;
firm in her resolve, she did not consume those particles of dust.
For even small things achieve their purpose through internal essence.
Even the pollen of flowers did not enter her mouth;
the wind was struck with wonder greater than that of uprooting Mount Sumeru.
Her head was covered with mud, even though she was filled with great waters.
Though shaken by mighty winds, though terrified by the flashes of lightning,
though covered in dust by the clouds, and though agitated by the thundering of the sky,
she remained firm in her resolve within her mind for thousands of years.

Like one asleep upon a silken pillow, the ascetic woman did not tremble. Then, when external movement had ceased and time had not yet returned, she reflected upon her own self-nature as conscious awareness.
The light of knowledge arose, which perceives both the higher and the lower;
it became pure, the supreme, purifying needle of consciousness.
Through that very intellect, she herself became one who has known what is to be known.
"When evil deeds are exhausted through austerity, the needle shall indicate its own face.
Thus she performed severe austerity for thousands of years,
facing upward, causing distress to the seven great worlds.
By her asceticism, which was as terrible as the fire at the end of an aeon, Mount Himavat became ablaze;
because of that, the entire world seemed to burn.
Then Vāsava [thought], "Whose asceticism has thus overwhelmed the world?"
He questioned Nārada, and he told him this:
"For seven thousand years, that long-practicing ascetic woman remained with a needle [in her body];
having realized the nature of her own body, she caused this world to blaze."
The *nāgas* hiss, the mountains split asunder, the celestial chariots of the *vaimānika* gods fall, and the clouds and oceans vanish;
the quarters of the sky, along with the sun, go to desiccation and become darkened. O Indra, behold this destruction brought about by the power of asceticism alone!
This is the chapter titled "The Power of Sūcī’s Asceticism."
The seventy-third canto:
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard the entire account of Karkaṭīka’s harsh conduct, Vāsava—
Śakra, his curiosity aroused once again, questioned Nārada:
"Having acquired that state of being a Piśācī with needle-like limbs through ascetic penance, by her— "
"O Sage, what powers were enjoyed by Karkaṭī in the lap of the Himalayas?
Nārada replied:
"Jīvasūcī became a Piśācī; she was as delicate as a grain of millet."
There was an iron needle; its own support was that self.
Having abandoned that support of the self, she—seated upon a chariot of ether and wind—entered the body by way of the path of the vital breath.
Within all the intestinal cords, sinews, fat, and blood,
she of the soiled limbs has settled inside like a bird within its nest;
and whichever channel a particular wind does not fill, she has entered that very one.
There, a stake was driven into the ground, as prominent as the top of a banyan tree.
With his body and senses, he likewise consumed those and many other human flesh dishes that were suitable for food.
With her many garlands disarrayed as she slept, her young face charming, and her cheeks marked by leaf-patterns pressed against the chest of her lover,
she was sported in the sorrowless forest paths by the female bird.
In rows of clouds arising from the flowers of the wish-fulfilling trees,
he drank the intoxicating liquor of the drops of nectar from the fragrant *mandāra* blossoms;
and in the groves of the celestial mountains, he was accompanied by swarms of bees nestled among the bees.
The chewed-off limbs of corpses were [seized] by the extreme greed of the vultures,
as if by a swift horse in battle with a sword-blade for its staff;
they were drawn into all the channels of the body's cavities, like streaks of wind through the quarters of the sky.
Like a crow in the pathways of the sky, she flies upward and downward;
just as the vital breaths, which are masses of wind, quiver in the void within the heart of the Virāj-self,
so too does she quiver in every bodily abode.
It has wandered through the bodies of all living beings due to the perversion of its conscious power (*cicchakti*),
like a lamp-light illuminating within one's own homes;
it has sported amidst the bloods, like the fluidity inherent in waters.
It surged within his bellies like the turning of whirlpools in the oceans;
it slept within his pure fat as Śauri sleeps upon his remaining limbs.
The fragrance of raw flesh was tasted within him, like nectar by the power of the wind.

"May I become a needle made of living beings," she thought with a low desire, as she beheld the trees, shrubs, herbs, and other plants— already enjoyed by the splendor of the forest breeze dwelling in her heart— and rendered powerless by that very act of consumption.

The mental needle was perfected— conscious, purifying, and sharp. By means of that invisible [needle], with the fierce wind as its swift horse and the iron needle as its dwelling, it roamed through the quarters, obstructing them.
Drinking, eating, sporting, laughing, giving, taking,
dancing, singing, and dwelling— all these were performed by infinite embodied beings through that invisible,
corporeal [power] whose body is mind and wind.
Nothing exists that cannot be accomplished by her, who is like the nature of space;
yet, being intoxicated and powerless, she has failed to chew the sweet-tasting morsels.
Like a female elephant tied to a post, this girl has merely tossed about in vain.
In the wicked rivers of the body, which abound with surging waves and are utterly deficient,
she— who causes distress through her violent currents— acts like a mad crocodile; yet,
being powerless to swallow the fat and flesh within the heart, she remains there.

Like a dancer who has long performed on the stage, repeatedly bending her limbs one after another, the intellect— distressed for a very long time by the thoughts of the wealthy, the aged, the sick, and the wise— has danced within the hearts of elephants, camels, deer, elephants, horses, lions, and the like.
By means of this [consciousness], which follows the unity of the winds both externally and internally,
and which is difficult to perceive as it abides within like a trail of fragrance,
she is rendered beneficial through mantras, medicinal herbs, austerity, charity, worship of the gods, and so forth.
Driven away like the high waves of a mountain river in spate,
her course unperceived like the flame of a lamp, she quickly vanishes;
O Mother, she finds rest there as if upon an iron needle.
Everyone seeks a refuge according to their own latent tendencies (*vāsanā*);
the very state of being a demoness was made into a refuge by her through the state of being a demoness.
Even after wandering through all directions, everyone returns to their own home in times of distress.
A dull-witted person approaches the iron needle as if it were the living needle.
Thus, though she strove and wandered through the ten directions,
she attained mental satisfaction, but never physical.
For properties can exist here only when there is a substratum (dharmin), not when it is absent;
indeed, that [pleasure] belongs to one whose body is seen to be satiated.
Now, if that [pleasure] arises from the recollection of a previous satiated body, [then...]
She became sorrowful, longing for the happiness of a belly filled with sweet food;
then, thinking, "I shall perform extensive austerity for the sake of my former body," she determined a place for her asceticism by herself.
She entered the heart of that young sky-vulture through the path of the vital breath,
like a doe moving playfully through the air.
That vulture [saw] her, having thus taken refuge within an iron needle.
Urged by her with her beak, he took up his activity as if it were his mind;
taking a needle, that vulture went to the mountain she had thought of,
swiftly driven from within by the ogress-like needle like a cloud by the wind.
There, in that desolate great forest, he placed her—
just as a yogi places his consciousness in a state free from all conceptual constructions—
at the tip of that single, minute toe, where she remained unconscious.
Like a deity established upon the summit of a mountain by a vulture,
she stood with one foot on a single grain of dust atop her massive peak,
her neck uplifted like a crest upon the mountain’s head.
Seeing the life-needle (jīvasūcikā) that had been inserted and left standing upright within the vulture,
it began to emerge from the bird's body to go outside;
with its consciousness turned upward, the needle departed along with the vulture's life-breaths.
Like a streak of fragrance carried by the wind, directed toward the breeze of the sense of smell,
the vulture went to its own place, like a porter who has laid down his burden;
he became free from inner agitation, as if his disease had been cured.
A support has been devised for the sake of austerity by one who is indicated as being iron;
indeed, the employment of objects befits one who is firm, for it shines forth. For truly, actions do not succeed for that which is formless without a support.
Thus, relying on her exclusive devotion to her support, she remained steadfast in her asceticism;
like a living needle piercing an iron needle, or a female spirit encircling a *śiṃśapā* tree,
she surrounded him on all sides, just as a whirlwind encircles a trail of fragrance.
From that time forward, O Śakra, this long-suffering needle remained in the vast forest for many groups of years;
therefore, O you who are skilled in what must be done, exert yourself for the sake of her boon.
"For that ascetic power, accumulated over a long time, is indeed sufficient to burn up the world.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Having heard this from Nārada, Śakra, while looking at the needle,"
Then he dispatched the wind throughout the ten directions of the horizon. Thereupon, the Wind, having become conscious of himself, went to behold her;
leaving the path of the sky, he moved about with great haste.
That consciousness, swift as the wind and indeed not limited by being all-pervasive, suddenly beheld, without obstruction,
the vast expanse of the earth extending to the seven oceans.
The Lokāloka mountain, whose rocks consist of various jewels;
the ring of the ocean of sweet water, together with the range of mountains at the edge of the quarters;
and the ring of Puṣkara-dvīpa, containing within it a circle of mountains.
The ocean-ring of wine, inhabited by aquatic creatures,
forms the perimeter of that [continent], while the Gomedha island serves as its boundary; within it lies a multitude of regions,
surrounded by the moat of the sugarcane-water ocean and containing various internal mountain ranges.
Krauñcadvīpa is the excellent seat (pīṭha), containing the sequence of internal mountains;
it has a necklace of pearls from the Ocean of Milk with a central gem,
and is encircled by the island called Śveta, which possesses the various elemental divisions.
The earth has an ocean of clarified butter as its surrounding moat, containing within it the abode of the immortals;
