it possesses the extent of the boundary of Kuśadvīpa and the hollows of vast great mountains; it is girt by an ocean of curds, containing within it the cities of the spies.
Śākadvīpa has the shape of a barley grain and contains its internal regions up to the edge;
it is surrounded by an ocean of salt water, containing cities and mountains up to its boundary,
and holds Jambudvīpa’s great Mount Meru crowded with the principal mountain ranges.
First, the wind-waves fall from the masses of wind;
by this sequence, they spread forth here at the edge by that very same process.
Thus the wind, having looked upon Jambudvīpa, gazes [further].
He reached that peak of the Himalayas where the ascetic Sūci was;
on the great and formidable summit, he entered that vast wilderness which,
like a second sky, was devoid of the activities of living beings.
Because of its proximity to the sun, it was devoid of any growth of grass and spread out entirely as dust, like the structure of *saṃsāra*;
it had reached the state of an ocean to be filled by the caravan of rivers from a mirage.
Resembling Indra’s bow and possessing the likeness of a river of mirage,
it was immeasurable at its edges and horizons, watched over by the world-protectors,
and contained nothing but circles of dust stirred by the movement of the wind.
Smeared with the saffron of the sun’s rays and anointed with the sandalwood paste of the moon’s beams,
she was like a playful woman of the sky singing the song of the wind’s whistling; meanwhile,
the wind traveled by a long path, wandering all around the surface of the earth which rests upon a single swelling portion sealed by the seven islands and oceans.

Worn out by old age, having reached that peak of the foremost mountain which seemed as if clinging to the sky with its body of bees, he— possessing a massive frame that filled the infinite quarters of space—
rested there.
The seventy-fourth canto, titled "The Description of the Ripening of the Needle-like Austerity," by Vasiṣṭha.
There, upon the great forested summit of that mountain with its upward-pointing peaks,
he saw her standing in the center, like a needle rising up with a flame;
performing penance on one foot for a long time, she was withering away as she drank in the heat.
Her skin was withered by constant fasting, and her belly had shriveled into a single mass; she would seize that very wind with her mouth opened wide once, and then, as she exhaled it,
she seemed to hold it incessantly within her heart.
Dried by the rays of the fierce sun, withered by the forest winds,
yet remaining unmoved from its place and bathed by the beams of the moon;
its summit formerly occupied by a single atom of dust.
Perceiving her to have achieved her purpose, he gave no quarter to another;
she was like a forest that had offered its guest-tribute, like a flame long since arisen,
like life-force established upon her head, and like a mass of matted locks.
Beholding that needle, Pavana, his mind overwhelmed with wonder,
bowed down and, gazing at her conduct as if terrified,
spoke before her: "O great ascetic needle, for what purpose do you perform this penance?"
Defeated by that mass of splendor, he was unable to say "no.
Thinking only, "Oh, how wonderful is the great ascetic power of the Blessed One, Mahāsūcī," Māruta departed for the sky.
Having leaped across the path of the clouds, having passed beyond the layers of wind,
having left the hosts of perfected beings below, and having reached the path of the sun,
he ascended above all spheres of discernment and arrived within the city of Śakra.
Purandara embraced him for the merit of having seen Sūci;
and when questioned by Śakra, who dwells in that assembly of gods, he said, "I have seen everything."
Vāyu said:
"In Jambudvīpa there is a lofty king of mountains named Himavat,
whose son-in-law is the Blessed One, the bearer of the crescent moon himself."

On its northern side, upon the back of the Great Peak (Mahāśṛṅga), stands a most beautiful female ascetic named Sūcī; she performs a severe penance for the sake of quelling her hunger with the wind and other such elements.
What need is there to say more? Here, for the cessation of hunger, she subsists on air and so forth.
By her, the cavity of her own belly was closed up and made solid;
with its mouth opened wide for the sake of warmth,
it was now covered by the particle of *rajas* so that the intake of cold air might be prevented.
By means of her intense asceticism, he abandoned his snowy form and assumed the form of fire; having become a cow, he attained a state difficult even for the gods to serve.
Therefore, arise quickly; let us all go together to the Grandfather.
"Know that this unbearable austerity is for the sake of obtaining those boons, not for his own ruin.
Thus addressed by Vāyu, Śakra, together with the hosts of gods,
went to the world of Brahmā and petitioned that Lord.
"I shall go to the peak of the Himalayas to grant a boon," Brahmā promised; having said this, Śakra returned to heaven. After that much time had passed, she became purifying.
Her needle, which scorched the celestial mansions with the heat of her own ascetic penance,
was ignored from beginning to end by the Goddess— she who was filled with wonder and turned away— as she beheld its reflection in the sunbeams entering through the openings of her ears.

By its steadfastness, Mount Meru was surpassed like a blade of grass by a needle of silk; thus, as if through a skillful means for growth, she entered her mother’s interior at midday, as if out of fear of the heat, just as day enters the womb of night at both its beginning and end.

On another occasion, as she was gazing from afar with a look of reverence, her eyes fell upon her [the other woman] nearby; due to the resulting distress, she sank into her limbs. In a moment of crisis, people indeed forget the respect and hospitality they once showed.
With her shadow as the measuring rod and herself as the third person,
she— purified by asceticism— made a triangle equal to Vārāṇasī.
By means of that triangle, which had the three castes as its moat, they departed.
Even the winds and the dust particles have attained supreme liberation.
Having realized the ultimate cause, they were born from themselves after reflecting upon the consciousness of the self;
for in this world, O Rāghava, there is no other supreme teacher than one who follows the process of his own contemplation.
The seventy-fifth canto, titled "Description of the Manifestation of the Ripening of Austerities," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, after a thousand years, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) arrived from the vault of the sky and spoke: "Daughter, choose a boon.
Sūcī, being devoid of the organs of action and possessing only the subtle constituent of the individual soul (jīva), remained there.
She said nothing to him; she reflected only thus:
"I am fulfilled, my doubts have vanished; what shall I do with a boon?
I am at peace, I am extinguished, and I abide in absolute bliss."

All that is to be known has been known, the webs of doubt have been stilled, and my own discernment has blossomed; what further need is there for anything else? Just as I am situated here, so indeed shall I remain.
Having abandoned even the distinction between the real and the unreal, what need have I for anything else?
For all this time I have been oppressed by a lack of discernment,
like a young girl by a Vetāla spirit arisen from her own imagination.
"Now, having become tranquil through my own inquiry,
what use have I for imagined objects, whether desired or undesired?
With this conviction, she [Sūci], who was free from the organs of action, [remained].
Seeing her standing there in silence, the Blessed One Brahmā, whose mind was serene, spoke again to her who was free from passion:
"Daughter, choose some boon; remain for a certain time upon the earth."
"After enjoying worldly pleasures, you shall thereafter go to the supreme state;
such is the certainty of destiny, whose nature is irreversible.
O most excellent lady, by this asceticism, may your resolve bear fruit."
Become fat once more, you who were that very same Rākṣasī of the snowy forest;
by means of that body which was previously separated from you in the form of a cloud,
O daughter, [be restored] just as the state of being a tree arises within a seed through the growth of a great tree.
You shall again attain union with that body which is the form of its seed;
by that very body you shall take delight, O daughter, like a sprout established upon a creeper.
And because you have known all that is to be known, you shall no longer experience suffering in this world.
Pure within and with winds stilled, like a circle of clouds in autumn;
if you should ever cease internal meditation and emerge outwardly in play, you will become the very form of meditation upon the Self of all.

At that time, O daughter, she who consists of the meditation and concentration that are the nature of worldly activity, and who sports in the movement of the body like the nature of the wind, becomes its adversary and obstructs the movement of one's own karma.
By means of this method, you shall ward off the affliction of the elements for the sake of allaying hunger.

You shall live in the world with righteous conduct, yet remain a subduer of unrighteousness; through your state of liberation while living, you shall be the sole protector of your own discernment within the body.

Having spoken thus, the god departed from the expanse of the sky. Then, a slight reflection born of internal deliberation arose within her: "Let this needle become mine—is this dispassion, or is it passion, in my retaining the meaning of the Lotus-Born One’s words?
First there was a span, then a cubit, then a fathom, then a branch, and then a wreath of clouds.

In an instant, she shone forth with her limbs beginning to stir, through the process of the sprouting of the seed of the tree of volition. Then, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), possessing their full powers, emerged from the body as the organs of action;
they were like fresh blossoms on the tree of volition, which had previously remained latent within the seed.
The seventy-sixth canto, titled "The Attainment of the Body of a Needle," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then that needle-like female demon Karkaṭī became once again minute, yet attained bulkiness like an autumnal streak of cloud;
having regained her own form, she was somewhat delighted.
Through that awakening, she cast off her pride like a garment;
remaining right there in meditation, she sat in the posture of the bound lotus. Having taken hold of pure consciousness, she stood firm like a mountain peak.
Then, after six months, she attained awakening from her meditation,
like a peahen at the roar of a great rain-cloud during the monsoon.
Having awakened, her mental activity turned outward, and she became intent upon hunger.
"As long as life lasts, this nature of the body does not cease.
Then she reflected with thought:
"That which belongs to another must be enjoyed by me only through [proper] means."
I consider death here better for embodied beings than that morsel of food which is censured by the noble or not acquired through righteous means;
if I must abandon this body, let it be so without anything earned unjustly.
I do not eat anything that is unjust, for food so consumed turns into poison. What would be gained by eating that which is not in accordance with worldly custom?
For me, there is no concern whatsoever regarding life or death.
"For I was indeed mind-only, consisting merely of the delusion of a body and so forth;
that has been stilled by my own realization—whence, then, can there be a body or the perception of a body?
While she remained thus in silence, she heard a voice from the sky.
Spoken by the Wind-god, who was pleased by the Rākṣasa’s renunciation of his own nature:
"Go, Karkaṭī! Awaken the deluded quickly with wisdom;
for in this world, the very nature of the great is the rescuing of the deluded."

"Even though being instructed by you, he who shall not attain awakening was born only for his own destruction; it would be right for him to be your prey. Having heard this, she said slowly, "I have been favored by you."
He rose from the mountain peak and gradually descended;
having quickly passed over the plateau and gone from the edge of the valley floor,
he entered the settlement of the Kirātas situated at the foot of the mountain.
A fine region, abounding in food, cattle, multitudes of people, wealth, crops, medicinal herbs, and meat;

with an endless supply of roots, drinks, and grains; filled with deer, insects, birds, and the like; possessing the luster of a mountain of shifting, crumbling collyrium; and situated at the foot of the Himālaya mountains.
Thereafter, that night-stalker proceeded through the night upon a path of dense and blinding darkness.
The seventy-seventh canto, titled "The Canto of the Logic-Subverting Illogic."
Vasiṣṭha said:
In the meantime, in that region of the Kirātas,
the night became as dark as a mass of darkness that could be grasped by the hand.
The interior of the sky was shrouded by a veil of dark blue clouds, devoid of the moon;
it resembled a mass of rising collyrium from a thicket of *tāla* groves.
Due to the density of the creepers, the hollows of the villages were rendered motionless by a singular, blinding darkness.
In that city crowded with house-courtyards, she was in the prime of her youth;
in the courtyards, the lamps were dimmed by masses of darkness,
yet the lines of hair on her body shone like lamp-flames emerging from the holes of the keys.
Like a female crab dancing with her own mate,
the intoxicated piśācī-skeletons and vetāla-s stood as motionless as wood;
the multitude of beings was like those in deep sleep or the dead, shrouded by a dense mist.
With the gentle movement of a soft breeze and the spray of autumn frost,
the lakes resounded with the calls of ruddy geese and the rippling of frogs;
within the inner apartments, the faces of women and men shone with the playful joy of lovers.
In the forests, it blazed with fires whose tangled crests were flickering flames;
in the fields, it was covered in stones that had met with ripening nourished by the sprinkling of water;
and in the sky, the circle of constellations revolved with their movements unperceived.
In the forests, the trees had their flowers and fruits fallen by winds blowing through;
in the ravines, there were the cries of owls and vultures and other birds; and along the edges, the villages were harsh with the lamentations of those oppressed by thieves.
In the villages, the villagers were unconscious; in the cities, the citizens were fast asleep;
in the forests, the winds were blowing; and in the nests, the birds were motionless.
In the caves, the herds of lions were sleeping; and in the thickets, the deer were panting.
In the forest, she was covered with a veil of frost, observing silence;
she possessed the luster of the interior of a cloud filled with soot, resembling the belly of a mountain of glass;
she was as dense as a mass of mud, and her blindness was as thick as a sword-cut wound.
Agitated by the winds of cosmic dissolution, flickering like a mountain of soot, thick with the belly of mountains and the great mud of the single ocean;
possessing claws like ten million glowing coals, she is beautiful in the state of deep sleep.
Thick with the sleep of ignorance and possessing the hue of a bumblebee’s back,
during that terrible night in the midst of the Kirāta people,
the king was then at that moment together with his minister.
The wise Sudhīrātmā departed from the city, where the citizens were still asleep,
and by way of heroic conduct, Vikrama entered a treacherous forest.
While those two— the king and the minister— were wandering in the forest, they came upon a female crab.
She saw the two of them, possessing steadfast courage, their faces turned upward toward the sight of the *vetāla*.
Then she thought: "Ah! Today I have found my prey;
these two are fools, ignorant of the self, for this body is indeed a burden for them."
The fool lives for the sake of suffering, leading to ruin both here and in the hereafter;
he must be destroyed with effort, for no calamity should be nurtured.
For one who does not perceive his own self, death is the life of the fool.
Because it is the cause for the accumulation of evil, its arising occurs through death.
Furthermore, at the beginning of creation, a rule was established by the Lotus-born One:
"The fool, not the self-possessed man, exists for the sake of devouring the predatory."
Therefore, these two, having become my food, must be eaten by me this very day;
for one who is unworthy indeed disregards a faultless gain when it has been obtained.
Lest these two ever become virtuous and noble-minded!
Indeed, the destruction of such a person does not please my own nature.
Therefore, I shall examine these two; if they are endowed with virtues, I will not make them food, for one should never harm those who possess virtue.
By one who desires unartificial happiness, fame, and long life,
those endowed with virtue should be honored by granting all that is desired.
Even if I am destroyed by this body, I shall not enjoy that which is devoid of virtue.
For the virtuous bring joy to the hearts [of others] even more than the gift of life itself. One should protect a person of merit even by the sacrifice of one's own life;
through the medicine of association with the virtuous, even death attains the state of friendship.
If even I, a rākṣasī, protect one endowed with such virtues,
then another might likewise follow that same pure reflection of the heart.
Those embodied beings who dwell here endowed with noble qualities—
Through contact with the moon of the earth’s surface, they cool [the world] intensely.
Death is the obscuration of qualities; life is the resorting to those possessed of qualities.
The fruit of life, which consists of resorting to the virtuous, is heaven, liberation, and so forth.
Therefore, I shall examine these two lotus-eyed ones at some point through the play of questioning, [to determine] whether they possess the knowledge of measurement;
first, having considered their possession of good qualities or even a trace of defects, and then [considering] whether there might be an even greater fault than the quality.
Then, according to the circumstances of the case, he should impose a punishment— either light or severe— upon the one deserving of punishment, provided that wealth is available.
The seventy-eighth canto, titled "The Deliberation on Rākṣasīs."
Vasiṣṭha:
Then that Rākṣasī, a blossoming creeper in the forest of the demon race,
let out a deep roar in the very midst of the darkness, like a streak of cloud.
At the end of his roar, he spoke these words, harsh with the syllable *praṃ*,
like the sound of hail and thunder following a peal of thunder:
"O you two, the moon and the sun, who traverse the path of the sky in this terrible forest!"
"O you two of great intellect, who are you, appearing like insects in the hollow of the stone-pedestal of the darkness of Mahāmāyā? Are you of evil mind or otherwise?
Having come into the path of my maw, you shall in an instant become experts in death."
The King:
O Bhūtaka, who are you? And where do you dwell in this body?
Show yourself! Who would fear the sound of your voice, which is like the humming of a female bee?
Those who seek wealth fall upon it with all their might like lions;
you, however, cultivate [your purpose] through both appearance and words alike—why do you fear us?
For those who procrastinate, nothing is accomplished except for their own ruin.
Vasiṣṭha said:
When the king had spoken thus, she reflected, "Well said," yet out of a lack of self-control even before her passion was manifest, she both shrieked and laughed.
Then the two of them beheld her, filling the quarters of the sky with sound,
her form revealed by a mass of light from her own boisterous laughter;
she resembled a mountain slope ground down by the fragments of the clouds at the end of an aeon.
The sky was set ablaze by the circling flashes of lightning from her own eyes;
she was like the surging flames of the submarine fire within the single ocean of darkness,
her dark neck thick with the swelling mass of roaring clouds.
Before him appeared a woman whose face resounded with the fury of battle, who struck the night-stalkers with cries of "Hā! Hā!", and who made the heaven and earth appear like pillars of soot;
she had hair standing on end, a veiny body, tawny eyes, and was composed of darkness itself.
It instills no small fear even in yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas;
it is terrifying with the whistling of the wind and its own mouth gleaming from within the mountain caves;
it has pestles, mortars, and firebrands for its limbs, and ploughs and winnowing baskets for its crest.
Like the peak of Mount Vaiḍūrya quivering at the end of an aeon,
like the Night of Doom arisen, laughing as she strikes the Lord of the Universe,
like a forest of dense, cloud-filled sky that has come to assume a physical form.
She was like a fleshly night, rich with great clouds;
by the configuration of her body, she was like a mound of mud risen up,
as if her form had resorted to darkness for the battle between the moon and the sun.
She bore two dark breasts, resembling a pair of hanging clouds from the clefts in the slopes of an sapphire mountain,
and adorned with mortars and ploughs;
she was naked, her great body smeared with the glow of glowing coals.
Seeing her, whose body was like a tree in bloom with her vine-like arms swaying in the breeze, the two great heroes remained just as undisturbed as before;
for there is nothing that can cause delusion to one whose mind is secluded.
The Minister:
O great Rākṣasī, why is this agitation of yours so full of laughter? For women are indeed light-minded, and they are prone to excessive haste even in matters of triviality.
Abandon this agitation; this undertaking does not befit you.
For it is the wise who, seeking to accomplish their own goals, engage with the objects of the senses.
O frail woman, thousands like you are as numerous as flies.
Like grass and leaves scattered by the whirlwind of our own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), [the world is dispersed].
Having cast off the fever of agitation, that goal is accomplished by the wise man through a mind that is equanimous and healthy,
and by means of practical reasoning.
Let the matter be settled by your own worldly convention, or else let it be so; for what occasion is there for delusion according to the law of Great Necessity (Mahāniyati)?
Tell me, what is your desire? What do you seek as a petitioner?
"Even in a dream, no seeker among us has ever gone before you without obtaining his desired object.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed thus by him, that rākṣasī then began to reflect.
"Aha! How pure is the conduct of these two lions among men!
I do not consider them to be ordinary; this is a wondrous marvel.
Indeed, their words, their faces, and their very glances reveal the certainty within."
Through the doors of their speech, their countenances, and their glances, the intentions of the wise become one with each other, just as the waters of rivers become one through their confluences.
By these two, my disposition has for the most part been understood; and by me, theirs has been understood.
"I do not think these two are to be destroyed by me, nor are they themselves indestructible.
I consider you both to be knowers of the Self; for without the knowledge of the Self, the mind—having its notions of existence and non-existence wiped away—becomes free from fear and death."
"Therefore, I shall ask these two about a certain doubt that has arisen;
for those who do not ask anything, even when they have encountered what is to be attained, are the lowest of men.
Having reflected thus, he proceeded to inquire, as various opportunities for doing so presented themselves.
Restraining her laughter, which sounded like the roar of clouds at an improper time, she said:
"O sinless ones, tell me who you two heroic men are.
From the mere sight of those with clear minds, friendship arises."
The minister said: "This king belongs to the Kirātas, and I have attained the position of his minister;
we are prepared to suppress people like you by means of a night-patrol."
For a king, the duty day and night is the suppression of wicked beings;
but those who abandon their own duty are fuel for the fire of destruction.
Rākṣasī:
"You are the evil counselor of the king; because of this evil counsel, he has become Arāḍa.
A true king may have a minister, and by means of a good minister, the king himself becomes excellent.
Therefore, at the outset, the king must be joined with discernment by a wise counselor."
Through that, one attains nobility; as is the king, so are the subjects.
For those possessing the entire web of virtues, knowledge of the inner self is supreme;
likewise should the king be, and likewise the minister who knows counsel.
Sovereignty and impartial vision—these arise through the science of kingship (*rājavidyā*).
He who does not know this is neither a minister nor a ruler.
If you two are virtuous and possess knowledge of that [science], you shall attain the highest good.
"If you two do not bring harm to your own nature, I shall not devour you.
By a single means, you two children shall escape from my side,
provided that you investigate with your intellect the essence of this cage of my questions."

"O Lord of the Earth, O Minister, ask me questions; I am here with great longing for them. Fulfill my purpose! For who in this world, having promised a request, does not incur the fault that leads to destruction?
The Chapter Named "The Deliberation of the Rākṣasī."
The seventy-seventh canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, that Rākṣasī began to answer the questions.
When the king said, "Let it be told," [the Rākṣasī replied: "O Rāghava, listen to these words of mine:
Of that one atom which possesses manifold numbers, like an ocean..."
Within, hundreds of thousands of cosmic eggs dissolve like bubbles.
Is space non-space? Is it nothingness or indeed something?
Who am I that has come to be so? And who are you that remains as "I"?
Who is it that does not go while going, and who is it that stands still while standing?
Who is a conscious being yet like a stone, and who is an artist within the sky?
And who is one who, without ever abandoning the nature of fire, is a fire that does not burn?
O King, from what does fire arise incessantly?
What is that which is without moon, sun, fire, or stars, yet is indestructible and illuminating?
And why does light proceed from that which cannot be grasped by the eye?
What kind of supreme light could there be for creepers, shrubs, sprouts, and the like, as well as for those born blind and others who lack eyes?
Who is the progenitor of space and so forth, and who is the giver of their inherent nature?
Who would be the treasury of the jewels of the world? In whose treasury is the jewel that is the world?

What is the atom? Darkness and light—what is the atom? What is that which both exists and does not exist? What is the atom that is both far away and not far away? What is the atom that is itself a great mountain?
What is a moment (nimeṣa) and what is an eon (kalpa)? What is an eon and what is a moment?

What is perception (pratyakṣa) and what is of an unreal nature? What is consciousness (cetana) and what is unconsciousness (acetana)? What is non-wind (avāyu) and what is wind (vāyu)? What is sound (śabda) and what is indeed soundless (aśabda)?

What is both everything and nothing? Who am I and who am I not? What could come to be? (3,79.11) Having attained through hundreds of efforts over many lifetimes, even what has been gained becomes as if nothing; yet surely everything is obtained. (3,79.12)
By whom, while living in health, has one’s own self been so utterly abandoned?
By what minute thing is Mount Meru confined within, and the three worlds reduced to a blade of grass?
By what thing, no larger than a tiny speck, is a distance of a hundred yojanas filled?
Who is it that, being so minute, is perceived even within hundreds of leagues?
By whose mere glance is the world made to dance like a child? Within the interior of which atom do the multitudes of mountains and lands exist?
What atom, not abandoning its atomicity, could possess a form larger than Mount Meru?
What atom, whose essence is a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, could be a towering mountain peak?
What atom is the lamp that bestows illumination upon both light and darkness?
Within which atom do all atoms of experience reside?
Which atom, though utterly devoid of flavor, tastes intensely?
By the renunciation of what atom is everything abandoned, and by what atom is everything supported?
By what atom, incapable of concealing itself, is the world concealed? By whose logic does the world depend upon the existence of an atom?
What atom is devoid of parts, yet possesses a thousand rays and eyes?
What is a moment, or a great aeon, or even hundreds of great aeons? Within the atom the worlds abide, like trees in a seed— manifest yet unarisen, from seed to fruit.
For whom does an eon exist, situated within a mere blink of an eye like that of a living soul?
Who is the agent who acts even without resorting to the status of an instigating agent?
Even the seer, for the sake of the manifestation of the visible, would lead himself into the state of being the visible.
Seeing the visible world, who does not see their own self, just as one sees with the eyes?
And who, seeing the visible world before them for the sake of perceiving the visible, does not see the indivisible Self in which the visible has dissolved?
Who illuminates the self, the seer, and the seen, as if they were objects of sight?
By whom are these three swallowed up, just as bracelets and other ornaments are swallowed by gold?
Why is there nothing separate [from it], like waves and so forth from the great ocean?

By whose will does duality exist as something separate, like the waves of the great ocean? From that single, non-existent source which is yet existent, and which is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth—
why does duality also emerge as non-separate, like the waves of the great ocean?

Who, having placed within himself— like a seed situated within its own body— the Self, the vision, and the visible, both existent and non-existent, transcending all sequence and extending through the three periods of time; who, having placed there the vast mass of the world, abiding in the past, present, and future, remains unmoved?
Within whom does this eternal [universe] reside, like a tree within its seed?
What is it that, though unborn and of an unreal nature, arises by itself as both the seed and the tree, and yet remains as the single tree even while appearing as the seed?
O King, compared to whom is even Mount Meru but a mere spider’s thread?
Within whose belly reside millions of Merus and Mandaras?
By whom has this universe, consisting of many consciousnesses, been spread out? What is its essence, that you thus leap about, strike, and protect it?

"By seeing what will you not come into existence, or rather, by seeing what will you surely continue to exist? Speak that which is not seen with partiality for the sake of its pacification. May this great doubt of mine, which is a foul-smearing mist upon the face of the splendor of my mind, be utterly dispelled—that doubt before which no root is severed, and which never reaches the speech of the wise."
O wise ones, if you do not bring him to me by means of reasoned discourse to pacify his doubts and diminish his uncertainty,
then in an instant, without obstacle, you shall suddenly become fuel for the fire in the belly of this Rākṣasa.
Afterwards, with my vast belly, I shall devour that entire circle of your country in a moment.
"Thus it happens to you; I think that for fools, even an exceedingly sweet [thing] leads only to destruction.

Having spoken thus with a voice as deep and resonant as a vast cloud, yet with words made manifest through her exuberance, that night-stalker remained silent, her form exceedingly formidable, like a circle of pure, autumnal clouds in the inner apartments.
The Eightieth Sarga, titled "The Question of the Rākṣasī," by Vasiṣṭha:
When this great question had been posed by the daughter of a great rākṣasa in the great forest at the dead of night, the great master of mantras spoke these words: The Master said:
Listen, O cloud-like one; I shall resolve this question of yours, just as a lion tears apart a rutting lordly elephant in due order.
O lotus-eyed lady, this Supreme Self has been described by you.
By this very turn of speech, which is suitable for awakening the knower of Brahman:
because it is ineffable and inaccessible, the Self is beyond the range of even the minds;
it is pure consciousness alone, an atomic self, subtler even than space.
Within the supreme, partless consciousness, existence itself remains as if non-existent;
even this existence shines forth like non-existence, and thus this world stands established.
Because it is a slight experience, it exists in the form of creation.
Having previously attained the existence of all things by virtue of being identical with them,
that very atom— which is infinite because it transcends the senses—
enjoys nothing and yet nothing is not enjoyed by it, because it is the self of everything.
From the manifestation of the conscious atom (*cidaṇu*), its manifoldness arises from its own nature, even though it is unreal, just as the state of being a bracelet arises from gold.
This atom is the supreme space; it is subtler than space and unperceivable.
Transcending the six senses with the mind as the sixth, he remains even while being the self of all.
Though he is the self of all, he is never empty;
he who says that what exists does not exist is considered a madman.
By no reasoning whatsoever is the non-existence of that which exists here logical;
it is revealed as the self of all, like camphor hidden within a hollow.
That very same atom of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) remains here as everything, though appearing as a solid mass.
Nothing exists as stainless because it transcends the nature of the senses;
yet that very same [reality] is both one and many, because it is the self-experience of all beings.
It alone sustains this world, and likewise the millions of worlds.
These creatures are the waves of water in the great ocean of consciousness;
they shimmer within that water like the appearance of circularity due to its fluidity.
Because it cannot be grasped by the mind, the senses, and so forth, it is atomic, empty, and possesses the nature of space.
Because it is attainable through self-awareness, even that which has the nature of space is non-empty.
Being you, I have become [you] through existence due to the perception of duality;
being you, I am born as one whose body is both vast and non-vast through the expansion of awakening.
Through the realization that swallows up everything consisting of "thou-ness" and "I-ness," one becomes spontaneously neither you,
nor I, nor the whole, nor the non-whole. Though this subtle atom has traveled across a multitude of leagues, it does not travel.
Through consciousness, the state of being joined with the multitude [of objects] resides within that atom.
Even though it has gone, it does not go; even though it has arrived, it has not come, because it dwells within the inner sheath of the space of its own existence, beyond space and time.
Where indeed does he go, whose accessible [Self] resides within his very body?
For what can a son, dwelling in the hollow of his mother's breast, be seen by her elsewhere?
Even if one’s great domain is accessible and remains inexhaustible as long as existence endures.
And since he is the internal dweller of the All-maker, how and where indeed could he go? Just as when a jar is tightly sealed at its mouth,
there is no going or coming of the space within it, so it is with the Self.
When both consciousness and insentience exist within it as its internal states, consisting of experience,
then it is indeed both— the conscious and the inert.
When the existence of the conscious stone is of a single nature, having consciousness as its very form...
Then, O Rākṣasī, that very consciousness, like a stone,
[remains] in the supreme sky, which is without beginning or end; by means of that single atom of pure consciousness,
this manifold and variegated triple world was created, though it was uncreated.
Through the cognition of that [fire], its existence is not abandoned by the form of fire;
thus, although all-pervading, it does not burn, yet it is the cooker of the substances of the world.
Even from the stainless sky, it manifests forms that are blazing.

Blazing with consciousness as its sole essence, fire is born from that [Pradhāna]. Because of its perception, it illuminates even the sun and other luminaries within Pradhāna; that primordial form of light is not destroyed even by the clouds at the end of a great kalpa.
Unattainable by the eyes, consisting of pure experience, the lamp of the house of the heart,
the bestower of existence to all, infinite— that is remembered as the Supreme Light.
From that which transcends the six senses, including the mind, illumination proceeds forth.

That subtle atom (*aṇuka*), which consists of the nature of experience and is a luminosity whose form is the perception of height, is that by which there occurs within objects— even for creepers, shrubs, sprouts, and the like, as well as for those lacking sense organs— the wonder of the visible and the invisible.

Because he is self-aware of time, space, action, existence, and essential nature, and because his self-nature is the void (*kha*), he is neither a master, nor an agent, nor a father, nor an enjoyer; indeed, he is nothing at all.
Yet, without abandoning his atomicity (*aṇutva*), that atom is the casket for the jewels of the universe.
The world, consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, exists within that consciousness.
It is that very [consciousness] which shines clearly everywhere throughout the entire universe;
when this world arises, it is then that supreme jewel.
Because it is difficult to comprehend, it is darkness; because it consists of pure consciousness, it is the seer of light.
It exists because its nature is awareness, yet it is non-existent insofar as it transcends the senses.
It is far away because it cannot be grasped by the senses, yet it is not distant because its nature is consciousness.
Because it is perceived by everyone, O Śailā, this very world, while being nothing but an atom (aṇu),
appears as this mere perception; therefore,
mountains and such are not real, and thus the state of being Mount Meru exists only within the atom.
For the appearance of a blink is called a "blink," and the appearance of an eon is expressed by the word "eon. Indeed,
the play of the activity of an eon appears within a single blink.
Indeed, within the space of a mere blink, the tumultuous activity of an eon arises like a great city extending for many yojanas within the mind;
it is like the construction of a vast metropolis appearing within a stainless mirror.
Where even millions of *yojanas*, mountains, oceans, and eons exist within a single atom,
how can there be duality or unity? Indeed,
the thought "I did this before" arises only when the intellect (*buddhi*) has emerged.
In an instant, the real and the unreal are seen to be like the delusions of a dream. Indeed, time is always very long in suffering, yet extremely brief in happiness;
for it was declared that for Hariścandra, a single night lasted twelve years.
Whatever certainty arises within, whether it be true or false, shines forth like the nature of bracelets and such in gold, or like waves in the ocean.
There is no moment of blinking, nor an eon; there is no nearness, nor any distance.
Thus, the mere reflection of the atomic consciousness remains as if it were other things;
yet between light and darkness, which are distant and near, lasting for a moment or an eon,
there is not even the slightest difference, as they both reside within the single sheath of consciousness.
Because it is the essence of the senses, it is direct perception; because it transcends them, it is beyond direct perception.
It arises as the very object of sight, yet by virtue of its consciousness, it is the seer itself, whose true nature is reality.
As long as there is the cognition of a bracelet, the state of being gold does not exist at all.
As long as there is the appearance of being an object of perception, that [pure reality] does not exist at all.
When the perceived state of being a bracelet has ceased, like the pervasive nature of gold remaining when the bracelet is destroyed,
only the stainless, awakened Brahman remains.
Because it is everything, this [Self] has the nature of existence; because it is difficult to perceive, it has the nature of non-existence.
It is conscious because its essence is consciousness, yet it is insentient because there is no possibility of anything being perceived by it.
In this Self, which consists solely of the wonder of consciousness and whose nature is that very manifestation, [all things appear].
In this world, which resembles a tree stirred by the wind, how can there be the conceptualization of consciousness and its objects?
Just as the appearance of a shimmering mirage belongs to one who is emaciated by heat,
so too is the appearance of the world as a single, plump, non-dual consciousness.
That which is fashioned from rays more subtle than the sun’s, being free from all affliction—
in that state, what notion of existence or non-existence could there be, such as one might have regarding a wall?
Just as gold shines in the sky when marked by particles of illusory dust;
In that same way, this world appears; how could there be a distinction between consciousness and its objects?
Just as in a dream, a city of Gandharvas, or a mental construction, one perceives walls that are neither real nor unreal—know that the long-lasting delusion of the world is likewise.
And thus, those who perceive the reality of things as they truly are, purified by the practice of cultivating such reasoning, emerge through the wall as if through space;
for there is no difference between the wall and space except for the absence of firm perception.
From the conceptualization of Brahman and the individual soul (jīva), that which has become established remains indeed established.
In the stainless space of appearances, the emptiness of sky, walls, and so forth,
shine forth through their solidification like rays from a mass of light.
The appearance of distinctness arises from its connection with its own creative wonder (*camatkāra*).
For the supreme manifestation (*pratibhā*) is the soul of all things, like a seed whose nature is the tree;
just as the seed contains the state of being a tree within it, so too is the manifold seen as one.
In this way, the world is the infinite Brahman, peaceful like the expanse of space.
Just as the non-dual state of space exists within the tree that resides inside a seed,
so too does the unagitated state of space exist within the world that resides inside Brahman.
All is peaceful, unborn, one, without beginning or middle; here there is no part whatsoever, nor any mental constructions in any way.
Remain established in that which is free from duality, tranquil, transcendent, manifold yet pure, appearing in form, sufficient as the single unfolding.
This is the chapter named "The Distinction of Questions."
The Eighty-first Sarga:
The Rakshasis said: "Oh, how truly sublime and purifying are the words of your minister!"
"O lotus-eyed King, let him speak now.
The King said:
"This wind arises from subtle sensation, and the wind [is perceived] through the vision of delusion."
Therefore, there is nothing such as air and so forth; there is only pure consciousness.
Because sound is a cognition of sound, "sound" and "the object of sound" are merely illusory perceptions.
Consequently, the view that there is a word and a meaning for the word here has gone far astray.
He is the atom, he is everything, and he is nothing; he is I, yet he is not I, for he alone is that.
For this very Self, who possesses all powers, his own intuitive flash (*pratibhā*) is the cause here.
The Self is to be attained through hundreds of efforts, and once this is attained, nothing more remains to be gained.

And this is indeed that which has been attained, the supreme name of something. As long as awakening— which scrapes away the very root— has not arisen, the creeper of saṃsāra continues to blossom for a long time throughout the springs of birth.
By this subtle self, as it were becoming visible in its own form,
consciousness was carried away by its own intellect, just as water is drawn off by heat;
by this [intellect], Meru is made manifold, and the three worlds are reduced to a blade of grass.
Having vomited out that which was situated within as consisting of *māyā*, it is perceived externally. Whatever exists within the atom of consciousness (*cidaṇu*) is seen outside;
for the example here is that of a lustful man [who experiences] the embrace of his desired object in his mental constructs.

At the beginning of creation, consciousness, possessing all powers, perceives everything instantly by itself, according to its own impelled nature, just like a mental volition. Whatever appears within the mind of one whose disposition is noble, that very thing manifests accordingly.
It is as if that child’s mind perceives it in that way; this is the illustration here:
even from the state of a mere atom, by this extremely subtle atom of pure consciousness alone, the entire universe is filled throughout.
This [self] is indeed subtle; it does not fit even within hundreds of *yojanas*.
Because it is all-pervading and its nature is without beginning or end, it takes the form of sensation (*vedanā*).
Just as a child is led astray by a rogue who acts as a guide, [so is the world led by ignorance].
Through the movements of glances from eyes with arched brows,
the world— including its mountains and grass— is incessantly made to dance by the pure light of consciousness, which always performs this dramatic representation through its own unfolding.
Because it possesses that very same infinite form, consciousness may exist externally as if enveloped by Mount Meru and other such objects, just as with a minute piece of cloth; yet,
because its nature is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, it is greater than Meru itself.
This supreme atom is subtle, being of the nature of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair;
indeed, a statement of equality between it and a [gross] atom— which is of the nature of the space of pure consciousness—
is not fitting, just as one would not compare Mount Meru with a mustard seed.

The state of being a minute atom through the power of illusion (*māyākalā*) is non-illusory supreme selfhood (*paramātmatā*); just as [the substance] gold remains the same despite its form as a bracelet, there can be no equality [of status] here between them.
By this lamp, which is of the nature of experience, light is made manifest.
For that [world] would exist even without this [consciousness], being preceded by its own existence and destruction.
If the entire world, beginning with the sun, were a single inert mass, then what would the Self be? What would its nature be? What would light be, or where, or what would it be?
That which is pure existence consisting of consciousness alone, established by itself within its own self—
that very same light is perceived by the individual soul as if it were situated externally.
The lights of the sun, moon, and fire are non-different from the mass of darkness.

In this matter, there is only this much difference: that while whiteness and blackness exist in color, the distinction between light and darkness is like that which exists between soot and mist, or between a cloud and frost; such is the established nature of those two.

It is said that when the sun of consciousness shines upon these two inert things for their perception, they attain a state of identity with the existence [of consciousness] thereby. The single sun of consciousness shines tirelessly day and night.
Neither setting nor rising occurs within or without, even inside stones and the like;
by that [Self], this triple world shines forth for the soul of celebrated nature—
a hut rich with various vessels of perception, yet possessing a hard interior.
By this [sun], which destroys the body of darkness, you are that very darkness;
yet by its radiance, all darkness is illuminated. Just as the day-lotus and the night-lotus are brought to light by the scorching sun, so too is everything revealed.
When the existence of light and darkness has been thus revealed by consciousness alone,
just as the sun, creating day and night, reveals form,
so too does consciousness, having brought about both being and non-being, reveal form.
Within the atom of consciousness exist atoms of diverse experiences,
just as within a sweet-tasting fruit reside the splendors of its leaves, flowers, and fruits.
All these atoms of experience arise from the atom of consciousness.
Like rows of mango groves variegated by the juice of honey and fruit,
the supreme atomic self— though utterly devoid of flavor due to its subtlety—
tastes itself as the sole generator of the existence of all-encompassing flavor.

Whatever flavor whatsoever, having established its existence within itself, does not exist by its own nature apart from that [consciousness], like a reflection in a mirror. By that atom of pure consciousness, which abandons everything it has assumed, [all else is relinquished].
The world is abandoned through non-perception, yet everything is supported by perception.
Even when unable to protect itself, consciousness covers the entire world by spreading its own atomic nature far and wide like a canopy.

Just as an elephant in a grove of durvā grass cannot protect itself for even a moment or in the slightest degree, so too [the one] whose form is the sky of the supreme self has overwhelmed the universe,
yet conceals his state of knowing in an instant.

Alas! Like a child, the dense illusion of this world is a mere speck within the Sustainer of the universe. This world lives by the grace of the atom of pure consciousness, just as a forest grove appears variegated through the infusion of the essence of spring.
This entire world has arisen from consciousness itself,
just as a forest grove appears in its variety when it is vibrant with the essence of the spring season.
Know for certain that this world is truly nothing but composed of consciousness.
Know this cluster of sprouts to be the very essence of spring;
because it is the quintessence of all constituent parts, it is the thousand-rayed one (the Sun),
that supreme atom which arises eternally without parts.
Since even within the perception of a single moment of the atomic consciousness (cidaṇu),
a flood of thousands of kalpas appears— just like childhood and old age in a dream—
therefore, that very atom of a moment is fully capable of containing hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Indeed, a single intuition unfolds through the play of all beings.
Just as the conviction arises, "I have eaten," even when one has not yet eaten,
so too does the determination of conceptualization arise in the blink of an eye.

Those possessed by latent impressions (vāsanā) are seen to have the conviction, "I have eaten," even when they have not eaten, just as one perceives one's own death in a dream. The worlds are established within the atom that is the conscious self (cidātman).
For it is from that very source indeed that the appearances of the world proceed.
Whatever exists in whatever substrate, from that very substrate it arises; that [substrate] is itself that [appearance].
Modifications and the like are observed in that which possesses form, but not in the stainless sky.
All beings that have been, those existing at present,
and those that will be, arise from the seed-potency like trees;
by this [consciousness], even a moment and an eon are as a single grain of husked rice.

This [Self] is not bound by these two; it is the subtle one, consisting of its own limbs, and conscious. Sitting like one who is indifferent, this ethereal Self is not touched even in the slightest by the states of being an enjoyer or a doer, even while creating the worlds.
For this world arises from the emergence of existence within the supreme atom of pure consciousness;
and where indeed could the states of being an enjoyer and an agent reside in that supreme atom?
The world is never created as anything at all, nor by anyone at any time.
And nothing whatsoever is dissolved; today there is not even a fragment of this [world] to be refuted.
Know, O Rākṣasī, that all this which appears as a single flavor, existing within the expanse of space, is designated by synonymous terms for the world, yet is ultimately nameless.
The atomic consciousness, for the sake of establishing the visible world, assumes an internal wonder of consciousness as an external form, while remaining established within itself by its own nature.
This [externalization] exists externally and internally in the word, but not in the actual object.
For the sake of instructing sentient beings within the three worlds, because it is of the nature of consciousness,
the Seer, entering the state of the seen, perceives itself;
like an eye falling upon its own object, it exists as the real, yet appears as if non-existent.
The seer does not attain visibility, for he is non-existent and unreal;
since there is nothing whatsoever within the self itself, how could it appear before one? Vision alone is the eye, and that is the latent impression (vāsanā); such is its own nature.
Having made the object of vision manifold in form, she arises as the seer.
Without the state of being a seer, the existence of the object of vision is in no way possible—
just as a son cannot exist without a father, or duality cannot exist without the ground of unity.
The seer alone becomes the object of sight; there is no such thing as the state of being a seer without that [object].
Just as there is no son without a father, and no state of being an object of enjoyment without an enjoyer.
For the seer possesses the capacity for the manifestation of the object of sight precisely because of its nature as consciousness.
Just as gold, when fashioned into the form of a bracelet, [is not distinct from the gold itself],
so too the visible object has no capacity to produce the seer, because of its insentience;
it is like the delusion of being a "bracelet" having no power in the production of the gold.

From volition, consciousness shines forth as the manifestation of the visible world, which is itself non-existent, causeless, and the ground of delusion— just as the illusion of a bracelet is nothing other than gold.
Indeed, when there is the appearance of being a bracelet, the nature of the gold does not cease to be gold.
In this way, while the object of perception remains present, the true nature of the perceiver shines forth.
For the perceiver, abiding as the object of perception, seems to abandon its state of being a perceiver—
just as gold, when perceived as a bracelet, [seems to abandon] its state of being pure gold.

In a single manifestation, there is no existence of both the seer and the seen. When the cognition of the Puruṣa shines forth, how could there be the arising of the cognition of a bound soul (paśu)? Seeing the object of sight, the seer does not perceive his own self.
For when the seer becomes the object of sight, existence and non-existence alone remain.
But for the seer from whom the object of sight has dissolved through awakening, only existence shines forth,
just as gold remains gold even when it is not recognized as a bracelet.
When the visible object does not exist, the seer does not exist; when the seer does not exist, the visible object does not exist.
Without these two, there is no unity, nor is there even non-unity between them.
Having understood all this as it truly is, [one realizes] the self which consists of pure consciousness.
Beyond the range of words, a certain state of well-being alone remains.
Then the self, the seer, and the seen are illuminated as by a lamp;
all this has been accomplished by that single atom of pure consciousness.
The triad known as the object, the means of knowledge, and the knower is swallowed up within the intellect,
just as the unreal forms of bracelets and the like appear within gold;
for just as water is not even slightly separate from its waves and so forth.
Likewise, from this atom of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-aṇu*), nothing indeed exists as separate,
because its essence consists of all-pervasive experience and it has the form of the experience of everything;
for when the experience of oneness is established as logical, its unity with all things is indeed realized.
By his will, there is a distinctness [of the world] like the waves of the great ocean,
for he possesses the attainment of objects according to his will and has realized the singular goal. The Supreme Self alone exists, unconditioned by space, time, and so forth.
Because he is the self of all, he is the self of all; because he experiences everything by himself, he exists as such.
He exists because his nature is consciousness, and he does not exist because of the lack of awakening.
In this Great Self, whose form is truth, neither duality nor unity exists.
If there were some second, then the oneness of the one would exist;
for duality and unity are established in relation to each other, like sunlight and shadow.
Indeed, where there is no second, how can there be oneness of the one?
When unity is not established, duality itself does not exist.
This being the case, that which remains here would be empty because it lacks any basis for subsistence;
therefore, its form is not distinct [from the substrate], just as fluidity is not distinct from water.
Vast with its manifold undertakings, yet in its essential nature undisturbed by change—
the world exists within Brahman like a tree within a seed;
though dual, it is not separate from Him, just as the state of being a bracelet is not separate from gold.
For when the awakening to the intellect of equanimity occurs, duality— whether existent or consisting of the non-existent—
is [seen as such]. Just as liquidity belongs to water, motion to the wind, and emptiness to space, so too duality is not separate from the Lord.
For this perception of duality and non-duality leads to suffering for one whose nature is subject to decay;
however, those who are skillful know that supreme state which is the non-perception of these two.
[The categories of] knower, means of knowledge, and object of knowledge, as well as seer, seeing, and the seen—these are the manifestations of duality.
This entire world is situated within this single atom of consciousness.
Why then is this atom of the world not eternally supported by its own limb— the atom of Mount Sumeru— just as movement is sustained by the wind?
"Aha! Is this a terrible illusion, or is it the supreme power of a magician?
For within a single atom exists the entire succession of the three worlds. Or rather, this state of being an impossible illusion has always been established.

The entire world exists as nothing more than the subtle atom of pure consciousness alone. Although it contains within itself the entire web of the universe, this [consciousness] remains as minute as an atom without losing its equilibrium, like a seed containing a vast tree within the interior of a vessel.
Just as the expansion of a tree, complete with its fruits and shoots, exists within the seed,
so too the entire world is perceived by the supreme vision within the atom of consciousness;
yet that [world] does not abandon its state as a tree with branches and fruit while remaining within the hollow of the seed.
Just as a tree stands [within a seed], so does the expanded universe reside within the atom of consciousness.
Like the shell of a seed containing the germ of non-duality, the world exists as a state of established duality;
he who perceives the world within the supreme atom of consciousness—he truly sees.
Neither duality nor non-duality, neither seed nor sprout;
neither gross nor subtle, neither unborn nor indeed born;
it neither exists nor does it not exist, it is neither pleasant nor agitated.
Within the atomic consciousness of the three worlds, there is either existence or nothing at all;
neither the world nor the non-world exists. When the supreme atomic consciousness—which is the self of all—is present, whatever arises therein in whatever manner, it manifests exactly so.
Though not yet arisen, this single Self, the supreme atomic soul, arises through the unfolding of self-awareness as if it were the totality of all selves within the void;
it arises even while not arising, like a seed becoming a tree.
The supreme reality, through the dissolution of the world and the emergence of its destruction,
remains like a tree that has not yet abandoned its state as a seed;
it is the supreme atom (aṇu) that abides, having neither relinquished nor not relinquished its vibration.
The lotus fiber is like Mount Meru when compared to the supreme atom;
indeed, the fiber in the lotus-stalk is visible, yet its supreme atomic nature remains unseen by the eye.
The lotus fiber is like Mount Meru to the supreme atom of the self.
From the density of that very [consciousness], the millions of Mount Merus and other worlds reside within;

by that great [consciousness] and by that atom, the entire manifestation of the universe is pervaded, extended, fashioned, generated, and created. Like space, the pervasive emptiness of the void is attained on all sides as something utterly transparent.

As if not abandoning its own form—which is more beautiful through duality—yet having attained oneness with that which resembles deep sleep due to the awakening of the Supreme, the world thus remains as the very mass of ultimate reality, free from coming, going, and staying. Indeed, this is the world as the condensed essence of the ultimate truth.
This is the chapter titled "The Condensation of the World into the Ultimate Reality."
The eighty-second canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard this from the mouth of the king, Karkaṭī and Vanamarkaṭī—
Having awakened to that which resides within the state [of the Self], she abandoned both stinginess and agitation.
She attained inner coolness, contentment, rest, and freedom from affliction,
like a peahen in the rainy season or a night-lily under the moonlight.
At those words of the king, Ānandā was greatly moved within her womb, just as a female crane is stirred by the roar of a rain-cloud in the sky.
The Rākṣasī said:
"Oh, how wonderful! This intellect of yours shines with such purity, illuminated by the sun of awakening whose essence has not set;
it is white, equanimous, and pure, like moonlight from the lunar orb."
"This tiny spark of discernment has been seen by me from your heart.
I consider those like you, who possess discernment, to be worthy of the world's worship and service;
through association with you, I have blossomed like a night-lotus at the sight of the moon."
Just as fragrance arises from contact with flowers, so does auspiciousness arise from association with the virtuous;
and just as the blooming of lotuses occurs through contact with the sun,
so too, by associating only with the great, suffering no longer afflicts one.
For who indeed, holding a lamp-flame in his hand, is overcome by darkness?
You two, who have arrived here in the forest like the sun upon the earth, are worthy of worship; therefore, tell me quickly what auspicious desire you seek.
The King said:
"O Mañjarī of the forest of the Rākṣasa clan,
you constantly afflict the people in my kingdom excessively, causing them a piercing pain in their hearts."
Since all people are now perpetually afflicted with severe cholera within my domain,
I have therefore gone out tonight on my nocturnal round;
for when the piercing pains in the hearts of men cannot be stilled by medicines, [I must act].
Therefore, I have come forth for the sake of the mantras and other teachings proclaimed by those like you;
and my endeavor is for the purpose of restraining people such as yourself who strike down the deluded world— may that endeavor attain complete success.
"O auspicious lady, you should indeed accept this much alone:
that henceforth you shall not take the life of anyone.
Rākṣasī:
"Very well, O Lord; from this day forward, I shall act thus without fail.
This is the truth; indeed, nothing at all must be harmed by me henceforth.
The King said:
"If it is so, O lotus-eyed one, who subsists solely on the flesh of others, what would be the use of maintaining your body while you remain intent upon my desire? Rākṣasī:

"O King, after six hundred years, having awakened from my meditative absorption, the thought of food arose; this desire for food is mine today. Now, having gone to the mountain peak, I shall remain there, motionless in that very meditation."
Remaining comfortably for as long as I wish, like a lifelike wooden statue,
I shall maintain this little body by binding the *dhāraṇā* that leads to immortality;
then, at the appropriate time, I shall relinquish it according to my will— this is my resolve.
"O King, from this moment until the abandonment of my body, I shall not harm the lives of others; therefore, listen to these words of mine.
There is a mountain named Himavat, pure as the rays of the moon in its luster."

I dwell there in the fierce cave-dwelling of the Golden Peak on the Heart of the Northern Quarter, which has previously touched both the eastern and western oceans— I, the Rākṣasī named Karkaṭī, like an iron pillar-line.
"Requested by Brahmā through ascetic penance with the desire to bring about the destruction of living beings, I [said]: 'May I be a life-taking cholera; may I be subtle.
Therefore, having obtained that boon, for many groups of years by me..."

People have been made to suffer from cholera by you through the piercing of their vital breaths. "One must not harm those who possess virtue"—this great mantra was established for my restraint by Brahmā; I remain here, bound by that vow.
Therefore, let this [teaching] be accepted by him; by that, all the thorns in the heart will find peace in this world—what need is there to speak of the delusion caused by me?
For I have indeed desisted from violence, even that which was previously committed by me.
Because of that, the hearts of people and their channels have fallen into a state of distress.
Those people whom I abandoned after having harmed their blood and flesh—
those who were born from those distressed channels are likewise of such a nature.
"O King, this mantra for *viṣūcikā* has indeed been perfected by you;
for there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished here by those possessed of spiritual power (*sattva*).
Therefore, for the complete pacification of the pains in the sheaths of the obstructed channels,"

"O King, quickly take up this mantra which has been proclaimed by the Brahmins. Come near the river; let us go there, O Lord of the Earth. Once you have sipped water and are self-restrained, I, who am firm in my vows, shall bestow it upon you."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, during that night, the ministers and the king of the Rākṣasas,
having conceived mutual affection for one another, went to the bank of the river.

Having thus ascertained the Rākṣasī’s friendship through both positive and negative concomitance, the two of them remained there, having sipped water for purification, dwelling at the edge [of the hermitage].
Then, that [instruction] which had been imparted by Brahmā was delivered to them by her in due order.

Out of affection, she bestowed upon him the Viṣūcikā-mantra, which grants success through recitation. Then, having established a bond of friendship and dismissed him, when that night-stalker was about to depart, the king spoke these words.
The King said:
"O Great Queen, you are our guru and our companion; may you be well-pleased.
O beautiful one with lotus-like eyes, we both earnestly invite you."
"You ought not to render our prayer in vain;
for the goodwill of virtuous people increases simply from the sight [of one another].
Having assumed a charming form endowed with modest beauty, [he appeared].
"Come to our house, O auspicious lady; stay there as you please.
Rākṣasī:
"O, can you provide food for one who has assumed the form of an innocent woman?"
"With what do you satisfy me, who have assumed the form of a rākṣasī? "Only the food of a rākṣasa brings me satisfaction, not the food of ordinary people;
this innate nature, established from before, increases until the end of creation."
The King said:
"O blameless one, remain for some days in my house in the form of a woman, adorned with garlands of gold, for as long as you desire."
Then, having brought from the districts hundreds of thousands of wicked thieves deserving of death,
he gave them to you for a fine meal;
abandoning his lovely form, he assumed the body of a *rākṣasa*.

"Taking those hundreds of men you have gathered for execution, lead them to a peak of the Himalayas; there, enjoy them as you please. For a meal of great delicacies in a secluded place indeed brings happiness."
Having woken from sleep, abandon your slumber and become once more possessed of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Even after you have again desisted from concentration and returned at another time, you shall not lead away other men to be executed; for this violence is not in accordance with the Dharma.
For even violence performed according to one's own duty is equal to great compassion;
and you, who have ceased from meditative absorption, will surely come to me.
For friendship that has taken root, even among the wicked, does not perish.
Rākṣasī: O King, you have spoken rightly; I shall do exactly as you say, my friend.
Who would not welcome the words of one who acts out of friendship?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, that playful Rākṣasī there transformed herself,
wearing necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and garlands of woven flowers.
"O King, come, let us go," said the king and the minister; having spoken thus, the two set out to go ahead, and she followed them during the night.
Then, having reached the king's palace, they spent that night together in private.
"Tell me, they spent [the night] with respect in a beautiful house.
At dawn, she stayed in the inner apartments amidst the playful charms of the women;
the Rākṣasī and the king's minister each attended to their own duties.
Then, within six days,
the king collected three thousand condemned men from the palaces of other kings as well as from his own circle of vassals, and he gave them to her.
At nightfall, she became that very same fierce black Rākṣasī;
she seized those thousands of victims within the circle of her arms,
as a row of clouds holds masses of rain-showers within its hollows.
Having taken leave of the king, she returned to that very peak of the Himalayas,
like a poor woman who has obtained gold returning home, though her body was still formidable. There,
having eaten to her heart's content and slept happily for two days, she remained.
She becomes awakened, exceedingly pure, and once again possesses the state of meditative absorption (samādhi).
She awakens either after five or three years;
thereafter she enters the mandala and is honored by that king.
There, having spent some time with conversations full of confidence, she took those condemned men and returned to her own abode; thus,
even today, that Rākṣasa woman remains in the forest as one liberated while living.
Remaining on that very mountain, her mind’s one-pointedness in meditation dissolved;
when that king had attained peace through his own renunciation of desires,
she remained for a long time, relishing her own morsels of food out of friendship with the lords of his kingdom.
The eighty-third canto, titled "The Friendship with the Rākṣasīs," by Vasiṣṭha.
In that Kirāta region, whatever kings there may be,
with each of them she develops supreme friendship.
There, all great portents as well as fears of Piśācas and other such beings [are dispelled].
And that Rākṣasī, perfected in yoga, wards off diseases;
she has not ceased from meditation for many groups of years,
and having arrived there, she devours the well-accumulated creatures destined for slaughter.
Even today, those who are to be executed there are delivered by the king for that purpose;
for who indeed would not be resolute in honoring a friend?
While she sat absorbed in meditation within that circle of Kirāta people,
When she did not return for a long time, for the sake of pacifying the people's affliction,
that goddess named Kandarā— who bore an inauspicious name—
was dispatched by [the king] into a deep cavern within the city.
From that time forward, whichever king was there,
he himself would establish the goddess Kandarā. That base king who does not establish Kandarā or her shrine [is likewise condemned].
The masses diligently strike down his collection of afflictions;
by worshipping him, people obtain their desired fruit there. Through failure to worship him, one's own mental disposition swells with misfortune.
That Goddess is worshipped with the customary rites of those to be executed;
even now, residing within her image, she bestows fruits upon those whose minds are fixed on her—
she who brings auspiciousness to all the world and has swallowed up the entire multitude of those condemned to death.
Victorious here is that goddess of long standing, the abode of Kirāta folk, who possesses supreme awakening.
The narrative of Sūcī is concluded;
this is the eighty-fourth canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus has this entire irreproachable narrative concerning the forest ogress Karkaṭī been told to you exactly and in due order.
Rāma said:
"How did that black ogress come to be called Karkaṭī, as proclaimed in the caves of the Himavat? Tell me this exactly as it happened, O Lord."
Vasiṣṭha:
There are many families of Rākṣasas by their very nature;
they are black, white, green, and brilliant.
There was a Rākṣasa named Karkaṭa who resembled a crab;
born from him, that Kṛṣṇā became a female crab (karkaṭī) with the form of a crab.
Recalling the question regarding the female crab, this has been told by me to you.
In the course of explaining the nature of consciousness through internal discourse, it has been established that this world—
though clearly unmanifest— is [nonetheless] produced from a single,
supreme cause, a state without beginning or end.
Just as future waves exist in water as both identical to and distinct from it,
so too do other present creations exist [within the source].
Just as fire, even while not yet blazing, performs its causal function within pieces of wood...
Just as the sun, never abandoning its constant state of rising and its inherent gentleness, performs for monkeys and other beings the removal of cold and so forth;
in that same way, Brahman, though not becoming a manifold agent, creates this world as if it were diverse.
Has this very creation already arrived in the future?
O consciousness of the wooden statue, you are as well-awakened as if made of wood!
Just as a fruit and such, though not different from the seed, appears as if it were something else when it has arisen.
Thus, even that which is non-different appears as if it were different.

Because there is no cutting off of the single existence, there is no distinction between the fruit and the seed, nor any difference whatsoever in reality between consciousness and its object, just as between water and its waves.
Without investigation, no distinction between these two is possible;
whatever has arisen from any cause perishes through investigation.
O scion of Raghu’s line, let this delusion depart just as it came.

Once awakened, you will understand this; simply abandon it. When the knot of delusion has been severed by hearing my words, you will yourself fully comprehend the reality behind the distinctions between knowledge, words, and their objects.
This misfortune and prosperity arise from the mind; that mind, as well as this [world] and everything else, will undoubtedly attain peace simply by hearing my words.
Furthermore, everything has arisen from Brahman, and everything is indeed Brahman alone.
"Once fully awakened by my words, O blameless one, you will understand sufficiently.
Rāma said:
"Therefore, O Brahmin, the word *iti* here [expresses] the fifth case (*pañcamī*) in the sense of distinction (*vyatireka*)."
"But surely, why do you say that everything is non-different from the Lord of Gods?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"In the scriptures, for the sake of instruction, there arises either a word born of [conventional] meaning or one born of [ultimate] reality."
This distinction, characterized by number and consisting in the exclusion of its counter-correlate,
is indeed perceived through conventional usage, yet it is not real;
it is like a *vetāla* conjured up for the sake of a child's purpose.
In that state where things abide according to their true nature, there is neither duality nor unity;
how could there be such a corruption of conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*) in it?
For the relationship of cause and effect is characterized by the distinction between property and owner.
The cause and that which possesses the cause, as well as the sequence of the constituent parts;
the delusion regarding difference and non-difference, transformation and so forth;
likewise the modifications of existence, knowledge and ignorance, and pleasure and pain.

Thus, this world, woven together from the fabrication of false conceptualizations, exists for the sake of awakening the ignorant; yet in reality, there is no duality. This duality arises from lack of understanding; once it is known, duality no longer exists.
When that is known, all mental agitation is completely stilled, and silence alone remains.
At the time of final realization, having attained awakening, you will know it as the supreme, one, beginningless and endless, undivided, and indivisible.
For those who have not awakened conceptualize through the manifestations of their own mental constructions;
this discourse exists because of instruction, for once [reality] is known, duality is no longer found.
Without duality, the relationship between the signifier and the signified cannot be established.

Neither duality nor silence regarding speech is possible; enough of this! O descendant of Raghu, having fixed your intellect upon the meaning of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya), disregard the diversity of words and listen to that which I say.
Arising from somewhere, the mind—like a city of the Gandharvas—is born;
it extends this mere illusion called the world as its own unfolding. O sinless one, just as the mind extends this illusory world, so it is.
Listen, O Rāma; I shall tell you this illustration for the understanding of creation,
by hearing which you yourself will become certain that all this is merely an illusion, and you will cast away latent impressions far behind.
The three worlds are nothing but a construction of mental ideation;
having abandoned everything, you, with a tranquil self, shall dwell in your own self alone,
intent on attending to the meaning of my words for the healing of the disease of the mind.
And you shall apply effort through the application of the medicine of discernment (*viveka*).
