This being so, it is the mind alone that expands here as the form of the world;
the body and so forth do not exist, like oil within grains of sand.
For the mind itself, when defiled by the afflictions such as passion and the like, is saṃsāra;
that very same mind, when liberated from them, is called the end of existence (bhavānta). The mind must be cultivated, guarded, investigated, and acted upon like a noble person.
To be brought forth, to be engaged in worldly affairs, to be moved about, and to be held with care—
thus the mind bears the manifold variety of the three worlds within itself;
like a peacock’s egg, it unfolds in due time.

That which is this conscious portion of the mind is the state of being the seed of all objects; and its insentient portion, my dear, is this world, which is a delusion. This earth and the rest did not exist at all at the time of the original creation.
Formless and unborn, he sees as if in a dream, yet he does not see;
through the long perception of creation and so forth, and through the perception of insentient things such as mountains,
the knower of the subtle perceives the body as subtle, empty, and unreal.
The mind, whose nature is its own object of perception, is pervaded by the all-pervading Self;
it is as pure and serene as the water of the underworld [Ātala] when struck by the light of the sun.
Due to a lack of awakening, the childish mind falsely perceives the world-ghost.
Through awakening, he beholds his own supreme form, free from all affliction.
Listen as I explain to you how the Self comes to be perceived— that which gives rise to the delusion of duality and unity— by means of the sequence of stories to be told.

For that which is spoken with charming metaphors and reasoning, and with speech whose words and meanings are sweet and innocent, spreads throughout the listener’s heart and pervades it, O dear one, just as water fearlessly permeates oil within water. [But] that which lacks metaphor, contains unpleasant words, has difficult meaning, is agitated, hurried, confused, or has its syllables swallowed— The provided text ends mid-sentence; however, based on the context of the *Mugdhabodha* (MU), the intended completion of the verse is as follows: ...is not pleasing to the ear, like a harsh sound. (Note: The translation reflects the standard interpretation of this verse regarding the qualities of effective and ineffective speech.)
It does not enter the heart of the listener, but perishes entirely like clarified butter offered into ashes.
O virtuous one, whatever narratives and discourses exist on earth, and whatever object of knowledge has been declared, however exquisite it may be,
they quickly attain clarity through the presentation of illustrative examples, just as the world is illuminated by the white-rayed moon.
The eighty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Sprouting of the Mind," by Vasiṣṭha.
O sinless Raghava, since you have asked, I shall relate to you that very account of creation which was formerly told to me by Brahmā. Indeed,
in the past, I questioned the Blessed One who was born from the lotus.
"How do these multitudes of creations come into being, O Brahmin?
Brahmā replied:
"For in this way, the mind itself manifests in such a manner as if it were a real entity."

Like vast and variegated whirlpools in a body of water, O dear one, listen to what occurred long ago in a certain past age concerning me, as I was awakened at the beginning of the day and desired to create the world. MU_3,85.3–4.

Once, at the end of the day, having withdrawn the entire creation, I alone, with one-pointed mind and established in my own self, passed that night. At the end of the night, having fully awakened and performed the twilight rites accordingly, I remained.
I directed my wide-ranging vision toward the sky in order to see the world of living beings.
As soon as I beheld the sky— neither pervaded by darkness nor by light, exceedingly vast, empty, and devoid of boundaries— [I realized the truth].
Having resolved, "I shall bring forth this creation," I began to gaze at the very sky with a mind that was pure and subtle. Then, within that vast expanse of space, I beheld there with my mind—
He beheld the various great undertakings of creation, whose maintenance was unimpeded,
which were mutually unseen [by one another], and which included Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra, along with gods,
asuras, gandharvas, kinnaras, uragas, and humans.
Mount Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Mahendra, and Malaya; together with the mountains,
the earth, the rivers, and the directions— ten in number and radiant—
they [the lotuses] possess the appearance of reflections therein, dwelling within the calyxes of the lotuses.
The ten lotus-born ones were stationed, mounted upon chariots drawn by royal swans;
they stood amidst those ten separate worlds,
which were rising up with rows of living beings, long and blazing with flames, and radiant with brilliant light.
The great rivers flow, and likewise the oceans roar;
the suns scorch, and the winds flash in the sky.
In heaven the gods sport, and on earth human beings sport.
The Dānavas and the serpent-beings dwell happily in the netherworlds (pātālas). Pierced by the wheel of time, the six auspicious seasons, together with all their sub-divisions,
adorn the earth on every side, filled with fruits according to the season.
The conditions of conduct, both auspicious and inauspicious, have everywhere attained maturity toward all directions, yielding the fruits of hell and heaven; indeed,
all classes of beings desire the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
They strive toward their desired ends at the proper time and in due order;
likewise, the seven worlds, the islands, the oceans, and the mountains,
observing the end of the aeon, quiver with a tremendous roar.
In some places it has become night, in others it remains steady;
established within the mountain thickets, the darkness is as swift as a spark of light—
a bee hovering within a blue lotus of the sky.
A shimmering web of stars became a profusion of filaments;
the dense mist at the end of the aeon settled within the groves of Mount Meru like the pure cotton-wool of the *śālmalī* tree inside the cavities of its seed-pods.

The earth bore the girdle of the Lokāloka mountain, which resounded with the roar of the ocean of battle; it was enriched by the sapphire-like fragments of darkness and adorned with its own jewels, while the cries of living beings formed a low, humming murmur like a musical accompaniment.
Established within the expanse of the world like a woman in her inner apartments,
the splendors of the year appear like garlands of lotuses and water-lilies, resplendent with rows of white days standing amidst nights.
The worlds of beings situated within the various divisions of many wombs appear individually,
ruddy with light, like pomegranate seeds in a cluster.
The triple-streamed river that flows through the three paths, moving upward, downward, and across, [is seen].
Lacking the sacred thread of the world, yet pure like a throbbing digit of the moon,
they move here and there, wither away, and spring forth again—
like lightning-flower clouds with trailing vines in the quarters of the sky at the end of the wind.
Adorned with rows of celestial chariots, gardens, and cities of the Gandharvas,
the path of the ocean, the earth, and the sky shines resplendently. In the intermediate realms, the hosts of gods, asuras, humans, and serpents [gather] with the Saṅgha.
Like gnats buzzing within udumbara fruits, they remain there;
while time, marked by ages, kalpas, moments, lavas, kalās, and kāṣṭhās,
flows on unperceived, awaiting the destruction of all.
Having thus beheld [this] with my own pure and supreme splendor, I was struck with great amazement, wondering: "What is this? How is this?
For how is it that I see nothing at all with my fleshly eye?"

Then, with my mind, I beheld that incomparable net of illusion in the sky. Having gazed upon it for a long time from the sky by means of the mind alone, I brought the Sun out from that web of the world and questioned him.
"Come, O Lord of the gods of gods! O Bhāskara of great splendor!
Welcome to you!"—thus was he addressed by me, and then he was questioned:
"Who are you? How did this come to be—is there one world or many worlds?"
"If you know this, O Blessed One, then tell it, O sinless one.
Thus addressed, that Arka then fully recognized me;
having paid homage, he spoke these words with a voice of irreproachable cadence: "MU_3,85.36–37"
Bhānu:
Why do you not know that I have always been the cause even for this visible piśāca? O Lord, why do you ask me?
Now, O all-pervading one, if your play consists in the sequence of my words,
then listen as I speak that which has arisen from the inconceivable:
reality and unreality are extended by [your] powers, which bestow the delusion of the distinction between the weight of error and truth.
O Great-Souled One, here the great mind, shining forth as the Self of the Lord through its most refined structures, manifests.
This is the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Union of Brahmā and Āditya."
Bhānu said: O Great God, on the previous day, at the foot of Mount Kailāsa, in a single corner of Jambudvīpa, within the realm of mental construction— MU_3,86.1.
In that beautiful realm, resplendent with no small measure of happiness, which was established by your sons who had produced offspring under the name Suvarṇajaṭa,
there lived a Brahmin of exceedingly virtuous soul, the most eminent among the knowers of Brahman.

Indu by name was of an exceedingly peaceful soul and born of the lineage of Kaśyapa. While he was dwelling constantly at that time within his own circle of kinsmen, no son was born to him, just as there is no grass in a desert.

That wife of his did not shine, like a straight, fair, and perfectly pure bamboo-creeper that has flowered but bears no fruit. Then that distressed couple went to the mountain for the sake of a son to perform austerities.
Having ascended the shoulder of Kailāsa like two forest trees firmly rooted there,
they performed severe penance, subsisting on water alone while remaining within that empty, uninhabited bower of Kailāsa.

Having drunk a single handful of water at the end of the day, they remained there, motionless, having adopted the lifestyle of trees and abiding by the vow of forest-dwellers. Thus they stood then in that place, devoted to the discipline of the forest trees.
When the two ages, Tretā and Dvāpara, had thus passed away,
the Lord who bears the crescent moon became pleased with them,
like the moon toward two night-blooming lilies scorched by the heat of the day.
He arrived at that place where the brahmin couple were,
a region of trees entwined with creepers, like the Lord Śiva arriving at the garden of flowers;
the couple beheld him mounted upon his bull, bearing the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
They beheld him with his face in full bloom, like the moon upon two night-lotuses. They bowed down before that god, the Lord, who was as stainless as snow,
appearing like the full moon risen between heaven and earth.
Then Śiva, the Lord, threatening the sound of the forest of fresh bamboo shaken by the wind, spoke these words, gentle yet majestic and radiating with a smile: The Lord said:
"O Brahmin, accept this boon quickly; I am pleased with your desire.
Be joyful, like a forest of trees overwhelmed by the essence of the spring month.
The Brahmin replied:
“O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, may my ten sons of great intelligence become fortunate,
so that sorrow no longer afflicts me.
Bhānu said:
Then, having said, "So be it," the Lord vanished;
having made a roar in the sky and the ocean, he became a great-bodied wave of the waters.
Then the couple, having obtained the boon from Śiva, went home satisfied.
Having gone there, they were like two gods; she and Maheśvara were like Umā and Maheśvara in the sky.
There, in that house, the Brahmin woman became pregnant with a noble fetus;
with her full belly, the dark-complexioned lady shone like a streak of cloud filled with water.

In due time, she gave birth to ten sons, as tender as the new moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight; like the earth in springtime, the lovely woman brought forth these young ones who were as fresh as new sprouts.
Having received the sacred rites of the Veda, those youths of great splendor attained full growth.
For in a very short time, like fresh clouds in the rainy season,
they reached the age of seven years and became masters of the sciences of speech;
they shone there with splendor like stainless planets in the sky.
Then, after a long time, those two parents of theirs,
being skilled in knowing their destination, abandoned their bodies and departed for their own realm.
Thereupon, those ten Brahmins were left without mother or father.
Leaving their home far behind, they went to the peak of Mount Kailāsa.
There, being anxious and deprived of their kinsmen, they reflected and said this to one another: "What might be the highest good in this situation?"
"O brothers, what here would be appropriate? What would be free from suffering?
What constitutes greatness, great sovereignty, or auspicious, great prosperity?
For how insignificant is this lack of sovereignty, since even the vassal kings have long been lords!"
What indeed is the excellence of a vassal? For kings are indeed great lords.
What indeed is the excellence of monarchs? Here, the universal emperor is the great lord. What indeed is the excellence of sovereignty? For Indra is here the great lord.

"What indeed is that thing called sovereignty over Indra which perishes in a mere moment for Prajāpati, yet does not perish at the end of a kalpa? What could that possibly be considered auspicious here?
While they were thus speaking, the eldest brother, who was highly intelligent, [spoke].
With profound speech, he spoke thus like a deer among herds of deer:
"O brothers, that which does not perish even at the end of the kalpa among all forms of sovereignty—that is what pleases me here: the state of Brahman, and nothing else."
Then all those excellent sons of the twice-born praised that which had been spoken with words inspired by Indra, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent!
And they said this: "O father, how is the removal of all suffering [attained]?"
"The lotus posture (padmāsana), worshiped by the world, enables one to attain the state of Viriñca.
Then that brother spoke again to his brothers of immense splendor:
"May you all fully uphold everything that I have said."
"Seated in the lotus posture, radiant, with the thought 'I am Brahmā,' may your meditation be long-lasting: 'I create, I destroy.
When the Eldest had spoken thus, those excellent ones said, "So be it."
With their minds dependent on meditation, they remained together with the eldest out of devotion;
those ten, intent on meditation, assumed forms as if created by the hand of a painter,
and with their minds fixed within, they reflected with great reverence.
Seated upon the lofty throne of the wheel within the calyx of a full-blown lotus,
I am Brahmā, the creator of the world, the agent, the enjoyer, and the Great Lord—
possessing great supernatural powers along with the primary and secondary limbs of the sacrificial rites and their sequential performance.

These excellent Vedas are joined with Sarasvatī and Gāyatrī. This heaven, adorned by the gods, possesses magnificent fortune; its cities are occupied by the world-protectors, and it is frequented by circles of perfected beings (siddhas).
This dark-blue orb of the earth, adorned with mountains, islands, oceans, and forests, serves as the earring for the three worlds;
it contains this cavernous interior of Pātāla, the abode of Daityas, Dānavas, and serpents.
This house, filled with throngs of immortal women, is like the hollow of a dense forest.
This is Indra, the mighty-armed one, whose tree-like arms are adorned with the thunderbolt;
alone he protects the city of the three worlds, the enjoyer of purifying sacrifices.
As if restraining the multitude of directions with the leather thongs of their blazing nets,
these suns of abundant rays shine forth in succession.
These guardians of the world protect the universe with unshakable conduct.
Just as cowherds [tend] a herd of cows with firm boundaries,
these creatures emerge, submerge, quiver, and fall in every direction like waves of water. (MU 3.86.45–46)
I create this creation and likewise withdraw it with due regard;
I abide within the Self and remain at peace as the Lord of the World.
This year has passed; this age has come to its end.
"This is that creation, and this is the time for dissolution.
This kalpa has passed today; this is the night of Brahmā.
Therefore, I remain within myself as the Supreme Lord, the perfect Self."
Thus, with their minds cultivated in this way, those ten sons of Indu remained with their mental activities turned inward, as if carved out of stone;
having attained the path of the Lotus-Seated One, the net of all other trivial activities had fallen away from them.
Seated upon thrones worn by the constant weight of elephants, they shone for a long time in that lotus-like assembly. The eighty-seventh canto, titled "The Concentration of the Moon."
Bhānu said:
"In that lineage of the Grandfather, they remained attentive,
their minds occupied by those actions and their devotion firmly fixed upon it."
Until their bodies were withered by the heat and the winds,
like severed lotus shoots in the summer;
there, the flesh-eating beasts dwelling in the forest devoured those corpses.
They rolled here and there like monkeys among choice fruits.
Then, with external objects stilled and their meditation fixed upon Brahman,
they remained until the end of the four ages, when the kalpa came to its destruction.
Then, as the eon wanes and the mass of suns blazes forth,
while the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds pour down rain with a harsh roar and the winds of the eon blow, he remains standing in the great ocean.
When the hosts of beings had perished, they remained just as they were.
Now that you have awakened and desire to see the cycle of existence,
they remain just as they were, elevated by their own sequence.
"O Blessed One, O Brahmin, these are the ten Brāhmaṇas of Brahmā.
These ten transmigrations are situated within the void of the mind.
Of these, I am one, whose abode is the ether."
O Lord, Bhānu has been appointed by you to the task of the divisions of time upon the earth.
This creation of the ten Brahmās born from the lotus has been described to you; it arose in the void, O Lotus-born One, and now do as you wish.

This entire world, which has arisen as the highest realm of existence, enveloped in various conceptual constructions and deluding the mind with its web of rays— all this is but a delusion within one's own consciousness. Thus ends the chapter titled "The Determination of the Ten States of the World."
The eighty-eighth canto:
Brahmā said, "O Brāhmaṇa, having spoken thus to me, Brahmā, Bhānu..."
"O Brahmin, best among the knowers of Brahman, he remained silent.
Then, after reflecting for a long time in my mind, I said to him:
'O Bhānu, speak quickly! What else shall I create?'"
"O Bhāskara, tell me: if these ten worlds indeed exist there, what purpose would another creation of mine serve?
Bhānu replied:
O Lord, what purpose could there be for you in creation, since you are devoid of effort and devoid of desire?
O Lord of the world, this creation of yours is merely a pastime.
O Lord, even though you are free from desire, creation proceeds from you.
Like the sun from water, like a reflection from the intellect;
when there is indifference toward the attachment to the configuration of the body,
O Blessed One, the desireless state neither longs for nor abandons.
Then, O God, O Protector of Beings, you create this world merely for your own diversion,
repeatedly withdrawing it again and again, just as the sun withdraws its light at the end of each day;
for you alone, there is only the eternal diversion of non-attachment.
The world thinks, "This must indeed be done," yet it is not out of intense desire that you create;
nor do you perform the daily activity of your own self.
By abandoning obligatory duties, what unprecedented result will you obtain?
For one should always perform whatever comes to hand while remaining unattached,
just as a stainless mirror performs the function of reflecting images;
just as there is no desire in the wise man regarding the performance of action.

In the same way, the wise person has no desire for the non-performance of action. Therefore, with this desireless state of being which is like deep sleep, perform your duties as they arise, like one who has awakened from sleep.
O Lord, the world finds satisfaction through the creations of the sons of the Moon;
yet, O Lord of the Gods, these creations will not satisfy you.
You behold these creations with the eye of the mind, not with the physical eye.
Who, indeed, seeing with the eye, knows that "this creation has been created"? O Supreme Lord, he by whom the creation was fashioned with his own mind—
he alone sees it with the eye of flesh, and no other.
And no one is able to destroy these ten cycles of transmigration, which arise from the ten dustless [senses] and have long endured due to the firmness of consciousness;
for it is indeed possible to restrain that which is performed by the organs of action.

No one is able to restrain that which is determined by the mind. O Brahmin, whatever resolve has taken firm root in a living being's heart cannot be overturned by anything other than that very resolve itself.
Whatever has been practiced for a long time with a firm resolve by the mind,
there is no destruction of that even by a curse, nor when the body has perished.
Whatever has been firmly established all around in the mind and has taken root, a person becomes of that very form here in this world, and not otherwise.
Because of that realization, I consider any other means here to be as utterly fruitless as a mass of rocks;
thus ends the eighty-ninth canto, titled "The Declaration of Aindavanishcaya."
Bhānu said:
"O Lord, it is heard that in ancient times there was a sovereign in Magadha known as Indradyumna, who was like a second Indra."
He had a lotus-eyed wife named Ahalyā, who was like a reflection of the moon’s orb, just as Rohiṇī is to the Moon. In that very city,
it is said, there lived a powerful eunuch.
There was another illustrious young brahmin named Indra. At one time, during the course of a conversation, the queen heard from Ahalyā that she had previously been the beloved of Indra.
Having heard that, Ahalyā became enamored of Indra;
full of longing, she wondered, "Why does Śakra not come to me, Ahalyā?
She [lay] upon beds of lotus stalks, garlands, and plantain leaves.
The young woman suffered intensely, like a creeper cut down in the forests;
she found distress amidst all those royal splendors,
like a fish scorched by the summer heat tossing about on dry land.
"This one is Indra, this one is Indra"— with such infantile prattle,
she even abandoned her sense of shame as she fell into a state of helplessness. Then, to that distressed woman of deep affection, her friend spoke:
"O Ālī, I have told you that there shall be no obstacle; I shall even bring Indra to you.
Hearing "I shall bring Indra to you," her eyes blossomed with joy, and she fell at her friend's feet like one lotus falling before another.
Then, when the day had passed and night had arrived,
that female companion went to that young Brahmin named Indra;
having awakened that young Indra in the proper manner, she [spoke].
He quickly brought Ahalyā near him at night;
then, adorned with many garlands and ointments, she took her pleasure with that Śilpin, Mahendra, in a certain secret chamber.
Then, by means of that [love] which was as charming as necklaces and armlets, the young woman was won over by passion,
just as a creeper is drawn by the sweetness of honey.
Thereupon, being devoted to him, she perceived the entire world as consisting of him alone.
She did not think much of her husband, who was filled with infinite virtues.
Then, after some time, that lion among kings discovered her infatuation with Indra— that moonlight from the sky of her face.
As long as she meditated upon Indra,
so long did her face shine like a full moon or a blooming white water-lily.
Thus, the king observed their mutual state of attachment.
Then, with many punishments, he carried out the execution of those two.
Yet, though both were cast away into the reservoir of water, being virtuous, they remained content there and laughed; they did not fall into despair.
Then the king asked them, "Are you weary? Are you not foolish?
They, having been pulled out from the body of water, said to the protector of the earth:
"Having wandered here, we have beheld one another’s irreproachable beauty of countenance."
"O protector of the earth, we do not lose consciousness even when our own limbs are being cut off;
even when cast into the fire, we remain entirely untroubled. Thus, with joyful hearts and gladdened by their mutual memory [of the Dharma], they spoke to one another."
Entangled in the elephant's feet, remaining there without even being wounded,
they spoke thus to one another, their memories refreshed by joy.
Struck by the goad, yet still unwounded, they indeed spoke in this very manner.
Thus, those two, unwearying though submerged in the mire, spoke as follows;
having been repeatedly pulled out from one net of instruction after another that had been devised,
they were questioned and spoke again and again of that very same matter.
Indra said, "O protector of the earth, this world is my beloved;
no painful commands trouble me in the slightest.
And for her, O King, the entire world is indeed composed of me alone."
Therefore, by our teaching, not even the slightest suffering afflicts us.
O King, we call it "mind" (*manas*), for the mind is indeed remembered as the person (*puruṣa*);
this body is seen to be merely a mental construction (*prapañca*).
By a sudden mass of blows applied all at once,
even the steadfast mind cannot be pierced in the slightest.
O Great King, what indeed are those [powers], of what nature are they, and whose are these powers?
By these means, even minds possessed of firm resolve are shattered.
Whether the body falls or rises, or whether it goes to ruin,
the mind remains as before when it has fallen upon the object it has cultivated.

O Lord of the Earth, no states of being whatsoever residing within the body are capable of shattering my mind, which is firm, established, and long immersed in its desired object; for that which has been cultivated by the mind with intense momentum cannot be overcome.
He beholds only that which is immovable, not the movement of the body; O King, no actions whatsoever— not even boons or curses—
are capable of disturbing the mind that is possessed of intense spiritual urgency.
For men are unable to move the mind— though it may be attached with intense force toward what they desire— just as deer cannot move a great mountain.
This dark-eyed Rāmā is established within the treasury of my mind.
In the lofty temple of the gods, like the divine goddess herself,
I do not experience suffering because of my beloved, who protects my life;
she is like a mass of clouds clinging to a mountain scorched by the heat of summer.
O King, wherever and in whatever manner I stand or move forward,
there I experience nothing other than the union with my beloved.
By means of the mind named Ahalyā’s Beloved, the mind [is directed] toward that which is called Indra.
This [mind] comes into close connection with nothing other than its own inherent nature (svabhāva).
For the mind of a wise man, O King, when intent upon a single task,
cannot be shaken even by the power of the best of curses, just like Mount Meru.
For it is the body, O King, that undergoes change through blessings or curses; but the steadfast mind, having arisen with the desire for victory, does not.
And these fragments of bodies here, O King, are not the causes of the minds, nor have they arisen [from them].
For the mind is the cause among these tiny bodies, just as water is the cause for the sap of all the creepers in every forest thicket.
Know, O Great-souled One, that the mind is the primary body here; by it the multitudes of bodies are conceived in this world.
Whichever primary body the man presides over, in that one his purpose bears abundant fruit, and not in any other.

O fortunate one, know that the mind is indeed the primary sprout of man; from it, bodies have spread forth like the shoots of a tree. When the sprout is destroyed, the beauty of the shoots does not arise again, yet the sprout itself does not perish when the leaves fall away.
Upon the destruction of the body, the mind quickly creates a multitude of various bodies, just as a forest is newly produced in the land of dreams.
When the mind is wounded, the body indeed does nothing at all; therefore, protect the jewel of the mind.
O King, in every direction I see only the deer-eyed woman, my beloved; because of her, I am eternally delighted.
As for the fruit of your pleasure-induced transformations—which yields suffering either for a moment or for a very long time—I do not perceive it to be anything at all.
The Ninetieth Sarga, titled "The Fabricated Words of Indra": Bhānu.
Then, having been addressed thus by Indra, that lotus-eyed king spoke to the sage named Bharata, who was seated at his side. The King said:

"O Blessed One, knower of all phenomena, do you behold today the immense audacity in the mouth of this evil-souled one, who has carried off my wife? O Great Sage, bestow upon him a curse that is commensurate with his sin."
"Indeed, that very sin which arises from killing one who should not be killed is [removed] by the renunciation of killing"—
having been addressed thus by the lion among kings, Bharata, the best of sages,
quickly reflected properly upon the sin of that evil-minded man.
"Go to your destruction, O evil-minded one, along with this woman of wicked deeds who has overcome you through her betrayal of her husband! Thus did Bhānu utter a curse.
Then, their minds still bound by affection, they both fell to the ground due to the curse, like two leaves fallen from a tree.
Thereafter, overcome by calamity, they entered the womb of deer.
Then both of them were again born as birds, deeply attached to one another.
O Lord, in this present creation of ours, we two have become a highly meritorious Brahmin couple, devoted to asceticism and bound together by mutual affection.
For that curse of theirs,
O Lord, was indeed effective only in assailing their physical bodies, not in restraining their minds.
Until this very day, they have remained bound by that very cause which refined their bodies.
Wherever the two of you are born as husband and wife,
having observed that lovely affection of theirs, which is permeated by the essence of unartificial love,
even the trees become permeated by the essence of affection and agitated by amorous gestures.
The ninety-first canto:
Bhānu said:
"Therefore, O Blessed One, O Sage, I speak this of the mind exactly as it has arisen."
"O Brahmin, it is impossible for the lineages of the sons of Indu— which are unseizable and indestructible even by formidable curses—
to meet their destruction;
nor is such a thing fitting for one so great-souled."

What is there in this world, or indeed in the various worlds, that could cause distress even to you, O Lord of lords, you who are a great soul? For the mind is the creator of the worlds; the mind is indeed remembered as the person (puruṣa).
In this world, that which is performed by the mind is truly performed; that which is performed by the body is not considered performed.
Whatever is accomplished through the resolve of the mind cannot be destroyed by physical substances, medicines, or punishments for a living being, just as a reflection in a gem cannot be harmed.
Therefore, let these remain here with their radiant and tumultuous creations;
you, having created the subjects here, remain as the infinite one even within the space of the intellect (*buddhyākāśa*).
The space of the mind (*cittākāśa*), the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), and the third, the [outer] space (*ākāśa*).
These three alone are infinite, illuminated by the space of consciousness.
O Prajāpati, create one, two, or even many worlds;
abide in yourself by your own will—what have you gained from the sons of Indu?
Brahmā said:
O great sage, when the solar net of the world had been thus described by me, I reflected for a long time and then spoke this.
O Bhānu, what you have said is correct; for indeed, the sky is vast, the mind is vast, and the space of consciousness is expansive.
Therefore, I constantly perform the work of creation according to my own will.
"O Bhāskara, I shall quickly fashion many nets of beings.
Therefore, O Blessed One, you yourself become the first Manu here at once;
urged by me, perform the creation as you desire."
Then that Prabhākara, of great splendor and best among those who practice austerity, having accepted my words, divided himself in two;
with one [form], he attained the state of the Sun in his former body.
Having assumed the state of my mind through his second form, he instantly spread a succession of days across the path of the sky in that creation; he then brought forth the entire,
expansive creation as it was desired by me.
Whatever indeed appears to his mind,
that very thing attains clarity, stability, and even fruitfulness.
It is said that by the power of such an appearance, having become an ordinary Brahmin...
The followers of Indu attained the state of Brahman; behold the power of the mind!

Just as those living beings of Indu reached the state of Brahman through their state of consciousness (*cittatva*), so too have we, being of the nature of consciousness, reached the state of Brahman through our state of consciousness.
For the mind is of the nature of manifestation, and that which is its manifestation appears as this body and so forth, resembling empty space; therefore, there is no perception of a body.
Mind-ness is the wonder of the Self, and it wonders by itself.
Whatever exists potentially within its own self, like the essence of a mirage,
that very thing appears as the mind, known by the name *ātivāhika*;
they describe that same thing, when it becomes dense through delusion, by the name "body."
This mind, whose latent impressions have become attenuated, is called by the name "jīva"; know that the jīva, which is the wondrous manifestation of the body, gradually becomes the Supreme.
There is no "I" here, nor is there anything else; only this consciousness exists as consciousness.
Like the union of Vasiṣṭha and Indu, the non-existent has come to appear as if it were existent. Just as the mind of Indu was Brahmā, so do I remain;
and this world, created by me, shines forth as nothing but my own volitional nature.
This is merely a play of the mind established as "I am Brahman";
know that the body and so forth are simply its own nature, arising from the void of the Self.
Through the contemplation that pure consciousness alone is the singular form of the Supreme Self, [the world is transcended].
Having become the individual soul (*jīva*) and having become the mind (*manas*), it vainly perceives itself as possessing a body.
This entire world, which appears as the form of consciousness (*cidvapuḥ*), is like the cycle of existence experienced by the son of Indu;
though it is fully accomplished, it is a long dream born of one's own power, arising from a lack of awakening.

The nature of the mind (cittva) becomes the manas, which arises like the moon or a lotus, appearing as the delusion of the forms of the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the delusion of the form of the double moon. The form of the "I" (ahaṃrūpa) is neither existent nor non-existent, and its existence and non-existence are likewise.
That which possesses the nature of being perceived is unreal, because it is opposed to that [reality].
Know the mind to be both inert and non-inert, having the nature of volition and a vast form;
it is non-inert because its essence is Brahman, and it is inert because it has attained the nature of the visible object.
That which consists of the reality of the experience of the visible world dissolves in its absence;
just as the state of being a bracelet exists within gold, so too does it reside within Brahman.
Because Brahman is everything, everything—whether insentient or consisting of consciousness—is Brahman alone.
From our own selves down to a stone, there is nothing that is neither insentient nor sentient.
Since wood and such things lack consciousness, perception cannot occur;
for perception arises only from a relationship with something similar [to the perceiver].
Know that through perception everything is indeed sentient;
for perception arises from a connection, and that connection exists between two things of equal nature.
There is no such thing as the "splendor" (śrī) of the meanings of words such as "insentient," "sentient," "peaceful," and so forth.
In that ineffable state, just as there are no trees or creepers in a great desert,
the perception of an object within consciousness is declared to be the nature of the mind (*manas*).
Here, the aspect of consciousness is the non-inert part, whereas the quality of being an object of cognition is the inert part.
The conscious portion here is the aspect of awareness, while the insentient is the object of cognition, which is indeed visibility;
thus, the individual soul (jīva), perceiving the delusion of the world, falls into agitation. By consciousness itself, this very being is thus rendered dual through its own purity.
Therefore, that very [consciousness] is the entire world; it is duality itself, having obtained its own portion.
Having perceived itself as something else through the form of the visible, consciousness—though partless—appears as if it were a single part, wandering as if afflicted by delusion.
There is no delusion, nor indeed is there anyone who experiences delusion; this is the certainty here.
Consciousness, resembling a full ocean, is established in this manner as consciousness.
Since it possesses universality, let there be insentience within this consciousness, yet you perceive that very sentience.
In this context, the "consciousness-portion" is the element of awakening, which arises from the non-arising of "I-ness" (ahantā) and insentience.

(MU 3.91.41) Not even the slightest trace of "I-ness" and so forth exists within the supreme reality (para-tattva), just as waves and the like do not exist separately from water; for that [reality] has consciousness as its essence. (MU 3.91.42)
Know that the object of cognition which appears as the notion of "I" has arisen like a mirage; therefore, it certainly does not exist at all.
Know that the state of the Self is free from disease, consisting merely of the transcendence of the state of "I-ness."
They know that consciousness is non-duality and so forth, just as coldness is the very nature of snow.
Consciousness alone perceives its own insentience, which is like one's own death in a dream;
because it is the self of all, performing all powers, it does not attain a state of mere equality.
The mind unfolds as the form of all things, such as objects and so forth;
this body of consciousness is not a manifold self, having a form as clear as the sky. One should always abandon the notion of a self that consists of the appearance of the body and other such things.
One should clearly discern that the nature of the mind is essentially manifestation;
for when the copper of the mind is purified and attains the state of the gold of ultimate reality,
there arises unartificial bliss— what then is the use of fragments of stones that are bodies?
That which exists can be purified; but by whom can a tree in the sky be washed?

If the ignorance regarding the body and so forth were real, then attachment toward it would be appropriate. However, for those here who are intent upon the unreal and whose intellects are fixed on the body and such, [this is not the case].
Those ignorant ones who teach such things are merely men with the minds of sheep.
Just as one might contemplate this within one's own mind, so it becomes in an instant;
the illustration for this is the conviction regarding the moon, the daughter of Ahalya, and the artificial Indra.
Whatever manifests in whatever manner as the mind, whose nature is its own self-reflection, that very thing arises as the body.
Having realized that this body exists, yet "I" do not exist, and that the true nature is the single consciousness, remain free from desire.
This body and this so-called "I" strive for the sake of the body alone due to their inherent nature; therefore, it goes to destruction.
Out of the power of imagining yakṣas and such, the fool experiences fear even when he has gone to a place entirely free of yakṣas, by some manner of reasoning.
The ninety-second canto, titled "The Instruction on the Sequence of the Descent of the Living Being."
Vasiṣṭha said:
O descendant of Raghu, having been addressed thus by me, that blessed Lord, the lotus-born creator of beings, set aside his previous words and was questioned further.

O Blessed One, you yourself have declared that the powers of curses, mantras, and the like are unfailing; how then have those very powers been rendered futile? By means of a curse or the potency of a mantra, even the mind, intellect, and senses [are overcome].
Indeed, all [distinctions] among living beings are seen to be utterly deluded. Just as wind and its movement, or just as oil and ghee, these two— the mind and the body— are always indeed inseparable.
Or perhaps the body does not exist at all, being merely a benefit to the mind;
it is experienced in vain, like a dream, a mirage, or a double moon. In this case, the destruction of both would necessarily follow upon the destruction of the one.
The dissolution of the body, however, is inevitable upon the destruction of the mind.
O Lord, how is it that the mind is not assailed by defects such as curses and the like?
Or how is it assailed? Tell me this, O Supreme Lord.
Brahmā said:
There is nothing within the vessel of the world that cannot be attained by people through pure human effort accompanied by virtuous action.
From Brahma down to the stationary plants,
all beings of every species in this world at all times possess two bodies for embodied souls:
one is the mental body, which is swift-acting and remains mobile.
But the other body, composed of flesh, is of no avail;
for wherever there is a body made of flesh, it falls under the control of everyone and is afflicted by all curses as well as by the accumulation of mental and physical ailments.

For this second body of those who possess a body here, called "mind," is almost mute, incapable, wretched, and perishing in an instant; it is as fickle as a drop of water on a lotus leaf, its state dependent on the gods and other powers.
Though he is dependent [on others], he is not dependent on any beings in the three worlds.
If, having relied upon his own manly power and maintained constant fortitude,
he remains unassailable by sufferings, then he is beyond reproach.
In whatever way the mind-body of embodied beings exerts itself,
in that very way it becomes, reaping exclusively the fruit of its own resolve.
No effort of human agency bears fruit for the physical body of flesh.
Every action performed by one whose mental body is thus established becomes entirely fruitful;
for one who remains mindful with a pure heart,
curses and the like are as fruitless as arrows shot at a stone.
Whether the body falls into water, fire, or mud,
that which the mind contemplates is certainly what it attains.
The excellence of human effort arises from the sublation of all [other] states of being.
O Sage, for the mind indeed bestows its fruit without obstacle upon the mind itself.
By the power of human effort, having inwardly made the mind consist of what is dear,
even when faced with the commands of a false Indra, no suffering or pain was seen.
Having made the mind free from passion and devoid of fever through human effort,
Māṇḍavya conquered the afflictions even while remaining on the tip of a stake; likewise,
even while staying in a blind well, he did so by means of mental accumulations of sacrifice.
The city of the gods was attained by the seer Dīrghatapas;
and through human resolve alone, the sons of Indu attained the state of Brahman by means of meditation— a state which is not even surpassed by me.
Others too, who are vigilant— the steadfast gods and great seers—
do not abandon their own inner inquiry even for a moment. Mental agonies,
physical ailments, curses, and likewise the visions of evil [do not affect them].
The blows of lotus petals do not break them, as if they were stone.
As for those who are indeed broken by curses and other such arrows of mental anguish,
I consider their minds to be lacking in manliness and incapable of self-discernment.

At no time in saṃsāra is there anyone, even in a dream, who possesses even the slightest attentive mind and remains uncorrupted by the nets of faults. Therefore, in this world, a person should [subdue] the mind with the mind itself through human effort.
One should join one's own [mind] with its very own [nature] on the purifying path.
Whatever appears to it becomes sufficient in that form;
in an instant, O Sage, the mind becomes swollen like a child’s ghost.
Immediately upon its manifestation, the mind abandons its prior state,
O Sage, just as a pot abandons the condition of a lump of clay immediately after the potter’s work;
in an instant, the mind attains the state of being an object of manifestation.

Just as water, whose nature is mere vibration, assumes the state of lofty waves, so too the mind— when its faculties are unpurified— perceives night even in the solar disc through mere mental construction, just as one with impaired vision perceives duality in the lunar disc.
Whatever this mind perceives, that very thing immediately bears fruit;
it experiences it along with joy and sorrow, and therefore that alone is real.
Following every moment of its intuition, even in the moon there appears a hundred crests of fire.
Upon seeing it, one experiences a burning sensation, and being burnt, one suffers intense remorse.
Yet the mind, following its own intuition, finds an elixir even in that caustic substance;
for upon seeing and drinking it, it reaches supreme satisfaction, leaps for joy, and exults.
Even in the sky, the mind perceives a great forest at every step of its creative intuition;
having seen it, it cuts it down, and having cut it down, it plants it once more.
O dear one, the mind thus quickly perceives whatever magical illusion it itself imagines.
Having understood that the world is neither non-existent nor existent, you must surely abandon this vision which possesses manifold diversities.
The Ninety-third Chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Mind."
Vasiṣṭha: This was previously told to me by the Blessed One;
that very thing has been recounted to you today.
Therefore, from this unnameable, all-pervading Brahman, first arises a slight degree of mentation (*manana*). Having itself attained density, it becomes the mind (*manas*).
That mind, preceded by the conceptualization of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), brings about the formation of the world-structure.
Then he becomes a person of light.
He gave himself the name "Brahman. Know that this Parameṣṭhin, by whom that name was given, is the principle of mind (manas-tattva).
That Blessed One Brahmā, whose form is the essence of mind, because he consists of volition (saṅkalpa), sees whatever he wills; thus,
by him this ignorance was imagined, consisting of the conceit of self in what is not-self.
By that Brahman, this world—consisting of mountains, grass, and oceans—was fashioned in succession.
Thus, this creation has emerged from the reality of Brahman in a gradual sequence; yet it appears as if it had come from something else.
Therefore, [it is established] that all things existing within the belly of the three worlds...
O Rāma, the origin of the world from Brahman is like that of waves from the ocean.
Thus, when the universe has arisen, that consciousness of Brahman which consists of the nature of thinking, having fashioned the ego (ahaṅkāra), attains the state of Brahman.

As for those other powers of consciousness which are indeed non-different from all powers, yet appear as if differentiated, they manifest through the mind in the form of the Grandfather (Brahmā) when the universe has been expanded;
these, revolving by the thousands, are called individual souls (jīvas).

Having risen from the sky and being enveloped in the subtle elements (tanmātra) within the firmament, they enter— by means of the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti)— into whichever among the fourteen kinds of elemental beings (bhūta-jāti) stands nearby, whether stationary or moving, and thus attain the state of seeds (bīja-tā).

Thereafter, they are born into the world from a womb; thereafter, they become partakers of the fruits of karma corresponding to the flow of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by chance, like the "crow and the palm fruit.
Then, bound by the ropes of karma and enveloped by latent impressions, they fall and rise again as their bodies wander about.
And thus are these classes of beings:
some, enriched by thousands of births, fall like leaves from a forest tree.
Whirled about by the winds of karma, they wallow in the hollows of mountains.
Some, having undergone immeasurable existences, are deluded by continuous ignorance;
though born long ago, they continue to wander here even for many hundreds of kalpas.
Some, having passed through only a few previous existences that were delightful,
dwell in this world devoted to virtuous deeds;
some, having realized true knowledge, have gone to the supreme state.
Like drops of ocean water tossed by the wind into the midst of the sea,
so is the origin of all seeds from the state of Brahman;
for it is transient, subject to manifestation and disappearance, and characterized by attachment to worldly existence.
Latent impressions (vāsanā) sustain the fever of distress caused by the imbalance of poisons;
they bring about a chaotic mixture of endless, perilous misfortunes and activities;
they wander through various directions, lands, times, mountains, and mountain caves.
Adorned with the most exquisite variety and fashioned with the whirls of its eddies,
this withered creeper of the world’s wilderness— once severed by the axe of perfect discernment and its agitated mind and body dissolved— is no longer able to sprout again, O Rāmabhadra.
The ninety-fourth canto, titled "The Vision of Origination," from the *Vasiṣṭha*.
"O Rāghava, listen as I describe this classification of the origins of superior, inferior, and middling objects from here and there.
For that which has arisen for the very first time in this very birth..."
The first arising of that [intellect] is held to be sattvic;
it is known as "this-for-the-first-time," born from auspicious practice,
resting upon auspicious worlds, and connected with auspicious actions.
If that [consciousness], which operates through the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of manifold saṃsāra,
were to attain liberation through a few [specific] entities while being thick with qualities,
it would provide the inference for what is to be done and what is not to be done based solely on the production of such a result.
Therefore, she is called "one with the nature of a king" by those of perfected self.
But if she is occupied with the habitual tendencies of the manifold cycle of existence,
being extremely turbid even after thousands of births, she becomes a partaker of knowledge.
Because she bestows the inference of dharma and adharma solely through the granting of such fruits,
she is called "the one belonging to inferior beings" by those of perfected self.
She herself, immediately following a multitude of infinite births beyond calculation, [is so designated].

If liberation is said to be uncertain, that is declared to be the state of extreme darkness (*atyantatāmasī*). O Rāma, the middling birth of a person— occurring within two or three lifetimes— is characterized by an intellect acquired from a non-remote birth and such causes.
In the same way, O best of kings, the *rājasī* [nature] in this world follows after its effects;
it is described by those of perfected intellect as a path whose stages of rebirth are not far removed.
For that [nature], by the mere fact of being born with it, is fit for liberation according to those seeking release.
By inferring from such effects, that which is characterized by both passion and purity (rājasasāttvikī) has been described.
If that very same [nature] becomes a partaker of liberation through only a few other births,
then it is indeed called "passionate-passionate" (rājasarājasī) by those who know that.
If that same [person], though seeking liberation for a long time, becomes a partaker of liberation only after hundreds of births,
then she is described by the virtuous as being of rajasic and tamasic nature, characterized by such undertakings.
If that same person has liberation in doubt even after thousands of births, [she is likewise so described].
That which is thus described as having such an undertaking is the state of extreme *rājasa* and *tāmasa*.
But that birth of men from Brahmā, after having experienced thousands of previous lives,
is said by the great seers to be "slow liberation" (*ciramokṣā*), for it is *tāmasa*.
If she is destined for liberation by that very birth,

it is said by those who know reality that she is "of the nature of tamas and sattva," as this indicates such an undertaking. If she is destined for liberation through only a few [favorable] conditions, it is said accordingly.
"Having the nature of *tamas* and *rajas*": by means of such functions of the qualities (*guṇa-vṛtti*),
those who were previously enriched by thousands of births, and even hundreds of births before that,
are then declared by the knowers of truth to be "the most *tāmasa* among the *tāmasa*" (*tāmasatāmasī*), being fit for liberation.
But if, even previously or even before, one has been rich in hundreds of thousands of births,
yet remains doubtful regarding liberation, that person is said to be "extremely tamasic.
All these classes of beings come together from Brahman.
Slightly stirred from their enjoyment, like waves from the ocean;
all these multitudes of living beings have emerged from Brahman through the vibration of his own splendor, like rays from a lamp.
All the multitudes of beings have indeed arisen from Brahmā,
like sparks from a firebrand whirled by its own force;
all the classes of living beings have likewise emerged from that Brahmā.

Like rays from the orb of the moon, all the visible perceptions of Brahmā have arisen in the form of Mandāra blossoms; just as the various beauties of the branches of a tree take on the very form of that tree.
All these individual life-forces (jīva-śakti) have arisen from Brahman,
just as bracelets, armlets, and necklets arise from gold;
O Rāma, all these multitudes of living beings have likewise emerged from Brahman.
Just as drops of water [emerge] from a pure and radiant waterfall,
O Rāma, the entire conceptualization of the succession of beings belongs to the Unborn alone,
just as the spaces within jars, bowls, and holes belong to space itself.
All worldly constructions have arisen from the state of Brahman,
just as spray, whirlpools, waves, and droplets arise from water.
O Rāma, all perceptions of the visible world have likewise arisen from Brahman.
Just as the waves of a mirage belong to the brilliance of the sun,
all objects of sight are not distinct in nature from the seer;
they are like the moonlight of the cool-rayed one, or like the self-luminosity of fire.
Thus, indeed, these various classes of beings in the worlds arise from that very source and enter back into that very same source.
Some classes of beings, having existed for a long time, emerge after the end of thousands of births.
Some remain fixed in the form of only a few past births.
Thus, in these diverse worlds, by the will of the Blessed One, various forms engage in worldly activity;
the splendors of beings come and go, fall and likewise rise, like clusters of sparks arising from a fire.
The ninety-fifth canto, titled "The Exposition that Everything Arises from Brahman," by Vasiṣṭha:
The agent and the object of action are non-different, having emerged simultaneously from the supreme state,
just as the flower and its fragrance emerge from a tree.
When all conceptual constructions have ceased, the individual soul exists within the stainless Brahman.
They flash forth in the vast sky like sparks from the darkness itself.
O Rāghava, where the conduct of unawakened people is observed,
there the assertions that "living beings are produced from Brahman" remain established.
"O Rāghava, it is not fitting for those who follow the conduct of the fully awakened to speak in this way— asking whether this world was born from Brahmā or was not born—
nor until some conceptual construction has been brought to prominence, O Rāghava."
In this world, the glory of both the teacher and the teaching does not shine as long as [duality persists].
Therefore, having accepted the wretched state of differentiation, it is taught that "this is Brahman" and "these are the individual souls"— this is merely an error of words.

Thus, through this vision, the world arises from the unattached Brahman; though born from that, it is that very reality itself, yet it remains difficult to comprehend. Like Mount Meru and Mandara, the multitudes of individual souls are as numerous as these.
Rising up again and again, they dissolve into that very supreme state;
others, beginningless and endless, flash forth by the thousands like sprouts upon trees in various forest thickets.
Floods of living beings will arise like new sprouts in the springtime,
and they will go to dissolution in that very same place like honey-vines in the summer;
they remain incessantly through the ages, both those same ones and many others.
The multitudes of individual souls are born and then dissolved within that Supreme;
O Rāghava, the person and his karma are inseparable like a flower and its fragrance—
having emerged from the Supreme Lord, they both slowly re-enter into Him alone.
Thus, in this world, these Daityas, Uragas, humans,
and gods flash forth again and again through arising, subsiding, and non-existence;
the cause of their wandering is nothing other than the forgetting of the Self.
"O virtuous one, no other is observed to bestow the fruit of the path of birth.
Rāma said:
"That which is consistent with reality is true, as seen by those who possess the vision of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)."

That which has been determined by those free from passion is called a scripture (*śāstra*). Those who are endowed with the qualities of great beings (*mahāsattva*), who are steadfast and possess equal vision, and whose instructions bear fruit— they are declared to be the virtuous (*sādhu*).
This entire view, however, leads to the accomplishment of all actions;
for by means of virtuous conduct, one always follows the scripture.
He who does not follow the scripture, which is established upon the proper conduct of the virtuous—
Everyone rejects him, and he sinks into suffering.
O Lord, in this world and in the Veda,
the sacred tradition always declares that action and the agent are joined together here in a reciprocal manner.
The agent is produced by action, and the action is measured by the agent;
this traditional teaching spoken in the Vedas is like that of the seed and the sprout in the world.
A living being is born from action, just as a new sprout arises from a seed.

Action arises for a living being just as a seed [sprouts] from a sprout. By whatever latent impression (vāsanā) an action is cast into the cage of existence, a fruit corresponding to that very impression is experienced.
This being the case, how indeed can you say that the arising of beings from the state of Brahmā occurs without karma, which is the seed of birth? By this position,
O Blessed One, [you have contradicted yourself regarding] birth and karma.

O Brahmin, although the world is disregarded [as real], it is nonetheless inseparable from these two; for while you have cleared away the notion in the world that action is the cause of results such as birth and so forth, there nevertheless exists the fruit of actions.
When confusion has arisen in the world and actions no longer yield their fruits, and when the "law of the fish" prevails, only destruction remains.
What, then, is accomplished by this? O Blessed One, tell me this according to the truth.
"O best among those who know the Vedas, sever this vast doubt of mine.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Excellent, O Rāghava! I have been well-asked this auspicious question by you."
Listen, I shall tell you that by which the arising of knowledge may become intense:
that which is the unfolding of the mind in the form of the perception of parts—
that is the seed of karmas, and its fruit alone exists.
For that very reality which is the mind, having arisen from the state of Brahman, is itself the karma of living beings; it exists as the individual soul (jīva) abiding in the form of a body.
Just as there is no difference here between a flower and its fragrance, even though they appear distinct.
In the same way, there is no difference between action and the mind, even though they appear distinct.
In this world, the wise have declared that "action" is the vibration of activity;
since the body was preceded by the mind, action is indeed the mind itself.
There is no mountain, no sky, no direction,
and no heaven where there is no fruit for the deeds one has performed oneself;
whether it be an action clearly committed in this life or in a previous one.
This supreme human effort is never fruitless.
Know that the mind arises from Brahman; know that action here is nothing other than that.
Know, O Raghava, that very [mind] is the seed of living beings, and nothing else.

Because it is the cause of the connection [between thoughts] through the transition from one place to another, the mind is indeed the prior cause; therefore, the wise know the mind to be action (*karman*). From Brahman, who resembles an undisturbed ocean, there arises that which possesses the nature of vibration.
Some say that the consciousness of living beings has departed from here;
yet the mind is the action, the mind is the life-force, and by that very [mind] the body is extended.
Therefore, action and the agent are not distinct, just as oil is not distinct from the sesame seed.
For the two entities consisting of the agent and the object are indeed eternally non-different;
they appear as distinct only due to a lack of realization, being imagined in vain.
O Rāma, there are two minds for the ignorant, but not for the wise.
The water of the ocean and the water of its waves are like the perception of difference held by the ignorant.
Know that these two are indeed synonymous terms for the activity of the mind;
yet, having abandoned their status as synonyms, they remain difficult to comprehend.
First, the mind, whose nature is action, proceeds from the Supreme,
just as a flower of various forms proceeds from a tree with its own fragrance;
here, the cognitions that designate agent and object proceed incessantly from the Word.
They proceed from that [Supreme Self] like waves from the ocean;
yet when they are withdrawn back into it, those things designated as "living beings" dissolve away after having vibrated, just as waves dissolve into the ocean.
Whatever action is performed by the mind, that alone shall bear fruit;
it is in the mind alone, not arising from the body, that the agent and the action reside. Therefore, the mind is the agent.
In a mirror whose expanse is illuminated by light, the reflection shines forth with ease.
When the reality of Brahman is fully realized, agency clearly resides in the mind;
just as qualities such as whiteness reside in their substrates like cloth,
so too does agency abide in the mind known as the individual soul (jīva).
Just as frost is not perceived when it is devoid of coldness and other qualities,
so too no mind whatsoever is perceived in the absence of karma.
Just as collyrium is spontaneously destroyed when its blackness has vanished, [so is the mind].
In the same way, when the karma consisting of vibration ceases, the mind is utterly destroyed.
The destruction of karma is the destruction of the mind, and the destruction of the mind is indeed the state of non-action;
this belongs only to the liberated one, never to the unliberated.
Just as fire and heat are always conjoined, so too are the mind and its activity;
in the absence of either one, both indeed dissolve.
Know that the mind is always this play of vibration, and that action is indeed of the singular nature of vibration.
"O Rāma, when action and mind have reached the state of being the possessor and the possessed, they indeed become one with each other.
This is the ninety-sixth canto, titled "The Demonstration of the Unity of Action and the Person."
Vasiṣṭha said: "The mind is indeed nothing but ideation; ideation consists of vibration.
Action is the form thus ideated, and everyone pursues that which is its fruit."
Rāma said: O Brahmin, you ought to describe in detail to me— though I am dull-witted, yet possess a form that is not dull— the nature of the mind when it has ascended to the level of volition.
Vasiṣṭha said:
They know that form of the infinite reality of the Self, the omnipotent Great Soul, which is endowed with the power of volition, to be the mind.
That reality which stands with its form oscillating between the perception of the inert and the non-inert, and which is grasped by neither—those know that to be the nature of the mind.
The certainty is: "I am not the self-luminous consciousness; I am miserable."
That which is always characterized by the activity of conceptualization, they know to be the form of the mind.
That state which flashes forth for men as something motionless in the midst of existence and non-existence, having become intent upon conceptualization— they know that to be the form of the mind.

In this world, a mind devoid of the power of action, which is of the nature of time, is not possible, just as a possessor of qualities cannot exist without those qualities. Just as the existence of fire and heat is not possible if they were separate.
In the very same way, it is so for action and the mind, as well as for the self and the mind;
[the self] exists by means of its own mental form, which is characterized by action as its fruit,
whose sole body is volition, and which possesses manifold expansions.

Whatever latent impression (*vāsanā*) is planted where and by whom, just as a creeper is planted, so does it bear fruit there for that person; in that very way, that same result is obtained. Furthermore, the vibration of the mind is said to be the seed of karma, and it is experienced [as such].

Its various activities are like the branches of a tree bearing diverse fruits. Whatever the mind intends, all these functions of the organs of action accomplish it; therefore, the mind is said to be action.
Mind, intellect, ego, consciousness, action, as well as imagination, transmigratory existence, latent impressions, ignorance, effort,
and memory; the sense organ, primordial nature, illusion, and activity— these and others as well.

The manifold splendors of sound are many and are the causes of the delusion of saṃsāra; they have been made to function as synonyms for consciousness (cit), which— having abandoned its expansive wonder through a chance occurrence like the "crow and the palm fruit"— follows after objects of thought (cetya).
Rāma:
O Brahmin, how have these various modes of the supreme consciousness come to be established as diverse objects when they are being conceptualized?

Vasiṣṭha: When consciousness, which is essentially conceptualization, has as it were attained a state of being with a stain, at that very moment the condition of the mind arises in the form of unfolding.
When she remains established after having ascertained the sequence of entities,
then this is called "fixed intellect" (buddhi), capable of grasping [objects].
When, through false conceit, she herself imagines existence [of objects], [she is called "doubtful intellect"].
Therefore, that which is called *ahaṅkāra* (ego) is said to be the bond of worldly existence.
When, like a child, it abandons this and takes up that, being fragile and having completely discarded discernment, then it is called *citta* (mind).
When, because its sole nature is vibration, it rushes toward the fruit of vibration— thereby indicating action, malice, or praise— it is then designated as "action" (*karman*).
By way of a chance coincidence (*kākatālīya-yogena*), it abandons the determination of a single substance.
When one conceives an object as desired, that is what is called "conception" (kalpanā) here.
When one internally determines that something previously seen or unseen was created in the past,
that is designated as "memory" (smṛti).
When the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) dwell within the powers of objects as if they were already enjoyed, with all other perceptions subsided, then it is called "subsidence" (*asta*).
There exists the stainless reality of the Self, marked by a second vision.
For that which has arisen, though it does not exist, is then called "ignorance" (avidyā).
It manifests for the destruction of the Self and causes one to forget that state;
by means of a web of false conceptualizations, that impurity is imagined.
Having heard, created, seen, tasted, smelled, and reflected, this [faculty] gladdens Indra; therefore it is known as an *indriya*.
Within the unperceived Supreme Self, there is the entire web of the visible world.
Because it is the source of all things, it is called "nature" (prakṛti) in the world.
It swiftly leads existence to non-existence, or non-existence to existence;
because it thus brings forth a flood of conceptual constructions—whether of being or non-being—it is called "illusion" (māyā).
In the world, that which has entered into the state of cause and effect through the activities of seeing, hearing, touching, tasting, and smelling is called "action" (kriyā).
When consciousness follows after the objects of thought, it becomes defiled.
These are the synonymous functions of that which possesses the nature of a throbbing form—
having attained the state of consciousness and having reached its natural ground—
which have grown intensely firm through hundreds of its own volitions.
Stained by the blemish of what is to be willed, following the net of dullness,

divided into numerical categories, and indeed agitated by its own conceptual constructions— this is *cit* (consciousness) which is called "the individual soul" (*jīva*) in the world and is also described as "the mind" (*manas*).

It is called "mind" (citta) and likewise it is called "intellect" (buddhi). The wise describe this defiled thing— which has fallen away from ultimate reality— as a collection of synonyms, turbid with various conceptual constructions.
Rāma:
O Brahmin, knower of reality, the single certainty that does not arise within me is this: could the mind be insentient, or rather, could it be sentient? MU 3.96.36
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāma, the mind is indeed neither inert nor has it attained the state of pure consciousness;
rather, that vision which is neither inert nor conscious when it has faded away is called 'mind'."
O Rāma, that turbid form which appears in the midst of existence and non-existence, and which is the cause of the world— this is called the mind (*citta*).
It exists without a permanent, singular, or certain nature.
That which is here called "mind" (citta), from that this world is born.
Between the inert and the conscious perceiver, that which is mounted upon a swing by its own imagination— when consciousness has become dimmed in form— that is what is called the mind (manas).
O Rāma, that which is the impure outflow of consciousness, its interior marred by stains, is called the "mind" (manas); it is neither inert nor composed of pure consciousness.
These various names have been fully assigned to it.

Just as an actor assumes various roles, so indeed does the mind, O Rāma, undergo other states of being as it moves from one action to another— whether as ego, mind, intellect, the individual soul, or any other.
Just as a man proceeds according to the power of his various undertakings,
so does the mind proceed according to the power of its karma.
O Rāghava, these designations of the mind which have been described by me—
These very [entities] have been described otherwise by disputants through hundreds of conceptualizations;
having superimposed upon them a reasoning favored as their own nature,
they have fashioned various names and songs for the mind, intellect, senses, and so forth.
For the mind (*manas*) of one is inert, while that of another living being is distinct;
likewise, for one disputant there is egoity (*ahaṃkṛti*), and for another, intellect (*buddhi*).
Egoity, mind, intellect, and views are merely conceptual constructs of creation.
O descendant of Raghu, that which has been described by me as being of a single nature is otherwise conceptualized by the Naiyāyikas;
it is conceptualized differently by the Sāṅkhyas, and yet again differently by the Cārvākas.
By the followers of Jaimini, the Ārhatas, the Buddhists, as well as the Vaiśeṣikas,
and by others of various kinds such as the Pāñcarātras and so forth—
indeed, by all of them— that supreme state of the Self must be attained.
Like travelers from various regions and times gathered in a single city,
those who desire to ascend [to the heights] dispute only with conceptual constructions, due to ignorance of the ultimate reality and their mistaken understanding of it.
Debate-proponents praise their own paths with a variegated vision,

like travelers on different routes praising their own way according to the diverse lands and times from which they arise. O Rāghava, they have falsely proclaimed [these views] for those whose minds are intent on ritual action.
Through objects presented by its own conceptual constructions, the mind itself adopts various methods of diversity;
just as a single person performing the acts of bathing, giving, receiving,
and eating assumes a variety of roles as an agent, so too does this mind.
Due to the influence of various effects, the agency of the mind is described by different names— such as "living being," "latent impressions" (*vāsanā*), and "karma.
This entire world is nothing but the mind, as is experienced by everyone.
For a man who is without mind in this world does not see, even though he is seeing.
Having heard, touched, seen, smelled, and tasted both the auspicious and the inauspicious,
it is indeed one possessed of a mind who experiences internal joy and dejection.
The mind is the cause of objects, just as light is for forms;
for one whose mind is bound is indeed bound, while one whose mind is liberated is indeed liberated.
Know that to be the best among the dull-witted by whom the mind is called "dull."
And understand that the mind is indeed inert, for it is consciousness that [perceives] it;
this mind which has arisen is neither conscious nor inert,
and from it the world has emerged, filled with various pleasures, pains, and the sense of "I."
For when the mind becomes one-pointed, saṃsāra dissolves;
the turbid cause of delusion presents the world through its own delusion.
Indeed, that which is called the "mind" is not insentient, nor is it the cause of saṃsāra.
And even that which is inert, possessing the nature of a stone, is not the cause of saṃsāra.
The mind is the cause of objects, just as the appearance of forms [is caused by light].
What world could there be for one devoid of consciousness, other than that which exists apart from the mind?
Therefore, O Rāghava, in this world, neither consciousness nor insentience of any entire class of beings dissolves;
through the influence of various states of karma, the mind assumes various designations.
Just as time proceeds by assuming various forms through the seasons, so too,

even if the activities of the ego and the senses disturb the body of those who are without mental constructs (*amanaska*), let there be other principles such as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the rest.

O Rāma, those distinctions among the philosophical systems that have been proclaimed by proponents and critics here and there through mental reasoning do not, in fact, contradict one another, nor are they distinguished from one another anywhere.
For all powers reside in the omnipresent God; indeed,
when even a slight power arises from pure consciousness as if it were inert, then manifold diversity comes into being.
Just as a thread is produced from a spider, and the insentient from the sentient,
so too does primordial nature (prakṛti) arise eternally from the supreme, ever-awakened Brahman.
Through the power of ignorance, various mental dispositions (bhāvanās) have come into existence.

Because the meanings of the various synonymous terms for consciousness differ, this impure consciousness has attained its renown among disputants here as "the individual soul" (*jīva*), "the mind" (*manas*), "intellect" (*buddhi*), and "egoity" (*ahaṅkṛti*). It is indeed that very same [consciousness] which is spoken of in the world by the multitude of names such as "sentience," "mind," and "individual soul"; truly, there is no dispute over this.
The ninety-seventh canto, titled "The Perception and Discursive Thought of the Mind," [from] Rāma.

O Brahman, it is from the mind alone that this so-called "external display" (āḍambara) is said to arise; for it is understood from the meaning of the scriptural statement that the mind itself is indeed action,
when it is embraced by a firmly established disposition.
"O Brahman, I consider the body in this world to be like a radiant covering produced by the fierce heat of the sun; it is merely the mind itself that has assumed form,
manifesting in some places as a human being and in others as a celestial being."
In some places it shone forth as a Daitya, in some it arose as a Yakṣa;
in some it attained the state of a Gandharva, and in others it took the form of a Kinnara. Through various forms of forests, mountain ranges, cities, and towns, [it appeared].
I believe that it is the mind alone that expands through its projected form.
This being so, the flood of bodies is comparable to a mere fragment of straw or wood;
what purpose is there in analyzing them? For us, it is the mind alone that must be investigated.
Therefore, I believe that this entire expansive and deeply agitated world is spread out [as an illusion],
and that apart from it, only the Supreme Self remains—
the Self which transcends all states, is omnipresent, and is the refuge of all.
By its grace, the mind runs and leaps about within saṃsāra.
Therefore, I consider the activity of the mind to be the cause regarding bodies;
for it is that [mind] which is born and dies, for such a quality does not belong to the Self.
I believe that through such reflection, the mind will reach dissolution;
