and by the mere dissolution of the mind, thereafter the highest good will come to pass. When that which is called "mind" has been utterly exhausted, along with its actions and its harmful agitation—
The living being is called "liberated" when he is not born again.
O Blessed One, you have described three types of births for men;
the primary cause of these is the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent.
How then can the mind— which is named pure consciousness (*śuddhacit*), yet which has arisen from that reality devoid of purity, expanded, and become the painter of the world— be so? Vasiṣṭha said:
For there exist three kinds of space, vast within:
the space of the mind (*cittākāśa*), the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), and the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*) as the third.
These indeed are common to all and are established everywhere.
But through the power of the pure reality of consciousness (*cittattva*), they have attained oneness with existence.
That which stands both outside and within, the knower who makes existence manifest,
all-pervading among all beings— that is called the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*).

The creator who is intent on the welfare of all beings, whose nature consists of the manifestation and withdrawal of all things, by whom all this is pervaded— he is called the space of consciousness (*cittākāśa*).
For he is one whose body is uninterrupted throughout the expanse of the ten directions.
This very self of beings is space, the substratum of wind, water, and the rest.
Both the space of the physical ether and the space of the mind arise through the power of the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*).
For consciousness is the cause of the entire flood of effects, just as the day [is the cause] of all that arises within it.
The conviction that "I am inert" or "I am not inert" is a defilement of the consciousness;
know that very thing to be the mind, by which space and the other elements are brought into being.
The conceptualization of the three spaces has as its object the unawakened self.
For conceptualization is indeed employed for the purpose of instruction regarding the object of the awakened, but not [regarding the ultimate reality itself]:
"The one alone is the supreme Brahman, all-pervading, filling everything;
it is awakened, stainless, eternal, and devoid of parts or mental constructions."
Through the distinctions between duality and non-duality, encapsulated within the structure of scriptural statements,
the ignorant alone are instructed, and never the awakened. As long as there is a lack of awakening regarding Rāma, there remains the conceptualization of the three spaces.
For that very purpose of awakening, they are taught by me:
from the stained space of consciousness (cidākāśa), the space of the sky, the space of the mind, and so forth, have issued forth,
just as mirages arise from a forest fire in the desert.
For when consciousness becomes defiled, it attains the state of *citta* and weaves the illusory nets of the three worlds, agitated in nature.
Indeed, this state of *citta* belonging to that defiled reality whose essence is consciousness is perceived by those devoid of awakening.
Just as there is no silver in mother-of-pearl, so too bondage here exists through ignorance, whereas liberation occurs by the power of awakening.
Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Majesty of the Consciousness-Sky."
Vasiṣṭha said:
O sinless one, whatever mind arises from whatever source, it constantly strives with effort for its own liberation.
There is a vast, empty, and silent wilderness that is yet terrifying,
wherein the sky is visible as nothing more than a mere corner;
in it dwells a single man with a thousand arms and eyes.
With a bewildered mind and terrified, he stands with his form expanded;
taking up many iron clubs with a thousand arms,
he strikes his own back and flees by himself alone.
Striking himself with his own self by means of firm blows,
he flees in terror even for hundreds of leagues;
crying out and running away, he goes far hither and thither.
Exhausted, with a helpless appearance and shattered feet and limbs,
he fell helplessly and quickly into a great blind well—
a deep cavity in the sky of the terrible darkness of the black night.
Then, after a long time, he emerged from the blind well;
striking with blows again and again, he fled from himself by himself.
Having gone even further away, he reached a thicket of *karañja* trees.
He enters it like a moth entering a fire filled with thorns;
then, having emerged from that thicket of *karañja* trees as if in an instant,
he flees from himself, striking himself with his own blows.
Having gone even further, that blind man quickly entered that very same blind well, his limbs and form shattered; then,
emerging from the blind well, he entered a grove of plantain trees.
Striking himself again and again with blows, he fled from himself;
having gone even further away, he entered a lovely plantain grove, cool as the rays of the moon, as if laughing.
Emerging from that grove of plantains in an instant,
he went from the plantain forest to a bright thicket of *karañja* trees;
from the *karañja* forest to a well, and from the well to another area of the plantain grove.
Having entered and even struck out at himself, he remained established within his own self. Observing him engaged in such personal conduct, I took hold of him by force and awakened him for a moment.
And when asked, "Who are you? What is this? For what purpose do you do it?
What might be your desired name? Why are you deluded in vain?"—O descendant of Raghu, he told me this when thus questioned.
"I am nothing, O Sage, nor is this anything; I do nothing at all.
I have been shattered by you; you are my enemy, O subduer of foes.
Seen by you, I am destroyed—for both suffering and for happiness."
Having spoken thus to me, he looked at his own limbs and stood there;
miserable, he wept with a piteous cry like a cloud thundering while raining.
In a mere moment, he ceased his weeping there.
Beholding his own limbs, which were as white as moonbeams, he laughed;
then, at the conclusion of that loud laughter, that man gradually cast off those limbs of his from all sides before me.
First his head fell, most terrible to behold;
then his arms, followed by his chest, and after that his belly.
Then, in an instant, that man and those limbs were gone in a state of total confusion.
Everything vanished like a dream to one who has awakened;
having reflected upon the power of destiny, I then prepared to depart. In a secluded place, I saw yet another man just like him.
Even while striking out on all sides at himself with his thick-set arms, he flees away by himself;
falling into a well, he rises from the well and runs toward it.
Again he falls into the interior of a thicket; again, afflicted, he flees.
Again he enters a clear, cool forest for a moment;
again, enraged and again, delighted, he strikes out by himself.

Having observed for a long time such conduct natural to him, I gazed upon him with wonder; then, having firmly grasped him, I questioned him in that very same manner. Thereupon, he wept and laughed in that same sequence.
Having reached a state of disintegration through his limbs, he became completely invisible.
Then, having reflected upon the power of destiny, I prepared to depart; however, in that secluded spot, I saw yet another man in the same condition.
Striking him in that very manner, he himself fled;
while fleeing, he fell into a great blind well.
There I dwelt for a very long time, waiting for him.
When that rogue had finally emerged from the well after a very long time,
I was ready to depart; then I saw once more a man of that same appearance and that same conduct, striving in exactly the same way.
Having quickly seized him in that very manner, I spoke to him again;
yet, O lotus-petal-eyed one, he did not understand it at all.
That fool knew nothing of me whatsoever.
"O wretched sinner, you wicked twice-born!"— having said this, he departed, having reached the limit of his own business.
Then, as I was wandering in that great forest,
I saw many such men who committed such offenses.
Some who have questioned me come to rest like those awakened from the confusion of a dream;
some do not welcome what I say, like the barking of dogs.
Some, having fallen into blind wells, do not rise up again.
Some did not emerge from the grove of plantain trees even after a long time; some vanished within the vast thicket of the *karañja* forest;
some found no place to stand, while others were intent on wandering aimlessly.
Such was that vast great forest, O scion of Raghu,
which exists even today, wherein those men remain as you have described.
And that forest, O Rāma, has been seen by you here while engaged in your worldly affairs.
But because of the immaturity of your intellect, O Rāghava, you do not remember that [forest].
That terrifying forest, whose limbs are crowded with various perils, dense with thick darkness, and avoided by people—
though it is frequented by those devoid of understanding who have come seeking rest, it is not resorted to by those who know the truth, like a small thicket of flowering shrubs.
The ninety-ninth canto, named the Canto of the Story of Citta;
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, what is that great forest? When and how was it seen by me?
Who were those men there, and what were they striving to do?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O mighty-armed Raghunātha, listen; I shall tell you everything:
that which is called the great forest is not far away, nor are those men far from you—this very path of saṃsāra, with its deep, hollow pits and its lack of essence."
Know that great forest, O Rāma, to be empty yet rich in transformations;
when it is filled by that one Reality alone which is attainable through the light of inquiry,
and is not joined with anything else, then it is indeed absolute.
In that regard, know that those great forms which expand forth are indeed the minds fallen into suffering;
O Mahāmati, I am the discerning witness of them.
"O Rāghava, those other [minds] were seen by me through discernment;
indeed, it is by means of discernment that those very minds are understood by me,
constantly through my own self-luminosity, like lotuses by the sun."
O great-minded one, having attained awakening through my grace,
some minds have reached the state beyond tranquility;
others, due to delusion, do not rejoice in me or in discernment.
Furthermore,
O scion of Raghu, those deep blind wells which are the dense hells are in fact their own minds; they fall into them and they leap out from within them due to the power of their own contempt.
That thicket of *karañja* trees is known as the passion for one's wife;

human existence, crowded with the thorns of suffering and characterized by the three kinds of longing, is like that thicket. Indeed, those minds which have entered the thicket of *karañja* trees [are lost].

Those [pleasures] were born in the human realm, yet they found their singular delight therein. O scion of Raghu, know that this grove of plantains, cool as the rays of the moon, is a heaven that brings joy to the heart.
You ought to know that the minds which have entered the grove of plantains are those solely devoted to heaven,
whereas those which have entered the interior of a blind well do not emerge.
O Rāghava, those minds are possessed of great sins;
O delighter of the Raghus, those minds born of the human species are not like those that have gone forth from the Karañja forest.
Some, fully awakened there, are released from their bonds;
others, assuming many forms, indeed pass from one womb into another. Some, purified by merit and by severe austerity, [attain liberation].
They maintain their bodies, which remain in their accustomed states;
by those ignorant men who insulted me as a "wicked twice-born," they have,
through their own minds, which lack self-knowledge, insulted their own discernment.
"‘I am ruined, you are my enemy’— what was quickly spoken by you was merely a lamentation from a failing mind.
O Rāghava, that which was wept with great wailing and many tears by the man was [but the voice of distress]."
As he was mentally renouncing that web of enjoyments, he wept.
For one who has attained partial discernment but has not yet reached the stainless state,
intense anguish arises as the mind relinquishes enjoyments.
With a compassionate awakening, he beheld his weeping limbs and thought in his mind: "Alas! Why should I depart, abandoning these?
This was the state of one who had attained partial discernment, but had not yet reached the stainless state.

For one who abandons the limbs of the mind, distress indeed increases. O Rāma, that laughter which was once joyful for a man through the intoxication of ignorance becomes, however, a state of contentment for the mind when discernment has been fully attained.
For one who has attained solitude and abandoned the wandering of saṃsāra,
as the mind relinquishes form, bliss indeed increases.
Those limbs which were seen by a man while laughing in derision—
"For those [objects] seen by the mind indeed bring about deception.
'I have long been deceived by things fashioned through false conceptualization'—
thus did he look upon his own limbs with a sense of derision in his mind."
For when the mind has attained discernment and rests in the expansive state,
the steadfast one looks upon its former wretchedness from afar and laughs at it. When I questioned him with great effort, he held himself firmly [in that state].
Thus it is shown that discernment forcibly seizes the mind.
It is demonstrated that when the limbs have fallen apart and vanished before one's eyes, the desire for objects subsides in the absence of the mind.
That which was described as the man possessing a thousand eyes and hands is indeed shown to be the infinite form of the mind;
for it is the mind that itself strikes at itself with a torrent of blows.
With the blows of various evil imaginings, one strikes at one's own mind.
When a person flees while striking himself,
that mind flees from the blows of its own latent tendencies.

It strikes its own mind by itself through its own will, and it flees away by itself; behold the manifestation of ignorance! For all minds are indeed scorched by their own latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Desirous of reaching that state, they flee by themselves;
the mind itself spreads out this extended suffering,
yet when its own self is utterly exhausted, it flees from that very suffering once again.
The mind comes to bind itself within the web of its own volitions and latent impressions,
just as the silkworm binds itself with threads of saliva;
it plays restlessly, attaining misfortune just as it pleases.
Not seeing one's own future suffering, like a child through its own mischievous play,
or like a monkey pulling out a wedge who does not see the bull’s testicles caught in the crack of a wooden post— indeed, the mind undergoes this very same suffering.
Through long-term protection of the mind and likewise through long-term cultivation,
one attains a state of natural composure through practice and no longer grieves.
From mental negligence, sufferings increase like mountain peaks.
By that power alone they perish, just as snow before the sun.

O noble-minded one, for as long as life lasts, the mind should be protected by a blameless mental impression (*vāsanā*) born from the meaning of the scriptures; indeed, like a sage, it should remain in silence regarding passion and other such afflictions.
Afterwards, that cool, unborn state—the purifier of purifiers—is attained; established in which, a person no longer grieves even amidst great calamities.
Thus ends the chapter named "The Narrative of Citta."
The hundredth canto:
Vasiṣṭha said:
"This mind has emerged from the supreme state of Brahman."

"O Rāma, for those who are awakened, the mind here is Brahman alone and nothing else— neither non-identical with it nor identical with it, just as a wave is not different from the ocean. For those who perceive the commonality of water, a wave is not something other than the sea."
For those whose minds are unawakened, the mind is the cause of the delusion of saṃsāra,
just as one who does not perceive the commonality between water and the waves of water perceives them as distinct.
This [teaching] is intended solely for the awakening of those whose intellects are unawakened.
The distinction between the signified and the signifier is merely conceptualized.
The supreme Brahman is all-powerful, eternal, perfectly full, and immutable;
there is nothing that does not exist within that pervasive Self, nor is there anything that is not contained therein.
For the Blessed One possesses all powers; whatever power pleases him, the omnipresent Lord manifests that very power extended throughout.
O Rāma, the power of consciousness belonging to Brahman is perceived within bodies.
The power of vibration resides in the winds; likewise, the power of inertia resides in stones. The power of fluidity resides in waters; the power of fire resides in flames.
The power of emptiness resides in space; and the power of existence resides in the state of being.
For the power of Brahmā, who is omnipotent, is seen extending in the ten directions:
the power of destruction in things to be destroyed, the power of grief in those who grieve,
the power of bliss in the joyful, and the power of valor in the great warrior.

The power of creation exists within creations, yet at the end of the aeon, everything is withdrawn. Just as a tree— possessing fruit, flowers, creepers, leaves, branches, twigs, and joints— is contained within the seed of the tree, so too does this [universe] abide within Brahman.
By the power of appearance alone, the mind— intermediate between sentience and insentience,
designated as "living being" or "other"— is seen within Brahman.
[It is like] various trees, creepers, shrubs, networks of shoots, and sprouts.
Just as potencies exist in the seasons, so do they abide in Brahman within this life.
Just as the earth, having cast forth the flowers of all seasons according to the distinctions of place and time,
yields its blossoms, so does the Creator of the world yield various minds.
In some places and at some times,
certain powers emerge from that [source] due to the diversity of place and time, like rice plants from the surface of the earth.
This is the conceptualization of that which is known as pure, non-conceptual consciousness alone.
"O Rāghava, this Brahman alone is I, you, and the world and the directions.
That Self, O Rāma, is all-pervading, its great form eternally manifest;
when it assumes even a slight power of thinking, it is called the mind."
Just as there is the illusion of a peacock's tail in the sky, or the notion of a whirlpool in water,
so too the mind and the individual soul (jīva) are merely a fraction of appearance within the Self.
This form of the mind which has been described as consisting of the nature of thinking— *The Mahāyāna-Uttaratantra-śāstra*, 3.100.18.
Therefore, O subduer of enemies, this is the power of Brahman; thus, it is indeed Brahman itself.
The distinction such as "this is that" or "I am this" arises from appearance;
when the mind is perceived as other than Brahman, delusion is the ultimate cause.

Whatever this state of mentation is, whether it consists of the existent or the non-existent, and whatever is expressed by words—all that is the power of the All-Powerful; they know that power to be Brahman itself.
That which is called the essence of the existence of the mind, which resides within the mind—
That which has arisen perishes by that very appearance, and not by another.
Know those things—such as the exclusion of opposites, number, form, and so forth—which are conceptualized by the words of the mind to have been born from Brahman; they are Brahman itself.
Just as the manifestation of this mind proceeds, so exactly does it become; in this regard, there is indeed the example of the lunar reflections.
Just as movement occurs in a great body of water that is itself unmoved and pure, [so it is with the mind].

O Rāma, for the knower, this individual soul (*jīva*), which is the cause of *saṃsāra*, always revolves within the Supreme Self as the all-encompassing consciousness; it is like the water of the ocean revolving within itself through its surges, waves, and billows.
There is no second [reality]; existence itself consists of the activity of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
It is like a conceptualization other than water in the ocean, where there are no other waves.
That which is thus born and perishes, that which goes and stands—[all this is but such].
Thus, this Brahman manifests as Brahman through Brahman alone;
just as intense heat within itself appears as a mirage,
so too does the Self, though devoid of variety, flash forth by itself in manifold diversity.
The cause, the action, the agent, birth, death, and duration—all is Brahman alone; there is nothing else apart from that, for all is merely a conceptual construction.
There is no greed, no delusion, and no thirst; [all beings] are stainless.
What greed, thirst, or delusion can there be for the Self within the Self? From where could they arise?
This entire world is the Self alone; the process of mental construction is the Self alone.
Just as gold arises in the form of a bracelet, so does this Self arise in the form of the mind.
O Rāma, that Brahman which is unawakened is called the mind (*citta*) and the individual soul (*jīva*).
When it remains unrecognized, the kinsman quickly becomes a stranger.
By its own volition, through its ignorant self consisting of consciousness, [it creates this state].
Emptiness has been made manifest by the living being, as if by the sky.
Here in this world, the very self shines as the living being, appearing as a non-self;
like the appearance of two moons due to faulty vision, both the existent and the non-existent have arisen.

Because these two— the perception of the objects of words such as "delusion" and so forth— are utterly impossible, and because the Self is indeed all-pervasive, where could the Self be bound, and where could it be liberated?
For one for whom bondage is eternally non-existent, the notion that "there is bondage" is a false conceptualization.
"For one for whom [liberation] is conceptual, that liberation is false and not real.
Rāma said: "Whatever certainty the mind reaches, that indeed becomes so, and not otherwise."
"Therefore, O Lord, how could there be any bondage that is merely conceptual?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"This conceptualization of bondage by the ignorant is itself a false conceptualization."

Their other conception of liberation has arisen entirely falsely. Thus, the notions of bondage and liberation are recorded as being constructed by ignorance; but in reality, O Mahāmati, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
The unreality of conceptual construction is [known] for one whose intellect is fully awakened,
O wise one, like that of a snake in a rope, but not for one whose intellect is unawakened.
For the wise man, there is no delusion whatsoever regarding bondage, liberation, and so forth.

O Rāghava, delusion regarding bondage, liberation, and so forth belongs only to the ignorant. First is the mind, followed by the views of bondage and liberation, and subsequently the construction of the manifold world known as the universe; this entire state of affairs has become established like a mere narrative intended for the unwise.
The one hundred and first canto, titled "The Description of the Arising of the Mind Preceded by the Treatment of the Mind," [spoken by] Rāma:
"O best of sages, why is this sequence of the narrative concerning the boy mentioned?
Tell me this in due order, for it is the cause for describing the nature of the mind.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
O Rāghava, a child of very simple intellect asked his nurse,
"Tell me some story that has reached the path of my ears.
O high-minded one, for the amusement of that child, the nurse—
He tells a narrative composed of clear and sweet syllables:
"In a certain vast and empty city, there were three auspicious high-souled princes, like brilliant stars in the sky."
Two were not born, and likewise one did not even remain in the womb;
they appeared like moons, possessing auspicious conduct and auspicious forms.
Then, once, for the sake of obtaining the most excellent gain, they gathered together.
Persistent, with dejected faces and hearts stricken by grief,
they emerged from that empty city with distorted countenances,
like Mercury, Venus, and Saturn clustered together in the sky.
With limbs as delicate as the śirīṣa flower, scorched by the sun from behind on the road, they fell into exhaustion like tender leaves withered by the heat of summer;
their lotus-feet were burned by the scorching sands of the path.
Lamenting, "O father! O mother!", they were like deer strayed from their herd;
with feet pierced by the tips of *darbha* grass and the joints of their limbs parched by ascetic heat, they traversed a long distance with bodies grey with dust.

On the way, they reached three trees whose branches were thick with clusters of blossoms, whose foliage was covered in fruits and new shoots, and which served as a refuge for flocks of birds and deer.
Among those three trees, two did not even slightly resemble trees.
For the third, the Svāroha, no seed at all exists. Having come to rest and being weary, they stayed there beneath a single tree on the slopes of the Pārijāta in heaven, like Śakra, Anila, and Yama.
Having eaten the fruits produced from nectar and drunk their juice,
and having fashioned garlands from clusters of blossoms, they rested for a long time and then departed.
Having traveled yet further, when midday had arrived, they proceeded on.
They reached three rivers, noisy with waves tossing to and fro.
Among them, one was completely dried up; not even a drop of water remained in the other two, which were as devoid of sight as the eyes of the blind.
In that river which was utterly parched, they bathed with great devotion,

like Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Hara when afflicted by the heat of the summer sun bathing in the celestial Gaṅgā. Having sported in the water for a long time and drunk the water which was like nectar, they departed.
Those princes went along happily with joyful minds.
Then, at the end of the day, as the sun was sinking,
they reached a city that was about to be newly constructed, resembling a mountain.

There they beheld three delightful cities, abounding in excellent wealth, which were like lakes of dark blue sky filled with lotus-beds of banners, and whose circular precincts resounded with songs heard from afar.
Like the peaks of a great mountain, there were houses made of jewels and gold;
among them, two dwellings were unconstructed and one was indeed without walls.
Those three men entered that beautiful, wallless mansion.
Having quickly entered and sat down, those fair-faced women, as they were sporting there,
came upon three vessels fashioned from molten gold; therein,
two had turned into shards and one had been reduced to powder.
Those far-sighted ones took that vessel in the form of powder; by those eaters of much food, one hundred *droṇas* were cooked there,
with ninety-nine *droṇas* of that [powder] and one *droṇa* of grain.
Then, hundreds of people and hundreds of brahmins ate,
as did those three princes who had attained supreme peace.
All three of those princes were to be born in that very city.
"O son, we are now happily engaged in the pursuit of hunting.
O sinless one, I have told you this delightful tale;
take it to heart, O wise one, and you shall become refined."
"O Rāma, this auspicious narrative was told by the nurse to the child;
and the child attained satisfaction through this auspicious tale.
Indeed, O Rāma, this has been related in connection with the discourse on the nature of the mind."
O lotus-eyed one, this narrative of the boy has been told to you by me;
this construction of saṃsāra has reached its present state through fierce volitions imagined in vain, like the story of the boy.
O sinless one, this very net of conceptual construction, whose nature is mere appearance,
unfolds in the form of the notions of bondage, liberation, and so forth. Apart from mere volition, nothing else exists here at all.
By the power of volition, it may be something, nothing, or indeed something else. Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions—
all this is fashioned by volition for the self, like a dream.
The three princes, the rivers, and likewise the city—
just as they were fashioned by thought (saṅkalpa), so too is the existence of these three worlds. It is merely thought that flickers forth on all sides, unstable.
The ocean, consisting of nothing but water, [is contained] within itself by its own self, as it were, in the water; so too,
that which was first produced in the Supreme Self as mere volition has now attained expansion through its activities, just like the day.
The entire world is merely the manifestation of the web of volition; know that the object of thought is indeed nothing but volition in its playful display.
Renounce this mere volition sufficiently, O Rāma, and by taking refuge in the certainty of the non-conceptual, attain peace.
This is the chapter titled "The Tale of the Boy."
The one hundred and second canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"By the power of his own volition, the fool falls into delusion, but not the wise man."
"You worship yakṣas while harboring the conceptualization of yakṣas; indeed, you are deluded like a child.
Rāma asked: "O best among the knowers of Brahman, who is this yakṣa that has been conceptualized, and by whom?"
Vasiṣṭha said: "By means of this very non-existent attachment to the elements, one always indeed incurs great delusion;
through this clinging to the elements, the Yakṣa assumes the form of the ego."
A vampire is here falsely imagined as if it were a child.
Since the one supreme reality alone exists in everything,
from where has this "I" come, and how indeed has it arisen?

In reality, there is no ego-sense within the Supreme Self due to its non-differentiation; yet, because of false vision, the jewel of the mind appears as the great undertaking of saṃsāra, like a river on a path in the intense heat of the sun. MU 3.102.5.
The jewel of the mind is perceived as the great undertaking of saṃsāra.
Just as water manifests by means of water itself, resting upon itself, so too does the Self manifest by means of the Self.
Therefore, O Rāma, abandon false perception, which is without support;
take refuge instead in right perception, which has its support in reality and is blissful.
With an intellect characterized by discernment and free from the agitation of delusion,
investigate the truth now and completely abandon what is false.
Having said that you are bound when you are actually unbound, why do you grieve in vain?

In the infinite reality of the Self, what is bound, how, and by what? In this all-pervading reality of Brahman— the undivided Great Self wherein there is no perception of diversity— what is bound and what is liberated?
Though you are not afflicted, why do you suffer because of the very existence of affliction when a limb is severed?
No suffering whatsoever arising from the modifications of difference or non-difference exists in the Self.
When the body is destroyed, wounded, or decayed, what injury has come upon the Self?
When the bellows are burnt, the gold situated within them is not destroyed.
Whether the body falls or rises, what loss has come upon us?
When a flower is crushed, what fragrance is lost? The scent takes refuge in the sky.
Let the glories of cold and heat, as well as pleasure and pain, fall upon the lotus-body;
what injury has befallen us when bees are merely hovering in the sky?
Whether the body falls, rises, or travels to the far reaches of space—let it be so.
What harm could there be to you from that which is of a nature entirely different?
O Raghava, just as the relationship between the clouds and the wind, or between the bee and the lotus, such is the relationship between your body and your self.
The mind, indeed, is the body of the entire world;
its self is consciousness, which never perishes.
O one of great wisdom, you think that this very Self perishes.
It is never destroyed; why then do you grieve in vain?
Just as the wind goes when the cloud has dispersed, or as the bee goes to the infinite space when the lotus has withered, so does the self go to the boundless void upon the dissolution of the body.
For one dwelling in this saṃsāra, even the mind does not perish;
what need is there to mention the destruction of the self for a living being without the fire of knowledge?
That which is the analogy of the jujube fruit in a bowl, and that which is the sequence regarding the jar and space—
That very same state belongs to both the perishable and the imperishable regarding the body and the self:
just as a jujube fruit comes into the hand when the bowl bursts,
so does the self enter the sky when the body moves.
Just as the space within a jar remains in the sky when the jar moves,
so does this embodied soul remain free from affliction when the body perishes;
for the mind is the body of living beings, concealed by space and time.
Covered by a shroud of death, he lies there; why this lamentation?
O mighty-armed one, when the concealment of place and time occurs at death, even a fool fears it; yet here, no one whatsoever is ever destroyed.

Therefore, O Rāma, abandon this latent impression (*vāsanā*) that persists as the false notion "I am," just as the lord of birds, desiring to soar through the sky, abandons his eggshell. For this mental power is that which binds one to the desirable and the undesirable.
Through this vain delusion, this has been imagined like a dream. This is ignorance; it is difficult to bring to an end; it indeed increases for the sake of suffering.
When not fully understood, it expands this world which is composed of the unreal.
This deluded person perceives space as if it were a wall, and fire as if it were frost; for by its very nature, it fails to see its own true form.
This world, which is truly non-existent, arises slowly through the process of manifestation as if it were real.
The expansive world is imagined by her, like a long dream; her very nature, consisting of mere creative ideation (*bhāvanāmātra*), has attained the state of an agent,
making the eye of the worlds agitated, as if it were a peacock feather in the sky.
O Rāma, lead this [mind] to its own true nature through inquiry, just as the sun, the lord of day, leads a stone of frost to its dissolution by his heat.
Just as the rising of the sun is beneficial for one who desires the disappearance of the frost; ||| MU_3,102.32 ||| so too is this inquiry for the sake of the cessation of ignorance.
Thus, for one who seeks the dissolution of the mind, the desired goal is indeed accomplished through such inquiry.
For ignorance, having set forth, is a vast and difficult-to-navigate wilderness of misfortune;
like a magical illusion or a sorceress’s trick, it rains down gold.
The mind alone performs this act of its own destruction;
for the mind dances the drama called "the slaughter of the self" solely for its own ruin. The consciousness beholds itself only for the sake of its own annihilation.

For the one of corrupt intellect does not perceive that destruction is at hand. By the mere absence of conceptualization, the mind quickly brings this state of its own conceptual construction to completion; affliction (kleśa) is of no use here.
Having quickly conceptualized its own nature and then, through discernment, rendered the mind free from conceptualization,
it abandons its form and undertakes the realization of the Self. The destruction of the mind is a great attainment, yet its arising is a great calamity.

Exert yourself toward the dissolution of the mind, but not toward the speed of the mind. In this forest, where the trees are dense thickets of incessant pleasure and pain and the great serpent Kṛtānta lurks, this entire mind— devoid of discrimination, O fortunate one— is the sole cause of great calamity for the master.
Vālmīki:

When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
The one hundred and third canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
The mind has arisen from that which is beyond, like a drop rising from the restless ocean.
Having attained expansion, it spreads this world here and there;
it quickly lengthens what is short and brings what is long to a state of shortness. It fully transforms one thing into its own nature, and likewise the other into the nature of the former.
Even that object which is merely the size of a span,
by means of its own perfected meditative cultivation, quickly becomes as radiant as the king of mountains;
for the mind, having attained firm stability, shines forth from the supreme state.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, it brings about and dissolves the worlds of saṃsāra.
Whatever is seen here— this entire world, both moving and stationary, enriched with every variety— all this has emerged from the mind.
Agitated by the power of place, time, action, and substance, the mind— like an actor due to its fickleness— passes from one state of being to another;
it quickly brings non-existence to what exists, and thoroughly brings existence to what does not exist.
It takes on exactly such pleasures and pains as it has cultivated;
just as the mind, being fickle, takes hold according to its resolve,
so does the aggregate of hands, feet, and other limbs always exert itself.
Then that very same action bestows the desired fruit of the mind’s intention instantly, just as a creeper, when watered at the proper time, yields its corresponding fruit;
or as a child, from the mud in a house, fashions a wonderful array of toys.

In this way, O Rāma, the mind indeed acts; through its conceptualization, it creates the world. Therefore, why is a single form imagined for those objects in the world, which are like the soft lumps of clay spat out by children at play?
Just as the time that brings about the seasons produces a change in the form of a tree,
so too does the mind here produce a change in those very objects;
likewise in a mental wish, in a dream, and in the fabrications of one's imagination.

When the mind is absorbed in its own playful activities, it makes a league (*yojana*) as vast as a world-system (*vyūha*) as small as a cow’s footprint; it turns an eon (*kalpa*) into a moment (*kṣaṇa*), and brings a moment to the state of an eon.
Therefore, the wise know that the sequence of space and time is dependent upon the mind.
Due to the intensity or mildness of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), and due to the distinction between its abundance or scarcity,
the mind does not linger for long, nor does it fail through incapacity;
[it avoids] delusion, agitation, misfortune, and movement to or from improper places and times.
These arise from the mind, just as sprouts emerge from a tree.
Just as the ocean is nothing but water and fire is nothing but heat,
so too this world of manifold agitation is indeed nothing but the mind.

This entire extended field of objects of cognition, together with its agents, actions, and instruments— rich with the seer, the act of seeing, and the seen— all that, for you, is nothing but the mind (citta).
The mind itself appears as the worlds, the realms, and the forests, manifesting through its own internal divisions.
Just as people perceive gold as being of a single nature, despite its various forms such as armlets, crowns, and bracelets, once they have abandoned the notion that it is anything other than gold;
so too is this the hundred and fourth canto, titled "The Greatness of the Mind."
Vasiṣṭha said:
In this regard, listen as I shall tell you this wonderful account of how the splendor of the world’s magic trick remains dependent upon the mind.
On this surface of the earth, there exists a vast and prosperous great country named Uttara-Pāṇḍava, crowded with various cities and forests,
where ascetics rest in dense groves of fresh jambīra trees.
The city of the grove was a pleasure-garden where creeper-swinging was performed by Vidyādharīs;
its mountains were tawny with masses of lotus filaments tossed up by the wind,
and it was adorned with forest garlands consisting of shimmering clusters of flowers.
Its forest borders were concealed by groves of *karañja* flower-clusters;
its sky resounded with the humming of villages hidden among date palms;
and it was tawny with fields of ripening rice stalks arranged in rows.
Adorned by forest regions resounding with the loud cries of peacocks,
its lotus groves humming with the frantic calls of cranes,
it was like an ear-ring for the mountain village, dark as a thicket of *tamāla* trees.
The banks of the river were reddened by *pāribhadra* trees in full bloom, where the warbling of flocks of diverse birds produced a sweet,
melodious sound; there, the God of Love was summoned by the soft songs of young girls in the fields.
With clouds of blossoms shaken from the trees by the wind blowing over the flower-strewn ground,
and honored by Siddhas and Cāraṇas emerging from their cave-dwellings,
he appeared as if beauty itself had been specially fashioned and summoned from heaven.
Adorned with groves of plantain trees as far as the singing *kinnaras*,
and white with flower gardens shaken by the force of the gentle breeze—
there dwells a most righteous king named Lavaṇa.
Born from the lineage of Hariścandra, he was like a second sun upon the earth.
There, the mountains shone with their peaks made white by the crest-ornaments of his fame, appearing as if they were smeared with ashes by Śiva.
From him, by whose mere remembrance the world of his enemies suffers a feverish affliction— having completely severed the entire circle of his foes with fragments from his sword—
and whose noble undertakings consist in the protection of the world of the noble, [he is the one].
People will long remember his life-story, just like that of Hari,
whose songs of praise for his virtues are sung by celestial nymphs upon the peaks of the king of mountains and in the abodes of the immortals, causing their hair to stand on end with joy.
The songs of his own Sundarī, long heard by the world-protectors,
are echoed by the swans of Viriñca through their own practice as hymns of praise for his virtues;
even in dreams, nothing is common to him who possesses such noble wonder.
O Rāma, have you ever seen or even heard of the rays of the defect of wretchedness?
He who does not know crookedness, by whom greed has never been seen,
and by whom nobility is maintained like Brahmā holding a rosary of beads— [by him alone can these rays be perceived].
When the lord of the day had reached the eighth part of the sky,
he once sat upon his throne in the assembly hall;
while he was seated there at ease, like the moon in the sky, O King.
While the armies of the neighboring kings were entering in great haste, and while the beloved women were singing and the monarchs were seated comfortably,
the sound of lutes, flutes, and cymbals was enchanting and full of joy.

While the king— whose hand bore beautiful fly-whisks and who was full of grace— rested like the preceptor of the gods and asuras, and while the circle of ministers had concluded the most excellent affairs of state; MU_3,104.23 while the ministers were occupied with the outstanding duties of the kingdom;
While the reports of various regions were being proclaimed by skilled spies and secret agents, while the sacred Itihāsa was being recited from the manuscript,
and while the bards stood bowed before him chanting auspicious hymns; (MU 3.104.24–25)
A certain magician entered that assembly with great pomp,
like a rain-cloud descending upon the earth with a torrential downpour;
he bowed before the protector of the earth, whose neck was as majestic as a mountain peak.
He approached his beloved like a fruit-bearing tree reaching the foot of a mountain;
he sat down before the king— who possessed a fine luster, broad shoulders, was laden with fruits, and bore flowers— just as a monkey settles upon the top of a tree.
Fickle and greedy for riches, he spoke with his neck outstretched to the king— who was like a lotus— to him who was like a breeze of fragrant pleasure:
"O Lord, first behold here this one performance of a donkey."
"Remaining seated on his very seat, he [beheld] the earth with wonder, like the moon from the sky," having said this, he whirled the peacock-feather whisk that causes dizziness—
a seed for various manifestations, like Māyā by the Supreme Self.
The protector of the earth beheld her, resplendent with a streak of brilliance,
like Śakra seated in his celestial chariot gazing upon the vine of his own bow;
at that very moment, the Saindhava vassal entered the assembly hall.
Like a cloud following the path of the sky strewn with the moon,
that excellent horse of supreme speed followed him,
looking up toward the world of the gods from the ocean like Uccaiḥśravas following Śakra.
Taking that horse, he spoke to the king, as the Ocean of Milk, filled with Uccaiḥśravas, spoke to the Lord of the Maruts:
"O Lord of the Earth, here is this jewel among horses, resembling Uccaiḥśravas."

"O Lord, this horse, swift and victorious by nature, has been dispatched to you by our master like the wind incarnate. For the auspicious splendor of an object truly shines when offered to the great."
When he had spoken thus, the magician replied,
like a *cātaka* bird to a mountain when the thundering of the clouds has ceased:
"O Lord, mount this noble horse and wander through the world."

The king gazed at the horse, which possessed no small splendor bestowed by its own majesty, just as the sun gazes upon the earth; he did so with eagerness, like a peacock toward a cloud signaled by its thunder, as the horse was addressed by him.
Then, with an unblinking gaze, the king, whose form was like a painting,
stood gazing at the horse as if it were fixed in a work of art;
having looked for a moment at the peacock-feather horse, he remained with his eyes closed.
Like a timid man who has seen the ocean and its mountains agitated,
he stood for two moments as if absorbed in meditation within himself;
the Sage, the Buddha, remained like one who has transcended passion and abides in supreme bliss.
"Awakened by someone, this king— who was once so powerful as to have been conquered by his own majesty— is now brooding over some anxiety out of fear.
Thus it was that there, the white chowries remained utterly motionless.
For those nights with their yak-tail fans were as if the rays of the moon had been paralyzed;
those members of the assembly shone, filled with wonder and motionless,
like lotuses whose filaments and petals have become rigid from the mud.
The clamor of the people in the assembly hall gradually subsided,
like the thundering of the sky with its clouds at the end of the rainy season. The excellent ministers, having emerged from the ocean of doubt, fell into deep reflection.
The people despaired, like the immortals before the Asura king when he wields his mace;
with their eyes fixed and their wonder wide-eyed, that multitude, settled in the delusion of worldly existence,
assumed the luster of a forest of closed lotuses while the lord of the earth stood there with motionless gaze.
In the narrative of Indrajāla, the hundred-and-fifth canto, titled "The Delusion of the King," Vasiṣṭha says:
Then, after two muhūrtas, the lord of the earth attained consciousness,
like a magnificent lotus released from the waters of the rainy season;
having awakened, he shook himself from his seat, still adorned with his armlets and crest-ornaments.
With the tips of his ears erect as if for the enjoyment of hearing, he sat upon his throne trembling like a mountain during an earthquake;
he was like Mount Mandara, the base of the underworld, shaken and agitated.
As he was falling, the attendants supported the king with their arms,
just as the principal mountain ranges support Mount Meru when it is shaken by the dissolution of the world.
Being held up by his attendants, that king’s mind became utterly distressed.
It bore the splendor of the moon agitated by ripples upon his face.
"What region is this? Whose assembly is this? the king wondered slowly, humming like a bee dwelling within the calyx of a sinking lotus.
Then the assembly spoke respectfully to the god, "What is this?
like a lotus-pond with humming bees upon seeing the sun eclipsed by Rāhu.
Then the chief ministers likewise questioned him.

"O Lord, while you remain in such a state, we are utterly distressed, like the gods when Mārkaṇḍeya was terrified by the dissolution of the world. Groundless delusions shatter even the mind that is otherwise impenetrable."

In which conceptual constructions— like sensual enjoyments that are delightful at first sight but bitter in the end— has your mind wallowed? It has been habituated to discourses of constant and noble conduct.
Why does your mind, though pure, sink into agitations? The mind that has base objects and is torn asunder amidst worldly activities takes on delusion; it does not expand through greatness.
For whatever mental state has arisen in him through constancy,
even amidst those things that intoxicate the body with pride, he follows that very state;
it is pure, awakened, captivating in its qualities, and possesses a noble object.
For even your mind appears variegated and, as it were, torn asunder.
Indeed, a mind that has not practiced discernment, which follows the dictates of place and time, falls under the power of spells and herbs; a mind of noble conduct does not.
"How can one who possesses constant discernment suffer from brokenness or decay? It distresses the expansive mind just as a whirlwind afflicts the mountain of the gods.
When these words had arisen, the radiance of that king’s face—

He adorned Śītāṃśu, just as fullness adorns the moon at the end of the month. With his eyes opened wide in wonder, the king shone like Mādhava when the winter season has passed and the abundance of flowers has blossomed.
Then, with a face marked by excessive agitation, wonder, and a weary smile,
he shone like the moon in the sky beholding Rāhu with death imminent;
and looking upon the magician, he spoke as if laughing:
Seeing Babhru, who was murderous in nature like Takṣaka in the form of a serpent, [the king said]:
"O fool! Why have you, with your matted locks, created this snare?
The ocean, though troubled by the movement of fish, returns to clarity in an instant."
How wondrous! For the hundredfold powers of the objects of the Divine are indeed marvelous; though my mind is exceedingly powerful, it has been cast into delusion by these [powers].
Where are we, lamenting over the course of events in the cycle of worlds?
Where are the far-reaching, ordinary calamities that bring delusion to the mind?
Even when the mind of one who possesses great realized knowledge remains within the body,
it may at times succumb to delusion for a moment, even in the case of the wise.
O members of the assembly, listen now to this wondrous narrative concerning that which was displayed here by my illusionist for a mere moment;
in that instant, I beheld many shifting states of affairs.

"In an instant, Indra was struck down and his creations destroyed, like those of the Lotus-born Brahmā. Having said this, while the members of the assembly looked up with wide-eyed wonder, the king, as if smiling,
began to describe the wondrous event.
The King: Here, on this earth crowded with various objects, teeming with lakes, rivers, mountains, and cities,
and constricted by great peaks and oceans, there is this region endowed with abundant wealth.
The hundred-and-sixth canto, titled "The Awakening of the King," Canto 106.
The King:
There is indeed this land, endowed with various forests and rivers,
like a younger brother born of the same womb as this orb of the earth;
and here I am, its king, whose conduct is approved by the citizens.
"Indra himself, as it were, has today taken his place in this assembly hall.
Yet, here is some juggler who has arrived from afar;
he has risen up from the subterranean realm like the illusionist Maya himself."

By this [horse], this peacock-feather whisk, shimmering with its rows of feathers, was made to whirl here like a streak of Indra’s bow by the cloud driven by the winds at the end of an eon. Having observed this flickering [whisk] while standing before this horse, I...
One man, with a bewildered mind, mounted [the horse] alone by himself.
Then, as Puṣkarāvartaka [stirs] a mountain agitated at the time of dissolution,
I too, having mounted my own horse, set out as it moved along.
Then, setting out alone with great speed for the hunt,
I was carried far by that horse, which was as restless as the wind, like a wave of the ocean at the end of an aeon rushing to shatter the parched earth.
Like a fool or a deluded person whose mind is dulled by the habit of worldly enjoyments, one perceives the mind—
which is actually devoid of possessions and empty— as miserable like the heart of a woman.
Consequently, it becomes as terrifying as the abode of the world when consumed by the fire of universal dissolution.
Exhausted by my journey, I reached a vast, boundless forest that was devoid of birds, free from salt-mists, treeless, and waterless;
it was like a second sky or a second eighth ocean.
Like a fifth ocean completely dried up and hollow within;
like the expansive mind of a wise man, yet like the impetuosity of anger in a fool;
devoid of contact with people and lacking the growth of grass and sprouts.
Having reached this vast wilderness, my mind has fallen into despair,
like a wanton woman who, having encountered poverty, finds herself without food, fruit, or kinsmen—
amidst the quarters of the sky flooded by the shimmering mirage-waters of the parched desert sands.
I spent that day there until the sun vanished, sinking in exhaustion;
I passed through that forest with great difficulty and weariness,
like one seeking solitude passing through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which has the appearance of a vast emptiness in its center.
Having passed that day, I reached a vast wilderness,
like the weary sun reaching the peak of the western mountain after wandering through the empty sky;
there, among the trees mostly *jambu* and *kadamba*, the birds warbled sweetly.
Where, in the thickets, the kinsmen of travelers seem to quiver;
where rows of young grass-tips appear densely upon the ground,
like the movements of joy within the heart of a crooked man who has attained the wealth of ill-gotten gains.
"Compared to that tasteless forest from which I previously fled, this place indeed brings some small measure of comfort;
for among living beings, illness is better than the ultimate suffering of death.
There, I reached the ground beneath a grove of *jambīra* trees.
Just as Mārkaṇḍeya [clung] to the Lord of Mountains while sporting in the single ocean,
there I grasped a creeper clinging to the trunk,
like a dark row of clouds by a mountain scorched by heat.
While I was hanging from this [branch], that horse galloped away,
just as a mass of evil deeds departs when people are clinging to the Ganges.
Having traveled a very long distance, I, being exhausted, took rest there.
The sun rests upon the lap of the western mountain as if upon the base of a wish-fulfilling tree;
together with the entire burden of worldly activity,
the sun has settled in the courtyard of the sunset mountain as if for a moment of rest.
When the entire interior of the world was gradually seized by darkness,
and the nocturnal activities had commenced in the forest,
I was in that soft thicket of slender grass.
Like a bird settled in its own nest, free from intense lethargy;
yet [the mind] of one whose discernment has fallen away due to calamity, whose hope is severed, whose memory is fading,
who is as wretched as one who has been sold, and who is as if submerged in a blind well.
There, a night equal to an eon passed for me, submerged in delusion,
like that of the sage Mārkaṇḍeya while being carried away by the single ocean;
at that time, I neither bathed, nor stood, nor did I eat.
The night has passed for me alone, as I stand at the forefront of calamities— sleepless,
devoid of fortitude, and trembling along with the [surrounding] shoots;
that night slipped away upon me through the extreme length of my suffering.
Then, as the streaks of darkness, along with the stars, the moon, and the night-lotuses,
fell into a state of fading like my own dejected face,
and as the shrieks of the *vetālas* ceased in the forest of human beings;
Along with the clicking and whistling sounds of my row of teeth, which were afflicted by the pain of the cold,
I saw myself submerged within, as if laughing at me,
like the eastern quarter at dawn, flushed red from drinking honey-wine.
In an instant, like an ignorant man [attaining] knowledge, or a pauper [finding] gold,
I beheld the Sun mounted upon a celestial elephant and intent on ascending into the sky;
then, rising up, I slapped my arm-guard.
Like a lion with an elephant's hide, impassioned by the dance of twilight,
I set out to roam that vast wilderness,
as Time roams the hut of the world when its hosts of beings have been consumed by the fire of the kalpa.
Nothing real is seen there in that withered jungle, just as not even a trace of virtue exists in the body of a fool;
they are merely restless, wandering like eunuchs, devoid of all apprehension.
The birds moved about uttering cries of "cī-cī," "kū-cī," and "cī-va.
Then, when the sun had reached the eighth part of its course through the sky,
the creepers appeared as if they had bathed, with every last drop of dew dried away.
Wandering here, I saw a girl carrying a vessel of boiled rice,
holding a fine jar of nectar like the Mādhavī creeper held by a Dānava;
she had eyes with shimmering pupils, was dark-complexioned, and wore non-white garments.
I arrived there like the moon at nightfall.
"O girl, give me this rice quickly for my great distress;
for through the removal of the suffering of the wretched, riches attain their full expansion."

This hunger, having grown great within me, O young woman, burns me like a black female serpent dwelling in a hollow gives birth to a tree that has already grown old. Yet, despite such begging, nothing at all has been given to me by her.
Just as wealth is given by Fortune, who is sought with great effort, to one who has committed evil deeds,
so too [this state] falls upon me alone after a long time— me, who am her constant follower, standing before her like a shadow, from one bush to another.
Addressed by her, he said, "Know me to be a Caṇḍālī, adorned with necklaces and armlets—
extremely cruel like a Rākṣasī, with the faces of a man, a horse, and an elephant. O King, you shall not obtain food from me merely by begging."
"O handsome one, from this lack of noble birth in a village dweller, [I have gained] as it were a certain gentleness"—
having spoken thus, she walked on, yet stumbling at every step, sinking into the bowers with her body gracefully bent, she said: *Muṇḍakopaniṣad-bhāṣya*, 3.106.47–48.
"I shall give you this food if you become my husband;
for people do not provide assistance for the sake of a common purpose without affection.
"In this place, my father, a Pukkasa, drives the draft-animals during the harvest."
Like a hungry Vetāla in a cremation ground, grey with dust—
this food belongs to him while he remains in the state of a master;
for beloved men are to be honored even at the cost of one's life.
Then I said to her, "O lady of virtuous vows, I shall become your husband;
for in times of distress, who considers the laws of caste, family lineage, or tradition?
Thereupon, she offered me half of one portion of rice.
Formerly, for Indra who possessed the fire, half of the nectar from the *mādhavī* vine was drunk;
that juice of the *jambū* fruit was consumed along with the rice of the *pukkasa*,
and there I rested, my mind carried away by delusion.
Having filled me like a pond, that dark rainy season has passed away,
as if taking with its hand my life-force that had stood outside,
and it has reached a state of terrible form, wicked onset, and terrifying presence.

She informed her father, who was of stout appearance, about his own purpose for him, as if he were Avīci itself because of his commands; she, clinging to him with her devotion, was like a female bee clinging to a *mātanga* elephant by its sound.
Having said "So be it" to her, when the end of the day had arrived,
he released the two tamed horses that were tied up, like the two servants of Kṛtānta;
while the quarters of the sky, tawny with frost and clouds, seemed as if they were covered in rising dust.
Like *vetālas* emerging from that forest, we set out at the end of the day;
in a moment, from the long jungle, we reached a hamlet at twilight,
like *vetālas* emerging from one cemetery to enter another great cemetery.

It was strewn with disemboweled boars, horses, monkeys, cocks, and crows; swarms of flies buzzed about the portions of raw flesh drenched in blood; and birds swooped down upon the web of moist entrails protruding for the sake of drying them.
In the garden groves, the hindquarters of dogs were caught in the thickets of *jambīra* trees;
in the courtyards, birds fluttered over heaps of heavy, drying fat,
while drops of blood flowed from hides smeared with gore that had been attached to leather water-bags.

We entered that terrifying settlement of outcasts, strewn with heads and entrails, where flies buzzed over lumps of raw flesh held in the hands of children, and where infants wailed as they were threatened by decrepit, fierce old Caṇḍālas.
The world was as if dead during that kalpa, like the attendants of Kṛtānta;
I remained there in my father-in-law’s new residence, seated upon a large seat made of plantain leaves, filled with agitation.
My mother-in-law, who had squinting eyes, spoke with tears welling in her gaze, saying, "This is my son-in-law," and she was welcomed by him.
Then, having rested upon a seat of antelope skin after eating the food of a Caṇḍāla, he sat there.
Like accumulated misdeeds that have been repeatedly experienced,
those words of affection— though not at all pleasing and indeed inauspicious— are seeds of endless suffering; having heard them, they are quite enough.
Then, on a certain day when the sky was cloudless and the stars were visible,
through various efforts and the offering of the wealth of her garments,
that terrifying young woman was given by him to me.
Dark-skinned as if by their own black deeds,
the executioners roared impetuously on all sides; with great quantities of strong liquor flowing forth,
they beat their sharp drums and displayed their merriment, like vast personifications of their own accumulated sins.
The one hundred and seventh canto, titled "The Marriage of Caṇḍālī," Canto 107.
The King:
What is the use of saying more here? From that time forth, my mind being captivated by his festival, I became a well-nourished Pukkasa there.
At the end of the seven-night festival, eight months passed by in due course.
Then, having flowered and become fully developed, she remained pregnant;
subsequently, she gave birth to a daughter who brought misery, like a calamity that brings about suffering. That girl grew quickly, becoming stout, like the swelling of a fool's thoughts.
Again, after three years, that woman of evil intellect gave birth to an unlovely son, who was like a misfortune and a creator of the snares of hope;
and she again gave birth to a daughter, and thereafter yet another child.
I became a man with a wife, an old outcaste in the forest. There, many years were spent by me together with her,
as if by a killer of a Brahmin perishing in hell along with his remorseful thoughts.
In the midst of the forest, rendered helpless by the afflictions of cold, wind, and heat,
my mind has long been tossed about like an old tortoise in a small pond;
my intellect, struck by anxiety for my wife, is being consumed by burning anguish.
The quarters of the sky were seen as if ablaze, filled with arduous labors;
and there was a load of wood carried through the forest by one wearing many worn-out scraps of linen cloth, appearing like misdeed personified.
The rainy seasons were spent on the floors of the dwellings of the wealthy— floors strewn with husks, worn out, damp, and smelling of rags for loincloths— by one who,
eager to provide for his wife, was himself decrepit from the cold winds.
In winter, like a frog hidden within the hollows of the forest, [the heart remains concealed].
Driven away by the spreading tide of the heat of various turbulent quarrels,
drops of blood were released from the eyes under the guise of tears.
In the forest, the nights— drenched by the downpour of clouds— were spent by him in the corner of a cave-dwelling made of stone slabs, as he feasted on the raw flesh of wild boars.
When time had come to an end, affection had faded, and his wife had become devoid of substance.
Due to the lack of affection from my kinsmen and their incessant quarrels,
filled with suspicion everywhere and like a restless child crying out for playthings,
I have spent these years in another's house with a miserable heart.
His face has reached a state of decay through the threats of fierce Caṇḍālas agitated by quarrels with Caṇḍālīs,
like the moon by the fangs of Rāhu.
The morsels of panther flesh have been chewed by his shriveled lips.
Like the tongues of hell-beings, they were seized and sold from the hells;
like fierce winter winds blowing from the caves of the Himalayas,
they were endured upon my naked body like arrows released by Death.
By one who was utterly worn out by old age and delusion, the roots of many withered trees were uprooted in abundance, as if they were the roots of his own virtuous deeds;
and in the forest, he carefully cooked raw meat in small earthen bowls.
By me, who possessed a wicked wife and was unclean, food was eaten by people; with my many faces contorted, I acted to destroy the splendor of those who received it,
as if selling my own portion of fortune to another for a price.
Having repeatedly cut off the flesh from his own body, which was composed of the limbs of a living being,
he sold it throughout the lands of the Vindhya forest-dwellers for the sake of prolonging his life,
as if selling his own accumulated sins arising from thousands of previous births for the sake of their increase.
Scattered and strewn over the grounds of the monastic circles and gardens,
the spade was seen by his direct vision, which was overflowing with affection;
like one fallen into the Raurava hell, that crow attained a state of tenderness.
As if entering into kinship with the thickets of the Vindhya caves, he—
possessing the form of a Pulinda— had leaf-patterns applied to his body;
he was gratified by one who had surpassed the speed of a domestic dog by striking it with a club.
My wife and children lived on wretched food obtained from village beggars;
I spent my nights with forest monkeys whose teeth chattered together as dry palm leaves rustled under a torrential downpour.
When I was vigorously rubbed by the cold with millions of hairs,
drops of water were held upon me during the rains like pearls; meanwhile,
my belly was emaciated by the agitation of hunger for the sake of pieces of roots and tubers.
In the great forest, a tumultuous quarrel was waged with his wife; in that woodland, he acted like a kinsman to a *vetāla*— one whose teeth chattered, whose eyes were squinted from cold,
and whose limbs were soiled with ink.
Wandering along the riverbanks with a fishhook in hand for the sake of fish,
he was like Kṛtānta, the noose-wielder, wandering through the worlds at the end of an eon for the sake of all beings;
and by means of many fasts, he drank the well-prepared broth of slaughtered deer.
The blood was warm as it issued then, like the milk from a mother’s breast.
From me, who stood in the cremation ground, red-stained and blood-drinking,
the forest *vetālas* fled in terror, as if pursued by Caṇḍikā.
A snare is spread in the forest for the purpose of binding deer and birds;
likewise, those consisting of sons, wives, and kin exist for the sake of increasing one's desires.
By me, through these worlds composed of illusion, like birds caught in a net of threads, [all beings are ensnared].
And the directions of those whose lives were well-spent were brought to decay by their own snares. There, when the mind had been granted excessive freedom and evil deeds arose,
hope was cast far away like a river in the rainy season.
Like a snake fleeing far away out of shame from the hand that grasps it,
compassion was cast off from the body as a slough by a serpent;
cruelty, roaring with a clamorous fury and raining down arrows, [took its place].
Just as the dark cloud at the end of summer is accepted by the sky,

so too have I long endured misfortunes, though they were avoided from afar by people like a pit is shunned by those who avoid the *kumañjarī* flowers, even when they appear blooming and unblemished in form.
In the hellish cremation grounds, whose corners are swarming with dogs and crows,
handfuls of seeds of evil deeds have been sown by the rains of delusion;
[all this was done] mercilessly by one who held a snare and a sword while dwelling in the caves of the Vindhya mountains.
Like Death himself leaping among living beings, he pounced upon the deer;
with my head resting against the walls of the necks of commoners, I slept, devoid of discernment, like Viṣṇu upon the remaining coils of Śeṣa.
With my body— its garment of fluttering leaves, its rising smoke of arrows— I have acted like a cave in the misty marshlands of the Vindhya mountains;
for a long time, I have carried upon my shoulder a patched cloak made from my dark body, thick with lice.
Like the earth ploughed by a boar in the summer, my strength was utterly exhausted;
many times I resembled Time itself, which has consumed the world with the fire of the cosmic dissolution, leaving the circles of living beings scorched by the forest fires that arise.
Just as iron fetters are difficult to grasp, so too did my wife give birth there to diseases and misfortunes, even though they were my sons;
and at that time, I had only one son, Tribālaputraka.

Sixty full kalpas were spent by me, led away by unceasing faults. O members of the assembly, during that long interval I was afflicted there, bound by the shackles of evil tendencies, crying out amidst violent trees, weeping in calamities, eating wretched food, and dwelling in ruined hamlets.
The one hundred and eighth canto, titled "The Description of Calamity," from the Episode of Indrajāla.
The King said:
Then, as time passed and my life was worn out by old age,
while I bore a beard like a mass of young grass covered in frost,
and while the juices— both flavorful and flavorless— were driven away by the winds of karma;
As the masses of days fall away like clusters of withered leaves,
amidst pleasures and pains that flow incessantly like volleys of arrows in battle,
and amidst quarrels and affairs as they come and go—
While the world-delusion revolves like a whirlpool of conceptual constructions,
and while the mind wanders like the mass of waves in the ocean,
the self becomes deluded, mounted upon the moving wheel of accumulated thoughts.
Like a blade of grass being swept away in the whirlpool of the ocean of time,
for this two-armed donkey who finds sole refuge in his village— a mere worm upon the wound of the Vindhya earth— his lifespan has thus come to an end within this multitude of years.
When my status as a king was forgotten, like a great fever in a corpse;
when my state as a Caṇḍāla became fixed, like a mountain whose wings have been clipped;
[I felt] as the end of an eon feels toward the world, or as a forest fire feels toward a forest.
Like a wave of the ocean reaching the shore, or like a thunderbolt striking a withered tree,
the circle of fierce Caṇḍālas suddenly took flight at the time of death;
then the marshlands of the Vindhya mountains, devoid of food, grass, leaves, and water, were reached.
When the mass of clouds does not rain, when visibility is lost and everything remains stationary,
when the wind blows carrying bits of glowing embers,
and when the leaves are withered, rustling, and enveloped by forest fires; MU_3,108.10 [in such times...]
In the forest regions, which were as if long abandoned by those who had gone forth into homelessness,
there suddenly arose a terrifying and unrestrained forest fire;
it dried up every thicket and reduced the grasses and shrubs to nothing but ashes.
Its entire body grey with dust, all its people hungry,
a region where food, grass, and water were absent, a circle of forest fires rising from the land;
a herd of buffaloes plunging into the waters of the shimmering mirage in the desert.
The sky was covered by clouds that resembled banks of sand raised by the wind;
the multitude of men were intent on hearing nothing but the sound of water;
and all people were wasting away from extreme dehydration due to the heat.
Intensely agitated by hunger as it devoured its own offspring, it had abandoned all regard for life;
with its circle of teeth rolling in the frantic effort of chewing its own limbs,
it swallowed a fierce mass of khadira-wood embers, mistaking them for morsels of flesh.
[He saw] fragments of forest stones swallowed by frogs and jackals;
a multitude of mothers, sons, and fathers clinging to one another in haste;
and forest śārikas with their beaks screaming from within the bellies of vultures who had swallowed them whole.
The surface of the earth was drenched with blood from the mutual mangled limbs [of warriors],
while the elephants were frantic and agitated by the fury of being devoured by lions;
it was terrifying due to the roaming of lions who were intensely focused on swallowing those in mountain caves.
A battle was waged by world-wrestlers intent on devouring one another;
the wind consisted of flying, leafless charcoal from trees stripped bare;
and the ground of the mineral-rich earth was licked by cats eager for the blood they had drunk.
The forest wind was adorned with the dense massing of thick flames;
the jungle was tawny with clusters of blazing fire that leaped everywhere;
and the thickets were swollen with smoke rising from the burnt-out hollows of pythons.
The sky was veiled by twilight clouds with flames flickering in the wind;
there were circles of ash-pillars whirled about by fierce gusts,
and the cries of children were raised as they were crushed by the tips of the tusks of screaming men.
It was filled with the great corpses of men whose teeth and skin had been severed by throngs of bewildered people;
its own fingers were stained crimson, as if seized by the speed of consuming flesh;
and it possessed the appearance of dense smoke-yellowed clouds amidst the sound of blue-leaved creepers.

It was filled with the flesh of flaming torches wandering through the sky, swallowed by circling vultures; it was agitated by the flight of worlds whose limbs were torn apart from one another, and its heart and belly were rent asunder by the crackling sound of blazing fires.

Having suddenly reached that place— a dry hollow where a forest fire was leaping with terrifying crackling sounds driven by the wind, and where trees were falling as embers due to the hissing of frightened pythons— that region [was filled with terror].
The world, consumed by the twelve suns and fires, underwent a transformation;

the region became like the pleasure-houses of the Fire, the Sun, and the Son of the Sun (Yama), with its clusters of trees possessing matted locks of blazing fire and its people driven away by the spreading force of the wind.
In the narrative of Indrajāla,
the chapter titled "The Description of the Sudden Occurrence," the one hundred and ninth chapter.
The King said:
While that painful reversal of destiny was occurring—
a calamity like an untimely and violent end of an aeon that bestowed extreme heat—
certain people, accompanied by their wives and friends, departed.
Like clouds in the autumn sky, they have departed for other lands;
with their sons, wives, and foremost kinsmen clinging to the limbs of their bodies,
some have withered right there like trees broken in the forest.
Some, having been devoured by tigers from the various directions,
emerged from their own dwellings like fledglings whose wings have not yet grown and are emerging from their nests, only to be seized by hawks;
others entered the blazing fire like moths.
Some fell into pits like rocks fallen from a mountain;
but I, having abandoned those people of my own, including my father-in-law and others,
and taking only my wife, emerged from that region with great difficulty.
Having deceived the fires, the winds, the guardians, and even the devourers,
I have emerged from the fears of death together with my wife;
having reached the edge of that region, I am there at the foot of a palmyra tree.
Having cast those sons from my shoulder like formidable calamities,
I am at rest, long exhausted as if emerged from Raurava;
I am like a lotus without water in summer, tormented by the heat of the forest fire in the hot season.
Then, while the Caṇḍāla girl rested at the foot of a tree in the cool shade and was fast asleep,
my one son named Thutthaka stood before me, embracing two young boys.
"He is our most beloved younger brother, full of grace," [he said].
With a distressed soul and eyes filled with tears, he said to me:
"O trusted one, quickly give me flesh and drink of blood this very moment."
Speaking thus again and again, that foolish son of mine reached a life-ending state, crying out once more from hunger. To him, I indeed said many times, "My son, there is no meat."
Nevertheless, that very evil-minded one continued to say, "Give me meat. Then, deluded by affection and overwhelmed by grief,
I said to him, "Son, let my cooked meat be eaten."
That too was accepted by him as he said again,
"Give it," for his livelihood was exhausted and his skin was slack;
deluded by affection and compassion, he did so in order to dispel all suffering.
Then, having fallen into the hands of Death, my enemy, I suddenly rose up;
having gathered wood scorched by the heat of summer from the forest,
I constructed a funeral pyre there for my own death.
Then that funeral pyre, with its flickering flames of fire, was set ablaze;
in an instant, amidst crackling and popping sounds, it stood there longing for me.
I said: "If my son falls into this pyre again..."
"Having cut off and cut off my flesh, you must eat me instantly," he said;
yet even as I was about to throw myself upon the funeral pyre,
the king rolled swiftly from this lion-throne away from me.

Then, by the sound of trumpets and the shouts of "Victory! on all sides, I was fully awakened; and with mindfulness restored, I stood there composed. Thus, this delusion was produced for me here by the magician.
Just as the soul, through ignorance alone, is endowed with hundreds of states,
so have I related this account of my own self to you;
just as Mārkaṇḍeya described to the noble kings the endless suffering of the kalpa.
Vasiṣṭha said:
When Lavaṇa, the lord of kings of immense splendor, had spoken thus,
that master of sorcery vanished on the spot in an instant.
