Then those members of the assembly, their minds overwhelmed with wonder, spoke as follows;
their eyes, resembling lotus petals, were busily glancing at one another:
"Aha! Truly, this illusion is marvelous and indeed extraordinary!"
"Who indeed is this one called Śāmbarika, and where has he gone ahead?
For the powers of the All-Powerful Ordainer are indeed manifold and hundredsfold,
since even this man of discerning mind is bewildered by his illusory power."
Where on one hand is this lord of the earth, who has fully understood the ways of the world; and where, on the other, are these vast agitations suited to the mental activity of ordinary people?
Nor is this a delusive illusion produced by a magician that would merely bewilder the mind.
"For these Shambarikas are indeed always greedy for wealth;
they strive for wealth with great effort, yet they do not vanish from sight.
Thus, caught upon the swing of doubt, we have been left reeling.
"O Rāma, it is said that I was indeed dwelling in that assembly hall at that time;
therefore, this was seen by me with my own eyes, not heard from a reliable source.
O Great-souled One, bring this mind of yours—which has its limbs nourished by excessive conceptualization—to a state of tranquility."
When the intrinsic nature has been brought to supreme tranquility, you shall attain that most purifying state. The hundred-and-tenth canto, titled "The Narrative of the Magician."
Vasiṣṭha:
Due to another cause, consciousness (cit) first falls into the state of being an object;
having reached the stage of ideation (kalanā), it undergoes further internal differentiation (kalaṅka).
O Rāma, while these delusions— which consist of such activities— exist though they are unreal,
one sinks for a long time into their dense emptiness.
Indeed, the withered activity of the mind, though itself unreal, spreads [these delusions] far and wide.
Like a child [fearing] a Vetāla, one regards suffering with thousands of faults; for indeed,
the stainless activity of the mind brings even that which is real to non-existence in an instant, just as the light of the sun dispels darkness.
It brings the distant near and the near to a state of distance;
the mind flutters among beings like a foolish child among fledglings.
Fearlessness is [the state] of the ignorant mind, which is possessed by latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
To a bewildered traveler from afar, even a tree stump appears as a demon. A mind stained by suspicion suspects enmity even in a friend;
a creature whose intellect is possessed by intoxication sees the very earth spinning.
For when the mind is agitated, lightning strikes from the moon;
nectar, when consumed with the perception of poison, undergoes the effects of poison.
One perceives the construction of cities and towns—which are unreal—as if they were real.

For even while awake, the mind enveloped by latent impressions (vāsanā) is indeed like a dream; it is the sole cause of delusion for living beings. Therefore, that intensity of mental impressions must be uprooted with effort by cutting them at their very root.
The deer-like mind of men, drawn by the snare of latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
falls into utter helplessness within the thicket of the forest of *saṃsāra*.
But when that impression of the living being has been severed by the wise one through discernment, [it no longer remains].
His light shines forth like that of the sun in a cloudless sky.
Therefore, O mind, know this person to be the mind alone, not the body;
for the body is inert, whereas the wise know the mind here to be neither inert nor non-inert.

O Rāma, descendant of Raghu, know that whatever is done by the mind is truly done; O Rāma, descendant of Raghu, know that whatever is abandoned by the mind is truly abandoned. The entire world is mind alone; the circle of mountains is mind alone.
The mind is space, the mind is earth, the mind is air, and the mind is the Great One (mahat).
If the mind does not unite with an object through its own nature,
then even these things such as the sun would never be luminous.
The mind takes on delusion, and because of that it is called "deluded";
when the body has fallen into delusion, one does not call the corpse "deluded.
The mind becomes the eye when seeing, and it attains the state of the ear when hearing.
Through contact it attains the state of skin; through smelling it attains the state of the nose;
through tasting it attains the state of taste. Amidst these various functions here, the mind alone moves within the body like an actor on a stage.
It makes the short long, and it goes from existence to non-existence;
it brings sweetness to pungency, and it turns an enemy into a friend.
Whatever appearance belongs to this mind as it proceeds through its various states—
For in this world, that alone is truly perceived which is experienced as such through its own nature;
indeed, by the power of mere appearance, the night of Hariścandra— who had a mind attached to the objects of a dream— lasted for twelve years.
By the power of the mind’s influence, an eon became a mere moment for Indradyumna while he was dwelling within the city of Brahmā; likewise,
through a pleasant mental state, even the Raurava hell becomes a state of bliss.
It is like the bondage of one who has already attained his own kingdom in the morning, yet remains tightly bound. When the mind is conquered, the entire host of the senses is likewise conquered;
it falls away just as a string of pearls is destroyed when the thread is burnt.
By the power of consciousness (cicchakti), which is omnipresent, of transparent form, immutable, eternal, subtle, acting as the witness,
pervading all states of being, and yet not differentiated by the objects of thought; ||| MU_3,110.26 ||| by that [power], [the Self remains].
Although it is mute and inert like the body within the existence of Rāma's self,
the mind leaps about within by its own vigor, free from mental constructions and desires,
through the play of external mountains, rivers, sky, oceans, and cities.
While awake, it transforms a desired object into the state of being polished by nectar,
yet it turns even nectar into poison in abundance for that which is undesired.
Having fully projected the self’s own wonder into all entities, [it manifests them].

The mind, however, creates within objects forms according to its own inclinations. Infused by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), the mind becomes air in its vibrations, light in its illuminations, and fluidity in its liquid states.

Upon the earth, the mind—pervaded by the power of consciousness—attains hardness; in empty states, it attains emptiness; and wherever desire is established, it goes there. It turns white into black and leads the black to whiteness.
Behold the power of this mind even without [the constraints of] place and time:
when the mind is attached elsewhere, the taste of even a most delicious food that has been chewed by the tongue is not experienced. (MU 3.110.33–34)
That which is seen by the mind is not truly seen; that which is not seen is the unperceived.
Just as a form in darkness cannot be seen, so too is the sense-faculty without the mind.
The mind is dispelled by means of the sense-faculty, but the sense-faculty is not [dispelled] by the mindless state.
The sense organs are produced from the mind, but the mind is not produced from the sense organs.
Those great-souled ones who perceive the absolute difference between the mind and the body, yet recognize their unity, are wise men worthy of homage. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.10–11)
With her hair-knot radiant with flowers and her eyes turned playfully,
the woman remained as if lifeless, clinging to limbs that were like wood or a wall,
while his mind was elsewhere, detached from passion in the forest.
Even when his own hand was being chewed by a flesh-eating beast while he remained in his body, it was not perceived [by him].
O Sage, through the extraordinary power of the mind, one is swiftly and effortlessly joined with great sufferings to make them pleasant, and with pleasures to make them painful.
Alas, when the mind is attached elsewhere, even a story being told with effort is cut short like a creeper severed by an axe.
When the mind has ascended to the mountain slope, even for a creature living as a householder, [the world is no more].
The suffering of wandering through chasms, clouds, and mountain caves is experienced [therein].
When the mind is exultant in a dream, cities and mountains appear within the heart itself,
created in an instant like [objects] in the vastness of space.
The mind, agitated in a dream, projects a series of mountains and cities within the heart itself,
just as the ocean, when stirred, produces a multitude of waves within its own waters;
just as the crests and ripples of waves arise from the water inside the sea.
In the same way, the mental constructions of other bodies, as well as the rows of mountains and cities seen in dreams, arise from the mind;
just as the beauty of leaves, creepers, flowers, and fruits exists within a seed,
so do the illusory manifestations of waking and dreaming exist within this mind.
Just as a golden ornament is not distinct from gold,
so the splendor of the activities of waking and dreaming is not distinct from the mind.
Just as the beauty of streams, droplets, waves, and foam is perceived as belonging to water, [so too is the world perceived as belonging to consciousness].
Thus, this manifold variety indeed belongs to the mind;
for this activity of one's own mind arises as the visions of waking and dreaming,
assuming various roles like an actor through the influence of aesthetic emotion (*rasa*).
Just as the state of being a Caṇḍāla appears to Lavaṇa through the power of perception,
so too this expansive world is merely the mental construction of the mind.
Whatever is perceived in any way, that very thing immediately comes into being.
The mind’s creation of mental constructs— do as you wish.
Having assumed the forms of various cities, rivers, and mountains for embodied beings,
the mind spreads this very delusion of waking and dreaming while remaining within them.
Due to its nature as a *surā*, it becomes a *daitya*; due to its nature as a *nāga*, it even becomes a non-serpent (*anagatā*).
By the power of mental appearance, the mind encounters calamity, just like the salt ocean.
From the state of being a man, it attains womanhood; again, from the state of being a father, it attains sonship.
Just as an actor quickly [assumes various roles] through his own volition, so too is the mind.
Through volition it dies; through volition it is born again.
Through long-continued practice, the formless mind attains the state of living beings.
The mind, deluded by its own thinking and driven by the wind of latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
enters the womb through volition (*saṅkalpa*) [and experiences] pleasure and pain, fear and fearlessness.
Pleasure and pain reside in the mind like oil in a sesame seed.

According to the influence of place and time, that [consciousness] may become dense or subtle. Through the movement of the oil within the sesame seed, it attains a manifest and eternal state; likewise, through the mind’s attachment to thinking, pleasure and pain become solidified.
O Rāma, by means of the designation of space and time, it is indeed *saṅkalpa* (volitional ideation) that is spoken of;
for it is under its influence that space and time have come into existence.
It is *saṅkalpa* that becomes tranquil, flares up, arrives, departs, rejoices, and leaps about.
When the body’s resolve has borne fruit, the body itself is no longer [the master];
through various surges of movement fashioned by its own volitions,
the mind gallops within this body like a horseman in an arena.
Therefore, that mind which does not allow itself to flow outward into fickleness attains self-discipline, like an elephant tethered at its post;
the mind of one who does not waver is like a supreme pillar of steel.

That person is a true being; others are but mere worms in the mud. O sinless one, he whose mind has attained steadiness and remains fixed on one point is followed by meditation upon the unsurpassed state.
When the mind is restrained, the agitation of saṃsāra attains peace,
just as the great ocean of milk becomes still when Mount Mandara ceases its churning.
Whatever expansions of the mind arise through the delusions of intentions for enjoyment, [they subside with restraint].
These very things are the sources of the sprouts of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra.

These deluded men, dull-witted and slow with intoxication and delusion, circle around like bees; their minds cut and shattered as they whirl in the rotation of the wheel, they fall into the vortex of the turning eddy, which is like a trembling blue lotus in its great, sluggish speed.
The One Hundred and Eleventh Chapter, titled "Description of the Mind," by Vasiṣṭha.

Listen to the excellent medicine for the treatment of this great disease of the mind: it is dependent upon oneself, easily accomplished by one's own means through proper method, and resides within one's own self.
It is quickly attained by one’s own human effort, which consists of self-awareness.

By effort, the vampire of the mind is conquered once its desired object has been abandoned. He who remains free from affliction while relinquishing his cherished object has truly conquered his mind, just as a rogue elephant is subdued by a well-trained driver.
The infant-like mind is nurtured through the effort of self-reflexive awareness;
it is joined to the real from the unreal and is likewise awakened.
Through the steady application of the scriptures, that which was heated by the fire of thought is cooled.

O Sage, cut away the mind with the mind itself, as one would cut iron with iron. Just as a child is effortlessly yoked here and there, so too can the mind be restrained within; what indeed is very difficult in this?
One should direct the mind, through its own conscious effort, toward virtuous action that brings about a future rise of prosperity;
for the experience of renouncing what one desires is dependent on oneself and is exclusively beneficial.
Fie upon that worm of a man for whom this has become difficult!
Having contemplated through one's own awareness that the unattractive is of an attractive form,
the mind is conquered without effort, just as a child is by a wrestler.
Through human effort, the mind is quickly conquered;
by means of a mind that is free from adversaries, one is established in the state of Brahman.
This depends solely upon one's own mind, is easily accomplished, and requires nothing more than its own mastery.
Fie upon those jackals among men who are unable to act!

Without the mantra of mental tranquility— which is to be accomplished solely through one's own manly effort and consists in the renunciation of what one desires— there is no auspicious state of existence.
By the mere subduing of the mind through the realization of one's own self-awareness,
let that which is without rival, without beginning or end, and immovable be sought here. Indeed,
in the splendor of the pacification of the mind, which has the attainment of the desired goal as its limb...

When the disease of the mind has been severed by the weapon of non-conceptualization, then all things—the instructions of the guru, the meaning of the scriptures, mantras, and other such means—become as straw; at that time, one attains Brahman, which is omnipresent and tranquil. (MU 3.111.14–15)
In this matter, which is to be accomplished through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which destroys the misery of conceptual constructions (*saṅkalpa*),

and which possesses a tranquil form like a clear cloud— what kind of affliction could there be for a person? Surely, disregarding destiny (*daiva*) as it is imagined by the conceptual constructions of the deluded, [one should proceed].
Through human effort and through realization, lead the mind to the state of non-mind. Following that singular, ineffable Great State for a long time,
having caused the mind to be devoured by consciousness, become even beyond the nature of consciousness itself.
Liberated through the cultivation of existence and endowed with supreme intellect,
one should remain undistracted and hold oneself within the consciousness that is beyond the mind,
having grasped the mind and brought it to the state of non-mind by relying on the highest human effort.
Come to that great state where you neither exist nor anything else exists.
O Rāma, just as a weak enemy is swiftly conquered through prowess, so too can the mind— which takes the form of the error of perception— be conquered by manly effort alone.

Freedom from agitation is the root of prosperity; from freedom from agitation proceeds the conquest of the mind by a living being, by which the conquest of the three worlds becomes as a blade of grass. In that [state], there is not even the slightest fear of weapons, fire, portents, or calamities.
If there is merely the exclusion of intrinsic nature, what difficulty could there possibly be in that?
But as for those lowest of men who are incapable of being overcome by self-awareness,
how will they conduct themselves in the states of worldly transaction?
"I am a man," "I have been born," "I live"—such are the false views;
these fluctuations of the mind, arising from what is unreal, pass away as they are fickle.
No one whatsoever dies here, nor is anyone at all born here.
One knows for oneself the death of the body and that the mind has gone to another world.
Having departed from here, the mind manifests in the other world with a different form;
since this does not perish until liberation, whence can there be fear of death?
Wandering through this world and the next in the form of the body, the mind remains until liberation; no other form of it exists.
For men, affliction consists in the assault [of suffering] upon a son, a brother, a servant, and so forth.
It is my conviction that the self is not the exclusion of one's own consciousness from one's own mind.
Having investigated again and again in all directions— horizontally, upward, and downward—
I find that there is indeed no means other than the pacification of the mind.
When the path has been traversed, purified, and cleared, and when consciousness (*citi*) has arisen in the heart,
rest is produced merely through the dissolution of the mind.
One meditates upon consciousness (*citi*) in the space of the heart by means of the stream of the wheel of consciousness.
Kill the mind without hesitation; then mental afflictions will no longer crush you.
If that which was once delightful has been perceived by your discernment as un-delightful, it is my conviction that the very limbs of the mind have been severed.
"This is that I am; this is mine; my mind is merely this much"—by the mere non-contemplation of that [mind], it is cut away as if by a sickle, like a scattered cloud in the stainless sky in autumn.
Likewise, the mind becomes free from latent impressions in the supreme reality that is beyond conceptual construction. Where swords, fire, and winds may cause fear,
what fear can there be regarding that which is under one's own control— gentle, pure, and free from conceptualization?
"This is better, this is not"—this conviction is established even among children and remains unimpaired.
One should employ the mind toward the noble and supreme good, as one would toward a beloved son.
[One should subdue] the five-faced elephant of the senses within the lion of the mind that nourishes the cycle of worldly existence.

Those who slay these [perceptions] conquer here and fall into the state of Nirvāṇa. These fearsome calamities, which cause agitation, are produced from the mental construction of conceptualization, just as a mirage arises from the heat of the desert.

Let the winds blow at the end of the eon, let the oceans become one, and let the twelve suns blaze; there is no harm for one who is free from the mind (*nirmanas*). From the seed of the mind arise [all things] that bestow the fruits of good and evil.
These groves of saṃsāra are but the sprouts of the seven worlds.
For the sake of accomplishing everything that is to be achieved solely through the state of non-conceptualization,
remain intent on steadfastness within the imperial sovereignty of non-conceptualization.
The mind, as it gradually wanes, bestows supreme bliss,

just as a charcoal whose limbs are being consumed grants its desired goal to one seeking the extinction of that charcoal. If the mind has the abode of Brahman as its intended object, [it attains that state].
That which was previously unmanifest becomes clearly distinguished and visible within the subtle atom (aṇu).

Having conquered the mind through the power of mere contentment— by the power of mere volition one brings about great misfortune, while by the power of the pacification of volition one successfully accomplishes one's goals— attain victory through that which is eternally arisen and free from effort.

May that which remains— the unborn state— be attained through the supreme purity of a tranquil mind, through equanimity esteemed by the knowers of the Self, and through a subdued and measured inner absence of egoism. This concludes the chapter titled "The Exposition of the Nature of the Power of the Mind."
The one hundred and twelfth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"In whatever object, by whatever means, and in whatever manner,"
The mind, endowed with intense agitation, perceives its desired object.
This intense impetuosity of the mind arises and perishes;
by its very nature, it is without cause, like a series of bubbles on calm water.
Coldness is like that of frost, and blackness is like that of collyrium;
restlessness is the form of the mind, which possesses a single nature that is both intense and non-intense.
Thus spoke Rāma.
"O Brahmin, how can the flickering of this excessively fickle mind— which has nothing but its own momentum as its cause— be forcibly restrained? Vasiṣṭha replied:
And here, a mind devoid of flickering is not seen anywhere;
flickering is the inherent nature of the mind, just as heat is the nature of fire.
For this flickering power of vibration resides within the very essence of consciousness.
Know that to be the mental power whose nature is the manifestation of the universe.
Just as the very existence of wind cannot be inferred apart from its vibration and touch,
so too the existence of the mind does not exist apart from its flickering movement.
But that mind which is devoid of flickering is said to be dead;
and that very state is called liberation (mokṣa), as it is well-known from the scriptures on austerity (tapas).
By the mere dissolution of the mind, the cessation of suffering is attained.
By the mere act of giving rise to mental desire, one attains supreme suffering.
The demon of the mind, having arisen, produces intense pain;
therefore, with effort, cast it down for the sake of infinite enjoyment of happiness.

This flickering of his which is called ignorance (*avidyā*)—known by the other name of latent impression (*vāsanā*)—destroy it through inquiry. By means of that ignorance, which is the latent impression, [the mind remains] within; therefore, [bring about] the peace of the mind.
Through its dissolution by means of renunciation, the supreme good is attained.
That which is the middle between existence and non-existence, the middle between consciousness and insentience— that is called the mind (*manas*), O Rāma, its form oscillating between the two.
For, by the power of firm habituation, the mind— seized by the contemplation of dullness through its very nature as dullness— attains a state of inertness;
whereas through the exclusive contemplation of discernment, the mind [attains] the nature of the aspect of consciousness.
Through the power of firm practice, the mind attains a stable oneness of consciousness.
By means of human effort, whatever state the mind is directed toward,
having reached that state, it becomes colored by that very practice.
Therefore, relying on human effort and mastering the mind with the intellect,
take refuge in the state free from sorrow and remain steadfast, free from doubt.
If the mind is not broken by the mind itself through the contemplation of existence—
"O Rāma, it is forcibly extracted; there is no other means than this.
Indeed, the mind alone is capable of firmly restraining the mind.
O Rāghava, who other than a king would be capable of restraining a king?"

For those seized by the crocodile of craving in the swift current of the ocean of saṃsāra, and being carried away by its whirlpools, their own mind alone is the boat. Having severed with the mind itself the mind— the bond that is the supreme fetter— [one is liberated].

He by whom the self has not been liberated cannot be liberated by another. Whatever latent impression (vāsanā) called "mind" arises within one who is permeated [by it], the wise person should abandon each of those; through that, the destruction of ignorance occurs.
Having abandoned the latent impression of the flood of enjoyments, abandon the latent impression of distress;
then, having abandoned both existence and non-existence, become happy as one free from conceptual construction. This non-contemplation of contemplation—this much is the destruction of contemplation.
This very dissolution of the mind is called the destruction of ignorance.
Whatever is perceived as an object, non-perception of it is better;
indeed, non-cognition is nirvāṇa, while suffering arises from cognition.
By that very effort of one's own, it is accomplished by a person in an instant;
therefore, one should constantly practice the non-contemplation of phenomena for the sake of prosperity.
Those things such as passion which are desired by the mind—having understood each of them to be without substantial reality, you [should abandon them].
Having abandoned that sprout of attachment whose seed has been destroyed, and being satisfied, do not undergo joy and sorrow.
The 113th canto, titled "The Proclamation of Portions of Instruction by the Sound of Hooves."
Vasiṣṭha:
Since this latent impression (vāsanā) has arisen while being eternally unreal,
like the delusion of a double moon, it is therefore proper, O Rāghava, to abandon it.
Ignorance exists only for one whose wisdom is destroyed; it is accepted as existing merely by name. Since its non-existence is established, how could it exist for one of perfect wisdom?
O Rāma, do not be ignorant; be wise and investigate correctly.
There is no second moon in the sky; it is perceived in vain through delusion.
Apart from the reality of the Self, nothing exists—neither a real entity nor a non-entity—just as there is nothing apart from the mass of water in the vast ocean garlanded with waves.

Do not superimpose these states of existence and non-existence—created by your own conceptual constructions and consisting of unreality—upon the Self, which is eternal, pervasive, white (pure), and stainless.
You are not the agent; why then do you have this sense of "mine" regarding these activities?
For when only one exists, what is done by whom, and how?
O wise one, do not become a non-doer; for what is to be accomplished by you here through non-doing?
There is something to be achieved and something to be attained; therefore, O sinless one, remain established in yourself.
O scion of the Raghus, you are an agent because of your non-attachment;
thus, though you are a non-agent, perform action like an agent due to that very non-attachment.
If it were true, it would be something to be adopted; if it were false, it would simply be something to be abandoned.
Because of being solely intent upon what is to be accepted, attachment to action is indeed appropriate.
But where everything is a magical illusion, consisting of *māyā* and devoid of reality—
there, O Rāma, what are those views of "what is to be rejected" and "what is to be accepted," and how could they exist?
O scion of Raghu, this ignorance is the tiny seed-grain of saṃsāra;
for though it is non-existent, it has attained expansion as if it were real.
This is that wheel which initiates the expansive and essence-less cycle of saṃsāra.
This latent impression (*vāsanā*) is to be understood as mental, bestowing delusion;
like a beautiful bamboo stalk that is hollow and pithless within,
or like a succession of river waves, it is impermanent and subject to destruction.
Even when grasped with the hand, it cannot be seized;
though soft, it has an exceedingly sharp point, rising like a wave from a mountain torrent.
Though it appears clearly manifest, it is of no use for any real purpose.
The river, established in the form of shimmering waves, is in some places crooked and in others straight; it is long, short, steady, or moving.
Since it arises from that [source], it has nonetheless attained distinction from it.
Though empty within, this beautiful essence is seen everywhere;
though not established anywhere here, it is perceived everywhere.
Though seemingly inert, it is as if composed of consciousness, subsisting on the vibration of another.
Not remaining still for even a moment, she gives rise to the suspicion of instability;
though her complexion is pure like a flame, she has a hollow darkened by soot.
She leaps about by the favor of another, and wastes away when not looked upon by him.
In pure light she is withered, yet in darkness she shines intensely;
like a vast mirage, she sports with manifold colors.
She is crooked, treacherous, slender, soft, and yet harsh as a thorn.
Lalanā is fickle, hungry, and thirsty like the tongue of a serpent;
she herself quickly perishes like the flame of a lamp when the oil is exhausted;
and like a streak of vermilion dust, she does not glow without passion.
Momentarily manifest, flickering, and assuming various forms within the dull-witted mind, she arises like a crooked flash of lightning, striking terror into the naive.
Having seized [the mind] with effort, she burns it; appearing again and again, she dissolves away.

Moreover, even when sought, it is not found; as fleeting as lightning, it brings misfortune even when it arrives unbidden though delightful. Like a garland of flowers out of season, it should not be welcomed for the sake of one's highest good.
Completely forgotten, this [world] which causes delusion for the sake of excessive pleasure has arisen only for misfortune,
like the fabrication of a bad dream;
by the power of mere appearance alone, the three worlds appear vast.
Having produced them in a mere moment, he holds them and devours them.
By this [power], Lavaṇa turned a single moment into a series of years,
and Hariścandra fashioned a night lasting twelve years.
Furthermore, for others who are separated from their beloveds and suffering the pangs of separation,
the night becomes as long as a year through her grace;
yet for one who is happy, it becomes short, while for one who is miserable, it attains length.
For time,
which is characterized solely by its own transformation, acts upon this [consciousness] through its mere presence,
just as a lamp acts upon its effects such as light; yet this is not so in reality.

Like a woman with breasts covered by her garment who, though adorned, is not truly a woman because she lacks the nature of womanhood, so too this [body], though firm in appearance, is incapable of performing any action;
it is like a kingdom of the mind, radiant in form but devoid of reality.
Even with its hundreds of thousands of branches, it is nothing at all from the perspective of ultimate reality;
like a mirage in the forest, it is a mere false display that deceives only those deluded deer and not human beings.
Like a mass of foam, it arises and perishes, yet remains uninterrupted;
though inert, it has a flickering form, and when grasped, it is nothing at all.
Though non-different from consciousness, it surely stands as if it were something else.
Like a short silkworm’s thread, she is as if insentient though resting upon the sentient;
turbid and fierce in its prison, grey with the spreading dust of *rajas*;
flickering like the wind at the end of an eon, it has pervaded the interior of the worlds.
Like a column of smoke clinging to the body, causing burning and perspiration,
it pervades the worlds, having internalized the sequence of aesthetic flavors (*rasa*);
like a very long stream from a cloud, it is composed of insentient matter.
It is like a strong rope made from a collection of worthless grasses;
it is described as being merely a mental construction, like a garland of lotuses upon the waves.
It is like a lotus stalk full of holes, matured in the mud, and insentient by nature.
Like a flame, it appears intent on increasing, yet it does not grow;
like the taste of poison, sweet at first but terrible in the end.
Like the wick of a lamp, once extinguished, I know not where it goes here.
Even when seen at the very beginning, like a mist, it is perceived as nothing at all.
Like a handful of dust spread out and then examined until its ultimate atomic constituents,
this [space] is seen as merely the blueness of the sky, entirely devoid of any objective cause.
Like the delusion of seeing two moons, it has arisen; like a dream, it has produced confusion.
Just as a stationary object appears to move to one traveling by boat, so too has this [delusion] arisen here.
When the mind is thus afflicted, those who are agitated perceive it as if for a long duration.
To people, the long delusion of the dream of saṃsāra appears;
even that which is pleasant and real is seen as non-existent,
while that which is unpleasant and unreal is seen as existent.
When this [mind] is afflicted by this [ignorance], various delusions arise and perish in the consciousness like waves in the ocean.
This powerful mental cultivation, mounted upon the chariot of objective entities, [proceeds].
The mind quickly seizes her, as a snare catches a bird.
Out of compassion, he leads his mother— whose eyes tremble and whose breasts drip with drops of milk—
to the state of being his wife, filled with overflowing joy.

The nectar, though already moist, quickly causes the orb of the moon to swell, flooding the three worlds with its outflow; it creates a frantic agitation like the onset of the movements of a mad, supreme vetāla.
Indeed, even a stump bestows [its form] upon one who approaches it with the mind;
for by her grace, at times such as the twilight, clods of earth, stones, and walls appear as serpents to the eyes in this world.
Just as a single moon appears as two when seen by two people,
and just as in a dream one travels across the ocean, though it is near at hand;
so too, time that is long becomes a mere moment, just as the night is desired to end.
To those separated from their beloveds, even a single moment appears like a year.
There is nothing that this haughty woman will not do;
yet, O Raghava, behold the power of her who possesses nothing at all.
One should diligently restrain consciousness by means of consciousness itself;
by blocking the flow of consciousness, this river of the mind dries up.
This world exists only through that which is non-existent—a fragile-bodied, utterly hollow [consciousness].
It is truly a wonder that the world has been blinded by false meditation (mithyābhāvanā)—
a state that is formless, devoid of beautiful consciousness,
and which perishes swiftly even while it exists. (MU 3.113.57–58)
By the flickering light that perishes within the midst of darkness,
possessing the nature of an owl's eye, the world has been wonderfully blinded;
she who performs exclusively evil deeds cannot endure being looked upon.
It is a wonder that the world has been blinded by one who does not even recognize her own body;
it is a wonder that the world has been blinded by that woman of noble intellect and virtuous conduct, who is eternally beautiful yet perpetually set in the sunset of worldly existence.

Always sustained by this [ignorance], which is perpetually agitated by endless suffering and devoid of true awakening, it is a marvel that the world has been rendered blind. It is thick with the clouds of desire and anger, and its mouth is the spreading darkness.
It is a marvel that the world has been blinded by this insentient body,
which serves as a blind well for the Self— dull, worn out by its own inertia, and uttering long, painful lamentations. (MU 3.113.63–64)
By this [Māyā], which shatters attachment to the Puruṣa, which is like a diseased woman,
whose illusory nature remains unimpaired, and which revolves through various intentions, the world has been wonderfully blinded—
she whom the Puruṣa is not even able to endure looking upon.
By that woman who is herself without refuge, the man is wondrously blinded. By that woman who possesses no consciousness at all, and who perishes even while not yet destroyed—
by that woman who is no man, the man is wondrously blinded.

O Lord, by what means does this latent impression (*vāsanā*)— which produces endless and difficult-to-restrain playfulness, which brings about pleasure and pain oriented toward decline and rise, and which is bound as a mental conception within the cave of the mind— come to dissolve? This is the chapter titled "The Description of Ignorance" (*avidyā-varṇana*).
The one hundred and fourteenth canto.
Rāma:
[Tell me] that which arises from the manifestation of ignorance, pertaining either to the world or to the person.
"O Brahmin, how indeed shall this great blindness be destroyed?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Just as a frost-lily perishes in an instant from the sight of the sun,"

Thus this ignorance perishes; it perishes through the vision of the Self. It is this very ignorance that, together with the embodied soul, causes one to oscillate within the abysses of saṃsāra amidst the thorny thickets of suffering.
As long as ignorance has not arisen for this [person], nor has that which brings about its destruction;
and as long as there is no desire to perceive the Self by oneself, which bestows the destruction of delusion—
for one who looks toward something beyond this, the destruction of one's own self proceeds.
O Raghava, just as a shadow seeking the experience of sunlight vanishes of its own accord when the all-pervading sun is seen,
so too [the ego] dissolves when the all-pervading Lord is perceived,
like a shadow when the twelve-fold host of suns has risen in every direction.
In this world, ignorance is merely desire; its destruction is called liberation.

And that [destruction], O Rāghava, is accomplished by mere non-mental-conception (asaṅkalpa). When even the slightest darkness of latent impressions (vāsanā) in the sky of the mind has been destroyed, [liberation is attained].
The darkness of ignorance diminishes through the great rising of the sun of consciousness.
Just as the night of darkness vanishes somewhere when the sun has risen,
so too does ignorance dissolve somewhere when discernment has arisen.
Through firm habitual tendencies, the bondage of the mind reaches density,
just as the conceptualization of a restless vetāla appears to a child at twilight.
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, whatever is seen here is ignorance, and that ignorance is destroyed by the cultivation of the Self. Of what nature is that Self said to be?
Vasiṣṭha replied:

That reality of consciousness (*cittattva*), which is free from the pursuit of objects, all-pervading in its generality, and inexpressible—that is the Self, the Supreme Lord. This world, beginning from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is as follows: [MU 3.114.12] *ābrahmastambaparyantaṃ tṛṇādi yad idaṃ jagat*.
All that is at all times only the Self; no ignorance exists, O sinless one.
Indeed, all this is Brahman—eternal, a mass of consciousness, and imperishable.
No other conceptualization exists apart from that which is called "mind."
Nothing is born and nothing dies in these three worlds;
nor does the existence of the modifications of being (bhāvavikāra) exist anywhere.
There is only that which appears as the absolute, the undifferentiated whole of all things, remaining unimpaired.
In this world, there exists only pure consciousness (cinmātra), free from the pursuit of objects of thought.

Within this eternal, pervasive, pure, and untroubled pure consciousness— tranquil, characterized by an equal enjoyment of all experiences, and whose self has arisen free from modification— [all things abide].
That which, having itself conceptualized what is attained through its own nature,
runs forth— the consciousness that is itself the object of thought, unfading yet appearing faded— that is known as the mind (*manas*).
[It arises] from the one, all-pervading, divine, and omnipotent Great Self.
The power of differentiation and limitation arises from the One like a wave from water;
though nothing exists within that single, vast, and tranquil [reality],
it attains its perfection in the Supreme Self through mere volition.
Therefore, this [bondage] which is established by volition perishes by volition alone;
it is destroyed by that very thing from which it was born, just as a flame of fire is extinguished by the wind.
Having attained the form of a desire for enjoyment through success achieved by human effort, [it is thus overcome].
By mere non-conceptualization, that ignorance is completely dissolved.
Through the very firm resolve "I am not Brahman," the mind is bound;
through the very firm resolve "All is Brahman," it is liberated once again.
Volition is the supreme bondage; non-volition is liberation. Having conquered volition within, do as you wish.
"I have seen here in the sky a lotus pond with golden lotuses."
She drinks honey from trembling lapis lazuli cups, her naked body fragrant;
with her circles of lotus-stalk arms raised high and their full curves revealed,
she laughs at the orb of the radiant moon’s rays.
In this way, the net of conceptual construction, though unreal, appears as if real;
just as it is imagined by a child for the sake of destroying his own mental composure,
so too does this ignorance exist here, binding one through the process of mental cultivation to the cycle of existence.
By the fickle and childish mind, it is imagined only for the sake of suffering:
"I am emaciated," "I am extremely miserable," "I am bound," "I possess hands, feet, and so forth.
Thus one is bound by worldly activity that conforms to such mental states.
"I am not suffering, nor do I have a body; what bondage can there be for this conscious Self?"—by such conduct that accords with this realization, one is liberated.
"I am not flesh, nor am I bones; for I am other than the body, the Supreme."
Thus, one who possesses such certainty is said here to have internal ignorance destroyed.
Now, the splendor of darkness stands above, like the radiance of a lofty vaidūrya peak on the summit of the divine mountain,
or as difficult to penetrate as the rays of the sun.
For just as blackness is imagined in the sky as something arising from its own nature by a person standing on the earth through the impulse of his own conceptualization,
so too is this ignorance merely imagined— the notion of a self in that which is not-self.
"O Raghava, this is neither the shadow of the sapphire of Mount Meru nor the radiance of darkness, [perceived] by an unawakened person, not by one who is awakened. Rama said:
"O Brahmin, tell me, what has caused this blueness of the sky?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O Rāma, the blueness of the void sky does not exist as a quality."
Furthermore, due to the presence of the radiance of other jewels, this light of Meru does not exist here;
because the cosmic egg consists of light, because the perfected light is expansive,
and because the far side of the egg is luminous, there is no possibility of darkness here.
O fortunate one, this emptiness alone is seen in its vastness;
it is not composed of reality, being like a companion to its own counterpart, ignorance.
When the perfection of the destruction of one's own views is attained, darkness—which had arisen as something non-existent—is itself extinguished.
That blackness of space is perceived as such due to the nature of the object.
Just as, through this understanding, one realizes that the blackness seen in the sky is not actually blackness,
so too [should one understand] the darkness of ignorance.
For the wise have declared that the absence of conceptual construction is the suppression of ignorance;
indeed, it is as easy to accomplish as [the absence of] a lotus in the sky.
This delusion of the world, having arisen like the color of the sky, [is likewise easily dispelled].
O virtuous one, I consider non-remembrance to be better than remembrance;
for just as a person perishes through the thought "I am destroyed" and is thereby overcome by suffering,
so too does a person attain happiness through the thought "I am awakened."
Likewise, one whose resolve is deluded falls again into a state of delusion;
yet, through a noble resolve for awakening, one pursues awakening.
From a momentary recollection of these [truths], eternal ignorance arises.
Through effort or through forgetfulness, the goal perishes in reality.
She is the creator of all states of being, the deluder of all beings;
she is the savior when one's own self is destroyed, but the destroyer when one's own self prospers.
Whatever the mind synthesizes, all the functions of the senses accomplish that in an instant, just as ministers carry out the command of a king.
Therefore, he who does not allow the mind to engage in synthesis regarding objects—
Through internal conscious effort, he attains peace.
That which did not exist at the very beginning does not exist even today;
that which appears here is Brahman—peaceful, one, and immovable.
Therefore, whose thoughts are there to be pondered, how, or from where?
Relying upon the supreme human effort with the highest intellect, one should remain in a state free from constraint— unchanging, without beginning or end.
One should thoroughly uproot from the mind the cultivation of hope for enjoyments along with its very root.
That supreme delusion which arises— the cause of old age and death,
in which hundreds of snares of hope flourish— is the manifestation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
"My sons, my wealth, I am he, this is mine"—
this single latent impression flutters about like a magic trick;
for in this very empty body, [the ego] is as flickering as the wind in a bamboo thicket.

But by ignorance and by latent impressions, O knower of reality, the notion of "I" and "mine" is projected externally. In the ultimate sense, however, I consider that apart from the reality of the Self, there is never anything at all such as "I," "mine," or "this."
Through the vision of creation, this very same ignorance— though appearing as something else, diverse, and accompanied by the mountains and the rows of peaks on earth— revolves again and again;
it arises through mere lack of knowledge and perishes through mere knowledge.
It is to be discerned as mere consciousness, like a serpent in a rope;
O Rāma, that which is ignorance for the ignorant is not ignorance for the knower, for his Brahman is established in its own majesty.
The two conceptualizations of the rope and the snake are both imagined solely by ignorance;
however, by the knower, only the one uncreated vision of Brahman is determined.
Do not be ignorant, become a knower, and abandon the latent impressions of saṃsāra.
Why do you weep like a stranger for that which is not the self, as if it were the self?
O Rāghava, what is this dull and mute body of yours,
for whose sake you are helplessly overwhelmed by pleasure and pain?
For just as there is no identity between wood and lacquer, or between a jujube fruit and its bowl, even though they are joined together, so it is with the body and the possessor of the body.
Just as when a bellows is burned, the burning does not affect that which is inside the bellows.
Likewise, O scion of Raghu, when the body of the wind is destroyed, the self does not perish. "I am suffering" and "I am full of happiness"—these are delusions;
when the mind is afflicted by these, there is unbearable torment in this world.
By this utterly false, useless, and mind-swelling mental fabrication—
which bestows suffering and is blinded by the impurity of great delusion—
one imagines the presence of the Raurava hell even within the lunar orb, though it is moist with nectar.
The suffering of burning and withering in hell is experienced. In lakes with cool waves and high, water-trembling *kahlāra* flowers, the greatness of an abundance of mirages is perceived.
The agitations of falling and rising within the construction of a city in the sky are experienced in dreams and similar states, bestowing various pleasures and pains;
yet, if the latent impression of saṃsāra did not fill the mind, [these would not occur].
How could the frenzies of waking and dreaming lead one here to calamity?
For those [frenzies] are seen as the decrees of misfortune in the Raurava and Avīci hells,
yet they flourish when false knowledge has increased in the grounds of the celestial groves.
Pierced by this [ignorance], even a mind as delicate as a lotus fiber instantly perceives the delusions of the whirlpools in the ocean of the entire world. Indeed,
when the mind is afflicted by this, one remains fixed even in the midst of a kingdom.
People pass through various stages of life that are not even fit for a dog-cooker (outcaste).
Therefore, O Rāma, having abandoned the latent impressions that bind one to existence and consist of all objective states, remain free from passion like a crystal.
While you remain engaged in your duties, let there be no coloring by passion,
just as a crystal assumes various reflections. If, indeed, you always act with effortless ease (*līlayā*), through a mind free from curiosity and attachment, [then you are truly liberated].
By what [means] can you, the Great One, whose nature is action in the world through your supreme intellect, be compared?
The one hundred and fifteenth canto, titled "Instruction on the Avoidance of the Faults as Previously Described."
Vālmīki:
Having been addressed thus by the venerable and high-souled Vasiṣṭha,
Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals, shone as if he had opened his eyes for the first time.
With his inner heart blossomed, he attained a magnificent splendor,
like a lotus that has been refreshed when the darkness has faded and it is bathed in the light of the sun;
his face was brightened by a gentle smile born of awakening and wonder.
And Rāma spoke these words, which were washed by the nectar of his inner radiance:
"Aha! How wondrous it is that mountains are bound together by threads arisen from lotuses!"
All beings are brought under control by that ignorance which does not truly exist.
This very form has attained the state of a diamond within these three worlds— that which,
though indeed real, appears as if unreal due to ignorance.

Out of compassion, tell me once more the true nature of this illusory actress of saṃsāra upon the stage of the three worlds, for the sake of my certain understanding. Furthermore, O Great-Souled One, this doubt dwells within my heart.
"O highly fortunate one, what calamity did that Lavana encounter?
O Brahmin, when the body and the embodied soul are either joined together or both unslain, who indeed is the transmigrator who alone enjoys the fruits of good and evil?"
Having thus brought about that unsurpassed calamity for Lavaṇa,
where has he gone with his fickle undertakings, and who was that magician?
Vasiṣṭha said:
O sinless one, the body is like wood or a wall, and is as if nothing at all;
it is conceptualized by this mind, which is like the light of a dream.
But the mind, having entered into living beings, is permeated by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).

Know, O wise one, that the mind wandering in saṃsāra is as fickle as a young monkey. For it is the mind that, as the agent of action within the body, assumes various forms and is designated by the names of ego, intellect, and life-force.

O Rāghava, for one who is unawakened and for one who is fully awakened, these endless experiences of pleasure and pain do not belong to the body at all. The unawakened mind constructs various conceptualizations based on manifold notions.
Following its various mental modifications and having assumed diverse forms,
it remains unawakened only so long as the end of sleep has not arrived; for one perceives the confusion of a dream only while dreaming, never once when awakened.
As long as the living being, agitated by the sleep of ignorance, has not been awakened,
so long does he perceive the delusion of the onset of saṃsāra, which is difficult to comprehend. For one whose mind is fully awakened, all that darkness dissolves away.
Just as there is blindness for a lotus that blooms in the light of day;

so too, that which is designated by the self-realized as the mind (*citta*), ignorance (*avidyā*), the mental organ (*manas*), the individual soul (*jīva*), and latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and which is called the "karmic self" (*karmātman*)—that is the embodied being (*dehī*) who is experienced through suffering. (MU 3.115.17–18)
The body is inert and not deserving of suffering; it is the living soul (*jīva*) that suffers due to a lack of inquiry.
This lack of inquiry arises from dense ignorance (*ajñāna*), and ignorance is the cause of suffering.
Through auspicious and inauspicious qualities (*dharma*), the living soul has become an object of experience.
Due solely to the defect of non-discrimination, this great state does not reside within the sheath.
Bound by the disease of non-discrimination, the mind, possessing manifold functions,
wanders like a wheel through various modes of existence.
It rises, it cries out, it kills, it eats, it moves, it leaps, it rejoices—
it is the mind alone within this body, and never the body itself;
just as a householder is in his home, or as a charioteer is in his chariot.
Just as a snake is within a bellows, so is the mind within this body;
like the wind in a tree,
the mind flickers with a restless form while remaining in the body, yet the body does not abide in the mind.
"In all pleasures and pains, and in all mental constructions,
know that the mind is the agent, the mind is the enjoyer, and the mind is the human being. In this regard, listen as I shall tell you this wonderful account."
Just as that Lavaṇa fell into the state of a Caṇḍāla through a delusion of the mind,
so too the mind experiences the fruit of its actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious; since you have surely understood this, listen further, O Rāghava.
O sinless one, in former times, Lavaṇa, born of the lineage of Hariścandra,
while seated alone in solitude, reflected for a long time in his mind:
"My grandfather was the great officiating priest of the Rājasūya sacrifice."

"I was born into his family; I shall mentally perform that sacrifice for him. Having reflected thus and having gathered the necessary materials from the very beginning, that lord of the earth entered the initiation for the Rājasūya sacrifice.
He honored and worshipped the officiating priests and the holy sages;
he paid homage to the deities and kindled the sacrificial fire.
As he was thus performing the sacrifice, within his mind in the midst of the grove—
A full year passed in the worship of divine sages and the twice-born.
Having given away his entire possessions as a sacrificial fee to all beings, beginning with the twice-born,
the king woke at the end of the day in his own grove.
Thus King Lavaṇa attained the Rājasūya sacrifice;
for he was endowed with a nourished mind and possessed its fruit.
Therefore, know that the mind is the person who experiences pleasure and pain.
Therefore, O Rāghava, apply yourself to that truth which is beginningless and effortless.
When the mind is full, the person is complete; when it is destroyed, he perishes.
As for those who hold the conviction "I am the body," enough with such so-called wise men!
When the mind is full of discernment and fully awakened, all sufferings are utterly dissolved for one whose intellect has become detached;
indeed, when the cluster of lotuses is revealed by the rays of the sun, the dullness, contraction, and darkness born of closing are long since dispelled.
This concludes the chapter titled "Instruction on the Experiencer of Pleasure and Pain."
The one hundred and sixteenth canto.
Rāma said:
"O Lord of the Earth, Lavaṇa has obtained the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice."
"What proof could there possibly be here in this conjuration of a web of imagination?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"When the illusionist arrived at the right time in the assembly hall of Lāvaṇī..."
At that time, I was staying there and witnessed it with my own eyes.
Then, when Śambara’s agent had departed from that place, I was questioned with effort by the members of the assembly and by Lavaṇa, asking, "What is this?"
Having reflected and seen what was said there, listen as I shall explain to you that which was intended by Śāmbarika, O Rāma:
"Those who are performers of the Rājasūya sacrifice [shall remain] for twelve years."

They encounter the suffering of calamity, consisting of various forms of conditions. Therefore, O Rāma, that messenger of the gods, appearing in the form of a juggler, was sent from the sky by Śakra to bring misery upon Lavaṇa.
Having bestowed the supreme station upon that performer of the Rājasūya sacrifice, he departed by way of his own celestial path, frequented by gods and siddhas.
Therefore, O Rāma, this is indeed directly perceived; there is no doubt in this matter.
For the mind is indeed the agent and the enjoyer of diverse activities;
by rubbing and purifying that very mind, like melting away a speck of frost with heat, you shall bring the jewel of the heart to dissolution through discernment and attain the supreme good.

Know that the mind alone is ignorance (*avidyā*), which creates the grand display of the entire world and its inhabitants. Through the power of its manifold web of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), it produces this [world].

Having understood that there is no difference between the terms "ignorance," "mind" (*citta*), "living being" (*jīva*), and "intellect" (*buddhi*), just as there is none between the words "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) and "sapling" (*taru*), [one realizes] that it is the mind alone.

Make it dissolve. But when the stainless solar orb of the mind has risen— which dispels the fierce darkness of all conceptual constructions— there is nothing, O Rāghava, that is not seen, nothing that is not attained, nothing that is not made one's own, nothing that is not relinquished, nothing that is not honored, and nothing that is not one's own.
That which does not belong to another— namely,
that everything is always everything— is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Thus, when there is awakening, the entire mass of phenomena becomes a single unity.

"Just as a collection of various unbaked clay vessels, when placed in water [dissolves], so too, upon the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, the end of all pleasure and pain is attained," thus it was declared by the Blessed One.
Rāma said:
"It has been stated by the Blessed One that when the activities of the mind are completely extinguished, the end of all pleasure and pain is reached."
"How then, O Great-Souled One, does the existence of this mind, whose nature is exceedingly fickle, come to be?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O Moon of the Raghu dynasty, listen to the method for the pacification of the mind."
Having understood this, you shall restrain the mind, just as a skilled horseman restrains a wild horse.
For it has been stated previously that, among all beings, there are three modes of origin for Brahman;
therein, first of all, the activity of the mind arises.
She becomes Brahmā;
having become composed of volition in the form of Brahmā, she perceives exactly what she wills,
and by that means she fashions this grand display of the worlds.

There, having remained for many eons with sluggish momentum, imagining the cycle of transmigration consisting of birth, death, pleasure, pain, delusion, and so forth, it dissolves of its own accord like a drop of frost exposed to the sun;
yet, by the power of a volition arising at the time of dissolution, it is born again in another form.
That too dissolves again;
again another arises, or that very same one arises— thus repeatedly following the course of saṃsāra,
it itself becomes tranquil and subsides.
In this manner, infinite millions of Brahmās have passed away and will pass away in this cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and in others;
there exist yet other infinite ones whose number is simply not known.
Within this perspective, [it is explained] how the individual soul (*jīva*), having come from the Lord (*īśvara*), is born and by what means it is liberated.
Listen:

the mental power of Brahmā, having arisen and supported itself upon the spatial power situated before it, follows the wind located therein and attains the state of dense volition (*ghanasaṅkalpatva*).

Then, having again attained the state of the five subtle elements (tanmātra) of the gross elements and becoming what is called the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), she becomes the subtle primordial nature (prakṛti);
through contact with the sky and wind, she assumes the form of frost and enters into rice plants and herbs,
or else she enters into the womb of living beings.
From that [the embryo] is born;
from that, the person (puruṣa) comes into being.
By that very person, as soon as he is born, the acquisition of knowledge must be undertaken starting from childhood.
The gurus must be followed;
then, in due course, a sense of wonder arises in a person just as it does in you.
In a man whose mental disposition is like yours, the discernment between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted arises.

When a person endowed with such discernment, whose ego has been integrated, abides in the foremost birth consisting of pure *sattva*, the sevenfold ground of yoga— which brings about the illumination of the mind— descends for his welfare in due order. This is the section titled "The Descent into a Birth of *Sattva*."
The one hundred and seventeenth canto.
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, what are the seven stages of yoga that bestow supernatural powers?"
"Tell me this in brief, O best among those who know all principles.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"The ground of ignorance consists of seven stages, and the ground of the knower likewise consists of seven stages."
There are countless other intermediate words between these two; yet these two creepers,
which are the great trees of Being and Consciousness, bear their own fruit by means of the juice of their own effort and sweetness, being firmly rooted at every step.
In that regard, listen to the sevenfold nature of the ground of ignorance;
thereafter, you shall hear of the sevenfold nature born from the ground of knowledge.
Liberation is abiding in one's true nature; its loss is the experience of "I-ness."
This has been declared in brief as the characteristic of knowing and not knowing that [reality].
For those who do not deviate from the true nature of pure consciousness alone,
there is no possibility of ignorance, because of the absence of the arising of attachment and aversion.
That which is the total loss of one's own nature and the immersion in perceived objects—

no delusion greater than this has ever existed, nor will there ever be. Indeed, that state which exists in the interval when the mind has moved from one object to another is [the gateway to liberation].
That state which is free from the mark of mental ideation is called abiding in one's own true nature (svarūpasthiti).
That state which is like the interior of a stone— where all volitional constructions (saṅkalpa) have completely subsided—
and which is liberated from dullness, sleep, and the like, is known as abiding in one's own true nature.

When the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*) and so forth have completely subsided, that non-inert state of mind which shines forth in the absence of differentiation is known as one's own true nature (*svarūpa*). Likewise, there is the seed-waking (*bījajāgrat*), the waking (*jāgrat*), and the great-waking (*mahājāgrat*).
"Waking-dream, dream-waking, dream-dream, and deep sleep"—thus is delusion sevenfold. Furthermore, these are interconnected with one another; hear now its characteristics under various names.
That which is the first volition of consciousness— indescribable, stainless,
and the receptacle for the future meanings of names such as "consciousness" (citi) and "living being" (jīva)—
exists in the form of a seed while awake; that is called "seed-waking" (bījajāgrat).
This is the ninefold state of cognition; now hear about the condition of waking.
When one who has thus been produced from the Supreme [Self] possesses a clear conviction that "this is I" and "this is mine," that is waking, prior to any mental construction.
"This is he," "I am this," "this is mine"— such a robust cognition arising from previous births is declared to be the "great waking state" (mahājāgrat),
which manifests even when unestablished or not yet established, sleepless, and not consisting of external objects.
That which is the kingdom of dreams for one who is awake is called "waking-dream" (jāgratsvapna).
Through various distinctions such as the double moon, silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, and the mirage, that state of waking, having reached the level of habitual practice, becomes manifold.

Even that which was seen by me for a short time is not real; for the conviction that arises at the end of sleep regarding an object experienced during the time of sleep is called a dream, whereas the great waking state remains established in the heart.
Because there has been no meeting for a long time, his great body is not fully blossomed.
A dream that has ascended to the state of waking has reached the stage of the "great waking" (mahājāgrat).
For that which occurs whether the body is wounded or unwounded is indeed considered the waking within a dream.

The state of the inert living being when the six conditions have been abandoned, which is rich with the awareness of future suffering, is called the state of deep sleep (*sauṣuptī gatī*). In that state, grass, clods of earth, stones, and so forth— [are all perceived as identical. // MU 3.117.22 //
All categories of objects— past, future, and present— are established;
O Rāghava, these seven states have been described by me as belonging to ignorance,
each of which here has a hundred branches of various manifestations.
The waking-dream, having long been firmly established, proceeds toward the state of waking itself;
it expands and unfolds through the differentiation of various objects.
Within its belly, moreover, exist the visions of the great waking state.

Within those as well, there are indeed others; thus the cycle of transmigration is dense. Even within these intermediate states of deep sleep and dreaming, because [the underlying ignorance] persists, this entire delusion remains as solid as a stone.

From one dream the world goes to another dream; from one delusion it goes to another delusion, just as a whirlpool falling downward moves from one body of water to another. Some cycles of existence persist as if they were waking states within a long dream.
Furthermore, some are repeated dreams, some are waking-dreams, and others are different;
I have called these the "ground of ignorance" (ajñānabhūmi) in seven steps, distinguished by various internal divisions of modifications and states.
Cross over this ground through your beautiful investigations, once the Self has been seen for yourself, pure with awakening.
The one hundred and eighteenth canto, titled "Description of the Stage of Ignorance," by Vasiṣṭha:
Listen, O sinless one, to this sevenfold stage of knowledge,
by knowing which you shall not sink again into the mire of delusion.
Proponents of various systems speak of the stages of yoga in many different ways.
But these very [stages] which bestow auspiciousness are certainly favored by me.
They know that awakening is knowledge; this consists of seven stages.
Liberation is said to be that which follows beyond the seven stages.
"Awakening to truth" (*satyāvabodha*) and "liberation" (*mokṣa*) are indeed synonymous terms.
Through the awakening to truth, this living being (*jīva*) does not sprout again in this world.
The first stage of knowledge (*jñānabhūmi*), called "the desire for virtue" (*śubhecchā*), has been thus described.
In this context, the second is *vicāraṇā*, the third is *tanumānasā*,
the fourth would be *sattvāpatti*, then the one named *asaṃsakti*; the sixth is *padārthābhāvanī*, and the seventh is known as *turyagā*.
Liberation stands at the end of these; in it, one no longer grieves.
Listen now to this definition of these stages:
"Am I truly deluded? I shall examine the scriptures and the company of the virtuous."

The desire preceded by dispassion is called "good desire" (śubhecchā) by the wise. That engagement in right conduct which is preceded by study of the scriptures, association with virtuous people, dispassion, and practice is termed "investigation" (vicāraṇā).
Through *vicāraṇā* (investigation) and *śubhecchā* (pure desire), there is non-attachment toward the objects of the senses; that state where,

due to the absence of even slight suffering, it is called *tanumānasā* (the thinning of the mind) is attained by virtue of the cessation of objective referents in the mind through the practice of the first three stages (*bhūmikā*).

When the pure self of *sattva* is established, it is declared to be the attainment of *sattva*. Through the practice of the four stages, by means of the fruit of non-attachment, that which is characterized by the wonder of established *sattva* is called "Non-attachment" (*asaṃsakti*).
Through the firm practice of the five stages (*bhūmikā-pañcaka*), by delighting in one's own self,
and by the non-contemplation of internal and external objects,
as well as by the long-term understanding of reality through effort directed by another;
The sixth stage of attainment is born, named the non-contemplation of objective entities (padārthābhāvanā).
Through long practice on the six stages, due to the non-perception of duality,
that state of abiding solely in one's own essential nature is to be known as the attainment that goes beyond the fourth (turyagā).

For this fourth state (turya) exists here among those liberated while living (jīvanmukta); beyond that is the state transcending the fourth (turyātīta), which pertains to those liberated after death (videhamukta). Indeed, those highly fortunate ones who have reached the seventh stage (bhūmikā)—
Those great-souled ones who delight in the Self have attained the supreme state;
liberated while living, they do not sink into the experience of pleasure and pain,
and they may or may not perform any action, whether worldly or noble.
Being awakened while standing by their side, they indeed practice the conduct that has come down through tradition in every action, like one who has woken from sleep and remains unhurt;
because they delight in the Self, no various worldly pleasures bring them any joy.
The activities of the world are like the beauty of forms and light to those who are fast asleep.
This sevenfold stage, however, is the domain of the wise alone;
it is not for animals, immobile beings, and the like, nor for the minds of barbarians and others.

Even those such as animals and barbarians who have attained this state of knowledge—whether they possess a body or are bodiless—are liberated; there is no doubt in this matter. For knowledge is the severing of the knot; when that occurs, there is liberation.
This [state] consists merely of the subsiding of cognitions such as that of water in a mirage.
But those who, having crossed over dense delusion, have not yet reached the purifying state,
remain in these stages, intent upon the attainment of their own true self.
Some belong to all stages; some belong to a single stage at the end;
some belong to three stages; some belong to five stages;
some belong to six stages; and some belong to one and a half stages.
Some reside in the four levels of existence; some are situated in two levels;
some partake of a portion of one level; some occupy three and a half levels;
some occupy four and a half levels; and others occupy five and a half levels.
Discerning men move through the worlds upon these stages, remaining within the specific states of the tenfold penetration of the heat of the household abode.
For those wise ones are like excellent kings; they conquer these ten states.
But the defeat of the armies of the world-elephants is treated as a mere blade of grass.
Indeed, those great ones who conquer on these stages are truly venerable; for they have conquered the enemies that are their senses.
They instantly attain that vast state where even the status of a sovereign emperor (*samrāṭ*) and a cosmic lord (*virāṭ*) is regarded as a mere blade of grass.
The one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Ground of Knowledge," by Vasiṣṭha.
Just as gold, through the consciousness of being a ring,
forgets its nature as gold and cries out in vain with a false sense of ego, "I am not gold," so it is with the self.
Rāma said:
"O Great Sage, O Lord, tell me correctly how the emergence of the consciousness of a ring arises from gold as being of the nature of 'I-ness'. Vasiṣṭha replied:
Only the existent can be said to undergo coming and going, never the non-existent;
for the state of being "I" and the state of being a ring are never truly absent from gold.
If it is said, "O gold, give up your state of being a ring and take on another," [the gold remains].
"That is given by one possessing waves; that exists, there is no doubt.
Rāma said: "If it is so, O Lord, let that be here; but what is this state of possessing waves?"
"By this very analysis of meaning, I shall know the form of Brahman.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāghava, if the formless nature of the unreal is being defined as having a form,"
Therefore, describe to me the qualities of the form of the son of a barren woman. This state of being a ring is a vain delusion, like an illusion whose nature is non-existent;
its very form is such that it is not seen when scrutinized.
In the water of a mirage, in the double moon, in the "I-not-I" (ahantā), in the circle of fire (alātacakra), and so forth—
the very nature of these things is such that, though being perceived, they are not apprehended as real.
He who perceives the form of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell perceives [the appearance] of silver.
It does not attain even the slightest atom, nor does it exist anywhere even in the most minute degree.
Through mere non-investigation, the unreal appears as if real,
just as the nature of silver appears in a mother-of-pearl shell, or water in the mirages of the desert.
The non-existence of that which does not exist becomes manifest when it is scrutinized;
yet when not scrutinized, it appears like an ocean of water in a mirage.
And that very non-existent thing performs a function and is stable.
For the ignorant, the encounter with the delusion of a *vetāla* leads only to death.
Just as nothing other than goldness exists in gold, apart from that single [nature], so too do the states of being a ring,
a bracelet, and so forth exist [in it], like oil and the like in sand.

In this world there is neither truth nor falsehood; whatever appears in a certain way, it performs its function exactly in that way, like a child’s perception of a yakṣa. Whether it be existent or non-existent, that which is firmly established in the heart [is what matters].
Each of those performs its own purposeful action, like poison performing the function of nectar.

For that very ignorance is indeed supreme illusion; it is this transmigratory existence which consists in the cultivation of a sense of "I-ness" toward that which is non-existent and without foundation.
O King, the state of being a worm and so forth exists [in the body], but the state of "I-ness" and so forth does not exist in the Self.
Precisely because of the absence of "I-ness," such is the case in that which is pure, peaceful, equal, and supreme;
therein there is no eternity whatsoever, nor is there any state of being Brahmā (Viriñca).
There is no such thing as being the cosmic egg, nor any state of being a god or the like;

there is no state of being another world, nor anywhere any state of being a creation; there is no state of being Meru, no state of being space, no state of being the mind, and no state of being a body.
There is no such thing as the nature of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), nor is there any causality anywhere;
there is no reckoning of seasons and times, nor the reality of existence and non-existence.
There is no "thou-ness," no "I-ness," no selfhood, no "that-ness," and no such things as being or non-being.
Nowhere is there any conception of difference, nor any coloring by existence or non-existence.
All is peaceful, without support, conscious, clear, eternal, and auspicious;
it is free from affliction, without appearance, nameless, and without cause.
Neither existent nor non-existent, neither middle nor end, neither all nor indeed everything;
ungraspable by mind or speech, it is both empty and non-empty, and perfectly eternal.
Rāma said:
"O Great Brahmā, all of this has now been understood by me; nevertheless, tell me further: what is being observed in this creation? Vasiṣṭha said:
Others say that the supreme state is established as "this-ness" (idantā) in this manner;
yet here, there is never any creation, nor any designation of creation whatsoever.
Like water within the waters of the great ocean, it is situated in the supreme state.

Like water, which is motionless despite its fluidity, the supreme state is free from movement. That state shines like the luminous Self, yet it does not shine; they know that while the shining of lights is manifest, the supreme is non-shining.
Just as water within the interior of the ocean manifests [in various forms] while excluding what is below and above,
so too this world appears as if manifold within the Supreme due to its consciousness;
yet, through its own consciousness, it perceives itself as if it were something other.
One awakens to what is called "creation," and through tranquility, one attains eternal peace.
But the firm conviction is that creation is merely a designation for the ultimate reality;
it neither exists nor does it not exist, just as space within space.
Due to the existence of consciousness, there is the manifestation of creation; due to the absence of consciousness, there is the dissolution of creation.
Just as the delusion of a bracelet exists within gold, so too does the supreme, utterly tranquil state exist within the Supreme.
When the cessation of the activity of consciousness occurs, the existent creation itself attains the state of non-creation.
Non-existence attains existence through itself when self-awareness arises.
Know that awareness is the agitation consisting of the emergence of the sense of "I" and the creation [of the world];
know that non-awareness is the supreme state of peace, which is not inert.
By this, there is no creation; this world is not manifold, for the one Self is of the nature of Śiva.
It is like an army made of clay by a craftsman through the work of his hands.
This [Self] is full, without beginning, infinite, and without rising.
When full, it remains full even through further fillings; it abides as it was from the very beginning.
