That which is perceived here as creation is Brahman situated within Brahman—space resting in space, the peaceful in the peaceful, the auspicious in the auspicious.
Just as a city reflected in a mirror appears both distant and not distant within the city and the people, so too does the Lord appear as both that and its opposite;
the entire universe, though always non-existent, arises as if existent, and though existent, it is eternally transcended.
Because it appears as something real through its manifestation, yet consists of non-existence because it lacks substantial reality;
in this creation— which resembles a city in a mirror, shines like water in a mirage, and appears as the delusion of two moons— what true reality can there be?
Just as a city appears in the sky due to the scattering of magical powder,
so does the cycle of existence appear— both substantial and insubstantial— within consciousness.
As long as ignorance has not been forcibly burnt away, root and branch, by the fire of inquiry like a withered creeper, [so long does it persist].
Dense with the spreading of its branches, it thus produces various dense forests of pleasure and pain.
The One Hundred and Twentieth Chapter, titled "Instruction on Liberation.
The One Hundred and Twenty-first Chapter.
Vasiṣṭha:
O Rāghava, listen to what the "I-ness" of ignorance—fashioned falsely like a golden ring—is like when it is on the verge of destruction. MU 3.120.1
When King Lavaṇa saw that wandering in such a manner,
he set out for that great forest on the second day;
I remember that very same misery which I experienced in that wilderness.
"Because it resides within the mirror of the mind, it may sometimes be attained," he decided.
Having thus resolved with his ministers, he set out for the Deccan;
once again, for the sake of world conquest, he reached the Vindhya mountain range.
Out of curiosity, she wandered over the entire coastal land of the eastern, southern, and western great oceans, like the sun traversing the path of the sky.
Then, in one region, she beheld her [own reflection] standing before her as if on a wall.
He beheld that formidable forest, like the earth of the world beyond. Wandering everywhere, he saw all those various occurrences;
having seen them and understood them, he was filled with wonder.
Having recognized those hunters born of the Pukkasa caste before him,
he wandered about again in great agitation, his mind overwhelmed with wonder.
Then, at the edge of the great forest, he reached a place grey with smoke.
He went to that very village where he had previously lived as a prosperous Pukkasa.
There he saw various people, various women, small huts, those groves, reservoirs of water, and those riverbanks.
And she described that untimely destruction— those trees, those enclosures, and likewise those very landscapes marked by that singular event—
to other elderly women who were overcome with grief and had tearful eyes.
O friend, among friends there are countless sorrows for those whose kinsmen have perished in the wilderness of untimely death.

There, in that region scorched by the fierce thunderbolts of drought, this old woman— her eyes overflowing with blazing tears, her body covered by a tattered garment, her breasts withered and her limbs emaciated— stands weeping, utterly exhausted.

"Alas, my son! You whose every limb was once covered with sons, and whose body was now worn out by three days without food—when the dog tore away your skin from your aged frame, how and where were those vital breaths of yours released?
[It is like] the support of a palm tree for a fine red fruit resting between teeth moistened by the rain."
I remember you, who laughed with delight before your own wife for the sake of a garland of *guñjā* berries.
When shall I ever again see my son’s terrifying leaps and bounds as he runs through the thickets of *kadamba*, *jambīra*, cloves, and *guñjā* bushes, while the wild jackals crouch and dart within?

Those graceful charms of betel-chewing women are not present upon the faces of those who have consumed the flesh from the mouth of their son, whose chin is as dark as the *tamāla* tree. Even the daughter, equal to the Yamunā river, has been led away by her husband Yama to his destination.
Like a *tamāla* creeper with its clusters of flowers by a forest-dwelling breeze;

Alas, my daughter, you who wear necklaces of *guñjā* berries, whose limbs are graced by full and swelling breasts, whose complexion is like dark collyrium shimmering in the wind— where now are you, amidst the leafy garments of the forest and the cloud-like lips that have not yet appeared?
"Alas, O Prince, as lovely as the moon! Having abandoned those playful women of the inner apartments, you have gone to find delight with my daughter; yet even she has not attained stability for you.
Amidst the surging waves of the river of worldly existence, you are mocked by the play of ritual actions."
What indeed was not rendered trivial by that king, since he was united with a Pukkasa maiden? She,
whose eyes were like those of a startled deer, and he, whose prowess was like that of a satiated tiger—
both went to destruction in a single step, just as hope perishes along with its object, or as gold [is lost] with the [melting] crucible.
I am one whose lord has died, I am one whose children have perished, I have gone to a wretched land, and I am fallen into misfortune;

I am born of an ill birth, I am in great distress, and I am myself visibly raised up by calamity. O Mind, [behold] my wife, who is sinking from hunger and whose source of livelihood consists of the insults of the lowly.
Driven by the force of grief, whose course is irresistible, women are always without a protector when deprived of their sole refuge.

For one who is tormented by fate, bereft of kinsmen, deluded, and established upon the great ground of mental anguish, that which is life is death; and that which would be death is the supreme form of life.

"For one who is separated from his people and living in a foreign land, endless sorrows arise, like the grass on a mountain during the rains, crowded with thousands of branches and sap. While she was speaking thus, the king comforted that woman— the elder wife of his own household— with the help of his female attendants.
He asked: "What happened here? Who are you, and who is your daughter? And who is your husband?
Then, with eyes full of tears, she replied: "This village is named Pukkasaghoṣa;
here lived my husband, a Pukkasa, and he had one daughter who was like the moon."

By the turn of fate, that wretched woman found her husband, who resembled the moon, arrived here as a king by the power of destiny; like a solitary female camel finding a broken jar of honey in a desolate forest, she obtained him.
Having enjoyed pleasures with him for a very long time, she gave birth to daughters and sons.
In this hollow of the forest, surrounded by trees, the gourd vine has grown large;
thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first canto, titled "The Lamentation of Caṇḍālī."
Caṇḍālī said:
"Then, after some time, O Lord of Men, there occurred in this village a terrifying suffering of drought that broke the spirit of the people."
Because of this great suffering, all those people from the village departed and went far away; they have met their death there.
Therefore, O Lord, we here are bereft and empty, sharing only in misery.
"Weep for those who are to be pitied; our eyes are choked with tears.
Having heard this from the mouths of the women, the king was struck with amazement;
looking at the faces of his ministers, he became as if fixed in a painting.
He reflected further upon that unsurpassed marvel;
becoming exceedingly filled with wonder, he questioned them again and again. [He asked: "By what appropriate mental honors of theirs does the destruction of suffering occur?"
Pierced by compassion and having perceived the high and low states of the world,
he remained there for a long time, reflecting upon the courses of destiny; then,
honored by the citizens, he returned to the city and entered it.
In the morning, in that assembly hall, the king asked me, filled with wonder:
"O Sage, how is it that this dream has become manifest?
To him, I explained the matter exactly as it was, through various arguments, in such a manner.
Doubt, driven from the heart like a cloud by the wind—
this great ignorance, O Rāghava, which causes delusion,
quickly leads the non-existent to the state of existence and the existent to the state of non-existence.
Rāma:
How can you speak thus, O Brahmin? A dream has attained the state of reality! This matter, like a burden of delusion, does not sit lightly upon my mind.
Vasiṣṭha: All this, O Rāghava, is indeed possible within ignorance,
just as the appearance of cloth in jars is seen in dreams, delusions, and the like.
The distant appears near, like a mountain within a mirror;
for a youth, the long night seems to pass quickly, as if it were his beloved.
Just as one's own death occurs in a dream despite being impossible [in reality], so too do these things appear.
The unreal arises as if real, like the movement of objects in the sky within dreams. That which is perfectly stable wavers violently during an illusion, like the upheaval of the earth;
the weak gains strength, like a mind agitated by intoxication.
The mind, enveloped by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), intensely contemplates whatever it may be;
that very thing it immediately experiences accordingly—neither existent nor non-existent.
At the very moment that false ignorance (*avidyā*), consisting of the sense of "I" and so forth, has arisen, [it perceives this].
At that very moment, the beginningless, middleless, and endless nature of delusion is proclaimed;
by the power of appearance alone, everything revolves:
a single moment becomes an eon, and an eon becomes a single moment.
To what state would a being with a perverted mind not fall?
By the power of its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the deer itself assumes the nature of a lion.
Poison, delusion, intoxication, ignorance, infatuation, egoism, and the like are all the same.

All causes for the attainment of results arise from the perversion of the mind. Like the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit, great undertakings and worldly transactions mutually enter into one another by the power of mental impressions (*vāsanā*).
Whatever occurred previously in the king Lavaṇa’s settlement—
whether good or bad— that has appeared in his mind;
just as the mind forgets even an extensive action once performed, [so too does he forget].
Likewise, one certainly remembers even that which was done as not done;
for indeed, one perceives in a dream, "I have not eaten," or "I have eaten," and the journey to another land, though unaccomplished, is understood.
Such is this worldly transaction of the village of the Vindhya Pukkasa,
appearing as it does to him like a former narrative in a dream;
or rather, it is like the delusion of a dream seen by Lavaṇa.
That very consciousness of the Vindhya-pukkasa reached the mind of the king;
the consciousness of the Vindhya-pukkasa ascended into the mind of the monarch,
just as the speech, name, and face of many may be identical.
Likewise, even in a dream, there is time, space, and action;
yet, insofar as it pertains to worldly convention, its existence consists in its manifestation.
The existence of all things is nothing other than their being perceived.
Within consciousness, the manifold succession of creation appears,
situated in the past, present, and future, just as a tree exists within the seed of a tree.
Its existence and non-existence are established as being neither existent nor non-existent.
For that which is real is indeed real because of consciousness; it is not composed of existence through a lack of consciousness.
Ignorance does not exist at all, just as oil and the like do not exist in sand.
What could "bitterness" be for gold? It would be something other than gold if it existed apart from its nature as gold.
A connection between ignorance and the pure self is not logically possible.
That connection which exists between similar things is manifest and provides experience;
therefore, a connection such as that between lacquer and wood does not exist between two equals.

When all this is composed of the ultimate reality (paramārtha), consisting solely of a single locus and not having the nature of mutual experience, then stones and other such things are perceived by consciousness as equal,
by virtue of their connection [to that reality].
When all things existing in the world consist of pure consciousness and pure existence,
then these shine forth in mutual relation while established in their own self-experience;
for a continuous connection between dissimilar things is not possible.
Without mutual connection, there can be no reciprocal experience;
for a similar object, having attained oneness with another similar thing in an instant,
sufficiently expands its single form through that very oneness, and not otherwise.
When consciousness (cit) is joined with that which has a visible form, it arises as sentience;
when the insentient (jaḍa) is joined with the insentient, it becomes solidly insentient.
And a unity between the conscious and the insentient can never occur anywhere, because of their essential difference.
If both the insentient (*cijjaḍa*) were to exist together in one place, they would never merge;
for because it consists of consciousness (*cinmaya*), there is no perception of the trace of consciousness (*cidāleha*) by means of the trace of consciousness.
Indeed, these various distinctions such as wood and stone do not possess the nature of consciousness.
For an object is experienced through another object by means of transformation;
it is like the tongue [experiencing] taste, and that [tongue] is unstable due to the arising of its own kind.
Know that identity is the relationship; there is no connection between the insubstantial and the substantial.
Therefore, because of that [consciousness], a stone or similar object is not considered to be insentient; rather,
it is consciousness itself that has assumed the form of a stone, a wall, or the like, and having merged with consciousness,
attained a state of oneness, produces the delusion of the seer, the seen, and so forth.
When wood, stone, and all else are entirely composed of the ultimate reality (paramārtha),
they are perceived as objects of sight, internally connected with that very self;
thus everything, rich in every variety, is spread out as if infinite.
"O best among those who know reality, know that this entire universe is nothing but pure Being (*sanmātra*).

Even though it is filled with the unreal universe and its hundreds of delusions regarding the characteristics of the world, O dear one, the wonder of Consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*) remains unfilled by anything whatsoever."
Just as the cities of human imagination do not see one another,
so too the creations existing within consciousness do not serve to perceive space or time;
for the state of being a creation is the perception of duality, which arises from the delusion of "I-ness" and so forth.
Just as there is the delusion of bracelets and the like upon the relinquishment of the cognition of gold,
so too the delusion of bracelets and the like occurs within the gold due to the presence of spatial distinctions and so forth.
But for one who is encompassed by Your vision, no further ignorance exists apart [from that].

Just as the great variety of bracelets and other ornaments is in truth the one stainless Brahman, so too this creation, due to its identity with consciousness, is nothing but Being; it is entirely non-existent [as a separate reality]. Like an army composed of clay is nothing but clay despite its variegated appearance, so this world is nothing but pure Being.

Water is one, yet it appears as waves and the like; wood is one, yet it appears as carved figures; clay alone is one, yet it appears as jars and the like; Brahman is one, yet it is the delusion of the three worlds.
Among the relationship between the seer and the seen, that which is the true nature of the seer—
This supreme state is devoid of the seer, the seeing, and the seen. When the mind has moved from one object to another, that form which exists in the interval of the consciousness—
consisting of non-inert awareness and reflection— become absorbed in that forever.
Become forever absorbed in that eternal form of yours which is neither waking nor dreaming nor sleeping, which is both insentient and yet not inert;
for that which is the heart of a stone is indeed inertness alone.
Whether unagitated or agitated, O Rāghava, become one with that [reality].
Nothing whatsoever arises here nor does anything dissolve;
whether unagitated or agitated, remain established in yourself as you please.
The person does not desire nor does he hate anything whatsoever within the body at any time;

remaining established in yourself, free from anxiety, you should simply attend to the functions of the body, just as you remain indifferent toward the affairs of a village that may arise in the future.
Do not remain within the fluctuations of the mind, having thus attained its true nature.
Just as a person from another land, just as a piece of wood, and just as a stone—
view the mind in that very way, being indeed without-mind, which is the true nature of the self.
Just as there is no water in a stone, and just as there is no fire in water, so too the mind does not exist within its own self; how then could it exist in the Supreme Self?
Since nothing whatsoever is perceived when examined, whatever is done anywhere by it [is likewise non-existent].
Thinking, "That which has been done is not [done]," become one who transcends the mind.
If you follow the mind, which is ultimately not your self,
why do you not follow a barbarian living on the frontier?
Disregarding it continuously from afar, remain at ease and free from anxiety, like a block of wood rendered inert by mud; [think]:
"My mind has truly ceased to exist; it is as if dead this very day."
Become resolute and as immovable as a stone statue.
Since our mind does not exist during contemplation, you are in reality devoid of it;
so why do you torment yourself with what is useless for the sake of that which is [already] useless?
For those of feeble intellect who have been utterly subdued by the non-existent yakṣa of the mind, a thunderbolt has arisen from the moon.
Abandoning the mind far behind, remain firm as you truly are.
Be liberated through meditation and endowed with the highest reasoning.
Fie upon those who follow after non-existence, whose minds take the form of non-being,
and for whom time is spent solely in the activities of wandering through forests in the sky!
With a mind completely dissolved, O high-souled one, become one whose self is stainless and who has reached the further shore of existence.
Though investigated for a very long time, not even the slightest impurity was found within the self by the self through the mind.
This is the chapter titled "The Demonstration of the Non-existence of the Mind."
The one hundred and twenty-second canto. Vasiṣṭha:
From the very moment of birth, a person, even with only slightly blossomed intellect, ought to be intent upon the company of the virtuous.
This torrent of the river of ignorance, falling in an unceasing flow, cannot be crossed except through contact with the scriptures on tranquility and with virtuous people.
Consequently, in a person possessed of discernment, the inquiry into what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted arises.
By that means, he arrives at the stage of discernment called "the desire for the auspicious.

Then, through the power of discernment, by means of investigation and right knowledge, as he abandons improper latent impressions (*vāsanā*), his mind attains attenuation from the latent impressions of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
By that, he has descended to the stage of discernment called *tanumānasī*.
At the very moment the right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) arises for the yogin, there is the attainment of *sattva*;
when, through the power of that [knowledge], the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have reached attenuation, then he is said to be "unattached."
"He is not bound by the fruit of karma.
Now, for that long he practices the thinning of mental cultivation toward the unreal,
even while acting and even while engaging in worldly transactions, though remaining amidst the unreal entities of saṃsāra.
Because the mind has been stilled within its own self through the power of practice, even while acting upon an external object, he does not act;
even while seeing, he does not see, nor does he take up that very object.
Therefore, he meditates intensely.

And because his latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are attenuated, he performs his duties merely like one who is half-asleep and half-awake, rather than with a cultivated mind. Thus, having ascended to the stage of yoga called "non-cultivation" (*abhāvanī*), with his mind withdrawn within, he practices for several years until,
even while acting in every respect, he abandons the mental cultivation of external objects.
He becomes the self of the fourth state (*turyātman*);
therefore, he is called "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*).
He does not rejoice in what is attained, nor does he grieve for what is not attained.
Free from all doubt, he simply continues with what has been attained.
O Rāghava, you too have known that which is to be known in its entirety;
I believe that, compared to all other tasks, your latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have become attenuated.

Whether your activity transcends the body or you remain within the body, do not fall into grief or joy; you are the Self, free from all affliction. While you, the Self, abide—pure, omnipresent, and eternally risen—[how can there be such fluctuations?]
Whence, O Rāma, are suffering and pleasure? Whence are death and birth?
Why do you, though having no kinsmen, grieve for the sorrows of your relatives? For while this [Self] stands alone and without a second, what indeed are kinsmen to the Self?
Only a mere accumulation of the atoms of the body is perceived;
because it undergoes change in place and time, the Self neither arises nor perishes. Why do you grieve, saying "I am perishing," when [the Self] is indestructible?
In the pure Self, which is beyond the power of death, how could there be destruction?
Just as the space within a jar is not destroyed when the jar is reduced to shards,
so too you do not perish when this body is destroyed.

Just as when a mirage-river has dried up, the heat [of the sun] does not perish, so too when the body is destroyed, the Self does not perish. Why does this desire arise in you? This internal delusion is purposeless.

Being non-dual, what second entity could the Self possibly desire? O Rāghava, in this world there is nothing whatsoever— whether audible, tangible, visible, delightful, or olfactory— that exists apart from the Self.

O Rāghava, all these powers reside entirely within that very Self, which possesses all power; they abide in the pervasive Manifested One like voidnesses in space. This triple world has arisen from the mind within the belly of the Woman of the Three Worlds.
In this world, the people have been deluded by a threefold process;
yet when the pacification of the mind— known as the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā)—
and that which is called the destruction of karma are accomplished, this illusion utterly perishes.
In this formidable water-wheel of saṃsāra, there is a firm, mechanical rope;
O Rāghava, cut that rope of latent impressions (vāsanā) with effort.
As long as it remains unrecognized, it bestows great delusion.
But when fully understood, she is called the Infinite, bestowing bliss and leading to Brahman.
Having come from Brahman and having enjoyed the cycle of existence here as a sport,
she remembers Brahman once more and dissolves back into Brahman alone.

O Rāghava, from Śiva— who is formless, immeasurable, and free from affliction— all beings have arisen, like objects made manifest from light. Just as a multitude of lines appears on a leaf, or a network of ripples in water;
Just as bracelets and the like exist in gold, and just as heat and the like exist in fire,
so indeed this triple world consists of both that [Brahman] and what is not that;
it is situated in that very [Brahman], born from that, and is indeed nothing other than that.
This very Self of all beings is called Brahman;
when it is known, the world is known, and when it is unknown, it remains unknown.
For the sake of the conventional usage of the scriptures, [the following is said] regarding this one whose form is expanded:

The names "consciousness" (cit), "Brahman," and "Self" (ātman) have been fashioned by those of perfected minds. Indeed, that pure experience which arises when the sense objects and senses are in contact, being free from joy and resentment— that is this very Self, the imperishable consciousness.
In that Self of consciousness, which is clearer than space itself,
the world is reflected as if separate within its own expansion;
yet the Buddhas recognize greed, delusion, and the like as enemies because they are distinct from it.
Then, at that very moment, those Buddhas proceed without any distinction from him. For you, who are indeed bodiless and consist of non-conceptual consciousness,
how could delusion— known as shame, fear, and despondency— have arisen?
O you of poor intellect, why are you, like a fool, overwhelmed by vain conceptualizations— such as shame and other defects born of the body— which are themselves unreal?
For how can there be any fragmentation of that which is of the nature of indivisible consciousness when the body undergoes fragmentation?
Even for one who lacks right vision, there is no destruction; how much less so for one of sound intellect?
O Rāma, that which exists even on the path of the sun, which is not contradicted by scripture or tradition—that is to be known as the *cit* (the conscious self), the *puruṣa*, and not the body.

Whether a body exists or not, O Rāma, this person—whether conscious or unconscious—abides throughout the three worlds; even when the body is destroyed, he does not perish. As for these various sufferings that you perceive, [they do not affect him].
All those [qualities] belong to the body, not to the ungraspable self which is consciousness (*cidātman*).
Since it has transcended the path of the mind and remains as if empty,
how indeed could that consciousness be affected by sorrows or joys?
Therefore, from this distinguished cage of a body, the self, which is consciousness,
departs with its habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), just as a bee leaves a lotus for the sky.
If the reality of the self were non-existent, then [it would not depart] from this cage of a body.
When something is lost, what indeed is lost that you should grieve for it, O Rāma? Contemplate the truth; do not experience delusion.
For the Self, which is free from desire and of faultless nature, there are no desires whatsoever.
In the conscious Self— which is the witness, impartial, pure, and free from conceptual construction—

the worlds appear of their own accord, like rays within a precious gem. Just as there is a connection between a mirror and a reflection even though the mirror has no desire [to reflect], so it is here.
Just as this [mirror] possesses the power of its own nature, so too does this [consciousness] possess the power of both consciousness and the world.
Just as duality and unity are established between a mirror and its reflection,
so too here are difference and non-difference established between the Self and the world.

Just as activity arises on earth by the mere proximity of the sun, so too is this world produced by the mere existence of consciousness. O Rāma, when the perception of it as a solid mass has ceased, such is the state of the world.
This has become like space even within your minds.
Just as the radiance of a lamp exists by its very nature through mere existence,
so too does this activity of the world arise from the inherent nature of the reality of consciousness (*cittattva*).
Formerly, the mind arose from the reality of the Supreme Self, and by it this world was spread out as a web of its own conceptual constructions;
just as emptiness within the stainless sky appears as a blue expanse, delightful with beautiful creepers.
But when the mind has dissolved through the destruction of volitional constructs, the mists of delusion regarding saṃsāra vanish.
When the internal [intellect] is established in pure consciousness alone—which is one, unborn, primordial, and infinite—it shines forth as clear as the autumnal sky.

Then, the mind, whose nature is action, first arises from volition; having assumed the form of the lotus-born [Brahmā], it expands this infinite and manifold world, just as a deluded child imagines the body of a ghost.
Unreal, yet appearing as if real, it is first perceived, then it comes into being, and then it dissolves again;
the mind itself, with its expansive and throbbing form, is like a succession of circles of waves in the great ocean.
The Chapter titled "The Description of Ultimate Reality."
The one hundred and twenty-third canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"Know this much for now: that which stands as the visible world is thus established."
"I" and so forth—formless, mere delusion, consisting of unreality;
without an agent and without a body, like a painting arisen in the sky; without a seer, yet accompanied by experience, it is a dream-vision occurring even in the absence of sleep. (MU 3.123.1–2)
The manifestation of the future city appeared like a painting come to life;
it shone with the glow of a forest fire and was situated like a whirlpool in the water.
Though possessing a real form, it was empty within, like solar radiance in the sky.
Like a net of jewel-light seen in the sky, it is without a physical basis; like a city of one's imagination, it is maturely experienced yet composed of unreality;
consisting of the manifestation of the meaning of a story, it neither exists nor is it situated anywhere.
Though devoid of essence, it appears to have an exceeding internal essence; like a mountain in a dream, it is a mere emptiness, radiant with form like the elemental ether,
standing before one like an autumn cloud— imperceptible in its destruction yet subject to decay.
Like a color in the expanse of the sky, it appears while being devoid of substance;

it has the form of dalliance with a woman in a dream, yet it is devoid of any real object. Like a garden of flowers in full bloom created by magic, it possesses the appearance of vitality but is actually sapless.
It was like light devoid of brilliance, like a painted sun or fire;
it was experienced as unreal and unsubstantial, like a kingdom of the mind,
or like a pond of variegated lotuses bereft of beauty and fragrance.
In emptiness, it shines forth with various colors and the nature of forms;
yet in the ultimate sense, it is dried up by the fragile sprouts of the elements,
spread out, inert, essence-less, and as brilliant as the trunk of a plantain tree.
Spread out like a circle of darkness visible to wide-open eyes,
it was utterly devoid of form, yet remained as if directly perceived;
vast like a bubble on the water, it was empty within, its body quivering.
Consisting of essence yet having a false essence, with its arising and decay uninterrupted;
spreading like mist, though grasped it is nothing at all;
inert, the locus of emptiness, empty—[this world] is for some like an atom.
"It is established that there exists something consisting of the unreal;
it is empty and non-existent, yet when being grasped, it appears in a form that is not real, like a sword risen from its scabbard.
Rāma said:
At the end of a great aeon (*mahākalpa*), the visible world remains like a sprout within a seed;
it arises again from that very source in the supreme state—tell me, what is this?
Those who understand thus—are they ignorant or are they knowers of reality? This is clear.
"O Blessed One, speak as it truly is for the sake of pacifying all doubts.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"This visible world exists within the Great Destruction like a sprout within a seed."
If one says that the other person’s ignorance is due to extreme childhood, [we ask]:
in the case of touch, what is unconnected? How can this be unreal?
This is a perverted cognition produced by the folly of both the speaker and the listener.
Listen now, for how indeed this deluded notion— that the world existed like a sprout at the time of the seed— is merely the senseless prattle of the ignorant.
For the seed itself would have to be visible, falling within the range of the mind and the other senses.
In the case of a banyan seed, grain, and so forth, the production of a sprout is observed; however,
how could that which transcends the six senses including the mind, and which is even more subtle than the ether,
be capable of being the self-arisen seed of the world?

How and in what manner can there be the state of being a seed for the Supreme Self, who is subtler than even space, beyond the reach of all senses, and yet exists as the Real? For that which is subtle appears as unreal to those who do not perceive it.
What kind of seed-nature could exist there? In the absence of a seed, how can there be a sprout?
Even from the void of the sky, in that supreme state which is pure and empty, how could the world, Mount Meru, the oceans, the heavens, and so forth exist?
How can that which is nothing whatsoever be something? What substance could exist there within that which is insubstantial? If it does exist there, why is it not perceived while being present?
Or else, how could something belonging to the nature of "nothingness" come into being, or from where could it arise?
Where, from what, and when could a mountain arise from the space within a jar, which is empty by nature?
How can anything exist in its opposite, as [darkness exists] in light or [heat] in shade?
How can darkness exist in the sun, and how can fire exist in ice?
How could Mount Meru reside within an atom? How could anything exist in that which is formless?
Where could there be a unity between that which has such a nature and that which does not, like shadow and sunlight?
It is logical that the sprout exists within the acorn and the like, for they possess form.
It is illogical to claim that the world exists as something of great magnitude within that which is formless.

Furthermore, that which is invisible to the intellect and all the powers of the senses—whether in another place or in another person—is simply non-existent; when there is no cognition of such a thing, it is called "nothing at all."
He whose understanding is utterly deluded claims that the effect has attained the state of being its cause;
by what means, indeed, could such an effect arise from that [cause] through its own multitudes of causes in the form of auxiliary factors?
Having cast far away this notion of the relation between cause and effect imagined by the dull-witted, [one should understand the truth].
Know that this very world, which is truth and devoid of beginning or middle, is precisely what remains so.
The one hundred twenty-fourth canto, titled "The Refutation of the Produced and the Producer."
Vasiṣṭha said: Now, O best among those who know what is to be known, I shall speak regarding this acceptance [of the truth]:
in the stainless, great space of consciousness, which transcends all mental constructions.
If that sprout of the world exists there [in the beginning], then tell me: by what auxiliary causes does it arise?
Or, in the absence of auxiliary causes, how can there be the emergence of the sprout?
And a barren woman’s daughter has never been seen here by anyone at any time.
Furthermore, that which was declared to exist in the absence of auxiliary causes—
the Self— is the very root cause, remaining thus within its own nature.
At the beginning of creation, Brahman alone abides within itself in the form of creation;
since it remains as it is, without form, where is there any sequence of produced and producer? Or else, how could earth and the other elements come from somewhere else and perform this act?
Its status as a cooperative cause (*sahakārikāraṇatva*) is refuted here by the same arguments as before.
Therefore, the statement that "the world remains quiescent [in its cause] and yet expands forth without those cooperative causes" belongs to a fool, not to a wise man.
Therefore, O Rāma, this world never existed, does not exist, and will not exist;
it is merely the clear space of consciousness that shines forth in this manner within itself.
When the absolute non-existence of this world is realized, [it is seen as such].
Then, O Rāma, this entire world is truly Brahman; it is not otherwise.
For that which subsides through prior destruction, mutual non-existence, and so forth, remains unappeased within the mind, since it does not truly subside at all.
Therefore, apart from the absolute non-existence of the world as it is perceived in every respect,
there is no other means for the total destruction of suffering.
This awareness of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) that "the world and so forth exist" [is what must be transcended].
This is that very "I," as well as this form, light, mind, and its parts;
this sun and so forth, the earth and so forth, and likewise this year and so forth;
this is the eon and this is the moment, and these two are death and birth.
This is the agitation at the end of a kalpa; this is the great dissolution at the end of a kalpa.
This is the commencement of creation; this is the sequence of existence and non-existence.
These are hundreds of thousands of kalpas; these are millions of cosmic eggs.
These are the multitudes of Brahmās and Indras; these are the powers of Viṣṇu and the others.
These have evolved, and these have come forth once again.
These are the networks of celestial abodes; these are the divisions of space, time, and measure.
The great consciousness is the supreme space, unobstructed and infinite;
it shines forth by itself as tranquil, just as it has always existed.
These [appearances] are but a thousandth part of a minute atom of the light of that great consciousness.
Being its very nature, they remain within; they neither come nor go.
That internal wonder which is spontaneously projected by consciousness appears as this manifestation of creation—a form of light that possesses no foundation.
They do not arise nor do they perish; they do not come nor do they go.
Like inscriptions within a great rock, these creations remain immovable, flashing forth by themselves within the stainless Self.
Like portions of space within the sky, they are formless within that which is formless;
like the fluidity of water, like the movements of the wind,
like whirlpools in the ocean, or like the qualities belonging to one who possesses them.
This entire world exists as a single mass of consciousness, established in this manner—
endless, peaceful, and pervasive, including its beginning, rise, and setting.
In the absence of causes such as auxiliary factors, the world is emptiness.
And that "the Self-existent One is born"— this, they say, is the blustering of a madman.
He whose stain of the subtle parts of all objects has been stilled, who has cast off the entire bed of conceptual construction,
who has long since dispelled the deep sleep of ignorance, who is fearless of existence, and who adorns the earth— he is truly awakened.
The one hundred and twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Presentation of the Seed of Memory," [spoken by] Rāma:

At the beginning of creation after the great dissolution, this first Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) is born as the very essence of memory; from that, the world likewise arises as the essence of memory. Vasiṣṭha said:
O scion of the Raghus, at the beginning of creation following the great dissolution,
this very first Prajāpati exists initially as the self of memory alone;
and because the world consists of his volition, it likewise becomes this world of memory.

"The city of Saṅkalpa belonging to the former Prajāpati shines as if it were established"— even though this is so, O Rāma, that stability of the former Prajāpati is not possible at all, just like a great tree in the sky.
Rāma:
O Brahmin, how could it be that memory of the past does not exist at the beginning of creation?
How is it that prior memory is destroyed by the delusions of the great dissolution?
Vasiṣṭha said:
O wise one, prior to the great dissolution, Brahmā and the others of old indeed attained nirvāṇa; they necessarily reached the state of Brahman.
Who is the rememberer of that prior memory? Therefore, O observer of noble vows, tell me:
since the rememberer has attained liberation, how could that memory remain without a root?
Thus, in the absence of a rememberer, how could that memory arise, and by what means?

For indeed, in the great aeon (*mahākalpa*), all beings are destined for liberation alone. That memory which arises spontaneously within the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoman*)—whether regarding what has been experienced or not experienced—is the mature splendor of the world; for in the absence of the visible, there is only the radiance of consciousness.
It is the radiance of consciousness alone that shines, pure and illuminating without beginning or end;
that which exists as this "world" and as the "Self-existent" (Svayambhū) is that very radiance of Brahman, established from time immemorial as its own innate manifestation.
That subtle body is Virāj, whose form is the universe.
Within a single atom, this world shines forth together with the three realms,
endowed with the succession of space, time, action, substance, day, and night.
Then, within each atom,
there likewise shines that very same form, radiant in appearance and similarly surrounded by mountain ranges;
even there, such a form extends in this way toward every atom.
"The visible world appears as light, my dear; this is not real.
Thus, for one who possesses right vision or false vision, there is no end anywhere.
But for this [right vision], O sinless one, it has dawned whether toward the awakened or the unawakened.
To one who has awakened, this is indeed only Brahman—solely peaceful and immutable;
but to one who has not awakened, it appears as a radiant duality accompanied by the worlds.
Just as this radiant world shines forth, expanded from the cosmic egg, so it is perceived.

Likewise, thousands of millions of others shine within every single atom; just as there is a figurine inside a pillar, and a figurine within its limbs, and a figurine within that figurine’s limb, so too is the figurine of the three worlds.
Just as atoms on a mountain are neither distinct nor countable,
so too are the atoms of the three worlds upon the vast Mount Meru of Brahman.
Even the minute atoms within the multitude of rays of the sun could be counted.
The atoms of the three worlds, which have no beginning or end, exist within the sun of consciousness;
just as atoms move within the rays of the sun, within water, and within dust,
so do the atoms of the three worlds move within the sky of consciousness.
Just as this elemental space consists of the mere experience of emptiness,
so too this space of consciousness consists of the mere experience of creation. However,
when creation is perceived as the referent of the word "creation," it leads one downward.
He is the Buddha, fully capable of attaining the highest good by virtue of being the referent of the word *brahman*.
The conscious self (*vijñānātman*) is the ruler, the seed of the universe, the primordial *brahman* itself, which is its own mere space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*).
Understand that whatever has arisen from that is to be known as nothing other than that very thing—merely the awakening of awareness within the internal consciousness.
The one hundred and twenty-sixth canto, titled "The Description of the Infinite World," by Vasiṣṭha.
The ocean of existence is crossed by means of this bridge, which is the restraint of the collection of the senses;
it cannot be crossed by any other action whatsoever in this world.
One who possesses discernment and has conquered the senses through the study of the scriptures and the practice of the company of the virtuous—

One realizes the absolute non-existence of this flood of perceptible objects. O best of embodied beings, I have thus explained to you all this regarding the nature of how the successions of the ocean of saṃsāra come and go.
What is the use of saying more here? The mind is the sprout of the tree of karma;
when that is severed, the tree of karma, with all its world-branches, becomes severed. O Rāma, this entire universe is the mind; when it is treated internally, [all is cured].
This entire existence, consisting of the web of births, has been thus treated.
Therefore, this world arises with the mind agitated by fragments of impurity;
apart from the mind, where indeed is a body ever seen?
The demon of the mind does not reach pacification even in hundreds of eons by any cause other than the absolute non-existence of the object of perception;
and this [non-existence] is indeed possible for the treatment of the disease of the mind.
The supreme and most excellent medicine is the absolute non-existence of the visible world.
The mind undergoes delusion; the mind dies and is born again.
Yet, by the grace of someone [else], it is bound and then liberated once more.
Thus the entire world throbs within the mind when it is agitated by thought,
like the city of the Gandharvas in the vast, empty sky.
This entire expansive world flashes forth and exists within the mind.
Just as fragrance resides within a cluster of flowers, or as something else resides within it;
just as oil is in a sesame seed, or as a quality is in that which possesses qualities;
or just as a property is in its substratum—so too does this [consciousness] abide in the mind.
Just as a mass of waves is in water, just as the delusion of two moons is in [the reflection of] the moon,
and just as a mirage is in heat, so is cyclic existence in the mind.
Just as a web of rays is in the sun, and just as light is in fire.
Just as heat exists in fire, so does this world exist in the mind;
just as coldness exists in frost, and as emptiness exists in space,
and as flickering exists in the wind, so does this world exist in the mind.

The mind is the world, and the entire world is likewise the mind; for these two are indeed never separated from one another. When the mind is constantly wounded, both of them are wounded, but when the world is wounded, the mind is not.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Description of the Sprout of Persistence."
The one hundred and twenty-seventh canto.
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, best among those who understand what precedes and follows!"
"How indeed does this vast cycle of existence (saṃsāra) reside within the mind?
"O sinless one, tell me clearly by means of a vivid illustration how this expansive manifestation appears so manifest within the mind."
Vasiṣṭha:
Just as the worlds of the sons of Indu,
though bodiless, remain firmly established in the minds of the sages, so too does this [universe] abide within the mind.
Just as King Lavaṇa, whose form was confounded by Indra’s magical illusions,
attained the state of a Caṇḍāla, so too has this [state] remained in my mind;
likewise, for a long time, Bhārgava [dwelt there] out of a desire to enjoy the pleasures of heaven.
"And how this lordship over enjoyments came to be established in his mind.
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, [this was] due to the son of Bhṛgu's desire to experience the enjoyments of heaven."
"How did sovereignty over enjoyments and the state of being a transmigrating being come to be?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Listen, Rāma, to an ancient account, a dialogue between Bhṛgu and Kāla."
On the peak of Mount Mandara, thick with *tāla* trees;
formerly, on a certain peak of Mount Mandara crowded with flowers,
the venerable Bhṛgu performed severe penance.

The radiant and highly intelligent young son Śukra, who possessed the luster of the full moon, attended upon him, just as light attends the sun. In that excellent forest, Bhṛgu remained steadfastly established in meditative absorption.
As if carved at all times from the surface of a forest stone,
the boy Śukra sported with ease upon beds of flowers, amidst silver lotus-pools, and on swings of *mandāra* trees.

At that time, it is said, Śukra remained between the realms of knowledge and ignorance, like Triśaṅku suspended between heaven and earth, having not yet attained the great state. Then, while his father was established in non-conceptual meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi), at one point—
He remained undisturbed in solitude like a king who has conquered his enemies;
there he beheld an Apsaras passing through the path of the sky,
just as Janārdana beholds Lakṣmī emerging from the midst of the Ocean of Milk.
She was entwined with garlands of *mandāra* flowers, her tresses fluttering in the gentle breeze;
her gait was as captivating as the call of a peacock, and she made the air of the sky fragrant.
She was a creeper upon the tree of beauty, her eyes rolling with intoxication.
Beholding his beloved, whose very presence had been rendered immortal by the moon-like splendor of her body,
his mind became tremulous with joy,
like the ocean when the stainless full moon is seen.

Having restrained his mind within his heart, Uśanas, though struck by hundreds of arrows from the mind-born god, became composed solely of celestial nymphs, as all other mental activities had dissolved away. This concludes the chapter titled "The Stumbling of Bhārgava" in the *Bhārgava-upākhyāna*.
The one hundred and twenty-eighth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, meditating upon her with his mind, he remained right there with his eyes closed.
"Alone, indeed, Uśanas has begun this kingdom of the mind:
'For here is this maiden in the sky, the abode of the thousand-eyed one;
and I have reached heaven, adorned with shimmering celestial nymphs.'"
These are the gods, beautiful with crests of soft *mṛdu-mandāraka* flowers,
their bodies radiant with the grace of molten gold.
These are those showers of blue lotuses created to delight your eyes.
These Maruts, charming and playful in their laughter, lovely with gazes like those of deer,
appear intoxicated; they possess forms comparable to the Cosmic Being (Viśvarūpa) as they reflect one another, illuminated by the Kaustubha gem.
These are those songs of the hosts of gods, sung in sweet, falsetto tones, whose melodies are heard by bees detached from the fragrance of Airāvaṇa’s temples.
This is that very lake where the sage Vairiñca wanders like a swan among golden lotuses.
The celestial ladies rest in the gardens on the banks of the Mandākinī.
These are those guardians of the world— Yama, Candra, Indra, Sūrya, Anila, Jala, and Anala— their bodies radiant with scattered, blazing, and intensely glowing rays of light.
This is that Airāvaṇa, whose face was scratched by the tips of the tusks of the gods' elephants, and whose trampling tusks pierced the circle of the lords of the Daityas;
these are those who, having once stood upon the surface of the earth, have now become stars in the sky.

The celestial beings of the aerial chariots (vaimānika), adorned with shimmering, beautiful necklaces, chowries, and earrings— these are those rows of celestial chariots, radiant with lovely gold and decorated with various gardens and jeweled mansions.
These are those very waves of the Gaṅgā’s waters, strewn with Mandāra flowers, by which the deities are drenched with spray from their impact against the surface of Mount Meru.
These [clouds] are tawny with clusters of Mandāra blossoms that have spread forth.
The rows of gardens belonging to Śakra are filled with throngs of Apsarases swaying like swings;
these are the breezes from the Pārijāta tree, fragrant with the nectar of Kunda and Mandāra blossoms, and resembling a mass of moonbeams.
This Nandana grove is filled with throngs of vine-like women eager for the sport of being enveloped by the mist of flower-pollen;
it is a place where celestial damsels dance, delighted by the sound of lovely songs.
"These two, with voices as melodious as lutes, are Nārada and Tumburu.
These are the performers of meritorious deeds, adorned with many ornaments,
dwelling happily in celestial chariots soaring through the sky."
These celestial women, their limbs intoxicated by passion and love,
serve the Lord of the Gods like forest creepers in a grove;
they are flowers from the clusters of moonbeams and bunches from the wish-fulfilling gems.
These wish-fulfilling trees are bristling with clusters of ripe jewels.
Here, then, I honor and salute this Śakra seated upon his throne, as if he were a second Lord of the Gods.
Having reflected thus, Śacīpati [Indra] mentally saluted Śukra; there he appeared like a second Bhṛgu himself. Then Śukra, having been honored by Śakra, rose up with respect.
Taking him by the hand, he was brought and seated nearby.
"O Śukra, this heaven is blessed and shines today because of your arrival;
O Śakra, please dwell here for a long time," he said to him in this manner.
Then, having sat down there, that descendant of Bhṛgu, with his face radiant,
eclipsed the splendor of the entire stainless moon;
that son of Bhṛgu, saluted by all the hosts of gods, remained by the side of Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices.
For a long time he attained incomparable satisfaction, and having abandoned human thought, he became fully liberated.
This concludes the one hundred and twenty-ninth canto, titled "The Royal Aspirations of Bhārgava," within the Bhārgava Episode.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus Śukra, having reached the city of the gods with his own mind,
forgot his former state and his previous calamity, except for his affliction.
Then, having rested for a moment by the side of the Lord of Śacī,
he prepared to roam through heaven, urged on by the inhabitants of the celestial realm;
and beholding the splendor of heaven, marked by their restless glances.
He went to see that woman, as a crane goes to a lotus pond;
there he beheld that lovely deer-eyed woman who had come to the edge of the forest, like a bee to a mango creeper.
Beholding her, whose form was curved with shimmering and restless grace,
his limbs began to dissolve like a moonstone at the touch of moonlight.
With every limb melting away, he gazed upon that lovely woman.
Just as the moonstone [draws in] the cool, playful moonlight from the sky,
she too, being gazed upon by him, became devoted to him,
like a female ruddy goose at the end of the night when called out by her mate.
Surely that same splendor which belongs to the sun and the lotus in the morning— when they have blossomed through their essence and are mutually enamored— was possessed by those two.
Because that place grants whatever is desired, she was [chosen] by Madana.
Having rendered her entire body helpless, she was surrendered to Śukra alone.
The arrows of Smara fell repeatedly upon her tender limbs,
like torrents from a fresh rain-cloud upon the petals of a lotus pond.
Shaken by love, with her curls swaying like a swarm of restless bees,
she became the companion of a flower-cluster tossed by a gentle breeze.
With eyes like blue lotuses and a gait like that of a swan or an elephant—
Madana agitated her, as a flood agitates a lotus pond.
Then, seeing her in such a state, Śukra, who was intent on his purpose, summoned Tamas, just as the Creator summons the dissolution of all beings.
That region of heaven became shrouded in darkness,
like the edge of the Lokāloka mountain on the earth where the world is enveloped in blinding gloom;
within that circle of darkness, shame was like a sharp-rayed sun.
When that [state] had become established for him, as if in the god of love for a pair of lovers,
all those beings departed toward their desired directions from that place,
like birds at the end of the day toward the world of mortals.
With long, white-cornered eyes and her passion thus fully aroused,
she approached the son of Bhṛgu like a peahen approaching a rain-cloud;
he was seated upon a prepared couch in the middle of a white chamber.
There Bhārgava entered, like Mādhava entering the Ocean of Milk.
Grasping his feet, that lovely-faced woman, as if helpless,
shone like a lotus-pond clinging to the foot of a divine elephant.
And he spoke these sweet, joy-inspiring words, filled with playful syllables and uttered with a voice radiant with overflowing affection:
"O you with a face like the orb of the pure moon, behold! [The god of love] has drawn his bow into a circle."
"Why does this bodiless one pursue me, a weak woman?
O Lord, protect me here—me, a weak and wretched woman who has sought refuge in you.
Know, O virtuous one, that consoling the miserable is the vow of those whose conduct is true."
O Great-minded One, those who are utterly deluded and ignorant of the gaze of affection disregard such advances,
whereas those who know the essence of flavor never do so.
An advance made by two people who are mutually enamored occurs unexpectedly and spontaneously.
O beloved, he renders insignificant even the nectar-like flow from the moon that has been tasted;
this sovereignty over the three worlds does not so delight the mind as does the mutual bliss of affection between two people who have first fallen in love.
O giver of honor, by the touch of your feet I have been comforted,
like a night-lotus at night touched by the rays of the moon;
O handsome one, I live through drinking the nectar of your touch.
Just as the restless female cakora bird is [refreshed] by drinking the essence of the moonbeams,
so do you embrace me— who am clinging to your feet like a bee— with your sprout-like hands, and place me within your heart, which is like a true lotus filled with nectar.
Having spoken thus, she whose limbs were as soft as flowers fell upon his chest;
her eyes, with their rolling bees, were like a cluster of blossoms on a tree.
There, in those forest glades, that couple, lovely in their dalliance, sported together.
Like two intoxicated bees upon lotus ponds shaken by the wind, white with filaments;
thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth canto, titled "The First Union," in the Bhārgava episode.
Vasiṣṭha:
Through those dear advances long imagined by the play of his mind,
the reunion with Bhārgava became a source of satisfaction for him.
Then, together with her— who was adorned with garlands of *mandāra* flowers and intoxicated by the wine of the gods— he, like a second spotless moon,
sported upon golden lotus-ponds where the swans were inebriated.
On the banks of the river of the gods, together with the *kinnaras* and *cāraṇas*,
the playful [deities] drank the elixir (*rasāyana*) flowing from the moon’s crescent, while dwelling within the thickets of *pārijāta* creepers alongside the gods.
He sported for a long time with eager throngs of Vidyadhara maidens upon the vine-swinging arbors of the beautiful Caitraratha grove,
just as the expanse of the Nandana garden was filled by Mandara as it churned the ocean.
He was driven into a state of extreme agitation by the attendants of Śambhu; and with a passion like that of a madman, he wandered through the caves thick with networks of young golden creepers,
as if through the lotus-beds of Mount Meru.
In the forest groves of Kailāsa,
that playful lover spent the night— white as the moon— with her amidst the songs of the *gaṇas*.
Having rested upon the plateaus of the Gandhamādana mountain, he remained there.
Adorned from head to foot by him with golden lotuses,
O Rāma, he sported with her with laughter upon the slopes of the Lokāloka mountain, which are enchanting with their various wonders.

In the groves between the *mandāra* trees, he dwelt for sixty years together with the young deer, his dwelling fashioned like a celestial palace. On the shores of the Ocean of Milk, accompanied by his beloved wife, he lived.
Half of the Kṛta Yuga was exhausted along with the inhabitants of Śvetadvīpa;
through the playful arrangements of gardens in that city of Gandharvas,
he came to imitate Time, which creates an infinite succession of worlds.
Then that Śukra dwelt again in the city of Purandara for eight cycles of four yugas in happiness with the deer-eyed woman; subsequently,
due to the exhaustion of his merit, he descended to the circle of the earth.
Together with that proud woman, he fell down, his form stripped away;
all his limbs were severed by others, his chariot and its delights stolen,
overcome by anxiety and ruined like a soldier struck down in battle.

As he fell upon the earth, his body shattered into a hundred pieces along with his long anxiety, like a mountain torrent crashing against a rock. When both bodies had thus crumbled away, those two minds remained shrouded in latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Struck by those two, they were like two birds deprived of their nest in the sky.
Then, their minds entered the web of rays belonging to the moon;
having quickly attained the state of frost, they then became rice plants.
That best of brahmins ate those cooked *śāli* rice grains in Daśārṇa;
and the king ate the *śaukra* rice grains born from the womb of Śukra’s wife in Mālava.
Formerly, Uśanas was born in Daśārṇa before that best of brahmins.
From that king of supreme fortune, she was born as a woman among the Mālavas.
There the boy grew up, and there that woman grew up;
they were like the former husband and wife born again upon the earth after falling from heaven.
Then, at sixteen years of age, there was a glorious young brahmin boy named Śukra Sāraṅga, endowed with youth, in his father’s house. That maiden,
a celestial woman of the asuras named Mālā, [was in] the royal palace.
Like a creeper in a choice forest, Bhṛṅgekṣaṇā attained full growth. Then the auspicious princess Mālā incessantly worshipped Śaṅkara, thinking, "May I obtain my destined husband from former times."
Then, at the sacrifice of the King of Mālava, she beheld Sāraṅga, who had come to the assembly of brahmins together with her father;
seeing him, she of faultless limbs was moved by her former affection.

Her limbs glistening with moisture like a moonstone upon seeing the moon, she shone brightly. Then, in the midst of the sacrificial assembly, that garland— the daughter of the King of Mālava— chose the son of the twice-born from Daśārṇa as her husband.

When he had gradually completed his marriage, the lord of Mālava, worn out by old age, handed over the entire kingdom to him and departed for the forest. Thereupon, Sāraṅga, together with her, [resided] in that realm of Mālava.

He ruled the kingdom with great happiness for a hundred autumns, like Śakra. Then, after a long time, due to the fickleness of the mind and by the power of destiny, that couple became mutually displeased with one another.
But Sāraṅga, worn out by old age, his body ready to fall, assumed the color of withered leaves due to the weakness of his breath,
caused both by his wife’s aversion and the extreme onset of senility.

With death near, free from desire and doubt, he rejoiced. Then, for him whose attachment to kingship had withered and who proclaimed the excess of suffering, delusion reached a state of extreme density, like a vetāla spirit in a forest.
Therefore, death abandons this person who has fallen into the blind well of delusion, who is incessantly attached to enjoyments,
who lacks discernment, who is ignorant, and who is devoted to the wicked—
his heart being swallowed by craving.
Like a frog [leaping upon] a bird that is crying out and helpless,
he then, having experienced the fruit of his own auspicious and inauspicious karma in the hereafter,
is born among fishers due to the power of his evil disposition.
There, performing the work of a fisherman for a hundred autumns,
he attained a state of world-weariness because his mind was worn out by suffering.
Then, reflecting that "saṃsāra is indeed suffering," he [approached] Bhāskara.
Through that [merit], he was born as a great king in the Solar dynasty (Sūryavaṃśa).
Then, by the power of his virtuous disposition, he attained some degree of knowledge;
having cast off his royal body, he became a teacher who instructs all.
Having indeed attained the perfection of the mantra, he then became a Vidyādhara;
for one kalpa he enjoyed the city of the Vidyādharas. Then, having brought about the time of the end of that kalpa, by means of his wind-form, he departed.
When his body had been cast off and he was born again as the son of a sage,
he then, through contact with other sages, became established in fierce asceticism;
blameless, he dwelt in the depths of Mount Meru for the duration of a Manvantara.
There, a son of a doe, having human form, was born to him;
through affection for him, he again fell into a state of supreme delusion in an instant:
"May this son have wealth, virtues, and eternal life."

Thus, through incessant anxieties, he abandoned his established state of truth. Because he had fallen away from reflection on the Dharma and was preoccupied with thoughts of wealth for the sake of his son,
Death carried him off— his life-span exhausted— just as a serpent seizes the wind.

With his consciousness departed along with his singular preoccupation with enjoyments, he attained the status of the son of the Lord of Madra and became the sovereign of the Madra land. Having ruled the kingdom in the country of Madra for a long time, he destroyed all his enemies.
There, old age overcame her, as a frost-bolt strikes a lotus;
yet she cast off that body of the King of Madra along with the latent impressions of her asceticism,
and thus he was born as an ascetic, the son of a forest-dweller.
Having reached the bank of the great river Samaṅgā,
O Rāma, that ascetic of great intelligence, free from all affliction, performed austerities;
having followed the succession of bodies, his mind rendered helpless by the various stages of birth.

That descendant of Bhṛgu remained happily on the bank of the Varaṇā river, firm like a tree. This concludes the one hundred and thirty-first canto, titled "The Experience of Various Births," within the narrative of Bhārgava.
Vasiṣṭha said:
While Śukra was thus reflecting, a great deal of time consisting of many years passed in the presence of his father.
Then, after a long time, his body— withered by wind and sun—
fell upon the earth like a tree whose roots have been severed;
yet his mind, with its flickering range, remained amidst those various states.
He wandered like a deer through the most variegated forest groves;
his mind, wandering, reeling, and agitated on all sides as if cast into a whirlpool,
found rest upon the bank of the river Samaṅgā.
Remaining bodiless, Śukra experienced that state of worldly existence— which is both fragile and yet extremely firm, and dense with endless occurrences—
while his wise body remained upon the peak of Mount Mandara.
Dried up by the spreading heat, she became nothing but skin;
with the whistling sound of the wind flowing through the cavities of her body, she seemed to sing a sweet warble (*kākali*) born from the bliss of the exhaustion of the suffering of movement.
Like a breath of exhalation following the recollection of the vital breath, it released tears;
having been tossed about upon the forest lands by the play of fierce winds,
the wretched mind rolled in the pits of the realms of existence.
She seemed to laugh with her row of teeth, white as exceedingly bright clouds;
she revealed her own empty form, natural to the eyes,
with the beauty of a hollow resembling an old well in a forest.
Scorched by the heat and drenched by the weight of the rainwater,
she was as if defiled by the dust raised by the wind, like the consequences of one's own evil deeds;
trembling like a dry piece of wood, she let out cries of distress at every fall.
Pierced by the falling torrent of rain at the onset of the clouds,
she stood on the bank of a mountain river flooded by the monsoon cascade,
like a forest stone hissing with the whistling of the piercing wind.
Crooked, with strings of dried entrails, foul-smelling, and making a hollow *jhāṅkāra* sound,
it was like the lute of the Goddess of the Forest, its belly made of empty hide;
for that holy hermitage was indeed devoid of passion and hatred.

And because of Bhṛgu’s great asceticism, wild beasts and birds did not devour him. The mind of that scion of Bhṛgu’s lineage practiced austerities, while his slender body— emaciated by restraints and observances and drained of blood by the wind— rolled for a long time upon those vast rocks.
In the Bhārgava-episode, the one hundred and thirty-second canto, titled "The Description of the Corpse of Bhārgava," Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, after a thousand divine years,
Bhṛgu, the supreme lord, ceased from his meditative absorption due to his ultimate awakening;
he did not see before him that son whose face was bowed down by humility.
He beheld before him a great skeleton, the very limit of the boundary of all virtues, standing like merit incarnate; it was as if Time alone were present,
appearing like misfortune embodied or poverty personified.
Its body was withered by heat; partridges quivered within the openings of its skin;
frogs rested in the shadows of the hollows of its dried-out internal organs;
and flower-creeping insects slept within the cavities of its eyes.
Like a swarm of silkworms trapped within a cage of bees,
[he laughs] at his former desire for enjoyment which yields desired and undesired fruits,
with a body whose interior is washed by the stream [of tears] and whose garland of bones is parched.
With his bright skull-bowl, possessing the luster of the full moon,
he mimicked the beauty of a linga smeared with camphor;
and with his straight, dried, white [skull-staff], which remained as nothing more than bone—
With his neck extended, as if lengthening his very form,
he bore a face whose boundaries were defined by a row of teeth that appeared like a stalk of lotus-fiber— pale and from which the flesh had been stripped away in the process of carving.
Surely, with her long neck and face turned upward,
she seemed to be watching her life-breaths as they departed into the belly of the sky;
her shanks, thighs, knees, and staff-like arms having attained a doubled length.
As if measuring out his own lack of peace due to the fear of the long journey’s fatigue,
with a belly that was deeply sunken, withered, and reduced to mere skin,
he seemed to demonstrate to the ignorant the extreme emptiness of the heart.
Beholding that withered skeleton, which was like the tethering post of an elephant,
Bhṛgu rose up without reflecting on what had preceded or followed; for at the very moment he looked, it appeared clearly to Bhṛgu.

In an instant, he thought, "Is this my son whose life has departed for so long? Then, even as he was still reflecting, the power of the future caused a most terrible anger toward Time (Kāla) to arise within him immediately.

"Why was my son taken away at such an untimely hour? Thus provoked to anger, the Blessed One began to cast a curse upon Time (Kāla). Then Kāla, having assumed his true form, appeared with the subjects he had devoured.
Assuming a physical body of a terrestrial nature, he approached the sage, glorious,
bearing a sword and a noose, adorned with earrings and clad in armor;
six-armed and six-faced, he was surrounded by a vast army of servants.
The sky bore the splendor of a mountain of blooming *kiṃśuka* trees by the leaping mass of flames arising from his body;
and by the circles of fire spat forth from the tip of the trident held in his hand, [the sky shone].
The quarters of the sky shone as if adorned with golden earrings.
The mountains,
their peaks shaken by the wind from his breath, moved and fell, reeling as if mounted upon a swing.
The orb of the sun, darkened by the radiance of his sword-blade,
appeared as if it were obscured by the smoke of a world consumed at the end of an aeon.
Approaching that enraged great sage, the mighty-armed one—
He spoke with consoling words, as deep as the ocean agitated at the end of an eon:
"O Sage, those who understand the state of the world and have seen both the higher and the lower are not deluded even by a cause; how much less so, O Supreme One, without a cause?"
"You are a Brahmin of infinite austerity, while we are merely the upholders of destiny;
therefore, O venerable one, you are honored by us, O holy man, and not according to our own will.
Do not exhaust yourself with penance through these agitated, great fires at the end of the aeon."

"What can you burn with your curse that I am not already burnt? O Sage, the cycles of saṃsāra have been devoured, tens of millions of Rudras have been swallowed, and hosts of Viṣṇus have been consumed; who has cursed us?"
"For we are the eaters, O Brahmin, while you and others are the food. This is indeed our own destiny; it was not by our own volition.
Fire moves upward of its own accord, and waters flow downward of their own accord."
The enjoyer goes toward the food, and creation itself goes toward its end.
O Sage, such is the form of this Supreme Self here;
by itself, within its own self, the Self unfolds through its own power.

By the vision that has destroyed all taint, there is neither an agent nor an enjoyer here; yet by the vision that has not destroyed its taint, many agents exist here. O Brahman, agency and non-agency are merely imagined constructs.
It is through wrong vision alone, and not through right vision,
that flowers in groves of trees and living beings in the worlds come and go of their own accord; it is only the agency of Fate that is imagined here.
Just as the agency and non-agency in the movement of the moon’s reflection are neither real nor unreal, so it is with respect to the creations of time;
through the false delusion of the mind, the world consists of agency and non-agency.
One who has a deluded vision imagines a rope to be something else, just as one with impaired sight perceives it.
Therefore, O Sage, do not give way to anger; such is the course of calamities. Let things be exactly as they are; look upon the truth without agitation.
We do not act out of a sense of power, nor are we overcome by pride; rather,
we abide solely in destiny, under the influence of our own habitual tendencies,
driven by the force of necessity toward the activities and pursuits determined by that very destiny.
The wise person should act accordingly, not being shrouded by the great darkness of self-conceit;
those skilled in action simply perform what must be done,
relying upon the state of deep sleep and free from any desire whatsoever.
Where is that vision consisting of knowledge, where is your greatness, and where is your fortitude?

For since the path is well-known to all, why do you wander in delusion like a blind man? Even while maintaining in your mind the state of seeing clearly through the three times, [why do you act thus]?

Without examining the course of the world, why do you become deluded like a fool? O omniscient one, without examining the state of your son arising from the ripening of the fruits of his own karma, why do you deserve to curse me in vain like a fool?
O Sage, for all embodied beings here, the body is of two kinds;
do you not know that one is the physical body and the other is called the mind? Of these, the physical body is utterly insentient and solely intent upon destruction.
But the mind is fixed on rising up; it is diminished or not by its own affliction.
O virtuous one, just as a chariot is driven by a skillful charioteer who exerts some effort here, so too is this body driven by the mind.
Having conceptualized what is non-existent, the existent body is destroyed in an instant by the mind, just as a clay figure is destroyed by a child.
In this world, the mind alone is the person; that which is performed by it is said to be "done."
That [mind] is bound because of conceptualization; when conceptualization ceases, it is liberated.
"This is the body, this is the eye, this is a limb, this is the head"—that which undergoes such expansive modifications is designated as the mind alone.
For it is the mind (*manas*) that lives as the so-called "living being," while the intellect (*dhī*) functions as the determiner;
the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) exists due to the sense of "I," and it is this [mind] that indeed undergoes manifoldness.
Through the latent impression of the body, the consciousness perceives other things as its own.
One perceives earthly bodies as if they truly exist; but if one truly beholds them as unreal, the mind,
having abandoned the conception of a body, attains supreme bliss.
While you remained absorbed in meditative concentration, the mind of your son traveled further and further away along the path of his own desires;
leaving this body in a cave of Mount Mandara, he followed the doctrine of Uśanas.
He departed for the abode of the gods like a bird taking flight from its nest;
there, amidst the groves of Mandāra trees, the dwellings of Pārijāta,
the thickets of the Nandana garden, and the cities of the world-protectors.
O Sage, for eight cycles of four yugas, that one of great splendor attended upon Viśvācī, the celestial beauty, just as a bee attends a lotus;
he was filled with intense passion for her, who had been fashioned by his own volition.
Then, when his merit was exhausted, like the mist of night,
he fell along with her like a fruit ripened by time, his flower-ornaments withered and his limbs perspiring, sluggish in his bracelets.
Having abandoned that divine body in the sky itself,
and having reached the elemental ether,
he was born upon the earth as a twice-born man among the Daśārṇas and a lord of the earth in Kosala.
In the great forest of Aṅga he was a fisherman; on the banks of the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā), a swan;
a king of the Sūryavaṃśa in Pauṇḍra; a solar deity among the Sālvas; a guide;
for a kalpa, a glorious and wise Vidyādhara; and then, the son of a sage.
Then that prince,
now a young ascetic, became known as Vāsudeva and dwelt upon the banks of the Samaṅgā;
furthermore, by his own power and through the force of his latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he manifested himself in various other forms.
This son of yours wandered through infinite births in various miserable states:
he became a cowherd in the Vindhya forest, a hunter among the Kekayas,
a local chieftain among the Sauvīras, and a guide among the Traigartas.
The bamboo thicket among the Kirātas, the deer in the Cīra forest,
the reptile beneath the palm trees, the Tamāla tree, and the wild cock— this very son of yours, having become the best among those who know the mantras, [has returned].
In former times, he recited the lore that bestows the status of a Vidyādhara.
By means of that, O Blessed One, O Brahmin, he became a great Vidyādhara in the sky,
adorned with necklaces, earrings, and armlets, and a dancer of manifold graceful sports.
He was like another flower-bowed god to the lotus-like heroines;
beloved by the Vidyādharīs, he was the ornament of the Gandharva cities. Having reached the end of his lifespan, he entered the splendor of the twelve suns.
He was reduced to ashes, like a moth in a fire.
Then, in the vast sky devoid of the creation of worlds,
his latent impression wandered like a bird without a nest.
Then, when time had arrived— the commencement of the grand display of saṃsāra, characterized by diverse undertakings at the end of the night of Brahmā—
his mental impression (*manovāsanā*), being tossed about like the wind, [arose].
