O sage, having attained the status of a Brahmin in this Kṛta age, that son of a Brahmin named Vāsudeva was born today on the surface of the earth;
he has been born among the wise, having studied all the Vedas.
"O Great Sage, having been a Vidyadhara for an eon,
your son now practices asceticism, standing on the bank of the river Samaṅgā.
Amidst the hollows of the *khadira* and *karañja* trees, which are formidable with their various and uneven growths, he dwells through the persistence of diverse latent dispositions."
Having entered into the world among decrepit wombs and into the most dense forest regions—
this is the one hundred and thirty-third canto, titled "The Words of Time," from the *Bhārgava-ākhyāna*.
Kāla said: "Today, on the bank of the most excellent river, where the wind resounds with the gurgling of a surging mass of wild waves,
your son performs austerities."
Wearing matted hair and a rosary, having conquered the delusions of all his senses,
he remained there for eight hundred years in steadfast austerity.
O Sage, if you wish to see that son of yours, who is but a delusion of the mind, [go there].
"Open that eye of discernment and look quickly!
When this was said by Kāla, the Lord of the World, who possesses equal vision toward all,
the sage reflected with the eye of knowledge upon what his son had intended.
And in a moment, by the power of his visionary intuition, he beheld the entire account of his son reflected upon the mirror of his intellect; then,
at the proper time, he saw her standing on the slopes of Mount Mandara and later situated at the peak of Time.
Having come from the bank of the Samaṅgā river, Bhṛgu entered his own body.

Then, looking at Kāla with a gaze smiling with wonder, the passionless sage spoke these words to the passionless Kāla: *vismayasmerayā dṛṣṭyā kālam ālokya kāntayā / vītarāgam uvācedaṃ vītarāgo munir vacaḥ //* MU_3,133.7*
Bhṛgu said:

"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, we are but children, unsullied [by worldly knowledge]; O God, only those like you possess the intellect that perceives the three times with stainless clarity."
Though it exists, this course of the world— rich in transformations, manifold in form, and appearing as something unreal— produces delusion even for the wise.
O Lord, you alone know that which dwells within you.
"The form of this mental activity is a creator of illusions.
O Blessed One, it is said that death does not exist for this son of mine;
therefore, seeing him dead, I have become filled with agitation."
"O Lord, Time has carried away my son whose life was not yet exhausted;
by the power of destiny, the desire for your curse arose in me.
Yet, we who understand the course of saṃsāra do not [suffer] from calamity."
"Or we go toward prosperity, indeed falling under the sway of joy and resentment.
Anger is to be directed at one who acts improperly, and favor toward one who acts properly;
this worldly condition, O Blessed One, is firmly established."
"This is to be done, this is not"—such is the course of the world for as long as one lives;
as long as fire exists, so long are there perceptions of heat, burning, and the like.
For one who regards the state of the world as something to be abandoned, thinking "this is to be done, this is not," [the cycle continues].

O Teacher of the World, the complete renunciation of this [world] is indeed what must be abandoned. O Blessed One, since we were agitated by you when we failed to consider that very same concern for our sons, we have incurred reproach because of that.
"O Lord, you have now reminded me of what my son intended;
therefore, this son was seen by me on the bank of the Samaṅgā.
I think that for living beings in this world, there are two bodies, O All-pervading One."
"The mind alone is indeed the body, by which this world is brought into being.
"Time:
O Brahmin, you have spoken correctly; for us, the mind alone is the body."

Having formed a mental resolve, it creates a body just as a potter makes a jar. Through delusion, the mind creates an uncreated form and destroys what was created in an instant by means of its own volition, like a child imagining a ghost.
And likewise, O great sage, during states of agitation, powers appearing as dreams, false cognitions, and the like—
manifesting with the form of a city of Gandharvas— are seen within the mind;
yet this is based on the perception of one with a coarse vision.

The mind and the body of a person are said to be the two bodies. O Sage, these three worlds are merely the construction of mental ideation; they have arisen as something vast that is neither existent nor non-existent, and nothing else.
Through the creeper-like limbs of the body of consciousness, fueled by the latent impression of duality,
this manifoldness has arisen from ignorance, like the appearance of two moons.
By means of the manifold latent impression of duality, the mind perceives the multitude of objects.
Everywhere it perceives things as divided— pots, pits, cloths, and so forth.
Thinking "I am thin," "I am extremely miserable," "I am deluded," and cultivating these and other such notions arising from its own conceptual constructions, the mind enters the state of saṃsāra.
"Thinking is an artificial form; this is not my [true] nature, therefore I do not fall [into it]. Through the renunciation of that [thinking], the mind becomes tranquil—the eternal Brahman.
Just as when the ocean is spread out, extended with many waves...
In the nature of water—which consists of a series of many waves made of subtle vibration;
which is even, clear, pure, sweet, and cool;
which is indestructible, vast, of great majesty, and manifest—*MU* 3.133.29–30.
Meditating on its own form as a triangular wave,
it naturally creates its own conceptualization through the thought, "I am triangular.
And falling away, it thinks, "My form has perished," [sinking] into the Talātala hell.
By means of that very meditation, one goes to the surface of the earth while meditating upon it;
and when rising forcibly upward, having meditated "I am rising," one conceptualizes that state through various mental constructs along with their corresponding names.

When reflected with the sun, it is perceived as "I am luminous"; when struck by a mass of dust, it is perceived as "I am impure. But when possessed of a net of jewel-like rays, it shines with radiant splendor.
Pierced by a heavy burden of frost, he perceives himself as cold;
yet, with his body blazing from the reflection of the forest fire on the mountain slopes, he cries out in distress, "Alas, I am burned! and trembles while clutching a fish.
With the reflections of its shores, mountains, birds, forests, and trees,
it shines as if possessed of a great undertaking and intense activity, thinking "I am here"; its flickering body, though produced by pure and radiant splendor, is already destroyed.
"I have been devoured in pieces," he cried out like one who has lost his protector;
yet those waves are not distinct from the watery mass of the ocean,
nor does their single form exist as anything real, though it appears to be so.
Nor do those qualities, such as inferior length and so forth, reside within those various things;
they are neither established in the ocean like waves, nor are they not established there.
They are merely rendered fragmented by the conceptualizations residing in their own respective natures.
Those that were lost are born again; those that were born are born yet again, only to be destroyed.
Through mutual contact, they undergo manifoldness to an extreme degree;
yet, they are essentially composed of the single form of water and are free from all affliction.
In exactly that same way, within this expansive, white, pure, and stainless Brahman— which has the singular form of Brahman alone,
possesses a vast nature, is omnipotent, and is without beginning or end— all things exist as if separate, though they are not actually distinct from it.
The various powers (śaktis) abide there, restless in their diverse modes of conduct;
for it is the manifoldness of the many powers that resides within its own body.
Just as a mass of waves exists within water, so too does Brahman, though expanded, remain within Brahman.
Because she takes on various forms, Destiny (niyati), though possessing a fixed form herself, assumes a hundredfold diversity as she presides over all things;
being insentient, she assumes insentience, and being composed of consciousness, she attains the state of consciousness.
O sinless one, for the Self established in its own true nature, the power whose form is latent impression (vāsanā) is none other than Brahman itself; therefore, this world expands in vast forms,
like an ocean overflowing with various movements and manifestations.

It assumes diversity of its own accord through dwelling in various forms; it is like the ocean’s water within the water itself, by means of itself and within itself. Just as the various waves are not distinct from the water, [so too is this].
Likewise, all these various manifestations are not separate from the Lord of All;
just as the stalk, flower, creeper, leaf, fruit,
and bud exist within a single seed, so do the powers reside within Brahman.
Just as there is a multiplicity of powers in the Puruṣa due to his being a manifold agent,
so too is there always and everywhere an omnipotence in the omniscient Self.
Just as a variety of colors is seen in the harsh sunlight, [so is the variety of manifestations in the Self].
In the same way, the Lord of Gods possesses a manifold power consisting of both the existent and the non-existent.
From the undifferentiated Śiva, this world arises in diverse forms;
from Him who is of a single color, it emerges like a streak of lightning from a cloudless sky.
From the non-inert, the state of inertness arises, caused by the contemplation of dullness;
just as a thread emerges from a spider, or as deep sleep arises from a person.
By his own will, Śiva, though devoid of mind, brings forth the power of the mental faculties for the sake of his own bondage.
Just as the silkworm weaves its own cocoon,
so does the Self, O Brahmin, by its own will, manifest its own form; having done so,
it attains liberation from saṃsāra, like an elephant from its tethering post.
Whatever the self constantly contemplates, once it has been cultivated by itself,
even the great [self] is quickly filled with that very power. The cultivated power leads the self to its true nature (ātmatā) in an instant.
Just as a great autumn mist quickly permeates even the infinite sky, so too the unborn [Self],
when that power has arisen, swiftly attains identity with it;
indeed, having reached that very state, the tree becomes one with that essence.
There is no liberation for the Lord, nor is there bondage for the Self.
I do not know from where these notions of bondage and liberation have arisen in the world.
For him, there is neither bondage nor liberation; he is perceived as being composed solely of that [Reality].

Alas! This world is eternally seized by the unreal and consists of illusion. As soon as the mind is imagined by the non-temporal (akala) Self through delusion, this Self is then enveloped by it like a silkworm in its cocoon.
But these powers of the mind, which are non-different in essence from it yet possess bodies imagined as distinct, emerge from this [Self] by the millions;
abiding in it and born from it, they appear as separate forms, like waves from the ocean.

They abide in that, they are born from that, and yet they appear distinct, like rays from the moon. In this vast ocean of the Supreme Self, which consists of vibration, whose waters are consciousness, whose expansive expanse is spread out, and which abounds in the essence of pure consciousness alone— *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* 3.133.65–66.
Some of these surging waves, which manifest their own nature through their inherent essence, stand superior to Hari, Brahmā, Rudra, and Cidvalana;
others are Yamah, Mahendra, Arka, Vahni, Vaiśravaṇa, and so forth.
The waves of restless craving strike, act, and persist; some of them—
belonging to the Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, gods, and others—
are fierce waves that leap up, fall down, and toss about.
Some exist in a certain state, such as those born from lotuses and the like;
some have arisen and then perished, such as gods, humans, and the like;
and there are those such as worms, insects, moths, snakes, and pythons.
Some of these flash like droplets within that great ocean;
others, such as the restless-faced deer, vultures, and *vañjula* birds,
flash within the mountain thickets as if upon the shores of the coastal forests.
Some have very long lives, while others have extremely short lives;
some have hollow bodies due to their own hollow mental cultivation;
and some, amidst the turmoil of the dream of saṃsāra, are cultivated with stability.
Some, struck down by their own conceptual constructions, imagine the world to be utterly stable. Others, possessing very meager contemplation and overcome by the defect of dejection,
are made firm in their suffering by the thought, "I am weak, I am extremely miserable, I am a fool."
Some have attained the state of stationary beings, some have reached the status of deities;
some have attained the state of men, and some have gone to the state of Dānavas.
Some remain in this world for many hundreds of kalpas, while others, being thoroughly purified, proceed to the Supreme Person.
For the cognitions of consciousness, which are like waves surging from the ocean of Brahman, possess "thinking" as their other name.
The one hundred thirty-fourth canto, titled "The Instruction on Yoga for Demonstrating the Operation of Saṃsāra," from the *Bhārgava-upākhyāna*.
Kāla:
O Sage, these cognitions that take the forms of gods, asuras, and humans are non-different from the ocean of Brahman; this is the truth, and everything else is false.
O Brahman, those who are stained by their own conceptual constructions through false meditation have descended to lower states because of the internal conviction, "We are not Brahman.
Even while remaining within the ocean of Brahman, they perceive themselves as distinct from Brahman.
Cultivating these [states], they become deluded within the terrifying realms of worldly existence.
O Sage, those cognitions which belong to Brahman and are not stained by manifold impurities—
know that these are either the seed of karmas, or indeed karma itself.
O Sage, by this internal process of mental construction (*saṅkalpa*), which is itself the form of volition,
and which is as formidable as a handful of seeds for the *karañja* trees of the web of karma,
these rows of stone-like bodies have been spread throughout the vast world.
They stand still, they leap about, they weep and they laugh;
from Brahma down to a blade of grass, like the wind through its vibrations,
they exult, they restrain themselves, they wither and they smile.
Among these, some are entirely transparent, such as Hari, Hara, and others;
some abide in slight delusion, such as serpents, humans, and gods;
and some abide in extreme delusion, such as trees, grass, and so forth.
Some, utterly deluded by ignorance, have become worms and insects;
others are carried away like blades of grass, far from the great ocean of Brahman—
these are those who have not attained the spiritual stages, just like serpents and men.
Some, having merely glimpsed the shore, fell into despair;
both those already born and those yet to be born are being buried by the old rat of Death (Kṛtānta).
Others, having reached the interior of the great ocean of the reality of Brahman, [attain liberation].
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Śiva, and the others have gone to that state of non-sorrow;
some, possessed of only slight delusion, remain having taken refuge in that very ocean of Brahman,
which is free from the flood of the disease of passion.
Some multitudes of beings are yet to experience the flood of births, while others have already experienced millions of such floods; some remain barren, abiding in the light or in darkness.
Some go from above to below, and likewise from below to the Great State.
Some [actions] lead higher and higher, some downward, and others even further down;
this activity, fraught with many joys and sorrows, comes into being here due to the failure to remember the Supreme State.
But through the realization of the Supreme State, it goes to its destruction, just as the pain of poison vanishes upon remembering the Lord of Birds.
In the Bhārgava episode, the chapter titled "The Description of the Detailed Origin," the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter; the time.
Among these various and diverse classes of beings— like waves in the ocean,
or like various creepers in the month of Mādhava—
those who have conquered the delusion of the mind and perceived the higher and lower worlds stand in the midst.
Yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras wander here as those liberated while living;
others, however, are like wood or walls—deluded and having attained the state of stationary beings.
Since their delusion is not yet exhausted, what is there to be deliberated regarding them?
In this world, for the sake of establishing the Self of beings who are awakening,
treatises have been composed and circulated here by those of refined intellect.
But as for those whose intentions are fully awakened through the exhaustion of their misdeeds, [they require no further instruction].
Their intellect proceeds with clarity in the investigation of the scriptures;
through the thorough examination of the true teachings, the delusion of the mind dissolves,
just as the darkness of night vanishes before the sun moving across the sky.
For a mind that does not diminish leads only to delusion and not to accomplishment;
like a mist, it obscures the vision, and like a Vetāla, it leaps about.
It is the vessel for the experience of pleasure and pain for all living beings.
In this world, O sage, the body is indeed the mind alone, and not that which consists of flesh.
This collection of flesh and bone that is perceived as the physical (ādhibhautika) realm—know it to be a mental construction; the body is not ultimately real.
O Sage, whatever your son has done with his mind and body, he alone has swiftly obtained the result; we are not at fault in this matter.
Whatever action a person performs by means of their own latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), that very thing they experience.

He attains that very thing in that manner; here, there is no agency for anything else. What indeed exists in this world that has the power to create that which is not conceived within by one's own mental impressions?
Whatever enjoyments there are in heaven and hell, and whatever desires for heaven and hell exist,
they are the outflow of the moon of one's own mental conceptualization, yielding the suffering of dullness.
What is the use of saying more here by one who merely composes strings of words?
"Arise, O Blessed One; let us go where your son resides.
Having experienced everything here with his mind-body, Śukra now stands as a perfected ascetic (sāmaṅga-tāpasa) due to his contact with the rays of the moon."
That vital breath (*prāṇa-pavana*), conjoined with consciousness (*citta*) and moving through the lunar rays,
having become the essence of the dew, exists as a man by way of its potency (*vīrya*).
Vālmīki said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord Kāla, as if smiling at the courses of the world,
seized Bhṛgu with his hand from [Bhṛgu’s] hand, as the sun seizes the moon;
saying slowly, "Oh, how wonderful is the established order of destiny!"

The Blessed Bhṛgu rose up like the sun from the mountain of sunrise. Those two treasuries of splendor, having arisen together in perfect union, then shone in that excellent forest thick with *tāla* and *tamāla* trees,
like the full moon and the sun, free from clouds, rising simultaneously in a cloudless sky to sport.

When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Consolation" within the *Bhārgava-upākhyāna*.
The one hundred and thirty-sixth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then the two gods, Kāla and Bhṛgu, [emerged] from a cave of Mount Mandara.
As they set out upon the earth toward the bank of the river Samaṅgā,
those two of great splendor, descending from the mountain,
beheld sky-dwellers sleeping in bowers formed by thickets of fresh golden creepers.
The celestial maidens were playing on swings formed by circles of creepers,
their gazes— so innocent and lovely like those of a doe— calling to mind blue lotuses;
they sat upon high stone slabs used as seats, which were occupied by lions.

They were like personified forms of energy, maintaining their shapes as if they were sheer vigor, looking upon the three worlds with effortless ease; these leaders of elephant herds had their trunks extended high like palm trees,
and, drowsy from the intoxication of rut, they appeared as if the very embodiment of pride itself.
He saw beautiful yak-tail fans, their handles reddened by the filaments of flower-pollen and their tails crimsoned by the wind,
being moved auspiciously by the king;
they were submerged in a continuous downpour of falling flowers.
He saw bees seeking refuge in the branches of *sarja* and date-palm trees; monkeys, fierce as they roamed about, whose cries were drowned out by the clashing of their mutual fruit-strikes,
and whose beautiful faces were as pale-red as mineral pigments.
They saw the perfected ones (siddhas) in grove-palaces whose roofs were covered by canopies of creepers,
being struck by celestial women with *mandāra* flowers;
they appeared as if veiled by a cloth of clouds whose waters had turned pale-red from mineral dust.
The rivers, whose banks were devoid of human contact as if they had been ordained into the Buddhist monastic life,
possessed masses of waves laden with *kunda* and *mandāra* flowers,
as if they had donned the finery of the spring season out of longing for the ocean.

They beheld here and there the abundant splendor of the king of mountains, seeing trees whose limbs were laden with clusters of flowers and shaken by the wind, appearing like intoxicated men reeling upon obtaining wine, their eyes being the swarming bees.
Having reached the earth adorned with cities and towns,
they in an instant arrived there at the river Samaṅgā, which was like a virtuous woman consisting entirely of flowers, with its waves shimmering with blossoms.
Then, on a certain bank of that river, Bhṛgu beheld his son,
who had undergone a transformation into another body and attained a different state—
one whose senses were stilled, established in meditative absorption, and whose fickle deer-like mind was motionless.
He appeared as if resting after a very long time for the sake of quelling his weariness for a very long duration;

he seemed to be contemplating the infinite courses of the ocean of worldly existence, which have been enjoyed for so long and abandoned for so long, and which are filled with an unceasing alternation of joy and sorrow.
Surely it has attained immobility, like a wheel that has spun excessively,
as if due to the extreme exhaustion of revolving through the cycles of the infinite world;
it stands fixed in solitude, lovely, and resorted to by its singular splendor.
He was intent on tranquility, having abandoned the agitation and attachment of the mind;
established in non-conceptual samādhi, he had desisted from the activity of dualities,
laughing at all the worldly courses of existence with a cool intellect.
Having known the entire course of events, with all curiosity vanished,
the web of conceptual construction cast aside, and having taken hold of the Great State;
resting in the Self, which is a state of infinite repose.

Bhrigu beheld his son, whose mind was perfectly awakened and steadfast, free from the conceptual constructions of what is to be rejected or accepted, remaining like a white jewel that does not grasp at reflections.
Beholding that son of Bhṛgu, Kāla spoke these words to Bhṛgu, sounding like the roar of the ocean: "This is indeed your son.
At these words, "May he awaken," he ceased from his meditative absorption.
Like a peacock at the roar of a rain cloud, Bhārgava slowly opened his eyes and beheld before him the two lords, Kāla and Bhṛgu,
who appeared like the two gods, the Moon and the Sun, come together in their full splendor.
Then, rising from their seats of *kadamba* creepers, those two beloved ones,
having come together like the Brahmins Hari and Hara, bowed to one another;
and having performed their mutual courtesies, they sat down upon a stone slab.

On the summit of Mount Meru, like Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, they were worshipped by the world. Then, the twice-born one named Śāntatapās, on the bank of the Samaṅgā river, spoke these peaceful words to them, beautiful as a stream of nectar.
By the sight of you two today, I have attained peace,
as if the world were simultaneously reached by the cool-rayed and the hot-rayed suns.
He who [is not reached] neither by scriptures, nor by austerity, nor by wisdom, nor by learning—
"The delusion of my mind has perished; it has been destroyed by the sight of you two.
Showers of pure nectar do not bring such inner happiness as these glances of the great ones bring us joy."
"O you two of immense splendor, who have purified this region with your feet,
as the moon and sun purify the sky?
To him who had spoken thus, Bhṛgu replied to his son from another birth:
"Remember yourself! You are awakened; you are not ignorant," [said Bhṛgu], O scion of Raghu.
Thus enlightened by Bhṛgu, he remembered his own states from previous births for a mere moment, his eyes opened wide in meditation.
Then, with a face smiling with wonder and a delighted mind,
that best of speakers uttered words slow with reflection:
"Victorious is the Destiny of the Supreme Self, whose undertakings are unceasing!"
By whose power this revolving wheel of the world turns;
my infinite past births, indeed unknown,
have been remembered as they were, rich in their respective conditions and appropriate to them.
I have experienced many activities of manifold splendor,
and infinite fruits of my various conditions extending even to the end of a kalpa;
I have witnessed the harsh exertions and the delusions of acquiring wealth.
For a long time, they dwelt on the peaks of Mount Meru, free from all sorrow;
there they drank the fragrant water of the Mandākinī, reddened by mandāra flowers and mixed with lotuses, upon the slopes of that mountain of the immortals.
I have wandered through the groves of living beings filled with blossoming golden creepers,
and upon Mount Meru, amidst peaks beautiful with the flowers and shade of wish-fulfilling trees.
There is nothing that has not been experienced, and there is nothing that has not been done.
There is nothing that has not been seen among the various perceptions of the desirable and the undesirable.
That which was to be known has now been known; that which was to be seen has been seen unimpaired. I am at rest, long weary; all my delusion has vanished.
"Arise, dear one, let us go; let us see that body situated on Mount Mandara, which is now completely withered like a dried-up forest creeper.
There is nothing here that I do not desire, nor is there anything that I do desire."
I wander about solely to behold the fixed arrangement [of the world].

Why do I follow that auspicious state frequented by the noble ones with a mind fixed on my singular devotion to it? Enough with these desired and undesired things; let them be. I shall engage in this worldly activity that is before me.
In the Bhārgava-episode, the one hundred and thirty-seventh canto, titled "The Description of a Subsequent Birth of Bhārgava," Vasiṣṭha said:
Reflecting thus upon the courses of the world, those knowers of reality moved away from that bank of the Samaṅgā river like shimmering rays of light;
gradually ascending into the sky, they departed through the hollows of the clouds.

They reached Mount Mandara, with its golden caves, by way of the path of the perfected ones (*siddha*). On the plateau of that mountain, Bhārgava beheld his own body from a previous birth, now dried up but still shrouded by fresh leaves.
And he said this: "O father, this is indeed that slender body which was formerly cherished by you with pleasant enjoyments.
This is that body of mine, for which [you once used] heaps of mandāra flowers."
Cool beds were prepared for me in the groves of Mount Meru; behold,
this very body of mine, once caressed by throngs of celestial women,
now lies upon the ground, crushed by the mouths of crawling reptiles.
This very body of mine, by which I long sported in the groves of the Nandana garden,
has now become a withered skeleton;
she who once took delight in the lofty arena of passion through contact with the limbs of celestial nymphs.
Deprived of the activity of the mind, my body here withers away.
Amidst those various diversions and in those various states,
having bound yourself with such mental impressions (bhāvanās), how is it that you remain at ease, O little body?

Alas! Where have you gone? Broken and reduced to the withered state of an ascetic, you have become a mere skeleton; yet you, O unfortunate one, still think of me. By that very body through which I once took delight in amorous pleasures—*mūlam etad vināśasya saṃsārasya ca viddhi bhoḥ / yad idaṃ kāminīnāma kamanīyakathāspadam // MU_3,137.11* "Know this, O friend: that which is called 'the beloved woman,' the locus of alluring talk, is the very root of destruction and of cyclic existence. *yad idaṃ svapnamāyābhaṃ kṛtaṃ cittena cetanam / tad eva pratyayāpekṣaṃ cittam ity abhidhīyate // MU_3,137.12* "That which appears like a dream or an illusion, produced by the mind as a conscious experience—that very thing, when dependent on conditions, is designated as 'mind' (*citta*). *tasmān na cittataḥ kiṃcid anyat tattvaṃ hi vidyate / cittaṃ hi jṛmbhate tādṛg vicitrābhir avasthitaiḥ // MU_3,137.13* "Therefore, no reality exists other than the mind; for the mind expands itself through such various states. *tasmān na cittato 'nyo 'sti mṛtyur nāpi ca janmanā / cittaṃ hi jāyate citraṃ citraṃ mriyate ca tat // MU_3,137.14* "Consequently, there is no death nor even birth other than the mind; for the mind is born in manifold ways, and in manifold ways it dies. *tasmān na cittato 'nyo 'sti kartā bhoktā ca kaścana / cittaṃ hi kurute karma tac ca vai saṃpramuñcati // MU_3,137.15* "Therefore, there is no agent or enjoyer other than the mind; for the mind performs action, and it indeed relinquishes it. *tasmān na cittato 'nyo 'sti karmabandhaḥ kathañcana / cittaṃ hi badhyate citrair bhāvair atha vimucyate // MU_3,137.16* "Therefore, there is no bondage of karma whatsoever other than the mind; for the mind is bound by diverse dispositions and likewise liberated. *tasmān na cittato 'nyo 'sti bandho mokṣo 'pi kaścana / cittaṃ hi jāyate baddhaṃ mucyate ca tathaiva tat // MU_3,137.17* "Therefore, there is no other bondage or liberation apart from the mind; for the mind is born bound, and in the same way, it is liberated. *tasmān na cittato 'nyo 'sti saṃsāro nāpi nirvṛtiḥ / cittaṃ hi jāyate saṃsṛtir nirvāṇaṃ ca tat tathā // MU_3,137.18* "Therefore, there is no cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) nor even cessation (*nirvṛti*) other than the mind; for the mind is born as cyclic existence, and it is likewise nirvāṇa. *tasmān na cittato 'nyo 'sti draṣṭā śrotātha veditā / cittaṃ hi darśanaṃ śravaṃ vedanā ca nigadyate // MU_3,137.19* "Therefore, there is no seer, hearer, or knower other than the mind; for the mind is declared to be seeing, hearing, and feeling. *tasmān na cittato 'nyo 'sti mantā boddhā ca kaścana / cittaṃ hi mananaṃ bodho vijñānaṃ ceti gīyate // MU_3,137.20* "Therefore, there is no thinker or cognizer other than the mind; for the mind is sung of as thinking, awareness, and consciousness. *tasmān na cittato 'nyo 'sti kāmādyāś caiva kevalāḥ / cittaṃ hi kāmakrodhādyair bhāvaiḥ saṃjāyate tathā // MU_3,137.21* "Therefore, there is nothing other than the mind, consisting solely of desire and the rest; for the mind is thus born along with the states of passion, anger, and so forth. *tasmān na cittato 'nyo 'sti kleśajālaṃ ca kevalam / cittaṃ hi kleśajālena sahaiva parivartate // MU_3,137.22* "Therefore, there is no net of afflictions (*kleśa*) other than the mind alone; for the mind revolves together with the web of afflictions. *tasmān na cittato 'nyo 'sti saṃkalpo vikalpa eva ca / cittaṃ hi kalpanāklṛptaṃ vikalpātmakam eva ca // MU_3,137.23* "Therefore, there is no intention or conceptualization other than the mind; for the mind is fashioned by imagination and is essentially of the nature of conceptualization. *tasmān na cittato 'nyo 'sti saṃsargaḥ saṅga eva ca / cittaṃ hi saṅgasambaddhaṃ saṅgād eva vimucyate // MU_3,137.24* "Therefore, there is no association or attachment other than the mind; for the mind is bound by attachment and is liberated from attachment itself. *tasmān na cittato 'nyo 'sti saṃsthānaṃ sthānam eva ca / cittaṃ hi sthānasambaddhaṃ sthānād eva vimucyate // MU_3,137.25* "Therefore, there is no location or stationing other than the mind; for the mind is bound to a place and is liberated from that very place. *tasmān na cittato 'nyo 'sti saṃskāraḥ saṃskṛtaṃ ca yat / cittaṃ hi saṃskṛtaṃ tena saṃskāraiḥ parivartate // MU_3,137.26* "Therefore, there is no formative force (*saṃskāra*) or anything conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) other than the mind; for the mind, being conditioned, revolves through those very formative forces. *tasmān na cittato 'nyo 'sti saṃkleśo vyavadānakam / cittaṃ hi saṃkliṣṭaṃ sat saṃkleśād eva śudhyati // MU_3,137.27* "Therefore, there is no defilement or purification other than the mind; for the mind, being defiled, is purified precisely from defilement. *tasmān na cittato 'nyo 'sti dharmo 'dharmo 'pi kaścana / cittaṃ hi dharmasaṃyuktaṃ dharmād eva vimucyate // MU_3,137.28* "Therefore, there is no merit or demerit whatsoever other than the mind; for the mind, joined with merit, is liberated from merit itself. *tasmān na cittato 'nyo 'sti buddho dharmo 'pi kaścana / cittaṃ hi buddhatāprāptaṃ buddha ity abhidhīyate // MU_3,137.29* "Therefore, there is no Buddha or even any Dharma other than the mind; for the mind, having attained the state of Buddhahood, is designated as 'Buddha'. *tasmān na cittato 'nyo 'sti saṃbuddho dharmakāyakaḥ / cittaṃ hi dharmatāprāptaṃ dharmakāya iti smṛtam // MU_3,137.30* "Therefore, there is no perfectly awakened one (*saṃbuddha*) or Dharm
I am terrified of that very [body] which has now become a skeleton. Behold, where there was once a necklace on my chest with the appearance of a cluster of stars, ants are now crawling upon it.

Behold, by that very body of mine which once captivated excellent women with its luster of molten gold, a skeleton is now being dragged along. Behold these [creatures] with their wide-gaping mouths, wearing the dried skins of ascetics.
In the forest, deer are terrified by the hideous mouth of my mother’s skeleton.
Behold how the cave of my corpse’s belly, being utterly parched,
shines with a web of rays from the sun, as if illuminated by discernment (*viveka*).
With her slender body completely parched, she lies supine upon the forest floor;
by the insignificance of her own self, she seems to lead even those dwelling in the sky toward dispassion,
for she is liberated from the craving for sound, form, taste, touch, and smell.
By means of non-conceptual samādhi alone is my body nourished on this mountain.
That fraction of bliss which the body attains when the vampire of the mind has been completely stilled—
even that is not reached by sovereignty over the world.
Behold, with all its worldly toil at rest and all curiosity vanished,
the body sleeps happily, the web of conceptual constructions cast aside.
The tree of the body was once agitated by the frantic agitation of the monkey-mind.
It moves with such speed that it cuts away its very roots.
Freed from the miseries of the mind, this body of mine— standing like supreme bliss— no longer perceives the agitation caused by elephants, clouds, or lions on the mountain.

I see no other source of welfare for living beings than the state of mindlessness (acittatva), which is like the arrival of autumn to the mist of delusion caused by the fever of all desires. Only those who have reached that state have arrived at the very limit of the enjoyment of happiness.

Those of great intellect and tranquil minds who have attained freedom from mental distress— by good fortune, I behold in this forest this body of mine, liberated from all states of suffering, perfectly stilled, free from fever, and devoid of thought.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, it is said that at that time the descendant of Bhṛgu repeatedly took on very many bodies again and again.
O Sage, since this body was produced by Bhṛgu, what great excellence has arisen in it, or is it merely a lamentation? Vasiṣṭha replied:
O Rāma, that very essence of Śukra which had entered the state of a living being was born as the son of Bhṛgu in the form of Bhārgava, consisting of the nature of karma;
for she, having first emerged from the Supreme State, united with him.
Having reached the state of the elemental ether and being stirred by the wind,
she entered the heart of Bhṛgu through the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths;
gradually attaining the state of semen, she became the body of Uśanas.
Having received the sacraments of a Brahmin, she then went before her father;
after a long time, she reached the state of a withered skeleton.
When that body of Brahmā first arrived here, [it was thus].
Then, in response to that lamentation, Śukra—
though free from passion and devoid of desire, having assumed the form of the Brahmin Samaṅgā— grieved for his own body; for such is the nature of that which is born of the physical frame.
However, under the guise of grief, that wise one demonstrated for the sake of attaining detachment that distinction between the body and the embodied soul;
for both the knower and the ignorant, this is the course of the body as long as life lasts.
Worldly convention proceeds either through capacity or incapacity at all times.
Those who have fully realized the goal and those who are ignorant, following the nature of cattle,
remain within worldly conventions like a forest thicket.
Just as the worldly person is ignorant, so indeed is the wise man;
the only difference here lies in their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which is the cause of bondage and liberation.
For as long as there is a body, there is suffering in suffering and pleasure in pleasure.
The wise, whose intellects are unattached, appear like those who are not awakened;
they are always happy amidst pleasures and sorrowful amidst painful conditions.
For these great-souled ones are seen to be truly cool within.
The reflections of a pillar tremble, but its form remains steady;
likewise, for the wise man, only the organs of action tremble, but his mind remains steady.
By means of this movement and stillness, the knower of reality abides amidst the activities of the world.
Like the sun reflected in waters, it remains pure even while appearing below.
One whose intellect is unawakened is indeed bound, even if they have abandoned worldly actions;
one whose intellect is awakened is indeed liberated, even if they continue to sport with delusion.
For one whose faculty of intellect is liberated is liberated even if the faculty of action is bound;

likewise, one whose faculty of intellect is bound is bound even if the faculty of action is liberated. In this world, there is the perception of pleasure and pain, as well as the perception of bondage and liberation.
The sense organs alone are the cause, like fires for illumination.
Engaged in conduct appropriate for the external world, yet devoid of internal conduct,
remain equanimous as if non-existent, with all desires completely stilled.
Free from all desires, abiding in the Self by means of the self, perform the actions that must be done; for your true state is indeed centered in the mind.
On the path of worldly existence, which is a pit with great whirlpools of mental and physical afflictions, [remain steadfast].
Do not fall into this blind well of "mine-ness," which bestows misery.
O lotus-eyed one, you do not exist in things, nor do things exist in you;
you are of the nature of pure awakening—remain firm, established in the Self.

O Great-Souled One, if you have attained the stainless state free from longing, in which the great darkness of the notion of "mine" has vanished, and if you thus prevail over the mind, then homage to you, the one of supreme intellect and the truly existent! The One Hundred and Thirty-Eighth Chapter.
Vasiṣṭha:
Then, having rebuked those words of Bhrigu’s son,
the blessed Kāla spoke these words in a deep resonance.
Kāla said:
"O Bhārgava, having cast off this body of a Samaṅgā ascetic, enter this body, O virtuous one, just as a king enters his city. (MU 3.138.2)
"O sinless one, having performed penance with this body of yours in a former birth, you must again assume the position of the lords of the Asuras when the end of the great aeon has arrived;
at that time, you shall assume the form of Bhārgava."

This [body] should be abandoned like a withered flower so that there is no further grasping. O high-minded one, having attained the state of liberation while living, remain in this body of its former form, acting as the teacher to the great lords of the asuras.
"May it be well with you both; we shall go to our desired direction.
There is not even the slightest thing that would not be desired by him.
Having spoken thus, as they were releasing the flower, he vanished from between them.
Like the sun, the radiant one, with its rays, [pervades] heaven and earth;
when that Blessed One had departed after speaking of that destiny,
Bhārgava reflected upon the unbreakable and fixed course of necessity.
Like the month of Mādhava entering a beautiful creeper that has been withered by the cause of time yet is destined to produce flowers and fruit, he entered that young body;
that Brahmin body lay upon the ground with its face and limbs turned pale.

She fell down quickly, trembling like a creeper whose roots have been severed. When her body, which was her son, had entered [the womb], the great sage performed a restoration with mantras and the water from his water-pot.
Then all the slender channels of that [vein] shone,
filled as if they were rivers whose hollows are brimming with floods of water during the rainy season;
she was like a lotus pond in the rains, or like a fresh creeper in the spring.
When she was full, her vital breaths began to sprout. Then Śukra arose, his life-force and breath flowing forth,
like a cloud filled with rain through the union of moisture and wind.
He of pure appearance first saluted his father,
just as a cloud newly risen greets a mountain with its thunder.
Then the father embraced his son’s body, as he had done in former times.

Bhṛgu beheld his former body, now possessed of a son, with a heart moistened by affection, just as a cloud, dripping with moisture, beholds a mountain slope after a long time. The conviction that "this one was born from me" carries away even a man of great intelligence.
The thought "this is my son" then drew even Bhṛgu [to him];
for this sense of "otherness" and "belonging to oneself" persists as long as physical form exists.
Then the father and son became mutually adorned by one another.
They were like the sun and the lotus-pond, both rejoicing at the end of the night;
like a pair of cakravāka birds joined after a long separation; or like the peacock and the cloud, whose deep affection increases with the arrival of the rainy season.
Having stayed there for a moment with that conversation, which was suited to their long-standing and firm longing,
those two of great intelligence then rose up and reduced the body of that Brahmin at Samaṅgā to ashes right then and there.
For who indeed, born into this world, does not follow established conduct?
Thus did those two, Bhṛgu and Bhārgava, established in that purifying forest,
blazing with ascetic power like the moon and the sun in the sky.
The two masters of the world, Cera and Jñātavijñeya, were liberated while living;
their penance was easy to perform and firmly established amidst the floods of place, time, and circumstances.
Then, in the course of time, that Śukra attained the status of preceptor to the Asuras.
Bhṛgu also established himself in his own appropriate, healthy state.
This Śukra, of noble fame, was first born from this supreme state in due order;
later, however, through a swift lapse of memory, he became thus utterly confused amidst various other conditions.
In the Bhārgava-episode, the chapter titled "The Rebirth of Śukra," the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter;
Rāma said:
"Blessed One, why is it that the inspired flash of insight belonging to the son of Bhṛgu became fruitful for him through his own experience, yet does not likewise occur for another? Vasiṣṭha replied:
Then, from the state of Brahmā, there first arose that pure intellect of Bhārgava, unstained by any other birth;
it was the pure abiding of the mind resulting from the complete cessation of all desires.

That is called *sattva*; it is declared to be this very stainless consciousness (*cit*). Whatever the mind, whose nature is pure *sattva*, contemplates in such a manner, that very thing quickly comes to be exactly so, just like a whirlpool in the water of the ocean.
Just as this delusion arose spontaneously for the son of Bhṛgu,
so too is each individual case here illustrated by the example of Bhṛgu’s son;
just as the seed brings forth its own sprout, leaf, and so on, in a wondrous manner.
Indeed, for all the hosts of beings, it is just like a whirlpool in a thicket of reeds;
for this entire universe that is perceived is exactly thus: each thing, having arisen falsely, likewise goes to its setting falsely.
Nothing in this world sets nor does it rise for anyone;
this is mere delusion, a magical illusion that expands in vain.
Just as this thicket of saṃsāra appears to us in our own perception, so it exists.
Likewise, thousands of them indeed exist unseen by one another;
just as the transactions of dream-cities and mental constructs are not seen separately from each other, so too are these delusions of saṃsāra.
In this way, there exist multitudes of cities whose forms consist of mental constructs within the sky;
yet they are not seen by one another except through the vision of knowledge.
For indeed, there exist piśācas, yakṣas, and rakṣasas of such a nature.
"O descendant of Raghu, our bodies consist of mere volition and are composed of pleasure and pain; in this very way, we and these others have come into being,
having forms consisting of our own volitions, conditioned by the state of false reality."
For the cycle of creation and transmigration exists among others in exactly this manner;
yet it is not real in an ultimate sense, for it is established within that which is non-substantial.
Thus, indeed, the entire universe arises individually and in vain.
Just as the spring juice [manifests] through the form of new buds,
so too this first [state], one's own volition (*svasaṅkalpa*), has attained great expansion;
it is thus conceived with such firmness that it appears as the ultimate reality itself.
Each individual thought that has arisen, abiding within the belly of its own inherent nature,
perishes as it perceives this world as having such-and-such an undertaking.
By the power of appearance it exists, but by the observation of the actual reality, it does not exist.
The long dream is the web of the world, the tethering post for the elephant of the mind.
For the existence of the world is indeed the existence of the mind, and the existence of the mind is the world;
in the absence of one, both are destroyed, and that occurs through the investigation of reality.
For the manifestation of a pure mind is indeed true;
for the application of saffron dye adheres to a stainless cloth.
Indeed, when not brought about by another, another quality necessarily increases.
When the mind is not assailed by volitional constructions, intuitive insight arises.
Just as gold does not maintain its brilliance when covered by a soiled garment,
so too a single-pointed vision does not attain stability when the mind is withered.
Just as a gem is purified by polishing and copper by the application of a proper method, so too does the purification of the mind arise from long and firm practice. Rāma said:
In this world, which is of the nature of a reflection, how could these sequences of time and action, along with their rising and setting, arise for the mind of Śukra? Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as this world was seen by Śukra through his father and mother,
so did it remain established in his mind, like a peacock within a peacock’s egg.
From the treasury of its own nature, that [world] was relished by him and arose through this gradual process.

Just as from a seed there arise sprouts, leaves, creepers, flowers, and fruits, so too the living soul perceives within itself that which is the essence of its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*). In this regard, a dream serves as the illustration; this world is simply a long-lasting dream.
"O Rāma, has this thicket of saṃsāra not indeed arisen individually?
At night, it is clearly manifest within one's own self, like the web of dreams of men in an army.
Rāma said:
"This flood of the forest of worldly existence comes together of its own accord;
or perhaps it does not. You ought to tell me this correctly.
Vasiṣṭha replied:

For a defiled mind lacking vigor does not deserve union with another, just as two pieces of iron that have not been heated do not adhere to each other; yet when they are purified and heated, they do melt together.
Similarly, pure principles of consciousness (cittatattva) coalesce with one another.
For waters of a single form attain unity, but not those that are turbid.
Indeed, the purity of the mind is the state of being free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which is a singular state consisting of the non-perception of unreal objects.
Having awakened from that state of deep sleep—the state of the Self—one attains union with the Supreme through the application of those subtle elements alone.
The one hundred and fortieth canto, titled "The Convergence of the Kingdom of Dreams," by Vasiṣṭha.

In all the thickets of saṃsāra, there is no difference in the manifestation of that which consists of the nature of the seed-form and parts, appearing as the mere subtle elements (*tanmātra*). Whether it be active engagement or cessation, it is preceded by the attainment of those very subtle elements.

Immediately after all living beings have entered into deep sleep, those individual souls who possess active engagement reach the state of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). Through their unity with these subtle elements, they perceive mutually imagined creations.
Through the single channel of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the variegated reservoirs of creation mingle with one another and attain density on all sides;
some remain in a separate state, while others undergo dissolution separately.
Some mutually joined world-clusters are situated there;
where thousands of world-clusters, numbering in the infinite, exist within every atom without touching one another— that is the forest named Brahman.
Having attained density, it does not enter into mutual union;
whatever has grown in whatever place and in whatever manner, that alone it perceives, and nothing else.
Due to the power of present mental constructions, there is a succession of individual lives.
The habitual tendencies of the successive creations have merged together;
the existence of the body has become deeply rooted, while the absence of the body has been forgotten.
Because of this deep-rooted identification with the body, the sky of consciousness has forgotten its true self.
Just as the pure vital breath (*prāṇamarut*), through the piercing of another's vital breath,
perceives the kingdom of the mind of the one to be pierced, so too does that which resides in man perceive the [various] creations.
It rests upon the three states of the self of all multitudes of living beings.

In this regard, the body is not the cause of what is called waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. Thus, the state of being a living soul within the Self— which consists of these three other states— shines forth as corporeality, just as the state of being waves appears in water heated by heat.

Having reached the state of the digit of consciousness (citkalā) and remaining in the state at the end of deep sleep, the awakened individual soul turns back from it; the deluded one proceeds toward creation.
Indeed, when there is purity of intrinsic nature, then loving-kindness (maitrī) proceeds.
The manifestation of one's own benevolence consists precisely in the oneness of the two;
an ignorant individual soul (jīva), having awakened from deep sleep, partakes in its own creation, while another, due to the omnipresence of consciousness, is led by the creation of another.
In every creation, there exist other creations of distinct forms;
within those as well, there are floods of further creations, like the layers of a plantain tree's leaf-sheath.
In each creation, it possesses the function of being thick with the foliage that fills it with other creations.
The pavilion of Brahma’s plantain leaves is naturally cool.
Just as there is no otherness within the plantain tree even amidst its hundreds of leaves,
so too there is no otherness within the reality of Brahman even amidst its hundreds of creations.
Just as a seed, having become a fruit through its sap, becomes a seed again, so Brahman,
having become the mind, becomes Brahman again through awakening.
The seed, having sap as its cause, unfolds into the state of a fruit.
The individual soul, having Brahman as its cause, expands in the form of the universe.
It is not appropriate to say what the cause of that essence (rasa) might be;
because it is without distinction, it is not appropriate to speak of anything further than its own inherent nature (svabhāva).
Furthermore, it is impossible to assert non-existence anywhere in that which consists of all things;
nor is there a cause or the like in that which is not a cause, or in the primordial cause.
Just as a seed, having abandoned its own form, is seen when it has become the fruit.
Brahmā abandoned his own body, yet the fruit and the seed remain established.
Since everything possesses the form of a seed, that state (the Śiva-principle) is formless;
it is not possible to equate them, and therefore there is no analogy for the Auspicious One.
Space itself is born from the nature of space, yet it is not born as something other than that;
therefore, know, O Brahman, that the world is neither born nor unborn, like the sky.
Seeing the visible, the seer does not perceive his own self.
For one whose consciousness is overwhelmed by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), how can its innate state arise?
When the delusion of water in a mirage exists, what is skillfulness? But when skillfulness exists, what is that mirage?
The seer, as pure as space, though all-pervading, does not see itself, just as one cannot see one's own eye; alas, what a delusion that the self has become an object of sight!
Even with effort, Brahman, which is as pure as space, is not found.
But when that which is visible is not seen as something visible, its attainment is very far off.
Where even something as gross as you are not seen without focused attention,
there the visibility of a subtle seer is cast far away indeed.
The seer remains only the seer and does not touch the state of being seen;
and while the object of sight is seen by him, O Rāma, the seer is not seen.
Only the seer alone exists as one; for here, the object of sight does not exist at all.

If the Seer, who is the self of all, remains as the object of sight, how can there be any state of being an object? Whatever is accomplished by a king endowed with all powers, in whatever manner, that very thing quickly comes to be so; he himself arises in that very form.
Just as a cluster of mango trees becomes radiant without ever ceasing its state of sapidity,
and remains exalted with its fruits, flowers, and leaves,
so too the radiance of consciousness, having become the individual soul (jīva), becomes the embodied being.
Without ever abandoning that state of pure consciousness (cinmātratā), consisting of the vision of seeing,
the earthy essence arises from its own self through thousands of various streams of non-dual forms; in the same way, consciousness arises through the delusions of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhrama).
No end can be perceived here to the trees of the efflorescence of consciousness, which shine by themselves within themselves and are rich with hundreds of branches of the visible world;
just as each individual cluster [of flowers] possesses its own internal wonder of flavor.
In this way, this consciousness experiences [the world] and perceives the cycles of transmigration as distinct.
Whatever individual cycle of transmigration arises for whichever living power (*jīvaśakti*) and in whatever manner,
that consciousness within it undergoes that very state of existence of beings and worlds accordingly.
Certain streams of living beings meet one another;
having wandered through saṃsāra on their own, they find peace after a long time.
In this same way, you perceive yourself through this subtle and supreme vision.
Thousands of world-nets exist even within the interior of a single atom;
they exist in walls, in space, in stone, in flame, in wind, and in water—indeed, in everything, like oil in sesame seeds. These are the targets of the cycle of existence.
When the mind attains purity, then the individual soul (jīva) becomes pure consciousness (citi).

That [consciousness] is both pure and all-pervading; therefore, there is a mutual merging of all [souls], beginning with those born from the lotus, which fulfills their own existence through delusion.
The world is a long, great dream that has arisen within itself.
Some successions of beings go from one dream to another;
therefore, their perception of walls and such remains most firmly established.
Whatever one contemplates anywhere, that quickly becomes fully manifest there;
even that which is seen by consciousness in a dream is truly real at that very moment.
Within the atom of consciousness, all atoms of experience exist.

Just as within a seed there exist the atoms of leaves, creepers, flowers, and fruits, so too does the supreme atomic consciousness contain the world within itself. Space is latent within space; abandon the delusion of duality and unity.
By means of its own atoms, designated as space, time, action, and so forth,
consciousness itself experiences the atoms within, since no other atom is possible;
it is itself the manifest, transparent mass of conscious atoms of everything.

From Brahmā down to the insect, experienced through the perception of a body, only something very slight is manifested here; yet in reality, there is nothing at all. The atoms of consciousness themselves, which are supreme, relish their own self-nature as duality.
The mass of conscious atoms (cidaṇu), possessing an expansive body, shines forth by itself,
emitting the fragrance of consciousness through the flower-like openings of the eyes and other senses;
some [of these] perceive others as external forms, which are in reality dense masses of consciousness.
Because consciousness (*citi*) is all-pervading and indestructible, it is the seed of all that is visible;
therefore, a certain person perceives the entire world in its completeness within [consciousness] alone.
Therein, through prolonged mental construction (*kalana*), one emerges and submerges.
There, seeing one dream after another again and again,
he rolled about in false pits like a stone fallen from a mountain peak;
some were closed in, while others remained in delusion within themselves.
Great masses of embodied beings, vibrating with the essence of their own self-awareness,
perceive within themselves the delusive agitation of the world and living beings;
by some of them, that [world] is perceived in such a way as something unreal, like a dream.
Because the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is the self of all, that which is visible is real within the Self;
for wherever the All-pervading One is present, there indeed everything arises.
Furthermore, within the creation that appears inside the individual soul (jīva)...
A cluster of living beings arises high up, and within that, another as well;
from one living being another is born, and within that too is yet another living being. Everywhere, like the fibers of a plantain leaf, the seed of life continues to live.

This infinite [reality] is equal to the transformation of the perception of the visible; just as the state of being a bracelet or other ornaments in gold vanishes through mere thorough understanding, so too for one in whom no inquiry arises—such as "Who am I? or "What is this?"—it is enough.
For him who is not liberated from its beginning and end, this long feverish delusion of living persists;
but for that person of right mind for whom discernment has borne fruit,
his greed for enjoyments diminishes day by day.
Just as medicine that is properly applied to the body brings about health,
so too does discernment, when directed toward the conquest of the senses, bear fruit.
Discernment exists only in words, shining like a fire in a painting.
For one by whom discernment has been abandoned, it leads only to suffering.
Just as the wind manifests its existence through touch and not through speech,
so too is his discernment understood to exist only through the attenuation of desire.
Know that the nectar in a painting is not truly nectar; know that the fire in a painting is not truly fire.
A woman in a painting is surely no woman at all; likewise, discernment in words is merely a lack of discernment.
Through prior discernment, passion becomes attenuated, and then enmity is uprooted entirely.
Afterwards, it is indeed exhausted; where that exhaustion exists, there is discernment.
Thus ends the chapter on Origination, titled "The Incarnation of Jīvaṣaṇḍaka," within the Bhārgava-episode of the *Mokṣopāya*.
4. Prakaraṇa: The First Creation; Vasiṣṭha:
Now, immediately after the section on origination, hear this, O Rāma: the section on persistence, which, when known, brings about liberation.
The seed of the individual soul is the Supreme Brahman, stable everywhere like space.
Therefore, even within the world that is the belly of the living being, there exists a living being in manifold ways.
Because of the nature of the single, dense mass of consciousness, various species of living beings exist within other living beings,
like insects within the belly of a man or like the layers of a plantain tree.
O Rāma, just as in the summer heat a worm may arise from a film of sweat,
so too, by virtue of its own consciousness, the void itself spontaneously becomes a living being, assuming whatever name corresponds to each particular form.
In whatever manner those living beings strive for the realization of their own selves, [so do they become].
In that very way, they quickly become so through various methods of worship:
those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods; those who sacrifice to the yakṣas go to the yakṣas;
those who sacrifice to Brahman go to Brahman. Therefore, one should take refuge in that which is not insignificant.
For that Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, because of the purity of his own consciousness,
was quickly bound by nature through the object of perception seen for the first time. That which is before him, fresh and unfading, is what the child perceives at first.
Consciousness attains that form; it becomes nothing else whatsoever.
Rāma said: "O Blessed One, you should explain the distinction between the states of waking and dreaming."
And how might there be waking while awake? How might there be dreaming while not awake?
Vasiṣṭha replied: That which is characterized by stable conviction is called waking.
That which has unstable conditions is declared to be a dream.
If waking were to last for only a moment, then a dream would endure for a long duration;
thus waking becomes dream-like, and a dream attains the state of waking.
The distinction between the states of waking and dreaming does not exist without stability and instability;
yet, the experience of all things is always equal in both.
That which attains stability is called the waking state.
Listen to how a dream, which consists of momentary destruction, comes to be:
"The life-element exists within the body by means of which one lives;
that which is called heat, vigor, the life-element, and so forth—know that, my dear, to be it. (MU 4.1.13–14)
When the body, through mind, action, and speech, becomes active in worldly engagement,
then that perfected *jīvadhātu* (vital principle) flows forth.
As it flows through the limbs, consciousness indeed arises from touch.
Because it is nourished, it receives the name "mind" (*citta*), wherein the delusion of the world is internally dissolved;
streaming forth through the apertures such as the eyes toward the external world, it perceives within itself a form rich with various shapes and transformations. (MU 4.1.16–17)
Because of its stability, that state is likewise understood as "waking";
this is called the sequence of waking. Now hear the sequence beginning with deep sleep:
when the body is not agitated by mind, action, or speech.
Then this pure element of life remains tranquil;
with the vital breaths (*vāta*) having attained equilibrium, it is no longer disturbed within the heart, like a lamp in a windless chamber that provides only light. (MU 4.1.19–20)
Consequently, consciousness does not move through the limbs, and for that reason it is not agitated;
it does not enter the eyes and other senses, nor does it go outside.
The living soul vibrates only within, like the consciousness of oil within a sesame seed.
The perception of cold is like that of snow, and the perception of oiliness is as it is in clarified butter.
The individual soul (jīva), remaining for a certain moment within itself in a state of tranquility,
enters the state of deep sleep— a condition that is serene, devoid of consciousness, and like a gentle breeze.
Having known this, when the mind has ceased, one who remains tranquil even while engaged in worldly activity—
awakened throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep— is said to possess the fourth state (turya).
When he is moved by the vital breaths that have attained gentleness from the state of deep sleep, [he emerges].
That is the element of life, that is consciousness; from that, it arises as the state of mind (citta).
Residing within its own interior, it quickly perceives the entire web of the world within itself alone—vast, yet through its various parts and sequential delusions—just as a seed [perceives] a tree.
When the element of life (jīvadhātu) is slightly agitated by the vital winds (vāta),
it then moves like the sky and perceives within itself a motion in the void.
When it is flooded by water, it then experiences the agitation of water and so forth.
Just as a flower experiences its own fragrance within itself, so too,
when one is overcome by bile or other humors, one experiences the entire expansion of the confusion caused by the heat of the fire-element and so forth entirely within, as if it were outside.

When one perceives external places and times as red and filled with blood due to their nature as mere experience, one sinks right there; or rather, whatever latent impression (*vāsanā*) one cultivates, that one sees within while asleep. *Māṇḍūkya-kārikā* 4.1.30.
Just as [water] agitated by winds through apertures such as the eyes flows outward, so too,
when the apertures of the senses are not invaded and he remains undisturbed within,
that consciousness which he experiences immediately is called a dream.
"The wise say that waking is when one whose sensory apertures are fully occupied perceives through external consciousness while being agitated.
Now that you have understood this, O one of great renown and vast intellect, you should here abide in the conviction of reality.
If the world does not exist, then the contemplation of death, destruction, and the defects of saṃsāra is certainly not to be cultivated.
The Second Chapter: An Inquiry into the Nature of Waking, Dreaming, Deep Sleep, and the Fourth State.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāghava, all this has been told to you by me for the purpose of defining the form of the mind, and not for any other reason whatsoever."
Whatever the mind, with firm resolve, contemplates repeatedly, that it becomes,
just as a lump of iron attains the state of fire through contact with flames.
The perceptions of existence and non-existence, of grasping and abandoning, are imagined by the mind.
They are neither unreal nor real; they are caused by the fickleness of the mind.
For the mind is the cause and the agent, the instrument for the existence of the world;
it is the defiled mind that expands this [universe] in the form of the manifold variety.

For the mind, O Rāma, is indeed the person; it must be directed onto the auspicious path, since all prosperities in the world are achieved solely through its conquest. If the body were truly the self, how could the high-minded Śukra have [said otherwise]?
It undergoes various divisions arising from many bodies.
Therefore, the person is indeed the mind, and the body is indeed the mind;
whatever this [body] consists of, that he undoubtedly attains.
Exert yourself to pursue that which is not void, effortless, free from limiting conditions, and beyond delusion; you shall attain its true nature.
The body falls into the state of the mind, but the mind does not go toward the activities of the body.
Let your mind here fly toward that [Truth], O fortunate one; by that truth, let it abandon all other untruth.
The third canto, titled "The Examination of the Form of the Mind."
Rāma:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, this great doubt of mine churns restlessly within my heart like a wave in the ocean.
In that which is unconditioned by space, time, and the like, pervasive, eternal, and free from affliction—
whence has this withered consciousness called "mind" arisen?
For there exists nothing else besides it, neither in the past nor in the future.
"From where, of what nature, how, and where does his stain exist?
Vasiṣṭha replied: "Excellent, Rāma! You have spoken well; you have become a partaker in liberation."

Your intellect, the supreme outflow of wisdom, is like a cluster of blossoms on the Nandana tree. Devoted to the investigation of what precedes and follows, this mind of yours shall attain that lofty state which was reached by Śaṅkara and the other great sages.
"But for this question of yours, O Rāma, the time is not yet right.
This question is addressed only where the final conclusion (siddhānta) is being told. You should ask me about this matter at the time of the final conclusion."
"Therefore, your doctrine will be as clear as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand.
This question of yours shines forth at the time for establishing the doctrine;
for the cry of the peacock is appropriate only in the rainy season, while the song of the swan is fitting in autumn."
The innate blueness in the sky shines at the end of the rainy season,
whereas during the rains it arises from thick and towering masses of clouds. This excellent determination of the mind, which was commenced as the subject at hand, [is now concluded].

"Listen, O observer of noble vows, to that by whose power the birth of living beings occurs. Thus, O Rāma, it has been determined by all seekers of liberation that this very *prakṛti*, characterized by the mental activity of the mind, is what constitutes action (*karman*)."
Listen to how that [mind], through its various characteristics,
has come to possess manifold names as eloquent speakers describe it with diverse philosophical perspectives:
"Whatever state the mind, flickering in its thinking, assumes..."
Just as the wind, dwelling in the midst of thick fragrances, carries each one of them; so too,
having determined that very object and conceptualizing it,
he colors his own sense of self with that internal coloring.
Taking that certainty as his basis, he attains flavor (rasa) in that very [object];
then, through being composed of that, he experiences it in the body and subsequently even in the faculties of perception.
For, O Rāma, whatever the mind is composed of, the body follows that, by virtue of its subjection to it.
It attains the state of being that very [object], just as the wind within a fragrance attains the state of being that fragrance.
When the sense organs of cognition are active, the group of organs of action then vibrates of its own accord, like particles of dust on the earth stirred by a gentle breeze.
When the group of organs of action is agitated, it fully manifests its own power;
thus, extensive action is produced from it, like a mass of dust from the wind.
For such is the activity of the mind; the mind is known as the seed of action.
The existence of these two is indeed non-different, just as that of a flower and its fragrance.
Whatever state the mind assumes through the power of firm habituation,
such is its vibration called "action," and in that same way it relinquishes its branches.
Likewise, he diligently brings about the action that yields its fruit;
then, having quickly experienced the very taste thereof, he is bound.
Whatever state he assumes, he perceives that very thing as reality.
The conviction arises in him that there is no other excellence than this. Indeed,
for the sake of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation,
they always strive with firm dispositions through their very own practice.
Having fully embraced their own doctrine through the mental faculties of the followers of Kapila and having determined it, they have fashioned scriptural perspectives;
for they believe that there is no other way to attain liberation. Thus is their mind cultivated.
Established in their own delusions regarding their respective rules, they remain intent on revealing their own views.
The proponents of Vedānta, through an intellect firmly rooted in the conviction "this is Brahman," having determined and formulated arguments endowed with tranquility and self-control, [proceed].

But for those whose minds are convinced that there is no other way to attain liberation, the proponents of Consciousness-Only (Vijñānavādins) remain fixed in their own restrictive delusions, further elaborating their own view according to a cognition whose very nature is a shimmering illusion. *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā-vṛtti* 4.3.27.

They reveal their own views through their own delusions regarding restrictive rules (niyama). By other schools as well, such as the Ārhata and others, various scriptural perspectives have been fashioned according to their own preferred desires and diverse modes of conduct. (MU 4.3.28–29)
Indeed, various styles of composition arise through their own mature certainties, like a multitude of gentle water bubbles rising from a causeless source;
for there is but one single mine for all these styles.
O mighty-armed one, the mind is like the ocean for jewels.
Neither the nimba tree nor the sugarcane are inherently bitter or sweet; neither the moon nor fire are cold or hot.
Whatever is practiced by the mind is perceived exactly in that way.
One should indeed strive for that unconditioned bliss;
the mind must be led to consist of that, and by this it is attained.
Abandoning the mind—which is trivial and situated within the puppet-show of saṃsāra—one should focus on the visible [reality].
One is not helplessly dragged away by the pleasure and pain born thereof.
O sinless one, do not contemplate the visible world— which is impure, unreal in nature, delusive, a cause of fear, a mere appearance, expansive, and a bond.
This is illusion; this is ignorance; this is mental cultivation that brings fear.
The wise know that "action" (karman) is the state of consciousness becoming identified with that [object].
Know that the mind's delusion consists in its total absorption in the unity of the seer and the seen.
And that which is false exists merely for the sake of delusion, like the act of digging a hole in the earth.
This experience of being identical with the visible world, which is the very nature [of the ignorant],
is called the wine of saṃsāra, or ignorance (avidyā), by the wise.
Afflicted by this, the world does not attain what is auspicious,
just as one whose eyes are blinded by a cataract cannot perceive the brilliant light of the sun.
And it arises spontaneously from conceptual construction, like a tree in the sky.

By mere non-mental-construction (asaṅkalpana), it perishes of its own accord. O Mahāmati, when mental cultivation (bhāvanā) has been exhausted through mere non-mental-construction, by its own clarity and through playful discernment (vimarśa).
When all objects have attained stability within the state of non-attachment,
when the vision of truth has become clear, and when the unreal has come to an end,
that Self— the pure essence of non-conceptual consciousness— is fully realized.
For whom there is neither non-existence nor existence, neither pleasure nor even suffering;
for whom the state of absolute oneness alone is perceived within,
through an indestructible contemplation and not by means of the mind, the senses, or visual perception.
He who is abandoned by infinite latent impressions (vāsanās), though they are non-different from himself, is like the sky [freed] from rows of clouds;
for just as the state of being a snake is attributed to a rope when it is indistinctly perceived, so indeed is this [state of bondage].

Bondage is imagined by that which is itself unbound, through the nature of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). Just as the sky appears different in day and night, an imagined object assumes another state through a further imagination of it.
Whatever is not void, effortless, free from conditions, and beyond delusion— that very thing,
through its conceptualization as such, conduces only to happiness.
Just as there is fear because one thinks "there is a lion inside an empty granary," so too does conceptualization lead to suffering when directed toward what is unreal.
Likewise, there is the fear that "I am bound within this empty body.
Just as when one looks inside an empty granary and no lion is found,
so too, when examined, nothing worthy of being bound in saṃsāra is found.
"This world" and "this I"— this delusion has arisen among the ignorant,
like a flickering shadow in the dark of night.
Through the power of conceptual construction, for a living being, there arise existence and non-existence, as well as the auspicious and the inauspicious.
In an instant they pass into non-existence, and again and again they return to existence.
Like a mother who has assumed the state of a housewife and hangs from one's neck,
she performs the duties of a wife, bestowing the bliss of sexual union.
Like a beloved taken as one's own mother, she hangs around the neck and causes one to utterly forget the state of intoxication caused by the god of love;
