and having observed the multitude of objects that yield fruits according to one's inner disposition, [one realizes this].
In this world, a single form is not declared for objects by the wise.
Through firm contemplation, whatever the mind intensely contemplates,
it perceives that very result in that form for that duration of time.
There is nothing that is not true, and there is nothing that is not false;
in whatever manner and by whatever means something is determined, it is perceived as such by that [means].
The mind, having imagined an elephant in the sky, perceives itself as that very elephant in the sky.
He pursues the female elephant of the forest of the sky who stands within the sky.
Therefore, O Rāghava, abandon volition itself— which consists of the nature of all things— and, being well-established, remain in the Self by means of your own self.
For a gem, due to its insentient nature, is incapable of the act of negating reflections; but such is not the case for one like you, O Rāma.
Whatever, O Rāma, is reflected here in the jewel of your mind—
Having determined that it is a non-entity, do not allow yourself to be colored by it; or, considering that very [entity] as real and non-different from the Supreme Self,
contemplate the Self, which is without beginning or end, by means of the self.
O Rāghava, may those objects that reflect in your mind not color you— your self being attached to others— just as they do not color a crystal.
Just as various new dyes enter a stainless crystal and become manifest, [so too do thoughts appear in the mind].
Indeed, let the desires for worldly existence enter you here in such a way that they manifest clearly.
The Fourth Chapter: The Doctrine of Consciousness (Vijñānavāda).
Vasiṣṭha:

For a person who has practiced inquiry, whose mind’s habitual tendencies have dissolved, who abandons discursive thought through the knowledge of the Self, and who has partially realized the Self— *Mokṣopāya* 4.4.1 [= *Mahārtha-mañjarī* 4.22.1].
For one who has abandoned the visible as something to be discarded and has attained that which is to be accepted;
who perceives the Seer while not perceiving the visible,
and who remains awake within the supreme reality even while living and not asleep— MU 4.4.2.
While sleeping on the path of saṃsāra, which consists of dense delusion,
he is devoid of taste even for flavors because of their ultimate and absolute insipidity; he is disinterested in enjoyments that are delightful when indulged in, being free from all desire.
When the dullness of the mind has fully worn away and attachment has dissolved, the self attains oneness with the waters,
just as a mass of snow melts in the heat;
even amidst those states that are surging with waves and restless in their inner turmoil.
Then, as the cravings subside like rivers at the end of the rainy season,
the net of worldly tendencies is torn apart— like a bird-net by a rat—
with the swift force of disillusionment that loosens even the most stubborn knots.
Just as water becomes clear upon reaching the *kataka* fruit,
so too does one's own nature become perfectly serene through the power of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*).
Free from passion, free from attachment, free from the pairs of opposites, and free from dependence.
The mind emerges from delusion like a bird from a cage.
With its wickedness and doubts stilled, and its restlessness and confusion gone,
the mind, its inner space fulfilled, shines like the full moon.
Having produced supreme beauty, with her raised and lowered parts cast far apart,
she rises everywhere as evenness, like a sea when the winds have subsided;
yet she is composed of darkness, deluded, with an interior shattered by dullness.
The latent impressions of saṃsāra become thin, like the night at dawn; when the sun of consciousness has been seen, the lotus-plant of wisdom— with its shoots of merit—
blooms with stainless radiance, like the sky at morning in embodied form.
Wisdom captivates the heart and is capable of delighting the world;
the fortunes of sentient beings proceed like the rays of the full moon.
What is the use of saying more here? The one of great intelligence has known that which is to be known.
It neither rises nor sets, being like the sheath of space which has no real existence.
For one who has realized the true nature of the Self through inquiry,
even these— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śaṅkara— become objects of compassion.

Even while manifesting outwardly, those whose inner mind is free from egoism cannot be reached by conceptual constructions, just as deer cannot reach the water of a mirage. Like waves, these worlds come and go on all sides.
Embrace the wise one within yourself; death and birth do not exist for him.
Manifestation and disappearance constitute transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), and nothing else follows this sequence.
Thus, when these two are clearly perceived as such, he delights in them and does not suffer.
Just as the space within a jar is neither born nor dies when the jar is decorated or defiled, so it is here with the Self-possessor (ātman) when the body is adorned or impaired;
once discernment has dawned, the heavy burden of false delusion subsides.
Latent impressions perish like a mirage in the desert when the clouds have vanished.
As long as one has not investigated "Who am I? and "How is this?", the grand spectacle of saṃsāra remains like darkness.
He truly sees who perceives this body— which arises from a mass of false delusions and is the very seat of calamities—
not as "mine," thereby transcending the error born of the influence of space and time through the contemplation of the Self.

He who perceives the pleasures and pains of the body as identical with the Self and everything else through the vision that is eternally undivided— he truly sees. He who perceives that all is nothing but the light of consciousness— he truly sees.
He who perceives everywhere— “I alone am” that which is the shoreless, limitless sky, endowed with space, time, and action— he truly sees.
Even though [the world] is conceptually imagined as millions of parts from the billionth part of the tip of a hair, [it is all I].

He who perceives that "I am subtle" and all-pervading, he truly sees. He who perceives within himself the non-dual Consciousness—which is omnipotent, infinite in essence, and abiding within all beings—he truly sees. (MU 4.4.27–28)

The wise one does not see [the body] as "I am the body," which is subject to birth, old age, and death, and agitated by the fear of mental and physical ailments; he alone truly sees. My majesty pervades horizontally, upwards, and downwards.
He who perceives that "there is no second to me," he truly sees.
All this is strung upon me like clusters of gems on a thread;
he who perceives that "I alone am the inner ruler of the mind," he truly sees.
Neither I nor anything else exists here; only Brahman exists, yet even that does not exist.
He who perceives the middle between existence and non-existence in this way—he truly sees.
Whatever name there may be in the three worlds, all that is but a single limb of me.
He who sees within that [the Self] is like a wave in the ocean— he truly sees.

That great-souled one for whom the notions of "selfhood" and "otherness," as well as "I-ness" and "thou-ness," have ceased through the realization of reality— he, the one with clear vision, truly sees.
"She is to be pitied, she is to be protected by me alone; she is my younger sister"—he who looks upon the three worlds with such high-sounding pity is truly seeing.
For he sees the body that consists of the Bhairava of Consciousness, free from the pursuit of objects of thought.

He who perceives the entire web of the world as filled [with the Self] truly sees. Whether it be pleasure or pain, existence or non-existence, or the various mental constructions of non-discrimination, he who certainly perceives that "I am not these" does not fall away from his state.

When the world is filled with the supreme reality of one's own self and devoid of anything else, the man of true vision perceives: "What is there for me to reject? What is there to be accepted? He realizes:
"This is simply pure Being—beyond reasoning, beyond appearance. (MU 4.4.38)
I bow to him whose reckoning of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted has perished.
He who, though pervading all beings like space, remains the one Self and does not undergo the coloring of objective existence— he is the Great-Souled One, Maheśvara.

I bow to that state which has been attained by you, O gentle one, who are free from the conceptualization of darkness and light, who have become the very self of time, and who are perfectly equanimous and established in well-being—
[that state] in whose various and beautiful manifestations of power, pertaining to the world, the calculations of rising and setting occur.

Salutation to that Śiva, possessed of supreme awakening, whose single infinite movement is an entirely equal flow. The fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Essential Nature Resting in the Unsurpassed State."
Vasiṣṭha:
He who clings to the supreme state remains established like the revolution of a wheel;
even while exercising sovereignty over the kingdom of the city of the body, he is not defiled.
For one who knows that, this great city of his own body—resembling a pleasure grove—is for the sake of enjoyment and liberation; it leads only to happiness, not to suffering.
Rāma said:
O Great Sage, how indeed can the body be a city,
and how is it that the yogi, dwelling within it, becomes the sole enjoyer of the bliss of sovereignty?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
O Rāma, this city of the body is delightful and endowed with all virtues;
for the wise man, it is rich in infinite diversions and illuminated by the sun of self-luminosity.
With the light emanating from the windows of the eyes, its interior world is made manifest.
Her shanks were as broad as the gateway of her hands;
she possessed a line of hair like a creeping vine and thicket, and was garlanded by the watchtowers of her skin;
her circle of thighs and shanks rested upon the resinous mounds of her ankles.
Its feet are divided by lines like a great stone first fashioned [by a craftsman];
it is beautiful with the boundaries of the joints, the essence of the veins, and the vital points of the skin;
the opening of the private parts is fashioned at the front of the two door-panels of the thighs.
Covered by the foliage of her shimmering rows of teeth,
she was graced by a garden-like face possessing the luster of her brows, forehead, and mouth;
her broad cheeks were strewn with the blue lotuses of her glances.
The lake of her chest has the budding lotuses of her breasts sewn within it;
the mountain of her playful shoulders is covered by the dense line of hair;
and the hollow of her belly holds the bowl of food consisting of her own cherished morsels.
Resounding with the turbulence of breath exhaled through the long cavity of the throat,
adorned with whatever objects are obtained as they pass through the marketplace of the heart,
it is a city where the citizens of the vital breaths flow incessantly through its nine gates.
Her mouth was a gaping pit filled with fragments of bone from teeth seen therein;
her tongue was a flickering flame of fire that devoured food as it moved within the cavity of her mouth;
and the hollows of her ears were like deep pits covered by a thick growth of hairy grass.
With the edges of its buttocks curved by chains and broad shanks for its back,
with the endless mud of the anus drawn up from within the water-wheel of the rectum,
it is the ground of the garden of the mind where the noble lady of self-reflection frolics.

The city of one’s own body belongs to the wise man; it is beautiful with all its splendors, featuring restless monkey-like sense organs bound firmly by the ropes of wisdom, and enchanting with the blossoming flowers of laughter in the garden of the mouth.
It leads only to happiness and not to suffering, and to the highest benefit.
For the ignorant, this [body] is a keeper of the storehouse for endless sufferings;
but for the wise, it is a keeper of the storehouse for endless happinesses.
O subduer of enemies, when this [intellect] is destroyed, nothing is lost for the knower;
when it remains, everything remains. Therefore, this [intellect] brings happiness to the knower, since the knower, having mounted it, moves about freely within saṃsāra.
Because it leads to the attainment of all enjoyments and liberation without exception, this [knowledge] is remembered as the chariot of the knower.
Since sound, form, taste, touch, smell, kinsmen,
and prosperity are indeed obtained by means of this very [knowledge], it is therefore the giver of gain to the knower.
O Rāma, when this [intellect] itself bears the web of the activities of pleasure and pain, then it is capable of supporting the weight of all things everywhere. Indeed,
governing the kingdom within that city of the body, one becomes free from delusion.
The Knower remains free from agitation, as if dwelling in his own city like Indra;
he does not cast the intoxicated horse of the mind into the abyss of arrogance,
nor does he surrender the daughter of Wisdom to the demon of greed and duality.
And he does not perceive any vulnerability in that enemy kingdom of ignorance; rather,
within the midst of the fear of the enemy that is saṃsāra, he cuts away its very roots—
roots that consist of the turbulent planet of desire, which revolves with craving as its core.
He does not sink into the gambling match of the senses where pleasure and pain are the stakes;
he performs his bath incessantly, both externally and internally, in an instant.
His course of thought proceeds gradually through the confluences and sacred fords of the rivers.
Invisible to all the people, with his face turned away from the spectacles of the city,
he dwells perpetually in bliss within the inner apartments under the name of meditation. This city is a source of happiness for him whose soul is eternally joyful.
Divine, bestowing both enjoyment and liberation like Amarāvatī for Śakra—
how could that city not bring happiness to the lord of the earth, by whose presence everything remains stable and by whose absence nothing is lost?

When the city of the body has perished, nothing at all is lost for the knower, just as when a jar is destroyed, the space within it—which had pervaded the interior of the jar—is not destroyed. Indeed, the wind touches only a jar that exists; it does not touch one that no longer stands.
In exactly that same way, the embodied one, while remaining right here within this city of his own body,
is the Lord; though he is omnipresent,
having experienced the state of being a man created by his own conceptual constructions, he attains the vision of the Self.
Even while acting, he does not act; though fully intent upon all activities, he sometimes presides over all his customary affairs.
At other times, he ascends a shimmering celestial chariot for sport.
The stainless mind, desiring to sport in the lovely state of the Unstruck Sound (*anāhata*),
dwells there and constantly delights in the ever-cooled-limbed Lokasundarī, who is the friend always residing within the heart.
Two beloved ones, Truth and Singleness, stood at his sides like the two Viśākhās beside the moon, gladdening his heart.
The wise man [beheld] all these worlds as if split by the saw of suffering.
Seated upon his throne, he gazes from behind as if from the back of the sun, like Vālmīki himself;
having long fulfilled all his desires and being beautiful with every perfection,
he shines like the full-orbed moon, never again to suffer diminution.
Even when enjoying a flood of pleasures, no weariness arises for him;
indeed, the *kālakūṭa* poison shines upon the neck of one who has conquered his afflictions.
For a pleasure enjoyed after full comprehension leads to contentment.
Once recognized and reassured, the thief attains friendliness and no longer remains an enemy.
For one who has gone far beyond the tumultuous crowds of men, women, and actors,
the glorious abundance of enjoyments is perceived like a mere spectacle on a journey.
Just as a village procession encountered unexpectedly on the road is beheld by travelers,
even so is the activity consisting of worldly transactions perceived by the wise.
Just as objects such as the directions and substances appear before one's eyes without effort, [so do they appear to the enlightened].

In the same way, one of steady intellect falls upon objects of action entirely free from passion. The senses never take away an object already attained, nor do they give up what has been attained; thus the perfect knower remains established.
Those who have not yet attained [the goal] do not shake the one of noble mind who has attained equanimity,
just as flickering blows from a peacock feather do not move a mountain.
With all doubt completely stilled and all curiosity dissolved, [he remains unmoved].
With the web of latent impressions completely destroyed, the Knower shines like a sovereign emperor.
Not contained within himself, he expands by means of his own self within the Self;
possessing no limit or boundary, the self-possessed one is like the ocean of milk.
With a mind free from madness and tranquil, he laughs at those creatures who are wretched in their craving for enjoyments and whose senses are dejected, as if they were madmen;
just as one who desires another's wife is laughed at by others.
In the same way, the wise man laughs at the sense organ that desires enjoyment.
When the mind, having fled toward sense objects, abandons its great happiness and equanimity,
one should bring it to tranquility through discernment, just as one restrains a lordly elephant with a goad.
That mental tendency which is allowed to flow toward enjoyments must be destroyed at the very outset, just like the sprouting of a poison plant.
For even the honor shown later to one who has been struck is of infinite value.
Even a meager watering acts like nectar for a rice crop scorched by the summer heat.
For one who is not in distress, neither ordinary honor nor great respect is truly perceived;
to full rivers, even the small flood of the monsoon rains appears insignificant.
Even when filled and benefited by another, it desires more;
even though the entire world is filled, the single ocean still takes up all the water.
That which follows as the adornment of the restrained mind—
One considers that very [state] highly because it has been attained after not having previously attained its expansion.
A king who is bound and then released is satisfied with even a single village;
but one who is neither bound by others nor oppressed does not value sovereignty much.
Pressing hand against hand and grinding tooth against tooth,
and as if crushing limb with limb, conquer your own sensory enemies! For men who are eager for victory and desirous of rising above others must exert themselves to conquer their adversaries.

First, the senses must be thoroughly conquered because they are enemies of the heart. On this entire earth, those men are truly fortunate and possess virtuous minds who are counted among the ranks of heroes for not being conquered by their own minds.

I salute that subduer of enemies who has attained peace, in whose heart-cavern the serpent of the mind— with its fierce poison of restless desires— has been rendered motionless, though it remains coiled there like a bracelet. This concludes the chapter titled "The Endowment with the Splendors of the City of the Body."
The Sixth Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
"The great king of hells is like an elephant intoxicated by its own evil deeds."
The enemies that are the senses are difficult to conquer; they are filled with the arrows and shafts of desire.
Those who, being ungrateful, first destroy their own body—their very abode—are the enemies of their own senses, which are great treasuries of evil deeds and are hard to overcome.
Having taken refuge in the physical body out of greed for the bait of sense-objects, the vultures that are the senses—
those fierce birds whose wings are what ought and ought not to be done— flit about; yet by whomsoever those rogues are caught in the net of the thread of discernment, [they are subdued].
They do not tear apart its limbs, as one would a mouthful of stone.
Those who take delight in sense objects that are pleasant only at first sight,
but which end in utter bitterness, fall into the hells.
In this city of the wretched body, one who possesses the wealth of discernment is not helplessly overcome by the enemies of the senses dwelling within;
likewise, kings who dwell in the fierce earthen cities [of worldly power] do not possess true happiness.
Just as those who have mastered their minds are lords within the city of their own bodies,
so for one who has brought the servants of the senses under control and well subdued the enemy that is the mind,
awakened insights flourish like blossoming flower-clusters in spring.
For one whose mental pride has perished and who has subdued the enemies that are the senses,
the latent impressions of enjoyment wither away like lotus ponds in winter.
As long as these impressions leap about in the heart, they are like ghosts at night.
As long as the mind has not been conquered through firm practice upon a single reality,

I consider the mind of the discerning person to be a servant because it performs desired tasks, a minister because it accomplishes what must be done, and a vassal king because it overcomes its own senses. (MU 4.6.10–11)
I consider the mind of the wise to be a tender woman because of its fondling, a purifying father because of its protection, and a supreme friend because of its trustworthiness.
That which is beheld by one’s own vision through the lens of scripture, well-pondered, and earnestly prayed for— [that alone is true].

Having cast off the self, the father of the mind bestows supreme perfection. Well-polished, well-refined, well-held, and well-awakened, the jewel of the mind, joined with excellent qualities, shines within the heart as something dear to the heart.
This counselor of the mind ordains actions for one of virtuous deeds that serve as axes for the tree of birth and which result in future prosperity;
thus, O Rāma, the jewel of the mind, though stained by much mud, [is purified].

Wash yourself with the water of discernment for the sake of perfection, and become possessed of light. Even though you are expanded by discernment, do not fall helplessly like an ordinary man into the terrifying realms of worldly existence which are full of calamities.
Do not disregard this mist of great delusion— this illusory cycle of existence that has arisen, crowded with hundreds of calamities; rather,
relying upon supreme discernment and perceiving the truth with your intellect.
Having fully conquered the enemies that are the senses, cross over the ocean of existence.
O Rāghava, let there not be for you the logic of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, while this body is unreal and pleasure and pain are likewise non-existent.

O Great-minded One, having thoroughly cast aside with a noble intellect that vain certainty of "I am this," resort to that other state; go there, drink, and eat, and being without a mind, you shall not be bound. This is the chapter titled "The Demonstration of the Attainment of Mindlessness."
The Seventh Chapter: While this wise one was dwelling in the world, delighting in the world yet striving for its welfare, he remained intent upon the supreme goal.
"O Rāghava, let not the logic of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa be yours; through the manner of Bhīma, Bhāsa, and Druṇa, may you be free from excessive sorrow.
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, you who remove the torment of worldly existence, why have you cited the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa? Awaken me, who am pure, with this noble speech."
Vasiṣṭha said: [He spoke of] the logic of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, and the condition of Bhīma, Bhāsa, and Druṭa, just as the rainy season, which removes the heat of density, [renews] the peacock.
"O Raghava, having heard that, do thereafter what you deem best.
"In a cave of the underworld, enchanting with all manner of wonders,
there lived a lord of Daityas named Śambara, a great ocean of illusory jewels."
The celestial city’s pleasure grove contained the mansions of the Asuras;
its own domain was adorned with artificial, supreme suns and moons;
and Mount Ramanaka was rich with lotuses fashioned from fragments of stone.
He whose acts of giving were fulfilled by the undertaking of infinite wealth; whose palace courtyards resounded with the songs of women surpassing the voices of the celestial nymphs;
and whose pleasure groves contained trees laden with fruits as large as the orb of the moon.
It was a delightful abode, dense with clusters of blooming blue lotuses;
its cranes were summoned by jewel-adorned swans,
and its golden lotuses formed buds upon the tips of the branches of golden trees.
A mass of mandāraka flowers produced from a thicket of karañja trees;
where Indra was conquered by infinite daityas made of jeweled mechanical devices;
and where garden pavilions were constructed with flames of fire as cold as snow.
He surpassed the Nandana grove with its gardens of flowers blooming in every season;
he took away the sandalwood from the Malaya mountains, which were infested by serpents through his illusory power;
and he eclipsed the women of his own inner apartments with the beauty of the world’s golden women.
The Lord, the wielder of the discus and mace, engaged in a contest for the sake of sport;
his own city’s sky was enriched by clusters of jewels flying up incessantly like stars,
and its courtyards were filled with heaps of various flowers reaching up to the knees.
In the nights, he was like a hundred moons for the entire expanse of the netherworld;
his excellence was sung in songs by the gazes of the statues on the palace pillars;
and the celestial elephants were put to flight by his illusory lord of elephants, Airāvaṇa.
The interior of his harem was filled with the excellence of the splendors of the three worlds;
he was blessed with every prosperity and endowed with all sovereign powers;
and his supreme commands were honored by all the Daitya vassals.
The host of asuras rested in the shade of his great forest-like arms;
he was adorned with earrings made of the finest jewels from the caves of all the oceans.
Of that god who had been cast down, whose form was harsh and terrifying—

There was a vast army of asuras, capable of destroying the gods. When that illusory force was asleep and had likewise departed to another region, the immortals, having found a vulnerability, entered that other part of the army.
Then, for the sake of protection, the Daitya Śambara appointed his own vassals— Dudrika, Hava, Drumā, and others— to his armies;
yet the leaders of the gods, finding an opportunity, slew even them.
Like hawks ranging through the sky agitating sparrows,
the best of the asuras again appointed other generals—
restless and raising fierce cries, like the waves of the ocean.

The gods quickly struck them down as well; therefore, filled with wrath, he went to the celestial realm (*triviṣṭapa*) to destroy the immortals. There, terrified by his magic (*māyā*), those gods vanished from sight.
Like the deer in the groves of Mount Meru at the time of the dissolution of the world,
he beheld heaven empty, with hosts of minor gods wailing and the faces of the goddesses drenched in tears, resembling the universe at the end of a kalpa.
Having stayed there in anger, Śambara took what he had obtained,
burned the cities of the world-protectors, and went to his own abode. Thus, when the hatred between the Dānavas and the gods had become even more firm, [the conflict intensified].

The gods, abandoning heaven, vanished from sight in all directions. Then, whichever commanders were appointed with great effort by the Daitya Śambara, those very ones the gods, intent on their task, slew.
Then Śambara, overcome with agitation and filled with intense rage,
burned like a grass-fed fire fanned by the wind as he gasped for breath;
yet, even after searching the three worlds, he did not find the gods.

As if through great effort, he created three terrible and exceedingly powerful Asuras by means of his illusory power (*māyā*), who were like Time itself embodied for the sake of protecting his strength. They appeared as if they had been fashioned from his very wicked deeds.
Created by magic, those terrifying beings with arms like wish-fulfilling trees emerged,
possessing massive bodies like mountains shaken by their wings;
they were distinguished by the names Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
They are the sole agents of whatever is attained, possessing the nature of pure consciousness alone;
and because of the absence of prior karmas, they are devoid of latent impressions (vāsanās),
having as their only activity the vibration of non-conceptual pure consciousness.
Bearing a slender portion consisting of the nature of thought— the seed of karma that is unripened and artificial—
these soldiers have arrived at their emergence within [the body] through a traditional succession, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit.
Those whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been cast off continue with their natural activities;
for they are just like children half-asleep, who merely move their own limbs. Indeed, they are likewise devoid of both latent impressions and the conceit of selfhood (*ātmābhimāna*).
They know neither retreat nor attack, nor flight;
they know neither life nor death, nor battle, nor victory and defeat.
Seeing only the soldiers before them intent on striking, [they fight].
Striking down their enemies in battle, they crushed mountains with their blows.
Śambara, his mind filled with satisfaction, thought within the city:
"My army, well-protected by the illusory Asuras, shall indeed be victorious."
For these [beings] are utterly free from the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the desirable and the undesirable;
therefore, they do not fear in battle, nor do they flee, remaining steadfast.
When even when struck by the gods these do not retreat, [then they have attained their goal].
Therefore, this exceedingly powerful army of mine is now stationed here.
My host, protected by the tree-like arms of the exceedingly powerful Asuras, shall attain full stability,
just as the golden ground of the divine mountain remains firm even when struck by the tusks of the celestial elephants.
The eighth canto, titled "The Origin of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa," by Vasiṣṭha.

Having thus resolved, the lord of the Daityas dispatched an army, accompanied by Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, to the surface of the earth to destroy the gods. The Daityas [issued forth] from the thickets of the ocean, from mountain caves, and from the divine mountain.
Urged on by Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭi, the Dānavas, with a terrifying roar like that of winged mountains,
filled the hollow of heaven and earth, striking the sun with their blows of the hands.
Then, from the groves and from the caves of the mountain of the gods,
the hosts of celestial dwellers arose in fear, as agitated as at the end of a cosmic dissolution;
thus there occurred between those two a battle featuring the banners of both gods and asuras.
Within the world, terrifying like a premature and violent dissolution at the end of an aeon,
heads fell from the sky down below, like mountains with the sun and moon cast away during the cataclysm; their darkness was swallowed by the brilliance exhaled from their earrings.
Resounding with the lion-roars emitted by the warriors,
they reeled like mountains laughing aloud as they were buffeted by the gales of the dissolution;
their movements were pained by the falling of weapons that resembled the blows of their own rocky peaks.
The slopes of the boundary mountains, where circles of lions wandered in fear,
overflowed with sparks of fire from weapons shattered by mutual blows,
like stars scattered at the end of a kalpa.
Upon the shores of a single vast ocean filled with floods of blood and flesh,
there were Vetālas as tall as *kalpa*-tree trunks,
clapping their hands loudly; they stood where the clouds of dust had been laid to rest by the downpour of gushing blood.

In the sky, the tips of their earrings were crushed by weapons struck down upon them; the quarters of space became devoid of gaps, filled by the Daityas— who possessed arms like wish-fulfilling trees and forms like the sun— by whom the great mountains had been shattered by their blows.
The mountains, their peaks shattered by the falling showers of blazing thunderbolts, were reduced to a mass of fragments like they had been consumed by the fire at the end of an aeon.
The gods gathered together with such splendor as if they had been nourished by the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
The Asuras fled after them, like winds following the clouds;
then the gods, having attacked them, seized them like old mice caught by cats.
Both gods and Asuras trembled in heaven like mountains swaying in a forest of blossoming trees.
They filled one another with showers of weapons in the ten directions,
just as the winds fill the forests of Mount Sumeru with masses of blossoms.
A terrible battle then took place between the armies of the gods and the dānavas.
Within the hollows of the earth and the openings of the *udumbara* trees, there were swarms of great gnats.
Then, with the circles of the world-guardians raising their trunks like uplifted noses,
the sky was filled with clouds of the cosmic age (*kalpa*), and a terrible clamor of battle arose.
Like a levelled courtyard on the earth, it was grasped as a solid mass within the sky;
thick and slow-moving like the belly of a great cloud, it could be seized by the fist.
Its flanks resounded with the clashing of weapons and rocks crushed at its initial impact.
Resounding with the harsh, gurgling cries of heartless beings whose hearts were bursting,
it was amplified by the roar of clouds rising at the time of universal dissolution;
it resembled molten gold produced by the friction of twelve suns.
Having rebound from the impact against the wall of the cosmic egg and returned to the earth,
it was like the floodwaters of a great river struck by a dam, [filling] the mine. It possessed the sound of the force of the wind from the wings of the moving lord of mountains, which had wings.
It filled the caves of the great mountains with its crashing roar as it struck them;
its waves resembled the agitation of the Milky Ocean when churned by Mount Mandara;
and the lands of the islands were shaken by the thundering slapping of its waves, which echoed like a deep resonance.
Between the two enraged armies there occurred a battle marked by the upheaval of dānavas,
crushing cities, villages, mountains, forests, and men;
the quarters of the sky were filled with mountain-like dānavas shattered by hundreds of great weapons.
The interior of the sky was filled with the dust of mountains pulverized by weapons struck against one another;
hundreds of the peaks of Mount Meru were shattered by the impact of circles of *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles;
and the lotuses that were the Daityas, Devas, and Asuras were cut down by the wind of arrows.
The old grass of gods and demons was whirled about by hundreds of revolving whirlpools;
the sky was enveloped by the surging waves of the flowing torrent of the army; and the multitude of celestial chariots fell, crushed by the falling mountain-like weapons.
A city in the sky flooded by a torrential flood of ocean waters brought by his hands;
carrying hundreds of rivers of great missiles—swords, spears, and pikes—as its whirlpools;
and a pavilion of the cosmic egg rendered inert by the violent crashing of mountain wings.
The city of the world-protectors lay prostrate under the torrential blows of the Daityas' heels;
the golden palace rang out with the tumultuous cries of women,
while mountains of Daityas rolled about, stirring up the waters of the intoxicated ocean like mountains.
The army was filled with the sound of battle cries released by warriors whose blood-stained garments resembled the sky, while herds of cattle fled in terror;
it was shrouded by clouds that were like the waters of the world-protecting oceans,
yet it was once again seen crowded with hosts of troops illuminated by the splendor of gods and demons.
It was terrifying with the loud clanging of many *pacāpacā* sounds produced by the coming and going of the mountain-like Dānavas who resembled the mountains of the *sapakṣa* (the same side),
and it was filled with the mountain-streams of Daityas whose peaks were shattered by the mountain-like weapons.
The entire earth, with its oceans and mountains, was dyed red with blood;
it was covered by countless asuras, elephants, horses, men, and chariots, along with ruined kingdoms, cities, forests, villages, and mountain caves.
In that arena where the ground was strewn with arrows shattered by sword-blows,
where celestial bards were driven away by the downpour of rain-like clouds from the end of the eon,
and where the elephant Airāvaṇa had its temples crushed by the blows of fists; MU_4.8.37.
The Kulaparvata mountains were pulverized and cast up by the crushing impact of the great thunderbolt;
the Dānavas were set ablaze by masses of flames from the blazing fire of his wrath;
and the submarine fire was extinguished by the ocean brought forth in a single hollowed palm.
A great mass of water solidified by the accumulation of lunar cold and the like,
with mountain ranges of ice melted by the flames of forest-fires;
a night at the end of an eon consisting of impenetrable darkness created by weapons.
It was a mass of illusory suns that illuminated and stripped away the vast veil of darkness;
it rained down showers of illusory fires like the falling rain at the end of an eon;
and it drew forth the friction of the clashing weapons of fire and wind joined together.
It was produced from the weapon of a rain of stones shaken down by a rain of thunderbolts;

it was rich in battles with the weapons of sleep and awakening, and possessed the weapon of a rain-storm and the weapon of drought. It bore the weapon of trees with saws and was accompanied by the conflict of the weapons of water and fire.

The battle was as difficult as that with the Brahmā-weapon; darkness was interspersed with the brilliance of fiery weapons. The entire sky was made dense by the multitude of weapons and missiles discharged from those arms, enveloped by showers of stone-like weapons and radiant with showers of fire-like weapons.
In a mere moment, chariots with banners brushing against the moon and thundering with the whirring of their wheels traversed the mountains of sunrise and sunset;
while great asuras were dying there from the incessant blows of thunderbolts.
Wherein other demons were being born from the great vidyā-mantras of Śukra and Amara;
and where, protected by auspicious planets and the great comet, there arose here and there floods of portents and calamities amidst battles that caused necks to craned in alarm.
Due to his irresistible enmity, he made the world— including its mountains, earth, oceans, and heavens— appear like a forest of blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees with the waters of blood;
he turned the great ocean into one filled with corpses as numerous as mountains.
Great corpses, dangling from the shoulders of entire tree branches,
were swaying; the surface of the sky was filled with forests of arrow-thickets as tall as palm trees, which, fanned by their own winds, bore shimmering flowers and fruits upon their wings.
With forest-arms as numerous as mountains,
they danced, making the fallen clouds, celestial chariots, and stars appear like stars;
they pierced the mountains with arrows, spears, maces, darts, and axes.
The sky was covered with fragments of walls fallen from the seven worlds; there were massive drums like clouds, incessantly intoxicated with sound,
whose thunderous resonance rising from behind reached the elephants at the bottom of the netherworld.
The long mountain of Dānavas was dragged away by the hands of Vināyaka;
the hosts of Siddhas, Sādhyas, and Maruts were rendered motionless on the slopes of every quarter;
and the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, gods, and Cāraṇas were fleeing.
The leader of the Gandharvas lay there, turned to a corpse, his body mangled and wasted;
the host of Daityas and Dānavas had for the most part achieved a semblance of victory;
the army of the gods was in agony, and Indra was utterly despondent.
With the great radiance of red weapons like fire arising from the northern quarter,
and with a fierce intensity of light and heat flashing at every moment,
winds blew at the faces of the directions, their bodies condensed by the falling of thunderbolts and scattering fragments of shattered rock.

The winds, signaling the time of universal dissolution for the gods, were voracious with their deep, rattling roars. The ninth canto, titled "The Description of the Battle between Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa."
Vasiṣṭha: While that terrible tumult of battle was then occurring,
the bodies of gods and asuras fell like fragments of mountains.
While streams of blood flowed like the floods of the Gaṅgā descending from the sky,
while the host of gods was entangled in the noose, and while there arose a dense roar of released lion-roars,
the serpent, having crushed the entire abode of the gods by dragging it with its own coils, [remained].
While Airāvaṇa—
his rut exhausted, his fury for battle on the battlefield spent, and his pride in his armor vanished— was intent on flight, the army of the Dānavas surged forward like the sun at midday.
With their weapons and limbs fallen away and blood flowing from them,
the divine armies fled like waters whose embankments have burst.
Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa pursued those [armies], even though they had long been hidden.
They followed after him with a loud clamor, like fires following after fuel;
yet, despite searching with great effort, the asuras did not find the gods,
just as lions do not find deer that have fled into a forest thick with nets of clouds.
When the hosts of immortals were not captured, Dāma, Vyāla,
and Kaṭa then went with joyful hearts to their lord residing in the treasury of Pātāla.
Then those deities, being despondent, recovered for a moment and departed.
Having conquered Brahmā of immeasurable splendor as a means to victory,
Brahmā appeared before them, whose faces possessed the beauty of being deeply flushed with red—
like the moon appearing over oceans whose waters have been turned crimson at twilight.
Having prostrated before him, those gods fully related to him that matter uttered by Śambara— the sequence of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
Having heard all of that and having reflected upon it, Brahmā, the knower of discernment, [acted].
Brahmā spoke these words, which were intended to reassure the host of gods:
"Indeed, at the end of a thousand years, by the power of Śambara, [the form] of Hari will gradually [emerge]."
"Wait for that moment when the Lord of the Immortals must die.
Today, O best of the immortals, while fighting these Dānavas— Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa— flee from them by means of illusory warfare."
"By virtue of their practice in battle,
the wondrous manifestation of egoism will enter into the hearts of these [demons] like a reflection in a mirror.
Having taken up these latent impressions (vāsanā), these gods— Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa— "
They will be easily conquered, like birds caught in a net;
but today, being free from latent desires and devoid of pleasure and pain,
they have become invincible even to the gods by destroying their enemies through fortitude.

Those who are bound by the threads of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and brought under control by the snares of hope fall into subjection in this world like birds tied with ropes. For those wise ones who are free from latent impressions, whose intellects are unattached to everything, [attain liberation].

They do not rejoice, nor do they become angry; those great-minded ones are difficult to conquer. Even one who possesses vast knowledge and great learning is overcome by a mere child if the knot of bondage within him is tied by the rope of latent desires (*vāsanā*).

One who forms conceptual constructions such as "this is that I" or "this is mine" becomes a vessel for calamities, just as the ocean is for waters. This is because his self has been cultivated through the notion of being limited to this much alone.
Though he is omniscient, he has everywhere fallen into a state of supreme wretchedness.
By him who has assigned a limitation to the infinite and immeasurable reality of the Self,
that very Self has been brought under his own control.
Whatever exists in the three worlds that is distinct from the self, toward that one’s mental cultivation becomes bound by way of regarding it as something to be acquired.
They know that mere attachment is the cause of endless sufferings.
The wise know that mere detachment from all pleasures is the cause [of liberation].
As long as Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa remain established in their worldly state without detachment, you will not be able to conquer them, just as winds cannot overcome gnats.

A living being overcome by internal latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that lead to wretchedness is defeated; otherwise, even a mosquito becomes like the immovable mountain [Meru]. Wherever latent impressions exist, there wretchedness follows.
For it is observed that the possession of qualities and defects belongs to what exists, not to what does not exist.
O Śakra, act in such a way that they cultivate within themselves their own latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in the form of "This is he," "I am this," and "This is mine," just as Dāma and the others did.
Whatever misfortunes people encounter and whatever states of existence or non-existence they undergo—
these are the bitter yet tender blossoms of the *karañja* creeper of craving.
Bound by the threads of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), this world revolves in transmigration.

That [craving], when fully grown, leads to extreme suffering; yet when it is uprooted, it leads to happiness. Even one who is steadfast, even one who is very learned, even one born of noble lineage, and even one who is great—a living being is bound by craving, just as a lion is bound by a chain.

For this bird of the mind that dwells within the tree of the body and rests in the abode of the heart, craving has been fashioned as a snare. Wretched through its latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), the world is dragged away by the End-maker (*kṛtānta*).
Like a bird bound by a string, you shall breathe incessantly, helpless.
Enough with the burden of weapons and the wandering through battle;
by means of reason alone, you must subdue the enemy's latent tendencies along with their errors.
When the enemy's fortitude was shaken from within, neither his weapons, nor his treatises, nor his missiles could prevail over you, O leaders of the immortals;
yet these— Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa— by virtue of their practice in battle, [overcame him].
They will grasp within themselves a latent impression (*vāsanā*) consisting of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*).
If those mechanical men (*yantrapuruṣa*) created by Śambara do not rely upon such a latent impression, they will attain invincibility.
Therefore, O immortals, awaken them first through the battle of reasoning,
until— by the power of practice— they become possessed of latent tendencies (*savāsanā*). Then, with their dispositions firmly fixed, they will become fit to be slain by you.
In this world, there are none whose hearts are not pierced by craving, and none who are not tender.
This entire universe, with its even and uneven aspects, has attained stability through its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
yet it moves like the mass of waves in the ocean. Therefore, in this case, that very [craving] must be treated.
The Tenth Sarga, titled "The Words of the Grandfather" within the Narrative of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa. Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord vanished on the spot,
like a wave of water that has made its sound upon the shore of the sea.
But the gods, having heard those words, departed toward their respective quarters.
Taking in the fragrance of the lotuses like breezes taking up a forest garland,
they rested for some days in their own lovely dwellings— which possessed steady splendor— just as bees rest within lotuses.
Having attained for a short time that auspicious state which brought about their own exaltation,
they raised a roar from their drums resembling the sound of clouds at the end of an aeon.
Then, in the sky, together with those Daityas who had risen from the depths of Pātāla—
A terrible battle, causing a great waste of time, broke out once more.

There blew forth a torrent of swords, arrows, spears, and mallets; multitudes of clubs, maces, axes, fierce discuses, and masses of thunderbolts, mountain rocks, fires, and trees; as well as weapons with the faces of serpents, Garuḍas, and other creatures.
The river, created by magic, with a dense torrent of great waters and weapons fashioned by illusion, swiftly surged forth in every direction;
it was a river possessing a deep roar like a flood of agitated waters, tossing millions of rocks, mountains, riverbanks, and trees.
It carried in its central current embers, spears, boulders, javelins, swords, lances, arrows, tomara-spears, and mallets.
By means of celestial palaces filled with waters like the Ganges, and by drawing forth showers of thunderbolts in all directions,

the host of gods, asuras, and siddhas— which consists of bodies as harsh as earth and other elements— is struck down and seized; yet that very same host, created by illusion, rises up again through its own inherent power, appearing as if it were merely a body of rays in the sky.

Then the faces of the quarters became like great oceans filled with floods of blood from mountains shattered by weapons resembling crags; they were filled with the forests of *kunta* and *tālī* trees uprooted by the gods, asuras, lords of the asuras, and the celestial mountains,
while spears, arrows, pikes, clubs, swords, and discs were vomited forth, and the mountains released by the gods and dānavas were swallowed up in sport.
Then there fell a rain of iron lions and bulls, their teeth and claws as fierce as saws that creaked like bellows, yet still endowed with life;

and a row of venomous serpents leaped up like a drunken ocean, appearing like the host of suns at the end of an eon that burns the quarters of the sky with the heat of the fiery poison from their blazing eyes, while they bore aloft long-stretched earth and mountains.

The entire world became a body of extreme distress, its atmosphere filled with the roaring of thunderbolt-wielding sea-monsters and the crashing waves of the ocean of the sky, while the lords of mountains were encircled by the swirling currents of rivers of various weapons.
The firmament was adorned with mountains of mountain-missiles and hand-weapons, and with high-elevated serpents, celestial women, and hosts of goddesses.
For a moment it was filled with oceans, for a moment with floods of fire, for a moment with suns, and for a moment with darkness.
With masses of mountain-like fires from weapons spreading through the sky, which was tumultuous with the *guḍaguḍa* roar of Garuḍas,
the world became such that the space between the heavens and the earth was ablaze like the unbearable time of cosmic dissolution.
The asuras leaped up from the surface of the earth into the sky like birds from a mountain slope;
the gods fell to the ground by their own excessive force, like rocks from a mountain shaken during the dissolution of the world.
With the great fires of conflagration clinging to the forest-like rows of trees that were their raised weapons fixed upon their bodies, they perished.
Then the gods and asuras attained the splendor of mountains tossed by the winds at the end of an eon within the expanse of the sky.
With streams of blood released from the bodies of the great mountain-like gods and asuras, swirling on all sides,
the ocean of the sky appeared completely filled, like its own body with hundreds of rising Gaṅgās reddened by twilight.

Those experts in the path of policy brought to rest their mutual downpours of mountains, showers of water, as well as showers of various fierce weapons, showers of terrible thunderbolts, and showers of fire; they had shattered the walls of all the great mountain kings.
And they simultaneously released showers of flowers upon all the quarters of the sky, as if from the limbs of the directions.

(MU 4.10.20) The gods and asuras, distressed by the agitation of the battle in the lake, their hands clutching weapons that were crushing each other’s limbs, and with their broad chests smeared with blood, roamed through the sky like a conflagration of firebrands, hurling [missiles] at one another. (MU 4.10.21)
Then, with severed heads, hands, arms, and thighs wandering like inauspicious locusts through the expanse of the sky,
the belly of the world became as if covered by fierce masses of clouds from the horizon to the sun, obscuring the mountain ranges at the edges of the quarters.
With its fire intoxicated, its waters agitated, its wind and sun obscured, its forests shattered, and its hosts of gods and demons destroyed, [the world was thus devastated].
The universe had its walls and corners shattered; it was as terrifying as the end of an eon at an untimely hour.

It whirled violently, with the horizons spun about by mountain peaks struck by massive weapons equal in size to itself—peaks that rattled with fierce winds from the depths of their caves as if crying out in pain, and that roared with the abundant, descending sounds of lions.

It wandered within the expanse of the sky like leaves of a forest scattered by the wind—amidst illusions, rivers, oceans, clouds, dense fires, and conflagrations; with trees, the corpses of gods and asuras, mountains, and floods of stones; and amidst the whirling of helmets, arrows, spears, maces, missiles, and weapons.
Suddenly, it was struck with the terrible blows of palms that were irresistible due to their size, equal to the wings of the king of mountains.
There arose a flood of oceanic waters filling the city of the gods, shattered by the mountain-like bodies of falling warriors;
the interior of the earth’s mountains was washed with blood, the atmosphere was filled with a deep *ghuṅghuma* roar,
and the entire expanse of the world-cave became agitated as if it were a whirlpool in a lake of blood.

Then, indeed, that battle became like this worldly existence (saṃsṛti): it caused transformations extending through infinite directions; it bestowed pleasure and pain directed toward decline and rise; and it was crowded with hosts of gods and asuras engaged in the act of combat.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Description of the Battle Again" within the narrative of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
The Eleventh Canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, by means of such tumultuous undertakings, the life-taking Asuras [proceeded].
Through battles raged with great fury where death was undertaken,
and through illusion, as well as by means of debate, alliance, and conflict;
through flight, fortitude, deception, and stratagem.
That battle was waged by the gods for thirty-five years through acts of treachery, combat with missiles, and frequent disappearances;
it lasted for eighteen years, five months, and seven days.
Rains fell upon the trees, fires, weapons, waters, thunderbolts, and mountains.
During this time, however, due to the firm habituation of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*),
Dāma and the others— whose minds were consumed by it— grasped at the notion "I am" (*aham iti*).
Just as a mirror becomes like the reflected object due to the excellence of proximity,
so too have they attained the state of egoism through the excellence of practice.
Just as an object that is very distant does not reflect in a mirror, [so it is with the Self].
In the same way, the latent impression of objective things does not arise from a lack of habituation.
When Dāma and the others were born, they were born with the latent impression of egoism;
consequently, they fell into a state of wretchedness, thinking, "This is mine," "Life is mine," and "Wealth is mine."

Seized by the latent impression of fear and struck down by the latent impression of delusion, they are bound by the snares of hope; therefore, they have fallen into a state of wretchedness. For, even though they are devoid of egoism, they have vainly fashioned for themselves the sense of "mine-ness."
Then, like the perception of a snake in a rope, Dāma, Vyāla,
and Kaṭa fell into a state of wretchedness, miserable with the craving "May this body-stalk remain firm from head to foot as mine. (MU 4.11.10–11)
"May my body be firm; may my wealth lead to happiness"—
as they fixed their minds on this, their fortitude vanished,
because their bodies were free from latent impressions (*vāsana*) and those enemies of the gods were devoid of attachment.
That state of being intent on striking was quickly wiped away.
Thinking, "How may we remain steadfast in this world?
they fell into dejection, like lotuses deprived of water.
But for those who possessed self-conceit regarding food and drink, their delight became terrifying and fraught with worldly existence, rooted in the nature of *bhava*. Then,
in that battle, they fell into a state of hesitation out of fear.
Agitated by the herds of rutting elephants like young deer in the forest, their hearts struck by the thought, "We shall die! We shall die!
they indeed wandered very slowly in that battle against the enraged Airāvaṇa.

For those who sought only their own bodies and were terrified of death, out of a lack of fortitude they placed their feet upon his head, thereby bringing about their own downfall. Then, their courage utterly withered, they set out to kill the soldier standing before them.
Like fires whose fuel is exhausted, they were unable to consume the oblation;
though striking at the gods,
those soldiers, having become mere Sudasyus, stood with all their limbs mangled by wounds like common men.

What need is there for much speaking here? With their minds terrified of death as the gods were exulting, the Daityas fled from the field of battle. While all those mountain-like Dānavas were fleeing in every direction,
In the abode of the Asuras, among those renowned as Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa,
that army of Daityas fell from the sky,
fleeing here and there like the cluster of stars shaken on all sides by the winds at the end of a kalpa.
In the groves of the Immortal Mountain, upon the rocks of its peaks,
on the shores of the oceans, and amidst the masses of clouds;
in the hollows of the ocean’s whirlpools, in chasms, and likewise in the rivers.
In the forests at the ends of the quarters, and in the blazing woods;
in villages and cities whose treasuries were destroyed by that war;
in wildernesses inhabited by fierce yakṣas, and in deserts where forest fires were rising.
On the mountains at the edge of the Lokāloka range and in the lakes,
in the cities of Andhra, Dramiḍa, Kaśmīra, and Pārasīka,
and upon the waves of various oceans and the masses of Ganges water;
In distant other continents and upon the creepers of the Jambū groves,
those enemies of the gods fell everywhere with the forms of mountains;
their limbs and feet were shattered, and their hands and arms were torn asunder.
With entrails like strings clinging to the branches, shedding streams of blood from their severed limbs,
their hooves and heads scattered about, and with enraged eyes protruding,
their armor and weapons were shattered by the force of their own weapons whirling around.
Their various garments fall away, tossed about as they plummet from afar;
they are struck with fierce terror by the *khaṭat-kāra* sound of their helmets striking against their necks;
and parts of their bodies hang down, pierced by points sharpened on stone.
With their armor pinned by the forceful impact of the tips of *śālmalī* thorns,
and their heads shattered into a hundred pieces by the collision with smooth stone slabs—
all of them, though fully armed, [fell] immediately upon the mere act of falling.
The lords of the Asuras went to destruction in all directions, like dust particles entering the ocean and dissolving into its waters.
In the narrative of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, this is the twelfth canto, titled "The Fall of the Asuras."
Vasiṣṭha said:
When the gods were thus gratified and the Dānavas had been slain,
Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and the others became distressed and overwhelmed with fear.

Blazing with fury like the fire at the end of an aeon, Śambara— whose armies had been destroyed— flared up against Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa. Then, out of fear of Śambara, they went to the seventh netherworld.
Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa stood there, having abandoned the assembly of Dānavas. There, Yama’s servants known as Kukuhās— capable of terrifying even Vetālas— stand as the guardians of the ocean of hell.

They gave their daughters to them in succession, who were like personified anxieties in dense form. Together with them, Dāma and the others spent their time there for a period of ten thousand years, having taken up endless evil tendencies.
"This woman is mine, delightful; she is my sovereign"—thus, for those bound by false affection, time passed away. Then, on one occasion, Dharmarāja arrived at that place.
By chance, for the purpose of investigating the affairs of the great hells,
three asuras did not bow down before this Dharmarāja, whom they had never known before, treating him as if he were a common servant leading to their own destruction.
Then, by the command of Vivasvat, these [beings] were placed by him upon the grounds of blazing chasms, with the movement of their eyebrows directed;
there, they, along with their friends, wives, and kinsmen, raised piteous cries.
Like trees with their leaves and branches burnt by forest fires,
they are born again through their own cruel latent impressions (vāsanā) as Kirātas and royal servants, appearing in the form of executioners.
Then, having abandoned that birth, they were born as crows among the Suhmas;
at the end of that, they attained the state of vultures, and from there they went to the state of cranes.
Then they became Śabaras among the Trigartas and sheep among the Barbaras.
Then, those of crooked intellect took birth as insects in Magadha. Having experienced a manifold succession of births there,
O Rāma, they have today become fish in a marsh in the forest of Kaśmīra.
Consuming the thin, sludge-like paste of mud boiled by forest fires,
they neither die nor live, worn out by the mire of old age;
having experienced the agitation of various wombs again and again.
Having come into being again and again, they have perished like waves in the ocean.

O Rāma, those who have entered the ocean of existence, driven by the wind of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), have for a long time been carried along like straw by the waves in the form of bodies; yet they have not even now attained peace. Consider the infinite and terrible magnitude of latent impressions!
The thirteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Previous Births of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa," by Vasiṣṭha.
Therefore, O high-minded Rāma, I speak this for your awakening;
let there not be for you the logic of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa as if it were mere play.
Through the pursuit of non-discrimination, the mind falls into such a calamity.
He effortlessly embraces that which leads to endless suffering.
Where, indeed, is the lordship over Śambara’s host— the destroyer of the immortals—
and where is the state of a fish, withered by the mud of waters scorched by heat?

Where is that great fortitude capable of routing the hosts of the immortals, and where is this state of being a lowly servant to the Kirāta king? Where indeed is that noble steadfastness of consciousness and sattva, free from egoism?
Where does this wicked imagination of egoism arise from the onset of false latent impressions?
This vast and spreading cluster of the thorny blossoms of saṃsāra, dense with its branching tendrils,
emerges solely from the sprout of egoism.
Therefore, O Rāma, diligently cleanse the ego within yourself;
having cleansed it by realizing "I am not anyone at all," become happy.
The orb of the moon of ultimate reality is shrouded by the cloud of egoism.
The elixir became cool and attained invisibility.
Having been seized by the demon of egoism, the three— Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—
though non-existent, attained existence as Dānavas through the greatness of Māyā.
"O Rāma, today the fish dwelling on the small pools at the edge of the Mahāpadma lake in Kaśmīra are greedily longing for bits of moss.
Rāma said:
The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being.
Tell me, how did those who were non-existent become existent?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"So it is, O mighty-armed one; for that which is non-existent never becomes existent at any time.
Yet this very thing sometimes becomes vast or minute.
Tell me, how can the non-existent abide as the existent? Or how can that existent abide as the non-existent?"
"By this very illustration, I shall bring about your awakening.
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, it is indeed true that we who stand here are truly existent beings."
"But you say that Dāma and the others, though non-existent, exist and remain here.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Just as Dāma and the others, O Rāma, exist here as consisting of illusion (māyāmayāḥ)..."
Just as the flood of water in a mirage appears to be real though it is unreal,
so too we ourselves— along with the gods, asuras, and dānavas— are unreal, yet we frolic, go forth, and come back again.
Your existence is indeed false, and my existence is likewise false;
though experienced, it is unreal in nature, just like one's own death in a dream.
Just as a deceased kinsman in a dream, though experienced, consists of unreality.
And the cognition that "this one is dead" occurs in this way regarding this world;
for this statement concerning the deluded does not shine forth [as true].
It ceases through practice, yet there is no denial of direct experience.
A conviction that has taken deep root within never perishes for anyone in this world at any time, even without the effort of repeated practice.
He who says, "This world is unreal; Brahman alone is real," [is liberated].
The deluded laugh excessively at him as if he were mad;
for where indeed could there be unity between one who is intoxicated and one who is sober, between the ignorant and the knower of reality?
It would be like the meeting of shadow and sunlight, or of blindness and light.
Even with effort, neither the knower nor the ignorant is able to deny an experienced reality that is true, just as one cannot deny the assault upon a corpse.
It is appropriate for the knower of reality to say, "Brahman is the entire world."
Because when ignorance is not experienced, one has experienced that very [Reality].
For this statement, O Rāma, shines forth with respect to the awakened object:
"In the form of 'I am the Awakened One,' there is indeed nothing at all."
The wise one, experiencing that "this supreme Brahman alone is peace," how could he possibly perform a negation of his own direct experience?
Apart from the Supreme, there is nothing whatsoever in the self that is "I."
Just as the state of being a ring and so forth does not exist in gold, so too the state of being Vasiṣṭha does not exist in me.

Apart from the nature of pure being, there is nothing at all in the Self; for the ignorant person who perceives the Self through notions such as "I am a wave," there is no ultimate reality, just as there is no such thing as a wave in gold.
The deluded person consists of the disease of false ego, while the wise person consists of the one true Self;
indeed, the denial of their respective natures is never possible. How could there be a denial of that which constitutes the very essence of someone? In that case, how could such a denial be possible?
For a person to say "I am a jar" is indeed mere madness.
Therefore, neither we nor Dāma and the others are real anywhere;
we and these others are unreal, for there is truly no possibility of our existence.
The pure realization of truth is the stainless space of awakening;
it is the reality that is all-pervading, peaceful, and neither sets nor rises. All is that truth, yet it is devoid of emptiness, abiding as if it were nothing at all.
In that sky, my dear, these innate visions shine as their own radiance;
just as the innate visions of one with cataracts appear like clusters of hair and such, so do these creations appear there.
He experiences himself in an instant exactly as he conceives it;
therefore, the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), though unreal, becomes real through that perception.
Consequently, in this triple world, there is neither reality nor unreality.
In whatever manner consciousness perceives its own form, it arises in that very way; of this there is no doubt.
Just as the rope and other such things [appear], so too have we arisen in this manner.
Whether real or unreal—what need is there for conceptualization regarding them, my dear?
In this infinite, all-pervading, and formless sky of consciousness, consciousness arises in whatever manner; in that very way, it shines forth there abundantly.
Wherever consciousness itself manifests by its own power in the form of a rope or other such things, [it appears as such].
Thus, through the experience of such forms, that world came to be established there;
the designation "world" was applied to the manifestation of one's own dream by the sky-like consciousness whose nature is space, just as the appearance of water in a mirage occurs to a traveler.
Where the sky of consciousness is awakened, there the designation "the visible world" (dṛśya) is applied;
where it is asleep by that very same [consciousness], there the designation "liberation" (mokṣa) is applied.
And that [sky of consciousness] is never anywhere asleep, nor is it ever awakened.
Let it be understood that the visible world is nothing but the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoma*).
The splendor of creation is indeed liberation (*nirvāṇa*), and liberation is indeed the splendor of creation;
there is no difference in meaning between these two words, just as with synonyms.
In the ultimate sense, one perceives the world as one's own form,
just as a person with cataracts sees a mass of hair;
yet that mass of hair is nothing at all, for it is merely the vision that exists in that manner.
This visible world is nothing at all; thus the sky of consciousness (cidvyoma) abides.
This entire universe exists everywhere, yet nothing exists here that has not been experienced as such by us.
This peaceful, single, and pervasive reality remains thus, free from doubt and devoid of differentiation; therefore, remain in this state.
This form of the Great Consciousness is dense like a solid stone-cavity, tranquil, and as clear as the sky;
the views that "it exists" or "it does not exist" do not apply anywhere. That which exists shines forth perfectly as it truly is. The Chapter on Nirvāṇa, the forty-seventh [verse] of the Fourth Book.
The Fourteenth Chapter:
Rāma:
Like children, yakṣas, and piśācas, [they treat] even the virtuous as if they were the wicked.
"How can there be an end to the suffering of Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and the others?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"At that very moment, for the sake of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, by those servants of Yama..."
Requested by Yama, he said: "Listen to this, O scion of Raghu!
When Dāma and the others shall experience separation [from their bodies] and hear their own stories, they will then undoubtedly be liberated."
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, where, when, and how will they hear this account of my own life? By whom will this sequence of stories be narrated?"
Vasiṣṭha said:
In a small pool on the shore of the Mahāpadma lake in Kaśmīra,
these two repeatedly experienced a succession of births as fish.
With restless intentions bound by time, they will come to their end and become cranes right there in that lotus lake. There,
amidst the garlands of white water-lilies and the clusters of lotuses, they shall dwell.
Upon the excellent creepers of moss and upon the undulations of the waves;
on the swaying cradles of blooming white lotuses and upon the vines of blue water-lilies;
amidst the streaks of clouds formed by masses of spray and within the movements of cool whirlpools.
Having enjoyed the pleasures of the lake and being ornaments of the world, they will dwell there for a very long time; then, having attained complete purity,
they will be separated from those [pleasures] as they have acquired the means for liberation.
Just as the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas [appear] through the attainment of differentiation by chance,
there shall arise within the region of Kaśmīra a city adorned by mountains,
known by the name Adhiṣṭhāna, which will be glorious.
In its center there will be a peak named Pradyumnaśikhara, like the small bud of a lotus within the whorl of its petals. Upon that summit of the mountain, a certain king will build a palace.
A great *sāla* tree that scraped the clouds, like another mountain peak upon a peak;
within the hollow of a breach in the wall on the northeastern corner of the house,
which was constantly marked by grass tossed up by the unceasing wind.
In Ālaya, there will be a Dānava named Vyāla who will become a *kalaviṅka* bird;
like a first-year student with little learning, he will chirp meaninglessly.
At that very time, there will be a king there.
One named Śrī Yaśaskaradeva, like another Indra in heaven,
will have a Dānava named Dāma within his palace; as a mosquito,
making a soft sound, he will dwell in a hole in the back of a large pillar.
At that time, in that very city called Adhiṣṭhāna,
there will also be a monastery named the Ratnāvalī-vihāra.
There, the minister of that local ruler will be known as Narasiṃha.
The bondage and liberation of his perception will become as clear as an amalaka fruit in the palm of one's hand.
In his house there shall be a toy-crow bird,
and a cat named Māyāsura, with a cage made of tinkling bells.
That Nṛsiṃha, the minister of the king, will relate this narrative composed in verses concerning Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and the others.
Having heard that story, Kaṭa— along with Krakara— will remember his own former existence.
The tranquil portion of the false "I" within will attain supreme nirvāṇa.
Likewise, the sparrow dwelling on the edge of the Pradyumna peak,
having come here and heard its own story, will attain supreme nirvāṇa.
Even a mosquito, having come to dwell within a wound inside the wood of the royal palace,
will attain peace through this very circumstance;
likewise, a sparrow from Pradyumna’s horn and a mosquito from the royal palace [will find peace].
And from the monastery, O Raghava, Krakara and the others shall attain liberation.
Thus has been told to you the entire sequence of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa;
this worldly existence is indeed an illusion, utterly void yet exceedingly radiant.
Unrecognized, it causes one to wander like a mirage-ocean;
recognized, it subsides like a mirage-ocean.
Thus, even from a high station, one falls downward through the power of ignorance regarding women.
Deluded and foolish, they fall like Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
Where is the capacity to endure the crushing of Mount Meru and Mandara by the knitting of a brow?
And where is the state of being a mere speck in a wound within the wood of a royal palace?
Where is the state of having the orbs of the sun and moon felled by a mere slap of the hand,
and where is the state of being a bird in a hole in the wall of a house on Mount Pradyumna?
Where is the lifting of Mount Meru with a hand trembling in the play of plucking flowers?
In the house of Nṛsiṃha on Mount Ārṣyaśṛṅga, what was the state of being a young partridge?
For the space of consciousness, its radiance merely falsely colored by passion (*rajas*),
does not abandon its own nature even while it perceives itself as if having a different form.

By its own delusion of latent impressions— which, though unreal, appears as if real— a living being wanders from one state to another, like the perception of water in a mirage. Those who cross the ocean of existence by means of the very notion that it is a flowing stream, [they truly cross].

Those who, through the scripture, remain free from latent impressions, established in the realization that "this visible world is unreal," and those who, regarding the doctrines of dry logic as mere shifting cries of stars,
quickly enter the waters of the abyss— they do not destroy what is auspicious. (MU 4.14.34–35)
O dear one, for those who proceed along the path established by their own experience and leading back to the scriptures,
there is no destruction, just as there is none for birds in flight.
"This shall be mine, this shall be mine"— such is the thought of the intelligent.

Because of his own wretchedness and misfortune, not even ashes remain near him. All calamities abandon that noble-souled one who always regards even the three worlds as a blade of grass, just as sap leaves a withered straw.

The lords of the world protect him in whom the wonder of pure being (*sattva*) constantly vibrates within, like the indivisible cosmic egg of Brahmā. Even in the face of a terminal calamity, one must never take delight in transgression.
Even Rāhu, though drinking the nectar by improper means, died.
But those who take refuge in the sun of true scripture and contact with the virtuous— which grants fierce illumination— do not again fall under the sway of the blindness of delusion.
All calamities inevitably come to an end and inevitably depart;
well-being inevitably comes to pass for one whose fame is to be purchased by their virtues.
This is true for those who have no discontent with their virtues and no lack of passion for sacred learning.
Those men who are not addicted to vices are like gods; others are merely cattle.
Hari surely dwells in the embodied form of those who are like oceans of milk, whose fame—like moonlight—illuminates the sky of the hearts of people.
All that was to be enjoyed has been enjoyed, and all that was to be seen has been seen;
what else remains but non-attachment toward further enjoyments for the sake of shattering worldly existence?
This should be done in due order, according to the scriptures, according to established custom, and according to the traditional way of life.
Remain steadfast; let go of this unreal craving for enjoyments within.
Cultivate intimacy with fame that reaches the very heavens through your virtues;
for objects of enjoyment never protect one who has fallen into the clutches of death.

Those whose moon-white glory is sung by beautiful Siddha women with melodies throughout the expanse of the sky—they alone truly live; all others are dead. Having exerted the supreme human effort and undertaken noble endeavor, they flourish.

Who would not possess success through conduct that is free from agitation and in accordance with the scriptures? (MU 4.14.49) One who moves according to the scriptures should not hasten for successes;
success ripened over a long period of time becomes more robust. (MU 4.14.50)
Let worldly affairs be conducted according to the scriptures— free from sorrow, fear, and fatigue, free from greed, and free from constraint— so that they do not perish.
The individual soul has fallen into disappearance within the decayed and dark wells of worldly existences.
"O you who possess many fallacies, let this [treatise] now be extracted from here.
