From this point forward, do not descend further and further downward.
Let this scripture be determined as a weapon for warding off calamities."
In battle, where elephants are violently torn asunder and lives are being cast away, what is the use of mere wealth? Noble ones, let the scriptures be consulted.
Let it be investigated with the thought: "This is a mango; this is a neem."

Go by your own will or through the instigation of another; do not go like cattle. This miserable, auspiciousless, and thoughtless state that bestows misfortune—a dense and long-lasting great sleep—must be abandoned; one must awaken.
Do not remain asleep like an old, sluggish tortoise;
rise slowly and accept exertion for the sake of pacifying old age and death.
The attainment of wealth leads to misfortune, and the flood of enjoyments brings about the disease of worldly existence.
In times of adversity, all forms of prosperity arise; everywhere, victory belongs to the one who is free from attachment.
For those engaged in worldly affairs, well-being is achieved through conduct that follows the ways of the world and through action that does not contradict the scriptures and established custom.
For one whose conduct is beautiful through self-discipline, whose life is lived in solitude, and who does not crave even the slightest pleasure amidst the sufferings of saṃsāra—
his lifespan, fame, virtues, and prosperity flourish together for the sake of the excellent fruit, like a spring creeper in full bloom.
The chapter titled "The Description of Right Conduct" within the narrative of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
Fifteenth canto. Vasiṣṭha:
Because of the fulfillment of all excellences, everything exists everywhere and at all times.
Therefore, it is indeed possible; one should not abandon one's own virtuous exertion.
By propitiating the Lord of the Lake with joy that brings delight to friends, kinsmen, and relatives, even death was utterly conquered.
Even the gods exist in a state of total inferiority, being crushed by the Dānavas—
who are rich in noble Dānava power— just as lotus ponds are trampled by elephants.
This occurred at the sacrifice of King Marutta, presided over by the great seer Saṃvarta.
Another creation, including both gods and asuras, was fashioned by Brahmā;
yet the status of a Brahmin was attained by Viśvāmitra, who was endowed with great excellence and who repeatedly applied himself to austerities that are otherwise difficult to achieve.
By Upamanyu, who was so unfortunate as to have obtained such a difficult-to-attain elixir as the water of the *piṣṭātaka* tree, the Ocean of Milk was reached; he who,
like Viṣṇu and Brahmā, struck down the champions of the three worlds as if they were mere blades of grass.
By the firmness of his extraordinary skill, Śveta measured out Time itself;
having won over Yama through his affection and made a verbal agreement,
Sāvitrī brought her husband Satyavān back from the other world.
There is no excellence in the world that does not have a manifest fruit;
therefore, one who possesses every excellence must necessarily be one who has investigated [the self].
Self-knowledge is [the cause] of all states of experiencing pleasure and pain.
Therefore, one who seeks excellence therein should cultivate that which uproots [the afflictions].
Through this extremely corrupt vision of the visible world, which seeks its objects by means of such [a view],
no happiness free from suffering and free from affliction is ever attained.
Non-quiescence is the supreme Brahman, and quiescence is the supreme state;
even though this is so, nevertheless, know this tranquility to be auspicious.
Abandoning self-conceit and resorting to eternal tranquility, [one attains it].
Having reflected with wisdom upon the state of nobility, one should practice the service of the virtuous.
Neither austerities, nor sacred fords, nor scriptures prevail for you in crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra as effectively as the service of the virtuous.
He whose greed, delusion, and anger diminish day by day as he engages in his own duties according to the scriptures— that is a virtuous person.
Through association with one who knows the inner self, his wisdom proceeds.
By means of which the absolute non-existence of this visible world is perceived;
through the absolute non-existence of the visible, however, only the Supreme remains.
Due to the absence of anything else, the individual soul (jīva) quickly merges into that very [Supreme].
The visible world has not arisen, nor did it exist, nor will it ever come to be;
even in the present, it does not exist at all. Only the supreme, which is beyond cognition, exists.
This has been demonstrated by a thousand arguments, and it is being demonstrated further still.
Indeed, I shall now demonstrate that which has been experienced by all:
how this entire triple world is quiescent, a mere expanse of consciousness.
Since this reality is devoid of existence and so forth, how could anything else possibly exist here in any way?
The beautiful, flickering consciousness performs a wondrous marvel within its own restless self;
for it realizes that this very world is nothing other than itself.
The experience of the three worlds is the orb of rays from the sun of consciousness.
O you who are free from self-praise, tell me: what difference is there between the moon and the sun?
Those two—the opening and the closing of this consciousness-vision by its very nature, which constitute the experience of the world—are themselves its rising and its setting.
The referent of "I," when not fully understood, is a stain upon the sky of ultimate reality;
but the referent of "I," when fully understood, becomes the very sky of ultimate reality.
When the sense of "I" is thoroughly understood, it no longer functions as the ego-subject at all.
Just as water becomes one with water, the world of the "I" and so forth merges into the self of the sky of consciousness.
In reality, this visible world consisting of the "I" and other phenomena does not exist at all;
why then must it necessarily remain for one who investigates the nature of the "I"?
Even for those of dull intellect, the notion of a ghost arises toward one who is not a ghost;
this occurs because children lack the investigation that comes from a pure inner faculty.
As long as the moonlight of consciousness remains within, densely veiled by the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), [the world appears as such].
The night-lily of ultimate reality does not yet blossom so long as this term "I," which possesses its own substantial meaning, has not been wiped away by consciousness itself. When that is done,
what room is there for the mere conceptualization of craving for hell, heaven, liberation, and the like?
As long as the cloud of egoism expands within the heart,
so long does the cluster of *kuṭaja* flowers of craving blossom.
When the sun of consciousness has been eclipsed by the standing cloud of egoism, [the mind remains obscured].
It reaches only a state of dullness and never attains clarity in any way.
This ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), falsely imagined by itself, is close at hand;
it leads only to suffering and not to joy, like a yakṣa that causes delusion in children.
The sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva), imagined in vain, bestows delusion and produces an endless cycle of saṃsāra, just as a false notion [leads one astray] regarding a rope and similar objects.
Greater than that is the vast delusion of thinking, "This is I. This is the supreme darkness.
Nothing that is useless in saṃsāra has ever existed, nor will it exist;
whatever comes here as pleasure or pain, like a whirling firebrand,
is merely the unfolding display of the wheel of egoism.

He who has planted in his heart the painful sprout of egoism finds for himself the forest of worldly existence, which possesses a thousand branches and is difficult to cut down. Egoism is the sprout of those inexhaustible trees that are births.
The branches of those [trees] spread out thousandsfold with the thought "this is mine";
objects arising from latent impressions appear like the crackling of wood split by the wind,
or like the rows of sound from crashing waves.
Devoid of the sense of "I," you should block the wheel of saṃsāra by restraining yourself— that wheel which has the great navel of egoism and which carries one along.
As long as the darkness of the sense of "I" expands in the forest of human existence, [so long does it bind].
So long do these female demons of anxiety, intoxicated by thought, continue to dance about.
For that lowest of men who is seized by the demon of egoism,
neither the Tantras nor the Mantras can bring peace to him, for he is without a protector.
Rāma:
Since pure consciousness, which is like a mirror and is stainless, abides as one's own self, the ego-sense is reflected therein; therefore, what is there to be said regarding the person?
Vasiṣṭha:
O Rāghava, the wondrous manifestation of egoism is not an inherent property of things;
this phenomenon is produced by latent impressions (vāsanā) and is stilled through human effort.

"I am not, nor does the glory of wealth belong to me; where do pleasure and pain abide?"—from such contemplation of the nature of things, egoism does not arise. "This splendor is a false magical illusion; what use have I for attachment or aversion?"
Thus, through internal reflection, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) does not arise.
"I am not in the Self, nor does the splendor of the visible world belong to this [Self]"—
by such a peaceful mode of conduct, the ego-sense does not increase.

"For when the view of 'I' as the world has ceased— along with the perceptions of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted— and when equanimity has become serene, the ego-sense no longer functions. Rāma:
"What is the form of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), O Lord, and how is it abandoned? How does one become embodied or bodiless when it has been relinquished?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
O Raghava, there are three kinds of egoism (ahaṅkāra) here in the three worlds;
two are superior and the other is to be abandoned—listen, for I shall tell you.
"I am this entire universe; I am the Supreme Self, the Infallible One."
The supreme consciousness that [realizes] "there is nothing else" is indeed called the ego-sense (*ahaṅkṛti*).
This exists for the sake of liberation and not for bondage; it belongs to one who is liberated while living.
The designation "ego-sense" applied to this is merely conceptualized, not real.
I am distinct from everything, conceived as even a hundredth part of the tip of a hair;
or rather, this supreme second egoity is consciousness itself.
It exists for the sake of liberation and not for bondage, for one who is liberated while living.
The designation "I-maker" (ahaṅkāra) applied to this [body] is merely imagined, not real.
The conviction "I am this which consists only of hands, feet, and so forth"—
this is the third kind of worldly ahaṅkāra, and it is indeed trivial.
This evil-souled one is to be avoided; he is known as the supreme enemy.
A living being struck by him does not grow again, for he is a powerful foe who inflicts manifold afflictions.

With his intellect diminished, the world sinks indeed into calamities. By long abandoning this wicked egoism through its very existence, a being who possesses the refined ego attains the state of liberation as the Blessed One.
Having determined that "I am not this body," which is the very form of the fault of worldly egoism—
the notion that "I am the body"— its abandonment is the teaching of the Great Ones.
Even while accepting the first two types of egoism as being non-worldly (alaukika), [the wise remain detached].
The third, worldly egoity, which bestows suffering, must be abandoned. Indeed,
because of this wicked egoity, Dāma, Vyāla,
and Kaṭa reached that state which causes pain even when mentioned in stories.
Rāma:
O Brahmin, having abandoned this third worldly egoity from the mind, what state must a person attain for his own benefit? (MU 4.15.61)
Vasiṣṭha:
This [woman], who bestows suffering, must first be abandoned;
for in whatever manner a man remains [detached from her], to that same extent he attains the Supreme.
If a person free from sin remains contemplating these [elements] in the previously mentioned state of egoity (ahaṅkṛti), he attains that supreme state. Furthermore,
having completely abandoned even those, being devoid of all egoity—

Even so, it remains established that one ascends only to the highest state. At all times and with every effort, worldly egotism must be abandoned by the person of great intelligence for the sake of realizing supreme bliss.
By abandoning the impure egoism that consists of diseases residing in the body, there is nothing else more supremely auspicious;
this alone is the highest state.
Indeed, having abandoned this gross worldly egoism through its very existence [as an object of contemplation], one attains liberation.

Whether standing still or engaged in worldly affairs, such a man does not fall downward. For a being whose ego-conceit has been stilled and who possesses great wisdom, the diseases of sensory enjoyment do not taste sweet, just as the juices of potent poisons do not appeal to one who is fully satiated.
When worldly enjoyments no longer provide satisfaction, what else indeed can the mind of a man turn toward but that which lies ahead as his highest good?
O Rāghava, it is precisely through the abandonment of the pursuit of egoism [that this occurs].
The ocean of existence is crossed by means of that which arises solely from human effort.

Thinking, "I am not, nor does anything whatsoever belong to me," and "everything, indeed, is entirely I," the great-souled one brings this venerable consciousness— which has found its footing in the mind— to its ultimate state and attains the supreme goal.
The sixteenth canto, titled "An Inquiry into Egoism," in the narrative of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa; [spoken by] Vasiṣṭha.
In this regard, listen as I tell you what happened after Dāma and the others had departed, concerning Śambara himself in his city which was like a mountain;
for thus everything fell from the sky, its established order utterly destroyed.

When Śambara’s army had perished like a mass of clouds in autumn, that Dānava—having spent several years with his forces defeated by the gods and once again intent on slaying the gods—reflected thus: *Muṇḍakopaniṣad 4.16.2–3
Those Asuras, Dāma and the others, whom I created through my illusory power (māyā),
have been filled with a false internal sense of ego due to their foolishness in battle. Now I shall create other Dānavas, arisen through my illusory power.
Furthermore, I shall make them knowers of their own scriptures and endowed with discernment; then,
through the thorough knowledge of reality, they will abandon the egoism arisen from false mental construction and will conquer those gods.
Having reflected thus, the lord of the Daityas created such lords of the Dānavas through his illusory power (māyā), just as the ocean produces bubbles.
They were all-knowing, knowers of what is to be known, free from passion, and devoid of sin.
Those supreme ones, who have cultivated their selves, act as sole agents according to what has been attained;
marked by the names Bhīma, Bhāsa, and Druṭa,
they view the entire world as if it were a blade of grass, possessing purified intentions.
Having reached the earth, those Daityas covered the sky,
roaring with weapons for lightning, like rain-clouds in the monsoon;
they fought against the gods for many series of years.
By the power of discernment, they never again succumbed to egoism.
As long as the latent impression of "this is mine" arises within them, so long does that [egoism] vanish into unreality through the inquiry, "Who is this? What am I? (MU 4.16.11–12).
"The body is unreal, the consciousness is pure; who am I?"—by such inquiry, fear and the like did not arise for them.
The body is non-existent; this pure consciousness alone abides within the Self.
"By resolving that 'I am not, nor is there another,' the Asuras became [liberated].
Then, by those heroes who were free from egoism, fearless of old age and death, who imitated what was attained and followed what was present— MU_4,16.15–16.15.
By those whose intellects are ever unattached, who have slain others yet remain non-slayers,
who are liberated from the net of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), who have accomplished their task yet are non-doers,
and who are devoted to their commitment, thinking, "This work is the duty of the Lord."
By those free from passion, devoid of hatred, and always possessed of equanimity,
that divine army was slaughtered, devoured, wounded, and scorched by the Dānavas— Bhīma, Bhāsa, Druṭa, and the others— just as the beauty of one's own entrails is consumed by those who eat.
Then the army of the gods, crushed by Bhīma, Bhasa,
and Druha, fled with great speed like the Gaṅgā falling from the Himavat.
That host of deities [sought refuge] with the God who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk.
She went for refuge to the mountain, like a row of clouds driven by the wind. Viṣṇu consoled that terrified army of the gods, as a lover consoles a solitary woman pursued by a serpent.
Then that host of gods dwelt in the cavern of the Milk Ocean for as long as the Blessed One did not set out for the sake of destroying the enemy.
Thereupon, a fierce battle took place between Śauri and Śambara.
Like an untimely end of an aeon in which the Kulaparvatas have been uprooted,
the Daitya Śambara, together with his army and mounts, was quelled in that battle;
slain by Nārāyaṇa, he departed for the city of Viṣṇu.
But Bhīma, Bhāsa, and Druṭa were brought to rest by Viṣṇu himself in that fierce conflict, just as lamps are extinguished by the wind.
For when they had reached peace, they were indeed devoid of all latent impressions (*nirvāsana*).

Then their movement ceased, like that of lamps being extinguished. Therefore, O Rāma, the mind is bound by latent impressions (vāsanā) and liberated when free from them; quickly attain the state of being free from impressions through discernment.
Through the correct perception of reality, latent impressions (*vāsanā*) dissolve;
and with the dissolution of latent impressions, the mind attains tranquility like a lamp [when its fuel is exhausted].
There is no reality whatsoever here that one can sufficiently cultivate as an object of thought.

"Therefore, cultivation does not exist at all"— this is the correct vision. That supreme state is where the two words "latent impression" (*vāsanā*) and "mind" (*citta*), which possess corresponding referents, have dissolved through the perception of reality.
"This entire world is indeed the Self alone; who could imagine what, or where?
There is no such thing as mental construction (bhāvanā) at all—this is the correct vision.
The mind, enveloped by latent impressions (vāsanā), has attained its state here [in this world]."
That very [mind], when liberated from those [forms], is said to be "liberated.
When the mind has taken on the forms of various pots and cloths,
that very [mind] must be quickly brought to stillness, like a false yakṣa that has arisen.
Just as the mind was transformed by the forms of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa,
so too has it been transformed by the forms of Bhīma,
Bhāsa, and Druṭa. O Rāghava, let the principle of Bhīma, Bhāsa, and Druṭa remain unshakable for you.
"O Rāghava, let not the maxim of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa be yours. This was told to me long ago by my father, the lotus-born Brahmā;
today it has been told by me to you, my most highly intelligent disciple."
Therefore, O Rāghava, let not the maxim of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa be yours;
rather, O sinless one, let the maxim of Bhīma, Bhāsa, and Druṭa be yours forever.
This path of worldly existence, fraught with the dense thicket of pleasure and pain, has been traversed through the mental habituation to becoming.
Even for one engaged in worldly affairs, because of constant non-attachment toward the elements of existence, [the world] perishes;
thus ends the seventeenth chapter, named the Narrative of Dāma and Others.
Vasiṣṭha:
Victorious forever are those heroes, the virtuous ones, by whom their own mind— reeling with the intoxication of ignorance and ever-outward toward sense objects— has been completely conquered.
For this saṃsāra, which bestows all manner of afflictions and suffering, there is only one remedy: the restraint of one's own mind.
Listen to the essence of all dharma, and having heard it, let it be firmly grasped.
Bondage consists merely in the desire for enjoyments; the renunciation of that is called liberation.
What is the use of other collections of scriptures? Listen to this alone:
whatever is pleasant, my dear, let all that be viewed as poison or fire.
The objects of the senses, which provide a poisonous enjoyment, must be investigated again and again;
for they are undesirable and should be abandoned, yet when indulged in, they bring about pleasure. A mind perfumed by latent impressions (vāsanā) gives rise to vast defects.
Just as ground strewn with the seeds of thorns results in the proliferation of thorns,
so too the intellect that contains unattached latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and is devoid of mental proliferation,
having seen neither passion nor hatred, gradually attains supreme tranquility.
The intellect, containing within it auspicious latent impressions (*vāsanā*), always gives birth to excellent qualities,
just as the earth containing superior seeds produces fruit-bearing sprouts in due time.
When the mind remains serene through the continuous contemplation of virtuous states, [the intellect brings forth these qualities].
When fortitude has grown within, like the release of Kīcaka;
when it remains with its foundation firmly established, like the radiance in the moon;
and when the tree of association with the virtuous has borne fruit and provides cool shade.
In the straight tree of samādhi, which drips with the excellent nectar of bliss,
the mind becomes free from dualities, devoid of desire, and untroubled; its restlessness, purposeless striving, greed, delusion, fear, and disease are all stilled.
One whose doubts regarding the meaning of the scriptures have been exhausted, from whom all curiosity has departed,
who has cast off the web of conceptual constructions, who is liberated while living and untainted;
who is effortless, free from reproach, independent, and devoid of mental anguish.

Having destroyed his own self— the charioteer whose offspring are the fierce senses, which is the cage of the wife characterized by craving, and which is unattached and free from knots, yet shrouded in the mist of sorrow— he accomplishes the supreme goal of the Lord.
One abandons by oneself those conceptual constructions that cause the body's plumpness; a good servant, for the sake of his master’s business, casts off his own body like a blade of grass.
The rise of the mind is its destruction; the destruction of the mind is the great exaltation.
The mind of the wise man goes to destruction; the mind of the ignorant man increases.
The wheel of the world is mind alone; the circle of mountains is mind.
The sky is mind, the body is mind, the friend is mind, and the enemy is mind.

That forgetfulness of the self-nature of consciousness which is turbid with conceptual construction is called the "mind" (*manas*); this is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) that partakes in cyclic existence.
It is characterized by the pursuit of objects of thought, while its true designation as "pure consciousness alone" (*cinmātra*) has been lost.
The essence of consciousness (cittattva), when slightly turbid with conceptualization, is called the individual soul (jīva).
When it has fallen into the realm of the objectified (cetya), has acquired established notions, and has come under the sway of ignorance,
that very same [consciousness] is further expanded and imagined as the mind (manas).
The transmigrating person is not the self, nor is it the body, nor the blood;
everything such as the body is insentient, while the embodied one is like space, untainted.
When the body is cut into pieces, there exists nothing other than blood and the like.
When a plantain trunk is split open, there is nothing found other than its leaves.
Know that the mind is the living being, the man; it has merely assumed a form.
By means of itself, it grasps itself as something fashioned by the fragments of its own conceptual constructions.

Just as a silkworm spreads out its own threads and weaves a web for its own confinement, so does a person spread out the threads of their own conceptual constructions to construct [the world]. Having abandoned this delusion of the body, [one may again exist] in another place and time.
It takes on another body, just as a sprout assumes the state of a leaf.
Whatever kind of latent impression (vāsana) this mind possesses, such it becomes;
with whatever mind a person sleeps, that he perceives in his dream at night.
A seed watered with sour juice becomes sour, and one colored with honey becomes sweet; yet when sprinkled with the paste of *prativiṣā*, it becomes pungent.
Likewise, through a great and auspicious mental impression (*vāsanā*), the mind becomes great.
Through the king’s imagination, a man becomes a partaker of Indra’s dream-state of sovereignty.
Through a base latent impression, the mind attains a fragile state of baseness;
like one healthy who, due to the delusion of a demon, sees demons at night.
When the mind is expansive in its purity, turbidity finds no footing;
likewise, when the mind is expansive in its turbidity, clarity finds no footing. When the mind is expansive in its turbidity, a fruit of that very nature is produced.
In the same way, when purity expands, a fruit of that very nature arises.
Even when exhausted, the most excellent person does not abandon their noble course,
remaining unremittingly diligent like the moon in its pursuit of fullness.
Here there is neither bondage nor liberation, neither one to be bound nor the act of binding;
this is merely an illusion arisen from delusion, like a creeper of Indra’s net.
It has the appearance of a city of Gandharvas, arising in the manner of a mirage.

This saṃsāra, consisting of unreality, appears like the illusory perception of two moons. Arising from the false conviction, "I am not infinite; I am miserable," it dissolves through the firm conviction, "I am infinite; I am supreme."
This cultivation of the notion of "cognition" within one's own all-pervading and pure Self—
this is that bondage in the world, fashioned by one's own conceptual construction.
It is devoid of the states of bondage and liberation, and is free from duality and unity.
"All this is indeed the reality of Brahman"—this is the ultimate truth.
When the mind has attained purity and is unattached to all views, having reached a state as if it were no longer a mind, it perceives Brahman; not otherwise.
When the mind has attained purity through the waters of the auspicious continuum,
it takes on the vision of Brahma, just as a white cloth takes on the dye.
O sinless one, by means of the true contemplation that "all this is indeed my self," [one attains this state].
When the portions of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted have been exhausted, what can be said of bondage and liberation?
For one whose mind is purified by the scriptures, dispassion, and discernment, the body falls away like a flaw in a noble gem, and its true luster emerges.

Know that one-pointedness of the mind, which arises from attaining oneness with an object, is a vision of imperfect knowledge and is momentary in its destruction. When one has abandoned all perceptions of the visible, both external and internal, [that is true one-pointedness].
When the mind remains withdrawn and has attained that state,
then this clear perception of the visible object is necessarily composed of unreality;
know that being absorbed in that [object] is the very nature of the mind, and nothing else.

Because it is perishable at its beginning and its end, it is likewise unreal in the middle; therefore, those with minds of false knowledge suffer even while [the treasure] is held in their own hands. The thought "this world is indeed the Self," when devoid of true being, bestows suffering.
Otherwise, this splendor of the visible world bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
To think that the water is one thing and the wave another is ignorance due to perceived diversity;
to realize that "this wave is indeed the water" is true knowledge due to perceived unity.
Suffering arises from ignorance in the form of that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be accepted;
however, through the absence of that [ignorance] due to knowledge, infinity remains.
And because it is fashioned by conceptual construction, the form of the mind is composed of unreality.
But when there is no destruction of that which is not made of clay, tell me, O Rāghava, what is the affliction?
Just as a kinsman who is not affectionate is viewed with a mind free from passion and hatred,
so too, behold, do you view the cage of the visible objects of your own self.
Just as one is not tainted by pleasures and pains due to a kinsman who is no longer affectionate,
so too is one [not tainted] because of the thorough realization of otherness regarding the collection of principles that constitute the self.
That beginningless and auspicious knowledge is the middle between the seer and the seen.
When that truth is realized, the mind becomes tranquil, just as dust settles when the wind has ceased.
When the wind of the mind is stilled, the dust of the body subsides;
once again, the mist of saṃsāra does not arise in the city of worldly existence.

When the rainy season of latent impressions has ended and all that remains has subsided; when dullness has been brought to rest and its tremors have ceased; when the mud of the heart has reached dryness; and when the creepers of parched thirst within the great forest of the heart have withered—MU 4.17.56.
When the dense thicket of false knowledge has been destroyed by the unimpaired *akṣakṣīṇa* trees,
the mist of delusion perishes like the night at dawn;
that dullness departs somewhere, just as poison destroyed by a mantra.
On the mountain of the body, the rivers from the nine apertures no longer flow; the fierce peacocks of volition, with their shimmering plumage, no longer dance.
The hollow of the sky of one's own consciousness attains supreme purity.
The sun of life, exceedingly pure and of great splendor, shines forth most brilliantly.
Freed from the heavy burden of dense delusion and having attained supreme solitude,
the great quarters of space, cleansed and stilled, shine with exceeding beauty.
The stainless Mañjarī of Joy shines intensely,
cooling the circle of the quarters like moonlight in the autumnal sky;
she abounds in supreme bliss through the manifestation of all perfections.

The ground of discernment, when well-purified, attains great fruitfulness. The interior of the world becomes exceedingly clear, beautiful with the supreme light, and filled with cool shade, encompassing mountains and forests.

The lake of the heart attains an expanded tranquility and a clarity as transparent as crystal, with its interior like the hollow of a pure and stainless lotus. From the calyx of the heart-lotus, the bee of one's own defiled egoism emerges.
Indeed, becoming fickle, he departs for some unknown place so as never to be seen again;
he becomes free from all expectations, all-pervading, the leader of all,
devoid of latent impressions, tranquil in mind, and the sovereign of the city of his own body.
When the mind has become a lamp for the self attained through inquiry and is entirely free from agitation, the one of steady intellect,
beholding the states of existence as tasteless and fraught with the fear of destruction, dwells without feverish anxiety within the city of the body.
This is the chapter titled "The Description of the Nature of Tranquility."
The Eighteenth Chapter.
Rāma said:
"Just as this universe is situated within the conscious Self that transcends the universe,"
"Tell me that again, O Brahmin, for the further increase of my understanding.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Just as unmanifest waves exist within water, awaiting their future emergence,"
Furthermore, because they lack any perceivable characteristics, creations likewise do not abide within the nature of consciousness.
Just as space, though all-pervading, is not perceived due to its subtlety,
so too the partless aspect of consciousness, though all-pervading, is not observed.
Just as a female statue within a gem remains neither non-existent nor existent, so too does this creation exist within the Self;
it is neither real nor unreal. Just as the sky is not touched by clouds that rest in the sky and are supported by the air, [so is the Self untouched by creation].
Consciousness, which has creation as its locus within consciousness, is likewise untouched by those creations; it is the supreme consciousness.
Just as fire is reflected only in oceans and not on the earth, so too consciousness is perceived only in the subtle bodies (puryaṣṭakas) and not in the gross physical bodies.
Free from all conceptual constructions and devoid of all perceptions,
this very consciousness (cit) is designated by such terms as "the indestructible self" (avināśātmatattva) and so forth;
it is subtler than a hundredth part of space, and its form is undivided within those who know.
Perceiving the single Self as the nature of the entire stainless universe,
the vast multiplicity consisting of waves and so forth does not appear at all apart from pure consciousness, just as it does not exist apart from the water in the ocean.
Because it gathers (cinoti) that which is gathered (cita), namely the object of thought (cetya), this [world] is established within the Self (ātman).
However, in the ignorant, a state of otherness arises from the conceptualization that "there is something else.
In the ignorant, there exists the form of the multitude of worldly existences (saṃsāra), which are fierce and of the nature of non-existence.
Among objects of knowledge, she is indeed of the nature of light; being the single essence of all,
by virtue of her own experience, she is eternally the illuminator of the sun and other luminaries,
the savorer of all states of being, and the creative power for those experiencing worldly existence.
It neither sets nor rises; it neither stands up nor remains still;
it neither goes nor comes; it is neither here nor not here—this very consciousness (cit), whose form is stainless, abides by itself within the Self.
O Raghava, in this way Consciousness expands through the manifold display known as the world;
just as light shines forth through masses of light and water through floods of water,
so does Consciousness manifest through the vibrating stirrings of creation.
By its own nature, it is named Consciousness (citi), all-pervading, arisen as the Self,
luminous yet non-luminous, partless yet bearing parts;
by virtue of its own spontaneous movement, it abandons the infinite state.
With the thought "I am this," one should proceed slowly to the state of command;
for when diversity has become firmly rooted through prior worldly existence,
one arrives at a state established upon the grasping and abandoning of existence and non-existence.
The subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) produces hundreds of vibrations, yet it neither acts nor does not act;
it rises upward like a mass of sprouts within the hollow interior of the earth-element,
while the ether (*vyoma*) assumes its own vacuity, which is not in conflict with any material form.
The wind possesses the sole property of vibration, just as water has the form of taste;
the earth is firm, fire is manifest, and the worlds are established in their positions.
Time exists through its reckoning in the acts of obstruction and permission.

The flower, with its gathered filaments, slowly reaches the end of the creeper; the joy of the sap within the hollow of the earth becomes grass upon the ground. The delicate fragments of essence situated at the root come forth as fruit.
These lines take their place within the rows of sprouts;
the atoms assume their arrangement in Indra’s bow.
Through this configuration, a union occurs that is ever new.
Masses of flowers and sprouts attend upon the spring;
the splendors of forest fires undergo the ritual of summer;
and rows of dark clouds strive for the season of the rains.
In autumn, entire masses of fruit follow after it; in winter, the ten directions become white with snow;
and in the cold season, cool breezes carry the water to the state of ice.
Time does not abandon this boundary consisting of the [four] ages;
creations pass away with the playful motion of the flood of waves in a river.
Necessity (niyati) maintains its course, bringing about stability and skillfulness.
The earth, whose nature is to support, remains steadfast until the dissolution;
within this world-system, there are fourteen kinds of beings with various modes of conduct and various forms of arrangement.
Again and again they dissolve, and again and again they are born,
like bubbles in water where a continuous succession of streams falls.
It comes, it goes, it remains, it cries out loudly, it acquires its own objects, and it runs about amidst the mass of births.
Like one driven mad, the wretched multitude has its thoughts directed toward what is prescribed; with its desires aroused, it is rendered deluded and helpless by destiny.
The nineteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Sun of Consciousness."
Vasiṣṭha: In this manner, all these series of worldly existences, consisting of both the stable and the moving, come forth from and return again to Brahman by its very nature.
All this has arisen from itself, having become the cause for one another;
perishing through mutual interaction, it dissolves by itself alone.
Like a ripple appearing like a pillar in the depths of unfathomable water, it arises from itself.
In this very way, both the non-existent and the existent are perceived as consciousness alone.
Just as rivers are seen in the sky during the heat of summer despite the sky being devoid of appearance,
even so these perceptions of creation are observed within the reality of the mind.

Just as, under the influence of intoxication, one's own self appears as if it were another, so too, due to its nature as consciousness, the element of consciousness remains as if it were non-existent.
This [consciousness] is neither existent nor non-existent; because of its abiding within that [object] and its not abiding therein, it is consciousness.
And the nature of gold in bracelets and other ornaments is neither more nor less [than the gold itself].
O Rāghava, that by which you perceive sound, taste, form, and smell—
this is the Self, the Supreme Brahman, which exists pervading everything.
Since there is no multiplicity apart from the all-pervading, stainless Self,
no second conceptualization exists anywhere other than that;
for, in the absence of any other aggregate, there is neither existence nor non-existence, neither good nor evil.
Creations are conceptualized either by the Self alone or within the Self;
for desire arises only when an object distinct from the Self is established.
Where nothing whatsoever exists apart from one's own Self, what indeed could the Self desire there?
What should he pursue? What should he approach?
"This is desired" and "this is undesired"—such conceptual constructions do not touch the self.
Therefore, because of its desirelessness, this Self does not perform even the slightest action, since the agent, the instrument, and the object are one;

it does not abide anywhere, since the support and the supported are one. Nor is inaction intended for a desireless Self, because a second [entity] upon which such a distinction could depend is impossible.
Therefore, O Rāma, you are not Rāma, nor are you Arāma; this is the established state of Brahman.
Completely freed from all dualities, become an agent free from the fever of anxiety.

Moreover, O Rāghava, tell me: having placed this manifold task before you and having accomplished it with vigor, what is there that remains for you to attain from the host of living beings? What is appropriate for you to seek?
Let your resolve rest in the state of non-agency; do not harbor desires, but remain healthy and pure, with a mind most firmly established and a sea of fortitude.
Even by a person striving with great effort, that which constitutes perfect fulfillment cannot be attained here, even if one travels very far.
Thinking thus, abandon with your intellect the multitude of objects; you are yourself the reality, the conscious self, in its ultimate sense.
The twentieth chapter, titled "The Instruction."
Vasiṣṭha:
This being the case, that agency which is observed among those who possess such knowledge—whether in sacrifices and the like, or in acts of killing and the like—is unreal;
it does not belong to the ignorant.
For what is called "agency" (kartṛtva)?
That which is the determination of the mental activity through internal resolve, or the conviction regarding its acceptability, is designated by the term "agency";
it is called agency because, by virtue of such effort, one becomes the experiencer of a corresponding fruit.
The person vibrates in accordance with latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and one experiences the fruit in accordance with that vibration;
the established doctrine is that being an experiencer of the fruit is itself what constitutes agency (*kartṛtā*). And so it is said:
Whether one is acting or not acting, whether in heaven or even in hell,
the mind experiences whatever kind of latent impression (vāsanā) it possesses.
Therefore, for men who do not know the true reality, the state of being an agent belongs to those both acting and not acting.
But this is not so for those who have realized the truth, because they are free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
For one who has realized the truth, whose latent impressions have become loosened, does not pursue the fruits even while acting;
with an unattached intellect, he performs merely the movement of the limbs.
Even when the fruit has been attained, one does not experience it as "this entire world is indeed the Self.
By what could anything distinct be experienced?
Therefore, the knower of reality, though acting, does nothing at all.
But the ignorant one, even though not performing the movement of the limbs, experiences the entire fruit of action consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion;
even while not acting, he acts with a submerged mind. (MU 4.20.7)
Whatever the mind does, that is what is done;
whatever it does not do, that is not done.
Therefore, the mind alone is the agent, not the body.
This saṃsāra has come from mind alone;
it exists as consisting of mind, as nothing but mind.
But for the wise, everything is utterly tranquil.
"It is not that it was non-existent;
rather, the Knower alone exists here.
For those who possess a self, that mind has reached supreme tranquility, like the water of a mirage when the rain-cloud pours down.
Like a drop of dew melted by the fierce heat of the sun,
it remains having reached the fourth state;
it is neither bliss nor the absence of bliss, neither moving nor unmoving, but steadfast.
The wise do not know the knowing-mind (*jñamana*) as being existent, nor non-existent, nor even as something between these two.
The knower of reality does not sink into the essence of vibration consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), like an elephant in a small pond;
the mind of the fool perceives only the field of enjoyment (*bhogabhūmi*), not the true nature of existence (*sattattva*).
Likewise, there is this further illustration:

even though he does not actually fall into a chasm, a man who is lying on his bed or sitting down experiences the suffering of falling into a chasm when his mind is permeated by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of such a fall.
But another, even while performing the act of falling into a chasm, experiences the pleasure of a bed or seat when his mind has attained supreme tranquility.
Thus, between two persons occupying the same seat, one who did not perform the act of falling into the chasm becomes its performer.
The second person, though the doer of falling into a pit, becomes a non-doer through the power of the mind;
therefore, the established conclusion is that a person consists of whatever his mind is.
Consequently, let your mind remain eternally unattached, whether you are a doer or a non-doer.
Let there be nothing apart from the reality of the Self wherein attachment is cultivated;
understand that whatever exists in this world has all gone as a mere manifestation of the pure reality of consciousness (*śuddha-cittattva*).
When such a state arises—wherein the person has known what is to be known and the certainty is born that "this Self is not the object of pleasure and pain"—[then liberation is attained].
When the certainty arises that views of a support and its supported do not exist apart from the self;
when the certainty arises that the seer, the seeing, and the seen are not perceived as distinct from the self;
and when the certainty arises that there is no striving or non-striving whatsoever apart from the self.
When the certainty arises that "I am not the body";
when the certainty arises that "I am that portion which is distinct from all objects, even as small as a thousandth part of the tip of a hair";
and when the certainty arises that "whatever this is, all that is indeed I."

When the certainty arises, "I am indeed the light of consciousness, all-pervading and illuminating all reality," and when the certainty arises, "I am not an object of pleasure and pain," the wise one remains amidst worldly affairs— whether in difficulties or ease— with a state of mind free from feverish distress, acting with effortless ease.
Only joy alone, like moonlight, adorns the regions of the world, not anxiety. Therefore, even while acting, the knower becomes a non-doer,
because the mind is untainted.
He does not experience the fruit of action, even that which is produced by effort such as the movement of hands and feet.
This mind is the seed of all actions, all desires, all states of being, all worlds, and all destinies;
when it is removed, all actions are removed.
All sufferings are exhausted;
all joys arrive.
Even by mental action, even by that which is performed with effort, the knower is not assailed, is not rendered helpless, and does not fall into passion.
Because it is non-distinct [from the Self].
Just as a child, while mentally constructing and destroying a city, experiences that mental construction within the city as a mere play, not as something to be grasped as real.
He perceives this as uncontrived happiness;
and perceiving even the destruction of the city— which was mentally willed— as if it were not done, he experiences even suffering with ease and does not perceive it as suffering.
Thus, even while acting, one who knows the ultimate reality is not defiled.
Since the quality of being "acceptable" (*upādeyatā*) in all things is dissolving within the world, what could be the cause of suffering?
Furthermore, nothing whatsoever that is acceptable can exist which is indestructible or distinct from the self.

Therefore, this Self is in reality both an agent and a non-agent, both an enjoyer and a non-enjoyer. This agency and enjoyment which are superimposed upon it must necessarily be due to the delusion of false vision and not to its true nature.
Through the investigation of things as they truly are, the states of being an agent and an enjoyer do not exist.
Views such as aversion toward or desire for the senses and their objects are seen by those who hold such views, but not by those who do not.
For those whose minds are unattached, there is neither liberation nor saṃsāra in this world.
But for those whose minds are attached, everything exists internally just as it is established.
For the knower, however, only the reality of the Self shines forth;
he does not entertain duality or unity regarding the establishment of duality or unity.
And it does not make a duality between existence and non-existence;
rather, it reveals that all power is non-different from the web of powers.
Therefore: (MU 4.20.22)
There is no bondage, there is no liberation; there is nothing to be bound, nor is there a binder.
This suffering arises from lack of awakening; through awakening, it dissolves away.
The notion of bondage in the world is conceived in vain; the notion of liberation in the world is likewise conceived in vain.
Having renounced everything, free from egoism, established in the Self, and acting upon this earth with a steady intellect, remain thus, O Rāma.
The twenty-first chapter, titled "The Imparting of Instruction."

Rāma: O Blessed One, since the Supreme Brahman, distinguished by such qualities, exists alone, tell me, O Great-Souled One, from where could there be the arrival of this creation, which takes the form of a variegated painting produced by ignorance?
Vasiṣṭha:
O Prince, it is this very reality of Brahman that revolves here.
Because it possesses all powers, therefore all powers are seen in Brahman.
Existence, non-existence, duality, unity, beginningness, and endness—
beyond these there is nothing else.
Just as in a mass of water, various masses of water, through successive surges and counter-surges, display a variety of forms and manifest themselves.

They go; likewise, the mass of consciousness itself, as a mass of consciousness, while piling up consciousness, piles up, sustains, generates, and exhausts all powers consisting of action, speech, and mind.
The origin of all living beings, of all perceptions on every side, and of all things in their entirety, occurs incessantly from Brahman.
The worlds come forth from the Supreme; having remained therein, they fully dissolve back into it.
"They are always composed of that very [consciousness], like waves in the ocean.
Rāma said:
"Venerable sir, this expression of yours is exceedingly profound."
Indeed, I do not comprehend the meaning of this statement:
"Where, indeed, is the reality of Brahman, whose mental and sensory functions have ceased;
and where is this fragile splendor of objects born from it?"—such is the construction of your words.
And if this commencement has fallen from Brahman, then it must be similar to that;
for whatever is born from something becomes similar to it,
just as a human is born from a human.
From lamp comes lamp;
from grain comes grain.
Therefore, that which has arisen from the unchanging must itself be unchanging.
"Now, if this [body] were distinct from the self, how could this taint accrue to that stainless one?
Having heard this, the venerable Brahmarṣi Vasiṣṭha said: Vasiṣṭha:

"O sinless one, this world exists as Brahman alone; there is no impurity here. Just as dust does not manifest in the ocean when it is stirred by the multitude of waves and billows, O scion of Raghu, no second conceptualization exists here."
Just as there is no heat apart from fire, and no fire apart from heat, so too there is no Brahman apart from pure consciousness.
Rāma said:
"Brahman is devoid of suffering and devoid of attributes; this world is the suffering born from that [ignorance]."
"O Brahmin, this speech of yours has an unclear meaning; I do not understand it.
Valmiki:
When Rāma had spoken thus, he reflected upon it with his mind.
Vasiṣṭha, that tiger among sages, in instructing the descendant of Raghu,
has brought about a supreme expansion [of understanding]; yet this intellect of his has not yet attained complete purity, for it is still being led forward toward the reality here.

But for the wise one whose mind is fully developed, who has known what is to be known, and who has reached the further shore of the words concerning the means to liberation through discernment— for him,
there is no fault whatsoever in anyone; indeed, it is enough to say that ignorance does not exist within his self.
Rāghava continues on until he has spoken and reached rest;
however, it is not fitting to speak thus to one whose intellect is only half-developed,
for such a person, contemplating the state of enjoyment through this view, perishes.
In one who has attained the supreme vision, the desire for enjoyment does not arise;
this is appropriate for Rāma at the time when the final conclusion—that "all is Brahman"—is established.
First, one should purify the disciple through qualities such as tranquility and self-restraint.
Afterwards, one should cause him to realize: "All this is Brahman; you are pure.
He who says "all is Brahman" to an ignorant person who is only half-awakened casts that person into the snares of great hells.
"It is fitting to say that for the Great-Souled One, whose awakening is fully realized, whose desire for enjoyment has perished, and who is free from expectations, there is no stain of ignorance.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One, the dispeller of the darkness of ignorance, [spoke].

Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages and a sun upon the earth, spoke: "O Rāghava, does the attribution of a stain exist or not exist in Brahman? Vasiṣṭha continued: "O Rāghava, the attribution of a stain exists or does not exist in Brahman."
At the time of the final conclusion, O sinless one, you shall know it yourself:
Brahman is all-powerful, all-pervading, omnipresent, the self of all, and everything itself.
Just as you see a magician performing various wondrous feats that bring about the appearance of existence and non-existence; so too does Brahman manifest.
They lead non-existent beings [to existence];
in the same way, the self,
though not consisting of illusion, appears as if it were consisting of illusion.
A supreme magician turns a jar into a cloth,
a wagon into a pit,
and produces a creeper from a stone.
Like the Nandana grove on the golden slopes of Mount Meru,
he produces a jewel upon a creeper;
like a cluster of gems upon the wish-fulfilling trees.
It superimposes a forest upon the sky,
as if it were a celestial garden;
it brings the forest to the state of the sky.
It carries the sky down to the surface of the earth like a person whose radiance has vanished,
resembling the vast courtyard of a royal palace in a city of the Gandharvas.
He places the sky upon the surface of the earth,
as if it were a reflection of space upon a jeweled pavement.
Is there anything in this world that has existed, exists, or will exist, which the Lord— though his form is unmanifest— does not assume by entering into the state of consciousness?
He does not show [this];
for everything indeed exists in every way, everywhere, and at all times. Thus, it is held that here there exists only a single reality.
Therefore, O Rāma, what occasion is there for pride, resentment, or wonder? A wise person should always abide in equanimity alone.
[One should abandon] the transformations caused by pride, wonder, delusion, joy, and resentment.
The knower of that, having moved into equanimity, never departs from it.
For in the world, diverse logical arguments are seen to exist within the bounds of infinite space and time;
yet he does not laboriously construct these arguments himself.
For the ocean does not intentionally create the arrangement of waves,
nor does it reject those that have arisen, just as the sea does not reject its own billows;
rather, [it is like] ghee [emerging] from milk.
Like atoms in a jar,
like threads in a cloth,
or like banyan seeds within a banyan tree, these powers, residing in the Self alone, have emerged into manifestation and are being incessantly carried away.
It is just like waves;
herein there is no agent, no enjoyer, and no destroyer.
When the reality of the Self—the witness, free from affliction—abides eternally undisturbed in its own equanimity, [the world appears].
In this way, the world comes into being by itself, just as light exists when there is a lamp, as day exists when there is the sun, and as fragrance exists when there is a flower. (MU 4.21.32)
This which is perceived is merely an appearance;
it is like the movement of the wind, neither existent nor non-existent, as it were.
In reality, the Blessed One is not the creator again of any worldly perceptions that have already perished.
Or he is the destroyer of what has been created;
[these things] are sometimes manifest, sometimes slightly manifest, and sometimes extremely manifest, like heaps of flowers in a forest.
For that object which is not one's own self perishes here in this world.
How can that object which is one's own self be destroyed?
Therefore, through the power of incorrect knowledge (*asamyagjñāna*), all things arise from Brahman;
and for those things that have descended [into manifestation], ignorance (*avidyā*) arises at the very same moment as their descent.
Through that [ignorance], ignorance attains firmness;

therefore, from this [root], the tree of saṃsāra— with its hundreds of thousands of trunks, entwined with various auspicious and inauspicious [twigs], and possessing many branches throughout the worlds— attains expansion.

Having severed with the sword of discernment this worldly existence— a poisonous tree whose form is blossomed with hopes, coiled by the terrible hoods of the serpent of suffering, sprouted with the shoots of old age, flowered with decrepitude, and radiant with the creepers of craving— you, O Lord of Elephants, now roam here as one liberated, having cut the shackles that bind the self.
As if released from a pillar.
Chapter Twenty-Two, titled "The Instruction on the Teaching of the Oneness of All."
Rāma:
O Lord, tell me in detail how these living beings arise from the state of Brahman— how many there are and of what nature they are.
Vasiṣṭha:
Just as the various classes of beings arise from Brahman, just as they go to their destruction, and just as they become liberated; MU 4.22.2.
O mighty-armed one, O sinless one, listen as I shall explain to you in due order how they increase, how they endure, and how they disappear.
The stainless power of consciousness belonging to Brahman, acting by its own will, brings about manifestation.
Possessing all powers, she herself becomes the object of cognition, consisting of the act of perceiving.
Having attained density through that very act of perception,
she subsequently conceives of whatever it may be, and that [conception] attains the state of being the mind.
By the mere volition of the mind, it instantly expands this unreal visible world like a city of Gandharvas, while abandoning the vision of Brahma; the nature of consciousness, though shimmering,
remains as nothingness alone.
Since that which is perceived exists as such, for us the perceived is nothing but space.
Having formed the mental resolve of the Lotus-born, one perceives the form of the Lotus-born;
thereafter, one conceives the world, beginning with his own Prajāpati.
Resounding with the emergence of fourteen kinds of infinite beings—
such is this notification, O Rāma, which has arisen as a mental creation;
it consists of mind alone, is empty, and has the mere void as its body.
A city of mere imagination, unreal and consisting of nothing but delusion—
herein exist certain classes of beings in a state of great delusion;
some have awakened knowledge, while others falter midway.
Among all the classes of beings on earth who are awakening and who proceed as those to be instructed,
these human births are indeed full of many afflictions and composed of suffering, for they are tormented by hatred and fear.
From among these, I shall first describe that which is characterized by both passion and purity (rājasasāttvikī):
That which exists is the immortal Brahman, all-pervading and free from affliction;
it is the manifestation of consciousness, called the infinite, beginningless, and devoid of delusion.
From a single portion of the existence of vibration within that motionless body,
it attains density, like the state of being a whirlpool arising from movement in the gentle ocean.
Rāma said:
What can be called a single part of the infinite reality of the Self?
How could there be any transformation, and how could there be a succession of parts?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
Therefore, this arrangement of words— “born from that,” “born from that”—

is for the sake of conventional usage in the treatises, O Rāma, and not in the ultimate sense. [Terms such as] being subject to modification, being a whole possessing parts, and so forth, have been taught merely as designations.
Succession does not exist in the Lord, even though its arising is perceived.
Without Him, there is no other conceptual construction, nor will there ever be;
from where could the meaning of the word "succession" and the expressions born of worldly convention arise?
Whatever conception, whatever object, whatever word, or whatever group of embodied beings there may be here—
because they are born from that and because they consist of that, each is held to be composed of that.
That which is born from it becomes that very thing, just as fire arising from fire is fire itself.
The conceptualization of difference arises when one says, "This is the produced" and "This is the producer.
This worldly condition—that "this has arisen from that"—is merely an excess in the power of action; thus, the produced is indeed the producer itself.
The confusion regarding words and their meanings— thinking "this is one thing" and "that is another"—
occurs only when there is speech, because once [the reality] has been cognized, there is no duality.
By that very power of the mind which brings about victory over that [confusion], the conventional designation proceeds spontaneously.

Through firm cultivation, the desired object is attained by that [meditation]. That which is said—"a second flame is born from a single flame of fire"—is merely a variety of expression; there is no truth in the literal meaning of this statement.
Those expressions such as "the produced" and "the producer" do not apply to those [entities] according to others;
for how could that which is one and infinite ever be born?
This is the very nature of an expression: that an expression, once uttered, immediately [ceases].
It is joined with meanings such as number and the exclusion of its counter-correlate.
That which is perceived within the Supreme like a mass of waves in the ocean,
appearing in the form of the conceptualization of words and their objects— that the wise know to be Brahman alone.
Brahman is consciousness, Brahman is the mind, Brahman is knowledge, and Brahman is the non-substantial;
Brahman is the object, Brahman is the word, Brahman is the directions, and Brahman is the elements.
"This is one, this is another, this is a part"—such distinctions exist within the two selves.

What truthfulness can there be here in speech that expresses false knowledge and conceptual constructions? For that splendor of conceptual construction— which arises from the fickleness of the mind when one thinks, "This flame has been produced from the flame of the fire"— is not established in reality.
The expression of conceptual construction, though unreal,
is imagined to have the nature of reality because one's vision is impaired by delusion, like the defect of the cognition of two moons.
From that infinite state of Brahman, which is all-pervading and all-encompassing...
Nothing else whatsoever is possible; it has been said that whatever exists is that very [reality].
Apart from the reality of Brahman, nothing at all can be established here.
Indeed, "all this is Brahman"—this alone is the ultimate truth.
O wise one, such will be your established conclusion (siddhānta).
Right here we shall set forth the cage of words explaining the meaning of that conclusion:
"In this [system], certain sequences beginning with ignorance exist, and not others."
When this ignorance is destroyed, you will know the entirety of all things.
Upon the destruction of the unreal, the real becomes manifest as it truly is;
the world, which is the object of perception, is seen exactly as it is when the darkness of night has vanished.

O Rāma, whose appearance is stainless, this entire world that has been spread out by false views will, through the pacification [of those views] before you—who possess unerring and boon-bestowing vision—become truly non-illusory; there is no doubt at all in this matter. This is the chapter titled "The Instruction on the Teaching that This Entire World is Brahman."
The Twenty-third canto: Rāma [was honored] by those [women] whose cool, pure, and radiant splendors were like the interior of the Ocean of Milk.
By your various and profound words here on all sides,

for a moment I fall as if into blindness, and for a moment I attain clarity; like a day in the rainy season when the power of the sun’s heat has subsided and the clouds are shifting, I fluctuate between darkness and light.
"How has the conceptualization of the infinite, the immeasurable, the all-encompassing, the singular, the luminous, and that whose essence never sets, come to be? Vasiṣṭha replied:
All my utterances are indeed statements of the meaning of things as they truly are;
they are not ineffective or of inconsistent meaning, nor do they cause contradictions between what precedes and what follows.
This is so when the vision of knowledge has become clear and awakening has arisen in its full expansion.
Once you are established in your own nature, you will understand this vision of my words exactly as it is;

enough with this arrangement of words, meanings, and sentences for the sake of instruction and the comprehension of the meaning of the scriptures— this is merely for a moment to prevent your confusion.
When you shall now know that truth which is absolutely stainless,
then indeed you will know the distinction between the signifier, the signified, and the word-meaning.
This proliferation of speech, which creates distinctions, is merely imagined for the sake of those who are to be instructed.
And that [agency] exists only in the ignorant, not in the wise; it is not ultimately real.
Not even the slightest impurity of conceptualization, such as effort and the like, exists in the Self.
This very world remains as Brahman—free from passion and beyond all dualities.
O sinless one, this must be explained again and again in detail through various forms of expression on the occasion of establishing the final doctrine;
for without such elaboration of speech, this ignorance is incomparable darkness.

It is impossible for one who is intent on destroying each other to make an effort [to realize the truth]. O Rāma, it is through ignorance itself— when it is most intense and strives toward its own destruction— that knowledge, which removes all defects, is attained.
For a weapon is quelled by a weapon, impurity is washed away by impurity,
poison is neutralized by poison, and an enemy is slain by an enemy.
Such is this illusion of beings (bhūtamāyā), which bestows joy through its own destruction.

Its intrinsic nature is not perceived; even as it is being observed, it perishes. It conceals discernment and brings forth the worlds in abundance, yet it is not known what this is—behold this great wonder!
When not looked at, it throbs; when looked at, it perishes.
This illusion dances about as long as its true nature remains unrecognized.
Oh, how wondrous indeed is this illusion that binds one to saṃsāra!
That which, though unreal, appears as if most real, destroys even the wise;
by whomsoever that illusion of saṃsāra— which spreads out extensive differentiation within that utterly non-differentiated state— is fully understood, he is the Supreme Person.

"By means of this cultivation that [the world] does not exist in the ultimate sense, you will become a knower; through the attainment of the object of knowledge, you shall understand its true intent. However, as long as you have not awakened, by my word alone—"

Let there be the unrestrained certainty that "ignorance does not exist," remaining unwavering. That great mental reflection which has reached the state of being perceived— whosoever has the internal certainty that "this is unreal," he is a partaker of liberation.
Whatever has come into the range of vision is but the manifestation of the mind alone;
he who possesses the internal certainty that "that which is real is Brahman" is also a partaker of liberation.
The third vision, which is both moving and unmoving, is characterized by fixed contemplation.
She is the snare that binds all beings and birds throughout the entire world.
He whose single certainty is that the world— whether perceived as real or unreal— is an error like a dream or a delusion,
and who observes it with an unattached soul, does not sink into suffering.
For one whose notions of selfhood reside within these notions of their own true nature—
which are in fact not his true nature— it is ignorance alone that exists. No defects whatsoever, such as being subject to modification and the like, pertain to the Great Self.

In the Supreme Self, these exist like dust particles in water. This manifestation of the world, consisting of the coloring of words and their meanings, has arisen for the sake of worldly transaction; it is not separate from the Self.
Without this conventional usage, these perspectives derived from the scriptures do not attain stability, just as cloth does not exist without its threads.
For the self, being carried along the path of ignorance, is not perceived here [in its true nature].
And that [knowledge] is attained through the meaning of the scriptures, apart from self-knowledge.
O Rāma, indeed, the further shore of the river of ignorance is not reached except by the attainment of the Self; for that is the imperishable and infallible state.
"From whatever source this ignorance, which causes delusion, was born,
it has surely attained its standing by remaining after completely veiling the true state.
O Rāma, let there be no inquiry for you as to 'from where was this born?'"

"How shall I destroy this?"— let this be your reflection. O Rāghava, when it has set and been exhausted, you will know from where it came, what it is, and how it perished, without any flaw in your understanding.
In reality, this [duality] does not exist; it merely appears when not investigated.
Who can know the form of that which is non-existent yet appears through delusion, and from where? Once this [delusion] has arisen and reached maturity, its unextended form leads only to error.
Only after you have forcibly destroyed this [ignorance] will you truly understand it. Neither heroes nor wise men exist in the three worlds who are not rendered helpless by ignorance.
Therefore, exert yourself in providing medical treatment for her in this infirmary,
so that she will not further involve you with the suffering of birth.
[She is] the sole companion of all calamities, the blossom upon the tree of ignorance.
Completely uproot ignorance, which gives birth to a caravan of misfortunes;

having forcibly cast away this false view— which bestows fear, despondency, and unbearable calamities, and is clouded by the great cataract that deludes the heart— become one who has reached the further shore of the ocean of existence.
The twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Discourse on Ignorance," from the Vasiṣṭha [Yoga-vāsiṣṭha].

O Rāghava, hear the medicine for this disease spread by ignorance— which, though it exists even in one who is angry and lacks [virtue], is destroyed by mere discernment. O Rāma, listen to that birth which is both passionate and pure (rājasasāttvikī) that I shall describe.
Listen to her as she speaks, for I have set out for the sake of investigating the mind, vigor, and discernment:
"That which exists is the immortal Brahman, all-pervading and free from affliction;
it is the manifestation of consciousness, called the infinite, beginningless, and devoid of delusion. (MU 4.24.2–3)
For the vibration of that [consciousness], whose body is the pulsation of consciousness,
indeed becomes dense from a certain point alone, like the movement of the gentle ocean.
Just as the water within the ocean, through its vibration, appears as if solidified by its own motion.

Thus, all power converges into one, attaining the state of the power of vibration (spanda-śakti). Just as the wind moves within the sky by itself through its own self, so too does the Self here, by its own power, attain a state of agitation within its very own self.
Just as a lamp, by the power of its own flickering flame, attains a state of height [and radiance] through the moon-like [element],
so too does this Self sport within its own body. Just as there is shimmering water, moving here and there, within the waters of the ocean;
In the very body of all-pervading power, vibration is thus playful;
just as an ocean of molten gold shines with circles of light,
so does the ocean of consciousness flash within the Self through its pure pulsations.
Just as the vibration of a pearl is perceived by the eye within the sky,
so does the radiant power of the consciousness of Brahman arise.
That power of consciousness, slightly agitated in form, exists within the great ocean of consciousness.
It vibrates as nothing but that very [Self], pure and transparent, just as a wave exists within the ocean. Though non-different from the Self, it appears as if distinct,
like the splendor of light reaching a state of density within the hollow of space.
For a moment, that Goddess, throbbing through her omnipotence,
gathers her own power by herself, just as the moon-gem gathers its coolness.
This power of consciousness (cicchakti), called "Light," has arisen from the Supreme Self.
She draws forth the powers of space, time, and action as her companions.
Without knowing her own nature, though she abides pervading the infinite state,
she— remaining undifferentiated— conceives of herself as having a limited form.
At the very moment that form was manifested by her, who is supremely beautiful, there followed perceptions such as names, numbers, and so forth;
yet consciousness remains in this very state, distinct from the self that persists.
Infinite, it quickly enters into that [object] like a wave from the great ocean.
Just as the distinction between bracelets and armlets is not different from gold,
so too the form of the Self, when one contemplates its own partial aspect through consciousness, is not distinct from it.
Just as a lamp [illuminates] lamps that have arisen by means of itself, so too consciousness (cit) is cultivated through its own nature, with only the distinctions of place, time, and degree;
then consciousness is fully ignited by the power of movement across space and time.

Chasing after volitional constructs, it enters the state of conceptualization. O mighty-armed one, the form of consciousness (*cit*), which assumes shapes fashioned by mental construction and serves as the locus for space, time, and action, is called the "knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*).
They say the field is the body; he knows that field in its entirety, both internally and externally, and for that reason he is called the "Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajña).
Even while fashioning latent impressions (vāsanās), he again falls into the state of egoism (ahaṅkāra).
When the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) has been determined, it is called the temporal intellect (*buddhi*).
That intellect, when permeated by volitional construction (*saṅkalpa*), moves to the domain of reflection (*manana*);
the mind (*manas*), characterized by dense conceptualization, gradually attains the state of the senses (*indriyatā*).
The wise know that the body consists of hands and feet, as do the senses;
this body is born in the world, it dies, and it lives.
In this way, the individual soul (jīva) is indeed a volition, entwined by the rope of latent impressions (vāsanā).
With its self enveloped by a web of suffering, it gradually attains the state of consciousness.
Just as a fruit, through the process of ripening,
gradually reaches a different state by way of its condition alone and not by its essential form, so too does the living being [attain a different state] due to the influence of impurity.
The living soul (jīva) has attained the state of ego (ahaṅkāra), and the ego has reached the state of intellect (buddhi).
Enveloped by the web of volitions (saṅkalpa), the intellect has come to the state of mind (manas);
for the mind consists of volitions and is intent upon grasping forms.
Excluded by its own opposite, it is attained even by others who desire it;
as cows run toward an intoxicated bull, so do the powers such as desire pursue him for their own detriment, just as rivers flow toward the ocean. (MU 4.24.29–30)
Thus, the mind, consisting of power (*śakti*), having attained a state of dense egoity (*ahaṅkāra*),
enters into bondage by its own will, like a silkworm in its cocoon;
through the pursuit of its own volitions, it encircles its body with fetters.
"I am bound by myself"— with such anguish he suffers in torment.
Perceiving "I am bound," the principle of pure knowledge (*vidyātattva*), while gradually abandoning [its own nature],
generates within ignorance (*avidyā*) the world-demoness of the wild forest.
And remaining within the web of those very elements imagined by itself,
it falls into a state of supreme helplessness, like a lion bound by chains;
yet, through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it assumes the agency of performing diverse actions.
Following after ever-new states fashioned by its own mere will,
it is sometimes called the mind (*manas*), sometimes the intellect (*buddhi*), sometimes knowledge (*jñāna*), sometimes action (*kriyā*),
sometimes this ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and sometimes it is known as the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*).
In some places it is called *prakṛti*, in others it is conceived as *māyā*;
in some places it is declared to be the *manas*, and in others it is established as *karman*.
In some places it is known as *bandha* (bondage), and in others it is clearly called *citta*.
In some places it is called ignorance (*avidyā*), and in others desire (*icchā*); this is consistent.
O Rāghava, this very mind here is bound, sorrowful, overwhelmed by thirst and grief, a dwelling place for disease, and afflicted.
Afflicted by old age, death, and delusion, struck down by the contemplation of worldly existence,
seized by what is desired and undesired, and stained by ignorance and passion;
its form constricted by craving, it is the fresh sprout of the tree of karma.
Having utterly forgotten the state of its own origin, it imagines imagined misfortunes;
bound like a silkworm, it has entered the state of a cocoon—
a mass composed of the collection of those subtle elements, which is the heat of infinite hells.
Though invisible, this entire cycle of existence is a poisonous and evil tree; it bears the weight of a burden equal to the king of mountains, is rich with the branches of old age and death,
and acts as a snare of desires.

Just as a banyan seed contains within itself a banyan tree devoid of fruit, so too [the mind] harbors within it that which is consumed by the flames of the fire of anxiety, chewed by the python of anger,
struck by the waves of the ocean of desire, and has forgotten its own grandfather.
Like a deer strayed from the herd, its mind struck by grief;
like a moth burnt in a blazing fire of sensual objects;
like a lotus with severed roots, it has reached a state of supreme witheredness.
With its hopes severed from its own abode, it is ill at ease due to attachment to foreign lands;
situated amidst enemies in the guise of friends and serpents in the form of sense objects,
it wallows in endless and extreme perils.
