Like a bird fallen into a terrible snare,
the mind— driven by sense objects— is swept away in the ocean of misfortune, bound within the net of the world that is as empty as a city of Gandharvas.

O Rama, who resembles an immortal, lift up my mind as one would pull a mātaṅga elephant from the mud. O Rama, forcibly extract my mind, which is submerged like a bull in the pond of thought, its very limbs torn and shattered.

O Rāma, he in whose human form no compassion arises for this world— whose appearance is struck down by the proliferation of the auspicious and inauspicious, and who is fainting from the despair of blazing old age and death— is a *rākṣasa* in this world.
The Chapter named "The Descent of Living Beings."
The Twenty-fifth Canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"In this way, living beings are struck down by the state of consciousness through the mental preoccupation with worldly existence."
From Brahmā, whose form is immeasurable, hundreds of thousands and even tens of millions have been born in the past; they are born even today in all directions beyond count,
and others will continue to arise like showers of spray from a mountain torrent.
Driven by the force of their own latent impressions, they have fallen under the power of hope;
with their intentions bound by themselves,
they wander incessantly in every direction and every land, whether on water or on dry ground, through most diverse conditions.
They are born and they die like bubbles in water.
Some are in their first birth, some have transcended the power of birth;
some have undergone innumerable births, while others are separated from their current birth by hundreds of lifetimes.
Some belong to future births, some have experienced great existences in the past, some are in present existences, and some have gone to non-existence;
some are being born again and again for thousands of eons.
Some rely upon a single womb, while others have resorted to another womb;
some are struck down by great suffering, some remain in the state of youth,
some have risen to the highest degree, and some have arisen like suns.
Some were kinnaras, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and mahoragas;
some were Arka, Indra, Varuṇa, Tryakṣa, Adho’kṣaja, and Padmaja;
some were kumbhāṇḍas, vetālas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas.
Some are known as groups of brahmins, kings, vaiśyas, and śūdras;
some are śvapacas, caṇḍālas, kirātas, khaśas, and pukkasas;
and some have reached the state of grass, herbs, leaves, fruits, and roots.
Some were parched by forest creepers, thickets, grass, and stones;
some were [sheltered by] *kadamba*, *jambīra*, *sāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees; and some were lords of the earth, intoxicated by the abundance of their wealth.
Some were clothed in rags and had adopted the silence of sages;
some were snakes, cattle, serpents, worms, insects, and ants;
and some were lions, buffaloes, deer, bears, yaks, and antelopes.
Some became cranes, ruddy geese, herons, ducks, and cuckoos;
some attained the state of lotuses, white water-lilies, night-blooming lilies, and blue lotuses;
and some became young camels, elephants, moths, bulls, and donkeys.
Some are born as bees, mosquitoes, ants, gadflies, or bamboo;
some are overcome by the force of calamity, while others have attained prosperity;
some reside in the city of heaven, and others dwell in hell.
Some are situated within the circle of stars, others within the hollows of trees;
some abide in the form of wind, and some abide in the realm of space.
Some are situated in the rays of the sun, and some are situated in the rays of the moon.
Some abide in the sweet juices of grasses, creepers, and shrubs;
some wander here as those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), vessels of auspiciousness;
some remain as those long-liberated, and others are surely fully matured.
Some, being deceitful, will attain liberation only after a long time;
others, possessing evil dispositions, hate their own state of isolation (kaivalya).
Some have been born in this world, while others are situated elsewhere.
Some are neither here nor elsewhere, but abide in the supreme state;
some are Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Mandara, and Meru;
and some are the oceans of salt water, curd, milk, clarified butter, sugarcane juice, and fresh water.
Some are vast directions, some are rivers of great velocity;
some are women with lovely eyes, and some are eunuchs;
some possess awakened intellects, while others have minds that are utterly dull.
Some are instructors of knowledge, while others have attained meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Living beings, rendered helpless by the influence of their own latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
remain in these various states with their mental dispositions firmly bound.
They dwell within the treasury of the world, falling down and leaping up again,
incessantly struck by Death like balls with the hand;
bound by hundreds of snares of hope, they carry the heavy burden of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
They pass from body to body like birds from tree to tree;
through the illusory upheaval of infinite and endless conceptual constructions,
they spread out this great world-illusion of Indra’s net.

The deluded wander in saṃsāra like masses of whirlpools in water, so long as they do not perceive their own blameless Self. Having seen the Self and abandoned what is unreal, and having attained true consciousness, [they are liberated].
Having reached the state at the proper time, they are not born here again.
Having experienced thousands of births, and then through knowledge or austerity,
some reach the station of Parameṣṭhin and go to the supreme state.
Some, having attained even the high status of Indra, return again to the state of an animal due to the meanness of their intellect;
and from the state of an animal, they may also attain the state of a human.
Some, being of great intelligence, arise from the station of Brahmā.

At that very moment, some enter that very same [Brahmāṇḍa] in a single birth; others enter other Brahmāṇḍas. Therefore, these multitudes of living beings attain the state of being born from the lotus, while others even attain the state of being Hara.
Some go to the state of animals, others even to the state of gods;
and others, O Rāma, do not return at all, just as it is here, so it is elsewhere.
For just as this world is vast, so indeed are other worlds.
There have been many [beings] in the past, and there will be many in the future.
Through various diverse successions and through various causes,
their manifold creations arise and pass away.
Some attain the state of Gandharvas, some go to the state of Yakṣas;
some proceed to the state of Suras, and some come to the state of Daityas.
By whatever means people are situated within this cosmic egg, [so do they remain].
By that very [power], other abodes remain indistinguishable in their arrangement;
through the force of their own inherent natures and by mutual friction,
creations revolve like waves in a river.
Through manifestations and disappearances, through emergences and submergences,
creations revolve like the waves of a river; from that Supreme One,
the multitudes of individual souls flow forth incessantly.
From that which is inexpressible and self-cognized, they flash forth instantly right there—
like perceptions of light from a lamp, like rays from the sun,
like sparks from heated iron, or like scintillations from a fire.
Just as the various seasons arise from time, as diverse fragrances from a flower,
as spray from a downpour of rain, or as waves from the ocean;
so too, by means of time, having repeatedly cast off successions of bodies after rising up again and again—

The multitudes of living beings go to dissolution in their own very place. This dense, far-extended, and lofty construction of the three worlds— a delusive illusion— exists, perishes, and grows in vain, like a wave in the ocean within the supreme state.
The twenty-sixth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Structure of the Aggregate of Living Beings," Canto 26;
Rāma said:
"By what sequence, O Blessed One, does that living being, having attained its own state of existence, take on a body— a cage of bones? Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O Rāma, have you not understood what I have already told you?
Where has your discernment gone, which ought to consider the preceding and the following?
For this world, consisting of the body and so forth, both moving and stationary—"
"This is merely a mental appearance, unreal, arisen like a dream.
For this long dream, O sinless Rāma, is seen as a sheer falsehood,
having the form of the delusion of two moons, like a mountain seen by one afflicted by vertigo."
With the sleep of ignorance utterly stilled and all mental projections dissolved, he whose mind is awakened no longer perceives the dream of saṃsāra while looking upon it. For,
O Rāma, this [dream] is always imagined by the very nature of living beings.
Until the attainment of the state of liberation, transmigratory existence exists within the self;
it is eternally imagined through one's own nature and exists within every self.
The flickering body of the individual soul is like a whirlpool in water.
Just as the sprout expands within the seed, just as the leaf is within the sprout,
just as the flower is within the leaf, and just as the fruit is within the calyx of the flower;
since the body, which is of the nature of conceptual construction, exists within the mind.
Therefore, O Rāma, that [mind] clearly exists here in this world as an external form.
Whatever manifestation indeed arises from this mind,
that very thing quickly becomes [external], just as a lump of clay becomes a jar.
O Rāghava, this world appears as nothing more than a mental construction; it is not real, like the water of a mirage.
And by means of this very appearance, this body is perceived before us.

Just as a child, terrified and bewildered, sees a Vetāla standing before him; so too, at the beginning of creation, that very manifestation of his mind which was the pervasive Brahmā remained within the abode of the lotus-bud.
Through the very sequence of that [Supreme Being's] volition,
this infinite creation has come into existence from him, like an illusion produced by a powerful magician.
Rāma said:

"O Brahman, tell me quickly in detail how the individual soul (jīva), having attained the state of the mind, reaches the state of Brahmā, and how everything else likewise comes to pass. Vasiṣṭha replied:
Listen, O mighty-armed one, to the sequence of the assumption of a body according to the Vedic tradition;
by that very illustration, you shall understand the state of the world.
The reality of the Self, unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, [manifests] through its own power.
That which, by mere play, assumes a body delimited by space and time— this very thing, known as the synonym "living being" (jīva), intent upon the immersion in latent impressions (vāsanā),
becomes the restless mind, oriented toward the perception and non-perception of mental constructs.

First, the mental power (*manaśśakti*), as it impels [the mind], instantly contemplates the pure contemplation of space (*ākāśabhāvanā*), which is oriented toward the sap of the seed-syllable of sound (*śabdabīja*). Then, the mind gradually attains a state of density, becoming a dense vibration.

It cultivates the vibration of the wind, which is intent upon the essence of the seed of touch. From the friction of those two— space and wind— which have been rubbed together by the vision of the mind and possess the natures of sound and touch, fire is produced.
The mind, having attained a state of density, then in an instant brings about luminosity with its stainless light; through that, the light increases.
The mind, possessing such a multitude of qualities, experiences the subtle element of taste.
In an instant, it gathers the coldness of the waters; from that, the cognition of water arises.
Then, in a moment, the mind impregnates itself with such a multitude of qualities, its own form becoming gross like fragrance, by which the earth shall emerge.
Then, this body, enveloped by the elements and subtle essences (*tanmātra*), casting off its attenuation,
appears as a spark of fire flickering in the sky;
it is joined with the faculty of ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and endowed with the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*).
That is called the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), and the bee-like mind dwells within the lotus of the heart of beings.
By meditating upon that radiant form with intense fervor,
the mind attains a state of grossness through its ripening, just like a mango fruit.
Then that light, shining like molten gold in a crucible within the stainless sky, assumes its own natural configuration;
and then the mind [rests] upon that mass of light which constitutes its own configuration.
One spontaneously cultivates a vast, firm, and expansive meditation,
consisting above of the seat of the head, below of the feet,
situated on the sides as the hands, and having the nature of the belly in the middle.
Then that child, with limbs clearly manifest and a form as pure as a mass of flames,
remains there, having assumed a body through the power of his own desire.
In this way, O Sage, the mind— its parts imagined through the influence of its own latent impressions— remains.
Just as the season brings its own nature to fullness, it leads the body to growth;
having reached manifestation through time, it becomes one of pure form,
established in intelligence, goodness, strength, energy, discernment, and sovereignty.
This very Blessed One is Brahmā, the sovereign lord of all worlds,
resembling molten gold, born from the supreme ether. Then,
abiding in that supreme ether, he possesses the most excellent form.
Abiding within itself, it fashions its own home through the play of the mind.
At times it imagines the absolute, infinite void, devoid of boundaries; at other times, the stainless water, without beginning, middle, or end.

Sometimes the Lord [dwells] in a forest adorned by the blazing flames of the fire at the end of an eon; sometimes in a lovely grove resembling the bud of his navel-lotus. Thus, throughout the course of many successive births, he assumes various and manifold forms.
He effortlessly fashions seats of various forms;
when he first descended from the station of Brahmā, he was known as Susama due to his very knowledge.
Upon the departure of the sleep of the womb, one perceives the body as radiant,
rich with the flow of prāṇa and apāna, and composed of material elements;
it is covered with millions of pores and endowed with thirty-two teeth.
It has three pillars, five deities, and is marked by feet below;
it consists of five parts, has nine gates, and its limbs are made smooth with a coating of skin;
it is joined with twenty fingers and marked by twenty nails.
Having two arms, two breasts, and two eyes— or indeed many eyes and arms—
it is the nest of the bird of the mind and the burrow of the serpent of passion;
it is the abode of the ogress of craving and the cave of the lion of life.

Beholding his own most excellent and lovely body— adorned with a lotus-face and serving as a tethering post for the elephant of pride— the Blessed Brahmā, whose vision is stainless regarding the three periods of time, reflected: *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* 4.26.44–45.
"In this vast hollow of space, marked by me and whose further limits are unseen, what was there first?"—
thus thought Brahmā, having been newly born with the vision of the stainless Self.

He beheld the numerous multitudes of creations that had passed away in manifold ways. Then he recalled all the Vedas, together with their contents, qualities, and sequences, just as a spring season recalls its flowers along with their fragrance.

He effortlessly fashioned diverse beings born of his volition, engaged in various activities and undertakings, like a Gandharva creating a city. For their sake, and for the attainment of heaven and liberation, as well as for the accomplishment of dharma, pleasure, and wealth—
He composed infinite and diverse treatises.
Thus, O Rāma, this creation has attained stability within this world-emanation,
like the splendor of flowers from the mind of Viriñca, as from the springtime.
By means of his mind alone, assuming the form of the Lotus-born [Brahmā] through various compositions and playful creative acts,
the son of Raghu brought about an incomparable state of the glory of creation here in this world.
The chapter titled "The Instruction on the Exposition of the Descent into Saṃsāra."
The twenty-seventh canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"In this way, all this is truly accomplished; not even the slightest thing exists."
The supreme manifestation of the mind is indeed empty, being mere space.
Neither space nor time are ever encompassed by this cosmic egg,
even though it possesses a great form, for its true nature is that of space.
This world, whose nature is mere conceptualization, is like a city seen in a dream;
wherever it appears, there is only the void, established as pure space.
Even the painting of colors without a wall is seen to be composed of unreality.
This uncreated [world] is indeed created, like a variegated painting in the sky;
everything from the body to the three worlds is imagined by the mind.
And this is the cause of transmigration, just as the eye is the cause in the act of seeing.
For this world, consisting of the sequence of jars, huts, and cloths, is a mere appearance;
it revolves, yet walls and other such things do not exist as separate, real entities.
Indeed, this body has been fashioned by the mind for the purpose of habitation.

Like a silkworm with its own cocoon, he himself [creates his own confinement]. There is nothing that the mind— slowed by its own volitions— does not do, nor is there anything it does not attain, however inaccessible or exceedingly difficult it may be.

In the Supreme Deity who possesses all powers, what indeed are those powers that do not exist, by which the inner cave of the mind is veiled? For the existence and non-existence of all things at all times [depend on Him].
O mighty-armed one, since the All-powerful Lord exists as the source of all things,
behold that lotus-born form attained by the mind through contemplation;
therefore, O Rāma, they know that manifestation to be endowed with all powers.
In creation, gods, asuras, humans, and moving beings are produced by one's own volitions;
upon the cessation of those volitions, they subside like a lamp without oil.
Everything is similar to space, manifested solely through the expansion of conceptual construction.

Behold the world, O one of great intelligence, as a very long dream that has arisen. Nothing whatsoever is ever born or dies here; from the perspective of ultimate reality, O wise one, everything proceeds as a falsehood.
In that forest of trees marked by lines, where nothing ever undergoes increase or destruction, who indeed could suffer any injury?
You, however, do not perceive your own body— which is but a product of delusion— with a discerning eye.
"O Raghava, why do you speak like an ignorant person, with a mind struck by evil?
Just as a mirage appears due to heat and the excessive agitation of the mind,
so too all these beings, beginning with Brahma, are seen though they do not exist."
All the multitudes of forms in the world are composed of false cognition; they arise like a wish-fulfilling thought and resemble the illusion of seeing two moons.
Just as one traveling by boat falsely perceives the movement of a stationary pillar, so it is with these appearances.
This constant succession of forms has arisen from unreality itself.
Know this to be a magical net, a cage constructed by illusion;
it is a creation of the mind’s own thinking, existing as neither real nor unreal.
This entire world is indeed Brahman; how, then, could there be any otherness? What kind of logical consequence (prasaṅga) would there be, what would it be, and where would it abide?
"This is a mountain," "this is a post"—such is the delusion of conceptual proliferation (āḍambara).
Through the firmness of mental cultivation, the unreal appears as if real.
This world, which begins with the fourfold display of manifoldness and is empty within, is merely the conceptualization of desire and thirst; O Rāma, abandon it and cultivate something else.
Just as a grand undertaking in a dream is merely an illusion and not a real entity,
know that this long dream is likewise constructed by the mind;
though it appears as a great enjoyment, it is being grasped as something devoid of reality.
Abandon this treasury of the serpent-like desires of the world, this ostentatious display of saṃsāra.
Knowing that this is unreal, do not fix your affection upon it. What wise person, having recognized a mirage, would continue to pursue it?

The deluded soul who pursues a woman composed of mere desires, rich in forms born of his own imagination, becomes only a vessel for suffering. Since this world does not exist as a real entity, let it go as it pleases; it is but a non-entity.
But he who abandons the real and pursues the unreal perishes.
This world is merely a delusion of the mind, like the fear of a snake in a rope; through the diversity of mental impressions alone, it revolves for a long time.
In this world, only the fool is deceived by unreal entities that arise like the shimmering moon reflected in water; one such as you, who knows reality, is not so deceived.
He who seeks happiness by cultivating this collection of qualities [is likewise deluded].
That dull-witted person attempts to wipe away his own dullness in a fire that does not reflect images.
This expansive cage of the visible world, which appears though it is utterly non-existent,
is a construction of the mind’s own imaginings, like a city within the heart.
This arises by the will of the mind and dissolves by its will;
it is seen falsely and extensively, like a city of Gandharvas.
O Rāma, when this world is destroyed, not even the slightest thing is destroyed.
Even though this world appears joined together, nothing at all is actually joined.
When the city of the heart, constructed by the mind, is destroyed, tell me: what has grown, what has been diminished, and for whom?
Or, when that city has expanded, tell me: what has increased and what has been lost?
Just as a city arises in the hearts of children for the sake of play,
so too does this world arise incessantly through the mind.
Nothing whatsoever is lost to anyone, just as in the waters of a magical illusion.
When this worldly existence, arising from prosperity, has thus fallen away or perished—
if that which was unreal remains unreal, then what indeed is lost for whom? Therefore, this so-called "worldly existence" provides no ground for joy or despondency.
If something is absolutely non-existent, what indeed can perish therein?
For in the absence of destruction, O Mahāmati, what possibility is there for suffering?
Or if something is absolutely existent, what indeed can perish of it?
This entire world is indeed Brahman; why then have pleasure and pain arisen?
Since this world-process, which creates nothing but delusion, is everywhere unreal, what is there for a wise person to accept or desire in this cycle of existence?
Since this entire triple world is everywhere real and consists of the essence of Brahman, what could there be in it that should be abandoned? O wise ones, let them abandon that which they deem so.
Whether the world be unreal or real, for the knower of reality, it is thus [the same] regarding pleasure and pain.
But the fool, having failed to attain it, is distressed by a third part [of his desire].
That which does not exist at the beginning nor at the end does not exist even in the present;
O Rāma, for him who longs for what is non-existent, only non-existence remains.
That which is real in the beginning and at the end is indeed real in the present;
for one for whom everything is indeed real, only existence remains.
That which is unreal—such as the moon within water, a lotus in the sky, and so forth—[is not so].
Only fools, through the delusion of their minds, long for these things; the noble do not.
For the fool finds satisfaction in objects that appear expansive but are empty of substance, leading to endless suffering rather than to happiness.
Therefore, O lotus-eyed Rāma, do not be a fool;
having perceived the impermanence here, take refuge in that which is eternal and most stable.
Having reflected that "all this, including myself, is unreal," let there be no despondency in you.
"Let there not be despondency in you upon seeing that everything here has indeed been completed by me.
Valmiki:
When the sage had spoken thus, the day passed away, and the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites.
Having offered her salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Application of Reality as it Is."
Vasiṣṭha said:
When wealth, wife, and so forth have perished, what occasion is there here for grief?
What lamentation can there be for that which is seen in an instant like a magical illusion and then vanishes?
Whether half of a city of Gandharvas is adorned or ruined,

or whether it pertains to the portion of ignorance such as a son and so forth, what sequence of pleasure and pain can there be? For when wealth, a wife, and the like are obtained, what occasion indeed is there for joy?
When a mirage has grown large, what joy can there be for one seeking water?
When wealth and wife have increased, sorrow is appropriate, not contentment.
When the illusion of delusion has grown large, who here can find any consolation?
By those very objects of enjoyment which, when excessively pursued, give rise to passion in a fool,
it is by those same objects that detachment arises in the wise man.
Fools who do not perceive the further shore find satisfaction in enjoyments.
But by looking beyond these, the virtuous attain dispassion.
Therefore, O Rāghava, you who know the truth, remain indifferent toward whatever is lost in the worldly affairs of saṃsāra, and accept whatever is obtained.
Not desiring future enjoyments and not being artificial toward those already arrived— this is the characteristic of a wise man.
For in this turmoil of saṃsāra, the self is like a hidden assassin.
Dwell thus as a perfectly awakened one, so that you do not fall into delusion.
Those of perverted intellect who do not see this sequence of the world’s grand display— which is constructed through conceptual proliferation— correctly and impartially, are destroyed.
By whatever means possible here, for one who finds no delight in the realm of the visible,
their stainless intellect is nowhere further sullied.
For one whose attachment to all things has ceased with the realization that "this is unreal," [the mind becomes pure].

Ignorance, being unreal, cannot embrace the Omniscient One. He whose intellect realizes, "I and this entire world are one," remains established having abandoned both attachment and non-attachment; he does not sink.
Having grasped with the intellect that pure state which is the middle between existence and non-existence,
do not grasp nor release the universe, including its internal and external aspects.
It is infinitely expanded, transparent, possessing all, yet devoid of all.

O Rāma, remain passionless like the sky, even while performing your duties. For the wise man who remains engaged in action without desire or aversion, his discernment is not defiled, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Whether your subordinate group of senses performs acts such as seeing and touching or does not perform them, you remain desireless and possessed of the Self;
for your mind does not dwell upon the objects of the senses, which are unreal in the sense that "this is mine."
"Let it not sink; let that which is not sunk remain as it is, or let it act.
O Rāghava, if the splendor of the objects of the senses does not please your heart, then you have realized true knowledge and have crossed over the ocean of worldly existence.
For you, whether possessing a body or being bodiless, liberation has been achieved through the power of reality, even though you have not tasted the objects of the senses and did not desire it;
for, by means of supreme wisdom, you have risen to the highest state from the multitude of latent impressions.
O Rāma, separate the mind from the self, just as one separates the fragrance from a flower.
In this ocean of saṃsāra, which is flooded with the waters of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), those who have boarded the boat of wisdom have crossed over; others have drowned.
Having investigated the reality of the self with an intellect that is exceedingly steady and sharpened like the edge of a razor, enter your own true state.
Just as the wise who know reality, whose minds are nourished by knowledge, [attain their goal].

O Rāma, one should dwell in that manner; one should not dwell like a fool. The great-souled ones who are liberated while living, ever-contented and high-minded, are to be followed in their conduct, and not the deceitful who are wretched in their pursuit of enjoyments.
Those people who know both the higher and the lower neither abandon nor desire the worldly affairs of the world; they conform to everything.
[They remain indifferent] toward power, pride, the qualities, fame, and fortune.
Nowhere in the world are the great ones, who perceive reality, ever miserable;
even in a profound void they do not suffer, for they are unattached like the gardens of the gods.
Like suns, the great do not abandon their natural course.

Free from desire, following the conventional usage as it has come to them, they move about without arrogance, established in their own nature, situated within the chariot of the body. You too, O Rāma, have attained this discernment that has now arrived.

By this power of wisdom, I know you are at ease, O Sundara. Firmly maintaining clear vision, free from pride and devoid of envy, dwell upon this seat of the earth; you shall attain supreme perfection.
Established in yourself, renouncing all that is beneficial [to worldly ends], with desires seen from afar,
dwell, O sinless one, having taken up supreme coolness within.
— Vālmīki:
Thus, by these pure words of the sage of pure intent, Rāma appeared as if polished;
filled within with the sweet, radiant nectar of knowledge, he attained a coolness like that of the moon.
This is the chapter titled "The Instruction on the Application of Discourse Based on the Realization of Things as They Truly Are."
The twenty-ninth canto:
Rāma said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, you who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedānta!"
I stand as if comforted by your pure words.
I do not reach satiety in hearing your noble, dispassionate, elegant, and appropriate words as you speak them.
O Blessed One, in the course of your discourse on the *rājasa-sāttvika* birth, you have described the origin of the Lotus-born One. Regarding this,
O Great-Souled One, a doubt arises within my heart.
O you who sever all doubts, let that be told quickly:
how is the diverse origin of the Lotus-born One described in the scripture— sometimes from a lotus, sometimes from space, sometimes from an egg, and sometimes from water?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāghava, many hundreds of Śaṅkaras and Indras, as well as thousands of Nārāyaṇas, have passed away, who were all characterized by the nature of Brahman."
Today, in many other diverse cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*),
thousands wander about, engaged in various modes of conduct and pastimes;
this occurs simultaneously in infinite worlds, both those existing within the current time and those arising at other times.

Many other [creations] will arise abundantly in the worlds. O mighty-armed one, the various origins of the celestial dwellers within those eggs, beginning with that which was born from the lotus, have been described in heaven.
Sometimes the creations belong to Śarva, sometimes they arise from the lotus-born;
sometimes they are indeed Vaiṣṇava, and sometimes they are fashioned by the Sage.
Sometimes Brahmā is born from the lotus, and sometimes he is born from the waters.
And sometimes he is born from an egg, and sometimes he is born from the sky.
In one egg he is the three-eyed Arka, in another Vāsava;
in one he is Puṇḍarīkākṣa, and indeed in another he is simply Tryakṣa.
In one creation, there was a land densely crowded with trees;
in another, it was packed with people; and in another, it was covered by mountains.
One land was made of clay, and another was composed of stone.
One was made of gold, and likewise another was made of flesh. Some of those worlds were right here, while others were otherwise;
some consisted of individual worlds within one another, and some even pierced through them.
In this great sky of the reality of Brahman, infinite worlds sink down and emerge like the multitude of waves in the ocean;
just as waves are in the sea, and as a mirage is in the desert.
Just as flowers are found on a mango tree, so are the glories of the universe present in the Supreme.
It is possible to count the motes of dust within the rays of the sun,
but the multitudes of worlds cannot be counted within the essence of Brahman, which is of a restless form.
Just as swarms of mosquitoes arise and perish again and again among the cane groves during the rains, so too do these creations of the world;
nor is it known from what time they have come into being.
These successions of creations, characterized by constant coming and going,
flash forth incessantly like waves;
indeed, each arose from what preceded it, and that in turn from what was even more prior.
Having come into being again and again, the gods, asuras, humans, and other such beings—
all these classes of living creatures— dissolve like the breaking of waves upon a river.
Just as this egg of Vairiñca [Brahmā], so too are the successions of world-eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*).
Like years, the tubes have been exhausted by the thousands;
yet others now exist within this present body,
beyond this city of Brahmā, in the vast domain of Brahman.

In Brahmā, there will arise many other splendors of the city of Brahmā; having come into being again and again, they will perish like spoken words. In Brahmā, there will be other successions of creations that have remained [before].
Just as jars [arise] from a heap of clay, and as sprouts [emerge] from a bud;
just as waves and currents of water exist within the ocean as far as the sea extends,
so do the splendors of the three worlds exist within the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) as far as Brahman extends.
Rich with vast forms and transformations, yet when scrutinized they are nothing at all;
rising up and sinking down, these glories are neither real nor unreal.
They are insentient, full of flavor, and slender—like strands of moss.
They possess the nature of waves, their bodies appearing and vanishing;
they are the diverse behaviors and activities of all millions of creations,
and these creations have manifold forms, transformations, and appearances.
O Rāma, all perceptions of creation, which are the domain of those who know reality, do not exist as something separate from the Lord of All, just as raindrops do not exist apart from water.
Creations emerge from the Divine like raindrops from a cloud.
Therefore, all [beings] have arisen from Him alone, like visions from light.
All the visions of creation are not distinct from the Lord of All;
they appear as if distinct, like the thorns of the *śalmali* tree.
O Raghava, when these creations have become either flourishing or degraded,
the supreme ether— garlanded by the subtle element (tanmātra) born from space—
sometimes first attains its firm foundation.
From that, Brahmā is born; he is the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) born from space.
At times, Vāyu first attains a firm foundation;
from that, Brahmā is born; he is the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) born from Vāyu.
Sometimes water first attains expansion;
from that, Brahmā is born, he who is the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) produced from the waters.
Sometimes the earth first attains expansion.
"From that, Brahmā is born— this terrestrial Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati).
When one compresses the four [elements] and the fifth increases,
then the Lord performs worldly activity through that very birth.
Sometimes, by the very nature of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), a certain person manifests spontaneously within water, air, or even in the vast expanse of fire. Then,
from the mouth or sometimes from the feet of that person, [the Veda] is born.
Sometimes from his shoulder or his back, sometimes from his eye or his hand,
and sometimes from the navel of this Puruṣa, a lotus is produced;
in that [lotus] Brahmā moves about, and he is celebrated as "the one born from the lotus" (Padmaja).
This is an illusion, a delusion like a dream, a false wheel of fabrication;
it is as fleeting as a kingdom of the mind and as beautiful as a ripple on water.
Tell me, how could this possibly exist here within pure consciousness? What is there for it to arise from?
If this is not being questioned as a mere fantasy of the ignorant,
then perhaps— due to the coloring of the principle of the mind within the pure sky—
a golden cosmic egg containing Brahman manifests of its own accord.
Sometimes this Person emits vigor into the water;
from that a lotus is born, or else the great cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
From that Brahmā is born, and sometimes he is indeed the Sun.
Sometimes Varuṇa was born as Brahmā, and sometimes Vāyu was born from the lotus.
Thus, O Rāma, within these diverse creations that lack any internal [substantiality],
various and manifold origins have proceeded from Brahmā.
O sinless one, for the sake of illustration, I have described to you the creation of a single Prajāpati; the origin of others is exactly the same.
According to the view of the wise, this world-process is but the unfolding of the mind.
O Lord, this sequence of creation has been described for your enlightenment;
thus, this sequence of creation has been recounted to you so that you may understand how these classes of beings, beginning with the *sāttvika*, have come into existence.
Again there is creation, again destruction; again suffering, again happiness;
again the ignorant, again the knowers of reality; again the views of bondage and liberation.
Again and again they bring about creation, like those who have drunk oil and remain in a state of wretchedness.
Like lamps that have been lit, they go out and they arise;
in the birth and destruction of bodies, even for those who are Brahman,
there is no difference whatsoever in their destruction once they have abandoned temporal limitation.

Again the Kṛta age, again the Tretā, and again the Dvāpara and Kali; everything revolves once more by the turning of the wheel of time. Again there are the beginnings of Manvantaras, and again the successions of Kalpas.
Again and again, the states of action occur every morning, just as throughout the day;
yet this entire world, whose internal intervals are measured by the divisions of light and darkness and the reckoning of time,
is again and again nothing at all.
Like sparks from fire upon a heated, unstruck iron ball,
these states of being always abide by their very nature within the space of consciousness;
sometimes unmanifest, sometimes having attained manifestation.
All this exists within the supreme reality, like the seasonal blossoms on a tree.
The vibration of consciousness alone is the self of all, eternally possessing such a form;
from it arises creation, just as the appearance of two moons arises from the eyes.
All accumulated perceptions of continuous creation come together;
though they reside therein, they appear as if not residing there, like rays from the moon.
Indeed, this so-called transmigratory existence never truly exists at any time.
Because the power of non-transmigration exists within the power of all;
and never at any time, O virtuous one, has this world been otherwise,
because the power of transmigration exists within the power of all.
"By means of the fuel of non-transmigration, one should contemplate time as lasting for the duration of a great kalpa;
it is appropriate [to think], 'Now saṃsāra will no longer exist.
O Great-minded One, from the perspective of the Knower's vision, all this is indeed Brahman alone."
"It does not exist" — this very [statement] regarding *saṃsāra* is indeed logical for us.
However, from the perspective of the ignorant, because *saṃsāra* is uninterrupted and incessant,
it is logical that this *saṃsāra-illusion* is eternal.
And because of having contemplated this again and again, O descendant of Raghu, even that statement— "the world has never been otherwise"— is not false.
Having seen the worlds as perishable and the beings falling incessantly in all directions, [he spoke thus].
Why is it not reasonable to say that this entire world is perishable?
Having seen the sun and moon rising at all times and the directions as stable and immovable,
the statement that the entire world is imperishable is likewise not false.
There is nothing that does not arise within that single, pervasive Self—
the inexpressible web of conceptual constructions—
again and again; this entire world, as well as death and birth, occurs repeatedly therein.
Again there is pleasure, again pain, and again the organs and their actions;
again the quarters of space, again the sky, and again the oceans and mountains;
creation arises again and again, like the light of the sun, eternally.
Again the Daityas, again the gods, again the succession of other worlds;
again the desire for heaven and liberation, again Indra, again the Moon;
again the god Nārāyaṇa, again the sons of Manu and the rest.

Furthermore, the lotus of the two worlds (rodasī) rises again, with the quarters as its moving and beautiful petals, the moon and sun as its stalks, Varuṇa and Vāyu as its filaments, and Mount Sumeru as its lovely pericarp; it is resplendent with the stars as its filaments and possesses a full, blooming interior.
Having ascended the forest of the sky, the lion of the sun leaps again to shatter the herd of elephants that is darkness with the mass of his rays as claws;
meanwhile, the moon, with hands as beautiful as swaying mango blossoms, [shines].
It produces nectar and joy, serving as an ornament for the faces of the quarters, the brides of the world. Yet again, driven by the wind of the exhaustion of merit,
those who were the guardians of the fruits of their meritorious deeds fall here with their limbs shattered from the celestial tree.

Furthermore, having made some rustling sound with its wings— the side of active performance— while undertaking the cycle of existence, the partridge of Time departs. Again, when Indra has gone, having tasted the kingdom of Keśara, the same occurs.
The six-legged bee that is the lord of the secondary gods approaches the lotus of heaven.
But again, Kali defiles time that has been purified by the performance of rites,
just as a rising wind of dust and refuse defiles the ocean containing the discus-bearer.

Furthermore, the wheel named Time, fashioned by the potter Time, revolves with force and without ceasing, having made all beings its earthen vessels. Once again, the world reaches a state of saplessness, its auspicious stability destroyed.
When the end of the eon has drawn near, the world becomes like a forest completely parched;
then, with the infinite bodies of beings burnt by the fires of the suns,
the earth, filled with the bones of all creatures, attains the state of a cremation ground.
Again, by the rains of the Puṣkarāvarta clouds, which take the form of the Kulācala mountains,
the world attains the state of a single ocean, with dancing ashes for its great foam;
then, when wind and water have subsided, it becomes empty of all things.
Then the world, like a previously unseen void, enters into emptiness.
Having enjoyed life for some more years with a mind of equanimity,
he, through his worn-out body, dissolves into Brahman within the supreme Self.
Again, at another time, he indeed expands the multitude of worlds within the void by means of his mind, just as a gandharva creates a city;
thus there is again the commencement of creation and again the occurrence of dissolution.
Moreover, O Rāma, all this revolves like a wheel. In this long-continued display of great illusion,
O Rāma, having determined what is real and what is unreal, that which is spoken here [is established].
O Rāma, this wheel of saṃsāra is like the story of Dāśūra;
its forms are fashioned by conceptual construction, yet it is empty of reality in actual fact.
This [world] is densely spread out with mental constructions that arise from the unreal, resembling the vision of two moons.
But that which is created by the unreal is not real; therefore, what is the source of this delusion regarding this world?
The thirtieth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Method for Determining the Existence and Non-existence of the World."
Vasiṣṭha said:
When those whose intentions are destroyed by enjoyments and power are preoccupied with manifold ritual activities, they do not regard the truth; then the deceitful do not see it.
But those who have reached the further shore of the intellect and are not enslaved by the senses—
they behold this worldly illusion as clearly as a wood-apple in the palm of their hand.
Now, having seen that worldly illusion, the discerning living being—
One casts off attachment consisting of egoism, just as a snake sheds its skin; then,
having attained non-attachment, one is not born again,
even though remaining for a very long time in the field, like a seed consumed by fire.
Fools strive for the benefit of the body— which is beset by mental and physical ailments and destined to perish this very day— but not for the sake of the Self;
you too, like a fool, pursue the desired ends of the ignorant body.
"Do not bring about suffering for yourself by making existence your sole refuge.
Rāma said:
"This wheel of saṃsāra is indeed like the story of Dāśūra."
"O Lord, why is it that the form fashioned by conceptualization is devoid of any real entity?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"This is for the purpose of describing and designating the true nature of the world-illusion."

O Rāma, listen to the narrative of Dāśūra as it is being described by me. On this surface of the earth, there is a great and glorious region known as Magadha, abounding with trees of various blossoms.
Spreading through groves of *kadamba* trees, with forests of *tāla* palms,
it was filled with flocks of various birds and was enchanting with every kind of wonder;
its borders were thick with crops, and it was adorned with the city’s pleasure gardens.
The banks of all its rivers were filled with *kamala*, *utpala*, and *kahlāra* lotuses;
it resounded with the humming of songs sung by women sporting on garden swings;
and the ground of its paths was dense with flowers gathered during the night.
There, on a certain mountain slope thick with *karṇikāra* flowers,
dense with groves of plantains, and adorned with clusters of *nīpa* trees;
where *cakora* birds and yaks were warbling, and the waters of the cascades resounded.
In that place where the nets of flowering mango creepers resounded with the songs of sweet-voiced cuckoos,
where the sky was covered by palm trees swaying in the play of the Pulinda women, and which was the very life of the jīvajīvaka birds amidst the expanse of blossoming lotus ponds.

On that holy, preeminent mountain, where the trees were filled with various birds, the wind vibrated with a profusion of flowers and was reddened by the pollen of their filaments; there, the *kāraṇḍava* ducks raised their cries and the cranes moved gracefully through the lakes.
There was a certain sage of supreme righteousness and great ascetic power,
named Dāśūra; endowed with the practice of great austerity,
he dwelt on Mount Kadamba, free from passion and possessed of great intelligence.
Rāma:
O venerable one, for what reason did that ascetic sage dwell on the back of the great kadamba tree in the forest, and how did he live there?
Vasiṣṭha said:
His father was renowned as Śaraloman;
like another Brahmā by name, he dwelt upon that very same mountain.
He had an only son named Kaca, who was like the son of Bṛhaspati;
together with that son, he spent his life in the forest.
Then, after consuming many ages like Śaraloman, he departed.
Having abandoned his body like a bird that has left its nest,
Dāśūra wept alone in that forest,
deprived of his father in his final state, as mournfully as a kurara bird.
With his heart tormented by grief due to the separation from his parents,
he surely fell into a state of withering, like a lotus in the winter;
then that boy, dejected in spirit, [was addressed] in the forest by a forest deity.
"O Rāma, O son of a sage, O one of great wisdom, having been thus consoled by her whose body was invisible, she said: 'Why do you weep like one ignorant?
Do you not know the flickering nature of this saṃsāra? (MU 4.30.25–26)
O virtuous one, such is the nature of the world at all times: the cycle of existence is unstable;

one is born, lives, and afterwards inevitably perishes. O sage, whatever is visible to the eyes, beginning with Brahmā and extending to this entire universe— The final line of the verse is: *“yad yat kiñcid dṛśor dṛśyaṃ brahmādikam idaṃ mune”* (O sage, whatever is visible to the eyes, beginning with Brahmā and extending to this entire universe).
Everyone must go there; there is no doubt about this destruction.
Therefore, do not indulge in useless despair over your father’s death, for the setting of one who has been born is inevitable, like that of the sun at the end of the day.
Hearing the voice saying "without a body," Śikhaṇḍin, his eyes reddened,
regained his composure as if at the sound of thunder;
then, rising and performing his necessary duties, he respectfully attended to his father's final rites.
He formed a firm resolve for asceticism for the sake of the highest perfection.
As he performed his penance in the forest through brahminical rites,
his mastery of the Vedas became characterized by infinite resolve.
But because his intellect had realized that which was yet to be known through his state as a true śrotriya,
his mind found no rest even on the pure surface of the earth;
for he saw that this entire surface of the earth was likewise entirely pure.
Seeing everything as if impure, he indeed found no delight anywhere at all.
Then, by his own volition alone, he resolved:
"The very top of a tree is perfectly pure; there my dwelling is appropriate."
"Therefore, I shall now perform such austerity by which I may attain,
like a bird, the power of staying upon the branches and the leaves of trees.
Having thus reflected, he kindled a most brilliant fire.
He offered as an oblation his own flesh, having cut it from the surface of his shoulder.
"May the entire throats of the host of gods not be reduced to ashes by the Brahmin's flesh now situated in my mouth."
Having reflected thus, the seven-rayed Lord, assuming a physical form,
appeared before him with blazing splendor, like the Sun appearing before the Lord of Speech.
He spoke words concerning the boon desired by the heroic youth:

"O virtuous one, take this deposited treasure, like a jewel from a casket," said Anala. Having honored him with words of praise, the young brahmin, adorned with offerings of water and flowers, spoke to him: MU_4,30.40–41. "Take this deposited treasure, O virtuous one, like a jewel from a casket. Having spoken thus, the young brahmin, having worshipped Anala with words of praise, addressed him while he was graced by the offering of water and flowers.
"O Blessed One, I do not attain that purifying ground which was once filled with living beings; therefore, let my station be upon the tops of the trees.
When this was said by the son of the sage, the fire-god, the mouth of all the gods, [replied].
"So be it," said the Lord, and having spoken thus, he vanished from sight.
When that god had disappeared, like a twilight cloud in an instant,
the prince, his desires fulfilled, shone like the full moon.
He, full of joy, laughed with the swift brilliance of the orb of his own face which he had attained,
surpassing the moon crowded with its full digits and the blooming white lotus with the beauty of his smile.
The chapter titled "The Bestowing of Boons upon Dāśūra" in the *Dāśūropākhyāna*.
The Thirty-First Canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then [he beheld] that which stood in the midst of the forest, kissing the circle of the clouds.
Its pavilion-like trunk was frequented by the horses of the sun weary at midday;
it seemed to measure out the belly of the quarters with its long, branch-arms,
gazing upon the directions with eyes of blossoming flowers.
With its hair-like tresses of bees swarming in no small measure, tossed by the wind,
it was as if wiping the face of the quarters with hands of tender shoots;
it was surrounded by thickets golden with dense clusters of blossoms from broad stalks.
He seemed to be laughing with his mouths, which were like those containing betel and garlanded with bees;
he was encircled by the pollen of flower filaments shimmering from the play of the creepers,
like the full moon surrounded by its radiance.
The world was like a lofty path of the Siddhas, crowded with creepers and vines where cakora birds warbled in the bowers and kinnaras sang; there,
peacocks hung down from their tails over those seated upon vine-seats.
The sky was adorned with quivers, like a firmament graced by clouds accompanied by rainbows;
it shone with white yak-tail fans raised and lowered at every shoulder,
like a year filled with full moons followed by *cakora* birds.
It seemed to be singing aloud with the sweet warbling of *kapiñjala* birds, the melodious cooing of cuckoos, and the powerful cries of *jīvajīvaka* birds;
and with flocks of *kādambara* geese sporting in their nests.
It was as if the world were covered by perfected beings (siddhas) resting within the hollows of heaven;
and it was frequented here and there by flower-clusters with hands as red as coral and eyes like bees, resembling the celestial nymphs (apsaras) inhabiting paradise.
With its flickering mass of flower-pollen, it was tawny with blossoms like a dark cloud streaked with lightning and adorned with Indra’s bow;
rich with the branches of a thousand arms, it filled the hollow of the sky.
It was like the dancing of the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa), with the sun and moon as its earrings;
with great serpents seated upon its base, it was filled with clusters of stars in the sky,
like another terrestrial sphere in its midst composed of creepers and flowers.
Like the grandfather (Brahmā) of all mountains, forests, and trees,
he was like a single treasury upon the earth for fruits, shoots, and flowers;
he bore a mass of buds concealed by the pollen of blossoms.
The sky, with its web of stars obscured by the rays of the sun, was like the marshy banks;
and the surface of the earth, crowded with trees whose branches were thick with nests and filled with fluttering birds,
resembled the countryside thronged with restless people.
Abounding with flower-clusters and beautiful banners, adorned with bowers of creepers,
white as *makkola* flowers, and strewn with heaps of blossoms;
it resounded with the warbling of cakoras, camaras, parrots, cuckoos, and śārikas.
Its arched windows were the hollows covered by dense clusters of blossoms; with its interior thickets slow with the intoxication of birds wandering about,
it was like the supreme inner apartment of all the forest goddesses.
It shone like a mountain with rivers falling upon it, with masses of flower filaments in which swarms of bees were drowning,
and with heaps of flower petals wandering about, tossed playfully by the gentle breeze.
With shoulders covered by growing [hair], like a mountain with white clouds;
with pillar-like knees rubbed by the temples of elephants,
he stood firmly planted like a great mountain on its broad base.
It was surrounded by a multitude of birds with variegated-colored wings that moved within the hollows of its trunks, like a horned beast surrounded by a herd of wild animals;
and with the trembling web of its fingers in the form of flower clusters, it performed a dramatic gesture.
It seems as if it were pointing out the creepers dancing in the forest breezes.
Only a certain person, devoid of hope and no longer seeking anything from me, departs satisfied,
as if watching one who dances amidst the swaying circles of flowering creepers.
Because it was the sole beloved of the creepers, it was overflowing with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*);
it seemed to sing in a low, warbling tone (*kākali*) through the humming of the intoxicated swarms of bees.
From afar, flowers were being cast down by the sky-faring *siddhas*.
Welcoming him, as it were, with the warbling of cuckoos and swarms of bees;
it seemed to laugh with the bright splendor of flower buds at the exuberance of fruits, blossoms, and creepers, and at the loftiness of the trees.
With its clusters of upward-reaching branches, it seemed as if it were trying to conquer the *pārijāta* tree; it rushed through the midst of the sky with its necks held high,
possessing dense, eyelash-like filaments and flower-clusters shimmering with bees at their centers.

It was like the thousand-eyed Indra himself, rising up from Pātāla with his incomparable hoods covered in clusters of shimmering flowers and a multitude of jewel-encrusted gems, as if intent on conquering the state of Indra or desiring to gaze upon the sky. MU_4.31.31–32.
With its form covered in dust, it was like a second Śaṅkara;
yet, by means of its fruit-bearing shade, it brought joy to all the sages.
It was provided with new flower-creeper arbors whose walls were formed by closely set leaves.
He beheld the Kadamba tree in the sky like a city, crowded with flocks of birds and celestial beings.
This concludes the thirty-second canto, titled "The Description of the Kadamba Tree," within the narrative of Dāśūra.
Vasiṣṭha said: Then that one of great intelligence, his mind slow with joy, beheld him who was adorned with fruits and shoots and resembled a mountain composed of flowers.
Śauri climbed the kadamba tree standing in the forest, which acted as a pillar for heaven and earth,
like a lofty kalpa-tree situated in the single vast ocean. There, upon the tip of a sprout on a branch reaching toward the sky, he sat.
Having attained the sky, he entered it like a Buddha emerging from the edge of a forest of *aiḍūka* trees.
Then, having sat down upon a soft seat of fresh sprouts,
he gazed for a moment at the quarters of the sky with eyes languid with curiosity.
The mountains, lovely with their single rows of rivers, have the great peaks for their budding breasts;
they possess the stainless sky as their fine hair and the swaying blue clouds as their locks of hair.
They are clothed in garments of dark-green grass, and their limbs are fair with the weight of flowers.
Adorning the city, they carried jars filled with the waters of the ocean;
they bore blossoming lotuses and breathed fragrant scents from their mouths.
They possessed the low, humming murmur of a village as their lute-like song, and the sound of waterfalls as their tinkling anklets.
With mountains for their heads, great oceans for their feet, rows of forests for their lines of body hair,
jungles for their thighs and hips, and the sun and moon for their earrings;
marked by rice-fields for their sandalwood paste and the movement of grain for their decorative marks.
With garments of clouds as white as snow clinging to their mountain peaks and breasts,
serving as mirrors for the fresh adornment of the floodwaters of the great ocean,
they possess the horripilation of heat from the multitude of trees within the inner apartments of the world.
Wearing garments dyed with menstrual blood, they were stained with the rays of the sun and saffron;
adorned with various flowers, they were anointed with sandalwood paste as white as moonbeams.
Seated upon the leaves of the creepers of the sky’s surface, they appeared like flowing streams of water from the rows of forests.

The beloved of the three worlds, delighted, beheld the ten directions adorned without interval by flowers. In the *Dāśūra-upākhyāna*, this is the thirty-third canto, titled "The Surveying of the Directions by Dāśūra."
Vasiṣṭha said:
From that time forth, he became renowned in that hermitage of ascetics as Kadambadāśūra, a hero in his rigorous austerity.
Standing upon that lotus leaf and gazing at the quarters for a moment,
he firmly assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) with his mind withdrawn from the directions;
though he did not yet know the supreme reality, he remained intent on the mere performance of the ritual action.
With a mind characterized by the offering of his own fruit, he performed a sacrifice;
within the forest, with his mind fixed upon the leaves and creepers situated in the sky, all the sacrificial rites were performed by him in succession.
There, for ten years, he worshipped the gods with his mind alone through sacrifices such as those involving cows, horses, and human beings, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
In time, his expanded consciousness attained a state of stainless purity.
By force, he descended within [himself] to that knowledge born of self-purification.
Then, with his veil shattered and the impurity of latent impressions dissolved,
the sage dwelt upon that sprout, freed from all taint.
Once, he beheld before him upon that creeper a forest goddess with large eyes, clad in garments of swaying blossoms,
possessing a face as lovely as a passionate woman's, and with eyes rolling from intoxication.
To her, whose limbs were faultless and who was exceedingly captivating with the fragrance of blue lotuses,
that sage spoke as she stood with downcast face,
like a cuckoo to a forest creeper bent low under a burden of flowers.
"Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, who agitates the god of love?
Why do you stand there like a flowering creeper upon a friend?"—
thus addressed, the fawn-eyed Gaurī, with her full breasts, [remained silent].
She spoke these charming words in a sweet voice to the sage:
"Whatever desires are difficult to obtain on this earth,
all those are swiftly attained through the very request of the great."
O Brahmin, I am a forest deity in this grove, which is filled with creepers, adorned by your *kadamba* trees, and serves as a playful abode for the vines;
it was on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, during the festival of Smara.

A gathering of forest goddesses took place in the Nandana grove; there, O Lord, I went— to that assembly of the beauties of the three worlds— which was adorned with fragrant flowers, bees, cuckoos, and swarms of bees.
Then, during the festival of love, I saw all my friends accompanied by their sons;
because I was childless, I was deeply distressed.
Yet you stand there, a great wish-granting tree for the entire multitude of seekers.
"O Protector, how indeed am I to be pitied like one who is helpless and childless?
O Blessed One, grant me a son; otherwise, I shall offer my body here as an oblation into the fire to pacify the burning pain caused by the loss of a son."
When the slender lady had spoken thus, the bull among sages smiled and, filled with compassion, gave her a flower from his hand and said:
"Go, O slender-limbed one; in a month, you shall behold the lotus-eyed one who is worthy of worship."
"You shall give birth to a beloved son, just as a fine creeper bears its flower;
however, because he was entreated by you while possessed by the sin of death,
his knowledge will be attained only with great difficulty."
Having spoken thus to the slender woman, whose countenance was bright with joy and who was eager with the prayer, "I shall perform service for you," the sage dismissed her;
she departed for her own abode, while he remained there with his own self.
Time, marked by seasons and years, passed away gradually. Then, after a long period, that very lotus-eyed woman approached the sage, bringing with her a son twelve years old.
Having prostrated and sat before the Sage,
she whose face was like the moon spoke with gentle words, like a female bee at a mango tree:
"O Blessed One, this is that auspicious boy, our son."
"O Lord, I have indeed made myself an expert in all the arts;
yet by this alone, that auspicious knowledge has not been attained by which one is no longer tormented within this machine of saṃsāra."
"O Lord, you alone must now compassionately teach him knowledge;
for who indeed would consign a son born into a noble family to ignorance?
To her who was speaking thus, the sage said, "O frail woman, [this is] my disciple, your son."
"Keep him right here," she said, and dismissed her. When she had gone, that wise youth remained self-restrained as an attendant to his father, like Aruṇa standing before the Sun.
Then, for a long time, that sage awakened his son there with various eloquent speeches,
employing hundreds of narratives and accounts, both based on actual experience and purely imaginary, along with illustrative examples.
Likewise, through accounts from ancient histories and the certainties of the Vedas and Vedānta,
one should constantly engage in detailed discourses with a lack of agitation,
until [the truth] is ascended upon experience and firmly rooted in the intellect of those of superior insight.

By virtue of his own experience, the great-souled Maharṣi, having had enough with a multitude of words whose meanings were merely conventional and lacking in aesthetic flavor, enlightened his son standing before him in the sky, just as a rain cloud awakens a peacock.
The chapter titled "The Enlightenment of the Son of Daśūra."
The thirty-fourth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, once upon a time, by that path he [saw] the river flowing toward Kailāsa.
I went to bathe, my form invisible, traveling through the path of the sky.
Having emerged from the hollow of the circle of the seven sages in the heavens,
O wise one, I arrived at night upon the space above the Dāśūra tree.
As long as I hear from the hollow of a bough in the forest a voice like the humming of a bee trapped within a lotus bud—
listen, O son of great intelligence, to this complete account of this matter.
I shall relate to you a most wonderful narrative.
There was a king of great heroism, renowned throughout the three worlds, named Svottha; he was illustrious and capable of subduing the entire world.
He whose instruction all the leaders in every world bear high upon their heads like a supreme crest-jewel;
he who delights solely in heroic deeds and dwells in various wonders.
No one in the three worlds has ever brought this Great Soul under his control;
his thousands of undertakings, which bestow both pleasure and pain,
cannot be counted at all, like the waves of the ocean.
The prowess of that one of great valor could not be overcome by anyone in the world— neither by weapons and missiles nor by fires— just as the sky cannot be grasped with a fist.
His playful activity, which was vast in its undertaking and radiant in its manifestation, [could not be surpassed].
Even Śakra, Upendra, and Hara do not imitate him even slightly.
O mighty-armed one, his three bodies are capable of filling the directions;
drawing the world toward themselves, they remain as the superior, the inferior, and the middling.
Born within that very vast expanse of space, he became possessed of three bodies;
there alone he took his station, like a sound, a wind, or a bird.
There, in that shoreless sky, a city was constructed by him.
It possessed fourteen great highways adorned with three divisions;
it was rich with garlands of groves and gardens, beautiful with pleasure-mountains,
encircled by strings of pearls, and graced by seven ponds.

In that very same, exceedingly vast city, which was illuminated by two lamps whose nature was both cool and warm and which were never exhausted, and which was crowded with the paths of merchants characterized by upward and downward movement, that king [resided].
Moving groups of charming door-keepers were arranged;
some were stationed above, some below, and some in the middle;
some vanished after a long time, while others perished quickly.
Covered with black roofing, adorned with nine doors,
with winds blowing incessantly, and provided with many windows;
illuminated by five lamps, having three pillars, and made of white wood.
Smoothly plastered and soft, crowded with rows of streets—
these [palaces] were constructed by that king through his illusory power (*māyā*), O Great-minded One;
within them dwell great *yakṣas* as guardians, who are constantly afraid of the light.
Then, as the multitudes of the lower realms were moving about, that lord of the earth engaged in various sports within them like a bird in its nests;
O son, he was there in three bodies together with those yakṣas.
Having dwelt there for a moment, sporting at ease, he quickly departs again and goes forth.
O child, sometimes a desire arises in him of restless mind, fixed in the thought: "I shall go to some city that is yet to be created."
As if possessed by a spirit, he rises up in agitation and runs;
he reaches that city as well, which is like one constructed by the Gandharvas.
Sometimes, a desire arises even in that dull-witted being.
Thinking, "I shall go to destruction," it perishes quickly;
then it is swiftly reborn from the void like a great wave from the water.
It expands its worldly activity intensely, yet again begins slowly.
Then, through that very same worldly activity, one is sometimes deeply distressed;
one grieves, thinking, "What shall I do? I am ignorant, I am suffering. And at other times, having attained joy, one comes of one's own accord to a state of plumpness.
Like the current of a river from the swelling flood of monsoon rains,
that lord of the earth, possessed of great majesty, drinks, leaps, moves, yawns, quivers, shines, and yet does not shine— resplendent like the Lord of Waters agitated by the force of the wind.
The thirty-fifth canto, titled "Description of the Manifestation Arising from Oneself," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, at that great night in Jambudvīpa, the son of pure intent questioned his father, who was seated upon the crest of the top of a kadamba tree. The son said:
Who is this king known as Svottha, whose form is like that of his father? Tell me truly what has been told by you;
where will this creation come to be, and where should one go while it is currently present?
"Because it contradicts both [your own] interests, your speech is for the sake of delusion. Dāśūra said:
"Listen, my son; I shall tell you this exactly as it is."

By means of this, you shall realize the true nature of the wheel of saṃsāra. This structure of saṃsāra, which arises from the unreal, is devoid of substance, and is pervasive, has been thus described by me.
The volition born from the supreme ether is said to arise from itself;
it is born by itself alone and dissolves by itself alone.
This entire expansive universe exists as its very nature.
By its birth it is born; when it perishes, it perishes.
They know Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and the others to be its very limbs—like the branches of a tree or the peaks of a mountain.
In the empty void, he created this city of the three worlds;
by the mere persistence of appearance, he attained the state of Viriñci,
within which these fourteen world-enclosures are spread out with vast light.
Where there are groves and parks, and successions of gardens;
where there are pleasure-mountains such as Sahya, Mandara, and Meru;
and where the moon and sun, with their cool and warm radiance, serve as lamps that are never extinguished by the wind.
There, rivers flow with moving, excellent pearl necklaces for their waves— waves as lofty and shimmering as the rays of the sun—
and with water like sugarcane juice and milk, and sprouts of jewel-lotuses.
Where the Aurvānala lotus-pools are the seven great oceans; where,
upon the earth below and in the sky above, there is the wealth and glory of merit and demerit,
and where men, gods, and Kirātas engage in excessive buying and selling.
In this very world-city,
the king Saṅkalpa has constructed various dwelling-places for his own sport;
some, named Gīrvāṇas, have been stationed in the upper regions.
Some humans, serpents, and other beings are situated directly below;
moving by the flow of the wind-mechanism, they are composed of flesh and clay,
with white bones for their wood, variegated, and made smooth and stainless by a coating of skin.
Some perish after a long time, while others are subject to swift destruction;
they possess the beauty of a covering formed by the waving black hair of their locks,
and are endowed with nine openings, chief among which are the ears, eyes, and nose.
With the winds of the vital breath flowing incessantly, they are cooled by heat;
equipped with a multitude of windows such as the ears, nose, mouth, and palate;
possessing thoroughfares in the form of limbs like the arms; and featuring the five sense-faculties as their small lamps.

O Great-minded One, within those bodies fashioned by illusion, the great yakṣas of egoism— terrified of the supreme light— dwell inside the chambers of the physical frames through the power of conceptual construction. By means of these great yakṣas of egoism, [the self is bound] within the huts of the body.
For he sports excessively with that which is unreal, arising from what is unreal—
just as a cat is in a granary, as a snake is in a bellows,
or as a pearl is in a bamboo stalk, so is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) in the body.
In the houses of bodies, volition rises for a moment and subsides for a moment like a lamp; it is like a wave in oceans. Then, it attains a city that is a new construction yet to be.

When one perceives right before oneself the object that was previously imagined, it quickly perishes by its own nature through the mere act of non-imagining. This destruction leads to one's supreme welfare; indeed, its own arising never occurs again.
It arises by its own mere conceptualization, like a child’s imaginary ghost;
it leads only to endless personal suffering and never to bliss.
This vast suffering of the world expands through the existence of the self.
Through its very non-existence, it destroys the blindness of a moment, just as darkness [is destroyed] by light.
One weeps because of one's own activity that brings about suffering,
like the monkey who pulled out the wedge while his testicles were pinned between two pieces of wood.
Having obtained but a tiny fragment of the bliss he had imagined, he remains with his neck held high,
like a young camel suddenly tasting a drop of honey fallen from the sky;
he himself attains detachment for a moment and experiences pleasure for a moment.

Like an unworthy child, one's imagination undergoes transformation in an instant. Having diligently rendered this [mind] stainless from all objective states, the wise have reached the supreme state; do as they did, my son.

However, this Intellect has three bodies— superior, inferior, and middling— known as *tamas*, *sattva*, and *rajas*, which are the cause for the existence of the world. For volition, being of the nature of *tamas*, is constantly characterized by natural activity.

Having fallen into extreme wretchedness, one goes to the state of a worm or an insect. For volition, when its nature is *sattva* and devoted to dharma and knowledge, stands as an empire; it presides over sovereignty not far from the state of absolute liberation (*kevalībhāva*).
For volition, which is of the nature of passion, exists within worldly activity;
it persists in saṃsāra, enamored of children and wife.
But having abandoned these three forms, O Mahāmati, [one is liberated].
Volition reaches its supreme state upon the dissolution of the self.
Having abandoned all views and restrained the mind with the mind, bring about the destruction of volition, together with its external and internal objects.
Even if you perform severe austerities for a thousand years,
or if you were to effortlessly crush yourself to pieces with a stone;
even if you enter the ocean or the submarine fire—
Whether you fall into a chasm or into the water of a sword’s edge;
whether Hara is your teacher, or Hari, or even the lotus-born Brahmā,
or the Lord of the World, the Lord of Speech, overcome by supreme compassion.
Whether you are situated in the netherworld, on earth, or even in heaven,
there is no other means for you than the cessation of mental constructs (*saṃkalpa*),
directed toward that beginningless, changeless, and supremely purifying bliss.
Exert yourself with supreme human effort toward the pacification of volitional constructs (*saṅkalpa*).
O sinless one, it is said that all states of being are woven upon the thread of volitional constructs;
when that thread is severed, I know not where those fragile things go.
The non-existent, the existent, and both the existent and non-existent—all this arises from volition alone and from nothing else.
Since both the existent and the non-existent arise thus from volition, what can be called "truth" in this world?
Whatever is willed in whatever manner, that very thing becomes so in an instant.
O knower of reality, never form any mental construct whatsoever. Be free from constructs and devoted to the ordinary activities as they arise;
for when constructs are utterly destroyed, consciousness moves toward the state of being unobjectifiable.

O sinless one, why indeed have you resorted to this great suffering by means of that which is unreal in form, through which this world— unreal in its very essence— is spread out as a futile misery resembling yourself?
That which leads to the absence of suffering is what the wise resort to here, and nothing else.
Having attained the realization of the ultimate truth, having forcefully cast away the web of conceptual constructions,
and with the fluctuations of the mind stilled as in deep sleep, realize that peerless state for the sake of expansive bliss.
The thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Inquiry into Saṃsāra and Conceptual Construction," is concluded. Chapter Thirty-Six.
"What kind of thing is this mental construction (*saṅkalpa*), dear father? How does it arise, O Lord?
How does it increase, and how indeed does it perish? Dāśūra said:

The wise know that the mind's orientation toward an object of cognition— which belongs to the infinite reality of the Self, whose nature is universal existence— is the sprout of volition (*saṅkalpa*). That very [sprout], having attained a slight degree of existence, reaches a state of density.
The mind, filling the void like a cloud, proceeds toward solid inertia;
the consciousness, while contemplating the object of thought as if it were distinct from itself,
attains the state of volition here, just as a seed attains the state of a sprout.
For volition is indeed volition; it arises of its own accord, and it grows rapidly by itself for the sake of suffering, not for the sake of happiness.
For you are merely volition, just as the ocean is merely water.
Apart from volition (*saṅkalpa*), there is no other reality of your transmigratory existence; it is unreal.
Indeed, you have arisen in vain through a chance coincidence (*kākatālīya-yoga*);
like a mirage or the appearance of two moons, you grow only in unreality.
Just as the perception of gold in one who has swallowed a piece of mother-of-pearl is false,
so too shall your internal conceptualization become unreal when it approaches you of its own accord.
