Having been born as something unreal, you grow up as something unreal.
And when this consciousness has arisen, you, though existing, dissolve into non-existence.
"This is I," "these are my objects consisting of pleasure and pain"—
thinking thus, "all is in vain," you are distressed within with a sense of self-attachment.
You are indeed non-existent and unborn; how can there be birth for one who is inert?
You are deluded in vain by your own power of volition. Do not form a volition, and do not contemplate existence while remaining in this state.
By this very state of being, you become fit for your own welfare.
No further effort on your part is required for the destruction of mental constructs (*saṅkalpa*);
by the mere absence of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), the mental construct perishes within the heart.
In the crushing of a *sumana* flower, there might be some degree of interference;
however, in the mere absence [of the flower], which is easily accomplished, there is no destruction of intention.
When treading upon a flower, the effort of moving the hand is employed for the sake of the son.

Even that [world] assists in this [liberation] once conceptual construction has ceased. By means of that [insight], conceptual construction is to be destroyed; through the reversal of the perception of existence, it is destroyed effortlessly, even in half a moment.

When one remains established in one's own self, wherein even the mere state of existence has been stilled, what could be accomplished that is otherwise unattainable? For who, if not the undeluded, would achieve such a thing? O Sage, by means of mental resolve alone, one should dissolve one's own mind within the mind through the mind itself.

Having pierced through [this], abide within your own self; what is so difficult in this? For when volitional construction (*saṅkalpa*) is stilled, O Great-minded One, this incomparable suffering of saṃsāra becomes stilled even from its very root.
For volition, mind, the living soul, consciousness, intellect, and latent impression—
O best of those who know the truth, these differ only in name, not in meaning.
Apart from the constituent part of volition, nothing whatsoever exists anywhere here.
Cut that very [grasping] from your heart; why do you grieve for anything else?
For just as this sky is empty, so too is the world empty, since both of these are extended forth from conceptual constructions arising from what is unreal.
All of this that has been established by means of what is unestablished is itself unestablished;
since the world is [merely] a mental construction, where, then, can cultivation find a footing?
Whether there is a firm conviction in its reality or not, upon what could a latent impression (vāsanā) be based?
Through the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), perfection is attained; consequently, nothing remains to be acquired.
Therefore, all this which is unreal should be viewed with a detached mind, not through [reifying] contemplation (*bhāvanā*); by that means, one is no longer stained by pleasures and pains.
Having determined that "this is not a real entity," no further attachment arises here;
when attachment is exhausted, joy and resentment, as well as existence and non-existence, are no longer born.
The mind falsely creates this delusion of clouds of pleasure and pain.

The mind is the living soul that vibrates intensely; it is the mental city, the world. It revolves through the past, the present, and the future, existing as the mind with its powers manifesting in the world through the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

The impure and fickle living being— a monkey in the forest of the heart— establishes this unstable state according to its own disposition, resembling itself in its restlessness. Having assumed a long form, they become short again in the blink of an eye.
And these volitions, which are like dull waves, cannot be grasped;
once slightly perceived, they increase and consume everything along with one's belongings.
Like the remnants of a fire, these volitions blaze up even from a mere blade of grass.
Manifestations that reveal the world, blazing yet momentary,
causing delusion and rooted in the insentient, these volitions are like fires of lightning.
As soon as this son was born, he should have been treated immediately.

There is no doubt in this matter: that which is non-existent never becomes existent anywhere. If the mental construction (*saṅkalpa*) were established as existent, it would then be difficult to cure; however, since it is truly non-existent, it is then very easy to cure.
If this impurity of saṃsāra were innate, like the blackness of charcoal,
then what wise person, O virtuous one, would ever apply himself to its cleansing?
Rather, it exists like the husk, the chaff, and the bran within a grain of rice.

Whenever it does so, it perishes through human effort. O son, even that which is unartificial, once attained, becomes utterly artificial for the knower, because this pervasive impurity of saṃsāra is easily eradicated by one who knows.
Just as the husk of rice or the blackness of copper is destroyed by action, my son, so too is the impurity of a person removed;
for the living soul, even though its impurity is innate like that of the rice grain, it is entirely removable.
It perishes indeed; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, be one who possesses effort.
That cycle of existence which has been produced in vain by false conceptualizations dissolves with little effort; for how can an unreal thing possibly be stable?

For one who investigates its own true state, saṃsāra comes to non-existence, just as blindness vanishes from the light of a lamp, or the appearance of two moons from one's own correct vision. "This is not yours, nor do you belong to it; O son, abandon this delusion."
Do not fixate your meditation upon what is seen as true when it is actually unreal.
Let there be no vain delusion within you that "these playful splendors are the magnificent power of my Guru.
Since you exist, these expansive playfulnesses are manifest; therefore, all this shines forth as the reality of the Self.
In the narrative of Dāśūra, the thirty-seventh canto, titled "The Treatment of Volition," Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard that conversation between the two there at night,
I, O descendant of Raghu, moon in the sky of the Raghu clan,
fell from the air onto the top of a *kadamba* tree thick with leaves, flowers, and creepers.
Silent, with his soul hushed as if by a rainless cloud, he was like the peak of a mountain horn;
there I beheld Dāśūra, a hero in the restraint of the senses,
endowed with supreme austerity and glowing like fire with its brilliance.
With his splendors issuing from his body, turning the trees to gold and scorching that region like the sun itself,
the son of the fisherman beheld me as I arrived and honored me with the offering of guest-water (*arghya*).
He honored him with supreme devotion as he sat upon a leaf-seat that had been offered;
then, together with that radiant fisherman, he engaged in conversations concerning the son’s life,
which were capable of delivering one from the cycle of existence.
I saw that tree, its hollows brimming with buds,
appearing as if with a smile of blossoming teeth and trembling petals from the wind;
while all the beasts and birds fell down at the will of Dāśūra.
It was like a forest being enjoyed, adorned with bowers of creepers;
it was covered by yak-tails as beautiful as the moon, flickering against the tips of the creepers,
resembling a mass of fragments of white clouds filling the autumn sky.
Adorned with pearl necklaces in the form of rows of frost-drops,
every limb was filled with an abundance of clear flowers;
it was completely anointed with unbroken streaks of sandalwood paste.
Adorned with vast, pure, and expansive red garments,
it made every effort like a gallant man dressed for a wedding, carrying a burden of flowers and the like, and accompanied by women who were like creepers.
Adorned with circles of creepers arranged in the form of well-bound braids,
and equipped with flower-clusters as if they were banners, it was like a city during a festival;
grey with the pollen of flowers shaken off by the scratching of deer.
It stood like a champion tree with its surrounding forest pushed aside;
it was like a young *sāla* tree upon which the mountains had cast their evening clouds, rendered pale-red by the pollen exhaled from the flowers of the peacocks.
With hands as red as coral, reclining in cool shade,
reeling with honey, and possessing the brilliance of frosty horripilation;
with a dense mass of flowers shaken by the forest breezes.
With eyes like buds heavy with sleep, bearing breasts like flower clusters,
clad in garments as red as saffron from the mass of pollen in the floral nets,
she reclined at the window that served as her dwelling within the bower of creepers.
With a multitude of forest goddesses, who were languid and graceful in their play upon swings of fresh flowering creepers,
and who were adorned with the warbling of cuckoos, [he was surrounded] from the top of his head down to the tips of his feet, along with all the bowers of creepers.
With smiling bee-eyes, they [embraced] the cluster of flower-buds that seemed doubtful [of their own existence];
languid with intoxication, their fatigue from lovemaking allayed by the morning dew,
they clung closely to one another, covered in the pollen of flowers.
It was surrounded on all sides by pairs of intoxicated bees dwelling within the interior of the flowers, making some indistinct sound appropriate for lovers;
[he went] with the desire to hear the humming of the city at the edge of the forest.
For a moment they listened with ears pricked up at the pleasant *ṭāṅkṛta* sounds of chewing;
for a moment they gazed upon the ocean-girdled earth, shimmering like the silken garment of the moon, with their heads resting charmingly against the edges of the leaves.

The interior of the *śāra* creepers was filled with deer sleeping within their leaf-cups, as if they were the personified offspring of the forest lands abiding there by way of policy; it was a place where birds, along with their young,
slept in utter confidence within their nests.
The circular clusters of fruit,

hanging down at their edges where they have ripened and fallen, held silent bees; and the clusters were darkened at their perimeters by circles of blue sprouts, which served as rosaries for those with lotus-like eyes.

The entire forest was made fragrant, with clouds formed from flowers and variegated by *kadamba* pollen; at its base, it was crowded with those seeking fruit. What more need be said here? Not even the slightest thing exists [that is not present].
There, on that tree, not a single leaf was seen that was neither inhabited nor eaten.
On every leaf, deer slept, having found rest in the thick, dense foliage;
and in every thicket, birds nestled, belonging to that sovereign of trees.
As I gazed upon that tree distinguished by such qualities,
that night became like a great festival.
Then, with other stories, his son was [entertained] by me.
Led once again to supreme awakening by those delightful illuminations of consciousness,
that night passed for us there in mutual conversation of various kinds, like a mere moment for a couple in love.
When the morning had spread its web of dew-drops born of the day's heat, and when the cluster of stars— the sprouts emerging from the forest of the sky— had slowly faded away, he,
accompanied by his daughter, followed after the region of the sky where the *kadamba* trees stood.
Having dismissed Dāśūra, I went to the river Harācala; having reached there, I performed my desired ablutions and, ascending to the vault of heaven,
entered the sky and stood composed in the midst of the sages.
O descendant of Raghu, this story of Dāśūra has been told to you;
though it possesses the appearance of reality, it is composed of the unreal, being like a reflection of the world.
This very story of Dāśūra is what has been related by me.
O Raghava, for you who perceive the world as a form of terrible evil—
therefore, having abandoned both unreal and even real attachment,
remain ever noble and self-possessed with the conviction that the doctrine of the Daśūra is the truth.
By this chariot of the discourse between Kadamba and Dāśūra, we shall go to the state of immortality;
before long you will reach that city, by which you shall become a lord over the worlds.
This is the chapter named "The Meeting of Vasiṣṭha and Dāśūra."
The thirty-eighth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Having resolved that "this does not exist," abandon attachment in every respect.
What reliance can there possibly be here for those who investigate upon that which does not exist?
If this which is being perceived exists, how has it departed from you? Let it remain; why do you falsely attribute the nature of a self to it?
Even if you possess the certainty that "this exists" or "this does not exist," how can attachment to mental cultivation be appropriate toward that which is both moving and unmoving?
O Rāma, O Great-minded One, this world neither exists nor does it not exist.
This manifestation here, appearing in such a manner, arises solely from itself;
it is not produced by an agent, nor is it a sequence uncreated by an agent.
Having reached the state of being both agent and non-agent, this manifests by itself.
Whether the web of the world be without a creator or possess a creator,
O sinless one, do not entertain a connection with this in your mind.
For that creator here is a self devoid of all senses, resembling something insentient.
At that time, I consider the world to be without an agent, occurring by mere chance like the "crow-and-palmyra-fruit" coincidence. Whatever arises through such a fortuitous conjunction,
only a fool— not anyone else— forms an attachment to its existence.
O Rāma, this world is never peaceful, nor is it subject to destruction;
for it is perceived incessantly and arises again and again.
O Rāma, this world never exists [as a reality], nor is it indestructible.
Because it is inferred from its constant state of depletion and its perishable nature,
when the agent here has transcended all sense-objects and is free from fever,
he never experiences weariness while acting.
Therefore, this mature destiny, consisting of the states of existence and non-existence,
remains just such— stable and long-lasting— and does not perish even though it arises from the mind.
Within infinite time, a certain portion is but a hundred autumns.
Why does one who possesses such a short lifespan as that still pursue worldly attachments?
If the phenomena of the world were stable, then such attachment would not be improper;
yet how indeed can there be a mutual union between the insentient and the sentient?
If the phenomena of the world are unstable, then even that attachment is not fitting; for this attachment, which is as unstable as water-foam at its end, brings you only suffering.
O mighty-armed one, the bond of attachment between yourself and the world-phenomena [is thus futile].
It does not shine like the stable and unstable, such as a mountain of foam;
though the Self is the creator of all, it acts as if it were not a creator and does nothing at all,
remaining perfectly indifferent like a lamp toward its own light.
While acting, he does nothing, like the sun performing its daily task;
while moving, he does not move, remaining established in his own self like the sun situated in its own station.
From whatever cause this world appears to have arisen, it is seen as such.

"O Rāma, if this has been ascertained by you with such skill, and investigated with a mind purified by valid means of knowledge, [then it is so]: like Arjuna and the wind, or like the expanse and the whirlpool of water. (MU 4.38.19–20)
Therefore, O virtuous one, meditation upon an object is not appropriate;
for what kind of meditation can there be regarding a firebrand-circle, a dream, or an illusion?
A being who has arrived by chance is not a vessel for affection.

Having realized that the web of the world is an illusion, one has no basis for attachment. Just as you do not conceive of a longing for a hot moon, a cool sun, or the water of a mirage, so too should you not conceive of a longing for worldly existence.
Just as you perceive a person created by imagination, a person in a dream, or the delusion of two moons,
so too should you perceive this entire collection of existing things.
Having abandoned internal attachment consisting of the mental cultivation of the splendor of phenomena, [perceive them thus].
"Whoever you are, O sinless one, sport in this world as you please. For the Self, which stands in the state of non-agency even while performing agency,
which dwells within all beings and yet transcends everything," MU 4.38.25–26.
This necessity unfolds by mere proximity,
just as luminosity appears without desire by the mere presence of a lamp,
or as *kuṭaja* flowers blossom of their own accord by the mere presence of clouds.
In the same way, by his mere presence, he himself [establishes] the three worlds;
just as when the sun remains in the sky devoid of all desire,
the splendor of worldly activity arises, so too does action occur when the Lord exists.
Just as light proceeds from a jewel that remains desireless,
so too does this multitude of worlds proceed by the mere existence of the Divine.
Therefore, both agency and non-agency reside in the Self.
Because he is free from desire, he is not an agent; yet, by his mere presence, he is an agent. Because he transcends all the senses, he is neither agent nor enjoyer, O protector of beings;
but because he is within the senses, he alone is indeed both agent and enjoyer.
O sinless one, only two states exist within the self: agency and non-agency.
Relying upon whichever of these you perceive as the better, remain steadfast.
Through this firm conviction that "I am a non-doer" in all circumstances, [the self becomes liberated].

Even while performing actions that have fallen into the stream of worldly life, you are not defiled. Through the realization that "I am a non-doer" in all circumstances, a person's desire for enjoyment becomes tasteless due to the lack of engagement of their own mind.
Where there is the conviction, "I do nothing at all here," who could either entertain the desire for a flood of enjoyments or abandon it?
Therefore, one should constantly kindle the contemplation: "I am eternally a non-doer."

That which is called supreme nectar remains as equanimity alone. Furthermore, O Rāma, if you desire to abide by means of this state of being a great agent with the thought "I do everything," they know that too to be the highest state.
Wherever I produce this entire worldly delusion, how could there be a sequence of passion and hatred for another, since that is utterly impossible?
Since this [world] is merely my own undertaking, what room is there for the sequence of sorrow and joy?
When the expansion of my own pleasure and pain occurs as the destruction and arising of the web of the world,
and one thinks within "I am the doer," what room is there for the sequence of sorrow and joy?
But when the play of exhaustion and exhilaration has itself dissolved through the singular agency of one's own Self, only equanimity remains—
that supreme, true state which exists as equanimity toward all things.

The mind established in that state shall no longer experience suffering. Or else, O Rāghava, having abandoned everything— both agency and non-agency— and having drunk in [the essence of] the mind, remain firm as you truly are.
"This is I," "this is not I," "I do this," "but this is not"—
a vision consisting of such continuous mental construction does not lead to contentment;
it is the path to the Kālasūtra hell and the snare of the Mahāvīci hell.
That state of "I am the body," which is like a row of sword-leaf forests,
must be abandoned with every effort even when total destruction is imminent;
it should not be touched by one seeking well-being, just as a Pukkasi woman carrying dog-meat.
When that streak of redness has been utterly cast away from the vision,
the supreme vision arises like moonlight when the clouds have vanished.
Having clearly realized within oneself, "I am not the agent, nor is this [body] 'me'," one becomes the agent itself and everything.

Having understood this, or having reached the certainty that "I am indeed someone such as this, or rather, I am nothing at all," remain established in your own true state— the supreme state where the best of men, the virtuous who know the path, abide.
The thirty-ninth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Investigating Agency," [spoken by] Rāma.
O Brahmin, what you have spoken is true and beautiful in its expression:
indeed, the Self is the non-doer yet the doer; it is the non-enjoyer yet the enjoyer, the sustainer of beings, the Lord of all, consisting of all, the stainless state of pure consciousness alone.
The Lord, whose very body is self-experience, dwells within all beings. O Master, through your words, Brahman has now become accessible to my heart,
just as the water of a mountain becomes cool by its cascading streams.
"Out of indifference and lack of desire, he neither enjoys nor acts;
yet, because he brings about the welfare of the entire world, the Lord both enjoys and acts.
However, O Blessed One, this vast doubt remains within my heart."
O Brahmin, cut through that with your speech, as the moon dispels darkness with its light.
"This is real, this is unreal; this is he, I am this, you are this;
this is one, this is a second"—such is the impurity of conceptual construction.
"How has this [world] come to reside for the first time within the pure Self, which is as vast and tranquil as the sun in the midst of mist? Vasiṣṭha replied:
O Rāma, I shall explain to you the establishment of the answer to this excellent question at the very time of the final conclusion; then indeed you will understand it.
O Raghava, having reached the occasion of the final conclusion regarding the means to liberation—
"You will become fully capable of hearing these questions and answers,
O Rāma, just as a youth is the proper vessel for the songs sung by beloved women;
so too, one who has attained insight is the vessel for these questions and sublime utterances."
Just as a discourse filled with passion becomes useless for children,
so too does a discourse arising from noble inspiration become meaningless for those of meager understanding.
At any given time, only something specific shines forth for a particular person.
The fruit of a tree appears only in autumn, not in the month of Mādhava; likewise,
the words of instruction from the elders take hold upon a pure cloth,
and discourses on sublime wisdom take hold in one who has realized the Self.
The answer to this question was previously stated by me in brief;
because it was not given in detail, it was not clearly understood by you. If you yourself realize the Self by means of the self, then [you will understand].

"O virtuous one, you know this sequence of questions and answers here; of this there is no doubt. However, O virtuous one, when you have attained awakening at the time of the final conclusion, this sequence of questions and answers must be explained by me in detail."

The self alone knows the self, for it has been made by the self through the self; being perfectly serene, the self attains the self. O Rāma, this investigation into the agent and the non-agent has been told by me.
To destroy the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the knower of that [reality] should become free from impressions.
For bondage is indeed the bond of impressions, while liberation is the exhaustion of impressions;
having abandoned the impressions, abandon even the desire for liberation.
Having first abandoned the tamasic tendencies perfumed by sense objects,
take up the pure tendencies known as the cultivation of friendliness and the other [divine attitudes].
Then, having renounced even those internally while engaging with them externally, [abide in the Self].
Within, become one whose entire desire is stilled, with consciousness alone as your latent impression.
Then, having abandoned even that [consciousness] along with the mind and intellect, remain firm in samādhi; abandon that by which you abandon.

Having completely uprooted and abandoned the mind, the intellect, the notions of time, light and darkness, as well as latent impressions and their impressioner— all preceded by the vibration of the vital breath— one becomes like the moon in the sky, with a tranquil intellect.
O you who possess true awakening, you shall indeed become that very state without delay.
Having completely renounced everything from the heart, O one of great intelligence,
he who remains free from agitation is liberated and is the Supreme Lord.
Whether he practices meditative concentration or performs actions— or whether he does not— such a person,
who has abandoned all objects through the heart and possesses the highest intention, is indeed liberated. For him there is no purpose in inaction, nor is there any purpose for him in ritual acts.
For one whose mind is not devoid of latent impressions through concentration and recitation,
the scriptures have been sufficiently investigated and long discussed with one another;
yet for those who have abandoned their impressions, there is no higher state than silence.
Having wandered through the ten directions, everything that was to be seen has been seen;
yet only a few people have perceived things as they truly are. Whatever is observed, and wherever one goes—
People do not strive for anything there other than what is desired or undesired.
Whatever undertakings there may be, whatever sequences of actions people perform, they are all for the sake of the body alone; nothing at all is for the sake of the Self.
In Pātāla, in the world of Brahmā, in heaven, and on the surface of the earth,
only a few virtuous ones are seen who have perceived the ultimate vision.
When that which is unreal has arisen, [the notions] "this is to be abandoned" and "this is to be accepted" [appear].
That wise person whose two certainties have dissolved is exceedingly rare.
Let him rule the world, or enter into fire or water;
apart from the attainment of the Self, a living being finds no rest.
Those of great intelligence who are heroes against the enemies that are their own senses, and who strive for the destruction of the fever of rebirth—those of great wisdom are to be venerated.
Nowhere do the five elements exist; a sixth is not found anywhere at all.
Where does one of steady intellect find delight—in the netherworld, on the surface of the earth, or in the sky?
For the wise man who crosses over by means of skillful means, saṃsāra is like the footprint of a cow;
but for one who has abandoned skillful means, it is like a vast, surging ocean.
For one whose consciousness has expanded, what can this entire universe— which is as clear as a *kadamba* flower bud—
bestow, and what can it consume, even when it is fully attained?
It is for this reason that those lacking such understanding engage in great battles.
Therefore, O Rāma, I consider that even for the sake of alms, this [body] brings about the destruction of hundreds of thousands of pairs;
and the sudden destruction of this, which is as delicate as the belly of a lotus, in the mere span of a *kalpa*,
is like a great thunderbolt striking a creeping vine.
What could there be in these three worlds that is superior even to a blade of grass for one who possesses a self— a portion of the Primordial Being— to which [all else] has been reduced?
On this side the earth is covered by hundreds of mountains, and likewise on that side by masses of water.
How small is this body of the earth that it could fill [the space of] the sublime [Self]?
There is nothing in this world, including the abodes of Pātāla and Hara,
which can serve any purpose for the wise person who possesses the Self.
For the wise man who has attained oneness, who is as pervasive as space, who is self-abiding and possesses the Self, and who remains established in the Self beyond the mind—
the mist of the web of bodies, grey with its hollows empty— [vanishes].
The three worlds, beautiful with their peaceful movements, are a vast forest;
all the principal mountain ranges are the foam upon the pure ocean of the expansive Brahman;
and the splendors of the world are the mirage of the great radiance of the sun of consciousness.
The successions of creations are the waves of the great ocean of the reality of the Self;
the insights of the scriptures are the rains from the ocean of the unsurpassed state.
The lights of the moon, sun, and fire are like jars, pieces of wood, and other such objects.
Likewise, the hosts of living beings must be illuminated by the radiance of the lamp of consciousness; for long they have remained with their true selves hidden, wandering in the forest of saṃsāra—
men, gods, and asuras— who are like deer devouring the grass of sensual enjoyments.
With door-bolts of bone fragments and covers of skulls, bound by chains of sinews,
these bodies of the world are caskets of flesh containing the jewels of worldly living beings;
they stand there, as innocent as young forest doeses, driven about by others.
To amuse the minds of children, women are like leather dolls;
yet a man of such noble mind and great intelligence does not waver even slightly before floods of enjoyments, just as a mountain is unmoved by the breath from a mouth.
O Rāma, it is said that the Knower of the Self abides in that exceedingly lofty state,
from which even the region of the moon and sun appears to us as if it were the netherworld (pātāla).
Those who possess excellent knowledge have brought these worlds, which were once without light, into the light.
Those carried away by the ocean of existence look upon crawling reptiles as if they were we;
none of these worldly states can delight one who knows reality, just as a rustic village harlot cannot please a sophisticated city man beloved by a noble woman.
No worldly phenomena whatsoever can delight one who knows reality,
even when they are close at hand, just as vast clouds cannot color the sky of his expansive heart.
No worldly phenomena whatsoever can delight one who knows reality.
Like female monkeys dancing for Hara, who desires Gauri’s dance,
none of these worldly phenomena can please one who knows reality,
just as the beauty of a reflection in a former state cannot affect a gem placed within a jar.

Beholding the world— which is like a reflection cast upon a wheel, or like the shimmering image of waves dancing upon the surface of water— the knower of reality finds no delight in the pleasures sought by it, just as a royal swan takes no pleasure in mere blades of kusha grass. This concludes the chapter titled "The Description of the Form of Fulfilled Intent."
The Fortieth Sarga. Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, listen now to this very matter which is appropriate, concerning your ancestors.
The purifying verses sung by Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati,
were those which the son of the preceptor of the gods once sang while staying in a certain thicket of Mount Meru;
at that time, through the power of his practice, he attained rest within the Self.
His mind, filled with the nectar of right knowledge,
found no delight in this visible world— which is composed of the five elements, withered, and of a fragile nature.
Consequently, as if weary of it, he turned away from anything other than the supreme reality of the Self.
Not seeing [anything], he spoke this with a single, faltering voice:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? What shall I grasp? What shall I abandon?
The entire universe is filled by the Self, just as it is by the waters at the end of a great aeon."

Suffering, the self, and happiness, as well as space, hope, you, and I—all this has arisen as consisting of the Self; alas, I have been lost through the Self! Within and without the bodies, below, above, and in all directions—
Thus the Self here, and thus the Self there; nowhere does anything exist that is not composed of the Self.
For the Self is situated everywhere, and everything is established within the Self.
All this is indeed the Self; thus, I bow down within the Self alone.
There is nothing where I am not, and there is nothing that is not in me;
what else could I desire? I simply abide in tranquility, for by means of the Self within the self, I bow with a soul completely filled.
By that I am pacified within; where else could I possibly rush?
I am fire, I am wind, I am the earth, I am the sky.
That which is not me does not exist at all; I alone am everything, pervasive.
"Filled with the form of the Great Terrifier that pervades the boundless sky,
consisting of all consciousness, full, I abide like a single ocean"—
thus contemplating this state within the bower of the Golden Mountain.
Then, pronouncing the syllable *oṃ* in sequence like the sound of a bell— contemplating its half-measure,
the very last portion, as soft as a young child's hair,
neither within nor without, but in the supreme heart.
Pure, with the stain of temporal succession removed, his mental fluctuations dissolved within his heart,
resembling the cloudless autumn sky, Kaca remained there in the form of a mountain of stone.
This was the chapter named "The Song of Kaca."
The forty-first canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"Apart from attachment to food, drink, and women, there is nothing else here [in this world]."

What great thing could one desire that is auspicious and non-deceptive? How could the virtuous find delight in those enjoyments and such things by which the animals, beasts, fools, and the wicked are satisfied?
Enough with those human donkeys in this world who place their trust in enjoyments— which are the total possessions of the wretched, fragile at the beginning,
middle, and end— for here are the hairs, and there is the blood; such is the body of a woman.
By this, dogs find satisfaction, not human beings.
Earth is but clay, trees are wood, the body is flesh, and a mountain is but stone;
the ground is beneath and the sky is upon the back—what in all this is unprecedented for the sake of pleasure?
All worldly perceptions, following after the contact with sense-objects and fragile at the touch of discernment, lead only to delusion when they are grasped as real;
for even in the case of every auspicious state, at its ultimate end, it comes to rest.
Impurity and suffering certainly exist, like soot from a flame.
The activities of the six senses, with the mind as the sixth, are impermanent due to their coming and going;
like creepers, they do not support the true state, just as they cannot support a great serpent king.
"This daughter is the beloved of my blood and flesh"—with such words, she affectionately clings to that heap of bones which she calls her own body; what logic is there in this?
O Rāma, all this is true, yet it is for the satisfaction of the ignorant man alone.
O Rāma, this unstable and unreal world brings no satisfaction to the knower. Even without consuming poison, that which inflicts the stupor of poison—
abandoning that attachment to objective existence, attain the state of a knower through the realization of the oneness of the Self.
When the mind has attained stability by perceiving a self in that which is not-self,
then this world-web, consisting of unreality, comes into being.
By the power of latent impressions, the form of the body is imagined by the mind of Brahman.
"As if [attaining] a golden luster for oneself by means of a wall infused with light," said Rāma:
"O high-minded Brahmin, having reached the station of Brahmā, the mind— "
"How does this world gradually attain such solid density?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"The lotus-born [Brahmā], first a mere infant, having arisen from the bed of the womb..."

He uttered the word "Brahman," and for that reason he is called Brahmā. Then, within himself, he established as the abode of his mind— which consists of a web of volitions and assumes imagined forms— the splendor of volition itself.
Then he first willed forth a great, blazing radiance,
which curled the quarters of the sky with its flickering garlands of fire and scattered a mass of harsh sparks resembling stars.
Its sky was turned into a golden forest by the edges of its reed-like tawny flames;
its own orb was matted with a network of golden creepers of fire-flames;
and it was adorned with shimmering, spreading, and fiercely radiant hand-ornaments and earrings.
Within that radiant light, the mind residing in that body fashioned the sun, which possesses the very form of the Self. Then,
from that light, the maker of day rose up.
Standing in the midst of a circle of flames, with blazing golden earrings,
bearing a mass of flaming matted hair, emitting wide-spreading fire,
his limbs were the play of flames, filling the entire circle of space.
Then the highly intelligent Brahmā, by means of a sudden and beautiful manifestation of his supernatural power (*vimānatva*),
instantly conceptualized those other particles of light and beheld them exactly as they were.
The wise one regards the volitions born within him as being like groups of words;
O mighty-armed one, this is the state of the Self-born One at every re-creation,
wherein gods and demons are fashioned anew each day and for every world.
Time and the divisions of time, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets;
the rivers, oceans, islands, the directions, the mountains, and the earth;
the gods, Daityas, humans, Nāgas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas.
This Brahmā fashioned them like waves from the ocean. The lotus-born one then ordained their respective regions, mountains, and supreme celestial chariots, as well as their distinct functions.
They too, having attained success through their mere volition and possessing all powers,
beheld in an instant before them whatever object they had conceived. Then they conjured up many other diverse multitudes of beings.
They [remembered] others there, and they [remembered] yet others, and they [remembered] various others as well;
then, having recollected the Vedas along with the qualities of the sacrificial rites,
Brahmā established the boundaries for the wife of the house that is the world.
Assuming a Brahmanic form, the Mind, possessing a great illusory body,
thus expands this creation, crowded with the succession of beings,
abounding in oceans, mountains, and trees, and arranged according to the sequence of the various worlds.
[She is] the sphere whose interior is the mass of matted locks consisting of Mount Meru, the earth’s surface, and the quarters;
[she is] pierced by pleasure, pain, old age, birth, death, and disease;
pierced by passion, hatred, and fear; and whose nature consists of the three qualities (guṇas).
Whatever was previously imagined by those minds born of Viriñca,
all that is seen exactly as it was, even today, through illusion (māyā). Thus, in all creations— or indeed in some of them— the Unborn (aja) [perceives].
One conceives of saṃsāra and perceives it as stable. Thus, this very delusion has falsely attained stability in the world;
it is itself incessantly imagined by the mind through its own volitional construction.
By the power of volition, all the activities of the world proceed;
by the power of volition, O Goddess, destiny remains fixed and established. When creation had been set in motion by the Lords of Creatures, that lotus-born one [established it].
Seated upon his lotus throne, the Lord Brahmā reflects:
"By the mere vibration of my mind, this wondrous creation has arisen—
vast, expansive, and subject to the transformations of worldly activity."

This entire web of mental constructs, which I have spread out as harmful, is enriched with Indra, Upendra, and Narendras; it is crowded with mountains and oceans; and its hollows are constricted by the netherworld, the earth, the quarters, and the divisions of the paths.
"Now I desist from this process of the arousal of conceptual constructions," having thus resolved and ceased from the perilous thicket of the objects of imagination,
he remembers the beginningless, supreme Brahman as the Self by means of the self.
Having reached that state which appears as such, with his mind dissolved therein,
he remains at ease, his self pacified, like one weary from a journey resting upon a couch. Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, he has attained supreme peace.
Like an unagitated ocean, he abides within himself by means of his own self.
Sometimes the Lord, the Master, ceases from meditation of his own accord,
due to the power of consciousness, like the ocean ceasing its movement of water because of its inherent gentleness.
He contemplates saṃsāra, which is fraught with pleasure and pain,
bound by hundreds of snares of hope, and afflicted by passion, hatred, and fear; then,
his mind overcome with compassion, for the sake of the manifestation of reality—
In this world, he composes various treatises of great significance,
which contain the essence of the knowledge of the supreme self (*adhyātma-jñāna*), include the Vedas and Vedānta,
as well as the Purāṇas and other works for the liberation of all embodied beings.
Furthermore, having taken that supreme state as his object— a state free from calamities—
he remains established in himself, his soul at peace, like the ocean when Mount Mandara has ceased its churning.
Having observed the activities of the world and having established them within their proper bounds, he abides.
Brahmā, seated upon his lotus throne, abides once again within his own self.
That body of his exists merely by the force of the impressions of birth,
remaining like the whirling of a potter’s wheel for the sake of no further rebirth.
To him, neither the abandonment of the body nor its grasping is pleasing;
there is no self and no other here, neither stability nor instability.
All undertakings regarding all states of being are equal in all modes of conduct.
Having the form of a full ocean, he remains truly liberated;
yet, at times, through mere spontaneity and devoid of all volitional constructions, he awakens for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds.
O Mahāmati, know that this meritorious state of Brahmā which I have described is the sattvic state among the hosts of gods;
it is that portion of the mind belonging to Brahmā in the supreme space of emission.

This very [power] first arises and attains the state of Brahman. But when the period of creation has reached its stage of stability, another supreme creative impulse arises; resorting to space and air, it enters the sprouts of medicinal herbs.
One attains the state of a woman, another the state of a man;
one attains the state of an animal, and another the state of a yakṣa.
Having taken up the sprouts of medicinal herbs through the conduit of the moonbeams, [she nourishes them].
Whatever being she approaches, she quickly becomes that very thing. Once born, by virtue of that association,
she is either bound or liberated in that very birth, according to the distinction of her own creative wonder (*svacamatkāra*).

Thus, O Rāmabhadra, this creation has indeed reached its current state; clearly, it is bound by the fetters of karma through manifest difficulties, distressed by the intensity of the burden of various appearing roles and pastimes under the guise of the calamity of *kalana*. This concludes the chapter titled "The Activity of the Lotus-born," the sixty-second [verse] of the fourth canto.
The forty-second canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
While this Blessed One, the Brahman, was established in the stainless state,
O mighty-armed one, while the Grandfather remained established in his creative ordinance,
this world— like a dilapidated water-wheel— was made to turn by his own arrangement,
using the rope of the thirst for life to draw up the jars of living beings.
And when living beings, arisen from Brahman, enter the cage of worldly existence—
only to have their latent impressions cut away and withered like water in a mass of water—
and when they return from the Lord, revolving within the midst of space and wind;
O Rāma, just as sparks fly from a flickering firebrand fanned by the wind,
so do floods of living beings incessantly emerge from the Brahman and likewise enter it from all sides, like waves in the ocean.
Arising from the state that is without beginning or end, they have entered the state of conceptualization;
others enter the elemental ether like the beauty of smoke entering a cloud. There, they attain oneness with the circles of the subtle elements of the gross elements.
Just as the fragrance of mandāra flowers is carried by sweet breezes, so too were they assailed by that fierce wind— which had attained the nature of their very breath—
just as the immortals are attacked by a host of Daityas.
By that wind arising from the vital breaths of the elements,
those odors are deposited within bodies, as if into the cavities of the nostrils.
Within those elemental bodies, the living beings attain the state of vitality.
Then, in the world, other beings are born and become manifest living creatures;
having entered the state of an embryo through the path of smoke and so forth, they attain the state of being animate, or else they remain for a long time in the state of stationary beings.

Some, dwelling within the hollows of *śālī* trees, attain virility by way of the path of the wind and are born as various beings possessing the nature of life-force. O Rāma, some lineage of living beings is born the very moment it arises.
Enveloped by those subtle elements alone,
she remains within the hollow of the sky as long as the blessed moon does not rise with its full orb,
flooding the world with its rays that quiver like waves of milk-water.
Then, upon those exceedingly beautiful moonbeams, she, like a restless bird, places her foot as it moves from one tree to another;
and from those moonbeams, she enters the sprouts of medicinal herbs.
Like bees [flocking] to lotus ponds, they [the people] flocked to the new clusters of night-lilies;
the fruits of medicinal herbs became exceedingly sweet within,
and even the sugarcane stalks attained fullness as if with juice.
Upon those fruits, a row of living beings sets foot, like a line of insects upon the weight of a mother’s breasts filled with milk, which have been brought down by the rays of the moon.
Those embodied beings by whom those circles of ripe fruits are eaten—
Having entered into those very [elements], they remain there unawakened;
with the web of latent impressions (vāsanā) fast asleep, the splendor of the individual soul (jīva-śrī) presides over the cage of the womb,
just as the splendor of the seed (bīja-śrī), with its leaves folded, presides over a jar.
Just as fire resides in wood, as a jar resides in clay,
and as clarified butter resides in milk, so does the individual soul reside within vitality.
By this sequential process, having returned from the Great Lord (Maheśvara), [one attains the state of the Supreme Self].
That man who is born on earth with a physical beauty never seen before is indeed of a *sāttvika* nature and possesses noble conduct;
if through that very birth he is a partaker of liberation, then he is *sāttvika*.
Now, having entered such a womb and experienced a succession of births,
if one has attained a birth for the sake of liberation, that person is characterized by both rajas and sattva. I shall now describe to you the sequence for a man in his final birth.
O Rāma, just as that one who is predominantly *rājasa* attains liberation; so too, he who is exceedingly *sāttvika* and has entered into transmigratory existence for the first time—
rarely, somewhere, and somehow— comes into being with a sinless nature.
O Rāma, in this world there arise men who are characterized by the qualities of passion (rājasa) and goodness (sāttvika);
therefore, they alone should be investigated, and one should proceed here according to their perspective.
Those who have first emerged from the Supreme Self as individual beings—
O Rāma, those men endowed with great virtues are difficult to find.
As for others who are variously mute, deluded, and of a tamasic nature— being equal to stationary beings— what is there to deliberate upon regarding them, O Rāma?

Having experienced only a few other births and having attained great fortune in this present life, this man has indeed reached a state of fitness for profound inquiry; he is one whose nature is both passionate and pure.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Descent of the Living Being," taught as an incidental discussion following the determination of the person to be investigated.
The forty-third canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"For those who abide in the qualities of passion and goodness (rajas and sattva) are indeed possessed of great virtues on this earth."
They are eternally joyful and uplifted, like moons in the sky;
they do not succumb to weariness, just as regions of space do not acquire impurity,
nor do they wither in adversity, like golden lotuses at night.

They do not desire anything other than their own nature, just as the sun does not seek another day; they always delight in their own right conduct, just as trees delight in their own seasonal flowering.
They possess within them a state of eternal fullness, as beautiful as the moon and undisturbed.
Even in times of adversity, they do not abandon their coolness, just as the moon does not lose its coldness.
They shine by their very appearance through the beauty of virtues such as loving-kindness,
like great trees graced by a creeper that smiles with clusters of fresh blossoms.
Those who are equanimous in pleasure and pain, gentle, and always virtuous toward the good,
maintain their boundaries like the ocean and possess expansive minds;
therefore, O mighty-armed one, their state is the removal of all calamities.
One should always follow [the path] and not be submerged in the ocean of calamity;
in this world, one should move about without weariness in such a way that one acts for the upliftment of the self like those characterized by passion and goodness (rājasa-sāttvika).
Having mastered the noble true treatises and having investigated them again and again,
one should quickly cultivate the perception of impermanence with a mind that is secluded and introspective.
That form which belongs to those dwelling in the three worlds is non-existent at the beginning and at the end.
One should quickly contemplate that alone among all things, and not anything else in vain.
Having abandoned false vision, which is futile, finite, and productive of endless suffering, one should remember this alone: the right view, which is meaningful and infinite.
"Who am I? How has this world come to be?"—thus should this extended cycle of existence be investigated with effort by one who is wise and virtuous.
One should not immerse oneself in worldly actions, nor should one dwell with the ignoble.
The destroyer of all [defilements] should be seen; death must not be treated with indifference.
By one who knows that, even if situated in a high position, a virtuous person of very great and cool disposition should be followed, just as the peacock follows the cloud.
Having performed pure inquiry into the ego, the body, and the arising of saṃsāra, a person should take refuge in reality alone;
having abandoned the body— its bones and flesh, its blood and other impurities— which is unlovely.
One should behold pure consciousness alone as the thread of the pearl necklace of all beings.
In that which is real, eternal, pervasive, pure, omnipresent, the source of all existence,
and auspicious— this entire universe is strung upon it like a multitude of gems on a thread.
That very same consciousness which exists in the sun, the ornament of the expanse of the worlds in the sky,
is that same consciousness within the belly of an insect dwelling in the hollow of the earth.
Just as there is no difference here in reality between the space within a jar and [the universal] space, so it is.
O sinless one, there is no difference between the funeral pyre and the shape of the body;
likewise, for all beings, bitter and pungent tastes are not otherwise.
Indeed, because experience is one, there is only a distinction of consciousness.
Since the reality that is pure consciousness alone exists eternally as one,
what ignorance is this of yours that you think, "this has been born," or "this has perished"?
Indeed, there is no such thing here that comes into being after having previously not existed.
And there is no such thing as a real entity that, having come into being, dissolves.
This is merely an appearance, O Rāghava; it is neither existent nor non-existent, but stands as if it were real due to a mind that is agitated and unpeaceful.
"Let there be delusion and confusion for you due to ignorance, thinking that what perishes is not real;
yet, having firmly determined that it is indeed unreal, may you be free from sorrow.
If the world is non-existent, why indeed is there delusion here? And if it were existent, what cause would there be for such bewilderment?"
Therefore, amidst the conditions of birth and death, remain ever tranquil like the sky, perfectly equanimous.
The forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Examination of Delusion."
Vasiṣ�ṭha: A wise and discerning person, from the very beginning, should dwell together with one of great intelligence, who knows the meaning of the scriptures, is wise, and is a virtuous man.
Whatever noble perceptions of supreme consciousness exist that destroy suffering,
they flourish like creepers in the springtime when a virtuous person is present—
when one who is dispassionate, dear to the heart, and great.
O mighty-armed one, having investigated through inquiry, the supreme state is attained. O Rāma,
a person who is honored by the study of the meaning of the scriptures, by association with virtuous people, and by the practice of dispassion,
shines like you as a vessel of realized knowledge.

But you, whose own conduct is noble, steadfast, and an ocean of a multitude of virtues, abide in a birth that is free from suffering, characterized by the *rājasa-sāttvika* quality. Once again, in this world that has been scorched by saṃsāra, you are no longer a vessel for suffering.

O Sage, you are one whose birth is in the West; you run in accordance with your own true nature. By your own stainless vision, the reality of the world has become manifest to you exactly as it is, like the object of the sun’s radiance.
Now, with the impurities burnt away by the fire of the poison of my words, may you become stainless, truly equal to an autumn sky from which the clouds have been dispelled;
liberated from the conceptualization of worldly existence and joined with supreme consciousness.
Make your mind a cluster of pearls, utterly transparent within your heart.
When the mind is freed from the reckoning of "this is mine" and "this belongs to another," and is devoid of all divisions, it is indeed liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Those men on earth who now follow your supreme conduct shall also attain freedom from sorrow;
those men who shall live according to the example of Rāghava’s life, they too shall reach that state.

They shall cross the ocean of existence by means of the small boat of their own mind. That virtuous person who possesses a mind equal to yours and maintains an even vision is fit for the insights of knowledge, just as the full moon is for radiant lights.

You have reached the state free from sorrow, following whatever has come to pass; remain as long as the body lasts with a mind devoid of passion and hatred. Outwardly, observe the conduct appropriate for the world, but inwardly, abandon all desires.
"Attaining supreme coolness, remain like the orb of the full moon.
But those who are born into other births and are devoid of virtue—
these indeed are not to be considered, for they possess the nature of jackal cubs."
O mighty-armed one, by cultivating those very natures of men born with a *sāttvika* disposition, a person attains a noble birth in a future life;
for whatever species and qualities a living being constantly pursues in this world, [he will attain them in the next].
Even one born of another species attains the state of that species in an instant.
All previous conditions, which follow the power of birth and karma,
are overcome by the resolute through human effort, just as brave men conquer their enemies.
One should rescue the intellect with fortitude, even when it is distressed by the defects of karma belonging to a previous birth of impurity, just as one rescues a bewildered doe from the mud.
Those who have taken refuge in other births— whether characterized by darkness (tamas) or passion (rajas)— [should likewise do so].
By the power of their own discernment, the virtuous attain the nature of the *sāttvika* class.
O Rāghava, whatever is directed toward the clear jewel of the inner mind, one indeed becomes composed of that; therefore, human effort triumphs.
Through human effort characterized by highly precious virtues,
those seeking liberation arise here in this later age of auspicious birth.
There is nothing on earth, nor in heaven among the gods, anywhere at all—
That which a person endowed with virtues does not attain through human effort—
why do you, possessed of undecaying fortitude, the momentum of excellent dispassion,
and wisdom firmly rooted, not attain that desired goal?
Having secured your own welfare through your great being by means of your intellect, become free from sorrow;

for by your very example, these people on earth shall likewise become entirely free from sorrow. When you, endowed with the great majesty of discernment in your final birth and delightful with the quality of expanded goodness—

O Rāma, O Rāma! Let her not entertain thoughts of delusion regarding the bonds of worldly existence; for surely, her very foot has been placed upon the activity established in the quality of goodness (*sattva*).
The Section on Stability is completed.
5. Section: Tranquility (*Upaśānti*).
The First Chapter.
Now, immediately after the section on "Establishment," hear this:
the section on "Quiescence," which, when known, brings about liberation.
Vālmīki:
While Vasiṣṭha was thus delivering these delightful and purifying words in that well-attended assembly, which was as still as the autumn sky studded with stars, [the sage continued].
And while the king remained silent within the assembly for the sake of hearing [the discourse],
the lotus-pool was as motionless as a windless place where the lotuses were still; likewise,
the playful women had their intoxication, delusion, and strength completely stilled.
As if long exiled, the [elephants] retreated inward toward tranquility;
as if from hearing [the news], the swans upon their lotus-hands dissolved away; and as if paralyzed, the fly-whisks with their silent *ghurghura*-bells fell motionless, like those struck by a curse.
While those kings who knew that reality were examining the subtle portion of consciousness with the tips of their index fingers resting upon the bridge of their noses,
Rāma blossomed like a lotus at dawn.
On the seat where darkness had been utterly abandoned, like the rising of the sun in the sky,
Daśaratha listened with rapture to the words of Vasiṣṭha,
as a peahen listens to the thundering of a cloud that rains down heavily.
Having withdrawn the mind, which is as restless as a monkey, from all enjoyments,
it is directed toward listening with effort while the minister remains present;
thus, through the words of Vasiṣṭha, one’s own Self is fully realized as stainless as a digit of the moon.
While Lakṣmaṇa was present, distinguished by his skill and the power of his training;
while Śatrughna, the crusher of enemies, had attained fullness of mind;
and while [Rāma] remained like the full moon of the Rākā night, having reached a state of perfect bliss.
When Sumantra had attained friendship and his mind became as cool as the rays of the moon,
his heart blossomed like a lotus at that very moment;
while the other sages and kings remained there in that same state.
As if their jewel-like minds were being washed clean and their hearts were heaving with joy,
there then arose the sound of midday conchs, as deep as the roar of the ocean and as resonant as the thundering of clouds at the end of an aeon, filling all the quarters of space.
By that great sound, the words of the sage were eclipsed,
just as the cries of the cuckoo are drowned out by the roar of a thundercloud.
Then, in that assembly, the sage caused his own voice to fade away.
"By what great person is this quality that has conquered the essence being proclaimed?
Having heard that midday sound for just a moment,
when the dense clamor had subsided, the sage spoke to Rāma.
"O crusher of enemies, I have thus described to you this day's ritual duties beginning with Rāma; tomorrow morning I shall explain the other matters that must be told.
This which has been obtained through destiny is the duty to be performed by the twice-born."
"That midday libation remains to be performed for us, yet our noble task is faltering.
You too, O fortunate one, skilled in proper conduct, arise and perform the entire ritual of the libation, including the bathing, giving of gifts, worship, and so forth."
Having spoken thus, the sage rose together with Daśaratha,
like the sun rising from the slope of the mountain of sunrise along with the moon and the assembly of stars.
When those two stood up, the entire assembly trembled to rise as well.
Touched by a gentle breeze, she whose eyes were like lotus petals rose up,
adorned by a swarm of bees rising from her ear-ornament;
she was like the army of elephants on Mount Vindhya, with their trunks and lotuses swaying.
The circles of their armlets were crushed by the mutual friction of their shoulders,
signaling the hour of twilight with clouds reddened by the powder of jewels;
the humming of bees was added by those wandering about from falling head-ornaments.
The sky was turned into a rainbow by the intense radiance of her crown;
with the moving clusters of blossoms from the creeper-like hands of her beloved serving as waving chowries,
she was like a forest grove where a herd of magnificent elephants is agitated.
With their garments mutually drawn by the splendor of the jewels on their glittering bracelets,
they were like a garland from the Mandara forest whose flowers are shaken by the wind;
with the camphor-dust of musk serving as frost, they were like pure clouds.
Like a row of autumn clouds spreading across the horizon, she reached out to all the kings;
with the cavities of the sky reddened by the mass of the shimmering jewels on their crowns,
she was like the twilight that brings about the gathering of the restless and trembling lotuses of worldly affairs.
Filled with water in the form of the rays of jewels, with lotus-faces in close proximity,
encircled by swarms of bees, and possessing the melody of the sound of anklets— that assembly, crowded with hundreds of kings, rose up like a lotus pond.
The creation, complete with a continuous succession of beings, arose as if it were new.
Then, having bowed to the king, the princes departed from the royal palace like waves of the ocean rendered rainbow-like by jewels.
Then the neighboring kings and ministers, experts in policy and discernment, bowed down to Vasiṣṭha and the lord of the earth and departed for their baths;
as did Vāmadeva and others, as well as Viśvāmitra and his followers.

Placing Vasiṣṭha at their head, they stood waiting for the bath. There, King Daśaratha, the subduer of enemies, having honored the assembly of sages, was dismissed by them and departed for his own business.
Those whose abode is the forest went to the forest; those who dwell in the sky went to the sky;
and the citizens likewise departed for the city, so that they might return in the morning.
The Lord, having been entreated with affection by the King and Vasiṣṭha, [consented].
Viśvāmitra spent the night in the residence of Vasiṣṭha;
there he was attended by Vasiṣṭha along with the foremost of brahmins, kings, and sages,
as well as by all the sons of Daśaratha, headed by Rāma.
The glorious one, honored by all the worlds, went to his own hermitage,
followed by a multitude of gods like the Lotus-born Brahmā proceeding to the world of Brahmā;
from that place, the sage [dismissed] Rāma and the others, the sons of Daśaratha.
He dismissed all those who had bowed at his feet.
Having sent away the sky-dwellers, the earth-dwellers, and the water-dwellers— those moving beings whose range of qualities he had praised—
he performed, in due order within his own home, those daily rites for the twice-born while the noble sage remained seated.
The Second Sarga, titled "The Description of the First Day," by Vālmīki:
Having gathered at the house, those heroic princes, radiant as the moon, performed every daily rite in their own dwellings without exception—
Vasiṣṭha, Rāghava, the kings, the sages, and the twice-born.
Thus they performed their respective duties then in the streets of their own homes;
they bathed in reservoirs filled with lovely lotuses, water-lilies, night-blooming lilies, and blue lotuses,
resounding with the cries of ruddy geese, swans, and cranes.
They gave gifts to the brahmins consisting of cattle, land, sesame seeds, gold, beds, seats, food, and fine garments; they dwelt in their own palaces,
which were variegated with gold and jewels and adorned with chowries.
Together with their sons, grandsons, friends, servants, kinsmen, and circles of companions, they worshipped the gods beginning with Acyuta, Īśāna, Hutāśa, and Arka; thereafter,
they partook of their appropriate meals.

At that time, it was day in this city; because only one-eighth of it remained, it was pleasant with a gentle breeze. Then, according to their respective desires appropriate for that hour, they performed their evening rites.
They brought him along with their kinsmen until the sun went to its setting;
they performed the twilight devotions well, recited the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn,
chanted holy praises, and sang delightful verses.
Then, as the moon— dispeller of the sorrow of the night-lily, bestower of dew, and rising as if from the Ocean of Milk like the consort of Indra— had ascended,
[the lovers] slowly spread flowers and scattered handfuls of camphor upon them.

The descendants of Raghu lay upon couches as beautiful as the long orb of the moon. Then, without Rāma, that night passed slowly for the others who were occupied with their activities there, like a beautiful young woman.
Rāma remained there, reflecting upon those very words of Vasiṣṭha—sweet and noble—which he had previously drunk in, just as a young camel recalls the milk it has tasted before.
"What indeed is this wandering in saṃsāra? What are these people? he wondered.
Do these diverse beings here come into existence or pass away?
What is the nature of the mind, and how is this projected?
From what does this illusion arise, and how is it withdrawn?
And if it has ceased, what quality or what defect could there be?
How, moreover, has this contraction come upon the Self, which is all-pervading?
What would have been said by the venerable Sage regarding the dissolution of the mind?

What has been taught regarding the conquest of the senses, and what has been said concerning the Self? It is the Self alone that expands this world of saṃsāra through its pervasive forms— such as the individual soul (jīva), the intellect (citta), the mind (manas), and illusion (māyā)— all of which are composed of unreality.
When these very threads bound by mind alone have come to an end, there is the cessation of suffering; how then are these [objects] easy for us to treat?
How can this female crane of the intellect be drawn away from its circling around the cloud-mass of enjoyments?
"I shall separate the stream of enjoyment from it, as a swan separates milk from water.
(MU 5.2.20) "Enjoyments cannot be abandoned; without their abandonment, there is no wisdom.
We are not masters over calamities—alas, a great crisis has arrived! (MU 5.2.21)
This very purpose, which is to be attained by the conquest of the mind alone, has been fully accomplished for me;
yet it remains as heavy as a mountain due to my folly, like a ghost haunting a child.
When, having attained my own peace and being freed from the agitation of saṃsāra, shall I...?
"Like a young girl who has found her beloved, my mind shall attain happiness.
When will my purifying mind become one whose agitation has subsided, from which all curiosity has vanished, and which rests in the shoreless state?"
When, having well-established myself in that state which is more cooling than even the moon full of its entire collection of digits,
and having abandoned this form so fragile through mental constructs to dissolve within the Self, shall I laugh at the world?

When will my mind attain peace, like a wave in water? When, having crossed the ocean of saṃsāra— turbulent with the waves of craving and garlanded with the crocodiles of illusion— shall I become free from the fever of suffering?
On paths that are pure and tranquil, we who are wise shall dwell, free from sorrow and possessing equal vision, seeking liberation for those who desire it.
[O you] who have scorched all limbs and cause terror to all the elements!
O mind, when will this long-lasting fever of saṃsāra be extinguished for us?
O intellect, like the trace of a lamp in a windless place, having ceased its flickering,
you shall attain peace immediately following self-illumination.
When will you effortlessly cross over your senses from their sufferings—senses whose bodies are scorched by wicked desires—as Garuḍa crosses the ocean?
This delusion has arisen clearly: "This is he," "I am this," "This is mine."
Like a dark cloud in autumn, when will this [distress] ever subside?
That delight which we find amidst the rows of Mandāra groves becomes as insignificant as a blade of grass compared to that state of our own which we shall attain— when indeed shall we reach it?
"Tell me, will the stainless visions of knowledge proclaimed by those free from passion ever find a place within you?
O father, O mother, O son! May I never again utter such words."
O mind, my kinsman, you are the vessel; you are the food for those who experience suffering. O sister, O enlightened one, quickly fulfill the request of your brother;
for our liberation from suffering, contemplate the words of the Sage.
"Calamity falls upon you with affection, like a daughter, as long as worldly existence persists;
therefore, O fortunate one, remain steadfast for the sake of the destruction of existence. These were the first words spoken by the sage Vasiṣṭha to those who had become dispassionate.
Then follows the conduct of one seeking liberation, and after that, the sequence of the origins;
then the section on stability, beautiful with various illustrations and containing the entirety of consciousness—remember all this correctly, O Mind! (MU 5.2.38–39)

Even if it has been performed a hundred times and investigated, if that which was done does not reach the human intellect, it becomes fruitless like an autumn cloud; therefore, wisdom alone is the essence of what must be accomplished.
This concludes the chapter titled "Instruction and Tradition."
The Third Canto.
Vālmīki:
By means of such extensive and noble reflection, he remained there.
That night passed away like a lotus longing for the sun;
when the quarters of the sky were somewhat tawny with darkness and somewhat reddened by dawn, and the stars had become sparse as if the directions themselves had turned pale.
Simultaneously with the sound of the morning trumpets,
the glorious Rāghava, whose face was like the moon, rose up like a lotus from a lotus pond.
Having performed all the morning rites together with his brother, he [set out].

Accompanied by a limited retinue, he went to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha. From afar, Rāma, with his neck bowed, prostrated himself before the sage who was established in meditative absorption in a secluded spot and devoted solely to the Self.
Having bowed to him, they stood in that courtyard endowed with humility,
as long as the darkness was not entirely severed and destroyed from the circle of the quarters.
So too did the kings, the princes, the sages, and the brahmins.
They arrived at the hermitage of Mauna, like immortals reaching the world of Brahmā.
That abode of Vasiṣṭha became crowded with people,
thronged with elephants, horses, and chariots, and beautified by the palaces of kings.
In an instant, the blessed Vasiṣṭha emerged from his meditative absorption;
with appropriate conduct, he received the people who bowed before him.
Then, accompanied by Viśvāmitra, the sage was followed by other sages.
The glorious one suddenly ascended the chariot, just as the lotus-born Brahmā ascends his lotus-throne;
surrounded by a vast army, he went to the house of Daśaratha’s son,
like Brahmā, adorned by all the gods, going to Indra’s city.
He entered the spacious and beautiful assembly hall of Daśaratha,
like a royal swan surrounded by a flock of swans entering a lotus pond.
At that time, King Daśaratha quickly took three steps toward him.
The one of great prowess rose from his lion-throne and went forth. Then all those kings, headed by Daśaratha, as well as Vasiṣṭha and the other sages, seers, and brahmins, entered there.
And the ministers, headed by Sumantra; the wise priests, headed by Dhaumya;
the princes, headed by Rāma; the sons of the ministers, headed by Suha; the vassal kings and other subjects; and the citizens, headed by Suhotra.
The musicians and so forth, as well as the servants and the citizens and their attendants,
all sat down in their respective appropriate places and upon their respective appropriate seats,
with their gazes fixed intently upon Vasiṣṭha.

When the clamor of the assembly had subsided and the bards were established in silence, and when inquiries regarding their welfare had been made within that gentle inner circle of the court— amidst the heat of the sun like a mass of vermilion dust, as if upon a young child— *MU_5,3.18*...
It rests upon the surface of the canopy, shining in the orb of the mirror;
it flickers among the rows of fringes, enters the hollows of the lotuses,
and moves within the ruby-laden pearl necklaces.
As sweet breezes blow, carrying a thick fragrance from the large flower-swinging cradles spreading in every direction,
amidst soft windows and grounds strewn with blossoms.

While the matrons were seated upon their couches watching, their eyes flickering with the rays of the sun entering through the lattice-work, and while the female attendants holding white chowries stood silent— having abandoned even a trace of fickleness— their own chowries appearing tawny by the mass of light from their jewels; (5.3.22–23)
In the courtyard grounds, whose surfaces are as beautiful as the rays of the sun reflected in a mass of pearls, a swarm of bees does not savor the cluster of *caṃpaka* flowers;
through delusion, it wanders about as if perceiving them to be drops of fresh sunlight, like a cloud in the sky.
He who has heard the flow of Vasiṣṭha’s holy words proclaims them with spreading wonder among the noble world.
In that assembly, there were words charming with soft syllables and mutual smiles, delightful with manifold virtues; while the distinguished throngs of royal sages,
Siddhas, Vidyādharas, noble Munis, and Brahmins from the quarters,
the city, and the sky entered silently, observing a vow of silence and bowing reverently on all sides as the conversation proceeded in hushed tones.

When the breeze blows—reddish-brown with the golden pollen of swarms of intoxicated bees drawn from the tender buds of blooming *kokanada* lotuses; resonant with the song of clanging bells set in motion; cool with the waters of the night it has drunk;
scented with the smoke of *aguru* and *tagara* mixed with the fragrance of sandalwood; and marked by the intense scent of fresh flower-garlands in the clouds— MU 5.3.27.

It moves along with fragments of lotus-whirlpools from the white canopy, marked by the pollen of swaying flowers, while the bees are signaled by their humming sounds. The Fourth Canto, titled "Description of the Layout and Colors of the Assembly Hall."
Vālmīki: With a voice as deep as a thundercloud, Daśaratha spoke these words— beautiful with confident phrasing— to the leader of sages.
O Blessed One, I hope you are free from the exhaustion born of yesterday’s composition of words— that exhaustion which surpasses even the emaciation caused by ascetic toil.
For yesterday you uttered a multitude of words that were full of bliss and profound in their discernment.
We have been comforted here by him as if by a rain of nectar.
Like rays of the moon, these stainless words of the great ones— composed of nectar and dispelling darkness— cool the inner self.
These well-spoken words are showers of nectar that bestow unprecedented joy, take refuge in the highest state, and utterly dispel delusion;
they are the ultimate, singular lamp for beholding the jewel of the Self.
He from whom the creeper of eloquent speech arises is that tree of the virtuous, and he is worthy of worship.
The well-spoken words of the virtuous wipe away every evil intention and every ill deed,
just as the rays of the moon wipe away a mass of darkness.
"O Sage, our thirst, greed, and other such fetters of saṃsāra have been thinned by your teaching, like dark clouds in autumn.
We have now begun to behold the stainless Self."
Like those born blind who do not perceive gold brought before their eyes by a physician,
we were like that; O you whose body is the autumn of your own speech, may the mist called the latent tendencies of saṃsāra in the sky of our hearts now begin to thin away.
O Sage, neither the blossoms of the *mandāra* tree nor the waves of the nectar-water delight the heart as much as the words of those possessed of noble intellects.
Whatever [deeds] Rāghava performs while being honored by great men—
In this world, that day alone possesses light; the remaining days are blind abodes of darkness.
O Rāma, whose eyes are like lotus petals, desiring to see the true nature of reality, awaken the Sage once more as he remains established in his grace.
When the king had spoken thus, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha, noble-souled, who was seated there facing Rāma, said this: Vasiṣṭha:
"O Raghava, sole moon of your lineage, O high-minded one, do you perhaps remember the meaning of what was said by me, having considered it from beginning to end—
that there are various types of births due to the differentiation of the qualities such as *sattva*?"
O crusher of enemies, do you remember the division of all things?
Do you remember the form of the God, the stainless Supreme Self, which is both the whole and the non-whole, being and non-being, eternally manifest?
O virtuous one, sole recipient of praise for your goodness, do you remember how this entire universe arose from the Lord of Lords, the Sovereign of all?
And do you remember the nature of ignorance—how it spreads out, yet is hollow and fragile? *Mokṣopāya* 5.4.18.
O one of noble mind, you remember correctly that which is both infinite and finite;
do you remember well that which was established through the investigation of salt and other examples—that the person is nothing other than the mind itself? (MU 5.4.19–20)
"O Rāma, have you reflected upon the entire meaning of the discourse? Has that which was investigated yesterday been fixed in your heart during the night?
Has it been repeatedly examined and firmly established within your mind?"
