A purpose bears fruit only when highly esteemed, not when its stability is struck down by indifference. O giver of honor, you are a vessel for words that are pure and refined, just as a bamboo with a hollow heart is the vessel for pearls.
Vālmīki:
Having been thus granted the opportunity by the sage of great luster, the son of the Lotus-Seated One,
Rāma spoke these words.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, this is indeed the manifestation of your own power,
that I have understood your most noble speech.
"Everything you have commanded is exactly so and not otherwise;
the meaning of your words was contemplated by me throughout the night, with sleep cast aside.
You are the sun for the earth, for the destruction of the darkness of worldly existence."
O Lord, that delightful mass of rays of speech you extended yesterday—
O one whose self is undepressed, I have taken all of it within me,
just as the ocean takes in a beautiful, holy, and variegated collection of jewels.
By whom would your instruction— not conducive to worldly harm, heart-pleasing, meritorious, and a means to bliss— not be borne upon the head for the sake of perfection? We,
whose veils of frost-like saṃsāra are being worn away, [follow it].

Through your grace, they have become serene, like days at the end of the rainy season. Your holy instruction has a beginning that is sweet upon its first appearance, it increases one's good fortune in the middle, and it results in unsurpassed fruit in the end.
May the flower of your speech— blooming, white, unfading, delightful, and arising from a joyful intention— be for us eternally auspicious and bestowing its fruit.
O you who are expert in all eternal scriptures, a single great lake of spreading waters of merit!
O you of extensive vows, now devote yourself intensely toward me, who have cast off all sin;
thus [ends] the fifth canto, named "The Question of Rāghava."
Vasiṣṭha said: O you of beautiful form, listen attentively to this beneficial Chapter on Tranquility, which is as lovely as the supreme philosophical conclusion. MU 5.5.1
O Rāma, this long-lasting illusion of saṃsāra is constantly sustained by men of rajasic and tāmasa nature, like a pavilion supported by sturdy pillars;
yet it is [overcome] by heroes such as you, who are established in sattva and strengthened by their virtues.

This mature illusion is cast off with ease, like the skin by serpents. O virtuous one, those born of the quality of goodness (sattva) who are wise, as well as those characterized by a mixture of passion and goodness (rājasasāttvika),
investigate this world from its beginning to its end, reaching the Supreme.
For those whose debts have been cleared through association with the scriptures and the company of the virtuous,
an intellect arises that resembles a lamp, capable of discerning the essential truth.
By means of one's own self, one should investigate the Self through inquiry itself.
As long as the knowable has not been realized, it is not yet attained.
O delighter of your lineage, you are the foremost among those possessed of wisdom, skill in means, and fortitude; you are of noble birth and a preeminent being among kings.
O wise one, observe for yourself among the views concerning the commencement of saṃsāra:
what is real and what is unreal? Be devoted to that which is real. How can there be reality in that which does not exist at the beginning and at the end?
"O Rāma, that which is eternal in the beginning and at the end is the truth, and nothing else.
For that deluded beast of a person whose mind is attached to an object that is non-existent in the beginning and at the end, by what means can discernment be produced?"
"In this world, it is the mind alone that is born; it is the mind alone that grows.
But through the vision of right perception, it is the mind alone that dissolves.
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, I have understood this: that in these three worlds, it is the mind alone that wanders in saṃsāra and is the vessel for old age and death.
Tell me with certainty what the means for its crossing over is."
"O Raghava, the darkness within the heart of the descendants of Raghu is being destroyed by you, who are like the sun.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Previously, O Raghava, [you were purified] by the scripture, by dispassion, and by your excellence."
In the same way, through association with the virtuous, the mind is led toward merit. When the mind, nourished by goodness, has attained detachment,
then one should follow those who are gurus, for they are indeed gurus of realized knowledge.
Then, having performed meditation, worship, and so forth as instructed by him,
he gradually attains that state which is supremely purifying;
through pure inquiry, he perceives the Self by means of the self.
Just as the moon, with its internal coolness, [cools] its own orb with its radiance,
so too a person is carried away like a blade of grass in the great ocean of worldly existence until the mind finds rest upon the shore of discernment.
The intellect of this person, who has fully understood reality through investigation,
casts all mental afflictions beneath it, just as fine sand is submerged in gentle water.
"This is gold, this is ash"— when this is clearly understood, [the truth becomes manifest].

The delusion of a goldsmith is not like that of one who knows the Self. For when it has long been understood that "this Self is imperishable and of an indestructible nature," what room is there here for delusion, and from where could it arise?
For when the essence of a gem is not recognized, one is bewildered regarding its value;
but when its essence is known and its value is beyond doubt, where indeed could there be delusion?
O people, the Self, being unrecognized by you, leads to the establishment of suffering.

But once fully understood, it leads to infinite happiness and peace. Having separated your own self from this body which has afflicted it as if by mingling with it, become established in your own well-being without delay.
O men, there is not even the slightest connection between this body and the stainless Self, just as there is none between a speck of mud and gold, even when that gold is situated within it.
The Self is distinct and the body is distinct; they are like a lotus leaf and the water [upon it].
With arms upraised, I cry out, yet no one hears me.
As long as the mind remains inert by nature, like a tortoise in a pit— stupid,
its body sluggish for enjoyment, and having forgotten the inquiry into the Self— [so long does this state persist].
As long as it is not awakened, the darkness of saṃsāra cannot be pierced even slightly, even by the moon together with fire, or even by twelve suns;
for when the mind is fully awakened, it discerns its own true state.
Like the rising of the sun [driving away] the night, the darkness within the heart flees;

one should constantly awaken the mind, which has been lying upon the bed of worldly enjoyment, for the sake of supreme enlightenment, so that it may transcend existence, for existence indeed bestows extreme suffering.

Just as the sky is not smeared by dust, and just as a lotus is not smeared by water, even though they are in contact, so too is the Self of yours [unaffected] by bodies. Just as mud and the like, though attached, remain distinct from gold; ||| MU_5.5.31 ||| so too is the Self distinct from the body.
The inert body does not undergo internal transformation in that same way as the Self.
One perceives the experience of pleasure and pain in the Self,
though it is as unreal as the appearance of two moons or the yellowness [of a conch] in the sky.
For pleasure and pain belong to the body, not to the Self which transcends all;
these indeed belong only to one who lacks knowledge, and when that [body] is destroyed, they belong to no one.
There is no pleasure for anyone, nor is there any pain for anyone.
"Behold everything, O Rāghava, as consisting of the Self, peaceful, and infinite.
These extended perceptions of creation that are seen here are like waves in water, or like feathers in the sky, within the Self. (MU 5.5.35–36)
Just as a gem spontaneously gives forth its own light-reflections without external cause,
even so this Self bestows creations;
O wise one, the Self and the world are neither one, nor two, nor are they non-existent.
All this that now unfolds is merely a manifestation.
Indeed, all this is Brahman; this entire world is the Self pervading all.
O sinless one, abandon the delusion that "I am one thing" and "this is another."
Within that eternal, dense mass of Brahman, no conceptual constructions arise;
they are like the waves in the ocean, O Rāma, which are not distinct from the water.
Since everything is pervaded by the one Supreme Self alone, conceptualizations do not exist apart from it.
The second alternative does not exist, just as there is no particle of frost in fire. Indeed, by contemplating the Self through the Self as consisting of consciousness alone,
this Self itself expands within itself as the web of the world.
There is no sorrow, there is no delusion, there is no birth, and no one who is born.
That which exists here exists as that alone; be free from the fever of passion, O Rāghava.
Equal-minded, self-abiding, steady-witted, tranquil, with a peaceful mind, you are a sage.
O Rāghava, be free from fever, silent, as pure as a precious gem;

be free from the pairs of opposites, eternally established in sattva, devoid of the concern for acquisition and preservation, self-possessed, non-dual, and sorrowless in soul. O Rāghava, be free from fever.
Solitary, with peaceful intentions, steady-minded, and resolute in purpose,
follow whatever comes to you and be free from feverish distress, O Rāghava; be free from passion, free from exertion, free from mental agitation, and cleansed of all impurity.
Neither a taker nor a renouncer, be free from fever, O Rāghava.
Having attained the state that transcends the universe, fulfilled by having obtained all that is to be obtained,
remain unagitated like the full ocean— be free from fever, O Rāghava.
Freed from the web of conceptual constructions and devoid of the ointment of illusion,
being satisfied in yourself by yourself, become free from the fever of passion, O Rāghava.
You are the one whose body is infinite, boundless, and limitless— the best among those who know the Self.
O Rāghava, be free from feverish distress, as steadfast as the summit of the earth-supporting mountain.
Delight in the magnanimity within yourself by means of the self, like the full ocean;
rejoice in the bliss within yourself by means of the self, like the orb of the full moon.
This entire manifold creation is unreal in nature; one who knows that truth does not pursue what is unreal.

You are a knower of that truth, you are one whose mental fluctuations have been stilled, you are free from affliction, and you are eternally risen. O beautiful one, remain with your sorrows extinguished!
Having been instructed by your Guru, protect this earth under your sole umbrella for a long time, maintaining it here through your vision of the established order.
Having delighted the world of kings with all his virtues, it is not fitting for him to abandon the kingdom, nor is there any passion for worldly activities here.
The Fifth Chapter, named "The First Instruction.
The Sixth Chapter.
Vasiṣṭha:
It is my conviction that he who engages in actions without the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of thinking, "I am performing this very movement," is liberated.
Assuming a human body, some of these, devoted to ritual actions,
go from heaven to hell, and again from hell to heaven;
others, devoted to evil deeds, have desisted from their own discernment.

They go from hell to hell, from suffering to suffering, and from fear to fear. Some, bound by the threads of their own latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and agitated by their karma, pass from the state of an animal to the body of an immobile being, and from there back to an animal body.

Some fortunate knowers of the Self, whose mental vision has been scrutinized and whose fetters of craving are severed, proceed to the absolute state. O Rāghava, having previously experienced only a few births...
He who is liberated in this very life is one characterized by both passion and goodness;
once born, he attains growth like the moon during the bright fortnight,
and prosperity follows him as the rainy season does the *kuṭaja* tree.
O Great-minded One, for one whose birth is their last, pure knowledges enter immediately, like pearls entering an excellent bamboo tube:
nobility, amiability, friendliness, gentleness, liberation, and wisdom.
They always resort to him, as women do to the inner apartments;
he who, while performing all his duties, remains equanimous whether they flourish or perish and their fruits are gained or lost, neither rejoices nor grieves at any time.
There, dualities come to an end like darkness at daybreak;
there, virtues attain purity like clouds in autumn.
All people desire him whose conduct is sweet with gentleness.
Like herds of deer in the forest toward a flute of sweet sound,
such glories of virtue pursue a man of his final birth from the moment he is born,
just as cranes follow a rain-cloud.
Then, endowed with all virtues, he follows the Guru alone; the Guru, in turn, directs him toward solitary seclusion for purification,
with a mind possessed of virtue and characterized by discernment and detachment.
Then he beholds the Lord, and then the Self, uniform and free from ailment.
Therefore, O Rāma, with a beautiful inquiry and a tranquil mind, one must first awaken the mind that is sluggish in its conceptualizing.
For those of great virtue who are born later awaken the sleeping deer of the mind first with songs of excellence.
Having diligently served teachers of renowned virtue and having investigated the jewel of the mind with a stainless intellect—
Having beheld for a long time this inner light within this world, the human being attains a stainless state.
This is the seventh chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Sequence."
Vasiṣṭha:
This general sequence has been declared for all living beings;
now hear this other specific detail, O lotus-eyed one. MU 5.7.1
O Rāma, for those embodied beings born into this turmoil of saṃsāra, there are these two supreme methods for attaining liberation:
first, by means of gradual practice as instructed by a guru; and second— [the rest of the verse follows].
It is declared that the bestower of perfection occurs either by birth or through successive births.
But for one whose mind has attained some degree of proficiency, the second [type of attainment] occurs suddenly through the self alone,
like the falling of a fruit from the sky.
In order to attain the knowledge that perceives the falling of fruits from the sky,
listen here to this ancient account which I shall relate to you.
Listen, O fortunate one, how those of great majesty, having removed the flood of obstacles consisting of former good and evil deeds, [attained liberation].
Like fruits that have fallen from the tree, those in their final birth attain supreme, stainless discernment.
This concludes the eighth chapter, titled "The Indication of the Sequence."
Vasiṣṭha said:
There was a powerful king of the Videhas named Janaka, a man of noble intellect whose every misfortune had vanished and whose prosperity was rising. MU 5.8.1
He was a wish-fulfilling tree for the caravans of supplicants, a sun for the lotuses that were his friends,
a spring for the flowers that were his kinsmen, and a god of love for women.
He was a cool-rayed moon to the night-lotuses that were the twice-born, and a sun to the darkness of his enemies.

An ocean of the jewel of benevolence, he dwelt upon the earth like Viṣṇu. Once, during the springtime— which made the young creepers blossom, was tawny with clusters of flower-buds, and caused the intoxicated cuckoos to dance with joy— *The Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, Chapter 5, Verse 8.3–4.
He went to the lovely pleasure grove, its expanse filled with blossoms and its women like graceful, swaying creepers, just as Vāsava goes to the Nandana garden;
in that delightful, excellent forest, where the breeze was fragrant with the scent of kesara flowers.
Moving as a companion from afar, he wandered through the beautiful groves. Then, in a certain thicket of *tamāla* trees, he heard words uttered by invisible *siddhas* in their own conversation.
O lotus-petal-eyed one, these songs, which consist of the contemplation of the Self, belong to those whose minds are eternally detached and who dwell in mountain caves;
through the union of the seer and the seen, there arises the certainty of the bliss of pure consciousness.
We worship that outflow arising from the reality of one's own Self;
having abandoned the seer, the seeing, and the seen, along with all latent impressions,
we worship the Self as the first manifestation of vision.

We constantly worship the Self, which is like a reflection or a mental creation, resembling a mere appearance; it is the effortless cultivation of non-existence, situated eternally between the two positions of "it exists" and "it does not exist. (MU 5.8.11)
We worship that Self which is the manifestation of all manifestations;
we worship our own Self, which shines like the letter *ha* without its head (*a*), which abides in all forms, and which is uttered incessantly.
Those who, having abandoned the Lord who dwells in the cave of the heart, go to another god,
are like those who desire a jewel while discarding the Kaustubha gem held in their own hand.
Indeed, it is by abandoning all other desires that this fruit is obtained.
By this, the root-stalks of the poisonous creepers of desire are severed.
That dull-witted man who, even after perceiving the utter insipidity of worldly objects,
again forms attachments to them, is no mere man— he is a donkey.
Again and again, one should strike down these faculties—whether they have arisen or not—with the thunderbolt of solitude, just as Indra strikes mountains with his thunderbolt.
Through the power of tranquility, the virtuous mind attains peace; that which brings about the bliss of peace is pure.
For one whose mind is stilled, there arises for a long time an excellent abiding in the bliss of one's own true nature.
The ninth chapter, named Siddhagītā.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard these songs sung by the hosts of Siddhas, the lord of the earth immediately fell into despondency, like a coward at the roar of battle.
He went toward his own home, drawing along his retinue,
like the monsoon flood following the trees on its banks as it flows toward the ocean;
having completely dismissed his retinue there, he returned to his own abode.
Alone, he ascended to the highest dwelling, like the sun upon a mountain.

Then, as restless as the wings of birds soaring upward, observing the courses of the worlds, he lamented thus in his distress: MU_5,9.4: "Then, as restless as the wings of birds soaring upward, observing the courses of the worlds, he lamented thus in his distress."

Alas, what misery! Amidst these most wretched states of worldly agitation, I am forced to wallow helplessly like one stone against another. Only some infinitesimal fraction of infinite time is lived by me.
I fix my attachment upon that; fie on me, of base mind!
How insignificant indeed is this kingdom of mine, lasting only as long as life!
Without it, why do I remain in such misery like one whose intellect is destroyed?
"I am infinite at the beginning and at the end, yet in the middle my life is fragile.
Like a child gazing at a painted moon, why do I remain here in vain, possessed of such stubborn persistence?
This world is a snare of illusion, woven by the magician’s net."
Alas, what misery! I am bewildered; by whom have I been utterly deluded?
Whatever object there is, whatever is delightful, whatever is noble and unartificial—none of that exists here at all. Upon what, then, is this resolve of mine based?
"Even that which is far away is not far when it dwells within my mind"—
having thus resolved, I abandon all mental cultivation directed toward external objects.
The state of worldly flux is as fragile as a whirlpool in water.
For even now, this attachment toward happiness is seen to lead only to suffering.
Year by year, month by month, day by day, and moment by moment,
pleasures are pierced by pain, while pains themselves recur again and again.
Repeatedly grasped, seen, questioned, and scrutinized,
there is nothing here that is not trivial upon which the virtuous may establish their abiding.
Those who today stand at the head of the great fall low within a few days.
O ruined mind, what kind of trustworthiness is this in you? (MU 5.9.15) I am bound though there is no rope; I am defiled though I am free from mud;
I have fallen even though I stand above—alas, my own self, your stability is destroyed! (MU 5.9.16)
Why has this delusion come upon me all of a sudden, even though I am wise—
like a dark cloud that obscures the light and eclipses the sun?
What are these great enjoyments of mine, and what are these my kinsmen?

I suspect that I am agitated by some cause, like a child terrified of ghosts. Why do I myself bind upon myself this state of agitation, which brings about old age and death, while seeking stability amidst worldly objects?
Whether it remains or passes away, what concern is mine regarding this prosperity?
For it has appeared thus in vain, like the fleeting beauty of a bubble.
Those great riches, those enjoyments, and those virtuous, affectionate kinsmen—
Everything that has come within the range of memory—even though it is present—is now gone; what stability can there be?
Where are the riches of the kings, and where are the worlds of the Brahmins? Those of the past have vanished; why am I so full of trust?
Millions of Indras have fallen away like bubbles upon the water;
the virtuous will laugh at me, who remain bound by hope for life. Tens of millions of Brahmās have passed away, as have the successions of world-creations.

The kings have departed like dust; what stability can there be in my life? If I continue to cling to this support—the empty delusion consisting of the body, which is a nightmare in the night of saṃsāra—then let me be cursed for such instability!
"Why have I, like an ignorant man, been struck down by this demon of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*), which has arisen in a false form and falsely claims, 'This is that very I'?
Why has my life been snatched away, snatched away by this long-lasting [delusion]?"
Even though I see it, I do not perceive it through the subtle line of Time.

While the lords of the world have been made into footstools and the wielders of the Śārṅga bow have become play-balls, you dance before me—swallowed by Time, the Kāpālika ascetic; what reliance can there be in me?
Day after day these days come and go even now;
yet, because the one truly existent reality remains undestroyed, no day has ever been seen to pass away.
These days are like cranes in a lake, present within the minds of all living beings.
Only enjoyments flash within me; I have no vision of even a single void-state.
Having reached what is more miserable than misery, having gone from sorrow to greater sorrow, even now I am not dispassionate—alas, shame on me, whose disposition is base! (MU 5.9.30–31)
Whatever firm attachments one has toward solid objects, those very things are seen to perish; what, then, is supreme in this world?
That which is pleasing in the middle, at the end, and at the first encounter—[is it not all the same?]
All that is indeed impure, defiled by the impurity of decay.
In whatever objects a person fixes his attachment, in those very things a swift and intense arising of suffering is seen for him. (MU 5.9.33–34)
Day after day, the dull-witted person here reaches a state that is ever more evil, ever more cruel, and ever more distressing;
struck by ignorance in childhood, he is smitten by passion in youth.

Afflicted by anxiety for his wife and children, what can that dull-witted man ever do? Why does my mind not perceive this worldly existence— tasteless due to the coming and going of things, corrupted by the inequality of conditions, and possessing only a semblance of essence while lacking true substance?
Even by performing hundreds of sacrifices such as the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha,
one attains heaven for some portion of a great kalpa, but nothing more.
What region is there in heaven, on earth, or in the netherworld that exceeds this?

Where these calamities do not rush in like ill-behaved bees— how indeed can these mental anxieties and physical diseases, which are serpents lurking in the hollows of one’s own mind and sprouting from the foliage of the body, be warded off?
Non-existence stands at the summit of truth; lack of delight stands at the summit of delights;
sorrows stand at the summit of pleasures. To which single one among these should I resort?
Common, lowly creatures are born and they die.
The earth was made dense by those very [beings], yet truly virtuous men are difficult to find.
(MU 5.9.42) With eyes like blue lotuses and adorned with supreme love, these playful women exist only for the sake of laughter, being subject to momentary destruction. (MU 5.9.43)
Those by whose closing and opening of their eyes the dissolution and emergence of the worlds occur—such persons have passed away; what need is there to count those like me?
There are things more beautiful than the beautiful, and more stable than the stable.
Is the splendor of these objects of the senses truly such as this, when they result only in anxiety?
And as for those various prosperities— if they are approved by the mind,
I consider them to be surely great calamities despite their grand undertakings.
If even those various calamities are regarded as agreeable by the mind,
then I consider them too to be great undertakings and complete successes.
For in this world, which is a mere transformation of the mind and as fragile as a drop of water, [all things are but mental constructs].
Whence comes this unprecedented string of syllables "this is mine"? When the stability of the world has come about by mere chance, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit,
these notions of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted have been vainly devised by a rogue.
Amidst these visions called "pleasure," which are limited in form and extent—
to what such things am I attached, like a moth to the flames of a fire?
It would be better to wallow in the fires of Raurava, where there is constant burning.
But stability does not exist within the processes of saṃsāra, which are neither cut nor shattered.
Saṃsāra itself is said to be the very limit of sufferings;
how, then, can happiness be found by one fallen into its midst?
Those who dwell in this cycle of existence, which is characterized by uncreated and great suffering,
perceive other sufferings as merely tolerable sweetness. Even I, though afflicted by mental anguish, am like wood or a clod of earth compared to those who remain thus.

Thus it has reached equality with the ignorant, who have not perceived the true reality. Of this tree of saṃsāra, which abounds in thousands of sprouts, branches, fruits, and shoots, the root is the mind.
I consider that [tree] to be nothing but volition; by the cessation of volition, I shall wither it away so that the tree of saṃsāra reaches its end.
Amidst the activities of the monkey-mind, which are charming only in their outward form, [I shall bring about this drying up].
Having fully understood them even today, I no longer delight in these insipid things.
Pierced by hundreds of snares of hope, and bringing the affliction of repeated falls and rises, I have experienced the cycles of worldly existence; now I shall desist.
"Alas, I am struck down! I am ruined! I am dead!"—thus I lamented again and again.
But now that I have gone [beyond this], I do not weep;
I am awakened, I am joyful, for I have seen the thief of my self.
"I shall slay this one called 'mind,' for I have long been slain by the mind. "For all this time, this pearl of my mind remained unpierced; now it has been pierced and is fit for the string."
The frost-like speck of my mind will surely soon dissolve through the heat of the sun of discernment for the sake of my long-lasting liberation;
I have been well awakened by the wise, the virtuous, and the perfected ones.
I follow after the Self, which is the means to supreme bliss.
Having found the jewel that is the Self in solitude and beholding it with joy,
I remain here, with all other things set at rest, like a cloudless autumn sky.

Having forcibly cast out from within the false flickering of "I am this" and "this is mine," I slay my exceedingly defiled enemy, the mind, and attain tranquility; homage be to you, O Discrimination! This concludes the chapter named "Janaka’s Reflection."
The Tenth Canto: Vasiṣṭha.
While he was thus reflecting, [Vasiṣṭha] entered before him.
The doorkeeper [spoke] at dawn, like Aruṇa ascending to the front of the Sun’s chariot:
"O Lord, upon whom the entire burden of the earth rests, supported by Your pillar-like arms!"
"Complete and then rise for the daily duties appropriate for a king.
These women, with jars of water containing flowers, camphor, and saffron,
stand ready in the bathing area like personified rivers."
This lotus pond, its groves of day-lotuses and night-lotuses frequented by wandering bees,
has been fashioned for the sake of women, with pavilions constructed from woven cloth. These grounds on the banks of the lotus pond are filled with parasols.
With fly-whisks, chariots, elephants, and horses, for those attending upon you at the time of your ablutions;
with caskets filled with every kind of flower and overflowing with gems and medicinal herbs— the grounds for your worship of the gods have been made ready.

O God, this assembly of twice-born men, having bathed, with purifying grass in their hands, and having recited the *aghamarṣaṇa* mantra, gazes only upon you— you who are worthy of sacrificial fees. O Supreme Lord,
they are protected by women holding waving chowries in their hands.
"The cool dining areas have been prepared by the lovely women;
rise quickly, may it be well with you, and perform your duty without fail.
Great men do not let the proper time pass for their own tasks."
When the lord of the doorkeepers had spoken thus,
the king likewise reflected upon the wondrous nature of worldly existence:
"How small indeed is this thing called the happiness of sovereignty!"
I have no need here for this which is subject to momentary destruction.
Having abandoned all false pomp and agitation,
I shall remain in solitude alone, like a completely stilled ocean.
Enough with these mostly worthless expansions of my enjoyments;
having abandoned all activities, I shall remain happily and alone.
O mind, this cleverness [of yours] arises from this agitation caused by the habituation to enjoyments.
Abandon [the mind] for the sake of pacifying the mire of the snare of dullness caused by birth and old age. O mind, in whichever states you perceive agitation,
by becoming utterly detached from those very states, you shall attain supreme bliss.
Whether engaged in worldly activity or withdrawn from it, again and again, for a long time and over a long duration,
your mind finds no satisfaction in any of the realms of enjoyment. Therefore, enough of this trivial preoccupation with enjoyments.
"By which an unartificial satisfaction arises, one rushes toward that which is spread out"—
having reflected thus, Janaka became silent indeed;
with his restless mind stilled, he was like a figure depicted in a painting.
Out of respect and fear, the doorkeeper did not speak again a word that was unfamiliar to the mental dispositions of kings; then,
having remained silent for a moment, Janaka [addressed] the life of men.
Again, he reflected with a mind established in tranquility:
"What is there in this world that is worth acquiring which I should strive to accomplish? Upon what object, free from destruction, shall I fix my steadfastness?"
What is the use of being intent on action, or even of being inactive?
For there is nothing that has arisen which is not subject to destruction. Whether this body possesses action or is devoid of action, it has originated from what is unreal.
What loss indeed can there be for me, who am eternal, stable, pure, and consciousness? (MU 5.10.23) I do not long for what has not been attained, nor do I abandon what has been attained.
Abiding in the self which is established in itself, let that which belongs to me remain mine. (MU 5.10.24)
I have no purpose here with what is done, nor any at all with what is not done;
for that which is to be attained by action or inaction—whether existent or non-existent—is nothing to one who is truly existent.
Whether I am acting or not acting, my actions are neither fit nor unfit.
There is nothing here that is desired which has attained the state of being worth adopting.
Therefore, let this body rise and perform its natural activity as it has sequentially arrived;
for what will it accomplish while its limbs remain motionless?
When the mind is steady, free from desire, equanimous, and devoid of passion,
the activity and inactivity of the bodily parts regarding their respective effects are equal in their results.
Thus, the mind’s status as both agent and enjoyer pertains to the glorious fruits born of action.
When that [distraction] has subsided, even what was done by men is as if undone.
The firm resolve that is rooted within a person regarding their actions attains identity with that [inner state].
My intellect has reached the state free from affliction; I shall completely cast away internal instability.
The eleventh canto, titled "Janaka’s Resolve," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having reflected thus, Janaka rose to perform the duties as they presented themselves,
remaining unattached like the sun at the beginning of the day;
he himself abandoned all mental impressions of the pleasant and the unpleasant by means of his own mind.
Having performed whatever duties were required for that day, preceded by the winning over of the noble ones, he remained awake as if in deep sleep;
then, alone, he passed the night in the very same manner, through the play of meditation.
Having made the mind equanimous and stilled the wandering toward sense objects,
he awakened his consciousness in this way as the night was fading away:
"O mind, your restless expansion is not for your own well-being."
"Come to peace, my dear; having attained the essence of happiness through tranquility, [you shall find rest].
To whatever extent you effortlessly conceive a flood of mental constructions, O little mind, to that same extent does this cycle of existence expand for you."
Just as a tree attains a hundred branches through watering, so too,
O rogue, do you attain endless mental afflictions through the desire for enjoyment. These creations of the cycle of existence arise from the play of the web of thoughts.
Therefore, having abandoned these various anxieties, attain tranquility. O handsome one, weigh this flickering creation of saṃsāra;
if you find its essence, then resort to it alone.
Abandoning all reliance on this visible world, O you who yearn for the vision [of reality], do not grasp at it, nor let it go; wander with a pure desire.
Whether this visible world be unreal or real, let it arise or let it set.
O virtuous one, fall into a state of helplessness; do not be affected by its qualities or defects.
There is not even the slightest connection between you and the object of perception, which exists only in appearance.
Indeed, what kind of connection can there be with that which has no real form?

This [relation] is non-existent, and it is not existent; for there can be no relation between two things that are both non-existent or both existent—this is a most wonderful and unprecedented string of syllables! If this non-existent thing becomes existent, even so, O handsome one, it is indeed [a marvel].

Tell me, what kind of attachment can there be between the existent and the non-existent, or between the dead and the living? O mind, if both you and the object of perception were truly real and eternally established, from where would the outburst of joy and sorrow arise?

Therefore, O fortunate one, do not be deluded; do not indulge in exultation. Abide in an undisturbed intellect and abandon the state of worldly existence, which burns pointlessly within oneself like a firebrand made of *tinduka* wood.
O evil-minded one, do not fall into dullness by encountering the impurity of delusion!
There is nothing here that is so exalted and supreme by which you might attain ultimate perfection;
therefore, O rogue mind, relying with force upon extreme fortitude, abandon your fickleness!
The twelfth canto, titled "Instruction on the Mind," by Vasiṣṭha.
Reflecting thus while there in his own kingdom, King Janaka performed all his duties and, being of steady intellect, was not deluded;
his mind did not leap forth toward any objects of worldly pleasure.
He remained forever established solely in that which is perfectly even and pure.
From that time forward, he neither grasped at the visible world nor abandoned it;
rather, he abided in the present, entirely free from doubt.
Then, by means of that mind which was constantly engaged in discernment,
he did not again take on any stain, just as the sky does not take on the darkness of night.
This was due to that lord of the earth’s continuous application of his own discernment.
Right knowledge, possessing infinite luster, attained purity within his mind.
The conscious self (cidātman), free from disease and with its portions of conceptual construction unpolished,
arose in the space of his heart like the sun in the sky.
He, whose self is infinite and who knows the self of all beings, saw all phenomena spread out like gems upon the loom of the mind as being identical with himself;
he was never elated, nor did he ever become distressed.
Because he engaged in worldly affairs as they naturally occurred, his mind remained always equanimous;
from that time forward, O giver of honor, Janaka became one liberated while living,
possessing mature wisdom and knowing the higher and lower realms of the world.
While ruling the kingdom of the Videhas, Janaka, the life of his people,
was not at all tormented by joy or sorrow, being no longer subject to them;
free from both virtue and vice, he neither sets nor rises.
He neither desponds nor exults because of gains or losses arising from his own kingdom;
even while acting, he does nothing at all anywhere,
since he always remains established in the state of one liberated while living.
Like King Janaka while he was in the state of deep sleep,
all mental constructions had completely set for him with respect to all existing things;
he did not pursue what was to come, nor did he dwell upon the past.
Even while remaining in the present moment, he stands as if laughing;
O lotus-eyed Rāma, by the power of his own inquiry alone, he has attained everything that is to be attained in its entirety, and not through any other desire.
To whatever extent the limit of all investigations is reached, to that same extent it is investigated by one’s own mind alone;
that state is not attained through a teacher, nor from the meaning of the scriptures, nor through merit.
O Rāma, that state which is reached through the company of the virtuous, when the heart has become clear through inquiry arising therefrom,
is attained by means of one’s own innate, affectionate, and straightforward wisdom alone,
and not indeed by any other action.
Blindness never pursues that person whose flame of the lamp of wisdom burns with a sharp point, moving across both the past and the future.
Those calamities which are difficult to overcome and crowded with waves of suffering—
O Mahāmati, one crosses over those [difficulties] by means of wisdom, just as one crosses over waters by means of a boat.
Even a slight misfortune afflicts a fool who is devoid of wisdom,
just as even a faint breeze shakes a sapless tuft of grass.
Even if he is without companions, lacks instruction, and is abandoned by others, one possessed of wisdom crosses over the ocean of saṃsāra like a boat, O Rāma; even without assistance,
the wise person reaches the end of their task.
One who lacks wisdom perishes even when undertaking a task of the highest importance.
Therefore, one should first increase one's wisdom through the study of scriptures and association with the virtuous,
just as one nurtures a creeper for the sake of obtaining fruit by means of watering, protecting, and tending it.
The tree of one's true purpose, with its vast root of the power of wisdom, bears fruit that is exceedingly sweet in due time, like the lunar disc in the month of Māsa. Indeed,
the very same effort that men exert in acquiring external objects [is applied to this].

That very effort should first be applied toward the increase of wisdom. One should avoid the dullness of wisdom, which is the ultimate limit of all sufferings, the supreme treasury of calamities, and the seed of the trees of saṃsāra.
Whatever is obtained from heaven, whatever from the netherworld, and whatever is acquired from a kingdom—
all that is attained, O Great-minded One, from the treasury of wisdom. By means of wisdom, one crosses over this terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
O Rāghava, neither by conduct, nor by sacred fords,
nor even by austerity do men dwelling on earth attain that divine prosperity which has arisen as the sweet fruit of the creeper whose flowers are wisdom.
By means of wisdom, those who drank the blood of wild elephants torn apart by their claws have defeated lions with jackals,
just as lions [overcome] deer;
even the status of a king has been attained by men through the power of wisdom, even if they were commoners.
In this world, the capacity for heaven and liberation is seen to belong only to the wise man.
All disputants, sporting with their own conceptual constructions,
overcome [their opponents] like the roar of the ocean over the cries of the Sugata, just as thunder over the calls of birds.
This wisdom is a wish-fulfilling gem for the discerning person, residing within the treasury of the heart;
like a celestial kalpa-creeper, it bestows the fruit of whatever is desired.
Through wisdom, the fortunate one crosses over saṃsāra, while the base one is carried away by it.

The trained one reaches the further shore; the untrained one perishes with the boat. Intellect, when properly directed, leads a man to the further shore; when improperly directed, it carries him through the cycle of existence like a boat on the ocean.
Defects arising from the multitude of desires do not afflict the discerning, unconfused, and wise man, just as arrows do not strike one who is well-armored.
My dear, by means of wisdom, this entire world is seen exactly as it is.
Neither misfortunes nor successes come to one who possesses right vision. The vast, dark cloud of egoism— the dull-natured veil over the supreme sun— is shattered by me through the wind of wisdom.
By one who desires to attain that incomparable state, this very intellect must first be nurtured;
for surely, by a farmer seeking to harvest the fruit, the ground itself is tilled first.
The Chapter entitled "The Majesty of Wisdom."
The Thirteenth Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, having thus investigated the self by means of the self, just as Janaka did, [you shall attain liberation].
You shall, before long, attain the station of those who have known what is to be known.
For those wise men of royal birth who are in their final incarnation attain by themselves that which is to be attained, just as Janaka did.
One should strive to conquer those enemies known as the senses to such an extent that this Self,
by means of the self, becomes serene within the self alone;
when the all-pervading God, the Lord of gods, the Supreme Self, is serene.
When [reality] is perceived by oneself, all views of suffering are exhausted;
the handfuls of seeds of delusion and the rains of various calamities—
those false views come to an end when that which is both supreme and non-supreme is seen.
O Rāma, like Janaka always, with a self that undertakes all [proper] activities,
having perceived the Self through wisdom, become prosperous and supreme.
For one who has constantly adopted inquiry and observes people as fickle, [there is no attachment].

In time, one’s own self becomes serene of its own accord, just as it did for Janaka. Neither fate, nor ritual actions, nor wealth, nor kinsmen provide refuge for men terrified by worldly existence, except through their own effort.
O dear one, those who are devoted to fate and intent upon such false conceptualizations as ritual action— their intellect is dull and perishable, and it cannot be followed.
Having resorted to supreme discernment, one should perceive the Self by means of the self.
With an intellect steadfast in dispassion, one should cross the ocean of saṃsāra.
O Rāma, this attainment of knowledge, which bestows happiness and uproots the tree of ignorance, has been described as being like the falling of fruit from the sky.
Like that of Janaka, who possessed true wisdom and was himself a man of discernment,
this embodied soul, being a god, attains full expansion like a lotus at dawn. Through inquiry, the mind, its mental fluctuations stilled, dissolves away.
Just as snow loses its color, form, and texture when struck by the sun, so too,
when the night of the notion "I am this" has dawned upon its destruction,
the all-pervading, expansive light of one's own self proceeds forth.
When this contraction of "I am this very one" has dissolved,
an expansion pervading infinite worlds arises;
just as the latent impression of egoism was abandoned by Janaka.
In the same way, O one of noble intellect, reflect within yourself and renounce [the ego].
When the cloud of egoism has perished, the stainless supreme sun of self-luminosity truly becomes manifest in the pure sky of consciousness.
The cultivation of the sense of "I" is nothing but profound darkness;
when that has subsided, illumination arises.
It is cultivated thus: "I do not exist, nor does another exist, nor is it the case that [anything] does not exist."

When the mind has attained tranquility, it does not sink into things that are to be grasped. O Rāma, know that this—the mind’s pursuit of what is to be acquired and its absolute avoidance of what is to be abandoned—is bondage, and nothing else. (MU 5.13.19–20)
Do not indulge in grief regarding things to be abandoned; do not be intent on things to be accepted.
Having abandoned the views of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, remain established in the remainder and attain self-abiding peace.
For those who maintain the position that "this is to be accepted" and "this is to be rejected," [there is no liberation].
Once dissolved, they desire nothing and do not renounce anything here, nor do others [cling].
As long as the mental calculation of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted has not ceased in the mind,
equanimity does not shine forth, just as moonlight does not appear in a cloudy sky.
When the mind is agitated by the thought, "This is non-existent" and "This is existent," equanimity does not arise therein, just as a flower-cluster does not appear on a withered tree.
Where there is the desire for what is appropriate and inappropriate, and which revels in gain and loss...
In that state, how could equanimity and purity—which cause the cessation of all longing—be absent?
While this single, stainless reality of Brahman exists, why is there the constant appearance of manifoldness? Wherein lies irrationality, and wherein lies rationality?
I suspect that on the tree of the mind there are two restless female monkeys, longing for what is desired and fearing what is undesired;
since they leap about therein, how can there be gentleness in it?
Freedom from desire, fearlessness, permanence, equanimity, and wisdom—[these belong to one who has cast them off].
Freedom from effort, inactivity, gentleness, and non-conceptuality; fortitude, friendliness, mindfulness, contentment, joy, and softness of speech—
these qualities belong to the wise man who is free from the notions of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, and to whom women go when they are in love.
One should forcibly withdraw the mind as it runs downward toward sense-objects,
just as water falling down is held back by a dam through the practice of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*).
Having abandoned these external objects, one remains— whether standing, walking, sleeping, or breathing.
In every way and at all times, one should ward off all internal [impurities].
The turbid web of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which has grasped the fish of craving,
has spread through the waters of *saṃsāra* and is stretched out with the threads of anxiety.
O dear one, cut through this with this sharp probe of wisdom,
just as the wind cuts through a cloud as it blows across the vast expanse of space.
This is the root of the tree of saṃsāra, the seat from which the sprouts of defects arise.
With steadfastness as firm as a draft-ox and with an intellect uplifted by fortitude,
having severed the mind with the mind itself and forgotten the final mind,
and having severed even the present mind, attain the state of one whose saṃsāra is destroyed.
When delusion has been forgotten, one does not grow again in saṃsāra.
Whether standing, walking, breathing, O Rāma, dwelling, rising, or falling,
having internally resolved that "this is indeed unreal," abandon all attachment.
Relying fully on equanimity, performing the duties that have arrived,
and not thinking of those not yet attained, dwell here indeed, O Rāghava;
just as a tree neither holds nor rejects the signs of all seasons.
O sinless one, perform your duties here as you see fit, or do not perform them;
you alone are the knower, you are the unborn, you are the Self, you are the Great Lord.
This reality, which is non-different from the Self, has been spread out and pervaded by you.
He who has abandoned all mental cultivation regarding this entire mass of visible objects from every side is not seized by the defects born of joy, resentment, and despondency;
he is liberated from passion and hatred, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal.
The yogi who has abandoned the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of cyclic existence is said to be "liberated.
Whatever he does, whatever he eats, whatever he gives, or whatever he destroys— therein,
for him whose mind is liberated, there is equanimity toward pleasure and pain.
Having abandoned the cultivation of likes and dislikes, one who proceeds toward duties with the conviction that "only what has come to pass must be done" does not sink anywhere.
The mind possessed of the certainty that "this world is merely the existence of consciousness" [is liberated].
O Mahāmati, when the conceit of enjoyment is abandoned, the mind attains tranquility; for the mind, being insentient by its very nature, pursues the principle of consciousness (cittattva),
just as a cat, out of greed for meat, pursues a lion in the forest.
For just as a jackal eats meat obtained through the power of a lion’s prowess,

so does the mind resort to the visible world obtained through the power of the vigor of consciousness (*cid-vīrya*). Thus, the mind— which is like a mere mental construction— subsists by the grace of consciousness.
Cultivating the one consciousness alone and having attained that very consciousness, even from this state, how could the mind—
which is indeed inert, devoid of consciousness, and abandoned by the lamp of awareness— arise as something insentient, resembling a corpse?
The power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*), which consists of wind and is touched by the essential nature of consciousness (*citsvabhāva*),

is described by those who perceive the scriptures as "mind" (*citta*) through the term "differentiation" (*kalanā*). Whatever agitated form belongs to consciousness, that very thing is called this "differentiation."
Having realized "I am consciousness alone," she goes to that very consciousness.
That consciousness which is devoid of an object of thought is the eternal Brahman;
that same consciousness, when accompanied by an object of thought, is called "mental construction" (kalana).
That Brahman which exists in an indistinct form is the mind;
having attained the state of non-existence through its own conceptualization, it appears as if existent within the heart.
When this conceptualization of consciousness becomes established here as "mind" (citta), [it arises].

At that very moment, having forgotten her consciousness, she remained as if inert. She became known as "Kalanā" (the Power of Thought-Construction), following after volitional constructs; she became possessed of differentiation and subject to the qualities of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted.
This very consciousness, as it were, having attained a state of insentience through its own power,
does not perceive its true form as long as it has not been awakened.
Therefore, [it is awakened] by means of scriptural inquiry, supreme detachment, and [the grace of the teacher].
By restraining the senses, one should personally awaken from conceptual construction (kalanā).
Through discernment and tranquility, the conceptual construction of all beings becomes awakened and attains the state of Brahman; otherwise, it wanders as the world.
One should awaken the mental construction (kalana) which is intoxicated by the wine of delusion, wallowing in the pit of sense objects,
and fast asleep regarding the realization of the Self;
for as long as it is unawakened and inert, it perceives nothing at all.
Though appearing within like a playful mental construction, it is composed of unreality.
By that supreme vision abiding within,
this creative ideation shines forth among all things, just as the power of fragrance manifests in flower clusters.
But this "calculation" (kalanā) which has been conceptualized throughout the three worlds—does it truly perceive anything? For it possesses the sole characteristic of eternal insentience.
Where indeed could an insentient calculation, which is like a stone, be conscious?
Like a lotus-pond awakened by the intense heat of the sun, this [intellect] is awakened only by another.
Just as a maiden made of stone does not dance even when urged,
so this mental activity in the body does not perceive anything at all.
Where was a battle with a gurgling roar ever waged by kings against mere painters?
Where were medicinal herbs ever awakened by the rays of variegated moonbeams?
Or where did corpses, their limbs possessed by spirits, ever leap about?
Where is the sweet-sounding song [performed] by the circles of forest stones?
Where is the darkness of the night dispelled by suns fashioned from books?
And where are shadows created by sky-forests consisting of mere mental constructs?
Where can action be performed by these minds— which are as dull as stones, arisen from a mass of false delusions, and consisting of a mirage?
Just as when the vast heat of the sun persists, there appears a river of mirage-water.
In this very same way, this kalanā manifests sufficiently within the Self while it exists.
O Rāma, know that this vibration of the mind which has been gradually perceived is the power of the winds residing within the body as the vital breaths.
This consciousness which is unassailed by the determinations of even a fragment of volition,
and whose nature and flavor are not projected [by objects], is this supreme self-luminous light.
That conceptualization which persists as "this is he," "I am that," or "this is mine"— [it is this consciousness].
The designation of that [intellect] as the self of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is called "the living soul" (*jīva*).

Intellect (*dhī*), mind (*citta*), and "living soul" (*jīva*)—these are conceptual designations imagined for the unreal mental construction (*saṅkalpa*), whether it be existent or non-existent; they are not so in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), O Rāma, according to those who know that [reality].
There is neither mind, nor intellect, nor even a living soul, nor a physical body here in the ultimate sense; only one's own Self exists here at all times.
This entire world is the Self alone, as is the succession of time.
It is clearer than eternal space; it neither exists nor does it not exist, yet it is indeed stainless.
Because of its clarity, it appears as non-existent, yet it is existent by virtue of its nature as pure consciousness.
The Self, which transcends all states, is experienced through one's own direct experience.
The mind is completely exhausted where there is the consciousness of the Supreme Self;
where there is the destruction of darkness, there light prevails.
Where there is even a slight inclination toward conceptualization within the pure consciousness of the Self, [there remains a trace of duality].
In that state, there is the forgetting of the self and the remembering of the birth of the mind.
The mind is said to consist of the volitions of the Supreme Person;
through the absence of volition, the state of "no-mind" arises, which is known by the name of liberation.
Such is the birth of the mind, the seed of the tree of saṃsāra:

namely, that the consciousness of the Self becomes oriented toward conceptual construction (saṅkalpa). The existence of the non-conceptualizing mind becomes stained by the mark of conceptual construction.
It is called "time" here; the mind does not exist as a separate entity like a jar. When the power of the vital breath (prāṇa-śakti) is restrained, that which is called the mind dissolves.
For the mental substance exists within the substance of the vital breath itself.
The vital breath (prāṇa), situated within the heart, perceives the experience of other places;
that which [perceives] this through the sensation of vibration is designated as the mind (manas).
Through dispassion, the practice of the instruments [of yoga], logical reasoning, and the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā)— MU 5.13.83–84ab.
And through the awakening to the ultimate reality, the powers of the vital breaths are obstructed.
(MU 5.13.84) Just as stones possess the power to consume food at times, the mind does not possess the power to perceive its own vibration. (MU 5.13.85)

Vibration (*spanda*) is the power of the vital breath (*prāṇa-maru*), and it is essentially mobile and insentient (*jaḍa*). Consciousness (*cit*), however, is the consciousness of one's own self; it is established in its own nature, eternally all-pervading.
The mind (*manas*) is conceived as the connection between the power of consciousness and the power of vibration.
That which has arisen as something false is called false knowledge (mithyājñāna).
This is indeed declared to be ignorance (avidyā); it is called illusion (māyā).
This is that supreme nescience (ajñāna) which bestows the poison of the higher world of saṃsāra.

If the conceptualization of mental constructs (*saṅkalpa*) is not performed through association with the power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*) and the power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*), then these fears of worldly existence (*bhava-bhīti*) are utterly destroyed.
When that power of vibration, which is inseparable from consciousness, is perceived by consciousness itself, [then fear ceases].
If consciousness is perceived as having an object, it immediately becomes "mind" (citta) due to that mental construction (saṅkalpa).
This state of being mind is falsely imagined within consciousness, like a ghost imagined by a child;
for consciousness itself is the reality of vibration, whose form is an undivided circle.
Since consciousness is all-pervading, with what else indeed could it be connected?
With whom could Indra, whose power is indivisible, have a conflict?
Thus, due to the absence of a correlate, no connection exists here.
Without a connection, for whom is that mind established, and of what nature is it? If there were identity between consciousness and its vibration, what indeed could be called the "mind"?
What is an army without the gathering together of a multitude of horses and elephants?
Therefore, there is indeed no such thing as a "corrupt self" within the three worlds;
the destruction of the mind arises from its thorough and correct understanding. O sinless one, do not thus conceive such harmful intentions in your mind in vain.
The mind arises falsely; it does not exist at all from the perspective of ultimate reality.
O Mahāmati, do not form any conceptualization whatsoever within;
for that which is called the "conceptualizing mind" does not exist anywhere here.
O Sage, through right perception, the mirage of conceptual construction— which arose from incorrect knowledge— has been completely stilled within the desert of your heart;
for the mind is always dead, being inert and devoid of intrinsic nature.
The world is killed by that which is dead; strange indeed is this wheel of folly!
(MU 5.13.99) He who has neither self nor body, neither a support nor a source—by him all this is devoured; strange indeed is this snare of ignorance! (MU 5.13.100)
If one is struck even by the mind of someone who lacks all [mental] faculties,
I think his head would shatter from blows with lotus petals;
for he is one who has been slain even mentally by one who is dull-witted, mute, and blind.
I think that fool is being burned by the rays of the full moon.
For the world overcomes one who exists as a hero;
this [world] slays only that which does not exist—therefore, delusion has arisen.

Composed of false conceptualization and existing only as a falsehood, it is not seen even when sought; what power, indeed, can it possess? Oh, how truly wondrous is this creator of illusory phenomena!

Since the world is overcome even by a mind that is excessively fickle, folly is the ultimate end of all calamities; for what calamity does not exist for the ignorant? Behold, through folly this creation is brought forth even by one who is unborn.
"Alas, what a pity! This creation is utterly deluded, having fallen under the sway of folly, since it is tormented even by this unreal life-force.
I consider this creation to be composed of fools and exceedingly fragile."
It is shattered into fragments by the stroke of a sword-like wave;
it is torn asunder by the fall of a blue lotus stalk as if by a mechanical device;
and it faints at the touch of the rays of the full-orbed moon.

He is bound by the enemy’s gaze released from their eyes, like threads of sight; he is overcome by the army of his own volitions (*saṅkalpa*). For it is said that this [army] is not held back by a mind that remains fixed anywhere.
One is vainly afflicted by another who is imagined, wretched, and miserable.
This creation consisting of the world of fools arises from the mind itself as something unreal;
that which is unable to bring [the mind] under control is not taught by Rāma.
Noble by nature, she is not capable of the subtle impact of wisdom;
she is not fit for the words of instruction, remaining as if perfectly complete in herself. Indeed, she fears even the slender sound of the strings of a lute.
Even toward a friend who is asleep, she fears the radiance of his face;
even from a person laughing loudly, she flees in utter terror.
This ignorance, it is said, has rendered her helpless, even by her own mind.
Overpowered by a mere fragment of pleasure, as if scorched by her own heart dwelling within her like an enemy, her intellect is distressed;
utterly deluded, she vainly fails to understand that truth which is unmistakable.
The Chapter titled "The Restraint of the Mind" (Manonivāraṇa).
The Fourteenth Canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Being carried away by the insubstantial waves of the ocean of worldly existence, [she...]
That people have conquered their own mind so that it is no longer mute— this [conquest],
which has as its noble fruit the attainment of the Self,
is not taught here in this treatise by means of these discursive explanations. (MU 5.14.1–2)

Indeed, what person of evil mind would show a forest variegated with diverse blossoms to one who is blind and does not see at all? Or who [would show it] to one whose nose is wheezing from leprosy, when it comes to discerning various fragrances?

A fool of little intelligence makes himself the authority for his own instruction. Who would take as an authority a person of dull wit whose senses are perverted, who is intoxicated, and whose eyes roll from the effects of liquor, to serve as a witness in the determination of dharma?
What rogue would ask a corpse lying in a cemetery about the method of debate? And who indeed instructs a fool when there is doubt?
For by such means, one remains unconquered even if one is mute and blind, staying within the cave of one's own disposition.
How indeed can that evil-minded one be instructed, he who is a wild beast of the mind?
Know that the mind is already conquered in reality because it does not exist;
that which does not exist at all, such as a stone in the vicinity, has long since ceased to be.
O Rāma, he by whom the mind—which though non-existent—is not conquered due to his evil intellect, dies from the stupor of poison as if having swallowed actual venom.
The Knower always perceives the Self; it is the powers of knowledge that vibrate.
What is called "mind" (manas) among the senses and their respective functions?
The power of the vital breaths (prāṇas) is vibration, while the power of the Supreme Self is consciousness;
since the senses possess their own inherent powers, who here is bound?
And since all powers belong to that Self who is indeed omnipotent,
from where could this distinction or otherness possibly arise?
What indeed is called the "individual soul" (jīva), by which the world here has been rendered blind?
Know that the mind itself is non-existent; what power can it possibly have?
Having seen the succession of sufferings of those whose vision has been consumed by the mind, my intellect, overcome with compassion, O Rama, suffers like one who is deluded.
Who indeed here, and from what cause, would feel distress, since it is only the fool who suffers?
For common people and the like are born only for the sake of suffering;
likewise, the unintelligent are born within dull bodies only for their own destruction.
Like bubbles in the oceans, they rise and perish without ceasing.
Behold, how many animals are slaughtered every day in every region by those who act like butchers; what cause for lamentation is there in this?
The wind daily destroys tumors in the thickets of *kṣupa* plants;
there are gadflies and mosquitoes—what lamentation can there be in this?
In every direction, among the great mountains and in forest after forest, there are multitudes of *pulinda* tribes.
Hundreds of thousands of living beings are being slain; what lamentation can there be in this?
(MU 5.14.19) A large fish daily devours a multitude of small aquatic creatures for its meal; what lamentation can there be in this? (MU 5.14.20)
Vultures, hawks, and other flocks of birds constantly prey upon the multitude of creatures in the sky; what lamentation can there be in this?
A fly, emaciated by hunger, devours a nit as small as a grain of dust.
The hungry silkworm eats that gnat, and the restless wasp eats the gnat;
the frog devours that wasp, and the serpent devours the frog;
the fierce donkey kills the serpent, and the mongoose tears that donkey to pieces.
The cat kills the mongoose; the dog tears apart the cat;
the bear kills the dog; the tiger tears apart the bear.
The lion overcomes the tiger, and the *śarabha* devours the lion.
The *śarabha* perishes when leaping over a rutting cloud;
clouds are dispersed by winds, winds are overcome by mountains,
mountains are crushed by the thunderbolt, and the thunderbolt is subject to the will of Śakra.
Indra is supported by Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu enters the state of a living being,
garlanded by birth, old age, and death, and possessed of the conditions of pleasure and pain.
Even those beings who possess massive bodies and are equipped with the weapons of knowledge [are likewise subject to this].
For indeed, they subsist upon the lice clinging to their limbs;
thus, this forest of living beings is constantly being torn apart and shattered.
Out of delusion, they are sufficiently consumed by one another, and likewise protected.
Various kinds of living beings perish incessantly,
and diverse beings are born incessantly in every direction.
Fish, elephants, sea-monsters, and others are born within the reservoirs of water.
Swarms of insects, scorpions, and the like are born within the earth;
birds and the like are born in the atmosphere and in the sky;
lions, tigers, deer, and the like are born in the forest paths.
Lice, ticks, and ants are born even from the limbs of living beings;
and species such as wood-boring insects and pythons are born among stationary things.
Within stones, insects, frogs, wood-borers, and the like are born.
Likewise, various swarms of insects are born even in excrement.
Thus, throughout countless other births and degradations,
may those who possess compassion feel either joy or distress incessantly.

In this incessant whirlpool of saṃsāra, which arises without ceasing during the seasons that flow without end, there is neither contentment nor sorrow for those who are thus engaged. Indeed, these very rows [of beings] are like the clusters of leaves upon a tree.
Arising again and again, the abundant births of living beings dissolve away.
He who, out of compassion, has set himself to wipe away the suffering of the foolish,
comes to great exhaustion, like one who rubs the rays of the sun with his hand and umbrella.
Men on this earth do not possess the same nature as animals;
what purpose is served by speaking words to one who is as motionless as a tree trunk in a dense forest?
What indeed is the distinction between those whose minds are intent on leaping about and the beasts?
Those of deluded mind are dragged along by the rope of their own thoughts, like cattle.
Seeing the calamity of fools who are submerged in the mud of their own minds and whose very selves are fashioned from the fragments of their own desires, even stones weep.
For those who have not conquered their own minds, there are infinite heaps of suffering;
therefore, one who has perfected wisdom does not engage in that cleansing.
O descendant of Raghu, for those who have conquered their own minds, sufferings [no longer exist].
Therefore, let him who has known what is to be known proceed here, for [the objects] are impossible to avoid. O mighty-armed one, the mind does not exist; do not vainly imagine this.
By imagining it, you are being struck down as if by a Vetāla spirit.

O subduer of enemies, as long as you remained forgetful of the reality of the self and were deluded, so long did the serpent of your mind remain aroused. Now, however, it has been understood by you exactly as it is.
The mind grows from conceptualization; therefore, abandon that very thing quickly.
If you take refuge in this visible world, then you possess a mind and are bound;
if you renounce this visible world, then you are without mind and are liberated.
This collection of qualities is relied upon solely for bondage;
it is abandoned alone for the sake of liberation. Do as you wish.
Meditating that "I am not this, nor is this mine," remain unmoving like a mountain.
The Lord of the Heart, whose heart resembles infinite space—
O Rāma, having abandoned the impurity of conceptualizing distinctions between yourself and the world, which consists of duality, remain steadfast, abiding in what remains.

Within yourself and within the world, amidst the various states of the seer and the seen, remain always contemplating your own self as that which is called "vision. Abandoning both the object of taste and the taster, abide in the state between the object of taste and the taster.

Meditating on that which abides at the end of the act of tasting, become eternally identified with the Self. Today, taking hold of the middle state— which is without support— between the object of experience, Rāma, and the experiencer himself, remain steadfast.

Having thus cultivated the self as devoid of the contemplation of existence and free from the state of both being and non-being, become yourself established in the Self. Abandoning this very existence of the self, you yourself contemplate the object of thought.
When that happens, O Rāma, you enter into a state of mind that brings extreme suffering.
Having forcibly severed this chain of the mind by means of the knowledge of one's true nature and through right reasoning,
O mighty-armed one, set free the lion of your own self.
When, having abandoned the state of the Supreme Self, you fall into impurity by pursuing an object of thought (*cetya*),

and when you form a volition (*saṅkalpa*), you then become that very object of thought. [This occurs] through the cognition of the body, which perceives the object of thought as something existing and distinct from the Self.

The mind becomes afflicted with suffering and perishes when that [object] is abandoned. When the realization arises that "this entire world is indeed the Self," where is the consciousness, where is the mind, what is the object of thought, and what is the act of thinking?
The wise know that the mere thought "I am the Self" or "I am a living being (jīva)" is what causes this beginningless and endless suffering to expand, O Rāghava.
There is no such thing as a "Self" called a *jīva*; there are only other forms of existence (*sattās*) anywhere.

Thus, the stilling of the mind is said to be the supreme happiness. O Rāghava, when the certainty arises that "this world is indeed the Self," the non-existence of the mind is born; of this there is no doubt.

When, through the realization of truth, it is established that "this is indeed one's own self," know, O mind, that [delusion] has completely dissolved, just as darkness vanishes before the light of the sun.
As long as the serpent of the mind remains within the body, so long does great fear persist.
When that has been driven away through yoga, whence can there be an occasion for fear? O sinless one, let this vampire of the mind, which has arisen from mere delusion,
be forcibly cast down by you with the mantra of perfect knowledge.
O best among the powerful, when the yakṣa of the mind has departed from the house of the body, remain free from mental anguish and devoid of agitation; there is no fear for you.
By merely realizing "I am indeed passionless and indeed stainless," the very existence of your mind dissolves.
You have reached the supreme state, the highest, free from suffering; remain thus within, with all desires completely stilled.
The fifteenth canto, titled "Description of the Nature of the Mind."
Vasiṣṭha said:

O Rāma, following after this impure existence of the mind—the seed-syllable of saṃsāra and the snare that binds the individual soul— * *cittasattām*: the existence of the mind; *apāvanīm*: impure; *saṃsārabījakaṇikām*: the tiny seed-grain of transmigration; *jīvabandhanavāgurām*: the net that ensnares the living being.
Having abandoned its own true nature, the self falls into a state of impurity;
it pursues anxious thoughts and assumes the stain of conceptualization. Fainting away, it brings about great delusion and causes fear.
Craving, appearing like a poisonous creeper, brings about only fainting;
whenever it arises, it bestows great delusion.
This craving is like the dark night of Kṛṣṇa, causing the affliction of endless blindness.
Hara and the other gods are capable of enduring the burning of the flames of the fire at the end of an aeon;
but none whatsoever are capable of enduring the burning of the flames of the fire of craving. This sharp, black, and very long [flame] always flows within one's own body.
The sharp blade of craving is cool to the touch, pleasant, and brings comfort; yet it is terrible.
O Rāghava, those things which are endless, difficult to restrain, and arrogant—these are the fruits of the creeper of craving, and they are suffering in this world.
Invisible, this craving—the wild bitch of the forest that dwells within the cave of the human mind—devours the flesh, bones, blood, and other parts of the body from men.
At one moment it attains exaltation; at another moment it falls into emptiness.
The monsoon river of craving quickly shatters the dull-witted.
A person struck down by craving—seeing only misery, with a ruined mind and destroyed vigor—falls into degradation; he becomes deluded, wails, and collapses. (MU 5.15.9–10)
The vital breaths moving within the cavity of the heart remain healthy for that man in whose hollow the black serpentess of craving does not dwell; indeed,
it is certain that wherever the course of the night of the black serpentess of craving has set, [there the breaths abide].
There, merits increase like the moon during the bright fortnight.
That tree of a man which has not been gnawed by the woodworm of craving always shines with the ever-blossoming flower of merit.
In the forest of the inner disposition, the river of craving and delusion flows for men, filled with infinite and turbulent waves, and crowded with eddies and whirlpools.
By means of this craving, all these people are driven like birds upon a stringed machine.
They are carried away, shattered, and gathered up in great numbers.
Even the most subtle roots, though as hard as tempered iron,
are cut down when desire strikes them like the edge of an axe.

The deluded person, following after craving, falls into a pit, just as a young deer, pursuing a dark blade of grass or a branch, falls into a chasm. Neither disease, nor old age, nor hunger consumes one so swiftly as does aging.
Just as thirst wastes away the emaciated body, so does thirst take the form of the heart.
By means of this thirst, which is like a female sorceress (kauśikī) dwelling in the heart and is inherently inauspicious,
the Blessed One Viṣṇu himself assumed the state of a dwarf when it took root there.
Indeed, by this very thirst, which is somehow knotted within the heart by fate,
one wanders through the sky day after day like the sun bound by a rope.
For one living in this world, it is a prison consisting of the form of all suffering.
Avoid craving as you would a cruel female serpent from afar.
By craving the winds blow; by craving the mountains stand firm;
by craving alone the earth supports all; the three worlds are enveloped by craving.
This entire course of worldly existence is strung together by the rope of craving;
those bound by ropes are released, but none who are bound by craving are ever liberated.
Therefore, O Rāghava, abandon craving by relinquishing all volitional constructions.
"By means of reasoning, it has been determined that the mind (*manas*) is not the formulator of intentions (*saṅkalpaka*).
O mighty-armed one, do not first entertain within your heart that dark and false hope, thinking 'I am indeed this [name]'. (MU 5.15.24–25)

O Rāma, if you do not cultivate this notion of selfhood within that which is not the self— a notion that gives rise to suffering— then you may be counted among the truly wise. Having severed this meritless sense of "I," which consists of egoism, by means of the very probe of self-realization;
O worthy one, through self-cultivation on the stage that is the end of existence, there arises the power that overcomes all fears born of worldly becoming.
The sixteenth canto, titled "The Description of Thirst."
Rāma:
O Blessed One, these words of yours are exceedingly profound, in that you say to me: "Do not seize upon egoism and craving."
