"O Lord, if I am to renounce the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra),
then I shall completely abandon this structure known as the body,
just as a great tree is supported by its massive trunk."
By means of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), this body is indeed maintained; likewise,
upon the destruction of the ego-sense, the body surely perishes,
like a great tree when its root is cut by a saw.
"How then can I abandon this, and how can I live, O Sage?
Having determined one single course of action, tell me, O best among speakers.
Vasiṣṭha replied:

O lotus-eyed Rāma, the abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanā) everywhere is said by the knowers of reality to be twofold by name: that which is to be meditated upon and that which is to be led away. "I belong to these objects, and these are my life."
"I am not anyone without these, nor indeed are these without me"—
having abandoned this internal conviction and reflected with the mind,
one should cultivate the realization: "I am not the object, nor is the object mine."

That which is truly the relinquishing of latent impressions (vāsanā)— performed as a mere play by means of an intellect that is inwardly cooled— is proclaimed as "that which is to be meditated upon" (dhyeya).
Having brought about the destruction of all latent impressions through an intellect that regards everything as the Whole (sarvikā), [one attains liberation].
He who abandons the body with a mind free from desire is to be known as one whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been exhausted.
He who, having effortlessly abandoned the latent impression consisting of egoism,
remains as one who has renounced all objects of meditation, is called liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).

O descendant of Raghu, know that he who has brought about the uprooting of mental constructions and reached the end of latent impressions (vāsanā) is liberated; he does not rely on the scriptures. Having abandoned the object of meditation—that is, the abandonment of latent impressions—they remain at ease.
Great-souled and virtuous people like Janaka are liberated while living;
having abandoned these latent impressions and attained tranquility,
they remain as those liberated in the body (videhamukta) within the supreme and non-supreme Brahman.
O Raghava, these two types of renunciation are equal and established in the state of liberation;
both have attained the nature of Brahman, and both are free from the fever of worldly distress—
provided they are liberated, grounded in supreme conviction, and solely pure, O sinless one.
One remains with a throbbing body, while another remains with a tranquil body.
One remains embodied yet liberated, free from the fever of passion;
the other, having abandoned the body, exists as one who is emancipated and whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are no longer subject to being led astray.
He who neither rejoices nor desponds when pleasure and pain arrive incessantly and in due time is said here to be liberated.
He for whom there exist neither desire nor aversion regarding internal perceptions of objects is [liberated].

He who moves like one in deep sleep is said to be liberated. He whose internal calculations of what is to be rejected or accepted, as well as the notions of "mine," "I," and "here," have completely perished, is called one liberated while living.
He who is not internally touched by joy, impatience, fear, anger, desire, miserliness, or [wrong] views is said to be liberated while living.
He whose mind remains always awakened, yet with its mental fluctuations stilled as if in deep sleep, is liberated while living.
"He who is always attended with joy like the moon endowed with its digits—he is remembered here as a 'liberated one' (mukta).
Vālmīki:
When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites.
Having offered her salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, it returned along with the rays of the sun.
Thus ends the seventeenth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Treatment of Thirst."
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, those who are liberated while in the body do not at all remain within the range of words here;
therefore, listen to these who are liberated while living.
They know that state as liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*), by which, through a pure thirst, these very duties that have been undertaken are performed;
whereas that state of a living being in which there is attachment to external objects due to thirst is [bondage].

The teachers call that bondage the firm fetter of saṃsāra. Surely, when conceptualization has been abandoned, the latent impression (vāsanā) that dwells within the heart and moves externally is here described as belonging to one who possesses a body while liberated in this life.
"O Rāghava, thirst that is swollen by the calamity of external objects is said to be 'bound';
thirst that is liberated from the calamity of all objects is called 'liberated.
That thirst which previously existed and continues to be eternal even in the present..."
The state of being free from suffering and devoid of fragmentation is remembered by the wise as liberation itself.
O Rāghava, O high-minded one, know that this internal mental disposition— "let this be mine"— is thirst, it is a chain, and it is the cause of conceptualization.
Having forever abandoned this [notion] regarding all things, whether they exist or do not exist, the great-minded one attains the most exalted state;
he abandons both the hope for bondage and the hope for liberation, as well as the condition of pleasure and pain.
Having abandoned hope for both the existent and the non-existent, remain like the unagitated great ocean.
O best among the wise, having realized the Self to be undecaying and immortal,
do not defile your mind with fears of old age and death.
This collection of objects does not belong to you, nor are you this, O Raghava;
this [world] is something else entirely, and you are another, the eternal one.
Whether the universe has arisen from the unreal or is eternally established in reality, [you remain distinct].
When you have attained that state, how can there be any union with craving?
Furthermore, O virtuous Rāma, as a person reflects within the mind,
a fourfold certainty of vast proportions arises.
"I am created by my mother and father from head to foot"— this is the single conviction, O Rāma, which leads to bondage through the perception of what is unreal.
I am subtler than even the tip of a hair, transcending all objective existents.

Thus, O scion of Raghu, the second certainty for the sake of liberation arises for the wise: "I am at all times unimpaired, the self of the objects within the web of the world. And the third certainty for the sake of liberation is as follows: [I am the Self alone]. *Mokṣopāya* 5.17.15–16.
"I and this world are non-existent, eternally empty and like space"—
this is the fourth conviction for the attainment of liberation.
Among these four convictions, the first is said to lead to bondage.
Three [types of people] are said to be intent on liberation when they are permeated by pure contemplation.
Among these, the first is bound by thirst that is fit for bondage;
the other three possess pure thirst, are transparent, liberated while living, and are playful.

O Mahāmati, that conviction which holds "I am indeed the Self, all is the Self"— taking hold of that, your mind shall no longer fall into despondency. The greatness of the Self pervades horizontally, upwards, and downwards.
By that internal certainty that "all is the Self," you are not bound. That which is called the Void, primordial nature, illusion, Brahman, consciousness,
Śiva, Puruṣa, and Īśa, is eternally said to be the Self alone.
All this is always indeed real; here, duality or anything else is never found anywhere.
The world is pervaded by knowledge, not by the other, which is blinding.
The ocean, whose self is infinite, has filled the space down to the netherworld with its waters.
The entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is filled with the Self.
All this is eternally the Truth; falsehood exists nowhere at all.
Just as the entire ocean is nothing but water, and not waves and such things separately.
Bracelets, armlets, anklets, and so forth are not separate from gold;
likewise, the millions of forms of trees and grasses are not distinct from the Self.
Through the play of creating the world, by means of the various manifestations of duality and non-duality— MU 5.17.26.
The power consisting of the Supreme Self manifests as non-duality alone.
Whether one's own or another's, in all things at all times—
whether when an effect has perished or increased— do not grasp at pleasure and pain.
Relying on the non-duality of existence and being essentially composed of the non-duality of being,
disregard the non-duality of action and become one who embodies both duality and non-duality. Through this contemplation of existence, [transcend] the terrifying grounds of worldly becoming.
Do not fall like a blind elephant into rivers filled with whirlpools.
Duality is not possible in the all-pervading Great Self; nor is unity possible in that Self whose nature transcends both duality and unity.
They say that non-duality is devoid of unity, eternally manifest, and that everything is neither anything at all nor its own essential nature.

I do not exist, nor indeed do the worlds exist; yet all this that appears is indeed the unchanging. Know that it is mere consciousness, peaceful, appearing as neither non-existent nor existent—neither the world nor "I" as being real.
It is the supreme nectar, the primordial light of all lights, unborn, undecaying, inconceivable, without departure, and free from modification.
May you have this firm conviction: that this entire reality—Brahman—is always arisen, devoid of the web of instruments, the life-force of the power of life (*jīvaśakti*), and the cause of all causes;

it is the Lord eternally risen, situated within the expansive light of consciousness, the seed of experience, to be taught as one's own essential nature; and that within the heart of consciousness, there is the tasting of this all-pervading Being, which is "you," "I," and the world. May this be your certainty.
The eighteenth chapter, titled "The Severance of Thirst. // MU_5,17.34 // Chapter Eighteen.
Vasiṣṭha:
O mighty-armed one, this is the natural state of the great ones who have liberated their intentions and remain unassailed by false views, as they move about here with effortless ease.
Even while dwelling in saṃsāra, the sage, whose mind is liberated while living,
laughs at the worldly courses of existence which are tasteless in their beginning, middle, and end;
remaining engaged in all ordinary activities, he maintains equanimity toward all mental states.
Relying on that object of meditation— the abandonment of latent impressions— he remains established;
free from agitation in all circumstances, nourishing all goals,
his soul delighted in the garden of discernment, he stands in the grove of awakening.
Taking as his support the state that transcends all things, with a heart as cool as the full moon,
neither agitated nor overly elated, he does not despair within saṃsāra;
remaining impartial toward all enemies, he is endowed with compassion and courtesy.
Acting according to the sequence of what has been attained among the foremost [of beings], he does not sink in saṃsāra.
He neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires;
established in silence, initiating only what is natural, he does not sink in saṃsāra.
When questioned, he speaks on the subject at hand; when not questioned, he remains like a pillar.
Free from likes and dislikes, he does not despair in saṃsāra.
When urged, he speaks what is agreeable to all, possessing refined speech.
Knowing the intentions of living beings, he does not sink in the cycle of existence.
Grasping the states of what is appropriate and inappropriate, he perceives the world's affairs— his own activity impaired by desire— as clearly as a wood-apple fruit within the hollow of a hand.

Having ascended to the supreme state, they look upon the fragile condition of the world as if laughing, with an intellect that is inwardly cooled— those great-souled ones who have conquered their minds and have seen both the higher and the lower.

O Rāghava, such is their intrinsic nature as it has been described to you. However, we— being fools whose own minds are unsubdued and who are mired in the mire of worldly enjoyments— do not know what their preferred doctrine might be.
To them, women adorned with gestures and expressions of passion were desirable; those very women were but flames of the fires of hell, though they possessed the luster of gold.
Furthermore, objects that are actually calamities appeared as gains, while the pursuit of meaningless things resulted only in torment.

Pointing out actions that bring about calamity and are accompanied by the onset of suffering, we are unable to describe those various types of conduct which result in bondage to fruits and are filled with pleasure and pain.

Firmly grasping the full vision that delights in the relinquishment of all objects of meditation, remain established in yourself through the state of liberation while living, and wander in the world, O Rāghava. Internally, having abandoned all expectations, be free from passion and devoid of latent impressions.
Outwardly, O Raghava, dwell in the world following all conventional conduct;
noble and of refined behavior, conforming to every form of social practice.
Inwardly, O Raghava, dwell in the world as one who has renounced everything.
Having examined all ten stages, O Rāghava, take as your object of devotion that very state which is most profound, and dwell in the world.
Internally maintaining freedom from desire, yet outwardly acting with a disposition directed toward hope.
Heated on the outside but cool within, wander in the world, O Rāghava.
With artificial agitation on the outside but free from agitation in the heart;
an agent on the outside but a non-agent within, wander in the world, O Rāghava.
You have understood the true inner nature of all things;
therefore, O Rāghava, wander in the world according to your will with that vision. Abiding in artificial joy and delight, yet free from the corruption of artificial distress.
O Rāghava, wander in the world with the cessation of all artificial exertion and agitation.
Having abandoned egoism, with a mind at peace and as radiant as the sky,
wander in the world, O Rāghava, free from the marks of any blemish.
Freed from hundreds of bonds of desire, equanimous in all conditions of life,
and engaged in your natural duties outwardly, wander in the world, O Rāghava.
In the ultimate sense, there is neither bondage nor liberation for the embodied soul.
This illusory splendor of the transformation of saṃsāra is false;
O Rāghava, this world is seen through delusion as mere error,
like water produced by a conviction in a vast mirage under the intense heat of the sun.
How could there be bondage for the Self, which is unbound, uniform, and all-pervading?
And in the absence of that [bondage], for whom is liberation prescribed?
This vast delusion of the transmigratory state arises from the non-knowing of reality.
Through the knowledge of reality, [ignorance] goes to destruction, just as the notion of a snake [vanishes] upon a rope.
You have known your own reality through this subtle intellect;
you have become free from egoism—remain stainless like the sky.
If you do not exist, then all notions of friends and kinsmen must be abandoned;
for what indeed can be the notion regarding that which is of an unreal nature?
If you do exist, then you are inferred to be possessed of an ultimate reality.

You have attained this state for the first time from the Supreme Cause. Since the Self has no connection with enjoyments, kinsmen, the world, or with auspicious and inauspicious actions, why do you grieve for it?

For you who have conceived the realization that "I am the one essence of the reality of the Self," there is no connection with worldly existences, O Rāma; why then do you fear the delusions of the world?
For one who is unborn yet remains a kinsman, there is no relation to the succession of joy and sorrow experienced by kinsmen.
What is your connection to them, O Rāghava, that you grieve for these?
If you existed in the past, so too will you exist now;
if you are standing here, you have understood this certainty.

Why then do you not grieve for those other, even more numerous, kinsmen who existed in the past and have long since passed away, belonging to the multitude of previous births? As you were before, so you are today, and so you will be hereafter.
O Rāma, even so, since you are of the nature of reality (*sad-rūpa*), why are you bewildered?
(5.18.39) If, having existed in the past and existing today, you will not exist again in the future, then even so, with *saṃsāra* exhausted, for what reason do you grieve? (5.18.40)

Therefore, it is not fitting to be sorrowful regarding the natural order of the world, nor is it fitting to be joyful; rather, it is proper to act in accordance with what must be done. O Rāma, do not fall into sorrow, and do not even resort to joy.
Attain equanimity toward all things; you are the Supreme Self, omnipresent.
You are infinite and of pure form, like space, with an exceedingly vast interior;
you are eternally pure and luminous, like the hollow within a flame.
Your body is the invisible, atomic form of all things in the world;
you abide within the heart, spread out like the single thread of pearls upon a necklace.
This very state of worldly existence is that which, having come to be, comes to be again.
This is by the ignorant alone, and not by the wise; you are wise, O Rāma, so remain steadfast.
For this very nature of this continuous cycle of worldly existence expands through ignorance; yet you are possessed of knowledge, O noble-minded one.
What else could form (rūpa) be, apart from mere delusion, except within delusion? For what other sequence could there be in a dream, apart from the dream itself?
This power of the All-Potent One is considered to consist of nothing but mere delusion.
This so-called "illusion of saṃsāra" is neither unreal nor composed of reality;
O Rāma, it is merely perceived as such due to a lack of discernment and the absence of true knowledge— this appearance shines with extreme brilliance.
In this world, no one is anyone's relative, nor is anyone anyone's enemy;
rather, by the will of the Lord of All, everything belongs to everyone at all times.
This entire universe is fragmented and shattered, yet it is entirely intermingled with one another.
The world moves incessantly like a torrent of waves upon the water.
It goes from below to above, and likewise from above to below;
it revolves around this unstable cycle of existence like the rim of a wheel.
Those dwelling in heaven go to hell, and those in hell go to the celestial realm;
people pass from one womb to another, and from one continent to another. The wise fall into wretchedness, and the wretched attain wisdom.
Beings quiver with the delusions of hundreds of falls and risings.
Here, nothing at all is obtained that is uniform, stable, self-abiding, pure, and free from affliction— just as a grain of frost cannot remain in fire.
O Rāma, whatever highly fortunate beings there may be— whether many or few—
they are all seen here to have perished within just a few days.
Such notions as "otherness," "one's own," "difference," "you-ness," "I-ness," and so forth, [are likewise transient].
O mighty-armed one, these are not real here, just like the vision of two moons and such;
"this is a kinsman," "this is another," "this is I," and "this is you"— O Rāma, let these false perceptions now dissolve for you.
Engaged in worldly affairs for the sake of play with these [faculties] whose vision is destroyed—
sport outwardly with ease, while they are severed at their very root within.
O you of noble vows, conduct yourself thus upon this path of saṃsāra.

You do not become weary from exertion as you would if you were bearing the burden of latent impressions (vāsanā). Just as this auspicious inquiry that brings about the destruction of latent impressions arises within you, so too do you attain peace.
"This is a kinsman, this is not"—such is the calculation of those with small minds;
but for those of noble conduct, the intellect is indeed free from all obscurations.
There is nothing where I am not, and there is nothing that is not mine.
Thus, for those who have ascertained the essential truth, the intellect is indeed free from all veils.
That which is great like the space of consciousness neither sets nor rises;
established in its own nature, it perceives everything, just as one standing in the sky sees the surface of the earth.
For indeed, O Rāma, all these classes of living beings are your kinsmen; there are none whatsoever with whom you have not been intimately acquainted in some form or another.
In this world, which is filled with the turbulence of hundreds of diverse births, the distinction between "kinsman" and "stranger" lasts but a moment.
In reality, it is merely the state of delusion that flutters about; thus, even though the three worlds are without kin, they appear as long-standing relatives.
The nineteenth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Nature of One Liberated while Living."
Vasiṣṭha said: In this very context, they cite this ancient history,
a dialogue between two sons of sages on the banks of the triple-pathed river (the Gaṅgā).
"‘This is a kinsman, this is not’—it is remembered from such introductory discourse.
Listen, O Rāghava, to this meritorious and wondrous history.
In a certain corner of this Jambudvīpa,"
There is a mountain named Mahendra, the great crest-jewel of the forest array; there,
gods and kinnaras rest in the shade of groves of wish-fulfilling trees,
and it has surpassed the sky with its lofty peaks that seem to overspread it.
He seems to sing the Sāmaveda with the resonant humming of echoes produced by those who have reached the interior of the Brahma-world and roam among his peaks and caves;
he whose peaks are agitated by clouds thick with water as they strike their summits.
It shines as if with locks of hair interwoven with the flowers of creepers;
it resounds through the mouths of its caves with the yawns of śarabhas eager to leap from the slopes, as if laughing at the clouds of the cosmic dissolution.
In a certain part of that vast and delightful jeweled peak, where the roar of waterfalls cascading through the mountain caves surpassed on all sides the playful splendor of the waves of the ocean.
The sages brought down the celestial Gaṅgā for the purpose of bathing and drinking.
On the bank of that river which flows through the three paths, where trees were in full bloom,
there were golden lotuses shimmering like the slopes of a mountain of jewels.
There was a sage named Dīrghatapas, whose wisdom had fully dawned, who was a mass of austerity and possessed noble intellect; he stood as if he were the very embodiment of asceticism.
To that sage were born two sons, as beautiful as the moon.
Puṇya and Pāvana were like two locks of hair belonging to the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati).
Together with those two sons and his one wife,
he dwelt on the bank of that river, which was lined with fruit-bearing trees.
Then, in time, between those two sons of his, the one named Puṇya became the possessor of knowledge; he was the elder by age and the elder in virtue, O Rāghava.
Pāvana remained half-awake, like a lotus at the dawn twilight.
Due to ignorance, he has not reached the end, remaining as if in a state of restless wandering.
Then, when unreckoned time— whose causes have been reckoned— has passed,
and when a multitude of years has been exhausted, the wretched body reaches the end of its lifespan.

Having abandoned attachment to this cycle of existence— which is filled with fragile beings and terrifying with its weight of events— the sage Dīrghatapas, his life worn out by old age, [departed from] the body, that nest for the birds of mental constructions.
Like a porter laying down his burden, he abandoned his dwelling in the mountain cave;
he attained that passionless state where all mental constructions and activities have ceased, a locus of consciousness empty of objects of thought, just as the fragrance of a flower pervades the air.
Then the sage’s wife, seeing his body— devoid of the vital breaths of prāṇa and apāna— rolling upon the ground like a lotus severed from its stalk,
[reflected] for a long time on the yoga-method practiced by her husband and bestowed upon her.
She cast off her unfading body like a female bee leaving a lotus;
she followed her husband who had become invisible to people,
like the moon that has set into the expanse of the sky.

When his parents had passed away, while the funeral rites were being performed with merit and undivided attention, Pāvana arrived in sorrow. With his mind stricken by grief, he wandered through the forest paths.
Without even looking back at his elder brother, Pāvana lamented.
Then, having performed the funeral rites for his mother and father, the noble-minded and virtuous Pāvana returned to the forest, overwhelmed with grief.
Puṇya said:
"My son, why do you turn your grief into density— an absolute cause of blindness,
a terrible producer of streams of tears, like a rain cloud in the monsoon season?"
O man of great wisdom, your father has gone together with your mother to his own supreme state, known as liberation.
That is the station of all living beings; that is the form of those who have realized the Self.
Now that he has attained his own true nature, why do you grieve for your father?
Why have you conceived such an illusion born of delusion regarding this state of being,
that even though your father is not to be mourned, he is mourned by you in this cycle of existence?
She alone was not your mother, nor was he alone your father;
you alone were not the son of those two who had countless sons. O son, thousands of mothers and fathers have already passed away for you.
Like the many downward channels of a flowing stream in forest after forest,
you alone are not the only son of those two who have countless sons;
O son, the multitudes of sons of men pass away like the waves of a river.
Countless hundreds of thousands of sons have passed away from our parents,
like clusters of leaf-buds on creepers and trees; likewise,
multitudes of friends and kinsmen pass away for a living being in birth after birth.
Like fruits that have fallen from a great tree season after season,
O son, if parents and children are to be mourned out of affection,
then why are those who have passed away by the thousands not mourned incessantly?
O illustrious one, this worldly delusion is seen as a proliferation;
but in the ultimate sense, O wise one, there is neither friend nor kinsman. For even in the slightest degree, O brother, nothing exists here in the ultimate sense.
Like a drop of water in a vast desert heated for a long time,
these splendors that you behold— unsteady as parasols and fly-whisks—
are but a dream, O one of great intelligence, lasting only three or five days.
But with the ultimate vision, my son, investigate the truth:
"Neither you are here, nor is this yours. Abandon the delusion within.
Furthermore, these views—"this one is dead" and "I have gone"—[are likewise to be abandoned].
They appear as arising from the fever of one's own conceptual constructions, but not through reality.

In the vast desert of ignorance, this world of infinite forms flashes forth like water in a mirage, produced by the heat of its own latent impressions and consisting of the restless waves of good and evil impulses.
The twentieth meritorious canto, titled "The Purification and Awakening."
Who is a father, what is a friend, who is a mother, and who are kinsmen?
By one's own intelligence alone, these are shaken off, just as the dust of the earth is by a whirlwind.
[The world] consists of the states of affection, hatred, and delusion toward kinsmen, friends, and children.
This conceptual proliferation is extended by means of mere self-perception alone.
One who is perceived as a kinsman becomes a kinsman; one who is perceived as a stranger becomes a stranger.
This state of affairs is dependent upon mental cultivation, like the condition of poison or nectar.
For the all-pervading Self, which exists as a single unity,
how can there be the false conceptualization that "this one is a kinsman" and "that one is a stranger"?
[Indeed, such distinctions arise only from] the body, which is a mere heap of blood, flesh, and bone— a skeletal frame.
"O son, reflect for yourself with your own mind: 'Who might I be?
For from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is neither you nor I;
it is only false cognition that prances about, thinking, 'I am meritorious' or 'I am purifying.'"

Who is your father, who is your friend, who is your mother, or who is your stranger? In this void of infinite play, tell me: what is yours and what is not yours? If you are that [void], then when others have passed away through many births, [what remains]?
As for those kinsmen and those riches—why do you not grieve for them as well?
(5.20.8) They existed in flower-filled meadows and among the deer; many were their fortunate kinsmen—how is it that you do not mourn for them? (5.20.9)
Those swans, the kinsmen of Haṃsa, dwelt upon the lotus-filled shores of the ocean-maidens; why do you not grieve for them?
They lived amidst the variegated forest groves with their shimmering wings outspread.
There were many tree-kinsmen; why do you not grieve for them? There were many lion-kinsmen upon the great peaks of the mountains; why do you not grieve for them?
In rivers, lakes, and lotus ponds, you had many fish as your kin; do you not grieve for them either?
In Daśārṇa, you were a tawny forest monkey.
Among the Tukhāras he was a prince; among the Puṇḍras, a forest crow;
among the Hehayas, an elephant; and among the Trigartas, a donkey.
Among the Śālvas he was the son of Saramā, and among the Śavaras, a tree-dwelling bird.
Having become a *pippala* tree on the Vindhya mountain, and having become a wood-worm in a great banyan tree;
having become a monkey on Mount Mandara, O Brahmin, you were born in a cave.
Having been a twice-born man among the Kosalas, and having been a partridge among the Vaṅgas.
"Having become a horse, you were born among the Tukhāras from a Brahmin in the forest;
you who were a worm within a *tāla* trunk, a gadfly on an *udumbara* tree, and a bird in the Vindhya forest— you, my son, are that same younger brother of mine."
That ant which dwelt for six months in a hole in the hollow of a birch tree in a cave of the Himalayas— that very one is this younger brother of mine;
and that scorpion which was in the cow dung in a wretched village on the border of Suhma— [that very one is this other brother].
O virtuous one, for a full year you have been my younger brother;
you are that very same person who, like a bee clinging to lotuses, once nestled against the breasts of the Pulinda women in the forest. You are my younger brother.
"In these and many other various wombs of beings,
you were born in this Jambudvīpa previously hundreds of thousands of times. In this way, [you have seen] the sequence of your own past latent impressions."
I behold with subtle intellect, purified by right vision:
"Many were my various wombs, slowed by delusion;
today I remember them all through the sight awakened by knowledge."
Having been a parrot among the Trigartas, a swan on a riverbank,
and a crow in a hamlet, I was born here in this forest;
having experienced the state of a Pulinda in the Vindhya mountains and having become a tree in the Vaṅga country.
Having passed through the state of a camel, I was born here in this forest.
He who was a *cātaka* bird on the Snowy Mountain, he who was the king in the region of Puṇḍra,
and he who was a tiger in the thickets of the Sahya mountains— he is indeed your elder brother here.
He who was a vulture for ten years, a deer for five months,
and a lion for a hundred years— he is indeed your elder brother here;
[he who was] a partridge in the Andhra village and a horse for the Tukhāra king.
This is being told to you by me, the son of the teacher from Śrīśaila:
"O brother, I remember all my former births, with their various intense efforts, their diverse conducts and activities, and their pleasures."
This being the case, among those born in the world, hundreds of fathers, mothers, brothers, and friends have passed away for both of us.
Which of them should we mourn, and which of them should we not mourn?
Or why should we grieve for our kinsmen? Such is the very nature of the world:
endless fathers pass away, and endless mothers pass away, like the leaves upon the trees of a forest for men wandering in this cycle of existence.
"What measure, my son, can there be here for either suffering or happiness?
Therefore, having abandoned everything and attained a state of well-being, remain so.
Abandoning the conceptualization of manifoldness that resides in the mind as 'I'..."
Go to that state—may you be blessed—which those skilled in the ways of liberation attain.
Here, the wise do not grieve over this state of constant flux, characterized by falling and rising; they simply apply themselves to the remedy.
Free from existence and non-existence, devoid of old age and death—remember your true self with an undistracted mind; do not be deluded in spirit.
For you there is no suffering, no birth, no mother, and no father.
O wise one, you are indeed the Self; for you are certainly not anyone else at all.
In this journey of saṃsāra, which presents various dramatic roles, only the ignorant are the actors, O virtuous one, endowed as they are with the aesthetic sentiments and emotional states.
Those with impartial vision, established in their own nature, perceive objects exactly as they are obtained;
but those who know that [reality] are merely observers, established in the duty of witnesses.
Even though they are agents, they are not agents, just like lamps at the onset of night.

Thus, those who possess that knowledge regarding the activities of illumination are not defiled by reflections— even those residing within their own forms— while they remain here in the world; just as mirrors, gems, and the like are not affected by reflections, so too are the great-minded ones unaffected by their effects.

In the center of the heart-lotus, by means of this very great jewel— the self which is free from the stain of all the diseases of worldly seeking and endowed with a pure nature— cast aside all agitation within yourself, O son, and attain complete satisfaction.
This is the chapter titled "The Attainment of Purifying Wisdom."
The Twenty-first Sarga: Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus was the purifying Puṇya then awakened by him.
He attained awakening and clarity, like the earth at dawn;
then both of them, accomplished and having reached the further shore of knowledge and realization, wandered blamelessly through that forest for as long as they desired.
Then, after some time, those two from Videha, having become free from attachment, attained the state of nirvāṇa and reached tranquility like extinguished lamps.
Thus, for those who have previously experienced bodies, there are endless [sorrows] arising from wealth and kinsmen.
"O sinless one, what is grasped from these hopes, or what is abandoned? Therefore,
O descendant of Raghu, for these endless cravings,
the only means is renunciation alone, and certainly not their preservation."
Thought increases through thinking, just as fire grows with fuel;
it perishes through non-thinking alone, like a flame without fuel.
Mounted upon the chariot of abandoning the object of meditation, one looks with a gaze noble with compassion.
"Beholding the world as wretched, do not remain [in this state]; arise, O Rāghava!
This is the pure state of Brahman—free from desire and devoid of affliction.
Having attained it, O mighty-armed one, even one who was deluded is no longer bewildered."
Taking solitude as your friend and a mature intellect as your sole companion, you will not be deluded even in times of distress,
for all objects of sense have been warded off and kinsmen cast aside.
No one can rescue another from distress except through their own fortitude.
Therefore, by means of dispassion, the sacred teachings, and qualities such as greatness,
one should with effort uplift one's own mind for the sake of overcoming calamity.
Neither from sovereignty over the three worlds, nor from a treasury filled with jewels,
is that fruit obtained which is attained from a mind augmented by greatness;
for as long as one remains within this belly of the world, amidst the oscillations of calamities and portents, [one suffers].
Men fall [into the cycle of rebirth] as long as their minds are not free from fever.
When the mind is fulfilled, the entire world is filled with the flow of nectar;
indeed, for one whose feet are covered by shoes, the earth is as if entirely covered with leather.
The mind that follows the power of desirelessness attains fullness through hopelessness;
yet the mind, like a lake in autumn, reaches emptiness through hope.
Thus the heart becomes empty, its hollow interior laid bare.
Like the ocean drunk by Agastya, for those whose minds are helpless before their desires,
that great inner forest of the heart shines forth when the restless monkey of craving no longer leaps about upon the vast tree of the mind. (MU 5.21.16–17)

For those whose minds are free from craving, the three worlds are but the calyx of a lotus seed, a league is but a puddle in a cow’s hoofprint, and a great aeon (*mahākalpa*) is but half a blink of an eye.
That coolness is found neither in the moon nor in the caves of the snowy mountains.
Neither Rambhā nor a row of sandalwood trees shines as much for minds free from desire as does the full moon, nor the full ocean of milk,
nor the lovely face of Lakṣmī, shines for a mind devoid of longing.
Just as a streak of cloud defiles the moon, or as ink defiles a plaster of nectar,
even so does this demoness of hope corrupt a man within.
The branches of the tree of the mind, known as "hope," spread across the quarters of the sky.
When those [tendencies] are severed, the great tree of the mind becomes formless.
When the great branches of craving are cut and the trunk of the mind comes to rest,
fortitude, which was previously of a single nature, attains a hundredfold branching.
When the mind has reached its dissolution through that unsurpassed fortitude,
O Rāma, that state is attained wherein no destruction exists.
[This occurs] when these fluctuations of the mind and these hopes have been stilled within the supreme substratum.
If you do not allow a sprout to grow, then you exist, O Rāghava.
When your mind, devoid of mental fluctuations, has reached the state of non-mind,
then you attain that pervasive inner existence which consists of liberation.

O Rāghava, when the mind is agitated within by craving— which is like the wing of a peacock— inauspicious things spread forth in abundance. It is said that "vartana" means "mode of conduct," yet the mind proceeds according to its underlying disposition (*āśaya*).
Therefore, having abandoned hope, which is a modification of the mind, proceed toward the state of mindlessness.
For whatever function a person performs, they are subject to decay without that very function;
therefore, for the sake of the pacification of the mind, one should bring its activity to cessation.

O Great-Souled One, having cast off the bonds of existence, become one whose mind is liberated, with all cravings stilled. When the cords of hope—which are like fetters for the mind—have fallen away, who is not liberated?
This is the chapter titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of the Cure for Thirst."
Canto Twenty-two: Vasiṣṭha said:
Or rather, O full moon of the sky known as the lineage of Raghu!
"Like a fire, through the distinction of the intellect, one attains stainless knowledge.
Rāma said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, by your grace, [this has been placed] within my heart."

Everything to be attained has been attained; I rest in the stainless state. O All-pervading One, like a vast cloud from the sky in autumn, the entire great darkness of delusion has departed from my mind, O Kṛṣṇa.
Filled with nectar, clear, cool-souled, and of great splendor,
I abide within, full of bliss, like the full moon at evening; yet,
O autumn season for the clouds of all my doubts, what indeed am I?
I do not reach satiety with these words of yours as you speak.
O All-pervading Lord, tell me again of the attainment of higher knowledge for the further increase of my own awakening; for the virtuous do not grow weary of one who is humble.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O Rāghava, I shall tell you the supreme account of Baḍi;
by hearing which, you will attain eternal awakening.
Within this treasury of the world, at some distant edge of the horizon,
there exists a realm situated beneath the earth known as Pātāla.
It is drenched by the nectar-like waters produced from the Ocean of Milk.
In some places it shines with no gaps between them, filled by the daughters of the Dānavas;
in other places it is crowded with serpents possessing hundreds of thousands of heads, whose weapons are the heavy burden of poison and whose tongues move with fierce cries.
In some places it was filled with the sons of Danu, who, like moving Mount Merus, were intent on uprooting the entire universe with their playful movements;
they were towering as they rested the circle of the earth upon the tips of their mountain-like shoulders and walls.
In some places it was sheltered by the tusks of world-elephants, which were like trees upon mountains;
in other places, the succession of living beings was scorched by the great *kaṭakaṭa* sound [of clashing weapons],
while certain quarters of the sky were filled with foul odors as the circles of hell resounded.
It was covered from the surface of the earth down to the seven circles of the netherworld (pātāla),
appearing in some places as if filled with oceans of jewels rather than netherworlds;
it was [strewn] with the dust from the lotus-feet of the gods and asuras as they slept upon their heads.
In one place it was sanctified by that Blessed One Kapila,
who desired the play of worship with infinite offerings provided by the Asurī;
in another place it was protected by that Blessed One Hāṭakeśa.
While that great burden was being sustained by the pillar of the Asura Dostambha,
there arose a Dānava king named Bali, the son of Virocana;
he was simultaneously occupied by all the gods, vidyādharas, and nāgas.
He whose massaging of the feet was desired even by the King of the Gods;
he who is the treasury of the jewels of the three worlds, the protector of all embodied beings,
and the upholder of the laws of the universe— to him Hari has bowed down.
By his name alone, the temples of Airāvaṇa withered away; like the *kekayī* plant, the veins of the serpent’s heart went toward him and fell into distress.
By the fierce heat of his majesty, the oceans became like those at the time of universal dissolution.
The seven [oceans], facing desiccation, attained a state of heat before his wrathful form;
the rows of clouds from the smoke of the sacrificial clarified butter,
enveloping the mountains, always served as armor for the hollow interior of this cosmic egg.

By the forceful descent of whose gaze all the quarters of space bend down like creepers weighed down by fruit, while the mountain ranges that serve as the ornaments of the entire expanse of the world are conquered in play; MU_5,22.23 he who has sportively won the entirety of the world’s vastness as his ornament.
That Daitya ruled the kingdom for ten billion years. Then, as many ages passed, revolving in their cycles,
amidst the great floods of gods and asuras rising up and falling down.
Bali, the leader of the Dānavas, felt a sense of revulsion toward enjoyments that had been constantly consumed and which existed within the belly of the three worlds;
he remained stationed at a window smeared with the tips of the peaks of Mount Meru.
Once, he reflected for himself upon the nature of worldly existence:
"Now that my power remains unimpaired, how long must this sovereignty be exercised by me here, and how long must I sport within the three worlds?"

What is the use of enjoying my vast kingdom, which causes wonder throughout the three worlds and is burdened with manifold pleasures? It is sweet only for the moment of its onset, yet it must inevitably come to an end.
What indeed is this mere enjoyment of pleasures that brings happiness?
Again there is the reckoning of days, again the persistence of the night;
again those very same actions lead only to shame, not to contentment.
"The beloved is embraced again and indeed enjoyed again;
this is a child's play that brings great shame here to the wise.
That very same flood of activities, as tasteless as a piece of dried meat, [is repeated] again and again."
Day after day performing [this], why does the wise man not feel shame?
Again a day, again a night, again a succession of tasks—
again and again, I consider this to be a mockery for the wise man.
Having reached the state of being wavy again, it returns once more to the state of being waveless;
just as water does, so too does this person undergo various actions.
This activity, which takes the form of the behavior of a madman, occurs again and again.

Like the play of a child, it repeatedly causes even the wise person to laugh. Even though this activity is constantly performed and its purpose has been accomplished, what goal could there be such that one would not engage in action again?
Furthermore, for how long must we carry out this great display here? Until what point is it to be maintained?
This childhood play is, in reality, infinite and utterly devoid of substance.
Those who seek the production of misfortune perform [ritual] action in vain through repeated effort;
I do not see any single, magnificent fruit here in this world for which there might be some other task to be done once that [liberation] has been attained.
"Without enjoyment, what could be absolutely delightful and imperishable?
I shall reflect upon this immediately. Having thought thus, that Baḍi meditated;
then, in an instant, the king of the Asuras said, "It has been remembered."
Reflecting within his own mind upon the matter with a frown on his brow:
"Long ago, it is said, my father, the venerable Virocana— knower of the true nature of the self and one who has seen the higher and lower worlds— was questioned here."

O Mahāmati, where all delusions regarding both all sufferings and all pleasures have ceased— what is that called the ultimate limit? Where is the delusion of the mind stilled, and where have all desires passed away?

"O Father, where is there rest for one who is without cessation? What has a person attained here that brings satisfaction compared to all other attainments? Having seen what, O Father, would one no longer need further vision?"
For even these exceedingly abundant enjoyments do not bring happiness;
they agitate the mind and cause even the virtuous to fall into delusion.
Therefore, O dear one, [seek] that something of mine which is beautiful with expansive bliss.
"Tell me of such a place where, staying there, I may find long-lasting rest.
Having heard this, he spoke from beneath the veil of flowers— resplendent and peerless as they vied with the rays of the moon— which had been placed over me by her in the past.

The speech of Virocana— equal to a potent elixir of vast form for the quelling of delusion— spoken by his father, who had been carried off to heaven, after he himself had planted the tree of the ocean in the courtyard.
This is the chapter titled "The Words of Virocana."
The Twenty-third canto:
Virocana said:
"O son, there is an exceedingly vast region with a wide hollow."
Wherein even many thousands of triple-worlds find room;
wherein there are neither clouds nor oceans, nor mountains;
neither forests, nor sacred fords, nor rivers, nor lakes.
Neither the earth nor space, neither the heavens nor the winds and so forth;
neither the moon and sun, nor the lords of the world, nor the gods, nor the dānavas; neither the bhūtas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, nor the shrubs, nor the splendors of the forest.
It is not wood or grass, nor beings that are stationary or moving;
it is not water, nor fire, nor space; it is not above, nor below, nor the earth;
it is neither light nor darkness, nor the "I," nor Indra, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the rest.
There is but one great king there, of immense splendor;
he is the doer of all, the goer everywhere, and the all, yet he remains silent.
By him, the minister has been appointed, intent upon all deliberations.
It quickly brings about what was not yet joined and thoroughly dissolves what was already joined.
Though it is itself ignorant, it is always able neither to enjoy anything nor to know anything at all; nevertheless, for the sake of the King alone, it performs everything.
He alone is the sole performer of all the king's duties;
the monarch himself remains entirely at ease in solitude.
Free from mental and physical afflictions, where is that place of great splendor?
How is it attained, or by whom was it mastered, O Lord?
Who is that counselor, or even that king of great power,
who has effortlessly torn asunder the snares of the world and remains unconquered even by us?
"This narrative is unprecedented and strikes fear into the hearts of the immortals; dispel for me the cloud of doubt from the sky of my heart by telling it.
O son, there the venerable minister was [approached] by the hosts of gods and asuras.

Even when combined and multiplied by a hundred thousand times, they cannot overcome it even slightly. My son, if this [knowledge] is mastered, neither the thousand-eyed Indra, nor Yama, nor the Lord of Wealth, nor even a god or an asura can prevail.
There, weapons such as swords, clubs, missiles, vajras, discs,
and maces become blunted, like the striking of a lotus against a stone.
He is not accessible to missiles or hand-weapons, nor to the fierce deeds of warriors.
By him all the gods and asuras were brought under control at all times.
Even though he was not Viṣṇu, by that very one the asuras such as Hiraṇyākṣa were cast down,
like the wish-fulfilling trees on Mount Meru by the wind at the end of an aeon.
Even the gods beginning with Nārāyaṇa, though all-knowing,
were overcome by him and cast into pits at his will;
yet, by his grace, Smara, possessing five arrows, remains full of pride.
Having traversed these three worlds, he strides about like a sovereign emperor.
Even if he is censured by the hosts of gods and asuras, even if he is devoid of virtue,
evil-minded, and ugly in form, through his grace that wrath expands its power.
That the hosts of gods and asuras engage in battle again and again is merely the play of that counselor who possesses the power of mantras.
O son, if that counselor were indeed [controlled] by that Lord alone...
It is conquered when it is easily won; otherwise, however, it is as immovable as a mountain. When that very lord, in due time, desires to conquer his own minister, he conquers him without effort.
If you have the power to conquer the wrestler who churns the three worlds and causes the three worlds to exult, then you are truly valiant.
When that sun has risen, the lotus-pools of the three worlds [will bloom].

These expand when it expands and dissolve when it has gone to dissolution. O steadfast one of noble vows, if you are capable of conquering that one [Self] with a single, delusion-free intellect, then you have truly succeeded.
When that is conquered, even those worlds that were unconquered become conquered;
but if it remains unconquered, these remain unconquered, even if they have been held for a long time.
Therefore, for the sake of infinite accomplishment and for eternal happiness, [one should strive].

Therefore, apply yourself with effort to its conquest, even through arduous exertion. For indeed, by that exceedingly powerful one, the three worlds— including the gods, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, mahoragas, and kinnaras— were brought under control on all sides as if in mere sport.
The twenty-fourth canto, titled "The Verses of Virocana," in the account of Bāli; the canto on Bāli.
"By what means, dear father, is that powerful one overcome?
Who is he? O you of great heroism, tell me everything quickly.
Virocana replied:
O son, listen as I speak of the ease with which even that minister— who is of an eternally invincible nature— is conquered, by which means he is brought under control.
My son, once he is seized through this method, he comes under one's power in an instant.
Without reason, he burns like a provoked venomous serpent.
Those who, having fondled him like a child, restrain him by means of reason—
having beheld that king, they attain their goal.
When that protector of the earth is seen, that minister comes under your control;
and when that minister is overcome, that king is seen once again.
As long as that king is not seen, so long is the minister not conquered.
As long as the minister is not conquered, the king is not seen.
When the king is not seen, the evil minister leaps about excessively for the sake of misery;
when the minister is not conquered, that king goes to utter invisibility.
Therefore, through practice, one should bring both together equally:
the audience with the king and the defeat of the minister,
by means of human effort and one's own gradual cultivation.
Accomplishing this pair, one attains that auspicious state.
O Lord of Daityas, when practice has borne fruit, you will reach that state if you do not grieve even slightly thereafter.
The virtuous dwell there, with all their exertions completely stilled, their intentions ever joyful, and all their doubts entirely pacified.
Listen, my son, what region that is; I shall reveal everything to you.
"By me, through the teaching, liberation—which destroys all suffering—has been declared to you.
O Mahāmati, the Blessed One, the Self, who transcends all states, is the King there; by him, the wise one named Mind has been made his minister."
The mind, through its all-pervasive nature, has undergone this universal transformation,
just as a lump of clay becomes a pot, or as smoke becomes a cloud.
When that [mind] is conquered, everything is conquered, and everything is attained.

One should know that it is difficult to conquer; it is conquered only through skillful means (yukti). [The disciple asks: "O Blessed One, what is the clear skillful means for the mastery of that mind?"
"Tell me that, O father, by which I shall conquer the terrible Virocana.
Virocana replied:
"O son, regarding all objects of the senses in every way,"

This lack of reliance is the supreme method for conquering the mind. This alone is the highest method; by this very means, the great elephant of one's own intoxicated mind is swiftly brought under control.
For this, O Mahāmati, is exceedingly difficult to attain and yet easily attained:
it is difficult to reach for one who has not practiced it, but when well-practiced, it is attained with ease.
O son, this detachment from sense objects is attained through gradual practice.
It blossoms everywhere, like a creeper watered by a sprinkling;
for it is not obtained, even if desired, by one of deceitful nature who has not practiced it, just as rice is not obtained if it has not been sown. Therefore, my son, one should gather this [wisdom].
So long do these embodied beings wander through sufferings, dwelling in the wilderness of saṃsāra, as long as they do not attain detachment from sense objects.
Without practice, no one attains such weariness with sense objects.

Just as a living being who has gone to another land does not return even from the furthest distance, so too, by constantly abandoning the object of meditation, the practitioner who still bears a body should increase their detachment from enjoyments through practice, just like a climbing vine.
"O son, without human effort no auspicious thing is attained here;
the fruit of all undertakings is obtained through human exertion alone.
Just as when the fruit of an action is fully realized, one experiences joy, resentment, and so forth," [so it is with all results].
In the world, that which is called "fate" (daiva) is not fate in any embodied form anywhere. It is the inevitable necessity, or what is known as destiny (niyati),
that is expressed by the word "fate" by men alone, and not by others.
That which is always present here, wherever it has reached fruition,
and which serves to destroy both joy and resentment— that is called destiny (*daiva*). Destiny, in the form of necessity (*niyati*), is overcome by human effort (*pauruṣa*).
Just as the delusion of a mirage vanishes through the play of correct knowledge,
so too whatever is conceptualized by human effort becomes exactly that;
for the sky, when perceived as having a surface, bestows the happiness of that very surface-ness.
Therefore, the mind alone is the agent here; whatever it conceives, that becomes so.
Whatever kind of destiny it intends, that becomes so.
It [conceives] certain things as restricted, others as unrestricted, and even some as indeterminate.

It acts upon the mind; therefore, this mind is that which joins one to destiny (niyati). While fashioning a destined course—sometimes bearing its true name—the individual soul vibrates within this sheath of the world, like the wind in the sky.
Making the mind sometimes devoid of necessity (niyati),
it flashes like the wind with the word "necessity" conventionally applied to the meaning of consciousness.
Therefore, as long as there is the mind, there is neither destiny nor necessity.
O virtuous one, when the mind has set, let that which arises be so;
for the individual soul is born as a person, and whatever it conceives in this world through its own human effort, that occurs for it exactly so and not otherwise.
"O son, nothing exists here apart from human effort (*puruṣārtha*).
Relying upon supreme human exertion, one should cultivate a lack of attachment toward enjoyments.
As long as there is no lack of attachment toward enjoyments, [human effort] does not arise here as the bestower of victory."
The final liberation that destroys existence is not attained as long as delight in sense objects,
which causes delusion, persists; for as long as that lasts, one remains swinging on the restless swing of the states of worldly existence.
O son, without practice, this wretched hope— which arises from the weight of the serpent of enjoyments— never ceases to cause suffering. (MU 5.24.40) Baḍi.
"O Lord of all Asuras, how does this internal lack of attachment to enjoyments come to abide within a living being,
bestowing upon him long life?
Virocana replied:
For one who beholds the Self, the fruit clearly bears further fruit:
the soul’s lack of interest in enjoyments, like a great creeper in autumn.
Through the vision of the Self, this detachment from sense objects arises in the highest state.
It comes to abide in the heart like the goddess Śrī within the hollow of a lotus.
Therefore, by means of most beautiful inquiry— the whetstone of wisdom—
one should perceive the Divine and simultaneously withdraw attachment from worldly enjoyment.
One who has not yet attained proficiency in the noble method should fill two parts of the mind with enjoyments and one part with the scriptures, and one part with service to the guru.
For one who possesses some degree of proficiency, one should fill one part with enjoyments.
One should daily fill the mind of one who has attained proficiency through service to the guru and reflection on the meaning of the scriptures:
two parts with detachment from the scriptures and two parts with meditation and worship of the guru.
The soul, having attained goodness and becoming fit for the sequence of discourse on knowledge,
takes on a stainless form,
just as a cloth receives the finest dye through gradual nurturing by means of logical arguments and purifying words.
One should protect the child of the mind by means of the transformation brought about by the meaning of the scriptures.
When it has matured in supreme knowledge and its stubborn grasping has slackened,
the mind shines forth coolly, like crystal permeated by moonlight.
Then, by means of supreme and straightforward wisdom, one should immediately observe the form of the body as being exactly the same as that of enjoyments and the Lord.
O son, through the power of the investigation of wisdom, it is always exactly the same.
One should cultivate the observation of the self and the abandonment of craving.
When the Supreme is seen, there is freedom from craving; and when craving is destroyed, there is supreme vision.
These two visions support one another, like a boat and its helmsman.
When the multitude of enjoyments has lost its flavor and the higher and lower deity is seen,
an eternal and infinite repose arises in the supreme Brahman;
bliss that has long borne fruit arises as an infinite tranquility.
Never, indeed, does detachment from enjoyments arise for living beings except through the soul’s finding rest;
it is not produced by austerities, nor by gifts, nor even by pilgrimages,
except through the contemplation of one's own true nature.
By no reasoning whatsoever does the intellect proceed toward the vision of the Self for the sake of a man's highest good, except through his own effort;
O son, this is apart from the attainment of the ultimate truth through the renunciation of enjoyments.
The supreme bliss of resting in the state of Brahman is not attained anywhere else in this world, from Brahma down to a blade of grass,
as one finds it, O virtuous one, by taking refuge in the Supreme Cause.
Relying on human effort and casting destiny far behind,
the wise man should censure worldly enjoyments, which serve as firm bolts barring the path to the highest good.
When the censure of enjoyments has matured, discernment arises.
When the rainy season has passed, he becomes glorious and stainless like the autumn season.
Through reflection there arises a revulsion for enjoyments, and from that revulsion comes further reflection; these two fulfill one another like the ocean and the clouds.
Censure of enjoyments, discernment, and the eternal light of one's own self mutually accomplish their purpose, just like very affectionate friends;
having first disregarded destiny, one attains human effort through exertion.

Pressing his teeth against his teeth, he should cultivate a lack of delight in sensual enjoyments. At the outset, he should acquire wealth through manly effort, in a manner that does not conflict with local customs and is beneficial to his kinsmen.
One should attract noble and virtuous people by means of wealth;
through association with them, there arises a disdain for worldly enjoyments.
Then follows reflection, and subsequently the mastery of the meaning of the scriptures of knowledge.
Then, in due course, the attainment of the supreme state arises.
O Lord of Asuras, when at the proper time you cease from the objects of the senses,
then, through the power of discernment, you shall reach the supreme state.
You will rightly attain rest within the utterly pure Self;
you shall no longer cast yourself into the mire of mental constructs for the sake of suffering.
My dear friend, by means of wealth acquired through a gradual process and with little reproach, acquire a circle of virtuous people with due honor.
Through the thorough disregard for sense-objects arising from association with that [Self], you shall attain your true selfhood by means of the power of right inquiry.
This is the twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Mind-Treatment."
Bāḍi said: "This was previously told to me by my father, who possesses beautiful discernment;
now, by good fortune, it has been remembered, and I have attained full awakening."
"Today, this clear distaste for enjoyments has truly arisen within me;
by good fortune, I enter the pure bliss of tranquility, cool as nectar.
(MU 5.25.2) Again filling the quarters [with fame] and again bringing back wealth, he remained.
Again, turning toward his beloveds, he said: "I am weary of abiding in worldly prosperity!
Oh, how truly delightful is this ground of tranquility, so cool within!
In tranquility, all perceptions of pleasure and pain come to rest."
I am stilled; I am completely extinguished; I dwell in happiness, established in tranquility.
This is my end; I rejoice like the reflection of the moon set upon the water.
My body, once nourished by the impetuous force of a wild dance of the mind—
Alas, the acquisition of wealth is a misery characterized by incessant agitation!
That I was formerly delighted by pressing limb against limb and flesh against the flesh of a woman— that was merely the manifestation of delusion.
Examples have been seen; that which was to be enjoyed has been enjoyed unimpaired;
the entire multitude of beings has been traversed—what, indeed, could be more auspicious?
Again, those very same things, those very same things, are there, here, elsewhere, and right here.
From here and there, among all things, there is nothing such as "new.
Having mentally renounced and abandoned everything by myself,
I remain pure within my own self, full like the ocean.
In the netherworld, on the earth, and in heaven, women, jewels, precious stones, and the like are the essence; yet even that is swiftly swallowed up by the void of time.
For such a long duration as this, I was formerly a child in the extreme.

For one who feels hatred toward the gods because of their trivial worldly desires, what noble purpose could there be for that Great-Souled One, by whom the world— known as the "world"— is merely a mental construction, which may be abandoned or taken up at will?
Alas! For a very long time, intoxicated by the pride of ignorance and like a child, I have pursued what is harmful with the thought that it was beneficial, like a dog;
what indeed [is there] in this triple world for one whose thirst is ever-surging?
"What was done by me in ignorance serves only to increase my remorse. Enough of this trivial past reflection;
human effort bears fruit through the treatment of the present."
Today, through the unity of my own self with the single cause that possesses infinite forms, I attain bliss from every side, as if entering the ocean for the sake of an elixir.
What indeed is this "I," and what is the Self? Such is the contemplation of the Self.
I shall surely question Uśanas, my protector, for the sake of quelling ignorance. I meditate upon the Supreme Lord Śukra, whose grace is swiftly aroused;
then, instructed by his speech, I abide by myself within the Self in that state of infinite manifestation, for the words of instruction bear fruit as an imperishable goal.
The twenty-sixth canto, titled "The Instruction on Yoga According to the Siddhānta of Baḍicitta," within the narrative of Baḍi; by Vasiṣṭha.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One, his eyes closed like those of a *baḍi* tree,
meditated upon Śukra, whose eyes were like lotus petals and whose abode was the sky;
for that descendant of Bhṛgu was perpetually absorbed in meditation upon the infinite consciousness that pervades all things.
Having understood that his disciple Baḍi was conscious and seeking his teacher in the city,
the Lord Bhārgava, whose self is the all-pervading and infinite consciousness,
brought his own body to Baḍi’s jeweled window.
His body touched by the mass of light radiating from the teacher’s form,
Bāḍi awoke at dawn like a lotus awakened by the rays of the sun.
There, with the offering of precious gems and heaps of *mandāra* flowers, he [honored him].
He honored that descendant of Bhṛgu by prostrating at his feet.
Then Baḍi spoke to his guru, who was resting upon a costly throne, his body strewn with precious offerings and adorned with a crest of mandāra flowers.
Bāḍi:
O Blessed One, this intuition arising from your grace impels me to speak before you, just as the rays of the sun urge one to perform their task.
I am dispassionate toward enjoyments, which bestow great delusion;
I wish to know that reality which removes great delusion.
What exists here? How much is this? Or what indeed is its nature?
"Who am I? Who are you? Or what are these worlds? Tell me quickly.
Śukra replied: "What is the use of speaking much here? I am one who strives to go to the ether (kha)."
O Indra among the lords of the Dānavas, hear the essence of everything in brief:
for here, only consciousness exists; this is mere consciousness and is composed of consciousness alone.
Consciousness you are, consciousness I am, and these worlds are consciousness—this is the summary.
Taking this firm resolve to heart, behold with an illumined intellect;
by yourself, through your own self, you shall attain the infinite state.
If you are capable, then through this certainty you shall obtain everything from this.
If that is not so, then even though much has been spoken, it is like an oblation poured into ashes for you.
The conceptualization of consciousness (*cit*) as an object of thought (*cetya*) is bondage; its cessation is called liberation.
That consciousness is non-objectifiable is indeed the Self—this is the summary of all established doctrines.
Adopting this certainty, behold with an illumined intellect;
you shall yourself, by means of the self, attain the infinite state.
I am departing for the ether; here these seven sages have gathered together.
"O King, I must remain there in the sky for some purpose of the gods;
for as long as this body exists, even for those whose minds are liberated,
the renunciation of whatever objects are encountered does not come naturally."
When the descendant of Bhṛgu had thus spoken, he then leaped with great speed along the path of the clearly visible ocean through the midst of the sky,
which was variegated with bees and agitated by the multitude of planets like restless waves.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Yoga of Instruction on the Sixty-four [Arts]."
The Twenty-seventh Canto:
Vasiṣṭha said:
When that son of Bhṛgu, who is honored in the assemblies of both gods and demons, had departed,
Bali, the best among the powerful, reflected in his mind:
"The Blessed One has spoken rightly: 'This triple world is indeed consciousness alone;
I am consciousness, these worlds are consciousness, the quarters are consciousness, and this activity is consciousness.'"
In ultimate reality, everything—both external and internal—is consciousness alone;
apart from consciousness, there is nothing whatsoever here or anywhere else. If this sun, known as the *arka*, were not perceived by consciousness, [it would not exist].

In this case, what distinction between light and darkness can possibly be perceived? (MU 5.27.4) If this earth, which is called "earth," were not perceived by consciousness, what indeed would be the earth-nature of the earth? That [nature] would have become something that has ceased to exist. (MU 5.27.5)
If these directions are not perceived as "this is this direction," then what indeed is the directional nature of the directions, or the mountain-nature of the mountains?
If this world is not perceived as "this is the world" by the perceiver, [what is its reality]?
In that case, what is the world-ness of the world, or what is the sky-ness of the sky?
If this body, shaped like a mountain, is not perceived by the consciousness,
then what indeed is the "bodiness" of the body for embodied beings?
Consciousness alone is the senses, consciousness is the body, consciousness is the mind, and consciousness is that seeking.
Consciousness is within, consciousness is without, consciousness is space, consciousness is existence, and consciousness is the persistence of becoming.
I am indeed the one consciousness alone—everything, including touch and all prior desires.
I do not experience any contact with the body through the body at all. Of what use is this body of mine, which is like wood or a clod of earth?
I am the singular Self of the entire world, consciousness itself, whose nature is pure awareness.
I am indeed consciousness in the sun within the sky; I am indeed consciousness in the cage of the elements;
I am consciousness among gods and demons, and in all things both stationary and moving.
Consciousness alone exists here; for no second conceptualization is found.
Since duality is impossible in the world, who is an enemy and who is a friend?
When the radiant head of the body named "the bound" is severed,
what part of consciousness would be severed, given that it pervades all the worlds?
Hatred that has been accumulated by consciousness becomes hatred and not otherwise;
therefore, all states such as hatred, whether existent or non-existent, are of the nature of consciousness. Even upon investigation, there is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from consciousness.
Anything else may be found within this vast interior of the three worlds.
There is no hatred, no passion, no mind, and no mental fluctuations for that which is pure consciousness alone; how could there be any conceptual construction for that which is utterly pure?
I am indeed Consciousness— omnipresent, all-pervading, consisting of eternal bliss,
transcending the construction of conceptual thought, and devoid of even a fraction of conceptualization. That which is called "Consciousness" is not a name for that which is nameless.

This power of consciousness, whose essence is sound, vibrates everywhere. I am the Supreme Lord, the seer who is free from the seen and the seeing, possessing a solitary and stainless form, eternally arisen and devoid of appearances.

"I am neither the doer nor the enjoyer; I am the stainless witness alone, consisting of the beautiful digits of time whose forms are devoid of conceptual construction. Arisen as a mere appearance, I am eternal and free from all that is manifested."
I am of the singular nature of light; by my own nature, I am victorious.
Salutation to my own nature—to that which is devoid of the coloring of objects of thought, liberated, the great Self, and the form of inward consciousness.

Salutations again and again to me alone, who am consciousness free from the object of thought, endowed with the appropriate method, whose form is the manifestation of all things, and who fills the entirety of the universe. [MU 5.27.24] The nature of consciousness, which is liberated from the object of thought, completely fills the entire world.
I am that pervasive pure consciousness alone, in which all objects of perception have been completely stilled.
I am infinite like space; yet, though more subtle than the subtlest atom, I am all-pervading.
These various states of pleasure and pain do not reach me.
That pervasive consciousness is a feeling that cannot be felt and is beyond thought;
the states of existence and non-existence found in the world are not capable of defining me.
Or rather, let these worldly states define me as such.

For these [objects] are indeed not distinct from me, according to my own conviction. (5.27.28) If an object is measured by means of another object that constitutes its very nature, then when it is taken away or given away, what loss has truly occurred to whom? (5.27.29)
At all times, I am everything indeed; I am the doer of all, united with all.
This object of thought is nothing other than myself, and not even the slightest thing has been produced.
What is there to be gained from volitions and conceptual constructions? Consciousness and the unconscious are but my single radiance.
"I shall first cause agitation; then I shall find peace within my own purifying self.
Thinking thus, the highly wise Baḍi remained established in meditation, contemplating the meaning of the half-mora that is half of the half-mora of the letter *a*.

With all volitions completely stilled and the multitude of mental constructions pacified, he is free from doubt; his thinking has cast away the object of thought and the thinker far behind. Devoid of the meditator, the object of meditation, and the act of meditating, he is mindless, with all latent impressions (vāsanās) stilled.
Having met with great calamity, Baḍi became like a lamp in a windless place;
with his mind stilled, he dwelt there for a long time in that jeweled window, as if carved out of stone.
With his desires stilled, with his accumulation of thought freed from the defects of mental construction and brought to fulfillment,
Bāḍi shone with stainless being, like the autumn sky when it is clear and free of clouds.
This is the chapter named "The Resting of Bāḍi."
The twenty-eighth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then those Dānavas, the followers of Baḍi, were there at that time.

In an instant, the ministers led by Dambha, the heroic feudatories beginning with Kukuha, the kings headed by Sura, and the strength-seizing demons starting with Vṛtra, ascended that lofty crystal palace.
Hayagrīva and others were his courtiers; Śukunda and others were his kinsmen;
Luḍaṅga and others were his friends; and Palmūla and others were his attendants.
Kubera, Yama, Śakra, and other gods brought him tribute.
Yakṣas, vidyādharas, and nāgas, all desiring an opportunity for service;
Rambhā, Tilottamā, and other excellent women bearing chowries;
rivers, oceans, mountains, and likewise the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Then, for the sake of serving him, many other Siddhas dwelling within the belly of the three worlds arrived at that place of Baḍi;
he was established in meditation, silence, and samādhi, as motionless as if depicted in a painting.
Respectfully, they beheld him whose multitude of crowns were bowed down.
Having seen him, those great asuras, for whom all that was to be done had been accomplished, prostrated themselves;
they became faltering with despondency, wonder, joy, and fear.
Then the Dānavas, having deliberated among their ministers as to what had been achieved,
thought of Bhārgava, their preceptor and the best among all who possess knowledge.
Immediately after this thought, the Daityas [beheld] the radiant Bhārgava before them.
They saw him as if it were a city of the Gandharvas, conjured and yet attained.
Being honored by the hosts of Asuras, he sat upon a great seat;
there Bhārgava beheld the lord of the Dānavas, established in the silence of meditation.
Having rested for a moment as it were, and having gazed with affection, he—
whose delusion of worldly existence was exhausted— surveyed the boat with his vision,
[illuminating] the Milky Ocean with hundreds of rays from his body and the brilliance of his teeth.
As if casting a glance at the assembly, the venerable Śukra spoke these words with a smile:
"O Daityas, how wonderful this is, that by your own very deliberation— "
"O best of Dānavas, this Lord Baḍi has attained stainless light and is perfected. Remaining exactly as he is here,
let him attain stability within his own self and behold the state that is free from all affliction."

O Dānavas, he who is weary has attained rest; whose wandering burden of thought is exhausted; from whom the mist of saṃsāra has been stilled—he is not to be awakened. For by him, upon the destruction of ignorance, his own true light has been attained.

When the agitation caused by the clouds has subsided, he will reach awakening by himself in due time, just as the mass of rays from the sun does in a day; like a sprout with its form dormant within the seed-capsule, he shall emerge through his own self-awareness.
