"Perform your respective duties, all you leaders of the Dānavas;
Baḍi will emerge from his meditative absorption after a thousand years.
When this was said by the Guru, [there arose] there [in them] that which is born of fear, joy, and despair.
The Daityas cast off their anxiety like trees shedding their withered blossoms; having seated themselves in the assembly hall of Virocana according to their former arrangement,
all the Asuras thereafter remained intent upon their respective duties.

Men went to the earth; the lords of serpents to the subterranean realm (rasātala); the planets to the sky; the hosts of gods to the triple heaven (triviṣṭapa); the quarters, the mountains, and the lords of waters to the caves; and those who roam the forests, those who roam the heavens, and others went to the firmament.
This is the chapter titled "Description of the Hook-like Samādhi."
The twenty-ninth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, after a thousand divine years, O best of asuras, [the one]...
The Blessed Baḍi was awakened by the sounds of celestial drums.
When Baḍi had awakened, that city then shone intensely,
like a bed of lotuses when the mass of suns belonging to Brahmā has risen.
He was indeed fully awakened; as long as the Dānavas had not yet arrived, he reflected for a moment in his meditation chamber:
"Oh, how delightful is this path, cool and pertaining to the ultimate truth!"
Having remained in this state for a moment, I have attained supreme rest.
Therefore, I shall dwell following this very path;
what need have I for external splendors enjoyed here by you?
"Even from the reflections in the lunar orb, the waves of bliss do not delight me within as much as these planes of the expansion of consciousness. Thus,
his mind, having dissolved, was once again directed toward finding rest.
The Daityas blocked his way, like clouds obscuring the moon.
Seeing them, his eyes became agitated with the thought of bowing to them;
his body was thus surrounded by those who resembled the great boundary mountains.

For me, whose mind is gathered and whose conceptual constructions have been exhausted, what is there to be accepted? Since the mind has fallen away, let it go entirely into the state of being that [very essence]. Why do I desire liberation, and by whom indeed was I bound in the past?
"Unbound, I desire liberation; what is this mockery of a fool?
There is no bondage, there is no liberation; my delusion has come to an end. What is the use of the play of meditation for me, or what would come to me through non-meditation?"
I desire neither meditation nor non-meditation, neither enjoyments nor the state of being without enjoyment; free from all feverish distress, I remain in equanimity.
I have no longing for the supreme reality, nor do I have any longing for the maintenance of the world.
I have no need for the vision of meditative absorption, nor have I any need for worldly power.
I am neither dead nor am I living; I am neither existent nor non-existent, but equal.
This is not mine, nor is that other mine; salutations to me, for I am indeed the Self.
"Let this kingdom of the world remain; I shall stay here established in my own state.
Or rather, let there be no kingdom of the world at all; I shall remain cool within the Self. What need have I for the vision of meditation, and what use have I for the glory of royal power?"

"Let that which comes come; I am nothing, nor do I belong to anything anywhere. Even if there is indeed nothing at all to be done by me now, why then should I not perform here some action that is appropriate to my nature?"
Having thus resolved, the self-perfected Baḍi, the best among the powerful,
gazed upon the Daityas as the sun gazes upon lotuses,
distinguishing each of those born of Danu by the direction of his glance.

He accepted their prostrations like the wind gathering the fragrance of flowers. Then Vairocani, there, performed all his royal duties with a mind whose essence consisted in the abandonment of objects of meditation.
He honored the gods, the twice-born, and his gurus with worship;
he paid due respect to his friends, kinsmen, vassals, and virtuous men.
Likewise, he satisfied his servants and the multitudes of supplicants with wealth.
Lalana cherished him with the offering of various riches.
Thus he dwelt in that kingdom under his complete sovereignty;
then, at one time, his mind became inclined toward sacrifice.

Having determined that Bali was not a seeker of the burden of enjoyments, Mādhava performed a great sacrifice that gratified the entire world and was honored by the hosts of gods and sages, together with the foremost figures such as Śukra.
To accomplish the desired goal of Bṛhaspati, the bestower of success went to his sacrifice.
Knowing what was to be done, he [Śiva] went to grant this forest tract of the world to Śakra— who was the eldest in age and worthy, yet solely miserable for the sake of enjoyments.
Having deceived Bāli here by the mere pretext of a step,
Hari bound the monkey at the bottom of the netherworld (pātāla), as if in a house within the earth.
O Rāma, today he stands once more for the sake of regaining the status of Indra.
With a body liberated while living, established in his own self, and with his intellect perpetually seated in meditation,
he remains like a fish in the depths of the underworld; though possessing the mind of one liberated while living,
he views both adversity and prosperity with an equal eye.
That wisdom neither sets nor rises in the face of pleasure and pain;
it remains equal and of a most steadfast form, like a series of variegated suns. Here, among living beings, there are thousands of appearances and disappearances.
Having observed for a long time that his mind had turned away from enjoyments,
and having ruled the three worlds for ten million years,
the mind of Baḍi eventually attained detachment and became completely stilled.
"Thousands of conjectures and refutations, and hundreds of notions of existence and non-existence, have been scrutinized by Baḍi; where, then, can he find consolation?
Having utterly abandoned his longing for enjoyments, Baḍi’s mind is now completely fulfilled."
Delighting in the self, he remains eternally today within the depths of Pātāla.
O Rāma, by means of this Baḍi, this entire world must be governed as his sovereign for many groups of years here.
No satisfaction arises in him from attaining the station of Indra,
nor does agitation arise in him from falling from his own station.
He is equal toward all states of being, and his disposition is always uplifted.
Taking up what has been attained, one remains healthy and established like space.
This attainment of supreme knowledge has been described to you by me;
having grasped this vision, may you too be uplifted.
O Rāghava, by means of human effort alone, through one's own discernment and the certainty that "I am eternal" like Bāli, one should attain the state free from duality;
having enjoyed the three worlds for ten million times two and eight years.
Even Bāḍi, the best of Asuras, fell into a state of distaste for worldly existence;
therefore, O subduer of enemies, having utterly abandoned the multitude of enjoyments that inevitably lead to distaste, proceed toward the state of non-distaste, which is eternal bliss.
O Rāma, these perceptions of the visible world, which produce various forms and transformations, are none of them yours; they are like rocks upon a distant mountain.
They run hither and thither, rolling through the worldly conditions of life.
Stabilize this mind by binding it within the hollow of the heart.
You alone are the sun of consciousness situated everywhere in the world;
who is another to you, and who is your own? Why do you stumble in vain?
You are Ananta, the mighty-armed; you are the primordial Puruṣottama.
You, whose body is consciousness, manifest through hundreds of forms of objective reality.
All this world, both moving and unmoving, is woven upon you.

Just as a multitude of gems [shines] within a pure, ever-risen pearl-string, so you are not born and you do not die; you are the unborn, sovereign Person (puruṣa). Pure consciousness—may the delusions of birth and death not be yours.
Having deliberated upon the relative strength and weakness of all the diseases of birth,
abandon craving for enjoyments and become merely an enjoyer.
While you remain as the Lord of the World, the ever-risen sun of consciousness, [all darkness vanishes].
All this that appears is the entire circle of the dream of saṃsāra.
Do not indulge in futile despondency; this longing for pleasure and pain does not belong to you.
You are pure consciousness, the self of all, the illuminator of all things.

Having first conceptualized that which was desired as undesired, and that which was undesired as desired, abandon both of those through the practice of that [equanimity]. When the perceptions of the desirable and the undesirable are abandoned, eternal equanimity arises.
By that [wisdom] residing in the heart, a living being is not born again.
From whichever objects the mind sinks, like a child,
one should pull it out from each of those and settle it upon reality (tattva).
Thus, having bound with one's whole being the intoxicated elephant of the mind that has arrived through habitual practice, the supreme good is attained.
Do not [be led astray] by the deceitful who lack knowledge of reality and whose intentions are destroyed by false views.

Do not attain equality with those fools who have been sold by their own deceitful intentions. In this world, there is nothing more painful than the ignorance of one who, though possessing nothing, remains fixed in his own convictions while hanging upon the words of others.
O high-minded one, quickly drive far away this cloud of non-discrimination that has arisen in the sky of your heart by means of the wind of discrimination,
through your own effort, until the Self is perceived.
As long as grace has not been bestowed, there can be no arising of discernment.
Even through the study of the Vedas, the Vedānta scriptures, their meanings, and the insights of logic,
this Self does not become manifest until one’s own direct vision occurs.

O Rāma, you, established in serenity within yourself by means of the self, have attained expansive awakening; you understand my words. This [awakening] belongs to you, the sun of consciousness, who is devoid of even a fraction of conceptual construction.
The pervasive extension of the Supreme Self as described by me has been grasped and expanded [in your mind].
With all volitional constructions dissolved, with doubts and delusions stilled,
and with the mist of curiosity exhausted, you have become one who is free from the fever of suffering.
Whatever you approach, protect, destroy, drink, leap, or expand through consciousness, by that very fact you are it; O Great Sage, may you be free from the suspicion of any stain upon your awakening.
The Chapter Named "The Attainment of Pure Consciousness" (Baḍivijñānaprāpti).
The Thirtieth Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, O Rāma, listen to this further sequence for the attainment of higher knowledge.
Listen, O Lord of Daityas, how the perfected Prahlāda attained realization through his own self.
There was an asura named Hiraṇyakaśipu, whose prowess equaled that of Nārāyaṇa, who had routed the gods and dwelt within the depths of Pātāla.
Having pervaded the entire expanse of the world, he seized the universe from Hari,
just as a royal swan plucks a lotus with its broad petals from a six-legged bee.
Having brought both gods and demons under his sway, he ruled over the realms of the worlds.
Like a female elephant that has driven away a swarm of swans from a lotus pond, he [Diti] was like a bee among bees.
Then that lord of the Asuras, exercising sovereignty over the three worlds,
in due time gave birth to sons, just as the spring brings forth sprouts.
They grew in no time at all, their splendor eclipsing the stars,
like a thousand rays of ten suns sporting as they pervaded the sky.
There was indeed a venerable lord named Prahlāda, who was the primary self (pradhānātman).
Among those highly precious jewels, he was like the Kaustubha;
with that son, who possessed every beauty, Hiraṇyakaśipu shone intensely, as the year does with the springtime.
Then that Daitya Mada, accompanied by his sons and endowed with great strength and a vast treasury, arrived; he was like an elephant whose temples were dripping with rut-fluid.
With the spreading heat of his aggressive advance, he scorched the three worlds.
Then, by the splendor of his new hands alone— which were like a multitude of suns at the end of an aeon—
the gods, headed by the Sun and the Moon, were no longer distressed by him;
they were like kinsmen toward a child who is restless with mischievous play.
They requested Śauri for the slaughter of the lordly elephant of the Daitya king;
for even the great do not tolerate repeated wrongdoing.
Then [there arose] a roar like the gurgling of the world overturned at the time of dissolution.
It is adorned with the splendor of vajra-nails resembling the tusks of a world-elephant;
its circle of upward-pointing crests blazes with a network of steady lightning flashes,
and it wears flaming earrings that issue forth from the hollows of the ten directions.
Its vast belly was formidable, containing the entire mass of the great mountain ranges;
it caused the shell of the cosmic egg to crack as it shook the trees of its arms,
and it drove away the mountains with the winds exhaled from its mouth and chest.
Proud as the fire of cosmic destruction rising in anger, intent on burning the three worlds;
causing the sun to tremble by the movement of his broad, thick shoulders and formidable mane;
and making the mountains tawny with masses of fire blazing from the pores of his skin.

Having assumed the body of a Man-lion (Nārasiṃha), Mādhava slew the great Asura with his fierce eye-sockets that shattered the great walls of the world-mountain, and with his claws that tore away every limb along with his *paṭṭiśa*, *prāsa*, and *tomara* weapons.
Like an elephant against a neighing horse,
he burnt the city of the Asuras with the flames vomited from his eyes,
together with all its living beings, like the fire at the end of an aeon consuming the entire web of the world.
When that Nṛsiṃha-māruti had become violently agitated,
roaring with the slapping of his arms like a turbulent single ocean,
those hosts of Dānavas fled in all directions like gnats.
They vanished from sight like lamps whose light has faded. Then, with the lords of the Daityas in flight and the circle of the inner apartments consumed by fire,
the surface of Pātāla became like the world at the end of a kalpa.
When the Lord, who had been honored by the frantic efforts of the gods, had gradually subsided after his untimely act of cosmic destruction and had departed elsewhere,
the sons of Danu who remained alive were protected by Prahlāda.
They returned to their own country, like birds to a dried-up lake;
there, having lamented the loss of their own selves as was appropriate for the occasion,
they performed the funeral rites for their lords and kinsmen.
They slowly consoled their own surviving people, whose captives had been carried off and whose circle of kinsmen and relatives had been consumed by fire— men who,
with their wretched appearances resembling figures in a painting, were motionless and dejected in spirit like lotuses struck by frost.

With their minds scorched by grief, those leaders of the asuras became like burnt trees, deprived of all bloom. The thirty-first canto, titled "The Death of Hiraṇyakaśipu," concludes with Prahlāda’s restoration to peace.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then Prahlāda, his soul overwhelmed with grief because the Dānava had been slain by Hari, remained silent and reflected within the cavern of Pātāla.
"What indeed could be our means [to stop] this very sprout of the Asuras which grows here with a sharp point, so that the monkey Hari might devour each one as it is born?
Never in Pātāla have the Daityas, though possessed of staff-like arms, [been able to do so]."
They became steady, like lotuses blooming upon the Himalayas;
rising up again and again, they vanished with their brilliant forms and gurgling sounds,
like the waves of the ocean that manifest for a moment before beginning their motion.
The enemies, who rob the entire world of its light and cause unprecedented delusions of darkness,
have reached full maturity; they fill the heart with gloom and cause the abundance of petals to contract.
His friends fell into distress, like beds of lotuses at night; the realm was overrun by the gods who wiped away the dust from their father’s footstool, as deer overrun a great forest.
Devoid of effort, their fortune departed, wretched and with their inner intentions laid bare,
the kinsmen do not shine, like lotuses whose petals have been scorched.
In the houses of the Asura heroes, they quiver amidst incessant winds.
Grey with ashes and frost, as if laden with the smoke of incense,
the walls of the Daityas’ inner apartments— whose door-panels had been removed—
became like emeralds, from which new sprouts of barley had grown.
Even the Dānavas, who were like intoxicated elephants in the lotus-pool of the three worlds, have fallen into such wretchedness as the gods; alas, what is impossible for Fate?
They are terrified by the fear of even a slight rustling of leaves, as if they had seen the enemy.
The wives tremble, shattered like does that have strayed into a village;
the trees, their clusters of blossoming jewels plucked by the claws of the lion-like men, now stand as mere stumps to serve as ear-ornaments for the Asura women.
There, in the Nandana grove, the wish-fulfilling trees were replanted, their leaves being divine garments and creepers, and bristling with clusters of jewels as blossoms.
Previously, the faces of the celestial captive women were gazed upon here by the Daityas.
Today, however, the faces of the Asura captives are being gazed upon by the gods.
I think that great rivers of blood from their slaughter will flow forth against the temples of the divine elephants,
like mountain streams cascading down rocky ridges.
Upon our temples,
the ashes from forest fires shine like dust in parched desert thickets;
while the winds, reddened by the nectar of blooming white mandāra flowers, blow.
Those regions on the peaks of Meru became inaccessible to the Daityas;
the beauties of the gods and Gandharvas, who had resided within the inner apartments of the Dānavas,
returned once more to their station on Meru like blossoms upon a tree.
Alas! The graceful charms of my father’s wives, now withered like waterless lotuses, are mocked with playful laughter by the celestial nymphs.
By those very same whisks with which my father was formerly fanned while intoxicated—
In heaven, the thousand-eyed Indra is fanned by those very [serpents]— what a hardship! This other calamity has come upon us, bringing wretchedness,
solely through the favor of that one Hari, who possesses such contemptible manliness.
The gods, having found rest in the dense shade of the forest of his arms,
are never distressed, like the peaks of the Himalayas which have taken refuge upon the formidable summits of Śauri’s valor and have thus attained prosperity.
They cause us, the sages, to burn with grief like monkeys;
therefore, the tears shed upon the lotus-faces of the Asura women— who were ever adorned for their auspicious rites— act like frost upon lotus plants.
This world, like a dilapidated pavilion with crumbling, broken, and falling walls,
is supported solely by his arms, which are like pillars of sapphire;
he is the sustainer of the celestial host as it sinks into the ocean of calamity.
Like a tortoise submerged in the belly of the Milk Ocean supporting Mount Mandara,
he alone has struck down all these foremost of asuras— my father and the others—
like the great boundary mountains toppled by the turbulent winds at the end of an eon.
This very one, Madhusūdana, the glorious and formidable friend of the host of gods, possesses a multitude of arms capable of such acts of destruction;
by his prowess, he is the heroic axe for the staff-like arms of the Daityas.
Śakra oppresses the Dānavas as a monkey torments young children.
Difficult to conquer is the lotus-eyed one, even when his weapons have been cast aside;
he, whose essence is like a diamond, cannot be shattered by the severing of missiles and weapons.
By him, many terrifying battles were practiced together with our grandfathers, in which mountains were hurled at one another amidst the fury of combat.
In those various, most horrific, and extensive wars against the Asuras, he was ever present.
"He who is not afraid now will surely encounter fear; what need is there for further words?
I consider this alone to be the clear means for attacking Hari;
apart from that, I believe no countermeasure exists."

With one's whole being, with all one's intellect, and with the full force of all one's exertion, that God alone is the refuge and the goal here; it is not otherwise. There is nothing superior to Him within the three worlds.
Hari has become the cause of dissolution, maintenance, and creation.
Therefore, from that moment of closing my eyes onward, I have always taken refuge in the unborn Nārāyaṇa; for everywhere I am permeated by Nārāyaṇa.
The mantra "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" accomplishes all purposes;
it does not depart from the treasury of my heart, just as the wind does not depart from the sky.
Hari is the quarters, Hari is the ether, Hari is the earth, and Hari is the world.
This Hari is of immeasurable self; indeed, I have become composed of Hari.
One who is not Viṣṇu, yet worships Viṣṇu, shall not partake in the fruit of that worship.
Having become Viṣṇu, one should worship Viṣṇu; for I stand here as this very Viṣṇu.
Having filled this infinite space, the son of Vinatā,
with his golden limbs, has become the seat for my own limbs.
Upon the single branch of his hand rest all the birds that are weapons.

These great emerald trees, strewn with the blossoms of the rays of my nails, and these four arms of mine— whose shoulders are bound with garlands of soft mandāra flowers and whose armlets were rubbed against Mount Mandara— are yours.

Holding beautiful chowries that resemble the shimmering flood of moonbeams, this Lakṣmī stands by my side; she rose from the depths of the Ocean of Milk. Having effortlessly acquired the entire world, she is like a blossoming cluster on the tree of the three realms.
This fame of mine, white and pure in its radiance, attends my side;
ceaselessly it effects the ever-new creation of the world-web. This illusion of mine, sporting with its own magical displays, attends my side.
This is she, who effortlessly overcomes the groves of the three worlds;
she, Jayā, shines at my side like a creeper upon the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
These two gods, the cool-rayed moon and the sun, are ever cool and warm for me.
The two eyes within my mouth have revealed the cycle of existence.
This pervasive radiance of my body, dark as a blue lotus and beautiful as a full rain-cloud, has turned the entire circle of the quarters into darkness.
In my hand is this conch, Pāñcajanya, whose sound vibrates;
it is like the sky personified as the essence of sound, established as if within the Ocean of Milk.
This [conch] has Brahmā as its bee, hidden within the calyx of its pericarp.
In the palm of my hand is the glorious Padma, born from the hollow of my own navel.
This is my mace, Gadā, with limbs variegated by jewels, resembling the peak of Mount Sumeru, adorned with golden armlets, heavy, and the crusher of Daityas and Dānavas.
This is my [chariot], of radiant form, pleasant to behold, and beautiful to look upon,
its edges wreathed in flames that turn the quarters of the sky a deep crimson;
this is my [chariot], dark-hued and blazing, as magnificent as a banner-bearing fire.
The sword Nandaka stands ready, bringing joy and acting as an axe for the trees that are the Daityas.
This [bow] is like the cloud Puṣkarāvartaka amidst the showers from my arrows;
it is the Śārṅga bow, possessing the luster of the lord of serpents and as beautiful as Indra’s rainbow.
I have long borne within my belly these infinite worlds—those that have perished after being born, and those existing now in their many varieties.
This earth is my two feet; this sky is my head.
This body of mine is the three worlds; these directions are my flanks.
I am manifestly Viṣṇu himself, with the luster of the belly of a dark cloud, mounted upon the mountain of Suparṇa, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
All these evil-minded ones flee from me,
like heaps of straw moving restlessly before the wind.
This one, dark as a blue lotus, clad in yellow garments and bearing a mace—
I am Lakṣmī’s lord, mounted upon Garuḍa, Acyuta himself. What person of contrary nature would approach me, who am capable of burning the three worlds,
like a moth approaching the wind-tossed fire at the end of an aeon for its own destruction?
These gods and asuras standing before me are unable to endure my fiery gaze,
just as those with weak eyes cannot bear the light.
These— Brahmā, Indra, Agni, Hara, and the others— [cannot endure] me, the Lord Viṣṇu.
They praise me with infinite speech arising from many mouths:
"I have become one whose sovereignty has expanded, possessing an unconquered form; indeed, by my supreme majesty, I have transcended all states of duality."
I bow to that body which is the singular form within the interior of the abode of the three worlds, which forcibly destroys all wicked beings,
which dwells amidst thick mountains, grass, and forests, and which removes every fear.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Transformation into Nārāyaṇa for the Liberation of Prahlāda."
The thirty-second canto:
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reflected thus, he assumed the form of Nārāyaṇa and [became] Prahlāda.
He reflected once more upon the means for worshipping the Enemy of the Asuras:
"From this body of Viṣṇu, which is both transcendent and immanent,
this other Viṣṇu stands outside through the flow of the vital breath."
Mounted upon Vainateya, with his fourfold power clearly manifest,
holding the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, he has four arms and a dark-complexioned body;
the glorious one, whose eyes are the moon and the sun, who delights in the beautiful Nandaka sword.
He who holds a lotus in his hand, whose eyes are wide, who wields the Śārṅga bow, and who possesses great splendor—
him I shall quickly worship, together with his retinue,
through a mental sacrifice delightful with all necessary offerings.
"Therefore, I shall worship this Mahādeva once again with a great external offering of abundant jewels. Having thus reflected, Prahlāda, bearing a heavy burden of ritual preparations, [proceeded].
In his mind, he worshipped Mādhava, the husband of Kamalā,
with collections of jeweled offering bowls, ointments such as sandalwood paste,
incense, various lamps, and ornaments of diverse splendors.
With garlands of *mandāra* flowers, clusters of golden lotuses,
thickets of *kalpavṛkṣa* creepers, circles of jewel-like blossoms,
sprouts of celestial trees, and various wreaths of flowers;
With *kiṅkirāta*, *buka*, *kunda*, and *caṃpaka* flowers,
with blue lotuses, white water-lilies, *kumuda*, *kāśa*, date palms, mangoes, *kiṃśuka*, *aśoka*, *madana*, *bilva*, *karṇikāra*, and *kirātaka* trees; MU_5,32.11-12.
With *kadamba*, *kukura*, *nīpa*, *sindhuvāra*, and *sayūthika* trees; with *pāribhadra*, *guggulu*, *vidula*, and clusters of *kuyyaka*;
with thickets of *priyaṅgu*, *pāṭa*, *pāṭala*, and *dhātupāṭala*.
With mangoes, hog-plums, bhavya fruits, and chebulic and beleric myrobalans; with the creepers, flowers, and tender shoots of *sāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees;
and with young mango blossoms together with saffron.
With *ketaka* flowers, *saptaparṇa* leaves, and clusters of *irāmañjarī*, with various *pālīvata* blossoms produced from diverse trees,
and with groups of *mālatī* and *mādhavī* vines arising from the *manoharā* tree;
With clusters of fresh *śephālikā* flowers, beautiful as gold,
and with various kinds of food— edibles, chewables, drinks,
lickables, and thick syrups; with juices, fruits, and sprouts of diverse flavors.
With silken garments, beds, and costly vehicles; with golden seats, songs, dances, and instrumental music; with throngs of noble women;
and by offering the full splendor of gardens, groves, and pleasure parks.
With all forms of beauty and honor, and even by offering himself,
Prahlāda worshipped Hari, his lord within the inner apartments, with supreme devotion characterized by the splendor of the entire universe.
Then, in that temple, the lord of the Dānavas worshipped Janārdana with an offering complete with external objects;
by means of those very external things visible to the eye, he worshipped the Supreme Lord in that same sequence.

Having worshipped him again and again, the Dānava became filled with satisfaction. From that time forward, Prahlāda continued to worship the Supreme Lord every single day with complete devotion in that very same manner.
Then, from that time forward, all the Daityas in that city became devoted to Viṣṇu and were indeed auspicious, for the king is the cause of conduct.
News of this reached the sky, the world of the gods, and then Hari.
"Having abandoned their hatred for Viṣṇu, the Daityas remain as his devotees.
O Rāghava, Śakra and the other gods, along with the hosts of Maruts, were filled with wonder: "How is it that the Daityas have indeed taken up devotion to Viṣṇu? (MU 5.32.25–26)
In the Ocean of Milk, seated upon the coils of the serpent, the gods, overwhelmed with wonder,
left the sky and approached Hari, who was resplendent in battle;
there they related to him this account of the Daityas.
And out of wonder at this unprecedented marvel, the gods questioned him as he sat:
"O Blessed One, what is this, that those Daityas who have always been our adversaries [now act thus]?"
For they have attained identity with You; thus it is perceived that "this is Māyā.
Where indeed are those utterly wicked Dānavas who shattered the mountains, and where is devotion to Janārdana, which is obtainable only through a great birth in the West?
"O Blessed One, this report that a common man has been born with such virtues is like a garland of out-of-season flowers— pleasing at first, yet causing distress.
For when something does not belong to its proper place, it does not shine there."
Just as a highly precious gem is found in the midst of a collection of glass trinkets,
so too does every living being attain a state corresponding to its own qualities.
Even among unborn beings who are alike, I do not think a dog would ever find delight anywhere else.
Iron spikes, even when plunged into the body, do not cause such pain as these views of substantial entities,
which are bound together by their dissimilarity;
for whatever is obtained in its proper sequence, appropriate, and irreproachable [is what truly causes suffering].
Only that lotus shines there in the water, but not on dry land.
Where is the base, low-born Dānava, always delighting in vulgar undertakings and inferior deeds—
a wretched being of trivial nature— and where is devotion to Viṣṇu?
Just as a lotus-pond situated on harsh, saline soil does not bring happiness here because it has a poor foundation,
so too, O Lord, the story that even the son of Danu was devoted to Mādhava does not bring us such joy. This concludes the chapter titled "The Speculation of the Gods" in the *Prahlāda-upākhyāna*.
The Thirty-third Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then the slayer of foes [Rāma], toward the roaring and exceedingly agitated world of the gods, spoke.
Mādhava spoke these words, like a cloud to a flock of peacocks:
"O blessed ones, do not be despondent; Prahlāda is truly devoted."
"This is his final birth; he, the subduer of enemies, is worthy of liberation.
From now on, this son of Danu must not undergo conception again, just as a burnt seed cannot produce a sprout."
The wise know that "the virtuous has become devoid of qualities" is a sequence leading to misfortune;
whereas they say that "the one devoid of qualities has become possessed of qualities" is the sequence that grants success.
O best of immortals, [these] are the diverse worlds belonging to themselves.
"Go forth; this daughter of Prahlāda has not been acquired for your own misfortune.
Having spoken thus to the gods there amidst the waves of the Ocean of Milk, Vasiṣṭha—
The god vanished like a cluster of *tāpiñcha* feathers on the bank; and that host of gods, having worshipped Hari, ascended into the sky like a mass of spray from the ocean tossed by Mount Mandara.
Then the gods felt affection toward Prahlāda;
for where great beings are not agitated, there the mind becomes full of trust. Day after day, he worshipped Janārdana, the God of gods.
"In thought, deed, and word, Prahlāda was devoted. Then, as he remained intent on worship, over time his virtues— foremost among them the power of discernment, bliss, and dispassion— increased.
He did not delight in a multitude of enjoyments, like a tree withered of its sap;
nor did he take pleasure in women, like a deer in desert lands. He found no delight in worldly talk, except for the discussion of the meaning of the scriptures.
No delight was born in him for what is seen, like a lotus plant upon dry land;
his mind found no rest in the coloring of the diseases of worldly enjoyment,
like a detached pearl in the depths of the underworld.
Having abandoned the accumulation of enjoyments yet not having reached rest,
his mind alone remained as if fixed upon a swing.
Then, from the hollow of the Ocean of Milk, the body of Kṛṣṇa [assumed] that state of supreme bliss.
He lived there with her, who was all-pervading and supremely beautiful.
Then, by way of the netherworld (pātāla), Viṣṇu, his foremost followers gladdened,
arrived at the temple of Prahlāda for worship.
Having recognized that the god had arrived, the lord of the Daityas honored the lotus-eyed one with redoubled luster and with great reverence;
he worshipped Hari, the god who had entered the hall of worship and stood visibly before him.
Prahlāda, supremely delighted, praised [him] with nourishing words: "Prahlāda said:
[I praise] that supreme light, the treasury of the abode of the three worlds, which is delightful and removes every blemish."
I take refuge in Hari, the unborn Lord, the Sovereign, the infallible one, the worthy refuge, the protector of the helpless.
I take refuge in him who resembles the petals of a blue lotus and a mountain, who is like the hollow of the cloudless autumn sky,
who has the luster of bees, darkness, and collyrium, and who holds a lotus, a discus, and a mace.

I take refuge in that lake of water which is my own heart-lotus: its body is as tender as a cluster of trembling bees; it possesses a conch-shell with the luster of a white lotus bud; it has the bee that is Brahmā humming within its ears;
and it is strewn with the stars that are clusters of white jewels, while its full orb of a moon is the broad face made white by a smile.

I take refuge in Hari, who is like the autumnal sky with the Gaṅgā of the mass of rays from the jewel on his chest; who is the white lotus of the lily-pond of the three worlds; the foremost lamp that dispels the darkness of delusion; the most inert yet non-inert reality of the nature of consciousness; and the remover of all the world's afflictions. MU 5.33.23 I take refuge in Hari, who is the white lotus of the lily-pond of the three worlds; the supreme lamp for the darkness of delusion; the most inert yet non-inert reality of the nature of consciousness; and the remover of all the world's afflictions. MU 5.33.23
I take refuge in Him who is fair as the pollen of a newly blossomed lotus, whose limbs are adorned with the form of a radiant lotus,
who resembles the crimson sky at the time of day’s departure, who is beautiful in garments like gold, and who—
though His play consists in incessantly striking out and creating the worlds— is eternally unborn, undecaying, and all-pervading.
I take refuge in the Child who lies at the foot of a tree, his noble body worn out by a hundred ages.

I take refuge in the All-pervading Lord who dwells in the lotus of the heart; he is the frost-fall for the lotus-pond of the sons of Diti, the ever-rising solar orb for the lotus-pond of the gods, and the flood of water for the lotus-pond of Brahmā.
Vasiṣṭha: Thus honored with words full of many virtues, Hari— the destroyer of demons, whose shoulder is graced by the presence of Śrī,
and whose body is like the petals of a blue lotus— replied to the lord of the Asuras with affection, just as a cloud responds to a joyful peacock.
In the *Prahlāda-upākhyāna*, the thirty-fourth canto, titled "The Arrival of Nārāyaṇa," the Blessed One said:
"O treasure-house of virtues, O great crest-jewel of the Daitya lineage, please accept my further request for a boon in order to pacify the suffering of rebirth. Thus spoke Prahlāda.
"O bestower of the fruits of all intentions, O you who abide within all worlds,
O Lord, instruct me in that which you know to be the most sublime.
The Blessed One said:
"O sinless one, may you possess that discernment which culminates in rest in Brahman, for the sake of completely pacifying all agitation and for the sake of the supreme fruit. Vasiṣṭha said:

Having spoken thus to the lord of the sons of Diti, Viṣṇu vanished like a wave of the ocean subsiding after emitting a gurgling roar. When the god Viṣṇu had disappeared, [he offered] a handful of flowers for worship.
Leaving behind his western seat adorned with jewels and gems, the Dānava then sat down upon a soft, excellent throne in the lotus posture; there,
intent on the performance of reciting hymns, he reflected with deep thought.
"I have been told by the Lord, the enemy of worldly existence: 'May you indeed become one possessed of discernment. Therefore, I shall quickly perform internal reflection within myself:
'What indeed might I be in this grand display of the world?'"
"I speak, I go, I stand, I exert myself, and I take"—
as long as there is this world with its trees, forests, and mountains, which is external and utterly insentient, how indeed could I be that? (MU 5.34.8–9)
Non-existent, yet arisen, mute, it quivers for a moment due to the vital winds;
in a short time, this body dissolves. I am not this insentient thing, which is merely conceptualized by the dull cavity of the ear that lasts but a moment.

I am not the insentient sound, which has an empty form and an empty existence. (MU 5.34.11) Tactile sensation is that which is perceived through the skin—which perishes in an instant—whether it be something reached or otherwise unattained; having attained my self through the clarity of consciousness, I am not insentient. (MU 5.34.12)
I am not the insentient taste, which acquires its nature through the tongue, which is trivial, fickle by its restless essence, characterized by slight vibration, and dependent on material substances;
nor am I that which is dissolved in the seen and the seeing, perishable, and subject to momentary destruction.

I am not the insentient form that has perished in the pure Seer alone; I am not the insentient scent, which is imagined by the utterly inert and perishable nose, being fragile and having no fixed substratum.

Free from possessiveness, free from mentation, peaceful, with the delusion of the five senses gone, I am pure consciousness alone, devoid of parts and their perception. I am this mere consciousness, free from objects of thought, the illuminator.

Pervading both the external and the internal, partless, stainless, and consisting of pure consciousness— now I have remembered all this as the truth: I am this all-pervading Self, the manifestation of non-conceptual consciousness.
By this consciousness, all these things, from jars and cloths up to the sun, are illuminated, just as by a lamp of supreme brilliance; by this,
these various functions of the senses flash forth here.
By means of this internal radiance, just as rows of sparks [are sustained],
these powers of mental reflection flash within;
by means of this all-pervading heat, just as mirages appear in the desert.
By this, the substantiality of these objects is established,
just as the possession of qualities such as whiteness is [revealed] by a lamp for garments.
For this alone is [the reality] of all beings while they are awake.
The Self, the experiencer of all, stands upon the ground like a mirror.
By the grace of this non-conceptual lamp of consciousness,
the sun is hot, the moon is cool, the mountain is solid, and water is liquid.
Through this [discipline], the status of being a "real object" (padārthatva) arises with great intensity for those things experienced continuously,
just as heat arises through intense application of fire.
[This occurs] regarding Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Rudra, who are the causes for the maintenance of the world.
This is the primordial cause; no cause for it exists. From this—causeless, uncreated, the cause of all causes—the world has arisen, just as coldness arises from ice.
Salutations again and again to this Self of mine, which is devoid of names such as "citta," "thinker," "seer," and "seen," and which is eternally manifest.
Within this non-conceptual conscious Self, all beings [are contained].
The qualities abide in and enter the Lord of Beings.
Whatever is indeed conceived by this conscious inner self, that alone comes to be everywhere; nothing else exists, even if it were present.
Whatever is perceived by consciousness attains its own true state;
whatever is not perceived by consciousness here has set, even though it exists.
These rows of hundreds of objects appearing as jars, cloths, and so forth—
The beings of the world are indeed reflected in this vast mirror of space.
Invisible to all living creatures, yet attainable by those whose minds have dissolved,
this supreme space is beheld by the virtuous who are absorbed in it.
In this world, which is subject to increase and decrease,

this multitude of visible phenomena— both existent and non-existent— abides like the reflection of the sun upon a growing or diminishing object. This diversity of the sprout of the perceptible moves toward its own arising.
From this tree of causes, which abounds with the bees of right conduct,
arises this lofty and unstable structure of saṃsāra,
rich with various trees and shrubs, like a forest range rising from a mountain.
This Self of consciousness, the illuminator, is undivided among all those existing within the belly of the three worlds, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
This very one am I— devoid of beginning or end, and possessing a form that is omnipresent.
Within all beings, both moving and unmoving, my own experience abides. These many bodies of mine— both stationary and moving— are beyond all counting.
This very one am I, the single Self, manifesting by the power of my own experience;
because I am the seer of all that is seen, I possess a thousand rays and eyes.
This very one am I in the sky, with the beautiful body of the sun.
I dwell even with another body made of wind that moves through me.
This body of mine is dark blue, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace;
for it sports here in this world as the ultimate limit of all auspiciousness.
I am born here, always seated upon the lotus throne,
established in non-conceptual meditative absorption, and have attained supreme bliss.
With the form of the three-eyed one, I am the bee at the lotus-face of Gaurī.
At the end of creation, I withdraw this world just as a tortoise draws in its limbs.
With my form as Indra, I protect these three worlds,
which have come to me by succession, like an ascetic protects his small hut.
I abide as the sap within the network of grasses, creepers, and shrubs;
from the soil of consciousness, I raise them up like a great creeper from a well.
For the sake of my own play, this beautiful and vast display of the universe has been spread out.
Like a child of noble birth playing with mud,
all this is offered to me; having reached me, it attains existence,
yet once abandoned by me, even though it exists, it is truly nothing at all.
Whatever reflection has come into me, the expansive mirror of consciousness, that alone exists and nothing else; therefore, nothing other than me is found here.
I am the fragrance in flowers, and I am the luster in lotus petals.
I am the aesthetic quality in complexions, and I am the experience within forms.
Whatever is seen here as this world, both moving and unmoving,
that supreme reality of consciousness— devoid of all conceptual construction— is I.

The power consisting of rasa (flavor/essence), which is of the nature of water and whose arising is manifested through the subtle flow [of the breath], exists just as it does in wood and walls; so too do I exist in all things.
I [perceive] that supreme state of existing within the interior of all objects.
Having approached the manifold variety of consciousness, I expand it by my own will.
Just as clarified butter exists within milk and the power of flavor exists within water,
so too do I abide within all beings as the power of consciousness.
This entire world, existing in the three periods of time, is situated within me alone as consciousness—
devoid of the conceptualization of objects of thought, like a mass of things upon the earth. It fills the entirety of the quarters and the interior, having abandoned the delusion of contraction.
Abiding everywhere, the sustainer of all, I stand as the Virāj and the Samrāj.
This vast sovereignty over the world has come to me unasked— a realm where Indra is unbound and the gods are shattered by weapons, yet without precedent.
"Alas! I am indeed expanded; I do not subside within myself by means of the Self in the Self.
Like the single ocean swollen by the winds at the end of an aeon, I find no end within the Self, though it is pure and self-arisen within."
Like a crawling serpent quivering in the ocean of milk,
this small Brahmanic hut called the world is very cramped;
my vast body does not fit within it, like an elephant in a wood-apple.
Beyond the abode of Viriñca, even at the end of the principles (tattvas), he seized my station;
yet my form continues to spread forth even now and does not turn back.
How could this internal sense of "I am named so-and-so" be without support?
"This smallness of mine was, it is said, merely due to my boundless form. The delusion that 'this is you' and 'this is I' is utterly false;
for what is the body, and what is the bodiless, in the case of consciousness whose form is shoreless?"
Wretched and of feeble intellect were my grandfathers,
who, having abandoned this empire, took delight in the splendors of wealth.
Where indeed is this great vision, filled out and expanded by Brahman?

Where are the pleasures that are as terrifying as crawling reptiles compared to the splendors of sovereignty? Victorious among all views is this pure, consciousness-filled vision, which possesses infinite and endless enjoyment and is graced by supreme tranquility.

Salutations again and again to me alone, who am the inner witness-consciousness, whose nature is immediate awareness, and who am the conscious Self liberated from the object of thought, abiding within all beings.
I, having been born, am victorious; the cycle of the world has withered away for me.
"This Self has been attained, this Self has been attained by me; I live and I triumph.
Having abandoned this eternal awakening, which is the supreme sovereignty, I find no delight in the unenjoyable splendors of royal power that are nothing but suffering."
Fie on that wretched worm of the Grandfather (Brahmā), ignorant of the Self, who lusted for this surface of the earth which consists of nothing more than wood, water,
and stone— a consumer of clarified butter made of ignorance through substances whose sole essence is ignorance.
What indeed was accomplished by that ignorant teacher who sought only to gratify himself?
Having spent a few years in this village of the world,
what worthy goal did Hiraṇyakaśipu actually attain?

Without tasting the bliss of tranquility, even one who tastes hundreds of world-empires would have tasted nothing at all in this world. By him who has attained nothing else, this supreme nectar has been reached.
Having attained the inner state, one who is completely filled has attained everything in its undivided entirety.
The fool, having abandoned the immeasurable state, falls back to the measurable; the wise man does not.
For the camel, having abandoned the excellent grass, goes toward the thorn, and no other [animal] does so.
Who, having abandoned this supreme vision, would delight in a scorched kingdom?
What wise man, having rejected sugarcane juice, would drink bitter neem water?
Indeed, all those who were my grandfathers were nothing but fools.
Having abandoned this view, those who take delight in the perils of sovereignty—
where are the blossoming grounds of Nandana, and where are these scorched desert lands?
Where are these peaceful visions of awakening, and where is the self-identification with worldly enjoyments?
There is nothing in the three worlds that is desired as a kingdom;
yet everything exists indeed within the nature of consciousness—why, then, is it not experienced?
[It is experienced] by the intellect that abides in all things, which is pure by its very nature and free from modification.
In every way, at all times, everything is obtained well from every source:
the solar power of light, the lunar flow of nectar,
the great majesty of Brahmā, and the sovereignty over the three worlds belonging to Śakra.
The supreme fullness belongs to Śarva, and the fortune of victory to Vaiṣṇava;
mental power moves swiftly, while the power of Vāyu is strength. The nature of fire is the capacity for burning, and the nature of water is the satisfaction of taste.

The perfection of silence, the great ascetic power, the science of Bṛhaspati, as well as the celestial chariot, the ability to travel through the sky, and stability; Pārvatī-like profundity, oceanic depth, and the great loftiness of Mount Meru.
The splendor of the Sugatas is equanimity; the splendor of the moon is gentleness; the splendor of spring is intoxication and languor;

the splendor of the *mādhavī* creeper is its nature of being composed of flowers; the splendor of autumn is the abundance of grain; the splendor of the Yakṣīs is their illusory power; and the splendor of the sky is its stainlessness.
Coldness consists of that which arises from frost and that which arises from the summer heat;
likewise, there are these and many other states consisting of place, time, and action,
arising from various forms and modifications, situated within the belly of the three times.
The various powers are created by consciousness— which is pure in its commitment, changeless, supreme, and free from the perception of parts—
through the vision of hundreds of all objects while consciousness itself is devoid of conceptual construction.
Just as the radiance of the sun shines forth simultaneously, so too does the earth—
resting within the treasury of all directions and encompassing the multitude of objects throughout the three times— experience [all things] in a single instant.
In that same way, the stainless Consciousness, whose nature is all-pervasive, gathers the splendor of the vast state of the entire objective world throughout the three periods of time;
it simultaneously perceives hundreds of temporal calculations belonging to the three times.
Pure consciousness alone remains, fully expanded through infinite experience;
for consciousness, which has perceived the infinite vision and has grasped the three times,
only fullness— another term for equanimity— remains.
Perceived simultaneously by consciousness— whether through the mild or the pungent— it attains a state of equanimity, like the experience of honey at its conclusion; thus,
by means of that subtle state of consciousness in which all mental constructs have been abandoned.
Through the non-dual nature of existence (*sattā*) which pervades all entities and is of a single form,
the splendor of the various objects of experience— though diverse and interwoven within one another—
is experienced with equality due to their simultaneous perception.
Relying on existence through existence, existence abandons its state of suffering;
but by perceiving existence through non-existence, existence abandons its state of contentment.
[This occurs] for one who has disregarded the three times and is free from the bonds of "is" and "is not."
When the mind has relinquished the object of thought, equanimity alone remains.
Because it is beyond the reach of words, it attains a state as if it were eternally non-existent;
it abides as if it had reached the stage of the established doctrine of selflessness.
The self thus becomes Brahman, whether as nothingness or as the totality;
merged in supreme tranquility, it is designated by the name "liberation" (mokṣa).
However, this world is fashioned by mental construction through its state of dull manifestation.
This consciousness does not see correctly, just as a cataract-afflicted eye;
for that consciousness which is internally enveloped by impurities consisting of desire and lack of desire is indeed unable to rise up, like a bird bound by a snare.
By the very act of conceptualizing, these people have fallen into the snares of delusion like birds caught by a hunter;
they are ensnared by the net of their own volitions and fall into the pits of sensory objects.
This path, free from affliction, was never seen by my grandfathers;
having quivered upon the surface of the earth for only a few days,
those wretched ones perished like mosquitoes in a crevice.
If they had known the truth, those wretched-minded beings, who long for the pleasures that result in suffering,
would not have fallen into the blind wells of existence and non-existence;
for living beings are [trapped] by the delusion of dualities arising from desire and aversion.
They have become equal to insects submerged in the crevices of the earth.
He for whom the mirage of conceptualization— appearing in the forms of what is desired and what is undesired—
is stilled by the cloud of the realization of truth, he truly lives.
Whence indeed could there be the perception of a stain upon this pure, uninterrupted, and stainless form of moonlight-like luster?
Let there be salutation to my own self, whose nature is uninterrupted consciousness.
O Lord, jewel illuminating the world, ah! You have been attained after a long time. You have been grasped, you have been found, and you have arisen after a long duration.
You have been lifted up from all conceptual constructions; whatever you are, you are—that being you, homage be to you!
Salutations to me, to you, to the infinite one; salutations to you, to me, whose nature is auspiciousness;
salutations to the God of gods, the supreme, the Supreme Self—whose own form is like the full orb of the moon from which all clouds have vanished and which is free from the veil of mental constructs.
I bow to that which is joyful in its own body, established in itself by itself, arisen by itself, and possessing its own innate flavor.
The thirty-fifth canto, named "The Yoga of Prahlāda’s Instruction."
Prahlāda said: "Om"—this is the form of that which has been called forth, devoid of all modification;
this very Self is all this, whatever exists within the world.
This conscious being, though transcending fat, bone, flesh, marrow, and blood,
and though situated within, illuminates the sun and other luminaries like a lamp;
it makes fire hot and tastes the nectar-like essence.
He experiences the perceptions of the senses as a sovereign enjoys his pleasures.
For even while standing, he is not seated; even while walking, he does not walk.
Though engaged in worldly affairs, he remains tranquil; though acting, he is not defiled.
In the past, today, and likewise now— in this world, in the next, and in both— he remains equal in all conditions, whether concealed or unconcealed,
through the various mental constructions of arising, subsiding, and non-existence.
He remains pervading the entire world from Brahmā down to a blade of grass;
he is eternally composed of constant vibration because he is ever-moving like the wind,
yet he is eternally inactive even as a pillar, and he is untainted even more than space.
Like the wind agitating sprouts, he agitates the mind;
like a charioteer driving his team of horses, he drives the row of senses.
Always acting as a laborer within the house of the body, he is as if deeply distressed.
Like a sovereign emperor, the all-pervading Lord, established in his own well-being, enjoys the objects of experience.
He alone is always to be sought after, praised, and meditated upon;
by means of him, one transcends old age, death, and delusion, and attains liberation.
This [Self] is exceedingly easy to attain and easy to know, like a trusted kinsman;
it is the bee within the lotus-cavity of the body of everyone.
Even without being drawn or summoned, it is obtained from one's own very body.
Even when summoned for but a moment, he appears before one in an instant. As he is being served, this man who possesses every prosperity does not exhibit pride or arrogance, like a lord of wealth.
Like fragrance in flowers, like oil in sesame seeds,
and like the essential taste in juices, the Lord resides within bodies;
yet, due to a lack of inquiry, this conscious being remains situated only in the heart.
He is not recognized for a long time, like a beloved kinsman who has come before one's eyes;
yet, when this Supreme Lord is fully known through inquiry,
supreme bliss arises, just as it does upon finding a dear person.
When this supreme kinsman, who bestows unrestrained bliss, is seen,
various insights arise through which bondage dissolves;
all bonds are severed on every side, and all enemies are destroyed.
Hopes do not tear at the mind, like wicked rats gnawing at houses.
When this is seen, the world is seen; when this is heard, everything is heard;
when this is touched, the world is touched; and when this is established, the world is established.
He keeps watch over those who sleep; he strikes down those lacking discernment;
he removes the calamity of the afflicted; and he bestows [the fruit of their merit] upon those who are not great-souled. He wanders through the worlds like a lamp for the stability of the universe.
This living being sports in enjoyments and flashes forth among objects;
yet, by means of the self, he experiences the self alone within himself through tranquility,
remaining present in all bodies like pungency in black peppers.
Formless, consisting of volition and calculation, it rests upon both the external and the internal;
it abides as the universal existence of the multitude of objects in the world.
This is emptiness in space, and this is movement in the wind.
In luminous bodies, he is light; in water, he is the supreme essence.
He is solidity in the earth, heat in the fire, coolness in the moon, and he is existence within the multitude of worlds.
Just as blackness resides in a lump of ink, whiteness in a particle of snow,
and fragrance in flowers, so does the master of the body reside within the body.
Just as existence is all-pervading, and just as time is all-pervading, [so is the Self].
Just as the all-pervading sky is omnipresent, so too is the Lord omnipresent.
Just as the sovereign power of a monarch extends to every land,
so the essence of the Self is free from form, light, and mental activity.
This very one is the eternal God, the awakener of the gods;
I am myself the Self, and indeed no other mental construction exists for me,
just as the sky is not affected by a tiny speck of dust or a lotus leaf by water.
Just as there is no connection between a stone and agitation, so there is no connection between me and sin.
Let the fortunes of pleasure and pain fall upon the body or not;
what injury can befall us when they fall upon a gourd?
Just as light reaching the wick of a lamp is not bound by the cord,
even so am I unbound, transcending the entire multitude of existents.
What connection indeed can there be for me with desires, with existence and non-existence, or with the senses?
With what is space connected, or by what is the mind grasped?
When the body is shattered into a hundred pieces, what injury is there for the embodied soul?
When a jar is broken, wounded, or destroyed, what loss is there for the space within the jar?
Like an invisible *piśāca*, the mind has arisen in vain;
what loss has befallen us when that inert thing is destroyed through awakening?
That mind of mine consists of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of pleasure and pain.
In the past there was nothing; today, indeed, a single state of bliss has been attained.
One enjoys, another takes [the fruit], while another faces a crisis of misfortune;
one observes—oh, what folly! To whom indeed does this cycle belong?
Nature experiences and the mind undergoes the body's distress;
the witnessing Self is merely present here through ignorance—what loss is there for me?
I have no desire for the persistence of enjoyment, nor for its cessation.
Let that which comes come; let that which departs depart.
I have no expectation for pleasures, nor do I have aversion toward states of suffering.
Let joys and sorrows approach or depart; who am I in relation to them?
Let the various latent impressions (vāsanās) in the body go to their setting or their rising;
I am not among them, nor do any of these belong to me.
For all this time, I have been [bound] by the vast enemy that is ignorance.
Having plundered the entire essence of discernment and utterly crushed him in solitude,
this one has now been completely destroyed by me, once he was recognized as my own, through the beautiful grace of Viṣṇu arising from within myself.
This demon of egoism, which dwelt within the hollow of the tree of my body,
has now been driven away by me with the mantra of supreme awakening.
Now that this great yakṣa of egoism is gone, this great tree of my body stands free of its haunt.

Having fully attained a state of merit, he shines like one in full bloom. With the poverty of delusion stilled and the defect of evil desires destroyed, I stand as the Supreme Lord through the accumulation of the wealth of discernment.
All that is to be known has been known, and all sights to be seen have been seen;
that which remains here to be attained has now been attained by me.
By good fortune, I have cast away all misfortune and am free from the serpents of the sense-objects.

I have reached the vast and elevated ground of ultimate reality, where the mist of delusion has been completely stilled, where the mirage of worldly desires has subsided, where all quarters are free from passion, and where the tree of tranquility provides cooling shade.
Through praise, prostration, petition, tranquility, and self-restraint, this Blessed Self has been obtained; it has clearly been seen and realized.
Having transcended the state of egoism, it has finally returned to my recollection.
The Blessed One is the self, Viṣṇu, the eternal Brahman.
[He dwells] amidst the pits of the serpents that are the senses, upon the ground of the chasms of death,
within the thickets of the *karañja* trees of craving, and amidst the clamor of desire.
Within the nets of the forest of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), amidst the interior wells of rebirth,
in the burning of the forest-fire of suffering, and bearing the coals of misdeeds—
amidst hundreds of thousands of states of falling and rising, and the delusions of sinking and emerging.
Through appearances and disappearances, and by being entangled in the snares of desire,
I have for a long time been utterly crushed by the enemy that is egoism—
like a man of little fortitude in the night, beset by a demon in the forest.

Indeed, by your own power of action, and through your very self under the designation of Śauri’s speech, the splendor of discernment has now been awakened. Once the Lord is awakened, that demon of egoism— MU 5.35.56. The following is a list of the main characters in the Mahabharata: Dhritarashtra - The blind king of Hastinapura who fathered one hundred sons with his wife Gandhari. He was the father of Duryodhana and the uncle of the Pandavas. Gandhari - The wife of Dhritarashtra and mother of the hundred Kaurava brothers. She was blindfolded from birth as a sign of her devotion to her husband's blindness. Yudhishthira - The eldest of the five Pandava brothers, known for his righteousness and adherence to dharma. Bhima - The second of the Pandavas, famous for his immense strength and appetite. Arjuna - The third of the Pandavas, a skilled archer and the closest friend of Krishna. Nakula - The fourth of the Pandavas, known for his beauty and skills in horsemanship. Sahadeva - The youngest of the Pandavas, noted for his wisdom and knowledge of astrology. Krishna (Vasudeva) - The divine incarnation of Vishnu, acting as the charioteer and advisor to Arjuna during the Kurukshetra war. Duryodhana - The eldest son of Dhritarashtra and the primary antagonist of the Pandavas. Shakuni - The cunning maternal uncle of Duryodhana, known for his gambling skills. Karna - A powerful warrior who sided with the Kauravas, though he was actually the eldest son of Kunti born before her marriage to Pandu. Draupadi (Krishnaa) - The wife of the five Pandavas, central to many of the epic's conflicts. Ashwatthama - The son of Drona and one of the most formidable warriors on the Kaurava side. Drona - The teacher of both the Pandavas and Kauravas, and a key military commander. Bhishma - The great-grandfather of the Pandavas and Kauravas, known for his wisdom and martial prowess. Abhimanyu - The son of Arjuna and Subhadra, killed early in the Kurukshetra war. Sanjaya - The bard and charioteer who narrated the events of the war to Dhritarashtra. Dhritarashtra's Sons (Kauravas) - The hundred sons of Dhritarashtra and Gandhari, led by Duryodhana. Other Notable Figures: Virata - King of Virata, whose kingdom the Pandavas lived in disguise during their thirteenth year of exile. Kichaka - Virata's brother-in-law and a villainous general. Draupadi's Siblings - The five sons of Draupadi, including Prativindhya, Sutasoma, Shrutakarman, Shatanika, and Shrutasena. Shikhandi - Born female, she became a man to challenge Bhishma in battle. Balarama - The elder brother of Krishna, a mighty warrior who did not participate in the war. Uttara - Virata's daughter, who disguised herself as a man to fight alongside Abhimanyu. The Mahabharata features a vast array of other characters, including gods, sages, demons, and various kings and warriors from different regions of ancient India. Each character plays a significant role in the epic's complex narrative of family strife, moral dilemmas, and the ultimate battle for the throne of Hastinapura. "O Lord, I do not see [it], just as one does not see darkness when a lamp is lit. O Master, I do not know the destination of that demon of egoism who dwells in the hollow of the mind, once it has been extinguished like a lamp."
As soon as you, O Lord, were seen, that thief consisting of intoxication and egoism became intent on flight, like the darkness at the rising of the sun;
for that demon of egoism had arisen from what was unreal.
I abide in peace, perfectly well, like a tree from which all serpents have departed. I am stilled;
I am extinguished; I am awake; I am possessed of awakening. I have been released by the thief; after a long time, I am finally at rest.
I have attained internal coolness, having quelled the deer-thirst of my desires;
I am like a mountain bathed by the heavy rains of the monsoon, its forest fires extinguished.
Through inquiry, I have cleansed this notion of "I" within the context of the ultimate reality.
What is delusion? What are the sufferings? What are the evil desires? What is the heat?
(63) Delusions such as hell, heaven, and liberation proceed only when there is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkṛti*), just as the activity of painting occurs on a wall and not in the sky. (64)
When the mind is swollen with the mass of egoism, the wondrous essence does not shine forth,
just as the coloring of saffron does not shine upon a faded garment.
But when the cloud of egoism has vanished and the rain of craving has ceased— MU 5.35.65.
In the autumn sky of the mind, there shines a clarity endowed with radiant beauty. To you, the Self— for whom the mire of egoism has vanished, whose interior is perfectly serene,
and who are an ocean of bliss— I offer salutation after salutation.
Salutations again and again to me, who am like a mountain of bliss, resting at peace; whose clouds of ego have vanished, and for whom the forest fire of desire has been extinguished.
Salutations to him in whom the fierce crocodiles of the senses have been stilled, and the submarine fire of the mind has been exhausted.
Salutations again and again to you, O Self, who are for me an ocean of bliss;
salutations within to you, O Self, who are for me a mind-unmaddened one, whose lotus of bliss is in full bloom and whose great waves of thought are stilled.
Salutations again and again to my own inner Self, who dwells within the hollow of the lotus for the sake of the position that consciousness is a manifestation, who is the swan in the minds of all,
whose form is fashioned by its parts yet is partless and infinite in essence.

Salutations again and again to you, the moon of the Self, who is eternally risen and utterly full. Salutations again and again to the sun of consciousness, which is eternally risen, cool, the dispeller of the great darkness of the heart, all-pervading, yet invisible.

Salutations again and again to the lamp of consciousness, which is ignited by the oil of its own nature, which has transcended the wick, and which is steadfast in its natural support. The mind, heated by the fire of reflection, is cooled by the coolness of the [higher] mind.
I have severed the internal [self] by means of the self, like iron forcibly [piercing] iron.
Having repeatedly severed the senses with the senses, and the mind with the mind, and having severed egoity with egoity, I remain as the Residue; thus I am victorious. (MU 5.35.75–76)
Having crushed existence with non-existence, having severed craving with non-craving,
and having crushed ignorance with wisdom, the ignorant one was joined by me to the Knower.
When the mind has been severed within the mind and has attained a state free from egoism, [he is liberated].
When all objective states have dissolved through the realization of Being, I remain established in myself, absolute.
My body remains as a machine consisting of the pure Self and its mere vibration— devoid of objects, devoid of ego, without mind, and free from desire.
This liberation has arisen for me, which is endowed with supreme tranquility and exerts its sole effort toward the infinite universe fashioned by play;
the vampire of delusion is stilled, and the demon of egoism has departed.
"Free from the form of the wicked, I have become one whose fever has departed.
Having cut the net of the rope of craving,
I know not where the bird of evil egoism has flown away from the cage of my body."
In this tree of the body, whose nest of dense ignorance has been shaken up,
I know not where the bird of egoism has flown away. Tawny with the ashes of enjoyments, it is stained by the long-standing wickedness of evil desires.
"By good fortune, my friend, the latent tendencies that were struck down by fear have died out.
For how long a time was I such a mind, by which I myself falsely fell into a state of firm egoism? (MU 5.35.84–85)

Today I am truly born; today I have become one of great intelligence, for I have been completely liberated from the great cloud of egoism by Kṛṣṇa. This Lord, the Self, has been seen and realized within me.
Seized and experienced within his own body, he was joined with that experience;
his mind has reached its resting place, free from thought, free from longing, and has cast aside the subtle delusion of egoism.
Devoid of effort, stripped of the coloring of passion, and free from curiosity, this mind has attained perfect tranquility.
The great calamities—difficult to cross over, alternating between even and uneven, most hard to endure, and productive of long-lasting faults—have come to an end.
Maheśvara has attained his goal; he is the imperishable consciousness, with the fluctuations of the mind vanished within.
This is the chapter titled "Reflection on the Attainment of the Self by Prahlāda."
The thirty-sixth canto: Prahlāda.
O Self, after a long time, you have returned to memory, though you transcend all states.
"By good fortune you have been found, O Blessed One! Homage be to You, the Self of Consciousness!
Having saluted and gazed upon You, I embrace You fully.
Who else in the three worlds, O Blessed One, could be a kinsman other than You?"
You strike, you protect, you give; you praise, you go, you leap about.
You have arrived, you are seen; what do you do? Where are you going?
O you who fill the entire universe with your own existence, O friend of all people!
"You are always perceived everywhere; where can you flee now?
The vast distance between us, separated by many births, has today become no distance at all. By good fortune, O kinsman, you have been seen!"
Homage to you who have accomplished all that was to be done; homage be to you, the creator and the destroyer. Homage to the eternal, stainless self, who performs the dance of saṃsāra.
Homage to him whose hands hold the discus and the lotus; homage to the wearer of the crescent moon.
Homage to the Lord of the Wise; homage to you, O Lotus-born One!

This distinction between us here, which exists only through the perspective of the signified and the signifier, is a mere unreal conceptual construction, like that between a wave and the water of the wave.
It is you alone who manifest here eternally through this infinite [power] that takes the form of the manifold variety of endless objects, and which sports with both existence and non-existence.
Homage to the Seer! Homage to the Fashioner! Homage to the one of infinite expansion!
Homage to you whose nature is all things; homage to you who go everywhere!
For many births, for a long time, I have been possessed by great sin, scorched by your illusion and smeared with it, enduring manifold and protracted sufferings.
The conditions of the world have been observed by you, and various illustrative examples have been seen;
yet you have not attained that by which anything at all could be acquired.
This entire world is merely earth, wood, stone, and water.
O God, there is nothing here besides you that, once attained, is not desired.
Today you have been found by me, seen, and reached;
you have been obtained and seized—salutations to you, for you shall not be released.
How is it that the God, whose body is interwoven with the network of rays from the pupils of his eyes, and who exists in the form of vision, is not seen within? And he who,
touching the skin-flower, perceives touch and fragrance, just as one finds oil in a sesame seed— how is he not seen?
This [consciousness] internalizes touch; how then is it not experienced?
When one, upon hearing a sound, internally reflects upon the supreme power of that sound and it produces horripilation on the body, how could that [power] be something situated at a distance?
To whom would he not be pleasing— he whose tongue, like a sprout, relishes objects even from his own past body? Taking up the fragrance of flowers with the hand of the nose, he delights the body.
Whose mouth does he not reside with affection when he anoints it? How indeed can that Self,
who is sung of through the Vedas, the Vedāntas, the established tenets, logic, and the songs of the Purāṇas,
be forgotten once He has been known?
O Lord, that very same row of enjoyments, though so auspicious, does not please me today within, now that You—
the supreme and the non-supreme— have been seen by me in Your own clarity.
By You, the stainless lamp, the sun has been made manifest.
By you, who are cool as frost, the moon has attained its chill;
by you these heavy mountains have been supported, and by you these sky-dwellers are sustained.
By you alone this earth is held firm, and by you alone the sky is covered.
"By good fortune you have attained me; by good fortune I have come to you.
O Lord, I am you and you are I; by good fortune there is no difference between us.
By means of the two synonymous words "I" and "you," [he spoke] of the Great Self.
O virtuous one, salutations again and again to both you and me, who are united.
Salutations to me, the infinite, whose nature is free from ego;
salutations to me, the formless; salutations to the abode of tranquility.
While abiding here in one's own Self—which is identical with me, the Self; which is even, pure, the witness, and devoid of attributes;
and which is unconditioned by space, time, and the like—the mind undergoes agitation as the perceptions of the senses flash forth.
The vast power (*śakti*) that flows as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the downward breath (*apāna*) shines forth;
it draws along the machines of the body, which are smeared with skin, flesh, and bone, and possess the mind as their charioteer. These machines are driven by the threefold wheel of desire.
I am this very embodiment of consciousness, established nowhere;
let the body fall or rise according to its own desired will.
After a long time, I have become "I," and after a long time, this attainment of my own self has arisen.

After a long time, I shall attain peace, just as the world does at the end of a kalpa. Having traveled through saṃsāra for so long upon the path of the vast cycle of existence, I am weary; I have come to rest like the wind at the end of a kalpa.
Salutations again and again to You, who transcend all and encompass all;
salutations indeed also to those who speak of You as "I" or as "me.
Possessing entirely infinite enjoyment, You are untouched by perceptions of defect.
Victorious is the witnesshood of the Supreme Self, which requires no prior accumulation [of causes].
O Self, you abide everywhere within this body, like fragrance in a flower, like fire in a mass of fuel, and like oil in a sesame seed.
You laugh, you watch, you give, you thunder forth, and you leap;
though your form is free from egoism, this illusory power of yours is wondrous.
O Lord, you are victorious, blazing with light and causing the entire world to unfold.
O Jayanta, as you close once more this world whose activity has ceased,
this entire circle of saṃsāra exists within your very atom;
just as the banyan tree exists within the banyan seed, it has been, it is, and it will be.
Just as a cloud is seen in the sky in the forms of horses, elephants, and chariots,
so too, O Lord, are you perceived through the delusions of hundreds of objects.
You are the sovereign of existence for the sake of bringing about the cessation of the manifold fluctuations of worldly becoming.
Become one whose self is liberated from becoming, cast out from both existence and non-existence.
Abandon pride, intoxication, anger, turbidity, and likewise cruelty;
the great do not sink into the common mire of the qualities (guṇas).
Remembering again and again those former states of long-standing wickedness, laugh with a white burst of laughter like a shower of pearls, thinking: "Who am I? What was that which occurred?
Those undertakings have departed; those wasted days are gone.
