In those [previous bodies], you were withered by the mass of flames from the fire of anxiety;
today, however, you are the king in the city of the body, with vast desires,
and are seized neither by sorrows nor by pleasures, like the sky cannot be grasped by hands.
Today, having conquered the horses of the senses and subdued the elephant of the mind,
you have shattered the enemies of worldly enjoyment on all sides and now preside over universal sovereignty.
You are a traveler upon the boundless sky, forever rising and setting.
O Lord, you are eternally the illuminator both externally and internally, like the sun; though always in deep sleep, you are perceived through your own power,
for the sake of the play of observing enjoyments, just as a lover is perceived by his beloved.

The honey of forms brought from afar by the bees of sight is drunk by you, having been taken possession of through the power residing in the window of the eyes. The winds of the vital breaths (prāṇa and apāna) exhaled from the hollow of the cosmic egg are inhaled by you.
In the city of Brahman, you are perceived at every moment through comings and goings.
You are the fragrance in the flower of the body; you are the nectar of immortality in the moon of the body. You are the sap in the tree of the body; you are the coolness in the frost of the body.
In you resides a consciousness-filled affection for this body, like ghee in milk;
you abide within this body like fire within wood. You are the supreme essence of waters, and the luminosity of all lights.
You are the perceiver of objects; you are the illuminator of lights.
You are the vibration of all winds; you are the rut of the elephant that is the mind.
You are the brilliance and the sharpness of the flame of the fire of wisdom.
By your power, illusion dissolves away somewhere like a lamp,
and like a lamp, it arises again from some source elsewhere; likewise,
the cycles of objects existing within the world-process [dissolve and arise] in you.
Just as bracelets, armlets, and earrings are merely arrangements of gold,
so too do you, by means of words such as "this one," "I," and "you," playfully praise and speak of yourself as the Self through the Self alone.

Just as a cloud driven by a gentle breeze is perceived in the sky by the gaze of elephants, horses, and men, so too are you perceived by the gaze of living beings. Just as a flame flickers within fires in the forms of horses and elephants, [so do you appear].
In that very same way, you dwell within all creations, inseparable from the objects of perception.
You are the unbroken thread stretched across the pearls of the cosmic eggs;
you are the field for the crops of living beings, who are watered by the elixir of consciousness.
That which was non-existent and unmanifest among objects is made manifest by you, just as the experience of the flavor of meats is revealed by a cook; yet,
even though the splendor of existing things exists, it does not abide in you when you are not present.

Just as the beauty and grace of a woman is of no avail to one whose eyes have closed, so too an object, even if it exists here, does not possess true existence for you if it has not been perceived by you;
nor does one's own beauty reflected in a mirror lead to satisfaction.
Without you, this body rolls upon the ground like a piece of wood or a clod of earth;
though it exists, it is as if non-existent, like the night without the sun.
Upon encountering you, the succession of pleasure and pain comes to an end.
Just as darkness, light, or even frost, having attained visibility, [are perceived],
so too do pleasure and the other [feelings] attain their existence only through your gaze,
just as white and other colors appear in the morning by the light of the sun.

Having attained their own nature, they perish at the very moment of their connection; like darkness before a lamp, they utterly vanish as soon as they are seen. Darkness is the absence of light, and thus it becomes manifest only when light is absent.
At the very moment of contact with the lamp, she arises and perishes.
In the same way, the fortune of pleasure and pain, upon seeing you who are free from affliction, is born;
as soon as it is born, it perishes through total destruction.
Because of its fragility, it is not capable of remaining here for even an atom of time,
just like a minute fraction of time known as a hundred-thousandth part of a blink.
Transient, perishable, and subtle, it is the mental state consisting of pleasure, pain, and the like.
By your grace it throbs; when you are seen, it dissolves.
Arising at the very moment of beholding you, perishing at the very moment of beholding you—it is as if dead though born, and as if born though dead; by whom can it be perceived?
How could an entity that is unstable even for a moment perform an action?
How, indeed, can a garland be woven from waves that take the form of lotuses?
If an entity were to perform an action after having been produced and then perished, [it would be impossible].
Then this world would begin to fashion a garland out of the qualities of lightning;
yet you, abiding in the minds of those possessed of discernment, neither grasp nor abandon this fortune consisting of pleasure and the like, remaining perfectly equanimous.
O you who are devoid of discrimination, O soul of existence, enough of this description of your form by chance, O abode of the stainless state! For you are effortless, partless, and free from egoism.
Agency has been accepted both by the existent and by the non-existent.
Victory to you of formidable form! Victory to you who are devoted to peace!
Victory to you who transcend all scriptures! Victory to you who are the foundation of all scriptures!

Victory to you, O Born! Victory to you, O Unborn! Victory to you, O Wounded! Victory to you, O Unwounded! Victory to you, O Being! Victory to you, O Non-being! Victory to you, O Conquerable! Victory to you, O Invincible! I exult, I am stilled, I remain, and I have transcended.
I am victorious; I conquer; I live. Salutations to me, and salutations be to you!

(MU 5.36.79) While you abide in me—my own self established in its true state, free from disease and untainted by the dye of passion—where are my kinsmen, where are calamities, where are prosperities, and where are existence and non-existence? I attain eternal peace. (MU 5.36.80)
The thirty-seventh canto in the *Prahlāda-upākhyāna*, titled "Self-Praise," by Vasiṣṭha:
While reflecting thus, Prahlāda, the slayer of enemy heroes,
attained the state of non-conceptual absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) which is supreme bliss.
Established in that non-conceptual absorption, he remained motionless, like a figure depicted in a painting.
Established in his own state, he shone as if carved out of a mountain;
and as he remained thus, a vast amount of time passed for him in his own home, like that of the enemy of the gods (Rāvaṇa) staying on Mount Meru in the world.
Even though the lords of the asuras were awakened, the one of great intelligence did not wake;
like a sprout within its sheath, even with abundant watering at the wrong time,
he remained for five thousand years with broad shoulders and a single gaze.
In the city of the Asuras, he was indeed tranquil, like a stone in a churning ocean;
through that state which was entirely transformed into the condition of supreme bliss,
he reached the state of manifestation that was as if devoid of bliss and without appearance.

After this much time, that realm of Rasātala became kingless and was tormented by the harsh law of the fishes (*mātsyanyāya*). When Hiraṇyakaśipu had perished and his son remained absorbed in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), [the situation continued].

There was no other king at all in the abode of the sons of Danu. Because of his meditative concentration, Prahlāda could not be awakened by those lords of the asuras, even with the dānavas' supreme efforts directed toward that end.
There, the enemies of the gods did not attain their blossoming form before their lord,
just as bees at night do not reach a lotus whose mass of light from its petals is shining; nor did the wind of consciousness perceive the interior of him who was devoid of perception.
The human-like activity of the earth was like that of the sun when it has set.
Then, while the Daityas were agitated and had departed for their desired directions,
they wandered at will from city to city in a state of lawlessness.
Due to that absence of kings, the circle of the netherworld became devoid of sovereigns; it was overturned by the law of the fish (*mātsyanyāya*), its succession of virtues had vanished,
and the cities of the weak were devoured by the strong, stripped of all order and restraint.
With all its women rendered helpless and their lives destroyed by one another,
the interior of the city was filled with harsh lamentations and wailing;
gardens and towns lay in ruins, rolling in the dust, tormented by futile calamities.
The host of gods was overcome by anxiety, their kinsmen were deprived of food and fruit;
helpless before an untimely calamity, the circle of the quarters was destroyed;
they were humiliated by the children of the gods and assailed by other elemental beings.

Devoid of living beings, lacking prosperity, with its hollows almost entirely ruined; filled with the cries of those who had lost their wealth and wives due to battles intoxicated by women of uncertain character;
resembling the belly of the fierce Kali Yuga—thus did that host of Asuras become utterly agitated.
The thirty-eighth canto, titled "Description of the Destruction of the Asura City," in the Narrative of Prahlāda. Vasiṣṭha said:

Then, Hari— the destroyer of enemies, who delights in protecting the order of the entire web of worlds— having risen from his bed upon Śeṣa in the city of the Milk Ocean at the end of his summer sleep, [prepared] for the sake of the gods.
Once, with his intellect, he surveyed the condition of the world;
having observed the realm of the gods and the earthly realm with his own mind,
he quickly proceeded to Pātāla, which was protected by his enemies.

There, while Prahlāda the Dānava remained established in steady meditative concentration, he beheld the calamity that had befallen the lord of his enemies as it reached its full maturity within the city;
[he saw it] like one lying upon the bed of serpents, reclining upon the Ocean of Milk.
Moving within the body of the one who holds the conch, discus, and mace,

seated upon the lotus throne, he— whose mind and body were exceedingly radiant and who resembled the great bee of the lotus of the three worlds— reflected thus: *padmāsanasthasya manaśśarīreṇātibhāsvatā / idaṃ sañcintayām āsa trailokyābjamahālinā //* MU_5,38.6
When Prahlāda has found rest in his station and the leader of the netherworld has departed,
alas, this creation has for the most part become devoid of Daityas.
In the absence of the Daityas, the host of gods has reached a state where there is no one left to conquer.
It will come to rest like a great river when the mass of clouds has vanished;
then it will reach that state called liberation, free from duality,
its conceit exhausted and devoid of passion, like a withered creeper reaching total dryness.
When the flood of gods has attained peace, all sacrificial and ascetic acts on earth,
which have the state of being a god as their fruit, will undoubtedly come to rest.
And when these acts have ceased, the world of mortals will reach its end.
Furthermore, there will be no consequence of non-cyclic existence, and the remaining purpose will also be fulfilled:
"This triple world which has been created by me shall reach its dissolution before its time at the end of the kalpa, like a drop of frost under the heat."
"What has been achieved by me here, who have brought about the destruction of my own sport, now that this appearance has thus dissolved and reached its end?
Then I too [disappeared] in this void where the moon, sun, and stars had perished."

"Taking with me the tranquility of my body, I shall abide in that state. For if the world were thus to come to rest so abruptly, I see no good in this; I think rather that the Dānavas should live on."
Due to the agitation caused by the Daityas, the gods' sacrificial rites and ascetic practices were then disrupted;
because of that, the established order of the world was overturned and the course of worldly existence became otherwise.
Therefore, having gone to Rasātala, I shall restore everything to its proper state.
In his own station, he is like the season renewing a tree;
yet, if I were to appoint any other lord of the Dānavas instead of Prahlāda,
I believe that he would utterly destroy the gods.
"But this body of Prahlāda is his final one; it is purifying and great.
He must dwell here with this very body until the end of the kalpa.
For such is the fixed destiny ordained by the Supreme Lord."
"A living being must remain here according to its destiny, just as Prahlāda did.
Therefore, having gone quickly to that very lord of the Daityas, I shall awaken him,
just as a rain-cloud awakens a peacock sleeping in a mountain cave with its thunder."
Let one who is liberated while living and established in samādhi assume the lordship of the asuras,
just as a gem that is free from mental activity reflects an image.
Thus, this creation, together with the gods and asuras, does not perish.
And it shall not be without a counterpart; that will be my play.
Although these two—the destruction and the arising of creation—are perfectly equal for me, nevertheless, let this proceed according to its established order; what does it matter to me otherwise?

That effort which, due to a corrupt intellect, is applied equally toward existence and non-existence, or toward their destruction or their persistence, would be like striking at empty space. Therefore,
I shall go to the netherworld to awaken the Lord of the Asuras.
I bring stability to saṃsāra; I accomplish my divine play (līlā).
Having reached the city of the Asuras, which is terrible with its arrogant conduct, I awaken the Daitya as the sun awakens the lotus.
I bring this entire world, established upon all things, to a state of stability, just as a powerful rite brings the flickering mass of clouds to rest upon a mountain.
In the *Prahlāda-ākhyāna*, the thirty-ninth canto, titled "The Inquiry Concerning the Supreme Lord," Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus reflected, O Rāma, the Soul of All moved from the Ocean of Milk toward that city,
together with his retinue, like a mountain accompanied by clouds;
he went through that very opening at the bottom of the Ocean of Milk, whose waters had been solidified.
He reached the city of Prahlāda, which was like another realm of Śakra;
there Hari saw the Asura seated within a treasury of golden palaces,
like the lotus-born Brahmā reclining in a mountain cave absorbed in meditative concentration.
There, shaken by that Vaiṣṇava splendor,
those Daityas fled far away like owls terrified by the rays of the sun.
Hari, accompanied by two or three principal Asuras, remained surrounded by his retinue.
He entered the abode of the Asuras, like the moon entering the sky with its stars;
seated upon the son of Vinatā (Garuḍa), fanned by chowries that were Lakṣmī herself,
surrounded by his own weapons and attendants, and praised by divine sages.

"O Great-Souled One, awaken!"— uttering these words, Viṣṇu blew his conch Pāñcajanya, making the quarters of the sky resound. By that great sound, born from the breath of Viṣṇu, [the world was filled].
Simultaneously, with the force of an ocean of clouds agitated at the end of an eon,
the demonic host fell to the earth in utter confusion,
like a row of royal swans at the roar of dark storm-clouds.
The host of Vaiṣṇavas, their joy aroused and their agitation gone,
rejoiced like a row of *kuṭaja* trees blossoming at the roar of a rain-cloud.
The lord of the Dānavas gradually became one whose self was fully awakened.
Like a kadamba tree in the forest, its flowers radiant with the sound of clouds;
then the power of breath (prāṇa-śakti), having arisen from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
gradually overcame the demon, just as the Gaṅgā overwhelms the entire ocean.

In an instant, the splendor of his vital breaths overran the asura on all sides, just as the solar radiance, immediately upon its rising, pervades the interior of the world. Then, as his nine apertures were set in motion by the vital breaths, his consciousness—
It became inwardly oriented toward consciousness, reflected upon the mirror of the vital breath.

When the intellect was thus oriented toward consciousness, the *cit* attained the state of the mind (*manas*), like the beauty of a face appearing as a double image reflected in a mirror, O Rāghava. (MU 5.39.14–15)
When his mind had slightly sprouted and his eyes were about to open,
they gradually became like two blue lotuses at dawn;
his consciousness was then focused upon the openings of the channels (nāḍī) touched by the prāṇa and apāna breaths.

Like a lotus afflicted by the wind, a trembling arose within him. In the mere space of a blink, his mind attained fullness, as it were a wave upon water when it is filled by the force of the vital breath.
Then, with his eyes, mind, breath, and body blossoming,
he shone like a lake of lotuses when the sun has half-risen. At that moment, as soon as the Lord said, "Awaken!"
He had become awakened, like a peacock at the roar of a thundercloud.
With eyes blossoming, his mind born anew, and his memory restored,
the Lord of the Three Worlds spoke to him just as he had formerly spoken to the one born from the navel-lotus.
"O virtuous one, remember Mahālakṣmī; remember your own true form.
Why do you bring about the cessation of this body so prematurely? For one who is free from the mental constructs of what is to be rejected or accepted, [what concern are] the bodily states?"
"What purpose of yours is served by existence and non-existence? Arise now!
You must remain here with this body for as long as this kalpa lasts, O blameless one, for we know destiny exactly as it is."

Remaining here in this very kingdom as one liberated while living, you must spend this body— free from anxiety— until the end of the kalpa. O sinless one, when your body has perished at the end of the kalpa, you shall abide in your own majesty.
One should dwell [in this state] even when the jar has shattered, just as the space within the jar remains in the sky.
This body of yours has become pure, enduring until the end of the eon, having perceived the higher and lower worlds, and sporting in the liberation while alive.
The twelve suns have not risen, nor have the mountains melted;
O virtuous one, the world has not been consumed by fire—why then do you abandon your body in vain?
The wind does not blow madly, turning the three worlds grey with ashes.
Why do you abandon your body in vain, O you who bear the mark of the playful skull of the god of love?
Like blossoms on an *aśoka* tree, the lightning-flashes of the Puṣkarāvarta clouds no longer flicker within the vessel of the world; why do you abandon your body in vain?
The quarters of the sky, with mountains resounding under torrential rains and blazing with flaming fires, do not crumble; why then do you abandon your body in vain?
This world does not end with the triad known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
Why do you vainly cast off this body that remains like a withered cloud?
The clouds of the cosmic dissolution do not roar in the sky with terrifying sounds like the crashing of great mountain peaks; why do you vainly cast off this body?

I, whose banner is the bird, dwell in the ten directions amidst the worlds filled with living beings; do not disregard the body. These are we, these are the mountains, these are the living beings, and this is you.
This is the world, this is the void; do not despise the body.
For one whose mind is agitated by the force of thick ignorance, sufferings cut him down, and for him, death alone shines forth.

"I am emaciated, exceedingly miserable, and deluded"—these and other such reflections rob one's mind; for such a person, death is preferable. Bound within by the snares of hope, one is led here and there.
Death shines for him whose mental activity is restless;
death shines for him whose heart is shattered by cravings that have stolen away his spiritual cultivation, just as gargatya-carpers destroy a wretched house.
For one whose creeper of mental fluctuations has grown as high as a palm tree in the forest of the mind,
death shines forth when it bears fruit through pleasure and pain. For one who possesses this wretched tree of a body, with its network of creepers being the line of body hair—
Death shines forth for him whom the flood of misfortune sweeps away;
death shines forth for him whose forest of his own body is being consumed by the forest fires of mental and physical ailments, while his flickering limbs act as its creeping vines.
For one in whose body the serpent consisting of desire and anger writhes like [the serpent] within a withered tree, death shines forth as his [only] prospect.
That which is this abandonment of the body is known in the world as "death."
For that reason, there is no cause for those who know the object of knowledge and the knower, whether by means of the existent or the non-existent.
The life of that wise man shines forth, who possesses the vision of reality as it is and whose intellect does not depart from the contemplation of the true nature of the Self.
He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not defiled, who is equal toward all things— for him life is truly radiant. He who,
with an intellect that is inwardly cooled and liberated from passion and hatred, [remains thus...]
For his life shines forth when he observes this like a witness;
the life of one who, having correctly understood what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted,
has placed the mind within the mind— that life truly shines.

When the mind is absorbed in that reality which resembles a non-entity and is stainless of false conceptualization, its life shines forth. Relying upon the true vision, this activity of the world proceeds as mere play.
The life of one by whom [the world] is rendered free of latent impressions (avāsana) shines.
The life of one who, even while moving about, feels neither satisfaction nor agitation upon encountering what is to be rejected or accepted, shines.
Like a flock of swans from a lake, pure and belonging to the bright fortnight,
from whom a flood of virtues flows forth— the life of such a person truly shines.
When he has entered the path of hearing, been seen, or come to mind, [he brings glory].
All beings find joy in him; his life is truly radiant.

O Lord of the Danavas, long life shines forth for him alone—like the fullness of the imperishable moon—by whose rising all the lotus-hearts of men, possessing swarms of living souls, blossom; it does not shine for anyone else.
The fortieth canto in the *Prahlāda-upākhyāna*, titled "The Application of the Presentation of Nārāyaṇa’s Words," [spoken by] the Blessed One:
The stability of the perceived body is called "life" by the wise;
the abandonment of the body for the sake of another body is known as "death.
O great-minded one, you are liberated from both of these two sides.
"Do you have death here, or do you have life?
"O crusher of enemies, this was spoken by me merely for the sake of illustration;
O All-Knowing One, you do not live, nor do you ever die."
Though residing in the body, you are bodiless because you are devoid of embodiment; you possess the vision of the disembodied.
Though residing in space, you are indeed not space, for like the wind, you are unattached.
O observer of noble vows, you are truly the body itself because you bring about the perception of touch.
Space is the cause of height by virtue of obstructing it.
You are awakened because you have known the reality of things; yet, insofar as you are limited by this muchness (*iyattā*), you do not exist [as a finite entity].
This form, which is delimited by such limits, is subject to suffering among the ignorant.
At all times, you are entirely nothing but the singular consciousness that is the light of the Intellect (*citprakāśa*).

What is this body, or what is this "non-body," which you either grasp or abandon? Whether spring should arise or the wind of universal dissolution (*pralaya*) should blow— [the state remains the same].
What has come upon the Self, which is devoid of both existence and non-existence?
Even when mountains are crumbling, even when the fires at the end of an aeon are burning,
and even when cataclysmic winds are blowing, the Self remains established in itself alone.
Let all beings remain, or let them depart together;
let them perish or let them increase—the Self remains only within itself.
It does not diminish when destruction is reached, nor does it increase when there is growth.
The supreme Puruṣa does not tremble while this body trembles.
Even when your delusion that "I am the body" and "the body is I" has perished,
why does this false conceptualization arise, such as "I abandon" or "I do not abandon"?
"Having done this, I shall do that; having abandoned this, I shall take up that"—such volitions, my dear, have come to an end for those who know reality.
For those awakened ones who are the agents of all, what indeed will they do anew?
Because they never perform new actions, they have attained the state of non-agency;
from this non-agency, non-enjoyment follows as a matter of course.
Indeed, who in these three worlds has ever gathered what was not sown?

When agency and enjoyership have been stilled, peace alone remains; having reached full maturity, that very state is called liberation by the wise. Awakened, consisting of consciousness, and pure, they remain pervading all things.
What should they abandon that has been taken up, or what should they take up that has been abandoned?
The relationship between the grasped and the grasper is a sequence of parts within the act of cognition;
being devoid of the constituent parts of the object of cognition, what could it grasp, and what could it abandon?
When the relationship between the grasped and the grasper has utterly ceased, peace arises;
having attained a state that is internal, it is designated by the name "liberation.
Noble beings like you, the best of persons, always remain established therein.
For they move through the worldly state with their latent impressions (vāsanās) resting in supreme awakening, due to the similarity between this and the movement of the limbs during deep sleep;
like those half-asleep, they perceive this world by means of an intellect established in the Self.
For those whose intentions are focused solely on their own self do not take delight in pleasant things,
because they find a single flavor in their own self even amidst sufferings.
Being eternally awakened and unattached, they engage in these activities.
Like reflections in a mirror, which appear according to what is encountered without being desired,
those who are established in their own self remain healthy while awake, yet they sleep within the state of saṃsāra;
with intentions resembling deep dreamless sleep, they act like children.
Having reached the state of the Unconquered, having enjoyed for but a single day the splendor of the Lotus-born,
O Great-souled One, go now to the supreme abode of Acyuta, which is endowed with a multitude of virtues— right here!
This concludes the chapter titled "The Enlightenment of Prahlāda" within the Narrative of Prahlāda.
The forty-first canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
By that ocean of the jewels of the world, who beheld the wonders of the three realms—
When this had been said by Padmanābha in a voice cool as moonlight,
that body named Prahlāda— his lotus-eyes blossoming,
firm, and having adopted a course of reflection— spoke these words softly.
Prahlāda said:
"O Lord, for a long time you have been seen by me within with a stainless intellect;
now, by good fortune, O Lord of Gods, you are seen again externally with the eyes."
O Maheśvara, in this infinite vision,
which is free from all conceptual constructions, I was like the sky within the stainless sky;
neither by sorrow, nor by delusion, nor by thoughts of dispassion was I affected.
Neither by the act of abandoning the body nor by the fear of saṃsāra [is there any cause for grief],
for when that One alone exists, whence can there be sorrow and whence destruction?
Where is the body, where is saṃsāra, where is stability, and where are fear and fearlessness?
"O Lord of my heart, I have dwelt thus in the vast and pure state solely by means of my own stainless will;
alas, I am now dispassionate and shall renounce this cycle of existence."
The anxiety of those with unawakened intellect brings about the transformations of joy and sorrow.
"In the absence of a body there are no sufferings; when my body exists, there are sufferings for me"—this serpent of the poison of thought devours only the fool.
"This is happiness, this is suffering; this does not exist for me, this exists"—the mind that wavers thus is indeed deluded, not wise.
Those blinded by the latent impressions of ignorance think, "I am this one, I am another."

To those of great intelligence, these nights are as far removed [from darkness] as they are to the suns. The false delusion of the mind that "this is to be abandoned" and "this is to be grasped" does not drive the wise person to madness within, as it does the ignorant person of corrupt intellect.
O lotus-eyed one, when you, the Self, are spread throughout everything,
how can there be a second conceptualization consisting of the categories of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted?
The entire world, which exists as a manifestation of consciousness, stands between being and non-being.
"What is to be abandoned? What is to be accepted?"— pondering thus whether anything is to be relinquished or not,
and investigating the seer and the seen solely by means of their own intrinsic nature,
I rested for a moment within myself, by the self, in the Self.
Freed from existence and non-existence, devoid of that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be accepted;
thus was I previously, and now I am situated in this state—
having attained my own peace, O All-pervading Self, as is the way of the virtuous.
"O Mahādeva, I shall do whatever pleases you.
O lotus-eyed one, you are indeed the one to be worshiped throughout the three worlds;
therefore, you ought to accept from me this worship offered according to the occasion."

Having spoken thus before the one who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk, the lord of the Dānavas presented a vessel for the guest-offering (*arghapātra*), like a king of mountains offering the full moon;
[the vessel] contained his weapons, the host of Apsarases, the gods, and the lord of birds.
He worshipped Govinda, who was preceded by the three worlds,
the Lord of the worlds who has pervaded all realms both within and without.
Having performed that worship, the Lord of Kamalā spoke to him as he sat there.
The Blessed One said:
"Arise, O Lord of the Dānavas, take your seat upon the throne;
I myself shall soon bestow the consecration upon you."
"May those Siddhas, Sādhyas, and hosts of gods who have assembled here upon hearing the sound of the Pāñcajanya conch, grant you auspiciousness!
Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed one [addressed] the Dānava on the lion-throne.
At the conclusion of his yoga, he joined [the body] together like a cloud upon the peak of Mount Meru.
Then Hari summoned the great oceans,
beginning with the Ocean of Milk, as well as the floods of rivers such as the Gaṅgā, and likewise the waters of all sacred fords (tīrtha).
Accompanied by all the assemblies of brahmin seers, as well as all the hosts of siddhas,
joined by munis and vidyādharas, and attended by the world-protectors,
the one of immeasurable soul consecrated the great asura in the sovereignty of the Daityas.
Being praised by the hosts of Maruts like Hari in a former creation,
and being praised by gods and asuras while he himself was praising them,
Madhusūdana spoke these words to Prahlāda after his consecration.
The Blessed One said: "O sinless one,
as long as Mount Meru endures, as long as the earth remains, and as long as the orbs of the moon and sun exist,
so long shall you remain a king, praised for your unimpaired virtues."
Having abandoned the fruits of the desirable and the undesirable with a mind of equanimous vision,
and being free from passion, fear, and anger, govern the kingdom.
In this kingdom, which is filled with enjoyments, you have beheld the unsurpassed ground.
You should not feel agitation regarding either heaven or hell; rather,
amidst the perceptions encountered through the conditions of place, time, action, and form,
remain established in your natural duty and dwell with all latent impressions abandoned.
Taking what is not given because it must be abandoned, and having relinquished the sense of "mine," you act with equanimity toward existence and non-existence; thus, acting here, you are not bound.
Having seen the cycle of saṃsāra and weighed the incomparable state of the Tathāgata, you have reached the peerless goal.
You know everything everywhere; what else remains to be taught?
While you, free from passion, fear, and anger, reign as king, the earth shall no longer drink the demonic blood of the greedy.

The beauty of his tears will not become an ear-ornament for the Asuras, just as a river with high waves and rapid currents does not reach the forest groves on its banks. From this day forward, the conflict between the Dānavas and the gods shall be completely stilled.
May the world remain at peace, like an ocean free from storms;
may the wives of the gods and asuras, withdrawn from one another, place their trust only in their own husbands and within their own inner apartments.
Having dispelled the darkness of the deep sleep of the long night of worldly existence, and with the glory of your noble intention ever-risen,
O son of Danu, enjoy for a long time the unconquered royal fortune, which is as delightful as the amorous play of celestial women.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Coronation of Prahlāda" within the Narrative of Prahlāda.
The forty-second canto: Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed one, together with men, gods, and kinnaras—
Like a second cycle of existence, it shook from the palace of the Asuras; meanwhile,
the mass of feathers on the king of birds' back was filled by the handfuls of flowers released by Prahlāda and the others.
Having reached the Ocean of Milk in due course and dismissed the celestial river,
Viṣṇu sat upon the seat of the serpent’s coils like a bee upon a white lotus;
while Śakra remained in heaven with the immortals.
In the netherworld, the lords of the Dānavas remained free from all feverish distress.
O Rāma, this attainment of awakening by the son of Prahlāda, which destroys every trace of impurity and is as cooling as the liquid moon, has thus been told to you in its entirety.
For those men in this world who, even though they have committed many evil deeds,
shall investigate this with their intellect, they will attain the state before long;
through such general investigation, their evil karma comes to an end.
Who does not attain the supreme state by investigating the statements on yoga?
Ignorance is said to be evil; it perishes through investigation.
Therefore, one should not abandon investigation, for it cuts away the very root of evil.
For those men who contemplate this perfection of Prahlāda,
the sins committed over seven lifetimes undoubtedly reach destruction.
Rāma said:
"How was the mind of the high-souled Prahlāda awakened, O Blessed One, when it had been transformed into the state beyond by the sounds of the Pāñcajanya conch? Vasiṣṭha said:
O you of faultless conduct, two kinds of liberation are possible in this world: one with the body and the other without the body;
hear now this distinction between them.
For one whose mind is unattached, regarding the abandonment or undertaking of actions—
Know that this very absence of seeking is liberation while living (jīvanmukti) in this world;

O Rāma, that same state, when the body perishes, is called liberation beyond the body (videhamukti), which is devoid of rebirth. Those established in that state do not return to the realm of the visible.
Like parched seeds, devoid of the sprout of further birth,
the pure latent impression (*vāsanā*) of those liberated while living becomes stainless in the heart;
it is purifying, supremely noble, and follows only the quality of *sattva*.

Constantly absorbed in meditation on the Self, they remain as if in a state of deep sleep. O scion of Raghu, even at the end of a thousand years, those who are liberated while living awaken within that very body by means of that [meditation] abiding within.
O mighty-armed one, Prahlāda attained awakening through his own internal, pure-sattva predisposition, awakened by the sound of the conch shell;
for Hari is indeed the Self of all beings, and whatever appears to him [is that very Self].
That occurs exactly so immediately; everywhere, the Self alone is the cause.
As soon as it was thought by Vāsudeva, "May Prahlāda attain awakening," that very thing was present in the twinkling of an eye.

Without cause in himself, yet by means of the cause of all beings, that body was assumed for the sake of creation; that is the form of Vāsudeva through his own self. By the vision of the Self, Mādhava is swiftly beheld.

"By means of the worship of Mādhava, one's own Self is quickly perceived. Taking hold of this vision for the sake of perceiving the Self as Rāghava, sport quickly as the Virāṭ-Self; you shall attain the eternal state."
O Rāma, this vast rainy season of worldly existence, which possesses the essence of pleasure,
bestows supreme dullness upon one who does not behold the sun of inquiry;
by the grace of Viṣṇu, the Self, this illusion (māyā) is exceedingly radiant.
But it does not afflict the wise, just as a yakṣī cannot harm one who possesses mantras.

By its own will, O sinless one, this infinite illusion (*māyā*)—which weaves the net of saṃsāra—is like the flame of a fire moved by a subtle breath of wind; it attains density within [the self] through the self's own will, and at the proper time, it returns to thinness through the self's own will.
The forty-third canto, titled "The Establishment of Prahlāda," [ends with] Rāma:
O Blessed One, Knower of all Dharmas, we have been brought to peace by the pure rays of your words,
just as medicinal herbs are revived by the rays of the moon.
These [words] are pure, soft, and longed for by the ears.
Your words, when grasped, adorn [the mind] like flowers held in the hand.
(MU 5.43.2) Prahlāda, if everything is obtained through human effort, why then did he not attain enlightenment without the grace of Mādhava? (MU 5.43.3)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Whatever was attained by the high-souled Prahlāda, O Rāghava, all that was achieved by him through human effort alone, and not otherwise.
The Self and Nārāyaṇa are indeed not distinct, like sesame seeds and their oil;
likewise, they are like whiteness and a cloth, or like a flower and its fragrance.
For he who is Viṣṇu is the very Self, and he who is the Self is Janārdana.
The words *Viṣṇu* and *Ātman* are synonyms, just as *viṭapi* and *pādapa* are;
by his own name Prahlāda, he himself was first appointed by himself,
through his own supreme power, to devotion toward Viṣṇu.
For Prahlāda indeed acquired this boon by himself;
he deliberated by himself and conquered his mind by himself.
Sometimes the Self awakens itself by its own power.
Sometimes he is awakened by means of the body of Viṣṇu, which is attainable through devotion.
Even though he has been worshipped for a long time and is supremely pleased,
Mādhava is not able to bestow knowledge upon one who lacks inquiry.
In the vision of one's own Self, analytical inquiry arising from human effort is primary;
causes such as divine grace are secondary. Therefore, be intent upon the primary cause.
Thus, having first forcibly assailed the five senses, [proceed].
Through practice and with every effort, make the mind possessed of discernment.
Whatever is attained by anyone, anywhere, is indeed obtained through the activation of one's own power; it is never obtained from any other source.
Relying on human effort and having leaped over the mountain of the senses,
cross the ocean of saṃsāra and go to the further shore, the supreme state.
If Janārdana were seen without human effort, [then what need would there be for exertion]?
Why does that Unborn One not rescue the multitude of beasts and birds?
If the Guru rescues the ignorant man even without his own human effort,
then why does he not rescue camels, tamed oxen, and bulls?
Nothing great is obtained from Hari, nor from the guru, nor from wealth,
which has not already been attained by oneself from one's own self when the mind is conquered and the serpent of the senses is subdued through practice and dispassion.
That which is attained by oneself is not attained from the three worlds.
Worship the Self by means of the self; honor the Self by means of the self.
Having beheld the Self by means of the self, remain established in the Self by means of the self.
For the sake of engaging fools who flee from the study of scriptures, effort, and inquiry,
"Vaiṣṇava devotion" has indeed been fashioned as a means for establishing them in auspicious states.
First, the primary rule is declared to be practice and effort.
But in its absence, the sequence consisting of the worshiper and the object of worship would be merely figurative.
(MU 5.43.21) If there is no invasion of the senses, what is the use of worship, the object of worship, and the act of worshipping?
If there is no invasion of the senses, what is the use of worship, the object of worship, and the act of worshipping? (MU 5.43.22)
For without inquiry and tranquility, Hari is not attained;
and for one endowed with inquiry and tranquility, what need is there for the Lotus-handed One?
Therefore, one should propitiate one's own mind by means of inquiry and tranquility.
When that [self] is realized, you are realized; if not, you are but a wild donkey in the forest.
Why is such affection and entreaty directed toward Mādhava and others, rather than being directed toward one's own mind?
Viṣṇu resides within every single person;
those who go outside, abandoning Him, are not wise.
The reality of consciousness (cittattva) dwelling in the cave of the heart is the primary, eternal body.
The form of the Self with the conch, discus, and mace in hand is its secondary (gauṇa) form.
For he who, abandoning the primary [form], pursues the secondary, is like one who,
having rejected a perfected elixir (rasāyana), seeks to accomplish something that must still be achieved.
But he who does not attain stability in this wondrous state of self-knowledge, O descendant of Raghu— his mind being intoxicated with madness,
lacking internal discernment of the Self, ignorant, and enslaved by the mind— [is lost].
He worships the Lord of the Immortals, who holds the conch, the discus, and the mace in his hands.
O Rāghava, through that worship and arduous austerity,
his mind attains purity in due time through the water of dispassion.
Through constant practice and discernment, the mind quickly becomes serene;
it gradually reaches the state of the mango tree itself, endowed with its own power.
Thus, the self attains this cultivated fruit by means of the self alone.
O destroyer of enemies, by means of the occasion known as the sequence of Hari’s worship,
whoever obtains a boon from Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor has thereby obtained for himself the fruit of the tree of practice.

The restraint of one's own mind is the ground for all supreme goals and for all long-enduring prosperities, just as the soil is the ground for the beauty of a harvest. Even for one intent on digging the earth or scraping away a mountain peak, [it is the mind that is the true source].

There is no other means here for the destruction of suffering than the restraint of one's own mind. Men wander upon this earth through thousands of births as long as the great ocean of the intoxicated mind does not reach tranquility.
Even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and the others, though worshipped for a long time and full of affection,
cannot protect one from the mental affliction that has overwhelmed them,
even after they have abandoned external and internal forms that appear radiant yet are unborn.

Quickly perform the contemplation of pure consciousness alone for the sake of ending rebirth. Taste that which consists of the one, stainless consciousness, free from objects of perception, infinite in form, and the essence of all—pure Being; thus you shall reach the further shore of the river of birth.
In the *Prahlāda-ākhyāna*, the chapter titled "The Conclusion of Prahlāda’s Rest" is the forty-fourth chapter. Vasiṣṭha:
This illusion called "saṃsāra" has no end;
it comes to an end only through the conquest of one's own mind, and not otherwise.
[This is for the purpose of perceiving the variety of the world’s illusory expansion.]
I shall relate this history; listen attentively, O sinless one.
On this surface of the earth, there is a province named Kosala, which is like a forest of wish-fulfilling trees on Mount Meru and a source of multitudes of jewels.
There lived a certain virtuous Brahmin known as Gādhi,
a supreme scholar and wise man who was like the Veda itself incarnate;
he shone with a mind that had been detached since childhood.
Just as the world is [illuminated] by a stainless and pure sky,
he— having fixed some cherished purpose in his mind and departed from his circle of kinsmen— went to the forest to practice austerities.
There, that king of brahmins reached a lake filled with blossoming lotuses,
which was as serene and pure as the sky studded with stars when the moon has appeared for the sake of ascetic penance. In that lake, the twice-born one beheld the sight of Āśaucī.
Submerged up to his neck in water, he lived like a lotus in the rainy season;
eight months passed for him while submerged in the waters of the lake,
his facial complexion shattered by bees mistaking his flesh for the filaments of a lotus.
Then, once he had been purified by ascetic heat, Hari approached him,
just as a dark cloud approaches the earth’s surface during the rainy season when it is afflicted by the summer heat.
The Blessed One said:
"O Brahmin, arise from the midst of the milk and take your desired boon;
the tree of your religious observance has borne the fruit you longed for.
The Brahmin said:
Salutations to Viṣṇu, the bee within the hollow of the heart-lotuses of countless beings, the sole lake for the lotus-pond of the three worlds!
O Blessed One, this illusion arising from you is of the nature of the Supreme Self.
"I wish to see this wondrous thing called saṃsāra. Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O Unborn One, you shall see this illusion, and then you shall abandon it."
Having spoken thus, he vanished from sight like a city of the Gandharvas.
When Viṣṇu had departed, that lordly Brāhmaṇa rose from the water,
his form cool and pure like the moon emerging from the waters of the Milky Ocean.
His soul became thoroughly satisfied by the sight of the Lord of the World,
like a night-lotus blossoming at the sight and touch of the moon.
Then, several days passed for him in that forest.
Filled with the bliss of beholding Hari,
he once began his bath in a lake where lotuses had blossomed,
while reflecting in his mind upon the words of Viṣṇu, like a great seer.
Then, during the ritual of bathing, he performed a circumambulation within the water for the sake of destroying all his sins; yet,
in that rite of being submerged in water, his mind forgot its meditation and mantras.
With the expansion of his consciousness overturned, he saw himself lying dead in the midst of the water within his own house, having met with an untimely end,
fallen like a tree into the interior of a cave by the force of the wind.
With the flow of inhalation and exhalation ceased, it has reached its end;
the movement of its limbs is stilled, like a grove in a windless place. Its face is pale and withered, like a sapless leaf from a tree.
It had become a corpse, devoid of joy like a lotus with its stalk severed;
its eyes were turned upward like the sky at dawn when the stars are sinking;
it was like a village beset by drought, grey on all sides with dust.
It was surrounded by distressed kinsmen, their faces drenched in tears, wailing piteously like ospreys around a tree;
with the lotus-faces of those present fading as the water flowed away from the breaking of the bridge.
He was held by his wife Nalinī, who shared his same nature, as she clung to his feet;
he was also seized by his mother, who was charming in her cries, wailing, and lamentations, and who grasped his chin, which was marked with fresh signs of puberty.
He was surrounded by other wretched people standing at his side with tear-streaked faces,
clinging to him like a tree covered in withered leaves dripping with frost,
as if intent on avoiding all contact out of fear of separation.
He was covered by limbs extended far out as if they were not his own;
with lips that did not touch one another and teeth that had slowly lost their luster, he seemed to laugh at his own life.
He was as if entered into silent meditation, as if carved from the mud;
he lay fast asleep as if for the sake of never waking again, resting profoundly.
The voices of his kinsmen, rising in the tumultuous clamor of their lamentation, [reached him].
As if listening with effort for the sake of discerning his state of affection,
[he was addressed] then by those whose gestures were agitated by lamentations like the waves of that moment,
who beat their breasts and were drenched by tears from their swollen eyes.
Gradually, by his own kinsmen who were agitated and making hoarse cries like female ospreys,
that inauspicious one was driven out so as never to be seen again;
he was led to the cremation ground, stained with the mire of congealed fat.
It was crowded with hundreds of skeletons, some dry, some half-dry, and others decayed and moist;
the sun’s rays were obscured by clouds of vultures, the darkness was dispelled by the fires of funeral pyres,
and the earth was made to sprout with the mass of flames from the mouths of hundreds of jackals.

There, in that blazing fire, they reduced that corpse to ashes— a fire where fierce crows, herons, and water-fowl bathed in flowing rivers of blood, and where aged birds were caught in a web-like network formed by the spread of strings still damp with gore.

Like the oceans receiving a flood of water from the submarine fire, the kinsmen [received him]; and the funeral pyre, possessing a mass of matted flames like a network of swelling tongues of fire, quickly consumed that corpse with crackling and popping sounds, as if it were dry fuel.

The fire, pervading the mass of clouds with a fragrance released by the intense crackling sounds of the burning, shattered the heap of bones on all sides— like an elephant crushing a bamboo grove from which its thick sap has been vomited out through the holes. This concludes the chapter titled "The Destruction of Gādhi" within the narrative of Gādhi.
The forty-fifth canto: Vasiṣṭha said:
Then Gādhi beheld him with his own intellect, which was profound and mature.
Remaining within the water itself, he beheld himself— distressed— within his own impure inner self,
situated in the womb of the women of outcaste dog-cookers living on the outskirts of villages as far as the circle of cremation grounds.
Overcome by the fear of dwelling in the womb, its delicate limbs tormented,
it sleeps within the heart of a dog-cooker like a sprout in dog-dung;
then, in due time, through gradual ripening, it is born with a dark complexion.
Like a dark cloud enveloped by filth during the rainy season,
he was a child brought up in the house of a dog-cooker (śvapaca), beloved by the dog-cookers;
he moved here and there like the surging waters of the Yamunā.
He had passed his twelfth year and stood sixteen years of age; with broad shoulders and noble limbs, he was as robust as a rain-cloud. Surrounded by a pack of dogs, he roamed from forest to forest.
He was slaughtering hundreds of thousands of deer, maintaining the traditional way of life of the forest-dwellers;
he stood there like a tamāla tree embraced by a creeper— the beloved wife of a hunter— adorned with clusters of breasts and hands like fresh sprouts.
He was sporting at the edges of the forests with that fresh beloved, Śyāmā, whose pure garland was her teeth in the form of a network of buds, and whose limbs were curved with abundant grace.
Dark as a bumblebee with his dark wife, like a bee with a female bee amidst a profusion of flowers; clad in the garments of fresh leafy creepers,
he appeared like the formidable Vindhya forest itself personified and arrived before him.
Resting in forest thickets, sleeping in mountain caves,
hidden in leafy bowers, and making his home among the shrubs;
adorned with *kiṅkirāta* flowers as ear-ornaments and decorated with garlands of jasmine.
Adorned with *ketaka* flowers as ear-ornaments and entwined with garlands of mango blossoms,
it was disheveled upon beds of flowers and wandered along the shores of the ocean;
it was expert in the bowers of the forest and highly skilled in the hunting of deer.
Then, upon the mountains, he brought forth sons who were the sprouts of his own lineage,
like thorns on a *khadira* tree whose final fruit is exceedingly harsh;
[he saw him] possessed of a wife, prosperous, yet standing with his youth already wasted away.
Gradually it fell into decay, like a parched field deprived of rain.
Then, having returned to that native village which had been plundered by the Huns,
he settled in a small hut made of leaves at a distance, like a lord of sages.
Having reached a state of decrepitude through old age, with his own body as his only son,
resembling a nearly withered *tāla* tree in a pit of sap;
he practiced the mature household life of a dog-cooker (*śvapaca*), surrounded by many kinsmen.
Then Gādhi beheld that [place], which had reached a state of supreme growth like a forest grove of *karañja* trees, belonging to him who possessed a wife,
yet who was the lord of the decrepit dog-cookers and the cause of his own delusion.
That wife of his was entirely carried away by that man of intense fury,
just as a mass of forest leaves is swiftly swept away by a gale-force wind;
he alone, emaciated by grief, laments in the wilderness.
Like a deer separated from its herd, devoid of hope and with tearful eyes,
he spent several days there with a mind overwhelmed by grief; then, like a bird leaving a pond whose lotuses have withered, he abandoned his own country.
Free from attachment and filled with contemplation, he wandered through many lands,
as if impelled by another, like a cloud driven by the wind.
One day, he reached the glorious city in the realm of the Kiras.
Moving through the empty sky like an immortal in his celestial chariot,
he beheld a path covered by the shimmering rays of dancing jewels, with its trees and creepers serving as women;
strewn with flowers up to the ankles, it was as beautiful as the interior of the Nandana grove.
In that city, he reached the royal highway, which was crowded with vassals, women, and citizens, and resembled the path to heaven;
there he saw the auspicious elephant, whose stall was constructed of jewels and gems.
He saw him moving restlessly like a pure mountain king,
wandering here and there for the sake of the kingdom now that the king was dead,
like a connoisseur of jewels upon the earth of gems, desiring to behold the *cintāmaṇi*.
That outcaste gazed for a long time with a gaze wide with curiosity at that elephant, who was like a mountain possessed of movement; then,
taking hold of him with his trunk as he looked on, that elephant—
They respectfully placed him upon their own shoulders, as Mount Meru bears the sun upon its slope.
When he had ascended onto the palanquin, victory drums resounded on all sides,
like the great oceans roaring when the clouds of the cosmic dissolution have ascended into the sky.
The king shone with his desires fulfilled, while the sound of the people crying "Victory!
arose like the chorus of birds awakening together in a garden;
thereafter, a dense clamor rose from the throngs of bards.
It was like the roar of oceans whose waters are tossed by the tide.
There, beautiful women restrained him for the sake of adornment,
just as waves rising from the Milk Ocean [restrained] Mount Mandara with their gems.
The proud women adorned him with necklaces strung with various gems of manifold radiance and power, just as the shores adorn a coastal mountain with various jewels.
They decorated him with necklaces whose touch was cool as frost.

The women, with their tremulous sprout-like hands, surrounded him with flowers of diverse colors and fragrances, as the splendor of spring surrounds a forest with its various blossoms; they were like the dark rainy season surrounding a lofty mountain peak with the floods of new rivers.
With ointments of various colors, tastes, and fragrances, they quickly anointed him with masses of radiance,
just as mountain slopes are covered by clouds born of mineral ores.
He, lovely as jewels and gold, took up the extended parasol.
Like Mount Meru filling the sky with twilight clouds, stars, the moon, and rivers,
he shone like a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), adorned with playful young creepers and strewn with flowers of jewels and silken garments.
Accompanied by their retinues, all the subjects approached him who was in such a state, just as travelers approach a blossoming tree by the roadside.
Having led him to a lion-throne, they consecrated him in due order.
Just as the immortals [mounted] Śakra upon the elephant Airāvaṇa,
so did that outcaste obtain the kingdom within the city of Kīra,
like a crow seizing a fat deer in the forest that has lost its life-force.
His lotus-feet were rubbed by the lotus-palms of the Kīra women;
with saffron unguents applied to all his limbs, he shone like an evening cloud.
Thus, accompanied by the women of the city, he blazed forth in the city of the Kīras.
Like a lion accompanied by a pride of lionesses in a forest in full bloom,
his body adorned with strings of pearls released from the elephants of Love slain by Hari, his anxiety and dejection stilled,
he took delight there in great pleasures, like an elephant scorched by the heat of the sun’s rays finding relief in the full waters of a lake.

With his royal majesty spread abroad and his commands established in every direction, having settled the affairs of the country within a few days and having fully assumed the burden of sovereignty by the subjects, he became the king there under the name Gavala. This concludes the chapter titled "The Attainment of the Kingdom" in the account of Gādhi.
The forty-sixth canto: Vasiṣṭha said:
Surrounded by playful women and honored by the circle of ministers, [the king...]
Honored by all his vassals, adorned with parasols and yak-tail whisks, following the instructions of the perfected ones, beloved, and having understood the sequence of the qualities of sovereignty,
he attained the great station there, free from sorrow, fear, and fatigue.
Having forgotten his own power, he was constantly [occupied] with hymns of praise and auspicious rites;
through a state of being filled with bliss, he was like one thoroughly intoxicated by spirits.
For eight years, the outcaste indeed ruled the kingdom among the parrots.
For that entire period, he maintained his noble conduct in its entirety;
then one day, having cast off his ornaments, he stood by chance like the sky when it is free of darkness, with the stars, moon, sun, and clouds [temporarily] removed from its luster.
He thought little of his many necklaces, armlets, garments, and other ornaments;
for a mind expanded by sovereignty does not delight in external acquisitions.
Clad in such attire, he alone went out into the outer courtyard.
Like the sun reaching its setting from the central region of the sky,
he beheld there a group of outcaste dog-cookers, dark as clouds, stout,
and singing softly like a flock of cuckoos at the onset of spring.
Shaking the *jhallarī* lute with the grace of his sprout-like hands,
he was like a tree to a swarm of bees that hum sweetly as they cling to it;
then, from that [lute], there arose an aged man with blood-red eyes.
Like a leader of dog-cookers [outcastes] seeing a glass horn filled with snow,
he suddenly cried out, "Kaṭañja! and, out of joy, placed his hand upon the knee-tip of the Kīra king as if it were a crow perched on a creeper.
And he said this to the lord of the parrots: "O friend, O Kaṭañjaka!
Where have you been staying? By good fortune you are seen today, after so long, O dear kinsman! Where did you spend all this time in the midst of the forest?"

Abandoned by his circle of kinsmen, he is all alone like a cuckoo. Does some king here, full of passion, honor you— who are skilled in the art of song and possess a melodious voice— just as one honors a cuckoo?
Or does he perhaps fill me with gifts of houses, clothes, and food,
as the spring fills the *tamāla* branch with the juices of its fruits and leaves?
By the sight of you today, I have attained supreme bliss.
Like the rising of the sun for a lotus, like the rising of the moon for the ocean,
the sight of a kinsman is the ultimate limit of all joys, of all great gains, and of all infinite restorations.
While the dog-cooker was thus speaking, the king,
for that time, showed his contempt through various gestures of victory;
meanwhile, the beloved subjects standing at the windows likewise [did so].
Knowing "This is a dog-eater," they fell into utter dejection;
the citizens did not shine, like lotuses under a shower of frost, like villages during a drought,
or like great mountains engulfed in forest fires.
The king disregarded that conversation concerning his own kinsmen,
just as a lion ignores the yowling of a cat perched on the top of a tree;
he quickly entered the inner apartments, where the people were dejected.
Like a royal swan, he withered the lotus-lake of his body;
he reached a state of exhaustion in every limb,
like a tree whose great hollow between its knees is filled with fire.
There he saw all the people with dejected faces,
like a net of saffron flowers whose base has been gnawed away by a rat. Then the ministers, the citizens, and the women [approached] that lord of the earth.

Even while he remained in his very home, they did not even touch him, just as one avoids a corpse; and his servants, though bound by deep affection, abandoned him from afar without offering him respect,
like those distressed by grief over the corpse of a child.
Those who were not agitated thought of him as one whose face was joyless, whose body was darkened, and who was bereft of splendor— like a parched wasteland;
for his body was smoking and he was in a state of intense torment.
The people did not approach his side, as if he were a mountain of fire.
The slender women, overcome by a lack of enthusiasm and deprived of their usual throngs,
reached only his commands, like droplets of water upon ashes.
Because of his appearance as a performer of cruel deeds and because he brought misfortune through his association,
people fled from him especially, as if from a *rākṣasa*.
Even while standing in the midst of the crowd, he remained all alone.
Deprived of the virtues of wealth and the like, he was like a traveler in a foreign land;
though he cried out loudly, the citizens gave him no greeting,
just as travelers ignore a hollow bamboo flute even when it is adorned with a net of pearls.
"Then, having resolved: 'We have all been defiled for a long time by our association with the dog-cookers;
we have not been purified by penances, so we shall enter the fire,' the citizens and ministers in the city [acted accordingly]."
They set hundreds of thousands of funeral pyres ablaze on all sides.
As those fires blazed around it like stars in the sky,
the entire city was filled with people overcome by supreme wailing.
The multitude of people ready to leap into the blazing sacrificial pits was held back by their wives, who were crying out piteously and shedding streams of tears; likewise,
the priests who had entered the fire-pits were restrained by the weeping of their servants.
The chariot-paths resounded and the pits echoed like a forest stirred by the winds;
it was filled with the thick scent of the flesh of eminent Brahmins illuminated by funeral pyres,
and a mist arose from the dust shaken up by a calamitous whirlwind.
The sky was covered by entrails tossed about by birds drawn there by the scent of long-standing fat wafted by the wind, resembling clouds obscuring the sun;
the circle of the city blazed with funeral fires fanned by the wind.
The quarters of the sky were overspread by a multitude of stars that were sparks of fire flying upward; the city was like a place where reckless thieves roam, where children and young boys cry out,
where terrified citizens have abandoned all hope for their lives, and where there is no stability.
With houses left unprotected and all their stores plundered by thieves,
and with citizens preoccupied with death as they abandoned their sons and wives—
while such a painful reversal of fate was thus unfolding.
While all people were perishing in a state resembling the end of an aeon, Gavala—
his intellect purified by contact with virtuous men in the kingdom,
yet his mind agitated by grief— reflected thus: *Muṇḍakopaniṣad-bhāṣya 5.46.43–44*
For my sake, this great calamity has arrived in this land—an untimely event equal to the end of an aeon, destroying all its leaders.
What use have I for a life of suffering? Death would be a great festival for me.
"For a wicked creature who is censured by the world, death is better than life.
Having thus resolved, Gavala, before the blazing fire,
fearlessly offered his body as an oblation like a moth.

When that body named Gavala had fallen into the mass of fire by force and reached a state of being a heap of scattered limbs, Gādhi suddenly attained consciousness within the water, due to the throbbing sensation of the burning fire scorching his own limbs. —
Vālmīki:
When the sage had spoken thus, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites;
the assembly, having offered salutations, departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
The chapter titled "The Loss of the Kingdom," occurring within the narrative of Gādhi.
The forty-seventh canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, after two muhūrtas, due to the agitation caused by the burden of Gādhi’s mental anguish, [the sage]...
The state of agitation subsided like the surging of the ocean reaching its shore;
due to that delusion regarding the creation of water, he desisted,
just as Brahmā ceases from the fashioning of the world at the time of the end of a kalpa.
Having become tranquil, his intellect awakened and firm, he gradually attained realization;
just as one whose intoxication has subsided regains consciousness when the effects of liquor have worn off, he perceived:
"This is that I am; this is what must be done; this is not."
When the night had passed and the veil of darkness was thinned,
he raised his face from within the water, his true nature restored,
like the god Mādhava at the end of winter when the lotus awakens.
Seeing this earth, which possessed forests, rivers, and the sky, as if it were something entirely different before him, he was struck with supreme wonder:
"Who am I? What am I seeing? What indeed have I done?"
Reflecting thus, he remained for a moment with his eyebrows knit in a frown.
Within that very instant, I perceived his agitation;
realizing this, he rose from the water like the rising sun.
And he thought: "Where is my mother on this bank? Where is my beloved, since I have met my death in the midst of my mother and my wife?
Alas, both my mother and father have perished for me, unfortunate as I am."
Like a leaf carried away by the wind, I am as consumed by fire as a creeper or a tree;
I am without marriage, and I do not even recognize the true nature of women,
who are like corrupting wine that agitates the twice-born.
Therefore, what indeed have I seen that is unreal—this frantic engagement in various undertakings, like a city of the Gandharvas?
Let this matter rest; for this state of being situated between the living and the dead is the very essence of kinship.
In this [world] consisting of illusion and delusion, not even the slightest bit of reality is perceived.
Thus, the mind of embodied beings perpetually wanders among endless false perceptions, like a maddened tiger roaming through forest thickets.
Disregarding that delusion of the mind,
Gādhi then spent several days in his own hermitage.
Once, a certain guest fond of food arrived at Gādhi's place.
Exhausted, he rested with him as Durvāsas once rested with Brahmā;
brought to supreme satisfaction by feeding on the juices of fruits and flowers,
that guest was refreshed by Gādhi just as a tree is by the spring.

Then, having performed their twilight devotions and completed their prayers, both of them reached their beds in due order and lay upon soft sprouts. Thereupon, a peaceful conversation began between those two ascetics.
Like the beauty of flowers belonging to a season appropriate for its own function within its two months, Gādhi then questioned his guest with words that arose from the context:
"O Brahmin, why are you so emaciated? Why are you so full of fatigue? (MU 5.47.19–20)
The Guest said: "O Blessed One, hear the cause of my extreme emaciation and fatigue;
I shall tell you the truth, for we are not speakers of untruth."
On this surface of the earth, in a bower of the northern quarter,
there is a great and glorious country, highly renowned by the name Kīra.
There I dwelt for a month, being honored by the people in that city.
Deluded by the vampire of his own mind, which craves endless flavors,
one among them once remarked there during the course of a conversation:
"O twice-born, it has been told to me that in this world there was once a king who was a *śvapaca* for eight years."
Then, when I questioned all the inhabitants of the villages, they said:
"A Chandala was the king here for eight years.
At the end of that time, he was recognized and quickly entered the blazing fire.
"Then hundreds of twice-born men entered the fire here.
Having heard this from their mouths, I emerged from that circle and,
O twice-born one, performed an expiation at Prayāga for the sake of purification.
"Having performed the breaking of my fast today on the third day at the conclusion of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, I have come here; therefore, I am exhausted and exceedingly emaciated.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus questioned again by that learned Gādhi, the twice-born one spoke this very same thing and nothing else.
Then Gādhi, filled with wonder, spent that night there.

When the sun, the great lamp of the world-house, had risen, and after he had performed his morning rites and the guest had departed upon taking his leave, he reflected thus with a mind overflowing with wonder: MU 5.47.30–31: When the sun, the great lamp of the world-house, had risen, and after he had performed his morning rites and the guest had departed upon taking his leave, he reflected thus with a mind overflowing with wonder.
"That which was seen by me in my agitation—that it was spoken by a twice-born man as truth—is indeed so; for what else could this sequence be but the illusory magic of Śambara?
That death of myself which I saw among my kinsmen—"
"That was surely an illusion; there is no doubt. As for the rest, I shall see its truth for myself.
Therefore, with an unwearied mind, I shall go quickly to the village on the borders of the Hūṇa territory to witness the account of that self-sacrificing dog-cooker."
Reflecting thus, he rose up with eagerness to go to another mandala,
as if the sun were intent on beholding the side of Mount Meru;
having emerged, he carried [the chariot] along the path with the speed of a monsoon torrent.
He traversed many lands like a gust of wind crossing over waves; he reached the Hūṇa territories, where the customs of the local people were trivial,
just as a camel seeking a thicket of thorns reaches a forest of *kārañja* trees.
There, with his consciousness remaining fixed in that very same posture, he saw before him a certain village, like a city of the Gandharvas;
at its edge, he beheld that very same dwelling of the outcaste.
Like the underworld beneath the three worlds, he saw in Pātāla a multitude of hells;
he beheld that city of the Lord of the Śvapacas, consisting of various imagined and expansive structures, like that of the Gandharvas.
In that very same arrangement, he saw the dwelling of a dog-cooker (śvapaca) as seen before;
it led his mind to an indescribable state of detachment—
its walls covered with barley sprouts washed over by the downpours of the rainy season.
With its roof-covering half-fallen and its caves barely visible,
that poverty appeared like solidified misfortune,
like malice with its limbs shattered, or like a state of wretchedness cut to pieces.
Its outskirts were covered with white bones of cows, horses, and buffaloes, crushed by the teeth of Gādhi,
which stood there as if to bear witness;
and in those very skull-bowls in which he had formerly eaten and drunk—
It was covered all over by those impure things, which, though consisting of nothing but non-existence, seemed as if they were full;
it was encircled on every side by those very dried-out strings of entrails, like long-reaching thirsts recurring with every season.
With a smile, he gazed for a long time upon that house of his own,
which was like a self-possessed man looking upon his former body that has become a withered corpse.
Then, filled with wonder, he approached the village.

Having bypassed the city of the Mlecchas like a traveler reaching an Ārya country, he there questioned the people: "O virtuous one, do you perhaps remember the former history of this village, concerning the succession of the Śvapacas at its outskirts?"
"For I have heard from virtuous people that all wise men clearly perceive even what occurred long ago as if it were in the palm of their hand;
in this regard, [he saw] an old, eminent *śvapaca* living in solitude."
"O virtuous one, if you know that single embodied form of Smara, which is as it were the very personification of darkness and sorrows, tell it to me;
for it is traditionally held that there is great merit in dispelling the doubts of a traveler."
"Again and again," the villagers replied when questioned by the twice-born Gādhi, with no small measure of smiles and agitation, like physicians to one who is afflicted.
"The villagers": [this indicates the subject of the following verse].
As you say, O Brahmin, so it is; it is not otherwise.
Here there was a dog-cooker (caṇḍāla) named Kaṭaṅkaṭa, of terrible appearance, who possessed a multitude of sons, grandsons, friends, servants, kinsmen, and his own kin.
Just as the wind strips away a great forest from a mountain laden with flowers and fruit,
so did death snatch away all that wife and family of that old man,
whose vast circle of followers had once been like the spreading foliage of a tree.
He who, having abandoned that region, went to the interior of the Kīra kingdom,
and there became king for eight years without agitation;
he who was then recognized by the people there and cast out from afar.
Just as a heap of filth or a poisonous tree in a village, so too does one enter the fire among people by oneself who has entered the fire through noble association— that is,
having entered into nobility from the noble.
"O Lord, why do you ask with such effort about a single dog-cooker?
Is he some kinsman of yours, or perhaps someone you have known?
While the villagers were speaking thus, Gādhi questioned them again and again.
He dwelt for one month in all those villages;
exactly as he had experienced that state of being a dog-cooker (śvapaca),
so it was described by all those villagers to him without any omission.
Then, having heard this from the mouth of Sakala without contradiction, and having carefully observed it exactly as it had been experienced,
Gādhi— his heart blooming like the spotless moon and his true form concealed— was struck with supreme amazement.
This is the chapter titled "The Direct Observation of the Events Concerning Gādhi."
The forty-eighth canto: Vasiṣṭha,
having rolled about in the dog-cooker’s dwelling, went forth again filled with wonder.
For Gādhi’s mind found no satiety in beholding such wonders.
There he surveyed the sites and dwellings,
just as the Lotus-born Creator surveys the worlds as they emerge from the upheaval at the end of an aeon.
Wandering like a *piśāca* in the forest where his dwelling was overturned and entwined with garlands of dry bones, he spoke thus to himself:
"These are those very rows of ivory from dead elephants that were fashioned into my enclosure."
Even today they remain for a kalpa, like the peaks of Mount Meru;
here, that monkey meat, cooked together with bamboo shoots,
was eaten by those intoxicated by spirituous liquor along with their outcaste kinsmen.
Having embraced a dark-skinned outcaste woman here upon a lion-skin,
he sleeps after drinking the bitter *maireya* wine mixed with the fresh ichor of elephants; meanwhile,
the female dogs of the household, nourished on oil-cake, [attend to him].
Here, bound with leather thongs upon a wooden frame of dead elephants,
was that triple-vessel of the elephant-pearls,
fastened with the fierce hide of a buffalo, beautiful as a rain cloud.
In these various places here, she played for a long time with the sons of the outcaste dog-cookers, like cuckoos sporting amidst a heap of mango leaves;
she followed the whistling of the flutes produced by the breath of those children as they grew.
Song was sung by those gratified by the wine prepared with the blood of dogs;
there, together with his family at the wedding festivities, the householder performed a dance accompanied by loud clamor, like the waves upon the ocean.
Here, a bamboo cage was constructed for the purpose of striking down others, holding crows, vultures, and other birds eager to fly away;
remembering such past deeds of his as a dog-cooker (cāṇḍāla), Gādhi [was filled with remorse].
With his head trembling in amazement and reflecting upon the movements of the constituent elements,
he who understood the proper course of action departed from that distant land after some time;
leaving the realm of the Hūnas, he gradually reached another region.
Having crossed the continuous succession of rivers, mountains, regions, and forests,
he reached the abode of the Kīras, situated against the snowy mountain.
There he arrived at the city of Mahīpāla, which was like unto a mountain.
His soul weary from wandering through the world, like Nārada returning to the heavenly realm,
he beheld the places he had previously experienced, seen, and frequented within the city, and with great respect, questioned the people.
"O virtuous one, do you perhaps remember the outcaste lord here?
If you know him, then tell me about him quickly and according to the facts.
The Nāgara replied:
O twice-born one, for eight years there was a *śvapaca* who became the ruler here;
