to him sovereignty had been entrusted by the elephant Navamaṅgala. At the end, having fully recognized [the truth], he entered the fire.
"O ascetic, twelve years have passed here.
Whatever Gādhi asks people out of curiosity,
he hears it from their very mouths and experiences it as well."
Then he saw in that city the king, together with his army and mounts,
having gone out from the palace to behold the god who wields the discus;
seeing him, the sky was shrouded by the clouds of dust raised by the host.
Remembering his former sovereignty, he spoke to himself in great astonishment:
"These are those very Kīra maidens, their skin resembling the interior of a lotus,
possessing the hue of molten gold, with eyes like trembling blue lotuses."
These multitudes of yak-tail whisks, white as the gathered rays of the moon,
resembling steady waterfalls and like heaps of *kāśa* flowers,
are being waved by beautiful women.
These are like the growths of flowers upon nine creepers;
these are like the successions of peaks of Mount Meru, with wish-fulfilling trees and dwellings formed by herds of rutting elephants.

These kings are your vassals, equal in majesty to Yama, Śiva, Indra, and Kubera, like the world-protectors (lokapālas) of Vāsava. These are those very women, rich in all jewels, spread out here to grant every desire.

The rows of houses were as beautiful as groves of wish-fulfilling trees and creepers. This kingdom of the parrot folk, which I enjoyed in the past, has today become as visible to me as the conduct of my own previous births.
"This which stands before me even as I am awake seems like a true dream;
I do not know what kind of illusion has arisen and expanded.
Alas! Indeed, by this long-expanding delusion of the mind, how can one be awakened?
I have been brought to a state of helplessness, like a small bird caught in a net.
Alas! What a pity; my mind, struck down by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is ignorant and spreads out webs of delusion even as it observes, just as it does for a child.
"For this great illusion was indeed shown to me by that wielder of the discus; now I have clearly remembered it in its entirety.
"Therefore, I shall now make such an effort in a mountain cave."
"Knowing the true state of the vital point of this extreme agitation," Gādhi thought thus and departed from the city to perform austerities;
having reached a cave in the mountain, he stood there like a weary lion.
There, for a year and a half, subsisting on a single ladle of milk,
the one of great splendor performed austerities for the gratification of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Then, the lotus-eyed Lord appeared before him in the form of water.
He, dark as a blue lotus, became serene like a great lake in autumn;
he approached that cave in the king of mountains, the abode of the twice-born,
and then remained in the sky with a complexion as clear as a rain cloud.
The Blessed One said:
"Gādhi, have you seen my most profound illusion?
Have you seen the activity of the snare of the world, which is of a binding nature?"
Vasiṣṭha said: "O blameless one, since you have attained this state so dear to the heart, what else do you desire as you practice austerity on this mountain slope?"
Seeing Hari speaking thus, Gādhi, the best of the twice-born,
worshipped his feet with a profusion of flowers for worship.
Having offered the guest-water (*argha*) and scattered flowers, he quickly bowed down and performed circumambulations.
The twice-born Gādhi spoke these words to Viṣṇu, like a *cātaka* bird to a cloud:
"O Lord, this illusion (*māyā*) consisting of profound darkness which has been displayed by you— "

Like the sun at dawn [reveals] the earth, lead that [truth] of mine to manifestation. O Lord, how is it that the mind, garlanded with the impurity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), perceives delusion even while awake, as if in a dream?
How has that which was perceived for a mere moment as a delusion within the water attained direct perception for me, O abode of the stainless state?
Through the lengthening or shortening of time, there is the coming into being and passing away of the body.
"How could these things remain here within my delusion that I am a *śvapaca*?
The Blessed One replied:
"This form is born of the self of one who, though standing in the depths, is shaken by his own mental anguish."
That which perceives vast delusions, though the mind has not seen reality, [is as follows]:
there is nothing at all external—neither sky, mountains, earth, nor the directions;
all this exists only within one's own mind, like a cluster of leaves within a sprout.
Just as fruits and the like expand outward from a sprout, so too do earth and the other elements manifest externally from the mind.
It is true that earth and the rest reside within the mind; they never exist outside of it.
The fruit exists within the sprout; therefore, from that [seed], the splendor of the fruit arises.
Just as a potter [fashions] a jar, the mind destroys and creates forms, light, mental attention, existence, time, and the sequence of actions.
This is experienced by all men, even down to children,
in their perceptions of agitation, passion, disease, and so forth, which are like dreams or delusions;
for hundreds of thousands of mental occurrences reside within the mind that is permeated by latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Just as fruits and flowers on a tree do not appear again when the earth is overrun by roots,
nor as leaves do not grow again on a tree that has been uprooted,
so too there is no further birth for the soul once it is devoid of its dwelling.
If, by that very mind in which the infinite web of the world is established,
the state of a dog-cooker (outcaste) was manifested, what cause for wonder is there in this?
You have understood the nature of the dog-cooker through the power of appearance.
Just as a great agitation, though diverse, produces transformation,
so too you have witnessed the delusion that a twice-born guest arrived, ate, slept, and told a story.
Rising up in that very same way, I go and reach the realm of the Hūnas;
"These are the Hūnas, these are the villages"—such is the delusion you have seen.
In this very same way, here is the former, overturned house of Kaṭañja.

"I was told by people that Kaṭañja had seen you; thus, you have the delusion that you saw him. Likewise, having reached the city of the Kīras, I was told by the Kīras that you have the delusion that you saw Śvapaca as their king."
Thus, O best of the twice-born, you have seen this entire web of delusion—
that which you perceive as real and that which you understand to be unreal.
Enveloped by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), what indeed is there that the mind does not see?
A purpose that would take a year to accomplish is seen accomplished in a dream.
O one of great intelligence, neither those guests, nor the Hunas, nor the Kiras, nor that city existed;
you saw all of this only through delusion.
O Brahmin, while traveling as a traveler to the land of the Hūnas, you rested in a certain cave, like a deer in a forest; likewise,
due to being bewildered by fatigue, you mistook this for that circle of Hūna territory.
"This is that house of the dog-cookers"—this was seen by you, but not as a reality.
In the very same way, you saw that city of the Kiras;
it was exactly so, and not otherwise, for you, O twice-born one, were seeking a magical illusion.
O Sage, though you have always dwelt amidst all things, you have perceived a delusion with your mind like one who is mad, wandering through the quarters of the world.
Therefore, arise; perform your own duty and remain with a tranquil intellect.
"Without their own karma, human beings do not attain prosperity here in this world.
Thus spoke Padmanābha, who was being honored by a multitude of ascetics dwelling in the forest, O Vasiṣṭha.
Surrounded by hosts of gods and sages with purified hands, he returned to his own abode, the ocean.
This concludes the forty-ninth canto, titled "The Narration of Gādhi’s Deeds and the Greatness of Māyā."
Vasiṣṭha said: Then, after Viṣṇu had departed, Gādhi wandered again among the Hunas and other peoples like a cloud in the sky, for the sake of investigating his own delusion.
Having thus learned of his own situation from the people,
he once again propitiated Hari while remaining in a mountain cave. Then, after a short time, Janārdana came to him.
"By a single act of propitiation alone, Mādhava becomes a kinsman.
Thus the Blessed One spoke to Gādhi, like a rain-cloud to a peacock, favorably saying: "What more do you desire? Why do you continue with ascetic toil? (MU 5.49.3–4)
Gādhi said:
"O Lord, I have been deluded for six months while in the land of the Hūṇas and Kiras;
there, my account does not correspond even in their stories."
"O Lord, have you seen the land of the Hunas through illusion? For what purpose was this said?
"To destroy delusion, not to increase it; for the words of the great are intended to dispel delusion.
The Blessed One replied:
By a stroke of chance, the condition of the outcaste was reflected in the minds of all the Hūnas and Kiras;
therefore, my dear friend, what they tell you regarding your own situation is indeed the truth.
For that which appears never again becomes non-appearance.
That house which was built by some dog-cooker at the edge of the village, and which you saw in that state reduced to fragments of brick— [that too does not become non-appearance].* *MU_5,49.8–9*
Sometimes a single intuition arises even for many people;
for the movement of the mind is as diverse as the occurrence of the "crow and the palm fruit" (a coincidence).
Indeed, it is observed that many human beings see the same dream.
Like those whose minds are sluggish from sleep, delusion,
or intoxication by liquor, many [beings] simultaneously perceive their actions within a single play, as deer do in a forest glade.

People strive [for their goals] just as trees bear fruit at the proper season. O Brahmin, that scriptural teaching which holds that "Time is the giver" of obstacles and permissions— that Time exists merely as a mental construction within the Self.
The Blessed Lord Time is formless; they know him to be Brahman itself, unborn.
He neither gives up nor takes anything from anyone at all.
But this worldly time, consisting of years, kalpas, and yugas—
The multitude of objects is conceptualized by him, and by those [objects] that multitude of objects is conceptualized;
with minds deluded by the confusion arising from a common appearance,
those multitudes of Hūṇas and Kiras perceived it in that manner.
"O virtuous one, being intent on your own duty and investigating the self with your intellect, remain right here until the delusion of the mind has vanished; I shall now depart.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the Sovereign, vanished from sight.
Gādhi remained in the cave with a mind made heavy by anxiety.
Then, after several months had passed on that mountain,
the twice-born one again propitiated the lotus-handed Lord.
And once, seeing his lord arrived, he bowed down to him; he honored him in his mind with deep longing and spoke to the Lord. Gādhi said:
"O Blessed One, as I recall that variegated state of my own existence among the Śvapacas,
and this illusion of saṃsāra, my mind is utterly bewildered.
Having said this, he quickly spoke according to the facts for the sake of dispelling his great delusion.
"Appoint me to this very same stainless task.
The Blessed One said:
"O Brahmin, this world is a grand display of the great sorcery of Māyā."
All manner of wondrous occurrences arise here in this vast world;
you have seen such things in the city of the Hūnas and Kiras out of delusion. This is indeed possible, for such illusions are seen by people.
The Hunas and the Kīras, like you, have likewise experienced such delusion; though it appears real, it is in vain because it arises simultaneously with other perceptions.
Listen now, O blameless one, as I shall explain this according to reality.
By this, your anxiety becomes thin, like the creeper of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
He who was formerly that outcaste named Kaṭañjaka in the Hūna region, he existed in that very same form and in that very same way in the past.
In that very same way, having become one whose vows were impaired, he went to another land and became King Kīra; thereafter,
he entered the fire while you were dwelling within the water, solely in your mind.
Such is the nature of the manifestation of the established order of worldly conduct:
that which has been seen and experienced is sometimes completely forgotten,
while at other times the mind perceives even the unseen as if it were seen.
Just as there is delusion regarding the existence of realms in dreams and mental fantasies,
so too, my dear, is it seen by the mind itself even while awake;
just as one who perceives the three times sees that which resides in the past and the future.
O Gādhi, your conduct is such that it brings forth inspired wisdom.
One who possesses self-mastery does not sink into the thought, "This is he, I am this, this is mine";
one who lacks self-mastery perceives in this way: "This is he, I am this, this is mine."
The knower of reality does not despair, thinking "I am indeed everything";
he does not grasp at objects with a sense of their division or their lack of ultimate purpose.
Therefore, amidst delusions and confusions that play with pleasure and pain, he remains unshaken.

Even when submerged, one does not sink, like a gourd vessel in water. As for you, however, your mind is seized by the net of latent impressions (vāsanā) and you are devoid of discernment; like one suffering from a great disease with only a little remaining, you have not attained well-being.

Because your knowledge is incomplete, you are unable to ward off the delusion of the mind, just as one who lacks the correct mantra cannot dispel a cloud. Whatever appears suddenly as a reflection within your mind alone—
Like a tree [overwhelmed] by the force of a torrent, you are instantly overcome by that very [mind].
If one remains here, having seized the spoke of the wheel of illusion at the navel of the mind from all sides, then nothing whatsoever can cause affliction.
"Arise! Practice austerities for ten years with an unwearied mind in a bower of this mountain; thereafter, you shall attain knowledge and the state of infinite being.
Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed one vanished on the spot.
Like a wind-cloud, like a lamp, or like the swelling of the Yamunā, [it vanished] in an instant.
Gādhi attained supreme detachment born of discernment,
just as a tree reaches a state of saplessness at the end of the autumn season.
With a mind released from the burden of great delusion, he gently censured the manifold and inconsistent activities of the Creator;
then, his soul moistened with compassion, he went forth for the sake of supreme glory through disciplined observance.
Like a rain-cloud that has become silent after raining upon a mountain for the sake of rest,
he, with all mental constructs cast aside, performed penance there;
through that, for ten years, he attained self-knowledge.
Thereafter, having regained his own true nature, the Great-Souled One— freed from fear and delusion, devoid of desire for the realm of enjoyment,
possessing the ever-rejoicing form of one liberated while living, and profoundly tranquil like the full moon— remained with a mind that was no longer agitated or incomplete.
The chapter titled "The Conclusion of Gādhi’s Story" is finished.
Fifty-fifth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"In this way, O descendant of Raghu, this [nature of reality] is exceedingly vast and difficult to comprehend."

Illusion, which produces great delusion, is treacherous and reaches to the very limit of the self. On one hand, there is the perception seen in the agitation of a dream lasting but two moments; on the other, there is the delusion of being a king among the outcaste dog-cookers for many years.
Where is this state of being perceived through agitation, and where is direct perception? Where is the unmistakable unreality, and where is the transformation into reality?
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, I say: enough with this claim that this is an extensive illusion.
"It yokes the inattentive mind to extreme peril.
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, how then can there be the blocking of this wheel of Māyā?"
"We act with forceful speed, causing the severing of all limbs.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāghava, of this wheel of illusion that has the form of saṃsāra..."
Know the mind to be the great hub of that which revolves and causes others to revolve.
When that [mind] is surely held fast by the intellect through human effort,
the wheel of illusion— its hub seized— is brought to a halt.
When the center of the mind is firmly grasped, the wheel of delusion does not revolve;
just as when a rope is held fast, the peg wrapped in the rope remains stationary.
O sinless one, why do you, who are an expert in the single combat of the wheel, not understand this?
A wheel held at its hub comes under control; it cannot be otherwise.
Therefore, O Rāghava, having firmly grasped the hub of the mind with effort, restrain the wheel of saṃsāra by blocking the movement of the self.
Without this method, this suffering of yours is endless;
but look, through this method, it has indeed reached its end in an instant—
provided one does not rely on any other supreme medicine than what is called the mere mastery of the mind.
Even with great effort, the great disease of saṃsāra is not pacified.
Therefore, O Rāghava, abandoning the practices of pilgrimage, charity, and austerity,
bring the mind itself under control for the sake of supreme welfare.
Samsara exists only within the mind, just as the space inside a jar exists within the jar.
When the mind is destroyed, there is no samsara; when the jar is destroyed, there is no space within the jar.
The space within the cavity of the jar-like mind is the space of the samsara of the mind.

Having destroyed that form which is like the incomparable sky, enter your own true nature. The mind, for a moment engaging with the present as it arrives in succession through external cognition, yet not engaging with the past or the future, attains the state of non-mind.
If you abandon every mental construction along with its underlying tendencies at every moment,
then you have indeed attained that purifying state of "no-mind.
As long as there is the fabrication of mental constructions, so long do the manifestations of the mind persist.

As far as the expanse of the clouds extends, so far do the drops of water exist in the sky. As long as there is a conscious mind and sentience, so long does there exist the conceptualization of volitional constructs.
As long as the world exists with the rays of the moon, so long do the fragments of frost persist.
If consciousness is devoid of the mind, then know that the roots of this miserable transmigratory existence have been burnt away from their very foundation; this is success.
For consciousness devoid of the mind is called direct self-awareness (*pratyakcetana*).
That which is of the nature of being without mind has no stain of conceptualization therein.
That is truth, that is the state of Śiva, that is the supreme existence;
it is omniscience and that is contentment, wherein indeed the mind is destroyed.
But wherever the mind is established, there too sorrow and happiness always come into its presence, like crows to a cremation ground.
Through the realization of the unreality of things, the establishment of all entities [is seen as such].
The seed of the creeper of saṃsāra does not arise from conceptual construction (saṅkalpa).
Through the yoga of continuous practice— consisting of the study of the scriptures and association with virtuous people—
the unreality of worldly phenomena is realized.
Having withdrawn the mind from its lack of discernment through one's own efforts and resolutions, it must be forcibly joined to the path of the scriptures and the conduct of the virtuous;
for the Self alone is the primary cause in the vision of the Supreme Self.
A jewel fallen into the bottomless depths is drawn out by means of another jewel.
One’s own self alone is capable of abandoning the sufferings experienced by itself;
therefore, the self alone is traditionally held to be the primary cause for the knowledge of the self.
Whether speaking, releasing, grasping, opening the eyes, or even closing them,
remain intent solely upon infinite consciousness alone, from which all mentation has been cast out;
abandon the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) such as "this is mine," "that is this," or "I am he."
Be intent solely on the pure consciousness residing within through single-minded devotion.
With a unified intellect until the body’s end,
remain devoted to meditative absorption by means of the continuous connection with your own self-awareness.
In flightings and in battles, in sorrows and in joys,
in waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, remain intent upon your own self-awareness;
having cast off the impurity of the object of perception and having thoroughly churned the sluggish mind.
Having completely severed the snares of hope, become intent upon self-awareness. With the conventions of "auspicious" and "inauspicious" stilled, the poison of hope extinguished,
and the view of "desired" and "undesired" destroyed, become intent upon the essence of pure awareness.
Not touching your own sensations— along with their agents, objects, and instruments— from within,
become intent upon pure self-consciousness alone, free from conceptualization and without support.
Indeed, while remaining in the waking state itself, cultivate that stable condition which belongs to deep sleep.

Reflecting that "all exists," become one whose body is the single essence of being (*sattā*). Released from the states of diversity and non-diversity, and joined with liberation within the heart-mind, become intent upon pure consciousness alone, like a lamp for the perception of all things.
Having abandoned both selfhood and otherness, and being undivided within the state of the world,
remain firm by supporting yourself like a diamond pillar. Having severed the internal mental bonds consisting of worldly expectations through your noble resolve, remain steadfast.
With an intellect that maintains singular steadfastness, proceed to a state where neither merit nor demerit exists.
Enough of this; as you attain the reality of self-awareness, even the most virulent *hālāhala* poison will become nectar for you.
Then arises the great delusion, the cause of the wandering in saṃsāra,
when there is a falling away from one's own pure and partless self-awareness.
At that time, the delusion which is the cause of the wandering in saṃsāra is utterly destroyed.
When you abide in self-awareness that is stainless and partless—
having returned to your true nature and crossed the great ocean of hope—
your consciousness will expand in every direction like the rays of the sun.

O Rāma, for one who beholds their own true nature and abides in the state of bliss, even a delicious elixir acts like a potent poison. We feel no shame before those men who have attained their own true nature.
The remaining ones, called "men," are long-armed donkeys; they become like dwarfs before the mountain, like elephants before a peak,
for one who has reached the supreme limit and stands exalted by his own self-awareness.
Within the boundary of the seer and the seen, even all the lights such as the sun do not assist one who possesses the divine eye of self-awareness;
these [lights] become non-entities, like lamps at midday.
The sun and other celestial bodies have attained their selfhood in the act of creating the great light;
yet the knower of reality remains supremely exalted above all those things possessed of splendor, rays, power, and even the greatest might, as well as all things endowed with loftiness.

Just as the sun, fire, the moon, gems, and stars shine with their radiance, so do the best of men, who have known all that is to be known, shine forth in the world. Compared to the worms in the crevices of the earth and even to donkeys, human beings [are superior].
O Rāma, those who do not know reality are considered even more contemptible than animals.
As long as one does not possess the Self, the body is a vampire of delusion;
those who know that truth maintain that it is only the knower of the Self who is truly joined with consciousness.

For one who does not know the Self is a wretched body; though moving about upon the earth, he wanders aimlessly like a corpse. But the knower of the Self is truly conscious. As the mind grows gross, the knowledge of the Self recedes far away.
When the stainless splendor of light has arisen like a great cloud,
the mind should be gradually emaciated by the renunciation of the enjoyment and non-enjoyment of pleasures;
by one who knows that, through the removal of their "flavors," it should be made like a withered leaf over time.
By this reliance on the mere body as a self within what is not-self,
and by means of sons, wives, and family, the mind attains stoutness;
through the transformation of egoism and the playful impurity of "mine-ness."
Through the thought "this is mine," the mind becomes swollen;
through the suffering of old age and death, which leads to vain exaltation,
and through the nest of the venomous snakes of the afflictions, the mind becomes swollen.
By drinking the milk of false hopes, by the force of the wind of enjoyments,
and by this grasping at existence, the serpent of the mind grows fat;
through the play of mental and physical afflictions, it finds its solace in the cycle of rebirth.

The mind attains fullness through the effort of rejecting what is to be abandoned and acquiring what is to be accepted. Through the swelling of enjoyments— which possess the nature of coming and going and which signal the imbalance of poison— the serpent of the mind becomes fat.

O you who are like the moon, quickly cut down with the saw of discernment this poisonous tree of the mind: its deep-rooted hollows are the physical body; its towering clusters of blossoms are the mass of anxieties; it is bent low by the fruits of old age, death, and disease; and its flowers are the blooming surges of sensual enjoyment.

Violently sever, without hesitation, the great branch of hope, whose leaves are tender conceptual constructions. [Sever] that fierce tumor of pleasure and pain, which is intoxicated for a moment by the bliss of resting while seated on one bank, yet is incapable of remaining still and is eager to churn the lotus grove of the succession of noble beings.

O Rāghava, lion among kings, tear apart with the row of sharp claws of your wisdom the elephant of the mind that dwells in the forest of the body— its long tusks being the chronic distortions— and which,
finding constant delight in unwholesome objects, is nourished by devouring the garland of the physical frame.

Drive far away that crow of your own mind— the essence of which is wicked conduct, harsh and shrieking, bold, cruel with a beak hardened by its actions, one-eyed, and exceedingly blackened by its parts; for it is arrogant and haughty within the nest-cavity of the body, and must be removed for the sake of pacifying faults.
Attended by the ogress of craving, resting in the great pits of ignorance,
and wandering for a long time through hundreds of bodies in the forest of its own cycle of existence devoid of consciousness—
from that house of its own conscious self, [it is liberated] by the independent mantras of discernment, dispassion, and the effort of the Guru.
As long as this demon of the mind has not been expelled, how can there be the realization of the Self in this world?

[The Self] destroys the flood of pride struck down by the auspicious and inauspicious, the poison of anxiety, and the bodice of the body; it is the constant food for pure breath and the destroyer of fear for everyone, O Rāma.

O Rāma, having brought the great serpent of the mind to stillness through the power of the mantra that censures the flood of enjoyments, and having utterly cast off fear, become one whose nature is fearless of worldly existence—
having abandoned the body which bears an inauspicious form by means of constant attendance upon the rows of corpses.
Afflicted by the exhaustion of wandering through the quarters, dwelling in the cremation ground with a wounded body,

and rushing in all directions for the bait of enjoyments, the vulture of the mind— with neck outstretched and its pride increased by its own stability— if it flies away from the tree of the body, then your victory is truly complete.

[The author] describes the person who wanders as a traveler through the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), mocking the world: wandering through forest edges and distant quarters, seeking fruits, restless with agitated limbs, and going from the birthplace to the place of rebirth.
[He sees him] upon the tree of the senses, whose eyes and nose are its flowers, whose arms and so forth are its branches, and whose fingers are its trembling leaves.
O dear one, for the sake of spiritual success, thoroughly subdue this great monkey of the mind as it leaps about;
it has arisen to destroy the harvest of good fruits, flashing with the lightning of attachment to radiant pleasures,
raining down a torrent of misfortunes, and tossed within by the whirlwind of latent impressions.

By the power of the fierce mantra that abandons both conceptualization and non-conceptualization, you must zealously dispel the cloud of the mind from the sky of the heart; having attained the great fruit, become wealthy and liberated.
[The mind] is knotted by actions created by itself, unbreakable by weapons and unburned even by blazing fires.

O Rāghava, having yourself severed with the weapon of mere non-visualization this noose of the mind— which inflicts supreme suffering upon oneself, which is a long chain through all other births, and which is a multitude of countless bodies threaded together— wander at your ease, free from fear.

With the speed [of its breath], it quickly [overcomes] the terrible python of conceptualization— which has scorched all people on the path with its hissing, makes the awakening of others extremely difficult to attain, withers the grove of living beings with the poison of desire, and whose long body is swollen like a piece of meat in the wind— sleeping within the cave of the body in a sluggish state.
Having burned away the great forest of desires by the force of the fire of non-desire, become free from fear.

O virtuous one, quickly lead the mind to tranquility with the pure mind, as one employs a weapon against a terrible weapon; abandon your fickleness forever, like a tree that has lost its monkey yet remains undiminished in its splendor.

Having resolved with his mind, "Enough, enough," he became free from fear and had all internal impurities stilled; seeing even his entire body as light as a blade of grass, he—having reached the further shore of saṃsāra—drank, moved about, and took delight with ease through the vision of what is to be abandoned.
This is the chapter named "The Application of Rāghava’s Intention."
Fifty-first Sarga. Vasiṣṭha said:
Upon those very long, slender, and shining dark-blue [waters],...

Do not abide in mental fluctuations that are like the edge of a razor. O you who are skilled in guidance, since this creeper of intelligence has been born in the great field at the proper time, lead it to growth by watering it with discernment.
As long as this bud of a body does not wither from the ashes of the Kali age,
lift it up while it has fallen upon the ground and hold it fast;
O knower of the single true essence of my words, do so through the singular contemplation of the meaning of my speech.

You shall attain happiness, just as the enemy of serpents [Garuda] did from the contemplation of the sound of clouds. O wise one, having repeatedly resolved through your steady intellect that the five elements are torn asunder and shattered, contemplate them within yourself.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, in what sequence did the sage Uddālaka sever that pentad of elements and investigate them within?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O Rāma, how in former times Uddālaka attained the supreme, unimpaired vision through the investigation of the multitude of beings.
In a certain corner of this world-old house,
on a stretch of ground named after the wind and the directions, crowded with mountains like jars,
there is indeed a certain plateau known by the name of the lordly mountain Gandhamādana.
It is strewn with flowers, grey with the smoke from camphor trees;
it is filled with birds of variegated colors and delights in its many forests.
Its banks are occupied by forest-dwellers, and it smiles with the filaments of its blossoms.

In some places it possessed great jewels set within it; in others, blue clouds like water-lilies; in some places it had a beautiful crest of mist; and in others, it was like a mirror reflecting a lake.
There, on a certain rising ridge covered with fruit-bearing trees, [he beheld her].
In that place where flowers were strewn as far as the ankles and which possessed great trees of glossy shade,
there lived formerly a sage named Uddālaka— a silent, dignified, and high-minded ascetic of unrestrained austerity who had not yet reached his youth.

At first, however, he possessed little wisdom or discernment; he had not yet attained rest in the supreme state, nor was his virtuous intention awakened. Then, through the gradual practice of austerity, the observances of the meaning of the scriptures, and the restraints, [he attained it].

What could that primary goal to be attained be, upon reaching which one no longer grieves,
and having reached which, no further connection with birth arises?
When shall I, having abandoned discursive thought, abide in that supremely pure state?

I shall find long-lasting rest, like a cloud upon the peak of Mount Meru. When will the latent desires for enjoyment within me come to peace, like the waves of the ocean with their sounds of restless surging?

"When will I laugh at the thought, 'Having done this, that other thing must also be done,' with a mind resting in the ultimate state? When will the web of conceptual constructions no longer cling to my consciousness?"
Just as water remains upon a lotus leaf, having abandoned all attachment;
when, by means of the supreme boat that is wisdom, shall I have crossed over the river of craving, with its many surging waves?
When shall I mock this action, composed of unreality and performed by beings belonging to the world of the Jagatī meter, like the fruitless play of a child?
When shall I [attain] the state where the mind, overturned by conceptual constructions, no longer swings upon its cradle?
The delusion within me will subside like the dizziness of one who has drunk a soothing elixir.
When shall I, laughing at the worldly courses of existence, attain inner contentment like the Virāj-self whose intellect is full?
Peaceful, of even conduct, gentle, and free from desire for all objects—
when shall I attain tranquility, like the great ocean released from its agitation? When shall I [renounce] this entire splendor of the visible world, which consists of hundreds of desires?

Seeing everything like one in deep sleep, I shall become inwardly expanded. When, with an intellect whose conceptual constructions are stilled, shall I perceive everything— both internal and external— as nothing but pure consciousness and contemplate it as such?
When shall I, with my mind and self stilled and having attained supreme consciousness, reach the highest light, as if from the disappearance of blindness from birth?
When, by means of the beautiful radiance of consciousness obtained through practice...
From afar I shall behold this slender digit of Time.
When, liberated from both the desired and the undesired, and devoid of what is to be rejected or accepted,
shall I find contentment, established in the state of self-luminous reality?
When will this night of my delusion, O Kṛṣṇa— strewn with the owls of vain hopes and whose heart-lotus is withered by dullness— come to an end? When,
in a cave of the mountain, shall I become one whose mind is utterly tranquil?
I shall attain equality with a stone through non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*).
When will my elephant-like mind— intoxicated by the great pride of self-identification—
be destroyed and brought to ruin by the lion of the realization of reality?
When will forest ants build their nest upon my head, which is rendered silent by rest in partless meditation? When will birds, their minds absorbed in meditation, perch fearlessly upon my chest?

When shall I find rest, standing upon the base of the mountain-stump? When shall I abandon the path through the forest of saṃsāra— thick with the *karañja* trees of craving and overgrown with the shrubs of birth— and go my way?
Thus, overcome by anxiety in the forest, the twice-born Uddālaka sat down again and again and practiced meditation;
yet his mind, as restless as a monkey, was being led away by sense objects.
He did not obtain the joy-bestowing stability of meditative absorption.
Sometimes, immediately after abandoning external contacts,
the monkey of his mind would experience agitation regarding the abiding in reality.
Sometimes, having abandoned internal sensations, the monkey-like mind, out of its restlessness, wanders toward external objects like one greedy for poison;
sometimes, seeing an inner light resembling the sun within itself, the mind [becomes absorbed].
O lotus-eyed one, when his mind has turned toward sense objects and become greedy for them,
it abandons the inner darkness of ignorance;
at times, that mind flies away like a frightened bird.

"Having abandoned external and internal objects of touch, as well as sleep, that mind attained neither darkness nor light; it reached a state of eternal stability. Thus, with his inner meditative states agitated, he wallowed in confusion.
Day after day in the formidable caves, like a tree broken by the wind,
he stood in the peril of mental deliberation with a mind that had been cut down and regrown;
his body swayed like a blade of grass upon the waves of the shore.
Then, with a troubled mind and devoid of delight,
the Lord of Day dwelt alone upon the mountain every day, like [Śiva] on Mount Mahāmeru;
and once, he reached a cave that was difficult for any living being to attain.
With all movement completely stilled, like the state of liberation,
it was undisturbed by winds, unvisited by beasts or birds,
unseen by gods or gandharvas, and as beautiful as the supreme ether.
Covered with a profusion of flowers, soft as tender grass,
it was as if fashioned from emeralds set within crystals of *jyotīrasa* stone;
its shade was made resonant by the songs of the *siddhas*, and it was illuminated by manifest jewel-lamps.
It was well-guarded by the forest goddesses like the inner apartments of a palace;
it did not admit light to the eyes, being neither too hot nor too cold,
like the golden-white radiance of the autumnal sun when it has risen.
She was not withered by the meager light, nor was she disturbed by harsh sounds or winds; her borders were thick with flower clusters like a young *mālāvatī* vine,
appearing like the very path of tranquility embodied in form, and possessing a beauty worthy of being the resting place for the Lotus-born One.
[She who is] delightful with the softness of a cluster of flowers and beautiful like the interior of a lotus— from all sides.
The fifty-second canto, titled "The Longing of Uddālaka."
Vasiṣṭha said:
That righteous-souled one entered that cave of Gandhamādana,
just as a bee enters a lotus-bud reached after a long wandering.
Intent upon attaining meditative absorption, he shone as he entered,
like the Lotus-born Brahmā entering his own city when he has ceased from the activity of creation.
He prepared a seat with dark blue leaves that had clusters of blossoms within them.
There, he spread a beautiful deer-skin upon his back, like a soft mass of clouds over a rain-cloud,
or like the sky, studded with stars, over the sapphire slope of Mount Meru.
There he sat down, causing his mental absorption to diminish,
like a rain-cloud that has become silent after raining upon a mountain peak, his inner body purified;
facing north, he assumed the very firm lotus posture like a Buddha.
Holding his testicles with his heels, he formed the *brāhma* añjali.
Having withdrawn [the mind] from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which cause the deer of the mind to roam about,
he engaged in this investigation for the sake of non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*).
O foolish mind, what purpose do you have in the activities of saṃsāra?
The wise do not pursue actions that yield only suffering in the end—
those who, having abandoned the elixir of tranquility, run after sensual enjoyments.
Having abandoned the grove of *mandāra* flowers, he goes to a poisonous jungle.
Even if you go to a hole in the earth or to the world of Brahmā,
you will find no peace there without the nectar of tranquility.
Abandon this state of being unfilled by hundreds of hopes, which bestows all suffering; go to the supreme, most beautiful state of ultimate bliss.
These various mental constructs consist of the nature of existence and non-existence.

Only for your own fierce suffering and never for your happiness— O fool, what is the use of these [objects] such as sound, whose functions have been destroyed? You wander incessantly and in vain, just like a female frog.
O mind-frog, what have you gained by wandering aimlessly through the world for so long in blindness? For whatever you obtain, and in whatever you find satisfaction, that is all you receive.

O fool, why do you not fix your mind upon that state of tranquility? O fool, having come to the state of being a listener, do not go to your destruction like a deer, following after sounds with a mind nourished by futile exertions.

O fool, having come to the state of skin, do not become bound by this longing for touch which leads to suffering, like a lordly elephant lusting after a female elephant. O blind one, having come to the state of the tongue, do not become blinded by greed for foul-smelling foods.

Do not meet your destruction like a fish greedy for a baited hook. O deluded one, do not go to your own burning by resorting to visual perception directed toward the forms of women and the like, like a moth lured by lust for light.

Resorting to the path of the nose within the hollow of the body-lotus, do not seek bondage by being intent upon fragrance, like a bee. The deer, the bee, the moth, the elephant, and the fish— each of these has been destroyed by a single sense-object.
O ignorant one, where is there happiness for one who is pervaded by all these misfortunes?
O mind, the web of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) woven within you leads to bondage;
it is an innate froth upon your own self, like a silken cocoon produced by a silkworm.
If, having arrived like an autumn cloud, you attain purity free from the affliction of impurity and become utterly tranquil,
then your victories shall be infinite.
[Those states] which bring about the conditions of decline and rise, and which cause torment at their conclusion—
Even though you know [the truth], if you do not abandon the worldly views, you will perish. Or for what purpose should I give this instruction to you?
For, O sinless one, there is no mind in a man who possesses discernment.
As long as there is density of ignorance, so long is there density of the mind;
as long as the rainy season is powerful, so long is there an abundance of mist.
As long as there is attenuation of ignorance, so long is there attenuation of the mind.
As long as the rainy season lasts, so long does the frost persist. As long as the pure mind, accompanied by discernment, has not reached attenuation,
I consider that [ignorance] to be as diminished as an autumnal cloud.

This is the instruction: whatever is done for one who is non-existent or perishing is equivalent to striking at the water of the sky with the wind. Therefore, I abandon you, who are wasting away and composed of unreality.
They say that the supreme folly is the instruction to abandon [what is not to be abandoned]. I am the non-conceptual lamp of consciousness, free from the latent impression of egoism;
I am not bound by you, the seed of egoism, for I am composed of unreality.
"This is that very me"— thus has a false view been clung to by you,
O fool, for your own destruction, like the cholera of the poison of doubt.
The subtle and intelligent abiding in the reality of the infinite Self is [the remedy].
Just as it is impossible for an elephant to be perfumed by the scent inside a wood-apple fruit, so too,
O Mahāskandhadeva, this profound and painful latent impression (vāsanā) upon which you rely is unreal; therefore, I do not follow after it.
What indeed is this vain delusion, like that of a child who does not investigate? It is a construction based on the continuous fabrication of the error "this is I.
When one analyzes [the body] bit by bit from the big toe up to the head, [it is found to be empty].
That which is called "I" is not found; who then am I?

Thus established, I behold that single [reality] which fills every corner of the directions throughout the three worlds—a consciousness that is itself beyond being perceived, its nature pervasive everywhere.
Its measure is not perceived, nor indeed is there any conceptualization of it;
it possesses neither oneness nor otherness, neither greatness nor minuteness.
If you consider that feeling—which is itself unperceivable—is the cause of my suffering, [then...]
"By means of this distinction born of discernment, you shall be slain by me:
'This is flesh, this is blood, these are the bones in the body;
these are your breath-winds—who is that "I" who stands here? (MU 5.52.39–40)
O mind, flesh is one thing, blood another, and bones yet others;
awakening is one thing, and movement another—wherein then does this "I" reside?
This is the nose, this is the tongue, this is the skin, and these are the two ears.
"This is the eye, this is the movement; who is this that stands as 'I'?"—in accordance with reality, there is no "I," nor you, nor even latent impressions (vāsanā).
This pure Self, the manifestation of consciousness, alone unfolds in its absolute simplicity.
"I alone am everywhere here, or else I am nothing at all here"—this alone is the vision consisting of reality; no other sequence exists.
For a long time, I have been crushed by the great "I-ness" of the rogue of ignorance.
Like a young animal found in the forest by a proud wolf,
by good fortune this thief of ignorance has now been recognized by me;
I shall never again take refuge in him who robs one of the true nature of reality.
Free from suffering, I am not one who is subject to suffering; he does not belong to me, nor do I belong to him.
Just as a cloud remains above it, I am nothing to the mountain.
Having never truly come into being, I do not say "I," nor do I stay, nor do I go.
Through the contemplation of the Self, I have attained freedom from egoism. Surely these [faculties]—the eyes and the rest—are entirely other than me and ignorant;
whether they go or remain in the body, they are none of mine at all.
Alas! Who am I, by what name, and how was I fashioned by whom—this vampire of a worldly child with a form as towering and incomparable as a palm tree?
For so long a time, I have been rolling fruitlessly in this pit.
I am like a deer on a desolate mountain, freed from water and grass.
If my eye has turned upward toward the vision of my own true interest alone,
then who could that "I" be, who am thus deluded by suffering?
If the sense of touch has turned its face upward toward its own essential nature called "touch," then what is this that arises as the so-called "I," like a wretched ghost?
When this faculty of taste is established in its own sequence among the flavors...
"How can this contemptible delusion—that 'I am an eater of delicacies'—possibly arise?
When the ear, which is devoted to the power of sound and is clever only in its own domain, is [withdrawn], what source can there be for that seedless suffering of egoism? (MU 5.52.54–55)
When the sense of smell, filled with its own self-centeredness, encounters its own fragrance,
I do not recognize that thief who thinks, "I am the smeller. This mental construction, which produces the appearance of an object, follows the same sequence as a mirage.
If that [object] does not exist, what is the basis for this agitation?
Even though these sense organs, such as the eye, are devoid of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they function spontaneously toward their own external objects; latent impressions are not the cause here.
"O mind, surely action is performed free from latent impressions (vāsanā);
here, those perceptions of pleasure and pain are experienced only as such [without attachment].
Therefore, having abandoned your own internal latent impressions, cast aside the foolish senses."
"Perform all your actions, O all of you, and you shall not encounter suffering. It was by yourselves that these latent impressions (vāsanā) were vainly cultivated for the sake of suffering,
just as children experience distress from the destruction of their playthings made of mud."

All perceptions, such as latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the like, are not distinct from the Self, just as waves are not distinct from water; this is true for the ignorant as well as for the wise, O sinless one.
You have been ruined by craving alone, you who are the prisoners of the senses in vain.
Like silkworms with their own innate threads,
you wallow here in the peril of old age and death through craving alone,
like travelers on a mountain path wandering in their vision into the depths of ravines.
In this world, latent impression alone is the cause for your bondage in one place,
just as a rope strung through empty shells appears extended to those who have been released [from their grasp]. Indeed,
this is constructed by mere imagination and is not real in substance.
By mere non-mental-construction, it is cut away as if by a sickle.
For this [notion] leads only to your own delusion and destruction,
like a gust of wind to lamps flickering even with their own light.

O mind, you are the treasury of all the senses; therefore, having surely attained oneness with all the senses, and having perceived the self as being of an unreal nature, remain in the state of Nirvana, which is singular, stainless awakening.
Having skillfully cast away the endless cholera of the poison of sense-objects and the latent impression of the ego's persistence, remain.
O Blessed One, through the reasoning that effects the avoidance of what is desired, may you be free from fear; for you are not a ground for fears.
The fifty-third canto, named the "Investigation of Uddālaka."
Uddālaka:
Whether its form is boundless or as minute as an atom, consciousness is unobjectifiable;
therefore, latent impressions and the like have no power to affect it.
By means of the mind, the intellect, the ego, and the deceptive senses acting as reflections,
the female vampire of emptiness, raised up by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is intent on causing terror;
yet from the very transformations produced by her, one should derive fearlessness toward those same things in abundance.
Furthermore, let them experience [birth and death] within; for I am indeed the untainted consciousness (*cit*). There is no birth or death for consciousness, since consciousness is all-pervading.
Tell me, what is it that dies? Or by what is anything ever killed? (MU 5.53.3–4)
There is no purpose in life apart from consciousness; that very consciousness is life itself.
What will this soul ever attain, if it lives having already died?
To say "one lives" or "one dies" belongs only to those who weave webs of false conceptualizations.
The limitation of the mind alone does not apply to the Self, whose nature is all-pervasive.
For he who has attained the state of "I-ness" (ahambhāva) is grasped by existence and non-existence;
but for the Self there is no "I-ness," so how could it have those states of existence and non-existence?
The sense of "I" is a vain delusion, and the mind is but a mirage; the entire collection of objects is insentient. For whom, then, could there be the cultivation of the notion of "I"?
The body consists of blood and flesh, and the mind has perished through inquiry.
Since all things such as the mind and so forth are insentient, how can there be the cultivation of the sense of "I"?
The senses remain entirely occupied with their own self-sustenance; and since objects abide merely in their state as objects, how can there be the cultivation of the sense of "I"?
The qualities (guṇas) abide in the qualities; nature (prakṛti) is established in nature.
Reality alone rests in reality—whence, then, can there be the conception of "I"?
[It is] all-pervading, residing in all bodies, consisting of all time, and great.
For only the supreme light, the very self of consciousness, remains.
Thus, what is its form? Or who is it? What is to be accepted? And by what is it made? What is its nature? Of what is it composed? Who am I? What do I grasp? And what do I abandon?
Therefore, it is said: "In this case, there is no such thing as 'I' which arises from existence or non-existence;
for one whose nature is free from egoism, with what could there be a connection, and how?
When egoism is absent, what connection can there be, between whom, and of what kind?"
When the non-existence of any relation is established, the conceptualization of duality dissolves.
Thus, whatever exists in this world has Brahman as its essence;
it is Brahman alone that exists, and that very same Brahman am I. Why then do I grieve in vain?
When one alone, the stainless and all-pervading state, is established, how could there even be the name of the stain of egoism, and from where could it arise?
Indeed, the splendor of objective entities does not exist at all; here, only the all-pervading Self exists.
And when the reality of objective entities is absent, no connection exists for anyone.

When the senses sport among the senses, the limbs among the limbs, and the mind within the mind, by what is consciousness—whose nature is undiminished—connected? To whom does it belong, what is it, and how?
Just as there is no mutual connection between pebbles and counting sticks,
so too there is none among the body, the senses, the mind, and consciousness, even when they are perceived together in one place;
for the great delusion of egoism arises from what is unreal and is thus futile.
This world is perverted by the notions "this is mine" and "this is I.
This wondrous manifestation of egoism arises from a failure to perceive reality;
it dissolves through the light of reality, just as a streak of frost vanishes under the heat.
Nothing whatsoever exists apart from the Self;
that reality is the Śabdabrahman—this I shall fully contemplate.
Of this delusion of egoism that has arisen, it is like the color attributed to space.
I consider that never remembering again is surely better than forgetting;
having completely forgotten the delusion of egoism along with its roots for a long time,
I abide as the true Self within the Self, like the sky in the autumn sky.
The latent sense of "I" bestows a mass of misfortune, causes evil deeds to blossom,
and spreads intense suffering;
it vibrates within the watery space of the heart when it is thickened by egoism.
The cluster of faults blossoms all around the grove of the body.
Death lies at the end of life, and life ends in death;
existence is cut off by non-existence—how bitter is this sensation of suffering!
"This has been gained; this I shall obtain"—this [thought] causes internal burning for the foolish, like the radiance of sun-gems in summer that never subsides.
The thought "this does not exist" or "this exists" runs toward the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
Just as a mass of clouds [does not moisten] a range of mountains with its dull nature, so too,
when egoism has been utterly exhausted, the sapless tree of saṃsāra no longer produces a sprout, remaining like a stone. (MU 5.53.30–31)
The black female serpents of craving for existence, having made their home in the tree of the body,
flee somewhere when the son of Vinatā— the discerning self— has arrived;
for when the universe has arisen from the unreal, we who are born from it are likewise composed of the unreal.
In the vibration of that which consists of non-existence, what sequence can there be for "you" and "I"?
This world arises at first without a cause from that which is causeless;
how can that which is causeless and yet swollen with manifestation be called "existent"?
In the past, for an infinite time, this body was unformed, like a pot [in its state] as clay; now it exists, and likewise it will come to an end in the future.
In the interim, it is merely a human lifespan, unstable for a short duration.
Just as water, having abandoned its initial and final states of gentleness, becomes waves; so too,
those who place their reliance upon this body— which is subject to momentary fluctuations and is prone to dissolution—
are ruined, for they possess false views.
All things exist both before and after, and on all sides;
since these lack any distinct middle, what reliance can there be on that which is devoid of form?
O mind, you are prior and subsequent, bodiless and tranquil.
Whether it be existent or non-existent, it is dissolved in the void; what is the point of your fierce agitation toward this middle state?
Just as in dream-transformations, just as in visions of delusion, just as in the playfulness of intoxication, or just as in the confusion caused by traveling in a boat.
Just as in the case of disorders of the humors, or in the impairment of the senses,
or under the influence of extreme agitation, joy, or the onset of afflictions,
the form of both the existent and the non-existent is seen to be shifting and subject to decay.
In this very way, O mind, this fluctuation of deficiency and excess occurs in due course; and it is constantly brought about by you through the arising of pleasure and pain,
just as it happens for lovers during the nights of separation and union.
You too, though non-existent, appear as if real;
like a mirage, how could that which you have created be real?
Whatever has this expansive appearance, all of it is the sphere of the visible.
Having determined that "this is non-existent," let the mind go to the state of no-mind.
When the firm conviction has taken root in the expansive mind that "this is non-existent," the latent tendencies for enjoyment wither away like lotuses in winter.

Surely, when the self has been seen by the mind— which has abandoned its lack of vigor and is free from passion— the mind itself becomes established in its own natural state. Having cast the components of its own consciousness into the fire of the Supreme Self, it [becomes] itself [liberated].
The mind, whose nature is burning, attains eternal purity.
Having perceived the body as something other [than the self], having abandoned the latent impressions of sense-objects,
and having accepted its own destruction, the mind conquers like a hero.
The mind is the enemy of the body, and the body is the enemy of the mind;
through a state of oneness, they perish like the container and its contents.
This occurs for those who possess passion and hatred, which are eternally and mutually opposed.
The destruction of these two by the scraping away of their roots is the supreme happiness.
That talk which speaks of finding delight in the union of these two is equal to the talk that the earth is being devoured by a woman made of iron in the sky.
Wherever two things that are inherently opposed are joined together,
there a succession of calamities falls like torrents of rain. For it is the base person who takes delight in the union of mutually contradictory things.
He should abandon that body in Patadvāra amidst a mass of fire and without water;
having touched the mind with its mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*), he gives his own sufferings to the body as if it were a child-demon, just as one gives wealth to a worthy recipient.
Afflicted by those sufferings, the body then desires to destroy the mind;
even a son kills his father when he has become an assailant. There is no enemy by nature, nor is there ever a friend.
It is said that a friend is one who bestows happiness, while those who cause suffering are known as enemies.
The body, experiencing sufferings, desires to destroy its own mind;
yet the mind, in an instant, makes the body a secure fortress for its own sorrows.
Thus, when suffering and pleasure are intertwined with one another, what arrival of happiness can there be?
For this body and mind are, by their very nature, pierced by each other.
Only when the mind itself is completely exhausted does the body cease to be a vessel for suffering.
Driven by the constant longing for its destruction, the body itself runs about;
yet this body, which is repeatedly lost to misfortune and is the very seat of calamities,
is swiftly reviled by the mind that has failed to attain self-discrimination.
For these two— the mind and the body— have indeed grown mutually robust,
being insentient in nature like a rain cloud and a lake during the monsoon;
having become one in essence, they exist as two for each other's mutual suffering.
When the mind is intent on worldly affairs, it is like wind and fire;
when that mind is diminished, the body becomes utterly exhausted at its very root. But when the mind increases, the body grows with a hundred branches, like a tree.
When the mind is destroyed, the body—devoid of latent impressions—is utterly destroyed;
yet when the body is destroyed, the mind is not destroyed. Therefore, one should destroy the mind.
Having cut down the forest of the mind, with its tree of volitions and its creeper of craving, [one attains liberation].
Having reached the vast expanse of the earth, I roam at my ease.
I perceive this mind of mine to be truly wasting away;
the web of latent impressions is subsiding like a cloud at the end of the rainy season.
This arrangement of the elements, known as the body, is my physical form;
as the mind perishes, let it remain only as something dissolving away.
Indeed, that very body for the sake of which the glory of enjoyments is desired [shall likewise vanish].
Neither is he mine, nor am I his; what purpose do I have for this mere fragment of pleasure?
Listen now to the reasoning regarding the sequence [of arguments] that "I am not the body":
even though all the limbs are present, why does a corpse not move?
Therefore, I am beyond this body, eternal, with a radiance that never sets;
having attained union with the Effulgent One, I perceive the Sun in the sky. I am the Knower; I have no need for pleasure, nor do I suffer from what is not beneficial.
Whether the body exists or not, I remain free from the fever of distress.
Where the Self is, there is neither mind, nor senses, nor latent impressions;
the vulgar do not stand near the mountain-king (the Self).
I have followed that path; I am alone, I am victorious.
I am free from desire, I am without parts, I am without effort, and I am without longing.
Now I have no connection with the mind, the body, the senses, or anything else.
Just as when oil is separated from crushed sesame seeds, so too for me,
who have moved away from this supreme state of my own by mere sport,
this auspicious retinue follows somewhat below me as I descend.
Well-being, vigor, existence, loveliness, truthfulness, and knowledge;
bliss, tranquility, wisdom, joy, and emergence;
fullness, magnanimity, truth, and radiant one-pointedness.
The state of universal oneness, fearlessness, and the exhaustion of the dualistic conceptualization—
these are eternally manifest, self-abiding, beautiful, and the source of auspiciousness;
they are the beloveds of me, who delights in the single Self, and are forever dear to my heart.
Since everything is possible for everyone, at all times and in every way,
therefore, with respect to everything, my desire and aversion, as well as pleasure and pain, have ceased;
this is evident through the absence of delusion, the state of being free from mental distress, and the mind’s freedom from conceptual construction.
I shall rest within my own self, as cool as a drop of cloud in the autumnal sky.
The fifty-fourth canto, titled "The Play of Uddālaka’s Reflection."
Vasiṣṭha,
having thus resolved with that expanded and pure intellect,
sat in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana) with his eyes half-closed.
He uttered the syllable *oṃ* with a piercing voice, its sound directed upwards,
like the resonant clang of a bell struck squarely upon its handle.
As he was pronouncing *oṃ*, his consciousness became oriented toward that very reality (*saṃvittattva*).
As long as the syllable Oṃ remains in the upward-stretching, expanded, and stainless Self—
within the first part of that which consists of three and a half measures, possessing a distinct resonance,
and wherein the body vibrates with the breath slightly agitated by the Praṇava.
The process of the departure of the vital breath, known as *recaka*, emptied his entire body just as Agastya, having drunk the waters, emptied the ocean;
the vital wind remained in the space filled with the essence of consciousness.
Like a bird that has abandoned its body and left its nest in the sky,
the flaming fire of his heart, blazing with intense heat, consumed his impure body,
just as a forest fire fanned by a gale consumes a withered tree.
This state occurs as long as one desires it during the first stage of the *praṇava*;
it does not happen through force, for *haṭhayoga* is indeed a source of suffering.
Then, on the occasion of the other parts, when the *praṇava* is established in equilibrium...
There occurred a state of the vital breaths known as the "motionless jar-retention" (niṣpandakumbhaka).
There, neither outside nor inside, neither below nor above, nor in the directions, did those breaths undergo agitation; they were as if half-stunned.

The fire that had consumed the body was instantly extinguished like a bolt of lightning; only white ash, pale as snow, remained visible. There, upon a bed of camphor, they appeared as if comfortably asleep.
The bones of the body were seen, motionless and white.
The wind, shaking that ash along with the bones,
joined them to its own body which was greatly swollen, as if it were observing the vow of the Three-Eyed One.
And that [cloud], stirred by a fierce wind, having covered the sky for a moment,
went away somewhere like an autumnal mist of clouds, containing ashes and bones;
such is this state in the subsequent stage of the *praṇava*, as long as one desires.

For haṭhayoga does not arise by force alone; indeed, it is a giver of suffering. Then, on the third occasion, there arose the practice of breath-control known as *pūraka* (inhalation), which brings peace through the filling [of the breath] with the *praṇava*.
At this moment, the vital breaths, situated within the nectar of consciousness,
attained coolness in the sky, beautiful like the touch of snow; gradually, remaining in the midst of the firmament, they took on the form of the lunar disc.
Like smoke rising into the expanse of the sky, as if from cool clouds;
when that lunar orb was filled with its full complement of digits,
like a mass of merit or a great ocean of elixir.
The vital breaths, possessing great streams of elixir,
took on the appearance of jeweled pillars, like the rays of the moon in the waters.
That stream fell from the sky onto the ashes of the physical body remaining upon Śeṣa.
Like the celestial river falling upon the head of Hara, she became a rejuvenating elixir;
with her body possessing four arms and resembling the orb of the moon,
she appeared like the Pārijāta tree emerging from the ocean when Mount Mandara was whirled about.
That body of Uddālaka, arisen as Nārāyaṇa,
shone beautifully and splendidly with radiance, like a blossoming mango tree.
His vital breaths, consisting of elixir, filled his body.
Like rivers filling a lake, or like sweet juices filling a tree,
the vital breaths, filled with reverence, filled the *kuṇḍalinī* within;
spreading out in crooked and winding courses, like streams filling the lakes of the mountain ridges.
The body of that twice-born man returned to its natural state,
like the surface of the earth washed clean at the end of the monsoon's onset.
Then, seated in the lotus posture, he established a firm stability within his body.
Having bound the five senses like an elephant to a post,
he applied his resolve toward the state of non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*),
just as a stainless autumn season seeks to bring its own nature to clarity.
With his thought, he drew his heart from afar— like a deer driven by the wind of its own mind, wandering through the quarters of the directions— as one pulls a stake with a rope;
for his mind was running downward, intoxicated, turbid, and agitated.
He forcibly restrained her, as a dam holds back swift-flowing water.
She half-closed her eyes, which were fringed with thick lashes,
like a lotus at twilight whose honey-bee-like pupils have become motionless.
The silent sage brought gentleness to the force of the inhalation and exhalation within his mouth,
like one who breathes in a favorable place at an auspicious time for the sake of well-being;
he diligently separated the vital breaths from them, just as oil is extracted from sesame seeds.
Withdrawing his senses from the objects of the senses like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs,
he gradually abandoned all external contacts far away as if they were enemies;
just as a gem covered in a cloth suddenly casts its radiance far off.
He caused the internal sensations of touch to dissolve, divested of their visual forms, just as a tree in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa sheds its sap that resides within the hollows of its branches; then,
by contracting his anus, he restrained the winds of the nine gates.
By closing her face, she was like other jars whose openings and cavities were covered;
the wise woman bore her firm neck, richly illuminated by the light of her jewel and clearly marked with flowers, like Mount Meru bearing the peak of its summit.
He held within the space of his heart the mind that had attained self-restraint,
like a mad elephant subdued by skillful means and confined in a pit in the Vindhya mountains;
having attained a stainless and exceedingly gentle state, like the autumnal sky.
It carried away the unshakable splendor of the full ocean and Mount Meru;
then it shook off the floods of conceptual constructions that had come into manifestation,
appearing before one like gnats shimmering in front of the wind.
As the mental appearances arose again and again according to his desire,

the hero severed them with his mind, just as one cuts away arrows with a sword in battle. When the flood of conceptual constructions had been completely cut down, he beheld [the reality] within the sky of his heart.
That darkness, which veiled the sun of discernment and was as black as flickering collyrium,
he likewise dispelled by means of the sun of his own inner self,
which had arisen through perfect knowledge, just as collyrium is quickly swept away by a favorable wind.
When the darkness had ceased, he beheld that lovely mass of light,
like the evening cloud at dawn when the nocturnal gloom has subsided.
He crushed that grove of land-lotuses like a young elephant.
And he drank a full draught of blood with speed, like a *vetāla*.
When his vital energy had subsided, the mind of the sage, reeling,
fell into sleep like a night-lotus, or like one who is intoxicated and unsteady.
Just as the wind disperses a mass of clouds, as the sun destroys the night-lotus,
or as the sun with its sharp rays dispels the night, he quickly tore that [illusion] apart as well. Upon the cessation of his sleep, his mind began to contemplate.
As a creature with dark eyes [sees] a peacock’s crest in the sky,
as the wind [dispels] a cloud, as the wind [scatters] mist,
and as a lamp [removes] darkness, so did that Pure Self quickly wipe away even that [ignorance].
When the consciousness of the void had collapsed, his mind became deluded,
like one intoxicated by liquor when sleep has dissolved away.
Yet that noble-minded one wiped away even that delusion of the mind.
Just as the sun dispels the dullness produced by the night from the world, so too the mind, having reached an indescribable state free from passion, darkness, sleep, delusion, and the like,
rested for a moment.
Having quickly rested, he fell into a state of bodily consciousness whose nature is pure awareness,
like the water of a lake dammed by a bridge flowing back toward its own source.
This occurred through the power of long-continued contemplation and the tasting of his own self-awareness.
Thereupon, it attained the state of pure consciousness, like gold taking on the form of an anklet.
Then, having abandoned its nature as the mind, the mind reached an expanded state of consciousness;
it quickly became something entirely different, like mud remaining within a jar.
Having abandoned the object of consciousness, the pure consciousness attained the state of universal consciousness (citsāmānya),
just as the singular awareness of the ocean remains when the distinctions of waves and the like have been cast off.
Then, having abandoned the mentalization of the multitude of elements, it became the vast, all-sustaining [consciousness].
Then he became that pure, pervasive expanse of consciousness (cidākāśa), having attained awakening.
There he reached the great bliss devoid of both the seen and the seeing—
an infinite, supreme savor, like an ocean of elixir.
Having completely transcended the body, he arrived at a certain state;
his self, consisting of the nature of universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*), became an ocean of bliss.
This swan of the consciousness of the twice-born remained in the stable lake of bliss.
He stood motionless in the sky like the moon full of its digits;
he became like a lamp sheltered from the wind, resembling a figure fixed in a painting,
and like an ocean whose tides have ceased, remaining as still as a cloud that has finished raining.
Then, while staying in that great world, Uddālaka beheld for a long time numerous Siddhas moving through the sky like immortals,
and various throngs of Siddhas arriving from all sides.
Those dense throngs of Apsarases, who bestow the status of Śakra and Ārka,
the twice-born man paid no heed to;
he, of profound intellect and unperturbed, regarded them as the mere frolics of childhood.
Disregarding the company of the Siddhas, he then remained for six months in that temple of his own bliss on the northern horizon like the sun;
that very state of liberation while living which the twice-born man had attained.
There the Siddhas, Suras, Sādhyas, and those beginning with Brahmā and Hara abide;
having been transformed by bliss, they have reached the state beyond bliss.
Neither in bliss nor in the absence of bliss did their consciousness then shine forth.

Whether for a moment or for a thousand years, once the mind has found its stability there, it finds no pleasure in the flood of enjoyments, just as one who has seen heaven finds no delight in the earth. That is the state, that is the peaceful goal; that is the eternal, auspicious supreme good.
For one who has attained rest therein, no further fatigue arises. Having reached that state, the virtuous do not return again to this perception of the visible world,
just as those who have obtained Caitraratha do not go back to the Khadira grove.
Having reached that state of great bliss, the minds of embodied beings no longer value the visible world, just as kings disregard wretchedness.
When the mind is rested in that state, it perceives the condition of the visible world as something already awakened.
"O sinless one, through hardship he attains awakening, or else he does not attain it at all. Then Uddālaka, having dwelt for six months in a place far removed from the realm of the Siddhas—
like the sun emerging from the belly of the clouds in the springtime— awoke.
With his self fully awakened, he again beheld the Siddhas of supreme splendor,
who were intent on prostration and possessed bodies like the orb of the moon;
they held chowries that whirled like clouds of pollen from white Mandāra flowers.
The successions of celestial chariots with their fluttering banners;
the sages like us, whose lotus-hands were marked by the purification of *darbha* grass;
and even the lords of the *vidyādharas*, surrounded by *vidyādharī* maidens.
Then they said to that high-souled sage Uddālaka:
"O Blessed One, look upon us with favor through our prostrations;
having ascended this celestial chariot, come to the city of the gods."
For heaven alone is the ultimate limit of the abundance of worldly enjoyments.
O Lord, enjoy your desired pleasures as is fitting until the end of the kalpa;
indeed, all ascetic practices are performed solely for the sake of experiencing the fruits of heaven and other such realms.
Behold these excellent women of the Vidyādharas, bearing necklaces and chowries, as they attend upon you like female elephants attending a male elephant.
O women of pure smiles, desire is the essence of dharma and artha; indeed, desire is the very essence of you all.
"Like blossoms in springtime, they become heaven itself.
While the Siddhas were speaking thus, the sage, having honored his guests according to the prescribed rule, remained composed and free from agitation.
That man of steady intellect neither rejoiced in nor abandoned that prosperity;
saying, "O Siddhas, depart," he became intent upon his own duties.
Then, devoted to his own work and having become indifferent toward enjoyments—
Having worshipped him, the perfected ones (siddhas) departed on their own after a few days;
and that sage, liberated while living, wandered at his pleasure through the forest edges and the hermitages of the sages for as long as he desired.
On the peaks of Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Himavat, and Vindhya,
and upon the lands of the islands, groves, cardinal directions, thickets, jungles, and forests— from that time forth, the twice-born Uddālaka attained his station.
He dwelt in the caves within the recesses of the mountains, absorbed in the play of meditation.
Sometimes after a day, sometimes after a month, sometimes after a year,
and sometimes after a multitude of years, he would awaken from his absorption in meditation.
From that time on, although Uddālaka was engaged in worldly affairs,
he remained perfectly composed, having attained oneness with the nature of consciousness (*cittattva*).
Through the practice of the singular density of the nature of consciousness, he attained the state of the Great Mind (*mahācitta*).
In this visible world, like a variegated sound, it neither sets nor rises.
With a mind stilled by the attainment of the acquisition of the supreme state, with the bonds of birth shattered and the swing of doubt destroyed,
one beholds that own body— beautiful as the autumnal sky, expansive, powerful, manifest, stainless, and beyond description.
He bore [it].
Chapter fifty-five, titled "The Resting Place of Uddālaka.
Chapter fifty-five.
Rāma said:

O Lord, the sole sun for the day of self-knowledge, the forest fire for the grass of my doubts, and the moon that extinguishes the heat of ignorance—what is this "Being-in-general" (sattāsāmānya)? MU 5.55.1
Vasiṣṭha:
