When the mind is completely dissolved through the contemplation of absolute non-existence,
then that which is the common nature of consciousness becomes the commonality of pure being.
When consciousness, devoid of the aspect of "this-ness," dissolves into itself,
it then becomes like non-existence, utterly transparent, and the universal of pure being (sattāsāmānyatā).
When all objects of perception have subsided and there is no mutual cognition [of subject and object], [that state is the supreme].
When they are meditated upon as having the same nature as one's own nature, then there is equanimity;
visible objects dissolve into the Self by the Self, like the limbs of a tortoise [withdrawing].
When they are not meditated upon at all, then there is the state of pure universal existence.
For this is the supreme vision, which always occurs for both the embodied and the disembodied upon liberation; it is comparable to the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta).
O sinless one, this exists for one who has emerged from meditation as well as for one established in samādhi.
For the wise man alone, and not for the ignorant, does that which is born of awakening arise.
All those noble-minded ones who abide in this vision are liberated while living;
they are like perfected alchemical elixirs on earth, or like winds in the path of the sky.
"O Rāghava, all of us beginning with myself, as well as Nārada and others,
and Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśvara, and the rest, have been seen established within this [state].
By taking hold of this path, which destroys all fear,"

This Uddālaka lived in the house of the world for as long as he desired. Then, after a long time, a firm resolve arose in his mind: "Having cast off this body, I shall remain liberated from the body."
Thus resolved, he sat upon a seat of young leaves within a mountain cave,
having assumed the lotus posture with his eyes closed;
he restrained the nine gates of the mind by means of the suppression of the anus.
Not heeding the contacts of the senses, with the mass of consciousness within his own limbs cultivated,
his vital breaths restrained and his neck held in a balanced posture,
his mouth shines as the root of the tongue touches the surface at the base of the palate.
With his gaze and mind joined together— neither outward nor inward, neither below nor above, neither upon an object nor in emptiness— and without his teeth touching his teeth,
he remains with the flow of his breath restrained and the complexion of his face clear.
With his limbs, consciousness, and awareness uplifted, his body became bristling with horripilation.
Through the practice of the consciousness of his own limbs, he attained the universal consciousness;
from that practice, he reached the supreme, flowing stream of bliss.
Then, through the relishing of that [bliss], the sequence of the state of the commonality of the withdrawn mind reached the universal sustainer,
the infinite self, the commonality of pure existence (*sattāsāmānya*). Abiding therein, with an experience of perfect equanimity, it attained supreme repose.
With the radiance of his face utterly innocent and free from both worldly joy and ordinary bliss,
his hair standing on end from the tranquility of supreme bliss, he had reached the goal and was fully liberated;
the delusion of worldly existence, such as the fluctuations of the mind, had long since been worn away.
That Great Being became like one fixed in a painting;
he was equal to the spotless autumnal moon when its digit is not yet full. Gradually, over the course of a few days, he came to rest within his own stainless self.
Like the sap of a tree at the end of autumn, he passed beyond the stage of birth within the stainless radiance of the sun’s rays.
Having transcended all conceptual constructions, free from transformation, and beautiful, his form was liberated from the adjuncts of all impurities and the play of stains.
He attained that primordial bliss in which the splendor of Indra is carried away like a blade of grass in a mass of water.

Pervading the limitless expanse of space and reaching all directions, full, having the nature of sustaining the worlds, to be served by those of great fortune, beyond description and qualities, true, primordial bliss, happiness that is not of this world, infinite— he became a Brahmin. When his mind had reached that primordial state, which is its own true nature, the body of the twice-born then remained seated for six months.
Scorched by the rays of the sun and made pleasant by the whistling of the wind, the mountain lute became one with its strings exceedingly thin and numerous.
Then, after a long time, the Mothers, accompanied by the daughters of the mountain, emerged from the sky toward that ground of the mountain;
for the sake of attaining their desired fruits, they all descended together like rows of flames from a fire, their hair tawny.
That skeleton of the Brahmin, dried by the rays of the sun, was suddenly grasped at the tip of her hand by the divine goddess Khiṅkhinī—
the goddess of gods, adored by all the wise— who, having performed a dance with nine jewels during the night, now assumed the luster of glass. Thus,
today Uddālaka’s body shines amidst a mass of shimmering peacock feathers, tossed about like fragments of fresh clouds, and entwined with clusters of Mandāra garlands.

In the forest of the heart, which is vast and spread out, this creeper of the mental fluctuations of Uddālaka— whose blossoms are the radiant splendor of the unfolding of self-bliss through discernment— rests like a bee within a cluster of flowers in a vine-thicket that is the playful ornament of the Great Fortunate Goddess Khiṅkhinikā; and subsequently, it approaches [the state of] the inner mass of flowers.
That tree which is once established, shining with beauty and possessing fine shade, never suffers separation from it and attains the highest union with its fruit.
The chapter named "The Liberation of Uddālaka."
Fifty-sixth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
O slayer of enemies, having thus reflected upon yourself by means of your own self in this sequence, [you shall attain liberation].
O lotus-eyed one, one attains rest in the expansive state;
the meaning of the scriptures is investigated by those whose minds are focused on the Guru for as long as it takes to reach the Supreme through the practice of dissolving all that is visible.

The meritorious state is attained through detachment, practice, the meaning of the scriptures, wisdom, and the sequence of preceptors and restraints; or else, it is attained by wisdom alone. For the intellect that possesses perfect awakening is sharp and free from blemish.
"Even one devoid of all requisites attains the eternal goal.
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, is there anyone known to possess such meditative absorption?"
"One who is awakened is at rest even while engaged in worldly activity;
another, having resorted to solitude, remains fixed in meditative absorption.
Of these two, O Blessed One, tell me which is superior."
Vasiṣṭha:
For one who perceives this collection of qualities as not being the self,
that inner coolness which arises is called samādhi.
Having ascertained, "I have no connection with visible objects," one becomes cool;
whether established in worldly activity or established in meditation,
O Rāma, these two are entirely equal if they are inwardly cooled.
That which is inner coolness is true wealth; that is the fruit of austerity.
If the mind of one established in the state of samādhi is restless with mental fluctuations, then that concentration of his is equal to the frantic dancing of a madman.
If the mind of one engaged in the frantic dance [of worldly activity] has its latent impressions (*vāsanā*) exhausted,
then that frantic dance is equal to the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of a Buddha.
He who engages in worldly affairs yet is awakened, and he who is awakened while dwelling in the forest— [they are the same].
Truly, these two persons have reached a state beyond doubt:
one whose mind has subtle latent impressions (*vāsanā*) does not act even when this [body] is acting,
just as a living being whose mind is far away does not act while listening to a story.
Even while not acting, the mind is indeed the agent,
as if one were standing on the brink of a chasm in a dream, though the limbs are motionless.
That state in which the mind is a non-agent is the supreme meditative absorption (samādhi).
Know that to be the state of absolute oneness; it is auspicious, supreme, and final liberation.
For the wavering or steadiness of the mind is the primary cause of memory;
therefore, through meditation and the vision of the meditator, make that very mind free from the sprout of desire.
The mind that is free from latent impressions (vāsanā) is declared to be stable, and that alone is meditation (dhyāna).
That indeed is the state of absolute liberation (kevalībhāva), and therein it is eternally tranquil.
Even a mind with attenuated impressions is said to be striving for the highest state.
The mind that is free from latent impressions (vāsanā) attains the state of non-agency;
however, this mind characterized by dense latent impressions conceives of itself as an agent and bestows all suffering. Therefore, one should cause those latent impressions to become attenuated.
He who, having become inwardly tranquil toward the world and free from sorrow, fear, and desire within,
remains established in his own self— that is known as *samādhi*.
Having completely renounced all states of being along with their mental constructions by means of the mind...

Whether you remain on a mountain or in a house, remain just as you are. For those householders whose minds are well-composed and whose faults of ego-conceit have been stilled, even their homes are like secluded forest lands.
For those whose minds and vision are concentrated, a dwelling in the forest and a dwelling in the city are equal,
just as for great beings here, all beings appear as great beings.
Even the blazing nets of people appear thus to one whose great cloud of the mind is being stilled.
O son of the protector of the earth, cities themselves are empty for one whose mind is intoxicated by worldly activity; even forests are deserted for such a person,
O slayer of enemy heroes, while cities filled with great crowds appear as mere wildernesses.
The mind that has emerged from meditation enters into a state of deep sleep when delusion subsides;

it reaches Nirvana. Whether you wish for Nirvana to be beyond all states of being or identical with the essence of all states of being, act according to your will. *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* 5.56.26. It is beyond the sphere of all existents, or else it is the soul of all existents.

He who always perceives the Self is said to be concentrated (*samāhita*). O Lord of Men, this world is never seen by the mind apart from the Self; it is exactly as it is in a dream, even while one is awake.
Just as people dwelling in a forest are as good as non-existent even while they are there because of their lack of connection [to it], so too, for the knower, even a village is like a forest.
With his mind always turned inward, he remains ever-awakened whether sleeping, walking, or reading.
One perceives the city, the countryside, and the village as if they were a forest.
Through constant abiding in the inward-turned state, everything attains the nature of space;
for this world, teeming with elements, is in every way useless [to such a one].
But when inner coolness is attained, the world becomes cool for those who remain alive, just as it is for men free from fever;
yet for those scorched by the thirst within, the world is filled with the burning of a forest fire.
Whatever exists within all living beings is situated outside as well.
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions—
these are portions of the reality of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) that have become established externally.
Like the hollow of a banyan seed, that which is within this Self shines forth externally, radiant like the fragrance of a blooming flower.
Neither externality nor internality exists anywhere for anything whatsoever.
Whatever appears in whatever manner, because it is consciousness, arises as reality in that very way.
The interior of the reality of the Self shines forth externally as the world;
like camphor with its fragrance, it is both contracted and expanded.
This Self vibrates as this expansive universe, both as "I-ness" and as the world;
it exists as the external and the internal, and yet that all-pervading Lord is neither non-existent nor existent.
That which is perceived as being outside is the external, and that which stands as being within is the internal.
When this Self is known as it truly is, one perceives its own nature within;
the world, both external and internal, is seen as peaceful and non-different from the Self.
However, while the sense of "I" and so forth persists in the body, there remains a great fear characterized by manifold breakages.

For one whose self is struck by mental anguish, heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions— all seem ablaze as if by the fire at the end of an aeon. But he who delights only in the Self, performing actions with his organs of action while remaining inwardly composed—

He who is not subject to joy or sorrow is said to be composed (samāhita). He who, seeing the Self as omnipresent, has a thoroughly tranquil intellect, neither grieves nor meditates [on worldly objects]; he is said to be composed.
He who, seeing the courses of the world with all their prior and subsequent limits,
laughs at these views— he is said to be composed. In me, the supreme equanimity, there is no "I-ness" nor the birth of the world.
Just as the elements of foam do not perish without dissolving back into the mass of waves,
so too he in whom there is no "I-ness" within, nor division and the like,
nor "mine," nor consciousness and unconsciousness— he exists; the other person does not exist.
He who, being as pure as the sky, conducts himself here with perfect self-restraint,
remains like a piece of wood or a clod of earth amidst the transformations of joy and anger;
he regards all beings as his own self and the wealth of others as a mere clod of earth.

He who sees [the object] by its very nature and not out of fear, he truly sees. An object, whether large or small, is not perceived as having the form of non-existence; nor is it experienced by the knower as having the form of existence, just as it would be by one who does not know it in its true state.
Endowed with such an intention and having attained the state of a Great Being,
let him stay or arise, let him go or meet death,
let him strike down or dwell in his own home, rich in supreme enjoyments or crowded with people.
Whether he dwells in a vast forest where all enjoyments have been abandoned, or dances with unrestrained drumming intent on drinking, or whether,
having renounced all attachments, he attains tranquility on a mountain— let him do as he pleases.
Let him anoint his body with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor;
or let him fall into a fire spreading with a mass of tangled flames.
Let him commit great evil, or even abundant merit.
Let him meet his death this very day, or at the end of a multitude of kalpas;
he is nothing, nor is anything done by that Great-Souled One,
for he incurs no stain, just as gold remains untainted even when immersed in mud.
The consciousness is stained by the objects denoted by the words "person" (*puruṣa*) and so forth,
which are themselves defiled and consist of the latent impressions of the sense of "I-ness," resembling the silver perceived in a mother-of-pearl shell.
Through right knowledge of things as they truly are, there occurs the cessation of all objective entities.
For that very internal stain of his has been pacified through non-existence;
since the evil habituation of "I-ness" produces for the person— the ground of birth for consciousness— various pleasures and pains.
Just as a householder finds relief when the delusion of a snake in a rope has subsided,
so too is internal equanimity held to arise when the sense of "I-ness" has been completely stilled.
Whatever one does, whatever one eats, whatever one gives, or whatever one offers in sacrifice— [all this is performed within that state].

For the knower, that [action] does not exist, nor does the knower exist therein; let him act or let him not act. For him there is no purpose through action, nor is there any purpose through non-action;
established in his very self according to his own nature, he is the Blessed One.
From that, desires arise—not like blossoms from a stone—but all those that do arise are that very same reality, just as waves are water.
This entire world and that [Self] are everything; there is no division whatsoever here.
He whose singular form is the purifier of the Supreme Person is "Being" (Sat); yet that Being is indeed nothing at all.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Investigation of Meditation."
Vasiṣṭha:
Just as the perception of sharpness exists within the sun-crystal because it possesses consciousness,
so too does this [consciousness] perceive "I-ness," duality, space, time, and so forth.
That which is the perception of sweetness within the saltiness of the self, due to its nature as consciousness,
exists as characterized by distinctions such as "I-ness," as well as by space, time, and so forth.
That which is the perception of sweetness within the self by the observer of the self, due to its nature as consciousness, exists inherently.
That which is the experience of solidity by the stone of the Self, due to its own intrinsic consciousness— manifesting as "I-ness," duality, and so forth, as well as the world and its like—
has attained the state of spatial and temporal distinctions and the rest. (MU 5.57.3–4)
That which is the experience of insentience by virtue of knowing itself as the self, mountains, and so forth,
is established as "I-ness" (ahantva), "duality" (bhedādi), "the world" (bhuvanādi), and so on.
That which is the transformation of the water of the self, due to its being fluid consciousness, [is the same].
Therefore, that which consists of the whirlpools and so forth, the "I-ness" and so forth, the distinctions and so forth, and the forms and so forth—
just as branches and such belong to the tree of the Self by its own nature— the perception of those [forms] appears clearly as "I-ness," "distinction," and so on, like the world and its contents.
That which is the perception of emptiness within the sky of the self due to its nature as consciousness—
that has been cultivated as the ego, duality, and so forth, as well as meditative cultivation.
That which is the perception of voidness within the sky of the self due to its nature as consciousness—
Thus, the "I-ness" (ahantā) and so forth, like the mind and the body, are illuminated;

that which is the self's own uninterrupted continuity, being devoid of gaps, appears as if situated outside due to its nature as consciousness, through the distinctions of "I-ness" and the rest. (MU 5.57.9–10)

Since it is by its own nature the knower of its own existence, that which is the singular awareness of existence is established as "I-ness" (*ahantva*), "differentiation" (*bhedādi*), or "consciousness" (*cetanādi*).
This is because the internal manifestation of the light of the Self occurs spontaneously.
Having understood that "I-ness" and so forth, as well as "knowledge-ness" and so forth, belong to the individual soul (jīva), he perceives it thus:
"That which exists within as the moon of the Self—the form of consciousness, the elixir of consciousness—is tasted by itself; therefore, 'I-ness' and the rest have arisen from that."

That which exists within the sugar-candy of the Supreme Self, consisting of the emergence of the sweetness of consciousness— that very thing is tasted by it internally through its own nature as "I-ness" (ahantā) and so forth.
Because of its consciousness, that which is the internal shining-forth of the jewel of the Supreme Self occurs spontaneously.
Internally, he perceives that very [state] as the nature of volition, thinking "I am," and so forth; yet,
because there is no object of knowledge here, he knows nothing internally, nor does he savor any flavor, for there is simply no flavor to be savored.
And he accumulates nothing within, since that which is to be accumulated is impossible;
nor is anything perceived, because that which is to be perceived is impossible.
This Self is a mere appearance of non-existence, infinite and of a full form.

He remains forever as a single, solid mass within himself, like a great mountain. By this turn of speech, O descendant of Raghu, I have demonstrated to you that there is no distinction between the "I-ness" and so forth, and the "world-ness" and so forth.
There is no mind, nor a thinker, nor the delusion of the world and so forth;
like the sky within a stone, it is therefore peaceful and becomes solely quiescent.
Just as water within water attains the state of whirlpools and the like due to its fluidity, [so does this occur].
Thus, through the knowledge of it, the knower attains the state of "I-ness" and so forth within the Self, which is pure consciousness;
just as liquidity exists in water and motion in the wind,
so do "I-ness," space, time, and the rest exist in the Knower, who is pure consciousness alone.
For when the Knower, through the expansion of knowledge, knows that which exists in the state of knowability—
namely, "I-ness" and so forth, as well as the "living self" and so forth through the functions of living—
it is known just as the cognition of the Knower arises through knowledge in its particular form.
Having realized that non-otherness itself is otherness, she then expands in that manner.
The life of the individual soul is knowledge; when there is the state of being a knower, there is the life of the living soul.
There is not even an atom’s worth of difference between the knower and the living soul, despite their apparent diversity.

Just as there is no difference between the Knower and the individual soul, O Rāma, so too there is no difference between the Knower and the world; know it to be peaceful and indivisible. All is utterly tranquil, unborn, one, without beginning or middle, a mere manifestation and tasting, beyond thought and beyond signs.
All is utterly tranquil; yet this perception consisting of sound is indeed for the sake of awakening, though it is merely in vain—this "Om.
The fifty-eighth canto, titled "The Dispelling of Duality."
Vasiṣṭha said: In this very context, they cite this ancient history,
the wondrous account of Suraghu, the lord of the Kirātas.
The fat of the northern direction, a mass of camphor from the earth,
the laughter gathered from Śiva, or perhaps the white radiance of the moon;
here on earth stands a peak of the Snowy Mountain, a mountain named Kailāsa.
He is the leader of the mountain range as if it were a fine cluster of pearls;
he is like the ocean of milk to Viṣṇu, like heaven to the Lord of the Gods,
and like the navel-lotus of the Lotus-born One to the Moon-crested Lord.
He shines with the swaying clusters of *rudrākṣa* beads along with the celestial nymphs (*apsaras*),
like the ocean with its waves of shimmering jeweled rods;
he is struck incessantly by the feet of the intoxicated wives of the *gaṇas*.
Where the blossoming *aśoka* trees shine like [the goddess] Aśokā; where,
as Śaṅkara wanders through the quarters among the *bhṛgu* stones, waterfalls flow forth and return incessantly, melting the moonstones.
It is here that the universe is encompassed by masses of creepers, shrubs, and trees, by ponds, lakes, rivers, and streams, and by terrified herds of beasts and flocks of birds;
at its base dwell the Kirātas known as the Hemajaṭas.
Like ants dwelling within the root-cavity of an excellent tree,
those insignificant beings live near him like insects in a forest at the foot of Mount Kailāsa, amidst thickets of tangled shrubs, subsisting on what is close at hand.
Among them there was a noble-souled king, a conqueror of enemy cities,
who was like the right arm of the Goddess of Victory and of his subjects;
he was named Suraghu, powerful and the destroyer of the pride of formidable enemies.
He was like valor incarnate, or like the wind embodied;
a Jina through the riches of his dispassion, a leader of the Guhyakas through his wealth,
a preceptor of Indra through his insights, and a teacher of the Asuras through his poetic compositions.
He performed his royal duties through the sequence of punishments and favors as they arose,
with an untiring soul, just as the sun traverses its days.
Then, however, he was overcome by the pleasure and pain born of those very actions.
"Or, like a bird caught by the neck in a well-set snare,
shall I, with my own vigor, further torment this distressed being as if it were pressed in an oil-press?
For the suffering that arises for me is born as suffering for all living beings alike."
"I bestow wealth upon him; through wealth, every person becomes possessed of joy, just as I am. Therefore, enough of my restraints!
Or rather, I shall exercise restraint only against one who has actually committed an offense."
This progeny does not exist without water, like a river.
Alas, what misery! This one was to be restrained, yet by fortune he is to be favored by me;
by fortune I am happy today, yet by misery I am sorrowful today.
Thus the king’s mind wavered and found no rest,
circling for a long time like a blade of grass in a great whirlpool of water.
Then one day, the sage Māṇḍavya came to his house.
Wandering through every corner of the quarters like Nārada for Indra,
he honored that great sage—
who was an axe to the trunk of the stubborn tree of doubt and was skilled in all things— and questioned him.
Suraghu said:
"O Sage, by your arrival I have attained supreme bliss,
like the surface of the earth when the month of Mādhava has arrived."
"Today, O Lord, I stand at the forefront of the blessed by virtue of the Dharma,
since I have been beheld by you, as a lotus is by the radiant sun.
Blessed One, Knower of all Dharmas, you have rested for a long time."
Therefore, cut through this doubt of mine, as the sun dispels the darkness.
For whom indeed does suffering not perish through association with the great?
Yet those who know suffering say that doubt is the supreme form of suffering.
The anxieties born from the rejection or acceptance of various beings, which reside within the bodies of my devotees,
torment me excessively, like the claws of a lion upon an elephant. Therefore, let equanimity arise in me, pervading all things like the rays of the sun.
O sage worthy of my respect, act accordingly out of compassion.
Māṇḍavya said:
O King, by means of your own method, which is within your own power and established in yourself—
This flimsiness of the mind dissolves like snow;
by means of self-inquiry alone, the fever of the mind within is quickly pacified,
just as a great mist vanishes with the mere arrival of autumn.
With one's own mind, one should inwardly investigate one's own sense faculties located within one's own body: what are they like, or what indeed are they?
Who am I? How did this come to be? What is it? And how do death and birth occur?
Reflect upon this within yourself; you will attain sufficient greatness.
Once your true nature has been fully understood through such reflection, the mental states of joy and resentment shall no longer be able to shake your mind, which remains as immovable as a mountain.
Having cast off its own form, your mind will attain peace and freedom from fever,
becoming like a wave that has returned to its original state within the water;
O sinless one, even while it persists, your mind will abandon its [dualistic] form.
O Kāla, they will become like the seasons when another season has arrived— devoid of blemish. All those illustrious ones will be objects of compassion,
like subjects on earth toward a father who has seen the truth and is well-pleased.
O King, with the self perceived by the lamp of discernment, you will surpass even the greatness of Mount Meru, the oceans, and the sky— that greatness which bestows the supreme goal.
And your mind, having attained such greatness, [will find no further purpose] in the cycles of worldly existence.
O virtuous one, he shall not sink, like an elephant in the hoofprints of cattle.
But the wretched mind, O King, sinks even in a trivial matter,
just as an aged mosquito sinks in the water of a cow's footprint.
Through the mental impression (*vāsanā*) of the mind, one sinks like a worm in the mud by means of that very wretchedness of one's own which clings to the mere appearance of objects.
O mighty-armed one, to that same extent everything is abandoned of its own accord.

Just as the ore is washed away until only the supreme gold remains, so too everything is scrutinized until only the Self is perceived. MU 5.58.42 As long as the other world exists, it is only the Supreme Self that remains; as long as the element is being purified, it is only the gold that remains;
so long is everything observed until the Self alone is discerned. MU 5.58.42
Having completely renounced everything— in every way, everywhere, and at all times— by means of a universalizing intellect, the Self is realized by the self through itself.
As long as everything has not been relinquished, the Self is not attained.

When all things have been relinquished, what remains is called the "self. O virtuous one, as long as something else has not been abandoned, one does not attain a thing that is truly universal; so what need is there to speak of attaining one's own self?
O King, that alone— and nothing else— is truly attained where one, having abandoned all other activities, falls of one's own accord with one's whole being for the sake of attaining one’s true self;
therefore, for the purpose of beholding the Self, one should renounce everything.

Having renounced everything whatsoever, that which remains is the supreme state. Having thoroughly cast aside from the mind all that is manifested as the reality within the world— consisting of the entire succession of causes and effects— and having likewise completely severed one's own bodily form, that which is auspicious [remains].
The fifty-ninth canto, titled "Māṇḍavya’s Instruction," within the narrative of Suraghu; Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus to Suraghu, O descendant of Raghu,
the Blessed One Māṇḍavya, adorned with silence, departed for his own quarter.
When the excellent sage had gone, the king went to a secluded and blameless spot.
He reflected deeply within himself with his intellect: "Who indeed am I?
"I am not Meru, nor is Meru mine; I am not the world, nor is the world mine.
I am not the mountains, nor are the mountains mine; I am not the earth, nor is the earth mine."
"This Kirāta territory is not mine, nor am I the territory;
this region is mine solely by virtue of my own convention.
That convention has been abandoned by me; neither am I the region, nor does it belong to me."
Now only the city remains; this indeed is the certain conclusion here.
Rich with banners, city-gates, and palanquins, crowded with servants and groves, and filled with elephants, horses, and vassals—neither am I that city, nor is the city mine.
Bound by futile conventions, destroyed when those conventions cease—
this multitude of enjoyments and this wife are not I, nor is all this mine. Thus [it is with] the retinue, the army, the vehicles, and the interior of the city.
"I am not the kingdom, nor is the kingdom mine; for this conventional designation is confusing. (MU 5.59.8) "I consider myself to be merely the body, joined with hands, feet, and so forth.
Therefore, let me first thoroughly investigate this very thing within. (MU 5.59.9)
Therefore, in this regard, I am not this flesh and bone, which are insentient;
nor do they enter into union with me, just as water does not with a lotus.
Flesh is inert, so I am not that; nor am I even the blood.
I am not the dull bones, nor do they ever belong to me.
I am not the organs of action, nor do the organs of action belong to me.
Whatever in this body is indeed insentient, that I am not, for I am consciousness.
I am not the enjoyments, nor are the enjoyments mine; nor am I the sense organs, which are inert and of an unreal nature, nor are the sense organs I.
The mind is the root of the defect of transmigratory existence, for it is indeed inert; I am not that.
Now, the view that "intellect" (buddhi) is the ego (ahaṅkāra) is composed of the mind (manomayī).
That body consists of the sheath of the elements (bhūtakośa), ending with the mind, intellect, and senses;
yet I am not thus [identified with] the body and so forth—I perceive what remains.

But the remaining [self] is the living consciousness (*cetanājīva*), and it perceives by means of the object of perception (*cetya*). If that [consciousness] is awakened by something else, it would not possess the nature of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattvavapuḥ*).
Thus, I abandon the object of sensation; for indeed, I am not that which is perceived.
I remain as pure consciousness, the remainder, free from conceptual construction.
This wonderful one—I am he who has attained his own nature, born in time as the knower of what is to be done.
This is that I, the infinite self; where is the end of this Supreme Self?
In Brahmā, Indra, Yama, Vāyu, and likewise in the hosts of all beings,
this very Blessed One, the Self, exists like a thread within pearls.
This power of consciousness (cicchakti) is stainless and free from the disease of the object of cognition (cetya).
Filling every corner of the quarters of space, she assumes a terrifying form;
she pervades all states of being, subtle, and free from both existence and non-existence.
Abiding as far as the world of Brahmā, she is the casket containing all powers.
She is the one most blessed with all beauty, the lamp illuminating all that is manifest;
she is the thread in the form of a stretched web for all those liberated from saṃsāra. She is enriched with all forms and transformations, yet she is devoid of all forms.
She has become the flood of all beings and has always attained the state of being everything.
Within the interior of the world, there are fourteen kinds of beings;
this worldly conceptualization, consisting of them, is essentially of the nature of sensation.
The state of all suffering and the course of existence is merely a false appearance;
the supreme consciousness, which manifests as all these various forms, is nothing other than the Self itself.
This very Self is pervasive within me; this is my awakening.
This very [mind], with its limbs assumed [as a body], creates the delusion of being a king.
By the grace of this [mind] alone, the mind— seated upon the chariot of the body— gallops, leaps,
and dances amidst the playful activities of the web of saṃsāra.
This mind, body, and so forth are in reality nothing at all;
when this fragile thing perishes, nothing whatsoever is lost.
This dance, consisting of the web of the world, is performed by the actors that are the minds.
By this single streak of light, as it were, she is seen.
Alas, my concern regarding the state of restraint and favor has been in vain;
it was centered solely upon the body, yet the body itself is nothing at all.
"Ah! I have indeed awakened; my false vision has vanished.
That which was to be seen has been seen in its entirety, and that which was to be attained has been attained by me. Whatever is seen here as this visible world, all of it is but this."
That is merely a portion of the outflow of consciousness; nothing else exists there that is eternal.
Where are those two [powers], of what kind are they, on what are they based, and what is their nature—the restraint and favor in the world, as well as the sequences of joy and resentment?
What is pleasure and what is pain? All this is the pervasive Brahman.
I was deluded in vain; by good fortune, I am now established as one who is no longer deluded.
In this light, what is there to grieve for, and why should one be bewildered?
What is being perceived? What is being done? Where is one staying? Where is one going?
This something called "this" shines forth as a manifestation of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*).
Obeisance, obeisance to You, O One devoid of objective reality (*nistattva*); You are the beautiful one who is both the seer and the seen.
"Aha! I have indeed awakened; I have fully understood; enough for me!
Homage to myself, the infinite, and to the arising of perfect knowledge! Free from passion, abiding in the objectless state, with the delusion of existence gone, I am devoid of all striving."
Then, having transcended the state of steady deep sleep, I dwell in the Self in absolute equanimity. This is the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Resting of Suraghu."
Vasiṣṭha:
Thus the Lord of Hemajaṭā attained the unsurpassed state through discernment and resolute effort, just as the son of Gadhi [Viśvāmitra] attained the status of a Brahmin.
He did not experience weariness in his activities, which involved endless forms of action,
even as they were performed again and again, like a lord throughout a succession of days.
From that time forth, he remained free from the fever of all worldly endeavors.
When his own task was completed, like a mass of water subsiding before him,
he— freed from joy and resentment and performing his natural duty—
possessing a noble and profound form, surpassed the splendor of the ocean.
He shone with a mental state possessing the qualities of deep sleep—
a state that was unwavering and luminous— just as a lamp shines by its own flame.
He was neither merciless nor compassionate, neither subject to dualities nor free from envy.
He was neither happy nor unhappy, neither desiring nor desiring to avoid;
through his constant vision of equanimity and his stainless, steady conduct,
he shone with inner coolness like the orb of the full moon.
Perceiving that the entire world is the manifestation of the essence of consciousness,
her mind shone forth in fullness, its glory of pleasure and pain stilled;
whether exulting, sporting, reeling, standing, walking, breathing, or sleeping.
Established in his own samādhi, he became awakened and attained absorption in consciousness.
Governing the kingdom with detachment, that lotus-eyed one remained for many hundreds of years with his form unimpaired.
Thereafter, overcome by that splendor, he himself abandoned this abode called the body, just as a drop of frost dissolves;
he entered that supreme, primordial cause, the Lord of Causes.
Like an ocean filled with a flood of water by a flowing river,

that great-souled one— having attained the stainless, singular form of splendor, having reached the state of the sky, and being stilled of sorrow— was fully sufficient for the supreme true nature, just as a pot is united with the space within it.
The sixty-first canto, titled "The Conclusion of the Story of Suraghu," ends. Vasiṣṭha said:
Holding fast to this view, the mind does not suffer,
like a child who has found a lamp while submerged in a terrible darkness.
Through the state of discernment, the mind attains tranquility even with a subtle body.
Just as one might cross a precipice by relying on a dense mass of sturdy grass,
having understood this purifying vision and cultivated it through exposition,
remain forever in one-pointed concentration, thereby adorning the surface of the earth.
Rāma:
O Lord of Sages, how can there be a single-pointed concentration, or what is its nature? For the mind is as restless as the plumage of a peacock struck by the wind.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen now to this wonderful dialogue between Suraghu, who was then awakened, and the royal sage Parṇāda.
I shall reveal to you this mutual conversation between the two whose souls had arisen from being awakened by the singular concentration on Rāghava.
There was a king of the Pārasīkas, a slayer of enemy heroes.
He was renowned by the name Parigha, like a bolt upon a chariot.
O descendant of Raghu, Suraghu became his supreme friend,
just as Mādhava is to Madana when he dwells in the Nandana grove.
Once, in Parigha’s realm, there suddenly occurred a great calamity,
born from the fault of the people’s evil deeds, like the end of an eon in this world of transmigration.
There, many populations perished, their lives destroyed by hunger.
Just as a succession of living beings perishes when a forest is ablaze with fire,
Parigha saw that suffering and fell into incomparable despair;
he abandoned his entire kingdom like a traveler leaving a burnt village.
Incapable of remedying the destruction of his subjects and possessing a state of detachment,
he went to the forest to perform austerities like the Lord of Jina Munis,
remaining unrecognized by the citizens in a certain distant forest.
With a detached soul, he dwelt there as if in another world;
practicing austerities with a peaceful mind and self-controlled, he made his home in a mountain cave and consumed only dry leaves that had fallen of their own accord.
Then, for a long time, consuming only withered leaves like a fire,
he obtained the name Parṇāda among the ascetics.
From that time forth, that best of royal sages was known by the name Parṇāda.

In Jambudvīpa, he became renowned among the dwellings of sages. Then, after a thousand years of asceticism performed with a resolute mind, he attained through the power of practice that knowledge born of self-purification.
Free from duality, devoid of passion, possessing equal vision,
effortless, and beyond compassion, he was one liberated while living, his intellect fully awakened;
he wandered at will through this small hut of the three worlds.
O virtuous one, together with those who were perfected and those still seeking perfection, he— like a bee toward a lotus—
once reached the palace of King Hemacūḍa,
which was constructed of jewels and resembled another peak of Mount Meru.
Having emerged from the pit of ignorance and having realized what is to be known, they both performed full mutual honors there toward their former friend.
"Oh, how indeed my auspicious and purifying [deeds] have borne fruit! he exclaimed.
"I have found you," they said to one another;
then those two of irreproachable form, their bodies embraced,
sat together upon a single seat like the sun and the moon upon a mountain peak.
Parigha:
My mind has attained supreme bliss through the sight of you;
like the orb of the moon emerging from the water, it has become cooled within.
Natural affection for a friend, upon separation, branches out into a hundred shoots,
like a tree that has been cut down and re-rooted on the bank of a pond.
Those confident conversations, those playful gestures, and that behavior—

O virtuous one, remembering my former state, I rejoice again and again. O sinless one, this knowledge has been attained by me through the grace of Māṇḍavya— knowledge born from the grace of the Supreme Self, just as it was attained by you.
"O lord of the earth, are you today free from suffering? Have you found rest upon the supreme mountain Meru, as it were?
O most auspicious one, do you, through delighting in your own self,"
Clarity arises in the mind like the water of a lake in autumn.
O fortunate one, O lord of men, do you attend to your duties with a gaze that is both very serene and profound? (MU 5.61.29–30)
Are the wise people in your lands free from mental and physical ailments, and do they dwell without the fever of distress, their rice harvests fully ripened?
Is the earth, bending under its weight like a fruit-bearing creeper, yielding abundant fruit?

The earth sustains its subjects abundantly with the fullness of your fruits. Is your purifying fame, like a cage of moonbeams, spread throughout the ends of the quarters in the form of a mass of frost?

I hope, O friend, that these quarters have been made free of gaps by you through your hundreds of virtues, just as the walls [of a field] are filled by the waters of a lake for the sake of the lotus stalks;
and I hope that those who dwell joyfully upon the posts in the corners of the rice fields are [content].
In every village, young maidens sang of your joy-bestowing fame:
"May there be well-being for you in your grain, your wealth, and your possessions;
likewise in your servants, your wives, your sons, and your cities."
Is this vine of your body free from mental and physical afflictions?
Does it bear fruit known as merit, as proclaimed for both this world and the next?
[For those things] which are pleasant at first sight but are ultimately and utterly hostile.
Is your mind free from passion toward the serpents of the sense-objects?
Oh, how long a time it has been since we two were separated;
by the power of time, we have been joined once more, like the spring season and the mountain slope.
O friend, those states of happiness and suffering born of union and separation, which are not seen by living beings, do not exist in this world. Thus,
throughout these exceedingly long states, they have undergone transformation.
"Furthermore, we too have been embraced [by this fate], for the destiny of the Ordainer is indeed manifold.
Suraghu said:
"O Blessed One, the course of this destiny is like the movement of a lamp's flame."
For who can understand the profound and wondrous course of destiny?
You and I, separated by great distances and into far-off conditions, have been joined together once more today; oh, what is impossible for Fate?
But we, O Great Being, now stand exceedingly well;
through the merit of your arrival, we have attained supreme purity.
For us, whose sins have been somewhat diminished by your coming, [the fruits] of the trees of merit [are now manifest].
Thus has our fruiting occurred that we are no longer distressed.
O royal sage, all our prosperities were already established in the city;
by your arrival today, they have branched out into a hundred directions.
O one of great majesty, your speech scatters sweetness all around like a heap of elixirs;
both your word and your gaze are meritorious, for association with the virtuous is indeed equal to the supreme state.
The Fifth Chapter, titled "The Meeting with Suraghu."
The sixty-second canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, for a long time, they remained there engaged in such confidential conversation.
Standing there, the one named Ayudha, filled with affection for his former friend, spoke:
"O King, whatever action is performed within this web of worldly existence," said Parigha.

O sinless one, for one whose mind is thus concentrated, there is happiness unlike any other. Do you perhaps practice that supreme samādhi— the highest state of tranquility and excellence— which is free from conceptual construction and is the ultimate place of rest?
Suraghu:
O Blessed One, tell me this which is free from all conceptual constructions:
what indeed is called that samādhi which is the supreme excellence of ultimate tranquility?
O Great-souled One, who indeed is that wise person who, while constantly acting in silence or even in speech,
is ever uncomposed in mind? And when, for whom, does such a state actually occur?
But those whose minds are eternally awakened, even while performing worldly activities,
are always in perfect samādhi, being established in that single reality of the Self.
This is true even for one who is seated in the lotus posture or has joined his palms in the *brahmāñjali* gesture.
For that which has the nature of never resting, what is meditative absorption (samādhi), or how could it be? [Suraghu:
O Blessed One, the realization of reality is a fire that consumes the straw of all desires.
This is declared according to the distinctions of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and not merely as remaining silent.
O virtuous one, by the word "meditative absorption," the wise refer to supreme wisdom (*prajñā*)—which is ever-satisfied and perceives the reality of things as they truly are. (MU 5.62.8–9)
Unshaken, free from egoism, and not falling under the sway of dualities,
the state that is more stable than Mount Meru is designated by the term "samādhi.
It is free from thought, devoid of desired objects, and divested of both the rejectable and the acceptable.

The complete movement of the mind is designated by the word "samādhi. From the moment the mind becomes endowed with absolute awakening, the concentration of that Great-Souled One remains uninterrupted from that point onward.
For once the mind has become awakened, meditative concentration is not severed again,
just as the lotus fiber drawn out by a child cannot be pulled back even from afar;
nor does the eye cease its perception of light throughout the entire day.
"May my wisdom last until the end of my life through such contemplation of reality.
Just as a river is not obstructed by its constant flow of water,
so the vision of discernment is not obstructed for even a single moment through awakening."
Just as the continuous flow of time does not forget its own movement at every moment,
so too the intellect of the wise does not cease to remember its own self everywhere.
Just as the ever-moving wind does not forget its course in all places, so the intellect of the wise remains ever-attentive to its true nature.
Just as the intellect of a wise man, having determined the object of thought, does not forget pure consciousness (*cinmātra*),

so too does the Intellect remain established while discerning its own movement through the divisions of time; O dear one, the Intellect likewise remains for a long time while discerning that which is devoid of any object of thought.
Just as an object devoid of existence is not perceived,
so for the knower, time devoid of the knowledge of the Self is not found.
Just as in the world of transmigration, a possessor of qualities cannot exist without those qualities.
For one who possesses a self cannot exist as such if devoid of self-awareness.
"I am always fully awakened; I am always stainless;
I am always peaceful in nature; I am always composed in meditation."
By what could a disturbance of my meditative absorption be produced, or how could it be so,
by anything distinct from myself that is eternally of the nature of non-existence?
Therefore, my mind has never at any time been other than composed of meditative absorption.
And it is not eternally non-concentrated, because it arises solely from the reality of the Self. The Self is omnipresent, eternal, and indeed everything in every way.
For what could that be which is non-concentration, and what is traditionally known as concentration?
The great ones, whose intellects are eternally concentrated and who possess perfect tranquility, abide free from the distinctions of the transformation of objects;
therefore, my elaborate discourse is not falsely proclaimed through the breaking down of the distinction between the unconcentrated and the concentrated.
Thus ends the chapter named "The Determination of Samādhi."
The sixty-third canto, "The Iron Bar":
O King, you have surely awakened; you have attained that supreme state.
With an inner heart completely cooled, you shine like the full moon;
filled with the honey of bliss and endowed with supreme splendor,
you shine like a lotus, cool, gentle, and sweet.
Stainless, expansive, full, profound, and with your intentions made manifest,
you shine like the ocean when it is released from the agitation caused by the force of the wind at the shore;
you are clear, filled with your own bliss, and have dispelled the clouds of egoism.
Clearly you shine like the autumnal sky—vast and profound.
You appear composed in every situation, you are content in every situation;
O King, you are free from passion everywhere, and you shine everywhere.
Having reached the further shore of discerning the essential from the non-essential through your great intelligence,
you know all this exactly as it exists, without exception;
O knower of the reality that distinguishes existence from non-existence, you whose disposition is joyful!
Your body remains free from the agitation of the states of passion and aversion;
like the ocean filled with nectar, you are completely satisfied by the distinction between the real and the unreal, O handsome one, so that there is no further decay.
Suraghu said:
O Sage, there is no object whatsoever in which we find anything worth accepting; for as much as this visible world exists, it is nothing at all.
And since there is nothing to be acquired, what indeed could there be that is to be abandoned?
Without the exclusion of its opposite, how can something be called "to be abandoned"?
Because all things are either non-existent or, from the perspective of time, not non-existent.

For a long time, my mental states— both the trivial and the non-trivial— have been utterly exhausted. Having observed here that, by the power of place and time, the trivial becomes non-trivial and the non-trivial becomes trivial, the wise should avoid both censure and praise.
In this world, praise and blame arise from passion; and passion arises from longing.
And that which is longed for by one of beautiful intellect is a most noble object.
Within the three worlds, these are women, mountains, oceans, and forest ranges.

The elements are utterly void; beyond that, there is no supreme essence. In this decaying world, which consists of soft masses resembling tumors of flesh, and which is empty and devoid of anything desirable—what indeed can be desired?
When desire has ceased, there is the destruction of aversion and passion, just as light and heat vanish when the splendor of day has passed.
Enough with these excessively prolix elaborations of speech; this single perspective is sufficient for happiness in this world.
If the mind within has its latent impressions fully stilled and is indeed joyful, that is the supreme foundation.
The sixty-fourth canto, named "The Firm Resolve of Suraghu."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus reflected upon the delusion of the world, Suraghu and Parigha honored one another; satisfied, they each returned to their own respective duties.
O Rāghava, having heard that very [teaching] which is the supreme cause of awakening,
become clearly established in this very awakening.
O steadfast one, by means of supreme wisdom whose sharpness is extended through inquiry, [realize the truth].

When the autumn season of the mind has arrived— vast and stainless, bringing joy and bearing fruit through the consensus of all the worlds— the dark cloud of egoism has utterly vanished from the sky of the heart. (MU 5.64.3–4)

One abides in the supreme Self, the most highly praised space of consciousness, which is the object of meditation, the refuge, perfectly equanimous, the source of all blissful prosperity, and supremely auspicious;
[he who] is eternally composed of the inner self, eternally inward-turned, and happy.
Through constant contemplation of consciousness, he is not afflicted by sorrow.
Even while intensely engaged in worldly affairs and possessed of passion and aversion,
he does not take on internal stain, just as a lotus does not take on a drop of water.
The sage who possesses right discernment and, having understood, has a mind that is inwardly peaceful,
is not afflicted by the mind, just as the king of beasts is not harassed by an elephant.
In the wise one, there exists no wretched mind that finds its sole refuge in worldly enjoyments.
Like a wicked tree in the Nandana grove, the mind of the wise man is like the body of the Himalayas.
Just as a human being is not pained by the death of a wife who has lost her passion,
so too the mind that has fully understood all ignorance does not grant suffering.
One whose delusion regarding the mind has been fully understood through the realization of the light of the world is not touched by sin, just as the surface of the sky is untouched by dust.
The mere thorough comprehension of ignorance is itself the great medicine.
It is like a lamp for the cataract of the disease spread by ignorance.
For as soon as ignorance is thoroughly understood, it is utterly destroyed;
moreover, the realm of enjoyment no longer tastes sweet.
Even while engaged in worldly affairs, the virtuous person whose mind is inwardly unattached and unified in thought is not touched by sin, just as water does not touch the eye of a fish.
When the light of the sun of consciousness has arrived, the night of ignorance has been utterly destroyed.
The ground of consciousness, having attained supreme bliss, shines for the knower.
When the sleep of ignorance has ceased, the person awakened by the sun of knowledge attains that enlightenment by which he is never again deluded.
Those days are lived joyfully, and those sequences of actions are truly fruitful,
in which the moonlight of consciousness arises within the sky of the heart through the contemplation of the Self.
A person who has crossed over delusion by means of constant contemplation of their own Self—

He attains an inner coolness as if by his own nectar, like the moon. Those are true friends, those are true scriptures, and those are true days, by which the clear arising of self-contemplation occurs for one filled with the radiance of dispassion.

Those wretched ones, who have incurred sin and for whom the contemplation of the Self is a mere trifle, grieve for a long time like creepers in the jungle of rebirth. Bound by hundreds of snares of hope and greedily longing for the bait of worldly enjoyments, they suffer.
With a form worn out by old age, distressed by sighs of grief,
bearing the heavy burden of suffering, living in the wilderness of birth,
smeared with the mud of evil deeds, and lying in the pool of delusion.
Bitten by the swarm of disease-biting insects, dragged by the excellent rope of craving, spurred on by the horse of the mind, and made motionless by the bonds of kin;
worn out by the decrepitude of children and wife, it sinks and rises again in the mire of misery.
Exhausted and deprived of rest, broken upon the long path,
worn out by coming and going, wandering in the wilderness of saṃsāra,
it has not found cool shade and is tormented by intense heat.
Resplendent in its outward form yet wretched, overcome by the senses as by draft-animals,
mounted upon the carriage of karma, exhausted by the lashings of misdeeds,
and difficult to bear due to the whirling cycle of appearance and disappearance;
Rolling in the vast forest of ignorance with broken limbs,
submerged in the pitfall of his own misfortunes, sinking down, destitute,
his body exhausted by the burden of karma, he utters piteous cries.
O Rāma, applying the greatest effort, one should forcibly rescue this bull of a living being from the pond of saṃsāra for a long time.
When the mind has been exhausted through the contemplation of reality, it is not born again.

Then the living soul may at last cross the ocean of existence. O Rāma, through contact with one of great majesty, the means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra is obtained, just as a firm boat is obtained from a navigator.
O Rāma, a wise person should not dwell in that desert-like land where there is no tree of a virtuous man— neither bearing fruit nor providing cool shade.
[But one should dwell] in that which has the leaves of affectionate and cooling speech, the shade of integrity, and is blossomed with smiles.
O Rāma, one finds great rest for a moment in the grove of the virtuous;
but in its absence— where the continuous fever of great delusion is imparted—
a wise person who has attained even a slight degree of discernment should not sleep here.
For the self alone is the friend of the self; by the self one should uplift the self.
One should not cast the self into the mud-swan of birth through arrogance.
What is this? How has it come to be? What is its root? What is its destruction?
The wise should therefore examine the suffering of the body with great effort.
Neither wealth, nor friends, nor scriptures, nor kinsmen can assist men in extricating themselves when they have sunk [into the mire].
By always dwelling together with the mind alone as his friend,
and by reflecting upon something [within] along with it, the self becomes uplifted;
through the effort of practicing detachment and self-reflection, which is born from that reflection.
The ocean of existence is crossed by means of the boat that is the light of reality.
One should not despise oneself, though one is constantly being pitied by people and scorched by evil desires; rather, one should lift oneself up with diligence.
One should uplift the elephant of the living soul, which is sunk in the mire of birth, from its great tethering post of egoism, with the rope of craving and the intoxication of the mind.
O Rāghava, by this alone is the self saved.
When delusion is cast aside and the ego-sense is wiped away,
by this much alone the true path becomes fully manifest;
for when the infatuation of the mind is discarded, the state of "I-ness" dissolves.
By this alone, O Lord of Gods, the Supreme Self is understood:
when the body is viewed as being equal to wood or a clod of earth.
When the cloud of egoism has perished, the sun of consciousness is seen.
Then, through its transformation, that state is fully attained.
Just as when darkness is completely dispelled, there is the self-evident perception of light,
so too, when the ego-sense is severed, there is the self-manifested vision of the Self.
That state which arises from the complete eradication of egoism, which is a source of perfect bliss,
is the supreme consciousness, full in form and all-pervading;
resembling a completely full ocean, it does not come within the range of our speech.

It does not take up a comparison, nor does it pursue attachment. If the fourth state (*turyā*)— which consists solely of the portion of the light of consciousness and has attained stability— is reached as a vision, then by means of that, [the world] is compared.
Not far removed from similarity to deep sleep,
that state is perceived as full in form, like the splendor of the sky within the ocean;
it exists within all states of being when the mind and ego have dissolved.
That supreme blissful body of the Supreme Lord arises;
through the perfection of yoga itself, it is not far from deep sleep.
O Rāma, it cannot be reached by words, but is experienced here within the heart alone.
When this entire infinite reality of the Self is established within the mind that has become firm through transformation,
and when all external things have subsided, the God of gods— who is the soul of all moving and non-moving beings— is experienced by oneself.
Following that comes the destruction of the latent impressions of sense-objects, and following that, the auspicious, supreme, and most radiant light.
And thereafter, by virtue of equanimity, there is a transformation into one's own true nature within the inconceivable form of the Great Ones.
This is the sixty-fifth canto, titled "The Instruction on Compassion."
Vasiṣṭha said:
O lotus-eyed one, if the Self is not perceived even after cutting through the mind with the mind itself, then one must abandon the notions of "mine" and "I. MU 5.65.1
The suffering of the world does not set, like the sun depicted in a painting;
calamity arrives with boundlessness, as vast as the great ocean,
repeatedly producing dull waves.
The rainy season of worldly existence, dark as a sapphire-blue tree, is agitated.
In this very context, they cite this ancient history:
a dialogue between a friend and a playful sun-bird on the peak of Mount Sahya.
There is a mountain that has conquered the sky with its height, the earth with its base,
and the netherworld with its foothills— a conqueror of the three worlds,
possessing an irresistible abundance of flowers and irresistible, pure waterfalls.

Guarded by Guhyakas as its treasure, it was named Sahya and possessed an unbearable radiance; it shone with golden slopes and ridges that were like the temples of a celestial elephant, with walls of mineral ore as pale-red as a mass of pearls.
In some places it was strewn with a profusion of flowers, in others with minerals even more variegated;

in some places it was strewn with blossoming lotuses, and in others its surface was variegated with gems. Here it possessed roaring waterfalls, and there it resounded with the whistling of bamboo reeds.
From here comes the wind from the Raṭadguhā cave; from there, the humming of bees.
On the mountain peak is a host of singing apsarases; in the forest is the soft warbling of birds.
On the plateau are intoxicated clouds; in the thickets is the cry of deer.
Guha was sung of by the Vidyādharas; the lotus-ponds were celebrated by the bees;
the Kirātas sang of its borders; and the forest trees were praised by the birds.
It was embraced by the gods upon its shoulders and embraced by men at its feet.
In the underworld (pātāla), it was encircled by nāgas like another house for the world;
in its caves it was resorted to by siddhas, and it was supported within by treasures;
it was inhabited by nāgas among the sandalwood trees and by lions upon the peaks of its summits.
His body was enveloped by clouds of flowers, and he was dusted with the pollen of those floral clouds;
the wind bore clouds of flower-petals and was as pale-white as flowering trees.
Tawny with clouds of mineral dust, he stood upon a surface of jeweled stones.
He was fully attended by hosts of celestial women as if they were made of wood;
there, the mountain peaks were like beautiful women approaching their lovers, draped in garments of cloud-blue silk and adorned with ornaments of mute jewels and lovely golden rocks.
There, on a ridge on the northern bank where the trees bent under the weight of their fruit,
where the waters of cascading torrents flowed through a network of jewel-like lotus ponds,
and which was bristling with clusters of blossoms released from the creepers of mango trees—
On the slopes of the quarters, densely covered with *vidula*, *aṅkola*, *punnāga*, and *nīpa* trees;
where the sun was hidden by the canopy of spreading creepers; radiant with the mass of rays from jewels;
where the ground was moistened by the flowing juice of the *jambu* fruit; and which brought delight to the heavenly realm.
Equal to the world of Brahmā, as delightful as heaven, and comparable to the city of Śiva,
there is the glorious and great hermitage of Atri, which removes the fatigue of those who have attained perfection.
In that great hermitage of Atri, there were two ascetics.
Like Śukra and Bṛhaspati in the path of the sky,
there were two sons born to those two who shared a single dwelling;
they were the sprouts of their lineage, pure of body, like two lotuses from the Sarasvatī.
Named Vilāsa and Bhāsa, they gradually grew up,
like two young shoots on a creeper and a tree, swiftly increasing for their parents.
They remained mutual friends, deeply affectionate and dear to one another.
Embraced like sesame seeds and oil, they remained together like the fragrance of flowers;
those two were never separated, like a deeply devoted husband and wife. Their minds became one, as if a single entity had attained duality.
Thus, those two of most enchanting form, rejoicing in one another,
remained in silence in their own hermitage like two bees upon a lotus;
having cast off childhood, they reached youth, becoming beloved by the people.
In a very short time, like the sun and moon risen together,
those two parents cast off their bodies and departed for heaven, leaving behind them,
like two birds flying out from their nest when afflicted by old age.
When their parents had passed away, the two of them became dejected of face;
with their limbs sinking and their vigor gone, they were like two lotuses pulled up from the water.
Having performed the funeral rites there, they broke out into lamentation.
"For the established order of the world is indeed inviolable, O giver of honor, even for the great.

Having performed the funeral rites, they were then overwhelmed by the agony arising from grief; lamenting piteously with voices of distress, they remained like figures in a painting, all their physical movements stilled, until the end of the day with hearts utterly vacant and motionless.
In the account of Bhāsa’s playful adventures, the sixty-sixth canto, titled "The Description of the Sahya Mountain," Vasiṣṭha said:
Then those two firm ascetics remained overcome by grief,
their entire bodies withered by penance like two trees in the forest;
detached from the world, the two brahmins spent their time in the wilderness.
Like two deer separated from their herd, they reached a state of supreme detachment;
thus, days, months, and years passed for them,
until gradually they both succumbed to old age like trees at the edge of a chasm.
Having failed to attain pure knowledge, those two ascetics, long grown old,
once happened upon one another and spoke thus to each other:
Vilāsa:
O great kinsman of this world, O light, welcome to you— you who are the fruit of the tree of life, the consolation, and the ocean of nectar!
For so many series of days have passed for you while separated from me.
"Tell me, O virtuous one, where have you spent [your time]? Is your austerity indeed stainless?
Is your intellect free from feverish distress? Have you become self-possessed? Has your knowledge borne fruit? Are you well? (MU 5.66.6–7)
When Vasiṣṭha had spoken thus, his friend, who was agitated by the ocean of worldly existence and had not yet attained great wisdom, replied with respect to his friend.
Bhāsa:
O virtuous one, welcome! Indeed, it is by good fortune that you have been seen today, O giver of honor.
But how can there be well-being for us who remain here in this cycle of existence?
As long as the object of knowledge has not been realized, as long as the realm of the mind has not been exhausted,
and as long as one has not crossed over from saṃsāra, how can there be any virtue for me?
As long as primordial wisdom has not been attained, and as long as equanimity has not arisen...
As long as awakening has not arisen, how can there be well-being for us?
As long as the hopes born of the mind have not been completely cut away,
like weeds by a sickle, how can there be well-being for us?
O virtuous one, without the attainment of the Self and without the great medicine of knowledge,
this cholera of miserable transmigratory existence arises once again. Its onset sprouts in childhood and its tender leaves flourish in fresh youth.
The wretched tree of saṃsāra approaches again, blossoming with old age. From this tree of the body, which is withered by age and where the cries of kinsmen act as bees,
there arises once more the cluster of blossoms that is death, white with the flowers of senility.
The series of years, having tasted the bitterness of the seasons and being stitched together by ancient days, is led away again, becoming almost devoid of flavor;
it dwells within the great caves of the mountain that is the body, where it is intensely pricked by the thorns of craving.

Furthermore, in activities that are like playful serpents, one is utterly deluded by long-lasting miseries that take the form of fragments of pleasure, through various auspicious and inauspicious deeds. Nights pass away and return, consisting mostly of the arrival of endless [suffering].
Life is wasted by base actions that initiate fruitless endeavors, sprouting from the onset of wicked desires and performed by a ruined agent;
for the intoxicated elephant of the mind has uprooted the hitching post of its latent tendencies.
Driven by the female elephant of craving, it runs far astray;
clinging to the leafy branch of the tongue within the cave-dwelling of the body-tree,
the greedy vulture grows ever stronger upon that wish-fulfilling gem of thought.
Lacking moisture, devoid of joy, and light, with limbs as fragile as falling petals and the color of withered leaves, this succession of days wastes away;
its physical splendor has set, and it is obscured by the dust of dishonor.
The face turns to a dusty grey, like a lotus struck by frost.
From the drying lake of the body, from which the waters of youth have flowed away,
the royal swan of life— irreversible— flees in an instant.
From the tree of life, shattered and shaken by the force of time’s wind,
the flowers of enjoyment fall downward like the leaves of the day.
Within these waters, which are inhabited by serpents of enjoyment and contain the croaking frogs of suffering, [the world remains].
The mind sinks far down into the blind wells of delusion.
Lust, clearly manifesting in various forms of attachment, flickering and fragile,
climbs high up like a banner atop a ruined shrine.
Within this mechanism of saṃsāra, the hoof of Death trims the life-hoping threads that are rooted in the vast pit of time.
Youth is a wave leaping with vigor, frothing with abundant exuberance.

The difficult river of life flows with great whirlpools that turn back; the boundless river of activity flows on, crowded with a multitude of waves consisting of the clamor of various arts and duties, and filled with agitated hollows.
Infinite rivers of kinsmen fall incessantly into the vast ocean of time,
into the deep hollows of which this jewel of a body is cast— the belly of a sea of mud that is destruction.
"O father, it is not known where the mind is drawn in birth after birth;
for a long time, the consciousness wanders in the wheel of anxiety, restless with its rapid circular motion, like a blade of grass in a whirlpool in the ocean."
Carried away by the great waves of mental activity within the infinite [ocean] of objects,
the mind— its inner disposition dancing with anxiety— finds no rest for even a moment.
"This has been done," "I am doing this," "I shall do that"— enough of this!
Ensnared in the net of time, the bird of my intellect has fainted.
This great malady of duality— the thought "this is a friend" and "this is an enemy"—
cuts through my vital organs as if they were fresh lotuses.
Moving within the single mass of waves that are the whirlpools of intoxication, with thought as its beak,
the fish of pride swells in an instant and in an instant suffers destruction.
Such non-self-related sufferings are indeed manifold.
Searching with the notion of a self, a person falls into wretchedness.
Falling into the midst of manifold pleasures and pains, broken by the vast precipice of old age and death,
this person rolls upon the mountain within the belly of the world and reaches a state of decay like a sapless leaf.
The sixty-seventh canto, titled "The Exposition of Impermanence," by Vasiṣṭha:
Thus they both exchanged inquiries regarding their welfare;
in time, having attained stainless knowledge, they then went to liberation.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, I speak of how there is a destination other than through knowledge.
For one whose mind is bound by fetters, there is no crossing over the cycle of existence.
For one of noble intellect, even this infinite suffering is as trivial as a cow’s footprint; for the enemy of serpents (the Garuda), the unfathomable ocean becomes like a mere puddle.
The great-souled ones, transcending the body, abide in their own self which is pure consciousness;
seeing their own body from afar, they laugh at it as the sun laughs at the common folk.
When the body is suffering and agitated, what harm has befallen us?
When the chariot is overturned and broken, what injury is there to the charioteer? When the mind has fallen into agitation, my dear, what has happened to the consciousness?
When a wave is soiled by dust, what change of nature occurs to the ocean?
What are swans made of iron, and what are stones made of milk?
What indeed are rocks made of wood, and what are the enjoyments of the Supreme Self?
What kind of connection could there possibly be between the eastern mountain and the western ocean?
In the vast expanse of the interval between consciousness and its bondage, what indeed is the difference?
Just as pieces of wood carried along in the current of a river are merely lifted onto its lap, so too are these bodies to the Self. What essential distinction can there be here between them?
Just as from the friction of wood and water, sparks and the like arise increasingly high,
so too do these fluctuations of the mind arise from the conjunction of the body and the self.
Due to the connection between wood and water, reflections [appear] from the wood.
Just as bodies are perceived in milk, so too [are they] in the Self.
Just as reflections in a mirror, water, and so forth are in reality neither unreal nor real, so too are bodies in the Self.
Just as one is never distressed by the clashing of wood, water, or stone,
so too there is no injury to the five [aggregates] whether they are joined together or separated.
Just as from water stirred by wood, trembling, sound, and so forth arise, [so it is with the aggregates].
In the same way, these [perceptions] arise from this body when it is awakened by consciousness.
These perceptions do not belong to the intellect or to the insentient; they belong to the body of consciousness.
For these are merely ignorance; when that ignorance is destroyed, they become that very [consciousness].
Just as there are no experiences for anyone regarding the union of wood and water,
so too there are no experiences for anyone regarding the union of the body and the embodied self.
Just as this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is seen by the ignorant as having attained reality, [so it appears].
To one who knows that, transmigratory existence has thus perished and attained unreality.
Just as those internal attachments are absent on the surface of a stone,
so too are the experiences of external enjoyments for one whose mental activity is unattached.
Just as there is no internal attachment between water and wood,
so too is there no internal attachment between the body and the embodied self.
The connection between water and wood is devoid of internal attachment.

Just as between the knower and the body, or between a reflection and water, pure consciousness (*saṃvitti*) abides everywhere, devoid of any object of cognition (*saṃvedya*). Any other consciousness marked by duality does not exist; it is a false consciousness.
That which is not suffering becomes suffering through internal perception;
clearly, a post becomes a vampire when it is conceived as a vampire.
For even a non-connection becomes a connection through internal determination.
Like sexual union with a woman in a dream, or like the breaking of a post or a vetāla; for a connection that is essentially unreal is like that between water and wood—
just so is the false connection between the body and the Supreme Self.
Without internal attachment, water is not agitated by blows from wood;
the self, free from internal attachment, is not burned by the sufferings of the body.
By the very notion of "body," the self remains under the sway of bodily suffering.

The wise know that by abandoning that [attachment], one becomes liberated from it. For, my dear, because they lack internal attachment, even leaves, water, stones, and pieces of wood do not experience suffering, even though they are joined together with one another.
Free from internal attachment, they go to the supreme state beyond suffering;
likewise, the self is entirely unattached even when joined with the body, senses, and mind.
For internal attachment indeed belongs to all embodied beings in this cycle of existence.
It is the seed-cause of the trees of old age, death, and delusion.
A living being possessed of internal attachment sinks in the ocean of saṃsāra;
but one freed from internal attachment has crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra.
The mind that possesses internal attachment is said here to have a hundred branches;
