the mind free from internal attachment is said to be dissolved.
Know that a mind that is attached is impure, like a shattered crystal.

Know that the mind has the luster of unbroken crystal; it is indeed unattached. A mind that is unattached and stainless is clearly liberated even while wandering in saṃsāra; but one that is attached remains bound, even if it is engaged in long-term ascetic practice.
The mind bound by internal attachment is fettered; freed from attachment, it is liberated. Internal attachment alone is the sole cause of bondage and liberation.
For one who is free from internal attachment, there is no sense of agency even while acting.
Just as there is a state of agitation and longing in a dream filled with pleasure and pain,
so too agency exists in the mind even for one who is bodiless,
consisting of states of agitated pleasure and pain, as in dreams and the like.
When the mind is not the agent, the state of non-agency becomes clear within;
for a person whose mind is empty, even while acting, does not perceive it as such.
You experience what is done by the mind, but not what is not done by the mind.
Nowhere is the body the cause, nor indeed is the mind the agent. The wise know the mind to be unattached and truly non-acting, even while it acts;
being unattached, it does not attain the state of being an enjoyer of the fruits of action.
One who is unattached to both the killing of a Brahmin and the horse-sacrifice is not tainted, just as one whose mind is fixed on a beloved woman far away is not affected by the duties at hand. Thus,
the individual soul, liberated from internal attachment and possessing a sweet disposition, remains untainted.
Whether performing external actions or not performing them, there is never anywhere a doer or an enjoyer.
That mind which is free from internal attachment is without agency;
it is disjoined [from objects], it is tranquil, it is joined [to its true nature], and it is untainted.
Therefore, one should certainly abandon that cruel internal attachment which clings to all objects and causes all suffering;
for the mind, when freed from the fault of internal clinging, attains peace and becomes like the primordial sky, possessing a stainless luster.
One attains a firm unity with the Self, which is free from all mental constructs, like a bee merging into the blue water of a lotus pond.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Investigation into Internal Attachment."
Rāma:
O Blessed One, what kind of association leads to bondage for men, and what is said to lead to liberation? And how is this [bondage] to be treated?
Vasiṣṭha:
When there is the complete abandonment of the distinction between the body and the embodied self, no mental conception remains.
But when one places trust in the body alone, that attachment is said to be worthy of bondage.

When there is a determination of limits regarding the infinite reality of the Self, that desire for pleasure is called an internal attachment worthy of bondage. "All this is the Self in its entirety; what then do I desire, and what shall I abandon?"—MU 5.68.3.
Know this to be the state of non-attachment, residing in the body of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta):
"I do not exist, nor does another exist; let there be happiness or let there be none"—the man who remains unattached within is said to possess liberation.

He does not rejoice in inaction, nor is he intent on the nature of ritual action; he who is perfectly equanimous and renounces the fruits of action is known as "unattached. For one whose mind is fixed solely on the reality of the Self, the mind no longer falls under the sway of joy or resentment.

He who does not come [under the sway of these] because he is unattached is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). That skillful renunciation of all fruits of action and the like by means of the mind alone, and not by means of physical action, is known as non-attachment (asaṃsaṅga).
O dear one, all activities, though they manifest in various ways, become healing when free from attachment and bring about the highest good;
however, by the power of attachment, all these result in vast heaps of suffering.
They branch out into a hundred shoots like trees with ravines and thorns.
When a donkey on the road, its nose pulled tight by a rope by the cart,
carries a load with a terrified soul, that is the manifestation of attachment.

That a tree endures the affliction of cold, wind, and heat while remaining fixed in one spot with its body— that is the manifestation of attachment. That a worm, its limbs tormented, is submerged in a fissure of the earth— [that too is the same].

That the impaired person wastes away his time is the manifestation of attachment to worldly things. That the deer abandons its body due to the affliction of the hunter’s arrows, even while subsisting on a diet of dūrvā grass sprouts, is the manifestation of attachment to worldly things.
That grasses and creepers reach the state of being cut again and again,
despite their various modes of movement, is the manifestation of attachment (*saṃsakti*).
Grasses, shrubs, and creepers [arise] from the connection with the essence of the netherworld (*rasātala-rasa*).
Whatever form they produce, that is the manifestation of attachment (*saṃsakti*). Like waves in a river, infinite beings arise again and again and dissolve; that is the manifestation of attachment.
That the river of saṃsāra—which is inherently tranquil, yet appears infinite and crowded with hundreds of objects—is intoxicated, is the manifestation of attachment.
For attachment, O Rāghava, is said to be of two kinds: barren and venerable.
To the deluded, attachment is everywhere venerable; to those who know reality, their own [nature] is venerable.
Attachment born of the body and other objects, which arises from a lack of awakening to the reality of the Self and bestows further saṃsāra, is called "barren" when it is firm.
Indeed, that attachment born of discernment, which has become true through the realization of the reality of the Self and is free from further saṃsāra, is said to be worthy of worship.
(The Lord) possesses a body with a conch, discus, and mace, through various powers.
By virtue of its attachment to that which is worthy of worship, it protects the three worlds.
By virtue of its attachment to that which is worthy of worship, the sun daily makes its journey as a traveler upon the path of the supportless sky.
Through the power of attachment to that which is worthy of worship, the Brahmanic body indeed manifests— a form conceived by a mind steady in the meditative absorption of a great eon,
adorned with splendor, and sportively absorbed in the faces of women.
By the power of attachment to the one worthy of worship, the body of Śaṅkara remains [in its state].
Likewise, the Siddhas who have realized the goal, the world-protectors,
and others remain within the multitude of worlds by the power of attachment to the one worthy of worship.
This other succession of elements maintains the multitude of bodily mechanisms,
revolving through old age and death due to the power of fruitless attachment;
the mind falls upon sense-objects like a vulture upon scraps of meat.
Merely through the power of a barren attachment, and due to the futile suspicion of taste,
the wind blows within the hollow of the universe by the force of clinging;
the five elements abide [thus], and this is the maintenance of the world.
In heaven are the gods, on earth are men, and in the netherworld are the serpents and asuras;
they all exist within the udumbara fruit of the cosmic egg like shimmering gnats.
They are born and they die; they fall and they rise.
Beings are incessantly and repeatedly swallowed by one another like droplets from a mountain torrent;
O dear one, the multitude, their limbs crushed by mutual devouring and shattered by dullness,
wanders about in confusion like a withered leaf in the wind.
The wheel of constellations in the sky, densely covered by swarms of gnats that are the earth,
quivers with a whirling motion like the flood of water from the elephants of the underworld; it is the ball of the boy Time, worn out by the states of decline and upheaval.
Even now, the moon does not abandon its body, which remains stained by its dullness;
nor does the host of gods in heaven cut through the thicket of the mind, which has become calloused from beholding the suffering of various cycles of ages.
"O Rāghava, behold this wondrous and variegated painting created by someone in the supreme void, solely through the power of latent impressions (vāsanā).
It consists of the world within the empty sky, using the singular stage of mental attachment."
Whatever is fashioned here as a manifold variety is never real.
For those whose minds are attached to this worldly existence and who engage in its affairs,
craving devours their bodies just as a flame of fire consumes blades of grass.
Who is able to count the number of atoms in the bodies of the Lord of Waters, which are attached to his mind,
as well as those in the pearl-necklace of the Gaṅgā from its base to its summit on Mount Meru?
Those whose minds are attached do not count their bodies as being like waves that have been released.
All successions of suffering come upon one whose mind is deeply attached,
just as great rivers, surging with dull waves, flow into the ocean.
For those whose minds are attached, these rows of delightful inner apartments are fashioned as the hells named Raurava, Avīci, Kālasūtra,
and so forth; they are like a heap of dry fuel for the fire of suffering for people whose hearts are clinging.
Know that by this [attachment] the blazing fires of hell burn;
O Rāma, whatever web of suffering exists within this world,
all of that is imagined for the sake of those whose minds are attached.
O Rāma, everything is pervaded by ignorance— which is characterized by the mind’s attachment, which is a burden to the body, and which seeks the states of both decay and arising;
yet all these manifestations of power exist through non-attachment to enjoyments.
They swell to a vast extent, like great rivers in the rainy season.
Know, O Rāghava, that attachment within the limbs is like glowing coals;
know, O Rāma, that freedom from attachment to the limbs is an elixir.
By means of the internal attachment, nature itself is consumed,
just as a medicinal herb is burnt by the fire produced from its own fruit;
it remains unattached everywhere yet appears attached, existing as if infinite.

The mind that is free from volitional construction and always luminous becomes conducive to bliss alone. He who abides with his own mind— having attained the rising of the vision of knowledge, having reached the cessation of the domain of ignorance, and being everywhere devoid of attachment— is liberated.
The sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Contemplating Attachment," by Vasiṣṭha.
At all times,
remaining with everyone in every situation and engaged in all activities, one whose mind is discerning should act without being attached to thoughts, nor to actions, nor to objects.
It is not in space, nor in the region below, nor in the directions, nor in the creepers;
it is not outside in the vast expanse, nor indeed in the functions of the senses;
it is not within, nor in the vital breath, nor in the head, nor in the palate.
It is not between the eyebrows, nor at the tip of the nose, nor in the mouth, nor in the hollow of the eyes;
it is not in darkness, nor in light, nor in this sky of the heart;
it is not in the waking state, nor in dreaming, nor in deep sleep, nor in the stainless state.
It is neither black nor yellow, nor red and so forth, nor even variegated;
it is neither stable nor moving, neither in the beginning nor in the middle, nor elsewhere;
it is neither far nor near, neither in the limb, nor in the object, nor in the self.
Neither in sounds, touches, or forms, nor in states of delusion or bliss;
neither in the activities of going and coming, nor in the calculations of time—
having rested solely in consciousness while slightly supporting itself upon objects of thought.
Let the mind, which finds its own essence in the Self, remain as if devoid of flavor in all circumstances.
Established therein and free from attachment, the living being has attained the state of the non-living;
let him neither engage in this entire worldly activity, nor let him engage in it.
Whether performing actions or not performing them, the living soul, engaged in the activity of delighting in its own self,
incurs no connection with the fruits of action, just as the sky is unaffected by clouds. Or else, having abandoned even that objective aspect, it becomes a tranquil mass of consciousness.

Let the living soul (jīva) remain perfectly tranquil within itself, like a glowing gem. O Rāmabhadra, the living soul that has attained extinction (nirvāṇa) within itself and whose nature is eternally manifest does not incur attachment while conducting worldly affairs on earth, due to its freedom from attachment to the fruits arising from action; it remains as if laughing at the body from afar.
The seventieth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Practice of Constant Conduct," by Vasiṣṭha.
Established in meditations of unattached bliss, those who have realized the Self remain even while engaged in worldly affairs, inwardly free from sorrow; for them,
whether the body is agitated or unagitated, there is consciousness without the perception of sensory objects.
The splendor of one whose mind is free from fever, resting upon consciousness devoid of objects of thought, is perceived in his face like the beauty of the full moon. By him,
the multitude of people is brought to clarity, just as water is purified by *katakaka* fruit.
Constantly absorbed in the vision of the Self, the knower remains established in his own nature even while being restless;
though agitated, he is seen to be in vain, like the reflection of the sun [in rippling water].
The great-souled ones, delighted in the Self, are awakened and possess supreme exaltation.
Tremulous with the tips of its feathers on the outside, yet as immovable within as Mount Meru;
the mind, having attained the state of the Self, does not undergo the coloring of pleasure and pain,
just as a smooth crystal does not take on the contact of dye.
The vision of cyclic existence has arisen for one who knows the higher and lower worlds;
it does not stain the true mind, just as a streak of water does not stain a lotus.
Absorbed in meditation on the self, the meditator has attained supreme awakening.
But one who is liberated from the impurity of *kalā* is called "unattached.
By delighting in the Self, the living being attains non-attachment in this world;
through the knowledge of the Self, attachment becomes attenuated, and not otherwise.

O Rāghava, while remaining awake, the living being becomes situated in deep sleep; in this vision, having transcended duality, it is eternally free from rising and setting. Having attained maturity in this state, one reaches the purifying fourth state (turyatā).
Just as the moon, through the power of transformation, attains the state of the new moon [amāvāsya] when it is eclipsed by the sun;
so too, that state of one whose mind has been extinguished, which exists within consciousness yet is devoid of the condition of being an object of thought,
is called "tranquil ideation"— it is deep sleep even while awake.
And having reached that state of sleep, a man who lives and conducts himself is never dragged by the thongs of pleasure and pain;
he who, while remaining truly awake, performs the activities of the world as if situated in deep sleep.
Like a mechanical puppet, it does not perceive pleasure or pain.
Attachment to the mind causes affliction by bringing about the torment of existence and non-existence;
once the mind has attained the state of the Self, what can afflict whom, and how?
The living being who remains established in the state of liberation while alive is not bound by actions performed with the effortless ease of one who has awakened from deep sleep;
O sinless one, relying upon that state of deep sleep, perform or do not perform [actions].
One's own [karma] has arrived by the power of the causes and conditions of the nature of action.
To one who knows, neither the grasping nor the abandoning of karma is pleasing;
those who have realized the Self remain following whatever has come to them.
Even while acting, you are not an agent through the intellect that abides solely in deep sleep;
and even as a non-agent, you are an agent—do as you wish!
Just as an infant does not move upon its cradle while perceiving nothing at all.

Likewise, O Rāghava, perform actions without considering their fruits and so forth. Because you abide in the state of consciousness that is beyond objects of thought, you possess the intellect of deep sleep even while awake;
whatever you do as one who has attained the Self, in that there is no sense of agency for you.
Having reached the state of deep sleep, the knower who has dispelled all mental impressions through self-knowledge alone attains an inner coolness, just as the moon does through its nectar.
Established in deep sleep, the one of great luster whirls like the orb of the full moon.

He remains the same in all conditions, like a mountain throughout the seasons. Established in deep sleep, the wise-souled one does not come to possess restlessness in external activities; he is like a mountain that has not been shaken by an earthquake.
Having become established in the state of deep sleep, with the body free from all taints,
either strike [the body] quickly or maintain it for a long time like a mountain.
O Rāma, this very state of deep sleep arises through the yoga of practice.
Being mature, she is called the Fourth (turyā) by those learned in the principles.
Here, consisting of bliss alone, with all afflictions exhausted,
the knower becomes one whose mind has utterly set, having attained the great awakening.
Abiding here, the Knower is delighted, reeling with supreme bliss;
he beholds this worldly construction as if it were a mere play.
Free from sorrow, fear, and exertion, he has transcended the agitation of saṃsāra.

One who has ascended to the state of the Fourth (turya) does not fall again, for he possesses the Self. With a steady intellect, he looks upon this person striving to attain his own holy station as one standing on a mountain looks down with a smile at those below.
But having attained an imperishable state in this fourth stage (turya), because of being completely absorbed in singular bliss, he has reached the state beyond bliss; indeed,
he is then the great bliss beyond bliss, transcending even the [limited] parts (kalā).

The yogi who has reached the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is called "liberated. Having shed all bonds of birth and being devoid of all mental identifications, that great soul attains an existence consisting of the supreme essence, like a lump of salt dissolved in water.
The seventy-first chapter, titled "Instruction on the Treatment of Attachment," by Vasiṣṭha.

O descendant of Raghu, as long as there is the reflective awareness of the fourth state (turya-parāmarśa), so long is it the domain of the state of absolute oneness (kevalatā) for one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and for words. Beyond this, [it is the domain] of those who are liberated while still possessing a body, as well as of words.
O mighty-armed one, that state is not within the reach of ordinary men, just as the sky is not.
For it is a path of rest even more remote than the distant;
it is accessible only to those liberated while in the bodyless state (*videhamukta*), like the tracks of the wind in the sky.
Having experienced the maintenance of the world for some time through the state of deep sleep,
and subsequently attaining the fourth state (turya), those who know that and are skilled in the Self, reeling with supreme bliss, reach the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta).
In that way, O scion of Raghu’s lineage, attain the state free from dualities.
O Rāma, remain engaged in worldly affairs as if in the state of deep sleep; for you, O subduer of enemies, neither decline nor agitation exist, like those of the moon in a painting.
Do not grasp at consciousness as being the body, whether in its dissolution or its stability;
for this is an error that expands, thinking "this is the body.
What purpose do you have in the destruction of the body? What purpose do you have in the preservation of the body?
Engage yourself in your natural activities; let this [body] remain as it is.
You have known that truth; you have realized that state.
You have attained your own true nature; be free from sorrow for the sake of your well-being.
Desired, undesired, and abandoned through the beauty of your cool radiance,
you shine like the sky freed from darkness, heat, and clouds;
your mind has attained its true self and no longer pursues misfortune.
A person perfected through yoga, mantra, and austerity descends from the sky as if onto the earth.
Here, there exists only pure consciousness, devoid of near and far;
let there be no delusion in you such as "this is he," "I am this," or "this is mine."
The designation "Self" is merely a conceptual construct imagined for the sake of conventional usage regarding the All-pervading Lord;
distinctions such as name and form have long since departed from Him.
Just as the ocean is nothing but water and not distinct from its waves and so forth, [so is the Self].

This entire universe is indeed the Self alone; the multitude of beings and so forth do not exist separately. Just as nothing other than the water of the entire ocean can be found, even so, nothing other than the Self can be found within the vast expanse of the world.
O wise one, where do you establish the notion "this is I"?
What is that "you," and what would belong to you? What is not you, and what would not belong to you?
There is no duality, nor is there a body; the consciousness has no connection with them.
It is possible for the stainless one [to be affected] by the veils of darkness, just as it is for the sun;
yet, O slayer of enemies, even if we were to admit duality,
there could be no connection between the omnipresent Lord and the body and other [factors], even though they exist.
Just as no connection is possible between the spreading of shadow and sunlight, or between light and darkness, so indeed it is with the body and the embodied self.
Just as cold and heat are eternally opposed to one another, [so are they].
In that same way, O Rāma, no connection is possible between the body and the self.

But how could there be a connection between these two—the insentient body and the sentient embodied one—given that their relationship is not one of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)? It is [merely] experienced as such.
The notion that the body is connected to the self, which is pure consciousness alone,
arises from a misconception as difficult to comprehend as the idea of water in a forest fire;
this false view perishes through the vision of truth.
Just as the ocean is correctly perceived through contemplation [to be distinct from its waves],

so too is the conscious self (cidātman)— pure, eternal, self-luminous, and free from affliction. Since the body, however, is impermanent and impure, how could it be connected with that [conscious self]?

The body undergoes vibration through the wind and is made full by the elements; however, there is not even the slightest connection between that [body] and the Great Self (mahātman). Even if a duality of the body were established, no connection with it is possible for the Great Self.
"But O wise one, if duality is unestablished, how can there be such a reckoning?"—this alone is the truth; therefore, my dear, take your stand right here:
there is neither bondage nor liberation for anyone, at any time, or anywhere.
"O Rāma, bring to firmness everywhere, both internally and externally, this clear conviction that everything is composed of the Self and is peaceful.
To think 'I am happy,' 'I am suffering,' or 'I am deluded'— these are known as false views."
If you maintain the notion that these [bodies] are real entities, then you will experience suffering for a long time.
That same sequence which applies to a mountain and a blade of grass, or to silk and a stone, is said to apply to the Supreme Self and its body as well.
Just as a unity between cold and heat is not seen even in discourse,
nor is there a union between the insentient and light, so too there is no such [union] between the self and the body.
Just as there is neither connection nor equality between light and darkness, [so it is with the self and the body].
O Rāma, for the self and the body are thus absolutely distinct:
the body moves by means of the wind; by that very [wind], it comes and goes;
and by that same [wind] moving through the channels of the body, it produces sound.
Just as sound consisting mostly of the letters ka, ca, ṭa, ta, and pa vibrates within the internal wind,
so indeed does it arise from the bodily cavities like that from a bamboo flute; likewise,
the movement of the pupils and the movement of the eyes are due to the wind.
The vibration of the senses is indeed nothing but the consciousness of the Self alone.
The state of the Self resides everywhere— in space, stones, walls, and so forth—
and it is perceived within the mind itself, like a reflection in a mirror.

Having abandoned the abode of the body, wherever the bird of the mind goes by the power of its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there alone the Self is experienced. Just as where there is a flower, there the perception of fragrance is established; so it is here.

For wherever the mind is, there the self-consciousnesses are likewise established. Just as space, which is omnipresent, is reflected in a mirror, so too the self, though omnipresent, is perceived within the mind.
Just as the place where water descends is its locus upon the surface of the earth,
so too the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone is the locus for the self's cognitions.
The form of the world, consisting of both the real and the unreal, is reflected within the internal organ.
Self-consciousness spreads this [world], just as the light of the sun spreads illumination.
Therefore, it is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone that is the cause for the manifestation of the elements;
but the Self, because it transcends all things, is the cause that is itself no cause.
The great-minded have said that non-investigation is ignorance and folly;
it is the essence of wandering in saṃsāra and the cause of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). Due to improper perception and delusion, the mind has grasped at existence.
O Raghava, by the thorough knowledge of the single reality of the self as it truly is, the mind— like a seed of delusion—
reaches a state of non-existence in an instant, just as darkness is dissolved by the sun.
Therefore, due to a lack of inquiry, the mind itself is the cause of saṃsāra;
it is known by such names as the individual soul (*jīva*), the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), consciousness (*citta*), and the intellect (*manas*).
Rāma said:
"O Lord, these many perceptions have become firmly rooted in the mind;
tell me how this is so, O giver of honor, for my spiritual perfection.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
All these entities are eternally of the single nature of the reality of the Self,
just as various waves and droplets are comprised within the one water. The Self, whose essence is solely vibration, resides here and there within them.
Just as water remains pure like the sky amidst turbulent waves,

so too does the Great Lord (Maheśvara) abide within them in an unchanging form, even when they have not yet attained the state of waves— just as the nature of water persists within the waters before they become waves.
Among those, entities such as stones are motionless and established in themselves;
however, beings such as humans are restless, quivering like the foam on wine.
Among them, within those bodies, by means of the Self which possesses all powers—
Because he has grasped the activity of ignorance, he has resorted to that ignorance.
That ignorance, when colored by the form of the infinite Self, is called the *jīva*;
it is the transmigrating being, an elephant trapped within the cage of the great delusion of *māyā*.
It is called "jīva" because of its vitality; the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) exists through the state of "I-ness" (*ahantā*);

the intellect (*buddhi*) by way of determination; and the mind (*manas*) by way of volitional construction. Primordial nature (*prakṛti*) exists as the state of being the source, and the body stands as the locus of experience.
The insentient exists by virtue of its nature as matter, while the sentient exists by virtue of its own self-existence.
That which is the supreme reality situated between the perspectives of the insentient and the sentient—
this very thing has come to be known through various designations as manifoldness.
Thus, O sinless one, the true nature of the individual soul (jīva) has indeed been proclaimed in many ways across numerous Vedāntic texts such as the Bṛhadāraṇyaka;
yet, by others— namely, those of evil discrimination and false reasoning— within these very designations, [it has been misinterpreted].
Objects have been vainly imagined by the deluded solely for the sake of delusion.
Thus, O mighty-armed one, this living soul is the cause of saṃsāra;
what has been done here by this mute and most wretched body?
Just as when the support and the supported perish together, one is destroyed by the destruction of the other,
so too, upon the destruction of the body and such, there is no destruction of the self.
Just as when the juice of a single leaf has been consumed, the [remaining] sap does not undergo destruction.
Just as the sap of a leaf passes through the interstices of the sun’s web of rays, so too,
upon the dissolution of the body, the embodied soul does not undergo destruction for anyone;
if it is free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*), it likewise abides in the sky at the station of the Self.

I think that for one whose ignorance leads to the delusion, "I am destroyed when the body is destroyed," a vampire has arisen from the slope of his mother’s breast. For he who would undergo absolute destruction is said to have been born already dead.
For the destruction of the mind would indeed be destruction; that is said to be liberation. Others say that one who has died is "destroyed," but that is false and not true;
having been separated by space and time, he is experienced once again.

Here, the living being (jīva), enveloped by latent impressions (vāsanā), departs after casting off the body; it is perceived by people like grass caught between the waves of a flood, under the designation of "death," though concealed by space and time.
Like a monkey that has left one forest tree and taken its stand upon another,
it abandons that as well and in an instant moves to yet another;
in a different, vast region and at a different time, O Rāghava.

Driven here and there by their own latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), living beings are led for a long time by that which they depend upon, like children by a cunning nurse. Enveloped by the rope of latent tendencies, they grow old within the hollows of mountains.
The *jīvajīvaka* birds exhaust their lives with extreme suffering.

(MU 5.71.70) Bearing the heavy burden of suffering brought upon them by an aged world, their lives worn out by old age and gasping for breath, these people fall for a long time into the depths of hell, driven by the persistence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced in their hearts. (MU 5.71.71)
Vālmīki:

When the sage had spoken thus, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
The seventy-second chapter, titled "Instruction on Saṃsāra," from the Vasiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa].
When the body is born, you are not born; when the body is destroyed, you are not destroyed.
You are the Self, the stainless Self; the body is nothing at all to you.
That which is like the analogy of the jujube fruit in a bowl, or the state of space within a jar—[that is your nature].
In that regard, the notion that "two [bodies] exist" when one has been wounded or decayed is a futile conceptualization.
Fie upon that blind-minded person who, when this perishable body has perished and returned to its own state [of dissolution], grieves, thinking, "I am perishing."
Just as the connection between a ray of light and its chariot is devoid of both attachment and agitation,
so too is the mind perceived as connected with the body, the senses, and pleasures;
it exists through a mutual dependence, like that between a lake, mud, stones, and water.
Just as is the relationship between Rāghava and his kin, so too is that between the body, the senses, and the self.
As is the union and separation of the ocean, the earth, and other such elements— devoid of desire and lamentation— so too is the union and separation of the body and the embodied soul.
Just as those terrified by the transformations of an imagined vetāla are entirely false imaginings, so too are affection, pleasure, and the like;
for individual beings are constructed from the mere aggregation of the five elements.
Just as various figurines [seem to emerge] from a single piece of wood,
nothing other than wood exists in a wooden man; likewise,
nothing other than the aggregate of the elements exists in the body.
O people, in the agitation, destruction, and arising of the five elements,
why have you fallen under the sway of joy, resentment, and despondency?
What excellence indeed is there for men, whether in that which is called "woman" or in any other name?
When the mere aggregate of elements has arisen, like a storm of arrows,
the variety of their arrangement serves only to satisfy the ignorant;
for those who possess true knowledge, however, there is the vision of the five elements exactly as they are.
Just as there is no passion between two stone statues situated upon the same rock, even though they are joined together, so it is between the mind and the body.
And just as the mutual disposition of clay figures might be when they meet, [so too is the relationship between the mind and the body].
May such a union of intellect, senses, self, and mind be yours;
[yet] these daughters of stone are not vessels for the bond of mutual affection.
Here, who is there to lament for the body, senses, self, and vital breaths?
Just as a wave thoroughly brings together masses of grass that have drifted hither and thither, so does the Creator bring beings together;
they are joined and separated just like blades of grass upon the waters of the ocean.
Having released internal mental construction, the Self likewise remains as the bodies;
the Self, through its nature as consciousness, persists while embracing the bodies,
just as water— though free from internal movement— remains within the whirlpool that turns the blades of grass.

Through awakening, having abandoned the state of being the mind, the self itself attains its own true nature, just as water, by the power of its own movement, abandons its turbidity and becomes clear, leaving behind the whirlpool. Then, one perceives the multitude of elements known as the body as something distinct.
Just as a creature situated within a whirlwind [overlooks] the circle of the earth, so too,
having abandoned the collection of separate elements, the unborn one transcends the body and attains supreme light,
like a sun-gem in the day.
Then he knows himself by himself, freed from the ailments of the means and objects of knowledge;
like one released from intoxication, he remembers his own consciousness within.
The Self alone vibrates in the sky of consciousness, appearing as if arisen through the nets of objective things.
Just as the infinite waters in the ocean consist of waves, droplets, and surges,
so too do those who possess such great awakening, who are free from passion and devoid of sin,
move about here as those liberated while living, having attained the state of great beings.

Just as great waves shine with various kinds of precious gems, so do the best of men shine through diverse worldly activities, yet remain free from latent tendencies (*vāsanā*). Neither the ocean is affected by the erosion of its shores, nor the sky by dust.
In this world, the self-possessed man does not wither through his own worldly dealings—
whether by those who have departed or those who have arrived, whether they are pure or impure, fickle or dull-witted.
For one who has realized the Self, there is neither passion for nor aversion toward the ocean of enjoyments.
Whatever mental cogitation exists anywhere in the entire world,
the wise know that to be the radiant play of the nature of consciousness (cittattva) directed toward an object of thought (cetyonmukha).
Whatever is "I," whatever is the elements and so forth, and whatever occurs within the three periods of time— [all this is that same consciousness].
That expansion of the relationship between the seen and the seeing unfolds [as follows]:
Whatever is seen, whether it be non-existent or existent, depends upon the single act of vision;
since the other [the seer] is untainted by that, whence can there be the states of joy and sorrow?
The unreal is indeed unreal, for the real is always real;
know that the real-unreal is non-existent—why then are you bewildered by its meaning?
Abandoning false vision, see correctly, O fair-eyed one.
One who possesses perfect vision and is mature never becomes deluded anywhere in this world.
That ultimate bliss which exists in the relationship between the seer and the seen,
consisting of pure experience, is therefore called the Supreme Brahman.
The unsurpassed consciousness of bliss arising from the relationship between the seen and the seer bestows saṃsāra upon the ignorant and liberation upon the wise, for it is the source of happiness.
The wise know that the bliss of the relationship between the seen and the seer is the very nature of the Self.
When that [consciousness] is enveloped by the visible and bound, it is said to be "bound"; when it is liberated from that, it is called "liberated.
When there is a healthy awareness of bliss arising from the connection between the visible and the seer, free from decay and excess, that is called liberation by the wise.
In the relationship between the seen and the seeing, there is an experience whose own object is [that very relationship];
by taking as its support that experience which is free from both the seen and the seeing, one attains existence and non-existence.
For this is the vision of deep sleep, which thus comes into full manifestation.

In this way, it attains the state of the fourth (turyatva); thus is liberation traditionally remembered. When the perception of the visible has been relinquished through the application of the supreme intellect, O Rāghava, there remains only the consciousness of the relationship between the visible and the seer.
The Self is neither gross nor subtle; it is neither perceptible nor conscious;
it is neither unconscious nor inert; it is neither non-existent nor composed of existence.
It is not "I," nor another, nor indeed one, nor many, nor possessed of multiplicity.
It is neither near nor far; it neither exists nor does it not exist.
It is neither unattainable nor attainable; it is neither non-omnipresent nor omnipresent.
It is neither a category of existence nor a non-category; it is neither non-pentadic in nature nor pentadic.
That which has come into the range of visibility, the domain of the six senses with the mind as the sixth—
whatever state may transcend that is, as it were, nothing at all.
Thus does the world appear correctly to the one who knows it as it truly is.

O Knower, everything consists of the Self; nowhere does anything exist that does not consist of the Self. In hardness, fluidity, motion, space, and vision—in all these elements of earth, water, air, ether, and fire—the Self alone is everything.
There exists only consciousness (citi), without which there are no objects at all;
know that to say anything exists as something distinct from it is the prattle of a madman.
All worlds, throughout the entire succession of time and kalpas, have gone and returned within that single [consciousness].
"O Great-Souled One, let your mind be thus: 'There is only the Self, and no other fabrication of parts exists,' and thereby transcend worldly existence.
This is the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Primary Nature."
Vasiṣṭha:
O Rāghava, by such a perspective of inquiry and through the abandonment of duality,
one's own true nature is attained by the knowers of reality, just as the wish-fulfilling gem is obtained by those who know it.
Now hear this other vision, O Rāma,
by which you shall behold the Self as immovable and become one who possesses divine sight:
"I am the ether, I am the sun, I am the quarters, and I am also what is below."
I am the Daityas, I am the gods, I am the mountains, and I am the great light; I am darkness, I am the clouds, and I am the earth, the oceans, and so forth;
I am the dust, the wind, and the fire—I am indeed this entire universe.
"I am indeed that very Self abiding everywhere throughout the three worlds;
who am I, and what is this other? For how can there be duality for that which is one?"—thus being certain within himself, he surely [perceives] the world as his own Self.
Seeing this, one is not helplessly overcome by joy or sorrow.
O sinless one, since this entire world is established as consisting of me alone, tell me, O lotus-eyed one: what could be one's own and what could be another's? MU_5,73.6–73.7
Apart from that Knower, what exists which,
upon its arrival, would cause joy, or upon its destruction, would cause despondency to the Knower who pervades the universe?
These two— egoity and the faculty of vision— are pure and characterized by the quality of goodness (sattva).
From the knowledge of reality, two [forms of] ultimate consciousness arise that bestow liberation:
the first is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkṛti*) that "I am the Supreme, whose nature transcends all atoms"; the other, O scion of Raghu, is said to be "I am everything."

But there exists, O sinless one, a third view of the ego, namely "I am the body"; know that this leads only to suffering and not to peace. Or else, having abandoned even these three for the sake of attaining all perfections—
Having taken hold of that state as you desire, remain firm in it;
for the Self, though its nature transcends all and surpasses the existence of all things,
exists indeed as the illuminator, filling the entire world with its own being.
Behold quickly through your own direct experience that you are indeed that which is eternally arisen;
abandon doubt and the knot of the heart, O best among the knowers of reality.
O Rāma, the Self does not exist through inference, nor through the words of authoritative persons, and so forth.
At all times, in every way,
and everything— whatever this vision is, whatever movement there is, and even that which is called consciousness and so forth— all that is the Lord Self, devoid of both the seen and the seeing.
That deity is neither existent nor non-existent; he is neither an atom nor is he great.
He is not even the middle between these two states of perception, yet he alone is all this in every respect.
He alone speaks this, and yet it is not possible for him to speak.

This is not other than that, nor is it this; behold the flawless illusion (*māyā*). This is not the Self, yet this too is the Self; the distinction in designations is itself imagined within one's own self by that very all-pervading power.
For it abides everywhere, radiant throughout the three times;
yet, due to its subtlety and its extreme greatness, it is not perceived as such.
While infinite objects exist, it reflects itself as the individual soul (jīva).

The Self, by the power of its own nature, [appears] spontaneously in the mirror of the *puryaṣṭaka*. (MU 5.73.21) Precisely through the emergence of the *puryaṣṭaka*, the Self is experienced by itself, always abiding in all things, like the wind in the sky through the movement of clouds. (MU 5.73.22)
The conscious self is all-pervading and omnipresent; it does not abide anywhere in particular.
Just as existence (sattā) belongs to all things, so too is Maheśvara.
When that subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) exists, the individual soul (jīva) manifests, but not a stone.
When there is wind, dust appears; when there is a lamp, vision occurs.
This desire of the *puryaṣṭaka* manifests within the Self alone, which is established in itself, just as the worldly longing of people arises when the sun has risen.
If, while the sun remains in the sky, this worldly activity— which exists only by virtue of its arising through that [sun]— perishes, what has happened to the luminous sun?
Likewise, if the Divine remains within the Self, what happens to this world-activity which exists only by obtaining its existence from His being?

The body goes to destruction; what of that is lost for the Self? This Self, which belongs to all and exists at all times, is neither born nor does it die; it neither desires nor abandons; it is neither liberated nor bound.
Arising from the awakening to the self, it takes on the nature of a self in that which is selfless;
this delusion, appearing like the mistaken perception of a snake in a rope, leads only to suffering.
Because it is beginningless, this [self] is not born; because it is unborn, it does not perish.
But it does not desire anything other than itself, because such a thing is impossible. Due to being unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, this [Self] is never bound;
even in the absence of bondage, there would be no liberation, and for that reason it is traditionally known as "non-liberation" (amokṣa).
O Rāghava, this Self is distinguished by such qualities as these;
yet, under the influence of lack of inquiry, this deluded world weeps for it.
He who has correctly perceived the entire sequence of the world from beginning to end—
Do not fall into grief, O wise one, like a person afflicted by folly. Having always abandoned the two mental constructions— the nature of bondage and liberation—
a wise man should conduct himself with self-silence, like a mechanical device.
Liberation is not on the back of the sky, nor in the netherworld, nor upon the surface of the earth;
for liberation is indeed the stainless mind awakened by perfect knowledge.
It is the self-effacement of the mind through non-attachment to all desires.

That is called "liberation" by the knowers of reality who perceive the Self. O Rāma, as long as pure awakening has not been aroused, so long is liberation desired through devotion out of the wretchedness of ignorance.

Having attained long-lasting awakening, when the mind has reached a state of vast expansion, even the ten types of liberation are not desired, much less a single liberation alone. This is liberation; this is bondage—this fragile conceptualization [is what binds].

Having renounced all, you are a great renouncer; you alone are both existence and non-existence. Having attained a state free from conceptual constructions, protect for a long time this circle of the earth—marked by the girdle of the oceans dug by the sons of Sagara—with internal detachment, your glory ever-risen.
The seventy-fourth chapter, titled "Inquiry into the Self," by Vasiṣṭha.

Through the play of conceptualization within the self, a body appears; it is like the notion of ugliness arising in the heart of one who does not see the face of a beautiful person. Under its influence, this vast and thick-waisted [universe] has come into being.
Māyā is the great power of intoxication, as it were, from a mere drop of the taste of wine. By this transformative power, which consists of both that and its opposite,
this entire universe has come into being, like water produced in a desert through the heat of the sun.
The mind, the intellect, the ego, the latent impressions, and even the senses—
thus marked by imagined names, the ocean of the Self surges with its waters.
The duality between the mind and the ego exists in speech, but not in reality.

That which is the mind is indeed the ego-sense; that which is the ego-sense is indeed the manas. Just as whiteness is conceptualized as distinct from snow, so too is the distinction between the mind and the ego-sense falsely imagined.
When one of the two— mind or ego— is destroyed within their interval,
both are indeed destroyed, just as when a cloth is destroyed, its whiteness perishes. Therefore,
having abandoned the hollow notion of liberation, as well as the notion of bondage and all desires, [one attains peace].
Through excellent detachment and discernment, one should simply cause the mind to subside.
If the thought "May there be liberation for me" arises, then the mind has emerged from its state of absorption;
when the mind is intensely intent on such thinking, it leads only to the defects of the body.
When the Self has transcended everything, or when it is extended in every form, what is bondage and what is liberation? How can there be rootless mental construction?
When the vital breath, by its nature of movement, strikes against the body—
Then the series of sprouts that are the hands, limbs, and girdle quivers,
just as the wind moves the rows of sprouts on a tree;
in the very same way, the vital air thoroughly moves the series of limbs within the body.
She is all-pervasive, subtle, unmoving, and cannot be moved;
she does not undergo vibration of her own accord, like the divine mountain [Meru] by the winds.
With all objects reflected within her, she remains solely established in her own self.
It illuminates these worlds through awakening, like a lamp.
In this regard, what is this vain delusion of yours that brings such extreme suffering—
the notion of "this is I," "these are my limbs," and "this is mine"— which belongs only to those of perverted intellect?
Due to its restless longing for the impermanent, like a mass of stones tossed about by the waves,
the activities of knowing, acting, and experiencing are perceived; therein,
this self is conceived as the thinker, the experiencer, and the agent.
Latent impression (*vāsanā*) arises from the heat of ignorance in vain, like a mirage;
though unreal, it appears real and drags on the intoxicated deer of the mind, which thirsts for sense objects, just as a mirage draws one in. (MU 5.74.17–18)
Once this [avidyā] is recognized in its true nature, it perishes and flees,
just as a Caṇḍāla girl flees from the midst of Brahmins once she has been fully identified.
When ignorance is thoroughly understood, it no longer drags the mind away.
A mirage, once fully understood, does not draw away one who is thirsty.
O Rāma, through the realization of the ultimate truth, latent impressions (vāsanā) fall away along with their very roots;
just as the mass of darkness dissolves when light arrives, so too does it vanish through illumination.
When the certainty that "ignorance does not exist" has arisen through the scriptures and reasoning,
ignorance dissolves like a drop of frost under heat;
thus, one who is certain thinks, "What is the use of enjoyments for the sake of this inert body?"
The man of knowledge shatters the cage made of hope, just as a lion tears apart a trap. O Rāma, when the entanglement of hope has indeed been cast off from the heart,
a person attains a beauty that has arrived and experiences joy like the moon.
He attains supreme coolness like a mountain washed by rain;
he possesses the highest bliss like a poor man who has obtained a kingdom;
and he shines with stainless splendor like the vault of heaven in autumn.
He does not overflow within himself, like the ocean at the end of a kalpa;
free from agitation, he becomes like a cloud that has ceased raining. Abiding in the Self as a knower, he remains like a tranquil sea.

He assumes supreme fortitude and, like the immovable Mount Meru, possesses steadfastness; he shines with a self-composed splendor like a fire whose fuel has been exhausted. He becomes extinguished within himself, like a lamp that has been calmed.
The man attains the supreme vision, just as one who has drunk the nectar of immortality.
Like a jar containing a lamp within, like a fire with its flame in the center,
or like a gem radiating brilliance, he becomes manifest from within.
He beholds his own self as the soul of all, omnipresent, the lord of all, the leader of all, possessing all forms yet formless;
he laughs heartily, having transcended those delicate days of the past.
In those [states], his mind— which was as fickle as a volley of Cupid’s arrows— was severed.
Having emerged from the arena of worldly conflict, with the fever of pride and passion stilled,
he sat devoted to the inner self, his mind full and pure.
Having wiped away the stains of the mire of desire, having severed the bond of birth,
liberated from the fear of the defects of dualities, he has crossed the ocean of saṃsāra;
having attained unsurpassed rest, he has reached the station of the state that cannot be attained.
Having attained the state from which there is no returning, he has reached the end of all karmas. Engaging in the undertaking of all desired goals, he desires nothing at all;
experiencing joy in everything that is approved, he rejoices in nothing at all.
He neither gives nor takes, neither praises nor blames;
he neither sets nor rises, and he neither rejoices nor grieves. Having renounced the fruits of all undertakings, he is free from all limiting adjuncts.

One who has completely renounced all desires is known as liberated while living (jīvanmukta). Having abandoned all longings with the mind, become silent like a raincloud that has shed its water entirely.
Likewise, a woman of excellent complexion, though clinging to one's limbs, does not bring such pleasure as the state of hopelessness,
cool as the moon, brings to the heart.
O Rāghava, even the moon, though pressed against one's neck, does not bring such pleasure.
Hopelessness brings such inner happiness, as if entirely cooled,
that the honey from flowers swaying with pollen does not shine as brightly as a man of noble mind who is silent and whose heart is equanimous through hopelessness.
Neither from the Himalayas, nor from pearls, nor from plantain trees, nor from sandalwood,

nor even from the moon is that coolness obtained which is attained through the absence of desire (nairāśya). Even more than sovereignty, even more than heaven, even more than the moon, and even more than Mādhava—

Even from the company of a beloved, hopelessness is the supreme happiness. O virtuous one, that ultimate bliss which renders the splendors of the three worlds as insignificant as a blade of grass is obtained through hopelessness.
Take hold of hopelessness— the axe for the *karañja* tree of desire, the station of supreme bliss,
and the flower-cluster of the tree of tranquility. The earth is but a cow’s footprint, Meru is a mere post, and desires are but small caskets.

O Rāma, for one whose form is adorned with hopelessness, the three worlds are but a blade of grass. The activities of giving, taking, gathering, wandering, and the display of wealth are laughed at by those supreme persons who are free from desire.
By whom can he be compared— he who has rendered the three worlds as mere straw, and in whose heart conceptualization never takes root?
"Let this be mine, let that not be mine"— such is the attachment within the heart.
How can people weigh that which has no self or lord?
Relying on desirelessness— the supreme good fortune of the intellect, free from stain and beyond all distress— attain the ultimate happiness.
O Teacher, know that this world is a false delusion of hopes;
it has arisen like the revolving of the rim of a wheel on a moving chariot. Why do you, O mighty-armed one, being learned, yet delude yourself like a fool?
"With a mind deluded by thoughts such as 'this is mine,' 'that is his,' or 'I am this,' [one fails to see the truth].
This entire world is indeed the Self; no diversity exists here.
Having realized that the world is of a single form, O Rāma, the wise do not suffer."
O Raghava, it is precisely through the vision of the flood of objects as they truly are that the supreme consolation of the intellect is attained— namely, the state of desirelessness (nairāśyam),
which stands free from contradiction regarding existence and non-existence at both the beginning and the end.
Taking that form as your object of focus, establish the stability of all things.
With a mind firm in the realization of selflessness, this most delusive illusion flees away like a doe from a lion, leaving the transmigrating being behind.
A man of steady intellect regards alike his beloved wife— restless with intense passion— and a trembling forest creeper, as well as a row of crumbling stones.
Neither worldly enjoyments gladden his heart within, nor do calamities cause him distress.
O dear one, the beauties of what is seen do not carry away the wise man, just as winds cannot move a mountain.
Even for a sage of noble intellect who has become a knower, though he possesses a young woman full of passion,
the arrows of Love are shattered into fragments within his mind.
One who knows his own true nature is not helplessly dragged away by passion and hatred;
for him, there is even no contact with these two, let alone their overcoming.
[He remains] with an equal vision toward things such as a swaying creeper, a woman, or a mountain rock.

He does not take delight in enjoyments, like a traveler in desert lands. With his mind liberated, the wise man enjoys the abundance of enjoyments that come to him effortlessly as a mere play, just as the eye perceives light.
Like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, a series of enjoyments such as women may arrive;

yet even when indulged in, my friend, they lead neither to suffering nor to satisfaction for the steadfast one who has correctly perceived the nature of reality and understands the slight fluctuations between pleasure and pain.
Like two surging waves against the king of mountains, they are unable to cause him any agitation.
Looking upon worldly enjoyments with ease, gentle, self-controlled, and free from feverish distress,
he takes refuge in his own state, which abides within all beings.
The Knower remains free from agitation even while possessed by agitation,
as he brings forth the worlds, like Brahmā himself who is solely devoted to his own self;
for calamities arrive according to desire, according to time, and according to sequence.
A mountain does not waver amidst pleasure and pain, just as it remains steady through the changing seasons.
O Rāma, even for one who is deeply immersed in the activities of the organs of action, nothing at all sinks him, provided his mind is eternally unattached and he possesses great wisdom.
Gold is said to be stained by an internal impurity, and not otherwise;
for a living being is said to be attached through attachment to worldly existence, and not otherwise. For the discerning person who perceives his own self as distinct from the body—
Even though his limbs have been cut apart, nothing at all has been cut away.
That which is known once, pure and radiant, remains known forever;
for a relative who has been recognized does not again fall into a state of being unknown.
Just as when the delusion of a snake has ceased, the notion of a snake no longer returns to the rope—
like a mountain torrent that has flowed away during the rains— so too gold, once its form purified by heating and returned to its own natural luster, is incapable of [assuming] impurity again.
Even though it is submerged in mud, the lotus takes up the filth once again.
When the knot of one’s own heart is destroyed, there is no further bondage by the qualities (guṇas);
for who can bind again with effort a fruit that has already fallen from its stalk?
Who has the power to join together again a stone and the mind, both of which have been reduced to fragments on all sides by the blows of ill-repute and critical inquiry?
Once ignorance has been fully understood, who would ever sink into it again?
Having understood the livelihood of the dog-cookers (outcastes), what twice-born man would look upon it?
Just as the ocean of milk ceases its churning when there is nectar-water,
so too the latent impression of saṃsāra ceases its mental deliberations.
Poisonous water is drunk with the suspicion that it is honeyed nectar;
as long as its true nature is not fully recognized, but once it is recognized, it is abandoned.
Even a passionate woman endowed with beauty and charm is like a painted beauty.

Because it arises from mere material substances, it is perceived by those who know reality as being exactly like the hair and lips of a woman in a painting, even though she is alive; for what attachment indeed can there be toward her? (MU 5.74.80–81)
Even if molasses has been experienced as sweet, it cannot be made otherwise by burning and cutting; likewise, the light of reality regarding the self cannot be altered.
A woman devoted to another, though preoccupied with her household duties, [remains focused on her lover].
Within that very state, he tastes the fresh elixir of the new commitment.
Thus, when the wise man has attained rest in the supreme, pure reality,
he cannot be shaken even by the gods together with the asuras.
By what powerful husband has a woman, devoted to another,
been made to forget the great festival of union with the beloved of her own imagination? The world is supported by the light of infinite consciousness, which is of a single flavor in all things.

By what can the intellect of that great-souled one who knows reality be made to forget? (5.74.86) Engaged in uninterrupted worldly activity amidst all manner of pleasure and pain, he remains dependent on his elders, yet is wearied by his husband and father-in-law. (5.74.87)

Just as a woman in love, languid with bliss due to the beauty of her beloved’s imagination, is not distressed by the nets of suffering even when she encounters misfortune; so too, one whose ignorance has dissolved is not troubled, even while engaged in the affairs of the world.
One whose conduct is governed by right view attains joy within the inner self.
Though his limbs are severed, he does not cry out; though tears flow from him, he does not weep.
Though he is burned, he is not consumed; even when destroyed, he does not perish.
Free from the conjunction of pleasure and pain, and undaunted even by calamities that thwart one's plans,
let him dwell— whether in the palace of a supreme city, on a vast mountain, in a forest, or in a grove of asceticism.
This concludes the chapter entitled "The Teaching on Dispassion."
The seventy-fifth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Janaka remained established in his kingdom, even while occupied with the affairs of state.
Always free from fever within and with an undisturbed mind,
your grandfather Dilīpa, though fully intent on all worldly undertakings,
enjoyed the earth for a long time solely through his inner state of detachment.
Having the appearance of one liberated while living, the unborn Māndhātṛ protected the kingdom forever;
though he remained for a very long time amidst various battles of forces and numerous affairs of state,
he did not abandon the supreme state.
Baḍi, residing on the seat of Pātāla, maintains his own daily existence;
ever-renouncing yet ever-attached, he stands in the state of one liberated while living. Namuci, the sovereign of the Dānavas, is always intent on the conflict between the gods.
In various modes of conduct and dwellings, he was never distressed within.
Having cast off his body in the battle with Vāsava, the high-minded Vṛtra,
though his mind was inwardly cooled, waged war against the gods.
Performing the duties of a Dānava and protecting the depths of Pātāla,
Prahlāda attained joy that was free from harm and reproach;
though solely intent on Śambara, he inwardly manifested as one with Śambara.
O Rāma, Śambara abandoned this Śambara, the snare of saṃsāra; Hari, with an unattached intellect, while engaging in battle with the Dānavas,
attained supreme consciousness and abandoned his body along with his mace.
The fire, though intent upon the entire network of ritual actions,
remains here as if liberated in order to enjoy the fortune of sacrifice for a long time;
likewise, the Soma, whose nature is equanimity, is being drunk by all the gods.
He does not incur attachment anywhere, even when traversing the sky like [the wind];
though Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, fought with Candra for the sake of his wife,
he remained liberated even while performing that wondrous sport in heaven.
Śukra, who illuminates the vault of the sky, who has attained the status of protector of all aims,
and whose mind is free from transformation, passes his time as the preceptor of the Asuras;
even though he has long been causing the limbs of the multitude of beings in the world to move about.

The wind, which always moves everywhere, is indeed liberated; likewise, O Rāma, Brahmā— whose mind is equanimous and whose intellect is untiring— though he ought to feel agitation at the state of the world’s constant flux, exhausts his vast lifespan.
Even the Blessed Lord Hari, though liberated, wanders here for a long time through the play of the cage of dualities such as old age, death, and battle; likewise,
even by the liberated Three-eyed One [Śiva], the blossoming cluster of the tree of beauty was enjoyed.
Gaurī is borne upon half the body [of Śiva] like a woman by her lover;
even though she is liberated, the three-eyed Gaurī has the white one bound around his neck,
like a cluster of perfectly pure pearls, stainless as the crescent moon.
The hero Guha, though liberated, being of profound intellect and the sole ocean of the jewels of all knowledge, undertook the sequence of battles against Tāraka and the others.
Bhṛṅgīśa offered his own blood and flesh to his mother.
O Rāma, with a mind that was indeed liberated, steady, and purified by meditation,
the sage Nārada— though his own nature was already free— wandered through this forest tract of the world as if in play, acting according to his purposeful disposition.
The self-possessed and powerful Viśvāmitra, whose mind is liberated while yet alive,
personally presides over the performance of the sacrifice prescribed by the Vedas;
Śeṣa supports the earth, and the sun creates the succession of days.
Indeed, it is precisely through liberation while living (jīvanmuktatā) that Yama exercises his office as the Lord of Death.
Furthermore, hundreds of others in this threefold world— yakṣas, gods, humans, and asuras— who have attained liberation, remain within the cycle of existence (saṃsṛti) as virtuous beings.
Established in worldly affairs among those who maintain various customs,
some are cool within, while others are deluded like stones;
having attained supreme awakening, some have come to the forest.
Just as Bhṛgu, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Sahadeva, and others;
some remain in royal power, adorned with parasols, chowries, and garlands—
such as Janaka, Śaryāti, Māndhātṛ, Magadha, and others.
Some abide in the sky, situated within the circles of celestial mansions,
such as Bṛhaspati, Uśanas, Candra, Sūrya, and the lords of sages;
some have attained the status of gods, stationed upon rows of celestial chariots.
Just as Agni, Vāyu, Varuṇa, Yama, Tumburu, and Nārada,
some who are liberated while living reside in the depths of Pātāla;
just as Baḍi, Suhotra, Andha, Prahlāda, Hlāda, and others.
Those of cultivated intellect always exist even among the animal births, while those of foolish intellect, O wise one, exist even among the divine births; for indeed,
everything exists by means of everything, everywhere, in every way, and at all times.
Indeed, it is possible within the Self, which is the soul of all and whose nature is both self and non-self;
for the ordinance of the Creator is manifold, its necessity is slow to manifest in infinite undertakings,
and due to the diversity of its structural parts, everything is seen everywhere.
"Vidhi, Daiva, Vibhu, Dhātṛ, Sarveśa, Śiva, and Īśvara"—
by these names the inner Self, the inward-consciousness, is designated.
Within the non-substantial there exists a substance, like gold within sand.
There exists a non-entity within an entity, like dross within grains of gold.
When examined through reasoning, what appears logical is seen to be illogical;
for it is out of fear of sin, O Rāma, that people engage in dharma.
O virtuous one, the eternal truth is perceived within the unreal;
through the practice of meditation upon emptiness, the eternal state is attained.
That which does not exist arises quickly through the play of place and time.

For even rabbits are seen possessing horns when they stand in the place of Śambara; and those things which appear as firm as the essence of a diamond have gone to destruction at the end of a kalpa, just like the moon, the sun, the earth, the oceans, the gods, and the mountains.
Seeing thus, O mighty-armed one, the sequence of existence, non-existence, and becoming,
abandon joy, resentment, dejection, and pride, and attain equanimity. Here,
the non-existent appears as existent, and the existent is also seen as non-existent.
Abandoning both the existent and the non-existent, quickly attain equanimity through that.
O Rāghava, in this world, the attainment of liberation is not possible at all; for millions of people remain submerged due to a lack of discernment and the failure to engage in it.

O Rāghava, liberation is indeed always attainable in this world through the practice of discernment; for by means of discernment, millions of people have become liberated. Through discernment and non-discernment, liberation becomes easy to obtain or difficult to reach.
Liberation comes through the attainment of the dissolution of the mind; therefore, kindle discernment. One who desires prosperity must exert effort toward the vision of the Self;
through the vision of the Self, the severing of the head of all suffering occurs.
Free from passion, free from attachment, liberated while living, and possessed of great intelligence—
many such as Suhotra and Janaka appear here in this world.
Therefore, O Rāma, you too, with an intellect made firm by the dawning of discrimination, [should act accordingly].
"O, wander as one liberated while living, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal!

There are two kinds of liberation found in this world for those who possess a body: one is with the body (sadeha), and the other is without the body (videha). Hear now the distinction between these two."
For the peace of the mind through non-attachment to objects is indeed liberation;
that state is possible for one of sinless character, whether the body exists or not.
O dear one, the highest sages know that the mere exhaustion of affection is absolute isolation (*kaivalya*).
That [state] occurs both when the body exists and when it has ceased to exist.
He who lives with his attachments gone is called liberated while living;
he who lives with attachments is bound; and the third is truly liberated.
Effort for the sake of liberation must be applied with diligence according to the proper method;
for one devoid of effort and method, even a cow’s footprint becomes difficult to cross. But for one who lacks resolute determination, there is only vast suffering.
Relying solely on delusion, one should make oneself subject to others;
yet, having summoned great fortitude with a resolute mind,
one should examine the self by means of the self for the sake of one's own long-term perfection.
For one whose resolve is expanded, the world becomes like a cow’s footprint; for one whose resolve is destroyed, even a cow’s footprint becomes the world.
That which the Sugata has attained is the supreme excellence, and that which some king has attained is stability.
That which the great have attained is the supreme state, the great fruit of the tree of the labor of spiritual effort.
The seventy-sixth canto, titled "The Consideration of the Liberated and the Unliberated."
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, these worlds arise from Brahman;
they attain stability through lack of discernment, my dear, and they come to rest through discernment.
Who is able to count the whirlpools of the water in the web of the world within the ocean of Brahman, or the motes of dust in the rays of light?
Know that improper perception is the cause for the persistence of the world.
Right vision is the sole cause for the pacification of saṃsāra.
For this terrible ocean of saṃsāra, O Rāma, is difficult to cross;
indeed, it cannot be crossed without both logical reasoning and effort.
For this ocean is full, filled with a mass of the waters of delusion;
it has bottomless whirlpools of death and a hollow turbulent with billows,
where the foam of wandering merit floats and the submarine fire of hell blazes.
It has waves agitated by craving, and the elephant of the mind;
it is a casket for the jewels of enjoyment, wherein the river of life is hidden;
it is infested with the serpents of angry diseases and resounds with the croaking of the crocodiles that are the sense-faculties.
Behold, O Rāma, these waves spreading forth, beautiful and flickering;
they are known as charming women, capable of drawing one toward their peaks.
Rich with the beauty of emerald and ruby, they are filled with blue-lotus eyes.
Studded with teeth like pearls, adorned with the foam of smiles,
encircled by hair like sapphire bracelets, rippling with the playfulness of their eyebrows,
expansive with the sandy banks of their hips, and graced with conch-like necks; (these women are like rivers).
Abounding with the jeweled plaques of foreheads, teeming with crocodiles in the form of amorous play,
with darting side-glances for their shimmering minnows, and colored powders for their golden sands—
from such a terrifying ocean of saṃsāra, with its restless waves...
If one who is submerged succeeds in crossing over, that would be the height of human effort.
When the great ship of wisdom is available and discernment serves as the helmsman, fie upon him who has not crossed over this ocean of saṃsāra!
He who, having traversed from the near shore to the far shore and having measured it on all sides,
plunges into the ocean of saṃsāra— he alone is known as a *puruṣa*.
Having reflected with the noble ones and having surveyed the ocean of saṃsāra with his intellect...
"O Rāma, after this, such play is fitting, and not otherwise. O virtuous one, you are fortunate here, for with a mind intent on inquiry,
you are a youth by whom this cycle of existence is being scrutinized."

He who, like you, first reflects upon the world with an exceedingly refined intellect does not sink in this worldly existence. Having first investigated these enjoyments with his mind, he perceives them as bestowing fear upon those who indulge in them.

O Rāma, they should be enjoyed last, like serpents by Garuḍa. Those prosperities which are pursued after one has investigated reality and perceived it are those that result in a future elevation for a living being; all others lead only to suffering.
The strength, intellect, and splendor of one who has perceived reality increase,
like the beauty and other qualities of a tree in springtime. This occurs through a mind that is constantly pure, equanimous, cooled by the infusion of the dense elixir [of knowledge].
O descendant of Raghu, having known the bliss of that which is to be known, he shines exceedingly like the moon;
thus ends the seventy-seventh canto, titled "The Demonstration of the Similarity between the Ocean of Saṃsāra and [the Self]."
Rāma:
O Sage, tell me again in brief of the wonder of the perceived reality within this noble narrative; for who could ever be satiated by your words?
Vasiṣṭha said: "The characteristics of one liberated while living have been described by me in many ways;
O mighty-armed one, listen further to this which is now being told."

Free from desire, the self-possessed one constantly perceives this entire world as if in deep sleep; unattached, he views it as if it were unreal in every respect. Having attained, as it were, absolute liberation, his mind remains as if in a state of profound slumber.

Rejoicing as if reeling, he stands having attained the vision of the Self. With a noble-minded intellect that is turned inward and equanimous, he does not grasp even what is given, nor does he take hold of what is already held in his hand.
Observing this succession of people— like the movement of mechanical puppets— with a gaze withdrawn within, the one of tranquil intellect laughs;
he does not look toward the future, nor does he dwell upon the present.
He does not remember the past, yet he performs everything;
while asleep he becomes awakened, and though awakened, he is like one who is asleep.
Though performing all actions within, he is as if doing nothing at all.
Internally renouncing everything and internally free from seeking,
even while performing external activities, he remains established in all things;
externally, though engaged in all worldly efforts, he is intent on acting as circumstances arise.
Following the course of action resulting from the sequence of his own karma,
possessing a nature that experiences complete happiness, and as if established within all hopes,
he performs all actions while having abandoned the delusion of agency.
Sitting like one who is indifferent toward the activities of the sequence of nature,
he neither desires nor hates, neither grieves nor rejoices;
intent upon the welfare of living beings, his mind remains unattached.
He behaves like a devotee toward the devoted, and stands like a rogue toward the rogue;
he is a child among children, an elder among the elderly, a hero among the heroic,
a youth among those engaged in youthful pursuits, and one who is sorrowful among the sorrowful.
Engaged in meritorious discourse, free from the disposition of wretchedness,
firm-minded, filled with joy, gentle, and renowned for his virtue;
wise, gracious and sweet, full, and possessed of the emergence of perfect intuition.
With all weariness and misfortune cast aside, he was a loving kinsman to everyone;
possessing the form of noble conduct, he was equanimous, a great ocean of happiness,
as affectionate and cool to the touch as the risen full moon.
He has no need for good deeds, nor for enjoyments, nor for ritual acts;
neither for evil deeds, nor for the renunciation of enjoyments, nor for kinsmen;
neither through the undertaking of actions and instruments, nor likewise through inactivity.
Neither by bondage nor by liberation, neither by the netherworld nor by heaven;
when the world is seen as it truly is, as consisting of the one Self,
then the mind never again becomes miserable for the sake of bondage or liberation.
For one whose web of doubt has been burnt away by the fire of right knowledge,
the bird of the mind flies forth freely and without hesitation.
For one whose mind is liberated from delusion and established in equanimity, [the bird of the mind flies forth freely and without hesitation].

It neither sets nor rises; like the sky, it remains so amidst all mental fluctuations. Just as a child seated within a cradle moves its limbs without any conscious coordination, so indeed does the body of the knower act.
Reeling like one intoxicated with bliss, he has rendered rebirth insignificant;
