through the realization that nothing is to be grasped, he no longer remembers what was done or left undone.
He grasps everything in every way, and yet he relinquishes it all.
Having no purpose that can be undertaken, he acts like a child;
even while engaged in activities according to the sequence of place, time, and action,
he is not affected in the slightest by the pleasure or pain resulting from those actions.
Although externally engaged with all worldly affairs, he nevertheless, through inner lack of striving, does not attribute reality to objects nor does he pursue their fruits;
he disregards the state of suffering and does not look toward the hope for pleasure.
He feels no joy at the success of his undertakings, nor does he grieve at their failure.
Even if the cool-rayed moon were to become the sun, or the lunar orb were to turn pitch black,
or even if fire were to spread downward, no sense of wonder would arise in him.
"These powers manifest here in this manner for the conscious self"—
having realized this, no curiosity arises regarding its wondrous webs.
It assumes neither pity nor dejection, nor does it pursue cruelty.
He does not pursue shame, nor does he fall into shamelessness;
never is his soul dejected, nor ever is it arrogant;
he is neither negligent, nor weary of spirit, nor agitated, nor filled with joy.

In his mind, which is vast and as stainless as the autumnal sky, anger and other such passions do not arise, just as new sprouts do not grow in the open air. While the existence of the world proceeds with beings incessantly falling and being born, [he remains unmoved].
Where and how indeed could there be happiness or suffering for this [being]?
Just as the succession of elements in water is as fleeting and unstable as foam,
where in this world, from whence, and what end could there possibly be for the occurrence of pleasure and pain?
Those men who have perceived the process of creation do not despair nor do they exult amidst the endless and incessant arising of living beings through existence and non-existence; for them,
each night, in every moment, is like the various visions seen in a dream.
Just as these worldly perceptions perish as soon as they arise, so too are they;
when there is incessant arising and incessant destruction,
what room is there here for compassion or joy toward this burnt-out cycle of existence?
In the absence of the auspicious, when the state of happiness has vanished,
what kind of distinct perceptions of suffering arise, how do they come into being, or what indeed are those experiences of pain?
That [perception] which, at the end of happiness, arises from its own cessation and expands its own seed— [that is the nature of suffering].
This state of suffering is now stilled; how could it exist once happiness has vanished?

When pleasure and pain have been exhausted, and what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted have perished, where can the desired and the undesired remain when the auspicious and the inauspicious have dissolved?
When the desire for enjoyments has been stilled through the destruction of both pleasant and unpleasant sights,
and when the continuity of hopelessness has matured, the mind melts away like snow;
once the mind is exhausted from its very root, what talk can there be of volitional construction?
When the sesame seeds themselves are completely burnt, whence can there be any notion of oil?
(MU 5.77.43) When all entities remain as a dense mass of non-existence through meditative cultivation, the Great-Souled One stands like the sky, free from all mental construction.
Delighting in his own self, having realized the single true form, the Knower remains, sleeps, and lives eternally satisfied. (MU 5.77.44)
The seventy-eighth canto, titled "The Description of Liberation while Living," by Vasiṣṭha:
Just as a circle of fire arises from the whirling of a firebrand,
appearing as something real though it is unreal, so too does the world arise from the vibration of the mind;
just as [an image] appears as if distinct from water due to the vibration of the water itself.
Just as a circular whirlpool is seen in the sky due to the movement of the eye, so too is the world seen from the vibration of the mind.
Just as a circle of peacock feathers or pearls appears as if real though it is unreal due to the movement of the eye in the sky, so too is the world seen from the vibration of the mind.
Rāma said:
"O Brahman, tell me that by which the mind either vibrates or does not vibrate; for that alone must indeed be treated."
Vasiṣṭha said: Just as whiteness is in snow, O Rāma, as oil is in sesame seeds, as fragrance is in flowers, and as heat is in fire; so it is with this.
O delighter of the Raghus, the mind and its vibration are likewise joined;
they are non-different, and the distinction between them is merely a false mental construction.
When either the side of the mind or the side of the mind's vibration is entirely dissolved, [the two become one].
Through the self-abiding of both the qualities and the possessor of qualities, both perish; of this there is no doubt.
O Rāghava, there are two methods for the destruction of the mind: yoga and knowledge.
Yoga is indeed the restraint of its fluctuations, while knowledge is correct discernment.
Rāma:
By what kind of practice, bound to the out-breath and in-breath,
and known as yoga, does the mind attain peace that bestows infinite bliss?
Vasiṣṭha:
That wind which vibrates everywhere within this body and its channels,
like water flowing through the furrows of the earth, is celebrated as *prāṇa*.
Due to the force of its vibration, as it undergoes a variety of internal activities,
names such as *apāna* and so forth have been devised by those of perfected self.
Just as a flower is the source of fragrance, or as snow is the source of whiteness.

In the same way, this chariot has become the support for the mind’s non-differentiation. Know that, O Rāghava, that consciousness which arises from the internal vibration of the vital breath and is intent upon the fabrication of volitions is the mind.

They know the vibration of consciousness to be the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa); from that very vibration of the breath arise the various movements of consciousness, just as waves arise from the movement of water. Those adorned by the scriptures say that the mind is the pulsation of the vital breath.
When that [mind] is restrained, the mind will surely become tranquil.
Through the cessation of the mind's vibration, this cycle of existence dissolves,
just as worldly activity ceases when the movement of the sun’s light comes to rest.
Rāma: How can the movement of the vital airs— such as the *prāṇa* and others— which move incessantly within the body-cave and course through its depths, be obstructed?
Vasiṣṭha:
Through contact with the scriptures and virtuous people, and through the yoga of the practice of dispassion,
one first develops a lack of reliance toward worldly activities and a firm reliance [upon the Self].
From the long-term, unified arising of meditation as desired,
and from the intense practice of this very reality, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is ceased;
through firm practice of the natural *āyāma* (breath control) such as inhalation (*pūraka*), performed without fatigue.
Through the application of one-pointed meditation, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is ceased.
By pursuing the reality of the sound at the conclusion of the utterance of the syllable *oṃ*,
when consciousness becomes as in deep sleep, the vibration of the vital breath is ceased.
When the recaka has been practiced and the breath has entered the vast space,
the movement of the vital breath no longer touches the apertures of the limbs and is restrained.
In the kumbhaka, as before, it remains for an infinite time.
Through practice, when the vital breath (prāṇa) is made motionless, the vibration of the vital breath is obstructed.
By exerting effort to press the uvula with the tongue as it reaches the root of the palate,
when the vital breath has ascended to the upper aperture, the vibration of the vital breath is obstructed.

When consciousness is dissolved through meditation in the subtle ether— which is called "nothingness" and is free from all temporal divisions— the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is arrested at the tip of the nose, in the stainless space extending twelve finger-breadths.
When right vision has been attained and [the mind] is stilled, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is obstructed.

(MU 5.78.26) Through practice, when the vital breath reaches the upper opening—the space twelve finger-breadths above the palate—and consciousness has dissolved, the vibration of the vital breath is obstructed. (MU 5.78.27)
When the light of the star has subsided at the midpoint between the eyebrows and has set,

the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) ceases within the consciousness that is the abode of the intellect. For the sage, this occurs through the long-term perception of the solitary void within the heart.
"Through meditation on the mind free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is ceased.
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, what is that which is called the 'heart' (*hṛdaya*) of living beings in this world?"
"All this is reflected within that which is like a great mirror.
Vasiṣṭha said: "O virtuous one, in this world, the heart of living beings exists in two ways."
Listen now to this distinction between what is to be accepted and what is to be rejected:
know that within the body, which is limited by its specific dimensions, that which is situated on one side of the chest is the heart; understand that it is the part to be rejected.
Pure consciousness alone is declared to be the heart to be accepted by men;
it is neither within nor without, yet neither without nor within.
That heart, which is the primary essence of each [state], is where this [consciousness] is fully established.
That is the mirror of all things; it is the treasury of all prosperity.
Consciousness alone is called the heart of all living beings;
it is not a mere physical part of the body, inert like a worn-out stone.

Therefore, when the mind is forcibly directed toward this pure heart, which consists of consciousness, and is rendered free of latent impressions (vāsana), the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇaspanda) is arrested.
By these means, as well as by others devised through various resolutions, [this state is attained].
The vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*) is restrained by means of the various instructions residing in the mouths of teachers.
Through practice, these methods of yoga become effective, without obstruction,
as the means for a fortunate person to shatter the cycle of existence.
When [the practice] has attained firmness through repetition and is marked by dispassion (*vairāgya*),
the extension of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) according to one's latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is considered fruitful.
[This occurs] at the locations of the eyebrows, the nose, and the palate, extending up to twelve finger-breadths.
Through practice, the breath becomes stilled like a mountain river far away;
by repeated and long-term practice, the uvula is touched with the tip of the tongue against the palate,
whereby the breaths flow sufficiently upward.

But these meditative absorptions, though abundant in conceptual construction, through constant practice quickly lead to a state free of conceptualization for the sake of supreme tranquility. The person who delights in the self becomes free from sorrow and possesses inner happiness.
It comes from practice alone and from nothing else; therefore, be one who practices.
When the movement of the vital breaths has reached its exhaustion through practice, the mind attains tranquility, and only nirvāṇa remains.
Birth is enveloped by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), while liberation is a mind free of latent impressions;
and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) takes hold of both, O Rāma—do as you wish.
The vibration of the vital breath takes the form of the mind, and from that arises the delusion of transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*).
When that very [mind] has attained tranquility, the fever of worldly existence is extinguished.
Through the total cessation of conceptual construction, that state remains for the living being,
from which all words, along with every form of mental fabrication, turn back.
That in which all is, from which all comes, that which is all, and from which all proceeds; that wherein this [world] is not, from whence this is not, that which is not this,

and that which is not of such a nature— [it is known] because of perishability, because of being conceptualized, and because of possessing qualities, [as opposed to] the Self which is devoid of qualities.
For there is indeed no example whatsoever to be seen that is equal to it;
it is the essence of all grains, the lamp of all splendors,
and the source of all desires, from which the moonlight of consciousness arises.

Having taken refuge in that state which is the ultimate limit of all things, the one of great intelligence [sees] those many rows of fruits of saṃsāra— which arise from the wish-fulfilling tree of conceptualization and, possessing manifold flavors, are born and fall without ceasing.
He who remains established with a steady intellect, knowing that [Reality], is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Having abandoned all longing and curiosity, with the conceptualization of "beneficial" and "harmful" completely stilled,
the supreme person, whose mind is liberated, continues to engage in all worldly activities.
The seventy-ninth canto, titled "The Description of the Bondage of the Species of Those Liberated while Living," [spoken by] Rāma.
"Thus has the pacification of this mind been described through the method of yoga;
now, O Lord, out of your grace, tell me of right knowledge.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"The Supreme Self exists here as the essence of beginningless and endless manifestation"—
the wise know that this expansive, singular certainty is right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
These hundreds of potencies for objects in the form of jars, cloths, and so forth...
The firm conviction that "only the Self exists and nothing else" is right vision (*samyagīkṣaṇa*).
Birth arises from incorrect knowledge, while liberation comes from right contemplation;
from incorrect observation a rope is seen as a snake, but not so from right observation.
Consciousness (saṃvit), when completely freed from the portion consisting of volitional constructs (saṅkalpa) and devoid of the object of cognition (saṃvedya),
exists here as nothing other than that which is liberated from these initial designations.
When known in its pure form, it is called the Supreme Self (paramātman).
But when the nature of the Buddha is impure, it is called ignorance by the wise.
Consciousness itself is the object of consciousness; there is no conceptualization of duality between these two.
O Rāma, the Self alone accumulates the self; indeed, nothing else exists.
The vision of things as they truly are in these three worlds is this much:
having ascertained that the Self alone is the entire universe, there is fullness.
Since everything is indeed the Self, upon what are existence and non-existence dependent, or where are they situated?
Where is the conceptualization of bondage and liberation? O Rāma, what else is there to be grieved for?
There is no mind other than this, nor any object of thought; it is Brahman alone that unfolds as all this.
Everything is the one supreme void; where is liberation, and who is bound?
This Brahman is of expanded form, vast and established as the Great; it has long since transcended duality. You are indeed the Self of existence by your very nature.
When the true form is correctly perceived, [there is no difference] between wood, stone, and cloth.
There is not even the slightest difference anywhere for one who is turned away from conceptual construction.
That which is peaceful at the beginning and at the end, the imperishable essential nature of both things and the self— be absorbed in that, O Rāghava.

Through the delusions of old age and death arising from the notions of duality and non-duality, the Self alone manifests as various selves, like water appearing as waves. Relying upon the pure Self with an intellect that is eternally established within, one remains steadfast.

What enjoyment is capable of deceiving that Lord of the Self who stands thus? For one who has performed extensive inquiry, the enemies such as enjoyments do not pierce him even slightly, just as gentle breezes cannot shatter a mountain.
Ignorance that lacks discernment, deluded and devoted to hope, swallows up sufferings here in this world like a heron seizing a fish from waterless ground.
The entire world is indeed the Self; ignorance exists nowhere at all.
Thus, firmly grasping this correct vision, remain steadfast.
There is no multiplicity within the mental constructions, nor any difference in reality, just as there is no difference from the water in various kinds of lakes.
One who consists of such singular certainty, having perceived the true meaning, is called a liberated person.
The Eightieth Chapter, titled "The Characteristic of Right Knowledge," by Vasiṣṭha:
For the discerning person who perceives this within,
O dear one, no longing ever arises even toward enjoyments standing right before them.
The eye exists for the purpose of seeing alone, whereas the individual soul [is the experiencer] of pleasure and pain.
The ox is merely for the burden; the enjoyer is the leader of wealth.
When the eyes are immersed in forms, what agitation can there be for the embodied soul?
What loss is there to the army commander when a donkey plunges into a pond?
O base one, do not relish this mire of form; do not honor it.
For it perishes in the blink of an eye and indeed destroys you as well. With whomsoever friendship is made and whomsoever is followed, [it is that very person who is destroyed].

By his own actions, even a wise man and a hero is swiftly bound. O eye, do not resort to this form— which arises and perishes, which is pleasing only for a moment, and which consists of unreality— for the sake of your own destruction, you who are indestructible.
Like a witness, you, the eye, remain; form abides within the self.
Light [arises] by the power of time; why do you alone suffer?
Vision is like a ripple on water, like a feather rising from the sky.

O mind, from what has this arisen that you throb with attachment to your own kind? O ego, in a mind whose nature is to throb like a fish in a small pool of water, you yourself are throbbing; from where have you emerged?
Since light and form are both eternally insentient and flash forth in mutual dependence as support and supported, O mind, your agitation is in vain.
Form, light, and mental attention are not connected to one another.
They appear as if attached, like reflections in the mirror of a face.
For these have become closely joined to the ignorant creature;
when ignorance has dissolved through knowledge, they remain separate, consisting of unreality.

For these— form, light, and mental attention— are closely bound to one another by the activity of the mind, just as pieces of wood are held together by lac. Through the diligent practice of the mind upon the thread of its own mental ideation, [one attains liberation].
When [the mind] reaches cessation through investigation, the cultivation of ignorance is severed.
With the destruction of ignorance, when the mind has perished,
none of these— form, light, and mental attention— ever again come together with one another.
The mind alone is the awakener of all the internal senses;
therefore, it is that which must be eradicated from within, like a demon from a house. O mind, you wander in vain; I have seen your end.
In the beginning and at the end you are utterly void; even in the present, you truly do not exist. Why do you dance about within through these five modes in vain?
This dancing belongs only to him who perceives you as "I."
"Your leaping about does not bring even the slightest satisfaction to my mind;
like the movement of a phantom man, you burn in vain amidst your activities.
Stay or go, O mind—you are nothing to me, O rogue; you may live on."
By nature you are eternally dead; through inquiry, you remain perfectly dead.
O brother, you are devoid of reality, insentient, and eternally of the form of death—O rogue!
Only the fool who lacks discernment is deceived by you, not the one possessed of inquiry.
We have now recognized you; it was through our own folly that we followed after you. Today you are as dead to us as darkness is to lamps.
For a long time, O deceitful one, you have occupied the house of my body.
Formerly, this [body] was obstructed and deprived of association with the virtuous.
Now that you, O rogue of a mind— dull-witted, resembling a corpse, and departed— have gone,
this house of the body stands fit to be inhabited by all holy men.
"You were already such a dullard and a rogue even before; you remain so now as well. You will not become anything else—O Vetāla, are you not ashamed?
Together with the ogresses of craving and the guhyakas of anger and the rest,"
"Depart, O vetāla of the mind, from my body-abode!
By good fortune, through the mantra of discernment, the intoxicated vetāla of the mind has emerged from the temple of the body, like a wicked wolf from a mountain cave."
Oh, how truly wondrous and great is this: by this dull, momentary, and treacherous mind, all these people have been rendered helpless!
What is your prowess? What is your strength? What is your support?
If you leap about, you likewise oppress this very people.
You are a deceitful soul; O base-minded one, you are not spared by me!
O ignorant one, today you have merely realized that you are dead.
For so long a time, thinking you were alive,
I have remained afflicted throughout the many calamities of the long nights of saṃsāra;
yet today I have realized that the mind, indeed, is dead and does not exist here.
Therefore, having abandoned hope for you, I remain alone within my own self.
By good fortune, I have today realized for myself that the mind is dead;
I have not spent my entire life in vain with this rogue.

Having expelled the rogue mind from the abode of the body in an instant, I now remain healthy within, free from the Vetāla; for a long time, I have been tormented by this Vetāla of the mind which I had acquired.

I myself created various transformations, which I then laughed at. By good fortune, after a long time, the mind-ghoul— towering as high as a palm tree and marked by the excellent sword of discernment— has finally fallen from the house of my heart.
Now that the Vetāla of the mind has been pacified and has gone to the pure state,
by good fortune I remain alone and at ease in the city of the body.
The mind is dead, thoughts are dead, and the Rākṣasa of egoism is dead.
Through the mantra of discernment, I remain equanimous, healthy, and alone.
What is my mind? What are my desires? What could my ego be?
By good fortune, this wife of mine has been entirely lost and rendered useless.
Salutations again and again to me alone— the one who has accomplished all that was to be done, who is eternal, whose nature is stainless, and who is known as non-conceptual consciousness.
For me there is no hope, no actions, no saṃsāra, and no agency.
I am neither the enjoyer nor the body; salutations again and again to me alone.
I am not the self, nor the ether, nor indeed am I this [body] myself;
there is no limitation for me; salutations again and again to me alone.
Salutations again and again to me alone, who am formless, ineffable, luminous, and of stainless nature; who abides solely as the Self by itself;
who is changeless, eternal, partless, and without a self.
Salutations again and again to me alone, who am everything for every purpose.
Salutations again and again to me alone, having attained whose being— impartial, all-pervading, subtle, and the sole illuminator of the universe— I have entered within.

Neither the earth with its mountains, nor the rivers, nor the limbs of the quarters, nor even "I" or "not-I"—the entire world, rich with all objects, belongs to me alone; salutations again and again to me!
[It is] free from mental construction, delightful through tranquility, manifesting the universe yet not the universe, and infinite.
I myself bow down to that unborn, undecaying, and sovereign form of the Imperishable Lord, which transcends all qualities.
The eighty-first canto, titled "An Investigation into the Relationship between the Seer and the Seen."
Vasiṣṭha:
Having thus reflected within with the intellect, O mighty-armed one, the knowers of reality further reflect in this manner; the Self is to be known by those great-souled ones.
"It is the truth that this world is indeed the Self alone, cleansed by the mind;
from where could the mind have arisen? Oh, how strange is that which is non-existent!
For it is always [non-existent] because of its being ignorance, because of its being non-mind, and because of its being mere appearance."
The mind that has died does not exist at all as anything other than a delusion, like a flower in the sky.
Just as the movement of a tree stump is real for a child traveling by boat but not for one who is awake,
so too is the mind unreal for one who is unawakened.
When the delusion of ignorance and bewilderment has subsided, we no longer perceive the mind, just as the shaking of a mountain ceases once the whirling of a wheel has ended.
Thus, the mind does not exist at all; there is only Brahman, whose nature is that very Self.
The various mental constructions of objects are unreal, for they have been abandoned by me.
My doubts are stilled; I stand free from the fever of anxiety.
Just as I remain, so do I remain, truly free from all longing.
In the absence of the mind, the qualities such as craving are forcibly exhausted,
just as various descriptions of colors vanish when light ceases.
The mind is dead, cravings have departed, and the cage of delusion is destroyed.
Free from egoism has arisen within me; I have awakened to the world.
The universe is indeed one and peaceful; even multiplicity is not real.
What else remains for me to contemplate within? Enough with this discourse!
I am the eternal Self, established as subtle, all-pervading, and gentle, having attained that pure state which is without appearance and without beginning or end.
Whatever exists here and whatever does not exist— whether it be mind and so forth, or the self and other non-entities— I am that.
Therefore, let the mind become clearer than that, peaceful, infinite, ungraspable, and pervasive;
or let it not be so, or let it attain fixed mindfulness within.
What use have I for deliberation, since my own self has arisen as partless?
Out of ignorance, my state was that "I am the investigator";
but now, through investigation, I have become immeasurable in form—where is this investigator now?
Even when the mind has ceased, this glory of my conceptual construction is utterly meaningless.

For what purpose does this arise for the sake of the activity of the mind-demon? Therefore, having thoroughly determined that "this is it," I shall utterly abandon this internal fabrication of conceptualization;
with a tranquil self, I remain within the Self, observing silence.
"Whether eating, walking, sleeping, or standing, O Rāghava, one who knows that [reality] should daily investigate it everywhere with wisdom through the mind.
Having investigated with his own mind, which is established in its own state and at ease,"
The wise remain free from agitation while engaged in their natural duties;
free from pride and intoxication, with joyful dispositions and a radiance equal to the autumnal moon,
these great-minded ones dwell happily here, moving about in the midst of ordinary worldly affairs.
The eighty-second canto, titled "The Demonstration of the Non-existence of Mind," by Vasiṣṭha.
"This very inquiry was performed by Saṃvarta in the past;
it was told to me on the Vindhya mountain by him, who had realized the Self.
Having taken hold of this view, with an intellect intent on inquiry—"
Cross over this ocean of saṃsāra by means of gradual progression.
Now, O Rāma, hear this other view which bestows the [highest] state,
as it was established without hesitation by the sage Vītahavya.
In former times, the immensely radiant Vītahavya wandered through the vast caves of the Vindhya mountains like the sun wandering through the caverns of Mount Meru;
[all this was due to] this terrible sequence of ritual actions that brings about the delusion of saṃsāra.
Due to the nature of mental and physical afflictions, he became weary with the passage of time;
desiring that noble state attainable through the portion of non-conceptual meditative absorption,
he— worn out by old age— retracted the succession of his own activities.

He entered his own leaf-hut, fashioned by Rambhā, which was as fragrant and golden-hued as a mango tree, like a blue bee entering a blue lotus. There, upon a level and pure seat spread with a well-laid deerskin, he sat.
He rested on the peaceful mountain like a cloud that has discharged its rain;
having assumed the lotus posture and placed his joined palms upon his heels,
he stood with a firm neck and motionless as a mountain peak.
Gradually withdrawing the light scattered across the quarters,
like the sun at evening drawing back its mass of radiance as it enters a cave in Mount Meru,
he successively abandoned both external and internal sensations of touch.
With a mind free from sin, he reflected thus:
"Alas! This mind is so fickle that even when withdrawn, it does not attain stability for even a moment, like the broad leaves of a tree tossed by the waves."
Agitated by unrestrained forms perceived through the eyes and other senses, it leaps up incessantly like a ball struck by the palm of the hand;
it quickly abandons one state and grasps another, its functions amplified by the sense organs.
From whatever it is restrained, toward that very thing it rushes like one possessed;
from a pot it goes to a cloth, from a cloth to a large cart—
the mind roams among objects like a monkey among trees.
These five gates of the mind, beginning with the eye, which are fully capable of being called "burnt senses"—for now, I shall examine them.
O, you hosts of ruined senses! What is this recklessness of yours here?
Fickle like the waves of oceans with their surging waters,
do not, O you of restless minds, act with such impulsiveness to your own detriment;
remember the vast nets of suffering that have occurred in the past.
"O forms, you are indeed merely inert and base;
through this inertia, an excessive longing leaps forth like a mirage for those whose nature is essence-less and who are always without vision."
This arrogance of the blind leads only to ridicule.
The unborn, blessed Lord, whose nature is consciousness, acts as the witness of all;
you, whose hosts of senses have been destroyed, why have you come here in vain?
These [senses], such as the eyes and so forth, which are devoid of form, merely whirl about falsely;
they are like a firebrand-circle, resembling the delusion of a snake in a rope.
Therefore, by that Self who possesses great knowledge, the eyes and other senses are rendered devoid of cognition.
Not even slightly connected with heaven, the netherworld, mountains, or trees;
like a traveler afraid of snakes or a twice-born man fearing *pukkasa* outcasts,
pure consciousness remains far away from the sense organs, free from all affliction.
This mutual agitation of yours exists merely by the presence of consciousness,
just as those engaged in their daily tasks remain at ease while the sun shines.
O mind, you wanderer, you Cārvāka, you beggar for the bellies of the four quarters!
Like a dog, wander through this world in vain for no purpose;
"I am conscious," such is your false mental impression.
O rogue, there can be no identity between consciousness and the mind, for they are utterly distinct.
"I am indeed living"—this drum of your egoism has arisen in vain for the sake of suffering; it is not real, being devoid of truth.
Abandon this agitation born of egoism, thinking "I am that."
O fool, there is nothing at all; why do you agitate yourself in vain?
Consciousness is the mind, without beginning or end, and nothing other than consciousness exists.
In this body, O great fool, what could that thing called "mind" possibly be?
O mind, this suspicion that you possess the status of an enjoyer or an agent has arisen like an elixir that results in poison; it is indeed in vain.
O dull-witted collection of sense-faculties, do not become an object of ridicule yourself.
You are not the doer, nor are you the enjoyer; you are inert and are awakened by another. Who are you in relation to enjoyments, or what are these enjoyments to you?
Since you, being inert, have no self at all, how can there be relatives, friends, and the like?

For that which is insentient does not exist at all; it is only the existent that is associated with non-existence, because of the impossibility of [insentience] possessing the states of being a knower, an agent, an enjoyer, or a thinker.
If you are of the nature of inward consciousness, then that very Self is your body.
O mind, how can your existence, consisting of both being and non-being, cause you such suffering? Or rather, those states of agency and enjoyership which you have falsely grasped—
listen, O rogue, how they shall be wiped away by me through reasoning.
First of all, you yourself are inert; of this there is no doubt.
What kind of agency can belong to that which is inert? For how could stones ever dance?
Therefore, having long relied upon that pure portion of His which is sovereignty, [you have come to this state].
"You live, you desire, you kill, you leap, you go, you dance.
Whatever is done by means of a power, that is done by that [power] alone. A sickle cuts by means of a man's power; yet it is the man who is said to be the cutter.
Whatever is drunk according to its capacity becomes [the drinker] through that very act;
the drink is consumed by the vessel, yet it is the person who is called the "drinker.
By your very nature you are utterly inert, and though repeatedly awakened by the Knower, you remain so.
Therefore, it is the Self alone that gathers the Self by means of the Self; for this must be so for us.
The Supreme Lord, the Self, awakens you incessantly;
indeed, the deluded are to be awakened by the wise even through hundreds of repetitions.
For it is the very existence of the Self alone that flashes forth here, having the singular form of pure consciousness;
and by means of that [existence] alone, the mind quickly remains established after assuming the objects denoted by words.
Thus, O mind, you have come into being through ignorance from the power of the Self.
But in the face of intense knowledge, [this egoism] falls away like snow in the heat of the sun.
Therefore, you are dead, you are deluded; in the ultimate sense, you do not exist.
Let there be no vain conceit that "I am that very thing," for it leads only to your unhappiness.
The mental constructions of the unreal are like the creepers of Indra’s net;
O dear one, here it is consciousness alone that unfolds as the power of Brahman.
Through the forms of the worlds of men and gods, the power of Brahman arises abundantly.
Like the shore leaping with masses of golden waves from the ocean, the world dances;
yet, O deluded one, that [world] consists of consciousness and arises from consciousness. Since you are eternally non-different from that supreme state, why do you grieve for anything else?
For that state is all-pervading, abiding in all beings, and indeed possessing all forms;
upon attaining it, everything is always swiftly attained.
There is no "you," there is no body; here, only the Great, radiant Brahman exists.
For whom indeed does suffering arise from the outflows of "I" and "you"?
If you are the Self, then the all-pervading Self alone exists here and nothing else;
if you are that which is other than the Self, namely the insentient, then you do not exist, for its nature is ignorance.
The self alone is the entirety of the three worlds; other than that, there is nothing at all.
If you are that "nothing" which is other than the self, then you are nothing. Why do you vainly strive with thoughts such as "I," "this," "that," or "it belongs to me"?
How can that which has no real form manifest? Who is killed by the horn of a hare?
O rogue, there is no third conceptualization other than the parts of consciousness and insentience;
it is like a third coloring between shadow and laughter.

O ignorant one, that which arises from the vision of truth, when the duality of mind and matter has perished, is indeed nothing but self-awareness alone. Therefore, O deluded one, you are neither an agent nor an enjoyer.
That alone is you, the Supreme Brahman; abandon this ignorance consisting of the sense of "I.
It is merely for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of instruction regarding the domain of the ignorant that it is said, "the Self acts through you as its instrument."
The instrument, being insubstantial in nature, inert, and without support,
neither vibrates nor moves without the awakening of an agent;
O ignorant one, no power whatsoever exists in an instrument that lacks an agent.
In the absence of a reaper, what capacity does a sickle have to act?
The capacity for the action of cutting with a sword-stroke resides in the person;
it does not reside in the utterly inert sword, even when all its parts are intact.
Therefore, my friend, you are not the agent; do not become a partaker of suffering in vain.
O fool, being afflicted for the sake of others does not look well among common people. A Lord who has been benefited by you is not one to be pitied in such a way.

For him there is no purpose whatsoever in action, nor any in inaction here; yet the one of small intellect suffers, thinking only, "I am serving him," while for the virtuous, no such personal interest exists.
If you thus follow the will of the Creator, the Lord of Experience,
then no desire whatsoever would arise here for him, for he is always entirely satisfied by the all-pervading Self of Consciousness, which shines with an uncreated radiance.
This [universe] is filled by the One alone; there is no other conceptualization.
By means of the manifestation of the one and the many, as the totality of that pervasive Self, what is created within the Self by the Self itself—what is desired?
But for one such as you, agitation arises in vain through mere sight,
just as the mind becomes intoxicated upon beholding a queen.
O handsome one, if there were a connection between you and that [object], then you would indeed be its agent.
But it has no connection with this [other], just as a stone has none with a flower.
That which is the identity [of two things] with a second, through their being that [second], is their oneness;
that is declared to be the understanding of connection, where there was previously duality and now there is unity.
Consisting of various types of arrangements and manifested through diverse forms and actions,
it is known to be manifold, serving as the cause for states of pleasure and pain. Furthermore,
a connection is observed between two equal [halves], as well as between two halves that are unequal.
And when that [Primal Nature] exists, there is another [Spirit] characterized by distinct qualities within the three worlds;
many substances indeed take recourse in the quality of another substance,
just as medicinal herbs [take recourse] in the coolness of the moon, or as great rocks [take recourse] in heat.
If, however, there is such a connection for you with the Supreme Self,
let that mutual intermingling of qualities be the seed of transmigratory existence;
[yet this occurs] through the self by means of the self which transcends the power of the mental construction of the mind.
There is no such relationship between you and the subtle aggregate of the senses.
Furthermore, another kind of relationship is clearly observed in the world through convention,
such as the identity of two flames of fire or even two bodies of water.
Even for an atom whose nature transcends the power of mental construction and ideation,
there is no such connection with the aggregate of the sense organs.
Furthermore, O thief, a connection is observed even between two halves of a single moment.
Just as in this world, between a woman and a man, there is a distinction due to the diversity of even a single part;
or like water and milk, which are distinct by some slight difference;
or like water and honey, or two varieties of honey that are diverse.

Between white and red, or between the two splendors of Aruṇa and the Sun, there may be such a connection; yet for you, whose self transcends the power of the mind’s mental constructions, there is no such connection with the subtle atoms of the group of senses.
There exists another kind of relationship between things that are utterly distinct,
such as that between wood and fire here, or likewise between a man and an elephant;
yet even such a relationship does not exist for you between the collection of sense-faculties and the atoms.
By means of the self, which transcends the self through the creative power of mental ideation,
there is no relationship with you as a self— neither in the manner of seed and sprout, nor likewise in the sequence of father and son, even though it takes the form of cause and effect.
Even other things would be constructed merely by the convention of mental designation,
such as "I am yours" or "you are mine," based on the internal conviction of two parties;
and there are many others in the world, such as the relationship between container and contained.
In this world, excellent connections arise for those who establish such bonds; yet,
because your self is an atom that transcends the power of mental construction and thought,
no connection at all exists between you and the nature of the sensory faculties.
What kind of connection could there be between you and this terrible cycle of existence that causes suffering,
which has never been seen by us before nor is it seen now?
It is neither a perfectly symmetrical creation nor one that is half-formed.
What kind of relationship could there possibly be with that which lacks any defining characteristic?
O virtuous one, how could the moon, consisting of elixir, ever be joined with the horn of a rabbit’s head, given that it is eternal while the other is indeed non-existent?

O fool, how can there be a permanent unity between existence and non-existence, between the senses and the self, between light and the insentient, or between that which is stained and that which is stainless? Or, if both were indeed non-existent, what kind of conjunction could possibly occur here?
Like a fragment of rock from the mountain of the hare’s head and its horn,
O mind, listen to this certainty as I speak the truth:
no connection exists between you and the Self, even in dreams.
That which is not composed of the Self cannot exist anywhere, because the Self possesses all forms; therefore, O Citta, you do not exist.
This mind is liberated from the objects of thought through the expansion of the web of the world.
The very being of Brahman, consisting of "I," "you," and so forth, dances about.

Though surrounded on all sides by every conceptual construction arising from itself, yet entirely free from them, the all-pervading Lord— whose vision is completely stainless— does not enter into association with you, O one of deceitful form and ruined mind.
The eighty-third canto, titled "Instruction on the Mind," from the Narrative of Vītahavya; [spoken by] Vasiṣṭha.
The highly intelligent Vītahavya, on the slopes of a cave in the Vindhya mountains,
further reflected with a mind as sharp as a razor’s edge upon this:
"In this world, which is complete in its arrangement yet entirely devoid of a collection of sense organs that are not foolish,"...
When all conceptual constructions have been overwhelmed, when all sprouts of existence have been overturned,
and when this total destruction has arisen against you with its full retinue,
surely the Self emerges like the sun from the darkness of a wound.
O Supreme Lord, although You are eternally risen, You do not rise for one whose self is enveloped by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), just as the sun does not rise for one who is blind.
When the impurity of latent impressions is completely stilled, You are destroyed along with Your very root.
Then Brahman, the dense mass of expanded consciousness, becomes manifest.
For bondage consists merely of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); its destruction is called liberation.
Arise through the playful severing of the rope of latent impressions!
When the all-pervading Lord is seen, the series of the senses together with their latent impressions perishes;
just as the perception of blindness vanishes when the sun has risen,
the row of the six senses, with the mind as the sixth, comes to an end upon the attainment of the Self.
And when the strength of the senses is destroyed, the Self is perceived by the self.
Therefore, for the sake of constant well-being, one should practice both;
for the attainment of the Self and mastery over the senses are accomplished only through practice.
The accumulation of qualities seen within the self perishes of its own accord,
like the nocturnal agitation of beings when the sun has risen.
That which perishes upon seeing that [Self] is perishable by virtue of being that [which is seen].
How can that which is insentient by nature enter into a relationship with the sentient?
Just as there can be no union between light and darkness, or between heat and cold,
so too there can be no conjunction between the living and the dead.
Where is he who has transcended all parts, and where is he endowed with all parts?
Where is the eternal one whose nature is pure light, and where is the impermanent one whose form is like darkness?
Where is the eternally subsided form, and where is the eternally risen body of consciousness?
Where is one who is unattached, non-dull, non-mute, and non-blind, and where is the dense mass of consciousness that illumines all?
The conviction that "the Self is joined with the collection of senses" leads only to misfortune,
as long as ignorance alone dances within the minds of the ignorant.

Since it is established that the attachment belongs to the knower of that [Self] and not to the senses, when the collection of organs has reached its dissolution, the world consists of the Supreme Self. By what reasoning does this thick doubt of yours flash forth so foolishly?
"The Self is stained"— thus has that ignorance of hers now perished.
For the fool who, thinking "the Self is joined with deceitful senses," took refuge within [the body], has fallen into a swoon of poison, as if he had swallowed poison himself.
When those suffering from the dullness of their senses, or when pleasures are destroyed,
what has happened to the Self, whose virtuous conduct is undiminished?
Thus, the attachment of the mind, the senses, and the Self is utterly impossible for us.
When the absence of any connection is established, how can there be the states of being an enjoyer or an agent?
Therefore, I am neither an agent nor an enjoyer; there is no liberation, nor is there bondage.
I do not exist, nor does another exist; there is only the stainless Self of pure consciousness.
"I am that very one; you are that very one; the world is that; the sky is that; the earth is that.
Since it is certain that everything is indeed that alone, why do you become deluded?
To fall away from pure consciousness is suffering; do not fall away from consciousness."

By this single meditation, one becomes a constant meditator who perceives the Self. Know that when the internal object— which bestows suffering— whether visible or invisible, is absent, the mind's orientation toward conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*) is a fall from consciousness that brings suffering.
O mind, what kind of agency can there be in insentient objects of perception, such as the body and the senses? How could a forest exist in the sky?
[This occurs] in that which has cast off the mire of mental constructions and whose nature is the destruction of thought.
Furthermore, agency is not possible in the Self, just as it is not in the sky or a limb.
This Self alone, though being one, appears within itself as manifold through various forms;
thus the world is needlessly distressed, like the ocean appearing as waves.
When all this shines forth as mere appearance within this Self that is consciousness,
there is no second conceptualization, just as there is none in a heated coal cast into the ocean.
[This applies] whether in the God who is devoid of conceptualization, or in the body, or in the insentient mind.
Consciousness, when freed from the object of consciousness, is the essence and the beautiful; it is nothing else.
There is no conceptualization such as "this is one thing" and "that is another," or "this is auspicious" or "this is indeed inauspicious," just as there is no forest in the sky.
This entire expanse is nothing but pure consciousness (saṃvinmātra), devoid of any object of cognition;
how, then, can there be the conceptual construction that "this is I" or "this is another" within the beginningless,
formless, all-pervading Self that is spread everywhere?
Who could attribute a name [to it], or who could draw the *Ṛgveda* in the sky? While the Lord—

who is the essence of all things and objects, who stands filling and overflowing the vast quarters of space— abides eternally arisen within the Self, and while the notions of "non-existence" have rightly departed due to its stainlessness, the fragments of pleasure and pain, along with my delusion, have indeed perished.
The eighty-fourth canto in the Vītahavya episode, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Controlling the Senses," by Vasiṣṭha.
Furthermore, the steadfast and excellent sage, having purified his own mind with wisdom, rightly awakened his guarded collection of sense-faculties with these words:
"O collection of my sense-faculties, listen to your own true purpose; I shall speak it most clearly."
Having heard this and attained its true nature, proceed to supreme freedom from suffering.
Your existence as a self is singular and leads only to unavoidable suffering;
therefore, by realizing that the self has no real existence, you should abandon it.
"By my instruction, this existence of yours has clearly come to an end;
for you have arisen from ignorance through me.
O mind, the very manifestation of your own existence leads only to extreme suffering."
The frolicking of creatures in the boiling cauldron leads only to burning on both sides.
Behold, O brother, while you exist, the multitudes of the rivers of worldly existence— turbulent with dull waves— enter the ocean of Time.
Successive waves of suffering fall from somewhere, like torrents of rain in a downpour, as they grapple with one another in a frantic scramble for precedence.
Boundless and quivering, they strive to uproot the very heart.
Causing lamentation, cruel, and a cholera-like plague of existence and non-existence,
the cluster of old age and death— brilliantly white— blooms upon the withered tree of the body, where coughing and labored breathing act as buzzing bees.
In this cave-like hollow of the body, which is entwined by the serpents of turbulent waves,
the whirlpool of anxiety digs its pit with restless claws; there,
the cricket of greed flutters its wings with its sharp beak of dualistic conflict.
From this withered tree of a body, he plucks the lotuses of virtue. The harsh, impure, and arrogant cock of desire scatters the refuse of the heart here and there.
In the great night of delusion, the fierce owl of ignorance flits about the tree of the heart like a Vetāla in a cremation ground;
these and many other such [fears] exist as long as this host of senses remains within you.
Like *piśācas* in the night, those possessing the splendor of inauspiciousness leap about;
but when you are present, O virtuous one, all auspicious splendors fully blossom with light, like lotus plants at dawn.
The sky of the heart shines here, its mist of delusion stilled;
it is free from dust, vast within, and encompassed by stainless light.
It is as unshakeable as a flood of stones fallen into the hollow of the sky.
The floods of conceptual constructions, which cause long-lasting impairment, no longer fall upon one.
The supremely purifying, cooling, and heart-gladdening friendliness arises from the heart,
like a cluster of blossoms from a fine tree.
Thought, which is internally riddled with fissures, possessed of dullness, and its own virtues concealed,
undergoes desiccation like a lotus plant scorched by frost.
Upon the destruction of ignorance, light attains clarity within.
When the cloud has subsided, it is like the orb of the sun in the sky during autumn;
the heart attains equanimity— clear, expansive, profound, unagitated, and unassailable— like an ocean when the wind has been stilled.
The Person dwells within, filled with a flood of nectar and consisting of eternal bliss, like the cool moon;
the entire world of moving and non-moving things rests solely upon a portion of consciousness.

The body is cultivated as full in form and languid with bliss. For those who have no attachments and have severed the snares of hope, there is no returning to birth, just as there is no return for burnt leaves.
By a man who has exhausted the great path of worldly existence, old age, and birth,
one rests for a long time upon the tree of the self so as not to wander again.
Such and other perfections of virtue arise in this manner.
But since you, O all-consuming one, are the destroyer of the momentary existence of all desires,
O mind, between these two sides whose natures are existence and non-existence,
accept at once that very one which you perceive to be the better.
O best among men, I consider the absence of your own self to be your happiness;
cultivate that very absence, for the abandonment of happiness is indeed folly.
If, however, there truly exists within you a consciousness that has been internalized, [then...]
Who would ever desire the absolute non-existence of you while you are still living?
But, O handsome one, I tell you in truth: you do not exist.
Therefore, do not be unhappy by maintaining the conviction that "I am living" when it is entirely false.
In the process of analysis, your existence does not exist at all; even that existence of yours which was due to delusion has now been utterly destroyed by investigation.
O virtuous one, your nature is precisely this: that it cannot withstand analysis.
When properly investigated, you are formless and non-existent;
yet through lack of investigation, you are born like darkness from the absence of light.
Through investigation, you are stilled, just as darkness is dispelled by light.
"O friend, for all this time my lack of discernment has persisted;
by that very fact, it has become excessively swollen, serving as the sole cause of suffering.
Through mere deluded imagination, I have become like a child possessed by a vetāla."
When your extreme conceptualization had perished, you became established in *bhava*;
now that your former form has gone to destruction, you have arisen as the eternal.
Through the grace of discernment, [you have attained this]. Salutations again and again to discernment!
You have become awakened through the ultimate awakening of the mind;
when the state of "mindedness" has perished, you abide as the Supreme Lord. Your former manifestation of essential nature has now attained a state of stability within the highest good.
Now you are Maheśvara, liberated from all latent impressions (vāsanā).
That which arises from a lack of discernment perishes through discernment;
just as darkness born of the absence of light comes to an end through light.
O virtuous one, even though you do not desire it, when this investigation has reached its conclusion,

this destruction— which arrives as a matter of course— is for the sake of the accomplishment of happiness. Therefore, by means of the arguments of our established doctrine, it is determined that the sword does not exist.
O Lord of the senses, may there be well-being for you;
[well-being] has come to you who were previously non-existent, who now have no form of existence, and who will have no future—may there be well-being for you, O self-mind! (MU 5.84.41–42)
I am attaining final liberation; I am at peace; by good fortune, I am free from the fever of suffering.
Abiding in the state of the Fourth (turya), I remain established in my own very self.
Therefore, there is indeed no transmigrating being, nor is there any persistence of the mind.
The Self indeed exists, and it certainly exists because nothing else is found;
yet, I think that the conceptualization "this is the Self" is not pure for one whose inner being is stainless—
for how can there be a conceptualization of a single entity through the exclusion of a counter-correlate?
Not uttering the conceptualization "this is my self" because of that [ignorance], I, as a silent sage, am extinguished within my own self like a wave in water.
With latent impressions stilled, with the portion of consciousness no longer dependent, with the movement of breath ceased, and with the defects of birth and destruction vanished;
Having attained that portion of perfect consciousness which is devoid of the object of perception, I am stilled; this very silence within is free from desire.
The eighty-fifth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Contemplating the Non-existence of the Mind," in the account of Vītahavya.
Vasiṣṭha:
Having thus reached this conclusion, that sage Vītahavya, free from worldly desires,
remained motionless in meditative absorption within a cave of the Vindhya mountains.
Beautiful with the bliss of all vibration having ceased to stir,
his mind set at rest, he became as lovely as a tranquil ocean;
within himself, the succession of his vital breaths gradually subsided.
Like the flickering of a mass of flames when the fuel has been consumed in the fire,
when the external object has reached a state of non-existence within and no longer persists externally,
his two eyes remain with their lashes quivering, as he abides in that which remains.
With his eyes like a very slight gleam reaching the edge of the nose,
he attained an equal beauty with lotuses half-closed in bud; that one of great intelligence maintained the posture with body, head, and neck held straight.
Then,
as he remained thus established for three hundred years,
it seemed to him as if half a muhūrta had passed while he was in the hollow of a valley in the Vindhya mountains— like one carved from stone or like a figure depicted in a painting.
For all that time, it is said, that self-possessed one did not wake;
being liberated while living and absorbed in meditation, he did not abandon that body.
For that duration, that fortunate knower of yoga remained unawakened.
With the unrestrained roars of clouds, gurgling with the weight of torrential rain;
with the cries of the lords of the surrounding regions engaged in the hunt;
with the shouts of bears and monkeys, and the sounds of elephants slapping their trunks.
With the roaring fury of lions, the thundering echoes of waterfalls,
the crashing of fierce thunderbolts, and the dense clamor of elephants;
with the yawns of intoxicated śarabhas and the quaking of the earth as its slopes collide.
By the sounds of forest fires burning and crackling, by the surging and tossing of masses of water,
by the blows from the surfaces of great rocks, by the sinking of the earth's surface,
by the falling surges of water and the heat as harsh as fire— *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* 5.85.12–13.
When the rainy season had passed and the time for its conclusion had arrived, he moved at his own will through that mountain cave in a very short time, like waves upon the water.
He was cast upon the surface of the earth by the torrential flood of the rainy season;
there he dwelt within a narrow cavity of the ground,
his shoulders buried in mud like a stone deep within a mountain.
When three hundred years had passed, the Lord himself,
whose nature is the Self, awoke while being pressed against the hollow of the earth;
his consciousness alone took hold of that body which was crushed by the ground.
But the vibration consisting of vital breath does not occur without the movement of the breath. Having arisen and attained maturity as a mental construction in the sky of the heart,
that [vibration], taking the form of his own mind, was experienced by him right within his heart.
In the lovely Kailāsa forest, at the foot of a *kadamba* tree,
he remained for a hundred years in the state of a sage, his stainless self liberated while living;
then for a hundred years he held the status of a *vidyādhara*, free from all mental afflictions.
The five-fold group [of senses], Indra, and those bowed down by celestial beings and *cāraṇas*—
Rāma said:
"O Sage, regarding these manifestations of his such as sagehood and the rest..."
"How can there be restriction and non-restriction regarding the constraints of space and time?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"This power of consciousness, which is the self of all, arises in whatever manner and wherever it may be."
In that very way, it quickly comes to be through its identity with that single nature.
Whenever, wherever, and however the Buddha is perceived, that restriction remains established as such,
because the sequences of restrictions regarding place, time, and so forth, are of that same essence.

Thus, having seen various worlds within the space of consciousness in his heart, Vītahavya was free from latent impressions (*vāsana*). For those possessing perfect awakening, this very *vāsana* is not truly a *vāsana*.
For one burnt by the fire of knowledge, what seed-nature can remain in that which is already burnt?
For a single kalpa, he served as an attendant to the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva),
who possesses pure vision regarding the three periods of time and is the master of all sciences.
Whatever kind of firm mental impression one possesses, that is what one perceives;
Vītahavya experienced this very state through the condition of liberation while living.
Rāma said:
"O best of sages, this being so, even for one whose mind is liberated while living,
there exist perceptions of bondage and liberation, just as they did in the case of Vītahavya.
Vasiṣṭha said:
This entire universe, as it exists, is peaceful and as pure as space;
for those liberated while living, it is Brahman alone—whence could there be any perception of bondage or liberation?
Thus, the sky of consciousness shines in whatever manner and wherever it may be.

In each respective place, in that manner, and to that extent, he finds that which is spread out. By means of his own nature as Brahman, O Rāghava, he experiences many worlds already experienced and indeed those yet to be experienced, through his identity with all things.
In those innumerable worlds, where the great-souled ones are formless and their conscious selves have vanished into the hollows of the earth,
he who was Śakra, having failed to realize the Self, is today a king among the Cīnas.
At this very moment,
he who was a swan dwelling in the lotus of Brahmā with an unawakened self has now become this lord of fishermen in a bower of the Kailāsa forest, intent on hunting in the Nīpa grove.
"That king who, unaware of his own self, was on the ground in the region of Saurāṣṭra—
he is indeed this very tree with its vast branches standing here in the village of the Andhras.
Rāma said:
"It is said that this creation of Vītahavya was purely mental; how then, O Vasiṣṭha, can you say that those embodied beings therein were merely an illusion and not the makers of their own bodies?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
If that world of Vītahavya consists solely of a single delusion,
then what is the nature of this which appears? My dear friend,
this [world] is merely consciousness, merely mind, and consists of delusion.
In reality, however, that is not the world, nor is this [world] anything other than that;
yet it is not the case that the existence of the world does not exist— for this Brahman alone shines forth as the past,
the present, and the future, as this and likewise as that.

This entire visible world is composed of the mind, which is pure consciousness alone. As long as this world is not fully understood to be of such a nature, it remains a firm and adamantine reality; yet, when truly known, it becomes the supreme ether.
For the ignorant, this very mind expands in such a manner through the play of its own surging manifestations, like water in the ocean.
By the sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) as it truly is, it is designated as "mind" (*manas*) solely because of its own nature as consciousness.
By him the visible world was expanded; thus it is both pervaded and yet not pervaded by anything at all. The eighty-sixth canto, titled "The Description of the World of Vītahavya’s Mind."
Rāma:
What then? Was Vītahavya staying in that interior of the forest? How did he extract his body, and how did he become perfected?
Vasiṣṭha: Immediately thereafter, the mind named Vītahavya, whose nature is infinite,
thus realized its own self-manifestation as the Self.
Once, when this entire assembly had spontaneously attained the recollection of their former births,
a desire arose in them all to behold their previous lives in their entirety. Then they beheld all their own bodies, each one having perished again and again.
Then, from among those who had not perished, it occurred to him to extract by chance that body of his which was situated within a cavity in the earth—
the body known as Vītahavya, which had been oppressed within that earthen hollow.

Seeing the mass of mud brought by the monsoon flood resting upon his own back, as well as the earth on the surface of his body covered with a network of grass, the one of great splendor, constrained within the cavity of the earth, [reflected].
Once again, he reflected with his intellect through supreme awakening:
"Because all my limbs are bound together, my body, though overcome by the vital breaths, is as mute as it is; it cannot move even in the slightest degree."
Therefore, having gone there, I shall quickly enter this body of Vivasvat;
thereafter, his attendant Piṅgala will extract my body from it.
Or rather, what need have I for him? I shall attain peace without any obstacle.
"I shall enter nirvāṇa; I go to my own state. What purpose is there for me in the play of the body?
Having reflected thus in his mind, O high-minded one, Vītahavya remained silent for a moment and then further reflected upon the ground.
For I have no preference for either the abandonment or the maintenance of this body;
as is the relinquishing of the body, so too is its preservation.
Therefore, as long as this body remains and has not yet reached dissolution into the subtle state, [I shall remain].
Having mounted him for that long, I shall move about a little; then,
in order to lift my own body, I shall enter my tawny, glowing form situated in the sky like a reflection in a mirror.
Thus that sage, assuming the form of the wind, entered the sun,
having become an eightfold city-body like fire entering a mass of fuel;
and the blessed Sun likewise [perceived] this leader of sages who had entered his heart.
Having seen it, that noble-minded one reflected upon the sequence of events;
he beheld the supreme body of the sage in a cave-region of the Vindhya mountains, covered with grass and stones, devoid of consciousness.
Knowing the sage’s intention, Bhānu, situated in the midst of the sky,
commanded his foremost host to lift the muni from the earth;
that consciousness of the sage Vītahavya took the form of the *puryaṣṭaka*.
Having quickly honored Ravi with a mind full of devotion, she prostrated before the venerable one;
then, permitted by the Lord of Light, she entered with due respect the golden-hued leader who was traveling toward a cave in the Vindhya mountains.
Leaving the sky, which was as beautiful as a forest grove with its elephants, that Piṅgala reached the Vindhya forest, radiant with clouds intoxicated by the rainy season like a garment;
he uprooted the treasures of the earth, having torn away the mountains with his claws.
Like a crane extracting a lotus stalk from the mud, [he drew out] the sage’s body.
Then, he entered his own subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) with silence,
like a bird exhausted from wandering across the sky returning to its nest.
Having quickly bowed to one another, Vītahavya and the sky-dweller,
those two storehouses of splendor, became intent solely upon their respective tasks;
Piṅgala went through the air, and the sage went to the pure lake.
Having the appearance of a star and the form of a blooming night-lily, Vītahavya quickly sank into the lake— which resembled the rays of the sun—
as a young elephant sinks into a lotus-filled pool at the edge of a forest.
Having bathed there, performed his recitations, and worshipped the Sun,
he shone forth once more as before with a body adorned by asceticism—
through that friendliness, equanimity, supreme peace, true wisdom, joy, compassion, and glory.
The sage, his mind liberated from all attachments, remained intent on his practice; having gone to the bank of a river in the Vindhya mountains, he took delight there for the entire day.
This concludes the eighty-seventh canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Samādhi by Vītahavya."
Vasiṣṭha: At the end of the day, that sage entered once again a certain vast and solitary cave in the Vindhya mountains in order to compose his mind.
Having seen the higher and lower worlds, he spoke with his mind while maintaining that very same continuity, remaining equanimous toward the senses:
"Previously, the group of my senses was clearly withdrawn by me."
Now there is no purpose for me in further extensive reflection.
Having severed the conceptualization of "it exists" or "it does not exist," like a tender creeper,
I remain established in my residual state, as immovable as a mountain peak.
Like the risen [sun] having set, and like the set [sun] having risen;
equal, appearing as the flavor of equanimity, I remain, having attained self-abidingness.
Though awakened, I abide in deep sleep; abiding in deep sleep, I am awakened.
Taking hold of the fourth state (*turya*), I remain until the end of my task, standing in a state of total stillness.

Steadfast like a tree trunk in a secluded spot, I abide within the limit of my own mind as it stands everywhere; indeed, free from all affliction, I remain in the equilibrium of the universal nature of pure being (*sattva-sāmānya*).
Having reflected thus, he remained in meditation for six more days;
then he attained awakening, like a traveler who has slept for a moment.
Thus perfected was the Blessed One Vītahavya, the great ascetic.
He lived for a long time in that state of liberation while alive;
he never took delight in anything, nor did he ever feel revulsion.
Likewise, he experienced neither agitation nor joy.
Whether walking or standing still, this discourse arose in his heart with his own mind for the sake of diverting his thoughts:
"O you who possess a tranquil mind, you who are the master of the group of imperishable senses..."
Behold, Ānanda, what kind of pervasive bliss has been attained!
Therefore, O best among the fickle, you must constantly maintain this very state free from passion and abandon all restlessness.
O you thieves of the senses! O you whose hopes are destroyed and whose names are ruined!
This self does not belong to you, nor do you exist within the self.
Depart quickly toward your own destruction; your hopes have been rendered fruitless.
"You, whose bases are fragile, are not capable of attacking [me].
This latent impression (vāsanā) of yours that 'we are the self' has indeed arisen from the forgetting of reality, like the perception of a snake in a rope that has been seen."
This notion of selfhood in what is not-self, this notion of reality in what is unreal, arose here through a lack of inquiry; through inquiry, it has come to an end.
You are one thing, we are another, Brahman is another, and agency is yet another.
The enjoyer is one thing and that which is consumed is another; what fault is there, and for whom, and of what kind?
Wood is produced from forests, as are ropes, bamboo, and hides, as well as axes with iron blades; in this way, the carpenter is intent upon his meal.

Thus, just as here in this world a chariot in the form of a wretched house is produced by chance (*kākatālīya*) through a collection of factors whose constituent parts possess their own inherent powers,
so too [the body] is produced by chance with its sense organs fixed in their respective capacities.
In the same way, this body is indeed [illusory]; what destruction can there be here for whom? (MU 5.87.21) Forgetfulness has been forgotten far away, and mindfulness has clearly been recollected.
What exists has arisen; what does not exist is non-existent; what is perishable has perished; and what is stable remains. (MU 5.87.22)
In this manner, that tiger among sages, the Blessed One of great asceticism, remained here for many groups of years through such contemplation,
until his concern reached its end for the sake of no further rebirth.
Delusion remained far removed from him, and he dwelt there forever;
relying upon the infinite consolation of meditative absorption arising from the vision of the multitude of things as they truly are, that man dwelt there eternally.
When the perceptions of attachment to what is to be abandoned and acquisition of what is to be taken up, as well as their respective relinquishment and grasping,
had ceased, that Blessed One, the son of Agastya, Vītahavya, free from all latent impressions, dwelt in that state which is the supreme, perfect Self and the source of inner peace.
Listen to how he attained the state of disembodied liberation (videhamuktatā) over time:
having dwelt here in this holy hermitage for thirty thousand seven hundred years, and likewise on Meru, the abode of the gods.
The sage Vītahavya, whose mind was free from desire and aversion,
attained the state of absolute liberation (*kevalībhāva*) at the border of Videha— the end of the cycle of birth and action—
through his supreme longing for the nectar-like flavor of renouncing attachment to worldly existence.

He entered a golden cave of the Vindhya mountains in solitude with her; beholding the web of the world as something from which there would be no further return, he sat there in the lotus posture and spoke within himself to his own self.
O passion, go to passionlessness; O hatred, proceed to freedom from hatred.
For a very long time, I have played here with you both.
O enjoyments, salutations to you; for hundreds of millions of births, I [have been bound by you].
He was cherished by you in this world like a child by those who fondle him.
Homage again and again to that bliss which caused me to forget even this supreme and meritorious path to Nirvāṇa.
"O Suffering, my self was earnestly sought by me when it was scorched by you;
therefore, this path has been pointed out to me by you—homage be to you!
By your grace, this cool state has been attained by me."
"O you who are suffering by the very name of 'suffering,' yet whose nature is bliss—homage be to you!
May it be well with you, O friend; from this life which is the pithless essence of *saṃsāra*, we shall depart from this bodily existence to our own abode."
Alas, how truly miserable is the fate of dull-witted creatures!
Even after having undergone hundreds of births, I shall be separated from my very body.
O friend, O body, you who have been my long-standing kinsman, you are not being abandoned by me.

By you alone has this destruction been brought upon yourself through the power of [misconceived] knowledge of the self. Having attained the realization of the Self, you have brought about your own ruin;
you are not broken by another in the body, for this was cultivated by you alone.
"O Mother Tṛṣṇā, you who have withered away alone and in distress while I was at peace, you must not cause me further suffering; I am departing.
O Lord Kāma, you must forgive those offenses born of my perversity and transgressions."
"O Faults, I am going to the absolute state of peace; give me leave, enough!
O Mother Thirst, after a very long time, this separation of us two has now occurred through the fault of *yoga*; this is our final salutation."

Homage be to you, who are to be served by those of well-performed deeds; by you, in the past, I was drawn out from the hells and established in heaven. To you, who have grown in the field of evil actions and who carry the trunk of hell—
Homage to the one who bears the weight of flowers that are the teachings, yet possesses branches of evil deeds!
Homage to you, that Delusion, with whom many evil births were long enjoyed together, but who from this day forth remains invisible!
Salutations to you, who possess a voice as sweet as a resounding flute, who are clothed in leaves,
and who are a companion in meditative absorptions for those practicing austerities in the caves;
you are the cause of consolation for one weary on the path of saṃsāra.

You were my affectionate companion, the remover of all sorrow. Distressed by every calamity and fleeing from my faults, I have relied upon you alone as my supreme friend for the sake of destroying my grief.
Salutations to you, the staff of wood, the sole friend in old age!
O body, depart, taking with you nothing more than this essence: your own skeleton and the threads of blood and entrails.
Salutations again and again to the various forms of bathing that agitate the milk-ocean;
salutations be to worldly transactions, and salutations be to you, the cycles of transmigration!
You here are my innate and former friends.
"Gradually my vital breaths have been extinguished; may it be well with you, I am departing.
Together with you, I have rested in many diverse wombs and wandered through mountain thickets and other worlds."
I have played within the city-pavilions, dwelt upon the mountains,
remained amidst the delights of worldly affairs, and set out upon various paths;
there is nothing in the treasury of the world that I have not experienced together with you.
Nothing was done, nothing taken, nothing consumed, nothing given, and nothing grasped.
Now, my dear ones, go each to your own direction;
I am departing, for all unions on the path of saṃsāra end in separation.
May this visual light enter the solar orb;
may the perceptions of the joy of fragrance enter the forest flowers;
and likewise, may the vital breaths and their tactile sensations enter the wind today.
May the series of sounds that reach the ears enter the hollow of space;
may the mind, its form withered, dissolve into the moon like clarified butter poured into fire;
and may all things such as pleasure and pain return to their own original state.
May craving, along with its impulses, wither away like a lotus pond in winter;
like a blazing fire whose fuel is consumed, like a lamp devoid of oil,
like an ocean without Mount Mandara, or like a day when the sun has set.
Like an autumn cloud at the end of a kalpa of creation, I come to rest of my own accord;
at the conclusion of the syllable Om, I am extinguished within the self by the self.
