With the entire succession of activities vanished, I abide in a state that transcends all conditions of the perceptible world.

With a mind pacified by following the peace of the *praṇava*, I remain here, free from the stain of delusion. The eighty-eighth canto, titled "The Instruction on Yoga for the Rejection of the Aggregate of the Senses."
Vasiṣṭha:
Thus he reflected within himself, with his thoughts and desires stilled;
slowly pronouncing the beautiful syllable Om, he reached the ground of its attainment.
Having abandoned all volitions— whether external or internal, subtle or even gross— conceived within the three worlds and fashioned by the imagination,
he remains with an unshaken form within himself like a wish-fulfilling gem.
He was like the full moon, like Mount Mandara at rest;
he was like a potter’s wheel brought to a halt from its spinning,
and like the ocean at its full tide— stilled, vast, and pure.
It is a mass of tranquil splendor and darkness, devoid of sun, moon, and stars;
clear, infinite, and free from smoke, clouds, and dust, like the autumnal sky,
together with the long-echoing thread of sound culminating in the *praṇava*.
Just as the wind leaves behind a mass of sensory elements and subtle essences like a scent,
so then did he abandon the state of pure darkness (tamas),
which had appeared within him like a flickering form rising up, just as a wise man casts off a trace of anger.
Then, having reflected for half a moment, that splendor which had appeared vanished;
and at that time, there was neither darkness nor light.
Having reached that state, he [perceived] that mind with his mind to be like a blade of grass.
In less than half a blink of an eye, he caused even that slight vibration to cease.
Then, his bodily consciousness became established in its natural state,
having attained a manifestation equal to the cognition of a newborn infant— unconditioned and pure.

In a time less than half of a half-moment, the Lord, who is beyond all calculation, abandoned the state of being an object of consciousness within consciousness, just as the wind abandons its power of motion. Then, having reached the stage of *paśyantī*, which consists of pure existence alone, he remained there.
Having reached the state of deep sleep, he stood as immovable as Mount Meru.
Then, having remained for a moment established in the station of deep sleep,
the Lord attained stability within that sleep and entered the form of the Fourth State (turya).
There he was both joyless and joyful, both existent and non-existent;
he was both nothing and something, as well as light and darkness.
He is that which is not composed of consciousness and yet is composed of consciousness, that which is described as "not this, not this."
Then that [state] came into being, which is beyond even the range of my words.
That most beautiful place, the supremely purifying state,
became the inner essence of all things, yet devoid of everything.
That which is the Void for the proponents of emptiness, the Supreme Brahman for the foremost knowers of Brahman,
mere consciousness for the knowers of consciousness, and that which is of pure nature;
[that is] the Puruṣa for those of the Sāṅkhya view, and the Lord (Īśvara) for the proponents of Yoga.
Śiva is the goal for those who mark time by the phases of the moon; Time is the goal for those who proclaim Time as the ultimate;
the Self is the goal for those who know the Self; desirelessness is the goal for those whose nature is such;
and the Middle Way is the goal for the Mādhyamikas whose minds are perfectly tranquil.
That which is the established conclusion of all scriptures, that which conforms to the heart of all,
that which is everything, always, and for everyone— that which is real, he remains as that reality.
He is the unsurpassed outflow, the lamp even of lights.
That which has self-experience as its sole measure— whatever that may be— that is where he abides.
That which is both one and many, both with taint and without taint,
both all and not-all— whatever that may be— that is where he abides.

Then, in an instant, that Lord— whose state is even more stainless than the nature of the sky— remained as the unborn, undecaying, beginningless, primordial, single state, both with parts and without parts, and partless.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Nirvāṇa for Vītahavya."
The eighty-ninth canto:
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reached the very limit of worldly existence, he has come to the further shore of the ocean of suffering.
Thus Vītahavya became a sage who had stilled his mind and was free from further mental activity.
For when he had thus become tranquil and attained supreme bliss,
he remained in his own transformative state, like a drop of water in the ocean.
Remaining thus motionless, that body fell into a state of withering;
having reached an inner state of saplessness, it became like a leaf at the end of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Having abandoned the nest of the heart situated within the tree of his body, [the vital breaths] departed.
Having flown into the sky like a stone released from a machine, the bird of the vital breath departed;
all the elements completely entered back into the elements themselves,
while the body— a mere machine of flesh and bone— remained upon the surface of the earth and forests.
Consciousness has entered the ocean of consciousness; the elements abide within the elements;
everything remains in its own true nature when the sage has attained tranquility.
This, O Rāma, has been told to you, which is enriched by hundreds of investigations.
"Find rest through the wisdom of Vītahavya;
discern this by means of such reasoning, kindled by your own inquiry. Having perceived the reality and its essence through such logic, arise and abide in it, O Rāghava. (MU 5.89.7–8)
O Rāma, all this that has been described by me to you,
as well as what I am now describing, and whatever else I shall describe in the future,
was indeed seen by one who perceives the three periods of time and who lives eternally for a long duration.
All of that has been investigated and seen by me myself.
Therefore, O high-minded one, relying upon this stainless vision, attain supreme knowledge; for liberation is obtained through knowledge.
From knowledge arises freedom from suffering; from knowledge comes the destruction of ignorance.
From knowledge alone, O Rāma, comes supreme perfection, and not from anything else in reality.
Having completely severed all bonds on every side through knowledge, [one attains liberation].
The lord of sages, Vītahavya, had leveled all the mountains of his mind;
his consciousness, which was Vītahavya himself, was the world of volitions,
and he experienced this very universe as that world.
Vītahavya said: "The mind alone is everything; I am the mind, you are the mind, and these mountains are the mind.
This entire world is the mind; what room is there here for difference or non-difference?

One who has realized the supreme truth, whose defects such as passion have been exhausted, and who has transcended all impurities and transformations by destroying the limiting adjuncts (upādhi), [is liberated]."
Having long followed his own nature as pursued by others, the discerning one attained the stainless, infinite state, with his sorrow stilled.
Thus ends the ninety-first canto, titled "The Resting of Vītahavya."
Vasiṣṭha: Like Vītahavya, having realized that which is to be known and thus led yourself [to that state],
remain engaged in actions, O Rāghava, free from passion, fear, and hatred.
For thirty thousand years Vītahavya dwelt like a sage, free from sorrow; in that same manner, O Rāghava, do you dwell. Other royal sages, of great intelligence, have known what is to be known.

O high-minded one, dwell as you do in your own kingdoms; likewise, dwell [here]. The Self is never grasped through the sequences of pleasure and pain, even though it is all-pervading, O mighty-armed one; why do you grieve in vain?
Many who have realized the self dwell here upon this earth;
none have fallen under the power of suffering like you, my dear friend.
Be at ease, be noble toward existence, be equanimous, and be happy.

You are all-pervading; you are the Self itself, and for you there is no rebirth. Like lions among trees, those such as you who are liberated while living do not fall under the sway of any fluctuations caused by joy or resentment.
Rāma:
By this very occasion, this doubt has arisen within me;
may you dispel it for me, as the autumn season does a cloud.
"O best among the knowers of the Self, why are powers such as traveling through the sky not seen here in the bodies of those liberated while living? Vasiṣṭha replied:
O scion of the Raghus, these acts such as traveling through the sky and so forth are indeed the innate powers of those objects;
for it is this manifold web of actions that is displayed and then concealed again.
O Rāma, this is the inherent nature of things; it is not the view of those who know the Self.

O Rāghava, even one who does not know the Self and is not liberated certainly attains such powers as traveling through the sky by virtue of the potency of substances, actions, rituals, time, and power.
This is not the domain of one who knows the Self, for the knower of the Self is himself possessed of the Self;
satisfied by the Self through the Self, he does not pursue ignorance.
Whatever worldly states there may be, they know them to be created by ignorance.
How indeed could one who knows the Self, having abandoned ignorance, sink into those [states]?
For those who, by means of reasoning, establish even ignorance as being of the nature of happiness—they are indeed products of ignorance; they are not knowers of the Self following such a sequence.
Whether one knows the truth or does not know the truth, for him who exerts himself in due order through time, substances, and actions, the status of Indra and other such states is accomplished.
But he here who knows the Self transcends everything and is free from all desire.
For one who is satisfied in the Self alone neither acts nor desires;
he has no need for travel through the sky, nor for supernatural powers, nor for enjoyments, nor for majesty, nor for honors, nor for hope, death, or life.
Ever-satisfied, with a tranquil self, free from passion and devoid of latent impressions,
the knower of that reality abides in the Self, possessing a form like space,
unaffected by unexpected pain or pleasure.
Free from attachment, he is satisfied with both life and death;
honoring the Self, he remains equanimous toward both the even and the uneven, like the ocean receiving the waters of rivers as they arrive in their course.
He has no purpose whatsoever here through action, nor any at all through non-action;
nor does he have any dependence on any being for any object of desire.
Yet, even one whose self is thus purified might still long for the nets of supernatural powers.
He accomplishes those [goals] in sequence by means of substances that effect success (*siddhi*).
"This succeeds in this way through logic alone"— this is the sequence of necessity (*niyati*),
which cannot be rendered futile even by the best of gods, such as the Three-Eyed One (Śiva).
This is the very nature of things, established by itself and not from another;
it never abandons its fixed character, just as the moon does not abandon its coolness.
Even if he were omniscient, or capable, or even Mādhava or Hara himself, [he could not alter this].
For indeed, no one at all is able to alter destiny.
O Rāma, those powers— such as traveling through the sky and so forth— are born from the inherent natures of substances, time, actions, and the application of mantras.
Just as poisons kill, honey intoxicates,
and the fruits of the *madana* tree cause vomiting when eaten,
so too do substances, time, and the sequence of actions [produce their effects] by virtue of their inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
Those born from the application of reason quickly and certainly accomplish the practice.
Therefore, O Rāghava, for one who has transcended this and is joined with reason,
there is neither agency nor non-agency in self-knowledge.
Substances, mantras, rituals, timing, and logical methods grant success to the virtuous;
yet none of these assist at all in attaining the state of the Supreme Self.
Only he who possesses some desire can effectively achieve success.
Because the knowledge of the Self is complete, no desire can arise anywhere.
For the attainment of the Self occurs when the entire web of desires has been stilled; O sinless one, how could a desire, which is opposed to that state, ever be born from it?
Whoever has a desire arises and exerts himself accordingly;
thus he attains that [result] in due time, whether he be wise or even ignorant.
Nothing whatsoever was accomplished by Vītahavya when he lacked the desire for it.
As soon as the desire arose, he strove and rose up like a tree from the forest.
In this way, the various powers (siddhis) born of time, action, substances, ritual application, and inherent nature,
which have been acquired through successive stages, are accomplished exactly according to one's wish.
O Rāma, those successions of fruits called "accomplishments" (siddhi), which were obtained by him, were acquired by him from the tree of his own diligent effort—
for those great ones who are eternally satisfied, who possess that knowledge, and whose selves are purified.
"For those who have reached the end of their desires, supernatural powers (siddhis) do not provide any further assistance.
Rāma said: "O Brahmin, this is my doubt: was that body of Vītahavya [the same as his current one]?"

Why was he not devoured by flesh-eating beasts, and why did he not rot upon the ground? O Lord, tell me truly how it was that Vītahavya attained the state of disembodied liberation (videhamukti) so swiftly at that very moment.
Vasiṣṭha:
O virtuous one, that consciousness which is enveloped by the thread of the impurity of latent impressions becomes here a partaker in the burning of the states of pleasure and pain.
But that body which remains, consisting solely of pure consciousness and freed from latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
no one here is indeed capable of cutting it; hear the reasoning by which the body of a yogi cannot be harmed by such delusions as cutting and the like.
It cannot be overcome, O mighty-armed one, even by many hundreds of years. Whenever and upon whatever object the mind falls,
it quickly becomes absorbed in that very thing at that very moment.
For the mind undergoes transformation upon seeing an enemy,
and spontaneously attains a state of affection upon seeing a friend.
But toward a traveler, a tree, or a mountain that are devoid of passion or hatred, [the mind remains indifferent].
It is experienced by itself that it becomes free from passion and aversion;
it takes up greed for what is savory, yet feels no desire for bad food, and it experiences a sense of distaste for what is pungent—all this is experienced by itself. (MU 5.90.46–47)
Whenever and wherever in the body of a yogi— which is enriched by the play of equanimous consciousness—
the violent mind falls upon anything, it immediately attains equanimity. Being equanimous, because it is liberated from the sense of real existence, it does not engage in cutting or other such acts.
Just as a traveler on the road [is drawn] into the useless village-work of the villagers,
so too, by approaching the body of a yogin, one indeed incurs a state of violence;
whatever occurs there, one quickly becomes of that very nature— of this there is no doubt.
Thus, although there were predatory beasts— tigers, lions, insects, and reptiles—
the body of Vītahavya, lying upon the surface of the earth, was not torn apart. Consciousness is found everywhere, even in wood, clods of earth, stones, and the like.
Established in the form of the universal existence (sattāsāmānya), like a child or a mute,
it is perceived merely as flickering and wavering;
subtle, it appears as a reflection within the eightfold cities (puryaṣṭaka) alone, like [reflections] in waters.
Because of that equal perception of earth, water, air, and fire, O Rāghava, the body of Vītahavya was not subjected to transformation.
Listen to something else, O Rāma: vibration is the cause of destruction.
In the maintenance of the world, a transformation arises either from the mind or from wind;
the vitality of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) exists through their vibration, and when that ceases, they become like stones.
Since [the yogi] remains established through *dhāraṇā*, his body is not destroyed.
Whether internal or external, the vibration of the mind arises from the vital breath;
for one in whom this does not exist, both transformation and decay remain far away.
O best among the knowers of reality, when vibration has subsided both within and without, [the state of peace is attained].
The elements never abandon their established state within the body.
When the vibration of the mind and the vital breath, which reside in the house of the body, has become completely stilled,
the elements attain a stability like that of Mount Meru, their nature becoming rigidly fixed.
And so it is observed in the world that when vibration ceases, there is a firm stability, such as the lack of movement in all the limbs of logs; likewise,
for the wise yogins, their bodies remain in the world for thousands of years.

They did not rot nor did they break apart, like fragments of indestructible diamond. At that very moment, listen, why did that Vītahavya, who was a knower of reality and supreme through his realization of what is to be known, not attain peace after casting off his body?
For those who have understood what is to be known, who are free from passion, and possess great intelligence— all of them, having severed their bonds, remain independent while abiding in the body.
Or likewise, [they transcend] actions, whether belonging to the past or to this life.
Or rather, their latent impressions (vāsanās) do not sufficiently restrain that mind.
Therefore, O dear one, for those who know reality, the mind— like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit—
quickly and effectively brings about whatever it contemplates.
By a chance occurrence, through his meeting with Vītahavya,
his life was now recognized and immediately made stable;
for when his intuition had turned toward the disembodied state, [he realized this].
Then he became liberated while in the body (videhamukta), established in absolute sovereignty.
His mind, freed from latent impressions (vāsanā) and swiftly attained a state of being unshackled, arose as the Self;
whatever it desires comes to be in an instant, for the Great Lord consists of all powers.
The ninety-first canto, titled "The Instruction on the Contemplation of Attaining Siddhi," [Vasiṣṭha said:]
For when the mind has become almost entirely subsided through investigation,
then the qualities such as loving-kindness arose in this Vītahavya.
[Rāma:]

"O Sage, you said that when the nature of the mind has vanished due to the arising of discernment (*viveka*), qualities such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) have arisen. But, O Lord, O Brahmin, once the mind has set, to whom do qualities such as loving-kindness belong?"
"Or where do they manifest? Tell me, O best among speakers.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"The dissolution of the mind is of two kinds: with form and indeed without form."
One who is liberated while living possesses form; one who is liberated from the body is formless.
Here, the existence of the mind leads to suffering, while the destruction of the mind leads to happiness;
therefore, having brought the existence of the mind to its end, one should achieve the destruction of the mind.
Know that the mind which is pervaded by the web of tamasic latent impressions (vāsanā) and which is the cause of birth, exists solely for the sake of suffering;
it highly esteems the collection of material qualities (guṇa), thinking "this is mine."
But that mind which does not know reality and is subject to suffering is called the individual soul (*jīva*).
As long as the mind exists, so long is there endless suffering;
when the mind has set for a living being, *saṃsāra* has reached its end.
Know that the mind which exists as suffering, deluded, and constrained by the very determination "I am," is the fresh sprout of the tree of suffering. Rāma said:
O Brahmin, whose mind is destroyed, or what would that destruction be like?
What would its destruction be like, and what would its state of being (sattā) be? Vasiṣṭha replied:
O scion of Raghu’s lineage, I have described the existence of the mind;
now, O best among those who know how to inquire, hear from me concerning its destruction.
That which neither the states of pleasure nor the states of pain can dislodge from its equanimity—[that is the steadfast one].
They know his mind to be dead when it does not follow the lord of mountains like exhalations;
they know his mind to be dead when the thought "I am he" or "I am not he" does not diminish that best of men within.
O virtuous one, this is the destruction of the mind; if such a mind has perished, know that this state of the destruction of the *citta* belongs to the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
O sinless one, understand that state of delusion to be "mind-ness" (*manastā*), when it perishes.

For at that time, the state called the destruction of the mind arises fully as pure being (*sattva*). O Rāghava, some have given the name "mind-ness" (*cittva*) to that play of being— the destruction of the mind— which is the very nature of one liberated while living.

O sinless one, the mind endowed with qualities such as loving-kindness becomes possessed of the highest latent impression (*vāsanā*); it is liberated from further birth and is *jīvanmukta*. That which is pervaded by a latent impression that is free from further rebirth—
O Rāma, that mind which is unattached while living is called *sattva*.
Because it has been experienced right now, one who has attained *sattva* is united with reality (*tattva*).
This dissolution of the mind, which possesses its own form, exists for the one liberated while living.
Loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy— like the radiance of the moon—
reside in every way and at all times within the destruction of the mind of one liberated while living,
which is like the Himalayan mountain named Sattva.
The riches of one's virtues blossom like clusters of blossoms in spring.
But that dissolution of the mind which I have described, O scion of Raghu,
exists only in liberation while in the body (videhamukti), being of an indivisible nature.
Even a being endowed with all the foremost virtues dissolves into that stainless, supremely purifying state of disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*),
which consists in the dissolution of the *sattva* within that domain of disembodied liberation.
In that state called Virūpākṣa, where the mind has perished, nothing at all exists:
there are neither qualities nor the absence of qualities; there is neither prosperity nor adversity, nor restlessness; there is neither rising nor setting, nor the perceptions of joy and resentment.
There is neither light nor darkness, nor anything at all; there are no twilights, days, or nights; there are not the ten directions, nor space, nor the nature of benefit, nor the nature of harm;
there is no latent impression, no construction, no desire, no lack of desire, and no passion.
That state is neither being nor non-being, nor even a middle between them;
it is like the sky when it is free from darkness by light, devoid of clouds, the moon,
the sun, or rain, clear as autumn, free from the twilight, and radiant without dust.
For those who have reached the further shore of both wisdom and the tumultuous display of saṃsāra,
that vast abode is like the sky for the winds;
it is where suffering is stilled, which is non-inert by nature, where all are in a singular sleep, slow with bliss, and where the sun has dispelled the darkness of *rajas* and *tamas*.
In that state dwell those who are vast, whose bodies are the expanse of space yet are formless, and in whom every fragment of the mind has dissolved.
This concludes the ninety-second canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Examining the Mind."
Rāma:
[I behold] the tree of another world, grown upon the mountain of the supreme etherial vault,
variegated with stars for its flowers and with gods and asuras for its birds.
Its blue clouds, with their edges garlanded by flashes of lightning, form its sprouts;
its shores glisten, delightful in every season and beautiful with the multitude of the moon and sun.
It is encircled by the ponds of the seven oceans and filled with hundreds of rivers.

O Brahman, this world-forest is inhabited by fourteen kinds of infinite beings; it stands with its net cast out, having been entered by the sprawling vine of worldly existence, which is as tender as a grape.
Of this row of fruits consisting of the suffering of suffering through the stages of old age and death—
a row whose roots have grown deep, watered by the libations of the moisture of delusion—
what is the seed? And what is said to be the seed of that seed?
Now, what is the seed of that [intellect], and what might be the seed of that as well?
O best among speakers, tell me all this in brief once more, for the increase of awakening and for the attainment of the essence of knowledge.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, know the body to be the seed of the creeper of worldly existence, wherein the great sprouts of good and evil are contained within as a dense internal potential.
Thick with the spreading of its branches and radiant with fruits and shoots,
by him this earth becomes flourishing like the earth in autumn;
[he is] the treasury of the states of existence and non-existence, a casket for the jewels of suffering.

The mind, following the dictates of desire, is the seed of this body. From the mind arises this entire web of limbs, both real and unreal; likewise, it is experienced by itself in the delusions of dreams.
Just as a city arises from the conceptualization of a gandharva, so too does a body— resplendent in form and complete with windows— arise from the mind.
Whatever expansive worldly object exists that has come within the range of vision, [it is likewise a mental construction].
That form is an expansion of the mind, just as the state of being a jar and so forth belongs to clay.
There are two seeds for the tree of the mind, which bears the creepers of its functions:
one is the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the second is firm conceptualization (*bhāvanā*).
When the vital breath vibrates, intent upon touching the channels,
then the mind consisting of pure consciousness quickly arises.
When the vital breath does not vibrate within the hollows of the pathways of the vessels, [the mind likewise ceases].
Due to the power of non-perception, the mind does not arise within him.
This very vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) is perceived through the gateway of the mind;
it has attained the state of the world within the void, just as blueness and other qualities appear to the vision within the sky.
The vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) constitutes masculinity; its cessation is called peace.
From the vibration of the vital breath, consciousness moves like a ball set in motion.
Consciousness, awakened by the pulsation of the vital breath, flashes forth within bodies.
Like a ball struck by the hand,
consciousness— which is inherently all-pervading— is awakened within the limbs by the vibration of the vital breath;
it takes on a form subtler than the subtlest, like a trace of fragrance carried by the wind.
Know, O Rāghava, that the restraint of consciousness is the supreme good;
it is the cause of equanimity, for therein no agitation exists.
Consciousness, as soon as it arises, quickly moves toward the object of perception with intensity.
From that perception, infinite sufferings arise for the mind.
When consciousness, having slept, remains in a state of non-awakening,
then that which was to be attained has been attained— that stainless state.

Therefore, through the vibrations of the vital breaths and likewise by the impelling of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), if you do not cause consciousness to swell, then you are unborn. Know that the swelling of consciousness is the mind; by it, this [universe] is extended.

Yogins perform the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇarodhana*) for the sake of pacifying the mind, by means of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), meditations (*dhyāna*), and applications devised through skillful methods— thereby tearing asunder and shattering the web of misfortune that destroys the lives of people. (MU 5.92.25–26)
O Rāghava, those possessed of knowledge declare this to be the bestower of the fruit of mental tranquility, the supreme cause of equanimity,
auspicious, the health of consciousness, and the restraint of the vital breaths;
it is both revealed and experienced by the wise.
Listen now to this other [account] regarding the arising of the mind from latent impressions (*vāsanā*):
The grasping of an object through firm habitual cultivation, having abandoned all prior and subsequent deliberation— that is proclaimed to be *vāsanā*.
O mighty-armed one, that very state which has been cultivated by oneself through intense spiritual urgency quickly becomes his own, as he is freed from the memory of all other things.
For such a person is indeed rendered subject to the power of that specific latent impression (vāsanā).

Whatever one perceives, one becomes deluded, thinking, "This is that; this is the real entity. Due to the helplessness caused by the onset of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), one abandons one's true nature and, with a distorted vision, perceives that error as if everything were under the influence of intoxication.
One who possesses incorrect knowledge alone becomes overwhelmed by mental anguish,
being brought under control by an internal latent impression (*vāsanā*) like a chronic fever (*viṣūcī*).
That which is incorrect vision is the cultivation of the notion of "self" with respect to what is not the self.
Know that which perceives reality in what is unreal to be the mind, O Rāghava.
Through the intense cultivation of the notion that objects of firm habituation are real,
the exceedingly restless mind arises as the cause of birth, old age, and death.
When nothing whatsoever— whether of the nature of what is to be abandoned or what is to be adopted— is perfumed [by latent tendencies],
and one abides having relinquished everything, then the mind is not born. When, due to the constant absence of such perfuming, the mind does not conceptualize, [the mind is not born].
Then, that state of mindlessness arises which bestows supreme tranquility;
when nothing whatsoever flashes within consciousness, like a cloud in the sky,
then the mind is not born within, like a lotus in the sky.
When no state of being is cultivated toward any object whatsoever in the world,
then, in the empty sky of the heart, the demon of the mind does not arise.
O Rāghava, I consider this alone to be the true nature of the mind.
When one contemplates the ultimate nature of reality through passion and aesthetic delight,
and when one naturally cultivates a vision that is incapable of any conceptual construction,
how could the arising of thought occur for one who is as pure as the expanse of space?
That which consists in not cultivating anything, that which consists in the cultivation of non-existence,
and that which is the seeing of things as they truly are— that is called "no-mind" (*acittatva*). That which, having completely abandoned everything within, abides in a cool disposition;
Even while abiding in its functional state, that mind is declared to be of the nature of non-existence.
For one in whom passion does not exist due to the absence of attachment to latent impressions (*vāsanā*), his mind has reached the state of non-mind; that is called true being (*sattva*).

He whose dense latent impressions (*vāsanā*) no longer cause rebirth is liberated while living; established in the state of pure being (*sattva*), he remains like the whirling of a potter’s wheel. Those whose impressions are like parched seeds, devoid of rebirth, [are likewise liberated].

Those whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are devoid of relish are indeed remembered as liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). Having attained a mind whose nature is pure being (*sattva*), they have reached the further shore of knowledge;
they are said to be "mindless" (*acitta*), and at the end of the body, they take on the form of space.
O Rāma, there are two seeds of the mind: the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) and mental impressions (vāsanā).
When one of these two is exhausted, both quickly perish.
Indeed, these two seeds are mutual causes for the birth of the consciousness.
O Rāma, just as water and its receptacle are inseparable,
so too are these two like the seed and the sprout, or like sesame seeds and their oil;
they exist eternally in a state of inseparability according to a sequence that depends upon time.
But they both produce together a mental state consisting of consciousness,
just as both the fragrance and the breeze together produce the pleasure of the olfactory faculty; likewise,
these two are equal in being the producers of the mind at that time.
Established like fragrance in a flower or oil in sesame seeds,
the vibration of the vital breath arises through the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), and by that [vibration], latent impressions are produced;
thus occurs the sequence of seed and sprout for the seed of the mind.

Because consciousness is being carried away by latent impressions through the activity of agitation, it awakens the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa); by that means, the mind (citta) is born. Since the vital breath has the nature of vibration, it vibrates once it has touched the cave of the heart.
By awakening that consciousness, the childish mind is brought forth.
For thus, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*) are the causes of the mind;
when one of these two is destroyed, O sinless one, there is the destruction of both and of the mind as well.
The great trunk of pleasure and pain bears the great fruit of the body; its form is sprouted by its effects, entwined by the creepers of conduct and vows,
coiled by the black serpent of craving, and serving as a dwelling for the cranes of passion and disease.

This tree of the mind— whose root is ignorance, which is very firm, and in which the birds of the senses are hidden— is indeed felled in an instant by that which is called the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
just as a gale blows down fruit ripened by time.
Whitening all directions and obscuring every vision,
it has the form of a shifting cloud and arises from the heap of ignorance;
having attained the mere blade of grass that is craving, its body takes the shape of a pillar.
Trembling, with its subtle body agitated and greedy for leaping upward,
it perceives the great light situated within and dissolves away;
and through the cessation of the movement of the vital breath, O Rāma, the dust of the mind is extinguished in an instant.

It is said that the seed of these two— the latent impression (*vāsanā*) and the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇapavana*)— is the object of perception, because from that [seed] they both manifest. Then,
through the craving for objects of perception within the heart, there arises the vibration of the vital breath and the latent impression.
Therefore, that which is to be experienced arises; this is said to be the seed of these two.

By the complete abandonment of the object of experience, the vibration of the vital breath and its latent impressions are swiftly destroyed along with their roots, like two trees when their roots are cut.
O Hero, know that consciousness is the seed of the object of cognition;
without it, the object of cognition cannot exist, just as a sesame seed devoid of oil.
Nothing exists as a separate object of cognition, whether externally or internally.
Consciousness, throbbing, first conceives an object of perception and then manifests it by itself.
Just as in a dream one experiences one's own death or residence in another land,
so too does consciousness manifest an object of perception through its own inherent power of wonder.
O descendant of Raghu, that which proceeds from consciousness due to its own volition attains the state of being the web of the world;
just as a child might perceive a Vetāla born of his own imagination.
Just as the state of being a person is perceived in a tree trunk, so too is [the world] perceived in consciousness.

They know this to be false knowledge; it dissolves through right knowledge, just as the state of being a snake in a rope vanishes upon seeing it clearly, or as the appearance of two moons disappears when one’s own eyes are examined.
"Pure consciousness alone is the three worlds; there is nothing else whatsoever"—when such a firm internal certainty has taken root, the wise know that to be right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Whatever appears to this [consciousness], whether previously seen or unseen, [is but its own manifestation].
Therefore, that consciousness must be cleansed with effort by one who possesses discernment.
For it is merely the failure to cleanse that constitutes the great cycle of transmigration;
whereas the mere cleansing of that is designated as liberation.
Consciousness leads to infinite suffering because it is of the nature of birth;
non-consciousness, which abides in non-inertness, leads to bliss because it is of the nature of non-birth.
Therefore, become non-inert, free from [worldly] bliss, and relinquished of consciousness.
"You, O scion of Raghu, are that very Self which is awakened and beyond perception.
Rāma said:
"O Lord, what is it like to be non-inert yet devoid of cognition?"
And if there is no consciousness, that is insentience; how then can it be averted?
Vasiṣṭha said:
He who is established in non-abiding everywhere, yet finds rest nowhere at all—

The living soul (jīva) perceives nothing when it is without consciousness, for it is indeed non-inert. He for whom no support in the form of an object of consciousness exists here is declared to be "without consciousness" (asaṃvit), even though he is performing hundreds of actions; yet he is non-inert.
The space of the heart is not tainted even slightly by that which is to be experienced;
he who is thus non-inert and free from objective perception is called liberated while living.
When nothing whatsoever is cultivated within the self due to the state of being free from latent impressions (nirvāsanatā), [that is liberation].
It remains steady, like the consciousness of an infant or a mute;
at that time, O wise one, it becomes free from dullness, an expansive state beyond [ordinary] perception, which, once attained, one is no longer defiled by.
Through the abandonment of all latent impressions by means of non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*),
a vast bliss unfolds like blueness from the sky.
Therein, the yogi who is absorbed becomes a consciousness devoid of objective perception.
Because it consists of that [Self], it too dissolves within, being without beginning or end.
Whether walking, standing, touching, or even smelling, he is said to be by means of that [Self]:
non-inert, with bliss dissolved, having abandoned [ordinary] perception, and happy.
Grasping this view with painful and ruined effort,
cross to the far shore of the ocean of suffering— you who are an ocean of boundless virtues.
Just as from a seed a great tree arises and in time pervades the sky, so too does this [view] lead to liberation.
In this very way, this object of perception arises from consciousness through its own volition.
When consciousness, having willed a volition, perceives it as a body,
that very consciousness becomes the seed of this entire web of births.
Having produced herself from herself and deluding herself again and again,
consciousness at the end leads itself to liberation everywhere, O Rāghava;
whatever this [consciousness] contemplates, that very thing it becomes in an instant.
Like an actor, having abandoned his role, he returns after a long time to his own body.
Whether as a god, a naga, an asura, a yaksha, a rakshasa, a male kinnara, or an elephant,
it is the Self alone that dances within this playful world-drama.
Just as the silkworm, having bound itself and wept,

eventually attains its state of isolation after a long time, so too consciousness (*saṃvit*) by its own nature attains its absolute freedom. Likewise, consciousness is the abundant water within the nets of the ocean of the world.
Just as the sky, having filled the circle of the quarters, appears to have attained the state of mountains and so forth—
[the sky], the earth, the wind, space, the mountains, the rivers, and the directions—
these are said to be the waves of this continuous stream of consciousness.
The entire world is mere consciousness; there is no conception of a second.
By such right knowledge, consciousness does not become anything else.
When it perceives nothing at all, it neither vibrates nor moves.
Then consciousness comes to rest in its own self and is no longer defiled.
Furthermore, O Rāma, it is said that pure existence (*sanmātra*) is the seed of this consciousness;
from pure being alone does it arise, just as luminosity arises from light.
In that regard, there are two forms of existence (*sattā*): one abides in various shapes, while the second is of a single form. Listen now to this distinction between the two:
it is described as "jar-ness," "cloth-ness," "that-ness," "you-ness," and "I-ness."
That which is the form of existence (sattārūpa), though established in various forms through differentiation,
abandons that differentiation and is extended as a single essence through existence;
thus, by means of the universal alone, the single form of existence is proclaimed.

Having completely abandoned all particularity, that which is pure existence (sanmātra), untainted, uniform, and the Great Form (mahārūpa), they know that to be the supreme essence of Being (sattā). Form never exists as a multiplicity of shapes within Being.
Therefore, that which is unperceivable arises; hence, this [world] is without a real substrate (*avastuka*).
But that form of Being (*sattā*) which is of a single nature and pure in essence never undergoes destruction, nor does it ever become forgotten.
Whether it be the existence of time, the existence of parts, or this existence of objects—
having abandoned the mental construction of such distinctions, become intent solely upon pure Being (*sanmātra*).
The existence of time and the existence of space, when free from all mental constructions, is simply Being.
Even if it possesses the form of the supreme reality, nevertheless, this [division] is not real.
How could that which is seen as the cause of multiplicity— the conceptualization of division that produces divergent views— be purifying?
Cultivating only the singular nature of the universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*),
remain complete, filled with supreme bliss, and filling the quarters of space. O Lord of the Wise, that which is the ultimate limit of mere universal existence—
That very [state] becomes his seed-state; from that, he proceeds.
That which extends to the universal of existence (*sattāsāmānya*), being devoid of conceptualization (*kalana*), is the primordial state, without beginning or end; for it, no seed exists.
Consciousness dissolves therein and remains changeless;
having attained that state, she does not return again to suffering.
That is the cause of all causes, yet no cause for it is found.
It is the essence of all essences; therefore, no essence exists beyond it.
Within that vast mirror of consciousness, all these perceptions of objects are reflected, just as trees on a riverbank are reflected in a lake.
In that Sustainer of Taste, all these entities find their relish;
they manifest clearly, like the six flavors upon the tongue. Therefore, taste that very state of the sky of consciousness, which is even more transparent than the clear.
And that is the complete tasting of all things born from one's own experience.
My dear, it is there that the multitude of worlds is born, exists, grows, is perceived, comes to rest, and dissolves. (MU 5.92.114–115)
That is heavy among the very heavy, that is light among the very light;
that is gross among the grossest, and that is subtle among the most subtle. That is farthest among the farthest, and that is nearest among the nearest.
It is the lowest of the low, yet it is the highest even among the high;
it is the splendor of splendors, the darkness of darknesses,
the reality of realities, and, my dear, the supreme vision of visions.
That is this and that, both something and nothing; it exists and it does not exist;
it is both visible and invisible; it is "I" and yet it is not "I.
O Rāma, with every effort, [one should seek] within that which is supremely pure.
O sinless one, act in such a way that you attain stability in that state.
That is the stainless, undecaying reality of the Self; upon realizing it, the mind attains peace.
Having realized the nature of that expansive Oneness, become forever liberated from worldly existence, eternally awakened for all time.
The ninety-third canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Discerning the Seed of Saṃsāra," [spoken by] Rāma.
"These are those seeds which have been proclaimed by you, O giver of honor.
By the application of which one quickly attains that state?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
Whichever remedy has been declared by me for each of these seeds of suffering,
by the application of that very one, the state is swiftly attained—
if, indeed, [one is established] instantly in the state situated at the pinnacle of the generality of existence (sattāsāmānya).
O knower of reality, by human effort and through the forceful abandonment of latent impressions,
you maintain for even a moment a state that is imperishable in nature;
in this very moment, you are fully capable of attaining that auspicious state.
Or, my dear friend, if you establish yourself in the form of universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*),
then by a slight additional effort here you will attain that state.
Or, O sinless one, if you remain established in the principle of pure consciousness (*saṃvittattva*) with full awareness.
Therefore, with great and supreme effort, you shall attain that state.
O Rāghava, meditation is not possible regarding an object of perception alone,
because this consciousness itself is always present everywhere.
Whatever you think, whatever you go toward, whatever you stand upon, or whatever you do—in each of those instances, consciousness remains; it is consciousness alone, or that very object itself.
Or, if you make an effort to completely abandon latent impressions (*vāsanā*), [you will find the same].
By that, all mental and physical afflictions instantly become slackened for you.
Indeed, this is considered more difficult than previous efforts;
the abandonment of latent impressions is harder to accomplish even than uprooting Mount Sumeru.
As long as the mind has not dissolved, so long there is no destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Knowledge of reality, the dissolution of the mind, and the destruction of latent impressions—
having become mutual causes for one another, these remain difficult to accomplish.
Therefore, O Raghava, with effort, through discerning manliness,
and having abandoned the desire for enjoyment from afar, one should take refuge in these three;
for all of these are equal as long as they have not been repeatedly and thoroughly practiced.

Even in hundreds of years, the attainment of that state does not occur. O Great-minded One, for the Sage who has practiced for a long time, the dissolution of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*), the knowledge of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the destruction of the mind (*manonāśa*) become fruit-bearing simultaneously.
Even if these are practiced individually for a long time,
they do not grant accomplishment, like mantras that have been broken;
for even when practiced over a long period, these do not yield results even for those of keen intellect.
Like soldiers who are unable to advance against the enemy one by one, these [faculties],
when brought together in concerted effort by the wise man,
cut down the enemy that is saṃsāra from its very roots, just like warriors.

The dissolution of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*), the cessation of the consciousness-ego (*vijñānamanonāśa*), and [the realization of the Self] must be cultivated with effort simultaneously for a long time; by that, my dear, you shall not suffer.
Through these three practiced for a long duration, the firm knots of the heart are severed.
They are severed entirely, like lotus fibers when cut;
O Rāma, the persistence of worldly existence practiced through hundreds of previous births is never exhausted except through the yoga of long-term cultivation.
Whether walking, hearing, touching, smelling, standing, waking, or sleeping,
always practice this triad for the sake of the supreme good:
the complete relinquishing of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Therefore, those who know reality should likewise practice this. Through the complete abandonment of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the mind attains the state of non-mind;
and through the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), do as you wish.
Through firm practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), by means of the method imparted by the Guru,
and through the yoga of sitting and non-sitting, the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇaspanda) is restrained.
[This occurs] through the manifestation of perfect knowledge and through detachment from the objects of the world.
Because one sees things as they truly are, latent predispositions do not arise.
That form which is stable and non-deceptive regarding things in their beginning and end—
knowledge that perceives that form causes latent predispositions to be exhausted.
Because one acts without attachment, because one has abandoned the cultivation of worldly existence,
and because one perceives the destruction of the body, latent impressions do not arise;
just as dust does not remain in the sky when the movement of the wind has subsided.
When the manifestation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) has perished, the mind no longer functions.
Indeed, that which is the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇapavana*) is itself the vibration of the mind;
from it the worlds are born, like dust from refuse.
The wise person should exert themselves intensely to conquer the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*),
sitting again and again with a one-pointed mind, over and over.
Or else, having abandoned this gradual method, if they would rather directly attack the mind itself—
If that is pleasing to you, you shall attain that state after a long time.
O blameless one, the mind cannot be conquered without a method,
just as a wild, intoxicated elephant cannot be controlled without a goad.
The mastery of inner knowledge, association with the virtuous,
the complete relinquishing of latent impressions, and the cessation of the movement of the vital breath—
these, indeed, are the well-developed means for conquering the mind.

By these means it is quickly conquered, just as the dust of the earth is by showers of rain. Those who, while these methods exist, seek to restrain the mind by force, are like those who cast away a lamp and try to destroy the darkness with collyrium.
Those deluded ones who strive to achieve mastery over the mind through force are like those who attempt to bind a frantic lord of elephants with lotus fibers.
Their own bodies remain for a long time as the abode of the intoxicated mind.
Those who abandon reason and seek purification are known as ruined;
out of fear they enter further fear, and from affliction they go to further affliction.
Like wretched beings, they do not attain peace.
For a long time, possessed by hundreds of mental anxieties, they waste their lives through delusions regarding sacred fords, austerities, charity, sacrifices, and the worship of gods—
like deer wandering upon mountain peaks, subsisting on fruits and sprouts.
With minds utterly bewildered, those wretched ones were as terrified as deer;
their intellects were shattered and their delicate limbs broken,
so that they could find no confidence anywhere, like a doe that has strayed into a village.
Their minds, tossed by great waves and carried away by the force of delusion,
are swept far away as they fall, like grass in mountain rivers.
By the power of fate, at some point, even a small portion of the reality of the Self may [be revealed] to you.
Stained by the states of suffering and its defects,
beings— whether in hell, heaven, or as humans— whether they perceive it or not, are constantly coming and going; like balls, they are tossed about by the very nature of their falling and rising.
From there they go to hell, and from there to heaven, or even right here;
they revolve through cycles of rebirth like waves upon a river.
Therefore, O descendant of Raghu, abandon these false views.
Relying upon pure consciousness, become steadfast and free from passion.
Only the one possessed of knowledge partakes in happiness; only the one possessed of knowledge truly lives;
only the one possessed of knowledge is strong. Therefore, become composed of knowledge.

O Great-Souled One, perceiving the single, supreme, primordial state of pure consciousness—which is devoid of all that is to be perceived—remain within your very heart, free from all mental constructs. Even while performing actions, remain without the sense of agency; thus, with your glory fully arisen, you shall attain the state of the non-doer.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Instruction on the Process for Eliminating the Seed of Saṃsāra."
The ninety-fourth canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Even with a slight degree of inquiry, there is restraint of one's own mind.
By whomsoever even a slight [effort] has been made, by him the fruit of birth has been attained. That minute spark of inquiry which flickers within their hearts,
through the power of practice, reaches a hundredfold expansion.
But the bright qualities resort to a man of somewhat mature discernment who is preceded by dispassion, just as birds resort to a full lake;
[they resort] to the wise one who investigates correctly and perceives things as they truly are.
Even though they may be extensive, the manifestations of ignorance do not prevail intensely;
for what can the objects of the senses, the mental fluctuations, or even anxieties and diseases do here to one whose mind is fixed on right vision?
Where are those clouds of Puṣkarāvarta, reddish-pink with lightning, filled with the winds of the dissolution and seized by your fist-like nets?
And where is the moon situated in the midst of the sky, O charming girl, now contained within this jewel casket?
A simple woman, mistaking them for lovely blue lotuses, has bound him with them.
Where are those elephants, whose heads are crowned with lotuses and swarms of bees rising from their temples, now crushed by the gnats that are as sweet as the breath of a charming woman?
Where are the lions, enraged in battle, their rows of claws flashing as they strike at elephants' pearls, now torn apart by deer?
Where are the towering forest trees, consumed by the exhalations of venomous serpents?
Hungry pythons, agitated, have swallowed young frogs;
where indeed can a wise man— who has attained the ground of stability, who knows what is to be known, and who possesses discernment—
be overcome by the bold thieves that are the sense-objects?
The enemies that are the sense-objects carry away the immature intellect,
just as fierce winds blow down a tender creeper whose stem has been severed. However,
they are not able to break the intellect that is matured by the power of discernment.
Like gentle breezes [shaking] a mountain that endures the turbulence of an eon,

the winds of anxiety cannot shake one who is firmly established in a stable state— provided he does not grasp at the surface of the earth and whose tree of discernment is in full bloom. (MU 5.94.13–14)

Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping, he whose mind is not intent on inquiry is said to be dead. "What might this world be? What might I be?"—thus one should reflect slowly and incessantly.
Examine it yourself through the vision of the inner self, or together with virtuous people.
By means of inquiry that transcends darkness, the supreme state is seen,
like a stainless jewel by a shining lamp.
Through knowledge, the destruction of all sufferings arises,
just as darkness is dispelled by the sun through its playful manifestation of light.
When knowledge has become manifest, the object of knowledge itself fully arises of its own accord.
When the sun has risen, it is like a stainless light upon the earth;
that investigation of the scriptures by which the reality of Brahman is awakened is called knowledge, which stands as if non-different from the object of knowledge.
The wise know that the knowledge of the inner sciences (*adhyātmavidyā*) is the limb of reflection (*vicāra*);
its object of knowledge exists within itself, just as sweetness exists within milk.
A person who possesses the light of perfect knowledge is himself composed of the object of knowledge.
It becomes filled with the bliss of intoxication, like one who has drunk *maireya* liquor.
The wise know the supreme Brahman to be the stainless object of knowledge, whose nature is both being and non-being;
by the mere attainment of knowledge, it becomes manifest of its own accord.
The man of knowledge, with joy arisen within, does not sink anywhere;
liberated while living, free from attachment, he remains as the sovereign Self alone.
The man of knowledge [is unmoved] by pleasant sounds such as the notes of the lute and the flute.
In the amorous songs of the beloved woman and in her cooing during sexual union;
in the humming of bees intoxicated by the springtime passion;
and in the thundering of clouds nourished by the onset of the rainy season.
Amidst peacocks with their crests dancing wildly and uttering sweet cries,
amidst clusters of blooming lotuses and the warbling of cranes,
and amidst deep-sounding drums held in hands grasping knives and other weapons;
O Rāma, he does not fix his attachment upon the sounds of any stringed, wind, or percussion instruments—
whether harsh or sweet—
just as the moon does not cling to lotuses.
The wise man [finds no distinction] between the tender leaves of young plantain trunks and his own hands,
between houses adorned with clusters of sandalwood, agalloch, and mandāra creepers,
and the ground strewn with silken garments, pearl necklaces, and white and blue lotuses resembling the moon.
Upon their hips, breasts, and arms, which possessed the luster of molten gold;
upon their thighs, which shone like golden archways at the abode of the God of Love;
and amidst the playful delights of the Nandana grove, where the creeper-like limbs of the daughters of the gods and Gandharvas entwined.

O Rāma, the wise man, his intellect unattached even to things within his own power, does not bind himself to the pleasure of touch, just as a swan finds no delight in the desert sands. The man of knowledge feels no attachment toward dates, *kharjūra* fruits, *kadamba*, *panasa* (jackfruit), and the like.
Among grapes, cucumbers, walnuts, lotus stalks, and citron trees; among the products of wine, honey, *maireya*, and *mārdvīka* liquor;
and among curd, milk, ghee, inspissated milk (*āmikṣā*), fresh butter, and boiled rice.
Among the six diverse flavors— whether in things to be licked or drunk, in luxuries, fruits, grains, roots, vegetables, or even meats— he,
whose form is satisfied and whose intellect is unattached, does not bind himself to any of them.
The wise man finds no relish or delight in Yama,
Candra, Indra, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others,
nor in the peaks of Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Sahya, or Dardura, as a Brahmin finds none in the flesh of his father-in-law.
Upon nets of silk and leaves, upon fruits such as the orb of the moon,
in groves of wish-fulfilling trees where goddesses sport upon swings,
and against walls of gold and jewels made of gems and pearls;
The illustrious one, whose mind is unattached, does not desire to behold Tilottamā, Urvaśī, Rambhā, Menakā, or Aṅgalatā;
he is full in spirit, silent, and self-respecting, like a weak man toward his enemies.
The wise one [discerns] among the *kunda*, *mandāra*, *kalhāra*, and *kumuda* lotuses;
among the *kamala*, *utpala*, *puṇnāga*, *ketaka*, *aguru*, and *jāti*;
and among the *kadamba*, mango, *jambīra*, *kiṃśuka*, and *aśoka* trees.
In *japā*, *atimukta*, *sauvīra*, *nimba*, and *pāṭala* garlands;
in sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, powdered musk, and *mṛgamada*;
and in saffron, water-lilies, *vaṅga*, *elā*, *kakkola*, *tagara*, and the like.
With a single-minded devotion to the delight of fragrance, he does not become attached to any particular scent;
possessing equanimity and remaining unshaken, he is like a bird amidst the sweet scents of honey.
Whether there is the gurgling roar of the ocean or the echoing resonance of a mountain, [he remains the same].
He is not disturbed even in the slightest by the roars of the lords of beasts;
nor does he tremble even slightly amidst the trumpeting of rutting elephants, the writhing of vetālas, or the shrieks of piśācas and yakṣas.
He does not tremble from the roar of thunderbolts, the sound of crashing mountains,
or the trumpeting of Airāvaṇa, because his mind is absorbed in meditative concentration; nor does he waver from the friction of whirling saws or the slicing of sharp swords.
It does not tremble in its essential nature even by the falling of a thunderbolt;
it experiences neither joy in a grove nor does it undergo weariness.
It does not experience weariness in deserts, nor does it attain joy there.
Toward enemies and friends alike, who are like heaps of glowing embers upon sands of fine grit;
toward soft, grassy ground covered with scattered flowers;
and toward beds of sharp razor-edges made of fresh blue lotuses.
On lofty mountain regions and at the depths of well-chambers;
on rocks heated by the sun's rays and on soft women;
amidst prosperity and fierce calamities, and in deaths as well as in festivals.
Even while dwelling [in the world], he experiences neither agitation nor joy;
with his mind eternally liberated within, he remains perfectly equanimous.
Even in the forest lands of hell, where the ground is studded with iron spikes, [he remains unmoved].
Amidst the endless showers of spears and javelins hurled at one another,
he does not fear, nor does he succumb to helplessness or dejection;
equanimous, with a self-composed mind, silent and steadfast, he stands like a mountain.
Even that which is impure, unwholesome, or even poison, mud, or artificial poison, once consumed, is quickly digested; and when moistened and digested, it becomes as if delicious, like fine food.
[This occurs] through the use of the paste of *nimba* and *prativiṣā*, milk, sugarcane juice, water, or food.
One whose intellect is unattached and who knows the truth remains equanimous toward tasting [flavors].
He neither rejoices nor becomes angry at wines such as *maireya* and *madirā*, milk, blood, fat, marrow, and spirits, nor at husks, bones, grass, hair, or food.
He regards even the slayer of his life and the giver of it with an equal gaze, one characterized by serenity and sweetness;
[he looks upon] all things, whether their bodies be stable or unstable, and whether they be pleasant or unpleasant.
He neither rejoices nor desponds, always kindled by equanimity; because he has abandoned all attachment, because the nature of the world remains ungraspable,
because he has truly known that which is to be known, and because his own mind is free from passion.
A virtuous person, with a mind free from sovereign pride, does not grant any scope to any sense organ whatsoever in its engagement with objects—
[the mind] which is ignorant of reality, restless, lacking self-possession, and unstable.
The crocodiles of the senses swiftly devour him, as lions devour a sapling;
he is carried away in the ocean of existence, tossed by the waves of latent impressions, crying out "Alas! Alas! while being swallowed by the sea-monsters of his own senses.
For one whose mind has found rest in the Self and has attained its footing through inquiry,
the floods of conceptual constructions cannot carry him away, just as torrents of water cannot move a mountain.
For those who have come to rest in the supreme state at the limit of all mental constructs, [there is no further movement].

For those who have attained their true nature, even Mount Meru is regarded as a mere blade of grass. To those whose minds are thus expanded, the entire world is like a fragment of withered straw; poison is nothing but nectar;
and a single moment is equal to a thousand aeons. In such a state, there is perfect equanimity for them.

Realizing that the world is nothing but pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*), those of joyful intellect dwell with the world situated within themselves, because it consists of consciousness alone. Within the cage of objects that constitutes the world, which is but a vibration of pure consciousness—

What is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted here for the sage who knows reality? O sinless one, abandon this other delusion that "all this is consciousness alone. Since you are the expansive embodiment of consciousness itself, what do you have to give up, and what do you seek?

That which arises from the earth as a future, delicate sprout is nothing but consciousness manifesting in that way; there is no such thing as a sprout. That which does not exist in the beginning or at the end is likewise non-existent in the present.

"Having perceived that this existence of consciousness is but a delusion for a mere fraction of time," thus thinking, abandon the intellect that follows after being and non-being; having reached the end of all objective states, become one whose form is the light of consciousness free from attachment.

Whether performing action with the body, the mind, the intellect, or even with the senses alone, you are not tainted, being free from attachment. Even while acting with a mind free from attachment, you are not tainted.
O mighty-armed one, just as in the states of one's desires,
he whose mind is free from attachment— though performing actions with his slender limbs— is not stained by pleasures or pains, as if they were but fragments of a dream.
One whose mind is free from attachment does not see even while looking with his vision;
this is experienced even by a child because the mind is fixed elsewhere. Even when a living being looks with a mind free from attachment, he does not see.
He does not hear even while hearing, nor does he touch even while touching;
he does not smell even while smelling, nor does he open his eyes even while opening them.
He does not fall at all into objects, even when forcibly cast down.
This is experienced even by those of immature intellect—by fools, indeed—even when their minds are fixed on another land while they themselves remain in their own homes.
Attachment is the cause of worldly objects; attachment is the cause of saṃsāra.
Attachment is the cause of hopes; attachment is the cause of calamities.
They know that the renunciation of attachment is liberation; from the renunciation of attachment comes freedom from rebirth.
O sinless one, having abandoned attachment to all things, become one who is liberated while living.
Rāma said:
O Sage, you who are like an autumnal wind that dispels the mist of all doubts, tell me briefly, O Lord: what is meant by "attachment"? MU 5.94.84
Vasiṣṭha: That impure latent impression (*vāsanā*) which, through the presence or absence of objects, produces the fluctuations of joy and resentment, is called attachment (*saṅga*).

In the bodies of those liberated while living, the latent impression (vāsanā) becomes pure, free from joy and sorrow, and brings about the state of no further rebirth. Know that this is called "non-attachment," which persists as long as the body exists.

Whatever action is performed by that [mind] leads only to bondage. Having thus abandoned attachment, which causes the agitation of one's own limbs, if you remain unperturbed even while acting, then you are a master over it.
If you do not undergo any change of state through the fluctuations of joy and resentment,
then, O Rāghava, being free from passion, fear, and anger, you are unattached.
This is the steady state of one liberated while living— a state of non-attachment and effortless ease.
Relying on equanimity, established in yourself, free from passion, O sinless one; with the mind of one liberated while living, silent, having restrained the grasp of the senses,
free from pride, intoxication, and envy, the noble one remains free from the fever of worldly existence.

For at all times, even amidst the entire range of existing things, he whose inner disposition is equanimous and whose being is undepressed performs nothing other than that which arises spontaneously from his natural activity and proceeds in due order.
Whatever is to be done by him, belonging to his own nature, that alone he performs as it stands within its natural sequence.

Free from attachment and worldly ties, he acts without weariness and delights within his own intellect. Whether encountering adversity or great prosperity, the one of great intelligence does not abandon his innate nature, just as the great ocean of milk does not lose its whiteness even when stirred by a gentle breeze.
Having attained either universal sovereignty or calamity, or the state of a crawling creature or the lordship of the gods,
he remains without the rise of weariness and with joy extinguished, uniform in nature amidst decline and prosperity like the moon.
With all agitation cast aside and all sense of duality discarded, his various and trivial efforts for diverse fruits have been stilled.

O you of undaunted spirit, investigate the Self so that you may become one who is intent upon the highest goal of existence. Then, through a mind purified by the play of the unfolding expansion [of consciousness], behold the stainless state free from fever;
for when you have attained the vision of the Self, you will no longer be bound here by the fetters of birth.
The chapter titled "The Reiteration of Instruction" is concluded.
Chapter Six: Peace. Chapter: Nirvāṇa.
Immediately after the section on tranquility, hear this:
the section on Nirvana, which, when understood, brings about liberation.
Vālmīki said:
While the prince remained silent, his sole delight being the act of listening as the leader of sages spoke such unrestrained words,
his mind was fixed on the meaning of the sage’s speech and all other activities ceased.
While the royal assembly stood motionless as if depicted in a painting,
the host of sages— moving their fingers in gestures of inquiry and knitting their brows— respectfully reflected upon the meaning of Vasiṣṭha’s words.
While the group of matrons, their eyes like bees blossoming with the joy of a wondrous gaze, had become like clusters of flowers upon the trees of their uplifted necks,
and while the sun stood in the sky at the fourth part of the day; MU_6.1.5.
O gentle one, when the wind— having attained a certain tranquility through the knowledge of what has been heard,
and having become still in its expansive movement as if intent on listening—
remains in silence, bestowing the sweet fragrance of the Mandāra flowers; (in that state, the Lord spoke).
As the rays of light entered through the windows into the interior of the house, they remained motionless as if intent on listening to the heat; they seemed to have come to rest,
like travelers in the long sky, within the coolness.
Upon the mountain kings, whose bodies were like the sun’s heat fading at day’s end, the dust of the nets of pearl-strings— like ashes rising from the mass of their radiance— seemed to proclaim peace;
while upon the lotuses of their playful hands and upon their crests [the pearls] lay as if to soothe them.
While the juices were drying up through desiccation, as if their functions had ceased like the minds of children who are ignorant of the world; while the toy birds were chirping;
and while the womenfolk were incessantly obstructing [the guests] for the sake of food.
The dust raised by the wind from the wings of wandering bees has now entirely settled upon the flower-dust;
the yak-tail whisks are like the eyelashes of the Goddess,
as if out of fear of the web of shadows released by the rays of light grasping at the tips.
As if flying through the lattice windows and entering the interior of the house,
there arose the sound of kettledrums, small drums, and conchs, filling the quarters of the sky, intent upon making known the existence of the fourth part of the day.
Because of that, even his loud words quickly vanished,
like the cry of a peacock at the roar of a thundercloud;
and the row of birds staying in their cages became agitated, their wings fluttering in distress.
Like a row of forests with its *tālī* palms trembling from an earthquake,
the young girl, terrified by fear, came to the space between her nurse’s breasts and cried out,
like clouds in the rainy season reaching the hollows of lofty mountain peaks.
Swarms of bees flew out from the crest-ornaments of the kings like droplets of water from rivers with stony, treacherous currents;
thus did that palace of Daśaratha become agitated at that time.
When the day had grown long as previously described and the sound of the conch shells had subsided,
that tiger among sages, slowly withdrawing the subject at hand, spoke in sweet tones to the scion of Raghu in the midst of the assembly.
[Vasiṣṭha:
O sinless descendant of Raghu, this web of words has been spread out by me;
having bound the bird of the mind with it, take hold of it and lead it to the state of the Self.
Have you grasped the meaning of my words in this way—having abandoned what is difficult to understand, like a swan extracting milk from water?
Having reflected upon this again and again with your own intellect in its entirety, [you will realize: MU 6.1.24.
"O virtuous one, you must now proceed by this very path.
By means of this very understanding, O Rāma, you shall not be bound while wandering;
otherwise, you will quickly fall downward, like an elephant into a pit in the Vindhya mountains."
O Rāma, if you do not act upon my words which have been well-grasped by your intellect,
then you will fall into a pit like a traveler who has abandoned his lamp in the night.
For worldly activity, as it occurs through non-attachment, serves to establish one's own self-realization.
Thus, adopting this established conclusion of the scriptures, may you be prosperous. O members of the assembly, O Great King Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and all you rulers of the earth,
for now let everyone attend to their daily duties.
"Let them do so, for this day has mostly reached its conclusion.
We shall deliberate upon what remains once we have returned in the morning.
Vālmīki said:
When that sage had spoken thus, the entire assembly then rose up,
their lotus-like faces blooming like a bed of lotuses;
the kings, having praised the king and offered salutations to Rāghava, [remained there].

Having offered their praises, those Vasiṣṭhas returned to their own abode. Accompanied by Viśvāmitra, the illustrious Vasiṣṭha rose from his seat to go to the hermitage, having been saluted by the sky-dwellers.
Kings beginning with Daśaratha and likewise sages,
having followed the sage for a long time as he spoke in a manner suited to each,
took their leave; some went to the sky, while others departed for the depths of the forest.
Some, like bees rising from a lotus, remained in Rājagṛha;
others, having offered a pure handful of flowers at the feet of Vasiṣṭha,
followed the king as he entered his inner apartments.
Having reached their own hermitage, the devoted Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Śatrughna honored the feet of their guru and returned to the royal palace;
all those listeners, having arrived at their respective dwellings, [did the same].
They quickly bathed and offered worship to the gods, the brahmins, and likewise to the ancestors;
then, in due order, they together partook of the food appropriate to the sequence of the duties of their respective castes, along with their attendants ranging from brahmins down to servants.
When the sun had set along with the activities of the day,
and the moon-maker had arrived together with the activities of the night,
they remained upon couches and seats provided with silken coverlets.
The kings of sages who dwell on earth, along with princes and great seers,
attentively and with one-pointed minds reflected, exactly as instructed, upon the means for crossing over saṃsāra as proclaimed by the words of Vasiṣṭha.
Then, after only a single watch, with their faces sealed in sleep,
Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Śatrughna went to that beautiful woman of their dream, like lotuses seeking the day. That lasted for exactly three watches.
They contemplated the unimpaired instruction of Vasiṣṭha.
Then, for half a watch with their eyes closed,
they fell in an instant into that dream-sleep which dispels fatigue.
Thus, for those of pure minds who possessed discernment and whose aspirations had been elevated by their attainment of the essence [of reality], the night then ceased;
the three watches passed away, and the moon, now dimmed, assumed the appearance of a face with a soiled countenance.
This concludes the canto titled "Description of the Day’s Activities."
The Second Canto:
Vālmīki:
Then she, whose face was like the moon in distress and who was veiled by a curtain of utter confusion, [spoke].
The dark night shone as it waned, like a latent impression (*vāsanā*) being dissolved by discernment (*viveka*).
In the east, the cluster of stars appeared as if destroyed by the light, while in the western mountain they bore the luster of *śephālikā* flowers used as ear-ornaments.

Drawing in particles of frost, having touched the orb of the moon, and eager to swallow the moonlight, the morning breeze blew. Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Śatrughna, having risen together with their attendants, [proceeded].
Having performed their twilight devotions, they went to the holy hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
There, after first offering a continuous stream of *arghya* water, they paid homage at the feet of the sage, who had emerged from his fire-sanctuary after performing his twilight devotions.
In an instant, that palace, which had been silent with sages, brahmins, and kings, as well as elephants,
horses, chariots, and vehicles, became densely crowded in a moment.
Then that tiger among sages, together with that very army—

Accompanied by Rāma and the others, he went to the palace of Daśaratha early in the morning. There, the king, having already performed his morning devotions and being aware of his arrival, went out a long distance to meet him and honored him with great respect.
Having entered the assembly hall, which was further adorned with multitudes of flowers, pearls, and gems, they all took their seats upon the thrones and other furnishings.
Then, at that moment, all those who had been there the previous day—
