The listeners, both those who move through the sky and those who move upon the earth, assembled together.
That assembly, O gentle one, having performed mutual salutations, entered;
with its perfectly equal expanse, it shone like a lotus pond when the wind has subsided.
When those brahmin-sages, royal seers, and ascetics had quickly settled according to their respective places, at ease and suited to that region,
and when the soft sound of "welcome" had gradually subsided into silence, [the king spoke].
While the bards seated in the corners of the assembly hall were silent,
as if rising in haste like rays of the sun that have suddenly appeared at the windows and entered within, eager to hear.
The jingling sound of the pearl necklace, produced by the touch of the listener's hand as he quickly enters, subsides like the sacred syllable *oṃ*;
it was like Kumāra to Śaṅkara, or like Kaca to the Teacher of the Gods.
Like Prahlāda toward Śukra, or like Suparṇa toward the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
Rāma slowly cast his gaze upon the face of Vasiṣṭha,
as the wind directs a bee hovering over a blooming lotus in the sky.

Then the sage Vasiṣṭha, skilled in speech, addressed these words in due order to the descendant of Raghu— who was himself an expert in the meaning of speech— using that very same discourse which had not been interrupted. Vasiṣṭha said:
"Do you remember, O delighter of the Raghus, the speech I spoke yesterday—
words of exceedingly profound meaning that reveal the supreme truth?
Now, O crusher of enemies, listen to something else for the sake of further understanding."

Listen to this which is being spoken by me for the sake of your eternal perfection. By means of mastery over dispassion and practice, as well as from the vision of reality, one crosses over saṃsāra; therefore, apply yourself to the practice of those very things.
When the difficult-to-comprehend [ignorance] has been destroyed through the correct awakening to reality,
and the immersion in latent impressions has dissolved, one attains the sorrowless state,
which is unconditioned by space, time, and the like, and whose two limits are unseen.
For the world is indeed only the one Brahman, which, though established as such, has appeared as if it were duality.
Where Brahman alone exists, unconditioned by any entities,
being peaceful and appearing with perfect equanimity— how could anything else exist there?
Thinking thus, having internally abandoned the notion of "I," you, the Great One whose body is liberated,
uniform, with a tranquil self, silent, and consisting of your own Self— become so. There is no mind, nor ignorance, nor the intellect, nor the individual soul.

And these mental constructions, O Rāma, are made by Brahman alone. Whatever prosperities, whatever perceptions, whatever cognitions, and whatever desires of consciousness there may be—Brahman alone is that which is without beginning or end; here, nothing exists that is not Brahman.

Whatever is seen—from the netherworld, the earth, and heaven, down to the three-eyed Śiva and up to a blade of grass—that is indeed the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is consciousness; for there is nothing else.
O kinsmen, [regard] prosperity, the body, and all things as indifferent, to be abandoned, or to be accepted [only as appearances].
Brahman alone, devoid of beginning and end, expands like the ocean.
As long as there is the fabrication of ignorance, as long as there is the latent impression of non-Brahman,
and as long as there is attachment to the web of the world, so long does the conceptualization of the mind and other faculties persist.
As long as there is the sense of "I" regarding the body, as long as there is the notion of "self" regarding this visible world,
and as long as there is the attachment that "this is mine," so long does the delusion of the mind and its like persist.
As long as that lofty state has not arisen from the peak of association with the virtuous...
As long as ignorance has not been completely destroyed, there remains the downward inclination toward the mind and other internal faculties.
As long as this world-creating principle has not reached a state of relaxation through the power of right vision, the emergence of the mind continues clearly.
As long as there is ignorance, blindness, helplessness, and longing for sense objects— the heightening of swoon and delusion— so long does the conceptualization of the mind and its states persist.
As long as the fragrance of the poison of desire vibrates within the forest of the heart.
In this state, the cakora bird of discursive thought no longer enters at all;
for one whose mind has no longing for enjoyments, who possesses cool and stainless bliss,
and whose net of snares of hope has been severed, the delusion of the mind comes to an end.
For that man who has abandoned thirst and delusion, whose consciousness is eternally cool,
whose mind is utterly tranquil, and who is awakened— where is the ground of the mind? To him,
he perceives the unreal as something unfamiliar, unregarded, and non-existent.

How could the mind-born [world] exist when one’s own body is as if distant? For one whose self has become the nature of the infinite consciousness (*cittattva*) through meditation, and for whom the world is dissolved within the parts of his own limbs, the delusion of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth is stilled. (MU 6.2.38–39)
When false vision has been stilled— its nature a mass of erroneous delusions—
and when the supreme sun, the singular vision of ultimate reality, has arisen,
[the ego] is burnt like a withered leaf so that it shall never be seen again.
Know that the mind has dissolved like a drop of ghee in fire.
Those great-souled ones who are liberated while living and who perceive the higher and the lower— the path of the mind they have traversed is called *sattva*.

In the bodies of those liberated while living, the latent impression (vāsanā) that functions in worldly affairs no longer belongs to what is called "mind" (citta), for it has reached the state of pure being (sattva). Indeed, the knowers of reality, being devoid of [ordinary] consciousness, remain eternally established in the state of pure being.
Wandering here at ease through their own play, they abide in sattva with effortless composure. Though engaged in worldly affairs, those established in sattva have their senses restrained;
they constantly behold the light of consciousness, for them there is no notion of duality or unity, nor any latent impressions.
For one who, through inward-turned focus, offers the entire three worlds as grass into the fire of consciousness,
those with cool dispositions move about within like fools. A mind made clear by discernment is called *sattva*.

It no longer bears fruit as delusion, like a burnt seed that does not sprout. That latent impression (vāsanā) within the deluded mind which is subject to rebirth is designated by the term "mind" (citta); it is overturned through awakening.

O Rāma, you have attained what was to be attained; having reached the state of pure being (*sattva*), your mind—consumed by the fire of knowledge—shall not sprout again. That which is pierced by an arrow, or likewise by an axe or fire, may grow back.
For the mind, when consumed by the fire of knowledge and made clear through awakening, does not [perceive duality].
Indeed, the world is merely the expansion of Brahman, and the world exists because it is the expansion of Brahman;
here, no difference exists between these two, the world and Brahman, which is a mass of consciousness.

The three worlds exist within consciousness, just as bitterness exists within a mirage; therefore, consciousness and the world are not distinct. Consequently, it is futile to speak of them as existent or non-existent. Since you are not composed of insentient matter, you are of the nature of space; why then do you weep?

If the worlds do not exist because they are not composed of consciousness, from where could mental constructions arise? (MU 6.2.53) If you are composed of consciousness, then investigate that entire state of consciousness:
it is pure being, without beginning or end; therein, my dear, from where could mental constructions arise? (MU 6.2.54)
You are the conscious self, you are partless, and you are devoid of near and far.
Remember your own expansive form; do not become limited by forgetfulness.
Having attained that state of your own being, you shall experience the arising of everything or of nothing.
Such is your form; you are peaceful; you are consciousness; you are of the nature of Brahman.
You are indeed the interior of the rock of consciousness; you are not non-existence, nor are you below that.
Whatever you are, you are that; yet you are not even like that. You are being, you are non-being, you are self-luminous.
That particular object which is within you is neither you nor another; it does not exist for you.
Therefore, you are "not-that" (atad) to this [world]. O you whose self is a mass of pure consciousness, salutations to you!
You are the stainless sky, your body being a solid mass of consciousness, swelling within the vast expanse of the rock that is devoid of beginning and end.
Be at ease, O ocean of the entire world that abides with the playful grace of the unaging sprout-cases; victory be unto you!
The third canto, titled "The Consolidation of Rest."
Vasiṣṭha said:
O sinless one, you are that consciousness which carries within itself infinite worlds, like the mass of water containing a multitude of future waves. *Mokṣopāya* 6.3.1.
O Self of Consciousness, liberated from the cultivation of existence and devoid of both being and non-being, tell me: where indeed could impressions and the like remain?
This individual soul shines forth by itself as "this" through its own latent impressions.
Now, let the relevance of the other two meanings be described here:
O ocean of consciousness, whose nature is great, tremulous, profound, and radiant;
you are named Rāma, for you are motionless, equanimous, and as gentle as the moon.
Just as heat is not distinct from fire, fragrance from a lotus,
blackness from lampblack, whiteness from snow, sweetness from sugarcane,
and light from that which possesses the quality of illumination, so too is experience not distinct from consciousness.
O friend, as waves arise from water, so does the world arise from the nature of consciousness.
Experience is not different from consciousness, nor is the "I" different from experience;
the individual soul (jīva) is not distinct from the "I," and the mind is not distinct from the individual soul.
The mind is not distinct from the senses, nor is the body separate from the senses;
the world is not distinct from the body, for there is nothing other than the world.
Thus, this great wheel has been revolving for a long time.
Nothing has been set in motion, neither quickly nor slowly;
this entire world is not manifold, but is indeed non-manifold, one and indivisible.
It exists as space within space, in nothing whatsoever, being itself nothing at all.
In the void, the void is fully expanded; Brahman is magnified within Brahman. Truth unfolds within truth; the full resides within the full.
Even while performing the acts of perceiving forms and mental attention, one does nothing at all.
The wise person acts toward that which is not to be grasped, for agency resides only in what is to be grasped.
Whatever is seized by the notion that it is to be grasped leads either to suffering or to pleasure;
but that which is not to be grasped through notions of existence or non-existence is a non-agent with respect to pleasure and pain.
Just as space is neither manifold nor non-manifold, and just as a mass of water is like water within space,
so too is the sequence of the self and the world essentially empty, even while being purposeful. One who is stainless within like the sky and skillful in right conduct externally—
One who remains as steady as a piece of wood or a clod of earth amidst the transformations of joy and anger—
he alone sees; he alone truly sees who perceives even that person who is an extreme enemy, envious and intent on killing, as an unfeigned friend.
He who scrapes away both affection and envy, root and all, like the current of a river uproots a tree, is the destroyer of the faults of joy and resentment.
If the true nature of the transformations of passion and hatred is not contemplated, [then one remains bound].
But those [objects] are non-existent even though they appear to exist; they are unenjoyed even though they are enjoyed.
He whose state of being is not characterized by egoism, whose intellect is not stained—even having slain these worlds, he does not slay, nor is he bound.
The realization of the existence of that which does not exist has been described;
through perfect knowledge alone, that [realization] undoubtedly perishes,
like a lamp whose oil has run out and is extinguished within when the essence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) has subsided.
Therefore, nothing at all was created by Citra, nor was anything won by him, even though he was wise and active.
For one for whom this entire collection of objects— whether existent or non-existent— is not to be grasped in any state,
neither for the burning of suffering nor for pleasure, he is indeed liberated here while still alive.
The Fourth Chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Oneness of Brahman," by Vasiṣṭha.

O sinless one, the mind, the intellect, the ego, the senses, and so forth—all this consists of pure consciousness that is beyond the object of thought; where, then, do things such as the individual soul (jīva) reside?
This manifold diversity was bestowed by the Great Self alone through its single nature.
Know that state to be non-differentiation, like the nature of gold remains unchanged whether it is a bracelet or otherwise.
As long as there is the delusion of ignorance, so long does the mind of saṃsāra exist;
once the destruction of ignorance has occurred, where would there be an object of thought or even a "mind" itself?
Through the practice of inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*), dullness likewise comes to an end,
just as the internal chill caused by water is dispelled by attending a fire.
When the onset of the poison of craving for enjoyments has subsided, [the mind becomes clear].

At that very moment, ignorance is destroyed, like blindness when darkness has vanished. By means of the mantra of the science of the inner self (adhyātma-śāstra), when it is cultivated within, the cholera-like poison of craving is exhausted, just as mist is dissipated by autumn.
O Rāma, know that when folly is destroyed, the mind along with its kin is likewise destroyed;
just as when the clouds have dissolved in the sky, the dullness subsides without obstacle.
When the mind has attained the state of non-mind, the delusion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) perishes.
O sinless one, when the thread is severed, the arrangement of pearls in a necklace falls apart; likewise,
those who do not contemplate the meaning of the scriptures for the destruction of their dense sins will sink their minds into the experience of being worms and insects.
The flickering of your lovely lotus-like eyes,
born of ignorance, has been stilled like the trembling of a lake caused by the wind;
you have attained stability in that which is devoid of both existence and non-existence.
Just as the wind moves through the vast expanse of the sky,
O best of the Raghus, I believe you have attained awakening through my words,
as one who was asleep from the slumber of widespread ignorance is roused by the beating of drums.
I believe that the words of a family preceptor surely carry weight even with respect to commoners;
O Rāma, how could they not carry weight with you, whose intellect is so exceedingly noble? For in your case, the fact that his speech is to be accepted has been realized by your own mind.
His words entered deeply within him, like water poured upon a heated field.
"O high-souled one, we are here indeed the eternal family preceptors and gurus of the scions of Raghu;
therefore, O noble one, this which has been spoken by us must be swiftly performed by you in your heart, like a necklace. (MU 6.4.14–15)
The fifth canto, titled "The Demonstration of the Non-existence of Mind," [ends here].
Rāma:
"Oh, how truly wonderful! Through the contemplation of the meaning of your words, O Lord, this entire web of the world has become peaceful for me, even though it stands before me.
I have myself entered into supreme bliss within my own self."

Like the surface of the earth scorched by a long drought being refreshed by rain, I am stilled; possessing a cool nature, I abide in pure bliss. I have attained serenity, like a lake free from all agitation.
O Sage, this entire circle of directions now appears perfectly clear to me;
I perceive it as it truly is, as if free from all mist. I have been born anew, my doubts dispelled, and the mirage of my desires has been stilled.

Free from dust and mist, cooled by rain and forest breezes, I have attained within myself that bliss which is devoid of end— a taste of the essence of elixirs where even the state of a Lord is regarded as a mere blade of grass.
Today I abide in my true nature; I am healthy, and I am joyful.
I delight in the world, yet I am Rāma. Homage to me! Homage be to you!
My doubts and my mental constructions have all set; everything has vanished for me.
Just as the wandering of a night-vampire ceases at dawn when the sun shines,
my mind has attained tranquility within my vast, stainless heart— cool as ice and adorned with the lotus— like a female crane in a lake.
Doubts such as "Why is there a stain upon my soul? or "How does it come to be? have surely been uprooted, like darkness before the sun.
For everywhere and at all times, everything is only the Self, manifesting in various forms.
Whence come these false imaginings that "this is one thing and that is another"?
"What was I like before, bound by the shackles of craving?"—
thus laughing at my inner self, I am filled with joy.
Ah! Now I have rightly remembered:
this is indeed that unborn one (aja) by bathing in the flood of the nectar of your speech whom I now stand before.
Oh, how I have ascended to the vast, purifying ground!
Even while remaining right here, where the sun appears as if situated in the netherworld (pātāla) to me—
who have attained true existence and am freed from the ocean of worldly existence— I bow to that which is eternally worthy of salutation; I conquer the self by the self within the self.

O Lord, by the power of experience, having clearly become like a bee within the calyx of the heart-lotus through your excellent word, I have attained here a state of my own that is free from sorrow and has long been awakened. The canto named "Resting as Rāghava."
The Sixth Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
O mighty-armed one, listen once more to my supreme word.
What I shall say to you, who are well-disposed toward me and desirous of your welfare—
listen even though you have already attained understanding, for the sake of increasing that understanding, so that even those of slight awakening may become free from suffering. (MU 6.6.1–2)
The ignorant man who does not know the Self, for whom the notion of "I" is fixed solely upon the body,
is overwhelmed by the arrows of the senses as if by a rising affliction born of anger.
But for the wise man who knows the Self, whose firm abiding is in his own true Self—
Like contentment itself, the friends of the senses do not strike down that blameless one.
For what reason would that embodied being take upon himself the flood of bodily suffering, he for whom there is no praise when acting for the sake of others, save only blame?
The self is not connected to the body, nor is the body in the self;
these two are mutually distinct, like light and darkness.
It exists eternally free from all modifications of being and is untainted.
The Blessed One neither sets nor rises; he is eternally risen.
Let that which happens to this body—which is inert, ignorant, worthless, ungrateful, perishable, and a mere mass of earth—be so.
When the Self is scrutinized, nothing whatsoever exists as separate from it;
for that which is insentient and of a non-existent nature—how, my dear, could anything possibly belong to it?
That which has been stated again and again is for the sake of a thorough understanding.
Rāghava is awakened to this by means of various diverse arguments:
"If the self, in reality, were to assume the qualities of the body, then why does it not take on the insentience of that corpse-like form? (MU 6.6.10–11)
If, in the ultimate sense, the body were to grasp the qualities of the Self,
then how could it not also take up the mental state— the nature of consciousness— which is eternally manifest?
For when one of two things is fully understood, the insentience of the other remains established.
Tell me, what kind of shared identity of pleasure and pain can there be between those two?
How could those two, who are always equal and possess identical actions, ever exist?
And how could two things that are both non-existent enter into a mutual relationship with one another?
How could the gross be of the nature of the subtle, and how could the subtle become gross?
When one arises, there is no existence of the second, like day and night;
knowledge does not turn into ignorance, nor does shadow turn into heat.
The existent Brahman does not become non-existent, even amidst diverse perceptions. There is not even the slightest attachment for the embodied soul, though it is omnipresent;
even while residing in the body, it is like a lotus in water.

There is not even the slightest connection between Brahman and the existence of the body; for although it resides within that [body], it does not participate in its functions, just as the sky is not affected by the wind.
Nothing whatsoever belongs to the Self, nor does anything belong to the non-existent body.
Therefore, O Raghava, this delusion of pleasure and pain is entirely in vain; from where could it arise?
Old age, death, calamity, pleasure and pain, existence and non-existence—these do not exist here even in the slightest degree. Be extinguished and be at peace.
The delusion consisting of falling and rising, which exists as the body,
is seen to be situated within Brahman alone, just as the state of waves exists within water.
For it is only by depending on the existence of the Self that the self comes into being here.

The body-machine has arisen from the mere existence of the essence of water, like a wave; O dear one, just as there is the presence or absence of agitation in a reflection of the sun and so forth due to the movement of its support, so it is for the embodied soul through the body.
O one of right vision, when the reality of the self is perceived as it truly is,
the delusion of ignorance consisting of the body comes to rest and dissolves;
for through the knowledge of the true nature of both the body and the embodied self, their existence is established as it really is.
Existence and non-existence arise from the Self like two objects from a lamp;

for those who possess imperfect knowledge, they vibrate within this world through their own cycles of birth and rebirth— empty at their core, they are but the winds of delusion that fan the fire of worldly existence.
Those of dull intellect, who have not reflected upon their own true purpose and have not realized consciousness, flutter like grass caught and released by a whirlwind;
being inert, they have not tasted the reality of the mind and are bound by the threads of their own vital breaths.
Driven and overcome like machines, they dance and quiver;
they take up and cast aside everything, from grass to wood, possessing sound, touch, form, and the rest, their limbs as tremulous as waves.

Though they are insentient, these beings of dull intellect appear to possess a throbbing form, abounding in the flow of intense emotions, and subject to movement, arrival, and departure, like great surging floods; yet, within all of them, this immutable consciousness remains ever-present.
However, due to ignorance, they have fallen into a state of extreme wretchedness.
For the streams of breath of the ignorant are seen to be merely for the sake of movement, like the bellows of a blacksmith; they quickly appear to be so, yet they accomplish no purpose.
The threatening roar from a fool is heard like the twang of a bowstring,
devoid of conscious awareness and intended only for slaughter;
even the fruit obtained from a fool is like that from a wild forest tree.
Resting upon that [body] is like resting upon a stone slab;
therefore, even an encounter with it in the forest would be the same as with a wooden post.
Whatever is done for its sake is like striking at empty space with clubs.
Whatever is given to that lowest of men is like casting it into putrid mud;
whatever conversation one has with him is like summoning a dog to a sacrifice.
Ignorance is the culmination of calamities; for what indeed is not a calamity for one who lacks knowledge?
This stream of saṃsāra flows by the power of ignorance. For the ignorant, fierce sufferings and even firm pleasures recur again and again at every age, like mountains.
For the ignorant person who persists in attachment to the body, wealth, wife, and so forth, this terrible suffering never ceases.
This is the case for one who has conceived the notion of a self in the corpse-like body, which is not the self.
How indeed can this illusion, consisting of the perception of the non-existent, ever perish?
For one of dull intellect whose mind is stunted by base dispositions, who is blind to reality and a fool regarding what is unreal, he stumbles at every step even though he possesses eyes.
Poison arises from the moon as fragrance does from a flower;
even as a thorn [arises] from milk and a blade of dūrvā grass from dry land.
The bodies are the female serpents of the silk-cotton tree, and the minds are the chains for the elephant.
The desires of the ignorant spring forth like rice plants after a good rain.
The splendor of hell, guarded by the serpents of evil deeds, welcomes the one who knows not the Self,
just as a peahen joyfully awaits a rain-cloud.
With eyes as restless as a hovering bee and trembling lips like sprouts,
this poisonous creeper that is a woman blossoms only for the sake of fools;
its tremors are but sprouts upon the ground of the hearts of the ignorant ocean.
The wicked tree of passion, its luster vanished, grows ever larger;

the forest fire of hatred blazes in the desert of the ignorant’s heart, with the body as its fuel, the sound of arrows its smoke, weapons its flames, and the soldiers its torches, bringing the calamity of anger.
In the lake of ignorance and stinginess, with slander as its lotus leaves,
the lotus-stalk of envy flourishes fully, where the bee of anxiety buzzes;
in every birth, there is the agitation of waves of intense and fierce suffering.
The submarine fire of repeated death approaches only the insentient one.
Birth inevitably leads to childhood, childhood to youth, youth to old age, and old age approaches death; this cycle occurs again and again for the fool alone.
In this world, which is like an ancient water-wheel, the ignorant have been reduced to fragments by rising and sinking on the rope of saṃsāra within the machine;
yet to the intellect of the wise, this world is as fragile as the distance of a cow’s hoofprint.
That very [intellect] of the one who is not great-souled is bottomless and without limit;
like unseen birds from the hollow interior of the sky of consciousness, the thoughts of the ignorant do not reach the further shore, as if they were birds in a cage.
Through the mere transformation of existence and the mere cessation of latent impressions,
the rims of the wheel of birth cannot be made clear. By the ignorant one, for the sake of the objects lying upon the bed of the senses, the body is reddened by the blood of passion.
In the forest of saṃsāra, this creation—composed of the mountain of the elements and consisting of mere fragments of clay and flesh—is spread out like a heap of meat;
yet, due to delusion, it appears as a captivating array of mental objects, both meaningful and meaningless. (MU 6.55–56)
Victorious is the wish-fulfilling tree of the imagination of the non-meager conceptualization,
from which there extends forth the continuous succession of leaves that are the worlds;
upon it they stand, shine, gleam, and sport.
Adorned with various arrangements, where abundant enjoyments are the birds;
wherein births are the joints, the web of karma is the buds,
merits and sins are the fruits, and the splendors of prosperity are the flower-clusters.
Due to the rising of the moon of ignorance, these women clearly become medicinal herbs that attain supreme splendor within this forest-thicket of saṃsāra;
they are thick with dullness, full of arts, and have their rise brought about by the darkness of time.
Victorious is the moon of ignorance, whose nature is born of emptiness, the lord of defects;

by the grace of this lunar ignorance—which abounds in the nectar of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which satisfies the *cakora* birds of the quarters, and which seeks the essence of the jewel of the mind— [The world is sustained. (MU 6.61–62)
The playful royal swans, their limbs cooled by frost,
shine like beloved night-lotuses with their flickering eyes as bees; they possess breasts as white as moonlight, amidst the shimmering darkness of their braided hair.
That women shine like the night is but the manifestation of the moon of ignorance.

O Rāma, these various and abundant fruits that have spread forth from the tree of ignorance are sweet only at first sight, fraught with misfortune, possessed of a beginning and an end, and fragile throughout their entire existence. (MU 6.64–65)
The seventh canto, titled "The Greatness of Delusion," by Vasiṣṭha.
The women, adorned with strings of pearls and jewels,
shone like the waves of the churned ocean of Kāma when the moon of intoxication has risen;
they possessed the beauty of a swarm of bees hovering over the interior of a golden lotus.

In the springtime, the lovely flowers that have taken root upon the ground in the groves of the garden appear like the smiles of the God of Love, swaying against the petal-like cheeks of women as they gaze.
Flesh-eating vultures, jackals, dogs, ravens,
and crows are compared to women;
[yet] they possess phalli as tall as golden jars and lotus buds.
The row of a woman’s breasts is seen as a box filled with blood;
the fleshy fragment called the lip, smeared with saliva, is compared to the liquid essence of honey and wine flowing from the moon of elixir.
The arms, shaped like *śālmali* thorns and resembling cruel bone-impaling spikes,
are described by auspicious poets using such terms as "arms" (*bāhu*) and "creepers" (*latā*). The beloved woman, beautiful as a cluster of plantain trunks, delights in her lover.

The beauty of the archway of the God of Love, manifested by the splendor of her thighs, shines forth. Even prosperity— which is sweet only at first sight, attended by pairs of opposites in the middle,
and unpleasant in its swift conclusion— is ardently desired.
The mind encounters suffering, and suffering branches out into a hundred directions;
upon these branches of suffering arise the splendors that are the fruits of various karmas—
dense in form like a woven net, resembling ropes intended for imprisonment.
Like creepers in the rainy season, the quarters of the sky are shrouded in dense thickets of spreading vines;
the mist of delusion, which distorts what ought to be done from what ought not to be done,
becomes as dark as the Yamunā during the rains, its fleeting glimmers obscured by gloom.
With the inner heart made bitter by the end of life, and bestowing various forms of transformation,
the sap of the poison of rebirth tastes devoid of affection. The rows of leaves of the people are shaken, withered, and decayed.
The winds of one's own karma blow forth various golden dust-particles.
This Time, though its belly is voracious and boundless, is not satiated even by eons, even as it devours the infinite worlds like ripened fruits.
Intoxicated by the wind of delusion and transformed by the poison of haste, these powerful calamities flash like serpents within the cave of the mind;
struck by the demoness of anxiety and lacking the rising moon of discernment.
The night of youth passes away shrouded in darkness;
the tongue becomes worn out by the fevers of vulgar entreaties,
like a lotus petal situated within the hollow of its bud withered by frosts.
The firm *śalmali* tree of poverty, with its massive trunk of a miserable life and crowded with the thorns of hardship, spreads out a thousand branches.
It serves as a dwelling for the temple-like mind, which is hollow within, yet lofty and ruined.
In the night of excessive begging, the owl of greed prowls about.
Having long seized the quivering mouse of youth with its two ears,
the old, decrepit female cat of old age tears it apart.
This creation, devoid of essence and having gradually surpassed the height of the mountains,
attains fullness like a mass of foam;
it is white with the flowers of appearances and adorned with the sprouts of the world.
The creeper of existence has blossomed, bearing the fruit of the meaning of the Dharma.
The beautiful house of the three worlds is sustained, with the great mountain of Meru as its pillars, the sun and moon as its windows, and the sky as its roof.
In the vast lake of saṃsāra, the bees that are living beings move about within the lotuses that are bodies, drinking the nectar of the nature of consciousness;
they are radiant with beauty upon the sapphire mosaic of the path of the sky.
Within the interior of the world-cage, the lamp of the sun flickers;
its body is bound by the threads of the quarters, while the aged bird of humanity is confined within the cage of the senses, fastened at the end of the pegs of its own latent impressions.
The creeper of worldly existence, long ago touched by the python of Time, throbs with a succession of leaves born from its ceaseless falling;
for some time it has remained unseen on its back by the net of Time.
For a moment, the thick mud of the fierce hells has been cast down and freed from its spikes; within the lake of the path to heaven,
where blue clouds are the water-moss and moon fragments are the lotus stalks,
the celestial swans sport.

The lotus-pond of activity is vast, filled with rows of various fruits, garlanded by the waters of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), abounding in the fragrance of vibration, and blossoming with its lotuses.
Within the puddle of worldly existence, the wretched little fish of creation flickers about.
It is swallowed by the deceitful, aged vulture that is Death;
like a row of foam upon a wave, it is both the same and yet different, fragile and transient.
Day after day, diversity arises like the crescent of another moon.
This wheel is turned around by the potter Time, who fashions from it many clay vessels for living beings that are subject to momentary destruction;
thus, countless and no small things have arisen within the immovable state.
The dense forests of the world have been consumed by the fire of the cosmic ages.
This worldly condition undergoes perpetual reversal through endless existence and non-existence, and through hundreds of states of pleasure and pain.
Her steadfast fortitude was not shattered by the upheavals of the turning of the ages, nor by the chains of latent impressions, nor by the falling thunderbolts of delusion;
even when assailed by the sons of Danu, those lords of enemies who had fled in their hundreds.

The latent impression (vāsanā) bears a body like that of Indra, stripped of its splendor and shattered by shame; this constant whirlwind of destiny (niyativātyā), scattering a continuous succession of the dust of created beings, perpetually enters the throat of the serpent of Time (kālavyāla).
All the waters of objective entities fall incessantly from every side, with their fruits as foam, into the mouth of the submarine fire of non-existence; meanwhile,
the diverse potencies of substances flash forth, arising spontaneously.
Endowed with their own nature alone, like the shimmering beauty of waters,
the lion of Death, with its mane bristling, devours even the vast and numerous young elephants of the world, which are filled with the pearls of living beings.
The mountains of the world-system are its fruits, the masses of clouds are its wings, and it sheds the waters;
these birds of the universe are born, they die, and they fly.
Upon the wall of consciousness, bright with vibration, by means of the five senses as its colors, [the world is painted].
The painter of destiny unfolds the variegated pictures of saṃsāra—
[a power] that moves incessantly, ordaining all activity,
whose parts are as subtle as a hundredth of a blink of an eye, which is pure, and whose sprouts are ever-encouraged.
Steadfast beings of the stationary class perceive, as if through meditation, the subtle movement of time that brings about their own arising;
[they do so] by means of that which arises from passion and hatred, and consists of existence and non-existence.

All classes of moving beings are worn out by the delusion of old age and death; bearing the weight of their own past misdeeds, rows of insects on the surface of the earth are tormented for a fixed period of time by destiny.
In an instant, this serpent of Time— possessing vast coils and an opening difficult to perceive— swallows everything while remaining invisible and at ease,
from the moment of a single *kṣaṇa* up to the end of a *kalpa*, by means of its coloring with light and darkness.

Having observed something at the proper time, it was embraced within his own body. Here in the sky of Time (kālakhe), the six planetary deities of the seasons move about, intense with cold, wind, and heat, radiant with blossoming flowers, and bestowing fruit.
In this begging bowl that is the cosmic egg, the blessed Kālī, who is Action itself,
repeatedly gives and gives the alms of all beings, desiring to receive them back.
Within the hollow of the lotus of the three worlds, where the mass of milk comes to rest...
The swarm of bees that is the multitude of living beings produces a great humming sound.
She has a dark-blue braid like the gloom of night, eyes as flickering as the sun and moon,
and she whose body is the earth, the best of mountains, and the abode of Brahmā, Upendra, Hara, Indra, and the rest.

Having the reality of Brahman as her sole father, with breasts hanging down, she has the power of consciousness (cicchakti) as her mother; she is gross yet tremulous, possessing the density of lightning. She has a lattice of stars for teeth, and her lower lip is redder than the twilight.
Holding the entire Padminī forest in her hand, with the city of Indra as her face;
having the seven oceans as her pearl necklace, draped in dark blue garments;
with Jambudvīpa as her great navel, and the beauty of the forests as the line of hair upon her body.
Having come into being again and again, the aged mistress of the three worlds perishes;
having been destroyed, she is born repeatedly, causing manifold delusions.
She is submerged by others and then raised up within the terrifying great ocean of time.
With the bubbles of the cosmic eggs bursting away at every moment of conceptualization,
the cranes of worldly existence have repeatedly alighted and flown away again and again from the unfathomable lake of time, vanishing in the blink of an eon.
Rising again and again only to perish, these continuous flashes of creation,
as delightful as the light of consciousness, quiver within the cloud of time;
with the crying creatures as their birds, they fall in an incessant, swift torrent.

From the Kāla-tāla tree, it is said, there emerge from the Uttāla tree the lords of the gods who protect the fruit of the cosmic egg; some of these leaders of the gods bring about the creation of Brahmā through their opening of the eyes,
while others effect the dissolution through their closing of the eyes, existing somewhere or other.
In a certain supreme city, there exist some Rudras by the thousands, for whom entire networks of kalpas are exhausted in the mere twinkling of an eye;
even they come into being or cease to be with his very blink.
For even such a Lord of Gods exists, for this state of activity is indeed infinite. In the void state of Brahman, which consists of infinite volitions,
what powers or diverse arrangements could possibly not exist?
Thus, this worldly process— which shines with the burden of the objects of thought and the mental constructions that are never exhausted— is the manifestation of ignorance.
It consists of prosperity and likewise constant adversity, as well as the afflictions of childhood, youth, old age, and death.
And those successions of pleasure and pain which constitute the bathing [of the soul] are merely the manifestations of the intense darkness of ignorance.
The eighth canto, titled "The Majesty of Ignorance."
Vasiṣṭha said:
In this forest grove of saṃsāra, situated upon the slopes of the mountain of consciousness, what kind of creeper indeed is this called ignorance— so blossomed and so widespread?
This slender body-staff, whose joints are the vast mountains, is enveloped by the skin of the cosmic egg;
it is that which makes the three worlds beautiful.
Pleasure and pain, existence and non-existence, as well as knowledge and ignorance—[all these belong to it].
In this regard, these are the vast branches, as well as the roots and fruits:
from pleasure, ignorance arises intensely, and that very same thing yields its fruit at the end;
from pain, ignorance arises intensely, and that very same thing bears its full fruit at the end.
This ignorance arises from existence (bhāva) and clearly bears fruit as that very same thing;
it attains being (sattā) through existence and bears fruit as that very same thing in an instant.
Through lack of knowledge (ajñāna), it attains growth, and that alone is recorded as its fruit.

Through knowledge one attains realization, and that very [knowledge] bestows it at the end. His body unfolds, possessing various kinds of splendor, bestowing the fragrance of latent impressions (vāsanā), and dense with a mass of young sprouts.
This [mind] is like a flower-grove of the day with the restless night as its bees;
it is constantly quivering, with living beings falling away like its petals.
Having repeatedly approached with speed, it is here and there [cut down] by the elephant of discernment.
Shaken free from the spreading of dust, it returns once more;
rich with emerging sprouts, bristling with newly formed shoots,
endowed with the flowers of every season, and abounding in all essential juices.
The river of births is densely packed with joints, leaking through the fissures of destruction;
it is filled with the essence of the expansion of enjoyments, yet it is eaten away by the woodworm of solitary reflection. Indeed, those successions of moons and suns blossom day after day.
O descendant of Raghu, those stars in the sky, which are tossed by the wind, are indeed her limbs;
they have reached the state of buds with their throbbing forms,
filling the hollow of the firmament.
The light of the moon, the sun, and fire is but her floral pollen;
for by this, she, fair-limbed as a woman, draws the hearts of men. She is a female elephant of the mind, with the warbling cuckoo of her fancies.
Variegated by the serpents of the senses and stained by the skin of craving,
it has attained height by taking refuge in the body of the dark-blue tamāla tree of the sky;
with the earth and heaven as its excellent pillars, it stands upon the ground of the garden of the worlds.
With the lower portion of the cosmic egg as its root-basin and its net-like structure,
she receives the watering of the waters of all the oceans, the milk, and other fluids;
she is a bee wandering through the three Vedas, colored by the blossoms of beautiful women.
Stirred by the wind of the vibration of consciousness, it is a vast-leaved plantain tree;
it is pervaded by the pythons of evil deeds, yet it possesses a bower of flowers that is the splendor of heaven;
it is densely packed with living beings like pheasants, bestowing various kinds of joy and intoxication.
Consisting of various flavors, variegated, smiling with various flowers,
pervaded by rows of various fruits, blooming with various colors,
encircled by various basins, and supporting various birds.
Harsh with various pollens, marked by various fragments of clouds,
budding with various creepers, rising from various forest tracts,
ascending various mountain slopes, and continuous with various mountains; MU_6,8.21–22.
Born and being born, dying and likewise dead;
uninterrupted and likewise interrupted, eternally non-cutting;
past and present, existing yet the locus of the unreal.
"Perpetually and eternally youthful, yet eternally having attained tranquility—
this is indeed a great poisonous creeper; when embraced, it causes the swoon of the poison of saṃsāra,
but when touched [with discernment], it perishes."
From here [comes] the flourishing, from here the dissolution, from here the growth, and from here the established order;
from here the waters, from here the mountains, from here the Nāgas, and from here the gods;
from here the earth-nature has arisen, and likewise from here it exists as radiance.

From here it has attained the state of the moon and the sun; likewise from here, the form of the stars. From here is darkness, from here is light, from here is space, and from here is the fertile earth.
From here is the treatise, from here are the Vedas, and from here is that which is free from duality.
From this [side] come merit, from this sin, and from this the dullness of the stationary state;
from this, through knowledge, they are utterly destroyed, and from this, through the cultivation of ignorance, they increase.
From this, they remain in a state of being worn away by merit, austerity, and charity.
Through this play of yoga, she has surely reached dissolution:
in one place she has flown away like a bird; in another she remains as a deity; in another she has become fixed as a pillar; and in another she has attained the state of the wind.
In one place she is merged in hell, in another she dwells in heaven;
in one place she has attained the station of the gods, and in another she exists as a worm.
In one place she is Viṣṇu, in another Brahmā, in another Rudra, and in another the Sun.
In one place fire, in another wind, in another the moon, and in another Yama;

whatever exists in the worlds, O dear one, whether it be pervaded by great majesty or reduced to the state of withered straw—know that all this visible world, even including Śiva and others who manifest their bodies, is ignorance (avidyā). The attainment of the Self occurs through the transcendence of that [ignorance].
The ninth canto, titled "The Play of the Creeper of Ignorance," ends here.
Rama.
"O Brahmin, having heard that even the pure forms of Hari, Hara, and others that have arisen are nothing but ignorance, I have fallen into a state of confusion. Vasiṣṭha said:

That which is untouched by any object of perception, peaceful, and the self of all— that exists here as Being, Consciousness, and Light, free from all conceptualization. From that [Light] arises *kalā*, whose nature is that of conceptualization.
Like a whirlpool arising from water through its throbbing form,
she is conceived as threefold— subtle, intermediate, and gross— and then,
by means of her own body which has subsequently attained the state of mind (manas), [she manifests again].
In these three states, this very same *prakṛti* is clearly designated by distinct names— sattva, rajas, and tamas;
know that *avidyā* is *prakṛti*, characterized by these three qualities.
This indeed is the cycle of worldly existence for a living being; its further shore is the supreme state.
Regarding this, these three qualities (guṇas) that have been mentioned are also considered to be of three kinds each:
sattva, rajas, and tamas; thus, each quality is further divided.
This ignorance is divided into nine kinds according to the distinction of its qualities;
whatever is seen here is entirely dependent upon it.
The seers, sages, perfected ones, nāgas, knowledge-holders, and gods—
"Know this, O Rāghava, to be the portion of ignorance that is characterized by *sattva*.
Of this *sāttvika* portion, the *nāgas* and *vidyādharas* are *tamas*;
the *munis*, *sādhyas*, and gods such as Hara and others are *rajas* and *sattva* respectively."
O Rāma, among the classes of beings born from the divine source, within the quality of *sattva* which is the nature of ignorance,
there exists a stainless state; those such as Hari, Hara, and others are indeed *sattva*,
for they are knowers of that [state] which is the *sāttvika* portion of *prakṛti*.

He does not become deluded again; therefore, he is called liberated. For this reason, O Great-minded One, these beings such as Rudra and others remain as portions of pure being (sattva) for as long as the world endures, until their bodies perish.
As long as they possess a body, these great-souled ones remain liberated while living;
at the end of the body, they shall abide as supreme lords, liberated beyond the body.
This portion, however, is merely ignorance that has attained the status of knowledge.
The seed attains the state of fruit, and the fruit attains the state of seed.
Ignorance arises from knowledge like a bubble from water;
ignorance dissolves into knowledge like a bubble into water.
Duality arises merely from the conceptualization of duality between milk and waves;
likewise, duality arises merely from the conceptualization of a distinction between the vision of knowledge and the vision of ignorance.
Just as milk and waves are one in ultimate reality, so too are they one.
In the same way, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is an identity between the vision of knowledge and the vision of ignorance.
Neither the state of ignorance nor the state of knowledge exists here as anything at all;
for that which remains here after abandoning both the vision of knowledge and the vision of ignorance is indeed what truly exists.
O scion of the Raghus, through the exclusion of their respective opposites, these two—knowledge and ignorance—do not exist. Remain firmly established in that which remains.
There is no ignorance and there is no knowledge; enough with this conceptual construction.
That which is neither something nor nothing, and which is called the consciousness of the intellect (*citsaṃvit*), remains as such.
That very same thing, when its manifestation is not known, is designated as ignorance (*avidyā*);
when it is known, that very same thing is termed the destruction of ignorance (*avidyākṣaya*).
Due to the absence of true knowledge, a false conceptualization called ignorance arises;
at the end, these two exist only in relation to each other, like a shadow and its object.
But when ignorance has dissolved, both conceptualizations vanish in an instant.
O Rāghava, these two dissolve, and that which remains is inexpressible.
O Rāghava, when ignorance is destroyed and the side of knowledge has also perished,
that which is left is either nothing at all, or it is this very expanse.
In this regard, it is seen that everything is seen, yet nothing at all is seen;
just as a banyan tree, though possessing flowers, fruits, and so forth, exists within its own banyan seed.
That [reality] is the manifestation of all powers and the casket containing all powers.
Even more empty than the sky, unknowable, and consisting of consciousness;
just as fire exists in a sun-crystal and ghee in milk,
so all this, arising in the sequence of space and time, is situated therein.
Just as sparks [issue] from fire, and as rays from the sun,
so do these flickering perceptions emerge from that which remains stable.
Just as the ocean is [the source] of waves, and as a pure gem is [the source] of its radiance...
The treasury of infinite cognitions and splendors is likewise eternal;
it abides within and without all things,
its nature indestructible at all times, just as space exists within jars.
Just as the magnet possesses agency with respect to the movements of iron,
even though it is itself a non-agent, so too is agency attributed to that [Self].
Just as inert iron moves by the mere proximity of the gem [the magnet], [so does the world move through the mere proximity of the Self].
By its very existence, this body likewise arises as an insentient form.

This entire world is situated therein, within that which is the sole seed of the universe, named Consciousness (citi), where "awareness" (saṃvit) is but a conceptual construction upon a further construction; it is like a mass of restless waves in water, the nature of consciousness being formless even more than the sky, wherein nothing at all exists.
The tenth chapter, titled "The Dispelling of Ignorance," by Vasiṣṭha.
Therefore, know this: this entire world, both moving and unmoving, is truly nothing at all; not even the slightest thing has ever attained the state of being a real entity.
In that regard, there is no conceptual construction whatsoever consisting of existence and non-existence.

Therefore, O Rāma, why do you strive for all this, beginning with the individual soul, which is ultimately vain? We do not find that "snake" within which is designated as "this well-awakened one," just as one does not find the snake in the delusion of a rope-snake.
The very Self, when not fully known, becomes the source of delusion for those who wander;
when known, it attains the state of Selfhood, which is the ultimate limit of all consciousness.
In the world, it is called "ignorance" (avidyā) when the pure consciousness is garlanded with the impurity of the object of thought.
Transcending the object of thought, it attains purity, freed from all limiting adjuncts.
For the person is indeed mind-only; when that [mind] is destroyed, he is not destroyed. When it persists, he persists; this Self does not perish, just as space remains even when a jar exists.
Just as a child, while walking, sees one who is walking, and while standing, sees one who is standing,
so too this mind perceives itself as agitated;
like a silkworm, it binds itself with the manifold threads of its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
And though it envelops the interior of the mind, one does not perceive it due to childishness.
Rāma said:
"Folly has reached a state of extreme density and remains ever-present."
"O Lord, what is one like who has attained the body of an immobile being and so forth?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"One who has not yet attained the state of mindlessness, yet has fallen away even from the state of possessing a mind."
Relying upon a neutral form, this consciousness remains within stationary beings;
there, where the sleeping puryaṣṭaka resides, it exists merely as pure existence, like one who is mute, blind, and dull-witted, bestowing suffering.
Rāma:

O best among those who know what is to be known, I consider liberation to be not far off for one in whom consciousness, through its state of non-dual existence, is established even in stationary objects.
Vasiṣṭha:

If that which is the awakening to the universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*), arising from investigating this with prior intelligence and perceiving things as they truly are, were liberation, then it would be eternal. (MU 6.10.13)
The complete abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanās) through thorough understanding— that which is supreme—
is known by the wise as the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya), the nature of which is the universal essence of existence.
Having deliberated with the noble ones and having examined the scriptures through spiritual contemplation (adhyātmabhāvanā), [one attains this].

That which resides in the universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*)— that they know as the Supreme Brahman. Know that state of deep sleep (*suṣuptatva*) to be the latent impression (*vāsanā*) wherein the dull-witted remain dormant within, like a sprout within a seed, which bestows birth once again.
With the mind withdrawn within and latent impressions (vāsanās) dormant on all sides,
deep sleep (*suṣupta*)— though characterized by insentience— is the giver of hundreds of miseries of birth.
Indeed, all these beings beginning with the stationary (*sthāvara*) possess the nature of insentience.

Having ascended to the state of deep sleep, they are yet fit for birth again and again. O virtuous one, just as flowers reside within seeds and jars within a heap of clay, so do their own latent impressions (vāsanās) abide within immobile beings.
Where the seed of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) exists, that is deep sleep (*suṣupta*), which does not lead to perfection.
Where the latent impressions are seedless, that is known as the Fourth State (*turya*), which bestows perfection.
This applies likewise to latent impressions, fire, debts, diseases, and enemies.
Even a tiny remnant of oil, enmity, or poison causes affliction; however,
one whose seeds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been burnt away, possessing the nature of pure universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*),
whether still embodied or disembodied, shall never again partake in suffering.
The power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*), whose nature consists of the seeds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and which possesses the character of sleep,
exists eternally as sapidity (*rasa*) within all things, from stationary objects to others;
it exists in seeds as a state of unfolding, and in inert things through their dullness.
In liquids, by way of fluidity; and in others, by way of solidity;
in ashes, possessing the luster of the sun; and even in dust, in the form of atoms; in dark objects, by means of remaining at their base; and in swords, by means of its sharp edge.
The power of the Self (ātmaśakti) abides in all objects— such as jars, huts, and cloths—
by taking recourse in the form of the universal existence (sattāsāmānya) everywhere;
thus, this [power] remains, having assumed the entire state of the perceptible.
Just as the rainy season with its thick clouds hangs over the sky,
so too has this true nature of it been described and investigated:
it is non-universal yet all-pervading, appearing as if real while being essentially unreal.
This view of a self is a non-vision that bestows the wandering of saṃsāra;
when it is seen, it brings about the destruction of all sufferings.
The non-perception of this [self], however, is called ignorance by the wise.

For ignorance is the cause of the world; from it everything proceeds. As long as ignorance is perceived as being devoid of form, it dissolves instantly, like a particle of frost in the heat of the sun.
Just as a person whose sleep is fading away finds that his sleep dissolves as soon as he reflects upon his own state with even a slight degree of mental activity,
so too does this non-entity vanish as soon as it is conceptualized as "What kind of thing is this?"
Ignorance is destroyed just as blindness is by light. When one approaches with a lamp in hand, desiring to see what is hidden by darkness, then all that darkness melts away like ghee in heat.
But the determination of the form of darkness is not perceived by lamps;
rather, only the destruction of gloom arises, possessing a stainless form.
In this way, when being observed, she goes away or flees somewhere.
For its lack of reality is seen through investigation to be of an unreal nature;
just as whatever is seen when light has arrived appears in that very way, so too,
since ignorance is itself non-existent, its non-existence is perceived.
As long as it is not illuminated, nothing at all is seen;
whatever is illuminated in whatever manner, that is how it is perceived.
Within this machine of blood, flesh, and bone, who indeed am I? Thus one reflects within oneself.

As long as it is investigated, everything quickly dissolves. When both the beginning and the end have been truly discarded as non-existent, that which remains within the heart in their entirety is known as the destruction of ignorance.
That which is both nothing and something, that which exists, is the eternal Brahman;
that is the reality, that is to be accepted, and that is the cessation of ignorance.
By its very name, its nature is known to be devoid of intrinsic being.
For the taste of sugarcane residing on the tongue is not perceived from anything else.
Ignorance does not exist anywhere; this is the undivided Brahman alone, by which the entire expanse of the conceptualization of existence and non-existence is adorned.
Ignorance is precisely this: the certainty that "this is not Brahman.
Its destruction is precisely this: the certainty that "this is Brahman.
When the web of appearances—such as pots, cloths, and carts—is declared here to be "not the All-pervading One," that indeed is ignorance.
If it is argued that the pervasive Lord is the web of appearances consisting of jars, cloths, and carts, then that ignorance has indeed vanished.
The eleventh chapter, titled "The Cure for Ignorance."
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, this is being stated by me again and again for the sake of awakening you;
without practice, O virtuous one, the realization of the Self does not arise.
This powerful ignorance, known by names other than "avidyā," has surely reached its full development through hundreds of previous births and now persists;
it is experienced by all the senses, both externally and internally.
Through that [process], the body attains an extreme density amidst both existence and non-existence.
But self-knowledge, which is beyond the range of all the senses,
reaches its pure being only when the six organs, including the mind, have ceased.

How indeed can that which remains transcending the powers born of the senses, and whose mode of being exceeds the scope of perception, ever become an object of direct experience for a living being? Therefore,
ignorance alone is eternally and thoroughly practiced by all embodied beings.
O sinless one, consciousness never [perishes] here or in the hereafter.
Therefore, by means of the primary portion of ignorance, one should burn away the other;
one should continue until, through mutual friction, it subsides of its own accord and becomes auspicious.
For nothing whatsoever anywhere yields fruit without practice;
whatever is attained in any field is the fruit of the tree of practice.
Even ignorance, though long practiced and deeply rooted, [is overcome] through effort.

Through firm practice of the knowledge of the Self and by remaining unperturbed, one should lead [the mind] to tranquility. Cut down this creeper of ignorance that has taken root in the tree of your heart with the stroke of the sword of the playful practice of knowledge, for the sake of perfection.

O Rāghava, dwell in such a manner as King Janaka did after he had known what is to be known— by means of the intense practice of self-knowledge. Adopt that very certainty which Marutta possessed in his deliberation upon what ought and ought not to be done.

Whether waking or even standing still, that knowledge possesses truth by virtue of its certainty; through which Hari descends upon the earth into various wombs for the sake of diverse modes of conduct— that is declared to be the state of knowing that [Reality].
O Rāghava, may that certainty which belongs to the Three-eyed One as he dwells with his beloved, or even to Brahmā who is free from passion, or to Bṛhaspati,
the preceptor of the gods, or to Bhārgava— may that certainty be yours.
Of Divākara, Śaśin, Pavana, and Anala;
of Nārada, Pulastya, and myself, as well as Aṅgiras;
of Pracetas, Bhṛgu, Kratu, Atri, and Śuka.
"O Raghava, may that resolve which belongs to other gods, chief brahmins, and royal sages who are liberated while living, become yours.
Rama said:
"O Blessed One, O Brahmin, tell me in truth that by which these heroes of great intellect remain steadfastly free from sorrow. Vasiṣṭha replied:
O mighty-armed prince, you who have understood everything that is to be known, listen clearly to what you have asked; this is the definitive conclusion regarding these matters:
whatever expansive web of the world is perceived here—
All that is the stainless Brahman; thus established, it expands.
Brahman is the direction, Brahman is the world, Brahman is the succession of beings.
I am Brahman; my enemy is Brahman; my friends and kinsmen are Brahman.
Brahman is ether, wind, and fire; Brahman is earth, water, and so forth;
Brahman is the three divisions of time, and all that is established in Brahman alone.
Just as the ocean increases within itself by means of a succession of waves, [so does Brahman expand within itself].
Thus, by means of the splendor of its categories, this Brahman increases in this manner.
Brahman is grasped by Brahman; Brahman is enjoyed by Brahman;
Brahman expands within Brahman through expansions by the power of Brahman alone.
If Brahman were of the nature of my enemy, and if Brahman were to do me harm, then that Brahman would be attached to [the state of] Brahman; what else could there be, and what could be done by whom?
For passions and the like are non-entities, mere mental constructs like trees in the sky.
For those whose conceptual constructions have been destroyed, what occasion is there here for further growth?
Indeed, within Brahman alone—though it is all-pervasive—there occurs movement, vibration, and so forth; since Brahman is the totality, how can there be pleasure or pain? (MU 6.11.26–27)
Brahman is the knower within Brahman; Brahman is established in Brahman.
Brahman vibrates within Brahman; there is no other self-existent entity here.
The pot is Brahman, the cloth is Brahman; "I am Brahman," and this entire expanse is Brahman.
Therefore, what purpose is there in the futile conceptualization of passion and dispassion?
When the Brahman of death has freely merged with the Brahman of the body,
what could so-called suffering be, other than resembling the delusion of a snake in a rope?

When one is established in Brahman—the bliss of enjoyment and so forth—within the Brahman that is the body, this [world] is fully accomplished as "I. Why then would there be the vain conceptualization [of duality]?
Just as the notions of "you" and "me" do not exist for two waves of water that are equally moving.
In Brahman, whose nature is vibration, the notions of "thou-ness" and "I-ness" do not exist in the same way [as they appear in the unenlightened state].
Just as when a whirlpool has ceased in water, nothing whatsoever dies anywhere,
so it is indeed when the Brahman-body has attained the state of Brahman.
Just as motion and stillness do not abide in water that is both moving and unmoving,
so too the inert and non-inert forms do not abide in the Supreme Self.
Just as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold, and as a whirlpool exists in water, [so do these forms exist in the One].
In this way, the nature of the Self consists of both being that and not being that.
Indeed, the delusion— "this living self must be of an insentient nature"—
belongs to one who does not know the Self, but never to one who knows the Self.
To the ignorant, the world consists of a flood of suffering; to the wise, it consists of bliss.
To the blind, the world is darkness; but to the one with eyes, it is light.
To the wise, the world has a single nature; to the dull-witted, it bestows the suffering of duality.
To a child, the night is filled with shimmering spirits; to an adult, it is merely empty space.
O Rāma, in this eternal, singular mass of Brahman that exists everywhere, nothing ever dies, nor does anything ever live.
Just as waves and the like in the great ocean neither perish nor are born during its surges and play, so too the multitude of beings [neither perishes nor is born] within the Self.
"This does not exist" and "this exists"— these are merely names for delusions within the Self by means of the Self.
Power alone, devoid of any external cause, flashes forth within like the rays of a crystal.
Through the nature of the power of the universe, Brahman itself remains established within its own self,
just as a cloud of water exists within water in the form of a web of waves and droplets.
How could there be the notion of death regarding Brahman through the destruction of the body?
For nothing such as a body exists apart from Brahman, just as waves and the like do not exist apart from the water in the ocean. (MU 6.11.43)
Whatever is a drop or a droplet, whatever is a ripple or a wave,
whatever is foam or a surge— that is just as water is within water. So too are the body, its mental construction, the visible world, and both the perishable and the imperishable.
Whatever structure and whatever meaning exist here, that is Brahman, existing as such within Brahman.
The various arrangements and structures of Brahman are like those of gold; they are not of a different nature. For the deluded, however, the perception of duality is merely in vain.
The mind, the intellect, the ego, the subtle elements, and the senses—all this is Brahman alone; there is no other self, nor do pleasure, pain, and the like exist.
[This is known] through speech arising from such meanings as "I am he" and "this is you."
Just as an echo resounds within a mountain, so does the Self expand within itself by means of its own resonance.
Brahman alone, when unknown, remains as if it has fallen into a state of ignorance;
for thus it is seen by the dreaming mind that the Self is dead by its own self.
If Brahman is not cultivated as Brahman, it becomes composed of ignorance of Brahman;
just as gold that is not refined as gold becomes mere clay.
But when Brahman is known as Brahman, it becomes Brahman itself in an instant.
Gold, once recognized as gold, becomes truly gold in an instant. For the Self,
which is Brahman and possesses all powers, whatever it intensely contemplates,
it immediately perceives that very thing in that manner by its own power, without external cause.
Those who know Brahman know this Brahman to be without action, agent, or instrument; causeless and free from affliction; self-effulgent and the Great Self.
That which is not fully understood is called ignorance (ajñāna).
Knowledge that has been fully understood becomes the destroyer of ignorance.
For even a kinsman, when not recognized as such, is called a stranger;
yet once recognized, he becomes a kinsman by destroying the delusion of being a stranger.

But when it is internally realized that "this is improper," that contemplation arises by which one indeed becomes dispassionate through distaste for what is improper. Likewise, when it is internally realized that "duality is unreal," that contemplation arises.
Therefore, by means of that [contemplation] through which one indeed becomes dispassionate toward this duality that is so utterly distasteful—
when it is clearly realized as "I am not this"— that very contemplation arises;
by means of which one certainly becomes dispassionate through [the realization of] the identity with false egoism.
When it is known that "I am indeed Brahman," the realization of Truth arises,
by which one is completely absorbed within that true, innate form.
When it is known that "everything here is Brahman," only Brahman remains.
Indeed, when the nectar is drunk, who indeed would not become composed of nectar?
Whatever the mind grasps, that it quickly becomes fully;
by the singular consumption of Brahman, one becomes Brahman itself in an instant.
When it is known that what is false is indeed in vain, the contemplation [of reality] arises,
by which all false perception is surely wiped away.
When it is known that everything is indeed real, the contemplation [of unreality] arises.
When that truth is extended and expanded, by means of which stability is attained within;

when it is according to reality, according to the true nature, according to its form, and according to its state—then, my dear, meditative cultivation reaches stability, and never otherwise. (MU 6.11.63–64)

Even when one's own kin have passed away for a hundred years and are forgotten, even though they remain as if unrelated, the mind nonetheless feels compelled to love them within. For even while the delusion of worldly existence persists— having been practiced through hundreds of previous births— [the mind still acts thus].
The self finds supreme bliss within the self alone when it is stainless; yet,
though the Supreme dwells eternally nearby,
the mind does not find peace within, even when that Supreme has become its kinsman, as if it were still dependent on an external bond.
Indeed, even when poison is placed in food in a most secret manner, memory— whether withdrawn or active—
manifests itself like that of the *cakora* bird;
for even toward one who has appeared after being practiced through hundreds of previous births, the highest friendship arises.
In this visible world which is devoid of self, this [notion] of a Self does not find clarity.
Indeed, even when the nectar of immortality is kept strictly hidden within one's food, does it not remain present to the memory?
It shines forth just as the moon shines even when shrouded by clouds on a night.
When the Self is eternal, true, and such as it is, it rejoices in itself alone,
even when the impurities of conceptualization have been obscured for a time by diversity or have been utterly destroyed;
thus, one should diligently wash away this stain with stains by means of the Self through the Self.
The impurity of evil contemplation is to be cleansed by the scriptures until it becomes white;
once evil tendencies have been stilled, knowledge and merit adhere to the mind,
just as saffron dye clings to a stainless white cloth.
The firm conviction is that everything— this entire manifold creation existing throughout the three periods of time—
is eternally, unitarily, equally, and purely Brahman alone. In every way, at all times, the universal is everything, including pots, cloths, and so forth.
"I know that this Brahman has produced the expansion of the world. (MU 6.11.75) "For me there is no suffering, no karmas, no 'mine' here, nor any desire;
I am equal, established in well-being, and free from sorrow—I am Brahman. This is the truth. (MU 6.11.76)
"I am the blood, I am the flesh, I am the bones, I am the body;
I am consciousness and I am the power of cognition; I am Brahman"—this is the truth.
I am the grass, I am the creeper, I am the shrub, and I am the forests.

I am the caravan leader of mountains and oceans; indeed, Brahman alone exists in this manner. The powers of the elements, preceded by taking, giving, and contraction—I am all of that, the conscious Self, Brahman, who assumes an expanded form.
I am the manifestation and the desire for growth of creepers, shrubs, sprouts, and the like;
yet the Supreme Brahman, whose essence is the *rasa* (taste/savor), is the peaceful one residing within the conscious self (*cidātman*).
In whom all is, from whom all proceeds, who is all, and who is from everywhere.
Thus, this firm conviction arises: "I am this very Consciousness, the one Self, the Supreme Brahman.

By such names as Consciousness (cit), Self (ātman), Brahman, Being (sat), Truth (satya), Righteous Order (ṛta), and Knower (jña), that all-pervading reality is designated—the pure Consciousness alone, devoid of any object of thought.
It is experienced as the stainless Brahman of consciousness— mere appearance, the awakener of all beings, omnipresent, and tranquil;
it is that which is accumulated by the entire collection of mental constructs belonging to the mind, intellect, and the host of senses.
Having abandoned all differentiation, I am the stainless Brahman-consciousness, my own manifestation.
I am the pure Brahman-consciousness that illuminates the reality of all causes— the world and its existence, including sound and the rest— and there is no decay for me.
I am the supreme immortal Brahman-consciousness, whose nature is the flow of a stream of pure consciousness falling incessantly; I am the light, the silence beyond the mind.
I eternally experience the form that flows without ceasing, the nectar of realization.
Day and night, I am the radiant Brahman-consciousness, untainted.
I am the Brahman-consciousness, free from latent impressions, peaceful like deep sleep, pure in nature as light, and appearing as the culmination of all enjoyment. (MU 6.11.87–88)

Where even a slight experience of the sweetness of sugar-candy and the like persists within the mind and other faculties, though they are unawakened— that I am the imperishable Brahman, Consciousness.
When the moon has risen for one whose mind is attached to his beloved...

I am the stainless *cid-brahman*, the self whose existence is conditioned by the moon; I am the pure *cid-brahman* who am that power situated in the sky, like a thread, which is perceived by people standing on the ground as they gaze at the moon fixed in the firmament.
Devoid of the conceptualization of pleasure, pain, and so forth, and likewise without a mind;
whose nature is the experience of reality, I am the eternal Self, the Consciousness-Brahman.
When the mind is fixed elsewhere, like a traveler on an unfamiliar path in the world, [the Self remains].
That consciousness which is free from fault—I am that all-pervading Brahman, the Pure Intellect (cidbrahman).

(MU 6.11.93) In the connection of earth, water, fire, air, and seed during the processes of sprouting, that power of emergence which exists within—I am that pervasive Brahman, the Pure Intellect. (MU 6.11.94)
The existence of the taste within dates, nimba fruits, and bimba fruits— which remains latent within them— is that very Brahman; I am that same consciousness,
whose inner state is free from both sorrow and joy, and in which the arising of mental construction has ceased.
In the matter of gain and loss, I am equal; I am the stainless Consciousness-Brahman.
As far as the earth extends to the pole star, so far is the line of vision stretched out;
I am that pervasive Consciousness, tranquil and pure, like the center of that space.
Even in the waking state, even in deep sleep, and even in dreaming, I am the ever-arisen,
beginningless and endless Brahman-consciousness, free from all affliction;
I abide like the sweetness inherent in hundreds of sugarcanes, which arise from the field of individual souls.
I am the Brahman of consciousness, uniform within all, abiding as the equal one. Pervading all, subtle in form within primordial nature (prakṛti), like the radiance of the sun,
I am that beloved Brahman of consciousness which illumines this entire expanse.

Like a mere fragment of the bliss of enjoyment, like the power of tasting nectar, I am inwardly measured solely by my own experience: "I am the Consciousness-Brahman, eternally existent and immutable.
Though its limbs are woven throughout the body, it remains hidden, like a fiber within a lotus stalk.

I am the stainless Brahman-consciousness, whose form flashes forth in cutting and breaking. I am the pervasive power of consciousness (cicchakti), which, though pervading the worlds, is like a streak of clouds; it is characterized by vibration, its subtle atomic forms are difficult to perceive, and it is all-encompassing.
I am consciousness, devoid of decay, characterized solely by the internal affection consisting of experience, like the essence of ghee within milk;
while the fashioning of bracelets, armlets, and bangles is not composed of that [gold].
