Like gold situated within its ore, consciousness (cit) resides in the body; I am the all-pervading Self that is Brahman.

That consciousness which exists both outside and inside the multitude of objects, such as mountains and the like, in the form of the universal essence of being—that consciousness am I, the untainted one.

That which is the unartificial mirror of all experiences, inaccessible to the traces of impurity— that is the Great Reality of Mind (cittattva). It bestows the fruit of all volitions and illuminates all splendors.
We worship the conscious self (cidātman), which is the ultimate limit of all that is to be grasped;
we worship the conscious self, in whom all parts find rest, who transcends all constituent parts, and whose form shines incessantly.
We worship the conscious Self, which always tastes itself within the pot, the cloth, the riverbank, the wall, and the body; which, though awake, remains in the state of deep sleep.
It is heat in fire, cold in ice, sweetness in food, and sharpness in the razor.
We worship the Self of Consciousness, which is black in darkness and white in the moon.
We worship the Self of Consciousness, which has entered into sweetness within sweet things and pungency within pungent things for the sake of the power inherent in objects.
In the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, and in the fourth state (turya) and that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta),
we ever worship the same Consciousness-Self everywhere.
It is the one in whom all volitions have been stilled and from whom every curiosity has departed.
We worship the conscious self (cidātman), from whom all agitation has ceased;
we worship the conscious self, who is free from curiosity, without support, effortless, indeed everything, partless, and devoid of egoism.
We worship the Self of Consciousness, which stands at the end of all things, yet is itself boundless and of a single form; it is the infinite beginning of consciousness,
the supreme thread stretched across those who have cast off the body of the three worlds.
We worship the conscious self (cidātman), which performs expansion and contraction;
we worship the conscious self, which, like a wondrous and vast net, encompasses within itself the bird of the world— both the subtle that is hidden within and the fierce that is without.
We worship that one Self of Consciousness, wherein all this exists and yet does not exist even in the slightest degree, which is both being and non-being;
it is the supreme cognition, the full ground of all perceptions.
We worship the conscious self (cidātman) abiding in all modes of existence.
We worship the conscious self, which drives the wretched machine of the body bound by skin, vital organs, and veins; which is partless, yet the support of all that has parts.
We worship the Self of Consciousness, which is partless yet possesses sixteen parts, devoid of the forms of mental construction, possessing all forms yet nothing at all.
It resides within the heart, throat, and palate, reaching the tips of the eyebrows and the nostrils.
We worship the conscious self (cidātman) which abides within the vital breath that is supreme in its coming and going;
we worship the conscious self which dwells within the hollow of the heart-lotus, which pervades the sheath of all limbs, and which is the mirror for the display of the worlds.
We worship the Self of Consciousness, which is without head, ending in the letter *ha*, luminous, indivisible, and the ornament of all beings.
Through the flickering of the breath at the mouth of the state of rest within the vessel of oil...
We worship the lamp of consciousness, which is both joined and liberated, existing both externally and internally.
We worship the Self of Consciousness— the root-fiber of the lotus in the lake of the heart, the colorer of all limbs, and the means of sustenance for all living beings.
We worship the Self of Consciousness— the nectar that is truth, which arose from the milk-ocean, which dwells within the heart of the moonless [sky], and which is incapable of being taken away;
it has manifested through sound, form, taste, touch, and smell.

We worship the tranquil Self of Consciousness, which is devoid of that very [duality]. We worship the Self of Consciousness, which possesses great majesty, which is unassailable by all agents, and which, though possessing agency, is yet a non-agent.
"All this is mine alone; everything is I, yet I am not, nor is anything else I.
For one who has realized this, the world is destroyed for me, or rather, it remains firm; thus, freed from fever, I become [peaceful].
This is the chapter titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Certainty for One Liberated while Living" (Jīvanmukta-niścaya-yoga-upadeśa).
Thus, having reached this certainty, those great ones were freed from sin; such was the twelfth canto by Vasiṣṭha.
"Abiding happily in the state where truth and untruth are stilled and equal," thus the wise ones of perfected intellect, whose minds are equanimous and free from passion,
neither reproach nor rejoice in life, nor likewise in death.
Thus, with their charm impossible to transgress like the arms of Nārāyaṇa,
they shone with unswerving forms like other Meru mountains;
they took delight in forest groves, islands, and cities.
Like gods in the celestial gardens and heavens,
they wandered through groves filled with flowers where the sport of swings abounded,
and upon the rocky peaks of Mount Meru adorned with various forest ranges.
They established kingdoms that had conquered their enemies, were adorned with chowries and parasols, possessed diverse wealth, and were characterized by wonderful conduct;
they all followed her in these various flavors of activity.

Adorned here with the procedures prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, they were engaged in delightful pastimes that captivated the dance of beautiful women— pastimes charming in their recreation and sustenance, and abundant in enjoyments.
They roamed through the grounds of the Nandana grove, which were filled with the songs of Apsarases, graced by lovely mango trees, and entwined with Mandāra blossoms; they dwelt there,
where all creatures were at rest and all was purified by sacred custom.
They crossed, in due order,

the waves of the ocean of battle— waves terrifying with the sounds of kettledrums, filled with wandering arrows, and where great elephants had been slain— amidst the household duties of sacrificial rites.
They remained amidst all dualistic modes of conduct— those characterized by human anxieties, those with hearts agitated and distracted, and those fierce with the turbulence of passion;
yet their minds were free from attachment, devoid of limiting conditions, and beyond delusion.

Unattached, supreme, and tranquil, he had reached the highest state of pure being (*sattva*). He did not sink at all, even amidst great perils that repeatedly approached him, just as the great mountain ranges do not submerge in the lakes.

O scion of the Raghus, he did not wither from the parching of sorrow, like a forest glade in the summer heat, for he was embraced by the supremely lovely Śrī, who sported like the splendor of the full moon upon a mass of water.

And they did not rejoice in floods of enjoyments, just as a medicinal herb does not rejoice in dewdrops. For those men, O Rāma, being entirely undistracted while constructing the cage of their duties, neither clung to nor abandoned the pleasant or unpleasant fruits that resulted.

They did not rejoice when their goals were accomplished, nor did they sink into despair when overcome by adversity; they did not exult upon attaining happiness, nor did they wither away in times of distress;
they did not become bewildered amidst delusions, nor did they drown in the succession of calamities.
They did not grieve with sorrow, nor did they weep like you;
performing only the actions required by their natural conduct,
they remained free from agitation, like other Merus.
Adopting that vision which destroys the sins of the descendants of Raghu,
and adorned with freedom from egoism, sport here at your ease.
Thus beholding this succession of creations exactly as they are, [you shall find peace].
Firm as Mount Meru and deep as the ocean, remain composed and free from delusion.
All this is indeed pure consciousness alone that has thus come to appear;
here there exists nothing whatsoever, whether real or unreal, anywhere at all.
Relying fully on your greatness, abandon this with indifference; O noble one, become one whose intellect is unattached everywhere, and thus bring about the destruction of worldly existence.
Why do you weep with such intense agitation and mourn like a fool?
"And the mind of one who is deluded by error is like a blade of grass in a gentle whirlpool.
Rāma said: "Oh, Blessed One! I truly perceive the correct form [of reality]."
"By your grace I have awakened, like a lotus at the touch of the sun. My delusion has surely vanished, like mist in autumn;
with all my doubts completely stilled, I shall carry out your word."

Free from intoxication and delusion, liberated from pride and envy, with a soul awakened long ago and sorrow long stilled, you speak with a clear and resolute intellect that does not again fall into suffering. O virtuous one, I shall perform without hesitation whatever you say.
This is the canto titled "The Description of the Certainty of Liberation while Living."
The Thirteenth Chapter: Rāma;
upon the arising of the dissolution of latent impressions through the play of perfect knowledge.
"O Brahmin, tell me how one rests in the state of liberation while living.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"The method for crossing over saṃsāra is designated by the word 'yoga'."
Know that this [attainment], which has the nature of the pacification of the mind, is of two kinds.
One kind of it is proclaimed on earth as the knowledge of the Self;
the second is the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa). Listen, for that is now being described by me.
Rāma:
Because one is easily attained and the other is free from suffering, which of these two is better—
that by the mere understanding of which further agitation no longer afflicts one?
Vasiṣṭha:
Although both modes have been declared by the word "yoga," nevertheless, this term has come to be firmly established primarily in the sense of that which is joined with the vital breath (prāṇa).
Thus, in the process of crossing over saṃsāra, both yoga and knowledge are declared to be equal means that yield a single result.
For some, yoga is unattainable; for others, the certainty of knowledge.
But for me, O virtuous one, the sequence born of knowledge is highly approved;
that which is known does not become unknown again even in dreams, for knowledge proceeds eternally in all states. (MU 6.13.7–8)

"Or perhaps [you think] that yoga does not easily succeed because it must be accomplished through the practice of *dhāraṇā*, specific postures, locations, and so forth; yet this alternative view is not sound.
O descendant of Raghu, both knowledge (*jñāna*) and yoga (*yoga*) indeed arise from effort."
In this regard, it has been said: "Your knowledge is stainless, with the object of knowledge situated within.
Mounted upon the chariot of prāṇa and apāna, dwelling in the secret cave of the body, O virtuous one—listen—this yoga is called the bestower of infinite perfection. MU 6.13.10–11.
O Prince, when the cessation of the throbbing of the breath from the mouth has occurred and the mind has reached its dissolution,
you shall dwell here in the supreme state, free from fear, with your composure stabilized through the practice of yoga.
This is the chapter titled "The Investigation of Knowledge and Yoga."
The Fourteenth Canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"Indeed, this [universe] exists somewhere within the infinite space."
The vibration that takes the form of the world is like a mirage in the desert;
therein, Brahmā, born from the lotus, became the cause,
remaining as the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) while revolving under the weight of the created beings.
I am his mind-born son, Vasiṣṭha, whose conduct is preeminent;
I dwell in every age within the circle of the stars that revolves around the Pole Star. Once, while I was standing in the assembly hall of Śatakratu in heaven—
Having heard from Nārada and others the story of those who live for a very long time, the sage named Śātātapa— silent, honorable, and high-minded— then spoke during a certain course of conversation.
In the sky situated in the northeast corner of Meru, within a pavilion made of rubies,
there is a glorious wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru) known as Cūḍa on its peak;
at the top of that wish-fulfilling tree, in the hollow of its southern branch—
At the edge of a vine of refined gold, there is a dwelling for birds.
In that vast hollow resides a glorious crow named Bhusuṇḍa,
free from passion, like Brahmā in his own lotus.
Just as he lives for a long time here within the treasury of the world, so shall that long-lived one dwell in heaven; no such being has ever existed before, nor will there ever be again.
He is long-lived, free from disease, illustrious, and possessed of great intelligence.
He whose mind is at rest is peaceful; he is beloved and skilled in the knowledge of time. If one lives here as that bird lives, then that life of men would be long and truly worth living.
Thus was Bhusuṇḍa described by him, who was questioned again,
exactly as it happened in the assembly of the gods by that embodiment of truth. Then, when the occasion for the discourse had ended and the host of gods had departed, [the conversation continued].
Out of curiosity, I went to see the bird Bhusuṇḍa. There,
where Bhusuṇḍa was situated, I reached in an instant that lofty peak of Meru, which was vast and composed of rubies.
With a brilliance like molten ochre and the splendor of fire,
as if delighting the quarters of the sky with the flavor of honeyed liquor,
he appeared like a mountain massed with the glowing embers of the conflagration at the end of an aeon.
Like smoke from sapphire stones that reddens the sky with its light,
he stood upon the mountain like a mass of all colors gathered together,
a single dense source for all the clouds of twilight.
As he was departing from Meru, the lovely submarine fire— the digestive heat of the body— issued forth through the *brahmanāḍī* and reached his head,
appearing like the goddess of the Sumeru forest dyed with fresh lac.
His hand, with its fingers like crests, was raised to the sky as if in play to seize the moon;
with its reddish garlands of flames,
it seemed to move through the air toward the heavens like a mass of clouds, or like the submarine fire situated within a mountain.
With its peaks like fingers as if touching the sky,
and with the tips of its shimmering rays for fingernails, it seemed to kiss the heights;
it possessed chasms of sparkling gem-stones and golden caves radiant with light.
A cloudless sky filled with the pollen of autumn flowers, where Vidyādharas and gods wandered;
where the wind was graced by the sounding of flutes, and jeweled-creeper women danced;
where the thundering clouds served as drums—such was the theater for the mountain’s performance.
Rich with clusters of blossoming flowers and swarms of humming bees, it was as if clearly manifesting a row of teeth through its succession of petals, as if in playful laughter; there,
groups of Apsarases were swinging on swings, their passion and intoxication unrestrained.
He was a sage resting upon a stone, with a divine couple taking refuge in his cave;
clad in fine silken garments and a white deerskin, wearing the Gaṅgā as his sacred thread,
he stood like a tawny ascetic holding a bamboo staff.
Resounding with the roar of the Ganges' cascades, it was filled with celestial beings dwelling in vine-arbors; it was made beautiful by the songs of Gandharvas and sweetened by fragrant breezes.
It was adorned with blossoming golden lotuses as its crest-ornaments and decorated with stars as its jewels.
The tawny head of Mount Meru seemed to have reached the very limit of the sky;

it was like a playful mountain for the world of celestial maidens, adorned with pure and variegated patterns fashioned by fate from heaps of jewels and flowers in white, green, yellow, pale red, and white— the fresh colors of gems and blossoms.
In the Bhuśuṇḍa Episode, the fifteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Summit of Mount Meru," Vasiṣṭha said:
Upon his head, where the locks of hair were like clouds filled with flowers,
I beheld the arrival of the Kalpa standing like a circle of crests,
enveloped by clouds of flower-pollen and bristling with clusters of jewels.
Its height having conquered the sky, it was fixed as if one peak upon another;
it had a profusion of flowers twice the size of stars, leaves twice the size of clouds,
dust twice the size of rays of light, and was as tawny as lightning doubled.
In the mountain valleys, the song of the kinnarīs was doubled by the humming of female bees;
the beautiful creepers were made to appear double by the presence of celestial nymphs swaying on swings;
and the excellent birds were doubled by the flocks of siddhas and gandharvas.
Its bark-garment was doubled by a clear frost of jewel-like luster;
its great, excellent fruit was doubled by the embrace of the lunar orb;
and its joints were doubled by clouds that seemed as if they had become silent and dissolved.
Its trunk was entwined with delicious creepers, its leaves provided rest for kinnaras,
clouds cooed within its groves, and the children of the gods slept upon its banks;
[he approached it] after driving away the large bees of beautiful form with the sounds of his bracelets.
With Apsarases and Bhramarīs holding flowers within their hands,
and accompanied by the best of Suras, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, and Vidyādharas,
it reached a state like that of the world-tree (Jagadvārkṣī), filling the entire sky.
A dense web of buds, dense with soft young shoots,
dense with blossoming flowers, and garlanded with dense fruits;
a mass of dense flower-clusters and dense clusters of jewels.
It was rich with seamless garments and jewels, and agitated by the blossoming of creepers;
it attained a supreme variety through masses of flowers of every season, fruits and shoots of every season, and heaps of pollen possessing every fragrance.
In its marshes, groves, leafy creepers, joints, and flowers, I saw birds nestled in their dwellings,
nourished by fragments of lotus stalks as white as the crescent of the moon.
They feed on the lotus-roots from the navel of Brahmā; they are the swans of Brahmā’s chariot,
the younglings of the geese that draw it, singers of the Sāman chants,
friends of the syllable *Oṃ* and the Vedas, and eaters of the fibers of the lotus-stalks of Brahmā.
[He saw] those who had vomited forth a multitude of mantras with the natural sound of the utterance "svāhā," resembling dark clouds with a single, very steady mass of lightning;
like gods who drink the clarified butter, [they were] the leaf-like supports for the creepers of the sacrificial altar.
He saw parrots as dark as fire, young peacocks with crests like the tips of flames,
and excellent peacocks whose plumage was guarded by Gaurī;
they were experts in the entirety of Śiva’s knowledge imparted by Skanda.
He saw the kinsmen of those great sky-birds who were born and perished in the very heavens— those who had built their nests there, whose forms resembled autumn clouds,
some born from the swan of Viriñca and others born from the parrot of Agni.
Others born from the *kaumārabarhis* tree, others born from the trees of the sky;
the two-beaked birds, the *bhāruṇḍas*, the golden-crested birds,
the sparrows, the cranes, the vultures, the cuckoos, the curlews, and the wild cocks.
O Raghava, I saw there many other birds and multitudes of beings— such as parrots, blue jays, and cranes— just like those on this earth,
perched upon a branch of the southern shoulder [of the tree] high in the distant sky.
Then, while stationed in the sky above Puṣpapattrā, I beheld a circle of black crows,
garlanded with clusters of blossoms,
appearing like a mass of clouds at the end of an eon in the forest of the Lokāloka mountain.
There, I saw as far as a single hollow in the trunk of a tree,
strewn with various flowers and filled with manifold fragrances,
where those who subsist on the offerings made to the dwellings of Śakra, Vāyu, Yama, and Soma resided.
In heaven, the crows of meritorious women cry out as omens of beloved things;
they stand in the assembly with undisturbed forms,
like clouds that have been dispersed by the wind and spread across a level plain.
Standing in their midst was the illustrious Bhusuṇḍa, of towering form;
like a lofty sapphire set in the center of pieces of fine glass,
he was full-minded, dignified, impartial, and beautiful in every limb.
By constant attention to the movement of the vital breath, he was inwardly turned and happy;
renowned as "Long-lived" because of that longevity,
he was known in the world as Bhusuṇḍa, whose long life was well-known.
His mind was matured by witnessing the states of the arrival and passing away of the ages;
and he grew weary of counting the succession of Indras throughout every kalpa—
the births of the world-protectors, of Viṣṇu, Indra, and Garuḍa.
He was a rememberer of the gods, asuras, and kings of the past;
his mind was serene and profound, his speech was elegant, gentle, and charming; he spoke without crookedness, was a man of knowledge, and was free from possessiveness and egoism.
A friend, a self-controlled one, likewise a companion, a servant, a son, a teacher, or a master—at all times, in every way, and eternally, everyone is always to be praised by everyone.
O gentle one, he is serene, sweet, full of flavor, and great-souled; he is heart-pleasing, like a lake possessing unbroken coolness within.
The knower of the activities within the hollow of the heart-lotus, never abandoning his stainless profundity, and possessing the glory of a manifest intention—
this is the sixteenth canto, named "The Vision of Bhusuṇḍa."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, with my body blazing, I descended before him from the sky like a star falling upon a mountain, slightly agitating the assembly.
The lake of blue lotuses at Vāyasa-āsthāna was instantly agitated by the gentle breeze of my landing, like the ocean by an earthquake,
immediately upon seeing me arrive unexpectedly.
Bhusuṇḍa, however, realized, "This is Vasiṣṭha who has arrived.
He rose up from the heap of leaves like a young elephant from a mountain and spoke in sweet syllables: "O Sage, welcome!"
With hands born from mere volition, the young cloud quickly offered me a handful of flowers like a heap of gold, saying,
"Here is a seat," and presenting a fresh leaf of the wish-fulfilling tree.
When the leader of the crows had brought [the food] and abandoned his service,
and when the birds— led by Bhusuṇḍa— had risen with their wings slightly fluttering,
they saw the sage seated there, his gaze directed toward his own seat.
Then, together with Bhusuṇḍa and his troop of monkeys,
I sat down upon a seat in that grove of wish-fulfilling creepers (kalpalatā).
Thereupon, having offered water for the feet and other honors, Bhusuṇḍa, with a joyful mind, [proceeded].
The highly effulgent Bhusuṇḍa spoke to me in words sweet with affection:
"O Blessed One, after a long time, you have shown us your grace!"
Since we, along with these trees, have been sprinkled by the nectar of your sight,
O Sage— most venerable among those worthy of honor— by whom are you now sent, impelled by the long-accumulated store of my merit? From where have you come?
I hope that while you have long dwelt in this great delusion,
equanimity remains unbroken within your pure mind.
For what purpose has your self been distressed by the hardship of coming here today?
"You ought to grant us the command we desire to hear from your words.
O Sage, by the mere sight of your feet, everything has been understood by me;
we have been brought together by you through the merit of your arrival."
"Because of our discussions concerning long life, we have come to your memory;
therefore, you have sanctified this tree with your feet.
O Sage, since your arrival has thus been made known, I ask you here about this."
"The desire to taste the nectar of your words is expanding within me.
Having spoken thus, that long-lived bird Bhusuṇḍa, who perceives the stainless reality of the three periods of time, replied: "This is what was said by me there."
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O great king of birds, what you say is true;
I have come today specifically to see you, the long-lived one."
"By good fortune, you are safe with your inner self cooled; O pure-souled one, you have not fallen into the terrifying snare of worldly existence.
Therefore, O Blessed One, sever this doubt of mine according to the truth."
In what family were you born? How have you come to know that which is to be known?
O virtuous one, how long is your lifespan, and what conduct do you remember?
By whom was this dwelling place of yours pointed out to you, O far-sighted one?
Bhusuṇḍa said: O Sage, I shall tell you all that you ask;
this story of ours should be heard by a high-souled person without agitation.
When those like you— whose forms are worthy of worship by the Lord of the three worlds, who are noble-minded and great— listen to what has been spoken,
any inauspiciousness perishes through that proclamation, just as the heat of the sun is dispelled by the power of a cloud’s body.
The Chapter named "The Meeting with Bhusuṇḍa."
The seventeenth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, O Rāma, that Bhusuṇḍa was neither delighted nor dejected in mind.
Beautiful in every limb and dark-complexioned like a rain-cloud in the monsoon,
his speech was smooth and deep, and he addressed others with a smile;
he held the three worlds in his hand as if they were a single pāli-fruit being weighed on a scale.
Having viewed all things as mere straw and having made the cycle of worldly existence an object of his knowledge,
he perceived the restless flux of the world and understood both the higher and the lower;
steadfast and possessing a tranquil composure, he was like Mount Mandara at rest.
Complete, equal, and pure, like an undisturbed full ocean;
his intellect rests in the state of the ground, he is tranquil, reeling with supreme bliss,
and he knows the manifestation and disappearance of those born into the cycle of existence.

Delightful in form with his impetuous speech, his words being pleasant, sweet, appropriate, beautiful, and heart-pleasing, he—like one who has personally assumed a new body—is the supreme excellence that removes all fear.
With pure speech, he spoke these words in due order: soft, clear, free from agitation, and bright with laughter.
Like a charming cloud revealing its entire nature through its sweet thundering, [he spoke].
This is the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Bhusuṇḍa."
Bhusuṇḍa said:
"In this world, there exists the eldest of all the inhabitants of heaven,
the God of gods named Hara, who is worshipped by the God of gods."
She whose eyes are like rows of bees, whose breasts are like lofty clusters of blossoms,
is like a playful creeper clinging to half the body of a mango tree. She who is white as snow and necklaces, and who is entwined with clusters of waves—
His matted locks are entwined with the Gaṅgā as if it were a garland of flowers;
the glorious moon, born from the Ocean of Milk and flowing with streams of nectar,
serves as his crest-jewel like a reflected image.
He who was made immortal by the flow from the moon on his head,
for whom the Kālakūṭa poison is an ornament upon his neck like sapphire,
and whose pure [garment] born of fire possesses great whirlpools of streaks of dust.
For whom a heap of atoms is but ashes, and whose white bathing water is [the very essence of purity];
whose very bones— polished, fashioned, stainless, and surpassing the moon—
are the jewels within his body, radiant with splendor.
Whose garment is the sky— dark blue as a mass of clouds, with cool shoots of foliage, variegated by the specks of stars,
and filled with the wandering female jackals like a mess of cooked human flesh.
Whose house is the cremation ground, white as snow, abounding in many spirits;
whose kinsmen and mothers are adorned with garlands of skulls, drink the fermented juice of yellow and red flowers, and are draped with wreaths of entrails.
Whose bracelets were serpents with smooth bodies and shimmering golden luster, their crest-jewels flickering; he who,
eager to swallow the world, scorched the lords of mountains with the mere cast of his glance.
His conduct was that of Bhairava, by whose playful sport the immortals were terrified;
he restored the living beings of the world to well-being, while his own mind remained fixed in its natural activity.
Even the movement of his hand, occurring by chance, brought about the destruction of the cities of the asuras.
Those who are single-minded in form, free from affection, passion, and hatred—
those kinsmen of his are like mountains, being both full of moisture and yet devoid of sap.
Their heads and hooves, their hooves and trunks, their trunks and tusks, and their arms and bellies [are likewise].
And whose playful attendants have the faces of bears, camels, goats, and snakes;
and for that lord of immortal splendor, whose face shines with three eyes,
the other retinue consists of the Mothers, just like his own Gaṇas.
Before him, the Mothers dance, bowed down by hosts of spirits;
they are the sole consumers of the infinite multitudes of beings belonging to the fourteen classes.
With faces like those of donkeys, camels, and crows, they drink blood, fat, and marrow.
Naked and wandering about, wearing garlands made from the limbs of corpses,
they dwell upon mountain peaks, in the sky, and in other worlds;
they reside in forests, in cremation grounds, and within the bodies of embodied beings.
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Aparājitā— these,
moving through the left channel, are dependent upon Tumburu and Rudra. Siddhā, Śuṣkā, Raktā, and Utpalā are likewise deities.
Resorting to the southern stream, they take refuge in Bhairava Rudra.
Of all the Mothers, these eight are indeed the leaders;
following them are other goddesses by the hundreds of thousands.
Raudrī, Vaiṣṇavī, Brāhmī, Vārāhī, as well as Vāyavī,
Kaumārī, Vāsavī, Saurī, and so forth— these [goddesses] are thousands in number.
Following them are other supreme goddesses who move through the sky (khecaryas).
Born from gods, kinnaras, gandharvas, humans, and asuras,
there are others who follow them, numbering in the tens of millions,
dwelling upon the earth; they bear the name Rūpikās and subsist on men.
Horses, elephants, donkeys, crows, camels, pythons, monkeys,
and such like mounts they possess as they roam throughout the three worlds.
Some among them follow the nature of beasts, remaining fixed in petty actions.
Some, having realized that which is to be known, abide in the state of liberation while living.
Among those most worthy mothers, O leader of sages,
there exists a mother renowned as Alambuṣā, O giver of honor.
And Vajrāśrituṇḍa, known as Caṇḍa, resembles a mountain of sapphire;
his vehicle is a crow, just as Garuḍa is the vehicle of Vaiṣṇavī.
Thus, those Mothers, endowed with the eight sovereign powers, possess fierce activities.
Once, having gathered together, they held a meeting in the sky;
having worshipped the two gods Tumburu and Bhairava, who are worthy of worship by the whole world,
and being gratified by blood and wine, they engaged in conversations of diverse meaning.
Then, in the course of their conversation, this talk arose:
"Does the god Umāpati look upon us with indifference?
Let us display our power to him, so that he may no longer disregard us."
"Upon merely seeing her great power, he will treat us with contempt.
Having thus resolved, those goddesses, having brought Umā herself under their control, respectfully sprinkled her while her face and limbs were pale.

On that day of Pārvatī’s consecration, there was a great festival; the goddesses turned her— who had been snatched away by illusion from her husband’s side and had met with ruin— into a ball of rice, as her hair hung disheveled.
For all of them, there arose a performance of dance and song that was enchanting;
others danced with unrestrained clamor,
their garments cast aside, their hips and bellies revealed by the wide flinging of their long limbs.
Others laughed with a loud clamor like the roar of a dense thundercloud and the sound of unrestrained cymbals,
their limbs quivering as they rattled the ḍamaru drums;
others, delighted by the drinking bout, sang so that the mountain caves resounded.
In the hollow of the world-pavilion, which resounded with the humming of bees,
others drank a beverage consisting of well-chewed, moist heads and hooves,
while the cavities of the sky rang with their playful *ghuraghura* sounds.

They drank, they rose up on high, they crossed over, they arrived, they stayed, they laughed, they filled [the space], they offered oblations, they fell, they leaped aloft, they danced incessantly, and the goddesses ate sweet flesh; with their frantic dancing, they turned the three worlds upside down.
The canto titled "Description of the Mothers' Conduct."
The nineteenth canto: Bhusuṇḍa.
While this festival was taking place, those excellent steeds of theirs—
In that same way, intoxicated, they laughed, danced, and even drank blood.
There, some women intoxicated by the wine of their lovers danced in the sky;
the white swans of Brahmā’s chariot and the crow who was the charioteer of Alambuṣā also danced.

As the female swans danced and drank the wine, their passion arose perfectly, like the tide upon the shores of the ocean. Having become intoxicated and filled with passion, all those female swans gradually—
Then that crow named Caṇḍa looked back;
indeed, this crow had become the beloved of seven young female swans,
and he took his pleasure with them one after another until they were mutually satisfied.
Then those queens, highly gratified, became pregnant;
and having performed their dance, they attained a state of perfect tranquility and freedom from pride. They offered the beloved Umā, who had become food, to the Lord.

"For the sake of food, Mahāmāyā gave those [beings] to the wielder of the trident. When the moon-crested Lord learned that "my beloved was given as food," he became enraged toward the host of Mothers.
Then those [goddesses], having brought her forth once more by the gift of their own limbs,
gave Pārvatī again through marriage to the Moon-crested Lord.
Then the goddesses, Hara himself, and likewise the retinue of these two—
With hearts full of contentment, they all departed toward their respective directions.
O Lord of Sages, those Brahmin geese became pregnant;
they recounted to the Brahmin goddess the entire account exactly as it had occurred.

"O calves, my daughters-in-law, you are now pregnant; you are no longer capable of the work of the chariot. Now, wander about at your own pleasure," said the queen, full of compassion, as she dismissed the female swans who were languid from pregnancy.

She remained at her ease in that non-conceptual meditative absorption, O Brāhmaṇī. Then, O Lord of Sages, those royal swans, languid from pregnancy, moved about within the lotus-pond of Brahmā’s navel-lotus.
Thus, when their wombs were fully matured, those women gave birth upon the tender petals of the navel-lotus to soft eggs, just as creepers produce sprouts.
When the time had arrived, twenty-one eggs emerged from there.
At the descent of the embryo, they split apart with a roar like cosmic eggs;
from those very eggs, O Sage,
were born we twenty-one brothers, the sons of Caṇḍa, who are crows.

They were born and grew up upon that lotus petal; having developed their wings, they became capable of flying through the sky. Then the blessed goddess Brāhmī, together with her mothers, the female swans, [departed from] there.
Having been properly propitiated for a long time and being devoted to meditative concentration,
the Blessed Lady herself, at that time, was moved by our supreme faith;
thus were we favored by her limbs, so that we now remain liberated.
Having resolved, "We shall remain in a secluded place, our minds fully content and tranquil, established in meditation," we went to our father's side.
Then we were embraced by our father, and Alambusā was honored by us.
They were seen by her with favor, standing there self-restrained.
Caṇḍaka said:
"O sons, have you [escaped] from that which is woven together by the threads of limitless latent impressions (*vāsanā*)?"
"Sirs, you have surely emerged from this net of saṃsāra.
Otherwise, we shall pray to the Blessed Lady, who is compassionate toward her servants,
so that you may become those who have reached the further shore of knowledge."
The crows said:
"Father, enough of what is to be known; by the grace of the Goddess Brāhmī, it has been understood.
However, we desire an excellent place for dwelling in solitude."
Caṇḍaka:

Listen, my sons who desire a nest; I shall proclaim this supreme, most stable, and purifying place, free from fault. Dwell there for a long time, fully satisfied and without fear, where all activity has ceased and delusion has vanished. MU_6,19.26
The twentieth canto, named the Origin of Bhusuṇḍa, and the fierce [twenty-first] canto.
There is a mountain named Meru, the support for all multitudes of jewels and the refuge for all the gods, possessing immeasurable and great height;
it is the lamp for the moving moon and sun, and the wife for the host of living beings.
The pillar of this pavilion of the cosmic egg is made of gold;
its golden capital is for the moon, and its jeweled pinnacle is like a finger. Resounding with the circles of continents and oceans, it is like an arm raised up from the earth.
Surrounded by the neighboring mountain ranges, seated upon his throne in Jambudvīpa, the king—
whose eyes were like the sun and moon— caused them to revolve within that assembly of mountains;
he was garlanded with clusters of stars like jasmine blossoms, and his single garment was the sky of the ten directions.
His body was supported by two *nāgas*, and he was adorned by the leader of the heavens;
he was fanned on all sides by the beautiful women of the quarters, who served as ornaments to the city,
with cool, thick fly-whisks dripping with spray.
His feet, sixteen thousand yojanas below the earth,
are worshipped by various asuras and great serpents;
his body, however, is eighty thousand [yojanas], with the sun and moon as his eyes.
He is honored by the dwellers of heaven— the gods, gandharvas, and kinnaras.
Just as kinsmen depend upon a householder, so do beings of fourteen kinds subsist upon him, whose former abode is no longer seen.
In the northeastern direction of this mountain, however, there exists a great peak made of ruby,
like another sun risen from the horizon;
upon its summit stands a vast wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru), surrounded by a multitude of beings.
He stands like a reflection in the mirror of the world’s summit.
Upon his right shoulder there is a branch with golden shoots,
densely covered with clusters of jewels and bearing fruits that shine like the orb of the moon.
There, O sons, a nest had previously been built by me, shimmering with jewels, in which I indeed took delight while the Goddess sat absorbed in meditation—
a nest covered with petals of jewel-like flowers and provided with fruits that were elixirs.
Its verandas were fashioned with wish-fulfilling gems as pegs;
it was filled with young crows whose behavior was guided by intelligence;
its interior was cool and pleasant, and it was strewn with heaps of flowers.
"Therefore, my children, go to that nest which is difficult even for the inhabitants of heaven to reach;
staying there, you shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation without obstacle.
Having said this, our father kissed us there and embraced us.
That meat which had been brought for the goddess and for us, he gave [to her].
Having eaten that and having saluted the feet of the goddess and our father,
we leaped from that place, the marsh of the Vindhya, away from Ālambusa.
Gradually ascending through the sky and emerging from the hollows of the clouds,
they mounted the mass of air and paid homage to the celestial wanderers;
then, bypassing the Lord of Day, they departed for the cities of other worlds.
"O Lord of Sages, having transcended heaven, we have reached the world of Brahmā.
Having first offered salutations there, we shall quickly report these words of our father exactly as they occurred to our mother and to the venerable Brāhmī."
Having been embraced affectionately by them and encouraged by their command,
"Go," we departed from the world of Brahmā after offering our salutations.
Radiant as the sun, we passed beyond the cities of the world-protectors.
Wandering through the sky, fickle, and moving upon the currents of the wind—
having reached this wish-fulfilling tree and entered our own nest,
O Sage, we remain established in silence, free from all affliction.

"Just as we were born, and as we have reached this state, and just as we have attained awakening with minds at peace—this very thing has been fully and unerringly told by me to you. Now, O Great-Souled One, instruct me regarding what remains.
This is the chapter named "The Attainment of the Abode" (Ālayalābha).
The Twenty-first Chapter: Bhusuṇḍa.
There was once, in a former kalpa, a world that had long been forgotten.

O Lord of Sages, this very event— which today extends so far back in time— has been described by me through my present state of existence as a result of past practice; for I previously perceived the world as being equal [to the present].
"Today my merits, accumulated over a long time,
have borne fruit, O Sage, since I behold you here without any obstacle.
This is the nest, these are the branches, this am I, and this is the tree."
"Today these [limbs] have attained purification through the sight of you.
Having accepted this water for the guest-offering and this water for the feet, offered according to my means,
and having surely brought them to a state of purity, O Sage, instruct me with what remains."
Vasiṣṭha:
Having said this, and having personally offered water for the hands and feet once more to that bird Bhusuṇḍa,
O Rāma, I spoke as follows.
"O Lord of Birds, why are those brothers of yours—possessed of such character and great intelligence—not seen here? For you alone are seen.
Bhusuṇḍa replied:
"O Sage, a great length of time has passed while we have remained here;
O Sinless One, the successions of ages have worn away like days.
And during this much time, all my younger brothers—"
Having cast off their bodies like blades of grass, they are absorbed into the supreme Śiva.
Though they be long-lived, great, virtuous, or powerful, all are swallowed up by Time, whose nature is beyond measure.
Vasiṣṣṭha said: "O dear one,
as the masses of wind, carrying the sun and moon mounted upon their shoulders, blow incessantly with great speed, I hope you are not distressed?"
O father, how is it that you do not grow weary after being for so long in the extreme proximity of the sun’s rays, which burn the forest groves of the great mountains of sunrise and sunset?
And likewise, [how do you endure] the cool rays of the moon, which turn water into stone?
"O dear one, are you not weary by those clouds of the kalpa that have come so very near, resting here incessantly? O dear one,
how are you not weary by these mists that can be cut away even with an axe?"
Established in the highest state, how is it that this lofty wish-fulfilling tree does not tremble amidst the uneven agitations of the world?
Bhusuṇḍa said:
"O Brahmin, this life of a bird is without support or home, despised by all the world, and insignificant among all living beings—
especially when spent in such remote and desolate forests."
Its existence has been fashioned by the Creator either in the void or in the path of the sky.
O Lord, how can there be freedom from sorrow for a bird born into this world, living, and bound by the snares of hope?

But we, O Blessed One, are always endowed with contentment in our own self; we are never deluded by the formless delusions of the world. Satisfied with our own nature alone, we are freed from painful exertions.
"O Brahmin, we merely pass the time here in our own abode;
we neither hasten the life nor the death of this body.
We remain exactly as it stands, with all our desires extinguished."
The state of the world has been observed, and the perspectives of worldly examples have been seen;
surely our flickering bodies have been abandoned by the mind.
[This occurs] in that which is constantly self-luminous and eternally free from distress.

O Brahmin, within the house of the Kalpalatā creeper, which is rich with the brilliance of clusters of jewels, I always perceive the movement of the divisions of time upon the summit of the Kalpa mountain;
through the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, I know time to be uninterrupted.
Even though day and night are indistinguishable here upon this lofty mountain peak,
I know through my own intellect the progression of the world's time and its state; having attained rest through awakening, I discern the essential from the non-essential.

O Sage, my mind has indeed become tranquil and free from restlessness. Like a common crow, I no longer fall into a state of helplessness due to the snares of hope arising from worldly affairs— those snares which are insubstantial and like the belching fumes of a corpse.
O Great Sage, through our intellect— which possesses the nature of supreme tranquility and is cooled by light— we behold the world as an illusion and have attained steadfastness; thus,
even amidst terrifying circumstances, our minds remain unshaken.
We fear the forms of mirages as they appear in their proper sequence.
This worldly condition, charming in its inception yet flickering, is repeatedly scrutinized; herein, nothing whatsoever is composed of reality.

"O Blessed One, do all these nets of beings inevitably pass away and come back again, or not? What cause for fear is there for us in this? [Thus asked] as the river of the net of beings entered the ocean of time.
Though we stand upon the bank of the river of saṃsāra, we remain undisturbed.
We neither abandon nor do we grasp; we neither stand nor are we stationary.
Though gentle, we are exceedingly harsh—such are we, established upon this tree.
We have been favored by you, the best of men, who are free from sorrow, fear, and fatigue; being satisfied, we remain here with our fever of anxiety dispelled.
Our minds are neither distracted here and there, nor are they agitated in their functions.
"O Blessed One, our minds do not grasp at the reality of external objects.
With our own self having become tranquil— changeless, free from agitation,
and stilled— we are full and waveless, like great oceans on the day of the full moon."
O Brahmin, because of your arrival, our hearts are now filled with joy;
all our desires have borne fruit, and we have attained supreme fulfillment.
This [teaching] is like a cooling elixir, bestowing the highest bliss.
Whom indeed does the moonlight of association with the virtuous not delight?
By what can this essence of bliss from the company of the good be compared, by which even the Ocean of Milk— whose waters were churned by Mount Mandara— might be surpassed?
I consider nothing to be more beneficial for oneself than this:
that the virtuous follow those who have renounced all desires. What can be gained from enjoyments that are pleasant only at first sight?
From the wish-fulfilling gem of association with the virtuous, every essence is obtained.
With speech that is affectionate, profound, smooth, sweet, noble, and steady,
you alone act as a bee within this lotus-bud of the three worlds.

O Holy One, I believe that even for one who has realized the Supreme Self, this birth today has become fruitful through the sight of you, by which my evil deeds have been pacified; for the company of the virtuous removes all fear.
The Chapter titled "Description of the True Nature of Bhusuṇḍa."
The Twenty-second Sarga:
Bhusuṇḍa said:
"During the terrible upheavals of the ages and amidst violent, turbulent winds,"
This firm wish-fulfilling tree never wavers;
it is inaccessible to all beings who roam through other worlds.
Therefore, we dwell happily under this lord of the forest.
When Hiraṇyākṣa swiftly seized the surface of the earth encircled by the seven continents, even then the tree did not tremble;
nor did the mountain of the gods (Meru) waver when its body was shaken.
At that time, the tree Druma did not tremble, even when the mountain was leaped upon from all sides;
nor did Druma tremble when Nārāyaṇa, bending Mount Meru by the support of his arms, lifted up Mount Mandara.
When the winds of calamity blew, uprooting the rocks of the great mountains and shaking the trees of Mount Meru,
even then that tree did not tremble.
When the orbs of the sun and moon flickered due to the agitation of the gods and asuras, [the tree remained unmoved].
At that time, when the world was utterly agitated, not even a tree shook.
When the rows of clouds at the end of an aeon fell— shaken by the winds from the caves of the mountain tossing in the Milk Ocean— not even a tree shook.
When Mount Meru stood on all sides, slightly uprooted within the arms of Kālanemi, then the tree did not shake;
nor did the winds from the wings of the Lord of Birds [blow] during that encounter with the assault for the nectar.
When the Siddhas fell [from the sky], the tree did not tremble;
when Garuḍa, drawing toward himself the form of Śeṣa because his single coil was not yet completed, went for the nectar, even then the tree did not tremble.
When the flames of the fire at the end of the eon, surging with mountains and oceans,
were cast aside by the hoods of Śeṣa, even then the tree did not tremble.
How could calamities come to those who abide in such a preeminent tree?
"O tiger among sages, it is indeed due to our own misfortune that these calamities have occurred.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O one of great intelligence, at the end of the eons, when fire, water, and wind are surging forth,"
"How do you remain free from fever even while the suns are thus blazing?
Bhusuṇḍa replied:
"When the activity of the end of the aeon approaches for the maintenance of the world,"
Like an ungrateful person toward a true friend, I then abandon that nest;
I remain in space alone, free from all conceptual construction,
with all my limbs motionless and extended, like a mind devoid of latent impressions.
When the suns scorch, turning the mountains into liquid,
I then remain with a steady mind, having fixed the *vāruṇī* concentration.
When the winds of dissolution blow, shattering the great lords of mountains, [I remain thus].

Then, having fixed the *dhāraṇā* on Pārvatī, I remain motionless in the sky. When the world, including Mount Meru and all else, has dissolved and becomes a single ocean, then, having fixed the *dhāraṇā* on Vāyu, one with an unshakable mind floats through the sky.
Having reached the far shore of the cosmic egg, in the stainless state at the end of the principles,
I shall remain for as long as the lotus-born Brahmā persists in the work of creation, staying in a state of deep sleep with an immovable form.
Then, having entered the cosmic egg, I abide in the abode of the birds.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Lord of Birds, just as you abide there, unshaken by meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās), so do I.
"Why then do other yogins not remain [in their state] at the end of the kalpas?
Bhusuṇḍa replied:
"O Brahmin, this destiny of the Supreme Lord is indeed difficult to transcend."
"I must indeed become such as this, while others must become such as they are.
The necessity of what is destined to happen cannot be weighed;
for whatever occurs in whatever way, that is the certainty of inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
"By the power of my own resolve alone, in kalpa after kalpa, again and again,
this tree becomes thus upon this very peak of the mountain.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O leader of birds, you shall indeed be exceedingly long-lived,
a hero endowed with knowledge and discernment, whose mental course is fit for yoga,
and who has witnessed the assembly of many various and numerous creations.
"What, O auspicious one, do you remember? What wonder is there in these three worlds?
Bhusuṇḍa replied:
"A vast mountain rock, rough and devoid of grass or creepers."
I remember this earth below, devoid of mountains, forests, and trees;
for ten thousand years and ten hundred years,
I remember this earth below, filled with the weight of a burden of ashes.
I remember the earth below, where the lords of the days had not yet arisen, where the orb of the moon was unborn, and where the light of day was undivided;
its hollows half-revealed by the radiance from the jeweled slopes of Mount Meru.
I remember the world as being like the mountain Lokāloka;
I remember the gods fleeing in all directions, like men dying in a great battle with the Asuras.
I remember this earth, which for fifty cycles of four ages was held by the intoxicated Kāśis and Daityas, having become the inner harem of the Daityas—
a realm where the entire circle of Asuras reached their ultimate end.
I remember this hut-like world, the remnant of the three deities who were not inert;
I remember this earth, dense with thick trees, where for half of the final four ages no human beings were seen to be fashioned.
Thus I remember this earth, complete with its full four ages, joined by dense and immovable [mountains], where the conduct of people had not yet begun—
where the six-faced Kārttikeya was not yet born, and the gods were not yet despoiled by intoxicated Tāraka.
I remember this hut of the world, overflowing with the victory of the Daitya faction;
I remember this earth, marked in its center by Mount Meru as its pillar, submerged up to its peak in the floodwaters during three cycles of the four ages.
Out of fear, I remember the sky as being composed entirely of darkness, with all its celestial chariots and sky-dwellers vanished, and deprived of its stars,
moon, and sun; it became a place where the western quarter was devoid of Agastya and had become a single vast mountain.
On the great Vindhya mountain, I remember that hut of the world;
I remember these and many other such events.
What is the use of saying much? Hear the essence in brief.
O Brahmin, I remember hundreds of countless Manus who have passed away, as well as numerous creations characterized by many beginnings, and hundreds of cycles of the four ages;
[I remember them] as consisting of a single deity, pure, and devoid of men and asuras.
And I remember a certain creation consisting of three worlds and a single heaven;
I remember a certain creation containing intoxicated Brāhmaṇas who drink liquor, Śūdras who consume forbidden spirits, and virtuous wives who have many husbands.
I remember a certain creation where the world was devoid of trees, where there were no oceans, and where the beings were born as gods;
it was without mountains or earth, and its immortals and humans dwelt in the sky.
I remember a certain creation rich with a light devoid of both moon and sun; I remember a certain creation without Indra, without a sovereign, without middle, low, or high,
wherein all the quarters of space were equal.
In the division of time at the beginning of creation, within the three worlds,
there is the manifestation of gods and asuras, the emergence of the encircling oceans and continents,
the configuration of the principal mountain ranges, and the distinct arrangement of Jambudvīpa.
The creation of the notion of the dharma of the castes, the division of the world-system, the arrangement of the circle of constellations,
the formation of the Pole Star,
the birth of the Moon, the Sun, and other luminaries, and the established positions of Indra and Upendra.
The seizing of Hiraṇyākṣa, the raising up of the earth by the Boar,
the establishing of kings, and the bringing forth of the Vedas;
the overturning of Mount Mandara and the churning of the ocean for the sake of the nectar of immortality.
"The Garuḍa with wings yet unfledged," "the origin of the oceans"—
such traditional accounts (smṛtis) as these, which follow a sequence of very brief past events, are indeed remembered even by children, my dear; why then such insistence on them?
He whose vehicle is Garuḍa, yet whose vehicle is not Garuḍa; he whose vehicle is white, yet whose vehicle is black;
he whose vehicle is a noble bull, yet whose vehicle is no bull—him I have conceived, I whose life is beyond calculation.
The chapter titled "The Narration of the Account of Cirajīvin."
The Twenty-third Chapter: Bhusuṇḍa.
Then, O Blessed One, among those born in the world beginning with you—
Among Bharadvāja, Pulastya, Atri, Nārada, Indra, and Marīci; among Pulaha, Uddālaka, and others, as well as Kratu, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras; and among Sanatkumāra, Bhṛṅgīśa, Skanda, Īśvara, and the rest.
In Gaurī, Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Gāyatrī, and many others;
on Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Himavat, Dardura, and so forth; and among Hayagrīva, Hiraṇyākṣa, Kālanemi, Bala, and the rest.
Among Hiraṇyakaśipu, Krātha, Baḍi, Prahlāda, and others; among Aṅku, Pṛthuprotha, Vainya, Nābhāga, and Keli; and among Nala, Māndhātṛ, Sagara, Dilīpa, Nahuṣa, and others.
Among Ātreya, Vyāsa, Vālmīki, Vatsa, Vātsyāyana, and others; among Upamanyu, Manīṣin, Maṅkin, Bhagīratha, Śuka, and others—
some of whom lived not long ago and some of whom are somewhat remote in time.
Thus, what need is there for calculation regarding the recollection of the creations of today?
O Sage, son of Brahmā, this is indeed your eighth birth;
I remember that in this very eighth creation you were united with me.
Sometimes you are born from the sky, sometimes you are born from water;
sometimes you are born from a mountain, and sometimes you are born from fire.
Whatever your form may be, whatever your conduct, and whatever your configuration of directions and dimensions—
I remember this creation as being exactly like three other creations;
I remember ten creations consisting of men and gods who were uniform in appearance and conduct, whose dispositions were identical, and who possessed stability for an equal duration of time.
The gods vanished for five days,
having been cast up like tortoises from the ocean during five creations, O Sage,
while the Suras and Asuras were thrown into utter confusion by the force of Mandara’s churning.

I remember this twelfth [event]: the churning of the ocean of nectar. Just as a crocodile seizes an offering mixed with the juices of all medicinal herbs from the shore, so Hiraṇyākṣa thrice led the earth down below.

Having become the son of Reṇukā, Hari brought about the destruction of the Kṣatriyas for the sixth time, even across many cycles of creation. And for a hundred Kali Yugas, there are a thousand incarnations of Hari as Buddha.
O Leader of Sages, I remember that you attained this state through your very birth as a Śākya king;
I recall thirty disturbances of the three cities, two destructions of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, and ten instances of Śukra’s defeat by you, O Moon-crested One.
O Sage, for the sake of the arrow, I remember those eight leaders of the fever-demons who agitated the hosts of the gods in the battles of Hari and Śarva;
these [battles] occurred according to the deficiency or excess of the intellects of men in each age.
"I remember the Vedas, endowed with their various ritual applications and diverse recensions;
O sinless one, my many recitations are focused and complete.
The Purāṇas proceed clearly, revealed for each respective age."
Furthermore, I remember those very same ones, as well as others, in age after age— those histories composed by celestial sages and brahmins—
and another history of great wonder called the Rāmāyaṇa.
I remember that science of knowledge (*jñānaśāstra*), which consists of one hundred thousand verses;
wherein, by means of wisdom, knowledge is placed in the hand like a fruit, with the instruction: "One should conduct oneself like Rāma, not like the dissolute Rāvaṇa. (MU 6.23.22–23)
This was composed by Vālmīki, and he will compose it again now;
today it remains unmanifest in the world, but in time it shall be known. It is preserved by that very same living soul named Vālmīki, or by another, without being impaired.

"This is being done for the twelfth time; it had fallen into oblivion. I remember that second work of equal length, named the Bhārata, composed by Vyāsa in former times, which has been forgotten in the world."
This [work], which was forgotten, is now being composed for the seventh time by a soul named Vyāsa, as well as by another; thus,
the narrative scriptures have been expounded in every age.
O Lord of Sages, I remember various arrangements [of worlds]—
those very same ones, those others, and yet others, in age after age; O holy one, I behold and I remember these multitudes of objects.
For the destruction of the Rākṣasas, Viṣṇu will now undergo his eleventh birth under the name of Rāma,
descending to the earth in the house of Vasudeva to remove the burden of the world.
"Now, O Lord of Sages, the sixteenth birth will take place.
With his man-lion body, Hari slew Hiraṇyakaśipu three times over, like a lion slaying an elephant."
This delusion of the three worlds is never non-existent,
yet it is never truly existent, persisting like a bubble on water.
This undesirable delusion of the visible world resides within consciousness itself.
It is born and dissolves quickly, as fickle as a wave upon the water.
I remember the three worlds— many of them arranged in uniformity, others in disorder, and some with forms that are half-similar.

O Brahmin, in every Manvantara, when the order of the world has been overturned, I remember those very same deeds and such other conducts, as well as those other beings and their respective actions here in this world.
When the settlement has changed, when the familiar people have departed,
my friends are now others, and my kinsmen are indeed different; my new servants are entirely different, and my supports are likewise distinct.

At times I dwelt in solitude, taking refuge in the creepers at the foot of the Vindhya mountains; at times I took refuge in the creepers of the wish-fulfilling trees on the peaks of Mount Meru; sometimes I made my home on the Sahya mountains, and sometimes on Mount Dardura.
Sometimes dwelling in the Himalayas, sometimes taking refuge in the Malaya mountains;
at times, reaching a mountain, a forest, a tree, and a branch through my former disposition alone, I build my nest.
O leader of sages, even though infinite ages have passed since today,
this tree has grown with the very same configuration as it had before;
its splendor remains exactly as it was when my father was still alive.
Having previously established its configuration, this world has now reached its present state.
Here, the northern quarter did not exist before, nor did this mountain;
formerly, the northern direction was quite different, as was Mount Meru.
When the night of Brahmā has come to an end for each individual embodied being,
at the conclusion of my meditation, while remaining in the sky, I perceive this creation and know it;
[I know] the movements of the stars from the sun onwards, and the positions of Meru and the other mountains of the quarters.
While that [Self] remains, its configuration appears otherwise, and the directions likewise appear otherwise.
I consider this world to be neither existent nor non-existent; it is merely an illusion of the intellect.
This expansion of the power of the wondrous play of the Self’s own vibration unfolds.

I remember how sons have attained the state of fathers, friends likewise the state of enemies, and men have attained womanhood— and women manhood— hundreds of times. In the Kali age, I recall the practices of the Kṛta age, and in the Kṛta age, the conditions of the Kali age.

O Lord of Sages, I remember in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages certain creations that were unrestrained in their conduct; those beings, who had not seen the Vedas nor understood the meaning of the Vedas, lived according to their own conventions— I remember some such [creations] here and there.

O Brahman, while meditating upon the Supreme Brahman, I remember two thousand cycles of the four ages during which the world— including gods, asuras, and humans— was empty. [I remember] regions with various distinct configurations, and the storehouse of beings filled with diverse activities.
I remember all those various, playful, and elegantly arranged costumes from the days of Brahmā.
The twenty-fourth canto, titled "A Description of the Long-Past Creation."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, O mighty-armed one, that best of crows was questioned by me once more for the sake of inquiry, while standing at the tip of the creeper of the wish-fulfilling tree.
"O King of Birds, how is it that death does not afflict the body even of those who move about within the treasury of the world and engage in worldly affairs? Bhusuṇḍa replied:

O Brahman, although you are omniscient and already know [the answer], you ask me out of a desire to learn; for masters always incite their servants to speak. Nevertheless, I shall explain to you that which you have asked of me.
They say that not violating the command [of the teacher] is the primary way to propitiate the virtuous.
Death does not seek to slay him in whose heart the succession of threads of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), strung upon the pearls of his faults, has not been woven.
Death does not seek to slay him whom mental agonies do not pierce— agonies that are saws to the tree of trust and woodworms to the creeper of the body.
Like a monkey leaping from one thicket to another, he remains unshaken.
Death does not seek to slay him whose mind is not restless. Death does not seek to slay him whom the serpents of the body-tree, the flames of the fire of the mind, and desires do not burn within.
Death does not seek to slay him whom the serpent of greed— whose abode is the cave of his own mind and whose flood consists of the poisons of passion and hatred— does not consume.
He has drunk the entire water of discernment and acts as the submarine fire for the ocean of the body.

Death does not seek to slay him whom anger does not consume. Death does not seek to slay him whom the bodiless god of love does not oppress— just as a harsh, formidable, and turbulent machine does not crush a heap of sesame seeds.
Death does not seek to destroy him who has taken firm rest in that single, stainless, and supremely purifying state.
O Brahmin, these are the great defects that cause the disease of saṃsāra.

They do not disturb even slightly the mind that is concentrated in one-pointedness. Sufferings arising from mental and physical ailments, and those entangled in great delusions, do not disturb the mind that is concentrated in one-pointedness.
It neither gives nor takes, it neither abandons nor begs;
while performing its very duties, the mind is one-pointedly concentrated.
It neither sets nor rises, and it is neither forgetfulness nor remembrance.
The mind, when concentrated in a single state, is neither asleep nor awake.
Thoughts born of the transformations of desire and anger do not afflict the mind that is concentrated in a single state, even for those whose heart-space has been blinded.
Those things which are ill-meaning, ill-initiated, of bad quality, poorly expressed,
and followed by a faulty sequence do not cut through a mind that is one-pointedly concentrated.
[But] those things which are auspicious, of vast meaning, great, and endowed with virtue—

All [faculties] indeed follow after the mind when it is unified in concentration. One should direct the mind toward that which is beneficial in its ultimate result, which is true, unfailing, free from delusion, and liberated from the state of ill-directed effort.
O Sage, that which has not been seen by the impure mind— which, through long-standing alienation, acts like a demon of desire— should cause the mind to perform its highest function;
for it has been urged for a long time in the beginning, the middle, and likewise at the end.
One should direct the mind toward that which is beautiful, sweet, and wholesome;
one should direct the mind toward that which is free from states of misfortune, determined by the wise from the beginning, conducive to virtue, and beneficial for the world.
One should direct the mind toward that which is exquisite, sweet, heart-pleasing, savory, cool, and undecaying; it is exceedingly sharp, thoroughly discerned, supreme,
and the primordial object of vision beyond the intellect, which is the ultimate immortality.
One should direct the mind toward that supreme state which possesses unsurpassed good fortune.
In heaven— along with the gods, the gandharvas, the vidyādharas, and the kinnaras, and together with the hosts of celestial women— there is nothing whatsoever that is stable or auspicious.
O dear one, on this earth— with its kings and lords of men, its mountains, cities, and provinces, and its oceans— nothing whatsoever is auspicious or stable;
nor is it so with the nagas, the hosts of asuras, and likewise the women of the asuras.
In the entire netherworld (pātāla), there is nothing at all that is auspicious or stable.
In this entire world— whether in heaven, on the expanse of the earth, in the netherworld, or upon the slopes of the quarters— there is nothing at all that is auspicious or stable.
In this body— along with its face, hands, shoulders, feet, and the circle of the thighs, and including its blood and flesh— there is nothing whatsoever that is beautiful or stable.
It is agitated by mental and physical ailments and enveloped by a flood of suffering.
In activities that are eternally trivial, nothing at all is beautiful or stable;
nor is there anything truly firm or auspicious in thoughts that agitate the mind, crush the heart, and imprison the living soul.
Within the heart, amidst the surging Mandara mountains of the waves of milk-like water,
and amidst one's own restless conceptualizations and mental constructions, nothing whatsoever is stable or auspicious;
for they are incessantly subject to coming and going and are exceedingly hot.
In activities characterized by diverse modes of conduct, nothing whatsoever is stable or auspicious.
Neither is sovereignty over the entire earth desirable, nor is the various forms of the gods;
nor is the status of a Naga beneath the surface of the earth desirable—indeed, that alone is desirable where the minds of the virtuous find their rest.
Neither is the investigation of confused treatises better, nor is the critical analysis of excellent poetry better,
nor is the savoring of the sequence of the finest narratives better— than that wherein the minds of the virtuous find their steady rest.
Neither is a long life filled with mental anguish better, nor is death better, than the state of profound delusion.
"Neither hell nor heaven is preferable, for the mind of the virtuous finds its abiding place in neither.
(MU 6.24.37) Thus, all the various sequences of the world have taken root in a man through the dullness of his flickering intellect;
how then can the great ones find long-lasting stability in objects that are established upon such extremely unstable conceptions? (MU 6.24.38)
In the *Bhusuṇḍopākhyāna*, the twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Sole Elimination of the Resolve for Samādhi," Bhusuṇḍa said:
O best of all-knowers, there exists but one vision alone— unfailing, free from delusion, most excellent, supreme, and exalted. Contemplation of the Self brings an end to all sufferings.
She removes the long-accumulated fatigue of the tormented cycle of existence;
she moves through the vast courtesan-like expanse of the stainless path of the mind. By her, all sufferings—which are the manifestations of the misfortunes of sentient beings—[are destroyed].
Just as darkness is completely overcome by moonlight, so too does an end arise within [the self].
O Blessed One, that contemplation of one's own self, which is free from all volitional constructions,
is easily attained by those such as you, yet it is difficult to attain for those such as we.
How can those of ordinary intellect reach this state, which transcends all time and rests upon the supreme limit?
O high-minded one, however, her friends are those who delight in the contemplation of the Self.
O Lord of Sages, among those various [states] which have attained some degree of similarity to self-reflection and are as cool as the moon—
companions to the contemplation of the Self— I have chosen one from among them.
This contemplation on the vital breath, which brings about the destruction of all suffering, increases all prosperity, and is the very cause of life, has been undertaken. Vasiṣṭha said:
To the bird Bhusuṇḍa who had spoken thus, I,
though already knowing this, again questioned him calmly and playfully:
"O destroyer of all doubts, O you of exceedingly long life!"
"O virtuous one, speak to me according to the truth: what is meant by 'contemplation of the vital breath' (prāṇacintā)?
Bhusuṇḍa replied:
"You are a knower of all the Vedāntas and the destroyer of all doubts."
"O Sage, you ask me about this crow for the sake of a joke;
or rather, I shall repeat this very thing that has been learned from you yourselves—what harm is there in doing so? (MU 6.25.11–12)
Listen to this "Concentration on the Vital Breath" (*prāṇasamādhi*) being described by me, which restores life to Bhusuṇḍa and grants Bhusuṇḍa his self-realization.
O Blessed One, first behold this beautiful mansion of the body.
It has the three *guṇas* as its great pillars, is enclosed by the nine gates,
and is protected on all sides by the householder ego (*ahaṅkāra*), together with the wife— the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*)— and the kinsmen— the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
With the hollow of the ear-cavity as its attic,
with hair as its roof-covering, with wide eyes as its windows,
with the mouth as its principal gate, and with the arms as its side-walls;
Its door-arches were adorned with garlands of ivory *ketaka* flowers; its gatekeepers were constantly rattling their tongues like snakes, and they stood upon the thresholds of the porticos,
their feet encircled by the light of their finger-rings.

O Leader of Sages, for this body-house— which is smeared with blood, flesh, and marrow, and entwined by a network of sinews; which has a framework of thick bones like timber, and is like a well-plastered wall that has been thoroughly swept— [what use is it to you?].
Within the hollow, soft interior, adorned with a wall of ribs,
there is a gentle machine composed of two lotuses made of bone and flesh;
it has upward and downward stalks, with sheaths meeting one another and shimmering petals.
By means of its constant vibration, moving through the entire sky,
the wind seizes the soft petals of that machine;
as those petals quiver, that wind increases in strength.
Like a mass of vine leaves struck by the wind on all sides,
that wind, having increased and divided itself into many forms,
then spreads throughout this body— upward, downward, and in all other directions.
Then, that wind of the heart, whose diverse movements and activities are expressed by those who know it through technical terms such as *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *samāna*, and so forth,
[emerges] from the hollow of the mechanism of the heart-lotus; all the powers of *prāṇa* [proceed] from there.
Extending upward and downward within the body like rays from the lunar orb,
these powers of breath go out and come in, they leap about, they carry away, they sport, and they quickly fly up and fall down.
This very breath, residing in the heart-lotus, is called *prāṇa* by the wise.
O Sage, a certain power of this [breath] causes the eyes to blink;
another takes on the quality of touch, and another flows through the nose.
One digests food, while another utters words.
What need is there for much speaking here? The Lord Vāyu performs everything within this little body, just as a mechanic operates a machine.
There, O Sage, two winds move upward and downward; they are known as prāṇa and apāna, those two manifest and excellent winds. Constantly following their course, O Sage, I remain established.
Of those whose bodies are respectively cold and hot, who are eternally travelers in the sky of the atmosphere,
who operate as the two drivers in the great machine of the body without weariness,
and who are the sun and moon in the space of the heart, having the nature of fire and soma; MU_6,25.32–33.
Of this mind, which is the guardian of the city of the body;
of this ego, which is the lord of the two chariot wheels; and of these two, called prāṇa and apāna, which are its praised and beloved horses as they follow after me.
The movements of the vital breaths within the body and the state beyond the body are both unobstructed; O Brahmin,
for those who are always of equal nature throughout waking, dreaming, and deep sleep,
the days pass as if one were established in deep sleep.
Even when their limbs are severed into a thousand pieces, subtler than even a single fiber of a lotus stalk,
the movement of those two remains difficult to perceive while they exist;
having understood that movement of the two winds as it proceeds incessantly within the heart, one should follow that movement as it is impelled.
But here, O Great-Souled One, that man of joyful mind is not born again, for his bonds have been destroyed.
The twenty-sixth chapter, titled "An Inquiry into the Vital Breath," within the Narrative of Bhusuṇḍa.
Bhusuṇḍa said:
O Sage, although you know everything, why do you ask me in jest? I shall speak according to what was asked; listen even to that word of mine.
O Brahmin, this *prāṇa* is the power of vibration, its movement is constant;
this *prāṇa* is situated above within the body, both externally and internally.
O Brahmin, *apāna* also is the power of vibration, its movement is constant.
Within the body, both externally and internally, this apāna is situated downward.
This is the supreme prāṇāyāma which proceeds for the knower of reality while he is awake and even while he sleeps; listen now to that which leads to the highest good.
The wise know that outward orientation of the vital breaths from the hollow of the heart-lotus, occurring spontaneously without effort, to be *recaka* (exhalation).
[This occurs] as they extend twelve finger-breadths outward from the heart.
The contact with the limbs that occurs when the vital breaths enter is called *pūraka*.
When the breath descends from the outside into the interior through the *apāna* without effort,
the contact that fills the limbs— those wise ones know that too as *pūraka*.
As long as the *prāṇa* has not arisen in the heart after the *apāna* has set,
that is the state of *kumbhaka* experienced by yogins.
Inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*) each exist in two ways.

O high-minded one, listen to those who have been described by those of expansive intellect as being naturally present at all times, gentle, and free from effort, located externally at the station of the rising of the apāna, known as the "end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta). MU 6.26.10
O Lord, from the exterior limit of twelve finger-breadths, the *apāna* breath has arisen; therein, by its very nature, occur the *pūraka* and other [breath-techniques].
Its state on the outside is like that of a pot already formed from clay situated within [the mold].
