The wise know that [retention] of the apāna in the ether to be *kumbhaka*. But those who know yoga know that the outward movement of the breath, reaching as far as the tip of the nose, is the first [type], external *pūraka*.

The wise know that movement of the breath which, having emerged even from the tip of the nose, extends as far as the *dvādaśānta*, is the secondary external inhalation (*bāhyapūraka*). When the *prāṇa* has subsided right here and the *apāna* has not yet arisen, [that interval is the kumbhaka].

They know that state of full equilibrium to be the external *kumbhaka*. That inward-turned state which occurs without the rising of the *apāna*— one should know that as the external *recaka*, which, when meditated upon, bestows liberation.
That supreme density of form which arises from the *dvādaśānta* and moves outward from the *apāna*— the wise know that to be the other type of *recaka*.
These external and internal [breaths], such as *kumbhaka* and the rest, should be performed without interruption.

Having realized one's own nature as consisting of prāṇa and apāna, one is not born again. O one of great intelligence, these eight winds, when recollected day and night, have been described by me as bestowing liberation solely through their own inherent nature.
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping,
these do not come to a stop, for the wind is mobile by its very nature;
whatever one does or whatever one eats, one does so while recollecting these through the intellect.
In that state, the person performing breath-retentions (*kumbhaka*) and other practices is not the agent within;
for, having completely abandoned the external mind in this intensely focused activity,
he attains the absolute state (*kevala-pada*) in just a few days.
For a person practicing this, the mind does not form an attachment to external sensory objects, just as a Brahmin does not take pleasure in a dog-cooking festival.
Those of perfected intellect who remain firm, having grasped this view—
Indeed, it is only those who are untiring that have attained everything that is to be attained.
Whether standing, walking, constantly waking, or likewise sleeping,
if this vision is maintained, then bondage is not incurred.
Through following the inward and outward breaths, when unblemished awakening is attained,
one who is healthy and whose intoxication and delusion have been stilled shall dwell here within the self.
Abandoning all undertakings, the wise person remains healthy even while acting.
Having mastered the movements of the prāṇa and apāna, one who is well-established prospers in happiness.
O Brahmin, the rising of the prāṇa proceeds from the lotus-machine situated in the heart;
at a distance of twelve finger-breadths, this prāṇa sets outside.
O great sage, the rising of the apāna occurs from the exterior at the *dvādaśānta*,
while its setting takes place in the lotus-machine situated in the heart;
for it is there, in the space of the sky at the *dvādaśānta*, that the prāṇa comes to its setting.
From that [place], this apāna immediately arises thereafter.
The prāṇa, directed toward the external space, flows like a flame of fire;
the apāna, directed toward the space of the heart, flows downward like water.
The apāna is the moon that nourishes the body from the outside;
the prāṇa is the sun or the fire that cooks this physical form within.
For the prāṇa, heating the space of the heart at every moment, [sustains it].
The supreme sun, having first heated the space at the tip of the mouth, subsequently heats [the rest].
Having filled the space at the tip of the mouth and the sky of the heart,
this moon of the *apāna* subsequently nourishes [them] immediately after a single blink of an eye.

Having reached that state where the digits (kalās) situated within the moon of the apāna are swallowed by the sun of the prāṇa, one no longer grieves. Where the digits of the sun of the prāṇa, situated within it, are swallowed by the moon of the apāna...
Having attained that state, the mind, once seized [by it], does not undergo birth again.
Prāṇa itself attains the nature of the sun within the space both external and internal;
thereafter, it attains the state of the moon, which provides nourishment.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*), having abandoned its state as the moon which nourishes the body,
instantly attains the state of the sun, which performs supreme desiccation.
It does not reach the state of the moon until it has completely relinquished its state as the sun.
First, the vital breath (prāṇa) should be examined within; one should not grieve over place and time.
Having known the constant setting and rising of the moon and sun within the heart, and having found the mind’s own natural support in the Self, the mind is never born again.

He who beholds the divine Sun within his heart— along with its rising and setting, its moon, its rays, and its conjunctions— he truly sees. For the sake of spiritual accomplishment, one must perceive that darkness which is neither diminished nor exhausted, yet remains external.
One should destroy the darkness within the heart; upon its destruction, supreme perfection is attained.
When external darkness is completely exhausted, the light that illuminates the world arises;
but when the darkness within the heart is exhausted, the supreme self-illumination arises.
One should diligently observe the sun of the vital breath (prāṇa), which destroys the darkness within the heart, brings about full knowledge, grants liberation, and possesses both rising and setting;
for it is there, in the hollow of the heart-lotus, that the moon of the downward breath (apāna) goes to its setting.
From that state, the sun of the vital breath (prāṇārka) rises within, facing outward.
When the apāna has set, the prāṇa rises from the heart-lotus,
just as sunlight quickly reappears in that very place once the shadow has vanished from its body.
When the prāṇa has set, the apāna rises from the outside in an instant,
like a shadow quickly appearing on a new spot when the sunlight has vanished from all sides.
O noble-minded one, know that the apāna has arisen on the ground where the prāṇa was born.
Know indeed that the prāṇa has perished in the birthplace of the apāna.
When the prāṇa has set and the apāna is tending toward its rise,
by resorting to external kumbhaka for a long time, one does not grieve again.
When the apāna has set and the prāṇa is slightly inclined toward rising,
by maintaining internal kumbhaka for a long time, one no longer grieves.
[That state] which is rooted in the exhalation of the prāṇa and reaches the limit of the filling of the apāna—

By practicing the *kumbhaka* that is established in itself, one does not suffer again. Having seen the *kumbhaka* established in itself— the support for the exhalation of the *apāna* and situated at the end of the filling of the *prāṇa*— one does not suffer again.
When both prāṇa and apāna have dissolved within,
by taking hold of that peaceful state through the self, one does not suffer.
[One perceives] the apāna intent on consuming the prāṇa, as well as the partless place and time.
Having investigated both externally and internally, one does not grieve again. When the breath, intent on consuming the downward breath (apāna), is thus [controlled] within the heart and externally,
and when one has fully perceived place and time, the mind is not born again.
In that state where the prāṇa is swallowed by the apāna and the apāna by the prāṇa, both externally and internally— behold those two, space and time!
For a moment, the prāṇa has set and is devoid of the rising of the apāna.
They know that external kumbhaka, which is accomplished without effort, to be that state.
When the downward breath (apāna) has subsided for a moment and is devoid of the rising of the upward breath (prāṇa),
that internal kumbhaka, accomplished without effort, is indeed the supreme state.
This is that very form of the Self; this is that supreme, pure consciousness itself.
This [Self], though appearing as both being and non-being, once attained, one does not grieve.
It abides within the vital breath, just as fragrance dwells within a flower.

We do not worship the out-breath (*prāṇa*), nor do we worship the in-breath (*apāna*); rather, we worship the conscious self (*cidātman*) situated at the end of the state where the out-breath ceases and reaching the limit where the in-breath ceases—the middle between the in-breath and the out-breath. We worship the conscious self.
We worship the conscious Self (cidātman), the foremost bearer, who is the supreme life-breath of the vital breath, the highest vitality of the living soul, and the sustainer of the body;
in whom is all, from whom is all, who is all, and who is everywhere.
And we worship that which consists of all, the eternal conscious self; we worship the conscious self, which is the meritorious illumination of light, the purifier of all purifiers,
and the non-deficient contemplation of both existence and non-existence.
In the mutual friction within the heart,
we worship the conscious self (cidātman) situated in the wind, both externally and internally, as well as in space.
Where the apāna has set and the prāṇa has not yet arisen for a moment— there [we worship it].
We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), which is free from the stains of temporal divisions;
where the apāna has not arisen and the prāṇa has set—
we worship that reality of consciousness, which is a vortex in the space at the tip of the nose.

We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), the support for the state of the yogi, which exists in the two locations where the out-breath (prāṇa) and in-breath (apāna) arise, situated both externally and internally;
it is mounted upon the chariot of prāṇa and apāna, yet it is extended beyond prāṇa and apāna.

We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva) which is the essential form of all powers. We worship that reality of consciousness which is the god of the heart and the kumbhaka of prāṇa, and externally the kumbhaka of apāna, purified by the portion of pūraka.

We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), which is to be attained through the contemplation of the vital breath (prāṇa), and which awakens one to the nature of existence as the reflective awareness of the inward and outward breaths;
it is that which is the vibration of the vital wind and the cause of the bliss of that vibration.
We worship that Reality of Consciousness (cittattva), which is the cause of all causes;

that supreme state which is devoid of the stain of all mental constructions, yet is forever surrounded by the multitude of creative powers (kalā); that highest station of the glory of experience, to which all the gods bow down, we take refuge in.
The twenty-seventh canto in the Bhusuṇḍa Episode, titled "Description of Prāṇa-Samādhi.
Bhusuṇḍa said:
For this rest in consciousness has been attained by me, through the meditative absorption of the vital breath (*prāṇa-samādhi*),
gradually, by this very sequence, within my own stainless self.
O great sage, I remain established, firmly grasping this vision.
I do not move even for a fraction of a moment, as immovable as Mount Meru.
Whether walking or standing, waking or sleeping—
even in a dream— this perfect composure of mine does not waver from the Self.
Established amidst the ever-changing and unstable conditions of the world,
I remain inward-turned, abiding by myself through the self alone.
Even the wind might be restrained, or even water from its course.

I do not recall anything being suppressed by this well-poised concentration more than the following of the prāṇa and apāna breaths and the beholding of the Supreme Self; through great austerity, I have attained the sorrowless, primordial state.
O Brahmin, until the great dissolution, I live with a steady mind, observing even today the rising and sinking of living beings;
I never think of what has been or what will be.
Taking hold of my own present vision, I remain here;
having abandoned all longing for the fruits of actions as they arise,
I abide solely in a state of pure awareness, like one in deep sleep.
Having abandoned thoughts consisting of existence and non-existence, as well as those accompanied by the desired and the undesired,
I abide in the Self; free from affliction, I live for a long time,
constantly recollecting the moment of the union of prāṇa and apāna.
I am content with myself alone; therefore, I have lived for a long time.
(MU 6.27.11) "I have obtained this today; I shall obtain that beautiful thing"—such thoughts do not occur to me; therefore, I live for a long time, free from affliction. (MU 6.27.12)

I neither praise nor blame anything anywhere at any time, whether concerning myself or another, O virtuous one; by that I live free from affliction. I am not delighted by the attainment of the auspicious, nor do I feel distress over the inauspicious.

My mind is always equanimous; by that I live free from affliction. Having resorted to supreme renunciation, I have indeed forever renounced everything, including life itself; by that I live free from affliction.

O Sage, my mind is now peaceful—its restlessness stilled, its sorrow departed, and its desires extinguished; by this I live free from affliction. To me, a piece of wood, a graceful woman, a mountain, a blade of grass, fire, snow, and the sky are all the same.
I see everything as equal everywhere; therefore, I live free from affliction.
"What has come to me today, or what will happen again tomorrow morning?"—such a fever of anxiety does not exist for me; therefore, I live free from affliction.
Amidst the sufferings of old age and death, and amidst the pleasures of attaining a kingdom, I neither fear nor rejoice; by that I live free from affliction.
"This one is my kinsman, this one is a stranger, this one is mine, and this one is another."
"Thus, O Brahmin, I do not know; by that I live, free from affliction.
Whether eating, moving about, standing, rising, breathing, or sleeping, I do not perceive 'I am the body'; by that I live, free from affliction."
Regarding this cycle of existence, I remain as if in deep sleep;
seeing it as if it were non-existent, I live free from affliction.
To me, gain and loss, whether they arrive at the proper time or not, are equal.
Like two hands situated upon my body, by that I live, free from affliction.
With a vision that is steady, straight, clear-sighted, tender, and innocent, I see everything with straightforwardness; by that I live, free from affliction.
I have abandoned all sense of "mine" regarding this body from its feet to its crown; for me, whose mire of egoism has been cast off, I live free from affliction.
Whatever I do and whatever I eat, having renounced that [sense of ownership] even while performing those acts, I remain untouched by them.
The mind adopts dispassion; by that I live, free from affliction.
O Sage, whenever I perceive anything whatsoever, at that very moment I bow down and do not become arrogant; by that I live, free from affliction.
Even as a lord, I do not commit aggression; I am neither tormented nor distressed.
Even as a pauper, I have no longing; therefore, I live free from ailment.
While this body is perishing in form, the Self, the abode of consciousness, remains undestroyed.
I laugh from afar at the multitude of beings; by that, I live free from affliction.
Being composed, I grant no internal contact to the mental fluctuations that are driven by the snares of hope; by that, I live free from affliction.
I perceive the non-existence of the world and the existence of the Self, like a wood-apple held in the palm of my hand;
having awakened from sleep, I see this, and therefore I live free from affliction.
Wasted, broken, slack, decayed, agitated, crushed, and gone to destruction—[all these I have transcended].
I see everything as if it were new; therefore I live free from affliction.
I am happy when people are happy, and I am sorrowful when they are sorrowful;
I am a dear friend to all, and therefore I live free from affliction.
In adversity I am immovably steadfast, and in prosperity I am a friend to the world;
I am neither present nor absent in states of being or non-being, and therefore I live free from affliction.
I do not exist, nor does anything else belong to me; I do not belong to anyone else.
Thus has my mind been cultivated; by that I live free from affliction.
(MU 6.27.35) "I am the world, I am the ether, I am the sequence of space and time; I am action"—such is my understanding; by that I live free from affliction. (MU 6.27.36)
"The pot is consciousness, the cloth is consciousness, space is consciousness, the banyan tree and the cart are consciousness;
everything is consciousness—such is my state of being, and by that I live free from affliction.
Thus I am, O tiger among sages, the bee upon the lotus of the three worlds.
A crow named Bhusuṇḍa is said to have lived for a very long time.

Beholding and contemplating the three worlds as waves tossed upon the ocean of Brahman— varied in form by the power of their arising and destruction, sometimes submerged, sometimes rising, and with all visible objects in a state of agitation— I have remained here for a long duration.
The twenty-eighth canto, titled "The Narration of the Causes of Longevity" within the *Bhusuṇḍopākhyāna*.
Bhusuṇḍa said:
"O Brahmin, this has been told to you: who I am and what I am here for.
It was done out of boldness solely to fulfill your command, O master of the further shore of knowledge.
Vasiṣṭha said:

"O Blessed One, how wonderful it is that you have related this account of yourself, which is an ornament to sacred learning and a cause for supreme amazement! Blessed are those who [hear of] the Great-Souled One, who is exceedingly long-lived."

They question you as they would a second lotus-born Brahmā. Today we are exceedingly fortunate that you have related in its entirety, exactly as it was, your own pure and unbroken account, which purifies the intellect.
Wandering in all directions, I have beheld the realms of the gods;
yet in this world, no one greater than you has been seen.
Having wandered here, perhaps some great person might somehow be found?
A fortunate soul such as you is not easily found anywhere in this world,
just as a pearl is produced only within a certain section of a bamboo stalk;
for in the same way, one like you is born only within a certain portion of the world.
Indeed, a very great and auspicious deed has been accomplished by me today:
that you, whose body is merit and whose soul is liberated, have been beheld by me. May there be welfare for you; enter now the auspicious cave of your own self.
"This is my time for midday; I shall go to the abode of the gods.
Having heard this, Bhusuṇḍa rose from his tree and took with both hands, which were prepared for the purpose, a fine vessel adorned with golden leaves.
With the pollen from the flowers of the wish-fulfilling creepers,
that one of perfected intellect filled that vessel with the moon as the offering of pearls;
with that vessel for the arghya and pādya offerings, he [honored] me as if I were the Three-eyed One.
The elder brother worshipped him with devotion from head to foot; then,
saying "Enough, O Lord of Birds," and expressing his distress at the trouble of following him,
I rose from my seat and leapt up like a bird.
Having followed me for a distance of one *yojana* in the sky,
that bird was forcibly restrained by me as I seized him by the claw with my own hand.
Then, when I had traveled a long way along the path of the heavens, he became invisible.
That lord of birds turned back; for the association of the virtuous is difficult to abandon.
When he and I had both vanished from sight in the sky like two waves in the ocean, I returned my memory to the sages.
Having reached the circle of the Seven Sages and being honored by my wife,
I dwelt there with Rāghava, my heart blossoming with wonder;
meanwhile, Bhusuṇḍa, whose beak was auspicious, remained in that abode of the Kalpa-creeper.
Equanimous, with a tranquil mind, venerable, and possessed of his own meditative absorption,
that wise one remains alive even today upon that very same leaf of a creeper,
staying right there on that golden tree of Mount Meru.
Long ago, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, two hundred years after it had passed,
I met with Bhusuṇḍa on Mount Meru beneath a tree on its peak.
Today, O Rāma, the Kṛta age having ended, the Tretā age is now unfolding.
O destroyer of enemies, you were born in the middle of this Tretā Yuga. Today, for the eighth time, you met that very Bhusuṇḍa, who remains unchanged in his ageless form, upon that same mountain.
Thus has this wonderful and supreme account of Bhusuṇḍa been told;
having heard it and reflected upon it within yourself, perform that which is appropriate.
He who, possessing a pure intellect, shall here reflect deeply upon this discourse of the noble sage Bhusuṇḍa—
"He shall forcibly cross over the wretched cycle of existence, which is thick with the fear of worldly becoming and flows with the stream of the unreal.
Thus ends the Bhusuṇḍa-episode; this is the twenty-ninth canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, O sinless one, have I related to you the account of Bhusuṇḍa;
by means of this wisdom, Bhusuṇḍa crossed over the perilous strait of delusion.
"O mighty-armed one, having firmly grasped this view preceded by the practice of [controlling] your own vital breaths, become one who has crossed the ocean of existence, like Bhusuṇḍa.
Just as [he did] through knowledge and yoga born of continuous practice..."

Bhusuṇḍa attained that which was to be attained; likewise, accomplish that state. The virtuous, whose intellects are unattached, attain a state like that of Bhusuṇḍa in the supreme reality by observing the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
"You have heard these various philosophical views;
now, relying upon your own intellect, do as you wish.
Rāma said:
O Blessed One, by you—the illuminator of the stages—with the rays of your wisdom, the entire darkness of the heart’s unrestrained wickedness has been wiped away.
We have awakened; we are filled with joy; we have entered our own true abode.
"We stand here as those who have known what is to be known, O sirs, like those who have reached the further shore.
Oh, how wondrous is the conduct of Bhusuṇḍa!
Blessed One, that which has been proclaimed by you bestows the realization of the supreme goal."
O Brahman, O Lord, regarding that which you have described in this *Bhuśuṇḍacarita* as the house of the body, constructed of flesh, skin, and bone—
by whom indeed was it fashioned, or from whence did it arise?
"How has it come to abide, or who is it that abides therein?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"For the sake of awakening to the ultimate reality and for the removal of defects..."
Listen, O Rāghava, to this which I shall tell you in its true essence: This body-abode, O Rāma, has pillars of bone, nine gates, and is plastered with blood and flesh; it was not created by anyone.

This is merely an appearance; it manifests in this very way, having the form of the delusion of two moons, established as both existent and non-existent. For in the process of the delusion of two moons, the state of being two moons is indeed existent.
And in reality, there is indeed only one moon; so too is the state of the body.
For at the time of the cognition of the body, this body exists as established;
yet in reality it is non-existent, and thus it is said to be of the nature of both being and non-being.

In the context of dreaming, a dream is real; at other times, it is indeed in vain. A bubble is real in the context of being a bubble, but false at other times. Likewise, the body is real within the limits of the body itself, yet unreal beyond those limits.
Water exists when the heat lasts until the appearance [of the mirage], and is non-existent at other times;
the body is likewise considered to exist when the appearance lasts, and non-existent otherwise.
Thus, this world now appears as nothing more than a mere manifestation.

Abandon the delusion that "this body, composed of flesh and bone, is none other than me"— a notion held within as the thought "I am named so-and-so. There exist thousands of bodies created by one's own mental constructs.

O Rāma, that body by which you wander the horizons in a dream while lying upon your bed— where is that body of yours now? And that body by which you traverse the interior of the celestial cities within the kingdom of the mind during the waking state— [where is it now]?

Or if you wander about Mount Meru, where is that body of yours located? And as for that dream within dreams wherein you wander across the slopes of the earth, O Rāma, where is that body of yours located?
By means of which body you wander here in the kingdom of the mind, amidst lands of great splendor— that body of yours, where does it abide?
In the kingdom of the mind, whatever diverse worldly activities there may be—
O mighty-armed one, where are those bodies with which you sport?
Where is that body by means of which you attain bliss through the union with your beloved, who is full of passion and playful? MU_6,29.25–26
O Rāma, just as these bodies are composed of the vibrations of the mind,
so too this body is known to be mental, having such a commencement.
This delusion that "this is wealth," "this is the body," and "this is the place"— [is likewise mental].

All that is but the manifestation of the mind’s vigor and its volition. Know this saṃsāra, O descendant of Raghu, to be either a long dream, or a long delusion of the mind, or even a long kingdom of the imagination.
When you attain supreme awakening through your own self-will,
you will then see this clearly, as it truly is— from above and below—
just as the existence of the world is merely a construction of dreams and mental volitions.
For in this very same way,
this certain mental construction of volition (*saṅkalpa*) arises within the mind itself, just as I previously described the birth of the lotus-born Brahmā. (MU 6.29.31–32)
Endowed with various arrangements and possessing infinite hundreds of diversions,
this world appears as nothing more than the fabrication of conceptual thought,
just as an imagined appearance arises in the mind when it has attained the state of Brahmā.
Just as one has conceived of a body, another body indeed remains in that very same way;
for that body which was long practiced in the previous flow [of thought] appears exactly so through the dissolution of latent impressions (vāsanā), arising in its own form.
O Rāma, if this very resolve is cultivated otherwise through human effort, it becomes otherwise here in this world. When one has cultivated the thought,
"I am he," and "this is mine," [the cycle of existence continues].
"O Rāma, this which appears is real; it arises from the firmness of one's contemplation.
Whatever is contemplated with intense force, that very thing is seen everywhere immediately, O Rāma, like a beloved wife who is exceedingly dear."
Just as the habitual engagement with the day is seen even in a dream,
so too is cyclic existence perceived when it has been habituated through conceptual construction. Just as the duration of a dream appears swiftly like that of a day, [so does the world appear].
Likewise, although this [world] exists at all times, it is perceived as enduring for a long duration.
Just as a river is seen in the sky when it is heated by the sun's glare,
so too the earth is seen through mental construction (*saṅkalpa*), even though it does not exist.
Just as a tuft of hair appears in the sky due to a visual distortion,
so too does this splendor of the world appear solely through faulty cognition.
Just as even a timid person does not fall into agitation regarding their own mental constructions, [so should one remain undisturbed].
Even regarding this world which is one's own mental construction, the wise person does not feel fear in such a way.
For this very nature of one's own appears in this manner at present through the persistence of the path of saṃsāra; what is there that shines forth, and who is it? What is it? MU_6,29.44-45.
That very [mind], having been somewhat purified, attains a state of stainlessness through that purification;
once it has reached that state, O Rāma, this flickering worldly delusion is no longer seen. By the mere act of right perception, its own nature attains purity.
It does not take on further impurity, just as gold does not lose its state of being copper.
This triple world is merely an appearance; it is neither existent nor non-existent.
The wise know that the correct perception is the abandonment of all other conceptual constructions.
Death, life, heaven, knowledge, and even ignorance—none exist apart from the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa). This realization of oneness is right vision.
The cycle of transmigratory existence consisting of "you," "I," and so forth, as well as these ten directions—[all are but this].
The wise know that right vision is the realization that everything is nothing but one's own manifestation.
Through seeing the reality of things as they truly are within this saṃsāra composed of the existent and non-existent,
the mind— due to that right vision— neither sets nor rises.
Having determined that all things are either non-existent or indeed existent,
the mind, through right perception, attains desireless peace;
it neither censures nor praises, neither rejoices nor grieves.
Through right perception, the mind attains the coolness of truth.
Since everyone, indeed, must inevitably die along with all their kinsmen,
why do you grieve in vain over the loss of relatives?
"Since it is certain that I must inevitably die," when such is the certainty regarding the attainment of one's own death, why do you grieve in vain?
(MU 6.29.54) For one who is born, some degree of personal power and so forth is inevitable.
"What is to be attained by a man"—what occasion indeed is there for joy?
For every man engaged in worldly affairs in this saṃsāra, misfortune leads to ruin; what occasion indeed is there for grief? (MU 6.29.55–56)
This web of living beings sinks, rises, and quivers like a mass of bubbles in the ocean;
what lamentation can there be for this?
For that which is real is always real, and that which is unreal is always unreal.
But when it is merely a diversity of actions, why this lamentation over it?
"I am not, nor have I been, nor shall I be now;
I am the body, and this is a defect of the mind—what else is there to lament? (MU 6.29.58–59)
"O friend, if I am indeed something other than the body— namely, the reflection of consciousness—
then what are this existence and non-existence of mine, on account of which one suffers?
Thus, through such certainty, the mind of the sage becomes firmly established in right knowledge within.
It neither sets nor rises, nor does it burn within.
He takes up that very state of transcendence, which abides in the unsurpassed station,
just as a partridge takes up a soft, stainless tip of grass.
For this reason, not even the slightest reliance should be placed upon this unreal world;
for by means of reliance, a living being is bound like an ox to a strong rope.
Having determined through the intellect that this is a firm, though unreal, dream, [one should remain unattached].

O sinless one, you should dwell here with a vision free from attachment. He for whom even that which "must be done" no longer appears as a task to be performed attains inner coolness, just as the world does at the end of the day.
"O sinless one, having abandoned the distinction among the multitude of categories of objects, behold this as a mere commonality of appearance.
O Rāma, it is a mere appearance, stained by the touch of thought."
Then, having abandoned even that, one becomes the supreme state, free from appearances (nirābhāsa).
Consisting of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), eternal, all-pervading, and devoid of everything,
one becomes absolutely stainless upon the relinquishing of appearance.
When it is realized that "I do not exist, nor do my enjoyments truly exist," this ostentation does not appear as something vain or leading to misfortune.
For when it is realized that "I alone am indeed everything, consciousness itself," [the same follows].
This empty clamor does not appear to lead to any purpose or benefit.
Both of these systems of philosophy are true and grant ultimate success;
O Rāma, whichever one among them you find more pleasing, take refuge in that.
Therefore, O sinless one, dwelling here by means of these two very visions, bring about your own welfare through the complete destruction of passion and hatred.
Whatever is appropriate in this world, whatever is in the sky, or whatever is in the beyond—
All that is attained, O Rāma, through the complete destruction of passion and hatred.
Whatever action is performed by a mind impelled by passion, O Rāma,
that very thing quickly reaches the state of perversity for the deluded.
In mental states obstructed by the defect of hatred, virtues find no footing,
just as deer do not set foot on scorched ground. Passion and hatred are two serpents that have taken up residence within the wind of the mind.
From that wish-fulfilling tree, what indeed is not obtained?
For those who are wise, self-controlled, clever, and learned in the scriptures—
if they are nonetheless filled with passion and hatred, then fie upon them as jackals!

"My wealth has been enjoyed by another; wealth has been enjoyed by me from another"—in worldly dealings such as this, what room is there for passion and hatred? Wealth, kinsmen, and friends come and go again.
Why would a wise man feel attachment or aversion toward these?
This is the supreme Lord’s illusion, whose manifestation consists of existence and non-existence;
like a serpent coiled within the structure of saṃsāra, it utterly consumes those who are attached to it.
O Rāghava, in reality I have neither wealth nor people; truth itself does not exist for me.
This world is perceived as a mere falsehood, enveloped in falsehood.
Everything is non-existent at the beginning and at the end, and even in the middle, it is unstable and filled with mental anguish.
Where indeed could a wise man find stability in a tree created by another?
One person imagines a woman in the sky, while another, far away, enjoys her;
such, my dear, is the construction of this world-process, and nothing else.
In this world, the wise know this restless and pervasive state of constant coming and going to be equal to the creation and destruction of a city of Gandharvas;
it has arisen as something entirely unreal, like a city seen in a dream or a city of one's imagination.
Through the perception of long duration, a conviction has arisen today for you.
This cloth does not exist, nor does this object existing on the surface of the wall;
this is merely a mental construction that has reached full development through habituation.
You are eternally established in deep sleep within the vast, eternal state;
indeed, no one at all is established in the supreme Self. While remaining situated right there, you have fallen away from that state of deep sleep, yet this entire world remains within it.

You behold this long dream of saṃsāra, a vast delusion. Having strayed even slightly from your own true nature— which is dense with the sleep of ignorance— you remain here, bewildered by the dream of worldly existence.
Therefore, O Supreme Person, abandon this pervasive sleep consisting of dense ignorance, just as one who has found a treasure abandons a cobweb;
awaken and behold the pure Self, ever-arisen.

Like a lotus at dawn [receiving] the sun, awaken to the non-conceptual manifestation of consciousness; awaken, awaken! O mighty-armed one, you are being awakened again and again by me—behold the stainless sun that is the Self.
O Rāma, you have been awakened by me with this exceedingly cool rain of the water of knowledge, which resounds with beautiful words, like one awakened by a dense cloud.
O Rāghava, attain the supreme awakening; you are indeed now fully awake.
Behold the truth, having abandoned this worldly delusion which is false:
"There is no birth for you, no suffering for you, no defect for you, and no delusion for you;
you are liberated from all mental constructs, established by your own self within the Self."
With the net of defects born from conceptual construction completely dissolved, possessing a tranquil state of being like the pure essence of deep sleep,
and beholding this most expansive and gentle form, abide, O Great-Souled One, in the Self that is total peace.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Ultimate Reality."
The Thirtieth Sarga.
Vālmīki:
While Rāghava was thus listening with a mind that was pure and equanimous,
When [the mind] has come to rest freely in its own self and attained supreme bliss;
when all those [faculties] situated therein have become characterized by tranquility,
their minds undisturbed, and they abide with the Self awakened.
When all vibration, sound, and worldly activity had been completely stilled, and the assembly hall stood serene upon the surface of the earth like the night,
while the gongs remained silent and suspended in the sky; MU_6.30.3.
As if listening to the words of the Sage, the pure banners remained motionless; the birds, their movements stilled and their beaks fixed, were silent;
and those within the inner apartments slept, as did the birds in their cages and dwellings.

While the members of the assembly— those who had attained expansion of intellect and were well-versed in the true nature of reality— were deliberating upon the meaning of the truth, she, endowed with innate bliss,
addressed them with a series of excellent words characterized by supreme tranquility.
Even toward those who remained humble through discipline, though they were like playful monkeys,
the Sage ceased his flood of words for the sake of Rāghava’s own inner repose, just as water stops flowing when its dam is breached by its own current.
Then, when half a muhūrta had passed and Rāghava had been awakened,
Vasiṣṭha, the best among speakers, spoke again on that very same matter.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, you have awakened perfectly; you have attained your own true self. Resting upon this very [realization], remain within; do not indulge in pride here.
For this wheel of saṃsāra has its hub in mere conceptual construction (saṅkalpa).
O descendant of Raghu, when the flow is obstructed, it is held back; yet,
once the mind and the navel have been awakened, this wheel of saṃsāra continues to whirl with force, even though one strives to restrain it.
Relying on supreme human effort, and through the proper application of strength and wisdom,
one should extinguish the very mind at the hub of the wheel of saṃsāra—
by means that are endowed with discernment and gentleness, and fortified by the sacred scriptures.
That which cannot be attained through human effort is not to be found anywhere.
Abandoning reliance on destiny alone— a notion devised by the ignorant understanding—
and resorting to one’s own exertion, one should first restrain the mind.
O sinless one, by means of the delusion consisting of ignorance that has proceeded from Viriñca, this world— which is indeed non-existent— is perceived as having the appearance of existence.
O sinless one, these are merely the false forms of the expansion of the delusion of ignorance.
All these bodies wandering here have arisen from the unreal.
O Rāma, a wise person should never undergo modification through pleasure and pain for the sake of a body that is like a body created by mere volition.

The person within the body is considered far more hollow than even a painted man, whose face is withered by suffering and moistened by tears, whereas [the painted man] is serene and free from moisture.
[The body] is withered by mental and physical ailments, naturally moistened by fluids, and subject to destruction.
The stability in the body is not as [great] as that in the painted man;
for indeed, the body situated in the painting perishes when it is destroyed, and not otherwise.
The body, being perishable by nature and subject to inevitable destruction, perishes of its own accord.
A person of variegated form attains a lasting splendor when protected;
however, the physical body, even when well-protected, perishes utterly and does not increase.
Therefore, this excellent body is one of variegated [mental] form, not a body produced by mere volition.
Those qualities which indeed exist in a painted body do not exist in a body made of mental constructs (saṅkalpa-deha).
O sinless one, what reliance can you have on this body composed of flesh, which is indeed far more insignificant than even an insentient painted body?
O Great-minded One, what reliance can there be on this body born of long-term volitions?
For it is indeed more hollow than even a body born of short-term volitions. A body born of short-term volitions is not seized by long-lasting pleasures and pains.
Born of long-held intentions, this body is afflicted by long-lasting suffering;
for the body consists of intention—it neither exists nor does it not exist.
Why then does this foolish person undergo such affliction for its sake in vain?
Just as there is no injury to you when a man made of a painting is wounded or destroyed,
and just as there is no injury to you when a person created by imagination is wounded or destroyed;
so too, there is no injury to you when that which consists of a kingdom of the mind is wounded or destroyed.
Just as when the second moon is wounded or diminished, there is no injury to you;
just as when the onset of a dream is wounded or diminished, there is no injury to you;
just as when the water of a dense cloud is wounded or diminished, there is no injury to you.
In this machine of a body, which is by its very nature perishable and fashioned merely from mental constructs, there is no harm for you when it is wounded or worn away;
for it is composed of long-lasting dreams, fashioned by persistent volition.
Whether the body is adorned or defiled, there is indeed no injury whatsoever to consciousness (cit).
Consciousness does not set, O Rāghava, nor does the Self (ātman) move;
Brahman does not undergo transformation—what loss is there for you in the destruction of the body?
For just as one standing upon a revolving wheel, even though he has left the wheel behind,
sees the entire circle of directions spinning due to being utterly deluded,
so too does one perceive through false cognition that has suddenly arisen and is surging forth.
In this very way, through habitual practice, this wheel of the body is perceived:
it is seen as whirling when it has been set in motion, as falling when it has been cast down,
and as being struck when it has been slain, all due to the power of evil latent impressions (*durvāsanā*).
Having abandoned the delusion born of ignorance and having beheld the true vision,
one should firmly adopt steadfastness and cast off this dense delusion.
This body, fashioned by mental construction through false knowledge, is neither real nor unreal.
Whatever is produced by the unreal can never be real.
The body arises from the unreal, like a snake [projected] upon a rope;
and though it is itself unreal, it performs the activities of the world.
O Rāma, that which is done by the insentient is said not to have been done;
therefore, although it acts, the body is never indeed the agent.
For the body is insentient and devoid of effort, and there is no desire belonging to the Self.
Therefore, there is no agent at all; the unborn one is merely its witness.
Just as a lamp situated in a windless place remains fixed within itself, so remain like a witness amidst all states of being in the stability of the world.
"Just as the sun, remaining in its own state, performs its daily tasks, so too, O Rāma, perform this royal installation.
For in this body-house, which has arisen as empty and insubstantial,"
When existence has become false, like a yakṣa imagined by a child,
the insubstantial and evil vampire of egoism— shunned by all the virtuous— having come from somewhere, has entered that which bears the name "mind."
"O Rama, do not become a servant to this evil-minded ego;
by being its servant, hell is obtained as the fruit.
Within the house of the body, the formless [Self] exists through the play of its own volitions."
The vetāla of the deranged mind leaps about with ease;
having entered the empty house of the body, that has been wrought by the yakṣa of the mind,
by which even the great ones, though established in meditative absorption, are terrified.
Having expelled the vetāla of the mind from the single temple of your own body,
you shall never again fear the empty city of saṃsāra;
for those who take delight in this house of the body, which is actually overcome by the mind, [remain subject to fear].
It is a marvel that even today they remain unshaken like stone; why is this?
O Rāghava, that fortitude which exists when one's house of the body is seized by the demon of the mind belongs to a demon alone—it does not belong to one who is free from demons.
O virtuous one, dwell without attachment in this house of the great yakṣa of egoism, where the body has been consumed; for indeed, this is not yours and is not stable.
Abandon the state of being a follower of egoism through your expansive intelligence.
Having brought the ego to its end, let one rely immediately upon one's own Self alone.
For those who are seized by the demon of the ego and seek only hell,
being blinded by the disease of delusion, there are neither friends nor kinsmen.
Whatever action is performed with an intellect impaired by egoism will have a result like that of a poisonous creeper— namely, death.
[One] who is devoid of discernment and fortitude [commits this] upon the great corpse of one's own egoism.

Know that he by whom [this state] has been embraced through folly has already perished instantly. O Rāghava, those wretched ones who have been brought under the sway of the demon of egoism have become fuel for the fires of hell.
The tree of the body, in whose hollow the serpent of egoism writhes, is quickly felled by the steadfast. Whether the demon of egoism remains in this body or departs, [it matters not].
Look upon him with a great mind, O best of the great! For once he has been shaken off, disregarded, and even mentally set aside by you,
that demon of egoism will do nothing to you here.
O Rāma, while this demon of the mind manifests within the abode of the body,
what has it ever truly brought to the Self, which possesses infinite splendor?
For those men who are overcome by the yakṣa of the mind, their calamities are vast indeed.
They cannot be fully enumerated even in hundreds of years.
"I am struck," "I am dead," "I am burned"—these are the wretched activities of the demon of egoism, O sinless one; they do not belong to another.
Just as space, though all-pervading, is not connected to anything here,
so too the Self, though all-pervading, is not joined with the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).
This moving machine of the body performs actions and takes up [objects].
O Rāma, that activity of egoism is joined to the rope of the wind.
Just as the sky, though itself a non-agent, is said to be the cause for the rising of trees,
so too the Self, abiding within itself, is the cause for the activities of the mind.
O Rāma, by the mere presence of the Self, the mind— though pure like the form of a wall—
shines forth as if having assumed a body, just as it does by the mere presence of a lamp;
for the Self and the mind are eternally and utterly distinct.

What connection could there possibly be between heaven and earth, which are like light and darkness? O descendant of Raghu, through ignorance, the mind— which is enveloped by its own powers of movement, vibration, and effort— is perceived as the Self.
The Self is indeed of the nature of light, eternal, all-pervading, and omnipresent;
know that the mind is deceitful egoism, while the Great One resides within the heart. O treasure of the Raghus, you are the Self; you are not the dull stone of the mind.
Cast away the delusion of the mind; why have you become attached to this?
For there dwells in the empty house of the body a demon named "mind";
this evil-souled one causes terror—do not touch it, O noble one.
Having dispelled the demon of the mind— which brings fear, is inauspicious, and robs one of the very essence of fortitude— be firm in yourself;
for one firmly seized by the yakṣa of the mind, neither the scriptures nor kinsmen can help.
Teachers are not able to protect a human being; yet,
when the vetāla of the mind has been completely stilled, teachers and the kinsmen of the meaning of the scriptures are able to rescue him, just as one might rescue a deer from a small mire.
In this empty city of the world, everything has been utterly corrupted by the intoxicated yakṣa of the mind leaping about within the house of the body;
the entire courtyard of the home is haunted by the vampire of the mind.

To whom would this wilderness of the world not cause fear, being utterly empty? Yet within this city of the world, the house of the body— where the demon of the restless mind has been stilled— is inhabited by only a few virtuous ones.
O descendant of Raghu, whatever direction one resorts to here is filled with the corpse-cemeteries of bodies and the intoxicated Vetālas of delusion;
in this wilderness of the world, for a moment, like a bewildered child—
Grasping for yourself a portion of fortitude, lift yourself up by means of your own self.
O Rāma, in this forest of old age where herds of living beings wander like deer,
do not seek stability through the sap of grass like a young fawn.
O young human-deer roaming this forest of the earth’s surface,
having shattered the elephant of ignorance, take recourse to the conduct of a lion. Other foolish human-deer roam in their own jungles within Jambudvīpa.

O sinless Rāma, dwell as they dwell; do not dwell otherwise. For a very short time in the winter, which brings with it the coating of mud, one must not plunge into that which has the form of a bride, like a buffalo into a small puddle.
One should cast away enjoyments and non-enjoyments and follow the path of the Noble One;
having investigated with the great Nobles, one should take refuge in oneself alone.
[This applies even] to that which is impure, trivial, unfortunate, and ill-formed.
One should not plunge into the grinding-mill of anxiety for the sake of the body.
One body is fashioned by one [agent], it is inhabited by another yakṣa,
and yet another is the experiencer of its suffering— strange indeed is this cycle of folly!
Just as the density of a stone is of one single form, so too is that of the Self; for, due to the universal commonality of mere existence alone, nothing else is possible.
Just as there is density in a stone, so indeed is there mentality in the Self.
Because there is no other consciousness apart from its own existence, it is non-different from mere being (*sattāmātra*).
Just as solidity belongs to a stone,
so too does this supreme Self possess a consciousness that is uniform in form, by virtue of having the nature of the universal of existence (*sattāsāmānya*).
O dear one, here in this world, neither insentience nor consciousness arises separately;
for these two are fashioned by false conceptualization, like a yakṣa seen by a child.
Just as from a single mass of sugarcane juice, there arise various distinct products...
"This is molasses, this is sugar-candy"— this delusion has arisen in vain.
Because the one Supreme Self exists in the form of pure being (*sattāsāmānya*),
this notion of "insentience" and "sentience" has likewise arisen in vain through ignorance.
This [error] perishes as soon as it is scrutinized; it is destroyed by scrutiny alone.
Like the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, it is neither existent nor non-existent;
therefore, that which does not exist here at all has no being, and that which exists here cannot be non-existent. (MU 6.30.94–95)
Because it is established in its own nature alone, because of the impossibility of either duality or unity,
and because there is no cognition of anything else, there is equality between the stone and the Self.
Just as the non-dual, infinite, singular Self experiences its own existence, [so does the stone].
Likewise, the Self is established in its own nature as neither insentient nor sentient;
because of the impossibility of anything else, and because of the absence of the conjunction of eternal duality or unity,
and because of the impossibility of an object of consciousness, the Self is neither insentient nor sentient.
The two perceptions—the inert and the conscious—are like the son of a barren woman or a tree in the sky;
they have neither arrived nor not arrived, and they are neither seen nor unseen.
The referents of the words "inert" and "conscious" are non-existent, like a snake in a rope.
How could those two [statements] of yours be true, if they were nothing more than mere lack of foresight?
Furthermore, that which was said— that the self is conscious and the stone is insentient—
is based on the cause of making known a meaning suitable for such speech.
By whatever reasoning one who is to be awakened is awakened to a higher awakening, that instruction should be imparted; yet the fool does not grasp that state suddenly.
"The mind is distinct from these various impaired senses, and no agent is seen here; this body is merely a house in vain."
Someone else entirely is leaping about; "I am this one who is devoid of intrinsic nature"—alas, enough of this great magical illusion!

Amidst the restless transmigrations and the play of the succession of beings, the Great-Souled One, whose sole activity is consciousness, delights after having investigated the reality of the Supreme Person, just as a minister sports with female serpents full of virulent poison.
"You are not the head, nor the eyes, nor the blood and flesh, nor the bones, nor indeed the mind, nor the collection of elements.

Do not fall into delusion; you are not the body. You are the serene consciousness, the all-pervading one who has attained all that is stainless. Thus ends the chapter titled "The Investigation into the Existence of the Body."
The Thirty-First Canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having firmly grasped this view, his efforts toward both suffering and desired objects have perished.
Abandoning even the eightfold sovereignty as if it were a calamity, remain [in this state]. Now, here is another vision that destroys great delusion—
difficult to attain yet easily attained, free from decline, and free from affliction.
Listen to that which was previously told by me in a cave on Kailāsa for the sake of pacifying the suffering of saṃsāra, by the Lord whose crest is the half-moon:
"There exists [the mountain] shining with a mass of moonbeams, reaching beyond the heavens."
There is a king of mountains named Kailāsa, the abode of Gaurī’s lover;
it is washed by the cascades of the Gaṅgā, its cave-dwellings resound with the songs of the Gaṇas,
and it is made beautiful by groves of mango and kadamba trees swaying in the gentle breeze.
The host of gods, restless in their play, uttered sweet cries like those of ruddy geese;
the region was tawny with groves of date palms entwined by the young feathers of peacocks.
There, clouds were concealed within the *tamāla* trees, and the clouds themselves were likened to plantain trees.

Thick with a web of bees, filled with the warbling of plaintive francolins, its caves resounded with the songs of *vidyādharas*, its golden ravines shimmered, the cries of *kāraṇḍava* ducks rang out loudly,
and it was like a cloud of countless flowers.
He is the outpouring of the cloud of liberation, served by perfected beings and celestial musicians;
he is beloved by the moon as his crest-jewel, and worshipped by the inhabitants of the three worlds.
His arms are like the wish-fulfilling trees of a perfect aeon, and his neck is like the peak of a beautiful mountain summit.
His eyes were like shining jewels, and his body hair was like rows of forests;
the beauty of his hair was like the hollows of glass, and his garment was like the expanse of his own forest;
the sky above his chest was reddened by the mass of filaments shaken by the wind.
There dwells the Blessed Lord Hara, who bears the crescent moon,
holds the trident in his hand, has three eyes, and is surrounded by a multitude of attendants;
he whose body is half-formed by Bhavānī, and who is the sole cause of all the worlds.
The crusher of the pride of Kandarpa, the possessor of the arts and the bearer of their excellence; he whose splendor follows the six-faced one, who has an intoxicated bull as his vehicle;
he who wears the skin of a rutting elephant, whose abode is delighting in the cremation ground.
In former times, while worshipping that Great God on that very mountain,
I once dwelt for a long duration on the bank of the Gaṅgā, having established a hermitage and settled into a life of ascetic conduct for the sake of penance.
Following the traditional conduct in due order and taking refuge in the lineage of merit,
he performed his ablutions for the sake of dwelling there; having constructed a hut with blue leaves,
he fixed stakes made from young trees and planted a fence of creeping vines.
Having gathered the foremost forest creatures as his provisions, having acquired a water-pot,

carrying a sewn bag for flowers, and having strung together his own rosary of beads; surrounded by a multitude of disciples and having compiled a compendium of the meaning of the scriptures— (MU 6.31.18)
Having arranged the collection of books brought there and having protected the noble deer,
O Rāma, as I was thus distinguished by such qualities and practicing austerities in a grove of the Kailāsa forest, time passed me by.
Then once, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, when half the night had passed and was coming to an end,
the quarters of the sky were perfectly still, as if established in the silence of a log.
In thickets and dense forests where the darkness could be cut through with a sword,
as the wind blew with the laughter of dew-drops falling like pearls,
and while the deer lay resting in their enclosures near the hermitage; MU_6,31.22–23.

While the night-blooming lilies, the medicinal herbs, the female cakora birds, and the creepers were licking the flow of nectar from the moonbeams upon their sprouts for the sake of their own nourishment— *amṛtāṃśukarasyandam ātmanaḥ parivṛddhaye / lihatsu śaśiraśmibhyaḥ pallaveṣv amṛtadravam //*— (MU 6.31.24).
While they were drinking the flow of nectar,

scattered by the rays of the moon, [the moon] spread across the third part of the sky— a peacock-feather fan whose blue cloud-fronds rested upon the mountain and whose clusters of stars were the *kṛttikās*.
When the reflection of the multitude of stars appeared on the mountain’s crystal grounds amidst clusters of blooming flowers, doubling their brilliance,
I lay upon a couch of young shoots with a mind freed from desire.
He contemplates the unshakable reality of the Self, appearing as stainless light,
within the second body— the sky containing the constellation of the Seven Sages—
and it seems as if that very light is approaching him from that direction for his sake.
When the three stars were positioned at the center of the sky’s vault above the house,

and when the three deer, pursued by the Kirāta, seemed to have entered into a state of constant delusion; and when the passion of love was redoubled by the fragrance of blooming night-lilies— *mṛgatraye kirātātte sadā bhramam ivāgate / utphullakumudāmodadviguṇoddāmamanmathe //* 6.31.30.
While the flocks of *cakravāka* birds had departed for other mountain lakes,
the female *cakora* birds sat upon stone ledges as if carved from the rock itself on every side,
drinking the cool nectar of the moonbeams.
In the forest, where a sweet breeze blows, cooled solely by the rain of moonbeams' spray,
and where songs arise from the rustling of clusters of leaves, [the hermitage] is like a young bride setting out for her first tryst with her lover.
This is the canto titled "Description of Vasiṣṭha’s Hermitage."
The thirty-second canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
At that time, when the first half-watch had passed, there—
Having extended my concentration and remaining with my gaze fixed on the external,
I suddenly beheld a radiance arisen in the forest,
as brilliant as the Ocean of Milk when it was churned and agitated by the striking of Mount Mandara.
Resembling a hundred white clouds, like a multitude of dancing moons,
it was like an immovable mass of snow tossed by the force of a fierce wind,
or like a mountain of pure crystal melted by the heat at the end of an eon.
Like fresh butter from a cloud, like a mass of *ketaka* flowers risen up;
like the whiteness of a conch shell flying aloft, like a white cloud gathered together;
like the surging foam of milk, like the essence of pearls uplifted.

Having beheld with wonder that mass of splendor which had entered the interior of the cave like the surge of the Ganges' waves, and which was as pervasive as the laughter of Śiva— capable of being grasped as a single whole like thick curd—
I manifested my own radiance in all directions.
Observed with the vision of the intellect, which shines with internal illumination:
as soon as I beheld that peak, he who bears the digit of the moon was wandering at his own pleasure and by chance upon his delightful mountain.
Adorned with a garland of troops concealed behind the rear ranks,
his hand placed in the hand of Gaurī, his vanguard urged forward by Nandin,
he followed behind the bull, surrounded by all those who roam at night.
Encircled by a garland of *kahlāra* lilies, with a crest made of *mandāra* flowers,
he has matted locks crowned by a digit of the moon and wears earrings made of the king of serpents;
resembling a moving mountain of snow, he grants all desired objects.
"Then, having perceived the Blessed One with my mind alone, I bowed down and paid homage to him with a *mandārava* flower offered by my mind. Having done this,
I [arose] from this bed in the cross-legged posture.
In an instant, I was raised up from there like a great corpse by a spirit;
having awakened the disciples staying there and received the water of honor (*argha*),
I, well-restrained, went before the Lord of the World, purified by his gaze.
There, having offered a handful of flowers from afar, the three-eyed god was saluted and worshipped by me after I had presented the guest-offering (argha). Then,
with that [gaze] which was soft like moonlight, straight, and cool—

With a glance that removes all suffering and leads to the eternal state, the Lord, whose crown is adorned with the crescent moon and who was seated upon a bed of flowers, looked at me and spoke these words in syllables white with a smile: *Muṇḍakopaniṣad 6.32.16–17* (adapted for meter) "Having beheld me with a gaze that dispels all affliction and leads to the eternal station, the Lord, whose diadem is formed by the half-moon and who sat upon a flowery mound, addressed me with words brightened by a smile."
Īśvara said:
"O Brahmin, bring water for the guest-offering and water for washing the feet; welcome to you.
O sinless one, we have arrived today as guests at your hermitage."
O Brahmin, you shine with the splendor of asceticism, which is ever characterized by profound delight, constant tranquility, and joyful magnanimity. Come,
sit here upon this seat of natural leaves.
When he who bears half of the half-moon had thus spoken— "O gentle one, born from the ocean, purifier through the accumulation of merit"—
I approached him and offered water for the feet, flowers, and the respectful oblation (arghya).
Before the feet, the hands, and the body of that Self-Existent One,
many garlands of mandāra flowers were strewn.
Then the blessed Gaurī, with just such an act of worship, [honored him].
Thus honored, together with her companions and the circle of attendants,
O Rāma, Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord, who are full of devotion and affection, graciously accepted that worship from me with great respect.
At the conclusion of the worship, the Lord, who bears a digit of the moon, addressed me as I sat there with words as cool as the rays of the full moon: Īśvara said:
O Brahmin, do your consciousnesses, which are characterized by tranquility and have attained rest in the Supreme, remain established in that state which brings about auspiciousness?
Are they capable of opening the eyes of the lotus, the water-lily, and the night-blooming lily?

O Brahmin, are your disciples free from illness and devoted to you? O Blessed One, is all well with the innocent deer in your hermitage— those who enjoy the portion of offerings and whose appearance is as dear to me as my own beloved?
I hope these lofty Mandāra trees are bestowing Mandāraka flowers for the sake of worshipping you and us;
and I hope the holy Mandākinī river is available for your ablutions.
With a single lotus stalk, she offers a blue and a red lotus.
O sinless Lord of Munis, you are never distressed by my inconsistent actions, nor even by the playful antics of my attendants.
O Sage, O Brahmin, while you dwell here on this lord of mountains, the followers of the Lord of Wealth— who inhabit the forests and wildernesses— do not disturb you,
even amidst the throngs of ill-behaved yakṣas and the restless night-stalkers.
"Even while dwelling within the hollow of this mountain, you remain free from agitation.
When the Lord of Gods, the sole cause of all worlds,
had spoken thus, O descendant of Raghu, I addressed him with words full of conciliation.
O Maheśvara, for those here who possess the auspiciousness of the recollection of the Three-Eyed One,
nothing at all is difficult to attain, nor are there any fears whatsoever,
for their minds are completely filled with the bliss of recollecting you.
There are none in the treasury of the world who do not bear devotion to you.
Those are the lands, those the provinces, those the directions,
and those the mountains where men abide with minds solely intent on the remembrance of you.
O Lord, the recollection of you is the fruit of past merit, the nourishment for present merit, and the seed for future merit— just like a tree; indeed,
by that [recollection], the past, the present, and the future become fruitful.
O Lord, mindfulness of you is auspicious throughout the three periods of time;
it is the supreme friend of the mind and the remover of the spreading tide of all calamities.
O Lord, mindfulness of you is the watering of the creeper of all prosperity.
O Lord, the remembrance of you is indeed the cause of great glories, of great deeds that are highly honored, and of all causes;
it is an ocean of the waters of discernment and the supreme mine of the jewels of merit.
O Lord, recollection of you is a flood of suns for the darkness of ignorance;
O Lord, recollection of you is a jar for the flood of the nectar of knowledge, the moon for the moonlight of fortitude, and the gateway to the city of liberation.
O Lord, the remembrance of you is an axe for the creeper of craving, a mountain of clouds of fortitude, and a forest fire for the thicket of wretchedness;
it triumphs, illuminating the entire pavilion of the mind’s cycle of existence.
O Lord, the remembrance of you is an unprecedented and supreme lamp. O Lord of Beings, by me who possesses the noble wish-fulfilling gem of the remembrance of you,
my foot has been placed upon the very crest of all calamities.
O Lord, remover of all suffering and fear, you have not been present before my mind here even for a moment;
O Giver of Boons, O Hero, O Maheśvara, you have been forgotten by me, and thus I dwell in happiness like Bhava himself.
Vālmīki said:

When the sage had spoken thus, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
Thus ends the canto named "The Meeting with Hara."
The Thirty-third Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
To him who had spoken thus, the blessed goddess Gaurī addressed these words:
The Goddess, the Mother of the World, spoke to me as a mother speaks to her beloved son:
"O Blessed One, tell [me how] she may become a partaker of abundant good fortune."
"Where is Arundhatī, the foremost among devoted wives and beloved?
Rise up and bring her here from this hermitage that removes my weariness;
I shall engage in various conversations with her as my sole companion."
When Pārvatī had spoken thus, that housewife herself went quickly to that very place and, with full confidence, brought her back;
she then conducted her in accordance with the proper conduct for women, treating her as equal to Arundhatī.
Gaurī became completely absorbed in her own task and attained perfect peace.
At that moment, O Rāma, I reflected thus with my intellect:
"Undistracted and with my mind serene, this Blessed One has been found by me."
"Whom shall I ask about this doubt— the Supreme Lord, the great ocean of all-knowledge, whose crest is adorned by the moon?
Having reflected thus, O sinless one, that Guru was questioned by me in this way.
Listen, I shall tell you everything that was spoken by the Moon-crested Lord:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, Cause of all causes!
By your grace, this boldness has clearly come upon me."
I ask you, O Mahādeva, that which I have; tell it to me quickly with a gracious mind, free from agitation and affliction—
that which destroys all evil and increases all that is auspicious.
"O Maheśvara, tell me truly the procedure for the worship of the gods.
Īśvara said:
"Listen, O Brahmin, to this supreme and unsurpassed method of worshipping the gods."
"I tell you that by performing which act you shall indeed be liberated at once.
Do you know, O twice-born one, who this Great God might be?
Neither the lotus-eyed one is the God, nor is the three-eyed one the God."
Neither is the god born from the lotus, nor the god who is the lord of the thirty-three;
neither the god Wind, nor the Sun, nor Fire, nor the Maker of Night.
Neither am I a Brahmin, nor a king, nor am I "I," nor are you, O best of the twice-born.
The deity does not exist in the form of the body; the deity does not assume the form of a painting.
The deity is not of the nature of mental construction, nor is the deity the intellect.
Unfabricated, without beginning or end, pure consciousness is called the deity.
How could that [consciousness] exist within an object delimited by forms and so forth?
The wise know consciousness to be the auspicious *cit*, uncreated and without beginning or end;
that very thing is expressed by the word "God," and one should worship it.
That alone exists from which everything bears the nature of both existence and non-existence.
For those who do not know the reality of Śiva, the worship of forms and the like is performed;
for one incapable of the path of yoga (*yojanādhvan*), the path of a *krośa* is devised.
The fruit obtained from Rudra and others is limited by such measures as "this much" and so forth;
the fruit of the Self is bliss—uncreated, without beginning or end.
He who abandons the uncreated fruit and pursues a created fruit [is lost].
Having abandoned the Mandara forest, he goes to the Karañja grove.
There, awakening, equanimity, and tranquility are indeed the supreme flowers;
they know the Self to be auspicious, pure consciousness alone, partless and stainless.
Know that when the divine Self is worshipped with the flowers of tranquility, awakening, and so forth, that indeed is the worship of the deity; mere worship of forms is not true worship.
People, however, abandon the worship of the deity which consists of self-realization.
Those who are attached to artificial images undergo long-lasting suffering.

For those virtuous ones who have known that which is to be known, O Brahmin, they do not perform the worship of deities—except for the meditation on the Self—which is like the play of children. (MU 6.33.24–25)
The Self alone is the divine Lord Śiva, the supreme cause;
He should always be worshipped incessantly with the offering of knowledge. You are this very Self, the imperishable living being, the space of consciousness.
Know that the worship of the worshipful, the worship, and one's own self-worship are not anything other than one's own nature (svabhāva).
O Lord, just as this world has the nature of being merely consciousness-space (cetanākāśamātra),
so too let it be explained how the state of being a living soul (jīva) and so forth belongs to consciousness alone.

Indeed, it is said that here there exists only the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), devoid of near or far; that which remains at the end of aeons is the unthinkable object of thought (*cetya*) that is impossible anywhere else.
Of that which shines forth by itself, of its own self-manifestation, however—
"Enough of this notion that 'this world' is known by itself through him.
Thus, like a city in a dream, the world shines as being of the nature of consciousness (*cidātmaka*).
In this way, the world consists of nothing but the space of consciousness; it is transparent and without a foundation.

Because it is absolutely impossible [for anything else to exist], the non-perception of objects is merely the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoma*). That which, due to its nature as consciousness, flashes forth at the beginning of creation—that is known as the "world.
Therefore, this world that appears here has the form of a city in a dream.
In that state, which is the very self of the sky of consciousness, what is there called "otherness," and from where could it arise?
Mountains are nothing but pure consciousness; the world and the ether are nothing but pure consciousness;
the Self and the individual soul (jīva) are nothing but pure consciousness; and the succession of all beings is nothing but pure consciousness.

O dear one, tell me: apart from the mere expanse of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), what distinct thing could possibly exist at the beginning of creation, within the perception of that creation, or in a dream-city?
Space, the supreme space, the space of Brahman, the world, and consciousness—all are one.
Thus, these are synonymous terms, just as *taru*, *pādapa*, and *vṛkṣa* are;
and this is experienced in dreams, mental constructs, illusions, and the like.
At that time, indeed, it is the space of consciousness alone that shines forth in the form of the world.
Just as this space of consciousness appears in the form of the world within a dream,
so too does that very same thing appear to us in what is called the waking state. Just as in a dream-city there is nothing other than the space of consciousness anywhere at all.
O dear one, nothing whatsoever arises here in this world from the very beginning;

since nothing else exists apart from this, therefore all of this— both the state of being consciousness and that which is perceived, as well as the non-perceived and the existing world— is established as such.
Just as in a dream, objects such as pots and cloths consist of nothing but the space of consciousness,
so too this creation at the very beginning of creation consists of nothing but the space of consciousness;
for apart from pure awareness alone, there is nothing else in the city of a dream.
Just as nothing exists at all in these three worlds,

so too are whatever perceptions there may be, whatever entities and non-entities, and whatever scriptures— along with their locations, times, and minds— all of that is merely the space of consciousness (*cidvyoma*).
This very deity has been described as that which is supreme from the perspective of ultimate reality;
it is you, it is I, and it is the entire world in its totality—
the whole multitude of beings, the universe, and whatever else exists, including yourself and me.
For the body is indeed the space of consciousness, which is the Supreme Self alone and nothing else.
Just as in the city of a dream, within the process of conceptualization, there exists no body whatsoever other than the space of consciousness,
so too here in this creation, O Sage, from the first and unique creation onwards, there has been no form other than that.
The thirty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of the World as Consisting of the Supreme Self," [spoken by] Īśvara.
Thus, this entire universe is nothing but the Supreme Self alone;
it is Brahman, the supreme ether, known as the Transcendent God. This very worship is the highest good; from it, everything is obtained.
That God is all-pervading, everything, and everything is established in Him. From Him,
that bliss is obtained which is uncreated, without beginning or end, non-dual, undivided, and not to be accomplished by external means.
"You are awakened, O best of sages; therefore, this is described to you.
You are not fit for the worship of the gods consisting of flowers and incense, O Great One—for those whose intellects are unrefined, who are childish and of feeble minds," so it was said.
For them, the worship of the gods is said to consist of artificial images;
for they indeed worship the god— who is imagined as having a form— with perfumes, unbroken rice grains, lamps, flowers, and so forth, all of which are falsely imagined.
Having performed worship with rituals fashioned by their own imagination,
the foolish undergo distress through offerings of flowers, incense, and fragments of food;
having performed the worship of the gods in vain with objects created by their own imagination.
From whatever source they may come, those of false selfhood offer their fruits here;
O Brahmin, I shall describe that worship which is fashioned for those of childish intellect— consisting of flowers, incense, and offerings— which is unfit for one such as you.
But for those such as us, O best among the wise, there is no deity at all;
the deity who is the support of the three worlds is the Supreme Self alone and none other. Śiva is beyond all states and transcends all conceptual constructions.
Enveloped by all conceptual constructions, yet neither universal nor consisting of the whole;
unconditioned by space, time, and the like, the creator of every kind of undertaking, whose form is pure consciousness and who is stainless—he is called "God," O Sage. (MU 6.34.11–12)
Consciousness transcends all parts (kalās), abides within all beings,
is the goddess who bestows existence upon all, and removes all torment.
O Brahman, that which is the middle between being and non-being is called God (deva).
That which is known by the names *paramātman* and *apara*, that Reality (*sat*) is declared as *om*.
By its nature as Great Being (*mahāsattā*), it has attained equality everywhere;
it is called the Great Consciousness (*mahācit*) and is heard of in scripture as the Ultimate Reality (*paramārtha*).
It abides everywhere in all seasons within creepers, like sap;
it exists in the form of the universal essence of being (*sattāsāmānya*), and also as the self of the Great Consciousness (*mahācittva*).
O sinless one, that consciousness-essence (*cittattva*) which is in Arundhatī is the same consciousness-essence that is in you.
That which is the essence of consciousness (cittattva) in Pārvatī, and that which is the essence of consciousness in the Gaṇas;
that which is this essence of consciousness of mine, and that which is the essence of consciousness in the three worlds—
those of supreme intellect who know reality know that to be the God.
