O Brahman, tell me: what essence can there be in any other god who is imagined as possessing feet, hands, and so forth, apart from pure consciousness? O Brahman, he does not stand at a distance, nor is he difficult for anyone to attain.
He is ever established in the body, and likewise everywhere in space. He acts, he eats, he sustains, and he moves;
he breathes, he is the perceiver, and he knows each and every limb.
Thus, by virtue of that [power], he becomes the lord of the city of the limbs within this city of the body— which is subject to various activities, manifest, bound to his own essential nature,
situated upon the mountain of the physical frame, and mobile— through his grace.
Thus, in this heart-cave, which is like a dense treasury, he is the Lord of the Cave (Guheśvara).

For the sake of conventional usage regarding that stainless Self— which transcends the existence of the activity of the six senses including the mind— the designation "Consciousness" (cit) has been conceived.
This very one is composed of consciousness, subtle, all-pervading, and stainless;
it produces this radiant manifestation and yet does not produce it.
That consciousness, which is utterly pure, performs the activity of the world for the sake of the world.

The wise one delights this [consciousness] with aesthetic flavor, just as a sweet creeper is delighted by its sap. Those beautiful wonders that exist within consciousness exactly as they are, indeed produce a sense of wonder; some of these are designated as "space."
Some are designated as "living beings" (jīva), some are designated as "mind" (citta);
some are designated as "time" (kāla), and some are designated as "space" (deśa).
Some are designated as "action" (kriyā), and some are designated as "substance" (dravya).
Some designate it as the transformation of existence and so forth, or as the dullness of the mind;
some designate it as luminosity and so forth, and some designate it as darkness;
some designate it as the sun, the moon, and so forth, while others designate it as the Yakṣas.
Just as a sprout is produced by the spring season through its own nature of being desireless,
in that very same way, this splendor of the world is generated by the conscious self (cidātman).
Indeed, throughout all these [manifestations], consciousness remains always and solely one.
Within the lotus-lake of the three worlds,
the intoxicated sovereign consciousness, like a bee, experiences the honey of its own volitions, which are gathered by the mind wandering amidst the lotuses of the body.
The world, including the gods, asuras, and gandharvas, along with its mountains and oceans,
moves steadily upon consciousness like a blade of grass in a whirlpool of water. It is a wheel of activity, restless and ever-shifting, consisting of the flickering movements of the mind.
The wheel of saṃsāra revolves within the wheel of consciousness as a vessel of delusion.
Consciousness, in the form of the four-armed one, struck down the host of asuras,
just as the sun destroys the heat with a mass of clouds bearing weapons.
O Brahmin, consciousness (cit), by virtue of its three-eyed nature marked by the bull and the moon,
has attained the state of being adorned by the lotus-cluster of Gaurī’s face;
and having reached the state of being adorned by the lotus of Viṣṇu, it has its mind subject to meditation.
It maintains the status of the primordial lotus-lake of the triple Veda.
O Brahmin, the conscious principle assumes numerous diverse bodies here,
just as leaves grow upon a tree or as bracelets and other ornaments are fashioned from gold.
Indeed, she whose feet are worshipped by the entire host of gods assumes the status of the crest-jewel of the three worlds through her playful sovereignty;
indeed, having attained the state of both gods and asuras within the grand display of the belly of the three worlds.
It falls, it rises, and it moves, by its own self like the water of the ocean.
The moonlight of consciousness, spreading its radiance in all four directions,
causes the night-lotus beds of the existence of all beings to blossom.

The Great Lakṣmī who is the mirror of consciousness receives the triple world reflected within her by means of grace, just as a pregnant woman carries her embryo within her womb. Consciousness [perceives] the great spheres of the fourteen elements.
The glory of water makes it become like the ocean;
it possesses flowers of diverse light, sprouts of dense volition,
has ascended the field of the sky, and bears the fruit of the flood of existence.
A mass of pollen from the net of living beings, colored by the essence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), enveloped in the skin of sensory perception, and crowded with the buds of mental activity;
she whose radiant form consists of the filaments of the countless triple worlds of the past.
Laughing with the exuberant play of incessant throbbing, she is roughened by the festivals of all seasons and entwined with inert mountains and the like;
she is coiled with the knots of birds and is devoid of both root and tip.
This mind is blossomed, its subtle body consisting of both the real and the unreal;
it is a manifold flower of the visible world, variegated and unable to endure close scrutiny. Indeed, by means of this [mind], even a mere shadow is produced everywhere here.
The object is conceived, expanded, sung, and even acted out;
by this Great Consciousness, the sun and other luminaries shine eternally,
and bodies take pleasure in one another through the delusions of consciousness and insentience arising from "you" and "me."
This wind of consciousness dances along the path of its wide-spread whirlpools;
it is the trace of dust in the net of the world, whose very existence embodies the visible.
Consciousness alone fully manifests this entire undertaking of the universe.
Just as a lamp, the crest-light of the illuminator of the three worlds, [reveals] the beauty of colors; so too,
having attained union with the stainless lunar orb of consciousness,
the splendor of all objects existing in the world becomes perceptible everywhere.
By the sprinkling of the elixir of consciousness (*cid-rasāyana*), the series of multitudes of objects attains both form and fruit, like a beautiful creeper watered by the rains.
By the shadow of consciousness alone, the insentience of everything either subsides or arises.
If these wonders of consciousness did not exist within this body— which is like a corpse and shrouded in darkness as a house is by gloom—
then who would they be, and what forms would they take, were the three worlds themselves their bodies? (MU 6.34.56–57)
In this house of the body, within the light of consciousness, the flickering young bride of the multitude of actions dwells, bearing her infant-like volitions.
Without the light of consciousness, for whom would she manifest, even while quivering at the tip of the tongue?
How, when, and in what manner does it manifest, and what is its nature?
Even if it has a sturdy trunk, well-formed branches, and is completely surrounded by the bees of curly hair,
how can the tree of the body shine without the blossom-cluster of consciousness?

"It grows, desires, and consumes; it is consciousness alone that acts as both the moving and the unmoving. Consciousness alone exists; nothing else exists. This entire world has arisen as mere consciousness.
Having spoken thus with a voice as clear as a flow of nectar, the Three-eyed Lord [Śiva] then—
Again, O Rāma, I questioned him with words radiant with humility and modesty:
"O Lord, if consciousness (*cit*) is all-pervading, one, and of the nature of that [Brahman],
then why is this [one] conscious of the manifold, while this [other] is not conscious at all?"
"How can this conception—that he was once possessed of consciousness but is now situated as one devoid of consciousness—be a matter of direct experience in the world? Thus [asks the opponent].
The Lord says:
Listen to this in its entirety, O Brahmin; I shall speak to you according to what you have asked.
This question you have raised is great, O best among the knowers of Brahman.
Consciousness exists here within the two bodies, consisting of the nature of all beings.
But that one which is oriented toward the object of thought is known as the supreme, non-conceptual state.
Though its essence is bound by volition within, it remains as if it were something else entirely—
like a woman who, having abandoned her vows, has fallen into immoral conduct.

For just as that very same man, out of anger, becomes like another in an instant here, so too does consciousness (cit), marked by conceptual construction (vikalpa), undergo a change in its own nature;
O Brahman, consciousness, seized by conceptualization, falls away from its true nature.
Gradually manifesting insentience, consciousness enters the state of objective ideation;
it attains the nature of a spatial atom,
and subsequently becomes the subtle element of air, consisting of the seed of sound.

Divided by space and time, and enveloped by the subtle elements (tanmātras), it sequentially becomes the individual soul (jīva), then quickly becomes the intellect (buddhi), then the ego (ahaṃkāra), and then the mind (manas).
Having attained the state of the mind, it takes hold of the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra).
Just as a twice-born man becomes an outcaste through the thought "I am an outcaste," so too does consciousness become an outcaste through the failure to awaken to its own nature.
Due to the dullness resulting from the lack of awakening to its own conceptualizations, consciousness assumes a variegated form and proceeds incessantly with those conceptualizations.
Consisting of infinite volitions and thickened by the volition of inertia,
consciousness enters the body due to its own dullness, just as water turns into the state of stone.
Therefore, it receives the designations "mind," "intellect," "delusion," and "illusion."
O Sage, having resorted to clever dullness, one is born in *saṃsāra*. Having attained a state of habitual delusion, one is tormented by the fetters of craving;
possessed of desire, anger, and fear, one falls excessively into existence and non-existence.
Having abandoned her own infinite enjoyments, subject to the fluctuations of limitation,
scorched by the forest fire of suffering, and her heart emaciated by the thunderbolt of grief;
she is rendered disintegrated by the void sense of "I am this."
Having placed her reliance solely upon the perception of difference, she has fallen into supreme wretchedness;
submerged in the great mire of delusion like an aged female elephant in mud,
her little body swings to and fro on the pendulum of existence and non-existence.
Dealing with the transformations of this essence-less and worthless saṃsāra,
her heart tormented by distress, she follows the disease of passion;
like a doe strayed from her own herd, she has fallen into a state of helplessness.
Her form, which had arisen through manifestation, has set with its concealment.
Like a young girl fleeing from illusory spirits (vetālī), she flees even from those terrifying visions that arise from her own imagination and vanish when they prove to be unreal.
Like a camel longing for a drop of honey, one craves conditioned happiness;
falling from one misfortune into another due to vice, one descends further and further.
Having fallen from one peril into a more dire peril, one reaches a state of supreme helplessness.
Fallen from suffering into further suffering, situated in calamity after calamity,
beset by a multitude of various misfortunes, their intentions subject to the power of worldly activity,
they pass from hardship to greater hardship, consumed by the heat of remorse.
Successively, as she encountered ever new bonds, she fell into a state of utter lack of skill; intent on creating various structures, she reached the state of a worm.
Terrified of Śaṅkara on all sides, she met with the loss of her life.
Like a small fish in dwindling water, she is intent on tossing about;
helpless in all matters during childhood, seized by anxiety in youth,
tormented by the suffering of death in old age, and finally dead, brought under the sway of karma.
She is born variegated with suffering, dies while facing rebirth,
acts under the sway of obsession, and swallows [the world] while bearing agony;
she goes forth tormented by exhaustion and becomes as fragile as a water bubble.
With her heart overcome, she weeps; tormented, she cries out aloud—
an Apsaras in the city of heaven, a Nāginī in the depths of Pātāla,
an Asurī in the caverns of the Daityas, and a human woman on the surface of the earth.
A *rākṣasī* is on the support of a *rākṣasa*, a *vānarī* is in a hollow of the forest,
a *siṃhī* is on the peak of the king of mountains, a *kinnarī* is on a principal mountain (*kulaparvata*),
a *vidyādharī* is on a divine mountain (*devagiri*), and a *vyālī* is in a pit in the earth.

A creeper on a tree, a female bird in a nest, a climbing plant on a mountain peak, and a doe in the forest; Nārāyaṇa reclines in the ocean, the lotus-born Brahmā is absorbed in meditation in the city of Brahman,
Hara is with his beloved on the mountain, and Hari is the preeminent god in heaven.

The sun of sharp rays creates the day; the cloud pours down water; the moon creates the night; and the great ocean holds the water. The wheel of the seasons revolves together with the circle of the constellations and time.
In one place, light arises for three days and nights, while in another there is total darkness; in one place there is the swelling sap of seeds, in another the silence of stone;
in one place a river flows with water, and in another the spreading of flowers.

In some places there is the ripening of rows of fruits; in some places, decoctions produced by fire and other means; in some places, coolness from snow, the moon, and so forth; and in some places, the void where nothing exists at all.
In some places it has a blazing form; in some places it is black; and in some places it is white.

In some places blue, then green; in some places fire, in some places earth—because she is the self of all, because she is omnipresent, and because she is impelled by all-pervasive power, she is of a single form due to her universality, yet more transparent than even the sky; she is that supreme [reality].
In whatever manner, by whatever means, in whatever place, and at whatever time the self accumulates [karma],
it quickly becomes exactly so, just as waves and the like arise from the rush of water.
A female swan, a curlew, a crane, a crow, a female lotus-bird, or a she-wolf— [each becomes what she has accumulated].
Pikī, Balākā, Hariṇī, Vānarī, Karīṇī, Śunī; Caṭikā, Vañjulī, Śārī, Makṣikā, Ṣaṭpadī, Śukī;
Dhī, Śrī, Hrī, Prīti, Ārti, Śabarī, Śarvarī, and Śaśī.
Wandering through these and other various wombs,
she revolves in *saṃsāra* like a blade of grass in a whirlpool of water;
she fears her own mental constructions as a female donkey fears its own braying.
There is no other [power] like this one— deluded, childish, weak, and fickle. O Sage, I have described to you this power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti),
who is helpless under the sway of natural conduct, wretched, and subject to the laws of the bound (paśu).
Having acquired the designation "the self of action," this [individual soul] of the Supreme Self is to be pitied;
it has itself fallen into agitation amidst an abundance of endless suffering.
By this [soul], the non-existent, perishable, and innate impurity has been assumed.
Just as the husk remains as something other than the rice grain, so too does [the world] appear as something other [than Brahman].
Deprived of infinite glory and tormented by misfortune,
she laments upon attaining the state of a living being, like a heroine abandoned by her husband.

Behold the power of devotion to the insentient: without the remembrance of one's own state, it moves backward from here toward a downward fall, like the buckets on the wheel of a water-drawing machine at a well.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Investigation into the Nature of Consciousness Directed Toward Objects."
Chapter Thirty-five.
Īśvara said:
In this way, one accumulates only falsehood through the mental cultivation of "I am suffering."

Just as a young bride, intoxicated and as if asleep, might think "I have fallen" and weep though she has not perished, so too does the consciousness (cit) possess a perverted intellect that thinks "I am dead," though it is indeed immortal. Just as she weeps thinking "I am lost" though she is not lost, such is the nature of consciousness.

Just as this world is seen by one whose mind is inverted due to the absence of a [real] cause, and which, though illusory, appears stable, so too does the delusion of "I-ness" appear to consciousness. For it is the nature of consciousness (*cittvam*) that serves as the cause for that consciousness to experience the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
Nor is there any cause for that, because of the impossibility of its being either identical to or different from consciousness.
For in this way, due to the absence of a cause and because the object of cognition is impossible,
it is not consciousness, nor is that an object of cognition, nor is that cognized by it.
It does not possess the nature of the seen, the seeing, or the seer, like oil in a stone;
it does not possess the nature of agent, object, or instrument, like darkness in the moon;
nor does it possess mind, the object of mind, or the means of measurement, like a new sprout in the sky.
Consciousness, the object of consciousness, and so forth do not exist [in the Self], just as the *khadira* tree does not exist in the Nandana grove;
nor do "I-ness," "you-ness," "that-ness," and so on, just as mountain-ness does not exist in the sky;
nor do "this-ness" and "other-place-ness," just as soot does not exist in conch-shells or eyes.
There is no diversity, nor is there any interval between them, like Mount Sumerus within a single atom;
nor is there the splendor of words for word-meanings, like a great creeper upon a salt-waste.
It is "not this, not this," and it is not like night within the orb of the sun.
Neither reality nor unreality exists in frost, just as heat does not;
neither emptiness nor non-emptiness exists in a tree within a stone casket.
Nor is there a "great emptiness" of emptiness, for it is like the absence of a hole in the sky.
Only the state of absolute oneness (kevalībhāva), which is self-abidingness itself, remains; no fault of anyone exists, for this is attained through the state of pure knowing.
Merely by the absence of the objects denoted by negation, the misfortune that had spread over consciousness [is removed].
The misfortune is pacified by the mere cultivation of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*).

Apart from the mere cultivation of the meaning of the negative particle, nothing else here is required—not even a blade of grass, nor even the three worlds; thus, this matter is entirely within your own power.
For this matter is indeed within one's own power, yet it remains difficult to accomplish because of a lack of cultivation;
for how indeed can that which is not accomplished by a person be obtained?
That consciousness which is free from conceptual construction and non-dual, though it pervades everything—

It is the supreme, singular, and transcendent light, the illuminator even of lights. It is this very one that brings illumination, all-pervading, eternally pure, ever-arisen, devoid of mind, changeless, and stainless.
Established in the pot, the cloth, the banyan tree, the wall, the cart, the monkey, the god, the asura, the ocean, the spirit, the man, and the serpent,
she remains like a witness; being ever-existent, she does not move anywhere.
A lamp exists solely for the purpose of illumination; it does not perform any further action.
Though she is pure, she appears as if stained; though free from conceptual construction, she is rich in conceptual constructions.
Though insentient, she is the essence of sentience; though not everything, she is indeed everything.
The supreme, subtle consciousness, free from conceptual construction, perceives its own self-awareness;
just as the wind causes the limbs, vital organs, and so forth, or a machine, to move, so too consciousness—
when enveloped by form, light, and mental attention— due to a lack of awakening [to its true nature], [engages in worldly activity].
Upon awakening, that very [consciousness] remains; for it is neither existent nor non-existent.

That supreme, utterly transparent Consciousness enters into the state of thought through the act of cognizing, just as a virtuous person becomes like a wicked one through the perception of evil people.

Just as gold that has become dark returns to its state of copper through the removal of impurities, and then attains its supreme state of brilliance once again; so too does the Intellect (cit). When the breath is stilled, it returns to its original state, just like a mirror.
Likewise, having come here to this creation, through awakening it returns to its own state of consciousness. From the non-recognition of its true nature, transmigratory existence proceeds;
but from the recognition of its true nature, this very existence, though unreal, comes to rest.

When, through its nature as consciousness, it gathers within itself that which is unreal— the sense of otherness— then, having attained as it were a state of "I-ness," it perishes as it were, though it is indestructible.
Like a stone from the edge of a mountain peak falling downward with a slight tremor, it descends.
Just so, from consciousness, there is a downward fall of the Great Consciousness (mahācit).
This existence of form and the rest is indeed the object of cognition; yet the stainless consciousness itself is the pure cognizer.
Duality and unity, which arise from non-awakening, dissolve through awakening.
The awakening of consciousness within the mind, senses, and so forth occurs by the mere presence of consciousness,
just as worldly activity proceeds by the mere presence of light;
from the wind [of the vital breath] comes the movement of the pupil, and its radiance is called sight.
Form falls outside of that [consciousness], yet the awareness of form is the supreme consciousness (cit).
Skin and wind are inert and insubstantial; their conjunction is called touch.
The cognition of touch is the act of thinking (manana), but the awareness of that [thinking] is the supreme consciousness.
The connection between the subtle element of smell and the wind is the cognition of smell;
yet the perception of these [objects], when devoid of the mind, is supreme consciousness itself. This occurs through the union of the power of hearing the subtle element of sound with the mind.
Consciousness resembling deep sleep is declared to be the supreme consciousness (cit).
The tendency toward action arises from volition; volition is the process of mental reflection (manana);
and mental reflection is the turbidity of consciousness itself. Consciousness becomes pure when it is the Self (ātman).
Consciousness, whose nature is luminosity, eternal, and established in its own self alone,
sustains this world within itself, just as a stone contains its internal structure;
it maintains this non-dual state, free from modification and the like.

It neither sets nor rises; it neither vibrates nor grows. Having entered into the state of living beings through volition, yet by its own nature free from volition, consciousness—remaining itself—manifests both the insentient and the non-insentient as objective existence.

The vital breath (jīva) is known as the chariot of this [intellect]; the ego-sense (ahaṅkṛti) is the chariot of the vital breath; the intellect (buddhi) is the chariot of the ego-sense, and likewise the mind (manas) is the chariot of the intellect. The vital breath (prāṇa) is the chariot of the mind, and the group of senses (akṣagaṇa) is the chariot of the vital breath.
The body is the chariot for the flood of the senses; the movement of the body is the chariot.
Movement is action, which is saṃsāra, the cage of old age and death. Thus has this wheel been set in motion, born of the manifestation of mental afflictions.
It appears within itself like a pervasive dream that is non-existent;
it does not possess even the slightest essence of reality, remaining like the water of a mirage.
O Lord of Sages, the vital breath (prāṇa) is known as the chariot of this mental construction.

Wherever the vital breath (prāṇamarut) is, there the faculty of thought (manana) is established. Wherever this mental activity (kalanā) resides, it causes that very place to tremble; just as wherever a whirlwind goes to the forest, that very place is made to swirl.
When the mind has merged into space, the vital breath does not stir;
when the fire has reached non-existence, it no longer shines like form.
When the vital breath is stilled, the mind does not perceive even the slightest thing within itself.
When the whirlwind has subsided, the dust indeed does not stir.
Where the wind of the vital breath goes, there the mind remains;
wherever the chariot follows, there the charioteer is present.

The mind, impelled by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), travels to another place in an instant, like a stone released from a sling; it is not otherwise so swift. Where there is a flower, there is fragrance; where there is fire, there is heat.
Where there is breath, there is the mind; where there is the moon (the vital essence), there is its radiance.
Consciousness arises from the vibration of the wind through contact with the channels by its own nature.
The expansion of consciousness is the mind; therefore, it resides within the cavity of the vital breath.
Consciousness exists everywhere—in both the insentient and the sentient—as clear as the sky;
yet it is experienced as if it were agitated by the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa). Abiding in insentient things by way of its nature as pure existence alone, it remains present.
Awakened by the vital breath (prāṇa), it arises as the nature of sensation within the insentient [body],
having previously leaped forth through various expansive manifestations.
But once thought (manana) has passed away, that very same breath does not quickly descend again.
O Sage, the Supreme Self is reflected within the city of eight (the subtle body),
just as a reflection is seen in a mirror and not in stones or other such things.
Know that the mind is the "city of eight," the sole cause of all effects.

That very [reality] is described through various other distinctions imagined according to one's own inclinations. Since that from which arises the fruit—the entire web of the disordered visible world—is experienced as being none other than that [reality], know for certain: the mind indeed revolves through the perception of the body, but all that is ultimately non-substantial; understand that to be your true self.
The thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Unity of Mind and Vital Breath," [spoken by] the Lord.

O Sage, listen: how does consciousness—which performs actions, is characterized by vibration, and seems to fall—attain what is called death for men? It is through those former volitions of the mind, as well as other personal mental intentions and desires in this life.
O Sage, that power which has attained the state of the mind— having become exceedingly dense through these various winds of karma, as if it were utterly inert—
is made to vibrate by this self-consciousness, O Brahmin, which stands as its witness.
O Sage, by the grace of this [intellect], that variegated world— though possessed of blemishes—
is both created and not created here as a city of Gandharvas.
Without the existence of the self, the individual soul remains mute, like a wall.
By its existence, it vibrates like a stone set in motion by the sky;
just as extremely inert iron vibrates in the proximity of a magnet,
so does this individual soul (jīva) vibrate when the all-pervading Supreme Being is present.
This individual soul (jīva) manifests sufficiently by its own inherent power alone;
it takes up a reflection from an external object, not even from one situated within itself.
Because it has utterly forgotten its true nature, this jīva has fallen into a state of insentience.
Due to delusion and the forgetting of its true nature, consciousness— like a noble twice-born man reduced to the state of a Śūdra—
has indeed forgotten its own essence and fallen into the condition of being a mere mind;
because its intellect is afflicted by delusion, it has become as if greatly dejected.

The body is moved by an inert and helpless power of thought, driven by the force of the vital breath, like a leaf by a succession of waves; it is moved by this wretched living soul and mind, which are themselves of the nature of karma.

The bodily machines are moved about like stones by the wind. For, O Brahmin, in the drawing along of the chariots of the bodies, the arising of the mind and the vital breath are made the two firm laborers by the Supreme Self.
In one place, having accepted the form of the insentient as well as the state of being a living soul,
and having mounted the chariot of mental desire with the vital breaths as its draft-horses;
in another place, it assumes the state of an arisen object, and in yet another, the state of a perished object.
Sometimes assuming the state of many objects, sometimes the state of various objects—
as if having gone elsewhere or as if divided, yet never abandoning its own station—
it exists like water taking on the form of waves; it is that very same [reality], ever-arisen, appearing both as being and as non-being.
The supreme form of the Self shines forth within the mental modifications (vṛttis),
just as the beauty of form residing in material objects depends upon this light.
When the stainless Supreme Self, which is the essence of consciousness (cittattva), remains present, [the world manifests].
The living being lives with its world, just as a house does when there is a lamp.
Mental anxieties and physical ailments indeed swell in this [body],
just as water becomes waves and waves become foam.
The living soul, like a bee in the lotus of the body crowded with mental and physical ailments,
falls into a state of helplessness, just as water turns into waves.
Because the power of consciousness possesses all powers, through the realization that "I am not the intellect," [the soul attains liberation].
Though independent, it falls into a state of helplessness, like the brilliance of the sun obscured by clouds.
Possessing hope yet rendered helpless by delusion, it does not find self-awareness,
just as one overcome by profound numbness fails to feel the crushing of his own limbs.
Through delusion, the contemplation of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) perishes for this [individual],
just as a being possessed by dense delusion loses the memory of its own purpose.
Then, due to delusion, there is no perception of the limbs or of the power of movement (spanda-śakti).
Just as a leper does not feel the movement of his limbs, so too,
when there is no consciousness in the vibration of the body, the lotus-leaf situated in the heart does not quiver,
remaining untouched like a wooden leaf outside.
When the lotus petal is motionless, these vital breaths within attain peace,
just as the powers of the wind outside cease when the palm-leaf fan is still.
When the internal breath is stilled through the absence of touch, the living soul reaches a state of profound silence.
Just as dust becomes invisible when the wind in the sky has subsided, so too the mind,
deprived of its chariot and lacking any support, is seen to exist as mere mind;
it remains within the Self like the seed of a tree that has not yet obtained earth, water, or other conditions.

Thus, when the entire collection of instruments has become impaired on all sides and the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka) has met its destruction, the body falls motionless. Through delusion regarding consciousness, the object of consciousness, and the lack of consciousness, latent impression (vāsanā) undergoes vibration.
When spoken to, it remembers one thing and forgets another on its own.
Through the vibration of the heart-lotus machine, the *puryaṣṭaka* clearly comes into being;
when the flow within the heart-lotus machine is blocked, the *puryaṣṭaka* perishes.
"As long as the *puryaṣṭaka* exists within the body, so long does that [individual] live;
when the *puryaṣṭaka* has ceased, O twice-born one, the body is said to be dead.
This occurs due to the obstruction by contrary impurities and under the influence of states of cutting and piercing."
When the mechanism of the heart-lotus no longer throbs within,
then the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) gradually attains peace in the ether,
just as a succession of winds ceases when the wind-mechanism is obstructed.
Due to the power of his own lack of self-awareness, the individual soul falls into a state of helplessness;
lacking strength, it can no longer set in motion the lotus-machine situated within the body.
This is so for those whose pure latent impressions (*vāsanā*) do not depart from their hearts.

Those whose life-force (*jīva*) is stable and of a single form are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) and possess long lives. For when the lotus-machine is restrained and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has attained peace,
this body, lacking fortitude, falls to the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of earth.
Just as the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) becomes merged in the wind of the sky,
even so, O Sage, the mind then attains dissolution right there. The mind, which has long been accustomed to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) residing in its habitual states, [is thus dissolved].
Here and there it perceives its own wandering through heaven, hell, and other realms.
Deprived of the mind and vital breaths, the body becomes like a corpse;
it is as if a house falls into utter desolation once the householders have gone far away.
The all-pervading consciousness, having become a living soul through its power of volition and residing in the mind,
assumes the body of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold subtle body) and becomes an embodied being of a transportable nature;
it remains established by embracing the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) within its own consciousness.
Through intense contemplation, one subsequently perceives a gross form as if it were a dream or an illusion; then, becoming absorbed in that very state,
one momentarily forgets everything regarding the nature of the subtle, transportable body.
Even though this body is unreal,
the artificial conception formed toward it leads the unreal to the state of reality, and even reality to the state of unreality.
For consciousness, becoming the individual soul through its partial aspect, becomes the mind.
The mind mounts the chariot of the city-of-eight, and from that, the world proceeds.
The city-of-eight, consisting of wind, thoroughly raises up the body;
for then the individual soul (jīva), residing in the heart, is said to be like a vampire (vetāla).
When the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) has perished and the mind dissolves into the ether,
then the body no longer vibrates and is said to be "dead.
By the power of its own nature, the living soul (*jīva*) falls into a state of incapacity through forgetfulness.
Due to enmity and the power of time, the leaf becomes as if worn out;
O Sage, when the lotus-machine is seized by the vital force (*jīvaśakti*) and obstructed, and the *prāṇa* reaches a state of total arrest, the human being dies. (MU 6.36.47–48)
Just as leaves that have grown, having lived out their time, fall from a tree one after another, so too do the bodies of men. The bodies of embodied beings are born and they die.
And as for the leaves of trees—what cause for lamentation is there in that?
These rows of body-bubbles quiver in the ocean of consciousness;
some here, others there—a wise person has no attachment to them.
Although consciousness is omnipresent, it is reflected in this mind; for no other [medium] can grasp an internal object except for a mirror.
In the vast, pure sky of consciousness, forms of serene appearance manifest, though they are not composed of that [sky].
The rivers of the torments of delusion caused by various bodies, noisy with clamor yet clearly beautiful;
this is the thirty-seventh canto, titled "Reflection on the Fall of the Body."
Vasiṣṭha said:
How has duality come to the great-souled reality of consciousness (cittattva), which bears the crescent moon as its crest, is infinite, and is of a single form?
And how, O Mahādeva, does that which has taken root through the passage of time come to cause the affliction of suffering when it is warded off by wisdom? Īśvara said:

When consciousness, which is all-powerful Brahman, exists as the one eternal reality, then this arising and subsiding of duality and unity is utterly rootless. Indeed, duality could only exist if there were unity; and if unity were real, there would be the form of duality.
At the time [of dissolution], there are only two: the form of consciousness and that which is of the nature of consciousness; yet even that [latter] is non-existent because it lacks oneness.
Here, due to the absence of one, both oneness and duality are absent;
for without the one, there is no second, and without the second, there is no oneness.
Because cause and effect share a single essence, they possess a single form;

for even that which ends in the fruit, such as a seed and so forth, is merely a conceptualization of transformation. And consciousness, consisting of that [essence], manifests by itself through the non-conceptualization of the object of cognition.
Therefore, that very [reality] does not differ from its modifications and so forth, because it is their essence.
This conceptualization of modification and the like, arising from that [reality] with respect to objects,
attains meaningfulness through various notions of cause and effect and so on.
A wave is not "non-water" within the water; therefore, he to whom this [distinction] belongs is like us.
He to whom that [distinction] belongs is like a rabbit's horn; he for whom [the distinction] is real is like a sprout from the sky.
Now that the realization of the reality of things has been achieved here, enough with your verbal fabrications.
"O twice-born one, it is said that speech, because it is verbal in nature, cannot easily be cut off from [the act of] exclusion and so forth.
Yet, the omnipotence of Brahman is not truly divided [from it],
just as the waves, foam, and masses of spray are not distinct from the water of the ocean."
Just as flowers, sprouts, leaves, and so forth belong to the creeper and nothing else,
so too do duality, unity, the state of being the world, "thou-ness," and "I-ness" belong to consciousness.
For whatever distinction there is— such as space, time, or modification— is fashioned by consciousness itself.
"That alone is consciousness"—this has been declared to you; no further question is appropriate here for you.
Space, time, action, existence, necessity, and other such powers are indeed of the nature of consciousness; they have descended from themselves by virtue of the existence of consciousness.
And this consciousness, which is here celebrated as the object of thought, is remembered by such names as "Brahmā" and so forth;
it is like water that, though possessing the capacity for the name "wave," remains as water while being rippled.
[It is the great ocean of the play of consciousness, from which the wave of the sense of "I" arises.]
That which has not yet attained the state of being an object of cognition, as if it were merely a state of rippling,
is this very Supreme Brahman, celebrated by such names as Satya, Īśvara, Śiva, Śūnya, Eka, Paramātman, and so forth.

That form of the Supreme Self which is beyond such categories as "word" (padātīta) is not fit for naming; it is stainless and is not an object of words. This which is seen belongs to that great consciousness, which is like a creeper.

Since fruits, sprouts, flowers, and so forth are not distinct [from it], they consist of that very essence. Because the Great Consciousness accumulates objects of thought, it becomes the "running" consciousness; it perceives itself as the individual soul (jīvatva) and that as the external world, seeing that non-dual reality as if it were two.
Having contemplated by its own nature that "I am indeed other than this," it attains, as it were, a state of otherness; its own selfhood consists of its own volition.
That form which possesses its own stain appears as a form with a stain through its stainless form.
Having encountered that which has fallen into saṃsāra,
this very conscious body itself attains the state of a living being through consciousness alone.
By the manifestation of the principle of consciousness (cittattva), the living being, consisting of that [consciousness], lives.
The consciousness of living beings, having attained the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*),
becomes fivefold through mental cultivation and fully perceives, "I am a substance. That substance, once consumed by living beings, quickly attains the state of vital energy (*vīryatā*).
Then, having become possessed of vital breath, it knows— that which consists of experience—
through the sequence of "I-ness" (ahantā) and so forth, by means of the rapid succession of the fivefold experiences;
whatever it knows, whether stationary or moving, that it becomes perfectly.
Through a chance coincidence (*kākatālīya-yoga*) and through the exhaustion of firm habitual practice (*abhyāsa*),
[the mind] abandons its previous form due to its connection with another latent impression (*vāsanā*).
By means of the self-awareness of duality, duality arises even for that which is actually one.
Like a man who, through contact with a *vetāla*, becomes radiant like a *vetāla* himself,
duality ceases for the self through the realization of non-duality;
just as agency ceases for a person through the resolve, "I do not act."
In the ultimate sense, duality does not indeed exist within the Self,
because it is eternally changeless and all-pervading.
For that which is fashioned by one's own volition perishes when volition ceases.
O Sage, it is like a kingdom of the mind, like a city of the Gandharvas;
affliction consists in the construction of mental constructs, not in their destruction.
Effort toward mental construction is for the creation of a city of the Gandharvas, but not for its dissolution.
Since this suffering has arrived merely through the intensification of one's own volitions, it can be destroyed by the mere absence of such volition; what cause for distress is there in this?
For by forming even the slightest volition, a person sinks into suffering.
By not forming any mental constructs whatsoever, one enjoys imperishable happiness.
If your consciousness remains free from the serpent of mental constructs,
then you will shine brilliantly in the pleasure grove of bliss.
Having brought about the destruction of the cloud of conceptualization with the winds of your own discernment,
attain supreme purity like the expanse of the sky in autumn;
drying up the intoxicated river of conceptualization with the machine of your intellect.
There, having consoled yourself as you are being carried along,
with your mind free from worldly existence, look upon yourself supported within the elemental ether— shaken by the wind of volition and wandering like bits of leaves and straw.
Having warded off the turbidity of your own volitions by means of yourself,
and having attained supreme serenity, become possessed of the highest bliss.
For the Self here, by virtue of its omnipotence, manifests whatever it intensely contemplates in whatever manner.
Then he sees that [world] as such, manifested by his own volition (saṅkalpa).
This world has arisen falsely as mere volition alone;
O Brahmin, it dissolves somewhere simply by the absence of volition.
The cluster of flames of birth, stirred by the wind of volitional thought,
is extinguished like a lamp upon contact with the wind of non-volition.
This thorny creeper of craving, having reached full growth—
By uprooting the root of conceptual construction, make it withered away.
The arising of appearances and the cessation of appearances—
just as a city of the Gandharvas, so too is the delusion of saṃsāra.
The king grieves as long as he forgets that "I am a common man," and as long as the memory "I am a king" has not arisen in his heart;
O Brahmin, the former memory perishes once the present one has been born.
Just as the rainy season, having arrived, causes the autumn to lose its clarity,
so too does the impulse of the mind increase whenever there is a flow of dense [thoughts].
Just as a high pitch of a stringed instrument overshadows the other notes, so too does that very [impulse] dominate the faculty of hearing.
"Meditate upon this single contemplation: 'I am one; I am the Self.
Endowed with that contemplation, you will indeed become that very thing sufficiently.
For in this way, this state of Brahman—which is non-dual, radiant, indivisible, the supreme goal, and the highest divinity—is realized."

The form of the object of worship, the act of worship, the excellent worshipper, and the worshipped itself— being of a single nature with the mind, it is like something that is both something and nothing.
The thirty-eighth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of the Deity."
Īśvara said:
Thus this universe stands, consisting of the existent and the non-existent, and having the nature of the gods;
it is free from the states of duality and unity, yet even that freedom from duality and unity is transcended.
The nature of consciousness, like a mirror with a stain, has entered into the state of transmigratory existence;
yet that which is unstained and non-transmigratory is non-different from it, being of a dual nature.
Consciousness, having acquired the stain through the thought "I am this," becomes bound.

Having understood this very digit (kalā) as non-different from one's own self, one is liberated. Because of the absence of the state of having the form of objects, consciousness abandons its duality and, while not being [inherently] existent, it instantly assumes the state of pleasure, pain, and so forth, [only] insofar as it is "existent."
Pure, partless, the one true existence—by such terms as these, it is called "liberated" from all names, words, and meanings; yet, though being the self of all, it is like space.
All is incomparable and peaceful at the end of the mind, where the three paths converge.
"This universe has been expanded by Brahman through the power of Brahman, which resembles the ether.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"When the mind is severed within the mind—that which is the source of all the senses—"
Then, what remains in the second or even the third step?
For as long as there is the existence of the self, so long does that very Great Existence persist.
When the dissolution of all things has occurred, what kind of existence could there be, and from where could it arise?

Īśvara: When the mind has been severed within the mind—within that which consists of one's own senses and limbs—through discernment, through meditative absorption, through practice, or through mastery; MU 6.38.9.

When the distinction between the conceptualization of duality and unity has dissolved within the perceived self, and when the web of the world— swollen with the appearance of reality— has gone to its dissolution,
there remains that whose nature is the perception of the shattering of the conceptualization of saṃsāra.
The existence of the living being, called consciousness, is like parched grain;
it is named Paśyantī, unconditioned, and having abandoned the chewing upon objects of thought,
it is like the treasury of the autumnal sky freed from the great clouds of the mind.
Pure consciousness, abiding as mere being, has fallen into the instability of the objectified non-conscious;
yet it is not far removed from its Lord, who purifies through the prostration at his feet.
Consciousness, conceived as the self of space, has dissolved all conceptual constructions.
Possessing all commonalities yet not descended into the ocean of worldly existence,
she is nourished by the expertise of the state of dreamless sleep;
having reached the further shore, she who was long exhausted now rests in that expansive state.
This first step has been explained to you when the mind has been stilled;
now hear, O best of Brahmins, the second step, which is most purifying for this power of consciousness.
This very power of consciousness, when liberated from the mind, is characterized by peace.
She is as beautiful as the vast sky freed from all darkness and stars;
she is like the internal disposition within a stone covered by a thick layer of deep sleep,
like the essence within salt, and like the power of vibration within the wind.
When, in due course, it reaches its ultimate transformation right there,
it then moves into the supreme space like the power of sound in the ether; indeed,
it surely abandons its orientation toward the object of thought, just as water abandons its turbulence.
Like a streak of wind it possesses movement; like a streak of flowers, fragrance.
Having abandoned both temporality and spatiality, while remaining stainless amidst all instability, it maintains an infinite, nameless existence that is neither inert nor non-inert.
[He saw] that certain [reality], which is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, which has reached the state of Great Being (mahāsattā),
which is endowed with the fourth part of the fourth state (turyaturya), stainless and free from affliction,
and which stands as if within the eyes of the large-eyed one.
"O you of noble vows, this second state has been described to you as being intent upon the tasting of all things, in every way and at all times.
Now listen, O best among those who know the states, for I shall speak of the third state."
This vision, through the dissolution of the perceived object, has reached the state of the Nameless Reality;
transcending the meaning of words such as "Brahman" or "Self," it arises as absolute purity alone,
characterized by stability in time and by its stainless nature as the essence of clarity.
Because it bears names such as "Beyond the Fourth" (turyātīta), it attains the supreme state.
That is the highest point beyond the high, the primordial matter (pradhāna) by virtue of its nature as Śiva;
it is eternal, one, indivisible, the third, and purifying state.
O dear one, though she has long been established in this state and has traveled far along the paths of all hopes,
she does not come within the range of my words.
O Sage, you have told me that she transcends the reckoning of the three paths.
"Abide eternally in this state," so says the eternal God.
O Sage, this entire universe consists of this [Self], because it is known as being composed of that;
through the realization of Truth, O Lord of Sages, there is neither "this" nor "not this."
Nothing whatsoever proceeds here, and nothing whatsoever ceases;
it is peaceful, appearing as an even equality, and is indeed non-material like the interior of space.
Because of its non-dual unity, its lack of agitation, and its dense, solid nature, it is thus.
And because they possess immutability and other such qualities,

there is no difference whatsoever— however slight— between the mountains, the cavities, and the worlds, whether eternal or non-eternal, for they are all of the nature of a mass of consciousness, like existing things that are as if non-existent.
The All is Being, Śiva, the Peaceful, transcending the play of speech;
it is "Om," and from that mere measure, from its fourth part, it is the supreme "Om. Thus said Vālmīki.

Having spoken thus, the Lord of pure vision, in whom all sounds had subsided and who was delightful in his tranquility, remained silent for a moment in that vast state of ultimate transformation, together with that sage, his own mental fluctuations having been completely stilled. Thus ends the chapter titled "The Instruction of the Supreme Lord."
The thirty-ninth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, in a moment, Hara [reached] Gaurī’s lotus-pond.
Intent on manifesting my transformation, he freely assumed an outward expansion;
he displayed three eyes arising from his face by the power of Time,
like a mass of sun-gems rising from the casket of heaven and earth.
Withdrawing his splendor like twelve suns risen at an improper time,
yet not destroying the night, the Lord spoke to me with honor:
"O Sage, having summoned your contemplation, let your own being be quickly measured."
Bring forth the goal that is to be brought forth, like the wind blowing.
Whatever is to be seen here has been seen; what is the use of these delusions regarding tranquility?
For I see nothing here, whether to be abandoned or to be acquired, for one who knows that [reality].
You have dissolved these conceptual constructions consisting of both the peaceful and the unpeaceful;
you have awakened to the state as it truly is—you alone are the seer of the self-nature of existence.
Or rather, this state of the visible world was [taught] quickly for the sake of awakening the ignorant.
"Relying upon what I have said, listen; what is the use of remaining silent?
Having spoken thus, the wielder of the trident, looking at me as I stood in external consciousness, struck me—just as the moon, which is not the moonlight itself, strikes the white lotus in a lake.
[Īśvara:
Consciousness is the cause of the bodies' own movements through its state of indifference;
it is the self of those things that are not the true reality, just as the empty sky is the basis for trees. (MU 6.39.9)
The body is perceived by consciousness, yet it is never set in motion [by it].
The master is merely the seer; he becomes the agent only when performing an action.
By means of the vital breath (prāṇa), this house of the body vibrates like a machine.
Having abandoned movement, which is devoid of vital breath, it remains like one who is mute.
The power that impels, the power that purifies, and the power that brings about the consciousness of the intellect—
embodied and clearer than even the ether— it is its own existence alone that is the cause here.
As the vital breath and the body perish, they are indeed characterized by separation;
yet the conscious self (cidātman), clearer even than space, does not perish—so why these delusions?
The principle of consciousness shines forth within the body composed of mind and breath.
A reflection arises in a mirror that has a stainless luster;
O Leader of Sages, even though an object is present before it, it does not produce a reflection in a mirror covered with grime.
Likewise, even when the body has lost its vital breath, although it still exists,
the all-pervading consciousness is not diminished with respect to its vibration of awareness and so forth.
Consciousness alone, being free from the stain of ignorance through awakening, is the supreme Śiva.
They know that God, who is devoted to that [practice] and likewise bestows the welfare of all beings.
He is Hari, he is Śiva, he is Aja, he is Brahmā, he is the Lord of the Gods;
he is the Supreme Lord whose body is wind, fire, moon, and sun.
He alone is known as the all-pervading Self, the Self, Consciousness, Awareness, and Sentience;
the Lord of Gods, the Sustainer of the Body, the Creator, the God of Gods, and the Sovereign of Heaven. From the great effulgence of Consciousness, certain things seem to arise.
Those who are known in this world as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the rest,
are like specks on heated iron or like drops from the ocean;
they have arisen from the Supreme State as if through a slight delusion.
While the seeds of delusion— the creators of the web of conceptual constructions— persist,
this thick ignorance arises with its hundreds and thousands of branches,
entangled like the roots of the Vedas, the meanings of the Vedas, the gods, and the multitude of individual souls.
Then, who would be capable of describing this infinite [nature] which has been repeatedly set forth, perfected through its place and time?
He who is considered the supreme father of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others—

Mahādeva is the root-seed, like a tree to its sprouts. He, who is designated as the reality of Brahman and so forth, is the sole creator of all perception, the bestower of existence to all, the radiant one; he is to be revered and worshipped by those who know him.
Having as its object a directly perceived reality, it is ever-arisen in every respect; because it consists of pure consciousness, it encompasses the entire range of objects.
For that [consciousness], no invocation, mantras, or the like are of any use whatsoever.

Constantly invoked, abiding in all things, that pure consciousness is attained from every side; O Sage, whatever state of objects you enter, from that very state you attain auspiciousness as your own true nature through the vision of the mind directed toward form.
Know him to be the first, worthy of worship, to be saluted, to be praised, the recipient of the guest-offering, and the Lord of the gods;
know him to be the ultimate limit even of the great things that are to be known.
Having thus beheld the Self, which removes old age, sorrow, and fear—

Like a parched seed, a living being does not sprout again. O observer of vows, having worshipped that primordial one known as the "living being" (*jantu*) among all beings—who bestows the state of a living being—you have become the unborn, supreme state consisting of the Self; why then do you sink into [false] views?
The fortieth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Deities," Lord Śiva said:
The lords of Rudra know the Lord to be the one, pervasive form of consciousness alone, abiding within the existence of all beings, consisting of self-experience, and pure;
He is the seed of all seeds and the essence of the continuous flow of transmigratory existence.
Know that the supreme action among all actions is the stainless element of consciousness (ciddhātu).
It is the cause of the multitudes of causes, yet itself uncaused and untainted;
it is the contemplation of all forms of contemplation, yet itself beyond being contemplated and devoid of the nature of becoming.
It is consciousness among the floods of consciousness, that which is perceived within the self of consciousness;
it is the unperceivable consciousness, the object of perception, the supreme, and the manifold radiance. It is the light of lights, stainless, invisible, and born of the light.
The wise know the flood of the seed of the living soul to be seedless, a mass of consciousness, and stainless.
Know that which consists of the unreal yet is composed of reality, which is peaceful and devoid of both the real and the unreal—
the continuum beginning with Great Being— to be pure consciousness alone and nothing else.
One becomes oneself possessed of passion—the impassioned one, the act of coloring, and the color itself;
even empty space quickly becomes a decorated wall.
Within this expansive consciousness, the worlds are but mirages in the desert.
They have vibrated, will vibrate, and are vibrating by the millions.
This world is accomplished solely through its own existence within this self-luminosity;
nothing else whatsoever is accomplished therein, just as heat is not distinct from fire.
They know this atom to contain within it the great Mount Meru;
this blink of an eye is said to contain within it a great aeon (*mahākalpa*).
Even though it is encompassed by an aeon, its nature as a blink of an eye is not abandoned.
By this [consciousness], which is subtler than even the tip of a hair, the entire earth—including the seven oceans surrounding it—is pervaded; yet one does not reach its end.
Without even performing the construction of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), it has attained the state of being the creator.
While performing great deeds, he does nothing at all;
though possessing substance, he is without substance, and though without substance, he possesses substance.
Though bodiless, he has a great body, and though having a great body, he is bodiless.
Even now this [time] is always morning, yet it has become "today";
it is not "not today" nor "not morning," but rather "today and morning" or "always.
*Huṇḍubhillighale mattaśulupiṇṭhilisālaghe*.
"Vellighilla, salāvola, lāsaguggulu, sussunī"—
such meaningless sentences are likewise true, for he alone is that;
there is nothing that does not exist as he, and there is nothing that does not exist as he.
Salutation to that Self of All, to whom everything belongs, from whom everything arises, who is everything, who exists everywhere, and who is eternally composed of all things.
By the dense thicket of the spaces between the petals, by the playful and restless deep thundering of Vilāsavatī, and by the darkness...
The prosperity of the Mālavas, who were garlanded with the feet of the wrestler, was as if it had been embraced by the creeping vine of Fortune;
thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of Maheśvara," and begins the forty-first chapter.
Even the glorious wealth of meanings of words such as "Lord" (Īśvara) is of the nature of truth within that Lord of All, who is the casket for the jewel of all existence.
What indeed does not shine within that jewel of supreme consciousness—
those diverse worlds which, though they appear, are merely reflected therein?
This very existence of consciousness, residing within the seed-syllable, consists of its own body.
Having perceived clay, time, water, and so forth, it brings about the impelling of the sprout.
Existing within the transformations of foam and whirlpools, taking the form of fluidity,
it produces the vibration of waters when there is contact with the sense organs.
This [power], abiding in the clusters of flowers as fragrance and form,
shining within the nostrils, brings about their full blossoming;
residing in the limbs of stone, it leads them to the state of true reality.
By the effortless stability of the Lord of Mountains, it maintains the state of being the support for creation;
and, having the nature of the sheath that is the vibration of the wind, it brings about the sense-organ of touch,
just as a father [protects] his own son from his own defeat.

Having meditated upon even one's own self— which is the condensed essence of all things without exception— for the sake of attaining the state of space (*kha*), one thoroughly renders that self as "space-ness" (*khatva*), as if it were nothingness (*nakiñcittva*). Within the interior of the sprout of space, [the self] appears like a reflection of its own existence.
She bears a stainless body called Time (kāla), which is marked by the moments of conceptualization and the blink of an eye.
Through her own unblemished transformation, extending up to the fifth lord Mahā-Īśāna,
she herself becomes Niyati (the Power of Destiny), determining that "this is thus" and "this is not."
When this stable witness, vast in its radiance like a lamp,
exists, the successions of the world’s manifold paintings are illuminated;
it is the ground for the theater of the city of the supreme ether.
"Beholding the world-process as her own dance, she remains like a witness.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Lord of the World, how do those powers of this Śiva exist?"
What then would their witness-hood consist of, or how much dancing could there be?
The Lord replied: "Of Śiva, the Supreme Self, who is by nature immovable and tranquil..."
O gentle one, O observer of noble vows, although everything is of the nature of pure consciousness and formless,
there exists the existence of will, the existence of space, and likewise the existence of time;
as well as the existence of necessity and the Great Existence.
The power of knowledge, the power of action, agency, and even non-agency— there is no end to such powers within the Self of Śiva. Vasiṣṭha said:
From where do these powers arise? How is there multiplicity among them?
O Lord, how does their emergence occur, and what is the nature of their difference and non-difference? The Lord said:
This which belongs to Śiva, who is of infinite form and whose essence is pure consciousness alone,
is indeed called "power" (śakti); it is not different from him even in the slightest degree,
because of the manifestation of [attributes] such as being the knower, the agent, the enjoyer, and the witness.
The powers (śaktis) assume various forms and many manifestations. Although he is one, he shines as many by himself through what is called Śiva’s power;
by means of the single Śiva, whose self consists of all powers, [he manifests] within those whose nature is Śiva.
When objects exist as desired, yet are conceived as mere witnesses,
these [beings] dance in this world within the theater of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*),
having been gradually trained by Time, as if by a dancer.
This succession of these [entities] is called "Necessity" (niyati);
it is designated by such names as "Action," "Nature," "Will," and "Time.
This is because everything, from the unmanifest down to Mahārudra, exists in this manner.
Niyati is said to be the rule that governs the movement of the lotus-born Brahmā down to the blades of grass.
Niyati is eternally free from agitation and supremely powerful;
she dances perpetually in the sky, performing the drama of the web of the worlds.
Rich with the playful display of various flavors, accompanied by shifting gestures and dramatic expressions,
it resounded with the gurgling of many Puṣkarāvarta clouds struck down in an instant by the fire of the cosmic dissolution;
it was a temple whose ground-globes were strewn with flowers of every season.
Again and again, it produced a profuse shower of sweat-water;
it created the illusion of dark-blue garments fluttering like the edges of clouds;
and it was crowded with the rings of the seven oceans, now full and now completely dried, yet still rich in jewels.
The sky was variegated by side-glances that were like days for the Yama-birds (crows);
the crests of the mountain ranges were busy with their repeated submerging and emerging;
and there was a triple string of pearl necklaces formed by the Gaṅgā, strung upon the revolving moon-stones.
With fourteen kinds of infinite, natural, and undulating hairs,
its sprout-like hands flicker like clouds at the twilight of the seen and the unseen;
it is as delicate as the ornaments of the world, ever-moving and shimmering.
He whose footsteps traverse the vast earth, the netherworld, and the expanse of the sky;
who causes the clusters of stars—like a mass of sweat-drops—to sink and rise;
and whose face is the sky, made radiant by the smile-like movement of the orbs of the moon and sun.
It shook the canopy of the door-panels of many cosmic eggs;
it possessed sprouts of pearls resounding through the shifting arrays of other worlds;
and it contained within it the various flavors of the presence and absence of the conditions of pleasure and pain.

In this essence of the long drama called saṃsāra, which is a play of destiny (niyati) enveloped in transformations, this one Supreme Lord remains as the eternally risen witness; he is neither distinct from that [destiny] nor distinct from him [the individual soul]. Chapter named "The Dance of Destiny" (Niyatinṛtta).
Chapter Forty-Two.
The Lord: This god is supreme; he is always to be worshipped by the virtuous.
Pure consciousness alone is the experienced self, all-pervading and the refuge of all;
it abides in the pot, the cloth, the banyan tree, the wall, the cart, and even in the monkey.
It is Śiva, Hara, Hari, Brahmā, Śakra, Vaiśravaṇa, and Yama.

The Blessed One, who is the self of all, both external and internal, is always worshipped by those of excellent intellect through two kinds of procedures. First, O one of great intelligence, he is worshipped externally according to the following sequence.
Listen to that by which, O knower of reality, you shall thereafter hear the internal sequence:
in all sequences of worship, there is no sacred thread (*pavitraka*) made of *darbha* grass here;
for here, worship is indeed meditation, and meditation is indeed worship.
Therefore, one should constantly worship with meditation that which is the support of the three worlds;

one should take refuge in one's own self, whose essence is the "I-consciousness," which is of the nature of consciousness, radiant as a hundred thousand suns, the illuminator of all appearances, and the internal light of consciousness.
Whose neck possesses the vast expanse of the infinite and supreme ether;
whose lotus-feet are the sheath of space with no space beneath them;
adorned by the circle of arms that span the extent of the infinite quarters of the horizon.
He holds supreme weapons of various kinds within his great world-abodes;
he rests within the multitude of successive cosmic eggs situated in the corner of the treasury of his heart;
his form is boundless, reaching beyond the supreme space of light.
One should contemplate this row of hairs on his body as the prosperity of all beings, headed by Brahmā, Indra, Hari, Rudra, and Īśa, and consisting of the foremost of the immortals;
they are the ropes of the machine of the three worlds that initiate various undertakings.

All the powers beginning with Will (icchā) are to be contemplated as residing within the body. Time, which has the single state of Ananta as its support, whose sole form is pure existence, and by whom the web of the world is manifested, is his doorkeeper.

One should contemplate Mahādeva, who possesses a thousand feet and eyes, as having become a mere limb within some corner of this body— the sphere of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), together with the expanse of the world and its mountains.
He has a thousand heads, is peaceful, and is adorned with a thousand arms;
he is enriched everywhere by the power of sight, possesses the power of smell in every direction,
consists of the faculty of touch everywhere, and is endowed with the sense of taste on all sides.
Pervaded by hearing everywhere, accompanied by the mind everywhere,
yet transcending thought in every respect, it is the supreme auspiciousness (śiva) everywhere;
it is the eternal creator of all, bestowing all things conceived by the will.
"Abiding within the interior of all beings, he is everything, the sole means for accomplishing all things.
Having reflected thus, one should then worship the Lord of Gods according to the prescribed rule.
O best among the knowers of Brahman, hear now this procedure for worship.
One should not worship the Lord, who is one's own self-consciousness, with offerings;
nor with lamps, nor with incense, nor by the presentation of an abundance of flowers;
nor by the giving of food and other gifts, nor with the anointing of sandalwood paste.
Nor by saffron and camphor, nor by various enjoyments, nor by others; rather,
he is worshipped solely by his own awakening— an ambrosia that is eternal, obtainable without effort, cooling, and imperishable.
This alone is the supreme meditation; this alone is remembered as the highest worship:
the uninterrupted awareness of pure consciousness alone abiding within, while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, and breathing.
While speaking, releasing, or grasping, one should become composed of pure consciousness.
Having worshipped this very Self, who is the Lord, with the nectar of meditation—
characterized by supreme savor— and with flowers consisting of one's own desires, one becomes liberated.
Indeed, his intended self-meditation (*ātma-dhyāna*) is the very offering of meditation itself;
they know that pure consciousness constitutes the meditation, the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), and the water for the feet (*pādya*).
They know that the perception of meditation is the flower, the incense, and the supreme lamp.

Without that other [means], this self is certainly not attained. O Sage, having attained clarity through meditation, this self enjoys the glory of happiness in all worlds, just as a king enjoys [pleasures] within his palace in his body.
O excellent sage, by means of this meditation, even one who worships the Lord for thirteen *nimeṣas* shall indeed obtain the merit of gifting a cow;
having worshipped the Lord for one hundred *nimeṣas*, he likewise attains that same fruit.

A person obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) by offering himself to himself through the power of meditation. He who worships for even a single ghaṭikā attains the merit of the royal consecration sacrifice (rājasūya).
By performing the midday worship in this manner, a person partakes in the merit of a hundred thousand Rājasūya sacrifices;
having worshipped thus throughout the day, he shall dwell in the supreme abode.
This is that supreme yoga; this is that supreme ritual action.
This external worship has been declared as the highest for oneself.
That man who, without weariness, shall practice this purifier— the cause of the destruction of all sins— even for a moment,
will be saluted by the multitudes of the worlds of gods and demons, for he has attained his place in the world as one who is like me, the essence of the universe.
The forty-third chapter, titled "The Outer Worship," Lord Śiva said:
I shall now describe that internal worship of the Self, which is the purifier of purifiers and the destruction of all darkness—
[a practice] for one whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping.
This worship, consisting of constant meditation, belongs to one who observes all proper conduct. One should always meditate upon this supreme Śiva, who resides within the body,
as the self by means of the self, the creator of all perceptions.
Whether lying down or rising, walking or standing,
whether experiencing various sensations on all sides or abandoning them on all sides,
or enjoying and relinquishing objects of pleasure that are abundant and expansive— [the wise remain equanimous].

Having abandoned external lingas and other such objects, one should worship the Linga of Consciousness— which is the creator of the multitude of external objects, the bestower of the essential nature of all effects, and which resides within the Lord of the body and the [subtle] linga—
by means of the perception of whatever objects are encountered.

But one whose mind has attained purity through the bath of awakening regarding objects that have entered the stream of consciousness should worship the Linga of Awakening with the constant offering of awareness. One should [meditate upon] the Sun in the sky, cultivated by the enjoyment of the contemplation of the Sun.
He is the ever-risen moon, cultivated through the expansive meditation on the moon;
his consciousness is eternally aware of the flood of objects that appear before him,
and he carries [the breath] through the bodily gates in the form of the vital breath (prāṇa) at the mouth.
He who has made the *rasas* flavorful, whose spirited horses are the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*svānta*),
who is mounted upon the chariot of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, and who dwells hidden within the inner cave;
he is the knower of all perceptions of the knowable and the doer of all actions.
One should meditate upon Śiva, the enjoyer of all that is to be enjoyed, the rememberer of all consciousnesses;
whose multitude of limbs is perfectly known, who is cultivated by the contemplation of existence,
the abundant illumination of appearances, and the omnipresent.
It is both partless and possessed of parts, situated within the body, and moving through space; it is both unstained and stained, eternally conscious of its own limbs and members;
it abides in the power of the mind’s reflection and arises between the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
Situated in the heart, throat, and palate, resting upon the seat of the eyebrows and nostrils,
it abides within thirty-six crores of planes, transcending the state of the *unmanā* (transmental) limit;
it causes sound and the other objects to arise within, impelling the bird-like mind.
It abides in the threefold path of speech, both conceptual and non-conceptual;
it is inwardly supported within all limbs like oil within sesame seeds.
It is free from the stain of parts, yet it is perceived through the multitude of mental constructions.
It is situated in a single part within one's own heart-lotus and throughout the entire body;
it is pure consciousness, possessing a stainless luster, free from the conceptualization of parts and their integration,
visible everywhere through direct perception, and consisting of the nature of one's own self-experience.
One's own inner consciousness, standing before one as the self,
quickly assumes the state of an object and, in an instant, becomes as if a duality;
it is possessed of hands, feet, and limbs, along with hair, nails, and teeth.

One should contemplate: "I am my own body, this divine manifestation of consciousness. (MU 6.43.20) The manifold and numerous powers of various behaviors, perceived by the mind, worship me as mental wives do their supreme husband. (MU 6.43.21)
This mind of mine is the gatekeeper who announces the three worlds;
this thought of mine is the female usher standing before me in her pure form.
Intellect is my power residing in my limbs, and activity resides in my other limbs.
And my various cognitions are the ornaments upon my limbs;
the organs of action are the gates, and the group of sensory organs are the women.
This is that very I, the infinite Self, consciousness devoid of all limitations.
"I abide as the single, filled self, full and filling all things"—
having thus taken refuge in the Goddess, who is the pure wonder of the Self,
one remains within like a god, completely full and undepressed in spirit.
He neither sets nor rises; he neither rejoices nor suffers. He experiences neither satiety nor hunger; he neither desires nor abandons.
He is even, with an even conduct, an even appearance, and an even form.
Having attained gentleness and being beautiful in disposition on all sides,
he remains as one and the same throughout his entire life, possessing uninterrupted great intelligence;
thus he performs the worship of the gods for very long days and nights.

The body, enveloped by the reality of consciousness, is proclaimed to be the deity. With whatever object is at hand, he worships that supreme reality of the body as pure consciousness, with an intellect purified by the sacred observance (*samaya*).
One should worship with every object obtained according to the prescribed order;
one should not exert even the slightest effort toward anything that is not already available.
O sinless one, one should always perform this daily in the morning through the pursuit of dharma, and thereafter through purposeful action.
Then, with the experience of sensual pleasures, one should worship the pervasive Consciousness;
one should honor the Fire with various kinds of food, drink, and delicacies, as well as with beds, seats, and vehicles, according to what is available.
One should worship the Self, awakened through every form of happiness— such as the playful intensity of enjoying beloved food and drink—
yet [one who is] overwhelmed by mental and physical ailments and characterized by delusion and agitation [should not].
One should worship the Self with whatever misfortunes and sufferings one encounters;
and one should worship the Self with the boundaries of prosperity, the activities of the world’s existence, and the living beings encountered who have passed away.
Whether through poverty or through sovereignty— which comes of its own accord like the flow of a stream—
