having realized the Self, one should worship it with the flowers of diverse activities,
which are characterized by the splendor of the surging waves of various conflicts.
One should worship the gentle Self with the playful display of passion and aversion;
one should worship the Self residing in the heart with a friendliness that captivates the hearts of the virtuous, which is as cool as the moon and possesses the quality of sweetness.
One should worship one’s own self as the Buddha by either renouncing or, out of attachment, enjoying enjoyments that are neither prohibited nor forbidden at all times,
whether they arise from a flood of desired or undesired things, and whether they are appropriate or inappropriate.
One should honor oneself with what has been renounced, what was sought in distress, and what has been obtained.
One should disregard what is lost again and again, and accept what is gained as it comes;
for this state of being free from change is indeed the supreme worship of the self.
Always maintaining supreme equanimity toward all perceptions, whether they be desirable or undesirable, one should practice the vow of constant worship of the Self.
One should perceive everything as auspicious, and one should likewise perceive everything as inauspicious.
A person devoted to the constant worship of the Self should make everything consist of the Self;
having realized that whatever is pleasant at first sight and whatever is difficult to endure at first sight are all entirely equal, one should observe the vow of the constant worship of the Self.
One should abandon the distinction between "this is I" and "this is not I," and having resolved that "all is Brahman," one should perform the vow of constant self-worship;
[seeing] at all times and in every form that which undergoes transformations in all modes.
One should honor the self by accepting everything, in every possible way.
Without desiring and without rejecting, the wise person should enjoy the grounds of experience as they arise by their own nature, just as rivers are received by the ocean.
One should not feel agitation toward views, whether trivial or significant,
just as one does not react to the falling and rising of various objects in the sky.
Whatever auspicious or inauspicious arises through the conjunction of place, time, and action, [one should remain unmoved].
With that very [offering] which has been accepted without modification, one should worship the Self.
Whatever wealth of ritual materials is prescribed in this rule for the worship of the Self,
all of these are permeated by the single essence of tranquility.

They are neither sour, nor pungent, nor bitter, nor astringent; though smeared with various flavors, when gathered together, they are indeed sweet. O Lord of Sages, that power of flavor which is delightful through its sweetness of equanimity— MU 6.43.52. That power of flavor which is delightful through its sweetness of equanimity, O Lord of Sages, [is the true essence].
Whatever object of thought is meditated upon by her becomes nectar in an instant.
Whatever indeed is contemplated within the flood of the nectar of equanimity attains a sweetness like that which has fallen from the moon.
Having become equanimous like space, that seat which is free from mental impressions (*ahṛllekha*),
changeless, and effortless— that is called the worship of the Divine.
One should become full like the full moon, possessing the radiance of tranquility and equanimity.
Though consisting of a single mass of pure consciousness and appearing like a stone,
the knowing worshipper is clear as the inner space within, yet performs his natural functions externally; free from the mist of passion, he remains complete.
When the clouds of ignorance have vanished, the autumnal sky of the Knower shines forth, its inner landscape invisible even in dreams, and the mist of egoism and the like stilled.
It is a universal state where the mind, the knower, and the known have set, a vast expanse like the sensation of a newborn infant.

O wise one, remain established in the supreme state, living as a living being whose mind and consciousness are perfectly stilled. (MU 6.43.59) Remain with a mind in which all cravings have been pacified, with the Lord of the body eternally honored by the delusions of pleasure and pain arising from the sequence of time, place, and the perception of objects. (MU 6.43.60)
The forty-fourth chapter, titled "Reflection on the Worship of Deities," spoken by Īśvara:
Whatever you do, whether according to your desire or according to your undertaking,
if it is within the auspicious Śiva who is pure consciousness, that is the worship of the Self by the gods. Through that alone one attains bliss, and likewise, [the Self] reaches manifestation.
Abiding in that very form by himself, the Lord himself—
within that auspicious Self, none of the objects denoted by terms such as "attachment" or "aversion" can possibly exist as distinct entities, just as particles of frost cannot exist within fire.

Whatever experience there may be—whether of kingship or servitude, pleasure or pain, and so forth—whether belonging to oneself or to another, know that each and every one of these is the worship of the Self.
Know that consciousness itself is the act of worship; for it is consciousness alone that knows the Self as the Self.
O Brahman, whether by way of being the self of jars and other objects, or simply by its own nature as the Self,
this entire world exists as the form of the Self— auspicious, peaceful, non-manifest, one, radiant, and all-pervading, appearing as the very cognition of the world.

Oh, how wonderful! It is as if the Self alone exists as other things, such as jars and the like; surely the Self, which is Śiva—the infinite one who is the soul of all—remains established within itself, as if it has forgotten its own nature.
For indeed, within the infinite Self who is Śiva, who is the soul of all, [all things abide].
The delusion known as the worshipper, the worshipped, and the act of worship has arisen in vain;
for a state of tranquility characterized by fixed form is not possible in the Lord,
since, O Brahmin, the sequence consisting of the worshipped and the worship is merely a mental construction.
The deity who is separated from the act of worshipping the worshipful is impermanent; he is not a fit vessel for lordship over the infinite, stainless Self,
which is omnipotent and whose nature is pure consciousness pervading the three worlds.
O Brahmin, apart from [the doctrine of] non-divinity, even the designation [of a supreme lord] is not tenable.
Those for whom the Supreme Lord would be limited by space and time—
they are our teachers, but they are not truly wise, O wise one.
Having abandoned that [worldly] view and likewise having taken hold of this one,
he is equanimous, with a healthy mind, peaceful, free from passion, and without affliction;
with an undaunted intellect, he [proceeds] on all sides with offerings of duty as they arise.
"Remain worshipping the Self, indifferent to pleasure and pain, or the auspicious and inauspicious.
When you, a virtuous man, have thus attained [this state], surely no suffering of birth or anything else will quickly touch your agitated life-force;
for it does not cling to one who is completely pure and whose limbs are like clear crystal, just as a blemish does not adhere within a stainless new palace."
The forty-fifth canto, titled "The Inquiry into Divinity," by Vasiṣṭha:
O God, what is Śiva called? What is the supreme Brahman called?
What is the Self (ātman) called, or even what is the supreme Self (paramātman) called?
That [reality] is something, yet it is nothing; it is both emptiness and pure consciousness.
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Three Worlds, what is this distinction such as 'it' and so forth called? Īśvara replied:
"There exists here something real that is without beginning or end and without appearance."
Vasiṣṭha said: That which remains as if nothing at all due to the non-appearance of the senses—
even though they are joined with the intellect and the other faculties— is [the state of non-duality].
"O Īśāna, how has that gone? Tell me, by what is it understood?
Īśvara said:
"He who is a seeker of liberation, whose portion of ignorance consists solely of the sattvic [element], is known as 'Kevala'."
By means of those very portions of ignorance that are characterized by *sattva* and are designated as the "scriptures" (*śāstra*) and so forth,
he remains here washing away ignorance— both the superior and the inferior—
just as a washerman skilled in technique removes dirt with dirt.

When the destruction of ignorance arrives later, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit (*kākatālīya*), the self perceives itself by means of itself; this is the certainty regarding its own nature.
Just as a child, having somehow rubbed away charcoal, washes it away...

One attains purity of the instruments [of action] just as one attains whiteness upon the destruction of the charcoal of blackness. By investigating the parts [of reality] through various portions rich in scriptural knowledge, the Tāmasa is destroyed by the Sāttvika; thus, from the dissolution of both, there is the emergence of the Self.
The Self alone perceives itself and investigates itself by means of itself;
the Self alone exists here, and there is no ignorance—those who know declare that ignorance is the destruction of ignorance.
Whatever object there is here, it is understood as nothing other than the Self.
The sequence beginning with the teacher’s instruction is not the cause of self-knowledge.
For the teacher is essentially the aggregate of the senses; Brahman is reached through the cessation of all the senses.
Whatever object is to be attained upon the cessation of something cannot be attained while that thing still exists.
O twice-born one, even those things that are not causes have become powerful causes for the attainment of self-knowledge through the sequence beginning with the teacher’s instruction;
this occurs when the sequence of the teacher’s instructions proceeds toward the awakening of the disciple.
Though it is indefinable and invisible, the Self becomes serene by itself.
O sinless one, the Self is not understood through the meanings of the scriptures, nor by the words of a teacher;
it is understood by itself alone, through the power of its own awakening, from within.
Without the meaning of the scriptures and the instructions of the Guru, the Self is not realized;
it is only through the existence of their conjunction that the knowledge of one's own Self is illumined.
Through the long-standing existence of the conjunction between the Guru, the meaning of the scriptures, and the disciple—
Just as the conduct of people proceeds according to the day and night, so does self-knowledge proceed.
There is the complete cessation of the organs of action and perception, as well as pleasure, pain, and the rest;
this is called the auspicious Self (Śiva-ātman), by names such as "That" (Tat) and "Being" (Sat).
That wherein this entire world does not exist, or rather exists only in its own true form—
that which is more transparent than space, infinite, and real— indeed exists here.
Because they do not find rest therein, seekers of liberation whose bodies are composed of ignorance [wander].
By those whose selves are stained by the blemish of various impure conceptions,
yet who stand not far from the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukta),
there is the composition of the meaning of the scriptures for the sake of awakening to the means of liberation.

By the world-protectors headed by Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra, together with the learned ones— those whose selves were purified for the sake of establishing the doctrines of the Purāṇas, Vedas, and Siddhāntas—
it was declared that consciousness (cit) is Brahman, Śiva, Ātman, Īśa, Paramātman, Īśvara, and so forth.
Conceptual designations are imagined in that which is devoid of concepts, within the Lord who is distinct [from them].
Thus is this reality of the world; it is one's own reality, named Śiva.
Worshipping it in every way, at all times, and with everything, O friend, remain in happiness!

In such expressions as "Śiva," "the Self," and "the Supreme Brahman," there is a distinction created by those possessed of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); for the knower, however, there is no difference in the reality itself.
O leader of sages, the knower who constantly performs worship of the deity in this manner—
To that supreme state where servants such as ourselves go,
Vasiṣṭha said:
"This [world] does not exist at all, yet it stands as if it were existing."
"O Blessed One, you should explain that to me in brief. The Lord said:
"Know that which is the referent of words such as 'Brahmā' and so forth to be nothing but pure consciousness."
Even the clear sky appears gross to her, like Mount Meru to an atom;
perceiving the object of knowledge, she attains the fitness for the state called *cit*,
and indeed, even when free from objects of knowledge, she truly abides in the stage that is the end of *unmanā*.
In an instant, because its state of being experienced has been brought forth, it follows after the "I-ness" (ahantā),
just as a man, by virtue of his humanity, assumes the form of a new elephant in a dream.
Once this [consciousness] has attained that "I-ness," its spatiality, temporality, and extensiveness [are likewise assumed].
Those very friends themselves become of the nature of emptiness; then,
conjoined with them, that existence termed "the living soul" (jīva) becomes a knower of movement, like a streak of wind.
The power of the individual soul (*jīva-śakti*), being of such a nature and delighting solely in certainty,
follows the state of intellect (*buddhi*) and remains situated in the station of the ignorant.
It is followed by the power of sound (*śabda-śakti*), the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).
Each one vibrates within, its form unmanifest;
this group, having quickly come together and conforming to the Veda,
becomes the mind— the seed of the tree of volition whose essence is emptiness.
The wise know that [the subtle body] to be the vehicle for the expression of the *ātivāhika* (conveying) body;
through the power of Brahman residing within, it perceives the Self by means of its own nature as the knower.
For while this [subtle body] is being perfected, these powers reside within the mind.
Simultaneously with it, as if following after, there arise even those that have not yet emerged:
the existence of wind, the existence of vibration, and likewise the existence of touch;
the existence of the skin, the existence of fire, and likewise the existence that illumines.
The existence of sight, the existence of water, and likewise the existence of taste;
similarly the existence of flavor, and likewise the existence of smell; the existence of earth, the existence of the body, and the full existence of the physical mass.
Existence in space, existence in time— all these are devoid of form.
Having thus embraced the entire multitude of existences within its own nature, the mind, assuming its own essential form,
vibrates like a seed that has reached the state of life, supported by its sprouts and so forth.
Know this to be the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), and this body is the subtle transport-body (ativāhika).
This [body] flashes forth like a division of rays due to the lack of higher awakening;
yet that which is endowed with limbs, when fully realized, is nothing at all.
It is neither born, nor is it of the nature of existence, nor is it consciousness and so forth, nor anything else. In the Supreme, the Supreme alone vibrates— the absolute Self, which is pure Being—
like the play of liquid water within the interior of a basin of water.
This world, which is essentially one with consciousness and its objects, appears as something separate when it is not realized;
yet, once fully understood, it becomes like a city of imagination.
Through the thorough knowledge of this consciousness, one attains the very state of Śiva.
Or how does that which is indeed unborn attain the state of being a real entity?
If this [self] finds its own end through volition, it attains atomicity by itself;
then these [beings], whose existence consists of those subtle elements, perceive the body of that atom.
He quickly perceives that very [self] as having attained both atomic and gross dimensions; he sees its apertures consisting of the subtle elements (tanmātra) according to their respective locations.
Then, through the cultivation of the singular conception of the form of the Puruṣa, [he perceives it] in the shape of a person.
Having seen [the body] like the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" coincidence, he becomes sufficiently satisfied and nourished.
Then, the living soul (jīva), remaining in this state, perceives the body situated before him as something utterly non-existent,
like a city of Gandharvas or a city in a dream.
Vasiṣṭha:
The world has the appearance of a city of Gandharvas and is like a city seen in a dream; since it leads only to suffering, what logic is there for its destruction?
Īśvara:
Suffering arises through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
and those impressions exist even though the world is non-existent, like the shimmering water of a mirage.
Therefore, what is being perfumed, by what, whose is the perfuming, or from where?
How, my dear, can the water of a mirage be drunk by a man in a dream?
But when there is a creator, they tolerate [the existence of] the mind, the intellect, and so forth.
When the world no longer exists, that which is real remains.
Where there is neither latent impression (*vāsanā*), nor that which perfumes (*vāsaka*), nor that which is to be perfumed (*vāsya*),
there is only the state of absolute isolation (*kevalībhāva*), in which all delusion has been completely stilled.
For one for whom even a yakṣa—whether real or unreal—is indeed empty, that [yakṣa] has dissolved through absolute liberation; what else remains?
Indeed, in this way, the mental impression is empty, like a ghost.
This world named "the universe" has arisen; upon its cessation, peace remains unimpaired.
One who is established in non-duality toward both the world and the water of a mirage—that mass of consciousness—cannot be pointed out by saying, "He is this."

Those who know reality teach here that the discerning one is the living soul (*jīva*), while the ignorant are deluded by what is unreal and devoid of noble liberation. Indeed, he who instructs the ignorant gives his daughter—who is as pure as gold—to a man seen in a dream.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Demonstration of the Falsity of the World."
The forty-sixth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, O Blessed One, that individual soul beheld the agitation of the body.
At the beginning of creation, what state indeed does the Lord, residing in the sky, attain? [The Lord:
In the supreme void beyond the highest, his body [assumes its form] according to the sequence previously described.

The living being perceives [the world] as fully accomplished, just like a man in an unreal dream. For, because the mass of consciousness is all-pervading, just as a man in a dream quickly effects his actions, so too does the living being perceive the body.
Then, from that [state], he is designated as the eternal, unmanifest Person (puruṣa);
because he effects [this] within himself, he is called the first Person.
Thus, in a certain creation, Sadāśiva is the first entity.
In one [instance] he is called Viṣṇu, from whose navel the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) was born;
in another he is the Grandfather, and in yet another he is the other [Viṣṇu].
He is the Puruṣa of volition (saṅkalpa-puruṣa), existing as a formal embodiment arising from volition.
Nourished by his initial resolve and assuming that form of mind,
whatever he imagines in whatever manner, he experiences that exactly and immediately;
yet all of that is unreal in nature, like a ghost in an empty place.
But through the vision of delusion, the state of the world as "I" arises as having the nature of reality.
Indeed, he who thus becomes the primal person as the creator and so forth,
rises and dissolves within the void at every moment.
In a mere blink of an eye, one fully experiences successions of aeons, great aeons, and their cycles,
through nothing more than the error of mental appearance.
In every single atom, in every void, and in every single moment—
Indeed, the states of creation, the intermediate kalpa, and the great kalpa, as well as existence and non-existence, come to be.
Through hundreds of latent impressions (vāsanās), some are seen by others as having common characteristics;
some are not seen by one another, and some do not perceive anyone else at all.
Some [creations] are not seen by another, even though they are perceived as having a non-existent nature;
those creations do not arise everywhere in Śiva.
They exist in the supreme ether, having the form of ether itself.
And being themselves of the nature of both existent and non-existent, they dissolve like mountains in a dream.
Neither by these creations is space occupied, nor time, nor agency;
nor are these of the nature of the real, neither for a kalpa nor for even a moment.
Nothing at all is born here, nor does anything whatsoever perish;
consciousness manifests as wonder within consciousness, by way of its own self-wondering.
The world is like the creation, descent, and ascent of a city in a dream.

It does not traverse space and time even by means of the mind. Just as the infinite expanse of space, time, and so forth is not truly traversed even when it is traversed by a mountain created through imagination, so too is the unreal world.
Just as that primordial Person, the creator of the world, comes into being,
so too does a worm here become [that same being] in this very sequence in an instant.
For in this world, the four classes of stationary beings likewise arise in this manner.
From Rudra down to the trees, they are produced at every moment.
Some exist as supreme or subordinate, while others are like atoms;
such is their sequence, whether creation exists or does not exist.
Through the cultivation of the true nature of this illusion of saṃsāra,
when its distinctions are stilled by practice, there arises the auspicious peace. The supreme consciousness lasts for no more than half of a hundredth part of a blink of an eye.
If it has rolled away from its own nature, then this state arises:
that [consciousness], whose form is knowledge, remains within itself like a stone in a casket;
therefore, it is celebrated by the term "Brahman," which is by nature beginningless manifestation.
When this creation has reached maturity, the Great Consciousness (mahācit) attains a new state of awareness by entering into union with space, direction, time, parts, and atoms; thus,
through the process of the evolution of the elements and their subtle constituents (tanmātra), it arrives at the state of being a living soul (jīva).
The world of beings— including gods, asuras, and others, as well as mountains, wild animals, plants, and insects—

exists like a garland upon that eternal, pervasive, and firm thread; the entire universe, woven from both the existent and the non-existent, rests within Him who is the architect of all and whose every limb is the universe.
It is neither far nor near, neither above nor below; it is not "those," nor "mine";
it was not in the past, nor today, nor in the morning; it is neither being, nor non-being, nor something situated in between.
Apart from the reckoning of experience, there is no knower of this while all conceptual constructions persist.
The garland of valid cognitions, possessing the vast power of its fruit, does not persist [in the absence of an object], just as fire does not persist in water.
O Sage, that which was asked has been explained; may it be well with you.
We shall depart for our desired region; arise, O Pārvatī!
Having spoken thus, that blue-throated one, while I remained with my handful of flowers still held out,
crossed into the expanse of the sky together with his retinue.
When that Lord of Umā, the sovereign of the three worlds, had departed, I stood for a moment, following him with recollection as before.
Out of a sense of fresh purity, I have accepted this seat of *darbha* grass for myself, just as one who is weary accepts the great learning of a scholar.
The chapter titled "An Inquiry into the Designation of the Supreme Self" is concluded. The forty-seventh chapter, the Dialogue between Īśvara and Vasiṣṭha, is finished.
Vasiṣṭha said: This has been declared by the Supreme Lord himself, and I know it as well;
O Rāma, you too understand how this is situated.
In this illusory cycle of existence (saṃsāramāyā), where the unreal is perceived by means of the unreal as something indeed unreal, what is real and what is composed of the unreal?
Whatever is conceptualized by whichever conceptualization, [that is so conceived].
Likewise, even though it exists as that which is like the Self, it is not experienced [as separate],
just as liquidity is in water,
as movement is in the wind, and as emptiness is in space; so too is the state of emanation within the Self.
From that time forward, performing the worship of myself according to that very same sequence until this day with an undistracted mind, I have remained thus,
O Rāma; by means of this ritual of worship, these latent impressions (*vāsanās*) were [purified] by me.
Even those devoted to worldly affairs pass their time without weariness;
the worship of the Self with the flowers of conduct and action, as they arise,
has never been interrupted for me, day or night.
When all embodied beings are equal in their relationship between the grasped and the grasper,
that state of attentiveness maintained by the yogi is the worship of the Self.
O Lord of the Raghus, with this vision and a mind free from attachment, [one attains it].
Dwell in this vast wilderness of saṃsāra and do not grow weary. When great suffering arises from the loss of wealth and kin, O observer of noble vows, rely upon this view and engage in reflection.
One should not be affected by pleasure or pain arising from the gain or loss of wealth and kinsmen;
indeed, all such perceptions of cyclic existence are constantly of this nature.
You already know how the various objects of the senses lead to turbulent and diverse destinies.
Just as they go, just as they come, and just as they fall into decline,
so too do affections and riches proceed;
in this very way they are lost through unexamined signs.
They do not belong to you, nor do you belong to them; you are stainless, while the activities of the world are [separate].
This world is merely such as it appears—why do you suffer in vain?
You alone are the form of the world, pure consciousness itself, manifesting in extended forms.

When one's own constituent parts have ceased to recur, what room is there for joy or sorrow? O Rāma, having attained a state of single-minded consciousness and reached the condition of deep sleep, from this day forward, may you become the very essence of the fourth state (turya).
Equal, appearing as equal, with a radiant body and noble intellect, remain always according to your own nature like the perfectly full ocean.
You have heard all this; you stand here with a fully perfected mind.

If you wish to ask anything else, O delight of the Raghus, then ask it. That which was asked by you in the first eon— namely, "From where does impurity come for Brahman, who is of infinite form?"— bring that forward again today.
Rāma:
O Brahmin, now my doubt has especially ceased;
everything that was to be known has been known, and an unartificial satisfaction has arisen.
"There is no duality, nor unity, nor even conceptual construction belonging to the Self;
at that time I possessed ignorance, but now it has been stilled. "That [notion] that there is a stain upon the Self arose through the power of my own ignorance."
That delusion which existed has now ceased through your grace.
The self is neither born nor does it die, nor is it ever defiled;
everything is composed of Brahman—this indeed is what I have realized.
From questions, from doubts, and from all that was desired,
my mind has emerged purified, like a craftsman's [wheel] from the turning of a lathe.
This has occurred as most of the essential instructions have been proclaimed by the virtuous.

Free from longing, I abide within myself like Mount Sumeru amidst gold. There is nothing that exists for me toward which there is hope; there is nothing desired; there is nothing to be accepted, rejected, or regarded as neutral.
"This is to be abandoned, this is to be accepted; this is real, and this too is unreal"—this delusion of thought has been stilled, O supreme Sage, through your skillful means.
I do not long for heaven, nor do I hate the Raurava hell.

For I abide in the Self alone, like Mount Mandara free from clouds; I am the Mount Mandara of Rāma, who has long been wandering in delusion but is now at rest, free from confusion, and who has scattered the succession of the three worlds like grains into the ocean of milk.

O Lord of Sages, for one whose heart is stained by the conceptualization that "this is non-existent" or "this is existent," the web of evil doubts blazes all the more intensely. For whomsoever this world is known as being "thus," [for him the doubt persists].
Whatever state of wretchedness he encounters in the world, that is not found [in you].
O Blessed One, by your grace we have crossed over the ocean of existence, which is stirred by the various and turbulent waves of inertial activity.
The limit of prosperity has been known, and the boundary of calamities has been seen;
we are undaunted amidst all essential things, we are full, we are supreme lords.
[We have subdued] the elephant of desire, which is supreme, impenetrable by others, and whose hopes have been shattered.

In the battle of saṃsāra, my mind has attained perfect fortitude; having reached a state where conceptual constructions have dissolved, its desires have vanished, and its essential courage is undaunted— my unsurpassed mind, joyful within, triumphs throughout the three worlds in its renowned form.
The forty-eighth canto, titled "Attaining Rest," by Vasiṣṭha:
Whatever you do with the mind alone, which remains unattached while engaged with present objects together with the senses— that is not truly done.
Just as an object at the very moment it is encountered brings initial satisfaction, so too [is the case for the mind].
Who has not experienced that after a single moment of attainment, it is no longer so? Just as an object brings satisfaction at the time of desire, it does not do so at any other time;
therefore, only a fool, and no one else, binds his satisfaction to a pleasure of a moment.
At the moment of desire, that which leads to satisfaction, the cause therein is desire alone;
yet satisfaction ends in dissatisfaction—therefore, abandon desire.
Even if you should ever attain that state through the passage of time, [it would be so].
Therefore, you must not plunge again into the form of the contemplation of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāvanā).
O Rāma, you have found rest upon the peak of the mountain of self-knowledge;
you ought not to fall once more into the great abyss of "I-ness."
For one who possesses the infinite, true vision that has spread forth and stands upon the summit of the Meru of knowledge,
how could there again be a fall into the abyss within the darkness of the womb?
This nature of yours is seen to consist of the truth of equanimity.
I believe that you have become one whose conceptual constructions are exhausted and who has transcended time;
O gentle Rāma, this nature of yours appears to me as firm,
an immaculate equanimity resembling the full ocean.
May hope turn into hopelessness, and may the tendency toward mental construction turn into non-existence; may the mind turn into a state beyond the mind for you who live without attachment.
Whichever perception of an object you encounter, remain established in that very state.
Brahman, in its form as the universal existence, is a mass of expanded consciousness.
As one whose self is unknown, you are bound; as one whose self is known, you are not bound.
Therefore, O Rāma, by your own effort, awaken yourself through your own self.

Know that state to be free from latent impressions (*avāsanatva*), as gentle as the sky, wherein an object does not please the senses, yet whatever comes before them is experienced as it is. Performing actions with internal faculties devoid of latent impressions— *MU* 6.48.13.

You do not undergo transformation even by hundreds of agitations, like the sky. O fortunate one, experiencing within yourself as a peaceful soul the triad of the knower, knowledge, and the knowable as a single unity, you shall no longer be subject to further rebirth.
The emergence and dissolution of saṃsāra occur through the opening and closing of the mind's eye;
by restraining the latent impressions and the vital breath, make the mind free from such opening.
Through the opening and closing of the vital breath, the emergence and dissolution of worldly existence occur.
Make that [mind] free from the opening [of the eyes] through practice and application.
The dissolution and emergence of actions occur through the opening and closing of the eyes of ignorance;
dissolve that forcibly by means of union with the meaning of the Guru’s teachings and the scriptures.
Just as the perception of pillars and clouds arises from the vibration of contact with wind and dust,
so too does this world manifest through the vibration of consciousness by way of being an object of cognition.
This course of the world is to be understood as arising from the vibration of the relationship between the seen and the seeing.
Just as the cognition of color arises from the contact with light, walls, and so forth,

[so does sensation arise]; yet in the absence of the vibration of the relationship between the seer and the seen, no sensation arises that manifests as existence, just as there is none in the minds of painted men.
Illusion arises from the vibration of the mind; in its absence, it dissolves. A wave arises from the vibration of water; by the absence of that [vibration], it subsides.
[This occurs] through the relinquishing of the portion of latent impressions, through awakening, or through the restraint of the vital breath.
When the mind has reached a state of motionlessness, how can there be the occurrence of movement?
By the mere cessation of the movement of consciousness, the mind attains the state of non-mind;
or else, by the suppression of the vital breaths, that very same supreme state is reached.
In the relationship between the seen and the seeing, that bliss which is supreme and essential—
through the exclusive realization of its end and through the vision of Brahman, there is the dissolution of the mind. Where the mind has not arisen, that is unconditioned bliss.
It is not possible [to find such bliss] in heaven and the like, just as one cannot find a house of snow in a desert.
The vast bliss born from the stilling of the mind is inexpressible by words;
free from decay and excess, it neither arises nor ceases.
Through awakening, the end of the mind occurs; from the absence of awakening, the mind arises.
Therefore, the splendor of delusion has reached a state of density, like a child’s phantom.
For even though this mind exists, it dissolves through awakening.
Even that which exists appears as if non-existent, just like copper when it has been turned into gold.
The mind of the knower is not called "mind"; the mind of the knower is said to be *sattva*.
Mind partakes in the difference between name and object; through awakening, it is like copper becoming gold.
The nature of mind is not possible; therefore, it dissolves.
Delusion subsides through awakening, for there is no non-existence of that which exists.
This [world] consisting of mind and so forth is a non-entity, being of the nature of conceptual construction, like the horn of a hare.
Because the Self is all-pervasive, therefore, through the awakening to that [Self], the mind dissolves.
Having attained the state of pure being (*sattva*) for some time during the maintenance of the world,
and having sported within the fourth state (*turya*), it consequently becomes transcendent of the fourth (*turyātīta*).
Brahman alone, through the flood of delusions consisting of the manifold wanderings of the world, exists thus as the one in many forms;
it is the Self of all and becomes everything else, O dear one, for nothing else exists—just as various structures exist within a gold mine, so too do mental states (*caitta*) and the like.
This is the chapter titled "The Indication of the Non-existence of Mind."
The forty-ninth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, for the sake of awakening, [I shall tell] this [story] which causes the hair to stand on end with wonder.
O Rāma, listen briefly to this unprecedented and delightful narrative:
there exists a vast, pure, and manifest great bilva fruit, which does not age even over the course of cosmic ages and measures thousands of yojanas in extent.
It possesses the essence of indestructible flavor, like the sweet core of nectar;
though ancient, it is as beautiful and soft as the crescent of the new moon.
It has withstood the mass of grass-like mountains such as the great Meru and Mandara, which were firmly arrayed against it.
It is not moved even by the force of the winds at the end of a great kalpa;
it is immeasurable in its extent, spanning hundreds of lakhs of millions of ten-thousand-yojanas—
the primordial fruit upon which the existence of the world depends.
In comparison to this *bilva* fruit, the universes nearby lose their charm before the mountain, appearing like a mere line of mustard seeds at its base;
it possesses a sweet, wondrous essence that overflows with streaming sap.
O Rāghava, there is nothing that surpasses this food of six flavors;
it never equals any other preparation even at the end of its cooking,
for it remains eternally cooked and is never afflicted by decay.

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and others like them are merely some who have grown old; they do not know the origin or the root of that which is like a tree whose sprout and growth of flowers remain unseen. MU 6.49.9 adṛṣṭāṅkuravṛkṣasya tv adṛṣṭakusumodgateḥ /
Only the fruit is perceived of that which has no trunk, roots, or branches;
whose production, transformation, and other modifications are not seen, as it possesses a pervasive grossness in the form of a single solid mass.
Within this great fruit, which is the essence of all fruits, there exists an expansive,
changeless, and distinct inner sap;
it is as dense as the interior of a stone, yet like the flowing orb of the moon.
The essence (rasa), which is the nectar of truth flowing forth and to be tasted through one's own self-awareness,
is the sprinkling that brings cool light to all forms of happiness;
it is like a mountain, like a mass of nectar, and the very cream of the abiding fruit of the Self.
Therefore, that supreme marrow which is a sweet wonder,
eternally undisturbed within and non-different from the body of the *śrīphala* fruit—
its own arrangement of variety is the very limb of the fruit of non-duality.
By that slender girl, though she was very young and [her body] stout,
through the notion "I am this," there was produced and cultivated a pure state of being other than the real and the unreal— a state in which distinctions and the like are impossible.
Immediately following the emergence of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkalā*),
that [power] proceeds through the atoms of the three worlds— consisting of the body, sound, and space—
in successive order; thus, that power of consciousness attains the form of the individualizing intellect (*saṃvit*).
The marrow does not abandon its own prior configuration;
by that power of consciousness (saṃvit-śakti), which there takes a flickering form,
the vision is thus expanded within its own supreme nature.
This is the great, infinite void; this is the great portion of time;
this is destiny exerting itself; this is action, characterized by vibration.
This is the expansion of volition; this is the wandering caused by the weight of hope.
This is the persistence of passion and hatred; this is the intellect that discriminates between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted.
This is "you-ness," this is "I-ness," this is "thine-ness," and this is the established order.
This is the flood of cosmic eggs, standing above, in front, and also below.
"This is in front, this is to the side, this is behind, this is near, or this is far away; this is a real thing, this is present, and this is also future"—
such is the abode of the many lotuses of mental construction situated within.
This circle of the pavilion for the play of the cosmic egg is the very core of the lotus-heart of Hari,
which has blossomed through the unfolding of infinite time;
it is the rosary of the lotus-eyes of the world.
This long path of the journey, strewn with the sprouts of the seeds of the Great Rudras in its hollows, manifests a longing to dispel the darkness;
this is Meru, the pericarp of the lotus of the world whose petals are the quarters of space.
This cluster of flowers of the Glory of Heaven possesses unrestrained fragrance; it is a bee-like god, greedy for the sweet nectar of the shimmering moon.
It belongs to the withered tree of the world, which has the dust of hell for its roots.
And this blue lotus of the sky has Tārā as its filament, stands upon the rim of the cosmic egg, and extends to the furthest limits of the shoreless and shoreless-less;
it is the river of action, with its series of rafts consisting of the waves of the wind.
This multitude of successions of beings, abiding within the whirlpools of creation and dissolution, is a lotus of Time: it has darkness for its bee, moments and eons for its sprouts,
radiance for its filament, and the sky for its mud.
"These views on the meaning of the scriptures are rich in the transformations of existence— rich in old age, death, and cholera, and rich in the transformations of knowledge and ignorance"—
this was the wondrous essence of that *bilva* fruit for him.
Within the very framework of its own conceptual construction, it thus maintains its established state;
peaceful, self-abiding, free from affliction, and abandoned by both the pleasant and the unpleasant,
it remains exactly as it is, having rendered both agency and non-agency as mere acts of creation.
Though appearing as many diverse things when perceived individually, it is indeed neither manifold nor multiple; rather, it is that very same one and that very same one.

Established in truth, possessing the single form of universal peace, the consciousness that is the self of all is the supreme power, the Great Consciousness itself. This concludes the chapter titled "The Description of the Conceptualization of the Existence of the Mind. (MU 6.49.36)
Fifty-fifth canto.
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, by you this [goddess] has been manifested in the form of a bilva fruit."
It is my conviction that this has been described as the "Great Mass of Consciousness Being" (mahācidghanasattā).
This entire expanse, beginning with the ego-sense (ahaṃtā), is of the nature of the marrow of consciousness;
there is not even the slightest distinction consisting of the conceptualization of duality or unity.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as the arrangement of Mount Meru and other features is the marrow within the gourd of the cosmic egg,
so too this arrangement of the world, beginning with the cosmic egg, is the marrow within the wood-apple of consciousness.
The creation known as the world is the wondrous manifestation of the marrow of the consciousness-wood-apple;
it exists within the tranquil interior of deep sleep, like a carving within a stone.
O moon-faced one, in this regard, listen to this marvelous and astonishing [account].
Listen to another delightful narrative being told by me:
there exists somewhere a great rock that is smooth, clear, soft to the touch, possessing vast dimensions, dense, and eternally without fissures.
Within it, there are also very many lotuses in full bloom;
some have their roots arising from the pericarp, while others have the pericarp within their roots;
some have their roots above, some have their roots below, and others are rootless.
And near them there are hundreds of thousands of conch shells,
and vast masses of discs arranged like lotuses.
Rāma said:
"This is true; I have seen that great stone of such a kind.
It exists, surrounded by its retinue, in Sāligrāma, the abode of Hari.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"You understand this thus; you have seen those stones.
Whatever stone is there, every one of them has such an interior.
But this stone of mine, which I describe to you, is truly unprecedented."
Within whose great interior both all that exists and all that does not exist reside;
this "intellectual stone" (cicchilā) has been described by me to you, within which the worlds dwell in space— this consciousness is like a stone due to its nature as a single, solid mass.
Even within one whose limbs are exceedingly dense and whose form is without interstices,
the Supreme Brahman exists within, like a vast wind in the sky.
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions—
It exists within that stone, yet it is not even slightly hollow.
Within this [stone], which is a single solid mass, the lotus of the world unfolds;
there is nothing other than this substance, nor anything dual in nature.
The past, the present, and the future are like a statue carved from a block of rock;
thus, all that exists there is the configuration of the object itself.
Even though the internal arrangement within the stone is manifold, it attains the state of a single mass.
Just as it maintains its form, so this consciousness, though a single dense mass,
appears as a lump; just as a lotus, though not distinct from the stone casket,
consists of its own form, so too the creation, though not distinct from the form of consciousness, consists of its own form.

Just as the lines of lotuses within a stone remain inside it during the state of deep sleep, so too does this series of worlds exist within consciousness. Like a row of lotus designs within a stone, or the pungency within black pepper, [so is this world].
Just as creation neither rises nor sets, so it is within consciousness.
Just as the inner core of a wood-apple is non-different from the outer rind and exists without interval,
so too the sphere of the universe, though rich with its various transformations, is contained within consciousness.
The statement that "the modifications and so forth are that very [consciousness]" is purposeless for one who has already awakened;
for it quickly attains that state of reality, like a drop of water in water.
Because consciousness is infinite, these modifications and so forth are simply consciousness.
And that [universe] is accomplished through speech, and it dissolves by merging back into that [speech].
This very Brahman is the transformation and so forth, yet it is devoid of the meaning of transformation and so forth;
because of its infinity, Brahman alone is both the rejection and the non-rejection of objects.

The state of Brahmā, the transformations, and so forth—know that all these were produced from Brahman alone in succession; understand that those who perceive them as something else are like one who seeks water in a mirage. The seed, situated within the flower and the fruit, ends with the seed itself and possesses no other nature.
Such is that existence of the seed which will become so later on.
That which is the state of being a mass of consciousness within the mass of consciousness is itself the sequence of the three worlds.
The unity of these two is their duality; in the absence of one, both are destroyed.
The world never arises as something other than this; it was never otherwise. Consciousness and the unconscious are never non-existent, nor are these two ever separate from one another.
Just as there are many lines within an indivisible great stone, [so is the world within the One].
The course of the three worlds within the mass of consciousness is neither different from nor non-different from it,

like veins and the like within a stone; for just as those do not differ from the substance of the stone because they are its very essence, so too the states of being a thinker, an agent, and so forth, belong to the consciousness of the world.
Just as the arising and ceasing, the movement and stillness of lotuses within a rock do not become objects [of perception],
so too the creators of the world do not become objects.
This [world] is never created, nor does it ever perish.
O Mountain-Dweller, it consists of the manifestation of subsidence and the experience of its own play;
for just as, wherever, and in whatever form [it appears], so indeed is that very thing.
Brahman, which is the self of all and everything, remains situated in the state of deep sleep.
Know that this great delusion of the world, rich with the manifold transformations of existence, is indeed like deep sleep— just as a lotus and such might exist within a stone. O gentle one,
the play of the world is eternally in a state of deep sleep, because its nature consists of the tranquil, uniform, and dense mass of consciousness, which is of the essence of space.
The states of creation do not differ from the stone of the lotus in any way whatsoever from the perspective of its sister [the earth].
The fifty-first canto, titled "The Instruction on the Casket of Stone."
Vasiṣṭha:
Just as the fruit of the *cittattva* is variegated and delightful, so too, its internal arrangement of its own being, occurring in due sequence, is established as "creation" (*sarga*). (MU 6.51.1)
Because space, time, action, and so forth are of such an extremely subtle nature,
it is not possible here to say "this is one thing" and "that is another.
This applies to those who understand the conceptual constructions of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding all words and their referents.
Otherwise, how could this be described as "this" [and that], given its singular nature?
Just as the internal arrangement of a fruit occurs through various successive stages, so too [the One] appears as manifold even while not manifold,
as if agitated even while unagitated.
Just as the existence of a fruit ends within itself, so too the mass of consciousness ends within consciousness.
The city of the world is reflected in consciousness as if in a mirror; it seems to shimmer, yet it does not shimmer, like a structure carved within a stone.
Within the supreme jewel of consciousness, even hundreds of millions of worlds exist,
just as infinite desired fruits are fully contained within a wish-fulfilling gem. This entire extended universe is indeed carved from the very limbs of that jewel of consciousness.

The pearl of the world shines forth, composed of its rays like anything else. Creating days and nights, consisting of perceptions and non-perceptions, this radiant sun of consciousness stands manifesting the substances of the world.
Like the playful movement of water in the whirlpools within the hollow of the ocean,
the three worlds exist in consciousness— neither manifest nor unmanifest.
The self-possessed one has a body consisting of the essence of pure, singular consciousness, like the solid interior of a stone.
The one who is dear to the gods remains engaged in worldly activity like a water-jar;
consciousness, though devoid of division, is a dense vibration like the interior of a stone,
and though non-dual, it appears as manifold like the interior of a stone.
That which exists in the stone body of the statue is the statue; that which does not exist in the stone body of the statue is the statue.
That which is the truth amidst both existence and non-existence is simply the radiant luster of consciousness.
The splendor of objects has its essence in the marrow; indeed, that alone is what it consists of.

Just as a lotus, having abandoned the various meanings of words such as "diverse," exists within the interior of a stone as something non-diverse, so too this world is diverse, yet it is non-dual because it does not consist of that [diversity].

Neither as manifold nor as one, neither manifold nor non-manifold, like the interior of a solid mass of stone or a dense cloud, this world is of an undifferentiated nature, just like the interior of a mass of consciousness.
Just as a pure expanse of water reflects the light of the sun resting upon its surface, so too is this [world].
Though it is truly existent, it appears as if non-existent; thus, consciousness is like a dense mass that seems both being and non-being.

My dear, just as the interior of a hollow tree trunk filled with water is prone to movement due to its fluidity yet remains motionless when still, so too is this interior of the mass of consciousness.

Know that the world— including the multitude of consciousness, stone, conch, and lotus, as well as that which consists of them and that which does not— is the interior of the rock of consciousness, containing the referents of words such as "lotus" and so forth. This mass of consciousness, though as solid as a great boulder, has a hollow interior.
Without openings, internal, non-dual, and transparent like the interior of water,
this world falls [into it] as if into the Brahma, like Soma into flowing water. This world exists within Brahman, appearing as if in deep sleep, non-different from it, like a lotus carved in stone.
The world is Brahman, like the bilva fruit within its husk; indeed, Brahman alone is the beautiful reality.
Just as emptiness resides in space and fluidity in water, and just as motion resides in the wind, so does this world reside in Brahman.
Just as the state of Brahman exists within Brahman, so too does this world abide;
no difference exists between these two, just as there is none between a tree and its trunk.
Those worlds which exist here are but the intestines of the form of Consciousness.
For them, there is never at any time existence, non-existence, and so forth, just as there is not for that [illusion].
Brahman alone appears as the world, just as water [appears] through the sun's rays;
through contemplation, Brahman alone becomes pure, just as water [becomes clear] through the heat of the sun.

The form of Mount Meru, of grass and shrubs, of the mind, and even of the entire world, when analyzed down to its atoms— that they know to be the Supreme. That very same collection [of atoms] is what is called the mind, Mount Meru, grass, and so forth.

For that which is essential even in subtlety is indeed more essential in grossness. Just as the power consisting of rasa exists within the constituent elements of the world by way of its atomicity, so too does the nature of Brahman exist as the essence of all things.
Just as the power of flavor arises from water in the form of grass and shrubs,
so too does that very Brahman-hood arise here in its manifold variety through practice.
That which is the atomicity of light within the play of forms—
That supreme selfhood consists of the nature of both qualities and the possessor of qualities, as well as the reality of the self.

Just as the hardness of the mass of feathers and wings exists within the essence of the hen's egg, so do mountains and other things exist within the principle of consciousness, which is their manifesting substrate.
In the principle of consciousness (*cititattva*), which consists of its own manifestation, there exists multiplicity,
just as there is a mass of various-colored tail-feathers within the fluid of a peacock’s egg.
For in this way, it is both manifold and non-manifold, just like the fluid contained within the egg.
In the same way, the existence of Brahman and the world are seen through the vision of discernment:
as both manifold and non-manifold, like the juice of the egg and the peacock;
thus the delusion of Brahman and the world has the nature of both non-duality and duality.

Know that supreme state to be one's own true being, from which the existence of both the existent and the non-existent arises, from which their persistence comes, and from which their form— both that and not-that— is derived. Indeed,
one who does not perceive the manifoldness within the manifold surely perceives what is impossible.
Behold the blazing fire of the entire world, like the fluid within a peacock's egg.
Just as the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*) exists within the world, so does the world exist within the principle of consciousness;
it is both manifold and non-manifold, yet one, just like the fluid within a peacock's egg.
The conscious self (cidātman) is the essence of the egg of the world-peacock, filled with the plumage of the delusion of various objects;
yet know that its form as a peacock is not a peacock here, for it is the state of pure existence—how then can there be any duality?
This is the chapter titled "The Instruction on Reality."
Fifty-second Sarga. Vasiṣṭha said:
In which this entire extended universe exists, its very self being unarisen.
And that state of non-egoity was described as being like the interior of a peacock's egg.
In that [state], nothing has arisen, yet everything exists therein;
it is inexpressible by words, and even the essence of the bliss of heaven does not exist there.
And likewise, the sages, gods, hosts, perfected ones, and great seers,
constantly relishing their own nature, abide forever in the fourth state (turyapada). These are they whose gaze is fixed with unblinking eyes.
They are established in the relinquishing of the vibration of attachment between the seen and the seeing; they for whom no mental cultivation remains, even while engaged in actions,
and who are established in the relinquishing of the vibration of the relationship between consciousness and its object.
The vital breath does not stir for them, as if their bodies were depicted in a painting;
having abandoned attachment to the mind and its mental factors, they abide in their own true state.
Just as armies accomplish their purpose through the movement of the commander of the army, so do they achieve their goals through the movement [of the breath].
In the same way, the mind and its mental factors bring about cyclic existence through their vibration.
Just as the clear lunar ray gladdens a sprout,
so does the Self gladden [the mind] within during the union of the seen and the seer.
The form of the moon's light that has traveled far from the orb and has not yet fallen upon the wall—
that is the form of pure consciousness.
It is not an object of sight, it is not fit for instruction, and it is neither near nor far.
That pure form of the Self is attainable through solitary experience alone.
It is neither the body, nor the collection of senses, nor the mind, nor mental impressions;
it is neither the individual soul (jīva), nor vibration, nor consciousness, nor even space.
It is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor situated in between; it is neither empty nor non-empty.
It is not space, time, substance, and so forth; that alone exists, and nothing else.
It is entirely free from all these, even though it resides within the sheath of the heart.
Wherever this invisible one vibrates, that is the state of the Self.
And that, neither today nor at the end of an aeon, can be altered by weapons, fire, wind, or the like;
being of the nature of existence, it never becomes otherwise, either here or in the hereafter.
Thousands of bodily jars are born and die;
yet there is no destruction of this space that is the Self, which exists both within and without.
And all of that—the body and so forth—is indeed the Self alone, O best of those who know the Self.

Having realized through your own perfected intellect that [the world] is entirely composed of the Self, pure, and yet situated slightly apart from pure consciousness due to the deformity of cognition—
though blazing amidst activities, remain extinguished and free from the sense of "mine."
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving— all that is Brahman, devoid of attributes, free from qualities, and characterized by a self that is free from "mine-ness";
it is eternally without parts, one, and absolutely pure.

Changeless, without beginning or end, eternal, peaceful, and of a uniform nature— having seen that all this, from the action of time and its instruments and causes, to the agent, the effect, birth, maintenance, dissolution, and transmigration, is indeed Brahman, why, my dear, do you still wander with attachment through the vision of a self?
The fifty-third canto, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of Brahman," [spoken by] Rāma:
"If there is no modification or the like within the expanded Brahman, O Brahman, then how does this world, consisting of existence and non-existence, appear? Vasiṣṭha replied:

That which is the reversal of its own nature, such that it does not return to its prior state, is described as "modification" (*vikāra*) and so forth; this is found in things such as milk. Milk returns once more to the state of milk [after curdling], but from the state of curd, it does not become milk again.
Brahman is indeed pure Brahman, without beginning, middle, or end;
therefore, Brahman possesses no transformation, just as milk and other substances do not [remain unchanged when they become curds].
For that which is without beginning or end and devoid of modification, there can be no sequential arrangement of parts.
Know that this transformation of consciousness which is observed for a moment at the beginning and end of an object is an illusion; there is no modification in that which is changeless.
Since consciousness exists only when there is an object of cognition, it does not exist in Brahman.
That which is designated by the word "Brahman" is the conscious self (cidātman) devoid of objective perception;
it is said to be exactly as it is at the beginning and at the end.
Any apparent difference in its state in the middle is merely the manifestation of ignorance.
The Self, however, is equal at the beginning, end, and middle; it is everywhere and at all times.
Even space undergoes change, but the reality of the Self never does.
Because its nature is light, because of its oneness, and because of its eternity, this is the Lord.
He never falls under the sway of the transformations of phenomenal existence.
Rāma said:
"While Brahman, which is eternally one and absolutely pure, exists..."
"What is the origin of ignorance, whose nature consists in the delusion of consciousness?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"This entire reality is the essence of Brahman; it was so, it is so, and it will be so."
It is certain that there is no ignorance [avidyā] in that which is changeless and without beginning or end.
As for the sequence of the signified and the signifier expressed by the word "Brahman," even there, no difference exists; rather, that sequence was established merely for the purpose of instruction.
You, I, the world, the quarters, the earth, the ether, fire, wind, and so forth, are nothing but Brahman—without beginning or end; there is not even the slightest trace of ignorance.
The wise know that this so-called "ignorance" is a mere delusion, being unreal by nature.
"Since that [object] does not exist, what kind of name could it possibly have?
Rāma said:
"In the section on instruction, what was this that you spoke of yesterday?"
"O Lord, this ignorance is determined to be thus and so. Vasiṣṭha said:
"O scion of Raghu, you have remained unawakened for all this time."
It is said that you have been awakened by these well-reasoned arguments which were merely imagined.
This entire sequence of conceptual constructions— such as "this is ignorance" and "this is the individual soul"—
was devised by the best among those skilled in speech for the purpose of awakening the unawakened.
As long as the mind remains unawakened,
it does not attain awakening even in hundreds of years, unless it is freed from delusion;
only by awakening it through reasoning is this living being united with the Self.
That which is accomplished through reasoning cannot be achieved even by hundreds of efforts.
That foolish person who tells an unenlightened man that "everything is Brahman" brings about suffering for his friend by mistaking a post for a human being.
The fool is awakened by means of reasoning; the wise man is awakened by means of the reality itself.
The fool attains wisdom not without being awakened by reasoning.
For so long you were unawakened, you have now been awakened by reasoning.
Now you are fully awakened; you are being enlightened by reality itself:
"I am Brahman; the three worlds are Brahman; you are Brahman; the ground of the visible is Brahman.
There is no second conceptualization; do as you wish."
The three worlds are merely the pinnacle of great consciousness that is beyond perception;
one who possesses such internal realization is not defiled even while acting within them.
"I am the Supreme Self—of the nature of light, conscious, and all-pervading"—this is sufficient.
O Rāma, if you are wise, remaining free from possessiveness and egoism while standing, walking, sleeping, or breathing, and if your experience culminates in the realization of Rāghava,
then become that peaceful knowledge of Brahman which abides in all beings.
Therefore, you are that very being which is without beginning or end, the luminous supreme state;
you abide as the one all-pervading Self, whose nature consists of pure consciousness.
That which is Brahman, the Self, the All-pervasive Lord, and that which is ignorance and primordial nature (prakṛti)—[all these are you].
That [Self] is non-different, eternally of one essence, just as clay is in hundreds of jars.
The nature of the Self is not different from it, just as the state of being made of clay is not different from the jars;
or just as air is merely vibration, so the Self alone is the primordial nature.

That which is the movement of the Self by itself, like the whirlpool of water, is indeed designated here by the word "prakṛti" (nature); for it is that very thing [which is so called]. Just as the single movement and the wind are distinct in name but not in essence, so too are these two.
Likewise, there is only one self-nature, which is divided by name but not by its actual being.
The distinction between these two arises from lack of understanding; through true knowledge alone it dissolves.
This lack of understanding consists of unreality and is an illusion, just like the delusion of a snake in a rope.
When this seed of mental construction falls and vibrates upon the ground of consciousness,

from it arises the sprout of the mind, which is the future grove of saṃsāra. This very sprout, when burnt by the fire of self-knowledge, cannot grow again even with the waters of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Even if it is carefully sprinkled with water, it does not become capable of producing a sprout;
for if the seed of conceptualization does not fall into the field of consciousness,
then the sprouts of the mind— the trees that bear the fruits of pleasure and pain— do not arise.
Duality in this world is unreal, acquired through ignorance and born of non-awakening; abandon it, for you have attained awakening which destroys that ignorance.
Through the power of the singular nature of the Self, you are one whose being is fearless; "there is no suffering at all"—this is the essence of our ultimate truth.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Yoga of Contemplating Saṃsāra."
Fifty-fourth canto.
Rāma:
"All that is to be known has been known; all that is to be seen has been seen without flaw."
"O Brahmin, we have been completely filled by you with the nectar of knowledge.
This fullness is of the nature of the Full; from the Full, the Full is replenished;
the Full is filled by the Full; the state of Fullness remains as Fullness itself."
O Brahmin, I ask this again merely as a sport for the further increase of my understanding; you ought not to be angry with me, just as a father would not be with his child.
[The senses are] hearing, sight, touch, taste, and smell.
O Brahmin, although it exists and is clearly visible,
why does a deceased being not perceive its own object? And why does a living being perceive all of its own objects?
How is it that external objects such as jars, though perceived within the body by the sense organs— even though those organs are insentient— are not, moreover, perceived [as being] inside?
For it is said that the jar and the sense organ are like two iron rods [joined together].
"How can existence arise between two things that are unattached and devoid of essence?
Even though I know this, I ask you again out of a desire for further distinction; therefore, please tell me everything quickly out of compassion. (MU 6.54.7–8)
Vasiṣṭha said:
O dear one, neither the senses, nor the mind and so forth, nor even objects such as a jar,
can exist here separately apart from the stainless consciousness.
Even from the sky, that consciousness, by its own nature, has through its own mental activity conceived its own form as the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city);
and that very same [consciousness], having attained the state of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), exists as this world.
The collection of its constituent parts consists of those senses and so forth, as well as the jar and other objects.

That principle of consciousness (*cittattva*), which by its very nature has attained the state of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*), possesses these as its own internal constituents; within it, the jar and other such things are reflected.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, tell me what is the nature of my subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), which possesses the majesty of creating a thousand worlds and serves as a mirror for them?
Vasiṣṭha:
That Brahman which exists is the seed of the world without beginning or end, free from affliction,
consisting of light, pure consciousness alone, and devoid of all parts or mental constructs.
When that [intellect] becomes oriented toward temporal succession (kalā), it is known as the individual soul (jīva).
Indeed, that soul clearly accumulates [karma] and vibrates within this body.
From the state of "I-ness" (ahambhāva) it is called the ego (ahaṅkāra), and from the act of thinking (manana) it is called the mind (manas).
From the determination of awakening comes the intellect (*buddhi*), and likewise the sense-faculties (*indriya*) from the vision of Indra.
Through the ideation of a body comes the body, and through the ideation of a jar comes the jar.
This self, whose nature is thus, is known as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*).
That consciousness which identifies with knowerhood, agency, enjoyership, witnesshood, and so forth, is called the *jīva*; for that is known as the "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*).
From time to time, the *jīva* becomes one thing and then another by its own nature.
Due to the arising of infinitesimal particles of latent impressions (vāsanā) produced by past actions,
it assumes a form through time by means of its nature as the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold subtle body),
just as a seed becomes a sprout through the power of latent impressions acting like water for irrigation.
"I am the body and so forth, or the immobile world, or the gods"—
thus one sinks into false knowledge, thinking "I am not the primordial conscious Self.
In this way, the living soul, tossed by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), wanders through the world for a long time.
Just as a piece of wood tossed by waves in the ocean moves upward and downward,
so too some person— due to their sattvic nature— immediately after being released from the bondage of existence,
realizes their own self and attains the state that is devoid of beginning and end.
After a long time, someone who has passed through various successions of wombs attains the supreme state of the Self by the power of self-knowledge.
O wise one, such is the living being that has entered into embodied existence.
Listen to how he perceives objects such as a jar through the eyes and other senses: because of the activity of that consciousness which has entered into the state of being a living soul,
the aggregate of the six organs beginning with the mind stands before it, as if it were a body.
When the object falls into the body of the sense-organ in the form of that organ itself,
then, through contact with the living soul (jīva), it attains oneness with the individual self (jīvātman).
In the perception of external objects, the constant connection of the sense-organ is the cause.
For one whose mind is thus endowed, and never for one who is liberated:
whatever is more transparent than that [mind] reflects within it;
joined with the *jīva*, it becomes external, and then the *jīva* lives through it.
When the pupils of the eyes possess the luster of freshly polished jewels,
then external objects are reflected therein; consequently,
through the power of that reflection, they become joined with the individual soul (jīva).
O Rāghava, an external object becomes knowable by the living soul;
for even a child perceives that which comes into contact [with it],
so why would a living being— not even a beast or an immobile thing— not perceive it?
Furthermore, O virtuous one, the rays of the eye are enveloped by the living soul (jīva);
they fully embrace the visible object, and through that, the soul perceives it.
This very same sequence occurs in the case of touch, giving rise to the cognition of contact.
In the case of taste and smell, it is said that their perception arises from contact with the *jīva*.
But sound, because it resides in space (*ākāśa*), enters the space within the ear and reaches the space of the *jīva* inside in an instant; thus do the perceptions of the sense organs occur.
Rāma: O Brahmin, tell me, what is the nature of this reflection which is seen in stainless mirrors, precious gems, water, and so forth?
Vasiṣṭha:
That which has long existed within the space of Brahman appears like a chance occurrence;
that which remains for a moment and that which remains for a while—this alone is what constitutes these worlds of yours.
Contemplating that objects are merely one's own existence, like [objects] in a dream, [one sees] the single,

manifold-souled sky of consciousness standing firm like a tree in a dream. Whatever cognition there is of the existence of external objects, and whatever notion there is of the world as being the Self of Brahman— [all these are but the sky of consciousness].
Both he and she—everything that exists—is established according to its perception.
First, when the state of being an atom is understood, then subtlety, and then space;
those [powers] which today the knower perceives as the sky, hands, eyes, and so forth.
From the very beginning of creation, the object is reflected in the stainless [intellect];
yet the state of being "aware" arises from the identity between the entire original image and its reflection.
That which exists as "this object" is merely a shimmering within the sky of consciousness.
That arrangement which was conceived at the beginning of creation has now reached its state of stability.

By the power of the manifestation within the space of consciousness, there occurs a mutual attribution of qualities among entities that are in fact non-existent— a reflection within that which is stainless.
That mutual bestowal of existence which occurs by its very nature between two things that are utterly inert, like between two individual souls, is called a reflection;
or [it occurs] between the conscious self and the inert, or between the great Being and that which is of an inert nature.

O best among those who know the objects of knowledge, know that the mutual projection of the existence of the original object (bimba) occurs due to the restriction of their primordial nature; it is a delusion of the eyes regarding the reflection.
The world is merely that much; therefore, let there be no conviction in you here [regarding its reality].

In the supreme ocean, there is no such thing as the wave of "I" and so forth, nor the whirlpools of creation and the rest, because of its oneness with that [ocean], transcending distinctions of space, time, and action.
One whose mind is eternally unattached, whose self is joyful, and who possesses infinite consciousness of peace beyond both pleasure and pain— [is liberated].
"Remain with your mind settled in equanimity, free from the illusion of all the diseases of existence.
This is the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Examining Sensory Perception."
Vasiṣṭha said:
"The eyes and other faculties were already fully formed before the emergence of the new [body],
just as you have heard all this regarding the lotus-born Brahmā."
Just as the consciousness of the senses has been described at the beginning of the eightfold city of Brahmā, so too does it always arise for every eightfold city.
Know that the living being (jīva) is the eightfold city; he is the emergence of the senses within the womb.
Whatever one meditates upon in whatever manner, that one quickly perceives in that very way.
Know that the senses and what are called the objects of the senses are one's own consciousness;
and how that becomes perfected has been explained to you regarding the initial state of the mind.
Pure consciousness is the knower of consciousness, the irreproachable awareness;
therefore, from this internal awareness of "I," the individual soul as the *puryaṣṭaka* has emerged.
Yet, because it is one, infinite, unknowable, and free from affliction, [it remains essentially unchanged].
Because it is non-different, because it is not manifold, and because it is not empty, there is the supreme state.
One perceives nothing such as "this is an object of thought" and does not attain the state of the mind (*manas*);
nor does one come to possess the nature of a living individual (*jīva*), nor does one consist of the subtle body of eight constituents (*puryaṣṭaka*).
There is no play of ignorance and the like; that which always exists as if it were non-existent is called the Supreme Self (paramātman), transcending the six senses including the mind.
From that [Self], the individual soul (jīva) is produced, whose form is consciousness and whose nature is thought.
"It is merely delusion," and so forth, is sung as an instruction;
for when the disease consisting of ignorance has arisen from some cause or other,
it dissolves through inquiry by means of the instruction of the teacher and the taught.
When all activity has become utterly tranquil, that knowledge alone remains,
wherein even the sky appears gross like Mount Meru within an atom,
and wherein even that which is arising and existent remains as non-existent.
The world, which is the object of the Knower, stands as if fashioned out of mud.
Indeed, this entire form of ignorance consists of the unreal;
for when it is truly perceived, it surely perishes and is no longer seen.
How indeed can that which is called "seen" be obtained when it is a non-entity?
Or by whom has the water of a mirage ever been attained, even with great effort?
That which is always non-existent is indeed non-existent; its appearance as real is due to ignorance.
Through knowledge, the object is seen as it truly is, and delusion perishes.
