For the sake of investigating ignorance— even though the "vital city" (puryaṣṭaka) of the individual soul and so forth are absolutely unreal— a conceptual construction is imagined within the self that has been so constructed.

Therefore, for the purpose of instructing him, this conceptualization of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth was formulated by the scriptures for the sake of awakening; listen to it with a one-pointed mind. Having attained, as it were, the state of being a living soul, it abides in the station of the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*).
Consciousness, free from the stain of temporal parts (kalā) and turned away from insentience,
experiences immediately and fully whatever it contemplates,
whether that be true or false, just as a child [fears] a yakṣa in the night.
In whatever way she contemplates the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) therein,
she perceives them as such within herself, arisen in that very manner and with corresponding openings.
From those very [subtle elements], the external pentad of gross elements (*bhūtapañcaka*) has arisen.
It perceives what is non-different as having the appearance of difference, just as a sprout [sees] a hundred branches.
Then, possessing the conviction that "this is internal" and "this is external," the individual soul (jīva) firmly establishes whatever it grasps in exactly that manner.
That manifestation of the self which is like a web of rays from the moon is,
by virtue of its appearing as an external touch, accepted as such [as real] by the unheroic (the ignorant).
That which is like the heat of a mirage, or like the emptiness of the sky— [that is the nature of the self].
The perception of the self by that [consciousness] is as if it were something other than itself, resting upon it.
Having attained certainty regarding this very point, the discipline is made very firm:
"By this, it must be thus; by that, it must be thus," without any breach.

This [Self], which is the regulator of its own volitions under various names such as "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) and so forth, exists at some place and at some time by its very intrinsic nature and not otherwise.
This entire duality has arisen from the non-dual Self alone; it is non-dual.
Just as a grove [is produced] by sweet water, or as a large jar [is produced] from clay;
so too, the arrangement, transformation, and so forth, occur here [in the world] due to the possibility of place,
time, and other such factors, but they do not occur in God, because place, time, and so forth are impossible for Him.
Just as the spring season, arising within itself in a grove with the thought "the flower is here, the leaf is here, I am," removes duality while there is non-duality;
so too does the one arise with the thought "the cloth is here, the wall is here, I am."
Within the Self, whose nature is creation, Brahman— though free from dualities— assumes duality.

Just as one remains thinking, "Today I am a sprout," "Today I am the brilliance of the sun," or "Today I am a cloud," so too does the Self abide, possessing both the forms of existence and non-existence.
"Who in this world has the power to refute the sequence proclaimed by the Lord of All, according to which 'this must be conceived as such'?
For in a clear mirror, one's own form does not reflect back upon itself."
However, because separation is impossible, it simply shines forth.
But within Brahman, the Self itself, abiding as the Self, shines and reflects;
though bodiless, it appears as duality by its very nature, owing to its consisting of consciousness.
Just as whatever manifestation is perceived by the nature of consciousness is never subject to deviation here, even though it is unreal; so too,
the two states of being gold and being a bracelet possess both real and unreal natures.
Just as the state of being gold exists in a vessel, so too do consciousness and non-consciousness exist in the Self.
Because consciousness is all-pervading, its conscious nature is eternally present in the mind, just as the nature of gold is in a bracelet; yet insentience also remains [in it] at other times.
When the mind itself firmly cultivates its own nature as being either conscious or insentient,
then it becomes exactly that state, in that very way.
At various times, the living soul, through its own consciousness, becomes this or that other state by itself.
Possessing a cultivated form within due to the arising of a minute seed of latent impression (*vāsanā*),
just as a village seen in a dream attains the nature of reality for a moment,
so too does this living soul (*jīva*) move from body to body, which are of the nature of mental appearances.

Just as in a dream a person may perceive a wall as a cloth, so too, for us, does one body become another body; it is entirely unreal. It is unreal that one dies, and it is unreal that one is born again.
Through its own manifestation, like a dream, the living being perceives itself as having another form;
by this much time, it spontaneously experiences for itself the firmly rooted, natural conviction: "This form must be abandoned by me."
"O best among those who know what is to be known, understand that the world is the dream of the living soul; for in a dream, both things seen and unseen are experienced.
That which is neither waking nor dreaming, and is devoid of designations and the like, is the reality perceived by the seer."

A dream does not differ from its own clear state of pure consciousness alone. Just as a person sees a great dream that has never occurred before, so too this consciousness perceives its own self-awareness as the manifold world.
Impressions formed in the past are quickly overcome by human effort alone;
indeed, through exertion today, yesterday’s evil deeds turn into good deeds.
Apart from liberation, the senses of living beings, such as the eyes and so forth, do not cease their activity.
They emerge and submerge solely according to place and time.
Because of the mental construction of that [self], the body stands as if at its head;
though composed of five elements and cultivated, it is unreal, like a great yakṣa conjured for a child.
The mind, the intellect, the ego, and likewise the five subtle elements—this is declared to be the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka); this is the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha).
The self of consciousness is indeed formless; its extreme density is like the nature of space.
The wind becomes his great ankle, and the body becomes his Mount Sumeru.
This [wind] exists in two states in succession, but when devoid of states, it partakes in liberation.
Its single state is that of deep sleep; its dullness has embraced its own arising.
The state other than this [waking] is dream-nature, characterized by the cognition of a body;
"this [self] wanders here until liberation," so it is said by all things, both moving and stationary.
For at one time it is situated in deep sleep, and at another time it is established in a dream.
This subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) persists for everyone when one is in the state of deep sleep, about to be awakened by future suffering; then,
with its form unmanifested, it remains like a stone in the sky.

In states such as those of stationary objects and in the conditions of the wish-fulfilling tree, this [self] remains in deep sleep, a mass of dense delusion like a solid stone. Its state of deep sleep is its insentience; this transmigratory existence, however, is its dream.
That awakening which belongs to it is liberation; that is the waking state, and that is the fourth state (turyatā).
For the awakening of the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed liberation, and it is said here to be of two kinds:
one is liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), and the second is liberation after death (*adehamukti*).
Liberation while living is indeed the state of the Fourth (turya), and beyond that is the Supreme, which is beyond the Fourth (turyātīta).
For liberation is the awakening of the living soul, and that occurs through the effort of the intellect.
The living soul has knowledge as its measure; whatever it knows within, it becomes identified with that.
Therefore, let him know the mere act of cognition; thus he quickly becomes absorbed in that.
This living soul perceives this very long delusion of a dream, falsely arisen within its own heart, which has become as solid as a crystal.
Within this atomic soul there exists nothing at all apart from its own fraction of consciousness;
perceiving that very consciousness as something else, one grieves in vain.
Within this atomic soul there exists nothing at all other than the Supreme.

Wherever the world is seen, alas, it is the unfolding of illusion (māyā). Just as the appearance of whirling arises for grains of rice boiling in water within a pot, so too does the false arising of transmigration occur for the atomic souls (jīvāṇu) within their own interior.

Its bondage consists in being possessed of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), while liberation would be the destruction of those impressions. From these impressions, its states of deep sleep and dream manifest.
This dense delusion of latent impressions is known as the "insentient" state of the self in deep sleep.
Accompanied by the dream that necessarily occurs within that state,
the individual soul (jīva), drowsy from the onset of latent impressions (vāsanā), perceives a delusion;
when its sleep of latent impressions is exhausted, it then awakens.

The attachment to the visible world and its visibility, which are said to be latent impressions (*vāsanā*), do not exist at all within the Self of all, just as the state of being a bracelet or other ornaments does not exist in gold.
This [world] came into being through lack of awakening; it dissolves through awakening.
For you, however, there is indeed the arising [of the world] from the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Having destroyed the dense delusion of one's own latent impressions, one reaches deep sleep; then, having attained a state of attenuated latent impressions, one perceives the cycle of existence as a dream.

This dense latent impression (vāsanā) of delusion is the individual soul (jīva) that experiences the state of stationary beings and so forth; one with moderate impressions is a lower animal, while a person with attenuated impressions is a human being.
When those things such as jars, which are "living" externally, are taken up by the life-force within, [they become objects of perception].
Because the two— the grasped object and the grasping subject— possess existence through their identity with the individual soul (*jīva*),
the self is then thoroughly swallowed by the self when it is encompassed within and without by consciousness.
At that time, the cognition of grasped and grasping, along with its arising, is like a mirage.
Nothing whatsoever is abandoned here, nor is anything at all grasped here;
the single Self of Consciousness shines forth, devoid of external or internal forms and divisions. The three worlds are but the wonder of Consciousness; enough with conceptualizations of duality.
We have been awakened; we know nothing other than that which is piled up in the funeral pyre, beginning with the external.

Just as the entire ocean is pure, free from all distinctions, sweet, clear, liquid, and a single unity, so too this primordial, supreme state is understood to be entirely without disease, having cast aside the entire collection of differentiated things.
The fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Investigation into the Perception of the Objects of the Senses," by Vasiṣṭha.
Know that this world, which is the dream arisen for the individual soul (jīva) and tender with various mental constructions, is neither real nor composed of unreality.
A dream does not occur for the individual soul in the same way it occurs for the Supreme Person (puruṣa).
Therefore, these worldly states are indeed the unity of waking and dreaming;
this long dream of the individual soul (jīva) appears both quickly and at length.
Know, O best among those who know what is to be known, that although it is unreal, it lacks substantial reality.
Like those moving from one dream to another,
living beings perceive what is utterly unreal for a long time as if it were solid reality;
the non-inert has fallen into inertness, and within that inertness, non-inertness has arisen.

The appearance of truth has arisen within the unreal due to the delusion of the individual soul's experience. Even while perceiving the entire illusory wandering of the three worlds within the post itself,
living beings— whose minds are like serpents— wander here, bewildered as if in a dream.
Because their own infinite consciousness (cit) is all-pervading,
whatever they contemplate and perceive attains the state of reality;
[this is] the auspicious path of non-attachment taught by Puṇḍarīkākṣa.

O mighty-armed one, by embracing whom the great sage Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, became liberated while yet living and spent his own life happily and free from suffering— embrace her and thus spend your life.
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, when will Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, appear?
And what kind of unimpeded power will Hari describe to him?"
Vasiṣṭha said:
There exists that which is pure being, designated by the name "Self," abiding within the Self like the great sky within the beginningless and endless ether.
In that stainless [consciousness], this delusion of saṃsāra is seen,
just as bracelets and the like are seen in gold, or waves and the like in water.
The fourteen kinds of classes of beings manifest abundantly therein.
In this web of saṃsāra, like birds caught in a net,
Yama, Candra, Ārka, Śakra, and the others— those who follow the course of transmigration—
have assumed the status of world-protectors, established within the five elements.
"This is merit and should be adopted; this, however, is evil and should be abandoned"—such is the established order fixed by the Veda and fashioned by their own conceptual constructs.
When this [order] had thus reached maturity and had been flowing for a very long time, [the following occurred].
In this world-order, which is like a river that flows on without interruption yet perishes,
there is the powerful world-protector named Yama Vaivasvata,
who stands ready to restrain those beings whose existence is marked by death.
O sinless one, until this very day, his mind has remained as steady as a mountain, fixed upon his own duty that has descended through the flow of time.
That Lord Yama observes a certain vow for each cycle of four ages.
Nevertheless, out of fear of the sin arising from the destruction of living beings,
he sometimes remains for eight years, or ten, or twelve;
sometimes for five or seven, and sometimes even for sixteen.
While he sat like one indifferent, established in his discipline,
death did not harm any living beings within the web of the world.
By him, the surface of the earth was rendered devoid of movement, with the flood of beings packed without any gaps.
"In the rainy season, the thicket becomes as if covered with sweat by the gadflies.
Then, O Rāma, those various beings exhaust themselves through many stratagems so that the gods may remove the burden of the earth.
In this way, thousands of Yamas and hundreds of legal systems have passed away,
as have infinite beings and worlds.
But today, Vaivasvata Yama is the one who is the leader of the ancestors.
But now, O virtuous one, when some of the ages have been exhausted,
you must perform the practice of vows here in this world for twelve years in your own form, in order to destroy sin, having cast far away all cruel deeds.
Therefore, this earth, crowded with mortal beings who are as if immortal,
will become distressed like a dense thicket under the weight of those who have become a burden;
the Earth, her limbs overwhelmed by the weight, will seek refuge in Hari.
Like a beloved wife overcome by bandits and distressed, she will seek her dear husband;
then Hari shall descend to earth with two bodies,
together with all the portions of the gods who have assumed the leadership of men.
The son of Vasudeva alone shall be known as Vāsudeva;
he will be the second body of Hari, while Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu,
shall become the one celebrated as Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma.
The king whose girdle is the ocean, that son of Pāṇḍu who knows the Dharma,
will be known as Duryodhana; his paternal cousin, Bhīma,
will become his firm adversary, like a brown snake to a mongoose.
As those two vie with one another for the earth,
eighteen terrifying akṣauhiṇīs, eager for battle, will indeed clash here;
through their destruction, Viṣṇu will bring about the "Bharata-ness" (the state of being the Bharata land) of the earth.
With the bodies of Rāghava and Arjuna, that wielder of the great Gāṇḍīva bow—
being Viṣṇu himself assuming the state of an ordinary being—
will possess a body subject to human attributes, filled with joy and indignation.
Seeing his own kinsmen situated in both armies and facing death,
he will fall into despondency and will not exert himself for battle.
[Therefore,] that body named Arjuna has been obtained solely for the accomplishment of the task at hand.
"O Rāghava, Hari will awaken you with a Buddha-body.
The Blessed One said:
"Your inner self is afflicted by the human condition; through the overwhelming power of despair and delusion, you have lost consciousness."
Having lost yourself by abandoning your own [nature] for another light, you do not indeed shine as that reality of the Self, O lion among kings.

Behold the infinite, unmanifest, and beginningless-and-endless Self within yourself, O conscious one! You are the expansive form of consciousness, unstained by defects; you are unborn, eternal, and free from affliction.
It is never born, nor does it ever die; having come into being, it will not cease to be.
Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.
Chapter named "The Incarnation of Nārāyaṇa."
The Fifty-Seventh Chapter.
The Blessed One said:
"He who knows him as a slayer, and he who thinks of him as slain—"
Both of them do not understand that this [Self] neither kills nor is killed.
Of the infinite, uniform, existent, and subtle Self, which is even subtler than space and the supreme Lord, what is there to be killed, how, and by whom?
"You are not Arjuna; you are not the slayer. Abandon this conceit entirely.
You are yourself the eternal Self, liberated from old age and death.
He whose state is free from egoism, whose intellect is not defiled—"
Even having destroyed these worlds, he neither kills nor is he bound.
Whatever consciousness arises within, that alone is experienced;
therefore, abandon the notion of "this is he," "I am this," and "this is mine."
And by this very [nature], O Bhārata, you think "I am joined" and "I am destroyed";
thus, being powerless, you are dragged hither and thither by pleasure and pain.
Actions are performed in their respective parts by the qualities (guṇas), which are portions of your own self.
One whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer.
Let the eye see, let the ear hear, let this skin touch, and let the tongue experience taste; who here remains as the one "I"? (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.7–8)
O Mahāmati, even when the mind is intent upon the activity of fashioning, there is no one here who possesses the affliction of "I"; who indeed could it be for you?
O Bhārata, that which is produced by the combination of many factors— [in that, who is the agent?]
For one who is seized by the pain of pride is taken only for laughter.
Yogis perform action with the body, mind, intellect, and even with the senses alone, having abandoned attachment, for the sake of self-perfection.

Those whose bodies have not been permeated by the powder of the poison of selflessness— though they may be giving or taking [things]— are these very ones who are free from the cholera of worldly attachment.
Nowhere does the body shine, being defiled by the impurity of the sense of "mine-ness."

Even one who is wise and possesses vast knowledge is like a man of immoral character if he is not free from possessiveness and egoism; but he who is without "mine-ness" and without egoism, who is equal in pain and pleasure, and patient—
even while performing what ought to be done or what ought not to be done, he is not tainted.
And this, O son of Pāṇḍu, is your own kṣatriya duty, the most excellent;
though it is exceedingly cruel, it leads to welfare and prosperity.
Even if it be contemptible, base, and consisting of unrighteousness, it is yet slender.
One's own action leads to one's welfare in this world, but the nectar of immortality does not do so in the same way.
(6,57.16) Even for a fool, his own action alone leads to his welfare; how much more so for one of noble mind?
A mind from which egoism has dissolved is not defiled, even if it has fallen. (6,57.17)
Established in yoga, O Dhanañjaya, perform actions while abandoning attachment;
if you are free from attachment and act as duties come to you, you will not be bound.
Having become one whose body is the peaceful Brahman, perform action that is permeated by Brahman.

With your conduct dedicated to Brahman, you shall become Brahman itself in an instant. With all your purposes dedicated to the Lord, with your self as the Lord, free from affliction, become the Lord— the Self of all beings— who adorns the surface of the earth.
Having renounced all volitions, equanimous, with a tranquil mind, a sage whose self is united through the yoga of renunciation— performing [actions], be one whose intellect is liberated. Arjuna:

O Blessed One, O All-pervading Lord, what is the distinction between the renunciation of attachment, the offering to Brahman, and the renunciation consisting of dedication to the Lord; and likewise, O Master, what is the distinction between knowledge and yoga?
"Tell me this in due order, which brings an end to great delusion.
The Blessed One replied:
"When all conceptual constructions have completely subsided, there is an exclusively intense awareness."
That which has the form of the meditation on "nothing whatsoever" (nakiñcid-bhāvanā), the wise know that to be the supreme Brahman.
Those of perfected intellect know the exertion toward that [Brahman] to be both knowledge and yoga;
they know the offering of all the world and the self as being Brahman—that is, *brahmārpaṇa*.

Empty within and empty without, resembling a heart of stone, it is tranquil and as clear as the expanse of space; it is neither non-existent nor merely a stone. Then, there arises a slight emergence, a subtle arising of something other.

This appearance of the world is as empty as space. This notion that "I am a part" has arisen individually within consciousness; since it is divided into millions upon millions of parts, what kind of grasping can there be toward it?

When the diversity of conceptual constructions flashes forth within that whose essence is pure consciousness— though it is not diverse despite its manifold variety— why do you still cling to [the notion of] oneness even in that single reality?
This [consciousness], though non-differentiated, stands as if it were differentiated.
The year is distinct and boundless; one realizes, "I am not [that].

(MU 6.57.30) Just as there is an "I" here, so too is there a pot and so forth here, and a monkey is here; space is likewise here, as are water and the like—why then this grasping at "I-ness"? (MU 6.57.31)
Thus, the complete destruction of duality through the knowledge of non-distinction—
that renunciation of the web of mental constructs is called non-attachment.
It is the contemplation of the oneness of the Lord regarding the entire web of conceptual constructions.
This very state, in which the appearance of duality has dissolved, is the offering to the Lord.
Due to non-difference, even the distinction among these resides only nominally within the conscious Self;
the entire world, as the referent of all words, is the one essence of consciousness—of this there is no doubt.
I am hope, I am the world, I am the sky, and I am action;
I am time, I am non-duality, I am duality, and I am the universe.
Fix your mind on me, be my devotee, sacrifice to me, and bow down to me.
"Thus, with your mind fixed on Me as your supreme goal, you shall come to Me alone, realizing Me as the Self.
Arjuna said:
"O Lord of gods, You have two forms: the higher and indeed the lower."
"What kind of form is that, and when shall I abide by resorting to it for the sake of perfection?
The Blessed One replied:
"O sinless one, know my two forms: the common and the supreme."
The universal form endowed with hands and other limbs, bearing the conch, discus, and mace—
this supreme form of mine, which is without beginning or end, unique, and free from affliction,
is expressed by such terms as Brahman, Ātman, and Paramātman.
As long as you remain unawakened, dwelling in the ignorance of selflessness,
so long remain devoted to the worship of the four-armed deity.
Once you have become fully awakened through that sequence, you will then know that supreme reality.
My form is without beginning or end, by which you shall not be born again.
Or, O crusher of enemies, if you have known me as the object of knowledge,
then quickly take refuge in that Self of mine, which is the very Self of your own self.
"That which I declare as 'this am I' and 'that am I'—that is this very reality of the Self; I shall explain it fully to you again and again.
"I consider you awakened, O virtuous one; you have found rest in the supreme state."
You are liberated from all mental constructs; become one whose sole essence is truth.
With your self united through yoga, behold the Self abiding in all beings and all beings within the Self, seeing with equanimity everywhere.
He who, established in unity, worships the Self residing in all beings—
regardless of how he conducts himself— is not born again.
Unity is the meaning of the word "all," and the meaning of the word "one" is selfhood.
That which is neither existent nor non-existent, and by which one quickly attains that state— that is the Real (Sat).
That light born of illumination which exists within the minds of those belonging to the three worlds, having ascended to the level of direct experience— this is the certainty that "this is the Self."
O Bhārata, that experience of taste which exists within the waters of the three worlds— both those produced from cows and those born of the ocean— that very one am I, the Self.
And that subtle experience which exists within all bodies, that too am I.
Liberated from that which is to be experienced, I am this very Self, all-pervading.
Just as clarified butter resides within all milk,
so does the Supreme abide within all objects and bodies.
Just as light exists within and without all the jewels of the oceans, so do I abide within bodies, though appearing as if not abiding there at all;
just as space exists within and without thousands of jars.
In that same way, I abide as the Self within the bodies of the three worlds;
just as a thread is the body that strings together hundreds of pearls, so do I stand as the unperceived Self within hundreds of thousands of bodies.
In this multitude of objects, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass,
that which is the universal existence (sattāsāmānya) is known as the unborn Self;
that very Brahman, appearing with a slightly manifest form, remains as Brahman alone.
Through the delusive process of "I-ness" and so forth, and "the world" and so forth, this very Self appears in the form of the world; what is it here that is killed or kills?
O Arjuna, how can this [Self] be tainted by the auspicious or inauspicious sufferings of the world?
He who sees that which does not perish when things perish— standing like a witness, impartial as in reflections in a mirror— he truly sees.
"This is I" and "this is I"— thus is this spoken by me.

Thus you are the Self, the Self of all; know me thus, O Pāṇḍava. All these transformations of creation and dissolution proceed from the conscious Self, which is its own cause and dwells within, like the movement of waves in the ocean.
Just as there is the nature of stone in mountains, the nature of wood in trees,
and the nature of water in waves, so too is the Selfhood of all things.
[One should see] the Self abiding in all beings, and all beings in the Self.
He who perceives the Self in that way as the non-agent, he truly sees.
O Arjuna, just as water remains the same amidst waves of various forms and transformations, or as gold remains the same in bracelets and other ornaments, so does the Self abide within all beings.
Just as various moving masses of waves exist in water,
or as bracelets and other ornaments exist in gold, so do the elements exist within the Self;
O Bhārata, the entire collection of objects, beginning with the elements, is the Great Brahman.
Know that which is entirely one to be present everywhere, not even slightly divided.
What object of change among the modifications of existence is there to be found in the three worlds?
Where are they, or where is this world? Why do you delude yourself in vain?
Having heard this, having understood it within, and having cultivated it with firm certainty,
the virtuous who are liberated while living move about here with minds whose essence is the equality of all things;
free from pride and delusion, having overcome the fault of attachment, they have turned away from desire through the knowledge of the supreme self.
Freed from the dualities consisting of the notions of pleasure and pain, those who are undeluded go to that imperishable state.
The fifty-eighth chapter, titled "Instruction to Arjuna."
The Blessed One said:
Listen once more, O mighty-armed one, to my supreme word,
which I shall speak to you, who are delighted by it, out of a desire for your welfare.
But the contacts of the senses with their objects, O son of Kuntī, which bestow cold, heat, pleasure, and pain, are fleeting and impermanent; endure them, O Bhārata.
For they do not belong to the Self alone, nor to anything else; where, then, is suffering, and where is pleasure?

In that supreme Self, which is without beginning or end and without parts, how could there be filling or fragmentation? Yet, within this infinite one, the constituent part known as "mere touch" (sparśamātrā) is established, just as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold, despite the latter having no prior configuration.
For he whom these contacts of the senses— which are illusory in nature— do not disturb, that steadfast man, equal in pleasure and pain, is fit for immortality.
Because the Self is all-pervading, however, these [contacts] appear as if they were established [within it].
But since they are of the nature of non-existence, how can that which is of the nature of non-existence not be endured?
Even in the slightest degree, pleasure and pain do not exist in that which is all-pervading;
since the reality of the Self is omnipresent, how could these two possibly have existence?
The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being;
pleasure, pain, and the like do not exist at all, for the all-pervading Supreme Self alone exists.
Having abandoned the notions of existence and non-existence regarding these two—the world and the Self—[one attains liberation].
Having abandoned both "nothingness" and the "middle," remain with your feet firmly planted in what remains.
O Arjuna, the self does not rejoice in pleasure nor does it languish in sorrows;
for the conscious self, even while situated within the body, is like a stone.
The insentient mind and so forth, having attained the state of a body, are the vessel of suffering;
yet when this [body] is wounded or perishes, there is not the slightest injury to the Self.
As for the insentient body and so forth, it is established that they are the experiencer of suffering and the like.
Therefore, my dear, know that this very delusion of illusion arises from the power of ignorance.
Nothing at all—neither the body and so forth, nor suffering and so forth—exists as something separate from the Self; for what could be experienced by whom? MU 6.58.12–13.
That which I am speaking of here— by that, O Bhārata, this delusion of yours, which arises from a difficult-to-comprehend [ignorance], shall perish through right awakening,
just as the fear of a snake in a rope perishes through knowledge when it was born of ignorance.
Likewise, the body and so forth, as well as suffering and so forth, perish when understood, for they are born of non-understanding.
But the unborn Brahman, which is the all-pervading universe, neither perishes nor is born;
know this to be the supreme truth—this indeed is the highest understanding.
You are a wave in the ocean of Brahman; having become something slight, you dissolve.
Today you quiver within the whirlpool of Brahman; you are indeed Brahman itself, free from all affliction.
The world, time, action, space, you, I, and the soldiers—all these are you.
In Brahman alone is there such vibration; herein the sequences of existence and non-existence do not abide.
Abandon pride, intoxication, grief, fear, envy, and pleasure and pain.
This duality is of the nature of the unreal; become one who possesses the nature of the Real.
Through the destruction of millions of human akṣauhiṇīs, by means of your experiencing self,
make the battle— which has been expanded by Brahmā— a Brahman, consisting of Brahman.
Remaining indifferent to pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat.
O Bhārata, attain oneness with the Brahman of battle;
becoming equal in gain and loss, and truly possessing nothing,
act with the natural spontaneity of a dull-witted man or like the wind that moves.
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give,
and whatever you shall do, O son of Kuntī— be firm in the conviction that all this is the Self.
Whatever one is inwardly composed of, that one undoubtedly attains.

To attain the truth of Brahman, become one who is composed of the truth of Brahman. Having become Brahman and disregarding the fruit, the knower of Brahman performs action exactly as it comes, solely because it is Brahman that has been contemplated.
He who perceives inaction in action, and action in inaction, he is wise among men; he is called a doer of all actions.
Let not the fruit of action be your motive, nor let there be attachment to inaction.
Established in yoga, O Dhanañjaya, perform actions while abandoning attachment;
do not rely on attachment to action, nor likewise rely on delusion,
nor even rely on inaction— remain poised in equanimity as you are situated.
Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever-contented and independent, even though fully engaged in action, he does nothing at all.
They say that attachment constitutes agency; therefore, even for one who is not the agent, that [agency] may exist.
Since foolishness resides in the mind, one should therefore abandon that foolishness.
By resorting to supreme knowledge of reality, no sense of agency arises at all in the high-souled one who is free from attachment,
even though he is engaged in all activities.
Because there is no agency, there is no enjoyership; because there is no enjoyership, there is equality and oneness.
From equality and oneness comes infinity, and from that, the pervasive state of Brahman is attained.
Having completely abandoned the sense of manifoldness, one reaches oneness with the Supreme Self.
Even while performing both action and non-action, you are not the doer, O Arjuna.
Those wise ones call him a sage whose every undertakings are free from desire and purposeful resolve, and whose actions have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge.
He who remains even-minded, gentle, firm, self-abiding, tranquil, and free from longing for any object— even when intensely agitated, he has attained a state of complete composure.
Free from the pairs of opposites, eternally established in purity, indifferent to acquisition and preservation, he is possessed of the Self.

And follow what you have attained, O you who adorn the surface of the earth! He who sits restraining his organs of action but continues to dwell upon the objects of the senses with his mind, being deluded in soul, is called a hypocrite.
But he who, O Arjuna, having restrained the senses with the mind,
engages in the yoga of action through the organs of action while remaining unattached— he is preeminent.
Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in stillness;
In the same way, he into whom all desires enter attains peace, but not the seeker of desires.
The Arjunopākhyāna, titled "Instruction on the Knowledge of the Self," is the fifty-ninth canto.
The Blessed One said:
One should not practice the renunciation of enjoyments, nor should one practice the cultivation of enjoyments;
one should remain perfectly equanimous, following exactly what has been obtained.
Do not conceive of a self in the body, which is non-self; do not conceive of a self in worldly existence, which is itself the self.
Instead, conceive of the self as the true self, whose nature is non-existence.
O mighty-armed one, upon the destruction of the body, nothing at all is destroyed.
For if there were destruction of the self, then destruction would occur; yet the self is never destroyed anywhere.
They know the self to be indestructible, without beginning or end, and undecaying.
Let it not be a source of excessive suffering for you that the notion "the self is destroyed" is difficult to comprehend.
Those supreme ones who have realized the Self are never destroyed;
for those who have not realized the Self are destroyed, as they falsely imagine the non-Self to be the Self.
Arjuna said:
"If this is so, O Lord of the World, O giver of honor even to the foolish,
then I consider that when the destruction of the body occurs, nothing at all has been lost.
The Blessed One said:
In the very same way, O mighty-armed one, nothing whatsoever perishes anywhere.
Only the Self exists, its nature being indestructible; what of it could perish, and where?
This notion that "this has perished" or "this is joined [to the world]" arises from nothing but delusion and error.
I do not see anything else in this way, such as the son of a barren woman.
There is no coming into being for the non-existent, nor is there non-existence for the existent;
the limit of both has been perceived by those who see the truth.
But know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded;
no one is able to effect the destruction of this imperishable.
These bodies are said to have an end, but they belong to the eternal embodied self.
It is indestructible and immeasurable; therefore, fight, O Bhārata!
(6.59.11) The Self alone exists; there is no duality. How can there be the arising of the non-existent?
It is imperishable and infinite; for the existent, destruction does not exist. (6.59.12)
"When duality and unity are both abandoned, that which remains as the residue—
the peaceful middle between being and non-being— that is the supreme state here.
Arjuna said:
"O Blessed One, since I am dead, what is the nature of the existence of men in this world?
And how, O Lord, do heaven and hell exist for people while they remain in this world?
The Blessed One replied:
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, and intellect— this living soul (jīva), whose self is born from these subtle elements (tanmātra), dwells within bodies.
It is dragged along by latent impressions (vāsanā), like a young animal by a rope.
It remains within the body like a bird in a cage.
By the power of time, when the body has reached a state of decay,
it departs due to the force of its latent impressions (vāsanā), just as sap flows out from the leaves of a tree.
Having taken hold of these— the ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and the nose—
it departs just as the wind carries fragrances from their source.
Its possession of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) alone constitutes its "body," and not anything else produced by logical reasoning.
When latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are abandoned, they are destroyed; when they are destroyed, that state [of liberation] is attained.
Previously, one possessed of latent impressions becomes nourished by them and wanders through various wombs;
the individual soul (*jīva*), having the form of a mass of delusion, is like a person created by *māyā*.

Under the influence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the living soul (*jīva*) departs from the body, taking with it all the sense-faculties along with their inherent natures, just as the wind carries fragrances away from a flower.
O son of Kuntī, when the living soul has departed, the body becomes motionless.
With its limbs motionless and its expansion stilled like a tree in a calm wind, the body—
devoid of movement and invisible due to defects such as cutting or piercing—
is said in the world to be "dead" when it is bereft of life.
Wherever that living soul, whose form is breath, abides in space,
there it perceives an expansive form through the habitual force of its own latent impressions (vāsanā).
For this body, though non-existent, is perceived by the living soul.
Upon its destruction, he likewise quickly perceives another [world] just like a dream. Just as he perceives their forms, so too does he perceive their destruction;
for indeed, at the beginning of creation, he was thus fully manifested through his own mental cultivation.

At the moment of sudden emergence, whatever appears before one remains until final liberation; for this consciousness, that very appearance is inseparable from it. The prior web of latent impressions is overcome by human effort.
Just as today’s effort quickly [overcomes] yesterday’s effort through present exertion,
so too that very moment of the preceding and succeeding eye-blinks, when perceived by a powerful human effort, clearly triumphs.
Even if the cosmic egg were to burst asunder or the wind of universal dissolution were to blow,
a wise person must not abandon human effort in accordance with the scriptures;
for the creation of hell, heaven, and so forth occurs entirely through the power of latent impressions (vāsanā).
The living being, whose intellect is clouded by ancient delusion, perceives that which has been practiced for a long time.
Arjuna said:
O Lord of the World, amidst the bewildering cycles of creation such as hell and heaven, [the soul remains bound].
"Tell me, what is the cause of this individual soul's birth and existence?
The Blessed One replied:
"Know that this individual soul, consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is merely a small body."

Its very existence, consisting of its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is the cause of cyclic existence (*saṃsṛti*). Cyclic existence persists only as long as the latent impression vibrates; therefore, since it is like a dream, the destruction of latent impressions leads to the highest good in this world.

Arjuna: O Lord of the gods, from what does this mature latent impression (*vāsanā*) arise— which, through the force of long-standing habit, causes the delusion of transmigratory existence— and how is it destroyed?
The Blessed One said:
O virtuous one, from the height of the delusion of ignorance, through the cultivation of the notion of a self in that which is not-self,
and due to the lack of knowledge regarding the self, latent impressions come into being.
O son of Kuntī, you have cultivated the self and have realized the truth.
Abandon the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) such as "this is he," "I am this," "these are people," and "these are mine.
When the latent impressions dissolve, the individual soul (*jīva*) dissolves of its own accord.
For whatever is swollen by the existence of something else dissolves upon the destruction of that thing.
When the body has reached dissolution due to the alteration of place and time,
what [entity] remains to serve as the vessel for birth and death?
O Mahāmati, know that very thing which is the turbid form of the self, consisting of its own imagined conceptualizations, to be the *jīva* characterized by latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
That which is the immutable form of the self, independent and free from conceptualization, [is the true nature].
Know that to be liberation, O Bhārata, which is free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) due to awakening.
Even while living, O mighty-armed one, having perceived reality as it truly exists and being released from the snare of latent impressions, one is designated as "liberated."
He who is not free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is surely not one who is devoted to all dharmas;
even if he were omniscient, he would be bound on all sides like a bird in a cage.
Even for one whose internal impressions do not flicker, though they may be subtle like a peacock feather in the sky that is difficult to see—*Muṇḍakopaniṣad* 6.59.43.
For he alone becomes liberated here; indeed, for the sinless one, latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are bondage, and their destruction alone is liberation.
The Sixtieth Chapter, titled "The Determination of the State of Being Alive," from the *Arjunopākhyāna*.
The Blessed One said:
"Thus, through the state of being free from latent impressions and liberated while living,
having attained inner coolness within yourself, completely abandon the sorrow for your kinsmen."
Free from fear of old age and death, with a mind as clear as space, having abandoned all thoughts of the desirable and the undesirable, you are free from passion, O sinless one.
This task has come upon you by the force of circumstance; perform it just as it has arrived.
Perform your duty without dejection; nothing here is lost.

For that which is performed as one's own duty, having fallen into the natural flow of events, is the very nature of one liberated while living; otherwise, it is the state of one not yet liberated while living.
"I shall abandon this action" and "I shall resort to this"—such is the nature of the mind of the deluded person, which is not stainless; but the mind of the wise person remains in equanimity.
Those whose minds are peaceful perform their duties as they arise in the flow of events.
Liberated while living, they remain in a state like deep sleep yet manifest as if half-awake;
by their very nature, the senses of the knower withdraw from the objects of the senses into the heart, attaining a steady dissolution like the limbs of a tortoise.
The universe, woven from the existent and the non-existent, stands like a garland upon the vast and firm thread of pure consciousness alone—upon that Viśvakarman whose very limbs are the universe.
When this thread is extended, the universe expands; when it is withdrawn, it vanishes from view.
Upon the canopy of consciousness, there exists a manifold web of diverse arrangements;
though non-different from it, it appears as if different, like a formless body within its own limbs.
This world stands as a variegated picture upon consciousness, like a painting on a ceiling-canvas.

Just as a painting, once completed, remains as the work of the painter, so too does the entire universe— both that which has arisen and that which has not— abide within the Self. Just as the painting to be executed flashes forth in the consciousness of the painter, [so does the world appear within the Self].
In the same way, the painter of the mind creates the picture of the three worlds— comprising the universe, existing within the Universal Self, and arising through the three periods of time—
without a wall, even though it is of the nature of space, yet clearly manifest with its various modes of existence within that very space.
First, a manifold and variegated painting was spread out by the painter that is the mind;
afterwards, a wall was made of the nature of space—oh, what a delusion!
Indeed, this is an unprecedented and supreme illusion, wherein both the sky and the wall [are one].

There is not even the slightest difference between these two, though they are clearly perceived. O lotus-eyed one, know that these walls which appear to be produced by the mind’s painting are, in truth, the emptiness of space itself.
Just as the destruction and arising of the world appear in the mind in an instant,
so too this world— both external and internal— is the void-self, a mere sky. Indeed,
truthfulness resides only in this long-standing kingdom of the imagination.

How could it be true even when illuminated? There is no such thing as an error that persists once it has been seen through. What is seen through delusion dissolves upon being illuminated, becoming as thin as a cloud in the sky during autumn.
The various figures painted by the artist-mind reside within the mind; like these painted dolls, the external triple world and so forth lack a foundation, as there is no wall [to support them].
These do not exist, nor do you exist; what is obstructed by what?
Having abandoned the delusion regarding the obstructed and the obstructor, become as pure as space.
What activity can there be for space? And activity itself is of the nature of space;
therefore, time, action, walls, parts, and so forth, are the pure sky.
Just as a painting residing in the mind, though appearing as a real form, is essentially of the nature of space and is more empty than the sky itself— know this entire world to be just so.
That painting which has been created upon the wall of the mind by the painter that is consciousness, [is likewise empty].

Everything is not in the slightest different from emptiness, which is like space. Know this, O friend: just as the manifestation and dissolution of the world appear within the mind, so too do these two occur in an instant as if they were situated outside.
In the kingdom of the mind during the first moment— named for its various worlds—
arising in an instant, the state of being an eon was imagined through delusion.
Just as the mind is capable of creating a kingdom of the mind that is utterly non-existent, so too is it capable of imagining such things.
In the same way, the powerful mind can transform a moment into an eon;
it turns a moment into an eon, makes the small great,
and quickly turns the non-existent into the existent— thus has this delusion arisen.
For a moment, an initial mental construction appeared by its own nature;
that which is of such a variegated character stands as this web of the world.
Since its ultimate state is nirvāṇa, this creation has arisen in the blink of an eye.

The essence of the vajra is here imagined merely through the power of creative intuition (pratibhā). This variegated world-picture, painted by the mind, exists within consciousness; though it has no wall and is not rich in colors, it stands manifest before us as if expansive.
Oh, how wonderful! This painting, though without a wall, has arisen brilliantly;
it is the world, beautifully colored, standing as a delight for the eyes. It is streaked with the ink of manifold darkness and colored by the various rays of light.
It possesses various limbs marked by stains, is colored by various passions,
is rich in the play of various views, and has eyes that experience various perceptions;
it has a formidable arrangement of various clouds and displays various forms, both foremost and last.
The sky is a blue lake where the stars and the sun and moon are blooming lotuses,
and the rows of clouds are clusters of leaves engaged in various arrangements;
within its own chambers, it depicts the gods, asuras, humans, and women.
This wall of space, white as a *akkola* flower, is the supreme light;

within this very space, the deluded puppet of the three worlds—charming to all—is fashioned by the painter of the flickering mind. This single-act performance is colored by the face of pure consciousness alone, and it is filled with playful activity.
Her creeper-like limbs are of gold, her mass of hair is thick, and she gazes upon the world by moving her eyes like the sun and moon;
she is clothed in the scriptures that govern the triad of dharma, artha, and kāma; the earth is her high hips and the netherworld her feet;
fierce with the four arms of Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, and Hari, she has truth and falsehood as her lofty breasts and the quarters of the sky as her slender body.
She whose belly is the great world, with its mountains serving as the petals of the lotus-seat upon the earth encircled by the ocean-mechanism;

she whose face is the night, flickering with the darkness of her eyebrows and the high laughter of her stars, while her rows of teeth are the formidable planets and her bristling hair is the host of the fourteen kinds of restless spirits; she who possesses the multitude of conch-shells that are the thundering clouds of the dissolution.

The three worlds, endowed with living beings, fashioned out of space itself— variegated, of the nature of the void, and created by the long-unseen extraordinary Artist— the mind, skilled in the art of painting, as a choice doll adorned with manifold graces.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Description of the World as a Painting."
The Sixty-first Sarga.
The Blessed One said:
"Know this, O Arjuna, for it is indeed a great marvel here that—"
First the variegated painting arises, and only afterwards does the wall appear.
When the painting appears without a wall, the vast wall is seen;
oh, how wondrous is this illusion! The stone has sunk, yet the gourd has floated.

In the three worlds, which are like a painting situated within the mind and whose nature is space, how can this "I-ness" arise as something having the nature of space within you, whose very self is space?
The space of creation is fashioned by space; in space, space dissolves back into space.

The void is experienced within the void; the void is spread throughout the void. That which is the long rope of saṃsāra, entwined with the cord of latent impressions (vāsanā), is unwound here, O Arjuna, by the very unraveling of those impressions.
Just as a reflection appears in a mirror, so does this [world] appear within Brahman itself;
it is inaccessible to cutting, piercing, and the like, because of its non-difference from its substratum.
Cutting, piercing, and so forth do not exist apart from Brahman, and Brahman is like space.
What, how, whose, and by what is this cut; or where is it split?
Brahmanhood shines like water within the flood of Brahman, as water within water;
it abides as perfectly equal, stainless as the sky, and peaceful within the Self.
Therefore, the relationship between the infused and the infuser does not differ even in the slightest;

thus, for you, the state of being free from latent impressions (avāsanībhāva) is indeed perfected through awakening. He who is not free from latent impressions is certainly not one who is devoted to all dharmas.
Even one who is omniscient may have his self bound, and even an ascetic may possess passion;
for him in whose seed of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) exists even a very small portion remaining on the ground of consciousness,
the vast forest of transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*) arises once again.
The seed of latent impressions, once scorched by the fire of the awakening to truth that has taken root in the heart through practice, does not sprout again.
But when the seed of latent impressions is burnt, it no longer sinks into objective things.
Pure amidst pleasure, pain, and the rest, like a gourd leaf upon water;
you have become one whose self is tranquil, free from the disease of worldly existence, liberated, with the great delusion of the mind shattered.
Having understood that purifying sacred learning through right knowledge, remain as the activity of the Self alone, in the form of singular peace.
The sixty-second canto, titled "Arjuna’s Rest":
Arjuna said:
"Delusion has been destroyed and memory regained by me through Your grace, O Acyuta.
I stand firm, my doubts dispelled; I shall do as You command.
The Blessed One said:
If the mental fluctuations have clearly subsided within the heart through awakening,
know that this mind has quickly become tranquil and attained the state of pure being (sattva).
In this state, it is devoid of the object "that" (the perceived), and is named the inward-facing consciousness (pratyak-cetana).
That reality which is remaining, liberated from everything, and entirely free from all things—
that state no afflictions of the world can disturb,
just as birds soaring in the sky cannot be troubled by the earth below.
Know this Self here to be inwardly conscious, appearing as pure and devoid of volition, inaccessible to those of defiled vision;
for one who stands in the state transcending all and is purified by consciousness, there is no latent impression (vāsanā).
The vision of ordinary people is unable to perceive that state, just as the eye cannot see a serpent.
When all these things, such as pots and cloths, have ceased upon its attainment,
what can poor latent impression (*vāsanā*) do there in the supreme state?
Just as a trace of snow dissolves upon reaching the Fire-Mountain (Avalokiteśvara),

so too does ignorance dissolve upon attaining the pure reality of the mind (cittattva). Where, then, is that wretched, trivial latent impression of passion (rajas) which binds one to worldly enjoyment?
As long as this ignorance, which undergoes various transformations of form, continues to throb— filling the entire web of the world like the vast wind of the principle of consciousness (cittattva)—
so long will it persist until this pure Self is fully realized by the self through itself.
All perceptions of the visible have ceased; pure reality alone has arisen, pervasive like the sky within that state of one's own self which fulfills all things.
That [reality] possesses every form, yet it is devoid of every form.
By what name indeed can that supreme reality, which transcends speech, be compared? Therefore,

having skillfully cast off the latent impression of the ego's persistence— which is like a cholera-like affliction caused by the poison of sense-objects— through the method of striving to abandon all that is desired, become free from disease, the very embodiment of the sole Lord of the world.
Vasiṣṭha:
When the Lord of the Three Worlds had spoken thus and remained silent for a moment before him,
then the son of Pāṇḍu will offer his words there, like a bee approaching a cluster of dark lotuses.
Arjuna: O Blessed One, through your word, this mind of mine has attained the supreme state, with all states of sorrow completely dissolved,
like a lotus-pond awakened by the sun, the lord of the world.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, Arjuna, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow who has Hari as his charioteer, will rise up and, free from doubt, perform the sport of battle.
He will turn the earth into a land where great rivers of blood flow swiftly from wounded elephants, horses, and charioteers;
he will shroud the sky—the eye of which is the sun—with a circular mass of clouds consisting of the spreading flight of his arrows.
The chapter named "Arjuna’s Rest" is concluded; the *Arjunopākhyāna* is finished.
The sixty-third canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having firmly grasped this vision which destroys the sins of the descendants of Raghu,
"Abide in that which consists of disinterested renunciation and the offering to Brahman.
Know that Self to be the Supreme, in whom is all, from whom is all, who is all, and who is everywhere; who is eternally composed of all."
Though situated at a distance, you are not distant; you are all-pervading and indeed your very self.
Abiding in that, you attain its nature; that alone is undoubtedly yours.
That which is stainless consciousness, entirely free from any object of cognition—[that is you].
Know that the appearance of consciousness, which is liberated from the object of thought, is the supreme state.
It is the highest goal beyond the high; it is the unsurpassed vision among all visions.
It is the greatness of all greatnesses, and it is the teacher of teachers, the greatest of gurus.
That is the Self, and that is consciousness; that is the void, that is Brahman, that is the supreme.
That is the highest good, that is Śiva, that is the peaceful; that is knowledge, the ultimate state.
This which is the inner conscious self, whose nature is the experience of all.
In whom all things find their relish through their own existence—He is the soul of the world, like oil in sesame seeds; He is the lamp of the house of the world;
He is the sap of the tree of the world; He is the protector of the cattle of the world.
He is the thread upon which the pearls of all beings are strung, the vast sky of the heart;
he is the pervasive, supreme pungency of the mass of all elemental peppers.
He is the substantiality in every object, and he is the emptiness of that which has no substance.
He is the existence of what exists and the non-existence of what does not exist;
He is the lamp for the house, its activities, and its vessels and utensils of the world.
By His light, which is like that of the moon, the sun, and the stars, this universe is made manifest.
Everything has emanated from this conscious Supreme Self;
by means of inquiry into one's own self-awareness, this very Self is attained by oneself.
All the states of the world are charming only so long as they are not subjected to inquiry.
Non-existent in reality and crumbling under scrutiny—
having first become what [I am], to whom in this web of the world, which consists of a mass of false delusions, do I cling, and how can I maintain such an unreal resolve?
"I am the beginningless and endless space of Brahman, amidst the mental constructions, volitions, and imaginings of beginning, middle, and end; what limit can there be to my self?"—
one who possesses such internal certainty, yet engages in ordinary worldly conduct externally.
Free from rising and setting, he remains infinite at all times. That equanimity which abides in perfect balance neither sets nor rises;
he whose emptiness is like that of space is the Great-Souled One, possessed of the true form in this world.

One who has ascended to the state of non-duality of existence, with an intellect as profound as deep sleep, does not experience agitation of the heart even while engaged in worldly activity, just like the person in a mirror. Indeed,
even for one who is active in the world, it is like the case of the person in a mirror.
He whose heart experiences even the slightest agitation does not possess liberation.
Only when non-differentiation is realized is it reflected in the jewel of the knower; due to the supreme purity of consciousness, worldly activity proceeds just as it came.
This very wonder of consciousness (*cic-camatkṛti*) alone appears as the world;
here there is neither unity nor duality, and even the teaching is composed of that.
Through its own wonders, it manifests as the signified and the signifier, the disciple, the inquiry, and the teacher.
Within the self by the self, consciousness, being already tranquil, performs its wonder within consciousness.
For the vibration of consciousness is transmigratory existence, while its lack of vibration is the supreme state;
by the calming of the vibration of consciousness, this cycle of birth and death comes to rest.

That which is the cessation of non-contemplation— the state of being devoid of any portion of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*)— within the Great Consciousness (*mahāciti*), though appearing as if non-existent by its own nature, is called the vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*).
That which is emptiness (*śūnyatva*) yet not insentient is said to be the supreme body of consciousness.
The non-contemplation of the meaning of "not" that occurs here is what is experienced as saṃsāra;
and that, consisting of a mere dissolution into non-existence, is essentially devoid of substance.
Only the state of absolute oneness (kevalībhāva), which is one's own true nature, remains.
The wise know that the very vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*) is what sets the wheel of saṃsāra in motion;
it is like bracelets and other ornaments being nothing but gold.
There is no vibration of consciousness separate from consciousness itself that could constitute transmigratory existence.
The vibration of consciousness is nothing other than consciousness itself; for it is the lack of awareness of that [consciousness] which is transmigratory existence.
This vibration of consciousness is merely a lack of awareness, arising like the state of being a bracelet [out of gold].
When this [lack of awareness] dissolves through mere awareness, pure conscious-gold remains.
By the mere realization of truth, the inclination toward enjoyment perishes;
indeed, the absence of such inclination is here the supreme characteristic of one who possesses knowledge. All these objects of enjoyment are by their very nature undesirable to the knower.
For who is ever satiated? Indeed, one craves even bad food.
Know this alone to be the supreme characteristic of true knowledge:
that there is, by its very nature, no longing for enjoyments whatsoever.
The certainty that consciousness alone exists, which is the undifferentiated vibration of all things and whose nature is the Self of all,
is what is remembered by the term "knowledge" when it has taken firm root within through one's own practice.
He who is not wise does not truly enjoy even the objects of enjoyment while they are being experienced.
To achieve success in accordance with worldly conventions, he strikes at the sky with clubs.
Without artificial means, success is not attained—
whether regarding the self or the world— even by the crushing of one's own limbs.

As long as this unrealized self, whose nature is vibration, pulsates in the form of movement, it perceives the delusion situated at the limit of the "citta" (the thinking mind) and the "acitta" (the non-thinking).
However, upon the arising of perfect awakening, its successive stages of vibration and non-vibration [come to an end].
As if departing somewhere, like an extinguished lamp, those [mental constructs] along with their designations vanish;
for the lamp of consciousness, whose nature is light,
there is not even the slightest talk here of movement or stillness by its very essence.

That form which belongs to the motionless [Self]— which neither was, nor is not, nor is intermediate, like the wind— is precisely that which, when its vibration is stilled, is characterized by the state of pure consciousness.
The vibration of this Consciousness is non-different from it, bearing the nature of the essence of pure Consciousness.
If consciousness, abiding solely in the self,
does not experience the realization of the meaning of the negation— as if it were in nirvāṇa— then even the name of the categories of bondage and liberation does not exist.
The thought "let there be liberation" is itself a bond; internal fullness is the cause of its destruction.
Even the thought "let it not be" is a bond for you; non-perception is the supreme good.
Know that which is without appearance and non-inert to be the supreme state.
The abiding state of the nature of the intellect (citta), which consists in being oriented toward the unobjectifiable,
is that vibration of the Great Consciousness (mahācit) whose essence is the conceptualization of words and objects;
this [vibration], which is subject to bondage, liberation, and so forth, subsides when it is scrutinized.
When the ego-sense (*ahambhāva*) has been completely stilled by mere observation and is left without a support,

we do not know by whom, what, or for whom one is bound or liberated. And if the conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*) itself is realized as non-different from consciousness (*citi*), [then there is no bondage].
Therefore, all that has arisen is without volition and without vibration, being unrestrained.
Because it is always of the nature of consciousness (*cit*), even while there is vibration, it is grasped by consciousness through its very lack of vibration;
thus, when one abides in the motionless mass of consciousness, saṃsāra is utterly destroyed.

In the awakened state, the vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*) is nothing other than the energy of consciousness itself; no vibration of consciousness remains apart from it. Thus, while traversing one dream within this long dream consisting of the visible world, one proceeds.
The Knower does not assume delusion, because his own consciousness is all-pervading;
that from which the existence of all consciousnesses incessantly and forcefully arises, in which all these chisels of manifold mental constructions strike,
and wherein all perceptions arise as something delightful to experience— realize that inner Self through meditation.
End: Chapter Sixty-four, titled "The Realization of the Inner Self."
Vasiṣṭha said:
They call this the supreme reality; know this as the highest state.
I know this as the one alone; this alone exists, and nothing else.
This very inner Self, which is the single mirror for all beings—
from this the world has arisen, as a tree from a seed—
having set aside the intellect, ego, mind, and so forth, which are insentient by nature.
Know that to be the supreme state where the experiencer comes to an end.
That which is pure experience alone, devoid of mind, intellect, and the rest, the auspicious one designated as Great Consciousness— that is this supreme state.
Abiding therein, these great forms— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others—
shine forth intensely with their manifold powers (vibhūtis), like subjects under a gratified king;
they sport for a long time in pastimes such as traveling through the sky and so forth.
By the very people dwelling therein, it is like heaven for the inhabitants of heaven.
Having attained that, my dear, one does not die; having attained that, my dear, one does not grieve.
Having attained that, my dear, one does not decay; having attained that, my dear, one is not bound.
If even a slight perception of the nature of pure existence (sattāsāmānya) of the Supreme Self— which is of the form of the boundless, ultimate space—
is cultivated, then in a mere moment, that living being becomes a sage whose mind is liberated.
Performing the actions of saṃsāra, he does not suffer again.
Rāma said:
"That in which mind, intellect, and ego have reached their dissolution..."
"What is this manifestation that is called the universal existence (sattāsāmānya), and of what nature is it said to be?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"It is that Brahman which, residing within all bodies, eats, drinks, and moves about."
It takes up, it destroys, and it consumes that which is devoid of both consciousness and the object of consciousness;
all-pervading, free from beginning and end, established, and powerful— that is called here the universal essence of existence (*sattāsāmānya*), the reality of all things.
It exists as space within the sky, and it exists as sound within sound;
it exists as touch within touch, and it exists as the skin within the skin.
It is dissolved as taste within taste, and it exists as suchness within the tongue.
Form is seen as form, yet it is dissolved in the eye as sight;
it is seen as smell in the nose, and it arises as fragrance in the scent;
it is nourished as the body in the body, and likewise as the element in the earth.
It exists as liquidity in water, as airiness in air,
as heat in fire, and as the intellect in the intellect;
it exists as the mind within the mind, and as the ego-function in the ego-function.
Established in consciousness by means of consciousness, it has arisen as the nature of the intellect within the intellect;
it is fixed as "tree-ness" in a tree, situated as "cloth-ness" in cloth,
established as "jar-ness" in a jar, and situated as "banyan-ness" in a banyan tree.
In the stationary as stationariness, in the moving as movability;
in stone as stoneness, and in the conscious as consciousness;
among the immortals as immortality, and among men as humanity.
And as an animal among animals, as a worm in the state of a worm;
through time as time, and as a season within a season—
by means of this [power], the all-pervasive Lord abides as those very things within the divisions of time such as the *tuṭi*, the moment, and the blink of an eye.
In the white, it is born as whiteness; in the black, it exists as blackness.
It exists as vibration in actions, and as restraint in destiny.
It exists as stability in stability, and it exists as destruction in destruction.
The Supreme Lord is established in manifestation through the form of arising;
He rests in childhood by means of childhood, in youth by means of youth,
in old age by means of old age, and in death by means of death.
Thus, the Supreme Lord is non-different from all objects, just as the mass of water in the ocean is not different from its waves, spray, and ripples.
This diversity, however, is unreal; for it is indeed by means of this Reality that [the world] exists.

Just as a child imagines a ghost through the nature of its own consciousness, so too is this entire world imagined by you, who are established everywhere and free from affliction. Since all this is pervaded by me, whose form is consciousness itself,
and who— through various manifestations— both conceives and does not conceive of the self, remain at ease, O Great-Souled One, with a mind in which everything has been stilled.
Vālmīki:

When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
The sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Manifest Power," [spoken by] Rāma:
O Sage, just as for us the circle of dream-cities and towns exists,
so too does the assumption of bodies exist for Padmajā and the others;
and in that same way, all this has arisen as being composed of unreality.
"How did such a firm conviction arise within us?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"The Prajāpati of the previous creation appears just like our own creation."
The self that appears as one's own individual soul exists, but it is not real.
Because consciousness is all-pervading, the soul is everywhere and transmigrates everywhere;
yet that [transmigration] is unreal, arising from false perception, and it destroys right vision.
This manifestation of his, which has arisen of its own accord, appears like a dream;
it is the very self whose sole nature is the notion of "I," and it remains exceedingly firm.
Just as in a dream, a person does not perceive its momentary perishability, so too [this ego] persists.

In the same way, even by Brahmā, this [creation] is not perceived as such during the dream of creation. Whatever appearance of a dream may belong to this primordial Person (agrapuruṣa), that very same thing would be the nature of the creation consisting of Rāma, ourselves, and others.
Whatever is born from a dream-person is of the nature of that dream-person;
for it is experienced that whatever is the seed, such is the fruit—
know that to be unreal which is accomplished by means of the unreal.
Even if an object were capable, it is not logical to have attachment to its existence.
Since existence arises from the cultivation of the notion of being even when an object is non-existent,
one must therefore abandon the cultivation of the notion of what is unreal.
Just as that which arises from a person in a dream is perceived with firm conviction by one who possesses firm conviction,
so too is the creation and so forth within the Self perceived with firm conviction.
This dream of creation remains manifest for no more than the blink of an eye.
In that very instant, our state of being as creators was imagined.
Just as this vast expanse of a long dream arises for Prajāpati,
so too do the beginnings of all creations arise for every individual being.
Through the very existence of the reality of consciousness alone, successions of creations and dreams flash forth,
just as whirlpools and eddies manifest from the fluidity of water.
When this splendor of creation is of the nature of a dream and not real, [how can it be otherwise]?
"Does this come into being, or does it not?"—thus [the world] has gone to dissolution.
Whatever is seen in whatever manner and of whatever nature, it exists in that very way;
for the principles governing the delusions of dreams are not subject to logical questioning.
There is nothing in this world that cannot occur within delusion;
for diverse perceptions of reality are seen throughout the three worlds.
Just as fire burns in the midst of water, such as the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*) in the ocean.
Cities exist in the sky like the dwellings of the celestial beings;
lotuses grow upon rocks as trees do upon the Golden Mountain; and all flowers are found in a single place, just as they are on the wish-fulfilling tree.
The stones bear fruit like clusters of gems;
there are living beings within the stones, just as frogs are inside a rock.
Or, water issues from the stones, as from a moonstone.
In the blink of an eye, a jar becomes a cloth, like one under a curse;
they perceive even their own non-existence, just as in a dream one perceives one's own death,
or as water flowing downwards is seen flying through the sky when it is within a cloud.
Water stands in the sky like a canopy, just as the celestial river [flows];
large boulders fly up like winged mountains.
Indeed, everything is obtained from a stone, just as from a *cintāmaṇi* jewel.
Thoughts bear fruit quickly, like those within the celestial gardens;
yet those very same thoughts do not bear fruit quickly, O Raghava, like liberation and other such states.
Even one who is insentient performs action, like a mechanical man.
Such and other various bewildering undertakings,
impossible even for the playful illusions of Śambara or the Gandharvas, have been seen;
they arise from place, time, action, substances, jewels, and the curses of Śambara.

Infinite beings born of illusion and gandharvas arise from truth; yet here, even the non-arising of those who have arisen is admitted. The establishment of the aspects of both arising and non-arising are like the delusions of a dream.
There is nothing that is not real, and there is nothing that is not false;
everything, by everything, everywhere, within this creation called "the dream.
Just as a creature whose intellect is immersed in a dream perceives stability, so it is here.
One whose intellect is immersed in the dream of creation perceives stability in that same way.
Moving from one delusion to another, passing from one dream to another,
the living soul becomes utterly bewildered here, taking hold of the conviction that things are exceedingly stable.
Just as a bewildered deer, encountering the interior of a pit due to the fault of falling into it,
goes toward delusion consisting solely of the fall, so too does the living being, deluded by the fall into the cycle of existence (saṃsṛti).
This is the chapter titled "The Description of the World as a Dream."
The sixty-sixth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"In this regard, O Rāghava, I shall relate this ancient history; listen to it."
Regarding what occurred concerning a certain conceited monk:
there was once a great monk who was devoted to the practice of meditative absorption,
constantly spending his entire day in his own religious observances.

That mind of his, purified by the practice of samādhi, instantly contemplates whatever it thinks of and quickly attains that state, just as water becomes waves. Once, having ceased from his meditative absorption, he remained with a single-pointed mind.
