Seated upon his own throne, he reflected for a moment on the sequence of actions to be performed. As he was thus reflecting, this intuition then arose spontaneously within him: "I shall quickly manifest the conduct of an ordinary person for the sake of sport."
Having reflected thus, his mind remained as a certain internal person, like water in a whirlpool that has merely abandoned its movement and configuration. Then,
by that mental-person, a name was assumed for itself according to its own desire.
"By chance, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit, it suddenly occurred to him: 'I am Jīvaṭa.
Then that Jīvaṭa, who was a man created in a dream, wandered for a long time through the streets of a certain city fashioned by his own dreaming mind.
There he drank the drink, intoxicated like a bee drinking the nectar of a lotus;
ground down as if by a stone, he fell into a deep sleep.
In that dream, he saw himself as a Brahmin, satisfied with the study and practice of the scriptures.
Endowed with mere flashes of intuition, like the mind reaching another location;
once, that best of the twice-born, through his dedication to his daily duties,
fell into a deep sleep, just as a tree reaches the state of a seed.
He too saw for himself in a dream that he had attained the status of a vassal lord,
surrounded by a canopy of clouds consisting of banners, chariots, elephants, horses, and armies. Having taken his meal as a vassal lord, he once fell into a deep sleep.
His internal activity fell asleep, like a tree within its state of seedhood.
In a dream, he beheld his sovereignty over the garlanded circle of the quarters,
cherished by a multitude of enjoyments as a season is graced by a profusion of flowers.
Once, while the king was at ease and his desires had subsided, he fell asleep; then,
as if his own future conduct were appearing as its cause within the effect,
he beheld in a dream within himself the irreproachable state of a celestial woman.
She was like a tree in full bloom with filaments, having attained the state of a flower-cluster.
She took delight among the celestial armies and in the grounds of the divine gardens,
like Lakṣmī, the beloved of Hari, amidst the restless waves of the Ocean of Milk.
Once that young woman fell asleep in a bower of garden creepers while intoxicated,
her mental activity stilled like a fragrance resting upon a lotus.
Then, in a dream, she beheld within herself [the form] arisen through the power of union.
The state of being a deer arose spontaneously within her, like the state of water becoming a whirlpool.
Once, while overcome by sleep, that fawn with trembling eyes beheld in a dream the state of a creeper, which had taken root within herself through habitual practice.
Even animals perceive dreams due to the nature of the mind;
in this regard, the unimpaired examples are the recollections of the parrot, the horse, and the elephant.
She became a creeper, resplendent with flowers, fruits, and tender shoots.
Sporting in the bowers of creepers within the forest grove of the forest goddess,
she— having ascended through a form shaped like a sprout situated within a seed—
clearly perceived by her internal consciousness the cutting down of herself.
After experiencing a state of dense insensibility for some time through a portion of deep sleep,
he then beheld himself situated as a bee;
that six-footed creature then wandered in the forest among the forest creepers.
Like a lover among young women, he sported among the blossoming lotus ponds; parting the bimba-like lips of the flowers, he tasted their floral honey,
sleeping upon beds of blossoms after enjoying the playful vine-women.
He became as distressed in the lotus pond as a stalk of lotus fiber;
for even the mind of one with dull intellect finds delight only in some particular thing.
Then an elephant came to that lotus pond to trample it.
The mind of the deluded expands only for the sake of the destruction of beautiful objects.
Like a bee through the crushing of a lotus,
he was reduced to powder as if his very existence had been rooted out by the discovery of another superior quality.
Due to his perception of the elephant's appearance, the bee— by the power of that perception of the elephant's appearance— beheld himself arisen in the state of a restless,
intoxicated elephant; indeed, he fell into a pit as deep as a dried-up ocean.
In that void thick with the density of darkness, like a living being in saṃsāra,
he became the king’s favorite, a great destroyer of enemy forces;
always intoxicated by the power of liquor, he was like a night-stalker reeling about.
Once, cut down by the sword of his enemy, he went to his end,
like the life-force within the self when its form has been severed by the blade of discernment;
beholding the jewels from the frontal globes of herds of elephants, which resembled bees emerging [from the lotuses].
Departing from that elephant, the living being quickly became once again a bee.
Frequenting the forest creepers, he returned once more to the lotus pond;
for the long-standing habituation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is difficult to overcome due to a lack of awakening.
There, by being trampled by the hoof of an elephant, he was reduced once more to dust;
yet through the awareness of a swan standing nearby, he became a *kalahaṃsaka* (a type of swan).
That swan, wandering for a long time among lakes filled with blooming lotuses, [attained his former state].
Once, accompanied by many swans, he shone brilliantly; there, within him, consciousness— consisting of the Brahman-swan, which was almost devoid of sound and meaning—
blossomed like a peacock in the primordial ocean of the cosmic egg.
As he was contemplating that [vision] from afar, he was struck violently by the son of Daśaratha;
through the continuous connection with that realization, he became a swan born from the lotus-born Brahmā.
There, awakened by the playful expressions of words concerning uninterrupted discernment, his vision of the purifying reality was attained.
"Indeed, he who stands liberated must necessarily become one liberated in body (videhamukta) at the time of the end of the age.
This is the sixty-seventh canto, titled "The Example of the Monk’s Saṃsāra."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Once, that bird beheld Rudra in the city of Rudra,
with the playful grace of an elephant trumpeting upon the stalk of Brahmā’s lotus.
There, the thought arose in him with the certainty, "I am Rudra";
for just as a reflection instantly appears in a fine mirror, so too did he,
whose body had become that of Rudra, cast off that [previous] form.
Just as the fragrance from a cluster of flowers spreads by following the wind,
so Rudra then wandered at his pleasure in the abode of Rudra,
distinguished among the assemblies of the Gaṇas by those various practices of Śiva’s city.
But Rudra, through that singular splendor of his unsurpassed knowledge,
beheld with his intellect his entire former history;
for the Blessed Hara is the embodiment of unobstructed consciousness.
Amazed by his own hundreds of dreams, he spoke of his own accord in private:
"Oh, how wondrous is this illusion that deludes the entire world! Though unreal, it appears as real, firmly rooted like water in a mirage."

For the first time, having transcended the objects of thought, I have attained the state of pure consciousness (cittatā), through the contemplation of the sky and other elements established in the previously perfected creation;
thus, abiding by my own will as a living being, I am colored by the subtle elements (tanmātra) of the gross elements.
In a certain previous birth, I was a monk who remained entirely unperturbed. Because of that state of being unattached, I once experienced a sense of pleasure while wandering freely outside,
my form agitated by playful gestures, as I cultivated the thought that this was true delight.
At that time, through the power of that practice and by the dissolution of all objective existents,
the monk experienced that very [state], having abandoned the arising of any other mental construction.
That wonder which has taken root in the mind alone unfolds.
The autumnal creeper abandons even the water it has drunk during the summer.
Having become a living being with worn-out latent impressions (*vāsanā*), that mendicant Jīvaṭa wandered through those regions like an ant in its holes.
Then, because of his devotion to the twice-born within himself, he perceived his own state as that of a twice-born;
for when there is a reversal of one's disposition, that very disposition grows exceedingly strong.
That Brahmin attained the status of a feudal lord, which he had constantly contemplated.
Just as a sap, when drunk continuously, reaches fruition in a tree, so too,
by virtue of his agency in matters of sovereignty, wealth, and dharma, he became a king; yet,
through his lustful nature, that king attained the state of a celestial woman.

Out of greed for her darting eyes, that passionate doe became a creeping vine in the forest; alas, the delusion of latent tendencies leads only to suffering for living beings! (MU 6.67.17) She remained constantly fixed in the mind as a vine within the woods.
The creeper necessarily experienced being cut; then,

through the constant cultivation of that state, she perceived within herself the condition of being a bee, which had been long practiced in her internal consciousness by means of the suppression of other states.
Having experienced the crushing of an elephant's hoof,
he then wandered again and again through the delusions of the great cycle of existence.
At the end of hundreds of such transmigrations, I stand here as this very Rudra.
In this turmoil of saṃsāra, which is produced by the mind alone,
I have wandered extensively through many such forest regions of saṃsāra, which, though appearing utterly tranquil, seemed as if they were not empty.
In one creation I was named Jīvaṭa;
in another, an excellent Brāhmaṇa; and in another, a lord of the earth.
Having become a swan in a lotus grove, I became an elephant in the marshes of the Vindhya mountains.
And on Mount Hehaya, I, Hariṇa, have reached this state; here,
infinite thousands of years and hundreds of four-age cycles, composed of days and seasons, have passed away.
From the supreme state that first flashed forth for me,
there arose the sequence of knowledge established in the state of a monk by virtue of my belonging to the genus of sentient beings;
and having repeatedly transcended even that, I attained the status of a *brahmahaṃsa*.
That very former practice bears fruit through the arising of association.
Whatever firm practice has arisen for this living being without obstacle,
even after hundreds of other births, it pursues that very same one.
Sometimes, through a chance occurrence like the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" maxim, due to association with the virtuous,
the individual soul's habitual practice of impure tendencies ceases;
for such association and the like are the sole cause for its own emergence [from bondage].
The habitual practice of past tendencies requires only a slight cause.
Whatever is practiced incessantly, even in another body,
is experienced as real— even if it is unreal— during both waking and dreaming states.
That very thing which performs purposeful action for both suffering and happiness arises from mental cultivation; therefore, victory consists in the cultivation and non-cultivation [of that].
Mental cultivation itself perceives its own self as "this body."
Like a sprout expanding into a thicket by the mere fact of its own existence, this mental cultivation (bhāvanā), when scrutinized, leaves nothing behind;
it does not exist at all. Therefore, let us have enough of that delusion.
Since this delusion, composed of the unreal, has arisen like a color in the sky,
it must in reality be cleansed away by mere non-perception;
therefore, it is better that this very existence— which is essentially non-existent and harsh in nature— be cherished.
"Let it proceed for the sake of diversion; what will that which is non-existent do to us?
Therefore, rising up, I shall look upon all those individual streams of existence;
by bestowing light upon some of them, I shall unify them."
Having reflected thus, Rudra went to that creation where the mendicant, staying in his monastery, lay asleep like a corpse. Then,
having awakened that mendicant by means of both his own mind and consciousness, he spoke.
The mendicant also reflected upon his own delusion;
having perceived Rudra as himself and likewise Jīvaṭa and the others,
though he was beyond amazement due to his awakening, he experienced wonder for the sake of maintaining [the state].
Then Rudra and the mendicant, both rising up together,
went to some place where Jīvaṭa’s worldly existence resided in a single corner of the space of consciousness.
Having gone there, they reached that abode, that island, and that mandala.
They saw that object, that city, and that tavern-house;
they saw Jīvaṭaka lying asleep, unconscious, like a corpse,
having cast off the burden of his body while wandering through the realms of existence.
Having quickly awakened him and directed him through both mind and consciousness,
those [beings]— Rudra, Jīva, and the mendicant— though uniform, became threefold;
though possessing awareness, they appeared as if unaware, and though filled with wonder, they remained without astonishment.
The bards stood silent for a moment in the painting, as if their gestures had been fixed;
then they all departed for that certain realm of the space of consciousness,
where the cycle of existence of the brahmins abounds with the humming of beings engaged in various undertakings.
Having gone there to that dwelling, that island, and that region,
they reached that district, that village, and the abode of the Brahmin.
There they saw the Brahmin sleeping in his house, surrounded by his wife.
Seized by the throat by the Brahmin woman, he remained as if his life-force had departed outside his body.
Having quickly awakened him and directed him with both mind and consciousness,
those many who were present stood there, some filled with wonder while others remained free from it.
Then they went to the assembly of neighboring kings, which was reflected in the sky of consciousness and perceived by them, and which was beautiful with the weight of its undertakings;
there they reached that palace, that island, and that circle.
They beheld the intoxicated Sāmanta sleeping upon a lotus-bed,
as white as gold, resting in the hollow of the breasts of a woman with golden limbs;
he was like a bee sleeping within a lotus-bud, accompanied by a female bee.
Surrounded by beloved women like a tree entwined with blossoming clusters,
he stood amidst the lattice of lamps like a mass of gold set with jewels;
having quickly awakened him and engaged him through both his mind and his consciousness—
Though they were many, they remained thus, filled with wonder yet free from astonishment.
Then, having awakened him there, they entered the cycle of the royal world;
thereafter, together with him, they wandered through other realms of transmigration.
Having attained that state of Rudra— the desire for the Brahman-swan— all of them came together and shone as the hundred supreme Rudras.
With a single consciousness, their bodies were distinct, yet they were both active in diverse ways and motionless.
Know that the Supreme Lord is of a single form and yet possesses many forms;
know that his hundred Rudras are composed of unobstructed consciousness,
pervading all of saṃsāra and remaining as the sustainer of the entire world.
"O Rāma, there are ten great hundreds of Rudras here;
know that this is the eleventh, established for the sake of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). For whichever transmigration arises for whichever individual soul,"
There, the multitudes of unawakened living beings do not perceive one another.
For the awakened meet with each other like waves and water in the ocean;
the unawakened, however, remain fixed in their own individuality alone, like clods of earth.
Just as waves of water mingle thoroughly with one another due to their fluidity,
so too do the multitudes of awakened living beings mingle thoroughly with one another because of their consciousness.
And these masses of living beings have each arisen individually within this cycle of existence.
Because the element of consciousness is all-pervading, however, these [objects] exist as if real even though they are unreal.
Just as, my dear, whatever is dug out of the earth is called "clay," so too,
whatever is projected from the all-pervading consciousness appears here as that very thing.
Just as you perceive the five elements everywhere here in this world,
so too does the nature of consciousness, which is the self of all beings, exist everywhere.
Even in the limbs of a multitude of carved statues situated upon stone pillars, [consciousness is present].
Just as that very stone is perceived [as various things], so too the world is perceived within the Consciousness;
yet in the supreme, pure state of non-perception, those worlds are merely perception.
This is entirely without cause, like the emptiness of the sky.
In the density of consciousness, perception is bondage, while non-perception is liberation.
Whatever may be pleasing to you, that alone you should quickly make firm.
Creation and non-creation, bondage and liberation, consist of perception and non-perception.
These two are non-different from the perspective of awakening; do as you wish.
That which does not exist simply because it is not perceived—what distress is there in its destruction?
Know that whatever is to be attained through silence has already been swiftly attained.
That which consists of mere perception is indeed the exhaustion of the perception of limbs;
therefore, practice that which is desired regarding both perception and non-perception.
Just as a ripple is a vibration in water, so is the manifold world a vibration in consciousness.
O descendant of Raghu, the only difference here is this:
while space, time, and essential natures exist in the water [of the ocean] as waves and so forth,
at the beginning of the world, space and the others do not exist and are merely constructed by consciousness.
The three worlds appear as radiant; this luminous consciousness is the accumulation that is the very nature of the single Intellect.
When established in speech, this becomes possessed of differentiation and is afflicted; but when its expression is stilled, it is the auspicious Supreme Self.
Here, the two words "consciousness" and "creation" are never distinct in their meaning.
To say that "the two waters of the Vīci hell" are not a fitting statement for one who knows is itself appropriate only in the case of ignorance.
The sixty-eighth canto, titled "The Search for Hundreds of World-Cycles," from the Narrative of Śata-rudra in the Dream State.
Rāma said: O Lord of Sages, what has transpired beyond this for Jīvaṭa, the Brāhmaṇa, and the others, ending with the Haṃsa, whose bodies were merely those seen in the dream of the mendicant?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having come together with Rudra, they all became awakened;
having mutually perceived the cycle of existence, those who are portions of Rudra remain in a state of happiness.
When that Rudra beheld that illusion manifested in such a way,
he dispatched his own partial manifestations once again to that very state of worldly existence.
Rudra said:
"Go quickly to your own abode; having enjoyed pleasures there together with your wives for some time, you shall come back into my presence.
You shall become portions of myself, my attendants (gaṇas), and ornaments of my city."
"Then, at the time of the great dissolution, we shall go to that state together.
Having said this, the Blessed Lord Rudra vanished from them and went into the midst of the other Rudras established in the cycle of transmigration.
Jīvaṭa, the Brāhmaṇa, and the others also departed for their own abodes;
then, having spent their bodies together with their wives over time,
they reached the world of Rudra and will become the foremost of his attendants (gaṇas).
"Sometimes they are seen in the sky, bearing the form of stars.
Rāma said:
"Those such as Jīvaṭa and the Brāhmaṇa are merely forms created by the mental constructs of the mendicant."
"How is it that truthfulness prevails regarding the objects of one's volition, while there is untruthfulness in those very objects?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O Unborn One, the truthfulness of volition exists within the Lord, and the untruthfulness of volition exists within you."
That which does not exist in something does not exist [therein], because that state is the self of all.
(6.68.10) Whatever is seen in a dream and whatever is perceived through mental constructs exists there in that very way; it is of that nature at all times. (6.68.11)
It is established by that very state consisting of that place and time,
just as one reaches another location by means of a movement consisting of that place and time;
just as [one goes] from one place to another without effort, movement, and so forth.
In that same way, a dream cannot be obtained without its reality; [so too] nothing is obtained apart from consciousness.
Whatever this consciousness perceives exists within the treasury of the intellect;
because it is the self of all, the intellect attains that very thing exactly as it appears, unimpaired.
O dear one, that state which is attained through the objects of thought and dream cannot be reached here without the highest practice and yoga.
However, for those whose insights into the knowledge of yoga have borne fruit and remain steadfast—

These [beings], such as Śaṅkara and others, see everything everywhere. He who desires this object present before him as well as that which is imagined in his thoughts incurs the loss of both, because he relies upon both.
For every desired task is accomplished by one who is single-minded;
for who, while traveling toward the southern quarter, reaches the northern direction?
Only those intent on the object of their resolve perceive that object of their resolve.
By those intent on the object situated in front, the object situated in front is understood.
When this [object] is established in the cognition situated in front, he who desires to attain that which is imagined would,
because of his lack of single-mindedness, destroy both at that time.
Therefore, because they are fixed upon a single object, the mendicant’s life-force attains the state of Rudra;
having attained it as the self of all, everything is obtained from that state as it truly exists.
For those whose life-force consists of the resolve of a mendicant, that world is distinct for each one individually.
And they do not perceive one another except through the knowledge of Rudra; therefore,
unawakened individual souls (jīvas) are born from the awakened soul,
like fools [born] from a wise man by his will, as if they were sons.
"May I be a Vidyādhara here; may I be a ewe here"—this is the illustration of the fruitfulness of single-minded meditation within this state of ritual action.
Unity and multiplicity, as well as folly and wisdom, [are likewise found therein].
Through the effort of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and meditation (*dhyāna*), it is possible to adorn both divinity and humanity simultaneously by means of the sequences of place, time, and action;
for the individual soul (*jīva*), possessing the nature of all-pervading power and being undecaying, such capacity truly exists.
Its nature, by its very essence, is both infinite and yet endowed with limits;
it possesses expansion and contraction like the *haṃsa* (the soul) of the conscious self (*cidātman*). Whatever it desires exists, my dear; indeed, it accomplishes it of itself.
By means of these sequences of place, time, and action, which they themselves have conceived,
yoginīs and yogins remain here and go elsewhere; they desire both this world and the next— this has been seen many times.
Kārtavīrya, remaining in his home, became a rain-cloud and showered;
Viṣṇu, remaining in the ocean of milk, is born as a man on earth. The Yoginīs go forth for the sake of cattle while remaining within the assembly of Yoginīs.
Śakra, remaining on his celestial throne, goes to the fertile earth for the sake of sacrifice.
In this same way, within this Self of the World, one thousand [beings] become one;
hundreds of devoted men attain union with him in that very body.
Just as one becomes a thousand, so too does this Janārdana;
alone, he enjoys thousands of beloved women at the same time.
In this same way, those such as the Bhikṣus, Saṅkalpa, Jīvaṭa, and the Brāhmaṇas [attain their respective powers].
By the power of their knowledge of Rudra, they go to cities created by their own volition.
Having enjoyed pleasures there for a long time and then reached the city of Rudra,
they attain the status of his attendants and shall remain there with all their retinues.

In those various worlds, cities, and towns, which serve as dwellings for ever-blooming new kalpa-latas and possess clusters of vast jewels, the Vidyādharīs— wearing spotless crowns— delight together with Rudra. This concludes the chapter titled "The Resting of the Mendicant."
The sixty-ninth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"In this manner has the delusion of consciousness been observed by this mendicant."
Thus, every single being perceives itself as dying separately; indeed,
for every living soul, a state consisting of death and birth occurs,
even though it has taken on a form within the nature of the space of consciousness.
The forest of the world-process proceeds individually and separately for each person,
just as a grove of flowers proceeds separately from the caravan of its fragrance.
Indeed, every living being who has died [perceives] their own individual manifestation separately.
Thus, even though his true nature is such, the embodied soul remains agitated until liberation.
O Bhikṣu Rāma, by this discourse I have explained to you that this living being (jīva) is the Self set in motion by the Supreme; it is not merely the individual soul alone.
The living being, whose life is worn out, passes from one delusion to another,
just like a stone fallen from a mountain peak, falling lower and lower.
Having fallen from the state of the Supreme Self, the living being perceives this dream as solid reality.
From this dream, one sees oneself entering yet another dream;
falling from dream to dream, this body within— shattered by illusion— perceives this world as solid as stone, though it is utterly false.
Sometimes, by some means, or perhaps at some time,
this [being] is released from the sleep of delusion by means of the body itself and becomes fully awakened.
Rāma said:
"Alas! How terrible is the delusion that arises for this living being, which, upon falling even slightly from its state, produces various forms of transformation.
This [delusion] is produced by the subtle Māyā, the fierce night of false knowledge."
"Ah! How truly terrible is the disparity resulting from one's fall from one's own station!
O Blessed One, you have stated that in every way and at all times, everything is possible within the maintenance of the world; and that very thing is now being experienced by me."
"O great-souled one, does that mendicant, whose self is distinguished by such qualities, exist anywhere or not? Look within and tell me quickly.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Having stayed here in this small hut of the three worlds during the night absorbed in samādhi,
I shall declare in the morning whether this mendicant exists or does not exist.
Vālmīki said:
While the Sage was speaking thus, the midday drum resounded outside, as deep and resonant as the thundering of clouds agitated at the time of universal dissolution.
They offered one after another handfuls of flowers at his feet.

Like trees laden with flowers stirred by the wind, the kings and the citizens [welcomed them]. Having honored the best of sages, that protector of the earth rose from his seat together with the sage, like the sun rising from the mountain of sunrise.
Thereafter, the assembly rose with mutual salutations,
and the sky-dwellers and earth-dwellers departed in due order,
as they had done the previous day, attending to their daily duties in their respective abodes according to the scriptures.
All those who move upon the earth and those who move through the sky performed what was appropriate for their own religious duties, reflecting upon the knowledge spoken by the Sage;
they passed the nights as if they were moments, and even as if they were eons.
In the morning, while the people were again occupied with a succession of tasks, the assembly of *siddhas* moving through the air and those dwelling on earth remained just as before,
arranged in their respective seats, honoring the venerable ones who were honored by one another’s conversation.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Description of the Wonder Within Awakening."
The seventieth canto by Vālmīki:
[the assembly] joined by the sage Vasiṣṭha and joined by Viśvāmitra and others.
With the hosts of *khecarīs* and *siddhas* stationed there, and with its sovereign leaders at rest,
that very assembly shone, together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa;
gentle and of perfectly even expanse, it was like a lotus pond when the wind has subsided.
Then the Lord of Sages spoke, even without waiting for a question;
for the virtuous, out of compassion, awaken others by their very power.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O King, moon in the sky of Raghu’s lineage, joy of the Raghus!
Yesterday, with the eye of meditation, I gazed upon that mendicant for a long time.
I wandered for a long while in meditation, desiring to see such a mendicant."

The seven vast continents as well as the mountain ranges of the world-system— how indeed could such a kingdom of the mind be perceived even externally, so long as no such monk has been found anywhere?
Then, when a third of the night remained, I again set out toward the northern region by means of my intellect, like a coastal wind driving across the ocean.
There, moreover, lies a great and glorious province named Cīna.

There, upon an anthill, stands a monastery dedicated to the Jina. In that monastery, within his own small hut, dwells a monk named Dīrghaśaya, who has tawny hair and whose future destiny is thus ordained.
And for twenty-one nights, while he remained in that state, his servants—
fearing the interruption of his meditation— did not enter his house, which was secured by firm bolts; indeed,
he remained there like one who has obtained a great abundance of food.
Thus, even today, such is the state of destiny that has come upon him:
twenty-one nights have passed for him while he was absorbed in meditation,
yet in his mind he experienced them as thousands of years.
In a certain former eon, there was once a monk such as this;
today, however, there is a second here, but a third is not to be found. Furthermore, I have searched with my fourfold mind.
"Such a third monk as that other one, who was like a bee in the lotus-heart of the world,
has not been found by us since this creation.
Then, I subsequently beheld other creations with ease."
As long as there exists even a single creation resting within some corner of space,
there will be a third monk or brahmin following such a course;
thus, in that very same arrangement, they shall exist in great numbers.
In the succession of creations, there will be, have been, and are entities;
likewise, those sages, brahmins, and kings who are in this assembly,
and many others as well, must necessarily possess such conduct.
"O sinless one, this Nārada must become someone else again,
and likewise Atri must now become someone else again;
thus, by means of his wife and his actions, he has been joined with various states many times."
Thus one must become Janaka, Vyāsa, and Śuka; furthermore,
one must become Kratu,
Pulaha, Agastya, Pulastya, Bhṛgu, and also Aṅgiras.
These very ones, as well as others of such a nature, will from time to time become the locus of such actions, because this illusion is so widespread;
they and many others will be born with conduct similar to theirs.
They revolve again and again in successive creations like waves in water;
some are exactly alike, some follow a sequence that is half-similar,
some are slightly similar, and some are never the same again.

Thus, this vast illusion that deludes the mind has neither a moment nor an aeon here; for it is active perception that expands. Where are the twenty-one days and nights, and where are the endless evil births?
Where indeed is their perception? Oh, how formidable is the course of the mind!
This [world] is merely a flash of intuition that has thus blossomed white, yet it is as restless as the waves of various quarrels, like a lotus at dawn.

This entire web of saṃsāra, though appearing impure, has arisen solely from pure consciousness, just as a mass of fire arises from a single spark. Thus, each individual cluster of appearances has arisen, and within those clusters there are further diverse clusters.
Indeed, all things—both themselves and one another—are not false, for they flash forth within this Universal Self, the cause of all causes.
The seventy-first canto:
Daśaratha says:
"O Leader of Sages, let these men sent by me go quickly and awaken that monk who has entered the Chinese Buddha-cottage. Vasiṣṭha said:
"O King, that body of the great mendicant, deprived of life, has become moist and discolored; it is no longer a vessel for life.
And as for the life-force of that mendicant, having become a swan born from a lotus,"

Established as one liberated while living, he will no longer be a vessel for the cycle of worldly existence. At the end of a month, those who have been forcibly expelled from his house will look within for the mendicant whose mind remains unshaken.
The monk remains liberated in that very body;
how can he be awakened when his little physical frame has perished in the monastery?
This illusion, composed of the qualities (guṇas), is difficult to understand and hard to transcend for one who lacks discernment.
One passes through time with ease, by means of the constant awakening to truth.
Just as the state of being a bracelet is unreal, though fashioned from gold,
arising solely from the cause of a mistaken appearance.
This illusion is measured as belonging to the Supreme Self alone;
like a wave in water, it perishes upon mere observation.
Even the Knower, passing from one long dream consisting of the visible world into another dream, [is not truly affected].
Thus, through discernment, the vision of the all-pervading Self does not admit of any otherness.
Whatever appearance may arise for this [Self], that is the Self alone from the perspective of awakening.
That very same [Self] arises as the vision of the thicket of *karañja* forests of saṃsāra.
Each individual being has arisen as a separate sphere of saṃsāra,
like a monk’s dream within sleep, or like a wave from the water.
This dream of the world has spread forth from the Lotus-born One himself from the very beginning.

In that very same way, the entire creation, extending back to the Grandfather (Brahmā), appears to every person as it has ascended upon their own mind, like the playful display of a dream. Thus, millions of cosmic eggs arise here for each individual.
Vibrating within the Supreme, each individual soul perceives delusion; and within the heart, it experiences a long, internal dream that appears as if endowed with objective reality,
solely due to the lapse in the perception of the universal commonality of pure consciousness.
Someone has become a vessel for the sufferings of old age and death;
whether it be the netherworld or the realm of Brahmā, that which is characterized by the wonder of consciousness remains ever-present,
having repeatedly brought it forth by the mere vibration of a portion of the mind.

The intellect, whose nature is vibration, having entered the Self by means of the Self under the name of "life," rolls about elsewhere as something quite different, becoming laden with agitation. O Supreme Self, why do you fear the Supreme Self itself?
Just as a child [is distinguished] from this reflection consisting of the living body and so forth,
so too the Supreme Brahman exists within Brahman itself through the very perception of the world;
it is like pure space within space, or like stainless water within water.
This world belongs to Brahmā alone, who exists in the form of the universe;
it fears that which is perceived as other than itself, just as a child fears its own reflection.
When vibration is rendered motionless through awakening, the designations of the mind dissolve.
That too, through complete transformation, dissolves like ghee in fire.
It is the vibration of consciousness alone that unfolds within the vibration of consciousness, which is the Self of all;
movement and stillness, unfolding and so forth, are merely imagined—here there is nothing real.
Here there is neither vibration nor non-vibration, neither unity nor duality;
there exists only pure consciousness alone, and everything exists exactly as it is,
when the objects of creation and the ego-sense have been stilled through the supreme transformation.
Even pure consciousness does not exist at all; even "it does not exist" is not found.
Through the contemplation of duality, duality arises as the mark of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
When everything has dissolved through the realization of non-duality, the Supreme alone remains.
This diversity does not exist due to lack of awakening; that lack of awakening exists because of a failure to investigate.
Furthermore, the observer himself does not exist at all; therefore, there is supreme fearlessness.
Consequently, there is neither dream, nor the glory of the waking state, nor deep sleep, nor the fourth state (turyatā).
There is neither bondage nor liberation, nor anything else consisting of conceptual construction.
There is only one peace called the world; this [world] is established within that peace.
Therefore, since ignorance is utterly unreal, where can there be the triad of the seen, the seer, and the act of seeing?
Even the vibration of this consciousness is indeed non-vibration because of its freedom from conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*);
consciousness, devoid of conceptual construction, is neither distinct in vibration nor non-vibration.
Conceptual construction—consisting of the forms of duality, unity, and so forth—is the mental cultivation of the mind (*citta*).
And that [stain] dissolves by mere non-contemplation, and Brahman remains.
That which appears as if it were a stain of volition upon the lunar orb of consciousness— know that this is not a stain, but rather the dense body of the mass of consciousness itself.
"Being neither existent nor non-existent, one should remain in that expansive state"—
thus has been made this compendium of the essence of the entire great awakening.
From the lunar orb of consciousness, which is the embodiment of nectar, arises the stain of volitional thought.
Purified by you through your being— which is characterized by the cessation of both existence and non-existence—
having brought the conceptualization of existence, non-existence, and so forth to the state of pure consciousness by means of consciousness,
remain at ease and in equanimity at the conclusion of the play of tranquility and radiance.

Vibration and non-vibration, as well as the parts consisting of conceptualization and non-conceptualization, are not other than consciousness because of its nature as consciousness; yet consciousness is nameless, partless, omniform, unobstructed, a peaceful existence, and stands like a single ocean filled with sentient beings.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Exposition of the Unity of Brahman."
The seventy-second canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Having become one who maintains the silence of deep sleep, and having shaken off the form consisting of duality and unity,
"O Beloved, O one whose nature is consciousness, remain, having firmly established yourself in that state.
Rāma said:
"I understand the silence of speech, the silence of the senses, and the silence of wood (the state of being like a log)."
"O Brahman, tell me, what is called the silence of deep sleep (*suṣuptamauna*), the lord of silences (*mauneśa*)?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O Rāma, here in this world, sages are declared by the best of sages to be of two kinds."

One is the wooden ascetic (*kāṣṭhatapasvin*), and the other is the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). A sage who has not cultivated his self, who is firmly resolved upon dry ritual action, and who has forcibly subdued the collection of his senses, is a wooden ascetic.

Having understood this as it truly is, one whose self is cultivated abides within the Self; though appearing like the world, he is inwardly satisfied, and such a one is remembered as a liberated sage.
Whatever state belongs to these two lords of sages who are both tranquil—
That which consists of the nature of mental certainty is remembered by the word "mauna" (silence).
Those who know mauna say that it is of four kinds:
silence of speech, silence of the senses, the wooden state, and the state of deep sleep.

Vocal silence is the restraint of speech; physical silence is the forcible subduing of the senses and the renunciation of all activities, characterized as being like a log of wood. Mental silence is the fifth, which belongs to the "log-like ascetic" who is as if dead.
Indeed, while living as one liberated while alive (jīvanmukta), there occurs that which is called the silence of deep sleep.
Among these three specific types of silence, the subject is the wooden ascetic (kāṣṭhatāpasa);
and the one whose intellect is liberated is the subject of the fourth state, the silence of deep sleep.

Silence of speech is indeed established as *mauna*, yet that [silence] is merely a fraction of the mind; when defiled, it leads to the bondage of the living soul. Those who remain there are the "wooden ascetics" (*kāṣṭhatāpasa*).
Whether by force or through the application of yoga, the restraint of one's own senses—this is true silence.
Those wood-dwelling ascetics staying there call that "the silence of wood.
Whether remembering or not remembering, whether touching upon speech or not,
the one who observes the silence of wood remains without even seeing that which is seen.
This triad of silences is known as the flickering of the movement of the mind;
it occurs among ignorant sages, but not among those who know reality, for [the latter] act with effortless ease (*līlayā*). Indeed, this triad of silences is not to be adopted by the wise.
Those who know that [reality] may perform it either with ease or with playfulness, or they may not do so at all.
But listen now to this "silence of deep sleep," which is established in the mind of one liberated while living, leading to the non-rebirth of the creature— this ornament for the ears.
Here speech is neither restrained nor abandoned in its threefold form;
the perceptions of all the senses are neither excited nor subdued.
Indeed, this perception of multiplicity neither stirs nor subsides.
It is neither mind nor non-mind, neither existent nor non-existent, neither space nor the earth.
That which is undivided, effortless, without beginning or end, and remains as it is— that, my dear, is the silence of deep sleep, whether one is meditating or running.
Having understood, as it truly is, this delusion of the world's diversity,
that which is a state of non-attachment and freedom from fear— that, my dear, is the silence of deep sleep.
This entire expanse is indeed one, though its nature consists of manifold cognitions.
O dear one, that which is infinite and thus situated is the silence of deep sleep.
That which is established as even and tranquil— neither space nor non-space, being all yet not being anything— is the silence like that of deep sleep.
All is empty, without support, peaceful, and mere representation;
neither existent nor non-existent—thus one remains established in the supreme silence.
Through the various manifestations of the states of existence and non-existence that arise falsely, [one remains unmoved].

The wise know that supreme silence to be the absence of mental reflection (*anāmarśa*) regarding consciousness. That which is the non-recurrence of the activity of consciousness— whether it be the non-existent or the existent, appearing within the mind in the form of its own fluctuations— is the imperishable silence.
"I do not exist, nor does another exist; there is no mind, nor anything mental"—this consciousness of non-consciousness is uninterrupted supreme silence.
"I exist and the world exists," yet this is merely the referent of the word "exists."
That which is merely the generality of existence is called the silence of deep sleep.
Since consciousness alone exists by virtue of its being, how could there be other constructions such as dreams?
Deep sleep is indeed infinite; therefore, that silence is all-pervasive.
Know this very state of deep-sleep silence to be like awakening because of its infinity;
it is the stainless fourth (turya), or even that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta). Thus, one who is absorbed solely in deep sleep is likewise absorbed in the fourth state.

Or indeed, the samādhi beyond the fourth (turyātīta) may even occur while one is awake. Established in the fourth state, with all mental fluctuations stilled and purified, even while engaged in worldly activity during the waking state—whether remaining in the body or having become bodiless—one should always be like the ether of Brahman; for that alone, O virtuous one, is what you truly are.

"Om! Sit as the One, with the latent impressions of worldly existence cast aside; there is nothing here that is real, such as 'you' or 'I'. Yet everything exists here like the interior of a stone; therefore, O Knower, remain established solely in the single digit of the treasury of the sky of consciousness.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Great Silence."
The seventy-third canto.
Rāma said:
"O leader of sages, from where has the state of there being one hundred Rudras arisen?"
"Tell me, are those hosts Rudras or not?
Vasiṣṭha replied: "A mendicant saw in a dream a hundred bodies, each consisting of a hundred [parts]."
Everything has been known by way of summary; therefore, it was said by me:
"Those who are the hundred forms in a dream are remembered as the hundred *gaṇas*. They themselves are the hundred *rudras*, for even the *rudras* are designated as *gaṇas*. (MU 6.73.2–3)
Rāma:
O Blessed One, how is it that from a single mind a hundred minds are produced,
like a hundred lamps lit from one lamp by means of the Śatarudriya-mantra recited in a dream?
Vasiṣṭha:
Whatever those whose true being is unobstructed conceive of in whatever manner, that very thing comes to pass immediately; this is not so for those whose consciousness is obstructed.

Because the Self of all is omnipresent, whatever is meditated upon in whatever manner and wherever, that very thing is experienced there by the knower of that [Self], not through the intellect. Rāma said:
Adorned with a garland of skulls, bathing in ashes, and clad in the directions as his garment,
O Brahmin, Maheśvara dwells in the cremation ground and is a lover.
Vasiṣṭha said:
For the great lords, the perfected ones, who possess bodies while already liberated in life, there is no restrictive rule regarding action here; for such a rule is devised only for the ignorant.
Indeed, the ignorant, because their minds are unsubdued, [require] the regulation of action.
For by the law of the fish, through greed, people indeed go to supreme suffering.
But those who know that do not sink into attachment toward desirable or undesirable objects,
because they have conquered their senses, attained awakening, and are free from this latent tendency.
They always perform actions that have become habitual like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence;
or some do not perform them at all, for they have no attachment whatsoever to anything.
Thus, Viṣṇu alone has arisen as the agent of such actions from the Supreme.

The Three-eyed One has such karma, and the Lotus-born has such karma. For one who possesses knowledge, there is nowhere any karma that is blameworthy or blameless, nothing to be accepted or rejected, and no distinction between what is one's own and what belongs to another.

Just as heat and other qualities have become established in fire and the like since the beginning of creation, so too have the activities of Hara and others, as well as the castes of the twice-born, become established through the power of convention once the creation had reached full development. Each of these has arisen separately by virtue of linguistic convention.
Therefore, conceptualizations regarding one's own interests have been fashioned from the fruits already experienced.
Hence, I have not spoken to you of the fourth silence concerning the disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*);
O scion of Raghu, the fifth silence of the disembodied one has not been mentioned by me.
The space of the Self, which consists of consciousness, is even more transparent than the sky;
the attainment of that is the supreme good. Listen to how it is attained:
through the awakening of perfect knowledge and by means of constant, one-pointed meditative absorption.
Those who have realized [reality] through enumeration alone are known as Sāṅkhyas; those who,
through the complete stilling of the vital breaths and other winds,
are disciplined and have attained the state that is free from affliction and without beginning or end, are known as Yogins of Yoga.
But that which is to be accepted by all is the peaceful, unconditioned state;
that is attained by some through *saṅkhyā* (enumeration) and by others through *yoga* from the body. He who sees Sāṅkhya and Yoga as one—he truly sees.
That very same supreme state which is attained by the followers of Sāṅkhya is indeed reached through Yoga as well.
Know that to be the highest station where the activity of the mind, once it has reached there, is no longer perceived at all, being entirely free from the snare of latent impressions (vāsanā).
They say that the mind itself is the latent impression (*vāsanā*), for it is the cause of transmigratory existence;
when it dissolves within the actions of becoming, it reaches a state of causelessness.
Indeed, the mind perceives the body just as a child perceives a ghost.
Having led the self to dissolution, one does not perceive it again.
The mind, having arisen in vain, is indeed non-existent due to a lack of observation;
like the form of one's own death seen in a dream, it is not found when scrutinized.
Due to the absence of the mind, there is no saṃsāra; where is joy without a flower?
Where, then, can there be the teacher and the taught, or bondage and liberation?
Through the intense practice of the single reality, the vital breaths (prāṇas) are dissolved.
"And the restraint of the mind is the cause of the meaning of the word 'liberation'.
Rāma said:
"O Sage, if indeed the dissolution of the vital breaths is the cause of liberation,"
"For indeed, only the dead are liberated; therefore, I believe all living beings [are already so].
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Among these three practices, the pacification of the mind is the best."
Know that very goal to be quickly attained, so that it becomes auspicious.
When the vital breaths, free from latent impressions, abandon this little body,
then they no longer go to union with the subtle elements in the ether.
Know that the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) consist precisely of the portion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) adhere to those [subtle bodies] which possess such impressions and are like the mind, and not to others.
If these vital breaths, accompanied by latent impressions, abandon the body...
Just as a fragrance [clings] to the air, that [mind] enters into union with space and wind for the sake of suffering.
Like a cloud with water, the mind does not become tranquil so long as it possesses latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Without the mind, the vital breaths do not come into being, just as rays do not exist without the sun.
The mind never abandons the vital breaths without knowledge,
just as a partridge does not leave the tip of a blade of grass without first leaving the rest of the grass.
Indeed, having attained its own dissolution through knowledge, the mind reaches a state free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
And one no longer grasps the vibration of the vital breath; from that, indeed, peace remains.
From the knowledge of the non-existence of all objects, [this] fully arises;
then, my dear, through the destruction of latent impressions, there occurs the dissociation of the vital breath and the mind.
Then the mind, being utterly tranquil, no longer perceives the state of embodiment;
having attained the state through its own dissolution, the wise know that the mind is nothing but latent impression (*vāsanā*).
For the mind is merely latent impression; its absence is the supreme state.

"And that is accomplished through knowledge; they say knowledge is discernment. O Rāma, the end of this cycle of transmigration proceeds by means of one's own mere discrimination, just like the illusion of a snake in a rope.
The practice of a single object, the restraint of the vital breath, and the dissolution of the mind—
when even one of these is fully accomplished, they all become perfected through one another.
Just as when the movement of a palm-leaf fan ceases, the wind is stilled.
When the movement of the vital breath has ceased, the mind likewise becomes stilled.
Upon the dissolution of the body, the vital breaths merge into the space and air;
and there, they perceive this very mind according to how it has been conditioned.
Just as the inhabitants of Videha perceive their bodies in the sky, so too do those endowed with the mind experience all conduct and everything else.
Just as fragrance subsides when the movement of the wind has ceased, [so does the mind subside].
Likewise, when the vibration of the mind is stilled, the vital breaths are stilled;
for the life-force and the consciousness of living beings are eternally inseparable,
existing as a mixture like the scent and the flower, or like sesame and its oil.
The vibration of the mind is the vital breath; the vibration of the vital breath is the mind.
These two always move together like a chariot and its driver.
Indeed, like the container and the contained, they perish in the absence of either one.
And by means of their own destruction, they accomplish the supreme task known as liberation.
Through the intense practice of a single reality, the mind becomes thoroughly stilled;
because its very nature is absorbed in that, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is also stilled.
Having investigated that reality of the infinite Self, one should lead the mind to identification with it;
then, through absorption in that, the mind itself becomes stable as that very [reality].
That alone is the supreme good, whether there is non-perception or perception.
Remain steadfast in either of those two, even if both are non-existent, or else in that which remains.
One should contemplate the state of being within a single, firmly established reality until,
through one's own practice, that being attains the state of non-being for all time.
Through the power of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), the mind dissolves along with the vital breaths, as if through the exhaustion of its own objects of enjoyment; only the Supreme remains.
When the mind becomes one-pointed, it becomes [that Supreme] in an instant.
Through the nature of long-term practice, the entire flood of particularities is stilled.
Having understood with a reasoning mind that this ignorance does not exist, the supreme state is attained through knowledge alone; therefore, its practice is excellent.
When the mind is stilled, this mirage of saṃsāra subsides, just as a great mist vanishes when the clouds have passed away.
Know that ignorance is nothing but the mind; therefore, bring about its destruction by means of that very mind itself.
For that experience of the self as mind, characterized by such form and name, is indeed the supreme state.
If the mind remains for even a moment in the supreme state of nirvāṇa,
know that it has been transformed into that very state and has attained its true savor therein.
If the mind has found rest in the state [of liberation] through Sāṅkhya or Yoga,
having attained the state of *sattva* for even a moment, it is not born again. The mind from which ignorance has fallen away is designated by the word *sattva*.
The seed of saṃsāra being thus burnt, it shall not produce a sprout again.

The knower, whose ignorance has dissolved away, who abides in the state of pure being (sattva) and whose latent impressions are stilled, beholds the light that is equal, void-like, and tranquil; he becomes extinguished [in peace].
O fortunate one, the mind that has dissolved the state of ignorance is here called "pure being" (*sattva*);
it does not return again to the state stained by the parts [of duality], just as copper that has attained the state of gold does not revert [to its former condition].
This concludes the chapter titled "An Investigation into the Union of Vital Breath and Mind."
The seventy-fourth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"The living soul quickly becomes non-living; the mind attains the state of being no-mind."
Through inquiry, that which ends in ignorance is declared to be liberation.
Like the water of a mirage, the world and the sense of "I" and so forth are perceived; though they are utterly non-existent, they vanish through inquiry even as they appear.
Upon the cessation of this dream of saṃsāra, listen to these auspicious questions uttered by the Vetāla, which have come to my memory through the force of circumstances.
In the great Vindhya forest, there dwells a Vetāla of massive form.
Out of greed and hunger, he came to a certain circle.
That vetāla had previously dwelt in a certain abode of the virtuous; through the constant offering of many oblations, he was happy due to his perpetual satiety.

Being without signs and without fault, he did not kill a man standing before him even when hungry; for attachment is the guide to justice. In due time, he went from his forest dwelling to another city.
Driven by hunger, he sought to devour people according to his own logic;
there he encountered the king who had gone out on a night patrol,
and that fierce night-stalker addressed him with a deep and terrible voice.
The Vetāla said:
"O King, you have now been caught by me, the Bhīma Vetāla!
Where will you go? You are destroyed; you shall be my food today!"
The King said:
"O night-stalker, if you devour me here by force against all justice, then your head shall split into a thousand pieces; of this there is no doubt."
The Vetāla said:
"I do not eat you; rather, this principle is being stated by me:
you are a king, and all the hopes of those who seek you must be fulfilled by you."
O King, fulfill this request of mine for the sake of my existence;
you ought to correctly explain these questions posed by me.
To whom do the fragile, atomic world-eggs belong, compared to the rays of the sun?
In what wind do the great particles of the vast sky manifest?
Moving from one dream to another by the hundreds and thousands,
who is it that abandons yet does not abandon its own pure and radiant essential nature?
Just as the trunk of a plantain tree consists of nothing but layers upon layers of leaves,
so too does that very atom consist of inner within inner, and inner within inner;
for it is indeed that [Brahman] which appears as the cosmic egg, space, the mass of elements, the solar orb, and Mount Meru.

If one does not abandon its atomicity, whose atoms would they be? And for which partless entity would the three worlds constitute marrow— dense, uniform, and situated within a stone of a great mountain that is itself an atom?
If you speak thus to me, O evil-souled one, then having swallowed you here, O self-destroyer,
I shall forcibly seize your orb like a fruit, just as the God of Death seizes the world.
The Chapter titled "The Question of the Vetāla."
The seventy-fifth canto. Vasiṣṭha:
When the Vetāla had spoken thus, he laughed and proceeded to answer the questions.
The king, whose face was white with the luster of his teeth, spoke these words:
The King said:
"O Citrāṅgadā, this universe is like a pepper fruit."
It is wrapped in successive layers of bark that have become like skin;
indeed,
there exists a lofty and vast branch with such fruits upon it, possessing trembling foliage.
Furthermore, there exists a great tree of vast form, difficult to perceive, upon which there are thousands of such branches;
where there exist thousands of such trees.
There is such a forest, lofty and filled with endless trees and shrubs;
and where there are thousands of such forests,
there stands a great peak, exceedingly high and vast in form.
Furthermore, there is a great mountain where there exist thousands of such peaks, filling the entire expanse of the quarters; and furthermore,
there is a place where there exist thousands of such mountains.
There exists such an exceedingly vast region with extensive hollows;
and where there are thousands of such regions,
there exists a great island surrounded by massive lakes and rivers.
Furthermore, where there exist thousands of such islands,
there exists a terrestrial surface endowed with various wonderful arrangements;
furthermore, where there exist thousands of such earths, [there exists a world-system].
There exists such a vast world, a cage of great worlds;
and where there exist thousands of such worlds,
there exists such a great cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), like a seat for a fierce display.
There exists an ocean, vast and with incessant movement, wherein a single wave consists of thousands of such cosmic eggs; and there exists another,
where a delicate ripple is as large as those oceans.
There exists such a great ocean, pure and consisting of its own playful manifestations; moreover,
there is some man of exceedingly lofty form whose belly contains the waters of thousands of such oceans.
There is another man who is the foremost of all beings, upon whose chest a garland made of hundreds of thousands of such men rests. There are thousands of such high-souled persons.
He from whom [all things] flash forth within the mandala like the network of his own body-hairs—
he is such a great sun who blazes within these visions;
all these various conceptualizations are his very radiances.
To this sun, the universe is like a mote of dust in its rays;
he is called the Sun of Consciousness, and he illumines all this. This supreme sun of pure awareness is the illuminator of all that exists.
These expanses of the world are but motes of dust belonging to that very sun of supreme consciousness; they shine and come into being through its light,
just as the splendors of the day appear from the sun.

When the multitude of living beings is but the self manifested as mere consciousness, and when the assembly of the three worlds unfolds like a pavilion, there are no traces whatsoever of the agitation caused by sinking or emerging; indeed, remain here in peace. This concludes the chapter titled "The Description of the Supreme Great Sun."
The seventy-sixth canto:
The King said,
"The existence of time, the existence of space, and the existence of movement are composed of consciousness."
Furthermore, the existence of pure consciousness and all such things are purifying. Within the great wind of the Supreme Self, the restless *rajas* vibrates;
like fragrance within a flower, it is by its very nature both identical to and distinct from that [Self].
In this great dream called the world, one passes from one dream to another;
yet Brahman, which is augmented by its own tranquility, does not abandon its peaceful form.
This [world] is an infinite manifestation, naturally augmented by volitional thought.
Just as it expands through various expansions, so does that which has been expanded;
and volition does not differ even slightly from this Supreme Self. Because it consists of consciousness, there is therein neither any expansion nor any means of expanding.
Just as a plantain trunk consists of nothing but layers within layers,
so too this entire universe, having been evolved from Brahman, is likewise [layered].
That which is designated by these terms such as "Brahman," "Self" (ātman), and so forth—
It is empty and indefinable; it is not nothing, yet it is not anything at all.
Whatever existence is conceptualized, each is constructed by experience.
Therefore, like a plantain trunk, that which is spread forth is pure consciousness alone.
Because of its subtlety and because it is unattainable, the Supreme Self is the supreme atom (*paramāṇu*);
yet, because of its infinity, that very same [Self] is said to possess the dust of Mount Meru and all else.
Even the world and so forth stand before this [Self], which is both more minute than an atom and infinitely vast.
He appears like an atom because he is immeasurable, yet like formless space;
he is an "atom" (aṇu) because he is unattainable, yet a "great mountain" because he fills all.
Though consisting of all limbs, the Person is devoid of limbs.
The three worlds are but the very marrow of this representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*);
O virtuous one, know that the three worlds are indeed the center of mere consciousness (*vijñānamātra*).
The worlds are mere consciousness, unmeasured by parts, peaceful, naturally delicate, and of infinite forms.
The station of the Vetāla-child must indeed not be transgressed; thus, O you who possess such pride, experience [the consequence] and remain in peace.
The seventy-seventh canto, titled "The Breaking of the Vetāla’s Riddle."
Vasiṣṭha:
Having heard this from the mouth of the king, the Vetāla attained peace through his purified nature and through an intellect there aroused by reflection.
Having become serene in body and having gone to a secluded place,
the blameless one remained in unwavering meditation, forgetting his agonizing hunger.
"O Rāma, this web of questions from the Vetāla has been told to you by me."

In this sequence, this entire world is situated within the very atom of consciousness. Through inquiry, the universe contained within the sheath of the atom of consciousness dissolves, like the anger of a Vetāla; that which remains is the Supreme.
Withdrawing the mind from all directions with a tranquil inner self,
making it fall into a continuous flow, remain without desire and with a peaceful intellect;
having made the mind itself as clear as space by means of the mind alone, the sage [should abide].
"Remain with a mind pacified by singular tranquility, with a disposition as pure as the sky.
For one of steady intellect, free from delusion, who follows what has naturally come to him,
even that which is difficult to accomplish is achieved— just like King Bhagīratha."

For one whose mind is entirely tranquil, whose conduct is completely satisfied, and who always abides within the Self— which is perfectly equanimous— desired objects, even those most difficult to attain, are accomplished, just as the ocean was filled by the grandson of Sagara at the descent of the Gaṅgā.
The Chapter named "The Tale of the Vetāla."
The Story of the Vetāla is concluded;
this is the seventy-eighth canto.
Rāma:
"O Lord, tell me how, through the wonder of his mind, Bhagīratha’s descent of the Gaṅgā was accomplished. Vasiṣṭha replied:
There was a king named Bhagīratha, supremely righteous,
who was like an exquisite tilaka ornament for the earth with its oceans and islands.
Immediately upon his resolve, seekers obtained whatever they desired.
From him, whose face was as serene as the moon, who— like a wish-fulfilling gem—
unceasingly bestowed wealth for the sake of establishing the righteous,
took taxes no more than a blade of grass, just as a "grass-gem" takes up only a blade of grass.

Even that which was strung with the essence of diamond, he shattered without even glowing, like a jewel of iron [breaking] an iron machine— the conduct of the wicked. For, smokeless, burning without heat, cool, and devoid of sharpness, it was sufficient even to pierce the heart.
He dispels the darkness of men like a jewel dispels the night-time gloom within houses;
scattering a shower of sparks born from his own prowess on all sides,
he blazes among his enemies like the fire produced by a sun-gem at midday.
With a soft, cool, and pleasant touch that gladdens the earth,
he flows affectionately toward his own kin like a moonstone melting at the sight of the moon;
he is the sacred thread of the universe, flowing through both heaven and the netherworld.
By him, the third quality of the flow of the Gaṅgā was fulfilled upon the earth;
by him, the ocean dried up by Agastya was filled by the flood of the Gaṅgā,
even as a great caravan of supplicants— though difficult to satisfy— is fulfilled.
By him, the friend of the world, his kinsmen dwelling in the netherworld were led to the realm of Brahmā by means of a flight of stairs made from the Gaṅgā;
and he who propitiated Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and Jahnu through his ascetic penance.
Though he experienced distress again and again, he did not falter, for his resolve was firm. Then, while that lord of the earth was in the prime of youth,
he reflected upon this worldly course of life, which is so full of confusion.

Then, by chance, even in his youth, there arose in his mind a tiny spark of reflection on the wonder of detachment from one's own self, like a creeper in a desert. Thereupon, that lord of the earth reflected in solitude.
This worldly course is eternally crowded with inconsistencies:
again day, again night, again the giving, receiving, and eating of that very same food which is tasteless like a piece of shell; thus one feels ashamed while performing such actions.

I consider that deed well-done by which, once attained, nothing remains unattained in this world; all else is but the cholera of karma. One who performs stale actions again and again does not feel shame.
"But who, being free from delusion, would act like a fool with a deluded mind?
(MU 6.78.18) Then once, his mind agitated and fearing the cycle of worldly existence, Bhagīratha questioned his teacher Tryuttala in private: (MU 6.78.19)
Bhagīratha: O Lord,
wandering for a very long time within the worldly states that are empty at their core—
like wandering through vast wildernesses— we are utterly exhausted.
O Blessed One, how does the end come about for all sufferings— such as old age, death, and delusion— which produce existence? (MU 6.78.21) Tryuttula:
O King, through the realization of the Knowable— which is of the nature of long-standing equanimity, pure, sporting in indivisibility, full, and filling the self—
all sufferings are exhausted and all knots are completely severed.
O sinless one, doubts come to rest and all karmas as well.
They know the Knowable to be the Self, whose nature is pure consciousness;
it is omnipresent and eternal, neither setting nor rising.
Bhagīratha said: "O Lord of Sages, I know that there exists only pure consciousness— omnipresent, tranquil, stainless, and immutable— and that nothing else, such as the body and so forth, exists."
"But in this matter, my understanding does not become clearer;
O Blessed One, how may I have such a mere realization?
Tryuttula said:
Through knowledge, the mind within the heart attains a state of rest in the object of knowledge;
then, having become the body of all, the living being is not born again.
Non-attachment and lack of possessiveness toward children, wife, home, and so forth—
Constant equanimity of mind in the occurrence of both the desirable and the undesirable;
the uninterrupted cultivation of the true being through union with nothing other than the Self;
dwelling in solitary places; and a distaste for the assembly of worldly people.

Devotion to the knowledge of the inner self and the vision of the goal of the knowledge of reality—this is declared to be knowledge; that which is otherwise is ignorance. [It is] the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra, appearing as the destruction of passion and hatred.
"But when the sense of 'I' is stilled, O King, knowledge is attained.
Bhagīratha said:
"In this body, it has long been firmly rooted, like a tall tree upon a mountain."
"Tell me, how is this great enjoyment consisting of the sense of 'I' abandoned?
Tryuttula replied:
"By means of human effort, having abandoned the cultivation of the flood of enjoyments,"
Having gone and investigated the truth of the funeral pyre, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) dissolves.
As long as the cage of the bodily mechanisms is not entirely shattered— including shame and all else—
so long does the ego-sense remain manifest, even when one has reached the state of possessing nothing.

If you remain motionless, having abandoned all mental constructs, then you yourself, with the dissolution of ego, are the supreme state. Having attained a state of absolute poverty, free from all desires, devoid of every distinction, and liberated from fear, you have surely gone beyond your enemies.
Having abandoned all prosperity,
with pride stilled and the notion of a body cast aside, he wandered for alms among those very people and has even forsaken me; if you are truly great, then you are indeed great.
The seventy-ninth canto, titled "The Instruction of Bhagīratha," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, having heard this from the mouth of his guru, Bhagīratha,
with the task committed to his mind, became intent upon his own duty. Then, after only a few days had passed, he—

He performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice for the sole purpose of attaining complete renunciation. Discerning between the virtuous and the non-virtuous, he gave away his entire wealth— cows, land, horses, gold, and so forth— to Brahmins, gods, the afflicted, and his kinsmen.
In just three days, having thus renounced everything,
King Bhagīratha was left with nothing remaining but his own clothes. Then, seeing him destitute of all possessions and his subjects and citizens distressed, [he spoke].
He gave his own kingdom to his enemy like a blade of grass to a woman parting her hair.
When his kingdom, city, palace, and realm were overrun by the foe,
he departed from his domain with nothing left but his lower garment.
Where he was not known by name, and where he was not known from his appearance—
there, in villages, forests, or distant places, the steadfast man dwelt.
Thus, in a very short time, all his desires were completely stilled.
Through supreme tranquility, he attained rest within his own self.
Wandering among the islands upon the face of the earth, at one time, by the turn of fate,
he reached that very city which had been seized by his enemy king.
There, that peaceful man begged for alms from those very enemies, as well as from the citizens and the ministers, following the sequence as it presented itself to him.
Those enemies, the citizens, and the ministers recognized him as Bhagīratha.
Then, filled with despondency, they honored him with worship.
Though entreated by his enemy, "O Lord, accept the kingdom," the sage did not accept it;
he disregarded everything except for a blade of grass as food.

Having spent a few days there, he departed for another place, lamented by the people who cried, "Alas, what misery! This is Bhagīratha! Then, in another place, his soul was tranquil, his mind fully rested, and he was happy.
Once, that Bhagīratha, who delighted in the Self, encountered his teacher Tryuttala. Having offered him his own hospitality,
he dwelt for some time with him on a mountain, in a forest, in a village, in a city, and among people.
Having attained equanimity, those two—the teacher and the disciple—stood as equals; established in themselves, they regarded the maintenance of the body as a mere diversion.
"Why is this body maintained? What is gained for us by its being cast off?"
"Let him remain as he is, according to his sequence and his conduct"—
having thus resolved, those two, traveling from forest to forest, remained there;
they rejoiced neither in what is not joy, nor in pleasure, nor in that which is neutral.
Wealth, women, riches, and the eightfold sovereignty—
though offered by even the Siddhas when they are pleased— they considered it as worthless as withered grass.
By their own karma alone, this body must endure until its end, regardless of one's desire.
"Let us remain here by our own karmic destiny alone," they said; then the two stood there.
The two supreme ones rejoiced at the arrival of the Sage, who was born from the sequence of his own noble conduct.
Free from desire for either pleasure or pain, the two self-controlled ascetics were naturally equal in all things, equanimous like space itself.
The Eightieth Sarga, named "The Liberation of Bhagīratha," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then once, in a certain district within a preeminent city,
death carried off a childless king like his own prey. There, the subjects were distressed, and the traditional order of the kingdom having perished, they [sought] a king.
They searched for one endowed with vast splendor of virtue.
Having found Bhagīratha staying in the city, subsisting on alms,
they recognized him, brought him back, and made him their sovereign with their army.
In an instant, Bhagīratha was mounted upon an elephant by his heavy army— like a lake filled with water during the rainy season—
and he was hailed with deep roars: "Victory to Bhagīratha, the Lord of the World!"
The great caves of the lords of mountains became completely filled.
While he was protecting the kingdom there, the original subjects, having lost their king, approached him with respect and spoke thus: "The lord has died. (MU 6.80.5–6)
The subjects said: "O King, he who was formerly made our sovereign by you has been swallowed up by Death, like soft meat by a fish."
"You ought to show favor by protecting each respective kingdom;
for it is not proper to abandon wealth that has come to you unsolicited.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus entreated, the king accepted those words and became the lord of the earth marked by all the oceans;
he was impartial, peaceful-minded, observant of silence, free from passion, and devoid of envy.
Delighting in the singular task of what must and must not be done, and filled with wonder,
he heard that the water of the Gaṅgā was capable of delivering his ancestors— who had perished in the depths of Pātāla and had once been as vast as the ocean— from their state of ruin.
At that time, it is said, the celestial river did not flow upon the earth;
therefore, the offering of a handful of Gaṅgā water became difficult for the ancestors to obtain. Then Bhagīratha brought her down from heaven to the earth.
From that time forth, the king observed a vow regarding the Gaṅgā.
Then, having renounced the kingdom, the peaceful monarch, intent on what was to be done for the sake of spiritual practice, went with his ministers to the dense forest for asceticism.
There, having propitiated Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and Jahnu again and again for thousands of years, he established the Gaṅgā upon the earth.
From that time forth, she— possessing waves of exceeding purity, clinging to the limbs of the Lord of the World which are as white as the moon— [flowed].
The triple-pathed river fell from the vault of heaven to the earth, like the vast succession of great merits descending for high-souled beings.
With its shimmering waves breaking and smiling with masses of foam, it was like the flow of dharma in liquid form, a cluster of blossoms of pure merit.
