From that time forth, during the reign of King Bhagīratha, the triple-pathed river became a highway for the spread of his fame upon the surface of the earth.
The Eighty-first Sarga, titled "The Descent of the Gaṅgā," by Vasiṣṭha.
Adopting this view, which was chosen by Bhagīratha, remain equanimous and composed;
with a tranquil mind, accomplish whatever task arises as it may.
Having first abandoned this [prior view] and then having embraced it yourself, [proceed].
"Remain peaceful within yourself, as immovable as Śikhidhvaja.
Rāma asked:
"Who was this person named Śikhidhvaja, and how did he attain that state?"
"O Brahmin, tell me this again for the further increase of my awakening.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"They existed previously in the Dvāpara age, and they shall exist now as well."
In that very same arrangement, the husband and wife were affectionate toward one another like kinsmen.
Rāma said: "O Blessed One, that which existed before is indeed exactly the same now."
"O best of speakers, tell me, for what purpose will this come to be?
Vasiṣṭha replied: "This is the destiny of the creation of the world, arising from the self-consciousness of Brahmā."
Such a state is indeed eternally unavoidable, born of its own nature:
that one thing, having existed manifoldly, comes into being again and again;
while another, having not existed at all, comes into being, and then ceases to exist entirely.
One [form] manifests clearly through similarity to a previous configuration;
another flashes forth through partial similarity to a previous configuration.
Just as waves in a lake are both similar and dissimilar, so it is with these.
In that same way, various other conditions are seen within the cycle of existence.
Therefore, O Rāghava, lord of men, there will again be a king of great splendor who shall be spoken of; hear this account of his.
In the past, during the Dvāpara age, when the seventh Manu had passed away,
in this fourth cycle of four ages within this current creation, in Jambudvīpa— situated not far from the tranquil Vindhya mountains and crowded with elephants— there occurred [this event].
In the city of the Mālavas, there was a glorious lord named Śikhidhvaja;
he was endowed with fortitude, generosity, and compassion, possessed of patience, tranquility,
and self-restraint, heroic, of auspicious conduct, honorable, and a mine of many virtues.
He is the performer of all sacrifices, the conqueror of all archers,
the accomplisher of all tasks, and the sustainer of the earth in a form never seen before;
he is graceful, affectionate, sweet, clever, and a delight to the wise.
He was handsome, blessed with virtue, majestic, and devoted to the Dharma;
he was a knower of things to be known, a giver of all prosperity,
an enjoyer free from attachment, and a perfect listener to all that is heard.
Disregarding floods of wealth and casting aside women like blades of grass, he—
though still a child— attained heaven while his father was alive; and having conquered the quarters through his supreme vigor, that self-controlled youth reached the age of sixteen.
Surely he adorned the circle of the earth with the perfection of excellent sovereignty;
wise and whitening the quarters with his fame, he remained free from anxiety while protecting his subjects according to dharma, together with his ministers.
Then, as the years passed and spring blossomed forth in full splendor,
while the flowers were unfolding and the moonbeams were shimmering,
[he dwelt] amidst the swings of clusters of blossoms within the inner sanctum of the forest boughs.
In that place, white as camphor-dust, with moving leaf-doors,
fragrant and possessing canopies of shimmering flower-clusters,
while pairs of bees sang loudly together in the dense thickets; (6.81.21–22)
As a sweet breeze, cool as the rays of the moon, blew— caressing the groves of plantain and *kandalī* trees and the tender foliage on the banks—
his heart became newly and intensely longing for his beloved.
Intoxicated by sweet liquors, fragrant with an abundance of flowers,
and swelling with the pride of spring, he indulged in this kingdom of his imagination amidst the swings of the garden groves and the playful lotus ponds.
When shall I place upon my lap, on the couch, my beloved and charming young woman, whose breasts are like lotus buds and who is adorned with flowers?
When, like a bee among the creepers of lotuses, shall I [embrace] my female bee upon the swings?
"I shall lead this young girl, who clings to my creeper-like arms, away from her restlessness.
When will that moon-beautiful woman, tormented by love for my sake, come to desire a bed of lotus stalks, jasmine garlands, and clusters of kunda flowers and moons?"
Thus becoming absorbed in thought and intent upon gathering flowers,
he wandered through the forest edges and flowery groves,
as well as upon the swings in the pleasure gardens at the water's edge and among the playful lotus ponds.
In houses surrounded by creepers, in various garden grounds,
and in places adorned with descriptions of the arrangement of forests and groves,
he took delight with his mind intent on stories filled with the sentiment of erotic love.
He worshipped the maidens, whose creeper-like tresses were tossed by breaths shimmering with charming smiles, and whose breasts were like golden jars;
thus did his wise ministers perceive his newly formed resolve.

Indeed, the ability to discern intentions from outward gestures is the supreme qualification for the office of a minister. Then, the thoughtful circle of ministers requested the daughter of the lord of Surāṣṭra— who was endowed with youth— for his marriage.
In accordance with the prescribed rites, he took as his wife that most excellent woman, endowed with beauty and youth,
who was like a reflection of himself;
she was known on earth by the name Cūḍālā, a beauty fit for a king.
Having obtained that husband, she shone like a lotus pond in full bloom.
Śikhidhvaja caused Cūḍālā, whose eyes were like blue lotuses,
to blossom with affection, just as the sun beautifies a lotus plant with its splendor.

The affection between those two, whose minds were dedicated to one another, increased like a young creeper nourished by the sprinklings of gestures, expressions, and amorous sports. With all affairs entrusted to his ministers, he lived in great happiness, having established his subjects in security.
Like a royal swan with a lotus-pond, he took delight with that beloved wife in the inner apartments,
upon swings, in walkways of sandalwood and aloe,
on swings adorned with *mandāra* garlands, and amidst plantain and *kandalī* trees.
In the outskirts of cities, at the edges of forests, on the horizons, and by the lakes;
in the wildernesses, at the close of day, and among the *jambu*, *jambīra*, and *śāli* trees—
everything they did for one another was a source of delight.

Like the beauty of heaven and earth, they were never separated due to their constant performance of the six seasonal sacrifices; and because of their mutual affection for each other's activities, they both became experts in the entire range of arts.
Having attained a state of mutual blending, these two assumed a single essential nature,
as if their respective forms had been transferred to one another while remaining intact within each other's hearts.
Even the mastery of all scriptures and the like, as well as artistic skill, issued from the mouth of the Lord.
Like a child taking up objects from a vessel, she became proficient in all matters;
she learned dancing, instrumental music, singing, and so forth from the mouth of Cūḍālā,
and thereafter she became exceedingly skilled in the arts.
In the Kali age, like the moon and the sun at the new moon, those two shone together with mutual splendor;
dwelling within each other's hearts, both remained as if established in unity.
Abiding thus, they were of one essence, each having no lover other than the other.
Like the inseparable fragrance and flower, like Śiva and Pārvatī dwelling upon the earth;
with intellects beautiful through their cleverness and experts in the meaning of all scriptures,
they were like Kamalā and the Lord of Kamalā who had descended to the world for sport.

Out of affection, they were gracious and sweet, possessing equal knowledge and insight; devoted to following one another's lead, they were experts in the ways of the world. Endowed with the full range of arts and skills, they were like shining elixirs of aesthetic flavor.

With their cool, smooth, and charming limbs, they were like two risen moons; that couple of unsurpassed splendor shone within the inner apartments, lovely with the playful enjoyment of sovereign luxury, moving slowly under the influence of blooming passion and love,
like a pair of royal swans in the hollows of a lotus grove belonging to Brahmā.
The eighty-second canto, titled "The Play of Śikhidhvaja," by Vasiṣṭha.
Thus, for many years, the couple, filled with intense longing,
took delight day by day in the endless sports of youth. Then, as many years passed in their recurring cycle, [the time came].
"Youth gradually ebbs away like water from a broken jar.
In time, a slight detachment, like that of an autumn leaf, touched the heart of this couple, even as they were still fully immersed in passion."
Overcome by the latent impression of dispassion and standing in solitude, he reflected upon this worldly course of the couple as being thus impermanent:
"What indeed in this delusion within the cavern of saṃsāra is truly captivating?"
In this world of worldly activity, as fragile as a mass of shifting waves,
death is as unavoidable as the falling of a ripe fruit; and old age stands ready to strike, like a frost-bolt upon a lotus.
Life flows away incessantly, like water from the palm of the hand;
while all other desires remain as brief as a gourd vine in the rainy season, craving alone has grown long.
Youth passes away just like the current of a mountain river.
Life is as unreal as a magician’s trick, its duration lasting but a moment.
Pleasures flee like arrows shot from a bowstring;
miseries fall upon the mind like bold vultures pouncing on raw meat.

The body is as fragile as a bubble in the waters during the rainy season; worldly activity is devoid of essence, like the pithless core of a plantain tree, and brings about detachment; youth has swiftly passed away, like a beloved mistress leaving one who desires her.
Discontent has come upon me by force, like a tree of enmity.
In this wretched cycle of existence, what indeed could there be that is truly auspicious,
such that having attained it, the mind is no longer tormented by the various conditions of life?
Having thus resolved upon that pair as the medicine for the disease of worldly existence,
he reflected for a long time upon the scripture esteemed as pertaining to the inner self (*adhyātma*).
By the sole mantra of self-knowledge, the cholera known as *saṃsṛti* [is cured].

Having resolved that [the world] would subside, they remained devoted to that alone; with their minds fixed on that, their life-breaths directed toward that, their conversations concerning that, and taking refuge in those who knew that,
they became intent on worshipping that alone and engaged in activities for its sake.
Right there, intensely absorbed in their practice and awakening one another,
they remained for a long time, filled with mutual delight and engaged in that same endeavor. Then, that young woman [sang] verses of pleasing cadence without ceasing.
Having heard from the mouths of those who know the inner self the meanings of the scriptures that are capable of delivering one across,
he reflected in this manner upon his own self day and night,
whether inactive or active, with a mind that was pure in its disposition.
First, let me examine my own self: "What might this 'I' be?
Whose delusion is this regarding the world, how has it arisen, and where does it reside?
First, the body is insentient and mute; the certainty is simply that "I am not this."
This is established even from childhood and is experienced at the time of death as well.
Furthermore, its group of organs of action is not distinct [from the self] in the sense of being composed of parts;
because there is no difference between a part and the whole, it is indeed insentient.
In this same way, the group of sense organs is seen to be entirely insentient,
since it is impelled by the mind, just as a clod of earth on the ground is driven by a staff.
And I consider the mind itself to be insentient, though it possesses the power of volition.
Like a stone propelled by slings, the intellect is driven by the determinations of the mind;
thus, the intellect, though essentially of the nature of determination, is insentient—this is the certainty.
Like a river in a channel, it is carried along at its own will by the ego-sense.
Egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) is likewise devoid of essence, insentient, and of the nature of a corpse;
it is produced by the individual soul (*jīva*), like a delusive spirit conjured by a child.
And the *jīva* is of the nature of mental construction, consisting of vital breath, and situated in the heart.
The essence of semen lives within by means of something else.
Ah! Now it is understood by him who is stained by the mental impression (*cetya-ullekha*):
the individual soul (*jīva*) lives by means of the living self, which is the form of consciousness and the nature of the Self.
The individual soul (jīva), possessing the objects of thought like a cloud, lives by means of its very nature as consciousness (cid-rūpa),
just as fragrance [lives] through the wind or the current of a river through the sky.
By taking refuge in the unreal, insentient portion of the object of thought, the body of consciousness becomes insentient.
For even fire, when it enters a great block of wood, abandons its own form. Whatever appears—whether existent or non-existent—the consciousness itself consumes from within;
completely casting off its own form, it becomes that very object in an instant.
"Thus, although this nature of consciousness is itself inert, void, and devoid of volition, it perceives by being directed toward an object of cognition, awakened by another.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā asked: "By whom is this consciousness made conscious?"
Thus he reflected, and after a long time he awakened to this:

"Aha! After a long time, that which is to be known—the state free from affliction—has finally been realized; for once the mind has been measured by the consciousness, one is never again pained by anything."
For these—the mind, intellect, senses, and so forth, ending with the play of consciousness—are indeed non-existent, yet they appear as if existent; oh, how they abide like a second moon!
Only the Great Consciousness exists here, which is called "Great Being."

Stainless, equal, pure, and having the nature of being devoid of ego; having the form of pure consciousness, it is auspicious, pure awareness alone, and infallible. Shining forth once and for all, stainless, and eternally risen, it remains established.

That which is designated by names such as *sat*, *Brahman*, and *Paramātman*—the objects of cognition, the insentient, the mind (*citta*), and so forth—is not different from Her, nor is She separate from them.
By Her this consciousness (*cit*) is perceived; She is the Śrī of Consciousness, and she is remembered as the primordial Consciousness (*cid*).
This consciousness, which is indestructible, is its unimpaired form;
it thus expands within itself through the forms of the objects of mind, intellect, and senses, like water through the movements of ripples, droplets, and waves.
The existence of all beings and objects in the world manifests within its own interior;
that which is this [manifestation] is indeed the supreme form of that Great Consciousness.
This very lioness of pure consciousness has arisen in perfect equanimity.

Existence remains as a single, non-dual reality, appearing as if it were manifold through the expansion of the world; for here in this world, no existence other than that [primordial one] is possible,
just as various golden ornaments are nothing other than gold.

Just as it arises, that Great Consciousness perceives itself by itself in such a form— through its own nature as consciousness and its fluidity— as the state of waves and so forth, like water. Because the world is of the nature of consciousness, the Great Consciousness arises, as it were, though it is actually without arising.
Just as a whirlpool in the ocean, though possessing form, is essentially nothing but water due to its fluidity;
so too am I pure consciousness alone, expanded yet devoid of the sense of "I.
For that [consciousness], there is neither birth nor death, nor are there the states of being or non-being.
The destruction of this sky of pure consciousness can never occur;
this conscious self is indivisible, unburnable, and eternally stainless.
Oh, after such a long time, I have become peaceful and fully extinguished!
With my mind exiled [from worldly objects], I dwell in liberation like the ocean without Mount Mandara.
Having taken refuge in the space of the Self— which appears as non-existent, yet is utterly pure, infinite, unborn, and immutable— I rejoice for a long time without effort.
This space is infinite, as are the multitudes of beings beginning with the mountains;
this entire universe, including the gods and demons, is composed of that [universe] and is uncreated.
Like an army made of clay or straw, everything is merely earth.
In that same way, the existence of the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing consists solely of pure consciousness (cinmātra).
This oneness, this duality, "I," "not-I," and so forth—what delusion and confusion is there here? How, for whom, from where, or where could they exist?
Therefore, I am infinite and effortless, abiding in the tranquil void;
having attained final nirvana, I am extinguished; I abide in truth, free from fever.
Whether it be insentient or sentient, whatever indeed one perceives as an object of thought—
That form, whose essence is pure existence, abides within the Great Consciousness as its own nature.
Therefore, here there is neither "I" nor "another," nor the possibility of existence or non-existence;
everything is peaceful, without support, and established as the absolute alone.
Thus, intent on inquiry, she realized through supreme awakening this reality of the Supreme Self as it truly exists;
with the playful movements of her mind—passion, fear, and delusion—completely stilled, she became tranquil like a streak of cloud in an autumn sky.
The Chapter named "The Awakening of Cūḍālā."
The eighty-third canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, day after day, by virtue of that delight in her own self, she—
She remained eternally established in her natural state through inward-turned awareness.
Free from passion, free from disease, free from attachment, free from the pairs of opposites, and free from desire,
she neither abandoned nor took up anything, moving according to the conduct inherent in her nature.
Having crossed over the ocean of existence, with the web of doubts stilled,
her inner self is completely filled with the supreme attainment of the Great Self;
she, who was long exhausted, now rests, having firmly established herself in the Self.
"Because she had transcended all comparisons, she reached a state beyond description.
Thus, that queen of his, Cūḍālā of excellent complexion,
in a very short time indeed attained the realization of all that is to be known.
Having understood how this world has come into being as some kind of illusory vibration of consciousness,
and how everything dissolves again, she shone forth;
having attained rest in that state where no delusion whatsoever is seen.
Free from agitation, she shone like a streak of clear autumnal cloud; with her gaze steady and undisturbed, she consoled herself within herself,
standing still like an aged bull that has reached the grassy peak of a mountain.

By virtue of her intense practice of self-discrimination, she shone with the dawning of the Self, like a beautiful flowering creeper that has newly sprouted. Then, on one occasion, Śikhidhvaja beheld her of faultless limbs.

Beholding her unprecedented beauty, he spoke with a smile: "O slender one, you shine forth even more than before, as if endowed with renewed youth, adorned again and again, like the sovereignty over the world."
O beloved, you shine most intensely, as if filled with the essence of nectar, as if having attained a state that is difficult to reach,
and as if overflowing with a flood of bliss;
you bear a beautiful body that is both serene and lovely.
O lovely woman, you have come surpassing the moon with some indescribable splendor.
My dear, I see your mind as tranquil yet powerful, free from the misery of worldly enjoyment, attained to equanimity, profound and serene.

O beloved, I behold your mind as something that treats the three worlds as mere straw, which has drunk in the entirety of the triple universe, which is radiant with infinity, and yet gentle; O illustrious one,
it cannot be matched by any object of worldly power or pleasure.
Your mind rivals Mount Meru and the beautiful Ocean of Milk;
through those very limbs of yours, tender as young plantains, lotus stalks, and new shoots,
you appear to have attained growth without ever losing your composure.
Thus, remaining in that very same configuration,
you have attained a different state, like a creeper at the change of seasons.
Have you drunk the nectar of immortality, or have you attained universal sovereignty?

"Or has a practice leading to immortality been attained through the methods of yoga? O lady with eyes like blue lotuses, what unattainable thing have you obtained that is superior even to sovereignty, the wish-fulfilling gem, or the three worlds?"
Cūḍālā said:
"Having abandoned this form of 'nothing-at-all,' I have come;
because of that, I remain as the Illustrious One (Śrīmatī), whose nature is 'nothing-at-all'."
Whatever there is, and whatever is nothing at all—I know that as it truly exists, according to its arising and according to its passing away; by that I abide as one who is illustrious.
I am satisfied by enjoyments even when they have not been experienced, as if they were already enjoyed and long since departed.
I do not rejoice, nor do I become angry; therefore I remain possessed of splendor.
I delight alone in the solitary heart that resembles space;
I do not delight in royal pastimes, and therefore I remain possessed of splendor.
For I abide in the Self alone, not in forests, gardens, or palaces;
nor do I dwell amidst floods of enjoyments or upon couches; therefore, I remain as the Illustrious One (Śrīmatī).
I am indeed the sovereign of the worlds, though my form consists of nothing at all.
Thus I abide in the Self alone; therefore, I am established as Śrīmatī. I am one thing, yet I am not this; I am not that other thing, nor am I this either.
I am everything, or I am nothing at all; therefore, I am established as Śrīmatī.
"That which I see, I do not see; that which I see is something else entirely"—thus I perceive correctly, and by that I abide in glory.
I seek neither pleasure nor wealth, nor misfortune, nor any other state.
I am satisfied with whatever is obtained; therefore, I remain possessed of splendor.

Together with my companions—who, through their knowledge of that [truth], have subdued both aversion and passion regarding the perspectives of the scriptures—I find delight; therefore, I remain possessed of splendor.
Whatever I perceive here with the rays of my vision, or with the senses, or with the mind—indeed, O dear one, that is nothing at all.
But when devoid of those, I perceive that which appears as "nothingness"; thus I see correctly, O Lord, and I have long been awakened. Chapter named "The Attainment of Cūḍālā’s Self" (MU 6.83.31).
The eighty-fourth canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
To that fair-faced woman who was speaking thus, resting within her own self, [he replied].
"O you who speak incoherent nonsense! You are a fool!"— saying this softly, the king,
suspecting his beloved to be deluded by a mind greedy for sensual enjoyments,
laughed and spoke, not having understood the meaning of her words.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O fair-complexioned one, you are a girl who prattles nonsense;
you take delight in the play of words. O daughter of a king, enjoy yourself!"
Having abandoned something, he who has gone to a state of "nothingness" that is directly present—

how indeed can he, having abandoned the reality of what is directly perceived, be considered beautiful? He who abandons enjoyments while thinking, "I am satisfied even without enjoying them," [is truly wise].

How indeed can he shine when he has abandoned food, drink, and the like as if out of anger? How indeed can he shine who, firm in intellect, stands alone by himself, having renounced all— vehicles, food, beds, and so forth?
How indeed can that person of wicked intellect shine, who possesses the conviction: "I myself am nothing at all, yet I am the Lord of the World"?
Having abandoned all social associations, he dwells alone with himself in solitude within his own self.
How indeed can he who stands like one staring into a pit appear beautiful?
How indeed can he who utters such ravings as "I am not the body," "I am something else," or "I am nothing at all"— for [in truth] everything is indeed [Brahman]— appear beautiful?
"That which I see, I do not see; that which I see is something else entirely"—how indeed can he who considers such talk to be unreal appear beautiful?
Therefore, you are deluded, you are childish, you are fickle, O playful woman!

"O beautiful one, play with various playful conversations; play! Having laughed with a loud laugh at his beloved in this way, Śikhidhvaja rose at midday to bathe and departed from the women's quarters.
"It is a pity that he did not find rest within himself and did not understand my words;
'He is but a king,' thought Cūḍālā, distressed by the failure of her own efforts.
Thus it was then, my dear, between those two whose dispositions were such.
With those royal pastimes,
O Rāma, that day passed away; in due course, many months, seasons, and years elapsed there for that affectionate couple.
Once, although she was eternally satisfied and free from desire,

Cūḍālā herself felt a longing for the sake of the power to travel through the air as a sport. Then, that princess, for the purpose of attaining the power of traveling through the air, [prepared herself].
Disregarding all enjoyments and having retired to a secluded place, she alone,
devoted to solitude, sat with her limbs settled in her own posture and practiced for a long time the upward-moving vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Rāma:
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving,
is experienced as the fruit of vibration, which is known by the name "action."

Tell me, O Brahmin, what playful movement of intense practice is this for me, who am endowed with singular effort, that has resulted in such things as traveling through the sky? Whether one knows the Self or does not know the Self, it is likewise performed effortlessly for the sake of attaining perfection.
"O Lord, tell me truly how one accomplishes this.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"My dear friend, in this world, the object to be accomplished can arise in three ways from all sides."

O Rāghava, that which is to be accepted, that which is to be rejected, and likewise that which is to be disregarded are all of the nature of the self. Indeed, by diligent effort, that which is to be accepted is accomplished;
having understood it, that which is to be rejected is abandoned; and that which is to be disregarded is the middle path between these two.
Whatever brings delight is acceptable to one of false understanding;
that which is the opposite is unacceptable, while the wise know that which is intermediate to be worthy of indifference.
When everything is composed of the Self for the wise man of right understanding who knows, [then all is equal].
At that time, only three positions are possible, none other:
either this entire universe is [created] at some point as a mere play, or it is not;
or He regards it with indifference, like a glance cast from the eye, or He does not.
O Rāma, that which is characterized by equanimity is to be accepted by the wise, yet it has become something to be rejected by the deluded;
it is to be abandoned by one of expansive dispassion. Listen now as to how the sequence of accomplishment (*siddhikrama*) occurs:
all accomplishments have their means of realization (*sādhana*) in place, time, action, and substance.

It gladdens the living soul here, just as spring gladdens the earth. Among these four, the ritual action of the first kalpa is for the sake of accomplishing success (*siddhi*) and so forth; for those stages are, in sequence, identical with that [first kalpa] for the practitioner.
The description of the sequence of practices involving pills, collyrium, swords, and so forth—
let that detailed exposition remain aside for now, as it would detract from the subject at hand.
[Now follows] the description of the sequence of practices involving gems, medicinal herbs, ascetic heat, and mantras.

Let this elaboration here rest for now, as it detracts from the subject at hand. Even the elaboration that [liberation] comes from residing on Śrīśaila, in a land of the Siddhas, or on Mount Meru and so forth, is merely born of ritual action and thus detracts from the subject at hand.

Therefore, listen to this practice of training in the vital breaths and other winds, which yields the fruit of supernatural powers, as it arises in the context of the story of Śikhidhvaja. Having completely abandoned all latent impressions (vāsanās) regarding objects other than the goal to be attained, along with their very roots.
Through the contraction of the gates such as the anus, through the sequence of actions such as assuming the proper postures,

through the purification of food and seat, through the contemplation of the meaning of the teachings of the virtuous scriptures, through right conduct, through association with good people, through the renunciation of everything, and through a comfortable posture— // MU_6,84.34-35 //
O Rāma of noble vows, through the intense practice of breath control over some period of time,
and by abandoning anger, greed, and the like, as well as the renunciation of worldly enjoyments,
the senses become thoroughly subject to one's command in the processes of relinquishing, grasping, and restraining.

For a man who knows that [Self] is the sovereign, all vital breaths are like servants. O Rāghava, all prosperities, from sovereignty up to liberation, are achieved by everyone through the subjection of the bodily winds.
Circular in shape and situated at the location of the *kanda*,
the channel named Antraveṣṭanikā rests upon hundreds of other channels;
it resembles the head of a lute and is like a whirlpool in water.
The first of the scripts is established in the form of the syllable Oṃ, existing like the curls of hair;
it is said to be present among all living beings, from gods, asuras, and humans, to deer, crocodiles, birds, insects, and everything down to those born from lotuses.
Her matted locks are coiled like the body of the lord of serpents sleeping from the cold;
her white earrings are like the moon melting away before the fire at the end of an aeon.
She is restless with the movement of water clearly visible below the opening between her eyebrows and her mind.
Constantly floating, as it were, upon streams of aesthetic flavor (rasa),
she remains within that interior which is as delicate as the core of a plantain tree; therein,
the power of the vital breath (vāta-śakti) vibrates with a radiant movement, like [the sound] in a flute.
She is called by the name Kuṇḍalinī because she flows in a coiled form;
she is the supreme power of living beings, bestowing the vitality of all powers.
Constantly exhaling in the form of a hissing serpent, she is like an enraged female snake.
Standing firm with her face turned upward, she has become the cause of the vital pulsations (spandas).
When the vital breath (prāṇānila) enters the heart, the seat of Kuṇḍalinī,
then consciousness arises within, which is the seed of the elements and their subtle constituents (tanmātras).
When Kuṇḍalinī vibrates within the body like a bee upon a lotus,
then consciousness arises within through the awakening brought about by a gentle touch.
By means of that gentle touch upon the channel of the penis and the umbrella of the linga, [consciousness arises].

Just as consciousness arises intensely, so does Kuṇḍalinī arise with speed. Within her, all the channels (nāḍīs) connected to the cavity of the heart arise and dissolve like rivers in the great ocean.
"Because it is eternally of the nature of wind and is ever intent on vibration,
it is declared to be the one primordial seed of all consciousnesses.
Rāma said:
For consciousness (*cit-saṃvit*) exists as all-pervading, indeed unconditioned by space, time, and so forth.
By what means does its manifestation clearly arise from the sheath of Kuṇḍalinī?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
O sinless one, truth—consciousness and awareness—is found at all times and in all places;
however, its manifestation occurs in certain instances due to the influence of the elements and their subtle causes (*tanmātras*).
Consciousness, though present everywhere, appears to fluctuate within bodies.
Though omnipresent like sunlight, it manifests most intensely within the essence of jewels.
That a thing is seen as one thing or another— now vanished, now dormant, and now swollen— is the manifestation of its own inherent nature.
O sinless one, listen further as I shall explain to you in due order how this process, consisting of pure consciousness, arises intensely within bodies;
how the entire collection of beings, both conscious and unconscious, as well as the whole of space [arises].
Everything is pure consciousness alone, pure existence alone, and pure emptiness, like the sky.
For that which is pure consciousness and pure existence is changeless and free from affliction;
it abides somewhere as consciousness itself, having created the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
That pentad has entered into a state of duality, from the louse-egg to the end, through its own self-awareness,
with its modifications and so forth contained within it, just as a hundred lamps arise from a single lamp;
[all this occurs] by the mere existence of itself, which takes the form of a fragment of volition.
In this world, five groups proceed; some of them attain the state of gods,
some the state of animals and so forth, some the state of gold and so forth,
some the state of stones and so forth, and some the state of material objects and so forth.
Thus it is established that the world is merely the vibration of the pentad;
O descendant of Raghu, pure consciousness (cit-saṃvit) exists everywhere here.
It is solely by virtue of the pentad that the designation "sentience" is applied to the body and so forth.
In water, there is that which is called inert motion, while in stationary objects and the like, there is that which is called inert matter.

Just as in oceans one perceives "this is water" and "this is a wave," or "this is the bottom," so too within the five elements, one perceives here consciousness in its restless form and there inert matter.
Just as one might wonder, "Is this ocean moving toward me from here?"—
a doubt that is unwarranted— so too is this group of five, consisting of both the insentient and the sentient.
The pentad beginning with the body is animate and throbbing with life, while mountains and the like are insentient.
O sinless one, the immovable and other things are set in motion by the wind through the power of their own nature. O descendant of Raghu, natures are not to be questioned;
why would anyone be ridiculed for asking what causes coldness and heat in snow and fire?

For the continuities of the five [aggregates], which have grasped portions of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and undergo transformations of intensified states, are indeed fit to be subjected to inquiry; for these [continuities],
being overturned by portions of latent impressions, are led from here and there.
By a wise man who is capable of inquiry,
whether regarding the inauspicious or the auspicious, that [consciousness] is what is questioned;
for it is the fivefold [group of senses] with awakened latent impressions that is so questioned, not the one with dormant latent impressions.
One should apply that [investigation] where the fruit of inquiry is experienced; one should not strike at the sky with one's fists.
For the heaps of the five categories, beginning with Meru, are as minute as the tips of blades of grass.
These beings, from insects up to Viriñca, are both stationary and moving;
some have dormant latent impressions (*vāsanā*), such as the species of stationary plants,
while others have awakened latent impressions, such as humans, gods, and so forth.
Some have the holes of their own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), such as animals and the like;
some have their impressions exhausted, such as these who partake in liberation.
These [distinctions] are produced by the mind, intellect, and so forth, within their respective cognitions alone.
By means of the five aggregates associated with hands, feet, and so forth, certain designations are established;
by others, such as animals and the like, other designations are fashioned;
and by still others, such as stationary beings, various forms of consciousness are produced in a different manner.

Thus, O virtuous one, these various fivefold aggregates manifest through forms that are moving or unmoving, sentient or insentient, in their beginning, middle, and end. For among these, O Great-minded One, there is but a single atom of volition.
The seed of these creations is the tree of space;
within them, my dear, the sense organs are indeed the flowers that possess the fragrance of their objects.
The flickering activities are the radiant, trembling clusters of blossoms, while desires are the bees.

The various worlds are its clusters and shrubs; Malaya and Meru are its sprouts; here, the clouds are the playful creepers, and the ten directions are its tendrils. Whatever beings exist at present and whatever shall come to be in the future—
O descendant of Raghu, those worlds are their innumerable fruits. Indeed, O Rāma, these five trees have such seeds;
they arise by themselves through their own nature and perish by themselves in the course of time.
They themselves undergo diversity and, due to long-standing dullness, they manifest;
yet, being well-discriminated, they come to rest like waves in the ocean.
From whatever cause they rise up, from that very cause they themselves subside.

These, like waves upon the ocean, arise from dullness and discernment. O Rāma, those masses of the play of the five [senses] which have reached dissolution through the power of discernment do not return here to existence; others wander repeatedly throughout the world.
The eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Discerning the Fivefold," by Vasiṣṭha.
This is the seed-syllable of the pentad which resides within the interior of Kuṇḍalinī;
in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇamāruta*), it vibrates within her at all times.
That Kuṇḍalinī, ending in the letter *s*, is stainless, consisting of the digits of vibration, touch, and consciousness.
She is called *kalā* because she is quickly measured by the act of measuring; she is called *cit* because she is consciousness.
Because of living, she has become the life-force (*jīva*) of living beings; because of thinking, she abides as the mind (*manas*).
Through volition, she herself is volition (*saṅkalpa*); through cognition, she is known as the intellect (*buddhi*).
Having entered into a portion of the ego (ahaṅkāra), this very power, known as the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka),
abides in the body as the unsurpassed life-force (jīvaśakti) called Kuṇḍalinī;
having assumed the state of apāna, it flows constantly downward.
The one with a similar name stands in the middle; the one called udāna is situated above.
Below, however, she exists in the form of apāna alone, while in the middle she is always in the form of soma.
In a healthy man, she remains in the back in the form of udāna alone.
If it goes downward despite every effort and is not held back by exertion,
then the person meets death through that [force] which has emerged with violence.
If the entire [breath] moves upward and is not restrained by the proper method, [the same occurs].
When that [wind] has been forcibly expelled, the person meets with death; however,
if it should remain entirely within the self, having abandoned its upward, downward, and outward movement,
then a disease arises for the living being due to the obstruction of the waste and the vital air.
From the impairment of the general channels, the occurrence of general diseases arises;
from the impairment of the principal channels, the occurrence of principal diseases arises.
Rāma said:

"O Lord of Sages, what is the cause of their destruction and what is the cause of their arising within this body—both mental afflictions and physical diseases? Please explain this to me quickly and accurately.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
Mental anxieties and physical ailments—these two are the causes of suffering.
One should know that the cessation of these is happiness; their destruction is called liberation.
Sometimes they arise alternately, and sometimes they arise simultaneously.
In turn, at times those two—mental distress and physical illness—occur within the little body.

They know physical suffering as *vyādhi* (disease), while that called mental distress (*ādhi*) consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). One should know that both have their root in delusion, which exists when the knowledge of reality has perished.

Due to the power of ignorance regarding reality, while passion and hatred incessantly undergo attenuation within the heart without the subduing of one's own senses, there arises the dense delusion of the blindness of dullness, thinking, "This has been attained; this has not. (MU 6.85.15)
Mental anxieties arise like mist in the rainy season, when desires throb violently because the mind has not been conquered through folly,
and by the consumption of bad food and the traversing of evil regions.
Due to the influence of adverse times, the manifestation of evil deeds,
the fault of associating with wicked people, and the arising of base thoughts;
or due to the depletion or the fullness [of the elements], there is an unpleasant flow within the channels.
When the vital breath (prāṇa) falls into a state of instability, like a traveler on a new path entering a wrong road,
disease arises in the body from the humors (doṣa) as the cause of its disordered state,
just as the alteration of the river's form occurs due to the rainy season and the summer heat.
Whether it be from a previous life or this one, whether auspicious or inauspicious, whichever cognition is predominant, that very one directs [the being] accordingly in that sequence.
In this way, mental afflictions and physical diseases arise within the five elements.
Listen, O upholder of the Raghu lineage, as to how they perish:
for there are two kinds of mental anguish (*ādhi*) here in this world—the common and the essential.
The common is said to be that which pertains to worldly transactions, while the essential consists of [the cycle of] birth.
Worldly mental afflictions (*vyāvahārika-ādhi*) perish simply by obtaining what is desired;

afflictions born of existence (*ādhibhava*) are destroyed by the exhaustion of their cause; and even physical diseases (*vyādhi*) are likewise cured. Yet, O Rāghava, without the knowledge of the Self (*ātma-jñāna*), no mental affliction is truly eradicated.

Indeed, through the further realization that it is a rope, the snake in the rope perishes. O Rāma, the destruction of the essence of mental and physical afflictions is the uprooter of them all, like a river in the rainy season uproots the creepers on its banks.
But diseases not born of mental afflictions are destroyed by substances, mantras, and auspicious rites—
as taught in the medical treatises and other sciences— just as heat is dispelled by clouds;
and bathing, mantras, medicinal herbs, and the means of instruction have all been mastered.
"By you, what else is taught in the medical treatises?
Rāma replied:
"How does disease arise from the primary cause, and how is it destroyed?"
Through another method, beginning with the power of mantras, merit, and so forth—
Vasiṣṭha says: "When the mind is disturbed, this body does not experience [objects] correctly."
For just as a person who is enraged does not see what is right before him,
so too, disregarding what has been attained, one pursues a path that is not the way,
having abandoned the natural path like a deer afflicted by an arrow.
Due to agitation, the vital breaths abandon their equilibrium and flow [irregularly] within the body, like waters on a riverbank disturbed by a herd of elephants;
when the prāṇa flows unevenly, the channels fall into disorder.
Just as when a king is improperly established, the order of the castes and stages of life [falters],
so too some channels reach fullness while others become empty;
for when the vital breath (prāṇa) has departed from a region, it is like rivers in all seasons [drying up].
Food that is under-digested, undigested, or even over-digested leads only to harm through the improper movement of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*),
just as the current of a river carries logs to wherever it reaches.

In the same way, the vital breath (prāṇavāta) leads the foods inward to its own abode. Those foods which remain in conflict within the body undergo disease as a result of their inherent nature of transformation.
In this way, disease arises from poverty, and it perishes through the absence of poverty.
Just as diseases are destroyed by mantras, hear now that procedure;
and how myrobalan fruits cause purgation by their very nature.
Through the power of cultivation, the letters *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and so forth, likewise [arise]. O virtuous one,
by means of pure and meritorious action and service to the holy,
the mind attains purity, just as gold is purified by a touchstone.
O Rāghava, when the mind is pure, bliss increases within the body,
just as clarity appears in the world when the full moon has risen in a cloudless sky.
When the *sattva* is purified, these vital breaths (*prāṇavāyus*) flow in their proper sequence.
In that way, they digest the foods, and by that, disease is destroyed.
Thus, O You, have been declared the sequence of the destruction and arising of mental and physical ailments.
Now, through the discourse on Kuṇḍalinī, hear what is relevant to the present subject.

Know that Kuṇḍalinī, situated within, is the primary support for the individual soul (jīva), which is otherwise known as the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka); she is like a flower-cluster to the fragrance [of the soul].
When one remains for a long time after filling her through the practice of inhalation (pūraka), [the breath] becomes steady.
Then there arises the stability of Mount Meru and likewise the swelling of the body.
When the internal space is filled by inhalation and the vital breath is not released,
it is led upward by consciousness alone, having endured the fatigue and exhaustion of the heat.
Like a serpent provoked to fury, it rises up and assumes the likeness of a staff;
having seized all the channels within the body, it becomes bound like a creeper.
Then, it completely floods this entire bodily void.
"Just as a leather bag, when tightly sealed and filled with air, carries a man across the water—
by means of such yoga, through the play of practice,
yogins attain the power of moving through the sky, just as the wretched attain a state of great fortune."
When the Kuṇḍalinī power, through the flow of the Brahmā-nāḍī,
moves outward and upward by twelve finger-breadths at the crown of the head by means of the practice of exhalation (recaka) which restrains the other channels;
He attains stability for a moment, and then there is the vision of the sky.
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, what kind of vision is this that occurs without the rays of the eyes?"
"And how could the true nature of the other senses be thus?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O mighty-armed one, there are no beings that move through the sky who can be apprehended by one who moves upon the earth."
They are perceived by the human senses through superhuman powers that transcend ordinary ignorance;
yet, O Rāghava, they are seen by the eye of the intellect situated close to higher consciousness—
those perfected beings moving in the sky like dreams, even while bestowing their own purposes.
The vision of the perfected ones (*siddha*) is just like the observation of dreams;
the only distinction is that upon attaining the perfected state, there is stability of the object.
Through the practice of exhalation (*recaka*), [the breath] moves from the mouth to the outside at the *dvādaśānta*.
"When the vital breath has been brought to a long-lasting stability, they enter the supreme city.
Rāma said: "Tell me, O Brahmin, how is it that the state of one's own nature does not waver?"
For compassionate speakers are not weary even when questioned about difficult matters.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Power, which is called the inherent nature of things, manifests according to the way it flashes forth from the Self.

It is certain that through creation and so forth, this [universe] likewise attains its state of persistence. Because ignorance is not a real entity, it possesses no power over real things; yet, my dear, a difference is indeed perceived, for autumnal fruit appears even in the spring.
"All this is indeed Brahman of such a nature; through this manifoldness of diversity, it is perceived for the sake of worldly transaction, while its existence is merely conceptualized.
Rāma said:
"How is this body brought to either minuteness or bulkiness, for the purpose of passing through subtle apertures and the like, or for the purpose of filling the sky? Vasiṣṭha replied:
Just as a cut occurs from the joining of wood and a saw,
and fire is born from their friction by its own nature,
so too the flesh-and-lotus machine situated in the belly is joined face-to-face with one another.
Its root is closed at the top and bottom, like the surface of heaven and earth;
within its own abode, the Lakṣmī Kuṇḍalinī is hidden,
like a string of pearls inside the casket of a ruby.
Like a garland of foam from a whirlpool, it constantly hisses;
like a female serpent struck by a staff, it is bent and writhing.
Situated between heaven and earth, it is like the very activity of existence, manifesting in the form of motion.
The bee within the hollow of the heart-lotus, awakened by the honey of consciousness,
[is stirred]; all that— the power-lotus and so forth— is constantly shaken in the heart by internal and external winds from all sides, like a mass of clouds by the winds.
Whatever appears in the sky by its own nature, my dear, the winds thoroughly cause that which is thin and soft to tremble;
struck by those winds, that lotus and so forth wavers.
Just as leaves and other parts [grow] on a tree through mutual friction within the heart, so too the body, being intent upon digesting all tastes and other elements,
generates fire from their mutual friction, like a dense bamboo thicket.
His body, whose very nature is cool and cold, attained intense heat;
it was as if the entire world were pervaded in every limb by the risen sun,
with its rays spreading everywhere and its brilliance appearing like a star.
The golden bee within the heart-lotus of yogis has attained the state of being meditated upon.
When that knowledge, consisting of light, is meditated upon,
it bestows such power that even at night, an object situated a hundred thousand yojanas away is seen.
For that fire, which dwells within the treasury of the heart-lake— abounding with clusters of lotuses made of flesh— the water is its fuel, dried up like that of the submarine fire (vāḍava).
That coolness of the lotus is called the moon, whose nature is apāna.

Thus that fire has arisen from the moon; for the body consists of Agni and Soma. The wise know that whatever is of the nature of heat is designated as the splendor of the sun and fire, while that which is of the nature of cold is called Soma; by these two alone is the world created.

The entire world, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, is produced by the duality of knowledge and ignorance; that very [reality] is thus divided. The wise know that which is conscious, luminous, and characterized by knowledge and so forth to be the sun and fire.
The wise say that non-existence, dullness, darkness, ignorance, and so forth, are Soma.
Rāma said:
"O Sage, I have heard it said that fire arises from Soma, which is of the nature of water."
"Now tell me, O best of speakers, about the origin of Soma.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Agni and Soma exist mutually as both effect and cause within their own established order."
In turn, these two are produced from one another as equals:
like the seed and the sprout, O dear one, and likewise like day and night; their existence is comparable to shade and sunlight, yet they exist as distinct entities.
For the coexistence of shadow and sunlight is perceived simultaneously;
however, their existence would be perceived as a solitary [object] alone, like day and night.
Furthermore, the causal relationship between these two is said to be of two kinds.
That which arises from the transformation of existence and is born from the transformation of destruction—
when the emergence of a second [entity] from one occurs, as in the case of a sprout and a seed,
that is the relation of cause and effect born from the transformation of existence.
When one perishes, the existence of the second occurs like day and night;
this is the relationship of cause and effect, born from destruction and transformation.
Since the transformation of the nature of existence is established in the sequence of clay and jar, [the effect exists within the cause].
Because perception is unimpeded, no other means of valid cognition is required.
Even non-existence, arising from a single entity and established through the sequence of day and night as the transformation of destruction, attains the status of a primary means of valid cognition.
Those who argue through logic that there is no agency in one's own destruction and so forth should be treated with contempt and cast out, for they deny their own direct experience.
O descendant of Raghu, even non-existence is indeed a valid means of knowledge, just like perception.
For the absence of fire is the proof of coldness among all living beings.
That portion of fire which, through the state of smoke,
attains the nature of a cloud by means of a transformation of its existing form— that fire is the cause of the moon.
Since fire attains the state of water due to its nature of destruction through coldness,
that fire, by way of transformation into destruction, has Soma as its cause.
Having drunk the waters of the seven oceans, the submarine fire [is extinguished] by the emission of smoke.
By attaining the state of a cloud, the sun produces that very [light] in abundance.
Having drunk the lord of the night again and again on the new moon day, the sun vomits it forth during the bright fortnight,
just as a crane spits out a lotus stalk.
Having drunk the cool Soma, which is like nectar and resides at the tip of the mouth,
it becomes the downward-moving breath (*apāna*) and fills the body with water.
That portion of water which, by its subtlety, passes into the state of solar rays, [proceeds further].
Through transformation into the form of fire, that water becomes the cause of fire.
Since water attains the state of fire due to heat by means of its nature of destruction,
that water becomes the cause of fire through the transformation of destruction.
Upon the destruction of fire, the moon is its transformation in the form of existence;
upon the destruction of the moon, fire arises as a transformation produced by friction.
Likewise, when fire reaches its end, it indeed becomes the moon.
Just as the day, having come to its end, indeed becomes night, so too,
between darkness and light, shadow and sunshine, and day and night, a form that is distinct from both is not perceived even by the wise.
Even that which is turbid as a union is the very body of these two;
for just as existence and non-existence are conjoined in a single thing, so too are these two.
Indeed, through both consciousness and inertia, the elements manifest forth.
Just as day and night on the surface of the earth arise from darkness and light,
so too has this existence of the world been commenced by the nature of consciousness and the nature of insentience,
like the lunar body formed from the two mixed elements of water and nectar.
O Rāghava, know the luminous fire and sun to be the form of consciousness (cidrūpa);
know the moon-body to be of the nature of inertia (jaḍātmaka) and the form of darkness (tamas).
When the stainless sun of consciousness is seen, the darkness consisting of worldly existence (bhavāmaya) shall perish.
Just as when the sun in the sky is seen outside, the darkness of the black night [vanishes],
so too when the inert lunar body is perceived, the light of consciousness becomes as if non-existent;
just as the mass of solar radiance [is obscured] by the moon shining at midnight.
Fire reveals the moon, and its own long-lasting radiance illuminates the body;
the moon, too, illuminates the fire while bestowing its own form upon the body.
Yet consciousness (cit), being inactive, unmanifest, and solitary, is not perceived.

Just as light is perceived by means of a lamp, consciousness is apprehended by means of the body itself. Through the mind's orientation toward objects of cognition, there is attainment; that very state is transmigratory existence (saṃsṛti). But for one who is free from objects of cognition, there is no attainment; that indeed is nirvāṇa.
Know that these two, Agni and Soma— the body and the embodied soul— are joined together like a wall and its light, possessing their very existence only through mutual dependence.
[This occurs] when there is an excess of *nirvāṇa* (extinction) and an excess of *jāḍya* (inertia).
O dear one, the abiding of both Agni and Soma occurs solely within the limbs.
Prāṇa is Agni, whose nature is heat; Apāna is the Moon, which is cool.
Like shadow and sunlight, these two are established as moving through the pathways of the mouth.
When the *apāna* has become cool, the hot fire of *prāṇa* enters its presence,
just as a reflection appears in a mirror; and in that same way,
the fire of consciousness [enters] the moon situated within the mechanism of the lotus by means of its radiance— that which consists of water.
Just as one perceives the light of a wall here externally through experience, so too,
whatever consciousness there was at the beginning of transmigration, characterized by cold and heat,
attained the designation of fire and moon; that alone is the creation of men here.
Where the sixteenth digit of the moon is swallowed by the sun for a moment,
and where it is a span’s length from the mouth at its tip— there, fix your feet.
Indeed, it is there in the sky of the heart that the moon has truly reached the solar station.
Surely, remain with pure stillness and establish your footing there.
Fire is said to be heat, and the sun is consciousness; the moon is declared to be coolness.
Establish your footing where these two exist as reflections.
O sinless one, you are a knower of the transits of the bodily moon, sun, and fire;
for here, even at night, you see an object situated a hundred thousand yojanas away. Indeed, in this context, external transits are considered as insignificant as blades of grass.

O dear one, if you perceive the transits, the northern solstice, the proper time, and likewise the equinoxes— whether internal or external— as if they were situated within the bodily winds, just as they are experienced, then you do not grieve here, having attained the supreme state. This concludes the chapter titled "The Yoga of Instruction on the Discernment of Agni and Soma."
The eighty-sixth canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as this [body] of yogis attains both minuteness and grossness, so it is.
O Rāma, listen now to this which I shall explain correctly regarding the body:
within the heart, a spark of fire arises from the interior of the lotus-petal sheath;
it throbs like a golden bee at twilight, or like a flash of lightning in a cloud.
Through the consciousness of growth, he increases rapidly like a whirlwind;
indeed, by virtue of his nature as pure consciousness, he rises like the sun.
Having attained growth in an instant, he possesses the luster of the first sun appearing through the clouds at dawn.
Just as fire melts gold, it melts the entire body along with its limbs;
through skillful means, it even melts stones and the like, which cannot otherwise endure contact with water.
The movement of fire is external, but that which is internal is especially so.
That liquid of the body is subsequently shaken off and carried away somewhere by the vital breath agitated by consciousness, just as mist is carried away by a whirlwind;
deprived of its supporting channels, it remains situated in the void alone.
The power (śakti) is Kuṇḍalinī, emerged like a streak of smoke from the fire;
she has embraced the ego (ahaṅkṛti) along with the individual soul (jīva), mind (manas), intellect (buddhi),
and the rest, and she possesses an inner, throbbing wonder, like a streak of incense smoke.
Whether in a wound, a wall, a stone, the sky, or the ground—
whichever [object] it is joined with, by that means it emerges fully in that very way.
If, my dear, that same consciousness [is applied], then through the sequential taking up of the *rasas*, [the result follows].

It attains fullness through rasa, just as frost is filled with water. Whatever form one contemplates while full of rasa, O Rāma, it quickly assumes that very nature, just as a painter’s lines take on a particular shape in his mind.
Then, by the power of firm resolve, it attains bones within;
like one seated in a mother’s womb, or like a sprout firmly established in the earth,
O Rāghava, it assumes its intended form and dimension.
The vital power attains [the state of] Mount Sumeru or even a blade of grass. You have heard of the accomplishment of powers such as atomization (aṇimā) through yoga;
now hear, as an ornament for your ears, that which is accomplished through knowledge.
There exists here only one pure, gentle, and unperceived Consciousness alone;
subtler than the subtlest, tranquil, neither the world nor the activities of the world. When it turns toward volitional thought, it perceives itself by means of itself through its own self.

Whenever it has fallen into a state of turbidity, it is called the "living soul" (jīva). This very body, though unreal, is perceived by the deluded soul through the error of its own volitions, just as a child sees a towering phantom.
But when perfect illumination has arrived by means of the lamp of knowledge,
the delusion of conceptualization in the living being perishes like an autumn cloud;
upon the destruction of all conceptualizations, this body attains peace.
Then, O Raghava, just as a lamp is extinguished entirely when its oil is exhausted,
and just as a living being does not see a dream upon the departure of sleep,
so too the individual soul, when the truth has been realized, no longer perceives the body.
Enveloped by the body, the living being remains in the unreal with the conviction that it is real;
yet, through the singular contemplation of reality, the illustrious one becomes bodiless, happy, and liberated.
That terrible darkness within the heart, which is difficult to pierce even with the light of the sun and other luminaries,
he perceives through the sun of knowledge— thinking "I am pure consciousness alone"— as being all-pervading, stainless, and identical with the Self by means of the Self.
In every manvantara, O Rāma, Hari of immeasurable soul assumes the state of a Buddha, relying upon some cause or other. Of that Lord of Sages known by the name of Buddha, O Rāghava...
Those who are devoted, wise, and desirous of the path to liberation—
whether they maintain that "emptiness," or "mere consciousness," or some intermediate state between these two exists—
they designate Brahman through the presentation of such reasons.
Indeed, among them, those who know consciousness, having brought duality to an end,
perceive the world as nothing other than a mere conceptualization of delusion;
others, the knowers of momentary flux, call this the Middle Way (*madhyama*).
They remain established in the view that "this is neither empty nor is there any consciousness whatsoever.
But others are proponents of emptiness who, through firm cultivation of the state of emptiness,
abandon all attachment with the conviction that the entire world is even more empty than space.
O Rāma, those whose intentions are as pure as the sky perceive only the single, lofty space; they do not see themselves or the world and its origins as separate.
They pass through stone walls as if through the unobstructed sky.
They cannot be pierced by weapons or winds, remaining as immovable as the regions of space;
though possessing forms as vast as Mount Sumeru, they abide like atoms within the rays of the sun, the fibers of a lotus stalk, and the clouds.
Having attained a state as if it were emptiness, with their meditations fixed upon emptiness,
they remain free from fever in that which is empty, like portions of the sky that are themselves empty;
and having realized the self within the empty, they cultivate whatever it is just as it is.
They see that very thing instantly through their own firm conviction. O Rāghava, by the persistence of firm conviction, even the deluded turn poison into nectar and nectar into poison as well.

Thus, in whatever way a firm cultivation is practiced here, one indeed becomes that very thing quickly; this has been observed again and again. When this body is seen through the reality of its true nature, it ceases to be a [solid] body.

But when seen through the state of unreality, the body attains the nature of space. O Rāma, you have now heard this method of knowledge for attaining the states of *aṇimā* and the rest; listen now to this other method.
Through the practice of exhaling (*recaka*), the individual soul (*jīva*) is drawn up from the abode of Kuṇḍalinī and joined with the vital air (*vāyu*), like fragrance extracted from a flower.
This body, devoid of movement, is then cast off like a piece of wood or a clod of earth.
What regard can there be for the body, for the living soul, for the mind, or for the lineage?
(MU 6.86.40) Whether in a stationary or a moving being, the living soul is properly introduced within according to one's desire, in order to fully enjoy its prosperity. (MU 6.86.41)
Thus, having enjoyed the glory of supernatural powers (*siddhi*), if that body remains, one may enter it again, or another body— whatever else is pleasing in this regard— or,
by means of the unexhausted [power] that has pervaded the space and wind in every direction from the body...

Having filled the world with consciousness, he then remains as the perfectly complete one. O Rāma, having known the Lord who is ever-risen and free from defect, whatever the light of consciousness desires in whatever manner, it obtains that very thing without delay; they know this state of attainment to be nothing other than the condition of being unobstructed.
The seventy-seventh chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Aṇimā and Other Powers," by Vasiṣṭha.

Endowed with the sovereign powers of the *aṇimā* and other qualities, that Cūḍālā, who was proud of her royal status, became thus— a virtuous woman possessed of intense meditative practice. She traveled by way of the path of the sky and entered the hollow of the ocean.
She moved across the surface of the earth like the Ganges, pure and cool;
she did not depart from her husband’s chest for even a moment, nor from his heart,
dwelling in all kingdoms as if she were Lakṣmī in all the worlds.
Moving through the sky, dark-complexioned and adorned with ornaments as flickering as lightning,
she wandered over the surface of the earth like a streak of cloud or a garland of mountains;
[she traversed] wood, grass, stone, earth, space, wind, fire, and water.
He entered everything without obstruction, like a thread passing through a pearl;
he roamed at his pleasure over the peaks of Meru, the cities of the world-protectors, and the hollows of the quarters, the sky, and the earth.
She engaged in conversation with those who had become animals, piśācas, and others, as well as with nāgas, gods, asuras, vidyādharas, apsarases, and siddhas;
and she diligently [instructed] that husband regarding the nectar of self-knowledge.
She awakened him many times, like a mother her young child;
yet that king, her husband, found no rest within himself,
remaining detached like a pearl fallen upon the surface of the earth.

Even after such a length of time, that king, being a fool, did not recognize Cūḍālā, who was endowed with such virtues, just as a child fails to recognize a science. "This wife of mine is both skilled in the arts and yet innocent, like a young girl."
In this way, the king perceived Cūḍālā as being nothing other than that [woman]; yet she,
having not yet attained rest within her own self,
did not reveal to the king the glory of her own spiritual perfection, just as one does not show a Śūdra the performance of a sacrifice.
Rāma:
Even Śikhidhvaja attained awakening from that great Siddhayoginī only with great effort; O Lord, how could anyone else awaken?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāghava, what is called the 'method of instruction' is merely the observance of formal rules; the true cause for awakening, however, is the pure intelligence of the disciple alone."
The object of knowledge of the self is not known through learning nor through merit;
the self alone knows the self, just as a snake [knows] its own tracks.
Rāma said:
This being so, O excellent sage, how is it that this is heard in popular tradition, and that the instruction of a guru is the cause for the knowledge of one's own self? Vasiṣṭha replied:
There lived in the marshlands of the Vindhya forest an extremely wretched merchant, a householder possessed of wealth and grain, who was like a worm in a sore.
Once, as he was traveling through the Vindhya jungle, [a coin] fell from him.
O Rāma, for the sake of a single cowrie shell found amidst a mass of grass and chaff,
he exerted himself with such miserliness that he winnowed all that grass and chaff on every side for three days.
From two cowries he becomes four and eight over time;
then, by his own mind, he imagines a hundred, a thousand, and yet another thousand.
Thus, in the forest, the wretched man remains untiring day and night.
Laughing at the people, he winnowed chaff for three days.
Then, at the end of those three days, from that thicket of bushes,
he obtained a great wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) resembling the orb of the full moon.
Having attained that, with a satisfied heart, he returned home happy;
having obtained all the prosperity of the world, he remained with all fears stilled.
Just as it was for the Kirāta through his search for cowrie shells, so it was for him.
Just as a jewel worth the entire world is obtained without weariness day or night,
so too is the knowledge of one's own self attained through the instruction of the scriptures; for by following the lineage of gurus, one seeks one thing and indeed obtains another.

Brahman transcends all the senses; it cannot be attained through the consciousness of the senses such as hearing, O sinless one, by means of instruction [alone]. Furthermore, without the instruction of a guru, there can be no realization of the reality of the Self.
By whom has the wish-fulfilling gem been obtained without the search for cowrie shells?
This teaching by the Guru regarding this highly precious reality has become the cause [of its attainment],
just as a cowrie shell becomes the cause for obtaining a gem.
Behold, O Rāghava, this illusion which deludes even the great:
one thing is sought with effort, yet another fruit is obtained.
A person performs one action, but obtains quite another result; and the fixed order of things (niyati) is observed.
Therefore, for one of infinite power, the successful passage through the succession of worlds occurs through non-attachment and indeed through indifference alone.
The Eighty-eighth Chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Kirāta."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thereupon, King Śikhidhvaja, lacking the state of knowledge of reality,
fell into a supreme delusion, like the surface of the earth falling into the blindness of night.
With his mind inflamed by the fire of suffering, he did not take delight even slightly in those splendors, even when they were brought before him, as if they were flames of fire; rather,
he found solace in solitary places, at the ends of the earth, by waterfalls, and in caves.
He arrived like a man of vice among those who have abandoned sensual pleasures;
O Raghava, like you, a king is made to perform his daily duties by his servants when entreated with all manner of conciliations, persuasions, and exhortations.
Always possessing unrestrained dispassion and a mind as tranquil as that of a wandering mendicant,
he remained amidst his royal splendors without enjoying them, even while censuring great luxuries;
yet he gave away in abundance gifts such as cattle, land, and gold.
Bestowing honor upon the gods, the brahmins, and his own kinsmen,
he practiced austerities such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* vows;
he wandered through sacred fords, forests, and shrines.
Even so, he did not obtain even the slightest freedom from sorrow,
just like one seeking treasure who digs the earth where no treasure lies;
day and night, he withered away by the endless fire of grief.

He reflected with deep thought upon the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra. Overwhelmed by anxiety and dejected, he viewed his kingdom as if it were poison; though it possessed great splendor before him, he saw nothing in it with his distressed mind.
Then once, when Cūḍālā had come into his lap while they were in a secluded place,
Śikhidhvaja spoke these words to her in a sweet voice:
Śikhidhvaja said:
I have enjoyed sovereignty for a long time, and I have experienced the heights of prosperity;
now, joined with dispassion, I am going to the forest. For me there are neither pleasures nor pains, neither calamities nor successes.
Beings embrace the sage dwelling in the forest;
there is no delusion caused by the ruin of one's country, nor the destruction of men in battle.
I consider the happiness of one living in the forest to be even greater than that of a kingdom.
Bearing clusters as breasts, with red shoots for hands,
dancing with their masses of blossoms, and wearing the white clouds as fluttering garments;
captivating with their own pollen as body-unguents, they have fashioned ornaments of flowers.
Adorned by the slopes of the golden mountain as if they were a beautiful hip,
they are draped with pearl necklaces in the form of rivers threaded with pearl-like waves;
they are embraced by their companions, the creeping vines, and possess the most charming young fawns.
Possessing a natural fragrance that is unrestrained, providing food in the form of fallen fruit,
with eyes like rows of bees, their bodies bent under the weight of blossoms;
having become a source of consolation, they possess cool and stainless limbs.
O fair-faced one, these forest paths delight me just as you do;
for the mind does not become so peaceful and contented in solitary retreats,
nor among the orbs of the moon, nor in the abodes of Brahmā and Indra.
"O slender one, you ought not to place an obstacle in this request of mine;
for noble women do not, even in their dreams, thwart the desire of their husband.
Cūḍālā said:
O Lord, an action performed at the proper time shines, and nothing else;
a flower shines in spring, and fruit shines in autumn.
For those whose bodies are worn out by old age, it is fitting to take refuge in the forest.
Therefore, this does not please me for young men such as you. O Great King, as long as we have not been abandoned by our youth, we shine at home like trees with a profusion of flowers.
"Like swans departing from a tree for a lake, we shall go together from our home to the forest, where flowers and safety abound and which is white with blossoms, even as we grow old.
O King, it would be a neglect of the protection of subjects to abandon them before the proper time has come."
Just as the great affliction of consumption does not leave the moon,
so too a king who acts prematurely is restrained by his subjects;
for masters and servants restrain one another from improper deeds.
Śikhidhvaja said:
Enough, O lotus-garlanded-eyed one, with this obstacle to my desire;
know that I am departing from here for a distant, solitary forest.
"You are but a child with faultless limbs; you must not come to the forest.
For even for men, O lady of tender limbs, dwelling in the forest is difficult to endure. Women, even those who are hardy, are not capable of living in the forest."
"Which flowers, indeed, are capable of enduring the heat of the sun?
You must remain here in this supreme kingdom, protecting it;
for when a husband has departed, the vow of a woman is the bearing of the burden of the household."

Having spoken thus to his beloved, whose face was like the moon, the self-controlled king rose up to bathe and performed all his daily duties. Then, having abandoned his royal activities, the sun went to the mountain of setting.
Like a forest inaccessible to all people, Śikhidhvaja [departed];
the radiance, withdrawing its extended form,
followed that very lord who had gone forth from his palace, like a devoted Cūḍālā.
The dark night arrived, making the world grey with ash,
as if out of envy toward Śiva who bore the celestial river;
while the quarters of the sky stood with the clouds of twilight for hands, she approached him who wore earrings.
As the couple proceeded toward the further shore of the forest of Meru— which was marked by the rising laughter of moonlight amidst the dark tresses of its shadows—
it became a celestial garden for their dalliance, like the splendor of day and the lord of day.
As they approached this shore— which was heart-warming yet bereft of its sharp rays—
the host of stars, like a pair of spouses belonging to the night and the lord of the night, were seen again shattered upon the pavement of the sky. And furthermore, the Mairava [host] was seen.
It was as if the quarters of the sky, like brides, had released their handfuls of auspicious parched grain.
The night— moon-faced, dark with gloom, cool, and smiling with white water-lilies—
attained her youth, her breasts being the buds of lotuses.
Having performed his evening devotions together with Cūḍālā,
the king lay down upon his bed like Mount Maināka in the ocean. Then, at the hour of midnight, when all sounds had ceased in that place—
While all people were hidden within the stone casket of deep sleep,
she lay fast asleep upon that bed of soft silk,
utterly stupefied by slumber like a female bee within a lotus.
