those branches of this tree of the mind, which reach from one distant place to another for those who know space and time, are long, far-reaching, and widespread.
The sense faculties and enjoyments, consisting of waves of existence and non-existence,
are its vast masses of branches, crowded with the fruits of the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Of such a mind, which is like a malignant tree, at every moment—
"While you are pruning the branches, apply yourself to the scraping of the roots.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"While I am performing the cutting away of the trunk, branches, and so forth of the tree of the mind,"
"O Sage, how shall I effect the complete eradication of the root? Kumbha replied:
"The various latent impressions (*vāsanās*) are the branches, endowed with fruits, trunks, and so forth."
They become severed within by the power of consciousness.
One whose mind is unattached, who is silent, whose speech and deliberations are stilled,
and who acts only when the time is right— he is one whose mental creeper has been severed within.

He who stands cutting down the web of the tree-like creepers of the mind through human effort is fit for the testing of its very root. Pruning the branches is secondary; the primary task is the cutting away of the root.
Therefore, O Great Sage, be intent upon scraping away the roots of the tree of the mind;
by thoroughly burning those roots,
the thicket of mental thorns will become mindlessness itself.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Sage, what fire, capable of burning its fuel and bringing about its purpose, could there be for the seed of the tree of the mind, which consists of the sense of "I"?
Kumbha said:
O King, this inquiry into one's own self, which takes the form of "Who might I be?",
is known as the fire for burning the seed of the wicked tree of the mind.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Sage, I have deliberated many times with my great intellect until I realized that I am neither the world, nor the earth, nor even the circle of the mandala.
Neither the bank of a river, nor a forest, nor a leaf-hut and the like;
neither the body and so forth due to their insentience, nor flesh, bone, blood, and so on;
neither the organs of action, nor the organs of perception.
There is neither mind nor intellect, nor even the sense of "I," because of its insentience.
Just as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold, so does the state of being an "I" exist in the conscious self;
yet that [ego] is insentient and non-existent by nature, therefore, O Sage, I am not that.
In the supreme state, the meaning of the word "self" and so forth does not exist as a specific configuration,
because of its absolute infinity, just as a great tree does not exist in the sky.
O Blessed One, even though he knows this, [he still engages in] the complete cleansing of the sense of "I-ness."
"O Great Sage, because I do not know what is within, I am tormented by it. Kumbha replied:
"O Lord of the Earth, if you do not [know] even such a small group as this,"
"Because of its insentience, O one of great intelligence, tell me who you are—that new [self] of yours.
Śikhidhvaja replied:
"O best of the wise, I am pure consciousness alone, the clear self-awareness."
"In that wherein these entities take delight, or by which they are created—
for such as I am, this clinging to 'stain' is surely causeless; yet, because I think 'I am the one who possesses causes,' I do not know how to abandon it."
"O Sage, since I am unable to wipe away this non-existent, non-self-defining impurity from my soul, I therefore undergo most grievous penance. Kumbha said:
"Tell me, O mighty-armed one, what is that great stain clinging to you,
by which you remain a transmigrating being, whether through existence or non-existence?
Śikhidvaja said:
That sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) which is the seed of the tree of the mind is my impurity;
yet I do not know how to abandon it, for as soon as it is abandoned, it returns to me again and again.
Kumbha said:
Whatever effect arises from a cause must exist everywhere;
however, that which is otherwise non-existent—appearing like a second moon—is not found at all, even though it is seen.
From that [cause], the effect consisting of the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) is born.
"Having investigated the cause, tell me quickly with your own mind.
Śikhidhvaja replied:
"O Sage, I know that the perception of 'I' is the cause of this defect."
O Lord of Sages, tell me how that [mind] attains tranquility.
Established as "I" due to the mind's orientation toward objects of thought, it remains in a state of suffering;
O Sage, speak of the cessation of those objects of thought for the sake of its pacification.
Kumbha said:
You are a knower of causes; tell me quickly the cause of this sensation, and then I shall instruct you in the sequence of what is a cause and what is not a cause.

Tell me, O Lord, how that which consists of the object of knowledge and the act of knowing, and which is devoid of both the thinkable and the thinking, has become a cause when it is in fact without a cause. Śikhidhvaja said:
O Sage, this existence of objects here— consisting of the nature of the cognizer and the cognized, and characterized by the perception of what is to be known— has the body and so forth as its cause;
through the reality of the object, perception arises in the form of the body and the rest.
Just as movement arises from the appearance of what is unreal, like a streak of wind; so too,
by means of that [realization] through which I no longer perceive the non-existence of the existence of things,
the seed of the mind— the perception of "I-ness"— is completely stilled.
Kumbha said:
If the existence of things such as the body were real, then that [consciousness] would belong to you;
but since there is no existence of the body and so forth, upon what is your perception based?
Śikhidhvaja said:
How could that which possesses any perceivable nature consisting of mental construction be of an unreal form? How could light be darkness?

O Sage, how can it be that the body— which is endowed with hands, feet, and so forth, which possesses the manifestation of the fruits of action, and which is constantly being experienced— does not exist? Kumbha replied:
O protector of the earth, that effect for which no cause exists is not found here;
the perception of such an effect is merely an illusion.
An effect can never exist without a cause.
Where indeed could that substance be produced which has no seed?
Know that whatever effect appears as if real at the outset, though it is causeless, is the delusion of the observer, comparable to the water of a mirage.
Know that this which has arisen from false delusion is indeed non-existent;
even with great effort, the water of a mirage cannot be obtained.
It is not logical to seek a cause for that which is unreal, such as the appearance of two moons.

To whom does the adornment of every limb of the son of a barren woman appear beautiful? Know, O King, that this body— a cage of bones and so forth— is entirely non-existent, for it is an effect that occurs without a cause and is therefore impossible.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Lord of Sages, why is the father not considered the cause of this body, which is endowed with hands, feet, and other limbs, and is constantly perceived?
Kumbha said: O King, due to the absence of a cause, there is no such thing as a "father.
That which is born from what is non-existent is itself called non-existent.
The seed is said to be the cause of things that are effects;
for indeed, my dear, no sprout can come into being in this world without a seed.
Therefore, there is no effect here whose cause cannot be established.
For in the absence of a seed, that [object] does not exist; its cognition, however, is an illusion.
Whatever necessarily does not exist because it is seedless is a delusion of the mind, equal to the perception of two moons, water in a mirage, or the son of a barren woman.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Among the grandfathers, sons, and fathers within the three worlds,
why is the Primordial Grandfather not the cause, since he was born first?"
Kumbha said: O King, even that primordial grandfather does not exist at all;
for since there is no cause, there can never be an effect belonging to anyone.
Because its cause— the seed of its own nature— is eternally absent, O Grandfather,
even though it appears as something primary, nothing other than an illusion exists;
it manifests solely as a form of delusion, like the water of a mirage.
"Even the grandfather's [perception] of its being a functional object is of the nature of an error," [says the text],
"due to the false cognition of this grandfather and the others.
But once that density has ceased, I shall then wipe away the rest.
Therefore, that which is the sky of consciousness within the Self, shining eternally and beautifully by its own nature as pure consciousness—that is this God.
By that very Self, the Self has declared itself to be "the Lotus-born" (Brahmā) and "the one whose form is space" (Ākāśarūpa); thus all this is peaceful.
The chapter named "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja. (MU 6.98.71)
The ninety-ninth canto:
Śikhidhvaja said:
"If this delusion shines forth, extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass,"
And that which is capable of purposeful action—that remains as the cause of suffering.
[The Jar says:
Thus, for the time being, this delusion of the world has reached a state of attenuation.

The wise know that ignorance has perished only when it has become loosened, like water that was solidified by cold being dissolved by heat. There is no arising without destruction; there is no emergence without the dissolution of the previous configuration.

That very attenuation of the awareness of creation is indeed the cause for the attainment of the cessation of creation and for the realization of the supreme state. For one in whom this attenuation is observed, [liberation] occurs spontaneously through gradual stages.
Through the dissolution of its former configuration, even its cessation becomes possible.
O King, by this very sequence, understand that this Primordial Being has arisen as a manifestation of delusion, like water appearing in a mirage.
Even in the absence of a grandfather, this continuity of beings is unreal;
that which is established by what is itself unestablished is never established at all.
For this perception of beings has arisen like the water of a mirage.
Through investigation, it dissolves, just like the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
As for the claim that an effect comes into being after having not existed due to the absence of its cause—
apart from false knowledge, no such form of that [effect] is logically possible.
False view has never been perceived;
by whom could jars ever be filled with the water of a mirage?
Śikhidhvaja said:
Why is the Supreme Brahman— the infinite, unborn, unmanifest Lord, peaceful and infallible— not the cause of the First Creator? Kumbha said:
Because it lacks the state of being a cause, and because it lacks the state of being an effect, Brahman is non-dual, one, and immutable in nature; it is neither an effect nor a cause.
It is without agent, object, or instrument; it is without cause and without seed.
How could Brahman, which is inconceivable and unknowable, be an agent?
Since it is without cause, it is devoid of the state of being an effect;
when it is non-dual, one, and without beginning or end, that is its true apprehension.
That which is inconceivable, unknowable, auspicious, peaceful, and immutable—how, for whom, by what means, as an agent, as an enjoyer, or at what time could it ever exist?
Therefore, nothing such as this world and so forth has been created; it does not exist.
There is no agent and there is no enjoyer; everything is peaceful, unborn, and auspicious.
Because of the absence of a cause, this world is not the effect of anything; and because it is not an effect, it does not exist—thus, creation is not found.
When the world is not the effect of any cause whatsoever, then the non-existence of all things is established; and when that is established, whose is the cognition?
Thus, in the absence of cognition, there is no cause for the sense of "I-ness."
"Therefore, you are pure; you are liberated. What talk can there be of bondage and liberation? Śikhidhvaja said: "Amen! I am awakened, O Blessed One; what you have spoken is most excellent."
Because of the absence of a cause, I know that there is no agent here, namely Brahman.
Due to the absence of an agent, the world does not exist; therefore, there is no perception of objects.
Consequently, there is no mind or the like, which is the seed of that [perception]; hence, there is no "I-ness" or anything else whatsoever.
This being so, I am pure, I am awakened, and yet I am not;
I bow to myself and pay homage to the Supreme, for from the perspective of awakening, there is nothing at all.
The perception of objects is indeed false; that which appears is simply non-existent.
Enough of this; I shall now rest in peace like the expanse of the sky.

Alas! This perception of the differentiation of the world’s objects—along with its divisions of place, direction, time, and its flood of parts and actions—has been stilled after a long time, or perhaps it has indeed remained as Brahman alone.
I am at peace; I am extinguished; I abide in the supreme state. I do not go, nor do I rise; I do not set. I remain as the self abides in its ultimate state—auspicious, pure, holy, and silent.
This is the chapter named "The Resting of Śikhidhvaja."
The hundredth canto:
Vasiṣṭha says,
"Having thus attained rest in Brahman, that Śikhidhvaja..."
For a moment, his mind became perfectly tranquil like an extinguished lamp;
having reached the cessation [of thought] through the transformation of non-conceptual meditative absorption,
he was suddenly awakened by Kumbha with the words, "This is but my own play."
Kumbha said: O King, you have awakened from the sleep of ignorance and stand as Śiva;
therefore, there is no task for you through either setting or non-setting [of the sun].

"O dear one, you have now become liberated while living— your self shining forth all at once, abiding as the nature of the state beyond desire, and entirely free from the perception of parts. Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus awakened by Kumbha, he became enlightened;
having emerged from the casket of great delusion, he shone intensely. With his intellect at rest in an instant, he beheld the nature of the perceptible world.
The liberated soul Śikhidhvaja spoke thus with ease:
"Although this is already largely known to me, let that which I ask about be explained."
O giver of honor, O destroyer of delusion, for the sake of further refined awakening, [tell me]:

how can there be a cognition called the seer, the seeing, and the seen within that which is auspicious, peaceful, without appearance, supreme, and the untranscendable Self, which is the soul of the universe?
Kumbha said:
"Well asked, O Great King; you shine with the light of awakening.
For this alone remains for you to learn regarding knowledge; therefore, listen to this."
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving,
all of it— abounding in every variety— is destroyed at the end of the aeon; thereafter,
there remains only that which is motionless and profound, neither light nor pervasive darkness.
At the end of the play of the great aeon, that which is real remains as the essence:
pure consciousness alone, stainless, beautiful, shining like the stainless sky, liberated from all mental constructions, and endowed with supreme splendor.
That which is uniquely arisen, utterly transparent, tranquil, pervasive, and radiant;
whose essence is the Supreme Self, a steady splendor consisting of pure consciousness alone;
inconceivable, unknowable, equal, auspicious, and unwavering.
Brahman is the fullness of nirvāṇa, as if overflowing with prosperity;
it is subtler than the subtlest, and more massive than the most massive;
it is weightier than the heaviest, and the best even among the most excellent.

Such is that supreme subtle [reality], compared to which this sky appears as gross as Mount Meru would appear next to an atom. Such is that supreme gross [reality], compared to which this world appears as such.

It appears like an atom in some places, or it does not appear at all. This sovereign kingdom of the world is so exceedingly great, yet when one realizes it to be thus— immaculate and tranquil— it becomes like a mere fragment of withered straw.
Such is that supreme good which exists in the Lord:
that the splendor of the multitude of objects in the world arises from the perception of its own existence.
O King, that alone is the one pervasive essence found here.
The One is grasped by the intellect as a single unity, yet not even as a single thing due to its state of non-duality.
Therefore, no such thing as a second conceptualization exists;
the reality of the Self alone shines forth, both undiminished and unimpaired.
Always abiding as everything, appearing as if in every form,
it is neither effect nor cause because it is inexpressible and unattainable;
since it cannot be reached by perception or other means of knowledge, it is a certain, singular, and supreme reality.

Everything consists of everything, subtle, and is nothing but pure experience. How can that which is beyond description— whether it has emerged from a perceiver or not, whether it exists or does not exist— possess causality?
Indeed, from that whose nature transcends all means of valid cognition, nothing whatsoever is born—neither seed nor cause—because it is unnameable.
It is the reality devoid of agent, object, and instrument; a mass of consciousness, indestructible.
The nature of the Self is without appearance, characterized by self-awareness.
Therefore, O Sage, nothing whatsoever is born from the supreme Brahman;
tell me, how indeed could there be a sequence of produced and producer in the Unmanifest?
Nothing whatsoever is born in the tranquil state, nor does anything whatsoever dissolve;
Brahman abides by its own existence, being neither seed nor cause.
It is pure experience alone; therefore, nothing other than that exists.
"For that very world, consisting of the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*) and so forth, is indeed infinite.
Śikhidvaja said:
"O Sage, O Auspicious One, I know that in Śiva there is no such thing as the ego-sense of the world."
"How does the perception of creation appear? Tell me this quickly.
Kumbha replied:
"That essence of consciousness, which is without beginning or end, abides within its own self-awareness."
The wise know that world to be that extremely transparent abode, which is pure being alone.

Know that the awareness of "I," which consists in the manifestation of its own conscious self and is devoid of the perception of any possible object of consciousness, is the Virāj-self in which the world is situated.
Just as no distinction exists between the wind and the movement of the wind,
so it is between pure consciousness and the sense of "I," which are comparable to emptiness and space.
Just as waves and the like arise in water with causes due to place and time, [so do appearances arise within consciousness].
"Others say that because there is no [fixed] place or time, the world is likewise without cause.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"In this world, let it be granted that waves and the like in water and so forth have a cause."
"Others [perceive] the world as 'I' and so forth; I do not consider it to be without a cause.
Kumbha said: "Now, O Lord of the Earth, you have understood this truth."
This world consists of "I," "you," and so forth, yet nothing exists here [in reality].
Devoid of the referents of the word "world," the world exists as the essence of Śiva;
it is fashioned within space itself, peaceful, or rather, subtler than space.
Just as emptiness exists in the sky, so does this [world] abide in Brahman—
neither in the form of an existent nor a non-existent entity, nor in any form whatsoever.
This world, being of such a nature, becomes auspicious through right knowledge.

By the power of right knowledge, even poison becomes nectar. Without right knowledge, the entire world is supremely a source of suffering; even nectar, when consumed with the perception that it is poison, acts like the essence of poison.
Because he is the Lord, whatever this conscious Lord perceives,
that very thing immediately comes to be as such, auspiciously manifesting in that form—
just like a flame or a mass of clouds with their various shifting appearances.
For the reality of Brahman remains exactly as it is, without any change in its nature.
That which exists within the Self as the supreme, steady consciousness-nature,
is perceived by that very [consciousness] as this world of "I-ness" and so forth.

Only the supreme Śiva shines here as the ultimate reality; whence could there be a world, an "I," and so forth? A question regarding this is simply not appropriate. A question is fitting only for that thing which actually exists.
But as for that which is not perceived at all, what is the use of an inquiry into its perception?
Just as the existence of gold is not found without its particular configuration,
so the Lord has no standing without the world and the sense of "I."
Because it is without cause, this [world] does not exist; rather, Brahman alone expands in this manner.
Even while not expanding, it remains here as the "I" and as the world.
By that which consists of me, the intention is mutually impelled by that very same [Brahman].
These states of being produce wonder, like a multitude of couples in the presence of the five-arrowed god.
Consciousness alone is consciousness; by consciousness alone is it accumulated.
Though it is not manifold, through its own self as if it were manifold, the Self appears as if it were not-self.
From the Full they draw forth the Full; from the Full they have made full things.
From the Full come full things, yet the Full alone remains.
Only pure consciousness shines forth when, by virtue of being pure consciousness, it manifests within itself.
Indeed, that name which was never manifested becomes manifest as the perception of creation;
consciousness itself, though non-existent, appears by its own nature as if it were "I," without ever abandoning its own stainless form.
Consciousness is formless, without beginning or end; the form of the mind is infinite.
It appears as the body of the Universal Sovereign, like the self-existent one himself.
Then it perceives this [world] as either non-existent or indeed existent, because of its own essential nature.
Through cultivation, the visible world attains density and gradually comes into being.
This [reality], which is tranquil, is free from the denotation of the word "nature" (svabhāva) in its form as the expansion of the universe; it is ineffable and one.
It is the reality of the essence of experience, devoid of the state of "world," consisting of the vision of its own innate wonder, established as the ultimate thing.
The one hundred and first canto, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," [spoken by] Kumbha:
There is no object consisting of consciousness, nor is there an external one, nor even emptiness;
because its essence is nothing but feeling, that object is spoken of according to how it is perceived.
Just as liquidity belongs to water, the state of being a knower belongs to consciousness without a cause.
That [Self] is non-dual, eternal, and infinite, remaining exactly as it is.

Because there is no exclusion of a counter-correlative (pratiyogin) for its own-being and existence, there is no non-existence; therefore, the establishment of existence and being does not depend on anything else.
If the supreme reality were something tranquil that could become fit for the state of being a cause,
how could it be immovable, without appearance, and beyond inference?
Therefore, Brahman is never at any time a cause nor a seed.
Therefore, the creation of any effect whatsoever does not exist. For no other way of accounting for this creation is possible;
apart from pure consciousness alone, a material creation does not exist.
Whatever is seen here is a mass of consciousness, unpierced by [duality],
wherein the sound and meaning of the word "world" and its aesthetic relish are impossible;
no effect arises from the absence of a cause, nor does any objective entity (padārtha) come into being.

That which consists of duality, unity, and so forth is like a flower in the sky; because it is established solely upon its own destruction, it cannot logically be unproduced (*aja*). When there is perception, destruction is certain, and for that which is destroyed, birth is likewise certain.
Or else, if you perceive this entire multitude of objects as always existing, eternal, and yet destroyed—if that is so, then this reality here is of a single form; why, then, is there distress?
Furthermore, whatever this perception is, it is the wondrous manifestation of the nature of consciousness.
There exists only the reality of consciousness; duality and unity do not exist at all.
Therefore, O King, since there is an absence of the existence of objective entities and since mental cultivation is impossible, the cultivation of the "I-ness" does not exist for you.
Since the state of "I-ness" is impossible, what else can be called the mind?
Thus, the mind does not exist in the form of an "I"; therefore, O Lord, be free from delusion. Free from latent impressions, with a tranquil mind, silent, and composed of the supreme ether.
Whether with body or without body, whether remaining stationary or moving—

because of the purity of the vision of all-as-Being, because of the established non-existence of objective entities, and because of the absence of mental cultivation within the mind, the "I" does not exist at all; therefore, there is Śiva.
Through the cultivation of the meaning of the Veda that "all is Brahman" and through direct experience,
because the perceived object is the sole reality, that which is called "mind" does not exist.
Therefore, you are that stainless, causeless, eternally liberated, eternal, complete, manifold-yet-one Brahman.
This world is empty, devoid of self-nature, unreal yet appearing real, without beginning or middle; it is everything, yet not anything at all—abide in this state as it truly is.
The hundred and second canto, titled "The First Awakening of Śikhidhvaja."
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Tell me that other [instruction] by which my understanding that 'the mind does not exist' may become clear through reasoning; I have not understood the Buddha's teaching skillfully."
Kumbha said:
"O royal sage, the mind does not exist at all, anywhere, or at any time;
that which appears as if it were a mind is the imperishable reality known as Brahman."
Where the world itself— which consists of the knower and the known— does not exist,
how can there be the mental constructions of "I," "you," "that," and so forth?
This very world that has arisen as something whatsoever does not exist at all.
"Brahman alone shines within the self; how is it that this is heard and understood?
This world was indeed impelled at the beginning of creation and the great dissolution;
however, this instruction was given by me elsewhere for the sake of your awakening."
Because causes such as the nature of grasping (*upādāna*) do not exist,
and because it is impossible for all entities to be without a cause,
the world— which is a self understood by the ignorant— does not exist.

Therefore, that which shines forth here is nothing other than the radiance of Brahman. It is incorrect to say that the God, who is ineffable and formless, creates this; such a statement lacks logical foundation and is not experienced as truth.
"The Lord who is inexpressible, non-obstructive, of the nature of space, and formless—
he creates the worlds"— such speech is merely for the laughter of the ignorant. By this very argument, O King, the mind does not exist.
O virtuous one, the world itself is not real; how then can the mind and its like, which are contained within it, be so?

For the mind consists merely of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and impressions exist only when there is something to be impressed (*vāsya*). That which is to be impressed is the world, and that very world is unreal; therefore, how can the existence of the mind be established?
That which shines as Brahman itself, by itself, through itself within itself—
that very [Brahman], by that same [Brahman], has been made to bear such names as "mind" (citta) and so forth;
this visible world is its garment, and it alone has arisen for us.

Since there is an absence of a cause, how could there be "mind-ness" even previously? Therefore, this world does not exist here; rather, it is only this expansive consciousness—which is of the nature of the mere void of consciousness and is called the supreme space—that shines forth.
Whatever supreme space shines slightly [within] the mirror of consciousness due to its own inherent clarity— that is the mind, and that has created the world.
This notion of "I," "you," and "the world" is not real.
Surely it appeared like a false dream, yet it was indeed productive of effects;
since this world does not exist, there is no latent impression (vāsanā) at all.
Therefore, what kind of mind could there be, where, from what cause, and in what manner, if its very essence is that [non-existent world]?
This world, which is perceived as an object by the unawakened, is merely mental;
it is non-existent, formless, and was never produced in the beginning.
It has not been produced at all, due to the absence of a cause, from the very start of creation and for all time.
Based on worldly experience and the treatises,
neither beginninglessness, nor non-origination, nor even stability can be established for this manifest world,
which possesses form and consists of gross, resistant shapes.
Because all causes are absent according to worldly experience, scripture, and direct perception,
the occurrences of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) cannot be denied;
and as for those who [deny] these things established by scripture, experience, and the meaning of the Vedas—

He who says that dissolution and the other states do not exist is indeed like a madman. One should not take refuge in that utterly deluded beast, whose speech is untruthful and for whom neither the worlds, nor the scriptures, nor the Vedas are an authority.

And for this visible [object] which possesses resistance, a cause that is non-resistant can never exist; nor can that which has form have a cause that is formless. Thus, while being observed in this manner, it is not the case that this does not appear.
And yet it is not incapable of causal efficiency, nor is this world [devoid of it] in this manner.
Therefore, this [world] belongs to that partless space of consciousness, which is unobstructed in form, formless, infinite,
and existing as the most ancient of the ancient.
That which is the peaceful, equanimous state of the tranquil Brahman, who possesses all forms—
its self-manifestation by its own nature assumes the form of creation and dissolution;
by that very [state], its own body is known for a moment as this world.
But in another moment, one remains as the awakened, eternal Brahman within one's own self.
Therefore, all this is indeed Brahman; where is this notion of a "world" and so forth?
Where are the mind and its like, where the body and its like, and where are the conceptual constructions of duality, unity, and so on?
All is without support, unborn, profoundly peaceful, and without beginning or middle; it exists as the inner self just as it is.
This is neither manifold nor even non-manifold; remain as you are, established in the silence of perfect stillness.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja."
The one hundred and third canto:
Śikhidhvaja says,
"O Sage, through your grace, my delusion has vanished and mindfulness has been regained by me."
I stand firm, my doubts dispelled, my mind at rest, and possessed of the Self;
having known that which is to be known, I am the great silent sage who has crossed the vast ocean of illusion.
Peaceful, free from the nature of egoism, a knower, I abide in a state beyond all affliction.
"Aha! For how very long a time have I wandered in the interim;
now, at last, I have reached this imperishable and unshakable state.
Such being the case, O Sage, the three worlds beginning with Sāhaṃ do not exist."
"This which appears as the intellect of a fool, I know that to be Brahman. Kumbha said:
"Where even the world does not exist, there the manifestation of 'I-ness' cannot occur."
Where is the accumulation of the sky of saṃsāra? From where? Of what kind? How?
O sage, remain silent with a peaceful mind, conducting yourself according to the natural state of things, like the movement of a whirlpool within the belly of a gentle ocean.
This exists as it is, peaceful in its nature as Brahman;
"I" and "this world" are but the stainless sky, consisting of the essence of words and their meanings.
This is without beginning or end, though designated by the names "creation" and "dissolution."
The sky, whose essence is merely the wonder of consciousness, shines forth brilliantly.
Just as gold remains when the perception of its particular forms has ceased,
so too does this Brahman exist when the world and all other objects have subsided.

Just as the volition of the self-arisen is its own destruction, so indeed are these two— bondage and liberation— established as dependent upon one's own awareness. The very volition "I am" leads to bondage that is utterly destructive.

The mere resolve "I am not" leads to liberation for one whose self is stainless. That which is the knowledge of the true nature of the meanings of the words "bondage," "liberation," and "resolve"— whether they be existent or non-existent— is called reality and absolute oneness.
The realization of "I am not" is success; the realization of "I am" leads to calamity.
He who possesses the self of pure awakening thinks, "I am indeed that which is not-I.
Through the mere absence of conceptualization, by means of the arising of perfect knowledge, [this state is attained].
The mental construction (*saṅkalpa*), being itself of an unreal nature, perishes by itself for the sake of perfection. For in Śiva, whose essential nature is inconceivable, there is no causality;
and due to the absence of a cause, neither an effect nor even a functional entity (*padārtha*) exists.
When the non-existence of objective entities is established, cognition is not possible;
due to the absence of its cause, the sense of "I" never arises.
In the absence of the arising of the sense of "I," for whom and of what nature could there be saṃsāra?
Due to the absence of saṃsāra, everything remains as the Supreme alone. That which appears here is real; it is the Supreme itself abiding within the Self.
The Supreme, full of the Supreme, unfolds as the equal [all] within the Supreme.
Therefore, know that the entire world remains as motionless as if carved from stone,
like Brahman existing in the form of rays of light;
for when the mental construction of the city has perished, what remains of the city of imagination?
Know that form of the world to be transparent, arising from space, and composed of both being and non-being.
He truly sees who perceives the world as motionless yet vibrating like a shadow-man, peaceful, devoid of mental construction, and free from the referents of the word "world."
The wise know that for one who possesses right knowledge— whose mental engagement with forms and light has become flavorless and whose cultivation [of them] has ceased— that is Nirvana.
Just as there is a wind that is motionless, and just as there is space that is not blue;

Just as gold exists in the form of its various arrangements, so does Brahman exist as the world. Though devoid of essence and appearing as non-existent, these forms, light, and mental attentions— which produce the cognition of the world— exist as having the nature of Brahman.
Just as water, though possessing many waves, is devoid of the word and the meaning of "wave," so too is Brahman, though appearing as creation, devoid of the word and the meaning of "creation.
Creation itself is the supreme Brahman, and the supreme Brahman is the vision of creation.
This eternal meaning of the sentence, however, is devoid of the meaning of the word "creation" (sarga).
When the meaning of the word "Brahman" is fully realized, how can there be a cognition of the meaning of the word "creation"?
And when the meaning of the word "creation" is fully realized, how can there be a cognition of the meaning of the word "Brahman"?
When there arises the dissolution of the cultivation of all words and their meanings,
that certain pure space of consciousness is designated by the word "Brahman.
This occurs when both [subject and object] are no longer perceived through the attainment of perfect vision.
Speech turns back from that which remains—undecaying and tranquil.
This entire flood of objective perception has been stilled; there exists this single, essential nature, whose form is like space.
The entire world, as it truly is, is of the nature of stone and of the nature of rock, yet its supreme essence is the nature of consciousness.
The one hundred and fourth canto, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja. Śikhidhvaja:
And thus, O Great Buddha, I understand that this very world is the effect corresponding to whatever its supreme cause may be. Kumbha:
Where there is causality, there the effect is appropriately established;
since that which is not a cause does not exist in the first place, how could an effect arise from it?
Herein there is no cause whatsoever, nor is there ever an effect.
All this existing world is auspicious, peaceful, and unborn.
An effect is born from a cause; therefore, that [effect] must possess the qualities of its cause.
But as for that which is not born at all in this world, how could there be any similarity to it?
Tell me, how can that which has no seed at all be born?
That which is inconceivable and inexpressible cannot possess the nature of a seed in this world.
All perceptions, by virtue of place and time, possess causes.
How can Brahman, which is without an agent, be the object of the two means of valid cognition?
O Śiva, there is no causality in that which is neither an agent, nor an object, nor an instrument.
Therefore, there is no perception of the meaning of the word "world" that is not itself a cause.
Brahman alone is its own true nature, which exists as that which is pervasive and sustains all;
yet that very same reality, when perceived by those of imperfect vision, appears as the accumulated world.
That which is pure consciousness, undecaying, and tranquil is proclaimed as the One.
By that very means, one perceives the unborn Brahman, the world, as being real, tranquil, and the true body. O Lord of the Earth, whatever state belongs to one's own mind,
that alone is declared by the wise to be its destruction, and it is so experienced.
"Know, O King, that the mind has the nature of destruction; it is essentially perishable.

The mental construct (*saṅkalpa*) that leads to momentary destruction is what is designated by the word 'mind. [This occurs] merely through the absence of such constructs, even without the arising of perfect knowledge."

Volition, being itself of an unreal nature, perishes by itself for the sake of accomplishment. O lotus-eyed one, how could that which is called "ignorance"— and whose non-existence is admitted by its very name— be something truly existing within the mind?
How can he who, raising his hands, repeatedly declares with a loud voice, "I am a Śūdra," become a Brahmin? Of what nature is his status as a Brahmin?
He whose constituent elements have dissolved and who cries out very loudly, "I am dead"—[how can he be a Brahmin]?
Know that, my dear, it is indeed dead; its being alive is merely an illusion.
Whatever exists here that appears in the form of an illusion is seen like a whirling firebrand, like a mirage, a double moon, or like a child’s ghost.
How indeed could that which consists of a mass of delusions be real?
Therefore, it is said that the mind is nothing but the error of ignorance.
Ignorance is called the mind; though non-existent, it appears as if existent.
It is a false delusion, formless like a mass of hair in the sky.
Thus, it is ignorance itself that is expressed by the word "mind";
the destruction of that [ignorance] is the destruction of the mind, and that indeed is the relinquishing of the mind.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Lord, what is ignorance like, and how is it destroyed?
O Blessed One, best among speakers, tell me this in brief."
Kumbha said:
O best of kings, that non-perception of a real object—
whether it be a jar or something else, whether seen or unseen— is traditionally known as ignorance (ajñāna).
Non-perception is ignorance, while perception is knowledge;
because ignorance is not perceived and knowledge is perceived, ignorance is destroyed by knowledge.
O virtuous one, the cognition of water in the mirages of the desert is a vain delusion.

From the knowledge that "this is not water," the perception [of water] dissolves. That mature ignorance which dwells firmly in the heart as "this is the mind" is destroyed along with its very root by the knowledge that "the mind does not exist."
Just as the state of being a snake in a rope, which arises from the delusion of ignorance,
perishes when the knowledge that "this is not a snake" is firmly established in the heart; so too does the internal arising of ignorance— manifesting as "mind," "intellect," and "I"— [perish].
To that extent, the mind and the intellect remain indeed like an illusion; of this there is no doubt.

As long as the internal realization "I do not exist" has not arisen through the dawning of knowledge, to that extent the mind and the intellect remain like an illusion; here there is no doubt at all that they do not exist.
As long as there is the delusion of a false yakṣa, so long indeed is a yakṣa seen;
when the delusion of a false yakṣa has subsided, how can there be the possibility of a yakṣa?
There is no mind, nor any mental factors associated with the ego-sense and the like.
In this world, there exists only one pure consciousness.
By that [consciousness], when it was deluded, the mind, volitions, and so forth were created;
whatever it had willed, all of that has been abandoned by it once it has awakened.
Whatever comes about through volition departs through volition,
O mighty-armed one, like a mass of flames in a fire driven by the wind;
for that [world] is composed of the singular, dense reality of the Self, which is the very being of Brahman.
The entire world is pervaded [by it], like water by the ocean.
There is no "I," nor is there another; there is no you, nor these [senses], nor the mind.
There are no sense organs, nor is there space; only the one stainless Self exists.
That very same [reality] is perceived in the form of jars and other objects;
what a false conceptualization it is to think, "This is the mind" and "This is I"!
Nothing at all is born or dies within these three worlds.
The Self alone shines forth through the nature of the conception of existence and non-existence.
The Self is everything—the supreme Brahman—manifest and all-pervading once and for all;
neither duality nor unity exist. Be free from delusion through truth.
O friend, you exist as the very form of the qualities of all the senses, like the sky;
O one of great intelligence, you are not burned, nor are you defiled anywhere.
O friend, nothing of yours perishes, nor does anything increase.
Of you, who are of the nature of the stainless sky, single yet possessing infinite forms— those powers of yours consisting of desire and non-desire are indeed yourself;
for the moon is not perceived apart from its rays.

You are that primordial, unborn reality of the Self—ageless, beyond the other, the supreme nature, at once stainless, eternal, ever of one form, free from all mental construction, yet manifesting through the play known as the creative arts; you are that which has arisen from the beginning.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Awakening to the Ultimate Reality of Śikhidhvaja."
The one hundred and fifth canto:
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus reflecting upon those unfeigned words of Kumbha, the king—
In that very state of his own self, he became transformed in an instant;
with his mind and eyes closed, his speech stilled and free from fear,
his form appeared motionless, as if carved out of a slab of stone.
Then, after only a moment, Cūḍālā in the form of Kumbha spoke to him as he awoke with wide-open eyes: "O mighty-armed one, Kumbha said:"
Have you found rest in happiness upon this vast, pure, soft, and stainless couch, which is the state of those free from conceptual construction?
Are you awakened within, and have you cast off all delusion?
"Is that which is to be known fully understood, or has that which is to be seen been truly seen?
Śikhidhvaja replied:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, I am adorned with great majesty."
I have beheld that great station situated above all; oh,
what an unprecedented union with those great-souled ones who have known what is to be known— a union consisting of unique nectar, which bestows the fruit of the essence!
O lotus-eyed one, that which I have not obtained even through birth— the great nectar—
has today been attained by me spontaneously in an instant through association with you;
it is infinite, primordial, and immortal.
"How was this state of the Self attained by me?
Kumbha replied: "When the mind has reached tranquility and remains with the desire for enjoyments abandoned,"
When the ripening of the impurities has been completed and the entire collection of the senses [is stilled],
the stainless words of the Teacher find rest in the mind,
just as drops of saffron-water [rest] upon a pure white cloth.

O lotus-eyed one, today the ripening of the infinite impurities (*kaṣāya*) accumulated within your tiny body— which are of the very nature of your own latent impressions (*vāsanā*)— has arisen. All the impurities of the bodies [of beings] are [consumed] by time.
O virtuous friend, when the impurities consisting of latent impressions have dissolved, they fall away like fruits from a tree through ripening;
whatever the Guru speaks within then enters [you] like an arrow into its quiver.
Now that the ripening of your impurities is complete, you have been awakened by me today;
therefore, O Great-minded One, the destruction of your ignorance has occurred this very day.
Today your impurities are cooked away, and today indeed your ignorance is utterly destroyed.
This very day you shall be instructed; this very day you have awakened.
Today there is the total exhaustion of all your auspicious and inauspicious karmas; through the instruction of the company of the virtuous, their destruction has been accomplished for you.
O Lord of the Earth, for as long as this was the former portion of this day,
so long did your ignorance exist, thinking "I am the mind. Now, through the awakening by my words, that [ignorance] has come to an end within the mind.
O King, when [the mind] is completely relinquished from the heart, you have become fully awakened.
As long as the existence of the mind remains in the heart, so long does ignorance persist;
once the mind is abandoned by way of its nature as mind, the dawning of knowledge occurs.
The mind that perceives both duality and unity is called ignorance;
the dissolution of these two perceptions is knowledge, and that is the supreme goal.
You are awakened, you are liberated, O King, for the mind has been abandoned by you.

For that which is truly existent has been grasped by you through its being; the state of non-existence has been abandoned by you. Free from sorrow, free from exertion, free from attachment, eternally self-possessed, of great exaltation, a sage, observing silence, established in your own nature, remain stainless.
Śikhidvaja said:
"Indeed, O Blessed One, the mental ground exists only for a foolish being;
for one who is awakened and knows that [reality], O Lord, it is said that there is no mind at all."
"Tell me in full, with other rays of speech, how these who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta) wander about,
as well as those men such as yourself whose minds no longer exist."
"O Knower of Dharma, please thoroughly wipe away this darkness of my heart with such means as these. Kumbha replied: "It is exactly as you say; it is indeed so and not otherwise."

For the mind of those liberated while living does not exist, like a sprout from stones. That dense latent impression (*vāsanā*) which is capable of producing rebirth is designated by the word "mind" (*citta*); that [mind] does not exist for the knower of reality.
Know that impression by which those who know That (Tajjña) perform actions here— call it "being" (sattva), though it is free from rebirth.
These great-souled ones, liberated while living, are established in being and have their senses restrained.
They dwell free from attachment, never remaining fixed in the mind.
They say that the deluded state is "mind" (*citta*), while the awakened state is called "being" (*sattva*).
For those who are unawakened remain fixed in the mind, whereas those of great intelligence remain fixed in being.
The mind is born again and again, but the *sattva* is not born again;
there is bondage for the unawakened, O King, but none for the awakened.
You have become possessed of *sattva*, a great renunciant, and you remain steadfast.
"I know that today you have completely renounced the mind.
"O King, freed from all latent impressions (*vāsanā*), you shine like a sovereign;
O Sage, I consider your mind to have attained equality with space."
You have attained supreme tranquility, pure and established in equanimity,
like the great ocean of milk when it is no longer agitated by the striking of Mount Mandara.
You have likewise abandoned all attachment to kingship as well as to asceticism.
From the forest and from the body, and even from the fruits of good and evil deeds—
free from effort, devoid of attachment, with a mind renounced and cleansed of latent impressions— you have attained perfection, O mighty-armed one, having reached the state of the great renouncer.
For this is that great renunciation wherein everything is abandoned:
heaven, liberation, the mind, and even the fruits of austerity and charity.
O virtuous one, let it be awakened by the intellect through the supreme awakening, kindled by wisdom.
How much suffering could austerity possibly destroy?
That happiness which is free from decay and excess, which consists of equanimity—that alone is real, that is the true reality; it is something unique, whereas heaven and the like are perishable.
Mounted upon the scale of existence and non-existence, pierced by mental and physical ailments, what joy is there in that which is called heaven? Even that remains subject to doubt.
Until the accomplishment of one's own true goal is attained, the section on ritual action may appear auspicious.
How could one who has not obtained gold abandon brass?
Through association with Cūḍālā and others, you may easily attain the state of a knower;
why then are you immersed in this useless asceticism?
O wise one, behold the beginning and end of this evil deed, which is to be accomplished through the various stages of life such as the *āśrama*s; do not take pleasure in its middle alone.
For it is from this that these [stages] have emerged, and into this that they dissolve.
Establish your footing there upon those portions of conceptualization which are of the nature of austerity.
All phenomena have arisen from the sky of consciousness, which is clearer even than the physical ether;
they dissolve back into that very same place—dwell there and take delight therein.
"This must be done, this must not"—such volitions are but droplets of the Brahman.
O Śikhidhvaja, having abandoned these droplets, take refuge in the full cloud.
Just as a female friend is entreated, so do you request what is desired by me.
Why, then, does a woman not likewise herself entreat her beloved?
Great-souled and wise men do not grasp these states fashioned by imagination, which are radiant only at first sight, just as they do not grasp reflections of the moon in water.
Whatever yields fruits such as heaven or liberation is all equal;
having abandoned that which appears as equal, become indeed that very Self which is free from longing, [beholding] the existent as existent and the perishing as perishing.
Grasping this flood of objects, remain with a mind that has become motionless.
For one whose mind is without vibration, worldly existence no longer afflicts here,
O virtuous one, just as misfortune arising from human agency does not affect a man of sound policy.

O Lord of the Earth, whatever sufferings manifest here in the three worlds, all of them arise solely from the fickleness of the mind. He whose mind is steady, peaceful, motionless, and free from instability— *Note: The verse concludes with the description of the one who has attained such a state.*

He is the all-pervading Lord, he is the possessor of great bliss; he is the vessel of universal sovereignty. Now, O knower of reality, having brought both movement and stillness into oneness within the mind, remain as you wish, having attained eternal unity.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Lord, how have these two—vibration and non-vibration—attained unity?
O dispeller of all doubts, tell me this quickly.
Kumbha said:
The entire world is a single reality, pure consciousness alone, like water in the ocean.
That very reality either vibrates or does not, just as pure water [appears] with its waves.
That which is sung of by such names as "Brahman," "pure consciousness alone," "stainless," and "truth"—
that very thing, O dear one, the deluded perceive as the world;
for thus does the cycle of worldly existence arise even while the entire creation remains utterly motionless.
For movement consists of waves and the like, whereas that which is motionless is the supreme state of equality.
If that very movement of consciousness is likewise cultivated as motionless,
then by virtue of its single nature, it is indeed that very same immovable Śiva.
When creation, which is essentially nothing but the vibration of consciousness, is seen correctly, it dissolves;
when seen incorrectly, it arises like the delusion of a snake in a rope.
Consciousness, designated as "consciousness," is with vibration, but this [ultimate] consciousness is pervasive and without vibration.
Established in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), it cannot be expressed by speech.
When the mind has attained purity over time through the yoga of continuous practice— arising from contact with the scriptures and virtuous people— it is like the risen moon.
This has appeared as such, spread forth by the words of one's own experience;
yet the true nature of one's own experience is known by oneself through oneself.
You have attained your own state, which is without beginning or middle; remain right here, established in this desired station.
O virtuous one, you have indeed been born as the Great Consciousness-Self, formless and indivisible, truly free from sorrow.
The hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja."
Kumbha said: "O Lord of the Earth, Śikhidhvaja, I have thus told you everything—
how all this has arisen and how it dissolves."
"O leader of sages, having heard this, understood it, and reflected upon it, remain as you wish, with the state clearly perceived within the state itself.
At this very moment, I am going to heaven; there, the sage Nārada—"*
He returns from the world of Brahmā to the assembly of the immortals.
If they do not see me there, he becomes angry;
for the venerable ones should never be made to feel agitation by one who is worthy.
With all mental constructs abandoned and desiring nothing whatsoever, you must dwell in the Self alone; this very vision is purifying.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, even as Śikhidvaja, with flowers in his hand, was about to offer a reply and a prostration, he vanished from sight;
just as an object that has appeared in a vision is no longer seen before one's eyes.
King Śikhidhvaja did not see Kumbha before him.
When Kumbha had gone, the protector of the earth was filled with supreme wonder;
reflecting upon that very marvel, he became as if fixed in a painting.
Thus he reflected: "How wondrous is the play of Fate, that I have finally been awakened by this one under the name of Kumbha! Where is Kumbha, the son of Nārada, and where am I, named Śikhidhvaja?"
"Only through the proper timing have I thus been awakened. Oh, how well and logically this has been stated by the son of the gods!
Oh, after a long time, I have finally awakened from the sleep of delusion!"
"Where was I, submerged in the foul mud of the web of ritual acts, practicing the false delusion of 'this must be done' and 'this must not be done'?
Oh, how cool, pure, and peaceful is this, my own true path! (MU 6.106.12)

Taking the form of an elixir, it cools my very being as it were. I am stilled, I am extinguished, and I abide in absolute bliss; I do not even desire mere consciousness, but remain established just as I am.

Reflecting thus, the king, with his intention to renounce the world in this manner, remained in silence alone, as if carved out of stone. Then, in that very state— silent, free from conceptual construction, and without affliction— *he remained.*

Having attained an immovable foundation, he stood firm like the peak of a mountain. There, his fear completely stilled, that great-souled one, whose mind was equanimous, found rest after a long time; having finally attained his own stainless self through yoga, that conscious soul then fell into a deep sleep.
The one hundred and seventh canto, titled "The Composure of Śikhidhvaja," by Vasiṣṭha:
Through non-conceptual absorption, he remained like a piece of wood or a wall;
O Rāma, hear now how Śikhidhvaja [was addressed] by Cūḍālā,
who was in the guise of Kumbha, regarding that husband of hers.
Having awakened [the prince] and vanished, he swiftly crossed the sky.
In the heavens, he cast off his illusory form as a son of the gods and assumed a beautiful, feminine appearance, charming yet artless.

Having reached her own city through the sky, she entered the inner apartments in an instant; she became visible to the world and performed the duties of a queen. After three days, she returned once more to the heavens.
Through yoga, Kumbha became [invisible] and went to the forest of Śikhidhvaja.
Then, while staying on that very forest ground, she saw the king absorbed in unwavering meditative concentration (nirvikalpa-samādhi), as if carved out from a tree.
"Aha! Indeed, O sir, by good fortune this one has found rest here in the Self;
he stands healthy, equanimous, and peaceful," he said before the Lord.
"Therefore, let me first awaken him from this state to the supreme state."
Why indeed does he abandon his body this very moment?
After having enjoyed for some time either this kingdom or the forest,
we two shall go together to peace once these bodies have been cast off.
"Before this [body] undergoes an irreversible transformation,
I shall awaken it by means of this practice of yoga.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā let out a lion’s roar.
When he did not waver, like a rock on a mountain, even by that roar which was repeated again and again before his lord and which inspired fear in the forest-dwellers,
then she caused him to move.
When the king was neither awakened nor even moved though he had been shaken and cast down, then Cūḍālā, in the form of Kumbha, reflected:
"Aha! This Blessed One has truly reached maturity in his own state."
Therefore, by what means shall I now awaken him?
Or rather, why should I awaken this great-souled one?
Let him remain as he pleases, having attained awakening while being bodiless (videha).
"I too, having abandoned this female body, shall go to the supreme state from which there is no rebirth; for what indeed is mine here?
Having reflected thus, she prepared herself to abandon her own body.
Then that great virtuous woman, Cūḍālā, reflected once more:
"I shall indeed examine this body of the lord of the earth to see if there remains within his heart even a trace of vital essence, the seed of awakening."
In time, this Blessed One will attain full awakening,
like a cluster of flowers nestled within the sap of their root-stalks during the spring.
Thus, wandering here, he alone becomes one who is liberated while living.

"I think he must be Māyika; my peace of mind does not depart," Cūḍālā thought thus. Then, having observed her husband with apprehension through both touch and sight, that woman of excellent complexion spoke.
"There remains indeed a residue of being in his heart, the cause for awakening:
this body has not yet lost its form; I shall not abandon this physical frame.
Rāma:

"O Brahmin, how is one who possesses a deeply tranquil mind— who stands like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, and whose only remainder is pure being— known to be a man of meditative absorption? Vasiṣṭha replied:
In whose heart there exists a cause for awakening— a subtle essence of being remaining within, like the flower and fruit within a seed— such a person,
freed from the flickering of the mind, possesses an unfluctuating, true consciousness.
For one who is free from duality and unity, whose body is established in equanimity and immovability,
the even distribution of experience neither languishes nor exults;
it neither sets nor rises, but remains perfectly balanced.
The body of one whose mind vibrates with notions such as duality and unity undergoes change; it never does so for one who is motionless.
Indeed, the vibration of the mind is the cause of the existence of the entire world.

O Rāghava, just as spring is the season for flowers, so is the mind the source of the fluctuations of emotion. For that body in which the mind vibrates repeatedly falls under the sway of joy, despondency, and delusion.

When the mind has attained tranquility, the physical body that remains for such a person—though possessed of vital strength—is no longer subject to the transformations of states of being, just as the sky is not affected by them. Just as waves and the like do not arise from a continuous flow of water that has become calm; so too, when the mind is stilled, the fluctuations of existence do not arise.
Thus no fault is seen in one whose being is established in equanimity.
There is no perception of a self apart from its own subsiding;
as long as the being remains in equilibrium, it merely subsides in due time.
But in that body where neither mind nor being is found,
O Rāma, it dissolves into the five elements like a mountain of fire or ice;
this very body of Śikhidhvaja was certainly abandoned by the consciousness.
And because it was endowed with a portion of his essence, it did not become a vessel for decay.
Beholding her husband’s body in such a state, that excellent woman did not abandon her own body, but reflected quickly.
Having entered the all-pervading, pure essence of consciousness (*cittattva*), I awaken it;
for this beloved awakening is about to occur, as he is established therein.
If I do not awaken him, he will eventually awaken by himself after a long time.
"Why should I remain here alone?"— thinking thus, I shall awaken him.
Having reflected in this way, Cūḍālā abandoned her body, that cage of causal elements, and attained stability in the primordial consciousness which is devoid of beginning and end.
There, having caused the conscious vibration of the living Lord,
she entered her own body again from the sky, like a bird into its nest;
then, shaped like a jar, she rose up and settled upon a bed of flowers.
That Sāman, having begun its course, resounded like a swarm of bees.
Hearing that sound of the Sāman, the consciousness of the king, endowed with the quality of sattva,
awakened within his body like a lotus in spring.
Then King Śikhidhvaja, having attained the perfection of inner being, caused that vision to blossom like the sun causes a lotus;
he beheld Kumbha standing before him, intent upon singing the Sāman hymns.
"Endowed with a most excellent form, like another Sāmaveda," [the king thought].
"Oh, how blessed we are that the son of the sage has returned!
Saying this, the king offered flowers to Kumbha.
"By good fortune, O Blessed One, we abide within your purifying mind;
for indeed, what great beings are not steadfast in their favors?
This alone is the means by which we are purified and the cause of our arrival."
"Tell me, which other [remedy] for removing sin could there be? Kumbha replied:
O subduer of enemies, from the moment I departed from your presence..."
From that time forth, my mind has remained here together with you alone.
O sinless one, I find no delight in the stages of heaven, nor in the celestial gardens,
nor on the peaks of Meru and Mandara, nor in the caves of Kailāsa.
I desire only union with you, which is made beautiful by your auspicious conduct,
like a tree longing for the month of Madhu, which resembles a flow of nectar.
Therefore, I remain here now in your presence.

Whatever is most desired, my dear friend, that stands at the very forefront of all beautiful things. I believe there is no one in this world who is such a kinsman, a trusted confidant, a well-wisher, a friend, a companion, or a trustworthy disciple as you are to me.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Oh, how the trees of merit have borne fruit for us on this mountain of our lineage,
since even you, though unattached, desire union with us!"
"This is the forest, these are the trees, and here I am, your attentive servant. O Lord, if heaven does not please you, then let it be dwelt in here.
Through the yoga-method bestowed by you, I have found rest.

O virtuous one, I think that heaven is just like this; for where is there rest in heaven? Relying upon that very same pure and luminous state of self-abiding, you may roam here as you wish, whether in heaven or upon the surface of the earth.
Kumbha:
Have you perhaps found rest in the supreme state of great bliss?
Have you perhaps completely abandoned this suffering consisting of duality?
O King, has your intense delight in volitions that are charming only at first sight been completely uprooted, like a creeper on a riverbank swept away by the current?
Have you reached a state of peace, transcending the conditions of what is to be abandoned and what is to be acquired, remaining in a perfectly equanimous stability?
"Is your mind established, free from agitation regarding whatever has been attained?
Śikhidhvaja replied:
"By your grace, O Blessed One, the state that transcends all objects of perception has been seen."
The limit of saṃsāra has been reached; the certainty regarding what was to be attained has been found.
After a very long time indeed, we have finally come to rest, free from ailment. Everything that was to be attained has been attained; we are satisfied and remain whole for all eternity.
Nothing at all needs to be taught to us;
we are entirely satisfied everywhere, established and free from the fever of worldly distress.
What was known and what was unknown, what was unattained and what was attained, what was abandoned and what was clung to—[all this is now resolved].
There is nothing such as "you-ness" in you, nor "I-ness" in me; it is like the sky, possessing nothing at all.

Free from worldly existence, devoid of delusion, fear, and attachment, eternally awakened, with an equanimous disposition toward all and entirely gentle, being the self of all yet liberated from all conceptual synthesis, I abide in peace, as clear as the expanse of space.
The one hundred and eighth canto, titled "The Yoga of Kumbha’s Return," by Vasiṣṭha:
Thus, those two, the knower and the known, sat together in the forest for three muhūrtas, conversing with one another on various topics concerning the inner self.
Then, rising from there, they bathed in a certain lake abounding with cranes.
They sported in lakes and in forests that were like the Nandana grove;
by means of that conduct and those conversations, those two forest-dwellers spent eight days in those woodland paths.
Then Kumbha said, "Let us go to another forest on the mountain. Thinking "So be it," the king agreed, and they both set out.
They traversed forests of many forms, jungles, and riverbanks.
Lakes, thickets of shrubs, peaks, and dense forests;
likewise rivers, regions, villages, towns, and cities;
desolate wastes, formidable mountains, groves, sacred fords, and sanctuaries.
Being exactly equal in affection, equal in dress, equal in strength,
and equal in energy, the two remained so as they bathed and likewise stood;
O Rāghava, they both worshipped the ancestors and the gods and partook of their meals together.
They lay together on the same bed and became equal in their understanding.
In groves of *tamāla* trees and thickets of *mandāra* blossoms,
that couple, with affectionate hearts like two friends, shone resplendently.
The mental construction of conceptualization— thinking "this is to be grasped" and "this is not"—
did not carry away those two, O Rāma, any more than a whirlwind carries away the mountain of the gods. Those two friends wandered here and there, at times grey with dust.
In some places their limbs were smeared with sandalwood paste, and in others they were anointed with ashes;
in some places they wore divine garments, and in others they wore rags;
in some places they were covered with sprouts, and in others they were adorned with flowers.
Within just a few days, because her mind was thus absorbed and due to the loftiness of her virtuous nature,
the king shone like Kumbha.
Then Cūḍālā [beheld] that Śikhidhvaja, who possessed the luster of a celestial being.
Seeing that he had attained such splendor, the proud woman reflected:
"This husband of mine is of irreproachable soul, and so too are these forest lands;
this state of being free from toil—only he who is not a man of desire is cheated of it."
For those whose minds are liberated while living, who remain with whatever comes to them regarding enjoyment,

that which arises as a state of one-pointedness would be merely a trivial and foolish delusion. [Likewise,] a husband of one's own, of blameless nature, freedom from disease, and fresh youth— these are likewise [not to be clung to].

She who does not desire her own home, which is like a lattice of flowers, is truly ruined. She who does not delight in the house of forest-flower creepers while her dear husband is under her control, that sorrowless woman is indeed a ruined and wicked woman.

"Fie upon that wicked woman who, having obtained a beloved husband as her wedded lord, does not take pleasure in him in private! Fie upon the knower of what is to be known who abandons even that which has come to him! [MU 6.108.19] Thus it was said by one who knows the truth.
"What blameless and noble purpose could one who knows [the truth] have accomplished?
Therefore, I shall quickly compose some new literary elaboration with my wisdom,
by which this lord of the earth, my husband and bestower of honor, may take delight in me."
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā, assuming the guise of Kumbha and standing amidst the thickets of the forest, spoke to her husband like a female cuckoo to a male cuckoo. Kumbha said:
"This is the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, a favorable day;
today, indeed, Hari’s assembly in heaven is a grand undertaking.
I must establish my presence there in the presence of my father."
For destiny, as it stands, must never be abandoned.
Today, you must wait for me here in this forest region,
sporting with the flowers of meditation and remaining free from agitation.
"I come today at the end of the day from the sky, free from conceptual thought;
even more than from heaven itself, union with you brings me satisfaction.
Having said this, Kumbha gave a cluster of flowers to his friend Mañjarī.
As if for her own pleasure, she [embraced] her beloved, born from the trees of the Nandana grove.
While the king was speaking thus, "You must return very soon," he leapt from the forest into the sky like a charming autumn cloud.

As he moved through the sky, Śikhidhvaja beheld that mass of flowers born from the flower-garlands, which was being scattered by the forest wind like a snowy cloud in winter. It vanished from sight as it traveled on.
For true affection is indeed difficult to abandon, like the sleepless yearning of a peacock for the rainy season.

At the conclusion of Śikhidhvaja’s vision, she, whose body was like a water-jar, cast off her form in the sky like a whirlpool in a mass of water, and that lovely girl returned to her own true nature.
By way of the celestial path, she reached her own city, which was as delightful as heaven, resembling a wish-fulfilling tree in full bloom with its fluttering banners;
and without being seen, she entered the inner apartments crowded with beautiful women.
She was like the Great Lakṣmī of the month of Madhu upon a tree with shimmering creepers.
Having swiftly accomplished all the royal duties there,
she leaped once more into the sky to go to Śikhidhvaja’s grove.
Having traversed the path of the sky, level with the rays of the sun,
she, remaining in the air, beheld the forest of Śikhidhvaja upon the mountain;
seeing that form of Kumbha, she quickly seized it once again.
And before Śikhidhvaja it fell away like a flower in the sky;
there, with its luster faded, it made his face appear weary of mind,
like the moon shrouded in mist or a lotus withered by the night.
Seeing him in such a form, Śikhidhvaja rose up;
his heart became distressed, and with great respect, he spoke these words:
"O son of a god, homage be to you! You appear as if troubled in mind."
"O Kumbha, abandon your agitation; please be seated on this seat.

For those who are virtuous and have known what is to be known do not resort to a state born of joy or dejection; established in their own self, they remain like lotuses untouched by the moisture of water."
When he was told, "Therefore, sit down," Kumbha, as he sat upon the seat,
spoke with a dejected voice that resembled the sound of a broken bamboo:
"Those who, throughout the various states of existence, maintain an even mind for as long as they live..."

Those who do not abide with the organs of action are not wise in reality; they are rogues. O King, those fools who do not know the truth, due to their very childishness, flee from the states that have been naturally assumed.
As oil exists within every sesame seed, so does the state of decay exist within every body.
He who does not fall into this bodily state cuts through the sky with a sword;
for this is indeed the unsurpassed means of avoiding the suffering of the body's decay.
That equanimity belongs to the mind through yoga, and not to the state of the organs of action.
O dear one, as long as the body lasts, one who understands should abide according to conduct by means of the organs of action,
but never by means of the organs of perception.
All beings, beginning with Parameṣṭhin, remain within the various states of the body with their intentions fully awakened; this is the certainty of destiny.
Indeed, all this visible world consists of those who are ignorant of reality, those who know reality, and elemental beings.
All of that indeed runs toward necessity (niyati), just as water flows toward the ocean.

Those who know this remain unimpaired as long as the body lasts, experiencing this necessity through the equality of the intellect and other faculties, as well as through the movement of the hands and other limbs.
But the ignorant, O dear one, struck by states of pleasure and pain through the agitation of all things and shattered by hundreds of thousands of bodily marks, submit themselves to destiny.
Thus, O dear one, it has been understood here by living beings that they must remain in this manner amidst pleasures and likewise amidst states of suffering.
That which manifests as the collection of both the knower and the ignorant is indeed this fixed play of destiny, which is difficult to transcend.
The one hundred and ninth canto, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Conduct for the Liberated while Living."
Śikhidhvaja said: "This being so, O illustrious one, how have you come to experience such agitation,
even though you are a god and a source of happiness even beyond heaven?"
Kumbha said: Listen, O lord of the earth, to this wonderful matter of mine;
I shall relate to you in its entirety what has happened to me today in heaven.
Sorrow, when disclosed to a friend, reaches a state of extreme attenuation;
it is like a thick, dull, and dark cloud that has released its rain.
Through a friend who inquires after one's welfare, the mind attains clarity.
Just as water is quickly purified by a cleansing agent (kataka) that has been applied with affection; so too,
having gone from here and given a cluster of flowers to you,
I have crossed the sky and arrived at the celestial realm (triviṣṭapa).
There, having stood in the assembly hall of Indra together with his father in due order,
and having risen at the time for departure, he was dismissed by his father; saying,
"I have come here to this world, having abandoned heaven and reached the sky," he departed.
I travel along the path of the wind together with the horses of the sun. Then, while the sun has gone by one way, I return by another path, appearing as if falling from the ocean of the sky.
Then, in the midst of clouds filled with water along the path ahead,
I saw the sage Durvāsas approaching swiftly—
clothed in a garment of rainclouds and adorned with a circle of lightning.

With his mass of limbs washed by the rain, he stood upon the surface of the earth in the shade of a great cloud like a woman going to meet her lover (*abhisārikā*). With haste, he rushed toward her as if toward the beloved goddess of ascetic splendor (*tapolakṣmī*).
Having paid him homage, I said while carrying [the load]:
"O Sage, you who are clothed in dark-blue clouds are like a woman going to meet her lover.
Upon hearing this, O giver of honor, he became enraged with me, the destroyer of his pride.
Widening his blood-red eyes, he spoke with a deep resonance:
"I am the grandson of the Lotus-born; why are you so arrogant?
For worthy men bow down because of their virtues, just as trees bend under the weight of their fruit."
"O wicked and deluded Devakumāra, you speak foul words to me, saying that you are like a courtesan going to meet her lover;
[yet] a beloved woman possesses breasts and hair, and is transformed by gestures and expressions."
"Go! Because of this ill-spoken word, you shall become a courtesan at night.
Having heard this inauspicious speech uttered by the decrepit Brahmin, I reflected for a moment; meanwhile, the sage vanished from sight.
"Thus, O virtuous one, with a troubled mind, I have arrived here from the surface of the sky.
I have told you all of this; I have become a woman of the night. How can I pass this state of womanhood at the ends of these days?"
At night, one who has entered the womb should say: "What have I done to my father? Alas, how strange is the course of destiny within this cycle of existence!
By fate, I too have become like others—a prey for young men."
"Alas! Because of my abduction, a quarrel now arises here between the divine youths in heaven, whose minds are agitated by passion,
and those who, with souls overcome by shame, [belong] to the gurus, gods, and the twice-born."
"How should I, as a woman of the night, properly conduct myself before you?
