Vasiṣṭha, the son of the Sage, having said this, remained silent for a moment.
Taking heart, Kumbha spoke again here, O descendant of Raghu:
"Why do I grieve like an ignorant man? What injury has been done to my self?
This body, which is distinct from me, shall experience [the consequences] according to how it came to be."
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Devaputra, what is the use of this lamentation for you?
Let that which comes come; the self of the body is not defiled."
Whatever sufferings or pleasures are ordained,
all of those belong to the body, not to the embodied soul;
yet if you, though unworthy of distress, nevertheless suffer on account of these effects.
O ornament of the scriptures, what other means could there be for others?
Furthermore, why did you say that one should speak with composure when in distress? Now, having attained equanimity, remain as you are, free from weariness.
Vasiṣṭha:
Having thus mutually consoled one another with such words,
those two affectionate friends remained together in the forest, both distressed within themselves.
Then the sun, the lamp of the world, went to its setting as if producing femininity in that jar, like a lamp extinguished by the exhaustion of its oil.
Along with the weight of worldly affairs, the lotuses underwent contraction.
The roads, together with the travelers, and the hearts of the wives of those on the journey—
like fishermen, they gathered all the birds into one heap;
thus the world, though rich with the jewel-net of stars, fell into darkness.
The lake of night-lotuses, rich with stars, reached its full bloom as if laughing;
it resounded with the cries of cakravāka birds and swarms of wandering bees.
Then those two friends rose up for the twilight hour, when the moon was beginning to rise.
Having paid their respects and performed their recitations in that manner, they remained within the thicket.

Then Kumbha, gradually assuming a feminine form there, spoke with faltering words to Śikhidhvaja who stood before him: *Muṇḍakopaniṣad-bhāṣya 6.109.34–35* (as per the source text provided) [Note: The provided text contains a citation from the *Muṇḍakopaniṣad-bhāṣya*, but the content describes a narrative involving Kumbha and Śikhidhvaja, which is characteristic of the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*. The translation reflects the Sanskrit verses as they appear.]
"I seem to fall, I seem to quiver, and I seem to melt away with my slender limbs;
O King, I think that out of shame I am turning into a woman.
Behold, O King, these hairs of mine are growing longer."
Like rows of shimmering stars at the end of the day amidst the darkness,
these two breasts of mine appear upon my chest,
opening wide like two lotus buds facing the sky in springtime.
"My garments have become so long that they reach down to my ankles;
look, friend, as if from the body itself of a woman, they grow longer and longer.
My ornaments of vast jewels and my various garlands likewise."
"Behold, my dear, how these [limbs] arise from my own limbs like flowers upon a tree. Behold, my dear, how this frost— beautiful as a mass of moonbeams—
has risen of its own accord upon my head like a silken turban on a mountain."
"O giver of honor, all the signs of a beloved have appeared within me;
alas, what a pity! I am despondent—what shall I do? For I am a woman.
"Alas, what a pity! Oh, virtuous one, I remain indeed a woman!"
"Consciously, I am experiencing within me the buttocks joined with the hips," he said in the forest, "O Kumbha! Having spoken thus, he became silent and dejected.
And the king, beholding him, likewise remained despondent in spirit.
In just a moment, Śikhidhvaja spoke these words:
"Alas! O lady of excellent complexion, this one has become a great being.
O virtuous one, you have known what is to be known; you understand the course of destiny."
Do not become distressed in heart regarding this inevitable matter.

My dear son, such conditions befall even the wise when they concern the body alone; however, for those who possess higher wisdom, these do not affect the mind, nor does the mind depart along with the body.
Kumbha said:
"So be it; I shall assume the female form of a night-walker.
I do not feel any distress—for by whom can destiny be transgressed?"
Having thus resolved, the two of them mutually diminished that grief and spent the night in silence on a single bed for a long time. Then,
at dawn, having spontaneously cast off their youthful forms, they departed.
Kumbha became one whose embodied form was cast off by breasts resembling jars;
thus that queen Cūḍālā, of excellent complexion,
having assumed the state of a jar for her husband's sake, subsequently returned to womanhood.
The virtuous maiden dwelt in the forest regions at night;
by day, she remained united with her husband and friend, assuming the form of a water-jar.
Her movement through yoga was unimpeded as she traveled across the peaks of Kailāsa, Mandara, Sumeru, Mahendra, and Sahya.
Adorned with garlands, necklaces, and large ornaments, that woman sported as she pleased together with her beloved friend and lord.
The hundred-and-tenth canto, titled "The Attainment of Womanhood."
Vasiṣṭha:
Then, after only a few days had passed, that virtuous woman, assuming the form of a water-jar, spoke thus to her husband: MU 6.110.1.
"O King, lotus-petal-eyed one, hear these words of mine:
every night I remain here as a woman.
Therefore, I wish to master such feminine arts."
"I give myself in marriage to some husband;
therefore, you alone among the three worlds please as my husband. Accept me in marriage to be your wife for all time, even at night."
"O virtuous one, I wish to enjoy the pleasure of women together with my dear friend who has come to me unbidden; do not be an obstacle to me.
This pleasure has proceeded in due order since the beginning of creation, is easily attained, and is delightful."
What fault can possibly arise for one who performs his duty as it naturally occurs?

Since there is a unity between desire and non-desire, and because all things are equal [in their nature], we have neither desire nor non-desire; therefore, this [action] is performed by us as something intended.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O friend, O one of great intelligence, by performing this deed I perceive neither good nor evil; therefore, do as you wish."
"With a mind that has attained equanimity, I see these three worlds as being of the very nature of space; act as you wish. Kumbha said:
"If this is so, O protector of the earth, then this very day is an auspicious conjunction;
for I have calculated all of this,
including that tonight, when the moon has risen with its full and stainless digits, this is the full moon of the month of Śrāvaṇa."
"O mighty-armed one, a birth shall come to both of us alone,
upon this delightful peak of the summit of Mahendra’s mountain,
adorned with jeweled palaces richly illuminated by islands of gems."
In that place, which was resplendent with tall trees bent low under the weight of their blossoms,
and enchanting with the dance of forest flowers and creepers like dancing women,
the stars in the sky at night were accompanied by their lord, the full moon.
"Let those whose eyes reach to their ears look upon us both.
Arise for the sake of our own marriage; O King, let us prepare from the hollow of the forest a collection of sandalwood, flowers, and other materials, combined with jewels."
Having spoken thus, Kumbha rose up together with that king and gathered flowers as well as a collection of jewels and other treasures.
Then, in just a moment, on a level and auspicious jeweled peak—
By those two, heaps were indeed made, rich with unguents and flowers;
those heaps of necklaces, garments, and supreme jewels shone like the treasuries of Fortune herself, accumulated by Kāma through the course of time.
Likewise, having prepared the necessary equipment for the journey, those two great friends went to the river Mandākinī in the Golden Cave to bathe; there,
he then respectfully bathed the great king.

Kumbha, preceded by auspicious rites, approached his beloved Cūḍālā— who possessed shoulders like the frontal globes of an elephant, who was destined to be a wife, and who was to become his future husband— and he bathed her while assuming the form of Kumbha.
Having bathed there, the two worshipped the gods, the ancestors, and the sages;
they were as indifferent toward the fruits of ritual action as they were toward the abandonment of such action.
Always satiated by the essence of knowledge, they remained so for the sake of maintaining the established order of the world.
Those two auspicious ones, incited by one another, partook of food;
having put on white garments produced by the wish-fulfilling trees and having eaten the fruits, they proceeded in due order to the place where the bridegroom was staying.

In this much time, as those two were longing for their birthplace, the sun suddenly entered the mountain of setting, as if to do them a kindness. Then, when the sequence of twilight rites had occurred and the recitation of prayers (*japa*) and the *aghamarṣaṇa* had been performed,
As if to witness the wedding, the sky became filled with a net of stars;
then the night, the sole companion of the pair of lovers, smiling with its clusters of white water-lilies,
arrived scattering a profusion of frosty mist.
On the mountain peak, the pitcher properly arranged many jewel-lamps,
like the Lotus-born [Brahmā] from the sky arranging the celestial lights joined with the sun and moon; thus,
at the onset of night, he adorned the king as he assumed the state of a woman.
With floods of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, with musk and saffron;
likewise with necklaces, armlets, and bracelets, as well as garments from the *kalpalatā* tree;
with garlands, crests, and various woven flower wreaths.
Likewise, with clusters of *kalpalatā* creepers, *mandāra* and *pārijātaka* trees, *santāna* trees laden with many jewels, and a crown in the form of the moon—
after such a length of time, Kumbha attained the state of a bridegroom.
Pressed against her firm breasts, he quickly became full of amorous playfulness.
He reflected thus: "I have become this bride;
for the sake of passion, my very self must be surrendered by me; indeed, the duty appropriate to the occasion must be performed."
"I am here, the beloved bride; this husband stands before me.
Come, O Kāma, take me! This is your time, O dweller in the heart!"—having thus reflected, she [beheld] her husband standing before her, adorned.
She spoke to Kāma as Rati might to him when he was rising like the sun:
"O bestower of honor, I am Madanikā by name; I am your wife. This salutation is made by me to you, my husband, with affection."
Having spoken thus, she of faultless limbs, her face bowed down with shame, respectfully prostrated before her husband with her head and its dangling locks.
And she said this: "O Lord, please adorn me with ornaments."
"Having gradually kindled the fire, take my hand in marriage.
O Lord, you shine exceedingly; you make me sick with love. In the wedding of Rati, you stand surpassing Madana himself."
O King, your garlands shine like the networks of rays from the moon;
the necklace upon your chest bears the luster of the flowing stream of the Gaṅgā on Mount Meru.
O monarch, you shine with your locks of hair interwoven with mandāra flowers.
Like a golden lotus with restless bees grey with pollen,
O Lord, you stand surpassing Mount Meru in your jewel-like nets of light, in flowers, in splendor, in stability, in brilliance, and in loftiness.
Speaking in this manner, those two— future husband and wife who had previously been a hidden couple— became mutually delighted.
King Śikhidhvaja [addressed] Queen Madanikā.
Having seated her upon a pure golden couch, he himself adorned her with ear-ornaments,
garlands, and decorations of gems and pearls;
with garments, ointments, and flowers, each placed in its appropriate position.
Adorned, that slender woman, intoxicating and bestowing delight,
shone like Pārvatī longing for her wedding, like a passionate woman beloved by Kāma.
Having adorned the Great Queen, the Great King spoke thus to her:
O fawn-eyed one, you shine like the Fortune newly arisen.
May that blessing which belongs to Śacī with Śakra, that which belongs to Lakṣmī with Hari,
and that which belongs to Gaurī with Śambhu, be yours.
With teeth like the sprouts of a lotus root and eyes like trembling blue lotuses,
you stand like a lotus pond, your form made fragrant and beautiful;
with hands like deep red young shoots, you bear breasts like flower clusters.
I consider you alone to be the fruit-bearing creeper of the wish-fulfilling tree of desire.
With limbs as pure and cool as snow, and a smile that radiates like moonlight,
you bring complete delight the moment you are seen, like the splendor of the full moon appearing.
"Therefore arise, O lady of beautiful hips; let us ourselves prepare the wedding altar in due order, with nets of jewel-like flowers and creepers.
Having spoken thus, the two lovely spouses then prepared it.
He prepared an altar for his own marriage in the jeweled cave of Mahendra,
adorned with clusters of pearls, blossoms with bees as their humming ornaments,
jeweled garlands with tinkling sounds, and fluttering Vaijayantī banners.
With threads of *kalpa*-tree creepers, with clusters of *kalpa*-blossoms, with bands of *kalpa*-trees,
and with heaps of *kalpa*-tree fruits;
with networks of *devadāru* creeper-veils, marked with *kāṇḍa-pratisara* amulets.
With showers of pearls, flowers, and parched grain resembling stars,
and with four great coconuts placed in the four directions as full jars filled with the waters of the Ganges; MU_6,110.57–58.
In the midst of that [fire-pit], they kindled a fire with sandalwood logs,
its flames blazing, circumambulated it from the right while standing on the south,
and sat down first upon seats of leafy sprouts facing the east, in front of the fire.

Having directed the lovely couple [to their seats], he himself entered. Śikhidhvaja, having offered sesame seeds, parched grain, and other oblations to the fire, rose up, raised his beloved by her hands, and took her in his own arms.
Shining with one another like two other newlywed auspicious couples,
that pair of husband and wife performed the circumambulation of the sacred fire.
[He gave her] his own inheritance, the entirety of his knowledge, his heart, and his unwavering love.
Those two, honoring one another with the radiant beauty of their smiling faces,
performed three circumambulations and offered parched grains into the fire; then,
seeing my wife from the sky, they gradually released their hands.
With smiling faces, the two lovely ones, like two newly risen moons,
entered upon a fresh bed of flowers prepared beforehand.
In that interval, the moon [descended] one-fourth from the surface of the sky.
He slowly caused her to ascend, as if to behold the beauty of these two;
on that plateau, O beautiful woman, the moon sent forth his flickering rays through the gaps in the creepers, as if casting glances all around to look at them.
While they were thus engaged in various conversations there as the moon rose,
that lovely couple remained for a moment.
Then, having risen, [they entered] a golden cave illuminated by blazing jewel-lamps.
The two lovers entered the secret chamber they themselves had previously prepared;
there they beheld a new couch fashioned of flowers,
surrounded on all sides by heaps of blooming golden lotuses.
Constructed from *mandāra* and other flowers, free from wilting,
and reaching a height equal to the stature of a man, it was fashioned from uniform blossoms;
it resembled the long disk of the moon and was as cool as a bed of frost.
Resembling a stream of milk from the ocean, white as a mass of moonlight,
it stood like the reflection of Ananta upon a jeweled wall—
fragrant, lofty, lovely, and free from decay.
That couple fell upon that heap of pure white flowers,
which was as level and expansive in its expanse as Mount Mandara in the Ocean of Milk.
Then, with various graceful expressions of speech tender in their prostrations, and with endearments and services appropriate for the occasion, they [honored him].
For those two who were so deeply in love, that long night passed as if it were but a moment, filled with ever-new joys.
Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh canto, titled "The Playful Marriage."
Vasiṣṭha: Then, within the interior of the world colored by the rays of the sun,
Madanī, the wife of Śikhidhvaja, once again assumed the form of a water-jar.
Thus, on Mount Mahendra, both Kumbha and Śikhidhvaja were married by their own choice; as a desirable and accomplished new couple,
they sported daily amidst the various forest groves.
Upon trees laden with the weight of ripened fruit and adorned with flowers and tender shoots,
the beloved couple remained inseparable throughout the day as they were even more dear to one another than a friend; at night, like two lamps of radiance, they stayed closely embraced.
They sported in forest groves and mountain caves,
amidst thickets of *tamāla* and *sāla* trees, and in the dense thickets of *mandāra* blossoms;
they dwelt upon the Sahya, Dardura, Kailāsa, Mahendra, and Malaya mountains.
And having traveled for three days each across the slopes of Gandhamādana, the Vindhya mountains, and the Lokāloka range, when her beloved had fallen asleep,
Cūḍālā performed her royal duties and returned once more to her own place.
Those two, the King and the Earth, remained together in mutual joy— friends by day and husband and wife by night—
adorned with various flowers for one month on a peak of Mount Mahendra, thick with *sarala* trees.
In cave-dwellings with walls of jewels, they were honored by gods and kinnaras;
and on the back of Mount Śuktimat, where the rising moon was within reach of the hand and the Mandāra groves formed a garland,
they stayed for month after month in vine-cottages.
For two months, on the southern slope of Mount Ṛkṣavat,
in the Pārijāta grove within a bower of celestial flower-clusters,
at the foot of Mount Meru beneath a Jambū thicket, on the bank of the Jambū river—
For one month they dwelt on the ground of Jambūphalarasa in the land made of Jāmbūnada gold; for ten days they stayed in the region of Uttarakuru;
and for twenty-seven days they remained in the areas situated to the north of Kailāsa.
Thus, in various other lands of kings,
those two illustrious ones remained together as affectionate friends and a loving couple.
Then, after several months had gradually passed, she—
Cūḍālā, having assumed the form of a son of the gods, reflected:
"Under the weight of divine enjoyments, I shall test Śikhidhvaja,
lest his mind ever again find delight in worldly pleasures."

Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā, through her illusory power (*māyā*), showed her husband Hari as he had arrived in the forest, accompanied by gods and celestial nymphs. Seeing Indra approaching, surrounded by his retinue, she [showed him].
While dwelling in the forest, Śikhidhvaja honored him as was fitting.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Why have you subjected yourself to the hardship of traveling from such a distance?"
"O King of the Gods, by your grace, you ought to tell me this as it truly is.
Indra replied:
"We have been brought here from the sky because of the excellence of your virtues."

Like birds drawn by a thread fastened to their hearts, though they have gone far away; arise and come to heaven! There all the celestial women stand, looking up at you, filled with wonder as they hear of your virtues.
These are chariots, this is a vehicle, and this is the horse Uccaiḥśravas;
this is the elephant Airāvaṇa—take whatever shelter you desire.
Furthermore, there are sandals, pills, swords, elixirs, and so forth.

"Having taken it, traverse the path of the perfected ones and take possession of the realm of heaven. For as long as an eon, divine enjoyments are to be experienced by you, liberated while living, in the abode of the gods; for that reason, I have come to you."
Virtuous people like you do not despise the prosperity that has arrived with insults, nor do they long for prosperity not yet attained.
By your coming today without hindrance and by your dwelling in happiness, [all is well].
"May heaven attain purity, just as the three worlds have been purified by Hari.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O leader of the gods and others, I know heaven and its celestial conduct."
But for me, heaven is certain everywhere, yet not restricted to any single place.
For I am satisfied everywhere and I rejoice everywhere, O Lord;
because my mind has no desires, I am full of bliss in all places.
"Surely there is something fixed in one place that leads to such a heaven;
O Śakra, I do not know how to go there, nor do I perform what is unknown.
Indra said:
"O virtuous one, for the noble who have known what is to be known and whose intellects are perfected,
I consider the enjoyment of pleasures to be appropriate, as it is the conduct practiced by the righteous.
When the Lord of the Gods had spoken thus, the king remained silent.
"Why do you not come to me in this way? Hari asked.
When Śikhidhvaja replied "Certainly" with some hesitation, Kāla said, "May it be well with you, O Kumbha," and vanished.

Then that entire host of gods, together with the Lord of the Thirty-three, vanished in an instant, having dissolved there like a mass of waves in the ocean when the wind has subsided— a sea whose roar of leaping crocodiles, foam, and lordly serpents had ceased.
This is the chapter titled "The Arrival of Śakra."
The one hundred and twelfth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Having brought that illusion to rest, Cūḍālā reflected thus:
"By good fortune, this lord of the earth is not carried away by the desire for enjoyments.
Tranquil and with an even enjoyment of all things, even in the assembly of Śakra,
he has conducted himself with composure and without arrogance."
"I shall reflect upon this once more with even greater detail and care,
through someone whose mind is captivating yet dominated by passion and hatred.
Having thus reflected, she [waited] at night when the moon had risen in the forest.
Surely my beloved Madanikā has adorned herself;
for as the wind, rich with flowers and thick with the fragrance of wine, blows,
Śikhidhvaja stands on the riverbank intent upon his twilight prayers.
Intoxicated with passion, she entered the inner chamber of the forest goddesses— a bower of *santānaka* creepers dense with clusters of blossoms—
where, adorned with garlands of flowers, she reclined upon a bed of flowers prepared for her.

She stood there holding the beloved *śiḍga* bird that she had intended for her neck. Having arrived and searched through the groves, Śikhidhvaja beheld that charming *śiḍga* upon Madanikā’s neck within the bower of creepers.
His shoulders were draped with locks of hair, his body was anointed with sandalwood paste,
and his crest-jewel was disarrayed by tossing and turning upon the bed; he lay upon a pillow formed by the arms of a young woman, which were golden-hued and doubled over him.
Then he beheld that couple, their faces smiling at one another, with their ears, outer corners of the eyes, cheeks,
and locks of hair all aglow; they were joined face to face, concealed by the garments of the wish-fulfilling creepers.
With their garlands and couches swaying, and agitated by the affliction of love,
they bestowed upon one another their own passion under the guise of cosmetic unguents;
intent on sexual union, filled with dense bliss, and possessed of unrestrained and intoxicated passion.
Striking each other with flowers and pressing their breasts against one another’s chests, he beheld them with an unchanging mind and was gratified; "Aha!
How happily these two youths remain," said Śikhidhvaja.
"Stay, my dear ones, as you please; remain happily as you are.
Do not create an obstacle to our pleasure," he said, and then he departed.
Then, after only a moment, she disregarded her own worldly expansion (*prapañca*).
She went forth, displaying her own body which was agitated by the battle of passion.
She saw the king seated upon a golden stone slab in a secluded spot,
established in meditative absorption, with his eyes slightly opened.
Having approached that place, her face bowed down with shame,
the weary and withered woman Madanikā remained silent for a moment.
After a moment, Śikhidhvaja ceased his meditation and spoke to her.
With an undisturbed mind, he spoke these clear and sweet words:
"O slender one, why have you come so quickly with your joy thwarted?
Whatever beings there may be, they all strive only for joy."
Go once more and satisfy that beloved with acts of affection;
for mutual love desired by both is indeed rare throughout the three worlds. O proud lady, I do not feel any agitation on account of this matter.
Whatever is most dear in the world, that should be given by one who understands.
O slender-limbed one, Kumbha and I stand here free from passion;
you are but a young girl born of Durvāsas’s curse, so do whatever you wish.
Madanikā: Thus it is, O noble sir; for this state of being female or male is fickle.
Since women possess eightfold passion, you ought not to give way to anger.
"I am a weak woman who has been carried off by him into the dense forest; while you are intent on your evening prayers, what can I, a wretched creature, do?"—
with these mere words, the weak woman brought about the confinement of the man.

As long as she does not place her own body into the embrace of another man, so long will her anger, her refusal, and her lamentation avail; but once a beautiful woman has united with the body of a stranger, what can her chastity accomplish?
"I am a weak woman, a child, foolish, and guilty;
you ought to forgive me, O Lord, for the virtuous are indeed forgiving.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O young woman, my anger does not dwell within me like a tree in the sky;

it is solely because of your blameworthy conduct that I do not desire you as my daughter-in-law. Yet, O lady, out of friendship, I treat you with the same equality as before in these forest retreats."
"Through freedom from passion, we shall always delight in austerity alone.
[Vasiṣṭha:
"While Śikhidhvaja remained there in such a state of equanimity,"
Cūḍālā reflected, her heart uplifted by that truth:
"Aha! Oh, this Blessed One has attained supreme equanimity;
free from passion, fear, and anger, he abides as one liberated while living."
Neither desires for enjoyments, nor even great supernatural powers,
nor pleasures, nor pains, nor calamities, nor successes draw him away. All things that are contemplated reach him, O blameless one.
I consider these lovely women of great supernatural power to be like another Nārāyaṇa.
Therefore, I shall remind him of my entire life story;
having abandoned this form of a jar, I shall become Cūḍālā once again.

Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā, whose body was unharmed, quickly cast off the form of Madanikā and revealed her own form, Cūḍālā, right there. She appeared as if she had emerged from that body of Madanikā.
She appeared like a pearl freed from its casket, cleansed of all impurity.
He beheld before him that lady of faultless limbs,
standing as his beloved Cūḍālā, yet appearing so tender with affection that he took her for Madanikā herself.

The king beheld his own beloved, as if she were a cluster of spring lotuses in full bloom, as if the Goddess Śrī had descended from the surface of the earth, or as if she had been revealed from an open casket of jewels. This concludes the chapter titled "The Elaboration of the Lover."
The one hundred and thirteenth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, seeing his beloved, his eyes blossomed wide with wonder.
Śikhidhvaja spoke these words with a voice overwhelmed by wonder:
"Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one? From where have you come, O beautiful lady? What is your purpose? For how long have you been here, and for what reason do you stay?"
"By your gestures, your conduct, your smile, your courtesy, and your grace, you are perceived as my wife Cūḍālā.
Cūḍālā said:
"In this very way, O Lord, know that I am Cūḍālā, of this there is no doubt;
today I have personally attained you with my own natural body.
This creation of bodies such as Kumbha was for the purpose of awakening you."
In this forest, conceptual proliferation has branched out into a hundred directions.
Since you abandoned your kingdom and went to the forest for asceticism out of delusion,
from that very moment I have been striving for your awakening.
"O Lord of the Earth, you have been awakened by me in this way through the body of Kumbha; yet, by means of illusion, nothing such as Kumbha or anything else is real.
You are enlightened and have known that which is to be known; through meditation, this [truth] has become indivisible."

"O knower of reality, you see everything; behold it quickly through meditation. When Cūḍālā had spoken thus, the king girded his loins and beheld the entire account of his own self through meditation.
From the time of his renunciation of sovereignty until the moment of seeing Cūḍālā,
he beheld his entire personal history through a single moment of meditation;
from the time of his complete abandonment of the kingdom, he [saw] the succession of moments up to the present.
Having beheld everything, the protector of the earth ceased from his meditative absorption.
Emerging from that concentration, his lotus-like eyes blossoming with joy,
he quickly extended his arms, which were radiant with horripilation.
With his limbs melting with radiant affection, rising tears, and throbbing longing,
he embraced his beloved for a long time, as a male mongoose embraces a female.
Whatever state of being arose during that embrace of theirs—
Indeed, it could not be described even in years by the tongues of Vāsuki;
for a long time those two lovers remained embraced, as if fixed in a painting, as if fashioned from clay, as if melting away, or as if carved out of stone.

In a mere moment, their two beloved arms— dripping with networks of sweat and thick with horripilation— gradually became slightly slackened. Their hearts, though filled with nectar, felt as if they were empty.
With his arms released and his eyes fixed on her invisible form,
let him remain for a moment; then, after staying silent in intense bliss, the king, his hand resting gently upon the chin of his beloved, spoke words tender with affection.
Oh, how sweet, tender, and lovely is this meritorious outflow of the conduct of noble women— more delicious even than nectar!
O slender-limbed one, how much [of it] can be measured by you, who are as charming as the young moon?
For the sake of my husband, I have long endured terrible suffering;
yet, by what can that intellect be compared, by which I have been delivered from this pit of saṃsāra so difficult to cross?

Arundhatī, Śacī, Gaurī, Gāyatrī, Śrī, and Sarasvatī— all these appear delicate in comparison to the slender lady’s splendor of virtuous qualities. O beautiful one, [your virtues] such as wisdom, grace, loveliness, forbearance, friendliness, and compassion— MU_6,113.22 O beautiful one, [your virtues] such as wisdom, grace, loveliness, forbearance, friendliness, and compassion—
Among lovely women, you alone are seen to possess the very first beauty of form.
I have been awakened by you through your supreme resolve;
by what recompense could my virtues ever equal such a service?
Even from the beginningless, profound, and infinitely treacherous mire of delusion,
noble women who are resolute in devotion to their husband enable him to cross over;
for neither the meaning of the scriptures, nor teachers, nor mantras, and so forth, are capable of such deliverance.
Just as these noble women of the family are full of affection for their husbands,
so too are friend, brother, well-wisher, servant, teacher, counselor, wealth, happiness, scripture, abode, and handmaid— all these belong to the husband for the woman of a good family.
Noble women should always be honored with every effort;
all happiness in both worlds is perfectly established upon them. When she has crossed to the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, free from desire, [she attains liberation].
"How shall I repay this service of yours? I believe that from now on, the entire world of noble women will be cited in discussions of female virtue."
I think that Arundhatī and the other virtuous women must surely have been provoked to anger by the Creator when he fashioned you, for you surpass them all with the web of your virtues;
you are a casket for the jewels of chastity, beauty, and goodness.
"Come, O you who excel in virtues, grant me once more an embrace!
Having said this to Cūḍālā, whose eyes were like those of a young deer, Śikhidhvaja embraced her firmly again,
as a mongoose might embrace its mate.
Cūḍālā said:
"O Lord, while you were intent upon a web of dry rituals and your own mind was agitated,
I indeed became thus— extremely distressed on your account."
"Therefore, my own purpose, which consists of awakening you, has been accomplished by me.
So, O Lord, why do you offer me this praise?
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O lady of beautiful limbs, just as you have accomplished your own auspicious purpose,
so now may all virtuous women of noble family accomplish theirs.
Cūḍālā said:
O Lord, in whom the entire web of the world has come to rest solely within a portion of the intellect,
do you today still perceive that former delusion which thinks:
"I am doing this," "I am not doing that," or "I shall obtain this from here"?
Do you perhaps laugh inwardly at that intellectual frailty which is as flimsy as a mere hope?
O Lord, those trivial reckonings of thirst and those wicked fabrications of conceptual thought are no longer seen in you today, just as mountains are not seen in the sky.
"Who are you, endowed with such a body today? What is your ultimate goal, and what do you seek?
O Lord, how do you perceive the sequence of the final stages of the body's condition?
Śikhidhvaja replied:
In the perception of the essence of garlands of blue lotuses filled with *sumana* flowers,
you alone know that which I have approached;
I am effortless, I am partless, I am as clear as the sky, and I am free from desire.
"I am the nature of the self that is peaceful; for a long time I have remained as the 'I'.
Since I have attained that state, O lady with the hue of the *caṇpaka* flower, even great men such as Hari and Jina appear pitiable."
I am established in my own state, resting in pure consciousness which is nothing at all;
I have had enough of delusion and am liberated from saṃsāra, O lovely-eyed one.
I am neither pleased nor distressed; I am neither this nor anything else.

"I am neither gross nor subtle; I am everything, O beautiful one. I am indeed equal to that light which has emerged from the orb of radiance, which has not fallen upon a wall, and which is free from decay and excess."
I am peaceful; I am equanimity itself; I am pure, free from ailment;
I am indeed in the state of final nirvana; I exist in the most excellent vow of truth.
That which truly exists, that alone I am; I am able to say no other than this.
O you whose outer corners of the eyes tremble like waves, you are my guru; homage be to you!
By the grace of the large-eyed one, I have crossed the ocean of existence;
I shall not take up impurity again, like gold that has been smelted a hundred times.
Established in myself, peaceful, gentle, self-controlled, free from passion, and possessing an undivided intellect;
transcending all and yet omnipresent, I abide like the sky.
O Great Being, Lord of Life, my beloved, such is my state.
"Now tell me, O Lord, what pleases you, O Great-minded One? Śikhidhvaja replied:
"I do not know how to refuse, nor do I know how to desire."
O slender one, whether you ever perform such an act, I do not know;
O beloved, my mind does not know how to perceive either the state of its destruction or its persistence, for it observes the excellent vow of the sky.
"O beautiful one, do exactly whatever you know;
I shall hold that very thing, just as a gem reflects its image.
O blameless one, with a mind free from desire, act according to what has been obtained."
"I neither praise nor blame; do whatever you wish.
Cūḍālā said:
"If that is so, O illustrious one, then listen to my thought."
O soul liberated while living, having heard this, you ought to grasp that very [truth] now;
through the realization of oneness everywhere, which arises from the destruction of ignorance,
we have become desireless and as pure as the sky.
Whatever is our seeking, such is this non-seeking;
for when there is the manifestation of pure consciousness alone, what distinction can there be between seeking and non-seeking?
Therefore, O Supreme Person, we who exist in the beginning, the end, and the middle—
Having abandoned sheer ignorance, they remain right here;
O Lord, having now spent this time according to our current practice, we shall gradually attain the state of bodilessness (*videhatā*) after some period of time.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O restless one, tell me, what are we like at the beginning, the end, and in the middle?
Or rather, how can we remain, having abandoned this singular delusion?
Cūḍālā said:
O best of kings, we remain as kings from beginning to middle to end;
having abandoned this single delusion, we abide once again as yours.
"Be king in your own city, established upon your own throne;
I shall become your queen, the most excellent among lovely women.
With the king, the intoxicated citizens, and dancing young maidens,"

O Lord, may our city soon become like a grove of springtime forests— adorned with banners, resounding with the music of drums, strewn with showers of flowers, and filled with shimmering creepers, clusters of blossoms, and the humming of bees.
When Cūḍālā had spoken thus, Śikhidhvaja smiled and addressed these sweet words, unperturbed and free from haste: Vasiṣṭha said: [Thus it was]. MU_6,113.66
Śikhidhvaja said:
"If that is so, O large-eyed one, then those lands of the Siddhas' enjoyments are under our control in heaven; why, my dear, do we not dwell there?"
Cūḍālā said:
"O King, I have no desire for enjoyments nor for riches; O Monarch, I rejoice simply by the power of my own nature in whatever comes to me."

Neither heaven, nor sovereignty, nor even liberation brings me such happiness as when I remain established in my natural state, undisturbed and with my faculties at ease. When the mental conceits of "this is happiness" and "this is not" have come to an end, [true happiness arises].
"I stand here at ease, equally established in the peaceful state.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O large-eyed one, you have spoken rightly with this equanimous wisdom."
"What indeed would be the purpose of either accepting or abandoning the kingdom? [He replied:
"Having abandoned concern for states of pleasure and pain and being free from envy, let us both remain exactly as we are, having attained composure."

Thus, by means of their conversation and discourse there, the day drew to a close for those two beloveds who had been husband and wife for so long. Then, having risen, the blameless pair performed their daily duties as was customary.
Though filled with longing, those two experts in action remained free from anxiety; disregarding the attainment of heaven, they stayed with their minds fully satisfied.
On that very same bed, through various acts of affection, they remained together.
That night passed for those two who were liberated while yet living.

As they remained unconscious of their own supreme bliss of enjoyment and liberation, that long night— filled with the playful expressions of affectionate words between the two lovers and deepening their longing— passed away like a mere moment.
The one hundred and fourteenth canto, titled "The Manifestation of Cūḍālā," by Vasiṣṭha:
Then, when the sun had risen and stood in the cloudless sky—
as if this jewel of the world had emerged from a casket—
the lotus-pool seemed to open its eyes at the edge of the dawn.
As the rays of the sun spread through the worlds like established customs,
the two spouses arose and, having performed their twilight rites,
remained seated upon soft and smooth leaf-couches, lovely as golden caves.

Then Cūḍālā, having risen there, took the jeweled pitcher held in her hand... [and] in private, she consecrated her husband upon a lion-throne provided by her own resolve within her own kingdom. She, his wife, consecrated him, her husband, on that well-prepared seat of a lion brought forth by her will.
Standing there, the slender Cūḍālā, possessing a divine form,
said: "O Lord, having merely cast aside your silence, you ought to gather this peaceful splendor—
the energies of the eight world-protectors."
"O Cūḍālā! King Śikhidhvaja was thus addressed in the forest;
saying "I shall do so," he attained the status of a great king. Then he spoke to the proud lady who stood in the position of a female door-keeper.
"O Queen, I shall consecrate you to the rank of Mahādevī.

Having said this, he then seated her upon the throne; and having performed her consecration for the position of Mahādevī, King Meghavāg spoke to his beloved: MU_6,114.10: "Having spoken thus, he established her on the throne; then, having consecrated her to the rank of Mahādevī, King Meghavāg addressed his beloved."
"O beloved, lotus-petal-eyed one, you ought to summon in an instant an army of immense power and unrestrained might, born of mere thought.
Having heard these words of her lover, Cūḍālā, of excellent complexion, [responded].
He marshaled an army as formidable as an autumnal cloud.
Those two beheld that host, teeming with horses and elephants,
its banners filling the sky and making the forests appear dense.
The mountain caves resounded with the blaring of musical instruments, while the deep hollows echoed;
intoxicated vassal kings surrounded it, and wild elephants fled from it; it was formidable, tearing asunder with the rising roar of great lions.
The victorious elephant trumpeted with a spray of ichor from the temples of wild elephants in the forest;
it was thick with the creaking of wheels from the collision of multitudes of celestial chariots,
and it shattered the veil of dust and darkness with the intense radiance of the jewels in their crowns.
There, upon that excellent Gandhadvipa, in a royal palace protected by haughty vassal lords, the king and queen ascended.
Then King Śikhidhvaja, together with his beloved queen, [proceeded].
Dragging along his army, which was crowded with foot soldiers and chariots, that exceedingly powerful one moved forward with impetuous force; with his army that shook the immovable,
he swiftly shattered the mountains by his speed, like a whirlwind dispersing clouds.
Therefore, that lord of the earth set out from Mahendra, the king of mountains; and along the way, he beheld mountains, regions, rivers, and villages together with their jungles,
while showing his beloved that collection of accounts concerning his own life.
In a very short time, he reached his own city, which was as beautiful as heaven.
There, his vassals, honoring his arrival, recognized him by the sound of "Victory! and went forth with their hearts stirred.
Accompanied by both armies, which had joined as one and resounded with the blare of trumpets, the king entered the city;
he was showered with handfuls of parched grain and flowers by the women of the citizens.
Traveling along the merchant's road, he saw a city most exquisitely adorned,
crowded with banners and flags, beautiful with nets of pearls,
filled with women devoted to dance and song— a city like heaven fallen upon the earth.
Then, having entered the palace accompanied by various royal auspicious rites,
he duly honored the multitude of subjects who bowed before him;
after celebrating a magnificent city festival for seven excellent days.
The king, honored by his inner apartments, performed the duties of royalty.
Having ruled the kingdom on the earth for ten thousand years,
the king, together with Cūḍālā, desisted from maintaining the body.
"O Rāma, having cast off the body like a lamp without oil, that great-minded one attained nirvāṇa so as not to be born again;
for ten thousand years he had remained with that equanimity."

Having thus governed his kingdom, he attained the state of nirvāṇa. Free from fear and dejection, liberated from pride and envy, performing his natural and innate duties with a mind free from attachment and passion— thus that noble one, possessing a vision of perfect equanimity, conquered death and ruled as a sole monarch for ten thousand winters.

Having enjoyed infinite pleasures on earth and having remained for a long time as the crest-jewel of all sovereign rulers, he indeed attained that supreme state of immortality, just as this man has done.
In the same way, following the course of events that has come upon you, remain free from sorrow regarding the multitude of duties; arise, arise through your own effort with resolute vigor!
Experiencing the supreme fortune of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The narrative of Śikhidhvaja is concluded;
this is the one hundred and fifteenth canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
This entire narrative of Śikhidhvaja has been told to you;
proceed by this path, and you shall never suffer weariness.
"Grasping this view which destroys the suffering of the descendants of Raghu,
remain with a mind eternally free from passion, firmly established in that state—
just as Śikhidhvaja ruled his kingdom in such a manner."

O Rāma, while governing the kingdom, become one who possesses both worldly enjoyment and liberation. O descendant of Raghu, understand this just as Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati, attained awakening through the very method of Śikhidhvaja.
Rāma said:
"This venerable Kaca is the son of the venerable Bṛhaspati;
O Blessed One, please explain this to me as you have awakened to it, in brief."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O King, how that glorious Kaca, born of the preceptor of the gods, attained supreme awakening just like Śikhidhvaja.
Having transcended childhood and being intent on crossing over saṃsāra,
Kaca, who understood both words and their meanings, spoke to Bṛhaspati. Kaca said:
"O Blessed One, Knower of All Dharmas, tell us how a living being, bound by the thread of life, may emerge from this cage of saṃsāra. Bṛhaspati said:
"My son, by renouncing everything, one crosses over this ocean of saṃsāra— which is a house for sea-monsters of misfortune— without agitation. Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard these most purifying words of his father,
Kaca abandoned everything and went to a solitary forest.
That departure of his did not cause Bṛhaspati any distress.
For the great are indeed equal-minded in both union and separation. Then,
O sinless one, when eight years had passed,
Kaca again reached his father in a certain great forest.
Having honored and bowed to him, and having embraced his son,
Kaca again questioned the Lord of Speech with a weary voice: Kaca said:
"Today it is the eighth year since I have practiced total renunciation;
yet even so, my dear father, I do not attain blameless rest.
Vasiṣṭha said:
While Kaca was speaking thus with a distressed mind in that forest,
Vākpati said, "Abandon everything," and ascended to heaven.
When he had departed, Kaca [cast off] from his body even the bark garments and all else without exception.
He abandoned the raining of clouds and so forth, just as the vault of heaven does in autumn;
he dwelt alone at the ends of the quarters, peaceful, his form empty, breathing like the autumnal sky which is devoid of moon, clouds, sun, and stars.
Again, after three years, with a grieving mind, he reached that very same father and teacher in a certain part of the forest;
having performed the sequence of worship with devotion, [the father] embraced his son.
He questioned him again with a voice faltering from distress:
Kaca said, "Father, everything has been renounced, even my patched garment, my bamboo staff, and my girdle of munja grass."
"Nevertheless, there is no rest in my own state; what shall I do?
Bṛhaspati said:
"They say that the mind is everything; by abandoning it, my son, you shall shine."
"Those who know renunciation understand that the renunciation of the mind is the renunciation of everything," said Vasiṣṭha;
having spoken thus to his son, the Lord of Speech swiftly soared into the sky.
Kaca, his mind unwearied, sought to abandon his consciousness;
yet even while reflecting thus in the forest, when he could not perceive that consciousness,
he then pondered this with an undaunted intellect.
[Kaca said:
"The entire collection of objects, beginning with the body, is not said to be 'all' in this context.
Why and wherefore should I abandon this which is useless and innocent?"
"I shall go into the presence of my father to recognize the great enemy that is the mind;
having recognized it, I shall quickly abandon it, and thereafter I shall remain free from the fever of affliction.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reflected thus, Kaca ascended to heaven;
having reached the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati), he affectionately paid homage and prostrated before him.
And in private, he asked him: "O Blessed One, what is the state of my mind?"
"Tell me the true nature of the mind, so that I may renounce it.
Bṛhaspati replied:
"Those who know the mind understand that the innate mind is the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra)."
"That which is this internal sense of 'I' in a living being is called the mind. Kaca said: "I think its renunciation is difficult; it does not attain perfection."
"How indeed is it fitting for him to be abandoned, O best of yogins?
Bṛhaspati replied:
"Even from the crushing of flowers, even from the closing of the eyes..."
The abandonment of the ego-sense is easy; there is not even the slightest affliction in this.
Kaca said: O Great-minded One, [this applies] to that which measures thirty-three great crores.
"O Guru of the host of gods, tell me quickly how this is so.
Bṛhaspati said:
"O son, listen as I explain this very matter to you."
An object established solely through ignorance perishes by means of knowledge.
In reality, O son, there is no such thing as the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*); for it is a false delusion. Though non-existent, it appears as if existent—a deceptive phantom like a child’s ghost.
Just as the state of being a serpent appears in a rope, and just as the notion of water arises in a desert,
so too does the false ego manifest from a deceptive appearance;
just as a duality that is utterly non-existent is perceived in the moon due to delusion.
In that same way, the ego vibrates; though it is not real, it appears as if real.
There exists a single, beginningless and endless, pure consciousness, stainless and all-pervading, clearer even than space, which is the knower of all.
In all places, at all times, and in every manner, that very same single reality shines within all living beings, like water in restless waves. In this regard,
what is this "I-ness," from where does it arise, and how has it emerged?
Where has a mass of dust ever arisen from the ocean? Where has water ever emerged from fire?
O son, abandon this vain notion of "I am he," which is trivial, limited in form, and rendered helpless by space and time.
Unconditioned by space, time, and the like, transparent, eternally manifest, all-pervading,
consisting of all objects yet having a single object, you are the stainless pure consciousness alone.
Like the sap of fruits, flowers, and petals situated in every direction, you abide at all times within all worlds.
O you whose form is existence, how can there possibly be any notion of "I" for you, who are the stainless conscious self, eternally and utterly infinite?
This is the one hundred and sixteenth canto, titled "The Awakening of Bṛhaspati’s Hair."
Vasiṣṭha:
Having thus attained the supreme yoga, this unsurpassed instruction,
the son of the preceptor of the gods became liberated while living.
Free from worldly existence, free from egoism, with the knots of the heart severed and the intellect profoundly tranquil—O Rāma, remain without modification, just as Kaca remained.
Know that egoism is unreal; do not rely upon it, nor abandon it.
Indeed, how can there be the relinquishing or grasping of a non-existent hare’s horn?
When the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is impossible, where are birth and death for you? By whom could a fruit be gathered from what has been sown in the field of the sky?
You are partless, with all mental constructs stilled, the essence of all beings, all-pervading,
subtler than even the subtlest atom, pure consciousness alone, and free from affliction;
just as waves and the like arise from water, or as bracelets and the like from gold.
That very consciousness, appearing as if it were not that, manifests as the sense of "I";
thus, through lack of awakening, the entire world remains as if composed of illusion.
Through awakening, O sinless one, everything becomes the form of Brahman.
Abandoning the notions of duality and unity, remain happy as one who abides in the remainder;
do not be miserable in vain like a deluded person.
This illusory nature of saṃsāra is exceedingly difficult to cross, yet it has been taken by you to be substantial.
Like autumn mist, it quickly reaches attenuation through awakening.
Rāma said:
"I have attained supreme inner satisfaction through the nectar of your knowledge."
Like a *cātaka* bird overcome by the fear of drought when rained upon by a gentle shower,
I feel as if sprinkled with nectar; I enter into a state of inner coolness and stand, as it were, above all incomparable riches.
I do not attain satiety while you speak these words,
just as a thirsty *cakora* bird finds no satisfaction in the rays of the moon.
O Lord, though I am already satiated, I ask you this further question.
Who indeed, even if satiated, would not drink the nectar-liquor standing before them?
O best of sages, what is said to be that thing named "the false man," which renders the multitude of real things in the world unreal? Tell me this quickly.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, listen to this beautiful narrative uttered by me, which produces laughter and leads to the awakening of the unreal person.
O mighty-armed one, there is a certain person consisting of illusion and machinery;
he is dull-witted like a child, foolish, and entirely hidden by ignorance.
Born somewhere in solitude, he remains right there in that void.
Like a mass of hair in the sky, or like a mirage in the desert;
therefore, nothing other than that exists there, and what does exist is that very thing itself.
That which appears as something else is a false appearance, and the dull-witted person does not perceive it as such.
As he grew old in that state, a fixed resolve arose within him:
"The void is mine, I am the void, the void is my own, and I protect the void.
Having established himself in the void, he diligently protects his cherished object of preservation.

Reflecting thus, he built a house for the purpose of protecting the sky. He fixed his mind upon its interior, thinking, "The sky is protected by me," and remained there, O descendant of Raghu, satisfied with that space within the house.
Then, in the course of time, that house of his went to ruin, just as one season passes into another, or as a wave is dispersed by the wind.
"Alas! O space of the house, you are destroyed; alas! Where have you gone in an instant?"
"Alas, alas! Your purity is broken!"—thus he lamented.
Having mourned for a long time, that foolish man once again dug a well in that very place for the sake of his donkey, becoming intent on the space within the well.

Then, in the course of time, even that well of his met its destruction; consequently, he became overwhelmed by the great sorrow of the voidness of the well. At the conclusion of his lamentations regarding the voidness of the well, he placed his water-jar right there.
Having become absorbed in the space within the jar, he himself attained liberation.
O scion of Raghu, in the course of time, even that jar was destroyed;
for whatever direction a wretched thing takes, that very direction perishes as well.

At the conclusion of his prattle regarding the space within the water-jar, he made a pit there for the sake of donkeys; because of that, he became devoted to the space of the pit. In time, even his pit met its destruction in the forest.
With that very darkness as his splendor, he grieved for the space within the jar.
At the conclusion of his grief for the space in the jar, he built a great four-winged mansion for the sake of protecting the donkey; then he became intent upon that [new] space.
Time, which devours all creatures, swiftly snatched that away from him as well,
like the wind blowing away a withered leaf; he became utterly consumed by grief for it,
and at the edge of the four-compartment palace, he built a dwelling for the sake of guarding his donkey.
The space within the granary, which had the form of a cloud, remained there as the supreme ether;
yet Time quickly snatched that away from him, like the wind a cloud.
Because of that sorrow for the space within the granary, he was consumed by feverish distress.
Thus, with his house, four-sided halls, jars, bowls, and granaries,
this endless time of his passes away.

Remaining thus, that man of deceitful intellect perceives the sky within his cave-like house as his own self through the notion of "self," rather than perceiving the house as being encompassed by the sky.
O friend, the deluded one goes from one state of existence to another, moving through a dense web of intense suffering to even denser suffering.
This concludes the one hundred and seventeenth canto, titled "The Protection of the Sky," within the narrative of the False Man.
Rāma:
O Lord, why have you spoken of this illusory man under the pretext of a false person? And why is the protection of the sky being mentioned?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, Rāma; I shall reveal this to you exactly as it is. Now, hear the narration of the story of the illusory man.
"O descendant of Raghu, know that this person who is said to consist of the machine of illusion is indeed the ego (ahaṅkāra), arisen from the empty sky.
O virtuous one, in whichever corner of this space this world is situated," so it was said.
Then, at the beginning of creation, that infinite, unreal void arises of its own accord. Then,
from the cavity of sound within the space of Brahman— which dwells within and is exceedingly difficult to perceive—
the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) emerges, like a vibration from the wind.
Having increased in the sky, that rogue imagines it to be his own self;
through the conceit of "self" in what is not-self, he then strives for that purpose. For the sake of protecting this non-self as if it were the sole self, he [creates] various kinds of bodies.
Having repeatedly seen these worlds perish again and again, he creates this universe once more.
He alone is the illusory person (*māyāpuruṣa*); he is indeed a false person.
Though non-existent, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) has arisen in vain through illusion.
Having formed bodies such as a house, a sacrificial pit, a four-sided hall, or a water-jar,
and thinking "the self has been protected," he directs his contemplation toward that space.
O Rāghava, these are the names of this very ego-sense.
Listen to those delusions concerning the origin of the world through which this living soul (jīva) falls into confusion:

it is known as intellect (buddhi), mind (manas), consciousness (citta), illusion (māyā), primordial nature (prakṛti), as well as volition (saṅkalpa), conceptualization (kalanā), time (kāla), and a portion of time (kalā). MU 6.117.10–11.
Through these and other such names, having attained multiplicity, the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), possessing a thousand forms, expands by means of imagined objects within the vast,
empty, elemental ether for the long duration of the world’s manifestation.

Experiencing pleasures and pains, the person remains in a state of utter delusion. Just as this illusory person, out of the suspicion that it is his own self, protects the space within a jar even though it is already attached to the universal space (ākāśa), so too, do not become afflicted by suffering.
The Self, which is more vast than even space, pure, subtle, auspicious, and benign—
how and by whom can it be protected, or likewise grasped?
For that which is merely the space within the heart abides like the space within a jar.
Beings grieve in vain at the time of dissolution, thinking "the self has perished";
for just as space remains undivided when jars and such things are destroyed,
so too the embodied self is eternally indestructible when bodies perish.
This Self is pure consciousness alone, subtler than even space;
for it is merely a portion of one's own experience, and like the sky, O Rāma, it does not perish.
Nothing whatsoever is ever born, nor does anything ever die anywhere at any time.
Brahman alone expands in the form of the world's manifestation.
Realizing that "all this is one, peaceful, devoid of beginning, middle, and end,
and free from existence and non-existence," be happy.

Having abandoned through awakening the entire locus of egoism—which is the abode of all calamities, unstable, lacking independence, prone to imminent downfall, devoid of discrimination, essence-less, and ignorant—you remain in the perfectly established state and attain the highest excellence.
The Chapter Named "The Narrative of the False Man. (MU 6.117.21)
The one hundred and eighteenth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Prior to the supreme Brahman, the mind first arose.
Consisting of thought and expansive, it has attained a state of stability while remaining situated right there—
O Rāghava, the mind is in Brahman like fragrance in the calyx of a flower, like a great wave in the ocean, or like a web of rays in the sun. (MU 6.118.1–2)
O Rāma, that state of the invisible reality of the Self has been reached through forgetfulness alone; it is not reached by any other method, just as the perception of a snake arises in a rope.
O descendant of Raghu, he who conceives of anything as existing apart from the Sun [of Consciousness]...
For this web of rays is indeed like something other than that shining sun.
Just as an armlet is conceived as distinct from gold, yet it is nothing but that gold for him; for it is not truly anything other than gold.
For one by whom the wave is perceived as distinct from the water,
only the notion of the wave remains for them, not the ocean.
For one by whom the wave is perceived as non-distinct from the water...
The realization of the commonality of water is called non-conceptual.
By one for whom the armlet is perceived as not distinct from gold,
that single great realization of gold alone is called non-conceptual.
For one who perceives a series of flames as distinct from the fire itself,
the cognition of "fire" vanishes and only the cognition of "flames" remains.
That state is likewise colored by the flickering net of flames.

The agitated mind, when focused upon that very state, attains stability. When one perceives the series of flames as non-different from the fire itself, he possesses the cognition of fire alone; he is called "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*).
He who is free from conceptual construction is great; he is a sage whose mind is completely dissolved.
That which is to be attained has been attained by him; he does not sink into worldly objects.
Having abandoned all diversity within the hollow of pure consciousness alone, he remains there.
O sinless one, when you, who are the portion of pure consciousness, are yourself freed from objective perception,
you quickly bring forth by your own self the power called *saṅkalpa*,
just as the wind brings forth its throbbing power of motion.
Then the mind, which consists of the fabrication of conceptual constructions, appears as if separate;
it becomes the self of the universe and itself fashions its own form. That mind, whose essence is volition, [perceives] this entire world just as it is.

Whatever it conceives, that very thing becomes for it in an instant. The mind— known by such names as ego, intellect, and consciousness— attains the state of a worm, the state of Brahmā, the state of Mount Meru, or likewise the state of an atom.
Having attained the state of Viriñci through his own volition, the mind extends the maintenance of the world;
subsequently, within that [maintenance], it itself undergoes manifoldness.
This expansive world is seen to be composed solely of volition.
Neither real nor yet unreal, it arises like a web of dreams;
just as a person’s kingdom of the mind shines forth with various undertakings,
so does this vast kingdom of the mind belonging to Brahmā expand.
Just as a dream is neither unreal because it appears, nor is it real, so too, O Sage, the world and the Brahma-realm are neither non-existent nor existent; for this [world],
which has attained density, is merely a false appearance.
Because it is cultivated through the perception of things as they truly are, this [delusion] dissolves.
If it is seen from the perspective of ultimate reality, then this is nothing at all;
but if seen from the perspective of what is not ultimate, it branches out into a hundred directions.
Just as the ocean, by its very nature, manifests a body consisting of waves, ripples, and surging waters, so does the all-pervading Lord manifest a body;
performing thousands of actions, he is the agent, yet apart from the vibration of consciousness, there is no other doer.
No one ever produces anything that was not already there; therefore, abandon the notion of difference.
Whether seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, speaking, acting, or sleeping, reflect thus:
"I do not produce anything new; this is the truth."
Whatever you do, that is in truth the stainless, pervasive pure consciousness;
it is Brahman whose form is expanded, and nothing other than that exists.
Since the entire multitude of objects exists with consciousness as its essence, [nothing else remains].
This entire world is indeed consciousness alone; there is no other conceptualization.
In this mere radiance of consciousness, which is called the web of the world, how can there be the false grasping that "this is one thing" and "that is another"?
Since everything arises from the single consciousness alone in all its various forms, even the object of cognition does not exist; therefore, whence can there be bondage and liberation?
Having forcibly cast aside all such thoughts as "this is liberation" or "this is bondage," one should remain free from the conceit of duality.
Silent, self-controlled, free from pride and intoxication, a great-souled one performing his own duty, remain indeed without egoism.
The hundred-and-nineteenth canto, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of the Ultimate Reality."
Vasiṣṭha said:
O sinless one, you are a great doer, a great enjoyer, and a great renouncer;
having abandoned all doubts, take hold of eternal fortitude.
Rāma said:
"What is meant by 'the great doer,' what is meant by 'the great renouncer,' and what is meant by 'the great enjoyer'? O Lord, explain this to me correctly."
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, in former times this triad of vows was declared as supreme by the one who bears the crescent moon upon his crest to Bhṛṅgīśa, whereby he remained free from all affliction.

Formerly, on the northern peak of Mount Sumeru, which resembled fire, Śaśikalādhara dwelt together with his entire retinue. The one of great splendor questioned him out of his own desire to know through wisdom.
O Rāma, Bhṛṅgīśa, bowing with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Lord of Umā:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, omniscient Supreme Lord!"
"O Lord, please tell me quickly out of compassion that which I ask:
beholding this structure of saṃsāra, as unstable as a wave, I am bewildered, being devoid of rest in reality."
Having firmly embraced which beloved internal certainty do I remain in this dilapidated house of the world, free from all feverish distress? The Lord said:
"Abandoning all doubts and relying upon eternal fortitude,
become a great renouncer, a great doer, and a great enjoyer, O sinless one.
Bhṛṅgīśa said:
Why is he called the great renouncer? Why is he called the great enjoyer?
Why is he called the great agent? Tell me correctly, O Lord. The Lord said:
One whose intention is free from the fear of the arising or passing away of merit and demerit,
who acts according to what has been attained, is called a "great doer" (mahākartā).
[For him,] passion and aversion, pleasure and pain, merit and demerit, and fruit and non-fruit [are no longer obstacles].

He who acts without any expectation at all is called a great doer (mahākartā). He who is observant of silence, free from the sense of "I," devoid of pride, and liberated from envy— he who acts without agitation is called a great doer.
He whose mind is not stained by doubt regarding dharma and adharma in matters both auspicious and inauspicious— he is called a great doer.
He who is everywhere free from attachment stands like a witness.

He who acts without desire in his task is called a great doer (mahākartṛ). He who is free from agitation and joy, who remains equanimous through his own pure will, and who neither grieves nor exults— he is called a great doer.
He who, at the time of action, is wise, whose mind is unattached,
and who abides in conduct appropriate to the task— he is called a great doer.
He whose intellect, by its very nature, never abandons internal equanimity—

For he who performs both auspicious and inauspicious deeds is called a "great doer" (mahākartā). He whose mind remains perfectly equanimous during birth, stay, and destruction, as well as during rising and setting, is called a "great doer."
He who hates nothing and praises nothing himself, and who enjoys everything as it is presented—such a one is called a great enjoyer.
Though taking, he does not take; though acting, he does not act.
Even while eating, he who does not eat is called a great enjoyer.
He whose intellect is unwearied observes the entirety of worldly activity like a witness; he who has abandoned desire is called a great enjoyer.
He whose mind does not deviate because of pleasures or pains, through ritual actions or their performance, or due to the delusive presence or absence of things— he is called a great enjoyer.
Old age, death, calamity, sovereignty, and even poverty— [these do not affect him].
He who knows that it is indeed delightful is called a great enjoyer. He who, like the ocean with its waters, receives great joys and sorrows with equanimity is called a great enjoyer.
Non-violence, equanimity, and contentment never depart from him, like rays from the orb of the moon; therefore he is called a great enjoyer.
Whether bitter, sour, salty, pungent, unrefined, refined, or excellent— [all tastes are the same to him].
He who eats even the lowest food with equanimity is called a great enjoyer.
He who perceives the flavorful and the flavorless, as well as sexual union and its cessation, with equal vision— that gentle one is called a great enjoyer.
He for whom equanimity is well-established toward alkaline substances, various kinds of sugar, and likewise toward what is auspicious or inauspicious— he is called a great enjoyer.
Having abandoned such conceptual constructions as "this is fit to be eaten" and "this is not fit to be eaten," [he remains equanimous].

He who eats with his longing departed is called a great eater. He who experiences adversity and prosperity, delusion and joy, the inferior and the superior, with an even mind, is called a great eater.
He by whom merit and demerit, pleasure and pain, anxiety, death,
and birth have been abandoned through wisdom— he is called a great renouncer.
All desires, all doubts, all laughter, and all certainties [have likewise been abandoned].

He by whom [the world] has been abandoned through wisdom is called a great renouncer. He by whom the existence of the body, the mind, the intellect, the senses, and the world is truly relinquished is called a great renouncer.
"I have neither body nor birth, nor am I affected by action, whether appropriate or inappropriate"—
he who possesses such certainty within is called a great renouncer (mahātyāgī). By him, dharma and adharma, as well as the mind, mental reflection, and all striving [are abandoned].
One who has completely renounced everything within is called a great renouncer (mahātyāgī).

Having abandoned the mind, meditation, austerity, and splendor, as well as the notions of "thine-ness" and "I-ness" regarding the auspicious and inauspicious, he who remains established in his own self is called a great renouncer.
He who honors his own mental construction neither desires it nor rejects it—
being free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding all this— he is called a great renouncer.
Whatever extent of perceived conceptualization is observed here in its entirety, [he remains beyond it].
He by whom that [desire] has been thoroughly abandoned is called a great renouncer.

He who does not desire what is desired, who is free from the pairs of opposites, whose intellect is unshaken amidst pleasure and pain, who is steadfast, self-abiding, gentle, and self-controlled— he is called a great renouncer.
"Even while performing his duties, he who does not abandon the state of being as if in deep sleep— he, being full, is called a great renouncer.
Thus was it said of old by the God of gods to Bhṛṅgīśa, O sinless one.
"O Rāma, remain established as you are, holding fast to this view. Thus spoke Hara, whose matted locks were adorned by a crescent moon set amidst a garland of fragments of glorious skulls,
on Mount Meru— which possesses a single peak made of the finest radiant jewels and which has the form of a blazing fire— O Rāmabhadra.
Adopting this perspective, perform your graceful and beautiful duties at the proper time with a disciplined intellect.
You are eternally risen, you are stainless, you are free from affliction; cast away all doubt, be happy—whatever you are, that you are.
The chapter titled "The Yoga of Instruction on the Great Creator and Others" within the Narrative of Bhṛṅgīśa.
The one hundred and twentieth canto:
O Lord of Sages, yesterday indeed a question was asked by me.
In the unfolding of this section on tranquility, it is said:
"How could there be any trace of defilement for the infinite reality of the Self? How could a mass of dust belong to the ocean of unfathomable form?"
"In this regard, O Brahmin, you said to me, 'When the time for the final conclusion has arrived, there shall be a word that answers this question, even though I am urging you at an improper time.
Therefore, O Blessed One, cut away this doubt from my heart today."
Just as the moon dispels the darkness of the night with its cool rays of speech,
by drinking the nectar of your words, the mortal diseases of my fragments of doubt have been utterly destroyed, like dust by a rain shower.
"Nevertheless, I ask you, who are as beloved to me as a modest young bride:
knowledge known by oneself does not shine without the words of a guru.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, lotus-petal-eyed one, you have remembered [your duty] well.
Indeed, what undertakings of a wise man ever come to naught?
Through qualities such as forbearance, magnanimity, and tranquility, you have attained the status of a worthy recipient.
Like the earth’s splendor through the autumnal beauty of the rice harvest,
you stand as a vessel for the pure words of the Siddhānta,
like one whose mind is colored by passion for the songs of a deeply impassioned throat.
Having heard the established doctrine of the knowledge of the Self today, like one who is half-awakened,
you shall not fall into the ruin of both worlds through the fault of dualism regarding ritual action.
For one who is not a great soul is incapable of understanding the established doctrine of the Vedānta from this [teaching].
One who thinks "all is Brahman" goes downward by the power of non-dual action;
however, a high-souled person like you, whose self is purified by qualities such as forbearance,
having resolved that "all is Brahman," fully attains the non-duality of one's own nature.
Disregarding the non-duality of action, he neither desires nor rejects it;
because he is solely absorbed in the reality of the Self, he attains pure equanimity.
This is the conclusion of all scriptures and all perspectives from every side.
Listen, O Rāghava, to the final doctrine which is the sole lamp of self-knowledge:
by the mere contemplation of which a living being is not born again, my dear;
such a one is truly destined for liberation, not otherwise, just as a seed scorched in saline soil cannot sprout.
For those who have attained supreme awakening declare this aloud:
"We ourselves know it, and the scripture stands thus:
there is no distinction between reality and unreality, just as there is none between a wave and water."
There is no difference between the real and the unreal, just as there is none between the sun of the waking state and that of the dream;
yet, while there is no difference in their existence (*sattā*), this perceived difference is merely imagined.
This conceptual construction is not true anywhere; therefore, everything is nothing but pure existence.
O dear one, no distinction between the real and the unreal is perceived within existence, just as there is none between a mountain range imagined in the mind and an actual external mountain range.
For the person is pure consciousness alone; that which is called a "body" does not exist.
Causal efficiency and the consciousness directed toward that object are fulfilled by the object itself.
That very [consciousness] appears with an imagined form, like a mountain or an elephant;
what other purpose could there be for an object whose body is unreal, through any other sequences?
All ritual actions have as their fruit the bliss of internal self-experience, just like the experience of wine and other such substances from all constituent ingredients.
Here there is only this one [reality]; there is no second conceptualization.
The pure, eternal Self exists, yet it is established as if it did not exist.
For it has neither impurity, nor a mark, nor disintegration, nor substantiality;
it has neither existence nor non-existence, nor "thou-ness," nor "I-ness."
"Only the Self exists here; there is nothing else. Abandon, O Rāma, the notion of anything other than that. Then, being free from duality and free from oneness, remain equal and eternally awakened.
Rāma said:
"Therefore, O Blessed One, tell me this: how do the mind, the intellect, and the other faculties exist, by means of which this scripture has been proclaimed by you to me here?
Vasiṣṭha said:
The aggregate of sounds has been devised for the purpose of conventional usage in the treatises;

this [aggregate], consisting of mind, intellect, and so forth, is false, O Rāma, from the perspective of ultimate reality. It is merely the existence of consciousness itself, and likewise consists of the nature of the supreme space.

Just as these waves, whirlpools, and so forth are nothing more than the mere state of water, so too the entire flood of objects in the world has the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) as its essence. Just as an army in a dream, or as the wind in its movement... [as in a dream]. MU_6,120.29–30.
There exists the eternal, pure-natured, infinite, and primordial Brahman; indeed, there is nothing else whatsoever that can be conceived as a fraction of it.
Meditate thus, having attained the state of stainlessness; reach Nirvana, with all your activities stilled and purified.
The flawless Brahman is the sole seed of all the effects of every kalpa, existing in the form of the ultimate atom.
