And that vast [reality], which nourishes all states of being, is like space; whatever exists is as if non-existent.
At no time or place does anything else whatsoever exist, whether as a reality or as an unreality.
O virtuous one, remaining within this firm conviction, abide free from the play of doubt.

Constantly inward-turned, performing indeed the entire multitude of activities situated outside, you never experience weariness; you attain a state of stability equal to the sky. This is the chapter titled "The Dispelling of Conceptual Construction."
The one hundred and twenty-first canto: Vasiṣṭha said:
"The existence of the ego-sense of Rāma gives rise to the delusion of worldly transmigration."
For the fool, this [world] is cultivated as a fierce yakṣa through the cultivation of the notion of a yakṣa;
but when egoism is stilled, this cycle of existence indeed ceases,
O dear one, like the mist that brings delusion at the end of the rainy season.
Just as the delusion of a snake in a rope comes to an end for a person through the words of a friend—
such as "This is not a snake, this is a rope"—
so too does the delusion of egoism reach its cessation through the speech of the Guru.
"Contemplate the non-existence of the ego," and so forth—
through such means, by the repeated study of the treatises on knowledge, and through the sequence of discourses with the virtuous,
the delusion of "I" in a living being comes to rest, just as blindness is cured by collyrium.
Even that which is gross and presently existing is subject to decay through friction;
for instance, my dear, even a stone in a well wears away by being rubbed with jars.
Thus, there is no cause for the persistence of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛti*), which is a product of ignorance (*avidyā*).
"What doubt can there be regarding its destruction through investigations that cause such destruction?
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all principles, regarding this mind called the ego-sense..."
Or, when the body is in a state of dissolution, what could be the mark of the *sattva*?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O dear one, when the body—acting as a bow—is extinguished by the rising of the ocean of discernment (*viveka*),"

In the mirage of one's own mind, the heat of saṃsāra does not exist. For even when they have arisen, the vast faults such as greed and delusion do not touch the pure intention, just as water does not touch a lotus.

The glories beginning with *muditā* (joy) never abandon the face [of the practitioner], just as floral beauties that bestow good fortune and happiness do not leave the honey. When the arising of joy occurs through the inquiry, "How indeed is this cycle of existence? [the result follows].
The being arises and the mind proceeds toward its dissolution.
When the mind, which consists of egoism, dissolves and evil action wavers,
the knots of latent impressions break apart completely and gradually, as if exhausted.
Anger becomes thin, like a cloud in autumn;
delusion assumes dullness, as darkness does at dawn;
and desire goes to exhaustion, like a long-distance traveler in the heat.
Greed flees elsewhere, like a serpent seeing a peacock;
the senses do not exult violently, as night-prowlers do during the day;
and distress does not surge intensely, like turbulent dust in the rainy season.
They do not roar out sufferings like elephants deprived of their youth,
nor do they rush toward pleasures as waters flow through a fierce dam.
Furthermore, these things such as pleasure and pain are seen either in the face [of experience]...
O virtuous one, they are indeed seen, yet they do not stain the mind.
As the mind dissolves, it becomes an object of longing for the hosts of gods;
the virtuous man proceeds, and the cool moonlight of equanimity rises within him.
This stainless body of Indra becomes peaceful, lovely, radiant, and unimpeded; it is composed, yet powerful and clear.
Though it is subject to existence and non-existence, diverse, and vast, [it remains thus].

The delusion of worldly existence brings neither joy nor sorrow to the wise. Woe to that lowest of men who, out of delusion, fails to engage with this reality— which is free from calamity and is to be realized through the light of the intellect.

O dear one, for one who desires to cross the ocean of birth—a mine of jewels of suffering—in order to attain long-deserved rest, the supreme means is this thought: "Who am I? How is this world? Who might be the other? What is the use of enjoyments?
This is the chapter titled "The Description of the Characteristics of the State of Sattva."
The one hundred and twenty-second canto: Vasiṣṭha said,
"Your first ancestor was the king named Ikṣvāku."
Listen now to how he who was born of the Ikṣvāku lineage attained liberation.
There was a king renowned as Ikṣvāku, born of the solar dynasty;
he was the lord of rulers of the earth, like Dharmarāja among the ancestors.

Though his very nature is as cold as snow, he blazes among his enemies at midday like the sun-stone mountain, even while not touching other objects; he who maintains a state of kinship toward his enemies and toward those of sinful intent.
By his dark-complexioned body, which was like the gaze of a distressed woman,
he manifested his solar lineage through his majesty as it spread among his enemies,
while his gentleness was revealed toward friends, the wives of brahmins, elders, and other kinsmen.
Resorting to whose lotus-face, his friend the bee-like brow considered Hari’s chest to be as delicate as a flower at night;
by whose cool and white fame the entire world was enveloped.
He creates the illusion of the rising full moon for the ruddy geese.
While protecting his sovereign kingdom through the expansion of his unimpeded power, he once, having retired to a solitary place, reflected thus in his mind: MU_6,122.8
Though he reflected upon it, he did not himself understand the cause of this phenomenal world— the abode of the agitation of old age and death, and of the fluctuation of pleasure and pain.
Like a child at the sound of a thundercloud, he was deeply distressed by that.
Then, on one occasion, he questioned Manu, the blessed Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), who had come from the world of Brahmā and was seated in his own assembly hall, receiving honor.
Ikṣvāku said:
"O Blessed One, he joins himself with audacity against one of such vast splendor;
yet it is solely through your grace that he has the power to question you."
I am constantly consumed within by a flickering, smoke-darkened, and burning doubt, like the ocean by the submarine fire. From whence has this creation come, and what is its nature? Tell me.
How and in what things do old age, affliction, and the calamity of death abide? And how might I be liberated from this treacherous delusion of saṃsāra, like a bird from a thickly spread net?
You alone know all the courses of this manifold world,
which is profound and exceedingly fickle, just as Varuṇa knows the depths of the ocean;
you are the axe for the tree of doubt and the sun for the darkness within the heart.
"You alone are the Supreme Lord, the moon that cools with the supreme nectar.
Manu said:
"Oh, how after a long time, discernment has blossomed!"
You have asked an essential question that cuts through the spread of misfortunes.
Listen to this as it was asked: it is the crossing of the ocean of saṃsāra, the supreme resting place for the intellect, and a great wind for the grass of the visible world.
Whatever is seen here, O King, that is not anything at all;
just like the appearance of a snake in a rope, this has arisen as something entirely non-existent.
It is like a city of Gandharvas, or like the perception of water in a desert.
Just as the nature of silver appears in mother-of-pearl, or duality in the ocean of nectar—
so all this, consisting of unreality, flashes forth as a false appearance,
like the whirling circle of fire seen by eyes dazzled by a flickering, blazing torch.
That which is not perceived by us as anything,
yet is remembered as "nothing," which transcends the six senses including the mind, and which is even less than space—
that indestructible reality exists here; that is what is called the Self.
That, that is the supreme Brahman; that, that is the pure, ultimate Reality.
It is the essence of the creeper of creation, which has grown in the forest of the void, possessing infinite beings as its leaves and the clusters of stars as its flowers.
That very pure consciousness which manifests by itself,
vibrating like the waters of an undisturbed ocean, has assumed the form of the web of the universe.
Thus, O King, the succession of creations has emerged from the Supreme.
Having entered as reflections into that very great mirror,
those many powers of vibration, arisen from their own nature,
subsequently become the causes for one another under the names of "living beings" (jīva) and so forth.

Some attain the state of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), some go to the state of elemental beings (bhūta), and others become various other things; such is the condition of the world. For the powers of Brahmā, having assumed their respective functions, are indeed themselves.
Having conceived the state of having limited life, they abide as the nature of the cognition of "I.
Like silkworms, they bring about their own bondage;
having attained a limited form, they become colored like crystals.
Bondage is not possible at all for those who have themselves become bound;
for the deluded, out of fear, perceive a yakṣa even in the breasts of their own mothers.
Arising from its own nature, it is without cause and without reason.
The creative powers of Brahman mutually become causes for one another.
There is neither bondage nor liberation; there exists only Brahman, free from all affliction.
There is neither unity nor duality; it is the manifestation of pure consciousness that unfolds.
Just as a single body of water manifests through the breaking of waves, so does this insubstantial mind manifest in various ways.
Having cast far away the conceptualization of bondage and liberation, remain established in your own true nature as one who has arisen as the very essence of fearlessness.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Manifestation of Creation" within the Instruction to Ikṣvāku.
The one hundred and twenty-third canto:
Manu said:
"When the consciousness of pure awareness, which is Truth, becomes oriented toward volitional intention (*saṅkalpa*),"
O King, just as water turns into waves, so do living beings undergo change. Those living beings wander here in this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) that has arisen from before,
moving from one body to another due to the performance of their own actions, like bees among lotuses.
Even though the Supreme Brahman is the self of all, it performs action only while acting,
just as the sun performs its daily activities without being fixed to a single place;
just as insentient iron moves in the proximity of a magnet.
In this same way, this creation flashes forth within the Supreme Self established in its own state. Just as a whirlpool arises from the movement of water,
so does this body spontaneously come into being within the living self (jīva), which consists of consciousness.
Just as a golden wheel appears from the whirling of a firebrand,
so too this body is perceived from the movement of one's own consciousness.
Just as the multiplicity of water is imagined due to the division of rivers and streams, [so is the diversity of the world imagined].
Thus, through the distinction of these forms, there is a multiplicity of the Supreme Self.
States of pleasure, pain, and delusion exist only in the mind, not in the Self;
the state of being a bracelet, a bangle, and so forth, exists in the mental conception, not in the gold.
The wise know that in a deluded living being, this is the conceptualization of "mind" (manas), "thought" (citta), and so forth;
but in one who knows the reality of things as they truly are, this is declared to be pure being (sattva).
Immediately after the body, this being attains the state of pure space (vyomatā) alone.
It no longer becomes a cause for the afflictions of old age and death.
Just as a reflection of a mountain might appear to throb even though it does not throb,
so too the conscious self, though not an agent, appears to be an agent within the body.
O gentle one, the Lord of the abode follows along with the bodily manifestations and transformations, just as the reflection of a face follows the changes in that face;
yet, just as the sun is seen to be wavering in water though it is not itself wavering, so too does He appear.
Likewise, the self is seen to be restless within the body, yet it is not truly restless.
Just as the space within jars does not perish when the jars are destroyed,
so too the self of anyone does not perish when bodies are destroyed.
Devoid of form, light, and mental attention, the Lord assumes a body through attachment to objects; just as a pure gem reflects [colors], so does the Lord assume a body.
Or rather, what need has a tree for form, light, and mental attention to possess sweet sap?
Just as consciousness intensely illuminates the entire circle of the visible world,
so too does the Self abide within the whole network of objects, just as sweetness resides in every sweet substance found throughout the three worlds.
Just as the sun moves when a living being moves and remains still when it stands still—
yet this is merely illusory and not real— so too is the self [perceived] here within bodies.
Just as mirrors and the like do not [truly] perish when their reflections vanish, [so it is with the self].
In the same way, when the body perishes, the Self does not perish.
Just as gold is not burned when the charcoal and other materials are consumed by fire,
so too pure consciousness (cinmātra) does not perish when bodies are destroyed.
Just as the invisible Rāhu is seen when he has seized the moon,
so too is the self, whose nature is pure experience, perceived through the object of cognition.
Just as a gem attains a state of luminosity that makes it capable of reflecting an image, [so does the self manifest].
In the same way, consciousness is indeed perceived by the object of perception through its reflection.
Know that state of consciousness which, being free from the web of volitions, remains established in itself— beyond both decay and excess— that is the supreme state.
When the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) is established in sattva, the Self is perceived within by itself;
for when a mirror is freed from impurity, the reflection appears.
The Supreme Lord is seen neither by the scriptures nor by the teacher.
The Self is perceived by itself through its own intellect established in *sattva*.
O sinless one, all these entities beginning with the body are of the nature of *prakṛti*; they are neither non-existent nor existent, except as a mere delusion.
Just as travelers on a road are seen by one who is free from passion and hatred with such an intellect,
so too should these— the senses and their objects— be viewed.
A virtuous person should neither show them respect nor treat them with contempt.
Let these [entities] remain as they are, resting solely in their status as mere objects.
One who possesses discernment must become identified with that which truly exists;
the Self alone exists for the worlds, not the web of objects such as the body and so forth.
Having thoroughly cast far away the entire collection of objects, such as the body and so forth, with a perfectly cooled inner organ, remain eternally absorbed in the Self.
For the Self alone is the friend of the Self; indeed, the Self alone is found within the Self.
The Self, which is the soul of all, is drawn forth by the Self alone through the experience of the Self. Just as there is no state of being the great ocean apart from water,
so too there is no state of being the world apart from the reality of the Self.
Just as the sun remains the same amidst hundreds of thousands of jars, so does the Self remain amidst the series of bodies;
it neither sets nor rises, remaining unchanged whether those bodies are destroyed or not.
The notion of "non-Self" is like the perception of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
O sinless one, that [thought] "I exist" is false, because the Self here is all-pervading.
The notion "I am the body" is the bond of saṃsāra,
because it follows the suffering of the body and because the object [of that notion] is devoid of essence.
"I am of the nature of nothingness, just like these [elements] such as space"—
this eternal realization is not a bond to saṃsāra.
Just as the son of the Sun [is perceived] both outside and inside pure water, so too is the Self.
Just as light exists everywhere, so does the Self abide in all things;
situated on the wall, in the sky, in the underworld, before one, and far away,
the Self never perishes throughout the three periods of time.
Just as space is inaccessible to cutting and the like, so too is the Self;
indeed, the only difference lies in the fact that the nature of the Self is pure consciousness.
Just as there is a variety of forms and parts in gold, such as bracelets and other ornaments, [so it is with the Self].
In that very same way, the world and its origins possess both that nature and a different nature from the Self;
just as water, extending to the edge of the ocean,
manifests as a continuous flood of waves that arise and perish within the water.
In this very way, the manifestation of the Self within the Self is observed amidst the web of various objects rushing toward the ocean of destruction—
the terrifying great ocean of time, seized by the submarine fire of dissolution.
The waves of creation, like the surging rivers of the world’s web, flow on; yet even for him who remains unfulfilled even today, there is one who is the drinker of that ocean of time—
O King, contemplate that Self as the Great Agastya, just as [the sage did with] the Vindhya mountain.

For the sake of conventional usage in the treatises by those striving to uproot cyclic existence, designations such as "self" and so forth have been applied to that reality which transcends words. No one perceives the falsity of the snake in the rope; [yet it is seen].
There is no bondage for the Self anywhere; do not, my dear, imagine it through delusion. Those who remove delusion say that delusion is merely the mental cultivation of that [bondage].
By abandoning that very cultivation, cast it off and attain freedom from the fever of suffering.
This indeed is that darkness; this alone is the supreme impurity:

namely, that volitional construction (*saṅkalpa*) of the Self, which was previously unbound, [arising] through bondage with respect to this web of the visible, such as the body and so forth, wherein there is the notion of "Self" in what is not the Self.
Having abandoned the [notion of] being a sentient being, remain hidden and established as you please. Just as a mother, forgetting her son who is fast asleep in the hollow of her breast,
weeps for the sake of her son, so does this person weep for the sake of the Self.
Failing to realize that the self is ageless and immortal, people weep in vain, crying:
"Alas, I am slain! I am helpless! I am lost!
while the so-called death resides within the body, distinguished by variations of place, time, and action.
The world grieves for itself; alas, how great indeed is this delusion!
(MU 6.123.52) If the body follows the variations of place, time, and action, then what has happened to this beginningless and indestructible Self? (MU 6.123.53)
One thing is what is eaten, another is what is vomited; this is the same as that which is experienced by the multitudes of people.
When the body, which is subject to destruction, perishes, the self is grieved for as if it were destroyed.
O protector of the earth, [this is the error regarding] the body and the self, which possess change and lack change respectively.
What kind of relationship could there possibly be between these two, which are like gold and its ash?
This Self remains, as if in sport, concealing its own nature through its own playful manifestations known as various forms and transformations that do not depart from it.
Through the mutual causality of creation, manifestation, and withdrawal,
consciousness flashes forth within itself by its own nature as that which is without cause;
the Self plays like a child with conceptual constructs fashioned in sport.
Having veiled itself with flickering blades of grass as if it were a gem,
the sun of consciousness spreads forth its light-giving radiance of vibration;
fashioning the days of the world, it is never exhausted.
The sequence of the world is nothing but the body itself, which is the element of consciousness whose nature is mere vibration;
even its structural arrangement exists as non-different from the self, like the configuration of an object.
By its very nature, consciousness performs the activity of the world through mere vibration.
Without vibration, he withdraws objects of perception as if they were a succession of waves;
seeing all things without distinction and being devoid of intellect and other faculties,
the child that is pure consciousness plays by himself with the toys of creation.

Just as a child who has developed an attachment to a toy grieves when it is lost because its true nature was forgotten, so too does the self here in this cycle of transmigration [grieve] when its own nature is forgotten.
Through the recollection of that consciousness which is both motionless and yet vibrates, it becomes conscious by itself.
The wise know its state of being as vibration when it is directed toward the object of knowledge;

yet, through the delusion of knowing vibration while actually being non-vibrant, consciousness grieves as if out of forgetfulness. Suddenly, by attaining liberation—which is characterized by non-vibration—it becomes tranquil.
Having veiled its own unwavering fourth state (turya) with waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, it grieves in vain; by not doing so, it does not grieve.
The throbbing of consciousness (citspanda), consisting of the mind, intellect, senses, and so forth, serves as the web of the world.
They arise like the movement of water, such as waves, droplets, and the like.
For volition is the vibration of consciousness; non-vibration is known as non-volition.
Know that Brahman is non-volition—that which is like nothing at all.
Just as water appears in various forms through its own vibrations, so too is the non-dual Brahman-consciousness expanded in this way.
But when there is no vibration of consciousness and no volitional thought, that is the fourth state (turya); it becomes that Brahman.
They call that liberation; O King, establish your footing in that.

If consciousness is devoid of volitional construction (*saṅkalpa*), O King, it is indeed the vibration of consciousness; yet when it is without that vibration, it is consciousness itself. Volitional construction is said to be vibration.
Having established the essence of consciousness (cittattva)—which is free from conceptualization and discursive thought—within yourself, with all doubts stilled;
and being the Lord whose nature is consciousness even in the absence of vibration (spanda), remain self-abiding and happy, and rule this kingdom.
The Chapter named "An Inquiry into Vibration" (Spandavicāra).
The one hundred and twenty-fourth canto.
Manu:
By means of his own emanations, the all-pervading Lord, like a child playing with movements, [created] his own...
It seems to delude beings at the end; therefore, O sir, be vigilant in this matter.
Having itself conceptualized duality, the Self grieves for a long time within various wombs;
yet, through its own conceptualization of non-duality, it attains liberation in due course.
In such a way that he is bound, his own power arises for him;
in such a way that he is released, his own power arises for him.
It is not obtained through verbal teachings, nor by the intellect, nor by austerity or sacred learning.
When desire arises, then the self beholds itself.
Oh, how wondrous is this illusion that deludes all directions, since the self does not perceive itself even though it is threaded through every limb! MU 6.124.4–5.
O Lord of the Earth, having seen the all-pervading and infinite Self,
one turns away from attachment to the body and is thereafter no longer stained by sufferings.
Just as the rays of the moon, sun, fire, heated iron, jewels, and so forth [are distinct from their sources],...
Just as leaves and such belong to trees, and as droplets belong to waterfalls, so too is this world—the intellect and the rest—imagined within the vast Brahman.
It brings suffering to those who do not know it; that very [Brahman] appears as if it were something other than itself.
Just as water, by virtue of its flow, assumes the form of a stream or other such arrangements,
so too does this primordial nature (prakṛti) undergo manifoldness through the power of vibration (spanda).
Just as the movement within the reservoir of river water is not perceived, [so it is with the movement of nature].
Likewise, the Self, constantly fashioning creation, is not perceived;
just as the movement of the interior of a vast, clear, and pure stream of water flowing incessantly,
even when its particles are divided by ripples, is not perceived.
Likewise, although it is omnipresent, unobstructed, infinite, and ever-existent, its existence is not perceived within a rope, the sky, or even a stone.
Just as the movement of the sheath belongs to the water itself when it is being drawn up by a gentle person, so too does the Self abide within.
Neither existent nor non-existent, and not separate from existence, such is the nature of the conscious body (*cidvapus*).
Wherever it itself attains the state of consciousness (*cittatā*), consisting of its own volition through its omnipotence, there this [universe] stands as if vibrating.
Where, by virtue of its own omnipotence, it spontaneously abandons its nature as consciousness— which consists of its own volitions— therein the Real remains as if utterly tranquil. Ikṣvāku said:
If that is so, O highly fortunate one, then this vast form of stone and the like,
this great portion of earth— whence has it arisen, and what is its essential nature?
Manu:
All powers indeed reside within Brahman, which is pure consciousness,
just as the vine, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth reside within the seed of a banyan tree.
From the Self, who possesses all powers, there arise two powers designated as the insentient and the sentient.

Just as hardness and fluidity reside in gold, the most excellent of all powers; so too, that single power called "inertia" (jāḍya), which takes the form of earth and the other elements, has come to possess the nature of form, light, mental attention, and objective domain for those two [consciousness and intellect].
This [intellect] is neither born nor ever dissolved;
it is eternally an integral part of Being, situated like the space within a vessel. For one who perceives this as non-different from Brahman, like a snake [superimposed] on a rope—
Delusion, which has arisen from what is non-existent, dissolves through awakening.
This [delusion] does not undergo the designation of a modification of being within the pure conscious self;
indeed, it abides in consciousness like waves and ripples in water.
That which is the non-existence of the existent, or the existence of the non-existent, is indeed a modification (*vikṛti*);
because it would entail an absolute difference in nature, such a thing does not exist in the Supreme Self.
O King, [this applies] by way of the non-existence of the existent and the existence of the non-existent.
Because its form has perished, it is designated by such terms as "modification" (vikāra) and so forth.
However, that which appears as the state of being a fruit in a sprout, or as the state of being ghee in milk, is merely the manifestation of existence; it vibrates like waves upon water.
Whatever is perceived in whatever manner and wherever, that exists in that very way there;
it consists of the distinctions of space and time, and likewise consists of consciousness.
Just as a single mountain remains one and the same even when situated in different places and times, so too does this [consciousness].
Even so, the seed, though ending in the fruit, is one; here there is no otherness.

Just as the state of being a banyan tree exists in the banyan seed according to its own timing and manner of emergence, so too does this glorious [manifestation] of the insentient and the sentient abide within the Self consisting of consciousness.
"O King, like a dream, the mind alone flashes forth as a mere appearance, taking on the form of a mass of mental modes that undergoes manifold transformations of existence. Ikṣvāku said:
Just as this gross form of mountains and so forth appears to this Supreme Self—
whether it be unreal or real— explain that to me once again.
Manu said:
Thus all is equal, peaceful, the pervasive and imperishable sky of consciousness;
it is without limit, without appearance, and has been, is, and will be.
It is that which is neither above nor below, neither direction, nor darkness, nor light.

And nothing else whatsoever exists, for all is always [that alone]. By that Supreme Lord, whose sole essence is pure consciousness and who is free from beginning, middle, and end, this very world was willed by himself through his own volition.
Then, he who is unborn, whose nature consists of volition and whose form is mind, remained there;
by that mind, this vast expanse of space was conceived. Through the condensation of the mind and space, the vibrating wind came into being.
Then, through contact with the wind of the mental sky, he perceived light;
subsequently, there existed water in the form of a volition consisting of portions of fire.
Then that aggregate of the four elements was perceived by the mind as an egg.
That [Brahman], having become the egg born of the lotus, behold, the two worlds (rodasī) were produced;
therein, this great world-system, beginning with Mount Meru, exists as a mere semblance of parts.
Thus, Brahman alone, being perfectly full, is perceived as the world.

Through vibrations, modifications of states, and so forth, it remains as if possessed of change. Just as a single river appears in various forms at different places and times, even while existing as a creeper, it remains established in its own nature as a seed.
Just as kernels remain within the hollow of a grain pod,
so indeed do all worlds abide within the infinite space of consciousness (cidvyoman).
These successions of creations have entered the hollow of the Brahman of consciousness.
They manifest as transformations, like waves in the ocean.
Just as something is seen by a vision falling into darkness,
so the world and the "I" appear as unreal through consciousness.

Just as even a wheel or similar object is seen in blinding darkness by virtue of a particular vision, so too at the beginning of creation, this unreal notion of "I" is perceived by consciousness (*citi*). Whatever manifestation arises from the great power of the mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), that alone [is the reality].
Therefore, that [reality] is here neither existent nor non-existent by its very nature, and yet it is that;
the single, supreme, and essential Being, full in form,
vibrates through these manifestations just as the ocean manifests through waves and the like.
He who remains with his desires stilled, contemplating that the entire world is composed of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), is happy, being armored by Brahman.
He does so through a state free from the sense of "I" (ahamartha), which is of the nature of non-existence.
One should contemplate that "everything is empty, without support, and the consciousness is at peace.
"This is pleasant, this is not"—this is the seed of your continuous stream of suffering.
When that seed is consumed by the fire of equanimity, whence can there be any occasion for suffering?
O King, by the mere absence of mental cultivation, the internal distinction between the pleasant and the unpleasant quickly dissolves through one's own extraordinary human effort.
By means of the non-cultivation of phenomena, one cuts down the forest of karma.
O Indra among kings, having attained the Supreme, remain free from sorrow!

Having become one who fills the entire expanse of the world, transcending all divisions, delighting in the dissolution of the play of mental constructs, possessed of the splendor of blossoming, ever-new, unborn, ancient, eternally ageless and stainless, with an expansive enjoyment that is equanimous, equal, tranquil, and pure— you are the fearless body of consciousness.
In the *Manūpadeśa*, the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Instruction on Creation, Tradition, and Yoga"; [thus ends] the instruction of Manu.
Just as whirlpools appear in a mass of water, or reflections in a gem;
just as objects appear in the sense organs, or light in fire;
and just as blades of grass appear in the wind, whose movement is difficult to perceive.
Thus the three worlds manifest within the self of experience, which is difficult to perceive,
just as liquidity and other qualities exist in water, or as motes appear in sunlight;
so too do the arrangements of objects and the floods of creation exist within the dense mass of consciousness.
Consisting of that [Brahman], yet not having its form, situated in it, and existing through its existence— these creations, though endless, are perishable like bubbles in the ocean.
Just as a gem is black when [the surface is] black, white when white, and red when red.
Because it is pure through the absence of latent impressions regarding color, it does not undergo passion;
likewise, when the mind is deluded, the Lord is deluded; when it is struck down, he is broken; and when it is joyful, he is joyful.
Because it is pure through the absence of latent impressions, it does not undergo passion. (MU 6.125.5–6)
The birth of the world arises from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and that [impression] is merely a conventional designation.
This notion of "this is mine" is utterly false; abandon it!
Just as the sky is not defiled by dust, smoke, darkness, fire, or clouds, so too is the Self.
Likewise, through the volitions of *prakṛti*, the sky-like essence of consciousness remains untainted.
My dear one, just as light reaching the earth is nothing other than the sun itself,
so too these volitions are nothing other than consciousness itself, because they consist of that very [consciousness].
The supreme Self is inexpressible and motionless like the wind;
it is perceived by the Self alone through the vibration of the Self, which is the nature of self-awareness.
That which is non-existent yet appears as an object of knowledge gathers [the world] because its nature is consciousness.
This capacity for consciousness belongs to it; from this, this cycle of transmigration has arisen.
Just as shimmering, clear water is not something other than mere water, so too Brahman, whose nature is pure consciousness, is nothing other than Brahman itself.
The supreme Self is indeed inexpressible; yet that which constitutes its expressibility is called "consciousness" (cit).
It is this very consciousness that has entered the state of the seer and the seen.
Just as whirlpools and the like arise from the movement of water, even though they have not [previously] arisen [as distinct entities].
Thus, although it does not arise, the Supreme Brahman appears as if arisen because it perceives the world;
its nature is that of the Self which cannot be designated, being motionless like the wind.
That which here consists of the essence of the meaning of the word "consciousness" (cit) is the world characterized by "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) and so forth.

Just as in clear water, due to the movement of its fluidity, whirlpools and the like are perceived, so too, because of its consciousness, the mind—though indescribable in its supreme state—is considered to consist of the world.
The sequence consisting of pure awareness, which has been described regarding the beginning and end of creation, is as follows: [text continues].
Just as whirlpools and the like arise from the movement of water with every blink of the eye,
so do the notions of "I-ness" (ahantā) and "this-ness" (idantā) and so forth proceed from the supreme consciousness through its own cognitive power.
Know that non-perception is supreme; perception is said to be creation.
Through the perception of the non-existent as existent, the visible world appears; yet even though it exists, it becomes non-existent through non-perception.
Just as from the opening of the eyes of consciousness, the non-existent creation appears as a manifestation.
Yet, due to the closing and opening of the eyes of consciousness, even though it exists, it does not shine forth;
just as the world of an illusionist's net appears from the scattering of illusory powder, so too this [world] arises in the void from the wondrous power of the powder of consciousness.

Just as water possesses the characteristic of whirlpools even during a mere blink due to its movement, so too, because of its consciousness, the Lord manifests the delusions of creation and dissolution in an instant;
this is true even for one who is living, whose mental impressions have long since been exhausted, yet remains in the form of pure consciousness.

He whose being consists of non-perception is said to be liberated. Those who are fully awakened remain without latent impressions (*vāsanā*), without conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*), and with actions occurring as part of the natural flow; for they consist of the essence of non-perception.

Though they perform actions, they are free from the latent impressions of volition; with their inner dispositions stilled, they are constantly absorbed as if in wood, resembling the interior of a stone.
There is not even the slightest difference between them and those in the dream of a dream-city.
Therefore, for one who knows Brahman, there is the realization of Brahman within both creation and dissolution.
Because of the knowledge of the manifestation of words, meanings, and mental constructs, and through the awakening to reality,
that internal awakening to non-existence is called "non-realization" (avedana).
The heart of the existent one is a perception that is not seen though it appears as something seen; it is conscious yet remains as if unconscious, and though not empty, it resembles emptiness.
At the outset, one should increase wisdom through the study of the scriptures and association with the virtuous.
This first stage is said to belong to the beginner yogin.

The second is investigation (*vicāraṇā*), the third is the cultivation of non-attachment (*asaṅgabhāvanā*), and the fourth consists in the dissolution of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) upon the attainment of the state of pure being (*sattvatā*).
The fifth stage consists of the nature of bliss, which is pure consciousness;
here, one who is liberated while living remains with the appearance of being half-asleep and half-awake.
And the sixth stage is of the nature of non-perception.

A state resembling deep sleep, consisting of a single mass of bliss, is the fourth stage (*turyāvasthā*), which is utterly tranquil; this is indeed liberation alone. It is equanimity, clarity, and gentle—this is the seventh stage (*bhūmikā*).

Furthermore, the state that transcends the fourth (turyātīta), which is of the nature of final nirvāṇa, is the seventh; it is fully matured and is not an object for those who live. Among those, the first three states are established as being simply "waking."
The fourth is said to be the dream state, wherein the world indeed appears as a dream.
The fifth is called deep sleep (*suṣupta*), due to its being a single mass of bliss.
And the sixth, characterized by the absence of perception, is known as the fourth (*turyā*).
The seventh stage, the supreme ground, is the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta);
it is the ultimate, indefinable, and inaccessible even to the great. It is endowed with its own unique arrangements of categories, which are not found elsewhere.
Likewise, the intellect [appears] through the words and objects of creation, but not as having the form of the objects of creation themselves.
Just as bracelets and the like exist within gold, so does creation exist within the supreme state;
however, although it exists, it is devoid of the objects denoted by conventional names.

Just as bracelets and other ornaments exist within gold, yet do not exist at all when examined [as distinct from it], so too does the creation exist within the supreme state; it is like a conceptual object.
Through the existence of the perception of movement, which is itself devoid of movement, [the world appears].

That consciousness which is the splendor of the sprout is called "the existence of the Self" (sātmasattā). You are that; you are consciousness, and you are the mind. Yet you are not that, nor are you consciousness, nor are you the mind.
Existence and non-existence do not belong to her; she is tranquil, and beyond her nothing else exists.
Just as emptiness is not distinct from space, and just as the state of being a wave is not distinct from water,
so too form and the rest are not different from that [consciousness], nor are the seer, the mind, or the stone.
Within that vision, we abide as the seer, the seeing, and the seen.
I have not even been taught the names of such things as consciousness, mind, or insentience.
I do not maintain a denial of everything, nor do I maintain a denial of anything;
for since distinctions such as "you," "I," or "self" are impossible, the world is the supreme, peaceful void.

Having ascertained that the nature of the "I"—which has for its object all things whose specific distinctions are stilled, and which is joined with both reality and unreality—is called "action," and that even this [ascertainment] "it does not exist" (nāsti) is here either joined with other meanings such as "I" or is itself devoid of them; therefore, enough! Let one sit upon the seat that completely uproots the sprouts of the born, the insentient, and the sentient.
Vālmīki:

When the sage had spoken thus, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
The one hundred and twenty-sixth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Practice of the Essential Nature of Nirvana," [spoken by] Manu.
For the knower whose connection to existence is completely stilled and whose latent tendencies of passion and hatred have vanished,
the senses move like figures on a loom driven by a shuttle,
or like grass that has been wrapped around and then released, or like waves that are free from latent tendencies.
In worldly transactions, those who possess their own essential nature are both the knowers and the objects of knowledge.
Just as a wave within a wave is rendered waveless through its own nature,
so too is action such as battle fashioned by the knower according to his own state.

When a wave is led to the state of being no-wave, its essence remains unimpaired; it is just like water joined with water—nothing at all is lost. When the living is led into the living by means of the living, its essence remains unimpaired.

Likewise, when the self has become truly itself, nothing whatsoever is joined or lost. Let there be consciousness within even a portion of a word; yet, having fallen away from that, it becomes "with-object" (sacetyā), reaching a futile extinction and arriving at non-existence.
Because his self is established in the Self that is pure consciousness alone, he does not accumulate pleasure or pain;
though engaging in worldly activity, the liberated one whose nature is Truth remains as if these were non-existent.
This much indeed constitutes the state of being liberated while living (jīvanmukti): that through the power of steady practice, [one remains unshaken].

When consciousness is reflected [in the mirror of the mind], it becomes neither for the sake of pleasure nor for the sake of pain. If, being established in yourself by the power of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), you do not accumulate that which is to be perceived, then you are undoubtedly liberated through this great equanimity.

When the sage, whose intellect has not previously been made its own by portions of pleasure and pain from enjoyments, remains delighting in the Self— that is declared to be liberation. Whether he is engaged in worldly affairs or tranquil, whether he is a householder or a mendicant.
Whether he possesses a body or is bodiless, let the person be of such a mind:
if consciousness is equanimous, untouched by pleasure and pain,
then let that body do whatever it does, as if it were unconscious.
When this body, which is like a mirage, is extended as the self of ignorance and is wounded,
how can there be a succession of pleasure and pain within that unreal delusion of existence and non-existence?
This infinite [reality] is pure consciousness alone, devoid of the appearance of insentience.

Therefore, one should take refuge in the stainless Self, whose object of knowledge is impossible [to perceive as an other]. That state which, for one who is awake and living, consists of the non-accumulation of mental objects and is an unwavering consciousness—like the interior of a stone—is the Fourth (turya); that is liberation.
The embodiment of consciousness experiences this world—which is projected by its own being as its very self—within itself alone as a false perception, like one whose head has been severed in a dream.
Where is that which is false? Where is the nature of reality? And where is the water in a mirage? It is not real.

Therefore, through the very non-perception [of this], this delusion is completely destroyed. (MU 6.126.17) The delusion of the world’s cycle of existence arises from the accumulation of the notion "I am.
From the non-accumulation of this very notion, there is neither "I," nor the world, nor delusion. (MU 6.126.18)

Just as fire [perceives] its own heat, cold its own chill, the wind its own motion, and the ocean its own fluidity, so does Consciousness perceive the world as its own. Just as pure water perceives itself as fluid, a stone its own internal striations, and sugarcane its own sweetness, Consciousness perceives the world as its own. MU 6.126.19. Just as fire [perceives] its own heat, cold its own chill, the wind its own motion, and the ocean its own fluidity, so [does Consciousness perceive the world].
The knower perceives that reality of the Self, which is non-different yet appears as if different; however, one who is ignorant of it does not perceive it.
This concludes the one hundred and twenty-seventh canto, titled "The Description of the Nature of Liberation."
Manu says:
How indeed could there be a stain upon the Self by the Self itself, and in what manner?
Therefore, the Self is truly unstained, because a second entity is absolutely impossible. (MU 6.127.1)
The conceptualization of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth exists, yet it is not distinct from the Self;
the Self itself is the power of latent impressions, just as waves are nothing but water.
The Self manifests as the transformations of existence through the form of the body and the senses.
Just as water assumes the state of a wave even though it is not subject to transformation,
so too the Unchanging One, by falsely imagining the process of transformation,
becomes as if transformed; it perceives its own intense manifestation with great intensity.
O King, that which is seen as a modification of the Self—which is itself unchanging—is truly real; yet it is also unreal. Reflect upon this yourself:
just as bracelets and other ornaments are transformations of gold, so too are they of the Self.
No modification can occur in that which is unchanging, because it is indestructible.
Just as the state of being a wave is not a modification of the water, so the world is not a modification of Consciousness.
This delusion arises from the perception of what is unreal; it belongs to the act of seeing itself, not to the reality.

Just as one does not grieve when gold that has become a bracelet becomes a staff, nor even over its transformation, thinking "the gold of the bracelet is dead," so too there is no grief when the sky of consciousness remains as a wall due to its state as a covering.

It is not logical that the consciousness of space should die while the consciousness of the wise man remains. If the consciousness of the body were to become the consciousness of space, and the consciousness of space were to become the consciousness of the body, then what would be the source of joy or despair?
When there is the certainty that "consciousness exists" through the manifestation of the inward-facing consciousness,
because there is no longer any perception of objects along with their modifications— which are born of delusion—
then, by the power of one's own self-reflection, [the world] is surely brought to its long-standing emergence.
If the heart is devoid of latent impressions (*nirvāsana*), how can there be transmigration for the living being?
When the destruction of transmigration— which is nothing but the diversity of one's own consciousness— is to be accomplished,
why does such an extreme agitation arise in living beings?

That living being who, by force, brings about the subsiding of mere consciousness while not falling into insentience and remaining pure, has crossed the ocean of existence. This fickleness of consciousness is what constitutes transmigratory existence and the bondage of becoming.
Peace comes from the subsiding of that [thought]; therefore, bring about its subsiding. That very consciousness which attains peace is the same as the intellect that dissolves;
that very drop of dew which exists is the same as that which dissolves in the heat.
I do not die, nor do I live; I am neither existent nor non-existent, nor am I space.
Realizing "I am nothing but consciousness," the living being does not grieve.
I am untainted, ageless, free from passion, and one whose latent impressions are stilled.
Thinking, "I am stainless, the space of consciousness," one does not grieve.
Thinking, "I am devoid of beginning and end, pure, awakened, ageless and immortal, peaceful, and of an appearance that is perfectly equanimous," one does not grieve.
"I am the lamp of consciousness that illumines all things in the world;
what are birth and death to me?"—thinking thus, one does not grieve.
[This is true] whether it be regarding grass, fire, the sky, the sun, or among men, serpents, and gods.
Thinking "whatever I am, that indeed I am," who would grieve?
(MU 6.127.21) "Transversely, upwards, and downwards, my greatness as consciousness is all-pervasive;
knowing this, who would be subject to decay, for it possesses infinite manifestations? (MU 6.127.22)
With my great fever of passion completely stilled, I have reached the supreme consummation;
now, who is this that is called "I," which has arisen as a mere false notion?
Indeed, by means of the Unborn (Ajena), the Self was known as "I am the awakened one, the Lord."
Resting in itself by itself, like water in the ocean of water,
Brahman has become Brahman alone— unshakable, having attained equanimity;
it is as if water, having abandoned the form of waves, has returned to its own placidity.
I am of the nature of non-ego; I have dissolved away; I am eternal. I am inwardly cooled; I am at peace, like a mirage in the rainy season.
I am blissful for all time; I am born as the great one whose body is unborn.
Knowing this, the living being, though intensely bound, is not truly fettered.
Seeing that "there is no bondage for me, nor is there liberation for me; I do not exist, nor does anything else," one does not grieve, because of seeing things as they truly are.
Even while acting, action does not lead to bondage for one who knows reality;
even while consuming poison, one who knows it is never destroyed.
Action performed previously in the body is burned away by the very root.
Just as dry grass is consumed by fire through the awakening of its presence,
so too is it experienced for oneself that an object which is pursued while bound by latent impressions brings pleasure and yields its fruits. MU 6.127.30–31.

That very object which leads to happiness quickly becomes a source of suffering through its destruction; thus, the inseparable connection between happiness and suffering is well established. Whether an object is pursued with attenuated latent impressions (*vāsanā*) or with intense latent impressions, [it results in the same].

That [action] leads neither to happiness nor to destruction; rather, in time, it yields suffering. For the yogin who performs an action while free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*), like a child who is not asleep, he is not joined with the fruit of that action.
O sinless one, whatever action is performed with a mind whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been exhausted does not sprout again, like a parched seed.
Action is fashioned by the multitude of instruments, such as the body and the senses.
In this case, how could there possibly be a single agent or enjoyer?
One [atom] sees, another enjoys, and yet another subtle atom experiences;
since pleasure, pain, and so forth belong to one, who here possesses the status of being the sole agent?
The Self is both the agent and the non-agent, abiding in equanimity;
like a mirror among reflections, it transcends the six organs including the mind.
Therefore, my dear, all things beginning with the body are insentient; nothing at all [belongs to the Self].
No one at all performs even well-performed actions;
even while the wise man performs an action, it is done with an intellect that is unattached.
No one does anything at all; the body merely vibrates.
Even when remaining silent, the fool, with a mind deeply attached to thoughts,
performs action as massive as a mountain, which is not exhausted even in ages.
He who sits restraining his organs of action but continues to remember with his mind—
For one whose self is deluded regarding the objects of the senses, agency here is endless. But he who, O sinless one, restraining the senses with the mind,
engages in the yoga of action through the organs of action— he, though not a doer, partakes in liberation.
Action performed without latent impressions does not touch the unborn agent,
just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf or a cloud to the vault of the sky.
When actions are devoid of latent impressions, their fruits do not pursue the agent.
Then karma, the sole cause of birth, does not touch the living soul.
The essence of karma, which is the seed of birth, is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) everywhere;
and when that [impression] comes into being, it beholds a body within the womb.
From that very [state] one is born again quickly, and through the sequence [of births], one wanders in saṃsāra.
Therefore, for the sake of your welfare, let there be an internal separation from mental impressions (vāsanā).
Having completely cast off all mental constructs (bhāvanā) regarding all existing things, remain uplifted.
Cool as the moon and full, you shine like the sun with its light.
The splendor of the cotton-wool of karma belonging to the body-thorn, once being performed, is completed;
yet, when fanned away by the wind of knowledge, it goes to dissolution somewhere.
For one who has attained self-knowledge and crossed over the ocean of existence,
even if they so desire, ignorance of the self does not return again;
just as a swift river, having traveled far from its place of origin, [does not return].
The intellect that has thus reached the Buddhas does not fall back into delusion.
For every skill of a living being perishes through lack of practice,
even if it was once fruitful and pleasing, like a creeper deprived of watering.
This digit of knowledge, once born within, increases day by day by its own force even among the virtuous, like sown rice;
just as clarified butter extracted from curd does not again attain the state of being curd.
Likewise, cognition extracted by knowledge does not return to a state of ignorance again.
Just as a true warrior emerges victorious after breaking through the array of the enemy's troops,
so the sun of knowledge emerges after tearing through the darkness of ignorance.
The stainless Brahman, a mass of consciousness, peaceful, and pervading all this, is non-dual; though appearing as if dual, it is eternally one and free from affliction.
The supreme Self, whose nature is consciousness, shines as one within all things, like clear water within its own ocean.
O dear one, know that this entire world is but a single portion of pure existence (sattā), in which the vast multitude of composite parts has been completely stilled.
This concludes the one hundred and twenty-eighth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Ultimate Reality."
Manu says:
From a supreme cause, a single Jīva first arose;
from that, the particles of Jīvas were born, like sparks from heated iron. (MU 6.128.1)
These hundreds of gods, nāgas, gandharvas, and vidyādharas,
who were once addressed [by others], now quiver as pure drops of nectar from the ocean of their own immortal self.
Yet, ensnared by the web of their own arbitrary volitions, they have fallen into bondage.
Just as silkworms become cocoons by turning their own saliva into thread,
so too do beings bind themselves to one another through their own volitions;
consequently, they experience sufferings just as grains are encased within their own husks.

When he is burned by the fire of knowledge, the husk of his own conceptual constructions is consumed; then they become pure, like fresh pearls. They are never again born in the world, nor do any of them ever arise.
Having ascended to that state of the Self, they are freed from their latent impressions due to the removal of delusion.

Know that the world is without cause by its very nature in its arising and destruction; it has attained the state of mutual causality through its parts in the course of worldly existence. (MU 6.128.6–7)
Just as the sky is neither placed within water-jars nor yet not placed therein,
so the Self is neither situated within all bodies nor yet not situated.
Just as there is the designation "jar-space" when both the jar and the sky exist, [so too is the designation of the individual self].
While both the self and the body exist, there is likewise the perception of the body;
yet, O King, there are no portions whatsoever of consciousness or unconsciousness.
There is only a certain existence designated as the "self" that manifests within the body.
Just as a vision shines intensely when fixed for a long time upon a clear sky,
so does the appearance of the body flash forth within the Self of pure Being, which is designated as the "Self" of individual souls.
Previously, those living beings who, through their own volitions, brought about the stable existence of the world—
Through association with that [individual soul], other powers of Brahman today attain the state of being living beings. Just as even one who is not a thief is bound due to association with a thief,
so too, through prior association with the individual soul, the portion of the Self attains the state of being a limited cognition.
As long as there is a sense of "mine" regarding one's own body and so forth, so long is there the seed of saṃsāra;
as long as there is hope for the enjoyment of sense objects, so long does the self bear the name "jīva.
When, through the power of discrimination and by virtue of knowledge, the destruction of both duality and unity has occurred—

The self, having cast off the state of being a living soul, attains the state of Brahman, free from affliction. Deluded, this multitude of beings, bound by the threads of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), revolves in the wheel of delusion consisting of old age, birth, and death, sharing in the experience of suffering.
"I belong to no one, nor do I belong to anyone; such am I.
Nothing whatsoever is mine"—by this internal certainty, abandon *saṃsāra*.
By the firm conviction that "everything is mine, and I belong to everything," [one attains liberation].

Abandon the agitation of worldly existence; be established in yourself, transcending becoming. Having long moved upward from below and downward from above, and again from below to above, do not become a water-jar on the rope of anxiety for the water-wheel of saṃsāra.
Those fools who, out of delusion, cling to the dense illusion of worldly convention— thinking "this is mine," "I am this"— go downward, to the lowest depths.
[Thinking] "I belong to this," "this is mine," "he is this," "I am such-and-such"— thus they conceive of the Self.
When you have abandoned delusion through wisdom, O unborn one, you shall proceed higher and higher;
do not, like a stone in the ocean, sink lower and lower, deluded.
Through awakening, go ever higher, like the moon rising above the milk-ocean.
Contemplating how things arise and perish like the foam upon water,
do not count yourself among the multitude of creepers, grasses, vines, and shrubs.
The light of consciousness, that sun of the intellect, radiates forth everywhere.

By him, the house of the world, together with the sun, moon, and stars, has been made manifest. Relying without delay upon that light which is your own self, remain, O King, filling the entire space; behold the body and all else!
Just as a crystal, by its very nature, radiates luster while remaining still,
so too does the sun of consciousness radiate the worlds with the light of consciousness.
That which is the vibration of consciousness as pure mind, by its own self, is stainless.
This expansive world is fully realized within the vast consciousness of that Supreme Brahman;
for there, Brahman alone is magnified as Brahman.
Therein, these conceptual constructions of "being" and "non-being," and so forth, do not exist.

Wherever it abides by means of the power of pure being (*sattva-śakti*), which transcends the mind through its nature as all-powerful Brahman, there indeed lies that state of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
Wherever Brahman unfolds through the power of the mind consisting of infinite potencies, [therein resides the liberated one].
There,
by means of that solitary yet deluded and bewildered power of the mind, one remains in a state of dissolution;
having reached such a state, one assumes the form of animals, piśācas, spirits, and the like.
Where the power of the mind, through extreme delusion, remained in a state like that of deep sleep, there it became like trees, shrubs, grass, and the like;
for the mind that has long been deluded and whose thousands of bodies have perished.
Know that it possesses parts such as stone, like some mountain;
just as a flower is pervaded by fragrance and molasses by sweetness,
so too is the world, including the mountains and the sky, pervaded by the reality of consciousness (cittattva).
Just as the water of the ocean is in some places agitated and in others gentle in form,
so too is consciousness in some respects motionless and in others characterized by movement.
When the nature of consciousness is thus seen as an all-pervading, undivided expanse, [it is realized].
At that very moment, those who have crossed over saṃsāra and attained the state of the Supreme Lord should cultivate this thought:
"Whatever Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Varuṇa are prepared to do,
I, whose body is consciousness, perform it all."
In whatever philosophical systems, however they may be described, O dear one, all that is indeed true; for everything is indeed all-pervading.
Whether it be a particular place or a foreign land, a time or a mental construction—

"You know all that as Brahman itself; do as you wish. Whatever form is conceived, the Lord of Consciousness assumes that very state, extended like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) to fulfill each and every desire.
Whatever is meditated upon by that radiant one,
that very thing is perfectly created, adorned, joined, and experienced.
This occurs for one whose own mind has attained the state of pure consciousness and has crossed over death.
By what can that supreme bliss be compared?
Death alone is the ultimate limit of all sufferings in the three worlds;
having conquered it, by whom can that supreme bliss be described?
Having fully understood all views and all forms of prosperity,
one stands for a long time above them, having realized one's own self—
even if they be infinite, vast, and capable of splitting even a diamond.
No defects whatsoever afflict the knower of reality, who is pure like the sky.
All perceptions of defects, such as old age, death, and birth,
terminate solely in the knowledge of the Self, just as all rivers end in the ocean.

Nature (prakṛti) strives for the destruction of suffering only so long as it does not perceive the Self; having perceived Him, it becomes tranquil. Just as reeds perish upon encountering a flower [of the reed-grass], so too does nature cease its activity.
Having thus attained their self-nature, the mind, intellect, senses,
and so forth— O Lord of the Earth, the entire world is void in the beginning and void in the end;
therefore, know that this is indeed of the nature of the void, and void even in the middle.

Meditate upon the world as being neither internal nor external, neither empty nor non-empty, neither of the nature of consciousness nor consisting of consciousness, neither of the nature of the self nor of the nature of another;
having attained this true nature, primordial matter (prakṛti) comes to rest.
Where could an entity that has deviated from its own nature remain after having undergone agitation?
O sinless one, liberation is said to be the breaking of the knot of ignorance;
there is no place called liberation, nor time, nor any other state of existence.
Through the destruction of egoism and delusion, this nature—which is called "cultivation" (bhāvanā)—dissolves. This itself is liberation;
it alone, gradually dissolving the body, becomes quiescent.
For one who has reached non-existence, there arises in regard to sense objects a discernment that transcends words.
Having understood this worldly delusion of things as it truly is,
and having cultivated [the truth] according to that knowledge, the wise man remains at ease.
With the fickleness of investigating the meaning of the scriptures stilled, with the curiosity for poetry of manifold sentiments ceased,
and with the delusion of all conceptual constructions entirely cast aside, you abide in eternal bliss, characterized by equanimity.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Instruction on the Yoga for Dispelling All Doubts."
The one hundred and twenty-ninth canto.
Manu:
Delighting in the self, free from sorrow, eternally inward-turned, he is happy.
Even while performing actions, he remains free from delusion;
always inwardly cool and undisturbed,
he shines like the full moon with a gentle form.
Equanimous, with a tranquil mind, silent, and with the cessation of speech and discursive thought,
he shines within the self-nature of consciousness like a fire whose fuel has been consumed.
Clothed in whatever [garments] and fed by whatever [food], he remains.
Sleeping wherever he may be, he shines like a sovereign emperor.
Abandoning the rules of caste, the duties of the stages of life, the conduct prescribed by the scriptures, and the ritual mantras,
he emerges from the snare of the world like a lion from its cage.
Having attained an indescribable splendor that transcends the domain of words and is free from the stain of desire for sense-objects— like the vault of the sky in autumn—
he was both profound and serene, like a great lake in his speech.
Intoxicated by the essence of supreme bliss, he rejoices in the Self by means of the Self.
Expanding according to his desire and performing actions according to his desire,
he attains supreme contentment, freed from the constraints of the meaning of the scriptures.
Renouncing the fruits of all actions, eternally contented, and without dependence,
one is stained neither by merit nor by sin, nor even by anything else;
just as a crystal does not undergo coloring by means of a reflection.
One who knows that [reality] does not, even through the internal results of karma,
experience attachment; though laughing or weeping intensely, and through the honoring or mutilating of the body, he feels neither burning nor delight, as if these were occurring in a reflection.
Devoid of praise and devoid of the *vaṣaṭ* call, free from the honoring of those worthy of honor,
he is both conjoined with and dissociated from all methods and sequences of conduct.
Therefore, the world is not agitated by him, nor is he agitated by the world.
He is seen as liberated from joy, resentment, fear, and anger, yet he is also seen as engaged with them; he is abandoned by the onset of passion and hatred, yet he is also joined with them;
through the play of effort and non-effort, he is neither attained nor does he enjoy [the fruits].
The Great-minded One does not ascend to the status of an object of knowledge for anyone;
nor is the One of Noble Intent ever made an object of knowledge even by a fool.
Indeed, he who has arisen as oneness, having shaken off infinite multiplicity—
Who indeed is capable of weighing that beginningless and endless consciousness?
Whether one casts off the body at a sacred ford or in the house of a dog-cooker,
O King— whether it be at any time whatsoever or even at this very moment.
At the moment of attaining knowledge, he is liberated and free from affliction;
let him do whatever he does, for he is devoid of sorrow, old age, and fatigue.
Indeed, the delusion of "I" leads to bondage, while liberation occurs when that delusion is destroyed.
Let this body be as it may; what loss is there?
Whatever the progeny does, whatever they take, wherever they sit for a moment, whatever they see, touch, or long for—that belongs to Him.

He is to be worshipped, he is to be praised, and he is to be saluted with effort; that Great Soul is to be reverently greeted by one who desires prosperity for the sake of spiritual power. That supreme purity is not attained through sacrifices, pilgrimages, austerities, or gifts.
O dear one, that which is attained through devotion by the virtuous who know the Self and for whom the disease of worldly existence has been exhausted—
this is the description of the nature of the liberated person,
the one hundred and thirtieth canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the blessed Manu remained silent,
honored by the joyful king Ikṣvāku.
Entering the sky, the illustrious one went to the abode of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Adhering to this vision, O Rāma, attain the state of delighting in the Self.
Rāma said:
This being so, O Blessed One, what unprecedented excellence does one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) possess, who is of right mind and the best among the knowers of the Self? Vasiṣṭha replied:
In some particular excellence of a limb, the mind of the wise man does not find satisfaction;
eternally content and tranquil in soul, he abides in the Self alone.
What unprecedented excellence indeed exists in this world for the virtuous man?
For all extraordinary powers in this world have already occurred by the hundreds in the past—

performed by rogues, perfected beings (*siddhas*), those who possess such knowledge, as well as others such as beasts and birds; what, then, would be unprecedented about traveling through the sky and so forth?
With all agitation stilled, engaged in his natural activities,
that knower of reality, contracting the body, remains established in the self, at ease.
He is neither superior nor common, neither unlearned nor highly learned.
"These people do not recognize whether one is well-behaved or ill-behaved, even if one is wise.
Rāma said:
"Even for one who follows worldly conduct and abides like a common person,"
"O Brahmin, tell me even a slight sign of one who has known that which is to be known.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"My dear friend, nothing at all unprecedented is observed in him compared to ordinary people."

And whatever diversity may belong to him is observed elsewhere as well. O Rāma, for one who knows reality here, there exists no manifest characteristic capable of being perceived by the world, such as *aṇimā* and so forth, or the absence thereof.
Just as an ignorant person engages in worldly affairs, so too does the knower of reality in this world;
he remains subject to the pleasure and pain that arise through the force of worldly convention.
There is only one distinction here, and that is invisible within the condition of ordinary people.
Whether the body exists or not, that state wherein suffering has internally ceased—
apart from this state of being free from suffering, which consists of one’s own direct experience—
no other sign of the Knower of Truth (tajjña) is found, such as the head or horns.
O Rāma, although he may be a great doer, a great enjoyer, and a great renouncer, he becomes a knower of that [Reality]; these qualities are common even to an ignorant person,
for it is generally observed that even an ignorant one experiences a diminution of passion, greed, and the like.

Austerity and charity, as well as fame— these are not the characteristics of one who possesses true knowledge. Indeed, for the knower of that [Reality], there is no sign whatsoever, for it is eternally distinct from supreme bliss established in self-experience, and is free from decay and excess.
Or rather, the mark of one who knows that [Reality] is seen as great agency;
O virtuous one, this common characteristic has been described by me in many ways.
Indeed, this alone is the sign of Him whose form is signless, who is stilled from the long wandering of worldly existence and is liberated.
The daily and skillful attenuation of passion, anger, dejection, delusion, greed, and calamities by one who knows that [Self].
This is the chapter titled "An Investigation of the Marks of One Liberated while Living," the one hundred and thirty-first chapter.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen further, O mighty-armed one, to my words in brief, which I speak for your enlightenment, like a cloud to a peacock. (MU 6.131.1)
Your instruction is to be accepted by me from my own ascetic penance;
for, O Rāma, those who inquire without prior understanding are indeed the teachers of the Raghus. One who is overwhelmed by the dense wandering practiced through hundreds of previous births—
Listen, O Jīva, how one is liberated from the cage of *māyā*:

Consciousness (*saṃvit*), when conditioned by the notion of "I" (*ahaṃbhāvanā*) and endowed with such designations as "Jīva," is here called the "I-notion" (*ahambhāva*), which is indeed false; it is consciousness alone that is declared to be real.

That which is false flashes for only a short time due to delusion, not for long—like mother-of-pearl mistaken for silver, a mirage, or a double moon. That which is false goes to its destruction; that which is real does not perish.
This is well known in the world even to children, like the necessity of food and so forth:
"The existence of the non-existent is not found, just as there is no oiliness in sand;
nor is the non-existence of the existent observed, even as much as a tiny speck from the powder of a frog."
Just as the dust of a frog becomes a frog during the rainy season and remains unperceived, so wherever the living being (jīva) is situated, it arises and does not perish.
Erase this [notion] by means of the intellect alone; it is merely a product of mental construction (bhāvanā).
Just as copper attains the state of gold through time, so too, O dear one, the individual soul (jīva),
freed from its attachment to the state of the world, attains the nature of the Supreme Self;
it is like copper that has been released from its blackness and attained the state of gold.
For all living beings, the mental construction of "I" and "mine" is the bond of worldly existence;
like a snare for birds, it acts as their sole support.
Apart from the reality of the Self, there is no such thing as "I" or "mine. (MU 6.131.11)
When certainty through reasoning has taken root, the mental construction (*bhāvanā*) surely dissolves:

"The body is a corpse—a flood of flesh and bones; the world is a void, a void, a mass of mountains; intellect and the rest are mere fragments of conceptualization; who am I? What is mine? And how? (MU 6.131.12–13)

O Lord of the People, when the dissolution of contemplation occurs, the limit of this consciousness— which is indeed infinite and pure, yet seemingly possessed of an unperceived mind— is brought to rest;
for right vision alone is the remedy for this contemplation.

Know that destruction is like the day [following] the night for one of infinite luster. When the latent impressions have been stilled, the individual soul attains oneness with the mass of consciousness,
just as clarified butter is merged in clarified butter, water in water, or milk in milk.

The individual soul (jīva), both non-identical with and identical to that [Lord], shines forth within the Lord, just as light exists within a flame or as a trace of fragrance exists in the earth. By whatever [nature] the soul contemplates oneness, that it becomes in an instant.
Whatever the mind of a living being is, that he becomes; who does not experience this? Through the contemplation of Brahman, the individual soul attains eternal Brahman-hood;
by whatever one contemplates as immortal, one becomes immortal oneself.
Through the contemplation of what is not Brahman, the living soul falls into wretchedness and perishes;
O dear one, by the very contemplation of poison, a human being becomes poisonous.
For the stainless consciousness of the Self, the impurity consists in the conceptualization of an object of cognition.
"Having wiped yourself clean, arise as the self of pure consciousness and act, O sinless one.
Rāma said:
"The multitude of beings, from the gods down to the insects and lice born of sweat,"
"Is all action indeed arisen from speech, or is it something else? Tell me this, Vasiṣṭha. Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O Rāghava, regarding these fourteen kinds of living beings..."
Some [of what] has arisen is with cause, due to one's own past karmas;
some has arisen without cause, like the luster of a fine gem.
Now, karma will arise from its own nature, and that which is taken as a cause [will likewise arise].
Rāma:
O sun to the darkness of the heart, O lord of the wind for the ocean of doubt—
for all beings born in the worlds, and those yet to be born!
"What has come about, how, and for what cause; and what has not come about, how, and for what lack of cause?
What has been born, what is being born, or how indeed will it be born?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
Unconditioned by space, time, and the like, it abides both in the void and in the non-void;
it is attainable through the experience of the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoman*), just as fragrance is in the wind.
Like the sun pervading the clouds in the sky, or like a sprout within a banyan seed.
Like motion in the wind, consciousness is imperceptible both in the void and in that which is not void.
In some respects, it is eternal, immovable, tranquil, and abides in a state of perfect equanimity;
like the farthest reaches of the cosmic egg or the sky, it is infinite and changeless.
In some places, due to a vibration arising from its own nature, it flashes forth with radiance like fire,
