having attained the state of the world through the form of the elements and subtle elements;
in other places, through the coloring of the elements and subtle elements already endowed with prior vibration.
It assumes the state of being a real entity, like the condition of one with golden armlets;
just as a Brahmin, by neglecting his own true nature through evil desire, gradually accepts the status of a Śūdra, so too does the Lord of Consciousness assume the state of dullness.
Thus, at every dissolution, beings indeed manifest in two ways:
those born from the vibration of the immediate consciousness (*adyacitspandajātāni*) and those born from the vibration of the long-enduring consciousness (*ciracitspandajāni*).
Among these, those born from the vibration arising from the nature of consciousness itself are indeed the individual living souls (*jīvakāḥ*).
These inclinations have arisen without an external cause, like the radiance of a genuine gem.
Now, they must attain causality through their own actions—
actions that pertain to bondage and liberation, to destruction and birth.
For those who, having come from the Lord, have already experienced other births,
their past karma is indeed the cause for being born in this life;
likewise, those living beings who have just now emerged from the state of Brahman.
For they, though not born from a cause, are the cause for future birth.
Such is this relationship of cause and effect between the individual soul (*jīva*) and karma:
the meritorious and fortunate soul is known to be uncaused, while [karma] is born from a cause.
Some are born meritorious, and some are fortunate living beings;
the meritorious attain fortune, but the fortunate do not attain merit.
Some fortunate ones, without even having attained merit, become liberated.
Some are liberated due to their merit, while others are not liberated even because of their merit;
such as plants, grasses, creepers, shrubs, insects, birds, and the like,
as well as gods, asuras, humans, serpent-kings, piśācas, venomous snakes, and so forth.
Some are fortunate, some are meritorious, and some will attain merit;
through merit some are liberated, and through fortune others are likewise liberated from that [bondage].
Just as the testing of a jewel or the movement of the wind, so it is with these states.
Just as heat belongs to fire and so forth, so does the world belong to pure consciousness.
Just as the [false] perception of a manhood in a tree stump arises from incorrect vision and ceases through correct observation,
so too does duality in the Self cease.
O descendant of Raghu, because pure consciousness— which is utterly pure, whose nature arises free from conceptual construction, infinite, and all-pervading— is itself space,
some [being] is born from space alone, and some dissolves into space alone.
The living soul, whose nature is mere volition, is like an old cloud in spring.
Having clearly perceived the Self, he who dissolves into the void itself is not seen again, just as snow melted by heat [is no longer visible].
But he who, not seeing his own Self,

vibrates intensely through actions consisting of mental constructs and fluctuations— he, though dissolved, is born again; he, being insentient by nature, attains grossness through the movements of volition.
Like a rain-cloud in the monsoon, this [consciousness] arises again and again even when it has been repeatedly diminished.
O scion of Raghu, for the sake of the great accomplishment, cast away even that mental resolve which is endowed with a portion of the nature of the Self, as if it were food smeared with poison.
Be for the sake of your well-being that which is free from conceptual construction, without beginning or end, indifferent, established, the single self of all, arisen as the space of consciousness;
for all living beings reach the supreme state without cause.
Thereafter, they become the causes for the states of bondage and liberation in this world.
For the state of conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*) is the cause of bondage; therefore, abandon it. Liberation, however, is the absence of conceptualization; practice that with your intellect.
But because it is without cause, being the cause of all causes,
the individual soul (jīva) becomes one with Śiva from the Unmanifest (avyakta) in the mere twinkling of an eye;
in that very twinkling, he himself attains the state of being the cause.
In this cycle of existence, amidst its various states which are like the shifting water upon waves,
you must remain vigilant at the meeting of the grasped and the grasper,
gradually abandoning the states of conceptual construction.
Do not become the nature of the object of perception, and do not become the nature of the perceiver.
Having abandoned all mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), become absorbed in that which remains.
For one who is constantly attentive to the relationship between the perceived and the perceiver...
Whether not acting or even while acting, one pursues liberation alone.
For the ignorant one, O Rāma, whose self consists of the forms of the grasped and the grasper, enters into ever-new bondage moment by moment through the power of mental cultivation (bhāvanā).
In the relationship between the grasped and the grasper, through one's own cultivation of attachment (*rasabhāvanā*),
the bondage of the living being increases in intensity with every moment.
Even in the absence of the cultivation of attachment, [bondage persists] within the relationship between the grasped and the grasper.
At every moment, this living being attains the state of selfhood and becomes a partaker of liberation. O sinless one, whatever object the group of senses falls upon incessantly,
there it is bound by attachment and there it is liberated by non-attachment.
If even a little of this world pleases you, then you are bound to the state of existence;
if nothing at all pleases you, then you are liberated from the state of existence.
[This is so] regarding this entire collection of objects, including both the stationary and the moving.
Let nothing from a blade of grass up to the gods be pleasing to you.
For men, attachment always leads to misfortune, while detachment leads to the highest good;
because it is finite, attachment joins a person with endless sufferings.
When you eat, when you act, or when you abandon [them], you are merely indifferent;
you are neither the doer nor the enjoyer. Therein, one whose mind is liberated is at peace. Nothing whatsoever is born here, and nothing whatsoever perishes here.
Everything is peaceful, without support, the pure and all-pervading expanse of consciousness.
The wise do not grieve for the past, nor do they worry about the future;
O sinless one, they always accept the present as it arrives in its due course.
The flowers of living beings, born upon the tree of Brahman, quiver;
they are as if produced from it and identical with it, like foam upon the great ocean.
Through mutual reflection, they are like waves of the ocean of consciousness.
Even though they are of a single nature, living beings attain duality for the sake of the world's maintenance.
Through firm contemplation, the living being attains the state of the mind,
just as clear water turns to stone due to extreme cold.
The snares of craving, delusion, pride, and the like are knotted within the mind,
just as birds are caught in a net or young calves in a tethering rope.
O Rāma, the wise person must cut through the mind with the mind itself.
Just as iron is forcibly heated by means of steel that has been sharpened by isolation,

so too does the diversity of the Self appear— though it is not other than the Self, nor produced by modification or the like, but born of its own inherent nature— just as the variegated patterns on a peacock’s tail-feather appear.
It is nothing at all, yet it is something; though its form is real, its essence is non-existent.
It is more imperceptible than space, and though it takes the form of the world, it is formless.
Though it has support, it is without support; it is changeless amidst the changing.
Even when there is appearance, that which is without appearance perishes; yet it does not perish with respect to the object.
O descendant of Raghu, remain firm in that reality where the grasped, the grasper, and the act of grasping have attained their true being.
Cut the mind with the mind itself for the sake of stilling the delusion of saṃsāra;
those skilled in cleansing wash away impurity by means of impurity itself. For one who has attained the state of no-mind, there shall be no further existence for you.
Know that existence is indeed mental construction; it does not cease merely because of the dissolution of dreams.
Having realized that everything is pure consciousness, the Self alone, and that no other conceptualization exists—whether the mind be present or absent—you are not born again.
That conviction that "everything is consciousness alone, the Self itself, and nothing else exists"—

know that to be the supreme reality, the state beyond the mind (*unmanastva*), which is unborn. Even while the mind exists, it becomes a state of non-mind through the singular contemplation of the nature of the Self.
That state of mindlessness bestows liberation whether a mental form is present or absent. When all things are perceived as consciousness and the views of attachment and aversion have perished,
how can there be further rebirth once mindlessness has arisen, even though the mind still exists?
The individual soul (jīva) forms the resolve for happiness, and from that it goes to suffering;
for the soul strives for prosperity, yet it encounters supreme calamity.
Having ascended to the deliberation of the mind, one abandons the purposelessness of mental construction.
Whatever the deluded self does, by that very act it perishes of its own accord.
Having attained discernment, the mind thoroughly destroys its own volitions;
for a wicked person, having attained prosperity, first slays his own kin.
A wicked person, having first arisen, burns his own kin, just as a forest fire, with its harsh crackling sounds, consumes the bamboos. Through expansion,
the creations contained within consciousness become visible.
Just as there are various rows of colors on a kadarkaka gem,
so too Brahman— the single Self, shimmering with all powers—
is concealed yet appears manifest in manifoldness, like a kadarkaka gem during its travels.
The mind, when illumined by pure consciousness alone, brings about this existence of the world,
just as a doorkeeper, when looked upon by a king, arranges the assembly of vassal lords.
The activity of the mind when colored by consciousness is what is called "saṃsāra."
Just as leaves, flowers, and fruit arise from a seed drenched with sap,
so does the universe emerge through the flickering of the wheel of consciousness by means of various shimmering and transitory entities.
Now, having realized this truth here, either restrain that very flickering, or else lead it to density.
The one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Perceivable Healing," by Vasiṣṭha.
The individual soul (jīva) has three forms: the gross, the subtle, and the supreme.
Among these, worship that which is its supreme form; abandon the other two.
When these two forms of his are unreal, they arise like the appearance of two moons.
Through inquiry alone these two perish, but the supreme form does not perish.
O Rāghava, that form of the individual soul which is indeed indestructible—that is you; remain there with a footing as firm as a mountain, and rejoice.
Rāma said:
O Blessed One, please describe to me accurately those three forms of the living being; I wish to know its form exactly as it is.
Vasiṣṭha:
This body, composed of hands and feet, which moves about for the sake of enjoyment—
this gross form of the living being (jīva) exists here for the purpose of experience.

Know, O Rāma, that the mind— which takes the form of consciousness according to its own volitions and persists as long as saṃsāra exists— is the subtle body (*ativāhika*) of the individual soul (*jīva*).
It remains mounted upon the chariot of the vital breath (*prāṇavāta*), whether this physical body exists or has ceased to exist.
This world, which is the form of his mind, wanders unrestrained;
just as a fragrance mounted on the wind leaves the flower behind and exists in the sky,
so too does the mind, residing in the vital breath, remain when bodies have perished.
Just as there are various knots in a protective thread,
or as there are joints situated upon the segments of a bamboo cane, even so,
O sinless one, do bodies exist within this very long thread of the mind.
Arising again and again yet subject to destruction like the waves of a river;
know that which is without beginning or end, the truth, pure consciousness, and free from conceptual construction— that is the supreme form of the individual soul, its first and third state.
From that the world is born, and into that very same [reality] it dissolves;
having vibrated slightly, it takes on that form, like a mass of waves in the ocean.
This is because the arising, destruction, and persistence of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep [occur within it].
"This is the pure fourth state (*turyapada*); remain here with your footing firmly established.
Rāma said: "O Brahmin, what is this perception of the connection between the grasped and the grasper that occurs without sleep?"
I know for certain, without a doubt, that she remains restless while awake;
and I understand that which manifests during the delusion of sleep— just as it does while waking— in the form of the consciousness of the grasped and the grasper, is what is called "dream."
O Lord of Sages, I indeed know that the state of deep sleep is that condition of delusion which, like a stone, renders one unconscious of the states of waking and dreaming;
it remains present throughout all three— waking, dreaming, and deep sleep— yet is unperceived.
"O best of Brahmins, what is that which is called the Fourth (turya) and that which transcends the Fourth?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Having abandoned both the sense of 'I' and the sense of 'not-I', as well as existence and non-existence..."
That which is unattached, equal, pure, and established is called the Fourth (turya).
That state of equanimity which is self-abiding, peaceful, and the condition of one liberated while living—
the state of being a witness during worldly activity— is designated as the reckoning of the Fourth.
But one who moves among sense objects with the senses free from passion and hatred, self-controlled and with a disciplined mind, attains the state of the Fourth (turya).
Internal equanimity, clarity, oneness, and freedom from conceptual construction [are its characteristics].
He by whom emptiness (*śūnyatā*) has been cultivated has reached the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*).
Even all the great ones— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the rest—
as well as certain men who are living, are liberated and established in the fourth state.
This is neither waking nor dreaming, because of the impossibility of volitional constructions (saṅkalpa);
nor is it the state of deep sleep, because of the absence of both insentience and its opposite.
Like the delusion of a snake in a rope, the mind does not stir here.
The commonality of existence (*sattāsāmānya*) is the single essence; here, being (*sattva*) is situated equally [in all].

O Rāma, the state of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), which is pure bliss delighting in the Self and in which all desires have been completely stilled, is designated by the term "the Fourth" (*turya*).
Just as this appearance of the world in a dream is but the manifestation of consciousness,
so too, through awakening, one becomes peaceful, unobstructed, and liberated from hatred and fear;
for the perceived and the perceiver are utterly non-existent, and the realization of Brahman as the Self has arisen.
Likewise, that which is free from passion and the like is called the Fourth (turya).
For those who are perfectly awakened, this world remains as it truly is—tranquil;
for the unawakened, they say the Fourth is dissolved, yet it remains steadfast.

That which lies beyond the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukta), which is not within the range of words, is called the peaceful liberation of the disembodied (videhamukti), which transcends the fourth state (turyātīta).
In the state of liberation while living, which is the fourth state, for some time by chance—
Abiding in the state of disembodied liberation (*videhamuktatva*), go to the plane beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*).
Having established your footing in the fourth (*turya*) and attained supreme equanimity,
be neither a non-doer nor a doer with respect to natural action.
Upon the abandonment of even a fraction of egoism, let peace alone be experienced;
when the fragile mind is wounded, the fourth state (turya) manifests.
That worldly activity here in this cycle of existence is the delusion of dreaming while awake; that which is dense ignorance is indeed [the cause].

Enveloped by delusion, that is the state of deep sleep; the state of liberation while living, due to the absence of latent impressions, is the fourth (turya); and that which is beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is here, O Noble One, the bodiless liberation (videhamokṣa), which cannot be described by speech.
The one hundred and thirty-third canto, titled "An Inquiry into the Fourth State," by Vasiṣṭha.
The reality of the mind (cittattva) is imperishable, devoid of agent, object, and instrument;
that which is called waking, dreaming, and deep sleep is but an unreal delusion imagined by it.
In this regard, hear now this account being told by me.
"O subduer of enemies, just as even one who is awake attains awakening like a wise man,
a hunter once questioned a certain sage who was standing in a forest observing the silence of wood, having seen a deer running away."
Later, having approached and pursued a deer pierced by an arrow, he asked that sage, "Where has the deer gone? The sage replied to him:
"O virtuous one, we are sages dwelling in the forest, whose nature is tranquility."
"We have no ego-sense that is capable of persisting in worldly affairs;
for, my friend, the mind performs all the functions of the senses.
That [mind] of mine, which consists of the ego, has surely long since dissolved away."
Just as the light of the moon, the sun, and fire,
while remaining indifferent, cause a craftsman to engage in a sequence of actions,
so too does the ego, known by the name "mind," [employ] the group of senses in men.
Established like a witness, he directs them toward their respective duties.
When he himself has become completely tranquil, like a cloud in autumn, who remains among the objects of the senses? Who is as if dead, and who is as if dancing?
"O leader of the forest, our minds have attained peace;
we stand here with deadened hearts, like wooden puppets. We possess neither ego nor passion, like trees that have withered away. (MU 6.133.10)
For egoism (ahaṅkāra) is indeed the root cause of all actions. Just as pearls settle upon a thread, or as subjects gather around a king, the sense organs enter into a state of union with the ego.
When the great cord of egoism is severed, the young children that are the senses wander here and there in all directions like subjects without a king;
O hunter, the minds devoid of egoism are fragile and prone to dissolution.
My senses do not cling to their objects, like a lotus in water;
my infant senses do not come into mutual contact,
like drops of cool frost without the lac of egoism.
No one perceives my faculty of cognition or the sequence of my faculties of action;
seeing and the other senses remain as if fixed in a painting, each within its own object.
O virtuous one, you have not seen the deer by means of that which the sense-organ reports.
Or rather, that which one knows how to describe when seeing it—that we do not possess.
Indeed, for me, whose ego has dissolved, none of these [sensations] exist.
Therefore, O hunter, who can tell you of my perception of the deer in its state of suffering?
For the mind is indeed the guardian of all the senses, just as a herdsman is for cattle;
and that mind of ours has dissolved into the state that is devoid of all objects.
How then can these [senses], whose forms are scattered here and there, [function]?
Or rather, O dear one, let them say of you that you have gone right here to the five elements;
for just as a herd of children is without a maker or a father and is fragile,
so too is this collection of senses, lacking stability and devoid of the latent impression of the sense of "I."
"I do not perceive any states known as waking, dreaming, or deep sleep;
I abide solely in the fourth state (turya), wherein no object of perception exists. Thus, by speaking the truth, he attained the state of being indefinable.
The hunter was led by the sage and departed for his desired destination.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, I say that there is no state other than the fourth (turya);
for the non-conceptual consciousness is the fourth, and that alone exists here, and nothing else.
O sinless one, when the living self has seen the truth and attained the state of Brahman, the senses become useless within the body, like figures on a painted wall; for there,
in the connection with the desired and the undesired, there is no arising of pleasure or pain.
That mind would not exist, O Rāma; they know that being to be the Fourth State (turya).
During the time of dreaming, the dream itself is indeed waking, because it is not grasped by the distracted [waking] state;
and the waking state attains the condition of a dream through that very quality of being remembered.
In the waking state, the dream is unreal; in the dream, the waking state is composed of unreality.
The stage of deep sleep, characterized by dense delusion, is the end of the transformations of waking and dreaming.
O dear one, this triad known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep arises from error.
Like a leather thong placed [upon a drum], the Fourth State (turya)— which is unconditioned and consists of pure consciousness alone— remains vibrating within the intellect (vijñāna). Within that,
this [phenomenal world] flashes forth through delusion, like the state of being a wave in water.
Through the knowledge of reality as it truly is, these three dissolve;
only the pure state of liberation while living (jīvanmukta), which is the fourth (turya), remains.
This state beyond the fourth is declared by the wise to be "liberation after death" (videhamukti).
It is beyond the scope of such statements as "Consciousness is Brahman" and so forth.
For the threefold form of the mind—known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—is indeed composed of the three natures:
the peaceful, the terrible, and the deluded; thus the mind exists here in this triadic state.
The mind that is fierce consists of the waking state; when it is peaceful, it abides in the dream state;
when it is deluded, it is situated in the state of deep sleep; and when it is devoid of these three, it becomes dead. Where the mind is dead, there the single *sattva* remains equanimous.

Know that to be the state of liberation while living (jīvanmuktatva), that to be the Fourth (turya), that the Great State (mahat-pada). In that Fourth State, which consists of pure being (sattva), these sages and perfected ones— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others— are established as those liberated while living.
That sage whom the hunter questioned for the sake of the deer was established in the fourth state, whose nature is the arising of pure being;
he did not perceive any movement of the mind, for his mind was as if dead.
Having reached the state of non-dual unity, in which all particular aspects are stilled,
abide as a self free from affliction in the fourth state (*turya*), which is liberated from the play of all mental constructs;
there abide the great sages, truly liberated while still embodied, whose sense of duality has been completely pacified.
The one hundred and thirty-fourth canto, titled "The Parable of the Deer-Hunter," by Vasiṣṭha:

This indeed, my dear, is the established conclusion: that even time, space, and so forth, as well as the world and everything else, do not exist apart from a portion of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
By its own spontaneous vibration, it produces a clear yet fragile appearance.
The world-form, like lightning in the night, is consciousness, as are time and space.
Wherever the lightning of consciousness flashes, that is the world and time-space;
that which remains without flashing is the tranquil, all-encompassing, and timeless state.
Rāma:
As long as the ocean is observed, so long does the lightning truly appear in the sky.
I do not ask for the cause of this; tell me rather the cause of the vibration of consciousness.
Vasiṣṭha:
Setting aside from afar the mere frolic of the caviller, the ignorant, and the wicked-minded, listen; such a thing is to be said only to one like this, not to a denier.
"The lightning remains indeed within the dense cloud, and it flashes there, flickering;
this is established even among children—by whom could it possibly be denied?
Rāma said:
O Lord, since it does not depend on a cause, would the vibration of consciousness not be either eternal or non-existent? For in this world, every vibration is indeed caused. Vasiṣṭha said:
In this world, what can be the cause for the vibration of a windless ocean, a lamp, or the like, or of jewels,
or even of the wind abiding in the void? In the same way, even though Rāma is not the universal self, his being such or not such is logically established.
Since it is by its own nature the eternal self of all, why then is anything not possible?
Consciousness is both motionless and moving; there is a distinction in words, but not in reality.
Know that Brahman is a single, undivided mass, non-dual, just as water is essentially fluid.
Just as the sight of a pearl necklace or a swan in the sky arises from its own nature,
so too does the delusion of the world arise from the vibration of consciousness, which is the reflection of the Intellect within the vision itself.
Just as when the eyes are closed, the vision moves by its own power...
This consciousness perceives the form of the stars, and likewise the object of thought appears like a visible thing.
Having abandoned all mental constructions and conceptualizations, it has attained its true nature as the Self;
behold, it remains as a pure mass of consciousness, like the single ocean at the end of an aeon.
O virtuous one, people such as ourselves are not those who have seen the further shore of the world’s existence;

therefore, our word should be accepted with the thought "Om," free from doubt. Abandoning the notion that "I shall say something because of my cleverness in raising objections," [you should accept this].
If you abide by my word, then you shall surely go to that state.
Otherwise, having attained the status of a pure logician through the stains of various manifold conceptual constructions, you will become like a blade of grass or a shrub.
Rāma:

If this is so, then, O Brahmin, I consider that this world—consisting of you, me, and him—is in reality nothing other than what is called the three worlds; there is truly no such thing as conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
I consider this world to be mere illusion, appearing like the accounts of Lavaṇa, Indu, Śukra, and others; there is nothing here that is real.
This being the case, O best of sages, there is indeed a total negation of everything.
Tell me, how can such a thing be appropriate? Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O Rāma, you are perfectly awakened; you already know things as they truly are."
There exists only the pure mass of consciousness, and you have realized that very thing.
The final conclusion of the spiritual sciences (*adhyātma-śāstra*) is indeed the negation of everything:
here there is no ignorance, no *māyā*; this is the peaceful Brahman, beyond succession.
Having determined that within the luminous consciousness— which is indeed tranquil, pure, equal to the self,

and the manifestation of all powers— there is that which is designated by the name "Brahman," some [conclude] its state as emptiness (*śūnyatva*), while others [conclude] it as mere consciousness (*vijñānamātratā*).
Some dispute among themselves regarding the nature of the Lord;
having conceptualized the world as expanded and brought it to a state of manifold branches,
some, through their own reasoning, move toward the Sāṅkhya doctrine and others.
Some, possessing firm certainty that "all this is the peaceful Brahman," having attained the state of the pure consciousness-ether, remain as if non-existent though they are existent.
Others, having determined that "there is neither Brahman, nor the world, nor anything else," [remain thus].
The followers of the Sugata and others remain as clear and pure as space;
yet some, having formed various conceptual constructions otherwise,
remain, become tranquil, are born, transmigrate, or perhaps do not.
Having determined that the mass of consciousness (cidghana) is devoid of all parts (kalā),
yet permeated by its entirety of powers (samagra-śakti), disputants indeed contend;
having conceptualized through synthesis (saṅkalpanā) a single reality that is free from all parts, they employ their own various designations.
Proclaiming their own manifestations of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), physicians dispute one another through the power of their learned controversies.
The one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Non-existence of Ignorance" (*avidyānāstitvanirūpaṇa*).
Rāma:
What is said to be the essence of the body, the senses, the intellect, and so forth, as well as of the movement of the mind;
and from what [source] does it arise? May that which is all-pervasive lead to my welfare.
Vasiṣṭha:
Whatever is seen here, this world consisting of "you," "I," and so forth—
all that is indeed mind alone, just as the ocean is nothing but water.
The mind exists as the world in the form of the body, senses, and so forth;
through six or five doors, the object of cognition falls upon embodied beings.
Since the mind arises from some source or other, it is like the manifestation of two moons.
Just as that which has been described to you many times as manifold and diverse—
this mind, enveloped by the designations of "living beings" and so forth, and maintaining the delusion of saṃsāra—
hear now how it may be extinguished for the sake of the highest good.
The mind, rich with transformations of its own nature, perceives this little body as something non-existent yet swollen, just as a deer sees the water of a mirage;
in that same way, the mind indeed perceives the body as flickering and restless.
The form of curd is indeed non-different from milk because it is its own self;
just as milk itself experiences the entirety of its arising, persistence, and destruction, so too does the mind perceive the body as being the very nature of curd.

For instance, O mighty-armed one, you have heard the account of Bhārgava, who was deluded by the son of Indu (Lavaṇa), when he was engaged in defining the form of the mind. Even the dull-witted mind attains intuition once it is freed from all consciousness.
Just as iron moves when brought near a magnet without any desire of its own, so too,
through the anointing by the rays of the sun of consciousness— which is eternally risen, stainless, and infinite—
the lotus of the mind blossoms, along with the rows of petals of the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*).
Just as a string of pearls, consisting of both existence and non-existence, is seen in the empty sky,
so indeed does the flickering mind flash forth within the nature of consciousness (*cittattva*).
Just as the arising of various forms in the void is a mere delusion, a mental affliction.
Likewise, this body exists in the mind like a city of Gandharvas;
just as this body is false in the mind, appearing like the illusory doubling of a moon,
so too are the senses within the body— do not be intent on such things.

Just as the senses are to the body like a yakṣa imagined by a child, so too the movement of the senses is inert; do not go beyond this. Just as the movement of the senses is of an inert nature, like that of the winds.
In the same way, this flickering mind, though non-existent as a perceiver of vibration, throbs;
for just as the mind is inert and unstable, having the form of an illusion regarding vibration,
so too does the intellect manifest as a mirage for this mind.
Just as the intellect (*buddhi*) belongs to the inner self (*svānta*), so too does the ego-sense (*ahaṅkṛti*) belong to the intellect;
it is unreal in nature, arisen in vain—do not be devoted to such things alone.
Just as the ego-sense stands to the intellect like a flower to a creeper.
In the same way, let the individual soul (jīva) not be solely intent upon the ego-sense (ahaṅkṛti).
Just as the soul here consists of latent impressions (vāsanā) within emptiness through the ego-sense,
so too consciousness (cit), endowed with the power of manifestation (sacamatkṛti), is joined with a portion of the soul.

O sinless one, even that [object] does not exist as a real thing by virtue of its own nature, but only through the power of mental construction (*saṅkalpa*). Do not contemplate this as being anything at all; nor do you [arise] from it, nor does it from you.
All these have mutually become causes for one another through delusion.
The mind, intellect, senses, and so forth, revolve like waves.
Just as in a vast empty forest, madmen wander about, agitated by the delusions of their own volitions, so too do the mind, intellect, senses, and so forth.
In the cycle of transmigration, the body is the essence; within the body, the flood of the senses is the essence.
Within the collection of senses, movement is the essence; in movement, the mind is held to be the essence.
In the mind, the intellect is indeed the essence; in the intellect, the ego-sense is the essence.

The essence within the ego is the individual soul (jīva); the essence within the soul is consciousness (cit) that is slightly turbid. But the essence within consciousness is the state of being beyond the object of thought, because of the impossibility of an object of thought existing in Śiva. Therefore, there exists no other essence more essential than this.
The non-conceptual manifestation of consciousness alone is the cause everywhere;
there is no other cause for it, as it is by its own nature eternally luminous.
Abandoning the former [state], remain forever intent upon that alone.

Indeed, the entire universe, whether with parts or without parts, is nothing but pure consciousness alone. Whether it is enveloped by all mental constructs or whether it is free from them, know, O Rāma, that this whole world is composed of pure consciousness.
Therefore, O dear one, if your consciousness does not waver day and night from this supreme essence, then you are unborn and auspicious.
For one established here, certain wicked distractions find no footing at night, O Rāma, like [the tracks] of a snake.
"Do not abandon her, who is like a great cave of nectar; remain right here, as firmly inscribed upon a stone.
The one hundred and thirty-sixth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Non-existence of the Living Being and Other Entities."
Vasiṣṭha said:
By the desireless, perfectly tranquil consciousness-sun,
the object of thought is perceived within itself during the processes of creation and so forth, like a string of pearls seen in the sky.
Immediately thereafter, that very same [consciousness] unfolds with a hundred branches,
assuming the state of being the cause of delusion and appearing as the web of the world through its own radiance.
Just as no other cause for this is logically possible apart from its own nature.
In the world of the pearl-string of the vision of emptiness, consciousness (*citi*) is likewise the non-perception of an object of consciousness (*cetya*).
There is no difference between consciousness and the object of consciousness, for that which is consciousness is indeed the object of consciousness.
That which is the vision is itself the pearl-string; the seed is known as the sprout.

Know that the seed itself is the fruit when all its particular attributes have been abandoned; because of the conceptualization of these attributes, there is no reality in this mental construction (*saṅkalpa*).
If reality were found in the mental construction, then that which is born from it would either be that [reality] itself or [unreal].
And that volition (saṅkalpa) has arisen from this very first Śiva.
Therefore, that which is the supreme state— the imperishable pure consciousness (cinmātra)—
is itself consciousness with conceptualization (savikalpā cit), and it is also that primordial object of cognition (cetya).
That alone is the calculation of the individual soul (jīva); that alone is the throbbing ego-sense (ahaṅkṛti).

That alone is the intellect (buddhi), that is the mind (citta), and that is the vibration of the senses. That is the body, that is the entire world, that is the directions, and that is heaven and earth.
Therefore, from the mountains, oceans, directions, and so forth, down to the grass, or the lotus-born [Brahmā] and others—
[it is all insentient]: the body is insentient, the collection of senses is insentient, the mind is insentient, the intellect is insentient,
the faculty of egoism is indeed insentient, and likewise, vibration is insentient.
He who is the experiencer of these is you; you are all-pervading.
And that is partless pure consciousness alone—do not deviate from this, your own state.
Thus, this is one and the same, devoid of beginning and end, and all-pervasive.
In this way, speech shines forth by its own nature; there is no other conceptual construction.
All is peaceful; this world shines as mere manifestation (jñaptimātra).
Neither "you-ness" nor "I-ness," nor the birth and death of the world, exist.
Abandon delusion; be equanimous, changeless, eternally awakened, without support, and free from the state of existence.
All is peaceful, immutable, and without beginning or middle—this alone is the truth. Let there be enough for you with this; let there be nothing else.
This is the chapter titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Realizing Truth."
The one hundred and thirty-seventh canto.
Vālmīki:
Having thus heard the words of Vasiṣṭha, his heart blossomed with understanding.
Sighing as it were with his heart, Rāma spoke these words:
"Alas! This burden has long been cast off from my mind by me, yet here I am still bearing it."
"This is that I am," "this is mine today," and so forth— like a snake shedding its skin, when this internal state of the mind (*antaḥkaraṇa*) attains transparency,
it shines like the autumnal sky, free from the turbulence of clouds.
Who would not be exhausted by bearing this burden, this immense burden, thinking, "This is I," or "This is mine today"—a burden even heavier than Mount Meru?
I am at peace; I am fully extinguished; I am awake and possessed of confidence.
"Like a great boulder placed upon the shoulder of a traveler,
I have been deceived for all this time— alas!—
since I did not attain this peaceful, cool, and serene path."
Therefore, O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, you ought to sever for me this one remaining doubt; for the noble do not tremble.
If indeed all this is eternally composed of the Supreme Self, then why is there such agitation?
"Why was this sequence established—'this is to be done' and 'this is not'?
Vasiṣṭha replied: Just as living beings have arisen, or rather, have not arisen, from the supreme cause..."
Whether they possess duality or are non-dual, you have already understood that.
Among them, those for whom duality remains firmly established by their own volition must,
without doubt, continue to wander through the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) for some time.
In this regard, some, even while still children, through the application of their own creative wonder,
know the Supreme Self and remain free from the fever of worldly distress.
Those living beings who have attained a physical body— both those who lack a Lord and those who acknowledge a Lord— [are included therein].

Having grasped the expansion of duality, they reach that state in the course of time. There is indeed an ultimate repose; it belongs to no one and yet belongs to everyone. After a very long time some realize it, while another knows it in a short time.
O Raghava, some attain the state of having known what is to be known in their youth; yet other people here come to know the supreme reality only when they are old.
Thus, both those who know that and those who do not remain exactly as they are.

In this worldly conduct, there are both men who are liberated while living and those who are bound. If their worldly existence proceeds with the thought, "This is to be done" and "This is not to be done," then that [existence] will not be brought to an end; rather, the "law of the fish" (the strong preying on the weak) prevails.
As long as anything whatsoever throbs with the impulse of creation, so long has this established order been ordained: "Let there be no suffering through the law of the fishes.
[It is] free from merit and sin, devoid of mind, without the sense of "mine," and without the activity of thought.
The one liberated while living remains merely to pass the time;
however, he whose mind is seized by illusion, under the influence of self-identification with latent impressions,
attains fruits both here and in the hereafter, and strives for that purpose.

To such an extent, from the child to the scholar, and including gods and humans, that mind is non-deceptive; for the self consists of that very mind. To that which has its sole seed in one's own volition and bears the branches of hell and heaven—
O Raghava, for one who desires the fruits [of action], there is both agency and non-agency;
however, as for that agency or non-agency which belongs to the knower of reality,
it never at any time enters the state of being an object of cognition for anyone.
Whether he be an agent or a non-agent, O dear one, the knower of reality is indeed liberated;
he does not sink again into ignorance, like a bubble of water upon the surface of the water.
Whether he be an agent or a non-agent, one who knows things as they are not is indeed bound.
Like a dog from a forest well, one never emerges from this delusion.
Free from the body, free from the mind, silent, peaceful, established in self, and desireless—even while performing actions, remain; arise and stand firm in that state.
In the ocean of Brahman, the individual soul (jīva) is a wave; in the ocean of the individual soul, the ego (ahaṅkṛti);
in the ocean of the ego, the intellect (buddhi); and in the ocean of the intellect, the turbid mind (citta).
In the ocean of the mind, latent impressions (vāsanā) are a wave; and in the ocean of latent impressions, transmigratory existence (saṃsṛti).
In the ocean of saṃsāra, the body is unstable; in the ocean of the body, life is unstable;
in the ocean of life, youth is unstable; in the ocean of youth, the collection of the senses is like a wave; and in the ocean of the senses, their flickering activity is like a surge.
Experience occurs in the ocean of vibration; then, within the ocean of one’s own experience, the surging of consciousness is like a wave—this is the perception of creation.
By means of this, sound, touch, form, and so forth are perceived.
O scion of the Raghus, because it is the essence of all things, this entire universe is that pure consciousness alone.
Unagitated, indefinable, and not intent upon the act of creation,
this ocean of consciousness is designated merely as "Brahman" by the wise.
Even though it is undisturbed, if that [consciousness] were to experience as if it were disturbed,
then, having ascended to the aspect of consciousness (cidaṃśa), Brahman remains as the creation (sarga).
For this great ocean of consciousness is indeed undisturbed and ineffable, being equanimous.
It cannot be described by anyone through any name or even through a fraction [of its nature]. And for him, O mighty-armed one, no agitation can ever arise,
because he has understood that the entire world exists as nothing other than the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
O sinless one, that which is the mere playfulness (*vilāsitā*) of that God within His own essential nature is designated by the words "disturbance" (*kṣobha*) and "consciousness" (*cit*).
In the great ocean of ultimate reality, consciousness (*cit*) takes the form of the subtle essence (*ala*) of the object of thought (*cetya*).
It throbs like a wave through vibration; from that, this world is born.
This ocean of pure consciousness is undisturbed, indefinable, and equanimous;
yet when agitated by the waves of the object of thought, it is designated as "consciousness" (cit) by the wise.
The object of thought is a wave in the ocean of consciousness, and it is not distinct from it;
for its sole essence consists of that alone, just as a wave is nothing but water.
Therefore, the elements that have arisen are merely that [consciousness] itself.
That very reality appears as if it were not that; it is both the whole and the partless.
This entire world is but the One, which is nothing and yet is everything. O mind, do not lead yourself into the delusion of manifoldness through diversity.
Just as there is no difference in a single body of water manifesting in the form of waves, so too there is no otherness in the manifestation of consciousness through the state of the elements.
Just as a seed itself is the stalk, the leaf, the flower, the fruit, and the sap; [so is consciousness].
Thus the Unborn One manifests the worlds as being devoid of transformation and the like;
the very existence of the seed, ending with its fruit, vibrates as if it were something else.
It is the existence of Brahman itself that expands, taking on the form of the world through non-dual unity.
Just as a seed remains until the end of its fruit through the single commonality of existence (*satta*),
so too does Brahman remain until the end of creation through the single commonality of existence.
This entire expanse is nothing but the single commonality of the existence of Brahman.

It has been declared that the world is truly one, like a tree or a forest. That which is transparent and conscious is the very vibration that constitutes this delusion of the world; and that which is non-vibration, my dear, is the supreme tranquility, Śiva.
Oh, the greatness of the pure shadow of consciousness, from whose mere vibration even the worlds arise, and from whose mere lack of vibration they dissolve! From its opening and closing,
the dissolution and emergence of all beings occur.

That which appears as various and manifold is this very Brahman, a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*). Just as the wind, though its nature is undivided, moves through its own inherent vibration, so too does this world proceed from that [Brahman]; therefore, the world resides within it and is indeed that itself.
Therefore, all is pure, without appearance, and a mass of consciousness within the imperishable;
even while the visible world appears, neither "thou-ness" nor "I-ness" exists for one who is free from the fear of worldly existence.
Here there is neither unity nor duality whatsoever; whether "thou-ness" or "I-ness," they exist or do not exist, yet are nothing at all.

And everything exists everywhere and at all times; even so, that which the Buddha has realized is present here as well. This is the one hundred and thirty-eighth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Oneness of Brahman."
Vasiṣṭha:
Having heard what I have said and having determined that it is indeed auspicious, and having taken all of this to heart, remain thus; listen, O Rāghava.
Having renounced everything, O sinless one, become one who observes the silence of wood;
free from latent impressions, free from mental construction, with the mind exhausted and the intellect stilled,
do not see even those coming before you, nor hear even the sounding drums.
Neither touching even the sky nor smelling even the breath and so forth;
though eating, yet not eating, with an interior as pure as space—
remain thus through consciousness alone, having attained the ultimate state of the inner self.
"Remain within yourself alone, with a tranquil mind, like one who is mute, blind, and deaf;
like a figure carved from wood or stone, or like one depicted upon a painted wall.
Thus, remaining by means of the organs of perception alone, be as steady as Mount Meru.
Seeking non-rebirth, you who possess a great resolve through meditative concentration,
perform your duty with the organs of action— which are as flickering as a machine,
resembling those half-asleep and half-awake, and restless in the habituation to their own tasks.
Like children or madmen pursuing fruitless desires,
they are devoid of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), free from mental constructs (*amananaiḥ*), and as unstable as the leaves of a tree.
Always inward-turned, delighting in one's own self, and possessed of a fully perfected intellect— *MU* 6.138.8.
Remaining in deep sleep even while awake, perform actions without slumbering;
just as a silent mechanical man acts, so should you perform your activity.
Let the limbs move and throb according to the nature of the wind—what concern is that for you?
Internally renouncing everything, even while acting externally with steadiness, you are neither the agent nor the enjoyer; you are neither this [body] nor anything else.
For one whose state is not characterized by egoism, whose mind is not defiled—

Whether slaying or causing to slay the world, he neither kills nor causes to kill. Those who are supreme say that he whose undertakings are all devoid of desire and purposeful intention, and whose actions have been burnt by the fire of knowledge, is liberated.
Thus, O Great-Souled One, when one is composed in this way, no further thought arises;
by relying upon this infinite Great Samādhi, remain and you shall attain immortality.
The Chapter Named the Great Samādhi.
The one hundred and thirty-ninth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"In that state, indeed, certain notions of oneness, duality, or plurality do not arise."
In that regard, O Rāghava, there occurs a collapse of exclusive concentration (*ekāntasamādhāna*).
But where there exists only the single universal of being (*sattāsāmānyamātra*), what could be concentrated upon, by whom, and with what? There, nothing perishes.
Abandoning the delusion regarding words and their meanings— such as "I am collecting" or "I am not collecting"—

remain silent like a piece of wood, being of the nature of consciousness itself while appearing as if non-conscious. Your state should be like that of the wind when unblown, or of water, a mountain, or space.
May that state of yours be free from latent impressions (avāsanānta), whether you are acting or not acting, O Consciousness (cit).
When the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) has dissolved like a fragment of frost upon the heat of the sun,
and because of the non-accumulation of objects of thought (cetya), it has internally attained the supreme state.
Smaller than the smallest and larger than the largest,
peaceful, beyond perception, and non-dual— this is the pervasive reality.
This very [reality] has arisen individually as each distinct cluster of transmigrations.
The Knower, whose domain encompasses the worlds of the gods, the asuras, the netherworld, and the intermediate regions,
perceives all creations arising from every other volition as if they were unbroken;
he beholds them just as one who has tasted sugarcane perceives all the juices of sugarcane as being imbued with experience.

All the puruṣas of the creation of volition are real in relation to one another, because they are essentially inseparable from the space of consciousness (cidvyoman) and because they experience that very reality by themselves. All fluctuations of movement cease, just as [the waves] do due to the liquid nature of water.
All interruptions of consciousness arise from the Self, whose nature is consciousness;
just as two gems of similar luster attain unity through their identity of essence,
so too do the diverse creations of volition reach oneness by becoming objects of cognition.
Whatever is observed in water, all that is liquid;
whatever is touched in the state of peace, all that is likewise consciousness (*cit*).
They know the stirring of consciousness to be the mind (*citta*), while the absence of such stirring is liberation (*nirvāṇa*).
Therefore, an object is not to be touched by the mind of one who has not known the Self.
The existence of the mind is supreme suffering; the non-existence of the mind is supreme happiness.
Therefore, O Self, you must know the mind, for peace cannot be attained through its lack of perception.
Having seen what is pleasant or unpleasant, one should remain as steady as a stone;
by this much effort of the self, the cycle of existence is conquered through one's own human exertion, which consists in not becoming submerged in the objects of the world.
The ocean of existence cannot be crossed by mere fate, any more than one can cross the footprint of a cow.
When the demon of the mind has arisen through the desire of consciousness to attain an object,
who is able to count the empty delusions of saṃsāra?
Therefore, holding back as if you have found [the truth] that which was previously running away from you,
remain like wood or a clod of earth, performing your duty as it comes to you.
There is no pleasure to be experienced, nor pain, nor even anything intermediate.
By such effort, however, the infinite end of suffering is attained.
The living soul, licking as a reality that which is non-existent— like the water of a mirage—
encounters this terrifying cycle of transmigration when the yakṣa of the mind arises.
Perceiving both the external and internal through consciousness, firm as a rock with regard to mental states, you shall,
by means of the yoga of the stages (*bhūmikā-krama*), be liberated from the ocean of existence.
Like the full orb of the moon within, the knower of that reality attains a bliss consisting of the glorious elixir (*rasāyana*).

Having realized the essential nature of all things in the three worlds, he does not perform any action even while engaged in one; thus, having attained [the goal], he acts as if he were not acting. The description of Nirvana, the one hundred fortieth canto.
Rāma:
How is the practice of the seven stages of yoga performed?
And what are the signs for the yogin regarding each stage?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Since this affliction of ignorance has arisen from whatever source it may be—
whether it be true or untrue— listen now to my treatment for it.

If this [world] were that very same undestroyed [reality] from the infinite beyond, then it would not have been born, nor would there be ignorance; therefore, it must arise solely from consciousness. Disregarding this position, those who sport according to their own volitions—
Even though ignorance persists here, hear the sequence for its total destruction:

A creature, having been born for the first time, possesses a consciousness like that of deep sleep; with a nature characterized by the suffering of future mental impressions, it becomes a dull-witted being whose awareness is like that of a worm.
If, for one newly born, there were no arising of the manifestation of existence,
then that very immediate consciousness of pleasure and so forth would be the supreme state itself.
By this much alone, the state of deep sleep is distinguished from the supreme state.
That state which is free from the flood of future latent impressions (*vāsanā*), insentient yet possessing the nature of a stone,

equal to the fourth state (*turya*), established in its own self, having the nature of existence, and with its impressions stilled— therefore, the state of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) is not comparable to deep sleep.
O Rāghava, through the practice of the continuous realization of the Reality that stands at the beginning, the child gradually emerges from the state of deep sleep;
this occurs for a person whose intellect has arisen slightly and who understands the meaning of the local dialects.
The notion arises: "I take this," or "I discard this.
One whose intellect is limited to this much, who falls within the sphere of his own elders, is merely an object for his own ritual manuals and actions; he is not fit for the [higher] injunction.
Therefore, one must be either directed by family elders or possess personal certainty regarding words and their meanings;
for it is by means of that knowledge that a person who understands words and their meanings abandons what is to be abandoned, possessing the wisdom of one who knows that.
One who adopts what is to be adopted and does not look toward the middle [path]—
whether due to discrimination or fear of elders— is called a "man" in this world, provided he engages with the meaning of the scriptures preceded by inquiry. (MU 6.140.13–14)
The person is of two kinds: one who is engaged in worldly activity and one who has withdrawn from it.
Listen now to the characteristics of these two, who are oriented toward heaven and liberation respectively.
Is this so-called *nirvāṇa* truly better for us, or is cyclic existence itself preferable?
He who performs what ought to be done is known as one who has "set out.
His intellect for liberation, which will come to pass after many future births, is comparable to a tortoise inserting its neck through the hole of a yoke floating upon the four oceans.
Alas, the condition of cyclic existence is essence-less; enough for me with it! What is the use of stale karmic actions, by which the day is spent?
What might be the supreme rest, free from decline and excess?
He who possesses such internal certainty is known as "one who has desisted.
Although he is still living in this very birth, being one who lacks discernment,
he is a person of clear intention whose domain lies within these stages of yoga.
"How may I, having become free from passion, cross the ocean of saṃsāra?
When the one of noble intellect is thus intent on reflection,
he seeks the company of the virtuous and also studies the authentic scriptures.
Day after day, he attains detachment within his meditations;
he delights in noble actions and strives for honor,
yet he feels hesitation toward vulgar and dull activities that are fickle.
He does not strike at the vital points; he acts for the sake of merit and happiness;
he performs gentle deeds that cause no agitation to others; and he pursues actions that are tender, full of affection and friendship, refined, and appropriate.
He utters words that are appropriate to the place and time;
at that point, he has reached the first stage.
Then, possessing the nature that is about to be described, he will attain firm mastery therein.

In temples of the gods, in the dwellings of Brahmins, and in forests, he constantly delights; from this, he attains the first stage. Through contact with the scriptures and virtuous people, he himself increases his wisdom.
Like the crescent of the moon in the bright fortnight, she is endowed with beauty.
Devoted to the Sarvāstivāda school, gentle and full of affection,
he serves the virtuous in thought, deed, and word.

For a long time, following those who know that [truth], he has constantly examined the scriptures, bringing them from wherever they might be found— both those already acquired and those yet to be obtained. He is a peacock for destroying the venomous speech of serpents, with his neck raised high upon the mountain peak of the rain-cloud of Dharma.
One desires the power of bathing, giving, austerity, and meditation.
Having ascended the first [stage], one should resort to the second by force;
for there is no other way to cross over the crisis than through human effort.
One who possesses such discernment regarding the crossing over of saṃsāra is said to have attained the stages (*bhūmikā*); the rest, however, are remembered as merely "noble" (*ārya*).
Only the very first stage has reached equality with the state of nobility.
But for the remaining stages, nobility deserves to be their servitude.
Having reached the other stage of yoga called "Investigation," the one of noble mind assumes the nature of the great ones.
He takes refuge in that preeminent scholar who is renowned for his primary expositions on the Vedas, the Smṛtis, traditional conduct, retention, meditation,
and ritual action; he who triumphs over the enemies that are the senses through the binding of desire and curiosity.

"Amidst these heroes who strike at my very body like most cruel [enemies], shall I suddenly take refuge in this woman of passion as something unprecedented? Thinking thus, he is as if overcome by shame; he does not abandon his modesty and his compassion.
One who knows the classification of categories and has mastered what is to be heard understands the determination of what ought and ought not to be done, just as a householder knows his own home;
[he likewise perceives] the excess of intoxication, pride, envy, greed, and delusion.
Like a snake casting off its skin even as it lies outside,
he abandons even the embrace of women, though they be fragrant with sandalwood and aloe, and though they approach him unbidden; he treats his own body with utter disregard.
One regards the wives of others as one's own mother, the wealth of others as a clod of earth,
and all living beings with compassion as one's own self;
whatever one does, whatever one eats, whatever one moves, and whatever one strives for— [all this is done for them].
Therefore, at the outset, one examines it for a long time with a beautiful discrimination of the intellect.
That which is of the nature of non-investigation neither comes nor goes, neither speaks nor acts,
neither gives nor takes, neither accumulates nor expends.

For the sake of conforming to worldly convention, that which is momentary and non-contradictory takes on portions of joy and dejection, like a firebrand at night moving through the air. [It perceives] a bad location, a bad position, bad association, and a bad refuge.
Even though it is visible, one casts off the body and such things like a blade of grass.
That which is beneficial for the future life, which is visible, free from mental anguish, and devoid of delusion— that alone the silent sage pursues, like a deer chasing the wind.
He beholds women— who possess charming smiles and playful gestures, who are full of coquettish expressions and emotions, yet whose destruction is imminent— like withered creepers.
Having attained such a state of mind through the study of the scriptures and service to teachers and the virtuous, [he remains thus].

He attains it completely, along with its secret, exactly as it is. Then he falls upon that third stage of yoga, which is of the nature of non-attachment, like a beloved falling onto a pure bed of flowers.
Having abandoned faulty interpretation, excessive interpretation, and deficient interpretation,
his intellect— purifying in this regard— grasps the meaning of the scriptural statements exactly as they are.
Here, the meaning of the scripture bears fruit for him as he cultivates inner non-attachment.
Like a skilled cook preparing a soup with perfect flavor,
he refines his extended life while seated upon stone beds and seats, resting in the hermitages of ascetics amidst purifying conversations on the inner self.
The wise man passes his time wandering through forest glades, graced by the tranquility of his mind and gentle with the happiness of non-attachment;
for the moonlight, laughing with its spreading radiance, does not delight him in such a way.
Their dwellings are strewn with flowers, like those who reside in mountain caves.
They spend the afternoon in the worship and feeding of gods, twice-born ones, gurus, the wise, and scholars, and the forenoon with the study of sacred texts and the company of the virtuous.
One whose manner of acquiring wealth and purpose is consistently righteous,
whose soul is satisfied by the nectar of contentment, shines through virtuous conduct—
just as one shines amidst lakes of clear water and blooming lotus ponds.
He bathes in many sacred rivers and in ponds whose waters are like nectar scattered by the rays of the nearby moon, where the land and water are as gentle as the fragrance of flowers;
while he takes delight on mountain plateaus with humming caves, the forest deities attend upon that high-souled one with wild fruits.
The one hundred and forty-first canto, titled "The Characteristics of the Three Stages," by Vasiṣṭha.
Through the practice of the treatises on knowledge and the performance of meritorious deeds,
this vision of reality becomes clear for a living being exactly as it is.
Having reached the third stage, the awakened one experiences it for himself.
"There are two kinds of non-attachment; hear this distinction between them.
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, first tell me the definition of non-attachment."
"You shall explain to me later its twofold nature.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"In the very course of explaining its twofold nature, [I shall state] its definition."
Listen further to that non-attachment by which evil is destroyed.
This non-attachment is of two kinds: the common and the supreme.
First, listen to the common one; it alone shall lead to supremacy.
"I am not the Lord of Action, nor am I any agent whatsoever, nor anyone at all"—
this non-immersion in objects,
known as "general detachment," arises through some divine will.
The cultivation of non-cultivation is called "general detachment.
[One thinks: "I am unborn, I am the immutable self, I am infinite, I am free from affliction;
I am a non-doer"—this state of desirelessness is called "general detachment."
In this very way do affections and riches arise;
in this very way they perish. Who has agency here, and what [agency] could there be?
They are pleasant at first sight but bitter upon being scrutinized.
By a chance occurrence like that of the crow and the palm fruit, pleasures come and go;
enjoyments are like the unevenly flickering hoods of serpents.
I am not these, nor are they mine; with a tranquil mind, I remain awake within the Self.
Enjoyments are the great diseases of existence; prosperities are supreme calamities; unions are indeed separations; mental anxieties are diseases of the intellect.
Time is intent upon devouring all entities, which are insubstantial by nature.
Even while deceiving itself, it consumes [the world] through delusion;

indeed, O wonder, there are countless worlds— though unreal, appearing as if real, and though endless, appearing as if they have an end— [all of which are] nets of rays from the jewel of consciousness.
They are not found through investigation; they do not exist at all, even though they appear as if standing before one like cities seen in a dream while awake.
Again and again, they are like the shadows of trees and creepers in a windy forest.
They are incessantly flickering, appearing and disappearing.
That internal non-contemplation of phenomena through a lack of reliance—
realizing "I am neither the doer nor the enjoyer"— is that universal state of non-attachment.

"I am not the doer, nor the enjoyer, nor the speaker, nor am I one who goes; for such is the universal lack of connection [to action] when the impulse proceeds from the will of the Lord. Whatever is performed with dedication to the Lord, having abandoned all latent impressions (*vāsanā*), [is liberation].
They call that state of non-attachment the supreme goal. O descendant of Raghu, this general form of non-attachment has been described to you;
now hear about this most excellent non-attachment, which is an elixir for the ears.
By this sequential yoga, through the union of the great-souled ones,
by the command of the virtuous, and through the internal application of their own self-awarenesses,
practice is carried forward by means of human effort.

Just as a myrobalan fruit held in the palm of one's hand, so too is the entire essence experienced. Whenever even a slight desire arises, by the falling away of that very desire, the essential state is attained; it is reached through no other means of cognition.
When the entire limit has been seen— the lamp illuminating the three worlds,
the essence on the far shore of the river of saṃsāra, the supreme cause—
I am neither the agent nor the Lord; I am not the agent, nor am I the Lord.
"I am not this, nor am I another; I am not this, nor am I something else"—
having indeed cast far away such contemplations on the meaning of words,
that silent, peaceful state which is maintained is called the highest non-attachment.
That which is situated neither within nor in the sky, neither below nor above, neither in the quarters nor on the earth;
neither in an object nor in a non-object, neither in the insentient nor in the sentient;
that which is seated, luminous, peaceful, free from latent impressions, and beyond mental cultivation.

That which is without beginning or end, unborn, and lovely is called the supreme attachment (śreṣṭhāsaṅga). That which is the bliss of consciousness without a mind, the seat within all states of being,
and which is like the essence of spring and other seasons, is called the supreme attachment.
They know the supreme state of non-attachment to be the absence of immersion in objects, the absence of mental cultivation in the heart, and the lack of sensation regarding pleasure and the like.
[This applies] toward actions, objects, thoughts, latent impressions, and notions of selfhood.
Non-perception and non-immersion are said to be the absence of attachment to excellence.
This occurs by its very nature on the ground of consciousness, which stands upon the mire of ignorance,
either through a chance coincidence or from the exhaustion of all karmas.
In the lake of the heart, which possesses the playful ripples of consciousness, he was born as a lotus stalk with a pure body, accompanied by the water-insects of anxiety;
sweet with the fragrance of contentment and possessing the stainless sprouts of virtuous deeds.
Settled within the tip of the stalk of the mind, free from the thorny obstacles of impediments,
the lotus of discernment has taken root within and been blossomed by the sun of inquiry;
having reached the third stage, it bears fruit that is free from attachment.
With an unattached mind, silent, a sage who has cast out pride,
he becomes one for whom even the appearance of non-existence has vanished; from this state, through the assembly of pure ones and the equality of his spiritual deeds, he attains the third stage.
By a chance occurrence like that of the crow and the palm fruit, the first stage arises.
That stage, as soon as it has arisen within, is like a sprout of nectar;
it must be protected and nurtured by the wise man through discernment, which acts like the sprinkling of water.
One should daily and with effort bring that very portion which shines forth through inquiry to its full development, just as a farmer tends to a sprout. For this [intellect],
when its interior is polished, is the sole ground for the birth of all other [virtues].
Like a sprout from leaves, once grown, it takes root in others.
This third [state] brings about non-attachment and carries one across existence;
when this has arisen, [the other] arises like a lotus at the light of the sun.
Having conquered enemies such as drought, disturbances, and unfavorable regions,
the creeper whose root is well-watered yields its fruit in full.
One whose mind is unattached, who observes silence, and who is free from pride and envy—
One who has seen through the autumnal clouds becomes worthy and transcends the three worlds.
For him who has known all that is to be known and whose succession of doubts has been stilled,
there is no purpose whatsoever here in what is done, nor any in what is left undone.

Having attained the third stage, he wanders here possessing ordinary non-attachment, unarrogant and perceiving the supreme state. In this third stage of the ground, he possesses the highest non-attachment.
When all mental constructions and conceptualizations have departed,
there arises a state in which the contemplation of the fruits of action does not cling to one whose mind is unattached— just as water does not adhere to a lotus leaf, nor does color stain a gem.
Acting outwardly in accordance with his natural state through a mind that is eternally unattached,

he remains inwardly entirely undisturbed, unconquered in his heart. Having attained this state of non-attachment, even if he were to desire it, he does not fall back into the cycle of worldly existence here.
O Rāma, desire does not arise in you, nor does it ever arise; for that is indeed the wondrous manifestation of pure being (*sattva*).
The chapter titled "An Inquiry into the Spiritual Stages" (*bhūmikā-vicāra*), the one hundred and forty-second chapter.
Rāma: How can there be a crossing for a foolish man, born of an evil lineage, who has set out [on life's path] but has not attained union with Yoga?
"O Blessed One, what kind of destiny awaits one who has died after having ascended to the first, the second, the third, or any other [level]? Vasiṣṭha replied:
For one who is deluded and has not ascended [to the higher path], saṃsāra extends as far as hundreds of future births, occurring by chance like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence;
or else, for a man who has set out [on the path] through association with the virtuous, it does not.
The mind of dispassion arises like a flowering creeper in a desert.
Thus, that mind of dispassion, having grown through the sequence of the stages (*bhūmikās*),
binds one to *saṃsāra* just as a river binds its bank.
Some, even through great efforts throughout many births, fail to attain discernment;
they remain like the buckets of a waterwheel, moving up and down.
But he who practices either the first or any other stage of yoga—
He reaches the exhaustion of his lifespan for the sake of a future birth.
Carrying that very excellent equipment which has been practiced within his intellect,
he goes to the presence of death, just as the current of a river flows toward the sea.
There, accompanied by those very friends and kinsmen who were composed of such virtues and whose nature was pure through their auspicious intentions,
he remained undaunted in spirit, no longer clinging to any worldly existences.
Remembering with supreme devotion that which is the cause of crossing over the world,
he who is like a chariot driven by the mind and impelled by virtuous latent impressions (vāsanā) abandons his body,
just as a flower sheds its fragrance when shaken by the wind.
Accompanied by the vital breaths, the fragrance of the living soul, having abandoned the lotus of the body,
has flown up and reached some unknown space;
for a single moment, it remains in the state of deep sleep.
Having cast off the burden of the body, he has entered into a deep sleep; yet,
awakening in an instant, he is filled by his own habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) through constant practice, just as a riverbed is filled with water.

Having recollected this through his own intellect and by means of that very method of self-contemplation, the virtuous one—possessing a body of space—should abide in the sky, accompanied by the city of eight constituents.
That space is neither far nor near; it is neither this nor the other.
They know that indescribable state of space to be beyond all characterization.
Then, within that space, the individual soul— composed of the vital breath—
gradually assumes its former state, just as a sprout takes up sap in the springtime.

The living being, remembering that very cultivation which has been constantly practiced until the moment of death, abandons this terrible burden, the body. Whatever state of being one remembers while departing from the body— having been constantly cultivated therein— [that state one attains].
He obtains the very fruit acquired through the power of his own human effort;
whatever has been constantly practiced by the living soul throughout its body, that he remembers at death, disregarding all other states, thinking: "This was done by me."
Terrified by the fruits of his own karma, he does not perceive even those things standing before him— namely, battle, kingdom, wine, gardens, recitation, weeping, and delusions—
regardless of whether a state whose fruit is imminent occurs through his own will or against his will.
Through the dissolution of all phenomenal existence, that very [Self] alone is perceived first.
"May there be auspiciousness for me now; may there never be inauspiciousness for me"—this hope, extending from insects to the immortals, is never exhausted.
For one who has known the Self, this internal mental cultivation comes to an end;
pure as the sky, tranquil, and wise, he attains final nirvāṇa and is stilled.
If he were insentient, then he would not perceive certain objects present before him at the time of death.
If it is not inert, then it is helplessly assailed by objects through habitual practice.
Thus, this living being (jīva), whose nature is like space and who is enveloped by latent impressions (vāsanā),
perceives that moment as a state of inertia when a whole eon has passed.
"I was not a living being before; having died, I am now among my kinsmen.
In that moment, he perceives that the entire eon has been exhausted there.
In just a brief instant, once the determination of the eon has arisen, that living being [perceives this].
In this world, one perceives: "I have indeed entered into this region.
"Previously I was a living being; now I am dead among my kinsmen.
Therefore, the rites such as the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) were performed for me by my relatives."
"By means of those [actions], having obtained a body, I experienced my good and evil deeds for a very long time; now I have arisen in this manner.
Thus, in just a moment, he became possessed of conviction.
In accordance with its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the living being (*jīva*) perceives the body as the self;
for a moment or for a very long time, being bodiless, it gathers, beholds, and approaches a little body, just as you [behold] a dream.
"By means of an inferior latent impression (vāsanā), I have become one who possesses the fruit of a corrupted self;
I am born miserable and base"—thus does Jīvaka perceive.
"By means of a preeminent latent impression, I am one who possesses a preeminent fruit."
Being born as the very Pradhāna, it accumulates itself by means of itself.
Thus, even though the individual soul (jīva) is bodiless, it attains the state of having a body and perceives the next world, which is fully developed through the sequence of space and time.
"This is that world beyond for me; these are the men who are the Kings of Dharma.
This one has been led away, this one is to be led; this is my true endeavor.
But these are merely the grounds of the world beyond; I speak the truth regarding what was done in the past.
"I have been questioned by this upholder of Dharma; this shadow is my witness.
This good and evil karma stands before me;
I am led away, and I shall go either to heaven or indeed to hell."
The living being possessing such conditions perceives the long delusion of saṃsāra in a mere moment as well as in a hundred years.
This great thicket of suffering arises from the hollow of the seeds of latent impressions (vāsanā).
The manifestation "I" arises from a false birth regarding the self:
"I am enjoined to suffering," or "I am joined to pleasure";
