"this year of mine has passed," or "this century has gone by."
This evil deed has been consumed, and these various riches of heaven have been enjoyed;
for while dwelling in other wombs, I have now stood here as a tree. I stand here as a creeper, and I have flourished here as a shrub.
"I was born as this donkey; I have become this parrot.
"I have become a monkey here; I have become a partridge here.
I am a bear here, I am a banyan tree here, I am a fish here, and then a tortoise."
For a hundred years here I am a beast, and for a hundred years here I am grass;
yet, through the deeds of a virtuous son— such as the offering of funeral cakes and other acts of kinship— a man attains human birth, and I shall become so once again.
Now I am a man whose evil deeds have been exhausted and who has attained perfection. I was placed within the womb of this mother;
when the eight months of gestation had passed, I was born from my father’s house.
"I am this child standing here; I have reached new youth;
now I am old age after a long time; now I am dead"—experiencing such things, the individual soul is worn out by its own delusions.

It is carried away again and again by the whirlwinds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), through the revolutions of their cycles; it is tossed about in this great ocean of saṃsāra, which is the single vast sea where the grass of living beings quivers amidst the waves of various latent impressions and the movements of diverse whirlpools.
The living soul is sometimes situated in deep sleep, sometimes as an insentient stationary being; sometimes withered by disease, and sometimes afflicted by mental agonies;
it is happy or miserable, existent or non-existent, a human, a serpent, an immortal, or an asura.

Having fallen into worthlessness, he becomes a crane, a crow, a parrot, a conch-shell, a partridge, a deer, or a bull; passing from sorrow to sorrow and from fear to fear, he takes delight in the ashes of enjoyments that are pleasant only at first sight.
"Though bodiless, formless, consisting of volition, and having the sky as his abode,
he assumes the state of a *piśāca* in some place through the cognition 'I am a *piśāca*'. Whatever is established in its nature during creation, that it pursues accordingly."
O sinless one, whether that living soul knows all things or does not know them,
due to the various delusions of conceiving itself as a yakṣa, a rākṣasa, a piśāca,
and so forth, I am not capable of calculating the number of its births here.
From the mere mental cultivation of objective categories, a succession of extreme sufferings arises for the ego-soul, along with dense delusions of reality and unreality. Thus,
these delusions of worldly existence are born from the void itself, having the void as their very nature.
These do not create even the slightest obstruction of space, time, or concealment.
I have traversed the uninterrupted successions of creations— both formless and possessed of form—
which are established in a sequence like the flow of water, and which arise in the sky through their own ethereal nature.
The one hundred and forty-third canto, titled "The Demonstration that Creation is of the Nature of Space," by Vasiṣṭha.
For an embodied being who has passed away while on a stage of yoga, former misdeeds are exhausted in accordance with the portions of that stage.
"In the past I was a living being; I died there among my kinsmen."
Then he perceives: "I have arisen here after a long time.
By means of such meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), he sees his body as having come into being, fully endowed with all its limbs, as if fashioned from mud.
Seeing his body fully formed with its swollen latent impressions (vāsana),
he then quickly accumulates and perceives the vast world of the hereafter;
thereafter, for a certain period of time, [he experiences] the remainder of his evil deeds.
Having enjoyed his well-earned merits, he goes to the abode of the virtuous;
there, in celestial palaces above and in the cities of the world-protectors,
as well as in the groves and bowers of Mount Meru, he delights in the company of beautiful women.
Accompanied by his beloved, he delights among the swings of *mandāra* petals, in the thickets of *punnāga* trees, at the edges of the *pārijāta* forests,
beneath the canopies of *santānaka* trees, and among the *pāribhadra* trees.
Accompanied by his beloved, he delights in groves of wish-fulfilling trees.
Those supreme persons who die while established on the stages of yoga,
their evil deeds exhausted, rejoice intoxicated in the abodes of the gods.
Upon well-spread carpets of *kalpa*-tree shoots and within soft golden vine-cottages draped with flowers,
the *vidyādharas* enjoy the exquisite pleasure of love together with the *apsarases* in the celestial cities.
This concludes the chapter entitled "The Consideration of Death for the Gods of the Half-Coursed Realm."
The one hundred and forty-fourth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, each individual has been described as a separate grove within the cycle of worldly existence.
Including the worlds of the gods, the asuras, and the netherworld (pātāla), along with the intermediate spaces,
the earth, and the sky; even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and the others abide in this very manner,
being composed of volition (saṅkalpa) and relying upon this resolve for creation.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and the rest were previously merely mental; this illusory state of creation has arisen falsely, consisting of mere conceptualization.
Whatever is perceived whatsoever is but the unreal sky of illusion.
These men of volition— Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, Kāma, and the others— have arisen like pillars made of plantain trunks that are hollow within;
they exist here as both unreal and real, according to whether they possess consciousness or lack it.
The creation, distinct from each being, has blossomed forth by itself;
it is as extensive as a city in a dream of volition or a kingdom of the mind.
This is due to the all-pervasiveness of the element of consciousness and because of the mutual delusion of experience.
In these creations, all classes of beings, whose nature is real,
some merge with one another, possessing unobstructed consciousness; others, however, undergo transformation as creations while remaining unaware of one another.

O Rāma, by this sequence, even those who were men in your dreams may fall into a creation like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, thinking, "We have reached this other place. MU 6.144.9. Thus, in this order, O Rāma, even those who were men in your dreams [attain this state].
And the persons of volition (saṅkalpapuruṣa) are indeed real because their consciousness is unbroken.
Due to consciousness being the essence of the mind, it remains as consciousness alone;
for it there is no obstruction, no piercing, no otherness, and no perishability.
Persons created by imagination are real, and the delusions of dreams are real;
because they perform functions with regard to present objects, nothing here is composed of unreality.
That which cannot be attained by one another and does not serve a purpose is not a real thing.
It is true that this person from another land belongs to us as well.
Whatever exists, in whatever manner, by whatever means, and wherever it may be, it remains exactly so, by that same means, and in that very place.
Since existence and non-existence do not apply here within the realm of truth, enough of this silence; remain silent no longer.

The world does not exist by its own nature; that which is perceived here is entirely nothing but the reality of Brahman when examined, or else it is nothing at all. Even if one were to concede for the sake of argument that creation and so forth exist, I say this: [it is still unreal].
Know this stomach to be the Brahman, consisting of that very [consciousness].
Just as sweetness exists within the sugarcane and pungency within black pepper and the like,
so too does the visible world— the three worlds consisting of egoity and the rest— exist within Brahman.
I am this undivided reality, devoid of the words and meanings "world" and "visible," and free from the referent of the word "this.
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions— [all these are I].
Although it is partless and conscious, its portions exist externally;
through the volition directed toward the Puruṣa, creation unfolds within the heart,
consisting of portions of mountains, heaven, earth, and rivers, like sap in the fiber of a sprout.

Consciousness, being of the nature of space, fully relishes the world— which is also of the nature of space— by means of internal enjoyment according to its own desire, as if it were merged within its own belly.
In a dream, no physical place is traversed, nor does a place enter the heart.
In the waking state, there is no external space, nor is there a waking state existing within that space.
O sinless one, neither internality nor externality exists;
there is neither non-conceptualization, nor indeed any movement of conceptualization.
That consciousness which, with its nature contracted, experiences this circle of the three worlds,
is designated by the name "dream. That [consciousness] which,
with its nature blossomed, [experiences] this circle of the three worlds...
That which experiences [objects] is established as the state of waking.
When consciousness, as if from fatigue, does not for some time experience its own self,
but remains as if quiescent, that is remembered by the name "deep sleep."
Furthermore, when consciousness does not perceive itself for the sake of no further delusion regarding nirvāṇa,
being a steady and uniform manifestation— that is called the Fourth State (turya), which is liberation. Within the lotus of consciousness, this fragrance of the world exists externally.
When that [consciousness] has expanded and vibrates within itself,
there is no difference between creation and consciousness, just as there is none between the wind and its movement.
Just as movement is nothing but the wind, so too the world is nothing but consciousness.
Just as the state of the wind remains when the notions of the word and meaning of "vibration" are abandoned,

so too is the stability of creation when the notions of the word and meaning of "creation" are abandoned. The notion of the word and meaning of vibration in the wind consists in the exhaustion of imagined conceptualization.

The cognition of the meaning of the word "creation" ceases when the conceptualization of the imagined is exhausted. That which arises from volitional construction (*saṅkalpa*) perishes through the absence of such construction;
this is established by direct experience—what is difficult in this?
There is no creation, yet there is consciousness; that [consciousness] is like space even while it exists.
By not conceptualizing the meaning of the word "void" (vicchabda), this very [reality] is understood by itself.
It is certain that there is no cognition of the meaning of the words "creation" or "non-creation."
Upon the complete cessation of the volition for creation, one quickly awakens by means of the Self alone.
Indeed, the realization of non-creation becomes fully manifest when the meaning of the word "creation" is forgotten; that which remains is the Nameless.
Perception is the consciousness of creation; non-perception is the absence of creation.
There is no difference between perception and non-perception other than through words.
Since everything has an infinite form, where is there difference, and where is there differentiation?
Where is there forgetfulness? Therefore, peaceful silence alone is auspicious.

That which has long been established like a tethering post, from which the web of conceptual constructions and mental fluctuations has been cast out, which is most excellent through the cessation of inquiry into the meaning of the scriptures—that is the primordial, auspicious, and imperishable state, free from all doubt.
The one hundred and forty-fifth canto, titled "The Demonstration of the Identity of Creation and Nirvana," [spoken by] Vasiṣṭha:
All emanations are the Self, and the entire space is the essence of emanation;
there is no difference between space and emanation, just as there is none between the wind and its movement.
The lights, which fill the infinite sky, move back and forth within the void.
Just as these [atoms] do not obstruct one another, so too are the creations [mutually non-obstructive].
Just as these atoms meet and yet do not meet within [space],
because of their subtlety and imperceptibility in the sky, so too are the creations [mutually non-obstructive].

Just as there is not even the slightest difference among waters that have merged together, so too there is no distinction between creations that are of the nature of a solid mass of consciousness, even when they are joined. Just as the individual atoms of mists are not perceived when they are intermingled, [so it is with these worlds].
Likewise, individual beings are not perceived as separate from the lives [of the Creator] within the creations.
Just as the water in a river flows, turbid with its constant submerging and surfacing,
so does the flood of creation flash forth in the heart of consciousness, both distinct and intermingled.
Just as gusts of wind, having mingled with one another,
do not obstruct or perceive each other, so too are the creations of their own nature.
Just as whirlpools of passion revolve within the realm of passion, so it is with these.
When the subtle, fierce wind has expanded, creations likewise [arise] in relation to one another;
because they consist of the nature of volition (*saṅkalpa*), they are neither perceivers nor obstructors of one another,
like portions of space within space, or like lights within their own radiance.
Some, having come together with one another, attain complete unity,
like mists within mists or rays of light within their own radiance;
yet others, though joined together, appear distinct from one another.
Like ghee churned from the ocean of milk, or like the rays of the sun shining upon jewels;
as the peaks of Meru and Mandara appear with full expansion in a dream,
so do creations exist within the principle of consciousness, even inside stones and other such things.
Consciousness is all-pervading, tranquil, and has the nature of universal existence;
it is devoid of the objects denoted by the word "creation," for indeed, creations are its very belly—
land, water, sky, and mountains, in their entirety, past, future, and present.
Everything is all-pervading and tranquil because the Great Consciousness is omnipresent.
Since it consists of pure awareness, even the waters within it contain creations;
these are not carried away by the mind-space, appearing as if endowed with reflections.

Within the existence of the five elements, both externally and internally, thousands of creations always exist, yet they never truly exist at any time. Everywhere, at all times, everything is the All, by means of the All, and in every way.
There is nothing that is not real, and there is nothing that is not false.
There is nothing at all that is false, nor is there anything that is real, nor is there a middle state.
The vast Brahman expands; it is Brahman, peaceful and devoid of ends.
Through the suppression of all [prior] states, a state ripens into fullness;
therefore, an excess of being prevails even between two closely joined creations.
In the absence of mutual attainment, the individual soul (jīva) is established through its state of deficiency.
But the equanimity of cyclic existence attains equality in both [aspects]. Great entities, though distinct in character, merge with one another through their commonality;
yet they remain distinct in their diversity, like rays of light of various colors.
The unimpeded succession of creations unfolds within the realm of atoms,
even within the interior of the king of mountains, within rocks, in fire, in water, or in the totality of all things;
though it is crowded with the manifestations of mountains, rivers, suns, directions, time, and kalpas, all of which are of the nature of mental construction.
The world is the mass-base of the great mandala within the belly of space, in the element of the void that is the density of consciousness.
And the sky, along with the moon, stars, mountains, sun, and so forth, is likewise boundless within her belly.
Yet, though they have attained corporeal forms through one another, their essence consists of sounds neither seen nor heard by each other.
The one hundred and forty-sixth canto, titled "The Demonstration of the Identity of the World and Space," by Vasiṣṭha:
Just as an army made of cloth, though clearly manifest and vast in its mobilization,
with infinite thousands of limbs, weapons, and so forth, is— relative to its own nature— insentient and thus incapable of any actual exertion; so too is this [world].
The non-material light, the contemplation [of which] transcends time, parts, and so forth— [it is] solely, purely, and peaceful, [leading to] perfect nirvāṇa within the self,
through what is seen, inferred, known, and by other means, free from the ten delusions.
Not touched even slightly, yet existing;
unreal in nature, it is the primordial state of "I" and so forth, and likewise the undivided world.
Everything is composed of the substance of Brahman, existing yet consisting of unreality.
It is devoid of form, light, mental attention, and the meaning of words;
it is free from objects inferred by another, and it abides within the self.
By virtue of non-duality within the self, it is neither real nor unreal.
Rāma:
O Lord of Sages, there may be others such as ourselves among the armies of books;
but who else could there be for us, other than the state of the infinite Brahman?
Vasiṣṭha said: There is indeed no other [self] for us that consists of the nourishment of Brahman;
it is a non-existent delusion that has arisen, which, when scrutinized, cannot be found.

That deluded person perceives these modifications of being— which are unreal and non-different from it— from afar, just as one who is alive perceives his own death. This very [self], though its nature is not to be seen, is like the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
That [object] which has been examined by us does not exist, just like the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; therefore,
it has surely reached a state of rootlessness,
because we perceive that the object standing before us is not [that which was previously imagined], being devoid of light.
But for those by whom it is not perceived, it expands with a hundred branches—
though being utterly unreal, appearing as real like an army of child-vetālas.
Rāma:
"From the beginning of creation until the end of the world, this delusion has persisted; nevertheless, what is the use of knowing this auspicious [truth] if it leads only to endless suffering?
Vasiṣṭha said:

O Rāma, that which is unreal ceases to appear the very moment it is scrutinized; but a real entity, O sinless one, does not perish even with great effort, nor indeed does it ever cease to exist. Ignorance, however, subsides immediately upon being known and no longer causes affliction.
It does not deceive within, like the ocean of water in a mirage.
That very thorough understanding of it is its complete destruction,
leading solely to the highest welfare, just as the perception of an enemy toward a friend [leads to one's ruin].
When fully understood, [the notion] dissolves; when unawakened, it clings, though by its very nature it does not exist at all, like the false perception of a yakṣa.
The realization that "ignorance does not exist" is what is called knowledge.
In one who has attained firm realization, this [ignorance] ceases; for the knower, that very state is Brahman and liberation itself.
That which is unreal is seen as unreal, but the real never ceases to be.
When the delusion of the unreal world is seen as unreal, then it quickly ceases.

The perfection of mere conceptualization dissolves non-conceptualization; it is like the state of the mind itself, with its soft-limbed form, whose existence and non-existence depend upon man. For one who is untiring in this [state] where birth and death depend upon the person—

When this [intellect] has been correctly awakened, liberation alone remains. Having drunk up that which consists merely of the conceptualization of mountains, heaven, earth, rivers, and so forth, by means of mere non-conceptualization, the skillful person attains nirvāṇa.
If mountains and such were real, by what could they be prevented?
There is no coming into being for the non-existent, nor is there non-existence for the existent.
Just as a multitude of wheels spreads out from a vibration in the water, though they are unreal; so too does this world appear.
In the same way, the circle of transmigratory existence manifests from volition within the sky of consciousness;
just as a single body of water, by the power of its own movement, forms a hundred whirlpools,
so too the supreme Self, the world-soul, appears as the manifold universe through the power of its own vibration.
When thoroughly investigated and searched, the wheel and so forth do not exist within the water;
likewise, neither creation nor anything else exists within the sky of consciousness, nor is there any conceptual construction.
Creation and liberation are attained solely through the volition of one's own effort.
Whichever of these two pleases someone, that person follows it.
Because of not having found [the truth], there is liberation; because of having found it, there is the wonder of birth.
There is indeed a reality to be known for us; do as you wish.
Who indeed would create a non-existent object of cognition that brings suffering and then experience it?
For it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off.
Who is such a liberated soul who, having created a phantom, [would then suffer]?
By that very same [means], he himself strikes down his own unharmed self, being afflicted by it. Or rather, for whomsoever the rising of this demon of creation is pleasing,
let him, my dear, raise it up through his own volition for the sake of his own destruction.
Having created the object of sight and having assumed the state of a seer, he binds himself;
yet he who desires happiness may dispose of his own self as he wishes.
We, however, are intent only upon declaring the matter exactly as it is.
Having heard this, let people accept what is true or what is untrue according to their own will.

O mighty-armed one, let those who seek creation here possess the reasoning for creation, and let those who seek liberation possess the reasoning for liberation; we have no attachment whatsoever to either.
He whose consciousness has turned away from creation— whether external or internal—
and whose nature consists in the realization of the non-existence of creation, is fit for immortality.
Through the conviction that creation is non-existent, the consciousness of creation ceases.
That which remains when the mental activity of "I-am-ness" has been eliminated is that which is nameless.
When one has thoroughly investigated and searched until no world of manifestation is found,
what else remains as the cause of delusion other than the mental activity beginning with "I-am-ness"?
If you enter the netherworld, traverse the sky, leap over the circle of the directions, and wander about, you are still one whose self is non-self.
There is no "I" other than delusion, nor is there any world-system other than that; it is like the wind that is not other than the movement, or a stream of water that is not other than the flow.
This is the chapter named "The Dissolution of Creation."
The one hundred and forty-seventh canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"Because they exist as effects produced by mere mental construction, these mountains such as Meru and the rest [are not real]."

There exist classes of beings, beginning with Brahmā, who are soft and light, even more so than a heap of silk; their bodies have the appearance of wind without movement, like a swarm of *piśāca* spirits.
Within the insubstantial self of day and night, where light and darkness are spread out like the laughter and frowns of a shadow upon a living being whose body is breath,
the world— though sought, it is unattainable— flashes forth in the supreme sky.
Like the illusion of a mass of hair seen by one with impaired vision,
these gods and demons perceive this flickering cycle of existence as a forest of severed trees inhabited by piśācas, or like a living being within a burnt-out body.
They breathe like bellows and whirl about like smoke in the sky;
they cogitate with the appearance of half-sleep, seeing what is deluded and turbid.
Dull-witted people quiver like waves driven by the current of a river.
Those whose nature is one perceive another, just as cuckoos perceive the state of crows.
Stationary beings arise upon the earth like ripples on water;
internal states undergo transformation like waters driven by the force of a current.
Experiences, residing within the Self like the sweetness of sugarcane,
are agitated and transformed by the impacts of the wind's touch;
though consisting solely of mental construction and being subtle, they encompass the entire circle of mountains and oceans.
When placed upon a scale, the earth does not weigh even half a *raktikā*.
Though the treasury of future and past beings resides within it, the sky has descended to the depths of the underworld;
yet, as in the case of a painted fire, only its coolness is experienced.
Smokeless by nature, supportless, and unagitated by wind or other elements,
the sky ascends upward with the clouds like kinsmen who have been instructed;
the oceans stand in heaven, and the stars have arisen from the earth.
The mountains dance with their arms; the sand emits oil.
Whatever is conceived by the imagination, it is exactly so and not otherwise.
Is that which consists of the fabrication of conceptualization real, or is it unreal?
Nothing is stable, nor is anything unstable; nothing is insentient, nor is anything sentient.
There is no "I," no "you," neither being nor non-being, neither gross nor the pervasive minuteness of the atom.
Everything is everything, in every way, at all times, and for everyone.
There is no form that does not consist of the manifold nature of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
A child has bound Airāvaṇa; mountains have been burnt by the luster of the moon;
and illusory men fight with streams of water as if they were clubs.
In the vast sky, which has been ploughed by the excellent plough, the fine rice-grains have been sown;
they have ripened, been harvested, and placed within vessels.
The rows of forest trees sing charmingly and dance with joy, as if they were lions.
Lotuses grow upon the rocks, and the stones give birth to young elephants.
Cities fly up high, while the suns beg on the earth.
Mountains act like cities, and the water-fowls sing softly.
Even this element of volition shines forth only when [the object] exists;
other things, even if they exist, do not shine forth if there is no consciousness.
And this element of volition, fashioned by an intense act of will, [shines forth].
Through the abandonment of prior volitions, that which is of the nature of truth is inferred.
Therefore, neither truth nor untruth exists here at all;
whatever is contemplated in whatever manner, that is seen there in that very way.
"Thus, all this either does not exist or exists through the reality of Brahman;
it is of the nature of space yet devoid of space, like the heart of a man in deep sleep.
Thus, with her very heart, she [perceived] the three worlds as a puppet in a doll-house.
It is neither produced nor unproduced; it is neither sustained nor unsustained.
In whatever manner, at whatever time, and in whatever place it finds delight through its own configuration, in that manner, at that time, and in that place, it is produced or not by its own will.
Thus, in this world of fragile form, whose nature depends upon one's own volition,

what cause for distress is there in the delusion regarding existence and non-existence, which is under one's own control? My dear friend, this [liberation] is accomplished through mere personal effort, even by a child.
I believe that either worldly creation or the attainment of liberation is accomplished with ease.
Having understood this through your intelligence, you— whose mind is free from affliction and who have transcended both existence and non-existence— are indeed beyond the reach of the mind.
Thus, having understood that the universe is entirely composed of delusion and is utterly devoid of essence,
remain established in the attainment of the abandonment of the referents of the word "universe," which is full of essence.
Herein there is neither truth nor untruth, neither non-substantiality nor substantiality.
By someone, somewhere, this something exists as if it were something else;
what indeed is that mental construction by which liberation becomes an object of words with clear manifestation?
This [liberation] is merely described within the scripture, but it is realized internally through some unique, innate reasoning of one's own.
The one hundred and forty-eighth canto, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Contemplating Transformation," [spoken by] Rāma:
O Blessed One, in the context of your discourse on death in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), you have stated this essential point;
now, illustrate it:
when a yogi has gone to the next world, he enters into a cycle of pure intentions (*śubhasaṃkalpa*).
"Having enjoyed pleasures in the city of the gods, what kind of being does one become once again?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Then, when the accumulation of good deeds and the evil deeds previously committed [are exhausted]..."
When their enjoyments are exhausted and utterly spent, yogins are born upon this earth in the secret homes of those who are pure, prosperous, virtuous, and noble;
they never behold the faces of the wicked, which are intent on backbiting.
In that regard, the wise, having touched the sequence of the stages of yoga practiced through prior impressions, leap up to the higher sequence of stages.
Therein, they are free from agitation, intoxication, exhaustion, delusion, envy, and confusion.
Having cast far behind them all attachments, they stand firm like gentle moons;
wise, blessed, and pure-minded,
they remain amidst the burden of worldly existence, having reached the third stage.
This supreme reality of the Self, which is Brahman, consists of seven aspects designated as waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth (turya), and that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta).
O Rāma, these first three stages are established as the state of waking.
And that state of Brahman is attained through a realization impossible for others to achieve.
In the third stage, the yogi clearly perceives this entire waking world— this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) agitated by hundreds of distinct activities.

The state of being a jar exists in the parts of the jar, the state of being a cloth in the parts of the cloth, and the state of being a banyan tree in the parts of the banyan tree; thus it abides in the three states.
Through the cognition of differentiation as it truly is, this world is perceived during the waking state.

In this state, for those joined in yoga, there arises nothing but noble-mindedness (*āryatā*). For one who has not yet realized reality, that intense contemplation of the nature of objects which remains unfading is "waking"; let it be unreal or let it be real.
One who performs what ought to be done and refrains from doing what ought not to be done,
remaining established in natural conduct— he is known as a noble person (ārya). According to custom, according to scripture, according to one's own mind, and according to how things truly are—

He who adopts worldly convention is remembered as a noble one (ārya). He who reaches what is attainable through the organs of action, does not desire what is unattainable, and is liberated from joy, resentment, and pride— he is remembered as a noble one.
In the first [stage], it has sprouted; then it has blossomed on the ground;
in the third, the state of nobility (*āryatva*) becomes manifest for the yogin.
Having died while in that state of nobility, the yogin [attains] those [realms] produced by pure intentions.
Having enjoyed even those pleasures that were mentally constructed, the practitioner of yoga is born again.
Rāma said: Whatever has been cultivated while in the body is experienced at the end of that body.
In that moment, what state of the age (*yuga*) is experienced by the living being?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Whatever is seen here, this world of both the stationary and the moving—"
O best among the knowers of Brahman, know that which abides through the divisions of the three times and is devoid of beginning and end— that is the state of *tilataila* (sesame oil) within Brahman;
just as oil resides within a sesame seed, so does this [Brahman] reside within Brahman.
Death, life, movement, dullness, consciousness, pleasure, and pain—
this [entirety] resides within Brahman, just as oil resides in a sesame seed.
Illusion, the individual soul, the mind, thought, effort, lack of effort, motion, and the world [are likewise contained therein].
Thus, this [universe] resides within Brahman, like oil in a sesame seed.
Just as the sesame seed itself experiences the oil situated within it,
so too does Brahman experience the world within its own interior.
Just as sesame seeds within contain oil—sometimes at one end, sometimes at the other;
sometimes little, sometimes much; sometimes withered, sometimes pure—so too does Brahman internally perceive: sometimes as insentience, sometimes as consciousness.
In some places it is mind and so forth, in others mountains and so forth;

in some places it is the nature of space, in some places emptiness, in some places vibration, in some places time, and in some places direction; in some places sound, in some places peace, in some places subtle, and in some places dense.
Darkness, radiance, auspiciousness, evil, "I," "you," those things,
here and there, that place, reality, unreality, what was before, today, existence,
non-existence, and power— thus the supreme state, though one and not manifold, exists as if manifold.
Like water in water with waves having the forms of staffs, wheels, and creepers; so,
within the all-pervading Self, something appears somewhere—
though it is non-dual, without beginning or end, like fluidity in water.
O Rāma, in that expansion of consciousness which is the flow of death— a momentary delusion of insentience that appears both as lasting and non-lasting— your question is not appropriate.
For whatever appears in that expansive nature of intuitive awareness, it appears exactly as it is.
That very thing is thus by that means; what, then, is there to be conceptualized here?
Is it not as with water and wind regarding their flowing and moving?
Since those two are of that very nature, such a question is appropriate for people like you.
"O Rāma, once the conviction of being a creation has been established within the Self that is Brahman, your question—'What is the earth? What is the sky? What is the ether?'—is not appropriate.
For those who have wallowed in the ocean of worldly existence, [only] from this pure state [can they emerge]."
In this matter, the cause is simply the latent impression (*vāsanā*) practiced by beings for a very long time.
Whatever— such as coldness, heat, and so forth— is practiced through consciousness at its own arising,
even though it is non-existent, the wise know that to be its "nature," appearing like a double moon.

Without even understanding their own inherent nature, those agitated by delusion remain fixed in the conviction that "the nature of things is not free from conceptual construction," because they fail to perceive the supreme reality where the notions of "self" and "nature" do not exist separately.
The statement that "intrinsic nature resides in Brahman" does not shine forth as being without foundation.
In this very way, entities proceed as if they were real existents;
in this very way, they cease as if they were engaged in activity.
Nothing whatsoever is ever born, nor does anything ever die;
everything is peaceful, ineffable, and as indestructible as if carved upon a mountain of rock.
When delusion has swollen through dense latent impressions (*vāsanā*), its very self becomes even more solidified.
A mere moment is inferred to be an eon because of suffering;
just as Brahmanhood exists in Brahman, so too these [moments] consist of that very nature.
Devoid of names, words, and objects, they abide as one's own direct experiences.
When examined, that latent impression which leads to long-lasting suffering is not found;
it dissolves through one's own effort by means of the realization "I am not.
The experience of "I-ness" is suffering, while the non-arising of "I-ness" is happiness.
Because of the absence of a heart made of stone, this supreme silence arises within you; by resorting to it and remaining established as you truly are,
a person attains this unbroken, unsurpassed state free from all obstacles.
There exists a vast stone named Brahmā, upon which stands the eternal statue of the three worlds;
she consists of the essence of existence, non-existence, passion, and so forth, and is both endowed with consciousness and silent as a wooden post devoid of mind.
This is the chapter titled "The Demonstration of the Non-existence of the World."
The one hundred and forty-ninth canto.
Rāma said:
"O Sage, this [world] is merely the conceptualization that is the seed of the sense of 'I'."
If it is thus that what is non-existent appears as if it were existent,
then tell me, O Brahmin: why is it said in the world, in the scriptures, in the Śruti, and in the Smṛti,
that "the body of the deceased arises as a physical mass and so forth"?
Vasiṣṭha:
Just as Brahman exists, so too does this creation exist, governed by its own laws;
though it is not other than that [Brahman], it has attained the state of being "other" through the cognition of being a creation.
In this context, the meaning of words such as "creation" and so forth refers to the elements and the like that have come into being.
Know that the "elementality" of the elements consists in their nature of conceiving "I-ness.
This conceptualization is essentially characterized by passion and aversion, and not by any other nature.

"This is thus, this is not thus"— in this way, she whose nature is a single essence is proclaimed as the one who possesses the measure and the object of measurement, the conceptualization of the meaning of the word "creation," and whose form is the sense of "I" (ahantva) in the form of the primordial Person (puruṣa) such as Brahmā.
And without the restriction that "this is to be done" and "this is not," she does not exist,
for her sole life-force consists in this very form of the self.
But for her who has attained the state of Brahmā and so forth, [the notions] "you" and "I" are her own nature.

Therefore, there is no otherness from that self-nature, the Supreme Self. Having attained the state of Brahmā and so forth, it remains established in its own essential nature; being of the nature of the Supreme, it neither ceases nor arises due to its desirelessness.
For this state whose nature is stainless, existence and non-existence are equal;
therefore, it remains equanimous, perceiving neither non-existence nor becoming.
When that consciousness has indeed arisen, consisting of the conceptualization of Brahmā and the rest, [it remains thus].
They have no desire for anything other than the Self, which is like that which is both quiescent and unarisen.
Thus, this entire [reality] remains quiescent, infinite like space;
we do not deliberate upon it for any indefinable length of time.
But when that mental being remains expanding by its own nature,
then the creation exists precisely as having that form;
just as a river, while flowing, possesses the nature of its own whirlpools and so forth.
Likewise, for the existence of volition (*saṅkalpa*), which consists of the world and so forth,
there is no existence apart from the arrangement of its structural form— such as "this is thus" and "this is that"— arising from the consciousness of creation.
When that which is endowed with the nature of Viriñca and the rest subsides within the Self alone,
then there is no sequence such as "this is thus" or "this is that.
Only Brahman remains— tranquil, all-pervading, and void.
Like a whirlpool in water, that reality is not deliberated upon by us.
But when it does not quickly subside, consisting as it does of its own essential existence,
it then flows forth through the vision of creation, [discriminating] "this is an effect" and "this is not."
That which is the proliferation of conceptual construction is seen as creation;
it spreads out like a circle of oil on water. That very structure of creation, which is the supreme cause of the existence of creation, [is thus perceived].
"That very thing is thus, but this is thus; this is an extreme expansion.
If 'this is thus' and 'that is thus' do not exist here, how could there be what is above, and how could there be what is below?"
When the manifestation within one's own self has been perfected as the locus for the existence of the world,
the conceptualization of forms such as Brahmā and others is like seeking water in vain on a desert path.
Therefore, sound, touch, and the other [sensory objects] are merely its own constituent parts.

Consisting of volition itself, they quickly transform into one another through forms, perceptions, and sensations, like waters of liquid essence. The object assumes existence, and the word follows after the object.
One [element] assumes the state of a substratum, while the other assumes the state of being supported; thus does the seasonal period, bearing its own seasonal nature,
bestow its fruit when the sequence that determines the existence of things has blossomed.

Necessity (niyati) attains stability of its own accord, just as water flows naturally toward a low place. Therefore, those [Vedas] are called "necessities" because they are contained within it; they bring about the world's existence in the form of objects, for the stability of the world is constrained by necessity.
Then, for the sake of the world's stability until the end of the kalpa, for the attainment of knowledge,
and for swift steadfastness,
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others fashioned the Vedas as a conceptualized destiny consisting of a mass of sounds.
They maintain [this practice] long-established in their hearts, like a calculation of meanings;
these elements, such as the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), are the constituent parts of that state designated as "Veda," and thus it has attained its established form.
Cultivated according to their nature, they bear fruit when established in the mind; like birds arising from the fluid of their eggs, they emerge and exist in time through the power of consciousness.
One whose self consists of the meaning of the *śruti* and *smṛti*, having died, [attains] that which has been cultivated as foremost.
It perceives everything as having the nature of reality, and that [perception] bestows its fruit upon it.
He by whom the course of the Śruti and Smṛti has not been cultivated even slightly,
falls into dense delusion after death, lacking self-knowledge.
And that man by whom even a slight degree of it has been cultivated, having experienced a fruit corresponding to that measure upon death, is born again in a future birth.
This is whether one has cultivated the path of the *śruti* and *smṛti* or not.

Once this self-existence has been cultivated, one is indeed liberated; of this there is no doubt. Whatever seed falls upon the ground of the mind, however slight it may be, will certainly in time bear its full fruit without fail.

Having heard of the fruits of giving funeral cakes and other offerings in this world, a man who has died will certainly attain them beforehand; he experiences them within himself exactly as his mind was cultivated.
The Chapter Named "The Determination of the Offering of Funeral Cakes."
The one hundred and fiftieth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
In this very context, they cite this ancient history.

Formerly, during the past sixth kalpa, in the eleventh Manvantara, within the fifteenth cycle of four ages (caturyuga), specifically in the Tretā Yuga, on the surface of the earth, there occurred a dialogue between the lord of the Daityas and the preceptor of the gods.

There was a Daitya named Bala, who was like personified strength itself in its arrogance; he crushed other Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas with his flashing pride. He had destroyed all cities and consumed the entire multitude of people.
Having traversed the entire earth and conquered all the lords of the gods,
he subdued the three worlds and took possession of Indra’s abode;
it was like a single small village seized by a bandit in a kingless land.
Śakra, together with his retinue, followed him into servitude,
along with the hosts of world-protectors, apsarases, siddhas, and vidyādharas.
Having seized the sovereignty of Indra from the Lord of Śacī, he protected the kingdom of the world.
He followed the entire conduct correctly and exactly as it should be.
Once, while seated in the assembly, in the course of a conversation that happened to turn toward the subject of human mortality, he questioned his preceptor, the Lord of Speech.
Bala:
How can there be a return for one who has been reduced to ashes and has become extinguished?
And how can there be perception of the next world without a body?
Bṛhaspati said:
Like the water of a mirage, the body appears to the living being;
though its nature is unreal, it manifests through its own consciousness, just as a wave appears in water.
In reality, this [self] is not burned, nor is it born in reality;
nor does it die in reality, yet it experiences suffering intensely.
Whatever the nature of this living being (jīva) becomes, that is the fruit it reaps.
Neither its falsity nor its truthfulness is of any consequence;

O King, by whatever reasoning one may employ, once both the imagining and the non-imagining have ceased, where is there any state of being a living soul, and where are the notions of bondage and liberation?
For even after perceiving [the body], I live for a long time with my body;
yet, when dead, the living self perceives "I am dead," like a bodiless being in a dream.
By means of the offering of funeral cakes and other rites, when further cultivated, one quickly sees [the deceased].
Then it perceives: "I am born," and "I am the experiencer of karma.
"This is death, this is disease, this is the arrival of dying;
this is life; these are my wombs that bestow pleasure and pain."
Thus the person perceives within himself, like the swirling of liquid water;
that which is unmanifested and manifested, born of his own creative wonder (*svacamatkāra*),
is the appearance of life and the appearance of death.
Furthermore, the appearances of otherness are established as belonging to the living soul alone.
In the ultimate sense, neither the body nor the state of being composed of elements exists;
this [world] appears as if real though it is unreal, a mere delusion.
Know that sensation is saṃsāra; the absence of sensation is the absence of saṃsāra.
Whatever the nature of the living being's saṃsāra may be, it perceives exactly in that way.
This much alone is the reasoning stated by the wise.
This is indeed experienced; why then is there such delusion? Within the living being (jīva) exists saṃsāra like oil in a sesame seed, permeating it entirely.
It is not seen that the jīva exists within another saṃsāra, as in the case of dreams and the like.
The state of being a bracelet exists in gold, but the nature of gold does not exist in the state of being a bracelet;
this [distinction] exists through non-investigation, but it is not found here under scrutiny. Through further scrutiny, some do not even perceive the gold itself.
Therefore, there is neither gold nor a living being, nor is the state of being a bracelet real as a part [of it].
O King, that which exists within is experienced only within;
not even the slightest external means or the like is required for this.

The water of a mirage, living beings, and so forth, as well as the experiences corresponding to them—such as sensations of pleasure and pain—are like that; whatever remains beyond these is beyond the reach of speech. Delusion alone has arisen falsely, and false delusion dissolves away.
The remainder is quiescent, beyond the reach of speech; that which exists is neither existent nor non-existent.
This living being, whose contemplation has been cultivated, thinking "I am dead," dies elsewhere while perceiving "I am born."
The living being experiences within itself the aggregates of space, time, action, and substance, which consist of its own mental constructs, just as water experiences the flow of liquid substances;
for the living being is also non-existent, because its nature is that of consciousness which transcends all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, neither the objects of experience nor the act of experiencing exists, nor does the experiencer.

The individual soul (jīva), though unreal, perceives—just as it appears in a dream—a body consisting of its own mental projections, including the earth, the sky, mountains, and the sun; or perhaps it does not perceive it at all.
If the individual soul perceives this [world], it is the manifestation of misfortune;
if it does not perceive it, then the Self alone remains—that auspicious state which is the supreme tranquility.
[That state] in which the restlessness of investigating the meaning of the scriptures has been cast aside, and the weight of the various burdensome activities of the multitude has dissolved.
The Lord [is] that which is entirely free from the delusion arising from experience— since such delusion is impossible— and which is the state of tranquil nirvāṇa.
This is the chapter titled "The Attainment of Quiescence," the one hundred and fifty-first chapter.
Balarāma said:
"O Teacher, it is by no means through any living being— whether existent or non-existent—
or through anything else, nor even through the body itself."
If the fruit of giving alms and other such acts is experienced [by someone else],
then it is my view that the agent has no connection with the fault [of the act].
— Bṛhaspati:

Tell me quickly: for one who holds the view that the sacrificial seat (*kriyāpīṭha*) consisting of the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and so forth belongs to a non-agent, how can a sense of contradiction arise from the mind?
Because there is no mutual dependence and because of the abandonment of ritual action, it is for the welfare of all beings.
Through that, a connection with great sin arises here.
For one who possesses the cognition "I am," there exists the ground of the mind;
whatever seed falls upon it, that necessarily sprouts.
Except for the case of one who is utterly deluded or a child possessing consciousness,
all this is indeed real until the dissolution of creation and the end of destiny;
so too is the entire sequence of duties to be performed, whether by one who is dead or by one who is living.
For that which has been cultivated by him everywhere indeed bestows all fruits.
Bala said:
"If this is so, O Preceptor of the Gods, there is nothing that has not been cultivated."
"I know him to be liberated with a mind like a stone," said Bṛhaspati:
"By whom nothing has been cultivated while remaining in the dullness of a stone."

He is liberated; of this there is no doubt, for liberation is indeed nothing but absolute oneness (*kevalatā*). It is not possible for a living being to be devoid of any mental conception while alive, because as long as one lives, one is indeed composed of some [mental] content apart from [pure] knowledge.
If, by whatever means or reasoning, there is the cultivation of "nothingness," then for one who has not yet ascended,
that which is to be attained will surely remain unascended.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, in ancient times in the city of the gods, Rāma was instructed by the preceptor of the deities, the leader of the asuras, who possessed supreme knowledge.
Therefore, I have related this to you today; reflect upon it here, for it is beautiful, explaining the giving of the *piṇḍa* and other rites.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Dialogue between Bala and Bṛhaspati."
The one hundred and fifty-second canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Whether it be true or false, whether by the unreal or by the real—let it be so.
Whatever is touched even slightly by the mind is necessarily experienced,
whether immediately or at a later time; for once it has been perceived by the mind,
its essence is inevitably experienced within, just as liquidity is experienced within water.
The mind, having once perceived an object that spreads over a period of time,
remains dull, forgetting it, like a lump of the essence of the juice within a peacock’s egg;
it never ceases to exist until it is consumed by the fire of knowledge.
An object once grasped by the mind remains there like the indigo dye on a cloth.

There is no mind without latent impressions (*vāsanā*), just as there is no lampblack without blackness; the flood of latent impressions, whose nature is the multitude of worldly objects, is what is called the "mind."
Furthermore, no existence whatsoever of this mind has been observed, just as darkness is not seen by a lamp; thus, only its non-existence remains.
Therefore, we know nothing other than the mere fact that "there is no mind, nor mental factors, and so forth."
Know that by this knowledge alone this cholera of worldly existence shall be pacified.
Just as the notion of "I-ness" arises in the void, so too does that mind arise;
when it is known that it has not arisen, the mind is stilled through the peace of that realization.
Yoga is defined as the means for the pacification of the mind;
it is said to consist of seven stages. Listen now to the sequence of those stages.
O Rāma, three of these stages have been described to you in their proper order.
Those who abide on the three stages are remembered as great persons.

Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, ever devoted to the inner self, with desires turned away, they are liberated from the pairs of opposites such as pleasure and pain; thus they have attained the three stages.
The One Hundred and Fifty-Third Chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Non-existence of Mind," by Vasiṣṭha:
When ignorance has been brought to exhaustion through the practice of the three stages,
and right knowledge has arisen in the mind— resembling the rising of the full moon—
for the yogi whose mind is disciplined, there exists that which is undivided and without beginning or end.
Those who have reached the fourth stage perceive everything as equal.
When non-duality has attained stability and duality has come to rest,
those who have reached the fourth stage see the world as if in a dream.

Those whose wisdom has not yet fully expanded regarding difference, but whose intellects are peaceful regarding non-difference, shine as knowers of what remains slightly; they have reached the fourth stage.
With the almost total dissolution of what remains slightly, their consciousness resembles that of one half-asleep.
Those who have reached the fourth stage act like children;
those who have reached the fourth stage perceive conceptualization as being as hard as mountains or as dense as the rays of the sun, yet consisting of the nature of mere imagination.
The world sinks into suffering through objects that are either desired or undesired;
therefore, one does not reach even the slightest bit of the fourth stage from this point.
As long as one remains within the first three stages, one is established in the state of waking.
Having attained the fourth stage, the world is seen as resembling a dream;
it appears like a supreme reflection, unstable and transitory.
From this point on, the observer no longer perceives the visible world as the fourth stage.
Rāma: O Sage, if you do not feel weary, please describe accurately the characteristics of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, as well as the fourth state and that which transcends the fourth.
Vasiṣṭha:

For one who has not yet realized the ultimate reality, that state of being absorbed in the contemplation of objects alone is the waking state; it remains unfaded, whether the object be unreal or real.

Even while awake, that which is experienced— whether unreal or indeed real— is joined with the nature of an unreal cognition, because it is destined to perish in an instant and its form has not yet fully blossomed, like that of one seated in the womb.
The best of men call that state "dream" because of the clouding of the intellect;
they call that "deep sleep" (suṣuptaka) the time when there occurs the inevitable cessation of both waking and dreaming experiences.
That which is the state of Buddhahood— tranquil, undifferentiated, beyond waking and dreaming, inexhaustible, not in deep sleep, and established in its own clarity— is called the Fourth (turya).
It is the manifestation of the non-objective for those who have realized the ultimate reality.
That which is free from the three states is established as the fourth (turiya).
These three preceding states are experienced by everyone;
however, this state of the fourth is not attained except by one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Only by one possessing right knowledge, upon the exhaustion of the three internal states,
is the fourth state experienced as the pure self of the space of consciousness.
That state which is experienced by those liberated while bodiless is the experience of that which transcends the fourth.
Through long practice in the state of the Fourth (turya), that [state] does not come within the range of speech;
for the state beyond the Fourth (turyātīta) is not the domain of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Therefore, there is no description of it, as it is nothing other than Brahman itself anywhere.
O you who are skilled in the knowledge of cause and effect, the state of waking is not the cause of dreaming or deep sleep;
for it is the Supreme alone that abides as the ground of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
Through the power of the mind's impurity, the state of waking becomes dream-like.
And the dream state becomes the waking state through the arising of the purity of the intellect.
Through dense delusion, even the waking state enters into the state of deep sleep;
and likewise, O Rāma, this is the very nature of transmigratory existence.
O Rāghava, for one who is prone to sleep as well as for one who is not, these three states persist until the attainment of the fourth state (*turya*), occurring sequentially and not simultaneously.
Furthermore, through the practice of the state of *turya*, the triad of states gradually [dissolves].
It subsides, like the delusion of clouds in a fully mature autumn;
for one established in the fourth state does not again enter the three states,
just as a seed long roasted does not become a sprout even while living.

One who perceives the world as a tree of shadows— luminous in form, yet devoid of trunks, pillars, branches, leaves, and so forth, appearing while being composed of non-existence and consisting of undertakings empty of objective reality— has reached the fourth stage from here.
Just as a child perceives [the world] from within the mud, the wise man perceives the three worlds in this very way;
the wise man perceives the state of the world as being without manifoldness, though appearing manifold, like the formation of waves— devoid of latent desires and consisting of mere vibration.
One who knows that [reality] perceives everything— unseen conduct, what is heard from afar, and momentary destruction— just as an ignorant person perceives an unknown land;
it is like the speech of one tongueless in a dream, comparable to the experience of meditative cultivation.
The wise one perceives the three worlds as merely a wandering between delusion and non-delusion.
Like mist from afar, appearing as a vast form yet being nothing at all when scrutinized by the keen eye, the wise one perceives the three worlds.

The wise one perceives the three worlds as being like an autumn cloud—vast, polished, yet truly nothing at all; devoid of functional activity and empty in essence. Its mandala is constructed from many colors that cannot withstand close examination.
The wise one perceives the three worlds as having the form of peacock feathers—
non-existent, causing delusion, yet appearing when observed, and having come to rest; the wise one perceives the three worlds as resembling a yakṣa seen by a frightened child.
He perceives even an extensive creation that has not yet been entered,
like the beginning of a narrative, as the fourth stage from here; it does not touch upon divisions of space and time, and though unreal, it appears as if real.

From this state, one perceives the world— which is a great roar yet composed of silence, a great undertaking yet devoid of action, gross yet unattainable by the organs of action— as having an unreal form, resembling an army of mental constructs; this is the fourth stage.
Having cultivated that which resides upon the wall of the mind, standing like a painted scroll, one perceives everything as non-creative; from this state comes the fourth stage.
It remains like a magical illusion, water, or a reflection in a mirror.
From this point, one always experiences the fourth stage (*bhūmikā*).
Due to ignorance regarding substance, state, action, and effort, the knower has become like a mute;
like a person sold into a wretched land, he perceives the three worlds.
Like one of small intellect perceiving a different location where there is actually no change in position,
the wise man perceives the three worlds— which are non-empty— as being empty;
he sees that which is not carried as being carried, that which is stable as moving, and the unreal as real.

The knower perceives the three worlds as if they were cities situated within the reflection of a river, or like [cities] submerged in the ocean; or, when [the body] moves due to the throbbing of a fish, the knower perceives the three worlds [as moving along with it].

Like the experience of forms by one blind from birth— which is neither non-existent nor composed of existence— the Knower perceives the three worlds as resembling forms seen by a blind man in the past,
inscribed by his own volition upon a single smooth, great wall.
To the Knower, the world appears like a variegated army, offering no obstruction;
though painted upon the wall of space and ungraspable even by the wind,
the Knower beholds the three worlds as a wondrous painting created by the mind.
Whether the object is visible or invisible, he who is awakened by the effort of another perceives only the external, not knowing what is within; his heart remains unconquered.
This is the chapter titled "The Instruction on the Fourth Stage."
The one hundred and fifty-fourth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
That which was like a fragment of an autumn cloud, having been severed, dissolves away.
He remains with only existence remaining, having transcended the fifth stage.
May he abide in that state which consists of the cultivation and non-cultivation of all words and their meanings,
and which is equal to the perfect existence of the growth of a seed and its sprout.
One should remain in that state which is free from the conceit of "I" and so forth, equal, all-pervading, and stable;
which is the unknowing of the knower, like the blooming of a flower;
non-dual, one, equal, peaceful, and the supreme mass of pure consciousness.
The wise one, perceiving [reality] as clear as the expanse of space, does not perish.

By means of the cognition of non-duality, he stabilizes the contemplation of the non-dual nature of all things previously perceived through the notion of difference; thus, he remains equanimous toward all objects, like one in deep sleep.
With the destruction of the veil that obscures the intensely luminous consciousness of deep sleep,
he neither sets nor rises, neither stands still nor moves;
with the appearance of duality dissolved, he has awakened within.
From this state, one remains in the fifth stage, which is indeed a dense state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*).
For one who perceives "I-ness," it never subsides;
it is like a bee in the calyx of the heart-lotus, a cholera-like poison known as *saṃsṛti* (transmigration).
Just as water [perceives] whirlpools and the like through its own mind, intellect, and ego,
so too does Brahman perceive the three worlds through space, time, and other factors.
For one who conceives of "I-ness" and "you-ness," that [state of duality] never ceases.

The beauty of the *ahantva* (I-ness) is like sesame oil; it is the virulent cholera of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). That which was the fragrance of worldly existence within the bud of *ahantva* now stands manifest externally as this world has blossomed.

Just as the fragrance of a lotus is never separate [from the flower], so too the state of "I-ness" (ahantva) is never separate from the nature of the self, which consists of both the seer and the seen. That state of "I-ness" belongs to one's own essential form.
It has freely given itself the two names "inner" and "outer.
When examined, it is not the state of "I," nor does it exist either inside or outside;
this is an illusion appearing in an unreal form, fleeing from one's own observation.
Just as the water of a mirage, though non-existent, appears when examined,
so too is the delusion of the "I" and so forth dissolved;
for the triad of the seer, the seen, and the seeing is like the water of a mirage.
"There is nothing for anyone other than this; this is the pervasive, peaceful, and auspicious [state].
Possessing such certainty, the Great Being, whose nature transcends both unity and duality, remains equanimous in auspiciousness, having reached the fifth stage from here.
Abiding in inwardness, even while engaged in outward activity,
he appears as if constantly asleep due to his perpetual tranquility. In this worldly transaction, he is neither within, nor in the sky, nor without.
Then, having dissolved the mind, he who is of the nature of space either rejoices or wanders;

like one in deep sleep, even while awake, he does not conceive the delusion of the visible world. Arising from the destruction of all objective states and no longer perceiving even his own consciousness within, the wise man stands firm like a painted man.
The one hundred and fifty-fifth canto, titled "The Yoga of the Fifth Stage," by Vasiṣṭha:
Practicing in this stage and becoming free from latent impressions,
he gradually descends to another stage, the sixth, which is designated as the Fourth (turyā),
wherein there is neither non-existence nor the nature of existence, neither "I" nor even the absence of egoism.
That state remains as pure consciousness alone, with the mind extinguished and all latent impressions gone;
free from knots, peaceful in its true nature, liberated while living, and beyond conceptualization.
It abides as stainless, once-and-for-all enlightened, having transcended both duality and unity.
Liberated while living, devoid of worldly flavor, undifferentiated, and as beautiful as the sky;
though not yet extinguished, he is extinguished, remaining steady like a painted lamp.
Because he is free from latent impressions and devoid of relish, he does nothing at all.
Even while acting in this manner, he remains like a piece of wood, being in fact a non-doer therein. One who is endowed with perfect vision and has attained the state of liberation while living,
seeing this world as it truly is, is not bound by actions.
While acting, he does nothing; though a goer, he does not go;
though eating, he does not eat; and though speaking, he does not speak.
Such is the agency and enjoyment of a man who perceives a dream while awake.
Know, O Rāghava, what those two states of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) are like:
equal-minded, tranquil in intellect, silent, free from latent impressions, the one liberated while living regards the seer, the act of seeing, and the object seen as being like space.

One whose mind is set on nirvāṇa perceives oneself and others, the mountain and the atom, the dog and the brahmin, and the sun— all as being like space. Perfected, one beholds the peaceful, supreme, singular, and uncreated radiance.
Where has it set? Where will it rise? What kind of form does it have here?
Having ascended the palace of wisdom, the wise man, beyond grief, looks upon grieving people;
like one standing on a mountain peak looking down at those on the ground, the enlightened one observes everyone.
He has no purpose whatsoever here through action, nor any through inaction;
nor does he have any dependence on any living being for any object of interest.
Like water poured into water, he has attained oneness with Brahman alone.
Even while awake, one for whom the appearance of duality has dissolved experiences the state of deep sleep;
perceiving this entire world of moving and non-moving things on all sides, he does not perceive them as such.
Having lost the sense of "I," though seeing, he does not see the distinctions of difference.
Like the space within broken pots and jars merging into the space of the sky, he has entered a single, uniform, unreal, and peaceful state within the Supreme.
Though not yet extinguished, he is as if extinguished; like a child, he moves about.
Released from the sense of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) remains established.
Although the diseases of existence—attachment and aversion—have reached their end, they do not affect him;
just as all beasts and birds do not perceive the sky.
With the mist of egoism completely stilled, its form serene and expansive,
it shines like the autumnal sky— though empty in essence, as if not empty—
having attained a state of gentleness, as if intoxication had subsided.
Deeply asleep upon the earth, he appeared as if led to heaven;
because he was entirely immersed in bliss, he reached a state beyond [ordinary] bliss;
and because his nature was pure consciousness alone, he remained as if devoid of consciousness.
Like an ocean without Mount Mandara, like a fire whose fuel is consumed,
and like a wheel whose delusion has ceased, he attained tranquility within his very self;
as if carved by Tvaṣṭṛ on a lathe, he assumed an unprecedented form.
In another season, like a tree, he arises as something else;
tranquil yet lovely, radiant yet beautiful with light,
as if carved from the orb of the moon, gentle and a source of delight.
Empty within and empty without, like an empty jar in the sky;
full within and full without, like a full jar in the ocean.
Freed from modification and the like, he is as if abandoned by death.
Like one who has emerged from a great disease, he has crossed the unfathomable ocean of existence;
his self exhausted by the fatigue of the long journey, he is like one who has awakened after a deep sleep,
or like a sleeper regarding the visible world as if it were a dreamless slumber.
Cool within and without, as if fashioned from frost;
filled within and without with light, like pure water;
clear within and without, appearing like a gem within itself.
Empty within and without, he was fashioned like the sky; having conquered through the state of mindlessness, he remained like a statue,
while the multitude of his active senses moved at will like a mechanical puppet.
With the thought "May I be," through the complete exhaustion of the internal craving for the existence of the self and the ego,
that living lamp, having gone out, dissolves into the Self alone—
eternally satisfied, blissful, free from suffering, and without dependence.
Free from attachment, devoid of purposeful intent, knowing, and without desire, he is not bound.
For him there is no body, nor karma and the like, nor the triad of the seen, the seer, and the act of seeing;
there is no life, no death, neither non-existence, nor existence-and-non-existence, nor even pure existence.
This [world] has become something or other, or perhaps it is nothing at all;
it is either pure sensation alone, or perhaps mere cognition.
Nothing exists other than this single reality, which, like a single object, encompasses both the internal and the external.
Though situated far, it is not far away, like an infinite thread spread out;
even amidst many states, it remains eternally one in essence, equal and stainless,
its glory of differentiated qualities stilled, like the Great Time (Mahākāla) which is yet devoid of parts.

They call that indescribable Essence, which is the unborn, immortal, beginningless, awakened, pure from beginning to end, auspicious, stainless, beyond speech, omnipresent, peaceful, and one; the Lord who is both outside and not outside, the supreme knower, the foremost manifestation, and the ultimate appearance.
The Chapter titled "Description of the Sixth Stage."
The one hundred and fifty-sixth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
The meanings of "I-ness," "bodiness," and so forth, have long since dissolved away.

Therefore, even though he is a knower, that one who is liberated while living has attained oneness with the sky. That state is beyond the reach of words; it is the ultimate limit within the realms of existence, and here it is the further shore of the boundless ocean of saṃsāra.

By some she was called Śiva; by others she was proclaimed as Brahmā; by some she was declared to be Jñapti (Consciousness); by others she was remembered as Śūnya (the Void). By some she was inferred to be Artha (the Object), and by others she was taken to be Kāla (Time).
By some it is conceived as the distinction between primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*);
by others, in various other ways through diverse conceptualizations of the self,
it is indeed taught as something entirely different, though it is eternally indefinable.
This state of absolute liberation from the body is realized only by those who are themselves liberated from the body,
and by such as they with their minds; it is not perceived by others, nor by those established in the *sattva* quality, nor by those established in the *citta*.
For liberation while in the body is not truly called "liberation without the body" (videhamukti).
Indeed, for those whose intellects are unattached, whose latent impressions have been destroyed through knowledge,
and who have reached the third stage (bhūmikā), the mind no longer exists.
The wise say that when there is ignorance, the mind becomes dense;
it is the cause that brings about further births and the growth of the trees of worldly existence.
Through knowledge, the mind’s sap is exhausted, and it is no longer composed of the latent impressions of rebirth.
That is called *sattva* by those who know it; those established in that state abide in the station of *sattva*.

Abiding in *sattva*, having reached the state of having their latent impressions (*vāsanā*) burnt away by the fires of knowledge, these individual souls (*jīvas*), being exhausted, no longer produce the sprout of saṃsāra.
That which is not perceived by these states—whether they be those of the mind or those of the pure essence—is this seventh stage; it is called the bodiless liberation.
O descendant of Raghu, these stages have thus been described by me to you.
Through the practice of these [stages], no suffering is experienced.
O Knower of Causes, establish your footing upon these stages while performing your own various duties without deficiency;
remain here for a long time as one liberated while living, and then, at the end, having become bodiless (videha), abide in the single, exalted state.
The one hundred and fifty-seventh canto, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of the Seventh Stage," by Vasiṣṭha.

There is an elephant-cow who is eternally intoxicated and moves with gentle, slow gait; she is intent on physical form and endowed with great tusks. If she is indeed slain, she will surely bring about misfortune upon misfortune.
Therefore, while these stages remain intact, a man may be victorious; but as long as that female elephant, intoxicated with rut, has not been conquered,
what warrior indeed could prevail in the deserts of Mara?
Rāma:
Who is that negligent female elephant? And what are those battlefields?
How is she being struck down, and where is her established position?
Vasiṣṭha:
Let this desire for Rāma be like a female elephant,
appearing in this form, intoxicated within the forest of the body, and causing manifold exultations.
With senses intoxicated like fierce young elephants, speaking with the sweet voice of a female elephant,
she is hidden within the thicket of the mind and wanders through the forest of her own desires;
by means of these expansions of karma, she causes every grove to flourish.

The rivers called "bodies" and "passions," from which pleasure and pain spread forth like spray, possess waves of fear; these very waves are the surges of pleasure and pain, while merit and demerit are their two banks.
One's own karmas, whether extensive and auspicious or inauspicious,
the existence and non-existence of things, the whirlpools of becoming, and the circular courses of life— these,
intoxicated by their own momentum, move upward and downward, with great roots and tips.
The playful movements are the endless comings and goings through the stages of existence;
death is the movement of the lotus stalks, and life is the succession of foam. The great waves are the performance of actions, and cravings are the tributary streams.
Heaven is a bed of rice and other grains; hell is a seat of mud.
Wife and children are minnows; the realms of enjoyment are crocodiles.
Wealth is a row of stones, difficult to grasp and possessing treacherous claws.

The next world is a great ocean, and mental anxieties are its circle of waves. By means of those rivers of passion, that serpent of desire moving within the heart destroys these wretched *jīvajīvaka* birds.

Impression (*vāsanā*), desire (*īhā*), mind (*manas*), consciousness (*citta*), volition (*saṅkalpa*), cultivation (*bhāvanā*), longing (*spṛhā*)— this collection of names resides within the treasury of one's own heart;
it flows forth with effortless ease when the lotus-pond of fortitude is churned.
One should conquer with one's whole being this desire, which is like a female serpent and consists of the self of all things;
for as long as the thought "let this be" expands within,
so long do the fierce cholera-like poisons of the great venom of miserable saṃsāra persist.
The mist of wretchedness persists only so long as the whirlpool of desire;
once this has vanished, the living soul shines like the autumnal sky.
Such alone is saṃsāra: the thought that "let this be."
But the pacification of this [suffering] is liberation; such is the summary of knowledge.
For the fool, who is seized by the grip of false attachments and craves "let this be," waves surge around like rivers in the rainy season.
For one whose mind has risen above desire, no instruction whatsoever finds a resting place within;
it is like a reflection of the earth’s surface in a mirror,
or like a pearl in a clear, stainless, and desireless form that produces serenity.
