The word of instruction comes to rest like a drop of oil upon a mirror. Even a desire that has arisen to the slightest degree, which brings about misfortune, must be severed by the weapon of the effort of one's own consciousness, just as a row of poison-sprouts is cut away.
A living being permeated by desire does not abandon its wretchedness,
just as water mixed with powdered clay does not abandon its state of mud.
The wise say that the skill of snapping the bonds of desire is the fourth [state].
That task must be performed with effort by the most excellent of noble ones, through the consciousness of magnanimity;
for those who are ignorant, the supreme state is attained by the cutting away of desire,
just as birds reach the highest station by breaking their bonds.
By mere non-perception, the sprout of desire for existence does not arise,
just as a sprout does not emerge from a seed-pod without the watering accomplished by one's own effort.
Know that what is called "non-perception" is simply sitting silently within.
Oh, what a lack of attention there is toward such a trivial matter!
Whether he is inactive or active, let the person remain with a full mind,
staying like a stone, not perceiving pleasure or anything else within.
Lead that fish of desire away from its bait of food— that woman by whom a hundred corpses were eaten with extreme vigilance—
having uprooted the mooring-post of her mental constructs with the ease of a rutting Airāvaṇa.
Taking your stand with ease, become a conqueror of the three worlds.
Having long reflected within your heart upon the supreme mantra joined with the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*),
quickly bring the poison of conceptual construction to old age, and may you conquer all the diseases of existence.
The one hundred and fifty-eighth canto, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Will," [spoken by] Rāma.

"O Brahmin, how is it possible that through the state of actionlessness and the abandonment of mental constructs, the body of an embodied being falls away so swiftly while he is still alive? Vasiṣṭha replied:
The abandonment of conceptual construction is appropriate for one who is living, but not for one who is dead.
Listen to its true nature, which is an ornament for the ears:
those skilled in conceptualization say that conceptualization is indeed the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāvana).
The cultivation of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is called the renunciation of conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*).
Those who know conceptual construction say that the very essence of the categories of existence is itself conceptual construction;
the cultivation of the meaning of the negative particle is called the renunciation of conceptual construction.
The highest [sages] say that the agitation of thinking "let this be" is volition (*saṅkalpa*);
the cultivation of the meaning of its negation is called the abandonment of volition.
Know that volition is remembrance; they know the auspicious state to be non-remembrance.
That which was previously experienced and that which was not experienced are both cultivated.
Having forgotten the cause— the memory of what was experienced and what was not experienced—
and having quickly forgotten everything, remain as a hidden great sage.
By the mere non-recollection [of objects], one remains amidst past actions,
like the movement of a half-asleep infant toward habitual occurrences;
it proceeds without volition, like a wheel turning in its flow.
O sinless one, act in your duties accordingly through the power of prior impressions;
being without a [separate] mind, you have entered into the impressions of pure being (sattva). Act in your own duties as they fall into the natural flow.
With arms upraised I cry out, yet no one hears me.
That supreme good which is free from all mental construction—why is it not contemplated within?
Alas for the power of delusion, that this destroyer of all suffering [is ignored]!
The wish-fulfilling gem called discernment, though situated within the heart, is abandoned by people.
Let there be non-perception and no mental construction; let one become absorbed in that very state.
This much is the supreme good; let it be experienced by oneself.

It is said, O Rāma, that by remaining in silence alone, that supreme state is attained, wherein even universal sovereignty is regarded as a mere blade of grass. Just as for a traveler whose sole focus is the destination to be reached, [the movement] of his feet [is effortless].
Move in your actions like one whose intentions are unknown;
having completely forgotten the enjoyment of the fruits of all deeds, move without sensation, as if asleep,
toward the task that has come down by the current of events.
Vibrate with thoughts free from volition, disregarding pleasure and pain;
like a blade of grass caught and released by the current,
let your internal cultivation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa-bhāvana*) be without attachment toward actions as they arise in the natural flow.
Like a wooden automaton performing actions for the sake of another,
let all your perceptions through the senses be devoid of sapor,
like creepers in the winter season, recognizable only by their outward form.

Remain like a tree in winter with a creeper— by means of the sap of the sun of awakening, by the existence of the six groups of senses that have ceased to quiver, and by being free from the trembling of the bodily machine;
maintain only those internal juices of knowledge, even though they are active.
Through one's own effort, the senses are quickly subdued, just as the winter season withers trees.
For one who acts with these active senses, or likewise for one who does not act,
this caravan of the miseries of saṃsāra never comes to rest.
If you vibrate without conceptual construction, like the movement of wind, flame, a machine, or water,
then you are fashioned for infinite well-being.
This alone is the supreme fortitude that wards off the fever of birth.

That state of agency in one's own habitual actions which is free from latent impressions (avāsana). Free from latent impressions and free from volitional construction (asaṅkalpa), following whatever occurs naturally,
move slowly in your actions like the whirling motion of a potter’s wheel.
Let there be no thought of the fruit of action, nor let there be attachment to inaction;

either abandon both of these, or take refuge in both. What is the use of saying much here? This is stated in brief: [let there be no thought of the fruit of action, nor let there be attachment to inaction]. Either abandon both of these, or take refuge in both. What is the use of saying much here? This is stated in brief.
Volitional construction is the supreme bondage; its absence is liberation.
Here, there is nothing whatsoever to be done, nor anything not to be done, anywhere.
Everything is Śiva—without beginning or end, infinite; remain as you were before.
Perceiving inaction within action and action within inaction,
you who know the nature of things as they truly are, remain at peace and as you please.
They know that yoga is the state of non-perception, a peaceful and imperishable abiding.
Established in yoga, perform actions without attachment, or else do not perform them at all.
They know yoga to be the absence of sensation, the unartificial cessation of the mind;
having become entirely absorbed in that, remain as you are, O sir.
In that state which is equal, peaceful, auspicious, subtle, devoid of both duality and unity,
pervasive, infinite, and pure— what indeed can exist, and by what means?
Let your volition rejoice within you like a sprout in a desert.
May your desire delight like a creeper within the hollow of a stone;
for one who is peaceful and free from sensation— whether living or not living—
there is no purpose here in what is done, nor any at all in what is left undone.
In that which is peaceful within, eternal, and of an undifferentiated nature, there is neither action nor inaction;
nor are there actions even in action, nor agency even in the agent.
Perceiving "I" and "mine," you are not liberated from suffering.
Unaware [of this], you are liberated; take that which is desired.
"I" and "mine" do not exist; that which exists is sufficient, it is the supreme Śiva.
Beyond the highest, however, is this Śiva—soundless and devoid of objects.
Whatever is seen as this world is indeed nothing at all; it appears like the state of being a bracelet in gold, yet it does not truly exist.
They know that the cessation of objects is simply non-perception; thereafter, that alone remains—the truth, the ultimate reality.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of the Cure for Desire."
The one hundred and fifty-ninth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Non-dual unity is free from mental construction, peaceful, and established within the Self.
Just as an army is composed of puppets, so too is the world composed of Śiva;
likewise, the mind, ego, intellect, and so forth, are likewise made of that [Śiva],
joined with the arrangement of time, form, action, sound, and power.
The sequences of form, light, and mind consist of nothing but the mud of Śiva;
because they are identical with Him and because He is infinite, what is perceived by whom?
Measurement, the object of measurement, the means of knowledge, space, time, the directions, and so forth—all are likewise.
The manifestation of existence and non-existence consists essentially of the mud of Śiva;
therefore, O Knower, remain with an unattached mind, like one observing the silence of a stone within its interior, extracting from the supreme ether the essence of "I" and "mine," and nothing else.
Rāma:
O Lord, for the knower who does not contemplate the unreal nature of "I" and "mine," what auspicious result arises from the renunciation of attachment to actions and from their performance?
Vasiṣṭha said:
O sinless one, tell me quickly what I ask of you;
if you know it in its true essence, then what is this so-called "action"?
"What is the extent of karmas, what is their root, and how is that which is to be destroyed thoroughly destroyed? Tell me how it is destroyed.
Rāma said:
That which is to be destroyed must surely be destroyed skillfully;
O Blessed One, it is by scraping away the root, not by cutting away the branches and such.
Indeed, a wise person should destroy their own karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
By the destruction of its root through grinding, that tree is utterly destroyed.
O Brahmin, I shall describe the roots of the tree of karma; listen to me, for by the grinding away of which it becomes rootless and does not sprout again.
O Brahmin, this body has arisen as a tree of karma;
it has grown in the forest of saṃsāra, endowed with the various creepers of its limbs.
Of this tree whose seed is karma, there is a succession of fruits consisting of pleasure and pain.
Of this life which has the waking state as its springtime and the deep sleep as its winter;
which produces clusters and bunches of the buds of purifying conduct;
which is lovely with the youthfulness of a moment and laughs at the flower of old age.
At every moment, its form is shattered by the monkeys that are its waves;
from within the belly of the winter of sleep, the petals of its dreams emerge;
and the succession of its leaves—its worldly desires—is withered by the autumn of its own old age.
For this world-grove, whose wife is a bed of grass,
the delicate limbs— the hands, feet, ankles, and so forth— are its reddish leaves;
they have slender stalks, possess beautiful lines, and are ever-moving.
The fingers are like young sprouts—ruddy, trembling in the wind, soft, and smooth in form; though smeared with sinews and bones, they are full of life.
Soft yet sharp-pointed, they grow repeatedly upon their stalks.
The sprouts, which have the form of the rays of the second moon, are the shells of the nails;
for they are the roots of the fully blossomed karma, appearing in the form of the body—
firm and knotted as the organs of action.
Bound together by sinews, bones, and knots, they are like bodies sunk in mud;
swollen with the essence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they consist of their own vital blood-essence;
they possess ankles, firm limbs, excellent skin, and are smooth.
Know that their roots are indeed the faculties of perception;
though they have gone very far away, those five pillars are steeped in the mud of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and they are both flavorful and great.
The root of those [senses] is the vast pillar of the mind, which pervades the three worlds;
it is drawn by the five streams of the channels and consists of the flowing essence of infinite objects.
They know its root to be the individual soul (*jīva*), whose nature is consciousness directed toward objects of thought.
Consciousness is the root of the individual soul (jīva), and it is the single cause of all roots.
But Brahman is the root of that [consciousness], and its root is not found,
because it is inexpressible, infinite, pure, and of the nature of reality.
For all actions, such perception is the supreme seed;
having willed their own form within, from that, movement proceeds.
O Sage, consciousness alone is said to be the primordial seed of actions.

When that exists, the great-branched śālmali tree of the body is born. If this object denoted by the word "consciousness" is permeated by meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), it becomes the seed of karma; otherwise, the supreme state remains to be attained.
If consciousness is permeated by the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the meaning of the word "consciousness," then it becomes the seed of karma; otherwise, the supreme state remains to be attained.
Therefore, in this world, cognition alone is the cause of the formation of karma.
"O Lord of Sages, you yourself have stated that this is the seed of actions.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O Rāghava, regarding this subtle action whose nature is perception—"
What is renunciation, and what is the practice, as long as this body remains?
Whatever is perceived by that [mind] immediately becomes both external and internal—
whether it has a true form or an untrue one— provided that delusion has been instilled.
If it is not perceived, then one is sufficiently liberated from this delusion;
whether the delusion be real or unreal, what is the use of this investigation?
This very consciousness itself blossoms within through the delusions of arising.
Through names such as latent impression (*vāsanā*), desire (*icchā*), mind (*manas*), action (*karman*), and volition (*saṅkalpa*),
the sense of self exists within the house of the body for both the awakened and the unawakened embodied being,
until the end of the body; yet its abandonment is not found.
How indeed could the abandonment of that which is living be possible?
When there is the cultivation or non-cultivation of the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) regarding the meaning of the word "action" (*karman*),
action itself, having relinquished its state as action, becomes unborn (*aja*) by its very nature.
For he who performs action without the possibility of renouncing it has not accomplished anything at all by that renunciation of the sense that "this must be done. Rather,
true renunciation is the spontaneous dissolution of the perception of "this-ness" through awakening.
The wise know that renunciation of the world is non-attachment and indeed liberation.
Since there is no perceiver when there is nothing to be perceived, the vision of the object of perception did not exist even at the beginning of creation;
it has never arisen. Therefore, what is perception, and where could it be?
That which is the very nature of perception, having completely abandoned its orientation toward the object of knowledge, is not perception;
it is not action, and is called the peaceful Brahman.
Consciousness, when expanded by the cycle of transmigration, is said to be action.
They know liberation to be insentient, and the wise one to be the object of cognition; such is the understanding derived from instruction.

Therefore, the renunciation of actions is not possible as long as the body exists. For those by whom action is abandoned do not become liberated, because they have not abandoned that which is its root.
The root of one's own karma is consciousness, which consists of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the mind;
and that [consciousness] cannot be eradicated until the body [is transcended], except through awakening.
O Rāma, this supreme inner faculty is solely rooted in karma.

Subtle consciousness is cut away by its own effort through the non-perception [of itself]. By that very means through which consciousness is warded off by the non-perception of itself, the scraping away of the root of the tree of saṃsāra is accomplished.
That which is non-conscious space is unborn and one; therein exists this [world], yet it is devoid of objective reality.
Since it is of the nature of space, they say that this very [space] is thus free from affliction and has consciousness as its essence.
The Chapter Named "Instruction on the Method for Burning the Seed of Karma."
The one hundred and sixtieth canto.
Rāma said:
"O Lord of Sages, how can the non-perception of sensation be brought about?"
The non-existent has no being; the existent has no non-being.
Vasiṣṭha said:
The non-existent has no being; the existent has no non-being.
At that very moment, the perception of sensation is easily understood by oneself.
Know that these two—the word "sensation" and its meaning—are like the delusion of a snake in a rope; they have arisen falsely and are equal to the water of a mirage.
But non-understanding of these two is better; understanding of them leads to suffering.
Therefore, O Rāghava, understand only that which is real; do not understand that which is unreal. For a living being, the understanding of the meaning of the word "feeling" causes supreme suffering.
Having set aside the understanding of the meaning of words and cognition, remain as you truly are.
On this occasion of universal awakening, when the emergence of nirvāṇa occurs through both cognition and the meaning of words, let there be the supreme "Om" alone; be stilled.
One who possesses discernment must destroy their own karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
this is accomplished through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), by realizing that such karma does not exist.
Through the grinding away of the root of karma, *saṃsāra* comes to rest.
When one has thoroughly investigated and searched until no further action remains,
the nature of consciousness is like the pith of a wood-apple; whatever various designations it assumes within itself,
it acts just as the wood-apple does, without differing even in the slightest degree.
Likewise, within the mass of Brahman, multiplicity appears as if it were manifold; yet since it appears as if manifold, it does not differ from it in the slightest.
Just as an internal arrangement is not separate from that which possesses the arrangement.
Likewise, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) and so forth is not separate from the other [term] even in the slightest degree.
Just as that which is internal is itself internal, and liquidity is not distinct [from water],
so too non-existence (*avittva*) is indeed existence (*vittva*), because the meanings of the negative particle are of that very nature.
Just as liquidity exists in water and light in fire,
so too, within Brahman, there is no consciousness that is not of its nature;
for consciousness is action, and that is rooted within it, like a phantom that causes delusion.
If that [consciousness] arises without a cause, then what has not arisen does not exist.
This consciousness is action; it shines like a vibration in the wind.
When this self is without cause, it appears both externally and internally along with its objects and thoughts.
The expansion of karmas is the body; it is the ego-sense, and it is transmigratory existence.
By becoming insentient through the absence of ego, it subsides like a motionless wind.
Through the cessation of perception, having become the infinite Self, even though it is a knower, it becomes like a stone.
In this saṃsāra, perform the uprooting [of existence] like the snout of a boar;
in this way, the abandonment of the sheath of the minute particles of the seeds of karma will be accomplished.
Not otherwise, O Rāghava—may there be eternal peace for you.
But when this minute portion of the seed of karma has been abandoned in the other self,
which does not exist for the living being according to those who know reality— those who are peaceful— nothing whatsoever is grasped, nor is anything abandoned.
They do not know what to abandon or to take up; therefore, they remain in peace.
With hearts as empty as space, those wise ones remain exactly as things are.
They act according to what arises, yet they neither cling to it nor do they act with effort.

The organs of action of those whose minds are peaceful vibrate with a movement that has fallen into the natural flow; they are like children who are half-asleep. Though they have attained the essence of the taste, they are utterly devoid of craving for it.
Neither within nor without do the wise or the ignorant remain, like those who are skillful.
The non-perception of action is its abandonment, and that is accomplished through awakening;
since it is not a real entity, what is there to be gained by doing or by not doing?

That which is without sensation, beyond being perceived, free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), settled, peaceful, equanimous, and without mental delineation— that is called the renunciation of karma. That which is not remembered again, being perfectly and long-forgotten, is [the true state].
Remaining like the interior of a pillar— that is called the renunciation of action.
Those of futile understanding who treat non-renunciation as renunciation— for them, stuck in the pit, the Creator will provide no protection.

The demoness of renunciation-of-action devours those ignorant ones who perform only half of their duty without having first abandoned action entirely. But those who have established themselves in peace by means of the total abandonment of action along with its very roots—
For them, there is no purpose whatsoever here in what is done, nor any in what is left undone.
Having utterly uprooted even the smallest portion of the seed of karma along with its root,
those who know that reality remain perfectly happy, eternally established in one-pointed concentration.
When an action occurs spontaneously, they move with slight effort, lacking absorption in it;
they are as if reeling like drunkards or as if driven by a machine.
They are like those afflicted by a passion for the playful goddess of liberation.
Having reached an indescribable state of realization that is like being half-asleep and half-awake,
that which is abandoned along with its very root is said to be truly abandoned;
whereas an abandonment that does not uproot the foundation is merely like the lopping off of branches.
The tree of karma, whose roots have not been uprooted, though its branches are lopped off at the tips,
grows again with a thousand branches for the sake of suffering.
My dear friend, the abandonment of karma is accomplished by means of this [insight] which is devoid of the nature of sensation.
Therefore, do not proceed by any other means than this; bring about this very state.
But those who, without thus renouncing action, are set upon something else, kill the sky—which is the nature of renunciation—by means of non-renunciation.
Through its very nature as awakening, the abandonment of action is spontaneously accomplished;
like a burnt seed, being utterly free from desire, even non-action becomes action itself.
Action performed by means of the organs of perception bears fruit because of the cultivation of its essence.
Like a rope that has been wound around and then released, another movement born of the body is fruitless.

When the renunciation of karma is established through awakening, one who is liberated while living and free from latent impressions— whether staying at home or in the forest— is at peace, whether remaining still or engaging in activity.
For one who is tranquil, even a secluded house far from the forest is a place of solitude;
for one who is not tranquil, even a lonely forest is a crowded city.
For the wise man of peaceful mind, there are no people to be found even in a dream.

For the wise one for whom the visible world has been extinguished, the forest ground is the heart itself—spotless, expansive, and delightful; it consists of the mind alone and is devoid of objective entities, with all particular objects stilled. The entire world is but a great wilderness.
For the ignorant man who possesses infinite volitions and for whom the world arises within his own heart,
the entire ocean of the earth revolves only within that very heart; for the dense, ignorant,
and wretched one, it is a state fraught with the perils of manifold dualities.

The circle of villages, with its vast forms and energetic undertakings, exists within the heart alone; the earth, consisting of various states of activity and transformation, along with its circles of cities, towns, and mountains, appears reflected in the heart— pure when it is pure, and impure when it is defiled, like a reflection in a mirror-case.
The One Hundred and Sixty-First Chapter, titled "The Teaching on the Cessation of the Visible," by Vasiṣṭha.

When the world, beginning with the "I-conqueror" (sāhan), has been stilled within awakening whose nature is the power of consciousness (saṃvit-kalā), renunciation—which resembles the extinguishing of a lamp—is accomplished; it is not otherwise.
Renunciation is not the abandonment of ritual action; rather, awakening is known as renunciation.
That which is the single essence of the manifestation of the non-world, devoid of "I-ness" and the like, and imperishable—
[one realizes] "This is he, this is I, this is mine," yet like a lamp without oil,
when [all is] stilled in supreme nirvāṇa, only the self that is pure awakening remains.
For one who does not possess the knowledge that "this is he," "this is I," or "this is mine"— that this [self] is peaceful— for such a person there is neither peace, nor renunciation, nor liberation.
When the destruction of even these notions— "this is mine" and "I am this very one"— has occurred, [then one attains peace].

Śiva is the essence of awakening and is peaceful; there exists nothing other than that. When the "I"-portion has been dissolved by consciousness, everything indeed comes to an end. Nothing whatsoever remains dissolved anywhere; it abides as a single, dense mass of nirvāṇa.
The notion of "I" subsides without obstacle precisely through the absence of the notion of "I";
since this [liberation] is to be accomplished by this much alone, why is there such torment? Furthermore, the delusion that "I am not" does not exist apart from the state of being conscious.
Since your consciousness is as clear as space, where then can this state of delusion exist?
There is no delusion, no act of wandering, no error, nor is there any deluded person.
This is merely a lack of vision; through true vision, this [delusion] does not exist for you.
Know that this entire expanse is merely consciousness alone, resembling the nature of the non-existent;
Om, enough! Remain in silence; thus everything is nothing but nirvāṇa.
By that very moment, in the blink of an eye, one perceives "I am" indeed.

Having quickly resolved "I am not" by means of that very [knowledge], one does not grieve. Having extinguished the sense of "I" with the meaning of the negative particle, like an arrow that has been shot, remain constantly intoxicated by the flow [of bliss], firmly established in that state.
If you perceive this non-selfhood as being devoid of any other object,
then, remaining unattached to all states of existence, become one who has crossed the ocean of saṃsāra—
provided that you possess the heroism to conquer even your own innate nature.
Tell me, what talk can there even be of such a person attaining the supreme state?
He who has previously conquered the sixfold group by himself through the knowledge of the highest truth is a vessel for the preeminent qualities; no other is anything but a human donkey.
He whose mental activity within himself is either being conquered or has already been conquered regarding sense objects— he is called a man among the discerning.
Whatever object falls upon you, like a stone in the ocean, [leaves no mark].
Therefore, flee from that very [notion] by cultivating the thought, "I am not this.

Even though you have understood through reasoning that "I am not," and even though you are the Knower who is pure consciousness (*jñaptimātra*) by virtue of knowledge, why do you still delude yourself like an ignorant person?
In this [consciousness], there is no reality of the "I" in the object of knowledge, just as there is no reality of bracelets and such in gold;
that [notion] exists only through delusion, and it is stilled for you by non-recollection.
Whatever state arises within you, like a vibration in the wind, [is likewise unreal].

"By means of the mental modification 'I am not,' lead that [ego-sense] to a state of having no substratum. "How could he who has already conquered greed, shame, pride, and delusion at the very outset engage in this useless and harmful pursuit?"
That which exists within you, the Supreme Self, is non-different from you, just as vibration is non-different from the wind; it is like vibration in the air.
Through the consciousness of non-creation, creation shines forth as existing within the Supreme.
For even a bad object shines by means of a particular arrangement.
But the Supreme Self never rises nor ever sets;
and since there is nothing other than this, what state could there be—neither existence nor non-existence?
The supreme is full within the supreme; the tranquil is tranquil within the tranquil; Śiva is Śiva within Śivā. Thus, this alone is spread out: neither "I," nor the world, nor the intellect.
Non-extinction is extinction within the tranquil; the tranquil is auspicious within the auspicious.
Even Nirvana does not exist within Nirvana, nor is it even that [which one attains].
Wounds from weapons are endured, and the pains of disease are borne;
what hardship is there in enduring merely the thought "I am not"?
The sprout "I" is imperishable for the multitude of objects in the world;
when that [sprout] is brought to rootlessness, the world has reached rootlessness.
By means of the referent "I," though devoid of essence, the world appears to possess essence, as if by a mere vapor.

The dark [intellect] is like a supreme mirror; it becomes perfectly clear upon the cessation of that [activity]. The referent "I" is like motion in the supreme wind; but upon the subsiding of that, it is indefinable, without appearance, infinite, unborn, and immutable.
Others hold that the referent "I" (ahamartha) presents a reflection of an external object before consciousness;
upon the dissolution of that [object], it remains without passion and without reflection.
The referent "I" presents a reflection of an external object before consciousness.
Upon the cessation of that [ego-sense], she becomes the supreme, solitary state, free from all appearances.
When the cloud of the sense of "I" has perished, the autumnal sky of ultimate reality shines forth,
pure and radiant with its own infinite, stainless splendor.

O dear one, if the copper of egoity is freed from the impurity of the sense of "I," it becomes the supreme, radiant manifestation, possessing the splendor of gold. Just as the beauty of an object beyond description attains a state that cannot be designated.
In this way, this non-egoity attains the state of Brahman.
When non-egoity is established, Brahman remains as if possessing a name, like a definable object;
it is as if peaceful, as if existent, as if non-existent, and likewise as if possessing designations.

If the sense of "I," which is the seed of the world, has been burnt away through the absence of objective thought, then what room is there for such mental constructions as "I," "you," or "the bondage of the world"?
The Supreme is Brahman, the Auspicious, and the Self; it is untainted by the stain of names.
Egoity arises from the sense of "I," just as the forgetting of the nature of clay arises from the state of being a jar.
From this seed of the referent "I" springs forth this existence, which is like a poisonous vine,
in which infinite worlds come and go as its fruits.
This earth with its mountains and rivers, along with the perception of forms, desires, and so forth,
is the internal wonder of the "I-sense," which is like the seed of a peppercorn.
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions— [all are contained within it].
Thus, I am the fragrance of the blossoming flower of the "I-sense" (ahamartha). The "I-sense," having spread forth, reveals the world,
just as the day, having begun, reveals the perception and cognition of existing forms.
Just as light is made manifest by the passing day,
so too is the non-existent world momentarily fashioned through the sense of "I.
This drop of foul oil known as "I" exists within the water that is Brahman.
That which has issued forth is this wheel of the three worlds that stands before us.
Aha! By a mere opening of its eyes, the I-consciousness experiences the worlds;

For when the object of "I" has expanded, transmigratory existence is experienced; but when it is dissolved within through the destruction of latent impressions, it is no longer perceived, just as the pupil is not seen by the eye itself.
When the "I-portion" is brought to a state of partlessness by eternal consciousness, [transmigration ceases].

This mirage of saṃsāra subsides entirely when this supreme reality—accomplished merely through the cultivation of self-awareness—is realized as one's very own nature. Once this is established, do not fall into weariness; do not wander in delusion.

O sinless one, I see no higher good for you than this: that which is to be accomplished by your own effort alone, through means such as being without assistance, and which is free from the perception of "I.

Forget your sense of "I" and remain, with your power diffused throughout all things, adorning the entire universe, taking the form of the mountains in every direction, the intermediate space, the earth, the oceans, the winds, and the paths of the sky.

The stainless self— established in its own nature, peaceful, free from sorrow, devoid of the impurities and parts of the instruments of perception, beyond conceptual proliferation, motionless, yet the essence of movement— is both with parts and without parts; such is the essence of the established doctrine.
The One Hundred and Sixty-Second Chapter, titled "The Abandonment of Egoism," by Vasiṣṭha.
For one who possesses mindfulness and, at the outset, has conquered the inherent nature of the senses,
everything is quickly accomplished when he engages in solitude.
But for that person of burnt intellect by whom the mere inherent nature within has not been conquered, [nothing is achieved].

The attainment of that supreme state is as difficult to find as oil from sand. For even a slight instruction takes root in a pure mind, like [an image] in the oil of a stainless mirror; but it does not take root in a superficial mind, just as a pearl does not adhere to a mirror.
In this very context, they cite this ancient history,
which was previously told to me by Bhusuṇḍa on the summit of Mount Meru.
Long ago, Bhusuṇḍa was questioned during a certain conversation.

"Once, in a secluded cave on the peak of Mount Meru, I asked a certain long-lived being who was of dull intellect and ignorant of the self: 'Do you remember me? To this question of mine, my dear, he replied as follows."
Bhusuṇḍa said: "Formerly, there was a Vidyādhara who was ignorant of the self, accustomed to pleasure,
dry, noble, and lacking in inquiry, residing on the peak of Lokāloka."
Through manifold austerity, self-restraint, and observance,
he remained with undiminished life-span for four previous kalpas.
Then, at the end of the fourth kalpa, discernment arose within him.
Like beryl from the Viḍūra mountain, [he was purified] by the fitness arising from the appearance of the clouds.
Reflecting upon repeated death, repeated birth, and old age, he thought:
"I am ashamed; what single thing could there be that is stable? Having thus considered it, he [proceeded].
Having become dispassionate in soul and realizing the lack of essence in worldly existence, he abandoned his own city of gold and came to me to inquire about it.
Having approached my presence, he offered a grand salutation.
Honored by me, the Vidyādhara spoke these blameless words at the opportune moment:
"The hearts of the virtuous are soft with compassion, yet as firm as stone in their steadfastness."
The limbs of weapons and the senses are skilled in cutting and piercing;
they are agitated, defiled, and bringers of calamity, possessing waves of suffering because they are like fires to the forest of the qualities (*guṇa*).
Having conquered these senses—which are dense with the darkness of the heart and composed of *tamas*—I indeed attain happiness; for what use have I for worldly objects?
The one hundred and sixty-third canto, titled "The Question of the Vidyādhara. The Vidyādhara:
"Tell me quickly that noble, effortless state, free from decay or excess, purifying, and devoid of beginning or end.
For all this time I have been asleep, insentient by nature."
Now I am fully awakened through my own faith, O Sage; rescue me, who am bound by the great malady of the mind, greedy for the functions of ignorance,
and sunk in the wretched delusion of "I am."
Even in one who is illustrious, evil anxieties— intent on destruction— fall swiftly,
just as frost falls upon a lotus with excellent and fresh petals.
Only worn-out creatures are born and die.
It leads neither to Dharma nor to liberation, like mosquitoes in a lotus. Through those very same states, those very same mockeries of trivial gain,
we have been deceived again and again, exhausted after a long time.
With my mind exhausted, I do not perceive even an atom of rest while wandering among the fragile pleasures of existence, like a traveler in desert lands. These things,
whose onset is sweet, are perishable and the causes of worldly rebirth.
"O father, these terrifying realms of enjoyment are subject to swift change;
I take no pleasure in this perverse fortune of the Vidyādharas, which is dominated by honor and dishonor and cherished by a wicked ego."
I have beheld the grounds of the Caitraratha garden, tender with blossoms,
where the splendor of every kind of wealth was provided by the Kalpa trees and creepers;
I have sported in the groves of Mount Meru and in the cities of the Vidyādharas.
He rested upon the rows of excellent celestial chariots and upon the grounds of the wind-girdles;
he rested among the divine armies and upon the vine-like arms of beloved women;
and he rested in the cities of the world-protectors, which were graced by the playful charm of captivating necklaces.
"Nothing whatsoever is suitable or good; everything has been burnt to ashes by the feverish heat of mental anguish, my dear son—I have realized this now.
By one who is restless in gazing at forms and greedy for the faces of women..."
"By this light, through the eye, I have been led toward fault and suffering.
Abandoning the conceptualization that 'this brings qualities' or 'this does not,' [the mind] runs even after a non-existent thing because it pursues mere form."
The rogue does not come to a cessation as long as there is misfortune; nor does the mind, intent on seeking the welfare of others, turn away until it has brought about the ultimate goal.
This sense of smell, clearly rushing toward objects on all sides, leads only to one's ruin.
"O father, just as I am unable to restrain this horse here,
so too have I been constrained by my sense of smell— which follows after pleasure and pain like a conduit for scented water— to these extreme vices, as if by an enemy."
For a long time, I have been excessively struck by this tongue, devoid of moral conduct, amidst the mountains of suffering hidden by greedy jackals; yet,
I am unable to restrain the skin’s greed for touch.
O Sage, just as the heat of the sun intensified by the summer season [overcomes all],
my faculties of hearing— desiring the objects of beautiful sounds—
yoke me to this perilous state, just as a deer's thirst for grass leads it to its ruin.
I heard the splendor of auspicious sounds— prostrations from those seeking his favor, the voices of humble servants, and the mingled resonance of musical instruments and song.
There were the goddesses Śrīs, women, the quarters of the sky, and the shores of the oceans and mountains.
I have seen women who captivate with their charm, adorned with jingling jeweled ornaments;
for a long time I have tasted the six flavors, which are sweet, delightful in their wonder, and endowed with excellent qualities, brought forth by submissive beloveds.
In the pleasure-grounds, they were touched on all sides without obstruction by silken garments, lovely necklaces, flower-strewn carpets, and gentle breezes;
those grounds were adorned with the medicinal herbs and flowers used for the anointing of their brides' faces.
O Sage, the fragrances wafted by the gentle breeze have been experienced;
likewise, that which has been heard, seen, touched, tasted, and smelled again and again—even there we find no satisfaction. Fie upon the manifestation of ignorance!
In this saṃsāra, which has such a meager essence and a fragmented form, and which is parched and tasteless— tell me quickly, what more shall I resort to?
Having experienced this mass of miserable enjoyments for thousands of years, [what else remains?]
From the realm of Brahmā down to a blade of grass, no satisfaction ever arises.
Having ruled a universal empire for a very long time, having enjoyed a multitude of women,
and having utterly crushed the hosts of enemies— what unprecedented thing has been gained by all this?
Those for whom there was no food for a day, and those by whom the three worlds were consumed—
even they, as well as others, have in no long time alike attained the state of ashes.
For that which has been obtained by someone, nothing further remains to be obtained.
One should exert effort toward its attainment even through arduous practice;
for no tree has ever been seen by living beings in this world upon whose summit the enjoyments long relished by beloved ones float in the sky.
For a long time, I have been deceived by my senses in these distant rows of forests of sense-objects, like a child by crafty rogues;
but today, I have recognized these as enemies within their own domain.
Alas! These things called the senses deceive me no longer.
In the empty wilderness of *saṃsāra*, the deceitful hunters—the objects of the senses—lure the bewildered deer of man with repeated assurances and then slay him.

In this world, there are perhaps only two or three who have not been bitten by these serpents of the senses and their objects, which are poisonous with uneven cravings; nor have they even seen such a thing.
[They have not encountered] the snare of thirst, trembling and coiled within the terrifying forest of worldly enjoyments.
Abounding in the fierce sword-blades of greed, marked by the clusters of spears of anger,
pervaded by chariots of the net of duality, protected by egoism,
crowded with the horses of active exertion, and agitated by the clamor of desire; (6,163.38–39)
O dear one, those who are prepared to conquer the army of wicked senses stationed at the very borders of the body are indeed the true warriors here;
for it is easy to pierce the temples of a rutting elephant Airāvaṇa.
The restraint of one's own senses by those who have not entered the wrong path—
O virtuous one, for a man of great manliness, great being, and great fortune,
the conquest of the senses is the ultimate limit of greatness in this world.
Even a man attains the highest status among the inhabitants of heaven only so long as he is not oppressed by his own wretched senses;
for as long as a living being has conquered his senses, he remains as lofty as Mount Meru.
If one goes astray when the senses are unsubdued, one falls even lower than a blade of grass.
Those great beings who have conquered their senses alone are truly men on this earth;
I consider all others to be merely moving machines of flesh.

O Sage, if I possess the effort to conquer this army of the five sense-faculties under the command of the mind, then I shall surely conquer it; for there is no way to overcome the diseases of the supreme senses except by casting off the desire for enjoyments.
Neither medicines, nor sacred fords, nor even mantras lead to peace.
I have been led to the utmost exhaustion by my rushing senses,
like a lone traveler in a great forest beset by robbers.
The sense-faculties are like muddy ponds— turbid, fraught with the misfortune of crocodiles, filled with foul-smelling moss and trivialities,
difficult to cross, and shrouded in dense mists.
The vital breaths are like endless nets, and the sense-faculties are like forests; the sense-faculties are like lotuses with hollows, their qualities exceedingly difficult to perceive;
they possess knots, and their limbs are inert, just like lotus stalks.
The senses are like briny waters: harsh, greedy for jewels, and tossed by surging waves;
they are as terrifying as fierce crocodiles and evil planets, causing agitation among kinsmen and intent upon other bodies.
The senses cause cries of lamentation at the time of death;
among those lacking discernment they are enemies, but among the discerning they are friends;
the senses are like forests that are dense, vast, and empty.

These great clouds and the senses are alike: they are clashing like thunder, pithless, soiled, and dull; they flash like lightning and are seized by petty creatures, avoided by those who have perfected themselves.
The senses are overwhelmed by passion and darkness, like pits that are exclusively skilled at causing one's downfall; they are filled with the venomous serpents of the afflictions,
and the senses are like the edges of abysses where one is caught upon rough thorns.

One's own senses are like demons: they are self-indulgent, ignoble, and delight solely in rashness; they undergo transformations in the darkness, are empty within, devoid of essence, crooked, and full of knots.
The senses are like wood that is difficult to burn yet uniquely suited for combustion;
they are dense with delusion and fiercely scorching, possessing deep, impenetrable thickets.
The senses are like wretched cities: vast in their openings yet utterly empty within.
Among infinite objects, the instruments for things such as jars are the wheels, which are full of delusion and mud; and the senses are the components of those wheels.
O you whose nature is to rescue, by the dawning of compassion, lift me up—me, who am thus submerged in calamity and possess nothing at all.
Whosoever indeed arise as holy men (*santa*) in the worlds, their company is said to be the supreme remover of sorrow.
The hundred and sixty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of Vidyādhara Dispassion."
Bhusuṇḍa said:
Then, O Brahmin, having heard those purifying words of his, I spoke this in response to what was asked, with speech consisting of very clear syllables.
Excellent, O Lord of the Vidyādharas! By good fortune you have awakened for the sake of the world's welfare;
after a long time, you desire to rise from the deep pit of the cave of worldly existence.
Your mind, worthy of purification, shines forth in its pure form.
Like a stream of molten gold by means of fire,
he grasps the meaning of the words of instruction with effortless ease;
just as an object is reflected without exertion in a stainless mirror.
"Whatever I say here, you ought to accept it all with the word 'Om';
we have searched for this for a long time, so there should be no hesitation in this matter. Whatever object pleases you within, having relied upon it as a real entity—"
Therefore, perceiving that it is tasteless, remain at ease, abandoning it without obstacle.
Realize true non-egoity, casting off ignorance;
you do not exist even when sought within for a long time—you are not perceived.

For you who are certain that "neither 'I'-ness nor the world exists," everything is Śiva; and that is neither for suffering nor for pleasure. Is the world born from ignorance, or is ignorance born from the world?
Even upon reflection, we do not know [how they differ], for these two are one;
because the universe is unreal like the water of a mirage, even though it appears to exist, it is non-existent.
And regarding that which shines forth, the certainty is simply this: "it is something within that very [reality]."
Like the water of a mirage, the universe, though existing, is non-existent because it lacks substantial reality;
that which shines here is Brahman—neither nothing nor something at all.
Like the water of a mirage, the universe is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor anything whatsoever.
By virtue of its appearance it is real, yet by virtue of its lack of substantiality it is always unreal.
Like the water of a mirage, the universe neither exists as reality nor does it exist;
though it appears, it does not exist here because of that [reality's] absence, and therefore there is Śiva.
Know that non-duality (*ahantva*) is the seed of the universe;
for from it is born this world-tree, with its ancient roots and its mountains, heavens, earth, rivers, and oceans.
From the subtle seed of non-duality, this tree of the world arises.
Its roots are the worlds, rich with the essence of the senses;
the stars are its young buds, the multitude of constellations is its mass of flower-buds;
the days are its clusters of blossoms, and the full moons are its abode of fruits.
Heaven and the other great realms are its vast branches and hollows;
the mountains such as Meru, Mandara, and Sahya are its rows of leaves;
the seven oceans, my dear, are its streams, and the netherworld (pātāla) is its root-cavity.
The joints are swarms of wood-boring insects, and the knots are rows of cities; ignorance is the soil of birth, and the elements are the birds;
perception is the great pillar, and the bliss of nirvāṇa is the forest fire.
Forms, light, and mental attention are its various modes of delight;
the vast forest is space, and the white clouds are its bark.
The seasons are its diverse branches, and the ten directions are its twigs.
Consciousness is a great flood of nectar, surging with the movement of the wind;
the flickering rays of the moon and sun are intent on sinking and rising;
and the lovely clusters of flowers are the delusions of bees amidst the darkness.
Filling the netherworld, the quarters of space, and the intermediate region, that which is non-existent stands as if it were real.
When the seed of the sense of "I" is consumed by the fire of non-egoity (anahantā), there is no further sprouting of that which was [previously] existent.
This is the chapter titled "The Description of the Seed of the World-Tree."
The one hundred and sixty-fifth canto:
Bhusuṇḍa said:
"O Vidyādhara, O support of the earth, O you whose dwelling is in a mountain cave!"

This world-tree, which is skillful in its movement and wandering through the garments of the quarters of space, arises from the seed of the sense of "I-ness. When that seed is consumed by the fire of knowledge, nothing at all arises again.
And when that [object] is being scrutinized, it is said that "I-ness" (ahantva) never exists at all;
knowledge is precisely this much, and by this very [knowledge], it is consumed.
And because of the absence of "I-ness," there is no "I-ness"—the seed of saṃsāra.
The supreme knowledge is that because the state of "I-ness" does not exist, "I-ness" does not exist;
for at the very beginning of creation, since this creation is indeed joined with non-existence,
whence could there be "I-ness," whence could there be "otherness," and whence the delusion of duality and unity?

Those who, having heard the words of their teacher, strive with diligent effort toward the radical abandonment of all mental constructs (saṅkalpa) for the sake of attaining the supreme state, are victorious. Just as a cook gains mastery over his craft through the study of his own treatise on cooking, so too does one attain victory through the act of "cooking" [the senses].
The discerning person [attains this] only through effort toward their own discernment, and not otherwise.
Know that this world here consists solely of the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*), and nothing else;
it exists neither in the vital breaths, nor outside, nor inside—it is not found anywhere at all.
The variegated world is perceived merely by the opening of the creative resolve (saṅkalpa);
when that resolve does not open, it dissolves like a painting on the mind of a painter.
There exists a pavilion with great pillars, fashioned from pearls and gems.
Adorned with lovely gold for many hundreds of thousands of yojanas,
O dear one, it was surrounded by a thousand jeweled pillars as lofty as Mount Meru;
rich with a thousand rainbows, it was as beautiful as the clouds at the twilight of the kalpa.
Where, amidst various arrangements, women, children, men, and other residents have been stationed here and there for the sake of sport; where,
amidst enemies filled with the seeds of past deeds and enveloped in supreme darkness, there are tumultuous sounds.
The caskets of other worlds are rich with the variegated beauty of darkness and light;
they are made fragrant by the scent of the clouds that hover like fluttering leaves,
and the playful lotuses in the hands of women are like swaying wish-fulfilling trees.
The great mountain ranges have become balls shaken by the breath of children;
the twilight clouds have become ear-ornaments; the autumn clouds have become fly-whisks;
and the clouds at the end of the eon have come to serve as fans.
The surface of the earth was the gaming board, and the starry sky was the canopy.
In this game of dice, where the essence of beings was at stake, the sun and moon were the dice;
on the courtyard of the sky, the inhabitants of the house of the world were the wagers.
In the very same way, this world-form, though being a mere mental construction (*saṅkalpa*), has arisen,
its essence consisting solely of the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*), like a painting on the mind of a painter.
Thus, that which is unreal alone manifests, while the real dissolves away.
It dissolves and does not manifest; everything both exists and does not exist.
This very world has never arisen, yet it appears as if arisen from somewhere—just as the state of being a bracelet and so forth exists within gold, so too is the vast hollow of saṃsāra.
This is merely the wonder of consciousness, which brings about the cessation of the shimmering of the insentient;
it is entirely dependent on itself, so do as you wish.
When one has attained indifference toward the giving of food, drink, and other such things, [one is liberated].
This is his final birth; he shall no longer sink into the mire of karmic actions. O pure-souled one, you have attained the second holy stage of discernment, which sanctifies the three worlds.
I know that you will not fall back down again with your mind in this world; therefore, do not abandon this stainless state.
The one hundred and sixty-sixth canto, titled "Description of the Illusory Pavilion," spoken by Bhusuṇḍa:
O sinless one, even though you are of the nature of consciousness,
remain as a tranquil mass of consciousness, like a ray of light within pure water;
for that which is insentient exists within the sentient only because of the sentient itself.
Even in the case of dissimilarity, it is similar [to its effect], like fire in the ocean;
that consciousness is the cause of both the sentient and the insentient by its very nature as consciousness,
just as wind is the cause of the destruction and arising of flames.
Let your rest be in the realization that "I am not," but rather "I am the form of consciousness. Then, whatever you become and however you exist, be exactly as that.
You, whose nature is consciousness, abide both within and without all beings.
Just as heat exists both within and without a mass of clear water,

O dear one, if your conscious form is fixed upon consciousness, [realizing] "I am not this," and that it is neither other than that nor different from it, then in what way can you be measured as having the nature of Brahman?
It was as if the entire realm of the gods, demons, the underworld, and the earth had arisen together;
it was as agitated as the very movement of various worldly existences through time.
Like a painted scene on a wall, the world stood there as if in silence.
Likewise, consciousness, variegated by its own painting, is established within the wall of space as the Self.
By that very [consciousness], it becomes manifold—whatever is painted upon consciousness by itself, whether insentient or sentient; do as you wish.
These wonders of consciousness flash forth in the void as this world,

like rays of the sun, unobstructed for those who know what is known through their own will; they appear like the illusory clusters of hair seen in the sky by those whose vision is clouded by darkness.
Thus the form of the world vibrates for those who remain within that which is indeed without self.
This world—consisting of "you" and "I"—is a mere appearance arising in the form of cognition; it has neither truly arisen nor ceased.
Like a city fashioned from the web of the sun’s rays, it is not real here, just as a creeper does not exist in the sky.
The one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Consciousness-Sound," [spoken by] Bhusuṇḍa:
If consciousness exists, then within that very consciousness there is non-consciousness, just as fire [exists] in water; thus, consciousness and insentience are not different in the slightest.
Therefore, because there is no distinction between experiencing and non-experiencing, one should remain established in one's own natural state.
Just like a cognition appearing in a painting or like [space] in the midst of the sky,
it is indeed without constraint; so too, because of its possession of all powers within Brahman, non-consciousness exists therein,
just as a future speck of foam exists in undisturbed, pure water.
Just as a fragment of foam does not dispel its cause [of water],
so too the creation and so forth of Brahmā do not dispel their cause.
Furthermore, there is no cause here for the arising of creation, since it is without a cause.
Therefore, nothing whatsoever is born, nor does the world and so forth perish.
Because of the absolute absence of a cause, the world is not born at all;
like water in a mirage, the world does not exist even though it is seen right before one's eyes.
Brahman is infinite, unborn, and tranquil; therefore, this notion of creation does not exist.
Because of the absence of a cause, this is indeed the undivided Brahman alone.
Hence, you are like the interior of a stone and like the expanse of space.

Because you are of the nature of the single, solid mass of Brahman, you are unborn and without parts. You are the Knower; whether you are something or nothing, remain perfectly at ease, free from doubt.
O appearance of consciousness within the unconscious, be stilled by yourself within yourself.
Because it is eternal and infinite, the Unborn has no cause that produces an effect; since the beginning of creation is impossible, that which exists is the unborn Śiva.
But for those who delight in ignorance, there is no Unborn whose nature is consciousness.
When universal destruction has occurred, what is there for them to deliberate upon?
For wherever there is the Supreme, there indeed exist worlds;
and such worlds, in the form of the meaning of the word "world," are already liberated.
In grass, in wood, in water, in a wall—in everything indeed the Supreme is situated;
and everywhere the flood of creation stands interwoven with one another.
It is not appropriate to say what the intrinsic nature of this Brahman is.
Because in the infinite, supreme reality, the notions of "one's own" and "not one's own" are utterly impossible;
and because an entity that depends upon non-existence cannot possibly exist,
those wicked utterances which, by their very nature, fixate upon the infinite do not find a footing there.

Since non-selfhood and non-existence are absolutely impossible in that which is eternal and infinite, once the existence of selfhood is established, the expression of "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) no longer holds.
O virtuous one, "I-ness" is not found; enough with this, what is being scrutinized by the intellect?
This [world] has arisen from somewhere as something truly non-existent, like a phantom yakṣa conjured by a child;
yet that which is liberated from the referents of the word "I-ness" is the Supreme.
When examined, however, that which is joined with the referents of the word "I-ness" dissolves away.

The difference between the world and Brahman, and their non-difference, are like the playful manifestation of synonymous words and their meanings; established as mere conceptualization, they are not real, just as [the difference and identity] exist between a bracelet and gold.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Instruction on the Yoga for Attaining Creation and Liberation."
The one hundred and sixty-eighth canto. Bhusuṇḍa said:
Weapons, which are as dear to him as his own limbs, are submerged within his limbless body.

He who, while awakening, remains well-composed, is established in the supreme state. One should apply oneself to practice with human effort and fortitude until the state of deep sleep arises regarding the manifestation of objects.

Just as water does not stain a lotus even when it clings to its petals, so too mental afflictions (*ādhayaḥ*), even when they have reached the limbs of one who knows the reality of things as they truly are, do not defile him in the slightest.
Without being conscious of weapons, women, or the sky even when they are clinging to his body, [he remains unattached].
He who perceives things as if they were unattached, with a tranquil self—he truly sees.
Just as poison, within itself, becomes the *ghughunthī* [a state of transformation], and there is no such thing as "being *ghughunthī*" apart from the poison itself. (MU 6.168.4–5)
Without ever abandoning its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), it presides over the state of being a living soul (*jīvatā*).
In that same way, the Self (*ātman*)— which causes the dissolution of everything through the mere knowledge of itself—
becomes the living soul, just as the very essence of death becomes the *ghughuntha* [a type of insect].
Not abandoning its own nature, consciousness assumes the form of the insentient.
Though non-different from Brahman, it appears as if different, arising like a ghost;
though situated within that [Brahman], it remains as it is, yet appearing as if not situated there, manifesting as the creation.
Just as a worm within poison does not abandon its poisonous nature, yet gradually it neither comes into being nor dies, even though it is born and also dies; so too,
by means of its own conscious object which is formless, [the Self] exists among all things.
The ocean of existence cannot be crossed by mere chance, as one might cross a cow’s footprint;
but that state which dwells within all things, surpassing all states,
and possesses an inner coolness— in that, what cause for contempt?
Let the existence of all objects in the world be quickly contemplated in their general nature;
for what stain can there be upon the stainless Self, consisting as it does of mind, ego, intellect, and so forth?
Just as you perceive objects such as jars and cloths, so too perceive the body as an object.
Likewise, behold the "I," the mind, the intellect, the sensations, and so forth;
O friend, behold this flood of the multitude of worldly objects joined with the mind, intellect, and the rest.
Remain as pure consciousness itself, devoid of [objective] cognition, through your consummate steadfastness.
"No one ever has any fault or merit whatsoever;
there is neither pleasure nor pain, neither existence nor non-existence, and there is neither an enjoyer nor an agent.
This is called the "creation" consisting in the knowledge of things as they truly are.
The one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter:
Bhusuṇḍa says,
"Just as there is the mental conception that space itself has become the sky,"
Mere delusion is of an unreal nature, as is the cultivation of the sense of "I.
Just as one who imagines "the sky was born in the sky" is a deluded conceiver, so too does the self— which is indefinable, real, and all-pervading— appear as if it were unreal.
The void is only the Self, whose nature is consciousness; that is its own inherent form.
That which appears as "this-ness" is neither "I" nor "not-I.
Such is the pervasive form of consciousness wherein even the gross void is fully contained.
For the consciousness of that [subtle atom] consumes it like Mount Meru within an atom;
therefore, the appearance of manifestation is more subtle than even the void.
That which knows its own nature exists as this very creation.
For one who knows the Self as that which has consumed egoity, the world is its own expansion,
just as the flow of water from the ocean takes the form of whirlpools and the like;
it is a peaceful expansion, like the motionless flow of water.
Having the form of the motionless wind and resembling the heart of space,
neither place nor time is applicable to the expansions of the world,
apart from the expansion of pure consciousness— which is dense, void, and free from appearances.
When even a mere atom has expanded, it appears as if the world has arisen within wood, space, a boat, water, or on land; likewise in sleep, waking, and dreaming.
Yet, expansion and non-expansion cannot possibly coexist with one another.
For, because it is exceedingly pure and free from agitation and the like, the Knower is always conscious [of this];
yet he does not perceive enjoyment and the rest, nor does he have the thought "I am" with respect to the self.
Like liquidity within water, he remains non-dual, established in the Supreme.

One who is free from conceptual construction does not perceive the group consisting of intelligence, modesty, fortune, womanhood, memory, fame, and splendor, just as one does not see the footprints of a snake in the dark.
The nectar-fluid of the pure moonlight of consciousness flashes forth from the orb of Brahman, which is like the disk of the moon.
Because space and time are impossible [independently], creation is not distinct from the Lord.
Even though space and so forth do not manifest, they shine radiantly within the Supreme;
the consciousness-nature, which consists of the world and so on, is like the multitude of whirlpools in water.

With the sounds of plunging and emerging, and with the movements of eddies and whirlpools, the river of creation flows on for a long time, its continuity unbroken yet gradually wasting away. Just as water moves by means of whirlpools, and just as smoke moves through the sky; MU_6,169.15 so does this world proceed by means of various states of existence. It is like a dream, like a city of the Gandharvas, or like a mirage in the desert. MU_6,169.16 This world is not real, nor is it unreal; it is neither existent nor non-existent. It is perceived by the ignorant, but not by the wise. MU_6,169.17 As a rope appears as a snake in the dark, or as a shell appears as silver, so does this world appear within the Self. MU_6,169.18 As a person sees his own reflection in a mirror, or his shadow in water, so does the mind perceive the world within itself. MU_6,169.19 As one sees a city in a dream, or a firebrand-circle in the air, so does the mind perceive the world when it is deluded by ignorance. MU_6,169.20 As a man perceives a double moon due to an eye disease, or hears a sound in the air due to a ringing in the ears, so does the mind perceive the world when it is clouded by false notions. MU_6,169.21 As a person sees a forest in a painting, or a city in a vision, so does the mind perceive the world when it is under the influence of mental constructs. MU_6,169.22 As a person perceives a ghost in the darkness, or a phantom in a cave, so does the mind perceive the world when it is obscured by the veil of nescience. MU_6,169.23 As a person sees a mirage in the heat of the sun, or a flame in a lamp, so does the mind perceive the world when it is stirred by the winds of desire. MU_6,169.24 As a person hears an echo in a valley, or sees a rainbow in the sky, so does the mind perceive the world when it is distracted by the objects of the senses. MU_6,169.25 As a person dreams of a kingdom in sleep, or imagines a treasure in a dream, so does the mind perceive the world when it is immersed in the sleep of ignorance. MU_6,169.26 As a person perceives a shadow in the light, or a reflection in a crystal, so does the mind perceive the world when it is colored by the impressions of past actions. MU_6,169.27 As a person mistakes a rope for a snake in the twilight, or a mother-of-pearl for silver on the shore, so does the mind mistake the Self for the world when it is blinded by the darkness of delusion. MU_6,169.28 As a person sees a city in the clouds, or a garden in the sky, so does the mind see the world when it is projected by the power of imagination. MU_6,169.29 As a person hears a song in the wind, or sees a dance in the waves, so does the mind hear and see the world when it is agitated by the fluctuations of the mind-stuff. MU_6,169.30 As a person perceives a scent in the air, or a taste in the water, so does the mind perceive the world when it is saturated with the flavors of sensory experience. MU_6,169.31 As a person feels a touch in the ether, or a form in the void, so does the mind feel and perceive the world when it is devoid of objective reality. MU_6,169.32 As a person experiences a dream-body in sleep, or a phantom-form in meditation, so does the mind experience the world when it is separated from the waking state. MU_6,169.33 As a person sees a vision in the eyes, or a hallucination in the mind, so does the mind see the world when it is deprived of the light of true knowledge. MU_6,169.34 As a person hears a voice in the silence, or a melody in the stillness, so does the mind hear the world when it is hushed by the cessation of mental activity. MU_6,169.35 As a person perceives a fragrance in the flower, or a flavor in the fruit, so does the mind perceive the world when it is attached to the objects of the senses. MU_6,169.36 As a person sees a star in the day, or a flame in the night, so does the mind see the world when it is alternately illuminated and obscured by the play of consciousness. MU_6,169.37 As a person hears a sound in the silence, or a movement in the stillness, so does the mind hear and move in the world when it is driven by the impulses of the ego. MU_6,169.38 As a person perceives a color in the light, or a shape in the shadow, so does the mind perceive the world when it is colored by the duality of subject and object. MU_6,169.39 As a person sees a reflection in a mirror, or an image in a lens, so does the mind see the world when it is focused by the lens of the intellect. MU_6,169.40 As a person hears a whisper in the wind, or a murmur in the stream, so does the mind hear the world when it is filled with the subtle vibrations of thought. MU_6,169.41 As a person feels a breeze in the air, or a ripple in the water, so does the mind feel the world when it is stirred by the currents of emotion. MU_6,169.42 As a person perceives a scent in the breeze, or a taste in the rain, so does the mind perceive the world when it is nourished by the moisture of desire. MU_6,169.43 As a person sees a form in the light, or a shadow in the dark, so does the mind see the world when it is caught between light and darkness. MU_6,169.44 As a person hears a sound in the silence, or a word in the speech, so does the mind hear the world when it is awakened by the resonance of the inner voice. MU_6,169.45 As a person perceives a dream in sleep, or a memory in waking, so does the mind perceive the world when it is sustained by the continuity of consciousness. MU_6,169.46 As a person sees a city in a painting, or a landscape in a scroll, so does the mind see the world when it is depicted by the brush of the imagination. MU_6,169.47 As a person hears a song in a dream, or a story in a tale, so does the mind hear the world when it is narrated by the storyteller of the mind. MU_6,169.48 As a person feels a touch in a dream, or a pressure in a hug, so does the mind feel the world when it is embraced by the arms of attachment. MU_6,169.49 As a person perceives a scent in a flower, or a fragrance in a perfume, so does the mind perceive the world when it is scented by the perfume of worldly pleasure. MU_6,169.50 As a person sees a vision in a trance, or a form in a statue, so does the mind see the world when it is molded by the clay of habit. MU_6,169.51 As a person hears a sound in a bell, or a note in a lute, so does the mind hear the world when it is tuned to the strings of the heart. MU_6,169.52 As a person perceives a taste in a drop of honey, or a flavor in a drop of wine, so does the mind perceive the world when it is sweetened by the honey of hope. MU_6,169.53 As a person sees a flame in a lamp, or a spark in a fire, so does the mind see the world when it is ignited by the flame of passion. MU_6,169.54 As a person hears a cry in the wilderness, or a call in the distance, so does the mind hear the world when it is summoned by the call of destiny. MU_6,169.55 As a person feels a chill in the frost, or a warmth in the sun, so does the mind feel the world when it is touched by the breath of life. MU_6,169.56 As a person perceives a scent in the incense, or a fragrance in
Likewise, due to its insentient nature, this third creation belongs to these two [the individual soul and primordial matter].
Just as the grain, knots, and so forth exist in wood when it is cut by a saw, so too does this creation exist within the Supreme, which is beyond space and time; such is its form.
From the plantain-stalk of saṃsāra— which is soft except for its sprouts of conceptual construction— not even the slightest thing can be obtained from within it, for it is as hard as stone.
[The world] is occupied by the movements of those whose heads, eyes, hands, and mouths are like the thousand hooves of a horse.
Extending only a few fathoms across various mountains, rivers, directions, and regions,
it is empty within and devoid of essence; though colored by many passions,
it is threatened only by the cleansing performed through manifest dispassion.
Including the gods, asuras, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and mahoragas;
vibrating with inert matter, self, and wind; and perceived by both the insentient and the sentient—it shines forth, beautiful and magnificent, like a great kingdom depicted in a painting on a cloth.
The world, beautiful yet unable to withstand critical inquiry, is a vibrant manifestation of conceptual construction.
Within the aspect of conceptualization— which is itself a vibration and whose form is mere appearance—
consciousness expands through delusion like a drop of oil upon water.
Through the spreading nets of heart-etching thoughts, through the revolutions of the whirlpools of creation,
and through the chewing upon dull latent tendencies mixed with spreading attachment—
she becomes intent upon the manifold form of "I" and so forth by means of conceptual construction.
This [creation] is not distinct from the Supreme, just as the nature of water is not distinct from water itself.
Knowledge is the eternal Self alone, which is designated as "creation.
Since it exists as "I," there is no other creation, nor is there a creator.
Just as the fluidity of water does not perceive its own vibration when that vibration has subsided,
so too the expansion of consciousness does not perceive the appearance of the world.
Just as the fluidity of water does not perceive its state as waves when it exists as whirlpools.
Likewise, in its state as the space of the conscious self (cid-ātma-vyoma), it indeed does not perceive "spaciousness" and so forth;
for the cognition of the conscious one is preceded by the creation of space, time, and other factors.
Because its nature consists of emanation, its similarity to the fluidity of water is not far-fetched.
Know that whatever perception there is—such as the mind, the sense of "I," or the intellect—is ignorance; it is quickly destroyed through diligent human effort.
Half [of this ignorance] is removed by mutual conversation, and a portion by investigations into the scriptures.
Through one's own effort, that which remains is brought to cessation by ignorance.
When the fourfold division of the self has been accomplished, as ignorance wanes in sequence,
that which remains simultaneously is the reality beyond names, being neither existent nor non-existent.
Rāma:
One part [of my time] is spent in mutual conversation, another part in the investigation of the scriptures, and a part in personal exertion; how then can that [suffering] of hers cease?
O Lord of Sages, why is it said that [the world] exists both simultaneously and sequentially? Tell me, is that which is called "nameless" real, or is it unreal? Vasiṣṭha replied:
One should investigate the nature of cyclic existence together with a virtuous person who is dispassionate, seeks to transcend saṃsāra, and is learned in the inner science;
having sought such a person from wherever they may be, one should associate with them who is free from passion and devoid of envy.
One should diligently honor a wise person who is a good man, self-knowing, and learned.

O best among those who know what is to be known, know that when union with a virtuous person is accomplished, half of one's ignorance has gone to destruction, due to the dawning of the highest and most excellent state.
Half of ignorance is destroyed through contact with the virtuous;
a fourth part by means of what is taught in the scriptures, and a fourth part through one's own effort.
One single desire that has arisen is warded off from enjoyments.
Thus, through one's own effort, the fourth part of ignorance goes to its destruction.
Impurity is destroyed by association with the virtuous, by the meaning of the scriptures,
and by one's own effort— either by each one individually, by all together at once, or even gradually.
That which remains when ignorance has been destroyed—whether it be nothing at all or indeed something—is called the Supreme; it is the nameless reality, both non-existent and existent.
This Brahman is a solid mass, undecaying, beginningless, infinite, and one; it is the very manifestation of volition, without beginning and without end.
Having thus awakened, with pride, the measurable, and delusion gone, remain extinguished, wandering in a state free from sorrow.
The one hundred and seventieth canto, titled "The Realization of the Identity of Volitional Conception and Creation."
Bhusuṇḍa said:
For the flood that is the expansion of the universe, neither space nor time is required for its maintenance, just as there is no support for light in the sky.
These three worlds are merely a manifestation of mental ideation;
