they are peaceful, subtle, light, and clearer even than the fragrance within the wind.
O virtuous one, for this atom of the world, which is in truth nothing but the wonder of consciousness—*MU_6.170.2*.
The fragrance of the wind and Mount Meru exist through connection with the experience of others;
for he toward whom this creation arises is indeed the one who perceives it here,
just as a man perceives his own arrangement of objects in a dream.
In this very context, they cite this ancient history concerning what occurred long ago within the belly of a mote of dust belonging to the king of the gods.
At some time, in some place, on some tree of paradise, something happened.
Upon a certain branch of the cosmic tree, they beheld the fruit that is the world,
filled with the humming of the swarms of gods, asuras, and spirits,
and possessing the formidable door-panels of the mountains, the flesh-like netherworlds, the heavens, and the earth.
Exceedingly beautiful with the wonder of consciousness, thick with the essence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), fragrant with the scent of diverse experiences, and captivating to the mind’s relish;
it reaches the millions of creepers of existence upon the great tree of Brahman.
It has the great stalk of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*), is brilliantly illuminated by the light of equanimity (*samāloka*),
has its mouth open toward the gateway of liberation, is enveloped by the veins of rivers and oceans,
resides within the sheath of the five elements (*mātrāpañcaka*), and possesses the shimmering spray of stars.
Worn out at the end of the eon, it was struck down by her in the form of the *kāla-kokila* bird;
having become peaceful, it departed and vanished somewhere.
There, Śakra, the lord of the immortals and sovereign of the three worlds, appeared.
Like a leader of bees settled upon a jar of honey,

through the teacher’s instruction and his own practice, that great-souled one, whose inner self was cultivated, became one whose obscurations were destroyed and who was the best among those who know what precedes and follows.
Then, at one time, when Nārāyaṇa and others of great prowess had for some reason retreated and remained hidden,
that lord of the gods alone fought with the great asuras by means of the flames of weapons erupting like fire.
Defeated by those great heroes, he fled away in haste;
pursued by his enemies, he ran with speed through the ten directions,
finding no place of rest, like a base man in the next world.
When his enemies were distracted in their movements, he seized a slight opening;
having brought his own mental resolve for action to a state of stillness within himself,
he entered a certain mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam.
Like a bee entering the interior of a lotus bud by virtue of its nature as consciousness,
he quickly found rest there; after a long time, he regained his composure, and then, having forgotten the battle, he attained perfect peace.
Then, in an instant, he experienced a constructed dwelling;
in that lotus-gleaming house, he took his pleasure as if in his own celestial realm.
As a householder, Hari then beheld a constructed city.
Then Hari saw within the city a palace with walls made of jewels, pearls, corals, and other precious materials; he also beheld the countryside surrounding it,
filled with various mountains, villages, cow-pens, towns, and forests.
Then Śakra, with such delight, perceived the world— consisting of mountains,
the earth, rivers, and regions, along with its activities and the divisions of time.
Then Śakra, with such delight, perceived the three worlds.
Adorned with the full weight of enjoyments, he remained there in the sovereignty of the gods over the earth including Pātāla, the sky, the celestial realms, the sun, and the mountains. Then,
he had a son named Kunda, who was exceedingly powerful.
Then, at the end of his life, having cast off the body, the blameless Śakra attained nirvāṇa like a lamp whose oil is exhausted.
Having fathered a virtuous son, Kunda became the king of the three worlds.
In due time, at the end of his life, he attained the supreme state.
His son likewise, having then established his own son in the kingdom,
went at the end of his life to the purifying, supreme state.
"Thus, O handsome one, thousands of grandsons have passed away;
even now, among them, a portion of the Lord of the Gods remains established in their kingdom.
Thus, up to this day, this lineage of the Lord of the Immortals, having been ordained, maintains its place as a dynasty in the world.
Even when that [atom] is wounded, dissolved, struck down, or lost somewhere in the sky— a space purified by the rays of the sun—
this concludes the story of Indra, titled "The Description of the Multitude of Creations within a Single Atom," the one hundred and seventy-first canto.
Bhusuṇḍa said:
Of that Śakra, there was a certain descendant born into his lineage who became the lord of the gods;
he was endowed with supreme qualities and glorious, and it was his body that appeared in the western direction.
Then, for that son of Indra’s lineage,
there arose an inspired realization of knowledge uttered by the words of Bṛhaspati.
Thereupon, having known what is to be known, he followed the course as it had been attained.
The sovereign lord of the Ājyapās exercised his rule over the worlds;
he fought with the Dānavas and conquered all his enemies.
With a mind that had transcended ignorance, he performed a hundred sacrifices.
Out of necessity, Bisavālā dwelt for a long time within the interior of a lotus stalk,
and she experienced hundreds of other various events as well.
At one time, a desire arose in that woman, who was endowed with the power of awakening.

"I shall perceive the reality of Brahman as it truly is through meditative concentration. Standing in solitude, he beheld it through focused application; his intellect was stilled by the renunciation of all external and internal faculties.
The Supreme Brahman is all-powerful, pervading all things, consisting of all entities;
it is everything, in every way, at all times, by means of all, everywhere, and omnipresent.
It has hands and feet on all sides, and eyes, heads, and faces on all sides.
Possessing ears everywhere in the world, it stands pervading all; free from the qualities of all the senses, yet endowed with the qualities of all the senses;
unattached, yet the sustainer of all; devoid of qualities, yet the experiencer of qualities.
It is both outside and within all beings, both the unmoving and the moving;
because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible; it is far away, yet it is near.
It consists of the moon and the sun everywhere, and it consists of the earth everywhere.
Everywhere it consists of mountains, and likewise everywhere it consists of oceans;
everywhere it is heavy with essence, and everywhere indeed it consists of space;
everywhere it consists of worldly existence, and everywhere indeed it consists of the world.
Everywhere indeed it is the essence of liberation; everywhere indeed it is the primordial consciousness;
everywhere it consists of all objects, yet from every side it is devoid of everything.
Whether in a pot, a banyan tree, a cloth, a wall, a cart, a monkey, or a man—
In the abode, in space, in trees, on mountains, in wind, in water, and in fire—
even within a mere atom— he beheld the three worlds, with their various modes of conduct, transformations, and diverse activities.
"Just as sharpness exists within a mirage, or emptiness within the sky,
so too do the three worlds— whether real or unreal— exist within the Self consisting of consciousness.
Meditating thus with pure consciousness, which is free from the sense of objective existence, one attains liberation.
By that very same sequence, Śakra attained nirvāṇa.
The son of that Śakra, a conqueror of enemy cities,
also became a practitioner of meditation in that same manner and by that very same sequence.

Beholding everything in one place through meditation for a long time, that noble-minded and great-souled one beheld this creation of ours. Then, wandering within this creation, he attained the status of Śakra among the Śakras.
He ruled the kingdom of the worlds, which was adorned with hundreds of wonderful events.
Know this as it truly is: that lord of the gods was born today itself into the lineage of Indra, having arisen from the family of the Vidyādharas.
Then, through the practice of focusing on the seed-syllable situated in his heart while facing eastward,
he experienced the account of the play of the lotus-fiber network and so forth,
just as this Śakra was described as having his dwelling within the interior of a mote of dust.
Moreover, one born of such a lineage may be wise, possessed of splendor, and even handsome;
likewise, hundreds of thousands of similar worldly transactions have occurred and continue to exist there and elsewhere in the sky.
"O dear one, this river of waves flows thus without interruption for a long time; though it appears as a mature stream, it is deluded and remains fixed in that very state.
Thus, this illusion is long-lasting, yet it has extended toward the face of its own cessation."
She who delights solely in the total dissolution that occurs merely by the contemplation of truth;
for this illusion, O sinless one, appears as something accomplished in some way, somewhere, and from some cause whatsoever.

From the mere wonder of the sense of "I," like rain from a cloud, there arises quickly a mist that perishes upon being observed. O you who delight in seeing what is desired, do not fall for this; behold rather the nature of reality as free from the visible, whose essence is mere manifestation.

Therefore, come to the realization that all objects are empty, and thus their nature is emptiness— a single void alone, free from even the slightest conceptual construction. The one hundred seventy-second canto, titled "The Demonstration of the Unity of Volition and Non-volition."
Bhusuṇḍa said:
Where there is "I-ness" and the world, it stands having arrived there previously,
even within the atom of Indra, like a mote of dust in the interior of a sunbeam.

The sense of "I," which identifies with the self, is declared to be the primordial root of this worldly delusion that has arisen like the color of the sky. From the minute seed-syllable of "I," moistened by the sap of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), this [world] arises.
Upon the mountain of Brahmā, in the forest of the sky, grows the tree of the three worlds:
a cluster of stars for its flowers, dark-blue mountains for its sprouts,
the full flow of rivers for its veins, and the essence of latent impressions for its excellent fruit.

This world is said to be the vibration of the water of egoity; it is the delicious essence of the spreading flow of latent impressions within the wonder of consciousness. It is like a shower of star-drops from a sky that is rooted in the infinite.
It has the great whirlpools of existence and non-existence, with various mountains as its waves;
it is the scribbled lines of the three worlds, foaming with flickering light;
it is the bursting bubble of the cosmic egg, thick with the pressure of its door-panels.
It is a firm mass of foam upon the surface of the earth, possessing a sphere of dense consciousness;
its nature consists of the immersion and emergence within the variegated flux of worldly existence,
a wondrous spectacle of the surging waves of old age, death, delusion, and the like.

The world should be understood as the vibration of the wind of egoity (*ahaṃtva*), which is the sole abode of the multitude of drops (*bindu*) consisting of the body and so forth that have arisen and perished. The world should likewise be realized as the fragrance of the moon of egoity.
The "I" and the world are never distinct, like the wind and its movement,
like water and its fluidity, or like fire and its heat.
The world exists within the referent of the "I," and the "I" exists within the heart of the world.
For these two arise from one another and exist like the container and the contained.
He who, through awakening and the cessation of ignorance, wipes away the "I-ness" which is the seed of the world—
by him the impurity of the world is thoroughly washed away, as if by water.
O Vidyādhara, that which is called "I-ness" does not exist at all;
because it lacks a cause and is devoid of substantial reality, it is like the horn of a hare.
[This is so] within the all-pervading, infinite Brahman, which is free from all mental constructions.
Because there is no cause for it, the state of being "I" (ahantva) is never real.
A cause is not possible in the case of non-entities such as a hare's horn;
therefore, the state of being "I" and so forth does not exist anywhere at all, just like the son of a barren woman.
Due to the absence of that [grasping], the world does not exist; due to the absence of the world, there is no state of being a mind.
What remains is indeed nirvāṇa; therefore, remain at ease in peace.
Thus, because of the non-existence of the world and the "I," which are established upon arising, [they do not exist].
Form, light, and mental attention—these may be either peaceful or otherwise for you.
But that which does not exist simply does not exist; the remainder is peaceful and you are fixed.
You are fully awakened; do not again produce this rootless delusion.
Pure, with the stain of temporal succession removed, you are auspicious, you are peaceful, you are eternally the Lord.
Like space, you are the standard of comparison for everything; the world, too, is merely the form of an atom.
This is the chapter titled "The Union of the World and the Self in Oneness."
The one hundred and seventy-third canto:
Bhusuṇḍa then relates how that leader of the Vidyādharas spoke thus to me.
His consciousness was completely stilled, and he possessed the transformation of meditative absorption;
even though I awakened him again and again from this or that state,
he did not fall back to the objects before his eyes, having attained supreme nirvāṇa.
He attained that supreme state through awakening to just that much, and not by any further effort, O dear one, from one desiring excellence;
therefore it was said by me: "If indeed the mind is pure..."
Instruction spreads like a drop of oil upon water.
"I am not [the ego]"—this exists within; therefore, do not contemplate otherwise for the sake of peace.
For this alone is the supreme expression of instruction; indeed, there is no other.
This very [nature] falls upon the mind of one who is unworthy and flees away,
like a pearl falling onto the surface of a smooth, upward-facing mirror.
But upon the calm mind of one who is worthy, it settles and attains its brilliance.
Having entered within [the heart], which is called "discernment" (vicāra), like a flame in a sun-crystal,
the intense conceit of "I" (ahambhāvana) is indeed the seed of the śalmali tree known as suffering;
by its power, that [seed] becomes the cause for the spreading of its branches.
"First there is 'I', then 'mine'; from that, desire proceeds—this [desire] which brings about hundreds of evils for its objects and is the cause of worldly existence.
O best of sages, even those who are thus deluded may live for a long time."
For indeed, O dear one, discipline is the cause of long life.
Those whose internal minds are pure, who bestow long-lasting existence,
reach the supreme state even when instructed only slightly.
Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus to me on the summit of Mount Meru,
that lord of birds became silent, his soul liberated, like a rain-cloud that has ceased its downpour.
Having taken leave of that Siddha, O Rāma, I returned again by the path of the Vidyādharas to my own abode, which was adorned by a circle of sages.
This account of the subduing of the Vidyādhara, arising from the story of Bali-bhuj, has now been told to you for the sake of swift enlightenment.
In this assembly with Bhusuṇḍa, the lord of birds, eleven great yugas have indeed passed for me.
The one hundred and seventy-fourth canto, titled "The Liberation of the Vidyādhara," within the narrative of the Vidyādhara.
Vasiṣṭha: Through the very absence of the sense of "I," the desire that bears fruit as the cycle of existence— which yields both auspicious and inauspicious results— surely subsides within.
Through the practice of non-identification with the self, having become one for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal,
and having stilled the afflictions of existence, a person does not suffer. [The mind],
having flown out from the hollow of its own being, is impelled by the power of supreme awakening.
I do not know where this stone of the object "I" quickly goes;
impelled by the heroic power of Brahman, it has flown out from the hollow of the sheath of egoism.
I do not know where this stone of the machine of the body quickly goes.
This sense of "I," having been dissolved within by the flame of the knowledge of non-egoity,
I do not know where it has quickly gone, as if it had flown away;
the essence of "I" has dissolved within by the flame of the knowledge of non-egoity.
I do not know where it quickly goes, having risen from the leaf of the body.
For once the intoxicating juice of the essence of egoity has been squeezed out from the leaf of the body,
it attains transcendence by way of the sun of non-egoity.
Whether on a bed, in mud, on a mountain, in a house, in the sky, on dry land, or in water;
whether gross, subtle, formless, or even entered into another form;
wherever she may be situated—whether sleeping, awake, or reduced to ashes—she remains as such.
Though dead, drunk, submerged, far away, or nearby,
this "I-ness" (ahaṃtva)— which resides within the seed-vessel of the body—
spreads in an instant this high-reaching network of branches called saṃsāra.
The great tree of the body, situated within the seed-vessel of the "I-notion," extends its multitude of branches— the various states of transmigratory existence— here and there in abundance.
Though the tree exists within the interior of the seed, complete with hundreds of branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, it is not perceived by the eye.
The body, too, is seen by the very act of seeing the visible world to be filled with the consciousness of all that is perceived, within the infinitesimal atom of "I-ness. Then,

for one whose body has attained "I-ness" apart from the physical form through investigations, and whose essence is the mere sky of pure knowledge— once that [body] is utterly consumed by the great fire of awakening, the tree of saṃsāra does not sprout again here from the womb of the seed of "I-ness," which has become non-existent.
The one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Union of Non-Egoity and Non-Existence," by Vasiṣṭha.
Death, which consists of the total destruction [of everything], never exists;
rather, the instability within one's own mental constructs is what is designated as "death.
Behold before me Mount Mandara and Mount Meru being carried away as if they were mere straw!
Even though they are unbridled by the winds of the quarters, like mountains reflected in a river,
these successions of existences— whether joined or unjoined, having the nature of the void— stand within the sky, one above the other and one within the other, like the layers of a plantain leaf.
Rāma:
"Behold, my city is being carried away"— I do not understand the meaning of this sentence at all as it truly is, O leader of sages.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Within the vital breath (prāṇa) is the mind (citta), and within the mind is the world;
it exists in manifold forms, just as a tree exists within a seed.
When a man has died, the vital breaths merge with the winds of space,
for they flow into the Self just as the waters of rivers merge into the waters of the ocean. Indeed, the worlds within them move freely here and there.
"Even those things whose sole essence is volition, when driven by the wind of space,
are seen by us everywhere as all the directions filled with winds containing vital breaths and throbbing with volitions."
Look here! Look! By means of the groups of worlds born of volition, Mount Mandara and Mount Meru are being swept away before me by the vision of the intellect.
Within the wind of space are the life-breaths of the dead, and within those life-breaths is the mind.
Know that the world exists within the mind, situated like oil within a sesame seed.
Just as those whose life-breaths have departed are carried through the sky by the winds of space in their mind-made forms,
so too are these worlds, which are its limbs, carried along.
Even the actual multitudes of sky, earth, and so forth, as well as the three worlds themselves—
whether being carried or not being carried— are perceived everywhere like a fragrance,
O descendant of Raghu, by the intellect alone and not by the eye.

In front of them, forms consisting of mental constructs exist everywhere and at all times, like cities within one's own dreams; being even more subtle than space and having conceptualization alone as their essence, they are not burned in the slightest.
Because they possess a firm nature within their own worlds,
those very [worlds] are sufficient for the portion of consciousness, just as you are;
they appear like cities in a reflection before the flow of the river of vital breath.
Those that are unbound are carried away, and those that are bound are not carried at all.
O Rāghava, fragrances situated within the limbs of the wind are carried along;
likewise, the worlds situated within the vital breath are carried by virtue of their ethereal nature.
Just as there is no difference in the space within when a jar is carried to another country,
so too there is no difference in the mind— which consists of movement and other such qualities— within the delusion of the three worlds.
Thus, this delusion of the world has arisen for you as something entirely unreal.
It neither perishes nor arises; it is solely of the nature of Brahman.
Even if it is carried by the winds, that movement is not perceived within it, just as the motion of a boat is not noticed by those situated inside its hold.

Just as movement, even when it has touched the body, is not perceived by those situated inside a boat, so too Brahman is not perceived by those who abide within it and have become identical with it. Just as a house extending for a league is experienced within a small space;
Whether it be the pillar of a Yakṣa’s tree, an atom, or the entire world,
a person of feeble character perceives even a minute thing as exceedingly vast;
just as a mouse regards the contents of its own two palms, or as a child views a mere patch of mud.
While this world called the "universe" is merely a delusion lacking any real nature, the ignorant person possesses a very firm mental construction consisting of a flood of various realms;
within that state of ignorance, there arises the thought: "This is to be rejected, this is to be accepted."
For whoever there may be, even for an omniscient one, there exists delusion regarding existence. For just as a conscious whole perceives its own parts,
so the individual soul perceives the three worlds as spread out within itself.
I am the imperishable, infinite, supreme space whose nature is consciousness;
these worlds are but the constituent parts of that void of mine.
Just as a sentient being contains within itself things such as razors and needles, so too does this [world] exist within me.
In the same way, the individual soul perceives within itself the wandering of the three worlds.
Just as an insentient or sentient lump of clay conceives of itself as a bowl, a water-jar, or other vessels, so too, my dear, does the individual soul conceive of the world as its own limb.
Just as the sprout, whether conscious or unconscious, conceives itself as a tree within its body,
so too this triple world is Brahman, devoid of the meaning of the word "tree. Or,
just as a mirror reflects what is conscious or unconscious, whether it be a reflection or not, [so is this world].
Nor does he perceive the city, nor likewise the triple world as Brahman;
for the triple world consists merely of space, time, action, and substance.
Therefore, there is no difference between the "I-ness" of the world and that of its Self.

That which is taught by means of an imagined analogy possesses a commonality with the object of comparison through only a single part of that analogy. Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving— *MU_6,175.33*— it is all like this.

This body of the individual soul (*jīva*) is said to consist of the subtlest atoms when it has not yet been released [from its state]. When all perceptions have been abandoned and one stands in the state that is the locus of pure existence,
there is not even the slightest difference between the detached soul and the interior of a stone.
Whatever specific manifestation there may be, wherever, in whatever manner,
whenever, and by whatever means— just as liquidity is the inherent nature of water; so too,
whatever portion of conceptual construction there may be, wherever, in whatever manner...
Whenever and by whatever means it is accumulated, it is thus called an "accumulation" (cita) here.
Because it lacks consciousness, there is no mental construction (saṅkalpa) in the mind, like a sprout in the sky;
but because the mind possesses consciousness, know that conceptualization (kalpanā) exists here only through the act of cognizing (citi).
The glory of conceptual construction that arises for those of unawakened disposition is not composed of reality,
because the sky of consciousness is all-pervading and infinite.
That all the fabrications of mental constructs are real is an unimpeachable notion held even by children.
Who could deny the internal object experienced in dreams and the like?

Whether it be a mental construction (*saṅkalpa*) or a non-construction, whatever is painted by the consciousness, even if experienced, it would be unreal; for us, only the unreal exists, not the real.
When truth is expressed as non-truth, one becomes liberated Śiva;
he possesses the blossoming that arises from the total dissolution of the subtle body (*ativāhika-deha*).
The worlds are carried by the winds through the sky like the down of a *śalmali* tree.
They are not carried away like stones, nor do they exist at all through mere conceptualization;
yet within this treasury of the multitude of all objects, even in the exceedingly vast sky, worlds exist.
With the manner of the breaking of waves spreading over agitated waters, they meet with one another everywhere in dense succession.
Some are mutually restricted yet unobstructed, constantly trembling and possessing the luster of the stainless sky like waters;
others are like the variegated webs of mind projected by a skilled painter, appearing as if they were both within and without, expanding in multitudes.
Some are intermingled with one another in the sky, while some are not intermingled with one another.
Because the supreme consciousness is all-pervasive, it manifests forms of infinite variety, gathered from the many directions of its own creative impulse.
These forms are as fleeting as the reflection of a city in turbulent waters, yet they resemble the vast cities existing within one's own mind.
Though seemingly stable, they are constantly perishing in an instant—mere transformations like the surging waves of the ocean of consciousness.
The waters of the rivers, though existing separately, become intermingled within the ocean;
just as the lights of the stars, sun, moon, and planetary spheres, though risen together, appear unified in the sky.
This is the chapter titled "The Instruction on the Analogy between the Web of the World and Space."
The one hundred and seventy-sixth canto.
Rāma:
O Sage, as for the nature of the living being (jīva) and likewise its assumption of form—
"Tell me how its state of being the ultimate reality (paramārthatva) is established, and what that state is.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"It is called Consciousness (cit), which has another name [for it], and which is marked by the objects of its own volitions."
The infinite space of consciousness is designated by the term "jīva.
It is neither an atom nor gross, neither void nor nothingness;
consisting of pure consciousness whose nature is self-experience, it is all-pervading and is called the jīva.
The wise know that the life-force (jīva) is the subtlest among the subtlest and the grossest among the grossest; it is indeed nothing more than a mere atom, yet it pervades everything.
Whatever the nature of any given object may be, the life-force exists therein in that very same manner.
Know that which appears as such to be established through the exclusive realization of its own self-nature.
O Rāma, in whatever manner, wherever, and whenever something is perceived, it immediately becomes of the nature of that very experience.
Just as there is vibration for the wind, so indeed is there an object of cognition for the living soul;
this is to be determined solely by one's own consciousness, not through the defects of instruction. Just as the wind, by its lack of vibration, though existing, attains the state of non-existence.
In the same way, the living being (jīva), though insentient [in its substrate], attains the supreme state while living.
Because the *jīva* consists of the essence of consciousness (*cidghana*), through the very act of self-awareness as "I," it remains having fashioned the powers of space, time, action, and substance.
Adorned with space, time, action, and substance, yet itself unadorned, unreal yet appearing as real, expansive yet having only that much for its body—
this perceived state of frost-like atoms, which consists of non-existent forms.
Then, perceiving within itself its own non-selfhood as being like one's own death in a dream,
and contemplating that state which resembles the transformation of one's own limbs in a dream,
it quickly forgets its conscious existence and attains that very [state of non-self].
Awakening in this manner, he then quickly perceives his own self as a state of swelling, like the orb of the moon; then,
within that very self which is the lunar orb, he perceives the fivefold consciousness.
Like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, that which was previously divided now perceives itself by its own power.
Then, this [consciousness] perceives the five distinct parts of the five cognitions; it also experiences those apertures which have those [parts] as their form.
Later, that Virāṭ Puruṣa shines forth with five limbs;
he is the consciousness of infinite forms, unmanifest in essence, and free from affliction.
This one, consisting of mind, arose from the Supreme as the first-born.
Clear as space, tranquil, consisting of eternal and infinite splendor; he is the self that is not composed of the five elements, yet resembles one whose nature consists of the five elements;
the Virāj-self, the single Puruṣa, the Supreme, the Parameśvara.
It arises by itself alone and dissolves by itself alone;
it expands by itself alone and undergoes contraction by itself alone—
whether through a flood of cosmic ages or in a mere moment— by means of its own volitional constructs.
Arising again and again by chance, it comes into being and then subsides.
This body, whose nature consists solely of mind, is the form of primordial matter (prakṛti).
It is called the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka), the subtle vehicle for all beings.
This [Self] is gross and subtle, of the nature of space, manifest and unmanifest, devoid of end;
it is both outside and inside of everything, being both nothing and something indeed.
O Rāma, its eight limbs consist of the five [senses] with the mind as the sixth.
The sense organs consist of both existence and non-existence;
therefore, these Vedas were sung by him along with the conceptualizations of words and their meanings.
By him, Niyati was established, and thus it remains even today exactly as it was placed.
The infinite space above is his head, and likewise the surface below is the soles of his feet;
the boundless ether is his belly—this is the sphere of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
The infinite intermediate worlds are his ribs, and the blood is the waters.

The mountains are masses of flesh, and the rivers are the continuous veins; the oceans are streams of blood, and the entrails are the very coils of the earth. The arms are the vast quarters of space, and the multitude of stars is the line of body hair.
The fifty aggregates of wind are the vital breaths (*prāṇavāyu*);
the fierce solar orb is bile (*pitta*) and the digestive fire;
the lunar orb is the individual soul (*jīva*), phlegm (*śleṣman*), semen, the white [element], and strength.
The mind, whose nature is the treasury of volition and whose essence is the supreme nectar,
is the root of the sheath of the body and the seed of the tree of karma;
it is the source of all states of being and the cause of bliss.
That which is called the lunar orb is said to be the sovereign *jīva*;
it is the seed, the root, and the cause of the body, karma, and the mind.
From this *jīva*, which resembles the moon, [the vital energies] stream forth throughout the three worlds.
Living beings, minds, actions, pleasures, food, and nectar—
these are the volitions of Virāj; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the Conqueror (Śiva),
and the others, as well as gods, demons, and sky-dwellers, are the wondrous manifestations of his mind.

When the conscious self-nature, while awakening, quickly contemplates the state of being like a particle of frost at the very beginning, it then remains right there. Therefore, O scion of Raghu, know that this alone is the abode of the living soul.
This body is experienced as consisting of five members. From the Virāj, from the Jīva, and from the Moon, the food-born bodies of embodied beings spread forth in the form of a diffusion of dewdrops.

These very [elements], having become the mind, cause living beings to live within the bodies of embodied beings; they exert themselves as the cause of action throughout successive births. Thus does the Virāj endure for thousands [of years] and hundreds of great kalpas.
Now, various modes of conduct have passed away and exist;
yet, by means of this Being— which consists of universal experience, which is non-different from the Supreme State,
and which possesses the great limbs free from all limits— the Puruṣa remains as the supreme Virāj.
The one hundred and seventy-seventh canto, titled "The Description of the Virāj Self," by Vasiṣṭha:
This person of volition (saṅkalpapuruṣa), whatever he himself conceives,
that very thing becomes for him in such a manner, like the sky consisting of the five elements;
the wise know that the entire world-born is indeed his volition.
Such is the nature of that which has emerged, directed toward the objects of the fivefold self;
it is the Virāj, the cause of the entire multitude of things in the world.
Therefore, the effects are indeed identical in nature to their cause.
Just as this Virāj is, so too does the Virāj expand within each individual self in its own self-awareness; it is one who possesses awakening, not one devoid of awakening.
Thus, from the crawling insect up to Rudra, such delusion has arisen.
Even within an atom, the expansion of the mountain exists like a tree within its seed-vessel;
from the level of a crawling insect up to Rudra, the Virāṭ resides within each individual self.
Even within the supreme atom, the infinite Self exists through awakening, but not through non-awakening.
Just as this expansion has come to be within the Virāj-self,
so too it is within every single being here, even one as small as an atom.
In the ultimate sense, there is nothing anywhere that is either gross or subtle.
Whatever is cultivated in whatever manner is experienced accordingly in that very place.
The mind is born from the moon, and the moon arises from the mind;
or rather, the individual soul arises from the living principle—this is but a single existence, like a body formed from liquid water.
They know the vital essence (*jīva*) to be the quintessence of semen, resembling a drop of frost;
from that alone does bliss and the mass of strength proceed.
The Self first perceives that reflection of consciousness within itself by means of its own self.

Therein, it assumes identity with that, and by that means, the consciousness of the individual soul (jīvasaṃvit) becomes one whose form consists of that. Furthermore, when this [consciousness] attains the state of dissolution into the five elements (pañcatā),
no cause whatsoever exists there, nor is there any state of being an effect.
Because there is no exclusion of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogivyavacchitti*) between the states of "selfhood" (*svatva*) and "existence" (*bhāva*),
the expression of essential nature (*svabhāvokti*) here does not follow the actual state of affairs.
The living being (*jīva*) is its own selfhood (*svam*) precisely because it is a living being, and [it exists] by itself precisely because of that living-being-ness.
Contemplating [the self] as being internal, external, and as an object of perception,
one is as if enveloped by mist; devoted to the objects of thought,
with the self obscured, one does not see the path, like one born blind.

Through this power of universal expansion (*jagajjṛmbhikā*), which is non-different from its own self, the individual soul (*jīva*) exists in a state of both unity and duality, just as the wind exists through the power of vibration (*spandaśakti*).
Thus, the pure, awakened, and beginningless-and-endless [Self] becomes the individual soul (*jīva*) possessed of latent impressions (*vāsana*).

One whose self is obscured does not perceive the primordial Self, just as a drunkard does not see himself. The liberation of the great knot of ignorance— which consists of the unreal false object of cognition and takes the form of the meaning "I"— is traditionally known as *mokṣa*.
Remain indeed without perceiving "I" on all sides, with dense consciousness departed;
having the single form of non-designatable, supreme consciousness, you are neither existent nor non-existent, yet always arisen as the eternal existent.
The chapter titled "The Instruction on the Yoga for Determining the Nature of the Living Being."
The one hundred and seventy-eighth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāma, one should always be a man of knowledge, not merely a kinsman of knowledge."
"I consider ignorance itself to be better than being a kinsman through knowledge.
Rāma said:
"What is meant by 'kinsman through knowledge,' and who indeed is called a 'knower'?"
"What is the fruit of being a kinsman of knowledge, and what is the fruit even of possessing knowledge?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"He who explains and recites the scripture for the sake of enjoyment, like a craftsman [displaying his skill],"
He who exerts himself but not in spiritual practice is called a "kinsman of knowledge.
He whose awakening is seen to bear fruit in the movement of action,
living by the craft of awakening, is called a "kinsman of knowledge."
Those who are satisfied with mere clothing and food as the fruit of the scriptures,
and who are kinsmen to those possessing a portion of knowledge, should be known as craftsmen of the scriptural meaning—
those who abide in the dharma characterized by worldly activity as is appropriate for their learning.
Because his knowledge is not far removed [from the truth], he is called a kinsman of knowledge (jñānabandhu).

They know self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*) to be true knowledge; as for whatever other forms of knowledge there may be, they are merely the semblance of knowledge (*jñānāvabhāsa*), because they do not perceive the essential reality.
Those who, without attaining self-knowledge, are satisfied with a mere fragment of other knowledge through arduous effort, are remembered as "kinsmen of knowledge.
One should not be content in this world without the cessation of the mental fluctuations regarding the object of knowledge that arise from [superficial] knowledge.
O Rāma, having attained the state of being a kinsman through knowledge, take delight therein; do not find pleasure in enjoyments, which are like diseases born of worldly existence.
One should perform blameless action for the sake of food; one should take food for the sake of sustaining the life-breaths.
The life-breaths should be sustained for the sake of inquiring into reality; reality should be inquired into so that there may be no further suffering.
The One Hundred and Seventy-ninth Chapter, titled "The Reflection on the Kinsman of Knowledge," by Vasiṣṭha.

He who, through knowledge, being established in the knowable, does not enjoy the fruit of action— whether it be accumulated or unaccumulated— is called a man of knowledge. He in whose actions right performance is seen after having known [the truth] is [a knower].

One whose nature is free from latent impressions is called a man of knowledge. He whose inner coolness is perceived by the wise as being truly unartificial due to his tranquility is called a man of knowledge.
That awakening which leads to non-rebirth is what truly bears the name "knowledge.
All else—the giving of clothing and food, established social roles, and living through crafts—is merely for the sake of sustenance.
One who is free from desire and mental constructs regarding duties that have arisen through the force of worldly continuity [is liberated].
He who stands with his heart like space is called wise.
Phenomena proceed as if without cause from no cause;
though non-existent, they remain as if existent.
Through manifestations and disappearances, through existences and non-existences, and through the arising and ceasing of things,
they subsequently become causes for one another through mutual causal operations—
whether it be of non-existent things such as a hare's horn or the water of a mirage.
Now, what could possibly be the cause for that which is unobtainable even through observation?
Those who search for a cause for non-existent things such as a hare’s horn are reaching for the shoulder of the grandson of a barren woman’s son.
This alone is the swift cause for the non-appearance of unreal things:
namely, that which is called "non-perception," which is the exhaustion of perception through its own exhaustion.
When the individual soul (*jīva*) does not perceive, it becomes like the insentient Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
But when consciousness awakens, it remains as the individual soul (jīva) alone.
This very Supreme Self, while awakening from its unconscious state, becomes the individual soul,
just as a mango tree attains the state of a *sahakāra* through the acquisition of sap.
But the conscious one, becoming awakened, remains as the very *jīva*;
the *jīva* lives on, worn out through decayed births and lifetimes.
Those who have attained the supreme vision, having seen the further shore of the splendor of the visible world—
Even though it exists, no pervasive perception of those things belongs to them.

Know that for those who have attained the supreme vision, there is always a state like that of water— without form, light, or mental construction, and characterized by motionlessness despite its inherent movement.
Know that for those who have attained the supreme vision, all movement and non-movement here are like water— devoid of sensation due to the absence of perception;
it is without form, light, or thought, like a rope released from its surrounding coils.

The Buddhas exert themselves in their activities like winds among the leaves of trees. Those who have attained the supreme vision and see beyond the cycle of existence do not praise ritual action, just as one drinking from a river does not praise a well.
O sinless one, those fools whose latent impressions are bound to action praise ritual acts prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti; because of that, they fall lower and lower.
Their senses fall upon sense-objects like bold vultures pouncing on meat.
Restraining those [senses] with the mind, one should sit disciplined and intent upon that.
There is no gold without its setting, nor does Brahman exist without creation;
however, the meaning of words such as "creation" and so forth has been explained in a manner consistent with reality, and therefore it is auspicious.

When total darkness has arisen at the end of the age, worldly activity becomes undifferentiated and devoid of appearance, just as it is within the mass of Brahman; just as within the belly of a cloud, there exists the state of both movement and stillness among the portions of the cloud.
The existence of beings within the Lord is likewise of the nature of self-awareness;
just as within water there is both duality and non-duality among the constituent parts of water,
so too within Brahman, the perception of beings is the self-vibration whose essence is self-awareness.
Just as the existence of the rays of light within the sky—which is of a nature both dual and non-dual—is essentially one's own consciousness, so too is the existence of all beings within the Lord.
Just as the pervasion of parts that have no other [external] components resides in the whole; [so does the Lord pervade all things].
In the same way, the non-dual creation appears within the partless Śiva;
within the world is the form of the "I," and within the form of the "I" is the world,
situated as they mutually envelop one another like the layers of a plantain leaf-sheath.
Through the apertures of form, light, and mental attention, the living soul perceives the creation as if situated outside itself, just as a mountain perceives a lake within it;
this living soul perceives itself as the world without cause.
In the same way, one who does not perceive that [nature] does not perceive the state of being bracelets and so forth.
Even while living, they do not live; even though dead, they do not die.
Though existing, those auspicious ones who know the higher and the lower are as if they do not exist.
The awakened one, even while performing all actions, does not perceive them,
just as a householder engaged in domestic chores remains with his mind fixed on the cattle-pen and its vessels.
Just as the Virāj resides in the heart, so too does it abide within every body like the moon.
The individual soul (*jīva*), like a drop of frost, becomes large when [the body] is large and small when it is small.
Through conceptualization, the "I" (*ahaṃ*)—which is the self (*ātman*)—attains the state of being a triangle;
by means of consciousness, it regards its own form as real, though it is in fact unreal.
In the triangular *karmakośa*, the essence of *śukra* (semen/seed) resides;
the self (*ātman*) is the "I" within the body, just as fragrance resides in a flower. Thus, the consciousness situated in *śukra* is the "I" from head to foot.
It spreads throughout the entire pavilion of the cosmic egg, just as moonlight does;
the water of sensation, released through the channel of the apertures of the senses,
pervades the three worlds like smoke filling the sky with the nature of clouds.
Although perception exists both externally and internally throughout this entire body,
nevertheless, within this semen there is a dense latent impression (*vāsanā*).
That living being (*jīva*), whose essence consists of mere volition (*saṅkalpa*), abides as that which is its own volition.
Having become [established] in the heart, that very [Self] quickly and clearly flows outward.
As long as one does not abandon this state— which is free from thought and comparable to the sky—
the delusion of "I" is not pacified by any state whatsoever.
But even when being contemplated, thought is like the sky of that which is to be cultivated;
through tranquility, you shall gradually achieve the pacification of the sense of "I.
Those who know that engage here in worldly affairs while remaining free from both the object of cultivation and the act of cultivating it.
Like men of wooden silence, they do not contemplate the light of form.
He who is the contemplation of nothingness is said to be liberated;
though living, he is as pure as space, while another is clearly bound.
The consciousness residing in the vital seed (śukra) as "I" alone spreads throughout the entire body from head to foot, just as the light of the sun pervades the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
It becomes sight for the eye, taste for the tongue, and hearing for the ear.

Having bound these five kinds of latent impressions (vāsanās) and the like, one sinks into them. The state of being a knower arises from a single part of the mind as if unimpaired, just as sap, though all-pervading, emerges in the form of a sprout upon the earth in the springtime.
For one who contemplates the non-existence of things that have not yet arisen here,
and who lacks effort, suffering never ceases and remains infinite.
Clothed in whatever [is available] and fed by whatever [is available], [one attains peace].
Wherever he may lie, the knower shines forth like a sovereign emperor.
Though endowed with all latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he is free from latent impressions;
though empty within, his self is not empty, like the sky filled with air.
Whether seated, reclining, or traveling, he remains awakened through effort;
like one who has woken from sleep, he is at peace, liberated from the mental constructions of the mind that lead to *nirvāṇa*.
For the person (*puruṣa*) is pure consciousness alone, and though all-pervading, he abides thus.
Just as the fragrance within the interior of a lotus is clearly present in the essence of the body,

they know the living being to be pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*); the expansion of that [consciousness] is the world, while its abiding in the Self is the non-world— this is the ground of the supreme teaching.
Become dispassionate toward all worldly objects, such as power and prosperity;
by making your heart like a stone, you will thus attain well-being. O virtuous one, let there be a hollowing out of your heart, as if it were not hollow at all.
O Raghava, because one who possesses an ignorant body lacks true knowledge, he is like a stone;

yet between the knower of that [Reality] and the ignorant person, there is no distinction whatsoever in regard to all things— whether existent or non-existent— in their actions, except for the state of being free from latent desires (nirvāsanatva).
This very consciousness, when it is opened, becomes the world;
when it is closed, it is the supreme reality, nameless and pervasive, like the eye [when closed].
The entire visible world perishes, and having perished, it is born again.
That which is neither destroyed nor arisen is the Real; be that, O Bhava!
Cultivation is devoid of any basis for cognition; even when cultivated, it does not exist.
Like water in a mirage, it does not produce the sprout of existence.

The cultivation of the thought "I am severed" through the vision of things as they truly are does not produce further internal burning, even when observed, just as a scorched seed does not produce a sprout. Whether performing action or not performing it, one who is free from passion is free from affliction.
The Sage, who is by nature eternally liberated, abides within the self;

when the mind is stilled, those whose attachments to enjoyments have been completely pacified find peace. Yet their minds are not destroyed by non-existence, for the mind itself is indeed the mine [of all experience].
The enlightened soul, free from all density and consisting of pure light alone, is known as the Supreme;
it is both other than and not other than [the individual], like the sunlight at midday compared to that in the afternoon.
This is so even when the mind of a person situated in one place has traveled far away.
That form which is partless in the midst is the form of the Supreme Self.
That which is beautiful, consciousness, the camphor of the sky, and which itself experiences wonder— that knows the world as infinite, internal, and unmanifest.

The lords of the world indeed bow down to, take delight in with joy, and even dwell in the sky over a person who has reached the imperishable peace, radiant with the cessation of wandering through existence, and who remains like a lamp that has been set aside.
This is the chapter titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Knowledge and Bliss."
The one hundred and eightieth canto:
Vasiṣṭha said:
"With the latent tendencies of hope cast aside, he has abandoned all worldly tendencies."
Arise and depart from this Prakṛti, just as Maṅki did from her embrace.
Long ago there was a Brahmin named Maṅki who was firm in his vows;
hear how he attained Nirvāṇa through my instruction.
Once, invited for the sake of your grandfather by someone, I descended from the expanse of the sky to the earth;
while traveling across the ground, I reached the city of your grandfather.
I have reached a certain vast wilderness, long-extending and scorched by great heat;
thick with dust-stirring thickets, its sands shimmering and hot,
its far shore and limits unseen, yet marked here and there by the presence of small villages.
It was characterized by the tranquility of the unagitated ether, wind, light, water, and earth;
it was pervasive, empty, and of great undertaking, like the stainless reality of Brahman;
yet it was like ignorance, possessing the delusion of a mirage born of total confusion.
It was a place that bound one in dullness, vast and empty, agitated by forest fires and mists. Then, while I was wandering through that great wilderness,
I saw before me a traveler speaking from exhaustion.
The traveler:
Alas! The sun, with its intense heat, leads only to exhaustion;
this wicked heat causes torment, like association with a villain.
The vital points seem to throb, and fire seems to flash in the heat;
the forest ranges, with their clusters of shrinking shoots, languish.
Therefore, I shall now enter this village standing before me.

"Having quickly dispelled your fatigue here, I shall carry you along the path with speed. Having reflected thus, when he desired to enter the Kirāta village situated ahead, I then spoke these words: MU_6,180.11–12. "Having quickly dispelled your fatigue here, I shall carry you along the path with speed. Having reflected thus, when he desired to enter the Kirāta village situated ahead, I then spoke these words: MU_6,180.12.
O friend on the path who has not yet fully understood it, O one free from passion, O you of auspicious form!
Welcome to you, traveler on the great forest road of the path to the gods.
For long have you wandered in this human realm, upon the highway of deserted villages.
O traveler on the road, though you rest, you shall find no rest;
for in this abode of the vulgar, fatigue only increases through resting,
just as thirst indeed increases all the more by drinking salt water.
These living beings are like deer who have the village as their sole refuge, trembling at the rustling of new leaves; they move about in a state of total disarray.
They do not stir in the face of inquiry, nor do they blaze forth in the light of direct experience.
They do not tremble before misconduct, as if they were made of stone or iron;
their manliness is entirely devoted to desire, wealth, passion, and hatred,
and these ruined intellects take delight in actions that are sweet only at first sight.
Noble by birth, lofty, grand, cool, and full of flavor—
wisdom does not find confidence here, just as a mass of clouds finds no rest in a desert.
Better is the state of being in a blind cave, better is the condition of a worm within a stone.
Better a crippled deer in the desert than association with vulgar people.
Vulgar pleasures are sweet for the taste of a moment but lose their charm the next instant; they are intent solely on destruction, like drops of poison.
In dilapidated dwellings, winds blow, scattering grains of ash;
the village scavenger-winds are busy with grass, leaves, and forests. O sinless one, when he had spoken thus, I was then addressed by him as follows.
Having been comforted by my words, as if bathed in the waters of nectar, the traveler said:
"O Blessed One, who are you? You are a full self, a great soul; how have you become one who possesses the Self?"
Beholding the world without agitation, like a traveler observing a village procession:
"Have you drunk the nectar of immortality? Are you a sovereign (samrāj) or a cosmic ruler (virāj)? For though devoid of all objects, you shine for a long time as if completely full."
You are empty, you are full; you are as if whirling, yet you are firm.
You are not everything, yet you are everything; you are nothing at all, or indeed something.
You are tranquil and lovely, radiant and unimpeded.
O Sage, why is this form of yours both serene and majestic?
Though you stand upon the earth, you appear as if situated in the sky above all the worlds;
you are seen to be free from attachment, yet firmly established in [the ultimate] reality.
Though it extends through all objects, it does not possess the nature of those objects;
like the pure moon, your mind remains composed of nectar—
possessing its digits yet free from stain, inwardly cool, radiant, and equanimous.
Filled with the supreme elixir, you shine like the full moon.
I behold this entire circle of worldly existence situated within your consciousness, its presence and absence dependent upon your will, like a fruit within a sprout.
"I am this brahmin named Maṅki, O illustrious one, born of the Śāṇḍilya lineage;
having traveled a very long distance on the occasion of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, I have now seen these holy sites."
After a long time, I prepared to go to my own home;
yet, having seen beings within the belly of the world flashing like lightning, my mind became dispassionate and I had no desire to go home.
O Blessed One, out of compassion, please tell me about yourself;
for the hearts of the virtuous are indeed profound and serene.
Indeed, by the mere sight of them, great beings establish friendship before one.

Like lotuses, all beings blossom and come to rest. I believe that you, through your purity, awakening, and compassion, are capable of dispelling this delusion of my mind, which arises from the wandering of saṃsāra.
Vasiṣṭha:
O one of great intelligence, I am Vasiṣṭha; I am a sage whose home is the sky.
For some purpose, I have come upon this path of the royal seer.
Do not fall into despair; you have entered the path of the wise.
For the most part, you have reached the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra.
Your mind is noble with the power of dispassion, and even your speech is such as this.
And the appearance of one who is not a great soul does not possess a tranquil form.
Just as a gem attains a state of purity through gentle rubbing,
so the mind attains discernment through the ripening of its austerities.
What do you wish to know? How do you wish to abandon saṃsāra?
I believe that what has been taught, you are accomplishing through your actions.
You possess stainless latent impressions (*vāsana*), an exalted mind, and a discerning intellect regarding the minds of worldly people.
"You are indeed fit to lead [the world] to that state which is free from sorrow; this is what is said here.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first canto, titled "The Meeting of Maṅki and Vasiṣṭha."
Vasiṣṭha said:
When he had spoken thus, "It is mine," Maṅki fell at his feet and,
with eyes full of joy, spoke these words on the path as he was being carried along.
Maṅki said:
"O Blessed One, I have wandered extensively through the ten directions;
yet I have not found another holy man who could destroy my doubts."
Today I have obtained the fruit of all the efforts of my body,
in that I have become a bee at your lotus-feet.
O Blessed One, I am weary from beholding the states that bestow the defects of saṃsāra.

Arising again and perishing again, there is constant wandering through pleasure and pain. O Sage, because all pleasures inevitably end in suffering, they are in fact nothing but extreme misery; therefore, suffering alone is better.
Because they end in firm suffering, pleasures cause me pain;
indeed, it is as if my very suffering has turned into pleasure for me. My age, along with my teeth, hair, and limbs, has reached a state of decay.
The intellect, intent on falling from its high station, lacks resolute determination;
it gives rise to evil intentions and does not shine clearly,
like the hollow of a rotten village tree filled with the roots of poisonous *pippala* and *padma* plants.
Through the increase of the thicket of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), day after day, the intellect becomes more wicked in its state— terrible and crooked like a thorny tree or creeper;
while life, filled with exhaustion, passes away like a night blinded by darkness.

Intoxicated and having reached the end of light, exhausted by constant anxiety, it takes no pleasure at all; though seemingly destroyed, it does not perish. Like a withered creeper, our craving has neither flowered nor borne fruit.
Karma, known as latent impression (*vāsanā*), is submerged in the vital point (*marman*) for the sake of misfortune;
life is worn out for the sake of further birth, yet the ocean of existence has not been crossed.
Day after day, the hope for enjoyment swells, bringing only fear.
In one whose nature is both full and incomplete, [the desire for wealth] is exhausted like a pit, a thorn, or a tree. Indeed,
the great calamities of Fortune, which causes the fever of anxiety to manifest,
are such that even what is called "success" expands through deception.
The mind— a hollow darkness flashing with internal jewels,
agitated by waves, empty, like a desolate and withered ocean— does not touch me, for I am intent solely on the objects of the senses; thus say those who possess discernment.
Like a *śleṣmātaka* tree full of thorns standing in impurity, the mind— though devoid of reality, yet characterized by great exertion and like a wind-blown, swaying arjuna tree—
leaps about in vain for the sake of suffering, failing to attain true delight.
The night of ignorance has not merely waned— that night which bore the moon and stars of contact with scriptures and the virtuous, and in which the yakṣa of the ego-sense flourished.
Rather, it has been destroyed by the lion that slays the intoxicated elephant of the darkness of ignorance, and by the fire that consumes the straw of karma.
The sun of discernment has not risen, nor has the night of latent tendencies come to an end.
This elephant-like mind of mine perceives the unreal as real;
the senses are tearing me apart—I know not what will happen.
Even the perspective of the scriptures, when resorted to by the wise for the sake of crossing over,
leads to blindness like a lack of vision if it causes the obsession of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Thus, in this state of extreme delusion, whatever action is undertaken here is truly dreadful.
"O dear one, tell that to me who asks for the sake of ultimate welfare.
When a virtuous person arrives, the mists of delusion subside as in autumn, and all directions likewise become clear;
let there be the word 'Truth,' sung by the company of the virtuous, through you who enlighten me and grant peace from worldly existence."
The Chapter on the Dispassion of Maṅki;
the one hundred and eighty-second chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
Perception, cultivation, latent impression, and conceptualization—
these are the meanings of words here that unfold as devoid of ultimate reality;
know that perception and cultivation are the basis for all defects.
In this very [world], there are calamities, just as there are creepers on a tree of sweet sap.
On the dense path of saṃsāra, which carries the onset of latent impressions (vāsanā),
a diverse and lofty succession of events unfolds.
For the discerning one, the delusion of saṃsāra, along with its latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
gradually perishes at the end of the month of Mādhava, like sapless wood in a forest.
Of this *saṃsṛti*-serpent, it is the latent impression that causes its swelling.
Just as a streak of nectar [emerges] from a dense thicket of plantains,
so does the essence consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā) arise within consciousness as the ocean of saṃsāra;
it is like the sap of the spring season existing within the forest upon the earth.
Apart from pure consciousness, which is stainless and void, nothing else exists;
just as in the infinite sky there is nothing other than emptiness anywhere.
As for that persistent appearance that "there is another essence consisting of sensation," [it is likewise unreal].
This is ignorance, this is delusion, this is the pervasive cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
Established through a lack of discernment,
it perishes in an instant through true insight— unreal in nature yet appearing as real, like a child’s phantom ghost.

Upon the awakening of the vision of all that is seen, they attain oneness with the essence of consciousness, just as the full flood of rivers from the entire surface of the earth becomes one in the ocean.
For just as a vessel made of clay cannot be found apart from the clay when it is empty of clay, [so too the world is not found apart from consciousness].

For that which is to be cognized is indeed composed of consciousness; however, that which is devoid of consciousness is not perceived. Whatever object is awakened within awakening is said to be awakening itself.
Awakening does not perceive what is non-awakening, because of their dissimilarity; therefore, it is not otherwise.
In the seer, the seeing, and the seen, each is nothing but pure awareness (*bodhamātratā*); that is their essence. Therefore, there is nothing else apart from that, just like a flower in the sky.
That which belongs to the same class attains oneness with what is of the same class.
Through that mutual experience, there arises the certainty of oneness.
If wood, stones, and so forth did not possess the nature of consciousness,
then they would never be perceived, just like non-existent things.

But when the entire splendor of the visible world is of the single nature of pure consciousness alone, then, though appearing as other, it is in fact not other, and being thus realized, it is known by consciousness.
This entire visible world pervading the universe is extended as nothing but pure consciousness.
Just as wind is mere vibration and the ocean is mere water,
so too these things— though mixed together like lac and wood—
are not mutually experienced as mixed; for mutual experience constitutes unity.
For mutual experience is unity, and unity is indeed mutual awareness;
it is like that of two waters or two milks, not like that of wood and lac.
"I" leads to bondage, while "not-I" leads to liberation.
O blessed one, when this much is within one's own power, why is there such incapacity?
Like the cognition of two moons or the perception of water in a mirage,
why have I arisen as something non-existent, while in truth I have not arisen at all?
"‘This is mine’ leads to bondage; ‘It is not mine’ leads to liberation.
Since this matter depends entirely upon oneself, why is there ignorance regarding it?
The analogy of the wood and the jujube fruit, and that which exists between the jar and the space [within it], [apply here]."
That relationship, moreover, is not identity; identity is the mutual awareness [of the two].
But identity is indeed mutual awareness, even when it has proceeded into parts;
whether that be non-inert or inert, it does not abandon its single form.
That which is non-inert does not become inert, for its essential nature is immutable;
and as for that which is seen to be both non-inert and inert, there is no identity between them in what is perceived.
Those who are overwhelmed by the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) consist of hundreds of perverse transformations.
In the deep cavern of the forest of saṃsāra, they dance, driven by wretched karmas;
dragged by the rope of latent impressions (vāsanā) and led far away by their own deeds,
they rush ever downward like rocks fallen from a mountain.
Driven hither and thither by the winds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
these human-straws encounter such miseries as cannot even be described.
Through delusion, people who are passionately attached fall with great speed into the hells, like balls struck violently by the palm of the hand.
There, having reached a state of complete decay through moisture, they again become like something else after the passage of time.
The chapter named "The Awakening of Maṅki," the one hundred and eighty-third chapter.
Vasiṣṭha said: Indeed,
for one fallen into the dense path of saṃsāra,
calamities descend like clouds at the onset of the rainy season, marked by their characteristic occurrences.
All these entities are indeed mutually unattached, like stones in a forest; the mental cultivation of them is merely a chain.
The mind stands dense with the trees of its own experiences, leading to blindness.
By the coloring of their dispositions, people are like a forest in spring.
Alas! How strange it is that, under the power of latent impressions, these helpless elemental beings experience pleasures and pains throughout their births.
Alas! How extremely perverse is this latent impression (*vāsanā*), by the power of which people experience within themselves this delusion that does not even exist—
[this delusion] which is delightful, like nectar, pure, and illuminating.
What difference is there between one who is cool toward all objects and the wise moon?
What difference is there between a fool who desires whatever comes first or last without reflection, and a child who has no sense of restraint?

Tell me, what difference is there between a cat and a fool regarding material things, when both, until the end of their lives, do not renounce what they have acquired, whether good or bad? Indeed, all these things— body, wife, wealth, and so forth— [are of the same nature].
They quickly crumble like a shallow bowl of sand that has dried fast;
even as they wander through hundreds of wombs from the peak of Brahma down to a blade of grass for the duration of an eon,
there is no peace of mind without tranquility.
Merely by reflecting upon this, even the scent of bondage does not afflict you,
just as the unevenness of a path does not trouble one who is looking ahead while walking. Desire shall not swallow up your mind, for it is now fixed in concentration.
What can a *piśāca* do against a Buddha who is ever-vigilant?
Just as the expansion of the eye is merely the perception of form,
so too this world exists as the very nature of the expansion of pure consciousness, including the sense of "I."
O Slayer of the Enemy, just as the eye’s concealment is the cessation of the perception of all forms, so too is the concealment of consciousness the cessation of all that is visible.
This world, along with me, is indeed non-existent; pure consciousness alone expands within the void.
Just as the wind, through its slight expansion, quickly produces vibration; so too,
even while not performing any action, this [intellect] conceives of the unreal as if it were real—
just as one perceives the state of being a pot within gold, which is inseparable from it and inherent to it.
Just as the sky is mere emptiness, just as the wind is mere movement,
and just as waves and the like are mere water, so too is the world mere consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*).
The three worlds are nothing but uninterrupted, partless pure consciousness.
Know that the peaceful one is like the sky, or like a mountain reflected in water.
In the liberated and tranquil knower,
there arises a coolness within which even these moons, kinsmen to the blazing fire, find their place.
In this world, which is empty, devoid of light, beyond all perception, and whose nature is the one, absolute, peaceful, and pervasive Śiva— what is produced by what, and in what manner?
That existence which is designated by the word "Brahman" is the innate form of everything.
Wherever there is no sublation whatsoever, everything there is composed of that [Reality] and is imperishable.
But as for this state of being a discrete object where sublation is experienced,
or that which is perceived as a sublation itself— we do not know it to exist, like a flower in the sky.
O Knower, remain as one whose mind has departed, tranquil like a great stone; free from the non-awakened mind, abide in the infinite, unborn, and imperishable silence.
For one who stands in their own state, which is like space, there is no perception of limbs and so forth.

Without the firmness of repeated practice, it exists like a transformation in a dream. Without any collection of material causes, the non-acting Brahman perceives the variegated world as if upon no wall at all; it is neither anyone nor anything whatsoever.
Whatever it expands, that is indeed its own self, situated there in that very way;
because of the absence of the visible, one who does not perceive that [object]—who, where, and what could he do?
"I am happy"—thus one is happy; "I am miserable"—thus one is miserable.
All things, even those of the nature of space, remain established in their own-being as if they were earthen.
For all entities, though their essence is the space of consciousness,
their earthenness exists for you only falsely, like that of mountains in a dream.
Existence, when delineated as "I," is subject to the transformations of the burden of delusion;
in the absence of that [delusion], there is a state of resting solely in one's own nature, characterized by tranquility.
Just as the referent of the word "bracelet" does not exist as something distinct from gold, [so too is the self not distinct from its true nature].
When it is thus non-existent as something separate, there is no "I-ness" for one whose nature is peace.
Extinct, mindless, silent, both agent and non-agent, and cool,
the Knower remains alone and tranquil, empty yet completely full.
Moving without latent impressions like the limbs of a mechanical puppet,
the knower remains exactly as he is, even while engaged in worldly activity;
just as a child lying on a couch may move or may not move at all.

For one who has thus known the Self—possessing the singular awakening that is free from conceptualization, devoid of hope, effort, and desire—how could there be any mental synthesis (anusandhāna)? Since his nature is the Self, which is peaceful and characterized by pure "I-ness" (ahantva), whence could such synthesis arise? (MU 6.183.33–34)
For one who is not a seer, for whom there is nothing to be seen, whose form is vision itself, and who is formless—how indeed could there be any mental synthesis for such a witness who is independent?
Dependence alone is dense bondage; independence alone is liberation.
When one has come to rest within that [consciousness] which is endowed with all sounds, what is there to be seen? When this body— though composed of earth— is as non-existent as one's own dream,
being in essence nothing but a delusion, from where, where, for whom, and what could there be any mutual dependence?
With all worldly desires stilled, with every curiosity departed,
and with sensation cast away, the wise man dwells in pure consciousness through his realization.
Thus, O Maṅkin, even great delusion is overcome by one who has heard this.
There he was completely cast off, like the skin by a snake;
performing his duties as they flowed toward him, he had discarded all latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Thus, at the end of a hundred years, he remained on the mountain in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Until now, he remains like a stone;
yet the yogi whose internal organ is stilled awakens when being instructed.
By this means, O Rāghava, through the path of discernment, one attains peace and may wander with an enlightened mind.
Let not your mind, filled with passion, fall into despondency; it shall vanish in an instant like a row of autumn clouds in a cloudless sky.
The one hundred and eighty-fourth canto, titled "The Conclusion of Maṅki’s Nirvāṇa."
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Become extinguished, O gentle one, with a peaceful soul, following whatever has been attained;
though existing, be as if non-existent, fashioned like a crystal."
When everything is established within that single, expansive Self,
how can there be the conceptualization of multiplicity— neither in the one nor in the many?
Everything is devoid of beginning and end, a void filled with the essence of consciousness.
In the arising and destruction of bodies, what impairment can there be for the consciousness-principle?
For the play of the world flashes forth due to the flickering of the wonder of consciousness;
through the absence of that flickering, they dissolve like waves into water.
Just as the suspicion that there is cloth in a white cloud does not bear fruit,
so too this suspicion that "I am this body" is not real. Do not remain immersed in what is unreal, which brings forth manifold fear.
O fortunate one, for the sake of your well-being, meditate today upon that Reality which is the source of infinite bliss.
"I am indeed the infinite space of consciousness; there is no limit to my self"—may this supreme Reality, in its true nature, be your object of praise.
O Rāma, you alone are such a one possessed of this certainty, the stainless one;
there is not even the slightest reality whatsoever of the meditator, the object of meditation, or the act of meditation.
The seer, the seen, and the seeing—these are merely manifestations of consciousness.
Therefore, there is nothing other than that consciousness to be studied or to be meditated upon.
When the new moon rises and the wind of dissolution blows,
the reality of the Self— equanimous and serene— is neither agitated nor stilled.
Just as to one traveling by boat, stationary objects such as stumps, trees, and mountains appear to move;
and just as there is the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl, so too is the body and so forth [perceived] by the mind.
Just as the body and so forth belong to the mind, so too does the mental belong to the body.
In that very way, the individual soul is in the Supreme; whence then can there be duality or unity?
All this is thus the peaceful Brahman, whose consciousness is expanded;
there is no such thing as the world and so forth, nor does any other delusion exist.

Just as a forest does not exist in the sky, nor moisture in sand, nor lightning in the orb of the moon, so too do the body and such things not exist in the mind. Since this [body] is non-existent, do not fear the delusion of the world.
Know this alone to be the supreme truth, O best among those who know the truth:
that the notion "the world exists" or "it does not exist for me"—that which was your delusion today—has been stilled by my instruction; what other cause for bondage could there be?

Just as pots, water-jars, vases, and the like are nothing but clay, so too this world is mind-only; and that [mind] is extinguished through investigation. In adversity and prosperity, in existence and non-existence, one's consciousness is characterized by the cessation of desire, joy, and dejection.
Released from the sense of "I" through equanimity, remain as you are, or dissolve away.
O moon of your own noble lineage, if you have correctly understood reality as it truly is and remain established therein,
then— freed from joy, sorrow, desire, and vice— remain as you wish, relying upon that [reality].
The one hundred and eighty-fifth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Practice of Conduct According to One's Own Comfort," [spoken by] Rāma.
"O Lord, tell me again the true nature of seeds and sprouts, of human actions that produce birth, and of those things signified by the term 'fate' (daiva). Vasiṣṭha said:
