This very vibration of consciousness, extending from fate, action, and so forth, up to the formation of jars and other objects, has attained the state of "personhood" (puruṣatā) in the world. Apart from the vibration of consciousness, what could manhood or action possibly be?
Indeed, this entire world, consisting of jars, wells, cloths, and so forth, is created by this very [consciousness].
The fortune of the world proceeds from the vibration of consciousness accompanied by latent impressions (vāsanā);
for the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) ceases through the vibration of consciousness devoid of latent impressions.
For they know that the vibration of consciousness is without substrate and is non-vibration;
even though it is a vibration, it is not a vibration [in the ordinary sense], since by it whirlpools and the like are not carried away in the waters.
There is not even the slightest difference between consciousness and the self, which consists of the vibration of consciousness.
Apart from a portion of conceptual construction, O Rāma, there is no duality between the person and his action in the process of creation,
just as the duality between a wave and the water arises from mental resolve and is not real; so it is here with the living being and his karma, which consist of the vibration of consciousness.
O Rāma, action alone is the person, and the person alone is the state of action;
know that these two are non-different, just as frost and coldness are.
Just as that which is frost is coldness, and that which is coldness is frost.
Whatever action that being performs, that being is that very action; whatever being there is, that is that very action.
These—divinity, action, man, and so forth—are synonyms for the essence of the vibration of consciousness (saṃvitspanda); they do not exist as separate entities from action and the rest.
Through vibration, consciousness becomes the seed of the world; through non-vibration, it attains seedlessness.
And that very [consciousness] is the sprout, because the glory of the sprout already exists within it.
Consciousness, by its very nature, is non-vibrating in some respects and vibrating in others.
It exists as infinite, like a single ocean, transcending the sequence of space and time.
The vibration of consciousness, possessing latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is here the causeless seed;
having become the cause, it gives rise to the series of sprouts that are the body and so forth.
Even regarding the movement of grass, creepers, vines, shrubs, seeds, and sprouts, the seed is nothing but the vibration of consciousness (*saṃvitspanda*); for that [vibration], no seed exists.
There is no difference between the seed and the sprout, just as there is none between fire and its heat.
Know that the seed itself is the sprout; know that action alone is the human being.
Consciousness, throbbing within the sheath of the earth, produces the sprouts of stationary things—whether gross or subtle, soft or harsh—just as milk produces bubbles.
Without the earth-receptacle, which is exceedingly delicate,
who would be capable of causing sprouts as hard as diamond to emerge? Consciousness, residing within the essence of the vital energy of living beings, extends throughout all that is mobile.
Just as the sap residing within a creeper produces flowers and fruit, so too,
if consciousness were omnipresent and not exceedingly powerful,
then who would be capable of causing the arousal of even the mountain-like demons?
For this is indeed the primordial seed of all moving and stationary beings;
it has no seed other than the mere vibration of consciousness.
[There is no seed] for the conceptualizations of seed and sprout, nor for action, the person, or karma.
There is a difference in name but not in substance between waves, ripples, and billows.

To that Great One, for whom duality in humans and their actions is understood through the analogy of the seed and the sprout, let there be constant salutation— He who is the wise one among the ignorant.

The essence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) residing within consciousness, which is the seed of birth, causes the sprout [of rebirth] to flourish; burn that away with the fire of non-attachment. Whether one acts or does not act, there is no sinking [into the cycle of existence] by means of the mind.

The wise know that non-attachment consists in [remaining unattached] toward actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious. Alternatively, the eradication of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) itself is traditionally known as non-attachment;
therefore, by whatever means possible, bring about that very state within yourself.

By whatever means you know them, through human effort, eradicate the latent tendencies (vāsanā) completely; this alone is supreme auspiciousness. By whatever method you understand it, through personal exertion, [act accordingly].

One must restrain the portion consisting of the sense of "I-ness"; this indeed is the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*). There is no other way to cross over *saṃsāra* than through human effort, in this state called the destruction of latent impressions, which consists of the absence of the sense of "I-ness."
Consciousness alone exists here at the very beginning; that is the sprout, and that is the seed.
That is karma, and that is the person (puruṣa); that is destiny (daiva), and that is the auspicious and inauspicious.
There is no other seed at the outset, nor is there a sprout, nor indeed a person.
Neither karma nor destiny and so forth arise independently; for indeed, there is no seed, nor is there even a sprout. O virtuous one, neither karma exists, nor does the person (puruṣa) exist;
yet, through this splendor of designation, the single Consciousness alone has arisen, like an actor appearing in the beautiful roles of gods, humans, and asuras.
Having cultivated this very certainty, O healthy one, and having utterly abandoned the doubt regarding the deliberation of human action,
remain indeed as you desire, with your body of consciousness, free from latent impressions and liberated from all mental constructions.
Established in pure consciousness alone— tranquil, free from all desires, and devoid of doubt— you shall accomplish every task.

Delighting solely in the Self, his desires completely fulfilled, free from fear, O Rāma, he is delighted by tranquility. The one hundred and eighty-sixth canto, titled "The Demonstration of Freedom from Fear."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Always remain inward-turned, free from passion and devoid of latent impressions,
contemplating everywhere the stainless, peaceful Brahman that is pure consciousness alone.

With wisdom as clear as space, established in the singular, dense mass of pure consciousness, he was equanimous, gentle, and equal in bliss; his heart was nourished by the True Brahman. Amidst sorrows, terrible calamities, perils, and abysses, [he remained unshaken].
Toward all things encountered— whether lowly or exalted— remain free from suffering; according to their sequence and their place, experience pain as one who is not pained,
like a fool overcome by latent tendencies, even unto tears and lamentation.
O gentle-souled one, in the company of beloved ones, at festivals, and at times of prosperity, experience joy like one who is deluded and overcome by latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Yet,
toward living beings in their death-related tasks, such as battles and the like, remain merciless.
Like a forest fire consumes grass, [burn away] the deluded mind overcome by latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Without weariness toward goals that come in due course, acquire wealth through reflection like a heron;
in the tasks of acquiring wealth, remain like one who is deluded and overcome by latent impressions.
O destroyer of enemies, forcibly shatter all your foes like the wind disperses empty clouds, as if they were deluded by the power of latent tendencies;
show compassion toward those people who are wretched and worthy of pity.
With a mind delighting in the Self, remain silent like one who is deluded and overcome by latent impressions. Be joyful amidst pleasures, be sorrowful amidst sorrows;
show compassion toward the miserable, and be courageous among the brave.
Always inward-turned and full of bliss, endowed with delight in your own self,
whatever you do, O sinless one, you are not the agent therein, being noble in tranquility through the constant internal state of the cultivation of the Self, O virtuous one.

O Rāma, even the Vajradhārā [thunderbolt] falls and becomes blunted against you. He who dwells at ease within the self— the cavity of pure self-consciousness alone, free from the construction of mental volitions— is the Great Lord, delighting in the self.
Weapons do not pierce it; fires do not burn it;
waters do not moisten it; and winds do not dry it up.
Embracing one's own self—which is well-supported, sufficient, undecaying, and immortal—[one is liberated].
"Remain with your intellect and self firmly established, like a temple supported by strong pillars;

perceiving that pure consciousness which possesses the supreme splendor of the fragrance of the flowers that are the multitude of objects in the tree of the world, remain inward-turned and unshakable."
For those who constantly perform external actions with inward-turned focus,
no latent impression (*vāsanā*) arises even while they live, just as it does not arise in stones.
Again, make the mind sleep within, released from its outward proliferation.

Performing all actions like the limbs of a tortoise, remaining without outward engagement; with a mind that is inwardly devoid of activity yet appears to possess outward activity, as if one who has just awakened from sleep, carry out your duties.
Like the consciousness of a child, a mute, or the like, your mind— having cast off internal latent impressions— is not defiled while performing its duties, being like the sky;
it is dissolved through the abandonment of mental fluctuations and spreads only slightly outward.

Remain free from fever, dwelling within with a mind that is profoundly asleep. When the dissolution and emergence of the mind arise through knowledge— purified of the stain of volitional construction— abide in pure consciousness, O sinless one, and neither act nor refrain from acting.
Moving through the waking state with a mental state like that of deep sleep, sleeping while engaged in worldly activity—
grasp at nothing whatsoever, and do not renounce anything either.
If you are as if in deep sleep even while awake, then you truly wake within deep sleep itself.

Because of the identity of waking and deep sleep, you are that which is free from affliction. Thus, by means of gradual practice, one should attain that state which is devoid of beginning and end, beyond duality, and transcending all things.
"Neither duality nor even unity— having reached this certainty that the world is thus, O Rāma, attain the supreme rest with a mind as clear as space. Rāma said:
"If that is so, O tiger among sages, then you yourself, who consist of the notion of 'I', are here called Vasiṣṭha; therefore, tell me why. Vālmīki said:

While Rāghava was speaking thus, Vasiṣṭha, the best among eloquent men, remained silent for half a moment, his movements composed. While he stood thus silent, the great assembly of courtiers wondered, "What will happen now?"
When the ocean of doubt had subsided, Rāma spoke again:
"O Blessed One, for what reason do you remain silent like me?"
"There is no principle in this world where the excellence of the virtuous comes to an end.
Vasiṣṭha said: "It is not because I am unable to speak that my capacity for speech has reached its exhaustion."
But, O sinless one, for this question of yours today, silence alone is the answer.
There are two kinds of questioners: the knower of reality and the ignorant.
To the ignorant, an answer should be given according to their ignorance; but to the knower, an answer should be given according to his knowledge.
For so long a time, O Mahāmati, you were one who had not realized that state, serving as a vessel for further conceptualizations;
but now you have become a knower of that, resting in the supreme state.
Clearly, you are not fit for the higher states accompanied by conceptual thought (savikalpa).

O best of speakers, whatever verbal expression there may be— whether its meaning be subtle or ultimate, and whether it be extensive or even very brief— [it is all within the realm of conceptualization].
"O virtuous one, every such [answer] is marked by errors such as the exclusion of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), distinctions in number, and so forth— just as light is marked by motes of dust.
Therefore, O handsome one, a knower of reality does not accept an answer that is stained with flaws."
There is no speech that is without flaw, yet you remain as one who knows it.
And what must be spoken by me to the wise disciple exactly as it is,
the wise know to be the silence of wood, which is devoid of an end.
They say that silence—unceasing and free from conceptual construction—is the supreme state. That very silence has been granted to you, O handsome one, who know that [state].
For, my dear, whatever a person consists of, such is what he speaks.
"I declare that the mere object of knowledge is non-existent, and I abide in the state beyond speech.
For how can one who stands in the state beyond speech grasp the impurity of speech?
Therefore, I do not speak the unspeakable; for speech is indeed marked by conceptual construction."
Rāma:
Disregarding those words that proceed from you which are full of faults,
tell me— who, preceded by the exclusion of opposites— are you?
Vasiṣṭha:
This being the case, O Rāghava, hear this as it truly is:
"Who are you? Who am I? Or what is the world?"—O best among those who know reality.
For now, I am this peaceful, stainless light of consciousness,
devoid of the perception of objects of thought and transcending all volitional constructions.
I am the clear space of consciousness, and you, indeed, are space itself.

The entire world and all space are nothing but space alone. My self consists solely of pure knowledge within the self that is composed of pure knowledge; liberated from the state of other consciousnesses, I know not how to speak of anything else.
Those intent on manifesting their own particular doctrines lead even those striving for liberation— who are bound solely by the notion of "I" and "self"— into a hundredfold branching of views,
whether they are living in a state of tranquility or engaged in worldly affairs.
That state which is like a corpse, they call the supreme state.
It is peaceful, without external means, infinite in its means, and equal;
it is neither pleasure nor pain, neither "I" nor "another"—this is the auspicious state of abiding.
This "I-ness" of liberation is the absence of the mark of mental cultivation;
yet that very [absence] is sought by means of that [cultivation]. It is like a person blind from birth looking for a variegated painting.
Whether in movement or in stillness, one should remain as motionless as a stone.
Know that this is the unconditioned, ageless state of Nirvāṇa belonging only to the non-inert;
and that is not known by another, but is experienced by oneself alone— just as a wise man, detached from worldly desire, experiences his own wisdom within himself.
Herein there is neither "I-ness" nor "thou-ness," neither egoity nor even otherness;
it is simply the state of absolute purity, the stainless and auspicious Nirvana.
They say that the very turning toward objects of thought is the consciousness of this conscious being.
This very cycle of existence is bondage, leading to abundant suffering.
Know that liberation is the supreme, peaceful state, the imperishable, wherein the conscious self attains its unconsciousness— that is, the nature of being turned away from objects of consciousness.
In that which is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, peaceful, and abiding as the tranquil Self, an object of consciousness is simply not possible; who could perceive what, and how?
Within the vision of thought and dream, there is nothing other than the nature of pure consciousness itself.
Just as no other form exists, so it is when [the Self] has gone outside;
these [faculties] such as the mind (manas) and the intellect (buddhi) have the nature of pure consciousness alone.
However, when they are conditioned by the objects denoted by the words "mind," "intellect," and so forth, they become insentient in nature.
In pure consciousness alone— which is uniform, clear, extended both internally and externally,
and undivided— why does the notion of duality expand, leading to such misfortune? What difference is there between pure consciousness and the void?
And that which lies between these, the wise know; it does not come within the range of speech.
Just as some appearance, consisting of both being and non-being, is perceived with effort in the darkness, so too has this [world] gone into Brahman.
"If I am pacified and free from latent impressions (vāsanā), I am indeed space itself;
yet I do not bind myself to latent impressions, for I remain as the very sky of consciousness.
Thus resolved within himself, the knower of reality appears like an ignorant man in outward appearance.

Though existing in the form of knowledge, it subsides of its own accord as if non-existent. The fire of ignorance blazes among living beings through the secret of cognition, fanned by the wind of nescience; yet for those who are awakened, it is extinguished by that very same [cognition].
That which is the ignorance of those who are not insentient, like that of pillars remaining in a state of stillness—they call that liberation: unmoving, seated, and without decay.
Having attained ignorance through [the realization of] the nature of knowing, the human being becomes a sage.
Through ignorance, having fallen into a state of unknowing, one goes to the condition of a beast or a tree.
The delusion consisting of ignorance—the notion that "I am Brahman" and "this is the world"—is unreal;
upon investigation, it is not found, just as darkness is not found by means of a lamp.
Even though the entire collection of sensory organs is present, one whose intellect is peaceful is without volition or perception;
he experiences nothing at all, whether internally or externally. Just as in deep sleep, his dream-like state dissolves within meditative absorption.
All that is visible is again perceived within the consciousness of the Knower as being of the nature of space alone.
Just as the quality of having a bottom is [illusory] in the sky, so too is the state of earth and the other elements in Śiva;
it is nothing other than mere delusion. As is the sky, so is Śiva.
Even though he is endowed with all latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he is free from latent impressions;
for his intellect is such that it perceives all this as non-existent.
[The world] arises from conceptual constructions (*saṅkalpa*) born of the past, the future, dreams, illusions, and sorcery.
Just as there are cycles of rebirth, so too, even though [the world] is seen [as such], why do you have any attachment to it?
There is no suffering and no pleasure, no merit and no sin;
nothing whatsoever has been lost by anyone, because an agent and an enjoyer are impossible.
Everything is empty and without support; even this notion of "mine" is like the double moon or a city in a dream. He to whom it belongs does not exist for us either.
Whether one remains solely within conventional discourse or is devoted to the silence of wood, [the same applies].

Remaining like wood or stone, one attains the state of Brahman. Regarding both tranquility and manifoldness, here in this auspicious reality which is of a non-dual nature, there exists no other logical principle than that of the whole and its parts.
In this stainless, all-pervading Brahman, there is no expression of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because neither the state of being an object nor the state of being a possessor is possible.
Nor is there non-existence, because it is perceived; nor is there existence in the Unborn (*aja*), because it is pure consciousness.
Because the view of grasped object and grasping subject is impossible, there exists nothing at all.

That which is equal, stainless, unassailable, cherished by the noble ones, auspicious, unborn, undecaying, seated in equanimity—that true state, such as it is, is peaceful. Remain thus; drink, move, eat; for this "you" does not exist.
The one hundred and eighty-seventh canto, titled "The Exposition of the Cultivation of Nirvana," by Vasiṣṭha:
The very sense of "I" (ahantā) is the supreme ignorance that obstructs the state of Nirvāṇa;
that this very thing is sought after by the deluded is the behavior of a madman. The sense of "I" alone is sufficient as the illustration of the ignorance of the ignorant.

For one who knows that and is at peace, the notions of "I" and "mine" do not exist. Having cast off the impurity of egoism, the knower remains free from fever— whether possessing a body or bodiless— like the stainless sky, having attained Nirvana.
Neither the autumnal sky, nor the still ocean,
nor the center of the full moon shines as brilliantly as the wise man does;
just as there is an extraordinary lack of agitation in the army during a colorful battle.
Likewise, for the wise one who engages in worldly affairs, there is a single equanimity.
Because of the oneness with nirvāṇa, for the wise one, even mental impressions (*vāsanā*) are not truly impressions.
Like lines drawn on a rope, the waves and so forth of the ocean are not different from the water.

Just as the ocean, despite its surging waves, is entirely nothing but water, so too Brahman—though appearing as the swelling of the visible world—is Brahman alone and nothing else. Internally it has subsided and is unagitated; externally it has subsided and is tranquil.
And he who is impelled by that [consciousness] is said to be liberated.

Consciousness, in the form of the ego and its emanations, vibrates within the supreme consciousness which consists of consciousness; like water in water or air in air, what is the nature of this apparent diversity?
Just as the various formations of elephants, horses, and so forth, which appear in the smoke spreading through the sky,
are not distinct from that smoke, so too are all creations [not distinct] from the Supreme State.
This is understood through an investigation into the delusion of consciousness, by one who delights in the non-attainment of delusion.
Be victorious; do not fall into despondency, for you possess that knowledge which belongs to the Knower.

Just as a sprout internally experiences the tree, the flower, and the fruit, so too the Knower, whose nature is the space of the Self, perceives the world within the "I-ness" of the Self; yet that space of the Self is itself both space and non-space.

Like the appearance of a staff in water or flames due to the presence of form, light, and the mind, these [truths], though existing, do not exist as such; they are like the unsteady movements of the deluded mind.
According to pleasure, according to undertaking, according to destruction, and according to arising—
"Remain peaceful according to the place and the time, free from decay.
Even while engaging in worldly affairs, remain peaceful amidst the attainment of the desirable and the undesirable;
like a corpse, you shall experience no internal change, being fully extinguished."
He who possesses the ego devoid of mental impressions (*vāsanā*) sustains the world for a long time;
whether living or not living, he is a conscious soul (*cijjīva*), the supreme state.
Consciousness itself, when carried away by the vehicle of insentience, serves only as a burden of suffering.

For men bound by the fetters [of worldly existence], like young calves in the ocean, they take refuge in that reality of liberation; yet the ignorant do not do so, as if because of a lack of experience.
How indeed can one who is living attain that which is said to be attained only by the dead?
Whatever is conceptualized, that very thing is subject to destruction by virtue of that conceptualization itself.
That state where this [conceptualization] does not occur is the true, imperishable station.
Realizing that "there is neither another nor am I," become fearless through such contemplation.
This is true by reason, just as even poison can become nectar.
Having investigated the entire body, from the inert physical form up to the mind, one realizes "I am not";
therefore, the truth is "I am not."

For those who have stilled all particularities and whose investigation has reached the end of the sense of "I," pure liberation arises; yet nothing whatsoever is destroyed. Indeed, there is nothing here other than the human effort consisting of the investigation into the renunciation of enjoyment.
"Since it is of service, let one's own Self alone be quickly saluted by the ignorant.
(MU 6.187.23) They describe such reflection free from latent impressions as liberation; yet that never occurs without awakening.
"The delusion of the world has been destroyed"—this is the supreme awakening here. Since there is no conviction in this matter, that [delusion] is bondage for a long time. (MU 6.187.24)

Having correctly understood that "the world is unreal," and being indifferent toward sons, wealth, wife, and body, he indeed becomes like a conscious stone; for there is truly no liberation other than this.
The chapter titled "The Application of Instruction on the Presentation of Ultimate Reality."
The one hundred and eighty-eighth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"In the universal self, which is the manifestation of consciousness, that very [reality] is experienced immediately."
Whatever is experienced internally, whether it be unreal or a real entity,
that very thing first appears through the force of habituation as if having the nature of an external object; one's own dream is the illustration for this.

All this is of the nature of consciousness (*cit-rūpa*), and consciousness is clearer even than the sky; yet there is nothing whatsoever that is non-consciousness, and therefore this is nothing at all anywhere.
There is no destruction, no non-existence, no object, no birth or death, and no space.
There is neither emptiness nor non-existence; everything is indeed Brahman alone, and yet not even that.
Upon the destruction of the world, the ego-sense, and so forth, nothing at all is destroyed.
For even when the unreal is destroyed—such as a mountain in a dream—what is it that perishes?
In a false appearance, such as a city of one's imagination, how could there be any destruction?
Likewise, in the case of the world, the "I," and so forth, no destruction exists when they are non-existent.
If it is asked, "Whence then comes the reproach of the world?"—that [reproach] applies to that which is not a real entity.
No determination is possible regarding sky-flowers; what could possibly be determined?
But this indeed is the determination here: that by not conceiving anything at all, you remain like a stone, exactly as you are and according to your natural state.

The world, whose nature is mere conceptualization, is extinguished entirely in an instant when joined with the meaning of "not" (nañ); such is the conclusion regarding the delusion of creation. This creation is indeed unrestrained, yet it is imperishable because its essence is Brahman.
Otherwise, this creation does not exist, nor does the state of being a creation; for those for whom no creation exists— just like unreal men in a dream—
that creation and those persons are like the waves of water in a mirage.
Regarding these things which, though non-existent, have attained as it were the state of existence,
we know no definitive conclusion, just as one cannot reach a conclusion regarding the words about the son of a barren woman.
There is a certain, unprecedented fullness, resembling the perfectly full ocean.
Those who know that do not fall into the perception of the parts of the seer and the seen;
like lamps in a windless place, like mountains, or like water that has become calm,
they remain established in their own natural state, whether possessing outward conduct or free from it.
Resembling a single, full ocean, an indescribable inner fullness arises;
a consciousness characterized by inner coolness is perceived in the knower as something truly unprecedented.
When examined, this so-called "person" here is nothing but latent impression (*vāsanā*), and that [impression] is not found to exist [independently].
And no one perceives that [darkness]; therefore, cyclic existence (saṃsāra) is pervasive. That which is established through non-perception does not exist because of perception;
for here, the example of blackness is clearly demonstrated by its non-apprehension.
The elements consist of the body, flesh, and so forth, and that is unreal, a delusion, and insentient;
the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*cetas*) are composed of those very [elements] and nothing else.
Having abandoned the state of being composed of the elements and so forth for the intellect, ego-sense, and consciousness, [one realizes their true nature].

If an absolute state of stability is attained, that is declared to be liberation. Since consciousness remains as such because it does not rest upon an object of thought, what kind of existence could there be here?
Therefore, what is the latent impression (vāsanā), from where, where, and of what nature is it?
And for one who has this delusion, that which is unreal is not found by right investigation;
like the water of a mirage, therefore, to whom would saṃsāra belong, what would it be, and from where?
Thus, if that is the case, then the very arising of the thought "to whom would it belong? is itself [unreal].
Once again, that very same delusion of saṃsāra proceeds.
Therefore, without relying on anything, one should remain equanimous like space;
non-recollection is the highest good here, and forgetting is supreme.
Here there is no seer and no enjoyer; there is neither existence nor non-existence.
This world remains as it is—quiescent, one, and ever-vibrant like the ocean.
When it is clearly realized that the entire visible universe is Brahman, which is Being, [all duality ceases].
When the reflection [of the mind] perishes like the drying up of water, auspiciousness arises;
whether it be a state of tranquility or worldly activity, it is seen as free from passion and hatred by one who has rested in the supreme reality and possesses equal vision.
Alternatively, only the state of peace remains for this Nirvana.
Indeed, how can the Sage, being free from latent tendencies (*nirvāsana*), engage in conventional discourse?
This is so as long as his Nirvana has not reached full maturity.

For that long he conducts himself, free from the arising of passion, hatred, and fear; but when passion, fear, and anger have departed, having attained nirvāṇa with a peaceful mind, the sage— though appearing like one who possesses no virtue— abides in the Self.
Just as the entire lotus plant exists within the seed of the lotus in its sheath, so too the delusion of dreaming is non-different from the Self; there is no externality.
Through the cultivation of externality, the external appears; through the cultivation of the nature of the Self, it is the Self alone.
This cultivation occurs within the supreme reality; for that [reality] is indeed that very thing.
This very same delusion of internal dreams and so forth is expressed as being external.
There is not even the slightest difference here, just as there is none between the milk in two different vessels.
In this same way, stability and instability, which consist merely of delusion and are pervasive,
possess those two relations of container and contained, just like water and its waves.
In dreams and similar states, there is the perception of otherness because of the cognition of otherness [of objects] from the self.
But when there is the awakening to non-dual existence, that [consciousness] does not arise as something other than that;
for that which is the form of the Supreme Self— devoid of conceptual construction and tranquil—
becomes this [consciousness] through its being that, whereas it would not be that through its not being that.
When the cognitions of dreams and the like have subsided, that pure, sovereign form exists;
it is not non-existent, nor does it fall within the range of speech.
When delusion has utterly dissolved, the liberated one alone realizes it.
The true nature [of the self] is not an object of instruction, even for the wise.
Having abandoned the body—which is characterized by fear, pride, despondency, greed, and delusion—as well as the dullness of thought, the senses, and the mind;
having cast off the "I" and all distinctions, it is fitting to abide solely in that one, unborn, and imperishable Nirvāṇa.
The one hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Method for Nirvana," by Vasiṣṭha.

When consciousness expands, then the delusion of the world and the sense of "I" arise as if they were real, though they are truly non-existent— just as the appearance of a rope arises from the movement of water.
Even when this delusion has arisen, it does not lead to distress, because one knows its true nature to be Brahman.
But for the supreme detriment, through the cultivation of the meaning of the word "world," consciousness assumes the experience of forms by its outward extension; likewise,
by its outward extension, it remains established in the delusion of the waking state.
It might spread for two months and yet be useless; however, because it lacks intrinsic existence (*svabhāva*), it is not real.
How can that which is unreal spread? Where does the son of a barren woman dance?
This [spreading], however, exists merely as a deluded experience based on direct perception alone.
It is indeed non-existent because it is not experienced by itself, like a yakṣa in a child’s imagination;
for one feels "I am this" and "I exist for the sake of suffering. Since there is no such feeling [of a real self], the self is not [the agent]; thus, bondage and liberation depend upon oneself.
That indeed is meditation, that is concentration for you: to sit without sensation, like one who is insentient though not insentient—equanimous, peaceful, and free from ailment.
[This state is reached] through the distinctions between duality and non-duality, and through the dispelling of the confusion caused by the construction of sentences.
Do not despair over suffering like ignorant men, O wise ones. Suffering clings to the unreal, like a dream, for one whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are dense—
just as forms, light, and mental attention are fashioned by conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*).
One whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have become attenuated does not experience suffering at all, remaining as if asleep,
as if devoid of conceptualization regarding forms, light, and mental attention;
when the latent impression itself reaches a state of extreme attenuation, it attains liberation.
Through the conjunction of place, time, and action, an object— as if reaching the state of non-existence—
attains extreme attenuation; it is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) itself that reaches liberation,
just as a cloud in the sky attains the state of emptiness through the dimension of an infinitesimal atom.
Through awakening, the cultivation of non-existence reaches a state of density;
just as foolishness turns into wisdom through the practice of associating with the learned,
so too does the conviction "I am not" arise within through sound reasoning, culminating in the nature of peace.
This awakening, which has deeply taken root in both the living and the dead, is known as "consciousness" (bodha).
Just as movement exists in the wind, this world and its like appear here;
it is pacified only through inquiry such as, "Who am I? How is this? MU 6.189.14–15.
"Nirvana is simply 'I am not'—how much delusion is there in this?
Through the company of the virtuous and through inquiry, this is quickly understood.
By associating with those who know reality, the bondage of 'I am' indeed perishes."

As darkness is dispelled by light, or as night by day, one should investigate for as long as one lives—through association with those who know reality—the questions: "Who am I? How is this visible world? What is the living soul (jīva), and what is life? *Mokṣopāya* 6.189.17–18.
Life shines as the world, yet it perishes through the thought "I am darkness. Let that [darkness] be dispelled by the light of reality through service to the sun of the Knower of That.
O friend, whatever person possesses excellence of awakening, attend upon each of them individually.
From attachment and worldly discourse, the demoness of disputation arises for them.
When the yakṣa of contention has appeared, even for the wise man— as it does for the fool—
the delusion "I am" arises, obstructing the primary liberation that has been described.
Therefore, a wise person should serve a learned scholar in private on each occasion;
having unified those points taught by him, one should reflect upon them with the intellect.
One should reflect upon the meaning of what was said with the intellect for the sake of increasing one's wisdom.
One should attain identity with that Reality which is free from all conceptual constructions.
Having brought the intellect to a state of supreme sharpness through union with the All-knowing One,
let this single creeper of ignorance be utterly reduced to fragments.
This matter is indeed possible; therefore, I shall relate it to you.
We were but children who experienced this, not perceivers of what is improper.
It was like the manifestation of clouds from the sky, or like the breaking of waves upon the great ocean.

It is not logical that anything perishes here at the time of destruction, for there is no mental construction whatsoever for one who is free from such thought. Indeed, all this is like the water of a mirage within the undisturbed, peaceful, and pervasive Brahman;
when investigated, even "I" does not exist—how, where, and from what source could the delusion of mental construction and the like arise?
The hundred-and-ninetieth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Realization of Truth," by Vasiṣṭha.
If one does not attain the state of a knower through one's own manly effort and one's own intellect— expanded by association with the virtuous— then there is no other means;
for that which is unconstructed and that which is constructed [are both overcome] by one's own counter-conception.
That very thing assumes otherness, just as nectar [assumes] the state of poison. Conceptualization ends in non-conceptualization; liberation is the abandonment of conceptualization.
And this is accomplished through the prior renunciation of enjoyments, and not otherwise.
For one who dwells within, neither with speech nor with mind, perceiving neither the word nor its object, the cessation of conceptual construction gradually increases.
Apart from the notion of "I," there is no other form of ignorance.

When this [ego] is stilled, there is no other liberation whatsoever because of its non-contemplation. Now, you arise and perish as something that possesses egoity and lacks a body; but when that has been abandoned for a long time at the very beginning of the world-process, you become stilled and you attain perfection.
Salutations to that Great Soul, from whose insentience all this exists as if it were real though it is unreal, and which is as tranquil as a stone;
from his insentience all this subsides, like [the waves] upon a stone.
For one whose mind has dissolved into the supreme state known as emptiness, this occurs through the cultivation of non-thought (*acitta*).
Whether this [state] exists or does not exist, that which is conceptualized leads to the increase of suffering;
whereas that which is not conceptualized leads to internal happiness, for the non-conceptual arises from the absence of conceptualization.
There are two terrible diseases for the embodied being: this world and likewise the next, by which one, afflicted everywhere, experiences dreadful sufferings.
In this world, the ignorant strive against disease with enjoyments that act as harsh medicines.
As long as one lives, one should provide medical treatment according to one's ability for any illness; however,
the best of men strive to treat the great disease of the next world with the nectars of tranquility, the company of the virtuous, and spiritual awakening.
Those who are attentive to the medical treatment for the next world conquer through the method of tranquility the great desire for the path to liberation;
whereas he who does not apply the medical treatment for the disease of hell even in this very life— [is lost].
Having gone to a place devoid of medicine, what will that sick man do? Let life not go to waste through medical treatments for this world alone;
let the next world be treated with the medicines of self-knowledge by those who are ignorant [of it].
Life is as fragile as a drop of water clinging to a leaf trembling in the wind;
let this great disease of the next world be treated with effort and speed.
When this great disease of the next world is treated with effort and speed, [one is liberated].
The disease consisting of the perceived world subsides by itself and immediately. They know that a living being is mere consciousness, and the world is its expansion;
even within the interior of a single atom, there exists that [expansion] as vast as hundreds of mountains.
That expansion of consciousness which consists of form, light, and the mind is experienced as being within space alone; therefore, the delusion of the world is not real.
Even when dissolutions are observed, the delusions of clouds that appear as the visible world [are likewise unreal].
They neither perish nor are they born, for their sole nature is mere delusion.
If the self, submerged in the ocean-mire of worldly enjoyment, is not pulled out,
there is no other means than the marvelous power of one's own human effort.
A person who has not conquered the self is deluded and entrenched in the mire of enjoyments alone;
he becomes a vessel for calamities, just as the ocean is for waters.
Just as childhood is seen to be the first stage of life, so too is it the foundation of all that follows.
In the same way, the renunciation of enjoyments by one who knows that leads to the pacification of passion.
Though the river of life for such a knower is full of waves, it flows calmly; it moves with equanimity, O gentle one, like a colorless painting fixed upon a canvas.
But for the ignorant, the rivers of life are exceedingly terrifying,
flowing along with whirlpools, eddies, agitations, and waves;
the impulses of creation surge forth, constituting mere fragments of the expansion of consciousness.
Like the vision of two moons, children, ghosts, deer in water, dreams, and delusions, thousands of creations appear as waves in the ocean of consciousness.
When investigated, they are unreal; yet they seem real due to the error of experience.
Even within the hollow of space, the worlds are experienced as if they exist due to the delusion of the expansion of consciousness;
yet they are not truly real,
for the delusion of creation is but a bubble in the water of the unfolding of consciousness.
It possesses the form of the modifications of existence such as "I" and so forth;
consciousness is liberation, while the world is the unfolding of consciousness.
It is neither internal nor external, neither unreal nor real—it is all of that.
The Lord is of the nature of consciousness, unborn, unmanifest, one, and immutable;
he is Brahman, devoid of both selfhood and the state of being, whose essence is peace even beyond the ether.
From this Brahman, who is without intrinsic nature, the perception of creation arises spontaneously.
Just as no external cause is required for the movement of the wind,
so too do the waves of Brahman appear within the ocean of Brahman like dream-experiences.
In reality, however, there is neither dreaming nor creation here.
It is one alone, without appearance, without mind, non-inert, and equal;
it is neither existent nor non-existent, neither space nor non-space—this is the non-dual and imperishable.
It is that which, while remaining exactly as it is, is by nature devoid of objective perception.
They call him the best of sages, in whom the agitation of consciousness has arisen [only to be stilled];
he for whom even that which exists is, as if made of clay, devoid of the nature of perception— him they call the best of sages, in whom the "I" and the world have dissolved away.

Just as a city of the imagination subsides through the absence of conceptualization, so too do the world, the "I," and sensations— which arise from sensation— subside through the absence of sensation.
With the exception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), all verbal referents are indeed accompanied by causes.
But the cause of one's own nature is the experience of that liberation.
Here, there is no inherent nature whatsoever belonging to any entity;
all experiences are indeed the state of the great ocean of consciousness.
These very experiences are the vibrations of the great wind of consciousness;
let it be understood that they are the emptiness of the sky of Brahman.
Like the wind and its movement are non-different, so too are Brahman and the creation; their apparent distinction is merely that.
But for those two, due to the absence of their own delusion, it is like one's own death in a dream.
Delusion persists only so long as the investigation into the true nature of reality remains unclear;
however, when the investigation becomes clear, delusion itself goes to the state of Brahman.
But delusion is indeed an unreal, non-existent thing; therefore, it is not found upon investigation.
Like the horn of a hare, it is utterly transparent; thus, Brahman alone remains.
It is without beginning, middle, or end, infinite, transparent, equal, auspicious, eternal, and truly one.

Abandoning the entire delusion of the burden of the transformations of old age and ignorance, come to the state of the sky. The hundred-and-ninety-first canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Presenting the Meaning of Truth."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Among those who encounter pleasure and pain, he who perishes is truly lost;
he who does not perish is indestructible—for him, enough with the instructions of the scriptures.
For whoever has the arising of desire, pleasure and the like necessarily exist for them;
if these are to be treated through equanimity, then desire itself must first be cured.
In the supreme state, the two delusions of "I" and "the world" do not exist at all.
This is peace, without support, all of it—the imperishable Nirvana.
"I," "Brahman," and "the world"—this is a delusion of verbal construction;
by whom indeed was this imagined within the entirely peaceful space?
"Here there is no 'I', nor the world, nor those things denoted by words such as 'Brahmā' and the like;
because the one, which is peaceful, is everything, who here could be an agent or an enjoyer, and from where?
Since it transcends all instruction, it is indeed the negation of everything."
This has been done, and that which is of the nature of truth remains here alone.
The movement of the perfected ones (siddhas) situated above is not perceived as something harsh,
just like the thundering of clouds in a dream for a man sleeping on one side.
Since there is no [separate] cognition, the conduct of the perfected ones (*siddha*) is not perceived as such;
for everyone experiences that which abides in cognition as its very nature (*svabhāva*).
Indeed, cognition itself is the self-nature, for everything shines forth as consisting of that.
Therefore, that I am the entire world, non-different from the Supreme Self.
Consciousness shines as the world, just as in the case of volitions and dreams;
it arises without diverse parts, just as water arises in the form of waves.
The arising of cognition is of a single nature, yet it appears as if it has attained multiplicity;
however, due to ignorance, that [multiplicity] is not perceived when scrutinized, because it lacks substantial reality.
Just as every whole is in fact nothing but its own parts.
This world is indeed Brahman—eternal, partless, and tranquil. Like bricks made of the gold of consciousness, it sustains millions of vessels within;
whatever that consciousness perceives, it knows as the world and so forth.

Brahman alone shines forth as this world; it exists as that pure reality, yet appears as the universe because its nature is consciousness, just as water, being fluid by nature, appears as waves and the like.
Whatever one perceives within oneself, one sees that very thing as the world and so forth.
Even that which is formless is its own form; that which does not perceive is not [the Self].
The statements regarding its being sentient and insentient are spoken for the sake of instruction—because it presides over its own body—and do not, in reality, have existence as their object.
The world is neither existent nor non-existent; it appears within consciousness through consciousness. Since that which is insentient does not shine forth, what indeed is our grasp here?
Sentience and insentience belong to the Self, like vibration and its absence.
It is not dependent on anything under its own control, it remains established in itself like a stone;
for that which is perceived, there is neither existence, nor a support, nor a cause—
this "I" which is you, this Yakṣa, I do not know from where it has arisen.
The very existence of this Yakṣa who thinks "I am he" does not exist in reality;
oh, how strange it is that you have been rendered helpless by him!
Like the "crow-and-palm-fruit" coincidence, the delusion "I" appears within Brahman.
One's own very form appears through a visual delusion, like a mass of hair in the sky. I am indeed Brahman, and the world is likewise; how then could there be destruction or origination?
Therefore, what basis could there be for joy or sorrow, where, and in what manner?
Because the Lord is the sovereign of all, this world appears as perceived;
yet that which is unperceived does not appear to us. Therefore, let it remain unperceived for you.
Like the "crow-and-palm-fruit" coincidence, the void of Brahman appears as the world due to its consciousness.
How could that [creation] be different from that [Brahman], being like a city of dreams or mental construction?
Just as waves and so forth exist in water, as a wooden statue exists in a tree,
and as jars and other objects exist in clay, so do all creations exist within Brahman.
That which is experienced within the formless, the structureless, and the pure—precisely that is declared here; what indeed am I, and what are the worlds?
Just as the various diversities of movement belong to the wind by its very existence, so it is here.
In Brahman, which is devoid of intrinsic nature, there is the world and so forth, as well as the "I" and so forth;
just as the state of trees, elephants, horses, deer, and so on is perceived in a cloud,
even though it lacks the form of such arrangements, so too are creation and the sense of "I" in the Supreme.
Emanation appears as if possessing parts within the partless, auspicious Supreme;
know it to be like that, resembling cause and effect.
Therefore, it is peaceful, effortless, free from limiting adjuncts, and devoid of delusion.
Since the world does not exist at all, remain equanimous like the sky.
There are no you, nor we, nor worlds, nor space and the other elements;
this Brahman alone remains, entirely peaceful and full.
In all things without exception, there is the state in which every distinction has been stilled;
realizing "I am that very Truth," quickly abandon [the notion of self] and cultivate yourself for liberation.
Know that perception is bondage; know that non-perception is liberation.
Remain as you are, according to your natural state and conduct, peaceful and free from sensation.
The seer does not become the object of sight, nor does consciousness (cit) become the object of thought (cetya).
Since there is no object of thought, in the absence of a world, who could perceive what, and how?
Due to the absence of the states of the seer and the seen, remain even while awake as if in deep sleep— resembling the expanse of the autumnal sky, comparable to non-existence. Likewise,
[remain] as the one Brahman in the form of consciousness, just as there is motion in the wind.

In this context, creation is the state of conscious awareness, and liberation is the realization of the oneness of Brahman. The vibration of consciousness, which is the wind of Brahman, is known as creation;
that in which there is no such vibration of consciousness is declared to be Nirvāṇa.
Just as a seed knows its own form within itself, such as the sprout and so forth,
so too does the Great Consciousness know its own form existing within itself as the state of creation.
Just as a seed exists as the sprout and so forth through the perception of the sprout and so forth, [so does the Great Consciousness exist as the world].
Just as the supreme consciousness (*cit*) appears as the light of creation even beyond the awareness of creation,
so too does the supreme consciousness appear as the light of existence.
All analogies, such as the seed and so forth, are of that very nature and consist of that alone.
Know this entire world to be the changeless Supreme Brahman, changeless, without beginning or end, and free from affliction;
its nature consists solely of one's own volition, and it perishes through the absence of that volition.
This modification of duality and non-duality is like a city of one's imagination.
Just as you have understood the difference between emptiness and space to be such,
know that the difference between Brahman and the creation is likewise devoid of self-nature.
That supreme being of Brahman, which is of the nature of great consciousness and is peaceful—that is this voidness;
I, you, and he are that. Do not fall downward, thinking "I am a man. Within this Brahman, which takes the form of the world, nothing at all is born.

Even though it has arisen and then perished, it does not truly perish, like a wave in water. An object exists as Brahman; indeed, Brahman alone abides within itself, as a whole resides in its parts, as space in space, or as water in water.
That form which exists within consciousness during the transition from one place to another in a duration of half of half a moment—that very nature should be worshipped.
The wise declare that the essential nature of consciousness is twofold: agitated and unagitated.
Be single-mindedly devoted to that supreme good for which you strive; do not set your mind on anything else.
This concludes the one hundred and ninety-second chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Ultimate Reality."
Vasiṣṭha said: That stainless form which exists in the interval between consciousness as it reaches one place from another distant place, in that very instant— that is the form of the Supreme Self.
While walking, hearing, touching, smelling, opening and closing your eyes, or laughing,
you should certainly remain constantly absorbed in this [state] for the sake of freedom from all affliction.
From that very state which is free from appearances, true, and devoid of latent impressions and desires...
Remain as you are, according to your natural conduct, unmoving like the mountain of the gods.
This is the nature of ignorance: it is not found when scrutinized;
if it were found upon scrutiny, it would be nothing other than supreme knowledge itself.
Since the object of cognition cannot exist anywhere apart from its arising through ignorance, how could it ever be perceived? Therefore, peace alone has arisen by its own power.
Truth and Brahman are one; the world is one, though it appears as many.
Everything appears as if it were not everything; the pure appears as if impure, though it is all-pervading.
The non-empty appears clearly as if empty, and the empty as if non-empty.
That which is expansive appears as if non-expansive, and that which is non-expansive resembles the expansive.
Changeless yet appearing as if changing, equal yet appearing as if unbalanced, peaceful yet appearing as if unpeaceful;
being real yet appearing as if unreal, invisible yet appearing as if manifest;
undivided yet appearing as if divided, free from dullness yet having entered into what seems dull.
Though unperceivable, it appears as if possessing the nature of the perceivable; though partless, it shines as if having parts.
Though not the "I," it appears as if it were the "I"; though indestructible, it appears as if subject to destruction.
Though stainless, it appears as if stained; though beyond being known, it conveys the state of being known.
In the light, the darkness appeared like a dense forest— both new and old, subtler than even an atom, yet containing within it the multitude of worlds;
though manifesting as the soul of all, it was perceived with great difficulty.
Though free from nets, it is richly endowed with nets in many ways, like the Lord of Fishermen; though devoid of illusion, it is the sun whose orb consists of the rays of illusion—
know Brahman to be the lord of the knowers, as the great ocean is of waters.
The great treasury of the jewels of the world is lighter than cotton on a scale;
it is like an illusion, a mirage, or the moon, not even within the range of vision;
though infinite and shoreless, it does not abide anywhere at all.
In the sky, intent upon the arrangement of forests and the creation of mountain ranges—
minuter than the most minute, yet more massive than the most massive;
the heaviest of the heavy, and the most excellent even among the most excellent.
Without agent, object, or instrument, without cause and without actor—
this world-casket is eternally fulfilled by its very emptiness within,
like a forest that is always empty.
Though as hard as the Ananta mountain, it is as soft as a fragment of space;
each day it is generally ancient yet fragile, and new;
light appears like darkness, and darkness spreads like light.
Even that which is perceptible is difficult to discern, and even that which is beyond perception is foremost;
the conscious form itself is insentient, and the insentient itself is of the nature of consciousness.
I alone am the state of non-I, and that which is not I is indeed I.
"That is indeed other than I, and I am indeed other than that.
Within this full ocean, these waves of the three worlds remain as if quivering, their very nature being fluidity.
He sustains the creation situated within his own body, just as frost [sustains] whiteness;
yet it is by him alone that the creation shines, just as whiteness [shines] by means of frost.
This Lord, though devoid of parts such as space and time, exists day and night.
The non-existent world spreads forth as it were, like a wave in water.
Within this vast forest of space, these withered clusters of worlds blossom, their five petals— the five elements— spreading wide.
This [Self], possessing an utterly stainless form, has itself become a mirror out of its own desire to behold its own reflection;
it is the fruit of the tree of the sky, whose brilliant effluences are the outpourings of its own will.
They experience wonder within consciousness at the sweet taste of perceiving creation;
as the inner and the outer, and through the manifold diversity within itself,
this very [consciousness] shines forth both internally and externally by means of the manifestation of existence and non-existence.

The splendor of objects possessing such forms produces wonder within this [consciousness] by its own will for this purpose, just as the tongue does within the cavity of its own mouth. That which is the fluidity of this water is called the world.

The splendor of all objects of experience subsides here within that very one who shines like the sun, just as she is the constituent part for perceiving the sweetness of consciousness and possesses the movement of the whirlpools of the worlds;
from her alone does it arise, like light from a luminous source.
This entire world is this very [consciousness], white like snow;
from it these perceptions proceed, like rays from the moon.
From this as its source and its coloring, this variegated world stands forth.
Know this to be pervaded by that which is tranquil, free from the modifications of existence and non-existence;
from this most excellent tree, which has ascended into the courtyard of the sky,
these visible branches— clusters of the network of worlds— proceed forth.

In this stage consisting of space, through the whirls of the dramatic performance of the worlds, there surely appears a river characterized by rising and falling, bearing various and infinite blossoms upon its unwavering banks. *Mugdhabodha* 6.192.35.
In this stage whose nature is the void, by means of the movements of the cosmic drama, [the river flows].
The dancer of destiny dances with incessant movement through her various modes;
the Great Kalpa, which is the opening and closing of the eyes of the world’s play,
repeatedly devours and then generates the child that is Time.
Even while the worlds are arising, he remains entirely tranquil,
like a mirror that does not desire the reflections appearing within it;
so too with beings currently existing and with creations yet to be.

This is the causeless seed, like a forest for trees; its opening is the splendor of the world, and its closing is the arrival of dissolution. Without opening or closing, it remains established in itself alone.
These many great lights arise, and these worlds undergo their states of creation, dissolution, and birth;
yet all of them are but the vibration of this one boundless Essential Nature, just as the wind itself subsides into its own state of stillness.
This is the chapter titled "The Description of the Nature of the Supreme Brahman."
The one hundred and ninety-third canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, the meanings here produce wonder, like whirlpools in water.
And all these entities are like water and its waves.
Since the nature of this entire universe consists of the knowledge of that which is to be known, what is the use of the exertion for another supreme tranquility?
What is the form of the Supreme Space? It is the very form of this world. What further effort toward cessation is required?
Just as the city of a child’s imagination in the sky is nothing at all to me, so too this entire universe is non-existent in reality, yet it appears real to the mind of a child.
It is devoid of form, light, and thought, like the army of a stone statue.
Form, light, and mental attention appear; what universality is there here?

Without the essence of form, light, and mental attention—which is nothing other than pure consciousness—not even that [consciousness] is found, being at best merely empty space; where, then, is universality?
Knowing is the delusion of the world, while not knowing is not a delusion; for knowing and not knowing depend upon you, just as thought and non-thought depend upon you.
This is because the sky of consciousness, whose form is vast, has the nature of the supreme ether.
No subversion of intrinsic nature is possible anywhere.
For this universe, which consists of that [nature], no alteration of intrinsic nature exists even when examined;
how then could such a thing ever come to be for it?
All this is indeed the space of consciousness; neither "you" nor "I" exists, nor even modifications such as these. Within pure awareness there is no ignorance, nor do I ever find it anywhere.
Everything is peaceful, auspicious, and pure—a mere delusion of "you," "I," and so forth.

"I do not see anything at all, like a forest born of the sky. Know this to be my word: that which is the emptiness of the space of consciousness abides of its own accord within yourself, in the space of your own consciousness."
They say that the supreme state is the existent which is seated without the impulse of desire,
like the stillness of a stone statue or one depicted in a painting.
He is a silent sage whose mind is at rest regarding all ordinary activities.
Like the vibration of a wooden puppet, his life appears to the wise man who is free from desire and undisturbed—
empty within, empty without, tasteless, and devoid of latent impressions—
like that of an old bamboo stalk.
He to whom the visible does not please, but for whom the invisible is pleasing within the heart—he, being peaceful both internally and externally, has crossed over the ocean of worldly existence.
Let the nets of words be spoken; he whose latent impressions have vanished is like a bamboo flute.
Let the flavors that have not touched the body be experienced through natural impulses and external prompts;
let the objects of touch be touched as they arise, without latent impressions (*avāsanam*). Like a peaked pavilion, remain unshaken, without desire and without the impulse of aversion.
Let the various webs of flavors be tasted without desire, fear, or seeking,
and without pride or longing, like a ladle that takes whatever it encounters.
Let the various forms appearing before you be seen without mental impressions (*vāsanā*), as they come to hand.
Free from taste, devoid of mental conceit, and without greed, like one with variegated eyes;
let fragrant flowers be smelled without desire and without latent impressions (vāsanā), remaining unattached even while moving, like the wind in a forest. MU 6.193.19–20.

If you say this, then having been made aware of their lack of essence and thus treated like diseases, those illnesses of enjoyment will not lead to the pacification of suffering; for you, there is no talk at all of such a thing.
He who, day by day, experiences pleasure while tasting the poison of enjoyment—
When the fire blazes upon his own head, he abandons the inexhaustible thicket of worldly existence.
Those adorned by the scriptures say that composure consists in desirelessness;
for the mind does not become tranquil through hundreds of enjoyments unless it is free from desire.
As the arising of desire is suffering and the stilling of desire is happiness, so it is experienced neither in hell nor in the world of Brahmā.
The wise know that the mind is merely desire; its stilling is called liberation.
Only so many are the scriptures, the austerities, the observances, and the restraints.
To whatever extent and in whatever manner desire arises for a living being, to that same extent does the handful of seeds of suffering sprout.
Just as the desires of a living being diminish through discernment,
so too do the cholera-like pains of suffering and anxiety subside.
Just as the desires of a worldly person full of passion grow more intense...
In that very way, the waves of the poison of sorrowful thoughts continue to surge.
If this disease of desire is not treated by the medicine of one's own effort,
then I believe there exists here another, more powerful remedy.

If it is not possible to bring about the complete pacification of desire, one should at least follow it even in a small measure; one who stands upon the path does not perish. But that lowest of men who makes no effort to diminish his desires [is lost].
Thus, day after day, he casts himself into the blind well.
Desire alone is the seed of transmigratory existence, which is characterized by the production of suffering;
once burnt by the fire of perfect knowledge, it does not sprout again.
For saṃsāra is merely desire, and nirvāṇa is the non-perception of that; let effort be made toward the non-arising of desire—what is the use of vain delusions?
Why are teachers, scriptures, and gurus sought after so fruitlessly?
Why is the samādhi that is free from the pursuit of desire not attained? For one who considers the mere non-pursuit of desire to be difficult to accomplish,
instruction from a guru, the scriptures, and so forth are surely useless.
Enough with this existence of men, which is transformed by the poison of desire and brings forth only suffering;
it is a snare in the wilderness of birth.
If this [existence] were not made unreal for others through the knowledge of the Self, [it would be truly wretched].
Let the pacification of desire be accomplished; by that, it is fully attained.
For Nirvana belongs to the one who is without desire, while bondage indeed belongs to the one who has desire.
One should conquer desire according to one's ability; what is so difficult in this?
Let that very desire— the seed for the thicket of *karanja* and *khadira* trees of old age, death, birth, and so forth— be instantly consumed within by the fire of tranquility.
For wherever there is freedom from desire, there is liberation.
One should destroy every arisen desire to the full extent of its reach and according to one's vital breath. For from whatever source desire arises, from that very source come the snares of bondage—
masses of suffering consisting of merit and demerit, filled with widespread afflictions.
When even a single moment of a virtuous person passes devoid of the cessation of desire,
it is right for him to lament for a long time, like one who has been plundered by bandits;
for in whatever measure the desire within this man subsides, [in that same measure he finds peace].

In that very way, his welfare for the sake of liberation increases. For one who lacks discernment regarding the self, the fulfillment of one's desires is nothing other than the watering of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra.

Born from the tree of the heart, with sheaths containing the seeds of their own pleasure and pain, desires—born from the mind’s latent tendencies through both the auspicious and the inauspicious as if from enmity—reach the man who is like a sacrificial animal; then, like the sharp-edged flames of the fire of evil deeds, they consume him with a crackling sound.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Description of the Seed of Saṃsāra."
The one hundred and ninety-fourth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"The application of the transformation caused by the poison of desire is known as Yoga."
For the sake of peace, listen once more to what was clearly stated before:

if something distinct from the self exists here, let it be accepted according to one's desire; but if this is not the case, and there is no otherness from one's own self, why is anything else desired?
The consciousness of space is partless, without components, subtle, and even more empty than space itself;
that very consciousness am I, the world, and the directions. Since it is the Reality (satī), what else could be desired by it?
Having the nature of space, within space itself, it is as if it knows, though there is neither an object of knowledge nor an act of knowing.
In this world-appearance whose nature is space, what object of desire can there be?

And as for the question, "How could there be a relationship between the grasped and the grasper?", that does not apply to us; for we do not know those to whom such a relationship might belong among those who are thus entangled.
The relationship between the grasped and the grasper is not found even when it is considered to reside in itself.
But how can that which is non-existent be obtained? By whom has a black moon ever been obtained?
This very "residing in itself" is what constitutes the existence of the grasper and the rest.
Through the observation of their intrinsic nature, I do not know where they go when they are unreal.
This indeed is the very nature of things: that the seer, the seen, and all forms of seeing, once known to be unreal, lead to nirvana, and the sense of "I" passes away within the self.
In nirvāṇa there is no visible object and so forth; in the visible object and so forth, there is no nirvāṇa.
There is no mutual experience of these two, just as there is none between shadow and sunlight.
Both of these are mutually unreal; here, nirvāṇa itself is indeed unreal.
For it is from this that Nirvana is experienced—free from decay and free from suffering.
But the visible world and so forth are merely illusory; they grant eternal and infinite happiness yet are unreal.
Therefore, let them be contemplated [as such], and do not remain in the unproduced Nirvana.
That which is perceived as resembling the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is not found;
even its causal efficiency (*arthakārya*) does not exist. What is there for you to deny here?
Because of its existence [as an object], there is great suffering; because of its non-existence, there is great happiness.
But the non-existence [of the self], when supported by reasoning, attains firmness through cultivation.
O lowest of men, why then do you bring about bondage for yourselves,
when the means for its clear increase are at hand and all calamities have subsided?

Since this all-pervasive reality consists of pure consciousness alone, the notions of cause and effect and so forth are merely sought out due to a lack of awakening; enough with these deer-like pursuits for us!
Indeed, while the one Self of all is pervasive and of the nature of space, [such distinctions are imagined].
What indeed is the sequence of the statements regarding cause and effect and so forth?
That which is the cause for the vibration of wind and for the fluidity of water,
that same [cause] is the cause for the emptiness of space and for the beginning of the creation of this conscious self (cidātman).
If the entire universe, including the relationship between cause and effect, is indeed Brahman alone, then let those who seek a cause for the worlds within Brahman feel ashamed.
There is neither suffering nor pleasure; the world is peaceful and composed of auspiciousness.

There is no difference from the state of being mere consciousness; therefore, how could desire arise? Just as in an army of clay bodies there is nothing other than mere clay, so too in the visible world, the ego, and so forth, there is nothing other than Brahman.
Rāma:
If that is so, O Lord of Sages, let that desire arise or let it not arise;
for it is Brahman itself—what purpose could there be in its injunctions or prohibitions?
Vasiṣṭha:
When knowledge has been fully awakened, desire is Brahman itself and nothing else. O Rāma, you have understood this as it is; that is the truth. However, listen to this: MU 6.194.22.
Whenever knowledge arises, desire subsides at that very moment;
it is by the very nature of things that it occurs, just as the night vanishes when the sun rises.
To the extent that there is the arising of knowledge, to that same extent there is the cessation of duality.
And how could the arising of desire occur once the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have dissolved? For one in whom this ignorance has been stilled, liberation is said to be stainless;
because of the distaste for all objects of perception without exception, desire does not arise in him anywhere.
He has no aversion toward the visible world, nor does he have attachment to it;
rather, the splendor of the visible world is experienced by him solely through knowledge, not by its own inherent nature.
This occurs either by way of a chance coincidence or through the instigation of another.

If he ever desires anything, whether rightly or not, that desire and non-desire of his are Brahman alone; there is no doubt in this matter. However, when there is desire, the contraction of the knower is necessarily perceived.
If knowledge has arisen in a living being, then desire for that object subsides;
these two cannot coexist in one place, like light and darkness.
Furthermore, the knower of reality is never an object of either prohibitions or injunctions.

For one whose desires and longings for all things have been stilled, who is there, what can they say, or for what purpose? This alone is the mark of a knower: the extreme attenuation of desires, which brings delight to all the world, or else their total non-arising.
When the visible world has become tasteless and no longer brings any relish whatsoever,
then desire does not spread, and at that very moment there is liberation.
He who, through awakening, remains established in the peace of non-duality and unity, [attains this state].
All states of being, such as desire and lack of desire, are of the nature of Śiva for him.
Through awakening, duality has set; he is free from non-duality and devoid of unity.
He is pure, free from agitation, tranquil, and established in the Self.
He has no concern at all for what is done, whether it be existent or non-existent;
he is never concerned with himself, nor with another, nor with these things of birth and death. And no desire arises in him who is awakened to nirvāṇa.
If it awakens, that very [state] is the pure, eternal Brahman.
There is neither suffering nor happiness; the world is peaceful, auspicious, and unborn.
Those who know recognize as awakened him who remains within like a stone.

Making suffering into happiness through meditative cultivation, as if turning poison into nectar—one whose self is firm in such certainty is called "awakened. That which is situated in the sky is the sky; that which is peaceful in the peaceful is the auspicious in the auspicious.
When the world exists within Brahman— which is empty when it is empty and real when it is real— then,
while the universe remains within the space of consciousness that is beyond perception,
in that which is gentle, perfectly even, tranquil, and auspicious, the delusion of "I-ness" comes to an end.
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving,
all that is the peaceful void, comparable to a city imagined by another's thought.
Within a city imagined by another's thought, one may come and go without obstacle.
Just as [the world] exists for you due to its emptiness, so too does it exist within this delusion of the world.
The appearance of mountains, heaven, earth, rivers, and the quarters unfolds within the self that is emptiness;
it consists of no seer, no object seen, and no instrument of seeing, like the waves of water in a mirage.
Like a dream or a conjured city, like a child’s ghost or a palm-tree trunk—
whatever is seen therein, how could it possibly be anything other than unreal?
It appears as "I" though it is entirely unreal, and yet it appears as if it were real.

Even without one who experiences delusion, this delusion flashes forth; it is non-existent. Neither non-existent, nor existent, nor both existent and non-existent—this world is something beyond the senses, inexpressible, appearing as if unshaken like the sky.
In this world, although for the knower both desire and non-desire are equally sufficient through tranquility,
nevertheless, I consider the arising of non-desire to be clearly superior for the sake of the highest good.
This cognition of "I" and "the world" is situated in the void like the void itself.

Just as there is no cause for the vibration of the wind within the self of consciousness (cidātman), so too there is no cause for the mind's movement within it. That which is the consciousness’s orientation toward an object of thought is the mind; that itself is transmigratory existence (saṃsṛti).
Its desire is bondage, and its freedom from desire is liberation. Having understood this principle, one should attain peace.
Whether there be desire or lack of desire, whether there be creation or dissolution,
there is no injury whatsoever to anyone, for indeed nothing exists here [in reality].
Desire and lack of desire, existence and non-existence, being and non-being, pleasure and pain— [all these are mere appearances].
