Thus, in this regard, no mental constructions whatsoever can arise in the void.
They call that person a partaker of liberation whose desires diminish day by day and who is never satiated with discernment and tranquility.
When the heart is pierced by the arrow of desire, a piercing pain arises;
where these [afflictions] prevail, neither your jewels, mantras, nor medicinal herbs have power.
He who has already previously performed the investigations into cause and effect—him [you must approach].
Through right discernment we do not perceive anything other than a mass of false delusions.
If we carry out worldly transactions by means of that which is unreal and illusory, then why is the mountain of concern for others not swallowed up? (MU 6.194.54–55)
If conventional discourse is carried out by means of what is non-existent— which perishes at the mere moment of observation—
then why is the sky not covered by a rabbit’s horn?
Because of the sense of "I," the space of consciousness instantly succumbs to an excess of insentience.

Just as water attains the state of stone, so the mind attains the state of a body due to its nature as mind. Because of its consciousness, it experiences this very condition of being embodied, even though it is unreal,
just as the power of consciousness remains undestroyed when one experiences one's own death in a dream.
Just as blueness is unreal in the sky because it lacks substantiality, yet real through experience, so too in this Lord, creation is neither non-existent nor composed of existence.
Just as [the distinction between] emptiness and the sky, or between movement and the wind, [is perceived despite their lack of difference].
Likewise, there is no difference between the creation and Brahman, as they are of one and the same nature.
Nothing here is born, such as the world and so forth, nor does anything perish;
it appears merely like a dream to one who has fallen asleep.

When the creation of earth and the other elements does not exist, being merely a form of mental appearance, what cause for agitation could there be regarding acceptance or rejection within the sky of consciousness?
There is no manifestation of a body endowed with the instruments of intellect and so forth.
Brahman alone, which is pure consciousness, thus abides within the Self.
The status of the intellect and other faculties as instruments is not real, because neither duality nor unity is possible;
for the meaning of the proposition "this is performed by that" is utterly impossible.
In consciousness, the multitude of mental constructions and activities appears without cause and without sequence,
just as in a dream there occurs in a single moment death, birth, and the crossing of oceans;
the sky itself becomes earth, the sky becomes mountains, and the sky itself becomes solid walls.
Space alone is the worlds; space is the vibration of consciousness in the perception of creation.
Upon the wall of the void, the painting of the universe—composed of the stage of consciousness—is spread out;
it neither rises nor sets, it neither tires nor ceases.
In the water of consciousness, which takes the form of the fluidity of the lofty waves of the universe—what has arisen, when, and how; and what has ceased, when, and how?
For the great space of consciousness is quiescent and characterized by the emptiness of the world.
Because the object of cognition is impossible, there are no such things as the descriptions of rising and setting.
Through the application of pure consciousness, mountains act like the sky and the sky acts like mountains,
within the existence of Brahman’s creation.
By the application of the powder of *saṃvit*, yogins in half a blink of an eye turn the world into space,
for indeed they turn space itself into the three worlds;
like the countless cities of the *siddhas'* resolve in the sky.
Likewise, there exist thousands of creations, yet they are the sky of consciousness (*cinnabhas*).
Just as whirlpools in a great ocean, though mixed with one another, remain distinct and are not separate from it; so too are those creations.
The vision of one interval of creation after another for the awakened yogi is indeed the attainment of other worlds of the perfected ones; such are the words of the wise.
All beings are imperishable, abiding in the supreme Śiva.
Like the manifestations of emptiness in the sky, the various creations are unrestrained;
these natural delusions of creation, whose innate fragrance is the ultimate reality,
neither arise nor subside, like lines carved within a stone.

Just as the fragrances of flowers, though meeting one another, remain unmixed, so too do these creations— being of the nature of space— remain distinct from one another as established planes for the perfected ones (siddhas).
This is because all objects exist within the experience [of consciousness], having the nature of the space of volition (saṅkalpa).
The declarations regarding curses and boons are true only for those whose delusions consist of subtle conceptualizations;
neither the doctrine of pure consciousness nor the doctrine of external objects is ultimately true.
These perceptions bear fruit for you exactly according to how they are perceived.
That which exists as the consciousness within consciousness shines forth as the world;
here, a distinction between them is not possible, just as there is none between liquidity and water.
Time, the worlds, the universes, and I—the group of senses—all these, as well as "there" and "thus," are all one.
The sky of consciousness is peaceful, unborn, and imperishable; it is the very self of the Lord, and indeed, passion and the other afflictions cannot possibly exist there.
This is the one hundred and ninety-fifth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Cessation of the Visible."
Vasiṣṭha said:
When awakened by self-knowledge, one perceives the world as false, like the sight of a mountain dance seen in the sky by an eye smeared with the ointment of illusion. *Mokṣopāya* 6.195.1.

The creation of Brahmā and the creation of the mind are considered these two to be similar, because they both consist of the nature of ultimate reality and are eternally undisturbed. Through their nature as cognition, they are not external; yet they appear as external through experience.
Therefore, know that the nature of the external object is itself real.
For us, there is indeed an identity between the doctrine of external objects (bāhyārthavāda) and the doctrine of consciousness (vijñānavāda),
because the existence or non-existence of all things is always established within the single nature of cognition.
Unshaken, characterized by the peace of ether, air, light, water, and earth, pervasive, empty, and of great undertaking—such is the reality of Brahman everywhere.
In that [Brahman] is everything; from that everything proceeds; it is everything; and it is everywhere.
Salutation to that Self of all, who is eternal and consists of everything.
When, due to its nature as consciousness, the object of cognition attains oneness with the consciousness of the perceiver,
then this [object] is perceived by the very limb that is the visible [perceiver], and not by any other consciousness.
When this very act of seeing— the seer, the instrument of vision, and the object seen— is nothing but pure consciousness (cinmātra),
then the experience of everything therein remains as its fully realized fruit.
For if the seer and the seen were not one within the nature of consciousness, [there would be no such experience].

Not knowing that taste of the visible object, the seer would not see it, just as a stone [does not perceive] an eye. Because of its nature as consciousness, the object of thought (citya) sinks into consciousness (citi), like water into water;
through this, experience occurs, and not otherwise, as in the case of two pieces of wood.
Just as wood does not perceive because of the absence of unity with its own kind,
so too the observer, though non-inert, would not know the object of perception;
for wood possesses the nature of being exactly what it is in its existence.
Therefore, they know only that [consciousness] and nothing else; thus, the visible world consists of consciousness and the conscious perceiver.
(MU 6.195.12) The nature of the great conscious Self alone exists within water, air, earth, and stone.
In these, there is no vibration, cognition, or the like, because of the absence of vital breath (*prāṇa*), the individual soul (*jīva*), and so forth. (MU 6.195.13)

The vital breath, the intellect, and the other faculties have attained their existence through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). This *bhāvanā* is the wonder of consciousness itself, and it arises according to one's will.
Through its state as the world or its state of peace, it abides as the reality of Brahman.
Just as the self [assumes] masculinity upon entering the semen and the embryo, so too the semen—
which consists of atoms of all the limbs— becomes whichever specific limb it is derived from; for that very atom exists within the semen as residing in its own self.

Brahman is the self of all atoms; since it is, in reality, subtler than an atom, whatever substance that may be, it becomes that very thing, yet Brahman remains only Brahman. Just as a substance is indeed a substance whether it extends horizontally, upwards, or downwards.
Everything is indeed Brahman, in whatever way and by whatever means it may be.
Just as there is only the state of being gold and no otherness within a hundred forms of gold,
so too there is only the state of peace for that which is peaceful, despite the multitude of egoistic creations.

Just as no disturbances of creation or dissolution affect you, who possess the formidable power of a dream existing at your side, so too, for me, these are but the void-self. Like the army of Putraka fashioned from the mud of the sky, it is merely a mental construction.
Just as that [emptiness] is merely quiescence, so too is this world;
it is nothing but the delusion of mental construction (*saṅkalpa-bhrama*) which, having grown within, exists as the world,
like a tree in the course of a kalpa arising from a seed moistened by water and soil.
For the wise one who is the non-egoic Self, though existing, as if non-existent,
even the beauty of women and such things are indeed like fragments of withered grass.
In the three worlds— including gods, asuras, and humans— I do not see anything [that can truly affect him].
Even for a great soul, the entire world with its single strand of hair is not enough to cause greed;
for one who has realized the Self, there are no doubts or dualistic conceptions regarding how things exist or where they may go.
For that Great Self, whose entire universe is but the void and who is himself devoid of self, from where, for whom, and how could there be any desire? For him,
all distinctions have been stilled, and he is characterized by the absence of longing.
Who is capable of conceiving existence as being like non-existence?
(MU 6.195.27) Nothing dies through the Maras, and nothing lives through living beings; for this world, which consists of pure consciousness, and for space, there is no such thing. (MU 6.195.28)
Birth and death are the false delusions of the world appearing;
even though they do not exist, they appear on the shore of a mirage-river belonging to that delusion.
As long as one has not investigated correctly, there is neither delusion nor an investigator.
Indeed, birth and death do not exist; there is only the peaceful and immutable.

He who has attained detachment from the visible world, who delights in the Self and has reached tranquility—he, though existing, appears as non-existent, having completely crossed the ocean of existence.
They know that which is like the extinguishing of a lamp, in which the mind and its perceptions have set, which has attained peace within itself alone, and which is truly stainless.
To such a one, the visible world, beginning with the intellect, does not naturally appeal.
The supreme ones call him liberated who is as peaceful as space.
Through lack of inquiry, "I" exists; through inquiry, "I" does not exist.
Since the referent of "I" is non-existent, where is the world, and where is transmigration?

Through the very act of consciousness perceiving itself, you perceive the world— which, like the forms of the intellect and so forth, consists of matter, light, and the nature of the mind— as a mere display in the sky; for you, whose mind is tranquil regarding all objects, exist as the self of all.
In every way, at all times, may every action be auspicious.
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give,
and whatever you see or strike as you go— may all that be the imperishable Śiva.
That which I am, that which you are, hope, and whatever [exists] such as action, time, space, and so forth;
that which the Lokāloka mountains are—that is the pervasive, auspicious sky of consciousness (cidvyoma).
That which is the perception of the world of forms, and that which is the threefold time of the universe—[all this is that].
That which consists of the afflictions of old age, death, and so forth—that is the auspicious Great Space of Consciousness.

Having become free from the desire for discernment, free from appearances, free from longing, and free from the mind—a sage without a self—you abide in nirvāṇa; you remain established just as you are.
May your movement, desire, thought, and perception be stilled; may you abide in the infinite as one beyond conceptualization.
Whether there be worldly activity for you or not, let it be like the wind through its vibrations and stillnesses.
May your state as a person be free from latent impressions, devoid of fragmentation, and peaceful.
Just as a wooden puppet is moved by means of a mechanical device or a treatise, let the world of beings be external to you; let that which is without essence remain outside.
Remain like a multi-colored lamp, with an ineffable supreme light within.

For one who is free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*), devoid of passion (*virasa*), and free from desire (*nireṣaṇa*), what indeed—other than the scripture (*śāstra*)—could be a cause for the diversion of his intellect?
Even the movement toward the meaning of the scriptures is sufficient for him; therefore, his essential nature consists in being without intentionality (*anabhisandhi*) regarding sensory perceptions.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Description of Nirvāṇa."
The one hundred and ninety-sixth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
A person who has developed the conviction that the cycle of existence is artificial and exhausted...
Being free from conceptualization, it does not perceive conceptualization; therefore, it is indeed non-existent.
Like the fading of breaths upon a mirror, the "I" that has somehow persisted is seen to be with its cause when one knows this, and it quickly perishes and is no longer found.
He whose obscurations are exhausted, in whom doubt has been stilled,
and whose self is filled with the supreme nectar— he shines by his very being alone.
By means of the wind that dispels the mist of all doubts and suffering, he shines forth.
The region shines with the intellect of the luminous one, just as the sky does with the full moon.
Free from wandering, free from doubt, having attained light and being unobstructed,
the wise man is known by the knower alone, as pure as the autumnal sky.
Free from conceptual construction and without support, peaceful,
and cool within, it bestows purity through contact, like the wind from the world of Brahmā.
This is the true nature of things regarding perceptions of what is unreal.
That which is the perception of creation is like the perception of a barren woman’s son in a dream.
This world that is experienced is indeed non-existent;
this very nature of things is the perception of what has no real form.
Since the transmigratory worlds themselves are unreal, how could there be any purpose [in them]?
The very words "heaven" and "liberation" are like the son of a barren woman.
The world is real as Brahman—uncreated and unconditioned.
It is neither unestablished nor otherwise uncomprehended;
for this is the very nature of reality, arising from the repose in the essential nature of the Self—
that which is the non-perception of "I-ness," creation, and the visible world.
When the conscious self has reached another region a hundred thousand yojanas away from here in a single moment, its form in the midst of the path is stainless,
like a windless breeze, consisting of pure space and light.

The wise know that the nature of the entire multitude of things is unconditioned, peaceful, manifest, and like the blossoming of a creeper. For the discerning one established therein, all objective perception dissolves.
In deep sleep there is no cognition of dreaming; in dreaming there is no cognition of deep sleep.
The delusions of creation and dissolution are like dreaming and deep sleep.
This delusion is not the true nature of reality; it is neither dreaming nor deep sleep.
Neither creation nor nirvāṇa is ultimately true or peaceful. If delusion— which consists of nothing but the unreal— is not perceived when scrutinized,
how indeed can that which is unreal, like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, ever be attained?
That which is not obtained does not exist; therefore, there is no possibility of delusion.
There is no perception of anything whatsoever that is other than intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Indeed, it is said that intrinsic nature alone is always pleasing to everyone.
Whether it be non-duality or indeed duality— let it be discerned through whatever discourse is appropriate.
Since great suffering exists in the absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*), while peace exists solely in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
one should reflect within with this understanding and perform whatever is desired.
It is logically established that a vast, gross thing exists within a subtle seed;
likewise, the supreme teaching is that the embodied universe exists within Śiva, who is formless.
Form, light, mental activity, cognition, ego-sense, and so forth, exist in the Supreme.

Like liquidity in water, they are of the nature of space and constitute its very essence. Just as a material object performs actions through its own constituent parts which resemble it, so too does the non-acting sky of consciousness act through the elements that are its own self.
Because the notion of "I" and so forth does not arise from the unconditioned Self, this word—devoid of any objective referent—is produced like [the sound] from a drum.
Whatever is perceived as illusory does not exist at all; it is eternally non-existent.
The world, which is formless in essence, is Brahman itself, established within Brahman.
For those for whom the world is a dream, they are like dream-people to one another;
they do not exist in the Self as false limbs, nor do they exist for us, being like flowers in the sky.
Within me, your Brahman is of a single form, peaceful like the expanse of space;
and yet, through those [forms], worldly activity proceeds within me as if they were inseparable from the vibrations in the wind.
But I, consisting of pure being, am for them like a dream to those who are dreaming.
They are surely non-existent to me, like dream-visions during deep sleep.
Whatever worldly transaction I have with them is Brahman abiding in Brahman;
let them see what they see—enough of that for them, and enough of it for me.
"I do not exist at all within myself; this pervasive reality of Brahman arises, as it were, for your sake—such indeed is this speech.
[It belongs] to Aniruddha, who, though bound, is of the nature of pure consciousness."

Neither the desire for enjoyment nor the desire for liberation flashes in the heart of one who knows that [reality]. Since this sequence of bondage and liberation for human beings depends solely upon their own nature, what a grievance! Alas, through delusion, there is the confusion of mistaking a cow’s footprint for the ocean.
When liberation is established as non-existence, consisting in the subsiding of all becoming,
neither wealth, nor friends, nor ritual actions are of any help;
it is like a drop of oil on a high wheel that does not fall into the water.

Thus, when the volition regarding the object of thought has ceased, consciousness remains as the world. Just as the state of a dream-event possesses a certain flavor during waking, so too does the existence of the web of the ego and the world possess that same flavor for the discerning one.

By that very practice of yoga, it [the ego] likewise attains such attenuation that neither "I" nor saṃsāra remains, and only peace is left behind. Whenever the sun of one's true nature reaches its stable state, at that very moment—
The darkness of worldly enjoyments dissolves; though they exist, they are no longer experienced.

This very [Self], devoid of the sense of "I," vibrates within the process of emanation, becomes manifest, and shines forth in that way, just as light proceeds from a lamp, for it is the source of the entire collection of instruments such as the intellect.
In the *Vasiṣṭhagītā*, the one hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Resting in One's Own Nature," Vasiṣṭha says:
They know that the very nature of an entity devoid of intrinsic being is the undiminished experience of the senses— such as form, light, mental attention, cognition, and so forth; for,
by virtue of the absence of an essence, there is the peace of abiding in the true nature.
When it arises, then creation appears like an illusion;
when it attains a state of rest in its own nature, consisting of tranquility,
then the visible world subsides, as in deep sleep within a dream.
Enjoyments are the great disease of existence; kinsmen are a firm bondage; the attainment of wealth leads to misfortune. Therefore, let there be peace within the self by means of the self.
The creation consists of the nature of non-selfhood; the oneness of self-nature is auspiciousness.
Let there be the supreme void; let there be peace here, and no more distress.
I perceive neither the self, nor the object of sight, nor the delusion of the world.
I have entered the peaceful Brahman; I am indeed Brahman, free from all affliction.
"You alone perceive that which expands from the meanings of the words 'you,' 'I,' and 'mind';
I, however, see only the peaceful, absolute, supreme ether.
Within the very Brahman, the supreme space, [reside] those consisting of form, light, and mind."
Delusions have arisen in you like the fluctuations of the wind during the dissolution of an eon.
The Self that is Brahman does not know the creation, nor does the Self that is the creation know Brahman;
one in deep sleep does not know the dream state, nor does one in the dream state know deep sleep.
Awakened, like one who has woken from the dream-like vision of Brahma and the world,
the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) possesses a tranquil intellect and knows both form and formlessness as they truly are;
the enlightened one fully understands all this exactly as it is.

And the pure self becomes tranquil, like a cloud in autumn. Whether established in memory or established in conceptual construction, the so-called "vow" (saṅgara) is merely the delusion of existence and non-existence; likewise, the delusion of the "I" and the world is nothing but error.
For even in the self there is no seer, since no one exists for whom it [the self] is perceived;
it is neither empty nor non-empty—it is this delusion that appears as such.
—From the *Vasiṣṭha-gītā*, the chapter titled "The Discourse on Resting in the Self."
The one hundred and ninety-eighth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
This creation, which consists of the perception of "I-ness" and so forth, has as its nature that which is non-nature.
Let Nirvana be realized by itself through its own singular nature.
Wherever the sun may be, there let there be light;
wherever there is a supreme distaste for sense objects, there let the intellect be awakened.
Without agent, object, or instrument; without the seen, the seer, or the act of seeing;
the world has arisen as a painting without a wall—ungraspable and without extension.
Yet nothing at all has arisen; it remains thus, quiescent within the quiescent.
That is indeed the supreme Brahman, free from ailment, truth, and immutable.
Who is able to count the painted figurines of the world in the sky, which are colored by the stage of the imagination consisting of nothing but the wonder of consciousness?
Rich with the transformations of rasa and bhāva, they dance with ever-new gestures;
generally flashing in the sky even toward every atom, they are of the nature of the ether.
Wearing the flowers of all seasons as their crest-ornaments, they have the quarters of the horizon for their many creeper-like arms.
The netherworlds are their creeper-like feet, and the world of Brahmā is their neck;
the moon and sun are their rolling eyes, and the clusters of stars are their body hairs.
The seven worlds are their slender limbs, and they are clothed on all sides in the pure garment of the sky.
The worlds, encircled by the oceans of the continents and girdled by the Lokāloka mountain range,
possess living beings whose lives are subject to change and whose vital breaths flow incessantly;
they are adorned with forests and groves arranged like necklaces and armlets.
The declarations of the Purāṇas and Vedas, which observe the fruits of ritual actions, [declare this]:
"This dance of the daughters of the three worlds which is seen before us is the fluidity of the water of Brahman; it is that very [fluidity] stirred by the wind of Brahman."
The very state of being without intrinsic nature is its cause, which is of the nature of a cause;
it is like the non-existence of a dream during sleep, even while one remains in that sleep.
O Bhava, while not actually asleep, abide in the state of deep sleep, contemplating the true nature of existence.
Even while awake, take recourse to this dream-state that is free from agitation.

Those who know reality recognize that state as one's own nature, wherein there is the condition of deep sleep even while awake—an experience devoid of flavor due to the absence of [dualistic] cognition; liberation consists in the transformation into that very state.
Without agent, object, or instrument; without the seen, the seer, or the act of seeing;
without form, light, or mental construction—Brahman stands as the world.
O Beloved, the Beloved shines forth; the Full is established in the Full.
Devoid of duality and unity, it shines as that which is free from duality and unity;
while existing, it is the true reality, established, and peaceful—the very self of creation, abiding by itself within the Self.
It is like the hollow of space and resembles the interior of a solid stone.
Though dense, it has the form of a belly filled with jewels; though like the sky, it is like a reflection— unagitated even when agitated, both non-existent and existent,
like a city yet to be built existing within the mind.
The nature of light is expanded by Brahman, and the mind is made non-dual.
Just as a city of one's imagination does not differ from the imagination itself,
so too this appearance of the world does not differ from ultimate reality.
Like a golden pedestal containing the arrangement of many future forms,
that state, though being perceived, remains established as peaceful and immutable;
it is free from disease, uniform in nature, and yet rich with the constant flux of destruction and arising.

Brahman alone—devoid of destruction or origination, undecaying, and appearing as if manifold despite its luster—shines forth through the emergence of creation that is free from rising and setting, having attained a state of dense tranquility.
Just as the sky shines by the power of its emptiness, it forcefully abandons the acquisition of its own nature; yet this occurs only for one who has not awakened.
The One Hundred Nineteenth Chapter, titled "The Giving of Instruction for the Purpose of Resting in One's Own Nature," by Vasiṣṭha:
Gold that has become tranquil is not different from the mind;
because it is indeterminate and stainless, how could there be the occurrence of creation and so forth?
When the lamp of the mind has gone out, [the appearances] vanish like an illusion, even while it remains in the sky.
Forms, light, and mental attention are waves of the fluid ocean of consciousness;
just as the movement of the wind is independent of any external cause,
and just as the radiance of light spreads forth, so too does this world exist within the Supreme.
Just as liquidity resides in water, emptiness in the sky,
and vibration in the wind, so too does this something consisting of the Self reside within the Supreme;
for this world that shines forth within the Great Consciousness, the Great Space.
That very consciousness shines forth as purity, like [the brilliance] in a gem.
Just as liquidity is in water, as emptiness is in the sky,
and as movement is in the wind, so does the world exist within the Great Consciousness.
Just as the wind perceives its own vibration, so does consciousness perceive the world;
herein, not even the slightest possibility exists for distinctions such as duality or unity.
Through lack of discrimination and through discrimination, the world appears as either radiant or perishable.
In enlightenment, that which is eternally non-existent in form, lusterless, and imperishable— nothing other than pure consciousness alone exists; it is devoid of beginning, middle, and end,
and is determined to be the very nature of the Great Pure Consciousness.
To some it is auspicious and peaceful; to some, the eternal Brahman;
to some, mere emptiness; and to some, mere cognition.
Therefore, contemplate that infinite self whose nature is consciousness as being nothing other than the object of thought.
Through reflection, one understands that knowability resides solely within itself;
just as there is no cause for the vibrations of the wind apart from its own existence,
so too there is no cause for the functions of the consciousness of creation apart from the pure Great Consciousness.
"Whether existence or non-existence is eternal, because it does not depend on anything else"—
if this were the case, then [space] would exist by virtue of the presence of duality or unity.
But who here could conceive of duality or unity in the great void?
The state of the infinite, singular, supreme ether-receptacle is omnipresent throughout the entire universe.
Just as the duality of motion and wind, or of sound itself, is not real,
so too the duality between the universe and the Lord of the Universe is essentially unreal in nature.

That which is pure Great Consciousness alone, in which duality is impossible and which manifests as the universe—that alone is this; it is not the universe, nor does it possess the state of being a universe.
Just as gold possesses reality at certain times through the existence of its spatial and temporal forms, [so too does the One appear as many].
For the world, which is distinct as "bracelet-ness" and so forth, it is not so for others.
Furthermore, since duality and unity are impossible here, how could there be the relation of cause and effect?
If such a relation were to exist, it would be merely a mental construction and not a real entity.
Just as emptiness exists in the sky, or fluidity in water, or as the void exists within the void, so indeed the primordial nature of the world is non-different from it.
Whatever is the form of Brahman, that is the form of the world; where, then, is duality or unity?
Whatever is the nature of space, that indeed is the nature of the entire void. Within the single, pervasive, pure, and all-encompassing essence of consciousness alone,
it remains as the very state of being stone within an army of stone statues.
How and where could the diversity of cause and effect possibly exist?
How could there be non-emptiness in the void, given that a second entity is impossible?
It is the Self of intuition alone, whose nature is light, that shines as creation within the Great Consciousness.
Like a daughter carved from stone, because of being composed of that [reality], one becomes identical with it;
having thus understood the universe as it truly exists, the world of the virtuous dissolves, and only its essence remains, appearing like the state of wooden silence.
Just as for one with eyes closed there is a mental delusion of perceiving forms,

so too in a dream— even though not present in the waking state— it exists as if real through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Having brought about the cessation of such cultivation, one remains as one is, having become like a stone.
Remaining inwardly unagitated, sit evenly within your own nature.
With the offering of your own discernment and the worship of whatever objects arise,
let your own nature— the Supreme Lord— be worshipped by the intellect for the sake of awakening.
One's own Self, when worshipped with discernment, immediately bestows the most excellent state;
here, the worship of Rudra, Upendra, and others is regarded as no more than a blade of withered grass.
When worshipped solely with the offerings and flowers of inquiry, tranquility, and the company of the virtuous, [it grants liberation].
The Supreme Lord is one's very own self, which brings immediate liberation to the practitioner;
when worshipped solely through the mere vision of truth, He bestows the unsurpassed goal.
Where the Self-Lord resides, what deluded person would seek refuge in another?
For one whose self is honored by the company of the virtuous, tranquility, contentment, and discernment,
weapons, serpents, poisons, and fires act like *śirīṣa* flowers;
even though acts of worshiping the gods, austerity, visiting sacred fords, and giving gifts have been performed to excess.
These [actions] turn to ashes due to their fruitlessness for those whose souls are destroyed by a lack of discrimination.
If even these are made fruitful through discrimination,
then why is that very discrimination not clearly cultivated within?
When the latent impressions have ceased through the cognition of reality as it truly is, an effort known by the word "discrimination" arises from the clarity of the self.
In that very manner, discrimination should be increased within by means of the nectar of tranquility.
Furthermore, as one gradually attains dryness through the absence of delusions—
by disregarding the existence of the body and seeing things as they truly are—
one should equally abandon shame, fear, sorrow, envy, pleasure, and pain.
The world, the body, and so forth do not exist at all in the beginning; how could they exist today?
If this is an effect, then its cause is likewise nothing but Brahman alone.
It is merely a pure appearance, and not a cognition like that of a jar or other objects.
Intuition is essentially of the nature of knowledge; therefore, everything is nothing but cognition.
Even cognition, which is the glory of the reality of the Self, subsides when it is fully understood.
In the absence of an object of knowledge, however, that which remains is the ineffable, eternal, and auspicious.
This entire expanse is bodiless and so forth, not the self of all, yet it is peaceful;
it consists solely of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the act of knowing, remaining in the silence of a stone.
With their internal organs stilled and clear like the interior of a stone statue, [they remain thus].
Whether moving or unmoving, remain established as the very form of consciousness (jña).
Possessing the true nature of the knower of the unknowable, and embodying the essence of both existence and non-existence,
you are the ground of both being and non-being, as transparent as the expanse of space.
Remaining as they are, and moving as they came,
the wise attain the supreme state, performing only the single action that has been reached;
or rather, they shine with inner faculties tranquilized by the renunciation of everything.
They remain in solitude alone, as if depicted in a painting.
When conceptual construction has ceased, for one who is awakened, the entire world— though always appearing as real— has vanished, like a city of one's own imagination or like a dream.

Like one born blind describing the experience of forms with eyes through scriptures, the ignorant person, describing nirvāṇa by means of instructions on a portion of conceptual construction while possessing a nature consisting of ignorance, suffers within and does not find peace. MU 6.199.46.
Through the teaching of a portion of conceptual construction, the world [is led] by its self which consists of ignorance.
Because of ignorance regarding this or that, one thinks, "I have accomplished my purpose.
Being ignorant of his lack of accomplishment yet believing he has achieved his goal, he is deluded by folly;
in another moment, through his own torments, he will realize his lack of accomplishment.
The wise know that which consists of conceptual construction to be no means at all,

because it yields suffering through the delusions of desiring existence and non-existence, even for a mere moment. Having fully understood the delusion of the world, one should remain without latent predispositions (*avāsana*).

For that state in which all objects have become devoid of passion is called Nirvāṇa. Beholding the true nature of the world— which consists of the essence of the flowing flood of the non-objectifying consciousness, which is the manifestation of the meaning of the narrative, which is entirely beyond the reach of the knower and the known, and which is perfectly pure— I attain final liberation.

Having cast beneath his feet that state of non-enlightenment which is understood through the scriptures to correspond to the experience of form by one blind from birth, you fell into this inner awakening and became one who has transcended existence. The Chapter Named "Instruction on Nirvāṇa" (MU 6.199.52)
The two-hundredth canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Through thorough knowledge, this world, beginning with the ego-sense (ahaṃtā), is realized to be unreal.
Through delusion regarding experience, one proceeds toward what is truly real with a contrary understanding.
For one who is freed from the fever of ignorance and whose self is cooled by awakening, this alone shall be the sign: that the water of worldly enjoyment no longer pleases.
Enough with other forms of thorough knowledge and the delusions regarding the signified and the signifier;
let that which is merely the non-perception of "I" be contemplated as nirvāṇa.
Just as objects experienced in a dream delight us, so too does this [state].

And yet, in this very same way, there is no such delusion as "I am not the world" within it. Just as a yakṣa, due to its own nature, sees a tree together with a city and its inhabitants— though these are entirely unreal— in the same way, the individual soul (jīva) perceives the cycle of existence (saṃsṛti).
Just as a yakṣa whose nature is delusion and the light of that yakṣa exist together as real entities yet are mutually false, so too are the delusions of "I-ness" and the world.
Because there is no obstruction in the forest [of the mind], one is freed from the yakṣa that takes the form of delusion.
Just as these fourteen elements manifest, so too do these [appearances].
By contemplating with the understanding that "I am merely a delusion and entirely false," the yakṣa attains the state of being no-yakṣa, and this mind attains the state of being no-mind.
Remain as you are, peaceful, with all doubts dispelled, free from grasping and rejecting, without the spreading of any desires, and established in your true state;
this pervasive reality, whose nature is the seer, is such that no object of sight can ever truly exist within it.
Alternatively, it need not be said that the Self is the seer; for what would be gained [by such a claim]?
Just as a branch or a thicket is merely the fullness of the essence of spring, so too is the state of manifestation (sargatā) of consciousness merely the weight of its own essential nature.
This appearance of the world is nothing but the perception of pure consciousness;
what room is there here for unity or duality? Enough—let Nirvana be dwelt in!
Let it be experienced as the sky of pure consciousness, and let the supreme nectar be drunk.

"Remain here, free from fear, in this grove that delights in the bliss of nirvāṇa. Why do you humans, like deer driven by the wind, wander with bewildered minds through these utterly empty wildernesses of saṃsāra?"
O you whose intellects are blinded by the delusion of the waters of a mirage in the three worlds, do not run with minds agitated by dense clouds, you whose intentions are corrupted!
You are like those who drink the water of a mirage through the mental activity of perceiving forms and light.
O men, do not let your lives pass away in vain like deer;
you are perishing through your craving for this world, which is but a city of gandharvas in the sky.
Regard those things that appear as pleasure as nothing but suffering, solely for the sake of liberation.

Let the world, which is like a hair-tuft appearing in the midst of the great sky due to delusion, be transformed into its true nature by you who perceive it without error. Human beings are as fragile as the tips of leaves tossed by the wind or as transient as ripples on water.
Do not lie upon the beds of the womb, ever new in each successive birth.
Rest peacefully in your own nature, which is without beginning or end and free from interruption.
Desist from that which lacks true nature due to the defects of the states of the seer and the seen.
This cycle of existence is understood by me to be such that even the slightest "I" does not exist;
yet as for that truth which is undifferentiated, it has no name.
Having forcibly snapped the iron chain of craving that bound me, [I am liberated].
"Stand like a lion above all within the cage of saṃsāra.
Liberation is merely the cessation of the delusion that grasps at 'self' and 'mine. For the yogin, that liberation is his very own being, regardless of how he happens to be situated."

The state of nirvāṇa, the state of latent impressions, supreme tranquility, and gnosis—these are the cool resting places for one weary on the path of saṃsāra. Known by the knower of that [reality], it is not known by the ignorant; known by the ignorant, it is not known by those who possess that knowledge.
This purpose of the world exists as something ineffable and distinct from those two [subject and object] in relation to one another.
When the delusion of universal manifestation has subsided, that [purpose] remains established yet is no longer perceived,
like a water-made doll submerged in the waters of the great ocean.
When delusion has subsided, for the one who is liberated and has attained nirvāṇa, the world exists exactly as it is, yet it is found to have dissolved; it remains just as it was,
like a heap of ashes from burnt grass carried away by the winds.
In this way, the world goes somewhere by resting in the true nature of the wise.
That world is the arrangement of the reality that is Brahman;
it is of the nature of the referent of the word "Brahman," and does not partake in the referent of the word "world."
Just as these objects appear to a newborn infant,
so do they appear to the wise man who remains with his latent impressions (vāsanā) exhausted.
That which is night for all beings, in that the self-restrained one keeps watch.
That in which all beings are awake is night for the sage who sees.
For the knower, waking remains as if in deep sleep for the sake of cessation;
his cravings for worldly pleasures are like those of one observing a painting while awake.
The experience of the world is like the perception of forms by one born blind;

for the wise man, it appears as something mostly illusory and unreal, appearing yet not appearing. The three worlds are objects for the utterly deluded mind; they are not real for one who has awakened to the true object.
The world of the three realms, being an object for the deluded, is not real even when awakened by the Buddha.
Just as when a dream is known to be a dream, the forms, perceptions,
and mental activities do not please the mind, so too may they not manifest in the waking dream.
Free from differentiation, fully composed, having reached the supreme cessation,
with an inner organ cooled, the knower remains extinguished. For the knower of that, who is liberated and unafflicted, there is a state of equanimity even without formal meditation.
Without water, no depression whatsoever can come into being.
(MU 6.200.37) The mental orientation is indeed the object; the mind itself is the coloring by the object.
This single manifestation alone consists of both the external and the internal. (MU 6.200.38)
Just as water, rippling with waves, carries everything toward the ocean— consisting of the confluence of hundreds of river currents—
so too does it carry all things, both internal and external, consisting of both the beneficial and the harmful, into a single unified mass.
It is the mind alone that vibrates, appearing as objects and thus expanded;
there is no duality between the object and the mind, just as there is none between water and its waves.
When one is absent, both come to rest, like the wind and its movement.
Surely, through the pacification of the one alone, since they are ultimately devoid of essence and identical in nature, both the object and the mind are simultaneously and swiftly stilled. Therefore,
an object whose nature consists of conceptual construction should not be pursued by one who possesses true knowledge.
And through right knowledge, the pacification of both [the object and the mind] occurs in this way.
For the knower, the object and the mind perish by themselves even while not yet destroyed,
just as one who hates earthenware ceases to fear its hostile nature once he knows it is merely clay.
Just as the object and the mind always remain exactly as they are for the knower,
when [the two] have merged, there is something else entirely unprecedented, consisting of non-existence.
Even the accumulated web of objects and the world, though existing within the domain of the knower, does not exist for the ignorant person.
To the knower, the world does not exist as something possessing consciousness, just as there is no dream for a man sleeping on his side, nor as there is no intoxicated yakṣa for one who is sober;
the ignorant person perceives the knower as ignorant, yet the wise know the all-pervading nature to be the true Self.
Know that the mind is like a wave of pure water of consciousness— devoid of the objects of the word "mind" and free from division or end. Therefore,
where indeed could the object and the mind possibly arise?
This delusion is indeed meaningless; remain established in that which consists of the true nature of things.
By those who abide in the nature of pure consciousness, like autumnal skies, the state of "mind" is no longer experienced within the boundaries of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
Having shaken off infinite multiplicity— which is impossible within the stainless state—
abide in the density of consciousness (cidghana), your own nature, in which all that is to be known has vanished like dust.
It is cognition alone that presides over both the internal and external states of objecthood.
Tell me, how can the object and the mind be like seeds, branches, and fruits?
Since the object of knowledge is non-existent, cognition itself has reached the ineffable state;
therefore, you are the Residue, whose nature is existence, with all particularities stilled.
The object itself is the mental construction (*manaskāra*), and that is an error consisting of non-existence;
the mind itself is the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of the object, and that too is an error consisting of non-existence.
Because it is the self of all, this mind of the Unborn is without cause.

Due to the experience of delusion, an object appears as if it truly exists, though it is entirely false. The mind alone manifests as the appearance of an object; unstable like a flash of lightning, it flickers restlessly.
You are essentially mere mental attention (*manaskāra*), and thus you wander in delusion within cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Through the thorough knowledge of the single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), you do not exist, nor do you wander in delusion.
For cyclic existence is indeed nothing but the mind; it is stilled through the awakening to the self.
People, possessing the form of an error regarding silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, suffer in vain.
But the state of non-existence is the supreme nature of consciousness, free from saṃsāra;
any existence other than nirvāṇa is suffering, for it is the delusion of "I am."
"I am of the nature of the water of a mirage, unreal and empty in essence"—
through such thorough self-knowledge, the notion of "I" quickly subsides.
Having known this, one becomes intent on wisdom regarding the reality of both external and internal objects.
Just as water does not abandon its own nature even when it assumes the state of waves;

and just as the existence of a tree, from its roots to the tips of its branches, is one and the same— so too, consciousness, changeless and stainless, shines as a single reality unto the end of all that is knowable.
Just as the single, stainless sky shines throughout a hundred thousand yojanas,
so too does that single, undivided knowledge shine, reaching to the very limit of all that is knowable.
Just as the sky is one, stainless, and all-pervading due to its emptiness, so it is with knowledge.
Likewise, having known that single, stainless consciousness even within the states of the objects of knowledge,

the Self— having become solidified through its own thought— is made into a stone by the object of thought, just as gold is turned into stone by means of mercury. Thus, the Self itself is made into the mind by way of being perceived as an object.
Without space or time, the Self, through awakening, leads the state of consciousness to non-awakening by means of awakening; this principle is thus well-established.
Here, although there is no possibility whatsoever for awakening and the like, [it occurs].
Nevertheless, they are conceived in this way for the sake of mutual understanding:
those of great power, free from conceit, apply themselves to the pacification of the state of delusion;
being free from error and tranquil through their very infinity, they become eternally composed in meditative absorption.
The two hundred and first canto, titled "The Instruction on the One-pointed Devotion to Brahman," Canto 201.
Rāma:
O Sage, tell me of that existence which, like a tree of meditative absorption, bears fruit throughout one's life, possesses both flowers and creepers, and bestows rest. Vasiṣṭha said:

Listen to the description of the tree of meditative concentration (*samādhāna*), which rises high above the forest of people who live in solitude, possessing a livelihood that is upright and flourishing, and endowed with flowers, leaves, and fruit.
It arises somehow through hardship, or even by itself.

The wise know that the seed of this [tree] is the weariness born from the newness of saṃsāra. They know its field to be the mind, which is ploughed by the plow of the web of auspicious deeds and drenched with sap day and night, and watered by the channels of the flowing breath.
Disgust for cyclic existence, which is the seed of meditative concentration, falls of its own accord upon the ground of the mind— a secluded forest that gives birth to those who dwell in solitude—
when the seed of meditation has fallen upon the ground of one’s own mind by means of great intelligence.
One should diligently and without weariness sprinkle oneself with these [waters]:
pure, unctuous, purifying, sweet, and conducive to one’s own welfare—
like the nectar of the moon, consisting of the milk of association with the virtuous.

Having recognized with great intelligence that the excellent waters of the meaning of the scriptures—which bestow inner coolness, which are full, pure, and as refreshing as nectar—have fallen upon the ground of his own mind and have spread through the channels of his intellect; The seed is disenchantment with saṃsāra; that which must be guarded from meditation with effort is [the mind].

Through the construction of the rampart of austerity, by being sprinkled with the performance of deeds for the sake of others, and by the planning of the expansion of fortitude through resting at sacred fords and shrines.
A guardian named Contentment, whose disposition is well-trained and who is constantly accompanied by his beloved Joy, must be appointed for this sprouted [seed].
He shall keep at bay the birds of hope stationed behind him— those birds of others' favor.
One should ward off these vultures of desire and pride as they swoop down upon us;
with the soft bristles of respectful conduct, like the rays of the sun of discernment that shed the light of propriety, one must wipe away this dust and darkness.
Prosperities and women are like waves, fragile in their enjoyment;
upon that [body] fall thunderbolts impelled by the clouds of evil deeds.
Through the mantras of fortitude, magnanimity, and compassion, as well as through recitation, ritual bathing, austerity, and self-restraint—
"Those [impurities] must be warded off by the wielder of the trident whose essence is the *praṇava*.
From this seed of meditation thus protected,
there arises a new sprout called discernment (*viveka*), glorious and exalted by its noble birth.
By that, the ground of consciousness shines, both luminous and non-luminous;
it becomes delightful with light, like the sky with the newly risen moon.
Therefore, from that sprout, both leaves unfold of their own accord.
The first is the study of the scriptures, and the second is association with the virtuous.
Then, he binds the very pillar named Steadfastness, which is highly elevated,
encased in the bark of contentment, and stained with the essence of dispassion.
One whose self is nourished by the essence of dispassion and who is endowed with the monsoon of the meaning of the scriptures attains supreme elevation in a very short time;
one who is made robust by the essence of dispassion through contact with virtuous people and the meaning of the scriptures [attains this].

It does not tremble even slightly due to the agitations of the monkeys of passion and hatred. Then, from that [mind], which is adorned with the forms of consciousness, these creepers— sporting with their juices— arise and spread across vast regions.
Clarity, truth, existence, steadfastness, non-conceptuality, equanimity, peace, loving-kindness, compassion, and the renown of nobility— by means of these creepers,
which are the leaves of his virtues, that tree of meditation flourishes mightily.
"By these flowers of fame, the ascetic becomes like a *pārijāta* tree;
thus this tree of knowledge, possessing creepers, sprouts, and blossoms,
rises higher day by day, yielding the fruit of future meditation."
Rich with clusters of flowers that are his fame, possessing the swaying foliage of his virtues,
spreading the essence of dispassion, and having the form of a blossoming cluster of wisdom—
he cools all directions like a rain-cloud in the monsoon.
It pacifies the heat of existence, as the moon does the heat of the sun;
it extends the shade of tranquility, as the arrival of the clouds does the shade;
and it disperses cessation, as a gentle wind does a cloud.
He fastens his own seat with his self, as steady as a mountain of the Kulaparvata range;
he fashions above it a vessel for the fruit, adorned with auspiciousness.
And as the tree of the fruit of discernment grows day by day—
In the forest of a man’s heart, which is enveloped by the canopy of shadow,
there arises a coolness that removes the heat of the ground—
a beauty like the interior of frost upon the branches of the flourishing tree of the intellect.
In this [state], the deer of the mind— exhausted by the intermediate stages, weary from birth, a traveler on the path long worn out, and agitated by clamor— finds rest;
it is sought after by enemies for the sake of the bodily comfort that consists of mere existence.
Concealing his self as a mere collection of diversities, he looks out from the corner of a thicket;
driven by the winds of latent tendencies spreading through the forest of saṃsāra,
he is perpetually deceived by the river of the "I-notion."
Worn out by long wandering through the vast and distant caves of wives,
he has fallen into a pit from the precipice of handling sons and daughters-in-law;
his limbs bruised in the narrow space by rolling upon the creeper of Fortune (Lakṣmī).

Seizing the river of the glory of craving, he is carried far away by its waves; intent on fleeing from the distress caused by disease and wicked hunters, his appearance is one of extreme terror at the sudden fall of the hunter that is Fate.
Apprehensive of the arrow-like pain from the sudden impact of tasting the *geya*,
intent on routing his enemies, and marked by the striking of stones;
he was violently whirled about by the rising and falling, the coming and going, and the tossing up and down.
Gradually pulverized by the blows of the stones of humiliation,
wounded by being caught in the snare of the arrows of craving,
his conduct fashioned by his own wisdom, he was untrained in the supreme deceit.
Having entered the village of the senses, he is intent on fleeing,
yet he is crushed by the fierce, thundering trampling of the great elephant of the senses, which is so difficult to restrain;
he is rendered unconscious by the poisonous hissing of the serpent of sense-objects as it vomits forth its venom.
He is trampled upon the ground, moist with fluids, by dogs of desire;
he suffers from the clear burning of eruptions scorched by the forest fire of anger;
and he endures a continuous flow of long-lasting miseries through the repeated coming and going of the winds of transmigration.
Afflicted by the defects of the *daṃśa* (bites) that grant a longing for what clings to one's own limbs,
long pursued by the jackals of blood and fat shimmering with greed for enjoyments,
and chased by the leopard of poverty vomited forth from the cave of one's own karma;
His body was wallowing in the pit of the mountain of blindness caused by the mist of delusion;
distressed by the trembling of his heart at the sudden appearance of the lion of the mind,
he looked upon death as one views a *buka* flower produced from a fire-drill.
Frequented by people from afar for the sake of quickly swallowing their greed,
it is surrounded on all sides by the snare of accumulated thoughts bestowed by desires;
it is embraced for a moment and then abandoned by its friend named youth.

O King, like a young deer in a lotus pond at the sun’s heat, the mind-deer sometimes finds a moment of peace in some place of supreme tranquility, even when threatened by winds as if provoked to fury amidst difficult terrains.

May that most peaceful tree—the deer of your own mind reach it—where, amidst the restful groves of *tāla*, *tamāla*, *bakula*, and other trees and shrubs, there are the smiles of the playful abundance of many flowers; a happiness of which the deluded do not even know the name.
The chapter titled "Description of the Mind’s Misfortune."
The two hundred and second canto:
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Thus, O slayer of enemies, this deer-like mind of yours has found its rest."

Therein alone he finds delight and does not go to another branch. Then, after this much time, that tree of discernment gradually and fully manifests the fruit residing within— the Self that is the ultimate reality.
That merit, which is the fruit of the tree of meditation, is seen by the deer of one's own mind standing below at the edge of that excellent tree;
it then climbs the tree in order to taste that fruit.
Having abandoned other desires and possessing an expanded resolve,
he who enters the essence of discernment casts off the mental fluctuations rooted in the elements;
having attained the supreme state, he no longer strives for anything lower.
Therefore, for the sake of the supreme fruit, he who has ascended to the state of discernment casts off his former formative tendencies (*saṃskāra*) like a snake sheds its skin;
beholding himself as having ascended to the highest station, he laughs aloud.
"What kind of wretched person was I for all this time?"— thus,
with his delusions regarding those [objects] such as compassion and so forth dispelled,
he shines like a sovereign emperor, casting down the serpent of greed from the various branches [of worldly existence].
Day after day, craving abandons the dense rows of clouds over the moon of the heart, the masses of darkness over the lotus of the face, and the black chains of infamy.
It disregards what has already been attained and does not long for what has not yet been reached.
He becomes one who is full of *soma*, cool within amidst all mental activities.
With his self seated upon the very sprouts of the meaning of the scriptures,
he remains looking down at the movements of the world, characterized by rises and falls.
Beholding his former haunts— thorny with heaps of flowers scattered by fearsome trees and creepers— he laughs inwardly at their wretchedness.
Amidst those very branches, as she flew up and down, [he saw her].
Moving with a captivating gait, he shines like a king.
He regards his sons, wives, consorts, friends, and wealth as if they were produced in another life or born of a dream.
In him whose mind is cool and pure, the great afflictions of passion, hatred, fear, madness, pride, and delusion are seen to be like those of an actor;
he even laughs at unreal things before him as if they were the antics of a madman.
He does not perceive any of the states of the river of saṃsāra, whose currents are as fragile as waves; he is indifferent to the desires for women, sons, and wealth,
resting in a state never before attained, like one who is already dead while still living.
Having fixed one's gaze solely upon that supreme, solitary, and pure Self which consists of awakening,
one ascends far toward that fruit;
nourished by the nectar of contentment, one repeatedly recalls the previous stages.
He does not suffer even at the loss of things that are beneficial or things that are harmful. In worldly affairs and in undertakings that bring about enjoyment,
he experiences supreme agitation, as if awakened from sleep.
Like a long-distance traveler who, having been overcome by the fatigue of ignorance for a long time, longs for a noble, uninterrupted, and unimpeded rest;
even as fire awakened by exhalation remains within itself as if without fuel.
Even when there is only the delusion of breath, one becomes tranquil while remaining within [the self].
One is unable to ward off the dissatisfaction that forcefully descends upon objects,
just as one cannot stop rain falling from a cloud.
Traversing that great path which bestows the fruit of the ultimate truth,
he reaches a certain ground that is beyond the reach of words;
for by the power of destiny, even when no actions whatsoever are performed, [that state] is attained.
He feels a distaste for enjoyments, like a traveler in desert lands;
reeling and intoxicated as it were, yet blissful while sleeping amidst the fluctuations of worldly existence,
he— silent and with his mind full within— attains an indescribable state.
Having attained such a state,
he gradually approaches that supreme goal, just as a bird reaches the path of the sun;
then, having abandoned all cognitions, he becomes equal to space.
One takes hold, then tastes, then eats, and then becomes fully satisfied.
From the daily abandonment of all objects, through an expansion that occurs day after day,
resting in one's own pure nature is called the attainment of the ultimate reality.
When the cognition of duality has dissolved, pure consciousness alone remains;
the wise know that to be Brahman—pure, one, and without beginning or end.
By one who is dispassionate toward the desire for worldly objects and has renounced the desire for wife and family...
One who is liberated from the desire for wealth rests in that state through the ultimate transformation of consciousness and the supreme reality,
which are mutually [united];
like a streak of snow by heat, the perception of difference dissolves.
For one who knows that and is liberated from affliction, no state whatsoever is possible without the perfectly equal intrinsic nature,
just as a statue remains with its limbs displayed exactly as they are within a garland of flowers.
Just as a pillar is neither existent nor non-existent, so is the stability of the universe in the Supreme.
Meditation cannot be performed [in this state], nor is it required;
for one who has awakened through the absence of ignorance remains here by himself.
He in whom an absolute tastelessness toward visible objects is perceived is a Buddha; for one who is not awakened lacks the power to abandon the visible.
That which is the awakening to the nature of the visible is an awakening that does not perish through further cognition.

That is described by the term "concentration" (samādhāna) by those who are well-concentrated. When a cognition arises in the mind in the form of the unity of the seer and the seen within a single concentration, then it rests of its own accord.
For people who know reality, the very nature of things is the distaste for the perceptible;

the supreme ones say that the relishing of the perceptible is precisely the state of not knowing reality. It is only for one who does not know that [reality] that sense objects are relished, but not for one who knows it.
For one who has drunk the nectar of immortality, pungent sour gruel no longer tastes sweet. For the wise man who is free from thirst, established in the Self, and has abandoned the threefold desire,
meditation proceeds spontaneously even though he does not will it.

Awareness flashes forth within craving; yet for one in whom that very craving does not exist, where could that awareness remain once it has cast off its own form? How could it be, and by what means? For the knower, awareness—which is without support and beyond study—cannot be defined by any limitation.
This infinite [state] arises spontaneously of its own accord for one who is free from craving; it is undivided and self-manifesting.
For one who is free from craving, meditation proceeds spontaneously as something infinite, like the stationary form of a mountain whose wings have fallen away.
Because it is known within the self that is pure consciousness, the state of non-concentration arises;
it cannot be obtained [otherwise], just as a *buka* flower does not exist in a blazing fire.
Supreme detachment from sense objects is declared to be concentration (*samādhi*).
Salutation indeed to that Brahmin among men by whom that [state] was attained.
(MU 6.202.46) Indeed, when freedom from craving for sense-objects has reached full maturity, neither gods nor asuras, even including Indra, are able to destroy one's meditation. (MU 6.202.47)
Therefore, let supreme detachment from sense objects be accomplished through diamond-like meditation (vajradhyāna).
Once duality has dissolved through gnosis, what is the use of the straw of other forms of bliss?
Just as the meaning of the word "universe" resides in the ignorant, it is not the object of those who know reality.

The meaning of the word "universe" resides in the knower of that [Reality], not in the domain of the fool; just as there is a difference between those two—the knower and the ignorant—so too is there a difference between the two universes they inhabit. O wise ones, rest in that place where both shine forth as one.

For those who have attained perfection on the stages of awakening, or for those who lack discernment regarding objects, existence and non-existence, as well as duality and unity, are not determined here by anyone else.
The means [to this] is twofold: the meaning of the scriptures is one, and association with the wise is the second.
Meditation is the third [step] toward Nirvāṇa, and among these, each subsequent one is superior.

The mirror of the individual soul (jīva) assumes the form of these [elements] as their great body; from their mutual friction, it arises in the world, whether in a state of distinction or non-distinction, in both equal and unequal proportions.
For those who have previously known the entire world as it rests upon the chessboard of the eightfold path,
and for whom the attainment of both [liberation and worldly success] brings an end to craving for enjoyment—
the moment their entire being is shaken by the whirlwind of wisdom and consumed by the fire of knowledge in the sky of the self— [they attain liberation].
I do not know where this cotton-wool of the world quickly goes when it reaches the supreme peace.
By that awakening, which is like a variegated fire, dullness is not extinguished;
by which the delusion of the world, though its roots have been severed, does not quickly dissolve.
Just as the perception of the world by the ignorant is illuminated by ignorance,
so too, through thorough knowledge, the non-perception of that [world] is illuminated by the wise.
For one who knows that, the perception of the three worlds remains devoid of both word and meaning.
Just as it remains, the cognition of the three worlds arises like a painting;
fashioned as if by emptiness and constructed as if by a dream,
the cognition of the world shines within the conscious mind like a pure illusion.
Surely for one who has taken root in awakening, neither the sense of "I" nor the persistence of the world appears;
rather, there is a certain state of being whose nature is the supreme manifestation.
The mind, consisting of both awakening and non-awakening, shines like wood that is both dry and wet.
Due to awakening, the world is one; due to insentience, it has come to possess multiplicity. Through mutual lack of awakening, one disputes; through awakening, one practices friendliness.
Whatever portion of this [self] is predominant, one remains established as being composed of that.
The Buddhas realize the true nature of the existence and non-existence of the world,
just as one who has reached the fourth state [turiya] realizes the nature of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
This very mind, which is but latent impression (*vāsanā*), perishes through self-investigation.

Therefore, because [the self] is not a substantial entity, its destruction does not occur in liberation. Thus, from the tree of meditation—which has naturally reached full ripeness over time and has gradually attained awakening—he partakes of the primordial fruit of supreme awakening, which is like an elixir; in this way, the deer-like mind is released from its fetters.
The two hundred and third canto, titled "The Narrative of Manohariṇa," by Vasiṣṭha: Vasiṣṭha said:
When the fruit of the ultimate truth is known, enjoyed, and fully digested,
then that deer of the mind quickly becomes the ultimate reality itself;
its state as a "deer" vanishes somewhere, like a lamp whose oil has been exhausted.
There, the ultimate reality alone remains, shining forth infinitely.
When the mind has attained the state of awakening upon reaching the fruit of the tree of meditation,
it maintains a stability as firm as a diamond, motionless like a bird whose wings have been clipped.
The state of the mind (*manastā*) vanishes somewhere, while pure awareness (*bodhatā*) remains—
indescribable, ending in non-differentiation, being all things, yet the self of all.
The existence of the mind is said to arise as awareness because it is not distinct from it.
It becomes beginningless and endless, bestowing the fruit of pure illumination.
Consequently, in that state, there remains only meditation— effortless, without beginning or end, and with all desires entirely cast aside.

As long as Brahman has not been realized and one has not come to rest in the supreme state, so long is that which is called "thinking" not understood as true meditation (dhyāna). Having attained oneness with the ultimate reality, I know not where the mind has gone.
Where are the latent impressions? Where are the actions? Where are the perceptions of joy and anger? Only the yogi is seen, who has attained exclusive devotion to meditation;
established in the adamantine concentration (*vajrasamādhi*), he is like a mountain impervious to opposing forces.
For the yogin who has become disinterested in all enjoyments, whose sensory perceptions and consciousness are stilled, for whom every visible object is devoid of flavor, who delights in his own self,
and who has gradually attained rest through the forceful dissolution of mental fluctuations; MU_6,203.10.

Who indeed can ward off a concentration that has arrived for its own sake? One whose disposition is thus cultivated contemplates the distaste for sense objects until he no longer perceives those enjoyments at all, just like a man in a painting.

Seeing that the objects of the world are devoid of intrinsic reality, the self-possessed one, through the power of being free from latent desires, is as if forcibly placed by another into the diamond-like concentration (*vajrasamādhi*),
just as a river’s flood arrives during the rainy season.
Our mind moves again toward that which has come by force alone.
For when meditation arrives by force through the cooling of all objects,
that resulting distaste for sense-objects born of knowledge is indeed *samādhi*, and nothing else.
The firm distaste for sense objects alone is declared to be meditation;
that very meditation, through its full maturation, becomes truly like the essence of a diamond. For that which is this thirstlessness for enjoyments is indeed the sprouted state of meditation.
That very [state], through the binding of the seat, becomes the graceful curvature of the shoulders.
When right knowledge has fully expanded and abandoned all latent impressions,
it becomes meditation, which is Nirvana, having arrived at the state beyond bliss.
If there is freedom from craving for enjoyments, what else is needed for the wisdom of meditation?
If there is no freedom from craving for enjoyments, what else is needed for the wisdom of meditation?
For the sage who has abandoned the tasting of the visible world and possesses perfect knowledge.
Non-conceptual meditative absorption proceeds without interruption.
He for whom the visible world no longer brings relish is known as a perfectly awakened one (sambuddha).
When enjoyments no longer bring relish, then right awakening has arisen.
How can there be the state of an enjoyer for one whose nature is at rest?
For the state of being an enjoyer is indeed without intrinsic nature; when that [nature] has perished, how and from where could it exist?
One should remain devoted to meditative absorption (*samādhi*) at the conclusion of hearing, reciting, and chanting.
One who has desisted from meditative concentration and is at peace should resort to the study, recitation, and chanting of the scriptures.
One should dwell in nirvāṇa, free from weariness, delightful through the subsiding of all doubts,
as serene as deep sleep, with a mind equally tranquil, pure within like the expanse of an autumn cloud.
The chapter titled "The Realization of Equanimity," the two hundred and fourth chapter,
by Vasiṣṭha:
Listen to this method for one who, utterly exhausted by the burden of saṃsāra and with his body rolling in perils, desires rest:
first, when a spark of discernment arises in his heart, [he should proceed].
Whether due to a cause or even without a cause,

she who is filled with world-weariness then resorts to virtuous men of noble character and high standing, just as one scorched by heat seeks out shade-providing trees along the road to relieve the fatigue of the journey.
Like a traveler avoiding sacrificial posts, he keeps ignorant people at a distance;
following the wise, he performs bathing, charity, austerity, and sacrifice.
His conduct is charming, appropriate, and unartificial.
It bears the world’s delight, like the nectar of the lunar orb. Following supreme wisdom, fulfilling the welfare of others,
and delighting in pure actions, a certain gentle being proceeds forth.
Pure, smooth, soft, and enchanting like a vessel of fresh butter,
his sweet new acquaintance brings happiness to people;
so too are the cool and purifying deeds of the discerning one.
Just as the networks of rays from the moon thoroughly cool people,
so too one does not find such fearless rest in groves of gardens filled with heaps of flowers as one finds in the company of the virtuous.
Like the waters of the Mandākinī, the [teachings] of the discerning, when united, wash away sins and bestow purity;
[they are intended] for those who are discerning, dispassionate, and seeking to cross over saṃsāra.
People attain a coolness as if they were in houses made of ice and crystal. Indeed,
that noble urbanity which exists in a discerning person is not found even among the fresh daughters of the gods and gandharvas.
The wisdom of one who performs appropriate actions gradually attains clarity;
it internalizes the meaning of the treatises, just as the surface of a mirror reflects an object.
That wisdom, permeated by the essence of the meaning of the treatises, attains the height of true insight.
Like a plantain tree in a great forest,
the discerning [intellect] shines with its own splendor; like a mirror, wisdom, possessing perfect purity, swiftly carries within itself all objects reflected therein in their entirety.
One whose self is purified by the company of the virtuous and polished by the meaning of the scriptures shines like a cloth cleansed by fire,
brightened by the brilliance of blazing gold and producing a stainless luster.

The world shines through a virtuous mind, just as it does through the sun. Likewise, the wise person pursues both scripture and the company of the virtuous in such a way that, through constant association, he quickly becomes like them.
Gradually attaining the state of a virtuous person and being permeated by the weight of the meaning of the scriptures,
he shines while casting enjoyments beneath him, like one who has emerged from a cage;
day by day, he abandons the misfortune of pursuing worldly pleasures.

By him that family shone like the circle of stars by the moon. A certain unprecedented splendor, never before seen and not born of worldly enjoyment, now manifested in his mouth, just as when Rāhu has died, a new luster appears in the moon.
To the great ones who have treated the three worlds as mere straw, that tree of worldly existence (kalpaviṭapī) becomes a mere object of mention, like the celestial tree in the sky to the gods.
Even a wise person feels inward shame at the pursuit of enjoyments.
He is supremely satisfied with the excellence of others' enjoyments.

Within himself, he mocks his own flickering activities, which are as fleeting as a river; with a face smiling with weariness, he regards his own births as lowly, like one who remembers his past lives.
Then virtuous men come to see him out of nothing but affection,
their eyes wide with wonder as if beholding the moon risen upon the earth; he,
who has forever disregarded worldly enjoyment, regards even that [visit] with a mind of propriety.
Even when he has obtained enjoyments that are appropriate for him, he does not value them highly.
Within him, a distaste for the cycle of worldly existence arises first, as his inner self awakens;
