this occurs in one whose dullness has worn away, like the ripening of an autumnal tree.
Then, desiring his own well-being, he himself seeks the company of the virtuous for the sake of future welfare, just as one seeking health resorts to a physician.
By means of that, having become noble-minded, he immerses himself in the meanings of the scriptures.
A great man among those who are greatly serene is like a mighty elephant in vast lakes;
for a virtuous person, having rescued one standing near him from calamities,
establishes him in prosperities, just as the sun places all things within its own light.
Abstention from taking what belongs to others occurs first;
for one who possesses discernment, contentment with one's own possessions arises. One who has desisted from taking the property of others is filled with the nectar of contentment.
The person of discernment gradually desires even to disregard his own interests. For he who once gave away only grains, oil-cakes, and vegetables when asked,
by that very same practice of yoga, eventually gives away even his own flesh.
Surely, for those whose thoughts have become sparse as they pursue solitude,
foolishness and lightness vanish like the water in a cow's footprint when it is run over.
Having first diligently practiced restraint from taking what belongs to others for the sake of others, one should proceed.
Then, through discernment, one should cultivate detachment from one's own interests.
Thereafter, by means of the rejection of enjoyments, the wise gradually effect the renunciation of their own interests for the sake of supreme self-rest.
There is no such suffering in the world, even among the millions of hells,
as that which consists in the lifelong command to acquire wealth—
whether while sitting, lying down, traveling, walking, enjoying oneself, or earning.
The wealthy are solely devoted to anxiety; fools do not perceive this.

Indeed, objects of desire are vast calamities, prosperities are continuous misfortunes, and enjoyments are the great diseases of existence—for those who have cultivated them with a perverted perspective.
One does not fall into such helplessness through the expansion of the poison of anxiety as long as one does not pursue a great misfortune for the sake of a trivial object;
for that which is pleasing for a long time brings unsurpassed happiness.

May he view the object with the vision of a blade of withered grass and attain peace. He is remembered as the Lord of the Caravan, the true goal for those subject to the manifold transformations of existence, to the acts of aging and death, and to the burning pains of wretchedness and wickedness.
In this world, for living beings subject to old age and death,
contentment is the elixir that brings about freedom from aging and immortality.
Spring, the Nandana grove, the moon, the celestial nymphs, and the god of love—
Thus, on one side, the nectar of contentment has gathered;
on the other, through contentment, the heart reaches fullness like a lake at the end of the rainy season—
deep, cool, pleasing, serene, and rich in flavor.
Having attained vigor, the virtuous person shines with contentment,
like a tree in full bloom through the power of spring;
he exerts himself as if crushing insects under the tread of his feet.
Wretched by nature and seeking wealth, passing from one misery to another,
those supplicants of deformed appearance find no stable composure, like those tossed by the waves who have fallen into a turbulent ocean.
Wealth and women are as transient as the crests of waves;

what wise man would take delight in them, which possess a shade like that of a serpent’s hood used as a parasol? Even knowing the hardships involved in acquiring and protecting wealth, [one should not pursue it].
One should not touch that fool who,
like a beast among men, harbors desire; for him whose external and internal undertakings the mind cuts away with the sickle of dispassion, his field shines forth clearly.

The state of the world, though unreal, appears as if real to the ignorant and even to the awakened one who knows it to be so; that which flashes forth there is merely the manifestation of a lack of practice.
Having attained association with the virtuous through weariness with saṃsāra, and having approached the scriptures by means of that [association]...

Having cast aside enjoyments by means of the realization of the meaning of the scriptures, he attains the supreme goal through the firmness of his dispassion. This concludes the two hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Beginning of Tranquility for Those Seeking Liberation."
Vasiṣṭha:

When world-weariness has taken root, when association with the virtuous is established, when the meaning of the scriptures has been contemplated by the intellect, and when freedom from craving for enjoyments has arrived; MU 6.205.1
When a distaste for sense-objects has arisen, when goodness has likewise emerged,
when illumination has become manifest, and when awakening has taken birth in the heart,
wealth is no longer craved by the discerning man, just as darkness is not desired.
Those who are still living are abandoned like parched, impure leaves;
wives and kinsmen are regarded with the gaze of a passionless traveler,
yet they are attended to according to one's ability and the demands of the time.
Even though the objects of the senses are repeatedly attached to the senses,
enjoyments are surely not experienced due to the tranquility of the mind.
[This occurs] in solitary places, at the ends of the quarters, by lakes, and in forests.
They dwell in holy places or in their own homes,
amidst the playful diversions of friends, in assemblies, gardens, dining halls, and the like;
yet they do not remain steadfastly engaged in disputes over scriptures or logic.
By one who is tranquil, self-controlled, delighting in their own self, and observing silence,
it is knowledge alone that is sought by the wise one who speaks exclusively of realized wisdom.
Thus, through the power of practice, one comes to rest in the supreme state.
Like water in a low-lying place, by one who is tranquil and discerning of his own accord,
consciousness alone arises as the object, peaceful within and without;
that a separate object exists is impossible— this indeed is the supreme state.
"There is neither the apprehension of objects nor is there emptiness apart from the nature of consciousness"—
thus they say that supreme state resides within inner experience,
when duality and unity have subsided through the awakening to the awakening of non-awakening.
They say that Nirvāṇa is the abiding peace, one’s own supreme state. For those who have found rest in mere self-awareness and are free from the mind,
sense objects do not please them, just as water does not for stones.
Having attained the state of cessation, free from mental construction and slow with silence, he remains established in his own nature alone, like a self-possessed figure depicted in a painting.
All objects are devoid of objective reality; the Great One alone exists, appearing as minute as an atom.
For the knower of the object of knowledge and the knower, the heart is indeed non-empty, though its nature is emptiness.
For the wise one, egoity, the activity of the world, the notions of space and time, and even knowledge and emptiness— though they appear to exist— are in fact not found.
By means of knowledge established in the stainless state, the darkness of the heart is not perceived— just as external darkness [is dispelled] by a lamp— nor are passion, hatred, fear, and the like.
Free from all taints of *rajas* and having attained the supreme state through *sattva*, [it remains] in every respect.
One should bow to that sun of the knowers of reality, whose nature is free from the form of darkness.
When the dissolution of duality has occurred and the mind has attained invisibility,
that state of one who has realized awakening does not fall within the range of words.
The Supreme Lord, propitiated by supreme and long-standing devotion day and night, grants liberation to one whose intellect is absorbed in Him. Rāma said:
"O best of sages, who is Īśvara, and how may he be propitiated through devotion?
Tell me this in truth, O foremost among those who know all truths.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
O one of great intelligence, the Lord is neither far away nor difficult to attain;
the Supreme Lord is one's very own self, whose singular essence consists of Great Awakening.
In him is everything, from him comes everything, he is everything, and he is everywhere.
He is eternally all-pervading within, containing everything; homage to that Self of all!
Therefore, these transformations of creation and dissolution are perceived from that which is without cause as their cause, like the various movements of the wind.
All beings, both stationary and moving, constantly worship him from every side by granting whatever they desire; he,
for his part, [grants] very many births according to their wishes and desires.
When he has been fully honored by him, he attains grace. Being pleased, Mahādeva himself— the Self, the Great Lord—
swiftly impels a pure messenger, whose intentions are auspicious, for the sake of awakening.
Rāma:
O Sage, by whom is this messenger impelled—by himself or by the Supreme Lord? And how does that messenger effect awakening? Tell me.
Vasiṣṭha said: Impelled by the Self, the messenger named Viveka (Discernment) dwells in the cave of the heart as a granter of boons, like the moon in the sky.
This very one gradually awakens the living being whose nature is latent impressions;
he delivers the undiscriminating person from that ocean of saṃsāra.
This self of awakening is indeed the inner self, the supreme, the Supreme Lord.

O Rāma, the syllable *praṇava* is the Veda-sanctioned designator of this very [Brahman]. It is constantly propitiated through the performance of recitation, oblations, austerity, charity, study, sacrifice, and ritual sequences by men, *nāgas*, gods, and *asuras*.
The sky is the head, the earth the feet, the stars the rows of body hair,
the elements the bones, and the ether the heart of this Supreme Lord;
because his essence is consciousness, he pervades everywhere, smells, and sees.
Therefore, this living being (jīva), bearing hands, ears, eyes, and feet on every side,
awakens the messenger of discernment, slays the demon of the mind,
and is led by the Self along a vast and indescribable path.
Having abandoned the flood of all conceptual constructions and having shaken off the peril of misfortune,
let the self itself be pacified by the self through its own human effort.
While this demon of a wandering mind is agitated by waves like clouds, [one must remain steadfast].
In the darkness of the night of saṃsāra, one's own self is the full moon; within the hollow of the ocean agitated by waves— the whirlpools of ignorance and death,
flickering with the waves of craving, and driven by the fierce winds of one's own mind.
In this treacherous ocean of saṃsāra, which is the support for the current of great dullness and is dense with the crocodiles of the senses, discernment (*viveka*) is a great ship.
Having first become well-pleased by the worship of one's chosen deity, the Self bestows discernment here as a messenger of purification.
Through association with the virtuous, the study of the scriptures, and the supreme realization of the ultimate truth, the soul is led to the one, primordial, stainless state.
This is the chapter named "The Majesty of Discrimination," the two hundred and sixth chapter.
Vasiṣṭha:
Within those whose discernment is fully nourished and who have cast off the impurity of latent impressions (vāsanā),
an unprecedented kind of greatness arises.
The fourteen worlds do not fathom the intellect of the great, which is noble in its vastness, possesses sublime boundaries, and is beautiful in its profundity; for the wise,
the conviction that "the world is a delusion of the mind" is firmly established.
As one moves between the external and the internal, the grasping for objects and delusion subside.

When the delusion of the world flickers like two moons, like heat-waves, like water, or like a mass of hair in the sky, how can there be a causal condition consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)?
When the causal conditions of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are stilled, only the void sky remains;
yet if even that state is unreal to the mind, it must be abandoned by the discerning one. Indeed, when these three are devoid of these three states, [the Self alone remains].
Whether appearing as if seeing or not seeing, that state is supremely exalted.
Like a mass of rays from variegated jewels, the world consists of manifold forms;
it is a mere appearance, neither consisting of water, nor solid, nor of earth.
The world exists as nothing but form, light, and mind, and is indeed empty,
arisen like a web of rays from various jewels set in the sky.
Herein, there are no real elements, no world-ness, and no emptiness.

This is the unfolding of the network of light from the Lord of Jewels known as Brahmā. The emanations and visions of Brahmā, consisting of the conceptualization of manifoldness, appear as if formless, like dense masses of suns at the end of an eon.
Thus, first of all, no solidified grasping at a mass exists;
in an imagined object, only emptiness is perceived, like [the appearance of] space.
In this state, which is devoid of substantial reality, how can there be a basis for existence?
What bird could ever rest upon a future tree in the sky?
There is no substantiality in the elements, nor does emptiness exist;
for this very reason, even the mind has set. What remains there is the Real (Sat); in that, my abiding is established.
Though non-different, it remains as the very same, yet the awakened one appears in diverse forms;
with various objects dissolved within, he is like a lump of gold.
For one who abides in this state, the manifold universe dissolves into the "I-ness" (sāhantva).
For the knower, that which is inexpressible and devoid of thought remains as the true nature of reality;
the intellect alone is distressed by its perceptions of higher and lower states.
Indeed, the true object is realized through the intellect when it has been cultivated even slightly.
The Virāj is devoid of vigor, being free from the relationship of cause and effect and the like;
O dear one, this world situated in the past, present, and future is indeed non-existent.
That by which it is known through the nature of consciousness is designated as the Knower.
For that which is non-dual and tranquil, the universe does not exist.
All these aforementioned specific instructions reach the experience of the knower, just as the accounts of the virtuous reach those who are present.
The elements possess no solid mass, nor is their emptiness a mere non-existence;
for this very reason, the mind does not exist, and your abiding therein is the reality that remains.
The consciousness of this conscious being consists precisely in its inward-turned orientation toward the object of thought.

That which has arisen leads to misfortune; that which has not arisen leads to the highest good. Remain eternally composed in the consciousness of its non-arising—whether with movement or without movement—casting aside all doubt regarding that state of being.
Having emerged and reached the state of externality, it attains there a state of solidification through its own self-perception alone; due to its insentience, it becomes like a stone in water.
Just like the objects in a dream and so forth, consciousness assumes a state of solidification through non-awareness.
Having become the mind through its state of being the grasper of that [object], it binds the body.
In all these states, no otherness arises for consciousness;
the distinction is merely imagined through the conceptualization of words.
Both externally and internally, it is the Self alone that appears through the perceptions of objects within consciousness;
for how could there be any other state of being an object of thought for that which is oriented toward itself?
Both externally and internally, it is the Self alone that appears through the perceptions of objects within consciousness.
Just as this mind exists through its internal and external states,
so too, because consciousness is like space, time, space, and the rest are its very form;
and all objects are of the nature of space, appearing like the void in a dream, lacking any objective reality.
Through the power of consciousness or its absence, the external object and the internal state may become either conscious or unconscious;
for that which is insentient and non-existent can never anywhere attain the nature of consciousness.
Consciousness does not enter the state of being an object, nor does it remain once it has reached such a condition.
It remains exactly as it is, not undergoing even the slightest change into something else.
When the transformation into pure consciousness alone has fully arisen,
even the memory of the words "awakening" and "non-awakening," or "object" and "meaning," will come to an end.

For the minds that possess subtle bodies (ātivāhika-deha), the perception of materiality (ādhibhautikatā) arises spontaneously through firm habitual conditioning (bhāvanā). This [perception] is cultivated by means of subtle bodies that have been refined by minds as clear as space.
The state of being a ghost created by actors is false; likewise, the delusion of being a ghost is false.
This delusion is pacified through the practice of not wandering [in error], once it has been recognized.
Indeed, madness is said to be pacified through the realization: "I am not mad."
Through the thorough understanding of delusion by oneself, latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) cease;
for when one has recognized a dream as a dream, what indeed could there be to cultivate?
Through the very thinning of these predispositions, cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) comes to rest.

Latent impression alone is the great knot; the wise are intent upon its severance. Just as a man's madness of ignorance is cultivated through habituation, so too it is pacified in time through the repeated practice of awakening.
Just as this subtle body (ātivāhikadeha) is led by the wise into a state of materiality through contemplation, so too, by grace, it is led into the state of pure consciousness;
likewise, even the subtle body is led to the plane of the individual soul (jīvapada).
Through firm practice of awakening, one should lead even the state of Brahman [to its true nature].
If the arising of the Self-existent One is understood as being of the nature of consciousness,
then how is it that the *ativāhika* (conveying) intellect is also understood?
If, with respect to that, the knot regarding the meaning of the sentence does not dissolve—
just as, for example, the mantra-words for the eradication of spirits [must be applied] to each individual thread—
then the world must first be understood as one with consciousness by means of the intellect, provided it is free from affliction.
Through ultimate transformation, even that [mind] is no longer perceived.
When the mind, both internal and external, is stilled, its true nature shines forth;
resting in that very state, which is cool and radiant like the sky, one attains peace.
Possessing knowledge and established in the sacrifice of knowledge, planting the sacrificial post of meditation,
he conquers the world and performs sacrifice with the singular fee of universal renunciation.
Whether a rain of embers falls or the wind of dissolution blows, [he remains steadfast].
Whether walking on the earth or moving in the sky, the knower remains the same within the Self. For one whose mind is stilled through freedom from craving and who has fully attained cessation,
no state of stability other than the adamantine concentration (vajrasamādhi) is possible.
The mind is not so pacified by the compositions of scriptures, nor by instructions, austerities, and self-restraint, as it is by the absence of thirst for external objects.
Let the fire of total dispassion toward all objects be kindled within the grass of the mind.
Through the realization that "prosperity is indeed calamity" by means of the winds of total renunciation,
delusion— both external and internal— as well as the grasping of a solid body and the perception of objects,
shines forth within the Self as pure consciousness alone, like a gem due to its nature as knowing.
Through visions of human beings, *nāgas*, gods, houses, and mountain caves,
consciousness itself expands excessively, like smoke in the sky taking on the form of clouds;
and those residing within the inert vessel of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) tremble and flee.
The rivers of their own transformations, with their essences falling through the power of the individual soul (*jīva-śakti*),
are like living beings— like aged fish— sporting in the waters of the sky;
ensnared by the net of delusion, they do not remember their station within the Self.
Having become condensed through density, the mass of consciousness (cidghana) within the courtyard of the sky flashes forth from its own self by itself in the form of various objects. Thus,
all these living beings are merely atoms of the wind of latent impressions (vāsanā).
Like withered leaves, they stand with necks upturned, as dull as bamboos sighing in the wind.

Having summoned human strengths and conquered sloth, having risen and shattered the dense cage of the snares of saṃsāra along with the accumulated flood of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), one should emerge; thus, one must not remain like an ignorant person.
The chapter named "Universal Quiescence," the two hundred and seventh chapter,
by Vasiṣṭha:
These multitudes of living beings seen throughout the ten directions,
designated by such names as men, nāgas, lords of the gods, and gandharvas—
some of them are awake in dreams, while others are awake in their conceptual constructions.

Some are established solely in the waking state; others remain in the long-standing waking state; still others are established in the dense waking state; likewise, others are in the waking-dream state;
and some are those whose waking has ceased—living beings are thus remembered as being of seven kinds.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, let the distinction between these seven forms of living beings be told to me for my understanding, like that between waters in the oceans.
Vasiṣṭha:
In a certain previous kalpa, in a certain world, in a certain place,
some living beings possessing the nature of life remained asleep within their bodies.
Know that for those who perceive a dream, this world is their dream; indeed, they are called "living beings awake in a dream.
That dream which arises of its own accord for those who are fast asleep in a particular place—
In this regard, they are ours, while we are the dream-men for them.
Because of their long duration, that dream has attained the state of waking;
those living beings who remain situated within it are the dream-awakened ones.
Because the All-pervading One is omniscient, everything exists everywhere;
therefore, we who are like those in a dream stand as dream-men for them.
Rāma said:
In those eons in which they were born, the constructions of the eons have ceased;
if that is so, how can there be a continued existence for those who are awakened?
Vasiṣṭha said:
In this world, they are either liberated from the delusion of dreaming or, having attained a state of wakefulness,
they conceive of other bodies and fully resort to them;
likewise, they perceive another imagined world-cycle that has been constructed.
Indeed, there can be no crowding in the sky of the appearance of conceptual construction.

Those who are like insects in the decayed udumbara tree of the world—which is of the nature of one's own conceptual construction—are called "those awake in a dream"; now hear about those "awake in their own volitions" (saṅkalpa-jāgarāḥ).
In a certain former aeon, in some world, somewhere—
remaining entirely sleepless within, devoted solely to their mental constructs,
or perhaps rolling about in meditation, following the sway of their kingdom of the mind.
Those who have attained firmness of resolve and whose prior experiences have dissolved,
for whom the state of waking has long since become mere volition,
and whose worldly activities have ceased therein— they are indeed "waking through volition" (saṅkalpajāgarāḥ).
Upon the subsiding of conceptual construction, they resort again to that [state] or another;
we are these "men of volition" (saṅkalpapuruṣa) who abide within their bodies. These are said to be those who wake through volition and sleep through volition.
O Jīva, for the sake of your life, listen to the states of pure wakefulness.
These first descended from Brahman, whose nature is expanded;
they are called the "purely waking" states because they existed prior to manifestation and remained unevolved.
Those very same beings, having passed into further births and remaining awake for a long time,
are said to have reached maturity as they move through the cycle of cause and effect.
It is those very same ones who, due to the influence of their evil deeds, become inert and enter the state of stationary beings.
Those who have attained density amidst the waking state are called "dense-wakers" (ghanajāgrat).

But those who, awakened by the meaning of the scriptures and by the company of the virtuous, have attained enlightenment and perceive the waking state as if it were a dream— they become "waking-dreamers" (jāgratsvapna).
"But those who have attained perfect awakening and are rested in the supreme state,
their waking and other states having ceased, have reached the fourth stage.
Thus, the sevenfold division of living beings has been described to you.
Having understood this, like the nature of the oceans, become intent on the highest good.
Abandon the delusion consisting of the enumeration of the world; you have fully attained the state of being a dense mass whose sole form is pure awakening.
This primordial reality is devoid of emptiness and liberated from non-emptiness—a body free from both duality and unity.
The chapter titled "An Investigation into the Seven Types of Living Beings," the two hundred and eighth chapter;
Rāma said:
O Brahmin, how does that which is purely waking, devoid of cause and devoid of action, blossom forth from the Supreme, like a tree from the sky? Vasiṣṭha replied:
O Greatly Intelligent One, no effect is perceived without a cause;
therefore, for that [unconditioned Self] which is alone and awake, nothing whatsoever can arise here.
Because of that impossibility, other distinctions of living beings exist as those possessing life.
None at all come into being, being thwarted by the absence of a cause.
Nothing whatsoever is born here; nothing whatsoever perishes here.
The arising of the conceptualization of words and their meanings occurs for the sake of instruction and the object of instruction.
Rāma:
Who creates bodies by means of the conscious faculties such as the mind and intellect?
Who deludes living beings with the bonds of affection, passion, and the like?
Vasiṣṭha said:
No one ever creates bodies,
nor does anyone ever delude living beings.
Awareness, whose nature is a manifestation without beginning or end, is established within itself;
it appears in the form of various objects, just as [the ocean appears] through its waves and so forth.
Nothing external exists, yet awareness flashes forth as if it were external.
Awakening arises from the heart like a noble tree from a seed.
O scion of Raghu, this entire universe exists within awakening itself,
just as a carved statue is manifest within a pillar.
Let it be understood that the world is the single Self, both external and internal, infinite in terms of space and time, and the expansion of the fragrance of awakening.
Let this alone be cultivated as the supreme world: the dissolution of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Let it be stilled; for who indeed brings the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) belonging to the next world?
[It is] the perfection of place, time, action, the world, form, mind, and self;
yet it is not devoid of the meanings of words such as "place" and "time," nor is it a void.
O Rāghava, in that void, movement belongs only to those who know the words and to those seers for whom the visible world has become stilled; it does not belong to others.
Indeed, those who have taken refuge in the pit of egolessness, which is both fickle and profound—
No one ever perceives that light.
This vision of the world, teeming with the infinite multitude of beings of fourteen kinds, is to the knower like a mere limb of his own body.
Due to the absence of a cause, creation is neither impelled nor does it cease;
whatever the nature of the cause may be, such is the effect that arises.
Whatever the nature of the effect may be in the cause, that is its state as a cause.
The effect alone is perceived, for the two [subject and object] do not exist apart from that perception;
just as waves, whirlpools, and so forth exist within the ocean, so too do the world, the mind, and the rest exist within Brahman, which is free from agitation. (MU 6.208.17–18)
The stainless Brahman, which is the self of all, exists as a single mass,
just as gold exists within various vessels in the form of the objects contained therein.
During the time of a dream, the dream itself is the waking state, because it is not grasped by the distracted [mind] of the waking world.
During the waking state, that which is actually waking appears as a dream due to the perception of what is unreal.
Established as mere mind, it stands like the water of a mirage;
when its reality is undermined by investigation, the waking state attains the nature of a dream.
Through right knowledge, the elements, along with the body of the knower,
release their bond to the physical seat, like clouds that have passed away;
just as a cloud that has begun to dissolve returns to the state of the sky.
In the same way, through the awakening to reality, the world together with the grasping for a self is pacified;
like an autumn cloud or like the water of a mirage,
the state of being visible dissolves through realization even while it is still appearing before one.
Just as gold, clarified butter, and fuel, when cast into a blazing fire, attain oneness within that fire,
so too do the world, the mind, and the vision [of the seer] attain oneness in consciousness.
Through awakening, the solidification of the three worlds reaches a state of attenuation.
Just as the notion of a *piśāca* appears to a child who has been awakened in his own home,
so too, within the self by the self, in consciousness which is infinite in form,
the world, the mind, and so forth appear; what indeed is this "solidification" (*piṇḍabandha*) here?
This world, which has arisen like a thought within the mind, is indeed nothing but the awakening of consciousness;
when that very world has subsided through awakening, what reality remains for the solidity of the physical body?
Through the realization of a dream, the world abandons the hardness of its material form.

It reaches a state of extreme fragility, like gold melted by fire. This very consciousness, as it exists, attains density even without space and time, having fashioned those two out of itself like gold.
While one remains thus awake through inquiry, the sapid essence— which exists as something fragile like a dream— attains attenuation, just as the moisture does at the end of autumn;
even while persisting, the splendors of the visible world reach a state of extreme fragility.
Like dreams, these things do not please the discerning man once they are fully understood.
Where, indeed, is the rest of the inner self, and where is this perception of sense objects?
How can there be unity between deep sleep and the waking state, or between shadow and sunlight?
The state of the seer and the seen is delusion; non-delusion is abiding in one's own self.
How could there be a unity of the existent and the non-existent, or of the natures of delusion and non-delusion?
When everything is established as mind-only, mere delusion, and the nature of a mere dream.
In this world, the notion of reality recedes from all objects.
To whom would unrealities be pleasing, even for one of no great intelligence?
Though they appear before one's eyes, they are like the waters of a mirage.

When the cognition of reality has dissolved, one whose mind is peaceful perceives the world as having the nature of the sky— devoid of substantiality, appearing like a mass of rays from clouds or a lamp—
and through the thorough knowledge of the world as a non-entity and empty, one turns away from it.
The cultivation of relishing is a form of delusion belonging to one whose self is a wandering mind.
Since that which is known to be non-existent—how could it be something to be adopted?
Having fully recognized a dream, who would go after the gold in the dream?
When the object of sight is fully understood as being like a dream, attachment to it ceases;
the severing of the knot of defects in the states of the seer and the seen proceeds.
Devoid of attachment, with a tranquil mind, and with the ego-sense extinguished, the adept attains liberation.
Free from passion and free from exertion, the one with the intellect of a Buddha remains at peace. When the essence has become tasteless, latent impressions dissolve,
just as the rays of a lamp vanish when its flame has been extinguished.
Through awakening, the sky is seen as being without clouds, like the mass of rays from a lamp;
the entire world is of the nature of delusion, like a city of the Gandharvas.
It is neither the self, nor space, nor emptiness, nor even cognition.
Beholding through ultimate transformation,

one sees that state where there is neither self nor emptiness, neither the world nor mental construction; where there is no notion of the arising of the mind or its objects, yet everything exists exactly as it is.
The perfectly awakened one, who was formerly a knower of the earth and other realms, has set through knowledge;
for the knower, [existence] has become nothing but emptiness, and though it remains, it is not found.
The gentle self becomes a single concentration, stainless as the sky.

He remains free from attachment; though remaining, he is like one who is non-existent. With his mind set on its cessation, silent, having reached the state of total restraint, he has crossed the ocean of saṃsāra and come to the end of all karmas.
Supreme ignorance, which is intent upon the creation of bodies, worlds, space, mountains, and the senses, dissolves;
when that has dissolved, all this [world], though it continues to exist, [vanishes].
With the internal organ most profoundly stilled, with conceptual constructions dissolved, one consists of the essence of one's own true nature.
The wise one, satisfied by the nectar of supreme peace, remains free from all veils. This is the chapter titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Rest," the two hundred and ninth chapter.
Rāma said:
O Sage,
tell me again, in due order, that sequence by which consciousness appears as the world, so that there may be a further cessation of non-consciousness.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Whatever is seen by the utterly deluded Dakṣa exists only in his own mind;
that which is not seen does not exist in the mind of one whose memory is so diminished.
The capable person perceives only the meaning of the scripture as it is consistent from beginning to end;
he does not act upon whatever object falls within the range of his vision.
Being devoted to the practice of what is possible and having a mind focused solely on the meaning of the scripture, he is a sage.
Having become thus, listen to this instruction, which is an ornament for the ears:
This delusion regarding the weight of the visible world is indeed called "ignorance" (avidyā);
in reality, it does not exist, just as water does not exist in a mirage.
For the sake of instruction and the one to be instructed, please listen to this for a moment by complying with my request;
do so without raising such conceptual doubts as "Whence does she come? or "How is she? MU 6.209.6.
Through awakening, you will yourself come to know that "this does not belong to them" and "it does not exist.
Whatever is seen here— this world, both stationary and moving,
rich with all its various transformations— all of it perishes at the end of the aeon.
The destruction of this [world], consisting of the division of its parts, is necessarily unavoidable;
for there is indeed a depletion of the ocean when it is drawn out drop by drop.
This being the case regarding the destruction of substances, because Brahman is identical with them, [it follows that] Brahman is destroyed.
Neither infinity nor existence is possible for this [consciousness]; it is utterly impossible.
The claim that "knowledge is like the power of intoxication" is not established for us;
because we disregard the body, that [knowledge] is not real, being like a dream.
The splendor of the visible object perishes, comes back, or appears as that very same thing, as something else, or as something entirely new;
in this way alone would the treatise be appropriately composed, and not otherwise.
If one says "that very same thing returns," how could there be the possibility of what has been destroyed, since there is no mention of it?
It would be logical to say that she has gone to another form of that same nature; for we [hold that] she was directed toward an object previously experienced.
If it is said that she existed as space itself, that is incorrect; how could she be that very same thing?
If she remained as space in that very way, then she did not undergo destruction.
When cause and effect are thus of one and the same nature, then,
due to the absence of the relationship between cause and effect, our tradition maintains that there is indeed identity.
But as for emptiness, which has reached the state of non-apprehension— that is simply destroyed.
If it were something else, then what kind of destruction would it be? Please tell us.
What basis is there for the cognition here that "that which was destroyed has arisen again"?
It must necessarily perish, and therefore this other thing proceeds once more.

If the existence of the seed persists until the burning [of the field], being a single entity whose parts consist of the fruit and so forth arising with middling height, how can there be the relation of cause and effect?
For here, space, time, action, and the self are established as one, just as they are perceived.
Therefore, the seed alone is the cause, and not the jar that performs the function of a cloth.
When names rest upon all philosophical systems, there is no difference in the underlying reality;
since this reality consists of the ultimate truth, what use have we here for dispute?
This is peaceful, without beginning or end, because upon investigation it is of that very nature;
it is like the sky, pure consciousness alone, as established by the authority of direct experience.
Just as this has never been experienced as existing, so too it is not being experienced now.
How this attainment of perfection is achieved is now described in due order:
when the entire visible sphere has perished at the end of a great kalpa,
including everything from the level of Mahādeva down to the mind, intellect, and the organs of action.
When even the sky has come to rest, when time’s duration is no longer perceived,
when the wind has gone elsewhere, and when fire has utterly ceased to exist;
when darkness has reached its destruction and water and the other elements have long since perished—
When the entire collection of words and their referents has reached its end, there remains that which is the nature of peaceful awakening— pure, real, devoid of anything to be awakened to,
beginningless and endless, an indescribable, stainless, and immutable reality.
The supreme state is inexpressible, unmanifest, beyond the senses, nameless,
the self of all beings, empty, both being and non-being;
it is neither air, nor space, nor the intellect and so forth, nor even a void.
It is neither nothingness nor the all-pervading self, but something else entirely—the supreme ether.
That is experienced by one who knows it, who stands in that state, and who is liberated;
for others, it is described solely through the scriptures as they have been handed down.
It is neither time, nor darkness, nor the self; it is neither being nor non-being, nor space or direction.
It is neither the middle between these two, nor an end, nor awakening, nor even the unawakened state.
This something, utterly translucent, is perceived by those who have reached the further shore of awakening.
By those who have reached the supreme state and whose expansions of saṃsāra have been stilled,
all those objects which were previously prohibited by me are now established here;
they are indefinable by my intellect, like the waves of the gentle ocean.
Just as all various carved figures remain within a great pillar without being carved out,
so do all phenomena abide there; yet they abide there, and yet they do not abide.

That which is not the self of all is indeed the self of all; it is both that very thing and yet not that. Just as this state is the self of all while being devoid of all objects, so do those who are transformed into oneness perceive it exactly as it is.
When the cessation of all objects has occurred,
that primordial state is perceived as devoid of all objects and yet completely full of all objects;
O Great Buddha, for you, it consists in the pacification of all objects.
Right knowledge has not yet arisen; doubt is the illustration here.
He who is awakened, who has attained the supreme manifestation which is free from appearances, whose internal organ is composed and who is at peace—he beholds that true nature.
This delusion of the world throughout the three periods of time— consisting of "this," "you," "I," and so forth—
exists therein like a network of ornaments within a mass of gold.
Just as a collection of vessels is not perceived apart from the mass of gold, [so too is this world not perceived apart from the Self].
Likewise, the world is not found to be separate from the dense mass of ultimate reality (paramārtha).
At all times, its nature is non-different, for it is perceived as being composed of its own constituent parts;
this world and the non-world are like the form of a bracelet made of gold.
Devoid of the referents of words such as "place" and so forth, this world—consisting of place, time, and action—exists there exactly as it is; yet everything therein both exists and does not exist.
It is like waves and the like in still water, or like the variegated work produced by a painter.
Just as a collection of vessels exists within a mass of iron, so does this [universe] abide in Brahman.
Just as this is here neither different nor non-different, neither non-existent nor existent,
so too is this [universe] eternally composed of that, pure, and peaceful within the Peaceful.
This puppet of the three worlds appears as if uncarved,
having attained visibility within the wood of Brahman, which is like a divine tree. Carved puppets fixed upon a pillar attain visibility.
In this [reality], the statues of the three worlds appear though they have not been carved;
within this very Akṣobhya, the waves of the vision of creation appear as showers of the nectar of dense consciousness in the lake of supreme flavor.
In that which is indivisible, they appear as if divided; in that which is unshakable, they appear as if shaken.
Within the dense mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), showers of creation appear as if manifesting though they are unmanifest.
Here, within every single atom, lies the entire circle of worldly existence (*saṃsāramaṇḍala*).
Even that which shines with radiant manifestations does not shine at all [in comparison to it].
Even the collection of categories such as space, time, and wind is but a limb; yet that [Reality] is without limbs.
Though it is the self of all, devoid of all modifications of existence, they call this the undecaying supreme reality of the Self.
The two hundred and tenth canto, titled "The Description of the Nature of Brahman," Canto 210:
Rāma.
Just as there is consciousness in the unconscious, as there is temporality in time,
as there is spatiality in space, and as there is insentience in the sentient;
just as there is the nature of wind in the wind, and the state of being an element in that which was not yet an element.
Just as there is vibration in that which is motionless, and materiality in that which is formless;
just as there is divisibility in that which is indivisible, and finitude in that which is infinite;
just as there is visibility in that which is invisible, and the state of being a creation within creations.
"O Brahmin, best among speakers, tell me this in its proper sequence from the beginning;
for those of limited understanding are awakened only through a systematic progression.
Vasiṣṭha said:
That infinite great space is called the mass of great consciousness;
it is the peaceful, singular, and uniform state, consisting of the dissolution of the knower and the known.
Even at the end of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśvara, and the rest, which is named the Great Dissolution (mahāpralaya).
When the meaning of the word has attained its conventional status, that which remains as pure [consciousness]—
therein, no cause for creation can be logically established,
such as impurity, the seed of forms, or the delusion of *māyā* and *moha*.
It is solely peaceful, utterly transparent, and devoid of beginning or end;
it exists even where space itself is as solid as a stone. And yet, it cannot be said that it does not exist, because it possesses the form of the Knower.
Nor is it appropriate to say that it "exists not," since it is perfectly quiescent.
When self-awareness has reached a hundred yojanas in a mere moment,
the form that exists within that [awareness] is the true form of that state.
In that state, this world-form which is seen vibrating— appearing as if it had a cause, as if its form were formidable, and as if possessed of distinctions—
all that is neither born nor exists, due to the absence of a cause.
It is neither endowed with form, nor is it the world, nor is it joined with duality or unity.
For that which is without cause, existence is not possible here;
who has the power to deny a reality that is itself eternally experienced?
Nor can that which is peaceful, without beginning or end, be the cause of the world—
that formless Brahman [be the cause] of the well-formed, visible world which is not of the nature of Brahman.
Therefore, in that case, the very appearance that has the form of the world is itself that [Brahman].
The sky of consciousness (cidākāśa), abiding within consciousness, shines by itself alone.
The world, consciousness, Brahman, all states of being, non-existence, delusion, and so forth—all is one: unborn, peaceful, non-dual unity, free from affliction.
From the Full, the Full flows forth; in the Full, the Full shines resplendent.
Only the Full has arisen from the Full; in the Full, the Full is established.
It is peaceful, even, devoid of rising and setting, free from form, unborn, and as pure as the sky.
All that is always both existent and non-existent; thus has this primordial Nirvāṇa, whose nature is supreme awakening, been described.
The chapter titled "Description of Nirvāṇa," the two hundred and eleventh chapter.
Vasiṣṭha said: That which is called the world is the pure sky; the existent Brahman is situated in the sky.
This sky shines within the sky; such is the unborn meaning of the word "world."
Through the meanings of words such as "you," "I," and "the world," Brahman exists within Brahman—
tranquil, with a perfectly uniform appearance, both situated and yet not situated,
unborn even though consisting of the ocean, mountains, clouds, and the earth.
This world remains as Brahman, just like the silence of a wooden log.
Established in its own self, it is a seer who is no longer a seer because of the absence of the seen;
it is an agent who is no longer an agent due to the absence of anything to be done, being devoid of instruments.
Therein is neither knower-ness, nor agency, nor insentience, nor the state of being an enjoyer;
there is neither emptiness, nor objectivity, nor even the meaning of negation.
True reality is like the interior of a stone—solid, one, unborn, and all-pervading.
Everything is peaceful, without beginning or end, and one, beyond both injunction and prohibition.
Death and life, truth and untruth, the inauspicious and the auspicious—
all are one, unborn space, just as the web of waves is nothing but water.
The division of consciousness itself undergoes both the state of being the object seen and the state of being the seer;
and this conceptualization is experienced in dreams, cities [of the mind], and the like.
Thus, the world exists within the pure supreme space like a city in a dream.
This shines forth as Brahman alone from the very beginning; therefore, it remains established as such.
Know this all to be of that nature and the self of all, which, like the consciousness of one traveling from one place to another, is unmarked in the interval.
In this very way, the middle state of the sky of consciousness— which is utterly tranquil—
remains established as if it were the world, just as water exists as waves and the like;
that which arises is already arisen, and that which does not arise is unarisen.
Just as there is no distinction in the space between two places for one who knows, so too there is no difference in the interval [between states].
Therefore, indeed, the cause of this creation, like the horn of a hare,
is not perceived at all even when sought with great effort.
That which appears without a cause has not truly appeared; it is of the nature of an error.
How can the reality of an error, which is unreal in form, be asserted?
Indeed, how can there be an effect without a cause?
That which is the vision of a virtuous son for one who has no son is an illusion, not reality.
But that which shines forth without a cause is the manifestation of *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature),
appearing in every form like a mental construction or a city of Gandharvas.

In the transition from one place to another, the body of the Knower shines forth through the intervening moments without ever abandoning its own essential nature, like the transformation of an object.
Consciousness itself shines in the form of objects, and it is subtler than space.
"In this regard, the experienced example is the mountain within a dream or a mental construction.
Rāma said:
"Just as a future great tree exists within the seed of a banyan."
"O Brahman, why then does such creation not exist within the atom?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Wherever there is a seed, there the branch of expansive form may arise."
And that [causal capacity] is produced by causes and expanded by auxiliary factors.
At the dissolution of all beings, what could be the formative seed? Or what would be its auxiliary factor, by virtue of which the world is born?
But as for that supreme Brahman which is utterly tranquil, what conceptualization of form could there be therein?
Even the connection with atomicity does not exist here; so what possibility is there for it to be a seed?
This refers to the cause—the seed—which produces both the real and the unreal.
Because it is impossible, how, by whom, from where, or where could the existence of the world [be established]?
It is also not fitting to say that the world resides within the supreme atom; "Mount Meru resides within a mustard seed" is merely the imagination of the ignorant.
When there is a seed, views of cause and effect proceed;
but for that which is formless, what is the seed, and where is the sequence of the produced and the producer?
Therefore, that which is the supreme reality is this very world as it stands.

Nothing is born here, nor does anything perish. Within the heart, which is the space of consciousness, the pure consciousness perceives the delusion of the world through its own cognitive power— as if impure within the impure, and as pure within the pure.
Its own form alone shines forth, like vibration in the wind;
for us, there are no such things here as the conceptualization of the words and meanings of "creation.
Just as emptiness exists in space, and just as fluidity exists in water.
This pure creation exists within the Self, which consists of nothing other than itself; this world,
whose nature is light and which is profoundly peaceful, is indeed Brahman spread out before us—
without beginning or end, the truth, neither arising nor perishing.
When one goes from one place to another, the body that exists in the interval between moments—
that which is called "the world"— is thus situated within the self as having the nature of space.
Just as movement is in the wind, fluidity in water, and emptiness in space, so is this world.
Likewise, this world appears as non-different from the Self;
indeed, the sky of consciousness is the very sky of the world. Thus, it remains in the Self without blemish, free from the marks of rising and setting.
Within that, everything is but a limb and is therefore non-different from it. Remain in that void which is tranquil like the firmament, where all conceptualization has been cast away.
The two hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Non-dual Unity," by Vasiṣṭha:

Existence and non-existence, grasping and relinquishing, the gross and the subtle, the moving and the unmoving— these were indeed not produced at the very beginning of creation, for they arose without a cause. However,
the formless element of consciousness can never, in any case, be a cause.
The power of the Self is the seed of all forms, just as the earth is for trees;
constantly contemplating its own nature, which consists of creative ideation,
the element of consciousness remains within itself, as if experiencing the process of creation.
Tasting its own nature, the element of consciousness, whose essence is like the sky,
becomes bound by the chatter of creation and dissolution, just as one who is intoxicated is agitated by his own turbulence.
At that time, when everything is unarisen and does not exist at all, yet it is nevertheless perceived.
Then know this to be Brahman alone—equal, peaceful, and equal to the non-existent. It is the sky of consciousness within the very sky of consciousness, like the fluidity of water within water.
Because it possesses the nature of consciousness, it shines forth; by that very shining, it has created the world.
Just as in a dream, the pure consciousness itself arises as the world and shines through its own crystalline transparency, so too does it shine here in the void of creation along with its beginning.
Just as the world becomes a dream through the crystalline transparency of consciousness, so it exists.
In the very same way, this so-called waking state exists as nothing but that space.
For at the initial creation, the dream of consciousness is designated as "waking";
and in the present night, the dream of consciousness is designated as "dream."
Just as the line of waves, having first set in motion upon the rivers, remains established even today exactly as it was, so too is the arrangement of objects in the creation of beings.
Or rather, just as the beauty of the waves has entered into the composition of the rivers' waters.
Likewise, when the existence of the seed of consciousness within the space of consciousness has reached the state of creation,
if there is then an infinite destruction for the deceased, that is indeed the bliss of sleep;
if he returns again to transmigratory existence, that too is indeed a new form of bliss.
If there is fear of evil deeds, that [fear] exists equally both here and in the next world;
therefore, for all beings, death and birth are equal in their resulting pleasure.
Whether it be death or life, they are alike when the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of those two are similar.

Thus, he whose mind is thus rested is said to be "internally cooled. Through the realization of the absolute non-existence of all that is perceivable, there arises a perception in which the object of cognition has been discarded, whether the creation exists or does not exist.

That which is neither an object of thought nor of the nature of consciousness, and which is unperceived even by the minds [of others]—the knowers of that have attained identity with its being; they are peaceful while remaining engaged in worldly activity.
That which is called "the world" is merely the shimmering of consciousness, like the glittering of a crystal.
In the utterly transparent supreme space, how can there be any perception of bondage or liberation?

This world consists merely of the vibration of the sky of consciousness; by its very nature as volition, it is composed solely of being, and is never anywhere composed of earth or other material elements.
Here there is no space, no time, no substance, no action, and no ether;
everything appears as if real—both that which is swollen and that which is not swollen, yet is unreal.
Thus, only the dense mass of ultimate reality shines forth here.
It is neither empty nor non-empty, clearer even than the sky;
it possesses form yet is formless, non-existent yet exceedingly radiant.
It is pure, singular consciousness alone, expansive like a city in a dream.
Thus this Nirvāṇa is spread out; within the sky of consciousness, it is both turbid and yet of an unturbid nature.
It appears as if manifold, yet it has not spread forth anywhere as manifold; it is emptiness, like fluidity in water or like the sky.
This is the chapter titled "The Description of Being Consisting of the Ultimate Reality."
The two hundred and thirteenth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Everywhere, at all times, everything, and in every way, exists within the sky-like consciousness.

It is well that pure emptiness arises everywhere like the sky; where there is consciousness (*vit*), there is the splendor of creation, and even in the non-sky there is consciousness. Since all things consist of consciousness (*cinmaya*), there is nowhere anything that is not consciousness.
Just as the collection of objects such as mountains, or cities and the like, appear in a dream,
so too is the ground of waking objects nothing but the one supreme void that is consciousness alone.
Listen here to this narrative of the stone, which is an elixir for the ears.
Whatever was previously seen by me, whether it be a painting or a natural object— because I have known all that is to be known, my mind was at one time full,
and I desired to abandon this world, which is a dense delusion of worldly activity.

Having attained single-minded devotion to meditation for the sake of long-term rest, having abandoned the state of worldly flux, seeking absolute solitude, and proceeding toward tranquility, I thought this in a certain abode of the immortals: MU 6.213.6: "I have reflected upon this in a certain celestial realm."
Remaining thus, he beholds the various, fragile states of existence within the world.
Indeed, this worldly condition is tasteless and merely beautiful on the surface;
I consider that it never bestows happiness upon anyone, anywhere, or by any means.
These perceptions of the visible world produce agitation within the observer through intense distress and weariness, bestowing both desired and undesired fruits.
What is this that is seen? Or what is it that is perceived? And who am I myself?

Everything is peaceful, unborn, the sky-like expanse, consisting of pure consciousness, and motionless. Therefore, having gone from here to that excellent region which is inaccessible even to all the lords of siddhas, gods, and daityas, one should conceal oneself by means of the Self.
Invisible to all beings, having attained the non-conceptual samādhi,
I dwell in a state that is even, clear, and peaceful, free from sensation. Therefore, what place could there possibly be that has reached absolute emptiness?
Where these five perceptions of external objects are not experienced—
those sounds, forests, waters, and voices that disturb the meditator—
I am unshaken even by them; therefore, for me, mountains are enemies.
The various regions between the lords of mountains were crowded with people, yet all those lands were perilous, infested by the serpents of sensual objects;
the bellies of the ocean-caves were filled with people who were like aquatic creatures.
Like cities filled with citizens engaged in various undertakings,
the shores of mountains and oceans, the cities of the world-protectors,
the mountain peaks, and the caverns of the underworld were all teeming with living beings.
The mountain caves and deep hollows sing with the whistling of the winds, dance with their hands of creepers, and laugh with flowers;
their lotuses sway as their stalks tremble at the touch of the silent fish-munis.
The lakes are indeed tasteless,

resounding only with the whirling of their waters; the windless earth, though deserted, cries out with the rustling of the wind as its banners of grass and dust are stirred by the movement of the breeze.
Therefore, in some remote corner of empty space,
I shall remain here, supporting myself through the blameless application of yoga;
having constructed a small hut there in a certain corner by means of imagination.
"Within that [space], which is as firm as the interior of a diamond, I abide without any mental impressions (vāsanā). Having reflected thus, I went into the sky, pure as a sword-blade;
and there I beheld all of it, with its vast expanse.
In some places there were throngs of wandering *siddhas*, in others thundering clouds;
in some places it was frequented by *vidyādharas*, and in others ruined by the tossing of *yakṣas*;
in some places excellent cities were wandering about, and in others battles had already begun.
In some places it bore liquid water, in others it was filled with dancing yoginīs;
in some places there were cities of Daityas soaring upward, and in others cities of Gandharvas;
in some places the hosts of planets were wandering, and in others it was crowded with stars.
In some places it resounded with the cries of flocks of birds, in some places it was stirred by great winds;
in some places it was enveloped by portents, and in some places it was adorned with auspicious signs.
In some places there were unprecedented throngs of beings, and in some places it was protected by *nāgas*.
In some places it was trampled by the chariot of the sun; in some places it was agitated by the chariot of the sun.
In some places it was scorched by the heat of the sun; in some places it was endowed with the coolness of the moon.
In some places it was unbearable for base people; in some places it was difficult to traverse due to the heat of fire.
In one place there were frantic *vetālas*, in another the terrifying *garuḍas*;
in some places there were clouds like those at the end of an aeon, and in others winds like those at the dissolution of the world.
Then, leaving those hosts of spirits behind, he went further and further away.
I reached a solitary place, empty and exceedingly vast,
where the wind was utterly still, where no living being was encountered even in a dream,
which was free from auspicious or ominous portents, and inaccessible to the lineage of the *siddhas*.
Then I constructed there a hut with a spacious interior,
its walls solid and without gaps, beautiful as a lotus bud,
and enchanting like the belly of the full moon’s orb when its limbs have been gnawed by woodworms.
Adorned with the splendor of the beauty of *kalhāra*, *kunda*, and *mandāra* flowers,
I then conceived in my mind that it was inaccessible to all beings; consequently, I became one who was unapproachable by all creatures.
Seated in the bound lotus posture, with a tranquil mind and observing supreme silence,
he determined his own time for rising at the end of a hundred years;
remaining in non-conceptual meditative absorption, he appeared as if fallen into the seal of sleep.
Pure as the moon, clear as the sky, it is as if carved out from the firmament itself.
When the mind contemplates that which is pure, it perceives it instantly;
or, like the manifestation of a boon granted by a curse, it perceives it after a long time when it has become fully expanded.
Then, after a hundred years, the seed of awakening had taken root in the field of my heart, blossoming through the timely watering [of practice]. Thereupon,
my vital principle (jīva) became fully awakened, possessing the realization of a perfectly enlightened one.
Like sap in a tree during spring when its body has withered through the cold,
that hundred of years passed for me like a mere blink of an eye; for even many transitions of time seem but a moment to those whose minds are focused on a single thought.
Then, the sequence of the sensory faculties expanded outward from me, like the sap of a tree in spring appearing in the form of flowers. Then,
the demon of the thought "I have arrived" spread forth toward me— who was filled with vital breath and possessed a portion of consciousness— as it approached.
Then, surrounded by women who fulfilled his every desire, he entered his palace from somewhere, like the wind that causes the trees at its peak to rise and bow.
The two hundred and fourteenth canto, titled "Vasiṣṭha’s Meditative Absorption" (*vasiṣṭhasamādhāna*), in the *Ākāśamandira*.
Rāma:
O Sage, tell me for the sake of pacifying my delusion: why does the demon of egoism afflict even you, in whom nirvāṇa has already arisen?
Vasiṣṭha said: "In this world, for both the knower of that [Reality] and the ignorant, the persistence of the body cannot occur without the sense of 'I',
for it is not possible for that which is supported to remain without a support."
But hear this distinction here from me, O one of tranquil mind, by which,
through what you have heard, the demon of the sense of "I" shall come to rest within you.
This demon of the sense of "I" has been brought forth by this infant of ignorance.

The end, being non-existent, was merely imagined; therefore, one has risen well [from it]. Even ignorance does not exist at all when examined by an investigator who, like a lamp, does not find its own nature, just as one does not find the nature of darkness.
Just as it is scrutinized, so it dissolves; for here, when ignorance is thus investigated, the demoness of nescience vanishes. While ignorance is manifesting, this eternal nescience arises.
The Yakṣī, whose nature is the delusion of the intellect, is indeed bodiless, just as [darkness] is at night.
When creation exists, there is the possibility of ignorance; it never exists when it does not exist.
Just as when a second moon exists, a second rabbit-marked [moon] is perceived.
This creation, however, because it is unborn, does not exist as something known by the ignorant;
it is not born due to the absence of a cause, being like a tree in the sky from the very beginning within the interior of the sheath of the supreme ether, which is free from affliction.
What indeed could be the cause for the perception of earth and so forth?
It is said that from the seed as the cause, the effect—the sprout—is born;
but where even the seed does not exist, how could the sprout arise there?
Without a cause, an effect indeed cannot arise;
when, by whom, or where in the sky has a manifest tree ever been seen?
Or if branches and such are seen in the sky through mental construction (saṅkalpa), [it is likewise unreal].
That volition has become such, yet here there is no substantiality of objects.

This very creation which is experienced at the beginning of the world within the space of consciousness is like the void of space appearing in an empty well— a creation whose persistence is unrestrained.
The space of consciousness alone shines as suchness within itself;
its very nature, called "creation," is consciousness because of its sentience, and that is the Lord.
Here, the creation experienced every day in a dream serves as the illustration.
Self-awareness itself flashes forth in a dream in the form of mountains and cities. Just as the nature of consciousness exists for you here like a creation in a dream,
so too did it previously appear in the great void as a creation where there was no creation.
The unknowable perception, pure, unborn, and undecaying, shines forth;
that which exists at the beginning of creation, without beginning or end—that very creation remains for you.
Here there is no creation, nor is this sphere composed of the collection of elements such as earth and the rest.
Everything is peaceful and without support; Brahman alone abides in Brahman.
That Brahman, whose self is all-potent, appears in whatever manner it shines forth;
without ever abandoning its own pure form, it becomes exactly like that.
Just as a dream-city for a living being is a manifestation of pure consciousness alone,
so too is the creation at the beginning of creation a manifestation of pure, stainless consciousness alone.
That which is situated within the sky of consciousness in the clear, supreme sky of consciousness—
"This creation is indeed his own nature," thus it was contemplated by him alone.
The intense manifestation of the stages of the object,
the subject, and the act of being, and everything else— all is but the pure sky of consciousness, established within itself by itself.
This being the case, whence is creation, whence is ignorance, and where is lack of knowledge?
Brahman is entirely peaceful and solid; where do egoism and the like reside?
This very pacification of the sense of "I" has been described to you.
The sense of "I," once fully understood, subsides like a demon.
When I have thus fully understood this entire sense of "I," then,
even though it still exists, it is as fruitless to me as an autumn cloud.

"Just as a painted fire is known to be fruitless when applied to things that can be burned, so too the creation and so forth of the sense of 'I' (ahaṃbhāva), once understood, shall reach fruitlessness. Thus, if there is equanimity toward the abandonment and the attachment to this "I-making" (ahaṃkṛti), [then one is liberated].
Then my state is like that of space within space—whether in creation or non-creation.
There is neither "I-ness" for me, nor is there "mine-ness" in the absence of "I-ness.
Therefore, know this to be the cloudless expanse of consciousness alone.

For those who possess the realization that "as it is for me, so it is for others," there is no delusion of the sense of "I," just as there is no [delusion of] fire-nature in a variegated fire. There is the certainty: "I do not exist, nor does another exist; or rather, everything exists."
Engage in your natural worldly conduct, yet remain like a stone in its silence.
Abide for a long time with a form as clear as the expanse of space, as if bodiless, with all objective states negated.
Indeed, from the very beginning until today, everything is nothing but consciousness; there is no visible world, for thus everything without exception is Śiva.
The two hundred and fifteenth canto, titled "The Investigation of the Ego by One Who Has Known What Is to Be Known," [ends]. Rama:
"Aha! O Blessed One, for our prosperity, you have once again proclaimed a vision that is vast, noble, expansive, stainless, and immovable—
omnipresent in every way, at all times, for everyone, everything, everywhere, and bestowing all things."
"It is indeed so"—this is the truth, established through equal experience.
"O Brahmin, I have this doubt; please dispel it.
O Blessed One, what is this that is called the 'Narrative of the Stone'?"
Vasiṣṭha:
To establish that everything exists everywhere and at all times,
I relate this illustration of the story of the stone to you.

It is demonstrated that even within the hollow of a stone whose body is entirely solid and without gaps, there exist thousands of creations; tell me how this is so. Within this great elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*), it does not abandon its own emptiness.
"It is being demonstrated that one may say, 'There are thousands of creations.
Rāma said:
'O Sage, if it is said that there are floods of creations upon walls and other such surfaces,'"
Why then is it not shown that the floods of creation shine there in the void?
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, all this which is primary has been described by me to you in its entirety.
This creation which is perceived is indeed like space situated within space;
for from the very beginning it was never produced, and even now it does not exist.
This visible world that appears is Brahman, abiding in Brahman.
There is not even an atom of earth that is not filled with creations;
nor do creations exist anywhere else, for that is simply the ether of Brahman.
There is not even an atom of water that is not filled with creations.
And those creations do not exist anywhere; that is merely the space of Brahman.
There is not even an atom of light that is not filled with creations;
nor do creations exist anywhere—that is merely the space of Brahman.
There is not even an atom of air that is not rendered without interstice by creations;
nor do those creations exist anywhere—that is merely the void of Brahman.
There is not even an atom of space that is not rendered without interstice by creations.
Nowhere do creations exist; that is merely the space of Brahman. There is no state of the great elements that is not permeated by creations;
nowhere do creations exist—they are merely the space of Brahman.
There is not even an atom that is a part of a living being which is not filled with creations;
nor do those creations exist anywhere—this is simply the void of Brahman.
There is not even an atom among mountains that is not densely packed with creations.
Nowhere do creations exist; that is merely the space of Brahman (brahmakha).
There is not even an atom of Brahman that is not filled with creations;
nor do those creations exist anywhere—that is merely the space of Brahman.
In the creations, there is not even an atom that is not the Self which is eternally Brahman;
thus, creation is indeed Brahman, and Brahman is indeed the state of creation—there is only a difference in words, not in reality.
Creation itself is the Supreme Brahman, and the Supreme Brahman itself is the state of creation.
There is not even the slightest duality here, just as there is none between fire and the heat of the sun.
These views expressed in such sentences as "these are the creations" and "this is Brahman" appear devoid of actual meaning, like the sound of wood being split.
Where there is not even the slightest duality or unity,
how and for whom could the meanings of words such as "creation" or "Brahman" appear to you?
This is the one, peaceful, beginningless and endless, pure, and untainted reality.
Even for one who engages in worldly activity, O dear one, the silence of the wise is as solid as a stone.
Thus, the entirety of nirvāṇa is like the sky, and the visible world—yourself, me, the masses of mountains, the gods, and the demons—is likewise.
Behold this world, my dear, as being exactly like the web of worldly transactions that appears within the mind of another being in a dream.
The two hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Nature of Brahman as Creation," [from] the Rāmāyaṇa.
Immediately thereafter, O Sage, what occurred during the hundred years while you were awakened from meditation within the hollow of the chamber of the vault of the sky? Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, having awakened from that meditation, I heard a sound there— soft,
with indistinct syllables, and heart-pleasing; it was neither from musical instruments nor from song,
but soft and sweet as if arising from the very nature of a woman.
Because my limbs were so small, that speech of mine was not resonant;
it took the form of the humming of a bee, pleasing like the vibration of a lute-string,
neither weeping nor recitation, but sounding like the hollow of a bamboo flute.
Having heard that, I immediately reflected upon it there; then,
looking with astonishment toward the ten directions for the source of the sound,
I saw this vast expanse of space, devoid of the paths where *siddhas* travel.
That portion is situated at a distance of hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*.
How, then, could there be the occurrence of such a sound here?
Even though I look with great effort, I do not perceive any source for this sound.
"This infinite space before me is empty and stainless;
though one searches here with effort for what has come to be, it is not seen. Having thought thus, I looked again and again.
When I did not see Śabdeśvara, I then thought this:
"Having become space itself, I have attained oneness with space;
within the treasury of space, I produce the objects of sound, which is the quality of space."
Having established this body-space here in its natural state through meditation,
I shall attain oneness with the space of consciousness by means of that space, like water merging with water.
Having thought thus, I sat in the lotus posture to cast off the body.
In order to establish myself in meditative absorption, I closed my eyes once more;
having abandoned both external sensory contacts and those internal,
I became, within the space of the mind, one whose nature consists of the vibration of pure consciousness.

Gradually abandoning even that, I reached the state of the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*); I became the sky of consciousness, the single mirror for the web of the world. Then, by that very nature, I attained oneness with the elemental ether.
He has merged like water with water, or fragrance with fragrance.
Then he becomes the great space, infinite and all-pervading;
though formless and without support, he has become the support of all objects.
As many as there are multitudes of the three worlds and hundreds of transmigrations,
therein I behold even countless hundreds of thousands of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*),
mutually unseen and pure voids.
Various activities and deliberations are indeed empty of one another,
like the dream-forms of sleeping men occurring at the same time;
though they involve great undertakings, they are unseen and mutually void.
Those being born perish; those growing do so in great numbers;
those existing, those past, and all those yet to be, as well as the various mental states, the great walls, and the cavities, [all likewise perish].
In the mind alone, various kingdoms have been created by diverse people—
kingdoms that are unobstructed in form, as well as those with a single obstruction,
those with five obstructions, and those with six or one obstruction.
There are mandalas with ten enclosures, sixteen enclosures,
twenty-four enclosures, and thirty-six enclosures; they are empty, yet filled with the elements, and composed of the five elements.
There are elements consisting of one earth and so forth, as well as those consisting of four earths and so forth;
others consist of three earths and so forth, and yet others consist of two earths and so forth;
likewise, there are seven great elements, and those composed of a single species.
But such worlds as these are contrary to the expansive experience of one like you;
they are perpetually shrouded in darkness and devoid of the sun and other luminaries.
Likewise, their creations are closed off and encompassed by a single lord.
O Mistress of beings with diverse characteristics, they possess various modes of conduct;
they possess conventions and behaviors handed down through a lineage of those blind from birth,
and likewise they are eternally luminous and composed of blazing fire.
