Likewise, filled solely with water and consisting solely of wind,
they remain motionless in the supreme ether and flow there perpetually;
being born, they nourish themselves, and once fully nourished, they flourish on all sides.

Others move horizontally, consisting of the creation of the mute; some consist solely of the creation of gods, others consist solely of men; some consist of hosts of *daityas*, and others are filled with gaps of worms.
Within each other, and within those [layers], and within their own sheaths, down to the subtle atom—
those things born and those being born are like the layers of a plantain tree;
they are not seen by one another, nor indeed experienced by one another.
Even though they are vast, the various and endless nets of dreams belonging to the soldiers are essentially of the nature of the clear sky;
they function independently of one another and do not exist in dependence upon each other.
And there are mutual, mutually infinite scriptures;
those which have various mutual arrangements, and those which are mutually distinct from one another;
mutual worlds of the hereafter, and mutually established cities of the perfected ones.
The great elements are of one kind, and the mountains are of another;
they are inaccessible and vast, possessing incongruous forms, yet they are described by those such as me for the sake of the experience and inquiry of those like you.
Like atoms being carried along within the solar orb of consciousness,
they become various nets of rays and earrings within the sky of ultimate splendor;
having repeatedly become this and that, they manifest in abundance.
Some became exactly like that, like forest leaves;
others there were half-like, and others even similar;
for some time, O sinless one, others were very similar.
Other fruits, whose time of ripening is unknown, grow spontaneously by the power of chance; they flourish and remain firmly established as infinite fruits of the great tree of ultimate reality.
They are indeed neither different nor non-different from that, for they are composed of that very essence.
Some are of short kalpas, some of long kalpas;
others are manifold and indefinite, while some are manifold and definite.
Those nets of emptiness, within the treasury of the supreme ether,
remain uncomprehended for a long time; they are firm for one whose faults are not recognized,
and are thoroughly enveloped by hundreds of oceans, suns, skies, and Meru mountains.
In the void of the wonder of consciousness, the nets of dreams appear turbidly;
because experience is of the nature of delusion and because there is an absence of causes,
earth and the other elements— which have no cause— exist and yet do not exist at all.
Like the abundance of water in a mirage or like the appearance of two moons in the sky,
things that have come into being are not real, even though they appear real through experience;
they manifest profusely within the very sky of the mind's conceptualization.
Driven by the winds of latent impressions and pierced by their own actions,
the gnats that are the gods and asuras are like fruits full of juice on the udumbara tree of space, swaying in the breezes.
For one whose nature is noble, who is the initiator of all undertakings,
and who is a child of the pure reality of consciousness, the cities of conceptual construction in the sky—
such as "you," "I," "he," and "this"— are indeed rendered utterly immovable by the intellect.
And like clay toys brought to perfection by the brilliance of the sun,
they were sustained by a destiny full of flavor and eternally satisfied,
just as forests of fierce fruit are graced by a streak of the essence of spring.
The great agents are non-agents, and the sense-voids are not even created;
their forms are spontaneously perfected and are indeed fashioned by the sky of consciousness alone.
They consist of the ultimate reality itself, yet they arise as if distinct from it.
Those very things which were unobtained are obtained, and those which were always non-existent are indeed existent.
The fourteen, ten, one, and other such classes of elemental beings—
those very same ones are within, while others and yet others are outside.
Even hells, heavens, the underworld, enemies, and friends—
consisting as they do of great undertakings— are empty from the perspective of ultimate reality,
like the waters of the ocean of milk which everywhere have oil for their essence.
Fragile as waves, both internally and externally subject to transformation,
and consisting of nothing but mere appearances, these rays of the sun that is the Self arise spontaneously from it,
like the vibrations of the wind.
The forms of trees are like those of leaves, intellect, ego, and mind;
though they do not exist, they appear as non-existent, just as a dream belongs to men who are elsewhere.
[They dwell] upon the pillows of the conceptual constructs of the Purāṇas, the Vedas, and established doctrines.
Deeply asleep in dense slumber, they bear the likeness of corpses.
In the great forest of ultimate reality, within the sky fashioned by the Gandharva of consciousness,
there are deep, secret houses illuminated by the lamps of the sun.
In the infinite sky, as worlds were being born and, without cause, falling apart,
I then beheld those worlds like the clusters of hair seen by one with cataracts.
This is the chapter titled "The Description of the Web of the World."
The two hundred and seventeenth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, wandering about in such a state and reflecting deeply, I roamed all around.
Having for a long time entered into the state of the unobstructed space of consciousness,
I later heard that sound resembling the resonance of a lute;
gradually it became distinct in its syllables, and from that it attained the form of an Āryā verse.
With my gaze following the direction from which the sound came, I beheld a woman whose side illuminated the sky with a radiance like a flow of molten gold;
her garlands and garments were swaying, and her eyes were fringed by disheveled curls.
Another woman, with her braided hair swaying, appeared like the Goddess Śrī herself arrived; her limbs were as fair as gold, she possessed the bloom of fresh youth,
and she was as beautiful in every limb as a forest goddess, exuding fragrance.
She, whose face was like the full moon, who smiled with a profusion of flowers,
whose countenance was unrestrained by youth, and who was graced with eyes like long-lashed lashes;
she whose abode was the expanse of the sky, as beautiful as the rays of the moon.
“Adorned with a string of pearls, lovely, and following after me—
this noble lady, sweet-voiced and gentle-smiling, recited this Āryā verse softly at my side. (MU 6.217.7–8)

"I revere you alone, O Sage, as the tree on the bank that provides support for those who are being deluded in the river of worldly existence— a stream of animal-like beings whose consciousness is emptied by what is falsely proclaimed.
Having heard this, I looked toward her, whose voice was so sweetly spoken.
"What is the use of this woman? he thought, and having disregarded her, he departed.
Then, beholding that illusion consisting of the entire multitude of worlds, I was struck with wonder;
disregarding it as well, I prepared to roam through the sky.
Then, having completely cast aside that anxiety caused by her, I, whose nature is space, set about contemplating the world-illusion as it abides in the sky; meanwhile,
all those worlds remained as intensely formidable as before within that void.
Just as it is empty in a dream, so it is in the narration of one's mental constructions.
They never see or hear anything whatsoever, nor do they ever perceive those beings born during the Kalpas and Mahākalpas as being together with one another.
[He saw] the Puṣkarāvarta clouds in their state of madness, the winds of calamity that had gone wild;
the pavilions of Brahmā shattered by the crashing of great mountain peaks;
and the abodes of Aiḍabiḍa bursting apart from the explosions of the blazing fire at the end of the aeon.
[He saw] the twelve suns, whose discs were intensely hot and fierce;
[hearses] the gurgling sounds of the widespread wailing from the hosts of falling celestial cities;
and [beholds] the formidable swallowing of the ranges of mountain ridges, such as Meru and others, as they resound.
[He saw] the great oceans of the sky agitated by the massive turbulence of their own downfall, resounding with the crackling *paṭa-paṭa* sounds of the blazing fires at the end of the eon,
and harsh with the gurgling cries from the dwellings of gods, asuras, and men.
When the great floods of the seven oceans have filled the abodes of the sun and the moon,
all the worlds do not perceive one another during the end of the aeon,
like those sleeping in a single chamber who, in a dream, experience the tumult of battle.

There, thousands of Rudras and hundreds of millions of Brahmās were seen by me, as well as hundreds of thousands of Viṣṇūs and vast multitudes of Kalpas. There, in certain places where there was no sun, on a ground devoid of day and night,
At the end of the years of the non-conceptual age (*akalpa-yuga*), there is the destruction and arising of the cosmic arrays (*jagad-vyūha*).
In consciousness (*citi*) everything exists, by consciousness everything is perceived; consciousness is everything, and everywhere consciousness is present.
Consciousness is the singular essence of all—this entire reality was seen by me therein.
If you say, "You are something," that is not so at all, my dear;
for she is emptier than space, yet she is not a mere nothingness.
Thus, this very space shines forth, designated as the "world."
For by that very sound-space, all is indeed the supreme space.
This perception of the visible is an illusion, like the blossoms on a tree in the sky;
I experienced there that it is nothing but a limb of the sky of consciousness.

In that infinite [reality], which is of the single nature of the space of consciousness, all-pervasive and consisting of pure awareness, this was experienced by me as being devoid of conceptual construction:
"The web of the world is the void of Brahman; the ten directions are the void of Brahman."

O lords of sages, within that Brahma-ether— wherein exist the divisions of time, space, substance, action, and so forth— I have seen, throughout one hundred and fifty cycles of worldly existence, those supreme sons of Brahmā named Vasiṣṭha who were like me.
All seventy-two Tretā ages, together with their Rāghavas,
were seen there; likewise, a hundred Kṛta ages and a hundred Dvāpara ages were seen through the emergence of their various divisions,
as well as those various stages of creation.
If, through awakening, that single, all-pervading Brahman-sky is perceived as utterly transparent, then no differentiation exists within Brahman; rather, this world is indeed Brahman.
That Brahman alone—unborn, without beginning or end—is everything, including you, me, and so forth.
That which is like the silence of a stone, unuttered,
yet which appears as a certain kind of luminous form— that is remembered as Brahman, the world.
It shines as the very existence of consciousness itself in the non-objectifying space of consciousness, appearing in the form of the world.
Formless within the formless, it resembles the experience of a dream.
Brahman is not other than the Self; everything has the nature of mere appearance.
Like light, its illumination neither acts nor does not act.
In those hundreds of thousands of worlds, O Rāma,
heat is indeed experienced there as clusters of moons, and the suns possess cool forms;
beings perceive things in darkness, but they do not perceive them in light.
The behaviors of the owl are like its own cry;
by virtue they perish here, yet by their sins they go to heaven.
They live by eating poison and die by eating nectar.
In whatever manner consciousness perceives, or in whatever way it arises spontaneously, so does that object—whether real or unreal—immediately attain clarity; for it is indeed real.
This is seen through the mass of roots appearing in the form of branches by those who shine like diamonds.
The forest sways in the sky with trees rich in flowers and leaves.
The sands, being pressed, exude an oily essence;
and from the surfaces of the stone slabs, lotuses arise in abundance.
In wood, stone, and on walls, restless statues,
together with the women of the house, sing and converse;
they hold up clouds aloft like great banners.
Every year, different kinds of fruits arise upon that mountain;
due to the fixed arrangement of various limbs,
all beings move about on the ground with their heads.
Some worlds below the three worlds are devoid of both treatises and Vedas, utterly lacking in dharma, acting on mere whim like animals;
some are devoid of the experience of desire, being without any female kind.
They were filled with beings whose hearts were completely parched, as if made of stone;
some were like those who subsist on air, possessing jewels and stones,
while others were ignorant of worldly objects, free from greed, and devoid of desire.
In some cases, one perceives and attains the self individually, and not otherwise;
for although the world consists of many beings, it is also a single being.
Just as it is with the nails, hair, and so forth, so too is its existence elsewhere.
One should cultivate the realization that the self of all beings is one with one's own self.
(MU 6.217.49) In some places, there is only a vast void, infinite, shoreless, and boundless;
yet even at the end of that which our consciousness does not reach, the world exists once again. (MU 6.217.50)
Some possess intellects that are utterly incapable of perceiving the meaning of the word "liberation" regarding the Buddhas; they are like a multitude of beings entirely composed of wooden machinery,
devoid of the circle of the stars and lacking the calculation of time.
Some hosts of spirits possess the essence of silent signs;
others are entirely devoid of the perception of visual forms or sounds,
like the futile brilliance of the sun’s heat— such was his singular reflection regarding these beings.
Some [beings] lack the consciousness of smell and are deprived of the fragrance of objects; some are mute because sound is useless to them and are devoid of hearing;
and some are utterly speechless because they lack the consciousness of speech.
Because they are devoid of the perception of touch, some parts are like mere stones; yet others, though consisting of pure consciousness alone, are seen to be engaged in worldly activity,
while still others are eternally ungraspable, like *piśācas*.

Some worlds there, consisting of earth, are fixed as single units and remain as solid masses; others, having the nature of space, shine forth in that void. Some are filled with water, and some are filled with fire.
The worlds, whose nature is space, shine there in the void; meanwhile,
other embodied beings remain within those [worlds] which are filled with the single foundation of the earth,
like frogs in the hollow of a stone or insects in the belly of the earth.
In other worlds entirely filled with water— where there is no ocean, earth, forest, or mountain— other beings wander constantly like fierce fish;
while in others entirely filled with fire, even those devoid of water and the like.
The elements, consisting of fire alone, throb intensely like a flame;
in others, though filled with air, the elements— even when they have ceased—
throb with limbs made of mere wind, like the wind from an *arjuna* tree.

In other creations, there exist living beings whose bodies consist of nothing but space and who themselves are of the nature of space; they conduct themselves in invisibility. Likewise, there are those falling into the netherworlds, those leaping into the sky, those remaining stationary, and others intent on wandering through the quarters of the horizon.
What indeed is there in the various worlds that has not been seen by me among the flickering bubbles in the ocean of the manifest?
The Description of the Multitude of Worlds; the two hundred and eighteenth canto.
Vasiṣṭha: Within the space of consciousness, these living beings flash forth like waves of water within the water, because they possess consciousness; they are none other than our own minds.
Those very minds of ours have become the forms of the vast sky;
those infinite worlds have themselves spontaneously come into being all around.
Rāma said:
When all the hosts of beings have attained liberation at the end of the great kalpa,
how and for whom does the consciousness of creation arise again?
Vasiṣṭha said:

Listen now to how this world is experienced again when, at the end of the great dissolution, after the destruction of the earth, water, wind, fire, and ether without exception, and when all beings from Brahmā down to the immovable have been liberated and transformed, [the world arises] just as it is perceived here.
That which is inexpressible, the solid mass of ultimate reality, pure consciousness— what the sages call Brahman— of that, this world is the heart; therefore, it is indeed non-different from it,
and He alone is the Lord.
Thus, it perceives as if its own heart and nature were the world;
yet the world exists only as a mental diversion, not in a real sense.
Thus we perceive something while investigating.
Therefore, what indeed perishes and what indeed is born?
Just as the supreme cause is indestructible, so too is that heart.
It is indeed indestructible;
and the great eons (*mahākalpa*) and so forth are merely its constituent parts.
In this case, mere non-comprehension leads only to weariness;
yet even that, when investigated, is simply not found.
Therefore, nothing whatsoever ever perishes anywhere, nor does anything ever arise; Brahman alone remains—tranquil, visible, and unborn.
That pure existence consisting of consciousness alone, which exists even in a space no larger than a thousandth part of an atom, [is this].
Indeed, this world is the body of that Great Consciousness;
how could it perish while she remains unperished? And she herself does not perish.
Just as the heart of consciousness appears in a dream in the form of the world, so too does this world appear within her.
In that very same way, the self of space alone has shone forth since the beginning of creation.
Creation is a part of the space of consciousness; these states of creation are its dissolutions and its arisings.
Since everything is space, what is perishable and what is imperishable?
For this supreme consciousness is indeed uncuttable, unburnable, un-dryable, and undissoluble; it is invisible to those who do not know it.
That which is its heart becomes that very thing.
Just as that [Self] is neither born nor destroyed, so too this experience of the world and so forth existing within it is neither born nor destroyed;
it merely, through the power of recollection and forgetfulness, seems to imagine the occurrence and non-occurrence of experiences by way of its own essential nature.
Whatever reality has a certain nature, it does not perish without that [nature] being destroyed;
therefore, know that the visible world, whose nature is Brahman, is imperishable like Brahman itself.
Great dissolutions are merely its constituent parts.
In the supreme void of pure consciousness alone, how could there be existence or non-existence?
How could there be the modifications of being and so forth, since these are absent in the void? O Rāma, the great kalpas and other such entities, as well as these worlds, [are likewise unreal].
In this very Brahman, which is of the nature of Brahman, consciousness is established.
Having set aside the visible world and conceived it as mere pure consciousness under its control,
one attains that by which one was fashioned— just as one might indeed strike down a spirit with the very thing that created it.

Just as the branches, fruits, shoots, flowers, and so forth are the parts (*avayava*) of a tree which is a whole (*avayavin*), so too [the following] are the [apparent] attributes of that which is the ultimate reality— a mass of space, transparent in form, and indefinable: namely, dissolution and great dissolution, destruction and emergence, existence and non-existence, pleasure and pain, birth and death, having form and being formless, and so on.
"The parts are such that,
just as this whole is indestructible and indefinable, so too are they.
Whether the parts and the whole are visible or invisible," (MU 6.218.19).
Between these two, which are of one essence, there is never any difference whatsoever.
For they are not distinct from its own essential nature;
just as the root is part of a tree, so too [are they] of that which is the solid mass of ultimate reality.
In some places it is consciousness;

in some places the trunk of creation; in some places the branches that are the other worlds; in some places the limbs that are the established orders; in some places the sprouts that are the categories of existence;
in some places the flower that is light; and in some places...
In some places it is the blackness of darkness; in some places the hollows of the sky; in some places the thickets of the dissolution; in some places the ankle-bones of the great dissolution;
in some places clusters of Hari, Hara, and other deities; and in some places the skin of dullness.
Thus, this formless thing, which is indeed of the nature of space, remains inseparable from its own nature within the Brahman that is the self of consciousness—Brahman being similar to itself.
From this [perspective] there is existence, from this non-existence; from this creation, from this destruction.
"Experiencing only its own nature, it remains as firm as the mountain Brahmācala.
Likewise, my dear, there are no passions whatsoever in the supreme space of Brahman,
just as there are no poisonous creepers upon the orb of the moon."
In the stainless supreme space, where could there be the taints of existence and non-existence?
Where could there be the conceptions of beginning, middle, and end, or the delusion of other worlds?
Only ignorance alone has arisen here as a defect.
That ignorance subsides entirely through the contemplation of its transformation;
it perishes when grasped by the awakening of pure cognition,
just as a lamp is extinguished by the very wind that caused it to flare up.
Ignorance, having been fully understood, is realized as never having existed at all; one understands that everything is indeed Brahman, which is neither bound nor liberated.
O Rāma, for it is through such awakening that liberation is said to be attained by means of one's own self-awareness.
Reflecting thus, one attains [liberation]; there is no doubt in this matter.

Having seen here that this web of the world is beginningless, unborn, and is Brahman appearing in this way, and perceiving through the vision of inquiry the eightfold lordship as a mere blade of grass within oneself, the individual soul (jīva) abides in the Self.
The two hundred and nineteenth canto, titled "The Realization of the Unity of the World and Space," [from] Rāma.
"That which was seen by you at that time with your body of the sky of consciousness—
how much more so when it was situated in only one part [of that space], or even while wandering in the atmosphere?
Vasiṣṭha said:
At that time, I was indeed the perfected, infinite Self, all-pervading like space.
In that state, what kind of going and coming could there possibly be?
I did not consist of staying in one place, nor did I possess the nature of motion.
Then, by him, this was seen within himself as being in the very void:
"Just as you perceive the limbs of the body from head to foot,
so too have I seen this with the eye of consciousness, which is itself eyeless."
Then, for that one whose nature is the stainless sky of consciousness, who is formless and established as partless, those worlds became like a network of limbs;
yet, just as space, they neither dissolved nor lost their substantiality.
In this matter, the proof for you is the delusion of the world seen in a dream.
The visible world experienced in a dream is nothing at all; it is merely space.
Just as a tree perceives its own leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth with the eye of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), so too have I seen this.
Just as the ocean, whose nature is infinite, knows all aquatic creatures,
as well as its waves, whirlpools, and foam, so too have I understood this;
just as the whole knows its own parts within itself.
"Having realized that these creations are not other than myself,
O Rāma, even now— having attained the singleness of pure awareness— I see those same creations within my body, in space, on mountains, in water, and on land."
Having attained oneness with pure awareness, he knows that this space which is before us— both within and without the house— is filled with the multitude of worlds,
just as water knows its own fluidity and ice knows its own coldness.
Just as the wind perceives its own vibration, so does one of pure intellect perceive this. O Rāma, whoever possesses a discriminating self and has attained oneness with pure consciousness,
that very person, whose singular self consists of this [pure state], perceives his own Self in such a manner.
When this view has matured, no cognition of a knower, a knowing,
or a known arises at all, because there is only the single nature of consciousness;
just as for one standing on a mountain peak, divine vision perceives objects extending for tens of millions of leagues.
"I have realized that I know entities both externally and internally; just as one who knows the location of treasures knows the earth's surface and the entities such as those treasures,
so too have I realized that which is not other than the Self, which is the visible."
Rāma:
O Brahmin, since the lotus-eyed one experiences such feelings toward you,
tell me, what did that beloved do— she who is so skilled in reciting the scriptures?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Reciting that very same noble verse and likewise filled with conciliation,
she stood near me with a body of light, like a goddess stationed in the sky.
Just as I am of the nature of space, so too is she of the nature of emptiness;
therefore, that woman was not seen by me with my former body.
I am the self whose form is space, and she has a body consisting of nothing but the void.
"The web of the world was then situated there as nothing but space.
Rāma said:
"Through the body, its postures, the organs of action, effort, and the vital breaths..."

“From where do words arise with their phonemes, and from where does such a form [arise] for those whose nature is like space? From where do color-form, light, and mental attention arise? O Blessed One, tell me the certain conclusion regarding that for one who has proceeded in such a manner.”
Vasiṣṭha: Just as forms, perceptions, and mental activities, as well as sounds, recitations, and words,
exist in the sky during a dream, so too do they exist there in the ether.
Through form, light, and mental attention, those [objects] arise in the dream within the sky of consciousness itself;
just as they arise, so too does that which is seen therein abide as having the nature of space.
Not only is that seen object so, but even we who are your objects are likewise.
And this entire world is just like the clear sky; for us, it is exactly so.
The great ultimate element, whose nature is consciousness free from any object of knowledge, shines forth by itself in this very way—this is the certainty regarding its own inherent nature.
What proof do you have for the existence of the body, its locations, and its organs?
Just as they [the gods] possess bodies and so forth, so too does this [our world] exist for us.
Just as that is, so is this; just as this is, so is that.
The non-existent has become as if existent, and the existent remains as if non-existent.
Just as in a dream the sky appears as the earth, oceans, mountains, and the activities of living beings,
so too are "I," "you," "she," and "this"— all are likewise the sky.
Just as in a dream, the clamor of battle and the coming and going of men are experienced even though they do not exist, so too are the multitudes of cyclic existence.
If you say that the splendor seen in a dream is [unreal], why then is this [the world] inconsistent?
This is inexpressible, for there is no other cause for the persistence of experience.
To the questioner who asks, "How is a dream perceived?", it is replied:
"Insofar as you see it"—this alone is the cause here, and nothing else.
From the very beginning of the first creation, the Virāj-self shines like a being in a dream within the void;
it is the supreme-non-supreme space within space itself.
I employ the word "dream" for the sake of your understanding.
But this visible world is neither existent nor non-existent; it is not a dream, but Brahman alone.
Then, O Raghava, that beloved woman, having made me one with her consciousness through our union, appeared in visible form and asked me this.
Just as worldly interaction arises in a dream with those born of the dream,
so too did my interaction with her arise at that time.
Just as this worldly interaction is like a dream, it is indeed nothing but empty space.

In the same way, know this world and the sky to be my very self. Just as the form of the world in a dream is nothing but space, so too is this world; the great dream called waking is the emergence of the void at the beginning of creation.
This expansive world is a dream, or rather nothing at all, or simply the pure void; it is established as the void of mere non-existence, consisting solely of the nature of consciousness.
There exists a perceiver of this dream who possesses form, such as yourself and others.

But the witness of this dream-creation is the stainless sky of consciousness itself by its own nature. Just as the stainless sky is the seer, so too the visible world, appearing within that vision in the form of a dream, shines forth intensely; therefore, the sky remains stainless.
A dream that flashes forth spontaneously within the heart from the formless sky of consciousness—
how could there be creation for it, and how could it possess form?
That which is the dream-world is merely the void of the one who possesses form.
How is it that the dream-creation of the formless sky of consciousness is not [itself] empty?
The sky of consciousness, without any collection of material causes and even without a wall,
perceives this uncreated dream of the world as if it were created.
Though the pavilion of creation, with its windows of the senses, was fashioned by the Brahmin Brahmā within the void using the soft clay of the space of consciousness, it was not truly created.
For the wise one who knows that there is neither agency nor worlds, neither the state of being an enjoyer nor non-existence, and that nothing at all exists, [remains as he is].
Adopting the silence of a stone, conduct yourself according to the natural flow of events; let the body remain here or not.
Thus ends the two hundred and twentieth canto, titled "The Unity of the World."
Rāma:
How could there have been conversation with that woman, whose body was in the form of an ass?
How were the phonemes *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and so forth, uttered therein?
Now, if you say it is like a dream, then I ask this of you as well:
from where do the phonemes *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and so forth, arise in a dream?
Vasiṣṭha said:
In dreams, the phonemes of one's own body— such as *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*,
and so forth— never arise at all, just like those of corpses;
for if there were the utterance of phonemes anywhere, the meaning would then become manifest.
The person lying awake by one's side would have experienced that [dream] while dreaming;
therefore, nothing in dreams is real—that is merely an illusion. It is simply the manifestation of the space of pure consciousness, arising by its own nature within the void.

Just as the sky of consciousness appears as if it has attained the state of the moon, blackness, a tree, a stone, or a song, so too does it appear as the letters *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and so forth. That which is called the manifestation of the sky of consciousness is indeed what is experienced in a dream.
Know that space alone is the manifestation of the sky, and nothing else.
Just as a dream exists, so does this waking state stand at the beginning;
just as this world is, so too is that space which is itself without form.
Then that beautiful consciousness shines so cleverly that this very thing,
as it has always been, appears as if it were a true, stable, and throbbing reality.
Rāma:
"Bhagavān, this is indeed a dream; how then does it exist as the waking state? Tell me, how has that which is unreal attained the appearance of reality? Vasiṣṭha replied:
Listen: how can there be worlds that consist merely of dreams?
They are neither other than this, nor are they real, nor do they remain stable or enduring;
they are like seeds experienced within the sky as if in a heap of seeds.
Those very same things are both different from one another and identical, yet not identical;
within each, others arise in the same way,
many and diverse, unseen by one another.
All of them do not perceive anything at all of one another;
like inert things gathered into a single heap, they even touch like seeds.
Because their nature is that of space, they do not perceive each other’s contact.
Moreover, their conscious forms remain continuous as if asleep;
like those who are asleep yet engage in the conduct and activities of the web of the dream-world,
the Asuras, though slain by the gods, persist within that dream-world.
Due to ignorance they have not attained liberation; due to dullness they have not become inert;
yet, apart from their existence within the world of a dream, how can they be possessed of bodies? They are as if asleep, engaged in the conduct and activities of the web of the dream-world.
The men were slain by men, yet they remained exactly as they were.
O Rāma, tell me: what can those who have been thus slain do?
Because of their lack of consciousness, they did not attain liberation; because they possessed consciousness, they did not remain like stones.
All this visible world, including the mountains and the earth, remains exactly as it is;
these beings experience it for a long time, just as we do with our own respect.
For them, the arrangement of the eons and the world is exactly as it is for us.

Our world-system is exactly like theirs; those dream-men of theirs are precisely who we are situated here as being. And those transmigrations of theirs, O Rāma, they know this single one to be identical with them.
Those dream-people are indeed real for them due to their experience,
because the conscious self (cidātman) is all-pervading, whether it be one's own or another's;
just as those dream-people are real within the self, so too are others.
For you as well, those people in the dream-city are indeed real in that very same way;
those citizens of your own dream-city whom you saw remain there even now, because Brahman is the self of all.
For even upon awakening, dream-states persist according to their established nature;
they are experienced either as such states or as the Supreme Brahman.
Thus, everything exists everywhere and at all times within the Supreme, being the Self of all.
Just as space is nothing whatsoever, nowhere, and cannot be destroyed; so too,
within the infinite supreme space, within the infinite arising of sensation,
and within the infinite aggregate of the mind, the multitude of worlds is infinite.
Toward every treasury of the space-element, toward every circle of cyclic existence, toward every house in another world, toward every island and mountain,
toward every expansion of a mandala, and toward every village and city.
For every living being, for every house, for every year, and for every age— however many beings have died, all those who were devoid of liberation remain there;
for them, there are as many separate, inexhaustible cycles of existence (saṃsāras).
Within them there are intermediate beings; again, beings toward other beings;
again, worlds toward other worlds; and again, beings toward other beings.
Thus, this delusion of the visible world is a delusion devoid of beginning or end.
For one who knows Brahman, according to the perspective of Brahman itself, there is no such thing as limitation whatsoever.

Since pure consciousness alone exists within the wall, the sky, the stone, the water, and the land—indeed, that constitutes the entire universe—wherever that [consciousness] is, there the world exists.
What room is there here for counting? For those who know it, that is the Supreme; for those with ignorant minds, it appears as the visible world.
The two hundred and twenty-first canto, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of the Reality of the World," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, having gazed upon that woman whose eyes were like blue lotuses and jasmine flowers, and who was radiant with grace, I spoke to her playfully: "Who are you,
O one with the luster of lotus petals, and for what purpose have you approached me?"
"To whom do you belong? What do you seek? From where have you come? And what is your dwelling?
The Vidyādharī said: "O Sage, listen; I shall tell you my own story exactly as it is."
"You ought to ask with confidence, for I am distressed and seeking compassion.
Within some corner-cavity of the supreme treasury of space,
there resides something of yours— this very house of the world."

The netherworld, the earth, and heaven— these three lower realms here have been made into the inner chambers of the single maiden of conceptual construction by her who has attained the status of Creator.
Therein, it is encircled by continents and oceans as if by bracelets.
The surface of the earth, rising from the netherworld like the forearm of the Fortune of the World,
stands at the edge of the islands and oceans, extending ten thousand yojanas in every direction, composed entirely of gold.
Self-luminous, bestowing the fruits of one's intentions, as pure as the sky, composed of wish-fulfilling gems, and transparent, its own radiance surpasses that of the world;
it is the ground for the playful pastimes of the Apsarases, immortals, and Siddhas.
She is beautiful with all enjoyments accomplished by mere thought.
At the end of that earth lies the famous mountain Lokāloka,
which bears the appearance of a bracelet encircling the wrist of the earth’s surface.
In some places it is eternally pervaded by darkness, like the disposition of one with a deluded intellect;
in other places it is eternally of the nature of light, like the mind of those possessed of purity (*sattva*);
and in some places it produces delight, like the company of the virtuous.
In some places it produces distress, like an association with fools;
in some places all its objects are manifest, like the mind of the wise;
and in some places it is extremely profound, like the mind of a foolish Vedic scholar.
In some places it had not yet reached the rays of the sun; in some places it had fully attained the splendor of the sun.
In some places it consisted of the world itself; in some places the quarters of the sky were not yet empty.
In some places it was pervaded by the cities of the gods; in some places it was filled with the cities of the Daityas.
In some places it was a dense abyss reaching into the netherworld; in others, it possessed peaks and high caverns.
In some places vultures circled over its chasms; in others, it was enchanting with its ridges.
In some places, the interior of Brahmā’s city was reached by the summits of its peaks.
In one place, it was like the wind at the end of an eon blowing through a vast empty wilderness; in another, it was like a grove of flowering gardens where throngs of vidyādhara women were singing;
and in yet another, it was as terrifying as the kumbhāṇḍas in caves deep within the netherworld.
In some places it was as beautiful as the Nandana grove, enchanting with the hermitages of sages;
in some places there were inexhaustible clouds of intoxication, and in others, clouds that were difficult to obtain;
in some places its surrounding regions were dense with interior caves and mountain chasms.
In some places, the ground was cleared of living beings by the expulsion of base folk;
in other places, the beauty of the resident population surpassed that of heaven;
and in some places, the stationary and moving things were unknown because of the wind blowing there constantly.
In some places it was terrifying with the roaring of winds maddened by the great desert; in other places it was adorned by the warbling of intoxicated cranes amidst the rustling lotuses;
and in yet other places it resounded with the gurgling of water-waves and the splashing of clouds.
In some places, it aroused passion through the playful swinging of intoxicated apsarases;
in other places, its horizons were possessed by the antics of piśācas and kumbhāṇḍas; and in some places, its slopes were made lively by the songs and dances of vidyādharīs and siddhas.
In some places, its banks were being washed away by rivers carrying torrents of rain from clouds;
in other places, it was covered with fine cloths in the form of various clouds brought and driven by the ever-flowing winds;
and in some places, there were circles of meditators seated within the calyxes of lotus blossoms.
In some places he was adorned with ornaments bestowed by all the beautiful women who were accomplished siddhas;
in other places he was beautiful in his conduct, produced by the heat of the sun;
and in some places he was like a night-stalker driven mad, hidden within the house of nocturnal darkness.
In some places, the earth was losing its people due to rising portents;
in some places, circles of cities were flourishing through the perfection of good governance;
in some places it was utterly desolate, and in others it was covered with inhabited lands.
In some places it was as deep as white clouds, in others as terrifying as the netherworld;
in some places it was like a great wish-fulfilling tree, and in others a waterless desert;
in some places there were herds of great elephants, and in others swarms of rutting lions.
In some places there were excellent gardens devoid of beings; in some places there were mad rākṣasas.
In some places there were thickets of karañja trees; in some places there were groves containing all seasons.
In some places there were lakes resembling the sky; in some places there were vast desert wastes.
Upon its peaks are stones resembling ordinary mountains, which, like clouds at the end of an eon, remain firmly established;
they are composed of jewels and as pure as the sky, shining with the white luster of the moon born from the Milk Ocean or the sun. They are the abodes even of the Vātaskandhas.
In those [mountains], where monkeys with beautiful tails rest incessantly,
I dwell upon the surface of a rock on the eastern peak in the northern region, my skin as firm as the essence of unyielding diamond.
There, by that rite, I was bound and fastened with stone-machines;
O Sage, I believe countless multitudes of ages have passed for me there.
Not only am I bound, but even my husband there is likewise bound.
Like a bee caught within a lotus bud at evening,
I have long experienced confinement with that husband of mine in the narrowness of a stone cavity;
many years have passed here.

Even now, due to the single fault of our own selves, we do not attain liberation; we remain for a long time in that very place, with our perceptions still unliberated. We two are not merely bound within that narrow space of stone.
Our entire retinue has been bound there without exception.
There dwells my husband, an ancient, aged twice-born man;
he does not stir from that single spot and he lives for hundreds of years.

"O best among those who know what is to be known, from childhood he has been a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), a reciter, yet indolent; he dwells alone in solitude, straightforward in conduct and free from fickleness. I am his wife, devoted to him."
"Without him, I am not capable of sustaining this body for even a moment.
Listen, O Brahmin, how I was won as his wife by him,
and how this unartificial affection of ours has grown."
Long ago, while my husband— though born as such, still a mere child,
possessing only limited knowledge, and alone— was dwelling in his own stainless abode,
he obtained here a wife worthy of his Vedic learning, one who truly embodied the fruits of her birth.
Having determined through long reflection, "From whence did she originate?",
that faultless-limbed, lotus-eyed one was produced by her own Lord, as stainless as moonlight by the moon.
With my mind, I became the mental wife, as beautiful as the interior of a mandāra flower; from that point on, I grew like a blossom in the springtime.
Clothed in my innate garment, I captivated the hearts of all living beings.
With a face like the orb of the full moon and like the sky with its stainless stars,
she possessed breasts like rising buds; endowed with every excellence,
she was like a creeper in a noble forest, radiant with her sprout-like hands.
She eternally captivates the hearts of all living beings;
with eyes as enchanting as those of a doe, she bestows the intoxication of passion.
She is solely devoted to playful dalliance, her eyes rolling with amorous sport.
She is constantly fond of song and instrumental music, and ever devoted to new dances.
Supreme in the enjoyment of good fortune, she is the dear companion of both prosperity and adversity.
She is inseparable from the snares of delusion, yet remains undaunted by success or failure.
"O dear one, it is not only the house of this twice-born man that I support;
indeed, I sustain this entire abode of the three worlds.
I am the wife who perpetuates the lineage and am capable of maintaining the household."
Bearing alone the singular weight of supporting the furnishings of the house that is the three worlds;
then I became a young woman, with breasts emerging and swelling, radiant with the essence of grace like a cluster of blossoms on a trembling vine.

Because of his prolixity, his status as a Vedic scholar, and his devotion to asceticism, my husband has not yet married me, despite some underlying motive. Consequently, though endowed with youth and full of the essence of grace, I remain unmarried.
Without her, I burn with grief as a lotus plant in fire;
though surrounded by lotuses swaying in the cool breeze,
I experience a burning in my limbs as if standing on a bed of glowing embers.
All the circles of gardens are filled with showers of flowers;
the desert lands, once barren with scorched sands, have become lush.
They are tender with clusters of large, shimmering water-lilies and lotuses.
The lakes, though full of the sweet cries of cranes, have become tasteless to me and devoid of moisture.
Adorned with garlands of lotuses, mandārakas, and water-lilies,
I experience intense burning, as if tossed upon thorns.
Lilies, blue lotuses, white lotuses, plantains, couches,
and palaces— all these, once my body has touched them, turn to ash in the heat of summer.
Whatever is beautiful, sweet, wonderful, or captivating to the mind—
Beholding that, my long eyes become filled with tears within;
and drops of tears, scorched by the fire of calamity,
fall and sink with a "chamaccham" sound into rows of lotuses and water-lilies.
In the charming garden groves, by the playful swinging upon the trunks of plantain and kandalī trees, I cover my face and weep;
[I weep] in the plantain-leaf pavilion strewn with heaps of frost.
I see the heat being cast off, terrifying like the embers of *khadira* wood.
Beholding within the swings of lotus stalks a female crane attended by her mate, yet with a dejected face, I inwardly reproach my own youth.
I weep over a beautiful object, I become indifferent toward a neutral one,
I rejoice at what is unattractive, and I am distressed— I do not know in what state I remain.
I have seen kunda flowers, mandāra blossoms, water lilies, and snow.
Like ashes from those consumed by the fire of passion, [my sighs] have been scattered toward every direction.

(69) While I lay upon a bed of dark-blue sprouts, lotus stalks, creepers, blue lotuses, white water-lilies, jasmine, plantain leaves, and *mālatī* flowers—drying it up with the tossing of my limbs—the days of my fresh youth have passed in vain. (70)
In the narrative of Pāṣāṇa, the chapter titled "The Description of the Vidyādharī’s Misfortune," the two hundred and twenty-second chapter: The Vidyādharī.
Then, after a long time, that passion of mine turned into detachment, like a sapless sprout in the stillness of autumn;
grown old, finding pleasure only in solitude, I became devoid of flavor and stripped of affection.

With a husband whose mind is crooked and who is a silent hypocrite, what else is there for me but life itself? Better is lifelong widowhood from childhood, better even death, better disease or calamity, than a husband of unlovely nature.
Such is the fulfillment of life and such is unbroken good fortune:
that a woman’s husband is young and a man of refined conduct and aesthetic sensitivity. A woman whose protector is tasteless is lost; and an intellect that lacks refinement is lost.
Prosperity enjoyed by the wicked is lost; a courtesan is robbed of her modesty. She is a true wife who follows her husband; she is true prosperity that follows the virtuous.
She is a true lute whose strings are tuned by passion; she is true wisdom that possesses equanimity.
Neither mental anxieties, nor physical ailments, nor calamities, nor misfortunes cause any affliction to the minds of a couple who are devoted to one another.
Even the blossoming flower-filled grounds of the Nandana grove [are no match for their joy].
They act like bows for women who have bad protectors or no protectors at all.
Indeed, all worldly conditions may be abandoned or taken up as one desires according to a slight degree of their qualities, with the sole exception of a husband in the case of a woman.
"O leader of sages, these sorrows have been experienced by me, who possessed firm youth, for many years; behold the manifestation of my misfortune!
Then, by that very process, my passion gradually turned into dispassion."
He became as sapless as a lotus withered by frost.
"O Sage, through your instruction, I desire the liberation of my own self, having cast off all attachment to worldly states by means of the latent impression of dispassion."
For those who have not attained their desired goals, whose minds find no rest in others,
and who are being carried away by deaths, death is better than life.
He, my husband, now seeks nirvana day and night.
"A king awakens his mind to conquer the mind by means of the mind itself, O Brahmin. Therefore, for the sake of quelling the ignorance of my husband and myself,
please remind him of his own nature with words that are consistent with reason."
When my husband remained fixed in his own self, disregarding me entirely,
he brought about for me a world-existence devoid of passion and flavor; consequently,
I was rendered helpless, stripped of the influence of worldly desires.
Having bound myself in the intense concentration (*dhāraṇā*) on the desired movement through space,
and having acquired by means of that concentration a course through the sky,
I practiced the concentration once more, which yields the fruit of association with the perfected ones (*siddhas*).
Then, by observing the front and back of my own world-space,
I remained there having bound a concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and that too attained perfection for me.
Then, having seen the heart of my own world, I went outside of it.
"I have seen the massive rock that forms the head of the Lokāloka mountain.
O Sage, even after all this time, neither my husband nor I ever had the slightest desire to see anything else."
"My husband, through his exclusive contemplation of the pure meaning of the Vedas, knows neither what has passed nor what is yet to come; oh, he is one whose desires have vanished!
Therefore, although my husband is a learned man, he has not attained the Supreme."
Today, both he and I desire to reach the supreme state through diligent effort.
Therefore, O Brahmin, you ought to make this request of mine bear fruit;
for among the great, those who seek their aid are never left disappointed.
O giver of honor, as I wander constantly through the assemblies of the Siddhas in the sky,
I see no one here other than you who possesses the fire of the power of dense ignorance.
O Brahmin, O mine of compassion, it is for this reason that the virtuous fulfill the desires of those who seek their aid even without being asked.
Therefore, you ought not to subject me to contempt here, for I have approached you having sought refuge.
The chapter titled "The Narration of the Conduct and Birth of the Vidyādharī," the two hundred and twenty-third chapter.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been asked by me, "Very well," she sat upon a seat prepared for her;
she remained poised in the sky, seated upon a seat mentally projected [by me].
"How can there be a dwelling for those like you within the interior of a rock?
How could there be movement there, or for what purpose would there be a place? The Vidyādharī replied:
O Sage, just as this vast world shines forth for you,
so does our world remain there, engaged in creation and dissolution.
Just as these [worlds] exist here, so do the conditions of the three worlds remain established there.
The broad rivers flow; the immortals dwell in the sky.
The nāgas flash in the underworld (pātāla); the mountains abide within the Self (ātman).
The waters act with deceptive guile; the winds blow in the atmosphere.
The oceans shine with their waters, yet living beings reach their end only gradually;
beings are born incessantly, and likewise they die without ceasing.
Winds blow, waters flow, and the gods in the sky both shine and do not shine.
The mountains stand firm, the planets rise together, and kings protect the earth.
The successive traditions of worldly activity among gods, asuras,
and humans have proceeded restlessly until the end of the kalpa, like rivers flowing into the ocean.
The day-lotuses in the lake of the earthly realm have been fully blossomed and then closed again, or opened once more, by the rows of flickering clouds, until the end of the kalpa; meanwhile,
the moon has engaged in a comparison on all four sides with sandalwood through its own radiance.
Creating night and the moon (Rohiṇī), it destroys even the darkness residing within the heart.
Delighting in the tasting of its own state, impelled by the mechanism of the vital breath (vāta),
this lamp called the Sun shines in the sky, the abode of heaven and earth.
Willed by Brahmā and unimpeded by the winds or the waters,
the wheel of the stars revolves incessantly in the sky like the whirling of a woodworm;
the fixed pivot grinds the grain of all beings from the beginning of creation until the end.
By destiny, the earth's gates were shaken, and the oceans roared like thunderclouds.
The surface of the earth was filled with islands, seas, and mountains; the sky with celestial chariots and cities;
and the entire circle of the netherworld (pātāla) with throngs of daityas, dānavas, and nāgas.
The blue orb of the sky is the earring of the Fortune of the three worlds;
it remains flickering for her who is restless in her conduct, with its shimmering jewels.
It is like the consciousness of movement belonging to the wind, devoid of intellect and the like.
Taking up the immobile and the mobile, as well as the subtle, it is born. The sage [assumes] silence through silences; he resorts to the mobility of a monkey through earth, waters, and winds;
he resorts to spatiality through spaces, and luminosity through fires.
Within trees, the earth, the oceans, the mountains, and the rivers,
living beings— worms, gods, asuras, and aquatic creatures— throb intensely, facing toward death and birth; Time impels all these subjects, including the gods, asuras, and gandharvas.
With arms like the Kalpa-tree, day after day, like a herdsman tending his cattle;
in the ocean of time— endless, vast, bottomless, and profound—
the revolutions of the seasons rise up again and again only to dissolve.
The fourteen kinds of elemental dust, tossed by the winds, dissolve into the space of destruction like autumnal clouds;
while the heavens awaken the world with the fly-whisks of the rays of the moon and sun.
Clad in the garment of the sky and crowned with a mass of stars,
the quarters of the horizon remained as if paralyzed, enduring the winds, earthquakes, clouds, and heat, never abandoning their own regions.
Through portents, the roar of clouds, earthquakes, and the seizing of planets—
whether unknown or known— the destiny of beings is understood.
The submarine fire blazes as it drinks the waters of the seven oceans.
Like a host of living beings throughout the duration of a kalpa across various worlds,
he enters the netherworld, ascends into the sky, traverses the circle of the directions, and wanders everywhere;
he circles the ranges of mountains and great oceans, as well as other continents, following the course of the movement of the winds.
The two hundred and twenty-fourth canto, titled "Description of the Interior of the Vidyādharī Stone. The Vidyādharīs:
"Come to that creation; let favor be shown, O Sage!
For when wonders have arisen, the great are indeed filled with intense curiosity.
Vasiṣṭha said:
When she said "So be it," I began to travel through the sky together with her—
just as fragrance travels with the wind, or emptiness with the void in the void.
Then, having traversed a long distance through that empty celestial path, I—
I attained that ethereal movement of the elements along with her.
Having transcended that movement of the elements here in the atmosphere, after a long time,
I reached the sky above the crest of the Lokāloka mountain, where white clouds gather.
Having emerged from that seat of clouds, white as the moon in the northern quarter,
I was brought by her to that lofty slab fashioned of refined gold;
yet, as I looked, I saw only a bright stone and not that world.
Then I said to that beloved woman: "Where is the ground of your creation, appearing like a high ridge of the world of fire made of refined gold?
Where are the moon, sun, fire, and stars, and where is the sevenfold series of worlds?"
Where are the oceans, the sky, and the directions? Where are the rising and sinking? Where is the mass of the great ocean, and where is the vast expanse of the starry firmament?
Where are the ranges of mountain peaks, and where are the lands of the great ocean?
Where are the seven circles of continents, and where is the ground of molten gold?
Where is the calculation of cause and time, and where is the wandering through the elements and the worlds?
Where are the Vidyādharas and Gandharvas, and where are humans, gods, and Dānavas?
Where are the sages, kings, and ascetics, and where is the sequence of right and wrong conduct?
Where are the nights of Yama and the cycles of time, and where is the wandering through heaven and hell?
Where are the notions of merit and sin, and where are the play of the digits of time?
"Where are the enmities between Asuras and gods, and where are the currents of hatred and affection?
While I was speaking these words, that woman of excellent complexion,
looking at me with eyes as wide as bees and filled with wonder, spoke to Śilā.
The Vidyādharī said:
"I see my entire creation here upon this stone,
like a city situated within the reflection of a mirror before me."
"In this philosophy, constant perception alone is the cause for me;
O Sage, I consider the absence of that [perception] to be the cause of your non-perception. Through this mutual discourse on the long-standing unity of the two, [we have reached this conclusion]."

The state of our bodies as a single identity with the pure *ativāhika* [subtle] form has been forgotten by us both. Because of this, although I have practiced for a very long time, I do not clearly perceive this world of mine, which has become like a dark complexion.
That which was formerly my own world, so exceedingly manifest to me,
I now see here as if reflected in a mirror, indistinct;
due to the mutual anguish of long-standing, futile longing for conversation with the Lord.

One's own innate health, which is most pure and pervasive, has been forgotten. That practice which shines forth from within through the essence of the pure sky of consciousness becomes identical with that very state; thus it is observed even in a child.
There is no scripture, no accomplishment, no logic,
and no art such that it cannot be mastered through practice by one whose exertion never sets.
By virtue of my constant practice within the continuity of my own world, the delusion of discursive speech [no longer affects me].
"Surely he has overcome both, for the powerful one is the victor over the two;
O Sage, for those seeking their desired object, there is no other refuge than the repeated performance of that action prescribed by one who knows it."
This mature delusion of ignorance here, consisting of the notion "I am," subsides through the cultivation of knowledge; behold the manifestation of practice!
Even the ignorant gradually attains the state of knowing that, and even a mountain is ground to powder.
"Even a wood-worm eats a great tree; behold the manifestation of practice! I am but a young girl, a disciple and a child, yet I see it; you do not see it.
Even an omniscient one sees the creation of stone; behold the manifestation of practice!"
In this way, indeed, the fully matured cholera of false knowledge is pacified by inquiry; behold the manifestation of practice!
O Sage, through practice even a pungent substance becomes agreeable.

To one person the neem tree is pleasing, while to another, honey is pleasing. Affection becomes dense toward those who are not kinsmen through the power of proximity and habitual practice; conversely, through lack of practice and distance, affection for kinsmen undergoes attenuation.
This subtle body (ātivāhikadeha), which is merely the pure space of consciousness,
attains the state of a material body through the power of the practice of mental cultivation (bhāvanā).
That material body [arises] from the cultivation of the practice of concentration (dhāraṇā).
Behold the manifestation of practice: like a bird, one moves through the sky.
Meritorious deeds may come to naught, mothers may come to naught, and fortunes may come to naught;
but practice never comes to naught.

Enemies who are difficult to subdue attain success and turn into friends; even poisons turn into nectar through the power of constant practice. That person is base who has abandoned practice regarding the desired goal.

Sometimes one does not obtain that which is most desired, just as a barren woman does not obtain her own son. Whatever object is highly cherished, one should abandon it through repeated practice and by means of reasoning, even at the cost of one's life, just as one abandons life itself.
That lowest of men who does not practice toward a desired object attains what is undesirable and reaches from one hell to another.
Those who resort to the lake cross the vast river of saṃsāra.
Only those who do not abandon the practice known as the inquiry into the Self manifest the desired object through the semblance of practice;
they reach it without obstacle, just as the light of a lamp reveals a jar.
Just as the wish-fulfilling trees, creepers, and wish-fulfilling gems bear fruit throughout the autumn months, so too do the stages of practice.
An object of desire that has been long practiced illuminates all beings with its radiance.
Just as they do not perceive the night on the earth called the body, so too [they do not perceive the darkness].
For the manifestation of all objects for every class of living beings,
the single sun of practice alone ever triumphs supremely.
Among the fourteen kinds of elemental beings (*bhūtajāti*), for no one whatsoever is the desired object accomplished without natural, uncontrived practice (*abhyāsa*).
Practice is said to be the repeated performance [of an action]. (MU 6.224.42)
That alone is the human goal here; without it, there is no other way.
Through one's own action, which consists of effort known as the practice of firm repetition, perfection arises from that very self-knowledge and not otherwise.
When the sun of practice shines upon the earth and in the forest, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished by a hero;
through practice, all fears on this earth—even in the most desolate mountain caves—become fearlessness.
This is the chapter titled "Praise of Practice."
The two hundred and twenty-fifth canto: The Vidyādharī said:
"Then, through the stainless concentration (*dhāraṇā*), one should practice the contrary [meditation] for the sake of awakening."
"By that [means], while making it manifest, the world will come to reside upon the mountain.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"When the Vidyādharī had spoken thus, which was consistent with reason, upon the earth..."
Then, having assumed the lotus posture, I arose in meditative absorption.
Having abandoned the cultivation of all external objects and being devoted solely to pure consciousness,
I first cast off that impurity consisting of the conceptualization of the meaning of discursive speech.
Then, having attained the state of the sky of consciousness, I reached the supreme vision,
just as the sky attains clarity upon the arrival of the autumn season.
Thereafter, through the intense and singular practice of focused attention on reality within the body, [I realized the truth].

Surely my delusion regarding the material world has now set. Then, the pure nature of the great space of consciousness— free from rising and setting, yet consisting of perpetual arising— seemed as if it had truly dawned.
Then I saw that it was like a stone in the sky;
yet in reality, it was neither space nor a stone, but that supreme reality itself—
solid in its ultimate sense, transparent, manifesting in such a way, and being of such a nature.
Through such meditation, my own self perceived itself in that very way,
just as in a dream one sees a massive rock situated within a house; yet,
like the sky, that rock was nothing but the pure firmament of consciousness.

A man who himself experiences dreams and then enters into the dream-state of another is like one who has awakened from ignorance within a dream; such a person is easily led astray. Those whose heads are severed while they are in the state of dreaming remain bound in the cycle of worldly existence.
Indeed, what can they possibly accomplish without the attainment of knowledge in due time?
Awakening occurs even for those possessed of great delusion once the time has come;
therefore, there is nothing whatsoever that is imperishable apart from the reality of Brahman.

Therefore, that pure mass of consciousness, the stone-like expanse of Brahman, was seen by me there; however, earth and the other elements were not real anywhere at all. That which is pure and ultimate in the original creation of the elements—[that alone was seen].

That very body of theirs, which was previously attainable through meditation, remains established today. For that which is the primordial, innate body of beings belonging to Brahman is what is called "the kingdom of the mind" or "volition" today.
That is the transportive body; it is supreme from the perspective of ultimate reality.
It is the first direct perception, that primordial manifestation of consciousness. That which is the first object of perception is the primary form of the individual soul (jīva).
What was called "mental perception" has today been declared by that same person of evil intellect to be "the perception of the yogi," and also "mental perception.
This is merely his own form of consciousness, which he has needlessly rendered as something else.
This which is called "present" is a perception arisen from the non-existent;
know, my dear, that such a perception is indeed a false perception.
Oh, how wondrous is this illusion, that what was previously perceived becomes hidden!
In this matter, which is not subject to sensory perception, the determination is based on the recognition of direct perception:
know that the state of possessing a subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*), which was first mentioned, is real and all-pervading; whereas the material body (*ādhibhautika*) is merely an illusion.
Just as the state of being a bracelet does not exist in gold even when it has been experienced,
so too the material nature of the subtle body does not exist.
That which was non-delusion has become delusion for those who wander in error, and that which was delusion has become non-delusion for those who have reached the truth.
Does the living being (jīva) know [this] without inquiry? This would surely be a state of delusion.
Through inquiry, this material body (ādhibhautika-deha) is not found;
however, it is said that the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) is imperishable in both worlds.
When consciousness rooted in the material body (*ādhibhautika*) is established within the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*),
it is as false as a mass of water in a mirage in the desert; thus,
material consciousness arises within the sequence of the subtle body.
Just as the notion of a person in a post arises due to the influence of the view of a body,
so too does the perception of silver in mother-of-pearl, water in heat-rays, and duality in the moon;
likewise, the material nature of the mind exists in the mental and the subtle (ativāhika) bodies.
That which is unreal is made real, and that which is real is made unreal;
oh, how great is the power of delusion born from the lack of reflection in this living being!
There exists only the direct perception of the yogi, yet there is also that which is mental.
For it is by these two alone that the conduct of both worlds is accomplished.
He who, having abandoned the primary means of perception, establishes himself in this unreality,
remains comfortably situated after drinking the water of a mirage within his own perception.
They say that pleasure is indeed suffering because it is experienced as perishing in an instant;
they know that which is unconditioned, without beginning or end, to be true pleasure.
Thus, let this perceptible reality be investigated through direct perception itself.

That which is primordial, that which is real, and that which is the presiding witness— let that be seen through direct perception. There is no one more utterly deluded than he who, having abandoned the perceptible experience of this world which grants the enjoyment of both worlds, clings instead to that which is illusory in nature.
For these beings, there exists only a subtle, transportable body (*ātivāhika*);
therein, the delusion of a material body is merely an unreal phantom.
How could that which consists of unarisen conceptual constructs be perceived as real?
How can that which is not itself real produce a real effect?
Where even perception itself is unreal, what else could be real there?
Where could that established entity exist which is proven by means of something unestablished?
If existence itself is directly perceived as non-existent, where indeed could inference and the other means of knowledge apply?
Where elephants are being driven away, what talk can there be of woolly creatures?
Therefore, because it is established by valid cognition, the perceptible does not exist anywhere at all.
Whatever else exists here as if it were real, that is but the dense mass of Brahman.

Just as in a dream the mountain seen by the dreamer is only empty space within the house and not anything else for anyone else, so too, for both of us who possess that same realization, that very stone is but consciousness.
"This is a mountain, this is the sky, this is the world, and this is I"—thus the Self, consisting of consciousness, itself performs a wondrous display within the void.
One whose self is awakened perceives this; one who is unawakened never does.
The comprehension of the meaning of the discourse belongs to the listener; it never occurs for one who does not listen.
This very delusion of one whose mind is unawakened has attained the status of reality, just as trees and mountains dance before a drunkard even though they remain perfectly stationary.

Having realized the nature of consciousness—the auspicious, direct perception, the single awakening whose form is unimpeded everywhere—those fools who resort here to other, fragile forms of perception are enough for me; let them be mere straws, those deceitful ones.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Description of the Impossibility of the Perceptible through the Establishment of the Means of Valid Cognition."
The two hundred and twenty-sixth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"The limb of the world is without appearance, invisible, yet it stands as if visible."

Through the supreme vision, that very Brahman, free from all affliction, is perceived. Therein, the delusions of mountains, rivers, streams, worlds, and other worlds appear reflected like images in the great void of the supreme mirror.
Having entered that creation without obstruction, she remained motionless;
I too entered there along with her by means of my volition.
While she, having reached the world of Brahmā, was making an effort,
Seated before Viriñca, most beautiful, the Vidyādharī said:
"O tiger among sages, my husband must be told: 'He protects me.'"
"In former times, I was brought forth by this undecaying one for the sake of marriage;
yet even now, though he is the Ancient Puruṣa, he has not married me, who have grown old. Because of that, I have come to a state of detachment."
Having attained detachment, he too desires to go to that state where there is neither the state of being a seer, nor the state of being seen, nor even emptiness; and now,
while this world has reached the great dissolution.
And he does not waver from his meditation, remaining as immovable as a mountain in its silence.
Therefore, O Lord of Sages, having awakened both him and me,
establish us upon the supreme path until the beginning of the creation at the end of the great kalpa.
Having said this to me, he spoke as follows to awaken him:
"O Lord, this lord of sages has arrived here at our abode;
this sage is the son of Brahmā in another world-house."
"Honor him who has come to your home with the hospitality due to a householder. Let this bull among sages be awakened with water for the guest-offering and water for the feet;
for great souls take delight in the worship of the great."
When she had said "So be it," he of great intelligence awakened from his meditative absorption;
like a whirlpool in the ocean arising from the nature of the fluidity of self-awareness,
he, skilled in discernment, slowly opened his eyes.
As spring appears upon the earth when the cold season has subsided, as flowers [reveal their scent],
so did those limbs gradually manifest his consciousness,
just as the clusters of new sprouts reveal the fresh sap of spring.
Multitudes of gods, *siddhas*, and *apsarases* gathered from all sides,
like restless swans at dawn approaching a lake in full bloom. He saw me arrived before him, as well as that graceful woman.
Then the venerable one spoke words as beautiful as the sound of the *praṇava*:
"O you who have seen the essence within the worthlessness of saṃsāra, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand, [I am] another world-Brahmā."
"O Sage, you who are a great ocean of the nectar of knowledge, welcome to you! You have reached this most distant path;
weary from the long journey, please sit upon this seat."
When he had spoken thus, O Blessed One, saying "I salute you," I sat down upon a jeweled throne that was revealed to my sight. Then,
the praises uttered by the immortals, sages, gandharvas, munis, and vidyādharas—
The praises were commenced, as well as the offerings, prostrations, and the rules for his maintenance.
Then, within a mere moment, when the agitation of all the hosts of beings had subsided, I spoke to that Brahmā.
"O Lord of the past and the future, what is this that she has approached me and speaks to us with words of wisdom, urging us diligently: 'You must awaken them'?
You, O God, are the Lord of Beings and have reached the further shore of all knowledge."
"O Bṛhaddyuti, tell me, what does she say to me?
O Lord, how is it that she, having been produced by you for the sake of being a wife,
has not been brought here to the state of a wife, but instead has been led back to bitterness?"
O Sage, listen; I shall relate to you this account of another world-existence exactly as it occurred,
for that which has transpired must be told in its entirety to the virtuous.
There exists, indeed, something that is unborn, peaceful, and undecaying;
from that, which is of the singular nature of the manifestation of consciousness, I have emerged as a manifestation.
I am always established in the Self, which is of the very nature of space.
"While the creation persists, my name shall be 'The Self-Existent' (Svayambhū).
But in reality, I am not born, nor do I perish in any way;
I am the space of consciousness, abiding unobstructed within the space of consciousness."
"That you are this, 'I am yours,' and this mutual conversation between us—
it is my conviction that it is simply one wave clashing against the crest of another wave.
Thus, by the power of time, I have come to possess such a clear form."
Due to its extreme delicacy, within the mere reflection of consciousness there exists, by its very nature,
a latent impression (*vāsanā*) of "I" that has neither arisen nor ceased; this alone shines forth here as distinct from mine, yours, and that of others.
But I, rejoicing in the non-existence of desire, am established in the Self;
by nature my form is unchanging, I delight in my own Self, and I am self-luminous.
[This is so] because of that delusion of "I," the latent impression, and the persistence of the world.
"This presiding deity has been perfected in the form of a body.
Thus she stands as the presiding deity of my latent impressions (vāsanā);
she is not my wife, nor was she created by me for the sake of being a wife."

Having grasped at existence through the power of being possessed by one's own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), thinking "I am the wife of Brahmā," she herself has gone to fruitless and extreme suffering; for indeed, this very thing is what constitutes the end of latent impressions within.
This is the chapter titled "The Attainment of Another Creation."
The two hundred and twenty-seventh canto:
Another World-Brahmā.
Today, I, who am the space of pure consciousness, [perceive] a state composed of another space.
"I wish to take another [consort], and for that reason this destruction has arrived here.
O Lord of Sages, she was indeed intended by me to be abandoned now during this time of the great dissolution; therefore, she has become bitter."
When, because of my being space, I become the supreme space,
then there is the state of the great dissolution and the total destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Therefore, this [desire], having become tasteless, runs toward my path.
What person of noble intellect indeed would not follow the Creator?
Here today marks the end of the Kali age and the reversal of the four yugas;
this very day has come the end of the subjects, of Manu, Indra, and the gods.
"Today indeed is the end of the kalpa and the very end of the great kalpa;
