today is the end of my latent impressions (vāsanā) and the very end of the space of this body. Therefore, O Brahmin, these latent impressions are now prepared to go to their destruction."
Where indeed could a trace of fragrance remain when the lotus pond has dried up?
Just as a restless wave arises from a line on the ocean of water,
so too does desire arise in vain from latent impressions (vāsanā) even in the absence of a cause.
From the very nature of the latent impression (vāsanā) of the body associated with conceit,
the desire to perceive the Self arises spontaneously for her; yet,
by means of the practice of concentration (dhāraṇā), she perceives the reality of the Self.
By her, whose mind was intent on the multitude of worlds, the creation of beings was seen as unrestrained;
by her, who is devoted to wandering through the sky, the stone upon the mountain peak was seen as the support of her own world, yet for us, it is of the nature of space.
This world of ours exists upon that stone-like mountain of your world;
within the objects of our own world, there are indeed other worlds as well.
We do not perceive them, for we remain fixed in the vision of duality.
But once they have attained oneness with awakening, we see them immediately through that very vision:
worlds exist everywhere— in a pot, a cloth, a banyan tree, a wall, in space, in wind, in water, and in fire— just as they always do within a stone.
The so-called world is indeed a vain delusion, comparable to a city in a dream; it is purely false. Where, then, is that which is of the nature of consciousness—does it exist or does it not?
For those by whom this [delusion] is fully understood, it attains oneness with the sky of consciousness.

Those who have departed do not become deluded, whereas the remaining ones are vessels for error. But by the practice of concentration on another [object], O Sage, they accomplish their own purpose through the power of their own dispassion; you have been seen by this very method.
Thus the power of consciousness unfolds like an insurmountable illusion;
this is the stainless power of Brahmā, devoid of beginning or end.
No effects whatsoever proceed here, nor do they cease.
The consciousness alone shines forth, illuminating substance, time, and action.
Know that this entire world— space, time, action, substance, mind, intellect, and so forth—
is nothing but a single limb of the rock of consciousness, devoid of rising or setting.
This consciousness alone remains as if in the form of a stone,
bearing within its own body the web of the universe, just as the wind possesses motion.
It perceives itself, which is a mass of pure consciousness, as the world.
Though without beginning or end, that consciousness, by virtue of its nature as consciousness, has transcended even that which possesses a beginning and an end.
This stone-like consciousness, though without beginning or end, appears through the realization "I am that which possesses a beginning and an end";
though formless, it stands as the body of the world, appearing as if it possessed form.
Just as in a dream, consciousness itself perceives its own form as a city in the void,
so too does this [consciousness] perceive the world-body as a stone.
Here, rivers do not flow, nor does the wheel of time revolve.
Objects do not transform within; it is this sky of consciousness that shines.
Within the sky of consciousness, the cognitions of the great eon and its end do not arise as separate forms, just as one body of water does not exist separately from another within water.
The worlds both exist and do not exist within the peaceful sky of consciousness, whose single form is omnipresent;

just as the spaces within the sky exist within the great expanse of the sky, so too, O Vasiṣṭha, if they exist, they are merely parts of that supreme ether. Therefore, O sage, go now to your own world and attain peace within your latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
"Let forms such as the intellect and other faculties proceed toward the Supreme; we ourselves shall proceed to the state of the Great Brahman.
This concludes the two hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Words of the Grandfather within the Stone," from the *Mokṣopāya*.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the blessed Brahmā, together with the inhabitants of the world of Brahmā,
sat in the bound lotus posture and entered into infinite meditative absorption.

With his mind completely stilled, he remained until the end of the half-measure following the syllable *oṃ*; though his form was fixed like a figure drawn in a painting, his sensations were not yet extinguished. Following him in that very same way, she remained absorbed in meditation.
The latent impressions (vāsanā), which had been entirely pacified, became like the form of space;
when that Supreme Lord, free from volition,
had reached a state of attenuation, I then beheld the form of the all-pervading, infinite sky of consciousness.

Just as his volition becomes tasteless in an instant, so too does the power of the earth— with its mountains, islands, and oceans— to produce grass, shrubs, creepers, and rice vanish with equal speed.
She began to set gradually,
as if entirely; for she bears the earth as but a single limb of that Virāj-self, due to the arising of non-perception of it.
Devoid of consciousness, she became tasteless and utterly decayed,
having fallen into the frailty of old age like a creeper at the end of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa; just as our own fingers become tasteless when they are no longer perceived by us.
Thus, due to the lack of consciousness on the part of Viriñca, the earth fell into a state of desolation;
it was overwhelmed by the weight of many great calamities occurring simultaneously,
while its human inhabitants were released from the hells that had been scorched by the coals of their own misdeeds.
It was filled with the wretchedness of famine, sudden calamities, distress, poverty, and misfortune;
it was crowded with women of immoral conduct and men devoid of restraint.
The sun shone there, grey with dust, mist, and fine particles of soil.
It was agitated by pairs of opposites, fools, great suffering, calamities, and diseases;
its territories were devastated by fires, floods, and wars;
and its common folk were reduced to miserable straits by drought and oppressive heat.
Where mountains and cities fell unexpectedly due to great portents;
where people wept at the destruction of children, Vedic scholars, the virtuous, and the noble;
and where bottomless wells suddenly appeared in the midst of unsuspected dry land.
The kings will be attached to women of mixed castes; all people will have the character of beggars; crossroads will have the character of corpses;
women will have the character of having but a single hair; and the lords of men will have the character of being addicted to drink.
The entire population will practice a conduct of suffering and be characterized by strife;
women will be of unrighteous character and devoted to hundreds of false doctrines;
all wealth will fall into the hands of the wicked, while the virtuous will be struck down by calamity.
The protectors of the earth were ignoble, showing no respect for the learned;
they were devoted to greed, delusion, fear, hatred, passion, disease, and the dust of worldly affairs.
These men approached those who should not be approached, and they struck down the virtuous twice-born with their wrath.
It is filled with the most wretched of people who cry out incessantly and piteously;
its cities, villages, temples, and dwellings of the twice-born have been devastated by bandits; though its undertakings seem sweet at first, it is fragile and brings forth the agony of future ruin.
Characterized by a failure of duty manifesting through the surge of indolence,
afflicted by the pain of every calamity, its multitude of quarters gradually destroyed,
with its cities and villages reduced to ashes, the entire realm became utterly desolate.
With garments as terrifying as clouds of weeping ashes and earrings,
her belly resounded with the loud wailing of the unfortunate as they began their tumultuous lamentation;
she was surrounded by a multitude of people, each as small as a mere fist, who were attached to the suffering of the masses.
"Devoid of moisture at its entire extremity and lacking the qualities of all seasons"—
thus, when the earth element has lost its perception of Brahman,
the earth becomes greatly distressed due to its imminent destruction.
Then, when the watery element, released from its conscious control and tending toward exhaustion,
became agitated in nature,
the oceans— transgressing their fixed laws and casting aside the noble boundaries of propriety— had their waters overflow.
Like madmen, they cried out as they proceeded toward transformation;
with the shifting arrangements of the agitation of their waves,
they stripped away the groves on the shore, while mountains were overturned and tossed about by the rolling eddies of the surging billows.
The mountains were completely enveloped by dense masses of water-spray in a great upheaval; their interiors were churned by powerful, surging, and restless sea-monsters (makaras),
while their bellies were filled with forests of trees being overwhelmed by leaping sea-monsters.

Aquatic creatures were struck down by lions fallen from mountain caves they had torn open; great clouds of sky-dwellers were shattered by leaping makaras; and there arose harsh, *ḍā-kāra* and *ṭāṅ-kṛta* sounds from the mutual clashing of waves.
The suns were washed by the hissing breath of the elephants that were the surging waves;
the mountain slopes were split asunder by the waves busily tossing one against another;
and the circles of wave-hands plundered the mountains on the banks.
Entering the roaring mountain caves like houses, the intoxicated elephants—
those kings intent on attacking the cities of their enemies— seemed as if they had slain their foes;
they terrified the sky-dwellers by their loud trumpeting that resounded through the firmament.
The forests were plundered and the groves laid waste,
while the sky was filled with waves resembling winged mountains;
shaken by mountain-like surges split apart by winds of great roar.
The waters resounded against the banks and the multitude of shifting mountains on the shore; they were tossed up by large, leaping whirlpools that hurled forth swarms of sea-monsters,
while mountain caves were swallowed up by the deep, sinking eddies.
The mountain ridges are jagged with boulders and rocks shattered by the crashing waves;
elephants are submerged in the water amidst the surging billows, their trunks hanging down as they are impaled upon the rocky caverns;
and tortoises are caught and pinned to the tree branches by the force of the tossing, swirling currents.
The clattering sounds of mountain ridges falling were heard by Yama, Indra, and the guardians of the earth, who stood with ears pricked up, overwhelmed by fear; meanwhile, mountains,
submerged and then resurfacing, were swiftly shattered by the lashings of the fish’s tail.
With their waters agitated by moss-like clusters of fresh blue lotuses,
and their waters mingling with the flames of the blazing submarine fire,
they seem to enter the great conflagration by their own nature at the destruction of the Lord.
Fighting like Mleccha mountain-elephants and water-elephants,
they seem to dance with the surges of waves as they pierce through the whirlpools of the water;
they are experts at the crashing impact of the mutual collision between the waters and the mountains.
Adorned by the circles of living beings in the forest thickets of Mount Vahadgiri,
they were thoroughly agitated by waves as radiant as the clanging of the trumpeting of wild lordly elephants— waves that resembled the subterranean realms of the Asuras.

Then there arose a sound like the trumpeting of the elephants of the quarters with upturned trunks, fierce as if the very interior of the palate of the netherworld were being split and crushed; the earth,
its pillars trembling, shook, stirred by the waters.
Like a trembling creeping vine of moss tossed by the surging ocean,
the sky— filled with the tumultuous roar of an irresistible thunderclap—
seemed to burst asunder and fall, while the quarters of the world resounded with the cries of the immortals.
Comets, shaped like swirling eddies, fell from the sky like golden jewels, great pearls, and vermilion serpents released from the earth.
From the quarters, the heavens, and the ground, there arose [meteors] that scorched the horizons.
Rows of various portents, with their massed tresses of flames from the Vala mountain,
and the two kinds of great elements— the material elements such as earth and the divine beings such as the immortals— released by Brahmā, all went into a state of extreme agitation on every side.
The worlds of the Moon, Sun, Wind, Indra, and Agni were filled with tumultuous cries;
with their lords having gone to the world of Brahmā,
they were intent on falling away, trembling with crashing sounds as rows of trees fell down.
The mountains experienced the intense swaying of the earth;
the caves of Kailāsa, Meru, and Mandara trembled from the earthquake.
Showers of gem-clusters fell from the *kalpa* trees, as they were loosened from their branches.

The world became scattered and shattered by the tumultuous cries of mountains, cities, oceans, and forests, which had struck one another by the apocalyptic winds of dissolution; it resembled the mass of the Triple City falling into the full ocean at the end of an aeon.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Disturbance at the End of the Aeon" within the Narrative of the Stone.
The two hundred and twenty-ninth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, when the Self-born One had withdrawn his life-breaths from the realm of space,
He abandoned his firm station within the wind-sphere in the Virāj-self;
for it is said that those [winds] were indeed his vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
When they too were overcome by him, who else could have maintained the station of the stellar sphere (*ṛkṣacakra*), which supports all beings?
When the wind of vital breath was overcome by Brahmā within the mass of air,
and having abandoned its stability, it fell into agitation, those [beings],
being without support, fell down like firebrands from a reed-thicket accompanied by wind.
Like clusters of stars falling from the sky or heaps of flowers from a tree onto the ground,
the rows of celestial chariots— whose roots were withered by the ripening of time and whose support, the wind, had subsided— fell down like the fruits of the world-tree.
When the fuel of conceptualization belonging to the realm of Brahmā turned toward pacification,
the movements of the perfected ones vanished like the flames of a blazing fire;
wandering through the sky for an eon like tufts of cotton driven by the winds of cosmic dissolution.
As their own power diminished, the lineages of the Siddhas fell silent;
the forests of wish-fulfilling trees and the cities of Indra and the other gods collapsed, as did the peaks of the mountain of the immortals, trembling from the earthquake.
Rāma:
You say that Brahmā, whose nature is mere volition, is the Virāj whose body is the universe;
what part of him is the earthly world, what is heaven, and what is the netherworld?
O Brahmin, how do these constituent parts abide within him,
or how does he himself abide within his own body? That Brahmā, whose nature is mere volition and who is formless, exists as this [universe].
"The world has arisen as such; this is my firm conviction, and nothing else can be said.
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"In the beginning, this was neither non-existent nor existent, but remained free from all affliction."
The supreme space of pure consciousness alone fills the entire expanse of the quarters;
it perceives its own spatial nature as this "object of thought.
Without ever abandoning its essential nature, it remains conscious by virtue of its sentience.
Know that the conscious individual soul (jīva) exists as the mind due to its density;
yet, within this vast net, nothing exists with a formal shape.
The pure space of consciousness remains in the Self as before, like the pure sky.
Whatever appears here is not other than Śiva;
therefore, that mind, expansive, vibrating with cultivated egoity,
and consisting of volition, remains as the undecaying, motionless space (ākāśa).
That which has been cultivated as the thought "I am the light of consciousness" experiences its own non-existent form within the void,
like space in space;
it perceives the self as cultivated, sees it, and experiences it as well.

It is established that the body is indeed empty, consisting of nothing but conceptual construction (saṅkalpa). Just as you perceive an imaginary city—which is itself empty—acting according to its own nature, so too the Unborn perceives the body; he has experienced it as mere space within space.
Because consciousness is pure, it experiences such an experience as it desires and then subsides by its own will. However,
when there is full realization of this state, then [the expansion] of those such as ourselves occurs.
Know this cycle of existence to be empty, though it stands as if real.
Through the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, latent impressions (vāsanā) are extinguished here;
from that non-duality and absence of ego, liberation remains as the residue.
Thus, he who is Brahmā is indeed this world that exists;
O Rāma, whatever is the body of Virāj-Brahmā, that is this world.
Whatever delusion has arisen from him, whose nature is the space of volition (saṅkalpa), [that is this world].
This world shines forth; it is called the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
All this is indeed space, consisting of the mental construction of volition.
In reality, however, the world does not exist, nor do "you-ness" and "I-ness" exist anywhere.
In the stainless void that is mere consciousness, how or by what could the world be born?
What exists here, and what is its auxiliary cause?
Therefore, this world is born as false and is perceived as false.

The false tastes as the false; the void perishes. Through the manifestation beginning with the world, pure consciousness alone tastes itself by itself, within the sky of the Self, just as duality [arises] from the movement of the wind.
Know this world to be the sky of consciousness— devoid of both duality and non-duality, neither something nor nothing, empty, transparent, and free from affliction.
Therefore, O Rāghava, I abide as one in whom all distinctions have been stilled.
Though existing, you are as if non-existent; therefore, remain exactly thus, free from the sense of "mine.
Without latent desires, with a peaceful mind, silent, and devoid of fickleness, do whatever comes to pass, or do nothing at all—what need is there for attachment?
That single experience which is beginningless and eternal is itself the visible world, and nothing else is the visible world.
Those extensive experiences that arise from the true experience are the great vision of the visible. This concludes the chapter titled "Nirvāṇa" within the narrative of the Stone.
The two hundred and thirtieth canto:
Rāma said:
"The cognition of the world as bondage or liberation is neither void nor composed of existence."
"It is said that this primordial reality neither sets nor rises.
O Brahmin, this Brahman has been taught by you; I have understood it sufficiently.
Speak further, for there is no satiety for me as I listen to this nectar."
O Lord, the perceptions of the agitation of creation and so forth, as well as the perceptions of emptiness and so forth—
none of them are real, nor are any of them unreal. This being the case, I have understood that which is the truth in all its entirety.
"Nevertheless, let the experience of creation for the sake of further awakening be described.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Whatever is seen here, this entire world of the moving and the unmoving—"
Everything, rich in all its various modes and characterized by place, time, action, and so forth— when that is destroyed, in that great destruction known as the Great Dissolution (mahāpralaya),
which involves the transformation of Brahmā, Upendra, the Maruts, Rudra, and Mahendra.
There remains something peaceful, utterly pure, unborn, and without beginning, from which words turn back; what else can be understood?
Just as Mount Meru appears vast in form compared to a mustard seed, [so does the world appear vast compared to that Reality].

Likewise, even space is gross compared to that which is void; in that primordial, supreme sky— which is immeasurable, uncounted, gentle, timeless, unchanging, eternal, peaceful, and whose nature is pure experience— [all else is contained].
Free from conceptual construction, profoundly peaceful, and of immeasurable form in space and time,
the great inner space of consciousness perceives, as it were, the state of an atom;
contemplating that very state within itself by its own nature, like a dream, even though it is unreal.

Then he understands the pervasive nature of consciousness, which is the meaning of the word "Brahman. Within himself, he experiences the state of being the Knower; and because of his consciousness, he perceives his own innate atomicity as consciousness.
Then, as it were, he beholds that very [atomicity], and thereafter he remains like a seer.

Just as in a dream one person sees his own death by means of himself, and the witness of that death is indeed dead, so too is the atom of consciousness within itself. Therefore, this state of consciousness is essentially one within, yet it appears as if dual.
Seeing, it remains in its own essential nature, yet it stands as if there were a seer and a seen.
The state of consciousness, though utterly empty and devoid of form, arises as if seeing a subtle body; thus, at that time, it appears as a duality, like a seer.
Perceiving the self as a luminous atom through its own power of experience,
it becomes aware of its own swelling, just as a seed becomes aware of its state as a sprout.
[It perceives] space, time, action, substance, the seer, the act of seeing, and the object seen.
They remain as entities possessing distinct natures, with their designations unarisen.
That atom of consciousness (*cidaṇu*) wherein [a thing] appears—that location has attained the status of "space.
When it appears, that is "time"; that which is the appearing is known as "action."
They know that the perceived object is *dravya* (substance); here, the state of being a perceiver is *upalabdhṛtā*.
Illumination is the state of seeing (*darśanatā*), and the cause of illumination is the faculty of sight (*dṛk*).
In this way, swelling (*ucchūnatā*) appears, whether measured or infinite, or else in succession.
Unreal, like the sky itself, and having the very form of the sky, it is beyond all means of valid cognition.
The manifestation of the atomic consciousness appears through its own spatial extension as entering the body;
that by which one sees is the eye, and that by which there is hearing is the ear.
That by which one smells is the nose; that by which one touches is the skin;
that by which one tastes is the tongue. This is the collection of the perceptible objects of the senses. Within the manifestation of the atomic consciousness, first of all, it is devoid of names.
This group of subtle elements (tanmātra) is the very form of space for them;
it exists as a single, compact mass of the space that is the reflection of the atomic consciousness (cidaṇu).
Helpless due to its own synthetic connection, it perceives the five sense organs.
In this way, the continuous pursuit of consciousness sufficiently nourishes the visible world;
that very process is called "knowledge" (jñāna) and is designated as "intellect" (buddhi).
Thereafter, having become established as the mind (manas), it reaches the state of the ego (ahaṅkāra).
The self has accepted that this atom of consciousness is delimited by space and time;
wherever there is a fresh perception of this entity,
at that point, through subsequent time, it will assign it the designation of "past."
In another location, he will establish what is known as "upward";
in this manner, he will gradually conceive of the designations of the directions and so forth.
[This constitutes] the cognition of the meanings of words for place, time, action, substance, and direction.
Though he himself remains as pure as space, he will become thus;
through his own experience, this consciousness assumes the form of space within space itself,
attaining what is called the *ātivāhika* body.
And for a long time, through that very cultivation there,
he grasps a full conviction regarding his own material nature;
this is the delusion that [the self] is fashioned by the void within the void itself, as if it were something stainless.
Like water in the river of torment, it is spread over with the unreal and the real;
it assumes the name of "conception" within its own body, which has the form of space,
providing in one place the meaning of the word "head" and in another the meaning of the word "foot."
In some cases, it consists of the meanings of words such as "chest" and "flanks," and is free from turbidity;
in other cases, it consists of the meanings of words such as "existence," "non-existence," "grasping," and "relinquishing.
It possesses a determined configuration and is constrained by space, time, and other factors.
When the multitude of senses has turned toward sense-objects and is pierced by them,
that subtle atom (aṇu) then perceives a form imagined by itself for the self—
one characterized by hands, feet, and so forth, and accompanied by the mental construction of the mind and other faculties.
In this way Brahmā is accomplished, and in that same way Hari is accomplished;
in this way Rudra is accomplished, and in this way even a worm is accomplished. Yet nothing at all has been accomplished; it remains exactly as it was, established in its own state.
In the void, the void sports; in cognition, cognition unfolds.
It is the reflection of bodies, the seed of the plants of the three worlds, the provider of the bolt for liberation, and the cloud that rains upon the essence of saṃsāra.

He is the cause of all effects and the leader in the performance of time and other such functions; he is that primordial Person who, though not arisen, has arisen by his own will. He has no body composed of the elements, nor are there bones in his little frame.
He cannot be seized by the fist by anyone at all.
Therefore, though his soul was as powerful as the roar of a lion in battle amidst clouds and oceans,
he remained truly silent, like a man fast asleep.

Just as the perception of warriors and soldiers seen in a dream by one who is awake exists neither as non-existent nor as existent when it has entered the realm of memory, so too does that [body] abide.
Though its vast body may measure many hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*, it remains thus.
Within a single atom, the unborn one contains the three worlds situated within a hair-tip;
though his nature consists of the multitude of qualities of the principal mountain ranges and he is composed of vast multitudes,
he does not fill even a single grain of rice on a scale.

Although he is as vast as the expansion of hundreds of millions of worlds, in reality he has not occupied even an atom’s worth of space, like a mountain in a dream. He is called the Self-Existent (Svayambhū), and he is called Virāj.
The Self of the cosmic egg, whose body is the world, is in reality composed of space;
he is called Sanātana and is also designated as Rudra,
possessing bodies such as Indra, Upendra, the Maruts, clouds, mountains, and networks [of stars].
Having first cognized a body manifested as a mere atom of light,
he gradually becomes an expansive consciousness and abides as the thought, "I am the Great One.
Through the perception of vibration, he experiences that which is called "vibration" (spanda).
That which is known as "wind" exists in the form of the mass of wind (*vātaskandha*);
through sensation, it is experienced as the movement of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths.
Therefore, that which is called the mass of wind in space is this very thing.
Because it is consciousness, those [worlds] imagined by that [consciousness], like demons by a child, though non-existent,
have attained the state of being abodes— just like sparks of fire.
The swing of the reversal of the prāṇa and apāna breaths arises within its belly.
It bears the name Vātaskandha; that vast heart is the world itself. It is the prototype of all bodies, the primary seed of everything belonging to the world that functions until the end of the aeon.
When bodies arise from this very desire of the Self of the world, then their internal state remains just as their external state is; for consciousness is,
as previously stated, the primordial seed of that [Self].
In the very same way, even today, that which is desired by him arises within the living being.
His phlegm, bile, and wind are the moon, sun, and wind;
his planets and constellations are the droplets of spittle within his vital breath.
We perceive its bones as mountain ranges and its dense fat as networks;
we do not see its head, feet, skin, or body apart from that [universe].
Know, O dear one, that the world is the body of Virāj, for it is the conceptualized form of the one whose nature is volition.
The sky, mountains, earth, oceans, and all else are the space of consciousness; therefore, they are utterly tranquil.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Description of the Nature of Virāj," the two hundred and thirty-first chapter.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen now to this wonderful arrangement, captivating in its diverse conduct, regarding the form that was assumed by him during that kalpa and that [act of] volition.
That which is the supreme space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) is the body of the Virāj-self;
it is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, yet its light body is the world.
Brahmā, fashioned by volition (*saṅkalpa*), [conceives] his own egg, which consists of volition.
He perceives that very space as radiant all around his body;
this resolve, which is Brahman and the Self, made its own egg twofold—
the luminous [egg] having a luminous form, like a mature bird [breaking] from a mature [shell].
He perceived that one part of the cosmic egg had reached far into space,
while the portion situated far below was not distinct from himself;
the upper portion of the Brahmāṇḍa is called the head of Virāj.
Its lower portion is called the feet; here, the middle is the infinite void (*kha*).
The junction of two vast, separated fragments is seen as an infinite, dark, and empty line of space.
The sky is his broad palate, and the stars are drops of blood;
gods, asuras, humans, and others are the sensations and vital airs within his body.
Within his body are the worms, the *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*.
The other worlds are the cavities and hollows within his body. The fragment of the cosmic egg is the expanse beneath him, the soles of his feet;
the hollows of Pātāla are the cavities of his knee-joints below.
The earth, with its many hollows and cavities, crackles *śala-śalā* with waters; it is a quivering mass of entrails encircled by oceans and islands.
The rivers, whose essence flows forth, are like veins that gurgle with water.
Jambudvīpa is his heart-lotus, with Mount Meru as its pericarp;
the hollows are the quarters of space, while the liver, spleen, and other organs are the mountains.
The soft, smooth, and banner-like tissues are the nets of fat, dense and pervasive.
The moon and sun are his eyes; the world of Brahmā is said to be his mouth.
His brilliance is declared to be the moon, and the Himālaya mountain is his phlegm.
Likewise, the world of Agni and the submarine fire (aurvāgni) are his bile, which is exceedingly difficult to endure.
The masses of wind are the great winds; the prāṇa and apāna breaths are situated in the heart.
His groves are the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpadruma*), and in some places there are swarms of serpents;
his infinite forests and pleasure gardens are the networks of body hair.
Above, the entire fragment of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) constitutes its vast head;
from it, a radiant flame rises from its crest, its light streaming through the cavity at the edge of the cosmic egg.
By that very mind, he is himself [the mind]; thus, no other mind is employed by him.
Indeed, it is the self alone that undergoes division; for whom, how, and from where could [the senses] exist?
It is this very self that has projected the existence of the senses elsewhere, since the entire collection of senses is indeed merely a mental construction.
Just as between a part and the whole, so too here between the sense organ and the mind,
there is not even the slightest difference, yet they are not identical, being two distinct bodies.
Whatever effects belong to the worlds, those indeed are his.

It is only his volitions, colored by duality through the movement of the male faculty (puṃvṛtti), that should be understood as his birth and death in this world; there are no others for him. Therefore, he alone is this world; he exists as the essence of volition, and nothing else.
The existence of the world depends upon its [the Self's] existence; by its death alone the world dies.
Just as the existence of the wind that moves is one and the same, so too is the existence of those two;
the existence of the world and the Cosmic Man (Virāj) is one, like that of the wind and its movement.
That which is the world is indeed Virāṭ; that which is Virāṭ is known as the world.
"World," "Brahmā," and "Virāṭ" are synonymous terms;
these are mere conceptual constructs, whose nature is the pure space of consciousness.
Rāma:
Since the Virāj is indeed of the nature of volition and is like space itself that has assumed a form,
how can this Brahman remain within its own body?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as you remain within your body through meditation exactly as you are,
so too does the Grandfather (Brahmā), whose nature is volition, abide within his own body.
Likewise, that splendor which belongs to the foremost of men within the inner city of Brahmā is like a reflection in the body of a daughter born of one's own self;
it is there that even you are fully capable of maintaining your presence until the end of the body.
What will Brahmā, the all-pervading Lord whose nature is volition, not accomplish there? For just as the mobile entity resides within the immobile seed,
why should that which consists of the imagination of consciousness not reside within one's own body?
May he be with form, having the nature of space, or may he be formless like the sky;
may he abide both outside and inside, for there is no distinction between the external and the internal.
Delighting in the Self, silent as a log of wood, though not insentient, he is as inert as a stone.
The Virāj, consisting of "I," "you," and so forth, abides within the Self.
Like a man wrapped in or casting off vines, grass, and wood, or like the sound of water rushing by with its limbs agitated,
the knower of reality remains with a mind as tranquil as the interior of a stone, even while moving through the manifold web of activities.
In the narrative of the stone, the chapter titled "The Description of the Nature of Virāj," the two hundred and thirty-second chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, with my eyes fixed upon Brahmā, who was established in the world of Brahmā above and absorbed in meditation,
I gradually beheld in the directions a second, stainless sun that had clearly risen in the midst of midday.
Like a conflagration in the face of the quarters, like a forest fire on a mountain,
like the world of fire in the sky, or like the submarine fire in the ocean—
then I beheld the blazing sun in the direction of the southwest.
The sun in the southern quarter; the sun facing the south-eastern direction;
the sun in the eastern quarter; the sun facing the north-eastern direction;
the sun in the direction of Kubera (the north); and the sun at the border of the north-western direction.
I was astonished by that sun in the western quarter;
while I, agitated, quickly reflected upon this calamity of fate,
the sun rose from the surface of the earth like the submarine fire (aurva) from the ocean.
In the eleventh [chapter], like a reflection of all the suns arisen together,
a triad of suns appeared in the sky and in the expanse of the quarters.
That blazing host of twelve suns, measuring twelve in number, arose.
It blazed intensely in every direction, like fire in a dry forest. Then there arose a summer day that withered the entire host of worlds—
a conflagration without fire, where clusters of glowing embers were suddenly invisible.
O lotus-eyed one, by that fireless burning of the fire,
my limbs became as if scorched by a forest conflagration and grew weary.
Then, having abandoned that place, I ascended far away.
The sky appeared to me like a ball struck by a firm blow of the palm;
standing in the air, I beheld the risen sun of fierce brilliance scorching even the ten directions with the heat of the twelve-fold host of Adityas.
With its vast, terrifying roars, the blazing forests and mountains were set ablaze;
the tumult of the seven oceans was brought to a boil by the great sound of "ka-ha-ka-ha";
and the interiors of the cities and the spaces between the worlds were packed thick with flaming firebrands.
The mountains were turned vermilion by the swelling mass of dense flames;
the firm lightning was like scattered great embers as it flew about;
and the circle of cities crackled with the swelling roar of snapping sparks.
The pavilion of the world’s assembly hall was filled with thousands of glass pillars and thick stone slabs from which columns of smoke rose as the earth split apart;
it resounded with an intense gurgling noise from the agonized cries of the great elements and living beings as they boiled.
It was fierce with the crackling *caṭacaṭa* sound of the falling cities of the world-protectors; the surface of the earth was strewn with showers of gems vomited by scattering stars;
and crowds of people were burning while fleeing from every dwelling place.
The horizons were difficult to behold due to the conflagration burning in every direction;
the great ocean, with its aquatic creatures, was steamed by the mass of boiling water;
and circles of serpents were seen wandering through the caves and crevices of the mountains.
The circles of cities were crushed and scorched by falling mountains; the bays, mountains, and thickets resounded with the "pa-ca-pa-ca" cry of falling birds;
and the oceans and mountains were feverish with living beings rising up in heat from the scorching sun.
The vidyādhara women were torn from their hearts and cast down;
the gods fled, exhausted by their cries and weeping, leaving no refuge.
The surface of the earth was scorched by the underworld, where the flames of the nāga-world were blazing.

The fierce aquatic creatures were tossed about in the mud and water of the dried-up ocean; as if by the submarine fire (Aurva), which, due to the lack of fuel, had suddenly leaped up in a thousand ways,
it rose a hundredfold and seized the courtyard of the sky.
Then there arose the Fire of the Kalpa, adorned with the garments of blazing-flamed *kiṃśuka* flowers,
as if for the sake of a wild dance (*tāṇḍava*), wearing a garland of flickering torches;
it was loud with the crackling roar of its flames, like a fierce warrior shouting aloud.
With arms raised in flames and hair like smoke, he acted as a dancer in the dilapidated hut of the world.
Forests, groves, cities, and towns blazed up, as did the provinces,
islands, fortresses, jungles, and dry lands.
All cavities are the great space; the ten directions are the sky, the head;
chasms, wells, water-wheels, watchtowers, whirlpools, and the edges of the quarters;
mountain peaks, hosts of perfected beings, mountains, and the oceans of the sea.
The lakes, rivers, gods, asuras, humans,
and serpents were filled with the sounds of "śa-na-śa-na" from men of inauspicious radiance; there were ogresses with fierce shrieks, their upward-pointing banners blazing with masses of flames.
With terrifying *bhāṅkāra* sounds— *bhaṃ bhaṃ bham*— and amidst profuse ashes,
flames issued forth from the caves of the chasms, mountains, and the earth. All the multitudes of living beings dwelling within the bellies of those flames became crimson.
The inauspicious [omens] brought the splendor of lotus-filaments resting upon dry land;
with masses of flames pervading the world that sang "dhag, dhag, dhag," beautiful as clouds of vermilion and possessing the fresh radiance of freshly shed blood.
It was strewn with red garments like the sky with evening clouds,
or as if covered by forests of blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees that had taken flight;
it was as if enveloped by the submarine fire, like forests of blooming *aśoka* trees.
The oceans, filled with the cries of land-lotuses, seemed as if they were uttering sounds;
the Himavat mountain, possessing arrangements of smoke and blazing flames of various colors, acquired the splendor of a terrace for a palace variegated with minerals.
The Vindhya mountain, which had become like the moon to the forest of Ananta through its arrangement of eternal youth that kindled a fire,
fell into a state of distress due to the forest trees that resembled glowing coals and leaped up as forests of flames from the mountains of sunrise and sunset.
Like Śiva agitated by arrows, Sahya became unbearable;
the sky was like a lake, its center shimmering with blackness, garlanded by swarms of wandering smoke, and its lotuses of flickering flames cleansed by the winds.
O Rāma, the peaks of the mountains in the sky, with their crests like tongues of fire, danced like passionless dancers whose hair was the banners;
the surface of the upper lid of the cosmic egg had the flames of fire placed upon its palms.
Then, from the frying pan-like earth where living beings were like grains popping in the heat,
the earth— reddened by the fire of its own moisture and mud, and adorned with the rows of bracelets that are the islands and oceans—
descended upon the heart and forearm of the Fortune of the World.
The mountains were utterly shattered with crackling sounds, the trees with the rattling noise of their falling,
and the lands with tumultuous roars;
the oceans took on the appearance of boiling water, thick with foaming and surging waves.
In the sky before the sun, they seemed to strike with the palms of their waves;
with their wave-hands tossing one against another, those stupified by delusion carried away the mountains of glowing coals on the trembling earth, as if they were enraged.
This fiery sound, fierce with its crackling *bhaḍabhaḍa* roar like flames, has reached these caves of those who feed on the void of hope;
it has shattered the walls of the cities of the world-protectors, reducing them to glowing embers and the like.
Even the ten directions fell into a state of helplessness, their movements abandoned;
Mount Meru, with its cave-dwellings containing trees thick and wet with molten gold,
gradually assumed a dwarfed form, as if shrinking from the heat in the sunlight.
In an instant, the Himavat fled swiftly from that fire,
becoming cool within and pure throughout, like a virtuous man escaping from a wicked person.
Even in that state, however, the Malaya mountain retained its stainless fragrance.
The noble-minded man does not abandon his supreme quality even in destruction;
even as he perishes, the Great One bestows joy and not sorrow.
Even when burnt, sandalwood serves only for the delight of those who live.
The supreme reality never becomes non-reality;
even when consumed by the fire of universal dissolution, gold does not perish.
Within that [reality], both gold and space are not destroyed even by the fire of dissolution.
The very form of those two is praiseworthy, for they do not perish even when everything else perishes.
Space is indestructible due to its omnipresence, and gold is imperishable due to its excellence;
yet I consider *sattva* alone to be true happiness, neither *rajas* nor *tamas*.
A cloud of fire arose, emitting a rain of burning coals scattered by the falling of shifting, lofty trees;

it was a mass of great smoke, like a mountain of clouds that had been consumed by fire. Amidst this, there were those whose bodies were vast yet empty, suffering from the emission of tongues of flame.
Not even ashes are seen anywhere of the dry leaves of the trees of the sky that have become like vessels,
nor of the clouds along with their waters when they are consumed by the flames of the dissolution;
just as no trace remains of the defects of ignorance once true knowledge has arisen.
Before the blazing fire could leap as far as Kailāsa,
Rudra, enraged at the end of the aeon, consumed it with the fire from his eye.
Amidst this, there arose the crackling sounds of trees bursting from the heat and massive boulders splitting apart.
The mountains seemed to fight with floods of clubs, stones, and clods of earth;
their namesakes, the mountains, shone like masses of clouds with crests of flames,
appearing as if they were groves of land-lotuses blooming all the way to the sky.
The creation, having existed for only a brief moment, entered the state of being remembered;
the end of the eon, spreading forth sufferings, entered the state of being forgotten. Utterly consumed by torment and affliction, they were intent upon the destruction of others.
The fires denied the existence of the worlds, as if they were non-existent.

Winds blew, their forms hardened by the falling of thunderbolts, wearing garlands of fragments of flickering firebrands and severed heads; like the winds at the time of universal dissolution, they licked the burning mountains and struck down thunderbolts.

The winds blew with such force that they bore along the heat of the ashes rising from the forest of blazing trees violently shaken and split apart; their flames were whitened by the sparks struck by the whirling firebrands amidst the clouds; they were darkened by the trickling drops of flame flickering between the falling peaks of fire; and their forms took on the appearance of a flood of extinguished embers.
The two hundred and thirty-third canto, titled "The Description of the Fire at the End of the Great Kalpa," by Vasiṣṭha:
Then, when the wind at the end of the aeon blows, shaking the mountains,
and by its force creates whirlpools in the sky with the waves of the oceans,
while the seas break their bounds and become dense with turbulence;
When the surface of the earth— dense with sins, overwhelmed by the calamity of the poverty of clouds,
devoid of even a portion of a lord of beings, and scorched by fire—
had at some point in time even descended into the underworld; MU_6,233.2–3.
When the heavens were no longer visible, when the multitude of created beings had perished, and when the quarters of the world were devoid of light and had become abodes of sorrow—
then, from some hollow in the sky, like hosts of arrogant demons, [they emerged].
The Puṣkarāvartaka clouds let out a deep rumbling roar,
as fierce as the shattering of the shell-walls of the cosmic egg when burst by Brahmā;
it was filled with the tumultuous sound of the ocean, intoxicated by the mutual clashing of the waves.
Intense with the thick clamor vomited forth from the cities of other worlds,
it resounded with the fierce, gurgling roar produced by the falling shoulders of the great boundary mountains;
slow with the whirlpools that filled the interior of the conch-shell of the cosmic egg.
It obstructs the heavenly realm and forms a thicket of spreading creepers upon the surface of the netherworld;
it delights in the effortless striking against the walls of all distant directions,
and it thirsts for the drinking-vessel of the liquor of the great dissolution.
It was amplified by the cries of Indra’s elephant Airāvaṇa as he frolicked during the onset of the dissolution;
it gathered a roar like that of the ocean of clouds agitated at the end of an aeon,
resembling the tumultuous sound of the churning of the Milky Ocean during the great dissolution.
In this formidable water-wheel of the cosmic egg, it is like a churning mechanism with a loud roar.
Then, wondering how this dense mass could remain while this fire of the kalpa exists,
I cast my gaze throughout the ten directions in astonishment.
As long as I do not see a single cloud anywhere in the quarters of space,
but only showers of firebrands like thunderbolts crossing with flickering flashes;
by that heat of the blazing fire, extending for many millions of *yojanas*—
All objects were reduced to ashes, even in the ten directions far away. Immediately thereafter, in a moment, I experienced in the distant sky a cool wind from above and a fire-like heat from below.
At such a distance along this path through the sky, the clouds of the kalpa remain;
they are within the range of the heat of those fires, but not within the range of my vision.
Then, from the direction of the western quarter, the wind of the kalpa arrived.
In that [wind] by which the Vindhya, Meru, and Himavat mountains were carried away like blades of grass,
the mountain-like flames— where the embers flew like birds and the forests were overrun by flickering torches— swiftly fled toward the direction of fire.
Clouds of glowing coals, resembling the hue of twilight clouds, surged forth;
masses of ash-clouds, intermingled with the dust of burning embers, wandered through the sky.
That mass of flaming mountains was seen moving toward the direction of fire.
It was as if a host of winged golden mountains were fleeing;
when the mass of the earth’s mountain ranges— whose nature was filled with the coals of the bodies of the Asuras—
had become a dense mountain of flames, the splendor of the luminaries shone forth.
In oceans that were oceans of fire, with waters boiling and surging;
in forests where the leaves had no memory [of greenness], and where the waters were trees of blazing fire;
and beneath the cities of the world-protectors, whose lords dwell in the world of Brahmā.
When men, women, children, and the elderly had been consumed by the fire and were falling from the pit—
within that fierce lake of the cosmic egg, which was like a lotus-pond at the end of an aeon, shimmering with flames for its foliage and containing the embers as its seeds— MU 6.233.23–24.
When the roots, the *nāgas*,
and the mountains had sunk into the great mire of glowing coals as far as the underworld (*āpātāla*),
the sky, its movement no longer visible, drew near to me like a herd of camels.
In an instant, a mass of clouds from the end of the aeon arrived, dark as collyrium;
it was like a mountain composed of lightning equal to the flames of the fire at the end of the aeon,
bearing the weight of the waters of the seven oceans resting upon a single corner.
The horizons were filled with a mass of frost shining against the walls [of the sky];
it was skilled at shattering the dense circle of the shell of the universe;
like the ocean agitated at the end of an aeon, it possessed the motion of circular whirlpools.
With its wide-spread roar like lightning moving through the water, it was as if the sky itself had arrived;
the world of the moon, dead and consumed by fire, became doubly cold,
having assumed another form as if come from the other world.
Bearing the entire Himālaya mountain in the form of a mass of snow, it held all the waters, trees, and mountains of the quarters frozen solid by its chill;
then, it shattered the sky with a hardness like the explosion of the cosmic egg.
Having first raised a violent dust-storm, a painful rain indeed fell,
terrifying with the fires of conflagration, the roar of the wind, and the flashing of lightning;
it resounded with the crackling and popping of thunderclaps that seemed to shatter the very shell of the universe.
With hundreds of hissing sounds from heaps of spray and the inexhaustible roar of its thunder,
it made the sky appear as if constructed from walls of cool droplets and mist;
it shone with the mass of beryl pillars that were the circle of the earth’s surface.
With torrents of rain, she was intent on shattering the mountain of the earth’s fortitude;
the city of burning coals was shattered by the crackling sounds of the earth splitting apart;
and the world was thrown into turmoil by the falling of beings due to the forceful impact of her thundering.
Then she became the mistress of the house of the world, which was filled with glowing embers;
she was welcomed by the earth, who blazed with the beauty of her tears.
That sky, with its display of leaping sparks, appeared like a vast expanse of gathered petals from the lotuses of the terrestrial realm.
Then there arose streams resembling swarms of wandering bees, with clusters of wings formed by shimmering, cool droplets.
That terrifying collision of water and fire filled the quarters with a rising, great *caṭa-caṭa* roar;
it was like a fierce battle between the forces of the great, as formidable as irresistible enemies, where sharp weapons strike against sharp weapons.
The Chapter titled "The Thundering of the Puṣkarāvarta Clouds," the two hundred and thirty-fourth chapter.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, at the end of the eon, when the earth, fire, and wind had undergone supreme agitation,
this triple world became radiant with clouds of ash resembling the flight of birds from a *tāpiñcha* forest.
The swirling of smoke circulates like the great eddies of a vast ocean;
it resounds with the playful, low humming of rising sparks from extinguished flames,
filling the intervals between the worlds with dense masses of scattered clouds of vapor.
With trumpets emitting rising, spreading cries of victory— characterized by long, surging *jhāṅkāra* sounds and the rhythmic *chamacchama*—
and with clouds of smoky ash swirling about like the tumultuous clouds at the end of a great aeon; MU_6,234.4.
It was bewildered by the swirling confusion of clouds of vapor, like a mass of fierce clouds of spray;
and by the gusts of wind, terrifying with the crashing sounds against the walls of the cosmic egg,
it scattered the heaps of the cities of Indra and the other gods flying through the sky.
The hearing of Antaka was rendered deaf by the *ṭāṅkāra* sounds of the violent collision of hundreds of millions of stones bursting forth from the surging waters, winds, and fires;
and by the incessant downpours of rain held in columns resembling pillars of the sky.
With multitudes of rivers whose waves were like the Gaṅgā, producing a deep "chamaccham" sound as they uprooted the wish-fulfilling creepers,
the entire ocean was being filled by those fearsome floods, like the sky by clouds.
With its orb of clouds appearing almost yellowed by the scorching suns, which resembled clusters of flower-buds resting upon a mass of *tāpiñcha* leaves;
it bore mountains, rivers, peaks, islands, and cities.
It was like the crushing of mountains caused by the agitation of the winds at the end of an eon;
fierce hosts of planets and stars, agitated and difficult to grasp due to their conflict,
fell down like doubled whirling firebrands as they were cast into the whirlpools.
It was battered by the impact of the collision between the ocean-born waters and the lord of mountains;
it was crushed by the edges of mountains overturned during the great dissolution,
and even by the thick clouds of the kalpa, dense with vapors hissed forth.
The ocean was congested and sluggish with a density of darkness that blinded the rays of the sun’s network;
it was filled with fragments of the shattered earth’s surface whose slopes were crumbling away,
and with mountains and cities being carried off and rolling along.
The horizons were shattered by deep-roaring thunderclaps and oceanic crashes, by gurgling winds that severed the clouds as they rose over the mountains,
and by harsh clanging sounds that acted like hammers upon the very surface of the shell of the universe.
The roar of the single ocean was struck by the fierce crashing of clouds at the end of an eon;
the sky was filled with fragments of heaven, the netherworld, and the earth, intermingled and scattered by the winds, remaining in their respective natures.
With gods and dānavas whose limbs were dead, half-dead, burnt, or half-burnt,
their weapons whirled about as they collided with one another,
tossed by the winds like the withered grass of other worlds scattered by the winds at the end of an aeon.
The pillar known as the Arjunavāta was set ablaze by smoky ashes;
its banks were overturned by the impact of drifting masses of stone,
while falling worlds produced a harsh, piercing sound of *tāra*, *tuṣkāra*, and *ṭāṅkṛta*.
Resplendent with the echoing roars from the caves of mountain ranges tossed about by the wind,
it was filled with whirlpools created by falling cities of the world-protectors,
like asuras amidst the winds that produce harsh thundering sounds.
It was filled with windows through which the winds blew, carrying away the forest groves;
and it bore within its celestial sphere a multitude of Daityas, Agnis, Suras, Nāgas, and Vivasvats,
appearing like a swarm of gnats in the sky.
With the masses of the best of mountains perishing as their celestial abodes were shattered,
the waters— producing the gurgling roar of whirlpools, sending water upward and fire downward,
and crushing the cities of the world-protectors with the impact of mountainous floods— [raged on].
The cities of the lords of gods, daityas, siddhas, and gandharvas were falling down;
mountains and other peaks were being pulverized until they took the form of extinguished embers, while the winds produced a shower of dust from all objects.
It shattered the ancient cities of the gods and demons, whose crumbling walls crumbled away;
with its jewels, it made the waters resound like the splashing of water-bearers.
Filling the sky, it flew over the palaces of the seven worlds.
It was filled with other oceans, as it were, revolving in circular motion like whirling forms,
crowded with palaces made of gold, crystal, lapis lazuli, and precious gems,
falling from the sky with rising jingling sounds.

Clouds of smoke and ash rose up, and masses of torrential streams fell; floods of waves surged upward, and the mountains of the earth sank down. Roaring with the gurgling sounds of whirlpools, they strove to crush one another.
The oceans, strewn with massive mountains like scattered leaves,
were tossed about; the world became difficult to behold, with the hosts of gods crying out, living beings perishing, and hundreds of banners whirling in portents of calamity.
The sky became densely packed with a continuous stream of beings— half-dead and half-alive, flickering like the wind, and the color of withered leaves;
the world was filled with torrents of thick, falling rain from the peaks of mountains.
It was filled with hundreds of rivers that had burst forth from the crumbling masses of the great mountain cities;
the fires within it were joined by hundreds of sounds of "shame, shame, and peace";
and its mountain slopes and riverbanks were tossed like cradles by the surging of the moving ocean.
A great forest of flames arising in moments across the sky and the most distant quarters, where islands and oceans were mingled according to the logic of a heap of grass and a river;
where the gods fell amidst the fragrance of the ashes produced by fires extinguished by rain.
In former times, the world existed as a being whose creation had been utterly forgotten;
it possessed unrestrained, surging sounds yet followed the sequence of their cessation;
its remnants shone with a longing for creation, though it was devoid of the worlds of the virtuous.
Constantly shaken by the winds of incessant error,
it is being purified again and again like a heap of seeds;
[it is purified] by the gold-dust produced from the fire of the mutual friction of firebrands.
The hollow of the sky, with its golden pavement, was filled with scattered dust;
the great fragments of the earth’s surface, along with the islands and oceans, had fallen away,
filling the seventh netherworld as the circles of the subterranean realms rolled about.
From the seventh layer of the netherworld up to the surface of the earth and its mountains,
until the sky became a single ocean filled with the winds of dissolution,
that single ocean then gradually increased, and quickly so, by means of hundreds of rivers.
In this world, anger is like dull waves in the mind of a fool;
first it is like a pestle,
then its limbs resemble a pillar, and then it flows with a current shaped like a palmyra tree, carrying away all essence.
Then, by a rain that fell with a singular downpour of fierce river-like currents and which thickened like clouds over the entire surface of the earth with its seven continents,
the fire, though capable of burning, was thus brought to subsidence.
Through the perspective of the scriptures, the virtuous, and the wise, folly brings about calamity.

(MU 6.234.47) The hollow of the cosmic egg became desolate, its mass of objects situated above and below turned upside down, with the marrow of the mountains resounding with a hollow *khaṇ-khaṇ* sound within; it was like a withered wood-apple fruit, tossed about in the play of a young child. (MU 6.234.48)
The two hundred and thirty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Puṣkarāvarta Clouds," by Vasiṣṭha:
When the surface of the earth was shattered by the calamities of wind, rain, and snow,
the force of the water increased like a sovereign at the end of an eon (kalā),
augmented by the falling torrents resembling the flow of the Gaṅgā.
Suddenly, with thousands of rivers as beautiful as Mount Meru and Mandara,
its caverns reaching to the path of the sun,
the single vast ocean swelled up, sluggish and motionless like a foolish lord.
Within its vast, swirling motion, it has swallowed mountains and grass;
with the tips of its quivering, lofty waves, it has engulfed the orb of the sun;
and Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Vindhya, and Sahya are its aquatic creatures.
With lotus-stalks hidden within the shifting mud of the earth,
it was congested by the twisting of forest groves half-burnt;
it was defiled by the soot-mud from the sweeping away of the ashes of the three worlds.
The sun was like a lotus-stalk grasping the massive streams that were the pillars of the sky;
the petals of the lotuses dissolved in the great ocean of the water of those streams;
and the clouds bore the appearance of having reached the edges of mountains of foam.
A ship filling the cities, towns, and fortresses of the wandering Indra, Agni, Arka, and Indu; a multitude of fierce gods, asuras, and men being swept away like logs;
slowly swelling in its progression, it licks the solar orb.
The great mountains were being washed away by bubbles produced by the intense downpour of the sound *tarat-tāratara*;
the wandering clouds of the end of the eon came to rest upon those whirling bubbles.
Beholding the western ocean with those eyes that were like rescuers,
its interior resounded with the *ghuṅghuma* roar of the floodwaters of the great dissolution,
as it swept away all the continents and mountains of the earth in a single current.
The mountain-like masses of water were stirred up by fierce winds into unprecedented floods;
the violent torrent of water roared with great *ghurughuru* and *gharghara* sounds,
tossed about by collisions and revolutions against the walls of the cosmic egg.
Making the hundreds of thousands of yojanas undulate and rise,
as if with blades of grass, while the mountains performed a swaying motion upon the waves, shattering the orb of the sun with the impact of their stones.
In the nest-like hollow of the vast ocean of the empty universe,
he seized the mountain-crows hidden within by means of his webbed hands,
while they were agitated by the sinking and surfacing of great beings, both dead and alive.
Dragging along waves that appeared like sprouts accompanied by reflections,
it bore upon the edges of its foam-mountains the remnants of the dead who had fallen from the city—
exhausted by the force of the waters— like mosquitoes.
Like Indra with his eyes, he beheld thousands of water bubbles, vast as the stainless sky of this very day, rolling about like a circle;
with those bubble-eyes that possessed the expansive expanse of the autumnal sky, they swirled.
He seemed to behold the torrents of rivers and the clouds that fill the self, as he performed, as it were,
embraces with his arms— the circular waves— of the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds,
which had risen up like winged mountains.
Satiated by devouring the three worlds, as if singing with gurgling roars,
as if dancing upon the formidable ridges of mountains with his wave-like arms for trees,
with rivers for clouds, and with the burnt-out mountains rising above and in the midst; MU_6,235.22.
Below, it was surrounded by mountain ranges and by nagas dwelling in the mud;
it was filled without interval by the falling torrents of the triple-pathed river (Ganges),
wherein the mountain peaks were submerged, raised up, and carried away like foam and bubbles.
With sky-dwellers crying out as fragments of heaven were being carried away,
and with the beautiful lotus-like faces of throngs of Vidyādhara women being swept along,
[the world] was submerged in the flood of the waters of the single ocean, which possessed the speed and gurgling roar of a rushing torrent.
When the collection of the three worlds was being swept away by the great waters,
there was no protector, nor even anyone who could offer a word of help;
for who is able to save that which has been swallowed by Time?
There was no sky, nor were there the quarters of space; there was nothing below, nor was there anything above.
There was neither being nor was there creation; there existed only the supreme, solitary water.
This is the chapter named "The Description of the Single Ocean."
The two hundred and thirty-sixth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
In the meantime, I, stationed in the sky, then cast my gaze [upon him].
In the world of Brahmā, in the world of Mahī, at dawn like the sun’s radiance,
I beheld there the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) established in meditative absorption, appearing as if carved from a mountain, accompanied by his principal retinue.
And there was an assembly of the Vedas and of sages of purified souls;
Śukra, Bṛhaspati, Śakra, Vaiśravaṇa, and Yama;
Soma, Varuṇa, and Agni, as well as other celestial ṛṣis.
The leaders of the gods, gandharvas, siddhas, and sādhyas—
whose forms were depicted in the work of painting— all remained intent on meditation,
seated there in the lotus posture as if they were lifeless.
Then these twelve Ādityas arrived at that very spot;
they stood there quickly in the same manner as before, with their bodies bound in the lotus posture (padmāsana).
Then, after only a moment, I no longer saw the Lotus-born One (abjaja).
Having first become awakened,
I did not see the entire host of people in the world of Brahmā, nor even that latent impression, as if they were a city seen in a dream passing before me upon waking.
At that time, O Brahmin, that city of Brahmā was utterly desolate,
like a town on earth destroyed by a sudden and violent calamity;
all those who were such as they were had then vanished somewhere.
The sages, the ascetics, the Vedas, the gods, the Vidyādharas, and the rest—
while standing in the sky, I perceived through my focused attention that they had all attained final liberation like Brahmā himself.
When latent impressions have dissolved, those who have reached the state of non-perception have returned to their own true nature, like people awakened from a dream-world.
This body, though its essence is space itself, appears clearly manifest through latent impressions.
But due to the absence of that [awakening], the dream does not appear to one who has awakened, just as it was before.
Just as a body situated in the intermediate space is perceived in a dream,
when one awakens and those latent impressions have subsided, nothing at all is observed.
Even while awake, when the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have likewise ceased,
neither the subtle body (*ativāhika*) nor the physical body (*adhibhautika*) is perceived here;
this experience of dreaming is the illustration in this case— by whom can it be refuted?
This has been established from childhood; it has been experienced, heard, and remembered.
Even if a deceitful person were to deny his own experience, he should be abandoned; for who indeed would try to wake a sleeping man with falsehood?

If you argue that a dream, which has the body as its cause, is not seen in the absence of a body, then for you there would likewise be no world beyond for those who are bodiless once this body has perished. If this were the case...
This creation would not have come into being, yet it certainly exists at all times.

Since destruction—which consists in the division of parts—is inevitable, it is impossible that this world was ever otherwise than it is now. Thus, the claim that it was not established as such at any time is untenable.

If you should say that this consciousness never arises from the body or the collection of elements at the destruction of the world— just as the power of intoxication [does not arise]— then [you must consider] those Purāṇas and Itihāsas which teach the total dissolution of all things.
Furthermore, O Mahāmati, the Vedas beginning with the *Smṛtis* would become useless regarding this matter due to their lack of authority;
how then could they possess authority even in other matters, such as the knowledge of dharma and so forth?
And this is not found in the world because it would lead to the annihilation of the universe;
moreover, my dear, let this be aside and hear another point from me:
that power of intoxication which is observed in one's own consciousness is seen in other places as well.
For those who have died, that state of having a body as a piśāca or other such being is not established.
If you argue that even this is a vain delusion that persists as long as the body is perceived, then for you, the very name "vain" would simply mean "true."
If that were so, why would this cognition— that there exists the other world with its heavens, hells, and so forth— not attain the status of truth?
If the appearance of a *piśāca* were true for one who possesses the instruction of a madman, [then why not this as well]?
If that which appears were not real, how could the nature of the next world be real? If you say, "A *piśāca* exists," and therefore consciousness has a real object,
then why would this [consciousness]— "the next world exists for the deceased"— not have reality?
If a ghostly cognition exists within the body by way of a chance occurrence like the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" maxim,
then why does the conscious awareness of the objects of the next world not exist as well, since its causes are present?
Whatever consciousness perceives internally, it experiences that very thing accordingly and sufficiently.

Whether it be true or false, let it be established by experience that there is a world beyond for the deceased; such a conviction may thus arise. Whether this body exists or does not exist, what is real and what is unreal in that regard?
Therefore, the innate nature (*svabhāva*), first manifesting, perceives consciousness;

subsequently, having understood the cause to be latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it beholds the delusion. Through the destruction of that [delusion], the affliction consisting of the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing comes to rest.
When that [Brahman] exists, this female demon called "saṃsāra" arises.
First, perception arises; from that comes the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of Brahman.
Know that its cessation is *nirvāṇa*, and its existence is the delusion of *saṃsāra*.
That [duality] has never arisen at all, because it is impossible in the Supreme Brahman;
and even that which appears to have arisen is indeed Brahman alone, the ultimate reality.
The wise know that the thorough realization of this much is Nirvāṇa.
Know that very lack of thorough knowledge regarding this, O Rāghava, to be bondage.
This [Self] is a mass of consciousness alone, whose nature consists of both shining and not shining;
it shines by itself within, or indeed does not shine at all by itself.

The view of bondage and the view of liberation consist merely in the subtle transformation of a portion of consciousness; how great, then, is the affliction in their realization? Awakening to consciousness is bondage, and its non-awakening is Śiva.
The world, though non-existent, appears as if real, its interior filled by the awakening of consciousness.
Non-inert awareness while asleep is called liberation;
that which is awakened is called bondage. Take whichever you desire.

Remain in peace, O you whose mind is as clear as the expanse of space— possessing the infinite impression of Nirvana, free from dullness, a continuous flow of pure awakening, unconditioned, devoid of doubt, non-dual yet not lacking unity, and having cast out all emptiness.
This is the chapter titled "The Demonstration of the Absence of Latent Impressions" (Vāsanābhāvapratipādana).
The two hundred and thirty-seventh canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
"Thus all those inhabitants of the world of Brahmā arrived."
The lamps became invisible, like wicks whose oil is exhausted. Then,
when Brahmā had attained absorption into Brahman, those twelve Ādityas,
with their blazing rays, consumed that world of Brahmā just as they consume the world.
Having burned the city of Viriñca and having entered meditative absorption like Viriñca himself,
they too attained nirvāṇa, like ten oil-less lamps. Then, the flood of the single ocean filled the interior of Viriñca’s city.
At night, he filled the earth with darkness as if it were a hollow metal tube;
the entire world, up to the realm of Brahmā, became filled with that fluid,
like a ripe grape fruit filled entirely with juice.
Then, by the masses of waves and mountain ranges that completely enveloped everything, the clouds of the kalpa were shattered and dissolved back into the water itself.
In that interval, I beheld there from the sky—
Then there arose from the midst of the sky a certain terrifying being,
resembling a cloud at the end of an aeon; black, filling the atmosphere,
it was like the darkness of the night accumulated since the beginning of time, risen up in bodily form.
Bearing a brilliant splendor like that of a million rising suns,
with faces radiant with eyes resembling three suns and intense with three steady flashes of lightning, he vomited forth masses of flames.

Having assumed a body that was five-faced, ten-armed, three-eyed, and holding a trident in its hand; a form as vast as the sky even though it had reached the end of non-existence, and dark like a fine sword, he remained standing like the ether itself.
It remained in the sky outside the cosmic egg filled with the single ocean,
like the void itself characterized by the arrangement of hands, feet, and other limbs;
it stirred the great single ocean by the turning of the breath from its nostrils.
Like Govinda [Viṣṇu] who agitated the Ocean of Milk with his staff-like arms,
he was like the flood of the waters of the Kalpa-ocean arisen in the form of a male;
he was ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra) incarnate, appearing without cause.
Like a great multitude of mountain ranges rising with the splendor of flight,
he filled the entire sky with the mass of his wings.
Then, by means of my trident and eyes, I recognized him, thinking, "This is Rudra."
Having recognized him from afar, the Supreme Lord was saluted.
Rāma asked: "Is that Rudra of such a kind? Is he Kṛṣṇa, or is he of great form?"
Why does he have five faces, and why ten arms? Where does he abide?
Why does he have three eyes, and why is his nature fierce? Why is he alone, and what is his purpose?
By whom was he impelled, what did he do, and where did he go? Tell me, O Sage.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O descendant of Kakutstha, this ego-sense named Rudra has likewise arisen;
its nature is the conceit of being unique, and its form is the pure sky.
That Blessed One has the form of space; he is great, stainless, and the color of space.
Because his essence consists solely of the space of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), he is called the self of space (*ākāśātmā*).
Because he has become the self of all beings and because he is omnipresent, he possesses a vast form.
Those five sense-faculties that are attached to it are said to be its faces, appearing in every form;
for the organs of action and their objects are its ten arms.
When he was completely abandoned by Brahmā, who had arrived at the supreme state along with the burdens of all beings, then he assumed a form. Yet he,
whose self is of the singular nature of space, possesses no physical shape.
Thus, that [Lord] is indeed perceived as mere illusion and does not possess a physical form.
He abides within the vast elemental ether that has become the space of consciousness,
and he dwells eternally within the bodies of all beings like the wind.
At that time, having abandoned all elemental beings and possessing a form of space,
he will experience agitation for a moment and, being diminished, shall attain supreme peace.
Those which are the three qualities, those which are the three times, and mind, ego, and intellect— [all these shall cease].
The syllables of the *praṇava* and likewise the three Vedas are situated within the arrangement of that Rudra’s eyes; by him,
the triple world has been grasped as a trident within the hollow of his hand.
Since nothing else whatsoever exists apart from that [Self], even among the multitudes of all living beings, therefore the body alone stands as the Self;
its purpose is its own nature, which consists in the perception of the existence of creation.
He is impelled by Śiva, who is of the nature of the space of pure consciousness;
and being swallowed by that very [Śiva], he shall attain supreme peace.
This Lord Kṛṣṇa is of the nature of the stainless ether-soul.
Having reduced the entire world to a single ocean at the end of the eon, he then drinks that up and attains supreme peace, so as never to return to existence again.
Immediately thereafter, I saw him there for as long as his exertion lasted.
He set out with the force of his vital breath to draw that great ocean toward him;
then, drawn by his breath, the great sea entered his wide-open mouth, which was filled within with garlands of flames, like the submarine fire entering the ocean.
Becoming the Vāḍava fire, that very ego (ahaṅkāra) as Rudra drinks up all that water in the ocean until the end of the kalpa;
in an instant, it is like water swallowed by Pātāla, or a hole by a serpent.
Like a fierce wind entering the sky, he entered his mouth with speed.
Rudra drank up that milk in an instant,
just as the sun, dark-bodied, consumes the darkness, or as contact with the virtuous destroys vice.

From the world of Brahmā down to the netherworld (pātāla), all became peaceful and empty; the sky was uniform, freed from dust, smoke, wind, clouds, and the elements. There, only four things were seen, as pure as the firmament.
These objects are motionless; hear about them, O delight of the Raghus.
First of all, there is that Rudra in the center, appearing in the form of black garments;
he stands without support in the void, motionless like the reflection of the ocean.
The second part remains far away, resembling the surface of the earth and the sky;
it is the portion of the abode of the cosmic egg situated below the seven netherworlds (pātāla),
