including the netherworlds, the terrestrial realm, the heavens, the great mountains, and the celestial dwellers.
There was a slight pervasion by the earthly portion, consisting merely of mud;
then, a third entity arose here, the region above the sphere of Brahmā.
Due to its distance and the cessation of sight, it appeared as dark as the sky.
That which lies between the two widely separated fragments of the cosmic egg is space—
beginningless and endless, the pure and all-pervading Brahman.
At that time, this fourth category of reality was clearly perceived by me.
"Apart from these four, there is nothing else whatsoever other than this.
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, what exists outside the door of the temple of Brahman?"
"Tell me, what are the obstructions there? How many are they established, and in what manner?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Beyond the two hemispheres of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), there is water ten times as vast."
Beyond that, there exists the infinite, expanded, and pervasive twilight sky;
beyond that, in the same manner, stands the fiery energy consisting of flames, tenfold in power;
and beyond that, in the same way, stands the purifying and stainless wind.
Then, in that very manner, the pure sky remained tenfold;
beyond that was the supreme, utterly transparent, infinite space of Brahmā.
Then, here and there in the sky, his other visions likewise appeared.
"Countless [worlds] shine, situated far apart, their own creations unseen by one another.
Rāma said:
"O Lord of Sages, above that fragment of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and below it—"
Where, how, and by whom is that water and so forth, which possesses such a vast form, supported?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
That earthly element among all things stands like a supporting pillar-jewel.
The parts run toward that very [source], just as sons run to their mother;
therefore, all objects hasten toward that which is nearest— the body of the earth called the cosmic egg— just as the thirsty run to water.
Therefore, depending upon that very [Self], water and the other elements remain established;
they do not abandon their own state of existence, just as the limbs [of a body] do not.
Rāma said:
"O Brahman, how do those two halves of the cosmic egg remain? Tell me:
what is their form, by whom are they supported, and how do they perish?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
The unsupported appears as if supported, and that which has fallen seems as if it were falling;
the world, though formless, appears with form like a city in a dream.
What indeed falls here, or by what is it supported?
Just as there is the manifestation of consciousness, so does this abide.
Just as a mass of hair [appears] in the sky, and just as there is emptiness in the sky,
or just as there is vibration in the wind, so is the world in the sky of consciousness.
Upon the funeral pyre stands the city of imagination, the house of the world called the cosmic egg;
it exists like the sky within the sky, utterly formless yet appearing as if having form.
Arising from the consciousness of its own fall, it remains falling day and night.
That which arises from the consciousness of one who is leaping remains even while leaping;
that which arises from the consciousness of one who is standing remains day and night while standing;
and that which arises from the consciousness of one who is walking remains day and night while walking.
The knower of destruction meets with destruction through the perceptions of great kalpas and the like;
it is born through the consciousness of birth, and through the perceptions of creation and so forth within the void.
Like a cluster of pearls appearing within the expanse of the autumnal sky, though unreal when seen, it arises with a form that appears exceedingly real.
Who here is capable of determining the number of these worlds, which flash forth in the sky through delusion?
The chapter titled "The Exposition of the State of Mere Delusion," the two hundred and thirty-eighth chapter.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, O Rāghava, I beheld that Rudra in the great sky at that time, having begun to dance like one intoxicated, possessing a vast form.
Like the sky having assumed a form, yet not abandoning its own inherent pervasiveness,
he was of immense stature, dark as a rain-cloud, and filling the ten directions;
his eyes were the sun, the moon, and fire, and his garments were the moving winds of the ten quarters.
A dense and long-reaching web of light, a tethering post for those of dark luster;
resembling the submarine fire, radiant with the weight of its surging waves of trembling arms,
it rose up as if suddenly from the waters of the single ocean by means of a bodily form.
Immediately thereafter, I saw that from his body there issued forth,
like a shadow, something that moved in accordance with his dancing—
even when the suns were absent, in the thick of great darkness.
"While he stood there, I thought to myself, 'How could this shadow have come to be? Even as I was reflecting quickly,
right before him, that woman— three-eyed and disheveled— stood there dancing."

Dark, emaciated, with veins showing on her limbs, decrepit and deformed in appearance, she was like a night that had assumed a physical form— black as crushed collyrium— crowned with a mass of forest fuel flickering in a fire filled with flames.
It was like the splendor of darkness embodied, like the radiance of the sky made manifest with form;
exceedingly long and with a terrifying mouth, it seemed intent on measuring the heavens,
and by the appearance of its long knees and arms, as if desiring to measure the quarters of the sky.
Emaciated as if by many fasts, with her great jawbones deeply sunken,
she was dark as collyrium like a line of clouds tossed by the wind;
when she was thus thin and powerless to rise, she was made very tall by fate.
It was as if bound by cords in the form of veins, long and reaching far;
indeed, she was so exceedingly tall that I beheld her head and hoof only with great effort, through repeated upward and downward movements over a long time.
With heaps of skulls, hooves, and hands strung together like strings of moist entrails, rootless and entwined with sinews like a thicket of thorns,
she possesses a universal form through the clusters of lotus-like heads of Yama, the Sun, and others.
She wore a garland of skulls, her gaze was stainless, and she vomited forth mountains of fire;
her ears hung down, her nose was flattened, and she had earrings made of human heads;
she spat out dried gourd-vines, and her long, dangling breasts were dark.
Her skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) is marked by the circles of Brahmā’s hair, which flows like a mass of Kumāra’s peacock feathers;
she illuminates the ocean of darkness with the pure radiance of her garland of moon-like teeth.
Dark and loud, like a streak of smoke, it whirled in circular eddies;
high up, it clung to the tree of the sky like a vine of dry pumpkins,
its limbs tossing about with a rustling *paṭapaṭa* sound caused by the winds.
With her arms raised like great waves, she shines with a dark and radiant splendor;
like a garland of waves upon the single ocean, she whirls in the eddies of her dance.
For a moment she takes the form of a single arm, and for a moment she is crowded with many arms.
With infinite, fierce arms, she is quickly the dance-pavilion of the world;
she is quickly of one-faced form, and quickly of many-faced appearance;
with infinite, fierce faces, she is quickly even faceless for a moment.
"Endowed with a single foot one moment, and very quickly endowed with a hundred feet the next;
at one instant rich with infinite feet, and at another moment appearing footless—
this is that Night of Time (Kālarātri), as I have inferred from her bodily form."
"This is indeed the Goddess Kālī"— thus was she determined by those moving about;
her three eyes resembled a fierce well filled with flames,
and the region of her forehead was like the peak of a blazing mountain of sapphire.
Her two formidable jaws were like the deep chasms at the summit of the world-illuminating sapphire mountain;
she wore a pearl necklace of stars strung upon the thread of the wind-bands,
and her broad, high arches shone like mountains of sapphire.
With her vulva as terrifying as a mountain of black glass, she was like a female crow;
with the flowers of her dancing vine-like arms— her bright, whirling circles of nails—
she seemed to whirl hundreds of full moons across the expanse of the sky.
With arms whirling like the clouds at the end of an aeon that pervaded the circle of the quarters, raining down great flashes of light from the tips of their fingernails like stars,
they appeared as if the trees of their arms were swaying, covered by the networks of their finger-creepers adorned with the flowers of their nails.
With her dark, massive forms that covered the entire expanse of the sky,
she approached, mocking with her moving multitude of shanks the great fires that had not yet consumed the roots of the *tāla* and *tamāla* trees.
With his hair reaching the far shore of the infinite great sky,
it seemed as if he were creating a vast canopy for the elephant of darkness;
by that wind of his breath, even the Meru mountains are carried along.
With a roar that resounded through the vast limbs of the sky and the quarters of the world with thick *ghuṅghuma* sounds,
he sang this song of battle-cry (*kṣveḍāgeya*) amidst the whistling blasts of the dense winds;
his face turned toward him as if in a constant conciliation, following his lead.

Then, as she grew in body through the intensity of her passion for dancing, she filled the expanse of the sky; and with my attention fixed, I beheld her as she held within her form the essence of playful, undulating movements.

The garlands of clouds at the end of the eon, formed by the Malaya, Kailāsa, Sahya, Mandara, and Meru mountains, served as her silk headbands; and the three worlds, situated between the spheres, were the circular mirrors before her.
The Himalaya and Meru mountains are her earrings, fashioned from silver and gold;
the great garland of the Brahmāṇḍa is her girdle;
and the principal mountain ranges are her flower-strings, with their peaks, forests, and cities as clusters of blossoms.
The flowing rivers, excellent islands, villages, and tender sprouts were seen upon her limbs; likewise, the cities and towns,
the three worlds, the seasons, and the sequence of months, days, and nights were all contained within her body.
Her pearl necklaces and the like are the rivers such as the Kālindī and the Tripathagā;
both dharma and adharma are the ornaments on her other two ears. Her four breasts are drops of the flowing water of dharma.
The Vedas are her nipples, with the meanings of all the scriptures as their fourfold arrangement.
She bears garlands of flower-strings that are the emerging masses of weapons: tridents, sharp-edged spears, barbed missiles, arrows, pikes, double-edged swords, and mallets.
The fourteen kinds of elemental beings, beginning with the gods,
which dwell within her body, exist as the rows of hair upon her;
and the cities, villages, and mountains likewise reside within her body.

As she dances, they dance along with her for the sake of renewed birth; at that time, this entire world, including all moving beings and excluding the stationary, dances. Thus have I realized that one remains established in happiness in the next world.
Having swallowed the world and placed it within her own body, she has attained satisfaction;
intoxicated, she dances about like a peahen that has consumed an old snake. The entire world appears as if situated within a mirror’s reflection.
Upon her expansive body, which bore the form of a donkey, the one assuming the form of a donkey beheld that beautiful dance of the world situated within the mirror of her body;
at that time, it was seen by me for a long duration, standing before me and undecaying.
The network of stars was flickering, the circle of mountains was whirling,
and the gods and demons were shaken by the wind like a swarm of gnats;
the sky was enveloped by islands and oceans that resembled the circles of wheels released in battle.

In which the great mountain ranges were like blades of grass tossed by the whirlpools of its playful surging; the sky resounded with the *ghuṅghuma* noise of the winds as they blew away the dark-blue cloud-garments;
and there arose a loud *paṭat-paṭa* clatter from the shattering of the cities upon the bones of the world’s pillars and mountains.
Just as the world is pervaded by objects— both mixed and unmixed— like reflections in a mirror,
so too is it filled with limbs that possess expansive forms and the delusions of the stage;
Meru dances, its great arms being the swaying, lofty principal mountain ranges.
With the mass of its clouds whirling and the hair of its trees— the winds— bowing down,
the oceans, though rushing, did not abandon their seal of boundaries;
they went from the earth to the sky, and from the sky to the surface of the earth.
Cities are seen rolling below with gurgling roars, along with their houses, watchtowers, and inhabitants; yet nothing at all rolls below that [city].
As it whirls about, the sun and moon, the days and nights, move skillfully within it.

The light from the tips of her nails shines like golden threads amidst the intervals [of her body]. The showers of perspiration born of her feverish distress gleam like clouds laden with frost, as she is clothed in the garments of her playful grace.
Her vast, well-formed circle of braided hair was the sky;
her feet were the netherworld (pātāla), her belly the earth, and her arms the cardinal directions.
Her coils of intestines were the islands and oceans, and all the mountains were her ribs.
The rows of her out-breaths and in-breaths were like swings, and her body was like a palanquin for the masses of wind;
as she danced upon that expansive form,
the Himavat, Meru, Sahya, and other mountains served as the swinging cradles.
As she twirled her garlands with arms whose qualities were like those of the Tarada mountain,
it was as if the cosmic dance (tāṇḍava) had begun once more at the end of an eon through her effortless play.
Her body was fierce, its hair-like scales belonging to the hosts of gods, asuras, and serpents.
She was unable to remain motionless, like a whirling wheel;
wearing the sacrificial thread of various manifestations of consciousness,
she moved through the sky, making a sound like the deep rumbling of clouds.
There, the ground becomes space, and space also becomes the ground; having formed these mental images, they exist within, yet nothing at all undergoes transformation.
Thick, resonant humming sounds emerge from the vast cavernous chamber of the nostrils.
There, fierce winds blow, producing deep rumbling sounds.
And her sky, with its hundreds of hands performing the four-fold whirling dance,
shines as if strewn with sprouts tossed up by a violent wind.
Due to the agitation caused by the whirling of the multitude of objects in that world-system,
even my firm vision was paralyzed by delusion, like an army in the heat of battle;
mountains were carried away as if by machines, and sky-dwellers fell down.
The palaces of the immortals roll about like dust in the moving mirror of that body;
the Meru mountains are scattered like leaves, the Malaya mountains like sprouts,
the Himalayas like particles of frost, and the earths like creepers upon the clouds.
The Sahya mountains were like birds upon the earth, the Vindhya mountains like Vidyādharas,
and the Ṛkṣavanta mountains wandered within like swans in the sky.
Even the continents were like blades of grass, and the oceans like bracelets.
The lotuses that dwell in the celestial realm were present in the water of her body—
her limbs, which resembled the clear sky and were like cities seen in a dream or through collyrium, possessed large shanks and a luster like that of a mirror filled with solidified paste.
Vindhya dances in the forest of the Golden Mountain; Sahya, the mountain on earth; Kailāsa, Malaya, and Mandara on the peak of Mahendra;
Gokarṇa in the courtyard of the sky; and all the forest lands of that [city] have attained mobility within the city of the Vidyādharas.
Then, within the body:
the ocean dances upon the mountain, and even the mountain leaps high into the hollow of the sky; the very firmament, encircled by the moon, sun, and stars, has gone beneath the earth.
The forested multitude of the six continents, mountains, and cities, strewn with blossoms, whirls like a blade of grass in the ocean amidst the world in the expanse of the quarters of the sky;
mountains, oceans, the regions at the ends of the directions, the intermediate worlds, and the circles of cities and towns wander in the firmament.
In the mirrors of rivers and lakes, there appeared, in succession, heaps of grass and leaves scattered by the wind;
fish swam in the desert as if in excellent water, and cities stood firm in the sky as if on the earth.
The earth was in the sky and the sky was below, filled with inexhaustible clouds and mountains whirled about by the winds of cosmic dissolution.
The multitude of stars revolves with the circular motion of a thousand lamps' mechanism, beautiful like a cloud raining down jewels;

within and without, a rain of flowers is released by the hosts of *vidyādharas* and immortals as if out of startled affection. The multitudes of days and nights, in their cycles of dissolution and creation, are like mere droplets.
Black and white objects shimmer all around, crowded together like the pure white and black circles of a mirror;
jewels, the orbs of the sun and moon, clusters of stars, necklaces bearing flickering luster, clear garments,
and swirling great cloths incessantly create the appearance of many firebrands.
At the time of the end of the eon, the various and excellent jewels of the three worlds, tumbling about, suddenly produce a clanging *jhana-jhana* sound with their revolutions;
these radiant ornaments, possessing manifold qualities, move continuously upward and downward.
[This occurs] when all the days and sunlight turn dark, as if by the waves of light from the swords of warriors intoxicated by battle.
Even though they are well-established, a clamor is heard from the circles of people as they tumble about in their various turnings.

(MU 6.238.82) The gods and asuras, headed by Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, Hara, Agni, Ravi, and Indu, rushing forward in their revolutions, come and go only toward one another, like flies and gnats tossed about by the wind. (MU 6.238.83)

In that [state], all phenomena— contraction and emanation, pleasure and pain, birth and non-birth, desire and lack of desire, prohibition and injunction, birth and death, delusion, and so forth— always manifest together and separately, even when they have reached a state of total intermingling.
[They are the] delusions of the arising, persistence, and destruction of entities, and the revolutions of the worlds through contraction, emanation, and the protection of the earth.
In this [world], not even the slightest number can be discerned of those ethereal bodies that shine forth falsely in the sky.

Therein, portents, the pacification of calamities, death, festivals, battles, impartiality, hatred, passion, fear, trust, and so forth, shine like a collection of jewels within a single casket; it is a succession of creations of various flavors, unimpeded and supreme.
Within her body, which consists of the ether of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), the arrangements of the world— which exist as its very nature and are characterized by clear experience—
vibrate everywhere, including the states of creation and dissolution, like the shimmering of a mass of hair floating in the sky perceived by one with impaired vision.
Thus the world is seen both agitated and unagitated, existing in a state of constant flux.
It stands like the reflection of a sprout being moved.

Even though they remain fixed in their dance-like posture, the purposes of the world within them abandon their stability and assume it anew at every moment, like the creations born of a child’s imagination.
Constantly being purified within the body of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*),
the heaps of the world’s mung-bean grains are shattered as they accumulate;
for one moment something is perceived, and for another moment nothing at all.
At one moment she is only the size of a thumb, and at another moment she fills the sky.
Because that Goddess is the power of consciousness (*saṃvit-śakti*), whose nature is the world;
she is infinite, possessing a pure body that is the treasury of the supreme space.

Consciousness (cit), whose body is the sky of the three worlds existing throughout the three times, shines forth in such a manner by means of that very form which exists as such—a form resembling the web of the world-painting situated within the mind of a master painter, shining with a swift radiance.
Because it consists of many conscious selves, its body is of the nature of emanation; because it consists of a single knowing self, its body is the one, utterly tranquil void.

Bearing a single form that is both closed and opened in a single blink, she shines as an infinite and beginningless body. Within her, that visible world—consisting of infinite stones, mines, lines, lotuses, wheels, and the like—shines forth, just as ripples appear in the ocean’s depths because it is consciousness, even though its body is merely the void of space. (MU 6.238.94–95)
The great goddess Bhairavī, filling the sky,
danced before that Bhairava-formed Rudra at the end of the eon;
the earth and its forests appeared like withered stumps, scorched by the fierce fire residing in his veins and vital points.
Shaken by the winds at the end of the eon, she dances like a garland of forest flowers;
she bears mortars, pestles, grass mats, plows, winnowing baskets,
and containers, as well as clubs, water-jars, cooking pots, jars, garlands, and wreaths.
Scattering and intermingling a mass of flowers from such networks of garlands,
she caused that vast expanse to be stirred by her dance;
and even as he was being thus honored by her, Ākāśabhairava likewise remained there.
In that very manner, assuming an expanded form, he then dances intensely:
"ḍimbaṃ ḍimbaṃ kuḍimbaṃ paca mana ḍuha mā jham prajham praṃ prajham praṃ tṛllaṃ tṛllaṃ tṛtṛllaṃ tṛkhalu khalumayaṃ khaṅkhamaṃ khaṅkhamaṅkham."
"Guṃ haṃ guṃ haṃ tu guṃ haṃ guḍulaḍuḍumuḍaṃ ḍāḍimāḍiṃ ḍuḍeti"— dancing with sounds as her musical instruments in the cremation ground of universal dissolution, may Kālī grant you prosperity!
Having bound the tawny mass of Brahmā’s matted locks upon the tip of her skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), she has fashioned a garland from the severed heads of the foremost Daityas.

May Bhairava protect you— he who, with his hand holding the great horn of Yama’s buffalo, filled with the wine of blood, bears upon his chest a crest of Tārkṣya feathers, while being praised by Kālarātri, who rejoices in the dissolution of the world.
In the *Pāṣāṇopākhyāna*, the chapter titled "The Description of Kālarātri," the two hundred and thirty-ninth chapter;
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, why does she dance at the destruction of all things? What is she?
Why does she wear a garland of winnowing baskets, plows, jars, and the like?
What has been destroyed so that the three worlds exist again? And what is it that resides within the body of Kālī?"
“Nirvāṇa dances about; how then has it come to pass? Vasiṣṭha replied:
“That is neither man, nor woman, nor that dance, nor those two.”
In that which has become thus and acts thus, there is no form, nor do those two exist.
That which is the beginningless sky of pure consciousness is the cause of causes;
it is infinite, peaceful, a mere manifestation, all-pervasive, and imperishable.
That is Śiva; he is perceived as Śiva himself in the form of Bhairava.

Abiding thus for the sake of the peace of the world, he is indeed the supreme space (paramākāśa). Because he is consciousness, he is such by virtue of the manifestation of his own nature, even without [external] power.
It is not logical for that [consciousness] to exist without its form, just as it is not possible for gold to exist without its [golden] nature.
Tell me, O wise one, how could pure consciousness exist without sentience?
Tell me, O wise one, how could black pepper exist without its pungency?
Look: how could gold exist without its bracelets and other ornaments?
How could an object persist without its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva)?
Tell me, how could the sweetness of sugarcane juice remain without it?
That which lacks sweetness is not indeed sugarcane juice;
likewise, that which is pure consciousness (cinmātra) yet lacks sentience is not called pure consciousness.
Furthermore, it is not possible for the space of pure consciousness to ever perish anywhere.
Nothing other than his own mere existence is tenable for him;
indeed, he must necessarily accept his distinctness from space.
Therefore, that which is his own unshakable abode is his mere existence.

Without beginning, middle, or end, its essence consists of all powers. O Rāma, this very thing is the creation of the three worlds, the end of the eon, the sky, the earth, and the directions; it is destruction, production, cessation, light, and darkness.
Birth and death, illusion, delusion, dullness, non-substantiality, and substantiality; discernment, bondage, liberation, the auspicious and the inauspicious;
knowledge and ignorance, embodied state and disembodied state, the momentary and the long-lasting.
You are restlessness and you are stillness; you are "I," and you are "it" and "the other.

You are the existent and the non-existent, as well as both existent and non-existent; you are ignorance and wisdom, space and time, the reckoning of actions and substances, and the imagination of play.
This entire expanse— consisting of form, light, mental attention, action, the intellect, the sense organs, fire, water, air,
space, earth, and so forth— is that very pure, untainted sky of consciousness.
Without abandoning its very nature as space, the Self of all remains established in this way;
and all this is undoubtedly just the stainless sky.
A mountain in a dream is an unimpeachable illustration here for its non-difference from that [sky].
This supreme space consisting of consciousness which has been described by me—this is called Śiva; he is the eternal one.
He exists as Hari, and he is the Grandfather (Brahmā).
The moon, the sun, Indra, Varuṇa, Yama, Vaiśravaṇa, and Anila; fire, the rain-cloud, and the ocean; "yesterday," "today," and "tomorrow"—these exist and do not exist;
they are merely the full manifestations of fragments from the treasury of the space of consciousness.
Through such perceptions, these things appear as they do due to false cultivation;
yet, through the realization of mere self-nature, they become exactly as they are.
Non-awareness and awareness—thus, the sky of consciousness alone abides within the Self.

Therefore, let there be peace, for there is no such thing as the emergence of difference from unity. As long as this living soul does not know its own supreme nature and attain absorption in it, so long does it act as a wave within the great ocean of its own saṃsāra.
But once it is known, he attains peace in such a way that there is neither that ocean nor those waves;
and all this, as it truly is, becomes peaceful, infinite, and his very supreme self.
The chapter titled "Description of the Nature of Śiva" in the Story of the Stone.
The two hundred and fortieth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
This which has been described by me is the supreme space of pure consciousness alone.
"This is that one called Śiva," so saying, Rudra then begins to dance.
O best of the accomplished, that form of his is no form at all;
rather, it is the void of pure consciousness alone that shines forth in such a manner.
I saw that very sky, peaceful and having that form; it was understood by me alone—no one else sees it as such. Just as that [was] the end of the aeon, that Rudra, and that Bhairavī.

Thus, everything has been fully understood by me as mere illusion. O Rāma, it is only the supreme void of the consciousness-ether that appears in such a manner through its particular arrangement, having assumed the form of Bhairava; nothing else exists.
"Since no understanding arises without the relationship between the signified and the signifier,
therefore, O Rāma, that which has been described by me to you as being present within you is precisely that which has ascended to the level of the signified."
For those whose perception of the material world has become firmly rooted, that which in an instant attains the nature of reality is not Bhairavī,
nor is he Bhairava, nor is there that destruction;
all of it is merely delusion, and only the sky of consciousness shines forth.
Like a city created in a dream, like the force of a desire in the ocean, like the delight in a caravan of goods described in a story, and like the play of a kingdom of the mind;
just as one perceives a city in a dream, or as one mistakes a clear sky for a string of pearls.
Just as a mass of hair appears in the sky, so does consciousness shine within the density of consciousness.
The pure space of pure consciousness alone flashes forth by itself within itself;
just as it is named, so it appears as the world, being that very self.
Just as the Self itself shines forth within the sky of consciousness as the world,
so too does that dance of Śiva at the end of the aeon shine forth therein.
O dear one, such is the form of Śiva and Śivā described as being formless.

Now listen; I shall explain to you the state of dance as non-dance: A conscious entity cannot remain anywhere without some movement caused by consciousness, just as an object cannot exist as a non-object.
Consciousness exists as Rudra by virtue of its own nature,
just as gold exists in the form of a decorative ornament through its arrangement.
Whatever is indeed consciousness, wherever it may be, that necessarily exists by its very nature.
For reality, born of its own nature, necessarily possesses the quality of vibration.
That very vibration which belongs to this Śiva, who is a mass of consciousness,
appears to us as a dance due to the influence of the immersion in one's own latent impressions.

"Therefore, know that when Rudra, who is auspicious at the end of the aeon, assumes a fierce form and dances swiftly, that is indeed his own inherent vibration of the mass of consciousness. Rāma said:
From the perspective of valid cognition, this visible world does not exist at all in reality;
or, if it does exist, it will all perish at the end of the aeon.
Then, in this great void at the end of the aeon, within this supreme ether—
"How does the mass of consciousness (cidghana) perceive what object, or by what name, it perceives?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O dear one, even then, this very [consciousness] exists for the sake of bringing to rest the cloud of duality and unity."
If there is no object of thought whatsoever within the sky of pure consciousness,
then nothing is perceived by anyone anywhere at any time; everything is tranquil, like the silence of stone, a dense mass of awareness, the very expanse of space.
And that which is called "the object of cognition" is merely the movement of its own nature (*svabhāva*),
because the tranquil nature of consciousness remains established in its own being.
Just as in a dream, consciousness itself appears internally like a city or a town.

It is not something like a city or the like; rather, it is simply the space of consciousness (*vijñānākāśa*). Within itself, by means of itself, that void of consciousness—sufficient as both knower and the known—knows its own self and its own manifestation from the very beginning of creation.
Within the sky of one's own nature, which is the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) shining with its own inner luster,
such conceptualizations as "this is he," "I am this," and "you do this" arise.
Therefore, there is no duality here, nor is there unity, nor is there emptiness.
If there is no cognizer and no cognition, that is indeed silence, or rather, it is not even that.
Since nothing whatsoever is cognized anywhere by anyone, due to the absence of anything to be cognized and so forth, the cognizer likewise does not exist; thus, only silence remains.
For non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in all verbal systems; and that is the silence of a living stone.
Therefore, remain simply silent.
While remaining unmoving from the silence of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-mauna*), perform the web of conventional conduct (*ācāra-jāla*) that is your own natural activity, just as it flows.
Remain peaceful, with a mind as clear as the expanse of the sky, free from pride, delusion, and intoxication, and with the life-force of the bodiless one (Aṅgaja) [Kāmadeva].
The chapter titled "The Description of Viśvarūpa in the Story of the Stone," the two hundred and forty-first chapter.
Rāma:
O Sage, tell me what follows: why does Kālī dance in this manner?
Is it her delight in wearing garlands made of winnowing baskets, ploughs, spades, clubs, and other such implements?
Vasiṣṭha said:
That Bhairava is the space of consciousness, designated as Śiva;
know that his power of vibration (spanda-śakti) is non-different from him and free from all affliction.
Just as wind and its movement are one, and just as heat and fire are one,
so too pure consciousness and the power of movement are always of a single nature.
Wind is characterized by its movement, and fire is characterized by its heat.
That [Śiva] is perceived in this way only through the power of vibration (spanda-śakti), and certainly not otherwise.
The wise know Śiva as Brahman—tranquil and even beyond the description of those who master speech.
It is that power of vibration which extends the appearance of the visible world by cutting off His [undifferentiated] nature.

Just as the will or the mental construction of a person possessing form creates a city of imagination, so too does the will of Śiva— though he is formless— create this universe. This very [will] is called consciousness (cit), arising as it does through its orientation toward the object of consciousness (cetyonmukhatā).

This very [entity] is called by the name "vāsanā," because from vāsanā arises the consciousness of the visible world. This is declared to be the "portion of the individual soul" (jīvakalā), for through its animation it is the desire for life;
as the nature of creation, it has itself attained the state of primordial matter (prakṛti).
She is called *Kriyā* because she brings about the experience of the appearances of the perceptible;
she is called *Śuṣkā* because she withers, having the form of the crest of the submarine fire (*vāḍavāgni*);
she is called *Caṇḍikā* because of her ferocity; and she is [called] *Utpalā* because of her lotus-like color.
She is *Jayā* because she is solely intent on victory, and *Siddhā* because she is the refuge of accomplishment;
she is called *Jayantī* because of her triumph, and *Vijayā* because she is the basis of conquest.
She is declared *Aparājitā* due to her heroism, and *Durgā* because her form is difficult to grasp.
She is celebrated as Sārā because she is the essence-power (*sāra-śakti*) of the syllable *oṃ*;
she is Gāyatrī because her nature is singing (*gāyana*); she is Sāvitrī because of her abiding in procreation (*prasava*);
and she is called Sarasvatī because she causes all philosophical views (*sarva-dṛṣṭi*) to flow forth (*saraṇa*).

Gaurī is so called because her body is fair-complexioned; she is ever attached to the body of Bhava. Furthermore, for all beings in the three worlds, whether asleep or awake, the syllable *am* is eternally uttered within their hearts; thus she is called *Amā*, the digit of the moon.
Because the two Śivas have the nature of space (*vyoma*), their body appears black;
for the sky is seen by them as flesh drawn forth by their vision.
The sky abides in the sky itself; therefore, those two are situated in the sky.
The two elder brothers were like the sky, with limbs that were non-material and as clear as the firmament.

Listen now to how, due to differences in the multiplicity or scarcity of hands, feet, shoulders, and heads, there arose diversity among them, such as the bearing of plows, winnowing baskets, garlands, and other items.
For that divine power of action, whose sole form is vibration,
assumes fierce bodies such as "one should give," "one should bathe," or "one should offer oblations";
likewise, the beginningless and endless power of consciousness shines within itself by means of its own self.
Possessing a form like space, peaceful, the beauty of the visible world, and having vibration as her form—
those various dramatic gestures and movements of that Goddess Kālī are indeed these modes of creation, old age, and death belonging to Brahmā.
This Action, through its vibration, creates and sustains within itself the series of villages, cities, islands, and provinces, which consist of imagined constituent parts.
Kālī is the lotus-pond; Kālī is Action; she is the Kālī of the cosmic egg.

The Goddess of Consciousness never at any time possesses this visible characteristic as a part of herself within her heart; for the Goddess of Consciousness is never anywhere possessed of visible parts. Apart from the state of Śiva, the very nature of Śiva is visibility.
Just as emptiness is an inherent part of space, movement of the wind,
and coolness is the very nature of moonlight, so too is activity an inherent part of consciousness.
Know that Śiva is peaceful, effortless, ineffable, and stainless.
Therein, due to its state of stillness, there is not even the slightest trace of the nature of vibration.
When that very activity, being of such a form, remains in that same state through the power of awakening after having ceased [its outward manifestation], it is then called Śiva.
When the establishment of the power of consciousness (citiśakti), the goddess of action, occurs within the self,
one is called Śiva at that very moment, precisely because of abiding in such a state.
[This is] the goddess of action, the power of consciousness, whose nature is ether, the Great Form.

These creations, consisting of groups of people and worlds radiant with light, together with their continents, oceans, earths, forests, groves, and mountains, possess no parts other than that which bears the form of the conceptualized [mind]. (MU 6.241.28–29)
The three Vedas, with their limbs and sub-limbs, along with the sciences, songs,
the meanings of injunctions and prohibitions, and the conceptions of the auspicious and inauspicious;
the sacrifices accompanied by sacrificial fees, fires, and the praise of cakes and clarified butter.
[There were] battlefields equipped with *kuṇāla* birds, mortars, grass mats, winnowing baskets, sacrificial posts, and so forth;
[battlefields] filled with collections of weapons— along with spears, arrows, and javelins—
and resplendent with *bhuśuṇḍi* missiles, clubs, darts, horses, elephants, and warriors.
There are fourteen classes of beings, beginning with the gods;
likewise, there are fourteen oceans and continents on earth, and fourteen worlds.
Rāma said:
"Tell me, O Kālīśarīrin: are those creations that exist within your limbs real in relation to your self, or are they unreal? Vasiṣṭha replied:
That [world] is indeed Rāma, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*); whatever is impelled by her is thus perceived within as if it were real,
though this entire universe is not reflected externally like a reflection in a mirror.
That [city] truly exists within consciousness; it is not unreal in reality.
Nevertheless, for one whose nature is consciousness, that city of volition may exist within as real.
How could it not come to be for purified consciousness through firm meditation?
Whether the creation exists in a mirror, or in a dream, or in a mental construction—
my view is that it is indeed real because it performs its function within the self.
If you say, "That [creation] is not for my sake," then why is it not so for you?
All things existing in other lands become useful at present; just as a village in another land serves the needs of one who has gone there,
so too all these things certainly serve the purpose of one who has attained that state.
Whatever is perceived as performing the function of all objects exactly as they truly are, that is real; it does not belong to anything other than the Self that has attained that state.
Therefore, all successions of creations reside within the sheath of the power of consciousness.

For one who has attained that state within the Self, all the multitudes of past, present, and future volitions and dreams are not real; yet they are all real [to him]. Otherwise, how could the Supreme Reality be the Self of all?
Just as for one who has been shaken while in a deep sleep, the city seen in a dream does not actually roll about, yet it is clearly inferred that it has rolled;
so too, as she moves, the world situated within her body rolls along with her.
It does not waver at all, remaining like a reflection in a mirror.
Though the great undertaking of the three worlds is real, it is merely an illusion;
tell me, what indeed can constitute the wavering or non-wavering of that which is merely an illusion?
When is the city of dreams real? When is the city of dreams false?
When is the city of dreams destroyed? When is the city of dreams established?
It is not merely that delusion alone exists; rather, the splendor of what is perceived extends even further ahead.
Understand that even this delusion of the world's splendor is unreal;
just as there is the experience of the three worlds in imagination, in a kingdom of the mind, in a dream, in conversation, or in error, so too was it previously experienced.
This delusion of "I" and "the world" shines forth as if within consciousness;
it subsides when thoroughly understood by that slender-limbed maiden who is the supreme ether.
This concludes the chapter titled "Description of Śiva and Śakti."
The two hundred and forty-second canto: Vasiṣṭha said:
"Thus that goddess dances with her long, staff-like arms."
Making the sky appear like a dense forest with her movements,
this actionless power of consciousness dances in that manner;
her ornaments are winnowing baskets, water-pots, mats, and the like.
Arrows, spears, clubs, lances, maces, swords, stones, and so forth;
as well as the multitude of categories of existence and non-existence, the arts, time, sequence, and the rest—
the vibration of consciousness holds the world within itself, like a mental construction of a city in the heart.
Or rather, that very [will] is the world; thus, as before, it is mere conceptualization.
Just as movement belongs to the wind, so is that will of Śiva.
As the wind is stilled when its movement ceases, so is Śiva when his will is completely tranquil.
Just as the formless wind spreads a display of sound and vibration within the space, so does the will of Śiva create the universe. Then,
when she dances there in that supreme ether, she manifests the world.
By a chance occurrence like that of the crow and the palm fruit,
Śiva himself, standing nearby, was touched by him from close at hand for a mere moment;
he was like the submarine fire, which, while carrying its own destruction, is touched by a flowing line of water.
As soon as that Śiva, the supreme cause, was touched,
Prakṛti then began to move; she gradually attained a state of attenuation,
casting off her infinite forms and becoming the size of a mountain.
Then she became the size of a city, and from that, Drumasundarī;
then she took on a form like the sky, and then the very form of Śiva.
Then she entered the river like a stream whose turbulence has subsided entering the great ocean.
Then he became truly one, separated from Śivā;
he was Śiva alone, in the auspicious and tranquil ether, beautified by peace.
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, that auspicious Supreme Goddess has been touched by Śiva;
for what purpose has she come to bring peace? Tell me this according to the truth.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, she is declared to be Prakṛti, the Supreme Goddess who is the will of Śiva;
she is renowned as the Māyā of the universe, the uncreated power of vibration (spanda-śakti). He is said to be the Puruṣa beyond Prakṛti, whose form is pure.
Bearing the form of Śiva, peaceful, and possessing the power of the supreme ether,
Prakṛti wanders through the cycle of existence in the form of a bee;
she is the Supreme Goddess, the power of consciousness (cicchakti), whose essence is mere vibration and whose will is sovereign.
As long as one does not perceive Śiva— the eternally satisfied, the disease-free, the non-inert state devoid of beginning and end, which has cast aside duality— [one remains bound],
because [the world] consists solely of the property of pure consciousness through a chance occurrence (*kākatālīya*).
The Goddess of Consciousness, having touched Śiva, becomes entirely identical with Him.
Nature, having touched the Puruṣa, completely abandons its nature as Nature;
having attained oneness within Him, it is like a river [losing] its form in the ocean.
For a river consists of nothing but water; when it has merged with the ocean, it quickly reaches that very ocean and dissolves right there.
O God, consciousness is the will of Śiva; having reached that very Lord, it becomes stilled.
Just as a sharp iron blade reaches its place of origin,
so too does Nature (prakṛti) swiftly enter the Person (puruṣa), just as one's own shadow enters the body of a person who has entered that shadow.
Having conceived its own nature as the eternal being called "Puruṣa," it wanders again in saṃsāra; for it does not attain that true state in this world.
A virtuous man dwells among a band of thieves only so long as he does not [recognize] them.
Having understood, one fully comprehends and does not delight in that [duality] again.
Consciousness delights in duality—which is, in fact, unreal—as long as it does not perceive the Supreme; but having seen That, it becomes one with It.
That consciousness, whose nature is nirvāṇa, is the supreme state;
having attained that reality, it reaches the state of oneness with it, just as a river reaches the state of the ocean within the ocean.
For so long, under the power of delusion, consciousness wanders through agitated creations belonging to the stages of birth.
As long as one does not perceive that Supreme, having then swiftly seen it, one sinks right there like a female bee into thick honey.

O Rāma, who indeed would abandon that reality of the Self once attained? And who, having obtained and experienced an elixir (*rasāyana*), would discard it—that by which all incessant sufferings consisting of birth, death, and delusion are stilled?
In the narrative of the stone, the chapter titled "Description of Prakṛti and Puruṣa," the two hundred and forty-third chapter; Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, Rāma, how he remained there in that great space;
having abandoned that delusion of a body, even that Rudra becomes tranquil.
Then that Rudra [beheld] those two fragments of the world as if they were depicted in a painting.
They remained there motionless while I stood watching;
then, in just a moment, that Rudra gazed upon those two fragments in the midst of the sky, as if with the sun of his eye he were beholding heaven and earth.
Then, in the mere twinkling of an eye, having brought those two fragments together with a snort from his trunk, he cast them as if into the depths of the underworld within his mouth; thereafter,
he alone remained in the sky like the sky itself throughout its entirety.
Having consumed the fierce and formidable circle of the cosmic egg,
he then, in a mere moment, became as light as a cloud;
thereafter he became like a tree, and then he became like a pillar.
Then he became the size of a staff, then the size of a span;
then I saw him in such a state, appearing like a grain of glass.
Then, becoming minute, he was seen by me from the sky with my divine vision.
"Having become a mere atom, he then vanished right there.
Thus, having come to rest like a fragment of an autumn cloud, even such a one of great undertaking disappeared before my very eyes. (MU 6.243.8–9)
Thus, when that shell of the universe, along with its coverings, had been swallowed by him—
as a leaf is swallowed by a deer tormented by hunger—
then the sky became stainless, and there remained only the peaceful, absolute Brahman.

"I beheld there, within the hollow of a fragment of stone, that vast delusion of the end of an eon— which was nothing but the space of consciousness, devoid of beginning, middle, or end— appearing like a reflection in a mirror."
Then, remembering that woman, that stone, and that delusion,
I stood at the palace gate like a commoner and was filled with wonder;
I looked again upon that stone of refined gold.
To whatever extent there are creations here, they exist everywhere within the body like the goddess Kālī;
they are seen by the eye of the intellect or by the divine eye, and not otherwise.
For everything that exists anywhere at any time is exactly as it is then.

If that stone is observed from afar with the physical eye, it is seen as nothing other than a single stone; there is no manifestation or anything else whatsoever. That stone remains in its singular form, a dense and solid mass.
"Vast and made of refined gold, it was as beautiful as an evening cloud. Then, overcome with wonder, I again scrutinized another part of the stone with that same supreme vision.
I beheld even that world-creation, sluggish and yet appearing as if hollow within, beautiful with its manifold objects; then once more,
I likewise observed another region.
To whatever extent and in whatever manner that region was enveloped by the fervor of creation,
in each and every place upon that stone,
I beheld the entire world reflected therein, as if in a mirror.
If that world were to enter me, I would see this entire visible universe within;
if it were not outside, I would see it reflected in a mirror. Then, with great curiosity, I [examined] all the rocks of that mountain.
The regions of the earth, as well as the grasses, shrubs, and so forth, were searched;
yet that world exists everywhere exactly as it is,
possessing its various forms, and is perceived by the supreme intellect alone, not by the eye.
In some places, he saw the Lord of Creatures being born from the first creation,
with the stars, moon, sun, days, nights, seasons,
and years being fashioned; in other places, he saw the circles of people inhabiting the surface of the earth.
In some places, certain regions were dug out by the four fierce oceans;
in some places, certain regions had no gods but possessed dānavas;
in some places, certain regions were inhabited by virtuous beings following the conduct of the Kṛta Yuga.
In some places, something was like a wicked being following the conduct of the Kali age;
in some places, something was well-established in its abiding state throughout the duration of a kalpa;
and in some places, something was as difficult to overcome as a battle between cities and daityas.
In some places, the earth was entirely without gaps due to a vast network of great mountains;
in some places, creation was incomplete, arising from a single lotus;
and in some places, the human beings on the surface of the earth were free from old age and death.
In some places, Śiva was present with his moonless head not yet produced;
the ocean of milk was not yet churned; it was filled with death, the gods, and the demons;
and it was devoid of nectar, the horse-unicorn, the physician, the sacrifice, Lakṣmī, and the poison.
In one place, a host of gods eager to destroy the great vidyās of Śukra and Amara;
in another, the lord of the gods intent on cutting out the limbs of embryos;
and everywhere, all subjects self-luminous because the nature of dharma never withers.
In some places there is the arrangement and persistence of certain things in a sequence different from before;
in others, there is the investigation of unprecedented Vedic scriptures, their meanings, and traditional practices.
In some places, there is the presence of inauspiciousness due to the agitation at the end of a kalpa.
In some places, a portion of the abode of the gods had been plundered by the hosts of Daityas;
in some places, there were Gandharvas and Kinnaras singing in beautiful gardens; and in some places, a partial reconciliation was being initiated between the gods and the Asuras.

Then, within my own body—which is the self of the great multitude of the universe—I experienced the entire display of the world: past, future, and present. All at once, I felt the churning of the Puṣkarāvarta clouds, agitated by the dissolution of the kalpa.
In one place, O gentle one, the continuous succession of all beings is well-established;
in another, the lords of gods, asuras, and men are agitated by battle; and in another, there is a mass of eternal, undifferentiated darkness where light cannot possibly exist.
In one place, it was free from darkness and resembled the interior of a beloved’s flaming hair;
in another, Madhu and Kaiṭabha were nestled within the stalks of lotuses;
and in another, the infant Brahmā slept within a casket of lotuses.

In one place, he saw Mādhava resting upon a towering tree in a single vast ocean; in another, he saw him motionless within the hollow of a stone, like the sky itself, vast in form and filled with the darkness of emptiness during the night of the kalpa.
It has the form of the belly of deep sleep— unperceived, without characteristics,
beyond ratiocination, and unknowable, like deep sleep in every respect;
in one place, the sky was filled with crows perched on mountains shaken by the flapping of wings.
In one place, it was brilliant with mountains melting from the impact of thunderbolts; in another, mountain ranges were being swept away by the surging, intoxicated ocean;
in another, it was tumultuous with the battle between the gods and Vṛtra, the Andhas, and Bāḍi.
In one place, the earth trembled from the shaking of intoxicated elephants in the netherworld;
in another, the ground was being trampled at the end of an eon by the head of Śeṣa.
In some places, the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa had been slain by another Rāma.
In one place, Rāghava was seen by the *rakṣasa* Rāvaṇa himself,
who stood with his feet on the ground while Rāghava’s head rested upon the peak of Mount Deva;
in another place, he was indeed assailed by Kālanemi as he gazed toward the far shore.
In some places it was constantly protected by the gods and dānavas alone; in other places it was protected by the immortals who had subdued the danujas;
and in others it was guarded by Viṣṇu joined with Jiṣṇu, and by the Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas.
In some places, he saw multitudes of akṣauhiṇīs destroyed by the host of Bhārata;
and in other places, Rāvaṇa slain by you yourself as the son of Daśaratha,
and the rākṣasas utterly exterminated by Rāma while intoxicated with battle.
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, tell me, did I exist previously?
And if I existed, how could it have been in this very same form?"
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, all states of being indeed revolve again and again,
just as beans being winnowed [separate] gradually by one means or another.
Some entities are equal in all respects, while others are equal only to one another;
some manifest as partial equals, like the waves of the ocean.
Again it is you, again it is I, and again these people appear repeatedly.
Never indeed do others arise at all within the Supreme, which is entirely undifferentiated. Or rather, the conclusion is that they are themselves the others, just as waves [arise] in the ocean;
in the same way, those wandering in existence are not truly born.
Infinite beings come and go here through the wanderings of existence;
they are the very same and yet others, both similar and dissimilar.
They possess cycles of return, and likewise, others do so on all sides.
Know that all beings are but droplets from the ocean of the world.
By means of wealth, kinsmen, age, action, learning, discernment,
and exertion— by those very things— certain embodied beings are born again and again.
Some embodied beings are equal to them by half; some are equal to them by a quarter; other living beings are dissimilar to them;
some are equal to all of these, while others are distinct from them by virtue of time alone.
Some are similar to time, while others are distinct from it;
by time their activities are agitated, and thus they go downward or upward again— countless other bodies, worn out by scratching, and yet others besides them.
Who is capable of fully calculating those elemental waters that flow within the ocean of worldly existence, which is as unstable as a whirling wheel?
This concludes the chapter titled "The Description of the Infinity of the World" within the narrative of the Stone.
The two hundred and forty-fourth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, having pervaded all with his body of pure consciousness, he remains infinite and free from affliction.
Having fixed my attention upon my own body, I then perceived something:
the entire creation had entered within me and remained there,
sprouting like a seedling in the heart of a grain of seed that has been sown and moistened within a granary.
Just as a sprout remains within a seed, desiring to emerge from the watering [of the soil],
so does the formless world exist within the mind— possessing consciousness yet devoid of shape—
just as the beauty of the visible world unfolds for one who has awakened from deep sleep.
Just as when one is awake after a dream has passed, due to the self-awareness of pure consciousness (cinmātra),

so too at the beginning of creation, the arising of the world is experienced within the Self— which is of the nature of the Void— as being non-different from itself, appearing in the form of its own internal aspect within the heart.
Rāma:
O you whose form is space, O Supreme Space, please explain further for the sake of precise understanding how the process of creation proceeds within space.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, Rāma, to how at that time my own state of being the Self-born was experienced by me there— this world, which is unreal yet appears as real, resembling a dream or a man created by magic.
Beholding that great cosmic upheaval of the Mahākalpa, I, whose form is space,
caused consciousness to emerge within another part of my body.
As soon as that stainless consciousness had emerged and remained for a moment, it was established.
At that very moment, I perceived there, as it were, a state of solidification;
O Rāma, just as you, through sleep, perceive the sky of consciousness— which is your own true nature—
as becoming somewhat dense when entering either the waking world or the dream-world.
First there is only the space of pure consciousness; from that arises the cognition "I am.

That [cognition] when solidified is called the intellect (*buddhi*), and when that intellect is further solidified, it is called the mind (*manas*). It perceives the subtle element of sound, and then the other subtle elements as well.
"Because of its grossness, the five sense-faculties arise; thus occurs the emergence of the group of faculties.
Just as the world of visible objects arises when one enters from deep sleep into the dream state, so too at the beginning of creation does the visible world appear in the blink of an eye."
In this infinite manifestation of the web of visible phenomena, which occurs simultaneously,
some speak of a sequence while others do not;
[yet all] have experienced the attainment of the lovely atom-fragment.
I am the conscious self, which in reality is indeed as pure as the sky. Just as the wind moves incessantly by its very nature within the ether,
so too consciousness perceives this entire form everywhere by its own inherent nature.
Whatever form was conceived by this supreme power, it is not able to make it otherwise, even with great effort. Therefore,
I saw that I had become as small as an atom.
Because it is of the nature of consciousness, that very thing quickly became established for me as being thus.
Then I perceived a form consisting of a subtle spark of light;
subsequently, while contemplating that very thing, I became, as it were, gross.

Thinking, "I shall first look at something," O scion of Raghu, I then experienced that very slight perception which arose from that subtle awakening as if for the sake of a faint glimmering. Whatever it was there, that is what I have perceived here today.
Listen to the principal names devised by those like you:
that through which one begins to see by means of an aperture is called the *cakṣus* (eye);
and that which I see is the *dṛśya* (the visible), while the act of seeing (*darśana*) is the fruit resulting from it.

"When I see that time, it is seen according to its sequence; mature destiny is what I see today, and that which I see there is the sky. 'I am situated in this place'—such is this mental construction."

Then, however, I perceived that the cause of this was merely the closing and opening of my eyes; from that, a slight awakening arose within me. Then, through the two openings, I beheld that which is space.
"Through those two apertures by which I saw, these two eyes are now situated; therefore,
a consciousness arose in me that 'I hear something,' and then I heard a slight, faint humming sound."
Then, from those two regions where the wind moves with an unceasing sound, like the natural resonance of a blown conch shell in the sky, I heard these two wounds of my ears.
"I have experienced some perception of touch here"—this very self, which consists of that mere perception, is known as this wind;
thus, the subtle element (*tanmātra*) of the sense of touch is established as being truly existent, even though it is [otherwise] non-existent. (MU 6.244.28–29)
That experience of tasting which was mine became the sense-organ for the relishable taste;
from my nose, the subtle element of smell arose, having the nature of space.
Thus, nothing at all was produced, yet everything here has been accomplished by me.
Thus, while I remained as the conscious one amidst the web of the senses and the subtle elements (*tanmātras*),
the five objects of knowledge arose from me by force,
having sound, form, taste, touch, and smell as their very bodies.
Formless, yet bearing such names, consisting of a solid nature and illusory in essence—
this very net of such a form which I was contemplating at that time is what is today called "ego" (ahaṅkāra) by people like you.
This very [element], when condensed, is designated as "intellect" (*buddhi*);
and that intellect, when further condensed, is designated as "mind" (*manas*).
In that state, I am established within the space that constitutes the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
The self of the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) consists of consciousness and has the nature of space;
I am emptier even than the wind, being merely pure space.
I am the form of emptiness for all existents, unobstructed.
Then, as I was cultivating that [state] and remained there steadfastly, the conviction arose in me: "I am embodied and nourished.
By means of that conviction, I then proceeded to produce sound.
Just as a man who has fallen asleep in a void might cry out while dreaming of flying,
so too was the sound previously produced by a child;
thus, this very syllable *oṃ* was subsequently brought to renown.
Therefore, know that whatever was spoken by me in the dream as if by a man— this very speech has now been brought here to the forefront.
I am indeed that Brahman, perfected, the creator of the emanation, and the teacher of the world.
Then, by means of my very mind-made [body], these creations were fashioned by me.
Thus have I arisen; I am not born from anything at all.
I have seen the cosmic egg, yet it is nothing whatsoever anywhere.
Thus, when this world of mine consisting of mind has come into being, nothing at all has truly come into being there; it is merely empty space.
In this way, all this is utterly void, being nothing more than mere cognition.
Indeed, these entities such as earth and the rest do not exist even in the slightest degree. The cognitions within consciousness appear like the waters of a mirage in the world;
there is nothing external, nor is there anything non-external—it remains just like that void in the sky.
In a desert there is no water at all, yet consciousness perceives it as such;
being rootless and internally tormented, it experiences this delusion like its own confusion.
In the same way, although the world does not exist at all within Brahman, consciousness perceives it as such.
Because it is consciousness itself, the delusion of error is indeed rootless;
this vast world appears as something non-existent within the heart alone,
like a mental construction, a kingdom of the mind, a story, or a city in a dream.
Just as one who is sleeping while another lies on their side perceives nothing at all unless they enter into that person's mind,
yet through entering that mind it is experienced; so too,
this entire world is perceived only through the entry of the mind.

Even though it appears in the form of a reflection in a mirror, it is otherwise non-existent. If it were perceived by the eye through its material nature, then nothing would be seen there; only the mountain itself would be visible.
If one observes with the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*) through the vision of supreme awakening, the creation is seen as nothing other than the stainless Supreme Self alone.
Everywhere, the manifestation of creation is perceived by the light of wisdom.

Brahman is indeed the Self; otherwise, this [world] is not perceived as anything at all. That which the pure intellect perceives through rational inquiry is not seen by Śiva with his three eyes, nor even by Indra with his hundred eyes.
Just as the sky is covered by creations, so too did I perceive the earth;
then I became a meditator, endowed with the concentration on the earth. By that concentration on the earth, I assumed the form of the earth itself.
Without even abandoning my form as the sky of consciousness, like a sovereign in an instant,
I entered the interior of the earth's constituent elements through the power of earth-retention;
within that body, I experienced the continents, mountains, grasses, trees, and so forth.
Then I beheld the surface of the earth, complete with its various forests and trees,
covered with various strings of jewels, and adorned with various cities;
it was rich with villages, thickets, and mountains, and its interior was hollowed out like the underworld (pātāla).
It is encircled by the oceans and continents embraced by the arms of the boundary mountains;
it is rich with the mass of grasses as its fine hair, with mountain thickets for its ankles,
supported by the frontal globes of the world-elephants of the quarters, and held up by the hundred heads of Śeṣa.
It is carried away by the protectors of the earth, yet it shines with the seasons;
its limbs are enjoyed by living beings, and it grows according to the established order.
It has the Himavat and Vindhya mountains as its sturdy trunks and Mount Sumeru as its noble neck.
Its body resounds with the pearl necklaces of the overflowing waters of the Gaṅgā and other rivers;
it possesses caves, dense thickets, and marshy banks, and the orb of the ocean serves as its mirror.
It is white with the desert wastes and saline plains, and it is more beautiful than the garment of the sky.
Filled with living beings and washed by great oceans,
adorned with flowering groves and sprinkled by masses of pollen;
it is constantly ploughed by farmers and fanned by cool breezes.
Scorched by the blazing suns and drenched by the rains of the monsoon,
he has broad peaks for his chest and hundreds of lotus-pools for his eyes;
he wears white and black clouds as a turban, and the ten directions serve as the chambers of his belly.
Terrifying with its formidable mouth, like a great trench encircling the world and its beyond;
its sole consciousness is the movement of infinite multitudes of beings;
it is pervaded both within and without by various distinct hosts of creatures.
Outside by gods, dānavas, and gandharvas, and inside by insects;
in the subterranean realms and the apertures of the senses by multitudes of nāgas, asuras, and worms;
and in the seven treasuries of the oceans by water-dwellers of various species.
It was pervaded by floods of rivers, forests, oceans, the ends of the quarters, mountains, islands, aquatic creatures, and terrestrial jungles;
it was encircled by various woods, circular fortresses, groves, creepers, lakes, streams, and clusters of lotuses.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Description of the Infinity of the World Contained within the Earthly Element," from the *Pāṣāṇopākhyāna* (The Narrative of the Stone).
The two hundred and forty-fifth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
O giver of honor, after that, while I was there upon the surface of the earth...
Day after day, this world resounds with the cries of rivers;
in one place, there is the piteous lamentation of women at a death,
and in another, the great bliss of a grand festival where women dance wildly.

In some places there was the terrible wailing of those suffering from the calamities of an irresistible famine; in other places, there was the deep affection resulting from the abundance of all kinds of crops;
and in some places, there was the fierce lamentation of regions scorched by great fires.
In some places, it was a region where cities and ports were being swept away by floods; in other places, it was a district plundered by fickle vassals;
and in yet other places, it was a realm inhabited by Rākṣasas and Piśācas of unrestrained cruelty.
In some places, its limbs bristled with the surging ripples of shimmering pools;
in others, clouds were tossed by winds emerging from the depths of its caves.
Its hair stood on end as sprouts emerged from the sheath of its own body, which was uplifted by the awakening of consciousness.

The earth’s surface sank and rose through the agitation caused by the movement of water and elephants; it trembled softly, marked by lines of shifting fissures and circles as the mountains, forests, and cities with their terrifying abysses and peaks shook.
In one place, there was the gathering of armies agitated by neighboring vassals in battle; in another, the entire circle of vassals sat together in gentle comfort.
In some forest, which was not empty, there arose the whistling sound of the swaying wind.
In one place there was a forest where crops were being sown, reaped, and ripened;
in another, a lake filled with blooming lotuses and crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks;
and elsewhere, a desert region where the wind blew white clouds of dust from its thick stalks.
In some places, there was the gurgling sound of rivers flowing with effortless ease as they rubbed against the testing-stones;
in other places, there was the swelling of seeds that had been sprinkled with water, manifesting their capacity to produce sprouts;
and in yet other places, there was the perception of the gentle quivering of the mouths of insects dwelling within.
"Awaken me quickly and protect me here"— such was the awakening, as it were.
By pressing against the ground with the expanse of its branches and surrounding foliage,
it sometimes supports a tree by firmly gripping the network of its roots.
In some places, [the mountains] were pressed against one another, crushing the limbs of the quarters of the horizon;
in other places, they were dense with mountain bones, tossed by the surging waves of the ocean,
and their peaks were crushed together by the contraction of parched foliage.
In some places, there was the dragging away by their own force with intolerant,
sun-like hands; in other places, there was a fall, harsh due to the dense firmness of their limbs, like the thunderbolt-strikes of elephants upon mountain peaks, mansions, and trees.
In some places, with eyes closed, it was a new, slow unfolding of the body,
marked by a subtle relish; in other places, there was the quivering of limbs,
resembling the rubbing of flies, lice, and bugs.
There is the effortless dragging away of spades, stakes, trees, enemies,
and ploughs; in some places there is cold that causes the limbs to shatter and the skin to wither, while the water has turned to stone and a harsh wind blows.
With its soft limbs submerged and swarms of insects clinging to its teeth, it was like an *udgālī* plant;
in some places, the roots of emerging lotuses and other plants were submerged in the water,
providing a pleasure from the coolness within while remaining harsh to the touch on the outside.

In one place, the mass of hair on her breasts was like a sprout of sleep; in another, it manifested as the play of passion. By the beds of soft lotus petals shaken by a very gentle breeze, the lakes provided a cooling relief for my limbs, as if for a man separated from his beloved.
In the narrative of Pāṣāṇa, the chapter titled "Description of the Intentions of the Earth-Sphere," the two hundred and forty-sixth chapter.
Rāma said:
"Having established the earth-dhāraṇā in order to behold the worlds, you have become capable of perceiving this world of the earth; how much more so, then, the mental one? Vasiṣṭha said:
"This is the mind, and I am the extensive surface of the earth;
this is not the mind, and yet in reality I am not that either.
There is nothing whatsoever that exists as a ground of the earth that is not of the nature of the mind."
Whatever you perceive as non-existent or existent, that is merely mind alone.
I am the pure space of consciousness; for me, who am that self, there is nothing other than it.
That manifestation consisting of pure consciousness is known by the name "volition" (saṅkalpa).
That is the mind, that is the surface of the earth, that is the world, and he is the Grandfather;
this sky of the mind shines forth like a city of volition in the void.
Thus, all that is extended is merely my volition, merely my mind.
It is established that this "earth-sphere" is nourished by the practice of *dhāraṇā*.
This is not indeed that earth-sphere; rather, it is something else, consisting of mind—a mere shimmering of space, an inconceivable manifestation of consciousness.
That very [element], being of the nature of mere space and having remained so for a long time,
abandons its mental state because it has acquired the status of the "this-notion" (idam-pratyaya).
This is the stable, very firm, and expansive sphere of the earth.
The cognition that "it exists" arises with respect to the sky itself due to long-standing perception;
by this same logic, this surface of the earth stands as if it were [real],
yet it did not exist in this way at the beginning of creation.
Just as consciousness alone shines in the void as the city in a dream, so too at the beginning of creation, consciousness alone exists as this world;
know that the three worlds are the kingdom of the mind of the child whose nature is consciousness.

This visible world, beginning with the surface of the earth, and this entire creation at all times, is nothing other than the volition of the Self whose nature is consciousness; the universe is composed of that [volition].
In reality, however, it has no substantial form, no true existence, and no luminosity.
The visible world exists when it is not fully known; once it is fully known, it is no longer found.
That very full knowledge of it is what you have been hearing for so long:
everything is pure consciousness, the void, shining by itself within itself.
The self of the earth-sphere and the self of the visible world are devoid of both duality and unity.
Just as a gem, by its very nature, produces rays of light such as white, yellow,
and so forth without acting, so too does the space of consciousness produce the world.
Since it performs no action and does not abandon its form, therefore this is not the mind; there is nothing here on the surface of the earth [other than it].
The sky of consciousness alone appears as the surface of the earth, continuous and without interruption.
Just as the sky exists within itself with its stainless surface,
so too did that state of mine then exist as the mere manifestation of its own nature,
utterly transparent like the orb of the earth, yet being the sky itself with its vast interior.
This terrestrial sphere and that [heavenly one]— both of these are the very nature of the Great Consciousness (mahāciti) shining forth,
just like a city in a dream.
Due to the conviction formed over a long period of time, they are perceived as stable.
It has been understood as it truly is: the uninterrupted expanse of consciousness alone.
This [world] is essentially mere space, and that [space] is also mere space.
Due to ignorance it is not fully known; due to knowledge, neither this nor that exists anywhere.
In the state of agitation, dreams, conceptual constructions, and the kingdom of the mind, there exist the networks of beings in the three worlds occurring throughout the three periods of time—
those that have been, those yet to be, and those currently existing.
O dear one, because they have attained the state of universal generality (*sattāsāmānyatā*), I alone am all those spheres of the earth; even though they are contained within me,
I have experienced them and seen them all in that manner.
This pure consciousness alone is the undecaying state, the reality of the Self; it maintains the nature of the pure Self without ever abandoning its presence within the body.
Yet, O dear one, though this world exists as it is, that which is awakened does not maintain even the slightest distinction regarding these worlds.
This is the chapter titled "The Demonstration of the Manifestation of the Visible," from the Narrative of the Stone.
The two hundred and forty-seventh canto.
Rāma said: "O Brahmin, tell me what happened next; at that time, by you, the worlds [were established]."
"Have you perhaps seen the circles of the earth within the heart, or not?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"By me, through the nature of the multitude of earth-circles belonging to the waking and dreaming states of the Supreme Self..."
Then that which was experienced in the heart was seen with the supreme vision:
how the entire web of the world remains exactly as it is everywhere—
consisting entirely of the visible, peaceful yet characterized by duality.
The worlds exist everywhere, and everywhere Brahman is established;
everything is empty, supremely peaceful, and all undertakings are sluggish.
Though the earth and other elements exist everywhere as gross forms, they are nothing at all.
Just as a dream-city is nothing but the sky of consciousness, so too that supreme reality is unborn;
it is not non-dual here, nor is there duality, nor is there non-existence, nor is there existence.
Where even "I" does not exist at all, how could anything be anywhere? What could possibly be there?
Even this perceived world, though experienced as "I" and so forth, does not exist at all;
or if it does exist, it is that unborn, nameless Brahman.
This world is like a city in a dream, appearing in the void of consciousness from the very beginning of creation.
What kind of existence and non-existence are there therein, where and from what do they abide?
Just as I saw those worlds assuming the form of the earth,
so too was that very same thing seen by me having become water.
Through the retention of water, having become water as if insentient yet actually sentient,
