it long made a gurgling sound within the depths of the ocean abodes,
within the stalks and channels of grasses, trees, creepers, shrubs, and climbing vines.
It was as soft and unobserved as a louse that has mounted upon your limbs;
it resembled a pillar when rising from all sides, and like a bracelet when that pillar was severed—
its interior carved out by the movement of a serpent through the clouds of its arrangement, as if by a soft snake entering an ear.

Having entered the heart through the mouth, which bears the exhaustion of the seasons, he fashioned a design of lines by means of his form as the nourishment resting upon the sprouts and fruits of the *vallī*, *tamāla*, *tāla*, and other trees.
The bodily constituents (dhātus) were covered, shaken, consumed, and torn away;
he slept upon beds of sprouts in the form of dewdrops,
simultaneously and without weariness in all directions.
Traveling along various lakes, rivers, and houses on an unceasing path,
he found rest here and there through the grace of his friend,
the bridge; for the wise find rest through the connection [with that friend], while the dull-witted do not, due to their lack of such reliance.
In reservoirs of water,
it was made to swirl by me with a whirling motion; yet, like a wicked man, it fell a hundredfold into abysses as a stone pillar turned upward upon the mountains with a whirling motion.
Having emerged from the wood in the form of smoke into the ocean of the sky,
it rested upon a cloud-bank together with the woman who was lightning, situated amidst a whirlpool of jewel-like sparks and sapphire-blue stars.
Like Viṣṇu with his body dark as a split sapphire, [he was seen] within all things;
even in this creation composed of atoms, he remained unperceived within the forms of composite objects,
like Brahman of pure essence dwelling within all entities.
Having attained contact with the subtle tips of the tongue, an exquisite experience was produced;
I consider that it belongs neither to the self nor to the body, but solely to knowledge.
Since that which has its own nature as its essence cannot be tasted by me, nor by the body, nor by anything else.
That coolness held within it is likewise unreal for one who lacks knowledge.
Having fully enjoyed clusters of flowers in all directions, which possess the forms of the essences of all seasons and provide manifold delights, he now offers only their leavings in his dwelling.
Residing within the joints of the limbs of the fourteen kinds of beings— though insentient, as if sentient, and though of an insentient nature, as if sentient—
he mounted the wind-god’s chariot in the form of a spray of mist.
O Rāma, in that state, as if by a mere fragrance, this entire world was experienced in its true condition, down to every single atom, throughout the paths of the stainless sky.
By me, who am non-inert yet as if inert, and by that state of being water,
all things within [the world] abide, both known and unknown.
Therein lie hundreds of thousands of worlds, with their hundreds of destructions and creations.
I have seen them grown like the seats made of plantain leaves.
Thus, whether the world or the non-world, whether with form or formless,
everything is but the sky of pure consciousness, more stainless than space itself.
Neither you nor this world exist as anything at all; rather, it is pure, supreme consciousness that shines forth here.
And yet, that too is nothing, nor is it a void; you are simply space. Remain free from doubt.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Description of the World Contained Within the Water-Atoms," from the Narrative of the Stone (Pāṣāṇopākhyāna).
The two hundred and forty-eighth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Thereafter, through the power of maintaining my vital energy, I became that very energy itself, invigorated by the concentration of radiance.
Endowed with diverse components such as the moon, sun, stars, and fire,
it is eternal because its nature is dominated by *sattva*, and thus possesses a luminous form like a king;
it illuminates all that is visible, excluding only the darkness of universal thieves, and is possessed of heat.
With lamps and other offerings, with smooth movements, and with hundreds of attendants, he made all matters manifest in every house like a divine king;
while the people rejoiced at the light of the world, their hair stood on end from the direct perception of his rays.
By those solely devoted to illuminating others, the dark garment cast far away;
it is invisible to the wretchedness of darkness which destroys all virtues,
yet constantly visible to everyone endowed with virtue.
It is the axe that fells the darkness of the *tama-tāla* tree, the state that brings about supreme purity,
and the life-sustenance for people through gold, gems, rubies, pearls, and the like; it is the wall, the limb,
and the lap upon which rest the white, black, crimson, and other colors.
Like a father to his sons, he was the progenitor of all the social classes.
His home was a state of intense affection for the earth, protected by the wind and pierced by lightning;
it was filled with profound joy and held its young sons like lamps.
In the subterranean realms (pātālaka), which consist largely of darkness, the purifying [element] is seen slightly;
on the surface of the earth, garlanded with beings, it is half-seen as consisting of passion (rajas);
and among those whose nature is goodness (sattva), the Great Being (mahāsattva) is eternally present in the abodes of the gods.
He is the lamp for the world’s dilapidated hut, a great well for the blinding darkness;
he is the stainless mirror for the brides that are the quarters of the sky, and the wind that disperses the frost of night;
he is the essence of the moon, the sun, and fire, and the saffron unguent of heaven.
The field for the crops of the days is darkness; the obstruction of waters is the rain.
The water splashing forth is that which washes the vast vessel of the sky’s crystal.
By bestowing existence upon objects and by means of their illumination as well—
Like a younger brother born of the same womb as the ultimate reality of pure consciousness,
it is the sun for the lotus-pond of action; it is the very life of the interior of the earth,
just as consciousness is the wonder of form, light, and mental attention.
Adorned with garlands of jewels—the innumerable stars situated in the vault of the sky;
surging with days, seasons, and years; foaming with the submarine fire and other such elements;
possessing waves such as the moon and the sun; great, yet internally cool and free from impurity.
Abiding within the cavity of the vast cosmic egg, it is eternally a single ocean, imperishable.

Just as the nature of gold exists in gold and other such things, prowess in men and others, the brilliance of gems and the like, and the radiance of the sun and other luminaries; [so too does that one reality abide in all].
In the orb of her moon-like face, where the eyelashes are the decorative markings,
there is a smile that is a manifestation of affection, flowing with a flood of the nectar of love;
it is a playful dancer upon her cheeks, arms, eyes, brows, and hands.
In women, there arises a playfulness born of their own invincibility;
in the minds of lions and other such beings, there is a valor that treats the three worlds as straw, strikes down enemies with a slap, and makes their heads as hard as adamant.
Amidst the warriors, there was a fierce roaming accompanied by the sharp, piercing *ṭāṅ* sounds of swords striking against armor and shields,
and the loud, crashing roars of their impact; among the gods,
there was the state of being an enemy to the Dānavas, and among the enemies of the gods, the state of being an enemy to the gods.
O Unborn One, I experienced benevolence toward all beings, including the stationary ones;
then, O Lotus-eyed Lord, I beheld you there, radiant as the sun,
within those lotuses in the hollows of space throughout the universe.
With its web of rays spread across the ten directions, it seized the world-bird as it perched upon the mountain-peak,
assuming the state of the sun; it beheld the surface of the earth like a village,
while the submarine fire was the whorl of the calyx within the sky-lotus amidst the ocean of darkness.
He is a lamp in the mansion of the cosmic egg, a tree for the rows of fruits that are the days;
his moon-like face has the form of a lake of elixir for heaven,
and it is the laughter of the night-demoness Night, the blossoming of the quarters of the night.
The multitude of eyes of Khaśakra [the Lord of the Sky] was the supreme object of comparison for all the glories of the world’s beauty; it was the beloved of the night, Rohiṇī, women,
and white water-lilies, and a cluster of flowers upon the creeper of the heavens.
The vast canopy of stars, like a swarm of moths in heaven,
was tossed about in the merchant’s path as if weighed in the palms of merchants;
its jewel-like nature was shaken by the hands of the ocean waves.
In the ocean of years, it is like a whirlpool of fish; in the mountain of years, a cluster of blossoms;
in the forest of years, a forest fire; and on the tree of years, a flash of lightning.
It is as fierce as wood being split, difficult to restrain, blazing, and driven by flames.
A great radiance, composed of shimmering gold, rubies, and pearls, resounded with a harsh roar like the conflagration at the end of an eon;
it eclipsed that [darkness], just as true wisdom is snatched away by the ignorant.
I have rested upon the lofty breasts of the women of the asuras, uragas, gandharvas, and lords of men in the form of pearl necklaces;
I have received a hundred kicks from their feet on the path, and I have served as a tilaka mark upon the faces of brides.
Behold the fickleness of states attained by me, who am like a firefly:
at times I have sported gracefully amidst the clouds like lightning, and here on earth like a fish in the oceans, moving through the sky amidst waters resounding with whirlpools.

In some places, with her body as tender as the buds of the *nīpa* tree, she acted as a lamp for the beloveds in their inner apartments, illuminating their amorous dalliances; in other places, she appeared as the flame of a mass of collyrium within the tresses of their hair.
Like the body of a tortoise withdrawn into its own shell, it is hidden within the void;
at the end of kalpas, due to the intense exhaustion from swallowing the entire world,
it is dissolved into the soot-black sky, like lightning vanishing when the clouds have closed in.
In some places, having drunk the waters until the end of the kalpa by means of the submarine fire (*vaḍavāgni*),
I was not satiated with the masses of water, just as the sky is never satiated with the worlds;
in other places, I existed as one whose teeth were flaming brands and whose arms were tongues of flame.
With its fierce mass of hair-like whirling columns of smoke, its turbulent energy,
and as it devoured living beings in the streams of the city’s ponds,
it produced crackling sounds like the letter *ṣṭa* from consuming objects such as wood.
In some places, like iron balls struck by weapons and stones,
particles of anger were vomited forth by me for the sake of striking and burning the slayers;
in other places, within the cavity of a great rock, I was a stone-jewel.
"Remaining for even hundreds of yugas, unseen by all beings.
Rāma said:
"O Sage, was happiness experienced by you in that state?"

"Furthermore, O giver of honor, tell me for my enlightenment: how does a man, though conscious, fall into a state of insensibility while asleep? Vasiṣṭha replied: "Just as a man goes [into this state] while sleeping..."

When the sky of consciousness assumes the state of being an object of perception, it likewise perceives its own insentience. When Brahman perceives itself as the earth and so forth, then it remains within as if asleep and inert; it cannot be otherwise.
In reality, however, this earth and so forth are neither of the nature of non-existence nor composed of existence;
like the seer and the seen, it appears as such, yet it is Brahman alone that remains uniform.
This is the true knowledge which has arisen unbrokenly in one.
For him there are no five elements, nor the delusion of the seer and the seen.
At that time, by me who am thus pure and of the nature of Brahman, that was performed;
apart from the form of Brahman, it is not possible to perform anything at all.
When all this visible world was known as the stainless Brahman,
then, abiding in the state of Brahman, my very self was perceived by me in this way. But when I again contemplated [the world] as consisting merely of the five elements, [I saw it otherwise].
If I were indeed insentient at that time, what could I possibly perceive?
Even though one is conscious, having firmly formed the thought "I am asleep," one enters into a state of dreamless sleep; such is the height of insentience that one perceives nothing at all.
But for one whose self is awakened by wisdom, that body which is material (adhibhautika) subsides; the stainless, transcendent (ativāhika) self consisting of pure consciousness alone arises.
By means of that subtle, transcendent body which is the self of consciousness, [he proceeds].

Or, by means of the Great [Vidyā], he remains as one whose self is Nirvāṇa according to his desire. Entering the heart even of stones—which are otherwise indivisible—by means of the body of awakening, he quickly emerges; he goes to the netherworld and to the sky.
Therefore, O Rāma, in the past, by me—
who was then infinite, consisting of consciousness and having the nature of the void—
those various [actions] were performed through the coming and going within the interior of the sky, the netherworld, and the diamond-hard rock.
For one who acts in such a manner, no obstacle arises quickly.
As long as he remains among insentient objects with a body consisting of pure consciousness,
he persists there in that state.
If, having moved by its own will, it then proceeds elsewhere,
it remains situated right there, just as the intellect does,
my dear; for they know the imperishable subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*) to be mere consciousness.
Now, you yourself experience that very state here as a Buddha:
through the realization that "I am of the nature of the void of pure consciousness" regarding the sun and other objects,
the Self itself is brought to its setting, being yet non-existent by way of the self.
It remained in the world of dreams and the like, as if shrouded in darkness or by night,
or as if veiled from other eyes, existing yet unattainable;
it was like a streak of waves clinging to its own body upon the river of burning coals.
With her body suddenly stiffened as if by the splendor of a kingdom of dreams,
she appeared like a streak of collyrium in a forest of fire, possessing the beauty of blossoming flowers,
the essence of full-blown land-lotuses, and the form of *kiṃśuka* and *aśoka* trees.

O Rāma, even within the interior of a single atomic particle, I have seen the glory of the universe in this very manner— blazing with a high-reaching mass of flames that had begun to spread, rising again and again, and turning like the fickle fortune of a wicked man.
And that [world] is neither other than nor distinct from the supreme sky of consciousness; in this regard, the multitude of mountains appearing here in a dream serves as your illustration.
The two hundred and forty-ninth canto, titled "The Description of the World as Composed of Atomic Particles of Fire," within the narrative of the Stone.
Vasiṣṭha:
Or rather, having assumed a wind-like state out of curiosity to observe the world,
I have attained the condition of air through steady concentration and a firm disposition.

I am perfected as the wind, the dancer in the presence of the vine-like women; I am the protector of the fragrance of the clusters of lotuses, blue lilies, jasmine, and other flowers. I am eager to carry away sprays of water and frost with effortless ease.
Delighted by the joy that refreshes all his limbs weary from sexual union,
he is skilled in the rhythmic dancing of grasses, shrubs, creepers, and vines;
he is adorned with the fragrance of flowers and the radiant luster of the fruits of climbing plants and medicinal herbs.
Gentle during auspicious times, it moves the tresses of women;
terrible during winds of portents, it is like a massive mountain tossing leaves.
In the Nandana grove, it is reddened by the pollen of the nectar of *kunda* and *mandāra* flowers.
In hell, he was a mass of glowing coals; on earth, he was as radiant as frost;
in the ocean, his movement was inferred by the lines of crooked whirlpools;
and in the sky, he was the lunar mirror polished by the passage of the clouds.
The chariot of Nakṣatra-kṣatrasainya, increased in its speed,
was intent upon supporting the celestial palaces where the perfected beings of the three worlds travel;
it moved as swiftly as the mind of his brother due to its rapidity of motion.
Though bodiless, he possesses all limbs; he is the sandalwood of the thrill of vibration.
Withered by the aging caused by the downpour of frosty spray, he is the intoxication of youth and fragrance, whose childhood consists of silence and softness.
Sweet with the fragrance of the Nandana grove, possessing a delightful and noble course of existence,
released from the beautiful Caitraratha forest, and having removed the fatigue of passion for lovely women;
he has long been weary from the swaying of his body upon the swing of the waves of the Gaṅgā.
Having his fatigue from lovemaking dispelled by his knowledge of the nature of exertion,

he long caused the creepers— the women of the spring forest— to tremble with their touch; they were bent low under the weight of flowers, their hands being the trembling leaves and their eyes the rolling bees.
Having long enjoyed the body of the lunar orb and slept upon the bed of full clouds,
he has shaken off the host of lotuses and is free from the fatigue of dalliance;
he is a sky-faring steed, the abode of all dust.
He is the great friend of the exultant elephants intoxicated with rut;
he is the herdsman of the clouds whose peaks are rich with the lightning-threads of his rain-showers;
he is the thread for the pearls of spray, and the enemy of the dust of the summer heat.
He is the fragrance of a flower in the sky, the brother of all sounds,
the water flowing through the channels of the veins, and the dancer upon the limbs and members of the elements.
He is the single soul who performs the actions of the vital points, the lion within the house of the cave of the heart.

He is the eternal, solitary traveler and the charioteer of the fire of consciousness; he is the plunderer of the jewels of fragrance and the ground of the city of celestial chariots; he is the moon that cools the darkness of burning and the ocean of milk for the coolness of the moon.
The driver of the machine of living beings by means of the rope of the vital and downward breaths;
he is both the enemy and the friend of lamps, delighting in wandering through the islands.
Though moving in front, his nature is invisible, like a city in a kingdom of the mind.
Oil from a palm-leaf fan, a tethering post for a trembling elephant;
in a mere fraction of a single moment, he caused all the mountains to tremble,
making the roar of the Ganges' current the only sound amidst the waves of his retinue.
The torrent of the river of heaven, which creates great whirlpools of dark water and dust,
possesses bees as its blue lotuses in the sky;
it sweeps away the withered grass that has been cast off from the bodies [of beings].
He is the sun for the lotus-forest of vibration, the sole rain-cloud for the downpour of sound;
he is the elephant in the forest of the sky, the whirlpool in the house of the body;
he is the kadamba grove of dust and the lover embracing the quarters of space.
Constantly and intensely engaged in drawing up the *rasa*, it never finds an opportunity for destruction through its six functions— solidifying, drying, supporting, moving, perfuming, and cooling—
and it acts like a brother to the *tejas*.
He is the one who effects the application of the bodily organs that perform seizing and taking;
he moves without obstruction through the pathways of the channels within the city of the body;
and by exchanging the vessels of the vital fluids, he is the great merchant of the jewel of life.
Devoted solely to the destruction and reconstruction of the city of the body,
and skilled in separating the essence from the dross,
the subtle portions, and the constituent elements within the body, I then beheld the entire world therein.
There, an undertaking of such a nature—clear, expansive, and very firm—was begun.
In this regard, for every single atom, the processes of creation seem as if they were being carried away;
yet nothing at all is actually carried away, for what can be carried away from the form of space?
Together with the moon, sun, wind, fire, Indra, Yama, Vaiśravaṇa, and Īśvara;
along with Brahmā, Hari, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and great serpents;
including the oceans, mountains, islands, the quarters of space, and the great abysses.
[He perceives] the sequences of action and time belonging to the lords of various worlds;
those situated within the realms of heaven, earth, the netherworld (pātāla), and other intermediate worlds;
and [those characterized by] the agitation of existence and non-existence, as well as old age and death.
Thus, O Rāma, at that time, I, in the form of the five elements, sported there within the interior of the lotus of the three worlds;
I drank and experienced the essence of earth, water, air, and fire.
At the root-nets of the trees, where living beings dwell, my body—
dense with elixirs and beautiful with the liquid of sandalwood—
rolled about as if upon beds of moon-disks and snow.
In all the groves of every season, he fully enjoyed the various fragrances and clusters of flowers throughout the quarters of the sky, offering the remnants to his own abode;
upon the soft, elevated, and depressed grounds of the celestial courtyard, which were well-spread with carpets.
He slept upon garlands of white clouds as if on beds of fresh butter,
reclining upon the limbs of celestial and Siddha women— limbs soft as flower petals and radiant with beauty— in which all traces of the latent impressions of passion were far removed.
In the lotus grove, formidable with white and red water-lilies,
a soft, playful clamor was made by the female swans;
[the region] was endowed with the root-grounds of the essential streams of autumnal rivers.
Upon his limbs were borne mountains that seemed like abodes of hair, teeming with shimmering beings;
they rested upon his limbs like mirrors, framed by the long threads of rivers flowing through the four directions and bounded by the oceans, as if reflecting his very form.
The world, bewildered by the creation of beings such as Siddhas and Vidyādharas, was perceived within my body— though appearing in the form of flies and gnats—
as having attained their bodies from the Sun and other luminaries through my grace and their own joy.
As if adorned with black, red, white, yellow, and green [garments],
the earth— marked by the ocean and consisting of the seven islands as its own form—
is established like a bracelet upon the forearm.
With his slender body touched by the wives of the Vidyādharas,
he experienced a thrill of horripilation within himself, even though he remained unseen;
[he perceived] the rivers as veins flowing with the essence of fluids, and the hollows as cavities.
The worlds themselves were the network of my bones, established as they were;
and within my heart, [the universe] resided like gnats inside a fig, with the countless elephants of space and the moving fly-whisks of the sun and moon.
O Rāma, even though I was then supporting the belly of the earth with my feet in the netherworld (pātāla) and the sky with my head, my state as a supreme atom (paramāṇutā) was not abandoned;
for I was the agent of all things everywhere, in all directions, at all times, and in every way.
It exists as the void-form, both entirely and partially;
it is somethingness and nothingness, with form and without form.
I have fully experienced it as both insentient and sentient.
Even regarding a single minute atom of the ocean, which has the Maināka mountain as its charming fish,
there are thousands of creations that have been experienced by me;
worlds borne upon my body, both hidden and manifest.
Like ancient cities reflected in a mirror by means of its non-inert nature,
so too has the state of water, wind, fire, earth, and space been produced by the existent Self through consciousness,
as if in dreams; alas, such is the unfolding of Māyā!
Furthermore, in that state, I beheld countless worlds within the hollow of space, even within every single atom;
for within every atom there is space, and within every atom there is a world situated.
Just as a multitude of creations in a dream consists of cities joined with other dreams;
I myself became the sky, the circle of the earth, and the ring of the continents,
yet even with my entire self, I did not pervade anything anywhere at all.
By drawing up moisture through the surface of the earth, I have caused all creepers, trees, and sprouts of grass to flourish, as if for the sake of my own purpose; yet within me,
who consists of the sky of pure awakening, there is nothing more stainless.
Some millions of worlds exist, and some do not exist at all.
Since they produce a beautiful wonder within consciousness by their own nature,
these perceptions of creation are merely its own internal wonders.
Whatever has been experienced, done, or seen anywhere, to whatever extent,
is not perceived here apart from the wonder of ultimate reality (paramārtha).
Each individual is, in essence, the universal form, the creator of all, and free from affliction.
The awakened one is the self of pure consciousness, because everything has Brahman as its essence.
He is all, present everywhere, the self of all, all-pervading, and the refuge of all;
this is the domain of the awakened, which I, being unawakened, do not know.
In the nature of consciousness, which is as clear as the expanse of space, that which shines forth as the succession of creations is its own inherent self-nature (*svatā*).

That very thing, within itself, is indeed like heat within fire; the perception of difference is merely like a sensation of warmth. Thus, there is no "being" (the finite), but only the infinite exists.
This concludes the demonstration of the identity between ultimate reality and creation, in the context of describing the world within the atoms of air.
The two hundred and fiftieth canto. Vasiṣṭha:
Then, having turned away from such a consciousness with effort,
I arrived at that place within the interior of the celestial hut;
yet there I did not see my own body situated anywhere.
I saw another certain perfected being (siddha) standing before me,
seated, established in meditative absorption, having attained the desired state—
like the sun at its gentle rising, or like a fire whose fuel has been consumed.
Seated in the bound lotus posture, peaceful, motionless in meditative absorption,
with the testicles situated between the two ankles, transcending all sense objects,
his neck gracefully curved with shoulders possessing a smooth and gentle expanse.
Beautiful in its posture, resting with a steady belly,
it was illuminated by the radiance of the two hands raised near the navel,
as if by the splendors of the heart-lotus situated outside.
With its eyelashes closed and all desires extinguished, it has attained a state of pure clarity;
like a lake at the end of the day with its lotuses shut, it is asleep. Its inner cavity of the mind is undisturbed and profoundly tranquil.
Maintaining a steady composure, he was like a sky from which all portents have vanished;

seeing that sage before me and not seeing my own body, I, with a beautiful mind, then thought this there: MU_6,250.8–9. Seeing that sage before me and not seeing my own body, I, with a beautiful mind, then thought this there: MU_6,250.9.
"Here in this Digambara [temple], some great Siddha has arrived;
for a long time, like me, he has been seeking a secluded place for rest in this vast sky.
With the thought that he might find here a secluded spot suitable for meditative absorption," [he approached].
"This hut has been seen by him, who possesses the power of true resolve.
Therefore, without considering my arrival,
he has established his residence here after casting aside that body of mine which had become a corpse."

"Let this matter rest here; I shall go to my own world," he resolved. Just as I was about to depart, because of the dissolution of my mental constructs (*saṅkalpa*), that hut vanished there and only empty space remained.

Then that perfected one, devoid of support, fell down while remaining in meditative absorption (samādhi). Just as the hut in my mental construction vanished instantly upon the cessation of that mental construction, so too did the city of dreams vanish when the dream-conception subsided.
Then that meditator fell from there like a torrent of water from a cloud,
like a cloud driven from the sky by the wind, like the moon at its waning,
like a meritless celestial being falling from his chariot, or like a tree whose roots have been severed.
Like a stone dropped from a height, he fell from there onto the earth.
As soon as the conceptualization— "As long as I am, so long shall this hut remain"—
was exhausted, the hut perished and he, having attained perfection, fell in an instant.
Then, out of curiosity regarding his noble character, I descended from the sky to the surface of the earth along with that Siddha as he was falling;
he fell by means of the circular movements produced by the swirling of the mass of wind.
Upon the earth, the delight of the gods, bounded by the seven continents and oceans,
he— due to the upward movement of his prāṇa and apāna breaths from the ether—
fell clearly with his head upwards, having assumed the lotus posture upon the ground.

He did not wake up; indeed, he seemed as if unconscious, like a body made of stone, or perhaps as light as one whose soul is deranged by wind. Then, I exerted myself with effort for the sake of awakening him.
Having made the sky a water-bearing cloud, a powerful roar was rained down;
by that falling of hailstones in that direction,
that peacock, as if in the rainy season, woke up from his sleep in the forest grove.
His bodily splendor was restored and his eyes were opened;
he appeared like a bed of lotuses in the rainy season, its very self blossomed by a downpour of rain. When the rain had completely ceased, I stood before him as he was thus awakened.
I questioned him who was pure by nature, yet withdrawn from the ultimate perspective:
"O leader of sages, where do you stand? Why do you perform this? Who are you? And why, though capable, do you not descend even from afar into my mind? (MU 6.250.26–27)
Thus addressed, he looked at me, recalled his former state,
and spoke these beautiful words, just as a *cātaka* bird addresses a rain-cloud.
The Siddha said:
"Wait for me while I recall my own history;
afterwards, I shall tell you the subsequent events of my life.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus and reflected quickly,
he remembered his own conduct exactly as it had occurred, like one remembering the day's events at evening;
then he addressed me with words as lovely and cool as the rays of the moon.
"Delightful, irreproachable, faultless, and the source of happiness.
The Siddha said: "O Brahmin, you have now been recognized by me; I salute you."
This transgression must be forgiven, for forgiveness is the very nature of the virtuous.
O Sage, for a long time I have wandered among the groves of the gods, deluded by the fragrance of enjoyments, like a bee among lotus ponds.
Then, as I was being carried away by the whirlpools of the wheel in the river of the visible world through the play of the waves of the water of the mind, I, being distressed, thought:
"I am agitated in the ocean of saṃsāra by the waves of the mental constructs of the visible."
In time, he became as agitated as a *cātaka* bird during a drought.
[He thought: "What indeed is there that is truly delightful in enjoyments, whose sole essence is mere consciousness?
I shall remain, free from agitation, in the sky of consciousness alone."
Apart from the mere [elements of] sound, form, taste, touch, and smell, there is nothing else whatsoever here; why then do you not delight sufficiently in this much?
This entire universe is merely the space of consciousness, or indeed, it is merely consciousness itself.
Why then do I, with my mind destroyed, take delight here in this unreal form, as if I were deluded?
Sense-objects are like the dangers of poison; they are deceptive, bestowing the delusion of desire.
These pleasures turn into tasteless distaste—who among those wallowing in them has not been ruined?
The mind is like a decayed little shrimp in the mud of a life that is worn out;
the great female crane of old age desires to seize it from the tree of the body.
This body is soon to perish, like a bubble upon the ocean.
Just as the flame of a lamp vanishes right before one's eyes while still flickering, so too does it disappear.
The river of birth and death has various turbulent waves, creates whirlpools and eddies, possesses great banks of mortality and rebirth, and is filled with the ripples of pleasure and pain.
Turbid with the effervescence of youth, frothing white with old age,
and possessing bubbles of happiness through the coincidence of chance,
this great current of worldly activity flows, agitated by the sluggishness of dullness.

Alas! This river called "life" is intensely hot, yet its roar is cool; it flows with the surging density of passion and hatred, its body tossing upon the surface of the earth, possessing great whirlpools of greed and delusion, and revolving through falls and rises.

New waters enter the river of saṃsāra, while the old ones flow away completely; so it is with riches that have come together. Enough with those who, having set out, turn back—their very nature is ruined.
What kind of reliance can there be here even upon those things that proceed as unprecedented?
(MU 6.250.47) The water of every river flows forth from the ocean and returns to it;
but the water of the river of the body, which is life, flows forth and does not return again. (MU 6.250.48)
Hundreds of existences revolve for every single body at every moment,
like the rotations of a potter’s wheel;
and the fourfold thieves roam about— those treacherous enemies that are the sense-objects.
They carry away the entirety of one's existence; do I remain awake here, or am I asleep?
Again and again, fragments of life fall away, yet no one perceives the days created by Time—alas! MU_6,250.51-52.

"This is for me today, and this tomorrow; this is for me now"—by such reckoning, alas, the world does not realize what has passed or what has been gained. It has eaten and drunk, and it has wandered through endless realms of existence.
Pleasures and pains have already been experienced; what else remains here to be accomplished?
Because of the repeated recurrence of the experience of pleasure and pain, and because all things are impermanent, we remain free from longing.
Multitudes of enjoyments have been experienced and the extreme impermanence of things has been witnessed; yet, not even a moment of profound rest can be found anywhere here.
I have wandered through the forest lands of Mount Meru, upon its lofty peaks.
"Has anything unartificial ever truly reached the cities of the world-protectors?
Trees everywhere are made of wood, living beings of flesh, and the earth of clay; since suffering and impermanence are likewise universal, tell me, how can one find consolation?"
Neither wealth, nor friends, nor pleasures, nor kinsmen are able to protect a person seized by time.
A person [in such a state] is like a mass of aged clouds within the hollows of mountains.
It sets, utterly empty within, as fragile as a heap of dust. These sensual pleasures are not delightful, nor are these prosperities charming;
even this life is as flickering as the sidelong glances of an intoxicated woman.
O Sage, where, for whom, how, or from whence can there be consolation?
For today or tomorrow, death places its foot upon the head of the sinner.
The body falls like a leaf; life is a state of decay.
Seized by a lack of steadfastness, the aesthetic flavors have become flavorless.
Our extended life has been spent merely in pursuit of joyless desires; not even the slightest thing capable of causing wonder for a man of spirit has been sought.
Today delusion has become dull; the body does not remain here.
Indifference alone is the highest state; attachment to staying is the lowest condition. This calamity has indeed arrived, bringing about great delusion.
One should consider this as eternal; one should not be attached here to this cycle of worldly existence.
By means of injunctions and prohibitions—whether prescribed by scripture or not—the world is led at will, just as water follows depressions and elevations.
Having stolen the entire essence of the fragrance of discernment from the flower-bud of the mind,
the winds of the objects of sense bestow a swoon.
Thus, that which is truly non-existent appears as if it has attained existence as a visible object.
Just as that which is real has become unreal in form, and that which is unreal has become real;
just as the wives of the ocean, swaying their bodies upon the earth,
run hither and thither, so do people run after sense-objects.

The arrows of the mind, once released, rush toward their target, the sense objects; they do not touch the bowstring again, just as ungrateful people do not return a kindness. Life itself is like a tempestuous wind, and friends are truly enemies.
Relatives are indeed bonds; wealth is indeed extreme poverty.
Pleasures are indeed extreme sufferings; prosperities are supreme calamities.
Enjoyments are the great diseases of existence; delight itself is supreme discontent.
All calamities and prosperities lead only to suffering;
life leads only to death—alas, illusion unfolds its power!
Through many revolutions of time, there is but a slight pleasure amidst the desirable and the undesirable.

Beholding the separations from those dear to him, a person reaches a state of decay. Sensual enjoyments—the pleasures of the sense objects—are like the hoods of venomous serpents; even when touched slightly, they bite, vanishing as soon as they are seen at every moment.
Life passes away for those who lack the attainment of the state free from exertion,
through terrible and painful efforts whose forms are fragile even at their conclusion.
For those whose thirst is bound by the hope for enjoyments, there is humiliation at every step.
Like wild elephants clinging to their tethering posts,
both prosperity and women are as transient as the crests of waves;
what wise man would take delight in them, which offer but the fleeting shade of a serpent’s expanded hood?
Truly, desires are enchanting; truly, worldly prosperities are delightful.
Yet, life is as fickle as the flickering sidelong glances of an intoxicated woman.
Those who take delight in sense-objects that are charming only at first sight—

They fall into hells that end in utter desolation. Wealth, obstructed by the defects of dualities, difficult to acquire, unstable, and unfit for those lacking spiritual capacity, has never brought me satisfaction.
Wealth is sweet only at first sight, ending in suffering;
it serves only to delude the world and perishes in an instant.
Excessively pleasant at the outset, they become utterly distasteful upon closer examination.
Pleasures are primarily fraught with calamities, like associations with the wicked;
the splendors of youth are as fleeting as the shadow of an autumn cloud;
and sense-objects are delightful only at first sight, yet lead to torment in the end.
The Ender (Death) stands as an encompasser even of the lives of the great;
the lifespans of embodied beings are as unstable as water hanging from the tip of a branch.
As one ages, the hair decays; as one ages, the teeth decay.
As one ages, everything decays; craving alone does not decay.
Amidst the entire forest of the body, which is dense with the enjoyment and non-enjoyment of pleasures, craving alone reaches its supreme bloom as a poisonous cluster.

Childhood passes away like youth, and youth passes away like childhood; these two are mutually comparable and analogous in their transience. Life slips away quickly, just like water from cupped hands.

Like the current of a river, that which has passed does not return. Having arrived suddenly from somewhere like a whirlwind, the body goes to its setting even as one looks on, like a wave, a cloud, or a lamp.
Delightfulness has been seen in what is unpleasant, and instability even in what is stable; truthlessness has been perceived in objects that are real—for this reason we are disenchanted here.
That which is happiness in the repose of the self, when the mind has attained the state of pure being (*sattva*), [is not found elsewhere].
Neither in the underworld, nor on the earth, nor in heaven, nor in any enjoyments whatsoever—
these five functions of the senses, even when their objects are entirely pleasing to the heart, do not attract me, just as variegated creepers do not entice a bee.
Today, after a long time, I have attained through my intellect this freedom from thirst for heaven and liberation, being devoid of egoism; by that,
this station of the sky has been reached for the sake of long-lasting repose in solitude.
Having come here just like you, I saw that hut.
Today this has been fully understood: that indeed it was your hut, and that you would come again—this is known without any doubt.
Then, however, I realized here through inference that this was some perfected being (*siddha*) who, having abandoned his body in this world, had attained *nirvāṇa* by means of the self.
O Blessed One, such was my experience; I am exactly as I have described.
I have told you everything; act according to what you understand.

O Sage, it is the very nature of even the minds of Brahmā and the other gods that as long as the Siddhas—intent on concentration—have not investigated and determined every object within their supreme intellect, they do not perceive any calculation of the three periods of time.
In the narrative of Pāṣāṇa, the chapter titled "The Description of the Gathering of Siddhas in the Pavilion of the Sky," the two hundred and fifty-first chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, upon that great ground as vast as the golden sky,
out of sheer affection for that perfected one, I said this to him:
"Not only by you, but even by me has this not been investigated."
A state of embodiedness that is devoid of pervasion is simply impossible;
for this reason, after deliberating upon your condition, I have made her firm.
It was not a hut in the sky by which you would have attained a stable station.
Therefore, O lotus-petal-eyed one, that which has passed away is indeed gone.
Having reflected upon and abandoned the past, behold the present state.
Arise; let us dwell as we are situated among the worlds of the perfected ones.
“O gentle ones, those who remain in their own abodes possess an excellent means for the realization of their own self.
Having thus resolved, the two of us leaped up like stars; we flew together through the sky in a single formation, like stones released from a catapult.
Then, having exchanged mutual salutations and taken our leave,
he departed for his desired destination, and I too went to my own desired place.
Thus, O Rāghava, I have related this entire account to you.
"Behold this wondrous variety of transmigrations!
Rāma said: "O Blessed One, this body of yours has become as minute as an atom upon the earth."
"By what body were you wandering through the worlds of the Siddhas?
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Ah, I remember; hear what happened to me thereafter in that abode of the world."
Wandering through the cities of the Siddhas and the cities of the world-protectors,
I reached Indra’s city; yet no one there saw me,
for I was devoid of a physical body, possessing only a subtle, transportable form.
O Rāma, at that time I indeed became one whose form was like the sky;
neither a support nor that which is supported, consisting essentially of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
I was neither a grasper nor a graspable object for those who understand reality as you do.
Nor does it anywhere act as an obstruction to space or time;
unimpeded by the flood of objects and directed toward its own self-experience,
it is the agent of worldly activity together with other such beings composed of mind.

O Rāma, the experience of dreams is an unassailable illustration in this matter; let there be enough of you who would deny such experience. Just as in a dream a man performing activities in his house is not seen [by others], [so too is the world].
Likewise, at that time, I was not seen even by those situated in the sky, though I stood right before them.
I perceive another who possesses the form and appearance of a king, yet no one perceives me, the subtle, transportable self (ātivāhikātman).
Rāma:
If you are not seen because of your bodiless state and your body is like the sky,
then how was it that you were seen by that Siddha in the Golden Forest?
Vasiṣṭha:
O Rāma, people such as ourselves obtain whatever objects they have intended; for one whose very nature is that of true desire does not obtain what has not been intended.
By a person of pure soul who is immersed in worldly affairs, the fact that the self is merely a transitory vehicle is forgotten in an instant.
At that time, I had formed the resolve: "Let him see me."
Therefore, he saw me as a vessel for the objects of his own volition;
a person, due to the state of having worn-out distinctions, is not a vessel for the objects of volition.
That very same person, because of having worn-out distinctions, becomes a vessel for the state of having true desires.
But when two Siddhas who possess mutually contradictory and desired powers encounter one another,
the one whose self is more exalted by a single superior quality is the victor, provided he possesses human effort.
As I wandered among the hosts of Siddhas in the cities of the World-Guardians, [I saw this].
When that subtle body (*ativāhika-ātman*) was forgotten amidst the flood of worldly affairs,
I then began to interact with the immortals in the sky;
yet no one there perceived me as I moved about restlessly.
O sinless one, even when I cry out most intensely, my voice is not heard by anyone in the worlds of the gods, like that of a man in a dream.
When I have set about to seize one thing, there is nothing else for me to seize.
Nothing at all is accomplished by one who possesses a body of mental ideation.
Thus, O descendant of Raghu, I have become a sky-demon;
this state of being a demon in a temple of the gods has been experienced by me in some inexplicable way.
Rāma:
Piśācas exist in this world; what is their form, what is their abode, what is their lineage, what is their conduct, what are they like, and what is their disposition?
Vasiṣṭha said:
There are piśācas in the worlds; hear what they are like: he who does not speak a word that arises in the course of conversation is no member of the assembly.
Certain *piśācas*, whose bodies are empty like the sky,
perceive forms endowed with hands, feet, and so forth, just like your own appearance;
they do so through a terrifying shadow that takes the form of a delusion regarding another object.
Having taken possession of their minds, they pierce the inner disposition of men; they swiftly kill, devour, and drink the blood of those who are weak-spirited, fickle, and living beings,
attacking their hearts and destroying their strength, flesh, and very lives.
Some are like space, some resemble mist;
some have the form of men in a dream, and even those with forms are of the nature of the void.
Some appear like men in a dream, while others have bodies of wind.
Some [beings] are entirely of the nature of delusion; all those consisting of intellect and mind are not at all fit to be grasped, nor are they able to grasp [anything].
Having a body as empty as space, they perceive a form of their own.
They experience pleasure and pain caused by cold, heat, and so forth;
they desire to drink, to eat, and to grasp, yet they are unable to do so.
They are possessed by desire, hatred, fear, anger, greed, and delusion.
Subjugated by mantras, medicinal herbs, asceticism, charity, fortitude, or righteousness,
beings are sometimes seen or even captured by someone somewhere through the power of a firm resolve or a propitiated mantra.
For they are of divine origin; thus, some possess the splendor of gods, some have a beauty equal to humans, and some possess the power of *nāgas*.
Some resemble dogs or jackals, dwelling in villages or the wilderness.
They dwell in water-channels, rubbish heaps, streets, and in hells;
these are proclaimed to be their abodes. Such are the characteristics of the Piśācas; now hear this concerning their birth.
Know that Brahman, which is non-objective and composed of consciousness, exists by its own nature as all-powerful;
though it is eternally awakened within, it appears as if it were conceiving objects of thought.
Know that to be the individual soul (jīva), and when it has become fully developed, it is traditionally called the ego (ahaṅkāra).
That egoism (ahaṅkāra), when nourished, is called "mind" (manas) by those who have declared the nature of the self;
this very [ego] is said to be Brahmā, whose form is the space of volition (saṅkalpa).
It is the non-existent seed of the non-existent world, devoid of any manifest shape.
Thus, with the mind established [in this way], Brahmā, though possessing a body, is like the stainless sky;
he is always existent yet of non-existent form, appearing in the shape of a person in a dream.
Devoid of material forms such as earth and the rest, he possesses a subtle, transportable body (*ātivāhika-deha*).
"How indeed could earth and the other elements exist in the sky for a person created by mere volition?
Just as your own mind perceives an imaginary city in the sky,
so too the mind perceives the state of Viriñca (Brahmā) as imagined within itself."
Whatever he knows as imagined, that he sees and also experiences. Why indeed does he not see that which is merely of such a nature? What he sees is like that: empty in essence, empty in the sky.
Brahman, or that which is in Brahman, is called Brahmā; this very world is so described.
Likewise, through long-term and singular contemplation, that manifestation of his becomes dense, established, nourished, and as beautiful as a very long dream.
Due to long-standing contemplation, that subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) of Brahmā— though it is of the nature of Brahman— experiences an extensive creation;
through its excellence, it has attained the state of a manifest material body (ādhibhautika-dehatā).

By that very [process], creation is said to be radiant with a continuous succession of distinctions. That Brahmā, whose self is nothing but Brahman, [remains so] even though those two— the Self and the world— are eternally unborn.
Just as between emptiness and space, which are indeed inseparable,
or as between the wind and its movement, which shine forth in a state of absolute identity,
one perceives that [the world] consists of the elements; yet that is merely false and not real.
Just as you [perceive] the person of volition (saṅkalpapuruṣa) as both existent and non-existent,
so too were the elements of the body created by him from earth and the other [elements].
These five designations, with consciousness as the sixth, abide as the world itself.
Just as this resolve of yours is indeed unreal while that [other] is real,
so too did he experience his own resolve as being truly real.
He himself is the space consisting of consciousness, and his resolve is the sky of consciousness.
Therefore, the entire world is a dream; where could destruction and origination reside?
Just as that mind is real, so too are its parts real;
likewise, the moons, Rudras, suns, Indras, and rays produced by it are real.
This being so, the web of the world is called the kingdom of the mind;
and that is empty, without support, like the sky, unclouded within consciousness.
Just as a city in a dream is space, and as a mountain of one's imagination is the sky.
Likewise, Brahman and the world are indeed the sky itself— pure and formless. Thus, for that which is immutable and shines forth as a mere appearance without ceasing,
the perceptions of creation, its beginning, middle, and end, have arisen here in vain and persist only as such.
O sinless one, tell me: in you, who are like the expanse of space, or in me, or even in the world, what could possibly be born or what could perish?
Why, then, do these meaningless and purposeless things exist for no good?

Tell me, why do passion, hatred, fear, and the like arise? My dear friend, in reality there is neither creation nor the beginning of creation, nor even non-creation; this has been manifested once and for all, and that is simply Being itself.
In the non-empty realm of vast extent, filled with the water of pure consciousness,
turbid with the mud of mental constructs and teeming with the frogs of future thoughts—
within that field of the inexhaustible sky, for the self that is space, there exists that which is of the nature of the sky.
From that seed was born this vast range of elemental rocks.
There is no field here whatsoever, nothing sown, no seed exists, and nothing has been born; yet everything remains established.
Those stone rings here that are well-nourished are the gods and so forth;
those which are brilliant in color are the ones established in the intellects of the Buddhas.
Those, however, which are half-ripened are the various classes such as humans, *nāgas*, and others.
Those which are solidified and devoid of passion become worms, stationary beings, and so forth.
Those which are not heavy, lacking fruits, empty in form, having reached dissolution,
bodiless yet possessing bodies, are known as Piśācas and the like.
For the will of one who possesses volition is never subject to questioning;
such was the will of Viriñca that it arose at that time, O Rāma.
Indeed, all classes of beings are of the nature of the space of consciousness.
Possessing subtle bodies (*ātivāhika-deha*) and devoid of the elements such as earth,
they— by virtue of long-term practice and through prolonged experience— attain the perception of the material world (*ādhibhautika-saṃvid*), just as dreams [attain] the waking state.
For in this way, these beings such as Piśācas and others— belonging to the category of elemental spirits—
dwell with contented minds, sporting within their own respective realms of saṃsāra;
some among them see one another, just as villagers see fellow villagers.
These classes of beings are as if they dwell in worlds that exist solely within a dream. Some, like those in a world created by a dream experienced by many men,
do not see one another, even though they are situated in various different forms.
Just as these low-born beings such as *piśācas* exist in this world,
so too do these *kumbhāṇḍas*, *yakṣas*, *pretas*, and others generally abide. Just as wherever there are *nāgas* here, water is found right there.
Likewise, wherever there are piśācas and the like, darkness remains there.
Even at midday, if a piśāca stands personally in a courtyard,
his very presence produces sufficient blinding darkness in that place.
The sun does not strike it, nor does anyone else perceive it;
he alone experiences it—behold the unfolding of illusion!
Just as the luminous orb is inseparably connected with the moon and other such bodies.

Likewise, the mandala of darkness (tamas) is non-different in essence from the piśācas and other such beings. Just as owls [perceive] light as lacking brilliance, so do the piśācas and others perceive that which is dominated by brilliance (tejas) as being dominated by darkness (tamas), due to their innate nature since the beginning of creation.
This birth of beings such as Piśācas has been described by me to you without departing from the established principles;
for it follows from the context that I was born in the worlds of the guardians of the celestial realm as one equal to a Piśāca.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Demonstration of the Identity of the World and Brahman through the Story of the Stone and the Context of the Piśāca."
The two hundred and fifty-second canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Thereupon, [he] whose body was the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) and who was devoid of the five elements—
Dwelling in the sky, I remained like a *piśāca* spirit;
neither the moon, the sun, Śakra, Hari, Hara, and the others, nor the gods, *siddhas*, *gandharvas*, *kinnaras*, or hosts of *apsarases* could see me.
"They do not approach me when I have approached them, nor do they listen to my words;
thus I have fallen into delusion, like a virtuous man who has been sold.
Then I thought: "We here are those whose desires are true."
"Let the hosts of gods behold me; therefore, in that celestial abode,
all those inhabitants there began to look at me first,
as if I had suddenly appeared before them like a tree conjured by magic."
Then, having attained the status of one who engages in worldly affairs within the abodes of the gods,
I remained established in my natural conduct, acting without hesitation.
By those who had not learned of my history, I was seen as one risen from the sky.
"By them, I am celebrated in the worlds as Vasiṣṭha the Pārthiva. By those Siddhas who saw me arisen from the wind while in my abode in the sky, I have been designated by the name Vātavasiṣṭha."
"O Vasiṣṭha, by those sky-dwellers who saw me in the firmament emerging from the rays of the sun, I am celebrated in the worlds as Taijasa;
and by those lords of sages who saw me rising up from the water,"

"I have been declared to be Vāri-Vasiṣṭha; such is the succession of my births. From that time forth, I have been celebrated in the world as a king in some places, as one composed of water in others, as belonging to others [the gods] in some, and as consisting of fire or wind in others."

Then, in the course of time, within that very subtle body (ātivāhika), my latent tendency toward a physical body (ādhibhautikatā) became firmly established, even though its nature was hidden from the intermediate space.
This state of being subtle and this physicality are both of the nature of space (kha).
Both of these are of one essence; therefore, my consciousness shines forth.
Thus, though I am the very sky of consciousness whose nature is this manifestation, I am the formless Supreme Space itself, yet appearing with form within you.
Even while acting, one who is liberated in this life remains as the very ether of Brahman;
likewise, even when freed from the body, he abides as nothing but Brahman. Even while acting in such a manner, my state of being Brahman does not depart.
Because nothing else of that nature is possible among you and others, I am indeed "I. Just as an ignorant person perceives a dream-man as a physical entity despite his being unborn and formless,
so too do I perceive the world.
In this very way, all the self-existent ones (svayambhuvaḥ) appear;
yet the creations are not born, though they are impelled as if already produced.
This is that same "I" here, like Vasiṣṭha in the ether, [appearing] as if having attained fullness.
Today, through the practice of your own self, you have attained the state of non-existence for yourselves.
All these beings are indeed of the nature of space and are self-existent;
for just as they are merely my mind, so too are these creations.
This creation, with me as its beginning, has— due to the fault of non-recognition—
attained a state as hard as adamant for the ignorant, like a vampire; yet once fully understood, it subsides in a very short time.
Just as affection for a kinsman who has gone far away diminishes through the thinning of latent impressions (*vāsanā*),

so too does the density of this creation consisting of the "I-sense" and so forth subside through thorough knowledge; just as the notion of something being worth grasping vanishes from the treasure seen in a dream.
All these perceptions of the visible world, once fully understood, subside—
just as the notions of grasping the water in the current of a mirage-river do—
merely by the study of scriptures such as the great *Rāmāyaṇa*.

This is attained eternally; what is difficult about this? But he whose intellect consists of the non-existence of the latent impressions of saṃsāra, yet remains dull and devoid of longing for liberation—he is a dog, a worm, or a monkey.
Rāma:
This very expansion of enjoyments— how would it be experienced by one whose intellect is liberated while living, and how would it be by one who indulges in ignorance?
Vasiṣṭha:
Merely by the contemplation of this great Rāmāyaṇa, which is like a sacred scripture,
a coolness arises within regarding all things, comparable to ice.
Liberation is the state of a cool mind; bondage is the state of a tormented mind.
Even regarding this, people have no desire—oh, the folly of the world!
By nature, these people are enslaved by sense objects, greedily craving one another, women, and wealth.
"Because one becomes happy through the vision of things as they truly are, and because of the investigation of the meaning of the scriptures for those seeking liberation.
Then, when the sage had spoken thus, the day passed away and the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites.
Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of night, it returned along with the rays of the sun.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Description of Vasiṣṭha’s Body" within the narrative of the stone. Thus ends the story of the stone.
